r3.06.03 Computation of stresses at the nodes by local smoothing r3.06.03 Computation of stresses at the nodes by local smoothing Summary: A local method is presented for computing stresses at the nodes from the stresses at the GAUSS points. It is used in the options SIGM_ELNO and SIEF_ELNO. This method amounts to computing the stresses at the vertices of an element by multiplying the stresses at the GAUSS points by a smoothing matrix, constant for each element type. For isoparametric elements of degree 2, the stresses at the mid-side nodes are obtained by averaging the values of the stresses at the 2 vertices of the edge. This smoothing method has two advantages: - the nodal stresses obtained have one order of accuracy more than by direct computation at the nodes, - the method is inexpensive in CPU time. This method has been generalised: - to the computation of the strains (option EPSI_ELNO) and of the internal variables (option VARI_ELNO) at the nodes in mechanics, - to the computation of the fluxes (option FLUX_ELNO) at the nodes in thermal analysis. 1 Preliminaries This method is based on the observation that there exist points at which the computation of the stresses, from the displacements in a primal displacement formulation, is more accurate. In the case of isoparametric finite elements of order 2 (SEG3 in 1D, QUAD8 and QUAD9 in 2D, HEXA20 in 3D), it is shown that the GAUSS points of the quadrature formula with {2}^{n} points ( n : dimension of the space) are such that one may hope, without this being formally demonstrated, for the computation of \sigma the same order of accuracy as for the computation of the displacement field u . The idea of the method is to compute, for each element, the stresses \hat{\sigma} at the nodes from {\sigma}^{k} at the GAUSS points, the latter being computed on each element by the formula: {\sigma}^{k}=D{B}^{k}u=D\sum_{i=1}^{\mathrm{NNO}}{B}_{i}^{k}{U}_{i} where: D is the elasticity matrix, {B}^{k} is the matrix relating the strains to the displacements at the GAUSS point k , {U}_{i} are the nodal displacements ( \mathrm{NNO} nodes) 2 Local least-squares minimisation method In general, one wishes to approximate, in the least-squares sense, the spatial distribution of the stresses by \sigma (x) , a polynomial function: \hat{\sigma}(x)=\sum_{\begin{array}{}i=0,\mathrm{...},p\end{array}}{a}_{i}{P}^{i}(x) The problem amounts to finding the coefficients {a}_{i} which minimise the functional: \chi =\int\int{(\sigma -\hat{\sigma})}^{2}\mathrm{dx}\mathrm{dy} The values of the function \sigma are known here only at the Gauss points: {\sigma}^{k}=\sigma ({x}_{k}) The minimum will be reached if and only if: \frac{\partial \chi }{\partial {a}_{i}}=0\begin{array}{}\forall i=0,\mathrm{...},p\end{array} Within the framework of the displacement finite-element method, the following smoothing function is chosen: \hat{\sigma}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{N}_{i}(x)\hat{{\sigma}_{i}} where: {N}_{i} is the shape function associated with node i on the finite element considered, \hat{{\sigma}_{i}} is the value of the stress at node i that is sought, n the number of nodes retained for the smoothing. The following system must therefore be solved: \frac{\partial \chi }{\partial \hat{{\sigma}_{i}}}=0\forall i=1,\mathrm{...},n éq 2-1 One may choose between two local smoothing methods: continuous smoothing or discrete smoothing. 3 Local smoothing methods (ref. [bib2]_ and [bib3]_) 3.1 Continuous local smoothing This type of smoothing leads to solving the system [] with the functional defined on the current finite element: \chi =\underset{e}{\int}{(\sigma -\hat{\sigma})}^{2}=\underset{e}{\int}{(\sigma -\sum_{i=1}^{n}{N}_{i}\hat{{\sigma}_{i}})}^{2} The minimisation leads to {M}^{e}\hat{\sigma}={F}^{e} with: \begin{array}{}{M}_{ij}^{e}=\underset{e}{\int}{N}_{i}{N}_{j}\mathrm{dx}\mathrm{dy}=\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{npg}}\bar{{N}_{i}}({\xi}_{k}){N}_{j}({\xi}_{k}){(\detJ)}_{k}{\omega}_{k}\\ {F}_{i}^{e}=\underset{e}{\int}{N}_{i}\sigma \mathrm{dx}\mathrm{dy}=\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{npg}}\bar{{N}_{i}}({\xi}_{k}){\sigma}_{k}{(\detJ)}_{k}{\omega}_{k}\end{array} | where | {\xi}_{k} are the GAUSS points in the reference element | | | --- | --- | --- | | | {(\detJ)}_{k} | the Jacobian of the geometric transformation between the reference element and the current element at the point {\xi}_{k} . | {\omega}_{k} : the weight associated with the point {\xi}_{k} {\xi}_{k} : the stress at the point {\xi}_{k} \bar{{N}_{i}}({\xi}_{k}) : the value of the shape function in the reference element at the point {\xi}_{k} Notes: - If the interpolation spaces of \sigma and of \hat{\sigma} are the same, one has \sigma =\hat{\sigma} . In practice, one retains for the space of \hat{\sigma} a space smaller than that in which \sigma is defined by the finite element. - One sees the link between the approximation at the GAUSS points of \sigma , where \sigma therefore converges better, and this smoothing procedure, whose justification is on the contrary continuous. - The way in which \sigma is computed at the GAUSS points does not come into play. The generalisation to non-linear problems is therefore obvious, although it cannot rest on the same justification. This method is nevertheless not retained, because it requires the solution of a linear system for each computation of \hat{\sigma} . 3.2 Discrete local smoothing In this case, the functional \chi is replaced by the summation: \tilde{\chi }=\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{npg}}{(\sigma ({\xi}_{k})-\hat{\sigma}({\xi}_{k}))}^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{npg}}{(\sigma ({\xi}_{k})-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{{\sigma}_{i}}{N}_{i}({\xi}_{k}))}^{2} The system to be solved is again written: \frac{\partial \tilde{\chi }}{\partial \hat{{\sigma}_{i}}}=0 , that is: \sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{npg}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}{N}_{i}({\xi}_{k}){N}_{j}({\xi}_{k})\hat{{\sigma}_{j}}=\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{npg}}{N}_{i}({\xi}_{k})\sigma ({\xi}_{k})\forall i=1,\mathrm{...},n that is, in matrix form: M\lbrace {\hat{\sigma}}_{\text{noeud}}\rbrace =P\lbrace {\sigma}_{\text{GAUSS}}\rbrace The matrices M (square n\times n ) and P (rectangular n\times \mathrm{npg} ) are then independent of the current element e . They may therefore be computed once and for all on the reference element. Notes: - This method is more economical than the previous one and gives comparable results [bib2], - Here again, the way in which {\sigma}^{k} is computed at each GAUSS point is immaterial (provided that the number of GAUSS points used for the computation of \sigma and that of \hat{\sigma} is the same). This method may therefore be used in the non-linear range . 4 Application of the method to the computation of the stresses at the nodes for various elements The local smoothing adopted in code_aster is the discrete local smoothing [r3.06.03-lissage-local-discret], which makes it possible to avoid the computation of integrals over the element. On all the 2D and 3D continuum elements, a smoothing space based on the shape functions relating to the vertices of the element has been chosen. The method therefore makes it possible to obtain the stresses at the vertices. In the case of elements of order 2, the stresses at the mid-side nodes are computed by taking the arithmetic mean of the two vertices "bracketing" the mid-side node considered. The mapping matrices making it possible to compute the stresses at the vertex nodes from the stresses at the GAUSS points are given below. These matrices may be square or rectangular. Indeed, the mapping matrices {M}^{\text{-1}}P are computed once and for all at the initialisation of each finite-element type (in AFFE_MODELE). Two types of matrix exist: - square matrices {M}^{\text{-1}}P , which are to be used when the number of GAUSS points used for the computation of the stresses at the GAUSS points {\sigma}^{k} is identical to the number of vertex nodes, - rectangular matrices {M}^{\text{-1}}P , which are to be used when the number of GAUSS points of {\sigma}^{k} is different from (in general greater than) the number of vertex nodes. 4.1 Square mapping matrices These matrices are used in the elements for which the number of GAUSS points of the computation of SIEF_ELGA/SIGM_ELGA is equal to the number of vertices. The option first computes the stresses at a number of GAUSS points equal to the number of vertices. The matrices {M}^{\text{-1}}P (given below) are then used to compute the stresses at the nodes. The elements concerned are: - in 2D: QUAD4, TRIA6, under-integrated QUAD8, - in 3D: TETRA4, PENTA6, HEXA8, PYRAM5 and under-integrated HEXA20. 4.1.1 Square mapping matrices for the 2D elements 4.1.1.1 r3.06.04 Fourier elements for axisymmetric structures r3.06.04 Fourier elements for axisymmetric structures Summary Fourier elements are intended to compute the response of a structure of axisymmetric geometry subjected to non-axisymmetric loadings decomposed into Fourier series. This document sets out a general theory of Fourier analysis with coupling of the symmetric and antisymmetric modes in the anisotropic case. The case of isotropic materials, or of materials orthotropic about the axis \mathit{Oz} , in which the modes are uncoupled, is studied separately. Fourier elements can be used in Code_Aster from the modelling AXIS_FOURIER. The support mesh cells of these elements are triangles and quadrilaterals of degree 1 and 2. 1 Introduction Fourier analysis is intended to compute the response of structures of axisymmetric geometries subjected to non-axisymmetric loadings. In this case, it is necessary to expand the loadings in Fourier series. Convergence is generally reached for 4 or 5 harmonics, but the rapidity of this convergence depends on the nature of the loading: the more regular the loading, the more rapidly the corresponding series converges. The most unfavourable case is that of a concentrated force, for which practice shows that one must go further (at least 7 harmonics). In Code_Aster , the decomposition of the loading into Fourier series is assumed to have been carried out beforehand by the user. Code_Aster makes it possible to compute the responses to this loading, harmonic by harmonic (modelling AXIS_FOURIER), and globally after recombination of the harmonics with one another (operator COMB_FOURIER). A first chapter will set out the general framework of anisotropy, with emphasis on the uncoupling of the modes in the orthotropic case. The second chapter explains the calculation of the stiffness matrix in the isotropic case. For the use of Fourier elements in Code_Aster , the reader is referred to the user's guide of the Fourier modelling U2.07.01. 2 Anisotropic Fourier analysis 2.1 General theory All the fields considered (forces, displacements, strains, stresses) are expressed in cylindrical coordinates with the following convention on the order of the components: | 1 | radial component along r | | --- | --- | | 2 | axial component along z | | 3 | tangential component along 	heta | Example: ({u}_{r},{u}_{z},{u}_{	heta}),({f}_{r},{f}_{z},{f}_{	heta}) The mesh is located in the plane (r,z) , the rotational symmetry being about the axis \mathrm{Oz} . r3.06.07 Diagonalisation of the thermal mass matrix r3.06.07 Diagonalisation of the thermal mass matrix Summary: In order to improve the regularity of the solution in transient thermal problems, one solution consists in “lumping” (that is: condensing onto the diagonal) the thermal mass matrix (capacity matrix). This possibility is accessible through the modellings PLAN_DIAG, AXIS_DIAG and 3D_DIAG for the phenomenon THERMIQUE. It is activated when calling the thermal analysis commands THER_LINEAIRE and THER_NON_LINE. When these modellings are used, only the linear finite elements (2D and 3D) have a lumped mass matrix. Indeed, direct diagonalisation does not give satisfactory results for quadratic finite elements, so it is not allowed The theoretical results are illustrated by the thermo-mechanical analysis of a cylinder subjected to a thermal shock. 1 Introduction Transient thermal analyses are considered in which abrupt variations of the loadings occur — for example, thermal shocks. In certain cases, it is noted that the temperature oscillates spatially and temporally. Moreover, if a temperature profile is observed at a given time instant of the transient, the temperature may at certain nodes exceed the min. and max. bounds imposed by the initial conditions and the boundary conditions. This physically unacceptable result violates what is called the “maximum principle”. The diagonalisation of the mass matrix can solve these problems of overshoot of the maximum. This is detailed in the note . Only the main results are recalled here. The maximum principle is recalled in the continuous case, then sufficient conditions are expressed that make it possible to verify it for the discrete equations. It is shown in particular that the diagonalisation of the thermal mass matrix is one of these sufficient conditions, and various methods for diagonalising \mathrm{M} are presented. Another sufficient condition depends on the thermal stiffness matrix (conduction). From this point of view, the thermal finite elements used in Code_Aster are studied more particularly. It follows that, in the case of linear elements, all the sufficient conditions for verifying the maximum principle are gathered. In particular, the diagonalisation of the mass does indeed make it possible to obtain a regular solution. On the other hand, for quadratic elements, the oscillations cannot be prevented. The solution proposed in Code_Aster is therefore described: the modellings developed in 2D (AXIS_DIAG, PLAN_DIAG) and 3D work with linear elements only. A numerical study of a thermal shock on a cylinder makes it possible to illustrate these results. 2 Maximum principle 2.1 Statement of the principle for the continuous case One of the possible statements of the maximum principle for the heat operator is given here (in the absence of source terms, and in homogeneous isotropic linear thermal analysis) . r3.06.08 Finite elements treating quasi-incompressibility r3.06.08 Finite elements treating quasi-incompressibility Summary: In certain situations, the mechanical behaviour of the material requires that the volumetric dilatation remain zero, in other words that the strain take place at constant volume: isotropic elasticity with a Poisson's ratio equal to 0.5 , perfect plastic flows in limit analysis … One proposes here to treat this condition of “incompressibility” or of “quasi-incompressibility” by using a formulation valid both in the compressible case and in the quasi-incompressible case. For this, one uses a 3-field variational formulation in which the unknowns are the displacement, the volumetric strain and the associated Lagrange multiplier (which would correspond to the pressure in the incompressible case). One proposes two versions of this formulation: one for small strains, the other valid in the presence of large strains. In the situation of a one-to-one relation between the pressure and the swelling, the case of Von Mises plasticity, it is possible to eliminate the swelling unknown. One then has a two-field displacement/pressure formulation. After a few reminders of the difficulties posed by the solution of incompressible problems, one describes the mixed finite elements implemented (in 3D and in 2D, plane and axisymmetric, in small and in large strains), and one also presents the main lines of the integration into code_aster (modellings INCO_UP , INCO_UPG , INCO_UPO ). This modelling is necessary in order to carry out limit analyses and in order to model elastic behaviours for Poisson's ratios close to 0.5 . It may also be useful in the case of modellings giving rise to large plastic strains and for which the traditional modellings may be insufficient and give rise to stress oscillations. 1 Difficulties linked to the treatment of incompressibility In certain situations, the mechanical behaviour of the material requires that the strain take place at constant volume. Materials possessing this property of non-dilatancy are often described as “incompressible” materials. We shall see that these problems pose two types of difficulty. The first difficulty is linked to the writing of the incompressibility condition, the second is linked to the numerical problems which this constraint gives rise to. These difficulties are found again when the material is quasi-incompressible. One reasons here in small perturbations, but the problem remains the same in the framework of finite transformations. 1.1 “Incompressible” and “quasi-incompressible” behaviours In the framework of continuum mechanics, a strain of isochoric type is characterised by the fact that the transformation gradient F is such that J=\det(F)=1 . If one places oneself in the framework of small perturbations, the preceding condition reduces to: 	ext{tr}(\varepsilon )=divu=0 The tensor \varepsilon is therefore purely deviatoric: \varepsilon ={\varepsilon}^{D} . It follows that, in the case of isotropic materials, the invariant 	ext{tr}(\varepsilon ) (or \det(F) ) does not intervene in the expression of the free-energy density \varphi ; thus, in the case of incompressible elasticity in HPP, one simply has: \varphi (\varepsilon )=\mu {\varepsilon}^{D}:{\varepsilon}^{D} This density makes it possible to express only the deviatoric part of the stress tensor: {\sigma}^{D}=2\mu {\varepsilon}^{D} In fact, the stress is defined up to a constant p which is the opposite of the mean pressure: \sigma =2\mu {\varepsilon}^{D}+pI Note: Incompressible isotropic elasticity is of course a limiting case of isotropic elasticity with a Poisson's ratio 
u = rac{E}{2
u }-1 tending towards 0.5 . It is not only the elastic materials whose Poisson's ratio is equal to or slightly less than 0.5 which involve the incompressibility condition. Thus, it also intervenes in the case of a rigid-plastic material ( rac{\partial \Phi }{\partial 	ext{tr}\sigma }=0) . Indeed, one has in this case: \dot{\varepsilon}=\dot{\lambda} rac{\partial \Phi }{\partial \sigma };\ \ \dot{\lambda}\ge 0;\ \ \Phi \le 0;\dot{\lambda}\Phi =0 which leads to the incompressibility condition 	ext{tr}(\dot{\varepsilon})=0 . Moreover, in the case of elastoplasticity, when the plastic strains become largely greater than the elastic strains, one finds oneself in a virtually incompressible case with 	ext{tr}(\varepsilon )\mathrm{\simeq }0 . Finally, the materials satisfying a constitutive relation of NORTON-HOFF type (law used for the limit analyses [:external:ref: R7.07.01 ]) also present the characteristic of incompressibility: \varepsilon (v)=\alpha {({\sigma}_{	ext{eq}})}^{n-1}{\sigma}^{D}\ \ 	ext{avec} \ \ n\ge 1 \ \ 	ext{et}\ \ \alpha >0 where {\sigma}_{	ext{eq}}=\sqrt{ rac{3}{2}{\sigma}^{D}:{\sigma}^{D}} is the Von Mises equivalent stress. 1.2 Some possible numerical solutions If one wishes to treat the incompressibility condition exactly, as we have seen, the stress is not completely determined from the strain (cf. ). It is therefore necessary to use a mixed formulation, that is to say to introduce (at least) one other unknown of the problem which will make it possible to determine the stress tensor completely. Several variants are possible, the simplest consisting in imposing the incompressibility condition by means of a Lagrange multiplier which is then the pressure p . Note: If one opts for a penalisation procedure, one is brought back to the quasi-incompressible case and therefore to the difficulties mentioned below. One may also, in particular in the case of linear elasticity, choose to make the material slightly compressible. In this way, the stress is entirely defined from the displacement and the use of a mixed formulation is no longer indispensable. On the other hand, the solution of these problems with the classical displacement finite elements poses numerical difficulties. Indeed, the kinematic constraint represented by a constant-volume strain is very strong, even too strong if the degrees of freedom of the element are not numerous enough. Thus, the 3-node triangle may present locking phenomena, that is to say that the “mesh” cannot deform. In a less extreme way, most classical elements, in particular linear ones, behave in an abnormally stiff manner. New elements must therefore be used in order to “relax” the system. These elements may rest on different types of formulation: - in displacement only - mixed: displacements / stresses, displacements / pressures, strains / stresses, displacements / pressures / volumetric dilatations, … In all cases, if one is not careful, one may have numerical difficulties. Several approaches are used in order to facilitate the deformation of the elements: - using under-integration makes it possible to improve the results but it presents a drawback: it may lead to the appearance of spurious or hourglass modes. In order to solve this problem, one may either enrich the stiffness matrix by means of stabilisation matrices which neutralise the hourglass modes, or use projection methods which consist in projecting, into a smaller space, the incompressibility condition so as to eliminate the locking phenomena. The best known is the B-Bar method , - enriching the element by means of additional degrees of freedom: one then speaks of enhanced-strain methods, incompatible modes,... 1.3 Option adopted and fields of application We have chosen here to opt for a formulation which covers the quasi-incompressible (up to the incompressible) as well as the compressible. For this, the term 	ext{tr}(\varepsilon ) is treated as an independent variable. With the associated Lagrange multiplier, this leads to a 3- or 2-field formulation. A large-strain version has also been developed on the same principle. In this case, the independent variable linked to the incompressibility condition is no longer 	ext{tr}(\varepsilon ) but J=\det(F) . The advantage of the 3-field formulation with respect to the 2-field version is that it makes it possible to use, in a transparent manner, all the elasto-plastic constitutive laws available in Aster (no need to separate the deviatoric part and the spherical part of the stress tensor). It is therefore not limited to elasticity or to Von Mises elastoplasticity. On the other hand, it introduces a large number of additional degrees of freedom. Whatever formulation is adopted, one will not be able to treat the case in which the Poisson's ratio is strictly equal to 0.5 , because one uses, for the computation of the elastic stress, the term  rac{E

Consequently, the incompressible formulations must be used : - in order to treat limit-analysis problems for which one assumes that the flow takes place at constant volume R7.07.01, - in order to treat elastic problems whose Poisson's ratio is greater than 0.45 . They may also be used: - in order to treat problems in which the plastic strains are large, which gives rise to oscillations at the level of the stresses (example: in the case of analyses on notched specimens). Of course, this formulation being more costly than the classical displacement formulation, it is to be reserved for the cases which pose a problem and in which one is interested in the values of the stresses (one may first try to use under-integrated quadratic elements, which already improve the solution). 2 Mixed variational formulation of the problem 2.1 Formulation in the framework of small strains Let a solid \Omega be subjected to: - an imposed displacement field u={u}_{0} on {\Gamma}_{u} - an imposed traction field t=\sigma .n={t}_{0} on {\Gamma}_{t} - a body-force field f on \Omega In the classical case of the displacement finite elements (modelling 3D or D_PLAN or AXIS in code_aster ), when the problem derives from an energy, the problem solved is the following: find u\in V with \sigma satisfying the constitutive relation, which minimises the potential energy: As we have explained in section [r3.06.08-difficulte-inco], this formulation is not suitable when one seeks to approach the incompressible solution, that is to say the condition div(u)=0 or 	ext{tr}(\varepsilon )=0 . Moreover, it lends itself better to the architecture of an analysis code in which the integration of the constitutive laws is well separated from the computation of the terms specific to the finite elements (the constitutive routines do not need to know of the existence of the two strain measures) but only the enriched strain). 3 Discretisation by mixed finite elements 3.1 Choice of the discretisation When one uses a mixed formulation, it is necessary to discretise both the space of the displacements, of the Lagrange multiplier p and of the “swelling” g . The experience acquired on mixed elements, in particular with 2 fields for the incompressible elements, makes it possible to know that the discretisation of these fields cannot be arbitrary, on pain of obtaining oscillation phenomena (in particular at the level of the pressures) or locking phenomena (elements which cannot deform, or which are too stiff). Thus it is necessary to have a number of pressure Gauss points large enough to verify the incompressibility condition almost everywhere and a number of pressure Gauss points small enough to have more degrees of freedom to compute than constraints to verify. One of the conditions necessary in order to obtain satisfactory results is the verification, by the finite element considered, of the LBB condition (LADYJENSKAIA, BREZZI, BABUSKA). One may find in and examples of elements satisfying the LBB condition. Here the problem is a little different when the 3-field formulation is adopted. In the present state, the discretisations used are not the same in the HPP version and in the large-strain version. 3.1.1 Small strains For the small strains, we have drawn inspiration from the classical practice of mixed formulations (e.g. ), by using an element of type \mathit{P2}/\mathit{P1}/\mathit{P1} for the 3-field formulation. In other words, the displacement is quadratic, and the pressure and the swelling are both linear. The finite elements used for the 3-field formulation are therefore the following: | in 2D: | u | 6-node triangle | 8-node quadrilateral | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | p,g | 3-node triangle | 4-node quadrilateral | | | | in 3D: | u | 10-node tetrahedron | 20-node hexahedron | 15-node pentahedron | | p,g | 4-node tetrahedron | 8-node hexahedron | 6-node pentahedron | | For each type of element, one uses a single family of Gauss points: - 3 points for the triangles - 4 points for the quadrilaterals - 4 points for the tetrahedra - 8 points for the hexahedra - 21 points for the pentahedra For the two-field formulation, an element of type \mathit{P2}/\mathit{P1} has been introduced. The displacement therefore has a quadratic interpolation, while the pressure is interpolated linearly. In the case of the use of a discretisation into linear triangles or tetrahedra, two stabilisation methods have been introduced. The first corresponds to the stabilised finite element \mathit{P1}	ext{+/}\mathit{P1} . The + corresponds to the introduction of an additional degree of freedom at the centre of the element in the interpolation of the displacements. This additional degree is commonly called a “bubble”. This stabilisation method works only on simplex elements (triangle in 2D and tetrahedron in 3D). It has the advantage of using very few degrees of freedom. The second stabilisation method corresponds to the Orthogonal Sub-Grid Scale (OSGS) method . The advantage of this method is that it works for all element topologies. Its principal drawback is that it introduces a third unknown (and therefore additional degrees of freedom) corresponding to the projected pressure field \pi on the space orthogonal to the displacement fields. It is also possible to use the linear mechanics operator MECA_STATIQUE; however this is strongly discouraged because the results obtained may be of mediocre quality. The small-strain version is accessible by using DEFORMATION=’PETIT’ under COMPORTEMENT, the large-strain version by using DEFORMATION=’SIMO_MIEHE’ or DEFORMATION=’GDEF_LOG’. The usable constitutive relations are those available respectively in small strains and in large strains SIMO_MIEHE or GDEF_LOG for the INCO_UPG modellings. The modellings INCO_UP and INCO_UPO are at present limited to the relations ELAS and VMIS_ISOT_XXX. It is therefore not possible to use the modellings with the commands: CALC_MATR_ELEM/CALC_VECT_ELEM/ASSE_MATRICE/ASSE_VECTEUR/RESOUDRE Given the form of the tangent matrix for the 3-field formulations (INCO_UPG), it is often necessary to use the MUMPS solver in order to solve the linear systems. It is recommended to use the reference-stress convergence criterion RESI_REFE_RELA except for the INCO_UPO elements because the option is not available. 4.4 Formulation of the elementary right-hand side terms The loads may be gravity, distributed surface forces, pressures. r3.06.09 Mechanical joint finite elements and coupled hydromechanical joint finite elements r3.06.09 Mechanical joint finite elements and coupled hydromechanical joint finite elements Summary: This documentation deals with the description of the linear and quadratic mechanical joint finite elements. The modellings in pure mechanics (xxx_JOINT) support both types of mesh, whereas the coupled hydromechanical modellings (xxx_JOINT_HYME) are implemented only for quadratic meshes. One proceeds to the elimination of fictitious pressure degrees of freedom for the quadratic modellings in pure mechanics. These modellings make it possible to simulate the evolution of a crack along a predetermined path. The second type of element also takes into account the interaction of the mechanics with a fluid flow inside the crack. One presents in turn the following points: 1. geometry of the elements 2. local frame of the joint and passage matrix from the global frame to the local frame 3. displacement jump in the joint 4. gradient of the fluid pressure 5. nodal vector of the internal forces together with the elementary tangent matrix 1 Geometry of the elements 1.1 Geometry of the linear 2D joint The 2D joint element is a four-node quadrangle (QUAD4) with two short sides and two long sides [12] and [34] (see figure1) which represent the two segments {\Gamma}^{+} and {\Gamma}^{-} of an interface (or lips of a crack) between two two-dimensional sub-domains. In order to distinguish the sides {\Gamma}^{+} and {\Gamma}^{-} , the local numbering of the nodes must necessarily be carried out as in the figure below: n t n1 n2 n3 n4 Y X Figure1: 2D joint element with the correct local numbering. By convention the face {\Gamma}^{-} is given by nodes 3 and 4 and the face {\Gamma}^{+} by nodes 1 and 2. The normal n is directed from the face {\Gamma}^{-} towards the face {\Gamma}^{+} . 1.2 Geometry of the quadratic 2D joint These elements are eight-node quadrangles (QUAD8); nodes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 carry mechanical displacement degrees of freedom. Nodes 6 and 8 carry pressure degrees of freedom in order to represent the fluid flow for the coupled hydromechanical modelling. They are eliminated for the purely mechanical modellings. > Figure2: HYME 2D joint element with the correct local numbering. By convention the face {\Gamma}^{-} is given by nodes 3, 4, 7 and the face {\Gamma}^{+} by nodes 1, 2, 5. The normal n is directed from the face {\Gamma}^{-} towards the face {\Gamma}^{+} . 1.3 Geometry of the linear 3D joint The 3D joint elements make it possible to represent a surface S between two volume sub-domains {\Omega}^{+} and {\Omega}^{-} . They are compatible with the mesh of the sub-domains. If the volume is meshed with HEXA8 elements, the joints to be used are also HEXA8 (eight-node hexahedra). If the volume is meshed with PENTA6 or TETRA4 elements, the joints to be used are PENTA6 (six-node pentahedra). In order to distinguish the upper surfaces {S}^{+} (associated with {\Omega}^{+} ) and the lower surface {S}^{-} (associated with {\Omega}^{-} ), it is necessary to impose a very specific local numbering of the nodes (see figure3). Figure3 : Diagram of the 3D joint elements HEXA8 and PENTA6 with the correct local numbering. By convention the face {\Gamma}^{-} is given by nodes 1, 2, 3, 4 for the HEXA8 (or 1, 2, 3 for the PENTA6) and the face {\Gamma}^{+} by nodes 5, 6, 7, 8 for the HEXA8 (or 4, 5, 6 for the PENTA6). The normal n is directed from the face {\Gamma}^{-} towards the face {\Gamma}^{+} . 1.4 Geometry of the quadratic 3D joint These joint elements can be used for the coupled HYME modellings or for the modellings in pure mechanics by the elimination of pressure degrees of freedom. In 3D they make it possible to represent a surface S between two volume sub-domains in pure mechanics {\Omega}^{+} and {\Omega}^{-} . They are compatible with the mesh of the sub-domains. If the volume is meshed with HEXA20 elements, the joints to be used are also HEXA20 (twenty-node hexahedra). If the volume is meshed with PENTA15 or TETRA4 elements, the joints to be used are PENTA15 (15-node pentahedra). In order to distinguish the upper surfaces {S}^{+} (associated with {\Omega}^{+} ) and the lower surface {S}^{-} (associated with {\Omega}^{-} ) it is necessary to impose a very specific local numbering of the nodes (see figure4). Figure4 : Diagram of the coupled HYME joint elements in 3D, HEXA20 and PENTA15, with the correct local numbering. For the HEXA20, the mid-side nodes 13, 14, 15, 16 carry pressure degrees of freedom for the fluid flow, and all the others carry mechanical displacement degrees of freedom. For the PENTA15, the mid-side nodes 10, 11, 12 carry pressure degrees of freedom for the fluid flow, and all the others carry mechanical displacement degrees of freedom. By convention the face {\Gamma}^{-} is given by nodes 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12 for the HEXA20 (or 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9 for the PENTA15) and the face {\Gamma}^{+} by nodes 5, 6, 7, 8, 17, 18, 19, 20 for the HEXA20 (or 4, 5, 6, 13, 14, 15 for the PENTA15). The normal n is directed from the face {\Gamma}^{-} towards the face {\Gamma}^{+} . 1.5 Automatic construction of joint mesh cells The command MODI_MAILLAGE used with the keyword ORIE_FISSURE makes it possible to impose the correct local numbering of the joint mesh cells in 2D or in 3D (see doc. U4.23.04). Furthermore, techniques are available for automatically creating joint elements in a mesh which does not contain any (see U2.05.07). 2 Local frame and passage matrix It is necessary to construct a local frame for the element in order to define the displacement jump \delta (input data of the constitutive laws: see R7.02.11 and R7.01.25). Furthermore, one defines the passage matrix R from the global frame to the local frame. This part is valid for the joint modellings in pure mechanics and for the coupled hydromechanical modellings. 2.1 2D case Let (X,Y) be the global frame. r3.06.10 Quadrilateral element with one integration point, stabilised by the “Assumed Strain” method r3.06.10 Quadrilateral element with one integration point, stabilised by the “Assumed Strain” method Summary: Despite all the potential of the linear isoparametric quadrilateral element for finite-element analysis, the application of a classical bilinear formulation to define its displacement field leads to poor results. If under-integration of the element makes it possible to improve its performance, it nevertheless gives rise to spurious modes which make the analyses unstable. The present document takes up the main stages of a stabilisation method for the analyses called the “assumed strain method” and explains the way in which it has been implemented in the analysis code Code_Aster . Numerous results based on the stabilised element are compared and commented on in order to conclude on the performance of the method. 1 Shortcomings of the 2D QUAD4 element: In order to highlight the need for a more efficient plane element, analyses based on two test cases have been carried out, which make it possible to highlight the locking of the 4-node isoparametric quadrilateral element. 1.1 Test case no. 1 The first series of analyses comes from the modelling of a clamped beam subjected to a shear force \mathit{fsy} at its free end [r3.06.10-modelisation-poutre]. This beam has the following material characteristics: E=100 , 
u =0.4999 . This test case is inspired by the one written in (plane-strain assumption). Modelling of a beam Boundary conditions: Displacements on \mathit{AD} : \mathit{Ux}(A)=\mathit{Uy}(A)=0 \mathit{Ux}(D)=0 \mathit{fsx}=8	imes L	imes y/{B}^{2} Forces on \mathit{BC} : \mathit{Fy}=\mathit{fsy}=1-4	imes {y}^{2}/{B}^{2} \mathit{Fx}=0 Geometry: L=100 B=50 This analysis was carried out seven times, multiplying the number of mesh cells on each edge by two each time: Number of mesh cells on an edge At the end of each analysis, the deflection at C was compared with that of the “exact” solution of Timoshenko beam theory. [r3.06.10-convergence-deformation] shows that the convergence of the analysis towards the theoretical solution is largely insufficient given the number of mesh cells used for the modelling. However, by carrying out the analyses in plane stress, it is observed that the results of the analysis converge towards the theoretical solution in a satisfactory way ([r3.06.10-convergence-contraintes], quadratic convergence). Convergence of the QUAD4 element in plane strain Convergence of the QUAD4 element in plane stress This loading is said to be bending-dominated. Through the first series of analyses, the impossibility for the QUAD4 of representing the bending strain modes [r3.06.10-modes-deformation-flexion] in plane strain and for a coefficient 
u close to 0,5 has been highlighted. This results in an excessive stiffness of the element due to the shear terms of the discretised gradient operator. Bending strain modes 1.2 Test case no. 2 Imposed displacement: \mathit{dy}=1 The second series of analyses is based on the modelling of a notched specimen [r3.06.10-modelisation-eprouvette] loaded by an imposed displacement. Material characteristics: 
u =0.4999 E=200\mathit{Gpa} {\sigma}_{y}=0,1 {E}_{T}=10 Plasticity criterion: Von Mises, plasticity with linear isotropic hardening. Modelling of a notched specimen For the display of the results, each QUAD4 has been cut into 4 zones each containing one Gauss point. It is the value of the stress at this point that is displayed. Reference solution: QUAD8 INCO_UPG (element treating incompressibility perfectly). {\sigma}_{yy} QUAD4 solution: The results show that the QUAD4 converges only at the cost of strong stress oscillations within each element. If these oscillations allow the element to reconcile its nodal displacements and its plastic strain at constant volume, they make the results unrealistic. 2 Under-integration of the QUAD4 Despite all the potential of the isoparametric quadrilateral element for finite-element analysis, the application of a classical bilinear formulation to define its displacement field leads to poor results. This is explained by various reasons: - it presents an excessive stiffness (“lock”), when a loading whose plane-bending part is significant. - the classical bilinear formulation of the displacement field is very sensitive to mesh distortion and presents severe “locking” when it is applied to an incompressible material. A solution to these numerical locking problems consists in computing the stiffness matrix by means of a reduced integration. The principle of this method is to consider, in the numerical integration scheme, fewer integration points than are usually required to evaluate the exact stiffness matrices of the element. Starting from the isoparametric QUAD4 element r3.03.02, the number of integration points as well as the weight and the coordinates of the latter are modified, in order to create the under-integrated element which will be called in this document: QUAS4 | QUAD4 | QUAS4 | | --- | --- | | Number of integration points: 4 | Number of integration points: 1 | | Weight of each point: 1 | Weight of the point: 4 | | Coordinates: (x,y)=(\pm  rac{1}{\sqrt{3}},\pm  rac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) | Coordinates: (x,y)=(0,0) | 2.1 Formulation At the centre, the discretised gradient operator used to compute the stiffness matrix has the following form: B={B}_{c}=\left[ egin{array}{cc}{b}^{{t}_{x}}& 0\ 0& {b}^{{t}_{y}}\ {b}^{{t}_{y}}& {b}^{{t}_{x}}\end{array}ight] eq 2.1-1 With  egin{array}{}{b}_{x}^{t}=N,x(0)= rac{\partial N}{\partial x}\mid \xi =\eta =0\ {b}_{y}^{t}=N,y(0)= rac{\partial N}{\partial y}\mid \xi =\eta =0\end{array} eq 2.1-2 and N represents ({N}_{1},{N}_{2},{N}_{3},{N}_{4}) , the vector of the shape functions. It is recalled that the vectors b represent the simplest form of the under-integrated discretised gradient operator introduced by Hallquist and which is based on the evaluation of the derivatives of the isoparametric shape functions at the origin of the reference frame (\xi ,\eta ) That is:  egin{array}{c}{b}_{x}^{t}= rac{1}{\mathrm{2A}}\left[({y}_{2}-{y}_{4}),({y}_{3}-{y}_{1}),({y}_{4}-{y}_{2}),({y}_{1}-{y}_{3})ight]=	ext{Constant sur l'élément}\ {b}_{y}^{t}= rac{1}{\mathrm{2A}}\left[({x}_{4}-{x}_{2}),({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}),({x}_{2}-{x}_{4}),({x}_{3}-{x}_{1})ight]=	ext{Constant sur l'élément}\end{array} eq 2.1-3 A=(1/2).((\mathit{x2}-\mathit{x4}).(\mathit{y3}-\mathit{y1})+(\mathit{x3}-\mathit{x1})\mathrm{\ast }(\mathit{y4}-\mathit{y2})) : Area of the element The stiffness matrix is written: {K}_{e}={K}_{c}=A.{B}_{{c}^{T}}.C.{B}_{c} eq 2.1-4 C being: - either the elastic constitutive matrix for the analyses in elasticity - or the tangent matrix for the analyses in plasticity. Note that during such analyses, it is the integration of the constitutive law at the Gauss point (at the centre in our case) which determines the value of the coefficients of C . Finally, the internal forces are written: {F}_{int}={K}_{e}.U={B}_{{c}^{T}}.{\sigma}_{c} eq 2.1-5 U : Vector of the nodal displacements. 2.2 Failure of the analysis in Code_Aster: spurious modes The analyses launched on test case no. 1 with such an element fail. The stage of the analysis which consists in inverting {K}_{e} in order to determine the nodal displacements cannot be passed. Indeed, at the centre, the stiffness matrix is singular. Displaying the kernel of {K}_{e} , one observes that its dimension is no longer three but five. Two vectors have been added to the kernel and have made the inversion of the stiffness matrix impossible. The appearance of these two additional vectors in the kernel of {K}_{e} is directly linked to the fact that the centre is chosen as the only integration point. In other words, there exist two nodal displacement fields other than the displacement fields corresponding to rigid-body motion which cancel the internal forces. These modes represent the hourglass modes of the QUAD4 [r3.06.10-modes-sablier]. Subsequently, one of the stages of stabilisation will consist in enriching the discretised gradient operator in order to make {K}_{e} invertible. Hourglass modes of the QUAD4 2.3 Graphical interpretation of the problem linked to under-integration The problem of the under-integration of the QUAD4 is linked to its hourglass nodal displacement modes (bending loading). [r3.06.10-modes] shows that, on such modes, the coordinates of the centre remain unchanged. If this is in agreement with beam theory (i.e. in pure bending, xx = 0 on the neutral fibre), classical finite-element theory does not make it possible to distinguish the deformed and undeformed state of an element in such a case. This is why these modes are also called zero-energy modes, which, at the level of Code_Aster , make the analyses impossible to carry out. Modes This problem originates in a value of the strain at the centre which is not representative of the strain of the QUAD4. The next chapter will describe the approach which will make it possible to compute the strain of the QUAD4 whatever the displacement modes of these nodes. 3 Stabilisation of the QUAD4 with one Gauss point The stabilisation of the QUAS4 is carried out in two stages: - Enrich the discretised gradient operator {B}_{c} and thus make it possible to compute the strain energy linked to the hourglass displacement modes ( hourglass modes ); - Interpolate a strain / stress field making it possible to account for the strain / the stresses over the whole element while integrating the QUAD4 at the centre ( assumed strain stabilization ). 3.1 Variational principle of the problem This is taken from the weak form of the Hu–Washizu variational principle: > \delta \pi (\upsilon , ar{\dot{\varepsilon}}, ar{\sigma})={\int}_{{\Omega}_{e}}{\delta  ar{\dot{\varepsilon}}}^{T}.\sigma d\Omega +\delta {\int}_{{\Omega}_{e}}{ ar{\sigma}}^{T}.(

This, as has been observed, is far from being the case for the QUAD4. The stability of this new element in the face of test cases as severe as those presented in this report is comparable to that of the under-integrated quadratic QUAD8 element. On the other hand, this element has the convergence of a linear element in terms of number of degrees of freedom. One must therefore mesh with a sufficient fineness to capture the stress gradients of the sought solution. r3.06.13 Mixed interface finite elements for cohesive-zone models (xxx_INTERFACE and xxx_INTERFACE_S) r3.06.13 Mixed interface finite elements for cohesive-zone models (xxx_INTERFACE and xxx_INTERFACE_S) Summary: This document presents a mixed interface finite element for cohesive-zone models. The corresponding keywords for the modellings in Code_Aster are PLAN_INTERFACE, AXIS_INTERFACE,3D_INTERFACE, PLAN_INTERFACE_S, AXIS_INTERFACE_S and 3D_INTERFACE_S. 1 Introduction This cohesive-zone model accounts for the phenomena of crack initiation, of propagation (in a given direction) and of final failure. The mixed interface element is introduced in order to discretise the cracking path, whose degrees of freedom are the displacement of the two lips of the crack, as well as the density of the cohesive forces. The construction of the finite-element model and the integration of the constitutive law CZM_TAC_MIX are detailed. This document is largely inspired by the article of Lorentz 5; the interested reader may refer to it for more details. 2 Construction of the mixed interface finite element 2.1 Principle of energy minimisation in fracture mechanics In their approach to fracture mechanics, Francfort and Marigo 5 describe the state of a structure O by a displacement field u which may admit discontinuities \delta =\left[\left[u\right]\right] across the surfaces \Gamma (u) . For a given loading the displacement is characterised by an optimality condition: it corresponds to the local minimum of the potential energy defined as the sum of the elastic strain energy, of the cohesive energy and of the work of the external forces: \begin{array}{}{E}_{\text{pot}}(u)={E}_{\text{el}}(u)+{E}_{\text{fr}}(\left[\left[u\right]\right])-{W}_{\text{ext}}(u)\\ {E}_{\text{el}}(u)=\underset{\Omega /\Gamma (u)}{\int}\Phi (\epsilon (u))d\Omega ;{E}_{\text{fr}}(\delta )=\underset{\Gamma (u)}{\int}\Pi (\delta )\text{dS}\end{array} where \epsilon denotes the strain tensor, \Phi the (volumetric) strain-energy density and \Pi the (surface) cohesive-energy density. In this formulation, the fracture mechanisms are considered as reversible. Irreversibility will be introduced in the following part, from internal variables. The characteristics of the problem are deduced from the minimisation, namely: - the prediction of the cracking path, since all the possible discontinuous displacements are taken into account; - a stress criterion for crack initiation (see 5). - the cohesive law relates the displacement discontinuity \delta to the traction vector t from the (generalised) derivative of \Pi ; - the contact conditions are handled via the cohesive energy, to which an indicator function forbidding interpenetration of the lips is added. However, taking all the possible discontinuous displacements into account leads to numerical difficulties linked to the discretisation of the functional space \text{BD}(O) . In particular, allowing discontinuities across each of the finite elements leads to a mesh dependence of the results. Alternative works are carried out, based on the regularisation of the discontinuities 5 or on mesh adaptation 5. The latter are however limited to surface energies of Griffith type (without cohesive forces) and lead to significant numerical difficulties. This is why a simplification is introduced in the model by considering that the potential displacement-discontinuity surfaces \Gamma are postulated a priori and that they no longer depend on u . 2.2 Search for a saddle point by a decomposition–coordination method Despite the postulate on the direction of cracking, the minimisation of the energy is not obvious given the non-differentiability of the surface energy. One relies here on the decomposition–coordination technique introduced in 5, which condenses the non-differentiability to a local level (Gauss points). 2.2.1 Augmented Lagrangian The relation between the discontinuity field \delta and the displacement field u is introduced explicitly into the minimisation; the total energy E therefore depends explicitly on u and on \delta : E(u,\delta )=\underset{\Omega \setminus \Gamma }{\int}\Phi (\epsilon (u))d\Omega -{W}_{\mathrm{ext}}(u)+\underset{\Gamma}{\int}\Pi (\delta )\mathrm{d\Gamma } The minimisation of the potential energy is then equivalent to the following constrained minimisation problem (the displacement belonging to the set of kinematically admissible displacements): \underset{\begin{array}{}u,\delta \\ \left[\left[u\right]\right]=\delta \end{array}}{\min}E(u,\delta ) The linear constraint \left[\left[u\right]\right]=\delta is treated by dualisation: a solution (u,\delta ) of corresponds to a saddle point (u,\delta ,\lambda ) of the following Lagrangian, where \lambda corresponds to the field of Lagrange multipliers: L(u,\delta ,\lambda )\underset{\mathrm{déf}}{=}E(u,\delta )+\underset{\Gamma}{\int}\lambda \cdot (\left[\left[u\right]\right]-\delta )\mathrm{d\Gamma } Finally, in order to gain coercivity with respect to \delta , which will prove necessary later, a quadratic penalisation term is added, having no influence on the solution since it is equal to zero when the constraint is satisfied. The augmented Lagrangian {L}_{r} , with the penalisation coefficient r , is then written: {L}_{r}(u,\delta ,\lambda )\underset{\mathrm{déf.}}{=}E(u,\delta )+\underset{\Gamma}{\int}\lambda \cdot (\left[\left[u\right]\right]-\delta )\mathrm{d\Gamma }+\underset{\Gamma}{\int}\frac{r}{2}{(\left[\left[u\right]\right]-\delta )}^{2}\mathrm{d\Gamma } 2.2.2 Characterisation of the saddle point The first-order optimality conditions for the augmented Lagrangian are written in the following way: \forall \mathrm{\delta \delta }\underset{\Gamma}{\int}\left[t-\lambda -r(\left[\left[u\right]\right]-\delta )\right]\cdot \mathrm{\delta \delta }=0\text{avec}t\in \partial \Pi (\delta ) \forall \mathrm{\delta u}\underset{\Omega \setminus \Gamma }{\int}\sigma :\epsilon (\mathrm{\delta u})+\underset{\Gamma}{\int}\left[\lambda +r(\left[\left[u\right]\right]-\delta )\right]\cdot \left[\left[\mathrm{\delta u}\right]\right]={W}_{\text{ext}}(\mathrm{\delta u})\text{avec}\sigma =\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial \epsilon }(\epsilon ) \forall \mathrm{\delta \lambda }\underset{\Gamma}{\int}(\left[\left[u\right]\right]-\delta )\cdot \mathrm{\delta \lambda }=0 The meaning of the subdifferential \partial \Pi is given in part 3. At this stage, one contents oneself with saying that t\in \partial \Pi (\delta ) means that t and \delta are related by the cohesive law. The equation therefore gives an interpretation of the Lagrange multiplier \lambda : apart from the penalisation term, these are the cohesive forces. The equation expresses the equilibrium of the forces in the volume and along the surface of the discontinuity \Gamma . Finally, it imposes the constraint between the displacement field and its discontinuities. 2.3 Discretisation of the finite element Since the trajectory of the crack \Gamma is defined a priori and thanks to the small-perturbation assumption, the spatial discretisation of the system can rely on an interface finite element. Suppose that the subdomains {O}_{-} and {O}_{+} (parts of O respectively below and above \Gamma ) are discretised by tetrahedra or hexahedra so that the nodes on each side of \Gamma coincide 1 . In this case, degenerate prisms or hexahedra can be used to discretise \Gamma and to connect the two lips {\Gamma}_{-} and {\Gamma}_{+} of the potential cohesive crack (see Figure 2.3-a). Figure 2.3-a : Discretisation by an interface finite element. Let a mesh be characterised by the parameter h (for example, the maximum size of the finite elements). In the domain O a quadratic interpolation with classical Lagrange finite elements (continuous P2) is adopted. The discretised space of the displacement fields {U}_{h} is written: {U}_{h}=\left\lbrace u;\forall x\in \Omega u(x)=\left[N(x)\right]\left\lbrace U\right\rbrace \right\rbrace where \left\lbrace U\right\rbrace denotes the vector of the nodal displacements and \left[N\right] the matrix of the quadratic shape functions. The trace of the interpolated displacement on {\Gamma}_{-} and {\Gamma}_{+} is also piecewise quadratic and the displacement discontinuity is expressed in the following way: \forall x\in \Gamma {u}_{\mid {\Gamma}_{-}}(x)=\left[{N}_{-}(x)\right]\left\lbrace U\right\rbrace ;{u}_{\mid {\Gamma}_{+}}(x)=\left[{N}_{+}(x)\right]\left\lbrace U\right\rbrace \forall x\in \Gamma \left[\left[u(x)\right]\right]=\left[D(x)\right]\left\lbrace U\right\rbrace \text{avec}\left[D(x)\right]\underset{\text{déf.}}{=}\left[{N}_{+}(x)\right]-\left[{N}_{-}(x)\right] where \left[{N}_{-}\right] and \left[{N}_{+}\right] correspond respectively to the trace of \left[N\right] on {\Gamma}_{-} and {\Gamma}_{+} and where \left[D\right] denotes the matrix of the quadratic shape functions which interpolates the displacement jump. Note that it may be useful to introduce a rotation into \left[D\right] in order to obtain the components of \left[\left[u\right]\right] in a local coordinate system and thus to distinguish the normal and tangential parts. The field of Lagrange multipliers \lambda is interpolated on \Gamma by piecewise linear shape functions (continuous P1), leading to the following discretised space of Lagrange multipliers {L}_{h} : {L}_{h}=\left\lbrace \lambda ;\forall x\in \Gamma \lambda (x)=\left[L(x)\right]\left\lbrace \Lambda \right\rbrace \right\rbrace where \left\lbrace \Lambda \right\rbrace corresponds to the nodal unknowns of the Lagrange multiplier and \left[L\right] denotes the matrix of the linear shape functions on \Gamma . In this way, the constraint \left[\left[u\right]\right]=\delta imposed by is satisfied only in the weak sense. Finally, the discretisation of the discontinuity field \delta \in {D}_{h} is based on the collocation points on \Gamma , of coordinates {x}_{g} . These points correspond to the Gauss points, of weight {\omega}_{g} , used to compute the integrals. A standard modelling, and a so-called under-integrated modelling, are distinguished here. - In the standard modelling, the Gauss points number 3 (segments), 6 (triangles) or 9 (quadrilaterals) per element. This corresponds to a discontinuous P2 interpolation of \delta . This choice has the advantage of limiting the risk of appearance of zero pivots in the tangent matrix, but it does not satisfy the LBB condition in the limit of an infinite penalisation parameter r . - In the under-integrated modelling, the Gauss points number 2 (segments), 3 (triangles) or 4 (quadrilaterals) per element. This corresponds to a discontinuous P1 interpolation of \delta . This choice better satisfies the LBB condition in the limit r\to \infty , but it is liable to give rise to zero pivots in the tangent matrix. These zero pivots appear when the stiffness of the elements in contact with the interface is not sufficient to ensure the coercivity of the formulation, in particular when the interface lies on a plane of symmetry, or between a volume and a structural element (bar, grid or membrane). The spatial discretisation, the notations as well as the diagrams of the finite elements for the under-integrated modelling are summarised in Figure 2.3-b. This poses a priori no problem for the meshing algorithms, at least for cracks having a simple shape, for example plane. 3 Integration of the cohesive law CZM_TAC_MIX The cohesive behaviour is determined by the cohesive-energy density \Pi (\delta ) . Although the variational formulation presented in the previous part is independent of the choice of the cohesive energy, a particular cohesive model is now considered, whose specific features are detailed. Its main characteristics are: - contact conditions (non-interpenetration of the lips); - perfect initial adhesion (no regularisation of the surface energy); - coupling between the failure modes (tension and shear); - total failure (zero cohesive forces beyond a certain damage threshold); - irreversibility of the failure. This means in particular that there is no final friction, nor any distinction between the failure mechanisms in tension and in shear. Note: The Code_Aster keyword corresponding to this cohesive law is CZM_TAC_MIX. For more details on this law (internal variables, input parameters, consistent tangent matrix) and on other cohesive laws, one may refer to 5 (R7.02.11). 3.1 Preliminary notations Because of the constraint of non-interpenetration of the lips of the crack, the normal direction n for the potential discontinuity surface \Gamma (opening/compression) must be distinguished from the in-plane directions (sliding, shear). No numerical method is necessary; indeed, the only equation to be solved (in ) is piecewise linear. 4 Conclusion An interface finite-element model is proposed in order to model the evolution of cohesive cracks along a predefined path. The latter is compatible with the use of classical volume finite elements. Its unknowns are the nodal displacements on the lips of the cohesive crack as well as the nodal Lagrange multipliers, corresponding to the surface density of the cohesive forces. The Lagrangian of the problem is augmented; this makes it possible to ensure a convexity condition (via the penalisation parameter) which guarantees the uniqueness of the solution during the local integration of the law. This approach nevertheless presents the following limits and drawbacks: - The potential trajectories of the crack must be postulated a priori. - Additional degrees of freedom, corresponding to the cohesive forces, are introduced. However their number remains small since they are limited to the potential trajectories of the crack. - The introduction of Lagrange multipliers leads to a mixed formulation: the solution of the problem therefore amounts to a search for a saddle point and no longer to that of a minimum as was the case in the initial energetic formulation 5. - It is necessary to augment the Lagrangian in order to have a local convexity property. This implies the introduction of a penalisation parameter, with no influence on the continuous problem, but which could affect the results of the discretised problem. However, the numerical examples in 5 show that this sensitivity remains weak and disappears with mesh refinement. - The local integration of the cohesive law relies on the computation of the displacement discontinuities from the cohesive forces. An inverse approach is generally adopted in the literature for interface elements. However a certain number of interesting properties emerge: - No regularisation of the cohesive law is necessary, in particular as regards the initial adhesion or the contact condition. - The choice of a quadratic discretisation for the displacements and a linear one for the Lagrange multipliers makes it possible to satisfy the LBB condition. The latter makes it possible to ensure the convergence of the solution with mesh refinement in terms of displacements and of cohesive forces (see the numerical example in 5). - The rate of convergence which would be obtained without an interface is not disturbed by the presence of the interface elements (see 5). - The search for a saddle point leads to a symmetric tangent matrix. - This interface model is compatible with the usual solution algorithms of Code_Aster such as the Newton method, the line search or the control of the loading. This is illustrated by 2D and 3D analyses in 5, thus demonstrating the robustness and the reliability of such a model. 5 Bibliography 1. Bourdin B., Francfort G.A., Marigo J.-J. r3.06.14 Introduction to the Hybrid High-Order (HHO) methods r3.06.14 Introduction to the Hybrid High-Order (HHO) methods Summary: This document presents the HHO methods for problems in non-linear mechanics (small and large strains) and linear and non-linear thermal analysis. The corresponding keywords in AFFE_MODELE for the mechanical modellings in code_aster are D_PLAN_HHO and 3D_HHO. An extension to non-local formulations is possible (D_PLAN_GRAD_HHO and 3D_GRAD_HHO). For thermal analysis, there are AXIS_HHO, PLAN_HHO and 3D_HHO. One must then choose between the formulations CONSTANTE, LINEAIRE, QUADRATIQUE, CUBIQUE or QUARTIQUE. More complete theoretical details are given in [1] and [9]. 1 Introduction The HHO methods have been developed for some years by Di Pietro, Ern and their collaborators. The first works concern the problems of linear diffusion [2] and of linear elasticity [3]. Since then, the HHO methods have been extended to different physics in order to treat both linear and non-linear problems (see [1] for the references that follow). A complete introduction and a review of the applications is given in [9] For linear problems, we may cite the works on the Stokes problem, on linear diffusion with variable coefficients, on advection-diffusion-reaction, on the Cahn-Hilliard problem, and on flows in fractured porous media. The use of curved meshes is considered for the linear-diffusion problem. For non-linear problems, we may cite the works on the Leray-Lions problem, on the stationary Navier-Stokes equations, on spectral problems, and on Bingham fluids. As regards solid mechanics more particularly, there has been the extension to the problem of non-linear elasticity in small strains, to the Biot problem, to the equations of Kirchhoff--Love plates, and the works carried out in [1] on hyperelasticity in large strains [4], plasticity in small [5] and large [6] strains and unilateral contact with Tresca friction. From a numerical point of view, particular attention has been paid to the implementation of these methods in a generic manner so as to include polyhedral meshes in any dimension. The HHO methods are non-conforming methods, like the discontinuous Galerkin (dG) type methods, but unlike the latter, they are formulated in terms of face unknowns (carried by the skeleton of the mesh). Unknowns in the cells are also added for stability and approximation properties (whence the term Hybrid). These cell unknowns can be eliminated locally by static condensation (or Schur complement). The term High-Order comes from the fact that the HHO methods make it possible to do low order as well as high order without modification of the method. The construction of the HHO methods rests on two ideas: 1. the local reconstruction of a gradient or of a potential from the cell unknowns and the face unknowns by "mimicking" an integration by parts; 2. a local stabilisation operator in order to impose weakly, on each face of the cell, the consistency between the face unknowns and the trace of the cell unknowns. The HHO methods present numerous advantages: 1. arbitrary order of approximation ( k \geq 0 for linear diffusion and k \geq 1 for linear elasticity); 2. use of polyhedral meshes with possibly non-conforming interfaces (see for examples of polyhedral meshes); 3. robustness with respect to the physical parameters (elastic incompressibility, dominant advection...); 4. attractive numerical costs thanks to static condensation, which makes it possible to eliminate the unknowns carried by the cells while maintaining a compact stencil; 5. local conservation of the fluxes on each face of the mesh. Examples of polyhedral meshes supported by the HHO methods. Point (3) is particularly relevant in the context of this manuscript, in which we are interested in the problems of solid mechanics, because the HHO methods will allow us to use a purely primal formulation (without addition of Lagrange multipliers, unlike mixed formulations) in order to eliminate the numerical locking arising from incompressibility, which is usually present for the H^1 -conforming methods. As for point (2) , one motivation is to be able to carry out a local refinement of the mesh without having to concern oneself with the possible presence of hanging nodes as in the H^1 -conforming methods. Indeed, as illustrated in this figure, the presence of hanging nodes is handled simply by treating the corresponding mesh cell as a polygon (or a polyhedron). Example of local refinement treated by the HHO methods (middle) and by the H^1 -conforming methods (right) starting from the same initial mesh (left). The HHO methods present more or less close connections with other numerical methods developed in recent years. For the low-order methods, there exist links with the Hybrid Finite Volumes and Mixed Finite Volumes methods, with the Mimetic Finite Differences methods (see [8] for a unified framework of the three previous methods), as well as with the Compatible Discrete Operator methods and the Gradient Schemes. For the higher-order methods, a connection has been established between the HHO methods, Hybridizable Discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) and nonconforming Virtual Element Methods (ncVEM). The main similarities and differences between the HHO, HDG and ncVEM methods are: - the reconstruction of the discrete operators for HHO replaces the flux equations for HDG, and these operators play the same role as the projection operators used by ncVEM; - the stabilisation operators for HHO and HDG are defined from a functional point of view (and are different in the case where the cell unknowns have the same degree as the face unknowns), whereas for ncVEM these operators are defined from an algebraic point of view while leading to quadratic forms equivalent to HHO. 2 Description of the method 2.1 Case of linear elasticity In this section we shall present the Hybrid High-Order (HHO) methods by means of the linear-elasticity problem. The aim is to describe the main principles of construction of the HHO methods. The domain \Omega_{0} deforms under the action of a body loading f \in {L}^{2}(\Omega_0;\mathbb{R}^{d}) and homogeneous Dirichlet-type conditions are imposed on the boundary \Gamma (for simplicity). Finally, it is important to recall that these convergence rates are one order higher than those obtained for {H}^{1} -conforming finite elements using polynomials of degree k in the cells. 3 Implementation The implementation in code_aster of new numerical methods that differ from the Lagrange elements can be difficult. We list the main reasons: - Limited number of geometric supports possible in the mesh: triangle and quadrangle in 2D, and tetrahedron, hexahedron, prism and pyramid in 3D (no support of polyhedral meshes); - Strong connection between the geometric support and the chosen element. The degree of approximation of the method is determined by the geometric support. For example, a linear approximation for triangles with 3 nodes (TRIA3) and a quadratic one for triangles with 6 nodes (TRIA6); - The finite-element unknowns are supported only by physical nodes of the mesh (and not by faces or cells of the mesh, as is the case for the finite-volume, discontinuous Galerkin and HHO methods). The main objective for the implementation of the HHO methods in code_aster is to reuse as much as possible the architecture of the code and not to modify the critical points of the code, which are: - The data structures - The finite-element catalogues - The locality of the elementary computations - The assembly operation We limit ourselves, for the implementation of the HHO methods in code_aster , to the geometric supports that already exist. Moreover, only the constant approximations k=0 (in thermal analysis only), linear k=1 , quadratic k=2 , cubic k=3 and quartic k=4 are implemented. The constant approximation, k=0 , is not available in mechanics because the kernel of the strain tensor includes, in addition to the constant translations, the rigid rotations. The various modifications are limited to two operators: - CREA_MAILLAGE: option MODI_HHO - DEFI_MATERIAU: option HHO 3.1 HHO unknowns and numbering We recall that the HHO unknowns, {\widehat{v}}_{T}=({v}_{T},{v}_{\partial T})\in {U}_{T}^{k} , that we compute are the coefficients of the polynomials of the cells and of the faces (these coefficients have a priori no physical meaning). Since the assembly must be carried out face by face (and cell by cell) and the HHO unknowns can be supported only by physical nodes of the mesh in code_aster , we need each face of the mesh to possess at least one node that is not shared with any other face of the mesh (typically a node located at the barycentre of the face) and that there be a node at the barycentre of the cell. This is the case in 2D for the triangle with 7 nodes (TRIA7) and the quadrangle with 9 nodes (QUAD9), and in 3D for the hexahedron with 27 nodes (HEXA27). These geometric supports correspond to the quadratic elements for the isoparametric elements. Unfortunately, there are not in code_aster tetrahedra, prisms and pyramids with this property. This is why we have added a mesh converter in CREA_MAILLAGE named MODI_HHO which makes it possible to transform a tetrahedron with 4 nodes into a tetrahedron with 15 nodes (likewise for the prisms (PENTA21) and the pyramids (PYRAM19)). The new nodes are located at the barycentre of the faces and of the cell. The face unknowns {v}_{F} for the faces F\in {F}_{h} are supported by the node that is located at the barycentre of the face F . These physical nodes of the mesh that support the face unknowns are named unknown_nodes . Moreover, since the faces are assumed plane, we use the vertex nodes to describe the geometry of the cells and of the faces; and to compute the various integrals. These physical nodes of the mesh that describe the geometry are named geometric_nodes . Finally, the nodes located at the midpoints of the segments are not used and are named empty_nodes . These different categories of nodes are illustrated here. These devices concerning the location of the HHO unknowns make it possible to reuse the data structures and the assembly without modifications. Different categories of nodes used for the geometric supports TRIA7, QUAD9, TETRA15 and HEXA27. Note (Static condensation): Static condensation (or Schur complement) makes it possible to eliminate locally the cell unknowns in the elementary contributions (in the end, a smaller problem composed only of the face unknowns is solved). One of the main difficulties is that the elementary contributions are computed locally to the element (cell or face) and then assembled directly into the global problem using the numbering. Whereas for the HHO methods, static condensation must be carried out before assembly in order to eliminate the cell unknowns. For reasons of simplicity, static condensation is not implemented, so as not to change the architecture of the code. However, it is possible to use it outside the operators with the HHO module in python. An example is given in zzzz513f. 3.2 Dirichlet boundary conditions The Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed strongly by modifying the matrix and the loading. The user must specify the imposed displacements on the Dirichlet boundary. However, it is not obvious for the user to give the values of the face and cell unknowns because these coefficients have a priori no physical meaning. We have added an automatic translator which computes the L^2 projection, {\Pi}_{F}^{k}({u}_{D}) , and imposes the value {v}_{F}={\Pi}_{F}^{k}({u}_{D}) from the displacement {u}_{D} given at the nodes of the face (in the continuous sense). In practice, in AFFE_CHAR_CINE, it suffices to give the conditions on DX, DY and/or DZ and the operator translates them automatically into conditions on the HHO polynomials. 3.3 Post-processing The HHO unknowns are the coefficients of polynomials. These coefficients have a priori no physical meaning. Thus, a post-processing must be applied in order to be able to visualise these results. We create a new NOEU field which will interpolate, in the sense of the Lagrange elements, the HHO unknowns in the field HHO_DEPL at the end of the analysis. The value of the displacement at a node of the mesh is the average of the values of the cell unknowns that contain this node. Note that this field is continuous, unlike the HHO fields. It must be carefully noted that this field is not in equilibrium with that of the stresses. It is there for purely visual purposes. The same post-processing is applied to the velocity and acceleration fields in the dynamic case. 3.4 Scope of use The HHO method can be used only in static and transient non-linear mechanics (STAT_NON_LINE/DYNA_NON_LINE) and in linear and non-linear thermal analysis (THER_LINEAIRE/THER_NON_LINE) The following features are excluded: - contact/friction - model reduction - macro-elements - computation of vibration modes or of buckling criteria The method can be used for the constitutive laws in small and large strains (model GDEF_LOG, PETIT, GREEN_LAGRANGE). Moreover, the HHO method cannot be used simultaneously with a standard finite-element method. The boundary conditions can be assigned only by elimination (AFFE_CHAR_CINE (_F)). Most of the body and surface loadings are available. The method works on all the 2D and 3D elements of the code. One must, where applicable, use CREA_MAILLAGE/MODI_HHO in order to make the mesh compatible. Certain parameters such as the stabilisation coefficient can be defined by zone in DEFI_MATERIAU/HHO. If no value is given, an automatic value is computed from the elastic parameters. 4 Bibliography 1. Pignet, Doctoral thesis, Hybrid High-Order methods for nonlinear solids mechanics, 2019. 1.
