r3.06.15 Stabilised mixed finite elements r3.06.15 Stabilised mixed finite elements Summary: These finite elements aim to complete the library of available finite elements by placing at the user's disposal a finite element having the following characteristics: - linear. The use of a linear finite element can, in certain cases, present advantages relative to a quadratic element: compatibility with linear structural elements; more diffuse damage with a local constitutive law, etc. - mixed. The finite element carries, as additional degrees of freedom, all the components of the strain tensor. This confers on it an accuracy far superior to that of the usual linear finite elements. - stabilised. The standard mixed formulations (\disp , \strain) can in certain cases exhibit spurious oscillations of the stress field. The finite element presented here introduces a stabilisation term making it possible to remove these spurious oscillations. These finite elements are available in AFFE_MODELE in 3D (modelling 3D_MIX_STA ) and in plane strain (modelling D_PLAN_MIX_STA ). They can be used only in small strains. Furthermore, two formulations are available: a standard formulation (formulation STA , taken from and ) and an incompressible formulation (formulation STA_INCO , taken from ) inspired by the B-bar method. 1 Equations of the problem The equations of the problem presented here are taken from and from . 1.1 Setting up the equations The equations of the problem are written in the classical way: \begin{split}\left \lbrace \begin{array}{ll} \divTensTwo {\left( \tensTwo{D} \strain \right)} + \vector{f} = \vectorZero \\ - \strain + \operGradSyme{\disp} = \tensTwoZero \\ \end{array} \right.\end{split} Here \operGradSyme{} represents the symmetric gradient operator and \tensTwo{D} represents the constitutive operator such that \stress = \tensTwo{D} \strain . The weak form of this system of equations is then written: Note \begin{split}\left \lbrace \begin{array}{ll} {\int}_{\domain} \transpose{\left(\operGradSyme{\dispVirt} \right)} \left(\tensTwo{D} \strain \right) \,d\domain = {\int}_{\domain} \transpose{\dispVirt} \vector{f} \, d\domain + {\int}_{\bound} \transpose{\dispVirt} \vector{t} \, ds \qquad \forall \dispVirt \text{ les déplacements virtuels}\\ - {\int}_{\domain} \transpose{\delta \strain} \strain \, d\domain + {\int}_{\domain} \ \delta \transpose{\strain} \operGradSyme{\disp} \, d\domain = 0 \qquad \forall \ \delta \strain \text{ les déformations virtuelles} \\ \end{array} \right.\end{split} A choice slightly different from is made here, where the authors choose to multiply the compatibility equation by the tangent operator. 1.2 Finite-element formulation 1.2.1 Standard formulation The displacement and strain unknowns are approximated by independent degrees of freedom. \discVect{U} and \discVect{E} denote the corresponding vectors containing the nodal unknowns. \discMatr{N_u} and \discMatr{N_E} denote the matrices containing the linear shape functions. One has \discMatr{B_U} = \operGradSyme \discMatr{N_u} where \discMatr{B_U} is the usual matrix of the derivatives of the shape functions. In practice, a node therefore has nine unknowns ( DX , DY , DZ , EPXX , EPYY , EPZZ , EPXY , EPXZ and EPYZ ) in 3D and six unknowns in plane strain ( DX , DY , EPXX , EPYY , EPZZ , EPXY and EPYZ ). A stabilisation parameter denoted \tau_{\strain} (lying between 0 and 1) is introduced, such that after discretisation: \begin{split}\left \lbrace \begin{array}{ll} \disp = \discMatr{N_u} \discVect{U} \\ \vector{\varepsilon} = (1 - \tau_{\strain}) \discMatr{N_E} \discVect{E} + \tau_{\strain} \discMatr{B_U} \discVect{U} \\ \end{array} \right.\end{split} \vector{\varepsilon} has been written for the strain degrees of freedom arranged in vector form so as to be homogeneous in notation with the displacements. The stabilisation parameter \tau_{\strain} makes it possible, among other things, to dispense with the inf-sup condition, and to choose linear discretisations for the displacement and strain degrees of freedom. It is observed that for \tau_{\strain} = 1 one recovers a usual linear finite element, and that for \tau_{\strain} = 0 one recovers an unstabilised mixed finite element. By inserting this discretisation into the weak form of the equations of the problem, one obtains: \begin{split}\begin{bmatrix} \discMatr{K_{\tau}} & \discMatr{G} \\ \discMatr{M_U} & \discMatr{M_E} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \discVect{U} \\ \discVect{E} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \discVect{F} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\end{split} The matrices \discMatr{K_{\tau}} \discMatr{G} , \discMatr{M_U} and \discMatr{M_E} are expressed in the following way: \begin{split}\left \lbrace \begin{array}{ll} \discMatr{K_{\tau}} = {\int}_{\domain} \tau_{\strain} \transpose{\discMatr{B_U}} \discMatr{D} \discMatr{B_U} \, d\domain \\ \discMatr{G} = {\int}_{\domain} \left(1 - \tau_{\strain} \right) \transpose{\discMatr{B_U}} \discMatr{D} \discMatr{N_E} \, d\domain \\ \discMatr{M_U} = {\int}_{\domain} \left(1 - \tau_{\strain} \right) \transpose{\discMatr{B_U}} \discMatr{B_U} \, d\domain \\ \discMatr{M_E} = - {\int}_{\domain} \left(1 - \tau_{\strain} \right) \transpose{\discMatr{N_E}} \discMatr{N_E} \, d\domain \\ \end{array} \right.\end{split} Note that the right-hand side is identical to that of a usual finite element for the displacement degrees of freedom, and equal to 0 for the strain degrees of freedom. 1.2.2 Incompressible formulation In , the authors propose an incompressible formulation for the stabilised mixed finite elements, a formulation inspired by the B-bar method. For this incompressible formulation, the matrix \tensTwo{B_U} is replaced by the following matrix \tensTwo{\overline{B}_U} \tensTwo{\overline{B}_U} = \tensTwo{B_U}^{\text{dev}} + \tensTwo{\overline{B}_U}^{\text{vol}} Here, \tensTwo{B_U}^{\text{dev}} represents the deviatoric part of \tensTwo{B_U} and \tensTwo{B_U}^{\text{vol}} its spherical part. One has \tensTwo{\overline{B}_U}^{\text{vol}} = \frac{1}{\text{npg}} \sum_{k=1}^{\text{npg}} \tensTwo{B_{U,k}}^{\text{vol}} \text{ avec npg le nombre de points de Gauss de l'élément considéré} It is therefore the average of the operator over all the Gauss points. This formulation is available under the name STA_INCO , only for the HEXA8 elements (in 3D) and the QUAD4 elements (in plane strain). Note A choice slightly different from is made here, where the authors use the following matrix \tensTwo{\overline{B}_U} = \tensTwo{B_U}^{\text{dev}} + \left( \tau_{\strain} \tensTwo{\overline{B}_U}^{\text{vol}} + \left(1 - \tau_{\strain} \right) \tensTwo{B_U} \right) However, tests (see Cook's membrane in small plastic strains) have shown that the choice finally retained here gave markedly better results for the treatment of incompressibility. 2 Precautions for use 2.1 Choice of the stabilisation parameter The choice of the stabilisation parameter \tau_{\strain} is left to the user. In , the authors recommend choosing \tau_{\strain} = \frac{h}{L} where L represents the characteristic length of the problem, and h the mesh-cell size. 2.2 Symmetry conditions In the presence of a plane of symmetry, it is necessary to impose symmetry conditions on the strain degrees of freedom (in addition to the usual boundary conditions on the displacements). For example, in plane strain, a plane of symmetry of normal X will result in an additional boundary condition EPXY = 0 on this plane. In 3D, a plane of symmetry of normal Y will result in EPXY = EPYZ = 0 . 2.3 Command variables The expression of the strain used as input to the constitutive law is recalled: \vector{\varepsilon} = (1 - \tau_{\strain}) \discMatr{N_E} \discVect{E} + \tau_{\strain} \discMatr{B_U} \discVect{U} In the expression above, \discMatr{B_U} \discVect{U} is constant per element whereas \discMatr{N_E} \discVect{E} is affine per element. It is therefore recommended to use adapted command variables in order to avoid any numerical locking. For example, in the case of temperature, it is recommended to use the following temperature as command variable: \tilde{T} = (1 - \tau_{\strain}) T + \tau_{\strain} \overline{T} With T an affine temperature and \overline{T} a temperature constant per element. In practice, the parameter \tau_{\strain} being small compared with 1, it would also be possible to use an affine temperature as command variable. 2.4 Discontinuities The stabilised mixed finite elements have nodal strain unknowns. For small values of \tau_{\strain} (which is often the case in practice), the strain and the stress are therefore almost continuous from one element to another. This element is therefore not suited to the modelling of strong discontinuities (such as, for example, prestressing in a civil-engineering structure). However, it is entirely possible to mix usual linear finite elements and stabilised mixed finite elements (see ). 2.5 Other uses In reference , the authors show that the stabilised mixed finite elements present good properties for the modelling of slender structures of plate type. In reference , the authors show that these finite elements make it possible to capture the cracking paths in the case of local damage models. However, this use of the stabilised mixed finite elements is not the subject of specific test cases and it is therefore not validated on EDF applications. 3 Validation The test case of Cook's membrane in elasticity (sslp104) compares the results obtained with those of reference . The test case of the clamped arch in elasticity (sslp108) is an example of implementation of the symmetry boundary conditions specific to the stabilised mixed elements. This test case is also originally taken from , but in the absence of the numerical values making it possible to recover the values of the original article, the results are compared with those obtained with standard quadratic elements. The test case of Cook's membrane in small plastic strains (modellings V and W of ssnp178) makes it possible to test the incompressible formulation by comparing it with results taken from the literature and obtained with other modellings available for this type of problem ( HHO and INCO_UPG ). The test case ssnp180 SCIENCE tests (modellings C and D) makes it possible to validate the use of the stabilised mixed finite elements on a structure representative of reinforced-concrete problems. 4 References Cervera, Miguel & Barbat, Gabriel & Chiumenti, Michele. (2025). Bending, Twisting, Merging and Branching Cracks: A Challenging Set of Problems. Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering. 32. 10.1007/s11831-025-10223-w. Cervera, Miguel & Chiumenti, Michele & Codina, Ramon. (2010). Mixed Stabilized Finite Element Methods in Nonlinear Solid Mechanics. Part I: Formulation. Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering. 199. 2559-2570. 10.1016/j.cma.2010.04.006. Saloustros, S., Cervera, M., Kim, S. et al. Accurate and locking-free analysis of beams, plates and shells using solid elements. Comput Mech 67, 883-914 (2021). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00466-020-01969-0

r3.07.03 Plate elements: modellings DKT, DST, DKTG and Q4G r3.07.03 Plate elements: modellings DKT, DST, DKTG and Q4G Summary: These modellings of plate finite elements are intended for analyses in small strains and small displacements of thin curved or plane structures. They are plane finite elements which do not take into account the geometric curvature of thin structures, unlike shell elements which are curved: parasitic bendings result, which can be reduced by using more elements so as to be able to approximate curved geometries correctly. The formulation is therefore simplified and the number of degrees of freedom reduced. These finite elements are reputed to be among the most accurate for the computation of the displacements and for modal analysis. For each of these different modellings several finite elements are available, according to the mesh cells: - the modelling DKT, according to the Love-Kirchhoff bending model, comprises the triangular (DKT) and quadrangular (DKQ) finite elements, which use fields with sub-points, in order for example to integrate the constitutive relation in the layers making up the thickness; - the modelling DST, with transverse shear energy in elasticity, comprises the triangular (DST) and quadrangular (DSQ) finite elements; - the modelling DKTG, according to the Love-Kirchhoff bending model, comprises the triangular (DKTG) and quadrangular (DKQG) finite elements, dedicated to “global” constitutive relations, which have only one layer and a single integration point in the thickness; - the modelling Q4G (also named 	ext{Q4}\gamma ) with transverse shear energy in elasticity, but with an interpolation other than for the modelling DST, comprises only the quadrangular finite element (Q4G). Note: In the document R3.07.09, one presents the modelling Q4GG, dedicated to thick plates. This modelling comprises the quadrangular finite elements (Q4G) whose theoretical description is given in the present document and the triangular elements (T3G) . 1 Introduction Shell and plate elements are used in particular to model thin structures where the ratios between the dimensions (thickness/characteristic length) are at most 1/10 . They therefore intervene in particular in fields such as civil engineering, PWR core internals, vibratory analysis, Euler buckling analysis, the analysis of thin structures in elastic multi-layer composite material... One restricts oneself to the framework of small displacements (even if it is possible but little recommended to use the updating ’PETIT_REAC’) and of small strains. Unlike shell elements, plane plate elements do not make it possible to take into account the geometric curvature of the structure to be represented and induce parasitic bendings. It is therefore necessary to use a large number of these elements so as to approximate the geometry of the structure correctly, and this all the more so as it is curved. On the other hand, one gains in simplicity of formulation and the number of degrees of freedom is reduced. Moreover, the formulations " Discrete Shear " (DST, DSQ and Q4g) or " Discrete Kirchhoff " (DKT, DKTG and DKQ, DKQG) of the kinematics, with or without transverse distortion respectively, allow good results in terms of displacements and of modal analysis. The support mesh cells of these finite elements are linear (triangles and quadrangles). The degrees of freedom of these finite elements are the translations and the rotations of the vertex nodes. The characteristics which one assigns to them are: the thickness, the shear coefficient, the offset, ... The manner in which these elements are implemented in code_aster as well as certain aspects of the use are given at [§5] of the present documentation. In particular one classifies these formulations: | modelling | finite elements | Use | | --- | --- | --- | | DKT | DKT, DKQ | Love-Kirchhoff model, dedicated to linear and non-linear constitutive relations with integration sub-point fields in the thickness, cf. §:ref:4.9 . | | DKTG | DKTG, DKQG | Love-Kirchhoff model, dedicated to “global” constitutive relations, which have only one layer and a single integration point in the thickness | | DST | DST, DSQ | model with transverse shear energy in elasticity | | Q4G | Q4g | model with transverse shear energy in elasticity | 2 Formulation 2.1 Geometry of the plate elements [1] For the plate elements one defines a reference surface, or mean surface, which is plane (plane x,y for example) and a thickness h(x,y) . This thickness must be small with respect to the other dimensions (extents, radii of curvature) of the structure to be modelled. [Figure 2.1-a] below illustrates our point. Figure 2.1-a One attaches to the mean surface \omega a local orthonormal frame \mathit{Oxyz} associated with the tangent plane of the structure, different from the global frame \mathit{OXYZ} . The position of the points of the plate is given by the Cartesian coordinates (x,y) of the mean surface and the elevation z with respect to this surface. 2.1.1 Intrinsic frame By taking the previous local frame \mathit{Oxyz} with as origin the first vertex of the element and as axis \mathit{Ox} the side joining vertices 1 and 2, one defines the so-called intrinsic frame. 2.2 Plate theory These elements rest on the theory of plates in small displacements and small strains. 2.2.1 Kinematics The straight sections, which are the sections perpendicular to the mean surface, remain straight; the material points situated on a normal to the undeformed mean surface remain on a straight line in the deformed configuration. It results from this approach that the displacement fields vary linearly in the thickness of the plate . If one denotes by u,v,w the displacements of a point q(x,y,z) along x , y and z , one thus has the Hencky-Mindlin kinematics: ( egin{array}{c}{u}_{x}(x,y,z)\ {u}_{y}(x,y,z)\ {u}_{z}(x,y,z)\end{array})=( egin{array}{c}u(x,y)\ v(x,y)\ w(x,y)\end{array})+z( egin{array}{c}{	heta}_{y}(x,y)\ -{	heta}_{x}(x,y)\ 0\end{array})=( egin{array}{c}u(x,y)\ v(x,y)\ w(x,y)\end{array})+z( egin{array}{c}{ eta}_{x}(x,y)\ { eta}_{y}(x,y)\ 0\end{array}) where u,v,w are the displacements of the mean surface and {	heta}_{x} and {	heta}_{y} the rotations of this surface with respect to the two axes x and y respectively. One prefers to introduce the two rotations { eta}_{x}(x,y)={	heta}_{y}(x,y),{ eta}_{y}(x,y)=-{	heta}_{x}(x,y) . The three-dimensional strains at any point, with the kinematics introduced previously, are thus given by:  egin{array}{c}{\epsilon}_{xx}={e}_{xx}+z{\kappa}_{xx}\ {\epsilon}_{yy}={e}_{yy}+z{\kappa}_{yy}\ 2{\epsilon}_{xy}={\gamma}_{xy}=2{e}_{xy}+2z{\kappa}_{xy}\ 2{\epsilon}_{xz}={\gamma}_{x}\ 2{\epsilon}_{yz}={\gamma}_{y}\end{array} where {e}_{xx},{e}_{yy} and {e}_{xy} are the membrane strains of the mean surface, {\gamma}_{x} and {\gamma}_{y} the strains associated with the transverse shears, and {\kappa}_{xx},{\kappa}_{yy},{\kappa}_{xy} the bending strains (or changes of curvature) of the mean surface, which are written:  egin{array}{c}{e}_{xx}= rac{\partial u}{\partial x}\ {e}_{yy}= rac{\partial v}{\partial y}\ 2{e}_{xy}= rac{\partial v}{\partial x}+ rac{\partial u}{\partial y}\ {\kappa}_{xx}= rac{\partial { eta}_{x}}{\partial x}\ {\kappa}_{yy}= rac{\partial { eta}_{y}}{\partial y}\ 2{\kappa}_{xy}= rac{\partial { eta}_{x}}{\partial y}+ rac{\partial { eta}_{y}}{\partial x}\ {\gamma}_{x}={ eta}_{x}+ rac{\partial w}{\partial x}\ {\gamma}_{y}={ eta}_{y}+ rac{\partial w}{\partial y}\end{array} Note: In plate theories the introduction of { eta}_{x} and { eta}_{y} makes it possible to symmetrise the formulations of the strains and, as we shall see later, the equilibrium equations. In shell theories one rather uses {	heta}_{x} and {	heta}_{y} and the associated moments {M}_{x} and {M}_{y} with respect to x and y . 2.2.2 Constitutive law The behaviour of the plates is a 3D behaviour in “plane stress”. Two theories including the strain due to the shear force exist and are presented in [2]. 2.2.3.1 The so-called Hencky theory This theory as well as that of Love-Kirchhoff which follows from it immediately rests on the kinematics presented in §2.2.1. The constitutive relation is the usual one and the shear correction factor is equal to k=1 . Note: When one does not take into account the transverse distortions {\gamma}_{x} and {\gamma}_{y} in the Hencky theory, the model obtained is that of Love-Kirchhoff (finite elements DKT(G) and DKQ(G)). The two rotations of the mean surface are then linked to the displacements of the mean surface by the following relation:  egin{array}{c}{ eta}_{x}=- rac{\partial w}{\partial x}\ { eta}_{y}=- rac{\partial w}{\partial y}\end{array} 2.2.3.2 The so-called Reissner theory (DST, DSQ and Q4g) The second theory, called Reissner’s, is developed from the stresses. The variation of the membrane stresses ( {\sigma}_{xx} , {\sigma}_{yy} and {\sigma}_{xy} ) is assumed linear in the thickness as in the case of the Hencky theory where this results from the linearity of the variation of the membrane strains with the thickness. However, whereas one assumes, in the Hencky theory, that the distortion is constant in the thickness and therefore the shear stresses, which violates the boundary conditions {\sigma}_{xz}={\sigma}_{yz}=0 on the upper and lower faces of the plate because of the constitutive law stated in §2.2.2., one uses within the framework of the Reissner theory the equilibrium equations in order to deduce from them the variation of the shear stresses in the thickness of the plate, respecting in particular the equilibrium conditions on the upper and lower faces of the plate. The internal energy of the model obtained after solution of the equilibrium equations in 3D, for bending only, with the variation of the plane stresses along z , brings out, for an elastic material, a relation between the stress resultants and the mean rotations and deflection. It is in this relation that the shear correction factor of k=5/6 appears instead of 1 in the relation which links the shear force to the distortion for a homogeneous and isotropic plate. The determination of the shear correction factors for orthotropic plates or laminated plates is described in the appendix. 2.2.3.3 Equivalence of the Hencky-Love-Kirchhoff and Reissner approaches If one assimilates the slopes of the mean surface { eta}_{x},{ eta}_{y} to the means of the slopes in the thickness of the plate and the deflection w to the mean deflection, the only difference between the Hencky theory and that of Reissner is the transverse shear correction coefficient in homogeneous isotropic elasticity of 5/6 instead of 1 . This difference is due to the fact that the starting assumptions are of a different nature and above all that the variables chosen are not the same. Indeed, the deflection on the mean surface is not equal to the mean of the deflections over the thickness of the plate. It is therefore normal that constitutive relations which involve different variables are not identical. The fact of having to solve at the finite-element level problems in displacements rather than problems in stresses by interpolation of the displacements leads us to use the equivalent approach in displacements of the Reissner problem formulated in stresses. 2.2.3.4 Notes Because of the previous equivalence one presents here only the displacement model for all the elements. In fact the elements DKT, DKTG, DKQG and DKQ rest on the Hencky-Love-Kirchhoff theory and the elements DST, DSQ and Q4G rest on the Reissner theory. The determination of the correction factors rests, within the framework of another theory, that of Mindlin, on equivalences of eigenfrequency associated with the vibration mode by transverse shear. One then obtains k={\pi}^{2}/12 , a value very close to 5/6 for the elements DST, DSQ and Q4G in the isotropic case. Within the framework of plasticity the problem of the choice of the transverse-shear correction coefficient arises because the equivalent approach in displacements of the Reissner problem formulated in stresses involves the non-linearity of the behaviour. One cannot therefore deduce, as is the case for elastic materials, a value of the transverse-shear correction coefficient. Plasticity (and other non-linear behaviours) is therefore not developed for these elements. 2.2.3.5 Computation of the shear stress and of the transverse distortion in code_aster The computation of the shear stress is carried out by considering: - the equilibrium equations in stress and in generalised force:  egin{array}{}{\partial}_{z}{	au}_{xz}={\partial}_{x}{\sigma}_{xx}+{\partial}_{y}{\sigma}_{xy}\ {\partial}_{z}{	au}_{yz}={\partial}_{y}{\sigma}_{yy}+{\partial}_{x}{\sigma}_{xy}\end{array} 	extrm{;}  egin{array}{}{\partial}_{x}{M}_{xx}+{\partial}_{y}{M}_{xy}={T}_{x}\ {\partial}_{y}{M}_{yy}+{\partial}_{x}{M}_{xy}={T}_{y}\end{array} - the free-edge conditions {\sigma}_{xz}(-h/2)={\sigma}_{yz}(h/2)=0 on the upper and lower faces; - relations linking the plane stresses to the derivatives of the moments:  egin{array}{c}{\partial}_{x}{\sigma}_{xx}=12/{h}^{3}\cdot z\cdot {\partial}_{x}\mathit{Mxx}\ {\partial}_{x}{\sigma}_{yy}=12/{h}^{3}\cdot z\cdot {\partial}_{y}\mathit{Myy}\ {\partial}_{x}{\sigma}_{xy}=12/{h}^{3}\cdot z\cdot {\partial}_{y}\mathit{Mxy}\end{array} That is, after analytical integration with respect to the variable z of {\sigma}_{xz}(z),{\sigma}_{yz}(z) and identification of the coefficients of the primitive: - the expression of the shear stress: {\sigma}_{xz}={T}_{x}\cdot 3/2h\ast (1-4{z}^{2}/{h}^{2}) {\sigma}_{yz}={T}_{y}\cdot 3/2h\cdot (1-4{z}^{2}/{h}^{2}) - the expression of the shear strain within the framework of the Reissner theory: {\gamma}_{x}={	au}_{xz}\cdot 2(1+

In the global frame, the degrees of freedom are the three displacements with respect to the three axes of the global Cartesian frame and the three rotations with respect to these three axes. Transfer matrices from the local frame to the global frame are therefore used for each element. Now, one has seen previously that the degrees of freedom of the plate elements are the two displacements in the plane of the plate, the out-of-plane displacement and two rotations. These rotations not being exactly the rotations with respect to the axes of the plate since { eta}_{x}(x,y)={	heta}_{y}(x,y),{ eta}_{y}(x,y)=-{	heta}_{x}(x,y) , this must be taken into account at the assembly stage in order to bring out the correct degrees of freedom {	heta}_{xi},{	heta}_{	ext{yi}} . 4.4.4.2 Fictitious rotations General case: The rotation with respect to the normal to the plate is considered not to be a degree of freedom. In order to ensure compatibility in passing from the local frame to the global frame, one therefore adds an additional local rotational degree of freedom to the plate, namely the one corresponding to the rotation with respect to the normal to the plane of the element. This implies an expansion of the blocks of dimension (5,5) of the local stiffness matrix into blocks of dimension (6,6) by adding a row and a column corresponding to this rotation. These additional rows and columns are a priori zero. One then passes from the enlarged local stiffness matrix to the global stiffness matrix. In the previous transformation, one has merely added the rotations with respect to the normals to the plane of the elements without modifying the strain energy. The contribution to the energy brought by these additional degrees of freedom is indeed zero and no stiffness is associated with them. The global stiffness matrix thus obtained nevertheless presents the risk of being non-invertible. To avoid this inconvenience, it is accepted practice to assign a small stiffness to these additional degrees of freedom in the enlarged local stiffness matrix. In practice, it is chosen between {10}^{–6} and {10}^{–3} times the smallest diagonal term of the local bending stiffness matrix. The user may choose this multiplicative coefficient COEF_RIGI_DRZ himself in AFFE_CARA_ELEM; by default it is equal to {10}^{–5} . For modal analyses involving both the computation of the stiffness matrix and that of the mass matrix, one must take a stiffness or a mass on the degree of rotation normal to the plane of the plate 103 to 106 times smaller than the smallest diagonal term of the stiffness or mass matrix for the bending terms. This makes it possible to inhibit the modes which may appear on the additional degree of freedom of rotation about the normal to the plane of the plate. By default, one takes a stiffness or a mass on the degree of rotation normal to the plane of the plate 105 times smaller than the smallest diagonal term of the stiffness or mass matrix for the bending terms 4.5.4 “Lumped” mass matrix The use of a “lumped” mass matrix has two advantages: it is simpler to implement numerically and it allows a better convergence . However the results are poorer than with the classical scheme (consistent matrix), for which the error is minimal [6] . The lumped mass matrix is in principle recommended only for transient analyses using an explicit time-integration scheme, which is used almost exclusively in fast dynamics. Unlike the analyses with implicit schemes, where at each increment (and at each Newton iteration in the non-linear case) one assembles and inverts a matrix, determined as a linear combination of the stiffness matrix, the mass matrix and the damping matrix, in explicit analyses only the mass matrix is assembled and inverted. Thus, by using a diagonal mass matrix the gain in terms of the CPU time of the solution as well as the gain in terms of the storage of the matrices are enormous compared with the use of a consistent mass matrix. Code_Aster not being a code specialised in fast dynamics, this advantage of the diagonal matrix is not exploited. The lumped mass-matrix option is therefore only a modelling choice, allowing possible comparisons with other analysis codes. Two methods are presented here for diagonalising a consistent mass matrix. It will also be shown in what way the choice between the two methods is conditioned by the choice of the consistent matrix between the classical one (§4.5.1) and the improved one (§4.5.2). The undoubtedly simplest technique for obtaining a lumped matrix is to retain the diagonal value for each degree of freedom as the sum of the entries of the row of the consistent matrix. Moreover, one recalls that the most important property of a lumped mass matrix is that it makes it possible to represent correctly a rigid-body motion. It is satisfied by the “row summation” method, written in equations in the following manner: {M}_{C}^{\alpha}=\sum_{ eta}{M}^{\alpha  eta } . Unfortunately the summation of the rows does not guarantee that all the terms {M}_{C}^{\alpha} are positive. Negative terms appear in particular when using the improved consistent mass matrix (mentioned in §4.5.2). For this reason and for most of the elements in Code_Aster, another approach has been chosen, due to Hinton (see [6]), in which the diagonal terms corresponding to the directions x , y , z , {M}_{H}^{\mathrm{\alpha x}} , {M}_{H}^{\mathrm{\alpha y}} and {M}_{H}^{\mathrm{\alpha z}} , are computed as: {M}_{H}^{\mathrm{\alpha x}}= rac{\underset{V}{\int}ho 	ext{dV}}{\sum_{ eta}{M}_{x}^{	ext{ββ}}}{M}_{x}^{	ext{αα}} {M}_{H}^{\mathrm{\alpha y}}= rac{\underset{V}{\int}ho 	ext{dV}}{\sum_{ eta}{M}_{y}^{	ext{ββ}}}{M}_{y}^{	ext{αα}} where the indices \alpha correspond to the node numbers. Although Hinton's method is generally more robust, it is unsuitable for plate and shell elements, since [eq. 33] does not make it possible to include the inertia terms, the terms {M}_{H}^{\alpha \cdot } defined in [eq. 33] necessarily having the units of mass and never of inertia. Consequently, for the elements treated here one modifies the computation of the consistent mass matrix used for the computation of the lumped mass matrix. One adopts the classical method described in §4.5.1 for the consistent mass matrix, then the “row summation” approach for the lumping. The affected option of code_aster is MASS_MECA_EXPLI and only for the DKT and DKTG elements. For the others the lumped mass matrix is not available. 4.5.5 Modification of the inertia terms The lumped mass matrix described in §4.5.4 is not very effective for an analysis in explicit dynamics, where the stability time step is strongly penalised by a poor conditioning of the mass matrix. The terms corresponding to the rotations, that is the inertia terms, are the main culprits, since they are much smaller than the translation terms, that is the displacements. For this reason, a method was proposed in [7] for modifying the problematic terms while avoiding degrading the quality of the solution. Although old and not entirely rigorous, the approach proposed in [7] is widely referenced by the literature of the field and has not really been the subject of remarkable improvements. One focuses on the terms due to bending, {	heta}_{x} , {	heta}_{y} and w(={u}_{z}) , the terms corresponding to the membrane being obtained in a classical manner and also applied to the 2D elements. The latter is defined by the knowledge of the 3 fields TEMP_SUP, TEMP_MIL and TEMP_INF given on the lower skin, at mid-thickness and on the upper skin of the shell. These elements are not exact at the nodes and one must mesh with several elements in order to obtain correct results. 5.2 Use and developments introduced These elements are used in the following way: - AFFE_MODELE ( MODELISATION = ’DKT’ .) for the triangle and the quadrangle of DKT type - AFFE_MODELE ( MODELISATION = ’DST’ .) for the triangle and the quadrangle of DST type - AFFE_MODELE ( MODELISATION = ’DKTG’.) for the triangle and the quadrangle of DKTG type - AFFE_MODELE ( MODELISATION = ’Q4G’ .) for the quadrangle of Q4g type One calls the routine INI079 for the position of the Hammer and Gauss points on the surface of the plate and the corresponding weights. - AFFE_CARA_ELEM ( COQUE=_F(EPAISSEUR=’EP’ ANGL_REP = ( ’ \alpha ’ ’  eta ’ ) COEF_RIGI_DRZ= ’CTOR’) In order to carry out post-processing (stresses, generalised forces,...) in a frame chosen by the user which is not the local frame of the element, one gives a reference direction d defined by two nautical angles in the global frame. The projection of this reference direction onto the plane of the plate fixes a reference direction \mathit{X1} . The normal to the plane fixes a second one and the cross product of the two previously defined vectors makes it possible to define the local triad in which the generalised forces and the stresses will be expressed. The user must take care that the chosen reference axis does not end up parallel to the normal of certain plate elements of the model. By default this reference direction is the X axis of the global frame in which the mesh is defined. The value CTOR corresponds to the coefficient which the user may introduce for the treatment of the stiffness and mass terms associated with the rotation normal to the plane of the plate. This coefficient must be small enough not to disturb the energy balance of the element and not too small so that the stiffness and mass matrices are invertible. One does not check whether the mesh cell is plane or not. The analysis takes into account the fact that the terms corresponding to the plate degrees of freedom are expressed in the local frame of the element. A transfer matrix makes it possible to pass from the local degrees of freedom to the global degrees of freedom. The elementary computations (CALC_CHAMP) currently available correspond to the options: - EPSI_ELNO and SIGM_ELNO which provide the strains and the stresses at the nodes in the user frame of the element on the lower skin, at mid-thickness and on the upper skin of the plate, the position being specified by the user. One stores these values in the following way: 6 components of strain or of stress: - EPXX EPYY EPZZ EPXY EPXZ EPYZ ou SIXX SIYY SIZZ SIXY SIXZ SIYZ - DEGE_ELNO: which gives the generalised strains per element at the nodes from the displacements in the user frame: EXX, EYY, EXY, KXX, KYY, KXY, GAX, GAY. - EFGE_ELNO: which gives the generalised forces per element at the nodes from the displacements: NXX, NYY, NXY, MXX, MYY, MXY, QX, QY. - SIEF_ELGA: which gives the generalised forces per element at the Gauss points from the displacements: NXX, NYY, NXY, MXX, MYY, MXY, QX, QY. - EPOT_ELEM: which gives the elastic strain energy per element from the displacements. - ECIN_ELEM: which gives the kinetic energy per element. Finally one also computes the option FORC_NODA for the computation of the nodal forces for the operator CALC_CHAMP. 5.4 Analysis in linear buckling The option RIGI_MECA_GE being activated in the catalogue of the element, it is possible to carry out a classical Euler buckling analysis after assembly of the elastic and geometric stiffness matrices. 5.5 Analysis in plasticity or other non-linear constitutive behaviour The stiffness matrix is here too integrated numerically. One calls the analysis option STAT_NON_LINE in which one defines, at the level of the non-linear constitutive behaviour, the number of layers to be used for the numerical integration. For the DKT modellings, all the plane-stress laws available in Code_Aster may be used. For the DST and Q4G modellings, only linear elasticity is usable. For the DKTG modelling, the only constitutive laws used are global laws (since there is only one integration point through the thickness), linking the generalised strains to the generalised stresses. These laws are, in version 9.4: GLRC_DM and GLRC_DAMAGE, as well as their coupling with elastoplastic membrane laws (KIT_DDI). The elementary computations currently available correspond to the options: - EPSI_ELNO which provides the strains per element at the nodes in the user frame from the displacements, on the lower skin, at mid-thickness and on the upper skin of the plate. - SIGM_ELNO which makes it possible to obtain the stress field through the thickness per element at the nodes for all the sub-points (all the layers and all the positions: on the lower skin, at the middle and on the upper skin of the layer). - EFGE_ELNO which makes it possible to obtain the generalised forces per element at the nodes in the user frame. - VARI_ELNO which computes the field of internal variables and the stresses per element at the nodes for all the layers, in the local frame of the element. 6 Conclusion The plane plate finite elements which we describe here are used in the analyses of thin structures, in small displacements and small strains, whose ratio of thickness to characteristic length is lower than 1/10 . As these elements are plane, they do not take into account the curvature of the structures, and it is necessary to refine the meshes in the case where the latter would be significant. They are elements for which the strains and the stresses in the plane of the element vary linearly with the thickness of the plate. Moreover, the distortion associated with the transverse shear is constant through the thickness of the element. Two families of plate finite elements exist: the DKT, DKQ elements (or DKTG, DKQG) for which the transverse distortion is zero and the finite elements with transverse-shear energy DST, DSQ and Q4G (or Q4g) for which it remains constant and non-zero through the thickness. One advises using the second type of elements when the structure to be studied has a ratio of thickness to characteristic length between 1/20 and 1/10 and the first ones in the remaining cases. When the transverse distortion is non-zero, the DST, DSQ and Q4G plate elements do not satisfy the 3D equilibrium conditions and the boundary conditions on the vanishing of the transverse shear stresses on the upper and lower faces of the plate, compatible with a transverse distortion constant through the thickness of the plate. It thus follows that, at the level of the elastic constitutive behaviour, a coefficient of 5/6 for a homogeneous plate corrects the usual relation between the stresses and the transverse distortion so as to ensure the equality between the shear energies of the 3D model and of the plate model with constant distortion. In this case, the deflection w has as interpretation the mean transverse displacement through the thickness of the plate. The non-linear behaviours in plane stress are available for the DKT and DKQ plate elements only. Indeed the rigorous taking into account of a constant non-zero transverse shear through the thickness and the determination of the associated correction on the shear stiffness with respect to a model satisfying the equilibrium conditions and the boundary conditions are not possible and therefore make the use of the DST, DSQ and Q4G elements rigorously impossible in plasticity. For the elements of the DKTG family, only global constitutive relations (moment-curvature relations and membrane forces – elongations) are available. r3.07.04 Volumetric shell finite elements r3.07.04 Volumetric shell finite elements Summary: In order to complete the library of plane-plate finite elements R3.07.03 currently available in Code_Aster (DKT, DST, Q4G...), it is proposed to introduce two volumetric, or three-dimensional, shell finite elements [bib1]. This modelling COQUE_3D U3.12.03 makes it possible to carry out analyses of shell structures of arbitrary shape with a better approximation of the geometry and of the kinematics. One will restrict oneself to the framework of linear kinematics. One therefore remains in small displacements and small strains. No restriction is made on the type of constitutive behaviour in plane stress. The two elements which are introduced are the 9-node quadratic Heterosis quadrilateral and its 7-node triangular counterpart. The formulation of the continuous problem is carried out in Cartesian coordinates, which makes it possible to avoid the explicit computation of the curvatures. These two elements have as their counterpart the 3-node line shell element presented in the document R3.07.02. These two new elements are validated on existing plate test cases, and on three new shell test cases developed in the validation documentation, the principal conclusions of which are presented briefly here. This note also presents in an annex how to take the anisotropy of materials into account. > Contents 1 Introduction Two volumetric shell finite elements with transverse shear are introduced into Code_Aster (the 9-node quadrilateral MEC3QU9H and the 7-node triangle MEC3TR7H) for the analysis of shell structures of arbitrary shape. To represent this type of structure, one previously used with Code_Aster plane-facet plate elements, which induced parasitic bendings, and shells of revolution which were too restrictive as regards the type of structure R3.07.02. The development was carried out for isotropic materials with linear kinematics, for small displacements and small strains. This formulation can be extended to anisotropic materials [Annex 1] and to non-linear kinematics (large displacements and large rotations) R3.07.05. For the solution of chained thermomechanical problems, one must beforehand use the 7- and 9-node thermal shell finite elements described in R3.11.01. The continuous mechanical problem is developed below by describing the shell kinematics of Hencky–Mindlin–Naghdi type (assumption of straight or plane sections) completed by a transverse distortion, and the thermo-elasto-plastic constitutive law. By means of a penalty parameter one can pass from a theory with shear to a theory without shear. The finite elements chosen are then presented; they are quadratic isoparametric elements making it possible to have a fine representation of a curved geometry and good estimates of the stresses. The interpolation and the integration method are also described. The development is finally validated on a few benchmark cases. The non-linear kinematics of these shells is treated in the reference documentation R3.07.05. 2 Formulation 2.1 Geometry of the shell For the volumetric shell elements \Omega one defines a reference surface \omega , or middle surface, which is skewed (with curvilinear coordinates {\xi}_{1}{\xi}_{2} for example) and a thickness h({\xi}_{1}{\xi}_{2}) measured along the normal to the middle surface. The choice of the HENCKY-MINDLIN-NAGHDI framework to describe the shell kinematics, presented in paragraph [§2], leads to expressions of the strains in which the derivatives are limited to order 1, unlike the LOVE-KIRCHHOFF model. One can therefore use a finite element of limited order while ensuring conformity (see p.110 of [bib7]). The degrees of freedom are the 3 displacements in the global frame and the 2 rotations in the local frame. The elements chosen are isoparametric quadrilaterals or triangles. The quadrilateral is represented below. The quadrilaterals give the best results (see p.202 of [bib8]). The best choice consists in taking, for these elements, quadratic interpolation functions (see p.224 of [bib8]) in order to model correctly the membrane, bending and shear effects. According to the results based on numerous test cases in the literature, the optimal choice is the quadratic isoparametric quadrilateral, which makes it possible to have a fine representation of a curved geometry and good estimates of the stresses. Among the elements with quadratic functions one chooses the heterosis element (Q9H), whose displacements are approximated by the interpolation functions of the Serendipity element and the rotations by the functions of the Lagrange element (cf. Annex 3). This choice is justified below. Figure 4.1-a: Representations of the isoparametric quadrilateral The figure [Figure 4.1-b] summarises the three families of elements named previously. Figure 4.1-b: Families of finite elements for the isoparametric quadrilateral Risks of membrane or shear locking appear when the thickness of the shell becomes small compared with its radius of curvature and the interpolation functions are of too low an order. To resolve them one uses a selective numerical integration [bib6]. For certain types of boundary conditions (clamping) with the Serendipity element the locking persists despite the selective integration. Moreover, for the Lagrange element, this type of integration leads to singularities in the stiffness matrix. The Heterosis element Q9H with selective integration does not encounter the problems mentioned and appears to be the most efficient for the modelling of very thin shells (see p.224 of [bib8]). It should be noted that this element possesses a deformation mode without associated energy if it is used alone. This mode disappears when one uses more than two elements [bib7]. For the triangular elements, the Heterosis element T7H is required for the same reasons but proves to be distinctly less efficient (see section 5 concerning the validation). To avoid this inconvenience it is accepted practice to assign a small stiffness to these supplementary degrees of freedom at the level of the enlarged local stiffness matrix. In practice, one chooses it between 10–6 and 10–3 times the smallest diagonal term of the local rotation stiffness matrix. In the global frame, the degrees of freedom are the three displacements with respect to the three axes of the global Cartesian frame and the three rotations with respect to these three axes. One therefore uses transformation matrices from the local frame to the global frame for the rotations of each element. Note: The external forces can also be defined in the user frame. One then uses a transformation matrix from the user frame to the local frame of the element in order to have the expression of these forces in the local frame of the element and to deduce the corresponding local elementary force vector. For the assembly one then passes from the local frame of the element to the global frame. 5 Validation In order to judge the relevance of the thick-shell formulation, the few application examples which follow concern both linear statics and the computation of eigenmodes. Three new test cases relating to the two finite elements described in the preceding parts have been integrated into Code_Aster . They enrich the test cases of the plate elements already present in the Code_Aster environment. A large part of these test cases has been listed in [bib10]. The three new test cases, two in statics plus one in dynamics, are classical validation examples taken from [bib3]. The reference solutions, analytical or numerical, taken from [bib3] are compared with the numerical results given by Code_Aster . For more information on these test cases, one should refer to the validation documentation indicated as a reference. 5.1 Test case in linear statics 5.1.1 Static test case no. 1 The first test case is that of a cylindrical panel subjected to its own weight V3.03.107. This test makes it possible to highlight membrane effects which are more important than the bending effects. It makes it possible to measure the performance of the shell elements relative to the DKT or DKQ elements, whose membrane interpolation is linear. 5.1.2 Static test case no. 2 The second test case is that of a helicoidal shell subjected to two types of concentrated loading V3.03.108. The helicoidal shape of the shell makes it possible to study the geometric representation of the finite elements. The concentrated loadings may be: - in the plane: the influence due to the membrane effects is then not important and the dominant behaviour is that due to bending, - out of plane: the membrane effects affect the behaviour of the shell. 5.2 Test case in dynamics This test case is a simplified model of a compressor blade, which is in fact a cylindrical panel V2.03.102. This test highlights the performance of the elements in dynamic behaviour through the data of the frequencies and of the eigenmodes. The frequencies and eigenmodes of the blade are experimental values which serve as reference results. 6 Thermomechanical chaining 6.1 Description For the solution of chained thermomechanical problems, one must use, for the thermal analysis, thermal shell finite elements R3.11.01 whose temperature field is recovered as input data of Code_Aster for the mechanical analysis. There must therefore be compatibility between the thermal field given by the thermal shells and that recovered by the mechanical shells. The latter is defined by the knowledge of the 3 fields TEMP_SUP, TEMP_MIL and TEMP_INF given on the lower skin, at mid-thickness and on the upper skin of the shell. Two volumetric shell finite elements supported on quadrilateral and triangular mesh cells have been introduced into Code_Aster . They were chosen with a very particular aim: to be able to represent a complete behaviour of curved structures, whereas until now one could use only plane-facet elements, which induced parasitic bendings and required the meshes to be refined. They are elements for which the strains and the stresses in the plane of the element vary linearly with the thickness of the shell. The kinematics chosen is a shell kinematics of Hencky–Mindlin–Naghdi type, making it possible to introduce the transverse-shear energy. The distortion associated with the transverse shear is constant through the thickness of the element. The variable correction on the transverse-shear coefficient k offers a flexibility of use making it possible to pass from the theory of HENCKY-MINDLIN-NAGHDI for k=1 , to that of REISSNER for k=5/6 and to that of LOVE_KIRCHHOFF (for very thin structures) if one chooses a value of k equal to {10}^{6}	imes h/L , h being the thickness and L a characteristic distance (mean radius of curvature, zone of application of the loads....). As in this last case one uses a penalty method in order to make the transverse-shear terms small, one can, if one takes a value of k that is too large, make the numerical system singular. In that case, one must decrease the value of k . The default value of k is 5/6 . One generally uses it when the structure to be meshed has a ratio of thickness to characteristic length lying between 1/20 and 1/10 . For smaller thicknesses, where the transverse distortion becomes small, one may wish to use a value of k={10}^{6}	imes h/L (in order to be able to make comparisons with DKT plate elements, for example). When the transverse distortion is non-zero, the shell elements do not satisfy the 3D equilibrium conditions and the boundary conditions on the vanishing of the transverse-shear stresses on the upper and lower faces of the shell, which are compatible with a transverse distortion constant through the thickness of the shell. It thus follows that, at the level of the constitutive behaviour, a coefficient of 5/6 for a homogeneous shell corrects the usual relation between the stresses and the transverse distortion so as to ensure equality between the shear energies of the 3D model and of the shell model with constant distortion. In that case, the deflection {	ilde{u}}_{3} has as its interpretation the mean transverse displacement through the thickness of the shell and not the displacement of the middle surface of the shell. For structures of small thickness, in order to avoid locking phenomena, one uses reduced under-integration for the membrane and shear parts of the stiffness matrix. The choice of finite elements fell on the Heterosis quadrilateral elements Q9H and the triangular elements T7H. Indeed, among the finite elements with quadratic interpolation functions, the performance of the Heterosis element Q9H is known. It is in particular superior to that of the Serendipity elements Q9S or of the Lagrange elements Q9. This performance nevertheless rests on the selective integration of the element, with reduced integration of the membrane and shear terms on the one hand, and normal integration of the bending terms on the other hand. By analogy with Q9H, one has taken the finite element T7H as the element of triangular shape. However, as far as possible, one will use the Q9H rather than the T7H, which is distinctly less efficient. The non-linear behaviours in plane stress are available for these elements. One points out, however, that the stresses generated by the transverse distortion are treated elastically, for want of a better approach. Indeed, the rigorous taking into account of a non-zero constant transverse shear through the thickness, and the determination of the associated correction on the shear stiffness relative to a model satisfying the equilibrium conditions and the boundary conditions, are not possible and therefore make the use of these elements, when the transverse shear is non-zero, rigorously impossible in plasticity. Rigorously, for non-linear behaviours, one should therefore use these elements within the framework of Love–Kirchhoff theory. Elements corresponding to the mechanical elements exist in thermal analysis; the thermomechanical chainings are therefore available with 7- and 9-node thermal shell finite elements. Extensions of the preceding formulation presented in the annex also make it possible to take into account the anisotropy of the materials and the kinematic non-linearity. r3.07.06 Treatment of the offset for the plate elements DKT, DST, DKQ, dsq and q4g r3.07.06 Treatment of the offset for the plate elements DKT, DST, DKQ, dsq and q4g Summary: The plate elements R3.07.03 are intended for the analyses of thin three-dimensional structures. The middle surface of these structures does not always coincide with the layout plane or the plane of the mesh. One therefore introduces the notion of offset of the middle surface with respect to the layout plane. It can be used for elements with account taken of transverse shear, or without this hypothesis. > Contents 1 Introduction With the aim of being able to analyse the behaviour of slender structures of plate type, or of curved surfaces approximated by facets, whose middle surface is offset with respect to the plane of application of the forces, one introduces the notion of offset of the middle surface with respect to the meshing surface. The displacement fields varying linearly through the thickness of the plate have as their origin the meshing surface, that is to say that, at the level of the meshing surface, only the translational degrees of freedom are necessary for the description of the displacement. The introduction of the kinematics into the expression of the strain work makes it possible to obtain the membrane, bending and transverse-shear stiffnesses of the offset element from those of the equivalent non-offset element and from the offset distance. The whole of the analyses (apart from the specific post-processing) is therefore carried out in a layout frame attached to the plane of the mesh. By default the results are therefore obtained in the frame of the mesh. For certain post-processings, it is possible to have these results automatically in other frames insofar as the user indicates the position of the post-processing plane with respect to the plane of the mesh. The offset distance between the plane of the mesh and the middle surface of the plate is given in AFFE_CARA_ELEM at the same level as the thickness. A positive offset d means that the middle surface of the plate is in reality at a distance dn from the meshed plate element, the direction n being given by the normal to the element (see [§4.1] of the Reference documentation R3.07.03 of the plate elements for the construction of this normal). The notation adopted is that of the note R3.07.03 on the plate elements DKT, DST, DKQ, DSQ and Q4G. 2 Formulation 2.1 Geometry For the offset plate elements, the reference surface is given by the layout plane or the plane of the mesh (the plane xy for example). The middle surface of the element is positioned with respect to this reference surface. The thickness h(x,y) must be small compared with the other dimensions (extents, radii of curvature) of the structure to be modelled. The figure [Figure 2.1-a] below illustrates the point. Concerning the value of the offset d , and because of the linearisation conditions of the bending adopted in the theory, one will take d such that an element of thickness d+h remains within the plate theory. Figure 2.1-a One attaches to the layout plane (the plane of the mesh) a local orthonormal frame \mathrm{0xyz} associated with the plane of the mesh, different from the global frame \mathit{OXYZ} . The position of the points of the plate is given by the Cartesian coordinates (x,y) in the layout plane (plane of the mesh) and the elevation z with respect to this plane. 2.2 Kinematics The straight sections, which are the sections perpendicular to the middle surface of the plate, remain straight. The material points situated on a normal to the undeformed middle surface remain on a straight line in the deformed configuration. It follows from this approach that the displacement fields vary linearly through the thickness of the plate. If one denotes by u,v,w the displacements of a point of the layout plane q(x,y,z) along x , y and z , the Hencky–Mindlin kinematics gives us: (\begin{array}{c}{u}_{x}(x,y,z)\\ {u}_{y}(x,y,z)\\ {u}_{z}(x,y,z)\end{array})=(\begin{array}{c}u(x,y)\\ v(x,y)\\ w(x,y)\end{array})+z(\begin{array}{c}{\theta}_{y}(x,y)\\ -{\theta}_{x}(x,y)\\ 0\end{array})=(\begin{array}{c}u(x,y)\\ v(x,y)\\ w(x,y)\end{array})+z(\begin{array}{c}{\beta}_{x}(x,y)\\ {\beta}_{y}(x,y)\\ 0\end{array}) | where: | u,v,w are the displacements of the layout plane; | | --- | --- | | | {\theta}_{x} and {\theta}_{y} are respectively the rotations of this plane with respect to the axis x and the axis y respectively. | One prefers to introduce the two rotations {\beta}_{x}(x,y)={\theta}_{y}(x,y),{\beta}_{y}(x,y)=-{\theta}_{x}(x,y) . The three-dimensional strains at every point, with the kinematics introduced previously, are thus given by: \begin{array}{}{\epsilon}_{xx}={e}_{xx}+{\mathrm{z\kappa }}_{xx}\\ {\epsilon}_{yy}={e}_{yy}+{\mathrm{z\kappa }}_{yy}\\ {\mathrm{2\epsilon }}_{xy}={\gamma}_{xy}=2{e}_{xy}+{\mathrm{2z\kappa }}_{xy}\\ {\mathrm{2\epsilon }}_{xz}={\gamma}_{x}\\ {\mathrm{2\epsilon }}_{yz}={\gamma}_{y}\end{array} | where: | {e}_{xx} , {e}_{yy} and {e}_{xy} are the membrane strains of the middle surface; {\gamma}_{x} and {\gamma}_{y} the strains associated with the transverse shears; {\kappa}_{xx} , {\kappa}_{yy} , {\kappa}_{xy} the bending strains of the middle surface, which are written: | | --- | --- | \begin{array}{}{e}_{xx}=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\ {e}_{yy}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\\ 2{e}_{xy}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\ {\kappa}_{xx}=\frac{\partial {\beta}_{x}}{\partial x}\\ {\kappa}_{yy}=\frac{\partial {\beta}_{y}}{\partial y}\\ {\mathrm{2\kappa }}_{xy}=\frac{\partial {\beta}_{x}}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial {\beta}_{y}}{\partial x}\\ {\gamma}_{x}={\beta}_{x}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\\ {\gamma}_{y}={\beta}_{y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\end{array} Note: - In the plate theories, the introduction of {\beta}_{x} and {\beta}_{y} makes it possible to symmetrise the formulations of the strains and the equilibrium equations R3.07.03. In the shell theories, one rather uses {\theta}_{x} and {\theta}_{y} and the associated couples {M}_{x} and {M}_{y} with respect to x and y , - the degrees of freedom which have been chosen are the displacements and rotations of the layout plane and not those of the middle surface. Indeed if one envisages the superposition of several offset plates in order to produce a sandwich material, there can correspond to the nodes of the mesh only a single displacement field and not the various displacement fields of the layers composing the material. 2.3 Constitutive law The behaviour of the plates is a 3D behaviour in “plane stress”. The transverse stress {\sigma}_{zz} is taken as zero because it is negligible compared with the other components of the stress tensor (plane-stress hypothesis). The most general constitutive law is then written as follows: (\begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{xx}\\ {\sigma}_{yy}\\ {\sigma}_{xy}\\ {\sigma}_{xz}\\ {\sigma}_{yz}\end{array})=C(\epsilon ,\alpha )(\begin{array}{c}{\epsilon}_{xx}\\ {\epsilon}_{yy}\\ {\gamma}_{xy}\\ {\gamma}_{x}\\ {\gamma}_{y}\end{array})=\text{Ce}+\mathrm{zC\kappa }+\mathrm{C\gamma } with e=\left(\begin{array}{c}{e}_{xx}\\ {e}_{yy}\\ 2{e}_{xy}\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right),\text{}\kappa =\left(\begin{array}{c}{\kappa}_{xx}\\ {\kappa}_{yy}\\ 2{\kappa}_{xy}\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right)\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}\text{et}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}\gamma =\left(\begin{array}{c}0\\ 0\\ 0\\ {\gamma}_{x}\\ {\gamma}_{y}\end{array}\right) where: C(\varepsilon ,\alpha ) is the local tangent stiffness matrix in plane stress; \alpha represents the set of the internal variables when the behaviour is non-linear. For constitutive behaviours (for example multilayers) for which the distortions are coupled to the membrane and bending strains, C(\varepsilon ,\alpha ) is put in the form: C=(\begin{array}{cc}H& {H}_{c\gamma }\\ {H}_{{c\gamma }_{}}^{T}& {H}_{\gamma}\end{array}) | where: | H(\varepsilon ,\alpha ) is a symmetric 3\times 3 matrix; {H}_{\gamma}(\varepsilon ,\alpha ) a symmetric 2\times 2 matrix; {H}_{c\gamma }(\varepsilon ,\alpha ) a 3\times 2 coupling matrix between the membrane or bending effects and the transverse shear. | | --- | --- | In the case where it is uncoupled, one has {H}_{c\gamma }(\varepsilon ,\alpha )=0 . The determination of {H}_{\gamma}(\varepsilon ,\alpha ) within the framework of Reissner's theory ([§2.2.3.2] of R3.07.03) is given in the annex. The elements DKT and DST are triangular isoparametric elements. The elements DKQ, DSQ and Q4gamma are quadrilateral isoparametric elements. They are represented below: Figure 4.1-a: Real elements The reference elements are presented below: Figure 4.1-b: Reference elements, triangle and quadrangle One defines the reduced frame of the element as the frame (\xi \eta ) of the reference element. The local frame of the element, in the layout plane (x,y) is defined by the user, by the keyword ANGLE_REP. The direction \mathit{X1} of this local frame is the projection of a reference direction \underline{d} onto the plane of the element. This reference direction \underline{d} is chosen by the user, who defines it by two nautical angles in the global frame. The normal N to the plane of the element ( 12\mathrm{\wedge }13 for a triangle numbered 123 and 12\mathrm{\wedge }14 for a quadrangle numbered 1234 ) fixes the second direction. The vector product of the two vectors defined previously \mathit{Y1}=N\mathrm{\wedge }\mathit{X1} makes it possible to define the local triad in which the generalised forces representing the state of stress will be expressed. The user must take care that the chosen reference axis does not end up parallel to the normal of certain plate elements. When this keyword is not present the offset is zero by default. 5.1 Application of the forces and couples All the analyses are done in the layout frame (plane of the mesh). If one defines forces or couples with respect to another frame, the user will have to make, for FORCE_ARETE and FORCE_NODALE, the transformations necessary in order to reduce to the mesh frame. For FORCE_COQUE the user will be able to specify the plane of application of the forces and the conversion towards the computation frame will be automatic. One thus introduces in AFFE_CHAR_MECA the notion of plane of application of the forces by the keyword PLAN under FORCE_COQUE. This plane of application is different from the reference plane or layout plane on which the mesh rests. For this keyword one will define the following four possibilities of application of the forces:’INF’ ‘MOY’ ‘SUP’ ‘MAIL’ . ‘INF’‘MOY’ and ‘SUP’ mean that one applies the forces on the lower, mean and upper skin of the plate respectively. ‘MAIL’ means that one applies the forces at the level of the reference plane or the plane of the mesh. By default the forces will be applied on the plane of the mesh of the plate. Concerned are the forces of type FORCE_COQUE of TE0032. In the frame local to the element, when the forces and the couples are applied on ‘MOY’ one uses the simple transfer relation: \begin{array}{c}{c}_{x}^{'}={c}_{x}-{\text{df}}_{y}\\ {c}_{y}^{'}={c}_{y}+{\text{df}}_{x}\end{array} in order to bring the forces and the couples back into the frame of the mesh where one does the analyses. In the frame local to the element, when the forces and the couples are applied on ‘SUP’ one uses the simple transfer relation: \begin{array}{c}{c}_{x}^{'}={c}_{x}-(d+h/2){f}_{y}\\ {c}_{y}^{'}={c}_{y}+(d+h/2){f}_{x}\end{array} In the frame local to the element, when the forces and the couples are applied on ‘INF’ one uses the simple transfer relation: \begin{array}{c}{c}_{x}^{'}={c}_{x}-(d-h/2){f}_{y}\\ {c}_{y}^{'}={c}_{y}+(d-h/2){f}_{x}\end{array} If the forces are given in the global frame of the element , one uses transfer relations of the type: {c}^{'}=c+(d+\varepsilon h/2)n\mathrm{\wedge }f where c is defined with respect to the frame ’INF’ ‘MOY’ ‘SUP’ with \varepsilon equal to -1, 0 and 1, respectively. When there is no offset, the previous formula reduces to {c}^{'}=c+\varepsilon h/\mathrm{2n}\mathrm{\wedge }f . Note: For loadings of type FORCE_ARETE or FORCE_NODALE the forces and couples can be expressed only with respect to the frame of the mesh. If the user knows them only with respect to the middle surface of the plate, he will have to carry out the change of frame himself in order to have the expression of the forces and of the couples with respect to the meshing surface. The relation to be used is {c}^{'}=c+\mathit{dn}\mathrm{\wedge }f where d is the distance between the computation plane and the loading plane, oriented by the normal to the shell. It is obvious that the user has an interest in the loading plane being the plane of the mesh, but it is not always possible to make these two planes coincide, as one can see on the left-hand part of Figure 2.1-a. 5.2 Application of the displacement boundary conditions For boundary conditions of displacement type the user will have to take care of the fact that they can be applied only on the mesh frame. The transfer relations with respect to conditions given on the middle surface are the following: \begin{array}{c}{\theta}_{\text{ref}}={\theta}_{\text{moy}}\\ {u}_{\text{ref}}={u}_{\text{moy}}-{\theta}_{\text{moy}}\mathrm{\wedge }\mathit{dn}\end{array} 5.3 Post-processings For the post-processings, the default results of generalised-force type are given in the frame corresponding to the layout plane. In order to have them in the other frames, the user will have to indicate the post-processing plane and the changes of frame will be automatic. For the post-processing of the generalised forces, one will be able to compute them in the middle surface of the shell via the command POST_CHAMP / COQUE_EXCENT. 6 Static and modal validation 6.1 Initial validation The first part of the validation consists in testing a simple plate subjected to forces and couples and whose plane of the mesh does not coincide with the plane of the middle surface on which the forces are applied. For the plate subjected to forces and couples, the results with and without offset must take account of the change of frame for the couples as indicated below. The displacements are linked in the following manner for a point situated at a height z with respect to the middle surface: u={u}_{\text{moy}}+{\theta}_{\text{moy}}\mathrm{\wedge }\mathit{zn}={u}_{\text{ref}}+{\theta}_{\text{ref}}\mathrm{\wedge }(z+d)n which is also written: \begin{array}{c}{\theta}_{\text{moy}}={\theta}_{\text{ref}}\\ {u}_{\text{moy}}={u}_{\text{ref}}+{\theta}_{\text{ref}}\mathrm{\wedge }\mathit{dn}\end{array} which allows us to establish the transfer relations between the displacements with respect to the middle surface and those with respect to the reference plane. For the generalised forces, in the two previous cases of the figure, one has the same results on the middle, lower and upper surfaces of the plate. 6.2 Test case SSLS111 : offset for simple plates This is a bending analysis of a bilayer constituted of two different isotropic materials. One studies the membrane–bending coupling. The reference analysis is that of a bilayer defined by DEFI_COMPOSITE composed of the two different isotropic materials ( no symmetry along z ). The other modelling is composed of two plates offset with respect to the mean fibre of the plate used with DEFI_COMPOSITE . The results, identical from one modelling to the other, are given in terms of displacements and of generalised forces. In addition one carries out, on the geometry of this test, a modal analysis for the two modellings: the natural frequencies found are identical. 6.3 Test case SSLS112 : offset for composite plates This is a bending analysis of a four-layer plate presenting a material non-symmetry with respect to its mean plane. The reference analysis uses a four-layer plate defined by DEFI_COMPOSITE. The other modelling uses two bilayers defined by DEFI_COMPOSITE but offset with respect to the mean fibre of the four-layer plate. The results, identical from one modelling to the other, are given in terms of displacements. 7 Conclusion The plate finite elements which we describe here are used in the analyses of slender thin structures whose ratio of thickness to characteristic length is lower than 1/10 . The middle surface of these structures does not coincide with the plane of the mesh (layout plane). The offset therefore corresponds to the distance of the middle surface with respect to the layout surface. A positive offset d means that the middle surface of the plate is at a distance dn from the meshed plate element, the direction n being given by the normal to the element. The values of displacements and of generalised forces obtained are given by default in the frame of the mesh. For the generalised forces, one can however define a post-processing frame — a frame associated with the middle surface — different from the layout frame. In the same manner, the applied forces are considered as being given by default in the layout frame. In the case of FORCE_COQUE, one can however specify a frame of application of the forces and couples — a frame associated with the middle surface — different from the layout frame. r3.07.09 Plate elements: Modelling Q4GG r3.07.09 Plate elements: Modelling Q4GG Summary This document presents the formulation of the thick-plate elements used in the modelling Q4GG. For this modelling, two types of finite element are available, depending on the mesh cells: - Quadrangular finite element (Q4G) - Triangular finite element (T3G) This modelling of a thick-plate element, like the modellings DKT, DKQ, DST, DSQ, DKTG and Q4G [7], is intended for analyses in small strains and large displacements of thin curved or plane structures. They are plane elements which do not take into account the geometric curvature of the structures, unlike the shell elements (COQUE_3D) which are curved: parasitic bendings result, which can be reduced by using more elements so as to be able to approximate curved geometries correctly. The formulation is therefore simplified and the number of degrees of freedom reduced. Note: The formulation of the quadrangular element Q4G used in the modelling Q4GG is described in document [7]. Consequently, one limits oneself here to the case of the triangular element T3G. > Contents 1 Introduction The details of the formulation of the thick-plate element T3G, as it was proposed in publication [6], are presented here. This element is constructed in a manner analogous to the element Q4G [7]. 2 Formulation 2.1 Geometry of the plate elements For the plate elements one defines a reference surface, or middle surface, which is plane (the plane xy for example) and a thickness h(x,y) . This thickness must be small compared with the other dimensions (extents, radii of curvature) of the structure to be modelled. The figure below illustrates the point. One attaches to the middle surface \omega a local orthonormal frame \mathit{Oxyz} associated with the tangent plane of the structure, different from the global frame \mathit{OXYZ} . r3.07.10 “Solid” shell finite elements – COQUE_SOLIDE r3.07.10 “Solid” shell finite elements – COQUE_SOLIDE Summary: In order to complete the library of plane-plate finite elements R3.07.03 currently available (DKT, DST, Q4G...), a solid-shell finite element is introduced. This COQUE_SOLIDE modelling (solid-shell element) makes it possible to analyse thin structures of arbitrary shape. This documentation is provisional; the elements are not sufficiently validated to be used in AIP studies and the COQUE_SOLIDE element is outside the qualification scope. Contents 1 Introduction There are several ways of defining what a plate or a shell is. The following definition will be adopted: “a plate (or a shell) is a mechanical structure which, ‘seen from afar’, is a surface”. In practice, this means that one of its dimensions (its thickness) is negligible compared with the other two. More fundamentally, from the mathematical point of view, only the curvature is a parameter that decides whether or not a shell theory applies; its thickness is not a founding assumption of the theory. The distinction between a plate (“ plate” ) and a shell (“ shell” ) rests on the idea that the plate is an initially plane structure whereas the shell is a fundamentally curved structure. To represent a curved component (a cylinder, for example), plate elements therefore proceed by “faceting” the surface, which introduces both a geometric error (approximation of the curvature) and a mechanical error since, for isotropic constitutive behaviours, this implies that plates do not exhibit coupling between membrane and bending strains. In general, a thin structure has a remarkable property: its mechanical strength (its equilibrium) depends essentially on its geometry. There is a very large difference in stiffness between a loading in its middle surface (membrane) and one normal to its middle surface (essentially bending). A thin structure is indeed much stiffer in membrane than in bending (it is much easier to deform a sheet by folding it than by stretching it). In practice, this property induces many modelling problems, a series of numerical “lockings”, that is, a poor representation of the various mechanical situations which cannot always be overcome by refining the mesh. The problem is fundamental, and the various situations that exhibit these lockings, and the means of removing them, will now be reviewed. 1.1 Limitations of classical isoparametric elements Classical 3D isoparametric elements exhibit a series of numerical lockings, due either to the poor representation of the various strain and stress modes representative of thin structures, or to properties of the material or of the constitutive behaviour (such as incompressibility or plasticity). To illustrate the locking situations that come from the thin-structure assumption, the analysis of a simple square plate in bending will be considered, represented by a single layer of 8-node cube-type elements (and therefore with a tri-linear approximation of the displacements). | | Structural properties Side: 1m Thickness: 0,1m Young's modulus: 210\mathit{GPa} Poisson's ratio: 0,3 | | --- | --- | | Figure 1.1-1: Example of a thin-structure analysis in 3D | | The maximum vertical displacement that should be obtained, from thin-plate theory (the result obtained with the DKT elements, for example), is 1.9 mm. For “solid” elements, several strategies exist to overcome this locking; see R3.06.08 or R3.06.14. 1.1.6 Methods for correcting lockings for COQUE_SOLIDE To overcome these lockings, three ingredients are proposed: - To remove volumetric and membrane locking, a method of reduced integration (RI) will be used, which consists in using an integration scheme less rich than the one classically used for 8-node bricks. Reduced integration will give rise to parasitic zero-energy modes (or “hourglass” modes), which will be eliminated by a stabilisation method; - To remove volumetric locking, an approach based on incompatible modes is also proposed, in its generic formulation known as “ EAS ” (Enhanced Assumed Strain), which will enrich the approximation in order to correct the pinching problem; - To remove transverse-shear and trapezoidal locking, the assumed-field method will be used ( ANS , “Assumed Natural Strain”). The EAS method (Enhanced Assumed Strain), whose formalism is based on the three-field Hu-Washizu formulation, was initially proposed by [Bib2, Bib3] in small strains, then extended to large strains by [Bib4,Bib5] before being applied to thermomechanical problems by [Bib6]. This method is a generalisation of the incompatible-modes method. It consists in reducing the order of the polynomials for certain strain components. This method makes it possible to reduce volumetric locking significantly. Recent work [Bib8], [Bib9] has shown that a single parameter is sufficient, which in addition makes it possible to be consistent with a reduced integration. Nevertheless, in certain configurations (compressive loading), instabilities appear; moreover, in the case of plate elements it is also necessary to overcome transverse-shear lockings. The EAS method will be combined with the ANS method and with the taking into account of pinching. The ANS technique (“Assumed Natural Strain”) consists in replacing the transverse shear strain by an assumed shear strain obtained by interpolation in the natural basis of the element (hence the qualifier “natural”). In addition to making the treatment of shear locking easier, interpolation in the natural basis gives elements that work with a more or less distorted mesh. 2 Kinematics 2.1 Description of the configurations The initial configuration {\Omega}_{0} and the current configuration {\Omega}_{t} are considered.
