The transverse shear strain is evaluated at the four points of the median edges of the middle surface of the solid shell. To interpolate through the volume, some authors propose to multiply the shear strain in the middle plane by the well-known Reissner function. This type of interpolation ensures that the static condition on the shear stress is satisfied on the upper and lower faces of the element. However, in non-linear problems (material and large strains), this interpolation becomes incorrect and it does not guarantee satisfaction of the static condition on the faces. Moreover, such an interpolation does not allow the element to handle frictional-contact problems naturally, since the shear strain is assumed to be zero on the upper and lower faces of the element. It has also been shown that such an interpolation leads to an ill-conditioned stiffness matrix. To avoid these drawbacks, the ANS technique has been applied following the work of [Bib13], [Bib8], [Bib9] and [Bib11]. | | | --- | | Figure 5.6-1: Points and nodes of the HEXA8 element | In the parametric space, each of the shear strains {\widehat{E}}^{u,\xi \zeta } and {\widehat{\epsilon}}^{\eta \zeta } is interpolated using the equivalent shear strain from four different tying points (figure ). 5.6.1 ANS method in small strains One recalls that the linear part of the strain tensor is written as a function of the displacements: \epsilon =\widehat{B}U On the matrix \widehat{B} , a specific interpolation is therefore written for the shear and normal components. r3.07.11 r3.07.10 Mixed hybrid finite elements via FENICSx – PLAQ_MITC r3.07.10 Mixed hybrid finite elements via FENICSx – PLAQ_MITC Summary: With the aim of completing the library of flat-plate finite elements R3.07.03 currently available (DKT, DST, Q4G...), one proposes to introduce a mixed hybrid finite element based on the MITC approach (in English, Mixed Interpolation of Tensorial Component ). This model makes it possible to carry out analyses on thin structures while respecting the Reissner-Mindlin assumptions. This documentation is provisional; the elements are not sufficiently validated to be used in AIP studies and the element PLAQ_MITC is outside the scope of qualification. Contents 1 Introduction The Reissner-Mindlin model constitutes a generalisation of the classical Kirchhoff-Love theory of thin plates. It was developed in order to represent better the effects of transverse shear in plates of moderate to high thickness. Whereas the Kirchhoff model rests on the assumption that the sections normal to the middle surface remain perpendicular after deformation, this assumption becomes too restrictive as soon as the thickness of the plate becomes significant relative to its in-plane dimensions. The Reissner-Mindlin theory introduces a field of rotations independent of the normals to the middle surface, which makes it possible to model more faithfully the real strains of thick plates subjected to complex loadings. It retains a relatively simple formulation, offering a good compromise between mechanical realism and numerical cost. The transverse-shear effects are modelled by a strain term defined as the difference between the gradient of the transverse displacement and the rotation field, weighted by a correction factor \kappa making it possible to adjust the shear energy. However, the direct discretisation of this model by means of standard conforming finite elements leads to numerical difficulties in the case of thin plates, in particular a phenomenon of transverse-shear locking (or shear locking , in English) which impairs the accuracy and slows the convergence of the simulations. In order to remedy this limitation, mixed formulations have been developed. These rest on the introduction of auxiliary fields for the shear, interpolated in suitable spaces (in particular of Nédélec type), and on the use of Lagrange multipliers in order to impose the compatibility constraints in a weak manner. The aim of the present document is to present the development and the integration of the new finite element PLAQ_MITC , designed to avoid transverse-shear locking and to improve the numerical accuracy in the case of thick plates. This element rests on a mixed formulation of MITC type ( Mixed Interpolation of Tensorial Components , in English) and relies on automatic code generation via FENICSx in order to simplify the development of the elementary functions, while ensuring their efficient integration. 2 Constitutive equations and assumptions 2.1 Assumptions of the Reissner--Mindlin model The Reissner-Mindlin model makes it possible to represent the mechanical constitutive behaviour of thick plates, by taking explicitly into account the effects of transverse shear. Unlike the Kirchhoff-Love model, it does not assume that the sections normal to the middle surface remain perpendicular after deformation. For what follows: - the transverse displacement is denoted w(x, y) , - the rotations of the fibres normal to the middle surface are described by an independent vector field \vector{	heta}(x, y) = \left(	heta_x (x,y), 	heta_y (x, y)ight) . The thickness h of the plate is assumed small compared with its dimensions in the plane, but not negligible, which authorises the introduction of a transverse-shear strain. The latter is defined by: \vector{\gamma} = \gradScal{w} - \vector{	heta}, where \gradScal{w} = \left( \cfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}, \cfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} ight) represents the gradient of the transverse displacement. 2.2 Elastic constitutive law The elastic constitutive behaviour of the material is described with the aid of the classical parameters: - Young's modulus E , - Poisson's ratio 
u , - a shear correction factor \kappa , generally taken equal to \cfrac{5}{6} for homogeneous plates. 2.2.1 Curvature tensor The curvature tensor 	ensTwo{\kappa} represents the spatial variations of the rotation field \vector{	heta} . It is defined as the symmetric part of the gradient of \vector{	heta} : 	ensTwo{\kappa} = \operGradSyme{\vector{	heta}} =  rac{1}{2} \left( \gradVector{\vector{	heta}} + 	ranspose{\gradVector{\vector{	heta}}} ight). 2.2.2 Bending energy The stresses due to bending 	ensTwo{M} are related to the curvature tensor by a linear constitutive law: 	ensTwo{M} = 	ensFour{D} : 	ensTwo{\kappa}, where 	ensFour{D} denotes the bending stiffness tensor, expressed by: 	ensFour{D} = D \left[ (1 -

The corresponding bending energy is given by: \psi_b =  rac{1}{2} 	ensTwo{M} : 	ensTwo{\kappa}. 2.2.3 Transverse-shear energy The elastic energy associated with the transverse shear is written: \psi_s =  rac{1}{2} S \left( \vector{\gamma}_R \cdot \vector{\gamma}_R ight) where S = \cfrac{E \kappa h}{2(1 + 
u)} and \vector{\gamma}_R denotes the "reduced" shear field, interpolated in a suitable functional space (for example of Nédélec type), in order to prevent the phenomenon of numerical locking during the discretisation by finite elements. 3 Variational formulations 3.1 Unknown fields and approximation spaces The modelling adopted rests on the Reissner-Mindlin theory, enriched by a mixed interpolation of MITC type (Mixed Interpolation of Tensorial Components), in the variant proposed by Durán and Liberman . This approach makes it possible to correct effectively the numerical locking linked to the transverse shear, thus ensuring a better accuracy in the reproduction of the strains, even for thin plates. The unknown fields are discretised in the following finite-element spaces: w^h \in P_1, \quad \vector{	heta}^h \in [P_2]^2, \quad \vector{\gamma}_R^h, \, \vector{p}^h \in \mathrm{NED}_1, where: - P_1 denotes the space of the linear Lagrange elements, that is to say the continuous functions whose restriction to each element of the mesh is a polynomial of degree less than or equal to 1; - [P_2]^2 denotes a space of vector fields with two components, each being a P_2 function, that is a polynomial of degree less than or equal to 2, piecewise; - \mathrm{NED}_1 corresponds to the Nédélec space of the first type, suited to the discretisation of tangential vector fields. On a quadrangular element, this results in the distribution of the degrees of freedom illustrated below: Distribution of the degrees of freedom for the fields w^h \in P_1 , \vector{	heta}^h \in [P_2]^2 and \vector{\gamma}_R^h, \vector{p}^h \in \mathrm{NED}_1 on a quadrangular element. This discretisation allows a faithful and stable representation of the various mechanical effects brought into play, while preventing numerical artefacts such as shear locking. 3.1.1 Nédélec functions These are vector functions principally associated with the edges of the elements. An important property is that they ensure the continuity of the tangential component of a vector field from one element to another. In our case, this makes it possible to guarantee that the projection of the field \gamma_R is consistent at the interface of the elements. Representations of the Nédélec functions 3.2 Energy of the system and variational coupling Let \Omega \subset \setR^2 be the plane domain occupied by the plate, discretised by means of a conforming mesh \mathcal{T}^h composed of quadrangular elements. The set of the edges is denoted \mathcal{E}^h and, for every edge E \in \mathcal{E}^h , \vector{t} denotes the unit tangent vector. The variational formulation adopted is expressed by the minimisation of a functional integrating the whole of the contributions of the system: - the bending energy, linked to the bending moments and to the curvature of the plate; - the transverse-shear energy, computed from a conforming field \vector{\gamma}_R^h ; - a weak coupling term, imposing the consistency between \vector{\gamma}_R^h and the field reconstructed from w^h and \vector{	heta}^h , via a Lagrange multiplier \vector{p}^h . The coupling term expresses, in weak form, the equality between the two representations of the transverse shear: the reconstructed field \vector{\gamma}(w^h, \vector{	heta}^h) and the conforming field \vector{\gamma}_R^h . This constraint, imposed on each edge E \in \mathcal{E}^h via \vector{p}^h , is written in the following variational form: \int_E \left( \vector{\gamma}(w^h, \vector{	heta}^h) - \vector{\gamma}_R^h ight) \cdot \vector{t} \, (\vector{p}^h \cdot \vector{t}) \measBound This coupling mechanism guarantees the consistency between the shear fields while ensuring the numerical stability of the scheme, and plays a key role in avoiding locking in the thin-plate regime. 3.3 Motivation for the use of MITC 3.3.1 Shear-locking problem In the Reissner–Mindlin model, when the thickness h tends towards zero, the expected constitutive behaviour is that of the Kirchhoff model, for which: \vector{\gamma} = \gradScal{w} - \vector{	heta} 	o \vector{0} However, with a standard discretisation using P_1 elements (continuous finite elements of degree 1) for the displacement w and the rotations \vector{	heta} , and under a clamped condition, one has: - \gradScal{w}^h \in \mathrm{P}_0 : piecewise constant field; - \vector{	heta}^h \in [\mathrm{P}_1]^2 : continuous field, zero on \partial \Omega . It then becomes impossible, except trivially, to obtain \gradScal{w}^h = \vector{	heta}^h . This approximation defect causes numerical locking: the discrete solution is too stiff and does not correctly reproduce the bending modes, in particular for thin plates. 3.3.2 Solution: the MITC elements The MITC elements ( Mixed Interpolation of Tensorial Components ) circumvent this locking by modifying the interpolation of the transverse shear. The principle consists in projecting the reconstructed shear \gradScal{w} - \vector{	heta} onto a suitable subspace (often defined on the edges or inside the elements), thus ensuring a weak compatibility between the fields. This technique limits the spurious constraints, restores the consistency of the model and allows a robust and uniform convergence, including in the thin-plate regime, without recourse to an excessive refinement of the mesh. 3.4 Weak variational formulation of the problem One seeks the stationary points of the functional \Pi by imposing that its directional derivative vanishes for every admissible variation 	ilde{q} = (	ilde{w}, 	ilde{\vector{	heta}}, 	ilde{\vector{\gamma}}_R, 	ilde{\vector{p}}) : F(q^h; 	ilde{q}) := D_{	ilde{q}}[\Pi(q^h)] = 0 \quad  orall 	ilde{q}. r3.08.01 “Exact” beam elements r3.08.01 “Exact” beam elements Summary : This document presents the beam elements of Code_Aster based on an exact solution of the equations of the continuous model carried out for each element of the mesh. The beams are straight: elements POU_D_T and POU_D_E. Curved beams will be modelled by means of a sufficiently fine mesh, to which a straight-beam model is assigned. The cross-section, constant or variable along the length, may be of arbitrary shape. The material is homogeneous, isotropic, linear elastic. The assumptions adopted are the following: - Euler assumption: the transverse shear is neglected, as is the rotary inertia. This assumption is verified for large slendernesses: element POU_D_E. - Timoshenko assumption: the transverse shear and all the inertia terms are taken into account. This assumption is to be used for small slendernesses: elements POU_D_T. - Saint-Venant assumption: the torsion is free. The treatment of the various loadings and of the quantities (grandeur) expected as results (stresses-forces) is also presented. Foreword This reference documentation of the beam elements was produced from work carried out by M.T.Bourdeix, P.Hemon, O.Wilk of the Institut Aérotechnique of the Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers, within the framework of an External Research and Development Contract with this laboratory. The volume of this document is due both to the precision sought and to the didactic character of the presentation, which is deliberately retained. 1 Notations The notations used here are not all identical to those used in U4.42.01, for reasons of compactness and of homogeneity with R3.08.03. One gives the correspondence between this notation and that of the user's documentation. \mathrm{DX},\mathrm{DY},\mathrm{DZ} and \mathrm{DRX},\mathrm{DRY},\mathrm{DRZ} are the names of the degrees of freedom associated with the components of the displacement u,v,w,{\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z} . | C | torsion constant | \mathrm{JX} | | --- | --- | --- | | {e}_{y},{e}_{z} | offset of the centre of torsion/shear | \text{EY},\text{EZ} | | E | Young's modulus | E | | \nu | Poisson's ratio | \mathrm{NU} | | G | Coulomb modulus = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu )} | | | {I}_{y},{I}_{z} | geometric bending moments with respect to the axes y,z | \mathrm{IY},\mathrm{IZ} | | {I}_{p} | polar geometric moment | | | {I}_{{\theta}_{x}} | polar moment of inertia about the longitudinal axis x | | | {k}_{y},{k}_{z} | shear coefficients | \frac{1}{\mathrm{AY}},\frac{1}{\mathrm{AZ}} | | K | stiffness matrix | | | M | mass matrix | | | {M}_{x},{M}_{y},{M}_{z} | moments about the axes x,y,z | \mathrm{MT},\mathrm{MFY},\mathrm{MFZ} | | N | force normal to the cross-section | N | | S | area of the cross-section | A | | u,v,w | translations along the axes x,y,z | \mathrm{DX},\mathrm{DY},\mathrm{DZ} | | {V}_{y},{V}_{z} | shear forces along the axes y,z | \mathrm{VY},\mathrm{VZ} | | \rho | density | \mathrm{RHO} | | {\sigma}_{{c}_{T}} | transverse shear stress | | | {\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z} | rotations about the axes x,y,z | \mathrm{DRX},\mathrm{DRY},\mathrm{DRZ} | 2 Introduction A beam is a solid generated by a surface of area S whose geometric centre of inertia G describes a curve C called the mean fibre or neutral fibre. The area S is the cross-section (transverse section) or profile, and one assumes that if it is evolving, its evolutions (size, shape) are continuous and progressive as G describes the mean line. For the study of beams in general, one makes the following assumptions: - the cross-section of the beam is undeformable, - the transverse displacement is uniform over the cross-section. These assumptions make it possible to express the displacements of any point of the cross-section, as a function of the displacements of the corresponding point situated on the mean line, and as a function of an increment of displacement due to the rotation of the cross-section about the transverse axes. This last one may be neglected (POU_D_E) or be the subject of a modelling (POU_D_T). The discretisation into “exact” beam elements is carried out on a line element with two nodes and six degrees of freedom per node. These degrees of freedom are the three translations u,v,w and the three rotations {\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z} . Figure 2-a: beam element and degrees of freedom. Given that the strains are local, a local basis depending on the element on which one is working is built at each vertex of the mesh. The continuity of the displacement fields is ensured by a change of basis, bringing the data back into the global basis. In the case of straight beams, one traditionally places the mean line on the x axis of the local basis, the transverse displacements thus taking place in the plane (y,z) . Finally, when we store quantities (grandeur) linked to the degrees of freedom of an element in a vector or an elementary matrix (hence of dimension 12 or {12}^{2} ), one stores first the variables for vertex 1 then those of vertex 2. For each node, one stores first the quantities linked to the three translations, then those linked to the three rotations. For example, a displacement vector will be structured in the following manner: (\underbrace{{{u}_{1},{v}_{1},{w}_{1},{\theta}_{{x}_{1}},{\theta}_{{y}_{1}},{\theta}_{{z}_{1}}}}_\text{sommet 1})(\underbrace{{{u}_{2},{v}_{2},{w}_{2},{\theta}_{{x}_{2}},{\theta}_{{y}_{2}},{\theta}_{{z}_{2}}}}_\text{sommet 2}) 3 The equations of motion In this chapter one presents the equations of motion of the beams in tension-compression, in torsion and in bending in the elastic domain. In each of the cases, these equations are deduced by application of the Lagrange equations, coming from Hamilton's principle, or else by writing the local equilibrium of a beam segment. We have chosen to recall both methods; the reader may refer to the one which is the most familiar. One restricts oneself here to the cases where the only loadings are distributed loadings (no concentrated forces). 3.1 Tension-compression Tension-compression is the translational motion along the longitudinal axis of the beam. 3.1.1 Local equilibrium equation One considers a segment of length \mathrm{dx} subjected to an axial force N [Figure 3.1.1-a] internal and an external force {f}_{\text{ext}} per unit length. Figure 3.1.1-a : Axially loaded beam segment. The beam has a cross-section S(x) and is made of a material of density \rho (x) and of Young's modulus E(x) . The fundamental principle of mechanics makes it possible to write: -\mathrm{N}(x)+\mathrm{N}(x+\mathit{dx})+\underset{x}{\overset{x+\mathit{dx}}{\int}}{\mathrm{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}(s)\mathit{ds}=\underset{x}{\overset{x+\mathit{dx}}{\int}}\rho (s)S(s)\frac{{\partial}^{2}\mathrm{u}(s)}{\partial {t}^{2}}\mathit{ds} where u is the displacement along the x axis of the segment Hence: \frac{\mathrm{N}(x+\mathit{dx})-\mathrm{N}(x)}{\mathit{dx}}+\frac{1}{\mathit{dx}}\underset{x}{\overset{x+\mathit{dx}}{\int}}{\mathrm{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}(s)\mathit{ds}=\frac{1}{\mathit{dx}}\underset{x}{\overset{x+\mathit{dx}}{\int}}\rho S\frac{{\partial}^{2}\mathrm{u}}{\partial {t}^{2}}\mathit{ds} Passing to the limit when dx \to 0 , one obtains: \frac{dN(x)}{dx} + {f}_{\text{ext}}^{(x)} = \rho S\frac{{\partial}^{2}u}{\partial {t}^{2}}(x) One retains only the first-order terms and one substitutes into , then one uses Hooke's law and the assumption that the beam is made up of longitudinal fibres working only in tension-compression in order to express the axial force by: N(x)=\text{ES}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} One thus obtains after simplification by dx : \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\text{ES}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x})+{f}_{\text{ext}}=\rho S\frac{{\partial}^{2}u}{\partial {t}^{2}} which represents the local equilibrium to first order of a beam, for a tension-compression motion. 3.1.2 Lagrangian method Taking up again the beam segment of the figure the total kinetic energy of the beam of length l is written: {E}_{c}=\frac{1}{2}{\int}_{0}^{l}\rho S{\left(\frac{\partial \mathrm{u}}{\partial t}\right)}^{2}\text{dx} One will denote for what follows {E}_{{c}_{e}}=\frac{1}{2}\rho S{\left(\frac{\partial \mathrm{u}}{\partial t}\right)}^{2} the elementary kinetic energy. The internal strain energy, thanks to Hooke's law, is written: {E}_{{p}_{int}}=\frac{1}{2}{\int}_{0}^{l}\text{ES}{\left(\frac{\partial \mathrm{u}}{\partial x}\right)}^{2}\text{dx} One will likewise denote {E}_{{p}_{{int}_{e}}}=\frac{1}{2}\text{ES}{\left(\frac{\partial \mathrm{u}}{\partial x}\right)}^{2} . One also has the work of the external force given by: {E}_{{p}_{\text{ext}}}={\int}_{o}^{l}{f}_{\text{ext}}u\text{dx} and at the elementary level {E}_{{p}_{{\text{ext}}_{e}}}={f}_{\text{ext}}.u The Lagrangian is given by: L={E}_{c}-{E}_{{p}_{int}}-{E}_{{p}_{\text{ext}}} and the Lagrangian density: L={E}_{{c}_{e}}-{E}_{{p}_{{int}_{e}}}-{E}_{{p}_{{\mathrm{ext}}_{e}}} For the one-dimensional continuous system, the Lagrange equation is written in this case: \frac{\partial L}{\partial u}-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial u'}\right)-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{u}}\right)=0 where {u}^{'} and \dot{u} denote respectively the derivative with respect to x and with respect to time. Its application obviously brings us back to the equation of motion of a beam in tension-compression . 3.2 Pure torsion (Saint-Venant torsion) Torsion is the rotational motion about the longitudinal axis of the beam. One assumes here that the centre of gravity coincides with the centre of rotation (of torsion) R3.03.03, and one neglects the warping of the cross-section. The case of the offset of the centre of torsion with respect to the centre of gravity is treated in [§ 5.1 ]. 3.2.1 Local equilibrium equation One considers a segment of length dx set in rotation under the action of a moment {M}_{x} [Figure 3.2.1-a] internal and of an external couple {\Gamma}_{x} per unit length. Figure 3.2.1-a : Beam segment in rotation about (\mathrm{Ox}) The segment is rotated by an angle {\theta}_{x} with respect to the undeformed position. We thus have: 3.2.1.1 Beam of circular cross-section -{M}_{x}(x)+{M}_{x}(x+\text{dx})+{\int}_{x}^{x+\text{dx}}{\Gamma}_{x}(s)\text{ds}={\int}_{x}^{x+\text{dx}}{I}_{{q}_{x}}\frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{x}}{\partial {t}^{2}}\text{ds} with {I}_{{q}_{x}}={\int}_{s}\rho {r}^{2}\text{ds} is the plane moment of inertia of the cross-section S about the axis of rotation (0,x) . As for tension, one obtains after division by \text{dx} and passage to the limit: \frac{d{M}_{x}}{\text{dx}}+{\Gamma}_{x}={I}_{{\theta}_{x}}\frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{x}}{\partial {t}^{2}} One introduces the constitutive law: {M}_{x}=G{I}_{p}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x} where G is the Coulomb modulus (or shear modulus) and {I}_{p} the polar geometric moment with respect to the centre of gravity of the cross-section. (One has moreover: {I}_{{\theta}_{x}}=\rho {I}_{p} for a material of homogeneous density). We then obtain the expression: \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(G{I}_{p}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}\right)+{\Gamma}_{x}={I}_{{\theta}_{x}}\frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{x}}{\partial {t}^{2}} which represents the local equilibrium to first order of a beam segment for a torsional motion. 3.2.1.2 Beam of arbitrary cross-section In order to take warping into account while remaining within the free-torsion assumption, in the case of non-circular cross-sections one is led to replace the moment {I}_{p} by a torsion constant C (lower than {I}_{p} ) in the torsion equation (R3.03.03 for the computation of C ). By definition, {M}_{x}=GC\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x} . One then obtains: \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(GC\frac{{\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}\right)+{\Gamma}_{x}=\rho C\frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{x}}{\partial {t}^{2}} When the centre of gravity of the cross-section is not the centre of rotation, this expression is not valid and the torsional and bending motions are coupled. 3.2.2 Lagrangian method We have in the same manner as in [§ 3.1.2 the kinetic energy (for example for a beam of circular cross-section): {E}_{c}={\int}_{0}^{l}\frac{1}{2}{I}_{{\theta}_{x}}{\left(\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial t}\right)}^{2}\text{dx} the internal potential energy {E}_{{p}_{int}}={\int}_{0}^{l}\frac{1}{2}{\mathit{GI}}_{p}{\left(\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial t}\right)}^{2}\text{dx} and the work of the external couple {E}_{{p}_{\text{ext}}}={\int}_{0}^{l}{\Gamma}_{x}{\theta}_{x}\text{dx} By applying the Lagrange equation to the variable {\theta}_{x} , one naturally arrives at giving the motion of a beam in pure torsion. 3.3 Simple bending Bending is the motion of translation and of rotation about an axis perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of the beam. One speaks here of simple bending (about \mathrm{Oy} or \mathrm{Oz} ). One restricts oneself to the case of straight beams. Curved beams are treated in [§ 8 ]. One describes the bending equation in the plane (O,x,z) , the extension to the plane (O,x,y) is immediate [Figure 3.3-a]. Figure 3.3-a : Bending of a beam in the plane (O,x,z) . The translation along the axis (O,z) is denoted w and the rotation about (O,y) is denoted {\theta}_{y} . 3.3.1 Local equilibrium equation One considers a segment of length \mathrm{dx} subjected to the shear force {V}_{z} , the bending moment {M}_{y} , an external force {t}_{{z}_{\text{ext}}} distributed uniformly per unit length, and an external couple {m}_{{y}_{\text{ext}}} distributed uniformly per unit length [Figure 3.3.1-a]. Passing to the limit when \mathrm{dx} tends to 0, one obtains: \begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial {V}_{z}}{\partial x}+{t}_{{z}_{\text{ext}}}=\rho S\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {t}^{2}}\\ \frac{\partial {M}_{y}}{\partial x}-{V}_{z}+{m}_{{y}_{\text{ext}}}=\rho {I}_{y}\frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{y}}{\partial {t}^{2}}\end{array} \begin{split}\begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial {V}_{z}}{\partial x}+{t}_{{z}_{\text{ext}}}=\rho S\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {t}^{2}}\\ \frac{\partial {M}_{y}}{\partial x}-{V}_{z}+{m}_{{y}_{\text{ext}}}=\rho {I}_{y}\frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{y}}{\partial {t}^{2}}\end{array}\end{split} One notes that the uniformly distributed force {t}_{{z}_{\text{ext}}} produces a term which is of second order in the equilibrium of the moments and is thus neglected. One then introduces the constitutive relations of strength of materials. {M}_{y}=EI_{y}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x} \text{ et } {V}_{z}={k}_{z}\text{SG}\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+{\theta}_{y}\right) The expression of {V}_{z} is due to Timoshenko [bib 4] where {k}_{z} is the shear coefficient in the direction z . It characterises the Timoshenko beam model; one will see later that the Euler beam model corresponds to a simplification of the Timoshenko model. {I}_{z} is the geometric moment of the cross-section with respect to the axis (O,y) . Consequently, one arrives at the two equations coupled in w and {\theta}_{y} for bending in the plane (O,x,z) . \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[{k}_{z}\text{SG}\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+{\theta}_{y}\right)\right]+{t}_{{z}_{\text{ext}}}=\rho S\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {t}^{2}} \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[EI_{y}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x}\right]-{k}_{z}\text{SG}\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+{\theta}_{y}\right)+{m}_{{y}_{\text{ext}}}=\rho {I}_{y}\frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{y}}{\partial {t}^{2}} When the beam is uniform, that is when the cross-section and the material are constant along the longitudinal axis, equations and reduce to a single equation in w . For this, one differentiates once with respect to the abscissa x the moment-equilibrium equation . EI_{y}\frac{{\partial}^{3}{\theta}_{y}}{\partial {x}^{3}}-{k}_{z}\text{SG}\left(\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {x}^{2}}+\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x}\right)=\rho {I}_{y}\frac{{\partial}^{3}{\theta}_{y}}{\partial x\partial {t}^{2}} One will note that this manipulation eliminates the presence of the term coming from a uniformly distributed external couple. Then, equation may be put in the form: \frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x}=-\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {x}^{2}}-\frac{{t}_{{z}_{\text{ext}}}}{{k}_{z}\text{SG}}+\frac{\rho}{{k}_{z}G}\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {t}^{2}} EI_{y}\frac{{\partial}^{4}w}{\partial {x}^{4}}+\rho S\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {t}^{2}}-\rho {I}_{y}\left[1+\frac{E}{{k}_{z}G}\right]\frac{{\partial}^{4}w}{\partial {x}^{2}\partial {t}^{2}}+\frac{{\rho}^{2}{I}_{y}}{{k}_{z}G}\frac{{\partial}^{4}w}{\partial {t}^{4}}-{t}_{{z}_{\text{ext}}}=0 It remains useful for this type of equation to recall the physical meaning of the various terms, so that during the simplifications one is aware of the neglected effects. EI_{y}\frac{{\partial}^{4}w}{\partial {x}^{4}} balances the loading density in the direction of the translation due to the bending moment. \rho S\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {t}^{2}} is the translational inertia term. \rho {I}_{y}\frac{{\partial}^{4}w}{\partial {x}^{2}\partial {t}^{2}} represents the rotary inertia of bending. \rho {I}_{y}\frac{E}{{k}_{z}G}\frac{{\partial}^{4}w}{\partial {x}^{2}\partial {t}^{2}} is an additional term of the rotary inertia due to taking the transverse shear into account (Timoshenko assumption). \frac{{\rho}^{2}{I}_{y}}{{k}_{z}G}\frac{{\partial}^{4}w}{\partial {t}^{4}} results from the coupling between the rotary inertia and the translational inertia coming from the shear force. The Timoshenko beam model (POU_D_T) takes all of these terms into account, in particular those which relate to the shear force. One can therefore model beams of small slenderness. The Euler beam model (POU_D_E) is a simplification since the shear-force strains are neglected as well as the rotary inertia (it comes into play in dynamic studies only for the high modes). These assumptions are justified in the case of a beam of sufficiently large slenderness. Consequently, for the Euler model, the equation of the bending motion, in the general case of beams of variable cross-section, is written: \frac{\partial}{\partial {x}^{2}}(EI_{y}\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {x}^{2}})+\rho S\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {t}^{2}}-{t}_{{z}_{\text{ext}}}=0 Moreover, it is indeed the shear force which causes the rotation of the cross-sections with respect to the neutral axis. Neglecting this effect thus amounts to writing that {V}_{z}=0 which leads to . {\theta}_{y}=-\frac{\partial w}{\partial x} which is the expression of the Euler assumption. The stiffness matrices are computed with the option RIGI_MECA, and the mass matrices with the option MASS_MECA for the consistent matrix, and the option MASS_MECA_DIAG for the diagonalised mass matrix. 4.1 Longitudinal motion of tension - compression A difficulty in writing the variational formulation comes from the fact that there may be, in structures composed of beams, concentrated loads (assimilable to Diracs). The equilibrium equation must be replaced by: \frac{dN}{dx}(x) + {f}_{\text{ext}}^{(x)} + \sum_{i=1}^{n_c}{f}_{i}^{c}{\delta}_{i}(x) = 0 One has omitted for simplicity the inertia forces, which would undergo the same treatment as the external forces {f}_{\text{ext}}^{(x)} . {\delta}_{i} represents the Dirac function localised at the point i , the {f}_{i}^{c} are the n_c concentrated forces applied to the beam. For the application of the finite element method, the equilibrium equation must be written in the form of the principle of virtual work which is in this case: \underset{G}{\int} N\frac{dv}{dx} \, dx = \underset{G}{\int}{f}_{\text{ext}} \, v \, dx + \sum_{i=1}^{ n_c }{f}_{i}^{c}{\delta}_{i}(v) All confusion being excluded, {\delta}_{i} denotes the Dirac measure associated with the point i and v is any kinematically admissible longitudinal displacement field. In practice, one assumes that there is no concentrated force inside the beam elements, but only at the end nodes. 4.1.1 Determination of the stiffness matrix It corresponds to the expression of the virtual work of the internal forces as a function of a given displacement. That is: {\int}_{0}^{\beamLength} {N \frac{dv}{dx}\,{dx}} for an element of length \beamLength . One introduces the elastic constitutive relation: N(x) = \youngModulus \beamArea \frac{du}{dx} By choosing as test functions: v(x) = {\xi}_{1}(x) = 1-\frac{x}{\beamLength} \text{ et } v(x) = {\xi}_{2}(x) = \frac{x}{\beamLength} corresponding respectively to the degrees of freedom {u}_{1} and {u}_{2} of the two nodes of the element, one obtains directly: {\int}_{0}^{\beamLength} {N \frac{d{\xi}_{1}}{dx}dx} = - {\int}_{0}^{\beamLength} {\frac{\youngModulus \beamArea}{\beamLength} \frac{du}{dx} dx } = - \frac{\youngModulus \beamArea}{\beamLength} \left[ u(\beamLength)-u(0) \right] and {\int}_{0}^{\beamLength} {N \frac{d{\xi}_{2}}{dx} {dx} } = {\int}_{0}^{\beamLength} {\frac{\youngModulus \beamArea}{\beamLength}\frac{du}{dx} dx} = \frac{\youngModulus \beamArea}{\beamLength}\left[u(\beamLength)-u(0)\right] The stiffness matrix of the element is therefore: \discMatr{K} = \frac{\youngModulus \beamArea}{\beamLength} \left[ \begin{array}{cc} 1 & -1\\ -1 & 1 \end{array}\right] Note \begin{split}\discMatr{K} = \frac{\youngModulus \beamArea}{\beamLength} \left[ \begin{array}{cc} 1 & -1\\ -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]\end{split} In the expression of the virtual work of the internal forces, u appears only for u(0) and u(\beamLength) . The displacement u has not been discretised inside the element. This is why the element is termed exact : one obtains the exact solution at the nodes, but only at the nodes. 4.1.2 Determination of the right-hand side The right-hand side is the expression of the virtual work of the applied forces. The right-hand side associated with the distributed loading and with the test functions introduced previously is: \left \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{f}_{1}\\ {f}_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrace \text{ avec } {f}_{1} = {\int}_{0}^{1} {{f}_{\text{ext}}\left(x\right)\left(1-\frac{x}{\beamLength}\right) {dx} } \text{ et } {f}_{2} = {\int}_{0}^{1} {{f}_{\text{ext}}\left(x\right)\frac{x}{\beamLength} {dx} } Note In AFFE_CHAR_MECA, one may introduce {f}_{\text{ext}} as an arbitrary function of x . At the level of the computation of {f}_{1} and {f}_{2} , on the other hand, the integration is carried out by assuming that {f}_{\text{ext}} varies linearly between the values taken at the end nodes. If one must model a non-linear variation of the distributed load, one must then discretise more finely. But let us insist on the fact that whatever the form of {f}_{\text{ext}}(x) (polynomial or otherwise), if one knows how to compute exactly the integrals {f}_{1} and {f}_{2} , the solution of the static problem will be exact at the nodes of the problem. The virtual work of the concentrated forces (given by assumption at the nodes of the elements) does not intervene directly at the element level. One introduces these concentrated forces in the form of nodal forces, directly into the assembled right-hand side vector. 4.1.3 Computation of the forces at the nodes of the beam The complete principle of virtual work is indeed written on the assembled system. On the other hand, by writing the integration-by-parts formula over the whole structure (beam \left[{x}_{0},{x}_{1}\right] ): {\int}_{\Gamma} {N \derivee{v}{x} dx} = \left[ N \left( {x}_{1} \right) v \left({x}_{1}\right) - N \left( {x}_{o} \right) v \left({x}_{o}\right) \right] + \sum_{i=1}^{N} { \left[ \vert N \vert \right]}_{i} {\delta}_{i} \left( v \right) - \sum_{j=1}^{M} {\int_{{\Gamma}_{j}} {\derivee{N}{x} v dx} } {\Gamma}_{j} representing all the intervals without discontinuity of the normal force, hence without a concentrated force, and {\vert N \vert}_{i} the jumps of N between these intervals. POU_D_T only). One distinguishes two types of cross-section variation: - linear or affine, - quadratic or homothetic. The distinction between the two types is readily conceived by taking the example of a rectangular beam: - if only one of the lateral dimensions varies, one assumes in a linear manner, then the area of the cross-section varies linearly, and is given by: S(x)={S}_{1}\left[1+(\frac{{S}_{2}}{{S}_{1}}-1)\frac{x}{L}\right] - when the two lateral dimensions vary (in a linear manner), the cross-sectional area evolves in a quadratic manner. S(x)={S}_{1}{\left[1+(\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{2}}{{S}_{1}}}-1)\frac{x}{L}\right]}^{2} Code_Aster makes it possible to treat the cross-sections ’CERCLE’, ’RECTANGLE’ and ’GENERALE’, but for obvious geometric reasons not all of these types of cross-section can admit both types of variation. The following table summarises the existing possibilities. | Cross-section | Constant | Linear or Affine | Quadratic or Homothetic | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | circle | yes | no | yes | | rectangle | yes | yes - along y | yes | | general | yes | no | yes | For the cross-section ’RECTANGLE’, it is the user who chooses the type of variation, by specifying ’AFFINE’ or ’HOMOTHÉTIQUE’ in AFFE_CARA_ELEM. One must indeed note that in the case ’AFFINE’, the dimensions can vary only along y. In the case of hollow circular cross-sections, for the cross-section to be considered homothetic, it is necessary that \mathit{EP1}/\mathit{R1}=\mathit{EP2}/\mathit{R2} . In the case of failure to respect the homothety, the solution given by Code_Aster is approximate. We consider in a general manner that the cross-section varies according to the formula [eq]: > S(x)={S}_{1}{(1\text{+c}\frac{x}{L})}^{m} [5.2-1] {S}_{1} is the initial cross-section at x=0 c is fixed by the knowledge of the final cross-section {S}_{2} at x=L . m gives the degree of variation: m=1 linear variation, m=2 quadratic variation. The moduli of Young (E) and of Coulomb (G) are assumed constant. The principle adopted by Code_Aster consists in computing equivalent cross-section characteristics, constant along the beam, from the real characteristics given at the two ends. These equivalent characteristics therefore depend on the phenomenon to which they contribute; in particular, they are distinct for the effects of stiffness or of inertia. 5.2.1 Computation of the stiffness matrix 5.2.1.1 Determination of the equivalent cross-section ( {S}_{\mathrm{eq}} ) The determination of the equivalent cross-section uses neither the method adopted in [§ r3.08.01-MatrRigiTC] in order to obtain the exact stiffness matrix nor an approximation of the solution by a polynomial function as described in [§ r3.08.01-MatrMassTC ]. In fact, the method employed departs from the finite element method and even from Galerkin's method; it consists in carrying out a solution of the problem of the beam of variable cross-section without imposed distributed forces, which makes it possible to express the forces at the ends as a function of the displacements. This method is “consistent” with that of [§ r3.08.01-MatrRigiTC] because the test functions defined in [§ r3.08.01-MatrRigiTC] are worth 1 or 0 at the ends of the beam, hence [eq] the nodal forces may be “assimilated” to forces. Moreover, this method makes it possible to obtain exact results for the static problem without a distributed force and leads, as we shall see, to a value {S}_{\mathrm{eq}} lying between {S}_{1} and {S}_{2} which, in the general case, guarantees the convergence of the approximate solution towards the exact solution (without however knowing the order of convergence). The cross-section of the beam being variable, the tension-compression equation in statics without an imposed distributed force is written: > \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[ES(x)\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right]=0 [5.2.1.1-1] with N(x)=ES(x)\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} We determine the stiffness matrix in the general case [eq]; we subsequently deduce from it the values of the equivalent cross-sections for the cases m=1 (linear progression) and m=2 (quadratic progression). By integrating [eq], we have: \text{E S}(x)\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}={C}_{1} or, taking into account the expression of S(x) : E{S}_{1}{(1\text{+c}\frac{x}{L})}^{m}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}={C}_{1} The constant of integration is determined from the values of the axial forces at the nodes. We integrate once more so as to obtain the forces at the nodes as a function of the displacements u(0)={u}_{1} and u(L)={u}_{2} : \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\frac{{C}_{1}}{E{S}_{1}}{(1\text{+c}\frac{x}{L})}^{-m} whence \text{u}(x)=\frac{{C}_{1}}{E{S}_{1}}\frac{L}{c}\ln(1\text{+c}\frac{x}{L}){\text{+C}}_{2}\text{} if m=1 and u(x)=\frac{{C}_{1}}{E{S}_{1}}\frac{L}{c}\frac{1}{(l-m){(1+c\frac{x}{L})}^{m-1}}+{C}_{2} if m\ge 2 One notes that the expression of u(x) is far from being polynomial. To model a curved beam, one must mesh the curved part with sufficiently many straight elements: 20 to 40 straight elements for a 90° elbow give entirely satisfactory results. This chapter is retained, because in the test-case database of Code_Aster the structures which present elbows are validated and compared with the theoretical solutions obtained with curved beam elements coming from the theory presented below. In order to compute the stiffness matrix for a curved beam element, we carry out the computation by passing through various stages. We start from the equilibrium equations which, once integrated, will give us a matrix (denoted {J}_{\theta} ) making it possible to determine the forces at one point of the beam knowing the forces at another point. This matrix will take into account the local change of basis. Then, by writing the potential energy of the element and by noting the decoupling of the bending in the plane of the element from the bending out of this plane, one determines the two flexibility matrices. Finally, the flexibility matrices having been computed, one obtains the local stiffness matrix by using Castigliano's principle, which must be recomputed in the global basis in order to be assembled. For the mass matrix, one considers only the reduced matrix (lumped masses), and one makes the simplifying assumption that the expression given for straight beams [§ 4.4 ] remains valid by considering a straight element of length R.\beta . It is therefore better in this case to model a curved beam by several curved elements. 9 Loadings The various types of loading developed for the beam elements "MECA_POU_D_E", "MECA_POU_D_T", in linear elasticity are: | Types or options | MECA_POU_D_E | MECA_POU_D_T | | --- | --- | --- | | CHAR_MECA_EPSI_R: loading by imposition of a strain (of thermal-stratification type) | developed | developed | | CHAR_MECA_PESA_R: loading due to gravity | developed | developed | | CHAR_MECA_FR1D1D: distributed loading by real values | developed | developed | | CHAR_MECA_FF1D1D: distributed loading by function | developed | developed | | CHAR_MECA_TEMP_R: 'thermal' loading | developed | developed | | CHAR_MECA_FRELEC: 'electric force' loading created by a straight secondary conductor | developed | developed | | CHAR_MECA_FRLAPL: 'electric force' loading created by an arbitrary secondary conductor | developed | developed | 9.1 Loading by strain OPTION: "CHAR_MECA_EPSI_R" One computes the loading from a state of strain (this option was developed in order to take thermal stratification in piping into account). The strain is given by the user by means of the keyword PRE_EPSI in AFFE_CHAR_MECA. The model takes into account only a work in tension-compression and in pure bending (no shear force, no torsional moment). One uses the following constitutive relations: N=\mathrm{ES}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x},{M}_{y}=E{I}_{y}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x},{M}_{z}=E{I}_{z}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{z}}{\partial x} Thus, one obtains the elementary right-hand side associated with this loading: - at point 1: {F}_{{x}_{1}}=E{S}_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x},{M}_{{y}_{1}}=E{I}_{{y}_{1}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x},{M}_{{z}_{1}}=E{I}_{{z}_{1}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{z}}{\partial x} - at point 2: {F}_{{x}_{2}}=E{S}_{2}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x},{M}_{{y}_{2}}=E{I}_{{y}_{2}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x},{M}_{{z}_{2}}=E{I}_{{z}_{2}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{z}}{\partial x} By giving oneself \frac{\partial u}{\partial x},\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x} and \frac{\partial {\theta}_{z}}{\partial x} for a beam, one can assign a loading to it. 9.2 Loading due to gravity OPTION: "CHAR_MECA_PESA_R" The gravity force is given by the magnitude of the acceleration g and a normalised vector indicating the direction n . The principle for distributing the loading over the two nodes of the beam is to take into account the shape functions \xi (x) associated with each degree of freedom of the element [§ 4 ]. We therefore have, for a gravity loading, an equivalent nodal force \overrightarrow{Q} : \overrightarrow{Q}={\int}_{0}^{L}\xi (x)\rho Sg\overrightarrow{n}\text{dx} Notes: The shape functions used are (simplifying assumption) those of the Euler–Bernoulli model. One must, of course, place oneself in the local frame of the beam in order to carry out this computation. Axial force (along x ) : \begin{array}{}{F}_{{x}_{i}}={\int}_{0}^{L}{\xi}_{i}\rho S\text{}g\cdot x\text{dx}\\ ({\xi}_{1}=1-\frac{x}{L},{\xi}_{2}=\frac{x}{L})\end{array} hence: {F}_{{x}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot xL(\frac{{S}_{1}}{3}+\frac{{S}_{2}}{6}) at point 1, {F}_{{x}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot xL(\frac{{S}_{1}}{6}+\frac{{S}_{2}}{3}) at point 2, for a cross-section varying linearly (S={S}_{1}+({S}_{2}-{S}_{1})\frac{x}{L}) and \begin{array}{}{F}_{{x}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot xL(\frac{3{S}_{1}+2\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}+{S}_{2}}{12}),\\ {F}_{{x}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot xL(\frac{{S}_{2}+2\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}+3{S}_{2}}{12})\end{array} for a cross-section varying homothetically (S{\left[\sqrt{{S}_{1}}+(\sqrt{{S}_{2}-\sqrt{{S}_{1}}})\frac{x}{L}\right]}^{2}) Torsional moment: Without taking warping into account, it is non-existent. - In the plane (xoz) : \begin{array}{}{F}_{{z}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot z{\int}_{0}^{L}{\xi}_{1}S\text{dx}\\ {M}_{{y}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot z{\int}_{0}^{L}{\xi}_{2}S\text{dx}\\ {F}_{{z}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot z{\int}_{0}^{L}{\xi}_{3}S\text{dx}\\ {M}_{{y}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot z{\int}_{0}^{L}{\xi}_{4}S\text{dx}\end{array} \begin{array}{}{\xi}_{1}=2{(\frac{x}{L})}^{3}-3{(\frac{x}{L})}^{2}+1,{\xi}_{2}=L\left[-{(\frac{x}{L})}^{3}+2{(\frac{x}{L})}^{2}-\frac{x}{L}\right],\\ {\xi}_{3}=-2{(\frac{x}{L})}^{3}+3{(\frac{x}{L})}^{2},{\xi}_{4}=L\left[-{(\frac{x}{L})}^{3}+{(\frac{x}{L})}^{2}\right]\end{array} hence, for a cross-section varying linearly: \begin{array}{}{F}_{{y}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot yL(\frac{7{S}_{1}}{20}+\frac{3{S}_{2}}{20}),{M}_{{z}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot y{L}^{2}(\frac{{S}_{1}}{20}+\frac{{S}_{2}}{30})\\ {F}_{{y}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot yL(\frac{3{S}_{1}}{20}+\frac{7{S}_{2}}{20}),{M}_{{z}_{2}}=-\rho g\cdot y{L}^{2}(\frac{{S}_{1}}{30}+\frac{{S}_{2}}{20})\end{array} and, for a cross-section varying homothetically: \begin{array}{}{F}_{{z}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot zL(\frac{8{S}_{1}+5\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}+2{S}_{2}}{30}),{M}_{{y}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot z{L}^{2}(\frac{-2{S}_{1}-2\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}-{S}_{2}}{60})\\ {F}_{{z}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot zL(\frac{2{S}_{1}+5\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}+8{S}_{2}}{30}),{M}_{{y}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot z{L}^{2}(\frac{{S}_{1}+2\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}+{\mathrm{2S}}_{2}}{60})\end{array} - In the plane (xoy) : \begin{array}{}{F}_{{y}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot y{\int}_{o}^{L}{\xi}_{1}S\mathrm{dx},{M}_{{z}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot y{\int}_{o}^{L}-{\xi}_{2}S\mathrm{dx}\\ {F}_{{y}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot y{\int}_{o}^{L}{\xi}_{3}S\mathrm{dx},{M}_{{z}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot y{\int}_{o}^{L}-{\xi}_{4}S\mathrm{dx}\end{array} hence, for a cross-section varying linearly: \begin{array}{}{F}_{{y}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot yL(\frac{7{S}_{1}}{20}+\frac{3{S}_{2}}{20}),{M}_{{z}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot y{L}^{2}(\frac{{S}_{1}}{20}+\frac{{S}_{2}}{30})\\ {F}_{{y}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot yL(\frac{3{S}_{1}}{20}+\frac{7{S}_{2}}{20}),{M}_{{z}_{2}}=-\rho g\cdot y{L}^{2}(\frac{{S}_{1}}{30}+\frac{{S}_{2}}{20})\end{array} and, for a cross-section varying homothetically: \begin{array}{}{F}_{{y}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot yL(\frac{8{S}_{1}+5\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}+2{S}_{2}}{30}),{M}_{{z}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot y{L}^{2}(\frac{2{S}_{1}+2\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}+{S}_{2}}{60})\\ {F}_{{y}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot yL(\frac{2{S}_{1}+5\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}+8{S}_{2}}{30}),{M}_{{z}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot y{L}^{2}(\frac{-{S}_{1}-2\sqrt{{S}_{1}{S}_{2}}-2{S}_{2}}{60})\end{array} 9.3 Distributed loadings OPTIONS: "CHAR_MECA_FR1D1D", "CHAR_MECA_FF1D1D", The loadings are given under the keyword FORCE_POUTRE, either by real values in AFFE_CHAR_MECA (option CHAR_MECA_FR1D1D), or by functions in AFFE_CHAR_MECA (option CHAR_MECA_FF1D1D). The various possibilities are: | | constant loading | linearly varying loading | | --- | --- | --- | | straight beam of constant cross-section | developed | developed | | straight beam of linearly varying cross-section | developed | no | | straight beam of homothetically varying cross-section | developed | no | For straight beams of constant cross-section, the distributed loading is composed of forces and of moments which are constant or vary linearly along the axis of the beam. In all the other cases the distributed load is composed solely of a constant force. The method used to compute the loading to be imposed at the nodes is that presented in [§ r3.08.01-VectFextTC ]. 9.3.1 Straight beam of constant cross-section For a constant or linearly varying loading, one obtains: {F}_{{x}_{1}}=L(\frac{{n}_{1}}{3}+\frac{{n}_{2}}{6}),{F}_{{x}_{2}}=L(\frac{{n}_{1}}{6}+\frac{{n}_{2}}{3}),{M}_{{x}_{1}}=L(\frac{{m}_{{t}_{1}}}{3}+\frac{{m}_{{t}_{2}}}{6}),{M}_{{x}_{2}}=L(\frac{{m}_{{t}_{1}}}{6}+\frac{{m}_{{t}_{2}}}{3}) {n}_{1} and {n}_{2} are the components of the axial loading at points 1 and 2, {m}_{{t}_{1}} and {m}_{{t}_{2}} are the components of the torsional moment at points 1 and 2, coming from the user's data placed back into the local frame. {t}_{{y}_{1}} , {t}_{{y}_{2}} , {t}_{{z}_{1}} and {t}_{{z}_{2}} are the components of the shear force, {m}_{{y}_{1}} , {m}_{{y}_{2}} , {m}_{{z}_{1}} and {m}_{{z}_{2}} are the components of the bending moments, at points 1 and 2, coming from the user's data placed back into the local frame. \begin{array}{cc}{F}_{{y}_{1}}=L(\frac{7{t}_{{y}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{3{t}_{{y}_{2}}}{20})-\frac{({m}_{{z}_{1}}+{m}_{{z}_{2}})}{2}& {M}_{{y}_{1}}=-{L}^{2}(\frac{{t}_{{z}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{{t}_{{z}_{2}}}{30})-\frac{({m}_{{y}_{2}}-{m}_{{y}_{1}})L}{12}\\ {F}_{{y}_{2}}=L(\frac{3{t}_{{y}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{7{t}_{{y}_{2}}}{20})+\frac{({m}_{{z}_{1}}+{m}_{{z}_{2}})}{2}& {M}_{{y}_{2}}={L}^{2}(\frac{{t}_{{z}_{1}}}{30}+\frac{{t}_{{z}_{2}}}{20})+\frac{({m}_{{y}_{2}}-{m}_{{y}_{1}})L}{12}\\ {F}_{{z}_{1}}=L(\frac{7{t}_{{z}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{3{t}_{{z}_{2}}}{20})+\frac{({m}_{{y}_{1}}+{m}_{{y}_{2}})}{2}& {M}_{{z}_{1}}={L}^{2}(\frac{{t}_{{y}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{{t}_{{y}_{2}}}{30})-\frac{({m}_{{z}_{2}}-{m}_{{z}_{1}})L}{12}\\ {F}_{{z}_{2}}=L(\frac{3{t}_{{z}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{7{t}_{{z}_{2}}}{20})-\frac{({m}_{{y}_{1}}+{m}_{{y}_{2}})}{2}& {M}_{{z}_{2}}=-{L}^{2}(\frac{{t}_{{y}_{1}}}{30}+\frac{{t}_{{y}_{2}}}{20})+\frac{({m}_{{z}_{2}}-{m}_{{z}_{1}})L}{12}\end{array} 9.3.2 Straight beams of variable cross-section The loading supplied must be constant. One uses a method similar to that used for the self-weight [§ 55 ]. The loading supplied must be constant along the element. The loading reduced to the nodes is equivalent to that which one can obtain by taking up again the results of [§ 9.3.1 ]. With a constant load, this becomes: \begin{array}{cccc}{F}_{{x}_{1}}=L\frac{n}{2}& {F}_{{x}_{2}}=L\frac{n}{2}& {F}_{{y}_{1}}=L\frac{{t}_{y}}{2}& {F}_{{y}_{2}}=L\frac{{t}_{y}}{2}\\ {M}_{{z}_{1}}={L}^{2}\frac{{t}_{y}}{12}& {M}_{{z}_{2}}=-{L}^{2}\frac{{t}_{y}}{12}& {F}_{{z}_{1}}=L\frac{{t}_{z}}{2}& {F}_{{z}_{2}}=L\frac{{t}_{z}}{2}\\ {M}_{{y}_{1}}=-{L}^{2}\frac{{t}_{z}}{12}& {M}_{{y}_{2}}={L}^{2}\frac{{t}_{z}}{12}& & \end{array} 9.4 Thermal loading OPTION: "CHAR_MECA_TEMP_R" In order to obtain this loading, one must compute the strain induced by the temperature difference T-{T}_{\text{référence}} : \begin{array}{}{u}_{1}=-L\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{référence}})\\ {u}_{2}=L\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{référence}})\end{array} ( \alpha : coefficient of thermal expansion) Then, one computes the induced forces: F=Ku . As K is the local stiffness matrix of the element, one must then carry out a change of basis in order to obtain the values of the components of the loading in the global frame. 9.5 Electrical loading OPTIONS: "FORCE_ELEC", "INTE_ELEC". This type of loading makes it possible to take into account the Laplace force acting on a principal conductor, due to the presence of a secondary conductor. The secondary conductor «\mathrm{2 }» is straight and it does not rest on a part of the Aster mesh if one uses the option "FORCE_ELEC". The secondary conductor is not necessarily straight and it may rest on a part of the Aster mesh if one uses the option "INTE_ELEC". The line density of the Laplace force exerted at a point M of the principal conductor by the secondary conductor is written: f(M)=\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1}\wedge {\int}_{2}\frac{{e}_{2}\wedge r}{{\parallel r\parallel }^{3}}\mathrm{ds} with {\parallel {e}_{1}\parallel }^{2}={\parallel {e}_{2}\parallel }^{2}=1 Note: In order to obtain the Laplace force, the vector returned following the computation carried out by one of these two options must be multiplied by the time function of intensity specified by the operator "DEFI_FONC_ELEC" .[U4.MK.10] 9.5.1 Finite or infinite straight secondary conductor OPTION: "FORCE_ELEC" U4.44.01 For a finite secondary conductor, we have: \overrightarrow{f}(M)=\frac{{e}_{1}}{2}\wedge \frac{n}{d}(\sin{\alpha}_{1}-\sin{\alpha}_{2}) with \begin{array}{}n=\frac{{e}_{2}\wedge d}{d}\\ d=∥d∥\end{array} For an infinite secondary conductor, we have: f(M)={e}_{1}\wedge \frac{n}{d} Three types of loading are possible: - infinite parallel straight conductor, - multiple infinite parallel straight conductors, - straight conductor in an arbitrary position, finite or infinite. For the case of an infinite parallel straight conductor, its position may be given in two ways: - either by a translation vector from the principal conductor to the secondary conductor, - or by the distance between the two conductors and by a point of the secondary conductor. One therefore obtains a loading which is constant over the whole principal element. One can thus use the technique presented in [§ 9.3 ] [§ 9.4 ] in order to compute the loading at the nodes. \begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{F}}_{1}=\mathrm{f}(M)\frac{L}{2},{\mathrm{F}}_{2}=\mathrm{f}(M)\frac{L}{2},{\mathrm{M}}_{1}={\mathrm{e}}_{1}\wedge \mathrm{f}(M)\frac{{L}^{2}}{12},{\mathrm{M}}_{2}=-{\mathrm{e}}_{1}\wedge \mathrm{f}(M)\frac{{L}^{2}}{12}\\ \mathrm{f}(M)=\mathit{cste}\forall M\end{array} For the case of multiple infinite parallel straight conductors , one must give directly the normalised "Laplace force" vector. This vector being usually given in the global frame, one must determine the "Laplace force" vector in the local frame of the principal element. Thus, in the same manner as previously, one computes the loading at the nodes. For the case of a straight conductor in an arbitrary position, finite or infinite , its position is given by two points {P}_{1} and {P}_{2} such that the current flows from {P}_{1} towards {P}_{2} . The loading is not necessarily constant along the principal element. The method chosen for computing the loading reduced to the nodes is of course the same as before. But here, the integration is done numerically by discretising the element into a certain number (in practice: 100 points between {P}_{1} and {P}_{2} ). One thus integrates: \begin{array}{}{F}_{1}={\int}_{0}^{L}f(M)\text{}\left[2{(\frac{x}{L})}^{3}-3{(\frac{x}{L})}^{2}+1\right]\text{dx}\\ {F}_{2}={\int}_{0}^{L}f(M)\text{}\left[-2{(\frac{x}{L})}^{3}+3{(\frac{x}{L})}^{2}\right]\text{dx}\end{array} \begin{array}{}{\overrightarrow{M}}_{1}={\int}_{0}^{L}-{\overrightarrow{e}}_{1}\wedge \overrightarrow{f}(M)\left[L(-{(\frac{x}{L})}^{3}+2{(\frac{x}{L})}^{2}-\frac{x}{L})\right]\text{dx}\\ {\overrightarrow{M}}_{2}={\int}_{0}^{L}-{\overrightarrow{e}}_{1}\wedge \overrightarrow{f}(M)\left[L(-{(\frac{x}{L})}^{3}+{(\frac{x}{L})}^{2})\right]\text{dx}\end{array} Note : As f(M)\cdot x=0 and ({e}_{1}\wedge f(M))\cdot x=0,(x={e}_{1}) one uses only the shape functions associated with the bending problem. 9.5.2 Secondary conductor described by part of an ASTER mesh OPTION: "INTE_ELEC", U4.44.01 The secondary conductor as a whole is not necessarily straight. But it is described solely by straight elements. Its length is necessarily finite. Its position may be completed by the use of a translation vector or of a plane symmetry (by a point and a normalised normal vector of the plane of symmetry) with respect to the principal conductor. Apart from the fact that one must sum the interaction of the various elements of the secondary conductor on the principal conductor, the method is the same as previously (case (\mathrm{iii}) ). Note: For the numerical integration, one uses 5 points lying between {P}_{1} and {P}_{2} . 10 Wrench of the forces - Wrench of the stresses (or generalised forces) - Nodal forces and reactions - OPTIONS: "EFGE_ELNO", "SIEF_ELGA", Wrench of the forces "SIPM_ELNO", "SIPO_ELNO", Stress tensor "FORC_NODA", "REAC_NODA". Nodal forces and reactions ◦ The option EFGE_ELNO makes it possible to compute the wrench of the forces at the 2 nodes of each beam element. ◦ The options SIPM_ELNO and SIPO_ELNO make it possible to compute the maximum values of the components of the stress tensor intervening in a beam model. ◦ The option SIEF_ELGA allows the computation of the nodal forces (option FORC_NODA and of the reactions REAC_NODA). Note: When one of these options ends in "_C", this means that the values of the displacements and of the forces are complex. 10.1 The wrench of the forces - OPTION: "EFGE_ELNO" One seeks to compute, at the two nodes of each “beam” element constituting the mesh of the structure under study, the forces exerted on the “beam” element by the rest of the structure. The values are given in the local basis of each element. By integrating the equilibrium equations, one obtains [§ r3.08.01-EffortNoeudTC ] the forces in the local frame of the element: {R}_{\text{LOC}}={K}_{\text{LOC}}^{e}{u}_{\text{LOC}}+{M}_{\text{LOC}}^{e}{\ddot{u}}_{\text{LOC}}-{f}_{\text{LOC}}^{e} where: {R}_{\text{LOC}}=(-{N}^{1},-{V}_{Y}^{1},-{V}_{Z}^{1},-{M}_{T}^{1},-{M}_{Y}^{1},-{M}_{Z}^{1},{N}^{2},{V}_{Y}^{2},{V}_{Z}^{2},{M}_{T}^{2},{M}_{Y}^{2},{M}_{Z}^{2}) | {K}_{\text{LOC}}^{e} | elementary stiffness matrix of the “exact” beam element, | | --- | --- | | {M}_{\text{LOC}}^{e} | elementary mass matrix of the beam element, | | {f}_{\text{LOC}}^{e} | vector of the “distributed” forces on the beam element, | | {u}_{\text{LOC}} | “degree of freedom” vector restricted to the beam element, | | {\ddot{u}}_{\text{LOC}} | “acceleration” vector restricted to the beam element. | One then changes the signs of the forces at node 1 [§ r3.08.01-EffortNoeudTC ]. - OPTION: "SIEF_ELGA" The option "SIEF_ELGA" is implemented for reasons of compatibility with other options. It serves only for the computation of the nodal forces and of the reactions. It is computed by: {R}_{\text{LOC}}={K}_{\text{LOC}}^{e}{u}_{\text{LOC}} . 10.2 The stress tensor - OPTIONS: “SIPM_ELNO”, “SIPO_ELNO”. One seeks to compute the maximum values of the components {\sigma}_{xx},{\sigma}_{xy} and {\sigma}_{xz} which are related to the forces by: \begin{array}{}N={\int}_{s}{\sigma}_{xx}\text{dS},\\ {V}_{y}={\int}_{s}{\sigma}_{xy}\text{dS},\\ {V}_{z}={\int}_{s}{\sigma}_{xz}\text{dS},\\ {M}_{T}={\int}_{s}(y{\sigma}_{xz}-z{\sigma}_{xy})\text{}\text{dS},\\ {M}_{y}={\int}_{s}z{\sigma}_{xx}\text{dS},\\ {M}_{z}={\int}_{s}-y{\sigma}_{xx}\text{dS}.\end{array} With the option "SIPM_ELNO", one computes the minimum and the maximum of the stress {\sigma}_{xx}\text{} over the cross-section. ◦ For a rectangular cross-section: \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{xx}^{{i}^{\mathit{Max}}}=\frac{{N}^{i}}{{A}^{i}}+(∣\frac{{M}_{Y}^{i}}{{I}_{Y}^{i}}\frac{{H}_{Z}^{i}}{2}∣+∣\frac{{M}_{Z}^{i}}{{I}_{Z}^{i}}\frac{{H}_{Z}^{i}}{2}∣)\\ {\sigma}_{xx}^{{i}^{\mathit{Min}}}=\frac{{N}^{i}}{{A}^{i}}-(∣\frac{{M}_{Y}^{i}}{{I}_{Y}^{i}}\frac{{H}_{Z}^{i}}{2}∣+∣\frac{{M}_{Z}^{i}}{{I}_{Z}^{i}}\frac{{H}_{Z}^{i}}{2}∣)\end{array} with {I}_{\gamma},{I}_{Z} : geometric moments of inertia with {H}_{\Gamma},{H}_{Z} : sides of the rectangle ◦ For a circular cross-section: \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{xx}^{{i}^{\mathit{Max}}}=\frac{{N}^{i}}{{A}^{i}}+(\sqrt{{({M}_{Y}^{i})}^{2}+{({M}_{Z}^{i})}^{2}}\frac{{R}^{i}}{{I}_{Y}^{i}})\\ {\sigma}_{xx}^{{i}^{\mathit{Min}}}=\frac{{N}^{i}}{{A}^{i}}-(\sqrt{{({M}_{Y}^{i})}^{2}+{({M}_{Z}^{i})}^{2}}\frac{{R}^{i}}{{I}_{Y}^{i}})\end{array} with R : radius of the cross-section ◦ For a general cross-section, an alarm message is issued in order to state that one does not know how to do so in this case. In order to recover these formulae, one uses the relations between the stresses and the strains and then those between the internal forces and (u,x;{\gamma}_{xy};{\gamma}_{xz};{\theta}_{x,x};{\theta}_{y,x};{\theta}_{z,x}) \begin{array}{}\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{xx}=E{\varepsilon}_{xx}\\ {\sigma}_{xy}=2G{\varepsilon}_{xy}\\ {\sigma}_{xz}=2G{\varepsilon}_{xz},\end{array}\\ \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\varepsilon}_{xx}=u,x+z{\theta}_{y,x}-y{\theta}_{z,x}\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{xy}={\gamma}_{xy}-z{\theta}_{x,x}\text{}({\gamma}_{xy}={V}_{,x}-{\theta}_{z})\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{xy}={\gamma}_{xz}+y{\theta}_{x,x}\text{}({\gamma}_{xz}={W}_{,x}+{\theta}_{y}),\end{array}\end{array} (\begin{array}{c}N\\ {V}_{Y}\\ {V}_{Z}\\ {M}_{T}\\ {M}_{Y}\\ {M}_{Z}\end{array})=(\begin{array}{cccccc}\text{EA}& & & & & \\ & {k}_{Y}\text{GA}& & 0& & \\ & & {k}_{Z}\text{GA}& & & \\ & & & \text{GJ}& & \\ & 0& & & {\text{EI}}_{Y}& \\ & & & & & {\text{EI}}_{Z}\end{array})(\begin{array}{c}u,x\\ {\gamma}_{xy}\\ {\gamma}_{xz}\\ {\theta}_{x,x}\\ {\theta}_{y,x}\\ {\theta}_{z,x}\end{array}) (The various types of motion are decoupled when one works with the principal axes (by definition)). One obtains: \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{xx}(x,y,z)=E\left[\frac{N}{\text{EA}}+z\frac{{M}_{Y}}{{\text{EI}}_{Y}}-y\frac{{M}_{Z}}{{\text{EI}}_{Z}}\right],\\ {\sigma}_{xy}(x,y,z)=G\left[\frac{{V}_{Y}}{{k}_{Y}\text{GA}}-z\frac{{M}_{T}}{G{J}_{X}}\right],\\ {\sigma}_{xz}(x,y,z)=G\left[\frac{{V}_{Z}}{{k}_{Z}\text{GA}}+y\frac{{M}_{T}}{G{J}_{X}}\right]\end{array} With the option “SIPO_ELNO”, the computation is somewhat different. One seeks the maximum effects of each force (N,{V}_{Y},{V}_{Z},{M}_{T},{M}_{X},{M}_{Y}) on the components {\sigma}_{xx} , {\sigma}_{xy} and {\sigma}_{xz} . One recovers the previous results in decomposed form. The result vector is written: \begin{array}{}({\sigma}_{{1}^{1}},{\sigma}_{{2}^{1}},{\sigma}_{{3}^{1}},{\sigma}_{{4}^{1}},{\sigma}_{{5}^{1}},{\sigma}_{{6}^{1}}\\ {\sigma}_{{1}^{2}},{\sigma}_{{2}^{2}},{\sigma}_{{3}^{2}},{\sigma}_{{4}^{2}},{\sigma}_{{5}^{2}},{\sigma}_{{6}^{2}})\end{array} with {\sigma}_{{1}^{i}}=\frac{{N}^{i}}{{A}^{i}} for the node i , (i=1,2) \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{{1}^{i}}=\frac{{N}^{i}}{{A}^{i}}\\ {\sigma}_{{3}^{i}}=\frac{{V}_{{Z}^{i}}}{{A}_{{Z}^{i}}},\\ {\sigma}_{{4}^{i}}=\frac{{M}_{{T}^{i}}}{{J}_{{X}^{i}}}{R}_{{T}^{i}},\end{array} for the rectangular cross-sections: \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{{5}^{i}}=\frac{{M}_{{Y}^{i}}}{{I}_{{Y}^{i}}}\frac{{H}_{{Z}^{i}}}{2},\\ {\sigma}_{{6}^{i}}=-\frac{{M}_{{Z}^{i}}}{{I}_{{Z}^{i}}}\frac{{H}_{{Y}^{i}}}{2},\end{array} \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{{5}^{i}}=\frac{{M}_{{Y}^{i}}}{{I}_{{Y}^{i}}}{R}^{i},\\ {\sigma}_{{6}^{i}}=-\frac{{M}_{{Z}^{i}}}{{I}_{{Y}^{i}}}{R}^{i},\end{array} for arbitrary cross-sections at the point ({R}_{{\Gamma}^{i}},{R}_{{Z}^{i}}) : \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{{5}^{i}}=\frac{{M}_{{Y}^{i}}}{{I}_{{Y}^{i}}}{R}_{{Z}^{i}},\\ {\sigma}_{{6}^{i}}=-\frac{{M}_{{Z}^{i}}}{{I}_{{Z}^{i}}}{R}_{{Y}^{i}}\end{array} In the case of a beam of hollow circular cross-section , the flexibility of thin shells is not taken into account; it may be necessary to correct certain quantities (grandeur) in order to take into account the ovalisation of the cross-section. Two coefficients are used for this: - a flexibility coefficient \text{cflex} (also used by the stiffness), which is applied to the inertias, - a stress-intensification coefficient \text{isigm} which is applied to the stresses. The correction coefficients are to be supplied under the keyword: POUTRE/SECTION=COUDE of the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM. It produces a field at the nodes in the command CALC_CHAMP by assembly of the elementary terms. For this computation, one usually uses in 3D R5.03.01, for example, the principle of virtual work and one writes: F={Q}^{T}\sigma where {Q}^{T} symbolically represents the matrix associated with the divergence operator. For an element, one writes the work of the virtual strain field: ({Q}^{T}\sigma )h={\int}_{\Omega}\sigma (u)\varepsilon (\mathrm{wh}) For the beam elements, one simply computes the nodal forces by assembly of the elementary nodal forces computed by the option SIEF_ELGA, which are expressed by: \left[{F}_{\text{LOC}}\right]=\left[{K}_{\text{LOC}}\right]\left[{U}_{\text{LOC}}\right][\text{§7}.1] - OPTION: “REAC_NODA” This option, called by CALC_CHAMP, makes it possible to obtain the reactions R at the supports from the nodal forces F by: R=F-{F}^{\text{char}}+{F}^{\text{iner}} {F}^{\text{char}}\text{et}{F}^{\text{iner}} being the nodal forces associated with the given loadings (point and distributed) and with the inertia forces. 11 Bar element Keyword ’BARRE’ A bar is a straight beam of constant cross-section comprising only the tension-compression degrees of freedom. r3.08.02 Modelling of cables r3.08.02 Modelling of cables Summary: Cables are flexible structures which can undergo large displacements. Their analysis is therefore non-linear. From the mechanical point of view, a cable can support no moment and is the seat only of a normal force called tension. The expression of the virtual work and its differentiation with respect to the displacements lead to the finite-element modelling: a stiffness matrix depending on the displacement of the nodes and a constant mass matrix. The static and dynamic iterative algorithms are presented. Two examples are given: one, static, is the search for the equilibrium shape of a cable subjected to a given horizontal tension; the other, dynamic, is the comparison between finite-element analyses and the results of short-circuit tests. Finally four annexes deal with: the calculation of the Laplace forces, the evolution of the temperature of a cable subjected to the Joule effect, the force exerted by the wind and the modelling of the stringing operation. 1 Notation | A | area of the straight cross-section of the cable. | | --- | --- | | B | strain matrix. | | {C}_{v} | volumetric heat capacity of the conducting metal. | | E |
