\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial {s}_{o}}1\right] | diagonal matrix \left[\frac{\partial}{{\text{ds}}_{o}},\frac{\partial}{{\text{ds}}_{o}},\frac{\partial}{{\text{ds}}_{o}}\right] . | 2 Introduction The essential characteristic of cables is that they are flexible structures , whose mechanical analysis is non-linear because they are liable to undergo large displacements . They undergo them during the stringing operation, when one adjusts sags in order to comply with environmental constraints. Subsequently, the cables may be set in large-amplitude motions under the impulse of the pressure of the wind , of the fall of ice sleeves , or, in the event of an incident, of the Laplace forces resulting from short-circuit currents. They then exert on their supports forces much higher than the static forces. This must be taken into account in the design of the structures. For the old structures, which may be subjected to increased short-circuit intensities because of the extension of the network, it must be verified that reliability is still ensured. 3 Mechanical assumptions Cables are considered as perfectly flexible wires, which can support no moment, neither bending nor torsional, and are the seat only of a normal tension. This tension plays the role of a generalised stress. One wishes to calculate the displacement field u({s}_{o},t) at the time instant t with respect to the reference configuration. The latter is a static configuration of the cable subjected, for example, to gravity and to the temperature {T}_{o} ; it is defined by the field of position vectors x({s}_{o}) . Figure 1: Segment of cable in the reference and displaced configurations As [bib1], one takes for the strain the Green measure of the relative elongation with respect to the reference configuration [Figure]: . g=\frac{{\text{ds}}^{2}-{\text{ds}}_{o}^{2}}{2{\text{ds}}_{o}^{2}} g must remain small . The right-hand side lends itself to calculation because it contains only squares of elementary lengths. One sees in the [Figure] that: > g=\frac{\partial x}{\partial {s}_{o}}.\frac{\partial u}{\partial {s}_{o}}+\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{\partial u}{\partial {s}_{o}})}^{2} [1] The constitutive relation is: > N={E}_{a}A\left[g-\alpha (T-{T}_{o})\right] [2] with: {E}_{a}=\lbrace \begin{array}{c}E\text{si}N>0\\ {E}_{c}\text{si}N\le 0\end{array} 4 Application of the Principle of Virtual Work If one does not take damping into account, the virtual work of the set of forces applied to a segment of cable during the virtual displacement \delta u is: > W(u,\delta u)={W}_{int}(u,\delta u)-{W}_{\text{iner}}(\ddot{u},\delta u)-{W}_{\text{ext}}(u,\delta u) [3] distinguishing the works of the internal forces, of the inertia forces and of the external forces. According to [eq]: > {W}_{int}(u,\delta u)={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}(N.\delta g)\mathrm{ds}={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}\left\lbrace N.\left[\frac{\partial (x+u)}{\partial {s}_{o}}.\frac{\partial \delta u}{\partial {s}_{o}}\right]\right\rbrace \mathrm{ds}={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}(N.B\delta u)\text{ds} [4] where: > B={\left\lbrace \left\frac{\partial}{\partial {s}_{o}}1\right\right\rbrace }^{T}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial {s}_{o}}1\right] [5] denoting by the upper index T the transpose of a matrix. > {W}_{\text{iner}}(\ddot{u},\delta u)=-{\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}(\rho A\ddot{u}.\delta u)\mathrm{ds} [6] In all cases, we consider the work {W}_{\text{ext}} as independent of u during a time step, because: - either it really is, in the case of conservative forces such as gravity; - or, in the case of the Laplace forces, the force applied to a cable element depends not only on the displacement of that element (classical follower force), but also on the displacements of the set of cables. One then considers that, during a time step, the force is constant and equal to its value at the end of the preceding time step. 5 Linearisation At equilibrium: > W(u,\delta u)=0 [7] If, to within a tolerance, the preceding equation is not satisfied, one seeks a correction \Delta u of u such that: W(u,\delta u)+\text{DW}(u,\delta u).\Delta u=0 \text{DW}(u,\delta u).\Delta u being the directional derivative of \text{W}(u,\delta u) in the direction \Delta u [bib] and [bib]. According to [eq], one obviously has: \text{DN}.\Delta u={E}_{a}A\mathrm{Dg}.\Delta u={E}_{a}AB.\Delta u According to [eq]: DB.\Delta u={(\left[\frac{d}{{\text{ds}}_{o}}1\right]\Delta u)}^{T}\left[\frac{d}{{\text{ds}}_{o}}1\right] . Therefore: > \begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{DW}}_{int}(u,\delta u).\Delta u={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}\left\lbrace {(B\delta u)}^{T}{E}_{a}AB\Delta u\right\rbrace \text{ds}\\ +{\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}\left\lbrace {(\left[\frac{d}{{\text{ds}}_{o}}1\right]\delta u)}^{T}N\left[\frac{d}{{\text{ds}}_{o}}1\right]\Delta u\right\rbrace \text{ds}\end{array} [8] According to [eq]: > {\mathrm{DW}}_{\text{iner}}(\ddot{u},\delta u).\Delta u=-{\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}(\delta {u}^{T}\rho A\Delta \ddot{u})\text{ds} [9] 6 Numerical implementation by finite elements One denotes by the lower index h the matrices discretised into finite elements. If v is a vector defined on the cable (position, displacement, acceleration, …) one has at the current point of a finite element of nodes i,j,\dots : v=\left[L\right]{v}_{e} {v}_{e} being the vector made up of the components of v at the nodes. Likewise: {\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial {s}_{o}}1\right]}_{h}v=\left[L'\right]{v}_{e}. According to [eq]: {B}_{h}={(x+u)}_{e}^{T}L{'}^{T}.L' The internal forces {F}_{int}^{e} of a structural finite element e are the forces which must be exerted at its nodes in order to hold it in its current deformed configuration. According to the theorem of virtual work for continuous media, the work of these point forces is equal to the work of the stresses in the element, that is to {W}_{int} , for every virtual displacement field. One therefore has, according to [eq]: {F}_{int}^{e}={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}N{B}_{h}^{T}\text{ds}={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}NL{'}^{T}L'\mathrm{ds}{(x+u)}_{e} . On the other hand, one replaces the inertia forces distributed in the element by point forces at the nodes {F}_{\text{iner}}^{e} such that their work is equal to that of the real inertia forces for every virtual displacement field. According to [eq], one therefore has: {F}_{\text{iner}}^{e}=-{\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}{L}^{T}\rho AL\mathrm{ds}.\ddot{{u}_{e}} Likewise, the distributed external forces are replaced by concentrated nodal forces {F}_{\text{ext}}^{e} equivalent in the sense of virtual work. The differential of the virtual work of the internal forces of a cable finite element is written, according to [eq]: , {D}_{h}{W}_{int}(u,\delta u).\Delta u={(\delta {u}_{e})}^{T}({K}_{M}+{K}_{G})\Delta {u}_{e} with: \begin{array}{c}{K}_{M}={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}{B}_{h}^{T}{E}_{a}A{B}_{h}\text{ds}\\ {K}_{G}={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}L{'}^{T}NL'\text{ds}\end{array} {K}_{M} and {K}_{G} are called the material and geometric stiffness matrices of the element. ({K}_{M}+{K}_{G})\Delta {u}_{e} is the principal part of the variation \Delta {F}_{int} of the internal forces at the nodes due to the displacement correction \Delta {u}_{e} . The differential of the virtual work of the inertia forces is deduced from [eq]: {D}_{h}{W}_{\text{iner}}(\ddot{u},\delta u).\Delta u=-{(\delta {u}_{e})}^{T}M\Delta {\ddot{u}}_{e} with: M={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}{L}^{T}\rho AL\text{ds} M is the mass matrix of the element. -M\Delta {\ddot{u}}_{e} is the variation \Delta {F}_{\text{iner}} of the inertia forces at the nodes due to the acceleration correction \Delta {\ddot{u}}_{e} . 7 Particular case of the two-node cable elements These elements are of the 1st degree: they are therefore straight in the reference position and remain straight in the deformed position. No moment is applied at their ends and they are the seat only of a uniaxial stress. They are therefore bar elements . In other words: modelling a cable by two-node elements amounts to assimilating it to a chain whose links (the cable elements) would be perfectly articulated with one another. By contrast, the cable elements having more than two nodes generally exhibit a curvature which varies with the strain. One therefore cannot treat them as bar elements. 8 Use in Code_Aster This paragraph indicates how one introduces the cables into the commands concerned of Code_Aster . | Command | Factor keyword | Keyword | Argument | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | AFFE_MODELE | AFFE | GROUP_MA | Name of the mesh-cell group supporting a cable. | | | | PHENOMENE | 'MECANIQUE'. | | | | MODELISATION | 'CABLE'. | | DEFI_MATERIAU | CABLE | E | Value of the modulus of the material. | | | | EC_SUR_E | Ratio of the compression modulus (very small and possibly zero) to the modulus. | | AFFE_CARA_ELEM | CABLE | GROUP_MA | Name of the mesh-cell group supporting a cable. | | | | SECTION | Value of the cross-section of the cable. | | | | N_INIT | Initial tension in the cable | | STAT_NON_LINE | COMPORTEMENT | GROUP_MA | Name of the mesh-cell group supporting a cable. | | | | RELATION | 'CABLE' | | | | DEFORMATION | 'GROT_GDEP' | 9 Static problem This problem is that of the search for the equilibrium of a structure of cables in an arbitrary position and subjected to a system of given forces. 9.1 Iterative algorithm The equilibrium equation, discretised form of [eq] and [eq] without the inertia term, which must be satisfied at each node, is: > {F}_{int}={F}_{\text{ext}} [10] Suppose that one has just calculated the displacement field of the cables, {u}^{n}({s}_{o}) , at iteration n : - if this field makes it possible to satisfy, to within a tolerance, [eq 9.1-1], one considers that the line: x({s}_{o})+{u}^{n}({s}_{o}) is the equilibrium shape of the cables; - otherwise, one calculates displacement corrections \Delta {u}^{n+1} by the linearised system: \left[{K}_{M}^{n}+{K}_{G}^{n}\right]\Delta {u}^{n+1}={F}_{\text{ext}}-{F}_{int}^{n} One uses for this the quasi-static non-linear algorithm described in R5.03.01, and which corresponds to the command STAT_NON_LINE. The displacement at iteration (n+1) is: {u}^{n+1}={u}^{n}+\Delta {u}^{n+1} One checks whether [eq] is satisfied by the field {u}^{n+1} and so on. 9.2 Example One wishes to calculate the equilibrium shape of a heavy cable [fig 9.2-a] one end A of which is fixed and the other, B level with A , is subjected to a given horizontal force. This problem is treated in [bib], where it is considered as highly non-linear. Extensional stiffness (E.A): 4.45 x 105 N, Weight per unit length: 1.46 N/m Figure 2: Equilibrium of a heavy cable subjected to a horizontal tension Initially, the cable, modelled by 10 elements of the 1st degree, is assumed weightless and has a straight horizontal position {\mathrm{AB}}_{o} . It is subjected simultaneously to the action of gravity and to the horizontal force F applied at {B}_{o} . The static equilibrium position \mathrm{ACB} is reached in 8 iterations only. 10 Dynamic problem This problem is that of the calculation of the evolution of a structure of cables. 10.1 Iterative algorithm of time integration The complete discretised form of [eq] and [eq], which must be satisfied at each node and at each time instant, is: > {F}_{int}(t)-{F}_{\text{iner}}(t)={F}_{\text{ext}}(t) [11] The time-integration algorithm is of Newmark type [bib] and [bib]. Suppose that the state of the cable (fields u,\dot{u}\mathrm{et}\ddot{u} at the nodes) is known at the time instant t and that one has just calculated an approximate value of these fields at the nth iteration of the time instant t+\Delta t . - If these values satisfy [eq], to within a tolerance, one takes them as the values of the fields at the time instant t+\Delta t . - Otherwise, one seeks the displacement correction \Delta {u}^{n+1} , to which correspond, according to the Newmark algorithm, the corrections of velocity and of acceleration: \Delta {\dot{u}}^{n+1}=\frac{\gamma}{\beta \Delta t}\Delta {u}^{n+1} and \Delta {\ddot{u}}^{n+1}=\frac{1}{\beta \Delta {t}^{2}}\Delta {u}^{n+1} such that: \left[{K}_{M}^{n}+{K}_{G}^{n}+\frac{1}{\beta \Delta {t}^{2}}M\right]\Delta {u}^{n+1}={F}_{\text{ext}}(t+\Delta t)-{F}_{int}^{n}(t+\Delta t)+{F}_{\text{iner}}^{n}(t+\Delta t) In the analysis of the motion of the cables, the Newmark algorithm may be unstable. This is why we use the so-called HHT algorithm, defined in [bib5, bib7], in which the two Newmark parameters are functions of a third parameter \alpha : \begin{array}{c}\gamma =\frac{1}{2}-\alpha \\ \beta =\frac{{(1-\alpha )}^{2}}{4}\\ \alpha \le 0\end{array} For \alpha =0 , the algorithm is that of Newmark, called the "trapezoidal rule". But for \alpha slightly negative, in practice: \alpha \ge -0.3 , numerical damping appears which stabilises the calculation. The determination of the initial acceleration and the initialisation of the fields at the beginning of a new time step are indicated in [bib]. 10.2 Comparison of calculations and of short-circuit tests In order to validate this modelling of the cables, we have compared dynamic calculations by Code_Aster with results of short-circuit tests [bib8]. These were carried out at the Laboratoire de Génie Electrique of EDF on an experimental structure representative of substation configurations [Figure]. Three cables tensioned between two gantries \mathrm{102 }m apart are short-circuited, in the foreground, by a shunt placed on insulating columns. At the level of the other gantry, they are supplied by a three-phase current of 35\mathrm{kA} for \mathrm{250 }\mathrm{ms} . One recorded the evolution: - of the tension of the cables at their anchorage on the gantries, by means of dynamometers; - of the displacement of the mid-points of the spans, marked by marker spheres, by means of high-speed cameras. One sees the glass cage of one of these cameras mounted on a gantry, on the left of [Figure]. Figure 3: General view of the short-circuit test installation The [Figure] gives the comparison for an anchorage tension and for the displacement of the middle of a cable. Figure 4: Comparisons of calculations by Code_Aster and of short-circuit tests 11 Conclusion The modelling of the cables presented above is efficient (reasonable number of iterations per time step or in order to reach a static equilibrium) and accurate: it is suited to the analysis of long cables. For short cables, by contrast, the flexural stiffness is not negligible, especially at the anchorages, and the modelling must be done by beam elements in large displacements and large rotations R5.03.40. 12 Bibliography [1] J.L. This magnetic field, acting on the current conveyed by another conductor, induces on the latter a force called the Laplace force. Figure 5: Arrangement of two neighbouring conductors Take a conductor (1) carrying the current {i}_{1}(t) [Figure A1-a], located in the neighbourhood of the conductor (2) carrying the current {i}_{2}(t) . At the point P of the conductor (1) , where the unit tangent oriented in the direction of the current is {e}_{1} , the linear Laplace force induced by the conductor (2) is: f(P)={10}^{-7}{i}_{1}(t){i}_{2}(t){e}_{1}\times {\int}_{{\Gamma}_{2}}^{}{e}_{2}\times \frac{r}{{r}^{3}}{\mathrm{ds}}_{2} One is interested only in the forces due to the very intense short-circuit currents, the Laplace forces in normal operation being negligible. f(P) can obviously be put in the form of the product of a function of time by a function of space. A1.1 Time function of the Laplace forces This function g(t) , is, to within a factor, the product of the intensities in the conductors (1) and (2) : > g(t)=2.{10}^{-7}{i}_{1}(t){i}_{2}(t) [12] where: > {i}_{j}(t)=\sqrt{2}{I}_{\text{ej}}\left[\cos(\omega t+{\varphi}_{j})-{e}^{-t/\tau }\cos{\varphi}_{j}\right] [13] with: | {I}_{\text{ej}} : | r.m.s. intensity of the current j; | | --- | --- | | \omega : | angular frequency of the current ( \omega =100\pi for a current of 50 Hz); | | {\varphi}_{j} : | phase depending on the time instant at which the short circuit occurs; | | \tau : | time constant of the short-circuited line depending on its electrical characteristics (inductance, capacitance and resistance). | Very often, one replaces the complete function g(t) [eq] and [eq] by its mean — which one calls the continuous part — neglecting the terms \cos(\omega t+\mathrm{...}) and \cos(2\omega t+\mathrm{...}) . Taking these terms into account would require a very small time step and the corresponding forces, at 50\mathrm{Hz} and \mathrm{100 }\mathrm{Hz} , have practically no effect on the cables whose oscillation frequency is of the order of one hertz. Therefore: {g}_{\text{continue}}(t)=2{I}_{\mathrm{e1}}{I}_{\mathrm{e2}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\cos({\varphi}_{1}-{\varphi}_{2})+{e}^{-(\frac{t}{{\tau}_{1}}+\frac{t}{{\tau}_{2}})}\cos{\varphi}_{1}\cos{\varphi}_{2}\right] A1.2 Space function This function is: h(P)=\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1}\times \int{e}_{2}\times \frac{r}{{r}^{3}}{\mathrm{ds}}_{2} The integral is calculated analytically when one divides the conductor {\Gamma}_{2} into straight elements. Along such an element {M}_{1}{M}_{2} [Figure A1.2-a], one has an effect: \begin{array}{}{r}^{3}={({y}^{2}+{r}_{m}^{2})}^{}\\ {e}_{2}\times r={e}_{2}\times {r}_{m}\\ {\mathrm{ds}}_{2}=\text{dy}\end{array} Figure 6: Laplace force induced by a straight element of conductor As: {\int}_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}\frac{\text{dy}}{{({y}^{2}+{r}_{m}^{2})}^{}}=\frac{1}{{r}_{m}^{2}}{\left[\frac{y}{{({y}^{2}+{r}_{m}^{2})}^{}}\right]}_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}} one has: \frac{1}{2}{e}_{1}\times {\int}_{{M}_{1}}^{{M}_{2}}{e}_{2}\times \frac{r}{{r}^{3}}\mathrm{dy}=\frac{1}{2{r}_{m}^{2}}{e}_{1}\times {e}_{2}\times {r}_{m}{\left[\frac{y}{{({y}^{2}+{r}_{m}^{2})}^{}}\right]}_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}} The bracket of the right-hand side is also equal to: \sin{\alpha}_{2}-\sin{\alpha}_{1} . A1.3 Implementation in Code_Aster The space function h(P) defined previously is calculated by an elementary routine which evaluates, for each of the elements of the conductor (1) , the contribution of all the elements of the conductor (2) which act on it. This contribution is evaluated at the Gauss points (1 only for the elements with 2 nodes) of the element of the conductor, (1) by the keyword INTE_ELEC of the command AFFE_CHAR_MECA. The elementary routine has 2 input parameters: - the loading map of the element of the conductor (1) comprising the list of the mesh cells of the conductor (2) acting on it; - the name of the geometry, variable in the course of time, which makes it possible at each time instant to evaluate the quantities {r}_{m},\sin{\alpha}_{1},\sin{\alpha}_{2} . The time function g(t) is calculated by the operator DEFI_FONC_ELEC which produces a concept of type fonction. Figure 7: wind velocity in the neighbourhood of a cable The regulations for the calculation of lines define the force of a wind by the pressure p which it exerts on a plane surface normal to its direction. For a cable, placed normally to the direction of the wind, these regulations prescribe taking for the linear force: {f}_{\frac{\pi}{2}}=p\mathrm{\varnothing } , \varnothing being the diameter of the cable. This amounts to considering that the cable presents to the wind a plane surface equal to its projected frontal area. One thus obtains an overestimate of the force because the cable, being cylindrical, presents a lower resistance to the air than a plane surface. If the velocity V of the wind makes an angle \theta with the cable, its component in the plane perpendicular to the cable has for modulus: \parallel {V}_{n}\parallel =\parallel V\parallel .\mid \sin\theta \mid . Therefore, the linear force is: {f}_{\theta}=p\mathrm{\varnothing }{\sin}^{2}\theta . Of course, the linear force exerted by the wind depends on the position of the cable: it is a "follower" force. It rests on pulleys placed at the bottom of the alignment insulators and it is retained by a force at the level of the second anchor support. Figure 8: Stringing of a cable in a section with two spans By acting on this force — or by moving its point of application — one adjusts the sag of one of the spans, the one which is the most subject to environmental constraints. Then one removes the pulleys and one fixes the cable to the insulators: the length of the cable in the various spans is then fixed. r3.08.03 Computation of the characteristics of a beam of arbitrary cross-section r3.08.03 Computation of the characteristics of a beam of arbitrary cross-section Summary: The principle of the computation of the various characteristic quantities of beam sections is presented. These are established from the geometric characteristics of the cross-section of the beam. These values are to be supplied to the operand SECTION:’GENERALE’ of the operator AFFE_CARA_ELEM U4.42.01. In order to determine them, numerical methods are presented, and implemented in the command MACR_CARA_POUTRE. In the case of the sections ’RECTANGLE’ and ’CERCLE’, the characteristics are computed directly in AFFE_CARA_ELEM by means of simplified formulae which are set out here. 1 The geometric characteristics Hypothesis: Only the cross-sections of homogeneous and isotropic beams are treated here (the same material characteristics for all the points and in all directions). The command MACR_CARA_POUTRE can also compute the geometric characteristics of a set of disjoint sections. 1.1 Arbitrary section 1.1.1 Principle Let a section (S) of area S in the plane (0,y,z) whose origin O is the centre of gravity G of the section, [Figure ]. Figure 1: section in the plane (0,y,z) The geometric moment of inertia of (S) with respect to the axis (\mathrm{Oy}) (which passes through the centre of gravity) is expressed by: {I}_{y}={\int}_{s}\mathrm{z²}\mathrm{dS} with [I]={\int}_{s}\mathrm{OM}\otimes \mathrm{OM}\mathrm{dS} One defines in a similar way the geometric moment with respect to (\mathrm{Oz}) by: {I}_{z}={\int}_{s}{y}^{2}\mathrm{dS} When the centrifugal geometric moment (often called the area product of inertia) defined by is zero, {I}_{yz}={\int}_{s}yz\mathrm{dS} the axes (\mathrm{Oy}) and (\mathrm{Oz}) are principal axes of the section (S) . One places oneself henceforth in this assumption; {I}_{y} and {I}_{z} are then called the principal geometric moments. In a general way, one must place oneself in the principal axes of a beam section for everything that concerns its characteristics, since the beam elements of Code_Aster are formulated in this frame. Starting from an origin located at the centre of gravity, it is sufficient, in order to pass from an arbitrary system of axes (G,y',z') to the principal system of axes (G,y,z) , to carry out a rotation of angle \theta such that [Figure]: \theta =\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Arctg}(\frac{2{I}_{y'z'}}{{I}_{z'}-{I}_{y'}}) Figure 2: Principal and arbitrary axes. The polar geometric moment with respect to the centre of gravity is given by: {I}_{p}={\int}_{s}\mathrm{r²}\mathrm{dS} where r is the distance from the element \mathrm{dS} to the centre of gravity [Figure ]. One naturally deduces {I}_{p}={I}_{y}+{I}_{z} . The polar geometric moment enters into the computation of the torsional stiffness of beams of circular section (Saint-Venant torsion). For the other section shapes, a torsion constant of the same dimension will be defined. Moreover, the geometric moments may be computed in another frame (P,y,z) , of arbitrary origin P different from the centre of gravity G (Huygens’ formula): \begin{array}{}{I}_{y}^{P}={I}_{y}^{G}+{(\mathrm{GP}.Z)}^{2}.S={\int}_{s}{z}^{2}\mathrm{dS}+{(\mathrm{GP}.Z)}^{2}.S\\ {I}_{z}^{P}={I}_{z}^{G}+{(\mathrm{GP}.Y)}^{2}.S={\int}_{s}{y}^{2}\mathrm{dS}+{(\mathrm{GP}.Y)}^{2}.S\\ {I}_{yz}^{P}={I}_{yz}^{G}+(\mathrm{GP}.Y)(\mathrm{GP}.Z).S={\int}_{s}yz\mathrm{dS}+(\mathrm{GP}.Y)(\mathrm{GP}.Z).S\end{array} in a general way, Huygens’ formula gives: \begin{array}{}\left[I\right]={\int}_{s}(\text{PG}+\text{GM})\otimes (\text{PG}+\text{GM})\\ \phantom{\left[I\right]}={\int}_{s}\text{PG}\otimes \text{PG}+{\int}_{s}\text{GM}\otimes \text{GM}\\ \phantom{\left[I\right]}+2{\int}_{s}\text{PG}\otimes \text{GM}\\ \phantom{\left[I\right]}=S(\text{PG}\otimes \text{PG})+{\int}_{s}\text{GM}\otimes \text{GM}\end{array} 1.1.2 Computation of the geometric characteristics by means of MACR_CARA_POUTRE This macro-command makes it possible to determine the characteristics of a beam cross-section from a 2D mesh of the section U4.42.02. It makes it possible to build a table of values, usable in the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM(SECTION: ’GENERALE’ U4.42.01). The geometric characteristics may be computed on the complete mesh, a half-mesh with symmetry with respect to Y or to Z , a quarter-mesh with two symmetries with respect to Y and to Z [Figure]. These characteristics are computed in the table for the whole mesh and for each mesh-cell group of the list specified by the user (case of a network of beams). The data correspond to a half or a quarter of the section if the keywords SYME_Y or SYME_Z are present. Figure 3 : Definition of the geometric characteristics. The results are gathered into four groups: - In the frame \mathit{OYZ} of the description of the 2D mesh for the mesh supplied by the user - area: A_M - position of the centre of gravity: CDG_Y_M,CDG_Z_M - area moments and product of inertia, at the centre of gravity G in the frame GYZ: IY_G_M, IZ_G_M, IYZ_G_M - In the same global frame, for the mesh obtained by symmetrisation if SYME_Y or SYME_Z: - area: A - position of the centre of gravity: CDG_Y,CDG_Z - area moments and product of inertia, at the centre of gravity G in the frame GYZ: IY_G, IZ_G, IYZ_G - In the principal inertia frame \mathrm{Gyz} . of the cross-section, whose naming corresponds to that used in the description of the beam elements of neutral fibre \mathrm{Gx} U4.24.01. - principal area moments of inertia in the frame \mathrm{Gyz} , usable for the computation of the bending stiffness of the beam: IY and IZ - angle of passage from the frame \mathit{GYZ} to the principal inertia frame \mathrm{Gyz} : ALPHA - characteristic distances, with respect to the centre of gravity G of the section, for the computations of maximum stresses: Y_MAX, Y_MIN, Z_MAX, Z_MIN and R_MAX. - In the global frame, at a point P supplied by the user: - Y_P, Z_P: point of computation of the moments of inertia - IY_P, IZ_P, IYZ_P: moments of inertia in the frame PYZ - IY_P, IZ_P: moments of inertia in the frame Pyz. 1.1.3 Computations carried out The list of the commands called by MACR_CARA_POUTRE is given in the document U4.42.02. The previous quantities are obtained by the call to POST_ELEM, for the option ’CARA_GEOM’. In addition, one may add there the keywords SYME_Y, SYME_Z, and ORIG_INER, which defines the point P . The computations are carried out in POST_ELEM, for the whole mesh, then possibly for each mesh-cell group, in the following way: - Loop over the 2D elements (modelling D_PLAN), with a call to the elementary option ’MASS_INER’. One obtains a CHAM_ELEM with one value per element (1 Gauss point) containing the components: {\int}_{\mathrm{élément}}\mathrm{dS},{\int}_{\stackrel{x}{\mathrm{élément}}}\mathrm{dS},{\int}_{\mathrm{élément}}\mathrm{dS} {\int}_{s}\mathrm{x²}\mathrm{dS},{\int}_{s}\mathrm{y²}\mathrm{dS},{\int}_{s}xy\mathrm{dS} , - Summation of the previous elementary quantities in order to obtain: A_M, CDG_Y_M, CDG_Z_M, IY_G_M, IZ_G_M, IYZ_G_M - Computation of A, CDG_Y, CDG_Z, IY_G, IZ_G, IYZ_G (taking SYME_Y, SYME_Z into account) - Computation of IY, IZ, ALPHA - Computation of Y_MAX, Z_MAX, Y_MIN, Z_MIN, R_MAX - If one specifies a particular point P (keyword ORIG_INER), one also computes the characteristics in the global frame of origin P : \mathit{PYZ} 1.1.4 Examples of use: solid rectangle (treated by the test SSLL107G) Geometric characteristics obtained LIEU A_M CDG_Y_M CDG_Z_M IY_G_M IZ_G_M IYZ_G_M 0.000003 1.00E-03 4.24E-18 -3.39E-18 2.08E-07 3.33E-08 2.65E-23 GR1 5.00E-04 2.20E-17 -1.25E-02 2.60E-08 1.67E-08 3.97E-23 GR2 5.00E-04 -8.47E-18 1.25E-02 2.60E-08 1.67E-08 5.62E-23 LIEU A CDG_Y CDG_Z IY_G IZ_G IYZ_G IY IZ ALPHA 0.000003 1.00E-03 4.24E-18 -3.39E-18 2.08E-07 3.33E-08 2.65E-23 3.33E-08 2.08E-07 9.00E+01 GR1 5.00E-04 2.20E-17 -1.25E-02 2.60E-08 1.67E-08 3.97E-23 1.67E-08 2.60E-08 9.00E+01 GR2 5.00E-04 -8.47E-18 1.25E-02 2.60E-08 1.67E-08 5.62E-23 1.67E-08 2.60E-08 9.00E+01 LIEU Y_P Z_P IY_P IZ_P IYZ_P IY_PRIN_P IZ_PRIN_P 0.000003 0.00E+00 0.00E+00 2.08E-07 3.33E-08 2.65E-23 3.33E-08 2.08E-07 GR1 0.00E+00 0.00E+00 1.04E-07 1.67E-08 -9.79E-23 1.67E-08 1.04E-07 GR2 0.00E+00 0.00E+00 1.04E-07 1.67E-08 3.31E-24 1.67E-08 1.04E-07 LIEU Y_MAX Z_MAX Y_MIN Z_MIN R_MAX 0.000003 2.50E-02 1.00E-02 -2.50E-02 -1.00E-02 2.69E-02 GR1 2.50E-02 2.25E-02 -2.50E-02 2.50E-03 3.36E-02 GR2 2.50E-02 -2.50E-03 -2.50E-02 -2.25E-02 3.36E-02 LIEU JX AY AZ EY EZ PCTY PCTZ RT 0.000003 - Figure 4 : rectangular section. In the case of the rectangular beam (operand SECTION:’RECTANGLE’), the computation gives: {I}_{y}=\frac{1}{12}\left[{h}_{y}{h}_{z}^{3}-({h}_{y}-2{\mathrm{ep}}_{y}){({h}_{z}-{\mathrm{2ep}}_{z})}^{3}\right] {I}_{z}=\frac{1}{12}\left[{h}_{z}{h}_{y}^{3}-({h}_{z}-2{\mathrm{ep}}_{z}){({h}_{y}-{\mathrm{2ep}}_{y})}^{3}\right] Figure 5 : circular section For the circular section (operand SECTION:’CERCLE’), one obtains: {I}_{y}={I}_{z}=\frac{p}{4}\left[{R}^{4}-{(R-\mathrm{ep})}^{4}\right] {I}_{p}=\frac{p}{2}\left[{R}^{4}-{(R-\mathrm{ep})}^{4}\right] 2 The shear coefficients and the shear centre The aim is to evaluate the coefficients {A}_{y}=\frac{1}{{k}_{y}},{A}_{z}=\frac{1}{{k}_{z}} appearing in the Timoshenko beam models with the shear strains taken into account. For EULER beams, these coefficients do not appear [U4.42.01 §7.4.2] and [R3.08.01 §2.3.1]. These coefficients are obtained for a linear elastic constitutive behaviour. In the case of arbitrary sections, the shear coefficients are to be supplied by the user in AFFE_CARA_ELEM, if the element chosen is a TIMOSHENKO beam (models POU_D_T, POU_D_TG and POU_D_TGM). In the case of circular or rectangular sections, the shear coefficients are computed by analytical methods of [§2.1]. In every case, they may be computed by MACR_CARA_POUTRE, from the plane mesh of the section. The numerical method used is set out in [§2.3]. This method applies to arbitrary sections (of homogeneous and isotropic material). In appendix 2, an extension of this method to the case of a network of parallel beams held between two rigid floors is described. The position of the torsion centre (or shear centre) is obtained only by numerical methods (cf. [§2.3]). For rectangular and circular sections, as for all sections with 2 planes of symmetry, the torsion centre coincides with the centre of gravity of the section. 2.1 Analytical methods Three analytical methods making it possible to compute shear coefficients, applicable to arbitrary sections, are described. The first two methods differ by the definition they propose of the shear coefficient, but rest on the same assumption, which consists in postulating the form of the distribution of the shear stresses in the section. 2.1.1 Assumption on the distribution of the shears: JOURAWSKI formula Consider for example the case of a beam of cross-section S , subjected to a shear force {V}_{y}={\int}_{s}{\sigma}_{xy}\mathrm{dS} . One writes the equilibrium of a prismatic part of the beam, lying between the cross-sections {S}_{x} and {S}_{x+a} and between the cutting plane located at the ordinate y and {y}_{\max} (ref.[bib]). The forces acting on this part of the beam are the stress vectors on the faces {S}_{x} and {S}_{x+a} , and those acting on the face located at y . Figure 6 : Beam section. Applying the resultant theorem, one obtains: \begin{array}{cc}{\int}_{{S}_{x+a}}{\sigma}_{xx}(x,y',z)\mathrm{dy}'\text{dz}-{\int}_{{S}_{x}}{\sigma}_{xx}(x,y',z)\mathrm{dy}'\text{dz}& =N(x+a,y)-N(x,y)\\ & ={\int}_{x}^{x+a}{\int}_{\frac{-b(y)}{2}}^{\frac{b(y)}{2}}{\sigma}_{xy}(\alpha ,y,z)d\alpha \text{dz}\end{array} To evaluate the right-hand term, JOURAWSKI proposed to consider only the average of the shears along z: {\bar{\sigma}}_{xy}(x,y)=\frac{1}{b(y)}{\int}_{-\frac{b}{2}}^{\frac{b}{2}}{\sigma}_{xy}(x,y,z)\text{dz} then {\int}_{x}^{x+a}{\int}_{-\frac{b(y)}{2}}^{\frac{b(y)}{2}}{\sigma}_{xy}(\alpha ,y,z)d\alpha \text{dz}={\int}_{x}^{x+a}b(y){\bar{\sigma}}_{xy}(\alpha ,y)d\alpha and letting a tend towards 0 , \frac{\partial N}{\partial x}=b(y){\bar{\sigma}}_{xy}(x,y) The beam equilibrium equations and the distribution of the bending stresses (in elasticity) give: N(x,y)={\int}_{{S}_{x}}^{}{\sigma}_{xx}(x,y,z)\text{dydz}={\int}_{{S}_{x}}^{}\frac{{M}_{z}(x).y}{{I}_{z}}\text{dydz} =\frac{{M}_{z}(x)}{{I}_{z}}m(y)\text{avec}m(y)={\int}_{y}^{{y}_{\max}}t\text{}b(t)\text{}\text{dt} hence {\bar{\sigma}}_{xy}(\text{x,y})=\frac{m(y)}{{I}_{z}b(y)}\frac{\partial {M}_{z}}{\partial x}=\frac{m(y)}{{I}_{z}b(y)}{V}_{y} The distribution of the shears along y is therefore given by the JOURAWSKI formula: > {\bar{\sigma}}_{xy}(\text{x,y})=\frac{m(y)}{{I}_{z}b(y)}{V}_{y}\text{avec}m(y)={\int}_{y}^{{y}_{\max}}t\text{}b(t)\text{}\text{dt} [1] in accordance with U4.24.01, with the notation of the [Figure]. The quantity m(y) represents the static moment of the part of the section (hatched) lying between y and {y}_{\max} : Figure 7 : beam section This distribution does indeed satisfy the boundary conditions along y of the three-dimensional problem: the shear is indeed zero on the lower and upper fibres ( y={y}_{\min} , or y={y}_{\max} ). But it takes into account only the average of the shears along z . Applying this formula to a solid rectangular section, one finds a parabolic distribution along y . Applying it to a beam of circular section, one finds a parabolic distribution in y and in z , which varies more slowly along z than along y . This remains valid for the other solid sections. For sections containing holes, care must be taken to consider only the material in the computation of b(y) . 2.1.2 TIMOSHENKO method Originally, TIMOSHENKO (ref. [bib]) proposed a simple definition of the shear coefficient, as being the ratio between the mean transverse shear stress in the section, denoted {\bar{\sigma}}_{\text{CT}} , and its maximum value ({\sigma}_{{\mathrm{CT}}_{\mathrm{Max}}}) . Since one always has the shear force by: > V={\int}_{s}{\sigma}_{\text{CT}}\text{dS} [2] one deduces: . {\bar{\sigma}}_{\text{CT}}=\frac{V}{S} Knowing that TIMOSHENKO proposes to write: > k=\frac{{\bar{\sigma}}_{\text{CT}}}{{\sigma}_{{\text{CT}}_{\text{Max}}}} [3] in order to determine k , it is sufficient to express the shear force V={\int}_{s}{\sigma}_{\text{CT}}\text{dS} [eq] as a function of {\sigma}_{{\mathrm{CT}}_{\mathrm{Max}}} . In the general case of arbitrary sections, there will naturally be two coefficients {k}_{y} and {k}_{z} , for each of the two principal axes. It remains to determine {\sigma}_{{\mathrm{CT}}_{\mathrm{Max}}} . For this purpose, TIMOSHENKO makes an assumption on the distribution of the transverse shear stresses: the transverse shear stress has a parabolic distribution in the direction of the shear force which produces it, with its maximum value at the centre and zero values at the edges. This is true according to the JOURAWSKI formula for a rectangular section. By extension, the method extends this assumption of a parabolic distribution to an arbitrary section This method is not applied in Code_Aster , except for hollow rectangular sections. The “energy” method is used in the other cases. 2.1.3 “Energy” method In reality, the definition proposed by TIMOSHENKO turns out to be little used in practice today; one prefers a formulation based on the internal energy due to shear in the section. The latter is written: {U}_{\text{CT}}={\int}_{s}\frac{1}{2}\frac{{\sigma}_{{\text{CT}}^{2}}}{G}\text{dS} where G is the shear modulus (equal to m ). The new definition of the shear coefficient is sometimes attributed to MINDLIN and is expressed by: > {U}_{\text{CT}}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{{V}^{2}}{k\text{SG}} [4] As a result, by substitution, one thus defines, for a section of homogeneous material, the shear coefficient by: > k={\frac{\left[{\int}_{s}{\sigma}_{\text{CT}}\text{dS}\right]}{S{\int}_{s}{\sigma}_{{\text{CT}}^{2}}\text{dS}}}^{2}=\frac{{V}^{2}}{S{\int}_{s}{\sigma}_{{\text{CT}}^{2}}\text{dS}} [5] By making an assumption on the stress distribution in the section, one can thus estimate the value of k . From the JOURAWSKI formula [eq], the previous expression may be written [bib]: > k=\frac{{I}^{2}}{S{\int}_{S}^{}\frac{{m}^{2}(y)}{{b}^{2}(y)}\text{dS}} [6] 2.1.4 COWPER method One may also take the three-dimensional effects into account in order to determine the coefficient k ; various formulations have been proposed, in particular by COWPER [bib] and taken up by BLEVINS [bib], based on the solution of the three-dimensional Saint-Venant problem. In this case, the coefficient k is a function of POISSON’s ratio, in general a first-order approximation. COWPER uses the three-dimensional equations of elasticity in the dynamic case to propose an expression of k giving good results in statics and in dynamics at low frequency. The approximation which makes it possible to arrive at the proposed formula consists in considering a stress distribution which is not parabolic, but results from the static problem (solved analytically) of the cantilever beam loaded transversely at its free end. It should be noted that the distribution obtained is strictly identical to the problem with a uniformly distributed transverse loading. 2.2 Particular case of the rectangular and circular sections Solid beams and tubes are distinguished. For the solid rectangular section, the shear coefficient is determined by the method based on the internal shear energy with a parabolic distribution of the stresses: > {k}_{y}=\frac{{I}_{z}^{2}}{S{\int}_{S}^{}\frac{{m}_{z}^{2}(y)}{{b}_{{}_{z}}^{2}(y)}\text{dy}} [7] Applied to the rectangular section, one obtains {k}_{y}={k}_{z}=\frac{5}{6} . Note that this value also corresponds to the COWPER method when POISSON’s ratio is taken equal to zero. For the rectangular tube, Code_Aster uses the TIMOSHENKO method, which leads to {k}_{y}={k}_{z}=\frac{2}{3} . In the case of beams of solid circular section, the energy method is used, which leads to {k}_{y}={k}_{z}=\frac{9}{10} . This value is also obtained by the COWPER method when POISSON’s ratio is equal to \frac{1}{2} . For circular tubes, thin-walled tubes and thick-walled tubes are distinguished. If one denotes by m=\frac{{r}_{i}}{{r}_{e}} the ratio of the internal radius to the external radius, a tube is thin-walled when m>0.9 , otherwise it is thick-walled. The shear coefficient of the thin-walled circular tube is given by the COWPER method, considering that m=1 and for a zero POISSON’s ratio, that is {k}_{y}={k}_{z}=\frac{1}{2} . For thick-walled circular tubes, an approximate formula of the COWPER method is used, which is written: k=\frac{1}{1,093+0,634m+1,156{m}^{2}-0,905{m}^{3}} Note that this formula does not ensure continuity with the limiting cases of the solid cylinder ( m=0 ) and of the infinitely thin-walled cylinder ( m=1 ). If the previous choices (made by AFFE_CARA_ELEM in the case of circular and rectangular sections) are not suitable, it is always possible to compute the shear coefficients numerically by means of MACR_CARA_POUTRE, whose method is specified in the following §. 2.3 Numerical method for computing the shear coefficients and the shear centre 2.3.1 Computation of the shear coefficients: This method is inspired by [bib], page 62. It makes it possible to determine simultaneously the shear constants and the torsion centre. It is implemented in MACR_CARA_POUTRE, from a plane mesh of the section. It currently works only for homogeneous and isotropic sections (for non-homogeneous sections, the method is similar [bib] but not available in Code_Aster ). As for the energy method, one compares, for a shear force V , the internal energy {U}_{1} due to shear in the section with the energy U2 associated with the MINDLIN model: {U}_{1}={\int}_{s}\frac{1}{2}\frac{{\sigma}_{xy}^{2}+{\sigma}_{xz}^{2}}{G}\text{dS}={U}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{{V}_{z}^{2}}{{k}_{z}\text{SG}} The shear coefficient is expressed by: {k}_{z}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{{V}_{z}^{2}}{{\text{SGU}}_{1}} One must therefore compute {U}_{1} and therefore the shear stresses (in elasticity) in the section in order to estimate the value of k . One places oneself in the principal inertia frame (G,y,z) , and one assumes that the beam is subjected only to a shear force {V}_{z} . It follows that: \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{xx}=z\frac{{M}_{y}(x)}{{I}_{y}}\\ \frac{\partial {\sigma}_{xx}}{\partial x}=z\frac{{V}_{z}}{{I}_{y}}\end{array} The equilibrium equations make it possible to write: \frac{\partial {\sigma}_{xx}}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial {\sigma}_{xy}}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial {\sigma}_{xz}}{\partial z}=0=\frac{\partial {\sigma}_{xy}}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial {\sigma}_{xz}}{\partial z}+z\frac{{V}_{z}}{{I}_{y}} On the other hand, the kinematics of the beam in bending/shear is: \begin{array}{}u(x,y,z)=u(x)+z{\theta}_{y}(x)+\tilde{u}(y,z)\\ v(x,y,z)=0\\ w(x,y,z)=w(x)\end{array} \tilde{u}(y,z) representing the axial displacement due to the warping of the section. The strains are written: \begin{array}{}{\varepsilon}_{xx}=\frac{\partial u(x)}{\partial x}+z\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}(x)}{\partial x}\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{xy}=\frac{\partial \tilde{u}(y,z)}{\partial y}\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{xz}={\theta}_{y}(x)+\frac{\partial \tilde{u}(y,z)}{\partial z}+\frac{\partial w(x)}{\partial x}\end{array} Using the constitutive relation of linear elasticity, the stresses are written: \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{xy}=2\mu {\varepsilon}_{xy}=\mu \frac{\partial \tilde{u}(y,z)}{\partial y}\\ {\sigma}_{xz}=2\mu {\varepsilon}_{xz}=\mu ({\theta}_{y}(x)+\frac{\partial \tilde{u}(y,z)}{\partial z}+\frac{\partial w(x)}{\partial x})\end{array} The shear components therefore satisfy: \frac{\partial {\sigma}_{xy}}{\partial z}-\frac{\partial {\sigma}_{xz}}{\partial y}=0 This relation makes it possible to introduce the stress function {\psi}_{z} such that the shear stresses in the section are written: \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{xy}=\mu \frac{\partial {\psi}_{z}}{\partial y}\\ {\sigma}_{xz}=\mu \frac{\partial {\psi}_{z}}{\partial z}\end{array} The equilibrium equation then makes it possible to obtain the function {\psi}_{z} by solution of a quasi-harmonic problem which is written: \begin{array}{}G\Delta {\psi}_{z}+f=0\text{dans}S\text{avec}f=\frac{{\mathrm{zV}}_{z}}{{I}_{y}}\\ G\frac{\partial {\psi}_{z}}{\partial n}=0\text{sur}\partial S\\ {\psi}_{z}=0\text{en un point}\end{array} This makes it possible to compute {\psi}_{z} then the shears. In practice, in MACR_CARA_POUTRE, one uses THER_LINEAIRE to solve the problem, by identifying {\psi}_{z} with the temperature. One chooses V=1 and G=1 ( G no longer appears in the expression of the shear coefficient). The boundary conditions of this steady thermal problem are: - source f equal to \frac{{\text{zV}}_{z}}{{I}_{y}} - zero flux on \partial S - zero temperature at a point of S One can then determine {U}_{1}^{z}={\int}_{s}\frac{1}{2}\frac{{\sigma}_{xy}^{2}+{\sigma}_{xz}^{2}}{G}\text{dS}=\frac{1}{2}{\int}_{s}G{(\nabla {\psi}_{z})}^{2}\text{dS} by an elementary computation on all the elements of the section, with the option ’CARA_CISA’ (computation of the gradient), then summation over these elements. One then computes {k}_{z}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{{V}_{z}^{2}}{{\text{SGU}}_{1}^{z}} The same computation is carried out with {V}_{y}=1 in order to determine {k}_{y}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{{V}_{y}^{2}}{{\text{SGU}}_{{}_{1}}^{y}} The result supplied is {A}_{y}=\frac{1}{{k}_{y}},{A}_{z}=\frac{1}{{k}_{z}} . 2.3.2 Computation of the coordinates of the shear centre The shear centre C is the point of the section where the shear stresses due to a shear force produce a zero torsion moment. This point is also called the torsion centre, because it remains fixed when the section is subjected only to a torsion moment. The torsion moment with respect to the point G is equal to {M}_{\text{xG}}={\int}_{s}({\sigma}_{xz}.y-{\sigma}_{xy}.z)\text{dS} : The torsion moment with respect to the sought point C is: {M}_{\text{xC}}={\int}_{s}({\sigma}_{xz}.(y-{y}_{c})-{\sigma}_{xy}(z-{z}_{c}))\text{dS}={M}_{\text{xG}}-{y}_{c}{V}_{z}+{z}_{c}{V}_{y} To determine the coordinates of the shear centre, one uses the previous computation [bib]: From the shear stresses determined for V=1 and {V}_{y}=0 , one computes: {M}_{{}_{\text{xG}}}^{z}={\int}_{s}({\sigma}_{xz}.y-{\sigma}_{xy}.z)\text{dS} One obtains: {y}_{c}=\frac{{M}_{{}_{\text{xG}}}^{z}}{{V}_{z}}={M}_{{}_{\text{xG}}}^{z} For V=1 and {V}_{y}=0 , one obtains: {z}_{c}=-\frac{{M}_{\mathrm{xG}}^{y}}{{V}_{y}}=-{M}_{{}_{\text{xG}}}^{y} 2.3.3 Example Let us take up again the example of the rectangular section [§1.1.4]. The shear coefficients obtained are identical to the analytical value (6/5). | \mathrm{LIEU} | \mathrm{AY} | \mathrm{AZ} | \mathrm{EY} | \mathrm{EZ} | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | whole | 1.20E+00 | 1.20E+00 | –8.72E-19 | 3.16E–18 | The components of the vector \mathrm{CG}=(\mathrm{EY},\mathrm{EZ}) expressed in the principal frame (G,y,z) are zero: the shear/torsion centre does indeed coincide with the centre of gravity. 2.4 Computation of the shear coefficients of a network The method described in appendix 2 makes it possible to compute shear coefficients of a beam equivalent to a set of parallel beams built in on a rigid floor and built in or pinned on another. 3 The constants related to torsion The torsion constant denoted \mathit{JX} must make it possible to take into account the warping of the (non-circular) cross-sections during a torsional deformation. It is used in the straight-beam models treated by Aster (EULER, TIMOSHENKO and warped TIMOSHENKO, or POU_D_E, POU_D_T and POU_D_TG). In the case of circular sections, the sections are not warped and the torsion constant is equal to the polar geometric moment {I}_{p} . The torsion constant C is defined as the moment necessary to produce a rotation of 1 radian per unit length divided by the shear modulus , that is: > C=\frac{{M}_{x}}{\mu \frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}} [8] \mathit{JX} has the same dimension as the geometric moments of inertia {I}_{y} and {I}_{z} , that is {m}^{4} . For a circular section, the definition [eq] is consistent since one has: {M}_{x}=\mu {I}_{p}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x} The determination of \mathit{JX} in the general case is done numerically (MACR_CARA_POUTRE) and reduces to a 2D Laplacian computation. The method presented here is detailed in ref. [bib] [§3.6.3] for simply connected sections. An original method for the computation of the torsion constants with sections containing holes is detailed in the appendix. The results are given here. 3.1 Computation of C in the case of arbitrary sections The complete solution of the problem is found in the appendix. Only the results are given here. According to the assumptions of the Saint-Venant pure torsion theory, there is no deformation of the mean line and no elongation along the longitudinal axis. The torsion is free, that is to say that it does not generate axial stresses. In other words, the sections may warp freely. If one remains in small displacements, one accepts that the angle of rotation of the cross-sections is equal to: > {q}_{x}(x)=\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}x=\Theta .x [9] Figure 8 : general section. If the point c is the torsion centre (which by definition remains motionless when the beam is subjected to torsion), the displacement field u(M) is given by [bib]: u(M)=\left[\begin{array}{c}u\\ v\\ w\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}x\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right]\wedge \left[\begin{array}{c}x\\ (y-{y}_{c})\\ (z-{z}_{c})\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}\xi (y,z)\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right] =(\begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}\xi (y,z)\\ -\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}x(z-{z}_{c})\\ \frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}x(y-{y}_{c})\end{array}) where \xi (y,z) is the warping function. HOOKE’s law is written: \sigma =2\mu \varepsilon +(E-2\mu )\mathrm{Trace}(\varepsilon )I where I is the unit matrix and the strain tensor is equal to \varepsilon =\frac{1}{2}(\text{grad}(u)+{}^{T}\text{}\text{grad}(u)) Neglecting the second-order terms, in \frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{x}}{\partial {x}^{2}} , one arrives at: > \sigma =\mu \frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& \frac{\partial \xi }{\partial y}-z& \frac{\partial \xi }{\partial z}+y\\ \frac{\partial \xi }{\partial y}-z& 0& 0\\ \frac{\partial \xi }{\partial z}+y& 0& 0\end{array}\right] =\mu \frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial z}& -\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial z}& 0& 0\\ -\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial y}& 0& 0\end{array}\right] [10] One has set: \varphi (y,z) stress function. One notes that the equilibrium relation divs=0 is then satisfied. Differentiating, one obtains: \begin{array}{c}\frac{{\partial}^{2}\varphi }{\partial {y}^{2}}=-\frac{{\partial}^{2}\xi }{\partial z\partial y}-1\\ \frac{{\partial}^{2}\varphi }{\partial {z}^{2}}=\frac{{\partial}^{2}\xi }{\partial y\partial z}-1.\end{array} Adding the two equations, one arrives at: > \Delta \varphi =-2 [11] It remains to establish the boundary conditions. One denotes by n the outward normal to the boundary ( \Gamma ), which may be multiply connected: With no external loading, one must have \sigma \otimes n=0 , which may be written: \mu \frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}\left[\begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial z}{n}_{y}-\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial y}{n}_{z}\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right]=0 where {n}_{y} and {n}_{z} are the two components of the normal. This writing may thus be put in the form n\wedge \text{grad}\varphi =0 , which implies that the vectors n and \text{grad}j are collinear. It therefore follows that \varphi (y,z) is constant on each connected component of the boundary ( \Gamma ). One may impose, for example, that \varphi (y,z) be zero on the outer contour: \varphi =0 on \partial {\Omega}_{0}=\Gamma \varphi ={\varphi}_{i} on \partial {\Omega}_{i} In the case where the sections contain holes, the constants {\varphi}_{i} are indeterminate. In order to allow the solution of the complete problem, equations must be added. These are obtained from the circulation of the warping function on each closed contour. One obtains the following conditions: {\oint}_{\partial {\Omega}_{i}}\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial n}\text{dl}=\mathrm{2A}(\partial {\Omega}_{i}) where A(\partial {\Omega}_{i}) is the area enclosed by the boundary (\partial {\Omega}_{i}) . These conditions reduce to classical conditions of prescribed flux (where l(\partial {\Omega}_{i}) represents the length of the boundary (\partial {\Omega}_{i}) ): \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial \underline{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{2A}(\partial {\Omega}_{i})}{l(\partial {\Omega}_{i})} Finally, the problem to be solved is written: \Delta \varphi =-2 on \Omega \varphi =0 on \partial {\Omega}_{0}=\Gamma \varphi ={\varphi}_{i} on (\partial {\Omega}_{i}) \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial \underline{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{2A}(\partial {\Omega}_{i})}{l(\partial {\Omega}_{i})} Once this problem has been solved, one obtains the torsion constant by: \mathrm{CT}=2{\int}_{\Omega}\varphi \text{ds}+2\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}{\varphi}_{i}A(\partial {\Omega}_{i}) . 3.2 Computation of the torsion constant in MACR_CARA_POUTRE This computation is carried out in MACR_CARA_POUTRE by the solution of a thermal problem. For this purpose the user must specify to MACR_CARA_POUTRE the mesh-cell group which defines the outer edge and, if the section contains holes, the mesh-cell groups which define the contour of each of them. One then solves a linear thermal problem (THER_LINEAIRE) on a plane mesh of the section in order to find the function j . One first places oneself in the principal inertia frame (CREA_MAILLAGE), from the coordinates of the centre of gravity and from the orientation of the principal frame computed previously. One then defines the boundary conditions in AFFE_CHAR_THER: - The source term is equal to –2 - The temperature of the outer edge is prescribed and is equal to 0 (TEMP_IMPO) - If the section contains holes (presence of one or more mesh-cell groups defining them): - On each mesh-cell group defining a hole, the temperature is constant (TEMP_UNIF) - The flux is equal to twice the area of the hole divided by the length of its edge. These quantities are computed beforehand . - The computation of \mathit{JX} is carried out in POST_ELEM by the keyword CARA_TORSION of the factor keyword CARA_POUTRE. In this case, one computes on each element the integral of j , (option CARA_TORSION on the plane thermal elements), then one carries out the sum over all the elements. Example: Let us take up again the example of the rectangular section [§1.1.4]. The solution of a steady thermal problem of unknown j makes it possible to determine the torsion constant and the shear stresses. The determination of the torsion radius \mathrm{Rt} is the solution of: \mathrm{Rt}=\mathrm{grad}(\varphi ).n (where n represents the outward normal vector to the edge under consideration of the section). \mathrm{Rt} varies along the external contour; indeed, for an arbitrary section, the shears due to torsion vary on the edge. One chooses to take the value of \mathrm{Rt} leading to the maximum shears on the external edge, that is to say the maximum value of \mathrm{Rt} (in absolute value) on the external contour. Moreover, if the section is cellular, one has several "several torsion radii": \mathrm{Rt}=2\ast A(k)/L(k) (where A(k) represents the area of the cell k and L(k) its perimeter). If one is content to seek the maximum value of the shear, one must take the maximum of the values \mathrm{Rt} obtained on the external edge and on the cells. The torsion radius is determined in MACR_CARA_POUTRE only by python commands. During the running of MACR_CARA_POUTRE the command POST_ELEM is called, so a new parameter \mathrm{Rt} is created for this command. 3.4 Torsion constant of the circular and rectangular sections Simplified expressions for these two types of section are described here. The computation of the torsion constants is then carried out directly in AFFE_CARA_ELEM. For the circular section the previous expressions remain valid. Taking a torsion function of the form \varphi (y,z)=\frac{1}{2}({R}^{2}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) one does indeed recover: \mathrm{CT}={I}_{p}=\frac{\pi}{2}({R}_{0}^{4}-{R}_{1}^{4}) For the rectangular section, the computation is naturally more complex but may be carried out by choosing a function which does indeed vanish at the edges, of the form: \varphi (y,z)=\sum_{i=0}^{+\infty }\sum_{j=0}^{+\infty }{A}_{ij}\cos\left[(\mathrm{2i}+1)\frac{\pi y}{{h}_{y}}\right]\cos\left[(\mathrm{2j}+1)\frac{\pi z}{{h}_{z}}\right] The solution leads to a torsion constant which is written: > \mathrm{CT}=\frac{{h}_{y}^{3}{h}_{z}^{3}}{{h}_{y}^{2}+{h}_{z}^{2}}c(\frac{{h}_{y}}{{h}_{z}})={h}_{y}{h}_{z}^{3}\left[\frac{c(\frac{{h}_{y}}{{h}_{z}})}{1+{(\frac{{h}_{z}}{{h}_{y}})}^{2}}\right] [12] where c(\frac{{h}_{y}}{{h}_{z}}) is expressed in the form of a series which takes the following values: \begin{array}{cccccc}\frac{{h}_{y}}{{h}_{z}}& 1& 2& 4& 8& +\infty \\ c(\frac{{h}_{y}}{{h}_{z}})& 0,281& 0,286& 0,299& 0,312& 1/3\end{array} In fact, Code_Aster uses a simplified formula (ref. [bib]) for the solid rectangular section, which is written: > \mathrm{CT}=\frac{{h}_{y}{h}_{z}^{3}}{16}(\frac{16}{3}-3.36\frac{{h}_{z}}{{h}_{y}}+0.280{(\frac{{h}_{z}}{{h}_{y}})}^{5}) [13] It is valid if {h}_{y}>{h}_{z} ; in the other case it is sufficient to exchange the respective places of {h}_{y} and {h}_{z} . One may consult on this subject the account by MASSONET of this aspect (ref. [bib]). One thus has: {\sigma}_{{T}_{M}}={M}_{x}\frac{{R}_{T}}{\mathit{JX}} In the case of circular cylinders, {R}_{T} is equal to the radius (external if it is a tube) of the section. For rectangular sections, the problem is distinctly more complex. Code_Aster imposes the torsion radius of the solid section by: {R}_{T}=\frac{\mathit{JX}4(3{h}_{y}+1.8{h}_{z})}{{h}_{y}^{2}+{h}_{z}^{2}} This approximate expression remains valid if the beam is not too flat. DHATT and BATOZ (ref.[bib]) give an expression with a more extended domain of validity, but in reality it is strictly speaking a series, numerical values of which are given by MASSONET (ref. [bib]). For the hollow rectangular beam, Code_Aster imposes an expression which is valid only if the wall is thin and of constant thickness {\mathrm{ep}}_{z} , that is: {R}_{T}=\frac{\mathit{JX}}{{\text{ep}}_{z}({h}_{y}-2{\text{ep}}_{y})({h}_{z}-2{\text{ep}}_{z})} This is an “adaptation” of the formula: {R}_{T}=\frac{\mathit{JX}}{2eA} where e is the thickness of the wall (constant) and A the area contained inside the mean line. This last expression is known under the name of BREDT’s first formula (Cf. ref. [bib] and [bib]). 4 Computation of the warping constant The warping constant is used by the beam model with warping (modelling POU_D_TG and POU_D_TGM), which it is important to take into account for beams of thin open sections (cf.[R3.08.04]). This coefficient (denoted {I}_{w} in R3.08.04, in {m}^{6} ) appears in the expression of the virtual work of the internal forces on the torsion terms: {W}_{int}={\int}_{0}^{2}({\theta}_{x,x}^{\text{ }}\mu .C.{\theta}_{x,x}+{\theta}_{x,xx}^{\text{ }}.E.{I}_{\omega}.{\theta}_{x,xx})\text{dx} Taking up again the approach of [§3.1], and placing oneself in a frame linked to the torsion centre C , the kinematics of the torsion of an arbitrary section is: u(M)=\left[\begin{array}{c}u\\ v\\ w\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}x\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right]\wedge \left[\begin{array}{c}x\\ y\\ z\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}\xi (y,z)\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right] =(\begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}\text{}\xi (y,z)\\ -\frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}xz\\ \frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}xy\end{array}) where \xi (y,z) is the warping function (which vanishes only in the case of a circular section). The expression of the stress field is (in elasticity): \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{xx}=E{\varepsilon}_{xx}=E\xi (y,z)\frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{x}}{\partial {x}^{2}}\\ {\sigma}_{xy}=2\mu {\varepsilon}_{xy}=\mu \frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}(\frac{\partial \xi (y,z)}{\partial y}-z)\\ {\sigma}_{xz}=2\mu {\varepsilon}_{xz}=\mu \frac{\partial {\theta}_{x}}{\partial x}(\frac{\partial \xi (y,z)}{\partial z}-y)\end{array} Unlike [§4], the second-order terms in \frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{x}}{\partial {x}^{2}} are no longer neglected. The first equilibrium relation {(div\sigma )}_{x}={\sigma}_{xx,x}+{\sigma}_{xy,y}+{\sigma}_{xz,z}=0 then implies the following condition on the warping function: \Delta \xi =0 On the other hand, with no external loading on the contour of the section , one must have \sigma \otimes n , which may be written: \frac{\partial \xi }{\partial y}{n}_{y}+\frac{\partial \xi }{\partial z}{n}_{z}=z.{n}_{y}-y.{n}_{z} , where {n}_{y} and {n}_{z} are the two components of the normal, or again in vector form: \text{grad}\xi .n=\frac{\partial \xi }{\partial n}=(n\wedge \text{CM}).x This determines the warping function up to a constant. To remove this indeterminacy, one writes for example the expression of the normal force (for a section where torsion produces warping): N=\underset{S}{\int}{\sigma}_{xx}\text{ds}=\underset{S}{\int}E\xi \frac{{\partial}^{2}{\theta}_{x}}{\partial {x}^{2}}\text{ds}=0 hence the additional condition on the warping function is \underset{S}{\int}\xi \text{ds}=0 . In practice, in MACR_CARA_POUTRE, one places oneself first of all in a frame linked to the torsion centre c . The Saint-Venant assumption consists in seeking a solution such that the stress tensor is of the form: \sigma =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{\sigma}_{11}& {\sigma}_{12}& {\sigma}_{13}\\ {\sigma}_{12}& 0& 0\\ {\sigma}_{13}& 0& 0\end{array}\right] The Saint-Venant principle is valid far from the sections of application of the forces. Indeed, except in particular cases of loading, the four terms assumed to be zero decay exponentially with {x}_{1} . To solve this elasticity problem, one chooses a formulation in stresses. The equations to be written are therefore the equilibrium equations and the compatibility equations. r3.08.04 Beam element with 7 degrees of freedom for taking warping into account r3.08.04 Beam element with 7 degrees of freedom for taking warping into account Summary: This document presents the element POU_D_TG, which is a straight-beam finite element with taking into account of the warping of the cross-sections. It makes it possible to analyse beams with thin open cross-sections, with restrained or free torsion. As regards bending, the normal and shear forces, this element is based on the element POU_D_T, which is a straight-beam element with transverse shear (Timoshenko model). For the element POU_D_TG, the cross-section is assumed constant (of arbitrary shape) and the material is homogeneous and isotropic, with linear elastic behaviour. The element POU_D_TGM is to be used for non-linear behaviours. This reference documentation relies on the general reference documentation of beams, in linear elasticity R3.08.01. It describes the specific features of the straight-beam element with warping POU_D_TG. 1 Field of use The development of the Timoshenko beam elements with warping (modelling POU_D_TG) in Code_Aster was carried out initially with the aim of computing the behaviour of pylons. It was mainly a matter of analysing structures formed of beams with a thin open profile (angles), for which the warping is significant. The non-linear behaviours are to be used with the element POU_D_TGM (multifibre beam). These non-linear behaviours concern only tension and bending. The shear due to the shear force, as well as the warping and the bimoment (force linked to the warping), remain linked by an elastic behaviour, for want of being able to express a non-linear behaviour on these quantities. The description of torsion with warping is valid for the use of the elements POU_D_TG and POU_D_TGM with the linear operators (MECA_STATIQUE, DYNA_VIBRA, ...) or the non-linear ones (STAT_NON_LINE, DYNA_NON_LINE, ...). 2 Notation The notation used here corresponds to that used in R3.08.01 and R3.08.03. One gives here the correspondence between this notation and that of the user's documentation. \mathrm{DX},\mathrm{DY},\mathrm{DZ},\mathrm{DRX},\mathrm{DRY},\mathrm{DRZ}\mathrm{et}\mathrm{GRX} are the names of the degrees of freedom associated with the components of the displacement u,v,w,{\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z},{\theta}_{x,x} . They are expressed in the global frame, except the degree of freedom associated with warping \mathrm{GRX} , which is expressed in the local frame. | Notation used | Meaning | Notation of the user's documentation | | --- | --- | --- | | S | area of the cross-section | A | | {I}_{y},{I}_{z} | geometric bending moments with respect to the axes x and y . | \mathrm{IY},\mathrm{IZ} | | C | torsion constant | \mathrm{JX} | | {I}_{\omega} | warping constant | \mathrm{JG} | | {k}_{y},{k}_{z} | shear coefficients | \frac{1}{\text{AY}}\frac{1}{\text{AZ}} | | {e}_{y},{e}_{z} | offset of the centre of torsion/shear with respect to the centre of gravity of the cross-section | \text{EY},\text{EZ} | | N | normal force on the cross-section | N | | {V}_{y},{V}_{z} | shear forces along the axes y and z | \text{VY},\text{VZ} | | {M}_{x},{M}_{y},{M}_{z} | moments about the axes x , y and z | \text{MT},\text{MFY},\text{MFZ} | | {M}_{\omega} | bimoment | \text{BX} | | u,v,w | translations along the axes x , y and z | \text{DX}\text{DY}\text{DZ} | | {\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z} | rotations about the axes x , y and z | \text{DRX}\text{DRY}\text{DRZ} | | {\theta}_{x,x} | derivative of the torsional rotation with respect to x | \text{GRX} | | E | Young's modulus | E | | \nu | Poisson's ratio | \text{NU} | | G=\frac{E}{2(1+\nu )}=\mu | Coulomb modulus (identical to the Lamé coefficient) | G | 3 Kinematics specific to torsion with warping The kinematics used to represent the displacement of the beam cross-sections is identical to that of the straight Timoshenko beams R3.08.01 as regards tension–compression and bending–shear. One details here only the torsion. Two possibilities are to be considered for the modelling of the torsional behaviour of non-circular cross-sections [bib], which always produces a warping of the cross-section. - The torsion is free (Saint-Venant torsion): the warping of the cross-sections is non-zero (it may even be significant for a thin open cross-section), but it is independent of the position on the axis x of the beam (constant as a function of x ) and there is no axial stress due to the torsion. - The torsion is restrained (Vlassov): the warping is non-zero, and moreover non-uniform axial stresses (whose resultant force is called the bimoment) exist in the beam. The element POU_D_TG makes it possible to treat these two configurations: the torsion may be free or restrained. The user will have access to the warping in both cases; on the other hand, the bimoment will be non-zero only in the case of restrained torsion. Note that at the location of the connection of the beams, the transmission of the warping depends on the type of connection. In general, the torsion in an assembly of beams is restrained. The warping may then be blocked at the connection points. Note: With elements without modelling of the warping (POU_D_T, POU_D_E), one can treat the case of free torsion (the displacements other than the warping will be correct), but not the case of restrained torsion. One can decouple the effects of torsion and of bending in a local frame (translated from the principal frame of inertia) having as its origin the centre of torsion. The centre of torsion is the point which remains fixed when the cross-section is subjected to the torsional moment alone. It is also called the shear centre because a force applied at this point does not produce a rotation about x . The displacements in the plane of the cross-section will therefore be expressed in this frame. The axial displacements remain expressed in the principal frame of inertia linked to the centre of gravity G , in order to keep a decoupling of the bending displacements and of the tension–compression. The displacement of an arbitrary point of the cross-section is then written in general form (free or restrained torsion): \begin{array}{}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}u(x,y,z)\\ v(x,y,z)\\ w(x,y,z)\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}_{G}(x)\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}z{\theta}_{y}(x)\\ 0\\ w(x)\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}-y{\theta}_{z}(x)\\ v(x)\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\omega (y,z){\theta}_{x,x}(x)\\ -(z-{z}_{c}){\theta}_{x}(x)\\ (y-{y}_{c}){\theta}_{x}(x)\end{array}\right\rbrace \end{array} Displacement = membrane + bending/ y + bending/ z + torsion with warping The components are expressed in the principal frame of inertia (centred at G ): x is directed along the axis of the beam, y and z are the two other principal axes of inertia. The term \omega (y,z){\theta}_{x,x}(x) represents the axial displacement due to the warping of the cross-section. \omega (y,z) is the warping function (expressed in {m}^{2} , but which has no obvious physical interpretation). The strains at an arbitrary point of the cross-section are then: \begin{array}{}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\varepsilon}_{xx}(x,y,z)\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{xy}(x,y,z)\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{xz}(x,y,z)\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}_{{G}_{,x}}(x)\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}z{\theta}_{y,x}(x)\\ 0\\ {\gamma}_{xz}(x)\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}-y{\theta}_{z,x}(x)\\ {\gamma}_{xy}(x)\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\omega (y,z){\theta}_{x,xx}(x)\\ ({\omega}_{,y}-(z-{z}_{c})){\theta}_{x,x}(x)\\ ({\omega}_{,z}+(y-{y}_{c})){\theta}_{x,x}(x)\end{array}\right\rbrace \\ {\gamma}_{xy}(x)={v}_{,x}-{\theta}_{z}\\ {\gamma}_{xz}(x)={w}_{,x}+{\theta}_{y}\end{array} \text{Déformation}=\text{membrane}+\text{flexion}/y+\text{flexion}/z+\text{torsion avec gauchissement} The term \omega (y,z){\theta}_{x,xx}(x) is zero in the case of free torsion: one has indeed {\theta}_{x,xx}(x)=0 , since the warping is independent of x . It is not negligible in the case of restrained torsion. The isotropic elastic constitutive law is written (making the assumption of plane stresses in the directions y and z ): \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{xx}(x,y,z)\\ {\sigma}_{xy}(x,y,z)\\ {\sigma}_{xz}(x,y,z)\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}E.{\varepsilon}_{xx}(x,y,z)\\ G.2{\varepsilon}_{xy}(x,y,z)\\ G.2{\varepsilon}_{xz}(x,y,z)\end{array}\right\rbrace The generalised forces in the cross-section are expressed as a function of the stresses for a homogeneous cross-section by [bib]: | N(x)=\underset{S}{\int}{\sigma}_{xx}(x,y,z)\text{ds} | Normal force | | --- | --- | | {V}_{y}(x)=\underset{S}{\int}{\sigma}_{xy}(x,y,z)\text{ds} | Shear force along y | | {V}_{z}(x)=\underset{S}{\int}{\sigma}_{xz}(x,y,z)\text{ds} | Shear force along z | | {M}_{y}(x)=\underset{S}{\int}z.{\sigma}_{xx}(x,y,z)\text{ds} | Bending moment about y | | {M}_{z}(x)=\underset{S}{\int}-y.{\sigma}_{xx}(x,y,z)\text{ds} | Bending moment about z | | {M}_{x}(x)=\underset{S}{\int}((y-{y}_{c}).{\sigma}_{xz}(x,y,z)-(z-{z}_{c}).{\sigma}_{xy}(x,y,z))\text{ds} | Torsional moment | | {M}_{\omega}(x)=\underset{S}{\int}\omega .{\sigma}_{xx}(x,y,z)\text{ds} | Bimoment (associated with the warping) | {M}_{\omega}(x) represents the generalised force associated with the warping. It is expressed in {\mathrm{N.m}}^{2} . One may give an illustration of it as in [bib] for a beam with an \text{I} cross-section (the bimoment acts here along z only): For an isotropic and homogeneous elastic behaviour in the cross-section, the generalised forces are therefore expressed directly as a function of the displacements by the following relations: \begin{array}{}N(x)=E.S.{u}_{,x}\\ {V}_{y}(x)={\text{Gk}}_{y}S({v}_{,x}-{\theta}_{z})\\ {V}_{z}(x)={\text{Gk}}_{z}S({w}_{,x}+{\theta}_{y})\\ {M}_{y}(x)=E.{I}_{y}{\theta}_{\text{y,}x}\\ {M}_{z}(x)=E.{I}_{z}{\theta}_{z,x}\\ {M}_{x}(x)=G.J.{\theta}_{\text{x,x}}\\ {M}_{\omega}(x)=E.{I}_{\omega}.{\theta}_{\text{x,xx}}\end{array} where {k}_{y},{k}_{z} are the shear coefficients. The warping does not intervene at the level of the shear forces, because these are expressed in the frame linked to the shear centre. Indeed, the warping function \omega is such that: \begin{array}{}\underset{S}{\int}\omega (y,z)\text{ds}=0\\ \underset{S}{\int}y.\omega (y,z)\text{ds}=0\\ \underset{S}{\int}z.\omega (y,z)\text{ds}=0\end{array} And the warping constant is expressed as a function of \omega by: \underset{S}{\int}{\omega}^{2}(y,z)\text{ds}={I}_{\omega} 4 Straight beam element with warping: stiffness and mass matrices The elementary stiffness and mass matrices for the element POU_D_TG are identical to those of the straight Timoshenko beam element (POU_D_T) as regards the tension–compression and bending–shear terms R3.08.01. The approach is identical; one simply recalls the result. This implies that, in the case of free torsion, one retains the properties of exactness of the solution at the nodes for the degrees of freedom of bending and of tension–compression. On the other hand, we shall see that, as regards restrained torsion, one carries out an approximation which does not make it possible to recover this property in the general case. The stiffness matrices are always computed with the option 'RIGI_MECA', and the mass matrices with the option 'MASS_MECA'. But the option 'MASS_MECA_DIAG' (diagonalised mass matrix) has not been implemented for this element (this option is mainly useful for problems of rapid dynamics, which is not the preferential field of use of this element). The degrees of freedom of the element are those of the Timoshenko beams, plus one degree of freedom per node making it possible to compute the terms relative to the warping: At each of the two nodes of the element, the degrees of freedom are: | u,v,w | translations along the axes x,y,z | \text{DX}\text{DY}\text{DZ} | | --- | --- | --- | | {\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z} | rotations about the axes x,y,z | \mathrm{DRX}\mathrm{DRY}\mathrm{DRZ} | | {\theta}_{\text{x,x}} | derivative of the torsional rotation along x | \text{GRX} | The local coordinates are expressed in the principal frame of inertia. It is used to treat buckling problems or vibrations of prestressed structures. In the case of a prestressed structure, therefore subjected to initial forces (known and independent of time), one cannot neglect in the equilibrium equation the terms introduced by the change of geometry from the stress-free state to the prestressed state. This change of geometry modifies the equilibrium equation only by the addition of a term which is a function of the displacements and of the prestress, whose associated matrix is called the geometric stiffness matrix and which is expressed by: {W}_{G}=\underset{{V}_{o}}{\int}\frac{\partial {u}_{k}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial {x}_{i}}{\sigma}_{ij}^{o}\frac{\partial {v}_{k}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial {x}_{j}}\text{dV} where {\sigma}_{ij}^{o} denotes the prestress tensor. This term appears naturally if one introduces the GREEN-LAGRANGE strain tensor into the virtual work of the strain: \begin{array}{}{E}_{xx}={\varepsilon}_{xx}+{\eta}_{xx}=\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}+\frac{1}{2}\left[{(\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x})}^{2}+{(\frac{\partial {u}_{y}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x})}^{2}+{(\frac{\partial {u}_{z}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x})}^{2}\right]\\ 2{E}_{xy}=2{\varepsilon}_{xy}+2{\eta}_{xy}=\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial {u}_{y}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}+\left[\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial {u}_{y}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}\frac{\partial {u}_{y}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial {u}_{z}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}\frac{\partial {u}_{z}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial y}\right]\\ 2{E}_{xz}=2{\varepsilon}_{xz}+2{\eta}_{xz}=\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial z}+\frac{\partial {u}_{z}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}+\left[\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial z}+\frac{\partial {u}_{y}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}\frac{\partial {u}_{y}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial z}+\frac{\partial {u}_{z}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}\frac{\partial {u}_{z}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial z}\right]\end{array} In the expression of these strains, the quadratic terms {(\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x})}^{2},\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial y}\text{et}\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial x}\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}}{\partial z} are neglected here, following the assumption commonly made by most authors [bib]. For a beam model, the initial-stress tensor reduces, in the local axes of the beam, to the components {\sigma}_{xx},{\sigma}_{xy} and {\sigma}_{xz} . Moreover, in order to be able to treat the problems of lateral-torsional buckling of thin beams, loaded essentially by bending moments and normal forces, one must add the assumption of moderate rotations in torsion [bib], [bib]. This is expressed by the following modification of the displacement field (only for the computation of the geometric stiffness): {u}_{x}^{\mathrm{3D}}(x,y,z)={u}_{G}(x)+z({\theta}_{y}(x)+{\theta}_{x}(x){\theta}_{z}(x))-y({\theta}_{z}(x)-{\theta}_{x}(x){\theta}_{y}(x))+\omega (y,z){\theta}_{x,x}(x) The origin of this expression cannot be detailed here. options | | | --- | --- | | CHAR_MECA_FR1D1D | distributed loading by real values | | CHAR_MECA_FF1D1D | distributed loading by function | | CHAR_MECA_PESA_R | loading due to gravity | |
