warping R3.08.01. There is therefore nothing particular to the element POU_D_TG. The other types of loading described in R3.08.01 are not available for this element. As regards the warping, it is possible to give boundary conditions involving the degree of freedom \mathit{GRX} (which makes it possible to model the restrained torsion: \mathrm{GRX}=0 ), but on the other hand nothing is provided for assigning a loading of bimoment type, whose physical interpretation is difficult to establish. Concerning the connection between elements, the transmission of the warping is an open question, as the reference [bib] points out: the continuity of the variable \mathit{GRX} from one element to the next (on which the warping depends directly) depends in fact on the technology of the connection between the various beams (weld in the axis, in which case the warping can be transmitted in full, connection by a gusset plate, ...). For an assembled structure such as a lattice, it seems more reasonable to assume that the torsion is restrained, therefore that the warping is zero at the ends. In order to assess the influence of this assumption, one may refer to the test SSLL102 (beam with an angle cross-section), whose modellings C and D use the element POU_D_TG, with free torsion for modelling C and restrained torsion for modelling D [V3.01.102B]. One observes that, for the bending loading, the difference in the displacement is small (2.5%), but for a torsional loading one obtains for this cross-section a non-zero lateral displacement (lateral-torsional buckling) whose value differs appreciably according to the assumption made: {u}_{z}=2.2{10}^{-5} for free torsion and {u}_{z}=2.62{10}^{-5} for restrained torsion. Likewise, the rotation varies strongly: {\theta}_{x}=3,79{10}^{-4} for free torsion and {\theta}_{x}=6,39{10}^{-4} for restrained torsion (GRX is zero at the ends). 6.1 Distributed loadings, options: CHAR_MECA_FR1D1D and CHAR_MECA_FF1D1D The loadings are given under the keyword FORCE_POUTRE, either by real values in AFFE_CHAR_MECA (option CHAR_MECA_FR1D1D), or by functions in AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F (option CHAR_MECA_FF1D1D). The loading is given only by distributed forces, not by distributed moments. The right-hand side associated with the distributed tension–compression loading is: \begin{array}{}\left[\begin{array}{c}{f}_{1}\\ {f}_{2}\end{array}\right]\end{array} with {f}_{1}={\int}_{0}^{1}{f}_{\text{ext}}(x)(1-\frac{x}{L})\text{dx} {f}_{2}={\int}_{0}^{1}{f}_{\text{ext}}(x)\frac{x}{L}\text{dx} For a constant or linearly varying loading, one obtains: \begin{array}{}{F}_{{x}_{1}}=L(\frac{{n}_{1}}{3}+\frac{{n}_{2}}{6}),\\ {F}_{{x}_{2}}=L(\frac{{n}_{1}}{6}+\frac{{n}_{2}}{3}).\end{array} {n}_{1} and {n}_{2} are the components of the axial loading at points 1 and 2 coming from the user's data, placed back into the local frame. If {t}_{{y}_{1}},{t}_{\mathrm{y2}},{t}_{\mathrm{z1}} and {t}_{\mathrm{z2}} are those of the shear force, one has: \begin{array}{cccc}{F}_{{y}_{1}}=L(\frac{7{t}_{{y}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{3{t}_{{y}_{2}}}{20})& & {M}_{{z}_{1}}={L}^{2}(\frac{{t}_{{y}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{{t}_{{y}_{2}}}{30})& \\ {F}_{{y}_{2}}=L(\frac{3{t}_{{y}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{7{t}_{{y}_{2}}}{20})& & {M}_{{z}_{2}}=-{L}^{2}(\frac{{t}_{{y}_{1}}}{30}+\frac{{t}_{{y}_{2}}}{20}),& \\ {F}_{{z}_{1}}=L(\frac{7{t}_{{z}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{3{t}_{{z}_{2}}}{20}),& & {M}_{{y}_{1}}=-{L}^{2}(\frac{{t}_{{z}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{{t}_{{z}_{2}}}{30}),& \\ {F}_{{z}_{2}}=L(\frac{3{t}_{{z}_{1}}}{20}+\frac{7{t}_{{z}_{2}}}{20}),& & {M}_{{y}_{2}}={L}^{2}(\frac{{t}_{{z}_{1}}}{30}+\frac{{t}_{{z}_{2}}}{20}).& \end{array} 6.2 Gravity loading, option: CHAR_MECA_PESA_R The gravity force is given by the magnitude of the acceleration g and a unit vector n indicating the direction of the loading. Notes (simplifying assumption): The shape functions used for this computation are those of the Euler–Bernoulli model. The approach is similar to that used for the distributed forces, provided that one first transforms the loading vector due to gravity into the local frame of the element. One obtains, in the local frame of the beam: \begin{array}{}{F}_{{x}_{i}}={\int}_{o}^{L}{\xi}_{i}\rho Sg\cdot x\text{dx}\\ ({\xi}_{1}=1-\frac{x}{L},{\xi}_{2}=\frac{x}{L})\end{array} whence: \begin{array}{}{F}_{{x}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot xL(\frac{S}{3}+\frac{S}{6})\text{}\text{au point 1,}\\ {F}_{{x}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot xL(\frac{S}{6}+\frac{S}{3})\text{}\text{au point 2}\end{array} Bending in the plane (\mathrm{Gxz}) : \begin{array}{}{F}_{{z}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot zL(\frac{7S}{20}+\frac{3S}{20})\\ {M}_{{y}_{1}}=-\rho g\cdot z\text{}{L}^{2}(\frac{S}{20}+\frac{S}{30})\\ {F}_{{z}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot zL(\frac{3S}{20}+\frac{7S}{20})\\ {M}_{{y}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot z{L}^{2}(\frac{S}{30}+\frac{S}{20})\end{array} Bending in the plane (\mathrm{Gxy}) : \begin{array}{}{F}_{{y}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot yL(\frac{7S}{20}+\frac{3S}{20})\\ {M}_{{z}_{1}}=\rho g\cdot y\text{}{L}^{2}(\frac{S}{20}+\frac{S}{30})\\ {F}_{{y}_{2}}=\rho g\cdot yL(\frac{3S}{20}+\frac{7S}{20})\\ {M}_{{z}_{2}}=-\rho g\cdot y{L}^{2}(\frac{S}{30}+\frac{S}{20})\end{array} 6.3 Thermal loading, option: CHAR_MECA_TEMP_R In order to obtain this loading, one must compute the axial displacements induced by the temperature difference T-{T}_{\text{référence}} : \begin{array}{}{u}_{1}=-L\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{référence}})\\ {u}_{2}=L\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{référence}})\end{array} ( \alpha : thermal expansion coefficient) Then, one simply computes the forces induced by F=\text{K u} . Since K is the local stiffness matrix of the element, one must then carry out a change of frame in order to obtain the values of the components of the loading in the global frame. 6.4 Loading by imposed strain, option: CHAR_MECA_EPSI_R One computes, as for the elements POU_D_T, the loading from a state of strain (this option was developed in order to take into account the thermal stratification in the piping). The model takes into account only work in tension–compression and in pure bending (no shear force, no torsional moment). The strain is given by the user with the aid of the keyword PRE_EPSI in AFFE_CHAR_MECA. By prescribing \frac{\partial u}{\partial x},\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x} and \frac{\partial {\theta}_{z}}{\partial x} on the beam, one obtains the elementary right-hand side associated with this loading: at node 1: \begin{array}{cccc}& {F}_{{x}_{1}}& =& E{S}_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x},\\ & {M}_{{y}_{1}}& =& E{I}_{{y}_{1}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x},\\ & {M}_{{z}_{1}}& =& E{I}_{{z}_{1}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{z}}{\partial x},\end{array} at node 2: \begin{array}{cccc}& {F}_{{x}_{2}}& =& E{S}_{2}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x},\\ & {M}_{{y}_{2}}& =& E{I}_{{y}_{2}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{y}}{\partial x},\\ & {M}_{{z}_{2}}& =& E{I}_{{z}_{2}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{z}}{\partial x}\end{array} 7 Wrench of the forces - Nodal forces and reactions 7.1 Options disponibles The various post-processing options available for the element POU_D_TG are: | Types or options | | | --- | --- | | EFGE_ELNO | wrench of the forces at the 2 nodes of each element | | SIEF_ELGA | force field necessary for the computation of the nodal forces (option 'FORC_NODA') and of the reactions (option 'REAC_NODA'). | | FORC_NODA | nodal forces expressed in the global frame | | REAC_NODA | nodal reactions | 7.2 The wrench of the forces 7.2.1 Generalised forces, option: EFGE_ELNO One seeks to compute, at the two nodes of each "beam" element constituting the mesh of the structure under study, the forces exerted on the "beam" element by the rest of the structure. The values are given in the local basis of each element. By integrating the equilibrium equations, one obtains the forces in the local frame of the element: {R}_{\text{LOC}}={K}_{\text{LOC}}^{e}{u}_{\text{LOC}}+{M}_{\text{LOC}}^{e}{\ddot{u}}_{\text{LOC}}-{f}_{\text{LOC}}^{e} where: {R}_{\text{LOC}}=(-{N}^{1},-{V}_{Y}^{1},-{V}_{Z}^{1},-{M}_{T}^{1},-{M}_{Y}^{1},-{M}_{Z}^{1},-{M}_{\omega}^{1},{N}^{2},{V}_{Y}^{2},{V}_{Z}^{2},{M}_{T}^{2},{M}_{Y}^{2},{M}_{Z}^{2},{M}_{\omega}^{2}) | {K}_{\text{LOC}}^{e} | elementary stiffness matrix of the beam element, | | --- | --- | | {M}_{\text{LOC}}^{e} | elementary mass matrix of the beam element, | | {f}_{\text{LOC}}^{e} | vector of the 'distributed' forces on the beam element, | | {u}_{\text{LOC}} | 'degree of freedom' vector restricted to the beam element, | | {\ddot{u}}_{\text{LOC}} | 'acceleration' vector restricted to the beam element. | One then changes the signs of the forces at node 1. Indeed, taking for example the case of tension–compression, one shows R3.08.01 that the forces in the element (option EFGE_ELNO) are obtained by: \left[\begin{array}{c}-N(o)\\ N(L)\end{array}\right]=\left[K\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}u(o)\\ u(L)\end{array}\right]-\left[\begin{array}{c}{f}_{1}\\ {f}_{2}\end{array}\right] 7.2.2 Generalised forces, option: SIEF_ELGA The option "SIEF_ELGA" is implemented for reasons of compatibility with other options. It serves only for the computation of the nodal forces. It produces a force field by elements. It is computed by: {R}_{\text{LOC}}={K}_{\text{LOC}}^{e}{u}_{\text{LOC}} 7.3 Computation of the nodal forces and of the reactions 7.3.1 Nodal forces, option: FORC_NODA This option computes a vector of nodal forces over the whole structure, expressed in the global frame. It produces a field at the nodes in the command CALC_CHAMP by assembly of the elementary terms. For this computation, one uses the principle of virtual work and one writes [R5.03.01]: F={Q}^{T}\sigma where {Q}^{T} symbolically represents the matrix associated with the divergence operator. For an element, one writes the work of the virtual strain field: ({Q}^{T}\sigma ){u}^{\text{ }}={\int}_{\Omega}\sigma (u)\varepsilon ({u}^{\text{ }})\forall {u}^{\text{ }} kinematically admissible For the beam elements, one simply computes the nodal forces by assembly of the elementary nodal forces computed by the option SIEF_ELGA, which are expressed by: \left[{F}_{\text{LOC}}\right]=\left[{K}_{\text{LOC}}\right]\left[{U}_{\text{LOC}}\right] 7.3.2 Nodal reactions, option: REAC_NODA This option, called by CALC_CHAMP, makes it possible to obtain the reactions R at the supports, expressed in the global frame, from the nodal forces F by: R=F-{F}^{\text{char}}+{F}^{\text{iner}} {F}^{\text{char}}\text{et}{F}^{\text{iner}} being the nodal forces associated respectively with the given loadings (concentrated and distributed) and with the inertia forces. 8 Bibliography [1] J.L. r3.08.05 A cable–pulley finite element r3.08.05 A cable–pulley finite element Summary: Pulleys play an important role in cable structures such as overhead electric lines. It is therefore useful to know how to model them in a manner which is at once realistic and efficient. The finite-element formulation of a length of cable passing over a pulley is presented: expressions of the internal forces and of the stiffness matrix. The pulley may be fixed or supported by a flexible structure. Its position on the cable at equilibrium is not known a priori: this position is that for which the tension of the cable is the same on either side. 1 Notation | A | area of the cross-section of the cable. | | --- | --- | | E | Young’s modulus. | | F | vector of the internal forces of the element. | | {F}_{n} | internal force at the node n . | | H | horizontal component of the tension [§An1]. | | {I}_{3} | identity matrix of order 3. | | K | stiffness matrix of the element. | | l | current length of the element. | | {l}_{0} | length at rest. | | {l}_{i} | initial length. | | {l}_{1} | \overrightarrow{{N}_{3}{N}_{1}} | | {l}_{1} | Euclidean norm of {l}_{1} | | {l}_{2} | \overrightarrow{{N}_{3}{N}_{2}} | | {l}_{2} | Euclidean norm of {l}_{2} . | | N | current tension of the cable constituting the element. | | {N}_{i} | initial tension (pretension). | | S | sag of a cable span [§An1]. | | s | length of a span [§An1]. | | T | current temperature. | | {T}_{i} | initial temperature. | | u | displacement vector of the nodes with respect to the initial position. | | {u}_{n} | displacement of the node n with respect to its initial position. | | w | weight per unit length. | | {x}_{n} | position vector of the node n in the initial configuration. | | \alpha | coefficient of thermal expansion. | | \varepsilon | current strain with respect to the initial configuration. | 2 Introduction Pulleys are used, during the construction of overhead electric lines, for the cable-stringing operation. The cable in the course of stringing [Figure 2-a] is fixed to one of the anchor supports of the section; it rests on pulleys placed at the bottom of the insulators of the alignment supports and it is retained by a force at the level of the second anchor support. By acting on this force — or by moving its point of application — one adjusts the sag of one of the spans, the one which is the most subject to environmental constraints. The pulleys are then removed and the cable is fixed to the insulators. The length of the cable in the various spans is then fixed, and it determines the subsequent behaviour of the line under static loadings (wind, ice overload) and in the dynamic regime (motion due to the Laplace forces created by the short-circuit currents). Figure 2-a: Stringing of a cable in a section with two spans The cable–pulley finite element presented here makes it possible to model the stringing operation and therefore to compute, in a natural way, the length of cable in the various spans. The idea of this finite element came to us some time after the conversation [bib1] and we presented its formulation in [bib2]. 3 Assumptions and definition of a cable–pulley finite element Figure 3-a: Length of cable passing over a pulley — real Take a length of cable {N}_{1}{N}_{2} passing over the pulley {N}_{3} [Figure 3-a]. This pulley is not necessarily fixed and may, for example and as is the case in the example of [§8], be mounted at the end of a cable. Figure 3-b: Length of cable passing over a pulley — modelled The pulley is assumed to be a point [Figure 3-b]. The following assumptions are made in addition: - The equilibrium position of {N}_{3} is not known, but it necessarily lies on the length {N}_{1} {N}_{2} deformed from its initial position. In the modelling of lines, the horizontal motions are of small amplitude and this assumption is generally not restrictive; - The two strands {N}_{3} {N}_{1} and {N}_{3} {N}_{2} are always rectilinear, like cable elements of the 1st order. It follows from this assumption that: {l}_{1}={x}_{1}+{u}_{1}-{x}_{3}-{u}_{3} eq 3-1 {l}_{2}={x}_{2}+{u}_{2}-{x}_{3}-{u}_{3} {l}_{1}=\sqrt{{l}_{1}^{T}{l}_{1}} eq 3-2 {l}_{2}=\sqrt{{l}_{2}^{T}{l}_{2}} The total length of the two strands is: - in the current position, where the temperature is T : l={l}_{1}+{l}_{2} ; - in the initial position, designated by the index i , where the tension is {N}_{i} and the temperature {T}_{i} : {l}_{i}={({l}_{1})}_{i}+{({l}_{2})}_{i} ; - in an unstressed position, designated by the index 0, where the temperature is {T}_{0} : {l}_{0}={({l}_{1})}_{0}+{({l}_{2})}_{0}. - The pulley is frictionless and therefore the tension is the same in the two strands. It follows from this assumption that the strain e is also the same, and one takes as its value the measure of the relative elongation of the length with respect to the initial state: \varepsilon =\frac{l-{l}_{i}}{{l}_{0}} eq 3-3 \varepsilon must remain small, so that the section A is considered as constant. One will note that, within the framework of the finite-element method, the line loads do not prevent the tension from being constant from {N}_{1} to {N}_{2} . These forces are in fact concentrated at the nodes {N}_{1} and {N}_{2} and on the axis of the pulley {N}_{3} . - The constitutive relation is elastic: N=\text{EA}\left[e-\alpha (T-{T}_{i})\right]+{N}_{i} eq 3-4 One calls cable–pulley finite element a length of cable {N}_{1} {N}_{2} {N}_{3} satisfying the preceding assumptions. 4 Internal forces of a cable–pulley finite element Let us recall the following definition: the internal forces of a structural finite element are the forces which must be exerted at its nodes in order to maintain it in its current deformed configuration. In the case of a cable–pulley finite element, the internal forces are deduced immediately from statics. One has indeed [Figure 4-a]: {F}_{1}=\frac{N}{{l}_{1}}{l}_{1} eq 4-1 {F}_{2}=\frac{N}{{l}_{2}}{l}_{2} and, in order to ensure equilibrium: {F}_{3}=-({F}_{1}+{F}_{2}). {F}_{1} and {F}_{2} having the same modulus, {F}_{3} is directed along the bisector of the angle ({N}_{1}{N}_{3}{N}_{2}) . Figure 4-a: Internal forces of a cable–pulley element {F}_{3} is applied to the axis of the pulley. The system F of the internal forces of the element is therefore: F=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{F}_{1}\\ {F}_{2}\\ {F}_{3}\end{array}\right\rbrace . 5 Stiffness matrix The stiffness matrix K of the element is the Fréchet derivative of F in the direction of the displacement \deltau of the nodes: \deltaf =K\deltau . K is computed by the following classical formula, used intensively in [bib3], [bib4] and [bib5]: \deltaf =\underset{\varepsilon \to 0}{\lim}\frac{\delta}{\delta \varepsilon }F(u+\varepsilon \deltau ) . eq 5-1 The detail of the computations is given in [§An1] and the final expression of K is the following: K=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{K}_{11}+\frac{N}{{l}_{1}}{I}_{3}& {K}_{12}& -{K}_{11}-{K}_{12}-\frac{N}{{l}_{1}}{I}_{3}\\ {K}_{12}^{T}& {K}_{22}+\frac{N}{{l}_{2}}{I}_{3}& -{K}_{22}-{K}_{12}^{T}-\frac{N}{{l}_{2}}{I}_{3}\\ -{K}_{11}-{K}_{12}^{T}-\frac{N}{{l}_{1}}{I}_{3}& -{K}_{22}-{K}_{12}-\frac{N}{{l}_{2}}{I}_{3}& {K}_{11}+{K}_{22}+{K}_{12}+{K}_{12}^{T}+(\frac{1}{{l}_{1}}+\frac{1}{{l}_{2}})N{I}_{3}\end{array}\right] eq 5-2 N is given by [eq 3-4] and [eq 3-3] ; \begin{array}{}{K}_{11}=(\frac{\text{EA}}{{l}_{0}}-\frac{N}{{l}_{1}})\frac{1}{{l}_{1}^{2}}{l}_{1}{l}_{1}^{T};\\ {K}_{12}=\frac{\text{EA}}{{l}_{0}{l}_{1}{l}_{2}}{l}_{1}{l}_{2}^{T};\\ {K}_{22}=(\frac{\text{EA}}{{l}_{0}}-\frac{N}{{l}_{2}})\frac{1}{{l}_{2}^{2}}{l}_{2}{l}_{2}^{T}.\end{array} K is symmetric , because of the symmetry of {K}_{11} and of {K}_{22} and of the global symmetry by blocks. But K depends on the displacements of {N}_{1},{N}_{2}\text{et}{N}_{3} through {l}_{1},{l}_{2}\text{et}N : the cable–pulley finite element is therefore a non-linear element. 6 Mass matrix This matrix obviously intervenes only in dynamic problems. The cable–pulley element is used in Code_Aster only for the quasi-static problems of cable stringing [§7]. Note: An example of a dynamic problem comprising a cable–pulley is nevertheless presented in [bib2]. The mass matrix of the element {N}_{1} {N}_{2} {N}_{3} is obtained by assembling the “consistent” mass matrices of the two-node cable elements {N}_{3} {N}_{1} and {N}_{3} {N}_{2} [bib6] and by adding the point mass of the pulley. It must be noted that, in the course of a dynamic analysis, this mass matrix must be updated because the lengths {l}_{1} and {l}_{2} vary. 7 Introduction of the cable–pulley element into Code_Aster The cable–pulley element is supported by a mesh cell SEG3. In the command AFFE_MODELE, under the factor keyword AFFE, one must define the arguments of the keywords as follows: | keyword | GROUP_MA | PHENOMENE | MODELISATION | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | argument | mesh-cell group of cable–pulley | 'MECANIQUE' | 'CABLE_POULIE' | The constituent material must be elastic. In the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM, the cable–pulleys are treated as cables. Since the cable–pulley element is non-linear [§5] and, for the moment, it is used only in statics [§6], it is accessible only through the operator STAT_NON_LINE. Under the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT, the arguments of the keywords are the following: | keyword | GROUP_MA | RELATION | DEFORMATION | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | argument | mesh-cell group of cable–pulley | 'ELAS' | 'GROT_GDEP' | Finally, the gravity force acting on the nodes {N}_{1}\text{et}{N}_{2} of a cable–pulley element [fig 3‑b] is a follower force, because it depends on the length of the strands {N}_{3}{N}_{1}\text{et}{N}_{3}{N}_{2} . For a structure comprising at least one cable–pulley element, one must specify this (follower) load in STAT_NON_LINE under the factor keyword EXCIT. An example of application is found in the test SSNL100A V6.02.100. Note: The cable–pulley element does not make it possible to take into account strain due to temperature. 8 Example of application This example is that of the stringing of a cable with two spans and with an imposed regulating tension. In [Figure 7-a], O is the anchorage of the cable on the left-hand anchor support. {P}_{1} is a first pulley placed at the foot of the suspension chain {P}_{1}C , fixed at C to the alignment support. {P}_{2} is a second pulley placed on the right-hand anchor support. O , {P}_{1} and {P}_{2} are, for simplicity, situated on a horizontal line. Figure 7-a: Equilibrium of a cable with two spans, subjected to a given regulating tension. {\text{OP}}_{1}={\text{P}}_{1}{\text{P}}_{2}=100m ; w=30N/m ; E´A=5x{10}^{7}N ; {N}_{p}=\mathrm{5 000}N In the initial position, the cable at rest, assumed weightless, is straight: the centre-line of [Figure 7-a]. For the finite-element modelling, this line is subdivided into: - ten two-node cable elements between O and {Q}_{1} ; - one cable–pulley element {Q}_{1} {R}_{1} {P}_{1} ; - nine cable elements between {R}_{1} and {Q}_{2} ; - one cable–pulley element {Q}_{2} {R}_{2} {P}_{2} . The cable is subjected simultaneously to gravity and to the regulating tension {N}_{p} exerted at {R}_{2} . The equilibrium position (solid line of [Figure 7-a]) is reached in 11 iterations by the operator STAT_NON_LINE of Code_Aster . The sags are 7.955m and 7.867m , respectively in the left-hand span and in the right-hand span. For an inextensible cable of a span of 100m , of line weight 30N/m and subjected to an end tension of \mathrm{5 000}N , the theoretical sag is 7.941m [§An2]. By acting on the regulating tension, one can adjust one of the two sags to a value fixed in advance. 9 Conclusion The cable–pulley finite element presented in this note, of a very simple mechanical formulation, has performances comparable to those of an ordinary cable element. It is very convenient and even indispensable for a realistic modelling of overhead electric lines. It should find other applications, notably in Robotics. 10 Bibliography 1. AUFAURE (EDF/IMA/MMN) | Initial text | | 10.1 | J.M.PROIX (EDF-R&D/AMA) | Modification of GREEN into GROT_GDEP | Computation of the stiffness matrix It is shown here how the formula [eq 5-1] applies to the computation of the first three rows of the matrix K [eq 5-2], those which relate to the force {F}_{1} . The other rows are obtained either by permutation of the indices, or by summation of two preceding rows. The first rows are therefore obtained by computing the derivative: \underset{e\to 0}{\lim}\frac{d}{\mathrm{de}}{F}_{1}(u+\text{ed}u) eq An1-1 and by factoring out the vector \deltau . According to the relations [eq 4-1], [eq 3-4] and [eq 3-3], one has: {F}_{1}(u+\varepsilon \delta u)=\left\lbrace \text{EA}\left[\frac{{l}_{1}(u+\varepsilon du)+{l}_{2}(u+\varepsilon \delta u)-{l}_{i}}{{l}_{0}}-\alpha (T-{T}_{i})\right]+{N}_{i}\right\rbrace \frac{{l}_{1}(u+\varepsilon \delta u)}{{l}_{1}(u+\varepsilon \delta u)} with, according to [eq 3-1]: {l}_{1}(u+\varepsilon \deltau )={x}_{1}+{u}_{1}+\varepsilon \delta {u}_{1}-{x}_{3}-{u}_{3}-\varepsilon \delta {u}_{3} and, according to [eq 3-2]: {l}_{1}(u+\varepsilon \deltau )=\sqrt{{l}_{1}^{T}(u+\varepsilon \deltau ){l}_{1}(u+\varepsilon \deltau )}. Consequently: \underset{\varepsilon \to 0}{\lim}\frac{d}{d\varepsilon }{l}_{1}(u+\varepsilon \deltau )=\delta {u}_{1}-\delta {u}_{3} \underset{\varepsilon \to 0}{\lim}\frac{d}{d\varepsilon }{l}_{1}(u+\varepsilon \deltau )=\frac{1}{{l}_{1}(u)}{l}_{1}^{T}(u)(\delta {u}_{1}-\delta {u}_{3}) and by permutation of the indices 1 and 2: \underset{\varepsilon \to 0}{\lim}\frac{d}{d\varepsilon }{l}_{2}(u+\varepsilon \deltau )=\frac{1}{{l}_{2}(u)}{l}_{2}^{T}(u)(\delta {u}_{2}-\delta {u}_{3}) Finally: \underset{\varepsilon \to 0}{\lim}\frac{d}{d\varepsilon }{l}_{1}(u+\varepsilon \deltau )=\frac{1}{{l}_{1}^{3}(u)}{l}_{1}^{T}(u)(\delta {u}_{1}-\delta {u}_{3}) By carrying the preceding expressions into [eq An1-1] and by factoring out the vector \deltau , one easily obtains the first three rows of K . Equilibrium shape of an inextensible heavy cable subjected to a given tension at the end Take a cable [Figure An2-a] one end of which is fixed at the point O and the other end P of which is subjected to the tension {N}_{p} . O and P are on the same horizontal line and a distance s apart. The line weight is w . One seeks the sag S . Figure An2-a: Heavy cable in equilibrium One finds in [bib7], p 6, the following well-known formulae: - equilibrium shape of the cable: z(x)=\frac{H}{w}\left[\cosh\frac{w}{H}(\frac{s}{2}-x)-\cosh\frac{\mathrm{ws}}{\mathrm{2H}}\right]; eq An2-1 - tension: N(x)=H\cosh\frac{w}{H}(\frac{s}{2}-x). eq An2-2 H is the horizontal tension, constant along the cable since the distributed external force — the weight — is vertical. H is computed by [eq An2-2] written at P : \cosh\frac{\mathrm{ws}}{\mathrm{2H}}-\frac{{\mathrm{2N}}_{p}}{\mathrm{ws}}\frac{\mathrm{ws}}{\mathrm{2H}}=0. \frac{\mathrm{ws}}{\mathrm{2H}} is therefore a root of the transcendental equation: \coshX=\frac{{\mathrm{2N}}_{p}}{\mathrm{ws}}X. This equation has two roots [Figure An2-b] if: \frac{{\mathrm{2N}}_{p}}{\mathrm{ws}}>{p}_{0}, with: {p}_{0}=\sinh{x}_{0} and: {x}_{0}=\text{cotanh}{x}_{0}{x}_{0}>0. Figure An2-b: Computation of \frac{\mathrm{ws}}{\mathrm{2H}} The smaller root, which corresponds to the greater tension of the cable, is the only useful one. The other root corresponds to a considerable sag of the cable, of the order of magnitude of its span. \frac{\mathrm{ws}}{\mathrm{2H}} having been computed, the sag is deduced from [eq An2-1]: S=\frac{s}{2}\frac{\mathrm{2H}}{\mathrm{ws}}(\cosh\frac{\mathrm{ws}}{\mathrm{2H}}-1) .

r3.08.06 Straight and curved pipe finite elements with ovalisation, swelling and warping in elastoplasticity r3.08.06 Straight and curved pipe finite elements with ovalisation, swelling and warping in elastoplasticity Summary: This document presents the modelling of a pipe finite element usable in piping analyses in elasticity or in plasticity. The pipes, curved or straight, may be relatively thick (ratio of thickness to radius of the cross-section up to 0.2 ) and are subjected to various combined loadings — internal pressure, in-plane and out-of-plane bending, torsion, extension — and may have a non-linear behaviour. This line element combines both shell and beam properties. The mean fibre of the pipe behaves as a beam and the surface of the pipe as a shell. The element produced is a straight or curved pipe element in small rotations and strains, with an elastoplastic behaviour in plane stress. Three modellings, corresponding to three different types of element, are available: - TUYAU_3M, which takes into account 3 Fourier modes at most, and which may be supported on mesh cells with 3 nodes or with 4 nodes. - TUYAU_6M, which takes into account up to 6 Fourier modes, and is supported on mesh cells with 3 nodes. 1 Introduction There exists an extensive bibliography on the modelling of piping, and numerous finite elements for straight and elbow pipes are available in the major finite-element codes. Reviews have already been carried out [bib1], [bib5], [bib6] in the past, which have been completed by incorporating the latest developments known in the field [bib11]. The important effects to be taken into account are the swelling due to the internal pressure and the ovalisation of the cross-sections by combined in-plane and out-of-plane bending. One places oneself in the assumption of small rotations and strains within the framework of this document. It is a line element with 3 or 4 nodes, of curved or straight beam type with local plasticity taking ovalisation, warping and swelling into account. The beam kinematics is enriched by a shell kinematics for the description of the behaviour of the cross-sections. This kinematics is discretised in M Fourier modes, the number M of which must at once be sufficient to obtain good results in plasticity and not too large in order to limit the computation time. The literature encourages us to use M=6 [bib9], [bib13] in plasticity. In elasticity, for thick pipes, one may be content with M=2 or M=3 . 2 The various shell and beam theories for straight or elbow pipe finite elements This chapter presents the elements of kinematics in three-dimensional curvilinear geometry, as well as their restrictions within the framework of beam and shell models. Indeed, in order to build the enriched piping finite element which meets the specification defined in the introduction, one exploits a technique of decomposition of the three-dimensional kinematics. The shell kinematics provides the description of ovalisation, swelling and warping, while the beam kinematics describes the general motion of the piping line. The various shell and beam theories used for each of the elements reflect the assumptions chosen a priori on the type of strains and of behaviours. 2.1 The pipe in beam theory 2.1.1 Case of an elbow pipe A first, relatively simple, approach amounts to considering the elbow represented below as a hollow beam of circular section. The beam is obtained by rotation through an angle \Theta of the circular section about \mathit{OZ} . A point of the beam is located by its distance r from the axis of the beam and by the two angles \theta , \phi where \theta is the longitudinal angle with \mathit{OY} indicated above and \phi the trigonometric angle with \mathit{OZ} measured on the circular section. Figure 2.1.1-a: Geometry and kinematics of the elbow in beam theory In the curvilinear coordinate system ( r , \theta , \phi ), the relations between the displacements u of the points of the elbow of position {r}_{0}=\text{OM}=-\text{R}{e}_{y}(\theta )+r{e}_{r}(\theta ,\phi ) and the Green–Lagrange strains are given by the following tensor in the natural basis ( r , \theta , \phi ): 2{f}_{\alpha \beta }=\frac{\partial ({r}_{0}+u)}{\partial \alpha }.\frac{\partial ({r}_{0}+u)}{\partial \beta }-\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial \alpha }.\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial \beta } , (\alpha ,\beta )\in \left\lbrace r,\theta ,\phi \right\rbrace . The unit vectors in the directions ( r , \theta , \phi ) are: {e}_{r}=\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial r},{e}_{\theta}=\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial \theta },{e}_{\phi }=\frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial \phi } where A=\sqrt{\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial \theta }.\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial \theta }}\text{et}B=\sqrt{\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial \phi }.\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial \phi }} . If one expresses the position of a point of the elbow in the local orthonormal toroidal basis ( {e}_{r},{e}_{\theta},{e}_{\phi } ) by ( {y}_{r},{y}_{\theta},{y}_{\phi } ) one has the following relations: {e}_{r}=\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial {y}_{r}},{e}_{\theta}=\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial {y}_{\theta}},{e}_{\phi }=\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial {y}_{\phi }} . The expression of the Green-Lagrange strain tensor in this basis is then: 2{\varepsilon}_{\alpha \beta }=\frac{\partial ({r}_{0}+u)}{\partial {y}_{\alpha}}.\frac{\partial ({r}_{0}+u)}{\partial {y}_{\beta}}-\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial {y}_{\alpha}}.\frac{\partial {r}_{0}}{\partial {y}_{\beta}} . The transformation relations between the expression of the Green-Lagrange strains in the curvilinear coordinate system and in the local toroidal basis defined previously are: \begin{array}{}{\varepsilon}_{\text{rr}}={f}_{\text{rr}}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{{f}_{\theta \theta }}{{A}^{2}}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\phi \phi }=\frac{{f}_{\phi \phi }}{{B}^{2}}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\theta \phi }=\frac{{f}_{\theta \phi }}{\text{AB}}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\theta r}=\frac{{f}_{\theta r}}{A}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\phi r}=\frac{{f}_{\phi r}}{B}\end{array} The use of this basis is particularly interesting because the constitutive relations in the orthonormal toroidal basis are simple to use. For the elbow above, if one considers that the strains remain small, one then obtains [bib4] after linearisation of the Green–Lagrange strains: \begin{array}{}{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{rr}}=\frac{\partial {u}_{r}}{\partial r}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial {u}_{\theta}}{\partial \theta }+\frac{{u}_{\phi Indeed, the cross-sections undergo a rigid-body motion, which precludes modelling warping, swelling and ovalisation. 2.2 The pipe in linearised shell theory 2.2.1 General case The elbow pipe is considered as a thin shell of revolution (portion of a torus). The mean surface is obtained by rotation through an angle \Theta of a circle of radius a whose centre is at a distance R from the axis of revolution \mathit{Oz} . One denotes by h the thickness of the elbow. One imposes that this thickness remain constant and that the section of the elbow be perfectly circular. A point on the mean surface is characterised by the two angles \theta ,\phi and its position -h/2\le \zeta \le +h/2 with respect to the mean surface, where \theta is the longitudinal angle, varying between 0 and \Theta , and \phi the angle measured on the cross-section. Figure 2.2.1-a: Geometry and kinematics of the elbow in shell theory One first places oneself within the framework of the linearised theory of shells with transverse shear as it has been described for example in Washizu [bib14]. It limits our study to the framework of small strains. Moreover, the large rotations of the mean surface are not taken into account. The displacements and rotations are thus defined with respect to the initial geometry of the elbow. If the displacements of the points of the mean surface in the three directions \theta axial, \phi circumferential and \zeta radial are denoted u,v and w those of any point of the elbow are written in the following way : \begin{array}{}{u}_{\theta}=u(\theta ,\phi )+\zeta {\beta}_{\phi }(\theta ,\phi )\\ {u}_{\phi }=v(\theta ,\phi )-\zeta {\beta}_{\theta}(\theta ,\phi )\\ {u}_{\zeta}=w(\theta ,\phi )\end{array} where {\beta}_{\theta} and {\beta}_{\phi } are the rotations with respect to the vectors {e}_{\theta} and {e}_{\phi } respectively. The strains at every point are thus given by [bib14]: \begin{array}{}{\varepsilon}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{{E}_{\theta \theta }+\zeta {\kappa}_{\theta \theta }}{1+\zeta /{R}_{\theta}}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\phi \phi }=\frac{{E}_{\phi \phi }+\zeta {\kappa}_{\phi \phi }}{1+\zeta /{R}_{\phi }}\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{\theta \phi }={\gamma}_{\theta \phi }=\frac{2{E}_{\theta \phi }+2\zeta {\kappa}_{\theta \phi }}{(1+\zeta /{R}_{\theta})(1+\zeta /{R}_{\phi })}\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{\theta \zeta }={\gamma}_{\theta \zeta }=\frac{2{E}_{\theta \zeta }}{(1+\zeta /{R}_{\theta})}\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{\phi \zeta }={\gamma}_{\phi \zeta }=\frac{2{E}_{\phi \zeta }}{(1+\zeta /{R}_{\phi })}\end{array} with: A=R+a\sin\phi ,B=a,{R}_{\theta}=\frac{R+a\sin\phi }{\sin\phi },{R}_{\phi }=a. where {E}_{\theta \theta },{E}_{\phi \phi } and {E}_{\theta \phi } are the membrane strains of the mean surface, {\kappa}_{\theta \theta },{\kappa}_{\phi \phi },{\kappa}_{\theta \phi } the bending strains of the mean surface and {E}_{\theta \zeta },{E}_{\phi \zeta } the transverse distortions. The strains of the mean surface are related to the displacements of the mean surface by replacing the displacement field of the preceding paragraph by that given above. One then finds: \begin{array}{}{E}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial u}{\partial \theta }+\frac{v}{\text{AB}}\frac{\partial A}{\partial \phi }+\frac{w}{{R}_{\theta}}\\ {E}_{\phi \phi }=\frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial v}{\partial \phi }+\frac{w}{{R}_{\phi }}\\ 2{E}_{\theta \phi }=\frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial u}{\partial \phi }+\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial v}{\partial \theta }-\frac{u}{\text{AB}}\frac{\partial A}{\partial \phi }\\ {\kappa}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\phi }}{\partial \theta }-\frac{{\beta}_{\theta}}{\text{AB}}\frac{\partial A}{\partial \phi }\\ {\kappa}_{\phi \phi }=-\frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\theta}}{\partial \phi }\\ 2{\kappa}_{\theta \phi }=\frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\phi }}{\partial \phi }+\frac{1}{{R}_{\phi }}(\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial v}{\partial \theta }-\frac{u}{\text{AB}}\frac{\partial A}{\partial \phi })]\\ 2{E}_{\theta \zeta }={\beta}_{\phi }+\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial w}{\partial \theta }-\frac{u}{{R}_{\theta}}\\ 2{E}_{\phi \zeta }=-{\beta}_{\theta}+\frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial w}{\partial \phi }-\frac{v}{{R}_{\phi }}\end{array} That is also: \begin{array}{}{E}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{1}{R+a\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial u}{\partial \theta }+v\cos\phi +w\sin\phi )\\ {E}_{\phi \phi }=\frac{1}{a}(\frac{\partial v}{\partial \phi }+w)\\ {\gamma}_{\theta \phi }=\frac{1}{R+a\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial v}{\partial \theta }-u\cos\phi )+\frac{1}{a}\frac{\partial u}{\partial \phi }\\ {\kappa}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{1}{R+a\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\phi }}{\partial \theta }-{\beta}_{\theta}\cos\phi )\\ {\kappa}_{\phi \phi }=-\frac{1}{a}\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\theta}}{\partial \phi }\\ {\kappa}_{\theta \phi }=\frac{1}{a}\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\phi }}{\partial \phi }-\frac{1}{R+a\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\theta}}{\partial \theta }+{\beta}_{\phi }\cos\phi )+[\frac{\sin\phi }{R+a\sin\phi }\frac{1}{a}\frac{\partial u}{\partial \phi }+\frac{1}{R+a\sin\phi }\frac{1}{a}(\frac{\partial v}{\partial \theta }-u\cos\phi )]\\ {\gamma}_{\theta \zeta }={\beta}_{\phi }+\frac{1}{R+a\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \theta }-u\sin\phi )\\ {\gamma}_{\phi \zeta }=-{\beta}_{\theta}+\frac{1}{a}(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \phi }-v)\end{array} In this theory there are therefore five unknowns; 3 displacements u,v and w as well as two rotations {\beta}_{\theta},{\beta}_{\phi } . If the Love-Kirchhoff assumption is applied (thin tube) the transverse shears are zero and there remain only the 3 displacements u,v and w since: \begin{array}{}{\beta}_{\phi }=-\frac{1}{R+a\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \theta }-u\sin\phi )\\ {\beta}_{\theta}=\frac{1}{a}(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \phi }-v)\end{array} 2.2.2 Case of the straight pipe If one applies these equations to the case of the straight pipe with: A=1,B=a,1/{R}_{\theta}=0,{R}_{\phi }=a. One recovers the more usual expression for this kind of geometry: \begin{array}{}{E}_{xx}=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\ {E}_{\phi \phi }=\frac{1}{a}(\frac{\partial v}{\partial \phi }+w)\\ 2{E}_{x\phi }=\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}+\frac{1}{a}\frac{\partial u}{\partial \phi }\\ {\kappa}_{xx}=\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\phi }}{\partial x}\\ {\kappa}_{\phi \phi }=-\frac{1}{a}\frac{\partial {\beta}_{x}}{\partial \phi }\\ 2{\kappa}_{x\phi }=\frac{1}{a}\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\phi }}{\partial \phi }-\frac{\partial {\beta}_{x}}{\partial x}+[\frac{1}{a}\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}]\\ 2{E}_{x\zeta }={\beta}_{\phi }+\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\\ 2{E}_{\phi \zeta }=-{\beta}_{x}+\frac{1}{a}(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \phi }-v)\end{array} In this theory there are therefore five unknowns; 3 displacements u,v and w as well as two rotations {\beta}_{x},{\beta}_{\phi } . If the Love-Kirchhoff assumption is applied (thin tube) the transverse shears are zero and there remain only the 3 displacements u,v and w since: \begin{array}{}{\beta}_{\phi }=-\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\\ {\beta}_{x}=\frac{1}{a}(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \phi }-v)\end{array} 2.2.3 Note One can introduce the shell kinematics directly into the 3D strain field. In that case one has: \begin{array}{}{\varepsilon}_{\theta \theta }={E}_{\theta \theta }+\zeta {\kappa}_{\theta \theta }\\ {\varepsilon}_{\phi \phi }={E}_{\phi \phi }+\zeta {\kappa}_{\phi \phi }\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{\theta \phi }={\gamma}_{\theta \phi }=2{E}_{\theta \phi }+2\zeta {\kappa}_{\theta \phi }\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{\theta \zeta }={\gamma}_{\theta \zeta }=2{E}_{\theta \zeta }\\ 2{\varepsilon}_{\phi \zeta }={\gamma}_{\phi \zeta }=2{E}_{\phi \zeta }\end{array} where the expressions {E}_{\theta \theta },{E}_{\phi \phi } and {E}_{\theta \phi } for the membrane strains, {\kappa}_{\theta \theta },{\kappa}_{\phi \phi },{\kappa}_{\theta \phi } for the bending strains and {E}_{\theta \zeta },{E}_{\phi \zeta } for the transverse distortions are given by the following expression in the general case: \begin{array}{}{E}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{1}{R+r\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial u}{\partial \theta }+v\cos\phi +w\sin\phi )\\ {E}_{\phi \phi }=\frac{1}{r}(\frac{\partial v}{\partial \phi }+w)\\ 2{E}_{\theta \phi }=\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial u}{\partial \phi }+\frac{1}{R+r\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial v}{\partial \theta }-u\cos\phi )\\ {\kappa}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{1}{R+r\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\phi }}{\partial \theta }-{\beta}_{\theta}\cos\phi )\\ {\kappa}_{\phi \phi }=-\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\theta}}{\partial \phi }\\ 2{\kappa}_{\theta \phi }=\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\phi }}{\partial \phi }-\frac{1}{R+r\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial {\beta}_{\theta}}{\partial \theta }+{\beta}_{\phi }\cos\phi )\\ 2{E}_{\theta \zeta }={\beta}_{\phi }\frac{R+a\sin\phi }{R+r\sin\phi }+\frac{1}{R+r\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \theta }-u\sin\phi )\\ 2{E}_{\phi \zeta }=-{\beta}_{\theta}\frac{a}{r}+\frac{1}{r}(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \phi }-v)\end{array} One notes that to order 1 in \zeta the two ways of proceeding give identical results. It is the definition of the membrane or bending strain which changes. In the first case it is independent of the position through the thickness and is computed for the mean radius of the cross-section of the pipe, whereas it depends on it in the case of the 3D approach. The term in brackets in the expression of [§2.2.1] represents a coupling between bending and membrane which appears when one expresses R+r\sin\phi and r as a function of R+a\sin\phi and a . In the remainder of our analysis we shall use this degenerated 3D expression of the shell kinematics. If moreover we use the Love-Kirchhoff assumption for the transverse shears, {E}_{\theta \zeta }={E}_{\phi \zeta }=0 one indeed recovers the following expressions of the rotations: \begin{array}{}{\beta}_{\phi }=-\frac{1}{R+a\sin\phi }(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \theta }-u\sin\phi )\\ {\beta}_{\theta}=\frac{1}{a}(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \phi }-v)\end{array} and: \begin{array}{}{\kappa}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{1}{R+r\sin\phi }[-\frac{1}{R+a\sin\phi }(\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {\theta}^{2}}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial \theta }\sin\phi )-\frac{\cos\phi }{a}(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \phi }-v)]\\ {\kappa}_{\phi \phi }=-\frac{1}{\text{ar}}(\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial {\phi }^{2}}-\frac{\partial v}{\partial \phi })\\ 2{\kappa}_{\theta \phi }=(\frac{\partial w}{\partial \theta }-u\sin\phi )[\frac{\cos\phi }{(R+r\sin\phi )(R+a\sin\phi )}+\frac{a\cos\phi }{r(R+a\sin\phi {)}^{2}}]\\ -\frac{{\partial}^{2}w}{\partial \theta \partial \phi }[\frac{1}{a(R+r\sin\phi )}+\frac{1}{r(R+a\sin\phi )}]\\ +\frac{\partial v}{\partial \theta }\frac{1}{a(R+r\sin\phi )}+(\frac{\partial u}{\partial \phi }\sin\phi +u\cos\phi )\frac{1}{r(R+a\sin\phi )}\end{array} the expressions for {E}_{\theta \theta },{E}_{\phi \phi } and {E}_{\theta \phi } remaining unchanged. One can easily extend this note to the case of the straight pipe. 2.3 Analysis of straight and elbow pipes In conclusion of the two preceding analyses one can model the pipe as a beam element whose section is a thin shell. This interpretation is made in most codes ([bib2], [bib8], [bib9], [bib10], [bib12], etc...). In the absence of warping of the cross-sections (i.e. the cross-sections remain plane) the axial beam displacement gives the new position of the cross-section and the ovalisation displacements (it then suffices to take u=0 in the thin-shell equations) make it possible to know how the latter deforms. The total strain is obtained as the superposition of the beam strains and of the ovalisation strains. The displacement field which one represents in the figure below is written: U={U}^{p}+{U}^{s} . In the first displacement field the image of the cross-section is an identical cross-section obtained by translation and rotation of the first. In the second displacement field, the cross-section is deformed. Figure 2.3-a: Decomposition of the displacement into beam and shell fields The finite-element modelling must therefore account for two different mechanical responses: that of the beam and that of the shell for ovalisation, swelling and warping. These last three modellings involve degrees of freedom which are not nodal (Fourier-series decomposition for example). 3 Mixed shell-beam elements for straight and curved pipes 3.1 Kinematics One decomposes the displacement field into a macroscopic “beam” part and a supplementary local “shell” part. V is the useful space of the three-dimensional displacement fields defined on any section of pipe. For the beam part, as in R3.03.03, one introduces the space T of the fields associated with a wrench (defined by two vectors): T=\left\lbrace v\in V/\exists (T,\Omega )\text{tel que}v(M)=T+\Omega \wedge \text{GM}\right\rbrace For the displacement fields of T , T is the translation of the section (or of the point G ), \Omega the infinitesimal rotation and the fields v are the displacements preserving the section S plane and undeformed (one again uses the assumptions of NAVIER-BERNOULLI). T is a vector subspace of finite dimension equal to 6. It possesses an orthogonal complement for the scalar product on V : . {T}^{\perp }=\left\lbrace v\in V/\underset{S}{\int}v.w=0\forall w\in T\right\rbrace Any field u of V is then decomposed in a unique way as the sum of an element of T and of an element of {T}^{\perp } : u={u}^{p}+{u}^{s}{u}^{p}\in T,{u}^{s}\in {T}^{\perp } . One then postulates for the surface displacements of the pipe defined in [§2.2] the following Fourier-series decomposition which satisfies the preceding orthogonality principle with the beam displacements up to order 3 in the thickness of the pipe: u(x,\phi )=\sum_{m=2}^{M}{u}_{m}^{i}(x)\cosm\phi +\sum_{m=2}^{M}{u}_{m}^{o}(x)\sin m\phi v(x,\phi )={w}_{\mathrm{n1}}^{i}(x)\sin\phi +\sum_{m=2}^{M}{v}_{\text{nm}}^{i}(x)\sin m\phi \cdots -{w}_{\mathrm{n1}}^{o}(x)\cos\phi +\sum_{m=2}^{M}{v}_{\text{nm}}^{o}(x)\cosm\phi w(x,\phi )={w}_{n}^{o}(x) (uniform radial expansion) \cdots +\sum_{m=1}^{M}{w}_{\text{nm}}^{i}(x)\cosm\phi \cdots +\sum_{m=1}^{M}{w}_{\text{nm}}^{o}(x)\sin m\phi where x is the curvilinear abscissa along the elbow or the straight pipe, indifferently, and M the number of Fourier modes. The rotations {\beta}_{x}(x,\phi ) and {\beta}_{\phi }(x,\phi ) are deduced from u(x,\phi ),v(x,\phi )\text{et}w(x,\phi ) by the Love-Kirchhoff relations of [§2.2.1]. Note: One may note that in the decomposition of v(x,\phi )\text{et}w(x,\phi ) the terms in \cos\phi \text{et}\sin\phi are not completely independent because of the orthogonality with the beam displacements. This moreover makes it possible to avoid rigid-body motions, for if {v}_{\mathrm{n1}}^{i},{v}_{\mathrm{n1}}^{o}\text{et}{w}_{\mathrm{n1}}^{i},{w}_{\mathrm{n1}}^{o} are independent, one can find a non-zero solution giving zero strains. Moreover in the expression of u(x,\phi ) one notes the absence of the terms in \cos\phi and \sin\phi already present in the beam part. If one neglects the variation of the metric with the thickness of the pipe the conditions of rigorous orthogonality between the beam displacements and those of the surface of the pipe are satisfied. In the contrary case, in order to satisfy this condition rigorously one would need a Fourier-series expansion of the rotations {\beta}_{x}(x,\phi ) and {\beta}_{\phi }(x,\phi ) starting at order 2. This is incompatible with the Love_Kirchhoff assumptions for these rotations. 3.2 Constitutive law The behaviour of the new element is a 3D behaviour in plane stress, because the global behaviour of the structure is that of a thin shell. It follows that {\sigma}_{\zeta \zeta }=0 and the constitutive law is written in general in the following way: (\begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{xx}\\ {\sigma}_{\phi \phi }\\ {\sigma}_{x\phi }\\ {\sigma}_{\zeta \phi }\\ {\sigma}_{x\zeta }\end{array})=C(\begin{array}{c}{\varepsilon}_{xx}^{p}+{\varepsilon}_{xx}^{s}\\ {\epsilon}_{\phi \phi }^{p}+{\varepsilon}_{\phi \phi }^{s}\\ {\gamma}_{x\phi }^{p}+{\gamma}_{x\phi }^{s}\\ {\gamma}_{r\phi }^{p}+{\gamma}_{\zeta \phi }^{s}\\ {\gamma}_{\mathrm{xr}}^{p}+{\gamma}_{x\zeta }^{s}\end{array})=C(\begin{array}{c}{\varepsilon}_{xx}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\phi \phi }\\ {\gamma}_{x\phi }\\ {\gamma}_{\zeta \phi }\\ {\gamma}_{x\zeta }\end{array}) In our case one will neglect the transverse shears for the shell part of our displacement field. It therefore follows that {\gamma}_{\zeta x}^{s}={\gamma}_{\zeta \phi }^{s}=0 . As moreover [§2.1.2] one has shown that {\gamma}_{r\phi }^{p}=0 it follows that {\sigma}_{\zeta \phi }=0 . For an elastic behaviour one thus has: (\begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{xx}\\ {\sigma}_{\phi \phi }\\ {\sigma}_{x\phi }\\ {\sigma}_{x\zeta }\end{array})=\frac{E}{1-{\nu}^{2}}(\begin{array}{cccc}1& \nu & 0& 0\\ \nu & 1& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& \frac{1-\nu }{2}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0& \frac{1-\nu }{2}\end{array})(\begin{array}{c}{\varepsilon}_{xx}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\phi \phi }\\ {\gamma}_{x\phi }\\ {\gamma}_{x\zeta }\end{array}) and C=\frac{E}{1-{\nu}^{2}}(\begin{array}{cccc}1& \nu & 0& 0\\ \nu & 1& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& \frac{1-\nu }{2}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0& \frac{1-\nu }{2}\end{array}) . 3.3 Strain work The general expression of the 3D strain work for the elbow element with the type of behaviour stated above is: {W}_{\text{def}}=\underset{0}{\overset{l}{\int}}\underset{0}{\overset{2\pi }{\int}}\underset{-h/2}{\overset{h/2}{\int}}({\varepsilon}_{xx}{\sigma}_{xx}+{\varepsilon}_{\phi \phi }{\sigma}_{\phi \phi }+{\gamma}_{x\phi }{\sigma}_{x\phi }+{\gamma}_{x\zeta }{\sigma}_{x\zeta })\text{dV} where l is the curvilinear abscissa which is equal to l=(R+r\sin\phi )\theta for an elbow where \theta is the angle travelled in order to describe the elbow. In the case of an elbow, one thus has \text{dV}=(R+r\sin\phi )d\theta rd\phi d\zeta and for a straight pipe \text{dV}=\mathrm{dxrd}\phi d\zeta where \zeta . is the position through the thickness of the elbow which varies between -h/2 and +h/2. In what follows the index d denotes the results for the straight pipe and the index c for the curved pipe. - Volume: \begin{array}{}{V}_{d}=\underset{0}{\overset{l}{\int}}\underset{0}{\overset{2\pi }{\int}}\underset{-h/2}{\overset{h/2}{\int}}r\text{dx}\mathrm{d\phi }\mathrm{d\zeta }=\mathrm{2\pi }\text{lah}\\ {V}_{c}=\underset{0}{\overset{l}{\int}}\underset{0}{\overset{2\pi }{\int}}\underset{-h/2}{\overset{h/2}{\int}}r\text{dx}\mathrm{d\phi }\mathrm{d\zeta }=\underset{0}{\overset{\Theta}{\int}}\underset{0}{\overset{2\pi }{\int}}\underset{-h/2}{\overset{h/2}{\int}}R+(a+\zeta )\sin\phi \mathrm{d\theta }\mathrm{d\phi }\mathrm{d\zeta }=2\pi R\Theta \text{ah}\end{array} . - Centre of gravity: The position of the latter is computed from the mid-point of the two end nodes of the pipe element, in the frame associated with the internal node of the element (cf [§2.1.1]). In the case of a straight pipe, the notion of centre of curvature has no meaning. O and G coincide with the internal node of the element and the middle of the segment joining the two vertex nodes. The intersection between the cross-section and the straight line issuing from the centre of this section directed by {z}_{k} is the trace of a generator represented below. Figure 6.1-a: Representation of the reference generator The origin of the \phi common to all the elements is defined with respect to the trace of this generator on the cross-section. The angle between the trace of the generator and the current position on the cross-section is then called \psi . 6.2 Connection of one element to the next The kinematics of [§3.1] is given in the plane of the elbow. The latter is determined by the arc of a circle generated by the axis of the elbow. The origin of the angles is the normal to the plane chosen as in [§2.1]. Defining the origin from a generator makes it possible to remove the problems of continuity of displacements from one element to another. Indeed if one postulates that the relative displacements of the cross-sections are of the type \sum_{p=1}^{M}{u}_{p}^{i}\cos\mathrm{p\psi }+{u}_{p}^{o}\sin\mathrm{p\psi } where \psi is the angle with the trace of the generator on the cross-section, the continuity of the displacements is automatically ensured from one element to the next. One denotes by Z the vector perpendicular to the plane of the elbow corresponding to the origin of the angles chosen up to now. One notes that the vectors Z and {z}_{k} are in the plane of the section k . \phi is the angle defined with respect to Z . If one introduces \psi the angle counted from the trace of the generator on the cross-section (therefore with respect to {z}_{k} ) one has the following relation: \psi =\phi -{\Omega}_{k} where {\Omega}_{k}=({Z,z}_{k}) is the angle between Z and {z}_{k} in the plane of the cross-section. Thus the displacements are henceforth of the type \sum_{p=1}^{M}{u}_{p}^{i}\cos p(\phi -{\Omega}_{k})+{u}_{p}^{o}\sin p(\phi -{\Omega}_{k}) . It is to be noted that for a given elbow the angle {\Omega}_{k} is identical whatever the cross-section chosen. It is on passing from one elbow to the next that the value of {\Omega}_{k} changes. Note : When the piping is made up of collinear straight elements, one arbitrarily chooses \Omega =0 . 6.3 Numerical implementation The piping line is meshed by straight or curved elements to be ordered. The first element indicates the beginning of the piping line. One determines for this element the associated triad {x}_{1},{y}_{1},{z}_{1} . If this element is straight, one chooses {\Omega}_{1}=0 , otherwise one computes {\Omega}_{1} as indicated in the preceding paragraph. If the first element is straight the triad associated with the first cross-section of the second element {x}_{2},{y}_{2},{z}_{2} is obtained by translation of {x}_{1},{y}_{1},{z}_{1} . If the first element is curved, the associated triad {x}_{2},{y}_{2},{z}_{2} is obtained by rotation of {x}_{1},{y}_{1},{z}_{1} in the plane of the elbow. In that case {\Omega}_{2}=0 if the second element is straight and {\Omega}_{2}=({z}^{2},{z}_{2}) if the second element is curved where {z}^{2} is constructed like the z of [Figure 2.1.1-a]. The remainder of the construction is easily deduced by recurrence from the preceding scheme. 7 Shell-pipe and 3D-pipe connections 7.1 Approach followed One adopts here an approach similar to the cases 3D-beam R3.03.03, and shell-beam R3.03.06: it consists in characterising the connection between an end node of a pipe element and a group of edge mesh cells of shell or 3D elements. This makes it possible to mesh part of the piping (for example an elbow) in shells or 3D elements, and the rest in straight pipes. Figure 7.1-a: Connection between a COQUE_3D mesh and straight pipes [HI75-98/001] Thanks to the kinematics introduced in the pipe element, the shell–pipe and 3D–pipe connections must make it possible to mesh in shell elements or in 3D only the elbow, without straight parts, since the damping of the ovalisation (and of the warping) is taken into account in the pipe element. The connection is expressed by kinematic relations between the degrees of freedom of the nodes of S (which represents the connection section, modelled by shell or 3D edge elements), and the pipe node N . For the connection to be effective, it is necessary R3.03.03 that it satisfy the following properties: 1. be able to transmit beam forces to the shell or 3D mesh, and be able to transmit all the degrees of freedom of the pipe element (or the forces dual to them), 2. not generate parasitic stresses in the shell or 3D elements, 3. not favour the kinematic relations or the static conditions with respect to one another, 4. admit arbitrary behaviours and work in dynamics. The linear relations will have the same form as in the shell-beam case, with additional equations specific to the degrees of freedom of the pipe. One has already introduced in [§3.1] the space T of the fields associated with a wrench (defined by two vectors): T=\left\lbrace v\in V/\exists (T,\Omega )\text{tel que}v(M)=T+\Omega \wedge \text{GM}\right\rbrace where for the displacement fields of T , T is the translation of the section (or of the point G ), \Omega the infinitesimal rotation and the fields are the displacements preserving the section S plane and undeformed (one again uses the assumptions of NAVIER-BERNOULLI). The displacement of the pipe is then equal to: \begin{array}{ccc}{u}^{t}={u}^{p}+{u}^{s}& {u}^{p}\in T& ,{u}^{s}\in {T}^{\perp }\end{array} where: {T}^{\perp }=\left\lbrace v\in V/\underset{S}{\int}v.w=0\forall w\in T\right\rbrace The approach consists in decomposing the shell displacement field {u}^{c} or the three-dimensional displacement field {u}^{\mathrm{3d}} into three fields: {u}^{c}={u}^{p}+{u}^{s}+{u}^{\epsilon} - a displacement field following a beam kinematics {u}^{p} (wrench), - a local displacement field of the section following the pipe kinematics {u}^{s} (Fourier series) defined in [§3.1], - a supplementary field {u}^{\epsilon} orthogonal to the first two in the sense of the scalar product. Note: When the Fourier-series decomposition of [§3.1] is infinite one has {u}^{\epsilon}=0 . In order to translate the equation above into linear relations, one shows that one must compute the following integrals, for the shell (or the 3D) and the pipe: - mean displacement: {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\text{dS} - mean rotation: {\int}_{S}\text{GM}\wedge {u}^{c}\text{dS} - mean swelling: {\int}_{S}\frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }.{u}^{c}\text{dS} - Fourier modes: {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS},{\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} , {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\wedge \frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} , {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\wedge \frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} , {\int}_{S}\frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }.{u}^{c}\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} , {\int}_{S}\frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }.{u}^{c}\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} . For the Fourier modes one will choose the relations simplest to exploit since some are redundant (see the note of [§6.7]). Note: One easily passes from the analytical expressions of the 3D–pipe connection to those of the shell–pipe connection. It suffices to substitute {u}^{\mathrm{3d}} for {u}^{c} in the set of connection integrals proposed above. One will therefore speak of this connection again only in [§7.8] dealing with the numerical implementation. 7.2 Kinematics of the pipe. In the curvilinear basis (o,x,y,z) associated with the cross-section of [§2.1] one denotes the displacements {u}_{1},{u}_{2}\text{et}{u}_{3} where: \begin{array}{}{u}_{1}(r,x,\phi )={u}_{x}(x)-{\theta}_{y}(x)r\cos\phi +{\theta}_{z}(x)r\sin\phi +u(x,\phi )+\zeta {\beta}_{\phi }(x,\phi )\\ {u}_{2}(r,x,\phi )={u}_{y}(x)+{\theta}_{x}(x)r\cos\phi -v(x,\phi )\cos\phi -w(x,\phi )\sin\phi +\zeta {\beta}_{\theta}(x,\phi )\cos\phi \\ {u}_{3}(r,x,\phi )={u}_{z}(x)-{\theta}_{x}(x)r\sin\phi +v(x,\phi )\sin\phi -w(x,\phi )\cos\phi -\zeta {\beta}_{\theta}(x,\phi )\sin\phi \end{array} . Once discretised this expression becomes: \begin{array}{}{u}_{1}(r,x,\phi )={\sum}_{k=1}^{N}{H}_{k}(x)({x}_{k}\cdot x){u}_{x}^{k}+{H}_{k}(x)({y}_{k}\cdot x){u}_{y}^{k}-\bar{{H}_{k}}(x)({x}_{k}\cdot y){\theta}_{y}^{k}r\cos\phi -\bar{{H}_{k}}(x)({y}_{k}\cdot y){\theta}_{y}^{k}r\cos\phi +\bar{{H}_{k}}(x){\theta}_{z}^{k}r\sin\phi +u(x,\phi )+\zeta {\beta}_{\phi }(x,\phi )\\ {u}_{2}(r,x,\phi )={\sum}_{k=1}^{N}\bar{{H}_{k}}(x)({x}_{k}\cdot y){u}_{x}^{k}+{H}_{k}(x)({y}_{k}\cdot y){u}_{y}^{k}+\bar{{H}_{k}}(x)({x}_{k}\cdot x){\theta}_{x}^{k}r\cos\phi +\bar{{H}_{k}}(x)({y}_{k}\cdot x){\theta}_{y}^{k}r\cos\phi -v(x,\phi )\cos\phi -w(x,\phi )\sin\phi +\zeta {\beta}_{\theta}(x,\phi )\cos\phi \\ {u}_{3}(r,x,\phi )={\sum}_{k=1}^{N}{H}_{k}(x){u}_{z}^{k}-\bar{{H}_{k}}(x)({x}_{k}\cdot x){\theta}_{x}^{k}r\sin\phi -\bar{{H}_{k}}(x)({y}_{k}\cdot x){\theta}_{y}^{k}r\sin\phi +v(x,\phi )\sin\phi -w(x,\phi )\cos\phi -\zeta {\beta}_{\theta}(x,\phi )\sin\phi \end{array} where u(x,\phi ),v(x,\phi ),w(x,\phi ),{\beta}_{\theta}(x,\phi )\text{et}{\beta}_{\theta}(x,\phi ) are discretised as in [§3.1]. The displacement at a node k of abscissa {x}_{k} at the pipe end is then written: \begin{array}{cc}{u}_{1}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )=& {u}_{x}^{k}-{\theta}_{y}^{k}r\cos(\phi )+{\theta}_{z}^{k}r\sin(\phi )+{\sum}_{m=2}^{M}({u}_{\mathrm{km}}^{i}\cosm\phi +{u}_{\mathrm{km}}^{0}\sinm\phi )+\zeta {\beta}_{\phi }({x}_{k},\phi )\\ {u}_{2}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )=& {u}_{y}^{k}+{\theta}_{x}^{k}r\cos(\phi )-\cos\phi {\sum}_{m=2}^{M}({v}_{\mathrm{km}}^{i}\sinm\phi +{v}_{\mathrm{km}}^{0}\cosm\phi )-\sin\phi {\sum}_{m=2}^{M}({w}_{\mathrm{km}}^{i}\cosm\phi +{w}_{\mathrm{km}}^{0}\sinm\phi )\\ & -{w}_{\mathrm{k1}}^{i}\sin2\phi +{w}_{\mathrm{k1}}^{0}\cos2\phi -{w}_{k}^{0}\sin\phi +\zeta {\beta}_{\theta}({x}_{k},\phi )\cos\phi \\ {u}_{3}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )=& {u}_{z}^{k}-{\theta}_{x}^{k}r\sin(\phi )+\sin\phi {\sum}_{m=2}^{M}({v}_{\mathrm{km}}^{i}\sinm\phi +{v}_{\mathrm{km}}^{0}\cosm\phi )-\cos\phi {\sum}_{m=2}^{M}({w}_{\mathrm{km}}^{i}\cosm\phi +{w}_{\mathrm{km}}^{0}\sinm\phi )\\ & -{w}_{\mathrm{k1}}^{i}\cos2\phi -{w}_{\mathrm{k1}}^{0}\sin2\phi -{w}_{k}^{0}\cos\phi -\zeta {\beta}_{\theta}({x}_{k},\phi )\sin\phi \end{array} For the pipe the angular-momentum vector \text{GM}\wedge u(M) and the swelling \frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }.u(M) have the respective expressions: \text{GM}\wedge u(M)=\lbrace \begin{array}{c}-{u}_{z}(x)r\sin\phi +{u}_{y}(x)r\cos\phi +{r}^{2}{\theta}_{x}(x)-\text{rv}(x,\phi )\\ -{\text{ru}}_{1}(r,x,\phi )\cos\phi \\ {\text{ru}}_{1}(r,x,\phi )\sin\phi \end{array} , and: \frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }.u(M)=-{u}_{z}(x)\cos\phi -{u}_{y}(x)\sin\phi +w(x,\phi ) . Note: The first component of the displacement field involves u(x,\phi ) in isolation. The same is true of the first component of the rotation vector with respect to v(x,\phi ) and of the swelling with respect to w(x,\phi ) . This note will be used in [§5.6] to link the Fourier modes to the degrees of freedom of the shell edges. 7.3 Shell kinematics The Love-Kirchhoff or Naghdi-Mindlin shell kinematics is written through the thickness: {u}^{c}(M)={u}^{c}(Q)+({\theta}^{c}(Q)\wedge n).{y}_{3} - {u}^{c}(Q) constitutes the displacement vector of the mean surface at Q , - {\theta}^{c}(Q) constitutes the rotation vector at Q of the normal along the directions {t}_{1} and {t}_{2} of the plane tangent at Q . This displacement and this rotation are computed in the global frame. It is possible by change of frame to have their expressions in the curvilinear basis (o,x,y,z) of [§2.1] associated with the cross-section of the junction between the shell and the pipe. For each node, the program computes the coefficients of the 9+6(M-1) linear relations which relate: - the 6 degrees of freedom of the beam node P of the pipe, - the 2+3\times 2(M-1) Fourier degrees of freedom of the pipe, - the swelling degree of freedom of the pipe, - with the degrees of freedom of all the nodes of the list of mesh cells of the shell edge. These linear relations will be dualised, like all the linear relations issuing for example from the keyword LIAISON_DDL of AFFE_CHAR_MECA. They are constructed as for the 3D-beam connection from the assembly of elementary terms. 7.4 Computation of the mean displacement on the section S It consists in computing the integral {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\text{dS} , where {u}^{c} is the shell displacement (comprising 6 degrees of freedom per node), S is the shell edge. The mean displacement on the section S is written: {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M)\text{dS}=h{\int}_{l}{u}^{c}(Q)\text{dl}+{\int}_{l}({\theta}^{c}(Q)\wedge n)({\int}_{-h/2}^{h/2}{y}_{3}{\text{dy}}_{3})\text{dl} that is {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M)\text{dS}=h{\int}_{l}{u}^{c}(Q)\text{dl} . Moreover one also has for the pipe part: {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M)\text{dS}={\int}_{S}[{u}^{p}(M)+{u}^{s}(M)]\text{dS}=\underset{S}{\int}(\begin{array}{c}{u}_{x}^{k}\\ {u}_{y}^{k}\\ {u}_{z}^{k}\end{array})\text{dS}=S(\begin{array}{c}{u}_{x}^{k}\\ {u}_{y}^{k}\\ {u}_{z}^{k}\end{array}) . One thus establishes that the mean displacement of the pipe section at node k is equal to the beam displacement of node k . One can thus link linearly the translational beam degrees of freedom at node k with the mean of the displacement degrees of freedom of the shell edge. One neglects in this expression the variation of the metric through the thickness of the shell. 7.5 Computation of the mean rotation of the section S \begin{array}{}{\int}_{S}\text{GM}\wedge {u}^{c}(M)\text{dS}={\int}_{l}{\int}_{-h/2}^{h/2}(\text{GQ}+{y}_{3}n(Q))\wedge ({u}^{c}(Q)+{\theta}^{c}(Q)\wedge n(Q){y}_{3})\text{dl}{\text{dy}}_{3}\\ =h{\int}_{l}\text{GQ}\wedge {u}^{c}(Q)\text{dl}+{\int}_{l}\text{GQ}\wedge ({\theta}^{c}(Q)\wedge n(Q))\text{dl}{\int}_{-h/2}^{h/2}{y}_{3}{\text{dy}}_{3}\\ +{\int}_{l}n(Q)\wedge {u}^{c}(Q)({\int}_{-h/2}^{h/2}{y}_{3}{\text{dy}}_{3})\text{dl}+{\int}_{l}n(Q)\wedge ({\theta}^{c}(Q)\wedge n(Q)){\int}_{-\frac{h}{2}}^{\frac{h}{2}}{y}_{3}^{2}{\text{dy}}_{3}.\text{dl}\end{array} that is {\int}_{S}\text{GM}\wedge {u}^{c}(M).\text{dS}=h{\int}_{l}\text{GQ}\wedge {u}^{c}(Q)\text{dl}+\frac{{h}^{3}}{12}{\int}_{l}{\theta}^{c}(Q)\text{dl} . Moreover one also has for the pipe part: {\int}_{S}\text{GM}\wedge {u}^{c}(M).\text{dS}={\int}_{S}\text{GM}\wedge \left[{u}^{p}(M)+{u}^{s}(M)\right].\text{dS}={\int}_{S}(\begin{array}{c}{r}^{2}.{\theta}_{x}^{k}\\ {r}^{2}.{\cos}^{2}\phi {\theta}_{y}^{k}\\ {r}^{2}.{\sin}^{2}\phi {\theta}_{z}^{k}\end{array})=I(\begin{array}{c}{\theta}_{x}^{k}\\ {\theta}_{y}^{k}\\ {\theta}_{z}^{k}\end{array}) where I is the inertia tensor of the beam. One thus establishes that the mean rotation of the pipe section at node k is equal to the beam rotation at node k . One can thus link linearly the rotational beam degrees of freedom at node k with the rotation degrees of freedom of the shell edge. One neglects in this expression the variation of the metric through the thickness of the shell. 7.6 Computation of the mean swelling of the section S It consists in computing the integral {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}.n\text{dS}={\int}_{S}{u}^{c}.\frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }\text{dS} , where n=\frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }=\frac{\text{GQ}}{\parallel \text{GQ}\parallel } is the normal to the shell mean surface. The mean displacement on the section S is written: {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M).n\text{dS}=h{\int}_{l}{u}^{c}(Q).n\text{dl}+{\int}_{l}({\theta}^{c}(Q)\mathrm{\wedge }n).n({\int}_{-h/2}^{h/2}{y}_{3}{\text{dy}}_{3})\text{dl}=h{\int}_{l}{u}^{c}(Q).n\text{dl} . Moreover one also has for the pipe part: {\int}_{S}\frac{\text{GM}}{\mathrm{\parallel }\text{GM}\mathrm{\parallel }}.{u}^{c}(M)\text{dS}={\int}_{S}\frac{\text{GM}}{\mathrm{\parallel }\text{GM}\mathrm{\parallel }}.[{u}^{p}(M)+{u}^{s}(M)]\text{dS}=\underset{S}{\int}{w}_{k}^{o}\text{dS} One thus establishes that the mean swelling of the pipe section at node k is equal to the swelling degree of freedom of the pipe at node k . One can thus link linearly the pipe swelling degree of freedom at node k with the displacement degrees of freedom of the shell edge. One neglects in this expression the variation of the metric through the thickness of the shell. 7.7 Computation of the Fourier coefficients on the section S It consists in computing the six integrals {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} , {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} , {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\wedge \frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} , {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\wedge \frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} , {\int}_{S}\frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }.{u}^{c}\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} and {\int}_{S}\frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }.{u}^{c}\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} , where {u}^{c} is the shell displacement (comprising 6 degrees of freedom per node), S is the shell edge. One has the following relation for the displacements on the section S : {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M)\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS}=h{\int}_{l}{u}^{c}(Q)\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl}+{\int}_{l}({\theta}^{c}(Q)\wedge n)({\int}_{-h/2}^{h/2}{y}_{3}{\text{dy}}_{3})\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl} that is {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M)\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS}=h{\int}_{l}{u}^{c}(Q)\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl} and {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M)\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS}=h{\int}_{l}{u}^{c}(Q)\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl} . Moreover one also has for the pipe part: {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M)\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS}=\underset{S}{\int}(\begin{array}{c}{u}_{1}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )\\ {u}_{2}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )\\ {u}_{3}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )\end{array})\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} . The first component of this relation then allows us to link linearly the Fourier coefficient {u}_{\text{kp}}^{i} to the components of the displacements of the shell edge in the following way: h{\int}_{l}{u}_{1}^{c}(Q)\cos\mathit{p\phi }\text{dl}={\int}_{S}{u}_{1}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )\cos\mathit{p\phi }\text{dS}=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}-\underset{S}{\int}{\mathit{r\theta }}_{y}^{k}{\cos}^{2}\phi \text{dS}& \text{si}p=1\\ \underset{S}{\int}{u}_{\text{kp}}^{i}{\cos}^{2}\mathit{p\phi }\text{dS}& \text{si}p\mathrm{\ne }1\end{array} Likewise {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M)\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS}=\underset{S}{\int}(\begin{array}{c}{u}_{1}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )\\ {u}_{2}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )\\ {u}_{3}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )\end{array})\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS} whence one deduces that: h{\int}_{l}{u}_{1}^{c}(Q)\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl}={\int}_{S}{u}_{1}(r,{x}_{k},\phi )\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS}=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\underset{S}{\int}{\mathrm{r\theta }}_{z}^{k}{\sin}^{2}\phi \text{dS}& \text{si}p=1\\ \underset{S}{\int}{u}_{\text{kp}}^{o}{\sin}^{2}\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS}& \text{si}p\ne 1\end{array}\begin{array}{c}\\ \end{array} One has the following relation for the rotations on the section S : {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}(M)\wedge .\frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS}=h{\int}_{l}{u}^{c}(Q)\wedge \frac{\text{GQ}}{\parallel \text{GQ}\parallel }\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl}+{\int}_{l}({\theta}^{c}(Q)\wedge n)\wedge n(\underset{-h/2}{\overset{+h/2}{\int}}{y}_{3}{\text{dy}}_{3})\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl} . The first component of this relation then allows us to link linearly the Fourier coefficient {v}_{\text{kp}}^{o} to the components of the displacements and of the rotations of the shell edge in the following way: h{\int}_{l}[{u}^{c}(Q)\wedge \frac{\text{GQ}}{\parallel \text{GQ}\parallel }{]}_{1}\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl}=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}-\underset{S}{\int}[{\text{ru}}_{y}^{k}{\cos}^{2}\phi +{\text{rw}}_{\mathrm{k1}}^{o}{\cos}^{2}\phi ]\text{dS}& \text{si}p=1\\ \underset{S}{\int}{\text{rv}}_{\text{kp}}^{o}{\cos}^{2}(\mathrm{p\phi })\text{dS}& \text{si}p\ne 1\end{array} Likewise one has: h{\int}_{l}[{u}^{c}(Q)\wedge \frac{\text{GQ}}{\parallel \text{GQ}\parallel }{]}_{1}\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl}=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\underset{S}{\int}[{\text{ru}}_{z}^{k}{\sin}^{2}\phi +{\text{rw}}_{\mathrm{k1}}^{i}{\sin}^{2}\phi ]\text{dS}& \text{si}p=1\\ \underset{S}{\int}{\text{rv}}_{\text{kp}}^{i}{\sin}^{2}(\mathrm{p\phi })\text{dS}& \text{si}p\ne 1\end{array} One has the following relation for the swelling on the section S : {\int}_{S}\frac{\text{GM}}{\parallel \text{GM}\parallel }.{u}^{c}(M).\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dS}=h{\int}_{l}\frac{\text{GQ}}{\parallel \text{GQ}\parallel }.{u}^{c}(Q)\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl} . This relation allows us to link linearly the Fourier coefficient {w}_{\text{kp}}^{i} to the components of the displacements of the shell edge in the following way: h{\int}_{l}\frac{\text{GQ}}{\mathrm{\parallel }\text{GQ}\mathrm{\parallel }}.{u}^{c}(Q)\cos\mathit{p\phi }\text{dl}=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\underset{S}{\int}[-{u}_{z}^{k}{\cos}^{2}\phi +{w}_{\mathit{k1}}^{i}{\cos}^{2}\phi ]\text{dS}& \text{si}p=1\\ \underset{S}{\int}{w}_{\text{kp}}^{i}{\cos}^{2}(\mathit{p\phi })\text{dS}& \text{si}p\mathrm{\ne }1\end{array} . Likewise, one has: h{\int}_{l}\frac{\text{GQ}}{\parallel \text{GQ}\parallel }.{u}^{c}(Q)\sin\mathrm{p\phi }\text{dl}=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\underset{S}{\int}-{u}_{y}^{k}{\sin}^{2}\phi +{w}_{\mathrm{k1}}^{o}{\sin}^{2}\phi \text{dS}& \text{si}p=1\\ \underset{S}{\int}{w}_{\text{kp}}^{o}{\sin}^{2}(\mathrm{p\phi })\text{dS}& \text{si}p\ne 1\end{array} One uses for all these relations the fact that \underset{S}{\int}\cos\mathrm{p\phi }\cos\mathrm{q\phi }\text{dS}=0\text{si}p\ne q. One neglects in this expression the variation of the metric through the thickness of the shell. Note: One may note that some of the relations established in this paragraph for p=1 are redundant with those established in paragraphs [§7.4] and [§7.5]. Of the six relations established from the computation of the integral forms {\int}_{S}{u}^{\mathrm{c.}}\cos\phi \mathrm{dS} , {\int}_{S}{u}^{\mathrm{c.}}\sin\phi \mathrm{dS} , {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\wedge \frac{\mathrm{GM}}{∥\mathrm{GM}∥}.\cos\phi \mathrm{dS} , {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\wedge \frac{\mathrm{GM}}{∥\mathrm{GM}∥}.\sin\phi \mathrm{dS} , {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\wedge \frac{\mathrm{GM}}{∥\mathrm{GM}∥}.{u}^{c}\cos\phi \mathrm{dS} and {\int}_{S}{u}^{c}\wedge \frac{\mathrm{GM}}{∥\mathrm{GM}∥}.{u}^{c}\sin\phi \mathrm{dS} , only two among the last four are linearly independent of the others. Thus the first two have already been established in [§7.4] and combinations of the last four give back those of [§7.5]. 7.8 Implementation of the method The computation of the coefficients of the linear relations is carried out in three stages: - computation of elementary quantities on the elements of the list of mesh cells of shell edges (mesh cell of type SEG2): - area = {\int}_{\text{elt}}1;{\int}_{\text{elt}}x;{\int}_{\text{elt}}y;{\int}_{\text{elt}}z . - summation of these quantities on ( S ) whence the computation of: - A=\mid S\mid - position of G . - knowing G , elementary computation on the elements of the list of mesh cells of shell edges of: {\int}_{\text{elt}}\text{Ni};{\int}_{\text{elt}}\text{xNi};{\int}_{\text{elt}}\text{yNi};{\int}_{\text{elt}}\text{zNi}\text{où :}\begin{array}{c}\text{GM}=\left\lbrace x,y,z\right\rbrace \\ \text{Ni}=\text{fonctions de forme de l'élément}\end{array} It must be noted that in the case of the shell–pipe connection, the integrals on the edge elements are to be multiplied by the thickness of the shell: \underset{\text{elt}}{\int}{N}_{i}=h\underset{l}{\int}{N}_{i} where l represents the mean fibre of the shell edge element.
