It assumes that the section of the pipe is circular. Unlike the elements POU_D_E, POU_D_T, R3.08.01 this element is not “exact” at the nodes for loadings or wrenches concentrated at the ends. One must therefore mesh with several elements in order to obtain correct results. 8.2 Modelling data The element is used in the following way: AFFE_MODELE ( MODELISATION = 'TUYAU_3M' ...) The mesh cells with 4 nodes are generated from the mesh cells with 3 nodes by means of: MAIL=CREA_MAILLAGE(MAILLAGE=MAIL,MODI_MAILLE=_F(OPTION='SEG3_4',TOUT='OUI')) One calls the routine INI090 for the shape functions, their derivatives and their second derivatives (for the shell part) at the Gauss points, as well as the corresponding weights. The characteristics of the section are defined in AFFE_CARA_ELEM AFFE_CARA_ELEM ( > POUTRE = _F(SECTION = 'CERCLE' ,CARA = ( 'R' 'EP' ),VALE = (.....) , ) , > ORIENTATION =_F(GROUP_NO=D,CARA=’GENE_TUYAU’,VALE=(X Y Z),), > TUYAU_NCOU=’NOMBRE DE COUCHES’, TUYAU_NSEC=’NOMBRE DE SECTEURS’,), ) R and EP represent, as for the classical beam elements, respectively the external radius and the thickness of the section. One also defines on one of the end nodes of the piping line the vector whose projection on the cross-section is the origin of the angles for the Fourier-series decomposition. This vector must not be collinear with the mean line of the elbow at the end node considered. One also defines at this level the number of layers and of angular sectors to be used for the numerical integration. AFFE_CHAR_MECA ( DDL_IMPO = _F ( DX=..,DY=..,DZ=..,DRX=..,DRY=..,DRZ=..,DDL de poutre UI2=..,VI2=..,WI2=..,UO2=..,VO2=..,WO2=..,DDL liés au mode 2 UI3=..,VI3=..,WI3=..,UO3=..,VO3=..,WO3=..,DDL liés au mode 3 WO=..,WI1=..,WO1=.., ,DDL de gonflement et mode 1 sur :math: W The loadings supported in AFFE_CHAR_MECA are: - the nodal forces (FORCE_NODALE), which work only on the beam displacements. - the internal pressure (FORCE_TUYAU= _F (PRES =.. )) - gravity, (PESANTEUR) - the line forces ( FORCE_POUTRE) The internal pressure working on the swelling degree of freedom \mathit{WO} , one then computes: {W}_{\text{pres}}={\int}_{0}^{l}{\int}_{0}^{2\pi }p{w}^{o}{r}_{{}_{int}}d\phi \text{dx}={\int}_{0}^{l}{\int}_{0}^{2\pi }p\sum_{k=1}^{N}{H}_{k}{w}_{k}^{o}{r}_{{}_{int}}d\phi \text{dx}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}{H}_{k}\left[{\int}_{0}^{l}{\int}_{0}^{2\pi }p{r}_{{}_{int}}d\phi \text{dx}\right]{w}_{k}^{o} 8.3 Analysis in linear elasticity The stiffness matrix and the mass matrix (respectively the options RIGI_MECA and MASS_MECA) are integrated numerically in TE0582. The computation takes into account the fact that the terms corresponding to the beam degrees of freedom are expressed classically in the global frame, and that the Fourier degrees of freedom are in the local frame of the element. In the case where the element does not belong to any elbow, this local frame is defined by the generator and the director vector carried by the mean fibre of the element as indicated in [Figure 8.3-a]. In the case where the element belongs to an elbow, the local frame is defined from the plane of the elbow as mentioned in [§2.1]. Figure 8.3-a: Local frame for a straight pipe 8.4 Non-linear analyses The tangent stiffness matrix (options RIGI_MECA_TANG and FULL_MECA) as well as the plastic projection (options FULL_MECA and RAPH_MECA) are integrated numerically in TE0586. All the plane-stress laws available in Code_Aster can be used: if they are not integrated directly, it is always possible to use a constitutive law formulated in plane strain, and to treat the plane-stress assumption by means of the method of De Borst. The pipe elements must be used only in small strains and small displacements. 8.5 Post-processing The elementary computations currently available correspond to the options: - SIEF_ELGA which provide the stresses at the integration points in the user frame. One stores these values in the following way: - for each Gauss point along the length, ( n=1,2 or n=1,3 ) - for each integration point through the thickness, ( n=1 , 2{N}_{\mathit{COU}}+1=7 ) - for each integration point on the circumference, ( n=1 , 2{N}_{\mathit{SECT}}+1=33 ) - 6 stress components: SIXX SIYY SIZZ SIXY SIXZ SIYZ where X denotes the direction given by the two vertex nodes of the element, Y represents the angle \phi describing the circumference and Z represents the radius. SIZZ and SIYZ corresponding to {\sigma}_{\text{rr}},{\sigma}_{\mathrm{r\phi }} are taken equal to zero. - EFGE_ELNO which makes it possible to obtain the generalised forces per element at the nodes in the frame of the beam. - VARI_ELNO which computes the field of internal variables per element at the nodes for all the layers and all the sectors, in the local frame of the element. - EPSI_ELGA which provides the total strains at the integration points in the local frame of the element. The computation is carried out in TE0584, and currently gives the values at the 693 integration points (for an element with 3 Fourier modes). These fields are called fields at integration “sub-points”. One stores these values in the following way: - for each Gauss point along the length, ( n=1,2 or n=1,3 ) - for each integration point through the thickness, ( n=1 , 2{N}_{\mathit{COU}}+1=7 ) - for each integration point on the circumference, ( n=1 , 2{N}_{\mathit{SECT}}+1=33 ) - 6 strain components: EPXX EPYY EPZZ EPXY EPXZ EPYZ where X denotes the direction given by the two vertex nodes of the element, Y represents the angle \phi describing the circumference and Z represents the radius. EPZZ and EPYZ corresponding to {\epsilon}_{\text{rr}},{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{r\phi }} are taken equal to zero. - The options SIEQ_ELGA and EPEQ_ELGA allow the computation of the invariants (von Mises, signed von Mises, trace) at each integration point (fields at “sub-points”). - EFGE_ELNO provides the classical generalised beam forces: N, VY, VZ, MT, MFY, MFZ. These forces are given in the local curvilinear frame of the element. - The command POST_CHAMP / MIN_MAX_SP makes it possible to extract, at each of the line Gauss points of an element, the maximum and minimum values of a component of a field. The min / max is taken over the set of sub-points of a point. 8.6 Test: SSLL106A It is a straight pipe of director vector (4,3,0) fixed at its end O and which is meshed with 18 TUYAU elements. The pipe is subjected to different types of load: - a tensile force, - 2 shear forces, - 2 bending moments, - 1 torsional moment, - an internal pressure. One computes the displacements at the point B , the strains and the stresses at certain integration points of the section containing B , as well as the first eigenmodes. This makes it possible to test the beam degrees of freedom, the swelling degree of freedom and modes 1 of the Fourier-series expansion. 9 Conclusion The elbow finite elements which we describe here are usable for piping analyses in elasticity or in plasticity. The piping may be subjected to various combined loadings — internal pressure, in-plane and out-of-plane bending, torsion, extension. For the moment, the element produced is a line element of beam type, straight or curved, with three nodes, in small rotations and strains, with a local elastoplastic behaviour in plane stress. It makes it possible to take ovalisation, warping and swelling into account. It combines the properties of shells and of beams. The beam kinematics for the axis of the elbow is augmented by a shell kinematics, of Love-Kirchhoff type without transverse shear, for the description of the behaviour of the cross-sections. This latter kinematics is discretised in M Fourier modes, the number M of which, which the literature encourages us to choose equal to 6 [bib8], [bib13], must at once be sufficient to obtain good results in plasticity and not too large in order to limit the computation time. In elasticity, for relatively thick piping (the ratio of thickness to radius of the cross-section greater than 0.1), one may be content with M=2 or M=3 . 10 Bibliography 1. r3.08.07 MEMBRANE and GRILLE_MEMBRANE elements r3.08.07 MEMBRANE and GRILLE_MEMBRANE elements Summary: This document describes the formulation and the implementation in Code_Aster of the MEMBRANE and GRILLE_MEMBRANE elements. The MEMBRANE elements make it possible to model a linear behaviour of an arbitrary membrane or a non-linear behaviour of isotropic membranes. The GRILLE_MEMBRANE elements are finite elements more specifically intended for the representation of steel reinforcement in a solid mass (for civil-engineering applications of the reinforced-concrete type). The main characteristics of these elements are the following: - membrane elements, with no torsional stiffness; - no rotational degrees of freedom, but, in return, no possibility of offset; - surface geometric support (triangle, quadrangle; linear or quadratic, and biquadratic only for the MEMBRANE elements); The GRILLE_MEMBRANE elements make it possible to model a non-linear behaviour of the reinforcing bars. 1 Introduction The MEMBRANE modelling makes it possible to represent the mechanical behaviour of a membrane that may be anisotropic in the linear regime and only isotropic in the non-linear regime. It makes it possible to model structural elements whose bending stiffness is negligible. The GRILLE_MEMBRANE elements make it possible to represent the possibly non-linear behaviour of reinforcing bars in a reinforced-concrete structure. The main constraint is that the reinforcing bars must be periodically distributed over a surface, and all oriented in the same direction. Note, however, that crossed reinforcing bars can be modelled by superposing two GRILLE_MEMBRANE modellings (see below). Elements of type GRILLE_MEMBRANE complement the possibilities for modelling reinforcement in Code_Aster , in addition to the GRILLE_EXCENTRE modelling. The differences between the GRILLE_MEMBRANE and GRILLE_EXCENTRE modellings are presented below. Recall that the GRILLE_EXCENTRE modelling is based on a DKT shell kinematics with a single layer through the thickness R3.07.03. This DKT foundation implies the presence of rotational degrees of freedom at the nodes of the GRILLE_EXCENTRE elements: although it allows the notion of offset, it is unnecessary when offset is not required (in that case it burdens the model unnecessarily, because not only do the rotational degrees of freedom lengthen the vector of unknowns, but a non-negligible number of these degrees of freedom must moreover be fixed by a double Lagrange multiplier). The GRILLE_MEMBRANE modelling is a modelling based on a “surface” kinematics; it requires no degrees of freedom other than the usual displacements (on the other hand, of course, this modelling does not allow the notion of offset to be used). The GRILLE_EXCENTRE modelling, based on DKT, requires geometric support elements of linear triangle or quadrangle type; the GRILLE_MEMBRANE modelling is developed from surface geometric supports, triangle or quadrangle, linear or quadratic. For both types of modelling, however, only one reinforcement direction is available per finite element. This makes it possible to model any type of reinforcement with several directions, by superposing one element per direction; the computational cost generated by these duplications is low: no duplication of the degrees of freedom (hence a constant matrix-inversion cost), duplication of the elementary calculations (but they remain simple, few in number in 3D — surface elements as against volume elements — and the elementary calculations for structures with a large number of degrees of freedom have a low cost compared with the inversion cost). 2 Linear formulation of the MEMBRANE elements For a membrane element, the strain energy can be written in the form: \Phi =\frac{1}{2}\int\sigma :\epsilon \text{ds} with \sigma la contrainte membranaire et \epsilon the membrane strain. The only difficulty is to obtain an expression of the type \epsilon =\mathit{BU} where U denotes the nodal values of the displacement. For this, a little differential geometry must be used. Denoting by a the natural basis (non-orthogonal; only the third vector, normal to the surface, is normalised) of the reinforcement plane and by g the contravariant metric associated with this basis (cf. R3.07.04.for more details). One starts from the expression of the contravariant derivative: | :math:nabla u=frac{partial {u}^{i}}{partial {xi}_{j}}={u}^{i}{ | }_{j}{a}_{i}otimes {a}^{j} | | | --- | --- | --- | with \left\lbrace {\xi}_{j}\right\rbrace an admissible parametrisation of the surface and {a}_{i}=\frac{\partial x}{\partial {\xi}_{i}} . Using the metric tensor g , one then has: | :math:nabla u=frac{partial {u}^{i}}{partial {xi}_{j}}={u}^{i}{ | }_{j}{g}^{mathit{jk}}{a}_{i}otimes {a}_{k} | | | --- | --- | --- | The reinforcement direction is then defined by the unit vector {e}_{1} , which is completed, for ease of presentation, into an orthonormal basis \left\lbrace {e}_{i}\right\rbrace . R denotes the change-of-basis operator between this basis and the natural basis such that: {a}_{i}={R}_{i}^{p}{e}_{p} Greek indices denote the indices taking values only in (1,2) , and one obtains: {\varepsilon}_{\alpha \beta }={(\nabla u)}_{\alpha \beta }=(\frac{\partial u}{\partial {\xi}^{j}}\cdot {a}^{i}){R}_{i}^{\alpha}{R}_{k}^{\beta}{g}^{\text{jk}} By definition of R : {R}_{3}^{1}=0 and by definition of g : {g}^{13}={g}^{23}=0 . One therefore obtains: {\varepsilon}_{\alpha \beta }={(\nabla u)}_{\alpha \beta }=(\frac{\partial u}{\partial {\xi}^{\delta}}\cdot {a}^{\gamma}){R}_{\gamma}^{\alpha}{R}_{\theta}^{\beta}{g}^{\delta \theta } If \hat{B} now denotes the derivative of the shape functions at the Gauss point under consideration, one has: {\epsilon}_{\alpha \beta }={R}_{\gamma}^{\alpha}{R}_{\theta}^{\beta}{g}^{\delta \theta }{\widehat{B}}_{\delta ,n}{\left({a}^{\gamma}\right)}_{i}{U}_{i,n} With n the node index. Hence the sought B : {B}_{i,n}={R}_{\gamma}^{\alpha}{R}_{\theta}^{\beta}{g}^{\delta \theta }{\widehat{B}}_{\delta ,n}{\left({a}^{\gamma}\right)}_{i} From B , one then has all the classical expressions for the strain: \varepsilon =\mathit{BU} for the nodal forces: F=\int{B}^{T}\sigma and for the tangent matrix: K=\int{B}^{T}\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \varepsilon }B 3 Non-linear formulation of the MEMBRANE elements The whole of the theoretical part, as well as the development of the membrane finite element, is based on the work of Anh LE VAN, published in his book Coques et membranes, Fondements de l’approche non linéaire [:ref: 1] . In this document, the following conventions will be observed, unless otherwise stated: - Latin letters ∈ {1,2,3} - Greek letters ∈ {1,2} - the Einstein summation convention is used - components referring to the initial configuration are written in upper case - components referring to the deformed configuration are written in lower case - tensors of order greater than or equal to 1 are written in bold - a subscript 0 will be used to indicate that one is on the initial configuration - the braces \lbrace \mathrm{❑}\rbrace denote a column vector - the brackets ⟨\mathrm{❑}⟩ denote a row vector - the square brackets [\mathrm{❑}] denote a matrix with more than one row and more than one column The study of membranes relies on many elements of differential geometry; the most important principles for the present study are therefore set out below. Differential geometry refers to the application of differential calculus to geometry; it arises in particular in problems involving the notion of curvature. It will be useful in taking account of the curved geometry of the membranes. 3.1 Differential geometry One works in the three-dimensional Euclidean space Ԑ equipped with the usual scalar product \left(\text{a},\text{b}\right)\mapsto \text{a}.\text{b} , the Euclidean norm \Vert .\Vert and an orthonormal global frame \text{ }(\text{O};{\text{e}}_{1},{\text{e}}_{2},{\text{e}}_{3}) . The first element to be made explicit is the local basis (or covariant natural basis); this basis is a priori neither orthogonal nor normalised. Let {\text{S}}_{0} be a surface, {\text{P}}_{0} a point belonging to this surface and ({\text{ξ}}^{1},{\text{ξ}}^{2}) a coordinate system of this surface. The covariant natural basis {(\text{A}}_{1},{\text{A}}_{2},{\text{A}}_{3}) is defined by (denoting by \text{}\times \text{} the vector product) : {\text{A}}_{\text{α}}=\frac{\partial {\text{P}}_{0}}{\partial {\text{ξ}}^{\text{α}}} One then writes, in the deformed configuration, denoting by \text{S} the surface and by \text{P} the position of the point {\text{P}}_{0} after deformation : {\text{a}}_{\text{α}}=\frac{\partial \text{P}}{\partial {\text{ξ}}^{\text{α}}} The first fundamental form can now be defined : {\text{A}}_{\text{α}\text{β}}\equiv {\text{A}}_{\text{α}}{.\text{A}}_{\text{β}} the matrix can then be constructed : \left[\text{A}..\right]\equiv \left[\begin{array}{cc}{\text{A}}_{11}& {\text{A}}_{12}\\ {\text{A}}_{21}& {\text{A}}_{22}\end{array}\right] this matrix is symmetric and invertible (because {\text{A}}_{1} and {\text{A}}_{2} are linearly independent). Its inverse is denoted: \left[\text{A}\ddot{}\right]\equiv {\left[\text{A}..\right]}^{-1}\equiv \left[\begin{array}{cc}{\text{A}}^{11}& {\text{A}}^{12}\\ {\text{A}}^{21}& {\text{A}}^{22}\end{array}\right] the dual basis ({\text{A}}^{1},{\text{A}}^{2}) of the basis {(\text{A}}_{1},{\text{A}}_{2}) is then defined by: {\text{A}}^{\text{α}}\equiv {\text{A}}^{\text{α}\text{β}}{\text{A}}_{\text{β}} This makes it possible to define the metric tensor : \text{A}\equiv {\text{A}}_{\text{α}\text{β}}{\text{A}}^{\text{α}}\otimes {\text{A}}^{\text{β}} In shell or membrane theory, it is the tensor \text{A} that takes the place of the identity tensor \text{I} in 3D. One writes: \Vert {\text{A}}_{1}\times {\text{A}}_{2}\Vert =\sqrt{\text{A}} where > , one calls \text{A} the Jacobian of the transformation. Finally, the curvature tensor is defined : \text{B}={\text{B}}_{\text{α}\text{β}}{\text{A}}^{\text{α}}\otimes {\text{A}}^{\text{β}}=\left({\text{N}}_{,\text{α}}.{\text{A}}_{\text{β}}\right).{\text{A}}^{\text{α}}\otimes {\text{A}}^{\text{β}} \text{B} is symmetric by definition; as its name indicates, it is used to measure the curvature of a surface at a point. 3.2 Assumptions In order to arrive at the equations characterising the behaviour of membranes, several assumptions are necessary. The aim here is not to re-derive how these assumptions are reached; they are therefore given directly without going into the details, which are given in [:ref: 1] . The assumptions are : - The displacements of the membrane are represented by the displacements of the mid-surface. - The Cosserat kinematic hypothesis is used : - Every point defined along a fibre remains, after deformation, along that same fibre. - There is no change of shape of the fibre through the thickness. - The thickness H of the membrane is very small; mathematically this is expressed by the conditions \text{H}|\text{tr}\text{B}|\ll 1 and {\text{H}}^{2}\left(\det\text{B}\right)\ll 1 . - A state of plane stress is considered \left[\text{σ}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{\text{σ}}^{11}& {\text{σ}}^{12}& 0\\ {\text{σ}}^{21}& {\text{σ}}^{22}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right] . - The mass density is constant through the thickness. - The stresses are constant through the thickness. - The second-order bending moment is neglected. 3.3 Equations governing the motion of membranes 3.3.1 Principle of virtual power The tool used to set up the equations of the membranes is the principle of virtual power (PVP), whose expression in Lagrangian variables is written: > , > virtual velocity field > , -{\int}_{{\text{Ω}}_{0}^{\text{ }}}{\text{Π}}^{\text{T}}:{\text{grad}}_{{\text{Q}}_{0}}{\text{U}}^{\text{ }}{\text{d}\text{Ω}}_{0}+{\int}_{{\text{Ω}}_{0}^{\text{ }}}{\text{ρ}}_{0}.\text{f}.{\text{U}}^{\text{ }}{\text{d}\text{Ω}}_{0}+{\int}_{{\partial \text{Ω}}_{0}^{\text{ }}}\text{T}.{\text{U}}^{\text{ }}{\text{d}\text{A}}_{0}={\int}_{{\text{Ω}}_{0}^{\text{ }}}{\text{ρ}}_{0}.\ddot{\text{U}}.{\text{U}}^{\text{ }}{\text{d}\text{Ω}}_{0} With : - \text{Π} : the first Piola-Kirchhoff tensor - \text{T}=\text{Π}.\text{n} : the nominal stress vector (on the boundary) - {\text{ρ}}_{0} : the mass density in the reference state - \text{f} : the body forces Time derivatives are denoted by the notation « \dot{\text{ }} ». {\text{Ω}}_{0} represents the initial volume and {\text{S}}_{0} will denote the initial mid-surface. These equations will not be used to code the finite element, but the static boundary conditions are necessary in order to understand the behaviour of membranes. The first step is to carry out integrations by parts using the divergence theorem in order to eliminate the derivatives {\text{U}}_{,\text{β}}^{\text{ }} and to bring out {\text{U}}^{\text{ }} . This could be anticipated, knowing that a membrane has no bending stiffness. Indeed, applying a couple to a membrane would produce a rigid-body motion. Moreover, a pressure applied to a flat membrane will also produce a rigid-body motion as long as the latter is not deformed and has not acquired a so-called “geometric” stiffness. To remedy this problem, an artificial “geometric” stiffness must be created at the beginning of the analysis by imposing a prestress which can be removed later. 3.3.3 Constitutive laws In order to relate the stresses in the material to its displacements, constitutive laws must be used. In the case of membranes, constitutive laws known as “hyperelastic” are used. Only two hyperelastic constitutive laws, among all those that exist, will be considered: the Saint Venant-Kirchhoff law and the neo-Hookean law. They will be characterised by their volumetric strain-energy density w as a function of the Green-Lagrange strain tensor \text{E} (such that \text{E}={\text{E}}_{ij}{\text{A}}^{i}\otimes {\text{A}}^{j} with {\text{E}}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\text{a}}_{ij}-{\text{A}}_{ij}\right) ) or of the dilation tensor \text{C} (such that \text{C}={\text{C}}_{ij}{\text{A}}^{i}\otimes {\text{A}}^{j} with > ). The second Piola-Kirchhoff stress, \text{Σ} , is then related to \text{E} or \text{C} by: \text{Σ}=\text{Sym}\frac{\partial \text{w}}{\partial \text{E}}=2\text{Sym}\frac{\partial \text{w}}{\partial \text{C}} with \text{Sym}\frac{\partial \text{w}}{\partial \text{E}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial \text{w}}{\partial \text{E}}+{\left(\frac{\partial \text{w}}{\partial \text{E}}\right)}^{\text{T}}\right) 3.3.3.1 Saint Venant-Kirchhoff law The standard hyperelastic material is characterised by the Saint Venant-Kirchhoff law. Its volumetric strain-energy density is expressed by: \text{w}\left(\text{E}\right)={\text{Σ}}_{0}:\text{E}+\frac{1}{2}\text{E}:\text{D}:\text{E} with D a fourth-order tensor called the elasticity tensor. 3.3.3.2 Neo-Hookean law The neo-Hookean law is another classical hyperelastic constitutive law; it is used in particular for the study of incompressible materials. This law gives better results when the body undergoes large strains. Its volumetric strain-energy density is expressed by: \text{w}\left(\text{C}\right)=\frac{\text{μ}}{2}\left(\text{tr}\text{C}-3\right)-\text{μ}.\ln\text{J}+\frac{\text{λ}}{2}(\ln\text{J})\mathrm{²} \text{μ} and \text{λ} are the Lamé coefficients; they are defined by: \text{λ}=\frac{\text{Eν}}{\left(1+\text{ν}\right)\left(1-2\text{ν}\right)} with \text{E} (resp. \text{ν} ) Young’s modulus (resp. r3.08.08 Multi-fibre beam element (straight) POU_D_EM r3.08.08 Multi-fibre beam element (straight) POU_D_EM Summary: This document presents the multi-fibre beam elements based on the solution of a beam problem for which each cross-section of a beam is divided into several fibres. Each fibre then behaves as an Euler beam. Several materials may be assigned on a single finite-element support (SEG2), which avoids having to duplicate the mesh cells (steel + concrete, for example). The beams are straight (element POU_D_EM). The cross-section may be of arbitrary shape, described by a “fibre mesh”, see u4.26.01. The assumptions adopted are the following: - Euler assumption: the transverse shear is neglected (this assumption is verified for large slendernesses), - the multi-fibre beam elements take into account the effects of thermal expansion, of drying and of hydration (right-hand-side terms) and, in a simplified manner, torsion. The normal-force/bending coupling is treated naturally, by integration in the cross-section of the uniaxial responses of the constitutive models associated with each group of fibres. An enrichment of the axial strain, solved by local condensation in the case of non-linear behaviours, allows good numerical results, whatever the evolution in the cross-section of the material centre of gravity of the cross-section. 1 Notation One gives the correspondence between the notations of this document and those of the user's documentation. \mathit{DX},\mathit{DY},\mathit{DZ} and \mathit{DRX},\mathit{DRY},\mathit{DRZ} are in fact the names of the degrees of freedom associated with the components of the displacement u,v,w,{\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z} . | E | Young's modulus | E | | --- | --- | --- | | \nu | Poisson's ratio | \mathit{NU} | | G | Coulomb modulus = \frac{E}{2.(1+\nu )} | G | | {I}_{y},{I}_{z} | geometrical bending moments with respect to the axes y,z | \text{IY},\text{IZ} | | {J}_{x} | torsion constant | \mathit{JX} | | K | stiffness matrix | | | M | mass matrix | | | {M}_{x},{M}_{y},{M}_{z} | moments about the axes x,y,z | \mathit{MT},\mathit{MFY},\mathit{MFZ} | | N | normal force on the cross-section | N | | S | area of the cross-section | A | | u,v,w | translations along the axes x,y,z | \mathit{DX},\mathit{DY},\mathit{DZ} | | {V}_{y},{V}_{z} | shear forces along the axes y,z | \mathit{VY},\mathit{VZ} | | \rho | density | \rho | | {\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z} | rotations about the axes x,y,z | \mathit{DRX},\mathit{DRY},\mathit{DRZ} | | {q}_{x},{q}_{y},{q}_{z} | external line forces | | 2 Introduction The analysis of structures subjected to a dynamic loading requires constitutive models capable of representing the non-linearities of the material. Numerous analytical models have been proposed. They may be classified into two groups: - detailed models based on solid mechanics and their description of the local behaviour of the material (microscopic approach) - models based on a global modelling of the behaviour (macroscopic approach). In the first type of models, one may find the classical finite-element models as well as the “fibre”-type models (having a beam-type element as support). Whereas the “classical” finite-element models are powerful tools for the simulation of the non-linear behaviour of the complex parts of structures (joints, assemblies, …), their application to the whole of a structure may prove impractical because of a prohibitive computation time or of the memory size necessary to carry out this analysis. On the other hand, a multi-fibre beam modelling (r3.08.08-fig-poutre-beton-arme) possesses the advantages of the simplifying assumptions of an Euler–Bernoulli beam kinematics while offering a practical and efficient solution for a complex non-linear analysis of composite structural elements such as those that one may encounter, for example, in reinforced concrete. Moreover, this “intermediate” modelling is relatively robust and inexpensive in computation time because of the use of 1D non-linear constitutive models. Reinforced-concrete beam with stirrups and reinforcement Modelling of a reinforced-concrete beam by a multi-fibre beam Finite-element support of a multi-fibre beam modelling 3 Element of beam theory (reminders) One takes up here the elements developed within the framework of the Euler beam elements (see r3.08.01). A beam is a solid generated by a surface of area S whose geometrical centre of inertia G describes a curve C called the mean fibre or neutral fibre. The area S is the right section (transverse cross-section) or profile, and one assumes that if it is evolving, its evolutions (size, shape) are continuous and progressive when G describes the mean line. For the study of beams in general, one makes the following assumptions: - the right section of the beam is undeformable, - the transverse displacement is uniform over the right section. These assumptions make it possible to express the displacements of an arbitrary point of the cross-section, as a function of the displacements of the corresponding point located on the mean line, and as a function of an increment of displacement due to the rotation of the cross-section about the transverse axes. The discretisation into “exact” beam elements is carried out on a line element with two nodes and six degrees of freedom per node. These degrees of freedom are the three translations u,v,w and the three rotations {\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z} (r3.08.08-fig-element-poutre). Beam element Given that the strains are local, one builds at each vertex of the mesh a local basis depending on the element on which one is working. The continuity of the displacement fields is ensured by a change of basis, bringing the data back into the global basis. In the case of straight beams, one traditionally places the mean line on the x axis of the local basis, the transverse displacements thus taking place in the plane (y,z) . Finally, when one stores quantities linked to the degrees of freedom of an element in a vector or an elementary matrix (therefore of dimension 12 or {12}^{2} ), one first stores the variables for vertex 1 then those of vertex 2 . For each node, one first stores the quantities linked to the three translations, then those linked to the three rotations. For example, a displacement vector will be structured in the following manner: \underbrace{u_1, v_1, w_1, \theta_{x_1}, \theta_{y_1}, \theta_{z_1}}_{\text{sommet 1}} \qquad \underbrace{u_2, v_2, w_2, \theta_{x_2}, \theta_{y_2}, \theta_{z_2}}_{\text{sommet 2}} 4 The equations of motion of the beams One will not take up in this document all the equations of motion of the beams. For further complements concerning this part one may refer to the documentation concerning the elements POU_D_E and POU_D_T . 5 Straight multi-fibre beam element One describes in this chapter the obtaining of the elementary stiffness and mass matrices for the straight multi-fibre beam element, according to the Euler model. The stiffness matrices are computed with the options 'RIGI_MECA' or 'RIGI_MECA_TANG', and the mass matrices with the option 'MASS_MECA' for the consistent matrix, and the option 'MASS_MECA_DIAG' for the diagonalised mass matrix. One presents here a generalisation in which the reference axis chosen for the beam is independent of any geometrical, inertial or mechanical consideration. The element works for an arbitrary cross-section (heterogeneous and without symmetry) and is therefore suited to a non-linear evolution of the behaviour of the fibres. and the strains in matrix form, with the enriched part: {\mathrm{B}}_{s}=\mathrm{N}.(\mathrm{U})+\mathrm{Q}.(\alpha ) \quad \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{B}.(\mathrm{U})+\mathrm{G}.(\alpha ) where \mathrm{N} and \mathrm{B} are the classical matrices of the interpolation functions and of their derivatives (see the equations and ) and: \mathrm{Q}={\left(\begin{array}{cccc}\frac{4x}{L}-\frac{4{x}^{2}}{{L}^{2}}& 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right)}^{T} \quad \text{et} \quad \mathrm{G}={\left(\begin{array}{cccc}\frac{4}{L}-\frac{8x}{{L}^{2}}& 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right)}^{T} {\int}_{0}^{L}\mathrm{G}(x)\text{dx}=0 Note \mathrm{G} has been chosen so that the element always passes the “patch test” (zero strain energy for a rigid-body motion) : After classical manipulations of passage from the continuous to the discrete, the system of equations , written for the whole of the structure, is approximated by: \left\{\begin{array}{c}{A}_{e=1}^{{N}_{\text{elem}}}\left({F}_{int}-{F}_{\text{ext}}\right)=0\\ {h}_{e}=0\text{}\forall e\in [1,{N}_{\text{elem}}]\end{array}\right. with: \left\{\begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{F}}_{int}={\int}_{0}^{L}{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.{\mathrm{F}}_{s}\text{dx}={\int}_{0}^{L}{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.{\mathrm{K}}_{s}.\left(\mathrm{B}.{\mathrm{U}}_{s}+\mathrm{G}.\alpha \right)\text{dx}\\ {\mathrm{F}}_{\text{ext}}={\int}_{0}^{L}{\mathrm{N}}^{T}.\mathrm{f}\text{dx}\\ {h}_{e}={\int}_{0}^{L}{\mathrm{G}}^{T}.{\mathrm{F}}_{s}\text{dx}\end{array}\right. {A}_{e=1}^{{N}_{\text{elem}}} denotes the assembly over all the elements of the mesh; \mathrm{f} is the distributed axial load on the beam element. The system of equations is non-linear, it is solved in an iterative manner (see STAT_NON_LINE). At iteration (i+1) , with \Delta {\mathrm{U}}^{(i)}={\mathrm{U}}^{(i+1)}-{\mathrm{U}}^{(i)} and \Delta {\alpha}^{(i)}={\alpha}^{(i+1)}-{\alpha}^{(i)} , the linearisation of the system gives (Newton correction iterations): \left\{\begin{array}{c}{A}_{e=1}^{{N}_{\text{elem}}}\left(\left({\mathrm{F}}_{int}^{(i+1)}-{\mathrm{F}}_{\text{ext}}^{(i+1)}\right)+{\mathrm{K}}_{e}^{(i)}.\Delta {\mathrm{U}}^{(i)}+{\mathrm{X}}_{e}^{(i)}\Delta {\alpha}^{(i)}\right)=0\\ {h}_{e}^{(i+1)}+{\mathrm{X}}_{e}^{(i)T}.\Delta {\mathrm{U}}^{(i)}+{H}_{e}^{(i)}\Delta {\alpha}^{(i)}=0\forall e\in [\mathrm{1,.}\mathrm{..},{N}_{\text{elem}}]\end{array}\right. with: \left\{\begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{K}}_{e}^{(i)}={\int}_{L}{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.{\mathrm{K}}_{s}^{(i)}.\mathrm{B}\text{dx}\\ {\mathrm{X}}_{e}^{(i)}={\int}_{L}{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.{\mathrm{K}}_{s}^{(i)}.\mathrm{G}\text{dx}\\ {H}_{e}^{(i)}={\int}_{L}{\mathrm{G}}^{T}.{\mathrm{K}}_{s}^{(i)}.\mathrm{G}\text{dx}\end{array}\right. The second equation of the system is local. It makes it possible to compute the enrichment degree of freedom \alpha independently on each element. One computes it by a local iterative method (iterations (j) for a fixed displacement {d}^{(i)}=\Delta {\mathrm{U}}^{(i)} ): {\alpha}_{(j+1)}^{(i)}={\alpha}_{(j)}^{(i)}-{\left({H}_{e(j)}^{(i)}\right)}^{-1}{h}_{e(j)}^{(i)} Thus, when one has converged at the local level, one has: {h}_{e}({d}^{(i)},{\alpha}^{(i)})=0 And one may operate a static condensation in order to eliminate \alpha at the global level. {\mathrm{K}}_{e}^{(i)}={\mathrm{K}}_{e}^{(i)}-{\mathrm{X}}_{e}^{(i)}{\left({H}_{e}^{(i)}\right)}^{-1}{\mathrm{X}}_{e}^{(i)T} From a practical point of view, this technique makes it possible to treat the enrichment at the elementary level without disturbing the number of global degrees of freedom. It is implemented at the level of the elementary routine charged with computing the options FULL_MECA, RAPH_MECA and RIGI_MECA_TANG. - In the particular case set out here, {H}_{e}^{(i)} is a real number, therefore very easy to invert. - Likewise, {h}_{e} and \alpha are also real numbers. - The computation of {K}_{e}^{(i)} is explained in r3.08.08-integration-cas-non-lineaire, the other quantities of the equation are computed according to the same technique. - Likewise the computation of {\mathrm{F}}_{int} is explained in r3.08.08-calcul-forces-internes, {h}_{e} in the equation is computed according to the same technique. Notes 5.5.3 Taking the eccentricity into account For an elastic behaviour, the enrichment of the axial strains makes it possible to take correctly into account the coupling between the normal force and the bending moments, and to make the response of the beam independent of the position chosen for the reference axis (see keyword COOR_AXE_POUTRE in the operator DEFI_GEOM_FIBRE, u4.26.01). It thus makes it possible to treat the case of eccentric beams. The numerical implementation of the enrichment of the axial strains presented in r3.08.08-implantation-numerique concerns the non-linear analyses with STAT_NON_LINE or DYNA_NON_LINE, for the options FULL_MECA, RAPH_MECA and RIGI_MECA_TANG. Indeed, the determination of \alpha is done by local iterations at the elementary level (equation ). In the case of analyses with the option RIGI_MECA (MECA_STATIQUE, modal analysis, non-linear analyses with an 'ELASTIQUE' prediction), one may determine \alpha explicitly as a function of the eccentricities of the elastic centre with respect to the reference axis: {e}_{y}=\frac{{\int}_{S}\mathit{Ey}\mathit{dS}}{{\int}_{S}E\mathit{dS}}=\frac{{K}_{\mathit{S13}}}{{K}_{\mathit{S11}}} and {e}_{z}=\frac{{\int}_{S}\mathit{Ez}\mathit{dS}}{{\int}_{S}E\mathit{dS}}=\frac{{K}_{\mathit{S12}}}{{K}_{\mathit{S11}}} One may then treat the static condensation in order to eliminate \alpha at the level of the elementary stiffness matrix. These computations have been done analytically and the matrix is implemented explicitly in Code_Aster (modification of some twenty terms if {e}_{y} and/or {e}_{z} are not zero). Given that the displacement is enriched, the mass matrix (see r3.08.08-matrice-masse-elment-multifibre) is modified. As for the stiffness matrix, the terms modified in the case where {e}_{y} and/or {e}_{z} are not zero have been computed analytically and programmed explicitly. The enrichment of the strains also modifies the computation of the options DEGE_ELNO and EPSI_ELGA . 5.6 Non-linear constitutive models that can be used The models supported are on the one hand the 1D constitutive relations of type VMIS_ISOT_LINE, VMIS_CINE_LINE and VMIS_ISOT_TRAC, CORR_ACIER r5.03.09 for the steels, on the other hand the model MAZARS_UNIL r7.01.08 dedicated to the uniaxial behaviour of concrete in cyclic loading. One may thus have several materials per multi-fibre beam element. Furthermore, if the behaviour used is not available in 1D, one may use the other 3D laws with the aid of the method of R.DeBorst r5.03.09. For example, one may treat: GRAN_IRRA_LOG, VISC_IRRA_LOG. However in this case, one can treat only a single material per multi-fibre beam element. Note The internal variables, constant per fibre, are stored in the sub-points attached to the integration point considered. Access to the post-processing of the quantities defined at the sub-points is done via the MED3.0 format, of Salomé. 6 Assembly-skeleton element The assembly-skeleton element is a generalisation of the multi-fibre beam element presented in the previous section. This element consists of an element having a beam kinematics, but in which batches of fibres are gathered into sub-beams which represent the guide tubes. These sub-beams are themselves multi-fibre, as shown in r3.08.08-fig-section-multipoutres . This element is accessible only within the framework of the kinematics of Euler beams. The assumptions adopted are the following: - the Euler assumption: the transverse shear is neglected (this assumption is verified for large slendernesses); - the element carries the usual displacement and rotation degrees of freedom of beams as well as three additional degrees of freedom modelling the rotation of the grid linking kinematically the guide tubes; - the rotations in the whole of the beams are all the same; - the skeleton element takes into account the effects of thermal expansion, of gravity and, in a simplified manner, torsion. These guide tubes are linked kinematically to one another by the grids of the fuel assembly, here considered as a rigid body. From these two assumptions, it is possible to describe the whole kinematics of this assembly of beams with the aid of nine degrees of freedom, as indicated on r3.08.08-fig-element-assemblage-combustible : - three degrees of freedom representing the displacement of the grid: ({u}_{x},{u}_{y},{u}_{z}) - three degrees of freedom describing the rotations of the guide tubes: ({\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z}) - three degrees of freedom modelling the rotation of the grid linking the guide tubes: ({\omega}_{x},{\omega}_{y},{\omega}_{z}) Diagram of the fuel-assembly element The position of a guide tube i with respect to the centre of the assembly skeleton is described with the aid of a pair of real numbers ({Y}^{i},{Z}^{i}) . By using the usual degrees of freedom (three displacements and three rotations) of a three-dimensional Euler beam and by assuming that the rotations in all the beams are the same, the kinematics of the guide tube i is written: {u}_{x}^{i}={u}_{x}\left(x\right)-{Y}^{i}.{\omega}_{z}\left(x\right)+{Z}^{i}.{\omega}_{y}\left(x\right) {u}_{y}^{i}={u}_{y}\left(x\right)-{Z}^{i}{\omega}_{x}\left(x\right) {u}_{z}^{i}={u}_{z}\left(x\right)+{Y}^{i}{\omega}_{x}\left(x\right) {\theta}_{x}^{i}={\theta}_{x}(x) {\theta}_{y}^{i}={\theta}_{y}(x) {\theta}_{z}^{i}={\theta}_{z}(x) Moreover, with a view to using beams with a non-linear behaviour, the cross-section of the beams is itself described with the aid of fibres (numbered from 1 to {N}_{f} ) and the multi-fibre beam theory is used here. Thus, for each beam i (varying from 1 to {N}_{p} ), the axial displacement of its fibre j is a function of the mean displacement of the cross-section of the beam, to which one adds the displacement imposed by the rotation of the cross-section. Since beam theory imposes that the cross-section of the beams remains straight, the axial displacement field of the fibre j of a guide tube i is written: {u}_{x}^{i,j}={u}_{x}^{i}-\left({y}^{i,j}-{Y}^{i}\right).{\theta}_{z}\left(x\right)+\left({z}^{i,j}-{Z}^{i}\right).{\theta}_{y}\left(x\right) By injecting into it the first equation : {u}_{x}^{i,j}={u}_{x}\left(x\right)-{Y}^{i}.{\omega}_{z}\left(x\right)+{Z}^{i}.{\omega}_{y}\left(x\right)-\left({y}^{i,j}-{Y}^{i}\right).{\theta}_{z}\left(x\right)+\left({z}^{i,j}-{Z}^{i}\right).{\theta}_{y}\left(x\right) Where the quantity ({y}^{i,j},{z}^{i,j}) corresponds to the position of the fibre j of a beam i with respect to the centre of the assembly of beams. The axial strain field of the fibre is subsequently determined by: {\epsilon}_{xx}^{i,j}=\frac{\partial {u}_{x}^{i,j}}{\partial x}={u}_{x}^{'}\left(x\right)-{Y}^{i}.{\omega}_{z}^{'}\left(x\right)+{Z}^{i}.{\omega}_{y}^{'}\left(x\right)-\left({y}^{i,j}-{Y}^{i}\right).{\theta}_{z}^{'}\left(x\right)+\left({z}^{i,j}-{Z}^{i}\right).{\theta}_{y}^{'}\left(x\right) The principle is to rely on the existing multi-fibre beams by passing from the degrees of freedom of the assembly-skeleton element to the i fields of “generalised multi-fibre beam displacements” constituting it, by using (). By proceeding thus (i.e. by treating all the beams individually), one determines a “local generalised displacement field” {U}_{i} for each of the beams i . One thus comes back, for each of the beams, to the determination of the fields with the aid of the six “classical” degrees of freedom along the element. Thus, one determines the generalised strains {D}_{i} on each of the beams i with {D}_{i}=B.{U}_{i} (cf. r3.08.08). Once this is done, one may: - determine the uniaxial strains on the fibres in the same way as for the Euler multi-fibre beams; - obtain the stresses by the constitutive law; - determine the generalised forces on the beam i as for an Euler multi-fibre beam from the stresses; - assemble the elementary matrix of the assembly skeleton from the matrices of each sub-beam; - finally one must construct the generalised forces of the assembly element from the generalised forces on the beams i . It is a matter of separating the moments caused by the rotation of the beams and those caused by the rotation of the grid. The implementation of this finite element is intended as an encapsulation of the multi-fibre Euler beam model. The discretisation of the skeleton element is carried out on a line element with two nodes and nine degrees of freedom per node. These degrees of freedom are the three translations (u,v,w) and the six rotations relative to the beams ({\theta}_{x},{\theta}_{y},{\theta}_{z}) and to the grids ({\omega}_{x},{\omega}_{y},{\omega}_{z}) . Skeleton element Given that the strains are local, one builds at each vertex of the mesh a local basis depending on the element on which one is working. The continuity of the displacement fields is ensured by a change of basis, bringing the data back into the global basis. In the case of straight beams, one traditionally places the mean line on the axis x of the local basis, the transverse displacements thus taking place in the plane (y,z) . Finally, when one stores quantities linked to the degrees of freedom of an element in a vector or an elementary matrix (therefore of dimension 18 or {18}^{2} ), one first stores the variables for vertex 1 then those of vertex 2 . For each node, one first stores the quantities linked to the three translations, then those linked to the six rotations. For example, a displacement vector will be structured in the following manner: \underbrace{u_1, v_1, w_1, \theta_{x_1}, \theta_{y_1}, \theta_{z_1}, \omega_{x_1}, \omega_{y_1}, \omega_{z_1}}_{\text{sommet 1}} \qquad \underbrace{u_2, v_2, w_2, \theta_{x_2}, \theta_{y_2}, \theta_{z_2}, \omega_{x_2}, \omega_{y_2}, \omega_{z_2}}_{\text{sommet 2}} 6.2 Determination of the stiffness matrix The stiffness matrix of the skeleton element rests directly on an assembly of the elementary matrices of each beam of the bundle of the assembly. One will therefore refer to the documentation relating to the straight multi-fibre beam element concerning the computation of these matrices. The stiffness matrices are computed with the options 'RIGI_MECA' or 'RIGI_MECA_TANG'. The skeleton element carries two nodes (indexed 1 and 2) each provided with nine degrees of freedom describing the three fields (U,\theta ,\omega ) . The whole of these degrees of freedom come to generate displacements/rotations on the multi-fibre sub-beams which for their part have twelve degrees of freedom. In order to differentiate the degrees of freedom of the skeleton element and of the sub-beams, one uses respectively capitals / lower case. For the displacements: {u}_{{x}_{1}}={U}_{{x}_{1}}-{\omega}_{{z}_{1}}{Y}^{i}+{\omega}_{{y}_{1}}{Z}^{i} \quad \text{et} \quad {u}_{{x}_{2}}={U}_{{x}_{2}}-{\omega}_{{z}_{2}}{Y}^{i}+{\omega}_{{y}_{2}}{Z}^{i} {u}_{{y}_{1}}={U}_{{y}_{1}}-{\omega}_{{x}_{1}}{Z}^{i} \quad \text{et} \quad {u}_{{y}_{2}}={U}_{{y}_{2}}-{\omega}_{{x}_{2}}{Z}^{i} {u}_{{z}_{1}}={U}_{{z}_{1}}+{\omega}_{{x}_{1}}{Y}^{i} \quad \text{et} \quad {u}_{{z}_{2}}={U}_{{z}_{2}}+{\omega}_{{x}_{2}}{Y}^{i} For the rotations: {\theta}_{{x}_{1}}={\Theta}_{{x}_{1}} \quad \text{et} \quad {\theta}_{{x}_{2}}={\Theta}_{{x}_{2}} {\theta}_{{y}_{1}}={\Theta}_{{y}_{1}} \quad \text{et} \quad {\theta}_{{y}_{2}}={\Theta}_{{y}_{2}} {\theta}_{{z}_{1}}={\Theta}_{{z}_{1}} \quad \text{et} \quad {\theta}_{{z}_{2}}={\Theta}_{{z}_{2}} If one denotes by {K}^{i} the matrix of size 12x12 corresponding to the beam i , one may compute for example the normal force {f}_{x}^{i} on the beam in this way: \begin{array}{c}{f}_{x}^{i}={K}_{1,1}^{i}.{u}_{{x}_{1}}+{K}_{1,2}^{i}.{u}_{{y}_{1}}+{K}_{1,3}^{i}.{u}_{{z}_{1}}\\ {K}_{1,4}^{i}.{\theta}_{{x}_{1}}+{K}_{1,5}^{i}.{\theta}_{{y}_{1}}+{K}_{1,6}^{i}.{\theta}_{{z}_{1}}+\\ {K}_{1,7}^{i}.{u}_{{x}_{2}}+{K}_{1,8}^{i}.{u}_{{y}_{2}}+{K}_{1,9}^{i}.{u}_{{z}_{2}}\\ {K}_{1,10}^{i}.{\theta}_{{x}_{2}}+{K}_{1,11}^{i}.{\theta}_{{y}_{2}}+{K}_{1,12}^{i}.{\theta}_{{z}_{2}}\end{array} This force is expressed as a function of the “local” degrees of freedom; one may also express it as a function of the “global” degrees of freedom, that is to say those of the skeleton element: \begin{array}{c}{f}_{x}^{i}={K}_{1,1}^{i}.\left[{U}_{{x}_{1}}-{\omega}_{{z}_{1}}{Y}^{i}+{\omega}_{{y}_{1}}{Z}^{i}\right]+\\ {K}_{1,2}^{i}.\left[{U}_{{y}_{1}}-{\omega}_{{x}_{1}}{Z}^{i}\right]+\\ {K}_{1,3}^{i}.\left[{U}_{{z}_{1}}+{\omega}_{{x}_{1}}{Y}^{i}\right]+\\ {K}_{1,4}^{i}.{\theta}_{{x}_{1}}+{K}_{1,5}^{i}.{\theta}_{{y}_{1}}+{K}_{1,6}^{i}.{\theta}_{{z}_{1}}+\\ {K}_{1,7}^{i}.\left[{U}_{{x}_{2}}-{\omega}_{{z}_{2}}{Y}^{i}+{\omega}_{{y}_{2}}{Z}^{i}\right]+\\ {K}_{1,8}^{i}.\left[{U}_{{y}_{2}}-{\omega}_{{x}_{2}}{Z}^{i}\right]+\\ {K}_{1,9}^{i}.\left[{U}_{{z}_{2}}+{\omega}_{{x}_{2}}{Y}^{i}\right]+\\ {K}_{1,10}^{i}.{\theta}_{{x}_{2}}+{K}_{1,11}^{i}.{\theta}_{{y}_{2}}+{K}_{1,12}^{i}.{\theta}_{{z}_{2}}\end{array} The generalised forces on the element are defined for the normal force by simple summation: {F}_{x}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{f}_{x}^{i} The tangent matrix is obtained by differentiating the forces with respect to the degrees of freedom. One therefore has, for example: \frac{\partial {F}_{x}}{\partial {U}_{{x}_{1}}}=\frac{\partial \left(\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{f}_{x}^{i}\right)}{\partial {U}_{{x}_{1}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}\frac{\partial {f}_{x}^{i}}{\partial {U}_{{x}_{1}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{K}_{1,1}^{i} And: \frac{\partial {F}_{x}}{\partial {\omega}_{{x}_{1}}}=\frac{\partial \left(\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{f}_{x}^{i}\right)}{\partial {\omega}_{{x}_{1}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}\frac{\partial {f}_{x}^{i}}{\partial {\omega}_{{x}_{1}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}\left(-{Z}^{i}.{K}_{1,2}^{i}+{Y}^{i}.{K}_{1,3}^{i}\right) One therefore sees that the first term of this matrix of the skeleton element is nothing other than the sum of the first terms of the matrix of the “sub-beams” making up the assembly. More generally, the elementary skeleton matrix is a linear combination of the terms of the tangent matrices of the sub-beams. One will not detail here the content of the whole of the matrix (18x18) whose useful stored part contains 171 terms. The ordering of the degrees of freedom is the following: ({U}_{{x}_{1}},{U}_{{y}_{1}},{U}_{{z}_{1}},{\theta}_{{x}_{1}},{\theta}_{{y}_{1}},{\theta}_{{z}_{1}},{\omega}_{{x}_{1}},{\omega}_{{y}_{1}},{\omega}_{{z}_{1}},{U}_{{x}_{2}},{U}_{{y}_{2}},{U}_{{z}_{2}},{\theta}_{{x}_{2}},{\theta}_{{y}_{2}},{\theta}_{{z}_{2}},{\omega}_{{x}_{2}},{\omega}_{{y}_{2}},{\omega}_{{z}_{2}}) And that of the forces: ({F}_{{x}_{1}},{F}_{{y}_{1}},{F}_{{z}_{1}},{M}_{{x}_{1}},{M}_{{y}_{1}},{M}_{{z}_{1}},{\mathit{MG}}_{{x}_{1}},{\mathit{MG}}_{{y}_{1}},{\mathit{MG}}_{{z}_{1}},{F}_{{x}_{2}},{F}_{{y}_{2}},{F}_{{z}_{2}},{M}_{{x}_{2}},{M}_{{y}_{2}},{M}_{{z}_{2}},{\mathit{MG}}_{{x}_{2}},{\mathit{MG}}_{{y}_{2}},{\mathit{MG}}_{{z}_{2}}) 6.3 Determination of the internal forces of the element A constitutive law is used, as within the framework of multi-fibre beam theory, in order to determine stresses on the fibres. One therefore has: {\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}=f\left({\epsilon}_{xx}^{i,j},\alpha \right) Where i is a functional of the strain of the fibre and of internal variables \alpha describing the constitutive law. The normal force in each of the fibres is subsequently obtained by integration of the stresses over the cross-section. Since the latter are constant per fibre: {f}_{x}^{i,j}={\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.{s}^{i,j} where {s}^{i,j} is the area of the fibre j of a beam {N}_{p} . One may thus reconstruct the generalised forces of a usual multi-fibre beam from the forces in the fibres constituting it, as done for the multi-fibre beam elements r3.08.08. For the normal forces i : {N}^{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{x}^{i,j} and for the shear forces i : {V}_{y}^{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{y}^{i,j} \textrm{et} {V}_{z}^{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{z}^{i,j} The bending moments of the beam i are written: {M}_{y}^{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{x}^{i,j}.\left({z}^{i,j}-{Z}^{i}\right) \textrm{et} {M}_{z}^{i}=-\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{x}^{i,j}.\left({y}^{i,j}-{Y}^{i}\right) Finally, the torsional moment {M}_{x}^{i}={G}_{x}^{i}.{\theta}_{x}^{i} is computed directly from the stiffness {G}_{x} on the assumption of a purely elastic behaviour. These forces therefore make it possible to establish an equilibrium in the different guide tubes constituting the skeleton. By introducing the equation into the principle of virtual work, one obtains: {\int}_{{V}_{0}}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.\delta {\epsilon}_{xx}^{i,j}.{\mathit{dV}}_{0}=\underset{0}{\overset{L}{\int}}\left({N}^{i}.\delta {u}_{x}^{'}\left(x\right)+{M}_{y}^{i}.\delta {\theta}_{y}^{'}\left(x\right)+{M}_{z}^{i}.\delta {\theta}_{z}^{'}\left(x\right)+{M}_{gy}^{i}.\delta {\omega}_{y}^{'}\left(x\right)+{M}_{gz}^{i}.\delta {\omega}_{z}^{'}\left(x\right)\right).\mathit{dx} With the normal force for the beam i : {N}^{i}={\int}_{S}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.\mathit{dS}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.{s}^{i,j}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{x}^{i,j} The bending moment with respect to y : {M}_{y}^{i}={\int}_{S}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.\left({z}^{i,j}-{Z}^{i}\right).\mathit{dS}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.\left({z}^{i,j}-{Z}^{i}\right).{s}^{i,j}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{x}^{i,j}.\left({z}^{i,j}-{Z}^{i}\right) And the bending moment with respect to z : {M}_{z}^{i}=-{\int}_{S}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.\left({y}^{i,j}-{Y}^{i}\right).\mathit{dS}=-\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.\left({y}^{i,j}-{Y}^{i}\right).{s}^{i,j}=-\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{x}^{i,j}.\left({y}^{i,j}-{Y}^{i}\right) The contribution of the beam i to the bending moment of the grid with respect to y is written: {M}_{g,y}^{i}={\int}_{S}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.{Z}^{i}.\mathit{dS}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.{s}^{i,j}.{Z}^{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{x}^{i,j}.{Z}^{i}={N}^{i}.{Z}^{i} And the bending moment of the grid with respect to z is written: {M}_{g,z}^{i}=-{\int}_{S}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.{Y}^{i}.\mathit{dS}=-\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{\sigma}_{xx}^{i,j}.{s}^{i,j}.{Y}^{i}=-\sum_{j=1}^{{N}_{f}}{f}_{x}^{i,j}.{Y}^{i}=-{N}^{i}{Y}^{i} These last two terms feed the generalised grid forces set out hereafter. The forces in the beams are assembled in order to describe the total force in the skeleton element. The normal force and the shear forces are obtained by summing the individual forces on the beams: these forces are computed by summation of the forces on each beam of the assembly bundle. One therefore has the normal and shear forces such that: N=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{N}^{i} \quad {V}_{y}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{V}_{y}^{i} \quad {V}_{z}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{V}_{z}^{i} And the torsional and bending moments of the beams: {M}_{x}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{M}_{x}^{i} \quad {M}_{y}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{M}_{y}^{i} \quad {M}_{z}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{M}_{z}^{i} The beams being rigidly linked to one another by the grids, the normal and shear forces in the beams generate, because of the eccentricity of the guide tubes with respect to the centre of the beam assembly, bending moments. The equilibrium of the forces having to be respected in the sense of the assembly skeleton, three new generalised forces are thus introduced and consist of moments applied to the rigid body. They represent the dual of the additional degrees of freedom presented in the description of the kinematics of the structure. The torsional and bending moments of the grids therefore take the values: {M}_{g,x}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{F}_{z}^{i}.{Y}^{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{F}_{y}^{i}.{Z}^{i} \quad {M}_{g,y}=\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{N}^{i}.{Z}^{i} \quad {M}_{g,z}=-\sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{p}}{N}^{i}.{Y}^{i} Thus, it is possible to describe the equilibrium in the skeleton with the aid of these nine generalised forces. 7 Application cases One may usefully consult the following test cases: - ssll111a: Static response of a reinforced-concrete beam (T-section) with linear thermoelastic behaviour, v3.01.111. - ssls143a: Cantilever beam with eccentric web, v3.03.143. - sdll130b: Seismic response of a reinforced-concrete beam (rectangular cross-section) with linear behaviour, v2.02.130. - sdll132a: Eigenmodes of a frame in multi-fibre beams; v2.02.132. - sdll150a: eigenmodes of a beam with eccentric web, v2.02.150. - ssnl119a, ssnl119b: Static response of a reinforced-concrete beam (rectangular cross-section) with non-linear behaviour, v6.02.119. - sdnl130a: Seismic response of a reinforced-concrete beam (rectangular cross-section) with non-linear behaviour, v5.02.130. - ssll102j: Clamped beam subjected to unit forces, v3.01.102. - ssnl106g, ssnl106h: Elastoplastic beam in tension and pure bending, v6.02.106. - ssnl122a: Multi-fibre cantilever beam subjected to a force v6.02.122. - ssnl504a: Bundle of multi-fibre beams v6.02.504. - ssnl504b: Skeleton element subjected to imposed displacements v6.02.504. - ssnl504c: Skeleton element subjected to force, moment, temperature and gravity loadings v6.02.504. - ssnl123a: Buckling of a multi-fibre beam v6.02.123. 8 Bibliography [bib1] J.L.
