The shear forces and the transverse shear stresses are obtained by writing the local equilibrium equations without body force: {\sigma}_{,j}^{ij}=0 Which makes it possible to write the shear force: {V}^{\alpha}\left({x}_{\gamma}\right)={M}_{,\beta }^{\alpha \beta }\left({x}_{\gamma}\right) And the shear stress: {\sigma}^{\alpha 3}\left({x}_{\gamma},{x}_{3}\right)=-{\int}_{-h}^{{x}_{3}}{\sigma}_{,\beta }^{\alpha \beta }\left({x}_{\gamma},z\right)\mathit{dz} Using the fact that {\sigma}^{\alpha 3}\left({x}_{\gamma ,+h}\right)={\sigma}^{\alpha 3}\left({x}_{\gamma ,-h}\right)=0 . The role of the pre-processing is to calculate the various quantities A , B , C , P , Q , R , \mathit{DM} and \mathit{DN} , from the description of the material (number, orientation and thickness of the various layers, local characteristics \rho \text{c} , k , \rho , L and d ). 3 Frames in the plane tangent to the shell. Matrix notation 3.1 Frames One considers the global frame of the structure (X,Y,Z) . In the case of laminated composites the orientation of the single layer is defined with respect to a reference direction {e}_{\text{réf}} in the tangent plane ( T ). This vector {e}_{\text{réf}} is determined by the projection of a vector {X}_{1} , given by the user under the keyword ANGL_REP of AFFE_CARA_ELEM, onto the tangent plane ( T ) at an arbitrary point of the shell. Figure 3.1-1: Definition of the local frame The vector {X}_{1} is defined by the user by two oriented angles: {\alpha}_{1} : between \mathrm{OX} and {X}_{1\text{proj}(X,Y)} {\alpha}_{2} : between {X}_{1\text{proj}(X,Y)} and {X}_{1} {\alpha}_{1} : takes one from the direction \mathrm{0X} to the projection, in the plane \mathrm{XOY} , of the vector {X}_{1} . {\alpha}_{2} : takes one from this projection to {X}_{1} itself: see figure . In the cases where, in a given zone of the shell, T is orthogonal to {X}_{1} , the user will have to define another vector (in practice for certain mesh cells). For a finite element of plane-facet type, contained in the tangent plane T , one defines the orthonormal frame ({V}_{1},{V}_{2}) local to the element by means of the numbering of the vertices. For example for the triangle: Figure 3.1-b : Local frame of the element ({V}_{1},{V}_{2}) The oriented angle {j}_{0}=({V}_{1},{e}_{\text{réf}}) makes it possible to pass from the frame local to the element to the reference frame. 3.2 Matrix notation In thermal analysis as in thermo-mechanics, the programming of the elements requires one to express the elasticity and conduction operators in the local frame of the finite element ({V}_{1},{V}_{2}) . One is accustomed to simplify the representation of the tensor quantities as follows. 3.2.1 Thermal analysis One represents the tensor quantities in the frame ({V}_{1},{V}_{2}) : {A}_{\alpha \beta }^{ij}\left((i,j)\in {(m,s,i)}^{2}\text{et}(\alpha ,\beta )\in {(1,2)}^{2}\right) In a vector form with six vectors, taking the symmetries into account (see r4.01.01-caracteristique-thermique): {A}^{ij}=(\begin{array}{c}{A}_{11}^{ij}\\ {A}_{22}^{ij}\\ {A}_{12}^{ij}\end{array})={\int}_{-h}^{h}{P}_{i}({x}_{3}).{P}_{j}({x}_{3}).(\begin{array}{c}{k}_{11}\\ {k}_{22}\\ {k}_{12}\end{array}){\text{dx}}_{3} Where k=\left(\begin{array}{c}{k}_{11}\\ {k}_{22}\\ {k}_{12}\end{array}\right) denotes the thermal conductivity vector built with the aid of the tensor (\begin{array}{cc}{k}_{\alpha \beta }& \begin{array}{c}0\\ 0\end{array}\\ \begin{array}{cc}0& 0\end{array}& {k}_{33}\end{array}) (see r4.01.01-notations-hypotheses), and of {P}_{i}({x}_{3}) , the Lagrange polynomials through the thickness. One does the same for {B}^{ij} and {C}^{ij} . Placing oneself in the element frame ({V}_{1},{V}_{2}) , one uses the transformation matrix {P}_{k}^{(m)} of the conductivity tensor k=(\begin{array}{c}{k}_{11}\\ {k}_{22}\\ {k}_{12}\end{array}) from ({V}_{1},{V}_{2}) towards the frame associated with {e}_{\text{réf}} []: {P}_{k}^{(m)}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{C}^{2}& {S}^{2}& 2\text{CS}\\ {S}^{2}& {C}^{2}& -2\text{CS}\\ -\text{CS}& \text{CS}& {C}^{2}-{S}^{2}\end{array}\right] It follows that the transformation matrix {({P}_{k}^{m})}^{-1} of the conductivity tensor from the frame associated with {e}_{\text{réf}} towards ({V}_{1},{V}_{2}) is given by: {P}_{{k}^{{(m)}^{-1}}}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{C}^{2}& {S}^{2}& -2\text{CS}\\ {S}^{2}& {C}^{2}& 2\text{CS}\\ \text{CS}& -\text{CS}& {C}^{2}-{S}^{2}\end{array}\right] 3.2.2 Thermomechanics One likewise represents in a vector form in the frame ({V}_{1},{V}_{2}) : - on the one hand, the normal stresses {\sigma}_{11},{\sigma}_{22} , the shear {\sigma}_{12} in the plane and the transverse shear {\sigma}_{13} and {\sigma}_{23} : \sigma =\left(\begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{11}\\ {\sigma}_{22}\\ {\sigma}_{12}\end{array}\right) - on the other hand, the corresponding strains: \epsilon =\left(\begin{array}{c}{\epsilon}_{11}\\ {\epsilon}_{22}\\ {\gamma}_{12}\end{array}\right) which are decomposed with the generalised membrane strains E and bending strains K : \epsilon \left({x}_{3}\right)=\epsilon \left(u\right)\left({x}_{3}\right)-{\epsilon}^{\text{th}}\left({x}_{3}\right) And for the thermal part: {\epsilon}^{\text{th}}\left({x}_{3}\right)=d\left({x}_{3}\right)\left({T}_{\left({x}_{3}\right)}-{T}^{\text{réf}}\right) Pour une ordonnée {x}_{3}\in ]-h,h[ , et: E=\left(\begin{array}{c}{E}_{11}\\ {E}_{22}\\ {E}_{11}\end{array}\right) Where d is the vector associated with the thermal expansion coefficients. For the elastic coefficients, one has {E}_{\text{LL}}^{(m)} , {E}_{\text{TT}}^{(m)} , {\nu}_{\text{LT}}^{(m)} , {G}_{\text{LT}}^{(m)} , {G}_{\text{LZ}}^{(m)} and {G}_{\text{TZ}}^{(m)} and the expansion coefficients {d}_{}^{(m)} and {d}_{\text{TT}}^{(m)} . In the axes of orthotropy (L,T) of the material m , the compliance matrix S is expressed by: {S}_{(m)}{\mid}_{(L,T)}={\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{1}{{E}_{\text{LL}}}& -\frac{{\nu}_{\text{LT}}}{{E}_{\mathrm{TT}}}& 0\\ -\frac{{\nu}_{\text{TL}}}{{E}_{\mathrm{TT}}}& \frac{1}{{E}_{\mathrm{TT}}}& 0\\ 0& 0& \frac{1}{{G}_{\text{LT}}}\end{array}\right]}_{(m)} The stiffness {\Lambda}_{(m)}={S}_{(m)}^{-1} being: {\Lambda}_{(m)}{\mid}_{(L,T)}={\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{{E}_{\text{LL}}}{1-{\nu}_{\mathrm{TL}}\cdot {\nu}_{\text{LT}}}& \frac{{\nu}_{\text{TL}}\cdot r4.02.01 Finite elements in acoustics r4.02.01 Finite elements in acoustics Summary: This document describes, for stationary linear acoustics at low frequency in a bounded medium, the equations used, the variational formulations which follow from them, and the corresponding translation into isoparametric finite elements by means of a usual formulation with one unknown p (acoustic pressure). This document corresponds to PHENOMENE='ACOUSTIQUE'. 1 Introduction One places oneself in the framework of linear acoustics, in a bounded medium, which considers a compressible fluid, with small amplitudes of perturbations or fluctuations of pressure and of density known. The equations to be solved are those describing the local equilibrium of the fluid and the conservation of mass, together with the linear viscoacoustic constitutive relation (of hysteretic type). A modelling option has been developed in Code_Aster , making it possible to study stationary linear acoustic propagation at low frequency, in a bounded medium, for propagation domains of complex topology, that is to solve, under the conditions stated, the Helmholtz equation. In order to know the paths of propagation of energy in the fluid, the acoustician has available the active acoustic intensity I : I= rac{1}{2}	ext{Re}\left[p{v}^{	ext{ }}ight] And the reactive acoustic intensity J : J= rac{1}{2}	ext{Im}\left[p{v}^{	ext{ }}ight] Where {v}^{	ext{ }} denotes the complex conjugate of the vibratory velocity. Knowledge of these quantities provides a very important complement of information in the solution of problems of every kind, for example the measurement of the powers radiated by machines, and the recognition and location of sources. The parameter k denotes the wave number of the problem treated; it may be complex or real, according to whether or not the propagation takes place in a domain comprising a certain attenuation modelled by means of a complex wave speed, for example if the material is “porous” [bib6]: k= rac{\omega}{c} with c denoting the speed of sound, which may be complex in the case of propagation in a “porous” or viscoacoustic medium, and \omega is a real number in every case, which denotes the angular frequency such that: \omega =2\pi f f is the working frequency of the harmonic problem. One assumes the solution of the problem to be sufficiently regular, p\in {H}^{2}\left(\Omega ight) . One multiplies the Helmholtz equation () without source term s by a test function \varphi . r4.02.02 Elements for linear fluid-structure interaction coupling with an inert fluid r4.02.02 Elements for linear fluid-structure interaction coupling with an inert fluid Summary: The elements described here make it possible to carry out computations of the frequencies and eigenmodes of a structure coupled to a fluid. They also make it possible to compute the acoustic response. After the formulation of the fluid-structure coupling problem, this document describes the approach followed in order to implement the new finite elements. 1 Introduction The vibratory behaviour of a structure is often modified if the structure is in the presence of a fluid: this is what is called vibro-acoustic coupling. One distinguishes the coupling cases into two categories: either the fluid is infinite (this is the case of submerged structures), or the fluid is contained in a bounded medium (this is the case of tanks more or less filled with fluid). The finite elements described here make it possible to solve coupling problems with a fluid of finite dimension. One denotes by {n}_{s} the outward normal to the fluid domain {\Omega}_{f} . At a given instant, the state of the fluid is defined by its (scalar) pressure field p and that of the structure by its (vector) displacement field {u}_{s} . One considers that the coupled system is subjected to small perturbations about its equilibrium state, in which the fluid and the structure are at rest. The fluid-structure interaction problem then consists in solving simultaneously two problems: - one in the structure subjected, on \Sigma , to a pressure field p imposed by the fluid; - the other in the fluid subjected to a displacement field u of the wall \Sigma . Note: if the sense of the normal, from fluid towards structure or from structure towards fluid, is of no importance (it is a convention), it is nevertheless imperative that this normal always be oriented in the same sense. It is strongly recommended to keep the orientation convention from the structure towards the fluid for all the modellings of the fluid-structure interface, in order to keep consistency with the other loadings on the structure (see in particular the case of loadings of type ONDE_PLANE). 2.2 Formulation of the vibro-acoustic problem 2.2.1 Description of the structure Assumption : the structure is homogeneous and obeys the laws of linear elasticity. In order to define the absorbing fluid elements, which take the BGT condition into account, one must assign the modellings '3D_FLUI_ABSO', '2D_FLUI_ABSO' or 'AXIS_FLUI_ABSO'. In order to choose the formulation ( u-p , u-p-\phi or u-\psi ), one will use the keyword FORMULATION in AFFE_MODELE. They lead to volume or surface elements, for the fluid part, and to surface or line elements for the fluid-structure interface or for the absorbing elements. 3.1 Euler buckling, geometric stiffness One considers the Euler buckling problem of an elastic solid in interaction with a fluid domain, modelled with the vibro-acoustic assumption. One models fluctuating fields. Euler buckling is therefore treated by searching for the vanishing of the natural vibration frequencies of the coupled system, including the presence of the geometric stiffness associated with the prestressed static state in the solid, controlled by a critical loading parameter to be determined. One admits at first that the geometric stiffness associated with the initial static state in the fluid is negligible. One therefore proposes to define a zero geometric-stiffness matrix in the fluid domain and on the fluid/structure interfaces. However, this method of analysis neglects the fact that the fluid pressure is a follower loading for the solid, which therefore introduces a non-linear term, which often has notable effects on the critical buckling loads. It is therefore preferable to treat the problem by a non-linear dynamic analysis associated with a stability analysis, by driving the mechanical loading: consult the document U2.06.11. 4 Bibliography 1. r4.02.03 Elasto-acoustic beam r4.02.03 Elasto-acoustic beam Summary: One presents a straight elasto-acoustic coupling element which applies to a structural element of Timoshenko beam type. This element makes it possible to carry out, in vibro-acoustics, the modal analysis of a straight pipe containing a pressurised fluid (water, steam…). One may also carry out response analyses to fluid sources (mass flow rate, volume flow rate, pressure) by modal recombination. The boundary conditions applicable to the nodes of these elements are of Dirichlet type: displacement, pressure or potential may be imposed there. > Contents 1 Notations | P | : | instantaneous total pressure at a point of the fluid | | --- | --- | --- | | p | : | pressure averaged over a cross-section | | \tilde{p} | : | fluctuating pressure | | u | : | displacement of the structure | | \Phi | : | displacement potential of the fluid | | {\rho}_{0} | : | density of the acoustic fluid | | {\rho}_{s} | : | density of the structure | | \omega ,f | : | angular frequency, frequency | | c | : | speed of sound in the fluid | | \lambda ,k | : | wavelength, wave number | | s | : | stress tensor of the structure | | \varepsilon | : | strain tensor of the structure | | \text{dV} | : | volume element | | \text{dA} | : | surface element | | \Sigma | : | interaction surface between the piping and the fluid | | {S}_{f} | : | cross-section of the fluid | | {S}_{s} | : | cross-section of the piping | 2 Introduction In order to be able to carry out dynamic response analyses of structures filled with fluid to fluids, 3D fluid-structure coupling elements have been developed in Code_Aster ( cf [bib2]). These volume elements have the advantage of allowing a fine description of the structure at particular locations, such as, for example, the junction between a main pipe and an instrumentation branch. On the other hand, their systematic use for the analysis of branched and complex networks would lead to prohibitive modelling costs (production of the mesh) and analysis costs. For this reason, and in order to facilitate simplified studies of the dynamic behaviour of piping, a straight elasto-acoustic beam element has been developed, making it possible to carry out, at a lower cost in manpower and in analysis, analyses of the overall behaviour of the straight parts of piping at low frequency. One finds below a presentation of the finite element for piping of elasto-acoustic beam type. The vibratory behaviour of piping networks is conditioned by the flow of the fluid which runs through them. 3 The elasto-acoustic beam model 3.1 Assumptions One studies at low frequency the vibrations of an elastic pipe, linear, homogeneous and isotropic, coupled to a compressible fluid. The effects due to the viscosity and to the flow of the fluid are neglected. Piping consists of slender bodies. Indeed, their transverse dimensions are very much smaller than their length: D\ll L , and the thicknesses are such that one may neglect the swelling and ovalisation modes of the pipe. One may use a beam model. At low frequency the acoustic wavelengths associated with the problems studied are large compared with the transverse dimensions and small compared with the longitudinal dimension of the circuit: \omega .L/c>1 and \omega .D/c\ll 1 . The compressibility acts indeed principally on the longitudinal displacements. Transversely, one considers that the fluid moves as a non-deformable solid, that is to say that it acts as an added mass. The pressure in a cross-section of the pipe then being constant, one says that the acoustic wave is plane. 3.2 Functional of the coupled problem One may write the variational formulation of the problem of fluid-filled piping from the equilibrium and constitutive equations of the fluid and of the pipe as well as from the boundary conditions. From the general functional of the three-dimensional coupled problem ([bib1], [bib2]), one may write the functional applied to the particular case of beams. The variational formulation of the 3D problem amounts to minimising the functional: F(u,p,\Phi )=\frac{1}{2}\lbrace {\int}_{{\Omega}_{s}}\left[\sigma (u):\varepsilon (u)-{\rho}_{s}{\omega}^{2}{u}^{2}\right]\text{dV} +{\int}_{{\Omega}_{f}}\left[\frac{{P}^{2}}{{\rho}_{0}{c}^{2}}(\frac{\mathrm{2P}\Phi }{{\rho}_{0}{c}^{2}}-{(\text{grad}\Phi )}^{2})\right]\text{dV}\rbrace -{\rho}_{0}{w}^{2}{\int}_{S}\Phiu .n\text{dA} with: \Omegas , the domain of the structure \Omegaf , the domain of the fluid \Sigma , the fluid-structure interaction surface. 3.2.1 Contribution of the piping The beam model used is that of Timoshenko with shear-force strains and rotational inertia of the cross-section. It corresponds to the modelling POU_D_T, whose elementary computations it takes up. One does not take into account the ovalisation effects [bib3]. The terms associated with the piping in the variational formulation are then written: {\int}_{L}\left[\sigma (u):\varepsilon (u)-{\rho}_{s}{\omega}^{2}{u}^{2}\right]{S}_{s}\text{ds} with: L , the mean fibre of the piping and {S}_{s} , the cross-section of the piping at the abscissa s (cf. [Figure 3.2.1-a]). Figure 3.2.1-a: geometry of the piping 3.2.2 Contribution of the fluid In this paragraph, one is interested only in the fluid part of the functional, that is to say, the coupling term set aside, in the term which is written in 3D: {\int}_{{\Omega}_{f}}\left[\frac{{P}^{2}}{{\rho}_{0}{c}^{2}}-{\rho}_{0}{\omega}^{2}(\frac{\mathrm{2P}\Phi }{{\rho}_{0}{c}^{2}}-{(\text{grad}\Phi )}^{2})\right]\text{dV} eq 3.2.2-1 One assumes that the pressure is decomposed into two terms: P(M(s),t)=p(s,t)+\tilde{p}(M(s),t) where p is the value of the pressure averaged over a cross-section: p(s,t)=\frac{1}{{S}_{f}(s)}{\int}_{{S}_{f}(s)}P(M(s),t)\text{dM} and \tilde{p} is a fluctuating-pressure term which corresponds to the contribution of the transverse modes. According to the assumptions of paragraph [§1], p satisfies the 1-D Helmholtz equation and \tilde{p} the Laplace equation (incompressible). The integral [eq 3.2.2-1] is therefore decomposed into two terms. 3.2.2.1 Term corresponding to the contribution of \tilde{p} In the motions perpendicular to the axis of the pipe, one considers that the fluid intervenes only through its added mass [bib4]; the term linked to \tilde{p} is therefore an inertia term: {\int}_{L}{\rho}_{0}{\omega}^{2}{({u}_{t})}^{2}{S}_{f}\text{ds} {u}_{t} being the transverse components of the displacement vector of the structure and {S}_{f} the cross-section of the fluid at the abscissa s . 3.2.2.2 Term corresponding to the contribution of p {\int}_{L}\left[\frac{{P}^{2}}{{\rho}_{0}{c}^{2}}-\mathrm{\rho 0}{\omega}^{2}(\frac{\mathrm{2P}\Phi }{{\rho}_{0}{c}^{2}}-{(\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial s})}^{2})\right]{S}_{f}\text{ds} 3.2.3 Coupling term 3.2.3.1 Current section According to the references [bib4] and [bib5], one shows that the coupling term C : C\text{=-}{\int}_{S}{\rho}_{0}\Phi \mathrm{u}.\mathrm{n}\text{dA}={\int}_{L}-\frac{{\rho}_{0}\Phi }{R}\mathrm{u}.j{S}_{f}\text{ds}+{\int}_{L}{\rho}_{0}\Phi \mathrm{u}.i\frac{{\text{dS}}_{f}}{\text{ds}}\text{ds} The equilibrium equations of the structure and the equation of propagation of the plane waves (Helmholtz) in the fluid are therefore coupled at the level of the bent parts and of the straight parts where there is a change of cross-section of the piping. In the case of a pipe of constant cross-section: R\to \infty and \frac{{\text{dS}}_{f}}{\text{ds}}=0 hence C=0 There is therefore no coupling between the beam motions of the structure and the longitudinal displacements of the fluid in the straight parts of the circuit. In this case, the fluid is characterised only by its added mass linked to the transverse displacements. 3.2.3.2 Pipe end In the case of a pipe end, one denotes \Sigmat =\Sigma +{S}_{f} , the total interaction surface between the fluid and the piping. In the case of a closed straight piping of constant cross-section, the coupling term C is then equal to: C\text{=-}{\int}_{S+{S}_{f}}{\rho}_{0}\Phiu .n\text{dA}\text{=-}{\int}_{{S}_{f}}{\rho}_{0}\Phiu .n\text{dA} This is the end effect. This term is added to the coupling term of a current section. Thus, a free node which realises a condition of zero flow rate through the cross-section [bib6] realises an acoustic end condition. Indeed, an incident plane wave is totally reflected on the end: the acoustic pressure in the duct obeys the Helmholtz equation with zero normal pressure gradient (the fluid and solid displacements being zero). \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\frac{{\partial}^{2}p}{\partial {x}^{2}}+{k}^{2}p=0\\ (\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}{)}_{{S}_{f}}=0\end{array} One seeks the solution in the form: p=A\cos(\omegat -\text{kx})+B\cos(\omegat +\text{kx}) that is to say in the form of a linear combination of an incident plane acoustic wave and of a reflected wave. The condition of zero gradient on the end, verified for all time instants, imposes: A=B The reflected wave is therefore "equal" to the incident wave (reflection coefficient equal to unity). 3.2.4 Functional of the coupled system in the case of piping In the particular case which we treat, of an unbent piping of constant cross-section, the functional of the coupled problem is therefore written in the following form: \begin{array}{cc}F(u,p,\Phi )=& \frac{1}{2}\lbrace {\int}_{L}\sigma (u):\varepsilon (u){S}_{s}\text{ds}-{\omega}^{2}{\int}_{L}\left[{\rho}_{s}{S}_{s}{u}^{2}+{\rho}_{0}{S}_{f}{({u}_{t})}^{2}\right]\text{ds}\\ & +{\int}_{L}\left[\frac{{P}^{2}}{{\rho}_{0}{c}^{2}}-{\rho}_{0}{\omega}^{2}(\frac{\mathrm{2P}\Phi }{{\rho}_{0}{c}^{2}}-{(\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial \sigma })}^{2})\right]{S}_{f}\text{ds}\rbrace -{\omega}^{2}{\int}_{{S}_{f}}{\rho}_{0}\Phi u.n\text{dA}\end{array} 3.3 Discretisation by finite elements The sought solution (u,p,\Phi ) minimises the functional F . The finite-element approximation of the complete problem then leads to the symmetric system: \left[\begin{array}{ccc}K& 0& 0\\ 0& \frac{{K}_{f}}{{\rho}_{0}.{c}^{2}}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}u\\ p\\ \Phi \end{array}\right]-{\omega}^{2}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}M+{M}_{f}& 0& {M}_{\Sigma}\\ 0& 0& \frac{{M}_{\text{fl}}}{{c}^{2}}\\ {M}_{\Sigma}^{T}& \frac{{M}_{\text{fl}}^{T}}{{c}^{2}}& {\rho}_{0}.H\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}u\\ p\\ F\end{array}\right]=0 K and M being respectively the stiffness and mass matrices of the structure, {K}_{f} , {M}_{\text{fl}} , H being the fluid matrices, respectively obtained from the quadratic forms: {\int}_{L}{p}^{2}{S}_{f}\text{ds},{\int}_{L}p\Phi {S}_{f}\text{ds},{\int}_{L}{(\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial s})}^{2}{S}_{f}\text{ds} {M}_{f} being the fluid matrix obtained from the quadratic form: {\int}_{L}{p}_{0}{S}_{f}{({u}_{t})}^{2}\text{ds} {M}_{\Sigma} being the coupling matrix obtained from the bilinear form: {\int}_{{S}_{f}}{p}_{0}\Phiun \text{dA} . By discretising p and \Phi linearly, one therefore has: p={p}_{1}\frac{L-x}{L}+{p}_{2}\frac{x}{L}\text{et}\Phi ={\Phi}_{1}\frac{L-x}{L}+{\Phi}_{2}\frac{x}{L} , L being the length of the element considered. In this case, the elementary stiffness matrix of the fluid is written: {K}_{f}=\frac{{S}_{f}L}{3}\left\lbrace {p}_{1}{p}_{2}\right\rbrace \left[\begin{array}{cc}1& 1/2\\ 1/2& 1\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{p}_{1}\\ {p}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace The elementary coupling matrix is written: {M}_{\Sigma}={r}_{0}{S}_{f}\left\lbrace {\Phi}_{1}{\Phi}_{2}\right\rbrace \left[\begin{array}{cc}-1& 0\\ 0& 1\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{u}_{1}\\ {u}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace The various elementary fluid mass matrices are written: {M}_{\Sigma}={r}_{0}{S}_{f}\left\lbrace {\Phi}_{1}{\Phi}_{2}\right\rbrace \left[\begin{array}{cc}-1& 0\\ 0& 1\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{p}_{1}\\ {p}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace {M}_{\Sigma}=-\frac{{S}_{f}}{L}\left\lbrace {\Phi}_{1}{\Phi}_{2}\right\rbrace \left[\begin{array}{cc}1& -1\\ -1& 1\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{\Phi}_{1}\\ {\Phi}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace 3.4 Implementation in Code_Aster On the principles which we have just described, a vibro-acoustic beam element, of Timoshenko type for the piping part, straight and of constant or variable cross-section (in this case, only the circular cross-sections are allowed), has been implemented in Code_Aster . It belongs to the modelling 'FLUI_STRU' of the phenomenon 'MECANIQUE'. This element possesses 8 degrees of freedom per node: the displacements and rotations of the piping, the pressure and the displacement potential of the fluid (cf. [Figure 3.4-a]). The formulation is written for local displacements in the local frame of the element constituted of the neutral fibre (axis X ) and of the principal axes of inertia (axis Y , axis Z ) of the cross-section. The two scalars p and \Phi (pressure and fluid-displacement potential) are invariant under a change of frame. On each node of this element, one may impose boundary conditions of Dirichlet type in pressure, fluid-displacement potential and displacements (translation or rotation). Figure 3.4-a: fluid-filled beam element To date, this element makes it possible only to compute the eigenmodes of a straight fluid-filled pipe and to carry out a harmonic response analysis. The effects of curvature or of an abrupt widening of the cross-section are not taken into account for the moment, but these fluid-structure effects, when one is dealing with fluids of low density such as the steam of an inlet pipe, do not seem to have a determining importance for the computation of the first modes: the correct mechanical representation of the elbow (flexibility coefficient) seems sufficient to compute these frequencies [bib7]. In modal analysis, one may cite the case of a straight fluid-filled pipe with a free end: Figure 3.4-b: fluid-filled beam, clamped–free the eigenfrequency of the tension-compression mode of this coupled fluid/structure system is given by the relation: \text{tg}(\frac{\omegal }{c})=\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{s}}{{S}_{f}}\frac{E}{{\rho}_{0}{c}^{2}}} One denotes by: E : Young's modulus of the solid material {S}_{S} : cross-section of the solid {S}_{f} : cross-section of the fluid One assumes here that the speed of sound in the fluid is equal to the speed of sound in the solid {c}_{S}=\sqrt{\frac{E}{{\rho}_{S}}} [bib7]. The transient response analysis for this type of finite element (u,p,\phi ) is not yet available in Code_Aster . 4 Bibliography 1. H.J.P. MORAND ; R.OHAYON Fluid-structure interaction. r4.02.04 Fluid–structure coupling with a free surface r4.02.04 Fluid–structure coupling with a free surface Summary: Fluid/structure coupling is presented here in the case where the fluid has a free surface. Free-surface elements have been implemented in Code_Aster in order to compute the sloshing modes of a fluid coupled to an elastic structure for a three-dimensional problem. > Contents 1 Notation | P | : | the stationary pressure in the fluid | | --- | --- | --- | | p | : | the fluctuating pressure in the fluid, | | {X}_{f} | : | the displacements in the fluid, | | {X}_{s} | : | the displacement field in the structure, | | g | : | gravity, | | \varphi | : | the displacement potential of the fluid, | | {\rho}_{f},{\rho}_{s} | : | the density of the fluid, of the structure, | | T | : | the stress tensor in the fluid, | | \sigma | : | the stress tensor in the structure, | | \varepsilon | : | the strain tensor in the structure, | | C | : | the elasticity tensor, | | c | : | the speed of sound in the fluid, | | H | : | the height of the fluid (or mean height), | | n | : | the outward normal of the fluid. | 2 Introduction In order to study the behaviour of structures filled with fluid, one may be led to take sloshing phenomena into account, that is to add to the coupled fluid–structure system the effect of gravity at the level of the free surface of the liquid. The structures concerned are, for example, the vessels of nuclear power plants of the fast-reactor line, and the fuel-storage pools [bib4]. The developments already carried out in fluid–structure coupling [bib3] have therefore been completed by the introduction of new surface elements which take into account, in their formulation, the effect of gravity. 3 Theoretical formulation of the problem The interaction problem of a structure with a heavy fluid amounts to solving three problems simultaneously: - the structure is subjected to a pressure field P imposed by the fluid on the wall \Sigma ; - the fluid is subjected to a displacement field {X}_{s} imposed by the structure on \Sigma ; - gravity acts on the free surface, where p=\rho gz . One will consider at first that the fluid is not heavy, before introducing gravity in paragraph [§3.2]. 3.1 Reminders on fluid–structure coupling In order to give a proper account of the fluid–structure interaction, we shall analyse separately the equations governing the behaviour of the fluid and those which govern that of the structure, without considering in this chapter the boundary conditions concerning the free surface. 3.1.1 Description of the fluid One considers that the system studied is subjected to small perturbations about its equilibrium state, in which the fluid and the structure are at rest: thus, P={p}_{0}+p and {\mathrm{X}}_{\mathrm{s}}={\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{s}}({x}_{0}=0) . This makes it possible to write [bib2]: \rho =-{\rho}_{f}div({\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{f}}) whence p=-{\rho}_{f}{c}^{2}div({\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{f}}) . With: - p the fluctuating pressure of the fluid, - \rho the perturbation of the density of the fluid, {\rho}_{f} the density of the fluid at rest, - {x}_{f}(r,t) the displacement field of a fluid particle. The fluid is: - perfect (that is, non-viscous) - barotropic: p=\rho {c}^{2} eq 3.1.1-1 - and irrotational: there exists a displacement potential \varphi , such that p={\rho}_{f}\frac{{\partial}^{2}\varphi }{\partial {t}^{2}} The behaviour of the Eulerian fluid volume is therefore described by the following equations: - constitutive law: {T}_{ij}=-p{\delta}_{ij} - equation of conservation of momentum in the fluid in the absence of a source: div(\overline{\overline{T}})={\rho}_{f}\frac{{\partial}^{2}{x}_{f}}{\partial {t}^{2}} eq 3.1.1-2 - equation of conservation of mass: \frac{\partial \rho }{\partial t}+{\rho}_{f}div(\frac{\partial {x}_{s}}{\partial t})=0 eq 3.1.1-3 By combining the equations of conservation of momentum [eq 3.1.1-2] and of mass [eq 3.1.1-3] written in the harmonic regime at the angular frequency w , one obtains, by virtue of [eq 3.1.1-1], the Helmholtz equation: \Delta p+\frac{{\omega}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}p=0 3.1.2 Description of the structure One considers that the structure is linear elastic and that one remains in the domain of small perturbations. In view of these assumptions, one writes: - the constitutive law in linear elasticity: {\sigma}_{ij}={C}_{ijkl}{\varepsilon}_{kl} - the equation of conservation of momentum in the structure in the absence of body forces other than the inertia forces: div(\overline{\overline{\sigma}})={\rho}_{s}\frac{{\partial}^{2}{x}_{s}}{\partial {t}^{2}} - the compatibility equation on the strain tensor: {\varepsilon}_{kl}=\frac{1}{2}({u}_{k,l}+{u}_{l,k}) 3.1.3 Description of the fluid–structure interface At the interface ( \Sigma ) between the fluid and the structure, since the fluid is not viscous, there is continuity of the normal stresses and of the velocities normal to the wall, and vanishing of the tangential stress (absence of viscous friction). These boundary conditions are written: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{ij}{n}_{i}={T}_{ij}{n}_{i}=-p{\delta}_{ij}{n}_{i}\\ \frac{\partial {x}_{f}}{\partial t}.n=\frac{\partial {x}_{s}}{\partial t}.n\end{array} 3.1.3.1 Formulation of the coupled problem Finally, the equation of the coupled fluid–structure problem is written, taking p as the variable describing the pressure field in the fluid and {x}_{s} the displacement field in the structure: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}{C}_{ijkl}{x}_{{s}_{k,\mathrm{lj}}}+{\omega}^{2}{\rho}_{s}{x}_{{s}_{i}}=0& \text{dans}{V}_{s}\\ \Delta p+\frac{{\omega}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}p=0& \text{dans}{V}_{f}\\ {\sigma}_{ij}{n}_{i}={C}_{ijkl}{x}_{{s}_{k,l}}{n}_{i}=-p{\delta}_{ij}{n}_{i}& \text{sur}\Sigma \\ \frac{\partial p}{\partial n}={\rho}_{f}{\omega}^{2}{x}_{{f}_{i}}{n}_{i}& \text{sur}\Sigma \end{array} The displacement fields {x}_{s} for the structure and the pressure fields p for the fluid which are sought minimise the functional: L({x}_{s},p,z)=\frac{1}{2}\underset{{V}_{s}}{\int}\left[{\sigma}_{ij}({x}_{s}){\varepsilon}_{ij}({x}_{s})-{\rho}_{s}{\omega}^{2}{x}_{s}^{2}\right]-\underset{\Sigma}{\int}p{x}_{s}nd\Sigma +\frac{1}{2{\rho}_{f}}\underset{{V}_{f}}{\int}\left[\frac{1}{{\omega}^{2}}(\text{grad}p{)}^{2}-\frac{{p}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}\right]\text{dV} 3.2 Action of gravity on the free surface 3.2.1 Formulation of the problem The linearised dynamic equations describing the small motions of a perfect fluid are recalled here. An Eulerian description of the fluid is chosen: \text{grad}P={\rho}_{f}(\mathrm{g}-\frac{{\partial}^{2}{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial {t}^{2}}) in {V}_{f} At equilibrium the fluid particle was at {M}_{0} and therefore: \text{grad}{P}_{0}={\rho}_{f}\mathrm{g} in {V}_{f} . r4.04.01 Metallurgical constitutive models of steels r4.04.01 Metallurgical constitutive models of steels Summary: This document presents the metallurgical constitutive models on heating and on cooling making it possible to describe the structural transformations of steels during thermal cycles exceeding temperatures of the order of 800°C . For the two types of transformation (on heating and on cooling) a detailed description of the available models is given and identification methods are supplied. Finally, one presents the hardness-computation model associated with the metallurgy. 1 Introduction The assembly and thermomechanical-treatment operations undergone by the metallic components of PWR plants can generate, in the materials of which they are made, stress fields, called residual, which exist before any service loading. The metallurgical transformations and principally the structural transformations are an important cause of these stress fields because they modify the behaviour (by modifying the physical characteristics) and generate thermo-mechanical loadings within the materials which undergo them (latent heats, strains due to the differences in density of the different metallurgical phases). These structural transformations are due essentially to the succession of a heating (often beyond 800°C ) and of a more or less rapid cooling of the parts during their manufacture. These thermal “cycles” may be intended (the case of heat treatments) or “undergone” (the case of welding). In all cases, they are very variable from one point to another of the part. The present document concerns the modelling of these structural transformations on heating and on cooling for low-alloy steels, and this at a scale which, while remaining “reasonable” for the metallurgist, is easily usable by the mechanical engineer. This type of modelling can be carried out for all the elements (PLAN, AXIS, 3D) of the PHENOMENE= "THERMIQUE" by the use of the operator CALC_META in “post-processing” of a thermal-evolution analysis. The constitutive relation dedicated to the steel, by difference with that dedicated to the zircaloys, to be used under the keyword COMPORTEMENT of the operator is the relation RELATION='ACIER' . For the definition of the metallurgical behaviour of the steel the supplying of the command DEFI_TRC and of the factor keyword META_ACIER under the command DEFI_MATERIAU is necessary. Finally, the definition of the initial metallurgical state can be carried out with the aid of the command CREA_CHAMP, under the factor keyword ETAT_INIT of the operator CALC_META. The metallurgy analysis is necessary for carrying out mechanical analyses which take into account the mechanical consequences of these metallurgical phenomena Elasto(visco)plastic modelling taking metallurgical transformations into account. The models presented (on heating and on cooling) are formulated within the framework of constitutive relations with internal (or memory) variables, and allow a simple and rapid identification based on the experimental diagrams. The choice of the variables and the forms of the evolution laws adopted are given and the description of the implementation of the models (identification method) is also presented. Finally, one presents the hardness-computation model which can, if necessary, complete the metallurgical analyses. Notes: - The basic metallurgical notions necessary for the understanding of the general problem and of the approach adopted are gathered in and where one will also find a bibliographical study of the problem. - This document is extracted from and where one gives a more detailed presentation of the models and of a few validation elements. More complete validation elements can also be found in for the cooling model and in for the hardness model. 2 Metallurgical constitutive model on cooling 2.1 Introduction On the basis of the dilatometry test [r4.04.01-Dilato], the mere knowledge, at a given time instant, of the temperature of a steel undergoing structural transformations does not make it possible to know its strain state. On the other hand, the behaviour of such a steel seems able to be described within the framework of constitutive models with internal variables. Indeed, if one introduces: - Z=\left\lbrace {Z}_{i}; \; i=1,p ightbrace the p -tuple of the proportions of the possible metallurgical constituents present at a point M and at a given time instant t (here, {Z}_{1}+{Z}_{2}+{Z}_{3}+{Z}_{4} will be the proportions of ferrite, pearlite, bainite and martensite and the proportion of austenite at M will be equal to {Z}_{\gamma} = 1-\left ({Z}_{1}+{Z}_{2}+{Z}_{3}+{Z}_{4}ight ) ); - The thermal strains of the austenite {\varepsilon}_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{th}}\left (Tight )={\alpha}_{\gamma}\left (T-{T}^{\gamma}ight ) and of the ferritic, pearlitic, bainitic and martensitic phases {\varepsilon}_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{th}}\left (Tight )={\alpha}_{\alpha}\left (T-{T}^{\gamma}ight )+\Delta {\varepsilon}_{\alpha\gamma }\left ({T}^{\gamma}ight ) noting: - The mean thermal-expansion coefficient of the austenite {\alpha}_{\gamma} ; - The reference temperature {T}^{\gamma} at which one considers {\varepsilon}_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{th}} zero; - The mean thermal-expansion coefficient {\alpha}_{\alpha} assumed identical for the ferrite, the pearlite, the bainite and the martensite; - The strain \Delta {\varepsilon}_{\alpha \gamma }^{\gamma} , at the temperature {T}^{\gamma} , of the ferritic, pearlitic, bainitic and martensitic phases with respect to the austenite (taking the latter as the reference phase); If one considers, in addition, that the strain of a multiphase mixture can be obtained from the strains of each phase by a linear mixture law, one can then describe the evolution of the strain state during a dilatometric test by: {\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{th}}\left (Z,Tight ) = \left (1-\sum_{i=1}^{i=4}{Z}_{i}ight ){\varepsilon}_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{th}}\left (Tight )+\left (\sum_{i=1}^{i=4}{Z}_{i}ight ){\varepsilon}_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{th}}\left (Tight ) that is {\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{th}}\left (Z,Tight ) = \left (1-\sum_{i=1}^{i=4}{Z}_{i}ight )\left[{\alpha}_{\gamma}\left (T-{T}^{\gamma}ight )ight]+\left (\sum_{i=1}^{i=4}{Z}_{i}ight )\left[{\alpha}_{\alpha}\left (T-{T}^{\gamma}ight )+\Delta {\varepsilon}_{\alpha\gamma }^{\gamma}ight] The problem then lies in the determination of Z or, more precisely and within the framework of simple materials with internal variables, in the determination of the evolution function f such that: \dot{Z}=f\left (T,Z,\cdotsight ) . In order to account for an effect of the cooling rate on the evolution of the structural transformations, we propose, within the framework of simple materials with internal variables, a modelling of the metallurgical behaviour of steels on cooling which includes, a priori, \dot{T} among its state variables. Schematic dilatometry curves 2.2 Assumptions 1. Assumption H1: A steel liable to undergo structural transformations is a simple material with internal variables among which one can choose the quadruplet Z characterising the metallurgical structure at a point and at a given time instant. One therefore models the structural transformations at a scale where the material point can be multiphase. This modelling scale, which may appear metallurgically coarse, is consistent with the notion of material point used in continuum mechanics and of which the dilatometry specimen, assumed homogeneous, is representative. 2. Assumption H2: The CCT diagrams completed by the Koistinen-Marburger martensitic-transformation kinetics completely characterise the metallurgical behaviour of an austenitised steel during continuous cooling. This assumption results directly from metallurgical practice and specifies the first of the objectives to be set for the model: to be compatible with all the experimental data relating to the metallurgical behaviour which accompanies the cooling of austenitised steels. Furthermore, this assumption also generates a “natural” choice and restrictions as regards the variables to be introduced into the model. 3. Assumption H3: The ferritic, pearlitic and (above all) bainitic transformations are impossible below the temperature of the start of the martensitic transformation {M}_{s} . This assumption, consistent with the representation of the CCT diagrams, makes it possible to decouple the diffusion transformations from the martensitic transformation. 2.3 Choice of the state variables Driving state variables In the thermo-mechanics of continuous media, the driving state variables are generally the temperature and the stress or strain state. However, because of assumption H2, the temperature is the only driving variable retained. Indeed, the influence of the stress state on the structural transformations does not appear in the CCT diagrams. Furthermore, there does not exist (apart from an effect of Le Chatelier type) a theoretical model even if experimental data relating to this influence under isothermal conditions have been obtained for certain steels. Internal state variables The first internal variable to be introduced is the quadruplet Z characterising the metallurgical structure and whose knowledge is sufficient, a priori, to describe from a mechanical point of view a dilatometric test. Besides the temperature T , its derivative \dot{T} and the stress state \sigma , the austenitic grain size d and the carbon content C of the transforming austenite also influence the metallurgical behaviour of steels on cooling. However, still because of assumption H2, one chooses not to introduce C as an internal variable. Indeed, the diffusion of carbon does not appear explicitly on the CCT diagrams, although it is implicitly taken into account, at least partially, in the very notion of metallurgical constituent. Furthermore, Giusti has shown that if taking C into account was theoretically possible, it led to evolution equations coupled between C and Z whose experimental identification “seems very difficult, not to say impossible”. Nevertheless, an effect of the carbon content on the decomposition of the austenite on cooling appears indirectly on the CCT diagrams. It is the phenomenon of stabilisation of the austenite which is expressed by a decrease of the martensitic-transformation temperature {M}_{s} [:ref:r4.04.01-ExempleTRC ]. Unlike the carbon content, the austenitic grain size d appears on the CCT diagrams which relate to austenitisation conditions to which there corresponds a value of d . We therefore choose to introduce d as an internal variable. However, the austenitic grain size, which results from the thermal history undergone on heating, no longer evolves on cooling and d intervenes only as a parameter in the constitutive model on cooling. Furthermore, the martensitic-transformation temperature {M}_{s} , which depends on the thermo-metallurgical history undergone, intervenes in the Koistinen-Marburger law adopted in assumption H2 in order to describe the martensitic transformation. One therefore chooses to introduce {M}_{s} as an internal variable. The memory character of the internal variables introduced here in addition to Z appears clearly: d characterises the thermal history undergone during the passage into the austenitic phase and {M}_{s} links the decomposition of the austenite to the conditions of its transformation into martensite. Finally, as it seems difficult to propose a simple form of dependence of the model with respect to these variables, one has chosen not to impose any particular form on the evolution functions {f}_{i} . The approach for computing the evolution rates of the metallurgical variables then uses interpolation techniques and rests on the fact that any experimentally known thermo-metallurgical history (a dilatometric test for example) is a particular solution of the differential evolution equation. 3 Identification and implementation of the model on cooling 3.1 Principle The identification of the model and the use of the experimental data constituted by the CCT diagrams in order to determine the value taken by the function f at a given thermo-metallurgical state (T,\dot{T},z;d) are based on the observation and the following assumptions: - the thermo-metallurgical histories appearing on a CCT diagram are all particular solutions of the differential equation. They therefore make it possible to compute, at each thermodynamic state encountered experimentally and present in a CCT diagram, the value taken by the function f . - the function f is regular; that is to say that if two points {E}_{k} and {E}_{j} are neighbouring with {E}_{k}=\left\lbrace T({t}_{K}),\dot{T}({t}_{K}),z({t}_{K});d({t}_{K})ightbrace , their evolution rates in z are likewise neighbouring, that is: {E}_{k} {\approx} {E}_{j} {\Rightarrow } f({E}_{k}){ rac{\left[T {-}{M}_{s}ight]}{T{-}{M}_{s}}}^{{+}}=\dot{z}({E}_{k}){\approx}f({E}_{j}){ rac{\left[T{-}{M}_{s}ight]}{T{-}{M}_{s}}}^{+}=\dot{z}({E}_{j}) One then determines the rates of the structural transformations of an arbitrary state by interpolation among all the “pairs” ({E}_{k},f({E}_{k})) defined by the CCT diagrams. 3.2 Integration of the experimental data into the model 3.2.1 Principle In general, a CCT diagram defines in a frame \left[\ln(t)-Tight] the structural transformations associated with a series of thermal histories plotted on this diagram [r4.04.01-ExempleTRC]. The integration of the experimental data then consists in recording for each history of these diagrams the successive values of \left ( T,\dot{T},z ight ) so that for any temperature T the model knows the values taken by the function f at (T,\dot{T}(T),z(T)) . In order to be able, from a reduced number of numerical data, to reconstruct in a continuous way the thermo-metallurgical evolutions, one formulates a few assumptions on the thermal evolutions and on the metallurgical behaviour of the steels. 3.2.2 Rules for the interpretation of the CCT diagrams Thermal evolutions In order to define the thermo-metallurgical histories present in a CCT diagram one must characterise their thermal evolutions. One can note that, in a frame \left[\ln(t)-Tight] and for temperatures lower than 820°C , the thermal histories of the CCT diagrams can, with a fairly good approximation, be deduced from one another by a horizontal translation [:ref:r4.04.01-ExempleTRC ]. It is therefore possible to define a thermal history {T}^{i}(t) from the data of a pilot curve {T}_{p}(t) and of the time instant (in seconds) at which this history crosses the isotherm 820°C by {t}^{i}(T)=\exp\left\lbrace \ln\left[{t}_{p}(T)ight]+\ln\left[{t}^{i}(820)ight]-\ln\left[{t}_{p}(820)ight]ightbrace where {t}^{i}(T) and {t}_{p}(t) denote the reciprocal functions of {T}^{i}(t) and {T}_{p}(t) . In fact, one has more readily information relating to the cooling rates of the thermo-metallurgical histories of the CCT diagrams than to instants of crossing of the isotherm 820°C . This is in particular the case of the welding steels, whose CCT diagrams are plotted in a frame “cooling rate at 700°C –temperature”. Taking into account, one can then express the instant of crossing of the isotherm 820°C as a function of {T}_{p}(t) and of {\dot{T}}^{i}(700) and one obtains as a characterisation of {T}^{i}(t) {t}^{i}(T)=\exp\left \lbrace F(T)-F(700)-\ln({\dot{T}}^{i}(700){F}^{'}(700))ight brace with F(T)=\ln\left \lbrace {t}_{p}(T)ight brace and, in particular {\dot{T}}^{i}(t(T))= rac{1}{{F}^{'}(T){t}^{i}(T)} Concretely, one interpolates the function F(T) by a polynomial of degree 5. An experimental thermal evolution is therefore completely defined by the data of the coefficients of the polynomial characterising its pilot curve and by its cooling rate at 700°C . The validation of this method of parameterisation of the thermal histories “read” on the CCT diagrams is presented in . Overall, and taking into account the relative inaccuracies of the plotting of the CCT diagrams, of the reading of {T}^{i}(t) and of the determination of {\dot{T}}^{i}(700) , the agreement between the thermal histories read and recomputed seems quite sufficient. If one has the recordings of the thermal evolutions of the CCT diagrams, one can define each experimental thermal evolution by considering that it is its own pilot curve. Furthermore, in the case where the dilatometric tests defining the CCT diagram used for the identification of the model are carried out with constant cooling rates, one characterises these cooling kinetics solely by their cooling rates at 700°C and a function F identically zero. Temperatures of the start and of the end of transformation A CCT diagram supplies, for a series of known thermal histories, the proportions of the different metallurgical constituents which have formed during cooling as well as the temperatures for which one observes on a dilatometric curve a significant variation of the global expansion coefficient of the specimen [r4.04.01-Dilato]. These temperatures are then considered as the temperatures of the start and of the end of the transformations. More precisely: - the temperatures of the start of transformation indicated on the CCT diagrams correspond to 1% of constituent already formed; - the temperatures of the end of transformation correspond to the final proportion of the constituent being formed minus 1%. Kinetics of the ferritic, pearlitic and bainitic transformations The observation of a dilatometric curve shows that, except in the neighbourhood of the temperatures of the start and of the end of transformation, the evolution of the strain as a function of the temperature is almost linear. Taking equation into account, the evolution of the quantity of transformed phase as a function of the temperature is then not very far from an affine function and one therefore assumes that: - for the ferritic, pearlitic and bainitic transformations, the transformation rate is, between the experimental temperatures of the start and of the end of transformation, a linear function of the temperature; - the rates of these transformations are twice as slow at the start (from 0 to 1% of transformed constituent) and at the end of transformation (from {Z}^{f}-1 \% to {Z}^{f} ) than between the experimental temperatures of the start and of the end of transformation. Martensitic transformations One assumes that the martensitic transformations are described by the Koistinen-Marburger law and the phenomenological equation expressing {M}_{s} . One then uses each CCT diagram in order to determine the coefficients  eta , A and {Z}^{s}_{\gamma} as well as the temperature {M}_{s,0} . Finally, in order to avoid the model systematically transforming into martensite the remaining austenite when one reaches the temperature {M}_{s} , one introduces an additional parameter, called TPLM, characterising (by its cooling rate at 700°C ) the slowest of the cooling kinetics which generates a martensitic transformation. More precisely [Martensitic transformation]: - {M}_{s,0} is considered as the temperature of the start of the martensitic transformation when the latter is total; -  eta is assumed constant and computed so as to satisfy, in the case of a total martensitic transformation, {Z}_{4}(M^f_s)=0,99 where M^f_s is the experimental temperature of the end of transformation; - A and {Z}^{s}_{\gamma} are determined by linear regression from the experimental thermo-metallurgical histories leading to a partial martensitic transformation. Evolution of the martensitic temperature ({M}_{s,0}-{M}_{s}) as a function of ({Z_1}+{Z_2}+{Z_3}) for the steel 16MND5 austenitised for five minutes at 900°C 3.2.3 Effect of the austenitic grain size on the kinetics of the transformations on cooling. The phase transformations proceed by nucleation and growth. The nucleation stage takes place essentially on the grain boundaries. The grain size of the austenite therefore plays an important role in the transformations on cooling. For this reason the CCT diagrams are established for given austenitisation conditions and should strictly speaking be used only for similar austenitisation conditions. The experimental results tend to show that the austenitic grain size modifies the transformation kinetics more than the temperatures of the start and of the end of the transformations, which is expressed relatively well by a translation of the CCT diagram along the time axis. To each point M of a CCT diagram there corresponds the n-tuple (T,\dot{T},z) . Translating the CCT along the time axis amounts to multiplying \dot{T} by a coefficient different from unity (the time axis is given on a logarithmic scale). One therefore defines an “effective” cooling rate {\dot{T}}_{	ext{eff}} : {\dot{T}}^{	ext{eff}}=\dot{T}\cdot \exp(a(d-{d}_{	ext{ref}})) with {d}_{	ext{ref}} the reference austenitic grain size of the CCT diagram (homogeneous to a length) and a a material coefficient (homogeneous to the inverse of a length). The evolution law adopted is therefore written: \dot{z}(t)=f(T,{\dot{T}}_{	ext{eff}},z,{M}_{s})=f(T,{\dot{T}}_{	ext{eff}},z){ rac{\left[T-{M}_{s}ight]}{T-{M}_{s}}}^{+}	ext{avec}z=\left\lbrace {Z}_{1},{Z}_{2},{Z}_{3}ightbrace . This expression has the advantage of limiting the interpolation to a single reference CCT diagram. Note One makes the assumption that the nucleation and the growth of the martensite are considered as instantaneous and that the density of the nucleation sites has little influence on this transformation. The effect of the grain size therefore does not concern the evolution of the martensitic phase and bears here only on the evolution of the ferritic, pearlitic and bainitic phases. 3.2.4 Input of the CCT diagrams Taking into account the previous assumptions, the input of the experimental data contained in the CCT diagrams therefore comprises: - For the CCT diagram: - the value of the austenitic grain size {d}_{	ext{ref}} of the diagram, which will be the reference grain size - the translation coefficient a for taking into account the effect of the austenitic grain size - the temperature of the start of the total martensitic transformation {M}_{s,0} - the value of the coefficient  eta of the Koistinen-Marburger law - the value of the coefficients A and {Z}^{s}_{\gamma} intervening in the equation - the values of the six coefficients of the polynomial of degree five interpolating the function \ln\left[{t}_{p}(T)ight] (if one knows explicitly the thermal histories, each of them is considered as being its own pilot curve and the definition of its six coefficients is to be renewed for each history) - For each thermal history of a CCT diagram: - the cooling rate at 700°C - the final proportions of ferrite, pearlite and bainite Z^{f}_{1} , Z^{f}_{2} and Z^{f}_{3} - the temperatures of the start of each transformation T^{d}_{1} , T^{d}_{2} and T^{d}_{3} - the temperatures of the end of each transformation T^{f}_{1} , T^{f}_{2} and T^{f}_{3} The CCT diagrams are introduced by the command DEFI_TRC. Furthermore, one also assumes that the whole of the ferritic, pearlitic, bainitic and martensitic phases transform in an identical manner into austenite. These assumptions are generally common to the whole of the austenitisation models , and . Consequently the model adopted is of the form: {\dot{z}}_{\gamma}=f(T,{Z}_{\gamma}) One recalls that the metallurgical-transformation model proposed by Leblond and Devaux and implemented in the Sysweld code is of the form (for the transformations on heating and on cooling): \dot{Z}(T,Z)=\lambda  rac{{Z}_{\mathrm{eq}}(T)-Z}{	au (T)} where, for the austenitic transformation, the parameter \lambda is taken constant. The elements of comparison with experiment presented in , and show that, provided the functions {Z}_{\mathrm{eq}}(T) and 	au (T) are identified from tests at different heating rates, this model allows a quite satisfactory description of the austenitic transformation of steels. Nevertheless, it seems that the identification of the function 	au (T) remains difficult . The austenitic-transformation model is of the form: {\dot{Z}}_{\gamma}(T,{Z}_{\gamma})= rac{{Z}_{\mathrm{eq}}(T)-{Z}_{\gamma}}{	au (T)} but with a simple form for the function 	au (T) , in order to keep a set of metallurgical models of easy and rapid identification. 4.2 Form of the model adopted In its continuous form, the model adopted is such that: {\dot{z}}_{\gamma}(T,{Z}_{\gamma})= rac{{Z}_{\mathrm{eq}}(T)-{Z}_{\gamma}}{	au (T)} where {Z}_{\gamma} denotes the proportion of austenite. Moreover, under certain conditions, an austenitic transformation initiated during heating may continue at the start of cooling. There does not therefore exist, strictly speaking, an austenitic-transformation model and a transformation model on cooling but a single model of metallurgical transformations which, according to the temperature considered and the sign of the rate of thermal evolution, is described either by the model of decomposition of the austenite, or by the model of formation of the austenite. The direction of the metallurgical evolution (that is to say formation or decomposition of the austenite) is determined as follows: - If the temperature is such that T(t+\Delta t) 0 , one uses the model of formation of the austenite - If the rate is negative or zero \dot{T}(t) \le 0 , one uses the model of decomposition of the austenite - If the temperature is such that T(t+\Delta t) \in \left[ {Ac}_{1}, {Ar}_{3} ight ] , one has four cases: - If the rate is positive \dot{T}(t) > 0 , one uses the model of decomposition of the austenite - If the rate is zero \dot{T}(t) > 0 and if z_{\gamma} \ge {Z}_{\mathrm{eq}} , one uses the model of decomposition of the austenite - If the rate is zero \dot{T}(t) > 0 and if z_{\gamma} {Ar}_{3} , one uses the model of formation of the austenite Note {Ar}_{3} is also a characteristic of the metallurgical behaviour on cooling already defined by the transformation model on cooling. 5 Identification of the model on heating 5.1 Determination of the function {Z}_{\mathrm{eq}}(T) The function {Z}_{\mathrm{eq}}(T) may be considered as the quasi-static solution of the differential equation and one chooses to define it (as in ) by the relation . The model chosen uses the assumption according to which the hardness of a multiphase material point is well represented by a linear mixture law of the microhardnesses of the constituents (here the phases austenite, ferrite, pearlite, bainite and martensite). r4.04.02 Elasto-(visco)plastic modelling taking metallurgical transformations into account r4.04.02 Elasto-(visco)plastic modelling taking metallurgical transformations into account Summary: This document presents the modelling implemented in code_aster for the mechanical analysis of operations that generate metallurgical transformations. The various mechanical effects resulting from the structural transformations to be taken into account, and their modellings, are presented. > Contents 1 Introduction Certain materials undergo structural transformations when they are subjected to particular thermal evolutions , , . This is, for example, the case of low-alloy steels during operations of the welding and heat-treatment type, or again the Zircaloy alloys of fuel cladding for certain accidental situations (LOCA). These transformations have a more or less strong influence on the thermal and mechanical evolutions. From the thermal point of view, the structural transformations are accompanied by a modification of the thermal characteristics (volumetric heat capacity, thermal conductivity) of the material that undergoes them, as well as by a production or an absorption of energy (latent heats of transformation) . However, the latent heats of transformation in the solid state are relatively small compared with the latent heats of liquid-solid change of state, and one may therefore, as a first approximation, consider the thermal and structural evolutions as uncoupled. This is currently the case for the thermal and metallurgical analysis options implemented in code_aster . U4.85.01 From the mechanical point of view, the consequences of the structural transformations (in the solid state) are of four types: - The mechanical characteristics of the material that undergoes them are modified. More precisely, the elastic characteristics (Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio) are little affected, whereas the plastic characteristics (the yield stress in particular) and the thermal expansion coefficient are strongly affected; - The volumetric expansion or contraction that accompanies the structural transformations results in a (spherical) “transformation” strain which is superimposed on the strain of purely thermal origin. This effect is brought out on a dilatometry test and, in general, it is grouped with that due to the modification of the expansion coefficient, and one speaks globally of the influence of the transformations on the thermal strain; - A transformation taking place under stress can give rise to an irreversible strain, even for stress levels very much lower than the yield stress of the material (at the temperature and in the structural state considered). This phenomenon is called “ transformation plasticity ”; - During the metallurgical transformation one may have a phenomenon of recovery of hardening . The hardening of the parent phase is not transmitted to the newly created phases. These may then be born with a virgin hardening state, or inherit only part, possibly all, of the hardening of the parent phase. Furthermore, the mechanical state also influences the metallurgical behaviour. The stress state may in particular accelerate or slow down the kinetics of the transformations and modify the temperatures at which they occur. However, the experimental characterisation of this influence, particularly in the case of complex situations (three-dimensional, under variable temperature and stress state), remains very delicate, and it is very common to consider the structural evolution as independent of the mechanical state. This is the case of the model of structural transformations implemented in code_aster . If the various couplings of mechanical origin are neglected, the determination of the mechanical evolution associated with a process involving structural transformations therefore requires two successive and uncoupled analyses: - An (uncoupled) thermo-metallurgical analysis allowing the determination of the thermal evolutions and then the structural ones; - A mechanical (elasto-viscoplastic) analysis taking account of the effects due to the thermal and structural evolutions; This document presents the mechanical modelling implemented in code_aster . The modelling is available for two materials: - Steel, which undergoes, around 850° , an austenite-ferrite transformation (passage from cold ferritic phases of face-centred cubic structure to a hot austenitic phase of body-centred cubic structure). Steel presents four possible ferritic phases: ferrite, pearlite, bainite and martensite; - Zircaloy alloys, which undergo, around 800°C , a transformation from a cold phase \alpha of hexagonal close-packed structure to a hot phase \beta of body-centred cubic structure ( \mathrm{cc} ). The models are identical for the two materials; only the number of phases changes. The model therefore comprises five phases for steel and three phases for Zircaloy. Modelling the behaviour of Zircaloy does indeed require considering two cold phases of different mechanical behaviour: a phase \alpha considered as pure and a phase \alpha mixed with \beta U4.85.01, . Nota Bene: The basic metallurgical notions necessary for understanding the general problem are gathered in . The elasto-plastic solution algorithm, without taking into account the effects due to the structural transformations, is set out in . This document is in part extracted from , where a more detailed presentation of the model and of a few validation elements is given. [Figure 4-1]). This phenomenon is called transformation plasticity and {\varepsilon}^{\text{pt}} denotes the corresponding irreversible strain . The model of transformation plasticity most frequently used is, originally, the three-dimensional generalisation of the one-dimensional phenomenological model established by Desalos . If, from a dilatometric test, one plots the difference between the elongation \varepsilon obtained for an applied stress different from zero and that obtained for a zero stress, as a function of the progress of the transformation, one observes that: {\varepsilon}^{\text{pt}}(\sigma ,b)=\varepsilon (\sigma ,b)-\varepsilon (0,b)=\mathrm{kF}(b)\sigma With: | k : | Constant homogeneous to the inverse of a stress; | | --- | --- | | F : | Normalised function ( F(0)=0 and F(1)=1 ); | | b : | Proportion of the transformed phase; | A three-dimensional and temporal generalisation of the preceding experimental model, for a single transformation, was proposed by Leblond , , , , in the form: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\mathit{pt}}=\frac{3}{2}K{\tilde{\sigma}}_{ij}F'(b)\dot{b} It rests on the following heuristic considerations: - The relation must be “incremental”, that is, it must relate the plastic strain rate to the transformation rate; - The transformation-plasticity strain rate must, as for classical plasticity, be proportional to the deviatoric part \tilde{\sigma} of the stress tensor \sigma . Transformation plasticity occurs without change of volume, hence a dependence on the stress deviator rather than on the stress field itself; - The transformation-plasticity strain rate must be zero outside the transformation ranges; - The integration of this relation in the uniaxial case at constant stress \sigma must recover the experimental relation. On the basis of experimental tests and for a transformation of bainitic type of a 16MND5 steel, for example, K={10}^{\text{-4}}{\mathit{MPa}}^{\text{-1}} and F(b)=b(2-b) . The phenomenon of transformation plasticity can exist during structural transformations under stress of ferritic, pearlitic, bainitic and martensitic type, which may possibly appear simultaneously. On the other hand, this phenomenon is considered not to exist during the austenitic transformation. To lighten the writing, one writes for transformation plasticity: {g}_{Z}^{\mathit{pt}}\left(Z,\dot{Z}\right)=\sum_{{k}_{f}=1}^{4}{K}_{{k}_{f}}{F}_{{k}_{f}}^{'}\langle {\dot{Z}}_{{k}_{f}}\rangle The general model implemented in code_aster is therefore: {\dot{\epsilon}}^{\mathit{pt}}\left(\sigma ,Z\right)=\sum_{{k}_{f}=1}^{4}{\dot{\epsilon}}_{{k}_{f}}^{\mathit{pt}}\left(\sigma ,Z\right)=\frac{3}{2}\tilde{\sigma}{g}_{Z}^{\mathit{pt}}\left(Z,\dot{Z}\right) Where \langle X\rangle denotes the positive part of a quantity. In code_aster, it is possible not to take the phenomenon of transformation plasticity into account. In the case where this phenomenon is taken into account, it appears as soon as there is a transformation, even if the structure yields. The model is more particularly dedicated to steel. Thus, for example, in the case of plasticity with linear isotropic hardening, one generally takes as the hardening variable the cumulative plastic strain denoted p . The hardening term is then written: R={R}_{o}p Where {R}_{o} is the linear hardening coefficient. This model is insufficient in two cases: 1. For viscoplastic materials, under the action of thermal agitation, a slow recovery of the crystalline structure of the metal occurs by annihilation of the dislocations and relaxation of the internal stresses; 2. During metallurgical transformations, there exist within the material atomic displacements of greater or lesser importance. These atomic displacements can annihilate dislocations that are at the origin of the hardening; 5.1 Viscous recovery of hardening 5.1.1 Single-phase model The phenomenon of viscous recovery of hardening, which leads to a partial evanescence of the hardening, is introduced into the modelling. The model used to describe this phenomenon is the following in the case of isotropic hardening: \dot{r}=\dot{p}-{g}^{\text{re},v} The evolution term of the hardening variable r therefore comprises a hardening term due to the plastic strain \dot{p} and a viscous-recovery term which will be denoted {g}^{\text{re},v} : {g}^{\text{re},v}=(\mathit{Cr}{)}^{m} The model thus makes it possible to describe the phenomenon of primary creep (hardening) and of secondary creep (stabilisation of the hardening) with the parameters C and m . In the case of kinematic hardening, the model will be written: \dot{\alpha}={\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\mathit{vp}}+{h}^{\text{re},v} With the recovery term which will be denoted {h}^{\text{re},v} : {h}^{\text{re},v}=\frac{3}{2}(C{\alpha}_{\mathit{eq}}{)}^{m}\frac{\alpha}{{\alpha}_{\mathit{eq}}} 5.1.2 Multiphase model In the multiphase case, the viscous part of the recovery is expressed by replacing the hardening variable by an average value over the phases: r\to \overline{r} With an average taken over the five phases: \overline{r}=\sum_{k=1}^{5}{Z}_{k}{r}_{k} And therefore: {\overline{g}}^{\text{re},v}=(\overline{C}\overline{r}{)}^{\overline{m}} In the case of kinematic hardening, according to ( ), one has: {h}^{\text{re},v}=\frac{3}{2}(C{\alpha}_{\mathit{eq}}{)}^{m}\frac{\alpha}{{\alpha}_{\mathit{eq}}} One proceeds in the same way as for isotropic hardening: \alpha \to \overline{\alpha} With: \overline{\alpha}=\sum_{k=1}^{5}{Z}_{k}{\overline{\alpha}}_{k} And therefore: {\overline{h}}^{\text{re},v}=\frac{3}{2}(\overline{C}{\overline{\alpha}}_{\mathit{eq}}{)}^{\overline{m}}\frac{\overline{\alpha}}{{\overline{\alpha}}_{\mathit{eq}}} 5.2 Metallurgical isotropic hardening recovery In the multiphase case, the hardening term is written for each phase: {R}_{k}={R}_{0,k}p Where {R}_{0,k} is the linear hardening coefficient of phase k . During metallurgical transformations, there exist within the material atomic displacements of greater or lesser importance. These atomic displacements can annihilate dislocations that are at the origin of the hardening. In these cases, the hardening of the parent phase is not transmitted to the phase produced; this is the recovery of hardening. The new phase may then be born with a virgin plastic state, or inherit only part, possibly all, of the hardening of the parent phase. The cumulative plastic strain p is no longer characteristic of the hardening state, and other hardening variables must be defined for each phase, denoted {r}_{k} , which take account of the recovery of hardening. The hardening term of phase k is then written: {R}_{k}={R}_{0,k}{r}_{k} 5.2.1 Two-phase model with one direction of transformation To define the variables {r}_{k} , the model proposed by Leblond is chosen. A two-phase volume element V is considered, which undergoes a metallurgical transformation and a plastic strain. Phase 1 is the parent phase, characterised by its volume fraction {V}_{1} , its phase proportion (1-z) and a hardening variable {r}_{1} . Phase 2 is the product phase, with its volume fraction {V}_{2} , its phase proportion z and its hardening variable {r}_{2} . The evolution equations of the {r}_{i} obtained by differentiation with respect to time are written: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\dot{r}}_{1}=\dot{p}\\ \\ {\dot{r}}_{2}=\dot{p}-\frac{\dot{z}}{z}{r}_{2}+\frac{\dot{z}}{z}\theta {r}_{1}\end{array} The parameter \theta characterises the proportion of hardening transmitted from the parent phase to the product phase, and \dot{p} is the equivalent plastic strain rate. Here p is no longer an internal variable of the problem as such. The only meaning of \dot{p} here is to be the plastic multiplier, and it is equal to the equivalent plastic strain rate. Sjöström obtains the same equations using a phenomenological argument which is reported here in order to make the model explicit . Let there be a time increment \Delta t , such that between t and t+\Delta t : - A fraction \Delta {V}_{2} of the parent phase transforms into phase 2 and is therefore added to the volume {V}_{2} of this product phase; - The volume element V undergoes a plastic strain \Delta p . | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{V}_{2},{r}_{2}(t)\\ {V}_{1},{r}_{1}(t)\end{array} | \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\Delta t\\ \Delta p\\ \Delta {V}_{2}\end{array} | \lbrace \begin{array}{}{V}_{2},{r}_{2}(t)+\Delta p\\ \Delta {V}_{2},\theta {r}_{1}(t)+\Delta p\\ {V}_{1},{r}_{1}(t)+\Delta p\end{array} | It is assumed that, during the metallurgical transformation, the transformed fraction \Delta {V}_{2} inherits only a part \theta {r}_{1} of the hardening of the parent phase 0\le \theta \le 1 . Then the hardening variables {r}_{i} at the time instant t+\Delta t are such that: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{r}_{1}(t+\Delta t)={r}_{1}(t)+\Delta p\\ \\ {r}_{2}(t+\Delta t)=\frac{{V}_{2}({r}_{2}(t)+\Delta p)+\Delta {V}_{2}(\theta {r}_{1}(t)+\Delta p)}{{V}_{2}+\Delta {V}_{2}}\end{array} That is, considering a standard incremental writing of the hardening variables such that: \Delta {r}_{i}={r}_{i}(t+{\Delta}_{t})-{r}_{i}(t) One obtains: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\Delta {r}_{1}=\Delta p\\ \\ \Delta {r}_{2}=\Delta p+\frac{\Delta {V}_{2}}{{V}_{2}+\Delta {V}_{2}}\theta {r}_{1}^{-}-\frac{\Delta {V}_{2}}{{V}_{2}+\Delta {V}_{2}}{r}_{2}^{-}\end{array} Equations () are obtained by passing to the limit.
