strain models The principal characteristic of the thermal evolutions concerned in this type of analysis is that they sweep a wide temperature range, which has an important effect on the mechanical behaviour of the material that undergoes the thermal evolution. One is in particular in temperature ranges where viscosity phenomena may no longer be negligible. It may therefore be necessary to use an elasto-viscoplastic constitutive model, especially when one remains in these ranges for a significant duration; for example during the stress-relief treatments associated with welding. A viscoplastic model is therefore chosen whose characteristics are such that it makes it possible to describe, with one and the same formalism and therefore without changing model: - A classical plastic behaviour, in order to model the cases at low temperature when the viscous effects are still negligible, or in order to model high-rate processes (welding); - A hardening viscoplastic behaviour at high temperature, in order to model the creep and relaxation effects associated, for example, with stress-relief treatments or with multipass welding; - A viscous-fluid type behaviour for temperatures higher than the melting temperature, in order to have a reasonable description of the molten zone. The viscoplastic model chosen does indeed degenerate, for certain limit cases, into a time-independent plasticity model, or into a viscous-fluid model. 6.1 Partition of the strain The total strain \varepsilon is written as the sum of four components: \varepsilon ={\varepsilon}^{e}+{\varepsilon}^{\mathit{th}}+{\varepsilon}^{\mathit{vp}}+{\varepsilon}^{\mathit{pt}} Where {\varepsilon}^{e} , {\varepsilon}^{\mathit{th}} , {\varepsilon}^{\mathit{vp}} and {\varepsilon}^{\mathit{pt}} are, respectively, the elastic, thermal, viscoplastic and transformation-plasticity strains. The strains of plastic type are purely deviatoric and the thermal strain is purely spherical. For the deviatoric part, one therefore has: \tilde{\varepsilon}={\tilde{\varepsilon}}^{e}+{\tilde{\varepsilon}}^{\mathit{vp}}+{\tilde{\varepsilon}}^{\mathit{pt}} And for the spherical part: \mathit{tr}(\varepsilon )=\mathit{tr}({\varepsilon}^{e})+\mathit{tr}({\varepsilon}^{\mathit{th}}) 6.2 Constitutive laws 6.2.1 Case of isotropic hardening One places oneself here in the framework of von Mises (visco)plasticity with additive isotropic hardening. The threshold function is written: f(\sigma ,r;T,Z)={\sigma}_{\mathit{eq}}-R(r;T,Z)-{\sigma}_{c}(T,Z) With {\sigma}_{\text{eq}} the Von Mises equivalent stress such that: {\sigma}_{\mathit{eq}}={(\frac{3}{2}\tilde{\sigma}:\tilde{\sigma})}^{1/2} R is the isotropic hardening term and {\sigma}_{c} is the initial critical stress. It corresponds to the minimum initial stress to be applied in order to have a viscoplastic flow. These two quantities may depend on the temperature and on the metallurgical phases. Equation () can be rewritten in the form: {f}^{\text{ }}=f-{\sigma}_{v}={\sigma}_{\mathit{eq}}-R(r;T,Z)-{\sigma}_{c}(T,Z)-{\sigma}_{v}=0 That is, in this model, the stress can be interpreted as the sum of a flow-limit stress (which itself decomposes into an initial limit stress and a hardening term) and a “viscous” stress depending on the strain rate and zero at zero rate: {\sigma}_{v}=\eta {\dot{p}}^{\frac{1}{n}} The (visco)plastic flow rate is written: {\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\mathit{vp}}={\dot{\tilde{\varepsilon}}}^{\mathit{vp}}=\dot{\lambda}\frac{\partial f}{\partial \sigma }=\frac{3}{2}\dot{p}\frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{eq}}} This tensor is purely deviatoric. The cumulative plastic strain \dot{p} is viscous and is written: \dot{p}={(\frac{\langle {\sigma}_{\mathit{eq}}-R(r;T,Z)-{\sigma}_{c}(T,Z)\rangle }{\eta})}^{n} With \eta and n the material viscosity coefficients. 6.2.2 Case of kinematic hardening In a manner equivalent to the case with isotropic hardening, the threshold function is written: f(\sigma ,X;T,Z)=(\tilde{\sigma}-X{)}_{\mathit{eq}}-{\sigma}_{c}(T,Z) With X the hardening tensor associated with the hardening variable tensor \alpha such that: X=\frac{2}{3}{H}_{0}\alpha {H}_{0} is the kinematic hardening coefficient. In a manner similar to the isotropic case, equation () can be rewritten by introducing the viscous back-stress: {f}^{\text{ }}=f-{\sigma}_{v}=(\tilde{\sigma}-X{)}_{\mathit{eq}}-{\sigma}_{c}(T,Z)-{\sigma}_{v}=0 The (visco)plastic flow rate is written: {\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\mathit{vp}}={\dot{\tilde{\varepsilon}}}^{\mathit{vp}}=\dot{\lambda}\frac{\partial f}{\partial \sigma }=\frac{3}{2}\dot{p}\frac{\tilde{\sigma}-X}{(\tilde{\sigma}-X{)}_{\mathit{eq}}} The cumulative plastic strain \dot{p} is viscous and is written: \dot{p}={(\frac{\langle (\tilde{\sigma}-X{)}_{\mathit{eq}}-{\sigma}_{c}(T,Z)\rangle }{\eta})}^{n} 6.3 Limit cases 6.3.1 Time-independent plastic model One wishes to describe an instantaneous elasto-plastic behaviour and to cancel the viscous effects. For this, the viscous parameters \eta and C will be taken equal to zero. - The thermal strain ( ) ; - The strain for transformation plasticity ( ) ; - The viscoplastic strain with kinematic hardening ( ); - Hooke's law; one obtains the following system to be solved: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\tilde{\varepsilon}={\tilde{\varepsilon}}^{e}+{\tilde{\varepsilon}}^{\mathit{vp}}+{\tilde{\varepsilon}}^{\mathit{pt}}\\ \sigma =A:{\varepsilon}^{e}\\ {\varepsilon}^{\mathit{th}}=({Z}_{\gamma}\left[{\alpha}_{\gamma}(T-{T}_{\mathit{ref}})-(1-{Z}_{\gamma}^{R})\Delta {\varepsilon}_{f\gamma }^{{T}_{\mathit{ref}}}\right]+{Z}_{f}\left[{\alpha}_{f}(T-{T}_{\mathit{ref}})+{Z}_{\gamma}^{R}\Delta {\varepsilon}_{f\gamma }^{{T}_{\mathit{ref}}}\right])\mathit{Id}\\ {\dot{\tilde{\varepsilon}}}^{\mathit{pt}}=\frac{3}{2}\tilde{\sigma}\sum_{{k}_{f}=1}^{4}{K}_{{k}_{f}}{F}_{{k}_{f}}^{'}\langle {\dot{Z}}_{{k}_{f}}\rangle \\ {\dot{\tilde{\varepsilon}}}^{\mathit{vp}}=\frac{3}{2}\dot{p}\frac{\tilde{\sigma}-X}{(\tilde{\sigma}-X{)}_{\mathit{eq}}}\end{array} Adding the expression of the viscoplastic law with isotropic hardening, that is: - The threshold function ( ), applying the mixture law to the hardening ( ) and to the critical stress ( ) ; One notes that, with an implicit discretisation, only two points differentiate the two types of behaviour, viscoplastic and time-independent plastic: - The form of the yield function, for which there is a complementary term in the case of viscosity (see 6.4.1.1 and 6.4.1.2 ); - The presence of the hardening-recovery term in the evolution of the hardening variable for the viscoplastic case. Moreover, classical incremental plasticity appears as the limit case (with no associated numerical difficulty) of incremental viscoplasticity when \eta ,C\to 0 and {\sigma}_{c}\to {\sigma}_{y} . This type of treatment has already been carried out by Lorentz R5.03.05. r4.04.03 Elasto(visco)plastic constitutive law in large strains with metallurgical transformations r4.04.03 Elasto(visco)plastic constitutive law in large strains with metallurgical transformations Summary This document presents a thermo-elasto-(visco)plastic constitutive model with isotropic hardening, with the effects of the metallurgical transformations, written in large strains. This model may be used for three-dimensional, axisymmetric and plane-strain modellings. One presents the writing of this model and its numerical treatment. In order to understand this document, it is practically indispensable to read the two notes R5.03.21 and R4.04.02 devoted to the constitutive models written, respectively, in large strains without metallurgical effects and in small strains with metallurgical effects. 1 Introduction This document presents a thermo-elasto-(visco)plastic constitutive law with isotropic hardening in large strains which takes into account the effects of the metallurgical transformations. This model may be used for three-dimensional, axisymmetric and plane-strain problems. This law represents an “assembly” of two models implemented in Code_Aster , namely a thermoelastoplastic model with isotropic hardening written in large strains (factor keyword DEFORMATION: ’SIMO_MIEHE’, cf. R5.03.21) and a small-strain thermo‑elasto-(visco)plastic model with the effects of the metallurgical transformations (factor keyword ’META_P_ _ ’ or ’META_V_ _ ’ of COMPORTEMENT of the operator STAT_NON_LINE). The first large-strain model has therefore been extended in order to take account of the consequences of the metallurgical transformations on the mechanics. In order to understand this document, it is practically indispensable to read the reference documents R5.03.21 and R4.04.02 which concern, respectively, the large-strain model without metallurgical effects and the small-strain model with metallurgical effects. Nevertheless, in order to make this note easier to read, we give a few reminders on these two models. In order to justify the extension of the model written in large strains to the large-strain model with metallurgical effects, we take up a few theoretical aspects extracted from [bib1] related to the writing of the large-strain model. One then presents the constitutive relations of the complete model, its numerical integration and the expressions of the tangent matrix (options FULL_MECA and RIGI_MECA_TANG). 2 Notations One will denote by: | \mathrm{Id} | identity matrix | | --- | --- | | 	ext{tr}A | trace of the tensor A | | {A}^{T} | transpose of the tensor A | | \detA | determinant of A | | \langle Xangle | positive part of X | | 	ilde{A} | deviatoric part of the tensor A defined by 	ilde{A}=A-( rac{1}{3}	ext{tr}A)	ext{Id} | | : | doubly contracted product: A:B=\sum_{i,j}{A}_{ij}{B}_{ij}=	ext{tr}({	ext{AB}}^{T}) | | Ä | tensor product: (\mathrm{AÄB}{)}_{ijkl}={A}_{ij}{B}_{kl} | | {A}_{	ext{eq}} | von Mises equivalent value defined by {A}_{	ext{eq}}=\sqrt{ rac{3}{2}	ilde{A}:	ilde{A}} | | {Ñ}_{X}A | gradient: {Ñ}_{X}A= rac{\partial A}{\partial X} | | {div}_{x}A | divergence: ({div}_{x}A{)}_{i}=\sum_{j} rac{\partial {A}_{ij}}{\partial {x}_{j}} | | \lambda , \mu | Lamé coefficients: \lambda = rac{\mathrm{E

One thus has: \Delta Q=Q-{Q}^{-} 3 Reminders on the metallurgical model and on the large-strain model 3.1 Model with metallurgical transformations We present here only the consequences of the metallurgical transformations on the mechanical behaviour. The determination of the mechanical evolution associated with a process involving metallurgical transformations requires beforehand a thermo-metallurgical analysis. This thermo-metallurgical analysis is uncoupled and makes it possible to determine the thermal evolutions and then the metallurgical ones. For the metallurgical constitutive models of steels, one may consult the document R4.04.01. For the study of the metallurgical transformations of steel, there exist five metallurgical phases: ferrite, pearlite, bainite, martensite (phases \alpha ) and austenite (phase \gamma ). The effects of the metallurgical transformations (in the solid state) are of four types: - the mechanical characteristics of the material which undergoes the transformations are modified. More precisely, the elastic characteristics (YOUNG's modulus E and Poisson's ratio 
u ) are little affected whereas the plastic characteristics, such as the yield stress, are strongly so, - the volumetric expansion or contraction which accompanies the metallurgical transformations results in a (spherical) “transformation” strain which is superimposed on the strain of purely thermal origin. In general, one groups this effect with that due to the modification of the thermal expansion coefficient \alpha , - a transformation taking place under stresses can give rise to an irreversible strain, even for stress levels very much lower than the yield stress of the material. This phenomenon is called “transformation plasticity”. The total strain \varepsilon is then written: \varepsilon ={\varepsilon}^{e}+{\varepsilon}^{	ext{th}}+{\varepsilon}^{p}+{\varepsilon}^{	ext{pt}} where {\varepsilon}^{e} , {\varepsilon}^{	ext{th}} , {\varepsilon}^{p} and {\varepsilon}^{	ext{pt}} are, respectively, the elastic, thermal, plastic and transformation-plasticity strains, - during the metallurgical transformation one may have a phenomenon of recovery of hardening. The hardening of the parent phase is not totally transmitted to the newly created phases. These may then be born with a virgin hardening state or inherit only part, or even all, of the hardening of the parent phase. The cumulative plastic strain p is then no longer characteristic of the hardening state and other hardening variables must be defined for each phase, denoted {r}_{k} , which take account of the recovery. The evolution laws of these hardenings differ from the usual laws so as to allow a total, or partial, “return to zero” of these parameters during the transformations. The expressions of the various constitutive relations will be found in the document R4.04.02. 3.2 Model written in large strains 3.2.1 General presentation This model is an Eulerian thermo-elasto-plastic constitutive law written in large strains which was proposed by Simo and Miehe ([bib2]) and which tends, under the small-strain assumption, towards the model with isotropic hardening and von Mises criterion described in R5.03.02. It makes it possible to treat not only large strains, but also, in an exact manner, large rotations. The essential characteristics of this law are the following: - just as in small strains, one assumes the existence of a relaxed configuration, that is locally stress-free, which makes it possible to decompose the total strain into a thermoelastic part and a plastic part, - the decomposition of this strain into thermoelastic and plastic parts is no longer additive as in small strains (or for the large-strain models written in strain rates with for example a Jaumann derivative) but multiplicative, - as in small strains, the stresses depend only on the thermoelastic strains, - in order to write the constitutive law, one uses the Kirchhoff stress tensor 	au which is related to the Cauchy tensor \sigma by the relation J\sigma =	au where J represents the variation of volume between the initial and current configurations, - the plastic strains take place at constant volume. The variation of volume is then due only to the thermo-elastic strains, - this model leads, during its numerical integration, to an incrementally objective model which makes it possible to obtain the exact solution in the presence of large rotations. 3.2.2 Kinematics We recall here a few basic notions of mechanics in large strains and of the constitutive model. r4.04.04 Metallurgical constitutive models of Zircaloy r4.04.04 Metallurgical constitutive models of Zircaloy Summary: This document presents the metallurgical constitutive models describing the structural transformations, on heating and on cooling, undergone by Zircaloy (fuel-rod cladding) between about 700°C and 1000°C . 1 Introduction The fuel claddings of pressurised-water nuclear reactors are made of zirconium alloy. These alloys undergo metallurgical transformations between 700°C and 1000°C , where they pass from a phase of hexagonal close-packed structure to a phase of cubic structure. In certain analysis cases, such as the scenarios of a core accident by loss of primary coolant (LOCA, APRP), the cladding reaches temperatures of the order of 1000°C and then undergoes metallurgical transformations. In order to analyse the mechanical behaviour of the cladding in these situations, it is necessary to take into account the influence of the metallurgy on the mechanics (modification of the mechanical characteristics). The present document concerns the modelling of the structural transformations of Zircaloy on heating and on cooling, and this at a scale which, while remaining “reasonable” for the metallurgist, is easily usable by the mechanical engineer. The metallurgy analyses in code_aster are carried out either during the integration of the mechanical constitutive law, or with the dedicated operator CALC_META, in “post-processing” of a thermal evolution analysis. In this second case, the choice of the model is made with the keyword RELATION= ‘ZIRC’ under COMPORTEMENT. This type of modelling can be carried out within Code_Aster for all the elements (PLAN, AXIS, 3D) of the PHENOMENE "THERMIQUE". For the definition of the metallurgical constitutive behaviour of Zircaloy, the entry of the factor keyword META_ZIRC under the command DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01 is necessary. Finally, the definition of the initial metallurgical state can be carried out by means of the command CREA_CHAMP, under the factor keyword ETAT_INIT of the operator CALC_META. The models implemented in Code_Aster in order to model the metallurgical transformations of Zircaloy are models developed by the CEA. These models have been identified on the basis of dilatometry and calorimetry tests for the cladding alloys (standard and new). For the mechanical constitutive behaviour with the effect of the structural transformations, one has the choice between several models: - either the same mechanical constitutive relations developed initially for the vessel steel 16MND5. These are all the relations declared in the operator STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword COMPORTEMENT of the type META_XX_XX. These are elastoplastic or elastoviscoplastic models, isotropic hardening (linear or non-linear) or kinematic, with or without taking into account the phenomena of transformation plasticity and of recovery of hardening of metallurgical origin (cf. R4.04.02 and R4.04.03). - or the law specific to Zircaloy. This is a threshold-free anisotropic elastoviscous model (Hill matrix). The keyword under COMPORTEMENT is META_LEMA_ANI (cf. R4.04.05); in this case, the metallurgical phase is an internal variable of the constitutive law and is determined during the integration of the latter. 2 Presentation of the model 2.1 Proportion at equilibrium Zircaloy has a hexagonal close-packed structure called phase \alpha , stable up to temperatures of the order of 700°C . Beyond about 700°C an allotropic transformation towards a cubic phase \beta begins, and it is complete in the neighbourhood of 975°C . The proportion of the phase {Z}_{\beta}^{\mathit{eq}} at equilibrium is given by the following equation, of Johnson–Mehl–Avrami type: \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}{Z}_{\beta}^{\mathit{eq}}=0& \text{pour}& T\le {T}_{d}^{\mathit{eq}}\\ {Z}_{\beta}^{\mathit{eq}}=1-\exp\left(-{(K(T-{T}_{d}^{\mathit{eq}}))}^{n}\right)& \text{pour}& {T}_{d}^{\mathit{eq}}\le T\le {T}_{f}^{\mathit{eq}}\\ {Z}_{\beta}^{\mathit{eq}}=1& \text{pour}& T>{T}_{f}^{\mathit{eq}}\end{array} where {T}_{d}^{\mathit{eq}} is the temperature of the start of the transformation \alpha \iff \beta at equilibrium, {T}_{f}^{\mathit{eq}} the temperature of the end of the transformation at equilibrium, T the temperature and K and n two material parameters. Equivalently, by inverting the equation , one obtains the equivalent temperature {T}^{\mathit{eq}} as a function of the proportion {Z}_{\beta} of phase \beta : \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}{T}^{\mathit{eq}}={T}_{d}^{\mathit{eq}}+\frac{1}{K}{\left(\log\left(\frac{1}{1-{Z}_{\beta}}\right)\right)}^{1/n}& \text{pour}0\le {Z}_{\beta}\le 0,99\\ {T}^{\mathit{eq}}={T}_{f}^{\mathit{eq}}& \text{pour}0,99\le {Z}_{\beta}\le 1\end{array} The temperature of the end of the transformation at equilibrium {T}_{f}^{\mathit{eq}} is chosen such that it corresponds to a proportion 0,99 of transformed phase \beta , that is: {T}_{f}^{\mathit{eq}}={T}_{d}^{\mathit{eq}}+\frac{1}{K}{\left(\log\left(\frac{1}{1-0,99}\right)\right)}^{1/n} 2.2 Evolution equation on heating The transformation on heating is the transformation \alpha \Rightarrow \beta . The temperature of the start of the phase transformation on heating {T}_{c} depends on the temperature rate on heating and is given by the equation: {T}_{c}={T}_{c}^{1}{({V}_{\mathit{ch}})}^{{T}_{c}^{2}} With {V}_{\mathit{ch}} the heating rate in °C/s and {T}_{c}\ge {T}_{d}^{\mathit{eq}} . The evolution model of the phase \beta on heating is given by the following differential equation (Holt model): | :math:frac{{mathit{dZ}}_{beta}}{mathit{dt}}={A}_{c}expleft(-frac{E}{RT}right){ | T-{T}^{mathit{eq}}({Z}_{beta}) | }^{M} | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | {T}^{\mathit{eq}}({Z}_{\beta}) is the equilibrium temperature corresponding to the instantaneous proportion {Z}_{\beta} of phase \beta and given by the equation . {T}_{c}^{1} , {T}_{c}^{2} , {A}_{c} , \frac{E}{R} and M are material parameters. 2.3 Evolution equation on cooling The transformation on cooling is the transformation \beta \Rightarrow \alpha . The temperature of the start of the phase transformation on cooling {T}_{r} depends on the temperature rate on cooling and is given by the equation: {T}_{r}={T}_{r}^{1}+{T}_{r}^{2}\ln({V}_{\mathit{ref}}) With {V}_{\mathit{ref}} the cooling rate in °C/s and {T}_{r}\le {T}_{f}^{\mathit{eq}} .
