r4.05.02 Stochastic approach for seismic analysis r4.05.02 Stochastic approach for seismic analysis Summary: This document presents a probabilistic analysis method for determining the response of a structure subjected to a random excitation of seismic type, from the cross-spectra of the excitation at the support points of the structure. The response is itself expressed in the form of cross-spectra. 1 Introduction Classically, the response of a structure subjected to a seismic excitation can be computed by two approaches: - transient dynamic analysis if the excitation is defined by an accelerogram (cf. [R4.05.01]). - analysis by the classical spectral method if the excitation is defined by an oscillator response spectrum (SRO) (cf. R4.05.03). Now, a seismic excitation is random by nature. These two methods are not initially designed to take this into account: in one case, many time analyses must be repeated for different excitations and then a statistical average taken (significant analysis cost); in the other case, very conservative hypotheses are made by considering averages (of simple or complete quadratic type, for example) for the maximum of the responses. A probabilistic analysis method has therefore been developed, also called the "stochastic approach to seismic analysis", based on the computation of the dynamic response expressed as power cross-spectra from the power spectral densities of the excitation. This method has in particular the advantage of taking better account of the correlations between the excitations at the various supports of the structure. The discussion of the various advantages of this method can be pursued in the reference [bib1]. The principle of the method and the notation adopted are therefore presented, starting from the classical approaches, then, in the third part, the probabilistic analysis proper. Finally, in the fourth part, the various methods for obtaining the exciting cross-spectrum will be presented. 2 Principle of the approach 2.1 Statement of the problem considered and general principle We place ourselves in the case of a multi-supported structure , that is to say that the structure has m support degrees of freedom, each being subjected to its own excitation (not necessarily equal everywhere). It is assumed that the structure is represented by a finite-element model comprising n degrees of freedom. The response is sought at a finite (and small) number of l degrees of freedom. It is assumed that the excitation quantity is of imposed-motion type and is expressed by a family of accelerograms {\mathrm{g}}_{j}(\mathrm{t}) for each of the support degrees of freedom j , j=1,m . The absolute motion of the structure is split classically into a rigid-body motion and a relative motion. The computation of the response in power cross-spectra is carried out by modal recombination . Following this modal analysis, a random dynamic response analysis is split into three parts: - definition of the exciting power cross-spectrum, - computation of the response power cross-spectrum. These first two parts are the subject of the command DYNA_ALEA_MODAL U4.53.22. The restitution of the response power cross-spectrum on the physical basis is carried out with the command REST_SPEC_PHYS U4.63.22. - computation of statistical parameters from the resulting power cross-spectrum. This last step is treated by the command POST_DYNA_ALEA R7.10.01 U4.84.04. 2.2 Decomposition of the motion The following decompositions and projections are detailed in the reference documentation relating to the solution by transient analysis of a seismic analysis R4.05.01. Only the main lines are retained here. Let {X}_{a} be the absolute displacement vector (of dimension n ) of all the degrees of freedom of the structure. The total response, called absolute {X}_{a} , of the structure is expressed as the sum of a relative contribution {X}_{r} and of the entrainment contribution {X}_{e} due to the anchor displacements (subjected to accelerations represented by an accelerogram {g}_{j}(t) at each of the support degrees of freedom j , j=1,m ). Let M,K and C be the mass, stiffness and damping matrices of the problem, restricted to the unsupported degrees of freedom. The equation of motion is then written in the frame attached to the relative motion: \begin{array}{c}{\begin{array}{}\text{M}\ddot{X}\end{array}}_{r}(t)+C\dot{X}_{r}(t)+{\text{K X}}_{r}(t)\text{= -}\text{M}\ddot{{X}_{e}}(t)+{F}_{\text{ext}}\end{array} {F}_{\text{ext}} : vector of the external forces In general the external forces are zero during an analysis of seismic responses. 2.3 Decomposition on the modal basis The computation of the response in power cross-spectra is carried out by modal recombination and calls, for imposed motion, on a modal basis which comprises both dynamic modes and static modes. Let \Phi =\left\lbrace {\phi }_{i,i=1,n}\right\rbrace be the (n,n) matrix of the dynamic modes computed for the associated conservative system, keeping the m supports fixed. Let \Psi =\left\lbrace {\psi}_{j,j=1,m}\right\rbrace be the (n,m) matrix of the static modes. The mode {\Psi}_{j} corresponds to the deformed shape of the structure under a unit displacement imposed on the support degree of freedom j , the other support degrees of freedom being fixed. The imposed displacement of the anchors {X}_{s}(t) is related to {X}_{e}(t) by the relation: {X}_{e}(t)=\Psi {X}_{s}(t) . The components of the acceleration of the anchor points {\ddot{X}}_{s}(t) are the accelerograms {g}_{j}(t) , j=1,m . One can therefore write \ddot{{X}_{e}}(t)={\Psi \ddot{X}}_{s}(t)=\sum_{j\text{=1}}^{m}{\psi}_{j}{g}_{j}(t)\text{} . The change of variable {X}_{r}(t)=\Phi .q(t) is carried out, q(t) being the vector of the generalised coordinates. By premultiplying the equation of motion by {}^{T}\text{}\Phi , one obtains — in the absence of external forces other than the seismic excitation — the equation projected onto the basis of the dynamic modes: {}^{T}\text{}\Phi M\Phi \ddot{q}(t)+{}^{T}\text{}\Phi C\Phi \dot{q}(t)+{}^{T}\text{}\Phi K\Phi q(t)=-{}^{T}\text{}\Phi M\Phi {\ddot{X}}_{s}(t) It is assumed that the damping matrix is a linear combination of the mass and stiffness matrices (hypothesis of Rayleigh damping constant over the structure, or Basile hypothesis allowing a diagonal damping). The basis \Phi which orthogonalises the matrices M and K therefore also orthogonalises the matrix C . Taking this hypothesis into account, the previous equation splits into n decoupled scalar equations in the form: for i=1,n where one has denoted: {\mu}_{i}={}^{T}\text{}{\Phi}_{i}M{\Phi}_{i} the modal mass {k}_{i}={}^{T}\text{}{\Phi}_{i}K{\Phi}_{i} the modal stiffness {\omega}_{i}=\sqrt{\frac{{k}_{i}}{{\mu}_{i}}} the modal angular frequency {\xi}_{i}=\frac{{}^{T}\text{}{\Phi}_{i}.C.{\Phi}_{i}}{2{\mu}_{i}{\omega}_{i}} the reduced modal damping" {p}_{ij}=\frac{{}^{T}\text{}{\Phi}_{i}.M.{\Psi}_{j}}{{\mu}_{i}} the modal participation factor of the support j on the dynamic mode i . The solution {q}_{i}(t) of this equation corresponds to the response of the dynamic mode i to the whole of the seismic excitation. The problem can further be decomposed by introducing the unknown {d}_{ij}(t) solution of the differential equation: {\ddot{\mathrm{d}}}_{ij}+2{{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}\dot{\mathrm{d}}}_{ij}+{\omega}_{i}^{2}{\mathrm{d}}_{ij}={g}_{j}(t) , this last equation corresponding to the response of the dynamic mode i to the acceleration . The relative displacement on the physical basis is then expressed: {X}_{r}(t)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{m}{p}_{ij}{d}_{ij}(t){\varphi}_{i} The information on the position of the support point is contained in the modal participation factor. 2.4 Harmonic response The total response of the structure has therefore been decomposed into a relative contribution and a differential contribution due to the displacements of the anchors, such that: \begin{array}{}{X}_{a}(t)={X}_{r}(t)+{X}_{e}(t)\\ \text{avec}\\ \lbrace \begin{array}{}{\ddot{X}}_{e}(t)={\Psi \ddot{X}}_{s}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}{\psi}_{j}{g}_{j}(t)\\ {X}_{r}(t)\text{= -}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{m}{{p}_{ij}d}_{ij}(t){\varphi}_{i}\text{}\text{où}{d}_{ij(t)}\text{est solution de}\text{}{\ddot{d}}_{ij}+2{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}{\dot{d}}_{ij}+{\omega}_{i}^{2}{d}_{ij}={g}_{j}(t)\end{array}\end{array} The solution of this last differential equation by the method of the Fourier transform involves the modal transfer functions {h}_{i}(\omega ) such that: . {h}_{i}(\omega )=\frac{1}{{\omega}_{i}^{2}-{\omega}^{2}+2i{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}\omega } One therefore obtains: {d}_{ij}(\omega )={h}_{i}(\omega ).{g}_{j}(\omega )\text{et}{\ddot{d}}_{ij}(\omega )\text{=-}{\omega}^{2}{h}_{i}(\omega ).{g}_{j}(\omega ) The total harmonic response of the structure is deduced from the previous formulae by modal recombination. \begin{array}{}{\ddot{X}}_{a}(\omega )={\ddot{X}}_{r}(\omega )+{\ddot{X}}_{e}(\omega )\\ {\ddot{X}}_{a}(\omega )={\omega}^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{m}{p}_{ij}{h}_{j}(\omega ){\varphi}_{j}(\omega ){j}_{i}+\sum_{j\text{=1}}^{m}{\Psi}_{j}{g}_{j}(\omega )\end{array} The complex matrix (n,m) , called the transfer matrix H(\omega ) , is then brought out, as follows: H(\omega )={\omega}^{2}P.h(\omega )\Phi +\Psi where P is the matrix of the participation factors, h(\omega ) the vector of the modal transfer functions {h}_{i}(\omega ) . The total response of the structure is {\ddot{X}}_{a}(\omega )=H(\omega )\ddot{E}(\omega ) where \ddot{E}(\omega ) is the vector of m lines made up of the Fourier transforms of the accelerations at the m support degrees of freedom. It is seen that this expression determines the response in acceleration. This then requires integrating the response twice in order to obtain the displacement; this problem is presented in [bib4]. One of the additional interests of the method proposed here is to avoid this difficulty. 3 The random dynamic response 3.1 Reminder on power spectral densities [bib2] 3.1.1 Definitions Let a probabilistic signal be defined by its probability density {p}_{x}({x}_{1},{t}_{1},\dots ,{x}_{n},{t}_{n}) . This probability density makes it possible to compute the moment functions of the signal. Moment of order 1, or expectation of the signal: {\mu}_{X}(t)=E\left[X(t)\right]=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}X{p}_{x}(x,t)\text{dx} Moments of order 2, or cross-correlation of two signals: {\rho}_{\text{XY}}({t}_{1},{t}_{2})=E\left[X({t}_{1})\overline{Y({t}_{2})}\right]=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}x\bar{y}p(x,{t}_{1};y,{t}_{2})\text{dxdy} When the signal is stationary, the cross-correlation depends only on \tau ={t}_{2}-{t}_{1} . It is written {R}_{\text{XY}}(t)=E\left[X(t)\overline{Y(t-\tau )}\right] Power spectral density and cross-spectrum {S}_{\text{XY}}(\omega ) , the power cross-spectrum or power cross-spectral density between two stationary probabilistic signals, is defined by the Fourier transform of the cross-correlation function, which is written: {S}_{\text{XY}}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{R}_{\text{XY}}(\tau ){e}^{-i\omega \tau }d\tau The inverse formula is written: {R}_{\text{XY}}(t)=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{S}_{\text{XY}}(\omega ){e}^{i\omega \tau }d\omega {S}_{\text{XY}}(\omega ) is generally complex and satisfies the symmetry relation: {S}_{\text{YX}}(\omega )=\overline{{S}_{\text{XY}}(\omega )} . When X=Y , {S}_{\text{XX}}(\omega ) is called the power autospectrum or power spectral density (DSP) . This function has the property of being real and always positive. 3.1.2 Relations between the DSP and the other characteristics of the signal Note: Most of the time, the signal is defined over a limited time, its Fourier transform does not exist, and an estimated Fourier transform over a period of length T is then defined by: {\hat{X}}_{T}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }\underset{-T/2}{\overset{T/2}{\int}}X(t){e}^{-i\omega \tau }d\tau . The following relations then hold with this estimated Fourier transform: \begin{array}{}{S}_{\text{XY}}(\omega )=\underset{T\to +\infty }{\lim}\frac{2\pi }{T}E\left[{\hat{X}}_{T}(w)\overline{{\hat{Y}}_{T}(\omega )}\right]\\ {S}_{\text{XX}}(\omega )=\underset{T\to +\infty }{\lim}\frac{2\pi }{T}E\left[{\hat{X}}_{T}(w)\overline{{\hat{X}}_{T}(\omega )}\right]\end{array} Link between the power autospectrum and the power of the signal: The power of a signal is equal to its variance. For a centred signal, the variance is: {\sigma}_{X}^{2}={R}_{\text{XX}}(0) . One therefore has: {\sigma}_{X}^{2}={R}_{\text{XX}}(0)=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{S}_{\text{XX}}(\omega )d\omega . 3.2 The equations of motion The total response of the structure is determined by the relation: {\ddot{X}}_{a}(\omega )=H(\omega )\ddot{E}(\omega ) , where \ddot{E}(\omega ) is the vector of m lines made up of the excitations represented by the Fourier transforms of the accelerograms {g}_{j}(t) at the m support degrees of freedom, H(\omega ) is the transfer matrix defined by H(\omega )={\omega}^{2}\text{ph}(\omega )\Phi +\Psi where p is the matrix of the participation factors, H(\omega ) the vector of the modal transfer functions {h}_{i}(\omega ) \Phi basis of the dynamic modes \Psi basis of the static modes it comprises n lines (= number of free degrees of freedom of the structure) and m columns. 3.2.1 "Cross-spectral-excitation" matrix NB: This designation "cross-spectral-excitation matrix" is abusive: it means "matrix of the power cross-spectral density of the excitation". It is assumed that the seismic excitation can be considered as a stationary signal — taking into account the ratios between the representative times — and centred. This makes it possible to use a certain number of results of probabilistic analysis. Interest is then in the stationary response of the system to a stationary excitation. {S}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(\omega ) denotes the matrix of the power cross-spectra corresponding to the excitation. Its data are set out in chapter 4. For the record, it is recalled here that it is computed from Fourier transforms of the accelerations. It is a matrix ( m\times m ). The term ij corresponds to the cross-spectrum between the signals {\ddot{E}}^{i} and {\ddot{E}}^{j} , that is to say again between the Fourier transforms of the accelerograms {g}_{i} and {g}_{j} . 3.2.2 Random dynamic response It has been seen that the power cross-spectrum between two probabilistic signals is the Fourier transform of the cross-correlation function of the two signals. It is applied to the total response of the structure: {S}_{{{\ddot{X}}_{a}\ddot{X}}_{a}}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{R}_{{{\ddot{X}}_{a}\ddot{X}}_{a}}(\tau ){e}^{-i\omega \tau }d\tau =\frac{1}{2\pi }\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}E\left[{\ddot{X}}_{a}(t){}^{T}\text{}\overline{{\ddot{X}}_{a}(t-\tau )}\right]{e}^{-i\omega \tau }d\tau One then works in the time domain in order to express the cross-correlation function of the total response {R}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}(t,t') . h(t) denotes the impulse response of the system: h(t)={\text{TF}}^{-1}[H(\omega )] and \ddot{e}(t) the inverse Fourier transform of the exciting DSP: \ddot{e}(t)={\text{TF}}^{-1}[\ddot{E}(\omega )] By inverse Fourier transform of the relation: {\ddot{X}}_{a}(\omega )=H(\omega )\ddot{E}(\omega ) one has {\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{\mathrm{a}}(t)=\mathrm{h}\times \ddot{\mathrm{e}}(t)=\underset{R}{\int}\mathrm{h}(u)\ddot{\mathrm{e}}(t-u)\text{du} \begin{array}{}{R}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}(t,t')=E\left[{\ddot{X}}_{a}(t){}^{T}\text{}\overline{{\ddot{X}}_{a}(t')}\right]\\ {R}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}(t,t')=E\left[\underset{R}{\int}h(u)\ddot{e}(t-u)\text{du}{}^{T}\text{}\overline{\underset{R}{\int}h(v)\ddot{e}(t'-v)\text{dv}}\right]\\ {R}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}(t,t')=E\left[\underset{R}{\int}\underset{R}{\int}h(u)\ddot{e}(t-u){}^{T}\text{}\overline{\ddot{e}(t'-v)}{}^{T}\text{}\overline{h(v)}\text{dv}\text{du}\right]\end{array} The system is assumed deterministic in this analysis, so the impulse response can be taken out of the computation of the mathematical expectation. It follows: {R}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}(t,t')=\underset{R}{\int}\underset{R}{\int}h(u)E[\ddot{e}(t-u){}^{T}\text{}\overline{\ddot{e}(t'-v)}]{}^{T}\text{}\overline{h(v)}\text{dv}\text{du} The excitation is assumed to be a stationary process, so the cross-correlation depends only on the time difference \tau =t-t' : {R}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(t-t'-u+v)=E[\ddot{e}(t-u){}^{T}\text{}\overline{\ddot{e}(t'-v)}]={R}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(\theta )\text{pour}\theta =t-t'-u+v=\tau -u+v whence {R}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}(t,t')=\underset{R}{\int}\underset{R}{\int}h(u){R}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(\theta ){}^{T}\text{}\overline{h(v)}\text{dv}\text{du}={R}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}(\tau ) which justifies the approach a posteriori. This expression is now substituted into the expression of the power spectral density of the response: {S}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{R}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}(\tau ){e}^{-i\omega \tau }d\tau =\frac{1}{2\pi }\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}\underset{R}{\int}\underset{R}{\int}h(u){R}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(\tau -u+v){}^{T}\text{}\overline{h(v)}{e}^{-i\omega \tau }\text{dv}\text{du}\mathrm{dt} By distributing the dummy integration variables, the respective Fourier transforms of h(u),{R}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(t-u+v),{}^{T}\text{}\overline{h(v)} are brought out, and one finally obtains: {S}_{{\ddot{X}}_{a}{\ddot{X}}_{a}}=H(\omega ).{S}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(\omega ).\overline{{}^{T}\text{}H(\omega )} with H(\omega )={\omega}^{2}\text{P.h}(\omega )\Phi +\Psi Taking into account the relations between the Fourier transforms of the displacement, of the velocity and of the acceleration, one also has: \begin{array}{}{S}_{{\dot{X}}_{a}{\dot{X}}_{a}}=\frac{-1}{{\omega}^{2}}H(\omega ){S}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(\omega )\overline{{}^{T}\text{}H(\omega )}\\ {S}_{{X}_{a}{X}_{a}}=\frac{1}{{\omega}^{4}}H(w){S}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(\omega )\overline{{}^{T}\text{}H(\omega )}\end{array} These relations make it possible to express the response of the structure by the DSP of the displacement or of the velocity. Notes: - According to the expression given to H(\omega ) , the DSP of the total, relative or differential displacement (respectively of the velocity or of the acceleration) is expressed: absolute motion: H(\omega )={\omega}^{2}\text{P. h}(\omega )\Phi +\Psi relative motion: H(\omega )={\omega}^{2}\text{P. h}(\omega )\Phi \text{} differential motion (i.e. entrainment): H(\omega )=\Psi - It is customary, during an analysis with Code_Aster, to restrict the matrix of the transfer function to the lines of the l observation degrees of freedom. This makes it possible to lighten the analyses accordingly as soon as l is small compared with n . 3.3 Application in Code_Aster The whole of the spectral approach for the seismic analysis is treated in the command DYNA_ALEA_MODAL U4.53.22. The data are grouped under three factor keywords and one simple keyword. The modal basis is made up of the dynamic modes computed by the command CALC_MODES U4.52.02, stored in a concept of type mode_meca recovered by the factor keyword BASE_MODALE, on the one hand; of the static modes computed by the command MODE_STATIQUE U4.52.14, stored in a concept of type mode_stat recovered by the simple keyword MODE_STAT, on the other hand. The factor keyword BASE_MODALE also has the arguments which make it possible to determine the frequency band or the modes retained for the analysis and the corresponding dampings. The data corresponding to the excitation are gathered under the factor keyword EXCIT (cf. paragraph [§4]): the type of excitation in the sense of the GRANDEUR is specified there: excitation in displacement or in force, the node or nodes NOEUD and components NOM_CMP excited, the name of the cross-spectra or autospectra INTE_SPEC, complex functions previously read or computed, respectively by the operators LIRE_INTE_SPEC U4.36.01 or CALC_INTE_SPEC U4.36.03 and stored in a cross-spectrum table of concept tabl_intsp which apply at each excited degree of freedom. Under the factor keyword REPONSE are found the data related to the choice of the discretisation. The command DYNA_ALEA_MODAL supplies the response in the form of a power spectral density on the modal basis. In order to obtain the restitution of the DSPs on the physical basis, REST_SPEC_PHYS U4.63.22 will be used, which makes it possible to specify the type of quantity of the response (displacement or force), at the "observation points" (node-component) of the result. In the presence of a response of displacement type, it will also be specified here whether the response corresponds to the absolute, relative or differential displacement. REST_SPEC_PHYS supplies a table of cross-spectra which contains, according to the user's request, the cross-spectral matrix in displacement {S}_{\text{XX}} , in velocity {S}_{\dot{X}\dot{X}} , or in acceleration {S}_{\ddot{X}\ddot{X}} for an expression in the absolute frame (index a ), the relative frame (index r ) or the entrainment frame (index e ). Each previous "combination" requires a specific call to the command REST_SPEC_PHYS. 4 Definition of the exciting power cross-spectral matrix The seismic excitation is, as has been said, random by nature. It may therefore be known not by its time expression but in frequency form by a power spectral density, also called a cross-spectrum. When there are several supports, they may be excited by identical or different excitations; the latter case is that of multi-support excitation. For m supports, the power cross-spectral density matrix of order m is defined, or by abuse of language the cross-spectrum of order m , which is a matrix ( m\times m ) of complex functions depending on the frequency. The diagonal terms represent the "auto-" spectral power densities — or autospectra — at the excitation points; the off-diagonal terms correspond to the cross-spectral densities between the excitations at two distinct support points (each line or column of the matrix in fact represents a support point in the physical mesh or a mode in a modal analysis). By definition of these terms, it follows that the power cross-spectral density matrices handled are Hermitian. (See [bib2] or the Reference documentation associated with the command POST_DYNA_ALEA R7.10.01) The various Code_Aster commands which make it possible to obtain a power cross-spectral density matrix are presented below. 4.1 Reading from a file The most elementary way of defining a power cross-spectral density matrix is to give, "by hand", the values at the various frequency steps. The operator LIRE_INTE_SPEC U4.36.01 is then used. LIRE_INTE_SPEC reads from an "excitation cross-spectrum" file. The format of the file in which the cross-spectral matrix is recorded is simple: the function of each term of the cross-spectral matrix is described successively; for each function, one line per frequency is given, indicating the frequency, the real and imaginary parts of the complex number; or the frequency, the modulus and the phase of the complex number (keyword FORMAT). Example of an excitation cross-spectrum file (for a matrix reduced to one term): INTERSPECTRE DIM = 1 FONCTION_C I = 1 J = 1 NB_POIN = 4 VALEUR = 2.9999 0. 0. 3. 1. 0. 13. 1. 0. 13.0001 0. 0. FINSF FIN 4.2 Obtaining a cross-spectrum from functions of time The power cross-spectral density matrix can be deduced from functions of time. The operator CALC_INTE_SPEC U4.36.03 in Code_Aster [bib3] is then used. From a list of N functions of time, this operator makes it possible to compute the power cross-spectrum N\times N which corresponds to them. For each term of the cross-spectral matrix ( N\times N ) the following approach is used [bib3]. To compute the cross-spectrum of two signals, the Wiener–Khintchine relation [bib7] is used, which makes it possible to establish a formula for computing the power spectral density by the Fourier transform of finite samples of the signals x(t) and y(t) . It then follows: {S}_{xy}(f)=\underset{T\to \infty }{\lim}\frac{1}{T}\mathrm{E}[{\mathrm{X}}_{k}(f,T).{\mathrm{Y}}_{k}\times (f,T)] where \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{X}_{k}(f,T)=\text{TF}{x}_{k}=\underset{0}{\overset{T}{\int}}{x}_{k}(t){e}^{-\mathrm{i2}\pi f}\text{dt}\\ {Y}_{k}(f,T)=\text{TF}{y}_{k}=\underset{0}{\overset{T}{\int}}{y}_{k}(t){e}^{-\mathrm{i2}\pi f}\text{dt}\end{array} are the discrete Fourier transforms of «x» and «y» . When one is interested in signals coming from measurements, one most often has only signals known in a discrete manner; likewise, a result of a transient analysis is a discrete signal. An approximation of the cross-spectrum of the discrete signals x[n] and y[n] defined on L points spaced by \Delta t , split into p blocks of q points, is obtained by the relation: \begin{array}{}{\hat{S}}_{xy}\left[k\right]=\frac{1}{\mathrm{pq}\Delta t}\sum_{i=1}^{p}{X}^{(i)}[k]{Y}^{(i)}\ast [k]\\ {X}^{(i)}[k]=\Delta t\sum_{n=0}^{q}{x}^{(i)}[n]{e}^{-\mathrm{2i}\pi \text{kn}/q}\\ {Y}^{(i)}[k]=\Delta t\sum_{n=0}^{q}{y}^{(i)}[n]{e}^{-\mathrm{2i}\pi \text{kn}/q}\end{array} The various blocks may or may not overlap. The values p and q are at the user's choice. This method is that of the WELCH periodogram [bib8]. The computation is carried out on a window which moves over the domain of definition of the functions. The user specifies in the command the length of the analysis window, the shift between two successive computation windows and the number of points per window. 4.3 Predefined excitations or excitations reconstructed from existing complex functions One may wish to define a power cross-spectral density matrix in various ways: - by a white noise: the values are constant - according to the analytical formula of KANAI-TAJIMI, useful in seismic analysis (filtered white noise), - or by taking up existing complex functions. The operator DEFI_INTE_SPEC U4.36.02 is then used. 4.3.1 Existing complex functions It is sufficient, under the factor keyword PAR_FONCTION, to give the name of the function for each pair of indices NUME_ORDRE_I, NUME_ORDRE_J, corresponding to the upper triangular matrix (because of its Hermitian character). 4.3.2 White noise A white noise is characterised by a constant value over the whole domain of definition considered. Under the factor keyword CONSTANT, this value (VALE_R or VALE_C) is given on the frequency band [FREQ_MIN, FREQ_MAX] for each pair of indices INDI_I, INDI_J, corresponding to the upper triangular matrix (because of its Hermitian character). In order to define the function completely, the interpolation and the extensions are specified. 4.3.3 White noise filtered by KANAI-TAJIMI [bib9] For a structure supported on the ground, it is common to take as excitation the power spectral density of Kanai–Tajimi. This spectral density represents the filtering of a white noise by the ground, considered as a single-degree-of-freedom system. The parameters of the formula make it possible to act on the central frequency and the bandwidth of the spectrum. Le spectre G(\omega ) s’exprime par la relation suivante: \begin{array}{}G(\omega )=\frac{{\omega}_{g}^{4}+4{\xi}_{g}^{2}{\omega}_{g}^{2}{\omega}^{2}}{{({\omega}_{g}^{2}-{\omega}^{2})}^{2}+4{\xi}_{g}^{2}{\omega}_{g}^{2}{\omega}^{2}}{G}_{0}\\ \begin{array}{cc}{\omega}_{g}=2\pi f& \text{pulsation propre}\\ {\xi}_{g}& \mathrm{amortissement}\mathrm{total}\\ {G}_{0}& \mathrm{niveau}\mathrm{du}\mathrm{bruit}\mathrm{blanc}\mathrm{avant}\mathrm{filtrage}\end{array}\end{array} The user must specify the natural frequency {f}_{g} of the filter, the modal damping {\xi}_{g} and the level of the white noise {G}_{0} (= VALE_R) before filtering; as well as, as for any function: the interpolation, the exterior profiles and the domain of definition (frequency band). By default a common ground is well represented by the values {f}_{g}=2.5\mathrm{Hz} and {\xi}_{g}=0.6 . Example of use for a white noise filtered by KANAI_TAJIMI: Interex = DEFI_INTE_SPEC ( DIMENSION : 1 KANAI_TAJIMI : ( NUME_ORDRE_I : 1 indices du terme de la matrice de densité NUME_ORDRE_J : 1 interspectrale de puissance FREQ_MOY : 2.5 fréquence propre AMOR : 0.6 amortissement modal VALE_R : 1 niveau du bruit blanc INTERPOL : ‘LIN’ interpolation linéaire PROL_GAUCHE : ‘CONSTANT’ prolongation PROL_DROIT : ‘ CONSTANT’ FREQ_MIN : 0. domaine de définition FREQ_MAX : 200. PAS : 1. ) ) ; 4.4 Other types of excitation The analyses of the previous paragraphs were carried out under the hypothesis of an excitation in imposed motion on a degree of freedom. With a few modifications it is possible to use the same approach for an excitation in force [§4.4.1] or by fluid sources [§ 4.4.2], the latter being expressed in a finite element [§4.4.3] or on a shape function of the structure [§4.4.4]. In the remainder of this paragraph, the random excitation is assumed known and supplied by the user in the form of a DSP, a power spectral density. 4.4.1 Case of the excitation in imposed forces Under the keyword EXCIT one has GRANDEUR = EFFO. When the excitation at the supports is of imposed-force type, the general equation of motion is: M\ddot{X}(t)+C\dot{X}(t)+\text{KX}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}{F}_{j} The response of the structure is then computed on a basis of dynamic modes \Phi =\left\lbrace {\phi }_{i,i=1,n}\right\rbrace , these modes being computed assuming the exciting supports free. No distinction is made, in this case, between absolute, relative and differential motion, and static modes are not used. The modal participation factor is defined in the form: {P}_{ij}=\frac{{}^{T}\text{}{\phi }_{i}{F}_{j}}{{\mu}_{i}} The transient, harmonic and random responses have the same expressions as the responses of the relative motion of the multi-support excitation in the general case [§3]. (Which corresponds to the absence of static modes). The exciting force is represented at each support degree of freedom by its DSP in the form of a term equivalent to {S}_{\ddot{E}\ddot{E}}(\omega ) . 4.4.2 Excitation by fluid sources Fluid sources appear, for example, in the study of a piping network. They correspond to active components or to connections of secondary piping. They are generally pressure sources or flow-rate sources. These various types of source are presented below according to their mathematical formulation and to what Code_Aster does in each configuration. These fluid sources are not directly seismic excitations but may be induced by an earthquake. The solution of the mechanical problem calls on the same methods, because of their random character, which justifies their presentation here. The modelling of the piping network is assumed to be carried out using the vibro-acoustic beams of Code_Aster . The response to fluid sources is computed within the framework of the response to imposed forces (cf. [§4.4.1]); in this framework one is interested in responses of quantity type "displacement" (GRANDEUR = DEPL_R under the keyword REPONSE). The pressure and force sources , for reasons of modelling of the fluid sources, are represented by dipoles [bib5]; it is therefore necessary to give two points of application . Volume flow-rate source: GRANDEUR = SOUR_DEBI_VOLU under the keyword EXCIT A volume flow rate is expressed in {m}^{3}/s , its power spectral density in {({m}^{3}/s)}^{2}/\mathrm{Hz} . A volume flow-rate source is considered, in the P-\phi formulation of the pipe elements with fluid, as an imposed force on the degree of freedom \phi of the node of application of the source R4.02.02. The user supplies the DSP of the volume flow rate {S}_{\text{vv}}(\omega ) ; the DSP {S}_{\text{vv}}^{'}(\omega ) applied as a force on the degree of freedom \phi is: {S}_{\text{vv}}^{'}(\omega )={(\rho \omega )}^{2}{S}_{\text{vv}}(\omega ) where \rho is the density of the fluid. Mass flow-rate source: GRANDEUR = SOUR_DEBI_MASS under the keyword EXCIT A mass flow rate is expressed in \mathit{kg}/s , its power spectral density in {(\mathrm{kg}/s)}^{2}/\mathrm{Hz} . The mass flow rate is the product of the volume flow rate by the density of the fluid. The user supplies the DSP of the mass flow rate {S}_{\text{mm}}(\omega ) ; the DSP {S'}_{\text{mm}}(\omega ) applied as a force on the degree of freedom \phi is: {S'}_{\text{mm}}\omega ={\omega}^{2}{S}_{\text{mm}}\omega Pressure source: GRANDEUR = SOUR_PRESS under the keyword EXCIT A pressure source is applied in Aster at a dipole {P}_{1}{P}_{2} . For a pressure source whose DSP is {S}_{\text{PP}}(\omega ) , expressed in {\mathrm{Pa}}^{2}/\mathrm{Hz} , Aster builds a power cross-spectral density matrix {S'}_{\text{pp}}(\omega ) which is applied as an imposed force on the degree of freedom \phi of the points {P}_{1} and {P}_{2} . {S'}_{\text{PP}}(\omega )={S}_{\text{PP}}(\omega )(\begin{array}{cc}{(\frac{S}{\text{dx}})}^{2}& -{(\frac{S}{\text{dx}})}^{2}\\ -{(\frac{S}{\text{dx}})}^{2}& {(\frac{S}{\text{dx}})}^{2}\end{array}) where S is the fluid cross-section, \text{dx} the distance between the two points {P}_{1} and {P}_{2} . Force source: GRANDEUR = SOUR_FORCE under the keyword EXCIT The force simply corresponds to the product of the pressure by the fluid cross-section of the tube: F=\mathrm{PS} . It is therefore also applied on a dipole {P}_{1}{P}_{2} . For a force source whose DSP is {S}_{\text{FF}}(\omega ) , expressed in {N}^{2}/\mathrm{Hz} , Aster applies, as an imposed force on the degree of freedom f of the points {P}_{1} and {P}_{2} , (a distance \mathrm{dx} apart), the power cross-spectral density matrix {S'}_{\text{FF}}(\omega ) such that: {S'}_{\text{FF}}(\omega )={S}_{\text{FF}}(\omega )(\begin{array}{cc}{(\frac{1}{\text{dx}})}^{2}& -{(\frac{1}{\text{dx}})}^{2}\\ -{(\frac{1}{\text{dx}})}^{2}& {(\frac{1}{\text{dx}})}^{2}\end{array}) 4.4.3 Excitation distributed on a shape function If the power spectral density of the excitation E(\omega ) corresponds to a force imposed on a shape function {f}_{i} , E(\omega ) gives the frequency dependence of the level of the excitation. The spatial weighting of the force is represented in Code_Aster by a field at the nodes which does not depend on the frequency: keyword CHAM_NO under the factor keyword EXCIT. This field at the nodes is an "assembled vector". From the theoretical point of view the computation formalism is the same as previously (excitation in imposed force [§4.4.1]), for a force vector on the right-hand side equal to {f}_{i} . 4.5 Applications These various types of excitation are taken up in the validation tests, and are presented by examples in the report [bib6]. In particular the excitations of fluid type are in the test: pipe subjected to random fluid excitations V2.02.105 (SDLL105). r4.05.03 Seismic response by the spectral method r4.05.03 Seismic response by the spectral method Summary: The study of the response of a structure under the effect of imposed motions of seismic type, with a single imposed motion (single-support) or a multiple one (multi-support) is possible in transient analysis (time history). One will refer to the note R4.05.01. For design studies, one may be interested only in an estimate of the maximum forces induced by the loadings, in order to evaluate the safety margin with construction regulations, without resorting to a transient analysis. The spectral method rests on the notion of oscillator spectrum of a seismic accelerogram. One details the method of construction of this response spectrum available in the operator CALC_FONCTION. One shows how this oscillator spectrum may be used to evaluate an upper bound of the response in relative displacement of a simple oscillator. This approach is justified if one does not wish to know the history of the displacements and of the forces, limiting oneself to the analysis of the inertial effects. The spectral method uses general notions of the modal recombination method R5.06.01. One describes the different combination rules that can be used in order to obtain a realistic but conservative upper bound of the maximum response of the structure. These methods are available in the operator COMB_SISM_MODAL. 1 Notion of an oscillator spectrum The spectral method for the study of the response of a structure under the effect of imposed motions of seismic type rests on the notion of oscillator spectrum of a seismic accelerogram A(t) . 1.1 Imposed motion defined by an accelerogram A(t) For an imposed motion s of seismic type, one may treat the problem in absolute displacement X or in relative displacement x such that: X=x+s . The general equations of motion of a simple oscillator are then written: Absolute motion and relative motion For the absolute motion m\ddot{X} + c\dot{X} + kX = c\dot{s}+ks and for the relative motion m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = -m\ddot{s} with the mass m , the stiffness k and the damping c . One retains the formulation starting from the relative motion for two principal reasons: - the seismic analysis of structures uses the stresses induced by the inertial effects of the earthquake, stresses computed from the strains of the structure which are expressed from the relative displacements; - the characterisation of the excitation signal may in this case be reduced to the accelerogram of the earthquake \ddot{s}=A(t) , a quantity supplied directly by the seismographs. The displacement signals s and velocity signals \dot{s} are in general not available in the geotechnical databases. For the determination of the response of a simple oscillator to an imposed motion and the conventional notations, one will refer to r4.05.03-A2. If the earthquake is defined by an accelerogram A(t) , an absolute acceleration applied at the base, the reduced equation is in this case \ddot{x} + 2\xi {\omega}_{0}\dot{x} + {\omega}_{o}^{2}x = -\ddot{s}=-A(t) The solution of this problem is the Duhamel integral presented in the annex x(t) = \frac{1}{\omega^{\prime}_{0}} {\int}_{0}^{t} { A(\tau){e}^{-\xi {\omega}_{0}(t-\tau )}\sin\omega^{\prime}_{0}(t-\tau) d\tau } = f(A,\xi ,\omega^{\prime}_{0}) with \omega^{\prime}_{0}={\omega}_{0}\sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}} 1.2 Oscillator spectrum of an accelerogram The notion of oscillator spectrum was introduced initially in order to compare with one another the effects of different accelerograms. The Fourier spectrum of a signal A(t) informs one about its frequency content. The response of a mechanical system to a motion imposed at the base depends largely on the dynamic characteristics of this system: eigenfrequencies and reduced damping (\xi ,{\omega '}_{0}) . r4.05.03-A details this aspect. If one wishes to know the maximum value of the response of a simple oscillator with the parameters, (A,\xi ,{\omega '}_{0}) one must evaluate the Duhamel integral which supplies the response of the oscillator to an excitation imposed at the base. Accelerogram 1.2.1 Oscillator spectrum in relative displacement From the Duhamel integral, one may define the oscillator spectrum of an accelerogram A(t) as the function of the maximum values of the relative displacement x(t)=f(A,\xi ,{\omega}^{\prime}_{0}) for each value of (\xi ,{\omega}^{\prime}_{0}) (recalling that \omega^{\prime}_{0}={\omega}_{0}\sqrt{(1-{\xi}^{2})} ). One thus defines the oscillator spectrum in (relative) displacement \texttt{SRO}^{x} \texttt{SRO}^{x}(A,\xi ,\omega^{\prime}_{0}) = {\vert x(t)\vert }_{\max} with x(t)=\frac{1}{\omega^{\prime}_{0}}{\int}_{0}^{t}A(\tau ){e}^{-\xi {\omega}_{0}(t-\tau )}\sin\omega^{\prime}_{0}(t-\tau )d\tau =f(A,\xi ,\omega^{\prime}_{0}) One observes, on the figure r4.05.03-fig-SRO_Deplacement, that beyond a certain frequency ( 35 \, {Hz} here), called the cut-off frequency of the spectrum, there is no significant dynamic amplification: the relative displacement is zero. Oscillator spectrum in relative displacement 1.2.2 Oscillator spectrum in relative pseudo-velocity For structures with a low reduced damping \xi i}^{nmode} \varepsilon_{i, j} \vert R_{i, I} R_{j, I}\vert } The modes are grouped according to the following rule: 1. Start a new group by adding the lowest eigenmode k (in frequency) which has not yet been grouped. 2. Increase the eigenfrequencies starting from k . 3. So long as \frac{({f}_{i}-{f}_{k})}{{f}_{k}} \le 10\text{\%} , add the i to the group. 4. Return to step 1. The correlation coefficient is equal to \varepsilon_{i, j} = 1 if the modes i and j belong to one and the same group and \varepsilon_{i, j} = 0 otherwise. 4.5.1.7 Combination with the "Ten percent" rule This method is very similar to the "grouping" method. It is also proposed by the American regulation U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC 1.92 Rev. 1). For a given direction I (with I=X,Y,Z ), the periodic response is: There is no notion of "group" in this method. The two modes are considered as "close" when the difference between two associated frequencies is less than or equal to 10%. In other words, the two modes i and j are close if \frac{({f}_{j}-{f}_{i})}{{f}_{i}} \le 10\text{\%} with f_i < f_j The correlation coefficient is equal to \varepsilon_{i, j} = 1 if the modes i and j are close and \varepsilon_{i, j} = 0 otherwise. The response obtained by the combination "NRC_TEN_PERCENT" is more conservative than that obtained by the combination "NRC_GROUPING". 4.5.1.8 Combination according to Gupta Gupta in , in order to take into account the correlations between modes due to the quasi-static part of the response, introduces the rigid response factor, which makes the correlation vary from 0 to 1 between the modal responses of intermediate frequencies between {f}_{1} and {f}_{2} , two frequencies to be determined (typically from 2 \text{Hz} to 20 \text{Hz} ). Gupta decomposes each modal response {R}_{r} into a dynamic part {R}_{r}^{p} and a quasi-static part {R}_{r}^{qs} {R}_{r}^{qs} = {\alpha}_{r}{R}_{r} and {R}_{r}^{p} = \sqrt{1-{\alpha}_{r}^{2}}{R}_{r} Thus, for each mode r , one assigns the rigid response factor {\alpha}_{r} to the modal response {R}_{r} . One has {\alpha}_{r}=0 for f\le {f}_{1} and {\alpha}_{r}=1 for f\ge {f}_{2} . The value {\alpha}_{r} is estimated for the frequency {f}_{r} according to the following formula: {\alpha}_{r} = \frac{\ln{f}_{r}/{f}_{1}}{\ln{f}_{2}/{f}_{1}} The combined dynamic response of the modal oscillators is carried out according to the 'CQC' combination: {R}_{d} = \sqrt{\sum_{{r}_{1}}\sum_{{r}_{2}}{\rho}_{{r}_{1}{r}_{2}}{R}_{{r}_{1}}^{p}{R}_{{r}_{2}}^{p}} The combined quasi-static response of the modal oscillators is carried out according to an algebraic combination: {R}_{qs} = \sum_{i=1}^{{N}_{r}}{R}_{r}^{qs} This combination is available only in the single-support case. 4.5.2 Contribution of the static correction of the neglected modes The contribution of the pseudo-mode may be combined quadratically because the independence from the contributions of the vibration modes is not contested. 4.6 Establishment of the directional response in multi-support 4.6.1 Computation of the global response The order of the combinations to be carried out differs according to whether the excitations of the supports (or of the groups of supports) may be considered as correlated or uncorrelated with one another. 4.6.1.1 Case with uncorrelated groups of supports The sequence of the combinations may be stated as follows, in order: - for each direction X , for each mode i and for each group of supports, one computes modal directional support responses (intra-group combination on the supports). Considering that the supports of one and the same group are correlated, one proposes a summation of the algebraic values; - for each direction X , for each group of supports j : - computation of the combined response of the modal oscillators (combination on the modes); - computation of the pseudo-mode {R}_{Xj}^{c} (static correction of the neglected modes); - computation of the entrainment motion {R}_{Xj}^{e} ; - computation of the directional support response: {R}_{Xj}=\sqrt{{{R}_{Xj}^{m}}^{2}+{{R}_{Xj}^{c}}^{2}+{{R}_{Xj}^{e}}^{2}} - for each direction (inter-group combination on the groups of supports): computation of the directional response, according to a CQS quadratic summation because the groups are assumed uncorrelated with one another; - computation of the total response (combination on the directions). 4.6.1.2 Case with correlated supports In the case where all the supports are correlated with one another (when one cannot exhibit uncorrelated groups of supports), one proposes the following scheme, which has the advantage of making it possible to establish a parallel between the treatment of the single-support case treated as such and the single-support case treated as a particular case of the multi-support case. The sequence of the combinations may be summarised as follows: - for each direction X and for each mode i , one computes directional modal responses (combination on the supports): the supports being assumed correlated with one another, one proposes a summation of the algebraic values or of the absolute values; - for each direction X : - computation of the combined response {R}_{X}^{m} of the modal oscillators (combination on the modes); - computation of the pseudo-mode {R}_{X}^{c} (static correction of the neglected modes, algebraic summation on the supports of the support pseudo-modes {R}_{Xj}^{c} ); - computation of the entrainment motion {R}_{Xj}^{e} (algebraic summation on the supports of the support entrainment motions {R}_{Xj}^{e} ) ; - computation of the directional response: {R}_{X}=\sqrt{{{R}_{X}^{m}}^{2}+{{R}_{X}^{c}}^{2}+{{R}_{X}^{e}}^{2}} , - computation of the total response (combination on the directions). 4.6.2 Separate computation of the primary and secondary components of the response Each component is the subject of a similar separate treatment. This approach is suited to the RCC-M post-processings in force for the seismic analysis of piping. 4.6.2.1 Primary component RIX (inertial response) The order of the combinations to be carried out differs according to whether the excitations of the supports (or of the groups of supports) may be considered as correlated or uncorrelated with one another. Uncorrelated groups of supports For each imposed motion \ddot{s}_{j} , one computes directional support responses (cumulation on the modes): {R}_{{IjX}} = \sqrt{{{R}_{j}^{m}}^{2}+{{R}_{j}^{c}}^{2}} with {R}_{j}^{m} the combined support response of the modal oscillators (cumulation on the modes) and {R}_{j}^{c} the contribution of the static correction of the neglected modes (support pseudo-mode). Then one combines the responses {R}_{{IjX}} (cumulation on the supports). Correlated supports For each imposed motion \ddot{s}_{j} , one computes directional modal responses (cumulation on the supports): {R}_{{IiX}} = \sqrt{{{R}_{i}^{m}}^{2}+{{R}^{c}}^{2}} with {R}_{i}^{m} the combined modal response of the modal oscillators (cumulation on the supports) and {R}^{c} the contribution of the static correction of the neglected modes (pseudo-mode). Then one combines the =responses {R}_{{IiX}} (cumulation on the modes). 4.6.2.2 Secondary component RII (quasi-static response) One combines the responses {R}_{{ej}} 4.6.3 Cumulation on the modes The criterion of choice of the method of combination of the contributions of the modes is the same as for a single-support excitation and one will preferentially use the CQC method. 4.6.4 Contribution of the pseudo-mode The corrective term by pseudo-mode may be combined quadratically. 4.6.5 Contribution of the entrainment motions The entrainment motion of the structure not being uniform, one may add a term to the computation of the directional response. This is not necessary if one chooses to consider this static contribution as a specific load case inducing secondary stresses. This term is defined from the maximum relative displacement which cannot be known from the absolute pseudo-acceleration spectra of the supports alone. {R}_{{ej}} = {\varphi}_{{Sj}}{\delta}_{j\text{max}} with {\varphi}_{{Sj}} the static mode for the support j , {\delta}_{j\text{max}} the maximum relative displacement of the support j with respect to a reference support (for which {\delta}_{j\text{max}}=0 ). 4.6.6 Cumulation on the supports This step is obligatory, but the choice of the method of combination of the directional responses remains very open. Indeed, the assumption of independence of the {\ddot{s}}_{j} depends strongly on the eigenmodes of the structure supporting the equipment studied. An analysis of the system studied is necessary in order possibly to group the supports by groups: for example, for a pipe connecting two buildings, either all the supports are considered as correlated with one another, or one may exhibit groups uncorrelated with one another (the group of the supports of building 1, that of building 2 and, finally, that of the intermediate supports), whose supports inside each group are correlated. Intra-group cumulation The excitations at the supports of one and the same group being assumed correlated with one another. By default, the cumulation is carried out algebraically according to the linear combination. For example, let us consider the support group m which contains nbAppui supports. The modal response along the direction X of this support group is combined as follows: {R}_{m,X} = \sum_{j=1}^{nbAppui} {R}_{m,jX} Other choices of cumulation by quadratic combination or by summation of the absolute values are available. Inter-group cumulation The groups of supports being constituted in such a way that they are uncorrelated with one another. By default, the inter-group cumulation is carried out by simple quadratic combination. By way of example, we assume that the structure possesses nbGr groups of supports. The modal response along the direction X is combined as follows: {R}_{X} = \sqrt{\sum_{m=1}^{nbGr} {R}_{{mX}}^2} Other choices of cumulation by linear combination or by summation of the absolute values are also available. 4.6.7 Single-support multi-support equivalence An analysis relating to excitations at the supports which are all identical may be conducted along two different paths, theoretically equivalent: - single-support analysis; - multi-support analysis with identical excitations at the supports. One draws attention to the fact that, if the results are indeed strictly equal in the absence of static correction via the pseudo-mode, they may present slight differences when the static correction is taken into account, because the respective treatments of this static correction are then not strictly equivalent. 4.7 Combination of the directional responses Three rules of combination of the directional responses are available. 4.7.1 Quadratic combination This combination corresponds to the assumption of strict independence of the responses in each direction. Let us recall that this combination rule has no geometrical meaning, although the three directions of analysis are orthogonal. R=\sqrt{{R}_{X}^{2}+{R}_{Y}^{2}+{R}_{Z}^{2}} The assumptions justifying the simple quadratic combination method, at this level, do not seem to have to be called into question in , but this method is not the most used. 4.7.2 Newmark combination This empirical combination rule is the most commonly used and leads in general to estimates slightly higher than the previous one. It assumes that when one of the directional responses is maximal, the others are at most equal to 4/10 of their respective maximum contributions. For each of the directions i(X,Y,Z) , one computes the eight values: {R}_{l} = \pm {R}_{X}\pm 0,4{R}_{Y}\pm 0,4{R}_{Z} which leads, by circular permutation, to 24 values and R=\max({R}_{l}) 4.7.3 Combination on the absolute values It must be noted that this rule is very conservative; it is used in certain specific cases (within the framework of PipingMaster). R = \vert {R}_{X}\vert +\vert {R}_{Y}\vert +\vert {R}_{Z}\vert 4.8 Warning on the combinations Several remarks are called for in order to warn the user about the way of using the combination methods and the combined quantities in a study note. Note 1 If one wishes to use arithmetic combinations (direction) and quadratic combinations (modes), the quadratic cumulations must always be carried out last. Note 2 Any quadratic combination applies only to the quantities for which, in instantaneous values, the cumulation has the meaning of a sum: combination of the components of displacement, or of generalised force or of stress of each eigenmode. The modal or directional quadratic combination therefore cannot be applied to stress intensities (principal stresses, von Mises, Tresca). Note 3 The results of a combination, whatever the cumulation rule, must not serve as data for computing other quantities: for example, a differential displacement between two points (or a strain) can be computed only from the modal differential displacements which one then combines. A fortiori the generalised forces and the stresses can be computed only mode by mode before any combination and not from inertia forces deduced from the acceleration fields obtained by combination of the modal accelerations. 4.9 Regulatory practices 4.9.1 Partition of the primary and secondary components of the response The different supports of a piping line may be animated by different motions. One and the same piping run may be distributed over different buildings, different levels or different pieces of equipment. It therefore undergoes a multiple excitation. This results in two types of loading: - an excitation whose frequency content varies from one support to another and which constitutes a primary loading according to the RCC-M classification, - Seismic Differential Displacements (DDS) inducing a stress state by displacements imposed at the supports and classified as secondary. The generalised moments resulting from these 2 loadings intervene separately in the RCC-M design inequalities and at several levels. With a view to a thorough RCC-M post-processing, it is therefore necessary to have available the primary and secondary components of the seismic response. In a more general manner, the method of combination of the support responses may differ according to whether one treats the case of the inertial or differential components. Moreover, the number of supports concerned by these two summations may not be equal. One is often led to impose overall differential motions even for supports associated with different user spectra. On the other hand, DDS formulated in rotation are sometimes to be considered. They cannot be associated with an inertial loading (limited to the translations). One therefore proposes two treatments: - Determination of the global response: - The inertial and static entrainment contributions are cumulated during the computation of the directional support responses. - Partition of the primary and secondary components of the global response: The two previous contributions are no longer cumulated during the computation of the directional responses and are the subject of 2 independent treatments: - The inertial component is obtained by suppressing the entrainment term {R}_{ej} in the computation of the global response. - The static component is determined by combining the entrainment terms defined under the keyword DEPL_MULT_APPUI . The methods of combination of these DDS load cases are entered in the keyword COMB_DEPL_APPUI . 4.9.2 Envelope-spectrum method Even if the piping is subjected to a multiple seismic excitation, the current practice is to come back to the analysis of a single-supported structure while keeping the DDS load cases. This simplified approach implies defining a single spectrum per direction for all the supports of the piping. For each direction, one then adopts an “envelope” spectrum of the different spectra at the supports. The spectra retained for the horizontal directions X and Y are identical. r4.05.04 Soil-structure interaction with spatial variability (operator DYNA_ISS_VARI) r4.05.04 Soil-structure interaction with spatial variability (operator DYNA_ISS_VARI) Summary: This document is a theoretical note describing the methods developed in the operator DYNA_ISS_VARI. This operator makes it possible to treat soil-structure interaction (SSI) problems in seismic analysis in which one wishes to take account of the spatial variability of the incident seismic field. Within the framework of a standard seismic study with soil-structure interaction by means of the Code_Aster /MISS3D chaining, one assumes that the seismic excitation does not vary spatially. However, the spatial variability may have non-negligible effects on the response of structures subjected to an earthquake. One observes in particular a reduction of the response in translation, which may make it possible to release margins in the SSI analyses. DYNA_ISS_VARI makes it possible to compute the response of a structure subjected to a seismic motion variable in space from a coherence function, from the impedance matrix and from the seismic force. The latter may be computed by the software MISS3D. More precisely, one constructs the spectral vectors of modal response (coming from a spectral decomposition of the coherence matrix) by way of a harmonic analysis in generalised components. On output, one obtains the spectral density of the modal response (for a unit excitation) or the time response (in acceleration). 1 Introduction In seismic analyses with soil-structure interaction, the current practice consists in considering a free-field motion that is uniform at every point of the surface of the soil. Recent observations of strong motions on seismographic arrays have nevertheless revealed spatial variations on fairly small scales. Taking the spatial variability of the incident field into account leads to a filtering of the translational motions for the high frequencies. The introduction of the spatial variability may thus lead to reduced floor spectra. The computation of the response is carried out in three steps: - Computation of the generalised matrices of the structure fixed on the interface. - Determination of the interface impedance matrices and of the seismic force by MISS3D: The software MISS3D rests on a substructuring method. The domain of the study is decomposed into subdomains — in our case the soil and the structure — coupled to one another by interfaces. One applies a multi-domain solution method and only the interfaces between domains need to be meshed by boundary finite elements. This makes it possible to model the structure (building) as well as the loadings applied to it entirely by Code_Aster . The code MISS3D, for its part, makes it possible to determine the interface impedances between soil and structure as well as the seismic force exerted by the incident field at the level of the interface. The solution of the dynamic problem and the post-processing are carried out again with Code_Aster . - Solution of the dynamic problem on a reduced basis (coming from the substructuring) in the frequency domain (DYNA_ISS_VARI) and post-processing. 2 Description of the command DYNA_ISS_VARI The operator DYNA_ISS_VARI U4.53.31 makes it possible to compute the response of a structure subjected to a seismic motion variable in space from a coherence function, from the interface impedance matrix and the seismic force. The latter may be computed with the aid of the Code_Aster /MISS3D chaining, cf. U2.06.07. On output from DYNA_ISS_VARI, one obtains, in generalised coordinates, the response spectral density or a time response to a time excitation. More precisely, one constructs the spectral vectors of modal response (coming from a spectral decomposition of the coherence matrix) by way of a harmonic analysis in generalised components. Then, one determines the power spectral density (PSD) of the modal response or else the time response in generalised components. The results that one can obtain by using the command DYNA_ISS_VARI (for the cases with or without spatial variability) are the following: - Computation of transfer functions between the seismic excitation and the response of the structure (the transfer functions are obtained by choosing an excitation by white noise). - Computation of the response spectral density for the case in which the seismic excitation is given by a spectral density (the Kanai–Tajimi spectrum is most often used to describe the seismic excitation, see also R4.05.02). - Computation of the time response in generalised components. The simulation of a realisation of the time response then makes it possible to determine floor spectra. 2.1 Seismic analysis with SSI in the frequency domain The software MISS3D is based on a frequency solution on the soil side; it makes it possible to determine the impedance matrices as well as the seismic force at the interface. The soil-structure interaction problem amounts to solving on the interface the harmonic dynamic equation: \left[\underset{\text{Equation d'équilibre du bâtiment}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{K}_{b}+i\omega {C}_{b}-{\omega}^{2}{M}_{b}}}+\underset{\mathit{Impédance}d'\mathit{interface}\mathit{sol}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{K}_{s}(\omega )}}\right]q(\omega )-\underset{\text{Force sismique}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{f}_{s}(\omega )}}=0 In equation (), q(\omega )\in {ℂ}^{m} is the vector of the generalised unknowns describing the displacement. In SSI analyses with MISS3D, one must supply a free-field accelerogram. The Fourier transform of this signal and the impedance matrix computed by MISS3D make it possible to determine the seismic force in the frequency domain, {f}_{s}(\omega ) . For what follows, one defines the complex displacement transfer function H(\omega )\in {\text{Mat}}_{\mathrm{ℂ}}(m,m) as: H(\omega ){f}_{s}(\omega )=q(\omega ) If the excitation is assumed to be a stationary Gaussian stochastic process, then the response is likewise a stationary Gaussian stochastic process. This is true because the transfer function is a linear filter. Thus, one may write the relation between the spectral densities of the seismic force and of the response: H(\omega ){S}_{f}(\omega ){H}^{\text{ }}(\omega )={S}_{q}(\omega ) Where {H}^{\text{ }} denotes the conjugate transpose of H and {S}_{f} is the spectral-density matrix of the seismic force, which may be evaluated from L realisations of the time seismic force {f}_{s}^{l}(t) : {S}_{f}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}{f}_{s}^{l}(\omega ){f}_{s}^{l}\text{ }(\omega ) In this expression, T denotes the time interval and W(t)=1/\sqrt{(T)} is the natural window on [0,T] (cf. [bib10]). It is an unbiased estimator of the spectral density [bib10]. Note : One may also write: {S}_{f}(\omega )=\underset{T\to \infty }{\lim}\frac{1}{2\pi T}E({f}_{s}(\omega ){f}_{s}\text{ }(\omega )) where E(\cdot ) denotes the mathematical-expectation operator. 2.2 Taking spatial variability into account DYNA_ISS_VARI is based on a probabilistic description of the incident seismic field by its power spectral density (PSD). The latter is generally constructed with the aid of a point spectrum and of a spatial coherence function. Thus, the cross spectral density of the free-field ground motion is written: {S}_{u}(x,x\text{',}\omega )=\gamma (x,x\text{',}\omega ){S}_{0}(\omega ) Where \gamma (x,x\text{',}\omega ) is the coherence function of the seismic signal between two points x and x' and {S}_{0}\in ℝ is the point spectral density of the free-field seismic motion. One assumes here that the spectral density is defined on the interval O=\left[-{\omega}_{s},+{\omega}_{s}\right] and that it is zero outside this frequency range. If one discretises with respect to the spatial variable, x and x' , one obtains the following spectral-density matrix: {S}_{u}(\omega )=\gamma (\omega ){S}_{0}(\omega )\in {\text{Mat}}_{ℂ}(m,m) In this expression, \gamma (of dimension m\times m ) denotes the coherence matrix and one denotes its components {\gamma}_{ij}(\omega )=\gamma ({x}_{i},{x}_{j},\omega ) . The elements of {S}_{u}(\omega )=\left[{S}_{ij}(\omega )\right]\in \text{Mat}(m,m) are the cross spectral densities, {S}_{ij}(\omega )=S({x}_{i},{x}_{j},\omega ) , m being the number of spatial discretisation points. In general, one assumes that the incident seismic field is homogeneous, that is that the stochastic description of the field depends only on the distance, d=\mid x-x'\mid , but that it is independent of the spatial position. The computation of the seismic response relies on the spectral decomposition of the coherence matrix \gamma (\omega ) . Let us specify that this is a spectral decomposition with respect to the spatial variable and not with respect to the time variable. Thus, one has: {S}_{u}(\omega )=\Phi (\omega )\Lambda (\omega )\Phi \text{ }(\omega ){S}_{0}(\omega ) Where \Phi is a matrix containing the eigenvectors {\varphi}_{k} of the coherence matrix \gamma and \Lambda is the diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues, \Lambda =\text{diag}({\lambda}_{k}),k=1,\dots m . In what follows, one will speak of POD modes (Proper Orthogonal Decomposition) to designate the {\varphi}_{k} . This makes it possible to distinguish them from the mechanical modes. From the expression of equation (), one defines: {s}_{u}^{k}(\omega )={\varphi}_{k}(\omega )\sqrt{{\lambda}_{k}(\omega )}\sqrt{{S}_{0}(\omega )},\forall \omega \in O Knowing that {S}_{u}(\omega )=\sum_{k=1}^{m}{s}_{u}^{k}(\omega ){s}_{u}^{k}\text{ }(\omega ) . The spectral density of the seismic force is obtained from the motion at the soil interface by the matrix transfer function G(\omega ) : {S}_{f}(\omega )=G(\omega ){S}_{u}(\omega )G\text{ }(\omega ) And thus: {s}_{f}^{k}(\omega )=G(\omega ){\varphi}_{k}(\omega )\sqrt{{\lambda}_{k}(\omega )}\sqrt{{S}_{0}(\omega )},\forall \omega \in \Omega In SSI studies with Code_Aster , the transfer function G(\omega ) is computed by MISS3D; this is described in more detail in section § 2.2.1 . Expression () is the input for the traditional seismic analysis, see equation (). The model is “reduced” if one can truncate expression () to K\le m POD modes. As has just been seen, the computation of the seismic forces with spatial variability of the incident field implies a spectral decomposition of the coherence matrix \gamma . For the remainder of the analyses, one retains only a reduced number of POD modes, namely K\le m modes. The parameter precision gives the share of the “energy” of the matrix that one retains by keeping only a reduced number of eigenvectors and eigenvalues of \gamma . If one designates by K the number of POD modes retained (one retains the K largest eigenvalues), one has: \text{precision}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K}{\lambda}_{i}^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{M}{\lambda}_{i}^{2}} The value 0,999 is taken by default for the precision. 2.2.1 Coherence functions The coherence function depends on the separation distance d between two points x and x' and on the frequency. In general, one expresses it by a modulus term and a phase term: \gamma (d,\omega )=∣\gamma (d,\omega )∣\exp(-i\theta (\omega ,d)) The term \exp(-i\theta (\omega ,d)) represents the phase shift due to the different arrival times of the waves. The amplitude term corresponds to “pure incoherence”. It may be evaluated from the PSDs (auto-spectra and cross-spectra) at the points x and x' : {∣\gamma (d,\omega )∣}^{2}=\frac{S{(\omega ,x,x')}^{2}}{S(\omega ,x)S(\omega ,x')} The coherence functions currently available in DYNA_ISS_VARI are the coherence function of Mita & Luco and the coherence function of Abrahamson (for rock). One does not introduce a phase term. The coherence function of Mita & Luco [bib5, bib6] is written: \gamma (d,f)=\exp\left[-{\left(\frac{\alpha \omega d}{{v}_{s}}\right)}^{2}\right] In this expression, {v}_{s} is the propagation velocity of the SH wave (typically 200-\mathrm{1000 }m/s ) and the parameter \alpha may vary from 0,1 to 0,5 depending on the cases but is generally taken equal to 0,5 . If one chooses \alpha =0.0 , then one carries out an analysis without spatial variability. One sees that the correlation length for the coherence function of Mita and Luco [bib5, bib6] is characterised by the expression (\omega \alpha /{v}_{s}{)}^{-1} . The generic Abrahamson coherence function [bib9] is written, for \omega =2\pi f : \gamma (d,f)={\left[1+{\left(\frac{f\tanh({a}_{3}d)}{{f}_{c}{a}_{1}}\right)}^{\mathit{n1}}\right]}^{-0.5}{\left[1+{\left(\frac{f\tanh({a}_{3}d)}{{f}_{c}{a}_{2}}\right)}^{\mathit{n2}}\right]}^{-0.5} Avec les valeurs suivantes des paramètres pour le mouvement horizontal: {f}_{c}=-1,886+2,221\ln(4000/(d+1)+1,5) {n}_{1}=7,02 {n}_{2}=5,1-0,51\ln(d+10) {a}_{1}=1,647 {a}_{2}=1,01 {a}_{3}=0,4 The Abrahamson coherence function for a rock or a medium soil (EPRI 1015110, 2007) is written, for \omega =2\pi f : \gamma (d,f)={\left[1+{\left(\frac{f\tanh({a}_{3}d)}{{f}_{c}(d){a}_{1}}\right)}^{\mathit{n1}(d)}\right]}^{-0.5}{\left[1+{\left(\frac{f\tanh({a}_{3}d)}{{a}_{2}}\right)}^{\mathit{n2}}\right]}^{-0.5} Pour le rocher, on a les valeurs suivantes des paramètres pour le mouvement horizontal: {f}_{c}=27,9+4,82\ln(d+1)+1,24{(\ln((d+1)-3,6))}^{2} {n}_{1}=3,8-0,04\ln(d+1)+0,0105{(\ln((d+1)-3,6))}^{2} {n}_{2}=16,4 {a}_{1}=1,0 {a}_{2}=40 {a}_{3}=0,4 This coherence function is an empirical model recalibrated from the 78 earthquakes recorded at Pinyon Flat (USA) by Abrahamson. It is also used for other types of soil, for which it is considered conservative. > For the medium soil, one has the following values of the parameters for the horizontal motion: {f}_{c}=14,3+2,35\ln(d+1) {n}_{1}(d)=2 {n}_{2}=15 {a}_{1}=1,0 {a}_{2}=15,8-0,044d {a}_{3}=0,4 2.2.2 Modelling of the seismic forces with Code_Aster - Case of a rigid foundation The interface modes are the six rigid-body modes. The modal seismic force computed by MISS3D is then written, for a unit excitation (white noise): {f}_{s}(\omega )={K}_{s}(\omega ){x}_{0} Where {K}_{s}(\omega ) is the modal impedance matrix and {x}_{0}=(1.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.) for a seismic excitation in the direction x , {x}_{0}=(0.,1.,0.,0.,0.,0.) for a seismic excitation in y and {x}_{0}=(0.,0.,1.0.,0.,0.,0.) for a vertical earthquake. The seismic force is non-zero only for the modal component in the direction of the earthquake (x,y,z) . Likewise, the coherence function is constructed only for the translational degrees of freedom in the direction of the earthquake. The other degrees of freedom are not affected. In order to take the spatial variability into account, one determines the modal participation for each POD mode characterising the spatial variability: {f}_{s}^{k}(\omega )={K}_{s}(\omega ){\Theta}^{T}{s}_{u}^{k} Where \Theta is the matrix containing the (mechanical) interface modes. - Case of a flexible foundation The interface modes are the d\times 6 unit modes relating to the d nodes of the interface. The modal seismic force computed by MISS3D is then written: {f}_{s}(\omega )={K}_{s}(\omega ){x}_{0} {x}_{0} is the modal participation vector comprising 1 for the degrees of freedom relating to the direction of the earthquake and zeros for the other directions. Likewise, the seismic force and the coherence function are non-zero only for the degrees of freedom in the direction of the earthquake. One constructs the coherence matrix and then the vectors {s}_{u}^{k} for the degrees of freedom in the direction of the earthquake: {f}_{s}^{k}(\omega )={K}_{s}(\omega ){s}_{u}^{k} - Case of an “arbitrary” foundation In these cases, corresponding either to an embedded foundation, or to a case of soil-fluid-structure interaction, or to a case in which the interface modes are arbitrary modes different from unit modes relating to the nodes of the interface, the modal participation vector {x}_{0} is no longer itself unitary, nor independent of the frequency, and one no longer has identity between the physical and modal coordinates of the interface. The modal seismic force computed by MISS3D is then written: {f}_{s}(\omega )={K}_{s}(\omega ){x}_{0}(\omega ) {x}_{0}(\omega ) the modal participation vector is therefore obtained by inversion of the seismic force {f}_{s}(\omega ) with respect to the soil impedance {K}_{s}(\omega ) ; the corresponding physical vector on the interface {X}_{0}(\omega ) is then written: {X}_{0}(\omega )=\Theta {x}_{0}(\omega ) where \Theta is the matrix containing the (mechanical) interface modes. In order to take the spatial variability into account, one determines the physical contribution on the interface for each POD mode characterising the spatial variability: {X}_{u}^{k}(\omega )={X}_{0}(\omega ){s}_{u}^{k} The physical vector on the interface {X}_{u}^{k}(\omega ) corresponds to a modal participation vector {S}_{u}^{k}(\omega ) such that: {X}_{u}^{k}(\omega )=\Theta {S}_{u}^{k}(\omega ) where \Theta is the matrix containing the (mechanical) interface modes. The corresponding seismic force will then be expressed as follows: {f}_{s}^{k}(\omega )={K}_{s}(\omega ){S}_{u}^{k}(\omega ) 2.2.3 Computation of transfer functions and of the response PSD By linear filtering, one obtains: {s}_{q}^{k}(\omega )=H(\omega ){s}_{f}^{k}(\omega ) Which makes it possible to reconstruct the response spectral-density matrix as: {S}_{q}(\omega )=\sum_{k=1}^{K\le m}{s}_{q}^{k}({s}_{q}^{k})\text{ } The model is reduced if one can truncate expression () to K\le m POD modes. For an excitation by white noise, one obtains directly the PSD of the transfer function on output. Note : Without spatial variability the seismic field and thus the seismic force are the same for the whole set of nodes of the interface (the foundation): {S}_{u}(x,x\text{',}\omega )={S}_{0}(\omega ) Warning: In the present state, DYNA_ISS_VARI can treat only the case of a shallow foundation. As for the interface modes, one may choose between a modelling by the 6 rigid-body modes (rigid foundation), arbitrary interface modes (flexible foundation) and a modelling by all the FE modes (flexible foundation). 2.2.4 Computation of the time response to an earthquake In general, it is possible to simulate trajectories of a stationary Gaussian process whose PSD one knows by using the spectral representation theorem. One could therefore obtain a realisation of the structural time response (stochastic process characterised by its spectral density {S}_{q}(\omega ) ) by the formula (cf. [bib4]): q(t)=\sum_{k}\sum_{n=0}^{{N}_{T}}H({\omega}_{n})G({\omega}_{n}){e}^{i{\omega}_{n}t}{\varphi}_{k}({\omega}_{n})\sqrt{{\lambda}_{k}({\omega}_{n})}\sqrt{{S}_{0}({\omega}_{n})}{\xi}_{n}^{k}\sqrt{\Delta \omega } where the {\xi}_{n}^{k} are independent complex random variables of reduced centred normal law and where \Delta \omega denotes the (constant) frequency step, {\omega}_{n},n=1,{N}_{T} are the frequencies coming from the discretisation. Under the hypothesis that one can approximate the point spectral density with the aid of a number of accelerograms, one has: {S}_{0}^{L}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}{u}_{0}^{l}(\omega ).{u}_{0}^{l}\ast (\omega ) Where {u}_{0}(\omega ) is obtained from the free-field accelerogram u(t) : {u}_{0}(\omega )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\underset{0}{\overset{T}{\int}}{u}_{0}(t){e}^{-i\omega t}\text{dt} Here, one does not use this method of generating signals from their PSD, because one is working with non-stationary processes of which one knows a realisation, namely the accelerogram at the input of the mechanical analysis. Given this context, one places oneself rather in a deterministic framework of signal filtering. Thus, one introduces a deterministic filter modelling the effect of the spatial incoherence. This filter is given by the matrix \Phi (\omega )\Lambda (\omega {)}^{1/2} . One can thus compute the frequency response and obtain the time response by inverse FFT. The frequency response is written: q(\omega )=\sum_{k}H(\omega )G(\omega ){\phi }_{k}(\omega \sqrt{{\lambda}_{k}(\omega )}{u}_{0}(\omega ) Considering equation (), one can check that the spectral density of the response q is that given by equation (). The model is “reduced” if one can truncate expression () to K\le m POD modes. 2.3 Results computed by DYNA_ISS_VARI In summary, the operator DYNA_ISS_VARI makes it possible to obtain the following results: - Computation of the spectral density of the modal response for a unit seismic excitation (in displacement). In order to obtain the response to a seismic excitation, one multiplies the PSD obtained for a unit excitation by the spectrum modelling the excitation (Kanai–Tajimi or other). - Computation of the transfer functions for a unit seismic excitation (in displacement). The transfer functions are given by the square root of the modulus of the response auto-spectra, \sqrt{\mid {\left[{S}_{v}(\omega )\right]}_{ii}\mid } (square root of the absolute value of the auto-spectrum [bib9] in physical coordinates). By comparing the transfer functions with and without spatial variability, one can determine margins linked to the incoherence of the seismic signal (cf. also [bib8]: “incoherence” margin factor in the seismic PSAs). - Computation of the floor spectra by way of the transient response (FONC_SIGNAL must be supplied). DYNA_ISS_VARI makes it possible to compute the transient response in acceleration. The oscillator response spectra (SRO) for a floor may be obtained in post-processing. 3 Other software: SASSI and CLASSI The two tools most used to carry out SSI analyses with spatial variability for the nuclear field are the software packages CLASSI and SASSI. The method implemented in Code_Aster is close to that of SASSI [bib8, bib9]. Just as DYNA_ISS_VARI in Code_Aster , SASSI makes it possible on the one hand to determine transfer functions (unit excitation) and on the other hand to compute time responses taking the spatial variability into account. The computation of the transfer functions is carried out according to the same principle in the two codes ( Code_Aster and SASSI): one carries out a spectral decomposition (POD) of the coherence matrix, one determines the response POD mode by POD mode in order to recompose from it the response PSD as described in this note. For the computation of time responses, there is a difference between the SASSI methodology and the implementation in Code_Aster. More precisely, SASSI introduces a random phase for each POD mode [bib9]: q(\omega )=\sum_{k}H(\omega )G(\omega ){\phi }_{k}(\omega )\sqrt{{\lambda}_{k}(\omega )}{e}^{i{\eta}^{k}(\omega )}{u}_{0}(\omega ) Where the {\eta}^{k}(\omega ) are uniform random variables on the interval [-\pi ,\pi ] . One then determines m responses and m SRO in order to retain the mean. However, the introduction of the random phase is not useful if one considers the problem as a (deterministic) filtering problem of a deterministic signal (the accelerogram) as described above. One can furthermore check that the expectation of expression () is equal to expression (). The method used by CLASSI is different, inasmuch as one remains within the framework of classical stochastic dynamics: one solves a linear filtering problem (as is the case for DYNA_ISS_VARI when no seismic signal is given). The PSD of the seismic excitation is approximated directly with the aid of an algorithm making the equivalence between the PSD and the SRO. The response SRO is obtained in the same manner from the response PSD, namely by determining the SRO corresponding to the computed response PSD [bib9]. 4 Bibliography 1.
