r4.05.06 Equivalent linear method for the propagation of waves in 1D r4.05.06 Equivalent linear method for the propagation of waves in 1D Summary This document describes the equivalent linear method and its implementation in Code_Aster in the command DEFI_SOL_EQUI U4.81.31. The equivalent linear method makes it possible to compute the response of a one-dimensional soil column (1D – one component) or of a multidimensional one (1D – three components), stratified horizontally, to the vertical propagation of shear waves (SV). It accounts in an approximate way for the behaviour of soils under cyclic loading. The solution method of the equivalent linear model is an iterative procedure, in which one evaluates at each iteration, for each soil layer, linear viscoelastic characteristics equivalent to those given by the degradation curves of the shear modulus G and of the increase of the hysteretic damping measured experimentally. The simplicity of the implementation, the quality of the results and the rapidity of the computations make it a method very widely used in engineering. The one-dimensional equivalent linear method is thus implemented in numerous analysis codes (SHAKE, FLUSH, CYBERQUAKE, DEEPSOIL, EERA,...). The application of the equivalent linear method remains valid as long as the volumetric strain of the soil can be neglected. In the contrary case, it is necessary to turn to non-linear models integrating the shear–mean-pressure coupling (or deviatoric strains–dilatancy) such as the cyclic elastoplastic model of Hujeux R7.01.23 (Cyclic constitutive law of Hujeux for soils). Traditionally the equivalent linear model is accepted up to distortion strains in free field of the order of {10}^{-3} (Guide ASN/2/01). This remains an order of magnitude of validity, which it is necessary to adapt to the situation and to the phenomena that one wishes to model. 1 Introduction Idriss and Seed (1967) [1] were the first to propose an equivalent linear approach for the analysis of the site response to a seismic solicitation. Later, Schnabel et al. (1972) [2] implemented this method in the frequency domain with the program SHAKE. The equivalent linear method has since been implemented in several analysis codes (SHAKE, FLUSH, CYBERQUAKE, DEEPSOIL, EERA,...) and in code_aster under the operator DEFI_SOL_EQUI, U4.84.31. This method is suited to the evaluation of the response of soil profiles made up of horizontal layers subjected to the vertical propagation of seismic waves. A 1D modelling – one component considers only the propagation of shear waves in a horizontal direction, whereas a 1D modelling – three components considers the vertical propagation of three plane waves (SV, SH and P). The degraded properties of the column are also given. 7 Choice of the weighting coefficient of the effective strain The weighting coefficient of the effective strain \chi is a key parameter linking the loading conditions during the earthquake to the laboratory tests which are carried out to measure the curves G/{G}_{\max} and D -gamma (Kramer, 1996 [7]). Its value is taken less than 1 . The introduction of this parameter into the theory of the equivalent linear model is practical because it makes it possible to adjust the computed results to a recorded response. However when one wishes to predict the response of a soil column, one must make the choice of a value of \chi . In the literature, the practices and the recommendations on the value of this coefficient are fairly different: - In the user's guide of SHAKE (2012 and earlier versions) [8], Schnabel et al. (2012) recommend taking it equal to a value of 0.65 . This value has today remained the reference value used in engineering practice without further consideration. However this recommendation remains empirical. - In the user's guide of DEEPSOIL (2012) [9], Y. Hashash recommends taking this parameter at a value of 0,65 . - In the user's guide of SHAKE91 (1992) [10], Idriss and Sun recommend varying this coefficient as a function of the magnitude {M}_{w} of the earthquake of the input signal, according to the formula: \chi = rac{({M}_{w}-1)}{10} - According to Idriss and Sun [10], the values of \chi are thus comprised in the interval [0.4,0.75] , which corresponds to earthquakes of magnitude {M}_{w} from 5 to 8,5 . - In the user's guide of EERA (2000) [5], this coefficient is denoted {R}_{y} and depends on the magnitude of the earthquake according to the formulation of Idriss and Sun [10] above. - Dickenson (1994) [11] shows that the response computed with \chi =0,65 can be slightly improved by using a value from 0,35 to 0,55 for earthquakes of magnitude {M}_{s}=6-7 , and between 0,55 and 0,7 for earthquakes of magnitude {M}_{s}=7-8 , {M}_{s} being the magnitude of the surface waves. - Yoshida et al (2002) [12] estimate that the value of \chi must vary according to the seismic level of the recorded signal and that it varies in reality between 0,2 and 1 . He specifies that there is no good method for the evaluation of \chi . Yoshida et al. show that the use of the weighting coefficient for the evaluation of the shear modulus and of the damping is at the origin of two defects in the theory of the equivalent linear model: - The overestimation of the maximum shear stress which implies an overestimation of the peak maximum acceleration. [12] illustrate the second defect of the equivalent linear method by the where the amplification (ratio of the FFTs of the accelerations) has been computed with SHAKE for an instrumented borehole in Tokyo Bay and compared with the measured ratio. The amplification computed by SHAKE is lower from 7\mathrm{Hz} . Yoshida et al. [12] show that the problem comes from the fact that the shear modulus and the damping are evaluated from the effective strain, and this for all frequencies. The shear modulus is then lower and the damping greater than necessary for the high-frequency domain, where the amplitudes are smaller than the effective strain. This point shows the simplification of using a single weighting coefficient of the effective strain for the behaviour at high and low frequencies. This is the reason why certain authors recommend varying \chi as a function of the magnitude. \chi must take low values for weak earthquakes and higher values for stronger earthquakes. Figure 7-2. Comparison of the amplification between SHAKE and the borehole measurements [12]. Points 1 and 2 are therefore contradictory since one would have to increase \chi in order to lower the overestimation of the maximum shear stress (and therefore of the peak acceleration) and reduce \chi in order to avoid the underestimation of the amplification at high frequency. The choice of \chi must therefore be made according to the problem posed, taking the two preceding remarks into account. Modifications of the equivalent linear model have been proposed to resolve these difficulties (FDEL model, Assimaki et al. [13], DYNEQ model Yoshida et al. [12]). In these models, the weighting coefficient of the effective strain, the shear modulus and the damping depend on the frequency. These models nevertheless remain little used in practice because of the mixed results. For the FDEL model, Assimaki et al [13] and Furumoto (2000) [14] show a good improvement of the results with respect to the classical model whereas Yoshida et al. [12] and Kwak et al. [15] put forward results less good than the classical model with the FDEL model. For the DYNEQ model, Yoshida et al. [12] show a definite improvement in the quality of the results obtained particularly in deconvolution with respect to the classical model (described here) and to the FDEL model. This improvement is nevertheless to be qualified by the works of Kwak et al. [15]. 8 Choice of the weighting factor of the effective water-pressure rise The weighting factor of the effective water-pressure rise {\chi }_{\mathit{ru}} is a key parameter making it possible to consider the effect of the water-pressure rise on the degradation of the shear modulus. The introduction of this parameter is practical because it makes it possible to adjust the influence of the increase of the water pressure in the shear behaviour of soils. During the thesis of Kteich (2018), a parametric study on the real case of the city of Urayasu was carried out in order to calibrate this factor by comparing the observations of liquefaction in the city with the predictions for various values of {\chi }_{\mathit{ru}} . The value making it possible to obtain all the observations of occurrence of liquefaction is equal to 0.6667. 9 Verification and validation The reader will refer to the user's documentation of the command DEFI_SOL_EQUI U4.84.31 or to the test cases ZZZZ412 (Validation of the command DEFI_SOL_EQUI), SDLS128 (Seismic solicitation of a soil column with the equivalent linear model, Comparison with SHAKE in deconvolution), SDLS141 (Seismic solicitation of a soil column – PRENOLIN benchmark comparison – Comparison with the Hujeux model at low strain), SDLX101e,h (Verification of the chaining MISS3D‑code_aster in the case of a large building), in order to have application cases. 10 Bibliography 1. r4.05.07 Non-linear soil–structure interaction with the Laplace–Time method r4.05.07 Non-linear soil–structure interaction with the Laplace–Time method Summary: This document is a theoretical note describing the Laplace–Time method ( cf . U2.06.05) developed in the operator CALC_MISS ( cf . U7.03.12) for the result type 'FICHIER_TEMPS'. It belongs to the framework of non-linear soil–structure interaction (SSI) analyses based on the Code_Aster –MISS3D coupling. The principle of the solution of such a non-linear analysis rests on a substructuring technique in which two subdomains are generally considered: on the one hand, a bounded non-linear domain corresponding essentially to the structural part (and possibly the soil surrounding the foundation) and, on the other, an unbounded soil domain with linear elastic behaviour. This domain decomposition makes it possible to apply the finite-element method ( Code_Aster ) for the transient modelling of the non-linear problem and a boundary-element method (MISS3D) for the computation of the impedance matrix representing the dynamic behaviour in time of the semi-infinite soil domain. In this framework, the Laplace–Time method makes it possible to compute the impedance operator in time from a particular sampling of the complex-frequency space (Laplace domain). In particular, this sampling is based on the characteristic polynomial of a second-order linear multistep method. Likewise, the Laplace–Time method makes possible the evaluation, at each time instant of the seismic analysis, of the convolution integral expressing the soil–structure interaction forces of the coupled system. 1 Introduction Dynamic soil–structure interaction (SSI) problems, or even soil–fluid–structure interaction problems, are often solved using a substructuring technique in which the complete system is decomposed into two or more subdomains. In particular, for the cases of non-linear SSI, it is decomposed into a linear domain (the far-field soil) and a non-linear domain (the building and possibly a part of the surrounding soil). The advantage of using this decomposition technique rests essentially on the possibility of using the numerical methods best suited to each domain. Thus, the linear far-field soil, which corresponds to an infinite domain, can be modelled with the boundary-element method (BEM, the English acronym) and the non-linear part, which is rather confined to a bounded domain, often of complex geometry for the structural part, with the finite-element method (FEM). This BEM–FEM numerical approach is indeed the one used in the code_aster –MISS3D coupling. In this framework, two particular features deserve to be recalled. First, the fact that any non-linear problem must in general be solved with a transient analysis. And second, the fact that MISS3D, based on a frequency formulation of the boundary-element method, makes it possible to model the unbounded linear soil by means of an impedance matrix (soil stiffness that depends on the frequency) projected onto a basis of modes representative of the kinematics of the interface between the linear and non-linear domains (also known, by misuse of language, as the SSI interface). In view of these two considerations, the coupled problem is formulated entirely in the time domain, but a convolution product coming from the frequency dependence of the impedance appears at the interface. To evaluate this convolution product, the literature proposes the time–frequency method or the hidden-variable method which, using the impedance function or its inverse, rest on a formulation in the frequency domain. Formulations of the impedance function in the Laplace domain are also found, which can be combined with convolution-quadrature methods. Nevertheless, the method developed in CALC_MISS (the Laplace–Time method), which is the one presented in this document, makes it possible to evaluate the convolution integrals by bringing out the inertia, damping and stiffness terms that characterise dynamic problems. 1.1 Problem statement: evaluation of the convolution integrals As mentioned previously, the Laplace–Time method proceeds by the evaluation of a convolution product. The main difficulty of its computation comes from the singular character of the convolution kernel (the impedance matrix), which indeed makes its evaluation difficult with a simpler and classical approach linked to FFT-type algorithms. To illustrate quickly the origin of this product, it will be assumed that the system is linear, so as to be able to start from the equations formulated in the Fourier domain: -{\omega}^{2}M\widehat{u}(\omega )+i\omega C\widehat{u}(\omega )+K\widehat{u}(\omega )+\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ {\widehat{Z}}_{s}(\omega ){\widehat{u}}_{\Gamma}(\omega )\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ {\widehat{F}}_{s}(\omega )\end{array}\right] where M , C and K are the mass, damping and stiffness matrices of the system, {\widehat{Z}}_{s}(\omega ) the soil impedance matrix, {\widehat{F}}_{s}(\omega ) the equivalent seismic force and {\widehat{u}}_{\Gamma}(\omega ) the vector of unknown displacements at the interface. Then, the convolution product appears directly on applying the Fourier transform to the previous equation: M\ddot{u}(t)+C\dot{u}(t)+Ku(t)+\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ {R}_{\Gamma}(t)\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ {F}_{s}(t)\end{array}\right] with {R}_{\Gamma}(t)={\int}_{0}^{t}Z(t-\tau ){u}_{\Gamma}(\tau )\text{}d\tau ,\text{}0\le t\le T and Z(t) the operator analogous to the soil impedance in time. If the structural part (plus possibly the near-field soil) were non-linear, the convolution product would also appear in the equations of the unknowns of the SSI interface, because the soil–structure interaction forces depend only on the nature of the unbounded soil domain, which itself is assumed always to be linear. 2 The Laplace–Time method 2.1 General principle Consider the particular case of two subdomains separated by an interface \Gamma : l’un noté :math: {\Omega}_{1} , which is unbounded and which presents a linear behaviour, and the other, {\Omega}_{2} , bounded and possibly non-linear. The interaction effects between the two subdomains can be represented on the interface by an impedance that is assumed to be defined in the Fourier or Laplace domain. In this framework, the global problem is solved in time in {\Omega}_{2} , taking into account the effects of the subdomain {\Omega}_{1} by means of an external force applied on the boundary. This interaction force, which brings into play the impedance function in the time domain Z(t) , corresponds to a convolution integral with the unknown field {u}_{\Gamma}(t) , which will be denoted (Z\ast {u}_{\Gamma})(t) . Thus, in a general manner, the evaluation of the interaction forces between the subdomains proceeds by the computation of a convolution integral between two causal functions, defined as: (Z\ast {u}_{\Gamma})(t)={\int}_{0}^{t}Z(t-\tau ){u}_{\Gamma}(\tau )\text{}d\tau ,\text{}0\le t\le T Let \widehat{Z}(s) be the Laplace transform of Z(t) ; it will be assumed that it is analytic in the complex half-plane \mathit{\Re e}(s)>{\sigma}_{0} and of slow growth for \mid s\text{|} large: | :math: | | widehat{Z}(s) | | le C({sigma}_{0}) | s{ | }^{mu}text{avec}C({sigma}_{0})text{et}mu in ℝ | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | In this framework, let \widehat{Z}(s)={\widehat{Z}}_{m}(s)\widehat{P}(s) with \widehat{P}(s) a polynomial function in s with matrix values 1 of degree m\ge \mu : \widehat{P}(s)=\sum_{p=0}^{m}{\Lambda}_{p}{s}^{p} If this polynomial decomposition is considered, the convolution kernel Z(t) , defined in the sense of distributions, can be expressed in the form of a differentiation operator of order p as: Z(t)=\left({Z}_{m}\ast \sum_{p=0}^{m}{\Lambda}_{p}\frac{{d}^{p}\delta }{d{t}^{p}}\right)(t) Consequently, the convolution product can finally be written as: (Z\ast {u}_{\Gamma})(t)=\sum_{p=0}^{m}({\int}_{0}^{t}{Z}_{m}(\tau ){\Lambda}_{p}{u}_{\Gamma}^{(p)}(t-\tau )d\tau ) with {u}_{\Gamma}(t) a causal function that is sufficiently differentiable. Using Lubich’s quadrature method, the previous equation can be expressed in the form of a discrete convolution. Indeed, if \Delta t denotes the discretisation time step, the latter can be written at the time instants n\Delta t ( 0\le n\Delta t\le t ) as follows: (Z\ast {u}_{\Gamma})(n\Delta t)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}({\Psi}_{1}^{n-k+1}{u}_{\Gamma ,k}+...+{\Psi}_{p}^{n-k+1}{u}_{\Gamma ,k}^{(p)}+...+{\Psi}_{m}^{n-k+1}{u}_{\Gamma ,k}^{(m)}) where the coefficients {\Psi}_{k}^{j} contain the contribution of the matrices {\Lambda}_{k} . 2.2 Application to soil impedance operators The soil impedance matrix, that is the spatially discretised version of the impedance operator, relates a displacement vector defined on the degrees of freedom of the soil–structure interface (or, in a generalised manner within the framework of the Aster–MISS3D coupling, on the FEM–BEM boundary) to the force vector defined on the same interface, denoted \Gamma in what follows: \widehat{Z}(s){\widehat{u}}_{\Gamma}(s)={\widehat{F}}_{\Gamma}(s) In a general manner, the soil impedance matrix, which is assumed analytic in the half-space \mathit{\Re e}(s)>{\sigma}_{0} for reasons of causality, can be expressed in the following form: \widehat{Z}(s)={\widehat{Z}}_{\mathit{sing}}(s)+{\widehat{Z}}_{\mathit{nsing}}(s) where {\widehat{Z}}_{\mathit{nsing}}(s) corresponds to the regular part of the impedance, whose inverse Laplace transform {Z}_{\mathit{nsing}}(t) , which exists in the classical sense, is defined as an exponentially bounded function, continuous in time, which vanishes for t 0 ): (Z\ast {u}_{\Gamma})(n\Delta t)=\sum_{0\le n\Delta t\le t}{\Phi}_{k}{u}_{\Gamma}(t-n\Delta t) where the coefficients {\Phi}_{k} correspond to the weights of the following power series: \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty }{\Phi}_{k}{\zeta}^{k}=\widehat{Z}({s}_{\Delta t}) The sampling points {s}_{\Delta t} of the dynamic soil impedance are given in the following section. Having arrived at this point, and taking into account that expression () is homogeneous with a force, it seems judicious to express this convolution not only in terms of displacement, but also as a function of the accelerations and of the velocities. The approach proposed belongs to this line of thought and rests on the factorisation of the polynomial part \widehat{P}(s) of the impedance: \widehat{Z}(s)={\widehat{Z}}_{m}(s)\widehat{P}(s)={\widehat{Z}}_{m}(s)({\tilde{M}}_{\Gamma}{s}^{2}+{\tilde{C}}_{\Gamma}s+{\tilde{K}}_{\Gamma}) Where {\tilde{K}}_{\Gamma} , {\tilde{C}}_{\Gamma} and {\tilde{M}}_{\Gamma} are respectively estimators of the stiffness, damping and inertia matrices of the soil. Thus, the convolution can be written by means of the inverse Laplace transform as follows: (Z\ast {u}_{\Gamma})(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}{\int}_{{\sigma}_{0}+iR}{\widehat{Z}}_{m}(s)\widehat{P}(s){\widehat{u}}_{\Gamma}(s){e}^{st}\mathit{ds} Consequently, the polynomial function \widehat{P}(s) being seen as a differentiation operator that acts on the displacement field, equation () becomes: (Z\ast {u}_{\Gamma})(t)=({Z}_{m}\ast {\tilde{M}}_{\Gamma}{\ddot{u}}_{\Gamma})(t)+({Z}_{m}\ast {\tilde{C}}_{\Gamma}{\dot{u}}_{\Gamma})(t)+({Z}_{m}\ast {\tilde{K}}_{\Gamma}{u}_{\Gamma})(t) where the interaction forces (denoted in what follows by {R}_{\Gamma}(t) ) are computed by convolutions with the accelerations, velocities and displacements of the interface. Taking a discretisation time step \Delta t>0 , the convolution integral becomes a particular case of equation () for m=2 : {R}_{n}=(Z\ast {u}_{\Gamma})(n\Delta t)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}({\Psi}_{2}^{n-k+1}{\ddot{u}}_{\Gamma ,k}+{\Psi}_{1}^{n-k+1}{\dot{u}}_{\Gamma ,k}+{\Psi}_{0}^{n-k+1}{u}_{\Gamma ,k}) where the matrices multiplying the displacement, velocity and acceleration vectors are given by: {\Psi}_{0}^{k}={Z}_{m}^{k}{\tilde{K}}_{\Gamma} {\Psi}_{1}^{k}={Z}_{m}^{k}{\tilde{C}}_{\Gamma} Indeed, in a manner analogous to the reasoning followed for equations () and (), the coefficients of the matrices {\Psi}_{0}^{k} , {\Psi}_{1}^{k} and {\Psi}_{2}^{k} correspond to the weights of the following power series: \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty }{\Psi}_{j}^{k}{z}^{k}={\widehat{Z}}_{m}({s}_{\Delta t}){\Lambda}_{j} With {\Lambda}_{0}={\tilde{K}}_{\Gamma} , {\Lambda}_{1}={\tilde{C}}_{\Gamma} and {\Lambda}_{2}={\tilde{M}}_{\Gamma} . To simplify the theoretical development, all the quantities already discretised in space (for example, with a finite-element method) are considered in what follows. 3 Computation of the impedance in time As mentioned previously, the Laplace–Time method is a numerical approach making it possible to discretise a convolution integral in time. 3.1 Implementation in code_aster Equation () shows that the numerical evaluation of the weights {\Psi}_{k}^{j} first proceeds by that of {\widehat{Z}}_{m}^{k} . In turn, the latter can be obtained from a Cauchy integral applied on a contour |z|=\rho : | :math:{Z}_{m}(kDelta t)=frac{1}{2pi i}{int}_{ | z | =rho }{widehat{Z}}_{m}left(frac{delta (z)}{Delta t}right){z}^{-k-1}dz | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | If this integral is expressed in polar coordinates z=\rho {e}^{i\theta } , then the trapezoidal rule is applied to the phase in order to discretise it in L identical steps of value \Delta \theta =\frac{2\pi }{L} , one obtains: {Z}_{m}(k∆t)\approx {Z}_{m}^{k}=\frac{{\rho}^{-k}}{L}\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}{\widehat{Z}}_{m}({s}_{l}){e}^{-i\frac{2\pi l}{L}k} where the operator defined in the Laplace domain is sampled on {s}_{l}=\frac{\delta (\rho {e}^{2\pi il∕L})}{\Delta t} with \delta (z)=\frac{3}{2}-2z+\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2} the characteristic polynomial of a second-order linear multistep method. Note that N and L are not necessarily equal, N being the number of time steps of the time window of interest (for example, as a function of the duration of the seismic signal) and L being the number of time steps of the computation of the impedance in time. If it is considered that {\widehat{Z}}_{m}({s}_{l}) is evaluated with a variability 2 {ϵ}_{\mathit{CQM}} , the coefficients {\widehat{Z}}_{m}^{k} will be computed with an accuracy 3 O(\sqrt{{ϵ}_{\mathit{CQM}}}) if L=N and {\rho}^{N}=\sqrt{{ϵ}_{\mathit{CQM}}} . With the values of L and \rho fixed, the weights of the series can be obtained from a classical FFT, which brings the complexity of the computation algorithm down to O(L\logL) instead of O({L}^{2}) . Nevertheless, the value of {ϵ}_{\mathit{CQM}} is not obvious to calibrate and depends in part on the nature of the problem to be solved. Indeed, values of {ϵ}_{\mathit{CQM}} that are too small, such as {10}^{-20} or {10}^{-30} , can lead to integration radii \mid z\mid =\rho that are too small. Since the Cauchy integrand contains a singularity at zero, values of the radius that are too small can result in a poor evaluation of the integral. In this respect, parametric studies have been carried out in in order to conclude that a good compromise is reached when {ϵ}_{\mathit{CQM}}={10}^{-10} 4 . Likewise, it will be noted that the dependence on {\rho}^{-k} leads, for large values of k , to inaccuracies on the coefficients {\widehat{Z}}_{m}^{k} computed. Knowing that the use of more accurate integration methods, of Simpson type for example, does not correct this problem, the idea is to widen the time range (i.e. L=\mathit{mN},m\in \mathrm{ℝ} ) over which the impedance is computed, in order to reduce the perturbations on the solution of interest. In this respect, it has been observed that, in general, the inaccuracies of {\widehat{Z}}_{m}^{k} propagate onto the response only beyond t\approx 0,7{T}_{\mathit{FIN}} , where {T}_{\mathit{FIN}} is the final time instant of the impedance computation 5 . 3.2 Main numerical considerations It has been seen previously that, in general, the singular part of the soil impedance can be approximated by a polynomial of order two. If the coefficients of this polynomial are real, it is easy to show that the soil impedance satisfies \widehat{Z}(\sigma -i\omega )=\mathit{conj}[\widehat{Z}(\sigma +i\omega )] in the analytic plane of the Laplace domain 6 . It will be noted that when a hysteretic damping is used in the soil (the case of MISS3D), the imaginary part of its static stiffness is non-zero and the assumption of real coefficients is no longer satisfied. A second interesting property, coming directly from the definition of the one-sided Laplace transform, is the following: \widehat{Z}(s=0)={\int}_{0}^{ꝏ}Z(t)\mathit{dt}\approx \sum_{k}^{N}Z(k\Delta t) for N chosen sufficiently large (~ a hundred time steps). Note that the soil impedance evaluated at s=0 corresponds to the static stiffness of the soil (real part), which is very different from the instantaneous stiffness of the soil. This must be well taken into account when a dynamic analysis ( Z(t=0)] is assembled on the left-hand side) is carried out following a static analysis ( \mathrm{\Re }[\widehat{Z}(s=0)] is assembled on the left-hand side) . To do this, CALC_MISS (TYPE_RESU = 'FICHIER_TEMPS') provides the keyword COEF_SURECH (cf. U7.03.12) initialised to 1.35, that is the equivalent of faire:math:L=mathrm{1.35N} in equation 23. This property is exploited in code_aster: the impedance is sampled on the upper half-plane, then completed numerically with the conjugate. Consequently, care must be taken with soils presenting very strong hysteretic dampings (greater than 25%). There exists in code_aster a macro-command (PRE_SEISME_NONL, cf. U4.63.02) making it possible to carry out the static–dynamic transition of a non-linear soil–structure interaction analysis. 4 Seismic analysis The seismic analysis of non-linear soil–structure interaction must be solved in the time domain. A few elements on the computation of the seismic force and the time discretisation of the equations of the coupled system are supplied below. 4.1 Computation of the seismic force in time The Laplace–Time method could also be applied for the computation of the seismic force; nevertheless the nature of the incident field developed in MISS3D invalidates the assumptions on the solution fields sought in the Laplace domain. In this framework, it cannot be guaranteed that the computation of the seismic force at complex frequency with MISS3D is correct for every type of foundation (surface and embedded) and stratigraphy. The approach recommended in the studies thus proceeds by the inverse Fourier transform of the seismic force evaluated by MISS3D in the frequency domain. 4.2 Time-integration scheme This part seeks to illustrate the numerical treatment of the convolution integral within the framework of a solution with a time-integration scheme of the Newmark family. Nevertheless, the reasoning also applies to the \alpha -HHT time-integration scheme, also available in code_aster. One will thus seek to solve in time the following linear dynamic problem, assumed discretised in space with the classical finite-element method: \left[\begin{array}{cc}{L}_{bb}(\cdot )& {L}_{b\Gamma }(\cdot )\\ (sym.)& {L}_{\Gamma \Gamma }(\cdot )\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}{u}_{b}(t)\\ {u}_{\Gamma}(t)\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ {R}_{\Gamma}(t)\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}{F}_{b}(t)\\ {F}_{\Gamma}(t)\end{array}\right] where a time differentiation operator {L}_{\mathit{\alpha \beta }}(\cdot ) is introduced for \alpha ,\beta \in \lbrace b,\Gamma \rbrace , \Gamma for the degrees of freedom of the interface as opposed to the rest of the degrees of freedom of the system, denoted b , and where the vector of soil–structure interaction forces, denoted {R}_{\Gamma}(t) , corresponds to the convolution integral that will be discretised with the Laplace–Time method. The solution of the coupled soil–structure system proceeds by the discretisation of all the quantities in time and by isolating the unknowns at the time instant t=n\Delta t , where the time step is denoted \Delta t . In particular, for the soil–structure interaction forces, it is interesting to start from equation () and to group the non-unknown terms corresponding to the time instants preceding t=n\Delta t into a single term, in order to separate them from the unknowns to be solved at time step n . The corresponding vector {R}_{n}\approx {R}_{\Gamma}(n\Delta t) is thus written as follows: {R}_{n}={\Psi}_{2}^{1}{\ddot{u}}_{\Gamma ,n}+{\Psi}_{1}^{1}{\dot{u}}_{\Gamma ,n}+{\Psi}_{0}^{1}{u}_{\Gamma ,n}+{R}_{\Sigma (n-1)} With {\Psi}_{0}^{1} , {\Psi}_{1}^{1} and {\Psi}_{2}^{1} referring respectively to the instantaneous stiffness, damping and inertia and {R}_{\Sigma (n-1)} depending only on the quantities computed at the previous time instants : {R}_{\Sigma (n-1)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}({\Psi}_{2}^{n-k+1}{\ddot{u}}_{\Gamma ,k}+{\Psi}_{1}^{n-k+1}{\dot{u}}_{\Gamma ,k}+{\Psi}_{0}^{n-k+1}{u}_{\Gamma ,k}) This grouping of terms makes it possible to introduce on the right-hand side the part of the convolution coming from the previous time instants, and on the left-hand side the terms bearing on unknowns. Indeed, this can easily be brought out by starting from a displacement formulation of an unconditionally stable Newmark integration scheme ( \beta =0.25 , \gamma =0.5 ) applied to equation (): \left[\begin{array}{cc}{\tilde{K}}_{11}& {\tilde{K}}_{12}\\ {\tilde{K}}_{21}& {\tilde{K}}_{22}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}{u}_{b,n}\\ {u}_{\Gamma ,n}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}{F}_{b,n}\\ {F}_{\Gamma ,n}\end{array}\right]-\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ {R}_{\Sigma (n-1)}\end{array}\right] where the matrix \tilde{K} corresponds to the Newmark operator that will have to be inverted at each time step, and the right-hand side to the sum of the equivalent Newmark vector and the known part of the discrete convolution product. In particular, the term \tilde{{K}_{22}} , which applies to the degrees of freedom of the interface \Gamma , is written: {\tilde{K}}_{22}=\frac{1}{\beta \Delta {t}^{2}}({M}_{22}+{\Psi}_{2}^{1})+\frac{\gamma}{\beta \Delta t}({C}_{22}+{\Psi}_{1}^{1})+({K}_{22}+{\Psi}_{0}^{1}) It will be noted that the terms {\Psi}_{0}^{1} , {\Psi}_{1}^{1} and {\Psi}_{2}^{1} play a role in the conditioning of the Newmark operator \tilde{K} and, consequently, their value has an impact on the convergence of the solution. Note also that \tilde{{K}_{22}} , remaining constant during the analysis, is computed only once. In code_aster, these instantaneous terms are assembled on the left-hand side via the operator MACR_ELEM_DYNA (cf. U4.65.01) and possibly a connection LIAISON_INTERF in the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA (cf. U4.44.01) if a reduced modal basis of the interface has been used. The term:math:{R}_{Sigma (n-1)} is modelled in code_aster during the non-linear dynamic analysis as a right-hand-side load obtained with the option “CHARGE_SOL” of the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA (cf. r4.05.08 Method for taking into account the Floor–Equipment interaction r4.05.08 Method for taking into account the Floor–Equipment interaction Summary: In seismic studies, one is often led to produce floor spectra for buildings in which the equipment is modelled by masses added to the floor. These additional masses affect the floor spectra. The method proposed here makes it possible to modify the floor spectra by taking into account the interaction of the masses and of the floor. 1 Introduction of the IPM method The problem of taking into account the dynamic coupling between the primary and secondary structures in the preparation of the vertical floor spectra is an important point of the dynamic study of the structure. On certain floor strips, equipment is sometimes installed whose total mass relative to that of the floor strip may reach a few percent, or even a few tens of percent. Now, the interaction between this equipment and the floor strip will in general tend to attenuate the amplifications observed, especially when there is coincidence between the frequency of the floor and the natural frequencies of the equipment installed on it. The investigations carried out in this respect have shown that the equipment/structure mass ratios were liable, in certain cases, to generate a dynamic coupling, described as Floor–Equipment Interaction, and having as its principal effect, when the natural frequencies of the equipment are close to those of the support, that of modifying the dynamic behaviour of the floor relative to the "rigid" case. This document forms part of an intention to produce realistic floor spectra taking into account the effects of dynamic coupling, as prescribed by the ASN guides ([1]). 1.1 Method The equipment–floor interaction rests on the principle that a heavy item of equipment placed on a floor modifies the behaviour of the floor. Simplifying assumptions are adopted for the modelling of the floor and of the equipment. Both will be represented by 1D oscillators in the vertical direction. The procedure described in this note leads to the construction of floor spectra corrected by the IPM. These floor spectra are obtained from the raw vertical accelerograms (that is to say, not taking the IPM into account) coming from a prior transient seismic analysis. 1.2 Taking account of the equipment in the modelling Before any modelling of a building, thought must be given to the taking into account of the equipment in the mass balance. Three rules may be set out concerning the taking into account of the equipment (or secondary structures) in the modelling [1]: - Small items of equipment (a few hundred kilograms) are not taken into account. They are in fact covered by the conventional live load on the floors; - If the mass of the equipment is small (see Figure 1) relative to that of its support, its dynamic behaviour has little influence on the dynamic behaviour of the supporting structure. One is content to represent this equipment by added masses in the building model; - For elements of significant mass having a sufficiently flexible support, the question then arises of the dynamic coupling between the structure and the equipment attached to it. To summarise, when an item of equipment is assumed to be uncoupled from the floor, its mass is simply taken into account in the floor model as a distributed or localised added mass. On the other hand, when an item of equipment is assumed to be coupled, it is necessary to take the equipment into account in the global model in order to characterise the coupling phenomena. A modal analysis of the equipment placed on the floor panel must be carried out; the principal modes must be extracted from it. The items of equipment are then represented in the global model as simple oscillators . However, it sometimes happens that certain items of equipment have been taken into account as an added mass without any stiffness being attached to them, because their relatively low mass, taken individually, did not justify it, or when the dynamic coupling of an item of equipment had been judged not significant by the modellers . The purpose of this method is to correct this shortcoming in the upstream modelling by an a posteriori taking into account of the dynamic coupling between the primary structures and the equipment. The equipment concerned may consist of a sum of small items of equipment whose total mass and modal characteristics satisfy the criterion set out in Figure 1 (for example: a row of electrical cabinets), or of a single item of equipment satisfying this same criterion in mass and in frequencies Figure 1: Coupling/uncoupling criteria [2] 2 Development of the method 2.1 Principles of the method The method proposed rests on the simple assumption that the response of the floor without Floor–Equipment Interaction (IPM) may be likened to the response of a 1D oscillator of frequency {f}_{1} , of mass {m}_{1}+{m}_{2} and of damping {\xi}_{1} (see Figure 2), where we have defined {m}_{1} as being the mass of the floor and {m}_{2} the mass of the equipment. It is the bending mode of the floor panels which is taken into account by the one-dimensional modelling of the floor. We furthermore consider that the modal mass mobilised by the bending mode is the total mass of the floor, which is a conservative assumption. The response of the floor without IPM amounts to considering that the equipment of mass {m}_{2} is rigidly linked to the floor. The equipment, for its part, is characterised by a set of 1D oscillators of variable frequencies and masses. We indeed assume that the heavy equipment placed on the floor possesses several natural frequencies in the vertical direction. The modal characteristics of the equipment (frequencies and participating masses) are to be determined by the user upstream of the analysis. These data may be found in the qualification notes or the design notes. A finite-element analysis may also supply this type of information. Each of the mechanical characteristics of the oscillators representing the equipment will bear the index i in the remainder of this document. From the mass {m}_{2} of the equipment and the mass {m}_{1} of the floor, one defines the mass ratio \lambda ={m}_{2}/{m}_{1} . The method used to obtain the corrected floor spectra rests on the following principle: - The accelerogram coming from the response analyses of the building and of the floors characterises the motion of the mass {m}_{1}+{m}_{2} in model A (see Figure 2); - The corrected accelerogram taking the IPM into account is computed by considering that the equipment is characterised by a series of simple oscillators; - From the corrected accelerogram, corrected floor spectra are computed for different values of the percentage of critical damping. For the computation of the corrected accelerogram, we employ a frequency-domain method based on the use of transfer functions. This method therefore assumes the computation of the Fourier transform of the initial accelerogram (or raw accelerogram). An inverse Fourier transform computation makes it possible to find the corrected accelerogram after having multiplied the FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) of the initial accelerogram by the transfer function between the motion of the mass {m}_{1} in model A and in model B. Figure 2: Descriptions of the models We define the following notations: - {\omega}_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{{k}_{1}}{{m}_{1}+{m}_{2}}} - {f}_{1}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{{k}_{1}}{{m}_{1}+{m}_{2}}} - {C}_{1} denotes the damping coefficient - {\xi}_{1}=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2({m}_{1}+{m}_{2}){\omega}_{1}} - {f}_{1}^{\ast }={f}_{1}\sqrt{1+\lambda } - {\xi}_{1}^{\mathrm{\ast }}={\xi}_{1}\sqrt{1+\lambda } - \lambda =\frac{{m}_{2}}{{m}_{1}} - {f}_{i}\in 0,40\mathit{Hz} - {m}_{i}={\alpha}_{i}{m}_{2} - {\Sigma}_{i}{\alpha}_{i}=1 - {\lambda}_{i}={\alpha}_{i}\lambda In these notations, we have denoted by {\alpha}_{i} the unit effective masses associated with each mode of the heavy equipment and by {\lambda}_{i} the mass ratio associated with each of these modes. We shall denote by N the total number of oscillators constituting the equipment placed on the floor. In model A, the oscillator has a mass {m}_{2}+{m}_{1} because we consider that the raw accelerogram, computed during a prior transient analysis, takes the added masses into account. This therefore assumes that the finite-element model of the floor incorporates the added masses of the heavy equipment. The analyses necessary for the modification of the floor spectra proceed in the following manner: - Identification of the parameters (frequency {f}_{1} and damping {\xi}_{1} of the support; dampings {\xi}_{i} of the heavy equipment, mass ratio \lambda , unit effective masses {\alpha}_{i} and frequencies {\lambda}_{i} ); - Reading of the accelerogram at the point of the floor under study \ddot{x}(t) ; - Fourier transform of the accelerogram, \hat{\ddot{x}}(\omega ) ; - Computation of the transfer function between the motion of the mass {m}_{1} in model A and in model B (see Figure 2), H(\omega ) ; - Product \hat{\ddot{x}}(\omega )H(\omega ) ; - Inverse Fourier transform, \ddot{y}(t) ; - Computation of the spectrum associated with \ddot{y}(t) at the desired damping \xi . We obtain, after the analyses, a series of spectra at the desired damping values. These spectra constitute the corrected floor spectra to be included in the collections of spectra. The analysis may be carried out for several points of the floor. 2.2 Computation of the transfer functions In this section, we propose to develop the equations leading to the correction of the floor spectra by the IPM. The transfer function between the points P of models A and B, see Figure 2 and Figure 3, is equal to the transfer function between the base and point P in model B divided by the transfer function between the base and point P in model A. 2.2.1 Transfer function for model B Below, the equations of motion for an excitation {\ddot{x}}_{b} at the base of model B:
