r4.06.02 Modal analysis by classical dynamic substructuring r4.06.02 Modal analysis by classical dynamic substructuring Summary: This report presents the theoretical bases of the methods of analysis by modal synthesis. We begin with the description of the RITZ transformation and of the methods of modal recombination which follow from it. Then, we present the modal synthesis which uses the classical techniques of substructuring and of modal recombination. We present, first of all, the techniques of classical dynamic substructuring of CRAIG-BAMPTON and of MAC-NEAL. The analysis tools by modal synthesis implemented in Code_Aster are then reviewed. One will detail the modal analysis by substructuring, then the harmonic response analysis and finally the time response analysis. One then presents the dynamic condensation by dynamic macro-elements in static substructuring. The last section of this document presents the principle of the computation of the force residual, making it possible to assess the quality of a reduced model for a given analysis. One also details the methodology developed for the quality indicator for the modal analysis for the generalised models. 1 Introduction Faced with the complexity of mechanical structures, often made up of an assembly of several components, the classical numerical or experimental methods of vibration mechanics prove costly, sometimes even unusable. In perfect consistency with the modular organisation of large projects, the substructuring methods appear as the most efficient means of carrying out the vibration study of the whole from the dynamic behaviour of the components [bib4]. In this report, we present, first of all, the theoretical bases of the methods of modal synthesis. They combine techniques of substructuring and of modal recombination. Each substructure is represented by a projection basis composed of dynamic eigenmodes and of static deflected shapes at the interfaces. Then, we present the two techniques of analysis by classical substructuring, implemented in Code_Aster [bib5]: the methods of Craig-Bampton, of Mac Neal and of interface modes. They are distinguished essentially by the use of different bases for the substructures. The specific case of the modal analysis of structures with cyclic symmetries by dynamic substructuring is addressed in the document R4.06.03. General notations: | {\omega}_{m} | : | Maximum angular frequency of a system ( {\mathrm{rad.s}}^{-1} ), | | --- | --- | --- | | \mathrm{nit} | : | Mass matrix arising from the finite-element modelling, | | K | : | Stiffness matrix arising from the finite-element modelling, | | \mathrm{q},\dot{\mathrm{q}},\ddot{\mathrm{q}} | : | Vector of the displacements, velocities and accelerations arising from the finite-element modelling, | | {\mathrm{f}}_{\mathit{ext}} | : | Vector of the forces external to the system, | | {f}_{L} | : | Vector of the connection forces applied to a substructure, | | \Phi | : | Matrix containing the vectors of a projection basis arranged in columns, | | B | : | Extraction matrix of the interface degrees of freedom, | | L | : | Connection matrix, | | T | : | Kinetic energy, | | U | : | Strain energy, | | \mathrm{Id} | : | Identity matrix, | | \lambda | : | Diagonal matrix of the generalised stiffnesses associated with the normal modes, | | {\mathrm{R}}_{e}(\omega ) | : | Residual dynamic flexibility matrix, | | {\mathrm{R}}_{e}(0) | : | Residual static flexibility matrix. | | \bar{\mathrm{M}}={\varphi}^{T}\mathrm{M}\varphi | : | is the generalised mass matrix, | | --- | --- | --- | | \bar{\mathrm{C}}={\varphi}^{T}\mathrm{C}\varphi | : | is the generalised damping matrix, | | \bar{\mathrm{K}}={\varphi}^{T}\mathrm{K}\varphi | : | is the generalised stiffness matrix, | | {\lbrace {\bar{f}}_{\text{ext}}\rbrace }_{o}={\Phi}^{T}{\lbrace {f}_{\text{ext}}\rbrace }_{o} | : | is the vector of the generalised external forces applied | | {\lbrace {\bar{f}}_{L}\rbrace }_{o}={\Phi}^{T}{\lbrace {f}_{L}\rbrace }_{o} | : | is the vector of the generalised connection forces applied, | | \eta ,\dot{\eta},\ddot{\eta} | : | is the vector of the generalised displacements, velocities and accelerations. | Note: The exponent k characterises the quantities relative to the substructure {S}^{k} and the generalised quantities are surmounted by a bar: for example {\bar{M}}^{k} is the generalised mass matrix of the substructure {S}^{k} . 2 Modal synthesis Dynamic substructuring consists in determining the behaviour of a structure from the vibration characteristics of each of its components ([bib3] and [bib4]). The methods implemented in Code_Aster use simultaneously the classical techniques of modal recombination and of dynamic substructuring. These methods, although different from that of the finite elements, adopt a procedure that is appreciably comparable but nevertheless introduce an additional approximation. They bring out three essential steps: Step 1: numerical study of each component by the determination of their vibration characteristics. The work consists in identifying eigenmodes and static deflected shapes by classical techniques of vibration mechanics. If one assimilates each substructure to a super-element, this step is similar to the elementary computation. Step 2: connection of the substructures. One uses the vibration characteristics determined previously for each component, and one takes into account the way they are connected. This work constitutes the substructuring step proper. It is akin to an assembly. Step 3: the solution and a recovery phase make it possible to obtain the sought solution in the physical frame of the global structure. 2.1 RITZ transformation The RITZ transformation is the subject of the reference documentation R5.06.01. We recall here its principle. For the problem of the numerical determination of the real eigenmodes of the undamped system associated with the structure, which we shall designate by eigenmodes , one reduces the matter to the solution of the following minimisation problem: Let \delta be a virtual displacement, one seeks: {\mathit{Min}}_{\delta}\frac{1}{2}{\delta}^{T}.(\mathrm{K}-{\omega}^{2}\mathrm{M}).\delta whose solution q satisfies: (K-\omega \mathrm{²}M).q=0 The RITZ method consists in seeking the solution of the preceding minimisation equation on a subspace of the space of the solutions. Consider the matrix containing the vectors of the basis of the subspace in question, arranged in columns. Restricted to this space of reduced dimension, the minimisation equation takes the following form: {\mathrm{Min}}_{p=\Phi \delta }\frac{1}{2}{p}^{T}.(K-{\omega}^{2}M).p That is, the sought solution: q=\Phi \eta which satisfies: (\bar{K}-\omega \mathrm{²}\bar{M})\eta =0 where \eta is the vector of the generalised displacements, \bar{K}={\Phi}^{T}K\Phi and \bar{M}={\Phi}^{T}M\Phi are called respectively generalised stiffness and mass matrices. After having solved the system, the obtaining of the eigenmodes in the physical basis is done by means of the relation. The RITZ transformation therefore makes it possible to replace the initial eigenvalue problem by a problem of the same nature, but of reduced dimension. The new generalised stiffness and mass matrices remain symmetric. However, this transformation must be used with caution. Indeed, the new basis being incomplete, an approximation is made at the level of the projection: one speaks of modal truncation. The accuracy of the final result then depends on the choice of the basis vectors and the relative error due to this reduction in the number of unknowns must be estimated. 2.2 Modal recombination A classical use of the RITZ transformation is the dynamic analysis by modal recombination. It is commonly used for the computation of the response of a structure to a low-frequency excitation. We shall limit ourselves here to the computation of the response to an excitation of a conservative structure. In this case, the finite-element method allows us to reduce the matter to the following matrix differential equation: \mathrm{M}\ddot{\mathrm{q}}+\mathrm{K}\mathrm{q}={\mathrm{f}}_{\mathit{ext}} If one applies the RITZ transformation, with as incomplete projection basis the first eigenmodes of the structure, the relation becomes: \bar{M}\ddot{\eta}+\bar{K}\eta ={\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}} where {\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}={\Phi}^{T}{f}_{\mathrm{ext}} is the vector of the generalised forces. The eigenmodes are orthogonal with respect to the mass and stiffness matrices. The differential equation therefore brings out diagonal matrices: the system is then constituted of uncoupled equations. Each of them is the equation of a single-degree-of-freedom oscillator of mass-spring type which brings out the generalised mass, stiffness and force relative to the mode j (respectively: {m}_{j} , {k}_{j} , {f}_{j} ), see Figure-a. If one considers the RITZ transformation [eq ], at the level of one degree of freedom, one has: {q}_{i}=\underset{j}{\Sigma}{\Phi}_{ij}{\eta}_{j} where: {q}_{i} is the i th coordinate of the vector q , {\eta}_{j} is the j th coordinate of the vector \eta , {\Phi}_{ij} is the component of the i th row and of the j th column of the matrix \Phi . It therefore appears that the response of the structure is expressed as the weighted recombination of responses of uncoupled single-degree-of-freedom oscillators. The RITZ transformation makes it possible, in this case, to define an equivalent scheme of the structure, which brings out the single-degree-of-freedom oscillators associated with the identified eigenmodes. Their stiffness and their mass are the generalised stiffnesses ( {k}_{j} ) and the generalised masses ( {m}_{j} ) of the corresponding modes. Figure -a: Principle of the dynamic analysis by modal recombination. Reserved essentially for studies that one improperly qualifies as low-frequency 1 , modal recombination consists in using the orthogonality properties of the eigenmodes of a structure in order to simplify the study of its vibration response. Besides the advantage of reducing the order of the numerical problem to be solved, the RITZ transformation on a modal basis, in this case, also makes it possible to uncouple the differential equations and to bring out a physical interpretation of the result obtained. Depending on the excitation frequency, one will use a modal basis that is more or less truncated. One must however estimate the truncation error in order to ensure the validity of the result. 2.3 Modal synthesis In a general way, the methods of modal synthesis consist in using simultaneously the dynamic substructuring (splitting into substructures) and the modal recombination at the level of each substructure. Often confused, by an abuse of language, with dynamic substructuring, modal synthesis is only a particular case of the latter. Dynamic substructuring consists in considering the displacement of a substructure in the overall motion, as its response to the connection forces which link it to the other components and to the external forces which are applied to it. Modal synthesis means that one computes this motion, at the level of each substructure, by modal recombination. One therefore uses a projection basis which characterises each substructure. Indeed, if the global structure is too large to be subjected to a modal analysis, the dimensions of the substructures make it possible to carry out this work. Modal synthesis requires that one first study each component separately, in order to determine their projection basis. In the remainder of this chapter, we present the types of modes and static deflected shapes used in the methods of modal synthesis with the aid of the following simple example: Figure -a : Principle of dynamic substructuring. The vector of the degrees of freedom of the substructure is characterised by an exponent which defines the number of the substructure, and an index which makes it possible to distinguish the internal degrees of freedom (index i ), from the boundary degrees of freedom (index j ). {q}^{k}=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{q}_{i}^{k}\\ {q}_{j}^{k}\end{array}\right\rbrace One is led, in order to study the substructure k , to define an impedance at the level of the connection degrees of freedom. Within the framework of the developments carried out in Code_Aster , it is either zero or infinite. The basis vectors used in the methods implemented in Code_Aster are: - the normal modes, - the constraint modes, - the attachment modes, - the interface modes, which one defines below. 2.3.1 The normal modes The eigenmodes or normal modes are advantageously used as a projection basis of the substructures for several reasons: - they can be computed and/or obtained experimentally, - they offer interesting orthogonality properties with respect to the mass and stiffness matrices of the substructure, - they are associated with natural frequencies of the structure. They can be of two types according to the condition given at the connection interfaces, cf. Figures-b and -c: - eigenmodes with fixed interfaces, - eigenmodes with free interfaces. Figure -b: Eigenmodes with fixed interfaces. Figure -c: Eigenmodes with free interfaces. Let us note that in the case of a free substructure, the existing rigid-body modes (or overall modes) form part of the transformation basis. 2.3.2 The static deflected shapes One defines an interface mode for each connection degree of freedom of each substructure. Depending on the cases, these may be constraint modes or attachment modes. The constraint modes are static deflected shapes which one joins to the normal modes with fixed interfaces in order to correct the effects due to their boundary conditions. A constraint mode is defined by the static deflected shape obtained by imposing a unit displacement on one connection degree of freedom, the other connection degrees of freedom being fixed. Figure -d: Constraint modes. The attachment modes are static deflected shapes which one joins to the normal modes with free interfaces in order to reduce the effect of the modal truncation. An attachment mode is defined by the static deflected shape obtained by imposing a unit force on one connection degree of freedom, the other connection degrees of freedom being free. Figure -e: Attachment modes. In the case of a substructure possessing rigid-body modes (here, substructure 2), its stiffness matrix is no longer invertible and it is not possible to compute its attachment modes. It is then necessary to fix certain degrees of freedom in order to make the structure isostatic, or even hyperstatic. 2.3.3 The harmonic deflected shapes A third projection basis has been introduced within the framework of the developments concerning the computation of the harmonic response by classical dynamic substructuring. It is the harmonic Craig-Bampton basis. The harmonic Craig-Bampton basis is constituted of eigenmodes with fixed interfaces and of harmonic constraint modes [bib8]. The latter are joined to the normal modes with fixed interfaces in order to correct the effects due to their boundary conditions. A harmonic constraint mode is defined by the response of the undamped substructure to a harmonic displacement, of unit amplitude and of given frequency, imposed on one connection degree of freedom, the other connection degrees of freedom being fixed. Figure -f: Harmonic constraint modes. This modal basis is more particularly suited to fluid-structure interaction problems, for which the static loadings are not applicable in Code_Aster (the added-mass effect is not taken into account). It can be used for any type of analysis (modal, harmonic and transient). 2.3.4 The reduced interface deflected shapes or “coupling modes” One defines an interface mode for the whole set of the connection degrees of freedom of each substructure. The interface modes are dynamic deflected shapes which one joins to the normal modes with fixed or free interfaces in order to correct the effects due to their boundary conditions. Concretely, the computation of the constraint modes consists in carrying out a condensation of the behaviour of the structure onto the interface degrees of freedom and thus in building an interface operator (Schur complement) which expresses the behaviour of the structure reduced to the interface. By a spectral analysis, one can then represent the deformations of the interface by linear combination of the eigenmodes of this interface operator. Figure -g: Interface mode. 2.4 Connection conditions between substructures 2.4.1 Introduction Consider the problem of two substructures {S}^{1} and {S}^{2} connected in a rigid manner and not subjected to external forces. For the motion of the complete structure to be continuous, one must impose the equality of the displacements of the two components at the interface and the action-reaction law: \forall M\in {S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}{{\mathrm{q}}_{i}^{k}u}^{1}(M)={{\mathrm{q}}_{i}^{k}u}^{2}(M)\text{et}{\mathrm{f}}_{L}^{1}(M)=-{\mathrm{f}}_{L}^{2}(M) where: {u}^{1}(M) represents the displacement field of the substructure {S}^{1} , {u}^{2}(M) represents the displacement field of the substructure {S}^{2} , {f}_{L}^{1}(M) represents the field of the connection forces applied to the substructure {S}^{1} , {f}_{L}^{2}(M) represents the field of the connection forces applied to the substructure {S}^{2} . Depending on the nature of the meshes at the interface, the preceding problem can be discretised differently. 2.4.2 Case of the compatible interface mesh In this part, we limit ourselves to the case of compatible meshes. This means that they satisfy the following properties: - the restriction of the mesh of each of the substructures {S}^{1} and {S}^{2} to the interface rests strictly on the same nodes at their intersection, - the finite elements associated with these connection mesh cells are of the same nature (linear, quadratic) on either side of the boundary. From then on, the condition [eq ] is strictly equivalent to the formulation below: {q}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{1}={q}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{1}\text{et}{f}_{{L}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}}^{1}=-{f}_{{L}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}}^{2} where: | {q}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{k} | is the vector of the degrees of freedom at the nodes of the interface {S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2} of the substructure k , | | --- | --- | | {f}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{k} | is the vector of the connection forces at the nodes of the interface {S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2} of the substructure k . | Indeed, the meshes of the two substructures and coinciding on the interface, the shape functions associated with the finite elements are the same at the interface. It is therefore sufficient to impose the equality at the nodes of the connection interfaces of each substructure in order to impose the equality over the whole connection domain. Let us introduce the extraction matrices of the interface degrees of freedom {B}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{k} : {q}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{k}={B}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{k}{q}^{k} By using the projection equation, the displacement continuity condition [eq ] and the formulation above applied to the two substructures, one obtains: {B}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{1}{\Phi}^{1}{\eta}^{1}={B}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{k}{\Phi}^{1}{\eta}^{1} That is: {L}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{1}{\eta}^{1}={L}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{2}{\eta}^{2}\text{avec}{L}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{k}={B}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{k}{\phi }^{k} where: {L}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{1} is the connection matrix of {S}^{1} associated with the interface {S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2} , it expresses the continuity of displacement between the two substructures from the generalised displacements at the interface, {L}_{{S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2}}^{2} is the connection matrix of {S}^{2} associated with the interface {S}^{1}\cap {S}^{2} . In the case of the eigenvalue problem of the global structure, equipped with its boundary conditions, one can write: \begin{array}{c}(\bar{K}-\omega \mathrm{²}\bar{M})\eta +{L}^{T}\lambda =0\\ L\eta =0\end{array} The generalised mass and stiffness matrices, the vector of the generalised degrees of freedom and the connection matrix which appear here, are defined on the global structure. They take a particular form for each method (Craig-Bampton, MacNeal, …) which will be made explicit later. The vector of the Lagrange multipliers \lambda is interpreted as the connection actions to which the interfaces are subjected. It is therefore a classical eigenvalue-search problem, with which a linear constraint equation is associated. In Code_Aster , this type of problem is solved by double dualisation of the boundary conditions [bib6]. Thus, one can show that this system is also the solution of the minimisation problem of the following functional, called the action integral : f={\int}_{a}^{b}F(\eta ,\dot{\eta},{\lambda}_{1}{\lambda}_{2})\cdot \mathrm{dt} where \mathrm{F}(\eta ,\dot{\eta},{\lambda}_{1}{\lambda}_{2})=\frac{1}{2}{\eta}^{T}\bar{\mathrm{K}}\eta +\frac{1}{2}\dot{\eta}\bar{\mathrm{M}}\dot{\eta}+{({\lambda}_{1}+{\lambda}_{2})}^{T}\mathrm{L}\eta -\frac{1}{2}{({\lambda}_{1}-{\lambda}_{2})}^{2} is the Hamiltonian. The variables of this functional are the generalised coordinates \eta , the associated velocities and the Lagrange multipliers {\lambda}_{1} and {\lambda}_{2} (in number equal to twice the number of connection equations). The last term of the functional imposes the equality of the Lagrange coefficients. The extremum is reached for the values of the variables which cancel the derivatives of f , whatever the real numbers a and b : -{\lambda}_{1}+L\eta +{\lambda}_{2}=0 {L}^{T}({\lambda}_{1}+{\lambda}_{2})+(\bar{K}-\omega \mathrm{²}\bar{M})\eta =0 {\lambda}_{1}+L\eta -{\lambda}_{2}=0 \left[\begin{array}{ccc}-\text{Id}& L& \text{Id}\\ {L}^{T}& \bar{K}& {L}^{T}\\ \text{Id}& L& -\text{Id}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\lambda}_{1}\\ \eta \\ {\lambda}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace -{\omega}^{2}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& 0& 0\\ 0& \bar{M}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\lambda}_{1}\\ \eta \\ {\lambda}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace The double dualisation therefore leads to a real symmetric matrix problem. One shows R3.03.01 that it makes it possible to render the matrix triangulation algorithms unconditionally stable. 2.4.3 Case of the incompatible interface mesh In this part, we consider the case of incompatible meshes. This means that they do not a priori satisfy the following properties: - the restriction of the mesh of each of the substructures {S}^{1} and {S}^{2} to the interface rests strictly on the same nodes at their intersection, - the finite elements associated with these connection mesh cells are of the same nature (linear, quadratic) on either side of the boundary. The method chosen to handle the mesh incompatibility is a method derived from that of the PPCM (“Plus Petit Maillage Commun”, least common mesh). This method is used within the framework of several types of problems in Code_Aster : handling of an incompatible mesh, projection of a field onto meshes of different natures… One therefore defines a “master” interface onto which one projects the nodes of the “slave” interface. The interpolation of the fields at the nodes of the slave interface (elements surrounded by {S}_{2} on the figure below) is done on the element of the master interface onto which each node is projected, with the aid of the shape functions of this element. Figure -a: One defines {\Sigma}_{e} as the interface restricted to one element and {n}_{e} the number of degrees of freedom of the element. By choosing the interface of the substructure {S}_{1} as master interface, the relation is rewritten: {u}^{1}(M)-\sum_{j=1}^{{n}_{e}}({\int}_{{\Sigma}_{e}}{E}_{j}^{2}(M)\xi (M)\text{dM}){q}_{j}^{2}=0 where \xi (M) are the shape functions of the element onto which the node is projected and {E}_{j}^{2} the restriction of the shape functions of the element j of the interface of {S}_{2} . This method makes it possible to couple substructures possessing meshes of different natures (linear with quadratic, …) and of different densities. One will however retain that the rule of good use consists in choosing as master the mesh of lowest density. Taking into account the conditions defined in the preceding paragraphs, the expression linking the degrees of freedom must be written again. Taking the interface of the substructure {S}_{1} as master interface, one has: {q}_{j}^{1}=\sum_{l}^{{n}_{e}}{\alpha}_{l}{q}_{l}^{2} Or again: {q}^{1}=A{q}^{2} where A is an observation matrix between the degrees of freedom of the two interfaces. The displacement continuity relations are expressed, with the generalised coordinates, by the following matrix relations: {L}_{j}^{1}{\eta}^{1}={\tilde{L}}_{j}^{2}{\eta}^{2} {\tilde{L}}_{j}^{k}=A{B}^{k}{\Phi}^{k} One can write this relation in matrix form: \left[{L}_{j}^{1}-{\tilde{L}}_{j}^{2}\right]\cdot \left[\begin{array}{c}{\eta}^{1}\\ {\eta}^{2}\end{array}\right]=0 The terms of the connection matrices are no longer equal to zero or one. They arise from the interpolations of the displacements projected onto the elements. Finally, by using the double dualisation, the matrix system obtained to be solved, in the case of the modal problem on the global structure, is: \Rightarrow \left[\begin{array}{ccc}-\text{Id}& \tilde{A}L& \text{Id}\\ {\tilde{A}}^{T}{L}^{T}& \bar{K}& {\tilde{A}}^{T}{L}^{T}\\ \text{Id}& \tilde{A}L& -\text{Id}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\lambda}_{1}\\ \eta \\ {\lambda}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace -{\omega}^{2}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& 0& 0\\ 0& \bar{M}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\lambda}_{1}\\ \eta \\ {\lambda}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace Where \tilde{A} designates the identity matrix \text{Id} if the substructure is the one whose interface is master and A , the observation matrix, if it is the one whose interface is slave. The double dualisation therefore leads to a real symmetric matrix problem even for the case of incompatible meshes. 2.4.4 Conclusion This method therefore makes it possible to treat the connection of interfaces corresponding to different types of modal basis without the management cost of an elimination which is always delicate. On the other hand, it is relatively simple. The major drawback of this formulation is that it leads to final assembled systems of dimensions larger than in the case of the elimination. Indeed, the coupling of the matrix equations has been done by introducing a number of additional degrees of freedom equal to twice the number of connection equations. This increase in the dimensions of the matrices can therefore be very large. Let us note that the Lagrange degrees of freedom introduced are, in this case, the forces applied to the interfaces in order to ensure the connection between the two substructures. 2.5 Elimination of the linear constraints The technique of double dualisation makes it possible to obtain uniformity in the taking into account of the constraints. This approach is indeed usable both for linear and for non-linear constraints, on the displacements or the stresses. It therefore allows, with great flexibility, the carrying out of a great variety of analyses. Nevertheless, within the framework of modal analysis in general, and of substructuring techniques in particular, the presence of the double Lagrange multipliers can constitute a drawback, linked both to the increase in the size of the problem with the number of constraints, and also to the numerical conditioning of the system thus obtained. The increase in the size of the problem is particularly clear in the case of the substructuring approaches, where, for the final problem, the great majority of the equations to be solved concerns the constraints. In order to circumvent this difficulty, a technique for the elimination of the kinematic constraints has been implemented on the basis of a QR decomposition of the connection matrices. 2.5.1 Case of linearly independent constraints The linear constraints associated with a dynamics problem can be written in the form of the linear system: \left[L\right]\cdot q=0 q designating the whole set of the degrees of freedom of the complete model (that is to say including all the substructures, in our case). The idea of the elimination consists in building a basis of the kernel of L , and in solving the problem projected into this basis. The construction of this basis is done simply from the QR decomposition of {L}^{T} . For a matrix L of size n\times N , where n is the number of constraints, and N the number of degrees of freedom, this decomposition is written: {\left[{L}^{T}\right]}_{N\times n}={\left[Q\right]}_{N\times N}\cdot {\left[R\right]}_{N\times n}=\left[{[{Q}_{1}]}_{N\times n}{[{Q}_{2}]}_{N\times (N-n)}\right]\cdot \left[\begin{array}{c}{[{R}_{1}]}_{n\times n}\\ {[0]}_{(N-n)\times n}\end{array}\right] {Q}_{2} is then directly the sought basis, as is shown in what follows. 2.5.2 Case of redundant constraints This decomposition also makes it possible to analyse what happens in the presence of redundant constraints (nodes constrained several times, “star” substructure, etc.). When the constraints are not all independent, one can write L in the form of a linear combination of {n}_{I} 7 - M=3(6+E(\frac{N}{d})+2) where E(.) corresponds to the integer part of the quantity considered. These M modes \tilde{{\phi }_{i}} are then lifted statically onto the model of the substructure, and then form the basis on which one seeks the interface modes: \tilde{\psi}=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\tilde{{\psi}_{i}}\\ \tilde{{\psi}_{\mathrm{c}}}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\tilde{{\phi }_{i}}\\ -{\mathrm{K}}_{\mathrm{cc}}^{-1}{\mathrm{K}}_{\mathrm{ci}}\tilde{{\phi }_{i}}\end{array}\right\rbrace One then projects the mass and stiffness matrices of the macro-element onto these vectors, \bar{\mathrm{K}}={\tilde{\psi}}^{T}.\mathrm{K}.\tilde{\psi}\text{}\bar{\mathrm{M}}={\tilde{\psi}}^{T}.\mathrm{M}.\tilde{\psi} and one seeks their eigenmodes: (\bar{\mathrm{K}}-{\omega}^{2}\bar{\mathrm{M}}){\eta}_{R}=0 The interface modes retained for the construction of the macro-elements are finally the first N vectors defined by: \psi =\tilde{\psi}{\eta}_{\mathrm{R}} The computation of the matrices \tilde{{\mathrm{M}}_{ii}} and \tilde{{\mathrm{K}}_{ii}} , and of the associated modes \tilde{{\phi }_{i}} is rapid and inexpensive in memory, and makes it possible to limit the lifting operation to the only vectors of interest in order to build the interface modes. Naturally, if one computes as many modes \tilde{{\phi }_{i}} as there are interface degrees of freedom, then the subspace described is identical to that described by the constraint modes. 3.4.4 Creation of the reduced macro-elements For each of the substructures, one has the bases of normal modes and the bases of the interface modes. The creation of the macro-elements is then identical to the case of the Craig-Bampton method. One establishes a partition of the degrees of freedom, distinguishing the vector of the internal degrees of freedom {q}_{i}^{k} and the vector of the connection degrees of freedom {q}_{j}^{k} : {q}^{k}=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{q}_{i}^{k}\\ {q}_{j}^{k}\end{array}\right\rbrace That is: {\phi }^{k} the matrix of the eigenvectors of the substructure {S}^{k} , {\psi}_{R}^{k} the matrix of the interface modes of the substructure {S}^{k} . The projection basis of {S}^{k} is characterised by the matrix: {\Phi}^{k}=[{\phi }^{k}{\psi}_{R}^{k}] The RITZ transformation (equation ) allows us to write: {q}^{k}=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{q}_{i}^{k}\\ {q}_{j}^{k}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\phi }^{k}& {\psi}_{R}^{k}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}_{i}^{k}\\ {\eta}_{j}^{k}\end{array}\right\rbrace ={\Phi}^{k}{\eta}^{k} {\eta}_{i}^{k} is the vector of the generalised degrees of freedom associated with the eigenmodes of {S}^{k} , {\eta}_{j}^{k} is the vector of the generalised degrees of freedom associated with the interface modes of {S}^{k} . Let us take an interest in the contribution of the component {S}^{k} from an energy point of view. The kinetic and strain energies are: {T}^{k}=\frac{1}{2}{q}^{{k}^{T}}.{M}^{k}.{\dot{q}}^{k}=\frac{1}{2}{({\Phi}^{k}{\dot{\eta}}^{k})}^{T}.{M}^{k}.{\Phi}^{k}{\dot{\eta}}^{k}=\frac{1}{2}{\dot{\eta}}^{k}.{\bar{M}}^{k}.{\dot{\eta}}^{k} {U}^{k}=\frac{1}{2}{q}^{{k}^{T}}.{K}^{k}.{\dot{q}}^{k}=\frac{1}{2}{({\Phi}^{k}{\dot{\eta}}^{k})}^{T}.{K}^{k}.{\Phi}^{k}{\dot{\eta}}^{k}=\frac{1}{2}{\dot{\eta}}^{k}.{\bar{K}}^{k}.{\dot{\eta}}^{k} These expressions bring out the projections of the mass and stiffness matrices onto the basis of the substructure. These matrices, called generalised, satisfy a certain number of properties by virtue of the orthogonality of the normal modes with respect to the stiffness and mass matrices; the upper left block of these matrices is diagonal. Moreover, we shall consider that these modes are normalised with respect to the mass matrix. The generalised stiffness and mass matrices therefore have the following form: {\bar{K}}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\varphi}^{k}& {\varphi}^{{k}^{T}}{K}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\\ {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{K}^{k}{\varphi}^{k}& {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{K}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\end{array}\right]{\bar{M}}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\text{Id}& {\varphi}^{{k}^{T}}{M}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\\ {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{M}^{k}{\varphi}^{k}& {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{M}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\end{array}\right] where {\lambda}^{k} is the matrix of the generalised stiffnesses associated with the eigenmodes of {S}^{k} . 3.5 Implementation in Code_Aster 3.5.1 Study of the substructures separately The projection basis of each substructure is composed of dynamic eigenmodes and of static deflected shapes. The dynamic eigenmodes of the substructure are computed with the classical operator of Code_Aster: CALC_MODES U4.52.02. In the case of the Craig-Bampton substructuring, the connection interfaces must be fixed. This is carried out with the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA U4.44.01. The operator DEFI_INTERF_DYNA U4.64.01 makes it possible to define the connection interfaces of the substructure. In particular, one specifies the type of the interface, which can be either "CRAIGB" (Craig-Bampton), or "MNEAL" (MacNeal), or finally "AUCUN" (no static modes computed). The operator DEFI_BASE_MODALE U4.64.02 makes it possible to compute the complete projection basis of the substructure. Thus, the dynamic modes computed previously are copied. Furthermore, the static deflected shapes are computed as a function of the type defined in the operator DEFI_INTERF_DYNA U4.64.01. If the type is "CRAIGB", one computes the constraint modes of the interfaces of the substructure. If the type is "MNEAL", one computes the attachment modes of the interfaces of the substructure. If the type is "AUCUN", one does not compute a static deflected shape, which corresponds to a basis of MacNeal type without static correction. The operator MACR_ELEM_DYNA U4.65.01 computes the generalised stiffness and mass matrices of the substructure, as well as the connection matrices. 3.5.2 Assembly The model of the complete structure is determined by the operator DEFI_MODELE_GENE U4.65.02. In particular, each substructure is defined by the macro-element which corresponds to it (coming from MACR_ELEM_DYNA) and the rotation angles which make it possible to orient it. The connections between substructures are defined by the datum of the names of the two substructures involved and of those of the two interfaces facing each other. In the case of the method of the interface modes, it is necessary to specify the option 'REDUIT' in order to allow the coupling between the macro-elements. The numbering of the complete generalised problem is carried out by the operator NUME_DDL_GENE U4.65.03. The generalised mass and stiffness matrices of the complete structure are assembled as a function of this numbering with the operator ASSE_MATR_GENE U4.65.04. 4 Modal analysis by classical dynamic substructuring 4.1 Introduction For the modal problems, the system studied is subjected to no external force. One does not take into account the dissipation in the solid. The method of modal analysis by substructuring, programmed in Code_Aster , which makes it possible to replace the global problem by a simplified problem, proceeds in four stages. First of all, eigenmodes and static deflected shapes are computed on each of the substructures composing the system. Then, the global problem is projected onto these fields, and one takes into account the couplings between the substructures, at the level of their interfaces. One can then solve in the classical way the reduced problem obtained. Finally, it only remains to deduce from it the overall solution by reconstitution. 4.2 Dynamic equations satisfied by the substructures separately We shall consider a structure S composed of {N}_{S} substructures denoted {S}^{k} . We assume that each substructure is modelled by finite elements. We have seen that in an analysis by dynamic substructuring, the vibration behaviour of the substructures results from the external forces which are applied to them, and from the connection forces which the other substructures exert on them. Thus, at the level of the substructure {S}^{k} , and in the case of the modal analysis we can write: {M}^{k}{\ddot{q}}^{k}+{K}^{k}{q}^{k}={f}_{L}^{k} The field of the connection forces is written in complex notation: {f}_{L}^{k}(t)=\left\lbrace {f}_{L}^{k}\right\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} The displacement field is written: {q}^{k}(t)=\left\lbrace {q}^{k}\right\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} The velocity and acceleration fields are written: {\dot{q}}^{k}(t)=j\omega \left\lbrace {q}^{k}\right\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} {\ddot{q}}^{k}(t)=-{\omega}^{2}\left\lbrace {q}^{k}\right\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} Finally the substructure {S}^{k} satisfies the following equation: ({K}^{k}-{\omega}^{2}{M}^{k})\lbrace {q}^{k}\rbrace =\lbrace {f}_{L}^{k}\rbrace The method of modal synthesis consists in seeking the unknown displacement field, coming from the finite-element modelling, on an appropriate space, of reduced dimension (Ritz transformation). We have seen that for each substructure, this space is composed of dynamic eigenmodes and of static deflected shapes: {q}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\varphi}_{i}^{k}& {\psi}_{j}^{k}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}_{i}^{k}\\ {\eta}_{j}^{k}\end{array}\right\rbrace ={\Phi}^{k}{\eta}^{k} {\phi }^{k} are the modal vectors associated with the dynamic eigenmodes of {S}^{k} , {\psi}^{k} are the modal vectors associated with the static deflected shapes of {S}^{k} , {\eta}_{i}^{k} is the vector of the generalised coordinates associated with the eigenmodes of {S}^{k} , {\eta}_{j}^{k} is the vector of the generalised coordinates associated with the static deflected shapes of {S}^{k} , {\eta}^{k} is the vector of the generalised coordinates of {S}^{k} . The equation is projected onto the basis of {S}^{k} taking into account . This allows us to write: ({\bar{K}}^{k}-{\omega}^{2}{\bar{M}}^{k})\lbrace {\eta}^{k}\rbrace =\lbrace {\bar{f}}_{L}^{k}\rbrace Assuming that the dynamic eigenmodes and the static deflected shapes are organised as the formula shows and considering that the eigenvectors associated with the dynamic modes are normalised with respect to the unit modal mass, the generalised mass and stiffness matrices take the following form: {\bar{M}}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}& {\varphi}^{{k}^{T}}{M}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\\ {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{M}^{k}{\varphi}^{k}& {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{M}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\end{array}\right]{\bar{K}}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\lambda}^{k}& {\varphi}^{{k}^{T}}{K}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\\ {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{K}^{k}{\varphi}^{k}& {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{K}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\end{array}\right] where: \mathrm{Id} is the Identity matrix, {\lambda}^{k} is the diagonal matrix of the squares of the natural angular frequencies of the basis. One shows, in the case of the Craig-Bampton method, that the normal modes and the constraint modes are orthogonal with respect to the stiffness matrix, whose off-diagonal terms are, from then on, zero. However, this property is not used in the algorithm programmed in Code_Aster . 4.3 Dynamic equations satisfied by the global structure The dynamic equations which the global structure satisfies are: (\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}{\bar{\bar{K}}}^{1}& & & & \\ & {}^{...}& & & \\ & & {\bar{\bar{K}}}^{k}& & \\ & & & {}^{...}& \\ & & & & {\bar{\bar{K}}}^{{N}_{s}}\end{array}\right]-{\omega}^{2}\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}{\bar{\bar{M}}}^{1}& & & & \\ & {}^{...}& & & \\ & & {\bar{\bar{M}}}^{k}& & \\ & & & {}^{...}& \\ & & & & {\bar{\bar{M}}}^{{N}_{s}}\end{array}\right])\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}^{1}\\ {}^{...}\\ {\eta}^{k}\\ {}^{...}\\ {\eta}^{{N}_{s}}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\bar{f}}_{L}^{1}\\ {}^{...}\\ {\bar{f}}_{L}^{k}\\ {}^{...}\\ {\bar{f}}_{L}^{{N}_{s}}\end{array}\right\rbrace To which one must add the connection equations (according to [eq ]): \forall k,l\text{}{L}_{{S}^{k}\cap {S}^{l}}^{k}\left\lbrace {\eta}^{k}\right\rbrace ={L}_{{S}^{k}\cap {S}^{l}}^{l}\left\lbrace {\eta}^{l}\right\rbrace This system is solved by double dualisation of the boundary conditions R3.03.01. Its final formulation therefore brings in the vector of the Lagrange multipliers \lambda and can be written in the condensed form: \begin{array}{c}(\bar{\mathrm{K}}-{\omega}^{2}\bar{\mathrm{M}})\lbrace \eta \rbrace +{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{T}}\lambda =0\\ \mathrm{L}\lbrace \lambda \rbrace =0\end{array} The problem defined by the equation is symmetric. On the other hand, its dimension is determined by the number of modes taken into consideration (dynamic modes and static deflected shapes). One is therefore led to solve a classical modal problem, of reduced size, with which a linear constraint equation is associated. Its solution therefore poses no problem. 4.4 Implementation in Code_Aster 4.4.1 Study of the substructures separately The dynamic eigenmodes are computed with the operator CALC_MODES U4.52.02. The conditions at the connection interfaces are applied with the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA U4.44.01. The operator DEFI_INTERF_DYNA U4.64.01 makes it possible to define the connection interfaces of the substructure. The operator DEFI_BASE_MODALE U4.64.02 makes it possible to compute the complete projection basis of the substructure. The operator MACR_ELEM_DYNA U4.65.01 computes the generalised stiffness, mass and possibly damping matrices of the substructure, as well as the connection matrices. 4.4.2 Assembly and solution The model of the complete structure is defined by the operator DEFI_MODELE_GENE U4.65.02. Its numbering is carried out by the operator NUME_DDL_GENE U4.65.03. The generalised mass, stiffness and possibly damping matrices of the complete structure are assembled as a function of this numbering with the operator ASSE_MATR_GENE U4.65.04. The computation of the eigenmodes of the complete structure is carried out by the operator CALC_MODES U4.52.02. 4.4.3 Recovery onto the physical basis The recovery of the results onto the physical basis is identical to the case of the modal analysis. It involves the operator REST_GENE_PHYS U4.63.31. In order to reduce the duration of the graphical processing during the visualisations, it is possible to create a coarse mesh by the operator DEFI_SQUELETTE U4.24.01. This mesh, ignored during the analysis, serves as a support for the visualisations. 5 Harmonic response by classical dynamic substructuring 5.1 Introduction For the harmonic problems, the system studied is subjected to a force that is arbitrary in space, but sinusoidal in time. The form of the loading, the excitation frequency and the modal properties each play an essential role. One must also take into account the dissipation in the solid, which one can express by the introduction of a damping matrix. The method of harmonic analysis by substructuring, programmed in Code_Aster , which makes it possible to replace the global problem by a simplified problem, proceeds in four stages. First of all, eigenmodes and static deflected shapes are computed on each of the substructures composing the system. Then, the global problem is projected onto these fields, and one takes into account the couplings between the substructures, at the level of their interfaces. One can then solve in the classical way the reduced problem obtained. Finally, it only remains to deduce from it the overall solution by reconstitution. 5.2 Dynamic equations satisfied by the substructures separately We shall consider a structure S composed of {N}_{S} substructures denoted {S}^{k} . We assume that each substructure is modelled by finite elements. We have seen that in an analysis by dynamic substructuring, the vibration behaviour of the substructures results from the external forces which are applied to it, and from the connection forces which the other substructures exert on it. Thus, at the level of the substructure {S}^{k} , we can write: {M}^{k}{\ddot{q}}^{k}+{C}^{k}{\dot{q}}^{k}+{K}^{k}{q}^{k}={f}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{k}+{f}_{L}^{k} In a harmonic problem, one imposes a dynamic loading, arbitrary in space, but sinusoidal of angular frequency \omega in time. One is then interested in the stabilised response of the system, without taking into account the transient part. The field of the external forces is written: {f}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{k}(t)=\left\lbrace {f}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{k}\right\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} The field of the connection forces is written: {f}_{L}^{k}(t)=\left\lbrace {f}_{L}^{k}\right\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} The displacement field is written: {q}^{k}(t)=\left\lbrace {q}^{k}\right\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t } The velocity and acceleration fields are written: {\dot{q}}^{k}(t)=j\omega \left\lbrace {q}^{k}\right\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t } {\ddot{q}}^{k}(t)=-{\omega}^{2}\left\lbrace {q}^{k}\right\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t } Finally the substructure {S}^{k} satisfies the following equation of motion: ({K}^{k}+j\omega {C}^{k}-{\omega}^{2}{M}^{k})\left\lbrace {q}^{k}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {f}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{k}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace {f}_{L}^{k}\right\rbrace The method of modal synthesis consists in seeking the unknown displacement field, coming from the finite-element modelling, on an appropriate space, of reduced dimension (Ritz transformation). We have seen that for each substructure, this space is composed of dynamic eigenmodes and of static deflected shapes: {q}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\varphi}^{k}& {\psi}^{k}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}_{i}^{k}\\ {\eta}_{j}^{k}\end{array}\right\rbrace ={\Phi}^{k}{\eta}^{k} {\varphi}^{k} are the modal vectors associated with the dynamic eigenmodes of {S}^{k} , {\psi}^{k} are the modal vectors associated with the static deflected shapes of {S}^{k} , {\eta}_{i}^{k} is the vector of the generalised coordinates associated with the eigenmodes of {S}^{k} , {\eta}_{j}^{k} is the vector of the generalised coordinates associated with the static deflected shapes of {S}^{k} , {\eta}^{k} is the vector of the generalised coordinates of {S}^{k} . The equation is projected onto the basis of {S}^{k} taking into account . This allows us to write: ({\bar{K}}^{k}+j\omega {\bar{C}}^{k}-{\omega}^{2}{\bar{M}}^{k})\left\lbrace {\eta}^{k}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{k}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace {\bar{f}}_{L}^{k}\right\rbrace Assuming that the dynamic eigenmodes and the static deflected shapes are organised as the formula shows and considering that the eigenvectors associated with the dynamic modes are normalised with respect to the unit modal mass, the generalised mass and stiffness matrices take the following form: {\bar{M}}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}& {\varphi}^{{k}^{T}}{M}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\\ {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{M}^{k}{\varphi}^{k}& {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{M}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\end{array}\right]{\bar{K}}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\lambda}^{k}& {\varphi}^{{k}^{T}}{K}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\\ {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{K}^{k}{\varphi}^{k}& {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{K}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\end{array}\right] One shows, in the case of the Craig-Bampton method, that the normal modes and the constraint modes are orthogonal with respect to the stiffness matrix, whose off-diagonal terms are, from then on, zero. However, this property is not used in the algorithm programmed in Code_Aster . We consider, as type of dissipation, only the viscous damping (it is the only one which is supported by the substructuring tools in Code_Aster ). Two methods are usable in order to take this damping into account: - the Rayleigh damping applied at the elementary level which consists in assuming that the elementary damping matrix {C}_{e} associated with each finite element of the model is a linear combination of the elementary mass and stiffness matrices {K}_{e} and {M}_{e} : {C}_{e}={\alpha}_{e}{K}_{e}+{\beta }_{e}{M}_{e} The damping matrix is then assembled {C}^{k} then projected onto the basis: {\bar{C}}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\varphi}^{{k}^{T}}{C}^{k}{\varphi}^{k}& {\varphi}^{{k}^{T}}{C}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\\ {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{C}^{k}{\varphi}^{k}& {\psi}^{{k}^{T}}{C}^{k}{\psi}^{k}\end{array}\right] - the proportional damping applied to the dynamic eigenmodes of each substructure. The resulting matrix is therefore an incomplete diagonal (one does not know how to associate a proportional damping with the static deflected shapes): {\bar{C}}^{k}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\xi}^{k}& 0\\ 0& 0\end{array}\right] 5.3 Dynamic equations satisfied by the global structure The dynamic equations which the global structure satisfies are:
