The treatments of the substructures are identical to the case of the modal analysis. The operator MACR_ELEM_DYNA U4.65.01 computes the generalised stiffness, mass and possibly damping matrices of the substructure, as well as the connection matrices. The Rayleigh damping is taken into account by completing the operand MATR_AMOR. The proportional damping is introduced by the operand AMOR_REDUIT. The harmonic loading is defined, at the level of the substructure, by the operators AFFE_CHAR_MECA U4.44.01 (application of the force on the mesh), CALC_VECT_ELEM U4.61.02 (computation of the associated elementary vectors) and ASSE_VECTEUR U4.61.23 (assembly of the loading vector on the mesh of the substructure). 5.4.2 Assembly and solution As in the case of the modal analysis, the model of the complete structure is defined by the operator DEFI_MODELE_GENE U4.65.02. Its numbering is carried out by the operator NUME_DDL_GENE U4.65.03. The generalised mass, stiffness and possibly damping matrices of the complete structure are assembled as a function of this numbering with the operator ASSE_MATR_GENE U4.65.04. The loadings are projected onto the bases of the substructures to which they are applied, then assembled from the numbering coming from NUME_DDL_GENE U4.65.03 by the operator ASSE_VECT_GENE U4.65.05. The computation of the harmonic response of the complete structure is carried out by the operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03. 5.4.3 Recovery onto the physical basis The recovery of the results onto the physical basis is identical to the case of the modal analysis. It involves the operator REST_GENE_PHYS U4.63.31 and possibly the operator DEFI_SQUELETTE U4.24.01 (creation of a "skeleton" mesh). 5.5 Conclusion The method of computation of the harmonic response by modal synthesis available in Code_Aster relies on that of modal substructuring, also programmed. It consists in expressing the whole set of the equations in a space of reduced dimension, constituted of modes of the various substructures, by a Rayleigh-Ritz method. The definition of these fields is that used for the modal substructuring and comprises normal modes as well as other static or harmonic ones. The procedure employed results in a projection of the matrices and of the right-hand side onto the restricted space. 6 Transient response by classical dynamic substructuring 6.1 Introduction The object of this reference documentation is to present the theoretical bases of the two methods of computation of the transient response by dynamic substructuring available in Code_Aster . The first consists in carrying out a transient analysis by substructuring for which the equations of the problem are projected onto the bases associated with each substructure. The difficulty resides in the double dualisation of the boundary conditions which leads to a singular mass matrix. In order to use the explicit integration schemes (which require the inversion of the mass matrix), one must therefore modify the treatment of the interfaces in the operator for the computation of the transient response. The second method consists in determining the eigenmodes of the complete structure by substructuring and in projecting onto this basis the equations of the transient problem. The step of recovery onto the physical basis of the final generalised results must therefore take this double projection into account. The operator for the computation of the transient response which receives the substructuring is the operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03. Relying on methods of modal recombination, it has been designed to solve transient problems in generalised coordinates and it is very efficient for large-size problems whose number of degrees of freedom it makes it possible to reduce. On the other hand, it supports the taking into account of localised non-linearities (at the nodes) which one wishes to generalise to the case of substructuring. In this report, we present the two methods of transient analysis by substructuring available in Code_Aster , as well as their implementation. 6.2 Transient analysis by projection onto the bases of the substructures 6.2.1 Dynamic equations satisfied by the substructures separately Let there be a structure S composed of {N}_{S} substructures denoted {S}^{k} . We assume that each substructure is modelled by finite elements. The vibration behaviour of the substructures results from the external forces which are applied to it and from the connection forces which the other substructures exert on it. Thus, for {S}^{k} , we have: {M}^{k}{\ddot{q}}^{k}+{C}^{k}{\dot{q}}^{k}+{K}^{k}{q}^{k}={f}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{k}+{f}_{L}^{k} The unknown displacement field, coming from the finite-element modelling, is sought on an appropriate space, of reduced dimension (Ritz transformation) according to the expression: {q}^{k}={\Phi}^{k}{\eta}^{k} The Ritz transformation, applied to the real and virtual displacement, leads to the transient dynamic equation of the substructure, and makes it possible to write: {\bar{M}}^{k}{\ddot{\eta}}^{k}+{\bar{C}}^{k}{\dot{\eta}}^{k}+{\bar{K}}^{k}{\eta}^{k}={\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{k}+{\bar{f}}_{L}^{k} The problem defined by the equation is symmetric. On the other hand, its dimension is determined by the number of modes taken into consideration (dynamic modes and static deflected shapes). One is therefore led to solve a classical transient problem but of reduced size. 6.2.2 Dynamic equations satisfied by the global structure The matrix writing of the dynamic equation satisfied by the global structure is written simply from the dynamic equations satisfied by each substructure: \begin{array}{}\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}{\bar{M}}^{1}& & & & \\ & \mathrm{...}& & & \\ & & {\bar{M}}^{k}& & \\ & & & \mathrm{...}& \\ & & & & {\bar{M}}^{{N}_{S}}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\ddot{\eta}}^{1}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\ddot{\eta}}^{k}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\ddot{\eta}}^{{N}_{S}}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}{\bar{C}}^{1}& & & & \\ & \mathrm{...}& & & \\ & & {\bar{C}}^{k}& & \\ & & & \mathrm{...}& \\ & & & & {\bar{C}}^{{N}_{S}}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\dot{\eta}}^{1}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\dot{\eta}}^{k}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\dot{\eta}}^{{N}_{S}}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}{\bar{K}}^{1}& & & & \\ & \mathrm{...}& & & \\ & & {\bar{K}}^{k}& & \\ & & & \mathrm{...}& \\ & & & & {\bar{K}}^{{N}_{S}}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}^{1}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\eta}^{k}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\eta}^{{N}_{S}}\end{array}\right\rbrace \\ =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{1}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{k}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{{N}_{S}}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\bar{f}}_{L}^{1}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\bar{f}}_{L}^{k}\\ \mathrm{...}\\ {\bar{f}}_{L}^{{N}_{S}}\end{array}\right\rbrace \end{array} To which one must add the connection equations: \forall k,l\text{}{\mathrm{L}}_{{S}^{k}\cap {S}^{l}}^{k}\left\lbrace {\eta}^{k}\right\rbrace ={\mathrm{L}}_{{S}^{k}\cap {S}^{l}}^{l}\left\lbrace {\eta}^{l}\right\rbrace \text{}{\mathrm{f}}_{{L}_{{S}^{k}\cap {S}^{L}}}^{k}=-{\mathrm{f}}_{{L}_{{S}^{k}\cap {S}^{L}}}^{l} This system can be written in the condensed form: {\bar{M}}^{k}{\ddot{\eta}}^{k}+{\bar{C}}^{k}{\dot{\eta}}^{k}+{\bar{K}}^{k}{\eta}^{k}={\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}^{k}+{\bar{f}}_{L}^{k} L\eta =0 \forall k,l{f}_{{L}_{{S}^{k}\cap {S}^{L}}}^{k}=-{f}_{{L}_{{S}^{k}\cap {S}^{L}}}^{l} 6.2.3 Double dualisation of the boundary conditions The condensed problem, given above, presents itself in the form of a transient system with which a linear constraint equation is associated (in force and displacement). In Code_Aster , this type of problem is classical and it is solved by double dualisation of the boundary conditions R3.03.01, that is to say by the introduction of auxiliary variables also called Lagrange multipliers in order to dualise the boundary conditions. After introduction of the Lagrange multipliers, the matrix system is put in the form: \left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& 0& 0\\ 0& \bar{M}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\ddot{{\lambda}_{1}}\\ \ddot{\eta}\\ \ddot{{\lambda}_{2}}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& 0& 0\\ 0& \bar{C}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\dot{{\lambda}_{1}}\\ \dot{\eta}\\ \dot{{\lambda}_{2}}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left[\begin{array}{ccc}-\text{Id}& L& \text{Id}\\ {L}^{T}& \bar{K}& {L}^{T}\\ \text{Id}& L& -\text{Id}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\lambda}_{1}\\ \eta \\ {\lambda}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}0\\ {\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace where {\lambda}_{1} and {\lambda}_{2} are the Lagrange multipliers. One observes that the introduction of the Lagrange multipliers renders the mass matrix singular. From then on, the use of the explicit integration schemes developed in the operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 is impossible because they require the inversion of the mass matrix. In order to render the matrix non-singular, it is sufficient to dualise, with the same Lagrange multipliers, the condition on the second derivative of the connection equations. Thus the displacement continuity condition is modified by the equivalent system: \forall t,L\eta =0\iff \mid \begin{array}{c}L(\eta +\ddot{\eta})=0\\ L\eta °=0\text{et}L\dot{\eta}°=0\end{array} where \eta ° and \dot{\eta}° are the generalised displacements and velocities at the initial time instant. The matrix system which follows from it is of the form [bib10]: \left[\begin{array}{ccc}-\text{Id}& L& \text{Id}\\ {L}^{T}& \bar{M}& {L}^{T}\\ \text{Id}& L& -\text{Id}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\ddot{{\lambda}_{1}}\\ \ddot{\eta}\\ \ddot{{\lambda}_{2}}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& 0& 0\\ 0& \bar{C}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\dot{{\lambda}_{1}}\\ \dot{\eta}\\ \dot{{\lambda}_{2}}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left[\begin{array}{ccc}-\text{Id}& L& \text{Id}\\ {L}^{T}& \bar{K}& {L}^{T}\\ \text{Id}& L& -\text{Id}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\lambda}_{1}\\ \eta \\ {\lambda}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}0\\ {\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}}\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace One observes that the mass matrix has the same form as the stiffness matrix. They are therefore invertible. This system is therefore perfectly equivalent to the equation (it satisfies at every time instant the connection conditions) and it can be treated, in this form, by the operator DYNA_VIBRA. 6.2.4 Treatment of the damping matrix One observes that the displacement continuity condition, formulated in the equation, results in an undamped second-order equation. During the solution by time step of a transient problem, any numerical error risks sustaining itself, thus reducing the stability of the algorithm. In order to optimise the damping of the numerical error, it is sufficient to dualise the condition on the first derivative of the connection equations with the same Lagrange multipliers multiplied by 2 (so as to render this damping critical): \forall t,\mathrm{L}\eta =0\mathrm{\iff }\mid \begin{array}{c}\mathrm{L}(\eta +2\dot{\eta}+\ddot{\eta})=0\\ \mathrm{L}\eta °=0\text{et}\mathrm{L}\dot{\eta}°=0\end{array} The matrix system which follows from it is of the form [bib10]: \left[\begin{array}{ccc}-\text{Id}& \mathrm{L}& \text{Id}\\ {\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{T}}& \bar{\mathrm{M}}& {\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{T}}\\ \text{Id}& \mathrm{L}& -\text{Id}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\ddot{{\lambda}_{1}}\\ \ddot{\eta}\\ \ddot{{\lambda}_{2}}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left[\begin{array}{ccc}-2\text{Id}& 2\mathrm{L}& 2\text{Id}\\ 2{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{T}}& \bar{\mathrm{C}}& 2{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{T}}\\ 2\text{Id}& 2\mathrm{L}& -2\text{Id}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\dot{{\lambda}_{1}}\\ \dot{\eta}\\ \dot{{\lambda}_{2}}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left[\begin{array}{ccc}-\text{Id}& \mathrm{L}& \text{Id}\\ {\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{T}}& \bar{\mathrm{K}}& {\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{T}}\\ \text{Id}& \mathrm{L}& -\text{Id}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\lambda}_{1}\\ \eta \\ {\lambda}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}0\\ {\bar{\mathrm{f}}}_{\mathit{ext}}\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace One therefore observes that the treatment of the numerical error on the connection equations leads to modifying the damping matrix of the transient problem. This modification is entirely comparable to that which is carried out on the mass matrix. By contrast, we have not wished to generalise this treatment to the case of the solution of undamped transient problems. That would have led us to create a temporary damping matrix. One might have feared increasing the computation times, without real benefit. Moreover, it is entirely possible for the user to define a damping matrix whose coefficients are zero. The modification of the latter being automatic, the undamped transient system will effectively be solved, while optimising the treatment of any numerical error intervening on the connection equations. 6.2.5 Treatment of the initial conditions Consider a substructure {S}^{k} characterised by its projection basis {\Phi}^{k} composed of normal modes and of static deflected shapes. One assumes that initially the substructure {S}^{k} is subjected to a displacement or velocity field (this in no way modifies the demonstration) denoted :math: . The Ritz transformation allows us to write: {\mathrm{q}}_{0}^{k}={\Phi}^{k}{\eta}_{0}^{k} where {\eta}_{0}^{k} is the vector of the generalised displacements (or velocities) of {S}^{k} to be determined. The vector of the initial generalised displacements (or velocities) is determined as follows: {q}_{0}^{k}={\Phi}^{k}{\eta}_{0}^{k}\Rightarrow {\Phi}^{{k}^{T}}{q}_{0}^{k}=({\Phi}^{{k}^{T}}{\Phi}^{k})\cdot {\eta}_{0}^{k} \mathrm{\Rightarrow }{\eta}_{0}^{k}={({\Phi}^{{k}^{T}}{\Phi}^{k})}^{-1}{\Phi}^{{k}^{T}}{\mathrm{q}}_{0}^{k} 6.3 Transient analysis on a global modal basis computed by substructuring The second method developed consists in solving the transient problem on the modal basis of the complete structure computed by substructuring. 6.3.1 Computation of the eigenmodes of the complete structure by substructuring Each substructure {S}^{k} is represented by a projection basis, composed of dynamic eigenmodes and of static deflected shapes, which we have denoted {\Phi}^{k} . The projection basis of the complete structure which results from it is denoted \Phi . The modal basis of the complete structure is computed by substructuring. Each mode obtained is therefore a linear combination of the vectors of the projection bases of the substructures: {\Phi}_{p}=\sum_{k=1}^{{N}_{S}}{\Phi}^{k}{\alpha}^{k}=\Phi \alpha where: | {\Phi}_{p} | is the matrix of the eigenmodes of the complete structure, | | --- | --- | | \alpha | is the matrix of the generalised modal coordinates of the structure. | The projection of the matrices and of the vectors constitutive of the transient problem, onto the basis of the eigenmodes of the complete structure computed by modal synthesis, makes it possible to determine: | the generalised mass matrix: | \bar{\bar{M}}={\alpha}^{T}\bar{M}\alpha | | --- | --- | | the generalised stiffness matrix: | \bar{\bar{K}}={\alpha}^{T}\bar{C}\alpha | | possibly the generalised damping matrix: | \bar{\bar{C}}={\alpha}^{T}\bar{C}\alpha | | the vector of the generalised external forces: | {\bar{\bar{f}}}_{\mathrm{ext}}={\alpha}^{T}{\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}} | By virtue of the orthogonality of the eigenmodes of the structure computed by modal synthesis, with respect to the matrices M and K , the generalised mass and stiffness matrices obtained above are diagonal: \bar{\bar{M}}={\alpha}^{T}\bar{M}\alpha ={(\Phi \alpha )}^{T}M\Phi \alpha ={\Phi}_{p}^{T}M{\Phi}_{p} \bar{\bar{K}}={\alpha}^{T}\bar{K}\alpha ={(\Phi \alpha )}^{T}K\Phi \alpha ={\Phi}_{p}^{T}K{\Phi}_{p} 6.3.2 Dynamic equation satisfied by the global structure The complete structure is subjected to the external forces which are applied to it. Thus, we can write: M\ddot{q}+C\dot{q}+{K}^{\bar{q}}={\bar{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}} The unknown displacement field, coming from the finite-element modelling, is replaced by its projection onto the basis of the eigenmodes of the structure, according to the formula: q={\Phi}_{p}\eta where \eta is the vector of the generalised coordinates of the structure. The Ritz transformation, applied to the transient dynamic equation of the structure, makes it possible to write: \bar{\bar{M}}\ddot{\eta}+\bar{\bar{C}}\dot{\eta}+{\bar{\bar{K}}}^{\bar{\eta}}={\bar{\bar{f}}}_{\mathrm{ext}} The step of recovery onto the physical basis requires that one take into account the double projection (onto the modal basis of the complete structure, then onto the projection bases of the substructures - cf. ). q={\Phi}_{p}\eta =\Phi \alpha \eta The problem defined by the equation is of an entirely classical form. One is led to solve a symmetric transient problem whose dimension is determined by the number of modes computed by substructuring and whose mass and stiffness matrices are diagonal. Let us note finally that the treatment of the initial conditions is identical to the case of the transient analysis by projection onto the bases of the substructures (cf. § 6.2 ). 6.4 Comparative study of the two methods developed The theoretical bases, associated with the two methodologies implemented in Code_Aster in order to carry out a computation of the transient response using the substructuring techniques, have been presented in the preceding chapters. We specify, here, their essential particularities. The first methodology consists in carrying out a computation of the transient response by substructuring. The equation satisfied by the complete structure is then projected onto the bases of the substructures. The accuracy of this method is therefore directly determined by the extent of these bases. The latter can be enriched without leading to prohibitive computation times because the substructures are, in principle, of relatively reduced sizes. Be that as it may, it is difficult to estimate the effect of the modal truncation from the sole knowledge of the modes of the bases of the substructures. On the other hand, the projection bases of the substructures are composed of modes which are not all orthogonal to one another (eigenmodes and static deflected shapes). The generalised mass and stiffness matrices constitutive of the final transient problem are therefore non-diagonal. Overall, their bandwidth can be determined from the number of static deflected shapes of the projection bases of the substructures. The duration of the integration in the transient computation operator DYNA_VIBRA will therefore be all the longer as there are interface degrees of freedom. On the other hand, the maximum integration time step admissible by the explicit integration schemes is determined from the maximum frequency of the projection basis. In the case of a transient analysis by substructuring, this frequency results, in principle, from the static modes whose diagonal terms are high in the generalised stiffness matrix and low in the generalised mass matrix. From then on, the integration time step cannot be determined a priori. Experience shows that it is very small, with regard to the natural frequencies of the bases of the substructures and that the use of the integration scheme with adaptive time step of DYNA_VIBRA is very profitable. The second methodology consists in carrying out a transient analysis on the modal basis of the complete structure obtained by substructuring. One knows that the step consisting in computing the eigenmodes of the structure can be costly in terms of computation time. This is all the more true when one considers non-linear forces because the projection basis must then be sufficiently extended in order to represent well the dynamics of the system. On the other hand, the modal basis on which the transient response is computed is generally of dimension smaller than that determined by the eigenvectors of the substructures (eigenmodes and static deflected shapes). The double projection therefore amounts to introducing a cut-off frequency. One must therefore expect this method to be less accurate than the preceding one. However, the computation of the eigenmodes makes it possible to estimate the effect of the modal truncation. On the other hand, it can make it possible to validate the models of the substructures if one has experimental results. Finally, the essential advantage of this method is that the mass and stiffness matrices used in the transient analysis are diagonal. The numerical integration is therefore very rapid. 6.5 Implementation in Code_Aster 6.5.1 Study of the substructures separately If one wishes to introduce a Rayleigh damping, the parameters and of this damping are defined, by the operator DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01. The treatments of the substructures are identical to the case of the modal and harmonic analysis. The dynamic eigenmodes are computed with the operator CALC_MODES U4.52.02. The conditions at the connection interfaces are applied with the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA U4.44.01. The operator DEFI_INTERF_DYNA U4.64.01 makes it possible to define the connection interfaces of the substructure. The operator DEFI_BASE_MODALE U4.64.02 makes it possible to compute the complete projection basis of the substructure (copying of the eigenmodes and computation of the static deflected shapes). The operator MACR_ELEM_DYNA U4.65.01 computes the generalised stiffness, mass and possibly damping matrices of the substructure, as well as the connection matrices. The Rayleigh damping is taken into account by completing the operand MATR_AMOR. The proportional damping is introduced by the operand AMOR_REDUIT. The transient loading is defined, at the level of the substructure, by the operators AFFE_CHAR_MECA U4.44.01 (application of the force on the mesh), CALC_VECT_ELEM U4.61.02 (computation of the associated elementary vectors) and ASSE_VECTEUR U4.61.23 (assembly of the loading vector on the mesh of the substructure). The operator CREA_CHAMP U4.72.04 which makes it possible to assign a field on the nodes of a model makes it possible to describe the initial displacement field and/or the initial velocity field of the substructure. 6.5.2 Assembly of the generalised model As in the case of the modal and harmonic analysis, the model of the complete structure is defined by the operator DEFI_MODELE_GENE U4.65.02. Its numbering is carried out by the operator NUME_DDL_GENE U4.65.03. The generalised mass, stiffness and possibly damping matrices of the complete structure are assembled as a function of this numbering with the operator ASSE_MATR_GENE U4.65.04. The loadings are projected onto the bases of the substructures to which they are applied, then assembled from the numbering coming from NUME_DDL_GENE U4.65.03 by the operator ASSE_VECT_GENE U4.65.05. The initial generalised displacements and the initial generalised velocities for each substructure are computed by the operator ASSE_VECT_GENE U4.65.05. This operator also carries out the assembly of these vectors as a function of the numbering coming from NUME_DDL_GENE U4.65.03. In the case of a transient analysis projected onto the "bases" of the substructures, the generalised assembled matrices and vectors obtained at the end of this step are used directly for the transient analysis. In the case of an analysis on the modal basis of the complete structure computed by substructuring, one must carry out specific operations which are presented in § 5.3 . 6.5.3 Computation of the modal basis of the complete structure and projection This chapter is specific to the transient analysis on a modal basis computed by substructuring. The modal basis of the complete structure is computed with the classical operator of Code_Aster: CALC_MODES U4.52.02. One defines a numbering of the final generalised problem with the operator NUME_DDL_GENE U4.65.03. The generalised mass, stiffness and possibly damping matrices are projected onto the basis of the eigenmodes of the structure with the operator PROJ_MATR_BASE U4.63.12. The generalised vectors corresponding to the external loadings are projected onto the basis of the eigenmodes of the structure with the operator PROJ_VECT_BASE U4.63.13. 6.5.4 Solution and recovery onto the physical basis The computation of the transient response of the complete structure is carried out by the operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03. The recovery of the results onto the physical basis involves the operator REST_GENE_PHYS U4.63.31; it is identical to the case of the modal and harmonic analysis. One can use the operator DEFI_SQUELETTE U4.24.01 in order to create a "skeleton" mesh. Coarser than the analysis mesh, it makes it possible to reduce the durations of the graphical processing. 6.6 Conclusion We have presented, in this report, the work carried out in order to introduce, into Code_Aster , the computation of the linear transient response by dynamic substructuring. The methods which have been chosen consist, for the first of them, in projecting the transient equations onto the "bases" of each substructure, composed of dynamic eigenmodes and of static deflected shapes and, for the second, in computing the eigenmodes of the complete structure by substructuring and in projecting the transient equations onto them. We began with an account of the theoretical bases on which the first method of transient substructuring relies in order to arrive at the matrix formulation of the final problem. In particular, an original treatment of the displacement continuity equation in order to render the mass matrix invertible and in order to ensure an optimal stability of the integration algorithm, has led us to modify the form of the mass and damping matrices of the transient problem. For the second method, the essential difficulty consists in recovering the results obtained in generalised coordinates onto the physical basis. Indeed, one must take into account the double projection: onto the modal basis of the complete structure on the one hand, and onto the bases of the substructures on the other hand. The developments carried out have resulted in modifications of the operators DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 and REST_GENE_PHYS U4.63.31. Their syntax has been very little modified, so that their use is identical during an analysis by substructuring and a direct analysis by modal recombination. 7 Dynamic condensation by dynamic macro-elements in static substructuring 7.1 Introduction The objective of the dynamic condensation of a model by static substructuring is to reduce the total number of degrees of freedom of a model constituted of several subdomains by condensing the solution of the subdomains of linear behaviour onto the degrees of freedom of their interfaces with subdomains of non-linear behaviour. The idea is then to represent each of these subdomains by a macro-element of static type in order to be able to use it in a mixed model also comprising finite elements for the non-condensed parts of non-linear behaviour in order to proceed to non-linear analyses by means of the non-linear computation operators STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03 or DYNA_NON_LINE U4.53.01. In the condensation of each subdomain, one also wants to integrate the dynamic part of its behaviour obtained by modal analysis and for that, one will therefore use dynamic macro-elements as the static macro-elements necessary in static substructuring. The principle of this conversion and their application is described in the documents [bib13]. 7.2 Classical problem and principle of the method Figure 7.2-a: Subdomains of the classical condensation problem. On figure 7.2-a above are schematised the possible subdomains which one can encounter within the framework of a classical problem of condensation by static substructuring: - the subdomains of type \mathit{E1} : subdomains of structure of constant linear behaviour condensed and modelled by a dynamic macro-element, - the subdomains of type \mathit{E2} : subdomains of structure of potentially non-linear behaviour not condensed and modelled by finite elements, - the subdomains of type \mathit{E3} : soil subdomain represented by a macro-element coming from the conversion of a complex soil impedance matrix. The basic principle of the condensation by macro-element consists in partitioning, for each subdomain of type \mathit{E1} , the degrees of freedom j of their interfaces denoted \Sigma with the subdomains of type \mathit{E2} as well as their other degrees of freedom i called "internal". The stiffness matrices K and mass matrices M are thus decomposed on these degrees of freedom: K=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{ii}& {K}_{ij}\\ {K}_{ji}& {K}_{jj}\end{array}\right] M=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{M}_{ii}& {M}_{ij}\\ {M}_{ji}& {M}_{jj}\end{array}\right] \begin{array}{}i\text{ddl internes}\\ j\text{ddl d'interfaces}\end{array} The principle of static substructuring amounts, for the matrix K for example, to condensing it only onto the degrees of freedom j of the interfaces \Sigma by correcting the initial term {K}_{jj} by a complementary term called "Schur complement" according to the principle of the so-called Guyan condensation [bib14]: \bar{{K}_{jj}}={K}_{jj}-{K}_{ij}^{T}{({K}_{ii})}^{-1}{K}_{ij}={\Phi}^{T}K\Phi The computation of the new term \bar{{K}_{jj}} amounts to a projection of the matrix K onto a basis of static modes \Psi of "constraint" type obtained by static response to unit displacements imposed at each degree of freedom j of the interfaces \Sigma : \Psi =\left[\begin{array}{}{\Psi}_{ij}\\ I\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{}-{K}_{ii}^{-1}{K}_{ij}\\ I\end{array}\right] The condensation onto the degrees of freedom j of the interfaces \Sigma of the mass matrix M and of the loads of the subdomains of type \mathit{E1} will be done in an analogous manner by the matrix product of the matrix and of the loading vectors onto the basis of static modes \Psi . One then observes that the terms {\Phi}^{T}K\Phi and {\Psi}^{\mathrm{T.}}M.\Psi can be obtained directly for each subdomain of type \mathit{E1} by means of the operator for the computation of a dynamic macro-element MACR_ELEM_DYNA U4.65.01 and that the projected load terms are obtained {\Psi}^{T}.F by means of the operator PROJ_VECT_BASE U4.63.13. 7.3 Condensation methods by complete or reduced basis According to the mode of computation of the modes of representation of the motions of the interfaces, two methods are currently used: 7.3.1 The computation method by complete basis The motion \mathrm{U} of any point of a subdomain of type E1 is expressed from the decomposition onto the static modes \Psi and onto a complement brought by the dynamic part of the motion expressed by eigenmodes \Phi : U=\Psi .{q}_{\Sigma}+\Phi .q With the method by complete basis, on the interface \Sigma , the eigenmodes \Phi have a zero contribution and the static modes \Psi have a unit value and therefore the displacement U of a point of the interface is expressed: U={X}_{\Sigma}={\mathrm{Id}.q}_{\Sigma} In this case, the physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma merge with the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} associated with the static modes \Psi . The generalised coordinates q associated with the eigenmodes \Phi being zero on the interface, their solution will be uncoupled from that of the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} . In the assembly of the matrices of the condensed problem, the terms of projection onto the eigenmodes {\Phi}^{T}.K.\Phi and {\Phi}^{T}.M.\Phi will be juxtaposed. In order to be able to "mix" physical degrees of freedom with generalised coordinates, one uses the device, transparent to the user, of passing the latter off as additional physical degrees of freedom taken from among the degrees of freedom internal to a domain of type \mathit{E1} . This alias is active in the model where the domains of type \mathit{E1} are condensed by macro-elements, but in order to have the true displacement of the degrees of freedom internal to these domains, it is obtained in post-processing after solution of the assembled global problem by means of the operator REST_COND_TRAN U4.63.33 by applying the initial relation: \mathrm{U}=\Psi .{\mathrm{q}}_{\Sigma}+\Phi .\mathrm{q} At the level of the assembly of a subdomain of type \mathit{E1} , the initial storage represented on figure 7.3.1-a comprises terms both on internal degrees of freedom and on the interface degrees of freedom with a non-complete fill-in profile. Figure 7.3.1-a: Initial assembly of the subdomains \mathit{E1} before condensation. After condensation by the complete method, most of the internal degrees of freedom disappear, but a very small part is devoted to representing the generalised coordinates associated with the eigenmodes and the terms of the static macro-element are added to the interface degrees of freedom with a complete fill-in profile this time. The resulting storage is represented on figure 7.3.1-b below. Figure 7.3.1-b: Assembly of the subdomains \mathit{E1} with the complete method. The assembly of the terms of the static macro-element is carried out by simple summation on the interface degrees of freedom and does not in general require an additional connection on the interface when one takes into account all the constrained static modes of the interface. It is not so in the particular case of the condensation onto a single interface node where there one must add a connection relation, rigid on the interface degrees of freedom. In the case of a subdomain of type \mathit{E3} , the post-processing by REST_COND_TRAN is useless because the displacement has no component on dynamic modes and the displacement at the interface is definitively obtained as soon as the global problem is solved. 7.3.2 The computation method by modal reduction With the method by modal reduction, the motion U of any point of a subdomain of type \mathit{E1} is still expressed from the decomposition onto the static modes \Psi and onto a complement brought by the dynamic part of the motion expressed by eigenmodes \Phi : \mathrm{U}=\Psi .{\mathrm{q}}_{\Sigma}+\Phi .\mathrm{q} But this time, on the interface \Sigma , the eigenmodes \Phi have a non-zero contribution because the static modes \Psi have a non-unit value and are in number generally very much smaller than the number of physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma which, in this case, do not merge with the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} associated with the static modes \Psi . One must therefore distinguish in the assembly and the solution the terms associated with the physical degrees of freedom and those associated with the generalised coordinates. In the same way as for the generalised coordinates q associated with the eigenmodes \Phi , one uses the device, transparent to the user, of passing the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} associated with the static modes \Psi off as additional physical degrees of freedom also taken from among degrees of freedom internal to a domain of type \mathit{E1} . But this time, the solution of the physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma will not be uncoupled from that of the generalised coordinates {\mathrm{q}}_{\Sigma} . In the assembly of the matrices of the condensed problem, the terms of projection onto the eigenmodes {\Phi}^{T}.K.\Phi and {\Phi}^{T}.M.\Phi will be juxtaposed. But one will then have to add a connection and therefore Lagrange degrees of freedom between the physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma and the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} . This connection is expressed by the relation: {X}_{\Sigma}=\Psi .{q}_{\Sigma} This relation is expressed by the repeatable keyword LIAISON_INTERF of the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA U4.44.01, which makes it possible to link each subdomain of type \mathit{E1} to a subdomain of type \mathit{E2} (cf. figure 7.2-a) by generating a particular case of LIAISON_DDL with the coefficients of the preceding linear relation. Then, in order to have the true displacement of the degrees of freedom internal to the domains of type \mathit{E1} , one proceeds in the same way in post-processing after solution of the assembled global problem by means of the operator REST_COND_TRAN U4.63.33 by applying the initial relation: \mathrm{U}=\Psi .{\mathrm{q}}_{\Sigma}+\Phi .\mathrm{q} After condensation by the modal reduction method, most of the internal degrees of freedom disappear, but a very small part is devoted to representing the generalised coordinates associated with the eigenmodes, another small part is devoted to the generalised coordinates associated with the interface eigenmodes. This time, the terms of the static macro-element are not added to the interface degrees of freedom which then retain a non-complete fill-in profile. But one then obtains a quadrangular block of Lagrange degrees of freedom between the physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma and the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} . The resulting storage is represented on figure 7.3.2-a below. Figure 7.3.2-a: Storage of the subdomains \mathit{E1} with the modal-reduction method. One will note that there is no imposed choice of computation for the reduction basis of interface modes \Psi . One possible choice will be that used in soil-structure interaction [bib15] by considering a basis of eigenmodes of the subdomain of type \mathit{E1} on a carpet of springs representative of the stiffness of the adjacent domains of type \mathit{E2} or \mathit{E3} . 8 Indications for the a posteriori control of the quality of the reduced model One of the principles making it possible to validate the quality of a reduced model consists in estimating, a posteriori, the deviation from equilibrium which may exist after the analysis. 8.1 General case for an analysis on a reduced model In order to characterise this deviation from equilibrium, one uses the principle of the force residual. This force residual {F}_{r} is computed - for the time responses: \left[{K}_{e}{T}_{r}\right]{q}_{r}(t)+\left[{D}_{v}{T}_{r}\right]\dot{{q}_{r}}(t)+\left[M{T}_{r}\right]\ddot{{q}_{r}}(t)-Bu(t)={F}_{r}(t) - for the harmonic responses: \left[({K}_{e}+j{K}_{h}+{K}_{v}(s))+s{D}_{v}+{s}^{2}M\right]{T}_{r}{q}_{r}(s)-Bu(s)={F}_{r}(s) where {K}_{e} is the stiffness matrix of the structure, {D}_{v} the matrix associated with the viscous dissipation, and M the mass matrix. One furthermore denotes by {q}_{r} the vector of the reduced degrees of freedom, and by {T}_{r} the associated reduction basis. The external-force term is defined by the product of a matrix of localisation of the forces B and of a vector u specifying the time evolution of the excitation. This writing makes it possible to separate the spatial and time components of a force often denoted f(t) . Concerning the harmonic response, {K}_{h} is the matrix representing the hysteretic behaviour, {K}_{v} the matrix representing the viscoelastic behaviour. One can also adopt the same procedure for the computation of the complex eigenmodes, detailed in the documentation on the construction of the reduced models in dynamics U2.06.04 If the solution obtained is exact, then the residual {F}_{r} is zero, by definition. Otherwise, one can build a measure of the deviation from equilibrium from the static response of the structure to this loading. One denotes by {R}_{r} the displacement residual associated with each complex mode computed. By definition, one has {K}_{e}{R}_{r}={F}_{r} A measure of the deviation from equilibrium is given by the elastic potential energy of the structure, that is {E}_{r}=\frac{1}{2}{∥{R}_{r}^{T}{K}_{e}{R}_{r}∥}^{2} An example of use of this technique is given in the documentation U2.06.04 8.2 Particular case of the computation of the modes of a generalised model The same principle can be implemented, but in a slightly more precise way, so as to bring out particular deviations from the various equilibria. 8.2.1 Presentation In the case of an analysis by substructuring with the use of interface modes, it is important to be able to determine more precisely the origin of an inaccurate analysis. The sources of inaccuracy are: - the poor representation of the displacements at the interfaces, for each substructure, - the dynamic behaviour of the internal parts, for each substructure, - the differential displacements (separation) which may appear at the interfaces between the sub - structures. The command CALC_CORR_SSD U4.52.16 makes it possible, on the basis of the computations of the works associated with these various forces, to build correction terms making it possible to improve separately the interface behaviours, and the internal dynamic behaviours of each of the substructures. NB: One will moreover have to take care, in the enrichment process, to orthogonalise separately the vectors with fixed interfaces, and the vectors with free interface, as is carried out in the test case SDLS122 V3.02.122, before concatenating them and building the modal bases. 8.2.2 Computation of the indicators and associated corrections In order to detail the construction of the various indicators and corrective terms built in the command CALC_CORR_SSD, let us consider a simple example constituted of the assembly of 2 substructures along a single interface. This approach is easily generalised, but leads to cumbersome notations. 8.2.2.1 Definition of the coupled problem For each substructure, one introduces the mass and stiffness matrices. One denotes by c the degrees of freedom associated with the internal parts ("complementary"), and by i the degrees of freedom associated with the interfaces. One also introduces the associated reduction basis, composed both of modes with fixed interfaces {\Phi}_{c} , and of interface modes {\psi}_{i} , lifted statically onto the rest of the structure, so that the corresponding displacements on the complementary degrees of freedom are {\psi}_{c}=-{K}_{\mathit{cc}}^{-1}{K}_{\mathit{ci}}{\psi}_{i} {K}_{S}={\left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{ii}& {K}_{\mathit{ic}}\\ {K}_{\mathit{ci}}& {K}_{\mathit{cc}}\end{array}\right]}_{S}/{M}_{S}={\left[\begin{array}{cc}{M}_{ii}& {M}_{\mathit{ic}}\\ {M}_{\mathit{ci}}& {M}_{\mathit{cc}}\end{array}\right]}_{S}/{T}_{S}={\left[\begin{array}{cc}0& {\Psi}_{i}\\ {\Phi}_{c}& {\Psi}_{c}\end{array}\right]}_{S} The reduced mass and stiffness matrices are written {K}_{\mathit{rS}}={T}_{S}^{T}{K}_{S}{T}_{S}/{M}_{\mathit{rS}}={T}_{S}^{T}{M}_{S}{T}_{S} Because of the introduction of interface modes, the compatibility relation of the interface displacements between the substructures 1 and 2 can no longer be written {q}_{i2}={q}_{i1} , but becomes, if the substructure 2 is slave: {\hat{T}}_{\mathit{iS}2}^{T}{T}_{\mathit{iS}1}{\eta}_{1}={T}_{\mathit{iS}2}^{T}{T}_{\mathit{iS}2}{\eta}_{2} One then defines a basis of the kernel of the constraints in order to eliminate the interface relations, on the basis of the elements present in section 2.5 {Q}_{i}=\mathit{Ker}(\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\hat{T}}_{\mathit{iS}2}^{T}{T}_{\mathit{iS}1}& -{T}_{\mathit{iS}2}^{T}{T}_{\mathit{iS}2}\end{array}\right])\mathrm{\Rightarrow } The complete model is then assembled, then projected onto a basis of the kernel of the constraints: {K}_{g}={Q}^{T}\left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{\mathit{r1}}& 0\\ 0& {K}_{\mathit{r2}}\end{array}\right]Q/{M}_{g}={Q}^{T}\left[\begin{array}{cc}{M}_{\mathit{r1}}& 0\\ 0& {M}_{\mathit{r2}}\end{array}\right]Q One denotes by \eta the generalised degrees of freedom associated with the problem thus obtained. One therefore has, if one denotes by q the physical degrees of freedom, q={T}_{r}{q}_{r}={T}_{r}Q\eta . 8.2.2.2 Deviation from equilibrium If one denotes by {Z}_{0}={K}_{g}-{\omega}_{0}{M}_{g} the dynamic impedance associated with the eigenmode of angular frequency {\omega}_{0} , and by {\eta}_{0} the associated reduced eigenmode, one has {Q}^{T}{T}_{r}^{T}\left[{Z}_{0}\right]{T}_{r}Q{\eta}_{0}=0 Under these conditions, the relation making it possible to quantify the deviation from equilibrium of this particular mode becomes: \left[\begin{array}{cccc}{Z}_{\mathrm{0cc}1}& {Z}_{\mathrm{0ci}1}& 0& 0\\ {Z}_{\mathrm{0ic}1}& {Z}_{\mathrm{0ii}1}& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& {Z}_{\mathrm{0ii}2}& {Z}_{\mathrm{0ic}2}\\ 0& 0& {Z}_{\mathrm{0ci}2}& {Z}_{\mathrm{0cc}2}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cccc}{\Phi}_{c1}& {\Psi}_{c1}& 0& 0\\ 0& {\Psi}_{i1}& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& {\Psi}_{i2}& 0\\ 0& 0& {\Psi}_{c2}& {\Phi}_{c2}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\mathit{Id}& 0& 0\\ 0& {Q}_{i1}& 0\\ 0& {Q}_{i2}& 0\\ 0& 0& \mathit{Id}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}_{\mathrm{0c}1}\\ \hat{{\eta}_{\mathrm{0i}}}\\ {\eta}_{\mathrm{0c}2}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{f}_{\mathrm{0c}1}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{0i}1}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{0i}2}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{0c}2}\end{array}\right\rbrace If the projection basis is of good quality, then the deviation from equilibrium must be small, and, ideally, one must even verify \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{f}_{\mathrm{0c}1}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{0i}1}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{0i}2}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{0c}2}\end{array}\right\rbrace \approx \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}0\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace the solver having to ensure \left\lbrace \begin{array}{cccc}{\phi }_{\mathrm{0c}1}& {\phi }_{\mathrm{0i}1}& {\phi }_{\mathrm{0i}2}& {\phi }_{\mathrm{0c}2}\end{array}\right\rbrace \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{f}_{\mathrm{0c}1}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{0i}1}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{0i}2}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{0c}2}\end{array}\right\rbrace \approx 0/{\phi }_{0}={T}_{r}Q{\eta}_{0} In order to be sure of having a model of good quality, one must therefore ensure the nullity of each of the terms, independently of one another. One must therefore verify the nullity of the works of the forces associated with the residual loads in each substructure, that is {\phi }_{\mathrm{0c}1}^{T}{f}_{\mathrm{0c}1}=0/{\phi }_{\mathrm{0c}2}^{T}{f}_{\mathrm{0c}2}=0 One must also verify the nullity of the virtual works associated with the residual forces at the interface: {\phi }_{\mathrm{0i}1}^{T}{f}_{\mathrm{0i}1}+{\phi }_{\mathrm{0i}2}^{T}{f}_{\mathrm{0i}2}=0 Finally, one must also verify the compatibility of the displacements, and avoid the differential displacements of interfaces (separations) {({\phi }_{\mathrm{0i}2}-C{\phi }_{\mathrm{0i}1})}^{T}{f}_{\mathrm{0i}2}=0 C is the operator of projection of the displacements of the master interface onto the slave interface. In the case of compatible interfaces, C is the identity matrix. In practice, in order to be more simply exploitable, the various works computed in CALC_CORR_SSD are divided by the natural angular frequency of the mode considered. This rescaling makes it possible to compare the error levels between the various modes. 8.2.2.3 Corrections associated with the residual forces Each of these terms makes it possible to define associated corrections. Thus, for each substructure k , one builds a subspace dedicated to the enrichment based on the principle of the static correction (cf. U2.06.04): {T}_{\mathit{Enrich}}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}0& {T}_{iI}\\ {T}_{cC}& {T}_{cI}\end{array}\right] With, {K}_{\mathit{cc}k}{T}_{cC}={f}_{\mathrm{0c}k} And \left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{iik}& {K}_{\mathit{ic}k}\\ {K}_{\mathit{ci}k}& {K}_{\mathit{cc}k}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{T}_{iI}\\ {T}_{cI}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{f}_{\mathrm{0i}}\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace In the case where the stiffness matrix would be singular for the substructure k , one regularises the problem by building a mass-shifted matrix K-{\alpha}^{2}M , where \alpha is a value small compared with the natural angular frequencies of the first flexible modes of the structure. 8.2.2.4 Corrections associated with the differential interface displacements In the case where the coupled modes computed do not perfectly ensure the continuity of the interface displacements, it is possible to enrich the displacements on either side of the interface. One must however here consider two cases, according to whether, for the substructure k , the interface considered is master or slave. If the interface is a slave interface, one then simply projects the displacement of the master interface onto the slave interface, and lifts this displacement statically onto the rest of the substructure. The complete reduction basis is then written {T}_{\mathit{Enrich}-\mathit{Slav}}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& {T}_{iI}& C{\phi }_{i\mathit{Mast}}\\ {T}_{cC}& {T}_{cI}& {T}_{c\mathit{Slav}}\end{array}\right]/{T}_{c\mathit{Slav}}=-{K}_{\mathit{cc}}^{-1}{K}_{\mathit{ci}}C{\phi }_{i\mathit{Mast}} In the case where the interface considered is master, one must then extrapolate the motions of the slave interface. The approach retained consists in building a basis of the modes of the master interface, and in seeking the best selection of them which makes it possible to reconstruct the displacements of the slave interface. This combination of interface modes is then lifted statically onto the complementary degrees of freedom of the substructure considered. If one denotes by R the extrapolation operator thus defined, the complete basis becomes, for a master interface: {T}_{\mathit{Enrich}-\mathit{Mast}}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& {T}_{iI}& R{\phi }_{i\mathit{Slav}}\\ {T}_{cC}& {T}_{cI}& {T}_{c\mathit{Mast}}\end{array}\right]/{T}_{c\mathit{Mast}}=-{K}_{\mathit{cc}}^{-1}{K}_{\mathit{ci}}R{\phi }_{i\mathit{Slav}} The construction of R is carried out as follows: - One computes the modes {\Gamma}_{i\mathit{Mast}} of the interface of the master substructure - One seeks the best linear combination of these modes which makes it possible to represent the displacements of the slave interface. One therefore seeks {\beta}_{0} which realises {\beta}_{0}=\underset{\beta}{\mathit{ArgMin}}{∥C{\Gamma}_{i\mathit{Mast}}\beta -{\phi }_{i\mathit{Slav}}∥}^{2} If the norm of the error is greater than 1e-6, then one computes a greater number of modes {\Gamma}_{i\mathit{Mast}} , and one iterates as long as the error norm is not satisfactory. R is then written formally R={\Gamma}_{i\mathit{Mast}}{(C{\Gamma}_{i\mathit{Mast}})}^{+} These corrections are computed for each interface of each substructure. One then separates each family of vectors into two families in order to be orthogonalised: - vectors whose interface displacements are zero - vectors whose interface displacements are non-zero NB: One will moreover have to take care, in the enrichment process, to orthogonalise separately the vectors with fixed interfaces, and the vectors with free interface, as is carried out in the test case SDLS122 V3.02.122 9 Bibliography 1. r4.06.03 Cyclic dynamic substructuring r4.06.03 Cyclic dynamic substructuring Summary: This report rests on the notions of analysis by modal synthesis described in the document R4.06.02. We address the methods of cyclic dynamic substructuring. Entirely devoted to the study of structures with cyclic repetitivity, they take the best advantage of the geometric particularities of the structure. The CRAIG-BAMPTON and MAC NEAL methods, developed in this framework, are presented. > Contents 1 Introduction In this document, we present a synthesis of the methods of cyclic dynamic substructuring. We give a definition of cyclic repetitivity (or cyclic symmetry) and we present the principal consequences of this property for the dynamic behaviour of the structure (nodal circles and nodal diameters, double modes). Then we present, in some detail, the two methods of cyclic dynamic substructuring implemented in Code_Aster . Improvements have been made to the classical methods by taking into account the presence of the nodes of the axis. These methods assume that the mesh of the basic sector is such that its traces on the right and left interfaces coincide (compatible meshes). The approach with the Mac Neal method is not implemented. It is assumed in this paragraph that the degrees of freedom carried by the nodes of the axis, in the same way as the right and left interface nodes, have been fixed for the computation of the dynamic modes of the basic sector and have been the subject of constraint-mode computations. Furthermore, the eigenvalues of the term {e}^{j\beta }{\theta}_{a} all having modulus 1, the conditioning of the global problem is not affected by this change. 4 Implementation in Code_Aster The treatment of the basic sector is identical to that of the substructures in classical substructuring. It involves the operators CALC_MODES U4.52.02, DEFI_INTERF_DYNA U4.64.01 and DEFI_BASE_MODALE U4.64.02. The eigenmodes of the structure with cyclic symmetry are computed by the operator MODE_ITER_CYCL U4.52.05 as a function of the projection basis of the basic sector defined previously and of the number of sectors of the complete structure. The recovery of the results onto the physical basis is identical to classical substructuring. It involves the operator REST_SOUS_STRUC U4.63.32 and possibly the operator DEFI_SQUELETTE U4.24.01. 5 Conclusion The principles of substructuring make it possible to set out the RITZ transformation and the modal recombination in order to arrive at the modal synthesis which integrates these two techniques. The rules for connecting the substructures are made explicit. Two methods have been developed in Code_Aster : that of Craig-Bampton and that of MacNeal. We present here their particularities, both in the definition of the initial modal basis and in its use. After having set out the definition of a structure with cyclic symmetry and the properties which follow from it, we have presented the methods of cyclic substructuring implemented in Code_Aster . They prove very advantageous for the computation of the eigenmodes of a structure with cyclic symmetry, such as the rotors of rotating machines, of whose geometric and mechanical characteristics they take full advantage. 6 Bibliography 1. r4.07.02 Modelling of turbulent excitations r4.07.02 Modelling of turbulent excitations Summary: The modelling of the turbulent excitations available in Code_Aster is described, together with the way in which they are taken into account in a dynamic analysis. The turbulent excitations are characterised by a spectral density of forces, specified by means of the operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB U4.44.31. Their taking into account in a dynamic analysis is done by projection of the spectrum onto the modal basis of the structure whose response one wishes to compute. The projection operations are carried out by means of the operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE [U4. 63.14]. > Contents 1 Principle of the analysis 1.1 Determination of a modal basis of the system under flow and projection of the excitation The computation of the dynamic response of a system to a turbulent excitation induced by a fluid flow is carried out by following the following stages: | | first, one computes the modal basis of the system out of flow by means of the operator CALC_MODES[U4.52.02], | | --- | --- | | | one then defines the characteristics of the configuration studied, for taking into account the fluid-structure coupling phenomenon, by means of the operator DEFI_FLUI_STRU[U4.25.01]. This operator makes it possible, for example, to supply the velocity profiles associated with the fluid-excitation zones, for configurations of the type ‘tube bundle under cross-flow’. It produces a concept of type [type_flui_stru] intended to be used by the operators implemented downstream in the command file, | | | the modal characteristics of the system under flow are then computed by means of the operator CALC_FLUI_STRU[U4.66.02]. One has as output a modal basis for each flow velocity, | | | the definition of the turbulent excitation is then done by a call to the operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB[U4.44.31]. The modellings available are the following: | - spectra of “correlation length” type, specific to configurations of the type “tube bundle under cross-flow”, for application to the vibrations of steam-generator tubes. The corresponding factor keywords are SPEC_LONG_COR_1, SPEC_LONG_COR_2, SPEC_LONG_COR_3 and SPEC_LONG_COR_4. These spectra are predefined; however, the user can adjust their parameters. This part is developed in paragraph [§2.2], - distributed turbulent-excitation model. The corresponding factor keyword is SPEC_FONC_FORME. The excitation spectrum is defined by its decomposition on a family of shape functions by supplying, on the one hand a cross-spectral matrix, and on the other hand a list of shape functions associated with this matrix. The associated concepts [interspectre] and [fonction] must be generated upstream. In the case of the component “control-rod cluster”, the user can also use a predefined turbulence spectrum, identified on the mock-up GRAPPE1. This part is developed in paragraph [§2.3], - localised turbulent-excitation model. The corresponding factor keyword is SPEC_EXCI_POINT. It is used in the case of an excitation spectrum associated with one or more point forces and moments. The definition of the excitation is then done by supplying: - a cross-spectral matrix of excitations (the associated concept [interspectre] must be generated upstream), - the list of the nodes of application of these excitations, - the nature of the excitation applied at each of these nodes (force or moment), - the directions of application of the excitations thus defined. This part is developed in paragraph [§2.4]. | | The projection of the previously defined turbulent-excitation spectrum onto the modal basis of the structure under flow is then carried out by means of the operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE[U4.63.14]. | | --- | --- | 1.2 Computation of the response to the turbulent excitation: frequency solution 1.2.1 Introduction The computation of the frequency response of the structure or of the coupled fluid-structure system is done in three stages: 1. computation of the cross-spectra of modal excitations, 2. computation of the cross-spectra of modal response, 3. recombination on the physical basis. First, one introduces for each mode the transfer function of the mechanical system (structure alone or coupled fluid-structure system). Each of the three stages above is then set out in detail. 1.2.2 Computation of the cross-spectra of modal excitations The cross-spectra of modal excitations {S}_{\text{QiQj}}(f,U) are determined by projection of the turbulent-excitation spectrum onto the modal basis of the mechanical system (structure alone or coupled fluid-structure system). This projection stage is set out in paragraph [§2] for the various models applicable to line structures. 1.2.3 Computation of the cross-spectra of modal response The cross-spectra of modal displacements {S}_{\text{qiqj}}(f,U) are then deduced from the cross-spectra of modal excitations {S}_{\text{QiQj}}(f,U) by means of the following relation: {S}_{{q}_{i}{q}_{j}}(f,U)={H}_{i}^{\ast }(f,U){S}_{\text{QiQj}}(f,U){H}_{j}(f,U) eq 1.2.3-1 where {H}_{i}^{\text{ }}(f,U) denotes the complex conjugate of the transfer function {H}_{i}(f,U) of the mechanical system considered. Given a frequency f and a flow velocity U , the transfer function {H}_{i}(f,U) of the mechanical system for the mode i is defined by: {H}_{i}(f,U)=\frac{1}{{M}_{i}{\omega}_{i}^{2}(-{(\frac{f}{{f}_{i}})}^{2}+\mathrm{2j}{\xi}_{i}(\frac{f}{{f}_{i}})+1)} eq 1.2.3-2 where {M}_{i} denotes the modal mass of the mode i,{\omega}_{i} and {f}_{i} denote respectively, at the velocity U , the angular frequency and the natural frequency of the mode i,{\xi}_{i} denotes, at the velocity U , the damping ratio of the mode i , and J denotes the complex number such that {J}^{2}\text{= -}1 . The computation of the cross-spectra of modal displacements from the cross-spectra of modal excitations and from the transfer functions is carried out by means of the operator DYNA_SPEC_MODAL U4.53.23. One deduces in particular from [eq 1.2.3-2] the relation linking the auto-spectra of modal displacements to the auto-spectra of modal excitations: {S}_{\text{qiqi}}(f,U)={\mid {H}_{i}(f,U)\mid }^{2}{S}_{\text{QiQi}}(f,U) eq 1.2.3-3 where {\mid {H}_{i}(f,U)\mid }^{2} denotes the square of the modulus of {H}_{i}(f,U) 1.2.4 Recombination on the physical basis Given a flow velocity U , the cross-spectrum of physical displacement {S}_{{u}_{1}{u}_{2}}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},f) at the points of abscissae {x}_{1} and {x}_{2} , at the frequency f , is obtained by modal recombination. This operation is written: {S}_{{u}_{1}{u}_{2}}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},f)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}{\phi }_{i}({x}_{1}){\phi }_{j}({x}_{2}){S}_{{q}_{i}{q}_{j}}(f,U) eq 1.2.4-1 Where N denotes the number of modes of the basis; {\phi }_{i}({x}_{k}) is the component at the discretisation point {x}_{k} of the shape of the i -th mode in the spatial direction considered. The recombination on the physical basis is carried out by means of the operator REST_SPEC_PHYS U4.63.22. The spatial direction considered is specified at the time of the call to this operator. 1.2.5 Statistical elements The modal variance {\sigma}_{i}^{2}(U) , associated with the velocity U , is expressed as follows: {\sigma}_{i}^{2}(U)=2\underset{0}{\overset{\infty}{\int}}{S}_{{q}_{i}{q}_{j}}(f,U)\text{df} eq 1.2.5-1 At the flow velocity U , the RMS value {\sigma}_{\text{RMS}}(x) of the response at a point x of the structure is given by: {\sigma}_{\text{RMS}}(x)=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\phi }_{i}^{2}(x){\sigma}_{i}^{2}(U)} eq 1.2.5-2 Where N denotes the number of modes of the basis and {\phi }_{i}(x) is the component at the point x of the shape of the i -th mode in the spatial direction considered. This operation is carried out by the operator POST_DYNA_ALEA U4.84.04. 1.3 Computation of the response to the turbulent excitation: time solution The time solution proceeds according to the following sequence of operations: 1.3.1 Factorisation of the cross-spectral density The operator GENE_FONC_ALEA U4.36.05 carries out the factorisation of the cross-spectral density of modal excitations {S}_{\text{QiQj}}(f,U) , before application of the Monte-Carlo method. 1.3.2 Generation of the random modal excitations The operator GENE_FONC_ALEA U4.36.05 generates random modal excitations {Q}_{i}(t) by carrying out draws by the Monte-Carlo method. The operator RECU_FONCTION U4.32.03 makes it possible to recover each of the evolutions {Q}_{i}(t) . 1.3.3 Modification of a modal basis and projection The operator MODI_BASE_MODALE U4.66.21 modifies the modal basis of the structure by substituting for the initial characteristics those obtained for a flow velocity considered. The operator PROJ_MATR_BASE U4.63.12 allows the projection of the assembled mass and stiffness matrices onto the new modal basis previously defined. 1.3.4 Definition of the obstacles The definition of the geometry of the obstacles is carried out, where applicable, by means of the operator DEFI_OBSTACLE U4.44.21. 1.3.5 Dynamic solution The transient dynamic analysis for the mode i(1\le i\le N) is carried out by means of a numerical integration scheme with the operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03. {M}_{ii}{\ddot{q}}_{i}(t)+{C}_{ii}{\dot{q}}_{i}(t)+{K}_{ii}{q}_{i}(t)={Q}_{i}(t) eq 1.3.5-1 Where {M}_{ii},{C}_{ii}\text{et}{K}_{ii} denote respectively the generalised mass, damping and stiffness associated with the i -th mode; {q}_{i}(t)\text{et}{Q}_{i}(t) denote respectively the generalised displacement and excitation associated with the i -th mode. 1.3.6 Ritz projection The recovery on the physical basis is carried out by means of a Ritz projection: U(x,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}{u}_{i}(x){q}_{i}(t) eq 1.3.6-1 U(x,t) denotes the assembled vector of the physical displacements; {u}_{i}(x) is the assembled vector defining the i -th modal shape and {q}_{i}(t) the generalised displacement along the i -th mode. This last operation is carried out by means of the operator REST_GENE_PHYS U4.63.31. 2 Turbulent-excitation models applicable to line structures 2.1 General principles 2.1.1 Assumptions It is assumed that the line excitation induced on the line structure by the turbulence of the flow can be modelled in the form of a stationary ergodic Gaussian random process of zero mean. This turbulent excitation is therefore entirely characterised by its cross-spectral density {S}_{f}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},\omega ) , where {x}_{1} and {x}_{2} are any two points of the beam and w denotes the angular frequency. The turbulent excitation applied to the structure is therefore characterised by its cross-spectral density {S}_{f} . In addition, it is assumed that the turbulent forces are independent of the motion of the structure. The turbulent excitation is identified experimentally on a reference mock-up. It is then applicable to any real component in geometric similarity with the reference mock-up. 2.1.2 Computation of the cross-spectra of modal excitations {f}_{t}(x,s) denotes the line density of turbulent excitation exerted on the beam; x is the current abscissa of a point of the beam and s the complex angular frequency (Laplace variable). The additional assumptions \mathit{H1} and \mathit{H2} are made: \mathit{H1} . The excited length {L}_{e} is smaller than the total length L of the beam. \mathit{H2} . The expression of {f}_{t}(x,s) does not depend on the origin of the excited zone {x}_{e} ; this is expressed by {f}_{t}(x,s)={f}_{t}(x-{x}_{e},s) . In this case, one can express the line density {f}_{t} in the following form: {f}_{t}(x,s)=\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{\rho U}}^{2}D\cdot {C}_{f}(\alpha ,\frac{D}{{D}_{h}},\frac{D}{{L}_{e}},{s}_{r}\text{,Re}) eq 2.1.2-1 with: \begin{array}{ccc}\alpha =\frac{x-{x}_{e}}{{L}_{e}}& {s}_{r}=\frac{\text{sD}}{U}& \text{Re}=\frac{\text{UD}}{u}\end{array} Where \rho denotes the mass density of the fluid, U is the mean flow velocity of the fluid, D and {D}_{h} are respectively the diameter of the structure and the hydraulic diameter, {C}_{f} represents the dimensionless coefficient of turbulent force, x is the current abscissa of a point of the beam, {x}_{e} denotes the abscissa of the origin of the excited zone, {L}_{e} represents the excited length, \alpha is the reduced space variable, s is the complex angular frequency (Laplace variable), {s}_{r} is the reduced complex angular frequency, \nu is the kinematic viscosity of the fluid, and finally “ \text{Re} ” denotes the Reynolds number. By the assumption of geometric similarity of the real component with the reference mock-up, one obtains: {f}_{t}(x,s)=\frac{1}{2}{\mathit{\rho U}}^{2}D\cdot {C}_{f}(\alpha ,{s}_{r}\text{,Re}) eq 2.1.2-2 Thus, the modal turbulent excitation {Q}_{i}(s) can be written in the Laplace domain (assumption \mathit{H2} ): {Q}_{i}(x)=\underset{{x}_{e}}{\overset{{x}_{e}+{L}_{e}}{\int}}{f}_{t}(x,s){\phi }_{i}(x)\text{dx}={L}_{e}\underset{0}{\overset{1}{\int}}{f}_{t}(\alpha {L}_{e},s){\phi }_{i}(\alpha {L}_{e}+{x}_{e})d\alpha eq 2.1.2-3 where {\phi }_{i}(x) is the component of the i -th modal shape in the spatial direction in which the turbulent excitation acts. By means of the expression [eq 2.1.2-2], one deduces: {Q}_{i}(s)=\frac{1}{2}{\mathit{\rho U}}^{2}{\text{DL}}_{e}\underset{0}{\overset{1}{\int}}{C}_{f}(\alpha ,{s}_{r}\text{,Re}){\phi }_{i}(\alpha {L}_{e}+{x}_{e})d\alpha eq 2.1.2-4 The cross-spectral densities of modal turbulent excitations are then expressed in the form: {S}_{{Q}_{i}{Q}_{j}}(f,U)={(\frac{1}{2}{\mathit{\rho U}}^{2}{\text{DL}}_{e})}^{2}\frac{D}{U}\underset{0}{\overset{1}{\int}}\underset{0}{\overset{1}{\int}}{\Phi}_{t}({\alpha}_{1},{\alpha}_{2},{f}_{r}\text{,Re}){\phi }_{i}({\alpha}_{1}{L}_{e}+{x}_{e}){\phi }_{j}({\alpha}_{2}{L}_{e}+{x}_{e})d{\alpha}_{1}d{\alpha}_{2} eq 2.1.2-4 | with | 1\le i,j\le N , where N is the number of modes retained in order to determine the response of the structure; | | --- | --- | | | {\Phi}_{t} : cross-spectrum of {C}_{f} between {\alpha}_{1} and {\alpha}_{2} ; | | | {f}_{r}=\frac{\text{fD}}{U} : reduced frequency. | Note: In what follows, one keeps the assumptions \mathit{H1} and \mathit{H2} and one denotes by {I}_{ij}({f}_{r}\text{,Re}) the integral: {I}_{ij}({f}_{r}\text{,Re})=\underset{0}{\overset{1}{\int}}\underset{0}{\overset{1}{\int}}{\Phi}_{t}({\alpha}_{1},{\alpha}_{2},{f}_{r}\text{,Re}){\phi }_{i}({\alpha}_{1}{L}_{e}+{x}_{e}){\phi }_{j}({\alpha}_{2}{L}_{e}+{x}_{e}){\mathrm{d\alpha }}_{1}{\mathrm{d\alpha }}_{2} eq 2.1.2-5 With the help of this notation, the cross-spectra of modal excitations are written: {S}_{{Q}_{i}{Q}_{j}}(f,U)={(\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{\rho U}}^{2}{\text{DL}}_{e})}^{2}\frac{D}{U}{I}_{ij}({f}_{r}\text{,Re}) eq 2.1.2-6 The expression of the auto-spectra of modal excitations is analogous: {S}_{{Q}_{i}{Q}_{i}}(f,U)={(\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{\rho U}}^{2}{\text{DL}}_{e})}^{2}\frac{D}{U}{I}_{ii}({f}_{r}\text{,Re}) eq 2.1.2-7 2.2 Spectra of “correlation length” type 2.2.1 Keywords The factor keywords SPEC_LONG_COR_i ( i varying from 1 to 4) of the operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB U4.44.31 give access to spectra of “correlation length” type. These spectra, specific to configurations of the type “tube bundle under cross-flow”, are predefined but the user can adjust their parameters. 2.2.2 Definition of the model 2.2.2.1 Cross-spectral density In the case of spectra of “correlation length” type, the cross-spectral density characterising the turbulent excitation is assumed to be able to be put in a form with separable variables such that: {S}_{i}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},\omega )={S}_{0}(\omega ){\varphi}_{0}({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) eq 2.2.2.1-1 In this expression, {S}_{0}(\omega ) represents the turbulence auto-spectrum and {\varphi}_{0}({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) denotes a spatial correlation function defined by: {\varphi}_{0}({x}_{1},{x}_{2})=\exp\cdot (\frac{-\mid {x}_{2}-{x}_{1}\mid }{{\lambda}_{c}}) eq 2.2.2.1-2 where {x}_{1} and {x}_{2} denote the abscissae of two observation points and {\lambda}_{c} represents the correlation length. Four analytical expressions are available in the operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB U4.44.31. These expressions each correspond to a particular representation of {S}_{0}(\omega ) . The user defines a turbulence spectrum by choosing one of these analytical forms, whose parameters he can adjust. 2.2.2.2 Modelling of the turbulence spectrum by an expression with separable variables - General case The function {\Phi}_{\text{tt}} introduced in the relation is modelled by a form with separable variables: {\Phi}_{t}({\alpha}_{1},{\alpha}_{2},{f}_{r}\text{,Re})=\sum_{n=1}^{{N}_{s}}{\varphi}_{n}({\alpha}_{1},{\alpha}_{2}){\Phi}_{n}({f}_{r}\text{,Re}) eq 2.2.2.2-1 Where {N}_{s} denotes the degree of the basis of the shape functions {\varphi}_{n} and {\Phi}_{n} is a function independent of the space variable. These two functions are stored in the database and can be selected by the user. The auto-spectra of modal excitations are given by [eq 2.1.2-7] by introducing: {I}_{ii}({f}_{r}\text{,Re})=\sum_{n=1}^{{N}_{s}}{L}_{ni}^{2}\cdot {\Phi}_{n}({f}_{r}\text{,Re}) eq 2.2.2.2-2 with: {L}_{ni}^{2}=\underset{0}{\overset{1}{\int}}\underset{0}{\overset{1}{\int}}{\varphi}_{n}({\alpha}_{1},{\alpha}_{2})\cdot {\phi }_{i}({\alpha}_{1}{L}_{e}+{x}_{e}){\phi }_{i}({\alpha}_{2}{L}_{e}+{x}_{e})\cdot {\mathrm{d\alpha }}_{1}{\mathrm{d\alpha }}_{2} eq 2.2.2.2-3 The principle of the computation is the following: one first computes the values of the {L}_{ni}^{2} by carrying out the computation of the double integrals; one then computes {\Phi}_{n}({f}_{r}\text{,Re}) for all the values of n; one finally obtains the expression of {S}_{{Q}_{i}{Q}_{i}}(f,U) by means of the equation [eq 2.1.2-4]. - Particular case: model used for the steam-generator tubes The particular case of the study of the steam-generator tubes corresponds to a particular case of the general case presented previously by setting \text{Ns}=1 .
