The values of the coefficients of the polynomial in {\tau}_{v} are the following: \begin{array}{}A=24.042\\ B\text{= -}50.421\\ C=63.483\\ D=33.284\end{array} 2.3 Distributed turbulent-excitation model 2.3.1 Keywords The factor keyword SPEC_FONC_FORME of the operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB U4.44.31 makes it possible to define an excitation spectrum by its decomposition on a family of shape functions. The user has the possibility of defining the spectrum by supplying a cross-spectral matrix and a list of associated shape functions. The concepts [interspectre] and [fonction] must then have been generated upstream. In the case of the component “control-rod cluster”, the user can also use a predefined turbulence spectrum, identified on the mock-up GRAPPE1. 2.3.2 Decomposition on a family of shape functions The distributed turbulent-excitation model assumes that the instantaneous line density of the turbulent forces {f}_{t}(x,t) can be decomposed on a family of shape functions {j}_{k}(x) of dimension K in the following way: {f}_{t}(x,t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}{\varphi}_{k}(x){\alpha}_{k}(t) eq 2.3.2-1 The coefficients {\alpha}_{k}(t) define at each time instant the decomposition of the turbulent excitation on the family of shape functions. The cross-spectral density of turbulent excitation between two points of the line structure of abscissae {x}_{1} and {x}_{2} is then written: {S}_{f}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},\omega )=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}{\varphi}_{k}({x}_{1}){\varphi}_{l}({x}_{2}){\mathrm{S\alpha }}_{k}{\alpha}_{l}(\omega ) eq 2.3.2-2 This formulation makes it possible to take into account an excitation whose spatial distribution is arbitrary. 2.3.3 Setting into equations 2.3.3.1 Application of a distributed turbulent excitation The length of application L is characterised intrinsically by the domain of definition of the shape functions associated with the excitation. The zone of application is determined by the data of the name of the node about which it is centred. {x}_{n} denoting the abscissa locating this node, the turbulent excitation is imposed on the domain \left[{x}_{n}-L/2,{x}_{n}+L/2\right] . The turbulent excitation being able, on the other hand, to be developed in a correlated manner in the two directions Y and Z orthogonal to the axis of the line structure, the shape functions are a priori vectors with two components. One therefore supplies, by convention in a table_fonction, two shape functions; the first is associated with the direction Y and the other with the direction Z . Each of the two functions is defined on the interval \left[0,L\right] . 2.3.3.2 Turbulent excitation identified on the mock-up GRAPPE1 The shape functions {\varphi}_{k} are the first 12 flexural modal shapes of the structure identified experimentally, distributed according to the two directions orthogonal to the principal axis of the beam. The general analytical expression of these shapes is the following: {\overrightarrow{\varphi}}_{k}(x)=(\begin{array}{c}{\varphi}_{\text{Yk}}(x)\\ {\varphi}_{\text{Zk}}(x)\end{array}) eq 2.3.3.2-1 with: {\varphi}_{\text{Yk}}(x)={A}_{\text{Yk}}\cdot \cos(\frac{{n}_{\text{Yk}}}{L}x)+{B}_{\text{Yk}}\cdot \sin(\frac{{n}_{\text{Yk}}}{L}x)+{C}_{\text{Yk}}\cdot \text{ch}(\frac{{n}_{\text{Yk}}}{L}x)+{D}_{\text{Yk}}\cdot \text{sh}(\frac{{n}_{\text{Yk}}}{L}x) eq 2.3.3.2-2 {\varphi}_{\text{Zk}}(x)={A}_{\text{Zk}}\cdot \cos(\frac{{n}_{\text{Zk}}}{L}x)+{B}_{\text{Zk}}\cdot \sin(\frac{{n}_{\text{Zk}}}{L}x)+{C}_{\text{Zk}}\cdot \text{ch}(\frac{{n}_{\text{Zk}}}{L}x)+{D}_{\text{Zk}}\cdot \text{sh}(\frac{{n}_{\text{Zk}}}{L}x) eq 2.3.3.2-3 where {n}_{\text{Yk}} and {n}_{\text{Zk}} denote wave numbers, L is the length of application of the excitation and the coefficients {A}_{\text{Yk}} , {B}_{\text{Yk}} , {C}_{\text{Yk}} , {D}_{\text{Yk}} , {A}_{\text{Zk}} , {B}_{\text{Zk}} , {C}_{\text{Zk}} , {D}_{\text{Zk}} are constant real coefficients characteristic of the shape function considered. The first 6 shape functions are associated with the direction Y and {A}_{\text{Zk}} , {B}_{\text{Zk}} , {C}_{\text{Zk}} , {D}_{\text{Zk}} are therefore zero, for 1\le k\le 6 . The last 6 shape functions are associated with the direction Z and {A}_{\text{Yk}} , {B}_{\text{Yk}} , {C}_{\text{Yk}} , {D}_{\text{Yk}} are therefore zero, for 7\le k\le 12 . This family of shape functions is therefore characterised by 5\times 12=60 real coefficients. The turbulent excitation identified on the mock-up GRAPPE1 is homogeneous in the two directions orthogonal to the axis of the line structure, the turbulence being uncorrelated between these two directions. The cross-spectral matrix \left[{\mathrm{S\alpha }}_{k}{\alpha}_{l}\right] identified on the mock-up GRAPPE1 is therefore a matrix of dimension 12\times 12 , constituted of two identical diagonal blocks of dimension 6: \left[{\mathrm{S\alpha }}_{k}{\alpha}_{l}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\left[{S}_{o}(\omega )\right]& \left[0\right]\\ \left[0\right]& \left[{S}_{o}(\omega )\right]\end{array}\right] By the property of Hermitian symmetry, this matrix is entirely defined by the data of the upper (or lower) triangular part of \left[{S}_{o}(\omega )\right] , that is 21 cross-spectra. For each of them, the characteristic parameters are the plateau level, the cut-off frequency and the slope of the spectrum beyond this frequency. The cross-spectral matrix of turbulent excitation identified on the mock-up GRAPPE1 is therefore characterised by 63 real coefficients ( 3\times 21 ). Note: The GRAPPE1 excitations are available at two reference flow rates . The set of the data characterising these excitations therefore represents 246 real coefficients ( [60+63]\times 2 ). 2.3.3.3 Projection of the excitation onto the modal basis One notes: {\phi }_{i}(x)=(\begin{array}{c}{\text{DY}}_{i}(x)\\ {\text{DZ}}_{i}(x)\end{array}) the i -th modal shape of the structure. Let {\beta}_{\text{ik}} be the coordinates of the i -th modal shape of the structure on the basis of the shape functions {\varphi}_{k}(x) : {\phi }_{i}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}{\beta}_{\text{ik}}\cdot {\varphi}_{k}(x) eq 2.3.3.3-1 The cross-spectra of modal excitations {S}_{{Q}_{i}{Q}_{j}}(\omega ) applied to the structure are then written: {S}_{{Q}_{i}{Q}_{j}}(\omega )=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}{\beta}_{\text{ik}}\cdot {\beta}_{\text{jl}}\cdot {S}_{{\alpha}_{k}{\alpha}_{l}}(\omega ) eq 2.3.3.3-2 For each mode i of the structure, the coefficients {\beta}_{\text{ik}} are determined by integrating the equation [eq2.3.3.3-1] premultiplied by the functions {\varphi}_{j} , over the domain of application of the excitation. One thus obtains: \underset{{x}_{0}-L/2}{\overset{{x}_{0}+L/2}{\int}}{\varphi}_{j}(x+L/2)\cdot {\phi }_{i}(x)\cdot \text{dx}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}{\beta}_{\text{ik}}\cdot \underset{{x}_{0}-L/2}{\overset{{x}_{0}+L/2}{\int}}{\varphi}_{j}(x+L/2)\cdot {\varphi}_{k}(x+L/2)\cdot \text{dx} \begin{array}{cc}\underset{{x}_{0}-L/2}{\overset{{x}_{0}+L/2}{\int}}{\varphi}_{j}(x+L/2)\cdot {\phi }_{i}(x)\cdot \text{dx}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}{\beta}_{\text{ik}}\cdot \underset{0}{\overset{L}{\int}}{\varphi}_{j}(x)\cdot {\varphi}_{k}(x)\cdot \text{dx}& \forall (i,j)\end{array} eq 2.3.3.3-3 For each i , the equation [eq 2.3.3.3-3] is written in matrix form: \left[\begin{array}{c}{a}_{\text{jk}}\end{array}\right]\cdot ({\beta}_{\text{ik}})=({b}_{ij}) eq 2.3.3.3-4 with: {a}_{\text{jk}}=\underset{0}{\overset{L}{\int}}{\varphi}_{j}(x)\cdot {\varphi}_{k}(x)\cdot \text{dx} that is: {a}_{\text{jk}}=\underset{0}{\overset{L}{\int}}({\varphi}_{\text{Yj}}(x)\cdot {\varphi}_{\text{Yk}}(\varphi )+{\varphi}_{\text{Zj}}(x)\cdot {\varphi}_{\text{Zk}}(x))\cdot \text{dx} and {b}_{ij}=\underset{{x}_{0}-L/2}{\overset{{x}_{0}+L/2}{\int}}{\varphi}_{j}(x+L/2)\cdot {\phi }_{i}(x)\cdot \text{dx} that is: {b}_{ij}=\underset{{x}_{0}-L/2}{\overset{{x}_{0}+L/2}{\int}}({\text{DY}}_{i}(x)\cdot {\varphi}_{\text{Yj}}(x+L/2)+{\text{DZ}}_{i}(x)\cdot {\varphi}_{\text{Zj}}(x+L/2))\cdot \text{dx} The solution of each of the systems of linear equations leads to the {\beta}_{\text{ik}} . The computation of the scalar products is carried out in the operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE [U4. 63.14]. Notes: 1. The functions {\varphi}_{k}(x) represent, in practice, the modal shapes recorded on the mock-up. The system (), with a dominant diagonal, is therefore well conditioned. In particular, when the mock-up line structure has a homogeneous line mass, the functions {\varphi}_{k}(x) are orthogonal and the matrix \left[\begin{array}{c}{a}_{\text{jk}}\end{array}\right] is diagonal. 2. Tests comparing the domain of application of the excitation with the domain of definition of the structure are carried out. 2.4 Localised turbulent-excitation model 2.4.1 Keywords The factor keyword SPEC_EXCI_POINT of the operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB U4.44.31 is used in the case of an excitation spectrum associated with one or more point forces and moments. The user can define the spectrum by supplying: - a cross-spectral matrix of excitations (the associated concept [interspectre] must be generated upstream), - the list of the nodes of application of these excitations, - the nature of the excitation applied at each of these nodes (force or moment), - the directions of application of the excitations thus defined. He can also use a predefined turbulence spectrum, identified on the mock-up GRAPPE2. 2.4.2 Foundations The localised turbulent-excitation model is a particular case of the distributed turbulent-excitation model. Thus, one assumes, as in paragraph [§2.3.2], that the instantaneous line density of the turbulent forces {f}_{t}(x,t) can be decomposed on a family of shape functions {\varphi}_{k}(x) in the following way: {f}_{t}(x,t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}{\varphi}_{k}(x){\alpha}_{k}(t) eq 2.4.2-1 The coefficients {\alpha}_{k}(t) define at each time instant the decomposition of the turbulent excitation on the family of shape functions. The cross-spectral density of turbulent excitation between two points of the line structure of abscissae {x}_{1} and {x}_{2} is then written: {S}_{f}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},\omega )=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{l=1}^{K}{\varphi}_{k}({x}_{1})\cdot {\varphi}_{l}({x}_{2})\cdot {S}_{{\alpha}_{k}{\alpha}_{l}}(\omega ) eq 2.4.2-2 The particularity of the localised turbulent-excitation model lies in the specificity of the shape functions {\varphi}_{k}(x) : {\varphi}_{k}(x)=\delta (x-{x}_{k}) makes it possible to represent a point force applied at the point of abscissa {x}_{k} {\varphi}_{k}(x)={\delta}^{'}(x-{x}_{k}) makes it possible to represent a point moment applied at the point of abscissa {x}_{k} \delta (x-{x}_{k}) and {\delta}^{'}(x-{x}_{k}) denote respectively the Dirac distribution and the derivative of the Dirac distribution at the point of abscissa {x}_{k} . Given the specificity of the shape functions, the projection of a localised turbulent excitation onto a modal basis is much simpler than in the general case (distributed excitation), since one can compute analytically the expression of the projected excitation. 2.4.3 Setting into equations 2.4.3.1 Application of a localised turbulent excitation One considers a turbulent excitation applied to a line structure and constituted of point forces and moments. This excitation is entirely characterised by the following data: - list of the nodes of application of the point forces and moments, - nature of the excitation applied at each node (force or moment), - direction of the excitation applied at each node. \text{Ainsi}{f}_{t}(x,t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}{F}_{k}(s)\cdot \delta (x-{x}_{k})\cdot {n}_{k}-\sum_{m=1}^{M}{M}_{m}(s)\cdot {\delta}^{'}(x-{x}_{m})\cdot {n}_{m} eq 2.4.3.1-1 is the expression of a localised turbulent excitation, characterised by K forces and M point moments, applied respectively at the nodes of abscissae {x}_{k} and {x}_{m} in the directions {n}_{k} and {\overrightarrow{n}}_{m} . One has: {n}_{k}=(\begin{array}{c}0\\ \cos\cdot ({\theta}_{k})\\ \sin\cdot ({\theta}_{k})\end{array}) and {n}_{m} defined in an analogous way. \theta represents the azimuth giving the direction of application of the force (or of the moment) in the plane P orthogonal to the neutral fibre at the node of application, as defined in the figure [Figure 2.4.3.1-a] below: Figure 2.4.3.1-a: Definition of the direction of application The generalised excitation associated with the i -th mode of the structure, {Q}_{i}(s) , being defined by: {Q}_{i}(s)=\underset{0}{\overset{L}{\int}}{\phi }_{i}(x)\cdot {f}_{t}(x,t)\cdot \text{dx} eq 2.4.3.1-2 where L represents the length of the beam and {\phi }_{i}(x) the shape of the mode i , one obtains, given the expression [eq 2.4.3.1-1]: {Q}_{i}(s)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}{F}_{k}(s)\cdot {\phi }_{i}({x}_{k})\cdot {n}_{k}-\sum_{m=1}^{M}{M}_{m}(s)\cdot {\phi }_{i}({x}_{k})\cdot {n}_{m} eq 2.4.3.1-3 The computation of the cross-spectra of modal excitations then leads to: \begin{array}{c}{S}_{{Q}_{i}{Q}_{j}}(s)=\sum_{{k}_{1}=1}^{K}\sum_{{k}_{2}=1}^{K}{S}_{{F}_{{k}_{1}}{F}_{{k}_{2}}(s)}({\phi }_{i}({x}_{{k}_{1}}).{n}_{{k}_{1}}).({\phi }_{j}({x}_{{k}_{2}}).{n}_{{k}_{2}})\\ +\sum_{{k}_{1}=1}^{K}\sum_{{m}_{2}=1}^{M}{S}_{{F}_{{k}_{1}}{M}_{{m}_{2}}(s)}({\phi }_{i}({x}_{{k}_{1}}).{n}_{{k}_{1}}).({\phi }_{{j}^{¢}}({x}_{{m}_{2}}).{n}_{{m}_{2}})\\ +\sum_{{m}_{1}=1}^{M}\sum_{{k}_{2}=1}^{K}{S}_{{M}_{{m}_{1}}{F}_{{k}_{2}}(s)}({\phi }_{i}^{'}({x}_{{m}_{1}}).{n}_{{m}_{1}}).({\phi }_{j}({x}_{{k}_{2}}).{n}_{{k}_{2}})\\ +\sum_{{m}_{1}=1}^{M}\sum_{{m}_{2}=1}^{M}{S}_{{M}_{{m}_{1}}{M}_{{m}_{2}}(s)}({\phi }_{i}^{'}({x}_{{m}_{1}}).{n}_{{m}_{1}}).({\phi }_{{j}^{¢}}({x}_{{m}_{2}}).{n}_{{m}_{2}})\end{array} eq 2.4.3.1-4 Note: When the user defines the turbulent-excitation spectrum, he must supply the cross-spectral matrix of the point excitations whose terms appear above. This matrix has dimension K+M (number of point forces and moments applied). 2.4.3.2 Turbulent excitation identified on the mock-up GRAPPE2 The turbulent excitation identified on the mock-up GRAPPE2 is represented by a resultant force and a resultant moment, applied at the same node in the two directions orthogonal to the axis of the structure. The line density of this excitation has the expression: {f}_{t}(x,s)=\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{\rho U}}^{2}{D}_{h}\left{L}_{p}\cdot {F}_{t}({s}_{r})\cdot \delta (x-{x}_{0})-{L}_{p}^{2}\cdot {M}_{t}({s}_{r})\cdot {\delta}^{'}(x-{x}_{0})\right eq 2.4.3.2-1 Where \rho is the mass density of the fluid, U is the mean velocity of the flow, {D}_{h} is the hydraulic diameter, {L}_{p} is the thickness of the housing plate (corresponding to the excited length), {x}_{0} is the abscissa of the point of application of the excitation, {s}_{r}=\frac{s\cdot D}{U} is the reduced complex frequency, {F}_{t}({s}_{r}) and {M}_{t}({s}_{r}) are the dimensionless coefficients representing the resultant force and the resultant moment. The quantities \rho , U , {D}_{h} and {L}_{p} make it possible to scale the excitation. By substituting the expression [eq 2.4.3.2-3] into the relation [eq 2.4.3.1-4] defining the modal excitation {Q}_{i}(s) , one obtains: {Q}_{i}(s)=\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{\rho U}}^{2}{D}_{h}\left[{L}_{p}\cdot {F}_{t}({s}_{r})\cdot {\phi }_{i}({x}_{0})\cdot (\begin{array}{c}0\\ 0\\ 1\end{array})+{L}_{p}^{2}\cdot {M}_{t}({s}_{r})\cdot {\phi }_{i}^{'}({x}_{0})\cdot (\begin{array}{c}0\\ 0\\ 1\end{array})\right] eq 2.4.3.2-2 The point force and moment identified on the mock-up GRAPPE2 being uncorrelated, the computation of the cross-spectra of modal excitations finally leads to: \begin{array}{cc}{S}_{{Q}_{i}{Q}_{j}}={(\frac{1}{2}{\rho U}^{2}{D}_{h})}^{2}\frac{D}{U}\cdot & {L}_{p}^{2}\cdot {\phi }_{i}({x}_{0})\cdot \begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}^{\prime}{\phi }_{j}({x}_{0})\cdot \begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}\cdot {S}_{{F}_{t}{F}_{t}}({s}_{r})\\ & +{L}_{p}^{4}\cdot {\phi }_{i}^{\prime}({x}_{0})\cdot \begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}^{\prime}{\phi }_{j}^{\prime}({x}_{0})\cdot \begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}\cdot {S}_{{M}_{t}{M}_{t}}({s}_{r})\end{array} eq 2.4.3.2-3 In this expression, D is the outside diameter of the structure, {S}_{{F}_{t}{F}_{t}}({s}_{r}) and {S}_{{M}_{t}{M}_{t}}({s}_{r}) represent respectively the dimensionless auto-spectra of force and of moment identified on the mock-up GRAPPE2. The operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE U4.63.14 computes the cross-spectra of modal excitations according to the relation [eq 2.4.3.2-3] above. The mock-up GRAPPE2 having been built in similarity with the reactor configuration, the following ratios are fixed and characteristic of this geometry: \frac{{D}_{h}}{D}\text{et}\frac{{L}_{p}}{D} One recalls that {D}_{h} and D denote respectively the hydraulic diameter and the outside diameter of the structure; {L}_{p} is the thickness of the housing plate, corresponding to the excited length. r4.07.04 Fluid–structure coupling for tubular structures and coaxial shells r4.07.04 Fluid–structure coupling for tubular structures and coaxial shells Summary: This document describes the various fluid–structure coupling models available from the operator CALC_FLUI_STRU. These models make it possible to simulate the fluid-elastic coupling forces in the following configurations: - tube bundles under transverse flow (essentially for SG tubes), - control-rod / housing-plate passage (exclusively for control-rod clusters), - coaxial cylindrical shells under annular flow (vessel / core-barrel gap, ...), - tube bundles under axial flow (fuel assemblies, ...). For each configuration, the fluid-elastic force model is presented first. The solution of the modal problem is then described. The solution methods used incorporate the specific features of the various fluid-elastic force models. 1 General presentation 1.1 Reminders The dynamic fluid forces acting on a structure in motion may be classified into two categories: - forces independent of the motion of the structure, at least within the range of small displacements; these are mainly random forces generated by turbulence or by the two-phase nature of the flow, - fluid forces dependent on the motion of the structure, known as “ fluid-elastic forces ”, which are responsible for the fluid–structure coupling. In this document, the four models of fluid-elastic forces implemented in the operator CALC_FLUI_STRU are considered. The computational aspects related to the implementation of these models are the subject of specification notes [bib. 1], [bib. 2]. 1.2 Modelling The dependence of the fluid-elastic forces on the motion of the structure is expressed, for small amplitudes, by a transfer matrix between the fluid-elastic force and the displacement vector . The projection of the equation of motion of the coupled fluid–structure system onto the modal basis of the structure alone is written, in the Laplace domain , as: \lbrace [{M}_{ii}]{s}^{2}+[{C}_{ii}]s+[{K}_{ii}]-[{B}_{ij}(U,s)]\rbrace (q)=({Q}_{t}) eq. 1.2- 1 | where | [{M}_{ii}],[{C}_{ii}]\mathit{et}[{K}_{ii}] denote respectively the diagonal structural mass, damping and stiffness matrices in air; | | --- | --- | | | (q) denotes the vector of generalised displacements in air; | | | ({Q}_{t}) is the vector of generalised random excitations (independent forces); | | and | [{B}_{ij}(U,s)] represents the transfer matrix of the fluid-elastic forces, projected onto the modal basis of the structure alone. This matrix depends in particular on , a characteristic flow speed, and on the frequency of the motion through the Laplace variable . | A priori, [{B}_{ij}(U,s)] is an arbitrary matrix whose extra-diagonal terms, if they are not zero, introduce a coupling between modes. Furthermore, the terms of [{B}_{ij}(U,s)] evolve in a non-linear manner with the complex frequency s . Each fluid-elastic force model is associated with a specific transfer matrix. In every case, the formulation of the modal problem under flow may be characterised by the relation [eq. 1.2-1]. For the various types of configuration that can be simulated with the operator CALC_FLUI_STRU, the representations of the transfer matrices of the fluid-elastic forces are set out in the remainder of this document. 2 Fluid-elastic excitation acting on tube bundles under transverse flow (essentially for SG tubes) Two methods for simulating the fluid-elastic excitation are available in Code_Aster . The first dates back to the late 1970s. It is very widespread in the scientific community, in which it is known as the “Connors method”. The results provided by this method depend to a large extent on the value assigned to one of its main input parameters: the “Connors constant”. Conservative values have therefore had to be determined for this constant on the basis of numerous tests carried out worldwide. The Connors method is well suited to the design of tubular bundles against the vibration risk at the design stage. It is described below in paragraph § 2.5. The second incorporates more physics than the Connors method. However, since a complete modelling of the phenomena is too complex relative to current knowledge, this second method remains based on a set of experimental correlations, known as fluid-elastic correlations. The implementation of this second fluid-elastic excitation model in Code_Aster is discussed in the specification note [bib.1]. The principle note of the FLUSTRU software [bib. 3] constitutes the theoretical reference documentation. It is recalled in outline in paragraphs § 2.1 to 2.4 below. 2.1 Description of the configuration studied A tube bundle excited by an external transverse flow is considered. External transverse flows tend to destabilise the mechanical system as the flow speed increases. An industrial case is that of SG tube vibrations. On this component, transverse flows are observed at the inlet of the tube bundle (single-phase liquid flow) and in the bent part of the tubes (two-phase flow) [Figure 2.1-a]. Figure 2.1-a: Diagram of a steam generator From the standpoint of fluid-elastic coupling, the study of the dynamic behaviour of the various tubes of a bundle subjected to a transverse flow is reduced to the study of an equivalent tube; the definition of the equivalent tube depends on the environment of the tube to be treated. When the tube considered has vibration characteristics appreciably different from those of its neighbours, this tube may be treated as a single tube, vibrating in the midst of a bundle of rigid tubes. Otherwise, the problem is more complex because a mechanical system with coupling between the tubes of the bundle must be considered, and therefore a large number of degrees of freedom. To treat this kind of configuration, a model was developed in the TTA Department, “the global model” [bib. 7]; this model allows the definition of a system equivalent to one degree of freedom, which represents the complete coupled system. The approach adopted for carrying out the analyses may be summarised as follows [Figure 2.1-b]: - Given the slender nature of the structures to be studied, the analysis of the fluid-elastic coupling in the tube bundle is performed by describing the tube through its curvilinear abscissa. - In the analysis, the fluid environment of the tube is characterised both by the physical properties of the fluid flowing inside the tube (primary fluid) and by those of the fluid flowing outside the tube (exciting secondary fluid). These physical properties, such as the density, may vary along the tube, as a function of the curvilinear abscissa. - The flow speed taken into account for the fluid-elastic coupling analysis is the component, normal to the tube in the plane of the tube, of the secondary-fluid velocity. This speed may vary along the tube. - In order to be able to take the various possible types of excitation into account, several excitation zones may be defined along the structure. In the case of the steam generator, for example, it is useful to distinguish, on the one hand, the zones in which the excitation is exerted by a fluid in the single-phase state, located at the tube foot, and, on the other hand, the zone in which the excitation is two-phase with a high void fraction, located in the bent part of the tube. - The coupling analysis is performed from the mechanical characteristics of the structure in “fluid at rest”. The fluid-elastic coupling forces are estimated from dimensionless correlations obtained on analytical similarity experiments. On each excitation zone, the appropriate correlations can thus be applied; the excitation zones must be disjoint. Figure 2.1-b: representation of the configuration to be studied For this fluid-elastic coupling configuration, the following notation will be used: | L | Total length of the tube | | --- | --- | | {L}_{k} | Length of zone k | | :math: | External diameter of the tube | | {d}_{i} | Internal diameter of the tube | | {\varphi}_{i} | Modal shape of mode i | | {\rho}_{i}(x) | Density of the external fluid at the curvilinear abscissa x | | {\rho}_{i}(x) | Density of the internal fluid at the curvilinear abscissa x | | {\rho}_{t} | Density of the tube (structure alone) | | {\rho}_{\mathit{eq}}(x) | Equivalent density at the curvilinear abscissa x | | U | Speed of the external fluid specified by the user in the operator DEFI_FLUI_STRU | | V(x) | Speed of the external fluid at the curvilinear abscissa x | | {V}_{k}(x) | Speed of the external fluid at the curvilinear abscissa x (excitation zone k ) defined by the product of U and a velocity profile specified by the user in the operator DEFI_FLUI_STRU | | {U}_{k} | Mean speed of the external fluid computed from {V}_{k}(x) for excitation zone k | | \overline{U} | Mean of the speeds {U}_{k} over all the excitation zones | 2.2 Stages of the analysis - The first stage of the analysis consists in computing the characteristics of the structure in “fluid at rest”. This is done by considering an equivalent mass of the tube; this equivalent mass groups together, on the one hand, the mass of the tube alone and, on the other hand, the masses added by the internal and external fluids. An equivalent density is thus defined along the tube as a function of the curvilinear abscissa by the expression: {\rho}_{\mathit{eq}}(x)=\frac{1}{({d}_{e}^{2}-{d}_{i}^{2})}[{\rho}_{i}(x).{d}_{i}^{2}+{\rho}_{t}.({d}_{e}^{2}-{d}_{i}^{2})+{\rho}_{e}(x).{d}_{\mathit{eq}}^{2}] eq. 2.2- 1 with {d}_{\mathit{eq}}^{2}=\frac{2.{C}_{m}.{d}_{e}^{2}}{\pi} eq. 2.2- 2 In the equation [:ref: éq. 2.2-1 ], the term {\rho}_{e}(x).{d}_{\mathit{eq}}^{2} represents the mass added by the external fluid. This term depends, through the parameter {C}_{m} , on the arrangement of the tube bundle (square or triangular pitch) and on the confinement of the bundle (reduced pitch). For fluid-elastic coupling analyses of tube bundles subjected to a transverse flow, analytical expressions determined from experimental results are commonly used to estimate the coefficient {C}_{m} . All of the data required to estimate the coefficient {C}_{m} are collected by the operator DEFI_FLUI_STRU. - Knowing the equivalent density of the tube, the elementary mass and stiffness matrices in water at rest are then computed by means of the equivalent-density profile, by the operator CALC_MATR_ELEM; the options MASS_FLUI_STRU and RIGI_FLUI_STRU are used. The operator CALC_MODES makes it possible, after assembly of the elementary matrices, to compute directly the modes in water at rest of the structure studied. - The fluid-elastic coupling forces are computed by the operator CALC_FLUI_STRU from the dimensionless correlations established on analytical similarity mock-ups. These coupling forces, [{B}_{ij}(U,s)] , which depend on the motion of the structure, are then taken into account in the general equation of motion [:ref: éq. 1.2-1 ] in order to compute the characteristics of the coupled flow–structure system for a given flow speed. 2.3 Expression of the transfer matrix of the fluid-elastic forces In the case of tube bundles excited by a transverse flow, the fluid-elastic coupling forces are forces distributed along the structure. They are characterised by dimensionless linear coefficients of added damping and stiffness, denoted respectively {C}_{d} and {C}_{k} . The expression of the coefficients of the transfer matrix of the fluid-elastic forces projected onto the modal basis of the structure in “fluid at rest” is then as follows: {B}_{ij}(U,s)=[(\underset{L}{\int}\text{}\frac{1}{2}{\rho}_{e}(x)V(x){d}_{e}{C}_{d}(x,{s}_{r}){\varphi}_{i}^{2}(x)\mathit{dx})s+\underset{L}{\int}\text{}\frac{1}{2}{\rho}_{e}(x){V}^{2}(x){C}_{k}(x,{s}_{r}){\varphi}_{i}^{2}(x)\mathit{dx}].{\delta}_{ij} eq. 2.3- 1 The dependence of the coefficients {C}_{d} and {C}_{k} on the motion of the structure and on the flow speed of the fluid is expressed by their evolution as a function of the complex reduced frequency , {s}_{r} defined by: {s}_{r}=\frac{s.D}{U} eq. 2.3- 2 The expression [:ref: éq. 2.3-1 ] shows that a diagonal transfer matrix is retained. This operation is performed by the operator CALC_MODES. This stage is indispensable because the fluid-elastic forces are projected onto this basis. - The second stage concerns the taking into account of the fluid-elastic forces by the operator CALC_FLUI_STRU. This stage is decomposed into 7 sub-tasks: 5.2.1 Pre-processing | 1°/ | By means of the topology of the mesh, deduction of the coordinates of the centres of the cylinders of the bundle, then verification of the correct arrangement of the cylinders with respect to one another (one verifies in particular that there is no overlap between two cylinders) and with respect to the rigid enclosure. | | --- | --- | | | | | 2°/ | Determination of the fluid excitation length, common to all the cylinders, as well as of an associated discretisation along the directing axis. | | | | | 3°/ | Construction of the tables giving the modal shapes in air of each cylinder of the bundle, for each of the modes taken into account for the fluid–structure coupling. For this purpose the shapes are interpolated at the points of the discretisation determined previously. | 5.2.2 Solution of the modal problem under flow | 4°/ | Solution of the perturbed fluid problem. The determination of the potential of the perturbed velocities requires the inversion of linear systems of high order, calling for the implementation of the Crout method. | | --- | --- | For each flow speed | 5°/ | Computation of the added mass, damping and stiffness matrices giving the transfer matrix of the fluid-elastic forces in the modal basis in air: full symmetric; a priori full and non-symmetric. | | --- | --- | | | | | 6°/ | Solution of the modal problem under flow; one solves the complete eigenproblem | One does not neglect the extra-diagonal terms of . After reformulation, the solution is performed by means of the QR algorithm: obtaining of the masses, frequencies and reduced modal dampings under flow , complex modal shapes expressed in the basis in air; of the latter, only the real part is retained after minimisation of the imaginary part (computation of a criterion on the imaginary part). | 7°/ | Recovery of the shapes under flow in the physical basis. is the matrix whose columns are the modal shapes in air, expressed in the physical basis. | | --- | --- | End of the loop on the flow speeds Notes: - Knowledge of the coordinates of the centres of the cylinders (pre-processing 1°) is necessary for the solution of the perturbed fluid problem (sub-task 4°). This solution leads to the estimation of the terms of the transfer matrix of the fluid-elastic forces (sub-task 5°), which involve the pressure and velocity perturbations. - The determination of a common excitation length and the creation of an associated discretisation (pre-processing 2°) make it possible to define a domain of integration over the structures for the projection of the fluid-elastic forces onto the modal basis. The interpolation of the modal shapes at the same points is therefore required (pre-processing 3°). - The dynamic behaviour of the bundle under flow may also be studied by means of a simplified representation of the bundle (with equivalent tubes). The stages of the analysis for taking the fluid–structure coupling into account are then identical to those described previously, the only differences appearing in the pre-processing. This second approach is described more precisely in the note [bib. 2]. In stage 1° of the pre-processing, the coordinates of the centres of the cylinders of the bundle are then specified directly by the user, who also establishes the correspondence between the cylinders of the bundle and the beams of the simplified representation given by the mesh. The eigenproblem that one solves is a complex problem. One therefore obtains an even number of complex eigenvalues conjugate in pairs. One retains only those whose imaginary part is positive or zero. The eigenvectors are complex, defined up to a complex multiplicative constant. r4.07.07 Identification of forces on a modal model r4.07.07 Identification of forces on a modal model Summary: The macro-command CALC_ESSAI brings together the Code_Aster features for analysis–test correlation. Within the scope of this documentation one describes the “force identification” feature, which is intended to make it possible to identify the forces applied to a structure in the form of an interspectrum, from the interspectrum of operating measurements, a modal model, identified or computed, and the choice of the location of the points of application of the forces. 1 Introduction, analysis hypotheses This documentation describes the methods used in the macro-command CALC_ESSAI. 1.1 Statement of the problem One considers a structure, which constitutes a dynamic system that one assumes to be linear (hypothesis H1). One assumes that this structure is subjected to an excitation assumed to be random (typical example: turbulent fluid forces), but which one can describe perfectly by means of its PSD (power spectral density, see the document “Modelling of turbulent excitations” R4.07.02, section 2.1). This vibration is measured at a certain number of points of abscissae {x}_{k}(1\le k\le \text{nmes}) . The forces applied to the structure are, for their part, not measurable. One therefore wishes to recover the forces from the measurement. This is an inverse problem, for the solution of which it is necessary to take a great many precautions in order to obtain a result which, if it is not exact, is nevertheless relevant. 1.2 Hypothesis of modal behaviour The structure is assumed to be linear (H1) , so one can describe its mechanical behaviour on a modal basis. Each mode i of the structure is defined by the following parameters: - {\omega}_{i} : natural angular frequency, {f}_{i} associated natural frequency, - {\xi}_{i} : reduced damping, - {m}_{i} : modal mass, - {\varphi}_{i}(\underline{x}) : mode shape. The flow exerts on the structure a force f(\underline{x},t) . One assumes that these forces are applied in one direction. The two measurement directions will be treated separately, assuming that they are not coupled. Displacement on a modal basis: one assumes that the motion of the structure is fairly well described by its first N modes: u(\underline{x},t)\approx \sum_{i=1}^{N}{q}_{i}(t).{\varphi}_{i}(\underline{x}) The generalised coordinates then satisfy the uncoupled equations: {m}_{i}({\ddot{q}}_{i}+2{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}{\dot{q}}_{i}+{\omega}_{{i}^{2}}{q}_{i})=\underset{0}{\overset{L}{\int}}{\varphi}_{i}(\underline{x})f(\underline{x},t)\text{dx}={Q}_{i}(t)\mathrm{\iff }{m}_{i}(-{\omega}^{2}{\stackrel{}{q}}_{i}+2{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}\omega {\stackrel{}{q}}_{i}+{\omega}_{i}^{2}{q}_{i})={Q}_{i}(\omega ),{}^{}1\le i\le N 2 Modelling and computation of the forces The assumed linearity of the behaviour of the structure allows the decomposition of the model on a modal basis: \underline{y}=\underline{\underline{C\Phi }}.\underline{\underline{{Z}^{-1}}}.\underline{\underline{{\Phi}^{T}B}}.\underline{f} Using the notion of interspectrum, favoured in the macro-command 1 : \underline{\underline{{S}_{yy}}}=\underline{\underline{C\Phi }}.\underline{\underline{{Z}^{-1}}}.\underline{\underline{{\Phi}^{T}B}}.\underline{\underline{{S}_{\text{ff}}}}.{\underline{\underline{{\Phi}^{T}B}}}^{H}.\underline{\underline{{Z}^{-1}}}.{\underline{\underline{C\Phi }}}^{H} (1) \underline{\underline{C}} and \underline{\underline{B}} are the observability and command matrices. \underline{\underline{C}} makes it possible to project a field defined on a model onto a more restricted field of sensors. \underline{\underline{B}} projects this same field onto the points of application of the forces. The matrices \underline{\underline{C\Phi }} and \underline{\underline{{\Phi}^{T}B}} are the mode-shape matrices defined on a sensor mesh and on a command mesh. They can be obtained with the operator PROJ_CHAMP or with the operator OBSERVATION, which makes it possible, in addition to the previous operator, to define for each node or node group unmeasured directions, or to define local frames. \underline{\underline{Z}} is the impedance matrix \text{diag}{(-{\omega}^{2}+\mathrm{2j}{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}\omega +{\omega}_{i}^{2})}_{1\le i\le N} associated with the basis of the mode shapes \underline{\underline{\Phi}} . This basis is in general defined on a model of good quality. A basis of good quality must indeed possess modal parameters close to reality. The mode shapes must also be close to reality, and furthermore be sufficiently regular. Thus, an experimental basis of mode shapes is defined on a reduced number of sensors, and is therefore not very regular (one risks a problematic solution of the inverse problem). One will prefer to it the basis of mode shapes of an updated numerical model or, better still, an experimental basis expanded onto a numerical model. This point is clarified below. Note on modal expansion One has an experimental modal basis ({f}_{i},{\xi}_{i},{m}_{i},{\underline{{\varphi}_{\exp}}}_{i}) . The modal parameters are assumed to be identified with a good approximation, but the mode shapes, of good quality, are defined only on a restricted number of sensors. One therefore attempts to extend this basis of mode shapes onto a numerical model which is sufficiently representative of the structure (but not necessarily updated). The expansion basis can be the basis of the modes of the numerical model (obtained with CALC_MODES). Carrying out a modal expansion therefore means finding the vector of generalised parameters \eta minimising: {\mathrm{\parallel }{\underline{{\varphi}_{\exp}}}_{i}-\underline{\underline{{\Phi}_{\text{num}}}}.\underline{\eta}\mathrm{\parallel }}^{2} The “correlation” tab of CALC_ESSAI makes it possible to carry out this expansion, thanks to the use of PROJ_MESU_MODAL. For more details on the principle of the expansion, one should refer to the documentation of PROJ_MESU_MODAL (U4.73.01). 2.1 Solution of the inverse problem Equation (1) of the direct problem can, under certain conditions, be inverted: \underline{\underline{{S}_{\text{ff}}}}={\underline{\underline{{\Phi}^{T}B}}}^{\oplus}.\underline{\underline{Z}}.{\underline{\underline{C\Phi }}}^{\oplus}.\underline{\underline{{S}_{yy}}}.{\underline{\underline{C\Phi }}}^{{H}^{\oplus}}.\underline{\underline{Z}}.{\underline{\underline{{\Phi}^{T}B}}}^{{H}^{\oplus}} The matrices \underline{\underline{C\Phi }} and \underline{\underline{{\Phi}^{T}B}} being rectangular, the sign \oplus denotes their Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse. This pseudo-inverse can be obtained by the use of an SVD algorithm (Singular Value Decomposition, cf. document R6.03.01). In CALC_ESSAI, two regularisation possibilities are available: 1. truncation of the small singular values: one denotes by {\sigma}_{\max} the largest singular value. The SVD consists in setting, for all the singular values lower than \varepsilon {\sigma}_{\max} , for a given \varepsilon , the value 0. They are therefore not taken into account in the inverse computation. The truncation eliminates information on the matrices to be inverted, but improves the conditioning; 2. Tikhonov regularisation: the inverse of the matrix of singular values is not equal to \text{diag}{(\frac{1}{{s}_{i}})}_{1\le i\le N} but to \text{diag}{(\frac{{s}_{i}}{{s}_{{i}^{2}}+\alpha })}_{1\le i\le N} . The parameter \alpha is called the Tikhonov parameter, and makes it possible to limit the divergence of the inverse solution. In CALC_ESSAI, one computes successively the interspectra: - of the generalised displacements (inversion of \underline{\underline{C\Phi }} ), - of the reconstructed physical displacements (in order to check the quality of the inversion), - of the generalised forces (multiplication by the impedance matrix), - of the physical forces (inversion of \underline{\underline{{\Phi}^{T}B}} ), - of the reconstructed generalised forces (for checking) - of the physical displacements by synthesis on the modal basis. A good criterion of the quality of the results of the inversion can be the comparison between the measured displacements and those reconstructed on the same modal basis which was used for the inversion (impedance matrix, and mode-shape matrices). The notion of interspectrum, or of PSD, makes it possible to describe random phenomena. For a deterministic phenomenon, \underline{\underline{{S}_{yy}}}=\underline{y}.\underline{{y}^{H}} , where H denotes the Hermitian operator. For a random signal, \underline{\underline{{S}_{yy}}} contains, on its diagonal, the spectral powers (auto-spectra) and, on its off-diagonal terms, the correlations between the signals. For example, in the case of a fluid force applied to a line-like structure, one readily imagines that the vortices created at the base tend to propagate along the structure. The off-diagonal terms therefore describe this propagation, together with the phase (see R4.07.02 for more details). 3 References 1. Perotin, R. Nhili, MEIDEE software version 2.1: principle note .
