r4.08.01 Computation of the thermal strain r4.08.01 Computation of the thermal strain Summary This document is devoted to the presentation of the computation of the thermal strain. It indicates the information required for the computation of the thermal strain and the various possibilities for the definition of this information by the user. 1 Introduction The values of the expansion coefficients are determined by dilatometry tests which take place starting from the ambient temperature ( 0°C or more generally 20°C ). Consequently, one generally has the values of the expansion coefficient defined with respect to 20°C (the temperature at which the thermal strain is assumed to be zero). Certain studies require a reference temperature different from the ambient temperature (zero thermal strain for a temperature other than the ambient temperature). A change of reference must then be carried out in the computation of the thermal strain (equation and figure below). {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}}\left(T\right)={\epsilon}_{m}^{\mathit{th}}\left(T\right)-{\epsilon}_{m}^{\mathit{th}}\left({T}_{\mathit{ref}}\right) Where {\epsilon}_{m}^{\mathit{th}} is the measured thermal strain (defined with respect to the ambient temperature) and {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}} is the computed thermal strain (defined with respect to a reference temperature). In code_aster , the thermal strain is computed by the following expression: {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}}\left(T\right)=\widehat{\alpha}\left(T\right)\left(T-{T}_{\mathit{ref}}\right) where \widehat{\alpha}\left(T\right) is the mean expansion coefficient (in the RCC_M sense) at the temperature T determined with respect to the temperature {T}_{\mathit{ref}} ( {T}_{\mathit{ref}} being the temperature at which one considers that {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}}\left({T}_{\mathit{ref}}\right)=0 ). In THM, the computation of the thermal strain is different. The thermal strain is evaluated by the following formula: {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}}\left(T\right)=\alpha \left(T-{T}_{\mathit{ini}}\right) The thermal expansion coefficient \alpha is necessarily a constant. The curve cannot be shifted. The thermal expansion coefficient must therefore have been evaluated at the ambient temperature. In addition, the reference temperature is given by THM_INIT/TEMP in DEFI_MATERIAU. 2 Computation of the thermal expansion coefficient 2.1 From the reference temperature The values of the thermal expansion coefficient have been determined by dilatometry tests carried out starting from the temperature {T}_{\mathit{ref}} . In this case, the keyword TEMP_DEF_ALPHA must not be specified in the command DEFI_MATERIAU u4.23.01. The equation is simplified, since {\epsilon}_{m}^{\mathit{th}}\left({T}_{\mathit{ref}}\right)=0 . Hence: {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}}\left(T\right)=\widehat{\alpha}\left(T\right)\left(T-{T}_{\mathit{ref}}\right) Where the values of the expansion coefficient \widehat{\alpha}\left(T\right) are entered under the keyword ALPHA (or ALPHA_ ) in DEFI_MATERIAU. 2.2 From a temperature different from the reference temperature The values of the thermal expansion coefficient have been determined by dilatometry tests which took place starting from a temperature {T}_{\text{def}} different from the reference temperature {T}_{\mathit{ref}} . Indeed, in general one has the values of the expansion coefficient defined with respect to the ambient temperature, 0°C or more generally 20°C , and certain studies require a reference temperature different from the ambient temperature. A change of reference must then be carried out (by the equation ). In this case, the user enters, under the keyword TEMP_DEF_ALPHA of the command DEFI_MATERIAU, the value of the temperature {T}_{\text{def}} , and under the keyword ALPHA (or ALPHA_ ) the values of the expansion coefficient \alpha \left(T\right) (defined with respect to the temperature {T}_{\text{def}} ). In the command AFFE_MATERIAU, under the keyword TEMP_REF, the user indicates the value of the reference temperature {T}_{\mathit{ref}} . The computation of {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}}\left(T\right) is carried out using the formula: {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}}\left(T\right)=\alpha \left(T\right)\left(T-{T}_{\text{def}}\right)-\alpha \left({T}_{\mathit{ref}}\right)\left({T}_{\mathit{ref}}-{T}_{\text{def}}\right)=\widehat{\alpha}\left(T\right)\left(T-{T}_{\mathit{ref}}\right) The computation of {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}}\left(T\right) requires the prior computation of the values of the function \widehat{\alpha}\left(T\right) . The function \widehat{\alpha}\left(T\right) remains defined (or entered) for the same values of T as \alpha \left(T\right) and keeps the same attributes (same type of interpolation ('LIN', 'LOG') and same type of prolongation ('CONSTANT', 'LINEAIRE', 'EXCLUS'). 2.2.1 Computation at temperatures different from the reference (to within a precision) The expression of \widehat{\alpha}({T}_{i}) is obtained using the equation . \widehat{\alpha}\left(T_{i}\right) = \frac{\alpha\left(T_{i}\right)\left(T_{i} - T_{\text{def}}\right) - \alpha\left(T_{\mathit{ref}}\right)\left(T_{\mathit{ref}} - T_{\text{def}}\right)}{T_{i} - T_{\mathit{ref}}} \quad \forall i \text{ tel que } T_{i} - T_{\mathit{ref}} \ge \text{Prec} The value of the precision is: - either specified by the user under the keyword PRECISION of the factor keyword ELAS_FO (command DEFI_MATERIAU u4.23.01), - or equal to 1. : default value. 2.2.2 Computation at temperatures close to the reference (to within a precision) The equation cannot be used directly. The equation is differentiated with respect to the temperature: \frac{\partial {\epsilon}^{\mathit{th}}}{\partial T}=\alpha '(T)(T-{T}_{\text{def}})+\alpha (T)=\widehat{\alpha}'(T)(T-{T}_{\mathit{ref}})+\widehat{\alpha}(T) Taking the value of the derivative at the temperature {T}_{\mathit{ref}} , one obtains: \widehat{\alpha}({T}_{\mathit{ref}})=\alpha '({T}_{\mathit{ref}})({T}_{\mathit{ref}}-{T}_{\text{def}})+\alpha ({T}_{\mathit{ref}}) It is considered that: \widehat{\alpha}(T_{i}) = \widehat{\alpha}(T_{\mathit{ref}}) \quad \forall i \text{ tel que } T_{i} - T_{\mathit{ref}} \ge \text{Prec} The value of the precision is: - either specified by the user under the keyword PRECISION of the factor keyword ELAS_FO (command DEFI_MATERIAU u4.23.01), - or equal to 1. : default value. Also, in order to compute \widehat{\alpha}({T}_{i}) one must first compute \alpha '({T}_{\mathit{ref}}) . 2.2.3 Computation of the derivative of the thermal expansion coefficient The computation of the derivative of the thermal expansion coefficient is carried out by an algorithm that treats three cases. First case: \forall i\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{tel que}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}|{T}_{i}-{T}_{\mathit{ref}}|\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}<\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{Prec}\text{avec}i\ne 1,i\ne N \alpha '({T}_{\mathit{ref}})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\alpha ({T}_{i+1})-\alpha ({T}_{\mathit{ref}})}{{T}_{i+1}-{T}_{\mathit{ref}}}+\frac{\alpha ({T}_{\mathit{ref}})-\alpha ({T}_{i-1})}{{T}_{\mathit{ref}}-{T}_{i-1}}\right) Second case: \forall i\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{tel que}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}|{T}_{i}-{T}_{\mathit{ref}}|\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}<\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{Prec}\text{avec}i=N \alpha '({T}_{\mathit{ref}})=\frac{\alpha ({T}_{\mathit{ref}})-\alpha ({T}_{i-1})}{{T}_{\mathit{ref}}-{T}_{i-1}} Third case: \forall i \quad \text{tel que} \quad \left| T_{i} - T_{\mathit{ref}} \right| < \text{Prec} \quad \text{avec } i = 1 \alpha'(T_{\mathit{ref}}) = \frac{\alpha(T_{i+1}) - \alpha(T_{\mathit{ref}})}{T_{i+1} - T_{\mathit{ref}}}

r4.09.01 Energy balance in thermo-mechanics r4.09.01 Energy balance in thermo-mechanics Summary: This documentation presents the writing of the energy balance for an analysis with Code_Aster . The computation of the energy balance can be activated in the operators STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03, DYNA_NON_LINE U4.53.01 and DYNA_VIBRA[U4.53.03] on a physical basis thanks to the option ENERGIE=_F(). This functionality therefore covers the thermo-hydro-mechanical analyses in quasi-statics and in dynamics. Excluded are the thermal analyses (operators THER_LINEAIRE, THER_NON_LINE and THER_NON_LINE_MO) and the modal analyses (operator DYNA_VIBRA on a modal basis). 1 Computation of the energy balance of an analysis The energy balance of an analysis can be very useful information. On the one hand, it makes it possible to take a critical look at the quality of the results, in the same way as an equilibrium residual in the Newton algorithm. On the other hand, it provides information on the physical phenomena involved and brings answers to the following questions: what is the energy transmitted to my system? What becomes of it? To do this, one establishes in what follows the writing of the energy balance for an analysis with Code_Aster on the complete model. We distinguish the nature of each energy term and we take care to define its origin. 1.1 Work of a force Let us consider the evolution at various time instants {t}_{i} of a deformable solid subjected to a variable external force \mathrm{F}(t) . Let {\mathrm{U}}_{i} be the displacement-field solution for each time instant {t}_{i} and {\mathrm{F}}_{i}=\mathrm{F}({t}_{i}) . The curve of the external force as a function of the displacement is given on the . From the energy point of view, the increment of external work supplied to the system between two consecutive time instants ({t}_{0},{t}_{1}) represents the area under the curve, which is computed by the trapezium method: {A}_{1}={\int}_{{t}_{0}}^{{t}_{1}}\mathrm{F}(t).\dot{\mathrm{U}}(t)=\frac{{\mathrm{F}}_{0}+{\mathrm{F}}_{1}}{2}.({\mathrm{U}}_{1}-{\mathrm{U}}_{0})={\bar{\mathrm{F}}}_{1}.{\Delta \mathrm{U}}_{1} where: - {\bar{\mathrm{F}}}_{1} represents the mean force over the time increment (the index is chosen as being that of the end time), - {\Delta \mathrm{U}}_{1} represents the displacement increment between {t}_{0} and {t}_{1} . Figure 1.1-1: Force–displacement curve. The increment of work of any force may therefore be considered as the scalar product of two vectors: the mean force over the time step and the displacement increment. This method of computing the increment of work of a force is practical within the framework of numerical simulation, since the solution is known at various time instants only, corresponding to the chosen time discretisation. 1.2 Energy balance Let us consider the dynamic equilibrium equation of a system in its form discretised in space: \mathrm{M}\ddot{\mathrm{U}}(t)+\mathrm{C}(t)\dot{\mathrm{U}}(t)+\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{U}(t),\dot{\mathrm{U}}(t),t)=\mathrm{L}(t) where: - \mathrm{U} , \dot{\mathrm{U}} and \ddot{\mathrm{U}} are the vectors of the displacements, velocities and accelerations at the nodes, - \mathrm{M} and \mathrm{C} are the mass and damping matrices, - \mathrm{R} represents the internal forces (in linear elasticity, this is the term \mathrm{K}\mathrm{U} ), from which one has removed what is considered as the damping forces, - \mathrm{L} is the vector of the external forces. This writing, inspired by R5.05.05, is here simplified with respect to the original writing which brings in Lagrange multipliers for the Dirichlet boundary conditions and the unilateral conditions. Note that the damping matrix \mathrm{C}\left(t\right) may depend on time if its construction is based on the tangent stiffness matrix and not the elastic one (option AMOR_RAYL_RIGI in the operator DYNA_NON_LINE). Each term of equation ( ) is homogeneous to a force. The energy evolution of the system between two consecutive analysis time instants {t}_{0} and {t}_{1} is translated directly by the work of each of these forces. Taking up again the notations of mean quantity (grandeur) and increment of quantity used in equation ( ), one obtains: - the increment of kinetic energy: \Delta {E}_{\mathit{cin}}={\int}_{{\mathrm{U}}_{0}}^{{\mathrm{U}}_{1}}{\left(\mathrm{M}\ddot{\mathrm{U}}\right)}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathrm{dU}={\int}_{{t}_{0}}^{{t}_{1}}{\left(\mathrm{M}\ddot{\mathrm{U}}\right)}^{\mathrm{T}}\dot{\mathrm{U}}\mathit{dt}={\left[\frac{1}{2}{\dot{\mathrm{U}}}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathrm{M}\dot{\mathrm{U}}\right]}_{{t}_{0}}^{{t}_{1}}={\overline{\dot{\mathrm{U}}}}_{1}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathrm{M}\Delta {\dot{\mathrm{U}}}_{1} One recovers an expression identical to equation ( ) by considering as force \mathrm{F}=\mathrm{M}\ddot{\mathrm{U}} , the operator \mathrm{M} being assumed constant. - the increment of energy dissipated by damping: \Delta {W}_{\mathit{amor}}={\overline{\mathrm{C}\left(\mathrm{t}\right)\dot{\mathrm{U}}}}_{1}^{\mathrm{T}}.\Delta {\mathrm{U}}_{1} As the damping matrix may be time-dependent, one must evaluate the quantity \mathrm{C}\left(\mathrm{t}\right)\dot{\mathrm{U}} at {t}_{0} and at {t}_{1} , then take its mean. This stage is neglected, and one in fact computes the following quantity: \Delta {W}_{\mathit{amor}}=\overline{{\dot{\mathrm{U}}}_{1}^{\mathrm{T}}}\mathrm{C}\left({t}_{1}\right)\Delta {\mathrm{U}}_{1} L'énergie dissipée par amortissement est donc calculée de manière approchée. - The increment of total strain energy: \Delta {E}_{\mathit{tot}}={\overline{\mathrm{R}}}_{1}^{\mathrm{T}}\Delta {\mathrm{U}}_{1} - The increment of work of the external forces: \Delta {W}_{\mathit{ext}}={\overline{\mathrm{L}}}_{1}^{\mathrm{T}}\Delta {\mathrm{U}}_{1} In the presence of frictional contact, an additional force term appears in the equilibrium equation, corresponding to the contact force. From the energy point of view, its contribution is computed easily in a manner similar to ( ), but it cannot be taken into account in any of the energies defined above. One therefore creates a new energy which represents the energy stored and/or dissipated by the link forces, which we name \Delta {W}_{\mathit{liai}} . The mechanical energy balance of the system is then written: \Delta {W}_{\mathit{ext}}=\Delta {E}_{\mathit{cin}}+\Delta {E}_{\mathit{tot}}+\Delta {W}_{\mathit{amor}}+\Delta {W}_{\mathit{liai}} Under the assumption that the solution is strictly exact, the left-hand term is equal to the sum of the right-hand terms. In reality, the numerical solution scheme induces discrepancies for various reasons: - the Newton algorithm is an iterative solution algorithm, whose convergence is detected when the relative equilibrium residual of the forces is lower than a certain criterion. By definition, the solution found is therefore correct to within a tolerance, which inevitably creates an equilibrium discrepancy in the energy balance. One can then improve the energy balance by tightening the convergence criterion, but the accuracy reached with the default criterion is generally satisfactory. - Among the numerical time-integration schemes, only some are not dissipative. Modifying the default values of these schemes, such as the Newmark scheme, leads to a numerical dissipation. The user may refer to the documentation R5.05.05 for more information on the dissipation of the numerical time-integration schemes. The energy balance finds here a first utility of importance: it makes it possible to quantify the energy dissipated by the numerical scheme. In shock analyses for example, it is common to use dissipative numerical schemes in order to filter the high frequencies. One thus defines the energy dissipated by the numerical scheme: \Delta {W}_{\mathit{sch}}=\Delta {W}_{\mathit{ext}}-\Delta {E}_{\mathit{cin}}-\Delta {E}_{\mathit{tot}}-\Delta {W}_{\mathit{amor}}-\Delta {W}_{\mathit{liai}} 1.3 Construction of the various energy terms An energy is considered as the work of a force. Numerically, the computation of an energy term consists first of all in building a global vector corresponding to the sum of all the forces whose contribution to the energy balance is stored in the same term. There exist numerous force vectors and we define in this part those which feed each of the energy terms. 1.3.1 Work of the external forces One defines as external work the work: - of all the forces associated with the commands AFFE_CHAR_MECA and AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F, with the exception of FORCE_SOL accounted for in the work of the link forces, - of the forces coming from the analysis by substructuring (use of macro-elements), - of all the forces associated with the commands AFFE_CHAR_CINE and AFFE_CHAR_CINE_F. In the strict sense of the term, the command AFFE_CHAR_CINE makes it possible to define boundary conditions of imposed displacement, whose work ought to be accounted for as link energy. For practical reasons, its contribution is added to the external work. In general, it is possible to recover the force corresponding to this imposed displacement. Certain cases may nevertheless pose a problem, as for example the test case ssnp155a (see § 2.1.2.1 ). 1.3.2 Work of the link forces One defines as work of the link forces the work: - of the contact and friction forces coming from the command DEFI_CONTACT, - of the force coming from the absorbing-boundary elements, - of the force coming from the option FORCE_SOL in the command AFFE_CHAR_MECA. 1.3.3 Work of the damping forces One defines as work of the damping forces the work: - of the damping force coming from the damping matrix (term \mathrm{C}\dot{\mathrm{U}}=(\alpha \mathrm{K}+\beta \mathrm{M})\dot{\mathrm{U}} ), - of the modal damping force (keyword AMOR_MODAL in the analysis operators). 1.3.4 Total strain energy The total strain energy groups all the contributions which require integrating a constitutive law. This may lead to arbitrary choices. For example, one accounts in the total strain energy for the contribution of the joint elements or of the cohesive elements, although it would be more natural to include them in the computation of the energy linked to the links. Likewise, when one uses constitutive laws to represent the contact with the discrete elements, the contribution is included in the total strain energy whereas it would be more in its place in the energy linked to the links. The rule is that, when it is a constitutive behaviour carried by finite elements defined in the model, then the contribution is added to {E}_{\mathit{tot}} . 1.4 Taking an initial state into account Let us consider the example of a mass–spring system subjected to an initial shock. In Code_Aster , the user can simply give an initial acceleration. This corresponds to the following equation: | \begin{array}{c}m\ddot{u}\left(t\right)+ku\left(t\right)=F\left(t\right)\\ u=0\\ F=0\\ \ddot{u}\ne 0\end{array} with as initial conditions: \begin{array}{c}u(0)=0\\ \dot{u}(0)=0\\ F(0)=0\\ \ddot{u}(0)\ne 0\end{array} | | | --- | --- | One notes that there is an incompatibility: the user supplies an unbalanced initial state. Strictly speaking, the equations of dynamics being of second order in time, there can be only a displacement or a velocity imposed at the initial time instant. If one wishes to impose an initial acceleration, one should in principle give the force which balances the equation of the system. The numerical scheme does not need it because this does not influence the solution. Nevertheless, this influences the computation of the energy balance because without this initial force, the balance is incorrect. Indeed, the energy equilibrium over the first time step is then written: \begin{array}{c}{W}_{\mathit{ext}}={E}_{\mathit{tot}}+{E}_{\mathit{cin}}\\ {W}_{\mathit{ext}}=0\\ {E}_{\mathit{tot}}>0\\ {E}_{\mathit{cin}}>0\end{array} The contribution of the external force which corresponds to this initial acceleration is missing. By taking it into account, one then obtains a non-zero term {W}_{\mathit{ext}} . In the general case, the energy balance can be correct only if the analysis starts from a balanced state. In the absence of an initial state, this condition is implicitly fulfilled. Particular attention must therefore be paid to the various possibilities of introducing a non-virgin initial state. 1.4.1 Case of the restarts from a state computed beforehand In this part, one is interested in restarts from a state computed beforehand, namely the use in ETAT_INIT of the keywords: - EVOL_NOLI for STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, - RESULTAT for DYNA_VIBRA. In order to compute each of the energy terms of equation ( ), one must therefore have available at the restart step: - the nodal vectors of displacement, velocity and accelerations, - the mass and damping matrices, - the internal forces resulting from the stress state, - the force vectors {\mathrm{F}}_{\mathit{ext}} , {\mathrm{F}}_{\mathit{amor}} and {F}_{\mathit{liai}} . The nodal vectors of displacement, velocity and acceleration, as well as the mass matrix and the internal forces, are always available. The damping matrix is in fact not necessary since one uses equation ( ) to evaluate the energy dissipated by damping, where this matrix is evaluated at the time instant {t}_{1} . Only the last three force vectors require particular attention. The vectors {\mathrm{F}}_{\mathit{amor}} and {\mathrm{F}}_{\mathit{liai}} must have been archived because it is impossible to recreate them. Thus, when one activates the computation of the energy balance, one automatically activates the archiving of two additional nodal fields named FORC_AMOR and FORC_LIAI. These fields are intended to be re-read in the event of a restart in order to initialise correctly the computation of the energy balance. Finally, concerning the vector {\mathrm{F}}_{\mathit{ext}} of the external forces, for STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, it is recomputed at the restart time {t}_{0} in accordance with the equilibrium equation ( ) of the system: {\mathrm{F}}_{\mathit{ext}}\left({t}_{0}\right)=\mathrm{M}\ddot{\mathrm{U}}\left({t}_{0}\right)+\mathrm{C}\left({t}_{1}\right)\dot{\mathrm{U}}\left({t}_{0}\right)+\mathrm{R}\left(\mathrm{U}\left({t}_{0}\right),\dot{\mathrm{U}}\left({t}_{0}\right)\right) In the case of an analysis with DYNA_VIBRA on a physical basis, one saves directly the external force FORC_EXTE. 1.4.2 Case of an analysis with an initial state given explicitly The user may be led to supply a non-virgin initial state in the form of a combination of the following fields: - a displacement field (keyword DEPL) - a velocity field (keyword VITE) - an acceleration field (keyword ACCE) - a stress field (keyword SIGM) - a field of internal variables (keyword VARI) The datum of the displacement, velocity and acceleration fields is automatically handled as in the case of an initial state coming from a previous analysis, by means of equation ( ). Note that the time schemes of the dynamics operators DYNA_NON_LINE and DYNA_VIBRA are led to compute an initial acceleration if the user does not supply one. This case is handled in the same manner. By way of example, in the case of the mass–spring system subjected to an initial acceleration, we build the following initial vector {F}_{\mathit{ext}} : {\mathrm{F}}_{\mathit{ext}}({t}_{0})=m\ddot{u}({t}_{0}) The datum of a stress field or of internal variables is also handled automatically, since these quantities (grandeurs) come into play in the computation of the term \mathrm{R}(\mathrm{U}({t}_{0}),\dot{\mathrm{U}}({t}_{0})) of equation ( ). 1.4.3 Initial energy state It is important to note that the energy balance is supplied in incremental form. Thus, it is possible to compute only a variation of the various energy terms between two analysis time instants. It is moreover this information which is useful in order to know the various energy transfers. When the initial state of an analysis is supplied from a result (see 1.4.1 ), the initial energy state is recovered. On the other hand, when the initial state is not given by a “result” data structure, one can neither recover nor compute the initial energy state. Consequently, the various terms of the energy balance are initialised to 0. 2 Help with use and applications 2.1 Advice In what follows, we indicate a few good practices facilitating the obtaining of a satisfactory energy balance. - Use a suitable formalism The set of the analyses presented falls within a Lagrangian configuration. Indeed, one brings in a mean-force term over the time step, obtained by summing a force written at the previous step with a force written at the current step. This does not pose a problem for the operator DYNA_VIBRA. But this may generate an incorrect energy balance for STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, when the formalism used, defined under the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT, is: - PETIT_REAC - SIMO_MIEHE In these two cases, it is advised to take small time steps in order to limit the discrepancy between the analysis configurations from one time step to the next. - Start from a balanced state A first precaution is to start from a balanced initial state. Equilibrium is ensured by computing the external force {F}_{\mathit{ext}} which balances the initial state (see § 1.4.1 ). In the majority of cases, this corresponds to reality. It is nevertheless strongly advised to start from an already balanced state when this is possible. - Use suitable convergence criteria Another important point to mention is the influence of the convergence criterion on the quality of the energy balance. The convergence of the analysis is ensured to within a tolerance, through the value of RESI_GLOB_RELA or RESI_GLOB_MAXI. When this criterion is too loose, the numerical dissipation may become non-negligible. In case of doubt, it is advised to re-run the analysis with a tighter criterion, in order to check that the energy dissipated by the integration decreases. - Prefer the command AFFE_CHAR_MECA to the command AFFE_CHAR_CINE The command AFFE_CHAR_CINE is particular. It consists, during the solution, in removing the degrees of freedom where a displacement is imposed. This functionality is of interest, since it makes it possible to reduce the size of the system to be solved. Nevertheless, it may pose a problem in the evaluation of the energy balance under certain conditions, admittedly rather rare. An example is given in part 2.1.2.1 . 2.2 A few applications In this part, we choose a few test cases in order to decipher their energy balance. The analyses are carried out with version 11.1.12 of Code_Aster . 2.2.1 Test case ssnp155a This test models a stamping of a sheet by a punch in a die (figure ). The structure is modelled in plane strains. One takes the symmetry into account in order to represent only one half. The punch and the die are modelled with boundary elements, on which one imposes a displacement by means of the command AFFE_CHAR_CINE. One then obtains at the end of the analysis an energy balance which is manifestly incorrect, since {W}_{\mathit{ext}} is zero and since {W}_{\mathit{sch}} ought to be very small compared with the other energy terms (table ). punch Figure 2.1.2.1-1: Geometry of the test case ssnp155a die | {W}_{\mathit{ext}} | {E}_{\mathit{tot}} | {E}_{\mathit{cin}} | {W}_{\mathit{liai}} | {W}_{\mathit{sch}} | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0 | 6,8808E+01 | 3,7883E-05 | 1,4873E-01 | -6,8957E+01 | Table 2.1.2.1-1: Energy balance of the test case ssnp155a at the end of the analysis The explanation is the following: the fact of using the command AFFE_CHAR_CINE removes from the solution the set of the degrees of freedom of the punch. In order to compute the contribution to the external work of the displacements imposed via the command AFFE_CHAR_CINE, one builds the vector of the displacements restricted to the nodes on which a displacement is imposed, and one uses equation ( ) with as force the vector of the internal forces. In this test case, the external work is solely that due to the imposed displacement of the punch. But as it is modelled only with boundary elements, which have no stiffness, their contribution to the vector of the internal forces is zero. One is therefore unable to recover the force which corresponds to the imposed displacement, and one obtains a zero external work. In order to obtain a correct balance, it is sufficient to use the command AFFE_CHAR_MECA to impose the displacement. With the latter, in order to guarantee the satisfaction of the imposed-displacement conditions, Lagrange multipliers are built corresponding in fact to the force to be taken into account in the computation of the external work. Another solution would have been to mesh the punch in order to be able to compute the internal forces there. In both cases, one then arrives at the energy balance indicated in the table below: | {W}_{\mathit{ext}} | {E}_{\mathit{tot}} | {E}_{\mathit{cin}} | {W}_{\mathit{liai}} | {W}_{\mathit{sch}} | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 6,8979E+01 | 6,8808E+01 | 3,7883E-05 | 1,4873E-01 | 2,2804E-02 | Table 2.1.2.1-2: Energy balance with use of AFFE_CHAR_MECA The equilibrium of the balance has clearly improved. Nevertheless, the term {W}_{\mathit{sch}} remains significant. This is in fact due to the use of a dissipative HHT scheme. When one uses a non-dissipative Newmark scheme, the term {W}_{\mathit{sch}} becomes negligible compared with the other energies (table ): | {W}_{\mathit{ext}} | {E}_{\mathit{tot}} | {E}_{\mathit{cin}} | {W}_{\mathit{liai}} | {W}_{\mathit{sch}} | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 6,8947E+01 | 6,8872E+01 | 1,6589E-02 | 5,7774E-02 | -1,4257E-08 | Table 2.1.2.1-3: Energy balance with use of AFFE_CHAR_MECA and of a non-dissipative scheme 2.2.2 Test case sdlv120a This test case, illustrated in the figure , models an infinite elastic bar in which one creates a compression wave by imposing a displacement at one of its ends. The other end of the bar is assigned elastic paraxial elements of order 0 intended to apply absorbing conditions at the boundary of the mesh, in order to account for the infinite medium. Figure 2.1.2.2-1: Geometry of the test case sdlv120a One then obtains the following evolution represented in the figure for the various energies involved: Figure 2.1.2.2-2: Energy evolution in the test case sdlv120a One observes that the energy brought in from the outside propagates in the bar in the form of total strain energy and of kinetic energy before being rapidly dissipated thanks to the absorbing-boundary elements. 2.2.3 Test case wtnv109a This test case models the effect of the mechanics and of the hydraulics on the thermal response. An element is stretched by imposing on it a displacement in the direction z , while applying to it a constant hydraulic pressure, which leads to a decrease in its temperature. We have chosen it in order to illustrate the influence of the convergence criterion on the equilibrium of the energy balance. In the table , one presents the energy balance with the default value of the criterion RESI_GLOB_RELA, namely 1.E-6 , then for a value of 1.E-12 . | RESI_GLOB_RELA | {W}_{\mathit{ext}} | {E}_{\mathit{tot}} | {W}_{\mathit{sch}} | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1.E-6 | 1,1296E+02 | 1,1303E+02 | -7,0833E-02 | | 1.E-12 | 1,1303E+02 | 1,1303E+02 | -2,3590E-12 | Table 2.1.2.3-1: Energy balance of the test case wtnv109a One notes that the equilibrium discrepancy, symbolised by the value of {W}_{\mathit{sch}} , has been reduced by a factor of 10.

r4.10.01 ZHU-ZIENKIEWICZ error estimator r4.10.01 ZHU-ZIENKIEWICZ error estimator Summary: This document sets out the method of estimation of the discretisation error proposed by ZHU‑ZIENKIEWICZ. This estimator is based on a continuous smoothing of the computed stresses, making it possible to obtain a better accuracy on the nodal stresses than the standard methods. Two successive versions of this estimator are described, each corresponding to a different smoothing. > Contents 1 Introduction Research on error estimators for the solutions obtained by finite-element analyses, and their coupling with adaptive meshing procedures, has grown considerably in recent years. The aim is to remedy the possible inadequacy of a modelling by automatically adapting the mesh to the solution sought, according to certain criteria (equal distribution of the discretisation error, minimisation of the number of nodes in order to reach a given accuracy, least cost). An a posteriori error estimator is presented here within the framework of linear homogeneous elasticity. Historically, this estimator, proposed by ZHU-ZIENKIEWICZ [bib1] in 1987, was widely used because of its ease of implementation in existing analysis codes and of its low cost. Nevertheless, the poor reliability of this estimator for elements of even degree was observed empirically (underestimation of the error) and led the authors to a modification of their method in 1992 [bib2], [bib3], with numerical verification of the asymptotic convergence of the estimator on all types of element. Nevertheless, the field of application of the 1992 version being for the moment more restricted (see [3.2]), both versions of this estimator have been implemented in Aster and are the subject of this note. 2 Principle of the method 2.1 Equations to be solved Consider the solution (u,s) of a linear elastic problem satisfying: - the equilibrium equations: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\text{Lu}=q\text{dans}\Omega \\ {\sigma}_{ij}{n}_{j}={\bar{t}}_{i}\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{t}\end{array} with L={}^{t}\mathrm{BDB} the elasticity operator - the compatibility equations: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\varepsilon =\text{Bu}\\ u=\bar{u}\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{u}\end{array} with \Gamma ={\Gamma}_{u}\cup {\Gamma}_{t} - the constitutive law: \sigma =D\varepsilon The problem discretised by finite elements consists in finding ({u}_{h},{\sigma}_{h}) , the solution of: {u}_{h}=N{\bar{u}}_{h} eq 2.1-1 satisfying K{\bar{u}}_{h}=\text{f} with K=\underset{\Omega}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}(\mathrm{BN})D(\mathrm{BN})d\Omega \text{f}=\underset{\Omega}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}\mathrm{Nq}d\Omega +\underset{{G}_{t}}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}N\bar{t}\mathrm{dG} where: {\bar{\text{u}}}_{h} represents the nodal unknowns of displacement N the associated shape functions The stresses are computed from the displacements by the relation: {\sigma}_{h}={\mathrm{DBu}}_{h} eq 2.1-2 2.2 Error estimator and effectivity index | One denotes | e=u-{u}_{h} | the error on the displacements | | --- | --- | --- | | | {e}_{s}=s-{s}_{h} | the error on the stresses | The energy norm of the error e is written: \parallel \text{e}\parallel ={(\underset{\Omega}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}\mathrm{eLe}d\Omega )}^{1/2} in the case of elasticity ={(\underset{\Omega}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}{e}_{\sigma}{D}^{-1}{e}_{\sigma}d\Omega )}^{1/2} eq 2.2-1 The global error above is decomposed into a sum of elementary errors, as follows: {\parallel e\parallel }^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\parallel e\parallel }_{i}^{2} | where | N is the total number of elements. | | --- | --- | | | {\parallel e\parallel }_{i} represents the local error indicator on element i . | The aim is to estimate the exact error from equation [eq 2.2-1] formulated in stresses. The basic idea of the method is to construct a new stress field, denoted {\sigma}^{\text{ }} , from {\sigma}_{h} and such that: {e}_{\sigma}\approx {e}_{\sigma}^{\text{ }}={\sigma}^{\text{ }}-{\sigma}_{h} The error estimator will then be written: {}^{0}\text{}\parallel e\parallel ={(\underset{\Omega}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}{e}_{\sigma}^{\text{ }}{D}^{-1}{e}_{\sigma}^{\text{ }}d\Omega )}^{1/2} The quality of the estimator is measured by the quantity \theta , called the effectivity index of the estimator: \theta =\frac{{}^{0}\text{}\parallel e\parallel }{\parallel e\parallel } An error estimator is said to be asymptotically exact if \theta \to 1 when \parallel e\parallel \to 0 (or when h\to 0 ), which means that the estimated error will always converge towards the exact error when the latter decreases. Obviously, the reliability of {}^{0}\text{}\parallel e\parallel depends on the "quality" of {\sigma}^{\text{ }} . The two versions of the ZHU-ZIENKIEWICZ estimator differ at this level (see [§3]). 2.3 Construction of an asymptotically exact estimator The characterisation of such an estimator is provided by the following theorem (see [bib 2]). Theorem If \parallel {e}^{\text{ }}\parallel =\parallel {u-u}^{\text{ }}\parallel is the error norm of the reconstructed solution, then the error estimator {}^{0}\text{}\parallel e\parallel defined previously is asymptotically exact if \frac{\parallel {e}^{\text{ }}\parallel }{\parallel e\parallel }\to 0 when \parallel e\parallel \to 0 This condition is realised if the rate of convergence with h of \parallel {e}^{\text{ }}\parallel is higher than that of \parallel e\parallel . Typically, if one assumes that the exact error of the finite-element approximation converges as \parallel e\parallel =0({h}^{p}) and the error of the reconstructed solution as \parallel {e}^{\text{ }}\parallel =0({h}^{p+\alpha }) with \alpha >0 then a simple calculation gives: 1-0({h}^{\alpha})\le \theta \le 1+0({h}^{\alpha}) and therefore \theta \to 1 when h\to 0 3 Construction of the recomputed stress field 3.1 1987 version The solution {u}_{h} resulting from equation [eq 2.1-1] being {C}_{0} on \Omega (because of the choice of {C}_{0} shape functions), it follows that {\sigma}_{h} computed by [eq 2.1-2] is discontinuous at the element interfaces. In order to obtain acceptable results for the nodal stresses, one generally resorts to an average at the nodes or to a projection method. It is this latter method which is adopted here. It is assumed that {\sigma}^{\text{ }} is interpolated by the same shape functions as {u}_{h} , that is: {\sigma}^{\text{ }}=N{\bar{\sigma}}^{\text{ }} eq 3.1-1 and a global least-squares smoothing of {\sigma}_{h} is performed, which amounts to minimising the functional J(\tau )=\underset{\Omega}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}(\tau -{\sigma}_{h})(\tau -{\sigma}_{h})d\Omega in the space generated by N . By differentiation, {s}^{} must satisfy \underset{\Omega}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}N({\sigma}^{\text{ }}-{\sigma}_{h})d\Omega =0 using equation [eq 3.1-1], one obtains the linear system: M\left\lbrace {\bar{\sigma}}^{\text{ }}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace b\right\rbrace with M=\underset{\Omega}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}\mathrm{NN}d\Omega and \left\lbrace b\right\rbrace =\underset{\Omega}{\int}{}^{t}\text{}N{\sigma}_{h}d\Omega This global system is to be solved for each of the components of the stress tensor. The matrix M is computed and inverted only once. 3.2 1992 version The constraint on the field {\sigma}^{\text{ }} differs from the 1987 version in the following way: it is assumed that {\sigma}^{\text{ }} is polynomial of the same degree as the displacements over the set of elements possessing an internal vertex node S in common. Let {S}_{K}=\underset{S\in K}{\cup}K denote this set, called a patch. For each component of {\sigma}^{\text{ }} , one writes: {\sigma}^{\text{ }}{\mid}_{{S}_{K}}={\text{Pa}}_{s} eq 3.2-1 | where | P contains the appropriate polynomial terms | | --- | --- | | | {a}_{s} the unknown coefficients of the corresponding monomials | | Example: | \mathrm{P1}P=\left[1,x,y\right] {a}_{s}{}^{t}=\left[{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\right] | \mathrm{Q1}P=\left[1,x,y,xy\right] {a}_{s}={}^{t}\text{}\left[{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}\right] The coefficients of the polynomial {a}_{s} are determined by minimising the functional: \begin{array}{cc}F(a)& =\sum_{i=1}^{N}{({\sigma}_{h}({x}_{i},{y}_{i})-{\sigma}^{\text{ }}{\mid}_{{S}_{K}}({x}_{i},{y}_{i}))}^{2}\\ & =\sum_{i=1}^{N}{({\sigma}_{h}({x}_{i},{y}_{i})-P({x}_{i},{y}_{i}){a}_{s})}^{2}\end{array} (discrete local least-squares smoothing of {\sigma}_{h} ) | where | ({x}_{i},{y}_{i}) are the coordinates of the GAUSS points on {S}_{K} . | | --- | --- | | | N is the total number of GAUSS points on all the elements of the patch | The solution {a}_{s} satisfies: \sum_{i=1}^{N}{}^{t}\text{}P({x}_{i},{y}_{i})P({x}_{i},{y}_{i}){a}_{s}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}{}^{t}\text{}P({x}_{i},{y}_{i}){\sigma}_{h}({x}_{i},{y}_{i}) whence {a}_{s}={A}^{-1}b with A=\sum_{i=1}^{N}{}^{t}\text{}P({x}_{i},{y}_{i})P({x}_{i},{y}_{i}) A may be very ill-conditioned (in particular on high-degree elements) and consequently impossible to invert in this form. To remedy this problem, the authors [bib4] have proposed a normalisation of the coordinates on each patch, which amounts to performing the change of variables: \begin{array}{c}\bar{x}=-1+2\frac{x-{x}_{\min}}{{x}_{\max}-{x}_{\min}}\\ \bar{y}=-1+2\frac{y-{y}_{\min}}{{y}_{\max}-{y}_{\min}}\end{array} where {x}_{\min},{x}_{\max},{y}_{\min},{y}_{\max} represent the minimum and maximum values of x and y on the patch. This method appreciably improves the conditioning of A and completely removes the previous problem. Once {\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{s}} has been determined, the nodal values are deduced from equation [eq 3.2-1] only at the nodes internal to the patch, except in the case of patches having boundary nodes. Internal patches: | | GAUSS points at which the stresses {\sigma}_{h} are computed according to equation [eq 2.1-2] | | --- | --- | | | | | | nodes of computation of {\sigma}^{\text{ }} {\sigma}^{\text{ }} | | | | | | internal vertex defining the patch | Boundary patches: The nodal values at the mid-side nodes belonging to 2 patches are averaged, and likewise for the internal nodes in the case of the QUAD9. Note: In the case of finite elements of different type, the choice of P in equation [eq 3.2-1] is delicate (problems of validity of {a}_{s} if the space is too rich, loss of superconvergence if it is not rich enough). A more thorough study seems indispensable. This is why the estimator \mathit{ZZ2} is for the moment limited to meshes comprising only a single element type. This restriction does not exist for \mathit{ZZ1} . The authors have shown numerically [bib3] that, with this choice of {\sigma}^{\text{ }} , their estimator was asymptotically exact for elastic materials whose characteristics are independent of the domain and for all types of element, and that the rates of convergence with h of \parallel {e}^{\text{ }}\parallel were improved relative to the previous version (especially for elements of degree 2: see test case SSLV110, Validation manual), whence a better estimation of the error. An illustration of these rates of convergence will be found in reference [bib 5]. 4 Implementation in Code_Aster and present limits of use 4.1 Implementation in Code_Aster The two previous estimators are implemented in Code_Aster in the post-processing command CALC_ERREUR U4.81.04. They are activated from options (ERZ1_ELEM for ZZ1 and ERz2_ELEM for ZZ2) and enrich a data structure RESULTAT. Furthermore, the computation of the stress field smoothed by one or other of the methods described in [paragraph 3] may be triggered separately from the computation of the error estimate (option SIZ1_NOEU for ZZ1 and SIZ2_NOEU for ZZ2). The error estimator supplies: - a field by element comprising 3 components: - the estimate of the relative error on the element, - the estimate of the absolute error on the element, - the energy norm of the computed solution {\sigma}_{h} . - listing outputs comprising the same information at the global level (over the whole structure) All the fields obtained may be visualised via the command IMPR_RESU. 4.2 Limits of use The theoretical framework is homogeneous linear elasticity. For ZZ1, the 2D modellings (plane stress and plane strain, axisymmetric) and 3D are permitted, whereas for ZZ1 only the 2D modellings (plane stress and plane strain, axisymmetric) are permitted. | Element types: | triangles with 3 and 6 nodes, | | --- | --- | | | quadrilaterals with 4, 8 and 9 nodes. | For ZZ2, the mesh must comprise only a single type of element. 5 Bibliography 1. r4.10.02 Residual error estimator r4.10.02 Residual error estimator Summary: The residual error estimator makes it possible to estimate the discretisation error due to the finite-element method on the elements of a 2D or 3D mesh. It is an explicit error estimator involving the residuals of the equilibrium equations and the jumps of the normal stresses at the interfaces, unlike the Zhu‑Zienkiewicz estimator, which uses an a posteriori stress-smoothing technique R4.10.01 and [bib5]. This estimator is implemented in Code_Aster in 2D and 3D elastoplasticity. 1 Introduction The residual error estimator was developed in 1993 by Bernardi-Métivet-Verfurth [bib1]. It is an explicit error estimator involving the residuals of the equilibrium equations (whence its name). It applies to elliptic problems (Poisson, Stokes, or linear elasticity) in dimension 2 or 3. These problems are assumed to be discretised by finite elements associated with a regular triangulation. Historically, the first explicit error estimator relating to equilibrium defects is due to Babuska and Rheinbolt [bib2] for 1D problems with linear elements. Gago extended this estimator to 2D and added to the formulae the traction jumps at the element interfaces [bib3] and [bib4]. New estimators were then proposed, in which the surface-traction defects on the boundaries of the domain were also taken into account, together with an improvement of the estimation of the inter-element jumps giving more reliable results. One is interested here in the residual estimator applied to the case of linear elasticity. The aim is, at the end of an elastic analysis, to determine the error map on the mesh with a view, possibly, to adapting the latter (by refinement and/or unrefinement) or simply for information. The adaptation can be done by chaining with the Homard cutting software. 2 Formulation of the residual estimator Let \Omega be an open set of {R}^{n} , n=2 or 3 , of boundary \Gamma , and T a regular triangulation of \Omega . In linear elasticity, the continuous problem is written: find (u,\sigma ) such that: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}div\sigma +f=0& \text{dans}\Omega \\ u={u}_{D}& \text{sur}{\Gamma}_{D}\\ \sigma .n={g}_{N}& \text{sur}{\Gamma}_{N}\end{array} {\Gamma}_{D} is the Dirichlet boundary of the mesh {u}_{D} is the displacement imposed on this boundary {\Gamma}_{N} is the Neumann boundary n the unit normal to {\Gamma}_{N} {g}_{N} is the loading applied on this boundary; it may be continuous or discretised. f is a force of body-force type (gravity, rotation); it may be continuous or discretised. {\sigma}_{h} is the stress obtained by the solution of the discrete problem: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}div{\sigma}_{h}+f=0& \text{dans}\Omega \\ {u}_{h}={u}_{D}& \text{sur}{\Gamma}_{D}\\ {\sigma}_{h}.n={g}_{N}& \text{sur}{\Gamma}_{N}\end{array} with the relation {\sigma}_{h}=\text{DB}{u}_{h} where: D is the Hooke matrix B is the linearised strain operator If K denotes a current element of the mesh, the error estimator (denoted \eta (\Omega ) ) is defined as being the root-mean-square of the local error indicators, denoted \eta (K) : \eta (\Omega )={\left[\sum_{K\in T}\eta {(K)}^{2}\right]}^{1/2} The local residual indicator The indicator is composed of three terms; the first represents the residual of the equilibrium equation on each mesh cell, the second term the jump of the normal stresses on the interfaces, the third term the difference between the normal stresses and the loading imposed on {\Gamma}_{N} if the element intersects {\Gamma}_{N} . Figure 2-a: Elements internal to a mesh - the first term of the estimator is the {L}^{2} norm of the residual of the equilibrium equation on the mesh cell K , multiplied by {h}_{K} which is either the diameter of the circumscribed circle for a triangular finite element, or the maximum diagonal for a quadrangle, - the second term is the integral, over S(K) defined [Figure 2-a], of the jumps of normal stresses integrated on each edge F of the element which has a neighbour, and multiplied by the square root of {h}_{F} , which is the length of the edge F , Figure 2-b: Elements located on the boundary of a mesh - the third term is the integral, over the intersection of each edge F of the edges \partial K of the current element K with the Neumann boundary {\Gamma}_{N} , of the jumps between the normal stresses of the element and the Neumann force {g}_{N} , multiplied by the square root of {h}_{F} , the length of the edge F . One therefore has the following formula for the residual estimator: \eta (K)={h}_{K}{\parallel f+div{\sigma}_{h}\parallel }_{{L}^{2}(K)}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{F\in S(K)}{h}_{F}^{1/2}{\parallel \left[{\sigma}_{h}.n\right]\parallel }_{{L}^{2}(F)}+\sum_{F\subset \partial K\subset {\Gamma}_{N}}{h}_{F}^{1/2}{\parallel {g}_{N}-{\sigma}_{h}.n\parallel }_{{L}^{2}(F)} eq 2-1 For the choice of the various terms of [eq 2-1], one refers to [bib1]. 3 Properties of the residual estimator | One denotes | {\eta}_{\text{EX}}(K) the exact error {\parallel u-{u}_{h}\parallel }_{{H}^{1}(K)} on the element K (unknown a priori) | | --- | --- | | and | {\eta}_{\text{EX}}(\Omega ) the global exact error {\parallel u-{u}_{h}\parallel }_{{H}^{1}(O)} | One then has the following properties ([bib1]): - whatever the element K , the elementary error \eta (K) is bounded above by the exact local error (multiplied by a constant independent of the triangulation), that is \forall K\eta (K)\le {C}_{1}\times {\eta}_{\text{EX}}(K) - the exact global error is bounded above by the estimated global error \eta (\Omega ) (multiplied by a constant independent of T ) that is {\eta}_{\text{EX}}(\Omega )\le {C}_{2}\times \eta (\Omega ) The constants {C}_{1}\text{et}{C}_{2} depend a priori on the type of finite element and on the boundary conditions of the problem. Kelly and Gago [bib3] proposed in 2D a constant {C}_{2} depending only on the degree p of the interpolation polynomial used: \begin{array}{cc}{C}_{2}={(\frac{1}{24{p}^{2}})}^{1/2}\text{soit}& {C}_{2}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{2p}\sqrt{6}}\text{pour les TRIA3 et QUAD4}(\text{degré 1})\\ & {C}_{2}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{4p}\sqrt{6}}\text{pour les TRIA6 et QUAD8}(\text{degré 2})\end{array} For 3D, one does not have an evaluation of the constant. One can nevertheless say that the estimated global error overestimates the exact global error in every case. This result is not necessarily true at the local level. 4 Implementation in Aster The residual estimator is implemented in 2D and 3D on all types of elements. It is computed by the command CALC_ERREUR by activating the option 'ERME_ELEM'. This option computes on each element: - the absolute error \eta (K) (see [eq 2-1]), - the norm of the stress tensor {\parallel {\sigma}_{h}\parallel }_{{L}^{2}(K)} which serves to normalise the absolute error, - the relative error {\eta}_{\text{rel}}(K)=100\times \frac{\eta (K)}{\sqrt{\eta {(K)}^{2}+{\parallel {\sigma}_{h}\parallel }_{{L}^{2}(K)}^{2}}} . Note: This definition of the relative error implies that in the zones where the stresses are very small, the relative error can be large and not significant. It is then the absolute error which must be considered. It also computes at the global level: - the absolute error \eta (\Omega )={\left[\sum_{K\in T}\eta {(K)}^{2}\right]}^{1/2} , - the global norm of the stress tensor {\parallel {\sigma}_{h}\parallel }_{{L}^{2}(\Omega )}={\left[\sum_{K\in T}{\parallel {\sigma}_{h}\parallel }_{{L}^{2}(K)}^{2}\right]}^{1/2} , - the relative error {\eta}_{\text{rel}}(\Omega )=100\times \frac{\eta (\Omega )}{\sqrt{\eta {(\Omega )}^{2}+{\parallel {\sigma}_{h}\parallel }_{{L}^{2}(\Omega )}^{2}}} . From the expression [eq 2-1], one sees that in order to compute the error indicator on the mesh cell K , one must know: - the possible loadings f on K and {g}_{N} on \partial K\cap {\Gamma}_{N} (or their discretisation {f}_{h} and {g}_{\text{Nh}} ), - the quantities {h}_{K} , {h}_{F} and n linked to the geometry of the element, - the stress field {\sigma}_{h} , - the list of the neighbours of K in order to recover the stresses on these elements, necessary for the computation of the 2nd term of [eq 2-1]. 1 and 2 can be computed or recovered easily. 3 must have been computed beforehand by one of the options 'SIGM_ELNO' or 'SIEF_ELNO'. Otherwise, a fatal error message is issued. 4 requires the computation of a particular mesh-cell–mesh-cell connectivity, in addition to the standard mesh-cell–node connectivity. This new object is stored in the data structure of type maillage. For the detail of the implementation in Aster , see [bib6]. For the validation of the estimator, see [bib7]. 5 Bibliography 1. r4.10.03 Spatial residual error indicator for transient thermal analysis r4.10.03 Spatial residual error indicator for transient thermal analysis Summary: In numerical simulations by finite elements, obtaining a raw result is no longer sufficient. The user increasingly requires a spatial error calculation with respect to the mesh . Methodological support and advanced “numerical-computational” tools are needed in order to gauge the quality of studies and to improve them. To this end, a posteriori spatial error indicators make it possible to locate, on each element, an error map on which the remeshing tools can rely: a first analysis on a coarse mesh makes it possible to recover the error map from the discretised data and from the discretised solution (hence the term “a posteriori”), the refinement then being carried out locally by ranking this information. The new a posteriori indicator (referred to as “pure residual”) which has just been implemented in order to post-process the thermal solvers of Code_Aster is based on their local residuals extracted from the semi-discretisations in time. Via the option ‘ERTH_ELEM’ of CALC_ERREUR, it uses the thermal fields (EVOL_THER) coming from THER_LINEAIRE and from THER_NON_LINE. It thus completes the range of advanced tools offered by the code, making it possible to improve the quality of studies, their pooling and their comparisons . The aim of this note is to set out in detail the theoretical, numerical and software work which governed its implementation. As regards the theoretical study we have, in a first stage, restricted ourselves to the linear thermal analysis of a fixed structure discretised by the standard isoparametric finite elements. In practice, however, the scope of use of this option has been partially extended to non-linear thermal analysis . The reader is given the theoretical and practical properties and limitations of the indicator obtained, while relating these considerations, which may sometimes appear somewhat “ethereal”, to a precise parameter setting of the operators concerned and to the modelling choices of the code. An attempt has been made constantly to link the various items addressed, while setting out, at least in outline, somewhat technical proofs that are rarely made explicit in the specialist literature. 1 Problem statement – Description of the document In numerical simulations by finite elements, obtaining a raw result is no longer sufficient. The user increasingly requires a spatial error calculation with respect to the mesh . Methodological support and advanced numerical tools are needed in order to gauge the quality of studies and to improve them. For example, the accuracy of the results is often degraded by local singularities (corners, heterogeneities…). One then seeks the right strategy for identifying these critical regions and for refining/coarsening them in order to optimise the local/global error compromise. And this with the greatest possible accuracy, automatically, reliably (the error calculation must itself be as little approximate as possible!), robustly and at the lowest cost. For each type of finite element, one generally has a priori estimates of the spatial error , . But these are verified only asymptotically (when the size h of the elements tends to zero) and they require a certain level of regularity which is precisely not attained in the problem regions. Moreover, these upper bounds underlie two types of strategy for improving the analysis: - the \text{p} -methods, which consist in locally increasing the order of the finite elements, - the \text{h} -methods, which refine locally in order to reduce the geometric characteristics of the elements. We are interested here in the second strategy, but through another class of indicators: the a posteriori error indicators . Since the founding work of I. BABUSKA and W.RHEINBOLDT , the importance of this type of indicator is well established and they are attracting growing interest, both in pure numerical analysis , , and in the field of applications , . They have in particular been implemented and used in N3S, TRIFOU and code_aster (for linear mechanics cf. r4.10.01, r4.10.02). For a survey of the existing indicators, one may consult the reference work of R. VERFURTH or the report of X. DESROCHES . To take up an argument of M.FORTIN (Cf. pp468-469), the development of a posteriori estimation is motivated principally by three reasons: - the first is the need to establish the accuracy of the results obtained by a finite-element analysis: how much credit should be given to them? Are all the phenomena and all the data involved properly taken into account in the modelling? - the second objective is to allow anyone to use an analysis code without having to intervene in the construction of the mesh in order to obtain the required global accuracy, - finally, the third line of study is more particularly oriented towards three-dimensional problems, for which the size of the meshes is limited by the available memory space and by the cost of the solution. These specifications bring out two dual problems : estimating the accuracy of the solution obtained on the principal parameters of the simulation, and proposing means of calculating a new solution which respects a minimum accuracy. The first problem is truly that of error estimation, whereas the second concerns the associated adaptive methods (refinement/coarsening, remeshing, displacement of points, boundary tracking…). These indicators thus make it possible to locate on each element an error map on which the remeshing tools can rely. Note: The name “indicator” is preferred to the usual terminology “estimator” (a literal translation of the English “error estimator”). In view of the fact that it has the same theoretical limitations as those of the finite-element solver (which it “post-processes”), that it is itself often marred by numerical approximations and that it is obtained via equivalence relations involving numerous constants depending on the problem… the information which it carries truly gives “only an order of magnitude” of the spatial error sought. Despite these restrictions, these a posteriori error maps remain no less important, and in any case they constitute the only type of information available in this field. A first analysis on a coarse mesh makes it possible to associate, with each element of the triangulation, an indicator calculated from the discretised data and from the first discrete solution. The refinement is then carried out locally by ranking this information. In short, and in a non-exhaustive way, the use of an indicator possibly coupled with a remesher: - provides a certain estimate of the spatial discretisation error, - procures a better distribution of the error due to local singularities, - makes it possible to improve the modelling of the data of the problem (materials, loadings, sources…), - makes it possible to optimise (the same accuracy at the lowest cost) and to make reliable the mesh-convergence process, - to estimate and to qualify an analysis for a given class of mesh. These considerations clearly show that the calculation of these estimators (which is ultimately only a post-processing of the problem considered) must: - be much less costly than that of the solution, - require only the discretised data and the calculated solution, - be capable of being localised, - be equivalent (in a particular form) to the exact error. We shall see that, with residual indicators, one can obtain only a global upper bound on the exact error together with a local lower bound on that same error . But these upper and lower bounds on the error complement each other because the first assures us that a solution has been obtained within a certain tolerance, while the second allows us to optimise locally the number of points in order to respect this accuracy and not to overestimate it. They involve constants which do not depend on the spatial and temporal discretisations. The aim of this note is to set out in detail the theoretical, numerical and software work which governed the implementation of an a posteriori error indicator making it possible to “post-process” the thermal solvers of Code_Aster. It is a pure residual indicator initiated by the option ‘ERTH_ELEM’ of CALC_ERREUR. As regards the theoretical study we have, in a first stage, restricted ourselves to the linear thermal analysis of a fixed structure discretised by the standard isoparametric finite elements. In practice, however, the scope of use of this option has been partially extended to non-linear thermal analysis. For further details on the scope of use and on the functional scope of the thermal indicator, and for an example of use, one may refer to [r4.10.03-mise-oeuvre-code-aster]. The a posteriori indicator which we propose is a pure residual indicator based on the local residuals of the strong equation semi-discretised in time . For certain elements of the theoretical study (and in particular its framework) we have drawn inspiration from the innovative work of C.BERNARDI and B. METIVET . They themselves extended, from the elliptic to the parabolic case, the results of R. VERFURTH . They were interested in particular in the calculation of indicators on the model case of the heat equation with a homogeneous Dirichlet condition, semi-discretised in time by an implicit Euler scheme. We have extended these results to the problems actually treated by the linear thermal operator of the code, THER_LINEAIRE. These are inhomogeneous mixed boundary-value problems (Cauchy-Dirichlet-Neumann-Robin), linear, with variable coefficients and discretised by a \theta -method. A thorough piece of work has therefore been carried out in order to grasp properly the theoretical mechanisms of the underlying thermal problem and in order to extrapolate the results of the preceding model problem . This is so as to try to approach the modellings and the scope of the code, while setting out mathematical subtleties that are often glossed over in the papers of the field. A particular effort has been made to put into perspective the choices made in Code_Aster with respect to past and current research, and to make explicit the general philosophy of these indicators. The reader is given the theoretical and practical properties and limitations of the indicators obtained, while relating these considerations to a precise parameter setting of the operator CALC_ERREUR involved in this post-processing. An attempt has been made constantly to link the various items addressed, to limit the recourse to long mathematical digressions, while setting out at least in outline numerous somewhat “technical” proofs that are rarely made explicit in the specialist literature. This document is organised around the following parts: - In a first stage, a theoretical study is carried out in order to underline what is at stake in the underlying thermal problem, and their possible links with the modelling choices of the code. First, one determines the minimum Abstract Variational Framework (CVA) (cf. [r4.10.03-contexte]) on which one will be able to rely in order to show the existence and uniqueness of a temperature solution field (cf. [r4.10.03-formulation]). By cross-checking these theoretical prerequisites with the practical constraints of the users, one deduces limitations as to the admissible types of geometry and of loading. One then studies the evolution of the stability properties of the problem (cf. [r4.10.03-discretisation]) in the course of the process of semi-discretisation in time and in space. - These controllability results are very useful for bringing out the norms, the techniques and the inequalities which enter into the genesis of the residual indicator. After introducing the notation usual for this type of problem (cf. [r4.10.03-notations]), a possible formulation of the indicator is obtained , together with the associated upper bound on the global error (cf. [r4.10.03-majoration]) and the lower bound on the local error (cf. [r4.10.03-minoration]). Different types of spatial indicator (cf. [r4.10.03-types-indicateurs]) are mentioned and several strategies for constructing indicators used in the parabolic case are set out in detail (cf. [r4.10.03-complements]). In the same paragraph, the temporal aspect of the problem is also examined through the contingencies of managing the spatial error with respect to that of the time step. - In a third part (cf. [r4.10.03-recapitulatif]), the principal contributions of these theoretical chapters and their links with the thermal solvers of the code are summarised. - Finally, one concludes by addressing the practical difficulties of implementation (cf. [r4.10.03-Difficultes-particulieres]), the necessary environment (cf. [r4.10.03-environnement]), the parameter setting (cf. [r4.10.03-résultats-calcul-erreur]) and the scope of use (cf. [r4.10.03-perimetre-utilisation]) of the indicator actually implemented in the post-processing operator CALC_ERREUR . An example of use taken from an official test case (TPLL01J) is also set out in detail (cf. [r4.10.03-exemple-utilisation]). Warning: The reader who is in a hurry and/or little interested in the theoretical mechanisms of the genesis of the error indicator and of the underlying thermal problem may, from the outset, skip to [r4.10.03-recapitulatif], which recapitulates the principal theoretical contributions of the preceding chapters. 2 The boundary-value problem 2.1 Context Consider a fixed body occupying a bounded connected open set O of {R}^{q} ( q = 2 or 3) with regular boundary \partial \Omega :=\Gamma :=\underset{i=1}{\overset{3}{\cup}}{\Gamma}_{i} , characterised by its volumetric heat capacity at constant pressure \rho {C}_{p}(x) (the vector variable x here stands for the pair (\text{x,y}) (resp. From the very first versions of the code, and before the introduction of THER_NON_LINE, it made it possible to simulate “pseudo” non-linearities. In view of its rather marginal use, this modelling will not be considered here. One is interested in the evolutions of the temperature at every point x of the open set and at every time instant t\in [0,\tau [(\tau >0) , when the body is subjected to boundary conditions and to loadings independent of the temperature but which may depend on time. These are a volumetric source s(x\text{,t}) , boundary conditions of prescribed-temperature type f(x\text{,t}) (on the portion of external surface {\Gamma}_{1} ), imposed normal flux g(x\text{,t}) (on {\Gamma}_{2} ) and convective exchange h(x\text{,t}) and {T}_{\text{ext}}(x\text{,t}) (on {\Gamma}_{3} ). Note: Non-linearities pose serious theoretical problems for proving the existence, uniqueness and stability of the possible solution. Property 13). 4.5 Complements The constant {K}_{3} , just like its preceding counterpart {K}_{2} , depends intrinsically on the type of boundary conditions enriching the initial heat equation as well as on the type of temporal and spatial discretisation . In an attempt to free oneself from this last constraint, SR.GAGO proposes (on a 2D model problem) a dependence of the constant {K}_{2} as a function of the type of finite element used . It is written {K}_{2}:=\frac{{\tilde{K}}_{2}}{\sqrt{24{p}^{2}}} where p is the degree of the interpolation polynomial used ( p=1 for the TRIA3 and QUAD4, p=2 for the TRIA6 and QUAD8/9). Whence the idea, once the global error indicator has been calculated, of multiplying it by this “corrective” constant \frac{1}{\sqrt{24{p}^{2}}} . This strategy has been implicitly adopted for the calculation of the error indicator in mechanics (option ‘ERME_ELEM’ of CALC_ERREUR, cf. [r4.10.02 §3]). We have not however adopted it for thermal analysis because this constant has been determined only empirically on the 2D Laplace equation. We do not wish in this way to bias the values of the indicators. Until now, only maps of spatial error indicators calculated at a given time instant of the analysis transient have been in question. But, in fact, there exist several ways of constructing an error indicator on a parabolic problem : - one may very well, first, semi-discretise the strong formulation in space and control its spatial error by a posteriori error indicators adapted to the steady case (in our case elliptic). One then applies a solver, of variable step and order, treating the ordinary differential equations (for example ), - a second strategy consists in semi-discretising in time and then in space and in determining the spatial error indicator at a given time instant (for example ) from the local residuals of the semi-discretised form. One applies a linear solver to the variational form making it possible to construct iteratively the solution at a given time instant from the solution at the preceding time instant, - another possibility consists in discretising simultaneously in time and in space on appropriate finite elements and in controlling their “space-time” errors in a coupled manner (for example ). This last scenario is the most attractive from a theoretical point of view because it proposes a complete control of the error and it makes it possible to avoid unfortunate decouplings as regards possible refinements/coarsenings driven by one criterion with respect to the other (cf. the following paragraph). It is however very heavy to put in place in a large industrial code such as Code_Aster . It assumes indeed, in order to be optimal, nothing less than a separate management of the time step by finite element. Which, from the point of view of the architecture supporting the finite elements of the code, is a real challenge! One therefore prefers the second scenario , which has the great advantage of being able to be implemented directly in a finite-element code because it relies above all on the solution of the fully discretised system. It is this type of indicator which has been put in place in N3S, TRIFOU and Code_Aster . Within the framework of a genuine “space-time” discretisation of the problem (scenario 3), one obtains, strictly speaking, a “space-time” indicator for each discretisation element K\times \left[{t}_{n},{t}_{n+1}\right] which is the weighted sum of three terms: 1. the residual of the calculated solution and of the discretised data with respect to the strong formulation of the problem ({P}_{0}) evaluated on K\times \left[{t}_{n},{t}_{n+1}\right] , 2. the spatial jump across \partial K\times \left[{t}_{n},{t}_{n+1}\right] of the associated trace operator (which naturally links the weak and strong formulations via Green’s formula), 3. the temporal jump across K\times \partial \left[{t}_{n},{t}_{n+1}\right] of the calculated solution. The solution which has been put in place obviously does not make it possible to bring out explicitly the temporal jump term . It reappears however implicitly , because of the particular method of temporal semi-discretisation, in all the terms in \theta of Definitions 10 and 12 . On the other hand, the fact of being interested principally only in the spatial discretisation and in its possible refinement/coarsening must not obscure certain contingencies with respect to the management of the time step .
