An ALARME therefore warns the user and urges him to switch to quadratic. 6.4 Scope of use This indicator has been developed, for the moment, only on the isoparametric elements (TRIA3/6, QUAD4/8/9, TETRA4/10, PENTA6/13/15 and HEXA8/20/27) and for the modellings PLAN, PLAN_DIAG, AXIS, AXIS_DIAG, 3D and 3D_DIAG . It therefore does not calculate the contributions of the structural elements of shell type (COQUE_PLAN, COQUE_AXIS, COQUE), of the pyramids (PYRAM5 and PYRAM13) and of the Fourier modelling (AXIS_FOURIER). Nor does it make it possible to calculate the jump terms of these elements with the authorised elements. However, if a mesh comprises licit and illicit elements, the calculation is not interrupted and, via OPTION –2 in the appropriate element catalogues, the user is warned that the said elements are not taken into account . Indeed, in order to carry out this post-processing, one must beforehand call, explicitly, the option ‘FLUX_ELNO’ (calculation of the heat-flux vector at the nodes) and, implicitly, ‘INIT_MAIL_VOIS’ (determination of the characteristics of the neighbourhood {\Delta}_{K} of an element K ). One is therefore dependent on their respective scopes of use . One must also keep in mind a few more minor rules which may however take on a quite particular importance for very precise studies: - The calculation of the indicator treats only the elements of the mesh belonging to the model designated by the keyword MODELE of the command CALC_ERREUR. One can thus work with (uncleaned) meshes comprising “rough mesh cells” to which one assigns a different model. - In a mesh of dimension q , one calculates the jump and loading terms only on skin elements of dimension q-1 . One therefore treats the relations of the TRIA/QUAD with the SEG and the relations of the TETRA/PENTA/HEXA with the FACE. For example, in the event of the presence of segments in a three-dimensional mesh, the option will not stop but it will not take into account their (possible) contributions. - The option ‘ERTH_ELEM_TEMP’ and its preliminary options do not know the PYRAM . Their contributions will be ignored. This gap comes from their introduction into code_aster being more recent than that of the preliminary options already cited. Note: In any case these elements are in the minority in a 3D mesh and are generated only by the free volumetric mesher of GIBI, which creates them locally in order to complete portions of hexahedral meshes. - In 2D, one must not accidentally insert a segment between two triangles or quadrangles , otherwise the jump term of these elements will not be calculated and one will wrongly enquire into the existence of a possible boundary condition. The calculation will not be interrupted but, at this interface, the value of the indicator will be incomplete. However, for particular needs (density of internal loadings localised in a structure, crack...), one may of course allow oneself this kind of situation. In 3D, the problem of course also arises when one inserts quadrangles or triangles between two contiguous FACEs. - the same type of imbroglio occurs when two points of the mesh are geometrically superimposed . Here again, the calculation ought not to be interrupted, but the value of the indicator will be incomplete at the level of this overlap zone, - If one works with a mesh which results from symmetrisation operations , one must try not to find oneself in the two preceding cases. Moreover, on either side of the axis of symmetry, the neighbouring mesh cells do not necessarily (in particular with the GIBI mesher) have orientations which meet the standard of Code_Aster (they ought to be reversed). The calculation of the indicator, for which this information is crucial (in order to define the outward normals to each mesh cell and the facing connectivities), detects the problem by calculating the Jacobian of each mesh cell. In 2D, a substitution algorithm makes it possible to get round the problem and to reconstruct the connectivity tables “nodes of the current element / nodes of its neighbours”. In 3D, the problem is much more arduous and particular to each element; the code therefore stops in ERREUR_FATALE in the event of a problem. - If one wishes to refine or coarsen one's mesh with MACR_ADAP_MAIL u7.03.01, the mesh must comprise only triangles or tetrahedra. Concerning the surface or volumetric loadings, “good practice” consists in using only mesh-cell groups. If one uses node groups, one must expect falsified calculations, because after a few refinements other points will probably have been inserted geometrically into the zone concerned by the GROUP_NO without being assigned any loading (one cannot modify the composition of a GROUP_NO during the session!). For point loadings or for recording points (on which, for example, POST_RELEVE_T will rely) the GROUP_NO is licit. On the other hand, it is not recommended to use directly mesh cells (MA) or nodes (NO) (outside a group), because in this case, as renumberings occur, HOMARD will probably lose track of them. It can retain the memory of the mesh cells or of the nodes only through a name of GROUP_MA or of GROUP_NO. Thanks to this mechanism, it can adopt a Lagrangian vision of the fate of these mesh cells or of these points! The calculation of the indicator operates indiscriminately on an EVOL_THER coming from THER_LINEAIRE or from THER_NON_LINE, steady or transient, isotropic or orthotropic, and on a fixed structure meshed by elements meeting the preceding criteria. In the non-linear case one takes into account the non-linearities of the materials and the modification of the problem into enthalpy. However one does not treat the possible contributions of non-linear loadings (FLUX_NL and RAYONNEMENT). The user is warned of this by an ALARME, just as he is warned that a boundary condition of type ECHANGE_PAROI is not taken into account. Indeed, in the linear case one recognises, for the moment, only the contributions of the loadings SOURCE, FLUX_REP and ECHANGE. For the taking into account of these loadings, particular overloading rules are applied (cf. r4.10.03-environnement). 6.5 Example of use In order to familiarise oneself with the use of this indicator in thermal analysis and with its possible coupling with the encapsulation of HOMARD via MACR_ADAP_MAIL u7.03.01, one may draw inspiration from the test case TPLL01J v4.02.001. In this other example taken from the HOMARD website, the coupling ERTH_ELEM/MACR_ADAP_MAIL u7.03.01 simulates the circulation of a “hot” fluid on either side of an elbowed metal part (at the top and at the bottom, via a time-dependent ECHANGE condition in AFFE_CHAR_THER_F). The circulation of the fluid takes place from left to right. Accuracy is required above all at the ends of the structure, at the level of the propagation of the fluid: thanks to the coupling of the error indicator with the refinement-coarsening tool, the mesh therefore remains fine at the edge of the part, in the zone where the “hot” fluid is concentrated. Finally it is coarsened at the rear, once the fluid has passed. One also observes that, as predicted by the theory (cf. notes [r4.10.03-formulation]), the solution of the thermal problem is “blunted” in the re-entrant corners and that the error indicator (even though it too is penalised in these zones) signals this state of affairs (even when the part has cooled down). Example: Use of the option ‘ERTH_ELEM’ coupled with HOMARD 7 Conclusion – Prospect In numerical simulations by finite elements, obtaining a raw result is no longer sufficient. The user increasingly requires a spatial error calculation with respect to the mesh. He needs methodological support and advanced “numerical-computational” tools in order to gauge the quality of his studies and to improve them. To this end, a posteriori spatial error indicators make it possible to locate, on each element, an error map on which the remeshing tools can rely: a first analysis on a coarse mesh makes it possible to recover the error map from the discretised data and from the discretised solution (hence the term “a posteriori”), the refinement then being carried out locally by ranking this information. The new a posteriori indicator which has just been implemented in order to post-process the thermal problems of code_aster is based on their local residuals extracted from the semi-discretisations in time. Via the option ‘ERTH_ELEM’ of CALC_ERREUR, it uses the thermal fields (EVOL_THER) coming from THER_LINEAIRE and from THER_NON_LINE. This new indicator completes the range of advanced tools offered by the code, making it possible to improve the quality of studies, their pooling and their comparisons. Indeed, error indicators in mechanics and a refinement/coarsening macro-command MACR_ADAP_MAIL u7.03.02 are already available. It remains to complete the scope of use of these tools and to extend them, in particular in order to manage better the non-linearities and the interactions between spatial error and temporal error. Note: Estimator by smoothing of the stresses of Zhu & Zienkiewicz (CALC_ERREUR+ OPTION‘ERZ1/ERZ2_ELEM’ r4.10.01) and pure residual indicator ( ‘ERME_ELEM’ r4.10.02). Subsequently, the prospects of this work are of several kinds: - From a functional point of view, the completeness of this indicator could also be improved by taking into account possible non-linear boundary conditions (FLUX_NL and RAYONNEMENT) and exchanges between walls (ECHANGE_PAROI). In the longer term, one ought also to be able to rely on structural finite elements (shell…), on pyramids, and to be able to treat convection-diffusion problems (operator THER_NON_LINE_MO r5.02.04). - From a theoretical point of view , when one uses new boundary conditions and/or when one relies on new modellings (shell, beam...), a “numerical-functional” study similar to that of this document ought to be carried out in order to judge the theoretical and practical limitations (with respect to code_aster ) of such an indicator and to derive its ad hoc formulation. - Let us recall finally that a host of a posteriori error indicators are available , and that rather few have been tested and validated on industrial cases. In order to refine diagnoses, to establish comparisons and to put in place remeshing strategies by class of problem, it would be interesting to extend the list of available indicators. Various residual indicators plus a local problem have thus proved more effective (but also more costly) during numerical tests (in the elliptic case) in N3S. Note: The indicator is the norm of the solution of a local problem, of the same type as the initial problem, but discretised on spaces of higher degree and whose right-hand side is the residual. According to the boundary conditions applied to this local problem, one distinguishes different types of them. They thus mix the “hierarchical bases” vision and the “residual” aspects of a posteriori error indicators. - The ideal consists in discretising simultaneously in time and in space on appropriate finite elements and in controlling their “space-time” errors in a coupled manner. This “space-time” indicator gives access to a complete control of the error and it makes it possible to avoid unfortunate decouplings as regards possible refinements/coarsenings driven by one criterion with respect to the other (cf. discussion [r4.10.03-complements]). It is however very heavy to put in place in a large industrial code such as Code_Aster . It assumes indeed, in order to be optimal, nothing less than a separate management of the time step by finite element. r4.10.04 Detection of singularities and computation of an element-size map r4.10.04 Detection of singularities and computation of an element-size map Summary: A method is proposed here which aims to improve the treatment of singularities in the mesh-adaptation strategies with the software HOMARD (in the case of refinement) or with the software GMSH (case of remeshing). This mechanism makes it possible, on the one hand, to detect the finite elements connected to singular zones and, on the other hand, to obtain, for a given global error, the size of the finite elements of the new mesh in the case of remeshing. This functionality is accessible in the command CALC_ERREUR through the computation options SING_ELEM (field constant per element) or SING_ELNO (field at the nodes per element). This option is valid only in mechanics. An error estimator in mechanics and the strain energy on each element must have been computed beforehand. Strictly speaking, this method is valid only in elasticity. > Contents 1 Introduction The objective of the option proposed here is to improve the treatment of singularities in the mesh-adaptation strategies proposed in Code_Aster. Indeed, the presence of singularities (present in practice in any analysis of real structures by finite elements) implies two sorts of difficulties which will be qualified here as “theoretical” and “practical”. The “theoretical” difficulties come from the fact that the contribution to the error in energy of the elements touching a singularity is of the form C{h}^{\alpha} ( C a constant, h the size of the element and \alpha the order of the singularity) whereas the contribution of the elements outside a singularity is of the form C{h}^{q} ( q depending only on the degree of interpolation of the shape functions of the element). The adaptation of the mesh must take this difference into account in order to be as efficient as possible. For example, in order to divide the contribution of the error by 4, one will have to take elements 16 times smaller in the case of a crack ( \alpha =1/2 ) and elements 2 times smaller in the case outside a crack with quadratic elements ( p=2 ). The “practical” difficulties come from the fact that, in singularity zones, the contributions to the error in energy are large. If one aims to obtain a small error in energy, these zones must therefore be refined very strongly. Now, one may wonder about the influence of these errors in energy on physical quantities of interest to the engineer (displacement at such a point, maximum stress in such a sensitive zone, etc.). In other words, it is not because the singularity zones cause large errors on the energy that they have a great influence on the analysis outside these zones. In practice, the error estimators quickly designate the singularity zones alone as being those to be refined: the singularity zones mask the other errors, for example a zone with a strong gradient which one would wish to refine. The Laboratoire de Mécanique et CAO of Saint-Quentin has developed a method making it possible, on the one hand, to detect the singularities, and on the other hand, to determine, for a given global error, the size of the finite elements of the new mesh in the case of remeshing. The use of these two pieces of information can be envisaged from two angles: - The finite elements considered as “singular” by the method can be excluded from the cutting process, - the new size of the finite elements is given to a remesher so that the latter builds the new mesh while respecting as well as possible this new size map. Currently, the software HOMARD cuts an element once (for example in 2D, a triangle is divided into 4 but no more). In order to continue the cutting, one must call HOMARD again. An evolution is therefore to be expected so that one can divide an element several times and thus respect as well as possible the size map of the new mesh. It is however possible to use the free mesher GMSH which takes a size map directly as input. Note: This document takes up as a whole the note resulting from a CRECO between the LMCAO and the AMA department, whose reference is cited in the bibliography ([bib1]). 2 Detection of the singularities 2.1 Principle of the method When the exact solution of the problem studied presents singularities, the order of convergence of the finite-element solution is modified and therefore also that of the error estimator. Consider, for example, a plane elasticity problem discretised with triangular elements of degree p . If the exact solution {U}_{\mathrm{ex}} is regular, one knows that ([bib2], [bib3]): {\parallel u-{u}_{h}\parallel }_{\Omega}={\parallel e\parallel }_{\Omega}\le C{h}^{p} eq 2.1-1 Where {\parallel e\parallel }_{\Omega}\le C{h}^{p} is the contribution to the error in energy, that is: {\parallel e\parallel }_{\Omega}\le \frac{1}{2}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\varepsilon ({e}_{h})K\varepsilon ({e}_{h})d\Omega eq 2.1-2 On the other hand, if the exact solution presents a singularity, for example if, locally in the neighbourhood of a point {M}_{0} , the displacement field is of the form (with r and \theta polar coordinates in the neighbourhood of the point {M}_{0} ): {U}_{\mathrm{ex}}={r}^{\alpha}V(\theta )+W\text{avec}0<\alpha <1 eq 2.1-3 Then, one shows that [Strang & Fix, 1976]: {\parallel {e}_{h}\parallel }_{\Omega}\le C{h}^{\alpha} eq 2.1-4 It follows that the rate of convergence of the global error in energy becomes independent of the degree p of the finite elements used and the same is true of that of the error measure (for example, if p=1\text{ou}2 then \alpha =1/2 for a crack). In order to obtain a good prediction of the optimised meshes, the previous observations lead us to use a convergence rate {q}_{E} per element such that the error estimator {\varepsilon}_{E} satisfies: {\varepsilon}_{E}=O({h}^{{q}_{E}}) eq 2.1-5 A simple way of defining these local coefficients consists in taking: - {q}_{E}=\alpha if the element E is connected to a singularity of order \alpha ; - {q}_{E}=q for all the other finite elements where q depends only on the type of finite elements used. The method presented in what follows therefore comprises three phases: - detection of the singular zones, in this case the singular nodes of the mesh; - numerical evaluation of the coefficient {q}_{E} for the elements connected to the nodes considered as singular (for the other elements, one then sets {q}_{E}=q ); - computation of the size-modification coefficient {r}_{E} . 2.2 Detection of the singular nodes The idea is to use the local errors. Indeed, experiments show that these local errors present a peak in the neighbourhood of a singularity. For each node i of the mesh, one therefore compares the mean error {\bar{m}}^{i} of the elements connected to the node i with the mean error \bar{M} over the whole structure. The node i is considered as singular if: {\bar{m}}^{i}\ge \beta \bar{M} eq 2.2.1-1 with {\bar{m}}^{i}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{\text{E connecté à i}}{{\varepsilon}_{E}}^{2}}{\sum_{\text{E connecté à i}}\mathrm{mes}(E)}} and \bar{M}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{\text{E}\in \text{structure}}{{\varepsilon}_{E}}^{2}}{\sum_{\text{E}\in \text{structure}}\mathrm{mes}(E)}} eq 2.2.1-2 where \beta is a coefficient greater than 1 and \mathrm{mes}(E) the area in 2D or the volume in 3D of the element E . The numerical experiments have shown that the singular nodes are well detected by setting \beta =2 in dimension 2, \beta =3 in dimension 3 for linear finite elements and \beta =2 in dimension 3 for quadratic finite elements. \begin{array}{l} {\bar{m}}_{1}^{i}\ge \beta \bar{M} \\ {\bar{m}}_{1}^{i}\ge {\bar{m}}_{2}^{i} \\ {\bar{m}}_{1}^{i}\ge 3\text{Min}({\bar{m}}_{2}^{i},{\bar{m}}_{3}^{i}) \end{array} - Layer 1: elements which possess the node i to be tested, - Layer 2: elements in contact (face, edge or node) with an element of layer 1, - Layer 3: elements in contact (face, edge or node) with an element of layer 2. Note 1: From a numerical point of view, the detection of the singular nodes differs between the 2D and 3D cases. The conditions given in what follows for this detection are not based on a particular theory but rather on the experience acquired in this field by the Laboratoire de Mécanique et CAO of Saint-Quentin. In 2D: a node i is considered as singular if it fulfils the following 3 conditions: \begin{split}\begin{array}{l} {\bar{m}}_{1}^{i}\ge \beta \bar{M} \\ {\bar{m}}_{1}^{i}\ge {\bar{m}}_{2}^{i} \\ {\bar{m}}_{1}^{i}\ge 3\text{Min}({\bar{m}}_{2}^{i},{\bar{m}}_{3}^{i}) \end{array}\end{split} Where {\bar{m}}_{1}^{i} , {\bar{m}}_{2}^{i} and {\bar{m}}_{3}^{i} are the means of the error for the elements belonging to layers 1, 2 and 3, respectively, with respect to the node i considered. The layers are defined as follows: In 3D: the node i is considered as singular if it fulfils the condition {\bar{m}}_{1}^{i}\ge \beta \bar{M} and if one of the nodes connected to the node i considered fulfils the condition {\bar{m}}_{i}^{\text{Noeud connecté à i}}\ge \beta \bar{M} . Unlike the 2D case, the node i is singular only if one of its neighbours is also (isolated singular nodes are forgotten in order to keep only the singular edges). Note 2: In 2D, only the vertex nodes are examined. In 3D, only the vertex nodes located on a boundary of the structure are examined (only for reasons of analysis time; this condition could therefore be modified). 2.3 Evaluation of the order of the singularity For each singular node i detected, the order of the singularity, that is to say the value of {q}_{E} which will be used for the elements connected to the node i , is determined by identifying the value of the energy density of the finite-element solution in the neighbourhood of the node i with the theoretical value in the neighbourhood of a singular point. 2.3.1 Case of dimension 2 In this case, one computes the mean finite-element energy, in discs A of centre i and of radius r : {\bar{e}}_{h}(r)=\frac{1}{2\mathrm{mes}(A)}\underset{A}{\int}\varepsilon ({u}_{h})K\varepsilon ({u}_{h})\mathrm{dA} eq 2.3.1-1 By identifying, by a least-squares method, this mean energy with the theoretical value in the neighbourhood of a singularity of order \alpha : e(r)=k{r}^{2(\alpha -1)}+c eq 2.3.1-2 one obtains numerically a value \bar{\alpha} close to \alpha . Figure 2.3.1-a: Numerical evaluation of \alpha In practice the numerical experiments show that it is sufficient to carry out the identification in a zone corresponding to 3 layers of elements around the singular point and to evaluate {\bar{e}}^{h}(r) for 5 to 8 values of r regularly distributed in this zone (10 values have been taken). 2.3.2 Case of dimension 3 In 3D the situation is more complex. The singular points are not, most often, isolated and it is therefore frequent to be in the presence of singular edges. Consider, for example, the case of a cube clamped on one face and subjected to tensile forces: all the points of the edges of the clamped face are singular [Figure 2.3.2-b]. Figure 2.3.2-b: Cube clamped in tension In this situation, the evaluation of the mean energy in balls A of increasing radius and centred on a singular node does not make it possible to identify {q}_{E} . Indeed, as the radius increases the extent of the singular zone contained in the ball A increases and one does not obtain a rapid decrease of {\bar{e}}_{h} [Figure 2.3.2-c]. Figure 2.3.2-c: Energy in concentric balls When the singular points are not isolated, the coefficient {q}_{E} must be identified by computing the energy density in coaxial cylinders built on the edges whose ends have been considered as singular [Figure 2.3.2-d] and cf. the note of [§ 2.2]. Figure 2.3.2-d: Energy in coaxial cylinders 2.4 Extension to stress-concentration zones In practice, it has been observed that the previous method, developed on cases presenting singularities, also makes it possible to take correctly into account the zones with strong stress gradients even if mathematically these zones do not correspond to singularities. 3 Construction of an optimal mesh 3.1 Generalities The objective of an adaptation procedure is to guarantee the user a level of precision on the global error while minimising the analysis costs. In order to evaluate the discretisation errors, a relative global measure of the error \varepsilon and the associated local contributions {\varepsilon}_{E} are used, with: {\varepsilon}^{2}=\sum_{E}{{\varepsilon}_{E}}^{2} eq 3.1-1 The idea is to use the results of this first finite-element analysis and the error estimators in order to determine an optimal mesh {T}^{\ast } , that is to say a mesh which makes it possible to respect the desired precision while minimising the analysis costs. The mesh {T}^{\ast } is then built with the aid of an automatic mesher and a second finite-element analysis is carried out. 3.2 Definition of optimality For a given global error {\varepsilon}_{0} , a mesh {T}^{\ast } is optimal with respect to an error measure \varepsilon if: \begin{array}{cc}{\varepsilon}^{\ast }={\varepsilon}_{0}& \text{précision demandée}\\ {N}^{\ast }& \text{nombre d'éléments de}{T}^{\ast }\text{est minimum}\end{array} eq 3.2-1 This optimisation criterion naturally leads to minimising the analysis costs. 3.3 Determination of an optimal mesh In order to determine the characteristics of the optimal mesh {T}^{\ast } , the method consists in computing on each element E of the mesh T a size-modification coefficient: {r}_{E}=\frac{{h}_{E}^{\ast }}{{h}_{E}} eq 3.3-1 Where {h}_{E} is the current size of the element E and {h}_{E}^{\ast } the (unknown) size which must be imposed on the elements of {T}^{\ast } in the zone of E in order to ensure optimality [Figure 3.3-a]. A possible choice for defining the size of an element {h}_{E} is to take the size of the largest side of this element. The determination of the optimal mesh is thus reduced to the determination, on the initial mesh T , of a map of size-modification coefficients. {E}^{\text{ }}\subset {T}^{\text{ }} E\subset T Figure 3.3-a: Definition of the sizes The computation of the coefficients {r}_{E} is based on the rate of convergence of the error: \varepsilon =O({h}^{q}) eq 3.3-2 where q depends on the type of finite element used but also on the regularity of the exact solution of the problem treated. For the “classical” error estimators, it is assumed that the rate of convergence of the error estimator is equal to the order of convergence of the finite-element solution. For the estimators in a quantity of interest, this rate of convergence is equal to twice the order of convergence of the finite-element solution ([bib4]). In what follows, in order to compute the size-modification coefficient {r}_{E} , the case of the regular solution ( q depends only on p , the degree of interpolation of the shape functions of the element) is distinguished from the case of the singular solution ( q depends only on \alpha , the order of the singularity of the displacement field). 3.4 “Classical” error estimators “Classical” error estimators denote the estimators which supply a norm ( L2 norm, H1 norm, energy norm) of the error in the solution. 3.4.1 Case of the regular solution First, it is assumed that the exact solution is sufficiently regular for the value of q to depend only on the type of finite elements used and to be equal to the degree of interpolation used p ( p is equal to 1 for linear finite elements and 2 for quadratic finite elements). In this case, in order to predict the optimal sizes, one writes that the ratio of the sizes is linked to the ratio of the contributions to the error by: \frac{{\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast }}{{\varepsilon}_{E}}=\left[\frac{{h}_{E}^{\ast }}{{h}_{E}}\right]={r}_{E}^{p} eq 3.4.1-1 where {\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast } represents the contribution of the elements of {T}^{\ast } located in the zone E , that is to say: {\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast }={\left[\sum_{{E}^{\ast }\subset E}{\epsilon}_{{E}^{\ast }}^{2}\right]}^{1/2} eq 3.4.1-2 {\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast } is the error of the element {E}^{\ast } computed on the mesh T . The square of the error on the mesh {T}^{\ast } can therefore be evaluated by: \sum_{E}{({\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast })}^{2}=\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2p}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2} eq 3.4.1-3 and the number of elements of {T}^{\ast } by: {N}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}} eq 3.4.1-4 Where d is the dimension of the space (in practice, d=2 or 3 ). Indeed, {r}_{E}=\frac{{h}_{E}^{\ast }}{{h}_{E}}={(\frac{V}{{{N}_{E}}^{\ast }})}^{1/d}{(\frac{N}{V})}^{1/d} with N the number of elements of T in E (hence 1), {N}_{E}^{\ast } the number of elements of {T}^{\ast } in the zone of E . One therefore has {N}_{E}^{\ast }=\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}} , that is {N}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}{N}_{E}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}} the total number of elements of {T}^{\ast } . The problem to be solved is therefore: \text{Minimiser}{N}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}}\text{avec}\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2p}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2}={\varepsilon}_{0}^{2} eq 3.4.1-5 It is an optimisation problem with a constraint on the optimisation variables. Introducing a Lagrange multiplier, denoted A , the problem [eq 3.4.1-5] amounts to making extremal the Lagrangian: L({\left\lbrace {r}_{E}\right\rbrace }_{E\in T};A)=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}}+A(\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2p}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2}-{\varepsilon}_{0}^{2}) eq 3.4.1-6 The extremality conditions give: \frac{\partial L}{\partial {r}_{E}}=\frac{-d}{{r}_{E}^{d+1}}+2Ap{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2}{r}_{E}^{2p-1}=0\forall E\in T eq 3.4.1-7 Whence: {r}_{E}={\left[\frac{d}{2Ap{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2}}\right]}^{1/(2p+d)} eq 3.4.1-8 Substituting into the second equation of [eq 3.4.1-5], one deduces A : A=\frac{d}{2p}{\left[\frac{\sum_{E}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2d/(2p+d)}}{{\varepsilon}_{0}^{2}}\right]}^{(2p+d)/2p} eq 3.4.1-9 The expression for A thus obtained is substituted into equation [eq 3.4.1-8] in order to obtain {r}_{E} : {r}_{E}=\frac{{\varepsilon}_{0}^{1/p}}{{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2/(2p+d)}{\left[\sum_{E}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2d/(2p+d)}\right]}^{1/2p}} eq 3.4.1-10 3.4.2 Case of the singular zones In order to predict the optimal sizes, a convergence rate {q}_{E} defined per element is used: \frac{{\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast }}{{\varepsilon}_{E}}={\left[\frac{{h}_{E}^{\ast }}{{h}_{E}}\right]}^{{q}_{E}}={r}_{E}^{{q}_{E}} eq 3.4.2-1 where {\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast } represents the contribution of the elements of {T}^{\ast } located in the zone E , that is to say: {\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast }={\left[\sum_{{E}^{\ast }\subset E}{\varepsilon}_{{E}^{\ast }}^{2}\right]}^{1/2} eq 3.4.2-2 The square of the error on the mesh {T}^{\ast } can therefore be evaluated by: \sum_{E}{({\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast })}^{2}=\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2{q}_{E}}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2} eq 3.4.2-3 and the number of elements of {T}^{\ast } is still evaluated by: {N}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}} eq 3.4.2-4 The new problem to be solved is therefore: \text{Minimiser}N\ast =\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}}\text{avec}\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2{q}_{E}}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2}={\varepsilon}_{0}^{2} eq 3.4.2-5 which is an optimisation problem with a constraint on the optimisation variables. Introducing a Lagrange multiplier, denoted A , the problem amounts to making extremal the Lagrangian: L({\left\lbrace {r}_{E}\right\rbrace }_{E\in T};A)=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}}+A(\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2{q}_{E}}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2}-{\varepsilon}_{0}^{2}) eq 3.4.2-6 The extremality conditions give: \frac{\partial L}{\partial {r}_{E}}=-\frac{d}{{r}_{E}^{d+1}}+2A{q}_{E}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2}{r}_{E}^{2{q}_{E}-1}=0\forall E\in T eq 3.4.2-7 Whence: {r}_{E}={\left[\frac{d}{2A{q}_{E}}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2}\right]}^{1/(2{q}_{E}+d)} eq 3.4.2-8 Substituting into the second equation of [eq 3.4.2-5], one obtains a non-linear equation in A (because {q}_{E} depends on the elements): \sum_{E}\left[{\left[\frac{d}{2A{q}_{E}}\right]}^{2{q}_{E}/(2{q}_{E}+d)}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{2d/(2{q}_{E}+d)}\right]-{\varepsilon}_{0}^{2}=0 eq 3.4.2-9 It is solved by Newton's method (the Lagrange multiplier is initialised by taking the Lagrange multiplier of the regular solution, that is to say the expression [eq 3.4.2-9] with {q}_{E}=p ). Once A has been computed, one deduces {r}_{E} from equation [eq 3.4.2-8]. 3.5 Error estimators in quantities of interest Error estimators in quantities of interest denote the estimators which supply an error on a precise physical quantity (quantity of interest) on a chosen zone. 3.5.1 Case of the regular solution In the case of the estimators in a quantity of interest, the value of q is equal to 2p [bib4] ( p is equal to 1 for linear finite elements and 2 for quadratic finite elements). In order to predict the optimal sizes, one writes that the ratio of the sizes is linked to the ratio of the contributions to the error by: \frac{{\epsilon}_{E}^{\ast }}{{\epsilon}_{E}}={\left[\frac{{h}_{E}^{\ast }}{{h}_{E}}\right]}^{2p}={r}_{E}^{2p} eq 3.5.1-1 where {\epsilon}_{E}^{\ast } represents the contribution of the elements of {T}^{\ast } located in the zone E , that is to say: {\epsilon}_{E}^{\ast }=\sum_{{E}^{\ast }\subset E}{\epsilon}_{{E}^{\ast }} eq 3.5.1-2 {\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast } is the error of the element {E}^{\ast } computed on the mesh T . The error on the mesh {T}^{\ast } can therefore be evaluated by: \sum_{E}{\varepsilon}_{E}\ast =\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2p}{\varepsilon}_{E} eq 3.5.1-3 and the number of elements of {T}^{\ast } by: {N}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}} eq 3.5.1-4 Where d is the dimension of the space (in practice, d=2 or 3 ). The problem to be solved is therefore: \text{Minimiser}{N}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}}\text{avec}\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2p}{\varepsilon}_{E}={\varepsilon}_{0} eq 3.5.1-5 Here again, it is an optimisation problem with a constraint on the optimisation variables. Introducing a Lagrange multiplier, denoted A , the problem [eq 3.5.1-5] amounts to making extremal the Lagrangian: L({\left\lbrace {r}_{E}\right\rbrace }_{E\in T}\text{;A})=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}}+A(\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2p}{\varepsilon}_{E}-{\varepsilon}_{0}) eq 3.5.1-6 The extremality conditions give: \frac{\partial L}{\partial {r}_{E}}=-\frac{d}{{r}_{E}^{d+1}}+2Ap{\varepsilon}_{E}{r}_{E}^{2p-1}=0\forall E\in T eq 3.5.1-7 Whence: {r}_{E}={\left[\frac{d}{2Ap{\varepsilon}_{E}}\right]}^{1/(2p+d)} eq 3.5.1-8 Substituting into the second equation of [eq 3.5.1-5], one deduces A : A=\frac{d}{2p}{\left[\frac{\sum_{E}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{d/(2p+d)}}{{\varepsilon}_{0}}\right]}^{(2p+d)/2p} eq 3.5.1-9 The expression for A thus obtained is substituted into equation [eq 3.5.1-8] in order to obtain {r}_{E} : {r}_{E}=\frac{{\varepsilon}_{0}^{1/2p}}{{\varepsilon}_{E}^{1/(2p+d)}{\left[\sum_{E}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{d/(2p+d)}\right]}^{1/2p}} eq 3.5.1-10 3.5.2 Case of the singular zones In order to predict the optimal sizes, one now imposes: \frac{{\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast }}{{\varepsilon}_{E}}={\left[\frac{{h}_{E}^{\ast }}{{h}_{E}}\right]}^{2{q}_{E}}={r}_{E}^{2{q}_{E}} eq 3.5.2-1 where {\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast } represents the contribution of the elements of {T}^{\ast } located in the zone E , that is to say: {\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast }=\sum_{{E}^{\ast }\subset E}{\varepsilon}_{{E}^{\ast }} eq 3.5.2-2 The square of the error on the mesh {T}^{\ast } can therefore be evaluated by: \sum_{E}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2{q}_{E}}{\varepsilon}_{E} eq 3.5.2-3 and the number of elements of {T}^{\ast } is still evaluated by: {N}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}} eq 3.5.2-4 The new problem to be solved is therefore: \text{Minimiser}{N}^{\ast }=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}}\text{avec}\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2{q}_{E}}{\varepsilon}_{E}={\varepsilon}_{0} eq 3.5.2-5 which is an optimisation problem with a constraint on the optimisation variables. Introducing a Lagrange multiplier, denoted A , the problem amounts to making extremal the Lagrangian: L({\left\lbrace {r}_{E}\right\rbrace }_{E\in T};A)=\sum_{E}\frac{1}{{r}_{E}^{d}}+A(\sum_{E}{r}_{E}^{2{q}_{E}}{\varepsilon}_{E}-{\varepsilon}_{0}) eq 3.5.2-6 The extremality conditions give: \frac{\partial L}{\partial {r}_{E}}=-\frac{d}{{r}_{E}^{d+1}}+2A{q}_{E}{\varepsilon}_{E}{r}_{E}^{2{q}_{E}}-1=0\forall E\in T eq 3.5.2-7 Whence: {r}_{E}={\left[\frac{d}{2A{q}_{E}}{\varepsilon}_{E}\right]}^{1/(2{q}_{E}+d)} eq 3.5.2-8 Substituting into the second equation of [eq 3.5.2-5], one obtains a non-linear equation in A : \sum_{E}\left[{\left[\frac{d}{2A{q}_{E}}\right]}^{2{q}_{E}/(2{q}_{E}+d)}{\varepsilon}_{E}^{d/(2{q}_{E}+d)}\right]-{\varepsilon}_{0}=0 eq 3.5.2-9 It is solved by Newton's method (the Lagrange multiplier is initialised by taking the Lagrange multiplier of the regular solution, that is to say the expression [eq 3.5.2-9] with {q}_{E}=p ). Once A has been computed, one deduces {r}_{E} from equation [eq 3.5.2-8]. 4 Use in Code_Aster 4.1 The commands The order of the singularity and the size-modification map are computed by the command CALC_ERREUR by activating the options 'SING_ELEM' (field constant per element) or 'SING_ELNO' (field at the nodes per element). The option 'SING_ELEM' computes, on each element, two components: - 'DEGRE': the order of the singularity, that is to say the value of the coefficient {q}_{E} (which is equal to p if the element is not connected to a singular node and which is equal to \alpha otherwise); - 'RAPPORT': the ratio between the current size {h}_{E} and the new size {h}_{E}^{\ast } of the finite element ( {h}_{E}/{h}_{E}^{\ast }=1/{r}_{E} ); - 'TAILLE': the new size {h}_{E}^{\ast } of the finite element ( {h}_{E}^{\ast }={r}_{E}{h}_{E} ). The computation of this option requires, beforehand, the computation of an error estimator (it is the absolute component which is used and this is hard-coded in Code_Aster ) and of the total strain energy. In the case where one of these options is not computed, an alarm message is issued and the option 'SING_ELEM' is not computed. The user can enter the optional keyword 'TYPE_ESTI' by indicating one of the following options: - 'ERME_ELEM' for the estimator based on the residuals; - 'ERZ(1 ou 2)_ELEM_SIGM' for the estimator based on the smoothed stresses (Zhu–Zienkiewicz version 1 or 2); - 'QIRE_ELEM' for the estimator in a quantity of interest based on the residuals; - 'QIZ(1 ou 2)_ELEM_SIGM' for the estimator in a quantity of interest based on the smoothed stresses (Zhu–Zienkiewicz version 1 or 2). If this keyword is not entered then the estimator based on the residuals 'ERME_ELEM' is chosen by default (alarm message issued). If the two Zhu–Zienkiewicz estimators are present, 'ERZ1_ELEM' is chosen. For the total strain energy, one uses: - With STAT_NON_LINE: 'ETOT_ELEM' which is the total strain energy on a finite element (valid for an elastic behaviour and for an elastoplastic behaviour 'VMIS_ISOT_XXX'). - With MECA_STATIQUE: 'EPOT_ELEM' which is the potential energy of elastic strain on a finite element and integrated from the displacements and the temperature (valid only for an elastic behaviour). The user must also enter the keyword 'PREC_ERR' which makes it possible to compute the precision {\varepsilon}_{0} of equation [eq 2.2-1] in the following way: {\varepsilon}_{0}=\text{PREC\_ERR}\ast {\text{Erreur}}_{\text{totale}} . The value of 'PREC_ERR' lies strictly between 0 and 1 (a fatal message is issued if this condition is not satisfied). For the option 'SING_ELNO', it is a copy of the values of 'SING_ELEM' to the nodes of the element. The prior computation of 'SING_ELEM' is therefore necessary. If 'SING_ELEM' is absent, an alarm message is issued and the option 'SING_ELNO' is not computed. 4.2 Scope of use The scope of use is the same (but more reduced) as that of the error estimator chosen, namely: - For the residual estimator: finite elements of continuous media in 2D (triangles and quadrilaterals) or 3D (tetrahedra only) for an elastoplastic behaviour, - For the Zhu–Zienkiewicz estimator: finite elements of continuous media in 2D (triangles and quadrilaterals) for an elastic behaviour. Strictly speaking (cf. [§2]), the computation of the order of the singularity is obtained from the theoretical energy at the crack tip [eq 2.3.1-2], an equation valid only in elasticity. The use of this option in elastoplasticity must therefore be handled with caution. 5 Bibliography 1. COOREVITS P.: Mechanism for the detection of singularities. First part. r4.10.06 Error estimators in quantities of interest r4.10.06 Error estimators in quantities of interest Summary: In this document, one presents the framework of error estimation in a quantity of interest. This framework is used with explicit residual estimators as well as with smoothing estimators. A number of quantities of interest are detailed, in particular their expression in terms of loading for the dual problem. > Contents 1 Model problem and notation 1.1 Equations An elastic solid, tied to a Cartesian frame of {ℝ}^{3} , occupies, in its natural state and before deformation, a bounded connected open domain \Omega of {ℝ}^{3} of regular boundary \partial \Omega with outward normal \overrightarrow{n} . Thus the estimators that have been developed over the last thirty years provide a reliable and accurate estimate of the error in global norms, such as the {H}^{1} norms, the {L}^{2} norms or else energy norms, by post-processing of the finite-element solution. This choice of global norms is imposed by the bilinear form. When the form is positive definite and symmetric, as is the case here, this induces a scalar product for which the associated norm is the energy norm; it is thus natural to estimate the error in this norm. The basic principle of this type of estimation is to use the approximate solution in order to estimate the discretisation error. In contrast to a priori estimation, a posteriori estimates can be made only once the approximate solution has been computed. A function \eta (h,{u}^{h},d) is an a posteriori error estimate if: \parallel u-{u}^{h}\parallel \le \eta (h,{u}^{h},d) where \parallel \cdot \parallel is a norm on the displacement fields, h the size of the elements, d a set of data of the problem and {u}^{h} the approximate solution. They provide a basis for mesh adaptation. Numerous estimators exist and may be classified into three categories: - Error estimators based on equilibrium defects, stemming from the work of Babuška and Rheinboldt ; - Error indicators constructed from smoothed stresses, stemming from the work of Zienkiewicz and Zhu ; - Error measures based on the concept of error in constitutive relation, stemming from the work of Ladevèze . In general, one must seek to construct an estimator whose asymptotic behaviour (when the size h of the elements tends to zero) follows that of the error. This behaviour is expressed by the existence of two constants {C}_{1} and {C}_{2} , depending on the data of the problem and on the discretisation but not on the size of the elements, satisfying the following relation (Ladevèze & Pelle, 2004): {C}_{1}\eta \le \parallel e\parallel \le {C}_{2}\eta where \eta represents the estimate of the measure \parallel e\parallel of the error e on the domain under consideration. Thus, in order to judge the performance of the estimators, there exist various intrinsic criteria. 2.2.1 Effectivity index The effectivity index \gamma is defined as the ratio between the error computed by an estimator {e}_{	ext{estimée}} and the true error {e}_{	ext{vraie}} : \gamma = rac{{e}_{	ext{estimée}}}{{e}_{	ext{vraie}}} Unless an analytical solution is available, the true error is computed as the difference between a solution obtained on a very fine mesh ( overkill solution) and the solution obtained on a given mesh. An effectivity index close to unity characterises a good estimator. If this property is reached when the size of the elements tends to zero, the estimator is said to be asymptotically exact. Nevertheless, the estimate must be sufficiently accurate ( \gamma close to 1) for fairly coarse meshes in order to be usable for the discretisations current in engineering. Finally, it is desirable to overestimate the error ( \gamma >1 ) in order to be usable as a stopping criterion in an adaptive process. Systematic studies have been carried out by Strouboulis and Haque and by Babuška on various test cases having an analytical solution or for which a reference solution can be determined on a very fine mesh. Overall, it emerges that the quality of an estimator depends on the topology of the mesh, on the regularity of the solution and on the regularity (flatness) of the elements. The single global index \gamma does not make it possible to account for the way in which the local error behaves: it may be that, in a few cases, the estimator is satisfactory for this criterion without succeeding in locating the zones where the error in energy is significant . 2.2.2 Robustness index In order to free oneself from the local behaviour of the estimator, another criterion has been defined by Babuška and Rodriguez . This approach makes it possible to highlight the discretisation error on a subdomain but also the distortion of the mesh elements and the regularity of the solution. Although it possesses mathematical bases, this technique seems complicated to implement for the complex meshes used in engineering. 3 Local error 3.1 Pollution error 3.1.1 Definition of the pollution error In order to define the pollution error, we shall provide a pragmatic definition by trying to understand what its behaviour may be and therefore its influence in the course of an adaptive process. The pollution error is estimated with the approximation error of the Green function associated with certain points. Another method has been used by Huerta and Díez (Huerta & Díez, 2000) and consists in finding an approximation of {e}_{\omega}^{	ext{pol}} by solution of the problem defining this error. Other work may also be cited (Ainsworth, 1999), (Oden & Feng, 1996). The industrial interest of the evaluation of this error being limited, we shall not develop these estimation methods any further. The numerous works on the computation of error bounds render the estimation of the pollution error unnecessary because it is included in the bounds. Moreover, for the estimation of a local error, as we have already indicated, the estimators in a quantity of interest make it possible to free oneself from the pollution error thanks to the dual problem. 3.2 Error in a quantity of interest 3.2.1 Quantities of interest Error estimates in the energy norm are too abstract to provide the users of analysis codes with sufficient information on the various aspects of the solution sought. It is then more useful to estimate an error in terms of quantities of interest; quantities having a physical meaning (an average of displacements in a subregion of the physical domain or an average of stresses on an interface or else, in the case of vibrations, one of the eigenfrequencies). Mathematically, they are characterised by linear or non-linear functionals in the space of functions to which the solutions belong. Several examples are given: the average of a component of the displacement on a domain \omega : Q(v)= rac{1}{\mid \omega \mid }{\int}_{\omega}{v}_{x}d\Omega the average of a component of the stress tensor on a domain \omega : Q(v)= rac{1}{\mid \omega \mid }{\int}_{\omega}{\sigma}_{xx}d\Omega One then seeks to compute the quantity {\varepsilon}^{Q} which may be expressed in the following form: {\varepsilon}^{Q}=Q(u)-Q({u}^{h}) In the case where Q is linear, the following equality is satisfied: {\varepsilon}^{Q}=Q(u-{u}^{h})=Q(e) In what follows, only the case of linear functionals will be considered because this corresponds to the framework of the simplified approach presented in what follows. From a mechanical point of view, this corresponds to the existence of a solution function of a dual problem, called the influence function, representing the influence of the forces of the reference problem on the total energy. The influence function is then used as a weighting of the equilibrium residuals of the reference problem. A simplified approach is presented, inasmuch as the framework is limited to linear elasticity and to linear quantities of interest. This is expressed by the fact that Q(\cdot ) is a linear form and that a(\cdot ,\cdot ) is a bilinear form. This approach makes it possible to understand better the necessity of using the error on the influence function and not only the influence function. The relation between the error in a quantity of interest and the residual may be expressed by the introduction of an unknown function \omega , called the influence function: Q(e)=\omega ({R}_{h}^{u}) Moreover, it is shown in that the previous relation becomes: Q(e)={R}_{h}^{u}(\omega ) By combining the previous relation with the residual equation: a(e,v)={R}_{h}^{u}(v) a relation between the error on the reference problem, the influence function and the error in a quantity of interest is obtained: a(e,\omega )=Q(e) This equality is necessarily satisfied when \omega \in V is the solution of the following problem: \lbrace  egin{array}{cc}	ext{Trouver}\omega \in V	ext{tel}	ext{que}& \ a(v,\omega )=Q(v)&  orall v\in V\end{array} This problem is called the dual or adjoint problem. This is why a finite-element approximation {\omega}^{h}\in {V}^{h} of \omega which satisfies  egin{array}{cc}a({v}^{h},{\omega}^{h})=Q({v}^{h})&  orall {v}^{h}\in {V}^{h}\end{array} is introduced. The simplest and most direct technique is to use the global estimators in the energy norm. By applying the Cauchy–Schwarz theorem, a relation between the error in a quantity of interest and the energy norms of the errors on the primal problem and the dual problem can be found: \mid Q(e)\mid \le {\parallel e\parallel }_{e}{\parallel \varepsilon \parallel }_{e} This expression thus allows us to estimate easily the error in a quantity of interest by using any error estimator in the energy norm, this without any additional development in an analysis code that has global estimators. Although this estimate is the simplest, it is also the coarsest: it does not take into account the local interactions between the primal error and the dual error (schematically this means that an error on the displacement does not result in an error in a quantity of interest). This can lead to heavy overestimates of the error in a quantity of interest. A somewhat different approach, called Dual Weighted Residual (DWR) , consists in considering the exact expression of the error in a quantity of interest: Q(e)=a(e,\omega -{\omega}^{h})={R}_{h}^{u}(\omega -{\omega}^{h}) The dual problem is solved by using a high-order approximation method. Another method, less costly, consists in using high-order interpolation functions defined on elementary patches of the domain. This approach leads to a guaranteed upper bound of the error. An “exact bounds” approach ( exact bounds approach ) uses the properties of the estimation based on the dual analysis. Thus, thanks to a displacement formulation of the finite-element method, a lower bound of the exact strain energy is obtained; thanks to a stress formulation, an upper bound of the exact complementary energy is obtained. From a practical point of view, this method is very costly since it implies solving the primal problem and the dual problem twice each. Other methods exist for estimating the error in a quantity of interest but, from an industrial point of view, only the approach using global estimators in the energy norm seems to be convincing. It does not require any additional development in order to access an indication of the error and it is also much less costly. 3.2.4 Bounds of the error 3.2.4.1 A new expression for the error Although very simple to obtain, the relation produces a considerable overestimate of the error. If e and \varepsilon are the errors of the finite-element approximations, respectively of the solutions of the primal and dual problems, then: Q(e)=a(e,\varepsilon )= rac{1}{4}{\parallel e+\varepsilon \parallel }_{e}^{2}- rac{1}{4}{\parallel e-\varepsilon \parallel }_{e}^{2} One introduces the scalar factor s\in R Q(e)=a(e,\varepsilon )= rac{1}{4}{\parallel se+{s}^{-1}\varepsilon \parallel }_{e}^{2}- rac{1}{4}{\parallel se-{s}^{-1}\varepsilon \parallel }_{e}^{2} The scalar s is chosen so that the quantities {\parallel se\parallel }_{e} and {\parallel {s}^{-1}\varepsilon \parallel }_{e} have the same amplitude, which implies choosing s=\sqrt{{\parallel \varepsilon \parallel }_{e}/{\parallel e\parallel }_{e}} . r4.10.07 Computation of the error in constitutive relation in dynamics under a frequency-domain formulation r4.10.07 Computation of the error in constitutive relation in dynamics under a frequency-domain formulation Summary: This document presents the principle of the computation of the error in constitutive relation (ERC). In this document, the solution of such a problem is restricted to the case of linear dynamics under a frequency-domain formalism. Several uses may motivate recourse to the solution of an ERC problem in linear dynamics: - The expansion of measured data onto a numerical model (field reconstruction), - The use of the ERC functional as a cost function in an updating or identification problem, - The spatial localisation of defects of a numerical model from measurements. The operator that solves the ERC is CALC_ERC_DYN u4.53.41. 1 Notations | \Phi (\cdot ) | : | Free-energy potential | | --- | --- | --- | | \underline{\underline{ϵ}} | : | Strain tensor | | \underline{\underline{\sigma}} | : | Stress tensor | | \Omega | : | Domain occupied by the structure | | \tilde{u} | : | Displacement boundary conditions on the boundary {\delta}_{u}\Omega | | \tilde{f} | : | Force boundary conditions on the boundary {\delta}_{f}\Omega | | \underline{\underline{C}} | : | Hooke tensor | | u | : | Displacement field | | \Re (\cdot ) | : | Real part | | {\xi}_{\omega}^{2} | : | Drüker error under a frequency-domain formalism | | (u,v,w) | : | Triplet of admissible fields associated with the ERC problem. | | {e}_{\omega}^{2} | : | ERC functional under an FE formalism in the field of linear dynamics, written in the frequency domain. | | \omega | : | Natural angular frequency | | f | : | Frequency | | [K] | : | FE stiffness matrix | | [M] | : | FE mass matrix | | [{G}_{r}] | : | Positive-definite norm matrix | | [H] | : | Observation matrix | | \Psi | : | Eigenmode | | \alpha | : | Regularisation-type parameter of the ERC functional. | | \gamma | : | Weighting-type parameter of the ERC functional. | | \widehat{u} | : | Measured displacement field. | | A | : | Matrix associated with the solution of the ERC problem. | | l | : | Vector of unknowns associated with the solution of the ERC problem. | | b | : | Right-hand side associated with the solution of the ERC problem. | 2 Introduction to energy functionals: case of the error in constitutive relation In the framework of simulation in general, and of mechanics in particular, one is often led to evaluate one or more physical quantities governing the system under study from measurements. In general, however, the quantities sought are not only inaccessible by measurement but may present a certain number of pathologies (incomplete, redundant, tainted with errors …). One therefore enters the framework of the solution of an inverse problem, whose aim is to establish a mathematical link resting on physical laws (a model), in order to recover the quantities sought that reproduce the experimental measurements as well as possible. Often, this takes the form of the solution of a minimisation problem in which a functional (cost function) is used, on the one hand, to quantify the discrepancy between the model and the measurement and, on the other hand, to resolve the potentially ill-posed character of the inverse problem. In mechanics, and in particular in the family of variational methods (as distinct from probabilistic methods), one classically distinguishes three approaches for the construction of the functionals that make it possible to solve the inverse problem in question: - methods based on least squares; - the approach resting on the Maxwell-Betti reciprocity theorem; - approaches based on the construction of energy functionals. Unlike least squares and the approach that invokes the reciprocity principle, energy functionals are based on the measure of the distance between the fields of admissible solutions constructed from the measurements and from the model. These techniques were first introduced by P. Ladevèze with the aim of estimating the quality of a solution obtained by the finite-element method. Thus, in [bib1], the concept of the Error in Constitutive Relation (ERC) was introduced. Since then, numerous applications have appeared, for example [bib2], [bib3] or [bib4]. The introduction of this notion may rest on 2 distinct principles: - The approach valid for Generalised Standard Materials (GSM) which, for a structure with a given constitutive behaviour, characterised by a free-energy potential \Phi (\cdot ) , quantifies the difference between two evolutions associated with force and displacement boundary conditions by the following residual: e(ϵ,\sigma )=\Phi (ϵ)+{\Phi}^{\ast }(\sigma )-\sigma :ϵ where {\Phi}^{\ast }(\cdot ) is the potential defined by the Legendre-Fenchel transform of \Phi (\cdot ) . It follows from the expression proposed by Fenchel between two quantities, primal and dual, coming from a given potential, namely: {e}_{\Pi}(x,y)=\Pi (x)+{\Pi}^{\ast }(y)-x:y An expansion of this expression for the discrepancy between two admissible pairs ({x}_{1,}{y}_{1}) and ({x}_{2,}{y}_{2}) leads to: {E}_{\Pi}(x,y)=\langle {x}_{2}-{x}_{1},{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}\rangle This error is always positive and becomes zero when the boundary conditions are compatible with the constitutive relation. Moreover, it makes it possible to define a distance that meets the necessary criteria of positivity and symmetry. It gives rise to the better-known expressions of the error in constitutive relation presented later. - The second approach is based on the stability principle in the sense of Drucker, defined for any pair of evolutions of the structure (starting from the same initial state) by the following inequality: {\int}_{0}^{T}{\int}_{\Omega}({\sigma}_{2}-{\sigma}_{1}):(\dot{{ϵ}_{2}}-\dot{{ϵ}_{1}})d\Omega \mathit{dt}\ge 0 If one places oneself in the framework of small perturbations, the response of the structure will be unique for any evolution issuing from the same history of the boundary conditions. This uniqueness property is satisfied for the constitutive laws frequently used (elasticity, plasticity, viscoelasticity, etc.) except for a few “singular” laws such as the damage laws. Indeed, the integration of the variational equation of the principle of virtual power entails the vanishing of the following expression: {\int}_{0}^{T}{\int}_{\Omega}({\sigma}_{2}-{\sigma}_{1}):(\dot{{ϵ}_{2}}-\dot{{ϵ}_{1}})d\Omega \mathit{dt}+{\int}_{0}^{T}{\int}_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}\rho {(\dot{{u}_{2}}-\dot{{u}_{1}})}^{2}=0 Under the assumption of the Drücker stability condition, this equation makes it possible to write the following inequality: {\int}_{0}^{T}{\int}_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}\rho {(\dot{{u}_{2}}-\dot{{u}_{1}})}^{2}\le 0\forall t\in [0,T],\forall x\in \Omega which results in the equality of the two velocities and thus the equality of the displacements everywhere in the structure and at every instant t (taking into account the identical initial states for the two evolutions 1 and 2). Next, the strain histories are equal (by differentiation), which will be followed by the equality of the internal stresses (by the constitutive relation). This assumption has been exploited to define a residual in the sense of an error in constitutive relation between two solutions described as kinematically admissible and statically admissible, respectively. A zero residual means that the two quantities, kinematically admissible and statically admissible, are compatible with the constitutive law. The constitutive relation therefore seems a good measure of the compatibility of a model with the displacement and force boundary conditions. Thus, numerous studies have been carried out on this approach in various fields (elastostatics, elastodynamics, etc.) based on the construction of a distance between admissible fields (with respect to the force and displacement boundary conditions) in the sense of the constitutive relation. Suppose, moreover, that one has constructed two solutions {S}^{1}({\sigma}_{1}) and {S}^{2}({ϵ}_{2}) issuing from two compatible evolutions of the displacement and force conditions respectively. The distance, in the sense of the constitutive relation, which makes it possible to evaluate quantitatively the discrepancy E between these two solutions must satisfy: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}E({S}^{1,}{S}^{2})=E({S}^{2,}{S}^{1})\forall {S}^{1,}{S}^{2}\\ E({S}^{1,}{S}^{2})\ge 0\forall {S}^{1,}{S}^{2}\\ E({S}^{1,}{S}^{2})=0\iff {S}^{1}={S}^{2}\end{array} A few classical formulations of the error in constitutive relation are proposed below by way of example. 2.1 Classical formulation of the error in constitutive relation: case of elastostatics The formulation of an energy functional of error-in-constitutive-relation type is particularly simple in the case of elastostatics. One considers that the laws governing the problem are: - The equilibrium equation: div\sigma =0 - The boundary conditions: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}u=\tilde{u}\mathit{sur}{\delta}_{u}\Omega \\ \sigma \cdot n=\tilde{f}\mathit{sur}{\delta}_{f}\Omega \end{array} - The constitutive law: \underline{\underline{\sigma}}=\underline{\underline{C}}:\underline{\underline{ϵ}}(u) Thus, the ERC functional is associated with a problem of searching for admissible fields described by: Find the statically admissible field {\sigma}_{s} and the kinematically admissible field {u}_{c} minimising: {\int}_{\Omega}({\sigma}_{s}-ϵ({u}_{c})):{C}^{-1}:({\sigma}_{s}-ϵ({u}_{c}))d\Omega under the admissibility constraints: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}_{c}=\left\lbrace u\in {H}^{1}(\Omega );u=\tilde{u}\mathit{sur}{\delta}_{u}\Omega \right\rbrace \\ {\sigma}_{s}=\left\lbrace u\in {H}^{div}(\Omega );\sigma \cdot n=\tilde{f}\mathit{sur}{\delta}_{f}\Omega \right\rbrace \end{array} In the static case, one can show that the statically and kinematically admissible solution fields are independent. This results in the possibility of their being computed separately as a Neumann problem and a Dirichlet problem respectively. 2.2 Modified formulation of the error in constitutive relation: dynamic case In the case of elastodynamics, it has been proved [bib5] that the “direct” extension of the previous formulation does not respect the spirit of the energy functionals for the dynamically and statically admissible fields because, besides the coupling through the constitutive equation, these fields are also linked by the equilibrium relation, which is now: div(\sigma )-\rho \ddot{u}=0 Thus, an approach known as the “modified ERC” is introduced by Feissel and Allix in [bib3], whose formulation is summarised below: Find the dynamically admissible field {\sigma}_{d} and the kinematically admissible field {u}_{c} minimising: {\int}_{0}^{T}{\int}_{\Omega}({\sigma}_{d}-ϵ({u}_{c})):{C}^{-1}:({\sigma}_{d}-ϵ({u}_{c}))d\Omega \mathit{dt}+{\int}_{0}^{T}({\int}_{{\delta}_{u}\Omega }{d}_{u}({u}_{c},\tilde{u})\mathit{dS}+{\int}_{{\delta}_{f}\Omega }{d}_{f}(f,\tilde{f})\mathit{dS})\mathit{dt} under the admissibility constraints: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}_{c}=\left\lbrace u\in {H}^{1}(\Omega );u=\tilde{u}\text{sur}{\delta}_{u}\Omega \right\rbrace \\ {\sigma}_{s}=\left\lbrace u\in {H}^{div}(\Omega );\sigma \cdot n=\tilde{f}\text{sur}{\delta}_{f}\Omega \text{et}div(\sigma )-\rho \ddot{u}=0\text{sur}\Omega \right\rbrace \end{array} where the terms {d}_{u} and {d}_{f} are positive-definite norms to be defined (typically {L}^{2} norms). 2.2.1 Frequency-domain formulation in a finite-element formalism The formulation presented below comes from the work in [bib6] and [bib7]. It is suited to cases of structural dynamics treated in the frequency domain and is particularly adapted to problems in an FE formulation in linear dynamics. Let us place ourselves in the case where one seeks periodic solutions of the dynamic problem cited above, of the form: \Re ({u}_{\omega}{e}^{i\omega t}) and \Re ({f}_{\omega}{e}^{i\omega t}) where \Re (\cdot ) denotes the real part and \omega the given angular frequency. The equilibrium equation is then written: div(\sigma )-{\omega}^{2}\rho {u}_{\omega}=0 Moreover, one denotes the admissible fields such that: - {u}_{c}=u is the kinematically admissible field - \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{d}=C:ϵ(v)\\ {\Gamma}_{d}=-\rho {\omega}^{2}w\end{array} are the dynamically admissible fields The Drüker inequality is now written: {\xi}_{\omega}^{2}(u,v,w)=\text{}{\int}_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}\text{tr}[C:{(ϵ(u)-ϵ(v))}^{\text{ }}(ϵ(u)-ϵ(v))]+\frac{1}{2}\rho {\omega}^{2}{(u-w)}^{\text{ }}(u-w)d\Omega where the sign \text{ } denotes the complex conjugate. This expression makes it possible to approach the writing of the error-in-constitutive-relation functional commonly used in linear dynamics under a formulation specific to the FE discretisation. Indeed, suppose that one is interested in the eigenmode search problem such that: ([K]-{\omega}^{2}[M])\Psi =0;\Psi \ne 0 where [K] and [M] are the stiffness and mass matrices respectively. In this context, the problem of searching for optimal admissible fields in the sense of a functional of modified-ERC type is formulated in the following way: Find the triplet of admissible fields (u,v,w) which minimises: {e}_{\omega}^{2}(u,v,w)=\frac{\gamma}{2}{(u-v)}^{\text{ }}K+\frac{1-\gamma }{2}{(u-w)}^{\text{ }}{\omega}^{2}M+\frac{1-\alpha }{\alpha}{(\mathit{Hu}-\widehat{u})}^{\text{ }}\mathit{Gr} under the constraint: \left[K\right]v-{\omega}^{2}\left[M\right]\text{w=}0 Where: [K] represents a real stiffness matrix [M] represents a mass matrix [H] represents an observation matrix [{G}_{r}] represents a symmetric positive-definite matrix serving as the norm of the errors in the observation space \omega =2\pi f : excitation angular frequency \widehat{u} observation of the displacements at the angular frequency \omega \gamma weighting parameter of the errors (u-v) and (u-w) \alpha weighting parameter of the functional, which can be likened to a regularisation term 2.2.2 Obtaining the admissible fields for the frequency-domain formulation in a finite-element formalism The constrained optimisation problem above can be transformed into an unconstrained problem by introducing the following Lagrangian: {E}_{\omega}^{2}(u,v,w,\lambda )={e}_{\omega}^{2}(u,v,w)+([K]v-{\omega}^{2}[M]w)\lambda Thus, obtaining the triplet (u,v,w)\text{} that minimises the associated constrained problem is achieved by seeking the saddle point of the Lagrangian given by: \partial {E}_{\omega}^{2}(u,v,w,\lambda )=0 which, considering the matrices [K] and [M] to be symmetric, leads to: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial {E}_{\omega}^{2}}{\partial u}=\frac{\gamma}{2}K+\frac{1-\gamma }{2}{\omega}^{2}M+\frac{1-\alpha }{\alpha}{H}^{\text{T}}\mathit{Gr}=0\\ \frac{\partial {E}_{\omega}^{2}}{\partial v}=\frac{-\gamma }{2}K+[K]\lambda =0\\ \frac{\partial {E}_{\omega}^{2}}{\partial w}=\frac{\gamma -1}{2}{\omega}^{2}M-{\omega}^{2}[M]\lambda =0\\ \frac{\partial {E}_{\omega}^{2}}{\partial \lambda }=[K]v-{\omega}^{2}[M]w=0\end{array} By simplifying the equations and seeking to obtain a symmetric system of equations, the search for the fields leads to the solution of the system of linear equations of the form: Al=b with, for each natural angular frequency {\omega}_{i} : {A}_{i}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}\gamma \left(\text{K+γ}/\left(1-\gamma \right){\omega}_{i}^{2}M\right)& -\gamma \left(K-{\omega}_{i}^{2}M\right)\\ -\gamma \left(K-{\omega}_{i}^{2}M\right)& \left(-\text{2α}/\left(1-\alpha \right)\right){H}^{T}{G}_{r}H\end{array}\right) ; and {b}_{i}=\left(\begin{array}{c}{0}_{n}\\ \left(-\text{2α}/\left(1-\alpha \right)\right){H}^{T}{G}_{r}{\widehat{u}}_{i}\end{array}\right) where the vector of the unknown fields is: {l}_{i}={\left(\begin{array}{c}u\\ u-v\end{array}\right)}_{i} Note that the field (u-w) is obtained directly by combining the second and the third equation of the saddle-point search, leading to: (u-w)=\frac{\gamma -1}{\gamma}(u-v) 3 Implementation in Code_Aster The operator CALC_ERC_DYN U4.53.41 has been developed in order to make it possible to solve the problem of searching for the optimal fields (u,v,w) associated with the constrained optimisation problem described in the previous section. In concrete terms, for a given list of frequencies, it solves the system of linear equations Al=b detailed above, which makes it possible to obtain the fields u and u-v sought. It should be noted that the field u-w is not proposed as an output of the operator, because it results in a trivial way from a proportional ratio with u-v . This operator also makes it possible to evaluate, if desired, the value of the functional {e}_{\omega}^{2} at the solution triplet (u,v,w)\text{} . This is particularly useful when one wishes to use the functional {e}_{\omega}^{2} in an updating or identification problem. The operator uses five mandatory keywords: - the keywords MATR_RIGI and MATR_MASSE correspond respectively to the real assembled stiffness and mass matrices of the model under study; - the keyword MATR_NORME: this keyword makes it possible to supply the generalised assembled matrix corresponding to the symmetric positive-definite matrix {G}_{r} serving as the norm of the errors in the observation space. - the keyword MATR_PROJ: this keyword makes it possible to give the projection matrix associated with the operator H . It is a geometric correspondence between the mesh associated with the mass and stiffness matrices on the one hand, and the mesh associated with the observations \widehat{u} on the other hand. The projection matrix requested here must come from an analysis with the operator PROJ_CHAMP U4.72.05 with the method 'COLLOCATION'. - the keyword MESURE: this keyword makes it possible to supply the fields which will be used as the observation \widehat{{u}_{i}} . This concept must contain as many order numbers as the number of frequencies which will be studied when the operator is called (operands FREQ/LIST_FREQ). Furthermore, the dimension of the fields contained in this concept must be consistent with the dimension of the norm matrix supplied under the operand MATR_NORME. In addition, the fields contained must not include degrees of freedom of Lagrange type. To this end, it is advisable to condition this concept by prior use of the operator OBSERVATION U4.90.03; - the keyword CHAMP_MESURE making it possible to define the type of field contained in the measurement; - the keyword FREQ / LIST_FREQ making it possible to define the frequencies at which the problem will be solved; - the keywords ALPHA and GAMMA corresponding to the weighting parameters of the functional which can be likened to a regularisation term ( \alpha ) and to the weighting parameter of the errors (u-v) and (u-w) ( \gamma ); - the keyword EVAL_FONCT making it possible to determine whether the value of the functional for the optimal triplet of fields will be evaluated and stored in the result; - the keyword SOLVEUR making it possible to choose the type of solver which will be used when solving the problem. r4.20.01 Indicators of unloading and of loss of proportionality of the loading in elastoplasticity r4.20.01 Indicators of unloading and of loss of proportionality of the loading in elastoplasticity Summary A set of scalar parameters, called indicators, is presented, making it possible to assess an unloading or a loss of proportionality of a loading in the course of its history. Two types of indicator are proposed: indicators in the form of scalar fields, making it possible to detect the zones of the structure undergoing unloadings or non-radial loadings, and global indicators integrated over a zone of the structure chosen by the user. The latter are intended more specifically for assessing the validity of the energy release rate in non-linear fracture mechanics. The indicators described in this document are available: - for the local indicators, under the command CALC_CHAMP, options DERA_ELGA and DERA_ELNO; - for the global indicators, under the command POST_ELEM, options INDIC_SEUIL and INDIC_ENER. 1 Introduction 1.1 Definition of a proportional loading Considering a structure subjected to a thermo-mechanical loading over the time interval [0,t] , this loading is said to be proportional (or, equivalently, radial) at the material point p if the stress field represented at that point by the tensor \sigma is proportional to a tensor independent of the time instant under consideration, the coefficient of proportionality being a monotonic function of time. Formally, this is expressed by:  orall 	au \left[0,tight],\sigma (P,	au )=\alpha (	au ){\sigma}_{0}(P),\alpha (	au )>0 a monotonic function on [0,t] . This definition implies, in particular, that the principal directions of the stresses remain constant, at the point under consideration, throughout the loading path (these directions may of course vary from one point to another). 1.2 Importance of proportional loading and usefulness of indicators For plastic materials, the mechanical fields depend on the whole history elapsed along the loading path. The flow rules therefore have an incremental character, and their integration depends on each loading case. A notable exception is precisely proportional loading, for which the flow rule can be integrated once and for all. For example, the Prandtl–Reuss plasticity law based on the von Mises criterion can be replaced by a non-linear elastic law (called the Hencky–Mises law). Strictly proportional loading cases are fairly rare. Indeed, a large number of conditions must be satisfied in order to realise such a case [bib1], and these are seldom verified for industrial structures. It may even be said that, for structures presenting geometric defects such as cracks, these conditions are never strictly verified. When the loadings are multiaxial, cyclic, or transient thermo-mechanical, certain portions of the loading path may be strongly non-proportional. It is then useful to locate these portions and to assess the extent of the loss of proportionality, in order for example to adjust the time discretisation of the elastoplastic problem for the portion under consideration, or to gauge the validity of certain post-processings (in fracture mechanics, for example). 1.3 Different types of indicator of loss of proportionality It seems difficult to define a single, simple quantity (grandeur) which could detect both spatial zones of loss of proportionality and portions of the loading path (temporal zones) at a material point. This is why scalar quantities are proposed, each with its own specificity: two, defined by fields measuring at each point the unloading and the deviation of the stresses between two time steps (local indicators), and two others of a more global nature, characterising, in a given zone of the structure, a non-proportional loading history. Note: These indicators are closely linked to the time discretisation of the problem. In particular, if this discretisation is too coarse, the unloading or the loss of radiality occurring during the time increment may very well not be detected. 1.4 Indicators of elastoplastic unloading Another application of the unloading indicators consists in alerting the user if, in the event of significant unloading, the choice of a kinematic hardening would provide a solution very different from the isotropic hardening that was used (cf. CR-AMA-11.035 [3]). This is of practical interest: in several studies, the behaviour very often chosen “by default” (because often only a tensile curve is available) is VMIS_ISOT_TRAC. Now, if local unloadings are possible, this may typically lead to overestimating the stresses (at imposed strain) or underestimating the strains (at imposed stress). It therefore seems relevant to warn the user if, when laws of von Mises with isotropic hardening have been used, there is a risk of obtaining incorrect results once the unloading becomes too large (and therefore no longer remains within the initial elastic domain). This may indicate that constitutive laws with kinematic hardening should be used (VMIS_CINE_LINE, VMIS_ECMI , VMIS_CIN1_CHAB, etc.). 2 Local indicators The aim of these indicators is to identify the zones of the structure where, at a particular time instant, either an unloading or a loss of radiality of the stress field occurs. They are produced in the post-processing of a static or dynamic analysis, 2D or 3D, using an elastic or non-elastic constitutive law. They take the form of fields of scalars, which may be examined by plotting their isovalues with a graphical post-processor. 2.1 Unloading indicators 2.1.1 Local indicator of total unloading This indicator measures, at the point M and between the time instants t and t+\Delta t , the relative variation of the norm of the stresses in the von Mises sense. It is written formally: {I}_{1}= rac{\parallel \sigma (M,t+\Delta t)\parallel -\parallel \sigma (M,t)\parallel }{\parallel \sigma (M,t+\Delta t)\parallel } . This quantity is negative in the event of local unloading at the point M. The norm \parallel \sigma (M,t)\parallel may be written in four different ways, according to the choice of the modeller: 1. \parallel \sigma (M,t)\parallel =\sqrt{ rac{3}{2}{\sigma}^{D}.{\sigma}^{D}} , where {\sigma}^{D} is the deviatoric part of the stress tensor (this norm is useful in plasticity with isotropic hardening). 2. \parallel \sigma (M,t)\parallel =\sqrt{ rac{3}{2}\sigma .\sigma } , where the whole of the stress tensor is considered, in order to detect for example decreases in the hydrostatic pressure. 3. \parallel \sigma (M,t)\parallel =\sqrt{ rac{3}{2}({\sigma}^{D}-X).({\sigma}^{D}-X)} , with X the back-stress tensor in the case of an elastoplastic law with kinematic hardening. 4. \parallel \sigma (M,t)\parallel =\sqrt{ rac{3}{2}(\sigma -X).(\sigma -X)} 2.1.2 Local indicator of elastoplastic unloading This indicator makes it possible to determine whether the unloading remains elastic or whether there would be a risk of plastification if a purely kinematic hardening were used. It is an “extreme” indicator, given that, for metals, isotropic and kinematic hardenings are both present. The option DERA_ELGA therefore computes (in addition to the components DCHA_V and DCHA_T) the components: I_decha=IND_DCHA : - IND_DCHA=0 initial value with no stress. - IND_DCHA=1 if elastic loading - IND_DCHA=2 if plastic loading - IND_DCHA=-1 if admissible elastic unloading (whatever the type of hardening) - IND_DCHA=-2 if improper unloading (plastification would have occurred with a kinematic hardening). VAL_DCHA: indicates the proportion by which the criterion is left (see below).
