It is written: {I}_{2}=1- rac{\mid \sigma (M,t).\Delta \sigma \mid }{\parallel \sigma (M,t)\parallel \parallel \Delta \sigma \parallel } , where the scalar product “.” is associated with one of the four preceding norms. This quantity is zero when radiality is preserved during the time increment. This criterion may also be interpreted as the quantity 1-\cos(	heta ) , where 	heta is the angle between \sigma and \Delta \sigma . This real-valued indicator ranges between 0 for radial loadings and 1. It is useful in particular for determining the validity of an elastoplastic solution in fracture mechanics. 2.2.2 Indicator of the error due to the time discretisation It provides a measure of the error \eta due to the discretisation in time, directly related to the rotation of the normal to the yield surface. The angle between {n}^{-} , the normal to the plasticity criterion at the beginning of the time step (time instant t-), and {n}^{+} , the normal to the plasticity criterion computed at the end of the time step, is computed as follows: {I}_{\eta}= rac{1}{2}∣∣\Delta n∣∣= rac{1}{2}∣∣{n}^{+}-{n}^{-}∣∣=∣\sin( rac{\alpha}{2})∣ . This indicator is directly linked to the norm of the variation of the normal to the plasticity convex (this can easily be generalised to any elastoplastic law with normal flow), and it may also be interpreted as the sine of half the angle between the two normals. This provides a measure of the error (see [4]). This criterion is operational for the elastoplastic von Mises behaviours with isotropic, linear kinematic and mixed hardening. It may be used to drive the automatic subdivision of the time step. 3 Global indicators These indicators are intended to detect whether, in the course of the history of the structure and up to the current time instant t , and for a zone of the structure chosen by the modeller, there has been a loss of proportionality of the loading (these indicators therefore leave a trace of the history, unlike the local indicators, which are instantaneous). They can be used only in the framework of an elastoplastic behaviour with isotropic hardening (in 2D or 3D). 3.1 Indicator on the plasticity parameters This quantity makes it possible, in the case of von Mises plasticity with isotropic hardening, on the one hand to know (on average over a zone {\Omega}_{S} of the domain \Omega ) whether the stresses and the plastic strains have the same directions and whether the plastic threshold is reached at the current time instant, and on the other hand whether, in the course of the history, the plastic strain has changed direction. This quantity is written: {I}_{3}= rac{1}{{\Omega}_{S}}{\int}_{{\Omega}_{S}}(1- rac{\mid \sigma .{\varepsilon}^{p}\mid }{({\sigma}_{Y}+R(p))p})d\Omega , where {\sigma}_{Y} is the initial plastic threshold, R the extension of the yield surface associated with hardening, and p the accumulated plastic strain. r5.01.01 Modal solvers and solution of the generalised problem (GEP) r5.01.01 Modal solvers and solution of the generalised problem (GEP) Summary: Whether it is to study the vibrations of a structure or to look for its buckling modes, the engineer often has to solve a modal problem: either generalised (GEP) or quadratic (QEP) Modal solvers and solution of the generalised problem (GEP). To do this, several methods are proposed via the operator CALC_MODES: inverse powers and Rayleigh coefficient, Lanczos, IRA, Bathe & Wilson and QZ. Each has its field of use, its advantages, its disadvantages and its development history. In order to treat large modal problems efficiently (in mesh size and/or in number of modes sought), one advises the use of the macro-command CALC_MODES with the option BANDE split into several sub-bands. It decomposes the modal analysis of a standard GEP (symmetric and real) into a succession of independent sub-analyses, less costly, more robust and more accurate. Even in sequential mode, the gains can be appreciable: factors of 2 to 5 in time, 2 or 3 in peak RAM and 10 to 104 on the mean error of the modes. Moreover, its multi-level parallelism can provide additional gains of the order of 20 in time and 2 in peak RAM, by reserving about sixty processors. In the first part of the document, we summarise the general problem of solving a modal problem, the various classes of methods and their variants in the public-domain libraries. All things that one must bear in mind before tackling, in the second part, the general architecture of a modal analysis. We then detail the numerical, software and functional aspects of each of the approaches available in the code. A specific chapter details the implementation of parallelism and of high-performance computing in the framework of modal analyses of standard GEP type. 1 Introduction A majority of studies concerning the dynamic behaviour of structures is carried out by performing a transient analysis on a modal basis. In order to compute these vibration modes, numerous algorithms have been developed over some sixty years. In order to cope with the continual increase in the size of the problems and with the degradation of the conditioning of the discretised operators, only the most efficient and the most robust in practice have been incorporated into the modal analysis operator CALC_MODES. The optimal fields of use of the search criterion of this operator can be separated. When it is a matter of determining a few eigenvalues (typically half a dozen) or of refining a few estimates, the criterion PROCHE , SEPARE or AJUSTE is entirely appropriate. It groups heuristic algorithms and those of power type (cf. §4). On the other hand, in order to capture a significant part of the spectrum, one resorts to the criterion BANDE , CENTRE , PLUS_PETITE or PLUS_GRANDE . The latter brings together the so-called “subspace” methods (Lanczos cf. §5/§6, IRAM §7, Bathe & Wilson §8) which project the working operator in order to obtain an approximate modal problem of reduced size (then treated by a global method of QR or Jacobi type). This operator also makes it possible to compute, in a robust manner, the whole spectrum of the problem thanks to the criterion TOUT . To do this, one uses a reference global method (QZ method cf. §9) which computes all the modes exhaustively. In view of its cost, it is however to be reserved for certain uses: a problem of small size (fewer than {10}^{4} degrees of freedom) or an algorithm benchmark. The various search criteria can moreover complement one another, because the methods implemented with PROCHE , SEPARE or AJUSTE are very efficient for optimising eigenmodes that have already almost converged. In one or two iterations, they can thus improve the eigenvectors computed a first time via BANDE , CENTRE , PLUS_PETITE , PLUS_GRANDE or TOUT . The projection onto the modal basis will only be the better for it! In the first part of the document we summarise the general problem of solving a modal problem, the various classes of methods and their variants in the public-domain libraries. This type of problem corresponds, in mechanics, in particular to: - The study of the free vibrations of a structure which is undamped and non-rotating. For this structure, one looks for the smallest eigenvalues or else those which lie in a given interval in order to know whether an exciting force can create a resonance. In this standard case, the matrix A is the stiffness matrix, denoted \mathrm{K} , real and symmetric (possibly augmented by the geometric stiffness matrix denoted {K}_{g} , if the structure is prestressed) and B is the mass or inertia matrix denoted M (real symmetric). The eigenvalues obtained are the squares of the circular frequencies associated with the frequencies sought. The system to be solved can be written: (K+{K}_{g})u={\omega}^{2}Mu where \omega =2\pi f is the circular frequency, f the eigenfrequency and u the associated eigen displacement vector. The eigenmodes (\omega ,u) are real. In the presence of hysteretic damping , \mathrm{K} becomes complex symmetric. Then the eigenmodes are potentially complex and unpaired. On the other hand, if K and/or M remain real but possibly non-symmetric , the eigenmodes are either real, or in pairs (\lambda ,\bar{\lambda}) . In the framework of linearised theory, assuming a priori that the stability phenomena are adequately described by the system of equations obtained by assuming the linear dependence of the displacement with respect to the critical load level, the search for the buckling mode u associated with this critical load level \lambda reduces to a generalised eigenvalue problem of the form: (\mathrm{K}+\lambda {\mathrm{K}}_{\mathrm{g}})\mathrm{u}=0 with K the stiffness matrix and {K}_{g} the geometric stiffness matrix. In order to fit into the “mould” of a standard GEP computation, the code computes, in a first stage, the real eigenmodes (-\lambda ,u) . Then it converts them to the format of a buckling analysis: (\lambda ,\mathrm{u}) . This type of problem is activated by the keyword TYPE_RESU=‘MODE_FLAMB’. It is to be reserved for real symmetric GEPs (otherwise the code detects it and produces a fatal error). Notes: - CALC_MODES makes it possible to automate the choice of the algorithm as a function of the search criterion, and to reduce the costs (CPU and memory) of a search for a significant part of the spectrum (only for a GEP with real modes) when one looks for the modes on a global band split into sub-bands. - The user can specify the class of membership of the analysis by initialising the keyword TYPE_RESU to 'DYNAMIQUE' (default value) or to 'MODE_FLAMB'. The display of the results will then be formatted taking this specificity into account. In the first case one will speak of frequency (FREQ) whereas in the second, one will speak of critical load (CHAR_CRIT). - In the presence of damping and of gyroscopic effects, the study of the dynamic stability of a structure leads to the solution of a modal problem of higher order, called quadratic (QEP): (K+i\omega C-{\omega}^{2}M)u=0 . It is solved by the two modal operators and is the subject of a specific note[Boi09]. Now that the links between structural mechanics and the solution of generalised modal problems have been recalled, we shall take an interest in the treatment of the boundary conditions in the code and in their effects on the mass and stiffness matrices. 3.2 Taking boundary conditions into account There are two ways, when building the stiffness and mass matrices, of taking the boundary conditions into account (this description in terms of a dynamic problem extrapolates easily to buckling): - Double dualisation, using Lagrange degrees of freedom[Pel01], makes it possible to enforce Cu=0 (CLL for Linear Boundary Condition), with C a real matrix of size p\times n ( K and M are of order n ). It entails the handling of larger matrices (called “dualised”) because they incorporate these new unknowns. The dualised stiffness and mass matrices then have the form \tilde{\mathrm{K}}=(\begin{array}{ccc}\mathrm{K}& \beta {\mathrm{C}}^{\mathrm{T}}& \beta {\mathrm{C}}^{\mathrm{T}}\\ \beta \mathrm{C}& -\alpha \mathrm{Id}& \alpha \mathrm{Id}\\ \beta \mathrm{C}& \alpha \mathrm{Id}& -\alpha \mathrm{Id}\end{array}) \tilde{M}=(\begin{array}{ccc}M& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}) with \alpha and \beta strictly positive reals (which serve to balance the terms of the matrix). The dimension of the problem has been increased by \mathrm{2p} , because to the n so-called "physical" degrees of freedom, one has added Lagranges. There are two Lagranges per linear relation assigned to the p boundary conditions. - The setting to zero of p rows and columns of the stiffness and mass matrices . This is valid only for blockings of degrees of freedom (simple Dirichlet, no proportionality relation between dofs). One cannot take a linear relation into account and one will speak of kinematic blocking (CLB for Blocking Boundary Condition). The stiffness and mass matrices become: \tilde{K}=(\begin{array}{cc}\bar{K}& 0\\ 0& \mathrm{Id}\end{array}) \tilde{M}=(\begin{array}{cc}\bar{M}& 0\\ 0& 0\end{array}) The dimension of the problem remains unchanged but one must however remove the participations of the blocked dofs from the components of the initial matrices ( \bar{K} is obtained from K by eliminating the rows and the columns of the dofs which are blocked; likewise for \bar{M} ). When one imposes boundary conditions, the number of eigenvalues (with all their multiplicities) actually involved in the physics of the phenomenon is therefore lower than the size n of the transformed problem: - {n}_{\mathit{ddl}-\mathit{actifs}}=n-\frac{3p'}{2}\text{avec}p'=2p (double dualisation), - {n}_{\mathrm{ddl}-\mathrm{actifs}}=n-p (kinematic blocking). On the other hand, in the modal analysis algorithms, one must make sure that the solutions belong to the admissible space . One brings oneself back to it via auxiliary treatments. Thus when one uses kinematic blockings (CLB), one must, in the various algorithms and at each iteration, use a “positioning vector” {\mathrm{u}}_{\mathit{bloq}} , defined by - if the i th degree of freedom is not blocked {\mathrm{u}}_{\mathit{bloq}}(i)=1 , - otherwise {\mathrm{u}}_{\mathit{bloq}}(i)=0 , and pre-multiply each vector handled {\mathrm{u}}^{1}(i)={\mathrm{u}}^{0}(i)\cdot {\mathrm{u}}_{\mathit{bloq}}(i)(i=\mathrm{1...n})\mathrm{\Rightarrow }{\mathrm{u}}^{1} This trick introduces the constraint of the blockings into the whole algorithmics and implicitly directs the search for the solution into the admissible space. Likewise, if one uses the double dualisation method, one needs a positioning vector of the Lagrange degrees of freedom {\mathrm{u}}_{\mathit{lagr}} defined like {\mathrm{u}}_{\mathit{bloq}} . It is used only when choosing the random initial vector. This makes it possible to enrich the modal analysis more rapidly by not limiting oneself to the kernel. Very often, they will be denoted by A and B in order to stay close to the usual modal notation without attaching oneself to such or such a class of problems. On the other hand, A being normal, its eigenvectors are orthogonal. In the case of the GEP \mathrm{A}\mathrm{u}=\lambda \mathrm{B}\mathrm{u} , this condition is not sufficient. Thus, let us consider the following generalised problem: \left\begin{array}{cc}1& 1\\ 1& 0\end{array}\right=\lambda \left\begin{array}{cc}1& 0\\ 0& -1\end{array}\right its eigenmodes are . {\lambda}_{\pm}=\frac{1}{2}(1\pm i\sqrt{(3)})\text{et}{u}_{\pm}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{\lambda}_{\pm}^{2}}}(\begin{array}{}-{\lambda}_{\pm}\\ 1\end{array}) If one adds the hypothesis "one of the matrices A or B is positive definite ", then the generalised problem has real solutions . One even has the following more precise characterisation (sufficient condition). Theorem1 Let A and B be two real symmetric matrices. If there exist \alpha \in \mathrm{ℝ} and \beta \in ℝ such that \alpha A+\beta B is positive definite, then the generalised problem has real eigen elements. Proof: This result is obtained immediately by multiplying the generalised problem by \alpha and by performing a spectral shift \beta . One then obtains the problem (\alpha A+\beta B)u=(\lambda \alpha +\beta )Bu . Since \alpha A+\beta B is positive definite, it admits a unique Cholesky decomposition in the form C{C}^{T} with C a regular matrix. The problem is then written {C}^{\text{-1}}B{C}^{-T}z=\mu z with z={C}^{T}u and \mu =\frac{1}{\alpha \lambda +\beta } , which allows one to conclude, because the matrix {C}^{\text{-1}}B{C}^{-T} is symmetric. On the other hand, in the non-Hermitian complex case (this is the case when taking hysteretic damping into account in Code_Aster), the eigenmodes may be complex: eigenvectors with complex components and eigenvalues \lambda real or arbitrary complex. - In the real non-symmetric case, the eigenmodes may be complex: eigenvectors with complex components and eigenvalues \lambda real or complex in pairs (\lambda ,\bar{\lambda}) . The following paragraphs detail them. 3.7.1 Determination of the shift The first operation consists in determining the shift as well as certain parameters of the problem. This is carried out in a more or less transparent manner depending on the computation option chosen by the user: - OPTION='SEPARE' or 'AJUSTE' => the shift is determined by the first phase of the algorithm and the number of eigenmodes sought per frequency band (supplied by the Sturm criterion) is bounded by NMAX_FREQ. - OPTION='PROCHE' => the shift is fixed by the user and the number of eigenmodes is equal to the number of shifts. - OPTION='PLUS_PETITE' => the shift is zero and the number of modes is parameterised by NMAX_FREQ. - OPTION='BANDE' => the shift is equal to the middle of the band fixed by the user and the number of modes is determined by the Sturm criterion. - OPTION='CENTRE' => the shift is fixed by the user and the number of eigenmodes is parameterised by NMAX_FREQ. Notes: - This phase does not concern the QZ algorithm. Indeed the latter computes the whole spectrum of the GEP. It is just after the modal analysis that one takes the user's desiderata into account (OPTION=’BANDE’ or ’CENTRE’ or 'PLUS_PETITE' or 'PLUS_GRANDE' or ’TOUT’) in order to select the modes sought. - For a GEP with complex modes ( \mathrm{K} complex symmetric or non-symmetric matrices), only the options ’CENTRE’, 'PLUS_PETITE', 'PLUS_GRANDE', ’TOUT’ are available (with Sorensen and QZ). 3.7.2 Factorisation of dynamic matrices In the second phase of pre-processings, one factorises [Boi08] “dynamic” matrices of the type Q(\sigma ):=A-\sigma B . That is to say that one decomposes the dynamic matrix Q(\sigma ) into a product of particular matrices (triangular, diagonal) which are easier to handle in order to solve linear systems of the type Q(\sigma )x=y . In the symmetric case, the decomposition is of the form Q(\sigma )=LD{L}^{T} , in the non-symmetric case, one has Q(\sigma )=LU , with U , L and D , respectively, upper triangular, lower triangular and diagonal. Once this (costly) numerical factorisation has been carried out, the solution of other linear systems comprising the same matrix but with a different right-hand side (problem of multiple right-hand sides type) is very fast. During this conversion, one filters and transcribes the results of the previous computation. Concerning the eigenvalues, one retains all the solutions computed: real, complex alone or in pairs. In CALC_MODES with OPTION='SEPARE’/'AJUSTE'/'PROCHE', two variants are available: the inverse iteration method ('DIRECT') and its acceleration by Rayleigh quotient ('RAYLEIGH'). They refine the eigenvalues previously detected by the heuristics (‘SEPARE’ or ’AJUSTE’) or the estimates supplied by the user (‘PROCHE‘). As for CALC_MODES with OPTION='BANDE'/'CENTRE'/'PLUS_ '/'TOUT', it allows the use of four distinct methods: the Bathe & Wilson method ('JACOBI'), the subspace methods of Lanczos type ('TRI_DIAG ' ) and Sorensen ('SORENSEN') and the global QZ method (‘QZ’). Concerning the eigenvectors, one forces their B -orthonormalisation only for a real symmetric GEP (otherwise one cannot define a B -inner product). With the Sorensen method and with QZ, this orthonormalisation is carried out explicitly, at the end of the modal analysis, via the IGSM algorithm of Kahan-Parlett (cf. appendix 2). For the other modal solvers, this step is included in their internal computation procedures. When one carries out an explicit reorthogonalisation, the latter concerns only the eigenmodes supposed to belong to the same eigenspace ( cf. note below). The theory assures us of the orthogonality of the other cases. This “targeted” orthogonalisation often makes it possible to gain at least 50% of the global computation time of the operator (sometimes up to 90%). One can of course only too strongly recommend not to deactivate these 'override' parameters! Notes: - When with the options 'BANDE','CENTRE','PLUS_ ' or 'TOUT' one activates the improvement procedure (keyword AMELIORATION='OUI' ), the Sturm test is not carried out at the end of the first solution step (by a subspace method). This is useless, since these modes are liable to be modified in the second step, that of improvement (by a few iterations of the inverse power method). It is only after this step that one carries out all the verifications: residual, Sturm test and membership of the initial band (if OPTION='BANDE' ). - The Sturm test can also be activated with the options ' PROCHE ', ' SEPARE ' and ' AJUSTE '. It does not then fulfil quite the same function. Indeed, these options serve to refine initial estimates of eigenvalues and to compute the associated eigenvectors: the presence of 'holes' in the spectrum computed is then possible and licit. On the other hand, the other options (' BANDE ' etc...) must compute all the modes specified, without omitting any: no hole in the spectrum is then tolerated. With 'PROCHE', 'SEPARE' and 'AJUSTE', the issuing of alarm or error messages does not therefore necessarily reveal a numerical problem but may be normal depending on the data setup. Thus if one specifies FREQ=(100.0,300.0) , the option ' PROCHE ' refines these values to (99.0, 299.0) and the spectrum of the mechanical problem normally also contains the value 200.0 , the Sturm test (if one activates it) will stop the computation on an error message whereas this absence of the value 200.0 is normal. The user did not ask for it to be refined! With the initial setting FREQ=(100.0, 200.0, 300.0) this alarm would no longer appear . In this framework, the activation of the Sturm test is therefore to be handled with caution. Functionally, it serves rather to defer the verification tests when one activates the keyword AMELIORATION at the end of a subspace method (cf. previous note). 3.7.5 Display in the message file In the message file are mentioned the pieces of information relating to the modes retained. One will therefore limit oneself to this case in the remainder of this chapter. In order to compute several eigenvalues of the generalised problem, one does not use the general method of inverse iterations as it stands . One can, for example, combine it with a deflation technique [11]_ so as to filter automatically the spectral information updated in order not to find it again at the next iteration. With the deflation by restriction [12]_ of Wielandt one builds iteratively the working operator (in the symmetric case), denoting by ({\mu}_{k},{\mathrm{u}}_{k}) the mode to be filtered {\mathrm{A}}_{k+1}={\mathrm{A}}_{k}-{\mu}_{k}{\mathrm{u}}_{k}{\mathrm{u}}_{k}^{\mathrm{t}} . This strategy, which does not apprehend the multiplicities, must be completed by a Sturm criterion. On the other hand, the fact of working in finite arithmetic and of not actually building the operator {A}_{k} at each iteration constrains one to blend this approach with high-performance orthogonalisation processes. All these complications have led to choosing another path, which breaks down into two parts: - The localisation of the eigenvalues (determination of an approximate value of each eigenvalue contained in an interval given by a bisection technique , refined or not by a secant method ). - The improvement of these estimates and the computation of their associated eigenvectors by an inverse iteration method . The search for an approximate value for each eigenvalue considered is selected in the factor keyword CALC_FREQ via OPTION: - If OPTION='SEPARE', in each interval of frequencies defined by the keyword FREQ, an approximate value of each eigenvalue contained in this interval is computed by using the dichotomy method (cf. §4.2.1). - If OPTION='AJUSTE', one first carries out the same operations as previously and then, starting from these approximations, one refines the result by the secant method. For these two options, one computes at the same time the modal position of each eigenvalue, which makes it possible to detect the multiple modes. Either one retains only the NMAX_FREQ lowest frequencies contained in the maximum interval specified by the user, or one computes all the values of this interval (if NMAX_FREQ=0). - If OPTION='PROCHE', the frequencies given by the keyword FREQ are considered as the approximate values of the eigenvalues sought. Notes: - Of course, as one has already specified, these options are to be used only to determine or refine a few eigenvalues. For a more extended search, one must use the other search options. - With the option 'PROCHE', one cannot compute multiple modes. - It is a costly algorithm because it makes much use of the Sturm test and therefore of its associated factorisations. - The bounds of the search intervals are supplied by FREQ or CHAR_CRIT depending on the initialisation of TYPE_RESU. We shall now detail the various algorithms (and their parameters) which are put in place in the first part of the process. 4.2 Localisation and separation of the eigenvalues 4.2.1 Bisection method As one has already seen previously, corollary 5bis of Sylvester's law of inertia (cf. § 3.5) makes it possible to determine the number of eigenvalues contained in a given interval by carrying out two decompositions LD{L}^{T} . This criterion can therefore lead to refining the interval until it encompasses only one eigenvalue. This driving being put in place, one passes from one iteration to the other by using the principle of dichotomy . On a starting interval [{\lambda}_{a},{\lambda}_{b}] , one therefore proceeds as follows, knowing pm({\lambda}_{a}) and pm({\lambda}_{b}) : Algorithm 3. Bisection method. One stops the process if one has cut the starting interval more than NMAX_ITER_SEPARE times, or if for a given interval one has ( (\frac{\mid {\lambda}_{a}-{\lambda}_{b}\mid }{{\lambda}^{\text{ }}})\le \text{PREC\_SEPARE} in this case one no longer refines the search in this interval). One finally obtains a list of frequencies. In each interval defined by the arguments of this list, there lies an eigenvalue having a certain multiplicity. As an approximation of this eigenvalue, one takes the middle of the interval. Notes: - One could have used as a criterion the change of sign of the characteristic polynomial, but besides the fact that it is very costly to evaluate, it does not make it possible, as it stands, to detect the multiplicities, - The initialisation of the process can be carried out empirically according to the user's needs. In order to encompass a part of the spectrum one can also use the regions of the complex plane of the Gerschgörin-Hadamard theorems (on \mathrm{A},{\mathrm{A}}^{\mathrm{T}} ...). In this respect, the bisection method can prove more efficient than a QR in the presence of a cluster. Its convergence, although linear, is indeed bounded by 1/2 whereas that of QR can tend towards 1[LT86]. Figure 4.2-1. Bisection method. 4.2.2 Secant method The secant method is a simplification of the Newton-Raphson method . At an arbitrary step, k knowing a value {\lambda}_{k} and by approximating the non-linear function p(\lambda ) by its tangent at this point, one determines the next value {\lambda}_{k+1} as being the intersection of this straight line with the \lambda axis, and so on, according to the iterative scheme > {\lambda}_{k+1}={\lambda}_{k}-p({\lambda}_{k})\frac{{\lambda}_{k}-{\lambda}_{k-1}}{p({\lambda}_{k})-p({\lambda}_{k-1})} Figure 4.2-2. Secant method. The tangent being approximated by a finite difference so as not to have to compute a derivative of p(\lambda ) , only the estimation of the polynomial is required. One considers that one has reached convergence when \frac{\mid {\lambda}_{k+1}-{\lambda}_{k}\mid }{{\lambda}_{k}} >}\varepsilon (i\le k) ). The numerical treatment of these problems has been the subject of numerous researches for thirty years and numerous palliative strategies have been developed. The choice of such or such a method depends on the type of spectral information required and on the computing resources available; the survey of JL.Vaudescal moreover proposes a very good overview of these variants: - Lanczos algorithm without reorthogonalisation , developed by J.K.Cullum and R.A.Willoughby[CW85] which consists in purging the spectrum computed of its spurious modes by studying the interlacings of the eigenvalues of the working matrix and of one of its sub-matrices. This variant admits a low extra computational and memory cost for determining the eigenvalues, but it complicates (sometimes greatly) the search for the eigenvectors. - Lanczos algorithms with total reorthogonalisation (B.N.Parlett) or selective (J.Scott) which consist at each step in reorthogonalising the last Lanczos vector obtained with respect to all the vectors already computed or simply with respect to the converged Ritz vectors (this variant thus makes it possible to drive dynamically the admissible loss of orthogonality). These variants are much more costly in computational complexity (the automatic reorthogonalisations) and in memory (storage of the previous vectors) but they prove more efficient and more robust. In the Newmann-Pipano variant[NP77] (METHODE='TRI_DIAG') of Code_Aster , it is the full reorthogonalisation strategy [22]_ which has been chosen: the vector {q}_{k+1} is therefore not quite computed as in the theoretical algorithm. Notes: - These problems of loss of orthogonality arise with all the more acuity as the size of the subspace increases. This is an additional argument for putting in place an iterative process limiting this size. - These strategies come in vector or block form; they are implemented in simple or iterative algorithms. The latter being able to benefit from explicit or implicit restarts, driven or automatic. The IRAM variant thus benefits from an implicit restart computed automatically. - The central point of these algorithms is constituted by the orthogonalisation method put in place. The whole process depends on its success and on its robustness. To the orthogonal transformations of Householder or Givens type, very expensive but very robust, one now prefers the algorithms of Iterative Gram-Schmidt type (IGSM) which are a better compromise between efficiency and computational complexity (cf. Appendix 2). This is moreover the choice which has been made for the Lanczos/Arnoldi variants put in place in the code. - The variant of selective reorthogonalisation with respect to the converged modes amounts to carrying out an implicit deflation by restriction on the working operator so as not to have to recompute them (cf. § 4.1). 6.3.2 Capture of multiplicities One has seen that in theory the Lanczos algorithm did not allow, whatever its reorthogonalisation strategy, the theoretical capture of multiple modes. In practice , for once, the rounding effects come to the rescue and "sprinkle" small components along almost all the eigenvectors. One can therefore capture multiplicities ; however they can be erroneous and require a complementary verification post-processing. Note: - In fact, only a block version (G.Golub & R.Underwood 1979) can allow us a correct detection of the multiplicities, at least as long as the size of the blocks is sufficient. This version has been extended (M.Sadkane[Sad93] 1993) to the Arnoldi algorithm but it would be a pity to deprive oneself of the Sorensen variant (IRAM) which is more efficient and more robust. 6.3.3 Lanczos phenomenon The success of this algorithm rested at the outset on what is called the “ Lanczos phenomenon ”. This conjecture predicts that for a sufficiently large subspace size ( m\gg n ) one is capable of detecting the whole spectrum (it being the subsequent task to separate the “wheat from the chaff”) of the working operator. In view of the low memory pre-requisites of a “basic” Lanczos ( roughly a tridiagonal matrix and a few vectors), this is particularly interesting for treating very large sparse systems (the other algorithms of iterated power type or QR themselves require the knowledge of the whole working matrix). We shall now detail (a little) a few elements whose interest goes far beyond the framework of this algorithm. 6.4 Complementary treatments 6.4.1 Detection of invariant subspaces In algorithm 8, the vanishing of the coefficient {\beta}_{l-1} prevents the normalisation of the new vector and requires an ancillary treatment called deflation . From the number of frequencies desired, one estimates the dimension of the computation subspace and one hopes that the eigenmodes of the projected standard problem will be a good approximation of those of the generalised problem. One verifies a posteriori the validity of the results (cf. §3.5) but one has no active control over this accuracy. If they are not satisfactory, one has as sole recourse only to carry out a new attempt by increasing the dimension of the subspace. Note: - The IRA method which we are going to tackle proposes a modulable and dynamic control of the accuracy of the results; it is an iterative method. 6.5.4 Detection of rigid-body modes An algebraic method computing the zero eigenvalues of the generalised modal problem has been introduced. Physically these correspond to the motions with zero strain energy of a free structure (cf. [BQ00] tutorial no. 2). Apart from the numerical difficulties of handling quasi-zero quantities, because of their multiplicities, their correct capture had until now often been problematic for the Lanczos implemented in Code_Aster : spurious modes appeared corresponding to missed multiplicities! This algorithm for detecting rigid-body modes, which one activates by initialising OPTION to ‘MODE_RIGIDE’ (default value ‘SANS‘), intervenes in pre-processing of the modal analysis proper (only with ‘TRI_DIAG’). It is based on the analysis of the stiffness matrix and breaks down into three phases: - Detection of the zero pivots of this matrix. - Blocking of these pivots. - Solution of a linear system of which the associated eigenvectors are solutions. During the Lanczos process it is then sufficient to orthogonalise, as they are determined, the basis vectors with these latter. However, the introduction of the IRA method reduces the interest (if not for comparison purposes) of such an option (which is not free in computational complexity since it requires inversions of systems). Why deprive oneself of such an algorithm which is in no way affected by the presence of these somewhat particular multiple modes! This method nevertheless remains useful as a fallback solution in the event of failure of IRAM. One can also envisage encapsulating it in an auxiliary operator (like INFO_MODE). Note: - This option ‘MODE_RIGIDE’ can be activated only with Lanczos for GEPs with real modes. 6.6 Field of use GEP with real symmetric matrices . A generalisation of this algorithm to the non-Hermitian case imagined by W.E.Arnoldi [Arn51] in 1951 makes it possible to solve this problem partially. It was brought back into fashion by Y.Saad[Saa80] in 1980 and an abundant literature covers the subject. Apart from the founding article and the papers of Y.Saad and M.Sadkane[Sad93], one recommends the updated and exhaustive survey of J.L.Vaudescal[Vau00]. This method being at the basis of the IRAM algorithm called “of Sorensen” (IRAM for ‘Implicit Restarted Arnoldi Method’), we shall first detail its operation, its behaviours and its limitations. Subsequently, we shall identify the issues which IRAM must answer (and it does so in most standard cases!) and we shall look into its theoretical and numerical inner workings. We shall conclude with the summary of its effective parameters in Code_Aster and with an example of a message file. 7.2 Arnoldi algorithm 7.2.1 Principle Its field of application covers all the pairs “working operator-(pseudo)inner product” . The counterpart of this openness is the fill-in of the Rayleigh matrix which becomes of upper Hessenberg form. This is not very prejudicial, because one can thus apply the QR algorithm to it directly. The first step of a good QR, apart from the balancing, consists precisely in reducing the working matrix to Hessenberg form. This makes it possible to gain an order of magnitude during the solution proper (cf. Appendix 1). The algorithm is very similar to that of Lanczos; it consists in progressively building a family of Arnoldi vectors {\mathrm{q}}_{1,}{\mathrm{q}}_{2,}\mathrm{...},{\mathrm{q}}_{m} by projecting orthogonally, at iteration k , the vector {\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma}{\mathrm{q}}_{k} onto the k previous vectors. The new vector becomes {\mathrm{q}}_{k+1} and thus, step by step, one ensures the orthogonality of this family of vectors. Unlike Lanczos, the orthogonality of the new vector with respect to all the previous ones is therefore ensured explicitly and not implicitly. The latter is managed by the Modified Gram-Schmidt algorithm (GSM) (cf. appendix 2) which proves sufficiently robust in most cases. Denoting by {\mathrm{e}}_{m} the m th vector of the canonical basis, the residual vector of the Arnoldi factorisation is written {\mathrm{R}}_{m}={b}_{m+1,m}{\mathrm{q}}_{m+1}{\mathrm{e}}_{m}^{T} . The Rayleigh matrix is then written: {\mathrm{B}}_{m}=\left[\begin{array}{cccc}{b}_{11}& {b}_{12}& ...& {b}_{\mathrm{1m}}\\ {b}_{21}& {b}_{22}& ...& {b}_{\mathrm{2m}}\\ 0& ...& ...& {b}_{m-1,m}\\ 0& 0& {b}_{m,m-1}& {b}_{\text{mm}}\end{array}\right] Apart from the form of this matrix and a lesser acuity to the orthogonality problems, this algorithm assures us of the same theoretical and numerical properties as Lanczos . However if one lets the size of the subspace grow indefinitely until convergence of the eigenvalues desired, the rounding effects will nevertheless take over again and one is heading for big trouble. Hence the necessity, as for Lanczos, of making this process iterative via restarts. Notes: - This method can be seen as an implicit variant of the Lanczos algorithm with total reorthogonalisation. - The implicit orthogonalisation of the algorithm can be conducted by more costly but more robust algorithms such as QR or IGSM. This is strongly required when the working operator presents too strong a defect of normality. - Because of the structure of {\mathrm{B}}_{m} , the memory complexity is more solicited than with Lanczos; on the other hand the computational complexity remains of the same order of magnitude O(\mathrm{nm}(c+3+m)) (with c the mean number of non-zero terms on the rows of the working matrix). - In order to improve this first point, Y.Saad[Saa80] has shown that the upper Hessenberg structure can see its extreme super-diagonals vanish if one carries out the reorthogonalisation only partially. - Vector algorithms having a natural tendency to miss multiplicities, one often prefers to use a block version (M.Sadkane 1993). But the size of the latter influences the quality of the results; it is for this reason that one prefers the vector or block versions of IRAM. - The choice of the initial Arnoldi vector is carried out in the same manner as for Lanczos. 7.2.2 Error and convergence estimates As regards the evaluation of the quality of approximation of the eigenmodes obtained, one has a criterion as simple and efficient as for Lanczos. Property 5 The Euclidean norm of the residual of the Ritz element (\tilde{\lambda},\tilde{\mathrm{u}}={\mathrm{Q}}_{m}\mathrm{x}) is equal to {\mathrm{\parallel }\mathrm{r}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2}={\mathrm{\parallel }({\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma}-\tilde{\lambda}\mathrm{I})\tilde{\mathrm{u}}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2}=\mid {b}_{m+1,m}\mid \mid {\mathrm{e}}_{m}^{T}\mathrm{x}\mid Proof: Trivial by taking the Euclidean norm of the Arnoldi factorisation {\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma}{\mathrm{Q}}_{m}\mathrm{x}={\mathrm{Q}}_{m}{\mathrm{B}}_{m}{\mathrm{x}+b}_{m+1,m}{\mathrm{q}}_{m+1}{\mathrm{e}}_{m}^{T}\mathrm{x} and as {\mathrm{q}}_{m+1} is normed to unity. Still focusing on the norm of the additional projector {\mathrm{\parallel }(\mathrm{I}-{\mathrm{P}}_{m})\mathrm{u}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2} one can generalise the convergence theorem 3 to the non-Hermitian case. Theorem 6 Let ({\lambda}_{1},{\mathrm{u}}_{1}) be the first (classical ordering, in decreasing order of modulus) dominant eigenmode of the diagonalisable {\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma} and let {\mathrm{q}}_{1}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}{\alpha}_{k}{\mathrm{u}}_{k} be the initial Arnoldi vector decomposed on the basis of eigenvectors; there then exists a Ritz mode ({\tilde{\lambda}}_{1},{\tilde{u}}_{1}) such that: \mid {\lambda}_{1}-{\tilde{\lambda}}_{1}\mid \le \frac{{\alpha}^{2}}{\beta}{\xi}_{1}{\delta}_{1}^{m} with \alpha =\frac{\beta}{{\mathrm{\parallel }{\mathrm{P}}_{m}{\mathrm{u}}_{i}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2}} , \beta the constant of theorem 1, {\xi}_{1}=\sum_{k=1,k\mathrm{\ne }1}^{n}\mid \frac{{\alpha}_{k}}{{\alpha}_{1}}\mid et :math: {\delta}_{1}^{m}={(\sum_{j=2}^{m+1}\prod_{k=2,k\mathrm{\ne }j}^{m+1}∣\frac{{\lambda}_{k}-{\lambda}_{1}}{{\lambda}_{k}-{\lambda}_{j}}∣)}^{-1} . This result extends in the same manner to the other modes. Proof: By taking up the demonstration of Y.Saad ([Saa91] pp209-210) and the result of theorem 1. These upper bounds, very different from those obtained with Lanczos, nevertheless guide the same phenomena: - If the initial vector has no contribution along the eigenvectors sought, one cannot capture them ( {\xi}_{i}\to +\infty ). - One has preferentially convergence of the peripheral modes of the spectrum, and this all the better as it is separated (property of {\lambda}_{i}^{m} ). - The decrease of the error is proportional to the increase of m (property of {\lambda}_{i}^{m} ). Notes: - When an eigenvalue is poorly conditioned {\xi}_{i}\to +\infty then one must increase m in order that {\lambda}_{i}^{m} decrease. - Analogous results have been seen in the case of a defective operator (cf. Zia 94). Armed with these lessons, we shall now summarise the issues which IRAM must answer. 7.3 The issues at stake The IRA algorithm attempts to bring an elegant remedy to the recurrent problems raised by the other approaches: - Minimisation of the projection space : it proposes at a minimum m>p+1 instead of the m=4p of Lanczos. - Optimal management of the extra costs of orthogonalisation establishing a compromise between the size of the subspace and the frequency of the restarts . - Transparent, dynamic and efficient management of these restarts. - Automatic taking into account of the spectral information . - Fixing of the memory pre-requisites and of the quality of the results . One therefore no longer has any question to ask oneself concerning the reorthogonalisation strategy, the frequency of the restarts, their implementations, the criteria for detecting possible spurious modes... “super-IRAM” takes care of everything! In short, it provides: - A better overall robustness . - Computational complexities O(\mathrm{4nm}(m-p)) and memory complexities O(\mathrm{2np}+{p}^{2}) improved (especially compared with a simple Lanczos such as that of Newmann & Pipano) for a fixed accuracy . - A more rigorous capture of the multiplicities, of the clusters and of the rigid-body modes (hence fewer parasitic modes !). Notes: - On this last point, only a block version of IRAM or a version incorporating “purge and lock” (capture and filtering techniques, cf. D.Sorensen & R.B.Lehoucq, 1997) can guarantee us a correct detection of the spectrum of a standard operator (i.e. not too poorly conditioned). - It seems that, in practice in Code_Aster , the ratio in computational complexity between IRAM and Lanczos/Bathe & Wilson is at a minimum of the order of 2 in favour of the former. With reasonable problem sizes (a few tens of thousands of dofs and p=O(100) ) the latter can rise up to 10 (without the encapsulation of CALC_MODES over several search sub-bands). In certain semi-industrial cases, it has made it possible to carry out a spectrum search which had failed with Jacobi and which was unapproachable with Lanczos (in view of the time allotted). - A class of algorithm called “Jacobi-Davidson” (cf. R.B.Morgan 1990) seems even more promising for treating pathological cases. It uses an algorithm of Lanczos type which it preconditions via a Rayleigh method. In the following paragraph we shall explain the operation of IRAM. 7.4 ‘Implicit Restarted Arnoldi’ (IRA) algorithm This algorithm was initiated by D.C.Sorensen[Sor92] in 1992 and is enjoying a real boom for the solution of large modal systems on parallel supercomputers. Its field of application is entirely general. It treats both real and complex problems, Hermitian or not. It is summarised as a succession of Arnoldi factorisations whose results automatically drive static and implicit restarts, via polynomial filters modelled by implicit QRs. First of all it carries out an Arnoldi factorisation of order m=p+q (in theory q=2 is sufficient, in practice q=p is preferable. It is moreover this last default value which has been retained (cf. §7.5) of the working matrix. Then once this pre-processing has been carried out it iterates a process of filtering of the undesirable part of the spectrum (numerically and methodologically, it is easier to exclude than to incorporate). It begins by determining the spectrum of the Rayleigh matrix ( via the unassailable QR) and it dissociates from it the undesired part (by referring to the criteria fixed by the user) which it then uses as a shift in order to put in place a series of q implicit QRs with simple shift (cf. Appendix 1). The factorisation is then written: {\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma}{\mathrm{Q}}_{m}^{+}={\mathrm{Q}}_{m}^{+}{\mathrm{B}}_{m}^{+}+{\mathrm{R}}_{m}\mathrm{Q} where {\mathrm{Q}}_{m}^{+}={\mathrm{Q}}_{m}\mathrm{Q} , {\mathrm{B}}_{m}^{+}={\mathrm{Q}}^{T}{\mathrm{B}}_{m}\mathrm{Q} and \mathrm{Q}={\mathrm{Q}}_{1}{\mathrm{Q}}_{2}\mathrm{....}{\mathrm{Q}}_{q} the unitary matrix associated with the QRs. After having updated the matrices, one truncates them down to order p {\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma}{\mathrm{Q}}_{p}^{+}={Q}_{p}^{+}{\mathrm{B}}_{p}^{+}+{\mathrm{R}}_{p}^{+} and thus, at the cost of q new Arnoldi iterations, one can recover an Arnoldi factorisation of order m which is viable. The whole subtlety of the process rests on this last chaining. Let us denote: \Phi ({\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma})=\prod_{i=1}^{q}({\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma}-{\tilde{\lambda}}_{p+i}\text{Id}) , the matrix polynomial of order q generated by the working operator. In fact, the implicit QRs have acted on the p first rows of the Arnoldi matrix, of the Rayleigh matrix and of the residual, so that the complementary factorisation of order q produces the same effect as a factorisation of order m initiated by the vector {\tilde{\mathrm{q}}}_{1}=\Phi ({\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma}){\mathrm{q}}_{1} . The initial vector has been implicitly modified (there is no actual construction and application of the polynomial) so that it preferentially generates the modes desired, by subtracting the components judged “improper”. As one has already remarked, this type of restart makes it possible to decrease the residual by lessening the components of the initial vector along the undesirable modes. In exact arithmetic, one would immediately have {\mathrm{R}}_{m}=0 and the process would stop there! Iteration after iteration, one therefore improves the quality of the modes sought by relying on auxiliary modes . Of course the latter is estimated at each step and conditions the appropriateness of simulating another restart or not. The process can be summarised (very macroscopically!) as follows: \begin{array}{c}\text{Factorisation d'Arnoldi d'ordre}m:{\text{AQ}}_{m}={\mathrm{Q}}_{m}{\mathrm{B}}_{m}+{\mathrm{R}}_{m}.\\ \text{Pour k= 1, NMAX\_ITER\_SOREN faire}\\ \text{Calculer}\underset{\begin{array}{c}\text{Conservées pour}\\ \text{amélioration}\end{array}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{\tilde{{\lambda}_{1}},\tilde{{\lambda}_{2}}...\tilde{{\lambda}_{p}}}},\underset{\begin{array}{c}\text{Utilisées comme}\\ \text{shifts}\end{array}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{\tilde{\lambda}}_{\text{p+1}}...{\tilde{\lambda}}_{\text{p+q}},}}\\ \text{QR avec shifts implicites,}\\ \text{Mise à jour}{\mathrm{Q}}_{m},{\mathrm{B}}_{m}\text{et}{\mathrm{R}}_{m},\\ \text{Troncature}\text{de}\text{ces}\text{matrices}à\text{l'ordre}p,\\ \begin{array}{c}{\text{AQ}}_{p}={\mathrm{Q}}_{p}{\mathrm{B}}_{p}+{\mathrm{R}}_{p}\mathrm{\Rightarrow }{\text{AQ}}_{m}={\mathrm{Q}}_{m}{\mathrm{B}}_{m}+{\mathrm{R}}_{m},\\ \text{Estimation qualité des}p\text{modes}.\end{array}\\ \text{Fin boucle}.\end{array} Algorithm 14. IRA method (known as Sorensen's). The maximum number of iterations is driven by the keyword NMAX_ITER_SOREN of the factor keyword CALC_FREQ. One must note that the Arnoldi algorithm is prudently completed by a total reorthogonalisation (triggered only if this proves necessary). This extra cost is all the more acceptable as it is implemented via the IGSM algorithm of Kahan-Parlett (cf. Appendix 2) which is particularly efficient. All this allows us to be assured of the good behaviour of the projection with respect to the initial spectrum. On the other hand, the evaluation of the quality of the modes is not carried out simply by building the p residuals {\mathrm{\parallel }{\mathrm{r}}_{i}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2}={\mathrm{\parallel }({\mathrm{A}}_{\sigma}-\tilde{\lambda}\mathrm{I}){\tilde{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2} via property 10. One has already mentioned that in the non-Hermitian case, they would not suffice for this task, in particular in the event of a strong defect of normality. In order to acquit oneself of it, without having recourse to other information [23]_ a priori , one uses the previous property completed by a criterion due to Z.Bai et al[BDK93] \mid {b}_{m+1,m}\mid \mid {\mathrm{e}}_{m}^{T}\mathrm{x}\mid where the i are the indices corresponding to the successive smallest values of \frac{{\mathrm{A}}_{ii}^{\sigma}}{{\mathrm{B}}_{ii}} , - Last vector {\mathrm{x}}_{q} , random vector. 8.4 Field of use GEP with real symmetric matrices . The others concern more the inner workings of the algorithm and they have been initialised empirically to standard values. 9 Global QZ method This solver is selected with SOLVEUR_MODAL= _F(METHODE='QZ')) 9.1 Introduction Most modal methods resort to a spectral transformation of “shift and invert” type in order to facilitate the search for a part of the spectrum and to transform the initial GEP into a classical SEP (r5.01.01-3.7.1). This approach is clever but it implies numerical factorisations of dynamic matrices of the type {{A}}_{\sigma}={({A}-\sigma {B})}^{-1} {B} (r5.01.01-3.7.2). The result of this factorisation is only a computational intermediate used many times in the algorithmics of the modal solvers. Now these factorisations are necessarily tainted with numerical errors linked to the conditionings of the matrices and to the backward error (the backward error measures the propensity of the algorithm to transmit/amplify rounding errors) of the direct solver (cf. Generalities on direct linear solvers and use of MUMPS). Hence the idea, in order to build a robust modal method, of avoiding this type of mechanism and of resorting only to: - Transformations which produce/propagate few rounding errors (called “backward stable”) of Householder or Givens type, - Canonical matrices easy to handle (triangular, diagonal or Hessenberg) and/or very well conditioned (orthogonal in real or unitary in complex). 9.2 GEPs and the QZ method This is the principle of the QZ method which treats the GEP directly. \begin{array}{c} \text{Trouver }(\lambda, u)\text{ tel que }\\ (A-\lambda B)u=0 \end{array} rather than an SEP resulting from its modification via a spectral transformation. This method in fact seeks to build the following generalised Schur decomposition (counterpart of the standard Schur decomposition). Theorem 12 (Generalised Schur Decomposition) Let A and B be two complex square matrices; then there exist two unitary square matrices Q and Z such that {Q}^{\ast}AZ=T and {Q}^{\ast}BZ=S are upper triangular matrices. The eigenvalues of the GEP eq:eq-r5.01.01-probGEP are then easily computed thanks to the (complex) diagonal terms of the matrices T and S For the proof, see [GL89] pp. 396 and [MS73]. This theorem therefore indicates that, once the Generalised Schur Decomposition has been unearthed, solving the GEP amounts to solving the equivalent GEP (and much simpler because triangular) \begin{array}{c} \text{Trouver }(\lambda, v)\text{ tel que }\\ (T-\lambda S)v=0 \end{array} They have the same spectrum, \lambda (A,B)=\lambda (T,S) , and one passes from the eigenvectors of one to those of the other, via the canonical transformation u = Zv On the other hand, the handling of pairs of the type ({\alpha}_{i},{\beta}_{i})=({T}_{ii},{S}_{ii}) , rather than directly an eigenvalue {\lambda}_{i}:=\frac{{\alpha}_{i}}{{\beta}_{i}} , is a numerical trick making it possible to apprehend better the complexity induced by the direct solution of a GEP. Indeed, depending for example on the rank of the matrix B , the spectrum can be: - finite: \lambda (A,B)=\left\lbrace {\lambda}_{1}\dots {\lambda}_{n}\right\rbrace , with possibly eigenvalues of very large values \pm \infty , - empty: ( \lambda (A,B)=\varnothing ), - infinite: ( \lambda (A,B)=\setR \text{ ou } \setC ). In the first two cases, the system is said to be “regular” as opposed to the last situation where it is said to be “singular”. To convince oneself of this, the examples below illustrate the three cases: \begin{split}\begin{array}{c} A:= \left[\begin{array}{cc} 1& 2\\ 0& 3 \end{array}\right], B:= \left[\begin{array}{cc} 1& 0\\ 0& 0 \end{array}\right] \Rightarrow \lambda (A,B) = \left\lbrace 1 \right\rbrace \\ A:= \left[\begin{array}{cc} 1& 2\\ 0& 3 \end{array}\right], B:= \left[\begin{array}{cc} 0& 0\\ 1& 0 \end{array}\right] \Rightarrow \lambda (A,B) = \varnothing \\ A:= \left[\begin{array}{cc} 1& 2\\ 0& 0 \end{array}\right], B:= \left[\begin{array}{cc} 1& 0\\ 0& 0 \end{array}\right] \Rightarrow \lambda (A,B)=\setC \end{array}\end{split} The representation of the solutions in (\alpha, \beta ) then makes it possible to manage these cases more cleanly. For example, the value \beta \approx 0 can be interpreted as an infinite eigenvalue \lambda \approx \infty (probably not to be retained in the working spectrum!). If in addition \alpha \approx 0 , one has an indeterminacy for computing the corresponding eigenvalue and this illustrates a singular or very poorly conditioned system. In the case of the GEPs, this situation appears when one treats the eigenvalues associated with the blocked dofs and with those of Lagrange (r5.01.01-3.2.1). The decomposition (\alpha, \beta ) then supplies a framework for filtering these numerical artefacts from the physical spectrum truly sought: {\lambda}_{\text{physique}}(A,B) := \left\lbrace -\infty \ll \vert {\lambda}_{i}\vert \ll +\infty, i=1\dots {n}_{{\text{ddl}}_{\text{actifs}}} \right\rbrace Notes - The QZ method is “backward stable” for solving a standard GEP. But it loses this property when one uses it on a linearised GEP, a computational intermediate for apprehending a QEP ([TM01]). - In the case of real matrices, one has a similar decomposition called “Real Generalised” with orthogonal square matrices Q and Z such that {Q}^{T}AZ=T is upper quasi-triangular (.i.e. block diagonal 1\times 1 or 2\times 2 ) and {Q}^{T}BZ=S is upper triangular. The philosophy of the computation remains the same, by introducing pairs (\alpha, \beta ) as intermediates, before the computation proper of the eigenvalues \lambda . A notable difference with the complex case comes from the fact that one can, even in the presence of complex modes, continue to work in real arithmetic. This strategy exploited by certain LAPACK routines has been used with the QZ method of CALC_MODES with OPTION among BANDE , CENTRE , PLUS_ or TOUT . In certain cases (SPD matrices, band structures…), the approach can be declined more efficiently (that is to say with a sparse storage, or even in parallel mode). For example, if the GEP has real symmetric matrices with B in addition positive definite (hence there exists a Cholesky factorisation such that B=LD{L}^{T} ), the GEP is solved directly via the equivalent real symmetric SEP \begin{split}(\text{GEP})\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c} \text{Trouver }(\lambda, u)\text{ tel que }\\ (A-\lambda B)u=0 \end{array} \right . \iff (\text{SEP})\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c} \text{Trouver }(\lambda, u)\text{ tel que }\\ \left({L}^{-1} \, A \, L^{-T}\right)\left({L}^{T}u\right) = \lambda ( D \, L^{T} u) \end{array} \right .\end{split} This canonical SEP is then solved in a robust and more efficient manner via an adapted QR (cf. appendix 1). This strategy exploited by certain LAPACK routines has been used with the QZ method of CALC_MODES with OPTION among BANDE , CENTRE , PLUS_ or TOUT . In the factor keyword SOLVEUR_MODAL , one takes TYPE_QZ=’QZ_QR’ . 9.3 The QZ method In the general case, the algorithm of the QZ method can be broken down into three steps: - Via Givens transformations (cf. appendix 3) or Householder 2x2, the two complex matrices A and B (resp. real) are decomposed in a form called “Generalised Upper Hessenberg”. That is to say that one determines two unitary (resp. orthogonal) square matrices {U}_{1} and {V}_{1} such that A={U}_{1}H{V}_{1}^{\ast} and B={U}_{1}R{V}_{1}^{\ast} (resp. A={U}_{1}H{V}_{1}^{T} and B={U}_{1}R{V}_{1}^{T} ) with H upper Hessenberg and R upper triangular. For example, with A:=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}10& 1& 2\\ 1& 2& -1\\ 1& 1& 2\end{array}\right]\text{ et }B:=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1& 2& 3\\ 4& 5& 6\\ 7& 8& 9\end{array}\right] , one finds \begin{split}\begin{array}{c}{U}_{1} := \left[\begin{array}{ccc} -0.12& -0.99& 0.03\\ -0.49& -0.02& -0.86\\ -0.86& 0.12& 0.49 \end{array}\right] \text{ et } {V}_{1}:= \left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1.00& 0.00& 0.00\\ 0.00& -0.89& -0.44\\ 0.00& 0.44& -0.89 \end{array}\right],\\ H:= \left[\begin{array}{ccc} -2.58& 1.54& 2.42\\ -9.76& 0.08& 1.92\\ 0.00& 2.72& -0.76 \end{array}\right] \text{ et } R:= \left[\begin{array}{ccc} -8.12& 3.63& 14.20\\ 0.00& 0.00& 1.87\\ 0.00& 0.00& 0.00 \end{array}\right]. \end{array}\end{split} - By generalising Francis's implicit double-shift algorithm (based on Householder transformations, cf. appendix 1), one finalises the transformation. One then unearths two unitary (resp. orthogonal) square matrices {U}_{2} and {V}_{2} such that H={U}_{2}{TV}_{2}^{\ast} and R={U}_{2}S{V}_{2}^{\ast} (resp. H={U}_{2}T{V}_{2}^{T} and R={U}_{2}S{V}_{2}^{T} ) with T and S upper triangular (resp. T upper quasi-triangular). By grouping these two steps, one establishes the result sought, as the product of unitary transformations remains unitary, \underset{{Q}^{T}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{({U}_{1}{U}_{2})}}A\underset{Z}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{({V}_{1}{V}_{2})}} = T \text{ et } \underset{{Q}^{T}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{({U}_{1}{U}_{2})}}B\underset{Z}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{({V}_{1}{V}_{2})}} = S - By using the diagonal terms of the triangular matrices obtained T and S , one deduces (after filtering and a few validity tests) the physical eigenvalues of the vibratory problem modelled. The right and left generalised Schur vectors (column vectors of Q and Z ) make it possible to go back up to the eigenvectors of the equivalent GEP then to the original eigenvectors ( via the transformation). This QZ method is recommended when one seeks to obtain in a robust manner the whole spectrum of a GEP. However, it is very costly in CPU time \vartheta (30{n}^{3}) against \vartheta (nm(m-p)) for IRAM with n the size of the problem, p the number of eigenmodes desired and m the size of the projection space. Moreover, it is very greedy in memory capacity because it requires the full storage of the matrices. Hence a memory complexity in \vartheta ({n}^{2}) against, for example, \vartheta (2 np+{p}^{2}) for IRAM. In short, this algorithm is to be reserved for small GEPs (fewer than {10}^{3} degrees of freedom), rather dense, of which one wishes to obtain a reliable estimate of the spectrum. As for the QR algorithm in Lanczos/IRAM or for Jacobi with Bathe & Wilson, it is rather to be exploited as an elementary brick of an algorithmic process which will have (considerably) reduced the size of the initial problem. For further information on the method, one may consult G.H.Golub[GL89] or the founding paper of C.B.Moler and G.W.Stewart[MS73] (1973) 9.4 Implementation 9.4.1 LAPACK Routines of the excellent linear algebra library LAPACK [Lap] propose dedicated routines (and drivers encapsulating them) for the solution of a GEP directly via a QZ. And this, for a wide panel of problems: SPD, real non-symmetric, complex Hermitian or arbitrary, single/double precision, full or band storage. On the other hand, the library proposes a whole panoply of routines for decomposing the solution, pre- and post-processing the data handled or even estimating the numerical errors which taint the solutions. It nevertheless remains very much linked to the full storage of the matrices; it works only In-Core and exploits no parallelism. On the other hand, it does not seem that there exists a public-domain package implementing a method of QZ type more efficiently than LAPACK. It is therefore on this library that the QZ method available in CALC_MODES with OPTION among BANDE , CENTRE , PLUS_ or TOUT is based. Let us note that many other products have made the same choice of LAPACK and of its QZ: eigenvalues module of Python/linear algebra, functions eig and qz for Matlab, spec for Scilab, MSC/Nastran, ... 9.4.2 Integration and post-verifications In the implementation which has been retained, the GEPs with real modes (real symmetric matrices) are treated in real arithmetic via the routines DGGEV and DGGEVX . The first routine is to be used during a standard run ( TYPE_QZ=’QZ_SIMPLE’ , default value). The second ( TYPE_QZ=’QZ_EQUI’ ), more sophisticated, is to be reserved for difficult solutions. In particular, it balances and permutes the terms of the input matrices in order to improve the spectral conditionings and therefore to decrease the numerical error on the solutions. Sometimes this pre-processing can be prejudicial by excessively increasing terms close to the machine precision, thus falsifying the results. For this reason, this option is not activated by default. In the very particular case of a real symmetric GEP with matrix B , in addition, positive definite (for example a dynamic computation without hysteretic damping with blocking boundary conditions modelled only by elimination without recourse to the double Lagrange), recourse to the LAPACK driver DSYGV is more efficient than the DGGEV/X . It must be activated explicitly via the keyword TYPE_QZ=’QZ_QR’ . For certain situations (buckling, double Lagrange, complex or non-symmetric matrix, linearised QEP), the non-SPD character of B can be detected a priori . A fatal error then stops the computation if the value QZ_EQUI has been chosen all the same. In the third and last case of a GEP with complex modes (complex symmetric matrices as in the case of hysteretic damping and/or real non-symmetric), the solution is carried out directly in complex arithmetic via the LAPACK drivers ZGGEV and ZGGEVX . As in real, the first is the default standard mode (activated by TYPE_QZ=’QZ_SIMPLE’ ) and the second, the expert mode ( TYPE_QZ=’QZ_EQUI’ ). At the end of the modal analysis, QZ returns pairs ({\alpha}_{i},{\beta}_{i}) and their associated eigenvector {u}_{i} , which one is going to sort and filter according to the following recommendations: - Mechanical verifications: If \vert {\beta}_{i}\vert is close to the machine precision, the mode is not retained (it doubtless corresponds to a blocked dof or to a blocking Lagrange) and an alarm message is issued (if INFO=2 ). Once all the sorts have been carried out, one makes sure that the number of physically acceptable modes (cf. formula (9.1-6)) does indeed correspond to the number of active dofs {n}_{\text{ddl}-\text{actifs}} . The latter is determined in the initialisation phase and is independent of the modal solver (r5.01.01-3.2.1). If the GEP has real modes, the non-verification of this criterion entails a fatal error. In the other cases, it is only reported by a dedicated display. It is then not necessarily synonymous with malfunctions. Everything depends on the subsequent sorting of the complex conjugate eigenvalues! - Numerical verifications: If \vert {\alpha}_{i}\vert \ge \Vert A \Vert or \vert {\beta}_{i}\vert \ge \Vert B \Vert , one does not retain the mode and an alarm message is issued. In the case of a real symmetric GEP (with TYPE_QZ=’QZ_SIMPLE’ or TYPE_QZ='QZ_EQUI’ ), one moreover verifies that all the eigenvalues have a very small imaginary part (lower than the value {f}_{\text{corrig}} supplied by SEUIL_FREQ , default value equal to 10^{-2} ). Otherwise, an alarm is issued. In the case of a real symmetric positive definite GEP treated via QZ_QR , one excludes the eigenvalues lower than -2{f}_{\text{corrig}} and greater than 0.5 \times {10}^{308} (0.5 maximum value representable on the machine). These arbitrary values result from numerical experiments on modal test cases of the verification base. When one finds an eigenvalue outside this band, an alarm is issued if INFO=2 . Then, once the modes coming from QZ have been filtered, they are going to be sorted and reordered according to the user's desiderata : - CALC_FREQ with OPTION='BANDE’ : option licit only with a GEP with real modes. One selects the eigenvalues situated in the frequency band desired by the user (keyword FREQ or CHAR_CRIT ). - CALC_FREQ with OPTION=’PLUS_PETITE’ : one retains the eigenvalue smallest in modulus. - CALC_FREQ with OPTION=’CENTRE’ : one selects the eigenvalues closest in modulus to the shift parameterised by the keyword FREQ or CHAR_CRIT . One retains NMAX_FREQ of them. - CALC_FREQ with OPTION=’TOUTE’ : one keeps all the licit eigenvalues coming from the previous filters. Finally, as for all the modal solvers of the code (cf. r5.01.01-3.7.2), the modes retained will undergo two last verifications: - Test on the norm of the residual of the mode (\lambda, u) . - In the standard case of a GEP with real modes, Sturm test for counting eigenvalues in the frequency band ad hoc . 9.5 Field of use This solver can be used for a GEP with arbitrary real matrices (symmetric or not) or with matrix A complex and B real symmetric. The user can specify the class of membership of the analysis (dynamics or buckling) by initialising the keyword TYPE_RESU . Depending on this value, one fills in the vector FREQ or CHAR_CRIT . 9.6 Display in the message file In the message file are mentioned the pieces of information relating to the method chosen (here QZ), to its variant (here QZ_SIMPLE ) and to the modes retained. In the most common case of a GEP with real eigenmodes, one specifies the list of frequencies {f}_{i} retained ( FREQUENCE ) and their error norm ( NORME D’ERREUR ). For a GEP with complex modes, unlike the QEPs one does not filter the conjugate eigenvalues. It keeps them all and displays them in increasing order of real part. However, the parallel efficiency of MUMPS in a modal analysis is more limited than for other types of analyses. One observes, in general, a parallel efficiency in time of the order of 0.2 to 0.3 and this, for a small range of processors: from 2 to 16. Beyond that one no longer gains anything. This is explained in particular by: - the quasi-singularity of certain working dynamic matrices, - a very unfavourable ratio “number of forward-back substitutions/number of factorisations”, - the significant cost of the analysis phase compared with that of the factorisation, - a very unfavourable ratio “time/memory cost of the linear solver”/“time/memory cost of the modal solver”. For further technical and functional information, one can consult the documentations R6.02.03, U4.50.01 and [U2.08.03/06]. In order to progress in terms of performance, one proposes to decompose the initial computation into more high-performing and more accurate sub-computations: this is the object of one of the functionalities of the operator CALC_MODES with OPTION='BANDE' and a list of n>2 values given under CALC_FREQ=_F(FREQ), detailed in the following paragraph. Generalities on the QR algorithm 12.1 Principle Algorithms of QR type were sensed by H.Rutishauser(1958) and formalised concurrently by J.C.Francis and V.N.Kublanovskaya(1961). This fundamental method is often involved in the other approaches better adapted to treating problems of large size (in particular the projection methods). \begin{array}{c}\text{Pour}k=1,...\text{faire}\\ {\mathrm{H}}_{k}={\mathrm{Q}}_{k}{\mathrm{R}}_{k}(\text{factorisation}\text{QR}),\\ {\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}={\mathrm{R}}_{k}{\mathrm{Q}}_{k},\\ \text{Fin boucle}.\end{array} Algorithm 1.1. QR theoretical. The process leads iteratively towards a matrix {\mathrm{H}}_{k} upper triangular (or block triangular) whose diagonal terms are the eigenvalues of the initial operator \mathrm{H}={\mathrm{H}}_{1} . The notation H is in fact not innocent, because one has every interest in orthogonally transforming beforehand (so as to modify only the form of the shifted operator and not its spectrum) the working operator A into upper Hessenberg form, that is in real arithmetic {\mathrm{H}}_{1}={\mathrm{Q}}_{{0}_{}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\text{AQ}}_{0} This can be carried out via various orthogonal transformations (Householder, Givens, Gram‑Schmidt...) and their cost (of the order of O({\mathrm{10n}}^{3}/3) ) is negligible compared with the gain that they make it possible to achieve at each iteration of the global process: O({n}^{2}) (with Householder or Fast‑Givens) against O({n}^{3}) . This gain of an order of magnitude can even be improved when the operator is symmetric tridiagonal (this is the case of Lanczos with a genuine inner product): O(\mathrm{20n}) . The convergence towards a simple triangular matrix is carried out only if all the eigenvalues have distinct moduli and if the initial matrix is not “pathologically” too poor in the eigen directions. The convergence of the i th mode (arranged classically in decreasing order of modulus) is then carried out in: \underset{\mathrm{j¹i}}{\max}\frac{\mid {\lambda}_{j}\mid }{\mid {\lambda}_{i}\mid } which can prove very slow if no complementary process is implemented. Notes: - The determination of the spectrum of the Rayleigh matrix with the Newmann & Pipano variant is carried out via a simple QR (or a QL in the symmetric case) of this type (with beforehand a balancing procedure). The only parameter accessible by the user is the maximum number of admissible iterations NMAX_ITER_QR. - For IRAM, this computation is carried out via a QR method with explicit double shift whereas the polynomial filters managing the restarts use a QR with implicit double shift. By precaution, no parameter is accessible for the user in Code_Aster! - One must not confuse the method, the QR algorithm, and one of its conceptual tools, the QR factorisation. - This class of algorithm is very much used for determining the complete spectrum of an operator, because it is very robust (it is the reference in this field). However it is very greedy in memory space which makes its use prohibitive on large systems. - The field of application of the QR algorithm is much more general than that of Jacobi (it is the second standard algorithm supplying the whole spectrum of an operator provided that one is ready to store it entirely) which is limited to Hermitian matrices. In order to accelerate the convergence of the simple algorithm which can be very slow (in the presence of clusters for example) a multitude of variants, based on the choice of shifts answering certain criteria, have seen the light of day. 12.2 The shift strategy This strategy consists in artificially bringing about a deflation phenomenon (cf. §4.1, §6.4) within the working matrix. This offers the triple advantage: - of being able to isolate a real eigenvalue or even two complex conjugate eigenvalues, - while reducing the size of the problem to be treated, - and while accelerating the convergence . In its version with explicit simple shift, the method is then rewritten in the following form: \begin{array}{c}\begin{array}{c}\text{Pour k}=1,...\text{faire}\\ \text{Choisir le shift}\mu ,\\ {\mathrm{S}}_{k}={\mathrm{H}}_{k}-\mu \mathrm{I},\end{array}\\ {\mathrm{S}}_{k}={\mathrm{Q}}_{k}{\mathrm{R}}_{k}(\text{factorisation}\text{QR}),\\ {\mathrm{H}}_{\text{k+}1}={\mathrm{R}}_{k}{\mathrm{Q}}_{k}+\mu \mathrm{I},\\ \text{Fin boucle}.\end{array} Algorithm 1.2. QR with explicit simple shift. Note: - This process generalises intuitively to several shifts. One then builds, for each global iteration k , as many auxiliary matrices {\mathrm{S}}_{k}^{i} as there are shifts {\mu}_{i} . The convergence of the process is greatly improved in the sense that the sub-diagonal terms vanish asymptotically in \underset{j\ne i}{\max}\frac{\mid {\lambda}_{j}-\mu \mid }{\mid {\lambda}_{i}-\mu \mid } In theory, if this shift \mu is an eigenvalue of the problem, then the deflation is exact. In practice, the rounding effects perturb this phenomenon; this is what is called the direct instability property of the algorithm . The main difficulty resides in the choice of the shift(s). On the other hand, one does not keep the same shift for all the iterations. One must change it when it is associated with a converged eigenvalue. Indeed, it will have numerically caused its eviction from the working spectrum by bringing about a deflation at the previous iteration. Since the 1960s a whole zoology of shifts has developed . While the simplest uses the last diagonal term {\mathrm{H}}_{n,n} that of J.H. Wilkinson [WR71] consists in determining analytically the eigenvalue \mu of the diagonal block \left[\begin{array}{cc}{\mathrm{H}}_{n-1,n-1}& {\mathrm{H}}_{n-1,n}\\ {\mathrm{H}}_{n,n-1}& {\mathrm{H}}_{n,n}\end{array}\right] closest to this term. This technique makes it possible to obtain a quadratic or even cubic convergence (in the symmetric case) and it proves particularly efficient for capturing double modes or distinct eigenvalues of the same modulus. However this strategy can prove ineffective in the presence of complex conjugate eigenmodes. The same author then proposed a variant including a double shift corresponding to the two complex eigenvalues {\mu}_{1} and {\mu}_{2} (determined beforehand) of the block in question. But besides the numerical difficulties in curbing the appearance of invasive complex components (which in theory have no reason to be), one has on the other hand a great deal of difficulty in preserving the “upper Hessenberg” character of the working matrix. At best, this slows the convergence of the QR algorithm; at worst, it completely falsifies its operation. In order to remedy these numerical disadvantages, J.C.Francis developed a version with implicit double shift . It is very well explained in GL89 and one will content oneself here with summarising it. In order to minimise the rounding effects, one would have to constitute directly the auxiliary matrix {\mathrm{S}}_{k} resulting from the simultaneous application of the two shifts {\mu}_{1} and {\mu}_{2} {\mathrm{S}}_{k}={\mathrm{H}}_{k}^{2}-({\mu}_{1}+{\mu}_{2}){\mathrm{H}}_{k}+({\mu}_{1}{\mu}_{2})\mathrm{I} before factorising it in QR form and building the new iterate {\mathrm{H}}_{k+1} \begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{S}}_{k}={\mathrm{Q}}_{k}{\mathrm{R}}_{k},\\ {\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}={\mathrm{Q}}_{k}^{T}{\mathrm{H}}_{k}{\mathrm{Q}}_{k}.\end{array} But the sole cost of the initial assembly (of the order of O({n}^{3}) ) makes the tactic inoperative. This variant, based on the implicit Q theorem, consists in applying to the working matrix particular Householder transformations making it possible to recover a Hessenberg matrix “essentially” equal to {\mathrm{H}}_{k+1} , that is to say of the type: . {\tilde{\mathrm{H}}}_{k+1}={\mathrm{E}}^{-1}{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}\mathrm{E}\text{avec}\mathrm{E}\text{=diag}(\pm 1,...\pm 1) The working matrix thus preserves , at least cost , its particular structure and its spectrum . All these variants are in fact very sensitive to the balancing techniques implemented in order to precondition the initial operator. The following paragraph will summarise this technique of “scaling” (“balancing” for English speakers) of the terms of the working matrix which is very much used in modal computation. 12.3 Balancing It is a matter of attenuating the rounding effects by curbing the range of expansion of the terms of the working operator , that is to say of avoiding that they become too small or, on the contrary, too large. On this subject, E.E.Osborne [Osb60] (1960) noted that generally the error on the computation of the eigen elements of A is of the order of \varepsilon {\parallel A\parallel }_{2} where \varepsilon is the machine precision. He then proposed to transform the initial matrix into a matrix \tilde{\mathrm{A}}={\mathrm{D}}^{\text{-1}}\mathrm{A}\mathrm{D} (with D a diagonal matrix), such that: {\mathrm{\parallel }\tilde{\mathrm{A}}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2}\ll {\mathrm{\parallel }\mathrm{A}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2} In fact one computes iteratively a succession of matrices {\mathrm{A}}_{k}={\mathrm{D}}_{k-1}^{\text{-1}}{\mathrm{A}}_{k-1}{\mathrm{D}}_{k-1} such that: {\mathrm{A}}_{k}\underset{k\to \infty }{\to }{\mathrm{A}}_{f} satisfying {\mathrm{\parallel }{\mathrm{a}}^{i}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2}={\mathrm{\parallel }{\mathrm{a}}_{i}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{2} with {\mathrm{a}}^{i} and {\mathrm{a}}_{i} , respectively, the i th column and row of {\mathrm{A}}_{f} . One moreover shows that the QL algorithm applied to the invertible operator A is equivalent to the QR algorithm applied to {A}^{\text{- }} (conjugate transpose matrix of the inverse of A ). The method put in place in Code_Aster is identical to the simple shift method of J.H.Wilkinson seen previously by adapting the search for this shift to the uppermost 2\times 2 minor.
