r5.02.04 Non-linear thermal analysis in a moving frame r5.02.04 Non-linear thermal analysis in a moving frame Summary The formulation and the algorithm of the stationary non-linear thermal convection–diffusion problem introduced within the command THER_NON_LINE_MO u4.33.04 are presented. The aim is to solve the heat equation in a moving frame tied to a loading and travelling in a given direction and at a given speed. The non-linearities of the problem come both from the characteristics of the material, which depend on the temperature, and from boundary conditions of radiation type. Problems of this type may be treated with models using plane, axisymmetric and three-dimensional structural finite elements. 1 Presentation of the problem The heat equation presents strong non-linearities under certain conditions. This is the case when the material undergoes phase changes: these are accompanied by an abrupt variation of the characteristic quantities (heat capacity, enthalpy). This non-linearity is all the more accentuated when one treats the convection–diffusion problem, in which the transport term depending on the enthalpy function appears. The aim of this modelling is to treat this latter problem in the steady regime (stationary case). In every case, one assumes that the velocity field is known a priori. The case of a moving solid is fairly frequent in practice. It concerns in particular welding applications or surface treatment, which involve a heat source travelling in a given direction and at a given speed. The thermal problem is then studied in a frame tied to the source. The partial differential problem results from the equation of the global thermal balance over any domain \Omega , which is written: \begin{array}{ccc}\frac{d}{\text{dt}}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\mathit{\rho \beta d}\Omega =& \underset{\Omega}{\int}\mathit{Qd}\Omega -& \underset{\partial \Omega }{\int}q.nd\Gamma \\ \text{accumulation}& \text{création}+& \text{entrée-sortie}\end{array} In this equation, O represents a connected domain, interior to the system studied, which one follows in its motion, \beta represents the specific enthalpy of the material and \rho denotes its density. Q is a volumetric heat source, q is the heat flux through the boundary \partial \Omega ( n being the outward normal), and d/\text{dt} is the material derivative . The first term of the equation is written (see for example ): \frac{d}{\text{dt}}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\mathit{\rho \beta d}\Omega =\underset{\Omega}{\int}(\frac{\partial (\rho \beta )}{\partial t}+div(\rho \beta V))d\Omega or again, taking into account the conservation of mass (\frac{\partial \rho }{\partial t}+div(\rho V)=0) : \frac{d}{\text{dt}}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho \beta d\Omega =\underset{\Omega}{\int}(\rho \frac{\partial \beta }{\partial t}+\rho V.\text{grad}\beta )d\Omega where V is the velocity vector of the displacement of the domain \Omega . V is entered under the simple keyword CONVECTION of the commands AFFE_CHAR_THER and AFFE_CHAR_THER_F. The second term of the right-hand side of the equation is written, taking into account the divergence theorem and Fourier’s law (q=-k(T)\text{grad}T) : \underset{\partial \Omega }{\int}q.nd\Gamma =\underset{\Omega}{\int}divqd\Omega =-\underset{\Omega}{\int}div(k(T)\text{grad}T)d\Omega where T is the temperature and k(T) is the thermal conductivity of the material, a function of the temperature. The equation having to be satisfied for every domain \Omega , one then has: \rho \frac{\partial \beta }{\partial t}+\rho V.\text{grad}\beta -div(k(T)\text{grad}T)=Q \quad \text{dans } \Omega Note: Let us note that the classical case with k(T)=k (constant) and V=0 , and where the specific enthalpy is a linear function of the temperature, \beta (T)=\text{CT} , gives back the well-known classical equation: \rho C\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}-\mathit{kDT}=Q in \Omega where \Delta is the Laplacian and C (constant) represents the specific heat. The partial differential problem treated by the command THER_NON_LINE_MO u4.33.04 consists in solving the equation in the stationary case (directly at the steady state) with boundary conditions on the boundary \partial \Omega . This problem is formally written in the following form: \begin{array}{cc}V.\text{grad}u(T)-div(k(T)\text{grad}T)=Q,& \text{dans}\Omega ,\\ +\text{conditions aux limites}& \text{sur}\partial \Omega \end{array} where we have adopted the notation, valid for all that follows, u(T)=\rho \beta (T) where \rho is constant, defining the volumetric enthalpy. 2 Boundary conditions. Reference problem to be solved One will refer, for example, to r5.02.01 for further information on the thermal boundary conditions of Dirichlet, Neumann and linear Fourier type, and to r5.02.02 for the boundary conditions of non-linear normal-flux type (non-linear Fourier). In an enthalpy formulation, the stationary thermal problem therefore consists in solving, in a domain O with boundary on \partial \Omega , V.\text{grad}u(T)-div(k(T)\text{grad}T)=Q \quad \text{dans } \Omega with k(T)\frac{\partial T}{\partial n}=\gamma ({T}_{\text{ext}}-T) \quad \text{sur } {\partial}_{1}\Omega k(T)\frac{\partial T}{\partial n}={q}_{0} \quad \text{sur } {\partial}_{2}\Omega k(T)\frac{\partial T}{\partial n}=\alpha (T)\quad \text{sur } {\partial}_{3}\Omega T={T}_{0} \quad \text{sur } {\partial}_{4}\Omega where: - {T}_{0} : is the temperature imposed on {\partial}_{4}\Omega ; - {q}_{0} : is the normal flux imposed on {\partial}_{2}\Omega ; - \gamma : is the heat-exchange coefficient; - {T}_{\text{ext}} : is the external temperature; - \alpha (T) : is the normal flux of non-linear Fourier type (radiation). The equations , represent the boundary conditions of the types, respectively: linear Fourier, Neumann, non-linear Fourier and Dirichlet. The reference problem , is strongly non-linear because of the non-linearities in k(T),u(T) (phase change) and \alpha (T) (radiation). 3 Variational formulation of the problem Let \Omega be an open set of {R}^{3} , with boundary \partial \Omega ={\partial}_{1}\Omega \cup {\partial}_{2}\Omega \cup {\partial}_{3}\Omega \cup {\partial}_{4}\Omega such that, for i\mathrm{\ne }j and i,j=1,\mathrm{...},4 , one has: {\partial}_{i}\Omega \cap {\partial}_{j}\Omega =\varnothing . Let furthermore \psi be a sufficiently regular function which vanishes on {\partial}_{4}\Omega : \psi \in V=\left\lbrace y\text{régulière}\text{et}\psi {\mid}_{{\partial}_{4}\Omega }=0\right\rbrace . Multiply by \psi the two sides of the equation , then integrate over \Omega . An integration by parts then gives: \begin{array}{ccc}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\mathrm{Qyd}\Omega & =\underset{\Omega}{\int}V.\text{grad}u(T)\mathrm{yd}\Omega -& \underset{\Omega}{\int}div(k(T)\text{grad}T)\mathrm{yd}\Omega \\ & =\underset{\Omega}{\int}V.\text{grad}u(T)\mathrm{yd}\Omega +& \underset{\Omega}{\int}k(T)\text{grad}T.\text{grad}\mathrm{yd}\Omega -\underset{\partial \Omega -{\partial}_{4}\Omega }{\int}(k(T)\frac{\partial T}{\partial n}y)\mathrm{dG}\end{array} since \psi is zero on {\partial}_{4}\Omega . Whence, taking into account the boundary conditions , and , the variational formulation of the reference problem, which is given by the following equation: \forall \psi \in V \begin{array}{}\begin{array}{cc}\underset{\Omega}{\int}k(T)\text{grad}T.\text{grad}\mathrm{yd}\Omega & +\underset{\Omega}{\int}V.\text{grad}u(T)\mathrm{yd}\Omega +\underset{{\partial}_{1}\Omega }{\int}\mathrm{gTydG}-\underset{{\partial}_{3}\Omega }{\int}\alpha (T)\mathrm{ydG}\end{array}\\ =\underset{\Omega}{\int}\mathrm{Qyd}\Omega +\underset{{\partial}_{1}\Omega }{\int}{\gamma T}_{\text{ext}}\mathrm{ydG}+\underset{{\partial}_{2}\Omega }{\int}{q}_{0}\mathrm{yd}\Omega ,\end{array} 4 Treatment of the non-linearities With a view to the numerical solution of the non-linear problem which we consider, it is necessary to treat all the non-linearities. In our case, let us mention the strong non-linearity linked to the enthalpy function u(T) , which takes into account the solid–liquid phase change, as well as the non-linearity linked to the possible presence of a boundary condition of non-linear normal flux (radiation). Recall that in the classical case of non-linear transient thermal problems without convection, that is V=0 , several solution methods are proposed in the literature. There exist both methods using enthalpy formulations and methods using temperature formulations, all having the aim of treating as well as possible the non-linearity linked to the enthalpy (phase change). We refer the reader to the reference for a summary of the principal methods encountered in the literature. However, let us note that, because of the difficulty linked to the presence of the transport term V.\mathit{grad}u(T) in the problem, none of these methods will be employed in what follows. As in every iterative process, the aim of the numerical scheme in view is to find a temperature field {T}^{n+1} at iteration n+1 , from the temperature field {T}^{n} , solution of the preceding iteration. 4.1 Treatment of the non-linearity linked to the enthalpy In order to treat this non-linearity, the strategy employed in this study was inspired by a technique for solving free-boundary problems , which was originally proposed in . Consider the enthalpy function u(T) as being given in a reciprocal form: temperature as a function of the enthalpy (the inverse of the function u(T) ). In other words, one will have to treat the following temperature–enthalpy relation: T=\tau (u) The reason for this choice will be clearer in what follows. Indeed, we shall have to treat a two-field problem: a temperature field and an enthalpy field. The discretisation of the inverse function makes it possible to increment the enthalpy field as a function of the current temperature field (and not the converse), as follows: The first-order expansion of the function \tau (u) is the following, {T}^{n+1}=\tau ({u}^{n})+\tau '({u}^{n})({u}^{n+1}-{u}^{n}) where \tau is the derivative of the function defined by with respect to its argument. In order to take this non-linearity into account, and starting from , one replaces {u}^{n+1} by an approximation as a function of the unknown temperature field {T}^{n+1} in the following way: {u}^{n+1}-{u}^{n}=\omega ({T}^{n+1}-\tau ({u}^{n})) where \omega is a relaxation parameter, constant over the whole domain and throughout the iterative process, representing the term \frac{1}{\tau '({u}^{n})} . Because of the non-convexity of the function \tau (u) , this relaxation parameter must necessarily satisfy the following condition , : \omega \le \frac{1}{\underset{n}{\max}\tau '({u}^{n})} In practice one takes \omega =\frac{1}{\underset{n}{\max}\tau '({u}^{n})} . Taking the approximation into account, the discretisation of the second term of the equation is expressed in the following way: \begin{array}{cc}\underset{\Omega}{\int}V.\text{grad}{u}^{n+1}\psi d\Omega & =\underset{\Omega}{\int}V.\text{grad}{u}^{n}\psi d\Omega +\underset{\Omega}{\int}\omega V.\text{grad}{T}^{n+1}\psi d\Omega -\underset{\Omega}{\int}\omega V.\text{grad}\tau ({u}^{n})\psi d\Omega ,\end{array} 4.2 Treatment of the non-linearities linked to the non-linear Fourier condition and to the thermal conductivity The non-linearity linked to the non-linear normal-flux condition is treated by considering the first-order expansion of the function (assumed sufficiently regular) \alpha (T) , which is given by: \alpha ({T}^{n+1})=\alpha ({T}^{n})+\alpha '({T}^{n})({T}^{n+1}-{T}^{n}) where (.)' denotes the derivative of the function (.) with respect to its argument. It appeared necessary to decide on a strategy for discretising the term k(T)\mathit{grad}T in the equation in order to be able to treat this non-linearity for the stationary problem which we consider. For this, we adopted the following approximation: \begin{array}{cc}k({T}^{n+1})\text{grad}{T}^{n+1}& =k({T}^{n})\text{grad}{T}^{n+1}-\left[k({T}^{n})-k({T}^{n-1})\right]\text{grad}{T}^{n}\end{array} This discretisation is in fact a simplification of the first-order expansion of the term k(T)\text{grad}T . It turns out to be effective, notably because of the weak non-linearity of the function k(T) in practice. Note Let us also note that the following purely explicit approximation: k({T}^{n+1})\text{grad}{T}^{n+1}\approx k({T}^{n})\text{grad}{T}^{n+1}, likewise gives satisfactory results. This observation has been verified from several numerical experiments. 5 Algorithm implemented in Code_Aster The numerical scheme employed for the solution of the reference problem , is deduced from the variational formulation and from the treatment of the various non-linearities, , , , discussed in the preceding section. The solution algorithm is constituted by the succession of two successive operations at each iteration of the analysis. Knowing the solution fields at iteration n : {T}^{n} at the nodes and {u}^{n} at the Gauss points, one seeks the solutions {T}^{n+1}\text{et}{u}^{n+1} at iteration n+1 as follows: \forall \psi \in V, \begin{array}{}\begin{array}{cc}\underset{\Omega}{\int}k({T}^{n})\text{grad}{T}^{n+1}.\text{grad}\psi d\Omega & +\underset{\Omega}{\int}\omega V.\text{grad}{T}^{n+1}\psi d\Omega \\ & +\underset{{\partial}_{1}\Omega }{\int}\gamma {T}^{n+1}\psi d\Gamma -\underset{{\partial}_{3}\Omega }{\int}\alpha '({T}^{n}){T}^{n+1}\psi d\Gamma \end{array}\\ =\underset{\Omega}{\int}Q\psi d\Omega +\underset{{\partial}_{1}\Omega }{\int}\gamma {T}_{\text{ext}}\psi d\Gamma +\underset{{\partial}_{2}\Omega }{\int}{q}_{0}\psi d\Omega \\ +\underset{{\partial}_{3}\Omega }{\int}(\alpha ({T}^{n})-\alpha '({T}^{n}){T}^{n})\psi d\Gamma +\underset{\Omega}{\int}\left[k({T}^{n})-k({T}^{n-1})\right]\text{grad}{T}^{n}.\text{grad}\psi d\Omega \\ +\underset{\Omega}{\int}\omega V.\text{grad}t({u}^{n})\psi d\Omega -\underset{\Omega}{\int}V.\text{grad}{u}^{n}\psi d\Omega ,\end{array} {u}^{n+1}={u}^{n}+\omega ({T}^{n+1}-\tau ({u}^{n})) At each iteration, a linear convection–diffusion problem is solved in order to obtain the field at the nodes {T}^{n+1} , and then a simple local correction is carried out in order to obtain the field at the Gauss points {u}^{n+1} . The stopping criterion adopted in code_aster involves the two solution fields at the same time: the temperature field, and the enthalpy field. The algorithm continues the iterations for as long as at least one of the relative variations of the iterates is greater than the corresponding tolerance given by the user: \begin{array}{}\frac{{(\sum_{i=1,...,\text{nddl}}{({T}_{i}^{n+1}-{T}_{i}^{n})}^{2})}^{1/2}}{{(\sum_{i=1,...,\text{nddl}}{({T}_{i}^{n+1})}^{2})}^{1/2}}>\text{tole 1}\\ \\ \frac{{(\sum_{i=1,...,\text{npg}}{({u}_{i}^{n+1}-{T}_{i}^{n})}^{2})}^{1/2}}{{(\sum_{i=1,...,\text{npg}}{({u}_{i}^{n+1})}^{2})}^{1/2}}>\text{tole 2}\end{array} where \mathit{nddl} is the total number of degrees of freedom at the nodes, and \mathit{npg} is the total number of Gauss points. \mathit{tole}1 is entered under the keyword crit_temp_rela of the factor keyword convergence of the operator ther_non_line_mo. \mathit{tole}2 is entered under the keyword crit_enth_rela of the factor keyword convergence of the operator ther_non_line_mo. 6 Principal computation options in Code_Aster The principal options of code_aster specific to the running of the algorithm , above are presented below. r5.03.01 Quasi-static non-linear algorithm (STAT_NON_LINE) r5.03.01 Quasi-static non-linear algorithm (STAT_NON_LINE) Summary: The operator STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03 makes it possible, in the case of a quasi-static loading, to integrate various types of non-linearities arising from the constitutive behaviour of the material, from large geometric transformations or from contact/friction conditions. The global solution algorithm employed is described here. The integration of the constitutive relations proper is described in the documents [R5.03....] and [R7.01....], (for example R5.03.02 for elastoplasticity), to which one may refer for more details. For analyses in large geometric transformations, one may consult for example the document R5.03.20 on non-linear elasticity in large displacements, or the documents R5.03.21, R5.03.22 on thermoelastoplasticity with isotropic hardening. For frictional contact, there are three documents: R5.03.50 on the discrete formulation of contact/friction, R5.03.52 for the hybrid formulation by contact/friction elements. For everything concerning piloting, one must refer to the document R5.03.80. 1 Presentation 1.1 General points STAT_NON_LINE is the operator of Code_Aster that makes it possible to carry out non-linear mechanical analyses when the inertia effects are neglected (if one wishes to take the inertia effects into account, one must use DYNA_NON_LINE, see R5.05.05). The analysis concerns a priori only the mechanical variables (displacements, stresses, internal variables), excluding any coupling with other physical phenomena (thermal, ...). Consequently, the associated fields that influence the mechanical behaviour (thermal, hydraulic, metallurgical fields) are computed beforehand by other operators (THER_LINEAIRE U4.33.01, THER_NON_LINE U4.33.02), or even by other codes (for example CODE_SATURNE for fluid mechanics, ...). There is an exception concerning the thermo-hydro-mechanical modelling (modelling known as 'THM'), for which STAT_NON_LINE treats the whole of the coupled problem of the diffusion equations of heat, of the pressure of the fluid(s) and of mechanical equilibrium R7.01.10. It should be noted that when one speaks of a computation time instant in this document, one almost always refers to a pseudo-time, which has no physical meaning and which serves only to parameterise the incremental algorithm. However, the time instant retains a physical meaning in viscoplasticity and when the command variables depend on it. 1.2 Types of non-linearities 1.2.1 Non-linear behaviours The non-linear constitutive relations are described in the documents [R5.03....], for the general behaviours, and [R7.01....] for the geomaterials. The choice of the type of behaviour is made by the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT. This leads, through the equilibrium equation, to a non-linear system that can be of two forms: - The system depends explicitly on the displacement field \mathrm{u} with respect to the reference configuration, and is parameterised by the computation time instant (through, among other things, the thermal evolution). - The system depends implicitly on the displacement field \mathrm{u} through an implicit differential equation (for example elastoplasticity, viscoplasticity, hypoelasticity, etc.). In this case, the constitutive relation is integrated as presented for example in R5.03.02: by linking a displacement increment \Delta \mathrm{u} computed from a given mechanical state (the mechanical state being represented by a displacement field \mathrm{u} , a stress field \sigma and a field of internal variables \alpha ) to the stress field at the time instant t of the analysis. The equilibrium equation therefore leads to a non-linear system in \Delta \mathrm{u} , but which is also parameterised by the computation time instant through the data of the problem (variation of the mechanical loading and thermal evolution, for example). 1.2.2 Large transformations In the cases where the small-perturbation hypothesis (moderate displacements and strains) is not satisfied, the method of solution of the problem must then integrate the evolution of the geometry of the problem, handle a particular kinematics and use an adequate formulation of the constitutive law. In practice, the small-strain hypothesis can be applied as long as the square of the modulus of the strain remains smaller than the accuracy of the analyses envisaged. Likewise, the small-rotation hypothesis can be applied as long as the product of the square of the rotation angle and the modulus of the strain remains smaller than the accuracy of the analyses envisaged. Various alternatives exist within Code_Aster ; our aim here is not to give a detailed presentation of them and we refer to the various documents dealing specifically with each problem. One should distinguish the formulations that operate on solid isoparametric elements (2D or 3D) and the formulations used for structural elements (beams, plates and shells). For the cases of the solid isoparametric elements, one finds three main types of formulation of the kinematics for the case of large strains: - The kinematics DEFORMATION=‘PETIT_REAC’ makes it possible to treat an arbitrary constitutive law in large strains. The law is written in small strains and the large strains are taken into account only by updating the geometry. This formulation is not incrementally objective. Moreover, one can use it only if the behaviour is isotropic, if the elastic strains are small compared with the plastic strains, if the rotations remain small (less than 10° ) and if one adopts a sufficiently fine discretisation in time. Moreover, the absence of the geometric contribution in the tangent matrix can sometimes make convergence difficult (see [R5.03.21 for more details). - The kinematics DEFORMATION=‘SIMO_MIEHE’ makes it possible to treat an elastoplastic constitutive law with isotropic hardening in large strains, the ductile failure law known as “Rousselier” or the elasto(visco)plasticity with phase changes for metallurgy (see R5.03.21, R5.03.06 and R4.04.03). This formulation is incrementally objective, with no limitation on the level of the transformations applied, but it is available only for the three constitutive laws mentioned and makes it possible to treat only the cases where the behaviour is isotropic. - The kinematics DEFORMATION=‘GDEF_LOG’ also makes it possible to treat any hypo-elastoplastic constitutive law. It is incrementally objective, with no limitation on the level of the transformations applied, and makes it possible to treat the case of anisotropic behaviours (see R5.03.24). In order to treat large elastic strains, one must employ another formalism, called via DEFORMATION = 'GROT_GDEP', which can be used for non-linear hyperelastic constitutive relations in large displacements (see R5.03.20 and R5.03.22 for the case of small strains) or for the hyperelastic constitutive law (see R5.03.19). Finally, for the structural elements (beam, plates or shells), specific formulations exist. One may mention: - The beams in large displacements (see R5.03.40) or the multifibre beams in large displacements (see R3.08.09). Keyword DEFORMATION='GROT_GDEP'. - The volumetric shell elements in geometric non-linearity (see R3.07.05). There are no structural elements (beam, plate or shell) usable in large strains in Code_Aster . 1.2.3 Unilateral contact and friction For contact and friction, one will refer to three documents: R5.03.51 on discrete contact with friction, R5.03.52 for the hybrid formulation by contact/friction elements and R5.03.53 on contact in large sliding with the XFEM method. 1.2.4 Boundary conditions and loadings It is possible to define non-linear boundary conditions, that is to say depending on the displacement of the structure. There are two main categories of non-linear boundary conditions: - For the Neumann loadings, it is essentially a matter of pressure: the latter having to remain normal to the surface, the fact that the structure undergoes large transformations implies that the loading depends on the displacements. One will consult on this subject the documents R3.03.07, R3.03.04 and § 3.2; - For the Dirichlet loadings, Code_Aster allows for the moment only the loading of type LIAISON_SOLIDE (see U4.44.01), which rigidifies exactly a part of the structure. One will consult on this subject R3.02.02; In both cases, it is necessary to specify explicitly that this loading is non-linear (one speaks of a follower loading) by means of the keyword TYPE_CHARGE in the factor keyword EXCIT defining the loadings (see U4.01.03). Note: in all generality, one can liken frictional contact to a mixed boundary condition (in displacement and in pressure) that is non-linear. 1.3 Statement of the quasi-static non-linear problem 1.3.1 General problem As a consequence of paragraph 1.1, one sees that it is legitimate to consider that the non-linear problem has a displacement as unknown and that it is parameterised by time. Let us therefore consider the quasi-static non-linear problem by the classical expression of the principle of virtual work. {\mathrm{v}}^{T}.{\mathrm{L}}^{int}(\mathrm{u},t)={\mathrm{v}}^{T}.{\mathrm{L}}^{\text{ext}}(t)\text{}\forall \mathrm{v}=0 where: - t represents the time-instant variable; - u is the displacement field taken from a reference configuration; - v is the kinematically admissible virtual displacement field; - {L}^{\text{ext}} is the external mechanical loading to which the structure is subjected (pressure, imposed force, ...); - {L}^{int} represents the internal forces of the quasi-static non-linear mechanics problem. In the linear case, one has {L}^{int}(u,t)=K.u , where K is the stiffness matrix of the structure. For the moment, the Dirichlet boundary conditions are not taken into account. In fact, more precisely, {L}^{int}(u,t) is related to the stress field \sigma by the operator of the work of the virtual strains {Q}^{T} according to the following relation: {L}^{int}(u,t)={Q}^{T}(u).\sigma In small displacements, {Q}^{T} is independent of the displacements; for large displacements, this is no longer the case. One gives oneself a discretisation of the time interval to be computed: t\to \left[{t}_{0},\cdots ,{t}_{i},\cdots ,{t}_{n}\right] The stress field {\sigma}_{i} at the time instant {t}_{i} is written \sigma ({u}_{i},{\beta}_{i},{t}_{i},{H}_{i-1}) , if one denotes {\beta}_{i} the fields of command variables and {H}_{i-1} the past history of the structure. For elastic behaviours, the history does not intervene: the set {H}_{i-1} is therefore empty. For incremental behaviours, the history is the set of the states (fields of displacements, stresses and internal variables) at the previous time instant: {H}_{i-1}=\left\lbrace {u}_{i-1},{\sigma}_{i-1},{\alpha}_{i-1},{t}_{i-1}\right\rbrace . In the general case, the dependence of the operator {L}^{int} is, as we have seen in [§ 1.1], implicit with respect to time: it results from the integration of the constitutive relation in time (for elastoplasticity problems, for example). The explicit dependence with respect to time appears in particular in the case of constitutive relations taking into account a phenomenon of hardening by time (time-hardening) or in the case of ageing. The formulation of the quasi-static problem consists in expressing the equilibrium of the structure (the internal forces are equal to the external forces) for a sequence of computation time instants {\left\lbrace {t}_{i}\right\rbrace }_{1\le i\le I} that parameterise the loading; one will denote the quantities at the time instant {t}_{i} by the index i (for example {\mathrm{L}}^{int}({\mathrm{u}}_{i},{t}_{i})={\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{int} ): {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{int}={\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{ext}} Which amounts to cancelling at ({\mathrm{u}}_{i},{t}_{i}) the vector {\mathrm{R}}_{i}({\mathrm{u}}_{i},{t}_{i}) called the equilibrium residual vector, defined by: {\mathrm{R}}_{i}({\mathrm{u}}_{i},{t}_{i})={\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{int}-{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{ext}} The state of the structure at {t}_{0} is assumed known. One carries out I increments (or steps) of load. The unknowns are computed incrementally by the global solution algorithm (even for elastic behaviours). From {\mathrm{u}}_{i-1} , a solution satisfying equilibrium at {t}_{i-1} , one determines \Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i} which will make it possible to obtain the solution at {t}_{i} : \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{t}_{i}={t}_{i-1}+\Delta {t}_{i}\\ {\mathrm{u}}_{i}={\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}+\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}\end{array} The increment \Delta {u}_{i} is first estimated by linearising the problem with respect to time about ({\mathrm{u}}_{i-1},{t}_{i-1}) (phase known as prediction or Euler). Then one uses a Newton method or one of its variants to solve equation () iteratively (one computes a sequence \Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n} where the exponent n is the iteration number). In addition to these variables, for the incremental constitutive relations, one needs to know at {t}_{i-1} the stress field {\sigma}_{i-1} and the field of internal variables {\alpha}_{i-1} (see R5.03.02 for an example). 1.3.2 Dirichlet boundary conditions We have imposed that the virtual displacement field be kinematically admissible, that is to say that it respects the boundary conditions in displacement (or Dirichlet conditions). In a general manner, the linear Dirichlet conditions are written: \sum_{j=1}^{r}{\alpha}_{j}{u}_{j}=\beta (t) With {u}_{j} the list of the r degrees of freedom, {\alpha}_{j} the coefficients and \beta the right-hand side, which may depend on time. In Code_Aster, there are two ways of taking these conditions into account: - By a method known as “kinematic” (definition by AFFE_CHAR_CINE), which uses a method of pseudo-elimination in the resulting linear system (see U4.44.03). In this case, one can define only simple boundary conditions such that r=1 ; - By a dualisation method (definition by AFFE_CHAR_MECA), which uses the technique of double Lagrange multipliers (see R3.01.01). It is possible to eliminate dualised boundary conditions by the use of a special method that is described in R3.03.05, but only by using the PETSc solver. We now describe the way of taking the dualised boundary conditions into account in the solution of a non-linear problem. In a first stage, we shall assume that the boundary conditions () can be written in the following discrete form: B.u={u}^{d}(t) \mathrm{B} is a linear operator from the space of the displacement fields onto a space of functions defined on a part of the boundary of the structure, {u}^{d} is a given function on this part. The dualisation of the Dirichlet boundary conditions B.u={u}^{d}(t) leads to modifying () in the following manner: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}^{int}(u,t)+{B}^{T}.\lambda ={L}^{\text{ext}}(t)\\ B.u={u}^{d}(t)\end{array} The unknowns are now, at every time instant t , the pair (u,\lambda ) , where \lambda represents the Lagrange multipliers of the Dirichlet boundary conditions. The vector {B}^{T}.\lambda is then interpreted as the opposite of the support reactions at the corresponding nodes. Denoting the quantities at the time instant {t}_{i} by the index i : \lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{i}^{int}+{B}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}={L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}\\ B.{u}_{i}={u}_{i}^{d}\end{array} The equilibrium residual vector {R}_{i}({u}_{i},{\lambda}_{i},{t}_{i}) is now: {R}_{i}({u}_{i},{\lambda}_{i},{t}_{i})=(\begin{array}{c}{L}_{i}^{int}+{B}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}-{L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}\\ B.{u}_{i}-{u}_{i}^{d}\end{array}) The unknowns are still computed incrementally by the global solution algorithm. From ({u}_{i-1},{\lambda}_{i-1}) , a solution satisfying equilibrium at {t}_{i-1} , one determines \Delta {u}_{i} and \Delta {\lambda}_{i} which will make it possible to obtain the solution at {t}_{i} : \lbrace \begin{array}{}{t}_{i}={t}_{i-1}+\Delta {t}_{i}\\ {u}_{i}={u}_{i-1}+\Delta {u}_{i}\\ {\lambda}_{i}={\lambda}_{i-1}+\Delta {\lambda}_{i}\end{array} 2 Newton method 2.1 Principle of the method The Newton method is a classical method for solving equations of the zero-finding type. Consider a vector function F non-linear in the vector x . One seeks the zero of this function, that is to say: F(x)=0 The Newton method consists in constructing a sequence of vectors {x}^{n} converging towards the solution x . In order to find the new iterate {x}^{n+1} , one approximates F({x}^{n+1}) by a Taylor expansion to first order about {x}^{n} and one expresses that F({x}^{n+1}) must be zero: 0=F({x}^{n+1})\approx F({x}^{n})+{F}^{'}({x}^{n})({x}^{n+1}-{x}^{n}) Or again: {F}^{'}({x}^{n})({x}^{n+1}-{x}^{n})=-F({x}^{n}) Finally: {x}^{n+1}={x}^{n}-{\left[{F}^{'}({x}^{n})\right]}^{-1}.F({x}^{n}) {F}^{'}(x) is the tangent linear mapping associated with the function F . The derivative at the point x in the direction h is defined as the following directional derivative: {F}^{'}(x).h=\underset{\theta \to 0}{\lim}\frac{F(x+\theta .h)-F(x)}{\theta} The matrix of {F}^{'}(x) in the bases chosen for the vector spaces concerned is called the Jacobian matrix of F at the point x . When F is a function from a Euclidean vector space into the reals, {F}^{'}(x) is a linear form, and one can show that there exists a (unique) vector, denoted \nabla F(x) and called the gradient of F , such that: {F}^{'}(x).h={h}^{T}.\nabla F(x) That is to say the scalar product of h and of the gradient of F . When one is close to the solution, the convergence of the Newton method is quadratic, that is to say that the number of zeros after the decimal point in the error doubles at each iteration (0.19 – 0.036 – 0.0013 – 0.0000017, for example). But this method (using the true tangent) has several drawbacks: - It requires the computation of the tangent at each iteration, which is all the more costly as the size of the problem is large (especially in the case where one uses a direct solver), - If the increment is large, the tangent (known as coherent or consistent) can lead to divergences of the algorithm, - It may not be symmetric, which obliges one to use particular solvers. It is for this reason that one can use other matrices in place of the tangent matrix: the elastic matrix, a tangent matrix obtained previously, the symmetrised tangent matrix, ... 2.2 Adaptation of the Newton method to the problem posed In a first stage, the Dirichlet boundary conditions are not taken into account. One must solve a system (non-linear because it depends on {u}_{i} ) of the form: {L}_{i}^{int}({u}_{i})={L}_{i}^{\text{méca}}({u}_{i}) R({u}_{i},{t}_{i})={L}_{i}^{int}-{L}_{i}^{\text{méca}} The internal forces {L}_{i}^{int} can symbolically be denoted {Q}_{i}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i} , where {Q}_{i}^{T} is the matrix associated with the divergence operator (expression of the work of the virtual strain field). The internal forces are then expressed: {L}_{i}^{int}={Q}_{i}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i}={\int}_{\Omega}\varepsilon ({w}_{i}):\sigma ({u}_{i}).d\Omega And the forces of the mechanical loading: {L}_{i}^{\text{méca}}={\int}_{\Omega}{f}_{i}.{w}_{i}.d\Omega +{\int}_{\Gamma}{t}_{i}.{w}_{i}.d\Gamma Where: - {w}_{i} denotes the virtual displacement field; - {f}_{i} denotes the body forces applied at the time instant {t}_{i} on \Omega ; - {t}_{i} denotes the surface forces applied at the time instant {t}_{i} on the boundary \Gamma of \Omega . The application of the Newton method leads to solving a sequence of linear problems of the type ( n is the number of the Newton iteration, i that of the time-instant variable): {K}_{i}^{n}.\Delta {u}_{i}^{n+1}={L}_{i}^{\text{méca},n}-{L}_{i}^{int,n} One denotes \delta {u}_{i}^{n+1}={u}_{i}^{n+1}-{u}_{i}^{n} the displacement increment between two successive Newton iterations. The matrix {K}_{i}^{n} is the tangent stiffness matrix at {u}_{i}^{n} and the vector {L}_{i}^{int,n} represents the internal forces at the {n}^{\text{ième}} Newton iteration of the {i}^{\text{ème}} load step. The quantity {R}_{i}^{n}=({L}_{i}^{\text{méca},n}-{L}_{i}^{int,n}) represents the unbalanced forces, which one calls the “equilibrium residual”. The matrix {K}_{i}^{n} is the matrix of the tangent linear mapping of the function {R}_{i}^{n} ; it is therefore: {K}_{i}^{n}={\frac{\partial {R}_{i}^{n}}{\partial u}\mid }_{({u}_{i}^{n},{t}_{i})}={\frac{\partial {L}_{i}^{int,n}}{\partial u}\mid }_{({u}_{i}^{n},{t}_{i})}-{\frac{\partial {L}_{i}^{\text{méca},n}}{\partial u}\mid }_{({u}_{i}^{n},{t}_{i})} In the absence of follower forces [§ 3.2], the second term is zero. There therefore remains of the matrix {K}_{i}^{n} only the derivative at the point {u}_{i}^{n} of the internal forces with respect to the displacements: {K}_{i}^{n}={\frac{\partial {L}_{i}^{int,n}}{\partial u}\mid }_{({u}_{i}^{n},{t}_{i})} A small error in the evaluation of the internal forces can have serious consequences, because it is their exact computation that guarantees, if one converges, that it will be towards the solution sought. On the other hand, it is not always necessary to use the true tangent matrix, whose computation and factorisation are costly. For example, a variant of the method uses the elastic matrix {K}_{\text{élas}} . The method using the true tangent matrix {K}_{i}^{n} (also called the coherent or consistent matrix) is called the Newton method; the methods using other matrices (such as, for example, the elastic matrix {K}_{\text{élas}} ) are called modified Newton methods or quasi-Newton methods. The choice between a tangent matrix (the last one obtained or a previous matrix) and an elastic matrix is made in Code_Aster by means of the keyword MATRICE= 'TANGENTE' or MATRICE='ELASTIQUE' of the factor keyword NEWTON. Moreover, it is possible to use an unloading matrix, that is to say a matrix with constant internal variables (the evolution of the non-linearities is therefore not taken into account in this matrix), below a certain time step, for certain constitutive laws. One will refer to the documentation U4.51.03 for the use of this functionality. The Newton method with a consistent tangent matrix can be illustrated simply with the aid of the diagram of d8.00.01-fig-newton. Figure 2.2.1-a One then continues with the loop of Newton iterations, which makes it possible, at convergence, to obtain the values of \Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i} , and therefore those of {\mathrm{u}}_{i} by application of equation (): {\mathrm{u}}_{i}={\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}+\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i} {\mathrm{u}}_{i}={\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}+\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i} 2.3 Euler prediction phase Experience shows that the convergence of the Newton method depends strongly on a judicious choice of the initial estimate: “the closer the initial estimate is to the solution, the faster the algorithm converges”. In order to start the iterative process of the method, it is therefore useful to determine a “good” initial increment \Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0} . For this, one linearises the continuous problem with respect to time: this is what is called the prediction phase. 2.3.1 Linearisation One will therefore linearise the system () with respect to time about {\mathrm{u}}_{i-1} . One begins by linearising the internal forces {L}_{i}^{int} : {L}_{i}^{int}\approx {L}_{i-1}^{int}+{\frac{\partial {L}^{int}}{\partial u}\mid }_{{u}_{i-1}}.\Delta {u}_{i}^{0}+{\frac{\delta {L}^{int}}{\delta t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}} One assumes that the mechanical loading does not depend on time (follower loads are excluded), therefore: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{L}_{i}^{\text{méca}}={L}_{i-1}^{\text{méca}}+\Delta {L}_{i}^{\text{méca}}\\ {u}_{i}^{d}={u}_{i-1}^{d}+\Delta {u}_{i}^{d}\end{array} By substituting back into the first equation of the system, one obtains for the equilibrium equation: {\mathrm{L}}_{i-1}^{int}+{\frac{\partial {\mathrm{L}}^{int}}{\partial \mathrm{u}}\mid }_{{\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}}.\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0}+{\frac{\delta {\mathrm{L}}^{int}}{\delta t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}.\Delta {t}_{i}={\mathrm{L}}_{i-1}^{\text{méca}}+\Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}} One has equilibrium at the time instant {t}_{i-1} , that is to say: {\mathrm{L}}_{i-1}^{int}={\mathrm{L}}_{i-1}^{\text{méca}} And there therefore remains: {\frac{\partial {\mathrm{L}}^{int}}{\partial \mathrm{u}}\mid }_{{\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}}.\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0}+{\frac{\delta {\mathrm{L}}^{int}}{\delta t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}.\Delta {t}_{i}=\Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}} One obtains the system of equations making it possible to compute predictive values \Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0} : {\frac{\partial {\mathrm{L}}^{int}}{\partial \mathrm{u}}\mid }_{{\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}}.\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0}=\Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}-{\frac{\delta {\mathrm{L}}^{int}}{\delta t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}.\Delta {t}_{i} 2.3.2 Prediction tangent matrix The quantity {\frac{\partial {\mathrm{L}}^{int}}{\partial \mathrm{u}}\mid }_{{\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}} denotes the partial derivative at constant time of {L}_{i-1}^{int} ; it can be expanded: {K}_{i-1}={\frac{\partial {L}^{int}}{\partial u}\mid }_{{u}_{i-1}}=({Q}_{i-1}^{T}.{\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial u}\mid }_{{u}_{i-1}}+{\frac{\partial {Q}^{T}}{\partial u}\mid }_{{u}_{i-1}}.{\sigma}_{i-1}) The matrix {K}_{i-1} is called the prediction tangent matrix. The dependence of the matrix Q with respect to the displacements is neglected under the small-displacement hypothesis: the term {\frac{\partial {Q}^{T}}{\partial u}\mid }_{{u}_{i-1}} , called the geometric stiffness term, therefore disappears from . This term is taken into account for the large transformations (see § 1.2.2). For the developers, let us specify that the computation of the tangent matrix during the prediction phase is carried out via the computation option RIGI_MECA_TANG. 2.3.3 Variants of the prediction There exist other prediction options available in STAT_NON_LINE. - One can use an elastic matrix {K}_{\text{élas}} in place of the rate tangent matrix {K}_{i-1} ; this is the option PREDICTION='ELASTIQUE' (option RIGI_MECA). - One can use a secant matrix {K}_{\text{sécante}} in place of the rate tangent matrix {K}_{i-1} ; this is the option PREDICTION='SECANTE' (option RIGI_MECA_ELAS). The secant matrix is an elastic matrix whose Young's modulus is used by applying the damage (see for example R5.03.25 for more details) - One can use a previously computed displacement increment in place of the estimate; this is the option PREDICTION='DEPL_CALCULE'. In this case one performs no inversion of a system and \Delta {u}_{i}^{0} is given directly. See the documentation U4.51.03 for its use. - One can use a displacement increment extrapolated with respect to the previous step. One computes the estimate of the displacement increment from the total increment obtained as the solution at the previous time step (weighted by the ratio of the time steps). This is the option PREDICTION='EXTRAPOL'. In these last two cases, in order to ensure that the initial displacement is kinematically admissible, one projects the estimate onto the set of the kinematically admissible fields (i.e. satisfying the Dirichlet boundary conditions) according to the norm given by the elastic matrix, which must therefore be computed. 2.3.4 Right-hand side vector of the command variables A command variable \beta (t) is a scalar quantity, a function of time and of space 1 , given a priori by the user via the keyword AFFE_VARC in the operator AFFE_MATERIAU. It is a parameter of the problem and not an unknown . The quantity {\frac{\delta {L}^{int}}{\delta t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}} denotes the partial differential, with respect to t and with u constant, of {L}^{int}=Q.\sigma (t,\beta (t)) . This particular notation is intended to draw attention to the fact that for {n}_{\mathrm{varc}} command variables, one writes the total differential: \frac{\delta \sigma }{\delta t}=\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial t}+\sum_{j=1,{n}_{\mathrm{varc}}}^{}\frac{\delta \sigma }{\delta {\beta}^{j}}.\frac{\delta {\beta}^{j}}{\delta t} If one takes as an example the command variable describing the temperature \theta : \frac{\delta \sigma }{\delta t}=\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial t}+\frac{\delta \sigma }{\delta \theta }.\frac{\delta \theta }{\delta t} One assumes that the temperature varies linearly between the two time instants: \frac{\delta \theta }{\delta t}=\frac{\Delta {\theta}_{i}}{\Delta {t}_{i}} The dependence of \sigma with respect to time and with respect to temperature makes it possible to write: {\frac{\delta {L}^{int}}{\delta t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}=\frac{\delta}{\delta t}({Q}_{i-1}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i-1})={Q}_{i-1}^{T}.({\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}+{\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \theta }\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}.\frac{\Delta {\theta}_{i}}{\Delta {t}_{i}}) Because Q does not depend on time and therefore \frac{\delta}{\delta t}({Q}^{T})=0 . The vector \Delta {L}_{i}^{\text{varc}} , whose expression is given by , is the temperature loading increment (beware of the change of sign!) that one has generalised to all the command variables : temperature, irradiation, metallurgical phases (see R4.04.02), ... \Delta {L}_{i}^{\text{varc}}=-{\frac{\delta {L}^{int}}{\delta t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}.\Delta {t}_{i}=-{Q}_{i-1}^{T}.({\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}.\Delta {t}_{i}+\sum_{j=1,{n}_{\mathrm{varc}}}^{}({\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial {\beta}^{j}}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}.\Delta {\beta}_{i}^{j})) One does not currently take into account the explicit dependence of the stresses with respect to time and therefore the first term of is zero. And therefore finally: \Delta {L}_{i}^{\text{varc}}=-{Q}_{i-1}^{T}.(\sum_{j=1,{n}_{\mathrm{varc}}}^{}({\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial {\beta}^{j}}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}.\Delta {\beta}_{i}^{j})) The loading increment of the command variables \Delta {L}_{i}^{\text{varc}} , arising from the differentiation of the internal forces with respect to the command variables, is an estimate of the effect of a variation of the command variables. In the case of temperature, if one denotes K the hydrostatic compression modulus and \alpha the thermal expansion coefficient, the thermal stress is written: {\sigma}_{i}^{\text{ther}}=-3.K.\alpha .\Delta {\theta}_{i}.I+{\sigma}_{i-1}^{\text{ther}} \textrm{si} \Delta {\theta}_{i}={\theta}_{i}-{\theta}_{i-1} Where I is the identity matrix. And therefore, by applying: \Delta {L}_{i}^{\text{ther}}=-({Q}_{i-1}^{T}.{\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \theta }\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}}).\Delta {\theta}_{i}=3.K.\alpha .\Delta {\theta}_{i}.({Q}_{i-1}^{T}.I) In the elastic case, these are the internal forces associated with a thermal expansion (it is not strictly speaking a loading; it is more akin to the effect of an initial strain). This estimate is used in the prediction phase and in the stopping criterion. If the thermal expansions take the structure out of the elastic domain (plasticity, for example), this estimate will be corrected during the Newton iterations. 2.3.5 Right-hand side vector of the mechanical loading The mechanical loading increment \Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}} is composed of the dead loads (independent of the geometry, such as gravity) and of the follower loads. In reality, there exist cases (the first load increment, for example) where {L}_{i-1}^{\text{méca}} is unknown. One recalls that the loading increment () is written: {L}_{i}^{\text{méca}}={L}_{i-1}^{\text{méca}}+\Delta {L}_{i}^{\text{méca}} One has equilibrium at the time instant {t}_{i-1} , therefore by applying: \Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}={\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}-{\mathrm{L}}_{i-1}^{int} The expression of the internal forces at the previous time step {L}_{i-1}^{int} implies either saving this vector from the previous analysis if it exists (restart of an earlier analysis), or integrating the constitutive law from the initial state given by the user (which can be costly). For the sake of simplicity and efficiency, one chooses not to reintegrate the constitutive law and one simply expresses the internal forces as the nodal forces by taking the stresses known at this time instant, that is: {L}_{i-1}^{int}={Q}_{i-1}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i-1} Whence the new expression: \Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}={\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}-{\mathrm{Q}}_{i-1}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i-1} The direct computation from () requires the user to take care of the consistency between the stress field, the displacement fields and the internal-variable fields (DEPL, SIGM and VARI in ETAT_INIT) with respect to the integration of the constitutive law in the case of a restart of an analysis. 2.3.6 Linear system By substituting back the expression of {\frac{\partial {L}^{int}}{\partial u}\mid }_{{u}_{i-1}} (equation ), of {\frac{\delta {L}^{int}}{\delta t}\mid }_{{t}_{i-1}} (equation ) and \Delta {L}_{i}^{\text{méca}} (equation ) into , the system of equations in prediction is written: {\mathrm{K}}_{i-1}.\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0}={\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}-{\mathrm{Q}}_{i-1}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i-1}+\Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{varc}} 2.4 Newton correction phase At the end of the prediction phase, we find ourselves with an estimate of the displacement increment \Delta {u}_{i}^{0} . If this estimate is exact (modulo the application of the convergence criteria described in § 2.5), then one obtains the converged solution for the time step {t}_{i} : {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{\text{convergé}}={\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}+\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0} But if this is not the case, one must find the value \Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i} of the displacement increment from the value {\mathrm{u}}_{i-1} obtained at the previous equilibrium (time instant {t}_{i-1} ): {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{\text{convergé}}={\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}+\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i} If the prediction phase has converged, one therefore has trivially: \Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}=\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0} Otherwise, one takes as initial value \Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0} obtained at the end of the prediction phase, before correcting by the iterations \delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n} of the Newton method. With a number {n}_{\mathrm{CV}} of Newton iterations that is sufficient (always with the arbitration of the convergence criterion): {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{\text{convergé}}={\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}+\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{n={n}_{\mathit{CV}}}\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{j} As long as one has not converged (if the number of Newton iterations is not sufficient), one denotes: \Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}=\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{n {\varepsilon}_{\text{pic}} ). Because of the change of slope between 1 and 2, the use of a secant or consistent tangent matrix leads to a very poor approximation, whence the interest of modifying it. The choice that is presented consists in constructing the tangent matrix as a linear combination of the consistent tangent matrix and the secant matrix, both being determined by the constitutive laws. Currently, the approach is available only for the softening constitutive law ENDO_ISOT_BETON. In order to manage the triggering of the tangent-secant option, one introduces an additional internal variable with respect to the existing internal variables, \alpha =({\alpha}_{1},\dots {\alpha}_{n},{\alpha}_{n+1}) (with n the number of internal variables of the model used). This variable accounts for the possible alternation between the elastic state and the softening state of a Gauss point. One initialises it at the first Newton iteration of each new time step, then one makes it evolve in order to know, at each Gauss point, the number of successive alternations between the two states. Having this information, one can estimate that, from a certain threshold onwards (for example {S}_{0}=3 alternations), the Newton algorithm will no longer be able to converge for the current time increment and that it is necessary to modify the tangent matrix. In order to modify the matrix, one relies directly on the way in which the consistent tangent matrix in ENDO_ISOT_BETON is constructed (see R7.01.04). It is a matter of summing the dissipative part and the non-dissipative part. {K}_{\text{tg}}={K}_{\text{sc}}+{K}_{\text{end}} where {K}_{\text{tg}} is the tangent matrix, {K}_{\text{sc}} the secant matrix (non-dissipative part) and {K}_{\text{end}} the damaging correction (dissipative part). For the modified matrix {K}_{\text{t-s}} , one replaces the expression {K}_{\text{tg}} in () by: {K}_{\text{t - s}}={K}_{\text{sc}}+\eta .{K}_{\text{end}} where \eta is a function of {\alpha}_{n+1} with values between 0 and 1. The function \eta retained in what follows is the following: \eta =\frac{1}{{A}^{({\alpha}_{n+1}-{S}_{0})}} where A is a constant and {S}_{0} the threshold on the value of the number of successive alternations undergone, from which the tangent matrix is modified. For {\alpha}_{n+1}={S}_{0} the matrix remains consistently tangent and for {\alpha}_{n+1}\gg {S}_{0} , it becomes secant. Values judged satisfactory for these parameters are A=1,5 and {S}_{0}=3 (default values). The choice of the evolution of the value of {\alpha}_{n+1} is essential for the performance of the algorithm. One chooses an increase of {\alpha}_{n+1} by G=1,0 , {\alpha}_{n+1}\to {\alpha}_{n+1}+G for each new alternation between an elastic state and a damaging state, then a decrease of {\alpha}_{n+1} by P , {\alpha}_{n+1}\to {\alpha}_{n+1}-P , when the state remains damaging twice in succession. The aim of the use of P is to allow the return to the consistent tangent matrix when a Gauss point remains damaging over several iterations, since the consistent tangent matrix makes the convergence quadratic, provided that one is close to the solution. The value of the rate of decrease P relative to the rate of increase G is crucial for the behaviour of the evolving algorithm. The overall idea consists in increasing {\alpha}_{n+1} when one is far from the solution, in order to have an operator closer to the secant than to the consistent tangent, then, once “close” to the solution, in switching to the consistent tangent matrix (which is the best in the sense of Newton). The ratio P/G (keyword TAUX_RETOUR – 0.05 by default) represents the third parameter of the algorithm, in addition to A (keyword AMPLITUDE) and {S}_{0} (keyword SEUIL). 2.7 Newton-Krylov method 2.7.1 General principle The Newton-Krylov method is one of the inexact Newton methods. It can be used only when the solver of the linear system () is iterative (as opposed to a direct solver). This approach does not modify the choice of the tangent matrix of the system as the previous methods do. It acts on the convergence criterion of the iterative solver used for the linearised system. By adapting as well as possible the convergence criterion of the iterative method to the Newton convergence, one avoids performing useless iterations (in the linear solver) and one thus gains in analysis time. 2.7.2 Implementation The general principle of the inexact Newton methods is to replace the condition that the solution increment \delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n} be the exact solution of the system () by a weaker condition. One requires that \delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n} satisfy the condition: ∥\begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{K}}_{i}^{n-1}.\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}-\left({\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}-{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{int,n-1}\right)\end{array}∥⩽{\eta}_{n}∥{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}-{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{int,n-1}∥ where {\eta}_{n} is called the forcing term . One can show that the method proposed is convergent and that when the sequence {\eta}_{n} tends towards 0 , the convergence is super-linear (see [ 8 ] p.96). The smaller this value is, the closer the solution will be to that obtained by an exact solution, but the less time one will gain in the solution of the linear system. One must therefore find a good compromise between solving the linear systems rapidly and not degrading too much the convergence of the Newton iterations. By examining condition (), one observes that it is identical to the relative convergence criterion of the iterative solvers used to solve the linearised Newton system. In order to check this condition, it is therefore a matter of using the forcing term as the convergence criterion of an iterative linear solver. As has been seen previously, one must also ensure that the sequence {\eta}_{n} tends towards 0 in order to retain the super-linear convergence of the Newton method. To this end, one will slave {\eta}_{n} to the decrease of the Newton residual by the evolution law ( cf. [ 8 ] p.105): {\eta}_{n+1}^{\mathit{Res}}=\gamma \frac{{∥{\mathrm{R}}_{i}^{n}∥}^{2}}{{∥{\mathrm{R}}_{i}^{n-1}∥}^{2}} where the constant is chosen such that \gamma =0.1 . This simple formula is not sufficient in practice, because one must guarantee an adequate decrease of {\eta}_{n} . For this, one determines {\eta}_{n} completely by the following expression: {\eta}_{n+1}=\lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}{\eta}_{0}& n=-1& \\ max(min(0.4{\eta}_{n},{\eta}_{n+1}^{\mathit{Res}}),{\eta}_{min})& n⩾0,& (1-\gamma ){\eta}_{n}^{2}⩽0.2\\ min(0.4{\eta}_{n},max({\eta}_{n+1}^{\mathit{Res}},(1-\gamma ){\eta}_{n}^{2}))& n⩾0,& (1-\gamma ){\eta}_{n}^{2}>0.2\end{array} where the constant is equal to {\eta}_{0}=0.9 and corresponds to the convergence criterion used for the first linear solution. {\eta}_{min} , for its part, is the value of the convergence criterion of the iterative linear solver supplied by the user (keyword RESI_RELA). To be more precise, a command variable is assigned to a mesh cell. It is therefore not a function of the geometry (and therefore of the displacements), but of the topology of the mesh. The infinite norm simply corresponds to the maximum component of the absolute value of the vector 3 Boundary conditions and loadings 3.1 Classification In the following paragraphs, we shall describe the set of the loadings possible in the operator and their classification. In the first place, one should distinguish three main categories of loadings: - The Dirichlet loadings (boundary conditions) apply to the nodal unknowns in the broad sense: this can be a displacement, a temperature or a pressure (for THM). They can be applied by elimination (AFFE_CHAR_CINE) or by dualisation (AFFE_CHAR_MECA). When the boundary conditions are treated by elimination, they are taken into account at the moment of the solution of the linear system, internally, and they therefore do not modify in any way the equations already described previously; - The Neumann loadings apply in general to the fluxes. They are conditions in forces, in general, defined on the mesh cells (except for the loading FORCE_NODALE). There is another distinction to be made between the follower loadings and those that are not. A loading is a follower loading when it depends on the geometry of the structure. Typically, pressure is exerted in the direction opposite to the normal. Therefore, when the structure deforms with the evolution of the load, the loading, expressed in an absolute frame, is transformed. There also exist follower Dirichlet loadings. These are boundary conditions that depend on the geometry because they are non-linear. The loads that do not depend on the geometry of the structure are called dead or fixed loads (for example, gravity). 3.2 Follower loadings In order to indicate that a load must be treated as a follower load in STAT_NON_LINE, one indicates TYPE_CHARGE='SUIV' under the keyword EXCIT. A mechanical loading {L}^{\text{méca}}({u}_{i}) comprising follower loads is therefore decomposed into two parts: {L}_{i}^{\text{méca}}({u}_{i})={L}_{i}^{\text{fixe}}+{L}_{i}^{\text{suiv}}({u}_{i}) The exponent {}^{\mathrm{fixe}} denotes here the dead loads, and {}^{\text{suiv}} the follower loads. The system of equations to be solved then becomes: {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{int}={\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{fixe}}+{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{suiv}}({\mathrm{u}}_{i}) The differentiation operations making it possible to write the prediction phase and the iterations of the Newton method therefore involve the derivatives of {L}_{i}^{\text{méca}}({u}_{i})={L}_{i}^{\text{fixe}}+{L}_{i}^{\text{suiv}}({u}_{i}) with respect to the displacements ({u}_{i}) . The prediction phase becomes: \left({\mathrm{K}}_{i-1}-{\frac{\partial {\mathrm{L}}^{\text{suiv}}}{\partial \mathrm{u}}\mid }_{{\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n-1}}\right).\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0}=\Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{fixe}}+\Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{suiv}}+\Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{varc}} And the Newton iterations consist in solving the system: \left({\mathrm{K}}_{i}^{n-1}-{\frac{\partial {\mathrm{L}}^{\text{suiv}}}{\partial \mathrm{u}}\mid }_{{\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n-1}}\right).\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}={\mathrm{L}}^{\text{fixe}}+{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{suiv},n-1}({\mathrm{u}}_{i})-{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{int,n-1} Thus, at the beginning of each load step (prediction) and at each Newton iteration, one must compute a stiffness matrix {\frac{\partial {\mathrm{L}}^{\text{suiv}}}{\partial \mathrm{u}}\mid }_{\mathrm{u}} and a vector {L}^{\text{suiv}} linked to the follower loadings. The only Neumann loads that can be treated as follower loads in the current state of the operator STAT_NON_LINE are: - The pressure for the modellings 3D, 3D_SI, D_PLAN, D_PLAN_SI, AXIS, AXIS_SI, C_PLAN, C_PLAN_SI R3.03.04 and COQUE_3D R3.03.07; - The gravity loading for the elements CABLE_POULIE R3.08.05, three-node elements comprising a pulley and two cable strands: the gravity force exerted on the element depends on the respective lengths of the two strands; - The centrifugal force in large displacements, which for a rotation speed \omega is given by: {\int}_{\Omega}\rho .\omega \wedge \left[\omega \wedge \text{OM}\right].d\Omega ={\int}_{\Omega}\rho .\omega \wedge \left[\omega \wedge ({\text{OM}}_{0}+u)\right].d\Omega . Available for the modellings 3D and AXIS_FOURIER; - The gravity loading for all the THM modellings of unsaturated porous media R7.01.10: indeed, the density depends on the nodal variables in order to take into account the constitutive relations of the geomaterials. 3.3 Dualised boundary conditions – Linear case We shall now take the dualised boundary conditions into account in the writing of the linear system to be solved. In a first stage, we shall consider only linear relations. One assumes the existence of a potential J(v) such that the minimisation of the latter makes it possible to express the mechanical equilibrium (in the weak sense) of the structure. If J(u) is this minimum then one has: \begin{array}{c}\text{Trouver}u\in V\text{tel que :}\\ \lbrace \begin{array}{c}J(u)=\underset{v\in V}{min}J(v)\equiv \lbrace {L}^{int}(u,v)-{L}^{\text{ext}}(u,v)\rbrace \\ \text{Avec :}V=\lbrace v\in {R}^{n}\text{tel que}\mathit{Bv}=0\rbrace \end{array}\end{array} - {L}^{int}(u,v) denotes the sum of the discretised internal forces. It depends on the solution sought via the constitutive laws, the large-transformation kinematics, etc. - {L}^{\text{ext}}(u,v) denotes the sum of the discretised external forces. It can depend on the solution as in the case of follower forces, of contact, etc. - V denotes the set of the admissible test solutions; - U denotes the set of the admissible solutions sought; - B is a linear operator from the space of the displacement fields onto a space of functions defined on a part of the boundary of the structure; Note: in mechanics, one can consider the presence of dissipative forces linked to the viscous character of the constitutive law or to the friction forces. In these cases the potential is replaced by the existence of a pseudo-potential of dissipation. One does not go into the details but one shows that one can come back within the framework of an optimisation problem thanks to the Legendre–Fenchel transformation. For the sake of simplicity, one keeps the general framework of the previous equation, because the rest of the developments is not affected by the existence of a pseudo-potential. In discrete form, the dualisation of the Dirichlet boundary conditions \mathrm{B}.\mathrm{u}={\mathrm{u}}^{d}(t) leads to the following problem [R3.03.01]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}^{int}(u,t)+{B}^{T}.\lambda ={L}^{\text{ext}}(t)\\ B.u={u}^{d}(t)\end{array} The unknowns are now, at every time instant t , the pair (u,\lambda ) , where \lambda represents the Lagrange multipliers of the Dirichlet boundary conditions R3.03.01. The vector {B}^{T}.\lambda is interpreted as the opposite of the support reactions at the corresponding nodes. Parameterising by the time instant {t}_{i} : \lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{i}^{int}+{B}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}={L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}\\ B.{u}_{i}={u}_{i}^{d}\end{array} Finding equilibrium therefore consists in cancelling at ({u}_{i},{\lambda}_{i},{t}_{i}) the equilibrium residual vector, which will be defined by: {R}_{i}({u}_{i},{\lambda}_{i},{t}_{i})=(\begin{array}{c}{L}_{i}^{int}+{B}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}-{L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}\\ B.{u}_{i}-{u}_{i}^{d}\end{array}) The unknowns are computed incrementally by the global solution algorithm, including the Lagrange multipliers of the dualised boundary conditions.
