It is necessary to introduce the contribution of the non-linear boundary conditions: {\parallel {\mathrm{Q}}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i}^{n}+{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}^{n}+{\nabla {\mathrm{C}}_{i}}^{n,T}.{\lambda}_{\mathit{nl},i}^{n}-{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}\parallel }_{\infty}\le \gamma The criterion RESI_GLOB_RELA (chosen by default) amounts to checking that the residual is sufficiently small, as previously, and this relative to a quantity representative of the loading. \frac{{\parallel {\mathrm{Q}}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i}^{n}+{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}^{n}+{\nabla {\mathrm{C}}_{i}}^{n,T}.{\lambda}_{\mathit{nl},i}^{n}-{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}\parallel }_{\infty}}{{\parallel {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{méca}}+{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{varc}}+{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}^{n}+{\nabla {\mathrm{C}}_{i}}^{n,T}.{\lambda}_{\mathit{nl},i}^{n}\parallel }_{\infty}}\le \eta If \textcolor{#000000}{C(.)} is non-differentiable then the general formalism does not change, with the exception of the correct definition of the generalised Jacobian of the non-differentiable function (see [R5.03.52] for example). 4 Line search The line search set out here concerns the line search in the absence of piloting. 4.1 Principle The introduction of the line search in the operator STAT_NON_LINE results from an observation: the Newton method with a consistent matrix does not converge in every situation, in particular when one starts too far from the solution. On the other hand, the use of matrices other than the consistent tangent matrix can, when they are too “flexible”, lead to divergence. The line search makes it possible to guard against such divergences. It consists in considering (\delta {u}_{i}^{n},\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n}) , no longer as the increment of the displacements and of the Lagrange multipliers, but as a search direction in which one will seek to minimise a functional (the energy of the structure). One will find an advance step \rho in this direction, and the update of the unknowns will consist in doing: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}={\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}\\ {\lambda}_{i}^{n}={\lambda}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n}\end{array} In the absence of line search (by default) the scalar \rho is of course equal to 1. 4.2 Minimisation of a functional In order to convince oneself better of the soundness of the line search, one can interpret the Newton method as a method of minimisation of a functional (in the case where the tangent matrices are symmetric). We insist on the fact that the equations obtained are rigorously those of the Newton method set out in [§ 2] and that only the way of arriving at them is different. Let us “forget”, in order to simplify the presentation, the dualisation of the Dirichlet boundary conditions and let us place ourselves under the small-strain hypothesis. One considers the functional: \begin{array}{}J:V\to ℝ\\ u\to J(u)={\int}_{\Omega}\Phi (\varepsilon (u)).d\Omega -{\int}_{\Omega}f.u.d\Omega -{\int}_{\Gamma}t.u.d\Gamma \end{array} where the free-energy density \Phi makes it possible to relate the stress tensor \sigma to the linearised strain tensor \varepsilon by the relation \varepsilon =\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial \sigma } in the case of hyperelasticity (one generalises this situation to the other non-linearities in the rest of the document). The functional J being convex, finding the minimum of J is equivalent to cancelling its gradient, that is: \nabla J(u).v=0\forall v\in V Which is exactly the Principle of Virtual Work, since: \nabla J(u).v={\int}_{\Omega}\sigma (u):\varepsilon (v).d\Omega -{\int}_{\Omega}f.v.d\Omega -{\int}_{\Gamma}t.v.d\Gamma Thus, solving the equations arising from the Principle of Virtual Work (basis of the problem formulated in [§ 1.3]) is equivalent to minimising the functional J which represents the energy of the structure (internal energy diminished by the work of the external forces \mathrm{f} and t ). 4.3 Minimisation method The minimisation is done iteratively, classically in two stages at each iteration: - Computation of a search direction \delta along which one will seek the next iterate, - Computation of the best advance step \rho in this direction: {u}^{n+1}={u}^{n}+\rho .\delta In a minimisation problem, the natural idea is to advance in the direction opposite to the gradient of the functional, which is locally the best descent direction since this direction is normal to the contour lines and directed in the sense of the decreasing values Figure 2-4.3-1 Figure 2 ‑ 4.3-1 However, it is possible to improve the choice of the descent direction by using this gradient method in a new metric. This is what will allow us to recover the classical equations of the Newton method. Let us take the simple example of a problem with two variables x and y for which the functional has the form of an ellipse whose minimum is at (\frac{\alpha}{a},\frac{\beta}{b}) : J(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}.{\mathrm{ax}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}.{\mathrm{by}}^{2}-\alpha x-\beta y By choosing as descent direction the inverse of the gradient of J , one passes from one iterate to the next (let us reason on x only) by: {x}^{n+1}={x}^{n}-{\text{ax}}^{n}+\alpha which does not point towards the solution, since the normal at a point of an ellipse does not in general pass through the centre of the ellipse Figure 2‑ 4.3-2 On the other hand, if one carries out a change of variables so that the contours of J become circles: \lbrace \begin{array}{}\bar{x}=\sqrt{a}.x\\ \bar{y}=\sqrt{b}.y\\ \bar{J}(\bar{x},\bar{y})=\frac{1}{2}.({\bar{x}}^{2}+{\bar{y}}^{2})-\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{a}}.\bar{x}-\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{b}}.\bar{y}\end{array} Figure 2 ‑ 4.3-3 The use of the inverse direction of the gradient of \bar{J} then makes it possible to obtain the solution in one iteration: {\bar{x}}^{n+1}={\bar{x}}^{n}-({\bar{x}}^{n}-\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{a}})=\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{a}}\mathrm{\Rightarrow }{x}^{n+1}=\frac{\alpha}{a} Thus, the use of the gradient method in the new metric allows an immediate convergence. In a more complicated case (convex functional but different from an ellipse), the convergence is not instantaneous but the change of variables makes it possible to reduce substantially the number of iterations necessary. 4.4 Application to the minimisation of the energy For simplicity, one will place oneself in the discretised linear case where the functional J is: J(u)=\frac{1}{2}.{u}^{T}.K.u-{u}^{T}.L One denotes K the stiffness matrix of the structure, and L the vector of the imposed loadings. In order to minimise J , we shall use the same descent method as previously by first carrying out a change of variables that is quite similar. The matrix K being symmetric positive definite, its eigenvalues are real and positive: one can therefore define the “square root” of K which will be denoted \sqrt{K} (also symmetric). One sets \bar{u}=\sqrt{K}.u ; the minimisation of J is then equivalent to that of: \bar{J}(\bar{\mathrm{u}})=\frac{1}{2}.{\bar{\mathrm{u}}}^{T}.\bar{\mathrm{u}}-{\bar{\mathrm{u}}}^{T}.{(\sqrt{\mathrm{K}})}^{-T}.\mathrm{L} By using a decomposition by the diagonal: K=P.D.{P}^{-1} With \mathrm{D} diagonal, therefore: \sqrt{K}=P.\sqrt{D}.{P}^{-1} Which leads to: \sqrt{{K}^{T}}.\sqrt{K}=P.\sqrt{{D}^{T}}.\sqrt{D}.{P}^{-1}=K By taking as descent direction the inverse direction of the gradient of \bar{J} , one obtains: {\bar{u}}^{n+1}={\bar{u}}^{n}-({\bar{u}}^{n}-\sqrt{{K}^{-1}}.L) That is, returning to the initial variables: {u}^{n+1}={u}^{n}-{K}^{-1}.(K.{u}^{n}-L) Or again: K.({u}^{n+1}-{u}^{n})=L-K.{u}^{n} One recovers the equations of the Newton method: the matrix K is the Hessian of the functional J (matrix of the second derivative) and the right-hand side is the difference of the loading and of the internal forces, also called the equilibrium residual. Thus the Newton method can be interpreted as resulting from the minimisation of the energy of the structure via a gradient method applied after a change of metric. 4.5 Determination of the advance step Let us return to the real problem, that of the solution of {L}_{i}^{int}({u}_{i})={L}_{i}^{\text{ext}} . This problem can be interpreted as the minimisation of the following functional: J=W({u}_{i})-{u}_{i}^{T}.{L}_{i}^{\text{ext}} where W({u}_{i}) corresponds to the discretisation, on the basis of the shape functions, of the internal energy of the structure: W={\int}_{\Omega}\Phi (\varepsilon (u)).d\Omega One has computed by the Newton method a displacement increment \delta {u}_{i}^{n} which, in the minimisation problem, is interpreted as a search direction, according to what precedes. One will compute the advance step \rho in this direction making it possible to minimise the value of the functional: \underset{\rho \in ℝ}{\text{Min}}\left\lbrace W({u}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {u}_{i}^{n})-{L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}({u}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {u}_{i}^{n})\right\rbrace In order to find the minimum of this scalar function of \rho which will be denoted f(\rho ) , one seeks the point where its derivative vanishes (this amounts to making the final residual and the search direction orthogonal): f'(\rho )={\left[\delta {u}_{i}^{n}\right]}^{T}.\left[{Q}^{T}.\sigma ({u}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {u}_{i}^{n})-{L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}\right]=0 f'(\rho ) is the projection of the residual onto the search direction. With the notations of [§ 2.2] and taking into account the support reactions, the scalar equation to be solved in order to determine the advance step \rho is written: f'(\rho )={\left[\delta {u}_{i}^{n}\right]}^{T}.\left[{Q}^{T}.\sigma ({u}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {u}_{i}^{n})+{B}^{T}.({\lambda}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n})-{L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}\right]=0 At the end of the line search, one updates the displacements and the Lagrange parameters by: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}={\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}\\ {\lambda}_{i}^{n}={\lambda}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n}\end{array} The convergence test bears: - On the maximum number of line-search iterations indicated by the user under the keyword ITER_LINE_MAXI of the factor keyword NEWTON (the default value 0 inhibits the line search, and \rho is then equal to 1), - On the criterion RESI_LINE_RELA given by f(\rho )\le \tau .f(0) , where \tau is equal by default to 0.1. The line search is in a way an “insurance” making it possible to guard against serious divergences of the Newton method. When the search direction is “bad” (if the tangent matrix is too flexible, for example), the line-search algorithm leads to a small value of \rho , which avoids moving too far away from the solution. It is not necessary to perform many iterations in the secant method (two or three are enough to avoid disasters) because each one is rather expensive (one must recompute the internal forces) and one does not have the ambition of finding at each Newton iteration the truly optimal value of \rho . 4.6 Computation of the line-search coefficient There exist two methods for computing the optimal \rho in the line search . 4.6.1 Secant method (METHODE=’CORDE’) In order that the determination of \rho should not be too costly, one uses a secant method whose maximum number of iterations is fixed by the user. The secant method can be interpreted as a Newton method in which the derivative at the current point is approximated by the direction joining the current point and the previous point: {\rho}^{p+1}={\rho}^{p}-\frac{{\rho}^{p}-{\rho}^{p-1}}{{g}^{p}-{g}^{p-1}}.{g}^{p}=\frac{{\rho}^{p-1}.{g}^{p}-{\rho}^{p}.{g}^{p-1}}{{g}^{p}-{g}^{p-1}} Where one has denoted {g}^{p}=f'({\rho}^{p}) . One starts from {\rho}^{0}=0 and {\rho}^{1}=1 . The secant method has an order of convergence of the order of 1.6. It is represented schematically in Figure 2-4.6.1-1. Figure 2 ‑ 4.6.1-1 4.6.2 Mixed method (METHODE=’MIXTE’) This method mixes several solution techniques in order to be more robust. It consists essentially in the application of a secant method (see the previous paragraph) between two predetermined bounds. It is in fact the application of the secant method with variable bounds. Here is the algorithm used: 1. One assumes that f'(0)>0 . If this is not the case, one changes the sense of the descent direction (by examining negative \rho , which amounts to defining f' as being equal to -f' 2. One seeks a positive {\rho}_{\max} such that f'({\rho}_{\max})<0 . The method is simply iterative by doing {\rho}_{n+1}=3.{\rho}_{n} with {\rho}_{0}=1 (bracketing or bounding stage) 3. One thus has the two new bounds between which the function changes sign. If one assumes that the function f' is continuous, there therefore exists a solution between these bounds. 4. One applies the secant method on this interval: one starts from {\rho}^{0}=0 and {\rho}^{1}={\rho}_{\max} . 4.6.3 Particular case: the Newton-Krylov method It has been specified above that the line search is carried out simultaneously on the unknowns \mathrm{u} and \lambda as shown by formula () of update of the variables. Now the functional to be minimised does not present a minimum as a function of the unknowns (\mathrm{u},\lambda ) ; it is indeed a Lagrangian which presents a saddle point, that is to say a minimum in \mathrm{u} and a maximum in \lambda (see R3.03.01). This way of proceeding is therefore not licit in the general case. That said, one can show that in the case where the system in prediction is solved “exactly” (at least to a numerically satisfactory accuracy), this approach is licit. This is generally the case in the usual use of Code_Aster . This is on the other hand not the case within the framework of the use of the Newton-Krylov method, where the linear systems are precisely solved in a deliberately inexact manner. In this situation, in order to circumvent the problem, only the unknowns \mathrm{u} are affected by the line search and the formula for updating the variables therefore becomes: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}={\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n-1}+\rho .\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}\\ {\lambda}_{i}^{n}={\lambda}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n}\end{array} Insofar as the functional to be minimised does indeed have a minimum in \mathrm{u} , the line-search procedure is licit. Insofar as the functional to be minimised does indeed have a minimum in \mathrm{u} , the line-search procedure is licit. 5 Piloting One will refer to the documentation R5.03.80. 6 Viscoelastic regularisation REGU_VISC In the presence of material instabilities, resulting for example from damage, the solution no longer depends continuously on time (or on the loading parameters) but exhibits jumps. Piloting is a technique for crossing these jumps, by allowing non-monotonic evolutions of the loading in order to recover continuity. But these techniques are not applicable when physical time intervenes, whether through a history of command variables (a thermal transient, for example) or in the constitutive behaviour of the material (viscosity). Viscous regularisation is another approach for recovering continuity. It consists in superimposing on the stresses arising from the constitutive law \sigma a stress of viscous origin {\sigma}_{\mathit{vis}} so as to penalise sufficiently the very rapid evolutions (whose limit is a jump of the solution): {\sigma}_{\mathit{tot}}=\sigma +{\sigma}_{\mathit{vis}};\frac{d{\sigma}_{\mathit{tot}}}{d\epsilon }=\frac{d\sigma }{d\epsilon }+\frac{d{\sigma}_{\mathit{vis}}}{d\epsilon } This is a numerical technique, with no a priori relation to a viscous reality of the material. One describes in the document R5.03.34 the viscoelastic constitutive law that governs the viscous stress {\sigma}_{\mathit{vis}} . 7 Bibliography 1. r5.03.02 Integration of the elastoplastic constitutive relations of Von Mises r5.03.02 Integration of the elastoplastic constitutive relations of Von Mises Summary: This document describes the quantities computed by the operator STAT_NON_LINE that are required for the implementation of the quasi-static non-linear algorithm described in R5.03.01 in the case of elastoplastic constitutive behaviours. These quantities are computed by the same subroutines in the operator DYNA_NON_LINE in the case of a dynamic loading R5.05.05. This description is presented according to the various keywords that allow the user to choose the desired constitutive relation. The constitutive relations treated here are: - the Von Mises constitutive behaviour with isotropic hardening (linear or non-linear) - the Von Mises constitutive behaviour with linear kinematic hardening (Prager model) The integration method used is based on a direct implicit formulation. Starting from the initial state, or from the previous computation time instant, one computes the stress field resulting from a strain increment. One also computes the tangent operator. 1 Introduction 1.1 Constitutive relations described in this document In the operator STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03 (or DYNA_NON_LINE U4.53.01), two types of constitutive behaviour can be treated: - incremental constitutive behaviour: factor keyword COMPORTEMENT, - non-linear elastic constitutive behaviour: factor keyword COMPORTEMENT. For each constitutive behaviour one may choose: - the constitutive relation: keyword RELATION, - the mode of computation of the strains: keyword DEFORMATION. For further details, consult the document U4.51.03 of the User's manual; the constitutive behaviours described here fall only under the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT. The relations treated in this document are: | VMIS_ISOT_LINE : | Von Mises with linear isotropic hardening, | | --- | --- | | VMIS_ISOT_TRAC : | Von Mises with isotropic hardening given by a tensile curve, | | VMIS_ISOT_PUIS : | Von Mises with isotropic hardening given by an analytical curve, | | VMIS_JOHN_COOK : | Von Mises with Johnson-Cook isotropic hardening, | | VMIS_CINE_LINE : | Von Mises with linear kinematic hardening. | 1.2 Purpose of the integration To solve the global non-linear problem posed on the structure, the document R5.03.01 describes the algorithm used in code_aster for non-linear statics and the document R5.05.05 describes the method used for non-linear dynamics. These two algorithms rely on the computation of local quantities (at each integration point of each finite element) that result from the integration of the constitutive relations. At each iteration n of Newton's method R5.03.01 one must compute the nodal forces R({{u}_{i}}^{n})={Q}^{T}{\sigma}_{i}^{n} (options RAPH_MECA and FULL_MECA), the stresses {\sigma}_{i}^{n} being computed at each integration point of each element from the displacements {u}_{i}^{n} by means of the constitutive relation. One must also build the tangent operator in order to compute {K}_{i}^{n} (option FULL_MECA). Before the first iteration, for the prediction phase, one computes {K}_{i-1} (option RIGI_MECA_TANG). The computation of {K}_{i-1} , which is required for the initialisation phase R5.03.01, corresponds to the computation of the tangent operator deduced from the rate problem. This operator is not identical to the one used to compute {K}_{i}^{n} by the option FULL_MECA, during the Newton iterations. Indeed, the latter operator is tangent to the problem discretised in an implicit manner. One describes here, for the constitutive relations VMIS_ISOT_LINE, VMIS_ISOT_TRAC, VMIS_ISOT_PUIS, VMIS_JOHN_COOK and VMIS_CINE_LINE, the computation of the tangent matrix of the prediction phase, {K}_{i-1} , then the computation of the stress field from a strain increment, the computation of the nodal forces R and of the tangent matrix {K}_{i}^{n} . 2 General notation and assumptions on the strains All quantities evaluated at the previous time instant are indexed by {}^{-} . r5.03.04 Elasto-visco-plastic constitutive relations of Chaboche r5.03.04 Elasto-visco-plastic constitutive relations of Chaboche Summary: This document describes the integration of the elasto-visco-plastic constitutive model of Chaboche with non-linear kinematic and isotropic hardening, with possible taking into account of viscosity. The implemented model has one or two kinematic variables, and takes into account all the variations of the coefficients with temperature, and has a hardening effect on the tensorial backstress variables. This version also makes it possible to model (in an optional manner) the viscous character of the material (Norton viscosity). It is integrated by the solution of a single non-linear scalar equation. This model is available in 3D, plane strain and axisymmetry. The plane-stress modelling uses a method of static condensation (de Borst). One also gives elements for identifying the coefficients of the constitutive relation. 1 Elasto-visco-plastic models of Chaboche available in Code_Aster For the analysis of structures subjected to cyclic loadings, the classical isotropic (linear or not) and linear kinematic hardenings R5.03.02 and R5.03.16 are no longer sufficient. In particular, one cannot correctly describe the stabilised cycles obtained experimentally on a tensile specimen subjected to an imposed alternating strain or to a tension–compression. If one seeks to describe precisely the effects of a cyclic loading, it is desirable to adopt more sophisticated modellings (but simple to use) such as the model of Saïd Taheri, for example, cf. R5.03.05, or else, if the number of cycles is limited, the model of Jean-Louis Chaboche which is presented here. In reality, the Chaboche model can be more or less sophisticated. The models developed in Code_Aster comprise either one kinematic variable (VMIS_CIN1_CHAB and VISC_CIN1_CHAB) or two (VISC_CIN2_CHAB and VMIS_CIN2_CHAB), and isotropic hardening. The choice of using two kinematic variables certainly complicates the model, but makes it possible to identify correctly the uniaxial tests over a wider range of strains [bib2], [bib7]. A certain number of identifications of the parameters of this model have been carried out mainly for the stainless steels A316 and A304 ([bib7], [bib8]). The models comprise 8 parameters (a single kinematic variable) or 10 (two kinematic variables), introduced in the command DEFI_MATERIAU: CIN1_CHAB (CIN1_CHAB_FO) = _F( ♦ R_0 = R_0, ◊ R_I = R_I, (inutile si B=0) ◊ B = b , (défaut: 0.) ♦ C_I = C_I, ◊ K = k , (défaut: 1.) ◊ W = w , (défaut: 0.) ♦ G_0 = G_0, ◊ A_I = A_I, (défaut: 0.) ) CIN2_CHAB (CIN2_CHAB_FO) = _F( ♦ R_0 = R_0, ◊ R_I = R_I, inutile si B=0 ou si effet de mémoire) ◊ B = b , (défaut: 0.) ♦ C1_I = C1_I, ♦ C2_I = C2_I, ◊ K = k , (défaut: 1.) ◊ W = w , (défaut: 0.) ♦ G1_0 = G1_0, ♦ G2_0 = G2_0, ◊ A_I = A_I , (défaut: 0.) ) The 8 or 10 parameters are real constants. All these parameters may depend on the temperature (keywords CIN1_CHAB_FO or CIN2_CHAB_FO) and the expected values are of function type. In the case where one wishes to introduce viscosity in addition (models VISC_CIN1_CHAB and VISC_CIN2_CHAB), one must also supply in the command DEFI_MATERIAU, under the keyword LEMAITRE (or LEMAITRE_FO) the parameters N and UN_SUR_K, which may depend on the temperature. LEMAITRE (LEMAITRE_FO) = _F( ♦ N = n, ♦ UN_SUR_K = 1/K The parameter UN_SUR_M of the keyword LEMAITRE (respectively LEMAITRE_FO) must obligatorily be set to zero (respectively to the identically zero function). It is also possible to take into account a memory effect of the largest plastic strain by means of the models ( VISC_CIN2_MEMO and VMIS_CIN2_MEMO). The keywords to be filled in are: MEMO_ECRO (MEMO_ECRO_FO) = _F( ♦ Q_M = Qm, ♦ Q_0 = Q0, ♦ MU = mu, ♦ ETA = eta, (défaut: 0.5) In the case of a non-proportional loading, it is necessary to enrich the model, by the data of two additional parameters: CIN2_NRAD = _F( ◊ DELTA1=:math: {\delta}_{1} (défaut= 1.E+0), ◊ DELTA2=:math: {\delta}_{2} (défaut= 1.E+0), avec :math: 0\le {\delta}_{1}\le 1 , :math: 0\le {\delta}_{2}\le 1 The constitutive laws are accessible in all the commands using the keyword COMPORTEMENT with the following relations: VISC_CIN1_CHAB, VISC_CIN2_CHAB, VISC_CIN2_MEMO, VISC_CIN2_NRAD, VISC_MEMO_NRAD,VMIS_CIN1_CHAB, VMIS_CIN2_CHAB, VMIS_CIN2_MEMO, VMIS_CIN2_NRAD, VMIS_MEMO_NRAD. Note : the model VISCOCHAB R5.03.14 also makes it possible to represent the effects described in this document. It furthermore comprises additional recovery and hardening terms. But its use in structural analyses is more costly in computation time (because one must solve, either by the Runge–Kutta method or by the Newton method, a system of 27 equations in 27 unknowns). Moreover, it poses robustness problems when the time step is large, because the Newton method may fail. This leads to numerous subdivisions of the time step. The models described in this document are optimised, insofar as they lead to solving a single scalar equation, and the solution method used is very robust (method of Brent or secant, cf. R5.03.14); it is therefore a model capable of integrating large time steps rapidly. In the remainder of this document, one describes the characteristics of the various models. One then presents the detail of their numerical integration in connection with the construction of the consistent tangent matrix. Finally, one also gives a few elements for the identification of the characteristics of the material. 2 Description of the models 2.1 Description of the models At every time instant, the state of the material is described by the strain \varepsilon , the temperature T , the plastic strain {\varepsilon}^{p} , the cumulative plastic strain p and the backstress tensor X . In the simplest case (a single kinematic variable, {\gamma}_{1}=\text{cste},{C}_{1}=\text{cste} ,R(p)={\sigma}_{y} ) the coefficients of the model {\gamma}_{1},{C}_{1} can be identified on a simple uniaxial tensile test, or else on a cyclic-hardening curve. Indeed in the uniaxial case, the model reduces in 1D to [bib2]: \begin{array}{c}{\text{dX}}_{1}={C}_{1}d{\varepsilon}^{p}-{\gamma}_{1}{X}_{1}\xi d{\varepsilon}^{p},\xi =\pm 1\\ \mid \sigma -{X}_{1}\mid ={\sigma}_{y}\end{array} which one can integrate (under monotonic loading) in the following manner: \begin{array}{c}{X}_{1}=\xi \frac{{C}_{1}}{{\gamma}_{1}}+({X}_{1}^{0}-\xi \frac{{C}_{1}}{{\gamma}_{1}})\exp(-\xi {\gamma}_{1}({\varepsilon}^{p}-{\varepsilon}_{0}^{p})),\xi =\pm 1\\ \sigma =\xi {\sigma}_{y}+{X}_{1}\end{array} the asymptote of the tensile curve of which makes it possible to obtain \frac{{C}_{1}}{{\gamma}_{1}} by: {\varepsilon}^{p}\to \infty {X}_{1}\to \xi \frac{{C}_{1}}{{\gamma}_{1}} hence \sigma \to \xi ({\sigma}_{y}+\frac{{C}_{1}}{{\gamma}_{1}}) and the slope at the origin of which supplies {C}_{1} (if {X}_{1}^{0}=0 ) : {\varepsilon}^{p}\to 0 {\dot{X}}_{1}\to {C}_{1}-{y}_{1}{X}_{1}^{0}\xi {X}_{1}^{0}={C}_{1}-{y}_{1}{X}_{1}\xi For a model with two kinematic variables, without isotropic hardening, a tensile curve still makes it possible to recover these relations: {\varepsilon}^{p}\to \infty \sigma \to \xi ({\sigma}_{y}+(\frac{{C}_{1}}{{\gamma}_{1}}+\frac{{C}_{2}}{{\gamma}_{2}})) and the slope at the origin is equal to {C}_{1}+{C}_{2} But apart from these simple cases a numerical identification is necessary in order to obtain the parameters. Solution of the equation f(p) = 0 It is a matter of solving a non-linear scalar equation by seeking the solution in a confidence interval. For this, one proposes to couple a secant method with a control of the search interval. Let the following equation to be solved: f(x)=0 , x\in \left[a,b\right] , f(a) 0 eq A2-1 The secant method consists in constructing a sequence of points {x}^{n} which converges towards the solution. It is defined by recurrence (linear approximation of the function by its chord): {x}^{n+1}={x}^{n-1}-f({x}^{n-1})\frac{{x}^{n}-{x}^{n-1}}{f({x}^{n})-f({x}^{n-1})} eq A2-2 Moreover, if {x}^{n+1} were to leave the interval, then one replaces it by the bound of the interval in question: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\text{si}{x}^{n+1} b\text{alors}{x}^{n+1}:=b\end{array} eq A2-3 On the other hand, if {x}^{n+1} is in the current interval, then one updates the interval: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\text{si}{x}^{n+1}\in \left[a,b\right]\text{et}f({x}^{n+1}) 0\text{alors}b={x}^{n+1}\end{array} eq A2-4 One considers that one has converged when f is sufficiently close to 0 (tolerance to be entered). As for the first two points of the sequence, one can choose the bounds of the interval, or else, if one has an estimate of the solution, one can adopt this estimate and one of the bounds of the interval. Note: This method works well if there is a single solution in the interval \left[a,b\right] . Without this being formally proved, one can note that f(0)>0 . One then seeks b such that f(b) 0 , one multiplies b by 10 and one tests whether f(b)>0 , and so on, until one finds a value b such that f(b)<0 . One is then sure that there is at least one solution on \left[a,b\right] .

r5.03.05 Viscoplastic constitutive relation of Taheri r5.03.05 Viscoplastic constitutive relation of Taheri Summary This document presents the implementation of the viscoplastic constitutive relation of Taheri, available for all the isoparametric elements (2D and 3D continuum) with the exception of plane stresses. After a presentation of the evolution equations of this law, the system obtained by implicit discretisation is described; it is shown in particular that it always admits a solution. This model is well suited to describing the response of austenitic steels under cyclic loadings, and in particular the phenomenon of progressive strain. On the other hand, because of its complexity (two yield surfaces, semi-discrete internal variable), it does not appear desirable to use it for different applications (a monotonic loading path, for example). 1 Description of the model The constitutive relation proposed by Taheri makes it possible to describe the response of austenitic steels under cyclic loadings: it is indeed well suited to representing the phenomenon of progressive strain. Before stating the equations proper, one may specify that this model differs from classical plasticity (von Mises criterion with kinematic and isotropic hardening) by two particularities, sources of difficulties in the numerical formulation. On the one hand, the evolution of the dissipative variables rests on two loading criteria instead of one: the first, classical, conditions the appearance of plastic strain, the second makes it possible to keep a record of the “maximum” hardening reached by the material in order to account for the ratchetting phenomenon. On the other hand, in order to represent progressive strain in a satisfactory manner, a semi-discrete internal variable has been introduced. Constant when the constitutive behaviour is dissipative, it evolves only in the elastic regime of the material. Original in appearance, this model nonetheless rests on physical bases, still set out in Taheri , . It is accessible, in an extended viscoplastic version (necessary in order to describe the constitutive behaviour at high temperatures), by the command STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword RELATION: VISC_TAHERI. 1.1 Plastic behaviour A detailed description of the constitutive law is given in Taheri et al. , . Briefly, the state of the material is described by its strain state, its temperature and four internal variables: | \varepsilon | total strain tensor | | --- | --- | | T | temperature | | p | cumulative plastic strain | | {\varepsilon}^{p} | plastic strain tensor | | {\sigma}^{p} | peak stress, memory of the maximum hardening | | {\varepsilon}_{n}^{p} | plastic strain tensor at the last unloading (semi-discrete variable). | The state equations which express the associated thermodynamic forces as a function of the state variables are written: \sigma =K\text{Tr}(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{\mathit{th}})\mathrm{Id}+2\mu (\tilde{\varepsilon}-{\varepsilon}^{p})\quad{\varepsilon}^{\mathit{th}}=\alpha (T-{T}^{\text{réf}})\text{Id} R=\text{D}\left[{R}^{0}+{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)}^{a}A{({\varepsilon}^{p}-{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p})}_{\text{eq}}^{a}\right]\quad\text{D}=1-m{e}^{-bp\left(1-\frac{{\sigma}^{p}}{S}\right)} \mathrm{X}=\text{C}\left[S{\varepsilon}^{p}-{\sigma}^{p}{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p}\right]\quad\text{C}={C}_{\infty}+{C}_{1}{e}^{-bp\left(1-\frac{{\sigma}^{p}}{S}\right)} | \tilde{a} | deviatoric part of a tensor a | | --- | --- | | R | isotropic hardening variable | | X | kinematic hardening variable | | K,\mu | bulk and shear moduli | | \alpha | thermal expansion coefficient | | {T}^{\text{réf}} | reference temperature | | S | ratchetting stress | | b,{R}^{0},A,a,m,{C}_{\infty},{C}_{1} | other hardening characteristics of the material | Note that the elastic moduli and the thermal expansion coefficient are entered by the user by the command DEFI_MATERIAU, keyword ELAS, while the hardening characteristics are set by the keyword TAHERI. These characteristics may depend on the temperature, by using the keywords ELAS_FO and TAHERI_FO. Let us also specify that an example of identification of the hardening characteristics on uniaxial situations is given in Geyer . The evolution of the internal variables is defined by two criteria. The first governs traditional plasticity with combined kinematic and isotropic hardenings: \text{F}={(\tilde{\sigma}-X)}_{\text{eq}}-R\le 0\text{ et }{\sigma}^{0}=\frac{\tilde{\sigma}-X}{{(\tilde{\sigma}-X)}_{\text{eq}}} | {(.)}_{\text{eq}} | equivalent norm: {a}_{\text{eq}}={\left(\frac{3}{2}\tilde{a}:\tilde{a}\right)}^{\frac{1}{2}} | | --- | --- | | \text{F} | plasticity criterion | | {s}^{0} | outward normal to the criterion \text{F} | This criterion is accompanied by the classical loading/unloading condition: \left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{si F} 0\end{array}\begin{array}{c}\text{}\dot{p}=0\\ \text{}\dot{p}\ge 0\text{ tel que }\dot{\text{F}}=0 \end{array}\begin{array}{c}\text{}(\text{élasticité})\\ (\text{plasticité})\end{array}\right. And the flow rule associated with the criterion \text{F} is: {\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}=\frac{3}{2}\dot{p}{\mathrm{s}}^{0} \text{ et donc }\dot{p}=\frac{2}{3}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{eq}}^{p} The second criterion governs the evolution of the peak stress. Geometrically, in the space of the stress deviators, it expresses the fact that the first yield surface (\text{F}=0) , represented by a sphere of centre X and of radius R , remains inside a sphere centred at the origin and of radius {\sigma}^{p} . It is written simply: \text{G}={X}_{\text{eq}}+R-{\sigma}^{p}\le 0 \text{G} maximum-hardening criterion According to the preceding geometric considerations, the evolution of the peak stress is: \left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{si }\text{G} 0\quad{\dot{\sigma}}^{p}\ge 0\text{ tel que }\dot{G}=0\end{array}\right. It must be noted that in the natural state of the material, the peak stress is not zero but is equal to the initial yield limit, namely: {\sigma}^{p}(\text{initial})=(1-m){R}^{0} Up to now, we have not mentioned the evolution of the semi-discrete internal variable {\varepsilon}_{n}^{p} . In fact, it evolves only in the elastic regime. More precisely, this variable takes into account the plastic strain state at the last unloading; in other words, at the beginning of each unloading, this variable should instantaneously take the value of the current plastic strain. However, in order to retain a continuous behaviour, one regularises the evolution of {\varepsilon}_{n}^{p} in the following manner: In the elastic regime: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{n}^{p}=\dot{\xi}({\varepsilon}_{n}^{p}-{\varepsilon}^{p})\left\{ \begin{array}{c}\text{si }{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p}={\varepsilon}^{p}\\ \text{si }{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p}\ge {\varepsilon}^{p}\end{array}\begin{array}{c}\quad\dot{\xi}=0\\ \quad\dot{\xi}\ge 0\text{ tel que }\dot{F}\text{=0}\end{array}\begin{array}{c}(\text{élasticité classique})\\ (\text{pseudo-décharge})\end{array}\right. In the plastic regime: \dot{{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p}}=0 The constitutive behaviour is thus completely determined. Before passing to the introduction of viscosity, the observation of the two yield surfaces calls for an important remark. One might think that the surface \text{G}=0 is effectively activated only in the plastic regime. In practice, this is not so. One may for example cite the case of a thermal loading: a cooling brings about (generally) an expansion of the yield surface \text{F}=0 , so that the peak stress is led to evolve in order to preserve \text{G}\le 0 , and this even in the elastic regime. 1.2 Taking viscosity into account In order to model the constitutive behaviour of stainless steels under cyclic loading when the temperature is of the order of 550°C , it is no longer possible to neglect the creep terms. In order to account for these viscosity effects while retaining the properties of the preceding model, a simple method consists in making the evolution of the plastic strain viscous. In other words, viscosity intervenes only in the plastic regime: no direct influence on the semi-discrete internal variable nor on the yield surface \text{G}=0 . To this end, following Lemaitre and Chaboche , one replaces the consistency condition by: \dot{p}=\left(\frac{\langle \text{F}\rangle }{K{p}^{1/M}}\right)^{N} | \langle \text{F}\rangle | positive part of F (Macauley brackets) | | --- | --- | | K,N,M | viscosity characteristics of the material | The viscosity characteristics of the material are entered in the command DEFI_MATERIAU, either by the keyword LEMAITRE if they do not depend on the temperature, or by the keyword LEMAITRE_FO in the opposite case. In the absence of one of these keywords, the constitutive behaviour is presumed plastic. All the other equations of the model are left unchanged. One will see that such an introduction of viscosity entails only minor modifications of the implicit integration algorithm of the constitutive law. 1.3 Description of the internal variables computed by Code_Aster The internal variables computed by Code_Aster are 9 in number. They are arranged in the following order: | 1 | p | cumulative plastic strain | | --- | --- | --- | | 2 | {\sigma}^{p} | peak stress | | 3 to 8 | {\varepsilon}_{n}^{p} | plastic strain tensor at the last unloading | | | | (arranged in the order xx , yy , zz , xy , xz , yz ) | | 9 | \chi | loading / unloading indicator (cf. r5.03.01-discretisation-conditions-coherence) | | | | 0 elastic unloading | | | | 1 classical plastic loading | | | | 2 two-surface plastic loading | | | | 3 pseudo-unloading | As for the viscoplastic strain tensor, it is not arranged among the internal variables but can be computed in post-processing by means of the command CALC_CHAMP, options ‘EPSP_ELGA’ or ‘EPSP_ELNO’, (cf. u4.61.02). 2 Numerical formulation of the constitutive relation In order to be able to treat plasticity and viscoplasticity in the same framework, one chooses to proceed to an implicit discretisation of the constitutive relations, (cf. r5.03.02). Let us note moreover that an explicit integration procedure is delicate for two reasons: on the one hand, the treatment of the semi-discrete variable is necessarily implicit and can lead to numerical oscillations (one pseudo-unloads, therefore one solves \text{F}=0 , and as a result, \text{F} may be (very small but) greater than zero, hence loading at the next step instead of continuing the unloading), and on the other hand, the equation is not differentiable when \varepsilon^{p} = \varepsilon_n^{\tilde{p}} 2.1 Implicit discretisation of the constitutive equations From now on, the following notation convention is adopted. Such a parametrisation at each time step makes it possible to dispense with the storage of \xi , provided of course that one keeps the values of {\varepsilon}_{n}^{p} . After this preliminary remark, one may turn to the consistency conditions. For the criterion \text{G} which governs the evolution of the peak stress, the discretised form of the consistency condition is: \text{G}(\Delta p ,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi )\le 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\ge 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\text{G}(\Delta p ,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi )=0 The consistency condition bearing on \text{F} is more delicate insofar as it governs the evolution of the plastic strain in the plastic loading regime and the evolution of \xi in the unloading regime. Once discretised, it is written: In the plastic loading regime (\xi =1) : \text{F}(\Delta p ,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =1)=0\quad \Delta p \ge 0\quad \Delta p \text{F}(\Delta p ,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =1)=0 In the unloading regime (\Delta p =0) : \text{F}(\Delta p=0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi )=0\quad 0\le \xi \le 1\quad \xi \text{F}(\Delta p=0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi )=0 In order to be able to select the constitutive-behaviour regime of the material, and therefore the equations to be solved, the first question is: Are we in a plastic situation or an elastic one? In fact, there exists a solution in the elastic regime (pseudo-unloading \xi >0 or classical elasticity \xi =0 ) if one can find a peak-stress increment such that: Incremental unloading condition with \xi =1 (scalar equation in \Delta {\sigma}^{p} ): \begin{array}{}\text{F}(\Delta p=0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =1)\le 0\\ \text{G}(\Delta p=0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =1)\le 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\ge 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\text{G}(\Delta p=0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =1)=0\end{array} In the case of plastic loading, that is to say when there does not exist a \Delta {\sigma}^{p} satisfying , one then has to solve the following non-linear system in \Delta p and \Delta {\sigma}^{p} : Plastic regime (non-linear system in \Delta p and \Delta {\sigma}^{p} ): \begin{array}{}\text{F}(\Delta p,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =0)=0\quad \Delta p\ge 0\\ \text{G}(\Delta p,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =0)\le 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\ge 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\text{G}(\Delta p,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =0)=0\end{array} On the other hand, in an elastic situation, two choices are still possible: pseudo-unloading (\xi >0) or classical elasticity (\xi =0) . The second case being more favourable, one begins by examining whether it is not feasible, that is to say whether there exists a peak-stress increment such that: Incremental condition of the classical elastic regime (scalar equation in \Delta {\sigma}^{p} ): \begin{array}{}\text{F}(\Delta p=0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =1)\le 0\\ \text{G}(\Delta p=0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =1)\le 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\ge 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\text{G}(\Delta p=0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi =1)=0\end{array} Finally, should it be a pseudo-elastic unloading, it remains to solve the following non-linear system in \xi and \Delta {\sigma}^{p} : Pseudo-elastic unloading (non-linear system in \xi and \Delta {\sigma}^{p} ): \begin{array}{}\text{F}(\Delta p =0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi )=0\quad 0\le \xi \le 1\\ \text{G}(\Delta p =0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi )\le 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\ge 0\quad \Delta {\sigma}^{p}\text{G}(\Delta p =0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi )=0\end{array} Let us note from the outset that the non-linear systems and can reduce to the solution of a simple scalar equation if \Delta {\sigma}^{p}=0 makes it possible to obtain a solution. One may summarise the algorithm for choosing the equations to be solved by the decision tree below. Decision tree for choosing the constitutive-behaviour regime 2.4 Bracketing of the solutions On reading the preceding paragraph, one will have noted the necessity of solving (numerically) a certain number of scalar equations or of non-linear systems. For this, it is always useful to have an interval on which to seek the solution. On the one hand, a bracketing of the solution demonstrates its existence (which greatly strengthens the chances of success of a solution algorithm!), and on the other hand, it allows an appropriate numerical treatment, hence a safer one. Concerning \Delta {\sigma}^{p} , a lower bound is of course 0. Moreover, the ratchetting stress S represents a limit beyond which the model no longer has any meaning. In fact, on examination of the material constants obtained by identification, cf. By examining the expression of \text{F} : \begin{array}{}\text{F}(\Delta p ,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi )\le {s}_{\text{eq}}-\text{D}{R}^{0}\\ \text{}\le {s}_{\text{eq}}^{e}-\frac{3}{2}(2\mu +\text{C}S)\Delta p -\text{D}{R}^{0}\\ \text{}\le {s}_{\max}^{e}-\frac{3}{2}(2\mu +{C}_{\infty}S)\Delta p -\text{D}({p}^{-}){R}^{0}\end{array} One deduces from it an upper bound for \Delta p , such that \text{F}(\Delta p ,\Delta {\sigma}^{p},\xi )\le 0 : \Delta p \le \frac{{s}_{\max}^{e}({\sigma}^{p})-\text{D}({p}^{-},{\sigma}^{p}){R}^{0}}{\frac{3}{2}(2\mu +{C}_{\infty}S)} {s}_{\max}^{e}({\sigma}^{p})=\max\left\{ \begin{array}{c}{\left[{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}-\text{C}({p}^{-},{\sigma}^{p})(S{\varepsilon}^{p-}-{\sigma}^{p}{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p})\right]}_{\text{eq}}\\ {\left[{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}-{C}_{\infty}(S{\varepsilon}^{p-}-{\sigma}^{p}{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p})\right]}_{\text{eq}}\end{array}\right. In particular, one can give a (crude) upper bound of \Delta p independent of \Delta {\sigma}^{p} : \Delta {p}_{\max}=\frac{{s}_{\max}^{e\max}-(1-m){R}^{0}}{\frac{3}{2}(2\mu +{C}_{\infty}S)} {s}_{\max}^{e\max}={\sigma}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{e}+({C}_{1}+{C}_{\infty})\max\left\{\begin{array}{}{\left[S{\varepsilon}^{p-}-{\sigma}^{p-}{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p}\right]}_{\mathrm{eq}}\\ {\left[S{\varepsilon}^{p-}-S{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p}\right]}_{\mathrm{eq}}\end{array}\right. One may then note that the systems and always admit a solution. Indeed, if for each system one writes respectively \Delta {\sigma}^{p}(\Delta p ) and \Delta {\sigma}^{p}(\xi ) the solutions of \text{G}=0 , then one has: - Non-linear system of plastic loading: \text{F}(\Delta p =0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p}(\Delta p =0),\xi =1)\ge 0\text{ et }\text{F}(\Delta {p}_{\max},\Delta {\sigma}^{p}(\Delta {p}_{\max}),\xi =1)\le 0 - Non-linear system of pseudo-unloading: \text{F}(\Delta p =0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p}(\xi =1),\xi =1)\le 0\text{ et }\text{F}(\Delta p =0,\Delta {\sigma}^{p}(\xi =0),\xi =0)\ge 0 3 Numerical solution methods The solution of the incremental equations confronts us either with a non-linear scalar equation, or with a non-linear system with two unknowns. The numerical methods employed are set out below. One also examines the computation of the tangent matrix, possibly used by the global algorithm of STAT_NON_LINE, (cf. r5.03.01). 3.1 Scalar equation: secant method The aim is to solve a non-linear scalar equation by seeking the solution in a confidence interval. For this, one proposes to couple a secant method with a control of the search interval. Let the following equation to be solved: \text{f}(x)=0\quad x\in \left[a,b\right]\quad \text{f}(a) 0 The secant method consists in constructing a sequence of points {x}^{n} which converges towards the solution. It is defined by recurrence (linear approximation of the function by its chord): {x}^{n+1}={x}^{n-1}-\text{f}({x}^{n-1})\frac{{x}^{n}-{x}^{n-1}}{\text{f}({x}^{n})-\text{f}({x}^{n-1})} Moreover, if {x}^{n+1} were to leave the interval, then one replaces it by the bound of the interval in question: \left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{si }{x}^{n+1} b\text{ alors }{x}^{n+1}:=b\end{array}\right. On the other hand, if {x}^{n+1} is in the current interval, then one updates the interval: \left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{si }{x}^{n+1}\in \left[a,b\right]\text{ et f}({x}^{n+1}) 0\text{ alors }b:={x}^{n+1}\end{array}\right. One considers that one has converged when \text{f} is sufficiently close to 0 (tolerance to be entered). As for the first two points of the sequence, one may choose the bounds of the interval, or else, if one has an estimate of the solution, one may adopt this estimate and one of the bounds of the interval. 3.2 Non-linear systems: Newton method and line search A Newton method is presented here, to which a line-search technique and a control of the descent direction have been associated so as not to leave the search domain (bounds on the unknowns). Let the following non-linear system: \left\{ \begin{array}{c}\text{F}(x,y)=0\\ \text{G}(x,y)=0\end{array}\right. \text{ avec }\left\{ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{\min}\le x\le {x}_{\max}\\ {y}_{\min}\le y\le {y}_{\max}\end{array}\right. If (x,y) is a point of the search domain, then one constructs a sequence of points ({x}^{n},{y}^{n}) which converges towards a solution (or at least, one hopes so) by the following process. - Determination of the descent direction A descent direction (\delta x ,\delta y ) is given by the solution of the 2 x 2 linear system: \left[\begin{array}{cc}{F}_{,x}^{n}& {F}_{,y}^{n}\\ {G}_{,x}^{n}& {G}_{,y}^{n}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}\delta x \\ \delta y \end{array}\right]=-\left[\begin{array}{c}{F}^{n}\\ {G}^{n}\end{array}\right] - Correction of the descent direction One corrects the descent direction (\delta x ,\delta y ) so that the points envisaged are in the search domain (with {\rho}_{\max} the maximum length that one allows oneself to travel along the descent direction): \left\{ \begin{array}{cccc}\text{si }x+{\rho}_{\max}\delta x {x}_{\max}& \delta x:=\frac{{x}_{\max}-x}{{\rho}_{\max}}\\ \text{si }y+{\rho}_{\max}\Delta y {y}_{\max}& \delta y:=\frac{{y}_{\max}-y}{{\rho}_{\max}}\end{array}\right. - Line search It only remains to minimise the quantity \text{E}=({\text{F}}^{2}+{\text{G}}^{2})/2 in the descent direction. Let us note that the norm \text{E} which one thus minimises is a measure of the error committed in the solution of the system: it is zero when (x,y) is a solution of the system . In order to minimise \text{E} , one will simply seek to cancel its derivative, that is to say to solve the scalar equation: \underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\left[E\left(x+\rho\,\delta x,\; y+\rho\,\delta y\right)\right]}_{\left(FF_{,x}+GG_{,x}\right)\delta x + \left(FF_{,y}+GG_{,y}\right)\delta y } = 0 \quad \text{et} \quad 0 \le \rho \le \rho_{\max} - Convergence criterion One considers that one has converged when the error \text{E} is less than a prescribed quantity (grandeur). Moreover, if the norm of the descent direction becomes too small (another quantity (grandeur) to be entered), one may think that the algorithm does not manage to converge. 3.3 Stopping criteria Up to now, the stopping values and the maximum numbers of iterations of the preceding solution methods have not been specified. Two cases must be distinguished. - When one seeks to verify the consistency conditions (scalar equation or non-linear system depending on the situation), one expects accurate results, whose relative tolerance \eta is set by the user in the command STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword RESI_INTE_RELA, (cf. u4.32.01). Depending on whether one seeks to solve \text{F}=0,\text{G}=0 or simultaneously \text{F}=\text{G}=0 , the stopping criterion is expressed respectively: \left|\frac{F}{R^0}\right| \le \eta \;\text{ou}\; \left|\frac{G}{R^0}\right| \le \eta \;\text{ou}\; \frac{1}{R^0}\sqrt{\frac{F^2+G^2}{2}} \le \eta {R}^{0} initial yield limit, supplied by the user, (cf. r5.03.01-comportement-plastique). Moreover, the user specifies a maximum number of iterations, still in the command STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword ITER_INTE_MAXI, (cf. u4.32.01). - When one carries out line-search iterations, one seeks to obtain a faster convergence (or at least a more reliable one). One must not however devote an excessive time to it. This is why one has fixed once and for all a maximum number of iterations equal to 3, a maximum bound {\rho}_{\max} equal to 2 and a relative stopping criterion of 1%: {\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho }\left[\text{E}(x+\rho \delta x,y+\rho \delta y)\right]\mid }_{\rho}\le {10}^{-2}{\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho }\left[\text{E}(x+\rho \delta x,y+\rho \delta y)\right]\mid }_{\rho =0} 3.4 Tangent matrix With a view to a solution of the (global) equilibrium equations by a Newton method, it is indispensable to determine the consistent matrix of the tangent constitutive behaviour, (cf. Simo et al. ). This matrix is classically composed of an elastic contribution and a plastic contribution: \frac{\delta \sigma }{\delta \varepsilon }=\frac{\delta {\sigma}^{e}}{\delta \varepsilon }-2\mu \frac{\delta \Delta {\varepsilon}^{p}}{\delta \varepsilon } One immediately deduces that in the elastic regime (classical or pseudo-unloading), the tangent matrix reduces to the elastic matrix: Elastic regime: \frac{\delta \sigma }{\delta \varepsilon }=\frac{\delta {\sigma}^{e}}{\delta \varepsilon } On the other hand, in the plastic regime, the variation of the plastic strain is no longer zero. The rules of composite differentiation make it possible to obtain: \frac{\delta \Delta {\varepsilon}^{p}}{\delta \tilde{{\sigma}^{e}}}=\frac{3}{2}\left[{s}^{0}\otimes \frac{\delta p }{\delta \tilde{{\sigma}^{e}}}+\Delta p \frac{\delta {s}^{0}}{\delta \tilde{{\sigma}^{e}}}\right]=\frac{3}{2}\left[{s}^{0}\otimes \frac{\delta p }{\delta {\sigma}^{e}}+\frac{\Delta p }{{s}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{e}}\left(\mathrm{Id}-\frac{3}{2}{s}^{0}\otimes {s}^{0}\right)\right] \otimes tensor product One may note that one has preferred to differentiate with respect to \tilde{\sigma}^{e} , knowing that one has: \frac{\delta \Delta {\varepsilon}^{p}}{\delta \varepsilon }=\frac{\delta \Delta {\varepsilon}^{p}}{\delta {\sigma}^{e}}.\frac{\delta {\sigma}^{e}}{\delta \varepsilon }=2\mu \frac{\delta \Delta {\varepsilon}^{p}}{\delta \tilde{{\sigma}^{e}}}.P\text{ avec }P:\left\{ \begin{array}{}S\to S\\ \varepsilon \to \tilde{\varepsilon}\end{array}\right. S space of symmetric tensors P projector onto the deviators Finally, it only remains to compute the variation of p . For this, one must distinguish whether it is a classical plasticity regime (\Delta {\sigma}^{p}=0) or a two-surface plasticity. Thus: Classical plasticity: \text{F}(p,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e})=0 {\text{F}}_{,p}(p,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e})\delta p =-{\text{F}}_{,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}}(p,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e})\delta {\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}\text{}\Rightarrow \text{}\frac{\delta p }{\delta {\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}}=-\frac{{\text{F}}_{,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}}(p,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e})}{{\text{F}}_{,p}(p,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e})} Two-surface plasticity: \text{F}(p,{\sigma}^{p},{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e})=0\text{ et }\text{G}(p,{\sigma}^{p},{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e})=0 \left[\begin{array}{cc}{\text{F}}_{,p}& {\text{F}}_{,{\sigma}^{p}}\\ {\text{G}}_{,p}& {\text{G}}_{,{\sigma}^{p}}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}\delta p \\ \delta {\sigma}^{p}\end{array}\right]=-\left[\begin{array}{c}{\text{F}}_{,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}}\\ {\text{G}}_{,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}}\end{array}\right].\delta {\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}\text{}\Rightarrow \text{}\frac{\delta p }{\delta {\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}}=\frac{\left|\begin{array}{cc}{\text{F}}_{,{\sigma}^{p}}& {\text{F}}_{,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}}\\ {\text{G}}_{,{\sigma}^{p}}& {\text{G}}_{,{\tilde{\sigma}}^{e}}\end{array}\right|}{\left|\begin{array}{cc}{\text{F}}_{,p}& {\text{F}}_{,{\sigma}^{p}}\\ {\text{G}}_{,p}& {\text{G}}_{,{\sigma}^{p}}\end{array}\right|} A careful examination of the expressions and makes it possible to observe that the variations of \text{F} and \text{G} with respect to \tilde{{\sigma}^{e}} are not necessarily collinear with {s}^{0} . Taking into account, one then deduces that the tangent matrix is in general not symmetric in the plastic regime. Rather than imposing the use of a non-symmetric solver, much more costly in computation time, one prefers to symmetrise this matrix. 3.5 Plane stresses The treatment of plane stresses adds a non-linear equation to be solved, coupled to the systems and , (cf. r5.03.02). Faced with this non-negligible difficulty and the absence of any expressed need, one has preferred not to offer the possibility of forcing a state of plane stresses at the level of the constitutive law. r5.03.07 Rousselier model for ductile fracture r5.03.07 Rousselier model for ductile fracture Summary The Rousselier model describes the damage due to the plastic growth of cavities in a metal. It makes it possible to model cracking and ductile fracture. The constitutive relation is elastoplastic or viscoplastic with isotropic hardening. It allows plastic volume changes and is written in small strains. The writing in large strains with a modified Simo and Miehe formulation, in the elastoplastic case only, is described in R5.03.06. This model is available in the command STAT_NON_LINE through the keyword RELATION='ROUSS_PR' or 'ROUSS_VISC' under the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT and with the keyword DEFORMATION='PETIT_REAC'. This model is implemented for the three-dimensional (3D), axisymmetric (AXIS), plane-stress and plane-strain modellings (C_PLAN, D_PLAN). The writing and the numerical treatment of this model are presented. 1 Introduction The mechanisms at the origin of the ductile fracture of metals are associated with the development of cavities within the material. One generally distinguishes three phases: - nucleation: this is the initiation or nucleation of the cavities, at sites which correspond preferentially to the second-phase particles present in the material, - growth: this is the phase which corresponds to the development proper of the cavities, driven essentially by the plastic flow of the metallic matrix which surrounds these cavities, - coalescence: this is the phase which corresponds to the localisation of the strain between the cavities in order to create macroscopic cracks. The Rousselier model [bib1], [bib2], [bib3] presented here is based on microstructural hypotheses which introduce a microstructure consisting of cavities and of a matrix whose elastic strains are negligible compared with the plastic strains. In this case, and in the absence of nucleation of new cavities, the porosity f , defined as the ratio between the cavity volume {V}^{c} and the total volume V of the representative elementary volume, is directly related to the macroscopic plastic strain by: \frac{{\rho}_{0}}{\rho}=\frac{1-{f}_{0}}{1-f} avec f=\frac{{V}^{c}}{V}\mathrm{\iff }\dot{f}=(1-f)\mathrm{tr}{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p} eq 1-1 where {f}_{0} denotes the initial porosity, {\rho}_{o} and \rho are respectively the density in the initial and current configurations (one takes in what follows {\rho}_{o}=1 ) and {\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p} the plastic strain rate of the total volume V . The construction of the model rests on a thermodynamic and phenomenological analysis which leads to writing the plastic potential F in the following form: F(\tau ,p,f)={\tau}_{\text{eq}}+{\sigma}_{1}{D}_{1}f\exp(\frac{{\tau}_{m}}{{\sigma}_{1}})-R(p) eq 1-2 where \tau =\sigma /\rho is the Kirchhoff stress, \sigma is the Cauchy stress, R the isotropic hardening as a function of the cumulative plastic strain p , {\sigma}_{1} and {D}_{1} material parameters. The presence in the plastic potential of the hydrostatic stress {\tau}_{m} authorises the plastic volume changes. In the case of nucleation of new cavities, one considers that the volume fraction created is proportional to the cumulative plastic strain. It is therefore sufficient to replace f by f+{A}_{n}p in the equations of the model. {A}_{n} is a material parameter. Equation [eq 1-1] is not modified. In the viscoplastic case, one writes the viscoplastic potential {F}^{\text{vp}} as a function of the plastic potential F : {F}^{\text{vp}}=\Lambda (F,p,f) eq 1-3 One will consider only the particular case such that: \dot{p}=\frac{\partial \Lambda }{\partial F}={\dot{\varepsilon}}_{0}{\left[\text{sh}(\frac{F}{{\sigma}_{0}})\right]}^{m} eq 1-4 which reduces to a power function (Norton-type law) when the two material parameters {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{0} and {\sigma}_{0} are very large. In what follows, one presents the constitutive relations of the Rousselier model and its numerical integration. 2 Notation One will denote by: | \mathrm{Id} | second-order identity tensor | | --- | --- | | \mathrm{II} | fourth-order identity tensor | | \text{tr}A | trace of the second-order tensor \mathrm{A} | | \tilde{A} | deviatoric part of the tensor \mathrm{A} defined by \tilde{A}=A-(\frac{1}{3}\text{tr}A)\text{Id} | | {A}_{m} | hydrostatic part of the tensor \mathrm{A} defined by {A}_{m}=\frac{\text{tr}\mathrm{A}}{3} | | {A}_{\text{eq}} | von Mises equivalent value defined by {A}_{\text{eq}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}\tilde{A}:\tilde{A}} | | : | doubly contracted product: \mathrm{A}:\mathrm{B}=\sum_{i,j}{A}_{ij}{B}_{ij}=\text{tr}({\text{AB}}^{\mathrm{T}}) | | \otimes | tensor product: (\mathrm{A}\otimes \mathrm{B}{)}_{ijkl}={A}_{ij}{B}_{kl} | | \lambda ,\mu ,E,\nu ,K | coefficients of isotropic elasticity | | \dot{p} | equivalent plastic strain rate \dot{p}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{\tilde{\dot{\varepsilon}}}^{p}:{\tilde{\dot{\varepsilon}}}^{p}} | Furthermore, within the framework of a time discretisation, all the quantities Q evaluated at the previous time instant are indexed by {-}^{} , the quantities evaluated at the time instant t={t}^{-}+\Deltat are not indexed and the increments are denoted by \Delta . One thus has: Q={Q}^{-}+\Deltaq The numerical solution is carried out by a \theta -method, with 0\le \theta \le 1 . For all the quantities, one defines: {Q}^{\theta}={Q}^{-}+\theta \Deltaq 3 Rousselier model We now describe the derivation of the equations of the Rousselier model presented in the introduction. 3.1 Derivation of the equations of the model One assumes that the specific free energy decomposes into three parts: a hyperelastic part which depends only on the elastic strain, a part linked to the hardening mechanism and a part linked to the damage: \Phi ({\varepsilon}^{e},p,f)={\Phi}^{e}({\varepsilon}^{e})+{\Phi}^{p}(p)+{\Phi}^{f}(f) eq 3.1-1 The Clausius–Duhem inequality is written (one does not consider the thermal part): \tau :\dot{\varepsilon}-\dot{\Phi}\ge 0 eq 3.1-2 an expression in which \dot{\varepsilon}={\dot{\varepsilon}}^{e}+{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p} represents the strain rate. The dissipation is also written: (\tau -\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}}):{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{e}+\tau :{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}-\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial p}\dot{p}-\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial f}\dot{f}\ge 0 eq 3.1-3 The second principle of thermodynamics then requires the following expression for the elastic stress–strain relation: \tau =\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}} eq 3.1-4 One defines the thermodynamic forces associated with the elastic strain, with the cumulative plastic strain and with the porosity in accordance with the framework of generalised standard materials: \tau ({\varepsilon}^{e})=\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}} eq 3.1-5 A(p)=\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial p} eq 3.1-6 B(f)=\frac{\partial \Phi }{\partial f} eq 3.1-7 There then remains for the dissipation: \tau :{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}-A\dot{p}-B\dot{f}\ge 0 eq 3.1-8 The principle of maximum dissipation applied from the viscoplastic potential {F}^{\text{vp}}(\tau \text{,A,B}) makes it possible to deduce from it the evolution laws of the plastic strain, of the cumulative plastic strain and of the porosity, namely: {\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}=\frac{\partial {F}^{\text{vp}}}{\partial \tau } eq 3.1-9 \dot{p}=-\frac{\partial {F}^{\text{vp}}}{\partial A} eq 3.1-10 \dot{f}=-\frac{\partial {F}^{\text{vp}}}{\partial B} eq 3.1-11 One assumes that {F}^{\text{vp}}(\tau ,A,B) is a function of the plastic potential F(\tau ,A,B) and that the latter decomposes into two terms depending respectively on the second invariant of \tau coupled to A and on the first invariant of \tau coupled to B : {F}^{\text{vp}}=\Lambda (F)=\Lambda ({F}_{\text{vM}}({\tau}_{\text{eq}},A)+{F}_{m}({\tau}_{m},B)) eq 3.1-12 By hypothesis, the first term decomposes additively like the von Mises potential: {F}_{\text{vM}}({\tau}_{\text{eq}},A)={\tau}_{\text{eq}}-A(p)-{R}_{0}={\tau}_{\text{eq}}-R(p) eq 3.1-13 In order not to obtain a trivial result, the decomposition of the second term must be multiplicative: {F}_{m}({\tau}_{m},B)=g({\tau}_{m})h(B) eq 3.1-14 Taking account of equation [eq 1-1], the evolution laws for \text{tr}{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p} and \dot{f} lead to the equality: \frac{g'({\tau}_{m})}{g({\tau}_{m})}=(\frac{-1}{1-f})\frac{{h}^{'}(B(f))}{h(B(f))} eq 3.1-15 The two sides of this equation are functions of the two independent variables {\tau}_{m} and f , so they are equal to a constant of dimension the inverse of a stress; this is the material parameter 1/{\sigma}_{1} . The dimensionless parameter {D}_{1} appears in the integration of g'/g : g({\tau}_{m})={D}_{1}{\sigma}_{1}\exp(\frac{{\tau}_{m}}{{\sigma}_{1}}) eq 3.1-16 The function B(f) and the inverse function f={h}_{1}(B) are unknown. r5.03.08 Integration of the viscoelastoplastic constitutive relations in the non-linear mechanics operators r5.03.08 Integration of the viscoelastoplastic constitutive relations in the non-linear mechanics operators Summary This document describes, for non-linear viscoelastic constitutive behaviours and viscoelastoplastic constitutive behaviours with a threshold, built on the basis of Lemaître's non-linear viscoelastic model, the ingredients required for the implementation of the non-linear mechanics algorithm, as in STAT_NON_LINE described in R5.03.01. The input data of all these non-linear viscoelastic constitutive relations integrated in Code_Aster generally have the same form. Only the way of introducing the main datum (the viscous strain-rate function) varies: it is presented according to the various keywords which allow the user to choose the desired constitutive relation. These quantities are computed by a semi-implicit or implicit integration method. From the initial state, or from the previous analysis time instant, the stress field resulting from a strain increment is computed. 1 Introduction The implementation of Lemaître's non-linear viscoelasticity model (keyword LEMAITRE) is described here; for certain particular values of the parameters it can reduce to a Norton viscoelastoplastic constitutive relation. A variant (depending on the fluence) of this Lemaître model has been added, with a view to the modelling of fuel assemblies (keyword LEMAITRE_IRRA). This model has the particular feature of including an additional anelastic strain: the growth strain. A viscoelastoplastic model with a threshold has been added. It is a material whose behaviour is purely elastic up to a threshold and then, once this threshold has been exceeded, the constitutive relation becomes a particular case of the Lemaître relation (LEMA_SEUIL). Finally, a viscoelastoplastic model with creep in the logarithm of the fluence has been implemented; it is accessed through the keyword VISC_IRRA_LOG. For each of these models, the material is assumed to be isotropic (except for the growth strain, which is uniaxial). They can be used in 3D, in plane strain (D_PLAN) and in axisymmetric conditions (AXIS). The constitutive equations of the models and their implementation in Code_Aster are presented in this note. 2 Continuous relation The small-perturbation assumption is adopted and the strain tensor is split into an elastic part, a thermal part, a known anelastic part and a viscous part. r5.03.11 Single-crystal and polycrystalline elastoviscoplastic behaviours r5.03.11 Single-crystal and polycrystalline elastoviscoplastic behaviours Summary: The aim of this document is to describe the integration of single-crystal and polycrystalline behaviours. This integration may be carried out explicitly (Runge–Kutta method with accuracy control and local subdivision of the time step) or implicitly (Newton method with local subdivision of the time step). These behaviours may be used for the analysis of microstructures (mesh of an aggregate, with a geometric representation of each physical single-crystal grain) or for an analysis of POLYCRISTAL type, a “homogenised” medium which, at every material point (integration point), contains several phases at once, in variable proportions. We also describe the types of analyses possible with these behaviours as well as the mesh generation procedure. 1 Introduction The general objective of the development of “micro-macro” functionalities in Code_Aster is to be able to modularly integrate models at several scales (with the possibility of choosing constitutive laws, localisation rules, types of microstructures). Which can lead to different types of analysis (polycrystalline analyses, use of a Berveiller-Zaoui type law or a “rule in  eta ” type law, analyses of multi-crystal aggregates with mesh of a microstructure, etc.). The approach presented here consists of allowing the decoupling, by modularity, of the different elements which constitute a constitutive law. This flexibility is accessible directly to the user. Furthermore, for the developer, it is possible to easily add a crystalline constitutive law by simply defining the partial derivatives of the problem, in terms of internal variables. This is sufficient if we are content with explicit integration; for implicit integration, the tangent operator must also be defined. More precisely, for the MONOCRISTAL behaviour aspect, at each integration point of a given finite element, the behaviour is that of a single crystal having a given orientation, and a certain number of slip systems. Each family of slip systems has its own local constitutive law. In the case of a polycrystalline model, it is assumed that at a material point (integration point of a finite element), several metallurgical phases are present simultaneously, each phase being able to consist of grains with given orientations, each grain having a certain number of slip systems (not necessarily the same for each phase). The representation of the material is based on a simplified self-consistent approach 5 or possibly extended for non-radial or cyclic loadings 4. Each family of slip systems has its own local constitutive law. We thus find separately the crystallographic structure, the law of crystal viscoplasticity and the scale transition rules. This mode of separation is also extended to the law of viscoplasticity itself, with a separation between elasticity, the criterion and the flow rule. 2 Formulation of single-crystal and polycrystalline behaviours 2.1 Principle of the constitutive laws of the single crystal The behaviours relating to the slip systems of a single crystal are (in all the behaviours considered) of the elasto-visco-plastic type. They can be constructed on phenomenological bases or on physical bases (dislocation dynamics). For each of the slip directions, the behaviour is one-dimensional . It can be broken down into three types of equations: - Flow relation: \dot{{\gamma}_{s}} represents the plastic slip of the system s \dot{{\gamma}_{s}}=g({	au}_{s},{\alpha}_{s},{\gamma}_{s},{p}_{s}) , with \dot{{p}_{s}}=∣\dot{{\gamma}_{s}}∣ and: - elastoplastic case, a criterion of the type: F({	au}_{s},{\alpha}_{s},{\gamma}_{s},{p}_{s})\le 0 and F\cdot \dot{{p}_{s}}=0 - elasto-viscoplastic case, \dot{{p}_{s}}=f({	au}_{s},{\alpha}_{s},{\gamma}_{s},{p}_{s}) - \dot{{\alpha}_{s}} represents the kinematic hardening in the case of a phenomenological law and the dislocation density for a physically based behaviour. Its evolution is the form: \dot{{\alpha}_{s}}=h({	au}_{s},{\alpha}_{s},{\gamma}_{s},{p}_{s}) - for phenomenological laws, isotropic hardening is defined by a function: R({p}_{s}) . These relationships become, after discretisation in time: - Flow rule: \Delta {\gamma}_{s}=g({	au}_{s},{\alpha}_{s},{\gamma}_{s},{p}_{s}) , with, \Delta {p}_{s}=∣\Delta {\gamma}_{s}∣ for elastoplastic behaviour a criterion of the type: F({	au}_{s},{\alpha}_{s},{\gamma}_{s},{p}_{s})\le 0 and F\cdot \Delta {p}_{s}=0 and for elasto-viscoplastic behaviour, \Delta {p}_{s}=f({	au}_{s},{\alpha}_{s},{\gamma}_{s},{p}_{s})\Delta t - Evolution of \dot{{\alpha}_{s}} : \Delta {\alpha}_{s}=h({	au}_{s},{\alpha}_{s},{\gamma}_{s},{p}_{s}) - Evolution of isotropic hardening: R({p}_{s}) The quantities ({	au}_{s},{\alpha}_{s},{\gamma}_{s},{p}_{s}) are evaluated at the current time for an implicit discretisation and at the previous time for an explicit discretisation. - the last internal variable is a plasticity indicator (threshold exceeded in at least one slip system at the current time step). 5 Numerical implementation in Code_Aster Generally speaking, single-crystal behaviours are integrated into Runge-Kutta methods for explicit integration, and into the “plasti” environment for implicit integration R5.03.14. The orientation tensors of the slip systems are all defined in the LCMMSG routine providing the global reference tensor for the nth system of the family provided whose name is provided by the calling routine. To add a new single-crystal behaviour, or simply a new flow or hardening law, the parameters must be defined in DEFI_MATERIAU. Depending on the case (flow, isotropic or kinematic hardening), the reading of these parameters must be added in the routines LCMAFL, LCMAEI and LCMAEC. For the integration, it is enough to write the increments of the internal variables in the routines LCMMFE (flow), LCMMFC (kinematic hardening) and LCMMFI (isotropic hardening), for the explicit integration to work. Implicit integration also uses the routines LCMMFE, LCMMFC and LCMMFI. It also requires the derivatives of the equations with respect to the different variables. The derivatives are written in the routines LCMMJF (derivative of the flow equation), LCMMJI (derivative of the isotropic-hardening relation) and LCMMJC (derivative of the kinematic-hardening relation). For more details on the architecture of the solution of the crystal behaviours, see D5.04.02. 6 Use These models are accessible in Code_Aster in 3D , plane strains ( D_PLAN ), plane stresses ( C_PLAN , by the De Borst method R5.03.03) and axisymmetry ( AXIS ). 6.1 Case of single crystal In the case of meshed microstructures, the different grains of a single crystal being represented by mesh-cell groups, it is necessary to assign the material parameters and the behaviours of the single crystals as well as their orientations to the different grains. The values of the parameters of the behavioural relations are provided using the DEFI_MATERIAU command. This is defined from the keywords MONO_VISC1, MONO_VISC2, MONO_DD_KR, MONO_DD_CFC for the flow, MONO_ISOT1, MONO_ISOT2, MONO_DD_CFC for isotropic hardening and MONO_CINE1, MONO_CINE2 for kinematic hardening U4.43.01. For example V6.04.172: MATER1=DEFI_MATERIAU( / ELAS =_F( E=..., NU=..., / ELAS_ORTH=_F( E_L=192500, E_T=128900, NU_LT=0.23, G_LT=74520,), # RELATIONS D’ECOULEMENT / MONO_VISC1=_F(N=10, K=40,C=6333), / MONO_VISC2=_F(N=10, K=40,C=6333,D=37,A=121), / MONO_DD_KR=_F(...), # ECROUISSAGE ISOTROPE / MONO_ISOT1=_F(R_0=75.5,Q=9.77,B=19.34,H=2.54), / MONO_ISOT2=_F(R_0=75.5,Q1=9.77,B1=19.34,H=2.54,Q2=-33.27, B2=5.345,), # ECROUISSAGE CINEMATIQUE / MONO_CINE1=_F(D=36.68), / MONO_CINE2=_F(D=36.68, GM=, PM=,), ); On peut ainsi dissocier, au niveau des données, l’écoulement de l’écrouissage isotrope et de l’écrouissage cinématique. Il faut maintenant définir le (ou les) type de monocristal étudié. Pour cela, on définit le comportement de façon externe à STAT_NON_LINE, par l’intermédiaire de l’opérateur DEFI_COMPOR, par exemple: MONO1=DEFI_COMPOR(MONOCRISTAL =(_F( MATER=MATER1, ECOULEMENT=MONO_VISC1, MONO_ISOT=MONO_ISOT1, MONO_CINE=MONO_CINE1, FAMI_SYST_GLIS=('CUBIQUE1',), _F( MATER=MATER1, ECOULEMENT=MONO_VISC1, MONO_ISOT=MONO_ISOT2, MONO_CINE=MONO_CINE2, FAMI_SYST_GLIS='CUBIQUE2',), ), _F( MATER=MATER2, ECOULEMENT=MONO_VISC1, MONO_ISOT=MONO_ISOT2, MONO_CINE=MONO_CINE2, FAMI_SYST_GLIS='PRISMATIQUE',), _F( MATER=MATER2, ECOULEMENT=MONO_VISC1, MONO_ISOT=MONO_ISOT2, MONO_CINE=MONO_CINE2, FAMI_SYST_GLIS='BCC24',), ), ) The DEFI_COMPOR operator calculates the total number of internal variables associated with the single crystal. Finally, to carry out a microstructure analysis, it is necessary to give, grain by grain, or by mesh-cell group (representing sets of grains) an orientation, using the keyword MASSIF of AFFE_CARA_ELEM. For example: ORIELEM = AFFE_CARA_ELEM ( MODELE = MO_MECA,MASSIF =( _F ( GROUP_MA='GRAIN1', ANGL_REP=(348.0,24.0,172.0),), _F ( GROUP_MA='GRAIN2', ANGL_REP=( 327.0, 126.0, 335.0),), _F ( GROUP_MA='GRAIN3', ANGL_REP=( 235.0, 7.0, 184.0),), _F ( GROUP_MA='GRAIN4', ANGL_REP=( 72.0, 338.0, 73.0), , …) Note 1: The orientations of the slip systems can be entered in nautical angles under the keyword ANGL_REP or in Euler angles under the keyword ANGL_EULER. Note 2: | For the same single crystal, the parameter values can be different from one family of slip systems to another. This is why we can define a different material by occurrence of the factor keyword MONOCRISTAL . But in this case, how can we provide transmit to STAT_NON_LINE the information stipulating that in a Gauss point (all those of the mesh-cell group concerned), we have several materials present? This is possible thanks to an evolution of AFFE_MATERIAU U4.43.03 and the material data structure D4.06.18):MAT=AFFE_MATERIAU(MAILLAGE=MAIL, AFFE =_F(GROUP_MA=’GRAIN1’, MATER=(MATER1,MATER2),), ); | | --- | The other data of the analysis is identical to a usual structural analysis. Finally, in STAT_NON_LINE, the behaviour from DEFI_COMPOR is provided, under the keyword COMPORTEMENT via the keyword COMPOR, obligatory with the keyword RELATION=’MONOCRISTAL’. COMPORTEMENT = _F( RELATION =’MONOCRISTAL’, COMPOR = COMP1 Clarifications that for explicit integration, (ALGO_INTE=’RUNGE_KUTTA’), it is useless to request the updating of the tangent matrix since it is not calculated. To begin Newton iterations of the overall algorithm, it may be useful to specify PREDICTION=’EXTRAPOLE’ U4.51.03. Examples of use can be found in the tests: SSNV171, SSNV172, SSNV194. 6.2 Case of polycrystal In the case of multiphase polycrystals, each phase corresponds to a single crystal. We will therefore use the parameters defined previously in DEFI_MATERIAU for the single crystal. Here, it is a question of defining, for each phase, the orientation, the volume fraction, the single crystal used, and the type of localisation law. This is carried out under the POLYCRISTAL factor keyword of DEFI_COMPOR. MONO1=DEFI_COMPOR(MONOCRISTAL=_F(MATER=MATPOLY, ECOULEMENT='MONO_VISC2', MONO_ISOT='MONO_ISOT2', MONO_CINE='MONO_CINE1', ELAS='ELAS', FAMI_SYST_GLIS='OCTAEDRIQUE',),); POLY1=DEFI_COMPOR(POLYCRISTAL=(_F(MONOCRISTAL=MONO1, FRAC_VOL=0.025, ANGL_REP=(-149.676,15.61819,154.676,),), _F(MONOCRISTAL=MONO1, FRAC_VOL=0.025, ANGL_REP=(-150.646,33.864,55.646,),), _F(MONOCRISTAL=MONO1, FRAC_VOL=0.025, ANGL_REP=(-137.138,41.5917,142.138,),), …… _F(MONOCRISTAL=MONO1, FRAC_VOL=0.025, ANGL_REP=(-481.729,35.46958,188.729,),),), LOCALISATION='BETA', MU_LOCA=80000,, DL=321.5, DA=0.216,); The keyword POLYCRISTAL makes it possible to define each phase by the data of an orientation, (provided by ANGL_REP or ANGL_EULER), of a volume fraction, of a mono-crystal (that is to say a model of behaviour and slip systems). The keyword LOCALISATION allows you to choose the localisation method for all the phases of the polycrystal. The keyword MASSIF allows you to choose a global orientation of the polycrystal under the keyword ANGL_REP if it is in nautical angles or under the keyword ANGL_EULER if it is in Euler angles. Finally, in STAT_NON_LINE, the behaviour from DEFI_COMPOR is provided, under the keyword COMPORTEMENT via the keyword COMPOR, obligatory with the keyword RELATION=’POLYCRISTAL’. COMPORTEMENT = _F( RELATION =’POLYCRISTAL’, COMPOR = COMP1 ) 6.3 Example As an example of implementation, we briefly present here an aggregate analysis, of cubic form (elementary volume) comprising 100 single-crystal grains, each defined by a mesh-cell group. The total number of elements is 86751. With mesh cells of order 1 (TETRA4) it has 15940 nodes. With mesh cells of order 2 (TETRA10), it has 121534. The loading consists of a homogeneous strain, applied via a normal displacement imposed on one face of the cube (direction z ). We achieve a strain of 4% in 1s and 50 increments.
