r5.03.12 Viscoplastic behaviour with memory effect and Chaboche recovery r5.03.12 Viscoplastic behaviour with memory effect and Chaboche recovery Summary: This document describes the integration of the elasto-visco-plastic constitutive model of Chaboche with an isotropic hardening comprising a hardening-memory effect and two non-linear kinematic hardenings, with possible taking into account of recovery and of viscosity. This model can be used by the relation VISCOCHAB of the keyword COMPORTEMENT. The model implemented has a hardening effect on the tensorial backstress variables and takes into account all the variations of the coefficients with temperature 1 . This constitutive law is integrated by the solution of a system of non-linear equations. This model is available in 3D, plane strain and axisymmetry. The modelling in plane stress is taken into account. except for the computation of the Jacobian 1 Elasto-visco-plastic model of Chaboche with memory effect and recovery The most complete elastoviscoplastic model of J.L.Chaboche superposes on the isotropic hardening two kinematic-hardening variables, and makes it possible to take into account the effects of cyclic hardening, creep, recovery and the memory of the greatest hardening. It is therefore well suited to cyclic loadings. Under certain loading conditions, structures can be subject to a phenomenon of progressive deformation, which may impair the functional capacities of the apparatus. In its original form, the model greatly overestimates the progressive deformation; in order to improve its representativeness, it has been modified by introducing radial-evanescence terms, so as to model this phenomenon better. The resulting model, named VISCOCHAB, is described in this document. Several studies have consisted in testing this constitutive law with respect to its capacity to model progressive deformations , , by comparing with tests , , , and with other models , in particular that of Taheri r5.03.05. In particular, identifications of the steels 316L and 304L have been made (respectively in and ). Recently, the thermal-fatigue studies have required the use of VISCOCHAB, in particular in order to take the memory effect into account. The model comprises 25 parameters (+ the 2 elastic parameters) introduced in the command DEFI_MATERIAU: VISCOCHAB (VISCOCHAB_FO) = _F( # écrouissage isotrope ♦ K = :math: k , ◊ B = :math: b , ◊ A_R = :math: {\alpha}_{R} , (défaut : 1.) # écrouissage cinématique ♦ C1 = :math: {C}_{1} , ♦ C2 = :math: {C}_{2} , ♦ G1_0 = :math: {\gamma}_{1}^{0} , ♦ G2_0 = :math: {\gamma}_{2}^{0} , ◊ A_I = :math: {a}_{\infty} , (défaut : 1.) # viscosité ♦ K_0 = :math: {K}_{0} , ♦ N = :math: n , # écoulement exponentiel ◊ A_K = :math: {\alpha}_{K} , (défaut : 0.) ◊ ALP = :math: \alpha , (défaut : 0.) # effet de mémoire ◊ ETA = :math: \eta , (défaut : 0.5) ♦ MU = :math: \mu , (défaut : 0.) ♦ Q_M = :math: {Q}_{m} , ♦ Q_0 = :math: {Q}_{0} , # déformations progressives (Burlet) ◊ D1 = :math: {\delta}_{1} , (défaut : 1.) ◊ D2 = :math: {\delta}_{2} , (défaut : 1.) # restauration ◊ M_R = :math: {m}_{r} , (défaut : 1.) ◊ G_R = :math: {\gamma}_{r} , (défaut : 0.) ◊ M_1 = :math: {m}_{1} , (défaut : 1.) ◊ M_2 = :math: {m}_{2} , (défaut : 1.) ◊ G_X1 = :math: {\gamma}_{\mathrm{X1}} , (défaut : 0.) ◊ G_X2 = :math: {\gamma}_{\mathrm{X2}} , (défaut : 0.) ◊ QR_0 = :math: {Q}_{r}^{\text{ }} , (défaut : 0.) ) These parameters are real constants. All these parameters can depend on the temperature (keywords VISCOCHAB_FO) and the expected values are of function type. There is no default value in this case. It will be noted that if C1 or C2 depends on the temperature, the computation of the Jacobian matrix is not exact, which can make the local convergence difficult if C1 or C2 varies strongly with T . The use of this constitutive law is accessible in the commands STAT_NON_LINE or DYNA_NON_LINE by the keyword VISCOCHAB of COMPORTEMENT. This complete model can be “degraded” by cancelling the effect of certain mechanisms (for example the recovery effect). For example, by cancelling the recovery effect and the radial-evanescence terms of the kinematic hardening (default material parameters), one recovers the Chaboche model with memory effect VISC_CIN2_MEMO . For details concerning the choice of the material parameters leading to the cancellation of certain effects, one may refer to the documentation of the command DEFI_MATERIAU. In the remainder of this document, the model VISCOCHAB is described precisely. The detail of its numerical integration is then presented, in connection with the construction of the consistent tangent matrix. 2 The model VISCOCHAB in Code_Aster 2.1 Description of the model At any time instant, the state of the material is described by the strain \varepsilon , the temperature T , the plastic strain {\varepsilon}^{p} , the cumulative plastic strain p and the backstress tensor X . The state equations then define, as a function of these state variables, the stress \sigma ={\sigma}^{H}\mathrm{Id}+\tilde{\sigma} (decomposed into hydrostatic and deviatoric parts), the isotropic part of the hardening R and the kinematic part X : {\sigma}^{H}=\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{tr}(\sigma )=K\mathrm{tr}(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{th}}) \text{ avec } {\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{th}}=\alpha (T-{T}^{\mathrm{ref}})\mathrm{Id} \tilde{\sigma}=\sigma -{\sigma}^{H}\mathrm{Id}=2\mu (\tilde{\varepsilon}-{\varepsilon}^{p}) R=R(p) X=(p,{\varepsilon}^{p}) where K,\mu ,\alpha and the coefficients of X(p) and R(p) are characteristics of the material which may depend on the temperature. More precisely, they are respectively the bulk and shear moduli, the thermal expansion coefficient, and the isotropic and kinematic hardening functions. As for {T}^{\mathrm{ref}} , it is the reference temperature, for which the thermal strain is considered to be zero. 2.1.1 Yield surface — viscoplastic potential The yield surface associated with the model VISCOCHAB is represented in the space of the principal stresses by: - its centre X , kinematic-hardening tensor, - its size {\alpha}_{R}R+k , k being its initial size and R the isotropic-hardening variable giving the evolution of this size, modulated by the coefficient {\alpha}_{R} , - its shape given by the Von Mises criterion applied to \tilde{\sigma}\text{-X} . \tilde{\sigma} is the stress deviator. The evolution of the plastic strain is governed by a flow law normal to a Von Mises plasticity criterion: F(\sigma ,R,X)={(\tilde{\sigma}-X)}_{\text{eq}}-{\alpha}_{R}R(p)-k\text{ avec }{A}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}\tilde{A}:\tilde{A}} The viscoplastic dissipation potential for the Chaboche model is written: {\Omega}^{p}=\frac{{K}_{0}+{\alpha}_{k}R}{\alpha (n+1)}\exp\left[\alpha {\langle \frac{F}{{K}_{0}+{\alpha}_{k}R}\rangle }^{n+1}\right] where \langle F\rangle is the positive part of F . One deduces from it the evolution law of the plastic strain: {\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}=\frac{\partial {\Omega}^{p}}{\partial \sigma }=\dot{p}\frac{\partial F}{\partial \sigma }=\frac{3}{2}\dot{p}\frac{\tilde{\sigma}-X}{{(\tilde{\sigma}-X)}_{\text{eq}}} having set: \dot{p}={\langle \frac{F}{{K}_{0}+{\alpha}_{k}R}\rangle }^{n}\exp\left[\alpha {\langle \frac{F}{{K}_{0}+{\alpha}_{k}R}\rangle }^{n+1}\right] Classically, \dot{p} is the cumulative plastic strain rate. The parameters {K}_{0} , {\alpha}_{k} and \alpha relate to the viscosity of the material (Norton viscosity). Equation can also be written in an equivalent way in the following form: \dot{p}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}:{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}} The unit normal to the yield surface is denoted: n=\frac{\partial F}{\partial \sigma }{\parallel \frac{\partial F}{\partial \sigma }\parallel }^{-1}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\frac{\partial F}{\partial \sigma }=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\frac{\tilde{\sigma}-X}{{(\tilde{\sigma}-X)}_{\text{eq}}} The evolution laws of the isotropic hardening and of the kinematic hardening are obtained from the thermodynamic potential and from the dissipation potential. 2.1.2 Formulation of the isotropic hardening The evolution of the isotropic-hardening variable R is given by: \dot{R}=b(Q-R)\dot{p}+{\gamma}_{r}{\mid {Q}_{r}-R\mid }^{{m}_{r}}\text{sgn}({Q}_{r}-R) This evolution law of the isotropic hardening involves a first term, linear as a function of the cumulative viscoplastic strain rate \dot{p} . This term is useful for describing the evolution of the loop (softening or hardening) under cyclic loading. This term supplies an asymptotic value of R (corresponding to the stabilised state) equal to the variable Q . This variable Q represents the cyclic hardening (the memory effect of the maximum strains). It is not a constant but it depends on the maximum amplitude of the strain (memory effect): Q=Q{}_{0}{}^{}\text{}+({Q}_{m}-{Q}_{0})(1-{e}^{-2\mu q}) One defines in strain space a yield surface inside which Q is a constant (non-hardening domain): f({\varepsilon}^{p},\xi ,q)=\frac{2}{3}{({\varepsilon}^{p}-\xi )}_{\text{eq}}-q\le 0 This criterion defines a domain characterising the maximum plastic strains, of which q measures the radius and \xi the centre, computed according to a normality law: {\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}:\frac{\partial f}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{p}}>0 The unit normal to the yield surface is denoted: {n}^{\text{ }}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial \sigma }{\parallel \frac{\partial f}{\partial \sigma }\parallel }^{-1}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\frac{{\varepsilon}^{p}-\xi }{{({\varepsilon}^{p}-\xi )}_{\text{eq}}} The evolution laws of the variables q and \xi are given in the form: \dot{q}=\eta H(f)\langle n:{n}^{\text{ }}\rangle \dot{p} \dot{\xi}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}(1-\eta )H(f)\langle n:{n}^{\text{ }}\rangle \dot{p}{n}^{\text{ }} The parameter \eta (which does not exist in the initial formulation 5 ) makes it possible to take the memory effect partially into account. If it is equal to 1/2, one recovers the initial formulation. If it is equal to 1, q is equal to the norm of the greatest plastic strain reached. If it is much smaller than 1/2, the memory effect is taken into account only in part. Note: The same expressions for Q , f , \dot{q} and \dot{\xi} are used in the laws VMIS/VISC_CIN1/2_MEMO which are simplified (and optimised) versions of VISCOCHAB cf r5.03.04. The evolution law of the isotropic hardening involves a second term, making it possible to take the effect of recovery into account. The variable {Q}_{r} is given by the equation: {Q}_{r}=Q-{Q}_{r}^{\text{ }}\left[1-{(\frac{{Q}_{m}-Q}{{Q}_{m}})}^{2}\right] Note that in the initial model of Chaboche , the coefficient {m}_{r} in equation is equal to 1. 2.1.3 Formulation of the kinematic hardening Before giving the expression of the hardening law of the model VISCOCHAB, the various stages which allowed its development are recalled. The simplest law is a linear hardening of the form: \dot{X}=\frac{2}{3}C{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p} To this law, one can add a non-linear recall term supplying an evanescent memory effect of the loading path (initial model of Chaboche): \dot{X}=\frac{2}{3}C\dot{{\varepsilon}^{p}}-\gamma X\dot{p} with \gamma ={\gamma}^{0}\left[{a}_{\infty}+(1-{a}_{\infty}){e}^{-\text{bp}}\right] It has been shown that such a law greatly overestimates the phenomenon of progressive deformation. This leads one to introduce a radial-evanescence term (term due to Burlet and Cailletaud): \dot{X}=\frac{2}{3}C{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}-\gamma (X:n)n\dot{p} In fact, this law now underestimates the phenomenon of progressive deformation. One can then combine the two equations and with the weighting parameter \delta \in \left[0,1\right] , in order to estimate the progressive deformations better: \dot{X}=\frac{2}{3}C{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}-\left[\delta (\gamma X\dot{p})+(1-\delta )(\gamma (X:n)n\dot{p})\right] In the initial model of Chaboche, one also finds an additional term which makes it possible to introduce the effects of recovery into the kinematic hardening, which finally gives the following law: \dot{X}=\frac{2}{3}C{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}-\gamma \left[\delta X+(1-\delta )(X:n)n\right]\dot{p}-{\gamma}_{X}{\left[{(X)}_{\text{eq}}\right]}^{m-1}X with \gamma given by the equation . For an exact taking into account of the dependence of the material parameters with respect to temperature, it is necessary to add an additional term in \dot{T} , which gives: \dot{X}=\frac{2}{3}C{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}-\gamma \left[\delta X+(1-\delta )(X:n)n\right]\dot{p}-{\gamma}_{X}{\left[{(X)}_{\text{eq}}\right]}^{m-1}X+\frac{1}{C}\frac{\partial C}{\partial T}X\dot{T} with \gamma given by the equation . The model VISCOCHAB proposed in fact comprises 2 kinematic-hardening variables {X}_{1} and {X}_{2} whose evolution laws are given by the equation . Summary: The evolution law of the hardening is of the form: \left\lbrace\begin{array}{l}X = X_{1} + X_{2} \\ \dot{X}_{i} = \frac{2}{3} C_{i} \dot{\varepsilon}^{p} - \gamma_{i} \left[ \delta_{i} X_{i} + (1 - \delta_{i}) (X_{i} : n) n \right] \dot{p} \\ - \gamma_{Xi} \left[ (X_{i})_{\text{eq}} \right]^{m_{i} - 1} X_{i} + \frac{1}{C_{i}} \frac{\partial C_{i}}{\partial T} X_{i} \dot{T}, \quad i = 1, 2 \end{array} \right. with {\gamma}_{i}={\gamma}_{i}^{0}\left[{a}_{\infty}+(1-{a}_{\infty}){e}^{-\text{bp}}\right]i=1,2 2.2 Implicit integration In order to carry out numerically the integration of the constitutive law, one performs a discretisation in time and one adopts an implicit Euler scheme, reputed to be appropriate for elastoplastic constitutive relations. This is the method used by default. It is also possible to carry out an explicit integration (see r5.03.12-integration-explicite ) by choosing the keyword ALGO_INTE=’RUNGE_KUTTA’. Henceforth, the following notation will be used: {A}^{-},{A}^{+} and \Delta A represent respectively the values of a quantity at the beginning and at the end of the time step considered, as well as its increment during the step. One therefore has the relation: \Delta A={A}^{+}-{A}^{-} . The problem is then the following: knowing the state at time {t}^{-} as well as the increments of strain \Delta \varepsilon (coming from the prediction phase (cf. requires knowledge of the tangent operator of the assembled system at the end of each increment. The tangent operator is denoted {M}_{c}=\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \varepsilon } . It is possible to determine this operator from the terms of the Jacobian J of the local system, already computed previously (see r5.03.12-expression-matrice-jacobienne). Indeed, the system \phi (\Delta Y)=0 is satisfied at the end of the increment and, for a small variation of \phi , considering this time \varepsilon as a variable, the system remains at equilibrium and one therefore checks d\phi =0 . By differentiation, one obtains: For the system (S1): \begin{array}{}\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta \varepsilon )}d(\Delta \varepsilon )+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta \sigma )}d(\Delta \sigma )+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta {X}_{i})}d(\Delta {X}_{i})\\ +\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta p)}d(\Delta p)+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta R)}d(\Delta R)=0\end{array} For the system (S2): \begin{array}{}\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta \varepsilon )}d(\Delta \varepsilon )+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta \sigma )}d(\Delta \sigma )+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta {X}_{i})}d(\Delta {X}_{i})\\ +\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta p)}d(\Delta p)+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta R)}d(\Delta R)+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta q)}d(\Delta q)+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta \xi )}d(\Delta \xi )=0\end{array} In what follows, the presentation is limited to the system (S1), but the approach is identical for the system (S2). One rewrites the system by putting the terms in \varepsilon on the right-hand side: \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta \sigma )}d(\Delta \sigma )+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta {X}_{i})}d(\Delta {X}_{i})+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta p)}d(\Delta p)+\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta R)}d(\Delta R)=-\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta \varepsilon )}d(\Delta \varepsilon ) With the notation defined previously, this system is written in matrix form: J.d(\Delta Y)=-\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta \varepsilon )}d(\Delta \varepsilon ) . Now \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial (\Delta \varepsilon )}=(\begin{array}{}\frac{\partial g}{\partial (\Delta \varepsilon )}\\ \frac{\partial {k}_{i}}{\partial (\Delta \varepsilon )}\\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial (\Delta \varepsilon )}\\ \frac{\partial r}{\partial (\Delta \varepsilon )}\end{array})=(\begin{array}{}-H\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}) where H represents the elastic modulus. Whence J.d(\Delta Y)=(\begin{array}{}Hd(\Delta \varepsilon )\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}) . The idea then consists in writing this system in blocks, by separating d(\Delta \sigma ) from the other variables Z={(d(\Delta {X}_{i}),d(\Delta p),d(\Delta R))}^{t} , which gives: \left\begin{array}{cc}{J}_{\sigma \sigma }& {J}_{\sigma Z}\\ {J}_{\sigma Z}& {J}_{ZZ}\end{array}\right\\ Z\end{array})=(\begin{array}{}Hd(\Delta \varepsilon )\\ 0\end{array}) By computing the Schur complement of {J}_{\text{ZZ}} , one finds that: \left[{J}_{\sigma \sigma }-{J}_{\sigma Z}{({J}_{\text{ZZ}})}^{-1}{J}_{Z\sigma }\right]d(\Delta \sigma )=Hd(\Delta \varepsilon ) , whence the expression of the tangent operator: {M}_{c}=\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \varepsilon }=\frac{d(\Delta \sigma )}{d(\Delta \varepsilon )}={\left[{J}_{\sigma \sigma }-{J}_{\sigma Z}{({J}_{\text{ZZ}})}^{-1}{J}_{Z\sigma }\right]}^{-1}H Note: Since J is not symmetric, the tangent operator {M}_{c} is not symmetric either. It is however symmetrised in Code_Aster.

r5.03.13 Viscoplastic behaviour with HAYHURST damage r5.03.13 Viscoplastic behaviour with HAYHURST damage Summary: The viscoplastic model coupled with isotropic damage, known as the Hayhurst model, is particularly suited to structural analyses in creep. The viscoplastic part of the model was proposed by Hayhurst et al. in [bib1], while the damage law was proposed by Charles Pétry in [bib2]. This model provides a satisfactory prediction of the drop in creep ductility through the application of limit criteria on strain and on damage. To date, this model has mainly been used at EDF R&D/MMC for creep-life predictions on grade 92 steel. Through the identification of specific parameters and the carrying out of structural analyses, this model also makes it possible to predict satisfactorily the creep behaviour and the life of welded joints [bib3]. This model is implemented in Code_Aster under the name HAYHURST; the rate equations are integrated numerically by an explicit Runge–Kutta scheme of order 2 with automatic subdivision into local sub-steps according to an estimate of the integration error (embedded Runge–Kutta method, see R5.03.14) or by an implicit Newton integration method. The test SSNV225 validates the integration of this model and is presented in the validation document V6.04.225, which also supplies experimental references related to the test case. 1 Introduction Applications in the fossil-fired thermal sector and certain nuclear technologies (GENIV, AGR) require the ability to predict the creep behaviour of materials, both in terms of viscoplastic strain and in terms of creep damage [bib1]. Moreover, from a “material” point of view, creep mechanisms must be taken into account in as physical a manner as possible so that the constitutive law is valid both in the dislocation-creep domain (high stresses) and in the diffusion-creep domain (low stresses). In the lower-stress domain, a drop in ductility is generally observed for tempered martensitic steels containing between 9 and 12% chromium. This drop in ductility can be modelled by means of an isotropic damage variable which causes failure of the material before significant plastic strains have had time to develop. In these situations, maximum-strain criteria cannot be applied, any more than damage-evolution laws strongly linked to strain, such as the LEMAITRE law. More generally, creep cavities appear in many families of metallic materials and can be observed on site by taking extraction replicas on the surface of the components under investigation. These cavities, associated with a reduction of the effective area resisting the forces in the material, can be correlated directly with damage of Kachanov type. In response to these modelling requirements, while remaining within a simple phenomenological mechanical framework, a constitutive law of Hayhurst type (with reference to its viscoplastic flow) was proposed in [bib2] and applied to creep analyses on a P92 steel commonly used in modern components of fossil-fired thermal power plants. This model, implemented in Code_Aster, is a viscoplastic constitutive model with double isotropic hardening, hyperbolic-sine viscosity, and coupled to Kachanov damage. It will be noted that the laws HAYHURST and VENDOCHAB are both viscoplastic laws with isotropic damage; the HAYHURST law nevertheless has its own advantages, detailed in the remainder of this document. Note: Reference [bib3] gives the application of this model to analyses of welded joints in P92 steel, and reference [bib4] gives preliminary work towards extending this model in order to take fatigue–creep interaction into account for the same material. 2 Formulation of the model 2.1 Theoretical framework In the initial formulation proposed in [bib1], two distinct damage variables, each with its own kinetics, are introduced. A variable \phi is in particular associated with microstructural evolutions depending only on time (i.e. static ageing of the material), whereas the variable \omega describes the cavitation mechanisms which develop under the combined influence of the viscoplastic strain and of the stress triaxiality. In the modelling retained in Code_Aster, the variable \phi is kept. In practice its identification is delicate, and microstructural ageing can be left out by setting the coefficient {k}_{c} to zero (cf. the equations in section 2.2). Furthermore, the variable \omega is renamed D because its evolution law differs from that proposed by Hayhurst (cf. [bib1]): the law used here is a hyperbolic sine. The advantages of this formulation are detailed in [bib2]. 2.2 Equations of the model The equations of the model are written: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\mathit{élasticité}:\\ \sigma Identification of the coefficients of the viscoplastic part of the model is carried out from creep tests at different stress levels. Once this identification has been carried out, the coefficients governing the damage can be identified from long creep tests at low stress for which a drop in ductility is observed (a drop in the strains at failure). A typical identification example is detailed in [bib2]. 4 Implementation in Code_Aster Use of the model HAYHURST is possible for 3D, axisymmetric and plane-strain modellings (3D, AXIS, D_PLAN, respectively). r5.03.14 Implicit and explicit integration of non-linear constitutive relations r5.03.14 Implicit and explicit integration of non-linear constitutive relations Summary This document describes two integration methods (one implicit and one explicit) for the solution of problems with non-linear constitutive behaviours in the operators STAT_NON_LINE R5.03.01 and DYNA_NON_LINE R5.05.05. The implicit numerical method presented is that of Newton, with or without line search. The explicit numerical method is that of Runge Kutta of order 2 with adaptive step. 1 Generalities on the integration of constitutive laws 1.1 Algorithm for the solution of the quasi-static problem When the constitutive behaviour of the materials composing the structure is not linear, the solution of the global equilibrium of the structure at each time instant is a non-linear problem whose variational formulation in the case of small strains can be written, in the quasi-static case, in the following form, deduced from the expression of the principle of virtual work (cf. R5.03.01): \lbrace \begin{array}{}{v}^{T}.{L}^{int}(u,t)={v}^{T}.{L}^{\text{ext}}(t)\text{}\forall v\text{tel que}B.v=0\\ B.u={u}^{d}(t)\end{array} Where: - t represents the time-instant variable - u is the displacement field taken from a reference configuration - v is the kinematically admissible virtual displacement field - the relation B.u={u}^{d}(t) corresponds to the boundary conditions imposed in displacements - {L}^{\text{ext}}(t) is the external mechanical loading to which the structure is subjected - {L}^{int} represents the internal forces of the non-linear quasi-static mechanics problem. {L}^{int}(u,t) is related to the stress field \sigma by the operator of the work of the virtual strains {Q}^{T} according to the following relation: {L}^{int}(u,t)={Q}^{T}(u).\sigma The dualisation of the Dirichlet boundary conditions B.u={u}^{d}(t) leads to the following problem [R3.03.01]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}^{int}(u,t)+{B}^{T}.\lambda ={L}^{\text{ext}}(t)\\ B.u={u}^{d}(t)\end{array} The formulation of the discretised quasi-static problem consists in expressing the equilibrium of the structure for a sequence of computation time instants {\left\lbrace {t}_{i}\right\rbrace }_{1\le i\le I} which parameterise the loading; the quantities at the time instant {t}_{i} will be denoted by the index i (for example {L}^{int}({u}_{i},{t}_{i})={{L}_{i}}^{int} ): \lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{i}^{int}+{B}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}={L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}\\ B.{u}_{i}={u}_{i}^{d}\end{array} This non-linear problem is solved by a Newton method (or quasi-Newton), cf. R5.03.01). The system to be solved is then written, for each iteration n of the correction phase: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{K}_{i}^{n}.\delta {u}_{i}^{n+1}+{B}^{T}.\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n+1}={L}_{i}^{\text{méca}}-{L}_{i}^{int,n}-{B}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}^{n}\\ B.\delta {u}_{i}^{n+1}=0\end{array} The vector of the internal forces {L}_{i}^{int,n} is computed from the stresses {\sigma}_{i}^{n} , the latter being computed from the displacements {u}_{i}^{n} by means of the constitutive relation of the material. In fact, in the case of incremental constitutive behaviours, {\sigma}_{i}^{n} is computed from ({\sigma}_{i-1},{\alpha}_{i-1}) and from the strain increment \varepsilon (\Delta {u}_{i}^{n}) induced by the displacement increment since the beginning of the iterative process. 1.2 Purpose of the integration This scheme requires, starting from the estimate of the displacements at iteration n , computing at each Gauss point: - the stress tensor {\sigma}_{i}^{n} which satisfies the constitutive law, and which makes it possible to compute {L}_{i}^{int,n} and the internal variables specific to each constitutive behaviour, - the consistent tangent constitutive operator {(\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \epsilon })}_{i}^{n} , in order to obtain the tangent matrix: {K}_{i}^{n}={\sum}_{e}{K}_{e,ì}^{n} with {K}_{e,i}^{n}={\int}_{{\Omega}_{e}}{Q}^{T}{(\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \epsilon })}_{i}^{n}Qd{\Omega}_{e} 1.3 Solution methods For each finite element, at each integration point, the constitutive behaviour must therefore be integrated, that is to say the stress tensor and the internal variables that are the solution of the problem must be computed, as well as the tangent operator. In the following paragraphs we present two general algorithms making it possible to compute the solution: either the solution by a Newton method, based on an implicit discretisation of the equations, or by a Runge-Kutta method of order 2 with error control, based on an explicit discretisation of these equations. Other solution methods, specific to each constitutive behaviour, are also employed. They are based on an optimisation of the system of non-linear equations, making it possible to reduce the number of equations to be solved, very often to a single equation. The method used then is a simple search for a zero of a function (see for example R5.03.02, R5.03.04, R5.03.16). For all these algorithms, it is possible, in the event of non-convergence, to proceed to a local subdivision of the time step. ; for this purpose, a linear interpolation of the displacement and of the command variables (for example the temperature) over the time interval is adopted, which leads, for every time increment, to: \forall \tau \in [:ref: {t}_{\text{i-1}},{t}_{i} ]T(tau )={T}_{text{i-1}}+frac{tau -{t}_{text{i-1}}}{Delta t}[T-{T}_{text{i-1}}] and {\varepsilon}_{ij}^{k}(\tau )={\varepsilon}_{ij}({u}_{\text{i-1}})+\frac{\tau -{t}_{\text{i-1}}}{\Delta t}[{\varepsilon}_{ij}^{k}({u}_{i}^{n})-{\varepsilon}_{ij}({u}_{\text{i-1}})] 2 Explicit integration of an incremental constitutive relation In order to solve the non-linear system relative to the constitutive law, one can use an explicit integration method of Runge Kutta type of order 2 (option ‘RUNGE_KUTTA’ of the operand ALGO_INTE of the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT) for incremental problems of non-linear constitutive behaviour. The relations currently concerned are: | VISCOCHAB | Elasto-viscoplastic constitutive behaviour of Chaboche, with two centres, with memory and recovery effect | | --- | --- | | VENDOCHAB | Viscoplastic constitutive behaviour with Chaboche damage | | POLYCRISTAL | Homogenised polycrystalline elasto-viscoplastic constitutive behaviour | | MONOCRISTAL | Single-crystal viscoplastic constitutive behaviours of metals | | HAYHURST | Viscoplastic constitutive behaviour with Hayhurst damage | The relation POLYCRISTAL is accessible only by the explicit method presented below. This type of integration makes it possible to implement very easily a new constitutive model [bib2]. The computation of the stress field from a given strain increment is described by following the evolution of the internal variables. 2.1 Use of an explicit method It is assumed that the system to be solved can be expressed in the form: \frac{dY}{dt}=F(Y,t;\Delta {\varepsilon}_{i}^{n},{\sigma}_{i-1}) where Y represents the set of the internal variables of the model, including the plastic-strain variation \Delta {\varepsilon}^{p} . Their time derivatives are assumed to depend only on the internal variables and on the stresses at the previous time instant, and on the total-strain increment supplied by the global Newton algorithm \Delta {\varepsilon}_{i}^{n} . This assumption rests in particular on the linear relation (Hooke's law) between the stress tensor at the current time instant and the elastic part of the strain tensor: \Delta \sigma =A(\Delta {\varepsilon}_{i}^{n}-\Delta {\varepsilon}^{p}) , which makes it possible to express \sigma as a function of \Delta {\varepsilon}^{p} in the differential equations \frac{dY}{dt}=F(Y,t;\sigma (\Delta {\varepsilon}_{i}^{n},{\sigma}_{i-1},Y)) One of the simplest techniques to implement in order to solve these differential equations is the use of explicit methods. For them to remain numerically efficient, it is indispensable to associate with them an automatic step control in order to retain a good cost-precision compromise. The explicit and embedded Runge and Kutta methods [bib1], [bib2] are undoubtedly the simplest integration schemes respecting these criteria. Their principle is to associate two integration schemes of different order in order to control the time step according to a required precision. Depending on the integration order chosen, several algorithms are available and the simplest scheme is a method of order two. One integrates according to the following scheme: - {Y}_{t+h}={Y}^{(2)} if the precision criterion is satisfied; - {Y}^{(2)}=Y+\frac{h}{2}[F(Y,t)+F({Y}^{(1)},t+h)] with {Y}^{(1)}=Y+hF(Y,t) The difference between {Y}^{(2)} (scheme of order 2) and {Y}^{(1)} (scheme of order 1, Euler) supplies an estimate of the integration error and makes it possible to control the size of the time step h , which is initialised to \Delta {t}_{i} for the first attempt. Thus, the method remains efficient if the constitutive behaviour remains elastic during the increment, and one naturally has local sub-steps independent of the global increment in order to integrate, with a better precision, the evolution of the internal variables at the Gauss points where the non-linearity of the constitutive behaviour is the most significant. 2.2 Control of the time step The strategy of the step control is defined from a norm of the discrepancy between the two integration methods: \parallel {Y}^{(2)}-{Y}^{(1)}\parallel and from the precision required by the user \eta (keyword: RESI_INTE_RELA). The criterion retained is the following, where one denotes Y=({y}_{1,}{y}_{2,}\mathrm{...}{y}_{N}) : \deltay (t)=\underset{j=\mathrm{1...N}}{\sup}\left\lbrace \frac{\mid {y}_{j}^{(2)}-{y}_{j}^{(1)}\mid }{\max[\varepsilon ,∣{y}_{j}(t)∣]}\right\rbrace F(0)+\omega F'(0) , then one models F(\rho ) by a polynomial of order 2 (quadratic interpolation): q(\rho )=[F(1)-F(0)-F'(0)]{\rho}^{2}+F'(0)\rho +F(0) The minimum of this polynomial is obtained for {\rho}_{q}=\frac{-F'(0)}{2[F(1)-F(0)-F'(0)]} . Note that if F(1) is much larger than F(0) , then the minimum of the polynomial is reached at 0. Now one does not wish to have an advance step that is too small, on pain of having to carry out a very large number of Newton iterations. For this purpose, a {\rho}_{\min}>0 is imposed (for example {\rho}_{\min}=0,1 ). An upper bound {\rho}_{\max} can also be imposed (for example {\rho}_{\max}=0,6 ). Thus, if {\rho}_{q} {\rho}_{\max} then {\rho}_{q}={\rho}_{\max} . Then one computes F({\rho}_{q})=\frac{1}{2}{\parallel f({x}_{k}+{\rho}_{q}.{d}_{k})\parallel }^{2} . If Armijo's rule is not satisfied, that is if F({\rho}_{q})>F(0)+\omega F'(0){\rho}_{q} , then one models F(\rho ) by a polynomial of order 3 (cubic interpolation): c(\rho )=a{\rho}^{3}+b{\rho}^{2}+F'(0)\rho +F(0) with \left[\begin{array}{}a\end{array}\right]=\frac{1}{{\rho}_{1}-{\rho}_{2}}\left[\begin{array}{cc}\frac{1}{{\rho}_{1}^{2}}& \frac{-1}{{\rho}_{2}^{2}}\\ \frac{-{\rho}_{2}}{{\rho}_{1}^{2}}& \frac{{\rho}_{1}}{{\rho}_{2}^{2}}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{}F({\rho}_{1})-F(0)-F'(0){\rho}_{1}\\ F({\rho}_{2})-F(0)-F'(0){\rho}_{2}\end{array}\right] where {\rho}_{1} and {\rho}_{2} are the last two failed values of \rho . The minimal point of c(\rho ) is: {\rho}_{c}=\frac{-b+\sqrt{{b}^{2}-\mathrm{3a}F'(0)}}{\mathrm{3a}} . The cubic interpolations are continued as long as Armijo's rule is not satisfied. In practice, the number of cubic interpolations is limited to 2. Figure 3.3.1-a : illustration of Armijo's rule 3.3.2 Implementation of the line search in PLASTI The system to be solved is: f(\Delta y)=0 The following Newton iterations are carried out: - updating of the variables at the time instant «+» - computation of the residual f(\Delta {y}_{i})=0 - computation of the Jacobian \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(\Delta {y}_{i}) - solution of the linear system \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(\Delta {y}_{i}).\delta \Delta {y}_{i}=-f(\Delta {y}_{i}) - line search: computation of \rho - updating of the solution: \Delta {y}_{i+1}=\Delta {y}_{i}+\rho \delta \Delta {y}_{i} For the line-search stage: The functional F(\rho )=\frac{1}{2}{\parallel f({y}_{i}+\rho .\delta \Delta {y}_{i})\parallel }^{2} is introduced. The parameters of the line search are fixed in the code: | Parameter of Armijo's rule | \omega =0,1 | | --- | --- | | Minimum bound for the relaxation | {\rho}_{\min}=0,1 | | Maximum bound for the relaxation | {\rho}_{\max}=0,5 | | Number of cubic-interpolation iterations | {\mathrm{it}}_{\max}=2 | Note: Some authors take even smaller values for \omega (for example {10}^{-4} ). 4 Implementation of a new constitutive model 4.1 Possible methods Using the previous architectures, a new constitutive model can be developed relatively easily: - the simplest method is the explicit integration, by the RUNGE_KUTTA method (see § 2); - the complete implicit integration by the NEWTON method in the PLASTI environment (see § 3) requires a little more development, in particular the computation of the Jacobian matrix; - it is nevertheless possible to use directly the development carried out for the explicit integration (2 routines), without an additional routine, in order to carry out analyses with implicit integration, the Jacobian matrix then being computed by perturbation. 4.2 Implementation of a new constitutive model by the explicit method In order to implement a constitutive model XXX, usable with ALGO_INTE_='RUNGE_KUTTA', it suffices to write 2 routines: - a routine for recovery of the material data, called by the dispatching routine LCMATE - a routine computing the time derivatives of the internal variables, called by the dispatching routine LCDVIN. The updating of the catalogues concerns only DEFI_MATERIAU and C_COMPORTEMENT, as well as the catalogue of the constitutive law (cf. D5.04.01). 4.3 Complete implementation of a new constitutive behaviour in PLASTI Without giving a precise computer description of the developments (see on this subject D5.04.01), one can nevertheless describe the architecture of PLASTI and the places where one must intervene in order to integrate a new constitutive behaviour. General architecture of PLASTI: - Call to the routines recovering the material parameters (at the time instant {t}_{i} because possibly depending on the command variables): LCMATE => specific routines for recovery of the material, common with RUNGE_KUTTA (§3) - Elastic integration over \Delta t : LCELAS=> by default, isotropic or anisotropic linear elasticity; if necessary, call to specific routines for the elastic computation XXXELA. - Evaluation of the threshold for the elastic integration: LCCNVX => call to the routines for evaluation of the threshold XXXCVX - If \mathrm{seuil}>0 , then solution by Newton: LCPLAS which calls LCPLNL, which carries out the Newton loop. Its structure is the following: - Initialisation: LCINIT => by default initialisation to zero: {y}^{0}=0 ; if necessary, call to the specific initialisation routines XXXINI - Newton iterations: - Incrementation of the solution {y}^{k}={y}_{i-1}+\Delta {y}^{k} - computation of the residual -f(\Delta {y}^{k}) LCRESI => call to the routines computing the residual XXXRES - computation of the Jacobian matrix \frac{\text{df}}{{\text{dy}}_{k}} : LCJACB => call to the specific routines XXXJAC - solution of the linear system \frac{\partial {f}^{l}}{\partial \Delta {y}_{k}}d(\Delta {y}_{k})\text{= -}{f}^{l}(\Delta {y}_{k}) by the Gauss method - incrementation of \Delta {y}_{k+1}=\Delta {y}_{k}+d(\Delta {y}_{k}) - convergence test LCCONV => by default, test on the relative error on the solution \mid {y}_{k+1}-{y}_{k}\mid |

r5.03.16 Elastoplastic constitutive relation with linear kinematic hardening and non-linear isotropic hardening. 3D modellings and plane stress. r5.03.16 Elastoplastic constitutive relation with linear kinematic hardening and non-linear isotropic hardening. 3D modellings and plane stress. Summary: This document describes an elastoplastic constitutive law with mixed hardening, linear kinematic and non-linear isotropic. The equations to be solved in order to integrate this constitutive relation numerically are specified, as is the consistent tangent matrix. This constitutive behaviour can be used for the modellings of 3D and 2D continuous media (AXIS, C_PLAN, D_PLAN), and for the modellings DKT, COQUE_3D and TUYAU. 1 Introduction When the loading path is no longer monotonic, isotropic and kinematic hardenings are no longer equivalent. In particular, one may expect to have simultaneously a kinematic part and an isotropic part. If one seeks to describe precisely the effects of a cyclic loading, it is desirable to adopt sophisticated modellings (but simple to use) such as the Taheri model, for example, see R5.03.05. On the other hand, for less complex loading paths, one may wish to include only a linear kinematic hardening, all the non-linearities of the hardening being carried by the isotropic term. This makes it possible to describe a traction curve precisely, while still representing phenomena such as the Bauschinger effect [ 1 ] (see for example the figure). The hardening characteristics are then given by a traction curve and a constant, called the Prager constant, for the linear kinematic hardening term. They are introduced in the command DEFI_MATERIAU: | Linear isotropic hardening | Non-linear isotropic hardening | | --- | --- | | DEFI_MATERIAU / ECRO_LINE SY: elastic limit D_SIGM_EPSI: slope of the traction curve PRAGER: (C: Prager constant ) | defi_materiau traction: (SIGM: traction curve prager: (C: Prager constant ) | These characteristics may also depend on the temperature, provided that one then uses the factor keywords ECMI_LINE_FO and ECMI_TRAC_FO in place of ECRO_LINE and TRACTION. The use of these constitutive laws is available in the commands STAT_NON_LINE or DYNA_NON_LINE: | Linear isotropic hardening | Non-linear isotropic hardening | | --- | --- | | STAT_NON_LINE COMPORTEMENT: RELATION:‘VMIS_ECMI_LINE’ | STAT_NON_LINE COMPORTEMENT: RELATION:‘VMIS_ECMI_TRAC’ | In the remainder of this document, one describes precisely the combined-hardening model. r5.03.17 Constitutive relations of discrete elements r5.03.17 Constitutive relations of discrete elements Summary: This document describes the non-linear behaviours of the discrete elements that are called by the operators for the solution of non-linear problems STAT_NON_LINE or DYNA_NON_LINE. More precisely, the behaviours described in this document are: - the thermoelastic behaviour ELAS, - the Von Mises-type behaviour with isotropic hardening used for the modelling of threaded assemblies DIS_GOUJ2E, accessible via the keywords DIS_GOUJ2E_PLAS and DIS_GOUJ2E_ELAS of the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT, - the bilinear elastic behaviour, accessible via the keyword DIS_BILI_ELAS, - the Von Mises-type behaviour with non-linear kinematic hardening, accessible via the keyword DIS_ECRO_CINE, - the non-linear viscoelastic rheological behaviour, accessible via the keyword DIS_VISC, - the non-linear elastoplastic behaviour, accessible via the keyword DIS_ECRO_TRAC, - the contact-type behaviour with impact and Coulomb friction, in explicit integration with penalty stiffnesses, accessible via the keyword DIS_CHOC of the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT, - the non-linear elastic contact-type behaviour DIS_CHOC_TRAC, in explicit integration with a non-linear stiffness given by a function, - the contact-type behaviour with impact of solids and Coulomb friction, in implicit integration, accessible via the keyword DIS_CONTACT, - the behaviours CHOC_ENDO and CHOC_ENDO_PENA, which make it possible to model a behaviour that takes into account a threshold for the impact force, as well as a variation of the stiffness and of the damping as a function of the relative displacement of the nodes of the discrete element, - the unilateral contact behaviour with Coulomb friction, used to model the translational and rotational behaviour of the set of grid-to-rod connection springs of the fuel assemblies, accessible via the keyword DIS_GRICRA. - the line-fitting behaviour, accessible via the keyword ARME, - the “Dashpot”-type behaviour, accessible via the keyword DASHPOT, - the non-linear behaviour which makes it possible to model a bending connection between a wall and a floor or a raft, accessible via the keyword JONC_ENDO_PLAS. The integration of the constitutive models mentioned above is detailed in this document. Other behaviours relating to discrete elements are available, but are not detailed here: - non-linear assembly of pylon angles, relation ASSE_CORN R5.03.32, - the non-linear elastoplastic behaviour of a rectangular shallow foundation subjected to a static or seismic three-dimensional loading, relation FONDA_SUPERFI R5.03.31. 1 Contents

r5.03.19 Hyperelastic constitutive laws r5.03.19 Hyperelastic constitutive laws Summary: Hyperelastic constitutive laws adopted for elastomers are described here. The compressible and incompressible cases are presented. For the models treating incompressibility, one proposes: - the hyperelastic model of Signorini type, which constitutes a generalised version of the Mooney-Rivlin laws, implemented natively, defined by RELATION='ELAS_HYPER', - the visco-hyperelastic model, whose hyperelastic part is of Signorini type, coupled to a viscoelastic branch of generalised Maxwell type, placed in parallel, implemented under MFront, defined by RELATION='ELAS_HYPER_VISC'. For compressible materials, one proposes: - the Hill law, implemented under MFront, defined by RELATION='HYPER_HILL'. These models are chosen in the commands STAT_NON_LINE or DYNA_NON_LINE, by means of the keyword RELATION under the keyword COMPORTEMENT. These relations are understood under large transformations via the keyword DEFORMATION='GREEN_LAGRANGE'. They are available for the 3D, 3D_SI, C_PLAN and D_PLAN elements. 1 Hyperelastic formulation 1.1 Kinematics One considers a solid \domain subjected to large strains. Let \gradTransfor be the transformation-gradient tensor taking the initial configuration {\Omega}_{0} to the current deformed configuration \domainCurr . One denotes by \posiRefe the position of a point in \domainRefe and by \posiCurr the position of this same point after strain in \domainCurr . \disp is then the displacement between the two configurations. One therefore has: \posiCurr = \posiRefe + \disp The transformation-gradient tensor is written: \gradTransfor =  rac{\partial \posiCurr}{\partial \posiRefe} = 	ensTwoUnit + \gradVector{\disp} Transformation from the initial configuration to the final one This tensor is not the best candidate for describing the strain of the structure. In particular, it is not zero for rigid-body motions and it describes the whole transformation: the change of length of the infinitesimal elements but also their orientation. Now a pure rotation motion does not generate stresses and it is therefore preferable to use a strain measure which does not take this rigid rotation into account. Let us consider an infinitesimal length element denoted \posiIncrRefe in the initial configuration and \posiIncrCurr in the final configuration. If the motion is a rigid rotation 	ensTwo{R} , one has: \posiIncrCurr= 	ensTwo{R} \posiIncrRefe The norm of this vector after transformation is therefore equal to \posiIncrCurr \cdot \posiIncrCurr = 	ensTwo{R} \posiIncrRefe \cdot 	ensTwo{R} \posiIncrRefe = \posiIncrRefe \left( 	ranspose{	ensTwo{R}} 	ensTwo{R} ight) \posiIncrRefe As the transformation is purely rigid, one has: 	ranspose{	ensTwo{R}} 	ensTwo{R} = 	ensTwoUnit 	ensTwo{R} is therefore an orthogonal tensor. The strain-gradient tensor may be written as the product of an orthogonal tensor and of a positive definite tensor (polar factorisation): \gradTransfor = 	ensTwo{R} 	ensTwo{U} The tensor 	ensTwo{U} (called the stretch tensor) is therefore a first measure of large strains. On the other hand, it requires the polar factorisation of \gradTransfor , which is a costly operation. One therefore prefers to use the right Cauchy-Green strain tensor: \ECGDroite = 	ranspose{\gradTransfor} {\gradTransfor} = 	ensTwo{U}^{2} This tensor is symmetric.
