r5.03.20 Non-linear elastic constitutive relation in large displacements r5.03.20 Non-linear elastic constitutive relation in large displacements Summary: The aim here is to describe a non-linear elastic constitutive relation which coincides with the elastoplastic Hencky-VonMises law (isotropic hardening) in the case of a loading which induces a radial and monotonic evolution of the stresses at every point of the structure. This model is chosen in the command STAT_NON_LINE by means of the keyword RELATION='ELAS_VMIS_LINE' or 'ELAS_VMIS_TRAC' under the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT. This constitutive relation is then extended to large displacements and large rotations, inasmuch as it derives from a potential (hyperelastic law); this feature is chosen by means of the keyword DEFORMATION='GROT_GDEP'. It is available for all 2D and 3D isoparametric elements. 1 Non-linear elastic constitutive relation: ELAS_VMIS_LINE and ELAS_VMIS_TRAC 1.1 Objective Within the framework of the global approach in fracture mechanics, the energy release rate can be given a meaning only for hyperelastic constitutive relations, that is, relations which derive from a potential, the free energy. In order nevertheless to be able to treat elastoplastic problems, a non-linear elastic constitutive relation is proposed which leads to results identical to those obtained by the plastic constitutive relation of Hencky-VonMises (isotropic hardening) in the case of a radial and monotonic evolution of the loading at every point. The definition of the material characteristics (keyword DEFI_MATERIAU) is identical to that of isotropic plastic behaviour. For further information on the model, one may refer to [bib1]. In order to illustrate the points in common and the differences between the plastic and elastic models, a tension then compression curve obtained for a one-dimensional bar is presented below. 1.2 Constitutive relation After integration in time of the Hencky-VonMises constitutive relation, formulated in strain rates and stress rates in R5.03.02, whose notation is adopted, the expression of the stresses as a function of the strains is: \lbrace \begin{array}{ccccc}\sigma =& K(\text{tr}\varepsilon )\text{Id}+& G({\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}})\tilde{\varepsilon}& & \text{éq 1}.2-1\\ -\text{si}& {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}\le \frac{{\sigma}^{y}}{2\mu }& & & \\ & G=2\mu & \text{et}p=0& & \\ -\text{si}& {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}>\frac{{\sigma}^{y}}{2\mu }& & & \\ & G=\frac{R(p)}{{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}}& \text{et}p\text{tel que :}& p+\frac{R(p)}{3\mu }=\frac{2{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}}{3}& \text{éq 1}.2-2\end{array} In a manner similar to plasticity, the hardening function R(p) is deduced from the data supplied by a simple tension test (linear hardening with the keyword ELAS_VMIS_LINE, or else defined by points with the keyword ELAS_VMIS_TRAC, cf. R5.03.02). As for the variable p , it deserves a few moments of attention. In the plastic model, its meaning is clear. It is the cumulative plastic strain, always increasing; it is an internal variable of the model. By contrast, in the elastic case, it no longer has the status of an internal variable, since there is no dissipation. Furthermore, it decreases during unloadings. In fact, its value coincides with that obtained in plasticity so long as the evolution of the loading is radial and monotonic. Besides the constitutive relation proper, it is necessary to know the value of the free energy for a given state for the computations of the energy release rate. Without proof, this potential, from which the constitutive relation derives, is worth: | If {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}\le \frac{{\sigma}^{y}}{2\mu } | \psi (\varepsilon )=\frac{1}{2}K{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}^{2}+\frac{2\mu }{3}{\varepsilon}_{{\text{eq}}^{2}} | | --- | --- | | If {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}>\frac{{\sigma}^{y}}{2\mu } | \psi (\varepsilon )=\frac{1}{2}K{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}^{2}+\frac{R{(p({\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}))}^{2}}{6\mu }+{\int}_{0}^{p({e}_{\text{eq}})}R(s)\text{ds} | > eq 1.2-3 1.3 Solution of the equation in p It could be observed in the previous paragraph that the expression of the stresses requires the solution of an equation in the variable p . Inasmuch as the hardening function R is increasing, this equation may be written by gathering the terms in which p appears into the left-hand side (which is then increasing with p ): More precisely, the left-hand side is piecewise linear in p . To solve the equation, it is then sufficient to run sequentially through each of the intervals until the one in which the solution lies is found. An affine equation then supplies the value of p . 1.4 Computation of the constitutive relation and tangent stiffness The computation of the stresses and of the tangent stiffness, that is, the variation of the stresses with respect to the strains, is performed according to the algorithm presented below. Adopting the convention of Code_Aster , the stresses and the strains are stored in a vector with six components, while the tangent stiffness is a 6\times 6 matrix. \left\lbrace \varepsilon \right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\varepsilon}_{xx}\\ {\varepsilon}_{yy}\\ {\varepsilon}_{zz}\\ \sqrt{2}{\varepsilon}_{xy}\\ \sqrt{2}{\varepsilon}_{xz}\\ \sqrt{2}{\varepsilon}_{yz}\end{array}\right\rbrace \left\lbrace \sigma \right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{xx}\\ {\sigma}_{yy}\\ {\sigma}_{zz}\\ \sqrt{2}{\sigma}_{xy}\\ \sqrt{2}{\sigma}_{xz}\\ \sqrt{2}{\sigma}_{yz}\end{array}\right\rbrace \left\lbrace 1\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}1\\ 1\\ 1\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace Constitutive relation: \left\lbrace \sigma \right\rbrace =K(\text{tr}\varepsilon )\left\lbrace 1\right\rbrace +G\left\lbrace \tilde{\varepsilon}\right\rbrace Tangent stiffness: \frac{d\left\lbrace \sigma \right\rbrace }{d\left\lbrace \varepsilon \right\rbrace }=K=\left[{K}_{1}\right]+\left[{K}_{2}\right] - \left[{K}_{1}\right]=\frac{\mathrm{3K}-G}{3}\left\lbrace 1\right\rbrace \otimes \left\lbrace 1\right\rbrace +G\left[\text{Id}\right] - \left[{K}_{2}\right]=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\left[0\right]& \text{si}{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}\le \frac{{\sigma}^{y}}{2\mu }\\ \frac{3}{2{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}^{2}}\left[\frac{2\mu {R}^{'}(p)}{{R}^{'}(p)+3\mu }-G\right]\left\lbrace \tilde{\varepsilon}\right\rbrace \otimes \left\lbrace \tilde{\varepsilon}\right\rbrace & \text{si}{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}>\frac{{\sigma}^{y}}{2\mu }\end{array} 1.5 Taking thermal strains into account In a manner identical to plasticity, the total strain is split into a mechanical part which satisfies the previous constitutive relation [eq 1.2-1], [eq 1.2-2] and a thermal part, a function of the temperature. Note furthermore that the various characteristics of the material may also depend on the temperature. \varepsilon ={\varepsilon}^{m}+{\varepsilon}^{\text{th}} \text{avec}\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\sigma =K(\text{tr}{\varepsilon}^{m})\mathrm{Id}+G({\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}})\tilde{\varepsilon}& \text{éq 1.5.1}\\ {\varepsilon}^{\text{th}}=\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{réf}})\text{Id}& \end{array} \alpha : thermal expansion coefficient {T}_{\text{ref}} : reference temperature It remains to complete the free-energy potential [eq 1.2-3] in order to include the temperature in it. Several choices are possible, depending on the way in which one wishes to define the entropy (derivative of the free energy with respect to the temperature). In our case, the potential adopted is: | If {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}\le \frac{{\sigma}^{y}}{2\mu } | \psi (\varepsilon ,T)=\frac{1}{2}K{(\text{Tr}(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{\text{th}}))}^{2}+\frac{2\mu }{3}{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}^{2} | | --- | --- | | If {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}>\frac{{\sigma}^{y}}{2\mu } | \psi (\varepsilon ,T)=\frac{1}{2}K{(\text{Tr}(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{\text{th}}))}^{2}+\frac{R{(p({\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}))}^{2}}{6\mu }+{\int}_{0}^{p({\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}})}R(s)\text{ds} | 1.6 Particular treatment of plane stresses Usually, one seeks to determine the stresses knowing the strains and the temperature. However, this is no longer quite the case under the plane-stress assumption, inasmuch as three of the components of the strain tensor are henceforth unknown, the dual quantities being fixed: | {\varepsilon}_{xz} , {\varepsilon}_{yz} and {\varepsilon}_{zz} | unknown | | --- | --- | | {\sigma}_{xz}={\sigma}_{yz}={\sigma}_{zz} | =0 | These unknown components must therefore first be determined. The method adopted is set out in [bib1] and R5.03.02. It may however be recalled here that the components xz and yz pose no problem, given the form of the constitutive relation [eq 1.2-1]: {\varepsilon}_{xz}={\varepsilon}_{yz}=0 On the other hand, the determination of the component zz requires the (numerical) solution of a non-linear scalar equation. Finally, one last warning is called for. Unlike plane strains, the solutions obtained under the plane-stress assumption are generally not exact, inasmuch as they do not satisfy the conditions of geometric compatibility (integrability of the strain field). They are only approximate solutions. 2 Elasticity in large transformations 2.1 Objective Henceforth, the aim is to take into account large displacements and large rotations, a feature accessible through the keyword DEFORMATION='GROT_GDEP' in the command STAT_NON_LINE. Let it be stated at once that one restricts oneself to isoparametric finite elements (D_PLAN, C_PLAN, AXIS and 3D) for which the discretisation of the continuous problem poses no particular difficulty, cf. [R3.01.00]. To this end, it is accepted that the second Piola-Kirchhoff stress tensor, S , derives from the Hencky-VonMises potential expressed by means of the Green-Lagrange strain E : \mathrm{S}=\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial E}\left(\mathrm{E}\right) Let us also recall the definitions of E and S . Further information may also be found in [bib1]. \begin{array}{}F=\text{Id}+\text{Grad}(u)\text{}E=\frac{1}{2}({}^{T}\text{}\text{FF}-\text{Id})\\ S=\text{Det}(F){F}^{-1}\sigma {}^{T}\text{}{F}^{-1}\end{array} Such a constitutive relation, said to be hyperelastic, makes it possible in all rigour to take large strains and large rotations into account. However, we limit ourselves to small strains, and this for two reasons. First, the constitutive relation adopted does not possess the right properties (polyconvexity) to ensure the existence of solutions, and nor does it control large compressions. Second, plastic behaviour differs markedly from a hyperelastic behaviour as soon as the strains become appreciable. It is for these reasons that we have chosen to retain the small-strain assumption, thus avoiding the controversy over large strains. 2.2 Virtual work of the external forces: dead-load assumption In order to treat the problem of the analysis of hyperelastic structures, one seeks to write equilibrium in variational form on the initial configuration. In particular, the virtual work of the external forces must be expressed on this same initial configuration, which requires the additional assumption of dead loads: it is assumed that the loading does not depend on the geometric transformation. Typically, an imposed force is a dead load, whereas pressure is a follower loading, since it depends on the orientation of the face of application, hence on the transformation. Under this assumption, the virtual work of the external forces is written as a linear form: {\mathit{dW}}_{\text{ext}}.\delta \mathrm{v}=\underset{{\Omega}_{o}}{\int}{\rho}_{o}{F}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d{\Omega}_{o}+\underset{{\partial}_{F}{\Omega}_{o}}{\int}{T}_{i}^{d}\delta {v}_{i}{\text{dS}}_{o} F : volumetric loading {T}^{d} : surface loading acting on the boundary {\partial}_{F}{\Omega}_{o} 2.3 Virtual work of the internal forces No proof of the expressions presented will be given here. For that, one may refer to [bib1] and R7.02.03. Here again, the initial configuration is chosen as the reference configuration, in order to express the work of the internal forces: | {\text{dW}}_{int}.\delta \mathrm{v}=\underset{{\Omega}_{o}}{\int}{F}_{\text{ik}}{S}_{kl}\delta {v}_{i,l}d{\Omega}_{o} | | --- | | with: \delta {v}_{i,l}=\frac{\partial {\mathrm{dv}}_{i}}{\partial {X}_{l}} | With a view to a solution by a Newton method, it is important also to express the second variation of the virtual work of the internal forces, namely: | {d}^{2}{W}_{int}.\delta \mathrm{u}.\delta \mathrm{v}=\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\underset{{\Omega}_{o}}{\int}\delta {u}_{i,k}{S}_{kl}\delta {v}_{i,l}d{\Omega}_{o} | Geometric stiffness | | --- | --- | | \mathrm{...}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}+\underset{{\Omega}_{o}}{\int}\delta {u}_{i,q}{F}_{\text{ip}}\frac{{\partial}^{2}\Psi }{\partial {E}_{\text{pq}}\partial {E}_{kl}}{F}_{\text{jk}}\delta {v}_{j,l}d{\Omega}_{o} | Elastic stiffness | 2.4 Variational formulation All the ingredients are now available for writing the variational formulation of the problem: {\mathit{dW}}_{int}.\delta \mathrm{v}={\text{dW}}_{\text{ext}}.\delta \mathrm{v} , \forall \delta v kinematically admissible 3 Bibliography 1. LORENTZ E.: A non-linear hyperelastic constitutive relation. Internal note EDF DER, HI-74/95/011/0, 1995. 4 Description of the versions of the document | Version Aster | Author(s) Organisation(s) | Description of the modifications | | --- | --- | --- | | 3 | E.LorentzEDF-R&D/MMN | Initial text | | 10.1 | J.M.Proix EDF-R&D/AMA | Change of vocabulary: GREEN becomes GROT_GDEP |

r5.03.22 Constitutive law in large rotations and small strains r5.03.22 Constitutive law in large rotations and small strains Summary: The formulation adopted to treat large rotations and small strains is described here. This formulation is valid for all the constitutive laws defined under COMPORTEMENT of the command STAT_NON_LINE and provided with the three-dimensional (3D), axisymmetric (AXIS), plane-strain (D_PLAN) and plane-stress (C_PLAN) modellings. This functionality is selected by means of the keyword DEFORMATION ='GROT_GDEP' under COMPORTEMENT. 1 Some definitions A few definitions of tensors related to large strains are recalled here. The deformation-gradient tensor F is the name given to the tensor that takes one from the initial configuration {\Omega}_{0} to the current deformed configuration \Omega (t) . \mathrm{F}=\frac{\partial \widehat{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial \mathrm{X}}=\mathrm{Id}+{\nabla}_{\mathrm{X}}\mathrm{u} with \mathrm{x}=\widehat{\mathrm{x}}(\mathrm{X},t)=\mathrm{X}+\mathrm{u} eq 1-1 where X is the position of a point in {\Omega}_{0} , x the position of this same point after deformation in \Omega (t) and u the displacement. Various strain tensors can be obtained by eliminating the rotation in the local transformation. This can be done in two ways, either by using the polar decomposition theorem, or by directly computing the variations of length and of angle (variation of the scalar product). In the Lagrangian description (that is to say on the initial configuration) one obtains: - By polar decomposition: \mathrm{F}=\mathrm{R}\mathrm{U} eq 1-2 where R is the rotation tensor (orthogonal) and U the right pure-strain tensor (symmetric and positive definite). - By a direct computation of the strains: \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2}(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Id}) with \mathrm{C}={\mathrm{F}}^{T}\mathrm{F} eq 1-3 where E is the Green-Lagrange strain tensor and C the right Cauchy-Green tensor. The tensors U and C are related by the following relation: \mathrm{C}={\mathrm{U}}^{2} eq 1-4 2 Constitutive laws in Green-Lagrange kinematics The Green-Lagrange tensor E can serve as the “kinematic input” to a constitutive law, which then relates the evolution of E to the PK2 stress (as the second Piola-Kirchhoff stress) S : \mathrm{S}=\widehat{\mathrm{S}}(\mathrm{E},\dot{\mathrm{E}}) eq 2-1 The latter is related to the Cauchy stress by the following relation: \sigma =\frac{1}{det(\mathrm{F})}\mathrm{F}\mathrm{S}{\mathrm{F}}^{T} eq 2-2 This kinematic choice is activated under the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT via the keyword DEFORMATION='GREEN_LAGRANGE', for the constitutive laws that allow it, that is to say those for which this kinematic choice is relevant (e.g.: Signorini behaviour, RELATION='ELAS_HYPER'). 3 Assumption of small strains and large rotations When the strains are small, there is no fundamental difficulty in writing the constitutive laws: the various “large strain” models lead to the same “small strain” model, and this both for isotropic and for anisotropic behaviours. Only the geometric difficulty associated with the finite rotation remains. To write the model in large rotations and small strains, one starts from the polar decomposition of F , that is \mathrm{F}=\mathrm{R}\mathrm{U} . Since the tensor U is a pure strain tensor and moreover a small one, the stress tensor {\sigma}^{\ast } associated with this strain history U can be computed by a small-strain constitutive law. It then suffices to subject this tensor {\sigma}^{\ast } to the rotation R in order to obtain the stress tensor \sigma associated with the strain history F , as follows: \sigma =\mathrm{R}{\sigma}^{\ast }{\mathrm{R}}^{T} eq 2-1 This scheme can be summarised as follows: \mathrm{F}\to \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{Id}+\epsilon \stackrel{\text{ldc}\text{HPP}}{\to }{\sigma}^{\ast }\to \sigma =\mathrm{R}{\sigma}^{\ast }{\mathrm{R}}^{T} eq 2-2 The drawback of this calculation chain is that it requires the polar decomposition of F . Two assumptions are made in order to avoid it. On the one hand, in order to avoid the computation of U , the HPP strain \varepsilon can be approximated by the Green strain E , taking advantage of the fact that the strains are small: E=\frac{1}{2}({F}^{T}F-\mathrm{Id})=\frac{1}{2}(U-\mathrm{Id})(U+\mathrm{Id})=\varepsilon +\frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon}^{2}\approx \varepsilon eq 2-3 {\sigma}^{\ast } is then deduced from this by the “small strain” constitutive law. On the other hand, in the same way, in order to avoid the computation of R , the HPP stress tensor {\sigma}^{\ast } can be approximated by the second Piola-Kirchhoff tensor S : \mathrm{S}=J{\mathrm{F}}^{-1}\sigma {\mathrm{F}}^{-T}=\text{Det}(\mathrm{U}){\mathrm{U}}^{-1}{\sigma}^{\ast }{\mathrm{U}}^{-1}={\sigma}^{\ast }+{\sigma}^{\ast }\text{O}(\epsilon )\approx {\sigma}^{\ast } eq 2-4 \sigma is then deduced by: \sigma =\frac{1}{J}FS{F}^{T} eq 2-5 Finally, in the presence of large rotations and small strains, it is sufficient to write the “small strain” constitutive law with, as input, the history of the Green strains E , and as output, the history of the Piola-Kirchhoff stresses S . This approach is valid both for isotropic and for anisotropic constitutive laws. As for the appropriate variational formulation, it is that adopted in hyperelasticity (behaviour ELAS, ELAS_VMIS_XXX under COMPORTEMENT with strains of type GROT_GDEP). For further details, refer to the associated reference document R5.03.20. One must however be sure that the problem under study does indeed induce small strains, because otherwise the simplifications [eq 2-3] and [eq 2-4] can no longer be made. Without this assumption, the discrepancy with a plastic behaviour increases rapidly with the intensity of the strains. Note: the GROT_GDEP model is used exclusively for certain structural elements (plates, shells) but also within the framework of a call to the MFront solver in the general case. In the other cases (standard isoparametric elements outside MFront), GDEF_LOG, SIMO_MIEHE or GREEN_LAGRANGE must be used, according to the behaviours, in order to activate the taking into account of large strains. 4 Bibliography 1. CANO V., LORENTZ E., "Introduction into Code_Aster of an elastoplastic constitutive model in large strains with isotropic hardening", Internal note EDF DER, HI-74/98/006/0, 1998

r5.03.24 Large-strain model GDEF_LOG r5.03.24 Large-strain model GDEF_LOG Summary: This document presents a hypoelastic large-strain formulation for constitutive laws of von Mises type, called GDEF_LOG in Code_Aster. This model, due to C. Miehe, N. Apel and M. Lambrecht [13], is a large-strain model based on a logarithmic measure, with a particular dual stress tensor. It is valid whatever the small-strain constitutive behaviour, and it has the advantage of supplying a symmetric tangent matrix. No modification of the kinematic internal variables is required. It allows an incrementally objective integration of the constitutive laws (as does the SIMO_MIEHE model). However, as with all hypoelastic laws, the constitutive laws are strictly speaking limited to small elastic strains. The capabilities of this model, and its advantages relative to the PETIT_REAC approximation, are illustrated in this document. 1 Introduction Most of the constitutive laws of Code_Aster can be used under the small-perturbation hypothesis (HPP), which makes it possible to identify the initial and current geometric configurations. However, when the strains become large (the limit is generally set at 5%), this hypothesis is no longer satisfied. The notions of material derivative and partial derivative are then different and, as a result, the incrementally formulated constitutive laws lose their objective character (independence of the mechanical state with respect to the observer); an inconvenient consequence is the possible evolution of the stresses under a rigid-body motion, contrary to physics. In order to recover objectivity, which is therefore indispensable if a reliable result is to be guaranteed, a large-strain strategy is possible. The purpose of this document is to present the formalism implemented in Code_Aster to treat constitutive laws with isotropic and kinematic hardening and a von Mises criterion. The GDEF_LOG formalism is presented, due to C. Miehe, N. Apel and M. Lambrecht [13], which is a large-strain model based on a logarithmic measure, with a particular dual stress tensor. It is valid whatever the small-strain constitutive behaviour, and it has the advantage of supplying a symmetric tangent matrix. No modification of the kinematic internal variables is required. 2 Formulation and assumptions This algorithm, due to C. Miehe, N. Apel and M. Lambrecht [13], is based on an energetic formulation, and the stiffness matrix is supplied in [13]. 2.1 Elements of kinematics The kinematic elements in the continuous case can be found, for example, in [3]. Interest here is in the case discretised directly in time, which makes it possible to define the quantities used in the formalism presented in this document. Consider a closed initial continuous domain {\Omega}_{0}\subset {ℝ}^{3} , each point of which is located by its coordinates X\in {\Omega}_{0} , subjected to a deformation field \varphi which takes it into the configuration \Omega : \varphi :{\Omega}_{0}\to \Omega \subset {ℝ}^{3} The coordinates of this point in the current configuration will be denoted x\in \Omega . The deformed configuration evolving over time, a family of fields {\varphi}_{n} is in fact defined, by means of the time discretisation, each corresponding to a time instant {t}_{n} of the evolution history of the domain. In the case of the large-strain formalism treated here, it is necessary to introduce four configurations for the domain and its evolution (cf. Figure 1): the initial reference configuration {\Omega}_{0} (that is to say the one for which the strains are zero), the configuration {\Omega}_{n} at the beginning of the current time step {t}_{n+1}={t}_{n}+\Delta t , the configuration {\Omega}_{n+1} at the end of this time step, and a mid-step configuration, {\Omega}_{n+\frac{1}{2}} , the formalism being integrated with a midpoint rule. Figure 1: Configurations required and deformation gradients From these configurations, the displacement fields and the deformation gradients for passing from one to the other are defined. The quantities taking the initial configuration into a given configuration are denoted in capitals (U,\mathrm{F}) and the quantities relating two deformed configurations to each other are denoted in lower case (u,\mathrm{f}) . Table 1 summarises the various quantities and their expressions. | Starting configuration | Arrival configuration | Displacement | Deformation gradient | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | {\Omega}_{0} | {\Omega}_{n} | {U}_{n} | {\mathrm{F}}_{n}={\mathrm{I}}_{d}+{\mathrm{grad}}_{0}{U}_{n} | | {\Omega}_{0} | {\Omega}_{n+1} | {U}_{n+1} | {\mathrm{F}}_{n+1}={\mathrm{I}}_{d}+{\mathrm{grad}}_{0}{U}_{n+1} | | {\Omega}_{0} | {\Omega}_{n+\frac{1}{2}} | | {\mathrm{F}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\mathrm{F}}_{n}+{\mathrm{F}}_{n+1}\right) | | {\Omega}_{n} | {\Omega}_{n+\frac{1}{2}} | | {\mathrm{f}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}={I}_{d}+\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{grad}}_{n}u {\mathrm{f}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}={\mathrm{F}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}\cdot {\mathrm{F}}_{n}^{-1} {\mathrm{f}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\mathrm{f}}_{n}+{\mathrm{I}}_{d}\right) | | {\Omega}_{n} | {\Omega}_{n+1} | u | {\mathrm{f}}_{n+1}={I}_{d}+{\mathrm{grad}}_{n}u {\mathrm{f}}_{n+1}={\mathrm{F}}_{n+1}\cdot {\mathrm{F}}_{n}^{-1} {\mathrm{f}}_{n+1}=\Delta \mathrm{F} | | {\Omega}_{n+\frac{1}{2}} | {\Omega}_{n+1} | | {\tilde{\mathrm{f}}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}={\mathrm{f}}_{n+1}\cdot {\mathrm{f}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}^{-1} {\tilde{\mathrm{f}}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}={\mathrm{F}}_{n+1}\cdot {\mathrm{F}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}^{-1} | Table 1: summary of the displacements and deformation gradients From these deformation gradients, it is possible to define the strain rates \mathrm{L} : {\mathrm{L}}_{°}={\dot{\mathrm{F}}}_{°}{\dot{\mathrm{F}}}_{°}^{-1} The spin-rate tensors \omega : {\mathrm{d}}_{°}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\mathrm{L}}_{°}+{\mathrm{L}}_{°}^{T}\right) and the strain-rate tensors \mathrm{d} : {\omega}_{°}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\mathrm{L}}_{°}-{\mathrm{L}}_{°}^{T}\right) with {}_{°} denoting the configuration n , n+1 or n+\frac{1}{2} . The Eulerian strain tensor between the configurations {\Omega}_{n} and {\Omega}_{n+1} is deduced from these definitions: {\mathrm{e}}_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left[{\mathrm{I}}_{d}-{\left({\mathrm{f}}_{n+1}\cdot {\mathrm{f}}_{n+1}^{T}\right)}^{-1}\right] The strain rate is then indeed related to the Eulerian strain: {\mathrm{d}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{\Delta t}{\tilde{\mathrm{f}}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}^{-1}\cdot {\mathrm{e}}_{n+1}\cdot {\tilde{\mathrm{f}}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}} The last quantity to be introduced for the algorithm is the incremental displacement gradient, relative to the configuration {\Omega}_{n+\frac{1}{2}} and defined by: {\mathrm{h}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}={\mathrm{grad}}_{n}u\cdot {\mathrm{f}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}^{-1} The latter makes it possible to determine the spin rate in the same configuration by the relation: {\omega}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2\Delta t}\left[{\mathrm{h}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}-{\mathrm{h}}_{n+\frac{1}{2}}^{T}\right] From these kinematic elements, it is possible to define hypoelastic constitutive laws whose integration is objective in large strains. The following section presents this type of formulation of the constitutive laws. 2.2 Hypo-elastoplastic constitutive laws In this section, the class of phenomenological plasticity models (here time-independent) with hypoelasticity is considered. It constitutes an ad hoc extension of the writing of the small-strain laws, which allows a certain generality and represents an advantage in the context of an analysis code: it will be seen in the following chapter that its numerical integration can be carried out in a manner equivalent to that of small strains. This class of models is to be contrasted with the hyperelastic class, based on the thermodynamic approach of continua. In this context, a free energy, which may for example be considered as a function of the temperature and of the Green-Lagrange strain, is defined; the evolutions of the stresses and possibly of the internal variables follow from it. One may cite, for example, the case of the Signorini hyperelastic law (cf. [4]) in elasticity and the Simo-Miehe formalism in hyperelastoplasticity (cf. [3]). A hypo-elastoplastic constitutive law is generally constructed in five steps. 1. In the same way as the additive split of the small strains, the strain rate \mathrm{d} is first split into an elastic part and a plastic part: \mathrm{d}={\mathrm{d}}^{e}+{\mathrm{d}}^{p} 1. A derivative of the Kirchhoff stress \tau =det(\mathrm{F})\sigma is then determined by an incremental relation depending on the elastic strain rate, with \stackrel{˚}{x} an objective derivative to be defined and \mathrm{C} the elasticity tensor.: \mathring{\tau}=\mathrm{C}:\left[\mathrm{d}-{\mathrm{d}}^{p}\right] 1. A convex reversibility domain defining the admissible stress space is constructed from a function f , with S the stress space and \mathrm{q} the set of the m internal variables representing the kinematic hardening of the material and \alpha the scalar variables (including the isotropic hardening): {{\rm E}}_{\tau}=\lbrace (\tau ,\mathrm{q},\alpha )\in S\times {ℝ}^{m+1}\mid f(\tau ,\mathrm{q},\alpha )⩽0\rbrace The evolution laws of these internal variables follow a normality principle (only associated constitutive laws are considered here), with \gamma \ge 0 the plastic multiplier, \frac{\partial f}{\partial \tau }(\tau ,\mathrm{q},\alpha ) defining the direction of plastic flow and g(\tau ,\mathrm{q},\alpha ) the evolution of the other internal variables: {\mathrm{d}}^{p}=\gamma \frac{\partial f(\tau ,\mathrm{q},\alpha )}{\partial \tau } \mathring{q}=-\gamma g(\tau ,\mathrm{q},\alpha ) The writing of the loading/unloading conditions, classically represented by Kuhn-Tucker and the consistency condition: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\gamma \ge 0\\ f(\tau ,q,\alpha )\le 0\\ \gamma f(\tau ,q,\alpha )=0\end{array} This class of model is therefore characterised by a strong analogy with the small-strain formalisms, with an incremental writing of the stresses which is not without raising some difficulties of numerical integration: indeed, in order to prevent stress evolutions under a rigid-body motion, an objective integration of equation () is required. 2.3 Strain and stress tensors The model is based on the logarithmic strain defined by: \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2}\log\left[{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{T}}.\mathrm{F}\right] The definition of this expression is supplied in appendix 2. The stress \mathrm{T} is defined in the logarithmic space as dual to \mathrm{E} , so that the mechanical power density {p}_{m} is expressed by their product \mathrm{T}:\dot{\mathrm{E}} . It is not a classical stress tensor, but it can be related to the usual tensors. Indeed, the mechanical power being written: {p}_{m}=\mathrm{T}:\dot{\mathrm{E}}=\Pi :\dot{\mathrm{F}} One obtains: {p}_{m}=\mathrm{T}:\dot{\mathrm{E}}=\mathrm{T}:\frac{\partial \mathrm{E}}{\partial \mathrm{F}}:\dot{\mathrm{F}}=\Pi :\dot{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{T}:{\mathrm{P}}_{\Pi}:\mathrm{F} With \Pi the first Piola-Kirchhoff stress tensor. This defines the projection tensor (of order four in 3D) {\mathrm{P}}_{\Pi} : {\mathrm{P}}_{\Pi}=\frac{\partial \mathrm{E}}{\partial \mathrm{F}} One therefore has: \Pi =\mathrm{T}:{\mathrm{P}}_{\Pi} The Cauchy tensor \sigma and the Kirchhoff tensor \tau will be written in the usual way: J\sigma =\tau =\Pi {\mathrm{F}}^{T} The second Piola-Kirchhoff tensor \mathrm{S} can also be computed as a function of \mathrm{T} : {p}_{m}=\mathrm{T}:\dot{\mathrm{E}}=\mathrm{S}:\dot{\Delta}=\mathrm{S}:\frac{1}{2}\dot{\mathrm{C}} With \Delta the Green-Lagrange strain tensor such that: \Delta =\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{I}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left({\mathrm{F}}^{T}\mathrm{F}-\mathrm{I}\right) There is a new form of the mechanical power: {p}_{m}=\mathrm{T}:\dot{\mathrm{E}}=\mathrm{T}:\frac{\partial \mathrm{E}}{\partial \mathrm{C}}:\dot{\mathrm{C}}=\mathrm{S}:\frac{1}{2}\dot{\mathrm{C}} One obtains for the second Piola-Kirchhoff tensor \mathrm{S} : \mathrm{S}=\mathrm{T}:\mathrm{P} If the chosen physics is particular, the model nevertheless makes it possible to retain the additive split of the elastic and plastic strains which is classical under HPP, with: {\mathrm{E}}^{p}=\frac{1}{2}\log({\mathrm{F}}^{p,T}.{\mathrm{F}}^{p}) Such a choice is always admissible. It simply amounts to adopting a definition for the elastic strain. Now, this definition proves consistent with a multiplicative split, in the absence of rotation (coaxial situation). Furthermore, plastic incompressibility is ensured because: \mathit{tr}{\mathrm{E}}^{p}=\log{J}^{p} The elastic energy {\psi}^{e} of the model also takes the same form as that of small strains but, adopting the notions of stress and strain specific to this formalism, one has: {\psi}^{e}=\frac{1}{2}{\parallel \mathrm{E}-{\mathrm{E}}^{p}\parallel }_{E}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{T}:{\mathrm{C}}^{-1}:\mathrm{T} This formulation has certain advantages: - the kinematic dimension of the model is confined upstream and downstream of the integration of the constitutive behaviour; this was one of the main factors in the choice of the formalism; all the constitutive models available in small strains are a priori available, provided of course that this has a physical meaning (hypoelastic large strains are well suited to metallic constitutive behaviours, and not to the constitutive behaviours of concrete); - if the HPP model admits an energetic expression, the same will be true of the large-strain model: the tangent matrix is therefore symmetric; - the only difficulty seems a priori to be concentrated in the definition of the logarithmic strain, but article [13] supplies a computation algorithm distinguishing the difficult cases (multiple eigenentities); - the model, according to the examples presented by the authors, gives results very close to those obtained by a classical formalism with a multiplicative split; - the model can be extended to cases of anisotropy (initial or induced). Moreover, article [13] supplies an expression of the tangent matrix in the configuration using \Pi (called nominal); however, since it is based on a formulation in terms of the first Piola-Kirchhoff stresses, which is non-symmetric, which is not classical and is never carried out in Code_Aster , it is preferred here to use the second Piola-Kirchhoff tensor to compute the internal forces and the tangent matrix on the initial configuration, referring to [15] for example. 3 Algorithm 3.1 Pre-processing > The logarithmic strain tensor computed by spectral decomposition: {\mathrm{E}}_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}\log\left[{\mathrm{F}}_{n+1}^{T}\cdot {\mathrm{F}}_{n+1}\right]=\frac{1}{2}\log{\mathrm{C}}_{n+1} That is to say that, if the {\lambda}^{(i)} are the eigenvalues of {\mathrm{C}}_{n+1} and {N}^{(i)} the associated eigenvectors, then the chosen strain measure is written: {\mathrm{E}}_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1,3}\log({\lambda}^{(i)}){N}^{(i)}\otimes {N}^{(i)} This measure makes it possible to obtain an additive split: \mathrm{E}={\mathrm{E}}^{e}+{\mathrm{E}}^{p} With: {\mathrm{E}}^{p}=\frac{1}{2}\log\left[{\mathrm{F}}^{p,T}\cdot {\mathrm{F}}^{p}\right] One may also write, between time instant n and time instant n+1 : {\mathrm{E}}_{n+1}={\mathrm{E}}_{n}+\Delta \mathrm{E} 3.2 Branching to the HPP constitutive law The HPP constitutive law must supply the stress tensor \mathrm{T} , defined by: {\mathrm{T}}_{n+1}=\widehat{\mathrm{T}}\left(\Delta \mathrm{E};{\mathrm{E}}_{n},{\mathrm{T}}_{n},{\beta}_{n}\right) where {\beta}_{n} represents the set of internal variables at time instant n and {\mathrm{T}}_{n} the stresses at time instant n . {\mathrm{T}}_{n} must therefore be recomputed as a function of the Cauchy stresses {\sigma}_{n} stored at time instant n . These stresses are written {\mathrm{T}}_{n}={\mathrm{S}}_{n}:{\mathrm{P}}_{n}^{\text{-1}} . However, this requires the transformation of {\sigma}_{n} into {\mathrm{S}}_{n} and the computation of {\mathrm{P}}_{n}^{\text{-1}} , which can be costly. It is therefore chosen to store the tensors \mathrm{T} as internal variables. Note The tensors \mathrm{T} being stored as internal variables, the user wishing to impose an initial stress state shall use the operands VARI and DEPL of the factor keyword ETAT_INIT of the command STAT_NON_LINE. Indeed, the stress tensor defined in the logarithmic space \mathrm{T} (and not the Cauchy stress \sigma ) must be given as input. The user wishing to use the GDEF_LOG formalism with an initial stress field (ETAT_INIT) is advised to refer to the test case ssnp159b (V6.03.159). 3.3 Post-processing The second Piola-Kirchhoff stress tensor is obtained by: {\mathrm{S}}_{n+1}={\mathrm{T}}_{n+1}:{\mathrm{P}}_{n+1} With {\mathrm{P}}_{n+1}={\partial}_{\mathrm{C}}\left({\mathrm{E}}_{n+1}\right) . This quantity is computed via an algorithm presented in [13] and recalled in appendix 2. It is also recalled that the Cauchy stress tensor is obtained by: J\sigma =\tau =\mathrm{F}\cdot \mathrm{S}\cdot {\mathrm{F}}^{T}=\mathrm{F}\cdot (\mathrm{T}:\mathrm{P})\cdot {\mathrm{F}}^{T} The tangent modulus, in the so-called "Lagrangian" configuration, is obtained by differentiation of {\mathrm{S}}_{n+1} : {\dot{\mathrm{S}}}_{n+1}={\mathrm{C}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ep}}:\frac{1}{2}{\dot{\mathrm{C}}}_{n+1} {\mathrm{E}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ep}}=\frac{\partial {\mathrm{T}}_{n+1}}{\partial {\mathrm{E}}_{n+1}} represents the tangent operator coming from the constitutive law and {\mathrm{L}}_{n+1} is the sixth-order tensor (in 3D) defined by: {\mathrm{L}}_{n+1}=4{\partial}_{\mathrm{C}\mathrm{C}}^{2}\left({\mathrm{E}}_{n+1}\right) The internal forces and the tangent matrix can then be computed on this configuration, on the initial configuration, as in [14]. Objectivity is preserved (stresses invariant under rotation for isotropic and kinematic hardening) and the accuracy is good (results identical to SIMO_MIEHE in the isotropic case). 4 Validity of the large-strain models It must also be stated that the formalism presented and studied here does not extend the validity of the constitutive laws into the large-strain domain; it only proposes an objective derivation of them. To clarify this statement, the case of an elastoplastic law with linear isotropic hardening may be considered. This type of plasticity law is physically valid in small strains; its use is extended to large strains, but its physical validity may rightly be called into question. Furthermore, an identification carried out on small-strain tests must potentially be reconsidered; Figure 2 presents a tensile curve modelled by a linear isotropic hardening: the tangent modulus must necessarily be defined with respect to the strain range considered. In small strains, it seems more appropriate to use {E}_{\mathrm{T1}} ; if the strains are larger, it seems more appropriate to use {E}_{\mathit{T2}} as the value of the hardening slope. But it is clear that it is the physical validity of the law itself that should be called into question. Figure 2: Identification in large or small strains 5 Comparison with PETIT_REAC 5.1 Approximation of large strains by PETIT_REAC The principle of the PETIT_REAC formulation simply consists in updating the geometry of the problem during the Newton iterations (and not at the end of each time step). This means that all the quantities appearing in the equations of the problem are evaluated on the current configuration. Nothing else is modified relative to the small-perturbation case. 5.1.1 Kinematic description The kinematic description is the same as that of the small perturbations. This means that a strain increment is computed by: \mathrm{\Delta \epsilon }=\frac{1}{2}({\nabla}_{{\Omega}_{i}}(\mathrm{\Delta u})+{\nabla}_{{\Omega}_{i}}^{T}(\mathrm{\Delta u})) {\Omega}_{i} being the updated configuration. The total strain is then the sum of each of these linearised strain increments, computed on different configurations. It is therefore delicate to give it a physical meaning, and it is better to use it as an indicator of the strain level reached. The hypothesis of an additive split of the strains is applied. 5.1.2 Elastoplastic constitutive relation In the expression of the elastic stress–strain relation, the necessity of using an objective derivative has been seen: \mathring{\sigma}=\mathrm{C}:[\dot{\epsilon}-{\dot{\epsilon}}^{p}] . With PETIT_REAC the objective derivative is replaced by the simple time derivative: it is therefore not objective. Consequently, the use of PETIT_REAC is not appropriate for large rotations, but it is appropriate for large strains, under certain conditions [10]: - very small increments; - very small rotations (which implies a quasi-radial loading); - elastic strains small compared with the plastic strains; - isotropic constitutive behaviour. 5.1.3 Equilibrium and tangent matrix In terms of finite elements, the solution by PETIT_REAC implies, at each load step, the solution of the same non-linear system as in small strains [11]: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{L}^{int}\left({u}_{i},{t}_{i}\right)+{B}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}={L}^{\mathit{ext}}({t}_{i})\\ B.{u}_{i}={u}^{d}({t}_{i})\end{array} With the sole difference that the internal forces are formally computed by: {L}^{int}({u}_{i},{t}_{i})={Q}^{T}({u}_{i}):\sigma where the operator Q depends on the displacements. In this framework, the computation of the tangent matrix leads to: {K}_{i}^{n}=\frac{\partial {L}^{int}}{\partial u}{\mid}_{({u}_{i}^{n},{t}_{i})}=Q(u):\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial u}{\mid}_{({u}_{i}^{n},{t}_{i})}+\frac{\partial Q(u)}{\partial u}{\mid}_{({u}_{i}^{n},{t}_{i})}:\sigma The first term is the contribution of the constitutive behaviour, similar to what was presented in small transformations, with the difference that this contribution is here evaluated in the current configuration. The second term is the geometric contribution, which is not present in small transformations. In the framework of the PETIT_REAC solution, this term is not present in the computation of the tangent matrix. One therefore has: {K}_{i}^{n}=Q(u):\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial u}{\mid}_{({u}_{i}^{n},{t}_{i})} The absence of the geometric contribution in the tangent matrix can sometimes make convergence difficult. 5.2 Comparison on an example The PETIT_REAC formalism (cf. [6]) is based on an update of the geometry for the computation of the strain increment, before integrating the constitutive behaviour in the same way as for small strains. This allows a simple treatment of large strains, but in a very approximate and non-objective manner, which can generate large errors. To be convinced of this, consider the alternating tension–rotation of a cube; for more details on the test, refer to [7] for example. Figure 3: Example of tension–rotation of a cube During the rotation phases, the stress must remain constant: a rigid-body motion does not generate stresses (in statics at least, and without viscosity). If the response obtained with a VMIS_ISOT_LINE constitutive behaviour is considered for the PETIT_REAC and GDEF_LOG strains, the PETIT_REAC strain type is shown to be inadequate whereas GDEF_LOG is valid (and supplies a response identical to SIMO_MIEHE). 6 Bibliography 1. r5.03.25 Regularised damage law ENDO_SCALAIRE r5.03.25 Regularised damage law ENDO_SCALAIRE Summary: This document describes the elastic brittle constitutive model ENDO_SCALAIRE, available only for the non-local modelling with a damage gradient GRAD_VARI. The damage is modelled in a scalar manner; the compressive and tensile loadings are not distinguished. Unlike the other damage laws introduced previously, this one behaves in a regular manner (no snap-back, finite elongation at fracture) at least in the one-dimensional cases. 1 Field of application The law ENDO_SCALAIRE belongs to a broad family of damage laws. It aims in particular to model an elastic brittle constitutive behaviour in a non-local version (GRAD_VARI R5.04.01 ) so that its behaviour, at least in the one-dimensional cases, is regular. The parameters of the law have been chosen in order to ensure both the absence of snap-back in the force-displacement response and the finite elongation of the 1D bar at fracture. The local version of the law is not implemented. The modelled material is isotropic elastic. Its stiffness may decrease irreversibly when the strain energy becomes large, without distinguishing tension from compression. The width of the localisation bands is controlled by a material parameter, entered in the operator DEFI_MATERIAU under the keyword C_GRAD_VARI of the factor keyword NON_LOCAL U4.43.01. Piloting of type PRED_ELAS R5.03.80 appears as the most appropriate mode of control of the loading level. 2 Variational formulation of the damage problem 2.1 Case of a generic law Two equivalent approaches may be used to describe the damage process of a brittle isotropic material. On the one hand, it is possible to derive the damage law within the framework of the generalised standard description. In this case it is necessary to define a free energy of the system, as well as the dissipation potential. The flow rule then establishes the evolution of the internal variables. As, for the description of damage, one needs only a scalar variable, the preceding description is simplified and may be reduced to a variational problem under the constraint of an increase of the damage [bib2]. In order to define a constitutive law with a damage gradient R5.04.01 it is therefore sufficient to express the total free-energy density (elastic+dissipation) as a function of the strain tensor \varepsilon and of the damage variable 0\le a\le 1 . The spatial distribution of the damage is then given by a field a(x) . The free-energy density is in general presented in the following form: \Phi (\varepsilon ,a)=A(a)w(\varepsilon )+\omega (a)+c/2{(
abla a)}^{2} eq 2.1-1 Here c is the non-locality parameter (C_GRAD_VARI), w(\varepsilon ) the elastic strain energy, \omega (a) the dissipation energy and A(a) the stiffness function. a=0 corresponds to the sound material and a=1 corresponds to the fully damaged material: A(1)=0,A(0)=1 . The evolution problem is henceforth a simple problem of minimisation of the Helmholtz free energy F\equiv \int\Phi (\varepsilon ,a)d\Omega under the constraint \dot{a}\ge 0 1 . {\min}_{(\varepsilon ,a)}F(\varepsilon ,a),	ext{où}F(\varepsilon ,a)=\int\left[A(a)\varepsilon :E:\varepsilon +\omega (a)+c/2{(
abla a)}^{2}ight]d\Omega where one has replaced w(\varepsilon )=\varepsilon :E:\varepsilon /2 by using the definition of the Hooke tensor. Two equations derive from the variational minimisation problem: \delta F(\varepsilon ,a)/\delta \varepsilon =0 2 and \delta F(\varepsilon ,a)/\delta a\ge 0 . The inequality in the second equation is linked to the presence of an imposed constraint. These two equations must be satisfied everywhere in the domain of integration \Omega . They are supplemented by a Kuhn-Tucker consistency equation \dot{a}\cdot \delta F(\varepsilon ,a)/\delta a=0 . On the boundaries \partial \Omega we obtain an additional normality condition 
abla a\cdot n=0 , where n is a normal vector. Finally, the damage variable and its gradient must be continuous inside the domain of integration in order to realise the minimum of the functional in question (see [bib2,4] for more details). 2.2 Constitutive relations The link between the variational formulation and the usual evolution laws is direct. The state of the material is characterised by the strain \varepsilon and the damage a , lying between 0 and 1. One defines the stress-strain relation, which remains elastic, and the stiffness is affected by the damage: \sigma =\delta F(\varepsilon ,a)/\delta \varepsilon =A(a)E:\varepsilon eq 2.2-1 with E the Hooke tensor. The evolution of the damage, always increasing, is governed by the following threshold function: f(\varepsilon ,a)=-\delta \Phi (\varepsilon ,a)/\delta a=- rac{1}{2}A'(a)\varepsilon :E:\varepsilon -\omega '(a)+c\Delta a eq 2.2-2 The consistency condition then takes its usual form: f(\varepsilon ,a)\le 0\dot{a}\ge 0\dot{a}f(\varepsilon ,a)=0 eq 2.2-3 One notes two particular features of this formulation. Firstly, the threshold function is non-local because of the presence of the Laplacian of the damage. Next, the absence of a flow condition is justified by the dual role of the damage a : on the one hand it appears as an internal evolution variable, on the other hand it fulfils the role of the Lagrange parameter \lambda \equiv a . r5.03.27 Mechanical behaviours for numerical simulations r5.03.27 Mechanical behaviours for numerical simulations Summary: The behaviour of the material is an essential input datum in most mechanical studies. In a numerical simulation this behaviour is taken into account by means of a model of greater or lesser complexity, assumed to reproduce sufficiently accurately the behaviour of the real material. The parameters controlling the model will have been adjusted beforehand from experimental data. Since every model is a simplified and inexact representation of reality, it is essential to ensure that the choices of formulation, and the set of parameters chosen, are relevant for the whole domain of loadings characterising the study. As soon as one leaves the simple cases in which a linear elastic behaviour or a plastic behaviour with isotropic hardening is sufficient, the choice of a constitutive model and its calibration for a given material is a long and delicate process, which requires relevant experimental data that are not always easy to collect. This document is complementary to U2.04.03, which gives advice to a user wishing to carry out analyses with non-linear behaviours of elastoplastic or elastoviscoplastic type, in order to choose a law suited to the modellings envisaged. 1 Some reminders on mechanical behaviour In mechanics, the term “constitutive law” may be used to group the models which govern the relation between the local states of stress and of strain, possibly taking previous states into account. Before discussing constitutive laws, it seems useful to recall briefly the main phenomena that may be encountered in terms of the behaviour of materials, with particular emphasis on the behaviour of metallic materials. In order to go further into the subject, the reader may refer to various reference works in the field, notably [bib2] and [bib3]. 1.1 Elasticity and plasticity The simplest constitutive law is linear elasticity, which corresponds to the ability of the material to recover its original shape when the loading is removed. The constitutive law which represents linear elasticity corresponds to a relation of proportionality between the stresses and the strains. For a large number of materials, elasticity may be considered as isotropic (the coefficient of proportionality is the same whatever the direction of loading). Certain materials (single crystals, textured materials), however, present elastic characteristics which differ according to the direction of loading. Certain materials, such as elastomers, possess a non-linear elastic behaviour. In this case, the stresses and the strains are no longer related by a relation of proportionality; the material nevertheless recovers its initial shape when it is not loaded. For most materials (including metallic materials) a linear elastic behaviour is observed for moderate loadings. When the loading continues to be increased, an irreversible plastic strain is progressively created and the linear relation between stress and strain is lost. Figure 1.1-1: Elastic and plastic behaviours 1.2 Influence of temperature When the same material is loaded mechanically at different temperature levels, an evolution of its response is observed both in the elastic domain and in the plastic domain. Generally, when the temperature increases, the total strain observed is larger for the same stress level. Figure 1.2-1: Influence of temperature 1.3 Viscosity If the same material is loaded at different loading rates, different mechanical responses are generally obtained in the plastic domain. Sensitivity to the loading rate reflects the viscous character of the material. Viscosity manifests itself in different ways according to the type of loading applied. With a monotonically increasing loading, one will be interested in the hardening modulus as a function of the loading rate. A strain step may also be applied to the material, and the progressive decrease of the stress at constant strain then observed. This is referred to as relaxation. A stress step may also be imposed, and a progressive increase of the strain at constant stress observed. This is referred to as creep. It will be noted that viscosity is generally a thermally activated mechanism. It will be all the more significant when the material is at a high temperature. More complex temperature dependencies may sometimes be found. This is for example the case of austenitic stainless steels, which present a significant viscosity at room temperature. This viscosity decreases as the temperature rises and becomes practically zero around 350°C , then it reappears and grows rapidly beyond 450°C . Figure 1.3-1: Manifestation of viscosity according to the nature of the loading 1.4 Cyclic behaviour The phenomena described so far are observable with monotonic loadings. When the applied loading is cyclic and the level of applied loading is sufficient to produce a plastic strain of the material, an evolution of the mechanical response is observed over the cycles. Depending on the material considered, this evolution may be of different kinds. Under a cyclic loading with a constant stress amplitude, an accumulation of strain is observed during the first cycles. If the stress amplitude is sufficiently high, strain continues to be accumulated at each cycle. This is referred to as progressive deformation, which may lead to rapid failure of the material. If the applied stress amplitude is more moderate, a stabilisation of the cyclic response is observed. Depending on the material (and the loading amplitude), the stabilisation may be of two types. If the stabilised cycle exhibits plasticity, one speaks of accommodation of the material. If the stabilised cycle is entirely elastic, one speaks of adaptation. Figure 1.4-1: Stabilisation of the cyclic response of the material Under cyclic loading, an evolution of the envelope of the loading path is generally observed over the cycles, as a result of an accumulation of hardening. Materials may be classified into two categories: 1. Softening materials, when the stress amplitude decreases for a loading at constant strain amplitude, or when the strain amplitude increases for a loading at constant stress amplitude. 2. Hardening materials, when the stress amplitude increases over the cycles for a loading at constant strain amplitude, or whose strain amplitude decreases for a loading at constant stress amplitude. Figure 1.4-2: Cyclic hardening and softening When the loading amplitude is constant, the phenomena of hardening or softening tend to die away with the accumulation of cycles, until a stabilisation of the response of the material is reached. If the material exhibits viscosity, the response of the material to a cyclic loading will depend on the loading rate. 1.5 Static recovery Certain materials also present a sensitivity to time in the case of a loading with plastification followed by an unloading and then a reloading. If the material is left at rest for some time before the second loading is applied, a recovery phenomenon is sometimes observed. Figure 1.5-1: The recovery phenomenon If the reloading is carried out immediately after the unloading, an elastic behaviour is observed until the maximum stress level before unloading is reached, and the response curve of the material then continues the initial curve before unloading. If the material is sensitive to recovery, and if the material is left at rest before being reloaded, a response of the material is observed which will be intermediate between the initial response of the material and the response obtained on immediate reloading. It is thus found that the material at rest progressively loses the memory of the hardening accumulated during the first loading. 1.6 Memory effect On certain metallic materials, and more particularly alloys with an \mathit{C.F.C.} (face-centred cubic) crystal structure, it is observed that the cyclic behaviour retains the memory of the maximum strain level reached during the life of the material. Figure 1.6-1: The hardening-memory effect Figure 1.6-1 describes the evolution of the stress amplitude as a function of the strain amplitude for a large number of cyclic tests on the same material. When an initially virgin material is loaded, the cyclic consolidation curve marked on the diagram is obtained. If the material is first hardened up to a relatively high strain level and is then cycled with a lower loading, the response corresponds to a “harder” material, as shown by the two curves A and B corresponding to different levels of pre-hardening. 1.7 Additional hardening The mechanical response of the material may sometimes be very different according to whether the loading is uniaxial or non-proportional multiaxial. One then speaks of multiaxial additional hardening. This phenomenon is illustrated by the following two figures. A 316L steel specimen is subjected to a combined loading of alternating tension and torsion (controlled in strain amplitude) with a phase shift of 90° between the two loadings. The stress levels reached (represented by the red points on the right-hand part of the figure) are about twice as high as those which would be reached on a specimen loaded with a radial or uniaxial loading of equivalent strain amplitude. | | | | --- | --- | Figure 1.7-1: Effect of additional hardening under non-radial multiaxial loading This test was simulated with two different constitutive laws. The blue curve corresponds to a constitutive model capable of reproducing the effect of additional hardening. The green curve is obtained with a similar constitutive law from which the account of additional hardening has been removed. The second formulation predicts distinctly lower stress amplitudes, which correspond to the response of the material for a radial loading. 1.8 Isotropic and kinematic hardening When the loading exceeds the yield limit of the material, it has been seen above that plastification is accompanied by a hardening which modifies the subsequent response of the material in the event of unloading or of alternating loading. If one places oneself in stress space, a threshold surface may be defined inside which the material remains elastic. When the loading path reaches this surface, plastic strain appears and the threshold surface adapts in such a way that the loading point remains on the surface as long as there is no unloading. Adaptation of the yield surface may take place in two distinct modes: If the surface expands while remaining centred on the origin (which corresponds to a state of zero stress), one speaks of isotropic hardening (see Figure 1.8-1). Isotropic hardening therefore corresponds to a variation in the size of the elastic domain. Figure 1.8-1: Isotropic hardening For a tensile loading followed by an unloading and then a compression, the material will retain an elastic behaviour up to a compressive level equivalent to the maximum loading reached in tension. If the yield surface moves so as to follow the loading, one speaks of kinematic hardening (see Figure 1.8-2). The elastic domain retains a constant size and translates so as to follow the loading. In the case of an alternating tension–compression loading, the elastic domain will correspond to twice the initial yield limit (in the absence of residual stress in the virgin material). Figure 1.8-2: Kinematic hardening The behaviour observed on real materials generally corresponds to a combination of kinematic and isotropic hardening. 2 Taking mechanical behaviour into account in numerical simulations In many cases an isotropic elastic constitutive law is sufficient, for example for a sizing study in which one is generally content to check that the maximum stress does not exceed a threshold value (yield limit, fatigue endurance threshold, etc.). The only behaviour parameters to be defined are Young's modulus E and Poisson's ratio \nu . For anisothermal studies, it is sufficient to replace the scalar parameters E and \nu by functions tabulated in temperature. When it is necessary to take the plastic behaviour of the material into account, the simplest solution is to use directly an experimental uniaxial tensile curve which will have been tabulated beforehand in the form of an evolution of the stress as a function of the strain. In the Code_Aster analysis code, formulations such as VMIS_ISOT_TRAC make it possible, during the solution, to generalise the uniaxial curve to multiaxial loading paths. This type of model has the advantage of a very simple implementation, in so far as one is dispensed from any step of identification of the parameters of a constitutive law, since an experimental tensile curve is used directly. It must however be borne in mind that these models implicitly incorporate the assumption of a purely isotropic behaviour of the material. Figure 2-1: Use of a tensile curve as a constitutive model Although real materials generally present a share of kinematic hardening, the approximation by a purely isotropic behaviour is not necessarily penalising, provided that the loading path at every point of the structure under study satisfies certain conditions specified below. In order to bring out the limits of the isotropic-behaviour assumption, the limiting case is considered of a material whose real hardening behaviour is purely kinematic, and a material point subjected to an increasing then decreasing uniaxial loading is considered. As long as the loading path at every point of the structure remains monotonic, the isotropy assumption has no effect. If a moderate local unloading is obtained, the model remains relevant. However, if the unloading becomes more pronounced, the model will predict an elastic response up to a compressive stress equivalent to the maximum tensile stress reached previously (the response of the model is represented by a solid curve on the figure). The real response of the material is represented by a dashed line. If the real material is purely kinematic, it is found that the onset of plasticity in compression occurs much earlier than predicted by the isotropic constitutive model, and that the discrepancy between the computed stress and the real stress may be significant. Figure 2-2: Discrepancy between isotropic behaviour and real behaviour The illustration presented here corresponds to a very unfavourable situation, notably because a material is assumed whose real behaviour is purely kinematic, but it is important, in any study using this type of behaviour, to be vigilant with respect to this type of error. It must also be emphasised that a small decrease in the global loading may result in a much larger unloading at certain points of the structure. It is therefore desirable to carry out a check on the whole stress field throughout the simulation. Anisothermal simulations are relatively simple with this type of data setup. Several tensile curves corresponding to different temperatures are supplied to the analysis code, and the code takes care of the interpolation in temperature between the various curves. If the study to be carried out requires account to be taken of a behaviour more complex than those addressed at the beginning of this chapter, it is necessary to use a constitutive law based on a mathematical formulation (generally in the form of a differential equation). Several steps are then necessary before carrying out the numerical simulation proper: 1. The choice of the formulation must be made consistently with the physical phenomena that one wishes to take into account. 2. The experimental data relevant to the calibration of the model are collected, with the aim of covering as well as possible the domain of loading undergone by the structure (supplementing them with additional tests if necessary). 3. The parameters of the model are then identified so that the numerical response is as close as possible to the experimental results. It is common to avoid the whole identification process when one has a law and a set of parameters obtained in a comparable study on the same material, or taken from a thesis or a paper. In that case, it is important to bear in mind that, whatever its complexity, a constitutive model offers only a simplified and therefore imperfect reproduction of the reaction of the material. It is usable only over a limited domain of mechanical loading, which generally corresponds to the range of loading covered by the experimental data used for its identification. The reuse of a pre-existing formulation and parameters may therefore prove risky if one does not also have precise information as to the domain of validity of the law that one wishes to use. By way of illustration, figure 2-3 compares the experimental and simulated loading paths for cyclic loadings at different amplitude levels. The constitutive law used was identified over a range of total-strain amplitude lying between \pm 0,2\text{\%} and \pm 0,7\text{\%} (with tests at intermediate loadings of \pm 0,3 and \pm 0,5\text{\%} ). This range of amplitude may therefore be considered a priori as the domain of validity of the law in terms of strain amplitude. The least heavily loaded test was carried out at an amplitude of \pm 0,15\text{\%} . This level is close to the limit of the domain of validity, and the constitutive law appears relevant despite a slight extrapolation. The test at \pm 0,4\text{\%} lies within the domain of validity. The interpolation between the results at \pm 0,3 and \pm 0,5\text{\%} used for the identification proves satisfactory. For the two tests at \pm 1\text{\%} and \pm 1,2\text{\%} , it is found that extrapolating the model towards loading amplitudes distinctly higher than the limit of the domain of validity leads to a significant underestimation of the simulated stress amplitude. It will be retained that knowledge of (and compliance with) the domain of validity of the law implemented are essential ingredients for the quality of the result of a numerical simulation. In the absence of precise information on the domain of validity of a “recycled” law, it is strongly recommended to confront the model with a few well-chosen experimental results before using it in a simulation. Figure 2-4: Estimation of the robustness of a constitutive law in the event of extrapolation outside its domain of validity. For anisothermal simulations, several strategies are possible. The simplest consists in having an isothermal constitutive law for which sets of parameters are identified for several temperature levels. During the simulation, the analysis code will carry out, at each integration point, a linear interpolation in temperature of each parameter of the law, and will then integrate the behaviour on the basis of the interpolated parameters. This solution is entirely satisfactory, provided that one makes sure that the evolution of each parameter as a function of temperature is reasonably regular. A more elegant alternative from the thermodynamic point of view consists in incorporating the effects of temperature directly into the formulation of the constitutive law. This approach may prove a little more complex, but it makes it possible in particular to propose a finer interpolation (and not necessarily a linear one) of the behaviour between the experimental data available at constant temperature. In general, it is important, during an anisothermal simulation, to make sure that the temperature range covered does not include a change of deformation mechanism for the material considered (or a change of phase). If this proves to be the case, the change of mechanism must be taken into account in the constitutive model retained. Other parameters may influence the mechanical behaviour of a material, such as the water content (for certain polymers or for concretes) or irradiation, whose effect on the behaviour at very high dose leads to swelling, an activation of creep and a hardening of the steel. The influence of these parameters is generally incorporated directly into the formulation of specific constitutive laws. 3 Bibliography 1.
