r5.03.28 Gradient damage law ENDO_FISS_EXP r5.03.28 Gradient damage law ENDO_FISS_EXP Summary: This document describes the elastic brittle constitutive model ENDO_FISS_EXP, available in non-local modelling with a damage gradient GRAD_VARI. The damage is modelled there in an isotropic manner, which preferentially implies modelling the cracks individually and not by homogenisation: the scale of discretisation must be suited to this choice. From the phenomenological point of view, the damage criterion is suited to the modelling of concretes, distinguishing in particular the states of tension and of compression. In addition, a restoration of stiffness in compression is introduced in order to reflect crack closure. On the other hand, the model is a priori not suited to modelling the damage of concrete in compression. Finally, it should be noted that the response of the model tends towards that of a cohesive law when the characteristic length becomes small compared with the size of the structure. It follows that the question of identifying this characteristic length does not arise provided that it is sufficiently small. And the model can give access to the quantities of interest of cohesive laws, such as, for example, the crack opening. 1 Field of application 1.1 Purposes The constitutive law ENDO_FISS_EXP , available in the command STAT_NON_LINE , has the objective of describing the quasi-brittle damage of concrete under mechanical tensile loadings. The damage is described there in an isotropic manner, which positions the model to describe the cracks individually and not in a homogenised manner. From the phenomenological point of view, the model aims more particularly to reflect: - the contrast between the elastic limits in tension and in compression, thus avoiding premature damage in compression under prestress, for example; - the specific shape of the damage surface in multiaxial tension, close to a Rankine criterion; - the impact on the stiffness of crack closure in the compression directions, which also reinforces the robustness of the simulations in the presence of surface-breaking cracks. Furthermore, the law ENDO_FISS_EXP falls within the framework of non-local models with an internal-variable gradient (modelling _GRAD_VARI ). The particular form of the law makes it possible to ensure a fundamental property: when the characteristic length of the model tends towards zero (in practice, when it becomes small compared with the characteristic size of the structure studied), the results tend towards those of a cohesive model, well suited to predicting the propagation kinematics and the crack opening. Consequently, except when seeking information at a sub-centimetric scale (which is not advised), the characteristic length does not appear as a parameter to be calibrated but may be fixed directly from the dimensions of the structure studied. The interested reader will find detailed elements on the formulation of the law and its physical validation in the reference [Lorentz, 2016]. 1.2 Material parameters The constitutive law relies on eight internal parameters (including the elastic constants), as will be seen in the presentation of the equations in the following chapter. However, thanks to the consistency with a cohesive law, these internal parameters may be reformulated in terms of quantities more accessible to the engineer. Besides Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, one will enter the tensile and compressive strengths (the latter being less significant for the problems targeted), the fracture energy and two parameters (one of which is optional) in order to describe the shape of the softening response. Finally, the characteristic length will be fixed on the basis of the dimensions of the structure or of the component studied. The command DEFI_MATER_GC takes charge of the transformation of these engineering parameters into internal characteristics of the law and replaces the command DEFI_MATERIAU. 1.3 Internal variables The degree of damage a, lying between 0 for a sound material and 1 for a fully damaged material, constitutes a priori the only internal variable of interest to the user. It is stored in first position (V1) in the table of internal variables stored by the code. By way of post-processing, component V3 corresponds to the impact of this level of damage on the stiffness in tension, namely A(a) . Finally, for information, questions of performance and of numerical robustness lead one also to archive, in the field VARI_ELGA, the state of the current time step in component V2 (0=elastic, 1=damaging, 2=saturated) as well as the level of strain reached at the end of the time step in components V4 to V9 (where the shear components are assigned a factor \sqrt{(2)} ). 2 Continuous model All the equations of the model are gathered in the table . The link between the internal parameters of the model and the quantities more accessible to the engineer is also specified there. The modelling choices call for a few remarks, which are set out below. Table 2-1: Equations of the continuous model 2.1 Stress–strain relation The function A(a) which enters into the stress–strain relation measures the impact of the level of damage on the residual stiffness (in tension). Its particular form is guided by consistency with a cohesive law. It plays the same role as the more classical form (1- a ) used in a number of models in the literature. Furthermore, in order to take account of the restoration of stiffness in compression, the elasticity law is no longer linear, even though it remains hyperelastic ( i.e. it derives from an energy) so as to avoid any spurious production or consumption of energy. It is similar to the formulation adopted for the law ENDO_ISOT_BETON R7.01.04; it takes account not only of the sign of the principal strains but also of that of the trace of the strains. From the practical point of view, it is therefore necessary to determine the eigenvalues of the strain tensor. Finally, in order to improve the robustness of the model and the convergence of the analysis, the jump in stiffness at the tension–compression transition has been regularised, by means of the infinitely differentiable function S(x) . It ensures a progressive transition between a zero value and a quadratic function; the rapidity (or abruptness) of the transition is controlled there by the parameter \gamma . A default value is proposed in the command DEFI_MATER_GC, which stipulates that 90% of the stiffness without regularisation is recovered for a strain (in compression) of the order of \mathit{fc}/E . 2.2 Evolution of the damage The presence of a term in the Laplacian of the damage in the threshold function, as well as a boundary condition on the damage field of zero-normal-gradient type on the boundary, reflects the non-local character of the model. More precisely, this corresponds to the non-local formulation with an internal-variable gradient as introduced in the booklet R5.04.01. From the numerical point of view, it allows an (almost) classical treatment of the constitutive law. However, the choice of a phenomenologically acceptable damage surface leads one to give up the existence of a single energy functional to describe the whole set of equations of the problem. Here, the evolution of the damage and the equilibrium of the structure result from the minimisation of two distinct energy functionals. From the practical point of view, the tangent operator is then no longer symmetric. 3 Numerical integration 3.1 Discretised equations The discretisation in time of the constitutive equations relies on an implicit Euler scheme, that is to say that the various variables of the problem are expressed at the final time instant of the time step. The expression of the stress at the end of the time step thus obeys the same relation as that in the table, the strain and the damage likewise being expressed there at the end of the time step. There remains the delicate part, which consists in computing the evolution of the damage. Integrating the damage-evolution equation is a problem which is admittedly scalar but non-linear. First of all, following the solution procedure proposed in [Lorentz and Godard, 2011] and taken up in the booklet R5.04.01, a term affine in the damage comes to replace the Laplacian term of the damage field in the threshold function g : \tilde{g}(a)=-A'(a)\Gamma (\epsilon )+\lambda +r(\alpha -a)-k At the stage of integration of the constitutive law, the quantities k and \alpha are considered known (as is the positive penalty coefficient r ), in the same way as the strains at the end of the time step, because they are expressed as a function of the nodal unknowns of the problem. Likewise, the value of the function \Gamma (\epsilon ) is also known, even though its computation also requires the solution of a non-linear equation, to which one will return further on. This is why the algorithmic threshold function above depends only on a . In the end, the problem to be solved consists in finding a\le 1 such that: \Delta a\ge 0\phantom{\rule{3em}{0ex}};\phantom{\rule{3em}{0ex}}\tilde{g}(a)\le 0\phantom{\rule{3em}{0ex}};\phantom{\rule{3em}{0ex}}\Delta a\tilde{g}(a)=0 where \Delta a=a–{a}_{n} denotes the damage increment during the time step. And if there exists no solution (less than 1 ), then a=1 (saturated damage). 3.2 Solution of the algorithmic evolution equation Since A is convex, \Gamma (\epsilon ) positive and r positive, the algorithmic threshold function is decreasing. There is therefore existence and uniqueness of the solution (important for the robustness of the numerical integration). In practice, one solves the problem in three stages: - If \tilde{g}({a}_{n})\le 0 then a={a}_{n} - If \tilde{g}(1)\ge 0 then a=1 - Otherwise solve \tilde{g}(a)=0 with {a}_{n}\le a\le 1 by a Newton method with controlled bounds 3.3 Effective computation of the gamma function According to the table , the computation of \Gamma (\epsilon ) refers to that of \chi (\epsilon ) , which is defined only implicitly: one must therefore solve a non-linear equation which is known to admit a unique solution, cf. [Lorentz, 2016]. For this purpose, one begins by introducing a few notations and a change of variable in which x is the new unknown: {\sigma}^{e}=\lambda \mathit{tr}(\epsilon )\mathit{Id}+2\mu \epsilon The space of the tensor s is generated by: \mathit{span}(s)=\lbrace {s}_{1},{s}_{2},{s}_{3}\rbrace With: {s}_{\beta}=\parallel s+({\beta}_{0}-\frac{1}{3})\mathit{tr}(s)\mathit{Id}\parallel The equation to be solved in order to determine x and therefore {\rm X} is thus written: {s}_{\beta}x+\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{3}\exp(2{s}_{i}x)}-{\gamma}_{0}=0 The left-hand side is convex. One estimates an upper bound {x}_{0} of the solution, then one solves the equation by a Newton method starting from {x}_{0} , which leads to a sequence of decreasing values which converge towards the solution of the equation by virtue of the convexity announced. It should be noted that the upper bound is obtained by one or the other of the two following relations, where {s}_{M} denotes the largest of the three eigenvalues of s : {s}_{\beta}x+\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{3}\exp(2{s}_{i}x)}\ge {s}_{\beta}x\Rightarrow x\le \frac{{\gamma}_{0}}{{s}_{\beta}} Or: {s}_{\beta}x+\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{3}\exp(2{s}_{i}x)}\ge \exp({s}_{M}x)\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\Rightarrow \phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}x\le \frac{\ln{\gamma}_{0}}{{s}_{M}} One will take the smaller of the two upper bounds for the sake of performance (or the only one if {s}_{M}\le 0 ). 3.4 Tangent matrix Determining the tangent matrix consistent with the chosen integration scheme raises no particular difficulty (differentiation of composite functions and differentiation of implicit functions) except that the eigenvalues of the strain enter into the computation of \Gamma (\epsilon ) and into that of the elastic law at the moment of distinguishing tension from compression. We examine here each of these points more precisely, with a view to dispensing with the derivative of the associated eigenvectors which, it is recalled, are not defined when the eigenvalues are not distinct. For the derivative of \Gamma (\epsilon ) , only the term which associates with x the norm of \exp(xs) requires a particular treatment. Now: \delta \parallel \exp(xs)\parallel =\frac{\delta \exp(xs):\exp(xs)}{\parallel \exp(xs)\parallel }=\parallel \exp(xs)\parallel \delta x+\frac{\exp(xs)}{\parallel \exp(xs)\parallel }:\exp'(xs):(x\delta s) At this stage, even though the derivative of the exponential (a fourth-order tensor) appears formally in the expression, it is not useful actually to carry out the differentiation. Indeed, the derivative of the exponential is symmetric because it is the derivative of the following isotropic scalar function (cf. [Silhavy, 2000] for the differentiability properties): f(S)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}{e}^{{A}_{i}} And therefore: \exp(A):\exp'(A)=\exp'(A):\exp(A)=\exp(2A) This last result is easily shown by noting that A and \exp(A) commute. In the end, the computation of the tangent matrix will pass through that of the tensor exponential, according to the relation above, without any need to differentiate the eigenvectors. And for the computation of the tensor exponential, one will rely on the method known as "scaling and squaring", see for example [Higham, 2005], which dispenses with the computation of the eigenvectors. As regards the stress–strain relation, it exhibits a trace term which poses no particular differentiation problem and an infinitely differentiable functional relation between the principal stress {\sigma}_{i} and the principal strain {\epsilon}_{i} . For the latter, one enters the framework of the derivative of tensor functions based on a scalar function of the eigenvalues: the article [Carlson and Hoger, 1986] then supplies the expressions of the (tensor) derivative whether the eigenvalues are distinct or not. 4 Description of the versions of the document | Version Aster | Author(s) Organisation(s) | Description of the modifications | | --- | --- | --- | | 13.2 | E.LORENTZ, EDF-R&D/AMA | Initial text | 5 Bibliography - Carlson D. r5.03.29 Plastic and viscoplastic ductile-damage constitutive laws GTN and VISC_GTN r5.03.29 Plastic and viscoplastic ductile-damage constitutive laws GTN and VISC_GTN Summary: This document describes the ductile damage model of Gurson – Tvergaard – Needleman (GTN). It is available in a local version and with a gradient of internal variables (GRAD_VARI or GRAD_INCO). The modelling of large strains is accessible via the GDEF_LOG kinematics. The constitutive behaviour can be time-independent (GTN) or viscoplastic (VISC_GTN). In the latter case, plasticity evolves according to a Norton model in which the threshold function appears. 1 Scope of application 1.1 Purpose Ductile damage of metallic materials results, broadly, from three mechanisms: the nucleation of cavities, their growth within an elastoplastic matrix and their coalescence. [Gurson, 1977] proposed a constitutive model of micromechanical inspiration able to account in a simple manner for the growth of cavities. It was completed in a phenomenological manner in [Tvergaard & Needleman, 1984] in order also to represent the stages of nucleation and coalescence: one then speaks of the GTN model. The evolution of the porosity (volume of the cavities relative to the total volume) results in a softening of the material, that is to say a decrease in the capacity to resist stresses. This often results in a localisation of the strains and of the porosity in bands of small thickness. The strong gradients which result then require an extension of the constitutive law in order to take distant interactions into account: one speaks of non-local formulations of the constitutive behaviour. Such an extension has been proposed for the GTN model [Zhang et al., 2018], which relies on the gradient of the hardening internal variable (GRAD_VARI, GRAD_INCO) according to [Lorentz & Andrieux, 1999]. This is the formulation introduced in code_aster. These phenomena generally take place at strain levels which require a non-linear kinematics. Here, it relies on the logarithmic strain (GDEF_LOG). Furthermore, at these strain levels, plasticity first induces a quasi-incompressible constitutive behaviour. In order to avoid the problems of numerical locking which may result, the use of a mixed formulation (GRAD_INCO) is recommended, possibly completed by a penalty term. The model is however also available in small strains (PETIT) as well as in the absence of a mixed formulation (GRAD_VARI), or even in a local formulation of the constitutive behaviour (standard finite elements). The rate effects of the loading can be taken into account through a viscoplastic formulation based on a Norton law (VISC_GTN), or else ignored (GTN). Let us add that viscous regularisation R5.03.34 is also recommended in order to stabilise the behaviour of fully broken points and therefore without resistance to stress. Finally, let us state that the elastic part of the model is expressed explicitly, that is to say that the stress is expressed as a function of the strain and of the plastic strain in the current state. There is therefore no incremental evolution of the stress; it does not contribute to defining the mechanical state of the system, it is a consequence of it. Note: for a point broken in the viscoplastic regime, the stress does not vanish instantaneously but it no longer depends on the strain, as will be seen later. In this very particular case, the evolution of the stress is purely incremental, which justifies the stress appearing (from the programming point of view) among the internal variables. On the other hand, it is not useful to supply it in the initial state given in STAT_NON_LINE/ETAT_INIT by SIGM; this value is ignored. 1.2 Material parameters The modular expression of the constitutive relation makes it possible to group the various parameters of the model by categories: - the elastic part is isotropic and depends on Young's modulus E and on Poisson's ratio 
u defined under the factor keyword ELAS (E, NU) of the command DEFI_MATERIAU; - the parameters of the isotropic hardening are defined under the factor keyword ECRO_NL (R0, RH, R1, GAMMA_1, R2, GAMMA_2, RK, P0, GAMMA_K). r5.03.31 Constitutive law FONDATION r5.03.31 Constitutive law FONDATION Summary: This document describes the non-linear elastoplastic behaviour of a rectangular shallow foundation subjected to a static or seismic three-dimensional loading. This constitutive law is assigned to 3D discrete elements made up of a single node in translation/rotation (DIS_TR) assigned a diagonal stiffness matrix (K_TR_D_N) by means of the relation FONDATION called by the operators for solving non-linear problems STAT_NON_LINE R5.03.01 or DYNA_NON_LINE R5.05.05. The keyword for defining the characteristics of the material in DEFI_MATERIAU is FONDA_SUPERFI. The law represents both the sliding mechanism, the mechanism of loss of bearing capacity and the mechanism of uplift of the foundation. Before one of the previously mentioned mechanisms comes into play, all the loading directions present a linear elastic behaviour described by classical stiffness characteristics. Three mechanisms, which can combine, are distinguished in the constitutive law: - the first representing the sliding between the underside of the foundation and the soil (treated as a plastic mechanism with hardening); - the second representing the phenomenon of loss of bearing capacity under the effect of too large a vertical load (treated, here too, as a plastic mechanism with hardening); - the third representing the phenomenon of uplift–re-contact of the foundation under the effect of a large moment (treated as a non-linear elastic mechanism). This matrix must be symmetric and diagonal in its local frame (the non-diagonal terms are ignored). The first stage consists, starting from the global force {F}^{O} at the beginning of the time step, in computing the tangent elastic rotational stiffness along x {K}_{\mathit{rx},\mathit{rx}}^{tan,o} and y {K}_{\mathit{ry},\mathit{ry}}^{tan,o} with the formulation seen in [§ 1.4 ]; one thus obtains the tangent elastic stiffness matrix: {K}_{élas}^{o,tan}=\left(\begin{array}{cccccc}{K}_{xx}^{ini}& 0& 0& 0& 0& 0\\ 0& {K}_{yy}^{ini}& 0& 0& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& {K}_{zz}^{ini}& 0& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& 0& {K}_{\mathit{rx},\mathit{rx}}^{tan,o}& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& 0& 0& {K}_{\mathit{ry},\mathit{ry}}^{tan,o}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0& 0& 0& {K}_{\mathit{rz},\mathit{rz}}^{ini}\end{array}\right) 2.1.3 Elastic trial From the tangent elastic stiffness matrix, one computes the force {F}^{élas}={}^{T}\left({F}_{x}^{élas},{F}_{y}^{élas},{F}_{z}^{élas},{M}_{x}^{élas},{M}_{y}^{élas},{M}_{z}^{élas}\right) which would be obtained if no plasticity mechanism is activated (also called “elastic trial”). That is: {F}^{élas}={F}^{O}+{K}_{élas}^{O,tan}\cdot \left({U}^{F}-{U}^{O}\right) 2.1.4 Computation of the plastic flow One now computes {f}_{\mathit{CP}}\left({F}^{élas},{Q}_{\mathit{CP}}^{O}\right) and {f}_{s}\left({F}^{élas},{Q}_{sl}^{O}\right) , see § 1.3 and § 1.2 . 2.1.4.1 If {f}_{\mathit{CP}}\le 0 et > Then no plasticity mechanism is reached, the foundation is in the elastic domain, the elastic trial corresponds to the force at the end of the time step: {F}^{F}={F}^{élas} and no plasticity variable changes: {Q}_{sl}^{F}={Q}_{sl}^{O}\text{ },{U}_{sl}^{F}={U}_{sl}^{O},{v}_{x,s}^{pl,F}={v}_{x,s}^{pl,O},{v}_{y,s}^{pl,F}={v}_{y,s}^{pl,O},\text{ }{Q}_{\mathit{CP}}^{F}={Q}_{\mathit{CP}}^{O}\text{ },{U}_{\mathit{CP}}^{F}={U}_{\mathit{CP}}^{O}\text{ }et\text{ }{v}_{z,\mathit{CP}}^{pl,F}={v}_{z,\mathit{CP}}^{pl,O} Figure 2.1-1: Illustration of the elastic trial without a failure mechanism being reached 2.1.4.2 If {f}_{\mathit{CP}}>0 et > Only the bearing-capacity loss mechanism is reached; r5.03.32 Constitutive law of the ASSE_CORN assembly r5.03.32 Constitutive law of the ASSE_CORN assembly Summary: This document describes the non-linear behaviour of the non-linear angle assemblies of pylons modelled by discrete elements DIS_TR. This constitutive law is assigned to the discrete elements by means of the relation ASSE_CORN, called by the operators for the solution of non-linear problems STAT_NON_LINE R5.03.01 or DYNA_NON_LINE R5.05.05. The law represents both the tensile behaviour of the assembly and the moment–rotation relation about the axis of the bolts perpendicular to the assembly. The other loading directions exhibit a linear elastic behaviour described by classical stiffness characteristics. Two phases, associated with two mechanisms, are distinguished in the constitutive law: the first represents the friction and the slip of the bolts up to the stop, and the second represents the plastification of the assembly up to failure. The plastic-type laws describing each of these phases have the same shape and present a concavity at their junction which makes convergence problematic and requires a particular numerical treatment in (gusset or cover plate), by bolts is shown schematically in [Figure 2-a]. Figure 2-a: local frame of the connection; the axis x coincides with the axis of the bar and the axis y coincides with the axis of the bolts The unidirectional behaviour of the assembly is modelled for tensile or flexural loading. The modelling adopted for the unidirectional behaviour under loading of the assembly subjected to a normal force or to a moment about y is represented by [Figure 2-b]. Figure 2-b: assembly mechanisms in normal force and moment Two phases of the behaviour, associated with two mechanisms, are distinguished: | mechanism 1: | friction and slip up to the stop (onset of shear of the bolts). | | --- | --- | | mechanism 2: | plastification of the assembly up to failure by shear of the bolts or tearing-out of the edge distances. | The friction limit surface (SLF) is the curve corresponding to the onset of slip in the spaces ({N}_{x}-{U}_{x}) and ({M}_{y}-{\theta}_{y}) . Friction is described by Coulomb's law. The ultimate limit surface (SLU) is the curve corresponding to failure of the assembly in the spaces ({N}_{x}-{U}_{x}) and ({M}_{y}-{\theta}_{y}) . Failure may be due, depending on the design of the assembly, to shear of the bolts or to tearing-out of the edge distances. Tests on the same geometry but with different bolt tightening torques show that the tangent stiffness of mechanism 2 at the stop point decreases as the SLF approaches the SLU. This justifies the physical modelling adopted for the assembly of the two mechanisms [Figure 2-b]. 3 Constitutive relation of the mechanisms The behaviour of mechanisms 1 and 2 is similar. It is non-linear, between an initially rigid tangent behaviour and an asymptotic limit behaviour. It is described by two essential parameters: the non-linearity parameter and the limit-surface parameter. The problem is that the junction between the mechanisms of the assembly law, on the constitutive law, presents a positive concavity (cf. [Figure 2-b]) which makes convergence problematic when, during a loading step, one passes from one mechanism to the other. In the subroutine TE0041, which computes, for each load increment, the elementary tangent stiffness matrix of a discrete finite element with 2 nodes possessing degrees of freedom in translation and in rotation, it proved necessary, in order to converge, to compute a secant stiffness directed from the initial state of zero force and displacement towards the state, at the end of the loading step, consisting of the imposed force and the corresponding displacement on the equilibrium curve of the constitutive law. For that purpose it was necessary, which was unusual at the level of this option, to know the internal iteration number of the numerical procedure computing the loading step, and then to estimate the force imposed on the element at the end of this step. Indeed, if one denotes by {F}^{+} the force imposed at the level of an element (unknown a priori, since only the assembled forces are known), by {U}^{+} the corresponding displacement on the equilibrium curve, and, for iteration i , the respective values U(i),F(i),Ks(i) of the displacement, of the force and of the secant matrix — standing in for the tangent matrix — computed at the end of the iteration, one knows on entry to the aforementioned subroutine only {U}^{i} , and the values at the beginning of the loading step F(0) and U(0) , because the values at the previous iteration i-1 have not been stored. The problem is that in this first iteration, the imposed displacement U(1) is different from the final displacement to be computed {U}^{+} in equilibrium with {F}^{+} , which is henceforth known (to within the equilibrium test of the previous loading step). The force computed at the end of this iteration F(1) must therefore likewise be different from {F}^{+} and such that F(1)={K}_{s}(1).U(1) , so that, starting from the pair U(1) and F(1) , one points with the secant {K}_{s}(1) at the pair {U}^{+} and {F}^{+} . One thus obtains at the beginning of iteration 2 a displacement U(2) very close to {U}^{+} , and one can then compute by the equilibrium relation F(2) , likewise very close to {F}^{+} , as well as the secant stiffness {K}_{s}(2)=F(2)/U(2) . If one has converged exactly at the previous loading step, 2 internal iterations are sufficient to converge exactly; otherwise a few additional iterations are required in order to satisfy the equilibrium test on the residual. r5.03.33 Plastic and viscoplastic constitutive laws with non-linear isotropic hardening VMIS_ISOT_NL and VISC_ISOT_NL r5.03.33 Plastic and viscoplastic constitutive laws with non-linear isotropic hardening VMIS_ISOT_NL and VISC_ISOT_NL Summary: This document describes the elastoviscoplastic constitutive model with non-linear isotropic hardening, available in a local version and with a gradient of internal variables (GRAD_VARI or GRAD_INCO). A modelling of large strains is accessible via the kinematics GDEF_LOG. The hardening function accumulates several terms (an affine term, two exponential terms, a power term, a Lüders plateau) capable of covering most of the non-linear responses of a metallic material; each can easily be cancelled, which offers a form of modularity to the constitutive relation (for example: linear hardening, or power-law hardening only). Finally, the behaviour may be independent of time (VMIS_ISOT_NL) or viscoplastic (VISC_ISOT_NL). In the latter case, plasticity evolves according to a Norton model in which the threshold function appears. 1 Domain of application 1.1 Purpose The constitutive law VMIS_ISOT_TRAC makes it possible to account for any form of non-linear isotropic hardening via the stress–strain response in a simple tensile test, given in the form of a sampled function. However, identification of this response may prove simpler if one adopts a predefined function depending on a small number of parameters. The user is then also spared the sampling stage, which is sometimes delicate when the function varies rapidly. The performance of the integration of the constitutive law also benefits, notably when the sampling required would have been particularly fine. This is the whole purpose of the constitutive law VMIS_ISOT_NL (plasticity) or VISC_ISOT_NL (viscoplasticity), dedicated to metallic materials. The hardening function R(\kappa) consists of the assembly of several elementary terms: R(\kappa) = \left \lbrace  egin{array}{cc} \widehat{R}(\varepsilon_{L}^{p})& 	ext{si }\kappa \le \varepsilon_{L}^{p}\ \widehat{R}(\kappa)& 	ext{si }\kappa \ge \varepsilon_{L}^{p} \end{array} ight. where \kappa denotes the hardening variable (which generally coincides with the accumulated plastic strain), \varepsilon_{L}^{p} fixes the limit of the Lüders plateau (zero in the absence of a plateau) and: \widehat{R}(\kappa) = {R}_{0} + {R}_{H}\kappa + {R}_{1}(1-{e}^{-{\gamma}_{1}\kappa }) + {R}_{2}(1-{e}^{-{\gamma}_{2}\kappa }) + {R}_{K}{({p}_{0}+\kappa)}^{{\gamma}_{K}} Cancellation of the affine term, of each exponential term or of the power term is carried out by setting respectively {R}_{H}=0 , {R}_{1}=0 or {R}_{2}=0 and finally {R}_{K}=0 , which makes it possible to obtain a simpler hardening function where appropriate. This constitutive model is compatible: - with a kinematics of small perturbations (HPP) or of large strains (GDEF_LOG); - with a plastic response independent of the loading rate (VMIS_ISOT_NL) or a viscoplastic response (VISC_ISOT_NL) on the basis of a Norton law; - with a local formulation or a formulation with a gradient of an internal variable in which the gradient of the hardening variable appears, cf. [Lorentz & Andrieux, 1999] and [Zhang et al., 2018]. Finally, it should be made clear that the elastic part of the model is expressed explicitly, that is the stress is expressed as a function of the strain and of the plastic strain in the current state. There is therefore no incremental evolution of the stress; it does not contribute to defining the mechanical state of the system, it is a consequence of it (in particular, the stress does not enter the definition of an initial state of the system). Note: > The practical consequence of this formalism is that an initial stress given in ETAT_INIT for STAT_NON_LINE will be ignored. 1.2 Material parameters The modular expression of the constitutive relation makes it possible to group the various parameters of the model by categories: - the elastic part is isotropic and depends on Young's modulus E and on Poisson's ratio 
u , defined under the factor keyword ELAS (E, NU) of the command DEFI_MATERIAU; - the parameters of the isotropic hardening are defined under the factor keyword ECRO_NL (R0, RH, R1, GAMMA_1, R2, GAMMA_2, RK, P0, GAMMA_K, EPSP_LUDERS); - the parameters of the Norton viscosity law, when it is present, are defined under the factor keyword NORTON (coefficient K and exponent N); - in a non-local formulation R5.04.01, the corresponding parameters must also be defined under the factor keyword NON_LOCAL (C_GRAD_VARI and COEF_PENA_LAGR). The parameters may depend on temperature (factor keywords _FO). The constitutive law is expressed in mechanical strains, that is it is compatible with the usual shrinkage terms, notably the thermal strain. 1.3 Internal variables The constitutive law relies on eight internal variables: on the one hand, the hardening level \kappa and the six components of the plastic strain (which it is therefore not useful to compute in post-processing); and on the other hand, for post-processing purposes only, the state of the current time step is also retained, with the values 0 = elastic, 1 = plastic with regular flow, 2 = plastic with singular flow (it will be seen below what this means). At the algorithmic scale of the constitutive law, the piloting introduces a strain affine with respect to \eta , namely \strain=	ensTwo{\strain^0}+\eta\,{\strain^1} where {\strain^0} and {\strain^1} are (tensor) quantities known at this stage. In view of, one then has: \stressCmp^e_{eq}(\eta) = 3\mu\,\Delta p + R(\kappa_n + \Delta p) where the right-hand side is a known quantity. Since \strain is affine in \eta , the same is true of {\stress^e} according to, so that solving reduces to finding the roots of a second-degree polynomial. The solutions \eta of the piloting equation are thus determined (0, 1 or 2 in number). 5 Bibliography Lorentz E., Andrieux S. (1999) A variational formulation for nonlocal damage models. Int. J. Plas. 15, 119-138. Zhang Y., Lorentz E., Besson J. (2018) Ductile damage modelling with locking-free regularised GTN model. Int. J. Numer. Methods Eng. 113, 1871-1903.

r5.03.34 Viscoelastic constitutive law REGU_VISC_ELAS r5.03.34 Viscoelastic constitutive law REGU_VISC_ELAS Summary: In order to regularise certain forms of quasi-static instabilities, a regularisation technique accessible in STAT_NON_LINE via the keyword REGU_VISC relies on the superposition of the constitutive stresses with viscoelastic stresses, the latter being able to confer on the system the expected stabilisation. The constitutive law REGU_VISC_ELAS governs the evolution of these regularisation stresses via a Maxwell model. It is accessible only through this regularisation functionality. 1 Field of application 1.1 Purpose In order to regularise certain forms of quasi-static instabilities, a regularisation technique accessible in STAT_NON_LINE via the keyword REGU_VISC relies on the superposition of the constitutive stresses with viscoelastic stresses, the latter being able to confer on the system the expected stabilisation, see [Lorentz, Drouet, Hamon, 2020]. Provided that sufficient stiffness is supplied, the evolution of the solution then becomes continuous with respect to time and the subdivision of the time step once again constitutes a response to possible convergence difficulties. Such a superposition is described in the figure below, where LDC represents the “true” constitutive law of the material and the Maxwell system of the lower branch corresponds to the viscous stiffness. The constitutive law REGU_VISC_ELAS describes the behaviour of this viscoelastic branch. This constitutive model is compatible: - with a small-perturbation kinematics (HPP) or a large-strain kinematics (GDEF_LOG); - with a local constitutive law or an internal-variable-gradient constitutive law in which the gradient of an internal variable is involved, see [Lorentz & Andrieux, 1999] or R5.04.01. 1.2 Material parameters The viscoelastic model relies on two parameters: the stiffness of the spring, denoted k , and the viscosity of the damper. Rather than entering the latter, it is preferred to introduce the characteristic time of the viscoelastic branch, denoted \tau . These parameters are entered under the factor keyword VISC_ELAS of the command DEFI_MATERIAU (keywords K and TAU). 1.3 Strain measures The constitutive model is fed by the mechanical strain (i.e. without the thermal-shrinkage terms and the others) if such is the case for the main constitutive law. Otherwise, it is the total strain (the displacement gradient). The kinematics PETIT and GDEF_LOG are both supported. The strain will be denoted \epsilon below, without loss of generality. 1.4 Internal variables The constitutive law introduces eight internal variables. They are, on the one hand, the six components of the stress in the viscoelastic branch, which accounts for the history effect of the model. And, on the other hand, two additional variables are computed essentially for post-processing purposes, in order to measure the extent of the viscous effects linked to the regularisation: they are the volumetric elastic energy stored in the spring and the volumetric energy dissipated by viscosity by the damper (accumulated over time). The internal variables are grouped in the following table. The corresponding indices do not correspond to the internal-variable number; indeed, they are stored after the internal variables of the main constitutive law (if the latter relies, for example, on five internal variables, those linked to the viscoelastic regularisation will be available under V6 to V13). | SIVXX - SIVYZ | 1 - 6 | Components of the viscous stress | | --- | --- | --- | | VISCELAS | 7 | Stored volumetric elastic energy | | VISCDISS | 8 | Volumetric energy dissipated by viscosity | 2 Continuous model 2.1 Constitutive equations The Maxwell model is written simply: {\sigma}^{v}=k(\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{v});{\sigma}_{v}=k\tau {\dot{\epsilon}}^{v} where {\sigma}^{v} denotes the viscous stress tensor and {\dot{\epsilon}}^{v} the viscous strain tensor associated with the damper. The viscous strain can be eliminated in order to obtain the evolution equation of the viscous stress: {\dot{\sigma}}^{v}+\frac{1}{\tau}{\sigma}^{v}=k\dot{\epsilon} The default initial state corresponds to a zero viscous stress. 2.2 Definition of the energies The volumetric energy stored in the spring of the viscous branch is: \text{VISCELAS}=\frac{1}{2k}{\sigma}^{v}:{\sigma}^{v} As for the volumetric energy dissipated by viscosity, it is written: \text{VISCDISS}=\frac{1}{k\tau }{\int}_{0}^{t}{\sigma}^{v}:{\sigma}^{v}\mathit{dt} 3 Numerical integration 3.1 Discretised equations The time discretisation of the constitutive equations relies on a first-order scheme. Let {Q}_{n} denote the value of a quantity Q at the beginning of the time step, \Delta Q its increment during the time step and (simply) Q its value at the end of the time step. The mechanical state at the beginning of the time step ({\epsilon}_{n},{{\sigma}^{v}}_{n}) is assumed known, as is the strain increment \Delta \epsilon (and therefore also the strain \epsilon ). The aim is then to compute the stress {\sigma}^{v} at the end of the time step. The discretisation of the stress–strain relation () is written as follows: {\dot{\sigma}}^{v}+\frac{1}{\tau}{\sigma}^{v}=k\frac{\Delta \epsilon }{\Delta t};{\sigma}^{v}({t}_{n})={{\sigma}^{v}}_{n} The right-hand side is then constant, so that the solution of this differential equation is written: {\sigma}^{v}={A}_{\Delta t}{{\sigma}^{v}}_{n}+{B}_{\Delta t}\Delta \epsilon ;{A}_{\Delta t}=\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta t}{\tau}\right);{B}_{\Delta t}=\frac{k\tau }{\Delta t}\left[1-\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta t}{\tau}\right)\right] The computation of the viscous stress is therefore explicit. 3.2 Tangent matrix The derivative of the expression () immediately supplies the tangent matrix: \frac{d{\sigma}^{v}}{d\epsilon }={B}_{\Delta t}{I}_{4} where {I}_{4} denotes the fourth-order identity tensor. From the perspective of a prediction by the tangent matrix, the zeroth-order term of the Taylor expansion of the discretised constitutive law () does not correspond to the viscous stress at the beginning of the time step but to: {\sigma}^{0}={A}_{\Delta t}{{\sigma}^{v}}_{n} This is the stress to be supplied to the option RIGI_MECA_TANG. 3.3 Computation of the energies The stored volumetric energy () is an explicit function of the viscous stresses and poses no difficulty. The volumetric energy dissipated by viscosity () introduces an integral which will be evaluated by a midpoint method (which is compatible with order 1 of the integration scheme of the constitutive law): \text{VISCDISS}:=\text{VISCDISS}+\frac{\Delta t}{k\tau }{\left[\frac{{{\sigma}^{v}}_{n}+{\sigma}^{v}}{2}\right]}^{2} 4 Description of the document versions | Version Aster | Author(s) Organisation(s) | Description of the modifications | | --- | --- | --- | | 15.2 | E.LORENTZ, EDF-R&D/ERMES | Initial text | 5 Bibliography - Lorentz E., Andrieux S. (1999) A variational formulation for nonlocal damage models. Int. J. Plas. 15, 119-138. - Lorentz E., Drouet G., Hamon F. (2020) Numerical stabilisation of a softening constitutive model by viscoelastic regularisation. Internal note EDF R&D 6125-1724-2020-01606.

r5.03.35 Integration of the viscoelastic constitutive relation of Maxwell (VISC_MAXWELL and VISC_MAXWELL_MT) r5.03.35 Integration of the viscoelastic constitutive relation of Maxwell (VISC_MAXWELL and VISC_MAXWELL_MT) Summary This document describes the development of the viscoelastic constitutive law of Maxwell. The Maxwell law (keyword VISC_MAXWELL) is a basic viscoelastic law. Its variant (keyword VISC_MAXWELL_MT) includes a variation of its parameters with porosity according to a Mori-Tanaka homogenisation law. This latter law is therefore available only for the poromechanical models (THM). 1 Introduction The implementation of the Maxwell viscoelasticity model (keyword VISC_MAXWELL) is described here. A variant of this model has been added for poromechanics (keyword VISC_MAXWELL_MT), which provides for the evolution of the parameters with porosity according to a Mori-Tanaka homogenisation model. This law was first developed and used within the framework of the thesis of G. Mélot [ 1 ] on bituminous materials. For each of these models, the material is assumed to be isotropic. They can be used in 3D, in plane strain (D_PLAN) and in axisymmetric conditions (AXIS). This note presents the constitutive equations of the models and their implementation. 2 Continuous relation The assumption of small perturbations and of an isotropic medium is adopted. The Maxwell model is represented by a purely viscous damper and a Hookean spring in series. This model takes into account a volumetric viscosity and a deviatoric viscosity. The equations are then simply: \begin{array}{c}{\dot{\epsilon}}_{v}(t)=\frac{1}{{\eta}_{v}}{\sigma}_{\mathrm{m}}(t)+\frac{1}{K}\dot{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{m}}}(t)\\ \dot{{e}_{ij}}(t)=\frac{1}{{\eta}_{d}}{s}_{ij}(t)+\frac{1}{2G}\dot{{s}_{ij}}(t)\end{array} with: {\epsilon}_{v} : the volumetric strain {\sigma}_{m} : the mean effective stress \sigma =\frac{1}{3}\text{Tr}\left(\sigma \right)I {e}_{ij} : the components of the deviatoric stress tensor {e}_{ij}={\epsilon}_{ij}-\frac{1}{3}{\epsilon}_{v}{\delta}_{ij} {s}_{ij} : the components of the deviatoric effective-stress tensor {s}_{ij}={\sigma}_{ij}-{\sigma}_{m}{\delta}_{ij} K : the bulk modulus G : the shear modulus {\eta}_{v} : the volumetric viscosity {\eta}_{d} : the deviatoric viscosity 3 Evolution of the parameters for the law VISC_MAXWELL_MT The behaviour of a porous medium is strongly affected by the proportion of voids that it contains. For certain materials (for example of bituminous-mix type) whose porosity is going to change considerably, it is important to include this variation in the viscosity. Homogenisation laws make it possible, among other things, to compute the mechanical properties of a porous material from the mechanical properties of the skeleton and from the porosity. The Mori-Tanaka method is appropriate for accounting for the interaction between the pores by modifying the strain boundary conditions at infinity within the framework of the Eshelby problem. In the thesis of G. Melot [ 1 ], this technique is applied, in the case of spherical pores embedded in an isotropic solid matrix, to the elastic part and then to the viscous part. The result is classical in elasticity and gives: \begin{array}{c}{K}^{\mathit{mt}}={K}^{s}\frac{4{G}^{s}(1-\mathrm{\phi })}{3\mathrm{\phi }{K}^{s}+4{G}^{s}}\\ {G}^{\mathit{mt}}={G}^{s}\frac{(1-\mathrm{\phi })(9{K}^{s}+8{G}^{s})}{9{K}^{s}(1+\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{\phi })+8{G}^{s}(1+\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{\phi })}\end{array} With {K}^{\mathit{mt}} and {G}^{\mathit{mt}} the effective parameters of the porous medium, of elasticity and of shear respectively, which will be used in the constitutive law. The mathematical derivation classically carried out in elasticity is then performed for the derivative of the strain tensor in place of the strain tensor. This makes it possible to obtain, in a similar manner, the following equations: \begin{array}{c}{\eta}_{v}^{\mathit{mt}}={\eta}_{v}^{s}\frac{4{\eta}_{d}^{s}(1-\mathrm{\phi })}{3\mathrm{\phi }{\eta}_{v}^{s}+4{\eta}_{d}^{s}}\\ {\eta}_{d}^{\mathit{mt}}={\eta}_{d}^{s}\frac{(1-\mathrm{\phi })(9{\eta}_{v}^{s}+8{\eta}_{d}^{s})}{9{\eta}_{v}^{s}(1+\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{\phi })+8{\eta}_{d}^{s}(1+\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{\phi })}\end{array} With {\eta}_{v}^{\mathit{mt}} and {\eta}_{d}^{\mathit{mt}} the effective viscosity parameters of the porous medium. 4 Integration of the constitutive relation A finite-difference time discretisation is used in order to obtain the expressions of the components of the effective-stress matrix. The calculation steps leading to the results are reproduced below. The following notation is used: \dot{{\sigma}_{{m}_{}}}=\frac{{\sigma}_{{m}_{n+1}}-{{\sigma}_{m}}_{n}}{\mathit{dt}} Where {{\sigma}_{m}}_{n} and {{\sigma}_{m}}_{n+1} are respectively the mean effective stresses at the previous time and at the current time, and dt the time step. Using the time discretisation of \stackrel{´}{{\sigma}_{{m}_{}}} and \stackrel{´}{{s}_{ij}} , the expressions of {\sigma}_{{m}_{n+1}} and of {s}_{i{j}_{n+1}} are sought: \dot{{\epsilon}_{{v}_{n+1}}}=\frac{1}{{\eta}_{v}}{\sigma}_{{m}_{n+1}}+\frac{1}{K}\frac{{\sigma}_{{m}_{n+1}}-{{\sigma}_{m}}_{n}}{\mathit{dt}}=\left(\frac{1}{{\eta}_{v}}+\frac{1}{K\mathit{dt}}\right){\sigma}_{{m}_{n+1}}-\frac{{{\sigma}_{m}}_{n}}{K\mathit{dt}} \dot{{e}_{i{j}_{n+1}}}=\frac{1}{{\eta}_{d}}{s}_{i{j}_{n+1}}^{'}+\frac{1}{2G}\frac{{s}_{i{j}_{n+1}}-{{s}_{ij}}_{n}}{\mathit{dt}}=\left(\frac{1}{{\eta}_{d}}+\frac{1}{2G\mathit{dt}}\right){s}_{i{j}_{n+1}}-\frac{{{s}_{ij}}_{n}}{2G\mathit{dt}} Which is equivalent to: {\sigma}_{{m}_{n+1}}=\left(\dot{{\epsilon}_{{v}_{n+1}}}+\frac{{{\sigma}_{m}}_{n}}{K\mathit{dt}}\right)\frac{K\mathit{dt}{\eta}_{v}}{{\eta}_{v}+K\mathit{dt}} {s}_{i{j}_{n+1}}=\left(\dot{{e}_{i{j}_{n+1}}}+\frac{{{s}_{ij}}_{n}}{2G\mathit{dt}}\right)\frac{2G\mathit{dt}{\eta}_{d}}{{\eta}_{d}+2G\mathit{dt}} Which finally is equivalent to: {\sigma}_{{m}_{n+1}}=\left(\mathit{dt}\dot{{\epsilon}_{{v}_{n+1}}}+\frac{{{\sigma}_{m}}_{n}}{K}\right)\frac{K}{1+\frac{\mathit{Kdt}}{{\eta}_{v}}} {s}_{i{j}_{n+1}}=\left(\mathit{dt}\dot{{e}_{i{j}_{n+1}}}+\frac{{{s}_{ij}}_{n}}{2G}\right)\frac{2G}{1+\frac{2\mathit{Gdt}}{{\eta}_{d}}} which can be written in incremental form: {\sigma}_{{m}_{n+1}}^{'}=\left(\Delta {\epsilon}_{v}(t)+\frac{{{\sigma}_{m}^{'}}_{n}}{K}\right)\frac{K}{1+\frac{\mathit{Kdt}}{{\eta}_{v}}} {s}_{i{j}_{n+1}}^{'}=\left(\Delta {e}_{ij}\left(t\right)+\frac{{{s}_{ij}^{'}}_{n}}{2G}\right)\frac{2G}{1+\frac{2\mathit{Gdt}}{{\eta}_{d}}} 5 Bibliography 1. Mélot, “Poromechanical modelling of the swelling of bituminous mixes by water uptake”, Thesis of the Université Paris-Est (2019) 1. Mori and K. Tanaka, “Average stress in matrix and average elastic energy of materials with misfitting inclusions” Acta metallurgica, vol. 21, n15, pp. 571-574, 1973.

r5.03.37 Homogenisation of periodic heterogeneous structures r5.03.37 Homogenisation of periodic heterogeneous structures Summary: The assumptions and the methods used in the command CALC_MATE_HOMO are set out; this command computes the homogenised linear thermal and thermoelastic properties for periodic heterogeneous structures with a rectangular pitch, with basic cells possessing symmetries with respect to orthogonal planes in Cartesian space. The case with hexagonal symmetry can also be treated. The framework adopted is that of the three-dimensional homogenisation of heterogeneous solids and also that of homogenisation in the theory of heterogeneous plates. A table of the homogenised linear thermal and thermoelastic coefficients is obtained, which may be used to define equivalent orthotropic materials, which may be parameterised by command variables, such as temperature or irradiation. All the thermal and thermoelastic corrector fields are also produced, so as to allow a subsequent use with a view to reconstructing the complete solution localised at the microscopic scale from the macroscopic solution. 1 Introduction Continuous media or heterogeneous structures are considered, whose geometric and/or physical properties vary “rapidly” and periodically in space with respect to the scale of the loadings applied, here with a rectangular pitch. They are therefore characterised by a three-dimensional “basic cell”, also called a “representative elementary volume”, possessing in the framework studied here geometric and material symmetries with respect to orthogonal planes in Cartesian space. One is interested in the “macroscopic” behaviour of these structures, in order to determine the overall response, but one also wishes to return to the “microscopic” scale on a “basic cell”, in order to access quantities of interest at that scale. These may be multi-perforated plates, fibre composites, made up of a repetitive pattern... The objective is to establish the homogenised properties in three-dimensional linear thermal analysis and, depending on the type of heterogeneous structure, cf. , in three-dimensional linear thermoelasticity, cf. , or in linear elasticity of a Love–Kirchhoff plate in bending–membrane, cf. . The “method of averages” is used for this, justified by an asymptotic expansion, cf. . In three-dimensional linear thermal analysis, it is accepted that sufficiently slow transients may be considered for the heterogeneous structure studied, so as to be able to separate the spatial scales as regards the effect of the time derivative of the temperature on the evolution of the macroscopic volumetric enthalpy. The effect of a thermal shock cannot therefore be treated in this way. Indeed, in one-dimensional stationary thermal analysis, under the action of a temperature imposed on the boundary {x=0} at {t=0} the solution is written: T(x,t) = T_{imp} \, \erfc \left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{t \, \frac{K_{cond}}{\rho_{cp}}}}\right) this solution brings out the thermal diffusivity coefficient \frac{K_{cond}}{\rho_{cp}} , which has the dimension of the square of a distance divided by a time. Take for example an ordinary steel of conductivity K_{cond} = 35 \frac{W}{m \cdot K} and heat capacity \rho_{cp} = 3.5 \frac{MJ}{m^3 \cdot K} , with a length of 3~cm ; the time derivative of the temperature becomes very small ( 0.01~\frac{°C}{s} ) beyond a duration of 90~s . This means that taking into account a transient whose duration is shorter will produce a solution that cannot be represented correctly at the homogenised scale for a basic cell of size 3~cm . In thermoelasticity, the following situations are distinguished: - three-dimensional heterogeneous solids, periodic in the three directions of Cartesian space; - slender three-dimensional heterogeneous solids, of plane or curved geometry: plate or shell, periodic in the two directions of the tangent plane. The standard case is adopted, cf. and r5.03.37-fig-introduction, where the periodicity pitch is of the same order of magnitude as the thickness of the plate or of the shell, and where this periodicity pitch is considered to be small compared with the mean curvature of the shell, so as to admit a Cartesian metric in the basic cell. Diagram of a periodic heterogeneous plate: periodicity pitch of the same order of magnitude as the thickness 2 Assumptions The assumptions adopted in the treatment proposed by the command CALC_MATE_HOMO are presented. The three-dimensional heterogeneous solid studied may be: - of arbitrary dimensions in the three spatial directions: a three-dimensional homogenisation is then carried out, cf. , . - slender, with one dimension small compared with the other two, of thin-plate or thin-shell type: a homogenisation is then carried out within the framework of the theory of heterogeneous plates, in Love–Kirchhoff kinematics, in bending–membrane, cf. , . The three-dimensional “basic cell”, or also “representative elementary volume”, corresponds to a periodicity pattern with rectangular pitch, constituting the geometry of the heterogeneous solid studied: - in the three spatial directions, for a three-dimensional homogenisation. The mesh of the three-dimensional basic cell is made up of three-dimensional mesh cells, on which isoparametric solid finite elements P1 or P2 will be assigned. Since the case is restricted to symmetries with respect to the planes of the spatial reference frame, the mesh is limited to the octant of the basic cell (X>0,Y>0,Z>0) ; - in two spatial directions, and over the half-thickness of the plate, along the third spatial direction ( Z ), for a homogenisation of plate or shell type. The mesh of the basic cell is made up of three-dimensional mesh cells, on which isoparametric solid finite elements P1 or P2 will be assigned. The dimension of the basic cell along the third spatial direction is used to define its thickness. It is however possible, in the case of a basic cell of the heterogeneous plate or shell, to treat a situation of a free boundary along the third spatial direction whose thickness is not plane: for this, a fictitious material will be added, with physical properties negligible compared with those of the other parts of the basic cell, in order to “fill” these voids so as to obtain a plane boundary. Since the case is restricted to symmetries with respect to the planes of the spatial reference frame, the mesh is limited to the octant of the basic cell (X>0,Y>0,Z>0) . Cases of periodic type with “hexagonal pitch” can also be treated by defining a periodic and symmetric “sub-cell” with square pitch. The basic cell, denoted C , is therefore bounded by plane boundaries, see r5.03.37-fig-celluleBase. It is made up of subdomains each carrying a given material and possibly one or more unmeshed cavities: see r5.03.37-fig-reseauPeriodique, which may intersect the boundaries of the basic cell. Mesh of a periodic basic cell. Diagram of the heterogeneous structure: positioning of the basic cell on the periodic lattice. The various materials constituting the basic cell are defined by characteristics of density, of isotropic thermal conduction, of heat capacity and of isotropic linear thermoelastic characteristics, which are defined as functions of command variables: temperature, or irradiation. The homogenised constitutive model produced will be, depending on the case: - homogenised three-dimensional non-linear thermal, - homogenised three-dimensional orthotropic linear thermoelasticity, - homogenised linear thermoelasticity in bending–membrane of a Love–Kirchhoff plate, without bending–membrane coupling because of the symmetry with respect to the mid-surface. - homogenised linear thermoelasticity in bending–membrane of a Mindlin plate with transverse shear, without bending–membrane coupling because of the symmetry with respect to the mid-surface. - homogenised linear thermoelasticity in bending–membrane of a Touratier plate with transverse shear, without bending–membrane coupling because of the symmetry with respect to the mid-surface. 3 Methods 3.1 Homogenisation in three-dimensional linear thermal analysis For homogenisation in three-dimensional linear thermal analysis, three thermal corrector fields {\zeta}^{i} are computed, each associated with three unit temperature gradients in each of the three spatial directions, homogeneous in the volume of the three-dimensional basic cell C . Since the mesh of the basic cell is restricted to the octant (X>0,Y>0,Z>0) , the conditions of material and geometric symmetry and of periodicity impose the following Dirichlet conditions: | Corrector | Dirichlet conditions | Wall considered | Imposed temperature gradient g | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | {\zeta}^{1} | T=0 | {x}_{\min} and {x}_{\max} | PRE_GRAD_TEMP=_F(FLUX_X=-1) | | {\zeta}^{2} | T=0 | {y}_{\min} and {y}_{\max} | PRE_GRAD_TEMP=_F(FLUX_Y=-1) | | {\zeta}^{3} | T=0 | {z}_{\min} and {z}_{\max} | PRE_GRAD_TEMP=_F(FLUX_Z=-1) | The three elementary heat-conduction problems on the basic cell C , which provide the three corrector fields, are written in variational form: \begin{array}{c}\text{Trouver }{{\zeta}}^{i}(x,y,z)\in {V}_{\text{pér}} \text{ tel que :}\hfill \\ {\int}_{C}{\tensTwo{K}}\cdot{\zeta}_{,j}^{i}\,{v}_{,j}\,{dV} = -{\int}_{C}{\tensTwo{K}}\cdot{g}_{j}^{i}\,{v}_{,j}\,{dV} \qquad \forall v\in {V}_{\text{pér}} \end{array} \begin{split}\begin{array}{c}\text{Trouver }{{\zeta}}^{i}(x,y,z)\in {V}_{\text{pér}} \text{ tel que :}\hfill \\ {\int}_{C}{\tensTwo{K}}\cdot{\zeta}_{,j}^{i}\,{v}_{,j}\,{dV} = -{\int}_{C}{\tensTwo{K}}\cdot{g}_{j}^{i}\,{v}_{,j}\,{dV} \qquad \forall v\in {V}_{\text{pér}} \end{array}\end{split} the space of admissible periodic fields {V}_{\text{pér}} being restricted here to those satisfying the Dirichlet conditions reported in the table above. Denoting by \vector{z} the position vector in the basic cell C , placed at the macroscopic point {\posi}_{0} , the microscopic temperature field is then written as the sum of the macroscopic temperature field {T}^{0} expanded over the basic cell via its gradient {\vector{g}}^{0}={\gradScal{T^0}} and of the contribution of the correctors: T({\posi}_{0},{\vector{z}}) = {T}^{0}({\posi}_{0}) + {\vector{g}}^{0}({\posi}_{0}) \cdot \vector{z} + \sum_{k}{g}_{k}^{0}({\posi}_{0})\,{{\zeta}}^{k}(\vector{z}) After the three corrector fields have been computed, the spatial average over the basic cell C of the heat capacity and of the isotropic thermal conduction coefficient is carried out. These terms correspond to the “rule of mixtures”, from which the contribution of the correctors is subtracted in order to obtain the components of the homogenised conduction tensor. To do this, the thermal-conduction dissipation energies {W}_{\text{ther}} associated with the linear combinations of the thermal corrector fields are computed; they are deducted from the terms of the rule of mixtures: {\vector{g}}^{0}\cdot {\tensTwo{K}}^{\text{hom}}\cdot {\vector{g}}^{0} = \frac{1}{\valeAbs{C}}\underset{\text{loi des mélanges}}{{\int}_{C} {\vector{g}}^{0}\cdot {\tensTwo{K}} \cdot {\vector{g}}^{0} \, dV} - \frac{1}{\valeAbs{C}}\underset{\text{contribution des correcteurs}}{{\int}_{C}{\gradScal{{\zeta}^{i}}} \cdot {\tensTwo{K}} \cdot {\gradScal{{\zeta}^{j}}}\, dV} with: {{\int}_{C}{\gradScal{{\zeta}^{i}}}\cdot \tensTwo{K}\cdot {\gradScal{{\zeta}^{j}}}\, dV} = {W}_{\text{ther}}({\zeta}^{i}+{\zeta}^{j})-{W}_{\text{ther}}({\zeta}^{i})-{W}_{\text{ther}}({\zeta}^{j}) The components of the orthotropic homogenised conduction tensor are expressed in the axes of the reference frame of the basic cell: {\tensTwo{K}}^{\text{hom}} = \left \lbrack \begin{array}{ccc}{K}_{11}^{\text{hom}}& 0& 0\\ 0& {K}_{22}^{\text{hom}}& 0\\ 0& 0& {K}_{33}^{\text{hom}}\end{array}\right \rbrack \begin{split}{\tensTwo{K}}^{\text{hom}} = \left \lbrack \begin{array}{ccc}{K}_{11}^{\text{hom}}& 0& 0\\ 0& {K}_{22}^{\text{hom}}& 0\\ 0& 0& {K}_{33}^{\text{hom}}\end{array}\right \rbrack\end{split} - The off-diagonal components of this matrix are zero as a result of the symmetries of the basic cell considered. - If the basic cell C has an additional geometric and material symmetry, with respect to a plane making an angle \theta =\pm \frac{\pi}{3},\pm \frac{\pi}{4} with the plane X=0 , or an invariance by rotation \frac{2 \, \pi}{3} about the axis \mathit{OZ} for example, then one will necessarily have {K}_{11}^{\text{hom}}={K}_{22}^{\text{hom}} . Notes 3.2 Homogenisation in three-dimensional linear thermoelasticity For homogenisation in three-dimensional linear thermoelasticity, six elastic corrector fields are computed, each associated with the six components of the symmetric second-order tensor of unit and homogeneous three-dimensional strain {\strain}^{0} in the volume of the three-dimensional basic cell, and one thermal-expansion corrector field, for a strain equal to the expansion coefficient in each subdomain of the three-dimensional basic cell. The mesh of the basic cell is restricted to the octant (X>0,Y>0,Z>0) . This same mesh is used for the underlying analyses and, consequently, the conditions of material and geometric symmetry and of periodicity, cf. , impose the following Dirichlet conditions: | Corrector | Dirichlet conditions | Wall considered | Imposed strain | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | {\chi}_{11} , {\chi}_{22} , {\chi}_{33} {\chi}_{\text{dil}} , {\chi}_{p}^{int} | {U}_{x}=0 | {x}_{\min} and {x}_{\max} | PRE_EPSI=_F(EPXX=-1) PRE_EPSI=_F(EPYY=-1) PRE_EPSI=_F(EPZZ=-1) PRE_EPSI=_F(EPXX=-ALPHA,EPYY=-ALPHA,EPZZ=-ALPHA) | | {U}_{y}=0 | {y}_{\min} and {y}_{\max} | | | | {U}_{z}=0 | {z}_{\min} and {z}_{\max} | | | | {\chi}_{12} | {U}_{y}={U}_{z}=0 | {x}_{\min} and {x}_{\max} | PRE_EPSI=_F(EPXY=-0.5) | | {U}_{x}={U}_{z}=0 | {y}_{\min} and {y}_{\max} | | | | {U}_{z}=0 | {z}_{\min} and {z}_{\max} | | | | {\chi}_{13} | {U}_{y}={U}_{z}=0 | {x}_{\min} and {x}_{\max} | PRE_EPSI=_F(EPXZ=-0.5) | | {U}_{y}=0 | {y}_{\min} and {y}_{\max} | | | | {U}_{x}={U}_{y}=0 | {z}_{\min} and {z}_{\max} | | | | {\chi}_{23} | {U}_{x}=0 | {x}_{\min} and {x}_{\max} | PRE_EPSI=_F(EPYZ=-0.5) | | {U}_{x}={U}_{z}=0 | {y}_{\min} and {y}_{\max} | | | | {U}_{x}={U}_{y}=0 | {z}_{\min} and {z}_{\max} | | | In the case where there is a cavity (or several) within the basic cell, the computation of another elastic corrector field {\chi}_{p}^{int} is also carried out, under the action of a unit pressure exerted within these cavities, so as to have complete access to the stresses at the microscopic scale. The six elementary elasticity problems on the basic cell C , which provide the six corrector fields, are written in variational form: the space of admissible periodic fields {\vector{V}}_{\text{pér}} being restricted here to those satisfying the Dirichlet conditions reported in the table above. The elementary elasticity problem on the basic cell C , which provides the thermal-expansion corrector field, is written in variational form: \begin{split}\left\lbrace \begin{aligned} & \text{Trouver } {\tensTwo{\chi}}_{\text{dil}}(x,y,z)\in {\vector{V}}_{\text{pér}} \text{ tel que : } \\ & {\int}_{C}\strain ({\tensTwo{\chi}}_{\text{dil}})\cdot \tensTwo{A} \cdot \strain (\vector{v})\, dV = -{\int}_{C}\alpha (x,y,z) \, \tensTwoUnit \cdot \tensTwo{A} \cdot \strain (\vector{v})\, dV \qquad \forall \vector{v}\in {\vector{V}}_{\text{pér}} \end{aligned} \right.\end{split} with {\tensTwo{A}} the elasticity tensor. r5.03.38 Isotropic multi-scale elasto-viscoplastic mechanical behaviour under irradiation: applications to irradiated reactor-pressure-vessel steels r5.03.38 Isotropic multi-scale elasto-viscoplastic mechanical behaviour under irradiation: applications to irradiated reactor-pressure-vessel steels Summary: This document presents the formulation of the constitutive law VISC_ISOT_PLAS. It is an isotropic elasto-viscoplastic flow model representing the multi-scale effects of plasticity as well as the effects of irradiation. A large-strain modelling is available through the GDEF_LOG kinematics. The parameters of the model comprise the elastic mechanical characteristics of the material (Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio) as well as the mechanical characteristics of the microstructure of the material considered: grain size and dislocation density for the unirradiated state, together with the concentration and size of the solute clusters for the irradiated state. The latter can be obtained directly from experiment by means of standard tensile tests. The law supplies the von Mises stress as a function of the cumulative (visco)plastic strain. The hardening is entirely isotropic, which restricts the use of the law to monotonic loadings with small unloadings. This modelling, developed mainly for needs specific to EDF, is above all designed to describe the monotonic mechanical behaviour of the steels of the pressure vessels of the French nuclear fleet of type 16MND5 (or of type A508 class 3) in the unirradiated and irradiated states. 1 Introduction The constitutive laws usually available to describe reactor-pressure-vessel steel are empirical in nature, fitted to the experimental behaviour defined at a given temperature, strain rate and irradiation state. Their predictive capability is consequently limited and does not offer a convincing demonstration of the extrapolation of their domain of validity. Multi-scale modelling represents a robust alternative by providing a physical constitutive description for each mechanism involved in plastic strain. In particular, taking into account the thermal activation of dislocation mobility makes it possible to predict, in a natural way, the effect of temperature and of strain rate. The present document describes the integrated equations of the crystalline behaviour, leading to an isotropic polycrystalline law as a function of the local temperature and strain rate of a reactor-pressure-vessel steel characterised by the parameters of its microstructure: grain size and dislocation density for the unirradiated state, together with the concentration and the size of the solute clusters responsible for irradiation hardening for the irradiated state. The law is designed to predict the monotonic behaviour of the steels of the pressure vessels of the French nuclear fleet of type 16MND5 (or of type A508 class 3) in the unirradiated and irradiated states. The parameters specific to each of the steels can be identified from tensile tests. 1.1 Summary of use The elements useful to a user are summarised briefly here. One should refer to the user’s guide for VISC_ISOT_PLAS for further details. First of all, this behaviour is used by default under the small-strain assumption. As for large strains, only the GDEF_LOG formalism is available for this law. Next, the list of material parameters is given, described in detail in the documentation of the keyword VISC_ISOT_PLAS(_FO). | YoungModulus | Young’s modulus, denoted E in what follows (in Pa ) | | --- | --- | | PoissonRatio | Poisson’s ratio, denoted 
u in what follows | | TAILLE_GRAIN | Mean grain size (in m ) | | D_DISLOC | Initial dislocation density (in m^{-2} ) | | C_AMAS | Concentration of the solute clusters (in m^{-3}) | | TAILLE_AMAS | Size of the solute clusters (in m ) | By default, all the physical data of the law are expressed in the International System of Units (SI), and an adaptation is possible when this is not the case for the units of length and of stress. We confine ourselves here to presenting the final constitutive equations and to describing the improvements made to the model since the publication of that article. 2.1 Notation and reminders on viscoplasticity Recall that viscoplasticity denotes the theory of continuum mechanics which makes it possible to describe the anelastic behaviour of a material whose strain depends on the rate at which the loads are applied to the solid under consideration. It is therefore a particular case of plastic behaviour, the material undergoing permanent irreversible strains when a certain load level is reached. However, the plasticity criterion here also depends on the history of the loading (and on its rate), generally through a scalar internal state variable called the equivalent strain. It makes it possible to measure the capacity of the material to harden under the effect of its plastic (permanent) strain without fracturing, independently of the direction chosen. One speaks of isotropic hardening, and the material is described as ductile, as is the case for many metals and alloys. The model involves the temperature explicitly, denoted T \left( ^{\circ} C ight) when it is expressed in degrees Celsius or T \left( K ight) in kelvin. r5.03.40 Static and dynamic modelling of beams in large rotations r5.03.40 Static and dynamic modelling of beams in large rotations Summary : This note gives a mechanical formulation of beams in large displacements and large rotations but with an elastic constitutive behaviour. The essential difficulty of the analysis of rotations lies in the fact that they are not commutative and do not constitute a vector space, but a manifold. At any time instant, the configuration of a beam cross-section is defined by the displacement vector of its centre of gravity and the rotation vector of the system of principal axes of inertia with respect to a reference position. As in the classical theory of beams, the internal forces are reduced to their resultant and their moment on the line of centres of the sections. One defines the associated strains. The linearisation of the internal forces with respect to the displacements leads to the usual stiffness matrix, which is symmetric, and, because of the large displacements and rotations, to the geometric stiffness matrix, which is arbitrary. The linearisation of the inertia forces leads, for the translational motion, to the usual mass matrix which is symmetric and, for the rotational motion, to a much more complicated matrix and without any symmetry. The time-integration scheme is that of Newmark. This modelling has been tested on five reference problems: three in statics and two in dynamics. This work was undertaken within the framework of a development of modelling tools for the components of lines and substations. The aim of the modelling is the dynamic study of conductors fitted with spacers (for the lines) or with downleads onto apparatus (for the substations) and subjected to the Laplace forces resulting
