Q,{Q}^{-1} | operator of passage from a rotation vector to the associated quaternion and its inverse. | 2 Introduction The essential difficulty of the mechanics of beams in large displacements lies in the formulation of the rotations. The rotation of a section with respect to a reference configuration is defined by the rotation vector ([bib3], [bib4] and [bib5]). The quaternions are used for the updating of this vector. In [bib4] and [bib5], the rotation increment is expressed in the reference configuration (total Lagrangian scheme). The computation of the mass matrices is complicated and cannot moreover be carried quite through to its end. But finally, all the matrices used are symmetric. In [bib1] to [bib3], the rotation increment is expressed in the last computed configuration (updated Lagrangian scheme). It is this scheme that we have chosen. The computation of the matrices is completed without excessive difficulty but they are not symmetric. Unlike [bib3], we have expressed the angular velocities and accelerations in the general axes and not in local axes. The matrices are thus more complicated, but one avoids the ambiguity which appears at the junction of two non-collinear beams. 3 Kinematics of a beam in finite rotations Figure 3-a: Evolution of a beam segment Let us follow the evolution of a beam segment from its initial position — or reference position — fig3‑a to its deformed position at the time instant t [fig 3-a] (b). The cross-section of the centre P of the beam in the reference position is located by the curvilinear abscissa s of P on the line of centres (or neutral fibre). One attaches to this section the orthonormal triad {E}_{1}\text{}{E}_{2}\text{}{E}_{3}\text{}:\text{}{E}_{1} is the unit tangent to the line of centres at P;{E}_{2}\text{et}{E}_{3} are directed along the principal axes of inertia of the section. As in [bib1] to [bib5], one makes the hypothesis that in the course of the motion the sections initially straight remain plane and do not change shape. From time instant 0 to time instant t : - P comes to P' and the position of P' is defined by the vector {x}_{o}(s,t) ; - the orthonormal triad {E}_{1}{E}_{2}{E}_{3} becomes the orthonormal triad {t}_{1}{t}_{2}{t}_{3}.{t}_{2} and {t}_{3} are still directed along the principal axes of inertia of the section and {t}_{1} is still the unit normal to this section. But {t}_{1} is not necessarily tangent to the line of centres at P' : in other words, there may be, in the deformed position, a slip due to shear, as in the Timoshenko model. The state of the section at the time instant t is therefore defined by: - the vector {x}_{o}(s,t) , which gives the position of the centre of gravity ; - the rotation vector which takes one from the triad {E}_{1}{E}_{2}{E}_{3} to the triad {t}_{1}{t}_{2}{t}_{3} , and which is defined in [§4.1]. The set of these two vectors constitutes the vector \phi (s,t) . 4 Rotation vector and rotation operator Appendix 1 gives preliminary results concerning the antisymmetric matrices of order 3. 4.1 Rotation vector Suppose that, in the system of general axes P\text{}{e}_{1}\text{}{e}_{2}\text{}{e}_{3} [fig 4.1-a], the point M' is deduced from M by the rotation of angle \alpha about the axis passing through P and of unit vector u . Let us set: \Psi =\alpha u \Psi is called the rotation vector taking one from M to M' . According to the Euler–Rodrigues formula [bib6] p. 186 and [bib7]: \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PM}'}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{PM}}+\sin\alpha (u\wedge \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PM}})+(1-\cos\alpha )\left[u\wedge \left[u\wedge \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PM}}\right]\right] . Figure 4.1-a: Representation of a finite rotation In general, the rotation vector of the product of two rotations is not the geometric sum of the component rotation vectors. The 2D case is a particularly simple exception: the rotation vectors, perpendicular to the plane, add algebraically. 4.2 Rotation operator Taking into account, the previous equation is written: \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PM}'}=\left[1+\sin\alpha \hat{u}+(1-\cos\alpha ){\hat{u}}^{2}\right]\overrightarrow{\mathrm{PM}} The expression in brackets defines the rotation operator R taking one from \mathrm{PM} to \mathrm{PM}' : R=1+\sin\alpha \hat{u}+(1-\cos\alpha ){\hat{u}}^{2}. One calls “Euler parameters” of the rotation the following four numbers: \begin{array}{cc}{e}_{0}=\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}& {e}_{1}=\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}{u}_{1}\\ {e}_{2}=\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}{u}_{2}& {e}_{3}=\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}{u}_{3}\end{array} One obviously has: {e}_{0}^{2}+{e}_{1}^{2}+{e}_{2}^{2}+{e}_{3}^{2}=1. Let us set: e=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{e}_{1}\\ {e}_{2}\\ {e}_{3}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}u. By using the relation , one easily puts the expression of R in the form: R=(2{e}_{0}^{2}-1)1+2({ee}^{T}+{e}_{0}\hat{e}). On the other hand, replacing \sin\alpha and \cos\alpha , on the right-hand side of , by their expansions in power series, one obtains: \begin{array}{cc}R=1& +\left[\alpha -\frac{{\alpha}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{\alpha}^{5}}{5!}+\text{...}+{(-1)}^{p-1}\frac{{\alpha}^{\mathrm{2p}-1}}{(\mathrm{2p}-1)!}+\text{...}\right]\hat{u}\\ & +\left[\frac{{\alpha}^{2}}{2!}-\frac{{\alpha}^{4}}{4!}+\frac{{\alpha}^{6}}{6!}+\text{...}+{(-1)}^{p-1}\frac{{\alpha}^{\mathrm{2p}}}{(\mathrm{2p})!}\right]{\hat{u}}^{2}\end{array} that is, by using and , the exponential form of the rotation operator: \begin{array}{c}R=1+\alpha \hat{u}+\frac{{(\alpha \hat{u})}^{2}}{2!}+\text{...}+\frac{{(\alpha \hat{u})}^{p}}{p!}+\text{...}\\ =\exp(\alpha \hat{u})=\exp(\hat{\Psi}).\end{array} It appears on that when \parallel \Psi \parallel \to 0 , R\approx 1+\Psi \wedge . R=\exp(\alpha \hat{u}) is obviously not computed by the expansion , but by the expression . Since {\hat{u}}^{T}=-\hat{u} , the transposition of all the terms of the right-hand side of gives: {\left[\exp(\hat{\Psi})\right]}^{T}=\exp(-\hat{\Psi}) that is: {R}^{T}={R}^{-1} and: {\mathrm{RR}}^{T}=1 The rotation operators, orthogonal according to the equation , form a group with respect to the multiplication operation — non-commutative in 3D — called the Lie group and denoted by \text{SO}(3) (Special Orthogonal group). 5 Passage from the local axes to the general axes The components of the vectors are expressed in the general axes {e}_{1}\text{}{e}_{2}\text{}{e}_{3} [fig 3-a]. The matrices of the operators which relate them are therefore valid only in these axes. But the mechanics of beams is formulated much more simply in the local principal axes of inertia {t}_{1}{t}_{2}{t}_{3} in the current configuration. One is therefore led to make the change of axes from the general triad {e}_{1}\text{}{e}_{2}\text{}{e}_{3} to the local triad {t}_{1}{t}_{2}{t}_{3} by the product {R}_{\text{tot}} of two rotations: - the rotation {R}_{o} , invariable, which brings the general axes ({e}_{1}\text{}{e}_{2}\text{}{e}_{3}) onto the local axes in the reference position ({E}_{1}\text{}{E}_{2}\text{}{E}_{3}) ; - the rotation R , depending on time, which brings the triad ({E}_{1}\text{}{E}_{2}\text{}{E}_{3}) onto the local triad in the current deformed position ({t}_{1}{t}_{2}{t}_{3}) , that is: {R}_{\text{tot}}={\mathrm{RR}}_{o} Given a vector v , of components known in the general triad, its components in the local triad are the components in the general triad of the vector: V={R}_{\text{tot}}^{T}v. One can therefore replace the computations bearing on vectors expressed in local axes in the current configuration, by the same computations bearing on the same vectors rotated by {R}_{\text{tot}}^{T} and expressed in general axes. In other words, this rotation {R}_{\text{tot}}^{T} makes it possible to replace the computations in local axes of the current configuration, by the same computations in general axes. 6 Internal forces, strains and constitutive law One places oneself within the framework of beam theory. The forces and the strains are defined by their reduction elements on the line of centres of gravity of the sections. Thus, the virtual work in the beam is computed by a simple curvilinear integral along this line. 6.1 Internal forces One calls internal forces on the section of centre P' and of normal {t}_{1} the forces exerted on this section by the part of the beam situated in the direction of {t}_{1} [fig 6.1-a]. These forces form a torsor whose reduction elements at P' are: the resultant f , the resulting moment m Figure 6.1-a: Beam segment reduced to the line of centres If \bar{f} and \bar{m} are respectively the external force and moment given per unit of undeformed length \bar{f} and \bar{m} are assumed independent of the configuration, that is to say “conservative” or “non-follower” —, the static equilibrium of the beam segment P'\text{}P'' of length \mathrm{ds} is written: \begin{array}{}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}+\overline{f}=0\\ \frac{\partial m}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial {x}_{o}}{\partial s}\wedge f+\overline{m}=0.\end{array} 6.2 Change of curvature at a point of the line of centres The local axes of the section of abscissa s are deduced from the general axes by the relation : {t}_{i}(s)=R(s).{R}_{o}(s){e}_{i}. By differentiating with respect to s : {t}_{i}'=(R'{R}_{o}+{\mathrm{RR}}_{o}'){e}_{i}, that is, by inverting the relation : {t}_{i}=(R'{R}^{T}+{\mathrm{RR}}_{o}'{R}_{o}^{T}{R}^{T}){t}_{i} . Let us set: R'{R}^{T}=\hat{\chi } The matrix \hat{\chi } is antisymmetric because differentiation with respect to s of gives: \hat{\chi }+{\hat{\chi }}^{T}=0 . One checks that the matrix {\hat{\chi }}_{0} defined by: {\hat{\chi }}_{o}={\mathrm{RR}}_{o}'{R}_{o}^{T}{R}^{T} is also antisymmetric. Therefore, by bringing in the axial vectors \chi and {\chi }_{0} : {t}_{i}'=(\chi +{\chi }_{o})\wedge {t}_{i} - \mathrm{ds}{\chi }_{o} is the rotation vector which takes one from {t}_{i}(s) to {t}_{i}(s+\text{ds}) when the beam undergoes a uniform rotation (R'=0) from its reference position to its current position. {\chi }_{o}(s) characterises the curvature of the reference configuration at the abscissa s . - \mathrm{ds}\chi is the increment of rotation from {t}_{i}(s) to {t}_{i}(s+\text{ds}) due to the variation of R along the beam. It is this vector \chi which characterises the change of curvature between the reference configuration and the current deformed configuration. 6.3 Virtual work in the beam and strain vector This paragraph is the extension to the three-dimensional case of an approach made in [bib8] on plane beams. The configuration of the beam at the time instant t is defined [§3] by the field \phi (s,t) : \Phi (s,t)=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{x}_{0}(s,t)\\ \Psi (s,t)\end{array}\right\rbrace . Let us compute the work W of the external line forces \bar{f} and \bar{m} in the following virtual displacement: \delta \phi (s)=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\delta {x}_{o}(s)\\ \delta \Psi (s)\end{array}\right\rbrace . One obviously has: W={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}(\overline{f}.\delta {x}_{o}+\overline{m}.\delta \phi )\text{ds} . The equilibrium equations make it possible to replace the external forces \bar{f} and \bar{m} by the internal forces f and m : W={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}\left[-\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}.\delta {x}_{o}-\frac{\partial m}{\partial s}.\delta \Psi -(\frac{\partial {x}_{o}}{\partial s}\wedge f).\delta \Psi \right]\text{ds} , that is, by integration by parts of the first two terms: W=-{\left[f.\delta {x}_{o}+m.\delta \Psi \right]}_{1}^{2}+{\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}\left[f.\delta {x}_{o}'+m.\delta \Psi '-({x}_{o}'\wedge f).\delta \Psi \right]\text{ds}. If one denotes by {W}_{\mathrm{ext}} the total work of the external forces on the beam — along it and at the ends — the previous equation is written: \begin{array}{c}{W}_{\text{ext}}={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}(\overline{f}.\delta {x}_{o}+\overline{m}.\delta \Psi )\text{ds}+{\left[f.\delta {x}_{o}+m.\delta \Psi \right]}_{1}^{2}\\ ={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}\left[f.(\delta {x}_{o}'-\delta \Psi \wedge {x}_{o}')+m.\delta \Psi '\right]\text{ds}.\end{array} According to the theorem of virtual work for continuous media, the right-hand side is the virtual work of the internal forces, which one denotes {W}_{int} . Following the idea of [bib8], let us seek to put the coefficients of f\text{et de}m in the form of the virtual increment of two vectors. Let us make the hypothesis that the vector {x}_{o}' tangent to the line of centres but not necessarily of unit length, differs from the unit vector {t}_{1} , normal to the section, only by an infinitesimal of the 1st order (of the order of \delta \Psi ). This implies that the beam lengthens little and undergoes a small slip. Then: {W}_{int}={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}\left[f.\delta ({x}_{o}'-{t}_{1})+m.\delta \chi \right]\text{ds} . Indeed, in the virtual displacement: - {x}_{o}' increases by \delta {x}_{o}'; - the unit vector {t}_{1} rotates by \delta \Psi ; - the vector \chi , defining the change of curvature [§6.2], increases by \delta \Psi ' . One therefore has: {W}_{int}={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}\left[f.\delta \varepsilon +m.\delta \chi \right]\text{ds}, with: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\varepsilon \\ \chi \end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{x}_{o}'-{t}_{1}\\ \chi \end{array}\right\rbrace . In the equation , \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}f\\ m\end{array}\right\rbrace and \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\varepsilon \\ \chi \end{array}\right\rbrace therefore appear respectively as a force torsor or of generalised stresses and the torsor of the associated strains . defines the elongation and the slip; \khi defines the change of curvature [§6.2]. One observes that, if \varepsilon must be small, on the other hand there is no limitation for \khi . Most beams fall within this framework. The relation is written: {W}_{int}(\phi ;\delta \phi )={\int}_{{s}_{1}}^{{s}_{2}}B\delta \phi .\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}f\\ m\end{array}\right\rbrace \text{ds} with: B=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\frac{d}{\text{ds}}1& {x}_{o}'\wedge \\ 0& \frac{d}{\text{ds}}1\end{array}\right] B is called the strain matrix . 6.4 Constitutive law According to [§5], the components in local axes of the generalised stress and of the strain are the components in general axes of the vectors: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}F\\ M\end{array}\right\rbrace ={\Pi}^{T}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}f\\ m\end{array}\right\rbrace ;\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}E\\ X\end{array}\right\rbrace ={\Pi}^{T}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\varepsilon \\ \chi \end{array}\right\rbrace One assumes that the constitutive law is elastic and that, in local axes, it has the same expression as for a Timoshenko beam: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}F\\ M\end{array}\right\rbrace =\text{DIAG}\left[\text{EA},{\text{GA}}_{2},{\text{GA}}_{3},{\text{GI}}_{1},{\text{EI}}_{2},{\text{EI}}_{3}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}E\\ X\end{array}\right\rbrace {A}_{2} and {A}_{3} being two areas depending on the size and the shape of the section. One sets: C=\text{DIAG}\left[\text{EA},{\text{GA}}_{2},{\text{GA}}_{3},{\text{GI}}_{1},{\text{EI}}_{2},{\text{EI}}_{3}\right]. C is called the constitutive matrix . 7 Elementary inertia forces The inertia forces applied to an element \mathrm{ds} form a torsor which admits, at the centre of gravity: - a general resultant, -\rho A\mathrm{ds}\ddot{{x}_{0}}(s,t) ; - a resulting moment equal to the opposite of the absolute rate of the elementary angular momentum H . In order to express the angular velocity, let us proceed as in [§6.2] and differentiate the relation: {t}_{i}={RE}_{i}, with respect to t , taking into account that {E}_{i} does not depend on time. One obtains: {\dot{t}}_{i}=\dot{R}{R}^{T}{t}_{i}. Let us set: \dot{R}{R}^{T}=\hat{\omega}. By differentiating the relation with respect to t , one sees that the matrix \hat{\omega} is antisymmetric. If one denotes by \omega the axial vector of this matrix, the relation is written: {\dot{t}}_{i}(s,t)=\omega \wedge {t}_{i}(s,t). \omega is therefore the angular velocity vector of the beam section of abscissa s at the time instant t . The rotation-angle increments {\Psi}_{i-1,i}^{n}\text{et}{\Psi}_{i-1,i}^{n+1} serve to compute the corrections of velocity and of acceleration from (\begin{array}{c}n\\ i\end{array}) to (\begin{array}{c}n+1\\ i\end{array}) . : Necessity of the transport into a reference space for the vector operations relative to the rotational motion The kinematic quantities (grandeurs), velocities and accelerations, in a given configuration lie in the vector space tangent to \mathrm{SO}(3) at the point defined by the rotation of the configuration with respect to the reference position. One can combine the quantities (grandeurs) relative to two distinct configurations only after having transported them into one and the same vector space taken as reference. The example which follows will make this necessity understood. Let us examine the angular velocity of a gyroscope at three time instants {t}_{1},{t}_{2} and {t}_{3} [fig A7-a]. Suppose that one passes from configuration 1 to configuration 2 by the rotation of angle -\pi about {e}_{1} , and from configuration 1 to configuration 3 by the rotation of angle -\pi /2 about the same axis. At 1, the angular velocity is carried by the axis of the gyro and has components (0,0,\omega ) in the general axes {e}_{1}\text{}{e}_{2}\text{}{e}_{3} . At 2, the angular velocity is likewise carried by the axis and has general components (0,0,–3\omega ) . One wishes to determine the general components of the velocity at 3, knowing that this velocity is the average of the velocities at 1 and 2. That the angular velocity at 3 is the average of the angular velocities at 1 and 2 does not mean that it is the average in the general axes, but in the axes attached to the gyro. In the example, since the gyro rotates about its axis, at 1 with the velocity \omega , at 2 with the velocity 3 \omega , then at 3 it rotates about this axis with the velocity 2\omega . Therefore, at 3, the general components of the angular velocity are (0,2\omega ,0) . Taking [§5] into account, one obtains the previous result by “transporting” the angular-velocity vector of configuration 2 onto configuration 1, taken as reference, that is to say by rotating this vector by the angle \pi about {e}_{1} . Its general components are then (0,0,3\omega ) . One takes the average of this vector and of the angular-velocity vector at 1, in order to obtain the vector of components (0,0,2\omega ) . One finally “transports” this last vector onto configuration 3 by rotating it by -\pi /2 about {e}_{1} , and one indeed arrives at the angular-velocity vector of general components (\mathrm{0, 2}\omega ,0) . r5.03.50 Discrete formulation of contact-friction r5.03.50 Discrete formulation of contact-friction Summary: This document describes the numerical methods used to treat contact/friction problems in large displacements in the operator STAT_NON_LINE or DYNA_NON_LINE by means of a discrete formulation. The available algorithms make it possible to treat the problem exactly (for contact) or approximately (for contact and for friction), without any restrictive choice on the underlying mechanical problem (kinematics or non-linear constitutive laws). This document also contains the theoretical elements for describing the solution of general unilateral problems (without pairing, such as seepage for example) usable by the keyword FORMULATION='LIAISON_UNIL'. 1 Introduction Two distinct solids are said to be in contact when they share a common surface which is part of their boundary. Treating unilateral contact consists in preventing one of the solids from “passing through” the other. Friction characterises the tangential sliding of one solid with respect to the other. In code_aster , only Coulomb dry friction is available. Contact in the discrete formulation in code_aster has the following characteristics: - The contact and friction laws are established from already discretised quantities: displacements and nodal forces on the meshed structures; - The contact/friction problem is solved by decoupling it from the problem of the equilibrium of the structure. In this document the various ingredients of the problem will be presented: - Description of the contact and friction laws; - Geometric pairing: this is the phase in which one links a node to another node, or a node to a mesh cell, in order to create a potential contact pair, that is to say one identifies the degrees of freedom for which discrete non-penetration relations will be written; - Establishment of the contact/friction problem; - Description of the algorithms available for solving the contact/friction problem. This document is therefore limited to the methods known as GCP, CONTRAINTE and PENALISATION. The formulation known as “continuous” (FORMULATION='CONTINUE' in DEFI_CONTACT) is the subject of the document r5.03.52. The formulation associated with the XFEM elements (FORMULATION='XFEM' in DEFI_CONTACT) is discussed in r5.03.53. This document also contains the theoretical elements for describing the solution of general unilateral problems (without pairing, such as seepage for example) usable by the keyword FORMULATION='LIAISON_UNIL'. 2 Mechanics of contact and of friction 2.1 Definition of the problem and notation Consider two solids which may come into frictional contact; the contact zone is either a point, a line or a surface. Let \left\lbrace n\right\rbrace be the outward normal to the surface of one of the solids in contact and \left\lbrace u\right\rbrace the displacement vector between the two solids. Then g=\langle u\rangle .\left\lbrace n\right\rbrace is the displacement projected onto this normal; it will be called the gap . From the Cauchy stress, one defines the pressure 1 p=\langle n\rangle .\left[\sigma \right].\left\lbrace n\right\rbrace and the tangential shear stress \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace =\left[\sigma \right].\left\lbrace n\right\rbrace -p.\left\lbrace n\right\rbrace as being exerted by one of the surfaces on the other. | | | --- | | Figure 2.1-a : definition of the local contact frame. | The shear force has, as its direction in the contact zone, a vector \left\lbrace t\right\rbrace lying in the tangent plane (\left\lbrace {t}_{1}\right\rbrace ,\left\lbrace {t}_{2}\right\rbrace ) indicated in the figure above. Equation defines the shear stress r exerted by the solid on the solid per unit contact area. \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace =\left[\sigma \right].\left\lbrace n\right\rbrace -(\langle n\rangle .\left[\sigma \right].\left\lbrace n\right\rbrace ).\left\lbrace n\right\rbrace =r.\left\lbrace t\right\rbrace \textrm{avec} r=\mathrm{\parallel }\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \mathrm{\parallel } 2.2 Signorini contact conditions The two variables defining contact have been introduced: - The signed distance between the two surfaces, or “gap”, g ; - The contact pressure p ; One then defines the three Hertz-Signorini-Moreau contact conditions - Geometric condition: impenetrability of matter (Signorini-Hertz). g \ge 0 \iff \left\{ \begin{array}{l} g > 0 \quad \text{pas de contact} \\ g = 0 \quad \text{contact} \end{array} \right. - Mechanical condition: intensility (Signorini-Hertz) p\ge 0\mathrm{\iff} \left\{ \begin{array}{c} p>0 \quad \text{contact} \\ p=0 \quad \text{pas de contact}\end{array} \right. - Energetic condition: complementarity/exclusion (Moreau) p.g=0\iff \left\{ \begin{array}{c} p=0 \quad \text{décollement} \\ g=0 \quad \text{contact}\end{array} \right. Graphically, the three conditions are represented in the figure below, where the hatched zones represent the excluded zones and the white zones or the black lines represent the allowed zones. | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | Impenetrability | Intensility | Complementarity | | Figure 2.2-a : graphical representation of the Hertz-Signorini-Moreau conditions. | | | Combining the three conditions gives the graph in the figure below. | | | --- | | Figure 2.2-b : graph of the unilateral contact condition. | The contact problem thus posed introduces a relation which is not single-valued ( p is not a function of g ), positive semi-definite and non-differentiable at p=g=0 . It is a problem which is mathematically difficult to treat. Contact is a reversible and conservative phenomenon for which an energy potential can be introduced and whose result does not depend on the loading path; it is similar to the Hencky elastoplastic model. The Signorini contact law is written: \left\{ \begin{array}{cc}g\ge 0& (a)\\ p\ge 0& (b)\\ p.g=0& (c)\end{array} \right. Notes: - Contact is assumed to be without adhesion, by virtue of the second condition (intensility). - The third condition allows the unilateral contact problem to be well-posed so as to be solvable by the classical techniques of constrained optimisation (introduction of the Kuhn & Tucker conditions), such as the active-constraint method. 2.3 Formulation of the friction problem 2.3.1 Definitions The friction criteria chosen are of the form: h(\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace )\le 0 where h(\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace ) is a convex function. The non-sliding domain is defined by the interior of the convex set. Two friction criteria of the form h(\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace )\le 0 are particularly used: the Tresca criterion and the Coulomb criterion. 2.3.2 The Tresca criterion The Tresca criterion is defined by the following function h(\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace ) : h(\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace )=\mathrm{\parallel }\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \mathrm{\parallel }-k\le 0 \textrm{avec } k \textrm{ une constante donnée} One denotes by C the convex disc of radius k centred at the origin defined by: C=\left\lbrace \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \text{tel que}\mathrm{\parallel }\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \mathrm{\parallel }\le k\right\rbrace The non-sliding condition is then defined by the membership of \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace in the interior of the disc C . In the case of sliding, for \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace lying on the boundary of C , the sliding direction \left\lbrace t\right\rbrace of \left\lbrace \dot{u}\right\rbrace is given by the normal to the criterion at \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace , as indicated on the . | | | --- | | Figure 2.3.2-a : friction disc for the Tresca criterion. | This is expressed by an expression for the sliding velocity analogous to the plastic multiplier: {\dot{u}}_{t}=\lambda .r With \lambda \ge 0 , that is to say that the sliding velocity is in the same direction as the tangential stress. 2.3.3 The Coulomb criterion The Coulomb criterion is defined by the following function h(\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace ) : h(\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace ,\mu ,p)=\mathrm{\parallel }\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \mathrm{\parallel }-k(\mu ,p)\le 0 \textrm{et} k=\mu .\mid p\mid The value of k depends on the contact pressure p and on the Coulomb friction coefficient \mu . Defined in this way, h is a cone. In the case of sliding, for \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace lying on the boundary of h , the sliding direction \left\lbrace t\right\rbrace of \dot{u} is not given by the normal to the criterion at \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace , but by the normal to the convex disc C of radius k=\mu .\mid p\mid . The Tresca criterion corresponds to a “slice” along the plane orthogonal to the Coulomb cone. | | | --- | | Figure 2.3.3-a : friction cone for the Coulomb criterion. | 2.3.4 Application to Coulomb friction Let us write the system of equations and inequalities which must be satisfied by these quantities in the case of the Coulomb friction criterion: \left\{ \begin{array}{cc}g\ge 0& (a)\\ p\ge 0& (b)\\ p.g=0& (c)\\ \mathrm{\parallel }\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \mathrm{\parallel }-\mu .\mid p\mid \le 0& (d)\\ \left\lbrace {\dot{u}}_{t}\right\rbrace =\lambda .\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace & (e)\\ \lambda .(\mathrm{\parallel }\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \mathrm{\parallel }-\mu .\mid p\mid )=0& (f)\\ \lambda \ge 0& (g)\end{array} \right. The first set of equations and inequalities (a–c) corresponds to the treatment of contact. The second set (d–g) corresponds to the description of friction obeying the Coulomb criterion. It involves several fields and links them together: the normal pressure p , the shear stress \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace and the tangential velocity \left\lbrace {\dot{u}}_{t}\right\rbrace . It may be understood as follows: \left\{ \begin{array}{cc}\text{Si}\mathrm{\parallel }\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \mathrm{\parallel } 0\text{et}\left\lbrace {\dot{u}}_{t}\right\rbrace =\lambda .\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace & (b)\end{array} \right. In the figure below the Coulomb cone has been represented. In stress space, the frictional-contact force can lie only inside the Coulomb cone: if it is strictly inside, the contact is sticking; if it is on the surface of the cone, the contact is sliding. | | | --- | | Figure 2.3.4-a : interpretation of the friction cone. | Another representation of this criterion can be given (see the figure below). | | | --- | | Figure 2.3.4-b : graph of Coulomb friction. | Friction introduces the notion of a threshold. The relation introduced by Coulomb friction is a relation which is not single-valued and is non-differentiable. Unlike contact, the relation is not associated 2 and cannot be derived directly from an energy dissipation potential. One will also note that friction links the relative velocity of the two surfaces and not the displacement. However, one can establish that in statics, if the problem is solved in incremental form (which is the case when one uses Newton as in code_aster ), the relative velocity may be replaced by the tangential displacement increment. 2.4 Formulation by differential inclusions The non-differentiable character of the friction relations leads us to introduce the notion of a differential sub-inclusion. One denotes by V the set of kinematically admissible displacements of the problem. The relation between the relative sliding velocity \left\lbrace \dot{u}\right\rbrace and the shear stress r expresses the two possible states of the system: no sliding, or relative sliding along the direction normal at \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace to the convex disc C . For the three criteria presented, the function \left\lbrace {\dot{u}}_{t}\right\rbrace (r) and its reciprocal \left\lbrace r({\dot{u}}_{t})\right\rbrace both belong to the subdifferentials of two conjugate pseudo-potentials {\Psi}_{c}(r) and {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}({\dot{u}}_{t}) , so that one can write: \left\lbrace \dot{u}\right\rbrace \in \partial {\Psi}_{c}(r) \textrm{et} \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \in \partial {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}(\dot{u}) The appearance of the differential inclusions comes from the non-differentiable character of the contact-friction laws. Indeed, {\Psi}_{c} denotes the indicator function of the convex disc C of radius k , centred at the origin, defined previously. It is such that: {\Psi}_{c}(r)=\lbrace \begin{array}{c}0\text{si}\left\lbrace r\right\rbrace \in C\\ +\infty \text{sinon}\end{array} The subdifferential \partial {\Psi}_{c}(r) of the function {\Psi}_{c} at r coincides with the outward normal to C at \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace . {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}(\dot{u})=k\mathrm{\parallel }\dot{u}\mathrm{\parallel } , where k is the friction resistance threshold; {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }} is the Fenchel conjugate of the indicator function {\Psi}_{c} . {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }} is positively homogeneous of degree one. This function is interpreted as the density of power dissipated in sliding. Using the notions of subdifferential, one can establish the following relations for associated \left\lbrace \dot{u}\right\rbrace and \left\lbrace r\right\rbrace : \left\{ \begin{array}{c}\dot{u}\in \partial {\Psi}_{c}(r)\mathrm{\iff }\left\{ \begin{array}{c}{\Psi}_{c}(r)=0\\ \dot{u}.(r'-r)\le 0,\forall r'\in C\end{array}\right.\\ r\in \partial {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}(\dot{u})\mathrm{\iff }\left\{ \begin{array}{c}\dot{u}\in V\\ r.(\dot{v}-\dot{u})\le {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}(\dot{v})-{\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}(\dot{u}),\forall \dot{v}\in V\end{array}\right.\\ {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}(\dot{u})+{\Psi}_{c}(r)=\dot{u}.r=k\mathrm{\parallel }\dot{u}\mathrm{\parallel }\end{array}\right. Notes: - The two conjugate pseudo-potentials presented are non-differentiable. - Once the normal reaction is known for the Coulomb criterion, one reduces locally to a Tresca friction criterion whose threshold is equal to k=\mu .|p| . - The local criteria adopted having a circular form, one deduces that \dot{u}\in \partial {\Psi}_{c}(r) implies that there exists a positive real \lambda such that \dot{u}=\lambda r . - The formulation of the problem in terms of velocity suggests an incremental numerical solution of the friction problem. The solution of the equilibrium problem will therefore be presented in incremental form. 2.5 Solution of the equilibrium problem Consider two solids of total volume \Omega dont la surface de contact est :math: {\Gamma}_{c} . To simplify, one will assume the existence of a differentiable strain energy in order to characterise the response of the two separate solids to external loads (in fact, one can show that the results given below are independent of this assumption). One denotes by V the set of kinematically admissible displacement fields, constrained by compliance with the contact and friction conditions on the interface. The equilibrium of the two solids in the absence of friction is written: Find U a kinematically admissible displacement field such that \left\lbrace U=\underset{v\in V}{\text{argmin}}\left[\Phi (\varepsilon (v))-W(v)\right]\right\rbrace \iff \left\lbrace \Phi (U)-W(U)\le \Phi (v)-W(v),\forall v\in V\right\rbrace In elasticity, \Phi (v)={\int}_{\Omega}\phi (\epsilon (v)).d\Omega is the strain energy. The function W(v) represents the work of the external forces. A necessary condition (which becomes sufficient if \Phi is strictly convex) for this equilibrium to be satisfied is that: D\Phi (U)-\mathit{DW}\left(U\right)=D\Phi (U)-{L}^{\text{ext}}=0 where D is the Gâteaux derivative operator and {L}^{\text{ext}} is the linear form associated with the external forces. With the introduction of friction, the problem must be approached in incremental form. One is led (see and ) to the following minimisation problem on the set \overline{V} of the kinematically admissible fields constrained by compliance with the contact and friction conditions on the interface: U known, find \Delta U\in \overline{V} such that U+\Delta U=\underset{\Delta v\in \bar{V}}{\text{argmin}}\left[\Phi (\varepsilon (U+\Delta v))+{\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}(\Delta {v}_{t})-W(U+\Delta v)\right] U+\Delta U is thus the solution of: \underset{\Delta v\in \bar{V}}{\min}\left[\underset{\Omega}{\int}\varphi (\varepsilon (U+\Delta v))d\Omega +\underset{{\Gamma}_{c}}{\int}k\mid \Delta {v}_{t}\mid d{\Gamma}_{c}-W(U+\Delta v)\right] where \Delta {v}_{t} is the tangential component of the relative displacement increment 3 of solid 2 with respect to solid 1 along the contact surface, with the conventions adopted in r5.03.50-formulation-frottement. Using the relations {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}(\Delta {v}_{t})=k\mid \Delta {v}_{t}\mid et :math: {\Psi}_{c}^{\text{ }}(\Delta {v}_{t})\ge r\Delta v if r\in C one deduces that U+\Delta U is the solution of the following \text{minmax} problem, on the space V of the kinematically admissible fields: \underset{\Delta v\in V}{\text{Min}}\underset{r}{\text{Max}}\text{}J(U+\Delta v,r) where the functional J is equal to: J(U+\Delta v,r)=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\phi (\varepsilon (U+\Delta v)).d\Omega +\underset{{\Gamma}_{c}}{\int}(r.\Delta {v}_{t}-{\Psi}_{c}(r)).d{\Gamma}_{c}-W(U+\Delta v) The presence of the indicator function in this expression indicates that the shear r on the contact surface {\Gamma}_{c} belongs to the convex friction disc C . 2.6 Variational formulation If \phi is convex, the \text{minmax} problem to be solved is put in an equivalent way in the form: Find \Delta U\in V and r\in C , a set of independent variables such that \delta J(U+\Delta U,r)\ni 0 This amounts to solving the following system of equations at equilibrium: \left\{ \begin{array}{cc}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial \varepsilon }(\varepsilon (U+\Delta U)).\delta \varepsilon .d\Omega +\underset{{\Gamma}_{c}}{\int}r.\delta {v}_{t}.d{\Gamma}_{c}-{L}^{\text{ext}}.\delta v=0& (a)\\ \underset{{\Gamma}_{c}}{\int}(\delta r.\Delta {U}_{t}.d{\Gamma}_{c}-\partial {\Psi}_{c}(r))\ni 0& (b)\end{array}\right. or again, in an equivalent manner: \left\{ \begin{array}{cc}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial \varepsilon }(\varepsilon (U+\Delta U)).\delta \varepsilon .d\Omega +\underset{{\Gamma}_{c}}{\int}r.\delta {v}_{t}.d{\Gamma}_{c}-{L}^{\text{ext}}.\delta v=0& (a)\\ \Delta {U}_{t}\in \partial {\Psi}_{c}(r)& (b)\\ r=({\sigma}_{1}.n).t\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{c}& (c)\end{array}\right. As in the previous section, {L}^{\text{ext}} is the linear form associated with the external forces. The linear form {L}^{\text{frot}} is associated with the shear forces exerted by solid 2 on the contact surface of solid 1 . One will also note that the variational formulation makes it possible to recover not only the equilibrium equations of the system but also the membership of \Delta {U}_{t} in the subdifferential of {\Psi}_{c} . 2.7 Stages of the solution of the contact-friction problem The discrete solution method implemented in code_aster is based on writing the interpenetration relations on the nodes of the meshes facing one another, which implies: 1. A discrete description of the contact surfaces (mesh); 2. The search for the minimum projection distance and for the position of this projection (the operation known as pairing); 3. The writing of the kinematic relations between the nodes; 4. Algorithms for the solution of the contact/friction problem; Each of these aspects will be detailed in the remainder of the document. For the formulations known as “discrete” (as opposed to the formulation known as “continuous”, see r5.03.52), code_aster solves the contact problem by methods which belong to the family of methods called the “status method” in the literature, with a decoupling of global-local type. The contact/friction algorithms act in two stages: 1. Geometric pairing problem - Identification: definition of the potential contact surfaces (cf. r5.03.50-definition-zones-potentielles) by the user 4. - Pairing: determination of the potential contact pairs (cf. r5.03.50-algorithme-appariement) by a method of searching for the minimum gap between a node and a facet (for node/facet pairing) or for the node closest to another node (for nodal pairing). - Kinematics: writing of the non-penetration relation by determination of the projection direction and evaluation of the coefficients (cf. r5.03.50-relations-cinematiques). The relation is written between the slave node and the master nodes. 1. Mechanical problem. Several types of algorithm are implemented in code_aster : - An algorithm based on the active-constraint method, usable for contact without friction only. This algorithm rests on the assumptions that the tangent matrix of the problem is symmetric and positive definite, and guarantees convergence in a finite number of iterations in this case , , . It must not be used outside this framework, that is to say in particular for non-symmetric matrices, for example in THM modellings or in large strains. It is the one used by default and it corresponds to ALGO_CONT='CONTRAINTE'. - A variant of the active-constraint method by means of an iterative solution by projected conjugate gradient. ALGO_CONT='GCP'. A method reserved exclusively for contact problems without friction. - A solution algorithm by regularisation of the contact and/or friction conditions, which one activates with ALGO_CONT='PENALISATION' and ALGO_FROT='PENALISATION' by choosing judicious penalisation coefficients. This implies a fortiori a parametric study on the value of these coefficients: they are not homogeneous to \left\lbrace u\right\rbrace , but have the dimension of a ratio of a force to a displacement, and it is difficult to give a general rule for the choice of their values. The user is strongly advised to check a posteriori that the unilateral condition is correctly taken into account by viewing the results in the zone concerned. If this is not the case, it is necessary to increase the contact penalisation coefficient until it is. This regularisation algorithm may be chosen in the case of a modelling involving a non-symmetric matrix, which therefore cannot be treated by the active-constraint algorithm. 1. Unilateral conditions. More generally, it is possible to use the algorithms ALGO_CONT='CONTRAINTE' and ALGO_CONT='PENALISATION' in order to impose inequality boundary conditions on any degree of freedom. These are defined by FORMULATION='LIAISON_UNIL' in DEFI_CONTACT (see the documentation u4.44.11), and take the algebraic form \left[A\right]\left\lbrace u\right\rbrace \le \left\lbrace d\right\rbrace . Instead of being built by pairing, \left[A\right] and \left\lbrace d\right\rbrace are fixed and built from the information given by the user in DEFI_CONTACT, but the rest of the treatment is essentially identical. The term “pressure” is an improper abbreviation of “contact-force density” Tresca friction, on the other hand, is indeed an associated law. \Delta {v}_{t} is the tangential component of the relative displacement increment in the quasi-static formulation; it becomes the relative velocity of the two surfaces in the dynamic formulation. There is no automatic mechanism for locating the surfaces in contact in code_aster 3 Geometric pairing problem 3.1 Introduction The first problem to be treated in the case of contact is to define, in a reliable and robust manner, which parts of the two surfaces are likely to come into contact. This is the operation known as pairing, common with the mixed hybrid formulation known as the “continuous” method presented in the document r5.03.52. Two types of pairing are available in code_aster : - Nodal pairing; - Master-slave pairing (or node-facet). Nodal pairing (APPARIEMENT='NODAL') imposes that the relative displacement between a slave node and the master node to which it is paired, projected onto the direction of the normal to the slave node, be less than the initial gap in this direction. The use of this formulation is not recommended because it requires compatible meshes (nodes “facing one another”) which remain so during the deformation (small-sliding assumption), and for which the master and slave normals are approximately collinear. Without these assumptions, the approximation made becomes hazardous and it is preferable to use the node-facet formulation. Master-slave pairing, chosen by the keyword APPARIEMENT='MAIT_ESCL', does not grant an equivalent role to the two surfaces: the surface ( {S}_{1} ) described under GROUP_MA_MAIT or MAILLE_MAIT is called the master surface and the surface ( {S}_{2} ) is the slave surface. The non-interpenetration conditions express that the nodes of the slave surface (stars in the figure below) do not penetrate the mesh cells of the master surface. One can see, on the other hand, that it is possible for the master nodes (circles) to penetrate the slave surface. | | | --- | | Figure 3.1-a : master surface and slave surface. | Note: - The slave nodes are by default all the nodes belonging to the contact mesh cells defining the slave surface. The keywords SANS_NO and SANS_GROUP_NO make it possible to give, zone by zone, a list of the nodes which must be removed from the list of slave nodes. This makes it possible to remove the nodes subjected to Dirichlet boundary conditions incompatible with contact (see r5.03.50-compatibilite-Dirichlet). 3.2 Definition of the potential contact zones code_aster having no mechanism for the automatic detection of the potential contact zones, it is therefore up to the user to define a priori the zones which he or she predicts will come into contact. These zones must be wide enough for no interpenetration to be observed. It should be noted that the pairing phase is in general an inexpensive operation (much less expensive than the solution of the mechanical contact problem) and that one can therefore define sufficiently extended zones without risking a penalty on performance, subject to observing certain precautions in order to ensure, in particular, the uniqueness of the projections. Consider the three solids in the figure below, represented in 2D. Three possible zones of interpenetration between the solids have been defined: one zone between solid A and solid B , and two zones between solid B and solid C . The user, who defines these zones in the command file, assumes here that outside these zones there is no risk of interpenetration, given the loading. | | | --- | | Figure 3.2-a : definition of three contact zones. | Each contact zone is defined in the operator DEFI_CONTACT, factor keyword ZONE. A zone consists by definition of two surfaces whose interpenetration one seeks to prevent: the first is defined under the keyword GROUP_MA_MAIT (or MAILLE_MAIT), the second under the keyword GROUP_MA_ESCL (or MAILLE_ESCL), that is to say by giving the boundary mesh cells which constitute them. These mesh cells are SEG2 or SEG3 for a 2D mesh, and TRIA3, TRIA6, QUAD4, QUAD8 or QUAD9 for a 3D mesh. Notes: - The boundary mesh cells required for contact will not be created by code_aster from the volume elements and must therefore already exist in the mesh file. - The choice of the surfaces which will be master or slave is important. Information on this subject is available in the documentation u2.04.04. 3.2.1 Particular case of contact for a cable or a beam in 3D It is possible in 3D to treat the contact between a SEG2 or SEG3 mesh cell (modelling a cable or a beam) and a surface. In this case, one must imperatively use the pairing method 'MAIT_ESCL' and give the segments under the keyword GROUP_MA_ESCL (slave mesh cells). The section of the beam can then be taken into account by the use of the keyword DIST_ESCL (cf. r5.03.50-introduction-jeu-fictif). 3.2.2 Case of nodal pairing One must choose as the slave surface the one which has the fewer nodes (an error message will stop you if your master surface contains fewer nodes than your slave surface), in order to maximise the chances of having an injective pairing (a master node is paired with only one slave node). The master node paired with each slave node is determined by a nearest-neighbour computation explained in paragraph r5.03.50-recherche-proche-voisin. One uses the normal to the master node in order to write the non-interpenetration relation. Even in the case of nodal pairing, the contact surfaces are defined in terms of mesh cells. The slave and master nodes are then the nodes of the mesh cells thus defined. 3.3 Orientation of the normals It is imperative that the contact mesh cells be defined so that the normal is outward: the connectivity of the segments must be defined in the order \mathrm{AB} , that of the triangles in the order \mathrm{ABC} , and that of the quadrangles in the order \mathrm{ABCD} , as indicated in the figure. For a better reading of the drawing, the boundary mesh cell used for contact has here been moved slightly away from the “face” of the 2D or 3D volume element on which it rests. One may use for this the operator MODI_MAILLAGE, options ORIE_PEAU_2D, ORIE_PEAU_3D or ORIE_COQUE. | | | Figure 3.3-a : numbering of the contact mesh cells in order to have an outward normal. | 3.4 Pairing algorithm 3.4.1 Principle The pairing algorithm proceeds in two stages: 1. For each slave node one searches for the nearest master node; 2. One then searches for the master mesh cell attached to the master node previously determined which is the closest to the slave node; In the case of nodal pairing, one obviously carries out only the first stage. 3.4.2 Search for the nearest neighbour of a node This phase is common to both formulations: node/facet and node/node. The method used to search for the master node closest to a slave node is very simple: it is sufficient to compute the distance (in the updated geometry, cf. r5.03.50-reactualisation-geometrique) between the slave node and the candidate master nodes. 3.4.3 Search for the paired master mesh cell The algorithm for searching for the master mesh cell which is paired with the slave node is the following: - Knowing the master node closest to the slave node P (see r5.03.50-recherche-proche-voisin), one examines in succession the master mesh cells containing this node. - For each mesh cell thus identified, one searches for the orthogonal projection M of the slave node P onto the master mesh cell. - The mesh cell minimising the distance \mathit{PM} is chosen to be paired with the slave node. Notes: - If the slave node projects outside a master mesh cell, one folds its projection back onto this mesh cell under certain conditions (see r5.03.50-traitement-projections). - If at least one projection takes place inside a master mesh cell, then this one will be preferred to a projection leading to a fold-back (whatever the distance measured) - If all the projections of the slave node take place outside their respective master mesh cell, the slave node is considered as not paired and will therefore be excluded from the solution phase 3.4.4 Computation of the projection of the slave node onto the master mesh cell 3.4.4.1 Notation The parts of the surfaces \partial {\Omega}^{i} liable to come into contact during the deformation of the two solids are denoted {\gamma}_{c}^{i} . One assumes the existence of regular charts denoted {\Theta}^{i} describing the surfaces {\gamma}_{c}^{i} . These charts are defined as follows: \begin{array}{cc}{\Theta}^{i}:& {\omega}^{i}\to \overline{{\Omega}^{i}}\\ & ({\xi}_{1}^{i},{\xi}_{2}^{i})\to {p}^{i}={\Theta}^{i}({\xi}_{1}^{i},{\xi}_{2}^{i})\end{array} where {\omega}^{i} is a bounded domain (of reference) contained in {ℝ}^{2} (it is the reference parametric space of the finite element). Furthermore, one denotes by {\varphi}^{i} the transformation of the solid {B}^{i} , defined by: \begin{array}{cc}{\varphi}^{i}:& \overline{{\Omega}^{i}}\to \overline{{\Omega}_{t}^{i}}\\ & \left\lbrace {p}^{i}\right\rbrace \to \left\lbrace {x}^{i}\right\rbrace \end{array} One always places oneself at a fixed time t . The master surface is denoted {\gamma}_{c}^{1} and the slave surface is denoted {\gamma}_{c}^{2} . Pairing is carried out by searching, for every point \left\lbrace {x}^{i}\right\rbrace ={\varphi}^{i}({p}^{i},t) of the boundary {\gamma}_{c}^{1} , for the point \left\lbrace \tilde{x}\right\rbrace of {\gamma}_{c}^{2} which is the closest. This amounts to solving the following constrained optimisation problem. For every point \left\lbrace {x}^{1}\right\rbrace ={\varphi}^{1}({\Theta}^{1}({\xi}_{1}^{1},{\xi}_{2}^{1}),t) with ({\xi}_{1}^{1},{\xi}_{2}^{1})\in {\omega}^{1} , and for every t\ge 0 , find \tilde{{\zeta}_{t}}=({\xi}_{1}^{2},{\xi}_{2}^{2})\in {\omega}^{2} such that: {\tilde{\zeta}}_{t}=\underset{({\xi}_{1}^{2},{\xi}_{2}^{2})\in {\omega}^{2}}{\text{argmin}}\left\lbrace \frac{1}{2}.∥{\varphi}^{1}({\Theta}^{1}({\xi}_{1}^{1},{\xi}_{2}^{1}),t)-{\varphi}^{2}({\Theta}^{2}({\xi}_{1}^{2},{\xi}_{2}^{2}),t)∥{2}^{}\right\rbrace The solution \tilde{{\zeta}_{t}} is the position in the parametric reference space of the projection M of the slave node P onto the master mesh cell. 3.4.4.2 Formulation of the minimisation problem In order to solve the non-linear problem, one proposes to use a Newton minimisation algorithm. The problem is reformulated in the following manner: for a given slave node one searches for the point (in parametric coordinates) which minimises the distance to a given master mesh cell (the one defined in paragraph r5.03.50-recherche-maille-maitre). One denotes by f the {L}_{2} norm of the distance between a slave node located at \left\lbrace {x}_{e}\right\rbrace and a point \left\lbrace {x}_{m}\right\rbrace belonging to the facing master mesh cell: f(\left\lbrace {x}_{m}\right\rbrace )={∥\left\lbrace {x}_{e}\right\rbrace -\left\lbrace {x}_{m}\right\rbrace ∥}^{2} One writes the functional in the parametric space, \left\lbrace {x}_{m}\right\rbrace being expressed from the {\mathit{nb}}_{\mathit{no}} nodes \left\lbrace {x}_{i,m}\right\rbrace of the paired master mesh cell: f({\xi}_{1},{\xi}_{2})=f(\left\lbrace \zeta \right\rbrace )={∥\left\lbrace {x}_{e}\right\rbrace -\sum_{i=1}^{{\mathit{nb}}_{\mathit{no}}}{\phi }_{i}(\left\lbrace \zeta \right\rbrace ).\left\lbrace {x}_{i,m}\right\rbrace ∥}^{2} It is this quantity which must be minimised. One applies the Newton algorithm to the stationarity conditions (Euler-Lagrange) of the minimisation problem thus stated, that is to say to the vector functional \left\lbrace \nabla f(\left\lbrace \zeta \right\rbrace )\right\rbrace , the expression of the first-order Taylor expansion, about the point \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{0}\right\rbrace : \left\lbrace \nabla f(\left\lbrace \zeta \right\rbrace )\right\rbrace \underset{\text{linéarisation}}{=}\left\lbrace \nabla f(\left\lbrace {\zeta}_{0}\right\rbrace )\right\rbrace +\left[H({\zeta}_{0})\right].(\left\lbrace \zeta \right\rbrace -\left\lbrace {\zeta}_{0}\right\rbrace ) Where \left[H\right] is the Hessian matrix of the second derivatives of f and \left\lbrace \nabla f(\left\lbrace \zeta \right\rbrace )\right\rbrace is its gradient. A minimum of f occurs when its gradient is zero. The iterative algorithm is then written: 1. Start from the initial point \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i=0}\right\rbrace on the master mesh cell. This starting point is simply chosen at \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i=0}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace 0\right\rbrace ; 2. Evaluate the gradient \left\lbrace \nabla f\left(\left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i}\right\rbrace \right)\right\rbrace and the Hessian matrix \left[H\left({\zeta}_{i}\right)\right] at this point; 3. Compute the descent direction \left\lbrace {d\zeta }_{i}\right\rbrace =-{\left[H\left({\zeta}_{i}\right)\right]}^{-1}.\left\lbrace \nabla f\left(\left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i}\right\rbrace \right)\right\rbrace 4. Compute the linear-search parameter \alpha (see r5.03.50-recherche-linéaire-algorithme-projection) 5. Compute the next point such that \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i+1}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i}\right\rbrace +\alpha \left\lbrace {d\zeta }_{i}\right\rbrace ; 6. If the process has converged, one stops, otherwise one loops to 2. Notes: - This problem is written without constraints; - One cannot guarantee the uniqueness of the solution; the Newton process will find the first point satisfying the stationarity conditions. - The existence of the gradient and of the Hessian matrix is ensured if the mesh cell is sufficiently regular, which is always the case on a finite-element mesh which is not too distorted. - The iterative process stops by a criterion on the displacement increment in the parametric space \epsilon =\frac{\sqrt{\langle {\zeta}_{i+1}\rangle \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i+1}\right\rbrace -\langle {\zeta}_{i}\rangle \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i}\right\rbrace }}{\sqrt{\langle {\zeta}_{i+1}\rangle \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i+1}\right\rbrace }} with \epsilon \le {10}^{-4} (a value which cannot be modified by the user). This value being estimated with respect to the parametric coordinates, there are no problems with the size of the mesh cells and the units used. - The maximum number of Newton iterations is fixed at 200 (a value which cannot be modified by the user). - If the maximum number of iterations is reached, one selects as the projection the iterate which has minimised the distance between the slave node and the master mesh cell (it is therefore not perfectly the orthogonal projection). - There exists a variant in which the search direction is not estimated by the Newton algorithm but is a fixed direction given by the user, which can be useful in certain difficult cases (a perfectly convex mesh cell which does not give a unique projection, for example). One activates it by the keyword TYPE_APPA='FIXE' and the vector is given by DIRE_APPA. - The projection onto the segment elements in 3D (the case of beams or cables) requires a definition of the normal by the user via the keywords VECT_MAIT/VECT_ESCL. 3.4.4.3 Expression of the tangent matrix and of the residual The expressions of the terms involved in the writing of the Newton algorithm described above are given below. One recalls the functional: f\left({\xi}_{1},{\xi}_{2}\right)=f\left(\left\lbrace \zeta \right\rbrace \right)={∥\left\lbrace {x}_{e}\right\rbrace {x}_{i,m}\right\rbrace )\end{array} 3.4.4.4 Linear search in the projection algorithm In order to improve the robustness of the projection algorithm, a linear-search phase is added in the Newton algorithm (cf. r5.03.50-formulation-problème-minimisation). The aim, given a descent direction \left\lbrace {d\zeta }_{i}\right\rbrace , is to determine an advance parameter \alpha which minimises a functional F associated with f . The linear-search algorithm used (linear search with backtracking and the Armijo rule) is the same as for the implicit integration of the constitutive laws r5.03.14. The functional F , associated with the distance functional f defined in , is the following: F(\alpha )=\frac{1}{2}{∥\nabla f\left(\left\lbrace \zeta \right\rbrace +\alpha \left\lbrace {d\zeta }_{i}\right\rbrace \right)∥}^{2} In order to choose \alpha , one will in fact not seek to minimise the functional F exactly but an approximation of this latter (quadratic, cubic). In order to know which approximation to use, one relies on the Armijo rule. For more details, one refers to r5.03.14 and which detail the implementation of such an algorithm. For the linear search implemented in the projection algorithm, the parameters chosen (hard-coded) are the following: | Parameter of the Armijo rule | \omega =0,0001 | | --- | --- | | Minimum bound for the fold-back | {\alpha}_{min}=0,1 | | Maximum bound for the fold-back | {\alpha}_{max}=0,5 | | Maximum number of cubic interpolations | {\mathit{it}}_{max}=2 | These parameters imply in particular that if the default step ( \alpha =1 ) does not satisfy the Armijo rule, that is to say that the descent direction chosen does not bring one closer to the orthogonal projection, then \alpha will be at most equal to 0,5 . This choice makes it possible to favour robustness (avoid following an erroneous search direction) rather than performance (values of \alpha greater than 1 ). For meshes of poor quality, with distorted mesh cells, the linear search has shown its usefulness, finding the correct orthogonal projection on difficult cases where an algorithm without linear search failed. 3.4.5 Treatment of projections outside the mesh cell There exist projections whose result is sensitive to purely numerical parameters or whose mathematical existence and uniqueness are not guaranteed. Under certain conditions, one can detect contact between two surfaces when there is none. The problem comes first from an incorrect and imperfect definition of the surfaces liable to come into contact. Take the case of contact in 2D (the contact surfaces are therefore segments) where a slave node must project outside the master surface (see figure): | | | --- | | Figure 3.4.5-a : projection outside a master mesh cell. | The user can choose to “re-project” this slave node onto the extended master mesh cell or not to do so (see figure). | | | --- | | Figure 3.4.5-b : principle of the tolerance zone for the projection onto a master mesh cell. | The limit value of this re-projection is fixed by the keyword TOLE_PROJ_EXT, which takes as its argument the value (referred to the reference element) of the extension of the master mesh cell within which one authorises the re-projection. By default, this value is fixed at 0.50 . This means that any slave node projecting at a distance greater than half the length of the master mesh cell will not be re-projected. In order to forbid re-projection completely, it is sufficient to set TOLE_PROJ_EXT to zero. This operator is valid in 2D and in 3D. In the 3D case, it is the extension of a surface contact mesh cell, and, since one reasons in the parametric space, the curvature of the edges of the elements is indeed taken into account. Likewise, if the contact surfaces are too extended, every slave node located behind the master mesh cell is paired. The notion of “in front–behind” is given by the orientation of the normals given by the user (see r5.03.50-orientation-normales). One can restrict this search for a paired mesh cell with the parameter TOLE_APPA, which specifies the maximum search distance of the mesh cells “pairable” with the slave node. 3.4.6 Case of the projection in a given direction When one uses the option DIRE_APPA, the user can force the projection algorithm not to search for the minimum distance between a slave node and its orthogonal projection onto the master surface, but simply to find the point of the master surface linked to the slave node by a given vector. In this case the algorithm is the following: 1. Start from the initial point \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i=0}\right\rbrace on the master mesh cell. This starting point is simply chosen at \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i=0}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace 0\right\rbrace ; 2. Build the Newton matrix \left[H({\zeta}_{i})\right] by the use of the direction given by DIRE_APPA; 3. Build the Newton right-hand side \left\lbrace R\left(\left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i}\right\rbrace \right)\right\rbrace by the difference between the slave node and its projection onto the master mesh cell; 4. Compute the descent direction \left\lbrace {d\zeta }_{i}\right\rbrace =-{\left[H\left({\zeta}_{i}\right)\right]}^{-1}.\left\lbrace R\left(\left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i}\right\rbrace \right)\right\rbrace 5. Compute the next point such that \left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i+1}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {\zeta}_{i}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace {d\zeta }_{i}\right\rbrace ; 6. If the process has converged, one stops, otherwise one loops to 2. There is no linear-search algorithm, unlike the previous case. 3.5 Kinematic relations 3.5.1 Definition of the contact matrix One carries out an idealised modelling of the contact phenomenon, in the sense that it assumes the boundaries of the bodies to be perfectly defined by a line or a surface: one then writes a discrete and linearised non-interpenetration condition. Let P be a slave node, M its projection onto the master mesh cell which was determined during pairing. In 2D, this master mesh cell has two nodes (SEG2) or three nodes (SEG3). In 3D, it may have three, four, six, eight or nine (TRIA3, QUAD4, TRIA6, QUAD8, QUAD9). The displacement of the point M is a linear combination of the displacements of the nodes of the finite element, with as coefficients the values of the shape functions \Phi at M . Let us place ourselves in the case where the master mesh cell is a SEG2 in order to simplify the presentation. One then has: \left\lbrace {u}_{M}\right\rbrace =\left[{\Phi}_{A}\left(M\right)\right].\left\lbrace {u}_{A}\right\rbrace +\left[{\Phi}_{B}\left(M\right)\right].\left\lbrace {u}_{B}\right\rbrace As a first step, one chooses to take as the direction \left\lbrace N\right\rbrace the outward normal of the master mesh cell (cf. ). | | | --- | | Figure 3.5.1-a : projection of a slave node onto a SEG2 mesh cell. | The normal gap is written as the difference between the slave node P and its projection M onto the master mesh cell: \langle N\rangle .\left[\left\lbrace {u}_{P}\right\rbrace -\sum_{j=1}^{{n}_{m}}\left[{\Phi}_{{B}_{j}}(M)\right].\left\lbrace {u}_{{B}_{j}}\right\rbrace \right]=d If one writes such a relation for all the contact pairs, one obtains the geometric non-penetration conditions in matrix form: \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right].\left\lbrace u\right\rbrace =d The matrix \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right] , called the contact matrix, contains one row per contact pair, and as many columns as there are physical degrees of freedom of the problem. Suppose that one has two contact mesh cells of type SEG2, according to the diagram of the . | | | --- | | Figure 3.5.1-b : writing of the contact matrix A on an example. | If one denotes for example {u}_{B} the displacement of the node B along the direction x , {v}_{B} the displacement of the node B along the direction y , and {d}^{1} and {d}^{2} the current gaps for the two pairs: \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right].\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}_{P}\\ {v}_{P}\\ {u}_{Q}\\ {v}_{Q}\\ {u}_{B}\\ {v}_{B}\\ {u}_{C}\\ {v}_{C}\\ {u}_{D}\\ {v}_{D}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{d}^{1}\\ {d}^{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace With the contact matrix \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right] : \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cccccccccc}{N}_{x}^{1}& {N}_{y}^{1}& 0& 0& -\frac{1}{2}.{N}_{x}^{1}& -\frac{1}{2}.{N}_{y}^{1}& -\frac{1}{2}.{N}_{x}^{1}& -\frac{1}{2}.{N}_{y}^{1}& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& {N}_{x}^{2}& {N}_{y}^{2}& 0& 0& -\frac{3}{4}.{N}_{x}^{2}& -\frac{3}{4}.{N}_{y}^{2}& -\frac{1}{4}.{N}_{x}^{2}& -\frac{1}{4}.{N}_{y}^{2}\end{array}\right] One has here considered only the degrees of freedom of the nodes involved in the contact; the matrix \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right] should be sparser. But in practice, one always reduces the contact matrix onto the active degrees of freedom. One therefore stores only the non-zero coefficients. 3.5.2 Definition of the friction matrix The notion of a contact matrix extends to the case of tangential sliding, on the tangent plane. It is the matrix of the kinematic friction relations \left[{A}^{\text{f}}\right] . 3.5.3 Choice of the normal In the previous paragraph, one chose to take as the direction \left\lbrace N\right\rbrace the outward normal of the master mesh cell. This is the default behaviour in code_aster . However, it is possible to choose other normals: - The slave normal NORMALE='ESCL'; - An average between the master normal and the slave normal NORMALE='MAIT_ESCL'; It is also possible to request the use of smoothed normals (LISSAGE='OUI'), that is to say that instead of using the master normal at the projection point, one can take a normal coming from the linear interpolation between the normals at the nodes of the master mesh cell. Likewise, the computation of the normals is always done via the shape functions of the element; this is what one defines as the “true” normal or the “automatic” normal. But it is possible to impose a normal on the master mesh cell, the slave mesh cell or on both in a different manner: - Directly (VECT_MAIT or VECT_ESCL='FIXE') - Indirectly by the use of a triad (VECT_MAIT or VECT_ESCL='VECT_Y'). In this latter case, the normal used will be the vector coming from the vector product between the tangent to the mesh cell and the given vector VECT_Y. Notes: - Since this is a pairing of node-facet type, the slave normal is itself computed by smoothing; the LISSAGE option therefore has no effect if one chooses NORMALE='ESCL'; - The use of predefined normals is mandatory in the case of beams; - The choice of a normal other than the master mesh cell must be limited to exceptional cases, such as when the mesh or the problems of compatibility of the contact with the boundary conditions have forced the user to take as master a coarsely meshed surface; - The use of TYPE_APPA='FIXE' for the search for the closest master mesh cell (see r5.03.50-calcul-projection-esclave-maitre) does not prejudge the choice of the normal in the writing of the non-penetration relation, which remains at the user's choice. But it is more consistent to choose a fixed normal (VECT_MAIT='FIXE'). 3.5.4 Coefficients of the contact matrix 3.5.4.1 Standard elements The values of the shape functions {\Phi}_{{B}_{j}}(M) of the master nodes at the point M for the various contact mesh cells are standard (see r1.01.01). 3.5.4.2 QUAD8 mesh cells The mesh cells of quadrilateral type with eight nodes present a defect. Indeed, the classical shape functions are not positive over the whole domain and lead to aberrant results when they are used in contact. The principal symptom linked to the use of the classical shape functions is the appearance of non-physical negative contact forces which cause oscillations (between the vertex nodes and the mid-side nodes). In order to avoid this phenomenon, code_aster proceeds to modify the QUAD8 element by imposing linear relations between mid-side nodes and vertex nodes and by finally using the shape functions of the QUAD4. In general, it is preferable to avoid using this kind of element and to prefer to it complete quadratic elements such as the QUAD9, because one considers the QUAD8 as linear elements and one furthermore introduces linear relations which can be a nuisance. 3.5.4.3 COQUE_3D elements The elements of type COQUE_3D are mixed non-isoparametric finite elements. They are based on quadratic mesh cells of type QUAD9 (respectively TRIA7) but, the mid-side node carrying no translation degree of freedom, one proceeds to a projection onto a QUAD8 (respectively TRIA6) and one therefore falls back on the defects mentioned in the previous paragraph. These finite elements are therefore not recommended in contact problems. 3.6 Introduction of a fictitious gap One may wish to model the contact between structures with certain particular features (“hole” or “bump”) which one does not wish to mesh (see figure). | | | | --- | --- | | Figure 3.6-a : holes and bumps. | | One solution consists in meshing the surface without these defects and in adding to it a distance given by the user (see figure). | | | --- | | Figure 3.6-b : meshed surface without defect. | One corrects the value of the gap: \langle N\rangle .(\left\lbrace {u}_{P}\right\rbrace -\left\lbrace {u}_{M}\right\rbrace ).=d-({d}_{\text{e}}+{d}_{\text{m}}) where {d}_{\text{e}} and {d}_{\text{m}} are given by the user respectively under the keywords DIST_MAIT and DIST_ESCL for each contact zone. Contact/friction (denoted C in the second column) is treated after each Newton iteration of the global problem (denoted G in the second column). Without taking contact into account, one will denote the solution vectors with a \text{~} , for example: \left\lbrace {\tilde{u}}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {u}_{i-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \delta {\tilde{u}}^{n}\right\rbrace 4.3.6.1 Case of dualisation The general procedure for the dualised case is the following: | At the Newton iteration n | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | G | Solution of the equilibrium problem without contact, equation | \to \left\lbrace \delta {\tilde{u}}^{n}\right\rbrace | | 2 | G | Update of the displacements without contact | \left\lbrace {\tilde{u}}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {u}_{i-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \delta {\tilde{u}}^{n}\right\rbrace | | 3 | C | Modification of the displacements in order to satisfy the contact conditions | \left\lbrace \delta {\tilde{u}}^{n}\right\rbrace \to \left\lbrace \delta {u}^{n}\right\rbrace | | 4 | C | Update of the displacements with contact taken into account | \left\lbrace {u}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {u}_{i-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \delta {u}^{n}\right\rbrace | | 5 | C | Computation of the contact forces | \left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{c},n}\right\rbrace and \left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{f},n}\right\rbrace | | 6 | C | Possible computation of matrices (case of sliding) | \left[{K}^{\text{g},n+1}\right] | | 7 | G | Computation of the internal and external forces with the modified displacements | \left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{ext},n}\right\rbrace and \left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{int,n}\right\rbrace | | 8 | G | Check of equilibrium | | The matrix \left[{K}^{\text{cf},n+1}\right] is computed only in the case of sliding. This implies that for the penalised methods, one will always need at least two Newton iterations, even in the elastic case: one iteration to solve the equilibrium problem without contact/friction and a second iteration to integrate the contact-friction conditions which will modify the global system. There exist several ways of choosing and computing this matrix. For more details see r5.03.01 The idea of transforming the Coulomb problem into a succession of Tresca problems is very widely justified in the literature (see for example) and is used in the majority of commercial codes. It is also the strategy adopted in the “fixed-point” version of the algorithm in the continuous formulation (see r5.03.52). 5 Algorithmic solution – Contact without friction 5.1 Contact links Each slave node potentially in contact has a status whose nature the algorithms will have to determine. A slave node is called a “potential contact link” or more simply a “link”. The term link alludes to the fact that the contact condition is the result of the imposition of a kinematic relation on the displacement degrees of freedom of the slave node. These links are gathered in various sets: - :math: is the set of the possible links (active and inactive); - {\Xi}^{\text{nc}} is the set of the slave nodes which are not in contact (inactive links); - {\Xi}^{\text{c}} is the set of the nodes effectively in contact (active links). One therefore has the following relations between the sets: - {\Xi}^{\text{c}}\cap {\Xi}^{\text{nc}}=\mathrm{\varnothing } because the nodes are in contact or not; - {\Xi}^{l}={\Xi}^{\text{c}}\oplus {\Xi}^{\text{nc}} because the nodes potentially in contact are so or not; 5.2 The dualised methods in contact 5.2.1 Equilibrium of the structure in the presence of contact One recalls that the equilibrium equation in the presence of contact is written: \left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{int}({u}_{i})\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}({u}_{i})\right\rbrace -\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{c}}\right\rbrace In the case of dualised contact, the contact force is written as a function of the contact Lagrange multiplier: \left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{c}}\right\rbrace ={\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{c}}\right\rbrace }_{\text{dual}}=[{A}^{\text{c}}{]}^{T}.\left\lbrace {\mu}_{i}^{\text{c}}\right\rbrace After linearisation of the equilibrium equation, one introduces the tangent matrix \left[{K}^{\text{m},n-1}\right] which will contain the contributions coming from the linearisation of the internal and external forces and the matrix \left[{K}^{\text{c},n-1}\right] for the contact forces; one finds \left\lbrace \delta {\tilde{u}}^{n}\right\rbrace , the solution increment of the equilibrium problem at iteration n but without application of the contact law: (\left[{K}^{\text{m},n-1}\right]+\left[{K}^{\text{c},n-1}\right]).\left\lbrace \delta {\tilde{u}}^{n}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{int,n-1}\right\rbrace -\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{ext},n-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{c},n-1}\right\rbrace We have seen that the contact forces in the dualised case do not depend on the displacement (see r5.03.50-linearisation). One therefore has \left[{K}^{\text{c},n-1}\right]=0 . This allows us to express the equilibrium of the structure with the contact forces taken into account (denoting \left[K\right]=\left[{K}^{\text{m},n-1}\right] and \left\lbrace F\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{ext},n-1}\right\rbrace -\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{int,n-1}\right\rbrace -\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{c},n-1}\right\rbrace in order to lighten the notation): \left[K\right].\left\lbrace \delta {\tilde{u}}^{n}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace F\right\rbrace The solution \left\lbrace {\tilde{u}}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace is obtained after equilibrium and before application of the contact conditions. It is written: \left\lbrace {\tilde{u}}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {u}_{i-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \delta {\tilde{u}}^{n}\right\rbrace In order to obtain the solution \left\lbrace {\tilde{u}}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace , we have not applied the contact conditions (Signorini's law) for the current Newton iteration n . On the other hand, the contact reactions computed at the previous Newton iteration n-1 are indeed taken into account in \left\lbrace F\right\rbrace . In order to solve completely the equilibrium problem with contact/friction, at iteration n , one must apply Signorini's law, which is expressed by the following system: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right].\left\lbrace {u}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace \le \left\lbrace {d}_{\text{ini}}^{\text{c}}\right\rbrace & (a)\\ \left\lbrace {\mu}_{i}^{\text{c}}\right\rbrace \ge 0& (b)\\ \langle {\mu}_{i}^{\text{c}}\rangle .(\left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right].\left\lbrace {u}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace )=0& (c)\end{array} One recalls the interpretation of the Signorini conditions: - Equation (a) represents the geometric non-interpenetration conditions, the inequality being understood component by component (each row relates to a potential contact pair). - Equation (b) expresses the absence of opposition to separation (the contact surfaces can experience only compressions); this is the condition known as intensility. - Equation (c) is the compatibility condition. When, for a given link, the Lagrange multiplier is non-zero, one has contact and therefore the gap is zero. When the gap is non-zero (the two surfaces are not in contact), the associated multiplier must be zero (no compression). The application of Signorini's law will modify the displacement increment \left\lbrace \delta {\tilde{u}}^{n}\right\rbrace (which becomes \left\lbrace \delta {u}^{n}\right\rbrace ), whence the solution obtained after equilibrium and after application of the contact law, which is written: \left\lbrace {u}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {u}_{i-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}\right\rbrace +\left\lbrace \delta {u}^{n}\right\rbrace 5.2.2 System reduced to the active links We are going to write the system making it possible to solve completely the equilibrium problem with Signorini's law taken into account.
