For the problems with friction, convergence results with uniqueness of the solution for the discretised problem are established in for small values of the Coulomb friction coefficient. The results are obtained by using a fixed-point algorithm associated with a Lagrange-multiplier method. For each contact problem solved, one studies the associated friction problem. Once the latter has been solved, one solves a new contact problem, and so on. These methods are however different from those presented here and one cannot therefore present theoretical convergence results for the latter. 7.1 Subdivision of the time step On the theoretical level, the convergence of the active-constraint method is ensured in a finite number of iterations. In practice, certain numerical artefacts can make this convergence delicate. A strategy has therefore been developed in order to ensure the robustness of the algorithm. During contact computations, in particular if the load steps carried out are too large, undesirable phenomena can appear: - The contact matrix is singular, - Oscillation of the active-constraint method: a node is detected alternately “stuck” then “separated”. In order to overcome these difficulties, the following strategy has been adopted. If: - The contact matrix is singular, - The number of active-constraint iterations is greater than a limit which depends on the number of potential links. This number is fixed at twice the total number of slave nodes for the active-constraint method, and at ITER_CONT_MULT times the total number of slave nodes for the other methods. Then one subdivides the time step, i.e. one returns to the previous load step and, instead of trying to reach the following loading level in one step as one has just done, one does several of them (For more details on this functionality of the operator STAT_NON_LINE, see the documentation U4.51.03). 7.2 Compatibility with the Dirichlet boundary conditions In the case of the methods with Lagrange multipliers, one can observe incompatibilities with the fact of imposing boundary conditions of Dirichlet type. Indeed, the problem must make sense physically. One cannot treat a contact problem in the direction of the axis z if all the points have a zero displacement along z . As we are going to see, treating such a problem leads to a singularity of the matrices of the type \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right].{\left[K\right]}^{-1}.{\left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right]}^{T} with the treatment of the Dirichlet boundary conditions by double Lagrange multiplier of code_aster . 7.2.1 Writing of the boundary conditions Taking inspiration from the reference documentation r5.03.01 of STAT_NON_LINE, the dualisation of the Dirichlet boundary conditions leads to the following system of equations to be solved: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\left[K\right].\left\lbrace \delta u\right\rbrace +{\left[B\right]}^{T}.\left\lbrace \delta \lambda \right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{int}\right\rbrace -\left\lbrace {L}_{i}^{\text{ext}}\right\rbrace \\ \left[B\right].\left\lbrace {u}_{i}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {u}_{i}^{d}\right\rbrace -\left[B\right].\left\lbrace {u}_{i-1}\right\rbrace \end{array} One then denotes \left[C\right] the stiffness matrix of the system such that: \left[C\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\left[K\right]& {\left[B\right]}^{T}\\ \left[B\right]& \left[0\right]\end{array}\right] This matrix possesses an inverse of the form: {\left[C\right]}^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\left[E\right]& \left[F\right]\\ {\left[F\right]}^{T}& \left[G\right]\end{array}\right] such that: \left[E\right].{\left[B\right]}^{T}=\left[0\right] . One thus checks that for each boundary condition l one has the property \left[E\right].{\left[{B}_{l}\right]}^{T}=\left[0\right] . 7.2.2 Return to the contact problem The matrix \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right].{\left[K\right]}^{-1}.{\left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right]}^{T} can also be written \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right].\left[E\right].{\left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right]}^{T} since the link vectors \left[A\right] involve only the displacement degrees of freedom. - It then follows that if a link vector J of the matrix \left[A\right] is a linear combination of the boundary conditions of Dirichlet type it satisfies the following property: \left[E\right].{\left[{A}_{J}\right]}^{T}=\left[0\right] . The matrix \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right].\left[E\right].{\left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right]}^{T} is then singular because it possesses a column of zeros. In practice, without particular treatment, one ends up in the code on a stop message of the type stop on a singular contact-friction matrix. The detection of these singular columns has been implemented in the code so as to eliminate from the contact-friction relations this type of relation and to avoid the stop described previously. - It then follows that if a link vector J of the matrix \left[A\right] contains a linear combination of the boundary conditions of Dirichlet type and is written \left[{A}_{J}\right]=\sum{\alpha}_{i}.\left[{B}_{i}\right]+\left[{\bar{A}}_{J}\right] , it satisfies the following property: \left[E\right].{\left[{A}_{J}\right]}^{T}=\left[E\right].{\left[\bar{{A}_{J}}\right]}^{T} . One can then have a matrix \left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right].\left[E\right].{\left[{A}^{\text{c}}\right]}^{T} which is singular because it possesses two identical rows. This detection is for the moment not available in the code and one ends up in the code on a stop message of the type stop on a singular contact-friction matrix. Note: This problem of compatibility between contact-friction and the boundary conditions does not appear with the regularised methods, inasmuch as one adds stiffness to the global stiffness and one does not carry out an elimination as in the computation of the Lagrange multipliers. 8 Conclusion Discrete modellings of contact-friction with 1D and 2D sliding surfaces have been implemented in code_aster . These modellings, usable with STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, are accessible under DEFI_CONTACT. The modellings proposed rely on the meshes of the surfaces coming into contact and make it possible to transcribe, node to node, the frictional-contact conditions between the surfaces after discretisation of the corresponding variational formulation. The method then extends without difficulty from small displacements to the case of large displacements. Indeed, the absence of the use of finite elements, between the surfaces which may come into contact, avoids the large distortion of the latter, in the case of large displacements. One can then use either direct node-to-node link conditions for meshes which are initially compatible, or node-to-node link conditions weighted according to a projection approach of master-slave type for incompatible meshes. In the case of 1D sliding surfaces one has been able to develop an algorithm using only Lagrange multipliers. The finite convergence of this type of algorithm is proved for unilateral contact without friction and, in the case with friction, for small values of the Coulomb friction coefficient. r5.03.54 Contact in small sliding with X-FEM r5.03.54 Contact in small sliding with X-FEM Summary: This document presents a new approach for treating contact problems in small sliding with the eXtended Finite Element Method (X-FEM) [bib1]. One considers the continuous hybrid formulation of contact problems between solids [bib2] and the solution strategy is similar to that already implemented in Code_Aster for the classical finite-element framework [bib3]. A new type of mixed contact element is introduced, specific to the X-FEM framework. The approach is implemented in Code_Aster in 2D and 3D, and treats both interfaces completely cut by a crack and interfaces with a crack front. It can be used with the command STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03. Friction of Coulomb type is taken into account. 1 Introduction In order to take frictional contact into account on the crack lips with X-FEM, we have chosen the framework of the continuous method [bib 1 ], [bib 2 ]. Unlike the discrete approaches where the contact problem is taken into account by assembly of nodal forces, the equations are here discretised by the finite-element method and the contact problem is taken into account by an assembly of elementary contributions. This approach has been developed by numerous authors, such as Alart et al. [bib 3 ], Laursen et al. [bib 8 ], Wriggers [bib 9 ], Curnier et al. [bib 10 ], Pietrzak [bib 11 ]. In this “continuous” approach, the contact conditions are seen as an interface law and not as boundary conditions. To the notion of interface law between deformable bodies, one can associate, on passing from the continuous formalism to the discrete model, the notion of contact element. The exact, and therefore rigorous, solution of the (non-differentiable) contact laws can be carried out via a hybrid contact element including the contact forces among the unknowns of the problem. In this framework, the hybrid formulation leads to a tangent matrix that is non-symmetric, not positive definite, ill-conditioned, with zeros on the diagonal. The difficulty of the problem lies in the non-differentiability of the system to be solved [bib 12 ]. The method proposed by Ben Dia is very similar, but one chooses to eliminate the non-differentiability of the contact by an active-constraint algorithm, and that of the friction by a fixed-point problem on the friction so as to obtain a sequence of regular problems possessing solution methods whose convergence is established. Numerous variants, according to the algorithms adopted and their arrangement, exist, but the convergence of the global scheme is not assured. One recalls that one starts from a Lagrangian formalism of the contact problem between two deformable solids, which one introduces into the principle of virtual work. A mixed displacement–pressure variational formulation is deduced by incorporating weak formulations of the contact laws. The equations are discretised by the finite-element method. The choice of the finite-element spaces of discretisation as well as the integration schemes (contact terms) are made explicit. With X-FEM, the crack lips are treated as a single geometrical surface of discontinuity which can be interior to the finite elements. The integration of the contact terms on this (non-meshed) surface then calls upon the quantities carried by the nodes of the elements crossed by it. In small displacements, no pairing is necessary because the points of the crack surface facing each other are intrinsically linked (they correspond to the same geometrical entity). The displacement jump is expressed as a function of the discontinuous enrichment degrees of freedom introduced by X-FEM. This document is organised around 6 principal sections, of which this introduction serves as section 1. The frictional-contact problem as well as the equations brought into play are introduced in paragraph [§ 2 ]. Starting from a Lagrangian approach to contact introduced into the principle of virtual work, paragraph [§ 3 ] arrives at an expression of the mixed displacement–pressure variational formulation. Paragraph [§ 4 ] evokes the choice of the finite-element discretisations of the contact-action fields. One specifies the solution strategy in paragraph [§ 5 ]. The expressions of the elementary contact and friction terms resulting from the X-FEM approach are detailed in paragraph [§ 5.6 ]. Paragraph [§ 6 ] is concerned with a particular compatibility condition of the displacement and pressure fields. An algorithm aimed at determining an adequate space of contact-pressure multipliers (that is, respecting the LBB condition) is set out. 2 Strong formulation of the frictional-contact problem 2.1 Formulation of the equations of the general problem One will denote by {r}^{1} and {r}^{2} the densities of the forces due to the possible frictional-contact interactions between the two surfaces. Failure to respect the LBB condition generates oscillations of the contact pressures, a phenomenon comparable to that encountered in incompressibility [bib 13 ]. Physically, in the case of Lagrangian contact, this amounts to wanting to impose the contact at too many points of the interface (over-constraint), making the system hyperstatic. To release it, one must restrict the space of the Lagrange multipliers, as is done in [bib 14 ] for the Dirichlet conditions with X-FEM. The algorithm proposed by Moës [bib 14 ] to reduce the oscillations is extended to the 3D case. Its aim is to impose equality relations between Lagrange multipliers. This algorithm has been the subject of an improvement in order to make it more physical and more efficient. In the case of penalised contact one finds the same oscillations. For a triangular mesh for example, one can show that there does not exist a combination of the Heaviside degrees of freedom that allows a rotation of the mean surface of the crack without generating oscillations of the displacement jump. For a high interface stiffness, as is the case in penalisation, this generates pressure oscillations. To remedy this, it is necessary to recover the explicit pressure in the degree of freedom \lambda , to apply the LBB condition to it and to bring it back up into the equilibrium, which explains the formulation given in § 3.3. The updating of the contact statuses is done as in the Lagrangian case, where \lambda and not {d}_{n} is tested in order to pass from a contacting state to a non-contacting state, this in order to avoid the oscillations on the contact statuses. 6.1 Description of the Moës algorithm for the linear and quadratic elements (algo1) The algorithm introduced by Moës [bib 14 ] is presented there with the aim of imposing Dirichlet conditions on an interface within the X-FEM framework. It shows that the Lagrange-multiplier technique for imposing Dirichlet conditions must be used with care, because the inf-sup condition is not always respected. The paper is restricted to the 2D case, but the algorithm presented is easily generalisable to the 3D case. The first phase is a node-selection phase, in which the selected nodes are those which are “important” for the approximation of the Lagrange multipliers. The other nodes are redundant and lead to oscillations of the Lagrange multipliers. Once the “important” nodes have been selected, equality relations are imposed between the Lagrange multipliers, in order to restrict the space of the multipliers. Thus, the Lagrange multipliers of the edges issuing from one and the same selected node are equal. More formally, let E and N be the sets containing all the edges and all the nodes of the mesh. The two ends of an edge e\in E are denoted ({v}_{1}(e),{v}_{2}(e))\in {N}^{2} . First of all, one begins with an initialisation phase (iteration k=0 of the algorithm). One first determines {S}_{e}^{0} , the set of the edges which are cut by the interface. r5.03.55 1 r5.03.55 LAC method – Local Average Contact 1 r5.03.55 LAC method – Local Average Contact Summary: This document describes the way of treating contact between solids (2D or 3D) in large transformations by a method of «mortar» type. The formulation is very accurate for the contact pressures obtained, in particular when the meshes are not matching or when the surfaces are curved. This formulation is available in the command DEFI_CONTACT under the name ALGO_CONT='LAC'. 2 r5.03.55 Contents 3 r5.03.55 List of illustrations 1 Introduction The finite-element method is currently used on a massive scale in computational mechanics to simulate problems of unilateral contact between two deformable objects. These are problems possessing a non-linear boundary condition, namely satisfying a non-interpenetration condition for the displacement field, a sign condition for the normal pressure on the contact zone and a complementarity condition between these two fields. In the general case, such problems lead to the handling of incompatible meshes (i.e. whose nodes of the contact zones of the objects considered are non-matching). The most widely used methods are based on algorithms of node-segment type in 2D and of node-facet type in 3D (in code_aster, these are the formulations DISCRETE and CONTINUE in mode INTEGRATION='NOEUD'). These methods are known to fail the patch tests in the general case of incompatible meshes and to lead to suboptimal mathematical analyses. On the other hand, the academic community has been very productive in this field over the last fifteen years. The most accomplished methods are the mortar methods adapted to contact. These methods consist in using a simple projection {L}^{2} onto a mortar space, i.e., a space of finite elements defined between the two objects. The various choices of mortar spaces generate a whole family of methods of mortar type. However these methods have important disadvantages when one considers their implementation in a generic way in an industrial code. The method proposed here gives numerical and mathematical results of as good quality as those obtained by the mortar methods while keeping the aspects (locality, analytical definition of the mortar spaces, etc...) that make the implementation in code_aster easier while preserving the current architecture of the code To do this, one will define a simple contact condition which consists in satisfying the contact conditions on average on each macro-element of a macro-mesh defined in a suitable way (which will have to be prepared by means of the option 'DECOUPE_LAC' of the operator CREA_MAILLAGE). 2 Theoretical formulation of the method 2.1 The contact problem 2.1.1 Strong formulation Consider the equilibrium problem of two solids in equilibrium in the figure , denoted by the index l=1,2 . Figure 1: Solids in equilibrium One seeks the displacement field u=({u}_{1,}{u}_{2}):\overline{{\Omega}^{1}}\times \overline{{\Omega}^{2}}\to {\mathrm{ℝ}}^{d} ( d=2 or d=3 ) such that ()-() are satisfied for l=1,2 : -div\sigma ({u}_{l})={f}_{l} \textrm{dans} {\Omega}^{l} \sigma ({u}_{l})={A}_{l}\epsilon ({u}_{l}) \textrm{dans} {\Omega}^{l} \sigma ({u}_{l}){n}_{l}={F}_{l} \textrm{sur} {\Gamma}_{N}^{l} {u}_{l}=0 \textrm{sur} {\Gamma}_{D}^{l} [{u}_{N}]⩽0 \textrm{sur} {\Gamma}_{C} {\sigma}_{N}⩽0 \textrm{sur} {\Gamma}_{C} {\sigma}_{N}[{u}_{N}]=0 \textrm{sur} {\Gamma}_{C} {\sigma}_{\tau}=0 \textrm{sur} {\Gamma}_{C} where [{v}_{N}]={\sum}_{l=1}^{2}{v}_{l}\cdot {n}_{l} . The equations () to () correspond to the mechanical problem considered (for simplicity, one places oneself in the framework of a linear elasticity problem) where A is a fourth-order tensor, elliptic, symmetric and with components in {L}^{\infty} coming from the constitutive law associated with the solid {\Omega}^{l} with a Dirichlet condition on the boundary {\Gamma}_{D}^{l} and a Neumann condition on the boundary {\Gamma}_{N}^{l} . To these equations, one adds the contact conditions on {\Gamma}_{C} , namely a non-interpenetration condition for the displacement jump [{u}_{N}] (), a sign condition for the normal pressure {\sigma}_{\mathrm{N}} the contact zone () and a complementarity condition between these last two fields (). The last equation () comes from the fact that one considers frictionless contact. 2.1.2 Weak formulation Starting from the equations () to (), one can introduce a weak formulation of the contact problem in the form of the following variational inequality: \textrm{Trouver} u \textrm{tel que } \forall v\in K \textrm{ ,} {\sum}_{l=1}^{2}{\int}_{{\Omega}^{l}}{A}_{l}\epsilon ({u}_{l}):\epsilon ({v}_{l}-{u}_{l})d{\Omega}^{l}⩾{\sum}_{l=1}^{2}{\int}_{{\Omega}^{l}}{f}_{l}\cdot ({v}_{l}-{u}_{l})d{\Omega}^{l}+{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{N}^{l}}{F}_{l}\cdot {({v}_{l}-{u}_{l})}_{N}d{\Gamma}^{l} where K\subset V is the convex cone of the admissible displacements ( K contains the non-interpenetration condition). One therefore uses the following spaces: {V}_{l}=\lbrace {v}_{l}\in {({H}^{1}({\Omega}^{l}))}^{d}:v=0\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{D}^{l}\rbrace V={V}_{1}\times {V}_{2} K=\lbrace v\in V:[{v}_{N}]\le 0\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{C}\rbrace One will denote subsequently: a(u,v)={\sum}_{l=1}^{2}{\int}_{{\Omega}^{l}}{A}_{l}\epsilon ({u}_{l}):\epsilon ({v}_{l})d{\Omega}^{l} And: l(v)=\sum_{l=1}^{2}{\int}_{{\Omega}^{l}}{f}_{l}\cdot {v}_{l}d{\Omega}^{l}+{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{N}^{l}}{F}_{l}\cdot {v}_{l}d{\Gamma}^{l} One introduces the equivalent mixed problem: \textrm{Trouver} u\in V \textrm{et } \lambda \in M \textrm{ tels que:} a(u,v)-b(\lambda ,v)=l(v)\text{}\forall v\in V b(\mu -\lambda ,u)\ge 0\text{}\forall \mu \in M With: b(\mu ,v)={\int}_{{\Gamma}_{C}}\mu [{v}_{N}]d\Gamma And: M=\left\lbrace \mu \in {H}^{-1/2}({\Gamma}_{C}):{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{C}}\mu \Psi d\Gamma \le 0\forall \Psi \in {H}^{-1/2}({\Gamma}_{C}),\Psi \ge 0\right\rbrace Note: The problems () and () are well posed. One therefore has existence and uniqueness of the solutions (u,\lambda ) . Furthermore, the solutions u of the problem () and u of the problem () are identical. 2.2 Discrete problems 2.2.1 Discrete variational inequality One considers the discrete contact problem from the point of view of the variational inequality (discretisation of the problem): \textrm{Trouver} {u}^{h}\in {K}^{h} \textrm{tel que} \forall {v}^{h}\in {K}^{h} a({u}^{h},{v}^{h}-{u}^{h})⩾l({v}^{h}-{u}^{h}) where {K}^{h}\subset {V}^{h} is the convex cone of the admissible displacements, a and l the bilinear and linear forms defined previously. To define a method, one must choose the discrete spaces {V}_{l}^{h} and the set {K}^{h} . Let {T}_{l}^{h} be a regular triangulation of {\Omega}^{l}\subset {\mathrm{ℝ}}^{d} , where d=2,3 . One then defines: {V}_{l}^{h}=\lbrace {v}_{l}^{h}\in {(C(\overline{{\Omega}^{l}}))}^{d}:{v}_{l}^{h}{\text{|}}_{T}\in {P}_{k}(T),\forall T\in {T}_{l}^{h},{v}_{l}^{h}=0\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{D}^{l}\rbrace where k=1,2 , {V}^{h}={V}_{1}^{h}\times {V}_{2}^{h} . One proposes to use the following contact condition: {K}^{h}=\left\lbrace {v}^{h}\in {V}^{h}:{\int}_{{T}^{m}}[{v}_{N}^{h}]d\Gamma \le 0\text{}\forall {T}^{m}\in {T}^{M}\right\rbrace where {T}^{M} is a macro-mesh of elements {T}^{m} to be defined according to the choice of {V}^{h} . This contact condition is inspired by methods of mortar type while keeping a local aspect. Indeed, the mortar projection matrix is no longer a full matrix because the inverse of the basis matrix of the space {P}^{0}({T}^{M}) is diagonal. This property ensures that the mortar projection matrices (matrix product between the inverse basis matrix of the space {P}^{0}({T}^{M}) and the coupling matrices between the mortar space and the approximation spaces) are local. However, one knows that the simple condition of type: {\int}_{{T}^{h}\cap {\Gamma}_{C}}[{v}_{N}^{h}]d\Gamma \le 0 is not stable for all the elements commonly used in engineering studies (in particular in 3D, where only the hexahedron with 27 nodes is naturally stable), and therefore does not lead to optimal mathematical analyses. However, by slightly widening the integration support, according to the cases, one manages to prove results of optimal convergence and of stability. 2.2.2 Discrete mixed formulation One introduces the equivalent mixed problem: \textrm{Trouver} {u}^{h}\in {V}^{h} \textrm{et } {\lambda}^{h}\in {M}^{h} \textrm{ tel que} a({u}^{h},{v}^{h})-b({\lambda}^{h},{v}^{h})=l({v}^{h})\text{}\forall {v}^{h}\in {V}^{h} b({\mu}^{h}-{\lambda}^{h},{u}^{h})\ge 0\text{}\forall {\mu}^{h}\in {M}^{h} with: {M}^{h}=\lbrace {\mu}^{h}\in {X}_{1}^{h}:{\mu}^{h}\le 0\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{C}\rbrace Where: {X}_{1}^{h}=\lbrace {\mu}^{h}\in {L}^{2}({\Gamma}_{C}):{\mu}^{h}{\text{|}}_{{T}^{m}}\in {P}^{0}({T}^{m}),\forall {T}^{m}\in {T}^{M}\rbrace One therefore obtains a «mortar {P}^{0} » method which will be automatically stabilised by the definition of the macro-mesh {T}^{M} . Note: The contact condition in {K}^{h} being fixed, the space of the Lagrange multipliers will always be a subspace of {P}^{0}({T}^{m}) whatever the type of finite elements used in the approximation space of the displacements {V}^{h} . One therefore notes that the order of the contact condition remains fixed for every approximation space considered (linear or quadratic); only the definition of the macro-mesh varies in order to ensure the good mathematical properties of the method. 2.3 Mathematical results We recall here the main mathematical results of the LAC method. The fundamental assumption of the method defines the way of constructing the macro-mesh is the assumption of the internal degree of freedom: Assumption of the internal degree of freedom: For every macro-element {T}^{m}\in {T}^{M} , there exists a degree of freedom {x}_{i} of {V}_{1}^{h} such that \mathit{supp}({\varphi}_{i})\subset {T}^{m} , where {\phi }_{i} is the basis function associated with {x}_{i} . Note: One notes that there exists a minimum size for the macro mesh cells making it possible both to satisfy the previous assumption and to guarantee the locality of the method. One also notes that the choice of the trace mesh used to define the macro-mesh is free; here, one has chosen mesh 1. One can now recall the two main convergence results of the LAC method. Theorem 1: Let u and {u}^{h} be the solutions of the continuous and discrete contact problems . One assumes that u\in ({H}^{s}({\Omega}^{1}){)}^{d}\times ({H}^{s}({\Omega}^{2}){)}^{d} with d=2,3 and 3/2 0 independent of {h}_{1} , {h}_{2} (where {h}_{1} and {h}_{2} are the discretisation parameters of the solid 1 and of the solid 2 respectively) and u , such that: {\Vert u-{u}^{h}\Vert }_{1,{\Omega}^{1},{\Omega}^{2}}\le C({h}_{1}^{s-1}+{h}_{2}^{s-1}){\Vert u\Vert }_{s,{\Omega}^{1},{\Omega}^{2}} Theorem 2: Let (u,\lambda ) and ({u}^{h},{\lambda}^{h}) be the solutions of the continuous and discrete contact problems . One assumes that u\in ({H}^{s}({\Omega}^{1}){)}^{d}\times ({H}^{s}({\Omega}^{2}){)}^{d} with d=2,3 and 3/2 0 independent of {h}_{1} , {h}_{2} and u , such that: {\Vert \lambda -{\lambda}^{h}\Vert }_{1/2,\ast ,{\Gamma}_{C}}+{\Vert u-{u}^{h}\Vert }_{1,{\Omega}^{1},{\Omega}^{2}}\le C({h}_{1}^{s-1}+{h}_{2}^{s-1}){\Vert u\Vert }_{s,{\Omega}^{1},{\Omega}^{2}} where {\Vert .\Vert }_{1/2,\ast ,{\Gamma}_{C}} is the dual norm of {\Vert .\Vert }_{1/2,{\Gamma}_{C}} . Note: In the remainder of this document one will adopt the following convention: one will call slave surface the surface on which one will have defined the macro mesh cells, that is the surface carrying the contact Lagrange multipliers in the case of the mixed formulation . The surface facing this last one will be the master surface. 2.4 Matrix formulation One considers the following matrices {C}^{E}\in {M}_{e,k}(\mathrm{ℝ}) , {C}^{M}\in {M}_{m,k}(\mathrm{ℝ}) and {M}^{\mathit{LAC}}\in {M}_{k}(\mathrm{ℝ}) , where {M}_{i,j} corresponds to the space of rectangular matrices of size i\times j and {M}_{i}={M}_{i,i} corresponds to the space of square matrices of size i , defined by: {C}_{ij}^{E}={\int}_{{T}_{j}}{\left({\varphi}_{N}^{E}\right)}_{i}d\Gamma {C}_{ij}^{M}={\int}_{{T}_{j}}{\left({\varphi}_{N}^{M}\right)}_{i}d\Gamma {M}_{ij}^{\mathit{LAC}}={\delta}_{ij}\text{|}{T}^{i}\text{|} where the {T}^{i} are the supports of the basis functions of {P}^{0}({T}^{M}) , the {\varphi}_{N}^{E} are the products of the normal with the basis functions associated with the slave surface and the {\varphi}_{N}^{M} are the products of the normal with the basis functions associated with the master surface. Let U be the displacement field and \Lambda the Lagrange multiplier; the matrix formulation of the problem is the following: \left[\begin{array}{cccc}{K}_{\mathit{NN}}& {K}_{\mathit{NM}}& {K}_{\mathit{NE}}& 0\\ {K}_{\mathit{MN}}& {K}_{\mathit{MM}}& {K}_{\mathit{ME}}& {C}^{M}\\ {K}_{\mathit{EN}}& {K}_{\mathit{EM}}& {K}_{\mathit{EE}}& {C}^{E}\end{array}\right]\times \left[\begin{array}{c}{U}_{N}\\ {U}_{M}\\ {U}_{E}\\ \Lambda \end{array}\right]=F With the following conditions: {M}^{{\mathit{LAC}}^{-1}}({}^{t}{C}^{E}{U}_{E}+{}^{t}{C}^{M}{U}_{M})⩽0 \textrm{dans } {\mathrm{ℝ}}^{k} \textrm{ ,} {M}^{\mathit{LAC}}\Lambda ⩽0 \textrm{dans } {\mathrm{ℝ}}^{k} \textrm{ ,} {M}^{{\mathit{LAC}}^{-1}}({}^{t}{C}^{E}{U}_{E}+{}^{t}{C}^{M}{U}_{M})\cdot {M}^{\mathit{LAC}}\Lambda =0 \textrm{dans } \mathrm{ℝ} \textrm{ .} Noting that {M}^{\mathit{LAC}} is diagonal positive definite, one has equivalence with the following formulation: \left[\begin{array}{cccc}{K}_{\mathit{NN}}& {K}_{\mathit{NM}}& {K}_{\mathit{NE}}& 0\\ {K}_{\mathit{MN}}& {K}_{\mathit{MM}}& {K}_{\mathit{ME}}& {C}^{M}\\ {K}_{\mathit{EN}}& {K}_{\mathit{EM}}& {K}_{\mathit{EE}}& {C}^{E}\end{array}\right]\times \left[\begin{array}{c}{U}_{N}\\ {U}_{M}\\ {U}_{E}\\ \Lambda \end{array}\right]=F With the following conditions: {}^{t}{C}^{E}{U}_{E}+{}^{t}{C}^{M}{U}_{M}⩽0 \textrm{dans } {\mathrm{ℝ}}^{k} \textrm{ ,} \Lambda ⩽0 \textrm{dans } {\mathrm{ℝ}}^{k} \textrm{ ,} {}^{t}{C}^{E}{U}_{E}+{}^{t}{C}^{M}{U}_{M}\cdot {M}^{\mathit{LAC}}\Lambda =0 \textrm{dans } \mathrm{ℝ} \textrm{ .} One solves the problem ()-() using an active-set strategy (active set) coupled with a Newton algorithm. 3 Implementation of the method This chapter presents the implementation of the «LAC» method (Local Average Contact) in code_aster . One will discuss more particularly the implementation choices linked to the new contact condition, avoiding the creation of new mesh-cell types in code_aster and fitting into the already existing formalism for the management of contact. It is therefore appropriate, for this first version of the implementation of the method, to adopt the meshed-contact strategy (one will define late contact elements making it possible to carry out the elementary computations of the contact contributions) and a generalised Newton type approach. The operators affected by the method are: - CREA_MAILLAGE; - DEFI_CONTACT; - STAT_NON_LINE. The proposed method implies the following developments: - A modification of the mesh on the slave contact zone (non-invasive in the volume) in the operator CREA_MAILLAGE; - A redefinition of the contact Lagrange multipliers, implementation of the space {P}^{0}({T}^{M}) in the operator DEFI_CONTACT; - A new pairing of «segment-segment» type in 2D and of «face-face» type in 3D, a new evaluation of the contact statuses and a new elementary computation, with an impact in the operator STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE. 3.1 Preparation of the mesh 3.1.1 Principles of the cutting The theoretical basis imposes that we satisfy the assumption of the internal degree of freedom (see § 2.3 ). For the sake of simplicity, of consistency between 2D and 3D, and in order not to «coarsen» the contact condition, one will use the local refinement method in the 2D and 3D cases. The factor keyword DECOUPE_LAC of the operator makes it possible to prepare this macro-mesh. In certain situations, the keyword will cut the surface mesh cells; in others, this will not be necessary. When one cuts a surface element one therefore arranges not to propagate this cut into the volume. This strategy makes it possible to limit the creation of too many mesh cells but can produce mesh cells of poor quality. Likewise, in order not to modify the user's initial choices, one will always propose a conforming subdivision: a triangle will be cut into triangles, a hexahedron into hexahedra, etc. 3.1.2 The 2D case In the 2D case, the slave contact interface is «1D». The latter is meshed either in SEG2 or in SEG3. First, one notes that the SEG3 associated with itself (macro mesh cell) satisfies the internal d.o.f. assumption; it will therefore not be necessary to cut the mesh cells having SEG3 on the skin (TRIA6, QUAD8 and QUAD9). In the SEG2 case, there exist two cuttings according to the type of the associated body mesh cell. In the TRIA3 case, one adds a node at the centre of the SEG2 mesh cell and one reconstructs the two new skin elements and the two new body elements. In the QUAD4 case. Given that one wishes to proceed to a conforming subdivision, one adds two nodes in the SEG2 mesh cell, and two nodes in the QUAD4 mesh cell. One can then reconstruct the three new skin elements and the four new body elements while supplying the information characterising the macro mesh cell. The results of these operations are presented in the table below (the contact surface is shown in blue). Note: Particular attention will be paid to the orientation of the new mesh cells created, to the conformity of the computation mesh created and to the updating of the mesh-cell groups. Knowing that one cannot update the node groups. Indeed, it is not possible to determine whether a new node enters an already defined node group or not. | | | | --- | --- | | TRIA3 | TRIA3 after DECOUPE_LAC | | | | | TRIA6 | TRIA6 after DECOUPE_LAC (no modification) | | | | | QUAD4 | QUAD4 after DECOUPE_LAC | | | | | QUAD8 | QUAD8 after DECOUPE_LAC (no modification) | | | | | QUAD9 | QUAD9 after DECOUPE_LAC (no modification) | 3.1.3 The 3D case In the 3D case, the slave contact interface is 2D. The latter can be meshed in TRIA3, TRIA6, QUAD4, QUAD8 and QUAD9. As in the 2D case, the QUAD9 mesh cell associated with itself satisfies the internal d.o.f. assumption; one can therefore directly supply the data structures containing the information relating to the macro-mesh without refining locally. In the other cases one will use two typical cuttings, one for the tetrahedral cases, and the other for the hexahedral cases. These two cuttings are conforming in the sense that one cuts an element by generating the same type of elements. The result of these operations is presented in the table below. | | | | --- | --- | | TETRA4 | TETRA4 after DECOUPE_LAC | | | | | HEXA8 after DECOUPE_LAC (Version 1) | | | | | | HEXA8 | HEXA8 after DECOUPE_LAC (Version 2) | | HEXA20 | Two versions (same as HEXA8) | | HEXA27 | HEXA27 after DECOUPE_LAC (no modification) | 3.1.4 Some remarks on the cutting The DECOUPE_LAC feature of the operator is capable of treating: - different types of mesh cell inside the same contact zone; - the multi-zone contact. Concerning the complexity of the computations on the new mesh one notes that one adds a certain number of nodes which will carry d.o.f. and potentially contact Lagrange multipliers. Let M be the number of mesh cells of the slave surface of the contact zone considered; then for (body) meshes in: - TRIA3 one adds M nodes and 2M mesh cells, - QUAD4 one adds 4M nodes and 5M mesh cells, - TETRA4 one adds M nodes and 4M mesh cells, - TETRA10 one adds 5M nodes and 4M mesh cells, - HEXA8 (version 1) one adds 8M nodes and 9M mesh cells, - HEXA20 (version 1) one adds 28M nodes and 9M mesh cells. Furthermore the aspect ratio and the configuration of the generated mesh cells may possibly disturb the post-processing of certain data on the slave surface (skin elements and body elements in contact). 3.2 Preparation of the contact The preparation of the contact data is ensured by the operator DEFI_CONTACT. This operator must take into account the new definition of the contact Lagrange multipliers, i.e. the space {P}^{0}({T}^{M}) . One must add for each macro mesh cell of the LAC surface a contact Lagrange multiplier (see figure ) knowing that it is not possible for code_aster to assign a degree of freedom to a physical entity other than a node. One will present here a device making it possible to define the space {P}^{0}({T}^{M}) locally on each computation mesh cell provided that one has an intelligent assembly of the matrix system. Figure 2: The three spaces of the contact zone (master, slave and LAC) 3.2.1 Illustration of the technique on the TRIA3 case The device lies in the fact that one knows for each mesh cell of the slave contact zone of the mesh given by DECOUPE_LAC what is the local number (in the connectivity) of the internal node of the macro mesh cell, see figure . Figure 3: Local numbering of the computation mesh, TRIA3 case (obtained by DECOUPE_LAC) One therefore knows on which node one must add the degree of freedom \mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C (see figure ); the local number of the node carrying the degree of freedom \mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C being fixed, one can define a single new element type making it possible to take into account the localisation of the \mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C . Figure 4: Assignment of the degrees of freedom on each new TRIA3 slave contact mesh cell Each degree of freedom \mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C is indeed common only to three elements, the three elements making up the macro mesh cell. Given that the basis function {P}^{0} associated with the contact Lagrange multiplier does not depend on the geometric vertices of the macro mesh cell, one can split the elementary computation on the macro mesh cell into an elementary computation on each mesh cell composing it. The first two points require an efficient and robust tool for the intersection of mesh cells in the case of straight mesh cells (linear and quadratic) and in the case of curved mesh cells (quadratic). 3.3.1 Algorithm for the solution of the non-linearities linked to contact One opts for the use of an algorithm of generalised Newton type, handling the geometric non-linearity, the active-set type strategy for the contact non-linearity and the constitutive non-linearity inside the same Newton loop. This algorithmic framework is already present in code_aster (see R5.03.52). It will therefore be sufficient to replace all the internal building blocks of the algorithm in order to implement the new method. One sets: U=\left[\begin{array}{c}{U}_{N}\\ {U}_{M}\\ {U}_{E}\end{array}\right] \textrm{;} K=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{K}_{NN}& {K}_{NM}& {K}_{NE}\\ {K}_{MN}& {K}_{MM}& {K}_{ME}\\ {K}_{EN}& {K}_{EM}& {K}_{EE}\end{array}\right] ; :math: C=\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ {C}^{M}\\ {C}^{E}\end{array}\right] Taking into account the initial «integrated gap» \overline{{G}_{0}} (see the definition in §), the problem is equivalent to: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\left[\begin{array}{cc}K& C\end{array}\right]\times \left[\begin{array}{c}U\\ \Lambda \end{array}\right]=F\\ ^{t}\mathit{CU}⩽\overline{{G}_{0}}\text{dans}{\mathrm{ℝ}}^{k}\\ \Lambda ⩽0\text{dans}{\mathrm{ℝ}}^{k}\\ ^{t}\mathit{CU}\cdot \Lambda =0\text{dans}\mathrm{ℝ}\end{array} One introduces the following function: A(U,\Lambda )=\Lambda +\max(0,\rho (CU-\overline{{G}_{0}})-\Lambda ) One can then show that is equivalent to: \left[\begin{array}{cc}K& C\end{array}\right]\times \left[\begin{array}{c}U\\ \Lambda \end{array}\right]=F \textrm{et} A(U,\Lambda )=0 The solution of the contact non-linearity then amounts to the search for the active constraints. Contact is active when the status of the point is active, which one will denote S{\Lambda}_{i}=1 . One obtains the following global algorithm: - Initial pairing: computation of \overline{{G}_{0}} - Loop over the Lagrange multipliers i=1..\mathit{dim}(\Lambda ) - If \overline{{{G}_{0}}_{i}}⩽0 then the point is not in contact, hence {\Lambda}_{i}^{0}=0 - Otherwise, the point is in contact, hence {\Lambda}_{i}^{0}=1 - Newton loop k=1 - While { S{\Lambda}^{k}\ne S{\Lambda}^{k+1},\forall k and {\Vert r\Vert }_{2}⩾\mathit{tole} (Newton equilibrium residual) - Computation of the elementary stiffness matrices and right-hand sides - Computation of the elementary contact matrices and right-hand sides - Loop over the Lagrange multipliers i=1..\mathit{dim}(\Lambda ) - If S{\Lambda}_{i}^{k}=1 then \left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& {C}_{k}^{E}& 0\\ {}^{t}{C}_{k}^{E}& 0& {}^{t}{C}_{k}^{M}\\ 0& {C}_{k}^{M}& 0\end{array}\right] - Otherwise \left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& 0& 0\\ 0& \mathit{Id}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right] - Assembly of the global system and solution: - \left[\begin{array}{ccc}{J}_{k}^{K}& {C}_{k}& 0\\ {}^{t}{C}_{k}& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& \mathit{Id}\end{array}\right]\times \left[\begin{array}{c}\Delta {U}_{k}\\ \Delta {\Lambda}_{k}^{a}\\ \Delta {\Lambda}_{k}^{\mathit{na}}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}{r}_{k}\\ \overline{{G}_{k}}\\ -\Delta {\Lambda}_{k-1}\end{array}\right] . - Update of the unknowns: - {U}_{k+1}={U}_{k}+\Delta {U}_{k} and {\Lambda}_{k+1}={\Lambda}_{k}+\Delta {\Lambda}_{k} - Pairing on the updated geometry, computation of \overline{{G}_{k+1}} - Evaluation of the new statuses: - Loop over the Lagrange multipliers i=1..\mathit{dim}(\Lambda ) - If {{\Lambda}_{k+1}}_{i}+\rho {{G}_{k+1}}_{i}⩽0 then the point is in contact, hence S{\Lambda}_{i}^{k+1}=1 - Otherwise, the point is not in contact, hence S{\Lambda}_{i}^{k+1}=0 - Computation of the Newton residual {r}_{k+1} 3.3.2 Pairing The aim of this phase is to handle the geometric non-linearity of the problem and that arising from possible large displacements. For each slave contact mesh cell, one seeks the master mesh cells likely to communicate with the slave mesh cell. One must also, during this operation, compute the mean «gap» between the two surfaces for each macro mesh cell. To do this, one will use four tools: - A search tool of linear complexity using the neighbourhood information at the level of the edges; - A tool for the projection of two mesh cells onto the same reference plane (reference parametric space of the slave mesh cell); - A tool for the intersection of plane mesh cells; - A tool for the computation of the mean distance between a triangle and a surface (3D case) or between two segments (2D case). 3.3.2.1 Search algorithm of linear complexity One adapts to the contact case the PANG algorithm for the computation of the mortar projection matrix for domain decomposition. This algorithm is of linear complexity once a starting pair of mesh cells has been found. It uses a restricted search on the neighbouring master mesh cells of the master mesh cells intersecting a slave mesh cell. Furthermore it uses the neighbourhood information at the level of the slave mesh cells to update the list of starting pairs of mesh cells. This algorithm allows an important gain in time with respect to a pairing of brute-force type (i.e. a double master–slave pairing loop). However it lacks robustness. Indeed, in the case of a pairing zone that does not possess a single connected component, it fails. One then detects only one of the pairing zones and the contact algorithm is consequently put in failure. One proposes a more robust but more costly version of the initial algorithm by associating with it a recursive search for a starting pair of mesh cells by brute force. 3.3.2.2 Projection tool This tool is already available in code_aster . Indeed, one of the tools of the pairing of the CONTINUE method (see R5.03.52) performs the orthogonal projection of a point of real space into the parametric space of a given mesh cell. One will therefore be able to project any master mesh cell into the parametric space of the slave mesh cell in order to carry out the intersection test. One notes two important points: - One restricts oneself to the case where the projection of the master mesh cell into the slave parametric space is convex ; - Given that one performs the projection into the parametric space of the master mesh cell, one will carry out only a purely 1D or 2D intersection. Furthermore, another routine is available in code_aster : the projection along an imposed direction. One notes that this projection algorithm will be useful for the mean «gap» tool. 3.3.2.3 Mean «gap» tool One introduces this tool in the 2D case described in the figure . The slave mesh is made up of two mesh cells ( E1 , E2 ) and therefore one macro mesh cell associated with a degree of freedom \mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C ; the master mesh is also made up of two mesh cells ( M1 , M2 ). One will describe the mean-gap tool on the first contact mesh cell. The result of these operations is described in the figure . Figure 19: Projection and intersection in the reference space of the slave mesh cell E1 Considering the intersection as a pseudo-element, one can bring back the Gauss points coming from a quadrature formula into the reference space of the slave mesh cell. One considers here for simplicity a quadrature formula with one Gauss point \mathit{Pg} ; its associated weight is the weight of the intersection. One then returns to real space in order to be able to estimate the distance to the Gauss points. These operations are described in the figure . Figure 20: Gap at the Gauss point, d One adds the following contribution in the component of the «integrated gap» vector, \overline{G} , corresponding to the degree of freedom \mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C of the contact mesh cell: {\overline{G}}_{\mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C}={\overline{G}}_{\mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}{d}_{i}{\omega}_{i}\Vert ({\partial}_{1}\sigma \times {\partial}_{2}\sigma )({\mathit{Pg}}_{i}){\Vert }_{2} where {d}_{i} is the signed gap at the i-th Gauss point ( {\mathit{Pg}}_{i} ), {\omega}_{i} is the weight associated with the i-th Gauss point in the reference space of the master mesh cell of the contact mesh cell, \sigma est la transformation de passage élément de référence élément réel et :math: N is the number of Gauss points defined on the intersection. By iteration over the contact mesh cells, one obtains the vector \overline{G} whose dimension corresponds to the number of degrees of freedom \mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C ; in our example there is a single component in the integrated «gap» vector. In the three-dimensional case, a tool for the triangulation of a convex polygon is necessary. Indeed, it is easier to compute the \overline{G} piecewise on a set of triangles (simpler definition of the quadrature formulae than on an arbitrary polygon). To finish the operation it suffices to divide each component of the integrated «gap» vector by the intersection weight found on the associated macro mesh cell. 3.3.2.4 Handling of quadratic meshes In the curved quadratic case, one cannot approximate the geometry of the master mesh cell in the slave parametric space. To simplify the algorithm, one will use a simple linearisation in place of the decomposition of the mesh cell into linear elements commonly used in the literature of mortar methods for contact. The slave geometry is for its part approximated exactly by its parametric space. Unlike the current approach consisting in using an auxiliary intersection plane (defined from the slave surface), one has chosen to carry out all the projection and intersection operations in the slave parametric space. This choice allows both the use of a pairing tolerance criterion independent of the modelling and the carrying out of only purely 2D or 1D intersections. By using this approach and by controlling the quality of the mesh, one prevents the appearance of the severe pathological cases that lead to fatal errors or to a non-convergence of the generalised Newton algorithm. Furthermore, unlike the classical mortar methods P2/P2 the LAC method is not confronted with the sign problem with respect to the basis functions of the space of the Lagrange multipliers. Attention must therefore be paid mainly at the level of the quality of the mesh, and more particularly of the mesh of the slave surface. Indeed, the algorithmic choices implemented in this first version of the implementation of the method do not take into account the case of non-convex intersections. If the slave mesh cells do not satisfy this constraint, one obtains irrelevant intersections; one then observes aberrant intersection coefficients (greater than one), which leads to a failure of convergence of the algorithm for the solution of the problem. 3.3.3 Computation of the contact matrices The computation of the elementary contact matrices is driven by the status field \mathit{S\Lambda } . If the constraint associated with the macro-element T is active, then one must compute the following contributions: {C}_{i}^{{M}_{\mathit{elem}}}={\int}_{T}{\phi }_{i}^{M}{\vec{n}}_{m}d\Gamma =\sum_{{M}_{c}}{\int}_{{M}_{m}\cap {M}_{e}}{\phi }_{i}^{M}{\vec{n}}_{m}d\Gamma {C}_{i}^{{E}_{\mathit{elem}}}={\int}_{T}{\phi }_{i}^{E}{\vec{n}}_{e}d\Gamma =\sum_{{M}_{c}}{\int}_{{M}_{m}\cap {M}_{e}}{\phi }_{i}^{E}{\vec{n}}_{e}d\Gamma where {\phi }^{E} and {\phi }^{M} are the slave and master basis functions, {\vec{n}}_{e} and {\vec{n}}_{m} the respective normals, {M}_{c} the set of contact mesh cells, and {M}_{E} the set of slave mesh cells. If the contact constraint associated with the macro-element T is inactive then there are no contact conditions to be satisfied on this macro-element and one sets to zero the associated degree of freedom \mathit{LAGS}\text{\_}C . Given that the macro mesh cell T does not exist as an element, one will compute «sub-elementary» matrices at the level of the contact mesh cells {M}_{c} (association of a slave and a master contact mesh cell). 3.3.3.1 Computation of the elementary contact matrices One in fact computes the elementary contact matrices {C}^{{M}_{\mathit{elem}}} corresponding to the integrals under the loop over the contact mesh cells (see equations). For each contact mesh cell, one must compute the following matrices: {C}_{i}^{{M}_{\mathit{elem}}}={\int}_{{M}_{m}\cap {M}_{e}}{\phi }_{i}^{M}{\vec{n}}_{m}\mathit{d\Gamma } {C}_{i}^{{E}_{\mathit{elem}}}={\int}_{{M}_{m}\cap {M}_{e}}{\phi }_{i}^{E}{\vec{n}}_{e}\mathit{d\Gamma } where {M}_{e} is the slave mesh cell of the contact mesh cell and {M}_{m} is the master mesh cell of the contact mesh cell. Given that the chosen contact condition corresponds to a zero gap only on average, one must proceed to a projection-intersection in order to define the integration support. To do this, one reuses the tools presented in the previous section. Following the scheme of the integrated-gap tool, one manages to obtain the coordinates and weights of a quadrature formula in the parametric space of the slave mesh cell of the contact mesh cell. By looping over the degrees of freedom of the master displacements, one can then compute the coefficients of the matrix {C}_{i}^{{E}_{\mathit{elem}}} . Then by using the projection onto the parametric space of the master mesh cell of the contact mesh cell one then obtains the integration support in the reference space of the master mesh cell, which makes it possible to compute (by defining an integration scheme) the coefficients of the matrix {C}_{i}^{{M}_{\mathit{elem}}} . 3.3.3.2 Choice of the normal The question of the choice of the normal has not yet been addressed. This choice not being unique, one proposes to use in our case two types of normal. Either one evaluates the normal at each master and slave Gauss point, or one uses a field of smoothed normals (keyword LISSAGE='OUI') computed on each deformed configuration (master and slave). These two choices make it possible to avoid the problem of the multiple definition of the normal at the vertices of the elements when one considers curved geometries. In the quadratic case, these two choices are relatively similar; on the contrary in the case of linear meshes, the smoothed normal field makes it possible to regularise the field of the normals and to approximate curved geometries better, see figure . r5.03.80 Methods of load piloting r5.03.80 Methods of load piloting Summary: This document describes the load-piloting methods available in Code_Aster (by a degree of freedom, by arc length, by strain increment and by elastic prediction). They introduce an additional unknown, the intensity of the pilotable part of the loading, and an additional equation, the piloting constraint. These methods make it possible, in particular, to calculate the response of a structure which would exhibit instabilities, of geometric origin (buckling) as well as of material origin (softening). 1 Introduction 1.1 Non-linearity and failure of Newton The Newton method presented in R5.03.01 fails on certain problems which exhibit a structural response that is not strictly monotonic as a function of the imposed displacements or loadings. In the figure , one presents the case where, for a given load level, several solution displacements exist. This problem is therefore not solvable with Newton if one pilots the problem by the loading. Figure 1.1-a : Non-monotonic response as a function of the displacement A second case (figure ) concerns geometrically non-linear problems (typically the buckling of thin shells and “gentle” snap-back problems). In this case, for a load level, one has several solutions in displacement and for a displacement level one has several possible loadings. This problem is not directly solvable by the Newton method, whether by piloting in loading or in displacement. Figure 1.1-b : Non-monotonic response in displacement and in loading The third case (figure ) describes damage problems in which sudden elastic returns (corresponding to the progressive damage of the material) make the curve very irregular (“sudden” snap-backs) Figure 1.1-c : Response with losses of stiffness Finally, there moreover exists a whole category of problems in which the loss of ellipticity of the problem creates bifurcations and therefore different solution branches (see figure ). In this case, what interests the engineer most is generally the dissipative branch and not the elastic branch. We shall see that techniques exist for selecting the “good” branches. Figure 1.1-d : Response with multiple branches 1.2 Problems with unknown loading intensity Piloting can also be used in the case where the problem exhibits, through its natural data setup, an additional unknown which is the intensity of the applied loading. Piloting makes it possible to treat the case where only the direction and the point of application of the loading are known, the intensity remaining an unknown of the problem. For example, in the figure , one sees the case of a cable stretched between two pylons. One knows that a loading which pulls the cable must be applied (one therefore knows the point of application and the direction of the loading) but one does not know the intensity \eta to be applied in order to obtain a given sag f . Figure 1.2-a : Example of a partially unknown loading 2 Principle of the load-piloting methods In general, the piloting functionalities available in Code_Aster make it possible to determine the intensity of part of the loading in order to satisfy a constraint bearing on the displacements. Their use is limited to simulations for which time does not play a physical role, which excludes a priori dynamic or viscous problems. It is also incompatible with problems expressing a unilaterality condition (contact and friction). One can distinguish several ranges of use, to which as many piloting methods correspond (factor keyword PILOTAGE): - Physical control of the forces by the displacement of a point of the structure: piloting by an imposed degree of freedom (TYPE='DDL_IMPO'); - Following of geometric instabilities (buckling), the response of the structure being able to exhibit a “gentle” snap-back: piloting by arc length (TYPE='LONG_ARC'); - Following of material instabilities (in the presence of softening constitutive laws), the response of the structure being able to exhibit a “brutal” snap-back: piloting by elastic prediction (TYPE= 'PRED_ELAS') or, more generally, by the strain increment, (TYPE='DEFORMATION'); - Analysis of the limit loads of structures (TYPE='ANA_LIM'), cf. [ref:R7.07.01 ]. More precisely, the piloting methods rest on the following two ideas. On the one hand, one considers that the loading (external forces and given displacements) decomposes additively into two terms, one known and imposed by the user ( {L}_{\text{impo}}^{\text{méca}} and {u}_{\text{impo}}^{d} ) and the other ( {L}_{\text{pilo}}^{\text{méca}} and {u}_{\text{pilo}}^{d} ) of which only the direction is known, its intensity \eta becoming a new unknown of the problem: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{L}^{\text{méca}}={L}_{\text{impo}}^{\text{méca}}+\eta .{L}_{\text{pilo}}^{\text{méca}}\\ {u}^{d}={u}_{\text{impo}}^{d}+\eta .{u}_{\text{pilo}}^{d}\end{array} On the other hand, in order to be able to solve the problem, one associates with it a new equation which bears on the displacements and which depends on the time increment: it is the piloting constraint, which is expressed by: P(\Delta U)=\Delta \tau \text{avec}P(0)=0 where \Delta \tau is indirectly a user datum which is expressed via the current time step \Delta t and a piloting coefficient (COEF_MULT) such that: \Delta \tau =\frac{\Delta t}{\text{COEF\_MULT}} The condition P(0)=0 is required in order to obtain a displacement increment which is all the smaller as the time step is small. Finally, the unknowns of the problem become the displacements u , the Lagrange multipliers \lambda associated with the boundary conditions and the intensity of the piloted loading \eta , named ETA_PILOTAGE. The non-linear system to be solved is henceforth written: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}{L}^{int}(u)+{B}^{T}.\lambda & ={L}_{\text{impo}}^{\text{méca}}+\eta .{L}_{\text{pilo}}^{\text{méca}}\\ B.u& ={u}_{\text{impo}}^{d}+\eta .{u}_{\text{pilo}}^{d}\\ P(\Delta u)& =\Delta \tau \end{array} - At present, follower loadings (i.e. which depend on the displacements) and Dirichlet conditions of type « DIDI » are not pilotable. - The loading no longer depends directly on time but results from the solution of the whole non-linear system. This implies that the piloted part of the loading must not depend on the physical time, but corresponds to a force which one adjusts in order to satisfy an additional kinematic constraint. Notes: 3 Solution of the global system The introduction of a new equation does not unduly disturb the method for solving the non-linear system. Indeed, one proceeds as in R5.03.01, that is to say that the solution is incremental. One denotes the time step i as a subscript and the Newton iteration n as a superscript. The non-linear problem is then solved in two stages: - A prediction phase which gives a first estimate of the displacements and of the Lagrange multipliers, denoted (\Delta {u}_{i}^{0},\Delta {\lambda}_{i}^{0}) ; - A Newton correction phase (\delta {u}_{i}^{n},\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n}) which corrects this first estimate; With a sufficient number {n}_{\mathrm{CV}} of Newton iterations, one obtains a converged result 1 : \lbrace \begin{array}{}{u}_{i}^{\text{convergé}}={u}_{i-1}+\Delta {u}_{i}^{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{n={n}_{\mathrm{CV}}}\delta {u}_{i}^{j}\\ {\lambda}_{i}^{\text{convergé}}={\lambda}_{i-1}+\Delta {\lambda}_{i}^{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{n={n}_{\mathrm{CV}}}\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{j}\end{array} The principle is therefore to linearise the system () which one writes at time step i : \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}{L}_{i}^{int}+{B}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}& ={L}_{\text{impo},i}^{\text{méca}}+{\eta}_{i}.{L}_{\text{pilo},i}^{\text{méca}}\\ B.{u}_{i}& ={u}_{\text{impo},i}^{d}+{\eta}_{i}.{u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{d}\\ P(\Delta {u}_{i})& =\Delta {\tau}_{i}\end{array} There will be no linearisation with respect to the piloting variable {\eta}_{i} . In this way, one preserves the whole methodology for updating the tangent operator already implemented for analyses without piloting. Moreover, the “banded” structure of the tangent matrix is retained. The solution scheme is therefore no longer strictly a Newton method (which is not troublesome, because we shall see that the piloting equation is, at most, of degree two). In prediction, if one linearises the system () without the piloting equation, with respect to time about ({u}_{i-1},{\lambda}_{i-1}) , one obtains (see the whole development in R5.03.01): \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}{\mathrm{K}}_{i-1}.\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0}+{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.\Delta {\lambda}_{i}^{0}& ={\mathrm{L}}_{\text{impo},i}^{\text{méca}}+{\eta}_{i}.{\mathrm{L}}_{\text{pilo},i}^{\text{méca}}-{\mathrm{Q}}_{i-1}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i-1}+\Delta {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{\text{varc}}\\ \mathrm{B}.\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{0}& ={\mathrm{u}}_{\text{impo},i}^{d}+{\eta}_{i}.{\mathrm{u}}_{\text{pilo},i}^{d}-\mathrm{B}.{\mathrm{u}}_{i-1}\end{array} In correction, one linearises the system () still without the piloting equation, with respect to time, but about ({u}_{i}^{n},{\lambda}_{i}^{n}) , one has: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}{\mathrm{K}}_{i}^{n-1}.\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}+{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n}& ={\mathrm{L}}_{\text{impo},i}^{\text{méca}}+{\eta}_{i}.{\mathrm{L}}_{\text{pilo},i}^{\text{méca}}-{\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{int,n-1}-{\mathrm{B}}^{T}.{\lambda}_{i}^{n-1}\\ \mathrm{B}.\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}& ={\eta}_{i}.{\mathrm{u}}_{\text{pilo},i}^{d}\end{array} One will bring the two systems together into a common writing, in order to simplify the presentation. The system to be solved is finally written: \left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{i}^{n-1}& {B}^{T}\\ B& 0\end{array}\right].\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{\delta u}_{i}^{n}\\ {\delta \lambda }_{i}^{n}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{\text{impo},i}^{n-1}\\ {u}_{\text{impo},i}\end{array}\right\rbrace +{\eta}_{i}.\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{\text{pilo},i}\\ {u}_{\text{pilo},i}\end{array}\right\rbrace Several remarks can be made: - The matrix {K}_{i}^{n-1} depends both on the current time step and possibly on the previous Newton iteration. The various ways of constructing it (quasi-Newton, elastic, secant, consistent, rate tangent, etc.) are described in R5.03.01; - One has assumed that the external loadings were linear (they depend only on the time step). One therefore does not consider follower loadings such as pressure or the centrifugal force, although from the theoretical point of view this poses no difficulty. On the other hand, the material may be described with a non-linear constitutive behaviour, which implies that {\mathrm{L}}_{i}^{int,n-1} depends on the Newton iteration (result of the linearisation of the internal forces). - The Dirichlet boundary conditions are always linear, which allows the matrix B to be constant over the whole transient. - With the right choice of the tangent matrix and of the right-hand side, formally, there is equivalence between (\delta {u}_{i}^{n=0},\delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n=0}) and the prediction increment (\Delta {u}_{i}^{0},\Delta {\lambda}_{i}^{0}) . One can now express the corrections of the displacements \delta {u}_{i}^{n} and of the Lagrange multipliers \delta {\lambda}_{i}^{n} as a function of {\eta}_{i} , subject to the solution of the linear system () with respect to each of the two right-hand sides. That is to say that one separates the two solutions: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{\delta u}_{i}^{n}\\ {\delta \lambda }_{i}^{n}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{\delta u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}\\ {\delta \lambda }_{\text{impo},i}^{n}\end{array}\right\rbrace +{\eta}_{i}.\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{\delta u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\\ {\delta \lambda }_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\end{array}\right\rbrace These two solutions correspond to the decoupling of the two loadings: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{i}^{n-1}\\ {u}_{i}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{\text{impo},i}^{n-1}\\ {u}_{\text{impo},i}\end{array}\right\rbrace +{\eta}_{i}.\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{\text{pilo},i}\\ {u}_{\text{pilo},i}\end{array}\right\rbrace One solves independently 2 : \left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{i}^{n-1}& {B}^{T}\\ B& 0\end{array}\right].\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{\delta u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}\\ {\delta \lambda }_{\text{impo},i}^{n}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{\text{cst},i}^{n-1}\\ {u}_{\text{cst},i}\end{array}\right\rbrace And: \left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{i}^{n-1}& {B}^{T}\\ B& 0\end{array}\right].\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{\delta u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\\ {\delta \lambda }_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{L}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n-1}\\ {u}_{\text{pilo},i}\end{array}\right\rbrace One can now substitute the displacement correction \Delta {u}_{i}^{n} into the piloting control equation of the system; there results a scalar equation in {\eta}_{i} : \tilde{P}({\eta}_{i})\underset{\text{déf.}}{=}P(\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}+{\eta}_{i}.\delta {\mathrm{u}}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n})=\Delta {\tau}_{i} The method for solving this equation depends on the nature of the piloting control adopted, cf. [§ 7 ]. Finally, all that remains is to update the displacement unknowns and the Lagrange multipliers: \lbrace \begin{array}{}\Delta {u}_{i}^{n}=\Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}+{\eta}_{i}.\delta {u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\\ {\lambda}_{i}^{n}={\lambda}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {\lambda}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}+{\eta}_{i}.\delta {\lambda}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\end{array} The notion of a “converged” result is described in more detail in [R5.03.01]. In practice, the factorisation of the matrix is performed only once and one solves the two systems simultaneously. 4 Piloting control equation 4.1 Piloting by control of a displacement degree of freedom: DDL_IMPO For this first type of piloting, the function P merely extracts a degree of freedom from the displacement increment. In particular, it is therefore a linear function: P(\Delta {u}_{i}^{n})=\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace =\Delta {\tau}_{i} Where the nodal vector \langle S\rangle is a selection vector which is zero everywhere except for the degree of freedom to be extracted, where it equals one: \langle S\rangle =\langle 0\dots 0\dots \underset{\text{noeud n, ddl i}}{1}\dots 0\dots 0\rangle Equation () then likewise reduces to a linear equation: {\eta}_{i}=\frac{\Delta {\tau}_{i}-\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}\right\rbrace -\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \delta {u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}\right\rbrace }{\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \delta {u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\right\rbrace } One will note that there is no solution when the piloted displacement correction \delta {u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n} does not make it possible to adjust the required degree of freedom, which can happen if, by mistake, one blocks the degree of freedom in question. In this case, the code will stop with ECHEC DU PILOTAGE. 4.2 Piloting by arc length: LONG_ARC Another very widely used form of piloting consists in controlling the norm of the displacement increment (with respect to certain nodes and certain components): one then speaks of cylindrical arc-length piloting, see Bonnet and Wood [bib1]. More precisely, the function P is expressed by: P(\Delta {u}_{i}^{n})={\parallel \Delta {u}_{i}^{n}\parallel }_{\text{ }}=\sqrt{(\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace ).(\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace )}=\Delta {\tau}_{i} Where, again, the nodal vector \langle S\rangle makes it possible to select the degrees of freedom used for the calculation of the norm (it equals one for the selected degrees of freedom and zero elsewhere). In this case one will note that \langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace is not a scalar, but a vector corresponding to the product of the components of \langle S\rangle by those of \left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n}\right\rbrace . In this case, the piloting equation reduces to a second-degree equation: \begin{array}{}{\eta}_{i}^{2}.\left[(\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \delta {u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\right\rbrace ).(\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \delta {u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\right\rbrace )\right]+\\ 2.{\eta}_{i}.\left[(\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}\right\rbrace ).(\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \delta {u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\right\rbrace )\right]+\\ \left[(\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}\right\rbrace ).(\langle S\rangle .\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}\right\rbrace )-\Delta {\tau}_{i}^{2}\right]=0\end{array} This equation may admit no solution. In that case, one chooses the value {\eta}_{i} which minimises the polynomial (). One then indeed verifies \tilde{P}({\eta}_{i})>\Delta {\tau}_{i} . In the contrary case, it admits two roots (or a double root). One chooses that of the two which minimises: - either the norm of the displacement increment ∥\Delta {\mathrm{u}}_{i}^{n}∥ ; - either the equilibrium residual R({u}_{i},{t}_{i})={L}_{i}^{int}-{L}_{i}^{\text{méca}} ; - either the angle formed by \Delta {u}_{i-1} and \Delta {u}_{i}^{n} (where \Delta {u}_{i-1} is the solution displacement increment of the previous time step), that is to say the one which maximises the cosine of this angle, whose expression is: \cos(\Delta {u}_{i-1},\Delta {u}_{i}^{n})=\frac{\langle \Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}+{\eta}_{i}.\delta {u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}\rangle .\left\lbrace \Delta {u}_{i-1}\right\rbrace }{∥\Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}+{\eta}_{i}.\delta {u}_{\text{pilo},i}^{n}∥.∥\Delta {u}_{i-1}∥} To calculate the angle, one uses only the unknowns corresponding to the displacements, to the exclusion of all the others (in particular the rotations in the structural elements). One notes that this last angular criterion selects the wrong solution when one passes from a loading phase to an unloading phase or vice versa, that is to say when the piloting coefficient {C}_{i} changes sign. The value {C}_{i-1} is therefore stored and updated at each converged time step, its initialisation for each call to STAT_NON_LINE being transparent to the user: {C}_{i-1} is thus initialised when the initial state is read, {C}_{i} having been included in the analysis parameters to be archived in the result concept. If {C}_{i}{C}_{i-1}>0 , one maximises criterion (). In the contrary case, one minimises it in order to select the displacement increment in the opposite direction to the previous increment. 4.3 Piloting by the strain increment: DEFORMATION Piloting by strain increment consists in requiring that the strain increment of the current step remain close in direction to the strain at the beginning of the time step, and this for at least one Gauss point of the structure. One thus requires, qualitatively, that at a minimum one point of the structure retain the strain mode which it had previously (for example, tension in a given direction). 4.3.1 Case of small strains For small strains, one can account for this requirement by means of the following choice of piloting function: P(\Delta {u}_{i}^{n})=\underset{g}{\text{Max}}\frac{{\varepsilon}_{g,i-1}}{\parallel {\varepsilon}_{g,i-1}\parallel }.\Delta {\varepsilon}_{g,i}=\Delta {\tau}_{i} Where the index g runs over the Gauss points of the structure (or only the mesh cells specified by the keyword GROUP_MA in PILOTAGE) and where the strain at a Gauss point is deduced from the nodal displacement vector via the use of the matrices “symmetric part of the gradient of the shape functions” {B}_{g} (not to be {A}_{g}^{(0)}=\frac{{\varepsilon}_{g,i-1}}{\parallel {\varepsilon}_{g,i-1}\parallel }\cdot {B}_{g}(\Delta {u}_{i}^{n-1}+\delta {u}_{\text{impo},i}^{n}) And: Instead of seeking a piloting parameter \eta which makes the criterion depart by a value \mathrm{\Delta \tau } with the damage coming from the previous time step, one seeks a parameter \eta which brings us back onto the criterion with a damage increased by \mathrm{\Delta \tau } . The elastic threshold function is therefore written {\tilde{f}}^{\text{el}}(\eta ,{d}^{-})=\mathrm{\Delta \tau }\Rightarrow {\tilde{f}}^{\text{el}}(\eta ,{d}^{-}+\mathrm{\Delta \tau })=0 ; - For the law ENDO_ORTH_BETON, see R7.01.09; - For the other damage laws of elastic type such as ENDO_SCALAIRE or ENDO_FRAGILE (with a local formulation or with gradients), just as for the law ENDO_ISOT_BETON, the elastic threshold function is chosen so as to seek a piloting parameter controlled by the damage value and not by the departure from the criterion. The elastic threshold function is written: \begin{array}{c}{\tilde{f}}^{\text{el}}(\eta )=\frac{1}{2}({e}_{0}+\eta {e}_{1})\cdot E\cdot ({e}_{0}+\eta {e}_{1})-s\\ \lbrace \begin{array}{cccc}\text{loi locale}& {e}_{0}={\epsilon}_{0}& {e}_{1}={\epsilon}_{1}& s=k({d}^{-})\\ \text{gradient d'endommagement}& {e}_{0}={\epsilon}_{0}& {e}_{1}={\epsilon}_{1}& s=k({d}^{-})-c\Delta {d}^{-}\\ \text{déformation régularisée}& {e}_{0}={\bar{\epsilon}}_{0}& {e}_{1}={\bar{\epsilon}}_{1}& s=k({d}^{-})\end{array}\end{array} 4.4.3 Illustration of the maximisation algorithm In order to illustrate our argument and in particular to understand why such a choice of {\varepsilon}^{\text{ }} makes it possible to solve the exact problem, one takes the example of a cohesive constitutive law CZM_EXP_REG or CZM_LIN_REG (cf R7.02.11) implemented on a joint element (cf R3.06.09). The displacement jump \delta is the primal variable (denoted generically \epsilon in what precedes), and \kappa the internal variable (denoted generically A ). The threshold function is then written: {f}^{\mathrm{èl}}(\delta )=\frac{{\parallel \delta \parallel }_{\mathrm{èq}}-{\kappa}_{i-1}}{{\kappa}_{\mathrm{REF}}}\text{avec}{\kappa}_{i-1}=\underset{v\in [0,{t}_{i-1}]}{\max}{\parallel \delta (v)\parallel }_{\mathrm{èq}};{\parallel \delta \parallel }_{\mathrm{èq}}=\sqrt{{\langle {\delta}_{n}\rangle }_{+}^{2}+{\delta}_{\tau}^{2}} Without detailing the proof, one can show that {\parallel \delta \parallel }_{\mathrm{èq}} satisfies a triangle inequality. This allows us to prove the convexity of the function: {f}^{\mathrm{èl}}(\eta )={f}^{\mathrm{èl}}(\delta (\eta ))=\frac{{\parallel {\delta}_{i-1}+\Delta {\delta}_{i}^{n}+d{\delta}^{\mathrm{cte}}+\eta d{\delta}^{\mathrm{pilo}}\parallel }_{\mathrm{èq}}-{\kappa}_{i-1}}{{\kappa}_{\mathrm{REF}}} We have plotted in a figure a qualitative graphical representation of the functions {f}^{\mathrm{èl}} for the various Gauss points of the joint elements, as well as the solutions of the exact global maximisation problem over the set of Gauss points: \underset{g}{\max}{f}_{g}^{\mathrm{èl}}(\eta )\stackrel{\mathrm{dèf}}{=}\underset{g}{\max}{f}^{\mathrm{èl}}({\delta}_{g}(\eta ))=\Delta {\tau}_{i} It then appears that the solutions \eta of this exact problem are identical to the solutions obtained with the algorithm for solving the piecewise affine equation, that is to say the solutions of equation () \underset{g}{\max}{A}_{1}^{(g)}\eta +{A}_{0}^{(g)}=\Delta {\tau}_{i} , with in our example: {A}_{1}^{(g)}=\frac{\partial {f}_{g}^{\mathrm{èl}}}{\partial \eta }({\eta}_{g}^{\text{ }});{A}_{0}^{(g)}=\Delta \tau -{A}_{1}^{(g)}{\eta}_{g}^{\text{ }} where {\eta}_{g}^{\text{ }} is a solution of the local equation {f}_{g}^{\mathrm{èl}}(\eta )=\Delta {\tau}_{i} We once again refer the reader to [3] for a rigorous proof. In general, selection by the residual is retained because of its robustness. However, choosing the solution which minimises the residual does not guarantee us the convergence of the Newton method. Certain cases have been exhibited for which the solution of maximum initial residual converges whereas this is not the case for the solution of minimum initial residual. Although the mechanical solutions are identical, one can thus obtain a significant difference at the same piloting step for problems with large instabilities, by changing for example the execution machine.
