r5.03.81 IMPLEX method r5.03.81 IMPLEX method Summary: This document presents a method for solving the non-linear problem, due to Oliver et al. [1], taking the place of the Newton method for certain damage and plasticity constitutive laws (ENDO_FRAGILE [3], ENDO_ISOT_BETON [4] and VMIS_ISOT_LINE [5] at the present time). It is based on an explicit extrapolation of the internal variables in order to determine the degrees of freedom (displacement) from which the constitutive behaviour is integrated implicitly. The vanishing of the residual is not checked. It thereby introduces an approximation of the solution but makes it possible to guarantee the robustness of the analysis. It is therefore up to the user to take a critical look at the results obtained, these not being converged in the classical sense of the term, and potentially being able to be far from the exact solution; one therefore advises carrying out several analyses with different load increments in order to make sure that the discrepancy in the results obtained is small. In cases of a sudden expansion of the damaged zone resulting in a strong snap-back of the global force/displacement response, the method, if it makes it possible to pass the instability, cannot be reliable in terms of the result. 1 Introduction One presents here a solution method, robust but approximate, of the incremental problem of non-linear quasi-static mechanics, for certain damage and plasticity constitutive behaviours. It is activated by the keyword METHODE = 'IMPLEX' of the operator STAT_NON_LINE, and it takes the place of the classical NEWTON method (cf. [2]). 2 Statement of the problem One places oneself within the general framework of the solution of a typical problem of non-linear mechanics discretised in space (K\in \Omega ) and in time (t\in [0,T]) , and written in displacement. Its solution, at the time instant {t}_{n+1} , consists in determining the displacements {U}_{n+1} (and therefore the strains \varepsilon ({U}_{n+1}) ), the internal variables {\alpha}_{n+1} and the stresses {\sigma}_{n+1} satisfying: 1. At the global level, the equilibrium of the forces: > {F}_{\text{ext}}({t}_{n+1})-{F}_{int}({\sigma}_{n+1}({U}_{n+1}),{t}_{n+1}) (1) 1. At the local level, the constitutive equations of the constitutive law considered for the material: State law: {\sigma}_{n+1}=\sum(\varepsilon ({U}_{n+1}),{\alpha}_{n+1}) Evolution law: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}f({\alpha}_{n+1},{\sigma}_{n+1})\le 0& \text{Convexe de réversibilité}\\ {\dot{\alpha}}_{n+1}={\dot{\lambda}}_{n+1}\ge 0& \text{Evolution des variables internes}\\ {\dot{\lambda}}_{n+1}f({\alpha}_{n+1},{\sigma}_{n+1})=0& \text{Condition de Kuhn-Tucker}\end{array} (2) with {F}_{\text{ext}} et {F}_{int} the external and internal forces, and \dot{{\lambda}_{n+1}} the multiplier (of damage or of plasticity). One considers in what follows a constitutive behaviour independent of physical time (no viscosity and no dynamic effect); the “pseudo-instant” {t}_{n+1} therefore represents the applied load factor. In the great majority of cases, each of equations (1) and (2) is relatively easy to solve. At the global level, the Newton method leads to a succession of linear problems of the type: {K}_{n+1}^{i}\delta {U}_{n+1}^{i+1}={F}_{\text{ext}}({t}_{n+1})-{F}_{int}({\sigma}_{n+1}^{i}({U}_{n+1}^{i})) (3) where the upper index represents the Newton iteration considered, \delta {U}_{n+1}^{i+1} is the displacement increment between two successive Newton iterations and {K}_{n+1}^{i} is the global tangent matrix. Note that this global tangent matrix is written (cf. [2]) \begin{array}{ccc}{K}_{n+1}& =& \frac{\partial {F}_{int}({\sigma}_{n+1}({U}_{n+1}))}{\partial {U}_{n+1}}\\ & =& {\text{A}}_{e=1}^{p}({\int}_{{\Omega}_{\varepsilon}}\nabla {N}_{e}.{C}_{{e}_{n+1}}.\nabla {N}_{e}d\Omega )\end{array} (4) where \text{A} is the assembly operator, p the number of elements of the mesh, {C}_{{e}_{n+1}} the local tangent operator (coming from the constitutive behaviour) and {N}_{e} the shape functions (for the element considered, denoted e ). The quantity {F}_{\text{ext}}({t}_{n+1})-{F}_{int}({\sigma}_{n+1}^{i}({U}_{n+1}^{i})) represents the equilibrium residual, which one must strictly speaking cancel. Determining \delta {U}_{n+1}^{i+1} therefore amounts to the inversion of the matrix {K}_{n+1}^{i} . If therefore the local elements coming from the constitutive behaviour (stresses, tangent matrix) are known and fixed, and generate a matrix K that is well conditioned, the solution is easy. Moreover locally, if the displacements {U}_{n+1} , and consequently the local strains \varepsilon ({U}_{n+1}) , are known, the solution of the majority of the constitutive laws, that is the determination of the stresses {\sigma}_{n+1} , of the internal variables {\alpha}_{n+1} and of the local tangent matrix {C}_{{e}_{n+1}} , is relatively easy. It is therefore in the simultaneity of these two laws that the difficulty of the implicit solution lies. The most classical solution method is the iterative Newton algorithm (cf. [2]). This iterative scheme does not always converge. Although this remains open to discussion (there exist other possible factors of loss of convergence, such as leaving the basin of attraction of Newton or the presence of bifurcations of the solution), the authors attribute this loss of robustness mainly to the singular character of the matrices, in particular for the damage laws, whose internal variables affect the stiffness matrices of the constitutive behaviour: in the cases of significant damage, close to or reaching failure, the softening leads to locally very “weak” tangent matrices, which may in the extreme no longer be positive definite. Through the assembly process (4), when the damage progresses in the structure, the global matrix K is deteriorated: it becomes too “flexible”, and its smallest eigenvalue tends towards zero. It then becomes singular and the algorithm diverges. The robustness of the analysis is then no longer ensured. In order to increase the robustness of the analysis in these situations, Oliver et al. [1] propose a particular solution method, named IMPLEX. The global equilibrium is then checked approximately with the help of a local tangent matrix (secant in the case of the damage laws) extrapolated explicitly and assembled, and the constitutive laws are solved implicitly from the approximate displacement field. The method is presented below. 3 The IMPLEX method The general elements of the IMPLEX method are presented here. For more details, one may refer in particular to [1]. The proposed method is based on two successive stages carried out in order to determine the set of the unknowns at the “pseudo-instant” (load) {t}_{n+1} . The first stage consists of an explicit extrapolation of the internal variables, then of the stresses, as a function of the quantities computed previously (at the load {t}_{n} ) and of the load step \Delta {t}_{n+1} . Thanks to this extrapolation, the local tangent matrix is evaluated and frozen; the solution of the equilibrium equation (3) makes it possible to determine the displacements, which one considers correct and which are therefore frozen in their turn. The second stage consists in carrying out the implicit integration of the constitutive behaviour, as a function of the degrees of freedom evaluated at the previous stage. The first stage is of explicit type, whereas the second is of implicit type, whence the name IMPLEX. At the end of these two stages, the equilibrium equation is not satisfied (it is satisfied in terms of the fields extrapolated at stage (1) only); however, the smaller the load increment, the smaller the error committed must be; one therefore advises carrying out the analyses with several different load steps in order to check that the difference between the responses obtained is small (response converged in terms of the load step). In what follows, the two stages are described. A balance of the key points is drawn up. 3.1 A method in 2 stages We shall here present in succession the 2 fundamental stages of the IMPLEX method, summarised in Table 1. 3.1.1 Explicit extrapolation and determination of the degrees of freedom This first stage concerns in particular the internal variable \alpha , whose evolution is governed by a law of type (2). At the beginning of the load step {t}_{n+1} , one has available all the information coming from the load step {t}_{n} and from the previous load steps. It is then possible to write the following Taylor expansions (the evolution of the internal variable is considered sufficiently regular to be able to do so): \begin{array}{}\lbrace \begin{array}{cccc}{\alpha}_{n+1}& =& {\alpha}_{n}+\Delta {t}_{n+1}{\dot{\alpha}}_{n}+O(\Delta {t}_{n+1}^{2})& \\ {\alpha}_{n}& =& {\alpha}_{n-1}+\Delta {t}_{n}{\dot{\alpha}}_{n-1}+O(\Delta {t}_{n}^{2})& \\ \Delta {t}_{n}{\dot{\alpha}}_{n}& =& \Delta {t}_{n}{\dot{\alpha}}_{n-1}+\Delta {t}_{n}(\Delta {t}_{n}{\ddot{\alpha}}_{n-1})+\Delta {t}_{n}O(\Delta {t}_{n}^{2})& \Rightarrow \Delta {t}_{n}{\dot{\alpha}}_{n}=\Delta {t}_{n}{\dot{\alpha}}_{n-1}+O(\Delta {t}_{n}^{2})\end{array}\\ \Rightarrow \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}{\dot{\alpha}}_{n}& =& \frac{\Delta {\alpha}_{n}}{\Delta {t}_{n}}-O(\Delta {t}_{n}^{2})\\ {\alpha}_{n+1}& =& {\alpha}_{n}+\frac{\Delta {t}_{n+1}}{\Delta {t}_{n}}\Delta {\alpha}_{n}-\Delta {t}_{n+1}O(\Delta {t}_{n}^{2})+O(\Delta {t}_{n+1}^{2})\end{array}\end{array} (5) with \Delta {X}_{i}={X}_{i}-{X}_{i-1} . By truncation, neglecting the second-order terms, one obtains the following prediction \tilde{{\alpha}_{n+1}} for the variable {\alpha}_{n+1} : > {\tilde{\alpha}}_{n+1}={\alpha}_{n}+\frac{\Delta {t}_{n+1}}{\Delta {t}_{n}}\Delta {\alpha}_{n} (6) Through (6), one notes that {\tilde{\alpha}}_{n+1} is indeed obtained explicitly, at the load {t}_{n+1} , as a function of the quantities (grandeurs) obtained implicitly at the load {t}_{n} . Figure 1 schematises this extrapolation process. The extrapolation error may be defined as the difference between the value of the extrapolated internal variable and its real final value; subject to a sufficiently regular evolution of the internal variable in order to carry out the Taylor expansions to a sufficient order, one can evaluate this error as: > {e}_{{\alpha}_{n+1}}=∣{\tilde{\alpha}}_{n+1}-{\alpha}_{n+1}∣\approx ∣{\ddot{\alpha}}_{n}∣\Delta {t}_{n+1}^{2} (7) This shows that in the case of a sufficiently regular evolution of the internal variable, the error decreases quadratically as a function of the load step. Once the internal variable has been extrapolated, one can determine the stress {\tilde{\sigma}}_{n+1}({\varepsilon}_{n+1},{\tilde{\alpha}}_{n+1}) and the local tangent operator {\tilde{C}}_{{e}_{n+1}} . In the particular case of the isotropic damage laws, it is the local secant operator which is used; the extrapolated stresses and this operator are then written: > \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}{\tilde{\sigma}}_{n+1}({\varepsilon}_{n+1},{\tilde{\alpha}}_{n+1})& =& (1-{\alpha}_{n+1}){C}^{\text{elas}}:{\varepsilon}_{n+1}\\ {\tilde{C}}_{{e}_{n+1}}=\frac{\partial {\tilde{\sigma}}_{n+1}}{\partial {\tilde{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}}& =& (1-{\tilde{\alpha}}_{n+1}){C}^{\text{elas}}\end{array} (8) These extrapolated local quantities serve for the assembly of the global tangent matrix {\tilde{K}}_{n+1} via (4), and for the determination of the internal force. The equilibrium equation in terms of the extrapolated field {F}_{\text{ext}}({t}_{n+1})-{F}_{int}({U}_{n+1},{\tilde{\sigma}}_{n+1},{t}_{n+1})=0 is then solved with this extrapolated matrix and the displacement field {\tilde{U}}_{n+1} obtained. It is solved by a classical Newton-Raphson method; it is therefore linearised by {\tilde{K}}_{n+1}\delta {\tilde{U}}_{n+1}={F}_{\text{ext}}({t}_{n+1})-{F}_{int}({\tilde{\sigma}}_{n+1},{t}_{n+1}) . In the case of the constitutive laws treated here (isotropic damage with secant operator and linear isotropic plasticity), the constitutive operator is constant during a time step (that is, independent of the current strain state {\varepsilon}_{n+1} ); the Newton-Raphson solution process becomes linear per time step and therefore converges in one iteration. This stage is however iterative in certain cases (non-linear plasticity for example), because of the non-constant character of the tangent operator. At the first iteration, one would then take {\varepsilon}_{n+1}^{0}={\varepsilon}_{n} . At the end of this first stage, the displacement field {U}_{n+1} is considered equal to the field obtained by the solution of the equilibrium equation written in terms of the extrapolated fields: {U}_{n+1}={\tilde{U}}_{n+1} . This displacement field will no longer be modified subsequently. | | | | --- | --- | | | | Figure 1: Schematisation of the extrapolation method 3.1.2 Implicit determination of the elements of the constitutive law Following the first phase, the displacement field is known. It is frozen for the load step and will therefore not be modified. One then determines the strain {\varepsilon}_{n+1}({U}_{n+1}) , then equations (2) of the constitutive law are solved implicitly in order to obtain the stress fields {\sigma}_{n+1} and of internal variable {\alpha}_{n+1} . This stage is identical to the standard solution of the equations of the constitutive laws. The only difference is the need to store \frac{\Delta {\alpha}_{n+1}}{\Delta {t}_{n+1}} in order to carry out the extrapolation of the internal variable at the next step. At the end of this stage, the displacement field {U}_{n+1} and the stress fields {\sigma}_{n+1} and of internal variable {\alpha}_{n+1} are therefore known. A major difference with respect to a classical implicit analysis is the fact that the real equilibrium equation is not satisfied; it is satisfied only in terms of the extrapolated fields. | Stage 1: Explicit extrapolation | Stage 2: Implicit integration | | --- | --- | | Extrapolation of the internal variables: {\tilde{\alpha}}_{n+1}={\alpha}_{n}+\frac{\Delta {t}_{n+1}}{\Delta {t}_{n}}\Delta {\alpha}_{n} | Frozen displacements: {\dot{U}}_{n+1}=0 | | Computation of the extrapolated stress: {\tilde{\sigma}}_{n+1}({\varepsilon}_{n+1},{\tilde{\alpha}}_{n+1}) Solution of the equilibrium equation in extrapolated fields: {F}_{\text{ext}}({t}_{n+1})-{F}_{int}({U}_{n+1},{\tilde{\sigma}}_{n+1},{t}_{n+1})=0 | Implicit solution of the constitutive laws: State law: {\sigma}_{n+1}=\sum(\varepsilon ({U}_{n+1}),{\alpha}_{n+1}) Evolution law: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}f({\alpha}_{n+1},{\sigma}_{n+1})\le 0\\ {\dot{\alpha}}_{n+1}={\dot{\lambda}}_{n+1}\ge 0\\ {\dot{\lambda}}_{n+1}f({\alpha}_{n+1},{\sigma}_{n+1})=0\end{array} | | Output of stage 1: {U}_{n+1} | Output of stage 2: {U}_{n+1} , {\sigma}_{n+1} , {\alpha}_{n+1} | Table 1: Summary of the IMPLEX method 3.2 Automatic management of the time step The IMPLEX method introduces, like all explicit methods, an intrinsic error which must decrease in a quasi-quadratic manner with the load step. The solution may therefore depend slightly on the load step selected by the user. The user may, if he or she wishes, use an automatic management of the load step via the command DEFI_LIST_INST, by specifying METHODE= 'AUTO' and MODE_CALCUL_TPLUS='IMPLEX' (cf. [9]). This method makes it possible to control the error while optimising the analysis duration, provided that the user has chosen a well calibrated first time step. The aim is therefore to minimise the error defined by equation (7). For this one will bound the increment of the extrapolated variable by a quantity (grandeur) denoted \mathit{Tol} : > \Delta {\tilde{\alpha}}_{n+1}=\frac{\Delta {t}_{n+1}}{\Delta {t}_{n}}\Delta {\alpha}_{n}\le \mathrm{Tol} (9) Whence: > \Delta {t}_{n+1}\le \frac{\mathrm{Tol}.\Delta {t}_{n}}{\Delta {\alpha}_{n}} (10) As the increments of the internal variable depend on the point considered, the time step will be chosen as the minimum value of expression (10) over the whole of the structure, that is finally: > \Delta {t}_{n+1}=\mathrm{Tol}.\Delta {t}_{n}{\mathrm{MIN}}_{x\in \Omega }(\frac{1}{\Delta {\alpha}_{n}(x)}) (11) One then adds conditions limiting the acceleration and the deceleration, as well as minimum and maximum bounds for the time increment. The acceleration (\mu ) and deceleration conditions are not modifiable and have been calibrated on concrete cases, whereas the minimum and maximum bounds may be modified by the user (the default values are given here). > \begin{array}{c}\Delta {t}_{n+1}\le \mu \Delta {t}_{n}=1,2\Delta {t}_{n}\\ \Delta {t}_{n+1}\ge 0.5\Delta {t}_{n}\\ \Delta {t}_{n+1}\le 10\Delta {t}_{0}\\ \Delta {t}_{n+1}\ge 0.001\Delta {t}_{0}\end{array} (12) Thus, the first time step \Delta {t}_{0} , supplied by the user, defines the bounds of the time increment. In order to choose it, one advises the user to have carried out preliminary analyses with the Newton method and to know the elastic limit of the structure; it would seem that the choice of a first time step equal to half the elastic limit allows a good efficiency of the method. Let us then show that the error committed is indeed controlled. For this one makes the assumption that equation 9 is satisfied. One therefore has \frac{\Delta {t}_{n+1}}{\Delta {t}_{n}}\Delta {\alpha}_{n}\le \mathrm{Tol} , and if one considers that the limiting acceleration and deceleration factors make it possible to write \frac{\Delta {t}_{n+1}}{\Delta {t}_{n}}\approx 1 , one has \Delta {\alpha}_{n}\le \mathrm{Tol} ; and step by step: > \forall n\in \mathbb{N},\Delta {\alpha}_{n}\le \mathrm{Tol} (13) Which finally makes it possible to write: > {e}_{{\alpha}_{n+1}}\approx ∣\ddot{{\alpha}_{n}}∣\Delta {t}_{n+1}^{2}\le \mathrm{Tol}{\mu}^{2}(1+\mu ) (14) The error is therefore controlled. 3.3 Key points of the method After this summary presentation, a few remarks are made here in order to understand the interest of the method and also its limitations. First of all, it is based on an extrapolation of the internal variables, determined from a Taylor expansion. The Taylor expansions being valid only for sufficiently regular functions, the method will be so as well. Thus, the crossing of the elastic limit, or the passage from a loading state to unloading, are points for which the method is strictly speaking not suited: the derivative of the damage is zero on the unloading side or on the elastic-limit side, and non-zero on the loading side. However, if the load steps are sufficiently small, the approximation may be made, inasmuch as the implicit correction takes place and therefore the extrapolation errors are partly smoothed out. In unstable situations however, for example when the damaged zone grows suddenly (which is in general characterised by a significant snap-back of the global force/displacement response), the method, although robust, cannot guarantee a reliable response, whatever the load increment used: it is not suited to this kind of situation. According to equation (8), in the case of isotropic damage laws, because of the limitation of \alpha to 1 and of the symmetric and positive definite character of the local elastic matrix {C}^{\text{elas}} , the local secant matrix {\tilde{C}}_{{e}_{n+1}} is always symmetric positive definite. As a result, by assembly, the global tangent matrix {\tilde{K}}_{n+1} remains well conditioned: the robustness problems mentioned in the introduction, linked to the increasingly singular character of K , must therefore be eliminated. Moreover, for a given load step and for the constitutive laws developed here (ENDO_FRAGILE cf. [3], ENDO_ISOT_BETON cf. [4] and VMIS_ISOT_LINE cf. [5]), the local tangent matrix is known by explicit extrapolation and remains constant throughout the load step. The linearisation of the equilibrium equation (1) by a Newton-Raphson method leads to a constant global tangent matrix {\tilde{K}}_{n+1} ; in other words, the equilibrium equation becomes linear at each load step, and its solution requires only one iteration. Next, and at the risk of being redundant, the method leads to external and internal forces that are not balanced at the end of each load step; they are balanced only at the end of the first phase, that is solely in terms of extrapolated fields: > \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}{F}_{\text{ext}}({t}_{n+1})-{F}_{int}({\sigma}_{n+1}({U}_{n+1}),{t}_{n+1})& \ne & 0\\ {F}_{\text{ext}}({t}_{n+1})-{F}_{int}({U}_{n+1},{\tilde{\sigma}}_{n+1},{t}_{n+1})& =& 0\end{array} (15) Consequently, during the analysis, one must not ask the algorithm to check the residual to within a tolerance, as it is usual to do (in implicit). From this point of view again, robustness is guaranteed, since the classical stopping criterion is irrelevant. Finally, this method has no other purpose than to increase the robustness of the analysis, and not the quality of the response obtained. Thus, it introduces an intrinsic error through the extrapolation. At best, one can obtain only results almost as good as those obtained by a classical implicit method of local solution. This error must decrease in a quasi-quadratic manner as a function of the imposed load step, subject to a sufficiently regular evolution of the internal variable (which in fact excludes the unstable propagations of damaged zones). The use of this method therefore requires a certain critical look. In order to guard against large errors, one recommends carrying out analyses with different and small load increments, in order to check that the solution does not differ too much from one increment to the next (in other words, that the solution is close to convergence in terms of load increments). Moreover, in the case of the crossing of unstable situations, the results obtained must be considered only for their qualitative aspect. 4 Practical aspects of use This solution method is activated by specifying, under the simple keyword METHODE of the operator STAT_NON_LINE, METHODE= 'IMPLEX' and by specifying the constitutive law used under COMPORTEMENT. Only certain constitutive laws are currently available with the IMPLEX method. Table 2 summarises the constitutive laws available according to the type of element considered. | Surface or volume elements | Bar elements | Membrane elements and grille_membrane | | --- | --- | --- | | ELAS | ELAS | ELAS | | VMIS_ISOT_LINE | VMIS_ISOT_LINE | | | ENDO_ISOT_BETON | | | | ENDO_FRAGILE | | | | | | | | | | | | TABLE 2: constitutive laws available with the method IMPLEX | | | For each constitutive law, the last internal variable is modified and corresponds in this case to the ratio \frac{\Delta \alpha }{\Delta t} . The method imposes an updating of the matrix at each increment (REAC_INCR = 1) and a single iteration. The equilibrium residual is computed, but no criterion is associated with it. One will be able to realise a possibly large error by seeing that the relative residual is high. For more information on the practical aspects, one will refer to [6] and [7]. r5.04.03 Second-gradient modellings r5.04.03 Second-gradient modellings Summary The second-gradient modellings arising from the work of Chambon et al. ([1], [2], [3]) and the second gradient of dilatation arising from the work of Fernandes et al. ([4], [5]), and of Gantier ([14]), are presented here. These modellings fall within the framework of media with microstructure and have as their numerical objective to give results that converge with respect to the fineness of the spatial discretisation, in order to avoid obtaining localised solutions. They must be used as soon as the mechanical rheological laws considered present a softening of the behaviour reflecting the damage or the degradation of a material before cracking. The second-gradient-of-dilatation modelling is, in fact, a simplified approach to the second gradient restricted to materials subject to the phenomenon of dilatancy. The numerical objective is to reduce the computation times significantly. It lends itself particularly well to geomaterials. Note: The second-gradient modelling has been withdrawn from the code. Only the dilatation-gradient modelling is available. > Contents 1 The second-gradient model 1.1 Brief presentation of media with microstructure At the origin of this theory, one finds the work of Mindlin ([6], [7]) within the framework of linear elasticity. This work was then taken up by Germain ([8], [9]), who gave an expression of it by application of the principle of virtual work, the basis of numerical methods with a view to an application by finite elements. This theory implies the definition of an enriched kinematics. In addition to the classical displacement field {u}_{i} , one considers the second-order tensor, denoted {f}_{ij} and called the microscopic kinematic gradient, which models both the strains and the rotations at the scale of the grains of the structure. One draws attention here to the fact that, within the framework of media with microstructure, the microscopic strain gradient has no reason to be linked to the gradient of any field depending on the macroscopic displacement. It is not necessarily symmetric. The microscopic strain gradient {f}_{ij} is a variable in the same way as the macroscopic displacement {u}_{i} , unlike the classical (macroscopic) strain field, which is obtained by derivation {\epsilon}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\partial {u}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}+\frac{\partial {u}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}}) An essential fact at the basis of the writing of this theory concerns the statement of the principle of objectivity or, equally, of material indifference: The virtual power of the internal forces of a system is zero in any virtual motion that rigidifies the system at the instant considered. Neglecting the expression of the external body forces for reasons of simplification of the writing, the consequence of the axiom of the virtual powers of the internal forces leads to the expression of the variational formulation, for any kinematically admissible field ({u}_{i}^{\text{ }},{f}_{ij}^{\text{ }}) \underset{\Omega}{\int}({\sigma}_{ij}\frac{\partial {u}_{i}^{\text{ }}}{\partial {x}_{j}}+{\tau}_{ij}({f}_{ij}^{\text{ }}-\text{}\frac{\partial {u}_{i}^{\text{ }}}{\partial {x}_{j}})+{\Sigma}_{\text{ijk}}\frac{\partial {f}_{ij}^{\text{ }}}{\partial {x}_{k}})\text{dv}=\underset{\partial \Omega }{\int}({t}_{i}{u}_{i}^{\text{ }}+{T}_{ij}{f}_{ij}^{\text{ }})\text{ds} where {t}_{i} and {T}_{ij} are respectively the traction forces and the double forces corresponding to the boundary conditions, on the boundary \partial \Omega , conjugates of the kinematic variables. The variational formulation () is another means of expressing the equilibrium relations, which are expressed \frac{\partial ({\sigma}_{ij}-{\tau}_{ij})}{\partial {x}_{j}}=0 \frac{\partial {\Sigma}_{\text{ijk}}}{\partial {x}_{k}}-{\tau}_{ij}=0 and one finds for the expression of the boundary conditions {t}_{i}=({\sigma}_{ij}-{\tau}_{ij}){n}_{j} {T}_{ij}={\Sigma}_{\text{ijk}}{n}_{k} where {n}_{j} denotes the outward normal to the boundary \partial \Omega . To complete the problem, one must define the constitutive laws which will link the static variables {\sigma}_{ij} , {\tau}_{ij} , {\Sigma}_{\text{ijk}} respectively to the history of the kinematic variables of \frac{\partial {u}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}} , \left({f}_{ij}-\frac{\partial {u}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}\right) and \frac{\partial {f}_{ij}}{\partial {x}_{k}} . These models have already proved that they were effective from the point of view of regularisation. However, they are complex in their use because of the different constitutive laws to be specified. Moreover, the discretisation by the finite-element method in 3D induces the addition of 9 supplementary degrees of freedom per node corresponding to the components {f}_{ij} . The computation times are then relatively large and consequently incompatible with the type of studies that we wish to carry out. 1.2 The second-gradient model Starting from the preceding model, expressed by the relation (), one can restrict the kinematics by forcing the microscopic gradient to be equal to the macroscopic gradient (see Chambon et al. As regards the latter, any relation could be considered, but until today, it is in general linear elasticity which has been chosen. 2 The second-gradient-of-dilatation model The principle of media with microstructure is based on taking the microscopic strains into account in order to introduce an internal length into the expression of the model. If the effectiveness of the regularisation brought by the second-gradient model is beyond doubt, the computation times of the simulations can become prohibitive. In order to reduce them within the particular framework of dilatant materials (for which the volumetric strain evolves as a function of the loading) one restricts the generality of the regularising effect to dilatant media with microstructure. 2.1 Dilatant media with microstructure The kinematics of these media is defined by the usual displacement field {u}_{i} , the microscopic volumetric variation denoted \chi and its gradients. By duality with this enriched kinematics, the static variables of the classical macroscopic stresses {\sigma}_{ij} , the microscopic dilatation stress \kappa and the vectorial double dilatation stresses {S}_{j} are introduced. The variable \kappa is the component conjugate to the relative volumetric strain (of the macroscopic field with respect to the microscopic one) {\epsilon}_{V}-\chi , while the components {S}_{j} define a vector which is the conjugate of the gradient of the microscopic dilatation \frac{\partial \chi }{\partial {x}_{j}} . For this one restricts oneself to applications considering dilatant materials. Now, discretising by the finite-element method the expression () has as a consequence the imposition that the field of the displacement unknowns as well as its divergence be continuous and differentiable. This amounts to taking into account C1-continuous finite elements. One then proposes to introduce the mathematical constraint () into the expression of the dilatant media with microstructure by means of a coupling of Lagrange multipliers and of penalisation. In THM, the second-gradient modellings available are detailed in the documentations U3.13.08 and U3.14.07. 4.3 Estimation of the regularisation parameter A1 (2nd gradient of dilatation) With the aim of characterising as well as possible the value to be assigned to the regularisation parameter, A1, of the 2nd gradient of dilatation, it is possible to determine an upper bound on this parameter as a function of the rate tangent matrix of any softening constitutive model. In this way, the user will be able to determine, as a function of the size of the mesh cells of the problem that he treats, the value of the parameter A1 best suited to his problem. This computation is based on an analytical \mathrm{2D} problem of a shear band [bib2 and bib11]. Failure in geomaterials is often characterised by the formation of zones with localised strains, reflecting a passage from zones of homogeneous strains towards non-homogeneous strain modes. The appearance of this phenomenon can be seen on the theoretical level as the spontaneous change of the strain mode, assimilated to a bifurcation of a branch of the equilibrium, that is to say the intersection of two branches of solutions that are functions of the control parameters. Within the framework of continuous media, it is possible to extract, under restricted conditions, bifurcation criteria making it possible to identify the control parameter causing the appearance of the shear band, as well as the potential orientations of the latter. On the other hand, for classical continuous media, the “post-localisation” regime, notably the width of the shear band, cannot be characterised. The experimental results nevertheless show that this width is an element intrinsic to the properties of the material, linked to its microstructure (shape and size of the grains, Desrues and Viggiani [bib12]) and to its initial state (void ratio and stress state). The use of the local second-gradient-of-dilatation theory makes it possible to enrich the kinematics of the medium, thus reflecting the effects of the microstructure at the global scale. In this section, we shall extract from a two-dimensional analytical problem the elements making it possible to characterise the width of the shear band during the “post-localisation” regime. The formulation of the problem in rate form is then written in the following form, considering the body forces constant: \underset{\Omega}{\int}{\dot{\sigma}}_{ij}{\dot{\epsilon}}_{ij}({u}^{\text{ }})+{\dot{S}}_{j}{\eta}_{j}({u}^{\text{ }})\mathrm{dv}=\underset{\partial \Omega }{\int}{\dot{F}}_{i}{u}_{i}^{\text{ }}\mathrm{ds}\forall {u}^{\text{ }}\in {\text{V}}_{0} {\dot{\sigma}}_{ij} , {\dot{S}}_{j} and {\dot{F}}_{i} are the time derivatives of the terms introduced in the equation. 4.3.1 Analytical solution The two-dimensional analytical problem addressed below was solved by [bib2] for a complete second-gradient model with the local elastoplastic Mohr–Coulomb model described by [bib13]. In other words, taking into account an enriched kinematics restricted to second-gradient media does not modify the value of the control parameter causing the appearance of a bifurcated solution in shear bands. 4.3.2 Numerical solution The elementary computation option PDIL_ELGA determines, for a given initial state of the stresses and internal variables, the value of A1_LC2 established according to the following formula: \text{A1\_LC2}=\frac{{a}^{1}}{{{l}_{c}}^{2}}=\frac{\left[{H}_{1211}{H}_{1112}-{H}_{1111}{H}_{1212}\right]}{3{H}_{1212}{(2\pi )}^{2}} for different orientations of the shear band. The explicit writing of the components of the stiffness tensor of the classical local model is obtained via the routines for the computation of the rate tangent matrices. A rotation of the shear band by an angle \theta implies a local rotation applied to the components of the stress tensor. It makes it possible to estimate the new components of the local constitutive tensor of the classical constitutive model, relating to the first gradient of the displacements. The angular discretisation used is first of 5° . Around the first maximum recorded, one carries out a discretisation at 1° then 0.2° . In this way, one ensures that one obtains a precise value of the parameter A1_LC2. The user can then define the value of A1 suited to the spatial discretisation of the structure studied, knowing that a minimum of 6 elements over LC appears necessary in order to guarantee the mesh-independence of the results. The numerical validation of the computation option PDIL_ELGA is carried in the test cases SSNV208A, SSNP125A and WTNV132C. 5 Verification The list of the validation tests for the second gradient: | Test case | description | | --- | --- | | ssll117 (modellings a and b) | Test of D_PLAN_DIL (see V3.01.117) | | sslv117 (modellings a to d) | Test of 3D_DIL (see V3.01.117) | | wtvn132 (modellings b and f) | Test of D_PLAN_HM_SI_DIL and D_PLAN_HMS_DIL (see V7.31.32) | | wtnl101c | Test of D_PLAN_THMS_DIL (see V7.30.101) | | wtnp119f | Test of D_PLAN_HH2MS_DIL (see V7.32.119) | | wtnl100i | Test of 3D_HMS_DIL (see V7.30.100) | | wtnv142b | Test of 3D_HM_SI_DIL (see V7.31.142) | | wtnv113k | Test of 3D_THMS_DIL (see V7.31.113) | | wtnv136e | Test of 3D_HH2MS_DIL (see V7.31.136) | 6 Bibliography 1. r5.05.01 Computation of an oscillator response spectrum r5.05.01 Computation of an oscillator response spectrum Summary: We present in this document the computation of an oscillator response spectrum (SRO). 1 Introduction When computing an oscillator response spectrum (SRO), one is led to compute the response of a single-degree-of-freedom oscillator to a seismic signal. This consists in solving a second-order differential equation whose time solution is given by a convolution product known as the Duhamel integral. The NIGAM method is an efficient method for solving this problem. In the frequency domain, the convolution product becomes a simple product and can be solved efficiently by means of the analytical transfer function. This document presents these two methods, which are available. The computation of an SRO can be carried out via the operator CALC_FONCTION, factor keyword SPEC_OSCI. 2 Mathematical definition of the response spectrum 2.1 Acceleration response spectrum The spectral acceleration is the name given to the maximum absolute response of a single-degree-of-freedom oscillator of natural frequency f excited at its base by an accelerogram. The oscillator response spectrum (SRO) is a function of frequency whose ordinates are the spectral accelerations. The equation of motion of a single-degree-of-freedom oscillator excited at its base by an imposed acceleration, \alpha(t) , is written: m \ddot{q}(t) + c \dot{q}(t) + k q(t) = -m \alpha(t) where q(t) is the relative displacement of the oscillator. Thus one has \ddot{q}(t) + 2 \xi \, \omega_0 \dot{q}(t) + \omega_0^2 q(t)=-\alpha(t) where \omega_0=\sqrt{ \frac{k}{m}} and \xi=\frac{c}{2\sqrt {k m}} . In the frequency domain this equation is written: -\omega^2 \hat{q}(\omega) + 2 \xi \, i\omega \, \omega_0 \hat{q}(\omega)+\omega_0^2 \hat{q}(\omega)=-\hat{\alpha}(\omega) Response spectra are generally expressed in spectral pseudo-acceleration {PS_{a}} . It corresponds to the product of the maximum of the absolute relative displacement |q(t)| of the simple oscillator by the square of its natural frequency f=\frac{\omega}{2 \pi} : PS_{a}(f)=(2\pi f)^2 \max_{T}|q(t)| where the spectral pseudo-acceleration is denoted {PS_{a}} and T is the duration of the observation. The response q(t) depends on the frequency of the oscillator f . This dependence is not mentioned explicitly in the expressions for the SRO, in order to lighten the notation. It is customary to work with the response spectra in pseudo-acceleration rather than to consider the absolute spectral acceleration. For a given frequency, the absolute spectral accelerations and the pseudo-acceleration coincide over a wide range of dampings. For higher dampings, beyond 20%, differences can be observed between the pseudo-acceleration and the absolute acceleration. The absolute spectral acceleration S_{a}(f) is readily obtained as the maximum value of the absolute acceleration response y(t) =\alpha(t) + \ddot{q}(t) : S_{a}(f) = \max_{T}|y(t)| The notable values of the acceleration response spectrum are: - the maximum frequency f_{max} , beyond which the spectrum reaches a constant value; one reaches the asymptote of the spectrum. This is the frequency beyond which the seismic signal no longer contains any frequency content. An oscillator whose natural frequency exceeds f_{max} follows the motion of its support. The acceleration associated with the asymptote is called the ZPA (Zero Period Acceleration), which corresponds to the maximum value of the entrainment acceleration. The ZPA corresponds to the value of the maximum absolute acceleration of the time signal (PGA) and does not depend on the damping of the oscillator. - the pseudo-acceleration at the peak (there may be several peaks) or of the plateau in the case of a smoothed and broadened response spectrum; - the pseudo-acceleration at low frequency is related to the maximum entrainment displacement. 2.2 Velocity and displacement response spectra The displacement response spectrum {S_{d}}(f) is defined as: S_{d}(f)= \max_{T}|q(t)| The pseudo-velocity response spectra PS_{v}(f) correspond to the product of the maximum of the absolute relative displacement |q(t)| of the simple oscillator by its natural frequency f= \frac{\omega}{2 \pi} : PS_{v}(f) = (2\pi f) \max_{T}|q(t)| = (2\pi f) S_{d}(f) The relative-velocity response spectrum is computed directly from the response of the oscillator: S_{v}(f)= \max_{T}|\dot{q}(t)| 2.3 Damping of the response spectra The response spectra also depend on the reduced damping of the oscillator (here this dependence has been omitted from the equations in order to simplify the notation). 3 Nigam time-domain method 3.1 Analytical solution of the response of a single-degree-of-freedom oscillator When computing the oscillator spectrum of an accelerogram R4.05.03, one is led to solve the following linear second-order differential equation: \ddot{q} + 2\xi \omega \dot{q} + {\omega}^{2}q = \alpha \left(t\right) where q(t) is the relative displacement, \alpha (t) is the acceleration of the motion imposed at the base, \omega is the angular frequency of the oscillator and \xi is the reduced damping of the oscillator. With initial conditions on q and \dot{q} . The solution of this equation is written in the form: q\left(t\right) = {\int}_{0}^{t} { h \left(t-\tau \right) \, \alpha \left(\tau \right) d\tau } + q\left(0\right)g\left(t\right) + \dot{q}\left(0\right)h\left(t\right) where q(0) and \dot{q}(0) are the displacement and the velocity at the initial time instant. We are interested in the expressions for h(t) and for g(t) according to the value of the reduced damping \xi . If \xi 1 (supercritical damping): h\left(t\right) = \frac{{e}^{-\xi \omega t}}{\omega \sqrt{{\xi}^{2}-1}} \, \sinh \left(\omega t\sqrt{{\xi}^{2}-1}\right) and: g\left(t\right) = {e}^{-\xi \omega t} \left[ \cosh \left( \omega t\sqrt{{\xi}^{2}-1}\right) + \frac{\xi}{\sqrt{{\xi}^{2}-1}} \, \sinh \left(\omega t\sqrt{{\xi}^{2}-1}\right) \right] 3.2 Numerical solution The time-domain numerical method implemented was proposed by Nigam and Jennings [bib2], and is more efficient than the Newmark method (see [Bib3]) in the case of subcritical damping , which corresponds to our initial seismic problem R4.05.03. One is therefore led to solve the differential equation: \ddot{q}\left(t\right) + 2 \xi \omega \dot{q}\left(t\right) + {\omega}^{2}q\left(t\right) = \alpha \left(t\right) with zero initial conditions and a subcritical damping, whose solution is written: q\left(t\right) = - \frac{1}{{\omega}_{d}} {\int}_{0}^{t} { {e}^{-\xi \omega \left(t-\tau \right)} \, \sin\left[{\omega}_{d} \left(t-\tau \right)\right]\alpha \left(\tau \right) d\tau } With {\omega}_{d}=\omega \sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}} . Assuming that \alpha (t) varies linearly inside each interval \Delta (t) as in figure r5.05.01-fig-approximationLineaire, one can write: \alpha \left(\tau \right) = \alpha \left(t-\Delta t\right) + \frac{\tau}{\Delta t} \left[ \alpha \left(t\right) - \alpha \left(t-\Delta t\right) \right] \text{ pour } \tau \in \left[0,\Delta t\right] Linear approximation of the function Note The time step \Delta t is not necessarily constant. Whence the equation to be solved (expressed in the new variable \tau ): \ddot{q}\left(\tau \right) + 2\xi \omega \dot{q}\left(\tau \right) + {\omega}^{2}q\left(\tau \right) = a+b\tau \text{ pour } \tau \in \left[0,\Delta t\right] Where a=\alpha (t-\Delta t ) and b=\left[\alpha (t)-\alpha (t-\Delta t )\right]/\Delta t . With the initial conditions: \begin{split}\left \lbrace \begin{array}{c} q\left(0\right)=q\left(t-\Delta t\right)\\ \dot{q}\left(0\right)=\dot{q}\left(t-\Delta t\right) \end{array} \right .\end{split} The solution of this equation is the superposition of a particular solution: {q}_{p}(t) = - \frac{a}{{\omega}^{2}} + \frac{2 \xi b }{{\omega}^{3}} - \frac{b}{{\omega}^{2}}\tau and of the solutions of the homogeneous problem: {q}_{h}(t) = {e}^{-\xi \omega \tau } \left[ {C}_{1} \, \sin({\omega}_{d}\tau ) + {C}_{2} \, \cos({\omega}_{d}\tau ) \right] Hence: q(\tau) = {e}^{-\xi \omega \tau } \left[ {C}_{1} \, \sin({\omega}_{d}\tau ) + {C}_{2} \, \cos({\omega}_{d}\tau ) \right] - \frac{a}{{\omega}^{2}} + \frac{2 \xi b}{{\omega}^{3}} - \frac{b}{{w}^{2}} \tau Differentiating q (with respect to \tau ) one has: \begin{array}{c} \dot{q}\left(\tau \right) = -\xi \omega {e}^{-\xi \omega \tau } \left({C}_{1} \, \sin{\omega}_{d}\tau + {C}_{2} \, \cos{\omega}_{d}\tau \right) +\\ {e}^{-\xi \omega \tau } \left( {C}_{1} \, {\omega}_{d}\cos{\omega}_{d}\tau - {C}_{2} \, {\omega}_{d}\sin{\omega}_{d}\tau \right) - \frac{b}{{\omega}^{2}} \end{array} The coefficients {C}_{1} and {C}_{2} are then determined by the initial conditions at the beginning of the interval (that is, for \tau =0 ): {C}_{2} = q\left( t-\Delta t\right) + \frac{a}{{\omega}^{2}} - \frac{2\xi b}{{\omega}^{3}} and: {C}_{1} = \frac{1}{{\omega}_{d}}\left[ \dot{q} \left(t-\Delta t\right) + \xi \omega q \left(t-\Delta t\right) + \frac{\xi a}{\omega} - \frac{2{\xi}^{2}-1}{{\omega}^{2}}b \right] Substituting {C}_{1} and {C}_{2} into the expressions for q and \dot{q} one obtains the matrix equality for \tau =\Delta t : \begin{split}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c} q(t) \\ \dot{q}(t) \end{array} \right\rbrace = A(\xi ,\omega ,\Delta t) \, \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c} q(t-\Delta t)\\ \dot{q}(t-\Delta t) \end{array} \right\rbrace + B(\xi ,\omega ,\Delta t) \, \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c} \alpha (t-\Delta t)\\ \alpha (t) \end{array}\right\rbrace\end{split} 3.3 Coefficients of the matrices of the system to be solved Coefficients for the matrix A : {a}_{11} = {e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t} \left[ \frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}}} \, \sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) + \cos\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) \right] {a}_{12} = \frac{{e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t}}{{\omega}_{d}} \, \sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) {a}_{21} = -\frac{\omega}{\sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}}}{e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t}\sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) {a}_{22} = {e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t}\left[ \cos\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) - \frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}}}\sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) \right] Coefficients for the matrix B : {b}_{11} = {e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t} \left[ \left( \frac{2{\xi}^{2}-1}{{\omega}^{2}\Delta t} + \frac{\xi}{\omega} \right) \, \frac{\sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right)}{{\omega}_{d}} + \left( \frac{2\xi }{{\omega}^{3}\Delta t} + \frac{1}{{\omega}^{2}} \right) \cos\left( {\omega}_{d}\Delta t \right) \right] - \frac{2\xi}{{\omega}^{3}\Delta t} {b}_{12} = -{e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t} \left[ \frac{2{\xi}^{2}-1} {{\omega}^{2}\Delta t} \, \frac{\sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right)}{{\omega}_{d}} + \frac{2\xi}{{\omega}^{3}\Delta t} \, \cos \left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) \right] - \frac{1}{{\omega}^{2}} + \frac{2\xi}{{\omega}^{3}\Delta t} \begin{split}\begin{array}{c} {b}_{21} = {e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t} \left( \frac{2{\xi}^{2}-1}{{\omega}^{2}\Delta t} + \frac{\xi}{\omega} \right) \, \left( \cos\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) - \frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}}} \sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) \right) -\\ {e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t} \left( \frac{2\xi}{{\omega}^{3}\Delta t} + \frac{1}{{\omega}^{2}}\right) \, \left({\omega}_{d}\sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) + \xi \omega \cos\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) \right)+\\ \frac{1}{{\omega}^{2}\Delta t} \end{array}\end{split} \begin{split}\begin{array}{c} {b}_{22} = -{e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t} \left( \frac{2{\xi}^{2}-1} {{\omega}^{2}\Delta t} \right) \, \left( \cos\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) - \frac{\xi}{\sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}}}\sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) \right) +\\ {e}^{-\xi \omega \Delta t} \left( \frac{2\xi }{{\omega}^{3}\Delta t} \right) \, \left( {\omega}_{d}\sin\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) + \xi \omega \cos\left({\omega}_{d}\Delta t\right) \right)-\\ \frac{1}{{\omega}^{2}\Delta t} \end{array}\end{split} with {\omega}_{d}=\omega \sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}} . 3.4 Computation of the acceleration Knowing q(\tau) and \dot{q}(\tau) , it is then possible to give the expression for the acceleration \ddot{q}(\tau) \ddot{q}(\tau) = - \left( 2 \xi \omega \dot{q}(\tau) + \omega^2 q(\tau) \right) + \alpha(\tau) with the expressions given by and . 4 Harmonic method 4.1 Computation of the displacement response One applies the Fourier transform to the seismic signal and to the equation of motion. The transfer function thus obtained is written h(\omega) = \frac{1}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 + 2 \xi \, \omega_0 \, i \omega)} Equation expresses the transfer function between an accelerogram and the relative displacement response of the oscillator forced at its base. The response in the frequency domain is thus written: \hat{q}(\omega) = h(\omega) \hat{\alpha}(\omega) The time response q(t) is obtained by the inverse Fourier transform of \hat{q}(\omega) . 4.2 Computation of the absolute-acceleration response The transfer function of equation must be replaced by the transfer function between an accelerogram and the absolute-acceleration response of the oscillator: h(\omega) = \frac{\omega_0^2+2 \xi \,i\omega \,\omega_0}{\omega_0^2-\omega^2+2 \xi \,\omega_0 \, i \omega} The response in the frequency domain is thus written: \hat{y}(\omega) = h(\omega) \hat{\alpha}(\omega) The time response in absolute acceleration y(t) = \alpha(t) + \ddot{q}(t) is obtained by the inverse Fourier transform of \hat{y}(\omega) . This is the HARMO method in CALC_FONCTION, factor keyword SPEC_OSCI. 5 Bibliography Gibert R.-J. - Vibrations of structures, Collection of the Directorate of Studies and Research of Électricité de France, no. 69, Eyrolles 1988. r5.05.02 Direct integration algorithms of the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’PHYS’ r5.05.02 Direct integration algorithms of the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’PHYS’ Summary: This document describes the time-integration schemes which are used to solve, in a direct manner, dynamics problems in linear transient mechanics . The NEWMARK and WILSON- \theta schemes are detailed, as well as the "central differences with a constant step" and "adaptive time step" schemes. 1 Introduction The aim of transient dynamic analysis is to determine, as a function of time, the response of a structure, given an external loading, or boundary conditions which are functions of time, when the inertia effects cannot be neglected. In a certain number of physical configurations, a transient analysis cannot be dispensed with in favour of a modal or harmonic analysis alone: - if the history of the phenomenon is important in the study, - if the external loading is complex (earthquake, multi-component excitations...), - if the system is non-linear (plasticity, impacts, friction ...). The methods of transient dynamic analysis which can then be used are divided into two broad categories: - the so-called direct integration methods, - the Ritz methods, including among others modal projection recombination. The direct integration methods are so named because no transformation is carried out on the dynamic system after the discretisation into finite elements. A presentation will be given of the direct integration algorithms used to solve a dynamic problem in mechanics for linear structures. These algorithms are employed in the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’PHYS’ The Ritz methods, on the contrary, carry out a transformation of the initial dynamic system, very often a projection onto a subspace of the initial discretisation space. The dynamic solution is then performed on a modified system, which only gives access to an approximation of the response of the initial system. They are presented in another document r5.06.04. 2 Implicit and explicit direct time-integration methods for a dynamic problem It is assumed that the structure under study has a linear constitutive behaviour and that the equations governing its dynamic equilibrium have been discretised by finite elements. A discrete system of second-order differential equations is obtained, which is to be integrated in time. In general, these equations take the following form: M.{\ddot{X}}_{t}+C.{\dot{X}}_{t}\text{}+K.{X}_{t}={R}_{t} - M is the mass matrix of the system, - C is the viscous damping matrix of the system, - K is the elastic stiffness matrix of the system, - R is the vector of the external forces applied to the viscous system. The system is of second order. Two classes of integration methods can be distinguished for integrating the equilibrium equations step by step: these are the explicit and implicit integration methods. Let us see what distinguishes them by examining the time integration of the following linear system: M.{\ddot{X}}_{t}+C.{\dot{X}}_{t}\text{}+K.{X}_{t}={R}_{t} This second-order differential system can be reduced to a first-order system: A.\dot{u}=B.u+F where: u=\left[\begin{array}{c}X\\ \dot{X}\end{array}\right]u=\left[\begin{array}{c}\dot{X}\\ \ddot{X}\end{array}\right]A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}I& 0\\ 0& M\end{array}\right]B=\left[\begin{array}{cc}0& I\\ -K& -C\end{array}\right]F=\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ R\end{array}\right] To integrate this differential equation, a discretisation {t}_{i} of the interval under study is used, together with a finite-difference formula to express the derivative \dot{u} . The methods in which, in the form written at time {t}_{i} , only the derivative \dot{u} involves the variable u at time {t}_{i+1} are called explicit integration methods. In this way, the determination of the quantities sought at the time instant {t}_{i+1} does not result from an inversion of a system involving the operator K . If, in addition, a "mass-lumping" is carried out so as to make the matrix M diagonal, the determination of {u}_{i+1} is particularly simple. These are the main characteristics of the explicit integration methods. The implicit or semi-implicit methods involve the discretisation of U in the form at a time instant later than {t}_{i} , generally {t}_{i+1} , so as to determine the variables of the problem at {t}_{i+1} . Their determination therefore requires the solution of a system involving the operator K . Two notions concerning the integration schemes are important: consistency and stability. The approximations used to obtain the differential operators define the consistency or the order of the integration scheme . One may indeed consider that the approximation with which the displacement is obtained at each time step is related to the order of approximation of the first and second derivatives with respect to time. The stability study of a scheme consists in analysing the propagation of the numerical perturbations over time. A stable scheme keeps a finite solution, in spite of the perturbations, whereas an unstable scheme leads to a numerical blow-up or a divergence of the solution. To carry out a stability study of an integration scheme, the latter is put in the form of a linear recursive system and the eigencharacteristics of this system are determined. If all the eigenvalues of the recursion operator are smaller than 1 in modulus, the scheme is stable; otherwise it is unstable (cf. ). Explicit integration schemes are generally conditionally stable, which means that the time step must be sufficiently small to ensure the stability of the scheme. Certain implicit algorithms have the particular feature of being unconditionally stable, depending on the choice of certain parameters, which is what makes them of interest and makes it possible to integrate the dynamic phenomenon with an arbitrarily large time step. The Wilson- \theta scheme and the NEWMARK scheme can be explicit for certain choices of their parameters. They are used for their unconditional stability properties, which are specific to implicit schemes. They will therefore be classified here in the category of implicit schemes, and the conditions under which they give the desired stability properties will be seen. Two explicit integration schemes have also been introduced. These are the DIFF_CENTRE and ADAPT schemes, both of which are based on the central-difference method. They are conditionally stable and, in order to be efficient, require a diagonalised mass matrix. Conditional stability leads to a control of the time step which, exploited in the case of the ADAPT scheme, allows the time step to be adapted according to the rapidity of the phenomena being modelled. 3 The WILSON-\theta scheme [bib1]_ 3.1 Presentation of the scheme It will be assumed in what follows that the solids are linear elastic. This method starts from the hypothesis that the acceleration is linear between t and t+\theta .\Delta t : {\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{\mathrm{t}+\tau }={\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}+\frac{\tau}{\theta \Delta the choice between several time-integration methods. In their default parameter setting, the Wilson and Newmark schemes are unconditionally stable implicit schemes. They therefore require an inversion of a linear system at each time step, but in return they offer a choice of time step which is restricted only by the fineness with which one wishes to describe the time evolution of the phenomena being modelled. The DIFF_CENTRE and ADAPT schemes are explicit, which saves them, in the case of a diagonal mass matrix, a costly matrix inversion. But the conditional stability of this type of scheme generally leads to the use of small time steps, conditioned by the smallest natural period of the system. It is therefore not guaranteed that the explicit schemes are systematically faster. This depends on the phenomena being simulated. If the physics of these phenomena requires a fine time discretisation, the time step used is naturally within the stability interval. Otherwise, the numerical stability constraints lead to a very costly inflation in the number of time steps. The ADAPT scheme takes advantage of information on the frequency content of the response in order to adapt the time step. The discretisation of time is therefore no longer imposed by the smallest natural period of the system but by its response. This can be an advantage when the frequency of the response evolves in time, as in the case of impacts. 9 Bibliography K.J. BATHE, E.L. r5.05.03 Harmonic response r5.05.03 Harmonic response Summary: This document presents the theoretical foundations of the computation of the steady-state regime of the response of a complex mechanical system, with linear behaviour, subjected to a harmonic dynamic excitation. The computation is carried out equally well directly on the system modelled by finite elements, or on the system represented by a modal basis; in the latter case, if the modal basis is the product of the substructuring technique, one will refer to the document R4.06.03. > Contents 1 Introduction In harmonic problems, the system studied is subjected to an excitation varying as the product of an arbitrary function of space by a sinusoidal function of time. Seeking the response consists in computing the field of the quantities represented by the degrees of freedom of the finite-element modelling of the system. When the system has a linear behaviour, the response of the field of the observed quantities tends rapidly (because of the dying-out of its transient component by internal dissipation) towards a steady-state regime: the resulting field finally varies harmonically like the excitation. It is this steady-state regime of the response which one proposes to compute. General notations: | t | : | time | | --- | --- | --- | | P | : | Current point of the model | | \omega | : | Angular frequency ( {\mathit{rad.s}}^{-1} ) | | j | : | Unit pure imaginary ({j}^{2}=-1) | | M | : | Mass matrix arising from the finite-element modelling | | K | : | Stiffness matrix arising from the finite-element modelling | | C | : | Damping matrix arising from the finite-element modelling | | q | : | Vector of the degrees of freedom arising from the finite-element modelling | | {\mathrm{f}}_{\mathrm{ext}} | : | Vector of the external forces on the system | | \Phi | : | Matrix of the vectors of the substructure basis | | \eta | : | Vector of the generalised degrees of freedom | 2 Harmonic equation We establish the dynamic equation in the case of a harmonic excitation for three kinds of mechanical systems: - pure structures (without fluid), - pure fluids (without structure) with a linear acoustic-type behaviour, - mixed structure and fluid systems in fluid–structure interaction. 2.1 Harmonic equation of structures The vibratory behaviour of a pure structure results from the external forces which are applied to it. The quantity to be computed is the displacement at every point P of the model. 2.1.1 Direct computation of elastic structures In the case of the direct computation on the finite-element model we may write: \mathrm{M}\ddot{\mathrm{u}}+\mathrm{C}\dot{\mathrm{u}}+\mathrm{K}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}\mathrm{u}={\mathrm{f}}_{\text{ext}}(P,t) where \mathrm{M} is the (real) mass matrix, C is the (real) damping matrix, K is the (real) stiffness matrix, {\mathrm{f}}_{\text{ext}}(P,t) is the (complex) vector of the field of external forces applied to S . Finally \mathrm{u} , \dot{\mathrm{u}} and \ddot{\mathrm{u}} are the (complex) displacement, velocity and acceleration vectors, functions of P and t . In a harmonic problem, one imposes a dynamic loading, arbitrary in space, but sinusoidal in time. One is then interested in the stabilised response of the system, without taking the transient part into account. The field of external forces is written: {\mathrm{f}}_{\text{ext}}(P,t)=\lbrace {\mathrm{f}}_{\text{ext}}(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} The displacement field is written: \mathrm{u}(P,t)=\lbrace \mathrm{u}(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} The velocity and acceleration fields are written by time differentiation of the displacements: \begin{array}{c}\dot{\mathrm{u}}(P,t)=j\omega \lbrace \mathrm{u}(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t}\\ \ddot{\mathrm{u}}(P,t)=-{\omega}^{2}\lbrace \mathrm{u}(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t}\end{array} Finally the structure S satisfies the following equation: (\mathrm{K}+j\omega \mathrm{C}-{\omega}^{2}\mathrm{M})\lbrace u\rbrace =\lbrace {\mathrm{f}}_{\text{ext}}(P)\rbrace 2.1.2 Computation on an elastic-structure modal basis The computation of the harmonic response by the modal-synthesis method consists in seeking the unknown displacement field, coming from the finite-element modelling, on an appropriate space of reduced dimension (Ritz transformation). One will refer to the documents R4.06.02 and R4.06.03. If one uses this method instead, equation () is projected onto the modal basis of S and one arrives at the following harmonic equation: (\overline{\mathrm{K}}+j\omega \overline{C}-{\omega}^{2}\overline{\mathrm{M}})\lbrace \eta \rbrace =\lbrace {\overline{\mathrm{f}}}_{\text{ext}}\rbrace where \overline{\mathrm{M}}={\Phi}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathrm{M}\Phi is the (real) generalised mass matrix, \overline{\mathrm{C}}={\Phi}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathrm{C}\Phi is the (real) generalised damping matrix, \overline{\mathrm{K}}={\Phi}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathrm{K}\Phi is the (real) generalised stiffness matrix and lbrace {\overline{\mathrm{f}}}_{\text{ext}}rbrace ={\Phi}^{\mathrm{T}}lbrace {\mathrm{f}}_{\text{ext}}rbrace is the (complex) vector of the applied generalised harmonic external forces. One has denoted by \Phi the (real) matrix of the modal vectors of the Ritz basis, lbrace \eta (P)rbrace is the (complex) vector of the generalised harmonic displacements. Once \lbrace \eta (P)\rbrace has been determined by () one carries out a restitution on the physical basis (cf. R4.06.02). 2.1.3 Direct computation of viscoelastic structures The constitutive law of a linear viscoelastic material is of the type L\sigma =Mϵ where L\mathit{et}M are linear differential operators in the time variable (see R5.05.04). In the harmonic domain, this constitutive law becomes of the type \sigma ={H}_{c}(\omega )ϵ where {H}_{c}(\omega ) is a complex tensor depending on the angular frequency. The discretised equation of the structure is then written, in the harmonic regime: ({\mathrm{K}}_{\mathrm{r}}(\omega )+j{\mathrm{K}}_{i}(\omega )-{\omega}^{2}\mathrm{M})\lbrace u\rbrace =\lbrace {\mathrm{f}}_{\text{ext}}(P)\rbrace One denotes by {\mathrm{K}}_{\mathrm{c}}={\mathrm{K}}_{\mathrm{r}}(\omega )+j{\mathrm{K}}_{\mathrm{r}}(\omega ) the complex stiffness matrix depending on the frequency. Particular case : if the damping is of hysteretic “global” type, the constitutive law is written \sigma =(1+j\eta )Hϵ where H is the real Hooke tensor and \eta is a global loss coefficient (cf. R5.05.04). Equation () is then written: ((1+j\eta )\mathrm{K}-{\omega}^{2}\mathrm{M})\lbrace u\rbrace =\lbrace {\mathrm{f}}_{\text{ext}}(P)\rbrace One notes that {\mathrm{K}}_{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm{K}+j\eta \mathrm{K} is a complex stiffness matrix, which no longer depends on the frequency. 2.2 Harmonic equation of acoustic fluids The document R4.02.01 describes the finite-element modelling of a fluid system (without transport) having a linear acoustic behaviour. The fluid system F undergoes a harmonic excitation of acoustic velocity on part of its boundary. The harmonic response is described by the following equation, in which the quantity to be computed is the acoustic pressure at every point P of the model. (\mathrm{K}+j\omega \mathrm{C}-{\omega}^{2}\mathrm{M})\lbrace \mathrm{p}(P)\rbrace =-j\omega \lbrace {\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{n}}(P)\rbrace where \mathrm{M} is the (complex) acoustic “mass” matrix, \mathrm{C} is the (complex) acoustic “damping” matrix (and in this instance that of the boundary {\partial}_{z}F where one applies an acoustic impedance) and \mathrm{K} is the (complex) acoustic “stiffness” matrix. One denotes by {\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{n}}(P,t)=\lbrace {\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{n}}(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} the velocity, with \lbrace {V}_{n}(P)\rbrace the (complex) vector of the field of normal acoustic velocities applied to the boundary {\partial}_{v}F of F where one applies acoustic velocities, and by \mathrm{p}(P,t)=\lbrace \mathrm{p}(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} the pressure, with \lbrace p(P)\rbrace the (complex) vector of the acoustic pressures. 2.3 Harmonic equation of fluid–structure systems The document R4.02.02 describes the finite-element modelling of a system F+S made up of a fluid part (without transport) F in interaction with a structure part S (interaction on F\cup S ). Fluid and structure have a linear behaviour. The fluid system F undergoes a harmonic excitation of normal acoustic velocity on part of its boundary. The harmonic response is described by the following equation, in which the quantities to be computed are: - the acoustic pressure at every point P of the fluid F , - the displacement at every point P of the structure S , - in addition, the displacement potential \varphi at every point P of the fluid F or other auxiliary variables described in R4.02.02. (K-{\omega}^{2}M-j{\omega}^{3}I)\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}u(P)\\ p(P)\\ \varphi (P)\end{array}\right\rbrace \text{=+}j\omega \lbrace {v}_{n}(P)\rbrace where \mathrm{M} is the (real) fluid–structure “mass” matrix arising from the domains F and S , I is the (real) fluid “impedance” matrix arising from the boundary {\partial}_{z}F of the domain F where one applies an impedance, and K is the (real) fluid–structure “stiffness” matrix arising from the domains F and S . The solution fields are of harmonic form. {v}_{n}(P,t)=\lbrace {v}_{n}(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omegat } is the (real) vector of the field of normal acoustic velocities applied to the boundary {\partial}_{v}F of F , u(P,t)=\lbrace u(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omegat } is the (complex) vector of the displacement field in the structure S , p(P,t)=\lbrace p(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omegat } is the (complex) vector of the acoustic-pressure field in the fluid F and \varphi (P,t)=\lbrace \varphi (P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omegat } is the (complex) vector of the displacement-potential field in the fluid F . 2.4 General harmonic equation In order to take into account all the cases of harmonic equations, the operator DYNA_VIBRA solves the following general harmonic equation: (-j{\omega}^{3}I-{\omega}^{2}M+j\omegac +K)\lbrace q\rbrace =\left\lbrace \sum_{i=1}^{k}{h}_{i}(f)\cdot {\omega}^{{n}_{i}}\cdot {e}^{j\pi \frac{{\varphi}_{i}}{180}}\cdot {g}_{i}(P)\right\rbrace where \mathrm{I} is the possible fluid “impedance” matrix, M is the “mass” matrix, C the “damping” matrix and K the “stiffness” matrix. The solution is \left\lbrace q(P)\right\rbrace . The right-hand side contains \left\lbrace {g}_{i}(P)\right\rbrace , which is a field vector at the nodes corresponding to one or more loads of force or acoustic velocity or potential or imposed motion, {h}_{i}(f) a real or complex function of the frequency f , \omega =2\pi f is the angular frequency, {n}_{i} is the power of the angular frequency when the loading is a function of the angular frequency, and {\varphi}_{i} is the phase in degrees of each component of the excitation with respect to a phase reference. By way of example, if one takes the case of a fluid system modelled in acoustics, without imposed degrees of freedom, simply excited on part of its boundary by a normal-velocity field {\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{n}}(P,t)=\lbrace {\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{n}}(P)\rbrace {e}^{j\omega t} , the terms of equation () become: (-{\omega}^{2}\mathrm{M}+j\omega \mathrm{C}+\mathrm{K})\lbrace \mathrm{p}\rbrace =-{\omega}^{}\left\lbrace {\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{n}}(P)\right\rbrace - no impedance component \mathrm{I} , - acoustic mass matrix \mathrm{M} , - Where applicable , a damping matrix \mathrm{C} arising from the acoustic finite-element modelling if there is an impedance on the boundary, - acoustic stiffness matrix \mathrm{K} , - the vector of the unknowns \left\lbrace \mathrm{q}(P)\right\rbrace is reduced to \left\lbrace \mathrm{p}(P)\right\rbrace , the vector of the pressures at the nodes - the loading \left\lbrace {\mathrm{g}}_{i}(P)\right\rbrace is \left\lbrace {\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{n}}(P)\right\rbrace , the normal-velocity field vector on the faces - {h}_{i}(f) is constant and equal to -1. - the power {n}_{i} is equal to 1 and the phase {\varphi}_{i} is zero 3 Bibliography 1.
