r5.05.04 Modelling of damping in linear dynamics r5.05.04 Modelling of damping in linear dynamics Summary: The linear dynamic analyses of structures subjected to imposed forces or motions require mechanical damping characteristics to be added to the stiffness and mass characteristics of the model. Several classical modellings are available, applicable to all the types of finite elements available: - the viscous damping model, - the hysteretic damping model (also called “structural damping”) for the harmonic analysis of viscoelastic materials. For the analyses using dynamic response methods by modal recombination, with a modal basis of real eigenmodes, it is possible to introduce modal damping coefficients. 1 Notion of mechanical damping 1.1 Damping models The motion of structures subjected to imposed forces or motions, variable with time, depends in particular on the damping properties, that is to say on the dissipation of energy in the constitutive materials of the structure and in the connections of the various structural elements with one another and with the surrounding medium. The physical phenomena involved in this dissipation of energy are numerous: friction, shocks, viscosity and plasticity, vibratory radiation at the supports. The constitutive models representing these phenomena are often poorly known and it is difficult to describe them explicitly at the elementary level. This is why the models most used are the simple models which make it possible to reproduce at the macroscopic scale the main effects on the structures [bib1] [bib2]. Those currently available are: - viscous damping: energy dissipated proportional to the velocity of the motion, - hysteretic damping (also called “structural damping”): energy dissipated proportional to the displacement such that the damping force is of opposite sign to that of the velocity. Note that Coulomb damping, which corresponds to a friction damping for which the energy dissipated is proportional to the reaction force normal to the direction of displacement, requires the contact to be modelled, which is outside the strictly linear framework. The non-linear operators can take it into account in all its generality [R5.03.50 & R5.03.52] whereas the operator for the transient solution in modal form can model Coulomb friction in the framework of point contacts R5.06.03. The values of the parameters of these models are deduced, when they are available, from experimental results. At the design stage, one limits oneself to the use of regulatory values. 1.2 General definitions for characterising the damping [bib1] 1.2.1 Loss coefficient The loss coefficient \eta is a dimensionless coefficient characteristic of the damping effect defined as the ratio of the energy dissipated {E}_{d}^{\text{cycle}} during a cycle to the maximum potential energy {E}_{p}^{\max} multiplied by 2\pi : \eta =\frac{{E}_{d\text{par}\text{cycle}}}{2\pi {E}_{p\max}} 1.2.2 Reduced damping By definition the reduced damping \xi is equal to half the loss coefficient observed for an excitation angular frequency equal to the natural angular frequency of the undamped system: \xi =\frac{\eta}{2} 2 Viscous damping model 2.1 Physical definition of viscous damping Classical damper devices (for example, by laminating a viscous fluid through the orifices of a piston driven by the vibratory motion) deliver forces proportional to the velocity of the motion and of opposite sign. Over a cycle, the work of these forces is positive: this is viscous damping. For a simple oscillator of stiffness k , of mass m and of viscous damping c , the applied external force balances the three components: the elastic restoring force \mathit{ku} , the damping force c\dot{u} and the inertia force m\ddot{u} , whence the dynamic equation in absolute motion: m\ddot{u}+c\dot{u}+\mathrm{ku}=f For this viscous damping model the energy dissipated during a cycle of angular frequency \omega is proportional to the vibratory velocity -\omega {u}_{0}\sin(\omegat ) associated with the displacement {u}_{0}\cos(\omegat ) : {E}_{d}^{\text{cycle}}={\int}_{0}^{2\pi }-c\omega {u}_{0}\sin\omega \mathit{td}\left({u}_{0}\cos\omega t\right)=\pi c\omega {u}_{0}^{2} and the potential energy for a sinusoidal displacement {u}_{0}\cos\omega t is: {E}_{p}^{\max}={\int}_{\pi /2}^{0}{\mathit{ku}}_{0}\cos\omega td\left({u}_{0}\cos\omega t\right)=\frac{1}{2}{\mathit{ku}}_{0}^{2} For a cycle of angular frequency \omega and of sinusoidal displacement {u}_{0}\cos\omega t , the loss coefficient is proportional to the frequency of the motion: \eta =\frac{c\omega }{k} 2.2 Harmonic oscillator with viscous damping The classical analysis of the undamped model associated with equation (), put in the form \left(k-m{\omega}^{2}\right)u=0 gives us {\omega}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} the natural angular frequency. The critical damping from which the differential equation () no longer has an oscillating solution is given by the formulae {c}_{\text{critique}}=2\sqrt{\text{km}}=2m{\omega}_{0}=\frac{2k}{{\omega}_{0}} which makes it possible to give a numerical interpretation of the reduced damping, which is often expressed as a percentage of the critical damping: \xi =\frac{\eta}{2}=\frac{c}{{c}_{\text{critique}}}=\frac{c}{2m{\omega}_{0}} 2.2.1 Response to a release from excitation Starting from a static deflection {u}_{\text{st}}=\frac{{f}_{0}}{k} , a release (freeing of the system) produces a free oscillatory motion {u}_{l}(t)={u}_{0}{e}^{-\xi {\omega}_{0}t}\cos{\omega}_{0}^{'}t which brings out the natural angular frequency of the damped system \omega {'}_{0}={\omega}_{0}\sqrt{(1-{\xi}^{2})} . Over time, the extreme amplitude ({u}_{1},{u}_{2}) decreases at each period by {e}^{-\xi {\omega}_{0}T}={e}^{-2\pi \xi }={e}^{-\delta } where \delta is the logarithmic decrement such that \delta =2\pi \xi . 2.2.2 Response to a harmonic excitation The response to a harmonic excitation of the form f(t)={f}_{0}{e}^{j\omega t} is written with a forced response, a permanent particular solution u(t)={u}_{0}{e}^{\left(j\omega t-\phi \right)} which is written with the reduced angular frequency \lambda =\frac{\omega}{{\omega}_{0}} \frac{{\mathit{ku}}_{0}}{{f}_{0}}=\frac{1}{1-{\lambda}^{2}+j2\xi \lambda }={H}_{v}\left(j\omega \right) where {H}_{v}(j\omega ) is the complex transfer function of a simple oscillator with viscous damping. The modulus of the response \frac{{u}_{0}}{{u}_{\text{st}}}=\frac{{\mathit{ku}}_{0}}{{f}_{0}}=|{H}_{v}\left(j\omega \right)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\left(1-{\lambda}^{2}\right)}^{2}+{\left(2\xi \lambda \right)}^{2}}} brings out a dynamic amplification with respect to the static response {u}_{\text{st}} . This amplification is maximum for \lambda =\frac{{\omega}_{0}^{'}}{{\omega}_{0}}=\sqrt{\left(1-{\xi}^{2}\right)} and gives the value of the maximum displacement \frac{{u}_{0\max}}{{u}_{\text{st}}}=\frac{1}{2\xi \sqrt{\left(1-{\xi}^{2}\right)}} . If one observes the vibratory velocity \dot{u}(t)=j\omega u(t) , the amplification of the vibratory velocity is maximum for \lambda =\frac{{\omega}_{0}}{{\omega}_{0}}=1 and the maximum amplitude of the velocity is {\dot{u}}_{0\max}=\frac{1}{2\xi }=Q , where Q is the mechanical analogy of the quality factor of electrical engineers. These properties are at the origin of the methods for measuring the damping characteristics of mechanical structures. 3 Hysteretic damping model 3.1 Physical definition of hysteretic damping For a sinusoidal excitation applied to an elastoplastic structure or to an elastic structure with friction, the force–displacement curve brings out a positive work of the external force which corresponds to an energy dissipated in the structure, which one can as a first approximation represent as below: In both cases the loss coefficient increases, in general, with the amplitude of the cycle. For small values of the loss coefficient (less than 0,2 ), the shape of the cycle has no appreciable influence on the motion and one can liken it to an ellipse [bib1]. In the particular case of a force–displacement relation whose cycle is elliptical in shape, the expression of the loss coefficient is simple. For an applied force F and a displacement u={u}_{0}\cosq the restoring force is {\mathit{ku}}_{0}\cos\theta , k being the “classical” stiffness of the mechanical system, and the damping force -{\mathit{hu}}_{0}\sin\theta , h being the stiffness phase-shifted by 90° , which leads to the constitutive relation F={\mathit{ku}}_{0}\cos\theta -{\mathit{hu}}_{0}\sin\theta . The energies, dissipated during a cycle and maximum potential, are: {E}_{d}^{\text{cycle}}={\int}_{0}^{2\pi }-{\mathit{hu}}_{0}\sin\theta d\left({u}_{0}\cos\theta \right)=\pi {\mathit{hu}}_{0}^{2} and: {E}_{p}^{\max}={\int}_{\pi /2}^{0}{\mathit{ku}}_{0}\cos\theta d\left({u}_{0}\cos\theta \right)=\frac{{\mathit{ku}}_{0}^{2}}{2} whence the loss coefficient: \eta =\frac{\pi {\mathit{hu}}_{0}^{2}}{2\pi \frac{{\mathit{ku}}_{0}^{2}}{2}}=\frac{h}{k} For a sinusoidal cycle \theta =\omegat , the hysteretic damping coefficient \eta =\frac{h}{k} is independent of \omega . It can be determined from a test under harmonic cyclic loading. 3.2 Harmonic oscillator with hysteretic damping The hysteretic damping model can be used to treat the harmonic responses of structures with viscoelastic materials. The energy dissipated per cycle in the form {E}_{d}^{\text{cycle}}={\int}_{0}^{2\pi }\sigma d\epsilon makes it possible to bring out a complex Young's modulus {E}^{\text{ }} from the stress–strain relation of a viscoelastic material \sigma ={\sigma}_{0}{e}^{j\omega t} and \epsilon ={\epsilon}_{0}{e}^{j\left(\omega t-\phi \right)} where {\sigma}_{0} and {\epsilon}_{0} are the amplitudes and \varphi the phase: {E}^{\text{ }}=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}=\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{\epsilon}_{0}}\right){e}^{j\phi }=\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{\epsilon}_{0}}\right)\left(\cos\phi +j\sin\phi \right) Denoting by {E}_{1}=\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{\epsilon}_{0}}\right)\cos\phi the real part and by {E}_{2}=\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{\epsilon}_{0}}\right)\sin\mathrm{\phi } the imaginary part, one obtains: {E}^{\text{ }}={E}_{1}+{\mathit{jE}}_{2}={E}_{1}\left(1+j\eta \right) with \eta =\frac{{E}_{1}}{{E}_{2}}=\text{tg}\phi where \phi is also called the loss angle. The classical analysis of equation () only makes sense, with a hysteretic damping model, for a harmonic excitation f(t)={f}_{0}{e}^{j\omegat } which leads to the equation: m\ddot{u}+k\left(1+j\eta \right)u=m\ddot{u}+\left(k+\mathit{jh}\right)u={f}_{0}{e}^{j\omega t} where the real part of the displacement u represents the displacement of the mass and h=k\eta . As previously [§ 2.2], the harmonic response can be written, with the reduced angular frequency \lambda =\frac{\omega}{{\omega}_{0}} , in the following form: \frac{{\mathit{ku}}_{0}}{{f}_{0}}=\frac{1}{1-{\lambda}^{2}+j\eta }={H}_{h}\left(j\omega \right) where {H}_{h}(j\omega ) is the complex transfer function of a simple oscillator with hysteretic damping. The modulus of the response \frac{{u}_{0}}{{u}_{\text{st}}}=\frac{{\mathit{ku}}_{0}}{{f}_{0}}=|{H}_{h}\left(j\omega \right)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\left(1-{\lambda}^{2}\right)}^{2}+{\eta}^{2}}} brings out a dynamic amplification with respect to the static response, an amplification which is maximum for \lambda =1 and gives the value of the maximum displacement \frac{{u}_{0\max}}{{u}_{\text{st}}}=\frac{1}{\eta}=\frac{1}{2\xi } . In conclusion, the reduced damping associated with hysteretic damping is: \xi =\frac{\eta}{2}=\frac{h}{2k}=\frac{h}{2m{\omega}_{0}^{2}} 3.3 A note on linear viscoelasticity Linear viscoelastic materials have constitutive laws of the type: L\sigma =Mϵ where M and L are linear differential operators in the time variable, that is to say of the type L=\sum{l}_{k}{\partial}_{t}^{{\alpha}_{k}} where {l}_{k} are real tensors and {\alpha}_{k} are the orders of differentiation, potentially non-integer. In order to compute the motion at a given instant t , one must know the dynamics of the previous instants: in this sense, the motion at the instant t depends on its history. If models with integer time derivatives require knowledge of the velocity, of the acceleration or of higher orders of the motion in order to compute the forces at a given instant, fractional-order models, for their part, need the whole history of the motion. Indeed, fractional derivatives have the characteristic of being non-local: for example the Grunwald–Letnikov derivative of f at x of order \alpha is defined as the limit when h\to 0 of the finite difference: \frac{1}{{h}^{\alpha}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}{(-1)}^{k}\left(\begin{array}{c}\alpha \\ k\end{array}\right)f(x+(\alpha -k)h) thus each point y >}{\omega}_{i} will be very little damped and the low-frequency modes \omega >}{\omega}_{2} are very damped. - complete proportional damping: \alpha and :math: beta From an identification on two independent modes ({\varphi}_{1},{\omega}_{1}) and ({\varphi}_{2},{\omega}_{2}) , one obtains for any other angular frequency a reduced modal damping \xi =\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha \omega +\frac{\beta}{\omega}\right)={\xi}_{1}\frac{\omega}{{\omega}_{1}}+{\xi}_{2}\frac{{\omega}_{2}}{\omega} . In the interval \left[{\omega}_{1},{\omega}_{2}\right] , the variation of the reduced damping is small and outside it one finds the addition of the previous drawbacks: the modes outside the interval are too damped. In none of the previous cases will one be able to reproduce an assumption of modal damping equal for all the modes. Methods have been devised in order to tend towards this objective [bib1]. 5.1.3 Global hysteretic damping The generalisation of the equation of the simple oscillator with hysteretic damping leads to the system of complex equations where F\left(\Omega \right) is a harmonic excitation. M\ddot{U}+K\left(1+j\eta \right)U=F\left(\Omega \right) Knowing the real stiffness matrix, it is possible to build a hysteretic damping matrix {K}_{h}=j\eta K , with a global loss coefficient \eta . As previously in solution by modal recombination, from a basis of real eigenmodes, one obtains {\phi }^{T}M\phi \ddot{q}+j{\phi }^{T}{K}_{h}\phi q+{\phi }^{T}K\phi q={\phi }^{T}F(t) where the generalised hysteretic damping matrix is diagonal {\phi }^{T}{K}_{h}\phi =\left[\text{diag}\eta {\gamma}_{i}\right] , like the generalised stiffness matrix {\phi }^{T}K\phi =\left[\text{diag}{\gamma}_{i}\right] . According to the definition of the reduced damping, the modal damping is constant for all the modes, whence \xi =\frac{\eta}{2} . Advantages: - easy to implement using the operators DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01 and ASSEMBLAGE(OPTION='RIGI_MECA_HYST') U4.61.21. One can also proceed by using the operator COMB_MATR_ASSE U4.53.01, after having assembled the stiffness matrix; - very useful for the validation of solution algorithms; - the damping actually introduced into the model is constant for all the modes of the structure, as required by construction regulations. Drawbacks: - this modelling is ill-suited to industrial studies, because it does not make it possible to represent the heterogeneity of the structure with respect to damping; - only the harmonic analysis (in complex variables) is possible. 5.1.4 Viscoelastic hysteretic damping The structure is damped by a viscoelastic material; the harmonic analysis then aims to solve the equation: \left(-{\omega}^{2}M+{K}_{r}(\omega )+j{K}_{i}(\omega )\right)U=F\left(\Omega \right) The determination of the complex modes is for the moment possible only by use of DYNA_VISCO U4.53.04, which makes it possible to compute the modes in air of an isotropic viscoelastic material whose Poisson's ratio is real. Advantages: - easy to implement using the operators DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01 and ASSEMBLAGE(OPTION='RIGI_MECA_HYST') U4.61.21; - the damping is physical. Drawbacks: - only the harmonic analysis (in complex variables) is possible. 5.2 Localised damping For the analyses requiring a modelling representing the heterogeneity of the structure, it is possible to assign damping characteristics localised on the mesh cells of the structure, in fact on elements of the model. 5.2.1 Damper elements It is possible to apply discrete damper elements: - on POI1 mesh cells: the damping is linked to the displacement (respectively the velocity) of the support node, - on SEG2 mesh cells: the damping is linked to the relative displacement (respectively the relative velocity) of the two connected nodes. The operator AFFE_CARA_ELEM U4.24.01 makes it possible to define for each discrete element: - a damping matrix of viscous type {a}_{\text{discret}} whose terms are assigned to the various degrees of freedom of the nodes concerned; several modes of description of the matrix are available. - a hysteretic loss coefficient {\eta}_{\text{discret}} multiplying the stiffness matrix of the discrete element assigned to the support mesh cell. 5.2.2 Damping assigned to any type of finite element The elastic material assigned to any finite element can be defined with damping parameters by the operator DEFI_MATERIAU U4.23.01. - Proportional viscous damping with two Rayleigh parameters \alpha and \beta . AMOR_ALPHA = :math: \alpha AMOR_BETA = :math: \beta For all types of finite elements (of continuous media, structural or discrete), it is possible to compute the real elementary matrices corresponding to the computation option 'AMOR_MECA', after having computed the elementary matrices corresponding to the computation options 'RIGI_MECA' and 'MASS_MECA'. The elementary matrix of the element i assigned the material {\alpha}_{j},{\beta}_{j} is then of the form: - for a finite element: {c}_{\text{elem,}i}={\alpha}_{j}{k}_{\text{elem,}i}+{\beta}_{j}{m}_{\text{elem,}i} - for a discrete element: {c}_{\text{elem},i}={a}_{\text{discret},i} - Hysteretic damping with a coefficient \eta AMOR_HYST = coef For all types of finite elements (of continuous media, structural or discrete), it is possible to compute the complex elementary matrices corresponding to the computation option 'RIGI_MECA_HYST', after having computed the elementary matrices corresponding to the computation options 'RIGI_MECA'. The elementary matrix of the element i assigned the material {\alpha}_{j},{\beta}_{j} is then of the form: - for a finite element: {k}_{\text{elem},i}^{\text{ }}={k}_{\text{elem},i}\left(1+j{\eta}_{j}\right) - for a discrete element: {k}_{\text{elem},i}^{\text{ }}={k}_{\text{elem},i}\left(1+j{\eta}_{\text{discret},i}\right) 5.2.3 Construction of the damping matrix The assembly of the elementary damping matrices is obtained with the usual operator ASSE_MATRICE U4.42.02 or by the command ASSEMBLAGE U4.31.02. One must use the same numberings and the same storage mode as for the stiffness and mass matrices (operator NUME_DDL U4.42.01). Note : the damping matrix obtained is non-proportional C\ne \alpha K+\beta M or {K}_{h}\ne j\eta K . 6 Use of the damping matrix 6.1 Use of the viscous damping matrix 6.1.1 Direct linear dynamic analysis The viscous damping matrix C , whatever its mode of construction and its proportional or non-proportional character, can be used for the direct linear dynamic analysis (keyword MATR_AMOR) with the operator DYNA_VIBRA. 6.1.2 Dynamic analysis by modal recombination For the analyses by modal recombination, one must project this matrix into the subspace defined by a set \phi of real eigenmodes, obtained on the associated undamped problem (K-{\omega}^{2}M)\phi =0 . This operation is possible with the command PROJ_BASE U4.55.11 or with the operator PROJ_MATR_BASE U4.55.01. For the computation of the dynamic response in imposed force or motion in the modal space, the following possibilities are available: - use of the generalised damping matrix {\phi }^{T}C\phi : - in transient analysis with the operator DYNA_VIBRA R5.06.04 and U4.54.03 and the keyword AMOR_GENE, - in seismic analysis by the spectral method with the operator COMB_SISM_MODAL R4.05.03 and U4.54.04 and the keyword AMOR_GENE, - in harmonic analysis with the operator DYNA_VIBRA R5.05.03 and U4.54.03 and the keyword MATR_AMOR. It is recalled that in the case of heterogeneous damping (use of the localised damping options), the matrix {\phi }^{T}C\phi is not diagonal. - use of the viscous modal damping by supplying a reduced modal damping constant for all the modes \xi or a list of values {\xi}_{i} . Several methods of identification of these coefficients are possible but there is no command for the systematic construction of the list of values. One can nevertheless mention the use of Basile's assumption (2{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}=\text{diag}\frac{{\phi }^{T}C\phi }{{\phi }^{T}M\phi }) , the regulatory practice RCC-G (or ETC-C) for seismic analysis with soil damping, exploitation of experimental results, ... - in transient and harmonic analysis with the operator DYNA_VIBRA R5.06.04 U4.54.03 and the keyword AMOR_REDUIT. - in seismic analysis by the spectral modal method with the operator COMB_SISM_MODAL R4.05.03 U4.54.04 and the keywords AMOR_GENE or LIST_AMOR, or also with the keyword AMOR_REDUIT. For the analyses by dynamic substructuring, with the use of a modal basis (Ritz basis) one will refer to R4.06.03 and R4.06.04. 6.2 Use of the complex stiffness matrix The complex stiffness matrix {K}^{\text{ }}=K+{K}_{h} , where {K}_{h} is an imaginary matrix (in the sense of complex numbers!), can be used for the direct harmonic analysis with the operator DYNA_VIBRA R5.05.03 and U4.54.03 and the keyword MATR_RIGI. For the analyses by modal recombination, no functionality is currently available for the use of the hysteretic damping model. 6.3 Complex modal analysis The viscous damping matrix C is indispensable for the complex modal analysis with the operator treating the quadratic eigenvalue problem R5.01.02 and CALC_MODES U4.52.02. It is recalled that the complex eigenmodes allow an approach better suited to the dynamic study of strongly damped structures (reduced damping \xi > 20%). No tool for dynamic response by modal recombination using a basis of complex eigenmodes is available. 7 Bibliography 1. “Damping”: Françoise GANTENBEIN and Michel LIVOLANT (CEA-DMT) in “Earthquake engineering” Collective work - Presses de l'E.N.P.C. (1985) 2. “Damping in structural analyses”: Forum IPSI - 2 AS Volume XVIII N°2 (June 1994)

r5.05.05 Non-linear dynamic algorithm r5.05.05 Non-linear dynamic algorithm Summary: The operator DYNA_NON_LINE DYNA_NON_LINE is used for the non-linear dynamic analysis of structures by direct time integration. The non-linearities may come from the material behaviour, from the constraints (frictional contact), or from large geometric transformations (large displacements and large rotations). The organisation of DYNA_NON_LINE is very similar to that of the non-linear quasi-static operator STAT_NON_LINE r5.03.01. A priori , all the constitutive relations developed in the framework of STAT_NON_LINE work in that of DYNA_NON_LINE. One presents here the general formulation of the non-linear dynamic problem in order to specify the links between the purely dynamic aspects and those already treated in other operators or formulations available in code_aster : management of the boundary conditions, of the fluid–structure couplings, of the damping, of the computation in a relative frame, then the properties of the numerical time-integration scheme, which is developed independently of any constitutive relation. One sets out how the latter is articulated with the Newton algorithm in order to treat the material and geometric non-linearities. Three complementary and efficient implicit time schemes are available: - the Newmark family, - the modified average acceleration (“HHT” in DYNA_NON_LINE, with the option MODI_EQUI='NON'), - the complete HHT scheme (“HHT” in DYNA_NON_LINE, with the option MODI_EQUI='OUI'), as well as its “without overshooting” version proposed in ('NOHHT' in DYNA_NON_LINE). The operator also proposes two explicit schemes: - the central differences, - the dissipative scheme of Tchamwa–Wielgosz. A few pieces of advice are given for proper use, which the documentation General advice on the use of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE complements. 1 Notation | Symbol | Description | | --- | --- | | u | continuous absolute displacement field | | K , {K}_{i}^{n} | stiffness matrix, tangent matrix | | M | inertia matrix | | R | vector of the internal forces | | L | right-hand-side vector of loadings (linear form) | | {L}^{\mathrm{abso}} {L}_{\mathrm{GR}}^{\mathrm{iner}} , {L}^{\mathrm{anel}} | right-hand sides due respectively to an absorbing boundary, to the non-linear inertial terms in large beam rotations, to anelastic chains (coming from command variables: temperature…) | | \mathrm{C} | damping matrix | | Q | assembled strain matrix | | {}^{t}V … | transpose of a vector V : dual linear form… | | t ; \mathit{\Delta t} | time; time step | | \alpha | parameter of the time-integration scheme of the \alpha method (and HHT) | | \beta ,\gamma | parameters of the NEWMARK time-integration scheme | | \Delta | increment of various quantities during the time step | | \delta | virtual variation of a field; increment of various quantities during the correction iterations | | i ; n ; j | index of the time step; index of the NEWTON iteration; component index | | \lambda ,\mu | LAGRANGE parameters: constraint reactions, contact reactions | | \mathrm{U},\dot{\mathrm{U}},\ddot{\mathrm{U}} | vector of displacement degrees of freedom and successive derivatives with respect to time | | \mathrm{P} | vector of degrees of freedom of barotropic fluid pressure perturbations | | \varphi | vector of degrees of freedom of the potential of barotropic fluid displacement perturbations | | \Phi | configuration: position vector: \mathrm{x},\mathrm{y},\mathrm{z} and possibly rotation vector, and other fields parameterising the system | | \dot{\Phi} | time derivative of the configuration \Phi with respect to time: translational velocity and possibly angular velocity | | \ddot{\Phi} | time derivative of \dot{\Phi} with respect to time: translational acceleration and possibly angular acceleration | | | Repeated-index convention: {U}_{d}^{k}\left(t\right){\Psi}_{k}=\sum_{k}{U}_{d}^{k}\left(t\right){\Psi}_{k} | 2 Non-linear dynamics: spatial discretisation of the continuous problem Solving a non-linear dynamic problem requires first describing the equations of the continuous problem, then presenting their spatial discretisation, here by finite elements, and finally describing the method of time integration, associated with the treatment of the material and geometric non-linearities. 2.1 Discretisation of the linear dynamic problem One denotes by u the field of absolute displacements with respect to the reference configuration, and parameterised by the time instant t , belonging to the affine space of the admissible fields {V}_{\text{adm}} . The direct method consists in solving the problem resulting from the finite-element discretisation of the displacement formulation. The discretisation of the virtual work of the inertia forces, in a field \delta v\in {V}_{\text{adm}}^{0} , the directing vector space of {V}_{\text{adm}} , is written: {\int}_{\Omega}\rho \ddot{u}.\delta vd\Omega {=}^{t}\delta V.M.\ddot{U} The discretisation of the virtual variation of the work dissipated by viscosity (damping brought by a dependence of the stresses on the strain rates) is: {\int}_{\Omega}c\dot{u}.\delta vd\Omega {=}^{t}\delta V.C.\dot{U} One specifies in r5.05.05-terme-inertie how the damping operator \mathrm{C} is built in DYNA_NON_LINE. The discretisation of the virtual work of the internal forces in linear elasticity is written: {\int}_{\Omega}\varepsilon (u).A.\varepsilon (\delta v)d\Omega {=}^{t}\delta V.K.U Finally, \mathrm{L} denotes the right-hand side resulting from the discretisation of the virtual work of the external forces. In linear elasticity, this therefore leads one to consider the following hyperbolic differential-algebraic system, for the degrees of freedom \mathrm{U} , with the initial conditions: \begin{array}{}\text{Trouver}U\in {ℝ}^{n}:\\ M.\ddot{U}+C.\dot{U}+K.U=L\\ U({t}_{0})={U}_{0}\\ \dot{U}({t}_{0})={\dot{U}}_{0}\end{array} accompanied by boundary conditions. The initial conditions are supplied to the algorithm by the keyword ETAT_INIT (operands DEPL and VITE). If the initial state results from a linear or non-linear static simulation, one does not take an initial velocity into account, and the displacement, as well as the state variables (stresses, internal variables), are extracted from the result of this simulation at the starting time instant considered. The dynamic equilibrium system becomes unstable if one can find a complex angular frequency \omega , whose imaginary part is negative, for which one can cancel the determinant of: -{\omega}^{2}\mathrm{M}+i\omega \mathrm{C}+\mathrm{K} . 2.2 Discretisation of the non-linear dynamic problem One now places oneself in a non-linear mechanical framework. One denotes the virtual work \underset{\Omega}{\int}\sigma (\mathrm{u},\dot{\mathrm{u}},t).\varepsilon (\delta \mathrm{v})d\Omega of deformation (also called that of the internal forces) of the non-linear mechanical problem. However one frequently adds to the internal forces coming from the constitutive law the internal forces of viscous damping built in a global manner, cf. [r5.05.05-amortissement]: C\cdot \dot{U} , where \mathrm{C} is the damping matrix. The virtual work of the internal forces is therefore written after discretisation: {}^{t}\delta \mathrm{V}.\left(\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{U},\dot{\mathrm{U}},t)+\mathrm{C}.\dot{\mathrm{U}}\right){=}^{t}\delta \mathrm{V}.\left({}^{t}\mathrm{Q}\left(\mathrm{U}\right).\sigma \left(\mathrm{U},\dot{\mathrm{U}},t\right)+\mathrm{C}.\dot{\mathrm{U}}\right) where one has deliberately distinguished the linear viscous forces (operator \mathrm{C} ) from the other internal forces. In the case of small displacements, the assembled strain operator {}^{t}\mathrm{Q} is constant (and defined on the initial configuration, coincident with the deformed configuration). The mechanical energy balance is written: \mathrm{L}.\delta \mathrm{v}={\int}_{\Omega}\rho \ddot{\mathrm{u}}.\delta \mathrm{v}d\Omega +{\int}_{\Omega}\sigma \left(\mathrm{u},\dot{\mathrm{u}},t\right).\epsilon \left(\delta \mathrm{v}\right)d\Omega The stress field \sigma at the time instant t is written in a general way \sigma (\mathrm{u},\dot{\mathrm{u}},\mathrm{Z},t,\mathrm{H}) , if one denotes by Z the field of command variables, such as for example T the temperature field, and by \mathrm{H} the past history of the structure up to the time instant t . For incremental behaviours, the history is the set of states (displacement, stress and internal-variable fields) at the previous time instant. In the linear case ( cf. r5.05.05-discretisation-dynamique-lineaire), the virtual work of deformation becomes: \mathrm{R}\left(\mathrm{U},\dot{\mathrm{U}}\right)+\mathrm{C}.\dot{\mathrm{U}}=\mathrm{K}.\mathrm{U}+\mathrm{C}.\dot{\mathrm{U}} where \mathrm{K} is the elastic stiffness matrix of the structure. 2.2.1 Inertia term One denotes by {}^{t}\delta \mathrm{V}.\mathrm{M}\left(\mathrm{U},\dot{\mathrm{U}},\ddot{\mathrm{U}}\right) , after discretisation, the virtual work {\int}_{\Omega}\rho \ddot{\mathrm{u}}.\delta \mathrm{v}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}d\Omega of the inertia forces of the system. One denotes by M the mass matrix of the system in small transformations. In large structural rotations (as for example beams, cf. r5.03.40), this virtual work is a non-linear function of U(t) and of its time derivatives (specifically of the rotation degrees of freedom); one therefore brings out the usual acceleration term with a non-linear correction: \mathrm{M}\left(\mathrm{U},\dot{\mathrm{U}},\ddot{\mathrm{U}}\right)=\mathrm{M}\left(\mathrm{U}\right).\ddot{\mathrm{U}}+{\mathrm{L}}_{\text{GR}}^{\text{iner}}\left(\mathrm{U},\dot{\mathrm{U}},\ddot{\mathrm{U}}\right) . In the other cases, \mathrm{M}\left(\mathrm{U},\dot{\mathrm{U}},\ddot{\mathrm{U}}\right)=\mathrm{M}\left(\mathrm{U}\right).\ddot{\mathrm{U}} , which may vary if one updates the geometry, or which is constant in small displacements. Note: case of the geometric update ( DEFORMATION='PETIT_REAC' ): For a dynamic problem with geometric update, having admitted conservation of mass, one notes that the mass matrix is not modified. Indeed: denoting respectively by det\mathrm{J}(\xi ) and \det{J}_{\mathrm{RG}}(\xi ) the determinant of the Jacobian matrix of the transformation from the real element {\Omega}_{e} to the reference element {\Omega}_{r} and that of the transformation from the updated real element {\Omega}_{\mathrm{RG}} to the reference element –cf. r3.01.00, §3.5– the virtual work of the inertia forces is written: {\int}_{{\Omega}_{\mathit{RG}}}{\rho}_{\mathit{RG}}\ddot{\mathrm{u}}.\delta \mathrm{v}d{\Omega}_{\mathit{RG}}={\int}_{{\Omega}_{r}}{\rho}_{\mathit{RG}}\ddot{\mathrm{u}}.\delta \mathrm{v}.det{\mathrm{J}}_{\mathit{RG}}(\xi )d{\Omega}_{r}={\int}_{{\Omega}_{r}}\rho \ddot{\mathrm{u}}.\delta \mathrm{v}.det\mathrm{J}(\xi )d{\Omega}_{r} because \rho_{\mathrm{RG}} = \rho \cdot \det J_{\mathrm{RG}}^{\mathrm{EL}} = \rho \cdot \frac{\det J}{\det J_{\mathrm{RG}}} as a consequence of the conservation of mass in the update (Jacobian {J}_{\mathrm{RG}}^{\mathrm{EL}} ). 2.2.2 Damping It is permissible to use discrete elements on which one places a damping behaviour via a matrix acting on the degrees of freedom, cf. u4.42.01, but the damping may also concern solid or structural models. The damping operator \mathrm{C} of the latter may be defined in code_aster in two ways in DYNA_NON_LINE, cf. also r5.05.04, u2.06.03: | 1) | a global way on a basis of eigenmodes ({\Phi}_{k}) , called modal damping (according to the BASILE hypothesis) established beforehand on the elastic structure, expressed on the “physical” basis of the finite-element modelling. One thus defines a coefficient per chosen mode. The keyword: AMOR_MODAL of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE makes it possible to supply it with the modal basis and the reduced damping coefficients (according to the BASILE hypothesis). Indeed, the dampings are determined experimentally by modal analysis on the resonances. The displacements \mathrm{U} are therefore projected onto the modes in order to obtain their generalised coordinates: {\eta}^{k}{=}^{t}{\Phi}_{k}.\mathrm{U} . The modal damping matrix is: \mathrm{C}=\left(\mathrm{K}{\Phi}_{k}\right).{C}_{\text{modal}}^{k}{.}^{t}\left(\mathrm{K}{\Phi}_{k}\right) with the scalar {C}_{\text{modal}}^{k}=2\frac{{\xi}_{k}}{{\omega}_{k}{.}^{t}{\Phi}_{k}.K.{\Phi}_{k}} where {\xi}_{k} is the modal damping factor at the angular frequency {\omega}_{k} and {k}_{k}{=}^{t}{\Phi}_{k}.K.{\Phi}_{k} is the generalised stiffness of mode k . Unfortunately this matrix may have a very full profile and make costly (the matrices C and K not having the same profile), as will be seen in [r5.05.05-schema-newmark], its integration into the left-hand side: one will then choose to treat these modal damping forces -\mathrm{C}.\dot{\mathrm{U}}\left(t\right) on the right-hand side by an explicit scheme. The validity of this modal damping modelling is acquired if one can neglect the couplings between eigenmodes. One must therefore make sure that the following criterion is verified: \underset{k,\ell }{\text{Min}}(\frac{{\xi}_{k}{\omega}_{k}}{\mid {\omega}_{k}-{\omega}_{\ell}\mid })\text{ ]: \Delta \hat{L}({t}_{i})=\hat{L}({t}_{i})-\hat{L}({t}_{i-1}) One also defines the increments of imposed conditions \Delta {U}_{d}({t}_{i}) , and one groups in \Delta {L}^{\text{anél}}({t}_{i}) the dependences of the stresses as a function of the various parameters or “command variables” Z of the constitutive law of the constitutive material: such as the temperature…: \Delta {L}^{\text{anél}}({t}_{i})=-{}^{t}Q({U}_{i-1}).\frac{d\sigma }{dZ}{\mid}_{({U}_{i-1},{\dot{U}}_{i-1},{\ddot{U}}_{i-1},Z)}.\Delta Z In the presence of modal damping the damping forces are carried over to the right-hand side. One then adds to \Delta \hat{L}({t}_{i}) the corresponding term: -C.{\dot{U}}_{i-1} . The term \Delta {L}^{\text{abso}}({t}_{i})=-{A}_{\text{fa}}\Delta \dot{P}({t}_{i-1})+\Delta {L}_{\text{abso}}^{\text{ordre}0}({U}_{\text{ent}}({t}_{i}),{\dot{U}}_{\text{ent}}({t}_{i}),\dot{U}({t}_{i-1})) denotes the contribution integrated explicitly from the solutions at {t}_{i-1} (in order to avoid having to treat a non-symmetric matrix, cf. r4.02.05) of an absorbing fluid boundary and of an absorbing elastic boundary, cf. and . One may also consult , and . 4.1.1 Generalities One defines with the aid of the methods of numerical analysis several types of properties for a time-integration scheme. Here is their meaning: 1. Convergence: the solution tends towards a limit when the time step \Delta t tends towards 0; 2. Accuracy: rate of convergence when the time step \Delta t tends towards 0; 3. Consistency and order of the scheme: the residual is bounded by {(\Delta t)}^{k+1} (example k=\mathrm{2 } : for the trapezoidal rule): a polynomial of order k+1 is integrated exactly; 4. The first, obvious, is that it must be adapted to the time sampling of the loadings applied to the system studied. Incidentally, it may be opportune to reconsider a modelling with a time dependence of the applied loadings that is too “violent”, by smoothing slope breaks for example. One advises, for reasons of accuracy (“Shannon”-type criterion on the cut-off frequency), a time step to be chosen such that: \Delta t\le 0,10{T}_{\min} where {T}_{\min} denotes the smallest vibration period of the system that one wishes to study. The space step of the finite-element mesh cells chosen also intervenes: the maximum time step \Delta t to be chosen is of the order of h/c , where c is the celerity of the elastic compression waves of the material and h a characteristic size of the mesh cells, if one seeks to describe partially high-frequency phenomena, for which however this numerical formulation of elastodynamics is not truly adapted (other numerical methods exist for doing so). Finally in the case of solids presenting rigid modes (free fall for example), in accordance with the note made in [r5.05.05-schema-newmark], it is appropriate to choose a time step \Delta t sufficiently small for the mass terms to be of the same order as those of stiffness (in the matrix \hat{K} , cf. ). Thus, one may choose: \Delta t\approx \sqrt{\frac{L}{50g}} where L is the diameter of the solid considered in “free fall” under the acceleration of gravity g . Thus the displacement increment g\Delta {t}^{2}/2 during this time step is small compared with the dimensions of the solid, or, in another way, similar to an elastic displacement under a field of action of the same magnitude. It is possible to have several dynamic analyses succeed one another, over successive time intervals, communicating by restarts by choosing as initial state the result of the last step studied previously, using very distinct time steps according to the a priori idea that one has of the response of the system studied. One does not possess a general result with this type of choice in terms of convergence… One also knows that the treatment of collisions is sensitive to the timing of the time steps, with respect to the “real” instants of shock: one will have to study the sensitivity of the response obtained. However, a “too small” time step may exacerbate the oscillations induced by the discontinuity. One may also turn towards the choice of an explicit scheme, of lower order (order 1), cf. for example even if such a choice leads one to take very small time steps. It is however advised to keep the time step constant during a phase of stationary linear dynamic response, in order to keep the properties stated previously. One wishes on the other hand that the high frequencies be attenuated by the computation because they may generate numerical instabilities and because the associated mechanical stresses are in general small. The curves giving the damping factor \xi as a function of \frac{\Delta t}{T} (period T=2\pi /\omega ) must therefore: - start from the origin with a horizontal tangent in order to give a very weak damping to the low frequencies, - be increasing functions in order to attenuate the high frequencies, and this all the more so as they are higher. Note The global algorithmic organisation is therefore unchanged with respect to the modified average-acceleration scheme: only the matrix of the system and the right-hand side are modified, and it is appropriate to store the vectors obtained at the previous steps. When \alpha =-1 (whence \beta =1 , \gamma =3/2 ), the HHT scheme then becomes explicit ( cf. ): \mathrm{M}{\ddot{\mathrm{U}}}_{i}+{}^{t}\mathrm{B}\,{\lambda}_{i}{+}^{t}\mathrm{A}\,{\mu}_{i}=\mathrm{L}\left({t}_{i-1}\right)-\mathrm{C}{\dot{\mathrm{U}}}_{i-1}-\mathrm{R}\left({\mathrm{U}}_{i-1},{\dot{\mathrm{U}}}_{i-1},t\right)-{\mathrm{L}}_{\text{GR}}^{\text{iner}}\left({\mathrm{U}}_{i},{\dot{\mathrm{U}}}_{i},{\ddot{\mathrm{U}}}_{i}\right) with: \ddot{U}(t+\Delta t)=\frac{1}{\Delta {t}^{2}}\left[U(t+\Delta t)-U(t)\right]-\frac{1}{\Delta t}\dot{U}(t) and \dot{\mathrm{U}}\left(t+\Delta t\right)=\frac{3}{2\,\Delta t}\,\left[\mathrm{U}\,\left(t+\Delta t\right)\,-\,\mathrm{U}\,\left(t\right)\right]-\frac{1}{2}\,\dot{\mathrm{U}}\,\left(t\right)+\frac{\Delta t}{4}\,\ddot{\mathrm{U}}\,\left(t\right) ensuring at the same time the greatest possible dissipation at high frequencies. On the one hand, by choosing for the simple keyword MODI_EQUI='NON', one uses the classical equilibrium equation where neither the terms of to “shifted” by \left(1+\alpha \right) or \alpha on the damping and the stiffnesses, nor the evaluation at {t}_{i+\alpha } of the right-hand sides are treated, which causes one to lose one order on the scheme (from 2 to 1). It is therefore in reality what one denotes in the literature the “modified average-acceleration method”, which is therefore limited to defining the optimal relation between the parameters of the Newmark scheme according to the to ; - On the other hand, by choosing for the simple keyword MODI_EQUI='OUI' (default value of the code), this amounts to adopting the complete HHT scheme presented above with shift of the internal and external force terms. Note One may use the following two variants with the factor keyword SCHEMA_TEMPS(SCHEMA='HHT'): With the complete HHT scheme (HHT with MODI_EQUI='OUI'), one treats the terms coming from the imposed displacements and follower forces as in the case of the average-acceleration scheme (HHT with MODI_EQUI='NON'). 5.3 Properties of the modified average-acceleration scheme One must have: \alpha \le 0 for the stability conditions of the scheme to be fulfilled, cf. [r5.05.05-proprietes-schema-newmark-problemes-non-lineaires]: the scheme is unconditionally stable . The “modified average-acceleration” scheme (also called the \alpha -method), therefore brings \beta ={(\gamma +\frac{1}{2})}^{2}/4 , which is the optimal choice for bringing a damping increasing on the high frequencies. When \alpha =0 , the “modified average-acceleration” scheme becomes again the “trapezoidal rule” and the damping is zero [r5.05.05-AmortHHHTOvershoot]. The value \alpha =-1 , that is \gamma =\frac{3}{2} and \beta =1 produces the strongest dissipation at high frequency, but destroys a great deal of the accuracy on the low-frequency modes. In practice, in the original “modified average-acceleration” scheme, one limits oneself to \alpha \in \left[-\frac{1}{3},0\right] , which ensures the monotonicity of the increase of the damping as a function of the frequency. The choice \alpha =-0.10 seems to be effective, even if it is possible to take values of \alpha higher in absolute value. Figure r5.05.05-AmortHHHTOvershoot, taken from , gives the variations of the numerical damping \xi as a function of \frac{\Delta t}{T} for a few values of \alpha , where T is the period of the system with 1 d.o.f. This figure calls for the following comments: 1. the “trapezoidal rule” ( \alpha =0 ) is attractive because it does not bring numerical damping for a system not physically damped, cf. [r5.05.05-schema-acceleration-moyenne], but it may be unstable in the non-linear case, 2. when \alpha \ne 0 , the curves do not have a horizontal tangent at the origin. As the “modified average-acceleration” scheme ( \alpha -method) brings a large artificial damping, certain users choose a time step, then determine the value of the parameter \alpha so that, in the frequency range which interests them, the numerical damping ratio is of the same order as the real mechanical damping ratio which, then, is not taken into account, 3. the error in time does not depend on \alpha , cf. . Numerical damping ratio as a function of the time step of the modified average-acceleration scheme One notes that one has for the small time steps \frac{\Delta t}{T} the following numerical damping: \xi = \vert \alpha \vert \frac{\pi \Delta t}{T}+o({(\frac{\Delta t}{T})}^{2}) which makes it possible to estimate in the targeted frequency range the mean numerical damping brought by the modified average-acceleration scheme ( \alpha -method), which is added to the physical damping possibly already present. Figure r5.05.05-ErreurHHTOvershoot, also taken from , gives the variations of the relative error in period as a function of \frac{\Delta t}{T} . The error is an increasing function of \vert \alpha \vert . Relative error on the period as a function of the time step of the modified average-acceleration scheme 5.4 Properties of the HHT scheme One must have: \alpha \le 0 for the stability conditions of the scheme to be fulfilled, cf. [r5.05.05-proprietes-schema-newmark-problemes-non-lineaires]: the scheme is unconditionally stable . When \alpha =0 , the HHT scheme becomes again the “trapezoidal rule” and the numerical damping is zero [r5.05.05-AmortHHHTOvershoot]. The value \alpha =-1 leads one to write the equilibrium at the previous step and is therefore not recommended. In practice, in the HHT scheme, one limits oneself to \alpha \in \left[-\frac{1}{3},0\right] , which ensures the monotonicity of the increase of the damping as a function of the frequency. The choice \alpha =-0.10 seems to be effective. The error in time increases less quickly than the numerical damping as a function of \alpha . Figure [r5.05.05-ErreurHHTOvershoot], taken from , gives the variations of the numerical damping \xi as a function of \frac{\Delta t}{T} for a few values of \alpha , comparing them with the modified average-acceleration scheme. One notes that: - the HHT method damps the low frequencies less than the modified average-acceleration scheme; - moreover, for a same value of the parameter \alpha , the numerical damping is distinctly more important, at “medium” and “high” frequency (\omega \Delta t>1) in the case of the modified average-acceleration type schemes, than for the HHT scheme. For example, for \omega \Delta t=2 , and for \alpha =-0.05 , one has a ratio of 2 on the values of numerical damping; - one therefore advises with the HHT scheme to envisage the taking into account of a physical damping [r5.05.05-terme-inertie], which one might not have taken into account by having chosen the modified average-acceleration scheme. Numerical damping ratio as a function of the time step of the HHT scheme, comparison with that produced by the modified average-acceleration scheme, cf. 5.5 HHT scheme and overshooting As mentioned in the paragraph r5.03.01-proprietes-schema-hht, the HHT scheme initially introduced in induces a damping in the high frequencies, while presenting a limited damping in the low frequencies. This makes it possible in particular to eliminate modes associated with high frequencies, for which the spatial and/or time discretisation is not sufficient. However, certain components of the numerical solution may be weakly damped (notably in the case of stiff systems), which induces the existence of oscillations altering the solution, leading to the phenomenon known under the name of overshooting . In particular, Hulbert and Hughes demonstrated the existence of overshooting in velocity in the case of the HHT scheme (see ). Moreover, Erlicher et al. showed that the entirety of the family of G-\alpha schemes (of which the HHT scheme is part) may present overshooting (see ). Furthermore, Bauchau et al. also propose a discussion relative to the effects of overshooting on the responses obtained with the HHT scheme. Thus, in spite of its appreciable numerical damping properties, the HHT scheme may be subject to overshooting phenomena. In this context, Kaiping proposed in a modification concerning the set of schemes of G-\alpha type, with a view to limiting the effects of overshooting. In particular, a new version of the HHT scheme, entitled NOHHT ( No Overshooting HHT ), was able to be proposed, via a modification of the coefficients of the scheme. One refers to for further details relative to this modification. The NOHHT scheme of may be used in u4.53.01, via the keyword SCHEMA_TEMPS. With a view to comparing the HHT and NOHHT schemes, one considers the elementary case (introduced in ) of a system with one degree of freedom, of mass m=1 kg, of natural period T=1 s, and endowed with a reduced damping \xi \in [0,1[ . In order to study the effect of overshooting in velocity, one computes the absolute error between the velocities obtained with the analytical solution of the problem and the numerical solution at the first time instant following the initial time instant, and this for several values of time step h > 0 . The results obtained in the cases \xi=0 (respectively \xi=0.5 ) are given in Figure r5.05.05-sdld32a-overshooting (respectively r5.05.05-sdld32b-overshooting). In the case of the classical HHT scheme, the error in velocity increases significantly when the chosen time step becomes large. On the other hand, this effect is appreciably limited in the case of the NOHHT scheme. This latter scheme therefore does indeed make it possible to limit the effects of overshooting. Study of the overshooting of the HHT scheme — Evolution of the absolute error in velocity as a function of the time discretisation, in the case without damping ( \xi=0 ) Study of the overshooting of the HHT scheme — Evolution of the absolute error in velocity as a function of the time discretisation, in the case with damping ( \xi=0.5 ) 6 The explicit schemes code_aster allows the use of two different explicit schemes: that of the central differences and that of Tchamwa–Wielgosz , which, for its part, is dissipative. These schemes, unlike the implicit schemes, are conditionally stable: there exists a limit time step that one cannot exceed on pain of divergence. These schemes are very well adapted to fast-dynamics problems, where one seeks to analyse the phenomena of wave propagation. Their cost becomes prohibitive, at least on a physical basis, when one must carry out numerical simulations over long times, as is the case when one seeks to obtain a vibratory response or when the imposed loading is of long duration: from several seconds, as, for example, in an earthquake. One must however point out that, compared with a solution with an implicit scheme, the explicit approaches cost much less on a time step. Indeed, whereas in implicit one must truly solve the assembled global system of large dimension at each step (or even at each iteration in the non-linear case), in explicit one dispenses with this very costly inversion by using a diagonal operator (based on the mass matrix alone, which therefore does not require an update: with the keyword MASS_DIAG = 'OUI'). With an explicit scheme, one can solve only in acceleration (keyword FORMULATION = 'ACCELERATION'). 6.1 The central-difference scheme This scheme (keyword SCHEMA_TEMPS, SCHEMA='DIFF_CENT'), the most common in fast-dynamics codes, is a particular case of the Newmark family. It is built by taking \beta =0 and \gamma =1/2 . This method of integration in time, which does not introduce numerical dissipation, is of order 2. Its stability time step (CFL condition: Courant Friedrichs and Levy ) is 2/\omega , with \omega which is the highest natural angular frequency of the structure considered. Notes On a physical basis, one can show that the critical time step is equivalent to the minimum time that a wave takes to cross the smallest finite element of the mesh. In practice, one approximates this value by computing the minimum, for all the finite elements, of: \Delta t=D/C with d which is the diameter of the largest inscribed sphere and c which is the celerity of the elastic compression waves in the element considered. This method of computation of the CFL condition, directly applicable on the solid elements, needs to be corrected for the structural elements. For the classical industrial applications, the CFL condition obliges one to take very small time steps (generally of the order of {10}^{-5}s . for metallic structures). On the other hand, on a modal basis, because of the strong truncation generally made for industrial cases, the critical time step, given directly by 2/\omega with \omega which is the cut-off angular frequency, will be much larger than on a physical basis. The explicit solution is always done in acceleration (the operator to be inverted then reduces to the mass matrix alone which one recommends “lumping”, hence making it diagonal). 6.2 The Tchamwa–Wielgosz scheme This recent scheme may be seen as the counterpart of the HHT scheme for the explicit case. The objective sought is the same: to introduce a high-frequency numerical dissipation, which does not disturb “too much” the low-frequency solution. This Tchamwa–Wielgosz scheme (keyword SCHEMA_TEMPS, SCHEMA='TCHAMWA') is not deduced from the Newmark family. Just like HHT, this scheme is parameterised by a real number, named \phi . If one takes \phi =1, the scheme does not dissipate. In practice it is recommended to choose a value of \phi between 1 and 1.1. The critical time step is that of the central-difference scheme divided by \phi . 6.3 Performance of the explicit schemes in code_aster code_aster is not a code dedicated to fast dynamics; it is a general-purpose code oriented towards implicit approaches. It is therefore not optimised for explicit solutions, in particular as regards the computation of the internal forces and the structuring of the objects generated, such as the solution data structure. It is therefore not recommended to use an explicit scheme for large-size problems, all the more so if one wishes to compute over a very large number of steps. 6.4 Explicit computations on a Ritz basis with subdomains in code_aster The comments of the previous paragraph are however to be qualified inasmuch as it is possible to proceed to explicit computations on a Ritz basis with subdomains (with “generalised” degrees of freedom) in Code_Aster . That is to say that one can by means of the factor keyword PROJ_MODAL carry out the computation with an explicit time-integration scheme on a modal (or Ritz) projection basis computed beforehand. This option intervenes in the case where one wishes to condense dynamically a part of the model with linear behaviour, by computing strictly by DYNA_NON_LINE only subdomains with non-linear behaviour. This, in order to reduce the size of the computational model. In this case, it is necessary to compute a Ritz modal basis on the whole model: the non-linear subdomain modelled for the computation calling on DYNA_NON_LINE and the other subdomains assumed linear and condensed dynamically. This basis must be orthogonalised with respect to the mass and linear stiffness matrices of the whole model. It must simply be representative of the motions activating the whole model. The modelled computational domain thus comprises a non-linear computational subdomain I and a series of linear subdomains E “external” to the computation which will be condensed dynamically. The matrices M , C , K , the forces F may be decomposed into a part associated with the domain I and a part associated with the subdomain(s) E . The equilibrium of the structure solved by DYNA_NON_LINE may then be written in terms of global finite-element degrees of freedom U : ({M}_{I}+{M}_{E}).\ddot{U}={F}_{I}^{\text{ext}}+{F}_{E}^{\text{ext}}–{F}_{I}^{int}(U,\dot{U})–{K}_{E}U-({C}_{I}+{C}_{E}).\dot{U} Let \lbrace \Phi \rbrace be a Ritz modal basis orthogonalised by elementary substructuring on the set of subdomains I and E . One then uses the Ritz transform: U = \Phi \, q and therefore by projecting by {}^{t}\Phi on the left one obtains: ({\tilde{M}}_{I}+{\tilde{M}}_{E}).\ddot{q}={}^{t}\Phi .{F}_{I}^{\text{ext}}+{\tilde{F}}_{E}^{\text{ext}}{–}^{t}\Phi .({F}_{I}^{int}+{C}_{I}.\dot{U})-{\tilde{K}}_{E}.q-{\tilde{C}}_{E}.\dot{q} The modes \Phi reduced to I are denoted \phi and the degrees of freedom U reduced to I are denoted u hence becomes for each time step: \tilde{M}.\ddot{q}={\phi }^{t}.{F}_{I}^{\text{ext}}–{\phi }^{t}.({F}_{I}^{int}(u,\dot{u})+{C}_{I}.\dot{u})+{\tilde{F}}_{E}^{\text{ext}}-{\tilde{K}}_{E}.q-{\tilde{C}}_{\mathrm{E.}}\dot{q} One therefore needs the generalised mass matrices \tilde{M}=({\tilde{M}}_{I}+{\tilde{M}}_{E}) diagonal as well as the matrices of the subdomains E : {\tilde{K}}_{E} and {\tilde{C}}_{E} full and the generalised vector {\tilde{F}}_{E}^{\text{ext}} which participate in the complementary terms to the standard dynamic problem reduced to the subdomain I which would be solved without dynamic condensation in the absence of subdomains E by DYNA_NON_LINE: \tilde{M}.\ddot{q}={\phi }^{t}.{F}_{I}^{\text{ext}}–{\phi }^{t}.({F}_{I}^{int}(u,\dot{u})+{C}_{I}.\dot{u}) At each time step, one evaluates and adds the complementary terms resulting from the dynamic condensation, cf. , to those of the standard dynamic problem without dynamic condensation and one solves with the explicit time-integration scheme in generalised coordinates q , having expressed with the explicit scheme the terms in \mathrm{u},\dot{\mathrm{u}} on the subdomain I . The knowledge of the orthogonalised Ritz modal basis \lbrace \phi \rbrace then makes it possible to obtain both the degrees of freedom u on the solution subdomain I and U on the whole model constituted of its subdomains. One will supply behind the keyword MODE_MECA only the modes \lbrace \phi \rbrace obtained by reduction of the Ritz basis to the non-linear computational domain I treated by DYNA_NON_LINE, behind the keyword MASSE_GENE the generalised mass matrix \tilde{M} , as well as behind the keywords RIGI_GENE AMOR_GENE the generalised operators of the subdomains E : {\tilde{K}}_{E} , {\tilde{C}}_{E} and finally with the factor keyword EXCIT_GENE {\tilde{F}}_{E} . An example of computation is supplied by the test case SDNV107A v5.03.107. The main nuance with respect to the restriction on the use of an explicit scheme for large-size problems consists both in the possibility of reducing the size of the computational model and in the use of a CFL condition on the time step linked to the maximum frequency of the projection basis, which makes it possible to reduce strongly the number of computation time steps. 7 Mass shift It is possible to enter a coefficient \mathrm{coef} behind the operand COEF_MASS_SHIFT in the keyword SCHEMA_TEMPS in order to carry out a “shift” of the mass matrix M which becomes: M'=M+\mathrm{coef.}K . The introduction of this coefficient makes it possible to invert in dynamics with an explicit scheme on a physical basis the mass matrix when the latter has zero terms for certain specific degrees of freedom, for example the pressure for the HM modelling elements. It should be noted that this shift is not necessary in dynamics with an explicit scheme on a modal basis (presence of the keyword PROJ_MODAL) because in this case the matrix to be inverted is the generalised mass matrix which is always invertible. The entry of this coefficient also makes it possible to improve strongly the convergence in dynamics with an implicit or explicit scheme whatever the type of modelling by imposing a cut-off frequency inversely proportional to the value of \mathrm{coef} . This practice, akin to the “selective mass scaling” method proposed by Lars Olovsson in numerous publications, makes it possible to satisfy the convergence criteria with larger time steps at the price of a distortion of the set of natural frequencies of the system, slight however for the low frequencies. A natural angular frequency of origin \omega then becomes \omega ' such that: \omega {'}^{2}=\frac{{\omega}^{2}}{1+\mathit{coef}.{\omega}^{2}} One notes from this expression that \omega ' tends towards a maximum value {\mathit{coef}}^{-0.5} . Thus, for example, for a maximum value in practice for \mathrm{coef}={10}^{-6} , the corrected maximum natural angular frequency of the system \omega ' is 1000r{\mathrm{d.s}}^{-1} , and a value for a natural frequency of origin of 30\mathrm{Hz} is corrected by this method to 29,481\mathit{Hz} . Notes : It is appropriate to point out that even if one activates the mass “shift” option, for the computation of the initial acceleration, it is always the non-shifted mass matrix which is used. The fact that it may be non-invertible does not however pose a problem, because in this case, one imposes the initial acceleration at 0 at every point. The stiffness matrix used for this “shift” is in practice that which is computed during the prediction phase of the Newton algorithm. 8 Example It is figure r5.05.05-fig-6-1 of the plane pendular motion of an extensible bar \mathrm{AB} of unit length, hinged at A to a fixed support, free at B and released without velocity in the terrestrial gravity field from a position defined by the angle {\theta}_{0} . One neglects all the phenomena of mechanical dissipation. As the amplitude {\theta}_{0} may be large — we shall take it of 90° — the point B undergoes large displacements and the problem is non-linear. The theoretical period is: T=1,6744s The computation of the motion of the pendulum by the HHT scheme ( \alpha -method) with \alpha =0 (“trapezoidal rule”) constitutes the test case SDNL100. Figure r5.05.05-fig-6-2 represents the evolution during one period of the elevation of the point B computed by the “modified average-acceleration” scheme with three values of \alpha . The period is divided into 40 equal time steps. The solid-line curve is relative to \alpha =0 . One observes practically no error. Large-amplitude pendulum “Modified average-acceleration” scheme, 40 steps of 0.0419 s The chain-line curve is relative to \alpha =-0,1 . One observes a damping ratio of about 2% whereas figure r5.05.05-fig-6-1, for \frac{\Delta t}{T}=0,025 , predicts 0.8%. This is because this curve was established in the linear case, whereas the motion of our pendulum is non-linear. The dotted curve is relative to \alpha =-0,3 . The damping ratio is about 5.8%, whereas that predicted by figure r5.05.05-AmortHHHTOvershoot is about 2.2%. The discrepancy is still due to the non-linearity of the problem. Finally, the chain-line curves and above all the dotted ones reveal a shortening of the computed period with respect to the theoretical period. 9 Conclusion The Newmark time-integration scheme and its variants called “modified average acceleration” and HHT, accompanied by the Newton method, make it possible to treat numerous types of non-linear dynamic problems, for material or geometric non-linearities. The treatment of highly non-linear and non-regular dynamic problems, such as the analysis of structures in large displacements or of frictional contact, is subject to numerical instability, even with time-integration methods unconditionally stable in the linear domain. One then succeeds in integrating the equations of motion with respect to time only by introducing artificial dissipation. The whole art is to dose this dissipation so that, in the range of frequencies which present a mechanical interest, it is roughly equivalent to the natural damping, without shifting too much the vibratory spectrum of the structure. Two explicit schemes are also proposed. One recommends that the users of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE read the documentation u2.06.13 whose role is to help to use these transient solution methods well. 10 Bibliography K.J. r5.05.07 Gyroscopic matrices of straight beams and of discs r5.05.07 Gyroscopic matrices of straight beams and of discs Summary: This document presents the formulation of the gyroscopic damping and stiffness matrices of the beam, solid and discrete elements. The beams are exclusively straight beams (Elements POU_D_T and POU_D_E). The cross-section is constant along the length and of circular shape. The material is homogeneous and isotropic. The discs are cylinders of revolution whose axis coincides with the axis of the beam. The disc is assumed undeformable. The assumptions adopted are the following: - Timoshenko assumption: transverse shear and all the inertia terms are taken into account. This assumption is to be used for low slenderness ratios (Elements POU_D_T). - Euler assumption: transverse shear is neglected. This assumption is verified for high slenderness ratios (Elements POU_D_E). The proper rotation speed (along the axis of the beam) may be constant or variable. In Code_Aster, the convention adopted defines the positive sense along the axis of rotation as being the usual trigonometric sense of rotation. 1 The straight beam element of constant circular cross-section A beam is a solid generated by a surface of area S , whose geometric centre of inertia G describes a curve C called the mean fibre or the neutral fibre. Within the framework of this modelling, only straight beams, of constant and circular cross-section, are taken into account. For the study of beams in general, the following assumptions are formulated: - The cross-section of the beam is undeformable, - The transverse displacement is uniform over the cross-section. These assumptions make it possible to express the displacements of an arbitrary point of the cross-section, as a function of an increment of displacement due to the rotation of the cross-section about the transverse axes. The discretisation into "exact" beam elements is carried out on a line element with two nodes and six degrees of freedom per node. These degrees of freedom are decomposed into three translations u , v , w (displacements along the directions x , y and z ) and three rotations {\theta}_{x} , {\theta}_{y} and {\theta}_{z} .(about the axes x , y and z ). In the case of straight beams, the mean line lies along the axis x of the local basis, the transverse displacements thus taking place in the plane (y,z) . For a dynamic analysis, the choice of the inertial frame as the reference system makes it possible to simplify the formulation of the differential equations governing their dynamic behaviour. This choice makes it possible to characterise the Coriolis effect (gyroscopic effect as seen from the rotor), which is added to the damping. Also, two other effects of apparent-stiffness type are added to the stiffness matrix: these are the centrifugal effect and the gyroscopic effect associated with the variation of speed. 3.1 Position in motion in the rotating frame In all generality, one will consider that the moving reference frame, whose origin is characterised by a translation \mathrm{s}(t){=}^{t}({s}_{x},{s}_{y},{s}_{y}) with respect to the inertial frame, rotates at the angular velocity \omega {=}^{t}({\omega}_{x},{\omega}_{y},{\omega}_{z}) about an arbitrary axis passing through the origin. It is important to note that the components of the rotation velocity are measured in the corotational frame. One will denote \omega ' the projection of this rotation velocity in the fixed frame, i.e. \omega ={t}^{}\mathrm{R}\omega ' where \mathrm{R}(t) is the change-of-basis matrix, formed of the direction cosines of the basis vectors of the inertial frame, expressed in the fixed reference frame. The position of a point P in the inertial reference frame (OXYZ), denoted \mathrm{y} , then has the expression: \mathrm{y}=\mathrm{s}(t)+\mathrm{R}(t)\left[\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u}(\mathrm{x},t)\right] where \mathrm{x} is the initial position of the point P in the inertial system and \mathrm{u} is the displacement vector resulting from the dynamic deformation of the structure at a given time instant t. The absolute velocity \dot{\mathrm{y}} of the point P is defined as being the first derivative with respect to time of the vector \mathrm{y} . It is written: \dot{\mathrm{y}}=\dot{\mathrm{s}}+\dot{\mathrm{R}}(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u})+\mathrm{R}\dot{\mathrm{u}} where \dot{\mathrm{s}} is the translational velocity of the origin O' of the rotating frame, written in the fixed frame. It is shown that the derivative \dot{\mathrm{R}} of the change-of-basis matrix may also be written as being the cross product between the rotation vector in the fixed frame \omega ' and the change-of-basis matrix \mathrm{R} , or else as being the product of the matrix \mathrm{R} and of the antisymmetric matrix \Omega which encompasses the three components of the rotation tensor in the inertial frame \omega : \dot{\mathrm{R}}=\omega '\mathrm{\wedge }\mathrm{R}=\mathrm{R}\Omega with \Omega =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& -{\omega}_{z}& {\omega}_{y}\\ {\omega}_{z}& 0& -{\omega}_{x}\\ -{\omega}_{y}& {\omega}_{x}& 0\end{array}\right] Inserting this definition into the expression of the absolute velocity, it follows that: \dot{\mathrm{y}}=\dot{\mathrm{s}}+\omega '\mathrm{\wedge }\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u})+\mathrm{R}\dot{\mathrm{u}} The absolute acceleration \ddot{\mathrm{y}} of the point P is defined as being the second derivative with respect to time of the velocity vector \mathrm{y} . It is written: \ddot{\mathrm{y}}=\ddot{\mathrm{s}}+\dot{\omega}'\mathrm{\wedge }\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u})+\omega '\mathrm{\wedge }['\omega '\mathrm{\wedge }\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u})]+2\omega '\mathrm{\wedge }\mathrm{R}\dot{\mathrm{u}}+\mathrm{R}\ddot{\mathrm{u}} with \ddot{\mathrm{s}} the translational acceleration of the origin O' of the rotating frame, written in the fixed frame and \dot{\omega}' is the instantaneous angular acceleration defined by the relation \dot{\omega}={t}^{}\mathrm{R}\dot{\omega}' . For the sake of clarity and without loss of generality, it will be assumed in the remainder of the document that the origin O' of the rotating frame is fixed, i.e. \dot{\mathrm{s}}=\ddot{\mathrm{s}}=0 . After pre-multiplication by the inverse transformation {t}^{}\mathrm{R} , one then obtains the absolute velocity and acceleration expressed in the moving reference frame: {t}^{}\mathrm{R}\dot{\mathrm{y}}=\dot{\mathrm{u}}+\omega \mathrm{\wedge }\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u}) {t}^{}\mathrm{R}\ddot{\mathrm{y}}=\ddot{\mathrm{u}}+\dot{\omega}\mathrm{\wedge }(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u})+\omega \mathrm{\wedge }[\omega \mathrm{\wedge }(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u})]+2\omega \mathrm{\wedge }\dot{\mathrm{u}} In this expression, which represents the theorem of the composition of the accelerations of a material point, one recognises the terms: - of relative acceleration \ddot{\mathrm{u}} , which contributes to the mass matrix; - of transport acceleration \dot{\omega}\mathrm{\wedge }(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u})+\omega \mathrm{\wedge }[\omega \mathrm{\wedge }(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{u})] (sum of the Euler effect due to the angular acceleration and of the centrifugal softening effect, which contribute to the stiffness matrix); - of complementary or Coriolis acceleration 2\omega \mathrm{\wedge }\dot{\mathrm{u}} , which contributes to the damping matrix. 3.2 Expression of the kinetic and potential energies In its general form, the kinetic energy is obtained from the absolute velocity \mathrm{y} as follows: \mathrm{T}=\frac{1}{2}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\dot{\mathrm{y}}}^{t}\dot{\mathrm{y}}\text{d}\Omega The expansion of the terms gives the following expression as a function of the displacement \mathrm{u} : \begin{array}{c}\mathrm{T}=\frac{1}{2}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\dot{\mathrm{u}}}^{t}\dot{\mathrm{u}}\text{d}\Omega +\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\dot{\mathrm{u}}}^{t}\Omega \mathrm{u}\text{d}\Omega -\frac{1}{2}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{u}}^{t}{\Omega}^{2}\mathrm{u}\text{d}\Omega -\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{u}}^{t}{\Omega}^{2}\mathrm{x}\text{d}\Omega +\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\dot{\mathrm{u}}}^{t}\Omega \mathrm{x}\text{d}\Omega \\ -\frac{1}{2}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{x}}^{t}{\Omega}^{2}\mathrm{x}\text{d}\Omega \end{array} The potential energy of the system (internal strain energy and work of the external forces) has the classical expression: \mathrm{U}=\frac{1}{2}\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\varepsilon}^{t}\Lambda \varepsilon \text{d}\Omega -\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\mathrm{u}}^{t}\mathrm{f}\text{d}\Omega -\underset{\partial {\Omega}_{\sigma}}{\int}{\mathrm{u}}^{t}\mathrm{t}\text{d}(\partial \Omega ) where \varepsilon is the vector associated with the strain tensor, \Lambda is the constitutive matrix and where \mathrm{f} and \mathrm{t} are, respectively, the vectors of the external body forces and surface forces. The displacement vector is approximated by the finite-element method. To this end, the classical shape functions described in the document R3.01.01 will be used. The displacement is then written in the form of the product of a displacement interpolation matrix, denoted \mathrm{B} , and of a vector of generalised coordinates \mathrm{q} . The kinetic and potential energies of the deformable body are then written as a function of the structural matrices as follows: \begin{array}{c}\mathrm{T}=\frac{1}{2}{\dot{\mathrm{q}}}^{t}\left[\mathrm{M}\right]\dot{\mathrm{q}}+\frac{1}{2}{\dot{\mathrm{q}}}^{t}\left[\mathrm{G}\right]\mathrm{q}-\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{q}}^{t}\left[\mathrm{N}\right]\mathrm{q}-{\mathrm{q}}^{t}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{B}}^{t}{\Omega}^{2}\mathrm{x}\text{d}\Omega +{\dot{\mathrm{q}}}^{t}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{B}}^{t}\Omega \mathrm{x}\text{d}\Omega \\ -\frac{1}{2}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{x}}^{t}{\Omega}^{2}\mathrm{x}\text{d}\Omega \end{array} \mathrm{U}=\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{q}}^{t}\left[\mathrm{K}\right]\mathrm{q}-{\mathrm{q}}^{\mathrm{t}}\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\mathrm{B}}^{t}\mathrm{f}\text{d}\Omega -{\mathrm{q}}^{\mathrm{t}}\underset{\partial {\Omega}_{\sigma}}{\int}{\mathrm{B}}^{t}\mathrm{t}\text{d}(\partial \Omega ) The first three terms of the kinetic energy bring out the matrices: - of mass \left[\mathrm{M}\right]=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{B}}^{t}\mathrm{B}\text{d}\Omega ; - of Coriolis \left[\mathrm{G}\right]=2\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{B}}^{t}\Omega \mathrm{B}\text{d}\Omega ; - of centrifugal acceleration \left[\mathrm{N}\right]=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{B}}^{t}{\Omega}^{2}\mathrm{B}\text{d}\Omega . The first term of the potential energy brings out the stiffness matrix \left[\mathrm{K}\right]=\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\nabla \mathrm{B}}^{t}\Lambda \nabla \mathrm{B}\text{d}\Omega . 3.3 Calculation of the equilibrium equations of the rotating system Leaving aside a possible classical dissipation function, characterised by the damping matrix, Lagrange's equations for the kinetic and potential energies of the solid are written as follows: \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\text{dt}}(\frac{\partial \mathrm{T}}{\partial \dot{\mathrm{q}}})-\frac{\partial \mathrm{T}}{\partial \mathrm{q}}+\frac{\partial \mathrm{U}}{\partial \mathrm{q}}=0 Inserting the expressions of the energies into Lagrange's equations, one finds: \begin{array}{c}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\text{dt}}\left[\left[\mathrm{M}\right]\dot{\mathrm{q}}+\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathrm{G}\right]\mathrm{q}+\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathrm{G}\right]\dot{\mathrm{q}}+\left[\mathrm{N}\right]\mathrm{q}+\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{B}}^{t}\Omega \mathrm{x}\text{d}\Omega +\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{B}}^{t}{\Omega}^{2}\mathrm{x}\text{d}\Omega +\left[\mathrm{K}\right]\mathrm{q}-\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\mathrm{B}}^{t}\mathrm{f}\text{d}\Omega \right]\\ -\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\text{dt}}\left[\underset{\partial {\Omega}_{\sigma}}{\int}{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{t}}\mathrm{t}\text{d}(\partial \Omega )\right]=0\end{array} Expanding the time derivative and taking into account the derivative of the transformation matrix in Lagrange's equations, one obtains, after simplification and rearrangement of the terms, the following matrix form: \left[\mathrm{M}\right]\langle \ddot{\mathrm{q}}\rangle +\left[\mathrm{G}\right]\langle \dot{\mathrm{q}}\rangle +(\left[\mathrm{K}\right]+\left[\mathrm{P}\right]+\left[\mathrm{N}\right])\langle \mathrm{q}\rangle =\langle \mathrm{r}\rangle \left[\mathrm{P}\right] is the angular-acceleration matrix, defined by \left[\mathrm{P}\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\dot{\mathrm{G}}\right]=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{B}}^{t}\dot{\Omega}\mathrm{B}\text{d}\Omega , with: \dot{\Omega}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0& -{\dot{\omega}}_{z}& {\dot{\omega}}_{y}\\ {\dot{\omega}}_{z}& 0& -{\dot{\omega}}_{x}\\ -{\dot{\omega}}_{y}& {\dot{\omega}}_{x}& 0\end{array}\right] \langle \mathrm{r}\rangle is the vector gathering the terms of the right-hand side. It groups the external excitations \underset{\Omega}{\int}{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{t}}\mathrm{f}\text{d}\Omega +\underset{\partial {\Omega}_{\sigma}}{\int}{\mathrm{B}}^{t}\mathrm{t}\text{d}(\partial \Omega ) and the centrifugal prestress -\underset{\Omega}{\int}\rho {\mathrm{B}}^{t}(\dot{\Omega}\mathrm{x}+{\Omega}^{2}\mathrm{x})\text{d}\Omega ). 4 Description of the versions | Aster version | Author(s) Organisation(s) | Description of the modifications | | --- | --- | --- | | 9.4 | E.
