r5.05.08 Modelling of cracked rotors by an equivalent stiffness as a function of the rotation angle r5.05.08 Modelling of cracked rotors by an equivalent stiffness as a function of the rotation angle Summary: This document describes a method for taking cracks into account in rotors modelled in 1D. It is based on theoretical developments described in notes [1] and [2] and published in [3], establishing, under certain hypotheses, the equivalence between a non-linear 3D model with a contact computation and a beam model in which the non-linearity due to the crack is simulated by an equivalent stiffness concentrated between two beam elements and a tabulated non-linear function of the angle of the bending moment with respect to the crack. This method, used in the shaft-line computation code CADYRO, has been extended and validated against experiment on the EUROPE test rig [4]. It is taken up in the operator DYNA_VIBRA of Code_Aster . 1 Introduction and objective For reasons of performance and of practical implementation, shaft lines in dynamics are not modelled by 3D finite elements but by beam elements, which naturally represent the slenderness of the rotors and which, in linear elasticity, approximate the real behaviour of the system at a low cost. However, one wishes to take into account, in the analysis of the dynamics of shaft lines, the impact of a crack on the rotor. If the 3D analysis, with a fine modelling of the behaviour of the crack by a contact algorithm, is conceptually conceivable, it is extremely demanding in computing resources. This is why one models the behaviour of the crack on the usual beam model of the shaft line by creating two nodes on the axis of the cracked rotor at the location of the crack and by introducing a non-linear “crack constitutive law” linking the mean rotations of the two nodes representing the lips of the crack to the bending moments applied to the beam. The crack constitutive law is tabulated from 3D analyses. One shows that it is not necessary to sweep the whole field of the pairs (\mathit{My},\mathit{Mz}) but that one analysis for each angle of the bending moment with respect to the crack is sufficient. 2 Hypotheses The hypotheses used to build the 1D crack model are: - the rotor has an isotropic elastic behaviour; - the crack may be of arbitrary shape but it is contained in a beam cross-section; - the lips of the crack are linked by a contact condition without friction; - the normal and shear forces are neglected (under certain hypotheses one can take the torsional forces into account, but within the framework of this element they are omitted); - the initial gap of the crack is zero; - the behaviour of the crack is quasi-static and the inertia effects are negligible. 3 Frames and notations By default the local frame of the beams in Code_Aster is the axis X . This convention is retained. The cracked-rotor element is characterised by: - its length \mathrm{2L} ; - its radius R ; - the position of the cracked section (at the middle of the rotor) One considers the following mechanical characteristics: - Young's modulus: E - Inertia of the uncracked beam: I One follows the classical description of beam kinematics. The cross-sections of the beam perpendicular to it remain straight and their rotation is described by: \theta =\left(\begin{array}{c}{\theta}_{y}(x)\\ {\theta}_{z}(x)\end{array}\right) The beam is subjected to a bending moment: M=(\begin{array}{c}{M}_{y}\\ {M}_{z}\end{array}) , which may open or close the crack. The strain energy of the cracked part of the rotor under the imposed bending loading is denoted {W}^{f}(M) . The strain energy contributed by the discrete element modelling the crack for a rotation discontinuity [\theta ] is denoted {W}^{d}([\theta ]) . The description of the cracked section, although averaged in the beam modelling, nevertheless requires a certain amount of attention, because the orientation of the response at the crack is not systematically the same as that of the force. It depends on the shape of the crack. Two angles are therefore defined in the frame of the cracked section: - \Phi , the orientation of the imposed force in the rotating frame; - \varphi , the orientation of the response in the rotating frame. Finally, one denotes by s(M) the local flexibility of the equivalent 1D element representing the crack and by k([\theta ]) its local stiffness. 4 Determination of the equivalent stiffness of the crack 4.1 Equivalent crack model One seeks in this chapter to determine the constitutive law M=f([\theta ]) relating, for the 1D crack element, the bending forces M to the strains expressed by the rotation jump [\theta ]=\left(\begin{array}{c}[{\theta}_{y}(x)]\\ [{\theta}_{z}(x)]\end{array}\right) of the lips of the crack represented by the two boundary nodes of the crack. 4.2 Strain energy 4.2.1 Formula for the strain energy at imposed force In [1] one establishes that the energy of the 3D model in quasi-statics is given by a “Clapeyron” formula: {W}^{f}({M}_{y},{M}_{z})=\frac{1}{2}\left({M}_{y}{\theta}_{y}(\mathrm{2L})+{M}_{z}{\theta}_{z}(\mathrm{2L})\right) On the 3D finite-element model, one can, thanks to this formula, compute the energy of the system for all the possible pairs ({M}_{y},{M}_{z}) and determine the equivalent stiffness k({M}_{y},{M}_{z}) for the cracked 1D beam element. However, exploring a space equivalent to {ℝ}^{2} would be too costly for a practical application. The properties of the energy functional of the elastic problem with contact make it possible to reduce the problem to a single variable. One shows that {W}^{f} is convex and positively homogeneous of degree 2 with respect to the applied moments: \forall \lambda \ge 0,{W}^{f}(\lambda {M}_{y},\lambda {M}_{z})={\lambda}^{2}{W}^{f}({M}_{y},{M}_{z}) This property is interesting because it means, in practice, that the contact zone on the lips of the crack is independent of the amplitude M of the bending. The energy is quadratic in M , as in the linear case. Its form depends only on the direction of ({M}_{y},{M}_{z}) . One can therefore rewrite the energy function with, as variables, the amplitude of the bending force \mid \mid M\mid \mid and its angle \phi . In the cylindrical frame the moment is written: \begin{array}{c}{M}_{y}=\mid \mid M\mid \mid \cos\varphi \\ {M}_{z}=\mid \mid M\mid \mid \sin\varphi \end{array} and the strain energy: {W}_{f}(M)=\frac{1}{2}{\mid \mid M\mid \mid }^{2}S(\varphi ) The problem reduces to the identification of S(\phi ) on the interval [0,2\pi ] . The energy is rewritten in a form which distinguishes the flexibility S(\varphi ) , contributed by the beams (sound and cracked parts), and the flexibility s(\phi ) , contributed by the crack: {W}^{f}(M)=\frac{L}{\mathit{EI}}{\mid \mid M\mid \mid }^{2}(1+s(\varphi )) By computing the strain energy on a 3D finite-element model of the cracked bar (figure ), one can determine s(\varphi ) . Illustration 1: 3D mesh of the cracked bar 4.2.2 Energy at imposed displacement It remains now to establish the relation between the energy and [\theta ] . One uses for this the energy at imposed displacement {w}^{d} . It possesses the same properties of convexity and of homogeneity of degree 2 as the energy at imposed force. Setting: \begin{array}{c}[{\theta}_{x}]=\mid \mid [\theta ]\mid \mid \cos(\phi )\\ [{\theta}_{y}]=\mid \mid [\theta ]\mid \mid \sin(\phi )\end{array} one obtains the following expression for the strain energy: {w}^{d}([\theta ])=\frac{\mathit{EI}}{\mathrm{4L}}{\mid \mid [\theta ]\mid \mid }^{2}k(\phi ) 4.2.3 Constitutive law of the cracked element One obtains M as a function of [\theta ] by differentiation of the energy: \begin{array}{c}{M}_{y}=\frac{\mathit{EI}}{\mathrm{4L}}\frac{\partial (k(\varphi )({[{\theta}_{y}]}^{2}+{[{\theta}_{z}]}^{2}))}{\partial {[\theta ]}_{y}}\\ {M}_{z}=\frac{\mathit{EI}}{\mathrm{4L}}\frac{\partial (k(\varphi )({[{\theta}_{y}]}^{2}+{[{\theta}_{z}]}^{2}))}{\partial {[\theta ]}_{z}}\end{array} with [\theta ]=\sqrt{{[{\theta}_{y}]}^{2}+{[{\theta}_{z}]}^{2}}(\begin{array}{c}\cos(\varphi )\\ \sin(\varphi )\end{array}) A few intermediate computations lead to the following relations: \left(\begin{array}{c}{M}_{y}\\ {M}_{z}\end{array}\right)=\frac{\mathit{EI}}{\mathrm{2L}}\left(\begin{array}{c}k(\phi )-\frac{1}{2}k'(\phi )\\ \frac{1}{2}k'(\phi )k(\phi )\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{c}[{\theta}_{y}(x)]\\ [{\theta}_{z}(x)]\end{array}\right) where \varphi =\arctan(\frac{[{\theta}_{z}(x)]}{[{\theta}_{y}(x)]}) 4.2.4 Relation between the stiffness of the crack and its opening angle The direction \phi of the mean opening angle of the crack [\theta ] is not a priori the same as \phi , that of the forces of the moments M . It is therefore now a matter of establishing a direct relation between the stiffness (or its inverse, the flexibility) and the opening of the crack. It is established in [1] and [2]. By exploiting the principle of complementary energy and thanks to the convexity of the strain energy, one shows that: {w}^{d}([\theta ])=\underset{M}{\mathit{Sup}}(\mathit{M.}[\theta ]-\frac{L}{\mathit{EI}}{\mid \mid M\mid \mid }^{2}s(\phi )) The function s(\phi ) was established in the previous paragraphs. A complementary mathematical treatment consists in applying to s(\phi ) a quadratic interpolation outside the nullity interval of s(\phi ) and a power interpolation at the bounds of the nullity of s(\phi ) . Furthermore, in the same way as the energy at imposed moment, the energy at imposed strain is convex and homogeneous of order 2. This implies that it does not depend on the norm of [\theta ] , but only on its direction \varphi . One can therefore limit oneself to identifying {w}^{d}([\theta ]) for \mid \mid [\theta ]\mid \mid =1 . The energy is then written: {w}^{d}([\theta ])=\frac{\mathit{EI}}{\mathrm{4L}}k(\varphi ) . If \lambda is the amplitude of the applied moment and \phi its direction, by identification one finds the formula giving the equivalent crack stiffness: k(\varphi )=\frac{\mathrm{4L}}{\mathit{EI}}\underset{M=1}{\mathit{Sup}}\underset{\lambda \ge 0}{\mathit{Sup}}(\lambda \mathit{M.}[\theta ]-\frac{L}{\mathit{EI}}{\lambda}^{2}s(\phi )) In practice this amounts to finding the domain [{\varphi}_{1,}{\varphi}_{2}] which the direction of the crack can have, then to maximising, for all the possible crack angles \varphi , the following expression: k(\varphi )=\underset{\phi \in [\varphi -\frac{\pi}{2,}\varphi +\frac{\pi}{2}]}{\mathit{Sup}}\frac{{\cos}^{2}(\phi -\varphi )}{s(\phi )} The derivative k'(\varphi )=\frac{dk(\varphi )}{d\varphi } is then obtained by means of a differentiation by Finite Differences of k(\varphi ) . 5 Bibliography 1. Stéphane Andrieux, “Determination of the biaxial-bending constitutive law of a cracked beam with account taken of contact on the cracks”; EDF R&D note HP-50/99/018/A (1999) 2. Christophe Varé, “Computation of a cracked-rotor model for the CADYRO code”; EDF R&D note HP-54/99/047/B 3. Stéphane Andrieux, Christophe Varé «A 3D cracked beam model with unilateral contact. Application to rotors »; European Journal of Mechanics A/Solids 21 (2002) 793–810 4. Carlo Maria Stoisser, Sylvie Audebert « A comprehensive theoretical, numerical and experimental approach for crack detection in power plant rotating machinery »; Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing 22 (2008) 818–844 6 History of the versions of the document | Version Aster | Author(s) or contributor(s), organisation | Description of the modifications | | --- | --- | --- | | 11.1 | TORKHANI | Initial version. |

r5.05.09 Computation of reconstructed signals and of the transfer-function matrix r5.05.09 Computation of reconstructed signals and of the transfer-function matrix Summary: This document presents the theoretical bases which made it possible to set up the macro-command CALC_TRANSFERT U4.53.51. The latter makes it possible to compute the transfer-function matrix between two points, but also to reconstruct the signals at a given point, knowing the signals at another point. > Contents 1 Introduction During linear dynamic studies, the user may be led to reconstruct an excitation signal knowing the signals measured at another point of the structure. The purpose of the present document is to present the theoretical elements which led to the creation of the macro-command CALC_TRANSFERT U4.53.51. In particular the equations which make it possible to determine the transfer-function matrix and those which make it possible to determine the reconstructed signals. 2 Theory In this chapter, one places oneself in a seismic example in order to present the problem, where one reasons in an absolute frame. 2.1 General principle During an earthquake, the recorded signals are generally measured on a structure. Thus, when one wishes to study the dynamic behaviour of this structure, the input signal is an unknown of the numerical model which must be determined (see figure 1). Figure 1 – Schematic representation of the problem In order to reconstruct the input signal knowing the output signal (a signal which is generally measured), one places oneself in the frequency domain and one seeks the transfer function \underline{\underline{H}}(\omega ) between the two points of our system (see figure 2). The input point corresponds to point E and the output point to point S in figure 1. Figure 2 - Diagram of the transfer function From several unidirectional dynamic analyses {\gamma}_{i},\mathit{avec}i=x,y,z , it is possible to obtain the transfer function by looking at the output \underline{S}(\omega ) and the input \underline{E}(\omega ) . Notes: Determination The input and output signals must be of the same nature (ACCE / ACCE or VITE / VITE or DEPL / DEPL. It is recommended to use white-noise type signals in order to excite the structure uniformly over the whole frequency range. Once the transfer-function matrix is known, and knowing the desired output signal, it is possible to reconstruct the input signal to be injected into the dynamic model in order to recover the output signal by solving the following matrix system: \underline{{E}^{\mathit{absolu}}}(\omega )=\underline{\underline{{H}^{-1}}}(\omega )\underline{{S}^{\mathit{absolu}}}(\omega ) Where: | \underline{{S}^{\mathit{absolu}}}(\omega ) | Vector containing the absolute accelerations measured at the output point S of the structure during the earthquake | | --- | --- | | \underline{{E}^{\mathit{absolu}}}(\omega ) | Vector containing the absolute accelerations to be applied at the input point E in order to recover the absolute accelerations measured at the output point S | | \underline{\underline{{H}^{-1}}}(\omega ) | Inverse transfer-function matrix | 2.2 Determination of the transfer-function matrix \underline{\underline{H}}(\omega ) In this paragraph, one proposes to present the equations which make it possible to determine the transfer-function matrix \underline{\underline{H}}(\omega ) in the three-dimensional case. In order to facilitate the data setup of the problem, one treats the problem in terms of acceleration (the latter can also be treated in terms of displacement or of velocity). Let {E}_{i}^{\mathit{absolu}} and {S}_{i}^{\mathit{absolu}} be the absolute accelerations computed respectively at the input and output points. One seeks to solve the following system: \underline{{S}^{\mathit{absolu}}}(\omega )=\underline{\underline{H}}(\omega )\underline{{E}^{\mathit{absolu}}}(\omega ) Where \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{S}_{i}^{\mathit{absolu}}={S}_{i}^{\mathit{relatif}}+{\gamma}_{i},i=x,y,z\\ {E}_{i}^{\mathit{absolu}}={E}_{i}^{\mathit{relatif}}+{\gamma}_{i},i=x,y,z\end{array} and \underline{\underline{H}}(\omega )=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}{H}_{xx}& {H}_{xy}& {H}_{xz}\\ {H}_{yx}& {H}_{yy}& {H}_{yz}\\ {H}_{\mathit{zx}}& {H}_{\mathit{zy}}& {H}_{zz}\end{array}\right) In order to determine the 9 unknowns of the problem, a system of 9 equations in 9 unknowns must be solved. This system is determined by carrying out three analyses with a unidirectional loading along the directions x, y or z so as not to neglect the possible coupling between directions. Harmonic analysis along X Let X\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{i}^{a},i=x,y,z be the absolute acceleration computed at the output point and X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{i}^{a},i=x,y,z the absolute acceleration computed at the input point for a unidirectional excitation {\gamma}_{x} . The system (E1) to be solved is the following: (\mathit{E1})\text{}\lbrace \begin{array}{c}X\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{x}^{a}={H}_{xx}X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{x}^{a}+{H}_{xy}X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{y}^{a}+{H}_{xz}X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{z}^{a}\\ X\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{y}^{a}={H}_{yx}X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{x}^{a}+{H}_{yy}X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{y}^{a}+{H}_{yz}X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{z}^{a}\\ X\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{z}^{a}={H}_{\mathit{zx}}X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{x}^{a}+{H}_{\mathit{zy}}X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{y}^{a}+{H}_{\mathit{zxz}}X\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{z}^{a}\end{array} Harmonic analysis along Y Let Y\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{i}^{a},i=x,y,z be the absolute acceleration computed at the output point and Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{i}^{a},i=x,y,z the absolute acceleration computed at the input point for a unidirectional excitation {\gamma}_{y} . The system (E2) to be solved is the following: (\mathit{E2})\text{}\lbrace \begin{array}{c}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{x}^{a}={H}_{xx}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{x}^{a}+{H}_{xy}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{y}^{a}+{H}_{xz}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{z}^{a}\\ Y\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{y}^{a}={H}_{yx}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{x}^{a}+{H}_{yy}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{y}^{a}+{H}_{yz}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{z}^{a}\\ Y\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{z}^{a}={H}_{\mathit{zx}}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{x}^{a}+{H}_{\mathit{zy}}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{y}^{a}+{H}_{\mathit{zxz}}Y\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{z}^{a}\end{array} Harmonic analysis along Z Let Z\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{i}^{a},i=x,y,z be the absolute acceleration computed at the output point and Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{i}^{a},i=x,y,z the absolute acceleration computed at the input point for a unidirectional excitation {\gamma}_{z} . The system (E3) to be solved is the following: (\mathit{E3})\text{}\lbrace \begin{array}{c}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{x}^{a}={H}_{xx}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{x}^{a}+{H}_{xy}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{y}^{a}+{H}_{xz}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{z}^{a}\\ Z\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{y}^{a}={H}_{yx}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{x}^{a}+{H}_{yy}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{y}^{a}+{H}_{yz}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{z}^{a}\\ Z\text{\_}{\mathit{sortie}}_{z}^{a}={H}_{\mathit{zx}}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{x}^{a}+{H}_{\mathit{zy}}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{y}^{a}+{H}_{\mathit{zxz}}Z\text{\_}{\mathit{entree}}_{z}^{a}\end{array} By grouping the systems (E1), (E2) and (E3) in the form of a global system (E), one obtains a system of 9 equations in 9 unknowns. r5.05.10 Dynamic analysis of structures with viscoelastic materials having frequency dependent properties r5.05.10 Dynamic analysis of structures with viscoelastic materials having frequency dependent properties Overview: This reference document tackles the way how advanced capabilities are introduced in Code_Aster to take into account frequency dependent properties of viscoelastic materials. Computing of harmonic response and modes of vibration (real or complex) is addressed. Having frequency dependent modes is a step forward for the modal projection method and for model updating with an experimental modal basis as a reference. An iterative method is used in order to compute frequency dependent modes. 1 Introduction ViscoElastic Materials (VEM) are intensively used to solve NVH issues. Damping pads and anti flutter products reduce the structure borne noise. Sealants and absorbing materials prevent the air borne transmission. Adhesives are common solutions to assemble parts. Whereas VEM are well known, the finite element analysis of their dynamic behavior is not straightforward. Most of the time, the use of a finite element software requires to simplify VEM as elastic materials. This simplification is not always the obvious thing to do and may lead to inaccurate results. This reference document addresses the finite element analysis of structures comprising VEM with frequency dependent dynamic properties. Conventional approaches are discussed and a method is proposed to overcome their limitations. The method computes frequency dependent modes using an iterative algorithm. The way how these modes can be used to improve the modal projection method is described. Implementation in Code_Aster is explained. 2 Finite element analysis 2.1 State-of-the-art From a simulation point of view, the frequency response of a structure comprising at least one VEM is obtained by solving the dynamic equilibrium equation: \left([{K}^{\text{ }}(\omega )]-{\omega}^{2}[M]\right)\left\lbrace u(\omega )\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace F(\omega )\right\rbrace , (2.1-1) with [{K}^{\text{ }}(\omega )] , the complex stiffness matrix as: [{K}^{\text{ }}(\omega )]=[{K}^{'}(\omega )]+i[{K}^{''}(\omega )] . (2.1-2) The frequency dependence of the matrix comes from the use of frequency dependent complex moduli to represent viscoelastic behaviors [1] . In many finite element codes, solving the system of Eq. () is not conventional because it needs to realize the stiffness matrix for each frequency step and to have computing procedures which are able to deal with frequency dependent matrices. The direct response approach consists in solving Eq. () for each frequency step as: \left\lbrace u(\omega )\right\rbrace ={\left([{K}^{\text{ }}(\omega )]-{\omega}^{2}[M]\right)}^{-1}\left\lbrace F(\omega )\right\rbrace \forall \omega \in [0,{\omega}_{max}] . (2.1-3) This method has the advantage of computing the exact response of the system. But, as it is necessary to compute and inverse a complex matrix at each frequency step, the computing time can become prohibitive for industrial structures with several million degrees of freedom. A few studies [2] [4] have shown the interest to solve Eq. () with dedicated modal response methods in order to improve the computational efficiency while maintaining the accuracy of the results. Modal response methods compute frequency responses by projecting the system of Eq. () on a modal basis [T] , with the assumption: \left\lbrace u(\omega )\right\rbrace =[T]\left\lbrace q(\omega )\right\rbrace . (2.1-4) The projection of the model on the considered basis leads to a low order model, that decreases significantly the number of degrees of freedom and consequently the computing time of frequency responses: \left\lbrace q(\omega )\right\rbrace ={\left({[T]}^{T}[{K}^{\text{ }}(\omega )][T]-{\omega}^{2}{[T]}^{T}[M][T]\right)}^{-1}{[T]}^{T}\left\lbrace F(\omega )\right\rbrace . (2.1-5) Using properties of elastic models (real and frequency independent stiffness matrix), the standard basis of the popular spectral decomposition method combines normal modes solving of the classical eigenvalue problem: \left([K]-{\omega}_{r}^{2}[M]\right)\left\lbrace {\Phi}_{r}\right\rbrace =\lbrace 0\rbrace (2.1-6) and a static correction to ensure a correct representation of the low frequency contribution of truncated high frequency normal modes [5] . Classically, [T] is composed by the normal modes between 0 and a minimum of 1.5\times {\omega}_{max} . However, frequency dependence of the VEM dynamic properties prevents from using the spectral decomposition method, because the modal basis [\left\lbrace {\Phi}_{r=1,N}\right\rbrace ] is only valid at the frequency {\omega}_{\mathit{ref}} , for which it has been computed. In practice, it has been demonstrated [3] the validity domain of the basis can be extended in a range around the frequency {\omega}_{\mathit{ref}} . If the VEM of the model give increasing moduli with respect to the frequency, the use of {\omega}_{\mathit{ref}}={\omega}_{max} will lead to a larger validity domain than for any other frequencies. Unfortunately, the validity domain of the basis may not extend over all the frequency range of interest. Inaccurate results may be obtained. To tackle this difficulty, static correction associated to the VEM can also be taken into account. This technique, presented in U2.06.04, leads to very accurate results, but its implementation for an industrial case is tricky. 2.2 Computation of frequency dependent mode For a frequency dependent real stiffness matrix, [K(\omega )] , the eigenvalue problem of Eq. () is written as: \left([K(\omega )]-{\left({\omega}_{r}(\omega )\right)}^{2}[M]\right)\left\lbrace {\Phi}_{r}(\omega )\right\rbrace =\lbrace 0\rbrace , (2.2-1) where the eigenfrequency, {\omega}_{r}(\omega ) , and the eigenvector, \left\lbrace {\Phi}_{r}(\omega )\right\rbrace , are frequency dependent too. For a fixed, given frequency, \omega ={\omega}_{p} , such eigensolutions can be obtained by solving the standard problem of Eq. (). Hence, the proposed method for solving the frequency dependent problem of Eq. () consists in using an iterative algorithm searching for: ∣{\omega}_{r}({\omega}_{p})-{\omega}_{p}∣ {\omega}_{2} . It means all the frequency dependent eigensolutions have been computed between {\omega}_{1} and {\omega}_{2} . The computing time of the proposed method is classically driven by the number of frequency dependent modes to be computed, the number of degrees of freedom of the model and the value of the convergence criterion ϵ . It is also dependent on the number of normal eigenvalues which are computed as solutions of Eq. () at each iteration. Having all the eigenvalues between {\omega}_{1} and {\omega}_{2} for each iteration is not necessary and could lead to prohibitive computing times. In theory, a minimum of two eigenvalues may be sufficient to run iterations: {\omega}_{n} to update {\omega}_{p} as described in Eq. () and {\omega}_{n+1} to continue when the procedure converges. In practice, this minimum number of eigenvalues will be determined by the capabilities of the numerical solver for Eq. (). It will be discussed for Code_Aster in section 3 . The proposed method can be naturally extended to the study of damped structures comprising VEM. The frequency dependent eigenvalues and eigenvectors are then computed as solutions of the following problem: \left([{K}^{\text{ }}({\lambda}_{r})]+{\lambda}_{r}^{2}[M]\right)\left\lbrace {\Psi}_{r}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace 0\right\rbrace , (2.2-5) with {\lambda}_{r=1,N} the complex eigenvalues, and \left\lbrace {\Psi}_{r=1,N}\right\rbrace the associated complex modes. In this case, Eq. () is rewritten as: ∣\tilde{\omega}{}_{r}({\omega}_{p})-{\omega}_{p}∣<ϵ.{\omega}_{p}\forall {\omega}_{p}\in [{\omega}_{1,}{\omega}_{2}] , (2.2-6) with \tilde{\omega}{}_{r}=∣{\lambda}_{r}∣ , the corresponding eigenfrequency in a structural damping model [6] . {\omega}_{p} will be updated by taking the value of the {n}^{\mathit{th}} eigenfrequency for which: \mid \tilde{\omega}{}_{n}-{\omega}_{p}\mid =min\mid \tilde{\omega}{}_{r=1,N}-{\omega}_{p}\mid . (2.2-7) Computing frequency dependent real or complex modes should be a step forward for comparison with experimental modal bases. Indeed, when structures comprising VEM are tested, their frequency dependent behaviors are physically measured. The proposed method could help to validate or to update finite element models with experimental references. 2.3 Improvement of the modal projection method The frequency dependent modes can be used to form the basis of the modal projection method for response computations of VEM. They will extend the validity domain of the basis over all the frequency range of interest. In combination to a static correction, either real modes will be used for weakly damped structures, or complex modes for highly damped structures [3] . The static correction will be determined with the stiffness matrix realized for \omega =0 . Real modes will be preferred to reduce computing times, since numerical solvers are much more efficient in this case. But for highly damped structures, the projection base composed with such modes may be insufficient to obtain accurate frequency responses. This can be improved using the modified Modal Strain Energy (MSE) method to reduce the errors [7] . So, frequency dependent real modes, \left\lbrace \widehat{\Phi}{}_{r}(\omega )\right\rbrace , become solutions of a modified form of Eq. () in order to take into account the damping matrix (imaginary part of the stiffness matrix) as: \left([{K}^{'}(\omega )]+\beta (\omega )[{K}^{''}(\omega )]-{\left(\widehat{\omega}{}_{r}(\omega )\right)}^{2}[M]\right)\left\lbrace \widehat{\Phi}{}_{r}(\omega )\right\rbrace =\lbrace 0\rbrace . (2.3-1) [{K}^{'}(\omega )] and [{K}^{''}(\omega )] are defined by Eq. () and \beta (\omega ) is calculated by the following empirical formula: \beta (\omega )=\frac{\mathit{trace}[{K}^{''}(\omega )]}{\mathit{trace}[{K}^{'}(\omega )]} , (2.3-2) where the trace for an N\times N matrix is defined as: \mathit{trace}[A]=\sum_{j=1}^{N}{A}_{jj} . (2.3-3) In the iterative algorithm, the use of the modified MSE method leads to calculate \beta ({\omega}_{p}) for each iteration and to search for the solutions of the resulting eigenvalue problem: \left([{K}^{'}({\omega}_{p})]+\beta ({\omega}_{p})[{K}^{''}({\omega}_{p})]-\widehat{\omega}{}_{r}^{2}[M]\right)\left\lbrace \widehat{\Phi}{}_{r}\right\rbrace =\lbrace 0\rbrace . (2.3-4) Another method to improve the real modes could be the use of residual modes whose purpose is to represent the damping of VEM in the modal projection basis [8] . The coupling with frequency dependent modes has been presented in U2.06.04. 3 Implementation in Code_Aster The approach to frequency dependent modes described above has been implemented in Code_Aster via a macro command, namely DYNA_VISCO. This script uses standard commands existing in Code_Aster for the conventional modal method. Python codes have been added for the new developments: - definition of a frequency dependent behavior, - computation of frequency dependent modes by the iterative algorithm, - frequency response computation with realization of the stiffness matrix at each frequency step. In the iterations, modes are computed as solutions of Eq. () via the standard CALC_MODES command. The modal extraction method are described in [9] . Five eigensolutions are searched around {\omega}_{p} for each iteration. This number is a good compromise between securing the convergence of the iterative algorithm and limiting the total computing time. In the case where the algorithm would not converge, the number of the searched eigensolutions will be automatically increased by the program. The user can define several VEM with different behaviors and choose the frequency dependent modes to be used: real modes or beta-modes. At this time of the implementation, it is also possible to compute frequency dependent complex modes, but they cannot be used as a modal basis for response computation. 4 References 1. Nashif, D. I. G. Jones, J. P. Henderson, Vibration Damping , John Wiley and Sons (1985). A-S. Plouin, E. Balmès, “Steel/Viscoelastic/Steel Sandwich Shells, Computational Methods and ExperimentalValidations”, IMAC (2000). 1. Merlette, S. Germès, F. van Herpe, L. Jézéquel, D. Aubry, “The use of suitable modal bases for dynamic predictions of structures containing high damping materials”, ISMA , Leuven (2004). 1. Abbadi, N. Merlette, N. Roy, “Response Computation of Structures with Viscoelastic Damping Materials using a Modal Approach - Description of the Method and Application on a Car Door Model Treated with High Damping Foam”, 5thSymposium on Automobile Comfort , Le Mans (2008). 1. Géradin, D. Rixen, Théorie des Vibrations, Applications à la Dynamique des Structures , Editions Masson (1996). D.J. Ewins, Modal Testing: Theory and Practice , Research Studies Press LTD. (1986). B-G. Hu, M. A. Dokainish, W. M. Mansour, “A Modified MSE Method for Viscoelastic Systems: A Weighted Stiffness Matrix Approach”, ASME Journal of Vibration and Acoustics 117, 226-231 (1995). 1. Bobillot, E. Balmès, “Iterative Techniques for Eigenvalue Solutions of Damped Structures Coupled with Fluids”, 43rd AIAA/ASME/ASCI/AHS/ASC Structures, Structural Dynamics and Materials Conference , Denver (2002). 1. D’Haene, J. Lu, “Influence of PVB mechanical properties on the vibrational damping of a windscreen”, ISMA , Leuven (2002).

r5.06.01 Model reduction in linear and non-linear dynamics: RITZ method r5.06.01 Model reduction in linear and non-linear dynamics: RITZ method Summary: This document presents the principle of model reduction by projection onto a reduced basis (Ritz method). The basis most commonly used is the modal basis. The truncation problems due to the use of a reduced basis are mentioned. Truncation corrections are proposed. The description and the properties of the algorithms for solving the system of second-order differential equations obtained in transient analysis are presented in the document R5.06.04. 1 Introduction Starting from a description of the geometry and of the materials of the structures, the finite-element method makes it possible to create an accurate and reliable model, but of large dimensions. In the case of a dynamics problem, one wishes to compute the response of a system for different time instants (transient analysis) or for different frequencies (harmonic analysis). The size of the finite-element model obtained is often irreconcilable with the number of analyses required in order to obtain all the desired results. For a restricted set of dynamic loadings, there generally exists a subspace of small dimension making it possible to describe the dynamic behaviour of the structure under specific loadings. The projection of the model onto a restricted basis is called the Ritz method or the Rayleigh-Ritz method. This document contains the following points: - a presentation of the Ritz methods, their use in the linear case, - a detail of the possible truncation corrections, - the generalisation to the non-linear case of the Ritz methods, - two simple illustrative examples. 2 Linear Ritz reduction methods 2.1 General description 2.1.1 Continuous formulation The Ritz method consists in projecting the displacement onto a restricted basis of functions satisfying the kinematic conditions of the problem: \tilde{u}(M,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\eta}_{i}(t){\psi}_{i}(M) eq 2.1.1-1 The displacement is described by a series of independent shapes \left\lbrace {\psi}_{i}(M);i=1\dots n\right\rbrace multiplied by amplitudes that are functions of time \left\lbrace {\eta}_{i}(t);i=1\dots n\right\rbrace . The difficulty consists in defining this family of shapes \left\lbrace {\psi}_{i}(M);i=1\dots n\right\rbrace which, unlike the shape functions of the finite-element method, are non-zero over the greater part of the structure. The quality of the approximation is linked to the fact that the displacements obtained have a good approximation in the subspace generated by \text{Vect}\left\lbrace {\psi}_{i}(M),i=1\dots n\right\rbrace . Projection onto a modal basis It is known that the eigenmodes \left\lbrace {\varphi}_{i}(M);i=1\dots \infty \right\rbrace generate the space of the kinematically admissible fields. The displacement is decomposed as: u(M,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}{\eta}_{i}(t){\varphi}_{i}(M) eq 2.1.1-2 The option most commonly used for the Ritz method then consists in taking as projection basis the first n modes: \tilde{u}(M,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\tilde{\eta}}_{i}(t){\varphi}_{i}(M) eq 2.1.1-3 The displacement obtained is an approximation of the real displacement. It may be of interest to add to the first n modes other shapes (see [§2.6.2]). 2.1.2 Finite-element approximation In the case of an approximation of the displacement by finite elements, the displacement is already approximated in the space of the shape functions: {u}^{h}(M,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{\text{Nh}}{q}_{i}(t){N}_{i}(M) eq 2.1.2-1 U denotes the vector of the degrees of freedom of the displacement: U(t)=\left[{q}_{1}(t),{q}_{2}(t),\dots {q}_{\text{Nh}}(t)\right] ; Ritz method in finite dimension If n >}{\omega}_{\max} nevertheless have a static contribution to the response of the system. It is often these modes that are not taken into account. By making a limited expansion in \omega in the neighbourhood of 0 . One obtains the principal part of the error, which is: {\hat{E}}_{(\omega )}=\hat{U}-\hat{\tilde{U}}=\sum_{i=p+1}^{n}\frac{{\Phi}_{i}^{T}.{\hat{F}}_{(\omega )}}{{k}_{i}}.(1-2j{\xi}_{i}\frac{\omega}{{\omega}_{i}}+0(\frac{\omega}{{\omega}_{i}})).{\Phi}_{i} eq 2.4-3 The error is all the smaller as the generalised stiffnesses of the neglected modes are large. In principle, therefore, all the most flexible modes will have to be taken until the residual flexibility of an additional mode is negligible in relative value with respect to the sum of the flexibilities already taken into account: \frac{1}{{k}_{n+1}}\text{ >}{\omega}_{\max} have a so-called static contribution to the response of the system in the domain \left[0,{\omega}_{\max}\right] . The correction techniques consist in computing this static contribution. 2.5.1 A posteriori static correction The truncation error, considering only the static response of the neglected modes (inverse transform of the principal part of the error), is: {E}_{(t)}=U-\tilde{U}\approx \sum_{i=n+1}^{\text{Nh}}\frac{{\Phi}_{i}^{T}.{F}_{(t)}}{{k}_{i}}.{\Phi}_{i} eq 2.5.1-1 But a priori the neglected modes as well as their generalised stiffnesses are unknown. On the other hand, one knows how to determine the complete static response of the system to a loading F ; the latter is: U={K}^{-1}.{F}_{(t)}\approx \sum_{i=1}^{\text{Nh}}\frac{{\Phi}_{i}^{T}.{F}_{(t)}}{{k}_{i}}.{\Phi}_{i} The correction that must be applied is therefore: \sum_{i=n+1}^{\text{Nh}}\frac{{\Phi}_{i}^{T}.{F}_{(t)}}{{k}_{i}}.{\Phi}_{i}\approx {K}^{-1}.{F}_{(t)}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{{\Phi}_{i}^{T}.{F}_{(t)}}{{k}_{i}}.{\Phi}_{i} The corrected solution of the response of the system is therefore: U=\tilde{U}+E\approx \tilde{U}+{K}^{-1}.{F}_{(t)}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{{\Phi}_{i}^{T}.{F}_{(t)}}{{k}_{i}}.{\Phi}_{i} eq 2.5.1-2 This correction is called a posteriori, because it does not intervene in the dynamic solution of the linear system and may be computed only much later. If {F}_{(t)} decomposes into k products of functions of time by functions of the space coordinates, this correction requires a factorisation of K and k solutions. This method has the advantage of not increasing the number of vectors taken into account in the basis. This method is applicable in the case of a narrow-band excitation, or at least one having a known cut-off frequency. The correction is exact in the low-frequency domain but may distort the response of the system at high frequency [§Annexe1]. 2.5.2 Addition of static modes to the basis Suppose that the loading F(t) is written: \mathrm{F}(t)=\sum_{j}{\alpha}_{j}(t).{\mathrm{F}}_{j} The second way of correcting the truncation error consists in adding to the basis of the initial eigenmodes static modes {\Psi}_{j} defined as the deformed shape under each given force {F}_{j} : {\Psi}_{j}={K}^{-1}.{F}_{j} eq 2.5.2-1 The new projection basis to be considered is the following: \hat{\Phi}=[{\Phi}_{1},{\Phi}_{2},...,{\Phi}_{p},{\Psi}_{1},{\Psi}_{2},...,{\Psi}_{m}]=[\Phi \Psi ] eq 2.5.2-2 The generalised components to be used are the following: \hat{\eta}=[{\eta}_{1},{\eta}_{2},...,{\eta}_{p},{\mu}_{1},{\mu}_{2},...,{\mu}_{m}]=[\eta ,\mu ] eq 2.5.2-3 The problem projected onto the completed basis is: \left[\begin{array}{cc}(\begin{array}{ccc}\setminus & 0& 0\\ 0& {m}_{i}& 0\\ 0& 0& \setminus \end{array})& {\Phi}^{T}.M.\Psi \\ {\Psi}^{T}.M.\Phi & {\Psi}^{T}.M.\Psi \end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\ddot{\eta}\\ \ddot{\mu}\end{array}\right\rbrace +\left[\begin{array}{cc}(\begin{array}{ccc}\setminus & 0& 0\\ 0& {k}_{i}& 0\\ 0& 0& \setminus \end{array})& {\Phi}^{T}.K.\Psi \\ {\Psi}^{T}.K.\Phi & {\Psi}^{T}.K.\Psi \end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\eta \\ \mu \end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\Phi}^{T}.F.\alpha \\ {\Psi}^{T}.F.\alpha \end{array}\right\rbrace eq 2.5.2-4 It is observed that the diagonal character of the generalised matrices has been lost, but the advantage obtained is that the basis completed with static modes makes it possible to represent correctly the low-frequency behaviour of the initial system. For example it is simple to show that at zero frequency the solution of this system is: \eta =0 and \mu =\alpha which is the exact solution of the initial static problem. Appendix 1 presents the comparison, on a discrete system with 3 degrees of freedom, between the exact solution, the solution projected onto 1 mode, the one projected onto one mode with a static correction, and the solution constituted by 1 eigenmode and 1 static mode. One notices that the addition of static modes makes it possible to extend beyond the interval \left[0,{\omega}_{\max}=\max({\omega}_{j})\right] the good dynamic representation of the system. This technique therefore seems very interesting; it has the merit of carrying out the correction immediately, which will be of interest for the non-linear methods, in which one needs knowledge of the physical displacements at each time step. The practical implementation of this technique is specified in U2.06.04. 3 Extension of the Ritz reduction methods to the non‑linear case 3.1 General problem The discretised non-linear dynamics problem without damping can most often be put in the following form: M.\ddot{X}+G(X)=F(t)\text{}X\in {R}^{n} eq 3.1-1 G(X) is a non-linear function of X which represents the internal forces of the system as well as all the other forces that depend on the displacement, F the vector of the external forces and M the mass matrix of the system. The tangent stiffness matrix of the system is by definition: {K}_{(x)}^{\text{tg}}=\frac{\partial G}{\partial X}(x) eq 3.1-2 It makes it possible to define at each time instant a modal basis by: (-{\omega}_{i(X)}^{{\text{tg}}^{2}}M+{K}^{\text{tg}}).{\Phi}_{i(X)}^{\text{tg}}=0 eq 3.1-3 The modes thus defined depend on X , hence on the time instant t . Knowing that the computation of the modal basis is very costly in computation time, the idea of wanting to project the model onto a modal basis at each time step, and then to solve, is of no interest compared with a direct solution. The method most commonly used consists in defining a projection basis by adding to the modes computed on an initial configuration shapes making it possible to project the non-linearity. Example: in the case where the non-linearity comes from a pointwise impact, it is proposed to enrich the modal basis with static modes making it possible to project the force undergone by the structure during the impact R5.06.04. The Ritz method always remains relevant in non-linear analyses, if the basis chosen makes it possible to project the displacements and the forces correctly. The non-linear problem projected onto an arbitrary basis \Psi is written: {\Psi}^{T}M\Psi .\ddot{\eta}+{\Psi}^{T}G(X)={\Psi}^{T}F\text{}\eta \in {R}^{n} eq 3.1-4 Two possibilities are then possible: - the non-linearities are localised and the non-linearity can be evaluated on the projection basis: G(X)=G(\Psi \eta ) . - The problem to be solved is a non-linear differential system in \eta of smaller size. Different strategies are possible for solving this problem, depending essentially on the integration technique that one wishes to use. - the non-linearities are global, and one must return to the space of the physical degrees of freedom in order to compute the internal forces: G(X) . This second method is more costly; it is much less common. Appendix 2 presents the comparison, on a system with 3 degrees of freedom with a non-linearity in {x}^{3} , between the exact solution and the solution obtained by the method above with 1 and then 2 modes. One notices that it is necessary to take more modes into account than for the linear problem. On the other hand, on this example 2 modes are quite sufficient to describe the system. 3.2 Indication of the projection error For non-linear problems the physical meaning of the number of modes to be taken into account is completely lost, and if the reduction methods always give a solution one must know the degree of confidence that can be granted to them. One way of proceeding, which is a little costly but indispensable, is to compute the residual of the initial system at each time step. It is defined by: R=M.\ddot{X}+G(X)-F(t) This residual vector is unfortunately not zero; it is only its projection onto the basis used that is. A norm can then be computed for this residual; the smaller the norm of the residual, the more confidence one will be able to grant to the solution. In order to use a relative value, it is of interest to compute the following fraction: r=\frac{\parallel R\parallel }{\max(\parallel F(t)\parallel ,\parallel G(X)\parallel ,\parallel M.\ddot{X}\parallel )} eq 3.2-1 Note: This indicator is not currently implemented in Code_Aster. 4 Use in Code_Aster In Code_Aster, the Ritz methods are usable in transient analysis essentially through the operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03. A phase of projection of the stiffness and mass matrices onto a basis of vectors is carried out by the operators PROJ_MATR_BASE U4.63.12 and PROJ_VECT_BASE U4.63.13. The generalised dynamic problem is then solved in the operator DYNA_VIBRA by an explicit integration scheme (EULER or DEVOGELEARE) or an implicit one (NEWMARK). The characteristics and properties of the integration schemes are presented in the note R5.06.04. For the structures for which the BASILE assumption does not apply (non-proportional damping) the damping matrix, which does not become diagonal, will also be projected. The integration of the coupled system is then necessarily done with the implicit scheme (NEWMARK) or the explicit scheme (EULER). The localised non-linearities are specified directly in the operator DYNA_VIBRA. Localised non-linearities of impact and friction type can be introduced (see R5.06.03 Modelling of impacts and friction), as well as modal forces that are functions of the displacement or of the velocity. The a posteriori static truncation corrections are available in the case of a single excitation (see R4.05.01 Seismic response). The addition of static modes can be done by using beforehand the operators MODE_STATIQUE U4.52.14 and DEFI_BASE_MODALE U4.64.02. When the problem includes non-linearities, only the explicit schemes can be used. For the global non-linearities [eq 3.1-4], it is possible to use the command DYNA_NON_LINE U4.53.01 with the operand PROJ_MODAL, which makes it possible to compute at each time step the internal forces as a function of the physical degrees of freedom, and then to project the problem onto a modal basis. An operation of return to the physical basis is then necessary in order to obtain the physical quantities (grandeur) such as displacement, velocity or acceleration on the structure. This operation is carried out by the operator REST_GENE_PHYS U4.63.31 for the whole of the structure, or RECU_FONCTION, (factor keyword RESU_GENE) U4.32.01 for the monitoring of a quantity (grandeur) at a node. In the case of global non-linearities (analysis with DYNA_NON_LINE) the operator REST_COND_TRAN U4.63.33 is used. More generally, the Ritz approach can be used in harmonic analysis by the command DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 and in power spectral density by the command DYNA_ALEA_MODAL U4.53.23. Finally, dynamic substructuring can be regarded as a specific Ritz method R4.06.02. 5 Bibliography 1. BATHE - WILSON: Finite Element procedures in Engineering Analysis 1. GERADIN, D.
