JACQUART (EDF R&D/AMA, EDF/CNPE de Tricastin) | | Consider the following discrete system with three masses: The stiffness and mass matrices are: M=(\begin{array}{ccc}m& 0& 0\\ 0& m& 0\\ 0& 0& m\end{array})\text{}K=(\begin{array}{ccc}k& -k& 0\\ -k& \mathrm{2k}& -k\\ 0& -k& \mathrm{2k}\end{array}) That is: {\omega}_{0}^{2}=\frac{k}{m} The eigenmodes and their angular frequency are: \begin{array}{c}\begin{array}{}{\omega}_{1}^{2}=0,198{\omega}_{0}^{2},{m}_{1}=1,841\text{}m,{\Phi}_{1}=(\begin{array}{c}1\\ 0,802\\ 0,445\end{array})\\ \end{array}\\ \begin{array}{}{\omega}_{2}^{2}=1,555{\omega}_{0}^{2},{m}_{2}=2,863\text{}m,{\Phi}_{2}=(\begin{array}{c}1\\ -0,555\\ -1,247\end{array})\\ \end{array}\\ {\omega}_{3}^{2}=3,247{\omega}_{0}^{2},{m}_{3}=9,296\text{}m,{\Phi}_{3}=(\begin{array}{c}1\\ -2,247\\ 1,802\end{array})\end{array} Let us compare the responses of the system modelled by a single eigenmode with or without static correction: It is observed that the static correction makes it possible to correct the response at low frequency; the model with 1 mode plus correction matches the exact solution perfectly at low frequency. On the other hand, at high frequency (beyond the first mode), this correction leads to overestimating the response enormously. The use of the static correction will therefore have to be used with caution and within the framework of a narrow-band excitation. Let us look at what the method of addition of a static mode gives. If a unit force is applied at point 1, the static deformed shape is: {\Psi}_{s}=\frac{1}{k}(\begin{array}{c}3\\ 2\\ 1\end{array}) The projected mass and stiffness matrices that one obtains are the following: \hat{M}=(\begin{array}{c}1,841m\frac{5,049}{{\omega}_{0}^{2}}\\ \frac{5,049}{{\omega}_{0}^{2}}14\text{}\frac{m}{{k}^{2}}\end{array}\text{})\text{}\text{et}\text{}\hat{K}=(\begin{array}{c}0,365k\text{}1\\ \text{}1\text{}\frac{3}{k}\text{}\end{array}) this system has as eigenfrequencies: {\omega}_{1}^{2}=0,198{\omega}_{0}^{2} and {\omega}_{1}^{2}=1,667{\omega}_{0}^{2} The response of the system modelled with one eigenmode and one static mode is the following: One notices that the correction is very good at low frequency (static-correction effect), and that the dynamics of the system are modelled well beyond the first mode taken into account. On the other hand the effect of the second mode is poorly represented (shift on the frequency). Consider the following discrete system with three masses: The stiffness and mass matrices are: M=(\begin{array}{ccc}m& 0& 0\\ 0& m& 0\\ 0& 0& m\end{array})\text{}K=(\begin{array}{ccc}k& -k& 0\\ -k& \mathrm{2k}& -k\\ 0& -k& \mathrm{2k}\end{array}) Let us make this system non-linear by adding a cubic internal-force term between \mathrm{x1} and \mathrm{x2} : F=k.{(\mathrm{x1}-\mathrm{x2})}^{3} Let us seek to evaluate the response of this system to a forced excitation of frequency close to the first eigenfrequency of the linear system (one has chosen \omega =0,18{\omega}_{0} ), with a large amplitude {F}_{m}=3.k . In this configuration, the response of the system cannot be evaluated by the response of the linear system (the cubic term is far too large); a non-linear analysis with pseudo-forces must be implemented, as was shown in [§3.2]. The curves of the transient results of this method can be seen in the report [bib8], taking into account one or 2 eigenmodes of the initial linear system. With a single eigenmode, one notices that a relatively large error is committed (sometimes reaching 50%); on the other hand it is satisfactory to observe that the extrema of the vibrations are predicted fairly well. One might have hoped that, by exciting below the first eigenfrequency, a single eigenmode would have sufficed to model the response of the system; one sees here that this is not the case. As is often observed for non-linear systems, the system also responds with superharmonics of the excitation frequency. On the other hand, by taking 2 eigenmodes to model the response of this structure with 3 degrees of freedom, a very satisfactory result is obtained (a few % error on the amplitude); to the eye one has difficulty distinguishing the difference. This shows that, by choosing a sufficiently rich projection basis, a complex dynamic system with non-linearities can be modelled very well thanks to a pseudo-force method.

r5.06.03 Modelling of impacts and of friction in transient analysis by modal recombination r5.06.03 Modelling of impacts and of friction in transient analysis by modal recombination Summary: This document describes the physical laws of contact with friction between structures and the modelling of them in the algorithm for transient analysis by modal recombination DYNA_VIBRA (TYPE_CALCUL='TRAN' and BASE_CALCUL='GENE') with COMPORTEMENT='DIS_CHOC'. For the various non-linear contact connections that can be used, the computation of the quantities defining the contact conditions is detailed. The usage schemes employed are described in R5.06.04. > Contents 1 Introduction The problems of impact with friction of interest to EDF concern, for example, the modelling of the vibrations of tubular structures held by supports with gaps, or separated by small gaps and thus able to come into contact. The tubes of the steam generators, the rods of the control-rod clusters and the fuel assemblies are examples of structures whose vibrations one wishes to model. The major consequence of vibrations in the presence of a gap is to cause impacts as well as friction between the structure and its supports, or between the structures, whence risks of wear. This document describes the type of non-linearities introduced by the presence of these gaps, as well as the modelling used to take them into account in the modal-recombination algorithm. 2 Contact relations between two structures Two relations govern the contact between two structures: - The unilateral contact relation, which expresses the non-interpenetrability of solid bodies, - the friction relation, which governs the variation of the tangential forces in the contact. For the present developments one will retain a simple relation: Coulomb's friction law. 2.1 Unilateral contact relation Let two structures {\Omega}_{1} and {\Omega}_{2} . One denotes by {d}_{N}^{1/2} the normal distance between the structures and by {F}_{N}^{1/2} the normal reaction force of {\Omega}_{1} on {\Omega}_{2} (see figure ). Figure 2-1: Normal distance and normal reaction The law of action and reaction imposes: {F}_{N}^{1/2}=-{F}_{N}^{2/1} The unilateral contact conditions, also called Signorini conditions (see [1]), are expressed as follows: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{d}_{N}^{1/2}\ge 0\\ {F}_{N}^{1/2}\ge 0\\ {d}_{N}^{1/2}{F}_{N}^{1/2}=0\end{array} Figure 2-2: Graph of the unilateral contact relation The graphical representation of the unilateral contact law in the figure expresses a force-displacement relation which is not differentiable. It is therefore not usable in a simple way in a dynamic analysis algorithm. If one restricts the study to the case of a tubular structure in the presence of a non-deformable support, one denotes by {d}_{n}\left({d}_{n}={d}_{N}^{1/2}\right) the normal distance to the support, and by {F}_{n} the reaction of the latter ( {F}_{n}={F}_{N}^{2/1}=-{F}_{N}^{1/2} see figure ). Figure 2-3: Normal distance and normal reaction between a structure and a support The expression of the normal contact conditions, expressing the limitation of the displacements due to the support, is: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{d}_{n}\ge 0\\ {F}_{n}\ge 0\\ {d}_{n}{F}_{n}=0\end{array} 2.2 Coulomb's friction law Coulomb's law expresses a limitation of the tangential force {F}_{T}^{1/2} of tangential reaction of {O}_{1} on {O}_{2} . Let {\dot{u}}_{T}^{1/2} be the relative velocity of {\Omega}_{1} with respect to {O}_{2} at a contact point and let \mu be the Coulomb friction coefficient; one has (see [1]): \lbrace \begin{array}{c}s=\Vert {F}_{T}^{1/2}\Vert -\mu {F}_{N}^{1/2}\le 0\\ \exists \lambda \text{tel que}{\dot{u}}_{T}^{1/2}=\lambda {F}_{T}^{1/2}\\ \lambda \le 0\\ \lambda .s=0\end{array} and the law of action and reaction: {F}_{T}^{1/2}=-{F}_{T}^{2/1} The graphical representation of Coulomb's law in the figure likewise expresses the non-differentiable character of the law and is therefore not simple to use in a dynamic algorithm. Figure 2-4: Graph of Coulomb's friction law If one restricts the study to the case of a tubular structure in the presence of a non-deformable support, only the tangential force {F}_{T}^{2/1}={F}_{T} is used; the friction law is expressed as follows: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}s=\Vert {F}_{T}\Vert -\mu {F}_{n}\le 0\\ \exists \lambda \text{tel que}{\dot{u}}_{T}=\lambda {F}_{T}\\ \lambda \le 0\\ \lambda s=0\end{array} A common extension of Coulomb's law, drawn from experience, consists in having two friction coefficients: one for adherence, denoted {\mu}_{s} , the other for sliding, denoted {\mu}_{d} , with {\mu}_{s}>{\mu}_{d} . One then has, in the adherence phase, \Vert {F}_{T}\Vert \le {\mu}_{s}{F}_{n} and, in the sliding phase, \Vert {F}_{T}\Vert ={\mu}_{d}{F}_{n} . 3 Modelling of contact/friction by penalisation 3.1 Model of the normal contact force The principle of penalisation applied to the graph of the figure consists in introducing a single-valued relation {F}_{N}^{1/2}={f}_{{\varepsilon}}\left({d}_{N}^{1/2}\right) by means of a parameter \varepsilon . The graph of {f}_{\varepsilon} must tend towards the Signorini graph when \varepsilon tends towards zero (see [2]). One possibility consists in proposing a linear relation between {d}_{N}^{1/2} and {F}_{N}^{1/2} : \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{F}_{N}^{1/2}=-\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}}{d}_{N}^{1/2}\text{si}{d}_{N}^{1/2}\le 0\\ {F}_{N}^{1/2}=0\text{sinon}\end{array} If one denotes {K}_{N}=\frac{1}{{\varepsilon}} (commonly called the impact stiffness ) one recovers the classical relation, modelling an elastic impact: {F}_{N}^{1/2}=-{K}_{N}{d}_{N}^{1/2} The approximate graph of the contact law with penalisation is in the figure . Figure 3-1: Graph of the unilateral contact relation approximated by penalisation In order to take into account a possible loss of energy in the impact, one introduces an impact damping {C}_{N} . The expression for the normal contact force is then written: {F}_{N}^{1/2}=-{K}_{N}{d}_{N}^{1/2}-{C}_{N}{\dot{u}}_{N}^{1/2} Where {\dot{u}}_{N}^{1/2} is the relative normal velocity of {O}_{1} with respect to {O}_{2} . In order to respect the Signorini relation (no adherence in contact), one must on the other hand check a posteriori that {F}_{N}^{1/2} is positive or zero. One will therefore take only the positive part {⟨\cdot ⟩}^{+} of the expression (): \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{⟨x⟩}^{+}=x\text{si}x\ge 0\\ {⟨x⟩}^{+}=0\text{si}x<0\end{array} The complete relation giving the normal contact force which is retained for the algorithm is the following: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\text{Si}{d}_{N}^{1/2}\le 0\text{alors}{F}_{N}^{1/2}={⟨-{K}_{N}{d}_{N}^{1/2}-{C}_{N}{\dot{u}}_{N}^{1/2}⟩}^{+}\text{et}{F}_{N}^{1/2}=-{F}_{N}^{2/1}\\ \text{Sinon}{F}_{N}^{1/2}={F}_{N}^{2/1}=0\end{array} 3.2 Model of the tangential contact force The graph describing the tangential force with Coulomb's law is non-differentiable for the adherence phase {\dot{u}}_{T}^{1/2}=0 . One therefore introduces a single-valued relation linking the relative tangential displacement {d}_{T}^{1/2} and the tangential force {F}_{T}^{1/2}={f}_{\xi}\left({d}_{T}^{1/2}\right) by means of a parameter \xi . The graph of {f}_{\xi} must tend towards the Coulomb graph when \xi tends towards zero (see [2]). One possibility consists in writing a linear relation between {d}_{T}^{1/2} and {F}_{T}^{1/2} for an incremental writing: {F}_{T}^{1/2}-{F}_{T,0}^{1/2}=-\frac{1}{\xi}\left({d}_{T}^{1/2}-{d}_{T,0}^{1/2}\right) With {\left(\cdot \right)}_{T,0} the quantities at the previous time step. If one introduces a tangential stiffness {K}_{T}=\frac{1}{\xi} , one obtains the relation: {F}_{T}^{1/2}={F}_{T,0}^{1/2}-{K}_{T}\left({d}_{T}^{1/2}-{d}_{T,0}^{1/2}\right) The approximate graph of Coulomb's friction law modelled by penalisation is in the figure . For numerical reasons, linked to the dissipation of parasitic vibrations (see [3]) in the adherence phase, one is led to add a tangential damping {C}_{T} in the expression for the tangential force. Its final expression is: {F}_{T}^{1/2}={F}_{T,0}^{1/2}-{K}_{T}\left({d}_{T}^{1/2}-{d}_{T,0}^{1/2}\right)-{C}_{T}{\dot{u}}_{T}^{1/2} This force must moreover satisfy the Coulomb criterion, that is: \Vert {F}_{T}^{1/2}\Vert \le \mu {F}_{N}^{1/2} If this is not the case, one corrects the friction force by the following formula: {F}_{T}^{1/2}=-\mu {F}_{N}^{1/2}\frac{{\dot{u}}_{T}^{1/2}}{\Vert {\dot{u}}_{T}^{1/2}\Vert } Figure 3-2: Graph of the friction law approximated by penalisation In the case of the extension of Coulomb's law with the distinction between the adherence coefficient {\mu}_{s} and the sliding coefficient {\mu}_{d} , the approximate graph of the law is modified (see figure ). Figure 3-3: Graph of the variant of the friction law approximated by penalisation 4 Types of contact connection modelled The developments presented here concern the implementation of non-linear connections with unilateral contact and friction between a node and an obstacle, or between two given nodes. The nodes in contact are assumed to belong to two slender structures of beam type, or to a beam and a non-deformable obstacle. The nodes on which the contact condition will bear are assumed to lie on the centre-line of the beams. 4.1 Connections between a node and a non-deformable obstacle 4.1.1 Node-on-plane-obstacle contact connections One considers a slender structure represented by elements of beam type. Its displacement is limited at a point by the presence of an obstacle constituted of two infinite half-planes in the direction Y (see figure ). Figure 4-1: Slender structures with node-on-plane contact In order to analyse the contact conditions, one places oneself in the frame perpendicular to the axis \mathrm{Xloc} , the direction of the neutral fibre or of a generatrix of the beam. Let \mathrm{NO1} be the node of the connection considered on the beam; the geometry of the node-on-plane contact connection (called PLAN_Y) is described in the figure (). Figure 4-2: Geometry of the node-on-plane-obstacle connection Let \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{Y}_{\mathit{loc}}\\ {Z}_{\mathit{loc}}\end{array}\right\rbrace be the coordinates of the node \mathrm{NO1} in the frame \left({Y}_{\mathit{loc}},{Z}_{\mathit{loc}}\right) ; the origin of this frame is the point ORIG_OBST. The normal distance {d}_{N} in this case, neglecting the rotations of the sections, is then expressed by: | :math:{d}_{N}=- | {Y}_{mathit{loc}} | +mathit{jeu} | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | The contact in this connection is supposed to take place whatever the offset in {Z}_{\mathit{loc}} between the two structures. The normal vector n in the frame \left({Y}_{\mathit{loc}},{Z}_{\mathit{loc}}\right) has components: n=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\mathit{sign}({Y}_{\mathit{loc}})\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace The other quantities {\dot{u}}_{N} , {F}_{N} , {\dot{u}}_{T} and {F}_{T} are computed in a general way as specified in [§ 3 ]. 4.1.2 Node-on-concave-circular-obstacle contact connections One considers a slender structure, represented by elements of beam type. Its displacement is limited at a point by the presence of an obstacle constituted of an infinite plane pierced by a circular hole (see figure ). Figure 4-3: Slender structures with node-on-circular-obstacle contact In order to analyse the contact conditions, one places oneself in the frame perpendicular to the axis {X}_{\mathit{loc}} , the direction of the neutral fibre or of a generatrix of the beam. Let \mathrm{NO1} be the node of the connection considered; the geometry of the node-on-circle contact connection (called CERCLE) is described in the figure (). Figure 4-4: Geometry of the node-on-circular-obstacle connection Let \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{Y}_{\mathit{loc}}\\ {Z}_{\mathit{loc}}\end{array}\right\rbrace be the coordinates of the node \mathrm{NO1} in the frame \left({Y}_{\mathit{loc}},{Z}_{\mathit{loc}}\right) ; the origin of this frame is the point ORIG_OBST. The normal distance {d}_{N} in this case, neglecting the rotations of the sections, is then expressed by: {d}_{N}=-\sqrt{{\left({Y}_{\mathit{loc}}-{Y}_{\text{ORIG\_OBST}}\right)}^{2}+{\left({Z}_{\mathit{loc}}-{Z}_{\text{ORIG\_OBST}}\right)}^{2}}+\mathit{jeu} One takes as normal vector n the vector: n=\frac{\vec{\text{ORIG\_OBST}-\text{NO1}}}{\Vert \vec{\text{ORIG\_OBST}-\text{NO1}}\Vert } With \text{jeu} a strictly positive distance. The other quantities {\dot{u}}_{N} , {F}_{N} , {\dot{u}}_{T} and {F}_{T} are computed in a general way as specified in [§ 3 ]. 4.1.3 Node-on-concave-obstacle contact connections discretised by segments One considers a slender structure, represented by elements of beam type. Its displacement is limited at a point by the presence of an obstacle constituted of an infinite plane pierced by a hole of arbitrary concave shape which can be discretised in polar coordinates by segments (see figure ). Figure 4-5: Geometry of the node-on-concave-obstacle connection discretised Let \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{Y}_{\mathit{loc}}\\ {Z}_{\mathit{loc}}\end{array}\right\rbrace be the coordinates of the node \mathit{NO}1 in the frame \left({Y}_{\mathit{loc}},{Z}_{\mathit{loc}}\right) ; the origin of this frame is the point ORIG_OBST. One searches for the contact facet closest to the node \mathrm{NO1} ; the normal vector n is defined as the direct orthogonal vector to the facet in the figure . Figure 4-6: Definition of the frame for the case of the node on a discretised concave obstacle Let \mathit{PNO}1 be the projection of the node \mathit{NO}1 onto the facet; the normal distance {d}_{N} in this case is: {d}_{N}=\vec{\mathit{NO}1-\mathit{PNO}1}\cdot n The other quantities {\dot{u}}_{N} , {F}_{N} , {\dot{u}}_{T} and {F}_{T} are computed in a general way as specified in [§ 3 ]. 4.2 Connections between two nodes of two deformable structures 4.2.1 Plane-on-plane contact connections The contacts between fuel assemblies, at the level of the mixing grids, constitute an example of plane-on-plane contact (see figure ). One therefore considers two slender structures, which may be modelled by beams of rectangular cross-section at the level of the contact zones. Figure 4-7: Slender structures with plane-on-plane contact In order to analyse the contact conditions, one places oneself in the frame perpendicular to the axis {X}_{\mathit{loc}} , the direction of the neutral fibre of the beams. Let \mathrm{NO1} and \mathrm{NO2} be the two nodes of the connection considered; the geometry of the plane-on-plane contact connection (called BI_PLAN_Y) is described in the figure . Figure 4-8: Geometry of the plane-on-plane connection Let \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{Y}_{\mathit{loc}}^{i}\\ {Z}_{\mathit{loc}}^{i}\end{array}\right\rbrace be the coordinates of the node {\mathit{NO}}^{i} in the frame \left({Y}_{\mathit{loc}},{Z}_{\mathit{loc}}\right) ; the origin of this frame is the point ORIG_OBST. (ORIG_OBST may be supplied by the user; by default ORIG_OBST is chosen as the midpoint of the nodes \mathrm{NO1} and \mathrm{NO2} ). The normal distance {d}_{N} in this case, neglecting the rotations of the sections, is then expressed by: | :math:{d}_{N}=- | {Y}_{mathit{loc}}^{1}-{Y}_{mathit{loc}}^{2} | -{D}_{1}-{D}_{2} | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | {D}_{1} and {D}_{2} are strictly positive distances. The contact in this connection is supposed to take place whatever the offset in {Z}_{\mathit{loc}} between the two structures. The normal vector n in the frame \left({Y}_{\mathit{loc}},{Z}_{\mathit{loc}}\right) has components: n=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\mathit{sign}({Y}_{\mathit{loc}}^{2}-{Y}_{\mathit{loc}}^{2})\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace The other quantities {\dot{u}}_{N} , {F}_{N} , {\dot{u}}_{T} and {F}_{T} are computed in a general way as specified in [§ 3 ]. 4.2.2 Circle-on-circle contact connections If one now considers two cylinders of circular cross-section, modelled by beam elements. The contact connection between two nodes of the centre-lines is assumed to take place between two circles, as the figure shows. Figure 4-9: Slender structures with circle-on-circle contact One places oneself in the frame perpendicular to the axis {X}_{\text{loc}} parallel to a generatrix of the cylinders. Let \mathrm{NŒUD1} and \mathrm{NŒUD2} be the two nodes of the connection considered; the geometry of the circle-on-circle contact connection (called BI_CERCLE) is described on the geometry of the figure . Figure 4-10: Geometry of the circle-on-circle connection The normal distance {d}_{N} has the expression: {d}_{N}=-\sqrt{{({Y}_{\mathit{loc}}^{1}-{Y}_{\mathit{loc}}^{2})}^{2}+{({Z}_{\mathit{loc}}^{1}-{Z}_{\mathit{loc}}^{2})}^{2}}-{R}_{1}-{R}_{2} One takes as normal vector from {\Omega}_{1} towards {O}_{2} the vector: n=\frac{\vec{\text{NO2}-\text{NO1}}}{\Vert \vec{\text{NO2}-\text{NO1}}\Vert } 5 Use of the localised non-linear impact and friction forces in modal recombination The non-linear forces expressed above are explicit functions of the position and of the velocity of the nodes on which the contact conditions bear. One chooses to use the pseudo-force technique in order to solve the projected dynamic problem. If the direct dynamic system is written: M{\ddot{X}}_{t}+C{\dot{X}}_{t}+K{X}_{t}={F}_{\mathit{ext}}(t)+{F}_{\mathit{choc}}({X}_{t},{\dot{X}}_{t}) The pseudo-force technique consists in projecting onto the basis of the linear system and in keeping the non-linear forces on the right-hand side. The projected dynamic system takes the form: {\Phi}^{t}M\Phi {\ddot{\eta}}_{t}+{\Phi}^{t}C\Phi {\dot{\eta}}_{t}+{\Phi}^{t}K\Phi {\eta}_{t}={\Phi}^{t}{\Phi}_{\mathit{ext}}(t)+{\Phi}^{t}{\Phi}_{\mathit{choc}}(\Phi {\eta}_{t},\Phi {\dot{\eta}}_{t}) The projected problem is integrated numerically by an explicit scheme. Recommendations are given in U2.06.04 for the choice of this basis. 6 Details on the use of the impact non-linearities with friction The impact non-linearities between a structure and an obstacle, or between two structures, have been introduced into the modal-recombination algorithms of Code_Aster : a first-order Euler algorithm and a fourth-order Devogelaere algorithm (see R5.06.04). These algorithms are used by the operator DYNA_VIBRA. The type of impact connection between the two nodes is specified by a specific command: DEFI_OBSTACLE. 6.1 Definition of the type of impact connection The type of impact connection is a generic notion, which contains no physical information such as a distance or any dimension. The type of connection simply specifies the geometric shape of the connection considered. The types of two-node connection with impact accepted by the command DEFI_OBSTACLE are described by the following keywords: PLAN_Y, PLAN_Z, CERCLE, BI_PLAN_Y, BI_PLAN_Z or BI_CERCLE (see figure ). Figure 6-1: Geometries of the impact connections The prefix specifies that it is a two-node connection. 6.2 Definition of the local frame for the contact conditions The structures treated, being regarded as slender cylinders (circular or rectangular cross-section), are modelled by beam elements. The contact is treated in a plane perpendicular to the direction {X}_{\text{loc}} of the generatrix of the cylinders. In order to define this change of frame completely, one introduces a local frame ({X}_{\text{loc}},{Y}_{\text{loc}},{Z}_{\text{loc}}) . The vector {X}_{\text{loc}} is the three-component vector supplied after the keyword NORM_OBST. By means of the first two nautical angles, one passes in a unique way from the global frame (X,Y,Z) to a frame having {X}_{\text{loc}} as its first basis vector (see figure ). A third rotation, whose angle is supplied after the keyword ANGL_VRIL, gives a unique correspondence between the principal frame and the local frame. Warning: the orientation of this local frame is important, because it is in this frame that the contact conditions are analysed, and that the local positions of the impact nodes are supplied. Figure 6-2: Rotations defining the local frame Figure 6.2-a: Rotations defining the local frame The operand ORIG_OBST makes it possible to define the origin of the local frame (\text{Orig},{X}_{\text{loc}},{Y}_{\text{loc}},{Z}_{\text{loc}}) . This operand is optional and in principle will not be used in the case of impacts between two nodes. The code then considers that the origin is situated at the middle of the segment joining the two nodes. 6.3 Definition of the nodes of the connections One specifies, after the keywords NOEU_1 and NOEU_2, the names of the two nodes of the structures on which the impact conditions will bear. If it is a connection between a node and an obstacle, only NOEU_1 is supplied. 6.4 Definition of the characteristic dimensions of the cross-sections The operand JEU is used for the contact conditions between a node and an obstacle. The operands DIST_1 and DIST_2 make it possible to specify the characteristic dimensions of the cross-sections of the structures surrounding the impact nodes. In the case of plane-on-plane connections, these are the thicknesses of material surrounding the impact node in the direction considered. In the case of circle-on-circle connections, these are the radii of the cross-sections surrounding the impact nodes. 6.5 Definition of the contact parameters The impact stiffness and damping parameters were introduced in § 3.1 and § 3.2 ; one specifies here the keywords making it possible to define them for a given connection: - The operand RIGI_NOR is mandatory; it makes it possible to give the value of the normal impact stiffness {K}_{N} . - The operand AMOR_NOR is optional; it makes it possible to give the value of the normal impact damping {C}_{N} - The operand RIGI_TAN is optional; it makes it possible to give the value of the tangential stiffness {K}_{T} ; - The operand AMOR_TAN is optional; it makes it possible to give the value of the tangential impact damping {C}_{T} ; - The operand COULOMB makes it possible to give the value of the Coulomb coefficient. Note: If a stiffness {K}_{T} is defined and the keyword AMOR_TAN is absent, the code computes an optimised damping so as to minimise the residual oscillations in adherence (see [3] ): {C}_{T}=2\cdot \sqrt{({k}_{i}+{K}_{T}).{m}_{i}}-2\cdot {x}_{i}\cdot \sqrt{{k}_{i}.{m}_{i}} , where i is the index of the mode predominant in the tangential direction in the response of the structure ( the largest modal mass normalised by the tangential displacement ). 6.6 Use of a unidirectional impact For obstacles of type PLAN_Y, PLAN_Z, BI_PLAN_Y or BI_PLAN_Z it is possible to activate the friction in a single direction of the plane of the obstacle. The operand UNIDIRECTIONNEL makes it possible to activate this unidirectional friction in order to cancel the friction in the direction given by the operand NORM_OBST. This option can be used both with friction of type COULOMB and with friction of type COULOMB_STAT_DYNA. With a friction COULOMB, the friction coefficient is zero along the axis supplied in NORM_OBST and mu in the perpendicular direction. With a friction COULOMB_STAT_DYNA, the adherence coefficient is zero along the axis supplied in NORM_OBST and mus in the perpendicular direction. The sliding coefficient is zero along the axis supplied in NORM_OBST and mud in the perpendicular direction.

r5.06.04 Time-integration algorithms of the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’GENE’ r5.06.04 Time-integration algorithms of the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’GENE’ Summary: This document describes the time-integration schemes which are used to solve, in the space of the modes, linear transient dynamics problems in mechanics, with, for certain schemes, the possible taking into account of localised non-linearities of the type impacts, friction, force-displacement and force-velocity relations, and the possible use of substructuring. The NEWMARK scheme (implicit, restricted here to the linear case), the DEVOGELAERE scheme, and four explicit schemes with an adaptive time step, ADAPT_ORDRE1 and ADAPT_ORDRE2, RUNGE_KUTTA_32 and RUNGE_KUTTA_54, are presented. 1 Introduction The aim of transient dynamic analysis is to determine, as a function of time, the response of a structure, given an external loading or boundary conditions which are functions of time, in cases where the inertia effects cannot be neglected. In a certain number of physical configurations, a modal or harmonic analysis is not sufficient and a transient analysis must be carried out. This is in particular the case if: - the history of the phenomenon is important in the study, - if the external loading is complex (earthquake, multi-component excitations, etc ...), - if the system is non-linear (plasticity, impacts, friction, etc ...). The transient analysis methods which can then be used are divided into two broad categories: - the so-called direct integration methods, - the Ritz methods, which include among others the recombination of modal projections. The direct integration methods are so named because no transformation is carried out on the dynamic system after the discretisation by finite elements. They are presented in the document R5.05.02, direct integration algorithms of the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’PHYS’. The Ritz methods, on the contrary, carry out a transformation of the initial dynamic system, by a projection onto a subspace of the initial discretisation space. The solution is then performed on a modified system which, if it is reduced, only gives access to an approximation of the response of the real system. Time-integration algorithms on a system in generalised coordinates are used to solve dynamic problems in mechanics for linear structures, with the possible taking into account of localised non-linearities such as impacts, friction, and force-displacement and force-velocity relations. Certain algorithms furthermore allow substructuring. These algorithms are programmed in the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’GENE’ U4.53.03. 2 Time-integration methods for a dynamic problem 2.1 Introduction It is assumed that the equations governing the dynamic equilibrium of solids have been discretised by finite elements. A discrete system of equations is obtained, which is to be integrated in time. To this end a discretisation \lbrace {t}_{i},i\in \mathrm{\mathbb{N}}\rbrace of the time interval of the study [0,T] is chosen and the equilibrium of the structure is written at the time instants {t}_{i} . In general these equations take the following form: \mathrm{M}.{\ddot{X}}_{t}+\mathrm{C}.{\dot{X}}_{t}+\mathrm{K}.{X}_{t}={\mathrm{R}}_{\text{ext}}(t)+{\mathrm{R}}_{\text{nl}}({X}_{t},{\dot{X}}_{t},{\ddot{X}}_{t}) eq 2.1 -1 where - \mathrm{M} is the mass matrix of the system, - \mathrm{K} is the stiffness matrix of the system, - \mathrm{C} is the damping matrix of the system, - {\mathrm{R}}_{\text{ext}}(t) is the vector of the external forces, - {\mathrm{R}}_{\text{nl}}({X}_{t},{\dot{X}}_{t},{\ddot{X}}_{t}) is the vector of the non-linear forces. The damping matrix \mathrm{C} is in general difficult to evaluate because the damping is often a function of the frequency. It is, however, common to simplify the taking into account of the damping by employing the proportional damping model, or Rayleigh model. The Rayleigh-Ritz reduction methods are presented in the document R5.06.01, Ritz methods in linear and non-linear dynamics. In the case where the term {\mathrm{R}}_{\text{nl}}({X}_{t},{\dot{X}}_{t},{\ddot{X}}_{t}) is not zero, the pseudo-force technique consists in projecting onto the basis of the linear system and in keeping the non-linear forces on the right-hand side. The pseudo-force technique is always associated with an explicit integration scheme. Consequently the taking into account of the non-linearities is available only for explicit schemes. The addition of the non-linearities does not modify the form of the equations. In the Ritz method, the displacement field {X}_{t} is replaced by its projection onto the modal basis such that {X}_{t}=\Phi {\eta}_{t} where {\eta}_{t} is the vector of the generalised coordinates and \Phi is the modal basis, most often reduced. The projected dynamic system takes the following form, with {\eta}_{t}\in {ℝ}^{p} : {\Phi}^{t}.\mathrm{M}.\Phi .{\ddot{\eta}}_{t}+{\Phi}^{t}.\mathrm{C}.\Phi .{\dot{\eta}}_{t}+{\Phi}^{t}.\mathrm{K}.\Phi .{\eta}_{t}={\Phi}^{t}.{\mathrm{R}}_{\text{ext}}(t)+{\Phi}^{t}.{\mathrm{R}}_{\text{nl}}(\Phi .{\eta}_{t},\Phi .{\dot{\eta}}_{t},\Phi .{\ddot{\eta}}_{t}) eq 2.1 -2 When Basile's hypothesis does not apply (non-proportional damping), the projected damping matrix is not diagonal. The integration of the coupled system is then necessarily carried out with one of the following three schemes: the implicit NEWMARK scheme, the explicit EULER scheme or the explicit schemes ADAPT_ORDRE1 and ADAPT_ORDRE2. The equation obtained in {\eta}_{t} is of the same form as the equation in {X}_{t} . Consequently, in the remainder of the document, the notation {X}_{t} will be used both for the displacement in generalised coordinates and for the displacement in the physical space. In the case of the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’GENE’, these are generalised coordinates. Two classes of method can be distinguished in the step-by-step integration of the equilibrium equations, the explicit integration methods and the implicit integration methods. Consider the following linear dynamic system to be integrated in time: M.{\ddot{X}}_{t}+C.{\dot{X}}_{t}+K.{X}_{t}={R}_{\text{ext}}(t) eq 2.1 -3 This second-order differential system can be reduced to a first-order system: N.{\dot{U}}_{t}=H.{U}_{t}+{F}_{t} eq 2.1 -4 where {U}_{t}=(\begin{array}{c}{X}_{t}\\ {\dot{X}}_{t}\end{array}) , N=(\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}& 0\\ 0& M\end{array}) , H=(\begin{array}{cc}0& \mathrm{Id}\\ -K& -C\end{array}) , {F}_{t}=(\begin{array}{c}0\\ {R}_{t}\end{array}) To integrate this system of differential equations, a discretisation \left\lbrace {t}_{i},i\in \mathbb{N}\right\rbrace is used, as well as a finite-difference formula to express the derivative {\dot{U}}_{t} . The integration methods in which only the derivative {\dot{U}}_{t} involves unknowns at time {t}_{i+1} will be called explicit integration methods. In this way the determination of the quantities sought at the time instant {t}_{i+1} does not result from an inversion of a system involving the operator H . If, in addition, a “mass-lumping” is carried out so as to make the matrix M diagonal, the determination of {U}_{t} is particularly simple. These are the main characteristics of the explicit integration methods. The implicit or semi-implicit methods involve the discretisation of {U}_{t} at a time instant later than {t}_{i} , generally {t}_{i+1} . The determination of the variables therefore requires the solution of a system involving the operator H . Two notions are important: consistency, or the order of the integration scheme, and stability. The approximations used to obtain the differential operators define the consistency, or the order of the integration scheme. One may indeed consider that the approximation with which the displacement is obtained at each time step is related to the order of approximation of the first and second derivatives with respect to time. The stability study of a scheme consists in analysing the propagation of the numerical perturbations in the course of time. A stable scheme keeps a finite solution, in spite of the perturbations, whereas an unstable scheme leads to a numerical blow-up or to a divergence of the solution. To carry out a stability study of an integration scheme, the latter is put in the form of a linear recursive system and the eigencharacteristics of this system are determined. If all the eigenvalues of the recursion operator are smaller than 1 in modulus, the scheme is stable. Otherwise it is unstable. Explicit integration schemes are generally conditionally stable, which means that the time step must be sufficiently small to ensure the stability of the time integration. Certain implicit algorithms have the property of being unconditionally stable, which is what makes them of interest and makes it possible to use an arbitrarily large time step. The schemes retained for the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’GENE’ are one implicit scheme, NEWMARK, and four explicit schemes, EULER, DEVOGELAERE, ADAPT_ORDRE1 and ADAPT_ORDRE2 (with an adaptive time step). The choice is made by the keyword METHODE: ‘EULER’, ‘DEVOGE’, ‘NEWMARK’, ‘ADAPT_ORDRE1’ or ‘ADAPT_ORDRE2’. 2.2 Implicit integration methods 2.2.1 Introduction The implicit methods involve the solution of a matrix system with the previously defined operator. If the solids are assumed to be linear elastic, this results in the solution of a linear system at each time step. The advantage of these methods is their unconditional stability, which allows them to integrate the equations of dynamics with a relatively large time step while correctly representing the behaviour of the lowest-frequency modes of the structure. An implicit version of the NEWMARK method, which has been programmed in DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’GENE’ for linear problems. 2.2.2 The Newmark method [bib1] 2.2.2.1 Presentation of the scheme Newmark [bib1] introduced two parameters \gamma and \beta for the computation of the displacements and velocities at the time step t+\Delta t : {\dot{X}}_{t+\Delta t}={\dot{X}}_{t}+\Delta t\left[(1-\gamma )\ddot{{X}_{t}}+\gamma {\ddot{X}}_{t+\Delta t}\right] {X}_{t+\Delta t}={X}_{t}+\Delta t\dot{{X}_{t}}+\Delta {t}^{2}\left[(\frac{1}{2}-\beta )\ddot{{X}_{t}}+\beta {\ddot{X}}_{t+\Delta t}\right] Consider the equilibrium equations at time t+\Delta t : M\cdot {\ddot{X}}_{t+\Delta t}+C{\dot{X}}_{t+\Delta t}+K{X}_{t+\Delta t}={R}_{t+\Delta t} Substituting the previous relations and eliminating {\dot{X}}_{t+\Delta t} and {\ddot{X}}_{t+\Delta t} , one obtains: \tilde{K}\cdot {X}_{t+\Delta t}={\tilde{R}}_{t+\Delta t} where \tilde{K}=K+{a}_{0}M+{a}_{1}C \tilde{R}={R}_{t+\Delta t}+C\cdot \left\lbrace {a}_{1}{X}_{t}+{a}_{4}{\dot{X}}_{t}+{a}_{5}{\ddot{X}}_{t}\right\rbrace +M\cdot \left\lbrace {a}_{0}{X}_{t}+{a}_{2}{\dot{X}}_{t}+{a}_{3}{\ddot{X}}_{t}\right\rbrace with: \begin{array}{cccc}{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{(\beta .\Delta {t}^{2})}& {a}_{1}=\frac{\gamma}{(\beta .\Delta t)}& {a}_{2}=\frac{1}{(\beta .\Delta t)}& {a}_{3}=\frac{1}{2\beta }-1\\ {a}_{4}=\frac{\gamma}{\beta}-1& {a}_{5}=\frac{\Delta t}{2}(\frac{\gamma}{\beta}-2)& {a}_{6}=\Delta t.(1-\gamma )& {a}_{7}=\gamma .\Delta t\end{array} 2.2.2.2 Complete algorithm of the Newmark method a) initialisation 1. initial conditions {\mathrm{X}}_{0} , \dot{{\mathrm{X}}_{0}} and \ddot{{\mathrm{X}}_{0}} 2. choice of \Delta t \gamma and beta and computation of the coefficients {a}_{\mathrm{1,.}\mathrm{..}},{a}_{8} (cf. above) 3. assemble the stiffness matrix \mathrm{K} , the mass matrix \mathrm{M} and the damping matrix \mathrm{C} 4. form the effective stiffness matrix \tilde{\mathrm{K}}=\mathrm{K}+{a}_{0}\mathrm{M}+{a}_{1}\mathrm{C} 5. factorise \tilde{\mathrm{K}} b) at each time step 1. compute the effective loading \tilde{\mathrm{R}} : \tilde{\mathrm{R}}={\mathrm{R}}_{t+\Delta t}+\mathrm{C}\cdot \left\lbrace {a}_{1}{\mathrm{X}}_{t}+{a}_{4}{\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}+{a}_{5}{\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}\right\rbrace +\mathrm{M}\cdot \left\lbrace {a}_{0}{\mathrm{X}}_{t}+{a}_{2}{\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}+{a}_{3}{\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}\right\rbrace 1. solve \tilde{\mathrm{K}}\cdot {\mathrm{X}}_{t+\Delta t}={\tilde{\mathrm{R}}}_{t+\Delta t} 2. compute the velocities and accelerations at time t+\Delta t {\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t+\Delta t}={a}_{0}\left({\mathrm{X}}_{t+\Delta t}-{\mathrm{X}}_{t}\right)-{a}_{2}{\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}-{a}_{3}{\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t} {\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t+\Delta t}={\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}+{a}_{6}{\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}+{a}_{7}{\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t+\Delta t} 1. computation of the next time step: return to b)1) 2.2.2.3 Stability conditions of the Newmark scheme The Newmark method is used quite widely in the field of mechanics, because it makes it possible to choose the order of the integration, to introduce or not numerical damping, and it possesses a very good accuracy. It is unconditionally stable if: \gamma >0.5 and \beta >\frac{{(2\gamma +1)}^{2}}{4} A positive numerical damping is introduced if \gamma >\frac{1}{2} and a negative one if \gamma # 2nd step by the BDF2 method t\to t+\Delta t 1. compute a prediction of the acceleration at time t+\Delta t {\tilde{\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}}_{t+\Delta t}={\mathrm{M}}^{-1}\left({F}^{\mathit{ext}}(t+\Delta t)-\mathrm{C}{\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}-\mathrm{K}{\mathrm{X}}_{t}\right) 2. compute the effective loading {\tilde{\mathrm{R}}}_{t+\Delta t} : \begin{array}{cc}{\tilde{\mathrm{R}}}_{t+\Delta t}& =-{a}_{2}\mathrm{M}\left({\mathrm{X}}_{t}-{\gamma}_{1}{\mathrm{X}}_{t+\gamma \Delta t}-{\gamma}_{2}{\mathrm{X}}_{t}-{\gamma}_{3}{\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}\right)\\ & -\left({a}_{1}\mathrm{M}+{a}_{2}\mathrm{C}\right)\left({\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}-{\gamma}_{1}{\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t+\gamma \Delta t}-{\gamma}_{2}{\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}-{\gamma}_{3}{\tilde{\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}}_{t}\right)\end{array} 1. solve \tilde{\mathrm{K}}\cdot \delta {\mathrm{X}}_{t+\Delta t}={\tilde{\mathrm{R}}}_{t+\Delta t} 2. compute the displacements, velocities and accelerations at time t+\Delta t {\mathrm{X}}_{t+\Delta t}={\mathrm{X}}_{t}+\delta {\mathrm{X}}_{t+\Delta t} {\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t+\Delta t}={\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}+\frac{1}{{\gamma}_{3}\Delta t}\left(\delta {\mathrm{X}}_{t+\Delta t}-{\mathrm{X}}_{t}+{\gamma}_{1}{\mathrm{X}}_{t+\gamma \Delta t}+{\gamma}_{2}{\mathrm{X}}_{t}+{\gamma}_{3}{\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t}\right) {\ddot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t+\Delta t}={\mathrm{M}}^{-1}\left({F}^{\mathit{ext}}(t+\Delta t)-\mathrm{C}{\dot{\mathrm{X}}}_{t+\Delta t}-\mathrm{K}{\mathrm{X}}_{t+\Delta t}\right) 1. computation of the next time step: return to b)1) The details of how these expressions are obtained are in [TARDIEU2021]. 2.2.3.3 Stability conditions The TRBDF2 scheme is of order two, implicit and therefore unconditionally stable, because \gamma \ge 1/2 . It introduces a frequency distortion which increases with the frequency. Furthermore, it is A-stable and, \gamma =2-\sqrt{(2)} having been fixed, its spectral radius is zero, and therefore this scheme is L-stable. 2.3 Explicit integration methods 2.3.1 Introduction Several explicit integration methods are presented: the second-order central-difference scheme, a fourth-order Devogelaere-Fu scheme and the adaptive time-step schemes ADAPT and Runge-Kutta. These three methods are available in the operator DYNA_VIBRA / BASE_CALCUL=’GENE’. The schemes are presented considering only linear forces. However the taking into account of the non-linear forces is readily deduced from them by the pseudo-force technique. 2.3.2 Devogelaere-Fu method 2.3.2.1 Presentation To present the Devogelaere-Fu algorithm, abbreviated as DEVOGE in Code_Aster , the dynamic problem is put in the form: \mathrm{M}.{\ddot{X}}_{t}+\mathrm{C}.{\dot{X}}_{t}=\mathrm{G}\left(t,{X}_{t}\right) where the matrix C is assumed diagonal. r5.07.01 Computation of non-linear modes with the operator MODE_NON_LINE r5.07.01 Computation of non-linear modes with the operator MODE_NON_LINE Summary: The operator MODE_NON_LINE makes it possible to compute the non-linear modes of an autonomous conservative linear system endowed with localised impact non-linearities. The numerical methods used for the computation of the non-linear modes are described here. 1 Introduction Non-linear modes are a mathematical tool which makes it possible to interpret non-linear dynamic phenomena. They are an extension of the eigenmodes R5.01.01 used to interpret linear dynamic systems. The operator MODE_NON_LINE makes it possible to compute the non-linear modes of dynamic systems with localised impact non-linearities. The definition of the non-linear modes will be recalled, then the impact non-linearities supported by the operator (unilateral, bilateral and annular contact) will be described, and finally the algorithm employed will be described. The latter is a combination of the harmonic balance method (EH) and of the asymptotic numerical method (MAN), which is called EHMAN (cf. [Bib1]). This documentation is not an exhaustive presentation of non-linear modes. It merely recalls the main assumptions under which non-linear modes may be sought using MODE_NON_LINE, together with the principles adopted for the representation of the non-linearities and the basic algorithmic elements. For a more complete presentation, and the details of the implementation, the reader is referred to reference [Bib1]. 2 Definitions of non-linear modes The first definition was given by Rosenberg in the 1960s, but it was at the beginning of the 1990s that the theoretically most solid definition of non-linear modes was given, using the theory of dynamical systems. Thus a non-linear mode is defined as “a two-dimensional invariant manifold of the phase space, tangent at a stable equilibrium point of the linearised system” (cf. [Bib2]). For conservative systems, a non-linear mode may be defined as a “family of periodic solutions”. This definition is much more attractive, because it gives access to powerful numerical tools such as continuation methods. This is why it is this definition that has been chosen here; consequently MODE_NON_LINE allows the computation of a family of periodic solutions. 3 Modelling It is assumed that, in the absence of contact, the structure under study has a linear behaviour and that the equations governing its dynamic equilibrium have been discretised by finite differences or by finite elements. A discrete system of second-order differential equations with n degrees of freedom is obtained. In general, these equations take the following form: \mathrm{M}.\ddot{\mathrm{U}}(t)+\mathrm{K}.\mathrm{U}(t)+{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(\mathrm{U}(t))=0, - \mathrm{M} is the mass matrix of the system, - K is the elastic stiffness matrix of the system, - {\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}} is the vector of the non-linear impact forces, One places oneself in the framework of localised non-linearities, that is to say that the forces are applied to a relatively small number of degrees of freedom. Let {I}_{\mathit{nl}} denote the set of the indices of these degrees of freedom, and {I}_{l} its complement, that is {I}_{n}=\lbrace 1,\dots ,n\rbrace ={I}_{\mathit{nl}}\cup {I}_{l} . The size of the vector {I}_{\mathit{nl}} is equal to {n}_{\mathit{nl}} . In order to be able to use the EHMAN algorithm, which combines the harmonic balance method (EH) and the asymptotic numerical method (MAN), a certain formalism must be adopted. It consists in rewriting the problem in the form of a first-order system, possessing non-linearities that are at most quadratic, that is a system in the unknown S of the form A(\dot{S})=C+L(S)+Q(S,S), where C is a constant, L is a linear form and Q a quadratic form. The terms on the right-hand side are in general grouped under the name R(S) ; the problem to be solved is then written in condensed form A(\dot{S})=R(S) To this end, two additional vectors of unknowns are introduced, {\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t) and \mathrm{Z}(t) , together with additional equations defining these vectors. The vector {\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t) describes the contact force and the vector \mathrm{Z}(t) is called the vector of auxiliary variables. The vector \mathrm{Z}(t) is of size {n}_{z} . This relatively abstract rewriting, detailed by means of examples, leads to the solution of a system of the form \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\dot{\mathrm{U}}(t)=\mathrm{V}(t),\\ \mathrm{M}.\dot{\mathrm{V}}(t)=-\mathrm{K}\mathrm{U}(t)-\left(\begin{array}{c}0\\ {\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(\mathrm{U}(t))\end{array}\right),\\ 0=\mathrm{G}({\mathrm{U}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t),{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t),\mathrm{Z}(t)),\end{array} where \mathrm{G} is a quadratic operator, which defines the contact implicitly. \mathrm{G} may be decomposed in the following way \mathrm{G}(\mathrm{S}(t))={\mathrm{G}}_{\mathrm{c}}+{\mathrm{G}}_{l}(\mathrm{S}(t))+{\mathrm{G}}_{\mathrm{q}}(\mathrm{S}(t),\mathrm{S}(t)). {\mathrm{G}}_{\mathrm{c}} is a constant mapping, {\mathrm{G}}_{l} a linear one and {\mathrm{G}}_{\mathrm{q}} a bilinear one. 3.1 Unilateral contact | | | The unilateral-contact non-linearity, in its non-regular form, is written: {\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t)=\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\alpha ({u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-g)\mathit{si}{u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)⩾g,\\ 0\mathit{si}{u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)⩽g,\end{array} where \alpha is the contact stiffness, g the gap between the node of the structure and the contact node. The regularisation proposed is written in the implicit form {\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t)({\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t)-\alpha ({u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-g))-\alpha \eta =0, where \eta represents the regularisation parameter. 3.2 Bilateral contact | | | The bilateral-contact non-linearity, in its non-regular form, is written {\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t)=\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\alpha ({u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-g)\mathit{si}{u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)⩾g,\\ 0\mathit{si}\mid {u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)\mid ⩽g,\\ \alpha ({u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)+g)\mathit{si}{u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)⩽-g,\end{array} where \alpha is the contact stiffness, g the gap between the node of the structure and the contact node. The regularisation proposed is written in the following implicit form {f}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)({f}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-\alpha ({u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-g))({f}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-\alpha ({u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)+g))-{\alpha}^{2}\eta {u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)=0, where \eta represents the regularisation parameter. It may be rewritten in a quadratic form, \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\alpha}^{2}{g}^{2}{f}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-\eta {\alpha}^{2}{u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-{f}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)z(t)=0,\\ z(t)-{({f}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-\alpha {u}^{\mathit{nl}}(t))}^{2}=0.\end{array} 3.3 Annular contact | | | One introduces z(t) , the radial distance from the equilibrium position ({e}_{x},{e}_{y}) of the impact node, whose current position is ({u}_{x}^{\mathit{nl}},{u}_{y}^{\mathit{nl}}) . z(t) is written z(t)=\sqrt{{\left({u}_{x}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-{e}_{x}\right)}^{2}+{\left({u}_{y}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-{e}_{y}\right)}^{2}}. The annular-contact non-linearity, in its non-regular form, is written {\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t)=\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\alpha (z(t)-g)\mathit{si}z(t)>g,\\ 0\mathit{si}z(t)⩽g,\end{array} where g denotes the radius of the ring (in other words the gap) and \alpha ( \alpha >0 ) denotes the associated stiffness coefficient. Introducing the components {f}_{x}^{\mathit{nl}} and {f}_{y}^{\mathit{nl}} of the non-linear force in the directions x and y , the regularisation proposed is written in the following implicit form \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t)\left({\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t)-\alpha (z(t)-g)\right)-\alpha \eta =0,\\ {z}^{2}(t)-{({u}_{x}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-{e}_{x})}^{2}-{({u}_{y}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)-{e}_{y})}^{2}=0,\\ {f}_{x}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)z(t)–{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t){u}_{x}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)=0,\\ {f}_{y}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)z(t)–{\mathrm{f}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t){u}_{y}^{\mathit{nl}}(t)=0,\end{array} where \eta represents the regularisation parameter. 4 Procedure for computing the non-linear modes One seeks the periodic solutions of the system \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\mathrm{M}.\ddot{\mathrm{U}}(t)+\mathrm{K}\mathrm{U}(t)+\left(\begin{array}{c}0\\ {\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(\mathrm{U}(t))\end{array}\right)=0,\\ \mathrm{G}({\mathrm{U}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t),{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t),\mathrm{Z}(t))=0,\end{array} by writing the vector \mathrm{U}(t) by means of a Fourier series truncated at order {H}_{l} (assuming that the influence of the higher harmonics is negligible), that is \mathrm{U}(t)={\mathrm{U}}_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{{H}_{l}}{\mathrm{U}}_{\mathrm{Ck}}\cos(k\omega t)+{\mathrm{U}}_{\mathrm{Sk}}\sin(k\omega t). The same expansion is performed for the vectors of unknowns {\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t) and \mathrm{Z}(t) , but with a different truncation order, called {H}_{\mathit{nl}} . One then has \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t)={\mathrm{F}}_{0}^{\mathrm{nl}}+\sum_{k=1}^{{H}_{\mathit{nl}}}{\mathrm{F}}_{\mathrm{Ck}}^{\mathrm{nl}}\cos(k\omega t)+{\mathrm{F}}_{\mathrm{Sk}}^{\mathrm{nl}}\sin(k\omega t),\\ \mathrm{Z}(t)={\mathrm{Z}}_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{{H}_{\mathit{nl}}}{\mathrm{Z}}_{\mathrm{Ck}}\cos(k\omega t)+{\mathrm{Z}}_{\mathrm{Sk}}\sin(k\omega t).\end{array} Nota Bene: The choice of a different order follows directly from the quantities represented. For a system with little impact, in the neighbourhood of the linear mode, the response \mathrm{U}(t) will be close to a pure sine. A small number of harmonics will therefore be chosen. One will increase {H}_{l} when seeking to obtain solutions associated with high energy levels. On the other hand, even for weak impact forces, the spectral content may be significant, in particular if the impact is stiff. A large number of harmonics must therefore be retained, and one will therefore in general have {H}_{\mathit{nl}}\gg {H}_{l} . In practice, one may begin by carrying out an analysis by choosing relatively low orders, in order to have an idea of the principal behaviour. On the other hand, with a small number of harmonics, one will not be able to capture the bifurcations correctly. The values of {H}_{l} and {H}_{\mathit{nl}} will therefore be increased gradually in order to bring out more complex behaviours. After a harmonic balance has been performed, an under-determined algebraic system is obtained whose unknowns are the Fourier coefficients of \mathrm{U}(t) , {\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{nl}}(t) and \mathrm{Z}(t) and the additional unknown, the natural angular frequency \omega . These unknowns are gathered into a single vector in order to put the system in the form (). The MAN may then be used as indicated in reference [Bib3]. To this end, the vector of unknowns S is expanded as a power series in a path parameter a S(a)={S}_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{{N}_{\mathit{MAN}}}{a}^{k}{S}_{k}, where {S}_{0} corresponds to the initialisation vector of the algorithm, and {S}_{k} for k=1,\dots ,{N}_{\mathit{MAN}} are the coefficients of the power series that remain to be determined. Next, the function R is expanded as a Taylor series, in the neighbourhood of the initialisation vector {S}_{0} 0=R(S(a))=R({S}_{0})+\frac{\mathit{dR}}{\mathit{dS}}({S}_{0})\left(\sum_{k=1}^{{N}_{\mathit{MAN}}}{a}^{k}{S}_{k}\right)+\frac{{d}^{2}R}{{\mathit{dS}}^{2}}({S}_{0})\left(\sum_{k=1}^{{N}_{\mathit{MAN}}}{a}^{k}{S}_{k}\right)\left(\sum_{l=1}^{{N}_{\mathit{MAN}}}{a}^{l}{S}_{l}\right) This relation is true for any a ; one then proceeds to the solution of a sequence of {N}_{\mathit{MAN}} linear systems possessing the same tangent matrix, depending on one another recursively. The solution of these systems makes it possible to obtain the vectors {S}_{k} . Note that this matrix can be computed analytically, since the function R is quadratic, that is \frac{\mathit{dR}}{\mathit{dS}}({S}_{0}){e}_{i}=L({e}_{i})+Q({e}_{i},{S}_{0})+Q({S}_{0,}{e}_{i}), where {e}_{i} is the vector of the canonical basis. A branch of solutions S(a) with a\in [0,{a}_{max}] is thus obtained, where {a}_{max} represents the domain of validity of the power series. From then on, the branches of periodic solutions which form the non-linear modes of the model may be obtained. The method also makes it possible to locate simple bifurcations by the detection of a geometric series in the power-series representation. 5 Bibliography [Bib1] E.H. r6.01.02 Generalities on the conjugate gradient: GCPC Aster and use of PETSc r6.01.02 Generalities on the conjugate gradient: GCPC Aster and use of PETSc Summary: In the framework of thermo-mechanical simulations, the bulk of the computational cost often comes from the construction and the solution of linear systems . The choice of the right linear solver is therefore essential, on the one hand for its speed, but also for its robustness and the memory space it requires. Each time, a compromise has to be struck between these constraints. For 60 years two types of solvers have competed for supremacy in the field, the direct ones and the iterative ones. Hence, as a precaution, a diversified offer from mechanics codes in this respect. code_aster is no exception to the rule. It offers three direct solvers (Gauss R6.02.01, the native multifrontal solver R6.02.02 and the external product MUMPS R6.02.03), iterative solvers of Krylov type (GCPC Aster and all those of the PETSc library). In this document , one details from a theoretical, algorithmic and code_aster modelling point of view, the fundamentals of the GCPC and of the other Krylov solvers implemented in PETSc . In particular, one highlights their links with the other linear solvers of the code and with continuous optimisation methods. One then goes on to their implementation difficulties, their parameter settings, their scopes as well as a few pieces of advice on use. For more details and advice on the use of linear solvers one may consult the specific user's guides U4.50.01/[U2.08.03]. The related issues of improving the performance (RAM/CPU) of an analysis and of the use of parallelism are also the subject of detailed guides: U1.03.03 and U2.08.06. 1 Problem statement In the numerical simulation of physical phenomena, a significant computational cost often comes from the construction and the solution of linear systems . Structural mechanics is no exception to the rule! The cost of constructing the system depends on the number of integration points and on the complexity of the constitutive laws, whereas that of the solution is linked to the number of unknowns, to the modellings adopted and to the topology (bandwidth, conditioning). When the number of unknowns explodes, the second stage becomes predominant 1 and it is therefore this latter stage that will mainly interest us here. Moreover, when it is possible to be more efficient on this solution phase, thanks to access to a parallel machine, this advantage can propagate to the phase of constitution of the system proper (elementary computations and assemblies, cf. U2.08.06). These inversions of linear systems are in fact omnipresent in the codes and often buried deep inside other numerical algorithms : non-linear scheme, time integration, modal analysis…. One seeks, for example, the vector of nodal displacements (or of displacement increments) u satisfying a linear system of the type \mathrm{Ku}=f (1-1) with K a stiffness matrix and f a vector expressing the application of generalised forces to the mechanical system. In general, the solution of this type of problem requires a (wider) questioning than it appears: - Does one have access to the matrix or does one merely know its action on a vector? - Is this matrix sparse or dense? - What are its numerical properties (symmetry, positive definite…) and structural properties (real/complex, banded, block…)? - Does one want to solve a single system (1-1), several simultaneously 2 or consecutively 3? Or even several different and successive systems whose matrices are very close 4? - In the case of successive solutions, can one reuse previous results in order to facilitate the next solutions (cf. restart technique, partial factorisation)? - What is the order of magnitude of the size of the problem, of the matrix and of its factorised form relative to the processing capacities of the CPUs and of the associated memories (RAM, disk)? - Does one want a very accurate solution or merely an estimate (cf. nested solvers)? - Does one have access to linear-algebra libraries (and to their MPI, BLAS, LAPACK… prerequisites) or must one call upon “in-house” products? In Code_Aster , one builds the matrix explicitly and stores it in MORSE format 5 . With most modellings, the matrix is sparse (because of the finite-element discretisation), potentially ill-conditioned 6 and often real, symmetric and indefinite 7 . In non-linear analysis, in modal analysis or during thermo-mechanical chaining, one often treats problems of the “multiple right-hand sides” type. Discrete frictional-contact methods take advantage of partial-factorisation capabilities. On the other hand, Code_Aster also uses scenarios of simultaneous solutions (Schur complements of contact and of substructuring…). As for the sizes of the problems, even if they swell from year to year, they remain modest compared with CFD: of the order of a million unknowns but for hundreds of time steps or Newton iterations. Furthermore, from a “middleware and hardware” point of view , the code now relies on numerous optimised and durable libraries (MPI, BLAS, LAPACK, METIS, SCOTCH, PETSc, MUMPS…) and is used mainly on SMP clusters (fast networks, large RAM and disk storage capacity). One therefore seeks above all to optimise the use of linear solvers with this in mind. For 60 years, two types of techniques have competed for supremacy in the field, the direct solvers and the iterative ones (cf. [Che05][Dav06][Duf06][Gol96][LT98][Liu89][Meu99][Saa03]). The former are robust and terminate in a finite number of operations (theoretically) known in advance. Their theory is relatively well completed and their declension according to many types of matrices and software architectures is very complete. In particular, their multilevel algorithmics is well suited to the memory hierarchies of present-day machines. However, they require storage capacities that grow rapidly with the size of the problem, which limits the extensibility of their parallelism 8 . Even if this parallelism can be decomposed into several independent layers, thus multiplying the performance. By contrast, iterative methods are more “scalable” when one increases the number of processors. Their theory abounds in numerous “open problems”, especially in finite arithmetic. In practice, their convergence in a “reasonable” number of iterations is not always secured; it depends on the structure of the matrix, on the starting point, on the stopping criterion… This type of solver has more difficulty in breaking through in industrial structural mechanics, where one often accumulates heterogeneities, non-linearities and junctions of models that undermine the conditioning of the working operator. On the other hand, they are not suited to solving efficiently problems of the “multiple right-hand sides” type. Yet these are very frequent in the algorithmics of mechanical simulations. Unlike their direct counterparts, it is not possible to propose THE iterative solver that will solve any linear system. The matching of the type of algorithm to a class of problems is done case by case. They nevertheless present other advantages which historically earned them a right of citizenship for certain applications. For an equivalent memory management, they require less than direct solvers, because one only needs to know the action of the matrix on an arbitrary vector, without truly having to store it. On the other hand, one is not subject to the “diktat” of the fill-in phenomenon which deteriorates the profile of the matrices; one can efficiently exploit the sparse character of the operators and control the accuracy of the results 9 . In the numerical-analysis literature, a preponderant place is often given to iterative solvers in general, and to the variants of the conjugate gradient in particular. The most seasoned authors agree that, even if its use gains “market share” over the years and the variants, certain fields remain refractory. Among these, structural mechanics, the simulation of electronic circuits… To paraphrase these authors, the use of direct solvers belongs to the domain of technique whereas the choice of the right iterative-method/preconditioner pair is rather an art! Despite its biblical simplicity on paper, the solution of a linear system, even a symmetric positive-definite one, is not “a long quiet river”. Between two evils, fill-in/pivoting and preconditioning, one must choose! Figure 1-1._ Two classes of methods for solving a linear system: the direct ones and the iterative ones. Lately the arrival of hybrid solvers [Boi08], which mix the two approaches in order to take advantage of their respective benefits, somewhat upsets the situation. On “frontier simulations” comprising tens of millions of unknowns, the conjugate gradient may find itself competed with by these new approaches (especially for problems of the multiple-right-hand-side type). But in fact it is generally present as the interface solver of these hybrids. The latter can be seen as particular preconditioners (multilevel, multigrid, DD) of a conjugate gradient or of any other Krylov methods (GMRES, BiCG-Stab…). On the other hand, given its simplicity of implementation (in sequential as in parallel) and its low memory occupation, it often remains the only alternative for tackling very large problems [10]_ . Notes: - The two great families of solvers must be seen more as complementary than as competing. One often seeks to mix them: DD methods [Boi08], preconditioner by incomplete factorisation (cf. § 4.2) or of multigrid type [Tar09], iterative-refinement procedure at the end of a direct solver [Boi09]… - For more details on the linear-algebra libraries implementing these methods and a few benchmark results confronting them, one may consult the documentation [Boi09]. But to really take advantage of these products, one must exploit them in parallel mode. The documentation [Boi08] illustrates a few aspects of parallel computing (hardware, methodology, languages, performance indicators) and specifies the different levels of parallelism that can be exploited in a code such as Code_Aster. Let us now turn to the set of chapters around which this note will be organised. After having set out the different formulations of the problem (linear system, minimisations of a functional) and in order to make the reader better feel the implicit subtleties of gradient-type methods, one proposes a rapid survey of their fundamentals: the classical “steepest-descent” then the general descent methods as well as their links with the CG. These reminders being made, the algorithmic unfolding of the CG becomes clear (at least one hopes so!) and its theoretical properties of convergence, orthogonality and complexity follow from it. Complements are rapidly sketched in order to put the CG into perspective with recurrent notions in numerical analysis: Petrov–Galerkin projection and Krylov space, orthogonalisation problem, equivalence with the Lanczos method and spectral properties, nested solvers and parallelism. One then details the “necessary evil” constituted by the preconditioning of the working operator , a few strategies often used and those retained for the native GCPC of Code_Aster and for the PETSc solvers. One concludes with the particular implementation difficulties in the code , the questions of parameter setting and of scope as well as with a few pieces of advice on use . Note: - The effective implementation and the maintenance of the iterative solvers in Code_Aster are the fruit of teamwork: J.P.Grégoire, J.Pellet, T.DeSoza, N.Tardieu, O.Boiteau… - In this document, a good number of figures have been borrowed from the introductory paper of J.R. Shewchuk [Sh94] with his kind permission: ©1994 by Jonathan Richard Shewchuk. For Code_Aster, see the ‘profiling’ study conducted by N.Anfaoui [Anf03]. Same matrix but several independent right-hand sides; cf. construction of a Schur complement. Problem of the multiple-right-hand-side type: same matrix but several successive and interdependent right-hand sides; cf. Newton algorithm without updating of the tangent matrix. Problem of the multiple-left-hand-side type: several successive and interdependent matrices and right-hand sides, but with matrices that are “spectrally” close; cf. Newton algorithm with updating of the tangent matrix. Also called SCC for ‘Symmetric Compressed Column storage’. In structural mechanics the conditioning \eta (K) is known to be rather poor. It can vary, typically, from 105 to 1012 and the fact of refining the mesh, of using stretched elements or structural elements has dramatic consequences on this figure (cf. B.Smith. A parallel implementation of an iterative substructuring algorithm for problems in 3D. SIAM J.Sci.Comput., 14 (1992), pp406-423. §3.1 or I.FRIED. Condition of finite element matrices generated from nonuniform meshes. AIAA J., 10 (1972), pp219-221.) The indefinite rather than positive-definite character is due to the adjunction of additional variables (called “Lagrange” variables) in order to impose simple or generalised Dirichlet boundary conditions [R3.03.01]. One also speaks of “scalability” or of scaling up. Which can be very interesting in the framework of nested solvers (e.g. Newton + GCPC), cf. V.Frayssé. The power of backward error analysis. HDR of the Institut National Polytechnique de Toulouse (2000). Everything is relative. The present limits are rather a few million unknowns for a PC and several hundred million for a computing-centre machine. The large CFD codes (for EDF: Code_Saturne, TELEMAC…) are thus completely backed by iterative solvers of conjugate-gradient type. They allow them to distribute streams of data/processing over thousands of processors and thus to manage, via parallelism, problems of very large size. 2 Descent methods 2.1 Positioning of the problem Let K be the stiffness matrix (of size N ) to be inverted; if it has the “good taste” of being symmetric positive definite (SPD in the English-language literature), which is often [11]_ the case in structural mechanics, one shows by simple differentiation that the following problems are equivalent: - Solution of the usual linear system with u the solution vector (of the displacements or displacement increments, resp. in temperature….) and f the vector expressing the application of generalised forces to the thermo-mechanical system ({P}_{1})\text{Ku}=f (2.1-1) - Minimisation of the quadratic functional representing the energy of the system, with \text{ } the usual Euclidean scalar product, \begin{array}{}({P}_{2})u=\underset{v\in {\Re }^{N}}{\text{Arg}\min}J(v)\\ \text{avec}J(v):=\frac{1}{2}\langle \text{v,Kv}\rangle -\langle f,v\rangle =\frac{1}{2}{v}^{T}\text{Kv}-{f}^{T}v\end{array} (2.1-2) Because of the “positive-definiteness” of the matrix which makes J strictly convex, the vector cancelling [12]_ \nabla J corresponds to the unique [13]_ global minimum u . This is illustrated by the following relation, valid whatever the symmetric K , J(v)=J(u)+\frac{1}{2}{(v-u)}^{T}K(v-u) (2.1-3) Thus, for any vector v different from the solution u , the positive-definite character of the operator makes the second term strictly positive and therefore u is also a global minimum. Figure 2.1-1. Example of a quadratic J in N=2 dimensions with K:=\left[\begin{array}{cc}3& 2\\ 2& 6\end{array}\right] and f:=\left[\begin{array}{c}2\\ -8\end{array}\right] : graph (a), level lines (b) and gradient vectors (c). The spectrum of the operator is ({\lambda}_{1};{v}_{1})=(7;{[1,2]}^{T}) and ({\lambda}_{2};{v}_{2})=(2;{[-2,1]}^{T}) . This result, very important in practice, rests entirely on this famous positive-definiteness, a somewhat “ethereal” property of the working matrix. On a two-dimensional problem ( N=2 !) one can form a clear picture of it (cf. figure 2.1-1): the paraboloid shape which focuses the unique minimum at the point {[2,-2]}^{T} of zero slope. - Minimisation of the energy norm of the error e(v)=v-u , more meaningful for mechanicians, \begin{array}{}({P}_{3})u=\underset{v\in {\Re }^{N}}{\text{Arg}\min}E(v)\\ \text{avec}E(v):=\langle \text{Ke}(v),e(v)\rangle ={(\text{Ke}(v))}^{T}e(v)={\parallel e(v)\parallel }_{K}^{2}\end{array} (2.1-4) From a mathematical point of view, this is nothing other than a matrix norm (legitimate since K is SPD). One often prefers to express it via a residual r(v)=f-\text{Kv} E(v)=\langle r(v),{K}^{-1}r(v)\rangle =r{(v)}^{T}{K}^{-1}r(v) (2.1-5) Notes: - The scope of use of the conjugate gradient can in fact be extended to any operator, not necessarily symmetric or positive definite or even square! To do this one defines the solution of ( {P}_{1} ) as being that, in the least-squares sense, of the minimisation problem ({P}_{2})'u=\underset{v\in {\Re }^{N}}{\text{Arg}\min}{\parallel \text{Kv}-f\parallel }^{2} (2.1-6) > By differentiation one arrives at the so-called “normal” equations whose operator is square, symmetric and positive > ({P}_{2})\text{''}\underset{\tilde{K}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{K}^{T}K}}u={K}^{T}f (2.1-7) > One can therefore apply a CG or a steepest-descent to it without too much trouble. - The solution of the problem ( {P}_{1} ) is at the intersection of N hyperplanes of dimension N-1 . For example, for the case of figure 2.1-1, it is expressed trivially in the form of intersections of straight lines: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\mathrm{3x}}_{1}+{\mathrm{2x}}_{2}=2\\ {\mathrm{2x}}_{1}+{\mathrm{6x}}_{2}=-8\end{array} (2.1-8) Figure 2.1-2. Solution of example no. 1 by intersection of straight lines. - Gradient-type methods stand apart from this philosophy; they fit naturally into the framework of minimisation of a quadratic functional, in which they were developed and intuitively understood. 2.2 Steepest Descent 2.2.1 Principle This last remark prefigures the philosophy of the method called “of the steepest slope”, better known under its English name of ‘Steepest Descent’: one constructs the sequence of iterates {u}^{i} by following the direction along which J decreases the most, at least locally, that is {d}^{i}=-\nabla {J}^{i}={r}^{i} with {J}^{i}:=J({u}^{i})\text{et}{r}^{i}:=f-{\text{Ku}}^{i} . At the i th iteration, one will therefore seek to construct {u}^{i+1} such that: {u}^{i+1}:={u}^{i}+{\alpha}^{i}{r}^{i} (2.2-1) and {J}^{i+1} Formally, at each iteration i of the algorithm, one thus seeks an increment {\delta}^{i}:={\alpha}^{i}{r}^{i} such that: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}^{i}:={u}^{0}+{\delta}^{i}{\delta}^{i}:={\alpha}^{i}{r}^{i}\in {K}_{i}\\ \langle {r}^{0}-K{\delta}^{i},w\rangle =0\forall w\in {L}_{i}={K}_{i}\end{array} (2.2-13) > This general framework constitutes what one calls the Petrov–Galerkin conditions. 2.2.4 Complexity and memory occupation The major part of the computational cost of algorithm 1 resides in the update (2.2-5) and, more particularly, in the matrix–vector product K{r}^{i} . On the other hand, one has already mentioned that its convergence was secured and took place in a number of iterations proportional to the conditioning of the matrix (cf. (2.2-11)). The computational complexity of the algorithm is therefore, if one takes into account the sparse character of the operator, of the order of \Theta (\eta (K)\text{cN}) where c is the average number of non-zero terms per row of K . Thus, with problems resulting from the finite-element discretisation of second-order elliptic operators [18]_ (resp. of fourth order), one has operator conditionings in \eta (K)=\Theta ({N}^{2/d}) (resp. \eta (K)=\Theta ({N}^{4/d}) ) where d is the space dimension. The computational complexity of the Steepest Descent in this framework is thus written \Theta ({\text{cN}}^{\frac{2}{d}+1}) (resp. \Theta ({\text{cN}}^{\frac{4}{d}+1}) ). As regards memory occupation, only the storage of the working matrix is possibly required [19]_ : \Theta (\text{cN}) . In practice, the computer implementation of sparse storage imposes the management of additional integer vectors: for example, for the MORSE storage used in Code_Aster , vectors of the end-of-row indices and of the column indices of the non-zero elements of the profile. Whence an effective memory complexity of \Theta (\text{cN}) reals and \Theta (\text{cN}+N) integers. 2.3 “General” descent method 2.3.1 Principle A crucial step of these methods is the choice of their descent direction [20]_ . Even if the gradient of the functional remains the main ingredient, one can perfectly well choose another version {d}^{i} than that required for the Steepest Descent. At the i th iteration, one will therefore seek to construct {u}^{i+1} satisfying {u}^{i+1}:={u}^{i}+{\alpha}^{i}{d}^{i} (2.3-1) with {\alpha}^{i}=\underset{\alpha \in \left[{\alpha}_{m},{\alpha}_{M}\right]}{\text{Arg}\min}J({u}^{i}+\alpha {d}^{i}) (2.3-2) This is of course only a generalisation of the 'Steepest Descent' seen previously and one shows that its choices of the descent parameter and its orthogonality property generalise \begin{array}{}{\alpha}^{i}:=\frac{\langle {r}^{i},{d}^{i}\rangle }{\langle {d}^{i},{\text{Kd}}^{i}\rangle }\\ \langle {d}^{i},{r}^{i+1}\rangle =0\end{array} (2.3-3) Whence the same “zigzag” effect during the unfolding of the process and a convergence similar to (2.2-6) with an error attenuation factor bounded from below by: {\omega}^{i}:=1-\frac{{\langle {r}^{i},{d}^{i}\rangle }^{2}}{\langle {K}^{-1}{r}^{i},{r}^{i}\rangle \langle {\text{Kd}}^{i},{d}^{i}\rangle }\ge \frac{1}{\eta (K)}{\langle \frac{{r}^{i}}{\parallel {r}^{i}\parallel },\frac{{d}^{i}}{\parallel {d}^{i}\parallel }\rangle }^{2} (2.3-4) From this result one can then formulate two observations: - The conditioning of the operator intervenes directly on the attenuation factor and therefore on the speed of convergence, - To ensure convergence (sufficient condition) it is necessary, at a given iteration, that the descent direction not be orthogonal to the residual. The sufficient condition of this last item is of course verified for the Steepest Descent ( {d}^{i}={r}^{i} ) and it will impose a choice of descent direction for the conjugate gradient. To remedy the problem raised by the first point, we shall see that it is possible to constitute a working operator \tilde{K} whose conditioning is smaller. One then speaks of preconditioning. Still in the case of an SPD operator, the unfolding of a “general” descent method is therefore written \begin{array}{}\text{Initialisation}{u}^{0},{d}^{0}\text{donnés,}{r}^{0}=f-{\text{Ku}}^{0}\\ \text{Boucle en}i\\ (1){z}^{i}={\text{Kd}}^{i}\\ (2){\alpha}^{i}=\frac{\langle {r}^{i},{d}^{i}\rangle }{\langle {d}^{i},{z}^{i}\rangle }(\text{paramètre optimal de descente})\\ (3){u}^{i+1}={u}^{i}+{\alpha}^{i}{d}^{i}(\text{nouvel itéré})\\ (4){r}^{i+1}={r}^{i}-{\alpha}^{i}{z}^{i}(\text{nouvel résidu})\\ (5)\text{Test d'arrêt via}{J}^{i+1}-{J}^{i},\parallel {d}^{i}\parallel \text{ou}\parallel {r}^{i+1}\parallel (\text{par exemple})\\ (6)\text{Calcul de la dd}{d}^{i+1}={d}^{i+1}(\nabla {J}^{k},{\nabla}^{2}{J}^{k},{d}^{k}\dots )\end{array} Algorithm 2: Descent method in the case of a quadratic functional. The designation non-linear conjugate gradient is here rather synonymous with “non-convex”: there is no longer any dependence between the minimisation problem ( {P}_{2} ) and a linear system ( {P}_{1} ).
