In the framework of a quadratic cost function of type (2.1-2b), it suffices just to substitute for step (1) the updating of the residual and the computation of the optimal descent parameter. The CG is only a Fletcher‑Reeves method applied to the case of a convex quadratic functional. Now that we have well initiated the link between the descent methods, the conjugate gradient in the sense of an SPD linear solver and its version, seen from the end of the telescope of non-linear continuous optimisation, we are going (at last!) to get to the heart of the matter and argue the choice of a descent direction of type (2.3-5) for the standard CG. For more information on descent-type methods, the reader may refer to the excellent optimisation works (in the French language) of M. Minoux [Min08], J.C. Culioli [Cu94] or J.F.Bonnans et al [BGLS]. The cancellation of the derivative is a particular case of the convex and unconstrained case of the famous Kuhn–Tucker relations characterising the optimum of a differentiable optimisation problem. It is called the “Euler equation”. Without this convexity, one is not assured of uniqueness. One must then come to terms with local minima! Whence a direct and visual link between poor matrix conditioning and a narrow and winding valley where the minimisation is mishandled. The positive-definiteness of the operator assures us of the “good nature” of the parameter {\omega}^{i} . It is indeed an attenuation factor because 0\le {\omega}^{i}\le 1 . That is \underset{i\to \infty }{\lim}\frac{J({u}^{i+1})-J(u)}{J({u}^{i})-J(u)}\le \alpha :={(\frac{\eta (K)-1}{\eta (K)+1})}^{2} The Lanczos method not computing these intermediate terms {\alpha}^{i} and {\beta}^{i} , but directly the tridiagonal terms, does not have access to this information. On the other hand, it can take into account symmetric matrices that are not necessarily positive definite. - Therefore, whether it is a matter of inverting a linear system or of determining part of its spectrum, these Krylov methods function on the same principle: progressively determine the basis vectors generating the projection space at the same time as the result of this projection. In the CG as in Lanczos, one strives to make this projection the most robust (orthogonality of the basis vectors), the most reduced (projection size = number of iterations) and the simplest possible (orthogonal projection). For the modal solver, another constraint is juxtaposed: approximate as well as possible the spectrum of the working operator by that of the Rayleigh matrix. In the non-symmetric case, one speaks of a projection that is no longer orthogonal but oblique and the rapprochements are then made between GMRES and Arnoldi. - In exact arithmetic, after N iterations, one has completely determined the whole spectrum of the operator. In practice, the problems of round-off and of orthogonalisation prevent us from doing so. But, if one is sufficiently patient ( m\gg N ), one is nevertheless capable of detecting the whole spectrum: this is what one calls the Lanczos phenomenon (cf. [Boi01] §5.3.1/5.3.3). - Paradoxically the loss of orthogonality is above all imputable to the convergence of an eigenmode more than to round-off errors! This analysis due to C.C.Paige (1980) attests that as soon as an eigenmode is captured it disturbs the orthogonal arrangement of the Lanczos vectors (in the case which concerns us, the residuals and the descent directions). In modal analysis, the numerical treatment of this parasitic phenomenon has been the subject of numerous palliative developments. As regards the CG, it must curb the effectiveness of the reorthogonalisation methods of the descent directions mentioned previously. 3.3.2 Nested solvers As has already been remarked, linear solvers are often buried deep inside other algorithms, and in particular, non-linear solvers of Newton type. For Code_Aster these are the most frequently used application cases: operators STAT_NON_LINE, DYNA_NON_LINE and THER_NON_LINE. In such a configuration, a linear solver such as the CG can play its trump card (with respect to a direct solver). Its iterative character proves useful for making the stopping test of the algorithm evolve (cf. step (5) algorithm 4) as a function of the relative error of the non-linear solver which encapsulates it: this is the nested-solvers issue (one also speaks of relaxation) [CM01][GY97][BFG] of which CERFACS is the “spearhead” in France. By relaxing at the opportune moment the precision required on the cancellation of the residual (for example a strategy in the case of a modal method of Krylov type + CG) or, on the contrary by hardening it (resp. modal method of power type + Gauss–Seidel + CG), one can thus gain in computational complexity on the CG without modifying the convergence of the global process. One must of course devise simple and inexpensive criteria so that the gain is substantial. This functionality could be inserted into Code_Aster (internal and automatic piloting of the value RESI_RELA). Note: - Certain authors have also asked themselves the question of the order of chaining of these algorithms: “Newton–CG” or “CG–Newton”? If from a computer-science and conceptual point of view, the question is quickly settled: one prefers the first solution, more readable, more flexible and which does not disturb the existing, from a numerical and algorithmic point of view, the share is more nuanced. It can depend on the “technical innards” deployed by the non-linear solver (tangent matrix, one-dimensional minimisation…) and by the CG deployed (preconditioner). Nevertheless, it seems that the natural order, “Newton–CG”, is the most efficient and the most evolutive. 3.3.3 Parallelism The CG, like many iterative solvers, lends itself well to parallelism. It is fairly scalable [23]_ . The principal elementary operations which constitute it (matrix–vector product, operation of [24]_ “daxpy and scalar-product type) decompose efficiently among different processors; only the parallelisation of the preconditioner (often based on a direct solver) can prove difficult (problems often called: ‘parallel preconditioning’). Moreover the linear-algebra libraries (PETSc, HYPRE, TRILINOS…) do not always propose a parallel version of their preconditioners. Concerning the preconditioners, one therefore has two criteria which tend to contradict each other: parallel efficiency and algorithmic efficiency. The codes therefore tend to favour preconditioners that are not very efficient from an algorithmic point of view [25]_ (Jacobi type) but not very greedy in memory and very parallelisable. The parallel gain (called speed-up) is immediately very interesting, but the sequential comparison point may not be very glorious [26]_ ! Another difficulty of parallelism also comes from the distribution of the data. One must see to it that the different rules which govern the data setup of the analysis (attribution of the boundary-condition zones, assignment of the materials, choice of the finite elements…) are not affected by the fact that each processor knows them only partially. This is what one calls the “consistency” of the distributed data [Boi08b]. Likewise, one must provide in the code the communications ad hoc during each global manipulation of data (stopping criteria, post-processings…). Notes: - Thus on a CRAY machine, J.P.Grégoire [Greg] adapted and parallelised, in shared memory and in distributed memory, an algorithm of preconditioned conjugate-gradient type. Four types of operations are carried out concurrently: the elementary vector operations, the scalar products, the matrix–vector products and the construction of the preconditioner (diagonal). Problems of ‘parallel preconditioning’ which have been solved only for the diagonal preconditioner, have unfortunately not allowed the porting of these prototypes into the official version of Code_Aster. - The direct solvers and the other iterative solvers (stationary methods Gauss–Seidel, SSOR..) are reputed less scalable than the Krylov methods (CG, GMRES…). We are moreover now going to tackle the thorny question of preconditioning for the CG. It will then become the Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient: GCPC. The Fletcher–Reeves and Polak–Ribière methods (cf. §2.3) also belong to this family of methods. Or extensibility in French. A method is said to be scalable from a strong point of view (this is the default criterion, ‘strong scalability’), if it makes it possible to solve a problem all the faster as one adds processors proportionally. Less commonly, one speaks of weak scalability (‘weak scalability’), when it is a matter of solving, in a comparable time, a larger problem by increasing by as much the number of processors (cf. [Boi08] §2.4). To take up a terminology proper to the BLAS library. An operation of DAXPY type makes linear combinations of vectors. Going so far as to tolerate convergences in thousands of iterations. Strictly speaking, to express a parallel gain, one should take as reference the best sequential computation. The latter calling upon a more efficient and possibly sequential preconditioner. The exercise nevertheless raises a difficulty: this operating point is often hard to exhibit. The size of the studies, taking into account the hardware characteristics of the machines, requires from the outset a computation distributed over tens of processors! 4 The Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (GCPC) 4.1 General description 4.1.1 Principle As one has been able to observe (and to hammer home!) in the previous paragraphs, the speed of convergence of the descent methods, and notably that of the conjugate gradient, depends on the conditioning of the matrix \eta (K) . The closer it is to its floor value, 1, the better the convergence. The principle of preconditioning is then “simple”; it consists in replacing the linear system of the problem ( {P}_{1} ) by an equivalent system of the type (left preconditioning): ({\tilde{P}}_{1})\underset{\tilde{K}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{M}^{-1}K}}u=\underset{\tilde{f}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{M}^{-1}f}} (4.1-1) such that, ideally: - The conditioning of it is obviously improved (this theoretical property, like the following one, are only very rarely demonstrated. They are often warranted only by numerical experiments): \eta (\tilde{K})\ll \eta (K) . - Just like the spectral distribution: eigenvalues more tightly packed. - {M}^{-1} is inexpensive to evaluate (as for the initial operator, one often only needs to know the action of the preconditioner on a vector): \text{Mv}=u easy to invert. - Or even easy to implement and, possibly, efficient to parallelise. - That it be as sparse as the initial matrix because it is a matter of limiting the additional memory footprint. - That it conserve for the working matrix \tilde{K} the same properties as the initial one: here, the SPD character. In theory, the best choice would be {M}^{-1}={K}^{-1} because then \eta (\tilde{K}={I}_{N})=1 , but if one has to invert the operator completely by a direct method in order to construct this preconditioner, it is of little practical interest! Although, one will see later that this idea is not as far-fetched as that. Put otherwise, the objective of a preconditioner is to pack the spectrum of the working operator; thus, as has already been mentioned, its “effective conditioning” will be improved together with the convergence of the GCPC. Graphically, this translates into a more spherical shape of the graph of the quadratic form. Even on a system with N=2 dimensions and with a “crude” preconditioner (cf. figure 4.1-1), the effects are noticeable. Figure 4.1-1. Effect of diagonal preconditioning on the paraboloid of example no. 1: (a) without, \eta (K)=3.5 , (b) with, \eta (\tilde{K})=2.8 . In the absolute, one can precondition a linear system on the left (‘left preconditioning’), on the right (resp. ‘right’) or by making a mixture of the two (resp. ‘split’). It is this last version which will be retained for our SPD operator, because one cannot directly apply the CG to solve ({\tilde{P}}_{1}) : even if {M}^{-1} and K are SPD, this is not necessarily the case of their product. The trick then consists in using an SPD preconditioning matrix, M , for which one will therefore be able to define another matrix ( M being real symmetric, it is diagonalisable in the form M={\text{UDU}}^{T} with D:=\text{diag}({\lambda}_{i}){\lambda}_{i}>0 and U an orthogonal matrix). The sought SPD matrix then comes from the associated decomposition {M}^{1/2}=\text{Udiag}(\sqrt{{\lambda}_{i}}){U}^{T} with {M}^{1/2} defined such that {({M}^{1/2})}^{2}=M . Whence the new working problem, this time SPD ({\hat{P}}_{1})\underset{\hat{\mathrm{K}}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{\mathrm{M}}^{-1/2}{\text{KM}}^{-1/2}}}\underset{\hat{\mathrm{u}}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{\mathrm{M}}^{1/2}\mathrm{u}}}=\underset{\hat{\mathrm{f}}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{\mathrm{M}}^{-1/2}\mathrm{f}}} (4.1-2) on which one will be able to apply the standard CG algorithm in order to constitute what one calls a Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (GCPC). 4.1.2 Algorithm In short, by substituting into algorithm 4 the expressions of the previous problem ({\hat{P}}_{1}) and by working a little at the simplification of the whole so as to manipulate only expressions in K , u and f , there comes the following unfolding. \begin{array}{}\text{Initialisation}{u}^{0}\text{donné,}{r}^{0}={\text{f-Ku}}^{0},{d}^{0}={M}^{-1}{r}^{0},{g}^{0}={d}^{0}\\ \text{Boucle en}i\\ (1){z}^{i}={\text{Kd}}^{i}\\ (2){\alpha}^{i}=\frac{\langle {r}^{i},{g}^{i}\rangle }{\langle {d}^{i},{z}^{i}\rangle }(\text{paramètre optimal de descente})\\ (3){u}^{i+1}={u}^{i}+{\alpha}^{i}{d}^{i}(\text{nouvel itéré})\\ (4){r}^{i+1}={r}^{i}-{\alpha}^{i}{z}^{i}(\text{nouveau résidu})\\ (5)\text{Test d'arrêt via}\langle {r}^{i+1},{r}^{i+1}\rangle (\text{par exemple})\\ (6){g}^{i+1}={M}^{-1}{r}^{i+1}(r\text{ésidu préconditionné})\\ (7){\beta}^{i+1}=\frac{\langle {r}^{i+1},{g}^{i+1}\rangle }{\langle {r}^{i},{g}^{i}\rangle }(\text{paramètre de conjugaison optimal})\\ (8){d}^{i+1}={g}^{i+1}+{\beta}^{i+1}{d}^{i}(\text{nouvelle dd})\end{array} Algorithm 5: Preconditioned conjugate gradient (GCPC). But in fact, the symmetric character of the initial preconditioned problem ({\tilde{P}}_{1}) is quite relative. It is inseparable from the underlying scalar product. If instead of taking the usual Euclidean scalar product, one uses a matrix scalar product defined with respect to K , M or {M}^{-1} , it is possible to symmetrise the preconditioned problem which was not so initially. As for Krylov methods in modal analysis, it is the pair (working operator, scalar product) that one must modulate in order to adapt to the problem! Thus, {M}^{-1}K being symmetric with respect to the M -scalar product, one can substitute this new working operator and this new scalar product into the algorithm of the non-preconditioned CG (algorithm 4) \begin{array}{}K\Leftarrow {M}^{-1}K\\ \langle ,\rangle \Leftarrow {\langle ,\rangle }_{M}\end{array} And (Oh surprise!) by working a little on the expressions, one recovers exactly the previous GCPC algorithm (algorithm 5). One proceeds likewise with a right preconditioning, K{M}^{-1} , via an {M}^{-1} -scalar product. Therefore, right preconditioning, left preconditioning or “split in the SPD manner”, all lead rigorously to the same algorithm. This observation will be useful to us later when one realises that the matrices supplied by Code_Aster (and also the preconditioners that one will associate with them) are not always in conformity with the ideal scenario ({\hat{P}}_{1}) . Notes: - This variant of the GCPC, which is by far the most widespread, is sometimes called in the literature: untransformed preconditioned conjugate gradient (‘untransformed preconditioned conjugate gradient’). As opposed to the transformed version which manipulates the entities proper to the new formulation. - The general descent methods and, particularly the non-linear CGs, are also preconditioned (cf. [§2.3]). This time with a preconditioner approximating the inverse of the Hessian at the point considered, so as to make spherical the graph of the functional in the neighbourhood of this point. 4.1.3 “Survey” of the principal preconditioners The solution often retained for its simplicity of implementation, its “numerical efficiency/extra computational cost” ratio for problems that are not too ill-conditioned, consists in preconditioning by the diagonal of the initial operator {M}_{J}:=\text{diag}({K}_{ii}) (4.1-3) This is what one calls diagonal or Jacobi preconditioning (JCG for ‘Jacobi Conjugate Gradient’) by reference to the stationary method of the same name. Notes: - It is a solution often retained in CFD (for EDF R&D: Code_Saturne, TELEMAC). In these fields, great attention paid to the non-linear solution scheme and to the construction of the mesh produces a problem that is often better conditioned. This is what made the reputation of the JCG, transformed for the occasion into a veritable “racing beast” dedicated to large parallel computers. - It is a solution proposed, in structural mechanics, by a good number of commercial codes: ANSYS, Zébulon, NASTRAN. It was present in Code_Aster but its lack of reliability led to its removal. - This principle of a “poor man’s” preconditioner extends to the descent methods by taking this time the diagonal of the Hessian. Another very widespread preconditioner is the SSOR (for Symmetric Successive Over Relaxation). Like the previous one, it is deduced from a classical iterative method: the relaxed Gauss–Seidel method. By decomposing the initial operator in the usual form K:=D+L+{L}^{T} where D is its diagonal and L its strictly lower triangular part, it is written (as a function of the relaxation parameter \omega ) {M}_{\text{SSOR}}(\omega ):=\frac{1}{\omega (\omega -2)}(D+\mathrm{\omega L}){D}^{-1}(D+{\mathrm{\omega L}}^{T})0 The “sinews of war” then being the spectral radius \rho \left[{({\text{FF}}^{T})}^{-1}B\right] which a judicious choice of \Theta (F) can contribute notably to bringing down. - This principle of incomplete factorisation generalises without difficulty to the standard case where the operator is written K=\mathrm{LU} with this time B=K-\mathrm{LU} . One then speaks of Incomplete factorisation of LU type (ILU for ‘Incomplete LU’). 4.2.2 Strategy retained in Code_Aster It is a preconditioner of ILU type (because we shall see in the following paragraph that the working matrices of Code_Aster often lose their positive-definiteness) inspired by the works of H. Van der Vorst [Van01]. The matrices remaining nevertheless symmetric, one can write K={\mathrm{LDL}}^{T} and B=K-{\mathrm{LDL}}^{T} . Note: - The matrix no longer being SPD but simply symmetric regular, one is not, a priori, assured of the existence of a factorisation {\mathrm{LDL}}^{T} without having recourse to permutations of rows and columns ( \mathrm{PK}={\mathrm{LDL}}^{T} with P a permutation matrix). A scenario which has not been provided for in the native linear solvers of Code_Aster (‘LDLT’, ‘MULT_FRONT’, ‘GCPC’) and would be difficult to implement efficiently given the MORSE storage of the matrices. Fortunately, one will see that a happy combination of circumstances makes it possible to unblock the situation (cf. §5.1)! Strictly speaking one should speak of incomplete factorisation of ILDLT type but in the literature and in the documentations of the codes, one already amalgamates ILU and IC, or even their variants, so there is no point in enriching the list of acronyms! This incomplete factorisation, in the direct line of the previous theoretical reminders, rests on two observations which we are now going to substantiate: - the notion of fill-in by levels, - the weak magnitude of the terms resulting from this fill-in. 4.2.3 Fill-in by levels The construction of the factorisation is carried out, row by row, via the usual formula {L}_{ij}=\frac{1}{{D}_{j}}({K}_{ij}-\sum_{k=1}^{j-1}{L}_{\text{ik}}{D}_{k}{L}_{\text{jk}}) (4.2-4) Whence the phenomenon of progressive filling of the profile (‘fill-in’ in English): initially the matrix L has the same fill as the matrix K , but in the course of the process, to a zero term of {K}_{ij} there may correspond a non-zero term of {L}_{ij} . It suffices that there exist a column k ( \tilde{\mathrm{K}}=(\begin{array}{cc}\bar{\mathrm{K}}& 0\\ 0& \mathrm{Id}\end{array}) (5.1-3) denoting by \bar{\mathrm{K}} its unchanged part. Each of the two approaches has its advantages and its drawbacks: genericity, modularity but increase in the size of the problem, degradation of its conditioning and loss of its positive-definiteness for the first. Unlike the second which decreases its size but which is circumscribed to certain types of boundary conditions and is, from the computer-science point of view, more delicate to implement. Note: 1. Other approaches were conceivable: simple dualisation, taking the boundary conditions into account in the variational formulation, projected conjugate gradient… 5.1.2 Consequence for the GCPC With AFFE_CHAR_CINE, the working operator \tilde{\mathrm{K}} remaining SPD, all the theory recalled in the previous paragraphs applies. On the other hand, with AFFE_CHAR_ACOU/MECA/THER (the most frequent case in practice), this is no longer the case, because it becomes simply symmetric and loses its positive-definite character. The consequences are then of three orders: - The global convergence of the GCPC (cf. (3.2-9)) is no longer guaranteed, - When it occurs, it is slowed down (cf. (3.2-11)) by a degraded conditioning, \eta (\mathrm{K})\ll \eta (\tilde{\mathrm{K}}) - The preconditioning can no longer be carried out via an \mathrm{IC}(p) , but rather by an \mathrm{ILU}(p) (cf. §4.2). It is still necessary that the factorisation {\mathrm{LDL}}^{T} always be possible without having to permute row or column! Fortunately, an adequate arrangement of the Lagrange multipliers with respect to the groups of degrees of freedom which they concern (they must encompass these degrees of freedom cf. [Pel01] §4), makes it possible to obtain without a hitch this incomplete factorisation (phew!). Notes: - In an EDF report B.Nitrosso [Ni92] shows that diagonal preconditioning is not conceivable (cf. §4.1), because it leads to the cancellation of the scalar product in the denominator of step (7) of algorithm 5: computation of the optimal conjugation parameter. Therefore, unlike Code_Saturne, Code_Aster cannot propose this unreliable option. - It remains nonetheless that, with dualised boundary conditions, the conditioning of the working operator is degraded and therefore the convergence of the GCPC is slowed down. Other commercial codes, like ANSYS [PLM], have already made this observation. 5.1.3 Memory footprint Taking into account the elements of §4.2, one has empirically noted an effective memory complexity of the GCPC with the Incomplete Cholesky type preconditioner ('LDLT_INC'), in \alpha times the size of K with: - \alpha =2,5 in \mathrm{ILU}(0) (default level in Code_Aster ), - \alpha =4,5 in \mathrm{ILU}(1) , - \alpha =8,5 in \mathrm{ILU}(2) . With the preconditioner using a single-precision factorisation issuing from MUMPS ('LDLT_SP'), the memory consumption is larger (at least \alpha >10 ). But in non-linear analysis, this factorisation can be kept during several system solutions (keyword REAC_PRECOND). The extra computational cost due to its construction is therefore finally smaller. Notes: - These figures are to be compared with the size of the complete factorisation which is of the order typically of \alpha =30 to 100 (this depends notably on the renumberer used in pre-processing). The disproportion of these figures illustrates well the principal competitive advantage of the GCPC with respect to the direct solvers: the memory occupation required. - However, unlike the direct solvers of Code_Aster, the GCPC has not been able to benefit from a memory paging. The whole matrix must be contained in RAM because it is used a great number of times via the matrix–vector product. Whereas the direct methods manipulate much larger objects but these are unloaded automatically and partially onto disk (software package JEVEUX and/or Out-Of-Core faculties of MUMPS). 5.1.4 Parallelism Unlike other solvers of the code (MULT_FRONT, MUMPS, PETSC) and for problems of ‘parallel preconditioning’, the native GCPC is usable only in sequential mode (cf. §3.3). For example, it does not benefit from the distribution of the tasks and of the data which the MPI parallelism set up around the direct solver MUMPS procures. Thus, a memory overhead of \alpha =30 with sequential In-Core MUMPS can very quickly come down to the level of a GCPC preconditioned by ILU(0) as soon as one uses a dozen processors and/or activates its Out-Of-Core faculties. 5.2 Scope of use All the operators generating real symmetric systems except those requiring obligatorily a singularity detection (modal analysis, stability and buckling ...). In non-linear analysis, if the problem is real non-symmetric, one can use this solver provided that one forces the symmetrisation (cf. §5.3). List of the Code_Aster operators that can use GCPC: - CALC_FORC_AJOU, - CALC_MATR_AJOU, - CALC_PRECONT \to Possible symmetrised approximation (cf. §5.3), - DYNA_VIBRA, - DYNA_NON_LINE \to Possible symmetrised approximation, - MACRO_MATR_AJOU, - ASSEMBLAGE, - MECA_STATIQUE, - NUME_DDL/FACTORISER/RESOUDRE, - MODE_STATIQUE, - STAT_NON_LINE \to Possible symmetrised approximation, - THER_LINEAIRE, - THER_NON_LINE \to Possible symmetrised approximation, - THER_NON_LINE_MO \to Possible symmetrised approximation. 5.3 Symmetric character of the working operator If the matrix is not symmetric two cases present themselves. Either the linear solver is inserted into a non-linear process (operators mentioned cf. list §5.2), or the latter is linear (the other operators). In the first case, one transforms the initial problem \text{Ku}=f into a new symmetrised problem \frac{1}{2}(K+{K}^{T})u=f . One supposes thereby that the encompassing non-linear solver (Newton algorithm) will compensate the approximation of the initial operator by \tilde{K}:=\frac{1}{2}(K+{K}^{T}) . This is moreover not the only approximation of this non-linear process… the choice of the tangent matrix is, for example, another. This symmetrised approximation does not harm the robustness and the consistency of the whole and avoids a more expensive non-symmetric solution. This operation is carried out by activating the keyword SYME=‘OUI’ (default ‘NON’) of the factor keyword SOLVEUR and it is legitimate for all the non-linear solvers of the code. When the problem is purely linear, one cannot expect any compensation from any encompassing process and this approximation becomes impossible. Recourse to the native GCPC is illegitimate and one must solve this non-symmetric system via the other linear solvers. The nature of the working operator is detected automatically; there is no need to notify it via the keyword SYME. 5.4 Parameter setting and printout To activate this functionality, one must initialise the keyword METHODE to ‘GCPC’ in the factor keyword SOLVEUR [U4.50.01]. Furthermore, two types of preconditioners are available (keyword PRE_COND): - PRE_COND='LDLT_INC': A classical Incomplete Cholesky (cf. §4.2) whose fill-in level is piloted by the keyword NIVE_REMPLISSAGE=k (k=0 does not mean “without preconditioning” but preconditioning of ILU(0) type). - PRE_COND='LDLT_SP': A single-precision factorisation carried out by the external direct solver MUMPS [R6.02.03]. This solution is, a priori , more costly than the first in terms of memory/time but the latter is shareable, in non-linear analysis, between different solutions of linear systems (keyword REAC_ITER). On the other hand, the robustness and the quality of this preconditioner can greatly accelerate the convergence of the GCPC. Notes: - To minimise the size of the profile of the working matrix and of its preconditioner (with the Incomplete Cholesky), a renumbering algorithm is available by default: ‘RCMK’ for ‘Reverse Cuthill Mac-Kee’ (cf. [LT98] §5.4.2). It can nevertheless be deactivated. - The principal “lever arm” for modifying the “CPU time/memory occupation” compromise of the GCPC remains the preconditioner and its different numerical parameters. Unlike the direct methods, one has had to fix a maximum number of iterations discriminating the converged iterative computations from the non-converged ones. This threshold (parameterisable) is arbitrarily fixed at half the degrees of freedom of the working problem \hat{K} . If after i =NMAX_ITER steps, the relative residual {\delta}^{i}:=\frac{\parallel {r}^{i}\parallel }{\parallel f\parallel } is not less than RESI_RELA, the analysis stops in ERREUR_FATALE. | Factor keyword | Keyword | Default value | References | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | SOLVEUR | METHODE=’GCPC’ | ’MULT_FRONT’ | [§1] | | | PRE_COND=’LDLT_INC’/ 'LDLT_SP' | ’LDLT_INC’ | [§4.2][§5.4] | | | NIVE_REMPLISSAGE=0,1,2… | 0 | [§4.2] | | | REAC_PRECOND | 5 | [§5.4] | | | RENUM=’RCMK’ or ‘SANS’ | ’RCMK’ | [§5.4] | | | NMAX_ITER= {i}_{\max} , maximum admissible number of iterations. Notwithstanding the fact that, unlike the native GCPC, certain PETSc solvers are adapted to non-symmetric systems. As a general rule, the use of the “simple” conjugate gradient (native GCPC or CG of PETSc) is not very robust on the Aster modellings. One prefers to it more sophisticated algorithms: GMRES… On large analyses ( >{5.10}^{5} degrees of freedom) very consuming in the solution of linear systems (operators STAT_NON_LINE, MECA_STATIQUE…), one has every interest in activating the parallelism induced by PETSc. The project began in 1991 and among its characteristics let us cite: some twenty developers (core-team: 9), one version per year, tens of thousands of users. One of the founding fathers of PETSc, William Gropp [WG], also works on the standardisation of the MPI language (MPICH). He is very active on the computer-science and algorithmic aspects of parallel computing. Data-preparation tools (cf. MURGE [MUR]) or macro-libraries (Numerical Platon, Arcane…) could in time relieve the host codes of these tedious contingencies which are the filling of the data structures proper to each external product. For the preconditioners with incomplete factorisation (ILU(k) cf. §4.2). RCMK for a renumbering algorithm of Reverse-Cuthill MacKee type. 7 Treatment of failures 7.1 Failures encountered Unlike a direct solver, an iterative solver will in general tend to fail during the phase of solution of the linear system: for example if the convergence criterion is not verified after the maximum number of iterations previously fixed. This can be caused by a preconditioner that is not robust enough or a quasi-singular matrix. Failures are also possible during the phase of construction of the preconditioner but are rarer: for example if MUMPS lacks memory during the single-precision factorisation in order to construct the preconditioner LDLT_SP. In this last case the solution is to relaunch the analysis with more memory or by increasing the value of PCENT_PIVOT. 7.2 Recovery in the event of failure Like the direct solvers, the iterative solvers of Code_Aster are capable of signalling the failure or the success of the linear solution. This functionality is exploited in the non-linear solver R5.03.01 in order to allow: - the cutting of the time step in the event of failure during the solution phase whatever the preconditioner - the updating of the preconditioner when LDLT_SP is used When LDLT_SP is used, one proceeds first to the updating, then one carries out again the current time step. If a new failure occurs, the time step is then cut. It is to be noted that no recovery is provided for in the event of failure during the phase of construction of the preconditioner. 7.3 Implementation The operator DEFI_LIST_INST makes it possible to activate the treatment of failures. In the presence of a cutting action (ACTION='DECOUPE') or of updating of the preconditioner (ACTION='REAC_PRECOND'), one activates in STAT_NON_LINE or DYNA_NON_LINE the capture of the errors in the iterative solvers. 7.4 Interception of the exception In the event of failure of the cutting strategy or of updating of the preconditioner, an exception is raised. It can be intercepted in the command file by using its name: ResolutionError. 8 Bibliography 8.1 Books/articles/proceedings/theses… [BFG] A.Bouras, V.Fraysse & L.Giraud. r6.02.02 Linear solver by the multifrontal method MULT_FRONT r6.02.02 Linear solver by the multifrontal method MULT_FRONT Summary: The multifrontal method MULT_FRONT is a direct method particularly well suited to the solution of linear systems whose matrix is sparse. This method comprises a preliminary renumbering phase intended to minimise the fill-in of the matrix during the factorisation. This phase also makes it possible to group the variables into "super-variables" or "super-nodes". The factorisation itself is carried out as a sequence of eliminations of super-nodes, in dense matrices. These dense matrices allow the use of optimised routines such as the BLAS, which obtain the best performance on vector or scalar machines. Once the factorised matrix is available, each solution of a system requires only an inexpensive "forward/back substitution". > Contents 1 Description of the method The multifrontal method is a direct method for the solution of linear systems, which is particularly well suited to systems having a sparse matrix. It factorises symmetric or non-symmetric matrices, not necessarily positive definite. In the most general case, the multifrontal method calls on the Gauss method with a search for pivots. The method implemented in Code_Aster factorises real or complex matrices, symmetric or not (a non-symmetric matrix is accepted provided that its structure remains symmetric), and uses the algorithm known as {\mathit{LDL}}^{T} or \mathit{L.U} , without a search for pivots. The solution of a linear system is carried out in three stages: - renumbering of the unknowns, - factorisation of the matrix, - forward/back substitution. In the case where several linear systems, with the same matrix, are to be solved, only the forward/back substitutions are to be performed. Likewise, if several matrices of the same structure are to be factorised, the renumbering of the unknowns will not have to be redone. This preliminary phase, which will ensure the performance of the factorisation, has a non-negligible cost; however, its relative weight (in computation time) decreases with the size of the matrices to be factorised. We shall follow the following plan: 1. presentation of the classical {\mathrm{LDL}}^{T} method adapted to dense symmetric matrices. Notion of elimination, 2. extension of the method to sparse matrices, notion of fill-in, 3. presentation of the multifrontal method. 1.1 LDLT method for dense matrices Let be an invertible matrix; it is known that there exists a unit-diagonal lower triangular matrix L and an upper triangular matrix U such that A=L\cdot U . The order of these matrices will be n . If is symmetric, this decomposition may be written: {A=\mathrm{LDL}}^{T} eq 1.1-1 where is a diagonal matrix and {L}^{T} the transpose of the matrix L , with unit diagonal. Let (i,j)\in {[1,n]}^{2} ; from [eq 1.1-1] one deduces the expression of the coefficients of L and D . Indeed one may write: {A}_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sum_{l=1}^{n}{L}_{\text{ik}}{D}_{kl}{L}_{\text{lj}}^{T} eq 1.1-2 L being unit-diagonal lower triangular, and D diagonal, [eq 1.1-2] becomes: > {A}_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{\min(i,j)}{L}_{\text{ik}}{L}_{\text{jk}}{D}_{kk} eq 1.1-3 There are many ways of computing the coefficients of and from [eq 1.1-3]. We shall see the method known as "by rows", usually used in Code_Aster , and the method "by columns" used in the multifrontal method. Method by rows The rows of L and D are computed jointly, one after another. Suppose these rows known up to order (i-1) , and suppose also that the coefficients of row i are known up to order j-1 ; [eq 1.1-3] is written, with j \mid \begin{array}{cc}\text{pour}i=j+1\text{à}n,\text{faire}& \text{éq 1.1-7}\\ \text{}\begin{array}{}{D}_{ii}={D}_{ii}-{L}_{ij}^{2}{D}_{jj}\\ \mid \begin{array}{}\text{pour}k=i+1\text{à}n,\text{faire}\\ \text{}{L}_{\text{ki}}={L}_{\text{ki}}-{L}_{\text{kj}}{L}_{ij}{L}_{jj}\text{(saxpy)}\end{array}\end{array}& \text{éq 1.1-8}\end{array} Let us make three remarks: 1. the operations [eq 1.1-7] are called the elimination of the unknown j . Indeed, after [eq 1.1-7], one will never again call on the terms of column j in the remainder of the algorithm. (Above, the definitive terms {L}_{\text{ki}} have been abusively confused with their programming name, which contains the values of {L}_{\text{ki}} modified in the course of the eliminations). One therefore deduces the general {\mathrm{LDL}}^{T} factorisation algorithm by columns. \mid \begin{array}{cc}\text{pour}j=1\text{à}n,\text{faire}& \\ & \\ \text{}\mid \begin{array}{}\text{pour}k=i+1\text{à}n,\text{faire}\\ \text{}{L}_{\text{kj}}={L}_{\text{kj}}/{D}_{jj}\end{array}& \text{/normalisation/}\\ & \\ \text{}\mid \begin{array}{}\text{pour}i=j+1\text{à}n,\text{faire}\\ \text{}{D}_{ii}={D}_{ii}-{L}_{ij}^{2}{D}_{jj}\\ \text{}\mid \begin{array}{}\text{pour}k=i+1\text{à}n,\text{faire}\\ \text{}{L}_{\text{ki}}={L}_{\text{ki}}-{L}_{\text{kj}}{L}_{ij}{L}_{jj}\end{array}\end{array}& \begin{array}{}\text{/élimination/}\\ \\ \\ \text{/saxpy/}\end{array}\end{array} eq 1.1-9 Before moving on to the notion of fill-in, it is appropriate to make right now a remark that will be useful later. If one looks at [eq 1.1-9], it appears that one can eliminate the unknown , even if the terms ({L}_{\text{ki}},k=i+1,n) and {D}_{ii} are not yet available. Indeed, it is sufficient to keep the terms (-{L}_{\text{kj}}{L}_{ij}{D}_{jj}) , and to add them afterwards to the terms {L}_{\text{ki}} . These terms ({L}_{\text{kj}}{L}_{ij}{D}_{jj}) , i ranging from j+1 to n and k from i+1 to n , form a matrix associated with the elimination of the unknown j , which will henceforth be called the frontal matrix j . 1.2 Sparse matrix and fill-in It is recalled that if the initial matrix contains zero terms, the successive eliminations cause fill-in, that is to say that certain terms {L}_{\text{ki}} are different from zero whereas the initial term {A}_{\text{ki}} is zero. Suppose that before the elimination of the unknown j , the term {L}_{\text{ki}} is zero; if {L}_{\text{kj}} and {L}_{ij} are both non-zero, [eq 1.1-9] shows that {L}_{\text{ki}} will itself become non-zero. This fill-in has a graphical interpretation. Suppose in this case that all the unknowns are represented by the nodes of a graph: one will connect the nodes k and i if and only if the term {A}_{\text{ki}} of the initial matrix is non-zero. If {A}_{\text{ki}} is zero with i connected to j and k connected to j , the elimination of j from the graphical point of view will then consist in connecting i and k . Figure [Figure 1.2-a] illustrates this interpretation. The dashed edges are those created by the elimination of j . They correspond to new non-zero terms of the matrix L . Figure 1.2-a: The elimination of node j connects all its neighbours to one another 1.3 Multifrontal method The multifrontal method is a direct method, of Gauss type, which aims to exploit to the maximum the sparsity of the matrix to be factorised. It seeks, on the one hand, to minimise the fill-in by using an optimal renumbering and, on the other hand, it extracts from the sparse structure of the matrix the information allowing it to eliminate (cf. page 5, remark (1)) unknowns independently of one another. Let us examine the simple case of figure [Figure 1.3-a], where the matrix has a single zero term, {A}_{21} . Figure 1.3-a Column 2 of does not undergo the effects of the elimination of unknown 1, because the coefficient (cf. [eq 1.1-9] seen previously). The contributions to columns 3 and 4 of , of the unknowns 1 and 2 are independent of their order of elimination (one must look in detail at [eq 1.1-9]). From this observation, one may introduce the notion of elimination tree presented by I. Duff [bib1]. The elimination tree of the matrix may be represented by figure [Figure 1.3-b]. Here 1 is indeed a leaf because there is no term for , 2 is also a leaf because , - a node has as father , if is the smallest row number such that . Here, 3 is the father of 1 and of 2. Notes: 1. from now on one uses the vocabulary of graph theory: tree, leaf, node... Here the tree is turned upside down, its leaves are at the bottom, 2. one will refer to [bib1] for more details and the proofs of the validity of the method, 3. in the example above, the order of elimination between the unknowns (3) and (4) is fixed by the initial numbering; one could have permuted the rows and the columns of the matrix and have 4 as the father of 1 and 2, 4. it must be noted that the construction of this tree must take into account the non-zero terms obtained by fill-in in the course of the elimination. (More details on this subject will be seen in [bib2]). One cannot build the elimination tree solely from the initial sparse matrix: one must also know the fill-in terms, as already mentioned previously. The numerical factorisation of the multifrontal method is preceded by an important phase: the simulation of the eliminations and thus of the creation of the non-zero terms. This simulation is also called the logical or symbolic elimination. This simulation takes place during the first phase: the renumbering. The four phases of the multifrontal method will be seen, the most important being the first and the fourth. First phase: The "minimum degree" renumbering. This renumbering has as its first aim to minimise the number of operations to be performed during the factorisation. To this end one simulates the elimination of the nodes and one chooses as candidate for elimination the node of the graph having the smallest number of neighbours. One uses here the notion of graph seen in figure [Figure 1.2-a]. The initial sparse matrix defines the graph on which one works. The latter is then updated at each elimination of nodes (creation of links). The simulation of the fill-in makes it possible to achieve the second aim , which is the construction of the elimination tree seen in the previous paragraph. The third aim achieved is the creation of the super-nodes . This is an important notion which we shall develop. A super-node (SN) is formed of the set of nodes which, in the course of the elimination, have the same neighbours in the sense of the elimination graph. In the course of the simulation of the elimination, one detects that, for example, the nodes , and are: - on the one hand, neighbours of one another (the terms , , ... are non-zero), - on the other hand, they have as common neighbours the nodes: (see [Figure 1.3-c]). They then form the super-node and will all be eliminated together during the numerical factorisation. The MM-F is a block factorisation method, when it uses the notion of "super-node". This notion has the following double advantage: - it reduces the (non-negligible) cost of the renumbering, - it reduces the cost of the factorisation by grouping the computations (use of linear-algebra routines of blas-2 or blas-3 type). One sees in [Figure 1.3-c] the structure of the columns (non-zero terms shaded) in a virtual global sparse matrix. In fact, such a sparse matrix is never assembled . One works in local dense matrices which are called the frontal matrices . There is one frontal matrix per SN (this notion will be seen again in the paragraph "Numerical factorisation"). Figure 1.3-c In summary, the first phase of the multifrontal method (the renumbering by the "minimum degree") consists of the following three actions: - a renumbering of the unknowns to be eliminated, in order to minimise the fill-in. One simulates the eliminations by updating each time the lists of neighbours of the nodes, - jointly with the previous action, one builds the elimination tree, and, - one detects the "super-nodes", which may be described as an equivalence class for the relation "have the same neighbours". Note: The elimination tree supplied by the renumbering is expressed in terms of super-nodes, because the numerical elimination to follow will be done by super-nodes. Second phase: The symbolic factorisation This phase is not as fundamental as the previous one. It is a technical phase intended to build certain pointers. These are in particular the arrays of global and local indices which establish the correspondences between the unknowns during the assembly of the frontal matrices. Third phase: The execution sequence This is also a technical phase. It was seen in the previous paragraph that the method consisted in traversing the elimination tree, performing an elimination at each node of the tree. The result of this elimination is a frontal matrix . The order of this matrix is the number of neighbours of the eliminated SN. The storage of the frontal matrices is costly in terms of memory occupation. The frontal matrix (result of the elimination of the ) will be assembled into the frontal matrix of node i , where i is the father of . This phase will be seen in more detail during the numerical factorisation). All the frontal matrices must be kept until they are used during the elimination of the "parent SN". One can then store the matrix of the "parent SN" in place of those of the "child SNs". There are several ways of traversing the tree while respecting the constraint: "the child must be eliminated before the father". The purpose of the third phase is to find the traversal order which minimises the memory space required for the storage of the frontal matrices ([bib2], page 2.12). Fourth phase: The numerical factorisation This phase is the actual factorisation, that is the computation of the matrices L and D . In what follows, these two matrices will be confused and, from the computer point of view, D will be seen as the diagonal terms of L . The numerical factorisation consists in traversing the elimination tree; for each "super-node", one performs: - the assembly, into the "mother" frontal matrix, of the "daughter" frontal matrices, - the elimination of the columns of the super-node. Let us see the following example with the graph and the elimination tree of [Figure 1.3-d] (nodes 8, 9, 10 do not appear in the drawing). Figure 1.3-d: Example of a graph and of an elimination tree In parentheses, one reads the numbers of the unknowns of the SN. The elimination of SN1 consists of: 1. the assembly of columns 1 and 2 of the initial matrix , into a working matrix, called the frontal matrix before elimination. This matrix is of order 5 , linked to the unknowns (1,2,4,5,6) . (Because 1 and 2 are linked to (4,5,6) only), 2. the elimination of SN1 (of columns 1 and 2 , according to the formulae [eq 1.1-7] and [eq 1.1-8] seen previously), 3. the storage of the two columns 1 and 2 of the matrix, in an array FACTOR, which contains the columns of the global factorised matrix, 4. the storage of the frontal matrix 1 of order 3 linked to the unknowns (4,5,6) . One does the same thing with SN2. These two eliminations are illustrated by figure [Figure 1.3-e], where one sees shaded with hatching the two frontal matrices. Figure 1.3-e The elimination of SN3 consists of: - the addition of columns (4,5,6,7) of the initial matrix, to the working matrix of order 7, linked to the unknowns (4,5,6,7,8,9,10) , - the assembly of the frontal matrices 1 and 2 into this working matrix, - the elimination of columns (4,5,6,7) , - the obtaining in FACTOR of four additional columns, - the obtaining of the frontal matrix 3 of order 3 (columns 8,9,10 ). One notes that the frontal matrix 3 can be stored in place of the frontal matrices 1 and 2 . The storage of these matrices requires a stack structure in which one pushes at the end of an elimination, and from which one pops during the assembly. It is the maximum length of this stack which is minimised during the execution-sequence phase. Figure [Figure 1.3-f] illustrates the elimination of SN3. Figure 1.3-f: Elimination of SN3 One notes that the coefficient {L}_{74} (white square in figure [Figure 1.3-f]) comes from the elimination of SN3, and that the initial term {A}_{74} is zero (dashed link in figure [Figure 1.3-d]). It was seen in paragraph 1.1 that the elimination of a column consisted of an operation of "saxpy" type, the addition to a vector of the product of a vector by a scalar. One easily sees that the elimination of a super-node, a group of columns, consists of an operation of "matrix-vector product" type. These operations consume the greatest part, in computation time, of the work of factorising the matrix. They are performed by subroutines of the BLAS library, supplied after having been optimised on most computers. One sees in figure [Figure 1.3-g] the column updated by the product of the matrix A\left[j+1:n,1:m\right] and of the vector A\left[j,1:m\right] . The factorisation being finished, one has the factorised matrix in the form of a compacted array of the non-zero terms only. This is a storage of "Morse" type. The global index array mentioned in the symbolic factorisation indicates, for each column of L , the row numbers of each stored coefficient. Figure 1.3-g: Update of the column by a matrix vector product 1.4 Forward substitution – back substitution The columns of L being stored in compacted form, the forward substitution is of "saxpy" type and the back substitution of scalar-product type, these two operations both being indexed. That is to say that the forward-substitution algorithm is roughly the following (having previously initialised by the right-hand side of the system): > \begin{array}{}\mid \begin{array}{}\text{pour}i=1\text{à}n\text{faire}\\ \text{}\mid \begin{array}{}\text{pour}k\in \text{colonne}i\text{faire}\\ x(\mathrm{global}(k))=x(\mathrm{global}(k))-{L}_{\text{ki}}\times x(i)\text{}(\mathrm{saxpy}\mathrm{indexé})\end{array}\end{array}\\ \mid \begin{array}{}\text{pour}i=1\text{à}n\text{faire}\\ \text{}x(i)=x(i)/{D}_{ii}\end{array}\end{array} The back substitution, for its part, is written in the form: > \mid \begin{array}{}\text{pour}i\text{variant}\mathrm{de}r\text{à}1\text{faire}\\ \text{}x(i)=x(i)-\sum_{k\in \mathrm{colonne}i}{L}_{\text{ik}}\cdot x(\mathrm{global}(k))\text{}:\text{}\text{produit scalaire indexé}\end{array} 2 Implementation and use in Code_Aster The use of the multifrontal method is accessible through the operator NUME_DDL, in the following way: nu = NUME_DDL (matr_rigi = matr, stockage = 'MORSE', renum = 'MD' ou renum= 'MDA', ou renum= 'METIS') ; Two other renumbering methods are available: approximate minimum degree (MDA), which is a variant of the minimum-degree method, and a nested-dissection method (METIS). They are described briefly in annexes 1 and 2. It is sufficient to replace the value of renum by MDA, or METIS. This method is also directly available under the keyword SOLVEUR in MECA_STATIQUE, STAT_NON_LINE, DYNA_NON_LINE, THER_LINEAIRE, THER_NON_LINE with the same logic. Then, one will use the operator FACTORISER, the call being the same as in the case of a matrix stored in profile mode. In NUME_DDL, one indicates that the matrix to be factorised is stored in MORSE mode and that one requests one of the two "minimum degree" renumberings, or a renumbering by nested dissection (METIS). In this case, NUME_DDL performs the first three phases seen previously: 1. renumbering, 2. symbolic factorisation, 3. execution sequence. Since a recent development, the renumbering is performed on the nodes (in the sense of the interpolation), and no longer on the degrees of freedom. This saves computation time and ensures that the initial order of the degrees of freedom inside the nodes is respected (this is sometimes necessary in the incompressible case, where the pressure must be numbered after the displacements). The numbering constraint on the "double Lagrange" multipliers bracketing the degrees of freedom affected by the boundary condition is also respected. In addition, NUME_DDL prepares the splitting into blocks of the factorised matrix. Indeed, it was seen that at each elimination, one stored in an array the columns of the factorised matrix. These columns will be used only during the forward/back substitution. They are never used for the computation of other columns. There is therefore no point in having them all in memory. They are stored, in Code_Aster , in the form of a collection of JEVEUX objects of variable length. These objects, blocks of columns, must nevertheless satisfy the following constraint: each block corresponds to an integer number of "super-nodes". One cannot therefore have the columns of the same "super-node" on several blocks. Since one does not know the memory space available during the numerical factorisation, one decides in NUME_DDL that the maximum length of each block will be the max. (over all the SNs) of the sum of the lengths of the columns of the \mathit{SN} . L{b}_{\max}=\underset{\mathrm{SNi}}{\mathrm{Max}}(\sum_{k\in \mathrm{SNi}}\mathrm{longueur}({\mathrm{col.}}_{k}))\text{},\text{}\text{(en abrégé)} The operator FACTORISER uses the pointers created by NUME_DDL and the initial MORSE matrix. It creates the factorised matrix in the form of a collection of JEVEUX objects, as was seen previously. A provisional data structure is also necessary. It concerns the frontal matrices. Two cases arise: - the stack of frontal matrices can fit entirely in memory (in a one-dimensional array); in this case, one allocates a JEVEUX object and the multifrontal algorithm then manages this space itself, by storing the "mother" frontal matrix in place of the "daughter" matrices, - it does not fit and, in this case, it is created in the form of a collection of JEVEUX objects, each frontal matrix being an object. For the elimination of "super-node" i one must have simultaneously in memory: - the block of the factorised matrix to which the \mathrm{SNi} belongs - the frontal-matrix object i as well as all the "daughter" frontal matrices of i which will be destroyed after their use. The frontal matrix i will itself be kept in memory until its use and its destruction. One could, as was done previously, release in the JEVEUX sense each frontal matrix after its creation. This can then lead, in the event of little memory being available, to a storage on disk which is prohibitive in volume. Indeed, a destruction of a JEVEUX object does not entail the destruction of its image on disk, and the sum of the lengths of the frontal matrices is enormous. In summary, one must be able to store simultaneously in memory: - a block of the factorised matrix, - the stack of frontal matrices, in a single object if it fits, in several objects otherwise. One therefore needs "enough" memory to use the multifrontal method. The second way of storing the stack allows execution when the memory is sufficient, but fragmented. When the memory is insufficient, one must relaunch the execution of FACTORISER with a larger memory. 3 Bibliography 1. I.DUFF: Parallel implementation of multifrontal scheme". Here is a simplified but essential description of it. 1. one forms the initial graph associated with the sparse matrix to be factorised, 2. one computes the number of neighbours of the nodes (their degree), 3. one numbers first (then eliminates from the graph) the node having the fewest neighbours (minimum degree), 4. one updates the graph of step 1, 5. one returns to step 2. The computation of the degree of the nodes is an operation costly in computation time. The "Approximate Minimum degree" method [bib3] proposes to reduce this cost. To this end, instead of computing the true degree of a node one contents oneself with an upper bound (often equal, according to the authors, to the true degree), of easier computation. Indeed, in the course of the elimination the true degree of node i is equal to {d}_{i} , the cardinal of the following set: {A}_{i}\cup \lbrace {L}_{e}\rbrace , where the union is taken over the set of the neighbours e , previously eliminated, of i (fill-in terms), and where {A}_{i} is the set of the initial neighbours. In the approximate method i is replaced by {d}_{i}=\text{card}({A}_{i})+\sum\text{card}\lbrace {L}_{e}\rbrace , that is to say that one neglects the intersection of the {L}_{e} . This method is described in [bib3] and the various variants of the "minimum degree" algorithm are set out in [bib4]. Reference documentation METIS The implementation of the renumbering module for sparse matrices METIS is described in the note [bib5], supplied in the METIS-4.0/Doc directory of the software. The algorithm used is described in [bib6] It is also possible to consult the following internet address: http://www.cs.umn.edu/~karypis METIS is principally a tool for partitioning graphs (meshes), aiming at the following 2 goals: - to partition a given graph into p subgraphs of sizes as close as possible, - to minimise the size of the boundaries between the subgraphs. The first goal aims at a good balance of parallelisation on p processors and the second aims at minimising the communications. METIS uses a multilevel graph-partitioning algorithm, proceeding in the following way: at each level one seeks separators (sets of edges), of minimal size, cutting the graph into equal parts. METIS applies this principle to the renumbering of the nodes of a graph by seeking at each step a separator dividing the graph into 2 subgraphs. One numbers first the nodes of the first subgraph, then those of the second, then those of the separator. One then applies the same algorithm to the 2 subgraphs in a recursive manner.

r6.02.03 General information on direct linear solvers and use of MUMPS r6.02.03 General information on direct linear solvers and use of MUMPS Summary In the context of thermo-mechanical simulations with Code_Aster , most of the calculation costs often come from the construction and solution of linear systems . To perform these solutions more efficiently, Code_Aster has chosen to integrate the direct method deployed in the MUMPS package (‘Multifrontal Massively Parallel sparse direct Solver; P.R.Amestoy, J.Y.L’Excellent et al; CERFACS/CNRS/ENS Lyon/IRIT/INRIA/Université de Bordeaux). This is in addition to its “in-house” multifrontal (C.Rose) and its other solvers: ‘LDLT’, ‘GCPC’ and ‘PETSC’. In distributed parallel mode and in Out-Of-Core, the Aster +MUMPS coupling provides CPU gains of the order of a dozen on 32 processors. And this, for RAM consumption , behaviour/functional scope and precision of results at least as good as those of the native multifrontal of the code. On large problems, by activating the BLR compressions, one can even gain a further factor of two or three. This product, via the parallelism it exhibits and its advanced features (pivoting, pre/post-processing, solution quality, …) greatly eases the running of standard studies. Moreover, it often remains the only viable alternative for exploiting certain modellings/analyses (quasi-incompressible, X-FEM, …) or for running very large studies (as an accurate direct solver or as a preconditioner, cf. option 'LDLT_SP' of 'GCPC'/'PETSC'). In the first part of the document we summarize the general problem of solving linear systems, then we approach the large families of sparse direct solvers and their variations in public domain libraries. All things to keep in mind before tackling, in the second part , the MUMPS package through its main characteristics and advanced functionalities. Then we detail the numerical, IT and functional aspects of its integration into Code_Aster . Finally, we conclude with some numerical results. For more details and advice on the use of linear solvers, you can consult the specific user instructions U4.50.01/[U2.08.03]. The related issues of improving performance (RAM/CPU) of a calculation and the use of parallelism are also the subject of detailed notices: U1.03.03 and U2.08.06. 1 General information about direct solvers 1.1 Linear system and associated solution methods In numerical simulation of physical phenomena, a significant computational cost often comes from the construction and solution of linear systems . Structural mechanics is no exception to the rule! The cost of building the system depends on the number of integration points and the complexity of the constitutive laws, while that of the resolution is linked to the number of unknowns, the models retained and the topology (bandwidth, conditioning). When the number of unknowns explodes, the second step becomes preponderant 1 and it is therefore the latter which will mainly interest us here. Moreover, when it is possible to be more efficient in this resolution phase, thanks to access to a parallel machine, we will see that this advantage can be propagated to the phase of constitution of the system itself (elementary calculations and assemblies). These inversions of linear systems are in fact omnipresent in codes and often buried deep within other numerical algorithms : non-linear diagram, time integration, modal analysis, etc. We seek, for example, the vector of nodal displacements (or displacement increments) u verifying a linear system of the type \mathrm{Ku}=\mathrm{f} (1.1-1) with K a rigidity matrix and \mathrm{f} a vector reflecting the application of generalized forces to the mechanical system. Generally speaking, resolving this type of problem requires (more) broad questioning than it seems: - Do we have access to the matrix or do we simply know its action on a vector? - Is this matrix hollow or dense? - What are its numerical properties (symmetry, positive definite, etc.) and structural properties (real/complex, in bands, in blocks, etc.)? - Do we want to solve a single system (1.1-1), several simultaneously 2 or consecutively 3? Or even several different and successive systems whose matrices are very close 4? - In the case of successive resolutions, can we reuse previous results in order to facilitate future resolutions (see restart technique, partial factorisation)? - What is the order of magnitude of the size of the problem, of the matrix and its factorisation in relation to the processing capacities of the CPUs and associated memories (RAM, disk)? - Do we want a very precise solution or simply an estimate (see nested solvers)? - Do we have access to linear algebra libraries (and their MPI, BLAS, LAPACK, etc. prerequisites) or should we use “in-house” products? In Code_Aster , we explicitly construct the matrix and store it in MORSE 5 format . With most modelling, the matrix is sparse (due to finite element discretisation), potentially poorly conditioned 6 and often real, symmetrical and indefinite 7 . In nonlinear, modal or thermo-mechanical chaining, we often deal with “multiple second members” type problems. Discrete contact-friction methods take advantage of partial factorisation capabilities and the domain decomposition method. On the other hand, Code_Aster also uses simultaneous resolution scenarios (Schur complements of contact and substructuration, etc.). As for the sizes of the problems, even if they increase from year to year, they remain modest compared to CFD: of the order of a million unknowns but for hundreds of time steps or iterations of Newton. Furthermore, from a middleware and hardware” point of view , the code now relies on numerous optimised and long-lasting libraries (MPI, BLAS, LAPACK, (PAR)METIS, (PT)SCOTCH, PETSc, MUMPS, etc.) and is mainly used on SMP clusters (fast networks, large RAM and disk storage capacity). We therefore mainly seek to optimise the use of linear solvers with this in mind. For 60 years, two types of techniques have been competing for supremacy in the field, direct solvers and iterative solvers (cf. [Che05][Dav03][Duf06][Gol96][Las98][Liu89][Meu99][Saa03]). The first are robust and result in a finite number of operations (theoretically) known in advance. Their theory is relatively well completed and their variation according to many types of matrices and software architectures is very complete. In particular, their multi-level algorithm is well suited to the memory hierarchies of current machines. However, they require storage capacities which increase rapidly with the size of the problem, which limits the scalability of their parallelism 8 . Even if this parallelism can be broken down into several independent layers, thus increasing performance. On the other hand, iterative methods are more “scalable” when increasing the number of processors. Their theory is full of many "open problems", especially in finite arithmetic. In practice, their convergence in a “reasonable” number of iterations is not always acquired, it depends on the structure of the matrix, the starting point, the stopping criterion… This type of solver has more difficulty breaking through into the mechanics of industrial structures where we often accumulate heterogeneities, non-linearities and junctions of models which corrupt the conditioning of the working operator. On the other hand, they are not suitable for efficiently solving “multiple second members” type problems. Except these are very common in the algorithms of mechanical simulations. Figure 1.1-1._ Two classes of methods for solving a linear system: the direct and the iterative. Unlike their direct counterparts, it is not possible to propose THE iterative solver that will solve any linear system. The suitability of the type of algorithm to a class of problems is done on a case-by-case basis. They nevertheless present other advantages which historically have given them the right to use for certain applications. With equivalent memory management, they require less than direct solvers, because we just need to know the action of the matrix on any vector, without having to actually store it. On the other hand, we are not subject to the “diktat” of the filling phenomenon which deteriorates the profile of the matrices, we can effectively exploit the sparse nature of the operators and control the precision of the results 9 . In short, the use of direct solvers is more of a technical matter while choosing the right iterative method/preconditioner pair is more of an art! Despite its biblical simplicity on paper, the solution of a linear system, even a positive definite symmetric one, is not “a long, quiet river”. Between two evils, filling/pivoting and preconditioning, you have to choose! Notes: - A third class of methods tries to take advantage of the respective advantages of direct and iterative methods: Domain Decomposition methods. - The two main families of methods should be seen more as complementary than as competitors. We often try to mix them: DD methods, preconditioner by incomplete factorisation (see R6.01.02 §4.2) or multigrid type, iterative refinement procedure at the end of the direct solver… 1.2 Linear algebra libraries To effectively solve a linear system, the question of using a library or an external product is now unavoidable . Why? Because this strategy allows: - Less technical, less invasive and much faster developments in the host code. - To acquire, at a lower cost, a wide scope of use while outsourcing many of the associated contingencies (typology of the problem cf. §1.1, data representation, architecture of the target machine, etc.). - To benefit from feedback from a varied community of users and the (very) advanced skills of international teams. These libraries often combine efficiency, reliability, performance and portability : - Efficiency because they exploit the spatial and temporal locality of the data and play on the memory hierarchy (example of the different BLAS categories). - Reliability because they offer tools to estimate the error made on the solution (estimation of conditioning and ‘backward/forward errors’) or even to improve it (for direct, balancing of the matrix and iterative refinement). Since the emergence in the 70s/80s of the first public bookstores [10]_ and private/manufacturers [11]_ and their user communities, the offer has multiplied. The trend is of course to offer high-performance solutions (vector, centralised then distributed memory parallelism, multilevel parallelism via threads) as well as “toolkits” for manipulating linear algebra algorithms and associated data structures. Let us cite non-exhaustively: ScaLAPACK (Dongarra & Demmel 1997), SparseKIT (Saad 1988), PETSc (Argonne 1991), HyPre (LL 2000), TRILINOS (Sandia 2000)… Figure 1.2-1._ Some “logos” of linear algebra libraries. Note: - To structure their use more effectively and offer “black box” solutions, macro-libraries have recently emerged. They bring together a panel of these products to which they add “in-house” solutions: Numerical Platon (CEA-DEN), Arcane (CEA-DAM)… Concerning more specifically direct methods for solving linear systems , around fifty packages are available. We distinguish “autonomous” products from those incorporated into a bookstore, audiences from commercial ones, those dealing with dense problems and others with hollow ones. Some only work in sequential mode, others support shared and/or distributed memory parallelism. Finally, some products are general (symmetrical, non-symmetrical, SPD, real/complex, etc.) others adapted to a very specific need/scenario. Note: - A more detailed internet resource but focused on sparse direct solvers is maintained by another big name in numerical technology: T.A.Davis[Dav], one of the Matlab contributors. 1.3 Direct methods: the principle The basic idea of direct methods is to decompose the problem matrix K into a product of particular matrices (lower and upper triangular, diagonal) that are easier to “invert”. This is called factoring [12]_ of the working matrix: - If K is SPD , it admits the unique “Cholesky factorisation”: K=L{L}^{T} with lower triangular L ; - If K is any symmetric and regular , it admits at least one “factorisation LD{L}^{T} ” : PK=LD{L}^{T} with L lower triangular with diagonal coefficients equal to unity, D a diagonal matrix [13]_ and P a permutation matrix; - If K is arbitrary and regular , it admits at least one “ LU factorisation”: PK=LU with L lower triangular than unit diagonal, U upper triangular and P a permutation matrix; | | | --- | Figure 1.3-1._ Principle of direct methods. Note: - For example, the symmetrical and regular matrix K below is decomposed into the following form LD{L}^{T} (without needing permutation here P=\mathrm{Id} ) > K:=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}10& & \text{sym}\\ 20& 45& \\ 30& 80& 171\end{array}\right]=\underset{L}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1& 0& 0\\ 2& 1& 0\\ 3& 4& 1\end{array}\right]}}\underset{D}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{\left[\begin{array}{ccc}10& 0& 0\\ 0& 5& 0\\ 0& 0& 1\end{array}\right]}}\underset{{L}^{T}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1& 2& 3\\ 0& 1& 4\\ 0& 0& 1\end{array}\right]}} (1.3-1) Once this decomposition is carried out, solving the problem is greatly facilitated. It is only expressed in the form of the simplest linear resolutions possible: based on triangular or diagonal matrices. These are the famous “ forward/backward algorithms ”. For example in the case of a factorisation LU , the system (1.1-1) will be solved by \begin{array}{c}\text{Ku}=f\\ \text{PK}=\text{LU}\end{array}\rangle \Rightarrow \begin{array}{c}\text{Lv}=\text{Pf}(\text{descente})\\ \text{Uu}=v(\text{remontée})\end{array} (1.3-2) In the first lower diagonal system (descent), we determine the intermediate solution vector v . The latter then serves as a second member of the upper diagonal system (ascent) of which the vector u which interests us is the solution. This phase is inexpensive (in dense, of the order of {N}^{2} against {N}^{3} for factorisation [14]_ with N the size of the problem) and can therefore be repeated many times while maintaining the same factorisation. Which is very useful when solving a multiple second members type problem or when you want to carry out simultaneous resolutions . In the first scenario , the matrix K is fixed and we successively change the second member {f}_{i} to calculate as many solutions {u}_{i} (the resolutions are interdependent). This makes it possible to pool and therefore amortize this initial cost of factorisation. This strategy is widely used, notably in Code_Aster : nonlinear loop with periodic updating (or no updating) of the tangent matrix (e.g. operator Aste r STAT_NON_LINE), subspace or inverse power methods (without Rayleigh acceleration) in modal calculation (CALC_MODES), thermo-mechanical chaining with material characteristics independent of temperature (MECA_STATIQUE), etc. In the second scenario , we are aware of all the {f}_{i} at the same time and we organize, in blocks, the descent-ascent phases, to simultaneously calculate the independent {u}_{i} solutions. We can thus use more efficient high-level linear algebra routines, or even play on memory consumption by storing the vector {f}_{i} hollowly. This strategy is (partially) used in Code_Aster , for example, in the construction of Schur complements of contact-friction algorithms or for substructuring. Note: - The MUMPS product provides for these two types of strategy and even offers features to facilitate the construction and resolution of Schur's complement. Now let's look at the factoring process itself . It is already clearly explained in the other theoretical documentation of Code_Aster on the subject[R6.02.01][R6.02.02], as well as in the bibliographic references already cited[Duf06][Gol96][Las98]. So we will not detail it. Let us just point out that it is an iterative process organized schematically around three loops: one “called in i ” (on the lines of the work matrix), the second “in j ” (resp. columns) and the third “in k ” (resp. stages of the factorisation). It is not only capable of detecting numerical singularities [23]_ of a matrix and to synthesize the information for external use (rank calculation, warning to the user, display of expertise, etc.), but in addition, despite this difficulty, it calculates a “regular ” solution [24]_ » or even all or part of the associated core . And in practice, how does MUMPS work? It is complementary to the parallelism and the algorithmic/functional range of the product . Its scope of use is almost complete. We don't have to choose between parallelism, this or that numerical refinement and these BLR compressions! All these functionalities are compatible and their gains are often cumulative [29]_ .
