BETON_UMLV is a linear viscoelastic constitutive model. In order to be able to represent the failure of concrete by tertiary creep, one proposes in Code_Aster to couple the creep model to a damage model, namely the MAZARS model (cf. R7.01.08). The coupling is carried out by assuming, on the one hand, that the creep strains are generated by the effective stresses (that is, those really seen by the material) and, on the other hand, that only a part of the creep strain (assumed constant) contributes to the evolution of the damage. The scheme is carried out while maintaining the direct link between the state of elastic strains and the state of stresses. 7.1 Implementation 7.1.1 Update of the internal variables of creep As for the rest of the document, one restricts oneself here to the description of the coupling between damage and basic creep. One therefore assumes, as previously, that the strain is written according to equation [eq 2-2]: \varepsilon ={\varepsilon}^{e}+{\varepsilon}^{f} where {\epsilon}^{e} , the elastic strain, also contains the contribution of the damage (micro-cracking) generated by the MAZARS model. Considering the spherical [eq 4.1-2] and deviatoric [eq 4.2-1] contributions of basic creep as well as that of desiccation creep, one obtains the increment of the creep strains \Delta {\underline{\underline{\epsilon}}}^{f} between the time instants n and n+1: \Delta {\underline{\underline{\varepsilon}}}_{n}^{f}={\underline{\underline{a}}}_{n}+{b}_{n}{\underline{\underline{\sigma}}}_{n}+{c}_{n}{\underline{\underline{\sigma}}}_{n+1} eq 6.1-1 with {\underline{\underline{a}}}_{n},{b}_{n}{c}_{n} the coefficients of the total basic creep in linear viscoelasticity. In order to introduce damage into the model, one assumes that the creep strains are generated by the effective stresses, denoted \underline{\underline{\sigma}}' in the remainder of the document. This makes it possible to associate the delayed strains with the sound part of the material, as proposed in [bib1]. One recalls that the effective stresses may be written as a function of the damage variable D or (see also the documentation[R7.01.08-B]) as an elasticity law: \underline{\underline{\sigma}}'=\frac{\underline{\underline{\sigma}}}{1-D}=\underline{\underline{\underline{\underline{E}}}}{\underline{\underline{\varepsilon}}}^{e} eq 6.1-2 Consequently, equation [eq 6.1-1] becomes: \Delta {\underline{\underline{\varepsilon}}}_{n}^{f}={\underline{\underline{a}}}_{n}+{b}_{n}\underline{\underline{\sigma}}{'}_{n}+{c}_{n}\underline{\underline{\sigma}}{'}_{n+1} eq 6.1-3 By using the elasticity law [eq 6.1-2] with equation [eq 6.1-3], one obtains the new relation for the creep-strain increment: \Delta {\underline{\underline{\varepsilon}}}_{n}^{f}={(1+c\underline{\underline{\underline{\underline{E}}}})}^{\text{-1}}\left[{\underline{\underline{a}}}_{n}+{b}_{n}\underline{\underline{\sigma}}{'}_{n}+{c}_{n}\underline{\underline{\underline{\underline{E}}}}({\underline{\underline{\varepsilon}}}_{n+1}-{\underline{\underline{\varepsilon}}}_{n}^{f})\right] eq 6.1-4 Thus, from all the quantities known at time instant n , it is possible to compute with relation [eq 6.1-4] the creep strain at time instant n+1 . Then, one easily obtains the effective stresses at time instant n+1 thanks to relation [eq 6.1-2], and the internal variables of creep with equations [eq 4.1-2] and [eq 4.2-1]. 7.1.2 Evolution of the damage One does not detail the MAZARS model here; the reader may refer to the Code_Aster reference documentation of the MAZARS model R7.01.08. The basic assumption is that the damage is driven by the elastic strain and a share of the creep strain. The strain tensor which drives the evolution of D is given by the following relation: \stackrel{˘}{\underline{\underline{\varepsilon}}}={\underline{\underline{\varepsilon}}}^{e}+\chi {\underline{\underline{\varepsilon}}}^{f} eq 6.2-1 with 0\le \chi \le 1 , coupling coefficient. The level of coupling increases with increasing \chi . There therefore exist two limiting cases: \chi =0 and \chi =1 . - If , \chi =0 there is an absence of coupling; the evolution of the damage depends only on the elastic strain and therefore one cannot have tertiary creep. - If \chi =1 the coupling is maximal; the damage depends on the total strain. This case generally leads to the premature ruin of the structure. r7.01.08 MAZARS damage model r7.01.08 MAZARS damage model Summary: This documentation presents the MAZARS constitutive model, which makes it possible to describe the elastic damageable behaviour of concrete. This model is 3D and isotropic, and is based on a damage criterion written in strain and describing the tension–compression asymmetry. The initial model does not account for the recovery of stiffness in the event of “crack closure” and does not take into account the possible plastic strains or viscous effects that may be observed during the straining of a concrete. The version implemented in Code_Aster takes the latest improvements into account. This reformulation of the Mazars model of the 1980s makes it possible to describe better the behaviour of concrete in biaxial compression and in pure shear. The \mathrm{1D} version of the model makes it possible to account for the recovery of stiffness in the event of crack closure; it is used only with multifibre beams R5.03.09. 1 Introduction 1.1 An elastic damageable constitutive law The MAZARS] constitutive model is a simple model, reputed to be robust, based on damage mechanics, which makes it possible to describe the decrease in the stiffness of the material under the effect of the creation of microcracks in the concrete. It is based on a single scalar internal variable D describing the damage in an isotropic manner, while nevertheless distinguishing tensile damage and compressive damage. The version implemented in Aster corresponds to the 2012 reformulation . The major modification with respect to the original model ] is the introduction of a new internal variable, denoted Y , corresponding to the maximum reached during the loading by the equivalent strain defined in the 1980s. Consequently, damage is no longer the internal variable in the revisited model. Moreover, its evolution law is simplified in order to eliminate the notions of tensile and compressive damage. Unlike the ENDO_ISOT_BETON model, this model does not make it possible to represent the phenomenon of crack closure (stiffness recovery). Furthermore, the Mazars model does not take into account the possible plastic strains or viscous effects that may be observed during the straining of a concrete. The \mathrm{1D} version of the Mazars model is described in the document R5.03.09 “Non-linear constitutive relations”. In this specific case, the model is capable of accounting for the phenomenon of crack closure. The \mathrm{1D} version of the model can be used only with multifibre beams. 1.2 Limits and regularisation methods Like all softening laws, the Mazars model raises difficulties related to the phenomenon of strain localisation. Physically, the heterogeneity of the microstructure of concrete induces interactions at a distance between the cracks formed ]. Thus, the strains localise in a thin band, called the localisation band, to form the macrocracks. The stress state at a material point can no longer be described solely by the characteristics at the point, but must also take its environment into consideration. In the case of this (local) model, no indication is included concerning the scale of the cracking. Consequently, no information is given on the width of the localisation band, which then becomes zero. This leads to a mechanical behaviour with failure without energy dissipation, which is physically unacceptable. Mathematically, localisation makes the problem to be solved ill-posed, because softening causes a loss of ellipticity of the differential equations that describe the straining process ]. The numerical solutions do not converge towards physically acceptable solutions despite the mesh refinements. 1.3 Coupling with thermal analysis For certain studies, it may be of interest to be able to take into account the modification of the material parameters under the effect of temperature. This is possible in Aster (MAZARS_FO combined or not with ELAS_FO). The assumptions made for the coupling with thermal analysis are the following: - thermal expansion is assumed to be linear, that is: {\varepsilon}^{\text{th}}=\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{ref}}){I}_{d} with \alpha = constant or a function of temperature, - thermo-mechanical interactions are not taken into account, that is, the effect of the mechanical stress state on the thermal strain of the concrete is not modelled, - concerning the evolution of the material parameters with temperature, they are considered to depend not on the current temperature but on the maximum temperature \mathit{Tmax} seen by the material during its history (an effect cited in the literature), - only the elastic (mechanical) strain induces damage. Note: Because of data-processing constraints, the initial value of \mathrm{Tmax} is initialised to 0. Consequently, material parameters defined for negative temperatures cannot be used (if necessary, this problem can nevertheless be circumvented by entering all temperatures in Kelvin instead of °C ). 1.4 Mazars law in the presence of a drying or hydration field The use of ELAS_FO and/or MAZARS_FO under the operator DEFI_MATERIAU makes it possible to make the material parameters depend on drying or on hydration. Furthermore, the strains related to endogenous shrinkage {\varepsilon}_{\text{re}} and to desiccation shrinkage {\varepsilon}_{\text{rd}} are taken into account in the model, in the following (linear) form (cf. R7.01.12): {\varepsilon}_{\text{re}}=-\beta \xi {I}_{d} {\varepsilon}_{\text{rd}}=-\kappa ({C}_{\text{ref}}-C){\mathrm{I}}_{\mathrm{d}} where \xi is the hydration, C the water concentration (drying field in the Code_Aster terminology), {C}_{\mathit{ref}} the initial water concentration (or reference drying). Finally \beta is the endogenous shrinkage coefficient and \kappa the desiccation shrinkage coefficient, to be supplied in DEFI_MATERIAU, factor keyword ELAS_FO, operands B_ENDO and K_DESSIC. As stated in the previous paragraph, the choice made in the implementation of the MAZARS model is that only the elastic strain induces damage. Consequently, if a concrete specimen that dries or hydrates freely and uniformly is modelled, a non-zero strain field and a perfectly zero stress field will indeed be obtained. The writing of the model is presented first, then a few data on the identification of the parameters. Finally, the principles of the numerical integration in Code_Aster are set out. 2 The MAZARS models 2.1 Original Mazars model The MAZARS model was developed within the framework of damage mechanics. This model is detailed in the thesis of MAZARS ] The stress is given by the following relation: \sigma =(1-D)\text{E}{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{e}} with: - E the Hooke matrix, - D the damage variable - {\varepsilon}^{e} the elastic strain {\varepsilon}^{e}=\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{\text{th}}-{\varepsilon}^{\text{rd}}-{\varepsilon}^{\text{re}} • {\varepsilon}^{\text{th}}=\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{ref}}){I}_{d} thermal expansion • {\varepsilon}^{\text{re}}=-\beta \xi {\mathrm{I}}_{\mathrm{d}} endogenous shrinkage (related to hydration) • {\varepsilon}_{\text{rd}}=-\kappa ({C}_{\text{ref}}-C){I}_{d} desiccation shrinkage (related to drying) D is the damage variable. It lies between 0 , sound material, and 1 , failed material. The damage is driven by the equivalent strain {\epsilon}_{\text{eq}} , which makes it possible to translate a triaxial state into an equivalence with a uniaxial state. Since extensions are of prime importance in the cracking phenomenon of concrete, the equivalent strain introduced is defined from the positive eigenvalues of the strain tensor, that is: \epsilon_{\text{eq}} = \sqrt{\langle \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \rangle_+ : \langle \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \rangle_+} \\ \text{où dans le repère principal du tenseur de déformations :} \\ \epsilon_{\text{eq}} = \sqrt{\langle \epsilon_1 \rangle_+^2 + \langle \epsilon_2 \rangle_+^2 + \langle \epsilon_3 \rangle_+^2} knowing that the positive part {\langle \rangle }_{+} is defined so that if {\varepsilon}_{i} is the principal strain in direction i : \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\langle {\epsilon}_{i}\rangle }_{+}={\epsilon}_{i}\text{si}{\epsilon}_{i}\ge 0\\ {\langle {\epsilon}_{i}\rangle }_{+}=0\text{si}{\epsilon}_{i} a) Original Mazars model b) Revisited Mazars model Figure 2.2-1: Comparison of the damage-initiation and failure surfaces of the Mazars models in the plane {\sigma}_{3}=0 and a C30 concrete Thus, a new formulation is proposed through 2 major modifications: 1. improvement of the behaviour in biaxial compression, 2. simplification and improvement of the behaviour in shear. The original Mazars model of the 1980s ] greatly underestimates the strength of concrete in biaxial compression. The first modification introduced by the revisited model therefore improves the behaviour in biaxial compression. This aim is achieved by correcting the equivalent strain when at least one principal stress is negative, by means of a variable \gamma : {\epsilon}_{\mathit{eq}}^{\mathit{corrigée}}=\gamma {\epsilon}_{\text{eq}}=\gamma \sqrt{{\langle \epsilon \rangle }_{+}:{\langle \epsilon \rangle }_{+}} with: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\gamma =-\frac{\sqrt{\sum_{i}{\langle {\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}\rangle }_{-}^{2}}}{\sum_{i}{\langle {\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}\rangle }_{-}}\text{si au moins une contrainte effective est négative}\\ \gamma =1\text{sinon}\end{array} The effective stress in the sense of damage mechanics is defined by: \underline{\underline{\tilde{\sigma}}}=\frac{\underline{\underline{\sigma}}}{1-D} The definition of - is similar to : \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\langle {\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}\rangle }_{-}={\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}\text{si}{\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}\le 0\\ {\langle {\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}\rangle }_{-}=0\text{si}{\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}>0\end{array} where {\tilde{\sigma}}_{i} is a principal effective stress. The improvement of the behaviour in shear is achieved by the introduction of a new internal variable: Y . It corresponds to the maximum reached during the loading of the equivalent strain. Its initial value {Y}_{0} is {\epsilon}_{\mathit{d0}} . Y is defined by the following equation: Y=\max\left({\epsilon}_{\mathit{d0}}\text{,max}\left({\epsilon}_{\mathit{eq}}^{\mathit{corrigée}}\right)\right) The loading function is: f={\epsilon}_{\mathit{eq}}^{\mathit{corrigée}}-Y The evolution of the damage is given by: D=1-\frac{(1-A){Y}_{0}}{Y}-A\exp(-B(Y-{Y}_{0})) In this expression, it is the variables A and B that make it possible to reproduce the quasi-brittle behaviour of concrete in tension and the hardened behaviour in compression. When r is equal to 1 (corresponding to the tension sector), the variables A and B are equivalent to the parameters {A}_{t} and {B}_{t} . Thus, is identical to . Conversely, if r is zero (corresponding to the compression sector), then A={A}_{c} , B={B}_{c} and is identical to . It gives, in the plane {\sigma}_{3}=0 , the evolution, as a function of the sign of the principal stresses, of the variables A , B , r and \gamma . In general {B}_{c} lies between 1000 and 2000 and {B}_{t} between 9000 and 21000 . - k introduces a horizontal asymptote in pure shear on the stress–strain curve if its value is different from 1 for {A}_{t}=1 , . The recommended value is 0.7 . Figure 3-1: Influence of the parameter {A}_{t} Figure 3-2: Influence of the parameter {B}_{t} One way of obtaining a set of parameters is to have the results of uniaxial tests in compression and tension (for tension, other types of tests may be used, “Brazilian” splitting tests for example). If strain-gradient regularisation is used (see § 1.2 ), it is recommended to fit the parameters of the law at the same time as the characteristic length {L}_{c} . A few authors (confer ) also suggest calibrating {L}_{c} by using experimental tests on several specimen sizes; indeed, the characteristic length is related to the size of the energy-dissipation zone, which could be the origin of structural size effects. 4 Numerical solution 4.1 Evaluation of the internal variable Y The computation of Y is very simple and follows an explicit scheme. The steps are the following: - Computation of the elastic and thermal strains - Computation of the principal elastic stresses and evaluation of \gamma . - Computation of the equivalent strain ( and ). - Computation of the variables r , A and B - Computation of the internal variable Y . - If Y\le {Y}^{-} then {Y}^{+}={Y}^{-} . If Y>{Y}^{-} then {Y}^{+}=Y . > Note: At present the variable stored during the analyses is {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}} so as not to modify the existing couplings with UMLV. A condition on the strictly increasing evolution of the damage allows this simplification in the case where \gamma varies. 4.2 Evaluation of the damage > The damage is computed in all cases with the equation . D=1-\frac{\left(1-A\right){Y}_{0}}{Y}-A\exp\left(-B\left(Y-{Y}_{0}\right)\right) It is important to specify that D is imposed to lie between 0 and 1, because it is possible to have values outside this range depending on the choice of the material parameters, as for the original model. 4.3 Computation of the stress After evaluation of D , one simply computes: \sigma =(1-D)\mathrm{A}{\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{e}} 4.4 Computation of the tangent matrix One disadvantage of the Mazars model is the absence of a tangent matrix. It is not possible to compute this matrix because of the use of the MacCauley operator in the computation of the equivalent strain , of \gamma and r . However, it is possible to use an approximation for radial loadings. The tensor \mathrm{M} such that \dot{\sigma}=\mathrm{M}\dot{\varepsilon} is sought, knowing that \sigma =(1-D)\mathrm{A}\varepsilon . The matrix is therefore the sum of two terms, one at constant damage, the other due to the evolution of the damage: \dot{\sigma}=(1-D)\mathrm{A}\dot{\varepsilon}-\mathrm{A}\varepsilon \dot{D} The first term is straightforward: it is the Hooke operator, multiplied by the factor 1-D . The second requires the evaluation of the damage increment \dot{D} . If a radial loading is imposed, the variables \gamma , r , A and B are constant. Setting: \dot{D}=\frac{\partial D}{\partial Y}\frac{\partial Y}{\partial (\gamma {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}})}\frac{\partial (\gamma {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}})}{\partial \varepsilon }\dot{\varepsilon} With \frac{\partial Y}{\partial (\gamma {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}})}\frac{\partial (\gamma {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}})}{\partial \varepsilon }=\frac{\gamma {\langle \varepsilon \rangle }_{+}}{{\epsilon}_{\text{eq}}} Under this radial-loading condition, the strain increment is written: \dot{D}=\left[\frac{(1-A){Y}_{0}}{{Y}^{2}}+\text{AB}\exp(B(Y-{Y}_{0}))\right]\frac{\gamma {\langle \varepsilon \rangle }_{+}}{{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}}\dot{\varepsilon} Notes: | 1. | Given the simplifications made, in the general case the tangent matrix is not consistent. Also, it may happen that updating the tangent matrix during the Newton iterations does not help convergence. In that case, it is sufficient to use only the secant matrix by imposing STAT_NON_LINE(NEWTON = _F(REAC_ITER =0 )). | | --- | --- | | 2. | In the general case, the tangent matrix is non-symmetric. It is possible to do so by means of the keyword SOLVEUR=_F(SYME = ‘OUI’) of STAT_NON_LINE . | | 3 . | The analytical expression of the tangent matrix is valid only for radial loadings ( \mathit{dr}=d\gamma =0 ). In the other cases, the quadratic convergence of the method is no longer guaranteed. | 4.5 Stored internal variables The following table indicates the internal variables stored at each Gauss point for the MAZARS model: | Internal variable | Physical meaning | | --- | --- | | \mathit{V1} | D : damage variable | | \mathit{V2} | damage indicator (0 if elastic, 1 if damaged, that is as soon as D is no longer zero) | | \mathit{V3} | \mathit{Tmax} : maximum temperature \theta reached at the Gauss point | | \mathit{V4} | {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}=\sqrt{{\langle \varepsilon \rangle }_{+}:{\langle \varepsilon \rangle }_{+}} the equivalent strain | Table 4.5-1 : Stored internal variables. 5 Features and verification The constitutive law MAZARS, keyword COMPORTEMENT of STAT_NON_LINE, associated material MAZARS, can be used in Code_Aster with various modellings: - 3D, D_PLAN, AXIS, C_PLAN (analytical formulation implemented; do not use the DEBORST method) - coupled with the THHM models (confer R7.01.11). r7.01.09 Constitutive law ENDO_ORTH_BETON r7.01.09 Constitutive law ENDO_ORTH_BETON Summary: This documentation presents the theoretical writing and the numerical integration of the constitutive law ENDO_ORTH_BETON developed by [bib1], which describes the anisotropy induced by damage in concrete, as well as the unilateral effects (different behaviour in tension and in compression). The validation of the model against experimental results is also proposed in this document. > Contents 1 Introduction 1.1 Characteristics of the damage of concrete Concrete is a complex material, formed of aggregates and of a paste ensuring the cohesion between these aggregates, and within which microcracks pre-exist, formed during the various stages of manufacture. Concrete is generally considered as an initially isotropic material, the microcracks having no preferred orientation. This isotropy is preserved if the applied loading remains in the elastic domain. From a certain level of loading, the microcracks will develop in particular directions, which induces the appearance of anisotropy in the non-linear phase. The cracks develop preferentially orthogonally to the directions of greatest tension or of smallest compression. The damage process is therefore expressed by a loss of stiffness generated by the decohesion of the material. The stiffness can be recovered when the cracks are closed (unilateral effect). To this is added another strong dissymmetry of the behaviour between tension and compression: the stresses sustained in compression are 10 times (or even more) greater than the stresses sustained in tension. Finally, let us point out other phenomena such as the formation of irreversible strains (caused for example by the locking of the crack lips by friction or the presence of degraded material between these lips) or phenomena of energy dissipation by friction of the crack lips. 1.2 Objectives of the law ENDO_ORTH_BETON Despite the existence of various anisotropic damage models for concrete, isotropic models are still used exclusively in design offices in order to account for the behaviour of concrete structures. This is due, for the anisotropic models, to the complexity of their numerical implementation, to the difficulty of identifying their sometimes numerous parameters, to the mismatch between the objectives of the model and those of the industrial study, to the difficulty of coupling the model with other physical phenomena (creep, plasticity), and in most cases to the long computation times required by the anisotropic models. The use of anisotropic models is moreover not necessary in the cases where the isotropic models describe the same behaviour of the structure. There are nevertheless cases where the anisotropic models can prove interesting, as soon as they predict a behaviour different from that of the isotropic models. The objective is to have available a simple anisotropic model (small number of parameters), numerically robust, and respecting the rules of thermodynamics (positive dissipation). It is obvious that a certain number of phenomena observed experimentally will not be able to be taken into account. A specification was therefore defined prior to the development of the model in order to define its framework. Two categories of requirements can be distinguished, the objective being to obtain a reasonable result whatever the loading. One concerns the physical consistency of the prediction of the model (1) to (4), and the other concerns the numerical robustness (5) and (6). The framework of our model is composed of the following points: 1. Account taken of the anisotropy thanks to the introduction of a symmetric tensor of order 2 representing the effects of the damage. It is therefore more accurate to speak of an orthotropic model, inasmuch as the use of such a tensor makes it possible to define only three principal directions of the damage. A tensor of higher order (4 or even 8) is necessary in order to account for the complete anisotropy. 2. Vanishing of the stress at failure. This leads us to define a free energy, a function of the strains, rather than a free enthalpy, a function of the stresses, because it seems easier to obtain a zero stress from finite strains than the converse. 3. Increasing and bounded eigenvalues of the damage. This point accounts for the irreversible character of the damage process (growth of the eigenvalues), of which failure constitutes the limit (bounded eigenvalues). It moreover makes it possible to reach failure in several directions. 4. Account taken of the unilateral behaviour of concrete: closure of the cracks in compression, dissymmetry of the damage thresholds between tension and compression. 5. Continuity of the stress/strain response, particularly at the open–closed transition of the cracks. Besides the fact that a discontinuity would be physically doubtful, it would lead to convergence problems of the numerical algorithm. 6. Respect of the framework of generalised standard materials. This makes it possible to ensure the thermodynamic consistency of the model (positive dissipation) and it provides pleasant mathematical properties for the numerical solution (existence and uniqueness of the solution of the problem of computing the stresses and the final damage at a fixed strain increment, called the “local projection problem” by analogy with plasticity). Note: | The framework of generalised standard materials (CSMG) as it is understood here is not strictly that defined by Halphen and Nguyen [bib11]. Indeed, the strict CSMG ensures the existence and the uniqueness of the solution of the global problem if the energy is convex with respect to all the variables simultaneously. This cannot be verified in the case of softening constitutive laws. The “degraded” CSMG that we define ensures only the existence and the uniqueness of the solution of the local projection problem (computation of the evolution of the damage at fixed strain). In order to respect the CSMG, one must verify the convexity of the free energy, on the one hand with respect to the strain, and on the other hand with respect to the internal variables: The convexity with respect to the strain is necessary in order to ensure the stability of the elastic problem. The convexity with respect to all the internal variables simultaneously is necessary in order to have the right mathematical properties for the local projection problem. In the case where several internal variables are used, the separate convexities with respect to each of these variables are not sufficient. The global convexity with respect to the strain and to the internal variables simultaneously is not required, since the strain increment is fixed for the local projection which makes it possible to compute the evolution of the internal variables. It moreover seems impossible to obtain this global convexity in the case of softening constitutive laws. The framework that has been defined omits a certain number of physical phenomena associated with the damage of concrete: appearance of irreversible strains volumetric dilatancy of the material in compression hysteretic behaviour for loading–unloading cycles, generated by the friction between the crack lips. | | --- | 2 Expression of the free energy 2.1 Account taken of crack closure If one seeks to take the closure effect into account, great attention must be paid to the continuity of the stresses as a function of the strains (which is an indispensable condition for a constitutive law in a finite-element analysis software), cf. [bib2]. Indeed, if one models this effect in too simplistic a manner, the constitutive law has a good chance of presenting a discontinuous response. One solution is to describe finely what one calls tension and compression, knowing that in tension (resp. compression) the crack will be considered “open” (resp. “closed”). A natural solution is to place oneself in a principal frame of strain. In such a frame, the elastic free energy is written ( \lambda and m denoting the Lamé coefficients): \varphi (\varepsilon )=\frac{\lambda}{2}{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}^{2}+\mu \sum_{i}{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2} eq 2.1-1 One can then define: - a volumetric tension or compression, according to the sign of \text{tr}\varepsilon , - a tension or compression in each principal direction, according to the sign of {\varepsilon}_{i} . The elastic free energy can then be written: \varphi (\varepsilon )=\frac{\lambda}{2}\left[{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{+}^{2}+{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{-}^{2}\right]+\mu \left[\text{tr}({\varepsilon}_{+}^{2})+\text{tr}({\varepsilon}_{-}^{2})\right] eq 2.1-2 with the following definitions for the positive and negative parts: {(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{+}=H(\text{tr}\varepsilon )\text{tr}\varepsilon ; :math: {(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{-}=H(-\text{tr}\varepsilon )\text{tr}\varepsilon ; \text{tr}({\varepsilon}_{+}^{2})=\sum_{i}H({\varepsilon}_{i}){\varepsilon}_{i}^{2} ; \text{tr}({\varepsilon}_{-}^{2})=\sum_{i}H(-{\varepsilon}_{i}){\varepsilon}_{i}^{2} where H is the Heaviside function. Note: A more detailed study of the properties of the positive and negative parts of a tensor is made in appendix 1. 2.2 Introduction of the damage variables Given the complexity of the damage mechanisms, and after having observed that it was difficult to describe the behaviour of concrete by using only a single damage variable, we have chosen to introduce two damage variables: - A tensor D of order 2 relating to the damage created in tension - A scalar d relating to the damage created in compression Note: The choice of a tensor of order 2 in order to model the tensile damage is relatively classical and intuitive. It makes it possible to describe the preferred orientation of the cracks orthogonally to the direction of greatest tension. The question of the damage created in compression (orthotropic or isotropic?) is much less clear. Suppose for simplicity that the cracks can be generated only in the planes orthogonal to {\overrightarrow{e}}_{1} , {\overrightarrow{e}}_{2} or {\overrightarrow{e}}_{3} . In the case of a simple tension in the direction {\overrightarrow{e}}_{1} , the cracks are created in the plane orthogonal to {\overrightarrow{e}}_{1} , which leads to a loss of stiffness in the direction {\overrightarrow{e}}_{1} . If one then applies a simple tension in the direction {\overrightarrow{e}}_{2} , one does not “see” the crack because the loading is parallel to the plane of the crack and the stiffness is not affected. The damage is therefore clearly anisotropic in tension. In the case of a simple compression in the direction {\overrightarrow{e}}_{1} , one creates cracks in the planes orthogonal to {\overrightarrow{e}}_{2} and {\overrightarrow{e}}_{3} . If one then loads in compression in the direction {\overrightarrow{e}}_{2} , one “sees” the cracks orthogonal to {\overrightarrow{e}}_{3} . The stiffness in the direction {\overrightarrow{e}}_{2} is therefore weaker than the undegraded normal stiffness, but it is stronger than the stiffness in the direction {\overrightarrow{e}}_{1} because the compression in the direction {\overrightarrow{e}}_{1} is sensitive to all the cracks, that is those orthogonal to {\overrightarrow{e}}_{2} and to {\overrightarrow{e}}_{3} . Consequently, the damage in compression seems less anisotropic than in tension, without however being completely isotropic. In the absence of a clear physical argument on the isotropic or anisotropic character of the damage in compression, we have chosen to take it as isotropic for reasons of simplicity. One sets B=I-D representing the integrity of the material in tension. One introduces the tensile damage into the “positive” terms of the free energy [eq 2.1-2] and the compressive damage into the negative terms. The free energy is now defined as follows: \varphi (\varepsilon ,\mathrm{\Beta },d)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\left[{(\operatorname{tr}(B\varepsilon))}_{+}^{2}+{(1-d)}^{2}{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{-}^{2}\right]+\mu \left[\frac{1}{4}\text{tr}({(\mathrm{\Beta \; \varepsilon }+\mathrm{\varepsilon \; B})}_{+}^{2})+{(1-d)}^{2}\text{tr}({\varepsilon}_{-}^{2})\right] eq 2.2-1 Note: The convexity of the free energy with respect, on the one hand, to the strain, and on the other hand to the damage variables simultaneously, is indeed respected. One will refer to [bib2] and [bib1] for a proof. 2.3 Bounds on the damage Failure, or the creation of a crack completely crossing the material element under consideration, imposes an upper bound on the damage. This bound is imposed on each eigenvalue of the tensile damage ( {D}_{i}\in \left[0,1\right] where the {D}_{i} denote the eigenvalues of D ), which makes it possible to reach failure in 3 orthogonal directions. A convex indicator function with respect to the damage, {I}_{]-\infty ,1]} for D or {I}_{[0,\infty [} } for B , is therefore used to control each of the eigenvalues of the damage (cf. [bib2 ]). Likewise, one uses an indicator on the value of the scalar compressive damage. One obtains the following expression for the free energy: \begin{array}{cc}\varphi (\varepsilon ,B,d)& =\frac{\lambda}{2}\left[{(\text{tr}B\varepsilon )}_{+}^{2}+{(1-d)}^{2}{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{-}^{2}\right]+\mu \left[\frac{1}{4}\text{tr}({(B\varepsilon +\varepsilon B)}_{+}^{2})+{(1-d)}^{2}\text{tr}({\varepsilon}_{-}^{2})\right]\\ & +{I}_{[0,\infty [}\left[\min({B}_{i})\right]+{I}_{]-\infty ,1]}\left[d\right]\end{array} eq 2.3-1 Note: It follows from this expression that once the damage is equal to 1 in a principal direction, this principal direction is henceforth locked and the damage can no longer evolve except in the plane perpendicular to this direction. The proof of this point is found in appendix 2. 2.4 Introduction of a blocked energy We propose to introduce a blocked energy in order to control better the evolution of the damage as a function of the loading, in the form used by [bib4]. The idea consists in introducing an additional term into the energy depending only on the damage, and not on the strain state. There then results an additional term in the derivation of the thermodynamic forces which control the evolution of the damage (cf. section [§ 3 ]). This additional term implies, on the other hand, no modification of the expression for the stress. The energy is written in the following manner: \begin{array}{cc}\varphi (\varepsilon ,B,d)& =\frac{\lambda}{2}\left[{(\text{tr}B\varepsilon )}_{+}^{2}+{(1-d)}^{2}{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{-}^{2}\right]+\mu \left[\frac{1}{4}\text{tr}({(B\varepsilon +\varepsilon B)}_{+}^{2})+{(1-d)}^{2}\text{tr}({\varepsilon}_{-}^{2})\right]\\ & +{I}_{[0,\infty [}\left[\min({B}_{i})\right]+{I}_{]-\infty ,1]}\left[d\right]+{\psi}^{\text{bloquée}}(B,d)\end{array} eq 2.4-1 where {\psi}^{\text{bloquée}}(B,d) is a convex function of the damage. One chooses to take this additional energy as zero when the material is sound. It must moreover be expressed by means of invariants of the damage tensor. One finally wishes the additional term in the expression of the thermodynamic forces to depend on the damage, which makes it possible to eliminate the choice of a term linear in the damage for the energy {\psi}^{\text{bloquée}}(B,d) . We have opted for the following expression: \begin{array}{cc}{\psi}^{\text{bloquée}}(B,d)& =\frac{{\gamma}_{B}}{2}\text{tr}({(\text{I - B})}^{2})+{\gamma}_{d}{d}^{2}\\ & =\frac{{\gamma}_{B}}{2}\text{tr}({D}^{2})+{\gamma}_{d}{d}^{2}\end{array} eq 2.4-2 where {\gamma}_{B} and {\gamma}_{d} are parameters of the model. Note: | One may ask oneself the question of the physical meaning of this additional energy. The evolution of the damage does indeed give rise, in the energy, to the appearance of an energy “blocked” by the system, and this energy is not zero when the material has failed. Consequently, if one draws up the energy balance of the creation of a crack, only part of the energy consumed corresponds to the dissipation of energy in the form of heat, whereas another part remains blocked. One can find a physical origin of this blocked energy in the case of compression. Indeed, if one releases the macroscopic stress, the cracks opened by the compression do not close completely, as proved by the existence of a residual macroscopic strain. There are therefore probably local residual strains and stresses which store energy (cf. [Figure 2.4-a] ), by analogy with plasticity. (One recalls that the law ENDO_ORTH_BETON does not describe the irreversible strains.). Figure 2.4-a Apart from the physical considerations, the interest of this blocked energy, equivalent to a hardening energy, is that the model remains well within the framework of generalised standard materials. The advantage, compared with a hardening energy, is that this energy will have a different effect on the two damage variables (we shall explain this point in the following section). | | --- | 2.5 Final expression of the free energy, of the stresses and of the thermodynamic forces associated with the damage variables The final expression of the free energy is written: \begin{array}{cc}\varphi (\varepsilon ,B,d)& =\frac{\lambda}{2}\left[{(\text{tr}B\varepsilon )}_{+}^{2}+{(1-d)}^{2}{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{-}^{2}\right]+\mu \left[\frac{1}{4}\text{tr}({(B\varepsilon +\varepsilon B)}_{+}^{2})+{(1-d)}^{2}\text{tr}({\varepsilon}_{-}^{2})\right]\\ & +{I}_{[0,\infty [}\left[\min({B}_{i})\right]+{I}_{]-\infty ,1]}\left[d\right]+{\psi}^{\text{bloquée}}(B,d)\end{array} eq 2.5-1 The expression of the stresses is deduced from the energy by differentiation with respect to the strains: \begin{array}{}\sigma (\varepsilon ,B,d)=\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial \varepsilon }=\lambda \left[{(\text{tr}B\varepsilon )}_{+}B+{(1-d)}^{2}{(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{-}I\right]\\ +\mu \left[\frac{1}{2}({(B\varepsilon +\varepsilon B)}_{+}B+B{(B\varepsilon +\varepsilon B)}_{+})+2{(1-d)}^{2}{\varepsilon}_{-}\right]\end{array} eq 2.5-2 The continuity of the stress results from the continuity of the eigenvalues of a matrix with respect to this matrix (cf. Ostrowski's theorem in [bib4]). Note: A defect nevertheless appears at the “open–closed” transition. The domains of activation and of deactivation of the crack-opening and crack-closure terms do not coincide. This is due to the fact that opening and closure are not associated with the separation into positive and negative parts of the same quantities (opening: damage combined with the strain, closure: strain alone). This does not however affect the continuity property. It moreover appears that this defect is limited to a zone close to the origin of the strains, where it does not generate any physical aberration, and that it has no incidence outside this interval (cf. [bib2]). The formalism proposed in [bib3], making it possible to ensure the continuity of the stress while taking into account the crack-closure effect, presents the same defect. One furthermore deduces from the free energy the expression of the thermodynamic forces associated with the damage variables: {F}^{B}(\varepsilon ,B)=-\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial B}=-\lambda {(\text{tr}B\varepsilon )}_{+}\varepsilon -\frac{\mu}{2}\left[{(B\varepsilon +\varepsilon B)}_{+}\varepsilon +\varepsilon {(B\varepsilon +\varepsilon B)}_{+}\right]+{\gamma}_{B}(\text{I - B}) eq 2.5-3 {F}^{d}(\varepsilon ,d)=-\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial d}=\lambda (1-d){(\text{tr}\varepsilon )}_{-}^{2}+2\mu (1-d)\text{tr}({\varepsilon}_{-}^{2})-2{\gamma}_{d}d eq 2.5-4 Each thermodynamic force is constituted of two parts: - A part depending on the strain and on the damage, which is derived from the elastic part of the energy. - A part depending only on the damage, which is derived from the blocked energy. This term will play the role of a hardening, and makes it possible to control the stress–strain response. One sees that the terms deriving from the blocked energy in each of the thermodynamic forces are independent of one another, which makes it possible to control more easily the evolution of each of the damage variables. 3 Evolution law of the damage variables 3.1 Evolution law In order for the model ENDO_ORTH_BETON to enter the framework of generalised standard materials, one must equip oneself with a dissipation potential. For reasons of simplicity, one rather defines the reversibility domain, as for the law ENDO_ISOT_BETON (cf. doc. R7.01.04). Note: From a formal point of view, generalised standard materials are characterised by a dissipation potential which is a positively homogeneous function of degree 1, the Legendre–Fenchel transform of the indicator function of the reversibility domain. One can therefore choose to define either a dissipation potential, or a reversibility domain. The first idea is to define two evolution criteria corresponding to each of the internal variables. This solution is entirely conceivable inasmuch as the thermodynamic forces are dissociated from one another. It turns out however that this solution has two drawbacks: - The first is of a “physical” order. Consider a specimen subjected to a uniaxial compression. One can imagine that the compression criterion alone is reached and that the tension criterion is not activated. Only the compressive damage then evolves. If one subjects this specimen, after unloading, to a tension in a direction orthogonal to the previous compression axis, the material behaves according to the model as a sound material, despite the creation, in reality, of microcracks parallel to the compression axis, hence perpendicular to the tension axis. - The second drawback is of a practical order. It is indeed easier to treat numerically a single criterion, involving a single Lagrange multiplier (cf. [Figure 3.1-a]), rather than two separate criteria, involving two Lagrange multipliers and able to create zones where the flow direction is not defined a priori (cf. [Figure 3.1-b]). Figure 3.1-a Figure 3.1-b One therefore decides to introduce a single criterion coupling the evolution of the two damage variables: g({F}^{B},{F}^{d})=\sqrt{\alpha {\parallel {F}_{-}^{B}\parallel }^{2}+(1-\alpha ){({F}_{+}^{d})}^{2}}-K(\varepsilon )\le 0 eq 3.1-1 where K(\varepsilon ) is a threshold depending on the strain state (this point will be commented on in section [§ 3.2 ]). The evolution of the damage variables is then determined by the Kuhn–Tucker conditions: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\begin{array}{}\dot{d}=0\\ \dot{B}=0\iff \dot{D}=0\end{array}& \text{pour}g 0,{\sigma}_{2} 0 , the damage variables evolve, respecting both the criterion and the normal flow. One therefore seeks (\Delta B,\mathrm{\Delta \; d},\mathrm{\Delta \; \gamma }) solution of the system: R(\Delta B,\Delta d,\Delta \gamma )=(\begin{array}{c}-\Delta B+\Delta \gamma \alpha {F}_{-}^{B}({B}^{-}+\Delta B)\\ -\Delta d+\Delta \gamma (1-\alpha ){F}_{+}^{d}({d}^{-}+\Delta d)\\ f(\varepsilon ,{B}^{-}+\Delta B,{d}^{-}+\Delta d)\end{array})=(\begin{array}{c}0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}) eq 5.1-2 This system is non-linear and requires the use of an iterative method. We have chosen to use a Newton–Raphson method. The index n represents the Newton iterations. Let {R}^{n}(\Delta {B}^{n},{\mathrm{\Delta \; d}}^{n},{\mathrm{\Delta \; \gamma }}^{n}) be the residual of the system at iteration n ; the linearisation of the system is written: {R}^{n+1}(\Delta {B}^{n+1},\Delta {d}^{n+1},\Delta {\gamma}^{n+1})={R}^{n}(\Delta {B}^{n},\Delta {d}^{n},\Delta {\gamma}^{n})+{({R}^{n}(\Delta {B}^{n},\Delta {d}^{n},\Delta {\gamma}^{n}))}^{\prime }:(\begin{array}{c}\Delta {B}^{n+1}-\Delta {B}^{n}\\ \Delta {d}^{n+1}-\Delta {d}^{n}\\ \Delta {\gamma}^{n+1}-\Delta {\gamma}^{n}\end{array}) eq 5.1-3 where {R}^{n}=(\begin{array}{c}-\Delta {B}^{n}+{\mathrm{\Delta \; \gamma }}^{n}\alpha {F}_{-}^{Bn}\\ -{\mathrm{\Delta \; d}}^{n}+{\mathrm{\Delta \; \gamma }}^{n}(1-\alpha ){F}^{dn}\\ f(\varepsilon ,{B}^{-}+\Delta {B}^{n},{d}^{-}+{\mathrm{\Delta \; d}}^{n})\end{array}) and {R}^{{n}^{\prime }}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}-I+\alpha \Delta {\gamma}^{n}\frac{\partial {F}_{-}^{B}}{\partial {F}^{B}}:\frac{\partial {F}^{B}}{\partial B}& 0& \alpha {F}_{-}^{B}\\ 0& -1+(1-\alpha )\Delta {\gamma}^{n}\frac{\partial {F}_{+}^{d}}{\partial {F}^{d}}\frac{\partial {F}^{d}}{\partial d}& (1-\alpha ){F}_{+}^{d}\\ \frac{\alpha {F}_{-}^{B}}{\sqrt{\alpha {\parallel {F}_{-}^{B}\parallel }^{2}+(1-\alpha ){\mid {F}_{+}^{d}\mid }^{2}}}:\frac{\partial {F}^{B}}{\partial B}& \frac{(1-\alpha ){F}_{+}^{d}}{\sqrt{\alpha {\parallel {F}_{-}^{B}\parallel }^{2}+(1-\alpha ){\mid {F}_{+}^{d}\mid }^{2}}}\frac{\partial {F}^{d}}{\partial d}& 0\end{array}\right] . This procedure is repeated until the residual is smaller than a convergence parameter. 5.2 Computation of the tangent matrix The tangent matrix is the tensor M of order 4 defined by: \delta {\sigma}_{ij}={M}_{ijkl}\delta {\varepsilon}_{kl}\iff {M}_{ijkl}=\frac{\partial {\sigma}_{ij}}{\partial \Delta {\varepsilon}_{kl}} eq 5.2-1 This matrix is not computed on the continuous problem but on the incremental problem. One therefore seeks the effects of a variation of the strain increment between two successive time steps on the variation of the final stress, taking into account the fact that the internal variables can also evolve. In the case of a constant threshold, the matrix is indeed symmetric, since the model is then indeed generalised standard and one uses an implicit integration scheme. 6 Validation The first step of the validation of the model is the comparison of the prediction with various experimental results for simple tests. Given the simplifying assumptions which have been made for our modelling, we shall of course not be able to reproduce all the experiments, in particular the triaxial compression experiments. One concentrates here on the simple tension tests, the simple compression tests, as well as on biaxial tests. 6.1 Identification of the parameters The identification of the parameters must be carried out in three successive phases: - One must choose a value for the coupling constant \alpha . It must be taken so that the scalar compressive damage remains negligible in a tension test. One decides to take it equal to 0,87 for all the tests of the present section in order to avoid the snap-back phenomenon in compression (cf. [§ 4.1.2 ]). - The second phase is the identification of the parameters {k}_{0} and {\gamma}_{B} . These parameters can be identified directly on the simple tension test because the other parameters of the model do not intervene in this test. - The third phase is the identification of the parameters {\gamma}_{d} , {k}_{1} and {k}_{2} on the simple compression tests and the biaxial tests. Strictly speaking, the identification of the parameters of our model for a material requires having available the experimental curves in simple tension, in simple compression and under biaxial loading. Unfortunately, all these results are generally not available simultaneously for a material. We shall therefore have to make a certain number of assumptions in order to calibrate our parameters. For example, we shall choose the parameter {k}_{2} for all the tests in such a way that the tensile stresses in the biaxial tests do not exceed the failure stress in tension. Moreover, we do not have available, for the compression tests, the failure stress in tension for the materials studied. We shall therefore take in an arbitrary manner parameters {k}_{0} and {\gamma}_{B} equal to those that we computed for the simple tension test. 6.2 Simple tension The experiments aiming to observe the behaviour of concrete under tensile loading are extremely difficult to carry out, which explains the relatively small number of results of simple tension tests. The difficulty lies in the fact that the damage concentrates in localisation bands corresponding to cracks, which has the effect of making the specimen under study inhomogeneous. As soon as strong heterogeneities appear, it becomes impossible to deduce a stress–strain curve from the force–displacement curve, and therefore to establish a constitutive law for the material. The PIED measuring apparatus ([bib6], [bib7]) makes it possible to measure a relatively homogeneous stress and strain field by limiting the localisation. This is why we use the results obtained by [bib6] in order to test our model. In the case of simple tension, only 3 of the 6 parameters of the model will play a role: - The coupling parameter \alpha . - The threshold constant {k}_{0} . - The blocked-energy constant associated with the tensile damage {\gamma}_{B} . - The parameters {k}_{1} and {k}_{2} have no influence on this test and the influence of the parameter {\gamma}_{d} is negligible. The parameter {k}_{0} governs the height of the stress peak and the parameter {\gamma}_{B} controls its width as well as the post-peak slope. The larger {\gamma}_{B} is, the less rapidly the damage evolves, which makes the non-linearity appear before the peak and increases the strain at the peak and its width. [Figure 6.2-a] shows the response of the model, compared with the experimental data of [bib6]. The computation is carried out on a single element so as not to encounter a localisation phenomenon. In order not to burden the notation, one will also denote by X , abusively, the matrix of this tensor in the fixed basis of the observer. Let moreover \tilde{X} be the (diagonal) matrix of this tensor in its principal basis: > \tilde{X}=(\begin{array}{ccc}{\tilde{X}}_{1}& 0& 0\\ 0& {\tilde{X}}_{2}& 0\\ 0& 0& {\tilde{X}}_{3}\end{array}) eq A1.1-1 Denoting by {U}_{i} the eigenvector associated with the i-th eigenvalue, and by Q=({U}_{1},{U}_{2},{U}_{3}) the change-of-basis matrix between the fixed basis and the principal basis of X , one has the relation: X=Q.\tilde{X}.{Q}^{T} eq A1.1-2 The positive and negative parts of the tensor X are defined by: {X}_{+}={P}_{+}:X=Q.{\tilde{X}}_{+}.{Q}^{T} with {\tilde{X}}_{+}=(\begin{array}{ccc}H({\tilde{X}}_{1}){\tilde{X}}_{1}& 0& 0\\ 0& H({\tilde{X}}_{2}){\tilde{X}}_{2}& 0\\ 0& 0& H({\tilde{X}}_{2}){\tilde{X}}_{3}\end{array}) eq A1.1-3 {X}_{-}={P}_{-}:X=Q.{\tilde{X}}_{-}.{Q}^{T} with {\tilde{X}}_{-}=(\begin{array}{ccc}H(-{\tilde{X}}_{1}){\tilde{X}}_{1}& 0& 0\\ 0& H(-{\tilde{X}}_{2}){\tilde{X}}_{2}& 0\\ 0& 0& H(-{\tilde{X}}_{2}){\tilde{X}}_{3}\end{array}) eq A1.1-4 where H is the Heaviside function. r7.01.10 THHM modellings. Generalities and algorithms r7.01.10 THHM modellings. Generalities and algorithms Summary The THM modules are those which treat the equations of continuum mechanics using the theory of porous media, possibly unsaturated, and considering that the mechanical, thermal and hydraulic phenomena are fully coupled. We present here the equilibrium equations, or conservation equations solved by these modules. We give a definition of the generalised stresses and generalised strains, making it possible to define in a fairly general way what a THM constitutive law is — at least what the modules considered regard as such — and making it possible to treat the non-linear equations exhibited within the framework of the algorithms of the operator STAT_NON_LINE. 1 Introduction The THM modules are those which treat the equations of continuum mechanics using the theory of porous media, possibly unsaturated, and considering that the mechanical, thermal and hydraulic phenomena are fully coupled. We present here the equilibrium equations, or conservation equations solved by these modules. We give a definition of the generalised stresses and generalised strains, making it possible to define in a fairly general way what a THM constitutive law is — at least what the modules considered regard as such — and making it possible to treat the non-linear equations exhibited within the framework of the algorithms of the operator STAT_NON_LINE. The THM constitutive laws proper are not developed in this document, but in the document R7.01.11. Chemical phenomena (transformations of the constituents, reactions producing constituents, etc.), as well as radiological phenomena, are not taken into account. The mechanical, hydraulic and thermal phenomena are or are not taken into account according to the constitutive behaviour invoked by the user in the command STAT_NON_LINE, according to the following nomenclature: | Modelling | Phenomena taken into account | | --- | --- | | KIT_HM | Mechanics, hydraulics with one unknown pressure | | KIT_HHM | Mechanics, hydraulics with two unknown pressures | | KIT_THH | Thermal, hydraulics with two unknown pressures | | KIT_THM | Thermal, mechanics, hydraulics with one unknown pressure | | KIT_THHM | Thermal, mechanics, hydraulics with two unknown pressures | Certain modellings (see documents U3.13.08 and U3.14.07) of THM are available with regularisation by a second gradient of dilatation. For the aspects relating to the second gradient of these modellings, refer to R5.04.03. 2 Presentation of the problem: assumptions, notation In this chapter, the aim is mainly to present the porous medium and its characteristics. 2.1 Description of the porous medium The porous medium considered is a volume made up of a solid matrix that is more or less homogeneous, more or less cohesive (very cohesive in the case of concrete, little so in the case of sand). Between the solid elements, one finds pores. One distinguishes the closed pores, which exchange nothing with their neighbours, and the connected pores, in which the exchanges are numerous. When one speaks of porosity, it is indeed the connected pores that one means. Inside these pores there are at most two constituents present in at most two phases. The system is considered closed. 2.2 Notation The quantities associated with a constituent c present in a phase p are denoted {X}_{c}^{p} . The index of the component c may vary from 1 to 2 and that of the phase likewise. These constituents may be (and will be indexed as such when needed): w for liquid water, \text{ad} for dissolved air, \text{as} for dry air, \text{vp} for water vapour. The porous medium at the current time instant is denoted \Omega , sa frontière \partial \Omega , and it is denoted {\Omega}_{0},\partial {\Omega}_{0} at the initial time instant. n denotes the normal at a point of \partial \Omega , the image of the normal {n}_{0} to \partial {\Omega}_{0} . We shall denote d(\partial \Omega ) (respectively d(\partial {\Omega}_{0}) ) the surface element of \partial \Omega (respectively \partial {\Omega}_{0} ). The medium is defined by: - parameters (position vector x , time t ), - variables (displacements, pressures, temperature), - intrinsic quantities (stresses and strains, mass supplies, heat, enthalpies, hydraulic fluxes, thermal...). For the solid phase, the small-displacement assumption is made. The various notations are set out below. 2.2.1 Descriptive variables of the medium These are the variables whose knowledge as a function of time and of place makes it possible to know completely the state of the medium. These variables fall into two categories: - geometric variables, - thermodynamic state variables. 2.2.1.1 Geometric variables In all that follows, a Lagrangian representation with respect to the skeleton is adopted (in the sense of [bib1]) and the coordinates \mathrm{x}={\mathrm{x}}_{s}(t) are those of a material point attached to the skeleton. All the spatial differentiation operators are defined with respect to these coordinates. The displacements of the skeleton are denoted u(x,t)=(\begin{array}{c}{u}_{x}\\ {u}_{y}\\ {u}_{z}\end{array}) . 2.2.1.2 Thermodynamic state variables The thermodynamic variables are: - the pressures of the constituents: given that we consider that there are at most two constituents, there will be at most two equations of conservation of mass, and therefore by duality at most two pressure variables, - the temperature of the medium T(x,t) . 2.2.1.3 Descriptive fields of the medium The principal unknowns, which are also the nodal unknowns (denoted U(x,t) in this document) are: - 2 or 3 (according to the space dimension) displacements {u}_{x}(x,t),{u}_{y}(x,t),{u}_{z}(x,t) for the modellings KIT_HM, KIT_HHM, KIT_THM, KIT_THHM, - the temperature T(x,t) for the modellings KIT_THH, KIT_THM, KIT_THHM, - two pressures {p}_{1}(x,t),{p}_{2}(x,t) for the modellings KIT_HHM, KIT_THH, KIT_THHM, - one pressure {p}_{1}(x,t) for the modellings KIT_HM, KIT_THM. 2.2.2 Quantities The equilibrium equations are: - the conservation of momentum for the mechanics, - the conservation of the fluid masses for the hydraulics, - the conservation of energy for the thermal problem. The equilibrium equations involve the generalised stresses directly. The generalised stresses are related to the generalised strains by the constitutive laws. The generalised strains are computed directly from the state variables and from their spatial and temporal gradients. The constitutive laws may use auxiliary quantities, often stored in the internal variables. These quantities are not described in this document, which does not deal with the constitutive laws proper. 2.2.2.1 Characteristic quantities of the heterogeneous medium - The Eulerian porosity: \phi . If one denotes by {\Omega}_{\varphi} the part of the volume \Omega occupied by the voids in the current configuration, one has: \varphi =\frac{{\Omega}_{\varphi}}{\Omega} eq 2.2.2.1-1 The definition of the porosity \varphi is therefore that of the Eulerian porosity. - The saturation of the phase p : {S}^{p} . If one denotes by {\Omega}^{p} the total volume occupied by the phase p , in the current configuration, one has by definition: {S}^{p}=\frac{{\Omega}^{p}}{{\Omega}_{j}} eq 2.2.2.1-2 This saturation is therefore finally a proportion varying between 0 and 1 . In the balance equations, it is clear that it is the product of the porosity by the saturation \phi {S}^{p} which will appear. One may therefore legitimately wonder why it is not this quantity which is taken as the unknown. The answer comes from the fact that it is the saturation {S}^{p} which appears more simply in the constitutive laws. - The Eulerian density of the constituent c in the phase p : {\rho}_{c}^{p} . If one denotes by {M}_{c}^{p} the mass of the phase p of the constituent c , in the volume \Omega of the skeleton in the current configuration, one has by definition: {M}_{c}^{p}={\int}_{{\Omega}^{p}}{{\rho}_{c}^{p}d\Omega }^{p}={\int}_{{\Omega}_{\phi }}{\rho}_{c}^{p}{S}^{p}d{\Omega}_{\phi }={\int}_{\Omega}{\rho}_{c}^{p}{S}^{p}\phid \Omega eq 2.2.2.1-3 The density of the phase p is simply the sum of the densities of its constituents: {\rho}^{p}=\sum_{c}{\rho}_{c}^{p} - The homogenised Lagrangian density: r . At the current time instant, the mass of the volume \Omega , {M}_{\Omega} is given by: {M}_{\Omega}={\int}_{{\Omega}_{0}}rd{\Omega}_{0} eq 2.2.2.1-4 2.2.2.2 Mechanical quantities - The strain tensor \varepsilon (u)(x,t)=\frac{1}{2}(\nabla u{}^{T}+\nabla u) , - The stress tensor which acts on the porous medium: \sigma . This tensor is decomposed into an effective-stress tensor plus a pressure-stress tensor \sigma =\sigma '+{\sigma}_{p}I . \sigma '\text{et}{\sigma}_{p} are components of the generalised stresses. This splitting is finally rather arbitrary, but it does correspond to an assumption that is fairly commonly accepted, at least for media saturated with liquid. 2.2.2.3 Hydraulic quantities - The mass supplies of constituents {m}_{c}^{p} (unit: kilogram per cubic metre). They represent the mass of fluid supplied between the initial and current time instants. They form part of the generalised stresses. {m}_{c}^{p}=J{\rho}_{c}^{p}\phi {S}^{p}-{\rho}_{c}^{{p}_{0}}{\phi }_{0}{S}_{0}^{p} eq 2.2.2.3-1 The mass supplies make it possible to define the global density seen with respect to the reference configuration: r(x,t)={r}_{0}+{m}_{\mathrm{lq}}(x,t)+{m}_{\mathrm{vp}}(x,t)+{m}_{\mathrm{as}}(x,t) , where {r}_{0} denotes the homogenised density in the initial state. - The hydraulic fluxes: {w}_{c}^{p} (unit: kilogram/second/square metre) in Eulerian representation {M}_{c}^{p} (unit: kilogram/second/square metre) in Lagrangian representation One denotes by {v}_{c}^{p} the velocity of the constituent c in the phase p , J the Jacobian of the material transformation and {v}_{S}=\frac{du}{\mathrm{dt}} the velocity of the skeleton. {\rho}_{c0}^{p},{\phi }_{0},{S}_{0}^{p} denote the densities, the porosity and the saturations at the initial time instant. By definition: {w}_{c}^{p}={\rho}_{c}^{p}\phi {S}^{p}({v}_{c}^{p}-{v}_{s}) eq 2.2.2.3-2 The Lagrangian form of denoted is obtained by writing: {M}_{c}^{p}.{n}_{0}d(\partial {\Omega}_{0})={w}_{c}^{p}.nd(\partial \Omega ) eq 2.2.2.3-3 The variables {m}_{1},{M}_{1} and {m}_{2},{M}_{2} each relate to a constituent of conservative mass . One sets in principle: \begin{array}{}{m}_{1}={m}_{1}^{1}+{m}_{1}^{2};{M}_{1}={M}_{1}^{1}+{M}_{1}^{2}\\ {m}_{2}={m}_{2}^{1}+{m}_{2}^{2};{M}_{2}={M}_{2}^{1}+{M}_{2}^{2}\end{array} Which we shall write: \begin{array}{}{m}_{\mathrm{constituant}}=\sum_{\begin{array}{}\mathrm{nb}\mathrm{phase}\mathrm{du}\\ \mathrm{constituant}\end{array}}{m}_{\mathrm{constituant}}^{\mathrm{phase}}\\ {M}_{\mathrm{constituant}}=\sum_{\begin{array}{}\mathrm{nb}\mathrm{phase}\mathrm{du}\\ \mathrm{constituant}\end{array}}{M}_{\mathrm{constituant}}^{\mathrm{phase}}\end{array} In the applications, one could for example have: - 2 constituents: air and water, - 2 phases for the water, - 1 phase for the air. One would then have: {m}_{1}^{1}\text{et}{M}_{1}^{1} : mass supply and flux of liquid water {m}_{1}^{2}\text{et}{M}_{1}^{2} : mass supply and flux of vapour {m}_{2}^{1}\text{et}{M}_{2}^{1} : mass supply and flux of dry air {m}_{2}^{2}\text{et}{M}_{2}^{2} : non-existent - The pressures: Since we consider that there may be two constituents other than the solid, there are two equations of conservation of mass, and therefore two associated multipliers, that is two pressures {p}_{1}\text{et}{p}_{2} . No assumption is made as to what these two pressures {p}_{1}\text{et}{p}_{2} mean. That will depend on the constitutive laws and on the way of writing them. For example one may choose: \begin{array}{}{p}_{1}=\text{pression capillaire}(\text{p}(\text{gaz})-\text{p}(\text{liquide}))\\ {p}_{2}=\text{pression de gaz}(\text{vapeur + air})\end{array} 2.2.2.4 Thermal quantities - The non-convected heat Q' (see below) (unit: Joule), - The mass enthalpies of the constituents {{h}^{m}}_{c}^{p} (unit: Joule/Kelvin/kilogram), - The heat flux: q (unit: J/s/square metre). 2.2.3 External data - The mass force {\mathrm{F}}^{m} (in practice gravity), - The heat sources \Theta , - The boundary conditions bearing either on imposed variables or on imposed fluxes. 2.3 Particle derivatives, volumetric and mass densities The description we make of the medium is Lagrangian with respect to the skeleton. One will find in [bib1] a definition of the notion of skeleton: “the matrix (solid part + occluded porosity) constituting the material part of the skeleton and the connected pore space of the elementary volume in question constitute the material point of the skeleton or particle of the skeleton”. Let a be any field on \Omega , let {x}_{s}(t) be the coordinate of a point attached to the skeleton which we follow in its motion and let {x}_{\mathrm{fl}}(t) be the coordinate of a point attached to the fluid. One denotes by \dot{a}=\frac{{d}^{s}a}{\mathrm{dt}} the time derivative in the motion of the skeleton: \dot{a}=\frac{{d}^{s}a}{\mathrm{dt}}=\underset{\deltat \to 0}{\lim}\frac{a({x}_{s}(t+\deltat ),t+\deltat )-a({x}_{s}(t),t)}{\deltat } \dot{a} is called the particle derivative and is often denoted \frac{\mathrm{da}}{\mathrm{dt}} (for example in [bib1]). We prefer to use a notation which recalls that the configuration used to locate a particle is that of the skeleton, with respect to which a fluid particle has a relative velocity. For a fluid particle the location {x}_{s}(t) is arbitrary, that is, the fluid particle which occupies the position {x}_{s}(t) at the time instant t is not the same as the one which occupies the position {x}_{S}(t') at another time instant t' . Let then A=\underset{\Omega}{\int}ad\Omega be a quantity linked to a volumetric density a , which density is itself carried partly by the solid grains and by the fluids . Let {{a}^{m}}_{c}^{p} be the mass density of a carried by the fluid phase p of the constituent c and let {a}_{s} be the volumetric density of a linked to the solid grains. All these definitions finally amount to writing: A={\int}_{\Omega}\mathrm{ad}\Omega ={A}_{s}+{A}_{\mathrm{fl}}={\int}_{\Omega}{a}_{s}d\Omega +{\int}_{\Omega}{a}_{\mathrm{fl}}d\Omega ={\int}_{\Omega}({a}_{s}+\sum_{p,c}{\rho}_{c}^{p}{\mathrm{jS}}^{p}{{a}^{m}}_{c}^{p})d\Omega eq 2.3-1 Following [bib1], we denote by \frac{{d}^{\mathrm{fl}}{A}_{\mathrm{fl}}}{\mathrm{dt}} the derivative of {A}_{\mathrm{fl}} if we follow \Omega in the motion of the fluid and \frac{{d}^{s}{A}_{s}}{\mathrm{dt}} the derivative of {A}_{s} if we follow \Omega in the motion of the skeleton. We then define: \frac{\mathrm{DA}}{\mathrm{Dt}}=\frac{{d}^{s}{A}_{s}}{\mathrm{dt}}+\frac{{d}^{\mathrm{fl}}{A}_{\mathrm{fl}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{{d}^{s}}{\mathrm{dt}}\int{}_{\Omega}\text{}{a}_{s}d\Omega +\frac{{d}^{\mathrm{fl}}}{\mathrm{dt}}\int{}_{\Omega}\text{}\sum_{p,c}{\rho}_{c}^{p}\phi {S}^{p}{a}^{{m}_{c}^{p}}d\Omega eq 2.3-2 The density {{a}^{m}}_{c}^{p} is transported with a relative velocity of ({v}_{c}^{p}-{v}_{s}) with respect to the skeleton. Taking into account the definition of \dot{a}=\frac{{d}^{s}a}{\mathrm{dt}} , and of the definition {w}_{c}^{p}={\rho}_{c}^{p}\phi {S}^{p}({v}_{c}^{p}-{v}_{s}) , one easily sees that the total derivative of A with respect to time is finally written: \frac{\mathrm{DA}}{\mathrm{Dt}}=\int{}_{\Omega}\text{}(\dot{a}+\sum_{p,c}\text{Div}({{a}^{m}}_{c}^{p}{w}_{c}^{p}))d\Omega eq 2.3-3 Note: In so far as we have made the assumption of small displacements of the skeleton, \dot{a}=\frac{{d}^{s}a}{\mathrm{dt}} may be identified with the partial derivative with respect to time \frac{\partial a}{\partial t} and {v}_{s} may be considered as zero. The internal forces R are expressed from a generalised principle of virtual work. In the case of “classical” continuum mechanics, that is when there is no constituent other than the solid, one is used to defining the internal forces by: {w}^{T}.R={\int}_{\Omega}\varepsilon (w).\sigma d\Omega \forall w , kinematically admissible displacement field. In this formulation, the strain field \varepsilon depends only on the displacement field and on its spatial derivatives, possibly in a non-linear way if one takes finite strains into account. One writes symbolically: R={Q}^{T}\sigma The constitutive law relates the stresses \sigma to the strains \varepsilon . Within the framework of the theory of porous media developed here, we try to stay as close as possible to this formulation by introducing generalised stresses \Sigma and generalised strains E ; The generalised strains depend only on the generalised displacement field U and on its spatial derivatives. The operator U\to E(U) is an operator of differentiation with respect to the coordinate field. The constitutive law makes it possible to compute \Sigma as a function of E . On the other hand, we cannot write directly {W}^{T}.R={\int}_{\Omega}\mathrm{\Epsilon }(W).\Sigmad \Omega , for the following reasons: - the equations we treat are evolutionary equations in time and the derivatives with respect to time of the quantities appear, - the equations are non-linear because of the transport terms linked to the Eulerian representation of the fluids: these non-linear terms appear only in the thermal equation, - the choice of the unknowns means that the non-linear transport terms appear in the generalised stresses. Take a transport term in equation [eq 4.3-1], {\int}_{\Omega}(\sum_{p,c}{h}_{c}^{mp}{M}_{c}^{p}+q).\nabla \taud \Omega , given that one has taken the pressures as the principal unknowns for the hydraulics, the quantities {M}_{c}^{p} linked to the velocities of the fluids belong to the generalised stresses, as do the enthalpies {h}_{c}^{mp} , and the transport term given as an example is linear in generalised strain and quadratic in generalised stress. This makes a difference with the formulation of the classical continuum theory where the large-strain terms are quadratic quantities of the strains. One thus avoids an update of the mass matrix. The elementary terms {M}_{ij}^{e} are completed on assembly by zero terms associated with the additional degrees of freedom specific to the coupled modelling. There results, on their expansion in the assembled mass matrix, an offset of degrees of freedom linked to the possible presence of the components 'PRESS1', 'PRESS2', and 'TEMPE' in the modelling. 7 Solution algorithm 7.1 Non-linear algorithm for the solution of the equilibrium equations In the general case of the modelling (variable coefficients, desaturation, convection) the variational problem presented above [eq 4.1-1] to [eq 4.3-1] is non-linear with respect to the displacement, pressure and temperature fields. After discretisation by finite elements, one obtains a non-linear matrix system. The matrix of the tangent operator moreover contains a non-symmetric term treated as such. One uses in all cases of modelling the non-linear solver STAT_NON_LINE based on a Newton-Raphson method, described in [bib5]. One introduces the vector functional: F(U)=R(U)-{L}^{\mathrm{meca}} eq 7.1-1 The associated tangent operator is denoted: DF=\frac{\partial F}{\partial U} . For the THM modules, the subject of the present note, the operator {L}^{\text{meca}} does not depend on the generalised displacements. All the terms depending on the generalised displacements have been introduced into R , and it is precisely for this reason that the displacements are found in the generalised strains. Let us note on this subject the very particular treatment of the term {\int}_{\Omega}r{F}^{m}.v of equation [eq 4.1-1]. According to [eq 6.3.4-1], {\int}_{\Omega}r{F}^{m}.vd\Omega ={\int}_{\Omega}({r}_{0}+{m}_{1}^{1+}+{m}_{1}^{2+}+{m}_{2}^{1+}+{m}_{2}^{2+}){F}^{m}.vd\Omega . We have chosen to split this term in two: The term {\int}_{\Omega}{r}_{0}{F}^{m}.vd\Omega is a contribution to {L}^{\mathrm{meca}} if the user has supplied the operand PESANTEUR of the loading used (defined by the command AFFE_CHAR_MECA), whereas the term {\int}_{\Omega}({m}_{1}^{1+}+{m}_{1}^{2+}+{m}_{2}^{1+}+{m}_{2}^{2+}){F}^{m}.vd\Omega , which depends on the generalised stresses, is a contribution to \mathrm{R} . 7.2 Passage from the nodal values to the values at the Gauss points As in all finite-element codes, the terms are computed by a loop over the elements and a loop over the Gauss points. A choice of discretisation in which the displacements, the pressures and the temperatures are interpolated with the same order of approximation leads to oscillations, especially for choices of time step that are too small with respect to the spatial discretisation. One will consult on this subject for example [bib10]. This problem is also related to the way of computing the so-called mass matrix, and one may consult on this subject [bib14].
