These differences concern only the writing of: - The energy equation - Henry’s law - Diffusion in the liquid - Diffusion in the gas Note concerning the enthalpies: It is necessary, in order to have consistency between the two models, that the user take {h}_{\text{lq}}^{{m}_{0}}=0 and {h}_{\text{vp}}^{{m}_{0}}={L}_{0} . 7.4.1 Energy equation The table above recalls the two formulations: | Notations Code_Aster | ANDRA notations | | --- | --- | | {h}_{\text{lq}}^{m} | =\frac{{\varphi}_{w}}{{\rho}_{w}{S}_{w}n} | | {h}_{\text{vp}}^{m} | =\frac{{\varphi}_{v}}{{\rho}_{v}(1-{S}_{w})n} | | {h}_{\text{as}}^{m} | =\frac{{\varphi}_{\text{as}}}{{\rho}_{\text{as}}(1-{S}_{w})n} | | {M}_{\text{lq}} | ={\rho}_{w}{f}_{w} | | {M}_{\text{as}} | ={\rho}_{\text{as}}{f}_{\text{as}} | | {M}_{\text{vp}} | ={\rho}_{v}{f}_{v} | By rewriting the energy equation of Code_Aster with these notations, one finds: \begin{array}{}\frac{d\phi }{\text{dt}}+\text{Div}({\phi }_{w}\frac{{f}_{w}}{{S}_{w}n}+{\phi }_{\text{as}}\frac{{f}_{\text{as}}}{(1-{S}_{w})n}+{\phi }_{v}\frac{{f}_{v}}{(1-{S}_{w})n})+\text{Div}(q)-(T-{T}^{0})\frac{d}{\text{dt}}\left[(1-n){\rho}_{s}{C}_{s}\right]\\ +3{\alpha}_{0}{K}_{0}T\frac{d{\varepsilon}_{v}}{\text{dt}}+3{\alpha}_{\text{lq}}^{m}T\frac{{\text{dp}}_{c}}{\text{dt}}-3({\alpha}_{\text{lq}}^{m}+{\alpha}_{\text{gz}}^{m})T\frac{{\text{dp}}_{\text{gz}}}{\text{dt}}-9{\text{TK}}_{0}{\alpha}_{{0}^{2}}\frac{\text{dT}}{\text{dt}}\\ =({\rho}_{w}{f}_{w}+{\rho}_{v}{f}_{v}+{\rho}_{\text{as}}{f}_{\text{as}})g+\Theta \end{array} The first line being that of ANDRA and the others being a priori negligible. 7.4.2 Henry’s law In the ANDRA formulation, Henry’s formulation is given by {\omega}_{l}^{a}=\frac{{P}_{\text{as}}}{H}\frac{{M}_{\text{as}}^{\text{ol}}}{{M}_{w}}{\rho}_{w} with the concentration of air in the water which one can reduce to a density such that {\omega}_{l}^{a}={\rho}_{\text{ad}} . H is expressed in \mathit{Pa} . In the Code_Aster formulation, recall that Henry’s law is expressed in the form: {C}_{\text{ad}}^{\text{ol}}=\frac{{\rho}_{\text{ad}}}{{M}_{\text{ad}}^{\text{ol}}} with {C}_{\text{ad}}^{\text{ol}}=\frac{{p}_{\text{as}}}{{K}_{H}} . {K}_{H} is expressed in \mathit{Pa.}{m}^{3}.{\mathit{mol}}^{-1} . One therefore has the equivalence: {K}_{H}=H\frac{{M}_{w}}{{\rho}_{w}} 7.4.3 Diffusion of the vapour in the air In the ANDRA formulation the flux of water vapour in the air as a function of the concentration of water vapour in the air or of the relative humidity is denoted: {f}_{{\text{Diff}}_{v}}=-{D}_{v}.\nabla {\omega}_{g}^{e} with the concentration defined as the molar ratio in the gas: {\omega}_{g}^{e}=\frac{{n}_{\nu}}{{n}_{g}} . In Code_Aster , this same flux is written: {f}_{{\text{Diff}}_{v}}={F}_{\text{vp}}\nabla {C}_{\text{vp}} with the vapour Fick coefficient {F}_{\text{vp}}=\frac{{D}_{\text{vp}}}{{C}_{\text{vp}}(1-{C}_{\text{vp}})} and {D}_{\mathit{vp}} the Fick diffusion coefficient of the gaseous mixture. {C}_{\mathit{vp}} is defined as the pressure ratio such that: {C}_{\text{vp}}=\frac{{p}_{\text{vp}}}{{p}_{\text{gz}}} . The perfect-gas law makes it possible to write that {C}_{\text{vp}}={\omega}_{g}^{e} hence \nabla {\omega}_{g}^{e}=\nabla {C}_{\text{vp}} and {f}_{{\text{Diff}}_{v}}={D}_{v}.\nabla {C}_{\text{vp}} . Hence the equivalence is written simply: {F}_{\text{vp}}={D}_{v} . 7.4.4 Diffusion of the dissolved air in the water In the ANDRA formulation the flux of dissolved air in the water is expressed {f}_{{a}_{{\text{ds}}_{e}}}={D}_{a}.\nabla {\omega}_{l}^{a} with {\omega}_{l}^{a}=\frac{{\rho}_{\text{ad}}}{{M}_{\text{ad}}^{\text{ol}}} . In Code_Aster, this same flux is written: {f}_{{a}_{{\text{ds}}_{v}}}={F}_{\text{ad}}\nabla {C}_{\text{ad}} with the dissolved-air Fick coefficient {F}_{\text{ad}}=\frac{{D}_{\text{ad}}}{{C}_{\text{ad}}(1-{C}_{\text{ad}})} and {D}_{\mathit{ad}} the Fick diffusion coefficient of the liquid mixture. {C}_{\mathit{ad}} is defined such that: {C}_{\text{ad}}={w}_{l}^{a} . Hence: {F}_{\text{ad}}={D}_{a} .

r7.01.12 Modelling of the thermo-hydration, drying and shrinkage of concrete r7.01.12 Modelling of the thermo-hydration, drying and shrinkage of concrete Summary Two types of phenomena, occurring at distinct periods in the life of a concrete, are described here: - on the one hand a thermo-hydration reaction generating a so-called endogenous shrinkage, appearing at the early age of the concrete (the first 100 days), - on the other hand an evaporation of part of the water not used in the hydration process, a phenomenon called drying and leading to a drying shrinkage. This phenomenon can last, depending on the dimensions of the concrete structure as built, from a few months to several years. These phenomena are modelled in the form of diffusion equations whose solution is represented by new variables making it possible to compute directly the strains of the endogenous shrinkage (due to hydration) and of the drying shrinkage (due to drying). 1 Introduction The behaviour of concrete, a material that is brittle in tension, heterogeneous and porous, is governed by numerous and complex physico-chemical phenomena. The losses of prestress induced by the delayed behaviour of concrete (shrinkage and creep) reduce over time the loading domain that the structure can support. These delayed strains, which appear in the concrete during its life, are composed of the early-age shrinkage (endogenous shrinkage specific to hydration and thermal shrinkage), of the drying shrinkage with the modelling of drying, and, as soon as it is subjected to stresses, of basic creep and drying creep. In the design rules, the delayed strains of concrete are generally based on empirical rules calibrated on a large number of results from the literature, taking into account the principal parameters, such as temperature, humidity, aggregate content and the water/cement proportion. The kinetics of the phenomena use equivalent times computed by means of an Arrhenius law in order to take account of ageing and temperature. A detailed analysis of the physico-chemical phenomena which are at the origin of the various delayed strains of concrete makes it possible to propose a modelling on the basis of an equivalent-continuum model is proposed (basic creep and drying creep are not treated here). 1.1 Phenomenological aspects of the behaviour of concrete at early age: thermo-hydration Early age is defined as the first 100 days of the life of the concrete. Endogenous shrinkage, or hydration shrinkage, and thermal shrinkage intervene from the first instants of setting (at early age), for a duration ranging from a few hours to a few days for thermal shrinkage, and from a few months to one year for hydration shrinkage, generally completed at the time of prestressing. Phenomena of restrained shrinkage or of differential shrinkage, in the formwork, can be at the origin of stresses or of cracks which must be assessed. In the liquid phase, concrete is a viscous fluid in which the solid grains are in suspension in the hydraulic binder containing solid particles (cements...). Following the formation of the first hydrates, the setting of the concrete occurs, some ten hours after its manufacture, which corresponds to the establishment of connected hydrate bridges between the cement grains throughout the material. At the very beginning, the grains are relatively dispersed in the mixing water. Over time, the hydration of the cement grains is accompanied by a consumption of this mixing water. Experimentally, one observes that the volumetric balance of the reaction is negative; this is the Le Chatelier contraction. Put simply, the total volume of the hydrates is nearly 10% smaller than the total volume of these constituents. Mechanically, at the scale of the cement grains, the phenomenon stops when the hydrate bridges formed between the grains are rigid enough to prevent a possible relative approach of the grains. The macroscopic consequences for the structures are practically non-existent, since throughout the duration of this phase the concrete is still deformable, and any contraction is compensated by a granular readjustment of the material against the walls of the formwork. Although of relatively small extent, and of insufficient mechanical effect to generate real cracking of the concrete, the stresses generated at the interface of two consecutive lifts can consume 50% of the tensile-strength margin of the material. The setting of the concrete, accompanied by the hydration of the cement, leads to an exothermic reaction. In massive structures the temperature can then rise to more than 50°C . Hydration is a thermally activated reaction, that is to say that the hydration rate increases with temperature. When the hydration rate decreases, the temperature falls, leading to a thermal shrinkage. In addition, the mechanical properties of the concrete vary as a function of its degree of hydration, and finally the consumption of water occurring during hydration leads to a capillary shrinkage. The various shrinkages can produce stresses much higher than the (low) tensile strength of the concrete and lead to cracking of the material. The computation of the temperature and degree-of-hydration fields is available with the command THER_NON_LINE. The computation of the mechanical fields taking endogenous shrinkage into account is carried out with the command STAT_NON_LINE. 1.2 Drying and drying shrinkage Modelling drying is important because the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of the material depend strongly on the humidity inside it. The objective is to propose a macroscopic modelling of the drying of concrete from a restricted number of parameters, easily measurable experimentally, from a non-linear transient diffusion law for humidity, chained to the temperature, dispensing with the complex mechanical, physical and chemical couplings at the scale of the material. On removal of the formwork, the concrete is immersed in an external environment which generally presents a degree of humidity of the order of 60 to 80% RH (relative humidity = ratio of the vapour pressure to the saturated vapour pressure for a given temperature). It then undergoes a genuine hydric shock (by analogy with a thermal shock). The concrete is then in thermodynamic disequilibrium with the atmosphere. Drying will allow it to recover a hydric equilibrium with the external medium. Physically, drying involves complex phenomena intimately coupled to one another, depending on the heterogeneous and granular structure of the concrete. At the macroscopic scale, it is possible to model drying as a non-linear diffusion phenomenon, with Darcy-type diffusion in the liquid phase, as long as there is continuity of the liquid phase, and with Fick-type diffusion in the gas phase, for the water vapour. Drying shrinkage is the primary macroscopic consequence of the drying of concrete. It is the direct continuation of the capillary-tension phenomena which are at the origin of endogenous shrinkage. By its intensity, the strains being of the order of 400 \times 10^{-6} to 800 \times 10^{-6} for 50% hygrometry and for ordinary concretes, it is one to three times larger than the elastic strain for a loading in the neighbourhood of 10 \text{MPa} . The modelling of thermo-hydration in the non-linear thermal operator is presented first, then the modelling of drying, and finally the introduction of endogenous shrinkage and of drying shrinkage into the non-linear mechanical operator. 2 Formulation of thermo-hydration 2.1 Thermo-hydration equation As mentioned in the introduction, the hydration of concrete is a strongly exothermic reaction. Taking it into account in the heat equation as a source term is therefore necessary (see [R5.02.02]). The right-hand side, which contains the internal heat sources, can then be enriched in the following way \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c} \rho\therCp\frac{d \temp }{dt} + \divVector{\therFlux} = Q \frac{d\xi} {dt} + \therSource \\ \therFlux = -\therCondTher \gradScal{\temp} \end{array} \right . where: - \therFlux is the heat flux, - \therSource is an internal heat source (in J s^{-1} {m}^{-3} ), - \rho \therCp is the volumetric heat capacity at constant pressure (in J {m}^{-3} K^{-1} ), - \therCondTher is the thermal conductivity ( W {m}^{-2} K^{-1} ), and, specifically to hydration: - \xi is the degree of hydration, by definition \xi \in \left[ 0;1 \right] ; - Q is the heat of hydration (in J {m}^{-3} ), that is the heat produced by the hydration of a unit volume of concrete. The evolution of hydration depends on the composition of the concrete and on the temperature; a high temperature accelerates the hydration reaction. Equation can be solved if the function \xi (t,\temp) , and therefore \frac{d\xi }{dt}(t,\temp) , is known. But the parameter \frac{d \xi}{d t} is preferred to the hydration itself, and the time t is thus eliminated. The corresponding function is called the affinity \frac{d\xi}{dt} = f^{\text{aff}} (\xi,\temp) The heat of hydration Q and the function f^{\text{aff}}(\xi ,\temp) must be supplied by the user under the keyword THER_HYDR of DEFI_MATERIAU. Their experimental determination is carried out by means of an adiabatic test. 2.2 Use of the adiabatic test for the determination of the affinity function and of the heat of hydration. In an adiabatic test, a sample of fresh and thermally insulated concrete is immersed in a calorimeter and the evolution of the temperature {\temp}^{\text{ad}}(t) is measured over time until hardening. This test can be used to determine the heat of hydration as well as the affinity function. Indeed, under adiabatic conditions the equation simplifies because \divVector{\therFlux}=0 . In addition, \therSource=0 because one considers that the only heat source is the hydration of the concrete. Integration of from the beginning ( \xi =0 ) to the degree of hydration \xi then gives the expression: Q\xi ({\temp}^{\text{ad}}(t)) =\ \rho \therCp({\temp}^{\text{ad}}(t)-{\temp}_{0}) If one assumes that \xi=1 (end of the test), one obtains the heat of hydration: Q = \rho \therCp \left( {\temp}_{\infty}^{\text{ad}}-{\temp}_{0} \right) where \temp_0 and {\temp}_{\infty}^{\text{ad}} are the temperatures measured at the beginning and at the end of the adiabatic test. Using this expression for the heat of hydration, one obtains the evolution of the hydration (and therefore of its derivative \frac{d \xi}{dt} ), in the form: \xi({\temp}^{\text{ad}}(t)) = \frac{{\temp}^{\text{ad}}(t)-{\temp}_{0}} {{\temp}_{\infty}^{\text{ad}}-{\temp}_{0}} The adiabatic test therefore supplies the functions \xi({\temp}^{\text{ad}}(t)) and :math:{temp}^{text{ad}}(t) . The parameters of the affinity function f^{\text{aff}}(\temp,\xi ) can be identified from the measurement points obtained during the adiabatic test, f^{\text{aff}}({\temp}^{\text{ad}},{\xi}^{\text{ad}}) . An expression for f^{\text{aff}}(\temp,\xi) has been suggested by in the form of an exponential of the temperature: \frac{d\xi }{dt} = f^{\text{aff}}(\xi,\temp ) = A(\xi) \, \exp\left(-\frac{{E}_{a}}{R \, \temp} \right) where \frac{{E}_{a}}{R} is the Arrhenius constant (a rather empirical parameter varying between 4000°K and 7000°K , and considered to be equal to 4000°K in the absence of additional information). For the adiabatic test one then has: A({\temp}^{\text{ad}}(\xi )) = \frac{1}{{\temp}_{\infty}^{\text{ad}}-{\temp}_{0}} \, \frac{{d\temp}^{\text{ad}}}{dt}({\temp}^{\text{ad}}(\xi)) \, \exp{\left( \frac{{E}_{a}}{R \, \temp^{\text{ad}}(\xi) }\right) } where the inverse functions {\xi}^{-1} , {({\temp}^{\text{ad}})}^{-1} have been used to eliminate the time parameter t . can also be written in the following way: \xi(t) = \frac{{\temp}^{\text{ad}}(t)-{\temp}_{0}}{{\temp}_{\infty}^{\text{ad}}-{\temp}_{0}} = \frac{Q(\temp(t))}{Q({\temp}_{\infty})} In fact, one can define in a general way the degree of hydration at each time instant t as being the ratio of the quantity of heat released up to the time instant t to the total quantity of heat released at the end of the hydration process. Note Within the framework of non-linear thermal analysis [R5.02.02], the first of the equations is often written in the equivalent form \frac{d\beta (\temp)}{dt}+\divVector{\therFlux}=Q\frac{d\xi (\temp)}{dt}+\therSource , \beta being the volumetric enthalpy. Indeed, in the command file, it is necessary to supply the enthalpy and not the volumetric heat capacity; see [R5.02.02]. 3 Discretisation of the thermo-hydration problem 3.1 Choice of the solution method The method chosen consists in solving globally the non-linear equation by making use of the non-linear thermal algorithm, and in solving locally the equation which represents the evolution law of a kind of internal variable representing the degree of hydration, this law being expressed by a function of the thermal state of the system. Indeed, there is no spatial differential operator for the variable \xi in the equations and therefore no need for a finite element. The relation represents a local law as in plasticity. One then keeps the same number of degrees of freedom as for classical thermal analysis. Such a decoupled process nevertheless leads to the computation of the same quantities several times. Indeed, suppose that \xi is discretised at the nodes of the elements. Consider the example sketched as follows: On node 1 , the evolution equation will be integrated four times. A possible solution would have been for the local computations to be carried out on nodal fields (Aster concept CHAM_NO) and not on fields of nodes by element, which is currently impossible. The solution which was finally adopted consists in computing \xi at the Gauss points of the element, which is all the more natural in that, for the mechanical computation, Young’s modulus depends explicitly on \xi . This nevertheless generates many local computations unless the finite element is strongly under-integrated. For example, if one considers a mesh comprising N 20-node hexahedral elements, there are about {4 \times N} nodes and {27 \times N} Gauss points. 3.2 Solution algorithm The weak formulation of equation is written in the following way: \int_{\domain} {\dot{\beta}(\temp) \, \tempVirt \measDomain} + \int_{\domain} {\therCondTher (\temp) \gradScal{\temp} \cdot \gradScal{\tempVirt} \measDomain } = \int_{\domain} {\therSource \, \tempVirt \measDomain} + \int_{\domain} { Q \, A(\xi) \exp{\left(-\frac{{E}_{a}}{R \, \temp} \right)} \, \tempVirt \measDomain } + \int_{\bound} { \Phi \, \tempVirt \measBound } for any virtual temperature \tempVirt . The development of thermo-hydration within the general algorithm of non-linear thermal analysis therefore consists in discretising explicitly, in the right-hand side, the term \int_{\domain} { Q \, A(\xi) \exp{\left(-\frac{{E}_{a}}{R \, \temp} \right)} \, \tempVirt \measDomain } . Denoting respectively by {\xi}^{-} , {\temp}^{-} , {\xi}^{+} and {\temp}^{+} the hydration and temperature variables at the beginning and at the end of the time step, one computes at each Gauss point the quantity: Q \, A(\xi^{-}) \exp{\left(-\frac{{E}_{a}}{R \, \temp} \right)} which is integrated directly into the right-hand side. After each solution of the current step, the variables are updated ( {\xi}^{+}={\xi}^{-} and {\temp}^{+}={\temp}^{-} ). The convergence test is active only on the temperature; the variable \xi does not enter the iterative Newton process used in non-linear thermal analysis. Taking hydration into account is in fact only taking into account a heat source known at the beginning of the time step. This purely explicit discretisation therefore requires the use of sufficiently small time steps. 4 Formulation of drying This part refers to the specification document for the development of drying , as well as to the thesis of L. Granger . 4.1 Modelling and equations of drying The modellings of thermal analysis or of thermo-hydration and of drying are decoupled at the solution stage. Drying is then presented as an operation chained to the thermal analysis. Since the equations making it possible to solve drying and non-linear thermal analysis are similar up to the coefficients, this decoupling makes it possible to integrate the solution of the drying analysis by using directly the solution module of non-linear thermal analysis, without adding new phenomena, new element types, or new computation options. The concentration or water content C , the computational variable in the modelling of drying, is assimilated, in terms of variable type, to a temperature. The transient temperature field, appearing in the drying equation, is only an auxiliary parameter on which the diffusion coefficient may depend. The phenomena of thermal analysis and of drying, within the framework of a modelling decoupled between thermal analysis and drying, are governed by the following equations: - equation of “classical” thermal analysis: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c} \rho\therCp\frac{d \temp }{dt} + \divVector{\therFlux} = Q \frac{d\xi (\temp)} {dt} + \therSource(\temp) \\ \therFlux = -\therCondTher(\temp) \gradScal{\temp} \end{array} \right . with \rho\therCp the volumetric heat capacity at constant pressure, \therCondTher the thermal conductivity, Q the heat of hydration and \therSource(\temp) the internal source. - equation characterising drying: \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} - \divVector\left( D(C,\temp) \gradScal{C} \right) = 0 where C ( {m}^{3}v / {m}^{3} or l/{m}^{3} ) is the computational variable (volumetric concentration or water content), \temp is the input variable of the analysis (the temperature), an auxiliary variable of the drying solution, D ( {m}^{2}/s ) is a diffusion coefficient, characterising the non-linearity of the equation, and depending both on the computational variable, C , and on the auxiliary variable, \temp . This diffusion law is given in various forms, according to the model retained (Bazant law, Granger law, Mensi law, Richards-Fick law, cf. r7.01.12-diffusion-usuelles and ). Equations and correspond to a chained thermal/drying analysis. One can therefore compute \temp without knowing the water concentration, then compute the latter, for which \temp is then a parameter (assuming that the thermal conductivity \therCondTher does not depend on the water concentration C ). Note also that the drying phenomenon is decoupled from the mechanical evolutions of the concrete. 4.2 Diffusion coefficient The material is described by the diffusion coefficient D , characteristic of the material, depending both on the temperature \temp and on the water concentration C . The equation of moisture migration in concrete comes from those of the mechanics of porous media. One should refer to for more detail. Classically, a diffusion law expresses a flux as the product of a quantity characteristic of the material by the gradient of an intensive quantity. The various quantities considered are defined by an average over the representative elementary volume, insofar as one can define this average for the material considered, so that the differentiation operators have a meaning. One therefore generally makes the assumption which consists in supposing that the liquid and gas phases are connected: - for the diffusion of vapour, one starts from the positivity of the dissipation associated with transport of the gas phase, distinguishing two phenomena, a permeation-type phenomenon (Darcy), related to pressure gradients, and a diffusion-type phenomenon (Fick), related to concentration gradients, - for the diffusion of liquid water, the positivity of the dissipation associated with transport of the liquid water, and Darcy’s law, make it possible to express the liquid flux as a function of the liquid pressure. Kelvin’s law, describing the coexistence of the two liquid and gas phases by writing the equality of the specific free enthalpies, leads to the expression of the flux as a function of the gradient of the degree of humidity. From the two preceding results, one obtains the expression of the total flux as a function of the gradient of the degree of water concentration. The classical experimental methods in drying problems generally give access to the water concentration, and very rarely to the relative humidity. It is therefore preferable to express the flux as a function of the water content, classically using the desorption isotherm of the concrete, which relates the water content, C , and the relative humidity, h . The relative humidity is the ratio between vapour pressure and saturated vapour pressure. The postulate of the local state stipulates that the current state of a homogeneous system in any evolution can be characterised by the same variables as at equilibrium, and that it is independent of the rates of evolution. In other words, the water content C and the relative humidity h are indeed related by the same relation as at equilibrium. This leads to the classical diffusion equation . This equation highlights the non-linear character of moisture diffusion in concrete. In industrial cases, the temperature is in general not uniform in the structure. It is therefore necessary to take into account a moisture diffusion coefficient which depends on the temperature. In practice, in the literature, the best-known authors (Bazant cf ) propose an expression for the diffusion coefficient of the type: D(C,\temp) = D(C,{\temp}_{0})(\frac{\temp}{{\temp}_{0}})\exp{(\frac{-{Q}_{s}}{R}(\frac{1}{\temp}-\frac{1}{{\temp}_{0}}))} with {Q}_{s}/R=4700{K}^{-1} and \temp in K . Note From the way things are presented, it would seem that one has not used the fact that drying is a phenomenon coupled with mechanics (that is to say that it is the cause of a drying shrinkage). In reality, we have made the assumption of a decoupling of the phenomena, when we used the sorption/desorption curve. In fact, during the measurement of the weight loss at equilibrium as a function of h , the specimen undergoes a shrinkage. At the microscopic level, everything happens as if the shrinkage, by modifying the porosity, were going to interact with the relative hygrometry inside the specimen, since the vapour pressure and h increase. This drying shrinkage being very small, it is usual to neglect it in the computations of the water content. There is therefore only a chaining between the computation of the water content and the mechanical computation of drying shrinkage. 4.3 Usual diffusion laws The diffusion law, a function of the two parameters C and \temp , can be defined freely by the user in the form of a nappe. However, several models found in the literature are also available. These models are presented below. 4.3.1 Law proposed by Granger D\left(C,\temp\right) = A \, \exp{\left(B \, C\right)} \left(\frac{\temp}{{\temp}_{0}}\right)\exp{\left(\frac{-{Q}_{s}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{\temp}-\frac{1}{{\temp}_{0}}\right)\right)} A (homogeneous to an area per unit time), B , {\temp}_{0} , {Q}_{s} and R ( \frac{Q_s}{R} in K ) are coefficients chosen by the user. D is a function of the temperature and of the water concentration. 4.3.2 Mensi law D(C)=A\ \exp{(B \, C)} A and B are coefficients chosen by the user. D is a function only of the water concentration. 4.3.3 Bazant law The Bazant law is expressed from the degree of humidity h , which is related to the water concentration by the sorption/desorption curve. The form of this law is the following: D(h) = D_1 \left(\alpha+ \frac{1-\alpha} {1+ \left( \frac{1-h(C)}{1-0.75}\right)^n} \right) Usually {D}_{1}={3.10}^{-10}{m}^{2}/s , \alpha lies between 0.025 and 0.1 , n is of the order of 6 . h(C) is the degree of humidity, which is expressed as a function of the water concentration by means of the sorption/desorption curve. The sorption/desorption curve can be introduced in the form of a standard tabulated function, knowing that in reality this curve presents a hysteresis, but can be considered as invertible if one takes account of only one direction of travel. 4.3.4 SECH_RFT law The SECH_RFT diffusion law is taken from the literature model RICHARDS_FICK_TEMPERATURE . This law models the permeation of water in liquid form and the diffusion of vapour in the gas mixture on the basis of the transport properties measurable in the laboratory (porosity, permeability, desorption isotherm, vapour diffusion), whereas the Granger law models only the permeation of water in liquid form by an empirical expression. It may be noted that in this law, unlike the others, the transport equation is written as a function of the degree of water saturation and not of the water concentration. The degree of water saturation S_r is related to the water concentration C (variable SECH) according to the following expression: S_r = \frac{C}{1000 \times \phi} With \phi corresponding to the porosity of the material. As for the other laws, it assumes that drying takes place at a gas pressure that is constant and equal to atmospheric pressure. The effects of temperature are better represented in the RFT model (especially for temperatures higher than 50°C). The hydric transport equation described by this model is a non-linear diffusion equation expressed as a function of the degree of water saturation S_r and which is written in the form: \frac{\partial S_r}{\partial t} - \divVector{D_{lv} \, \gradScal{S_r}} = 0 With D_{lv}= D_l + D_v . The coefficients D_l and D_v are, respectively, the diffusion coefficients of liquid water and of water vapour. The coefficient D_l , describing the transport of liquid water, is given by Darcy’s law: D_l(S_r,\temp) = \frac{ K_l(\temp) \, K_{rl}(S_r)} {\phi\eta_l(\temp)} \, \frac{\partial P_c} {\partial S_r} (S_r,\temp) The coefficient D_v(S_r, \temp) describing the diffusion of water vapour in the gas phase is given by Fick’s law: D_v(S_r,\temp) = \frac{D_{v0}(S_r,\temp)\, P_v(\temp)} {\phi } \left( \frac{M}{\rho_l R \temp} \right)^2 \frac{\partial P_c} {\partial S_r} (S_r,\temp) With - P_c(S_r,\temp) , capillary pressure determined by the desorption isotherm of water as a function of saturation, calibrated by the Leverett model. Its expression is given in DEFI_MATERIAU (BETON_DESORP). - K_l(\temp) , the intrinsic permeability to the liquid (homogeneous to an area), which is defined by the following relation: K_l(\temp) = K_0 \exp{\left[ \exp \left( \frac{\temp-\temp_0}{\temp_c} \right) -1 \right]} - K_{rl}(S_r) the relative permeability to water, which can be determined by a Muallem-Van Genuchten type law: K_{rl}(S_r) = \left(S_r\right)^p \left(1-\left(1-S_r^{1/\beta}\right)^\beta\right)^2 - D_{v0}(S_r, \temp) , the effective vapour diffusion coefficient, which is written D_{v0}(S_r, \temp) = D_0(\temp) R_m(\phi, S_r) - D_0 , the free-vapour diffusion coefficient (homogeneous to an area per unit time): D_0(\temp) = 0.217\cdot10^{-4} \left(\frac{\temp+273.15}{273.15}\right)^{1.88} It is specified that this expression is associated with the unit m^2/s . It is however possible to use this law for another system of units thanks to the keywords UNITE_LONGUEUR and UNITE_TEMPS (see DEFI_MATERIAU). - R_m(S_r, \phi) , the Millington resistance factor: R_m(S_r, \phi) = \phi^a D_{rv}(S_r) - D_{rv}(S_r) , the relative vapour diffusion coefficient: D_{rv}(S_r) = \left(1-S_r\right)^b - P_v(S_r,\temp) , the vapour pressure: P_v(\temp) = h(S_r, \temp)\cdot P_{vs}(\temp) - h(S_r, \temp) , the relative humidity determined by the desorption isotherm of water as a function of saturation: h(S_r, \temp)= \exp{\left(Pc(S_r, \temp) \frac{M}{\rho_l(\temp) R \temp} \right)} All these expressions depend on several parameters. Fixed parameters - R the perfect-gas constant ( R = 8.3144 J/mol/K ) - M the molar mass of water ( M = 18 · 10^{-3} kg/mol) User parameters of the material SECH_RFT - K_0 , the intrinsic permeability of the liquid at the reference temperature (homogeneous to an area), which corresponds to the parameter PERM_IN . - \temp_c [K] the thermal activation temperature, which corresponds to the parameter QSR_K . - a , first Millington coefficient, which corresponds to the parameter A_MIL . - b , first Millington coefficient, which corresponds to the parameter B_MIL . - p , pore interaction factor, which corresponds to the parameter VG_M_P . User parameters of the material BETON_DESORP - \temp_0 [K] the reference temperature. The corresponding material parameter is TEMP_0_C [°C] (which is converted into degrees kelvin). - \phi , the mean porosity, which corresponds to the parameter PORO . - \beta , Van Genuchten parameter, which corresponds to the parameter VG_N . Non-parameterisable quantities depending on the temperature - \eta_l(\temp) [Pa.s] , the dynamic viscosity of liquid water, of expression: 0.6612(\temp-229)^{-1.562} - \rho_l(\temp) [kg/m^3] , the density of liquid water, of expression: 314.4+685.6 \Bigl(1. -\bigl( \frac{\temp-273.15}{374.14}\bigr)^{\frac{1}{0.55}}\Bigr)^{0.55} - Pvs(\temp) [Pa] , the saturated vapour pressure of Rankine, of expression: Pvs(\temp)=101325\,\exp\left(13.7-\left(5120/\left(\temp+273.15\right)\right)\right) These expressions, just like the values of R and M , are given for information together with their units. They are globally involved in the formulae in the form of ratios and therefore do not interfere with the units of the analysis. Only \eta_l(\temp) is adapted to the system of units of the analysis according to the value of the material parameter UNITE_TEMPS. 4.4 Modelling of the boundary conditions The boundary conditions are in general expressed by a non-linear relation between the water-concentration flux {w}^{\text{fl}} (of dimension l/{m}^{3} \times m \, s^{-1} ) and the water concentration. These conditions are therefore analogous to the so-called exchange conditions in thermal analysis. One may for example use the formula proposed by L. Granger page 181: Its expression is the following: {w}^{\text{fl}} = \frac{0.5\beta } {{(C_0-{C}_{\text{eq}})}^{2}} \left[C-(2 \, C_0-{C}_{\text{eq}})\right] (C-{C}_{\text{eq}}) where: - {C}_{\text{eq}} is the water concentration for a humidity of 50% RH, - C_0 is the water concentration for a humidity of 100% RH, - \beta (of dimension l/{m}^{3} \times m/s ) is a coefficient, which can be defined experimentally and can evolve according to the cracking of the exchange surface (), - C is the current concentration (unknown) on the exchange surfaces. Note The temperature is always entered in degrees Celsius in the data setup. The conversion into degrees kelvin is done internally 5 Integration of drying in Code_Aster These developments concern the 2D elements, the axisymmetric elements and the 3D isoparametric elements, with any number of nodes, linear and quadratic. 5.1 Introduction of the notion of behaviour into the non-linear thermal operator The operator THER_NON_LINE is used for the solution of non-linear thermal problems. But the same solution module is used to solve drying and hydration problems, because of the analogy of the equations. The notion of behaviour has been added in the non-linear thermal operator, with a nomenclature and a syntax analogous to those of the non-linear mechanical operator. For drying it implies a notion of topological entity, on which this behaviour is applied. This can be useful when there are several types of possible diffusion laws, or when one wants to carry out a purely thermal analysis on one part of the mesh, while on another part one carries out a thermo-hydration analysis (on the other hand, the simultaneous use on the same mesh of drying-type behaviours and of thermal or hydration-type behaviours would not make sense). A ‘drying’ behaviour is associated with each of the diffusion laws, as they can be found in the literature, just as a specific material is associated with each of the diffusion laws, in order to define their characteristic coefficients. The solution of drying is identical, up to the coefficients, to that of non-linear thermal analysis, and no modification has been made to the solution algorithm. For drying, five distinct behaviours are defined under the keywords SECH_GRANGER, SECH_BAZANT, SECH_MENSI, SECH_RFT or SECH_NAPPE, in order to characterise each of the possible diffusion laws. They can be assigned to complementary parts of the mesh, during the same analysis. The simultaneous definition of several ‘drying’ behaviours associated with different topological entities requires several occurrences of the keyword COMPORTEMENT. The topological entity must then be identified by supplying the keyword GROUP_MA. In parallel with the ‘drying’ behaviours, in the operator DEFI_MATERIAU, materials make it possible in a first stage to define the values of the coefficients of the diffusion laws, non-linear functions of the water content and of the temperature. The user can choose the law (or laws) of his choice, and defines the value he wishes for each of these coefficients. The keyword SECH_GRANGER makes it possible to define the diffusion law of liquid and gaseous water in its most classical form among the expressions in the literature. Four coefficients as well as a reference temperature {\temp}_{0} characterise this law. The keywords SECH_MENSI and SECH_BAZANT make it possible to define the laws of Mensi and of Bazant, by means of the appropriate coefficients. The Bazant law, being expressed from the degree of humidity, requires the definition of a desorption curve making it possible to convert the water content into a degree of humidity within the framework of this modelling. The keyword SECH_RFT makes it possible to define a law of type RICHARDS_FICK_TEMPERATURE. It is described in section r7.01.12-sech_rft. Finally, the keyword SECH_NAPPE makes it possible to use a diffusion law, from a tabulated function of two variables, which will be interpolated in the analyses from the values of the water concentration and of the temperature. This last possibility has the drawback of not removing the ambiguity between these two variables associated with an identical type, 'TEMP'. It is necessary, for drying, to introduce as input to the analysis a concept of type [evol_ther], representing the evolution of the temperature field of the concrete structure, within the framework of a chained thermal/drying analysis. Indeed, the drying analysis requires the preliminary computation of the temperature and possibly of the hydration, because the diffusion coefficient D(C,\temp) depends on the temperature. 5.2 Implementation of the boundary conditions for drying 5.2.1 Expression of the boundary conditions The boundary conditions are expressed in the form of a humidity flux on the surfaces in contact with the external medium according to the expression . 5.2.2 Delimitation of the drying analysis by means of the boundary conditions The drying analysis is defined on the whole of the mesh where finite elements are assigned. In order to make the drying analysis effective only on a portion of the mesh (this with the aim of keeping the same model for the drying analyses and for the mechanical analyses and of facilitating the restarts of the analysis), the boundary conditions will be used. Indeed, drying takes place only if there is exchange with the outside. It is therefore the assignment of the boundary conditions which makes it possible to “localise” the analysis. The absence of drying on a portion of the structure will be expressed by the absence of boundary conditions on the exchange surfaces concerned. 5.2.3 Implementation in Aster The boundary conditions can be defined, as in thermal analysis, in the form of a non-linear normal flux formulated from a tabulated function of the computational variable, and interpolated during the analyses. This makes it possible to avoid creating new computation options, analogous to the non-linear thermal options which compute the left-hand side and the right-hand side, and which can be used directly for drying. It is then sufficient to choose a tabulated function corresponding to the expression of the flux, given by the equation . By means of a predefined function (FORMULE), the expression of the flux, given in polynomial form and as a function of the computational variable, is transformed into a tabulated curve, by means of CALC_FONC_INTERP. One therefore does not create a new computation option for the treatment of the boundary conditions. 5.2.4 Example of the setting up of the boundary conditions The sequence of commands, described in the example which follows (taken from the test HSNA100 V7.20.100), implements the creation of a boundary condition CHARSE05 on a mesh-cell group L_INT. The FORMULE is the numerical expression of the normal flux of water concentration which takes up the equation . BETA=3.41557E-08 C_0=105.7 C_EQ_I05=69.1 C_EQ_E05=69.1 C_EQ_I10=51.6 C_EQ_E10=69.1 FL_INT05 = FORMULE(NOM_PARA='TEMP', VALE='''(0.5 BETA / ((C_0 - C_EQ_I05 ) 2) (TEMP - (2. C_0 - C_EQ_I05 )) (TEMP - C_EQ_I05 ))''') LIST0=DEFI_LIST_REEL(DEBUT=0.,INTERVALLE=(_F(JUSQU_A = 200.,PAS = 10.))) HU_INT05=CALC_FONC_INTERP( FONCTION=FL_INT05, LIST_PARA=LIST0,NOM_PARA = 'TEMP', NOM_RESU='FL_INT05', PROL_GAUCHE='LINEAIRE', PROL_DROITE='LINEAIRE', INTERPOL='LIN', TITRE='FLUX D HUMIDITE' ) CHARSE05=AFFE_CHAR_THER_F(MODELE=MOTH, FLUX_NL=_F( GROUP_MA = 'L_INT', FLUN = HU_INT05)) Note It is important that the interpreted function and the tabulated function do not bear the same name, so that the right and left interpolations are properly defined, because the right and left exclusions do not “overload” the extensions of an interpreted function transformed by means of the operator CALC_FONC_INTERP. 5.3 Numerical integration of drying The heat equation leads, in the case of a normal-flux boundary condition on the boundary \Gamma , to the variational formulation: \int_{\domain} {\dot{\beta}(\temp) \, \tempVirt \measDomain} + \int_{\domain} {\therCondTher (\temp) \gradScal{\temp} \cdot \gradScal{\tempVirt} \measDomain } = \int_{\domain} {\therSource(\temp) \, \tempVirt \measDomain} + \int_{\bound} {\therCondTher (\temp) \, \frac{\partial \temp}{\partial n} \, \tempVirt \measBound } In an analogous way, the equation governing drying leads, in the case of a normal-flux boundary condition on the boundary \Gamma , to the variational formulation: \int_{\domain} {\dot{C}(\temp) \, \tempVirt \measDomain} + \int_{\domain} { D(C,\temp) \gradScal{C} \cdot \gradScal{\tempVirt} \measDomain } = 0 + \int_{\bound} { D(C,\temp) \, \frac{\partial C}{\partial n} \, \tempVirt \measBound } The solution of drying is integrated into the operator THER_NON_LINE, by replacing \rho \therCp by the constant function equal to the identity, and the conductivity by the diffusion D(C,\temp) , the temperature appearing as a constant in the computations (auxiliary variable). Depending on the diffusion law chosen, one must compute the value of the diffusion coefficient as well as its derivatives, according to the temperature and the water concentration at the current time instant, at the current point. One should refer to the documentation of the non-linear thermal operator R5.02.02 for further details on the numerical integration of non-linear thermal analysis. Within the framework of drying, the boundary conditions are given in terms of normal flux, and lead, as in thermal analysis, to a term in the left-hand side and to a term in the right-hand side. 6 Formulation of endogenous and drying shrinkage 6.1 Endogenous shrinkage Within the framework of a formulation of shrinkage in terms of strain, the total strain increment can be decomposed into the sum of a thermal component, of a component representing the endogenous shrinkage, and of a component representing the drying shrinkage, added to the mechanical component (elasticity, creep, ...). The simplest way of representing the drying shrinkage \strain_{\text{dess}} is to put it in the form: \begin{align}\begin{aligned}\Delta \strain_{\text{dess}} = \left( -\kappa \left( {C}_{0}-{C}^{+} \right ) +\kappa \left( {C}_{0}-{C}^{-} \right )\\\right) \, \tensTwoUnit = - \kappa \, \Delta C \, \tensTwoUnit\end{aligned}\end{align} \Delta {\epsilon}_{\text{dessiccation}}=\left[-\kappa \left({C}_{0}-{C}^{+}\right)+\kappa \left({C}_{0}-{C}^{-}\right)\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}\right].\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}{I}^{d}=-\kappa \Delta C.\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}{I}^{d} eq 6.1-1 where C is the water concentration, {C}_{0} the initial water concentration and \kappa a coefficient characterising the shrinkage, assumed constant. One can model the endogenous shrinkage in the form: \Delta \strain_{\text{endo}} = -\beta \, \xi \, \tensTwoUnit where \xi is the hydration and \beta a coefficient characteristic of the material whose dependences are poorly known. Drying and endogenous shrinkages can therefore enter a constitutive law by replacing in it the usual terms \Delta \strain -\Delta \strain_{\text{ther}} by \Delta \strain -\Delta \strain_{\text{ther}}-\Delta \strain_{\text{dess}}-\Delta \strain_{\text{endo}} . These terms are taken into account for the elastic and elastoplastic behaviours of Von Mises type and for several concrete models (BETON_UMLV, BETON_BURGER, BETON_DOUBLE_DP, ENDO_ISOT_BETON, MAZARS). One then has, for example, in 1D elasticity: \delta \strainCmp = \frac{1}{\youngModulus(\xi)} \, \Delta \stressCmp = \Delta \strainCmp_{\text{ther}} + \Delta \strainCmp_{\text{endo}} + \Delta \strainCmp_{\text{dess}} The mechanical parameter \youngModulus (Young’s modulus) depends principally on the hydration variable \xi . This formulation of drying shrinkage and of endogenous shrinkage has the advantage of using directly the water content C , which one can relate to the weight loss by simple integration over the volume. If one used the relative humidity h , it would have to be translated back into terms of water content by means of the desorption isotherm of each of the various concretes. These parameters can be defined in a relatively general framework, as functions of the various computational variables and auxiliary variables (temperature, hydration, water concentration, or constants) in order to leave the user the choice of defining freely the dependences of the parameters. It remains the user’s responsibility to use the functions in order to reproduce the expression of Young’s modulus. For more detail on these formulations, and on the means of computing the coefficients \kappa and \beta , one should refer to the thesis of L. Granger, , pages 99 onwards, and pages 210 onwards. For the mechanical analysis the variables \xi (the hydration) and C (water concentration) are data, as is the temperature in a thermomechanical analysis. 6.2 Integration of shrinkage into the mechanical constitutive laws Thermal analysis and drying are decoupled from the mechanical solution, just as drying is an operation chained to thermal analysis and to hydration. This decoupling makes it possible to integrate shrinkage into the solution operator of non-linear mechanics, without adding new phenomena, behaviours, element types and computation options. In addition, it makes it possible to introduce shrinkage in a simple way into all the non-linear constitutive laws. The syntax of STAT_NON_LINE is not modified. In the current version of the non-linear mechanical operator, shrinkage has been integrated into the elastic behaviour (ELAS), into the Von Mises elastoplastic behaviour (VMIS_ISOT_ ) and into the models specific to concretes: MAZARS, ENDO_ISOT_BETON, BETON_DOUBLE_DP, GRANGER , BETON_UMLV_FP. It consists in removing the shrinkage terms from the total strain, before the solution of the equilibrium equations at the Gauss points, in the same way as thermal expansion is taken into account. The coefficients \kappa and \beta characterising endogenous and drying shrinkages are defined under the keyword 'ELAS_FO' in DEFI_MATERIAU (operands K_DESSIC and B_ENDOGE respectively), as constants. The other mechanical characteristics, Poisson’s ratio and Young’s modulus, can also be defined as functions of the new variables HYDR and SECH, which have been added to the catalogues of the two operators DEFI_FONCTION and DEFI_NAPPE. The results, of type [evol_ther], coming from a non-linear thermal analysis, or from a thermo-hydration analysis, and from a drying analysis, and corresponding respectively to the thermo-hydric fields of type 'TEMP/HYDR', or to the drying field of type 'TEMP', are transmitted to the mechanical analysis by means of the operator AFFE_MATERIAU (keyword AFFE_VARC). The mechanical analyses associating these fields make it possible: - to compute the endogenous and drying shrinkages, in the case where the associated material characteristics will have been defined beforehand in DEFI_MATERIAU, - to interpolate Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio when these are functions of the hydration or drying variables. - In the presence of a drying field, it is necessary to supply the keyword VALE_REF in the command AFFE_MATERIAU. This value defines the drying value for which the drying shrinkage is zero. - One must therefore take care to be consistent with the drying values used (in particular at the initial time instant!) - Drying and hydration are not taken into account for the structural elements. For this type of element, it will be necessary to define zero coefficients \kappa and \beta , otherwise the analysis will stop in fatal error - The behaviours FLUA_PORO_BETON, ENDO_PORO_BETON and BETON_RAG take these effects into account but differently Notes 6.3 Tangent matrix The computation of the tangent matrices of the various non-linear constitutive laws is not affected by the addition of endogenous shrinkage and of drying shrinkage, because one neglects the derivatives, with respect to the hydration and drying variables, of the terms of the equilibrium equations, just as the derivatives of these same terms with respect to temperature are usually neglected. These derivatives appear at second order. 7 Bibliography GRANGER, L.: Delayed behaviour of concrete in the containments of nuclear power plants: analysis and modelling. The following are specified: - the description of the model, - the integration of the law in code_aster , - the description of the routines introduced. 1 Notation The notation used here is the notation usual in soil mechanics, to which is added the notation specific to the writing of the parameters of the CJS law. geomechanics usage, the sign convention adopted is that of continuum mechanics, i.e. tensile stresses are counted as positive. 2 Introduction The CJS model is an elastoplastic constitutive law suited to the modelling of granular materials. It was developed at the École Centrale de Lyon (, , ). The CJS version implemented in code_aster is a hierarchical model comprising several levels of complexity. In its most complete expression, the model has two yield surfaces: one is activated by isotropic loading, the other by deviatoric loading. The first undergoes isotropic hardening and the second mixed hardening (isotropic and kinematic). The elastic law is of non-linear hypoelastic type. 3 Description of the CJS law 3.1 Partition of the strains The global strain increment is decomposed into three parts, relating to each of the mechanisms involved: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}={\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{e}+{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{ip}}+{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}} where {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{e} , {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{ip}} and {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}} are respectively the elastic strain increment, the isotropic plastic strain increment and the deviatoric plastic strain increment. 3.2 Elastic mechanism The elastic part of the law is of hypoelastic type, whose general expression is: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{e}=\frac{{\dot{s}}_{ij}}{2G}+\frac{{\dot{I}}_{1}}{9K}{\delta}_{ij} where {I}_{1} is the first stress invariant: {I}_{1}=\text{tr}(\sigma ) , s is the deviatoric part of the stress tensor, and where K and G are respectively the elastic bulk modulus and the elastic shear modulus. These depend on the stress state according to: K={K}_{o}^{e}{(\frac{{I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}}}{3{P}_{a}})}^{n} , G={G}_{o}^{e}{(\frac{{I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}}}{3{P}_{a}})}^{n} {K}_{o}^{e} , {G}_{o} , {P}_{a} and n are parameters of the model. {P}_{a} is a reference pressure equal to -100 kPa. 3.3 Isotropic plastic mechanism The corresponding yield surface {f}^{i} is, in principal-stress space, a plane perpendicular to the hydrostatic axis, namely: {f}^{i}(\sigma ,{Q}_{\text{iso}})=-\frac{({I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}})}{3}+{Q}_{\text{iso}} where {Q}_{\text{iso}} is the thermodynamic force which depends on the internal variable q according to: {\dot{Q}}_{\text{iso}}={K}^{p}\dot{q}={K}_{o}^{p}{(\frac{{Q}_{\text{iso}}}{{P}_{a}})}^{n}\dot{q} {K}_{o}^{p} , {P}_{a} and n are the parameters of the deviatoric plastic mechanism ( {P}_{a} and n are identical to those of the elastic mechanism). The normality rule makes it possible to express the evolution of the plastic strain and of the hardening variable as a function of the evolution of the plastic multiplier {\lambda}^{i} : {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{ip}}={\dot{\lambda}}^{i}\frac{\partial {f}^{i}}{\partial {\sigma}_{ij}}=-\frac{1}{3}{\dot{\lambda}}^{i}{\delta}_{ij} and \dot{q}=-{\dot{\lambda}}^{i}\frac{\partial {f}^{i}}{\partial {Q}_{\text{iso}}}=-{\dot{\lambda}}^{i} Taking the second equation into account, the hardening law can also be written in the form: {\dot{Q}}_{\text{iso}}=-{\dot{\lambda}}^{i}{K}_{o}^{p}{(\frac{{Q}_{\text{iso}}}{{P}_{a}})}^{n} 3.4 Deviatoric plastic mechanism The yield surface of this second plastic mechanism is a convex surface with ternary symmetry defined by the equation: {f}^{d}(\sigma ,R,X)={q}_{\text{II}}h({\theta}_{q})+R({I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}}) with {q}_{ij}={s}_{ij}-{I}_{1}{X}_{ij} {q}_{\text{II}}=\sqrt{{q}_{ij}{q}_{ij}} h({\theta}_{q})={(1+\gamma \cos(3{\theta}_{q}))}^{1/6}={(1+\gamma \sqrt{54}\frac{\det(q)}{{q}_{\text{II}}^{3}})}^{1/6} . The scalar R and the tensor X represent respectively the mean radius and the centre of the yield surface in the deviatoric plane. s , q and X are deviatoric tensors. \gamma is a parameter which reflects the asymmetric behaviour of soils in compression and in extension. \theta is the Lode angle. This yield surface evolves according to two types of hardening: isotropic hardening and kinematic hardening. The coordinates of \text{HM} are: \text{HM}=(\rho \sin{\theta}_{s},\rho \cos{\theta}_{s}) Lode angle in the deviatoric plane The principal components of the deviator are therefore: {s}_{1}=\rho The term {\phi }_{o} is expressed as a function of the failure characteristic of the material. 3.4.3 Evolution law of the deviatoric plastic mechanism In granular materials, a volume change can occur for a purely deviatoric loading. This volume change is linked to the discontinuous nature of the material and to the kinematic conditions which result during loading. This particular phenomenon does not allow the deviatoric plastic strains to be defined from the normality rule alone. This is why the deviatoric plastic mechanism is non-associated. There therefore exists a potential function governing the evolution of the strains: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}={\dot{\lambda}}^{d}{G}_{ij}^{d} The potential function is defined from the following kinematic condition: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{v}^{\text{dp}}=-\beta (\frac{{s}_{\text{II}}}{{s}_{\text{II}}^{c}}-1)\frac{\mid {s}_{ij}{\dot{e}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}\mid }{{s}_{\text{II}}} where \mathrm{\beta } is a parameter of the model and {s}_{\text{II}}^{c} represents the characteristic stress state. A surface, of shape identical to the yield surface in stress space, separates the contractant states from the dilatant states. This surface, called the characteristic surface, has the equation: {f}^{c}={s}_{\text{II}}^{c}h({\theta}_{s})+{R}_{c}({I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}}) where {R}_{c} is a parameter corresponding to the mean radius of this characteristic surface. The kinematic condition can also be written in the form: \begin{array}{}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{v}^{\text{dp}}+\beta (\frac{{s}_{\text{II}}}{{s}_{\text{II}}^{c}}-1)\frac{\mid {s}_{ij}{\dot{e}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}\mid }{{s}_{\text{II}}}={\dot{\varepsilon}}_{v}^{\text{dp}}+\beta (\frac{{s}_{\text{II}}}{{s}_{\text{II}}^{c}}-1)\frac{\mid {s}_{ij}{\dot{e}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}\mid }{{s}_{ij}{\dot{e}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}}\frac{{s}_{ij}{\dot{e}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}}{{s}_{\text{II}}}\\ ={\dot{\varepsilon}}_{v}^{\text{dp}}+\frac{{\beta }^{'}}{{s}_{\text{II}}}{s}_{ij}{\dot{e}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}\\ ={{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{v}^{\text{dp}}+\frac{{\beta }^{'}}{{s}_{\text{II}}}{s}_{ij}\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}=0\end{array} where {\beta }^{'}=\beta (\frac{{s}_{\text{II}}}{{s}_{\text{II}}^{c}}-1)\text{signe}({s}_{ij}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}) . It is then possible to seek to express this kinematic condition from a tensor n in the form: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}{n}_{ij}=0 that is, after decomposition of each term into deviatoric and hydrostatic parts: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}{n}_{ij}=({\dot{e}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}+\frac{1}{3}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{v}^{\text{dp}}{\delta}_{ij})({n}_{1}{s}_{ij}+{n}_{2}{\delta}_{ij})={n}_{1}{s}_{ij}{\dot{e}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}+{n}_{2}{\mathrm{dt}\varepsilon }_{v}^{\text{dp}}=0 One deduces the relation \frac{{n}_{1}}{{n}_{2}}=\frac{{\beta }^{'}}{{s}_{\text{II}}} , which, added to the normalisation condition n:n=1 , leads to the expressions: {n}_{1}=\frac{\frac{{\beta }^{'}}{{s}_{\text{II}}}}{\sqrt{{\beta }^{'2}+3}} and {n}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\beta }^{'2}+3}} , that is {n}_{ij}=\frac{{\beta }^{'}\frac{{s}_{ij}}{{s}_{\text{II}}}+{\delta}_{ij}}{\sqrt{{\beta }^{'2}+3}} The evolution law of {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}} must be such that the kinematic condition is satisfied. It is therefore proposed to take the projection of {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}} onto the strain hypersurface of normal n , namely: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{dp}}={\dot{\lambda}}^{d}(\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {\sigma}_{ij}}-(\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {\sigma}_{kl}}{n}_{kl}){n}_{ij})={\dot{\lambda}}^{d}{G}_{ij}^{d} with {G}_{ij}^{d}=\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {\sigma}_{ij}}-(\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {\sigma}_{kl}}{n}_{kl}){n}_{ij} . Moreover, for the computation of the potential, one may note that: \begin{array}{}\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {\sigma}_{ij}}=\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {q}_{kl}}\frac{\partial {q}_{kl}}{\partial {\sigma}_{ij}}+R{\delta}_{ij}\\ =\left[\text{dev}(\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {q}_{kl}})+\frac{1}{3}\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {q}_{\text{mm}}}{\delta}_{kl}\right]\left[{\delta}_{\text{ik}}{\delta}_{\text{jl}}-{\delta}_{ij}(\frac{1}{3}{\delta}_{kl}+{X}_{kl})\right]+R{\delta}_{ij}\\ ={Q}_{kl}{\delta}_{\text{ik}}{\delta}_{\text{jl}}-{\delta}_{ij}(\frac{1}{3}{Q}_{kl}{\delta}_{kl}+{Q}_{kl}{X}_{kl})+\frac{1}{3}\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {q}_{\text{mm}}}\left[{\delta}_{\text{ik}}{\delta}_{\text{jl}}{\delta}_{kl}-{\delta}_{ij}(\frac{1}{3}{\delta}_{kl}{\delta}_{kl}+{\delta}_{kl}{X}_{kl})\right]+R{\delta}_{ij}\\ ={Q}_{ij}-({Q}_{kl}{X}_{kl}-R){\delta}_{ij}\end{array} 3.4.4 Failure surface The failure state results from the non-linear nature of the hardening laws and from the existence of limit values associated with the hardening variables R and X . The limit of R , denoted {R}_{m} , is reached when r tends to infinity. The limit of {X}_{ij} is reached when {\dot{X}}_{ij} becomes zero. Under these conditions: {Q}_{ij}=\phi {X}_{ij} and {Q}_{\text{II}}=\phi {X}_{\text{II}\lim}\Rightarrow {X}_{\text{II}\lim}=\frac{1}{{\phi }_{o}h({\theta}_{s})} at the failure state one therefore has (r7.01.13-fig-rupture): {q}_{\text{II}}=\frac{{s}_{\text{II}}+{I}_{1}{X}_{\text{II}\lim}\cos\alpha }{\cos({\theta}_{s}-{\theta}_{q})} Substituting this expression and the value of R at failure into the equation of the yield surface at failure, one obtains the equation of a limit envelope for the yield surfaces: {f}^{r}={s}_{\text{II}}h({\theta}_{s})+{R}_{r}({I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}})=0 with {R}_{r}=\frac{\cos\alpha }{{\phi }_{o}}+\frac{h({\theta}_{s})}{h({\theta}_{q})}{R}_{m}\cos({\theta}_{s}-{\theta}_{q}) , mean radius of the envelope, which is determined from the mechanical characteristics at failure of the material. The value of {\phi }_{o} can then be deduced from it: {\phi }_{o}=\frac{\cos\alpha }{{R}_{r}-\frac{h({\theta}_{s})}{h({\theta}_{q})}{R}_{m}\cos({\theta}_{s}-{\theta}_{q})} with \cos\alpha =\frac{{q}_{\text{II}}^{2}-{s}_{\text{II}}^{2}-{({I}_{1}{X}_{\text{II}})}^{2}}{2{s}_{\text{II}}{I}_{1}{X}_{\text{II}}} Representation of the failure, characteristic and yield surfaces in the deviatoric plane Moreover, {R}_{r} is linked to the maximum friction angle and depends on the mean stress and on the relative density. In order to take into account the dependence of the maximum friction angle on the mean stress and on the relative density, one considers the relation: {R}_{r}={R}_{c}+\mu \ln(\frac{3{p}_{c}}{{I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}}}) where {R}_{c} and \mu are parameters of the model. {p}_{c} is the critical mean stress, that is the minimum mean stress (it is negative with our sign convention) known by the material during its history. It depends on the initial relative density according to the classical notion of the critical line in the plane (e,\ln\mid p\mid ) : {p}_{c}={p}_{\text{co}}\exp(-c{\varepsilon}_{v}) where {p}_{\text{co}} is the initial critical pressure and 1/c is the slope of the critical-state line in the plane (\mid {\varepsilon}_{v}\mid ,\ln\mid p\mid ) . 3.5 Hierarchy of the model 3.5.1 Summary description of the three CJS levels From the complete description of the model given above, one deduces three levels of increasing complexity whose characteristics are summarised in the following table: | | Elastic mechanism | Isotropic plastic mechanism | Deviatoric plastic mechanism | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | CJS1 | linear | not activated | activated, perfect plasticity | | CJS2 | non-linear | activated | activated, isotropic hardening | | CJS3 | non-linear | activated | activated, kinematic hardening | 3.5.2 Summary of the CJS parameters Moreover, one can also summarise the correspondence between the different levels of the model and the parameters associated with each of them: | | n | {K}_{o}^{e} | {G}_{o}^{e} | {K}^{p} | \gamma | \beta | {R}_{c} | A | b | {R}_{m} | \mu | {p}_{\text{co}} | c | {p}_{a} | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | CJS1 | | \times | \times | | \times | \times | | | | \times | | | | \times | | CJS2 | \times | \times | \times | \times | \times | \times | \times | \times | | \times | | | | \times | | CJS3 | \times | \times | \times | \times | \times | \times | \times | | \times | \times | \times | \times | \times | \times | In code_aster , the elastic parameters of the CJS model ( {K}_{o}^{e} and {G}_{o} ) are taken into account directly in the elastic characteristics of the material, that is through the Young's modulus E and the Poisson's ratio \mathit{NU} . In each case, the aim is to compute, from the fields known in the minus state {\varepsilon}^{-} , {\sigma}^{-} and from the strain increment \Delta \varepsilon , the new stress state {\sigma}^{+} . In the sequence of computations, one begins by making the assumption that only the non-linear elastic mechanism intervenes. An elastic prediction is therefore carried out. This prediction is then used to compute the yield functions {f}^{i} and {f}^{d} ; one seeks to know whether one then goes beyond the thresholds: - if {f}^{i}\le 0 and {f}^{d}\le 0 , the elastic prediction is retained as the new stress state, - if {f}^{i}>0 and {f}^{d}\le 0 , one carries out the integration of the non-linear elastic and isotropic plastic mechanisms, - if {f}^{i}\le 0 and {f}^{d}>0 , one carries out the integration of the non-linear elastic and deviatoric plastic mechanisms, - if {f}^{i}>0 and {f}^{d}>0 , one carries out the integration of the non-linear elastic, isotropic plastic and deviatoric plastic mechanisms. On exit from the elastoplastic computation, when only one plastic threshold has initially been exceeded, each of the yield functions is recomputed. Indeed, it is possible that, in seeking to return onto one of the thresholds, one then exceeds the other threshold not initially activated by the elastic prediction. In that case, one then solves by integrating all the mechanisms. 4.1 Choice of the internal variables The variables q , r and \alpha are equivalent to the associated thermodynamic forces {Q}_{\text{iso}} , R and X . relaxation procedure inside the Newton iterations is taken into account. This makes it possible to avoid certain oscillation problems in the computation of the solution {Y}^{p+1} which finally lead to the non-convergence of the numerical integration. Thus, at iteration p+1 , instead of updating the unknown {Y}^{p+1} by a complete increment {\mathrm{\delta Y}}^{p+1} {Y}^{p+1}={Y}^{p}+\delta {Y}^{p+1} one sets {Y}_{m}^{p+1}={Y}^{p}+{\rho}_{m}\delta {Y}^{p+1} and one seeks, by performing a loop over sub-iterations m , to determine an optimal value of the scalar {\rho}_{m} . This value is sought by considering the rotation of the normal, in the deviatoric plane, to the surface {f}^{d} , in the course of the sub-iterations. This normal, denoted {\tilde{n}}_{m} , is expressed from the stresses contained in the term {Y}_{m}^{p+1} by {\tilde{n}}_{m}=2h{({\theta}_{q})}^{5}{q}_{\text{II}}\frac{\partial {f}^{d}}{\partial {q}_{ij}}=(2+\gamma \cos(3{\theta}_{q})){q}_{ij}+\frac{\sqrt{6}\gamma }{{q}_{\text{II}}}\frac{\partial \det(q)}{\partial {q}_{ij}} Starting from the initial value {\rho}_{0}=1.0 , the process set up consists of the following stages: - computation of the normals {\tilde{n}}_{m-1} and {\tilde{n}}_{m} - computation of the rotation angle {\phi }_{m} between these normals: \cos{\mathrm{\phi }}_{m}=\frac{{\tilde{n}}_{m-1}:{\tilde{n}}_{m}}{\sqrt{{\tilde{n}}_{m-1}}\sqrt{{\tilde{n}}_{m}}} - test on the evolution \cos{\mathrm{\phi }}_{m} : if \cos{\mathrm{\phi }}_{m}\le \text{TOLROT} then {\rho}_{m+1}=\text{DECREL}{\rho}_{m} and m=m+1 otherwise end of the sub-iterations and {Y}^{p+1}={Y}_{m}^{p+1} 4.7 Subdivision of the time step As for most constitutive relations, the possibility of locally subdividing (at the Gauss points) the time step has been introduced for the CJS model in order to facilitate the numerical integration. This possibility is managed by the operand ITER_INTE_PAS of the keyword CONVERGENCE of the operator STAT_NON_LINE. If itepas, the value of ITER_INTE_PAS, is equal to 0, 1 or -1 there is no subdivision (note: 0 is the default value). If itepas is positive the subdivision is automatic; if it is negative the subdivision is taken into account only in the event of non-convergence with the initial time step. The subdivision consists in carrying out, after the elastic prediction phase, the integration of the plastic mechanism or mechanisms involved with a strain increment whose components correspond to the components of the initial strain increment divided by the absolute value of itepas. 4.8 Miscellaneous notes 4.8.1 Computation of the term \cos({\theta}_{s}-{\theta}_{q}) The term \cos({\theta}_{s}-{\theta}_{q}) appears in the expression of {\varphi}_{o} . We have adopted for its computation the same method as that used at the ECL. That is, we determine the angles {\theta}_{s} and {\theta}_{q} in the following way: {\theta}_{s}=\frac{1}{3}\text{Arctan}(\frac{\sqrt{\text{1-}{\cos}^{2}(3{\theta}_{s})}}{\cos(3{\theta}_{s})}) and {\theta}_{q}=\frac{1}{3}\text{Arctan}(\frac{\sqrt{\text{1-}{\cos}^{2}({\mathrm{3\theta }}_{q})}}{\cos({\mathrm{3\theta }}_{q})}) then we take the cosine of the difference. These expressions of {\theta}_{s} and {\theta}_{q} are also used for the computation of: \frac{\partial \cos({\theta}_{s}-{\theta}_{q})}{\partial {\sigma}_{kl}}=-\sin({\theta}_{s}-{\theta}_{q})(\frac{\partial {\theta}_{s}}{\partial {\sigma}_{kl}}-\frac{\partial {\theta}_{q}}{\partial {\sigma}_{kl}}) with \frac{\partial {\theta}_{s}}{\partial {\sigma}_{kl}}=-\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{1-{\cos}^{2}({\mathrm{3\theta }}_{s})}\frac{\sqrt{54}}{{q}_{\text{II}}^{3}}({t}_{kl}-3\frac{\det(q)}{{q}_{\text{II}}^{2}}{q}_{kl}) 4.8.2 Computation of {R}_{r} The failure radius introduced in the CJS3 model is given by the formula {R}_{r}={R}_{c}+\mu \ln(\frac{3{p}_{c}}{{I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}}}) In fact, when \frac{{I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}}}{3}>{p}_{c} , one must lock {R}_{r} at the value of {R}_{c} . The dilatancy domain disappears and one does not allow {R}_{r} to decrease below {R}_{c} . Consequently, one introduces, in place of the preceding formulation, the following expression {R}_{r}={R}_{c}+\mu \max\left[0,\ln(\frac{3{p}_{c}}{{I}_{1}+{Q}_{\text{init}}})\right] 4.8.3 Tension Without cohesion, the tension domain which corresponds to positive stresses is inadmissible for soils. From the point of view of the integration of the CJS model, when the stress state tends towards the apex of the cone of the yield surface, the numerical risk of tipping into this forbidden domain increases. Now when one projects or when one makes a prediction at a point of this domain, the numerical computation leads either to an erroneous result or to a fatal error. Indeed, tension manifests itself numerically by a positive value of {I}_{1} . This value then poses a problem at the moment of evaluating certain quantities such as {(\frac{{I}_{1}^{+}+{Q}_{\text{init}}}{3{P}_{a}})}^{-1.5} ; moreover it would generate, from a theoretical point of view, a negative value of {q}_{\text{II}} according to the equation of the deviatoric yield surface. Such a phenomenon has been detected at several levels: in a particular way in the elastic prediction with the CJS1 model, and in a general way in the local Newton iterations involving the deviatoric mechanism. The same response has been provided in order to overcome this pathology: it consists in virtually projecting the stresses in the elastic domain onto the hydrostatic axis by setting: \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{11}={\sigma}_{22}={\sigma}_{33}=-1\text{kPa}\\ {\sigma}_{12}={\sigma}_{13}={\sigma}_{23}=0\end{array} One thus repositions the stress state in the compression domain while moving little away from the inadmissible initial prediction envisaged, and in the hope that structural considerations will allow the global computation to converge. Moreover the internal variables do not evolve and one assumes that one has returned to the elastic domain 5 Tangent operator The tangent operator called by the option RIGI_MECA_TANG corresponds to the tangent operator deduced from the rate problem and computed from the results known at time instant t. r7.01.17 Barcelona model r7.01.17 Barcelona model Summary: This document presents the formulation and the numerical integration of the elastoplastic Barcelona constitutive model [bib2]__, designed to describe the mechanical behaviour of unsaturated soils, in particular clays. This model is an extension of the modified Cam-Clay model [bib1]__ taking into account, in a schematic manner, the effects of the capillary pressure on the elasticity, the reversibility domain, and the hardening mechanisms observed experimentally on unsaturated soils. The Barcelona model comprises a total of sixteen parameters. The constitutive equations are solved by means of a time-implicit integration method, implemented in the tool MFront [bib5]__. Use of the model is necessarily linked to the HHM environment r7.01.11. 1 Notation The notation and sign conventions used are those of continuum mechanics. A bold character represents a second-order tensor and an open-face character a fourth-order tensor. For a second-order tensor \boldsymbol{a} , its decomposition into deviatoric and volumetric parts, denoted respectively \boldsymbol{a}_d and a_v , is written as follows: \boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{a}_d + \frac{a_v}{3}\boldsymbol{I},\quad\text{avec}\quad a_v = \boldsymbol{I}:\boldsymbol{a},\quad \boldsymbol{I}:\boldsymbol{a}_d=0 where \boldsymbol{I}=\boldsymbol{\delta} denotes the second-order identity tensor. One also writes a_m=\cfrac{a_v}{3} . For a second-order tensor \boldsymbol{a} of the same nature as a strain, its von Mises equivalent norm is denoted by a_{eq}=\sqrt{\cfrac{2}{3}\boldsymbol{a}_d:\boldsymbol{a}_d} . For a second-order tensor \boldsymbol{A} of the same nature as a stress, it is written A_{eq}=\sqrt{\cfrac{3}{2}\boldsymbol{A}_d:\boldsymbol{A}_d} .
