r7.01.19 Modelling of the creep/plasticity coupling for concrete r7.01.19 Modelling of the creep/plasticity coupling for concrete Summary This is a coupling model between the constitutive behaviours modelling creep, of GRANGER type, and the plasticity models, either general (von Mises law with isotropic hardening) or specific to concrete, of BETON_DOUBLE_DP type, implemented in the general solution algorithm of DYNA/STAT_NON_LINE. The coupling is carried out by a chaining of the solution of the equations of the two models during an iterative algorithm, which will take place at each Gauss point, at each iteration. It is therefore a "strong" coupling, since the equations of the creep law and of the plasticity law are satisfied rigorously at each instant. This chaining makes it possible to dispense with the complete development of a genuine coupled creep/plasticity solution, by using the existing models and without intervening in their solution, but it has the disadvantage of a higher computational cost. 1 Introduction This is a coupling model between the constitutive behaviours modelling creep, of GRANGER type, and the concrete models modelling the phenomena of plasticity, either general (von Mises) or specific to concrete, of BETON_DOUBLE_DP type, implemented in the general solution algorithm of STAT_NON_LINE R5.03.01. The existing models are used, with the objective of chaining the solution of the internal equations of the two models during an iterative algorithm, which takes place at each Gauss point, at each iteration. It is therefore a "strong" coupling, since the internal equilibrium equations of creep and of plasticity are satisfied rigorously at each instant. This chaining makes it possible to dispense with the complete development of a genuine coupled creep/plasticity solution, but it has the disadvantage of a higher computational cost. Indeed, at each Gauss point, and at each iteration, one must a priori solve several times the equilibrium equations of plasticity and those of creep, until the equilibrium between creep and plasticity is obtained. But this makes it possible to couple a creep law with any plasticity law, for a moderate development cost. On the other hand, in the case of the law BETON_DOUBLE_DP, in post-peak tension, the hardening curve is linear, and the local solution algorithm converges in a single iteration. The computational cost therefore remains limited. The couplings available by this procedure are, in the version of Code_Aster relating to this document: - for the creep law: GRANGER_FP, GRANGER_FP_V, GRANGER_FP_INDT - for the plasticity law: ELAS, VMIS_ISOT_LINE, VMIS_ISOT_TRAC, VMIS_ISOT_PUIS, ROUSS_PR, BETON_DOUBLE_DP Note: the coupling between the creep law BETON_UMLV_FP and the damage laws MAZARS and ENDO_ISOT_BETON is in fact a constitutive law written specifically in order to take into account the coupling between these two models, which does not fall under the principle described in this document. This coupling is described in R7.01.06. 2 Principle of the creep/plasticity coupling The coupling is carried out during the solution internal to the Gauss point, within the framework of an iterative algorithm in which the creep and plasticity computations are chained. In order to carry out such a coupling, one integrates into the local solution of the operators STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE a module making it possible to compute successively, from the same initial state (stresses and internal variables, strains and strain increments), the solution of creep and of plasticity. The principle is the following: during the solution at the Gauss point, from the initial state in stresses, internal variables and strains, a creep computation is performed. The creep strain increment computed during the solution of creep is then subtracted from the total strain increment, and supplied as an argument of the solution of plasticity. The solution of plasticity is carried out from the same initial state in stresses, internal variables and strains, except for the total strain increment, from which the creep strain increment has been removed. When the plastic strain increment has been computed, after solution of plasticity, one can correct the value of the strain at the input of the creep computation, and reiterate the chained creep/plasticity computation, until convergence of the solution is obtained, that is, the stability of the stresses and of the creep and plasticity strains. The stresses computed by means of the creep equations are a priori not identical to those of the plasticity equations. Their equality is not formally written in the equations. But when the creep/plasticity equilibrium is reached, one can show that the stresses at the output of creep are indeed equal to the stresses at the output of plasticity (cf. paragraph 3.2). Since the coupling is solved by chaining the solutions of creep and of plasticity during an iterative algorithm, this allowing a low cost of software development, computation of the tangent matrix is carried out exclusively from the plasticity model, without taking creep or the creep/plasticity coupling into account, as a simplification. The creep strains then constitute a loading for the plasticity computation. This assumes that the evolution of creep is slower than the evolution of plasticity. This simplification, all the more relevant when the analysis step is judiciously chosen, makes it possible to converge towards the (global) solution with a number of global iterations slightly larger than in the case where the tangent matrix is computed exactly, but it in no way alters the result of the (converged) analysis. 3 Formulation of the equations 3.1 Formulation of Granger creep in Code_Aster (Reminder) The modelling of creep in Code_Aster , according to the model of Granger , is presented briefly in this paragraph. For more detail, one will refer to [R7.01.01 and V6.04.142]. The expression for the creep strain applied to a linear viscoelastic material, by applying the Boltzmann superposition principle for a non-constant loading history \sigma (t) , can be written in 1D: {\epsilon}_{\text{fl}}(t)=\underset{\tau =0}{\overset{t}{\int}}f(t-\tau )\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \tau }\mathrm{d\tau }=f\ast \frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial t} \ast represents the convolution product J(t,{t}_{c})=f(t-{t}_{c}) is the creep function, an increasing function of (t-{t}_{c}) and zero for (t-{t}_{c}) negative. One can show that any linear viscoelastic body can be modelled by a series arrangement of Kelvin models and that the creep function can then be put in the form: f(t)=\sum_{s=1}^{r}{J}_{s}(1-\exp(-\frac{t}{{\tau}_{s}})) {\tau}_{s} and {J}_{s} are positive coefficients, identified on the experimental creep curves. A series arrangement of Kelvin models is used, whose coefficients are identified from experimental creep curves. It is shown in practice that the creep curves of concrete are reproduced satisfactorily with a series of 8 models. The following creep function is therefore used: J(t,{t}_{c})=\sum_{s=1}^{s=8}{J}_{s}(1-\exp(-\frac{t-{t}_{c}}{{\tau}_{s}})) which leads to the expression: {\varepsilon}_{\text{fl}}(t)=\underset{\tau =0}{\overset{t}{\int}}\left[\sum_{s=1}^{s=8}{J}_{s}(1-\exp(-\frac{t-\tau }{{\tau}_{s}}))\right]\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \tau }d\tau By differentiating this expression in the case of a single Kelvin model ( s=1 ), one easily obtains the following equation: {\tau}_{s}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{fl}}(t)+{\varepsilon}_{\text{fl}}(t)={J}_{s}\sigma (t) which can also be written: \sigma (t)=\frac{{\tau}_{s}}{{J}_{s}}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{fl}}(t)+\frac{1}{{J}_{s}}{\varepsilon}_{\text{fl}}(t) or again: \sigma (t)=\mu {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{fl}}(t)+K{\varepsilon}_{\text{fl}}(t) with \mu =\frac{{\tau}_{s}}{{J}_{s}} and K=\frac{1}{{J}_{s}} This formulation can be extended to the case of the series expansion in 8 Kelvin models (or more), subject to a few mathematical developments, which gives: \sigma (t)=\sum_{s=1}^{s=8}\left[{K}_{s}{\varepsilon}_{\text{fl}}^{s}(t)+{m}_{s}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{fl}}^{s}(t)\right] The rheological model of creep is represented in the figure below, in the case of a single Kelvin model: In order to simplify the presentation of the coupling in the paragraph which follows, only the first term of the Kelvin series decomposition is taken into account, and one writes: \sigma (t)=\mu {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{fl}}(t)+K{\varepsilon}_{\text{fl}}(t) Moreover, for the presentation, \mu and K are assumed constant, that is \mu ={\mu}^{-} and K={K}^{-} . 3.2 Formulation of the creep/plasticity coupling in 1D The creep/plasticity coupling corresponds to the rheological model below, in which creep, characterised by the coefficients K and \mu (stiffness and viscosity), and plasticity are modelled in series. In particular the coupling BETON_UMLV_FP / ENDO_ISOT_BETON is described in R7.01.06. 4 Integration algorithm of the creep/plasticity coupling 4.1 Algorithm at the Gauss points In order to introduce the creep/plasticity coupling into Code_Aster , the following approach is adopted: an iterative algorithm is used in which, at each Gauss point, creep is chained to plasticity. The creep equation is solved at each iteration (k) by means of an estimated value of the plastic strain increment, which is subtracted from the total strain increment. An estimated value of the creep strain increment is thus obtained, which is subtracted from the total strain for the solution of plasticity at iteration k . A new estimate of the plastic strain increment is thus obtained, which makes it possible to carry out the creep computation at iteration k+1 . The creep/plasticity chaining is carried out iteratively, until a stable solution is obtained, that is, a variation in relative value of the stress lower than a convergence criterion. Insofar as the solution of creep in Code_Aster is programmed in an incremental manner , the simplification consists in replacing \Delta \varepsilon by \Delta \varepsilon -\Delta {\varepsilon}_{\text{pl}}^{k} in the calling arguments of the solution of creep. There is therefore no intervention to be made in the creep solution module. The same is true of the solution of plasticity, in which \Delta \varepsilon is replaced by \Delta \varepsilon -\Delta {\varepsilon}_{\text{fl}}^{k} in the calling arguments of the solution of plasticity. 4.2 General flow chart The flow chart of the solution can be outlined as follows: Note : \mathrm{Vi} denotes the internal variables The creep computation has as its only objective to supply the creep strain, which enters as an additional loading of the plasticity computation. The stresses computed during the solution of creep are neither stored in memory nor used for the plasticity computation. At creep/plasticity equilibrium, they are equal to the stresses coming from the plasticity computation. The internal variables of the creep computation are on the other hand retained from one iteration to the next, because the creep computation at iteration n requires knowledge of the internal variables at iteration n-1 . These variables also make it possible to compute, at each time step, the creep strain whose increment is used for the plasticity computation. The same is true of the internal variables of the plasticity model. 4.3 Treatment of the internal variables The simultaneous solution of the two models, creep and plasticity, requires a particular treatment of the internal variables, analogous to what is done in the THM environment (cf R7.01.10): the dimension of the array of internal variables is the sum of the numbers of variables of each model. The information required in order to recover these variables at each computation instant is transmitted to the lower-level routines. For the accumulation of two coupled mechanical laws, the total number of internal variables is stored in the behaviour map, as well as the name of the laws. The internal variables of the various laws follow one another in the array of internal variables: first those which concern creep, then those relating to plasticity. 4.4 Management of the constitutive behaviours and taking into account the subdivision of the time step The chaining of the constitutive laws requires computation of the creep strain increment from the internal variables of the model, which is then subtracted from the total strain increment before calling another law. The constitutive behaviours therefore cannot be permuted. The first law to be coupled must be a creep law of type GRANGER_FP ( Granger law) or GRANGER_FP_V ( Granger law with ageing) or GRANGER_FP_INDT ( Granger law independent of temperature). The order of the constitutive laws defined by the user must respect this logic. The second law must be a non-linear mechanical law, of type BETON_DOUBLE_DP, or more generally an elastic law ELAS, or an elastoplastic law . The number of laws of the coupling is limited to two, the first being a creep law, and failure to respect these modelling choices leads to a «Fatal» stop. The solution module of the coupled creep/plasticity constitutive behaviour is presented as a new law. At present, the creep law is not integrated into the automatic subdivision of the time step of Code_Aster , because of an explicit solution, unlike the plasticity laws. During the solution of the coupling, the plasticity law benefits from the automatic subdivision of the time step, according to the same conventions as the subdivision applied to the uncoupled plasticity laws (systematic subdivision, or only in the event of non-convergence, or no subdivision). 4.4.1 Convergence criterion The creep/plasticity chaining is carried out in a loop, in the coupling module, until convergence of the solution. When the creep strain increment and the plasticity strain increment are stable from one iteration to the next, the stresses coming from the creep computation are equal to the stresses coming from the plasticity computation. One could establish a convergence criterion in strain, but it is more logical that the convergence criterion be computed from the stresses, which constitute the output argument of the elementary computations at the Gauss points (together with the internal variables). This model is developed in 1D and 3D; it is elastoplastic and damageable, with isotropic hardening, and it is based on the Lemaître model. This behaviour is used for analyses predicting the load-bearing capacity of reinforced-concrete structures affected by corrosion in the case of unidimensional loading. It is implemented under the name CORR_ACIER in 3D and in 1D (for the elements BARRE and multifibre beams). It also works with the option DEBORST for plane stresses (shell elements); the equations are integrated numerically by an implicit scheme of M. Ortiz and J.C. Simo, with the plastic multiplier obtained by linearising the threshold function with respect to the internal variables and by imposing satisfaction of the criterion at convergence. 1 Introduction This document presents a constitutive law for steel subjected to corrosion in civil-engineering structures. This law was formulated on the basis of the Lemaître model (plasticity coupled with damage). Following tensile tests carried out on corroded bars, an influence of corrosion on the plastic strain at failure is observed (the plastic strain of the corroded bars decreases as the degree of corrosion increases). r7.01.21 Constitutive law (in 2D) for the steel–concrete bond: JOINT_BA r7.01.21 Constitutive law (in 2D) for the steel–concrete bond: JOINT_BA Summary: The constitutive law JOINT_BA describes the phenomenon of degradation and of failure of the bond between the steel bars and the concrete, in reinforced-concrete structures. This documentation presents the theoretical writing within the thermodynamic framework and the numerical integration of the law, as well as the parameters which govern the model. For its use, one will rely on the joint-type finite elements (see the document[R3.06.09]) already existing in the code. 1 Introduction The constitutive law JOINT_BA describes the phenomenon of degradation and of failure of the existing bond between the steel bars (smooth or ribbed) and the concrete surrounding them. A key point for the design of reinforced-concrete structures, the modelling of the steel–concrete bond has as its aim the representation as well as the simplification of this complex phenomenon of interaction between the two materials, which develops in the interface and which undergoes an increasing degradation when one exceeds certain strength thresholds, specific to each material. The structural models which do not take the effects of the bond into account are generally incapable of predicting the localisation of the cracks as well as the networks created. Moreover, the degradation of the stiffness of the bond increases the vibration period, reduces the energy-dissipation capacity and leads to a significant redistribution of the internal forces (according to Bertero , 1979, cf. ). The constitutive law JOINT_BA is described within the framework of the thermodynamics of irreversible processes: the writing and the use of a “ classical ” material model coupling cracking and friction makes it possible to integrate in a robust manner fine non-linear mechanisms concomitant with the particular description of the slip kinematics. This last point allows us not to resort to the classical modellings of ‘contact’ type very often used in this context despite the numerous sources of numerical instabilities. Thus, under monotonic loading the taking into account of the normal-force–shear coupling makes it possible to treat cases of strong multiaxial confinement; under cyclic loading, the hysteretic behaviour and the corresponding dissipations are expressed thanks to the coupling between the damage state and the kinematic hardening. The use of an implicit scheme makes it possible to obtain a robust implementation. The paragraph r7.01.21-breve-description describes in brief form the phenomenon of the steel–concrete bond. The paragraph r7.01.21-ecriture-theorique presents the thermodynamic writing of the constitutive law, whereas the paragraph r7.01.21-integration-numerique specifies the numerical-integration stage of the law. The parameters which govern the model and which can be obtained from the properties of the materials involved are described in the paragraph r7.01.21-parametres-loi. 2 Brief description of the steel–concrete bond Conceptually, the bond phenomenon corresponds to the physical interaction of two different materials, which occurs over an interface zone, allowing the transfer and the continuity of the forces and of the stresses between the two bodies in contact. In the case of reinforced-concrete structures, this phenomenon is also known as the «tension stiffness» which develops around a reinforcing element, partially or totally embedded in a volume of concrete. The tensile forces which appear inside the reinforcement are transformed into shear stresses on the surface, and are transmitted directly to the concrete in contact, which will finally balance them, and vice versa. The response of the assembly will depend on the capacity of the concrete to deform as much as the steel, since the steel will tend to slip inside the concrete surrounding it. The bond phenomenon corresponds to this capacity of the concrete to deform and to degrade locally by creating a kind of layer, or envelope, around the reinforcement, whose kinematic and material properties differ from those of the rest of the concrete or of the reinforcement used. The phenomenon can be decomposed into three well-defined mechanisms: - a bond of chemical origin, - a friction mechanism between two rough surfaces (steel–concrete or concrete–concrete), - a mechanical action created by the presence of the ribs of the steel bar on the neighbouring concrete. From this decomposition, one can deduce clearly that for a smooth bar, the predominant mechanism is the friction between the two materials, whereas for a ribbed bar (commonly called in French «armature HA: Haute Adhérence»), the dominant mechanism is the mechanical interaction between surfaces. When the reinforcement is constituted by strands with steel cables, it is possible to control or to combine the various mechanisms since they are a direct function of the surface of the cables. The bond will undergo a different degradation according to the type of loading applied, whether monotonic or cyclic. Moreover, among the most important parameters which influence the behaviour of the bond, one may cite: 1. the characteristics of the loading, 2. the geometric characteristics of the steel bar, 3. the spacing between active bars, 4. the characteristics of the concrete, 5. the confinement by passive reinforcement, 6. the lateral pressure. When studying a cylindrical bar embedded in an infinite medium, one can identify the surface of discontinuity where one will place the effects of the bond, which develops in a certain zone of cracked and crushed concrete around the steel bar. At a given moment, this surface will correspond to the cylindrical crack created during the coalescence of the shear cracks. Looking at the crack network, one may suppose that, under ideal conditions, the cracking plane is always perpendicular (normal direction) to the surface of the bar and parallel (tangential direction) to its longitudinal axis (see r7.01.21-fig-liaison-elements-finis). This allows us to project the components of the displacement onto the normal and tangential direction of the cracking plane, and consequently to obtain the corresponding strains and stresses. Real description of the bond phenomenon and finite-element simplification: coordinates in the local frame of the interface element used as the support of the law JOINT_BA 3 Theoretical formulation The formulation presented here has been developed within the framework of the thermodynamics of irreversible processes; it gives the constitutive relation between the normal force, the shear stress and the slip, taking into account the influence of the cracking of the concrete, the friction and the various couplings in the phenomenon. For this, the constitutive relations which link the stress tensor and the strain tensor must include: - the cracking of the interface material by shear - the inelastic strains due to the slip - the hysteretic behaviour due to the friction - the coupling between the tangential response and the normal stresses 3.1 Presentation of the model One places oneself within the framework of a plane formulation in 2D, in the local frame defined in r7.01.21-fig-liaison-elements-finis. The stress tensors \sigma and the strain tensors \varepsilon are written: \begin{aligned} \varepsilon =\begin{pmatrix}{\varepsilon}_{N}& {\varepsilon}_{\tau}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\tau}& 0\end{pmatrix} et :math: \sigma =\begin{pmatrix}{\sigma}_{N}& {\sigma}_{\tau}\\ {\sigma}_{\tau}& 0\end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} where {\sigma}_{N} is the normal stress and {\sigma}_{\tau} is the tangential stress of the interface element; {\varepsilon}_{N} corresponds to the normal strain and {\varepsilon}_{\tau} to the tangential strain. The normal strain in the direction tangential to the interface is considered to be zero. This mode of strain for a bond element is one of zero strain energy. The normal and tangential behaviours being considered as decoupled at the level of the state, the thermodynamic potential obtained from the Helmholtz free energy is expressed in the following way: \begin{array}{c}\rho \cdot \psi =\frac{1}{2}[{\langle {\varepsilon}_{N}\rangle }_{-}E{\langle {\varepsilon}_{N}\rangle }_{-}+{\langle {\varepsilon}_{N}\rangle }_{+}E\cdot (1-{D}_{N}){\langle {\varepsilon}_{N}\rangle }_{+}\\ +{\varepsilon}_{T}G(1-{D}_{T}){\varepsilon}_{T}+({\varepsilon}_{T}-{\varepsilon}_{T}^{f})G\cdot {D}_{T}({\varepsilon}_{T}-{\varepsilon}_{T}^{f})+\gamma {\alpha}^{2}]+H(z)\end{array} where \rho is the density, E is Young's modulus, {D}_{N} is the normal-damage internal variable and {D}_{T} the tangential-damage internal variable, the two being linked to cracking and lying between 0 and 1. G is the stiffness or shear modulus, {\varepsilon}_{T}^{f} is the irreversible strain induced by slip with friction of the cracks, \alpha is the kinematic-hardening internal variable, \gamma is a material parameter and z , the pseudo «isotropic hardening» variable by damage, with its consolidation function H(z) . {\langle \rangle }_{-} and {\langle \rangle }_{+} define respectively the positive and negative parts of the tensor considered. One may remark in the equation that in the normal direction, the damage will be activated upon the appearance of the positive strains produced by tensile forces, whereas if the strains are negative because of the effects of compression, the behaviour will remain elastic. As regards the tangential part of the behaviour, one can recognise a classical elasticity–damage coupling as well as a new term making it possible to associate, with the damageable-elasticity state, a state of slip with friction. The coupling between slip and cracking is possible thanks to the presence of the damage variable as a multiplier in the second term of the right-hand side of the equation . The state laws are obtained classically by derivation of the thermodynamic potential, and thus make it possible to define the associated thermodynamic variables. The normal stress is expressed as: {\sigma}_{N}=\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}_{N}}= \left\{ \begin{array}{ccc}E\cdot {\varepsilon}_{N}& \text{si}& {\varepsilon}_{N}\le 0\\ & & \\ (1-{D}_{N})\cdot E\cdot {\varepsilon}_{N}& \text{si}& {\varepsilon}_{N}>0\end{array}\right. and the total tangential stress as: {\sigma}_{T}=\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}_{T}}=G(1-{D}_{T}){\varepsilon}_{T}+G\cdot {D}_{T}({\varepsilon}_{T}-{\varepsilon}_{T}^{f}) One can also define the tangential stress due to slip with friction (strain {\varepsilon}_{\tau}^{s} ): {\sigma}_{T}^{f}=-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}_{T}^{f}}=G\cdot {D}_{T}({\varepsilon}_{T}-{\varepsilon}_{T}^{f}) Note: Such a formulation departs considerably from a classical formulation of plasticity–damage coupling. The assumption leading to the introduction of the damage into the stress by slip is based on an experimental observation, which is that all the inelastic phenomena in a brittle material come from the growth of the cracks. The rate of energy restored by damage–friction can be written as: -\mathrm{\Upsilon }=-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {D}_{T}}=\frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon}_{T}\cdot G\cdot {\varepsilon}_{T}-\frac{1}{2}({\varepsilon}_{T}-{\varepsilon}_{T}^{f})\cdot G\cdot ({\varepsilon}_{T}-{\varepsilon}_{T}^{f})=-({\mathrm{\Upsilon }}_{\mathrm{DT}}+{\mathrm{\Upsilon }}_{\text{fT}}) In this last expression, {\mathrm{\Upsilon }}_{\mathrm{DT}} corresponds to the rate of energy restored by damage and {\mathrm{\Upsilon }}_{\text{fT}} to the rate of energy restored by friction of the cracks. The state law of the kinematic hardening leads to the definition of the back stress: X=\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial \alpha }=\gamma \alpha Concerning the hardening law of the isotropic damage, it is expressed by: Z=\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial z}=H'(z) We must now set out in a more detailed way the evolution of the damage mechanism in the bond, in other words specify the expression of H(z) . For a small value of damage, the mechanism which predominates is the interaction of the concrete with the ribs of the steel bar, whereas for a much larger value, it is the friction between the concrete and the steel which prevails. During the evolution of the damage, 2 principal phases can be identified: 1. the first phase corresponds to a stable growth of transverse cracks linked to the presence of ribs on the steel (apparent positive hardening of the evolution law), 2. the second brings into play only the coalescence of these transverse cracks, leading one to consider only the friction mechanisms (negative hardening towards a residual friction stress). 3.2 Analysis of the damage in the tangential direction The evolution law of the damage is divided into three stages: - region of perfect bond, - region of transition from small strains to large slips, - region of maximum bond strength and degradation down to the ultimate residual strength. In order to identify these regions, one establishes two thresholds: 1. the perfect-bond threshold {\varepsilon}_{T}^{1} , 2. the continuity threshold before coalescence of the cracks {\varepsilon}_{T}^{2} . Thus, taking up again the expressions linked to the damage, namely that of the energy-restitution rate and that of the internal variable associated with the isotropic hardening , one may note: 1. a true separation between the damage and the friction of the cracks (which makes it possible to modify only the evolution law of the damage without affecting the «friction» part), 2. the partition into two parts of the isotropic hardening, since one has two different stages in the damage. Moreover, Young's modulus is recovered from the elastic data supplied by the operator ELAS, which must always appear in the command file. These parameters, or the analytical expressions which make it possible to obtain them, have been obtained or determined from the numerical simulation of the experimental tests carried out by Eligehausen et al. , 1983, Cf . The carrying out of multiple simulations has made it possible to determine a relation between the geometric and material characteristics of the materials in question (steel and concrete) and the parameters which govern the interface model. 5.1 The initial parameters 5.1.1 The parameter « hpen » The joint element operating on the notion of a displacement jump, it is necessary to introduce a characteristic dimension of the degraded interface zone making it possible to define the notion of strain in the interface. To this end the principle of penetration between surfaces has been introduced: the parameter « \mathit{hpen} » makes it possible to define this zone surrounding the steel bar. This parameter corresponds to the maximum possible penetration, which depends on the thickness of the compressed – crushed concrete. At the same time, « \mathit{hpen} » governs the energy dissipation in the element as well as the kinematics of the slip. In order to give the user a reference for the choice of this parameter, one proposes to compute it from the diameter of the bar {d}_{b} and the relative area of the ribs {\alpha}_{\text{sR}} defined by: {\alpha}_{\text{sR}}=\frac{k\cdot {F}_{R}\cdot \sin\mathrm{\beta }}{\pi \cdot {d}_{b}\cdot c} where k is the number of ribs on the perimeter; {F}_{R} the transverse area of a rib; \mathrm{\beta } is the angle between the rib and the longitudinal axis of the steel bar; and c is the distance between ribs measured centre to centre. Finally, « \mathit{hpen} » will be computed with the expression: {h}_{\text{pen}}={d}_{b}\cdot {\alpha}_{\text{sR}} According to Eligehausen et al. , the reinforcement commonly used in the United States has values of {\alpha}_{\text{sR}} between 0.05 and 0.08 . For the smooth bars, given that one needs a small value of « hpen », one proposes values of {\alpha}_{\text{sR}} between 0.005 and 0.02 . The following table gives the values of « \mathit{hpen} » as a function of the diameter of the bar: | Diameter ( \mathit{mm} ) | Relative area | \mathit{Hpen} ( \mathit{mm} ) | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 8 | 0.01 | (0.08) 0.1 | Smooth commercial bar | | 8 | 0.08 | 0.64 | Ribbed commercial bar | | 20 | 0.08 | 1.50 | Ribbed commercial bar | | 25 | 0.08 | 2.00 | Ribbed commercial bar | | 32 | 0.08 | 2.54 | Ribbed commercial bar | The unit of «hpen» must of course correspond to the unit used for the mesh. 5.1.2 The parameter G or stiffness modulus of the bond Generally, because of the difficulty of measuring the shear strains, the stiffness modulus of a material is computed from Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, common parameters obtained experimentally. However, for our case, the interface is a pseudo-material whose characteristics must depend on the properties corresponding to the materials in contact, steel and concrete. Given that the material which one expects to damage is the concrete, one proposes to use initially for the bond the same value of G as for the concrete under study, but it may be higher, up to a value similar to the value of Young's modulus E , when one increases the value of «hpen». In the case of reinforcement with stiffnesses higher than those of the usual commercial bars (because of a special layout or geometry of the ribs), one can make a correction of the chosen value, by multiplying the stiffness modulus by a correction coefficient computed from the relative areas of the commercial bars, with the expression: {C}_{\text{arm}}=\frac{({\alpha}_{\text{SR}})\text{barre}}{({\alpha}_{\text{SR}}){\text{barre}}_{\text{comm}}} Then, the stiffness modulus of the bond G will be: {G}_{\text{liai}}={C}_{\text{arm}}\cdot {G}_{\text{beton}} In the last expressions, {G}_{\text{lia}} is the stiffness modulus of the bond; {G}_{\text{beton}} is the stiffness modulus of the concrete; {C}_{\text{arm}} is the correction coefficient by reinforcement; ({\alpha}_{\text{SR}})\text{barre} , relative area of the ribs of the bar concerned; and ({\alpha}_{\text{SR}}){\text{barre}}_{\text{com}} , relative area of the ribs of the commercial bar of the same diameter (preferably, 0.08 ). 5.2 The damage parameters 5.2.1 The elastic strain limit {\varepsilon}_{T}^{1} or perfect-bond threshold In order to define the perfect-bond threshold, one considers that the shear damage must be initiated when a certain strain threshold is exceeded. Consequently, one proposes to adopt the limit tensile strains of the concrete, that is, between 1\times {10}^{-4} and 0.5\times {10}^{-3} , which correspond to the shear stresses between 0.5 and 4\mathit{MPa} in perfect bond. 5.2.2 The damage parameter {A}_{\mathrm{1DT}} for the passage from small strains to large slips In this region, the evolution law of the damage is expressed in terms of strains and its construction depends on the elastic slope defined for the linear behaviour (shear stress versus strain) in the region of perfect bond: this parameter controls the value of the stress with respect to the slip in the passage from small strains to large slips. The determination of the value of this parameter is a key and delicate point of the model, since the evolution of the damage must take place with certain conditions noted by several researchers; for example: - the strength of the bond is directly proportional to the compressive strength of the concrete. However, as one increases the strength of the concrete, the behaviour becomes stiffer, leading to the brittle failure of the bond, - the particular stiffness of the reinforcement, which is linked to the diameter and to the quantity of ribs on the surface, must increase the strength of the bond, - the relation between the elasticity moduli of the two materials concerned must directly govern the kinematics of the bond. From the numerical simulations which one has carried out, one has observed that this value lies between a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 5, and that it will have to be adjusted as a function of the reference test chosen. Optionally, one proposes an expression which makes it possible to adopt an initial value and which depends on the characteristics specific to the materials: {A}_{{1}_{\mathit{DT}}}=\frac{1}{(1+{\alpha}_{\text{SR}})}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{f'c}{30}}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{E}_{a}}{{E}_{b}}} In the last expression, {E}_{b} will be computed with the expression supplied in section A.2.1,2 of BAEL'91: {E}_{b}=11000\times {(f'c)}^{1/3} In the last two expressions, one has: 1. f'c , compressive strength of the concrete in \mathit{MPa} ; 2. {E}_{a} , elasticity modulus of the steel, in \mathit{MPa} ; 3. {E}_{b} , elasticity modulus of the concrete, in \mathit{MPa} ; 4. {\alpha}_{\text{sR}} , relative area of the ribs of the bar concerned. The r7.01.21-fig-croissance-resistance-liaison gives a graphical comparison of it. Comparison of {A}_{\text{1DT}} : growth of the strength of the bond 5.2.3 The damage parameter {B}_{\mathrm{1DT}} This parameter has as its aim to soften the shape of the behaviour curve, as well as to facilitate the transition from the elastic slope towards the non-linear region. It may have a value lying between 0.1 and 0.5 (never greater than 0.5 since that is the equivalent of the square root of the formula). One may advise adopting the value 0.3 for ordinary computations. (See r7.01.21-fig-modification-courbure). Comparison of {B}_{\text{1DT}} : modification of the curvature 5.2.4 The strain limit {\varepsilon}_{T}^{2} or threshold of the large slips According to several authors, the large slips are overall greater than 1\mathit{mm} of displacement, but this is an indicator which depends on the shape and the dimensions of the specimens tested; therefore, one proposes that this strain never exceed 1.00 (dimensionless value). In a more precise way, one proposes to apply the following expression: {\varepsilon}_{T}^{2}=\frac{1}{{({h}_{\mathrm{pen}})}^{2}}\cdot (1-\frac{{({A}_{\mathrm{1DT}})}^{n}}{C+{({A}_{\mathrm{1DT}})}^{n}})=\frac{1}{{({h}_{\mathrm{pen}})}^{2}}\cdot (1-\frac{{({A}_{\mathrm{1DT}})}^{4}}{9+{({A}_{\mathrm{1DT}})}^{4}})\le 1.0 In this expression, one has applied a sigmoid function whose coefficients C and n make it possible to adjust the kinematic effect of {A}_{\mathrm{1DT}} on the slip, that is, when the bond becomes more resistant because of an increase in stiffness, the slip is reduced gradually. One has adopted the values 9.0 and 4.0 respectively, but they are always optional. The choice of the value of the strain limit {\varepsilon}_{T}^{2} is very important because it introduces a greater or lesser brittleness of the response by translation of the threshold of passage from small strains to large slips. This brittleness is linked to the stiffness of the concrete by way of the parameter {A}_{\mathrm{1DT}} . It must be noted that the following parameters which govern the damage must also be adjusted at the local level in order to ensure the correct continuity of the shear behaviour of the bond and thus to be able to obtain the desired or expected response of a real steel – bond – concrete system. 5.2.5 The damage parameter {A}_{\mathrm{2DT}} The damage, such as it has been conceived in the model, obeys two evolution laws which are expressed with the aid of a single classical scalar variable which will ensure the consistency of the damage. The parameters of each of the 2 laws are independent and numerically stable, but they are liable to generate serious errors in the continuity of the behaviour if one does not pay attention to the shape of the local stress–strain curve: see the case of the curve shown in the graph of r7.01.21-fig-a-endommagement-rupture-liaison, with a value {A}_{\text{2DT}}=1\times {10}^{-3}{\mathit{MPa}}^{-1} . We are not able to propose an analytical relation for the choice of this parameter, but the experience acquired allows us to state that the value of this parameter must lie between 1\times {10}^{-3} and 9\times {10}^{-2}{\mathit{MPa}}^{-1} approximately. Comparison of {A}_{\text{2DT}} : damage and failure of the bond 5.2.6 The damage parameter {B}_{\mathrm{2DT}} This parameter, which completes the damage-evolution law in large slips, controls not only the growth of the strength of the bond or the shape of the behaviour curve at the peak and in the post-peak region, but also the kinematics of the response, which implies the determination of the slip for the maximum shear stress as well as the amplitude of the curve at the peak of the behaviour. Thus, although the values of the damage parameters {A}_{\text{2DT}} and {B}_{\text{2DT}} will have to be adjusted at the same time when one constructs the behaviour curve of the bond in order to respect the continuity of the shape, one can say that the value of {B}_{\text{2DT}} is inversely proportional to the slip amplitude at the peak, that is, a value of 0.8 allows wider large slips at the peak than a value of 1.2 , for example. For practical cases, one recommends using a value lying between 0.8 and 1.1 in order to reproduce a consistent behaviour curve (See r7.01.21-fig-b-endommagement-rupture-liaison). Comparison of {B}_{\text{2DT}} : damage and failure of the bond 5.3 The damage parameters in the normal direction 5.3.1 The strain limit {\varepsilon}_{N}^{1} or threshold of the large displacements In a way similar to the elastic behaviour in the tangential direction, one considers that the decohesion must be initiated when a certain strain threshold is exceeded. We propose to adopt a value between {10}^{-4} and {10}^{-3} . 5.3.2 The damage parameter {A}_{\mathit{DN}} This parameter essentially controls the slope of degradation of the normal stress with respect to the strain due to the opening of the interface. We propose to use a minimum value of 1\times {10}^{-1}{\mathit{MPa}}^{-1} , which corresponds to a degradation similar to that of the concrete. Nevertheless, if one wishes to have an even more brittle behaviour of the bond, it suffices to increase this value. 5.3.3 The damage parameter {B}_{\mathit{DN}} In combination with the previous parameter, this parameter controls the damage of the bond, in particular the shape of the behaviour curve in the post-peak phase. We propose to use a value equal to 1, or 1,2 for more pronounced curves. Behaviour of the bond in the normal direction during the opening of the interface (normal tension on the bond) 5.4 The friction parameters 5.4.1 The material parameter \gamma of crack friction One of the assets of the model proposed here is that it is capable of taking into account the effects of the friction of the cracks, which, in the case of monotonic loading, is manifested by a positive contribution to the shear strength of the bond; moreover, in the cases of cyclic loadings, it is obvious that the shape of the hysteresis loops depends directly on the choice of the value of this material parameter. However, the corresponding values have not been calibrated, since we have not yet simulated tests with cyclic loadings in order to validate them. Temporarily, one proposes to use values lower than 10\mathit{MPa} , with a maximum value of \alpha equal to 1.0{\mathit{MPa}}^{-1} . 5.4.2 The material parameter \alpha of kinematic hardening On [r7.01.21-fig-effets-boucles-hysteresis-cyclique], one can see that the decrease in the value of \alpha increases the hysteretic dissipation, but also the shear strength and the residual pseudo-plastic strain. This is very important for the cyclic modelling of the bond since, in reality, when one exceeds the peak of maximum strength, one remarks that at the moment of unloading there is no longer any elastic contribution of the slip, that is to say that the residual pseudo-plastic strain corresponds exactly to the total slip reached. In other words, once all the cracks in the potential failure layer, longitudinal and tangential to the steel bar, have been connected, the only strength which will prevent the displacement of the reinforcement is the friction strength of the bond, produced by the contact and the interlocking of the asperities between the concrete–concrete surfaces. As previously, our experience is limited: one proposes to use a maximum value of 0.1{\mathit{MPa}}^{-1} which gives correct results for applications under monotonic loading, and which seems suitable for cyclic loadings. Comparison of \alpha : effects on the hysteresis loops under cyclic loading 5.4.3 The confinement-influence parameter c In our model, the influence of the confinement has been taken into account thanks to the application of this parameter, which controls these effects on the bond, and which is manifested by an increase in the maximum shear stress as well as by the increase in the maximum displacement at the peak when the confinement increases. For the calibration, we have carried out simulations with confinements of 0 , 5 , 10 and 15\mathit{MPa} , always using a value of 1.0 for this parameter. One has remarked that if one wishes to produce a kinematic translation of the slip caused by the confinement, it suffices to adopt a value of 1.2 or 1.5 (dimensionless). Optionally, it is advised to keep the value of 1.0 for ordinary computations. 5.5 Summary of the parameters In order to facilitate the use of the law, the following table presents a synthesis of the set of parameters of the constitutive model. One recalls that the values or the expressions proposed have only an indicative value, and that an arbitrary combination may give inaccurate and unexpected results with respect to the expected behaviour of the bond; r7.01.22 Viscoplastic constitutive law VISC_DRUC_PRAG r7.01.22 Viscoplastic constitutive law VISC_DRUC_PRAG Summary: This document describes the viscoplastic constitutive law VISC_DRUC_PRAG based on the elastoplastic Drucker–Prager model and taking viscosity into account according to a power law of Perzyna type. Its field of application is argillite, which is the host rock of the storage concept. The proposed model comprises a single viscoplastic mechanism. The criterion hardens with the cumulative viscoplastic strain, passing through three thresholds: elastic, peak and ultimate. The flow is non-associated, the flow potential being a Drucker–Prager potential hardening according to three levels: elastic, peak and ultimate. Between the thresholds, the hardenings are linear. This law can be used in a purely mechanical modelling just as it can be used in a THM modelling. It is available in 3D, plane strain and axisymmetric conditions. It is integrated by the solution of a single non-linear scalar equation. > Contents 1 Notation \sigma denotes the effective stress tensor in small perturbations, written in the form of the following pressure | 2 Introduction This document describes the integration of the viscoplastic constitutive law VISC_DRUC_PRAG in Code_Aster. This law comprises a single viscoplastic mechanism. The viscoplastic criterion hardens with the cumulative deviatoric viscoplastic strain, passing through three thresholds: elastic for a zero viscoplastic strain, a so-called peak threshold for a so-called peak viscoplastic strain (a parameter of the model) and an ultimate threshold for a so-called ultimate viscoplastic strain (a parameter of the model). Between the thresholds, the hardening functions are linear. In Code_Aster there exists another law based on the Drucker–Prager model and used in elastoplasticity in an associated form under the name DRUCK_PRAGER or non-associated under the name DRUCK_PRAG_N_A (see R7.01.16). 3 Formulation of the viscoplastic model VISC_DRUC_PRAG This model is based on a viscoplastic formulation of Drucker–Prager type, where the loading surface f(\sigma ,p) is defined by: f=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}{s}_{\mathrm{II}}+\alpha (p){I}_{1}-R(p) \alpha (p) and R(p) are functions of the cumulative deviatoric viscoplastic strain p , A viscoplastic flow potential g(\sigma ,p) is introduced: g=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}{s}_{\text{II}}+\beta (p){I}_{1} For the evolution of the criterion f and of the potential g three distinct thresholds are distinguished, corresponding to three values of the hardening variable: an elastic threshold, a peak threshold and an ultimate threshold. Between these thresholds, the hardening is linear. Between the elastic threshold and the peak threshold, the hardening is positive; after the peak the hardening is negative and becomes constant after the ultimate threshold. r7.01.23 Cyclic constitutive law of HUJEUX for soils r7.01.23 Cyclic constitutive law of HUJEUX for soils Summary: The constitutive model known as “Hujeux”, designed at the MSSMat laboratory of the ECP , is one of the cyclic elastoplastic models of soil mechanics (granular geomaterials: sandy clays, normally consolidated or over-consolidated, gravels…) best suited to simulations of geotechnical structures under earthquake loading. It has moreover been used for many years, so that its parameterisation is well mastered. This multi-mechanism model (spherical — for a consolidation path — and deviatoric) with memory variables is characterised by eight hardening loading surfaces, defined for monotonic paths and for cyclic paths. The mechanisms are defined by fixed planes, which induces an orthotropy of the soil behaviour. Inside these reversibility surfaces, the material is non-linear elastic. The hardening is governed by several variables and the normal flow rule is adopted for the consolidation mechanisms, whereas the flow rule for the deviatoric mechanisms is non-associated, following the Roscoe dilatancy rule. As with other soil constitutive models, the hardening is positive in the pre-peak phase and negative in the post-peak phase, which corresponds to the effect of dilatancy; these effects induce the “liquefaction” behaviour of the soil. The plastic strain tensor results from the accumulation of the contributions of the various active mechanisms. The volumetric plastic strain couples the mechanisms. The equations of the model are described, then its parameterisation, then its numerical integration according to a general implicit Newton scheme. Users have the possibility of accessing three implicit integration schemes for the Hujeux model: 'SPECIFIQUE', 'SEMI_EXPLICITE' and 'BASCULE_EXPLICITE', the last two being variants of the 'SPECIFIQUE' scheme introduced in order to provide more flexibility for the local integration of the behaviour during dynamic studies. 1 Theoretical formulation 1.1 Hujeux constitutive relation The model described here is the model known as Hujeux. The model was developed by the École Centrale Paris (LMSSMat laboratory) in the 1980s in order to represent the rheology of soils for alternating loadings, for example under earthquake. This constitutive relation of soil mechanics is a multi-mechanism model, characterised by twice four hardening loading surfaces: three linked to deviatoric mechanisms and one to a spherical consolidation mechanism, defined for monotonic paths and for cyclic paths. The deviatoric mechanisms are defined on three fixed planes, which induces an orthotropy of the soil behaviour. The spherical mechanisms reproduce the strong non-linearity of geomaterials on a consolidation path. Each of these planes, indexed by k , is defined by the basis vectors ({{e}_{i}}_{k},{{e}_{j}}_{k}) , taken from the orthonormal basis ({e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}) of three-dimensional space. The indices are denoted: {i}_{k}=1+\text{mod}(\text{k,}3) \text{ et } {j}_{k}=1+\text{mod}(\text{k+}1,3) Note: In a 2D plane-strain situation, the plane \text{k=}3 corresponds to the plane ({\mathrm{e}}_{1},{\mathrm{e}}_{2}) of the model. The model comprises a non-linear elasticity controlled by the Young's modulus depending on the confining pressure. A three-dimensional limit criterion close to that of Mohr–Coulomb is considered in order to take into account the influence of the effective mean stress on the stiffness of the soil and on the failure characteristics. The concept of critical state is also integrated into this model in order to represent the coupling between the deviatoric stresses and the volume variations and to formulate the isotropic hardening linked to the granular medium. A kinematic hardening is added in order to represent the cyclic behaviour of soils and is coupled to the density hardening of the soil. The Hujeux model is expressed in effective stresses — defined as the difference between the total stresses and the water pressure in the case of saturated soils — in the case of hydromechanical coupling: that is to say, one does not take into account the hydrostatic pressure of the fluid which may circulate in the pores, the latter being computed in the THM modellings. 1.1.1 Definition of the state variables and expression of the free energy 1.1.1.1 State variables The variables used to describe the state of the material point are the following: - \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} : strain tensor, - \boldsymbol{{\varepsilon}^{p}} : plastic strain tensor; one denotes in particular {\varepsilon}_{v}^{p}=\text{tr}{\varepsilon}^{p}=\boldsymbol{{\varepsilon}^{p}}.\boldsymbol{I} the volumetric plastic strain, \boldsymbol{\mathrm{I}} being the identity tensor, - {r}_{k}^{m} : the “mobilisation factors” of the deviatoric mechanisms on a monotonic path: this is a hardening in the pressure–shear plane, - {r}_{k}^{c} : the “mobilisation factors” of the cyclic deviatoric mechanisms: this is a mixed isotropic and kinematic hardening in the pressure–shear plane. - {r}_{4}^{m} : the mobilisation factor of the consolidation mechanism on a monotonic path: this is a hardening of the spherical consolidation mechanism (scalar), - {r}_{4}^{c} : the mobilisation factor of the consolidation mechanism on a cyclic path: this is a mixed isotropic and kinematic hardening (scalar), accompanied by a certain number of discontinuous history variables, described below. The various mechanisms of elastoplastic evolution involve hardening variables: the mobilisation factors associated with each of the mechanisms and the volumetric plastic strain {\varepsilon}_{v}^{p}=\text{tr}({\boldsymbol{\varepsilon^{p}}}) , common to all the mechanisms and coupling them. The latter modifies the loading surfaces even if they are not active, because of the hardening produced on the other activated loading surfaces: see [§ 1.1.2 and 1.1.3]. One denotes by \boldsymbol{\sigma} the (effective) stress tensor, the confining pressure being: p(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\frac{1}{3}\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) . By convention in code_aster, the case of compression corresponds to negative stresses (and strains). For each plastic mechanism in the plane k , one denotes by: {\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{(k)}={\boldsymbol{P}}_{(k)}\cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot {\boldsymbol{P}}_{(k)} the stresses in the plane k , where {\boldsymbol{P}}_{(k)} denotes the (symmetric) tensor of projection onto the basis plane ({e}_{{i}_{k}},{e}_{{j}_{k}}) , of normal {e}_{k} : {\boldsymbol{P}}_{(k)}={e}_{{i}_{k}}\otimes {e}_{{j}_{k}}+{e}_{{j}_{k}}\otimes {e}_{{i}_{k}} with {i}_{k}=1+\text{mod}(k,3) and {j}_{k}=1+\text{mod}(k+1,3) , that is: {\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{(k)}={\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{{i}_{k}{i}_{k}}.{e}_{{i}_{k}}\otimes {e}_{{i}_{k}}+{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{{j}_{k}{j}_{k}}.{e}_{{j}_{k}}\otimes {e}_{{j}_{k}}+{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{{i}_{k}{j}_{k}}.{e}_{{i}_{k}}{\otimes}_{s}{e}_{{j}_{k}} then the confining pressure in the plane k : {p}_{k}({\boldsymbol{\sigma}})=\frac{1}{2}\text{tr}({\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{(k)}) One also defines the deviatoric stress tensor {\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)} in the plane k , with the aid of the second-order identity tensor in the plane: {\boldsymbol{I}}_{(k)}={\delta}_{{i}_{k}{j}_{k}}{e}_{{i}_{k}}\otimes {e}_{{j}_{k}} : {\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})={\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{(k)}-{p}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}).{\boldsymbol{I}}_{(k)} One does indeed have \mathrm{tr}({\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)})=0 . Finally, one denotes the (von Mises) norm of the deviatoric stress tensor {\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)} : {q}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})={\parallel{\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\parallel}_{\text{VM}}^{\text{2D}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)\alpha \beta }.{\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)}^{\alpha \beta }} Moreover, several memory variables of the irreversible history retain, during certain phases of the evolution, the values of the state variables at the beginning of these phases, and govern the subsequent evolutions, recording the value of this variable at the beginning of the path on which a cyclic mechanism is triggered: - {p}_{H} : discontinuous scalar memory variable, recording the value of the confining pressure p(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) , - {\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{vH}}^{p} : discontinuous scalar memory variable, recording the value of the volumetric plastic strain, - {p}_{\text{kH}} : discontinuous scalar memory variable, recording the value of the “confining pressure of the plane k ” {p}_{k} , - {\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)H} : discontinuous tensorial memory variable, recording the value of the stress deviators {\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)H}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) in each plane k , whose expression is given in [eq 1.1.1-5], - {\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)H}^{c} : discontinuous tensorial memory variable, recording the value of the “modified” stress deviators {\boldsymbol{S}}_{(k)}^{c}(\boldsymbol{\sigma} ,{\varepsilon}_{v}^{p}{\text{,r}}_{k}^{c}) in each deviatoric plane k , whose expression is given in [eq 1.1.2-12]. Note: The formulation of the Hujeux model by orthogonal planes does not make it possible to represent axisymmetric states correctly; cf. . 1.1.1.2 Free energy One denotes the free energy by the sum of an elastic contribution and a hardening contribution: \begin{array}{}F(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} (\overrightarrow{u}),{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{p}},{r}_{k}^{K})={F}_{\text{él}}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} (\overrightarrow{u}),{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{p}})+{H}_{\text{écr}}({\varepsilon}_{v}^{p},{r}_{k}^{K})\end{array} for K=m,c ; \text{k=}1,...,4 . The thermodynamic dissipation is obtained by difference from the density of strain power, this in an isothermal process: D=\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}(\dot{\overrightarrow{u}})-\dot{F}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}(\overrightarrow{u}),{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{p}},{r}_{k}^{K})=\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot{\dot{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{p}}-{\dot{H}}_{\text{écr}}({\varepsilon}_{v}^{p},{r}_{k}^{K}) In so far as one does not solve the thermal coupling, one cannot differentiate the density of dissipated power from the rate of hardening energy, corresponding to a stored-energy term. However \boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot {\dot{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{p}} is not necessarily positive, unlike D . As will be seen below, the elastic part of the Hujeux law is non-linear: one cannot easily extract the expression of the potential {F}_{\text{él}}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} (\overrightarrow{u}),{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{p}}) . As the Hujeux constitutive law possesses a particular non-linear elasticity, cf. For a given loading increment and a given set of variables (initial displacement field, stress and internal variable), one solves the discretised global system ([eq 2.2.2.2-1] of ) which seeks to satisfy the equilibrium equations. code_aster uses a Newton method , initiated by a prediction step (Euler trial) which supplies an estimate \Delta {\boldsymbol{U}}_{i}^{0} of the displacement increment, whence the prediction '\boldsymbol{U}_{i}^{0}={\boldsymbol{U}}_{i-1}+\Delta {\boldsymbol{U}}_{i}^{0} , followed by correction iterations n=1,\mathrm{...} , which give corrections \delta {\boldsymbol{U}}_{i}^{n+1} of the displacement increment, whence the update {\boldsymbol{U}}_{i}^{\text{n+}1}={\boldsymbol{U}}_{i}^{n}+\delta {\boldsymbol{U}}_{i}^{\text{n+}1} , which must converge towards the solution {\boldsymbol{U}}_{i}={\boldsymbol{U}}^{+} . The option FULL_MECA moreover computes the tangent operator {\boldsymbol{K}}_{i}^{n} , at the global correction iteration n (on request via the command STAT_NON_LINE, factor keyword NEWTON, keyword MATRICE='TANGENTE' and REAC_ITER), from the stresses {\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{i}^{n} and from the tangent matrix of the local problem discretised in time: {{\boldsymbol{K}}_{i}^{n}=\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{R}}{\partial \boldsymbol{U}}\rvert }_{({\boldsymbol{U}}_{i}^{n})} The solution of these global systems of equilibrium equations gives us increments \Delta {\boldsymbol{U}}_{i}^{n} , therefore strain increments \Delta {\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_{i}^{n} . One therefore seeks locally (at each Gauss point) the increment of the stresses and of the internal variables corresponding to \Delta \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} and which satisfy the constitutive law. The evolution of the stresses and of the internal variables is obtained by solution of a system of differential equations, by local integration, under the initial conditions at the beginning of the time step, described in [§ 2.2]. The multi-mechanism elastoplastic constitutive equations presented in [§ 1] do not make it possible to demonstrate by a simple analysis the uniqueness of the solution of the structural equilibrium problem, discretised in time. The integration scheme must have a certain influence on the computed solutions. 2.2 General scheme of local integration The local integration schemes chosen for the implementation of the Hujeux law in code_aster are fully implicit, formulated on the incremental problem, for reasons of computational accuracy. They use an elastic prediction then correction iterations. Their aim is to produce, a strain increment \Delta \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} being supplied, the value of the stresses and internal variables at the time instant {t}_{i}{\text{=t}}^{-}+\Delta t . [fig. 2.2-a] presents the general organisation common to the local integration algorithms. Note: The evolutions of the computed quantities of the Hujeux model through an implicit integration are reputed to be sensitive to perturbations of the data of the integration algorithm (for example according to the choice of the computing platform or of the choice of spatial discretisation…). This is why various provisions have been taken in order to limit this sensitivity: see below the description of the tolerances introduced on the increments. One must note that, because of the multi-mechanism character with memory variables of the Hujeux model, the effective activation of the mechanisms not being a differentiable process, the rate formulation does not constitute the limit of the incremental formulation in time. code_aster does not propose an explicit integration for this model, cf. R5.03.14, although this method is used in the literature, cf. . The available implicit integration algorithms are 3 in number and are distinguished according to the following terms: - ALGO_INTE = 'SPECIFIQUE', this is the 1st implicit integration scheme developed in code_aster. It is the most robust integration scheme, because it carries out for the user the local subdivisions necessary in order to ensure as far as possible a convergence of the integration scheme. - ALGO_INTE='SEMI_EXPLICITE', this consists in relying on the integration strategy of the 'SPECIFIQUE' scheme but in accepting, during the iterations of the global Newton scheme, Gauss points that have not reached the local convergence criterion imposed by the user. Nevertheless, the global convergence is accepted only when the local integration is ensured for the whole set of Gauss points. - ALGO_INTE="BASCULE_EXPLICIT", this consists in this case in accepting the local non-convergence of the behaviour if the global Newton has converged. This strategy has been implemented for the purpose of speeding up the computation in dynamics but does not prove worthwhile for highly non-linear modellings. The process of local subdivision of the time step is available in order to reduce significantly the possible situations of non-convergence, and to save correction iterations. It consists in solving the local behaviour on linear subdivisions of the strain increment \Delta \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} proposed by the global solution. The local subdivision can be activated in the non-linear mechanics operator of code_aster (factor keyword COMPORTEMENT and keyword ITER_INTE_PAS, cf. U4.51.11. 2.2.1 Prediction phase One begins by establishing the elastic prediction {{\sigma}_{ij}^{+}}_{é} (approximate tangent elastic trial – Euler): {{\sigma}_{ij}^{+}}_{é}={\sigma}_{ij}^{-}+{C}_{\text{ijrs}}({\hat{p}}_{é}).\Delta {\varepsilon}_{\text{rs}} The tensor {C}_{\text{ijrs}}({\hat{p}}_{é}) , defined by [eq 1.1.1-11], is obtained from an expression discretised by an approximate scheme of the confining pressure: {\hat{p}}_{é}=\frac{1}{2}({p}^{-}{\text{+p}}_{é}^{+}){\text{=p}}^{-}+\frac{1}{2}{K}_{0}.{\lvert\frac{{p}^{-}}{{P}_{\text{réf}}}\rvert}^{n}.\text{tr}\Delta \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} This choice makes it possible to limit the risk of having a confining-pressure predictor producing stresses too far from the expected values, because of the exponential non-linear form of the elastic law [eq 1.1.1-11]. One begins with a first step of “re-prediction”. A re-subdivision of the strain increment \Delta \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} — additional to that possibly requested by the user via the keywords of the non-linear mechanics operator of code_aster — is introduced in such a way as to bound the following increments, associated with the prediction {\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{é} , by a simple homothety: \Delta {p}_{k}({\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{é})/{p}_{k}({\boldsymbol{\sigma}}^{-})\le 5\text{\%} \Delta {q}_{k}^{K}({\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{é})/{q}_{k}^{K}({\boldsymbol{\sigma}}^{-})\le 5\text{\%} \sum_{i,j}({\sigma}_{ij}^{\text{é}}-{\sigma}_{ij}^{-})/\sum_{i,j}{\sigma}_{ij}^{-}\le 50\text{\%} The purpose is to avoid possible excursions during the correction iterations towards loading paths that are too remote, which may lead to divergence (by leaving the convergence domain of the Newton algorithm). 2.2.1.1 Potentially activated plastic mechanisms {M}^{\text{pot}} The elastoplastic mechanisms {M}_{k}^{K} , for \text{k=}1,...,4 and K=m,c , are activated or deactivated according to the type of loading followed. A family of potentially active mechanisms is thus determined beforehand at the beginning of the current step from the state reached previously, and serves to compute the evolution actually followed. The initial choice of the potentially activated mechanisms at the start of the time step considered results from the converged mechanical state reached at the time instant {t}^{-} : the activation state of the various mechanisms (monotonic or cyclic) at the time instant {t}^{-} and the values of the variables {\boldsymbol{\sigma}}^{-} and {\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{-} . One denotes by {M}^{\text{pot}} the set of potentially activated plastic mechanisms cf. [fig. 2.2-b], and by {M}^{\mathrm{act}} the set of plastic mechanisms actually activated during the integration, cf. [fig. 2.2-c]. This definition makes it possible to reduce to the strict minimum the size of the system of local non-linear equations to be solved at each step. One uses the elastic prediction [eq 2.2.1-1] in order to establish a re-estimation of {M}^{\text{pot}} with the aid of the evolution \dot{{\mathrm{f}}_{k}^{K}} for \text{k=}1,...,4 and K=m,c , of the thresholds of the mechanisms and thus to define the situations of loading in the plastic regime or of unloading. One therefore initialises {M}^{\text{pot}}:={M}^{\text{act}}({t}^{-}) , and one records the history variables of the “parent” cyclic mechanisms {\alpha}_{H}^{-} , from the situation at the previous time instant {t}^{-} . One computes for all the mechanisms {M}_{k}^{K} two quantities helping the decision: {c}_{k}^{K}={\mathrm{f}}_{k,\boldsymbol{\sigma} }^{K}({\boldsymbol{\sigma}}^{-}+\Delta {\sigma}_{\text{élas}})\cdot{C}({\hat{p}}_{é}).\Delta \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \text{ et } {g}_{k}^{K}{\text{=f}}_{k}^{K}({\boldsymbol{\sigma}}^{-}+\Delta {\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{\text{élas}}) If it is a cyclic mechanism {M}_{k}^{c} then one also computes {c}_{k}^{m} for the associated monotonic mechanism {M}_{k}^{m} .
