represented by a tensor of the type: \boldsymbol{\sigma} =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{\sigma}_{xx}& {\sigma}_{xy}& {\sigma}_{xz}\\ {\sigma}_{xy}& {\sigma}_{yy}& {\sigma}_{yz}\\ {\sigma}_{xz}& {\sigma}_{yz}& {\sigma}_{zz}\end{array}\right] This symmetric tensor is diagonalisable, with {\sigma}_{1}\ge {\sigma}_{2}\ge {\sigma}_{3} the eigenvalues (or principal stresses) of \sigma such that: \boldsymbol{\sigma} =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{\sigma}_{1}& 0& 0\\ 0& {\sigma}_{2}& 0\\ 0& 0& {\sigma}_{3}\end{array}\right] The Mohr representation makes it possible to represent the action of this stress state on any facet of normal n rotating about the point M (Figure 1). Indeed, the stress vector acting on this facet is written: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{n}={\sigma}_{n}.n\\ \tau ={\sigma}_{n}-\left({\sigma}_{n}.n\right)n \end{array}\right. Decomposition of the stress vector acting on a facet of normal n The Mohr representation makes it possible to represent in one and the same diagram the components ({\sigma}_{n},\tau ) : \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{n}={\sigma}_{n}.n\\ \tau =\sqrt{\tau .\tau }\end{array}\right. This is illustrated in Figure 2. This representation leads to the very important result which one highlights by the following proposition: Proposition 1 Any stress state at a point M acting on a facet of arbitrary normal rotating about M coincides exactly , in the Mohr representation, with the whole of the green zone comprised between the three Mohr circles. One considers this result sufficiently well known that one need not explain it any further. It is very important because it defines the domain of physical validity for any stress state , and one will show that in the Hujeux law, this constraint is not respected in 3D! Domain of definition of an arbitrary stress state in the Mohr plane 8.2 Plasticity criterion of Mohr–Coulomb type Before coming to Hujeux, it is appropriate to explain the relation between the Mohr representation and a failure criterion of Mohr–Coulomb type. The expression of the Mohr–Coulomb criterion is the following: \underbrace{\frac{{\sigma}_{1}-{\sigma}_{3}}{2}}_{R}-\sin\left(\mathrm{\phi }\right)\underbrace{\frac{{\sigma}_{1}+{\sigma}_{3}}{2}}_{C}\le 0 with the principal stresses {\sigma}_{1}\ge {\sigma}_{2}\ge {\sigma}_{3} . Its representation in the Mohr plane is illustrated in Figure 3. The meaning of this criterion is to compare the stress state at the point M, represented by the circle of centre C=\frac{{\sigma}_{1}+{\sigma}_{3}}{2} and of radius R=\frac{{\sigma}_{1}-{\sigma}_{3}}{2} , with the failure line of angle \mathrm{\phi } . It is appropriate to note two important points: - The stress state at the point M is represented by the circle of centre C and of radius R in the Mohr plane, and not by a point, because this circle is the locus of the pairs ({\sigma}_{n},\tau ) for the whole set of planes of normals n\perp {n}_{2} rotating about M; - The tangency of the circle and of the failure line is obtained thanks to the term \sin\left(\mathrm{\phi }\right) , as one can deduce from a relatively simple geometric analysis. Representation of the Mohr–Coulomb criterion in the Mohr plane One summarises what has been established by this analysis by the following proposition: Proposition 2 In a criterion of Mohr–Coulomb type, one compares the stress state at the point M represented by a circle of centre C and of radius R in the Mohr plane with a failure line of angle \mathrm{\phi } . The mathematical expression of such a criterion is of the form: R-\sin\left(\mathrm{\phi }\right)C\le 0 . 8.3 Expression of the Hujeux plasticity criterion The Hujeux plasticity criterion is a criterion of Mohr–Coulomb type. One begins by decomposing the stress tensor by projection onto the three fixed planes of the Cartesian frame, proceeding as follows: {\boldsymbol{p}}_{\vec{{e}_{i}}}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} \right)=\boldsymbol{\sigma} -\boldsymbol{\sigma} .\left(\vec{{e}_{i}}\otimes \vec{{e}_{i}}\right)-\left(\vec{{e}_{i}}\otimes \vec{{e}_{i}}\right).\boldsymbol{\sigma} +{\sigma}_{ii}\vec{{e}_{i}}\otimes \vec{{e}_{i}} where {\boldsymbol{p}}_{\vec{{e}_{i}}}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} \right) is the projection of the tensor \boldsymbol{\sigma} onto the plane of normal {\vec{e}}_{i\in \lbrace x,y,z\rbrace } . Reciprocally, one will have the inverse of the projection operator: \sigma ={\boldsymbol{p}}_{\vec{{e}_{i}}}^{-1}\circ {\boldsymbol{p}}_{\vec{{e}_{i}}}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} \right)={\boldsymbol{p}}_{\vec{{e}_{i}}}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} \right)+{\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} .\vec{{e}_{i}}\right)}_{T}\otimes \vec{{e}_{i}}+\vec{{e}_{i}}\otimes {\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} .\vec{{e}_{i}}\right)}_{T}+{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{ii}\vec{{e}_{i}}\otimes \vec{{e}_{i}} {\boldsymbol{p}}_{\vec{{e}_{i}}}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} \right) is called the reduced tensor and may be expressed in each plane of the Cartesian frame according to the normal considered: | | {e}_{x} | {e}_{y} | {e}_{z} | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | {\boldsymbol{p}}_{\vec{{e}_{i}}}\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} \right) | \left[\begin{array}{cc}{\sigma}_{yy}& {\sigma}_{yz}\\ {\sigma}_{\mathit{zy}}& {\sigma}_{zz}\end{array}\right] | \left[\begin{array}{cc}{\sigma}_{xx}& {\sigma}_{xz}\\ {\sigma}_{\mathit{zx}}& {\sigma}_{zz}\end{array}\right] | \left[\begin{array}{cc}{\sigma}_{xx}& {\sigma}_{xy}\\ {\sigma}_{yx}& {\sigma}_{yy}\end{array}\right] | Representation of the reduced stress tensors in each orthotropic plane of the Cartesian frame Representation of the reduced stress tensors in the Mohr plane The Hujeux criterion is then written as follows: R-\sin(\mathrm{\phi })C\le 0 with: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}R=\sqrt{{\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{xx}-{\sigma}_{yy}}{2}\right)}^{2}+{\sigma}_{xy}^{2}}\\ C=rF\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{xx}+{\sigma}_{yy}}{2};{{\varepsilon}}_{v}^{p}\right)\frac{{\sigma}_{xx}+{\sigma}_{yy}}{2}\end{array}\right. It is clear from proposition 2 that the Hujeux criterion is a criterion of Mohr–Coulomb type. Consequently, it is possible to represent the reduced stress tensor by a Mohr circle in the Mohr plane. The meaning of the criterion is then to compare the circle of centre C and of radius R with the failure line of angle \mathrm{\phi } . Notes : How is this formulation justified? According to our understanding, it seems that: - The Hujeux criterion is derived by analogy with the Mohr–Coulomb criterion applied to triaxial loadings; - The decomposition of the stress tensor, being bijective and invertible, is justified mathematically, and is therefore satisfactory to the mind. 8.4 Validity of the Hujeux criterion In order to show that the decomposition of the stresses used in the Hujeux law is not physically valid, it is sufficient for us to find a counter-example to proposition 1. Now, finding one in 3D is relatively trivial: it is sufficient to consider an arbitrary 3D stress state. Let for example the following stress state: \sigma =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0.6& -0.1& 0.05\\ -0.1& 0.4& 0.1\\ 0.05& 0.1& 0.3\end{array}\right] (in MPa) One obtains the following principal stresses: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{1}=0.6416\\ {\sigma}_{2}=0.4445\\ {\sigma}_{3}=0.2139\end{array}\right. (in MPa) Whence one deduces the Mohr circles. One then computes the Hujeux circles in the Mohr plane. To do this, one computes for the first circle: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}R=\sqrt{{\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{xx}-{\sigma}_{yy}}{2}\right)}^{2}+{\sigma}_{xy}^{2}}\\ C=\frac{{\sigma}_{xx}+{\sigma}_{yy}}{2}\end{array}\right. And so on for the other two. Finally, it is interesting to characterise the locus of the real stresses ({\sigma}_{n},\tau ) in the Mohr plane given by a normal {n}_{i\in \lbrace x,y,z\rbrace } rotating about the point M in the orthotropic plane of normal {\vec{e}}_{i\in \lbrace x,y,z\rbrace } . The expression of the normals is the following: {n}_{x}=\left(\begin{array}{c}0\\ \cos\left(\theta \right)\\ \sin\left(\theta \right)\end{array}\right);\phantom{\rule{4em}{0ex}}{n}_{y}=\left(\begin{array}{c}\cos\left(\theta \right)\\ 0\\ \sin\left(\theta \right)\end{array}\right);\phantom{\rule{4em}{0ex}}{n}_{z}=\left(\begin{array}{c}\cos\left(\theta \right)\\ \sin\left(\theta \right)\\ 0\end{array}\right) One then computes: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{n,i}={\sigma}_{n}.{n}_{i}\\ {\tau}_{i}={\sigma}_{n,i}-\left({\sigma}_{n,i}.{n}_{i}\right){n}_{i}\end{array}\right. The real stress is written: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{n,i}={\sigma}_{n,i}.{n}_{i}\\ {\tau}_{i}=\sqrt{{\tau}_{i}.{\tau}_{i}}\end{array}\right. The solutions are presented in Figure 5: - The Mohr circles are represented by black dashed lines; - The Hujeux circles are represented by coloured solid lines; - The locus of the real stresses in the orthotropic planes is represented by coloured dashed lines of the same colour as the corresponding Hujeux circles. According to proposition 1, it is clear that the Hujeux circles do not correspond to a real stress state about the point M. The corresponding real stress state should rather be the one given in dashed lines, which does indeed satisfy proposition 1. One concludes from this that the Hujeux criterion, which compares the Hujeux circle with a straight line in the Mohr plane, does not represent either the phenomenological action of a real mechanism. Representation of the stress state at the point M in the Mohr plane: the Mohr circles are represented by black dashed lines; the Hujeux circles by coloured solid lines; the locus of the real stresses in the 3 Cartesian orthotropic planes by coloured dashed lines with the same colour as the corresponding Hujeux circles. Note It is interesting to note that one recovers the Hujeux circles by proceeding as follows: {y}_{x}=\left(\begin{array}{c}0\\ -\sin\left(\theta \right)\\ \cos\left(\theta \right)\end{array}\right);\phantom{\rule{4em}{0ex}}{t}_{y}=\left(\begin{array}{c}-\sin\left(\theta \right)\\ 0\\ \cos\left(\theta \right)\end{array}\right);\phantom{\rule{4em}{0ex}}{t}_{z}=\left(\begin{array}{c}-\sin\left(\theta \right)\\ \cos\left(\theta \right)\\ 0\end{array}\right) One then computes: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{n,i}={\sigma}_{n,i}.{n}_{i}\\ {\tau}_{i}={\sigma}_{n,i}.{t}_{i}\end{array}\right. with {\sigma}_{n,i}=\sigma .{n}_{i} 8.5 Conclusions - The stress state used to form the Hujeux criterion is purely theoretical, but non-existent . In this sense, it does not express a real mechanism for a three-dimensional stress state; - On the other hand, for a “plane” stress state, that is to say one contained in a plane perpendicular to a principal stress, the Hujeux circle coincides perfectly with the Mohr circle. This is the case for example of plane-strain or plane-stress problems, for which the Hujeux criterion therefore remains valid; - The formulation of a valid 3D criterion requires the use of the stress invariants ( {I}_{1},{I}_{2},{I}_{3} or the principal stresses). 9 Appendix 4: Internal sub-stepping strategy of the Hujeux law The internal sub-stepping programmed in the Hujeux law occurs at a double level: - at the level of the generic subroutine REDECE, entry point of all the constitutive laws (LdC) in code_aster; - at the level of the Hujeux law itself. The routine REDECE manages in a generic manner the internal sub-stepping for all the constitutive laws. The flow chart of the routine is given on the following page. The idea is based on the interception of a return code sent by the LdC: - IRET = 0 if the integration of the LdC has succeeded - IRET = 1 if it has failed - IRET = 2 if it has failed When the integration of the LdC has failed, and if IRET= 2, one leaves the routine directly. When the integration of the LdC has failed, and if IRET= 1, one attempts an internal sub-stepping as a function of the value of ITER_INTE_PAS: - ITER_INTE_PAS = -1, 0, 1: one leaves the routine - ITER_INTE_PAS > 1: one sub-steps by ITER_INTE_PAS over 3 levels - ITER_INTE_PAS < -1: one sub-steps by –ITER_INTE_PAS over 3 levels Let us note that the maximum number of sub-steppings is thus: \text{NB\_MAX}=\text{ITER\_INTE\_PAS}\times ({2}^{0}+{2}^{1}+{2}^{2})=7\times \text{ITER\_INTE\_PAS} Moreover, as in the routine of the Hujeux law, there is also a sub-stepping by ITER_INTE_MAXI , the maximum number of sub-steppings for the Hujeux law is thus: \text{NB\_MAX}=7\times \text{ITER\_INTE\_PAS}\times \text{ITER\_INTE\_MAXI} Finally, the consistent tangent matrix recovered is averaged over the whole set of sub-stepping steps. This makes sense only if the latter presents sufficient continuity properties from one sub-step to the next, which is generally not the case of multi-mechanism laws. r7.01.24 Viscoplastic constitutive law LETK r7.01.24 Viscoplastic constitutive law LETK Summary: The L&K law describes an elasto-visco-plastic behaviour of rocks. Elastoplasticity is characterised by a positive hardening in the pre-peak regime and a softening behaviour beyond the strength. Viscoplasticity expresses the effect of time on the behaviour. It is described by a Perzyna power law. The initiation of the elastoplastic or viscoplastic phenomena is triggered as soon as the corresponding threshold is crossed. The behaviour linked to each phase is described by the evolution of these various thresholds. This evolution is governed by plastic or viscoplastic hardening functions. For the elastoplastic mechanism, a loading surface evolves through various thresholds: - A damage threshold coincident with the initial viscosity threshold, - A macroscopic peak threshold, defined from laboratory tests, - An intermediate threshold, termed the cleavage limit, determined analytically, - A characteristic threshold defined as the envelope of the damage threshold and of the cleavage limit, also called the contractancy/dilatancy limit (this limit is coincident with the maximum viscoplasticity threshold), - A residual strength threshold. For the viscous mechanism, a viscoplastic surface evolves through: - An initial threshold coincident with the damage threshold - A maximum viscosity threshold considered coincident with the contractancy/dilatancy limit 1 Notations 1.1 Generalities \sigma denotes the effective stress tensor in small perturbations, written in the form of the following vector: (\begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{11}\\ {\sigma}_{22}\\ {\sigma}_{33}\\ \sqrt{2}{\sigma}_{12}\\ \sqrt{2}{\sigma}_{13}\\ \sqrt{2}{\sigma}_{23}\end{array}) One denotes: | {I}_{1}=\text{tr}(\sigma ) | first invariant of the stresses | | --- | --- | | s=\sigma -\frac{{I}_{1}}{3}I | deviatoric stress tensor | | {s}_{\mathit{II}}=\sqrt{s.s} | second invariant of the deviatoric stress tensor | | {\sigma}_{\max} | major principal stress | | {\sigma}_{\min} | minor principal stress | | \tilde{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon -\frac{\text{Tr}(\varepsilon )}{3}I | strain deviator | | {\varepsilon}_{V}=\text{tr}(\varepsilon ) | volumetric strain | | \cos(3\theta )={2}^{1/2}{3}^{3/2}\frac{\det(s)}{{s}_{\text{II}}^{3}} | \theta being the Lode angle | | {\dot{\gamma}}_{p}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{\tilde{\dot{\varepsilon}}}_{ij}^{p}{\tilde{\dot{\varepsilon}}}_{ij}^{p}} | cumulated plastic deviatoric strains | | {\dot{\gamma}}_{\text{vp}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{\tilde{\dot{\varepsilon}}}_{ij}^{\text{vp}}{\tilde{\dot{\varepsilon}}}_{ij}^{\text{vp}}} | cumulated viscoplastic deviatoric strains | | {\xi}_{p} | plastic hardening parameter | | {\xi}_{\text{vp}} | viscoplastic hardening parameter | | {G}^{\text{visc}} | function driving the evolution of the viscous strains and describing the flow direction | | \tilde{G}=G-\frac{\text{Tr}(G)}{3}I | deviator of G | | G=\text{Tr}(G) | trace of G | | {\tilde{G}}_{\mathit{II}}=\sqrt{\tilde{G}\cdot \tilde{G}} | norm of \tilde{G} | | \psi | dilatancy angle | | {f}^{d} | elastoplastic loading surface | | {f}^{\text{vp}} | viscoplastic loading surface | 1.2 Sign convention - Implicit integration scheme The integration of the LETK model according to the implicit integration scheme is carried out under the PLASTI environment. The integration of the LETK model under the implicit scheme is currently available only by computation of a perturbed local Jacobian matrix ( 'NEWTON_PERT' ). The solution algorithm follows the following logic. It uses an elastic prediction then correction iterations if the viscous and/or plastic thresholds are activated. The scheme aims to produce the variation of the stresses and of the hardening variables under the effect of a strain increment. The local subdivision of the model can be activated under this integration scheme by the keyword ITER_INTE_PAS of the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT , cf U4.51.11). 4.3.1 Elastic prediction phase This phase is similar to that presented in section 4.2.1 . The exceeding of the plasticity and viscosity thresholds is tested with respect to this stress state. The expression of the thresholds tested is made explicit in § 3.2 . - If none of the thresholds is activated, the prediction is considered valid with respect to the models. An update of the internal variables is undertaken in order to display the activation state of the various thresholds. - If one threshold among the two to be considered (plasticity and/or viscosity) is activated, the solution of a local system of non-linear equations must be initiated. The dissipation mechanisms defined as potentially active must lead to the exceeding of the associated thresholds (plasticity and/or viscosity) 4.3.2 Correction phase: non-linear equations to be solved This step consists in solving the system of local non-linear equations established on the basis of the viscous and/or plastic mechanisms. After convergence, the stresses and internal variables of the model are updated. The unknowns of the system of non-linear equations are the stresses {\sigma}_{n+1} , the plastic multiplier {\lambda}_{n+1}^{p} , the plastic hardening variable {\xi}_{n+1}^{p} and the viscous hardening variable {\xi}_{n+1}^{\mathit{vp}} . The vector of unknowns therefore comprises at most, for \mathrm{3D} modellings, 9 unknowns. The non-linear equations to be solved are the following: - The incremental state equation, \mathit{E1} : {\underline{\underline{\sigma}}}_{n+1}-{\underline{\underline{\sigma}}}_{n}-{C}^{e}({\underline{\underline{\sigma}}}_{n+1}):(\Delta \underline{\underline{\epsilon}}-\Delta \lambda {\underline{\underline{G}}}^{p}-\Phi ({f}^{\mathit{vp}})\cdot {\underline{\underline{G}}}^{\mathit{vp}})=0 - The Kuhn–Tucker condition, \mathit{E2} : \lbrace \begin{array}{cccc}\text{Si}& {f}^{d}\le 0& \text{alors}& \Delta \lambda =0\\ \text{Si}& {f}^{d}=0& \text{alors}& \Delta \lambda >0\end{array} - The incremental evolution of the plastic hardening variable, \mathit{E3} : {\xi}_{n+1}^{p}-{\xi}_{n}^{p}-\Delta {\xi}^{p}=0 , with \Delta {\xi}^{p} evolving according to the conditions specified in § 3.4.2 . - The incremental evolution of the visco-plastic hardening variable, \mathit{E4} : {\xi}_{n+1}^{\mathit{vp}}-{\xi}_{n}^{\mathit{vp}}-\Delta {\xi}^{\mathit{vp}}=0 , with \Delta {\xi}^{\mathit{vp}} evolving according to the conditions specified in § 3.4.1 . r7.01.25 Constitutive laws of dam joints: JOINT_MECA_RUPT, JOINT_MECA_FROT and JOINT_MECA_ENDO r7.01.25 Constitutive laws of dam joints: JOINT_MECA_RUPT, JOINT_MECA_FROT and JOINT_MECA_ENDO Summary: This document describes surface laws making it possible to model the fracture and the friction between the lips of a crack or of a joint. The law JOINT_MECA_RUPT represents only the damage phenomenon; it is based on a cohesive formulation of fracture. The law JOINT_MECA_FROT is an elastoplastic version of a Mohr-Coulomb friction law. The law JOINT_MECA_ENDO is a more complete law; it combines the two mechanisms: damage and plasticity are coupled through the free energy. This last law is written in the generalised standard formalism. In mechanics these laws are based on the modellings of the standard joints XXX_JOINT. The laws are dedicated to the modelling of dams, more precisely of the concrete/rock joints or of the joints between the monoliths of a dam. Depending on the type of loading the use of one or the other law may be chosen for different parts of the structure. In order to be able to simulate the behaviour of real dams certain specific features of construction have been introduced, in particular keying and sawing. Keying is an industrial procedure of injection of concrete under pressure between the monoliths of a dam. It is an intermediate stage of the construction of an arch dam; it serves to reinforce its watertightness after the construction phase of the vertical monoliths. Sawing is a similar procedure during which the dam is sawn in order to release the compressive stresses. Each procedure is defined via the keywords PRES_CLAVAGE and SCIAGE in DEFI_MATERIAU. Keying and sawing are not activated for the moment for the law JOINT_MECA_ENDO. The effect of hydrostatic pressure due to the presence of fluid in the joint is taken into account via the Terzaghi stress. All the laws admit either the modelling without coupling (pressure imposed in the option PRES_FLUIDE), or a coupled hydromechanical modelling (XXX_JOINT_HYME) which activates the propagation of the uplift pressures at the dam-rock interface. 1 Introduction The incidents which have occurred on concrete dams (Bouzey 1895, Gleno 1923, Malpasset 1959), as well as the results of monitoring, have shown that their stability, and consequently their safety, depends very largely on the hydromechanical behaviour of the weakest zones of the valley-dam assembly. Localised at the discontinuities in the structure and in the rock, these weak points are principally the faults of the abutment zones, the construction joints in the dam, the concrete-rock contact of the foundation and the joints between the monoliths of the dam. The mechanical behaviour of these zones at risk is strongly non-linear, but thanks to their surface character, industrial studies on large structures are complex but feasible. In addition to these difficulties, the mode of construction of dams, the keying/sawing techniques used and their multiple drainage points make them structures whose finite-element modelling is all the more complex in a conventional analysis code. The three constitutive laws described in this document make it possible to take into account the principal non-linearities of the behaviour of the structures: the crack-opening phase (JOINT_MECA_RUPT/ENDO) and the sliding phase of its lips (JOINT_MECA_FROT/ENDO). The law JOINT_MECA_ENDO is the most complete law; it is capable of representing the evolution of the state of the joint by combining the two phenomena of fracture (thanks to the damage variable) and of friction (thanks to the plasticity variable). Dam under construction Visualisation of the construction monoliths 1.1 The joints — weak links of the structure As mentioned previously, the joints of dams have a varied origin (r7.01.25-fig-image-physique-joint). In a general way, one can imagine the joint as a rough discontinuity possibly reinforced by a filling material. Physical image of a joint Different types of joint of a dam Coulomb's friction law, which uses only a single parameter (friction coefficient), captures only a tiny part of the very complex mechanical behaviour of such a structure. Indeed, apart from friction, the joint exhibits the following important phenomena: the loss of tensile strength, the elastic behaviour at very small displacement, the progressive disappearance of the shear-stress peak for a cyclic loading. The relevance of these phenomena depends strongly on the physical state of the joint, in particular on its level of roughness, on the mean size of the asperities, on the mechanical properties of the filling materials and of the rock matrix. The standard parameters in mechanics such as Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, or again the friction coefficient all influence the behaviour of the joint, but are not the only ones to be identified in order to capture the phenomena described above. The complete modelling of the joint therefore requires the introduction of a law depending on numerous parameters. The implementation of such a law in an implicit analysis code being an important technical challenge, we propose simpler laws, depending on few parameters but which nevertheless make it possible to capture the essential behaviour of the joint in most current conditions of use. These latter are named JOINT_MECA_RUPT, JOINT_MECA_FROT and JOINT_MECA_ENDO. They make it possible to model the behaviour of the joints which one finds between the monoliths of an arch dam and/or at the interface between the gravity dam and its foundation. We give a succinct description of them below, before detailing them in the parts which follow. 1.2 Mechanical constitutive laws (without hydraulic coupling) 1.2.1 Fracture behaviour JOINT_MECA_RUPT The law JOINT_MECA_RUPT is an elastic softening law, whose normal behaviour is founded on the cohesive formulation of fracture. It opens the possibility of modelling fracture in mode I (tension) and takes into account the coupling between the normal opening and the tangential stiffness. This law captures well the behaviour of real joints at small displacements, as long as the sliding regime is not reached. In order to identify the regimes in which it is applicable one can take up again the physical image of the joint (r7.01.25-fig-image-physique-joint). These are two rough interfaces possibly containing a filling material between their lips; this may be either clay, or elements of the rock for the cracks between the dam and the foundation, or keying grout for the monolith joints. A loading of the crack first brings into play the properties of the filling material and the geometry of the asperities which define the behaviour of the structure at small displacements. As long as the filling material is not damaged or the asperities are not broken, the behaviour of the joint remains elastic both in opening and in shear. However the normal and tangential stiffness parameters, denoted {K}_{n} and {K}_{t} , are not equivalent, because they bring into play two distinct physical phenomena. The first is linked principally to the stiffness of the filling material, the second depends rather on the bending stiffness of the asperities. The joint presents a tensile strength, denoted {\sigma}_{max} , which can be related to the filling materials, but also to the transverse frictions between the asperities of the two lips of the crack. The tensile strength is often quite low, not exceeding that of concrete {\sigma}_{max}\ll 1\mathit{MPa} . As a first approximation the normal stiffness can be estimated from the Young's modulus of the filling material E and from the joint thickness e , which gives {K}_{n}=E/e\simeq 10\mathit{GPa}/1\mathit{cm}={10}^{12}\mathit{Pa}/m . For sufficiently thick joints the elastic behaviour is isotropic and the tangential stiffness can be taken close to the normal stiffness {K}_{t}\simeq {K}_{n} . The fracture of the joint takes place in a progressive manner. Indeed, the joint is first damaged by partially decreasing its stiffness before breaking completely. In order to quantify this phenomenon we introduce a dimensionless penalisation parameter in fracture {P}_{\mathit{rupt}} , which represents a relative opening in softening with respect to the elastic opening. For low values of {P}_{\mathrm{rupt}} , the fracture is sudden. For large values {P}_{\mathit{rupt}}\gg 1 the transition is more progressive, but this significantly increases the initial dissipation energy. The details of this behaviour will be presented in the following parts. In practice the value is taken close to {P}_{\mathit{rupt}}\simeq 1 , which introduces a non-negligible softening phase without departing too far from the sudden-fracture behaviour. Normal and tangential behaviour for the extreme joint profiles: smooth joint \alpha =0 Normal and tangential behaviour for the extreme joint profiles: infinitely rough joint \alpha =2 In order to model the different types of profiles of the monolith joints of dams (represented in the figures r7.01.25-fig-joint-lisse, r7.01.25-fig-joint-rougeux), we introduce into the user interface an additional parameter \alpha \in [0,2] . The latter links the normal opening of the joint with the decrease of its tangential stiffness. Physically it reflects the depth of the asperities and varies continuously between 0 and 2 . The value \alpha =0 corresponds to the smooth interface without asperities (the tangential stiffness drops to zero as soon as the joint opens normally, see r7.01.25-fig-joint-lisse). The value \alpha =2 represents another extreme case, where the interface is very rough with an infinite depth of the asperities, that is the equivalent of the profile of a crenellated monolith joint (r7.01.25-fig-joint-rougeux). In this case the tangential stiffness is not affected by the normal opening. The default value is fixed at 1 , which represents an intermediate situation. Realistic joint profile corresponding to the intermediate roughness \alpha =1 1.2.2 Sliding behaviour JOINT_MECA_FROT If one loads the joint further in pure shear, it will end up sliding with a certain friction coefficient. Before passing into this plastic regime, one observes experimentally a peak of the friction force. This phenomenon is linked to the fact that in order to be able to slide, the asperities must leave their embedded position (dilatancy). During this phase the frictional contacts are not necessarily parallel to the surface of the lips, which increases the effective friction coefficient. This “exit” procedure is moreover accompanied by the increase of the normal displacement of the joint r7.01.25-fig-contrainte-cisaillement. If this cycle is repeated several times, the stress peak attenuates and disappears completely. One notes that the deeper the asperities, the more important the friction peak. In the limit case even at a non-zero normal opening the joint can reveal the elastic behaviour in tangential slidings (this case is treated by JOINT_MECA_RUPT with \alpha =2 ). The law JOINT_MECA_FROT does not take into account all the complexity of sliding and in particular the peak; it represents only the phenomenon of ultimate sliding, characterised solely by the friction coefficient \mu and the adhesion c . This latter is linked to the tensile strength {R}_{t}=c/\mu . The loss of tensile strength is not modelled by this law. As the yield surface is assumed fixed, once one reaches in tension the apex of the cone one continues the evolution in perfect plasticity with the normal stress locked at the value of {R}_{t} . This behaviour is clearly not physical for the brittle filling material and can be considered only as an approximation of the real behaviour. The law JOINT_MECA_FROT is written in an elastoplastic formalism with the elastic phase identical to that of the law JOINT_MECA_RUPT. Typical tangential behaviour: shear stress and normal opening as a function of the tangential opening (TEGG/EDF measurements) The yield surface for the law JOINT_MECA_FROT is a cone of revolution about the axis of the normal stress. It remains fixed in the course of the evolution. Coupling behaviour of fracture and friction JOINT_MECA_ENDO The first two laws JOINT_MECA_RUPT/FROT are very basic and they reproduce only a single phenomenon at a time, either fracture or sliding. Each of the laws can be used in various parts of the structure according to the local loading defined upstream of the study. The advantage of such an approach lies in the simplicity of the laws used, because they depend only on a reduced number of parameters. However in many situations the local change cannot be defined upstream of the study, see the cases where certain zones of the structure are loaded both in fracture and in sliding. The law JOINT_MECA_ENDO has been introduced in order to treat this type of situation; it combines the phenomena of fracture and of sliding. As for the law JOINT_MECA_FROT it is an elastoplastic law with a conical yield surface, but kinematic hardening is introduced in addition, whose damaging character makes it possible to represent the softening both in tension and in shear. This is easily illustrated by the representation of the evolution of the yield surface in the stress domain r7.01.25-fig-chargement-normal. The motion generated by the activation of the kinematic hardening of the yield surface spreads the elastic zone: the stress increases at first following the loading direction. However thanks to the damaging character of the coupling, the amplitude of the hardening decreases and the surface returns to its initial position for the ultimate loadings (completely damaged). This makes it possible to represent the peaks of tensile strength as well as that of sliding. Motion generated by the kinematic hardening of the yield surface for the law JOINT_MECA_ENDO, for the normal loading Motion generated by the kinematic hardening of the yield surface for the law JOINT_MECA_ENDO, for shear 1.3 Hydromechanical coupling In order to assess the stability of dams it is important to be able to model the propagation of the uplift pressures between the rock and the foundation of the dam. Two possibilities are offered to the user. First, an uplift-pressure profile can be imposed, as an input parameter of the loading. This simple possibility makes it possible to study the stability of the dam for a conservative hydraulic loading (the least favourable). On the other hand, the speed of the computation presents a non-negligible advantage. One can thus test an extreme hydraulic profile without spending more time than in the pure mechanical computation. Moreover, this feature makes it possible to carry out a hydromechanical chaining computation. The latter consists in starting with a mechanical computation with an initial pressure state in the joints. According to the damage of the latter, the pressure profile (whose form is given a priori ) is updated. Once the pressure is modified, the mechanical state of the joints evolves again, which can generate the fracture of some of them. The fluid then propagates more easily and the pressure profile again undergoes an evolution. This process is chained by means of a fixed-point loop in the command file in order to obtain converged mechanical and hydraulic states. Shift of the normal constitutive relation for the law JOINT_MECA_RUPT Taking the hydrostatic pressure into account. Shift of the normal constitutive relation for the law JOINT_MECA_FROT From the theoretical point of view, the introduction of the fluid into the joint modifies the normal mechanical stress {\sigma}_{n}\to {\sigma}_{n}-p (Terzaghi's law). In practice, the constitutive law in question is shifted downwards according to the value of the pressure p at each integration point. These laws also accept a coupled hydromechanical modelling, named xxx_JOINT_HYME. The difference from the model with hydromechanical chaining (presented above) bears on the more precise taking into account of the action of the mechanics on the hydraulics. Indeed, in the chained model the profile is given a priori . In the coupled model, the opening of the joint modifies the flow law of the fluid; the pressure profile is an unknown of the problem. During the hydromechanical coupling, in order to model the flow, the mechanical law is enriched by taking into account the cubic Poiseuille flow, which is regularised for very small crack openings. Thus, the pressure profile is no longer imposed, but computed during the simulation. In addition to the standard mechanical equation one simultaneously solves the following flow equation: div\overrightarrow{w}=0;\overrightarrow{w}=\frac{\rho}{12\bar{\mu}}{\delta}_{n}^{3}\overrightarrow{\nabla}p where \overrightarrow{w} corresponds to the hydraulic flux, {\delta}_{n} is the normal opening of the joint, and finally \rho and \bar{\mu} denote respectively the density and the dynamic viscosity of the fluid. Note The hydromechanical modelling is available for all the constitutive laws JOINT_MECA_RUPT/FROT/ENDO. 1.4 Keying procedure Keying is a key stage during the construction of an arch dam. It consists in an injection of concrete grout under pressure between the monoliths of the dam. It is therefore important to be able to model this process correctly. In practice the pouring of the concrete is decomposed into several stages where the concrete is injected at different places and at varied pressures. From the mechanical point of view keying is interpreted as a placing in compression of the lips of the keyed joint up to {\sigma}_{n}=-{\sigma}_{\mathit{nc}} (pressure of the injected concrete, keyword PRES_CLAVAGE). This option is included directly in the parameters of the constitutive law. Physically keying is accompanied by a solidification process of the injected grout; the procedure is modelled by the modification of the thickness of the joints concerned. If the joint is in strong compression initially, keying does not influence it. If on the other hand the joint is open or not sufficiently compressed ( {\sigma}_{n}>-{\sigma}_{\mathit{nc}} ), keying will result in the change of the joint-thickness parameter denoted {\delta}_{\mathit{nf}} . And, consequently, in a translation of the normal stress. The normal behaviour of the joint after keying can be modified. Thus, the tensile strength can be restored (Figure ) either partially or completely according to the damage of the joints before the keying procedure. The procedure implemented consists in not restoring it; it keeps its current value. Note The modelling of keying is available for the moment only for the basic laws JOINT_MECA_RUPT/FROT. In view of the current numerical implementation the phenomena of sawing and of keying cannot be chained on the same joint. Illustration of the keying procedure 1.5 Sawing procedure It has been shown by in situ tests that the concrete of certain hydraulic structures in France has suffered damage due to the alkali-aggregate chemical reaction unknown at the time of the massive construction of dams before the war. The most notable example is the Chambon dam situated on the Romanche, which after 80 years of existence was the victim of the phenomenon of concrete disease (AAR); consequently every fifteen years it must undergo a particular treatment. Microsawing operations on the structure make it possible to prolong its service life. As its name indicates, this procedure consists in sawing the dam in order to release the compressive stresses, which have developed over time. It is therefore important to be able to model this process correctly. From the numerical point of view, sawing is very close to the keying procedure: the joint thickness evolves in the course of the operation. Nevertheless, apart from the fact that this time the joint thickness decreases, its evolution is also driven by the displacement which is to be compared with the pressure driving during the keying procedure. The sawing phase is characterised by the saw thickness entered under a keyword SCIAGE. Illustration of the sawing procedure This option is included directly in the parameters of the constitutive law. In practice, in order to make the phenomenon close to physical reality, the sawn thickness is decreased by the initial opening of the joint before the operation. If the joint is in strong initial opening, sawing will not influence it. If on the other hand the joint is compressed, it will undergo complete sawing. Numerically it will result in the change of the joint-thickness parameter denoted {\delta}_{\mathrm{nf}} , and, consequently, in a translation of the normal stress, such that: {\delta}_{\mathit{nf}}=max(0,{\delta}_{n}^{-})-{\delta}_{\mathit{scie}} One also considers that the joint in its final state is completely damaged by the sawing. The latter, even if it is subsequently placed in tension, will therefore develop no tensile strength. The procedure is explicit; combined with the elastic unloading for the global structure which it generates, it results in the rapid numerical convergence of the modelling. At most one puts two Newton iterations, of which the first serves to update the thickness of the joints and the second is a linear unloading phase. Note The modelling of sawing is available for the moment only for the basic laws JOINT_MECA_RUPT/FROT. In view of the current numerical implementation the phenomena of sawing and of keying cannot be chained on the same joint. 1.6 Choice of parameters and the limits of application The constitutive laws JOINT_MECA_RUPT/FROT are simple, robust, depending on few parameters. These laws do not make it possible to model the behaviour in the fracture-friction transition phase. For the friction law, which presents a non-zero tensile strength, the fracture of the joint is not implemented. Unlike these simplified behaviours, the law JOINT_MECA_ENDO is a more complete law; it is capable of representing the evolution of the state of the joint by combining the phenomena of fracture and of friction. The laws introduced have the non-negligible advantage of being based on a theoretical formalism proven in the scientific literature. Certain parameters are specific to the given law, others (such as hydraulic coupling) have a universal character. Evolution of the sliding cone due to hardening 3.1 Implicit discretisation of the friction law The elastoplastic version of the friction law is formulated in rate form, which facilitates its numerical discretisation. The incremental version of the law remains strictly equivalent to the continuous version provided that the increments of change are infinitesimal. In order to limit the number of loading steps, we adapt the continuous version of the law to finite increments, in an implicit manner, that is to say that the sliding conditions are written in the final equilibrium state. The algorithm used is that of the radial return with elastic prediction. By convention we denote by a sign «-» the variables at the previous equilibrium state; the current state is denoted by the usual variables without an additional sign (see ). Coulomb friction law The continuous equations of the law are written in discretised form: \left\{ \begin{array}{c}\lambda ={\lambda}^{-}+\Delta \lambda \\ {\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}}={\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}-}+\Delta {\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}}\\ \vec{{\sigma}_{t}}={K}_{t}({\vec{\delta}}_{t}-{\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}})\\ {\sigma}_{n}=min({K}_{n}{\delta}_{n},{R}_{t})\end{array}\right. With the following law: \left\{ \begin{array}{c}f(\vec{\sigma},\lambda )=\parallel {\vec{\sigma}}_{t}\parallel +\mu {\sigma}_{n}-c-{\rm K}\lambda ⩽0\\ f(\vec{\sigma},\lambda )\cdot \Delta \lambda =0;\Delta \lambda ⩾0\\ {\Delta \vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}}=\Delta \lambda \frac{{\vec{\sigma}}_{t}}{\parallel {\vec{\sigma}}_{t}\parallel }\end{array}\right. In a Newton algorithm the displacement jumps \vec{\delta}=({\delta}_{n},{\vec{\delta}}_{t}) as well as the internal variables at the previous instant {\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}-} and {\lambda}^{-} being known, in order to solve the law it is enough to obtain the stress values \vec{\sigma}=({\sigma}_{n},{\vec{\sigma}}_{t}) and all the internal variables at the current instant (in our case {\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}} and \lambda ). The evolution equation of the law for the normal component is completely decoupled from the tangential motion, and can therefore be solved immediately: {\sigma}_{n}=min({K}_{n}{\delta}_{n},{R}_{t}) We thus obtain a set of five equations and one inequality, in order to obtain five scalar unknowns: \vec{{\sigma}_{t}}={K}_{t}({\vec{\delta}}_{t}-{\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}-}-\Delta {\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}}) And: \left\{ \begin{array}{c}f(\vec{\sigma},\lambda )\equiv \parallel {\vec{\sigma}}_{t}\parallel +\mu {\sigma}_{n}-c-{\rm K}{\lambda}^{-}-{\rm K}\Delta \lambda ⩽0\\ f(\vec{\sigma},\lambda )\cdot \Delta \lambda =0;\Delta \lambda ⩾0\\ {\Delta \vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}}=\Delta \lambda \frac{{\vec{\sigma}}_{t}}{\parallel {\vec{\sigma}}_{t}\parallel }\end{array}\right. In order to simplify this mathematical problem let us look in more detail at the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker condition f(\vec{\sigma},\lambda )\cdot \Delta \lambda =0 . There are two possibilities: either one slides \Delta \lambda >0 , or one is in the elastic domain \Delta \lambda =0 . If one is in the elastic domain, then \Delta {\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}}=0 and one obtains the elastic solution if and only if: {f}_{\mathit{el}}({\sigma}_{n},{\vec{\sigma}}_{\tau}^{-},{\lambda}^{-})\equiv {K}_{t}\parallel {\vec{\delta}}_{\tau}-{\vec{\delta}}_{\tau}^{\mathit{pl}-}\parallel +\mu {\sigma}_{n}-c-{\rm K}{\lambda}^{-}⩽0 In practice if is satisfied then the elastic prediction is the solution of the problem: \left\{ \begin{array}{c}\lambda ={\lambda}^{-}\\ {\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}}={\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}-}\\ \vec{{\sigma}_{t}}={K}_{t}({\vec{\delta}}_{t}-{\vec{\delta}}_{t}^{\mathit{pl}-})\\ {\sigma}_{n}=min({K}_{n}{\delta}_{n},{R}_{t})\end{array}\right. If the condition is not satisfied, then \Delta \lambda >0 and one is in the sliding phase. These terms are equivalent to the parallel distribution of discrete characteristics of type DIS_T on each segment joining each pair of vertex nodes facing one another from one face of the element to the other (see figure r7.01.25-fig-amortissement). The entries of the matrix \mathrm{C} are computed directly for the degrees of freedom of the vertex nodes. Consequently, if the number of vertex nodes of a face of a joint element is {n}_{s} , one assigns, for the mechanical damping matrix, the local characteristics {A}_{n}.\mathit{Surf}/{n}_{s} or {A}_{t}.\mathit{Surf}/{n}_{s} distributed in the local frame of the element on each of the diagonal terms. Their opposite values are assigned to the coupling terms. It is therefore as if one had {n}_{s} damping discretes of type DIS_T assigned on SEG2 mesh cells. Isotropic hardening on the tangential plane In the previous attempts , , at an introduction in explicit version , it appeared that these modellings generally prove to be of poor numerical performance; their extension to 3D is also rather delicate 4 Theoretical formulation of JOINT_MECA_ENDO One of the key points in the precise description of the interfaces between rocks is the identification of their elastic domain (also called the yield surface or the criterion). Because of their softening nature, not only rocky contacts but also any kind of analogous interface involving similar materials such as concrete, clay or soil can generally be classified according to their strength under various mixed-mode loadings. This approach is closely linked to the basic safety rules in industrial applications, where it is accepted as a first approximation that geomaterials could present an unstable failure once the critical load is reached. Throughout the last century, specific testing machines and the corresponding measurement protocols were set up in order to harmonise and standardise the experimental characterisation of the brittle interfaces cited above. To mention only a few, the simple tension test, or again shear at a fixed compression, are both well-documented experiments which are carried out in practice in order to catalogue the strength of materials by locating only a few points of their multidimensional elastic surface. This reduced “single-point” view of the strength of materials has been increasingly scrutinised in recent times, and multiple developments have been adopted. For example, the constant improvements of finite-element software allow new types of modelling, with loadings going beyond the elastic domain in order to explore a more subtle post-peak behaviour. While the complexity of the post-peak description could be reached through various theoretical formalisms, most of them still rest on the initial definition of the yield surface, and the question of this shape of the elastic domain remains the cornerstone of any identification of a non-linear model. Even though considerable progress has been made over the last decades, this precise identification of the yield surface remains today a rather difficult task. A common characteristic of geomaterials is their high strength under compressive loads. In current industrial applications it is precisely this property of higher compressive strength that is exploited in order to increase the overall robustness of the structure. As the interfaces considered are composed of geomaterials it is natural to assume a similarity between the corresponding yield surfaces. For geomaterials, according to their physical origin, a wide variety of criteria defining the elastic domain are employed in order to model their mechanical behaviour. The simplest surface, admitting an infinite strength in hydrostatic compression, is the one in the shape of a linear cone. It was introduced for the first time more than a century ago as the combination of Coulomb's friction hypothesis with the Galileo-Rankine tension cut-off principle. The initial description in principal stress, commonly called the Mohr-Coulomb form, was then generalised in the work of Drucker and Prager to a smoother deviator-trace relation. The direct relation between the shear and compression loadings, which is the principal signature of these linear criteria, made possible the development of various constitutive relations based on the same simplified dependence. We retain at this stage that the linear conical surface is commonly used to this day for the modelling of geomaterials. With many large infrastructure projects under way, more complex criteria emerged as new experimental data became available. For wider ranges of loadings, the dependence of shear strength on compression seemed to depart from the linear curve. In 1980 Evert Hoek and Edwin T. Brown propose a new particular form of criterion, of quadratic shape. It reproduces the Mohr-Coulomb type singularity for a low tensile loading while simultaneously taking into account the reduction of the shear strength under high compression. This purely empirical criterion has been widely used in the design of underground excavations. More recent work on rock joints seems to show the same modification of the yield surface. The law JOINT_MECA_ENDO attempts to capture this phenomenon partially: starting from the linear elastic yield surface, the latter evolves thanks to kinematic hardening, and the tensile strength is captured by the damaging coupling of the hardening amplitude. The apparent shape of the yield surface is no longer linear and, as a result, it approaches the yield surfaces of real joints. We also have the advantage of being able to represent the cohesive-zone model and the elastoplastic model within one and the same formalism, which we describe briefly below. Like the previous laws, the law JOINT_MECA_ENDO also accepts a coupled hydromechanical modelling; the HM coupling in it is identical and these two phenomena can be treated separately. We describe here the mechanical part of the law, which unifies the two mechanical phenomena: fracture and friction. It is based on the modellings XXX_JOINT (R3.06.09). Note : The next two sections present the general theoretical concept. On a first reading one may omit them and pass directly to the following section, which provides enough elements to understand the numerical implementation of the law. 4.1 Generalised standard model for the joints The theoretical framework chosen to model the coupling between fracture and friction of the joints of concrete dams is based on the generalised standard model , , . This model makes it possible to guarantee good thermodynamic properties by operating exclusively with energetic notions. Initially developed to represent three-dimensional phenomena, we adapt it to the joint model. In interface mechanics, two physical quantities are typically introduced. The first is the vector of the Cauchy stress density, which characterises the state of the local forces, while the second is the displacement-jump vector, which makes it possible to measure the relative position of the lips on either side of the interface, up to a certain reference configuration. If the reference configuration is known, the two quantities are objective and experimentally measurable. Consequently one of the aims of interface mechanics is to establish a link between these two quantities, which is called the material constitutive relation or the constitutive law. Following the original ideas of Cauchy and in the simplest manner, we can postulate that the stress is a bijective function of the displacement jump. Not all bijective stress-jump relations are however admissible from a thermodynamic point of view. For example, the work of the internal forces for constitutive relations with a non-symmetric tangent operator depends on the loading path, which is physically inadmissible for a fully reversible elastic process. Hyperelasticity restricts this stress-jump relation by admitting the existence of a scalar strain-energy density function from which the stress is derived. The mechanical loading of a hyperelastic material is regarded as a reversible process with zero dissipation, the only state variable being the displacement jump. In this sense, the hyperelastic formalism is conservative and compatible with a general thermodynamic description. The ideas are similar for extending the notion of thermodynamically admissible laws to behaviours in the presence of variables which record the loading history. In order to take proper account of the process of energy dissipation, which is very much present in the case of friction of the lips, it is necessary to introduce at least one additional state variable. This is generally done via the sliding vector, called the plastic displacement jump. The latter is intended to decompose the total displacement jump into elastic contributions and irreversible plastic contributions. Although this plastic variable has a clear physical meaning of residual strain for the fully unloaded system, it is generally not directly observable, which is why it is also called an internal (hidden) state variable. In order to capture not only the irreversible slidings, but also to take into account the attenuation of the roughness of the interface in the sliding phase, another internal variable must be introduced. We choose here to introduce a scalar damage variable, whose particular feature is that it is contained within the bounds [0,1]. Zero corresponds to the sound state and one to the completely damaged state. The thermodynamic description of interface mechanics rests either on the definition of the Helmholtz free-energy density, or on the Gibbs free energy , . As was explained above, for the isothermal evolution in the presence of plasticity and of damage, this function depends on three state variables, two of which are hidden. We choose a Helmholtz description with the total displacement jump. The projection onto the interface of the Cauchy stress tensor is then the dual conjugate of the total displacement jump \vec{\sigma}=\partial \psi /\partial \vec{\delta} , while the energetic response of the system to the evolution of plasticity and of damage is captured by the corresponding generalised forces \vec{X}=-\frac{\partial \psi }{\partial \vec{p}};Y=-\frac{\partial \psi }{\partial \alpha } . Most elastoplastic models admit an additive separation of the elastic and plastic strains. This leads to the simplest quadratic form of the free energy describing the residual plastic state. We adapt the same hypothesis for the joints: \psi (\vec{\delta},\vec{p})=K\frac{{(\vec{\delta}-\vec{p})}^{2}}{2} where K is the tensorial elasticity modulus, assumed constant. Note that we adopt abbreviated notations in order to simplify the description. In particular, in this linear elastic case, the generalised plastic force and the Cauchy stress are equal: \vec{\sigma}=\vec{X} . By adding the quadratic plastic term in the free energy one introduces de facto a kinematic hardening, because \psi (\vec{\delta},\vec{p},\alpha )=K\frac{{(\vec{\delta}-\vec{p})}^{2}}{2}+H(\alpha )\frac{{\vec{p}}^{2}}{2} \textrm{et} \vec{X}=\vec{\sigma}-H(\alpha )\vec{p} H plays the role of kinematic-hardening amplitude. In order to reproduce the softening phenomenon we assume that the hardening amplitude decreases with the development of plasticity. The reversible elastic domain, characterised by the absence of evolution of plasticity and of damage, is defined in the space of the observable stresses: \vec{p}=\text{const et}\alpha =\text{const}\to \vec{\sigma}\in \text{domaine élastique} . Thermodynamically, one must ensure that the rate of energy dissipation is positive: \text{D}=\vec{\sigma}\cdot \dot{\vec{\delta}}-\dot{\psi}\ge 0 where \dot{} corresponds to the time derivative: \dot{\psi}=\partial \psi /\partial t . Considering first the elastic unloading, we obtain the relation \vec{\sigma}=\frac{\partial \psi }{\partial \vec{\delta}} as a consequence of the process with zero dissipation \text{D}\left(\vec{p}=\text{const};\alpha =\text{const}\right)=0 , thus reducing the second thermodynamic principle eq. to the following direct inequality: \text{D}=\vec{X}\cdot \dot{\vec{p}}+Y\cdot \dot{\alpha}\ge 0 . In order to obtain a complete description of the material, one must introduce the evolution laws of the hidden variables: \dot{\vec{p}}\text{et}\dot{\alpha} . This is done either via a dissipation potential, or via a plastic potential, or directly via an explicit flow rule. For an arbitrary flow, the proof of the positivity of the dissipation rate eq. is a significantly difficult task. This is why additional restrictive hypotheses are commonly introduced. For example, if the evolution of the hidden variables depends exclusively on the generalised forces (\dot{\vec{p}};\dot{\alpha})\iff (\vec{X};Y) , the dissipation rate of the material becomes an exclusive function of these forces \text{D}=\text{D}(\vec{X};Y) . The principal advantage of such a description is that the positivity of the dissipation is independent of the loading path: it depends exclusively on the choice of the functions which drive the flow. Thus the whole of the model can be analysed in the space of the generalised forces. We draw on the recent work of by introducing the Helmholtz free energy for the interfaces in the following form: \psi (\vec{\delta},\vec{p},\alpha )={K}_{n}\frac{{({\delta}_{n}-{p}_{n})}^{2}}{2}+{K}_{t}\frac{{\Vert \vec{{\delta}_{t}}-\vec{{p}_{t}}\Vert }^{2}}{2}+{A}_{n}(\alpha )\frac{{{p}_{n}}^{2}}{2}+{A}_{t}(\alpha )\frac{{\vec{{p}_{t}}}^{2}}{2} with {A}_{n}(\alpha )={B}_{n}\cdot {(1-\alpha )}^{3}/\sqrt{\alpha} and {A}_{t}(\alpha )={B}_{t}\cdot {(1-\alpha )}^{3}/\sqrt{\alpha} . We use the decomposition of the displacement jump into a normal part and a tangential part \vec{\delta}=({\delta}_{n},{\delta}_{t1},{\delta}_{t2})=({\delta}_{n},{\vec{\delta}}_{t}) . The two stiffnesses under normal loading {K}_{n} and tangential loading {K}_{t} characterise the surface and the filling materials of the crack (the same meaning as for the laws JOINT_MECA_RUPT and JOINT_MECA_FROT). The two amplitudes of kinematic coupling (normal {B}_{n} and tangential {B}_{t} ) are likewise material parameters. The expressions of the stresses and of the generalised forces give the following set of equations: \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{n}=\frac{\partial \psi (\vec{\delta},\vec{p},\alpha )}{\partial {\delta}_{n}}={K}_{n}({\delta}_{n}-{p}_{n})\\ {X}_{n}=\frac{\partial \psi (\vec{\delta},\vec{p},\alpha )}{\partial {p}_{n}}={K}_{n}({\delta}_{n}-{p}_{n})-{A}_{n}\cdot {p}_{n}\end{array} \textrm{et} \begin{array}{c}\vec{{\sigma}_{t}}=\frac{\partial \psi (\vec{\delta},\vec{p},\alpha )}{\partial {\delta}_{t}}={K}_{t}(\vec{{\delta}_{t}}-\vec{{p}_{t}})\\ \vec{{X}_{t}}=\frac{\partial \psi (\vec{\delta},\vec{p},\alpha )}{\partial \vec{{p}_{t}}}={K}_{t}(\vec{{\delta}_{t}}-\vec{{p}_{t}})-{A}_{t}\cdot \vec{{p}_{t}}\end{array} Y=-{A}_{n}'{p}_{n}^{2}/2-{A}_{t}'{\Vert \vec{{p}_{t}}\Vert }^{2}/2 Where {A}_{n}'=\frac{d{A}_{n}(\alpha )}{d\alpha } . By choosing the elastic domain as the intersection of two domains defined in the spaces of the generalised plastic stress (cone of revolution about {X}_{n} ) and of the generalised force dual to the damage variable, we obtain the following flow law: \begin{array}{c}{f}_{X}(\vec{X})=\Vert \vec{{X}_{t}}\Vert +\mu {X}_{n}-\overline{c}\le 0\\ \dot{\vec{p}}=\dot{\lambda}\frac{\partial {f}_{X}}{\partial \vec{X}}\\ {f}_{X}(\vec{X})\dot{\lambda}=0;\dot{\lambda}\ge 0\end{array} \textrm{et} \begin{array}{c}Y=-{A}_{n}^{I}{p}_{n}^{2}/2-{A}_{t}'{\Vert \vec{{p}_{t}}\Vert }^{2}/2\le {D}_{1}\\ \dot{\alpha}\ge 0\\ (Y-{D}_{1})\cdot \dot{\alpha}=0\end{array} {D}_{1} is a material parameter which plays the role of penalisation in fracture, like {P}_{\mathit{rupt}} for the law JOINT_MECA_RUPT. It can be shown that, with our choice of the softening function, the evolution of the damage variable and of plasticity is simultaneous (see the thesis of Fontana, ). This simplifies the description for the discretised version of the law: \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{n}={K}_{n}({\delta}_{n}-{p}_{n}^{-}-\Delta {p}_{n})\\ \vec{{\sigma}_{t}}={K}_{t}(\vec{{\delta}_{t}}-{\vec{p}}_{t}^{-}-\Delta \vec{{p}_{t}})\\ \vec{{X}_{t}}={K}_{t}(\vec{{\delta}_{t}}-{\vec{p}}_{t}^{-}-\Delta \vec{{p}_{t}})-{A}_{t}({\alpha}^{-}+\Delta \alpha )\cdot ({\vec{p}}_{t}^{-}+\Delta \vec{{p}_{t}})\\ {X}_{n}={K}_{n}({\delta}_{n}-{p}_{n}^{-}-\Delta {p}_{n})-{A}_{n}({\alpha}^{-}+\Delta \alpha )\cdot ({p}_{n}^{-}+\Delta {p}_{n})\\ Y=-{B}_{n}\cdot S'({\alpha}^{-}+\Delta \alpha )\cdot {({p}_{n}^{-}+\Delta {p}_{n})}^{2}/2-{B}_{t}\cdot S'({\alpha}^{-}+\Delta \alpha )\cdot {\Vert {\vec{p}}_{t}^{-}+\Delta \vec{{p}_{t}}\Vert }^{2}/2\end{array} where we have introduced the scalar function S(\alpha )={(1-\alpha )}^{3}/\sqrt{\alpha} . The thresholds are easily expressed in implicit discretised form: \begin{array}{c}{f}_{X}(\vec{X})=\Vert \vec{{X}_{t}}\Vert +\mu {X}_{n}-\overline{c}\le 0\\ \Delta {p}_{n}=\mu \Delta \lambda \\ \Delta \vec{{p}_{t}}=\Delta \lambda \frac{\vec{{X}_{t}}}{\Vert \vec{X}\Vert }\\ {f}_{X}(\vec{X})\Delta \lambda =0;\Delta \lambda \ge 0\\ Y=-{B}_{n}\cdot S'({\alpha}^{-}+\Delta \alpha )\cdot {({p}_{n}^{-}+\Delta {p}_{n})}^{2}/2-{B}_{t}\cdot S'({\alpha}^{-}+\Delta \alpha )\cdot {\Vert {\vec{p}}_{t}^{-}+\Delta \vec{{p}_{t}}\Vert }^{2}/2\le {D}_{1}\\ (Y-{D}_{1})\cdot \Delta \alpha =0\end{array} The resolution of this system of equations is carried out by the standard procedure of elastic prediction. In the damaging plastic phase, we obtain a system of implicit equations with the following four unknowns \Delta {p}_{n};\Delta \vec{{p}_{t}};\Delta \lambda ;\Delta \alpha . In this part we shall speak of the hydraulic part of the law, as well as of the coupling itself; all the details of the mechanical part of the law have been described previously. 6.1 Hydraulic modelling The fluid flows from the zones of high pressure towards those of low pressure. A theoretical way of taking steady flow into account is to associate with the given hydraulic state an energy 1 H(p(x)) depending on the pressure distribution. The first hypothesis consists in assuming that the energy depends explicitly on the pressure variation and not on the pressure itself H=H(\nabla p(x)) . By taking the simplest possible convex form of this dependence on the gradient, one thus obtains the energy H=C{(\overrightarrow{\nabla}p)}^{2}/2 where C is a parameter of the law, which does not depend on the pressure. By computing the generalised forces corresponding to the pressure-gradient field one obtains Fick's first law. The hydraulic flux is proportional to the pressure gradient: \overrightarrow{w}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial \overrightarrow{\nabla}p}=C\overrightarrow{\nabla}p In this energetic formalism one seeks the pressure field at equilibrium by minimisation of the hydraulic energy \underset{p(\overrightarrow{x})}{\min}\underset{\Omega}{\int}H(\overrightarrow{\nabla}p(\overrightarrow{x}))d\Omega . This gives an equilibrium equation resembling that of mechanics div\overrightarrow{w}=0 . Within the framework of this model the solution of the hydraulic equilibrium equation is equivalent to the solution of a mechanical problem in quasi-statics, where the hydraulic flux is equivalent to the stress \overrightarrow{w}\iff \sigma , the pressure field corresponds to the displacement field p(\vec{x})\iff u(\vec{x}) and finally the pressure gradient is akin to the strain field \overrightarrow{\nabla}p\mathrm{\iff }\varepsilon . 6.2 Influence of the hydraulics on the mechanics The presence of the fluid in the joint adds a hydrostatic stress and thereby modifies the normal mechanical stress {\sigma}_{n}\to {\sigma}_{n}-p . By imposing a large pressure one is able to break the joint by a simple hydraulic effect. One can shift the mechanical law downwards as a function of the value of the pressure p at each point in order to take the effects of the pressure into account; see figures r7.01.25-fig-joint-rup and r7.01.25-fig-joint-frot. 6.3 Influence of the mechanics on the hydraulics In the case of fluid flow through a crack the hydraulic flux must increase with the opening ( {\delta}_{n} ) of the latter ( \overrightarrow{w}~O({\delta}_{n})\overrightarrow{\nabla}p ). In Poiseuille's law, which was found empirically for the laminar flow of a viscous and incompressible fluid, the dependence of the flux on the opening is cubic (the law is often called the cubic law). The hydraulic part of the law uses this type of coupling. The equations to be solved are written in the following manner: div\overrightarrow{w}=0;\overrightarrow{w}=\frac{\rho}{12\bar{\mu}}{\delta}_{n}^{3}\overrightarrow{\nabla}p In the case of a fluid flow through the junctions of a dam, one observes non-negligible fluxes even for the closed joints. It is then necessary to define a minimum thickness {\epsilon}_{\min} , keyword OUV_MIN, below which the flux reaches its minimum value. We regularise the flow equations in the following manner: \vec{w}=\frac{\rho}{12\bar{\mu}}\max{({ϵ}_{min},{ϵ}_{min}+{\delta}_{n})}^{3}\vec{\nabla}p For a non-zero pressure gradient the flux never reaches the zero value, \min\overrightarrow{w}~{\epsilon}_{\min}^{3}\overrightarrow{\nabla}p , which corresponds to the flow through the permeable walls of the closed joint. 6.4 Hydromechanical coupling The hydromechanical coupling brings into play the two mechanisms described previously: on the one hand the fluid acts by pressure on the lips of the joint, on the other hand the more open the crack the easier the fluid flow. In the absence of external forces the hydromechanical computation is presented schematically in this form: \left\{ \begin{array}{cc}\vec{w}=\vec{w}(\vec{\delta}(u),\vec{\nabla}p);& div\vec{w}=0\\ \vec{\sigma}=\vec{\sigma}(\vec{\delta}(u),p);& div\vec{\sigma}=0\end{array}\text{}\Rightarrow \text{}\vec{Y}=\vec{Y}(\vec{X});div\vec{Y}=0\right. The solution of the hydromechanical equilibrium equations is equivalent to the solution of the mechanical problem in quasi-statics, where one introduces the generalised stresses \overrightarrow{Y}=(\overrightarrow{w},\overrightarrow{\sigma}) , and the vector field of the unknowns \overrightarrow{X}=(p,u) . 6.5 Tangent matrix Since the generalised forces depend on u only through \overrightarrow{\delta}(u) , in order to compute the tangent matrix of the hydromechanical coupling, it is necessary to know only the following four terms: \frac{\partial \overrightarrow{\sigma}}{\partial \overrightarrow{\delta}} \textrm{,} \frac{\partial \overrightarrow{\sigma}}{\partial p} , \frac{\partial \overrightarrow{w}}{\partial \overrightarrow{\nabla}p} et :math: \frac{\partial \overrightarrow{w}}{\partial \overrightarrow{\delta}} The first term is the same as in pure mechanics; it is given in equation . The second term is trivial, because the only non-zero component is equal to \partial {\sigma}_{n}/\partial p=-1 . The diagonal hydraulic term takes a simple form because the hydraulic flux depends only on the pressure gradient: \frac{\partial \vec{w}}{\partial \vec{\nabla}p}=\frac{\rho}{12\bar{\mu}}\max{({ϵ}_{min},{ϵ}_{min}+{\delta}_{n})}^{3} In the last term only the derivative with respect to the normal opening is non-zero: \frac{\partial \overrightarrow{w}}{\partial {\delta}_{n}}=\frac{\rho}{4\bar{\mu}}{({\epsilon}_{\min}+{\delta}_{n})}^{2}\overrightarrow{\nabla}p This quantity is equal to zero for a closed crack {\delta}_{n}<0 . The tangent matrix thus formulated is not symmetric. We use a simplified notation; the exact term would be: rate of energy density. 7 Features and validation Two constitutive laws JOINT_MECA_RUPT and JOINT_MECA_FROT are introduced. They are validated on the elementary test cases ssnp162 and the pseudo gravity-dam ssnp142 .
