r7.01.26 Constitutive law BETON_RAG r7.01.26 Constitutive law BETON_RAG Summary: This document presents the constitutive model BETON_RAG, used to estimate the long-term behaviour of structures affected by the alkali-aggregate reaction. It also details the formulation and the numerical treatment of the model. 1 Introduction A certain number of civil-engineering structures of the EDF generating fleet, mainly dams, present pathologies of swelling of the concretes due to the alkali-aggregate reaction (AAR). In order to assess the safety and operating margins of these installations, and to control the maintenance costs, EDF and the Laboratoire Matériaux et Durabilité des Constructions (LMDC) of the Université Paul Sabatier (Toulouse III) have developed a numerical model, Grimal , making it possible to simulate the mechanical behaviour of the structures affected by the AAR. The aim of this model is to evaluate the strains and the anisotropic damage (cracking) of the structures affected. Indeed, recent experimental research confirms that the swelling due to the AAR becomes strongly anisotropic when the stress state becomes deviatoric. Moreover, the kinetics and the amplitude of the reaction depending strongly on the water content and on the temperature of the concrete, the model takes these environmental phenomena into account. Furthermore, compressive and tensile creeps play a significant role in the behaviour of the structures; they have therefore been treated in a specific manner. In code_aster , the model is used under the name BETON_RAG. 2 Description of the model 2.1 General principle A large part of the mechanical model presented here and of the couplings which enter into it is inspired by the model developed in the thesis of E. Grimal . The alkali-aggregate reaction and its effects are modelled using a phenomenological approach. This approach takes into account the various important phenomena evolving within the concrete and influencing the chemical reaction. The main developments proposed in this model concern the interactions between the pressure of chemical origin and, the delayed strains on the one hand and the anisotropic strains induced by the presence of oriented cracks on the other hand. The effects of humidity on the development of the alkali-reaction as well as on the capillary pressure inducing the shrinkage of the matrix are also considered. The dependence between the evolution of the swellings and the stress state is then a consequence of all these elementary phenomena; the mechanical effects of the alkali-reaction are therefore the consequences of an internal “long-term” loading due to the evolution of the chemical pressure ( {P}_{g} in figure r7.01.26-fig-2-1), combined with the external loading {\sigma}_{i} . Principle of the constitutive model of concrete subjected to a swelling pressure {P}_{g} , in addition to the external stress {\sigma}_{i} , loads the cement matrix. The latter is considered as a damageable visco-elasto-plastic medium (VEPD module in figure r7.01.26-fig-2-1). The next paragraph presents how the pressure due to the formation of gel is evaluated, in accordance with the environmental conditions and the strain state. Then, the mechanical model is set out within the framework of the thermodynamics of irreversible processes. 2.2 Evolution law of the internal pressure The pressure {P}_{g} due to the formation of gel in the porosity is evaluated by making the hypothesis that the stress state does not modify the chemical progress of the alkali-aggregate reaction. In accordance with the various available modellings, studied in the bibliographic part Ulm , Lemarchand , Coussy , the concrete is considered as a porous medium made up of a solid matrix and of gel occupying a part of the connected porosity. This porosity is formed of two types of pores, those initially connected to the reaction sites and those generated by the volumetric strain modifying the porosity ( {b}^{g}\mathit{tr}(\varepsilon ) in the equation ). The porosity connected to the reaction sites is written in the form {\varphi}_{0}={A}_{0}{V}^{g} , in which {A}_{0} is the progress from which the initial connected porosity is filled. Thus, as long as the volume of gel created ( {\mathit{AV}}^{g} ) is less than {A}_{0}{V}^{g} , the gel lodges in the connected porosity and {P}_{g} remains zero. {P}_{g} will increase only from the moment when all the porosity is filled: {\text{AV}}^{g}\ge \langle {A}_{0}{V}^{g}+{b}^{g}\text{tr}(\varepsilon )\rangle Taking these remarks into account, an expression relating the gel pressure and the volume of gel created ( {\mathit{AV}}^{g} ) is proposed: \mathit{Pg}={M}_{g}{⟨A.{V}_{g}-{⟨{A}_{0}.{V}_{g}+{b}_{g}\mathit{tr}(\varepsilon )⟩}_{+}⟩}_{+} In this expression: - {V}_{g} is the maximum volume of gel which can be created by the chemical reaction. - A is the progress of the chemical reaction, increasing from 0 for the sound concrete to 1 when the reaction is completed. - {M}_{g} is comparable to an elasticity modulus of the gel and {b}_{g} may be comparable to a Biot coefficient for the gel. The various positive parts allow: - a taking into account of the influence of the volumetric strain induced by an external loading on a variation of the connected porosity, - an increase in the pressure of chemical origin if and only if the gel manages to fill the connected porosity. Note: The pressure output by the model in the internal variables corresponds to the effective pressure, that is to say the product {b}_{g}{P}_{g} . 2.3 Progress of the reaction The progress of the reaction A mentioned previously is a function of the temperature and of the water content of the concrete. The evolution law used to evaluate the chemical progress is inspired by the work of S. Poyet . He shows that the gel created during the time ( t ) and its creation kinetics are proportional to the degree of saturation ( \mathit{Sr} ) of the concrete, the degree of saturation being defined by: \text{Sr}=\frac{C}{{C}_{\text{sat}}} In this expression, C is the concentration of free water contained per unit volume of concrete and {C}_{\mathit{sat}} is the value of C when the concrete is totally saturated. In order to take the effect of temperature into account, the Arrhenius law is used to model the thermal activation (Capra ). Finally, the following law is proposed: \frac{\partial A}{\partial t}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}=\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{\alpha}_{0}.\exp\left[\frac{{E}_{a}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{{T}_{\mathit{ref}}}-\frac{1}{T}\right)\right]\frac{{⟨{S}_{r}-{S}_{r}^{0}⟩}_{+}}{\left(1-{S}_{r}^{0}\right)}{⟨{S}_{r}-A⟩}_{+} In this law, {\alpha}_{0} is a kinetic parameter, {E}_{a} is the activation energy of the alkali-aggregate reaction (usually of a value close to 47000J/\mathit{mol}/°K Lombardi ), R is the perfect-gas constant ( 8.31J/\mathit{mol} ), {T}_{\mathit{ref}} (in kelvin) is the absolute temperature of the test allowing the identification of {\alpha}_{0} , T is the temperature of the material point. The term \langle \text{Sr}-A\rangle means that the chemical affinity of the reaction is conditioned by the degree of saturation of the concrete, Poyet having shown in his thesis that the progress A (which is a normalised variable) cannot exceed a limit value very close to the degree of saturation; he explains this by the fact that only the fraction of aggregate in contact with water can lead to the reaction. Consequently the amplitude of the reaction is proportional to the degree of saturation {S}_{r} . In the same way, the path travelled by the ions in order to reach the reactive silica is all the greater as the degree of saturation is low, which leads to a decrease in the kinetics. This kinetic effect of the degree of saturation is taken into account by means of the term \frac{⟨\mathit{Sr}-{S}_{r}^{0}⟩}{\left(1-{S}_{r}^{0}\right)} , in which {S}_{r}^{0} represents the saturation threshold from which the evolution of the chemical reaction becomes possible. Figure r7.01.26-fig-2-2 presents a few examples of variations of the progress A for various humidity states. The greater {S}_{r} is, the greater A is, A being maximal ( A=1 ) when the concrete is saturated ( {S}_{r}=1 ). If the concrete remains in an unsaturated state ( {S}_{r} 0 ) if the model is used in a classical hydromechanical approach. {\sigma}_{0}^{s} is the effective spherical stress on the solid skeleton. This level involves a purely elastic component of the concrete and can be schematised and written in equation form in the following way: {\sigma}_{0}^{s}={k}_{e}{\varepsilon}_{e}^{s} - Level 1: This level corresponds to a part of the microporosity weakly connected to the open macroporosity and subject to reversible water movements. The associated viscoelasticity is modelled by a Kelvin-Voigt solid (see r7.01.26-fig-2-8): {\sigma}^{s}={k}_{r}{\varepsilon}_{r}^{s}+{\eta}_{r}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{r}^{s} - Level 2: This level corresponds here to the interfoliar nanoporosity of the CSH. This level ensures the irreversible character of the viscous strains of the CSH. In this last expression, {\varepsilon}_{i}^{s} is an irreversible strain. {\sigma}_{i}^{s}={\eta}_{i}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{i}^{s} The rheological diagram of r7.01.26-fig-2-8 makes it possible to establish the equation: {\dot{\varepsilon}_{i}^{s}}=\frac{{k}_{r}^{s}{\varepsilon}_{r}^{s}+{\eta}_{r}^{s}{\dot{\varepsilon}_{r}^{s}}}{{\eta}_{i}^{s}} Since the damper linked to \eta_{i} is not placed in parallel with a spring, under constant stress it can lead to creep strains proportional to the duration of the loading. In order to avoid the divergence of these strains, a viscous non-linearity is considered. Physically, this corresponds to a consolidation of the specimen and to entanglements of the CSH sheets. This requires the introduction of an internal variable corresponding to the maximum of the norm of the irreversible creep strain tensor reached before the time step i (see equation ). \Vert \varepsilon_{éq,\, irr,\, i} \Vert = \underset{t \leq t_i}{\max}\left(\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{irr}^f:\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{irr}^f}\right) In this equation, {\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}_{irr}^f denotes the complete irreversible creep strain tensor, comprising the spherical and deviatoric parts. The symbol : corresponds to the doubly contracted product. The initial irreversible viscosity \eta_{irr}^0 is multiplied by an exponential increase factor depending on the norm of the irreversible creep strain tensor \Vert \varepsilon_{éq,\, irr,\, i} \Vert according to the equation , where \kappa_{irr} is a parameter controlling the equivalent irreversible strain for which the viscosity increases so much that there is no longer any significant evolution of the irreversible creep strains. \eta_{irr} = \eta_{irr}^0 exp\left(\frac{\Vert \varepsilon_{éq,\, irr,\, i} \Vert}{\kappa_{irr}}\right) 2.5.1.2 Deviatoric creep In accordance with the observations of Acker , , Bernard et al. , the viscoelastic aspect of the deviatoric behaviour is attributed to the interfoliar shear of the CSH sheets. This shear occurs at two scales: - A nanoscopic viscoelastic scale corresponding to the water weakly bound to the sheets, - A microscopic scale corresponding to free water weakly adsorbed between the sheets and subject to desiccation. Finally, the part of the cement paste made up of better crystallised hydrates (portlandite and hydrated calcium aluminate) has an almost elastic behaviour. The deviatoric viscosity therefore keeps a multi-scale character; one then proposes to represent it in a manner similar to the spherical branch, which moreover simplifies the implementation of the model (rheological equations similar to those of the deviatoric branch). The system governing the strains of the deviatoric rheological model is written, for each component i,\,j of the deviatoric strain tensor: {\dot{\varepsilon}_{irr,\,i,j}^{d}}=\frac{{k}_{r}{\varepsilon}_{r,\,i,j}^{d}+{\eta}_{r}{d}{\dot{\varepsilon}_{r,\,i,j}^{d}}}{{\eta}_{irr}^{d}} In this equation, the variables linked to the irreversible creep have been renamed {toto}_{irr} in order to bring more clarity with respect to the introduction of the indices i,\,j . One can specify at this stage of the modelling that the systems of rheological equations admit an analytical solution for a loading in total strain linear as a function of time. We shall take advantage of this solution in the implementation of the numerical verification test cases. 2.5.2 Module dedicated to the modelling of the anisotropic AAR swelling (VDt) The VDt module (figure r7.01.26-fig-2-3) models an increase in the anelastic strain when the concrete is subjected to a tensile stress induced by the AAR leading to damage. We know that in the presence of the AAR, the following strain–damage relation must be respected (figure r7.01.26-fig-2-3): {\varepsilon}_{i}^{\text{vdt}}={\varepsilon}_{0}\frac{{d}_{i}^{\text{RO}}}{1-{d}_{i}^{R0}} In this equation, {\varepsilon}_{0} is a parameter identified on a large number of tests and on concretes of various natures (Sellier ). Usually, its value is close to 0.35%. {d}_{i}^{\mathit{R0}} is a principal value of the tensor of the damages due to the tensile stresses induced by the AAR. Here, it will be evaluated in the following way: {d}_{i}^{R0}=min\left\lbrace {d}_{i}^{t};1-\exp\left(-\frac{1}{{m}^{t}}{\left(\frac{{b}_{g}.{P}_{g}}{{\sigma}^{\text{u t}}}\right)}^{{m}^{t}}\right)\right\rbrace In this expression, {d}_{i}^{t} is a principal value of the tensile damage tensor. {m}^{t} and {\sigma}^{\text{u t}} are parameters of the damage evolution law. We shall return to the choice of the damage variables and of their evolution law in the following chapter. 2.6 Damage model After having given the broad principles of the model, we shall first recall the thermodynamic concepts on which we must base our formulation. Secondly, we propose the free-energy potentials and the complementary laws defining the model. This presentation makes it possible to verify the dissipation conditions imposed by the thermodynamics of irreversible processes necessary for the convergence of the analyses. 2.6.1 Principle of the modelling The alkali-aggregate reaction causes swellings of the structure. These swellings can be very different according to the loadings of the damaged structures. The expansion considered isotropic in unrestrained swelling becomes a strongly anisotropic expansion as soon as the concrete is subjected to a deviatoric stress state (Multon , ). The microcracking generated by the intra-pore pressure is then prevented in the loading direction and the swelling appears systematically associated with the directions where the compressive stresses are the weakest. This phenomenon is particularly visible in beams where the cracks orient themselves parallel to the reinforcement. A macrocracking mechanism, due to the opening of the cracks in the direction where the material is the most damaged, amplifies this anisotropy. The micro- and macrocrackings generated lead to a drop in the elastic modulus of the concrete; this drop is usually modelled by damage theory. We present below the principles of the damage model which we shall apply to the stresses coming from the rheological scheme presented in the previous chapter. In order to simulate the behaviour of concrete degraded by the alkali-aggregate reaction, an anisotropic damage model, based on a realistic cracking criterion, must be used. This damage model must be formulated within the thermodynamic framework (Lemaitre ). The thermodynamic framework makes it possible to avoid possible inconsistencies of formulation which would lead to problems of physical representation and of numerical convergence. To this end, a thermodynamic free-energy potential from which the constitutive laws of the material derive must be proposed. In the case where the mechanical dissipation can be decoupled from the other dissipations (thermal, hydric or chemical), the dissipation condition is given by the Clausius-Duhem equation (equation ). This relation expresses the fact that the power of the “external forces” is at each instant greater than the recoverable power stored by the material; a part of the power of the “external forces” being dissipated mechanically by decohesion, friction, etc. The Clausius-Duhem equation for an isothermal mechanical transformation is classically written: \sigma :\dot{\varepsilon}-\rho \dot{\psi}\ge 0 In this expression, \sigma is the stress tensor, \varepsilon that of the total strains and \rho \psi the volumetric free-energy potential. The latter is chosen so that the dissipation is zero in the case of perfectly elastic loading. This restriction implies that the stresses \sigma derive from the free-energy potential with respect to the elastic strains {\varepsilon}^{e} , that is: \sigma =\rho \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}} With the usual hypothesis of partition of the total strain: {\varepsilon}^{e}=\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{\text{an}} Where {\varepsilon}^{\text{an}} is the anelastic strain. Two internal variables, linked by this partition equation, are thus defined: the anelastic strain {\varepsilon}^{\text{an}} and the thermoelastic strain {\varepsilon}^{\text{e}} . In our model, {\varepsilon}^{\text{e}} is the strain at level 0 of the rheological scheme; {\varepsilon}^{\text{an}} contains the strains {\varepsilon}_{\mathit{vdt}} and {\varepsilon}_{\mathit{vep}} presented in figure r7.01.26-fig-2-3 as well as the thermal strain if applicable. The micro- and macrocrackings generated by the stresses lead to a drop in the elastic modulus of the concrete; this drop is usually modelled by damage theory. We present below the principles of a damage model The model proposed is based on a tensorial representation of the damage. This representation is formulated so that the unilateral aspect of the behaviour can be treated simply and independently in each of the three principal directions of the effective stresses. The effective stress tensor is estimated from the principle of equivalence in elastic strain, at level 0 of the rheological scheme (figure r7.01.26-fig-2-3): \tilde{\sigma}={R}^{0}:{\varepsilon}^{e} With {R}^{0} the fourth-order elasticity tensor of the sound concrete, computed from the Young modulus and the Poisson ratio of the uncracked concrete. The apparent stresses are linked to the effective stresses by the damage tensor D : \sigma =(I-D):\tilde{\sigma} In this expression, ( I-D ) is an integrity tensor, also of fourth order, made up on the one hand of the identity matrix ( I ) and on the other hand of the damage tensor. By treating the cracking phenomenon from the fourth-order damage tensor D , the free-energy potential takes the following general form: \rho\psi=\frac{1}{2}(I-D):{R}^{0}:{\varepsilon}^{e}:{\varepsilon}^{e} In indicial notation this last relation is written: \rho\psi=\frac{1}{2}{(I-D)}_{ijkl}{R}_{\text{klmn}}^{0}{\varepsilon}_{\text{mn}}{\varepsilon}_{ij} Thus, the previous equations lead to writing the Clausius-Duhem relation in the following form: \sigma :{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\text{an}}-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial D}:\dot{D}-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {V}^{\text{an}}}:{\dot{V}}^{\text{an}}\ge 0 Where the {V}^{\mathrm{an}} are the internal variables associated with the anelastic strains. Or again with the indicial notation: \underset{{\phi}^{\text{an}}}{\underbrace{\sigma_{ij} \dot{\varepsilon}_{ij}^{\text{an}} - \rho \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial V^{\text{an}}_{ij}} \dot{V}^{\text{an}}_{ij}}}\quad\underset{\phi^D}{\underbrace{\underset{Y_{ijkl}}{\underbrace{- \rho \left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial D}\right)_{ijkl}}} \dot{D}_{ijkl}}}\ge 0 This last relation makes it possible to define the dissipation by anelastic strain {\phi }^{\text{an}} as well as the dissipation by mechanical damage {\phi }^{D} . It also makes it possible to define the thermodynamic forces {Y}_{ijkl} called energy-release rates. A simple way of ensuring the positive character of the dissipation whatever the state of the material and of the loading is to postulate the decoupling of the dissipations by anelastic strains and by damage; one must then verify separately {\phi }^{\text{an}}\ge 0 and {\phi }^{D}\ge 0 , or again: \left\{ \begin{array}{c}{\sigma}_{ij}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{an}}-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {V}_{ij}^{\text{an}}}{\dot{V}}_{ij}^{\text{an}}\ge 0\\ -{Y}_{ijkl}{\dot{D}}_{ijkl}\ge 0\end{array}\right. In viscoelasticity, the condition of dissipation by anelastic strain leads to choosing, for the viscosity laws, positive coefficients. In plasticity, one postulates the existence of a dissipation pseudo-potential ( {\phi }^{\text{ }\text{an}} ). The latter being a positive convex function in stress space and zero at the origin, so that the positivity of the dissipation is automatically verified. The flow law of the anelastic strains can be written in the form: {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{an}}=\dot{\lambda}\frac{\partial {\phi }^{\text{ }\text{an}}}{\partial {\sigma}_{ij}} Where \dot{\lambda} is a positive scalar called the plastic multiplier. The latter is computed so that the increase in the anelastic strain leads to a relaxation of the stresses, this making it possible to verify the plasticity criterion, itself also expressed in stress space. It remains to verify the positivity condition of the dissipation by damage. One can for this draw inspiration from the formalism briefly described previously for plasticity. That is to say, give oneself a dissipation pseudo-potential that is convex and zero at the origin in the space of the energy-release rates, from which the increments of the components of the damage tensor derive. One then has the following damage evolution law: {\dot{D}}_{ijkl}=-\dot{\lambda}\frac{\partial {\phi }^{\text{ }D}}{\partial {Y}_{ijkl}} The “damage multiplier” \dot{\lambda} having to be computed so as to verify the damage criterion. The construction of the pseudo-potential being arduous, the use of a more rational means, making it possible to ensure a form of the damage tensor consistent with the physical phenomena at the origin of the damage, is regularly used. For this, one calls on homogenisation theory. The damage tensor D is estimated there from the constitutive law of the sound material ( {R}^{0} ) and from that of a representative elementary volume (REV) of cracked material ( {R}^{D} ); one then has: {D}_{ijkl}={\delta}_{\text{ik}}{\delta}_{\text{jl}}-{R}_{\text{ijmn}}^{0}{R}_{\text{mnkl}}^{{D}^{-1}} The representativeness of the constitutive law of the equivalent damaged material will depend on the quality of the homogenisation of the REV. The unilateral character of the behaviour of the concrete is induced by the restoration of stiffness linked to the re-closures of the cracks. In the case of a cyclic uniaxial loading with change of the sign of the stress, one can observe experimentally the creation of tensile cracks perpendicular to the loading axis and of compressive cracks parallel to the loading axis. The losses of stiffness in tension and in compression are therefore attributed to at least two orthogonal networks of cracks. When the stress passes from tension to compression, the tensile cracks are closed and the compressive cracks are activated. When the stress passes from compression to tension, the tensile cracks open and are activated in their turn. In order to model “physically” the unilateral behaviour of the concrete, it is convenient to reason from a tensorial description of the crack network. The losses of stiffness in tension or in compression can thus be treated in each direction of space as a function of the sign of the stresses and of the orientation of the cracks: if a principal stress is positive, the most active cracks will be those whose orientation is globally perpendicular to the stress, whereas if the principal stress is negative, the most active cracks will be parallel to the stress. 2.6.1.1 Anisotropic damage by tension The various reasons briefly stated previously lead us to propose a damage model based on a representation of tensile cracking by a second-order tensor estimated from the effective tensile stress tensor {\tilde{\sigma}}^{t} and not from the extensions. These are here the effective stresses in the sense of damage; they must not be confused with the effective stresses in the sense of the mechanics of porous media, which affect the whole solid skeleton, whereas the effective stresses in the sense of damage affect only the undamaged part of the solid skeleton. The effective tensile stress tensor is obtained from the principal effective stresses, themselves coming from the application of the principle of equivalence in strain to the rheological model used for the solid skeleton: {\tilde{\sigma}}^{t}=\langle {\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}\rangle .({\overrightarrow{e}}_{i}\otimes {\overrightarrow{e}}_{i}) Where {\overrightarrow{e}}_{i} is the eigenvector associated with \langle {\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}\rangle which is the positive part of the effective principal stress {\tilde{\sigma}}_{i} . Using the principle of equivalence in strain stated by Lemaitre , the effective tensile stresses make it possible to define the associated elastic strain tensor {\varepsilon}^{\text{et}} : {\varepsilon}^{\text{et}}=\frac{1+{\nu}^{0}}{{E}^{0}}.{\tilde{\sigma}}^{t}-\frac{{\nu}^{0}}{{E}^{0}}\text{tr}({\tilde{\sigma}}^{t}).\mathit{Id} The cracking criterion retained for the tensile damage is that of Rankine; the threshold stress tensor is denoted {\sigma}^{R} ; the criterion expresses in each principal direction {\overrightarrow{e}}_{i} of the effective stress tensor the non-exceeding of the normal component of the threshold stress: {f}_{i}=\langle {\tilde{\sigma}}_{i}\rangle -{\sigma}^{R}:({\overrightarrow{e}}_{i}\otimes {\overrightarrow{e}}_{i}) The updating of the threshold stress tensor is in accordance with the consistency condition which is written simply: {\sigma}_{ii}^{R}=\sup\left({⟨\tilde{{\sigma}_{i}}⟩}_{+},{\sigma}_{ii}^{R}\right) where the {\sigma}_{ii}^{R} are the terms of the diagonal of the tensor {\sigma}^{R} expressed in the principal basis of the effective stresses. Admitting that the “equivalent” cracks, and therefore the damages, have the same principal directions as the threshold stresses, one can define the damage tensor in the basis of the principal stresses of {\sigma}^{R} : {d}^{t}={d}_{i}^{t}.({\overrightarrow{v}}_{i}\otimes {\overrightarrow{v}}_{i}) The damage {d}^{t} represents a set of three orthogonal networks of plane cracks coexisting within one and the same representative elementary volume. The terms {\overrightarrow{v}}_{i} are the eigenvectors of {\sigma}^{R} and {d}_{i}^{t} the eigenvalues of the damage tensor estimated from the eigenvalues {\sigma}_{i}^{R} of {\sigma}^{R} , and from the following evolution law inspired by the Weibull law (Sellier ). Damage evolution laws: {d}_{i}^{t}=1-\exp\left(\underset{{\beta}_{i}}{\underbrace{{-\frac{1}{{m}^{t}}{\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{i}^{R}}{{\sigma}^{\text{ut}}}\right) }^{{m}^{t}}}}}\right) In this expression {m}^{t} is a parameter all the greater as the material is brittle, {\sigma}^{\mathit{ut}} is also a “material” parameter; it is comparable to a cohesion; in practice {m}^{t} can be identified from the experimental damage measured from the peak of the constitutive law, {\sigma}^{\mathit{ut}} is directly linked to the strength. We shall give the relations between the parameters of the model and the measurable quantities (grandeurs) in the following paragraphs. Introducing the cracking index defined by: {\beta}_{i}=\frac{1}{{m}^{t}}{\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{i}^{R}}{{\sigma}^{\text{ut}}}\right) }^{{m}^{t}} There comes the relation between the damage and the cracking index: \frac{1}{1-{d}_{i}^{t}}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}=\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{e}^{{\beta}_{i}} This last relation will be practical for the construction of the free-energy potential. The internal variables introduced at this level will also make it possible to memorise the cracking state. It is also necessary, from this point of view, to note that the damage is an increasing and continuous function of the cracking index, which is itself an increasing function of the threshold stress. As the latter can only increase, the principal values of the damage tensor can only grow. As regards the normal strain-stress relations, the passage from the damage tensor to the constitutive law of the damaged material must express on the one hand a decrease in the Young modulus in the direction normal to the crack and on the other hand an attenuation of the Poisson effect between the direction orthogonal to the plane of the crack and the directions contained in its plane. In order to respect these conditions, we propose to use the following constitutive law: {\varepsilon}_{ii}^{e}=\frac{{\sigma}_{ii}^{t}}{{E}^{0}(1-{d}_{i}^{t})}-\frac{{\nu}^{0}}{{E}^{0}}({\sigma}_{jj}^{t}+{\sigma}_{kk}^{t}) Or again as a function of the cracking indices: {\varepsilon}_{ii}^{e}=\frac{{\sigma}_{ii}^{t}}{{E}^{0}}{e}^{{\beta}_{i}}-\frac{{\nu}^{0}}{{E}^{0}}({\sigma}_{jj}^{t}+{\sigma}_{kk}^{t}) In this expression {E}^{0} is the Young modulus of the sound material and {\nu}^{0} its Poisson ratio. The relation is written in the principal basis of the damages. It must be noted that this law is expressed here as a function of the apparent stresses and not of the effective stresses; it is this particular writing which makes it possible to benefit simply from an attenuation of the Poisson effect as a function of the cracking in the directions j and k as well as from the symmetry of the compliance tensor of the constitutive law. The shear slip-stress relations are also written in the principal damage basis; the relation proposed is the following: {\varepsilon}_{ij}^{e}=\frac{{\sigma}_{ij}^{t}}{2{\mu}^{0}(1-{d}_{i}^{t})(1-{d}_{j}^{t})} Which one can also express as a function of the cracking indices: {\varepsilon}_{ij}^{e}=\frac{{\sigma}_{ij}^{t}}{2{\mu}^{0}}{e}^{{\beta}_{i}+{\beta}_{j}} The shear slip-stress relation involves the damages on the two principal directions of cracking loaded in shear; the combination of the damages is of the weakest-link type. Besides the interaction between damages which this writing provides, one can attribute to it a statistical meaning by considering that the damages are comparable to probabilities of encountering surface discontinuities on the facets (Sellier ). Under this hypothesis, the weakest-link theory indicates that the probability that a shear stress passes over two orthogonal facets is equal to the probability of having simultaneously two orthogonal unfailed surfaces. Neglecting the statistical dependences between the two cracking planes, this probability is equal to the product of the probabilities of having on each of these two facets a continuity of the material; one deduces from it the denominator of the equation . Finally, the last reason for which we have adopted this form for the damage of the shear coefficient is that the resulting constitutive law presents the response expected from the test of rotation of the principal directions (known as the Willam test). In order to express the free-energy potential as a function of the elastic strains, it is necessary to ensure the invertibility of the stress-strain relations proposed previously. For this, let us express the apparent normal stresses as a function of the elastic strains: {\sigma}_{ii}^{t}=\frac{{E}^{0}}{{D}^{n}}\left[\left({e}^{{\beta}_{j}+{\beta}_{k}}-{\nu}^{{0}^{2}}\right){\varepsilon}_{ii}^{\mathit{et}}+{\nu}^{0}{\varepsilon}_{jj}^{\mathit{et}}\left(\nu +{e}^{{\beta}_{k}}\right)+{\nu}^{0}{\varepsilon}_{kk}^{\mathit{et}}\left(\nu +{e}^{{\beta}_{j}}\right)\right] with {D}^{n}={e}^{{\beta}_{i}+{\beta}_{j}+{\beta}_{k}}-{\nu}^{{0}^{2}}\left({e}^{{\beta}_{i}}+{e}^{{\beta}_{j}}+{e}^{{\beta}_{k}}\right)-2{\nu}^{{0}^{3}} One shows that {D}^{n} is always positive if the following two conditions are verified: \left\{ \begin{array}{c}{\beta}_{i}\ge 0\forall i\in \left\lbrace 1,2,3\right\rbrace \\ \nu \le 0.5\end{array}\right. The condition on the Poisson ratio is verified; it is the same for the condition on the {\beta}_{i} , given the evolution law of the damages proposed previously. The invertibility of the normal strain – normal stress relation is therefore assured whatever the level of damage. As regards the relations between the shear rates and the shear stresses, the inversion is immediate and one has: {\sigma}_{ij}^{t}=\frac{{E}^{0}{\varepsilon}_{ij}^{\mathit{et}}}{(1+{\nu}^{0}){e}^{{\beta}_{i}+{\beta}_{j}}} As the denominator of this expression lies in the interval [1,+\infty [ the invertibility is there too assured. By integrating the stress-strain relations with respect to the elastic strains associated with the effective tensile stresses, one obtains the elastic free-energy potential associated with the effective tensile stresses. This potential, denoted \rho {\Psi}^{t} in what follows, is here expressed in the principal basis of the damages: \rho {\Psi}^{t}=\rho {\Psi}^{t(n)}+\rho {\Psi}^{t(s)} With {\rho\psi}^{t(n)} the potential of the free energies associated with the extensions: {\rho\psi}^{t(n)}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{{E}^{0}}{{D}^{n}}\left( \begin{array}{c}({e}^{{\beta}_{j}+{\beta}_{k}}-{\upsilon }^{{0}^{2}}){\varepsilon}_{ii}^{{\text{et}}^{2}}+({e}^{{\beta}_{i}+{\beta}_{k}}-{\upsilon }^{{0}^{2}}){\varepsilon}_{jj}^{{\text{et}}^{2}}+({e}^{{\beta}_{j}+{\beta}_{i}}-{\upsilon }^{{0}^{2}}){\varepsilon}_{kk}^{{\text{et}}^{2}}\\ +{\mathrm{2\upsilon }}^{0}({\varepsilon}_{jj}^{\text{et}}{\varepsilon}_{ii}^{\text{et}}({\upsilon }^{0}+{e}^{{\beta}_{k}})+{\varepsilon}_{kk}^{\text{et}}{\varepsilon}_{ii}^{\text{et}}({\upsilon }^{0}+{e}^{{\beta}_{j}})+{\varepsilon}_{jj}^{\text{et}}{\varepsilon}_{kk}^{\text{et}}({\upsilon }^{0}+{e}^{{\beta}_{i}}))\end{array}\right) And {\rho\psi}^{t(s)} that associated with the elastic shear strains: {\rho\psi}^{t(s)}=\frac{1}{2}{G}^{0}({e}^{-({\beta}_{i}+{\beta}_{j})}{\varepsilon}_{ij}^{{\text{et}}^{2}}+{e}^{-({\beta}_{i}+{\beta}_{k})}{\varepsilon}_{\text{ik}}^{{\text{et}}^{2}}{e}^{-({\beta}_{j}+{\beta}_{k})}{\varepsilon}_{\text{jk}}^{{\text{et}}^{2}}) The potential can also be expressed simply as a function of the apparent stresses {\sigma}^{t} associated with the effective tensile stresses. That is, as regards the potential associated with the extensions: {\rho\psi}^{t(n)}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{ii}^{{t}^{2}}}{{E}_{i}}+\frac{{\sigma}_{jj}^{{t}^{2}}}{{E}_{j}}+\frac{{\sigma}_{ii}^{{t}^{2}}}{{E}_{i}}+2\frac{{\upsilon }^{0}}{{E}^{0}}({\sigma}_{ii}^{t}{\sigma}_{jj}^{t}+{\sigma}_{ii}^{t}{\sigma}_{kk}^{t}+{\sigma}_{kk}^{t}{\sigma}_{jj}^{t})\right) The {E}_{i}={E}^{0}(1-{d}_{i}^{t}) being the Young moduli of the damaged material. And for the potential associated with the shears: {\rho\psi}^{t(s)}=(1+{\upsilon }^{0}){E}^{0}\left( \frac{{\sigma}_{ij}^{{t}^{2}}}{{E}_{i}{E}_{j}}+\frac{{\sigma}_{\text{ik}}^{{t}^{2}}}{{E}_{i}{E}_{k}}+\frac{{\sigma}_{\text{kj}}^{{t}^{2}}}{{E}_{k}{E}_{j}}\right) The cracking indices {\beta}_{i} being able to be linked bijectively to the principal tensile damages {d}_{i}^{t} , the expression of Clausius-Duhem can be expressed as a function of the cracking indices. For more clarity we here momentarily disregard the role of the anelastic strains, by assuming a damageable elastic transformation involving only the effective tensile stresses: \sigma :{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}^{\text{et}}-\left( \underset{-{\varphi}^{\text{Dt}(n)}}{\underbrace{\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{t(n)}}{\partial {\beta}_{i}}{\dot{\beta}}_{i}}}+\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{t(n)}}{\partial R}:\dot{R}+\underset{-{\varphi}^{\text{Ft}(s)}}{\underbrace{\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{t(s)}}{\partial {\beta}_{i}}\dot{{\beta}_{i}}}}+\frac{\partial {\psi}^{t(s)}}{\partial R}:\dot{R}+\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{t}}{\partial {\varepsilon}_{I}^{\text{et}}}{\varepsilon}_{I}^{\text{et}}\right) \ge 0 In this expression, {\varepsilon}_{I}^{\text{et}} is a principal value of the tensor of the strains associated with the effective tensile stresses, {\varphi}^{\text{Dt}(n)} is the dissipation associated with the normal strains and {\varphi}^{\text{Dt}(s)} that associated with the shears. R is the passage matrix from the principal basis of the elastic strains to the principal basis of the damages; \dot{R} can be interpreted as a rotation rate of the damage tensor if the principal directions of strain do not rotate. Taking into account the form of the free-energy potential associated with the shears then makes it possible to compute the dissipation due to the damage associated with the shears. One has: {\phi }^{\text{Dt}(s)\dot{\beta}}={\dot{\beta}}_{i}\underset{\ge 0}{\underbrace{\left( \frac{1}{2}{G}^{0}({e}^{-({\beta}_{i}+{\beta}_{j})}{\varepsilon}_{ij}^{{\text{et}}^{2}}+{e}^{-({\beta}_{i}+{\beta}_{k})}{\varepsilon}_{\text{ik}}^{{\text{et}}^{2}})\right) }} This expression is always positive since {\dot{\beta}}_{i} is positive; the positivity of the dissipation associated with the shears is therefore verified. As regards the dissipation associated with the normal strains, one can remark that by using the stress expressions of {\psi}^{t(n)} and of {\varepsilon}^{\text{et}} in the Clausius-Duhem equation, one has: \sigma :{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\text{et}}-\rho {\dot{\psi}}^{t(n)}=\left( \underset{-\frac{{{\sigma}_{i}^{t}}^{2}}{{E}_{i}^{2}}}{\underbrace{\sigma :\frac{\partial {\varepsilon}^{\text{et}}}{\partial {E}_{i}}}}-\underset{-\frac{1}{2}\frac{{{\sigma}_{i}^{t}}^{2}}{{E}_{i}^{2}}}{\underbrace{\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{t(n)}}{\partial {E}_{i}}}}\right) \dot{{E}_{i}}=\underset{\le 0}{\underbrace{-\frac{1}{2}\frac{{{\sigma}_{i}^{t}}^{2}}{{E}_{i}^{2}}}}\dot{E}_{i}\ge 0 Which implies that {\dot{E}}_{i}\le 0 . Now {\dot{E}}_{i}=-{E}^{0}{\dot{d}}_{i}^{t} and {\dot{d}}_{i}^{t} being positive, the second principle is also verified for the damage associated with the normal strains. In the case of non-radial loading, the Clausius-Duhem relation contains the terms due to the evolutions of the principal damages, which are always positive as we have just seen, as well as terms due to the rotations of the damage directions. The latter express a drawing together of the orthotropy directions of the material and those of the loading. From an analytical point of view, this second transformation is analogous to a rotation of the principal directions of strain without damage. It therefore takes place without dissipation; the following relation must therefore be respected at each instant: \left( \sigma :\frac{\partial {\varepsilon}^{\text{et}}}{\partial R}-\rho \frac{\partial {\Psi}^{t}}{\partial R}\right) \dot{R}=0 Which implies: \sigma :\frac{\partial {\varepsilon}^{\text{et}}}{\partial R}=\rho \frac{\partial {\Psi}^{t}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{\text{et}}}:\frac{\partial {\varepsilon}^{\text{et}}}{\partial R} Now, by construction, \sigma =\rho \frac{\partial {\Psi}^{t}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{\text{et}}} , so this condition is identically respected and the rotation of the damage directions does not entail any complementary dissipation but induces a variation of the free-energy potential compatible with the evolution of the loading. We have just presented the principles of an orthotropic damage model in effective stress; the latter falls within the thermodynamic framework and moreover benefits from a direct numerical solution method in accordance (no sub-iterations at the Gauss points). Indeed, the computation of the damage as a function of the effective stress is direct, as is that of the apparent stress as a function of the effective stress and of the damage. 2.6.1.2 Isotropic damage by compression Under tensile loading, the criterion usually used is that of Rankine (principal tensile stress); this criterion accounts for a propagation of cracks in mode I . In compression, the criteria of Mazars or of Drücker-Prager are commonly employed; the Mazars criterion involves the notion of extension of the REV, the Drücker-Prager criterion accounts for the unfavourable effect of the stress deviator. In practice, failure in compression is induced by the elastic heterogeneities leading to the appearance of local fields of self-equilibrated stresses whose positive part causes the initiation and the propagation of cracks (figure r7.01.26-fig-2-9). By their origins, these induced positive stresses can exist only in the directions orthogonal to the compressive stresses which generate them. When these self-stresses reach the tensile strength a crack initiates and the compressive damage appears. In ordinary concretes, this damage appears progressively and it is possible to observe multiple vertical cracks distributed over a wide localised and inclined shear band (figure r7.01.26-fig-2-10). Cracking pattern as a function of the loading path (Torrenti ) The cracks parallel to the free edges are initiated in the neighbourhood of the aggregates by the induced self-stresses; they crack the concrete forming small “columns” which perish by lateral instability as figure r7.01.26-fig-2-10 shows. Appearance of “columns” in the neighbourhood of the aggregates (Torrenti ) Thus, the propagation of the compressive cracks can be likened to a phenomenon of multiple instabilities in compression along a shear band. Now the phenomena of mechanical instability are very closely linked to the conditions of lateral restraint of the compressed element. The instability always occurring in the direction of weakest restraint, this explains the cracks parallel to the unloaded edges in figure r7.01.26-fig-2-9. Besides the failure mode described above, it is important to recall how sensitive the compressive strength is to confinement, as the various biaxial and triaxial tests of the literature show. Given on the one hand the complexity of the failure mode in compression and on the other hand the sensitivity to confinement, it is usual, in order to model the damage of concrete in compression, to adopt a macroscopic isotropic Drücker-Prager criterion if one reasons in terms of stresses, or a Mazars criterion if one reasons in terms of strains. We have chosen here to adopt the Drücker-Prager criterion in order to be consistent with the formalism in effective stresses introduced during the presentation of the tensile damage model. The stresses at the origin of the compressive damage are therefore assumed to be the negative effective stresses {\tilde{\sigma}}^{c} ; the latter are defined in the principal basis of the effective stresses by: {\tilde{\sigma}}^{c}=\tilde{\sigma}-{\tilde{\sigma}}^{t} Where \tilde{\sigma} is the effective stress coming from the rheological model and {\tilde{\sigma}}^{t} the effective tensile stress defined by the equation . The equivalent Drücker-Prager stress is then written: {\sigma}^{\text{ceq}}=\sqrt{{J}_{2}}+{\delta}_{\text{hom}}\frac{{I}_{1}}{3} Where {I}_{1} and {J}_{2} are the first two invariants of the effective compressive stress tensor: \left\{ \begin{array}{c}{J}_{2}=\frac{1}{6}({({\tilde{\sigma}}_{1}^{c}-{\tilde{\sigma}}_{2}^{c})}^{2}+{({\tilde{\sigma}}_{1}^{c}-{\tilde{\sigma}}_{3}^{c})}^{2}+{({\tilde{\sigma}}_{2}^{c}-{\tilde{\sigma}}_{3}^{c})}^{2})\\ {I}_{1}={\tilde{\sigma}}_{1}^{c}+{\tilde{\sigma}}_{2}^{c}+{\tilde{\sigma}}_{3}^{c}\end{array}\right. The flow is carried out by considering that the damage threshold stress memorises the maximum value of the Drücker-Prager stress: {\sigma}^{\text{DP}}=\sup({\sigma}^{\text{DP}},{\sigma}^{\text{ceq}}) The damage then evolves non-linearly as a function of the threshold stress: {d}^{c}=1-\exp\left( -\frac{1}{{m}^{c}}{\left( \frac{{\sigma}^{\text{DP}}}{{\sigma}^{\text{uc}}}\right)}^{{m}^{c}}\right) The free-energy potential associated with the effective compressive stresses is written very simply because of the isotropy hypothesis of the compressive damage: \rho {\psi}^{c}=(1-{d}^{c})\frac{1}{2}\left[{\lambda}^{0}{(\text{tr}({\varepsilon}^{\text{ec}}))}^{2}+2{\mu}^{0}\text{tr}({({\varepsilon}^{\text{ec}})}^{2})\right] The dissipation associated with the compressive damage is written: {\phi }^{\text{dc}}=-\underset{{Y}^{c}}{\underbrace{\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{c}}{\partial {d}^{c}}}}{\dot{d}}^{c} The energy-release rate {Y}^{c} being negative and the damage strictly increasing, the positivity of the dissipation by compressive damage is assured. 2.6.1.3 Coupling of the tensile and compressive damages The predominant isotropic character of the compressive damage is linked to the “quasi-random and therefore statistically isotropic” complexity of the cracking paths generated during the degradation process. It is obvious that the cracks created will affect the tensile behaviour. A simple way of accounting for the decrease in the elastic moduli in tension as a function of the compressive damage is to consider that the isotropic compressive damage also reduces the tensile free-energy potential, which becomes: \rho {\psi}^{t\text{ }}=((1-{d}^{c})\underset{\rho {\psi}^{t}}{\underbrace{(\rho {\psi}^{t(n)}+\rho {\psi}^{t(n)})}} The term \rho {\psi}^{t} being positive, the positivity of the dissipation by compressive damage remains assured: -\rho \left(\frac{\partial {\psi}^{c}}{\partial {d}^{c}}+\frac{\partial {\psi}^{t\text{ }}}{\partial {d}^{c}}\right)\dot{{d}^{c}}⩾0 And the term (1-{d}^{c}) also being positive, the dissipation by tensile damage remains positive. Free-energy potential associated with the macroscopic elastic strains The partition of the strains as a function of the sign of the effective stresses having been done in equations and , the free-energy potential is the sum of the free energies associated with the effective tensile stresses on the one hand and with the effective compressive stresses on the other hand: \rho \psi =(1-{d}^{c})\underset{\rho {\psi}^{t}}{\underbrace{(\rho {\psi}^{t(n)}+\rho {\psi}^{t(s)})}}+\rho {\psi}^{c} Free-energy potential associated with an expansive internal chemical reaction If the model integrates a pressure ( {P}_{g} ) created by the expansive chemical reaction of progress A , the free-energy potential, at imposed temperature and at a given instant, becomes a function of A : \rho \psi ({\varepsilon}^{\text{ec}},{\varepsilon}^{\text{et}},A,{d}^{t},{d}^{c},{V}^{\text{an}}) In this expression {V}^{\mathit{an}} represents the internal variables associated with the anelastic phenomena. The Clausius-Duhem inequality therefore becomes: \sigma :({\dot{\varepsilon}}^{e}+{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\text{an}})+{P}_{g}(\dot{A}{V}^{g})-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}}{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{e}-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {d}^{t}}:{\dot{d}}^{t}-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {d}^{c}}{\dot{d}}^{c}-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial A}\dot{A}-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {V}^{\text{an}}}{\dot{V}}^{\text{an}}\ge 0 In this expression, the term {P}_{g}(\dot{A}{V}^{g}) is the mechanical power supplied to the solid skeleton by the chemical reaction. If one envisages a physical transformation of the REV without damage or anelastic strain, hence without mechanical dissipation, this energy must be found entirely in the free-energy potential, which is written: {P}_{g}(\dot{A}{V}^{g})=\rho \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial A}\dot{A} On the other hand the physical considerations lead us to express the gel pressure as a function of the volume fraction of matter in excess with respect to the volume of the voids connected to the reactive site on the one hand and of the total strains on the other hand, equation . Respect of the two previous relations leads to proposing for the part of the potential due to the gel the following form: {\Psi}^{g}=\frac{1}{2}{M}^{g}{b}^{{g}^{2}}{\left(\frac{A-{A}^{0}}{{b}^{g}}{V}^{g}-\text{tr}({\varepsilon}^{e}+{\varepsilon}^{\text{an}})\right)}^{2} This form of potential is close to that proposed by Ulm et al . The derivative of this potential with respect to the elastic strains gives the part of the macroscopic stress induced by the internal gel pressure in the solid skeleton: {\pi}^{g}=-{b}^{g}{P}_{g}=\rho \frac{\partial {\Psi}^{g}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}} 2.6.1.4 Free-energy potentials associated with the water pressures In a saturated medium, the intra-pore pressures act on the solid skeleton by deforming the walls of the pore network; the Clausius-Duhem equation is written, in the absence of damage and of anelastic phenomena: -({P}_{w}-{P}_{\mathit{w0}}){\dot{\varphi}}^{w}-\rho \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {\varphi}^{w}}{\dot{\varphi}}^{w}=0 In this expression {\varphi}^{w}=\frac{{m}^{w}}{{\rho}^{\mathit{w0}}} is the normalised water mass supply, {m}^{w} being the mass supply and {\rho}^{\mathit{w0}} the density of the water defined at the reference pressure {P}_{\mathit{w0}} . Moreover the physical considerations lead to expressing the water pressure in the form (Coussy ): {P}_{w}-{P}_{\mathit{w0}}={M}^{w}({\varphi}^{w}-{b}^{w}\text{tr}(\varepsilon )) An admissible form for the free-energy potential associated with these equations is then: \rho {\psi}^{w}=\frac{1}{2}{M}^{w}{b}^{{w}^{2}}{\left( \frac{{\varphi}^{w}}{{b}^{w}}-\text{tr}(\varepsilon )\right)}^{2} The derivative of this potential with respect to the elastic strains gives the part of the macroscopic stress induced by the water pressure: {\pi}^{w}=\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{w}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}}=-{b}^{w}({P}_{w}-{P}_{\mathit{w0}}) If the reference state is defined for the material saturated at atmospheric pressure ({P}_{\mathit{w0}}=0) , then the previous expression is valid only if the fluid mass supply is positive. Otherwise, the concrete desaturates and the water pressure is no longer governed by the relative compressibilities of the various phases but by the capillary phenomena. The mean water pressure {P}_{w} is therefore a function of the capillary pressure and of the degree of saturation {S}^{w} . Besides the variation of pressure in the water induced by the capillary phenomena, it is also necessary to consider the action of the interfaces of the fluid with the gaseous medium and the solid. Indeed, these interfaces are subject to capillary tension phenomena which themselves also act directly on the solid skeleton. In the case where the intra-pore gas pressure is in equilibrium with the atmospheric pressure (Coussy ), the part of the macroscopic stress induced by these two phenomena can be put in the following general form: {\pi}^{w}={b}^{w}{f}^{{w}_{({S}^{w})}}{P}^{c} Where {f}^{w} is a function taking into account on the one hand the decrease in the volume of water and on the other hand the increase in the number of solid sites subjected to the interfacial surface tension. In the present modelling, we are interested in structures situated in a partially saturated zone; in this case we propose to use a function {f}^{w} linear of the form {k}^{w}\cdot {S}^{w} ; the contribution of the hydric effects in the macroscopic stress then has the following form: {\pi}^{w}=-{b}^{w}{S}^{w}{k}^{w}{P}^{c}=\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{w}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}} Considering that the variation of the porosity \varphi due to the strain remains small compared with {\varphi}^{w} , one can admit that for the unsaturated medium \varphi \approx {\varphi}^{0} . If on the other hand one admits that the capillary pressure curve {P}^{c}({S}^{w}) is almost insensitive to the strain state of the solid skeleton, then: {\pi}^{w}\approx {b}^{w}({\varphi}^{0}+{\varphi}^{w}){k}^{w}{P}^{{c}_{({\varphi}^{0}+{\varphi}^{w})}}=\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{w}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}} If the capillary pressure curve admits an equation of “Van Genuchten” type then {\pi}^{w} takes the following form: {\pi}^{w}={\text{-b}}^{w}({\varphi}^{0}+{\varphi}^{w})(a{({({\varphi}^{0}+{\varphi}^{w})}^{-b}-1)}^{(1-\frac{1}{b})}) Where a and b are two calibration constants. The free-energy potential can then be put in the form: \rho {\psi}^{w}=-{b}^{w}({\varphi}^{0}+{\varphi}^{w})(a{({({\varphi}^{0}+{\varphi}^{w})}^{-b}-1)}^{(1-\frac{1}{b})})\text{tr}(\varepsilon ) The thermodynamic force associated with the variation of the water mass is obtained by derivation of this potential with respect to {\varphi}^{w} . 2.6.1.5 Dissipation due to the anelastic strains The Clausius-Duhem equation brings out the anelastic strains {\varepsilon}^{\text{an}} in the term \sigma :{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\text{an}} . This is the power of the external forces of the anelastic strain field; the evolution of these strains induces an evolution of the associated internal variables {V}^{\mathit{an}} possibly causing a variation of the free-energy potential: \rho \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial {V}^{\text{an}}}{\dot{V}}^{\text{an}} This last term represents the elastic energy blocked in the solid skeleton by the anelastic strain. In our model the anelastic strains have a viscoelastic or viscoplastic origin and can directly be used as internal variables, that is {V}^{\text{an}}={\varepsilon}^{\text{an}} . Thus, in the particular case of a purely anelastic transformation, the dissipation reduces to: {\phi }^{\text{an}}=\sigma :{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\text{an}}-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}^{\text{an}}}{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\text{an}}\ge 0 In the model proposed here we have adopted the principle of partition of the total strain into an elastic part and an anelastic part, which makes it possible to express the elastic strains as a function of the anelastic strains and to conclude that the thermodynamic force associated with the anelastic strain is the stress: \rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}}=-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}^{\text{an}}}=\sigma The second principle is therefore verified if \sigma :{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\text{an}}\ge 0 . In the model studied here, the anelastic strain associated with long-term creep or with the expansive chemical reaction is proportional to the stress, which one can write in abbreviated form {\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\text{an}}=k\sigma , where k is a positive coefficient depending on the internal variables for each component of the strain tensor. Thus the anelastic dissipation due to the long-term strains is a viscous dissipation of the form k{\sigma}^{2}\ge 0 . Concerning the AAR strain, we authorise its evolution only if the dissipation computed numerically over the time step is indeed positive. 2.6.1.6 Total free-energy potential and state laws The free-energy potential of the solid skeleton is obtained by summing the energy contributions of the various phenomena studied previously: \psi ={\psi}^{t\text{ }}+{\psi}^{c}+{\psi}^{g}+{\psi}^{w} The state laws are obtained by derivation of the total potential: \sigma =\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}} If one expresses the stresses in the principal basis of the tensile damages, one has for the diagonal terms of the stress tensor: {\sigma}_{ii}\phantom{\rule{4em}{0ex}}=\phantom{\rule{4em}{0ex}}\begin{array}{c}\left(1-{d}^{c}\right)\frac{{E}^{0}}{{D}^{n}}\left[\left({e}^{{\beta}_{j}+{\beta}_{k}}-{\nu}^{{0}^{2}}\right){\varepsilon}_{ii}^{\mathit{et}}+{\nu}^{0}{\varepsilon}_{jj}^{\mathit{et}}\left(\nu reference temperature. Let us note that in the equation , a reference strain {\varepsilon}^{0} is also present; it is a non-zero reference strain corresponding to a stress-free state. It can be associated only with a volumetric variation of the solid skeleton of chemical origin (chemical shrinkage linked to hydration for example). Indeed, the hydric shrinkage strains or the swelling strains by internal expansive products are manifestations of the intra-pore pressures appearing via the elastic and anelastic strains; they must therefore not be confused with this “imposed reference chemical strain” which is not accompanied by internal pressures and therefore cannot create damage in free strain. The elastic and anelastic strains are obtained by solution of the system of rheological equations presented in the previous chapter. If the solution of the system of equations of the rheological model is direct (without non-linearity requiring numerical sub-iterations at the Gauss point in the finite-element implementation), then the solution of the whole model is direct for the given total strain field. Let us recall that this aspect of the model meets the objective of ease of implementation and of reduction of the analysis time which we initially set ourselves. As we mentioned in the previous paragraph, the effective stresses and the strains referred to in the chapter devoted to the damage model come from the rheological scheme. Currently, the effective stresses used in the damage model come directly from the rheological model for which the integration of equations and is carried out with the viscoelastic characteristics of the sound material. The coupling between the damage and the rheology is therefore immediate. r7.01.27 Constitutive law BETON_REGLE_PR r7.01.27 Constitutive law BETON_REGLE_PR Summary: This documentation presents the law BETON_REGLE_PR implemented by the company Sixense-NECS within the framework of the free code_aster community. It is a regulatory law [bib1], written by combining two 1D laws. 1 Presentation of the law BETON_REGLE_PR The constitutive law is of the “twice 1D” type in the principal strain frame (coincident with the principal stress frame). Only a 1D behaviour is described, which is of non-linear elastic type. In compression, it is the parabola-rectangle law defined by the regulations [bib1]; the stress is given by the following relations: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\sigma ={\sigma}_{y}^{c}\left[1-{\left(1-\frac{\epsilon}{{\epsilon}_{0}}\right)}^{n}\right]\text{si}0 {\epsilon}_{0}\text{(partie rectangle)}\end{array} In tension the law is of triangular type [bib2]: \sigma =E\epsilon \text{si}\epsilon \le \frac{{\sigma}_{y}^{t}}{E}\text{avec}\sigma ={\sigma}_{y}^{t}+{E}_{T}\left[\epsilon -\frac{{\sigma}_{y}^{t}}{E}\right] The associated material parameters are as follows: E : Young's modulus; {\sigma}_{y}^{t} : the peak stress in tension ( {f}_{t} ); {E}_{T} : the tangent modulus (generally between \frac{-E}{3} and \frac{-E}{10} ); {\sigma}_{y}^{c} : the maximum stress in compression ( {f}_{c} ); n : the exponent of the hardening law in compression; {\varepsilon}_{c} : the strain at which {\sigma}_{y}^{c} is reached. The stress-strain response is given in the following figure: Figure 1-a : 1D stress-strain curve So that the slopes at the origin in tension and in compression are identical, the parameters can be chosen in such a way that: \frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \epsilon }(\epsilon =0)=E={f}_{c}\frac{n}{{\epsilon}_{c}} 2 Description of the internal variables There is no internal variable for this model. 3 Elementary stiffness matrices The tangent and secant stiffness matrices are available for this law. By default in code_aster, the tangent matrix is used. To use the secant matrix, or unloading matrix, the keyword PAS_MINI_ELAS must be added with a value greater than the interval between two analysis time instants, in the factor keyword NEWTON of the non-linear operators. The secant matrix is computed from the secant modulus in each principal direction i : - {E}_{i}^{s}={\sigma}_{i}/{\varepsilon}_{i} if {\epsilon}_{i}\ne 0 - {E}_{i}^{s}=E if {\epsilon}_{i}=0 4 Limitations of the law The law BETON_REGLE_PR has two important limitations: - the model is elastic: unloading is therefore not taken into account in the formulation of the law. The loading and unloading paths are therefore identical. It is therefore not recommended to use this law for non-monotonic, cyclic or dynamic loading cases. - the model does not represent the Poisson effect: the law is of the “twice 1D” type, in which the behaviour in the two principal directions of strain is treated independently. 5 Functionality and validation 5.1 Functionality The law is available only in 2D and is accessible with the modellings D_PLAN, C_PLAN and DKT. 5.2 Verification & Validation The law BETON_REGLE_PR is verified by the following test cases: | SSNP129 | V6.03.129 | Validation of the law BETON_REGLE_PR on a DKT element | | --- | --- | --- | | SSNS114 | V6.05.114 | Degradation of a reinforced-concrete plate under various loadings with the law BETON_REGLE_PR | The validation of the law was also carried out by comparison with the experimental results obtained on a reinforced-concrete slab subjected to its self-weight and to a pressure at the centre of the slab [bib1]. 6 Bibliography 1. r7.01.29 Constitutive law ENDO_HETEROGENE r7.01.29 Constitutive law ENDO_HETEROGENE Summary: This documentation presents the theoretical writing and the numerical integration of the constitutive law ENDO_HETEROGENE which takes into account the effect of the heterogeneity of the rock on its failure probability. This model has been integrated as a non-local damage law (with stress gradient) based on a two-threshold model. 1 Introduction – Field of application The constitutive law ENDO_HETEROGENE aims to model the damage of heterogeneous materials and has been developed specifically for geomaterials (for example argillite). This law is based on a probabilistic model of rock fracturing developed within the framework of a collaboration between the BRGM and the LMT-Cachan around the thesis of Nicolas Guy [bib1]. This model takes into account the effect of the heterogeneity of the rock on its failure probability. The initial distribution of micro-defects is indeed given as a function of this heterogeneity from a classical Poisson-Weibull model. The model then rests on the consideration of two thresholds: an initiation threshold and a propagation threshold based on the regularised stress intensity factor. Regularisation of the stresses allows us: - to obtain results independent of the spatial discretisation - to evaluate the two thresholds from the same quantity (grandeur), i.e. the regularised stress - to compute the “regularised” stress intensity factor without mesh refinement and with good accuracy. Finally, this model supplies explicitly a cracking path and takes account of the interaction of the cracks with one another. 2 A few general points on probabilistic models of crack-network formation By way of introduction, we specify here the framework within which this model is developed and we recall a few basic notions. In order to explain the formation of cracks, one assumes that they all initiate on pre-existing defects, modelled by cracks possessing a given size. In other words, the start of propagation is considered as the initiation. The Weibull model is widely used to study the degradation and the failure of materials with brittle behaviour [bib8] or quasi-brittle behaviour [bib3]. During the failure of a rock specimen, one may consider that it is the failure of the most critical defect, the local failure, which leads to the failure of the structure, i.e. the global failure. In other words, the failure of the weakest link leads to the failure of the chain (i.e. the structure). Within the framework of the weakest-link assumption, the global failure probability {P}_{F} of a domain Ω is related to the failure probability {P}_{\mathit{F0}} of each element {\Omega}_{0} of area {S}_{0} , by : {P}_{F}=1-\exp\left[\frac{1}{{S}_{0}}{\int}_{\Omega}\ln(1-{P}_{\mathrm{F0}})d\Omega \right] The cumulative probability of local failure PF0 may be written for example from a Weibull law [bib9] : \ln(1-{P}_{\mathrm{F0}})=-{(\frac{\langle {\sigma}_{1}-{\sigma}_{u}\rangle }{{\sigma}_{0}})}^{m} This Weibull formalism is widely developed in the documentation R7.02.06. One simply recalls that for a given crack of size a and in mode I , the expression of the stress intensity factor may be rewritten in the following manner: K=Y\sigma \sqrt{a} If one looks at an application of rock-mechanics type, one can show that a crack network can be formed in a geological medium (around a cell for example) following the application of an internal pressure, if a crack can initiate [bib5]. This is due to the decrease of the stress intensity factor when the size of a crack becomes large with respect to the diameter of the cell. The computation of the stress intensity factor for a crack breaking out on the inner edge of a hollow cylinder subjected to an internal pressure p\int shows two different trends as a function of the crack size [bib1]. In the first part, the effect of the crack size with respect to the level of the applied stress is predominant and K increases with it. On the other hand, in the second part, the effect of the decrease of the level of stress applied to the crack becomes more important than the effect of the increase of its size and K decreases as a function of the crack size. A crack can initiate as soon as K reaches the toughness ( {K}_{\mathit{IC}} ). The crack propagates as the internal pressure increases. When the internal pressure reaches its maximum value, the crack continues to propagate and stops when the value of K becomes lower than {K}_{\mathit{IC}} , neglecting dynamic effects. These results show that an isolated crack propagates up to a given size for which the value of the stress intensity factor becomes lower than the toughness of the rock. When a first crack stops, another can initiate on a second initiation site. The second crack will stop at the same length as the first, a third crack can initiate, and so on. This means that a crack network can form. Let us assume that all the cracks initiate from initial defects distributed in a random manner in the rock mass. A Poisson point process is considered in order to describe the distribution of the initiation sites. Among all these potential crack-initiation sites, only a fraction will give rise to cracks. When the value of the stress intensity factor for a defect (a crack) exceeds a critical value ( {K}_{\mathit{IC}} ), the crack begins to propagate. When a crack is initiated, the presence of this crack creates a stress-relaxation zone around it. In order to explain the initiation of a crack, one must model the interaction of the zones (i.e. the volume, the area or the length) affected by the decrease of stress and the other sites which can create cracks. If the site lies in a stress-relaxation zone, the microscopic stress is lower than the applied macroscopic stress. In this case, this site cannot give rise to a new crack. In this approach, the obscuration zone (i.e. stress relaxation) is the key quantity (grandeur) for describing the formation of a crack network. The obscuration zone is defined as a zone in which the stress level is lower than the applied stress. The shape and the size of this zone can be defined with the help of numerical simulations. One says that the potential defects are screened by the neighbouring cracks. 3 Development of the law ENDO_HETEROGENE We have chosen in Code_Aster to represent the formation and the propagation of the cracks by an integrated isotropic damage model. The damage-elasticity coupling law being given classically by: \underline{\sigma}=(1-d)\underline{\underline{C}}\underline{\epsilon} With \bar{\sigma} the stress tensor, \underline{\varepsilon} the strain tensor, \underline{\underline{C}} the isotropic elasticity tensor and d the damage variable. One places oneself in the framework recalled in section 2 . The presence of cracks in the structure is modelled by lines of broken elements (i.e. for which the damage d is such that d=1 ). For the sound elements, d=0 . The failure of the elements may be caused by two phenomena which are distinct here; namely the initiation of a new crack from the element considered or the propagation, through the element considered, of a crack which has initiated in another element. These two types of failure are described by two types of different threshold functions in this approach. Moreover, for constitutive laws corresponding to brittle materials, the introduction of a heterogeneity of the material projected onto the mesh has the effect of introducing a dependence on the size of the zone (and this even with the use of classical non-local models [bib1]). Furthermore, a local damage law cannot describe a brittle behaviour of weakest-link type. In order to remedy this problem, it is proposed here to: 1. modify the local law in order to represent a brittle failure of weakest-link type in a heterogeneous material 2. introduce a regularisation operator based on the gradient of the stresses. It is shown that a non-local description with stress gradient is, on the one hand, very close to the non-local models with strain gradient and, on the other hand, allows us to compute correctly the stress intensity factor, which is the key parameter for describing the propagation of macro-cracks. One introduces a regularised stress such that \underline{\bar{\sigma}}-{l}_{c}^{2}\Delta \underline{\bar{\sigma}}=\underline{\sigma} With \underline{\bar{\sigma}} the regularised stress tensor and {l}_{c} the characteristic length. One will consider the so-called natural Neumann boundary conditions, namely (\nabla \underline{\bar{\sigma}}).n=0 with n the outward normal to the edge considered. One considers a perfectly brittle constitutive law of the type: d=H\left(\langle \bar{{\sigma}_{1}}-{\sigma}_{y}(\mathit{el})\rangle \right),\dot{d}\ge 0 Where {\sigma}_{y} is a stress associated with the yield stress. The two thresholds will therefore be written as a function of a stress regularised over a characteristic length {l}_{c} which will be large compared with the size of the elements. One will endeavour in the present part to justify the choice of the two thresholds as well as the manner in which they are coordinated. 3.1 Initiation of the cracks As said previously, the initiation of new macro-cracks is represented by a Weibull model. With a view to describing in a relevant manner the cracking spacing, a scatter on the material parameters (Weibull modulus, scale parameter) specific to each finite element is introduced. By carrying out beforehand a random draw on a uniform distribution for each finite element in order to draw from it a value of the failure probability of each element P(\mathrm{el})\in [:ref: 0;1 ] , one can describe the stress for which a crack will initiate in a finite element by the following equation: {\sigma}_{a}(\mathrm{el})=\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{({\lambda}_{0}{Z}_{\mathrm{el}})}^{1/m}}.{\left[-\ln(1-P(\mathrm{el}))\right]}^{\frac{1}{m}} With {Z}_{\mathrm{el}} the size (the volume or the area according to the dimension) of the finite element, m the Weibull modulus and \frac{{\sigma}_{0}^{m}}{{\lambda}_{0}} the scale parameter. The use of a Weibull model to describe the initiation of new cracks has a definite advantage with a view to obtaining results independent of the mesh. Let us consider two different partitions of the domain {Z}_{\mathrm{do}} each made up of subdomains {Z}_{\mathrm{di}}^{1} and {Z}_{\mathrm{di}}^{2} . One may write: \sum_{i=1}^{\mathrm{n1}}{Z}_{\mathrm{di}}^{1}={Z}_{\mathrm{do}}=\sum_{i=1}^{\mathrm{n2}}{Z}_{\mathrm{di}}^{2} where \mathit{n1} and \mathit{n2} denote the numbers of subdomains in the two cases. The probability of initiation of the first crack of a subdomain for a loading \sigma is written: {P}_{\mathrm{asdi}}=1-\exp\left[-{Z}_{\mathrm{sd}}{\lambda}_{0}{(\frac{\sigma}{{\sigma}_{0}})}^{m}\right] where {Z}_{\mathrm{sd}} is the size (volume) of a subdomain. The probability of initiating the first crack over the set of subdomains {P}_{\mathrm{aesd1}} for a loading \sigma can be deduced from it: {P}_{\mathrm{aesd1}}=1-\prod_{i=1}^{{n}_{\mathrm{sd}}}\left[1-{P}_{\mathrm{asdi1}}\right]=1-\exp\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{{n}_{1}}{Z}_{\mathrm{di}}^{1}{\lambda}_{0}{(\frac{\sigma}{{\sigma}_{0}})}^{m}\right]=1-\exp\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{{n}_{2}}{Z}_{\mathrm{di}}^{2}{\lambda}_{0}{(\frac{\sigma}{{\sigma}_{0}})}^{m}\right]={P}_{\mathrm{aesd2}} Because: \sum_{i=1}^{{n}_{1}}{Z}_{\mathrm{di}}^{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{{n}_{2}}{Z}_{\mathrm{di}}^{2}={Z}_{\mathrm{do}} The equation allows us to recover a probability of initiation of the first crack over a domain of size {Z}_{\mathrm{do}} independent of the subdivision into subdomains. Finally one may write the evolution law of the damage d related to the initiation of a new crack in an element: d=H(\langle \bar{{\sigma}_{1}}-{\sigma}_{a}(\mathrm{el})\rangle ),\dot{d}\ge 0 where H is the Heaviside step function and \bar{{\sigma}_{1}} the maximum principal regularised stress. 3.2 Propagation of the cracks We shall show in this part that the non-local approach proposed allows us to compute correctly the stress intensity factor for cracks modelled as a series of broken elements. Indeed, it is possible to link a criterion in stress intensity factor, coming from fracture mechanics, to the regularised stress. One may consider that the asymptotic solution of the stress field at the crack tip is a good approximation of the fields that one will be able to find at the tip of a propagating crack. The stress field given by the Westergaard solution may be written in a frame at the crack tip such as presented on the Figure as a composition of elastic fields (for a plane problem): \underline{\underline{\sigma}}(r,\theta )={K}_{I}\underline{\underline{{f}_{I}}}(r,\theta )+{K}_{\mathit{II}}\underline{\underline{{f}_{\mathit{II}}}}(r,\theta ) With {K}_{I},{K}_{\mathrm{II}} the stress intensity factors in mode I and \mathit{II} , and \underline{\underline{{f}_{I},{f}_{\mathrm{II}}}} the associated weight functions (equation and ) in mode I and \mathit{II} . \underline{\underline{{f}_{I}}}(r,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi r}}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\left(1-\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\sin\frac{3\theta }{2}\right)&
