\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\left(1-\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\sin\frac{3\theta }{2}\right)& \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\sin\frac{3\theta }{2}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right] Figure 3.2-a : Definition of a frame at the crack tip The regularised stress at the crack tip can be estimated by \underline{\underline{\bar{{\sigma}_{p}}}}({K}_{I},{K}_{\mathit{II}})=\sum_{i=1}^{\mathit{II}}\left[\frac{{K}_{i}}{\pi {l}_{c}^{2}}{\int}_{\frac{-\pi }{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{\int}_{0}^{{\%}_{c}}\underline{\underline{{f}_{i}}}(r,\theta )r\partial r\partial \theta \right] Which can finally be written in the following form: \underline{\underline{\bar{{\sigma}_{p}}}}({K}_{I},{K}_{\mathit{II}})=\frac{{\Gamma}^{2}(3/4)}{5\pi \sqrt{\pi \mathit{lc}}}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{\mathrm{4K}}_{I}& {\mathrm{4K}}_{\mathit{II}}& 0\\ {\mathrm{4K}}_{\mathit{II}}& {\mathrm{6K}}_{I}& 0\\ 0& 0& \bar{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{33p}}}\end{array}\right] where \bar{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{33p}}}=-\nu (\bar{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{11p}}}+\bar{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{22p}}}) in plane strain and \bar{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{33p}}}=0 in plane stress. Moreover one recalls that \Gamma is the Gamma function, such that \Gamma (a)=\gamma (a,\infty ) and \gamma (a,b)={\int}_{0}^{b}{t}^{a-1}\exp(-t)\mathrm{dt} the incomplete gamma function. Concretely \Gamma (3/4)=1,225416 . Then, on the basis of the expression of the regularised stress at the crack tip, it is possible to propose an evolution law associated with the propagation of a macro-crack bearing on the maximum principal stress of the type: d=H\left(\langle \bar{{\sigma}_{I}}-{\sigma}_{p}(\mathit{el})\rangle \right),\dot{d}\ge 0 With: {\sigma}_{p}(\mathit{el})=\frac{6{\Gamma}^{2}(3/4)}{5\pi }\frac{{K}_{\mathit{Ic}}}{\sqrt{\pi {l}_{c}}} {\sigma}_{p}(\mathrm{el}) is the failure threshold of an element by propagation of a crack at the macroscopic scale and {K}_{\mathrm{Ic}} the toughness of the material. For a loading in pure mode I, the threshold proposed corresponds to a threshold of stress-intensity-factor type coming from fracture mechanics. The threshold proposed has in particular the advantage of being independent of whether one places oneself in plane stress or plane strain for a 2D problem and it comes close to a criterion in stress intensity factor in mode I for a 3D problem. One notes that in practice the criterion presented is a mixed-mode criterion; indeed, if one observes the failure threshold by propagation of a crack at the macroscopic scale under a loading composed for example of modes I and II in plane stress one obtains at the crack tip \bar{{\sigma}_{\mathit{Ip}}}=\frac{6{\Gamma}^{2}(3/4)}{5\pi }\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi {l}_{c}}}\left[{\mathrm{5K}}_{I}+\sqrt{{K}_{I}^{2}+{\mathrm{16K}}_{\mathit{II}}^{2}}\right] which also depends on the level of loading in mode \mathit{II} . 3.3 Coordination of the thresholds The two-parameter Weibull model describes the initiation of the cracks with a very conservative character. Indeed, using a two-parameter Weibull model amounts to assuming the existence of a non-zero probability of crack initiation as soon as the maximum principal stress becomes positive. On the other hand, the use of a crack-propagation criterion in stress intensity factor on a crack at the microscopic scale amounts to assuming the existence of a non-zero initiation threshold. For example, let us consider the case of a zone which has a dimension of the order of {l}_{c} and which is contained in a larger zone loaded uniformly. If one assumes the existence of a Weibull initiation threshold {\sigma}_{a} , one can associate with it a crack length by a fracture-mechanics criterion: {\sigma}_{a}(\mathit{el})=\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{({\lambda}_{0}{Z}_{\mathit{el}})}^{1/m}}{[-\ln(1-P(\mathit{el}))]}^{1/m}=\frac{{K}_{\mathit{Ic}}}{\sqrt{\pi a(\mathit{el})}} With a(\mathrm{el}) the half-length of the largest crack in the zone considered. For the sake of consistency with the propagation threshold {\sigma}_{p} , care must be taken that the use of a Weibull model to describe crack initiation does not imply assuming the presence, in a zone considered, of a crack larger than the size of the zone considered. Furthermore it seems reasonable to assume that a given element will be more easily broken by the propagation of a macro-crack than by initiation of a new crack. In this way, we shall also guarantee that the initiation sites which lie in the neighbourhood of the tip of a crack will be screened by it. This assumption amounts to setting the following inequality: {\sigma}_{a}(\mathit{el})\ge {\sigma}_{p}(\mathit{el}) which is equivalent to: a(\mathit{el})\le {\left(\frac{5\pi }{6\Gamma (3/4)}\right)}^{2}{l}_{c} in order to define a critical value of the initial-defect size. One can interpret the previous inequality as follows: one cannot assume that an initial crack of a size comparable to the macroscopic scale is contained in a zone of a size comparable to the microscopic scale. In practice, if there exist initial cracks of half-length greater than about {l}_{c} they will not be able to be taken into account by the initiation model proposed; one will on the other hand be able to represent them by a line of broken finite elements. The Weibull model will therefore be used to represent the initiation of cracks from initial defects of size lower than 2{l}_{c} . The characteristic length {l}_{c} appears as a transition scale between the microscopic scale of crack initiation and the macroscopic scale of crack propagation. The characteristic length can then be interpreted as being of the order of magnitude of the largest cracks initially present at the microscopic scale. Moreover one notes that if each finite element does not contain an initial defect larger than itself and if the characteristic length {l}_{c} is larger than the size of the finite elements, then the inequality is automatically satisfied. In order to carry out a coordination of the thresholds, a locating of the elements is necessary. To this end, a criterion bearing on the neighbourhood of a finite element has been developed. Within this framework, the propagation criterion will be checked only on elements which lie in the direct neighbourhood of a crack already initiated. This model therefore requires knowledge of the neighbours of an element. The details of this locating are explained in the following chapter. 4 Numerical integration 4.1 Initialisation In order to carry out an analysis using the two damage thresholds, it is necessary to define beforehand a set of parameters. The parameters characterising the material are the following: Young's modulus E , Poisson's ratio \nu , the toughness {K}_{\mathrm{Ic}} , the Weibull modulus m , the characteristic length {l}_{c} and a nominal initiation stress at the scale of the characteristic length. The nominal initiation stress at the scale of the characteristic length is introduced in place of the scale factor. One can express it by: {\sigma}_{{l}_{c}}=\frac{{\sigma}_{0}^{m}}{{({\lambda}_{0}{l}_{c}^{3})}^{1/m}} With {\sigma}_{0}^{m}/{\lambda}_{0} the scale factor and m the Weibull modulus. The nominal initiation stress at the scale of the characteristic length {\sigma}_{{l}_{c}} gives us an idea of the order of magnitude of the initiation stress of a domain of a size {l}_{c}^{3} which is possibly made up of several finite elements during an analysis. More precisely the initiation probability corresponding to a loading of {\sigma}_{{l}_{c}} is about 0.63. In addition to the parameters characterising the material, one specifies the thickness of the modelled structure {E}_{\mathrm{ps}} . It is possible to use a variant of the surface Weibull model instead of the volume one, for which the unit of the scale factor is the MPamm² instead of the MPamm3. In this case, one must specify that the structure has a thickness of {E}_{\mathrm{ps}}={l}_{c} During the initialisation phase one computes for each element the value of the initiation threshold (stored in as an internal variable). As shown on the , the computation of the initiation threshold {\sigma}_{a} is carried out for each finite element and consists of several steps. - For each finite element, one begins by computing the size of the elements {Z}_{\mathrm{el}} as a function of the position of the nodes and of the thickness {E}_{\mathrm{ps}} . Then, one computes the propagation threshold by the equation . - The initiation threshold (itself also an internal variable) is then computed (equation ) with P(\mathrm{el})\in [:ref: 0;1 ] a number drawn at random on a uniform probability density. If the consistency condition of the two thresholds (equation ) is not satisfied, one starts again after having drawn at random another value for P(\mathit{el}) . In order to make the two thresholds consistent, one carries out here a truncation of the Weibull distribution. Other choices could have been envisaged; one carries out here a truncation for the sake of simplicity. One notes that the choice of carrying out a truncation on the Weibull distribution obliges one to choose a realistic characteristic length. Indeed, if the characteristic length chosen is inconsistent ( i.e., small) with the Weibull parameters used, one can truncate the major part of the Weibull distribution. In this case, the description of the initiation is not faithful to the Weibull parameters considered. One will refer to section 4.4.2 for the choice of the parameters. Figure 4.1-a : Diagram of the initialisation of the analysis 4.2 Solution of the global problem The global problem bears on the computation of the displacements and of the regularised stresses. The constitutive law which makes it possible to compute at each Newton iteration the stress and the damage is implemented according to an implicit scheme. The problem is discretised with the help of the new particular finite elements introduced into Code_Aster as described on the figure . Figure 4.2-a : Nodal unknowns of a triangle element The finite elements used are quadratic in displacement and linear in regularised stresses; they therefore comprise 21 degrees of freedom for a triangle element for a plane problem (28 for a quadrangle). Two sets of shape functions and derived shape functions are associated with the displacements ({N}_{u}\mathit{et}{B}_{u}) and with the regularised stresses ({N}_{\bar{\sigma}}\mathit{et}{B}_{\bar{\sigma}}) . Two equations govern the global problem, one corresponds to the classical equilibrium; the other corresponds to the computation of the regularised stresses (for more details on the development of non-local gradient problems, one will refer for example to R5.04.01). The integral formulation of the problem is: \forall {u}^{\text{ }}\in {V}_{\mathit{ad}}{\int}_{\Omega}\underline{\sigma}:\underline{ϵ}({u}^{\text{ }})d\Omega ={\int}_{G}{u}^{\text{ }}.{T}_{G}\mathit{dG}+{\int}_{\Omega}{u}^{\text{ }}.{f}_{V}d\Omega With {V}_{\mathrm{ad}} the space of admissible displacements, {T}_{G} the forces imposed on the edge G, {f}_{V} the body forces and: \forall \underline{{s}^{\text{ }}}\in {[{H}^{1}(\Omega )]}^{6}{\int}_{\Omega}(\underline{{s}^{\text{ }}}.\underline{\bar{\sigma}}+\nabla \underline{{s}^{\text{ }}}.{l}_{c}^{2}\underline{\bar{\sigma}})d\Omega ={\int}_{\Omega}\underline{{s}^{\text{ }}}.\underline{\sigma}d\Omega One will denote in the part which follows \sigma ,\varepsilon \mathrm{et}\bar{\sigma} , the writing in vector form of the tensors of stresses, strains and regularised stresses; one denotes by u the displacement vector. The global solution amounts to the vanishing of a residual bearing on the displacements which can be written for each of the elements (for more details, one will refer to R5.03.01): {F}^{u}={F}_{int}+{D}^{T}\lambda -{F}_{\mathit{ext}} With {F}_{i}={\int}_{\Omega}{B}_{u}^{T}\sigma d\Omega ,{F}_{e}={\int}_{\Gamma}{N}_{u}^{T}{T}_{g}\mathrm{dG} the external loading in forces with {T}_{G} the nodal reactions. D is such that \mathrm{Du}={u}^{d} with {u}^{d} the imposed displacements and \lambda the Lagrange multipliers for Dirichlet boundary conditions. One also minimises a residual bearing on the regularised stresses: {F}^{\bar{\sigma}}={K}^{\bar{\sigma}\sigma }\bar{\sigma}-{F}^{\sigma} With {F}^{\sigma}={\int}_{\Omega}{N}_{\bar{\sigma}}^{T}\sigma d\Omega \mathrm{et}{K}^{\bar{\sigma}\sigma }={\int}_{\Omega}({N}_{\bar{\sigma}}^{T}{N}_{\bar{\sigma}}+{l}_{c}^{2}{B}_{\bar{\sigma}}^{T}{B}_{\bar{\sigma}})d\Omega . In order to minimise the residuals presented one uses the following tangent matrix: K=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\frac{\partial {F}^{u}}{\partial u}& \frac{\partial {F}^{u}}{\partial \bar{\sigma}}\\ \frac{\partial {F}^{\bar{\sigma}}}{\partial u}& \frac{\partial {F}^{\bar{\sigma}}}{\partial \bar{\sigma}}\end{array}\right] With: \frac{\partial {F}^{u}}{\partial u}={\int}_{\Omega}{B}_{u}^{T}\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \epsilon }{B}_{u}d\Omega \frac{\partial {F}^{u}}{\partial \bar{\sigma}}={\int}_{\Omega}{B}_{u}^{T}\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \bar{\sigma}}{N}_{\bar{\sigma}}d\Omega \frac{\partial {F}^{\bar{\sigma}}}{\partial \bar{\sigma}}={\int}_{\Omega}({N}_{\bar{\sigma}}^{T}{N}_{\bar{\sigma}}+{l}_{c}^{2}{B}_{\bar{\sigma}}^{T}{B}_{\bar{\sigma}})d\Omega \frac{\partial {F}^{\bar{\sigma}}}{\partial u}={\int}_{\Omega}-{N}_{\bar{\sigma}}^{T}\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial \epsilon }{B}_{u}d\Omega 4.3 Implementation of the constitutive law The sound finite elements ( i.e., for which d=0 ) can be found in different situations. Either they are at the tip of a crack, in which case they are subjected to the propagation threshold, or they are not at the tip of a crack, in which case they are subjected to the initiation threshold. Thus the position of the crack tips and their assigned elements are stored during the analysis. The Figure represents the evolution of the state of the finite elements during the initiation and the propagation of a crack. Initially, if all the finite elements are sound, they are all subjected to their failure threshold by initiation. If there is initiation of a crack in a given element, the element considered is broken ( i.e., d=1 ) and it points if possible to two neighbouring elements as shown on the Figure (a). At the following Newton iteration, the pointed finite elements are no longer subjected to their failure threshold by initiation but to the failure threshold by propagation. | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | | | | Figure 4.3-a : States of the finite elements If the pointed finite elements undergo a loading such that they break, each of them will then if possible point to a neighbouring finite element which will then be subjected to the failure threshold by propagation. As shown on Figure b, if a boundary finite element does not find an appropriate neighbouring element to point to, then nothing happens. Then, the propagation of the initiated crack can continue according to the level and the orientation of the loadings. The figure makes it possible to observe more precisely the method of pointing to the neighbouring elements during the initiation phase (figure (a)) and during the propagation phase (figure (b)). If in a structural analysis the loading level reached is sufficient to generate the initiation of a crack in the finite element {A}_{\mathit{el}} , then one makes the assumption that the crack considered initiates at the centre of the element and the damage of the finite element considered is equal to d=1 . One then defines two crack tips {B}_{\mathit{pt}} and {C}_{\mathit{pt}} which are the intersections of a straight line {\Delta}_{{A}_{\mathit{el}}} and of the edges of the finite element considered. One defines the straight line {\Delta}_{{A}_{\mathrm{el}}} as passing through the point {A}_{\mathit{pt}} and being perpendicular to the vector \overrightarrow{{n}_{{\mathrm{IA}}_{\mathrm{pt}}}} which corresponds to the direction associated with the maximum principal regularised stress at the point {A}_{\mathit{pt}} at failure \bar{{\sigma}_{{\mathit{IA}}_{\mathit{pt}}}} . Each of the crack tips is then taken in charge by a finite element neighbouring the finite element {A}_{\mathit{el}} , namely the elements {B}_{\mathit{el}} and {C}_{\mathit{el}} . The elements {B}_{\mathrm{el}} and {C}_{\mathrm{el}} are then subjected to the failure threshold by propagation. As shown on figure (b), if one reaches the propagation threshold at a crack tip {D}_{\mathit{pt}} taken in charge by an element {D}_{\mathit{el}} , then the damage of the element {D}_{\mathrm{el}} passes to d=1 . One then moves the crack tip along a straight line {\Delta}_{{D}_{\mathit{el}}} defined as passing through {D}_{\mathrm{pt}} and being perpendicular to \vec{{n}_{{\mathit{ID}}_{\mathit{pt}}}} the direction associated with the maximum principal regularised stress at the point {D}_{\mathrm{pt}} at failure \bar{{\sigma}_{{\mathit{ID}}_{\mathit{pt}}}} . The crack tip is then positioned at the point {E}_{\mathrm{pt}} and taken in charge by the finite element {E}_{\mathrm{el}} . The neighbourhood-management method developed makes it possible to manage several cracks simultaneously. It also allows each of the cracks defined to branch according to the structural problem as well as according to possible interactions with other cracks of the same structure. The integration into Code_Aster of the system described is summarised on the figure . Moreover, the internal variables used are described in section 4.5 . Figure 4.3-b : Locating of the neighbouring elements Figure 4.3-c : Integration of the initiation and propagation thresholds into Code_Aster The integration method of the neighbourhood-management system presented considers a finite element as being pointed only if it was pointed during the previous Newton iteration. Consequently each crack tip can lead to the failure by propagation of one element per Newton iteration. Moreover, the implementation of the material behaviour is analytical, which guarantees the stability of the converged states. Indeed, during a loading step, each crack tip can lead to the failure by propagation of as many elements as is necessary in order to reach equilibrium. Consequently, the model presented makes it possible to represent the propagation of macro-cracks even in the unstable phase. Let us consider the case of a structure subjected to a loading increment containing {n}_{\mathit{pf}} crack tips numbered from 1 to {n}_{\mathit{pf}} . If during the loading step no new crack initiates but each crack tip i must break {n}_{\mathit{elt}} elements in order for one to reach a stable state, then the number of global Newton iterations required to solve the problem on the loading increment is {n}_{\mathit{it}}=max({n}_{\mathit{eli}}) . One can deduce from this that the duration of the simulations depends only little on the number of cracks present in the structure. 4.4 Material parameters required for the law 4.4.1 Keywords In summary, 5 material parameters are required for the law, to be defined in the keyword ENDO_HETEROGENE of DEFI_MATERIAU: 1. WEIBULL: parameter m of the Weibull model, 2. SY: nominal initiation stress, 3. KI: stress intensity factor {K}_{i} , 4. EPAI: thickness {E}_{\mathrm{ps}} 5. GR: Seed of the random draw defining the initial defects The characteristic length is entered under the keyword LONG_CARA of DEFI_MATERIAU. 4.4.2 Identification advice The classical Weibull model is based on the weakest-link assumption: the global failure of the structure corresponds to the local failure, and therefore directly to the heterogeneities. The parameters of the Weibull distribution are found experimentally with splitting tests, characterised by an unstable propagation of the first defect which suddenly takes the specimen to failure. The weakest-link assumption is therefore valid in this case. As we have seen, the ENDO_HETEROGENE model considers more complex types of cracking, with the formation of a crack network. For this reason one introduces the concept of initiation, distinguishing it from propagation; the weakest-link assumption and the application of the Weibull model indeed stop at the finite element. However, the experimental calibration procedure of the Weibull parameters by splitting tests is still valid because it is a completely experimental procedure and because it applies to a case where the weakest-link assumption is valid; on the other hand, this corresponds only to the initiation of cracking for ENDO_HETEROGENE. A more complicated step concerns the determination of the remaining parameters: the toughness in mode I and the characteristic length. The two parameters are used by the ENDO_HETEROGENE model for the computation of the propagation threshold. The fracture-mechanics law used is non-linear precisely because of the presence of {l}_{c} . On the contrary, in the experimental tests the propagation is associated with the toughness alone, when one refers to a linear fracture-mechanics model. The two concepts of toughness used therefore do not seem to coincide, because they are not associated with the same theoretical model. One must therefore take with caution the toughness values coming from the classical tests. As regards the characteristic length alone, one can see this value as a key for the passage from the small scale, that of the micro-defects, to the large scale, that of the macro-cracks. An empirical rule for choosing it consists in taking a length lying between the length of the smallest defect and that of a macro-crack. One could therefore make an a priori choice of the characteristic length, and then choose the toughness accordingly. 4.5 Description of the internal variables The model has 12 internal variables which need to be stored at the previous time: 1. \mathrm{VI}(1) : damage d , 2. \mathit{VI}(2) : indicator (0 sound element, 1 pointed element, 2 broken by initiation, 3 broken by propagation), 3. \mathrm{VI}(3) : initiation stress {\sigma}_{a} , 4. \mathrm{VI}(4) : propagation stress {\sigma}_{p} , 5. \mathrm{VI}(5) : number of the pointed element number 1, 6. \mathrm{VI}(6) : number of the pointed element number 1 if initiation, 7. \mathrm{VI}(7) : Newton iteration of failure, 8. \mathrm{VI}(8) : current Newton iteration, 9. \mathrm{VI}(9) : X coordinate of the crack tip (after failure by propagation), 10. \mathrm{VI}(10) : Y coordinate of the crack tip (after failure by propagation), 11. \mathrm{VI}(11) : coordinate X of crack tip 2 at initiation, 12. \mathrm{VI}(12) : coordinate Y of crack tip 2 at initiation, 5 Functionalities and verification The constitutive law is inseparable from the modelling D_PLAN_GRAD_SIGM. One can therefore do only plane modelling. The description of the parameters as well as the identification advice are given in section 4.4 . The constitutive law ENDO_HETEROGENE as well as the modelling D_PLAN_GRAD_SIGM are verified by the following test cases: | SSNV147 | Modelling of crack initiation with the ENDO_HETEROGENE model | V6.03.147 | | --- | --- | --- | | SSNV148 | Computation of the stress intensity factor by regularisation of the stresses with ENDO_HETEROGENE | V6.03.148 | Note: In a parallel analysis, when one carries out an analysis on several processors with the law ENDO_HETEROGENE, nothing guarantees the uniqueness of the solution because of the initiation thresholds generated in a random manner. One may have a machine sensitivity of the order of 1.E-3%. In certain cases, there may be numerical problems of non-convergence. r7.01.31 Constitutive law for reinforced-concrete plates GLRC_DAMAGE r7.01.31 Constitutive law for reinforced-concrete plates GLRC_DAMAGE Summary: This documentation presents the theoretical formulation and the numerical integration of the constitutive law GLRC_DAMAGE [bib1]. It is written in a global manner in terms of resultant forces and moments for finite-element modellings of plates. This law incorporates the elastic and damageable behaviour in bending coming from the concrete and the elastoplastic behaviour coming essentially from the steel reinforcement, on the basis of the material characteristics of the two materials and of the composition of the cross-section of the reinforced-concrete plate. The result is a cyclic damageable elastoplastic behaviour, suited to dynamic studies of reinforced-concrete structures. The present GLRC_DAMAGE model does not take membrane damage into account and is therefore not very accurate when the loads on the plate are dominated by membrane effects. On the other hand, the failure of a plate depends above all on the behaviour of the steel, modelled by the elastoplastic part of the model. One therefore considers that failure should be represented correctly even in membrane. A model similar to this one, GLRC_DM, is capable of representing membrane/bending damage better, but does not take into account the yielding phase of the steels and therefore cannot be used to simulate failure. Note: The orthotropic elasticity induced by the orthogonal network of reinforcement is taken into account only within the framework of a linear analysis. For the non-linear analysis, this model must not be used . This constitutive law is used mainly for the chaining of analyses between code_aster and Europlexus. Warning! It must be used only in the direction from code_aster towards Europlexus, and not in the other direction. 1 Introduction 1.1 Global constitutive models The global models represent the evolutions of the material within the structure under study – beam and plate – on the basis of a relation between the generalised strain quantities (extension, curvature, distortion) and the generalised forces (membrane forces, bending, shear forces). These models are « fitted » beforehand with the aid of a frozen local analysis (for example with the aid of the results of a limit analysis of the cross-sections), as a function of the characteristics of the concrete and steel materials constituting the plate and of the distribution of these within the cross-section, cf. []. The schematic principle is as follows: d(\epsilon ,\kappa ,\gamma )\underset{\begin{array}{c}\mathit{loi}\mathit{globale}\mathit{de}\mathit{comportement}\\ \uparrow \\ \mathit{analyse}\mathit{locale}\end{array}}{\to }d(N,M,T) This local analysis must take the various couplings into account: for example, the evolution in bending depends on the value of the applied normal force. The non-linear equilibrium of the structure is treated at the global level on the generalised forces, via the plate kinematics considered. Figure 1.1-a : Reinforced-concrete slab. Since the local analysis is implemented only in pre-processing (within the framework of a monotonic-load analysis), one has no immediate means of returning, in the course of the analysis, to the local analysis of the stresses from the generalised internal forces. Indeed, the dissipative character of the irreversible constitutive laws requires one to store, in the course of the cycles, the evolution of the internal variables at every time instant if one wishes to compute the stresses at a particular point. One could envisage launching in parallel the three-dimensional constitutive law according to [eq 1.1-1] and integrating through the thickness in order to return to a global behaviour, but the cost and the complexity of such an approach seem an obstacle. It should be noted that this could be a means of estimating the error committed by a global constitutive law. On the other hand, this approach has not yet been adopted in Code_Aster . This type of model can usefully be validated by comparison with a direct analysis carried out with a local model. 1.2 Objectives of the law GLRC_DAMAGE The initial formulation of the global reinforced-concrete plate model GLRC_DAMAGE, established by Koechlin in 2002, is found in [bib1], [bib2] and [bib3]. This model was first developed for dynamic applications with collapse under impact of reinforced-concrete structures. The elastoplastic response of the model is essential for this type of application. Indeed, the dissipation of energy by yielding of the steels is significant. Taking into account the damage by cracking of the concrete makes it possible to make the first phases of the non-linear behaviour more accurate. Within the framework of seismic applications, one may expect a reversed situation: the damage and the response after cracking are essential, whereas it is rare to go as far as mobilising the generalised yielding of the steels. It nevertheless seems advantageous to have one and the same model in order to treat these two families of applications. The formulation of the model is established within the framework of the thermodynamics of irreversible processes. It combines plasticity with hardening, brought in particular by the steels, and the damage brought by the concrete cracking during the bending of the plate. The plastic behaviour is constructed on the basis of the limit analysis in bending of a reinforced-concrete plate. It is described with the aid of the framework of generalised standard materials. On the basis of experimental results, cf. [bib1], a linear kinematic hardening has been chosen in order to treat the cyclic behaviour. The damage is introduced in order to represent the loss of elastic stiffness which takes place by cracking of the concrete before the yielding of the steels. The damage threshold is assumed constant. This behaviour is assumed independent of the loading rates (the dissipations are instantaneous). 2 Formulation of the model One presents below the formulation of the model GLRC_DAMAGE, under the formalism of the thermodynamics of irreversible processes. One must note that the use of this model is associated with that of a plate element. If one chooses the family of finite elements DKT (supported modelling: DKTG), one adopts the Love-Kirchhoff theory, that is to say that one considers no transverse distortion through the thickness of the plate. The model GLRC_DAMAGE could be usable with the thick-plate finite elements Q4G, but this extension has not yet been carried out. The mesh cell of the finite element is assumed to be placed on the mid-surface of the slab (at z=0 ). With a view to being able to use the constitutive model GLRC_DAMAGE in two different types of analysis, one has chosen, according to the case: 1. for a linear elastic analysis of a reinforced-concrete plate: to take into account the orthotropy induced by the orthogonal network of steel reinforcement, as well as the bending–membrane coupling in the case of unequal reinforcement layers, via a homogenised steel–concrete elastic behaviour; 2. for a non-linear damageable elastoplastic analysis of a reinforced-concrete plate: to neglect the orthotropy and the bending–membrane coupling in the elastic phase. This assumption makes it possible to simplify the model, by supposing that, in the presence of strongly non-linear phenomena, the orthotropic elasticity becomes negligible, especially when modelling failure. Moreover, in practice one expects the walls, shear walls and the other structural elements to be reinforced more or less equally between the two principal orthogonal directions. This has the effect of reducing the effect of the elastic orthotropy. On the other hand, one very often chooses asymmetric reinforcement in order to optimise it as a function of the direction of the loading due to self-weight. This tends to induce a membrane–bending coupling in elasticity in addition to that in plasticity. However, even if the model neglects the asymmetry in elasticity, its influence in elastoplasticity, the predominant behaviour at failure, can be controlled through threshold functions, which themselves may be asymmetric. The model is defined by the description of the state variables, which represent the mechanical system at each material point of the middle surface of the plate, the surface density of free energy which encompasses the form of the constitutive relations and the type of hardening, the expression of the plasticity and damage criteria, and the irreversible evolution laws, deduced from Drücker's principle of maximum work. 2.1 State variables The global state variables are the following. First of all the global strain variables: 1. a membrane strain tensor: \epsilon defined in the tangent plane of the plate. 2. a curvature tensor: \kappa defined in the tangent plane of the plate. Then the internal variables: 1. two damage variables associated with the upper part, {d}_{1} and the lower part, {d}_{2} of the plate. They are each capped at a value, {d}_{1}^{max} and {d}_{2}^{max} . 2. two plastic curvature tensors associated with the yielding of the steel layers, upper and lower {\kappa}_{1}^{p},{\kappa}_{2}^{p} . 3. two plastic membrane strain tensors associated with the yielding of the steel layers, upper and lower, {\epsilon}_{1}^{p},{\epsilon}_{2}^{p} . 4. a second-order tensor of kinematic-hardening internal variables \alpha . 2.2 Free energy: linear elastic case The surface density of free energy is an additive expression of the elastic membrane and bending contributions: {\Phi}_{e}^{S}=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon :{H}_{m}:\epsilon +\frac{1}{2}\kappa :{H}_{f}:\kappa +\epsilon :{H}_{\mathit{mf}}:\kappa The tensors {H}_{m} , {H}_{f} , {H}_{\mathit{mf}} (bending–membrane coupling in the case of unequal reinforcement layers through the thickness) are described in [§3.1]. In the present state of the model, one assumes that: {H}_{\mathit{mf}}=0 therefore that the plate is symmetric and that there is no elastic membrane–bending coupling. In the model, the membrane–bending coupling can appear only as a result of an evolution towards elastoplasticity (cf. §2.5). 2.3 Free energy: damageable elastoplastic case In this case, one neglects the elastic orthotropy induced by the reinforcement in the two directions of the plane, as well as the elastic bending–membrane coupling (for unsymmetric reinforcement layers). One therefore treats the steel reinforcement as an isotropic elastic membrane, cf. []. The surface density of free energy is an additive expression of the elastoplastic membrane contributions, the damageable elastoplastic bending contributions, and the kinematic hardening: {\Phi}_{\mathit{epd}}^{S}(\epsilon ,{\epsilon}^{p},\kappa ,{\kappa}^{p},{d}_{1,}{d}_{2,}\alpha )={\Phi}_{e,m}^{S}(\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p})+{\Phi}_{\mathit{ed},f}^{S}(\kappa -{\kappa}^{p},{d}_{1,}{d}_{2})+{\Phi}_{p}^{S}(\alpha )+H({d}_{j}-{d}_{j}^{max}) with the hardening energy: {\Phi}_{p}^{S}(\alpha )=\frac{1}{2}\alpha :C:\alpha where C is a Prager kinematic-hardening tensor. In practice the tensor C is diagonal, with a coefficient {C}_{m} in membrane and another {C}_{f} in bending; one therefore has: C=(\begin{array}{cccccc}{C}_{m}& 0& 0& 0& 0& 0\\ 0& {C}_{m}& 0& 0& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& {C}_{m}& 0& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& 0& {C}_{f}& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& 0& 0& {C}_{f}& 0\\ 0& 0& 0& 0& 0& {C}_{f}\end{array}) In [eq 2.3.1], H denotes an indicator function of the domain of admissibility of the thermodynamic potential. Concretely, it serves to limit the evolution of the damage above {d}_{j}^{max} . The {d}_{j}^{max} are identified by [eq 3.2.11]. The membrane and bending energy densities are given by: 1. In membrane: {\Phi}_{e,m}^{S}(\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p})=\frac{1}{2}(\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p}):{H}_{m}:(\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p}) 1. In bending: {\Phi}_{\mathit{ed},f}^{S}(\kappa -{\kappa}^{p},{d}_{1,}{d}_{2})=\frac{{\lambda}_{f}}{2}\mathit{tr}{(\kappa -{\kappa}^{p})}^{2}{\xi}_{f}(\mathit{tr}(\kappa -{\kappa}^{p}),{d}_{1,}{d}_{2})+{\mu}_{f}\sum_{i=1}^{2}{\tilde{(\kappa -{\kappa}^{p})}}_{i}^{2}{\xi}_{f}({\tilde{(\kappa -{\kappa}^{p})}}_{i},{d}_{1,}{d}_{2}) where one introduces the Lamé parameters in bending {\lambda}_{f} and {\mu}_{f} : \begin{array}{c}{\lambda}_{f}=\frac{{h}^{3}}{12}\lambda \\ {\mu}_{f}=\frac{{h}^{3}}{12}\mu \end{array} h being the thickness of the plate and \lambda , \mu the Lamé coefficients of the homogenised material. {\tilde{(\kappa -{\kappa}^{p})}}_{i} denotes the i -th eigenvalue of \kappa -{\kappa}^{p} . One will subsequently denote by {\kappa}^{e} the elastic curvature-variation tensor defined according to the assumption of partition of the bending strains by: {\kappa}^{e}=\kappa -{\kappa}^{p} . And finally, one defines the characteristic function of the bending damage {\xi}_{f} : {\xi}_{f}(x,{d}_{1,}{d}_{2})=\frac{1+\gamma {d}_{1}}{1+{d}_{1}}H(x)+\frac{1+\gamma {d}_{2}}{1+{d}_{2}}H(-x) In this expression H is the Heaviside function and \gamma a damage parameter lying between 0 and 1. This function {\xi}_{f} characterises the reduction of the stiffnesses by damage. It is decreasing for {d}_{1} , {d}_{2} positive. It is convex (thanks to the choice of \gamma , identified by the procedure described in [§3.2.2]) in order to ensure the stability of the « material » of the reinforced-concrete slab. 2.4 Damageable elastoplastic constitutive law The damageable elastoplastic constitutive law (state law) supplies the dual variables: the membrane forces, the bending moments, which are second-order tensors defined on the tangent plane of the plate, the damage forces and the irreversible hardening tensors. They are written: 1. Membrane force: N=\frac{\partial {\Phi}_{\mathit{epd}}^{S}}{\partial \epsilon }={H}_{m}:(\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p}) 1. Bending moment: M=\frac{\partial {\Phi}_{\mathit{epd}}^{S}}{\partial \kappa }={H}_{f}^{d}(\kappa -{\kappa}^{p},{d}_{1,}{d}_{2}):(\kappa -{\kappa}^{p}) The membrane elasticity tensor {H}_{m} is given in [§3.1], whereas {H}_{f}^{d} is the damageable elasticity tensor which depends on the damage variables {d}_{1} , {d}_{2} and also on the signs of certain components of {\kappa}^{e}=\kappa -{\kappa}^{p} (of the trace and of the eigenvalues, in particular). One recalls that in [eq. 2.4.1] and [eq. 2.4.2] the elastic membrane–bending coupling is neglected (see [§2.2]). Moreover, because of the presence of the eigenvalues of the elastic curvatures in the expression of the free energy (see [eq. 2.3.4]), one computes the generalised stresses by using equations [eq. 2.4.1], [eq. 2.4.2] in the principal frame. The details of the transformation between the frames are available in R7.01.32. One also specifies that, according to the assumption of isotropic elasticity, the membrane–bending coupling is due solely to the elastoplastic process through {\epsilon}^{p} and {\kappa}^{p} (cf. §2.5). Note: One observes that the principal frame of the moments is the same as that of the elastic curvatures. Likewise, the principal frame of the membrane forces is the same as that of the elastic strains. In the absence of damage, {\xi}_{f}(x,{d}_{1,}{d}_{2})=1 : one indeed recovers an isotropic elastic plate behaviour. 1. Damage forces, for j=1,2 : {Y}_{j}=-\frac{\partial {\Phi}_{\mathit{epd}}}{\partial {d}_{j}}=\frac{1-\gamma }{{(1+{d}_{j})}^{2}}(\frac{{\lambda}_{f}}{2}\mathit{tr}{({\kappa}^{e})}^{2}H({(-1)}^{j}\mathit{tr}({\kappa}^{e}))+{\mu}_{f}\sum_{i}{({\tilde{\kappa}}_{i}^{e})}^{2}H({(-1)}^{j}{\tilde{\kappa}}_{i}^{e})) One observes that the {Y}_{j} defined by [eq. 2.4.3] are positive (it is a restitution of surface energy, whose SI unit is J/m²) if \gamma \in [0,1] . 1. Irreversible plasticity forces and moments: {N}^{p}=\frac{\partial {\Phi}_{\mathit{epd}}^{S}}{\partial {\epsilon}^{p}}={H}_{m}:(\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p})=N 1. Kinematic-hardening back-stress tensors: {X}^{m}=\frac{\partial {\Phi}_{\mathit{epd}}^{S}}{\partial {\alpha}_{m}}=-{C}_{m}:{\alpha}_{m} 2.5 Criteria – threshold surfaces 2.5.1 Plasticity criterion The plasticity criterion of Johansen with kinematic hardening is duplicated for the plasticity of the upper part (index 1) and of the lower part (index 2) of the plate. This criterion couples the membrane plasticity with that in bending. If x and y denote the directions of the orthogonal reinforcement of the concrete plate, for j=1,2 , the criterion is written: \begin{array}{ccc}{f}_{j}^{p}(N-{X}^{m},M-{X}^{f})& =& -({M}_{xx}-{X}_{xx}^{f}-{M}_{\mathit{jx}}^{p}({N}_{xx}-{X}_{xx}^{m}))\\ & \times & ({M}_{yy}-{X}_{yy}^{f}-{M}_{\mathit{jy}}^{p}({N}_{yy}-{X}_{yy}^{m}))+{({M}_{xy}-{X}_{xy}^{f})}^{2}\le 0\end{array} The {f}_{j}^{p} define a convex domain (cf. [bib4]) of reversibility, parametrised by 4 functions: {M}_{\mathit{jx}}^{p}({N}_{xx}) and {M}_{\mathit{jy}}^{p}({N}_{yy}) . These functions are constructed with the aid of the limit analysis of reinforced-concrete beam cross-sections representative of the cross-section of the plate under study, taken in the direction of the reinforcing bars, cf. [bib1, bib2]. One observes that only the differences between the loading state and the hardening back-stress tensors intervene in the expression of the criterion. This is characteristic of models with kinematic hardening. The dissipation potential associated with this criterion is given by: \begin{array}{c}{\Psi}_{\mathit{tot}}=N:\dot{\epsilon}+M:\dot{\kappa}-{\dot{\Phi}}_{\mathit{epd}}={\Psi}_{p}+{\Psi}_{d}\\ {\Psi}_{p}=N:{\dot{\epsilon}}^{p}+M:{\dot{\kappa}}^{p}-{\dot{\alpha}}_{m}:{C}_{m}:{\alpha}_{m}-{\dot{\alpha}}_{f}:{C}_{f}:{\alpha}_{f}\\ {\Psi}_{d}={Y}_{1}{\dot{d}}_{1}+{Y}_{2}{\dot{d}}_{2}\end{array} 2.5.2 Damage criterion The brittle damage criterion without hardening is defined by a scalar. This criterion is duplicated in order to distinguish positive bendings from negative bendings. It is written: {f}_{j}^{d}({Y}_{j})={Y}_{j}(\kappa ,{d}_{j})-{k}_{j}\le 0 This criterion represents a convex domain (cf. [bib2]) of reversibility parametrised by the thresholds {k}_{1} and {k}_{2} which define the appearance of the first bending cracks in the reinforced-concrete plate. Their SI unit is J/{m}^{2} . They correspond to a limitation of the surface density of elastic energy. This criterion is associated with the positive dissipation potential: {\Psi}_{d}({d}_{j},{\dot{d}}_{j})={k}_{j}{\dot{d}}_{j}\ge 0 This damage criterion is basic, but it is its combination with the effect of the damage on the elastic stiffness, cf. the function {\xi}_{f}(x,{d}_{1,}{d}_{2}) [eq. 2.3.5], which acts on the response of the model. 2.6 Plastic flow laws The plastic flow law is written (according to the normality rule with respect to the criterion [eq. 2.5.1]): {\dot{\epsilon}}^{p}={\dot{\epsilon}}_{1}^{p}+{\dot{\epsilon}}_{2}^{p}={\lambda}_{1}^{p}\frac{\partial {f}_{1}^{p}}{\partial N}+{\lambda}_{2}^{p}\frac{\partial {f}_{2}^{p}}{\partial N} {\dot{\kappa}}^{p}={\dot{\kappa}}_{1}^{p}+{\dot{\kappa}}_{2}^{p}={\lambda}_{1}^{p}\frac{\partial {f}_{1}^{p}}{\partial M}+{\lambda}_{2}^{p}\frac{\partial {f}_{2}^{p}}{\partial M} {\dot{\alpha}}^{m}={\dot{\alpha}}_{1}^{m}+{\dot{\alpha}}_{2}^{m}={\lambda}_{1}^{p}\frac{\partial {f}_{1}^{p}}{\partial {X}^{m}}+{\lambda}_{2}^{p}\frac{\partial {f}_{2}^{p}}{\partial {X}^{m}}=-(-{\dot{\epsilon}}_{1}^{p}-{\dot{\epsilon}}_{2}^{p})={\dot{\epsilon}}^{p} {\dot{\alpha}}^{f}={\dot{\alpha}}_{1}^{f}+{\dot{\alpha}}_{2}^{f}={\lambda}_{1}^{p}\frac{\partial {f}_{1}^{p}}{\partial {X}^{f}}+{\lambda}_{2}^{p}\frac{\partial {f}_{2}^{p}}{\partial {X}^{f}}=-(-{\dot{\kappa}}_{1}^{p}-{\dot{\kappa}}_{2}^{p})={\dot{\kappa}}^{p} where the {\lambda}_{j}^{p} are the plastic multipliers, positive or zero, for the positive bendings and the negative bendings. They are shared by the membrane flow and by that in bending. One deduces from [eq. 2.6.3] and [eq. 2.6.4], in the manner usual for linear kinematic hardening, that the hardening internal variables in membrane and in bending are equal respectively to the plastic strains and to the plastic curvatures. From this there follow the following relations on the back-stress tensors in membrane and bending: {X}^{m}=-{C}_{m}:{\epsilon}^{p} {X}^{f}=-{C}_{f}:{\kappa}^{p} It must be noted that this choice of a Prager tensor {C}_{m} identical both in tension and in compression is open to criticism. Indeed, in plastic compression, the concrete and the steel intervene, whereas in tension only the steel contributes (the concrete having failed). The plasticity criteria [eq. 2.4.1] may be reached at the same moment (for particular regimes of biaxial bending), so the flow may take place from the two criteria reached at once. The consistency condition gives two additional relations: \begin{array}{ccccc}{\lambda}_{j}^{p}{\dot{f}}_{j}^{p}(N,M)=0& \text{si}& {\lambda}_{j}^{p}>0& \text{alors}& {\dot{f}}_{j}^{p}(N,M)=0\end{array} 2.7 Evolution law of the damage variables The evolution law of the bending damage is written, for the positive bendings and the negative bendings (according to the normality rule with respect to the criterion [eq. 2.5.3]): {\dot{d}}_{j}={\lambda}_{j}^{d}\frac{\partial {f}_{j}^{d}}{\partial {Y}_{j}} The {\lambda}_{j}^{d} are the damage multipliers, positive or zero. One recalls that the {Y}_{j} , defined by [eq. 2.4.3], are positive by construction (energy restitution). The consistency condition gives two additional relations: \begin{array}{ccccc}{\lambda}_{j}^{d}{\dot{f}}_{j}^{d}({Y}_{j})=0& \text{si}& {\lambda}_{j}^{d}>0& \text{alors}& {\dot{f}}_{j}^{d}({Y}_{j})=0\mathrm{\iff }{\dot{Y}}_{j}=0\end{array} The two damage variables may evolve simultaneously. 3 Parameters of the law With global models such as GLRC_DAMAGE one seeks to have a simpler representation of the non-linear phenomena, by using numerical methods that are more efficient and more robust. Consequently, it is difficult to attribute a physical meaning to all the parameters of the model, because most of them encompass several phenomena. Thus, it is strongly recommended that the parameters of the model be validated by a comparative study between the GLRC_DAMAGE approach and a finer approach, such as modellings by multifibre beams, multilayer shells or 3D, on a part sufficiently representative of the structure to be analysed. Failing which, the error of an analysis using the model GLRC_DAMAGE cannot be estimated or controlled. In any case, the parameters of the law are determined in a simplified manner with the aid of the analysis of the monotonic behaviour of a reinforced-concrete cross-section, except for the linear elastic behaviour, where it is also possible to resort to a homogenised plate approach, cf. for example [bib4]. One assumes that the set of parameters describing the elastic behaviour is identifiable independently of the plasticity and damage parameters. Moreover, the homogenisation methods allow us to determine the global elastic behaviour with very good accuracy. One considers in [§3.1] two approaches for homogenising the elastic behaviour: in one of them one makes the assumption of an equivalent isotropic medium and in the other the orthotropy is taken into account. At present, only the isotropic approach is available in Code_Aster . Moreover, it is only the isotropic approximation which can be used in combination with plasticity and damage. In principle, an extension to orthotropic behaviours in linear and in non-linear analysis could be envisaged within an equivalent theoretical framework. The limitation to the isotropic cases was chosen on the one hand because the phenomenon of orthotropy was judged negligible at failure, the simulation of which is the principal aim of the model, and on the other hand in order to lighten the formulation of the model and the identification of the parameters. The parameters of the non-linear behaviours are more delicate to determine than the elasticity parameters. For the damage this is simpler, because their number is smaller. On the other hand, for the plasticity, the user must supply a function, determining the limit yield moment as a function of the membrane force. Moreover, the kinematic hardening is given by four Drucker tensors, each having three parameters. In this version their number is artificially reduced by assuming that these tensors are the same for the two plasticity thresholds. If the behaviours in elasticity and with damage can be identified without having a reference modelling (or a test), for the plastic behaviour this is strongly discouraged. One associates these values with the moment–curvature slopes, for the two loading directions j=1,2 , and with respect to the elastic slope, see also []: \frac{{p}_{2,j}}{{p}_{\mathit{élas}}}=\frac{1+\gamma {d}_{j}^{max}}{1+{d}_{j}^{max}} whence, for j=1,2 : {d}_{j}^{max}=\frac{{p}_{\mathit{élas}}-{p}_{2,j}}{{p}_{2,j}-{p}_{f}} In the operator DEFI_GLRC one supplies QP1 and QP2 for {p}_{2,1} and {p}_{2,2} . 3.2.4 Identification of the plastic behaviour parameters For the behaviours in elasticity and with damage, it is possible to obtain the values of the parameters analytically from the material and geometric properties of the reinforced concrete. In order to characterise the parameters of the plastic behaviour, it is imperative to refer to a finer modelling (multifibre beam, multilayer shell or 3D). Software of the MOCO type (see [bib10]) is recommended for the automatic identification of the GLRC models. In the long term, it is planned that such a tool be integrated into Code_Aster . In the current version, the identification of the elastoplastic part is left entirely to the care of the users. For the identification, it is more reasonable to identify the parameters of the non-linear behaviour from tests, numerical or experimental, with a monotonic loading. For example, one may use a test with homogeneous curvatures and bending moments. Such a test is pseudo-one-dimensional and can be represented entirely with a single graph, on which one can identify the damage and plasticity thresholds as well as the slopes corresponding to the various loading phases, see . In order to measure the effect of the membrane force the monotonic bending test must be combined with a membrane loading. Figure 3.2.4-a : Monotonic uniaxial bending. On the , one distinguishes five phases: 1. elastic phase characterised by the slope {p}_{\mathit{élas}} 2. phase corresponding to the damage of the concrete (slope {p}_{f} ), 3. recovery of the stiffness due to the steels after the maximum damage has been reached (slope {p}_{2} ) 4. yielding of the steels (slope {p}_{p} ). 5. elastic unloading: the value of the unloading slopes lies in the interval [{p}_{\mathit{élas}},{p}_{f}] for phases i) to iii) and is equal to {p}_{2} for phase iv). In order to describe the plastic behaviour one must supply the functions {M}_{\mathit{jx}}^{p}({N}_{xx}-{X}_{xx}^{m}) and {M}_{\mathit{jy}}^{p}({N}_{yy}-{X}_{yy}^{m}) , j=1,2 , as « aster » functions, FMEX1, FMEX2, FMEY1, FMEY2 in DEFI_GLRC. It is recommended to define symbolic functions by the command FORMULE, which must then be transformed into discretised functions by the command CALC_FONC_INTERP. In addition to these functions, one must also supply their first and second derivatives, which, on the other hand, can be computed by the operator CALC_FONCTION. Typically, these are functions close to parabolic functions. For a given direction, say x , the two functions {M}_{\mathrm{1x}}^{p} and {M}_{\mathrm{2x}}^{p} define the elastic domain, as in the . Figure 3.2.4-b : The elastic domain lies between the two bending-moment/membrane-force curves. The graph presents a comparison between the thresholds used by the model GLRC_DAMAGE and those obtained by a multilayer computation on the case of a beam. 4 Numerical integration of the constitutive law The law GLRC_DAMAGE was initially designed for fast-dynamics analyses resorting to explicit time-integration schemes. The version of the model is almost identical to the initial version and is therefore not optimised for static analyses or for implicit dynamics. Consequently, the model is liable to be insufficiently robust and insufficiently efficient for an analysis with large time steps. It is planned that the numerical integration of the model be improved. 4.1 Evaluation of the damage The damage model used in GLRC_DAMAGE has been extended to the membrane–bending coupling and placed in the model GLRC_DM (see R7.01.32). One therefore refers the reader to R7.01.32 for the details concerning the numerical integration of the damage part. The computation in GLRC_DAMAGE is simpler, because one neglects the influence of the membrane energy on the evolution of the damage. 4.2 Evaluation of the plastic flow The integration of the elastoplastic part is the most delicate part of the model. For the moment, one does not have a method with a satisfactory robustness for large increments of (pseudo)-time. One summarises below the particular features of the model presented in [§2], which one can hardly solve by the classical approaches, based on Newton's method. - Double cones: The elastic domain of each of the threshold functions defined in [§2.5.1] is not convex and can be represented by a double cone in the space of the generalised stresses (see ). Obviously, it is only the cone close to the origin which represents the true elastic domain. Thus, the resolution of the plastic admissibility must be carried out by adding two inequalities: {g}_{1}^{p}(N-{X}^{m},M-{X}^{f})=({M}_{xx}-{X}_{xx}^{f})-{M}_{\mathrm{1x}}^{p}({N}_{xx}-{X}_{xx}^{m})+({M}_{yy}-{X}_{yy}^{f})-{M}_{\mathrm{1y}}^{p}({N}_{yy}-{X}_{yy}^{m})\le 0 {g}_{2}^{p}(N-{X}^{m},M-{X}^{f})=({M}_{xx}-{X}_{xx}^{f})-{M}_{\mathrm{2x}}^{p}({N}_{xx}-{X}_{xx}^{m})+({M}_{yy}-{X}_{yy}^{f})-{M}_{\mathrm{2y}}^{p}({N}_{yy}-{X}_{yy}^{m})\le 0 With the inequalities and , one eliminates the non-physical solutions of the plastic-admissibility equations, {f}_{j}^{p}(N-{X}^{m},M-{X}^{f})\le 0 , {\lambda}_{j}^{p}\ge 0 . The functions {g}_{j}^{p} define the two planes, {g}_{j}^{p}(N-{X}^{m},M-{X}^{f})=0 , separating the non-physical cones from the cones determining the elastic domain. On the other hand, the introduction of the inequalities into the system prevents us from using algorithms of Newton type without important modifications. - Apexes of the cones : the other drawback, also linked to the shape of the elastic domain in the space of the generalised stresses, comes from the two apexes of the cones of the elastic domain (see ). This property can also make the convergence of the iterative algorithm difficult. Because of the two drawbacks mentioned above one cannot apply the radial-return algorithm, the one most often used for the solution of plasticity problems. In its place one has implemented a « cutting plane » algorithm, combined with bisection. The details of the algorithm are available in [bib1]. Figure 4.2-a : Plastic threshold in the space of the generalised stresses in the form of two double cones. 4.3 Evaluation of the tangent operator At present, the tangent operator of the model GLRC_DAMAGE is not consistent and does not guarantee the quadratic convergence of the global Newton process. Its implementation is based on an older version of the model. 4.4 Internal variables of the model We list here the internal variables stored at each Gauss point in the implementation of the model. | Internal-variable number | physical meaning | | --- | --- | | V1 | EXXP plastic membrane extension | | V2 | EYYP plastic membrane extension | | V3 | EXYP plastic membrane extension | | V4 | KXXP cumulative plastic curvature | | V5 | KYYP cumulative plastic curvature | | V6 | KXYP cumulative plastic curvature | | V7 | Cumulative plastic dissipation | | V8 | D1 damage variable of the upper face | | V9 | D2 damage variable of the lower face | | V10 | Damage dissipation | | V11 | orthotropy angle | | V12 | orthotropy angle | | V13 | orthotropy angle | | V14 | NXX kinematic back-stress membrane force | | V15 | NYY kinematic back-stress membrane force | | V16 | NXY kinematic back-stress membrane force | | V17 | MXX kinematic back-stress moment | | V18 | MYY kinematic back-stress moment | | V19 | MXY kinematic back-stress moment | 5 Verification The constitutive law GLRC_DAMAGE is verified by the following test cases: | linear static | SSLS126 | Bending of a reinforced-concrete slab (model GLRC_DAMAGE) supported on two sides: elastic beam regime | V3.03.126 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | linear static | SSLS127 | Bending of a reinforced-concrete slab (model GLRC_DAMAGE) supported on 4 sides: elastic plate regime | V3.03.127 | | non-linear explicit dynamics | SDNS106 | Transient response of a reinforced-concrete slab: model GLRC_DAMAGE | V5.06.106 | 6 Bibliography 1. r7.01.32 Constitutive law for reinforced-concrete plates GLRC_DM r7.01.32 Constitutive law for reinforced-concrete plates GLRC_DM Summary: This documentation presents the theoretical formulation and the numerical integration of the constitutive law GLRC_DM, which can be used with the modelling DKTG. It belongs to the so-called “global” models used for thin structures (beams, plates and shells). The non-linear phenomena, such as plasticity or damage, are directly related to the generalised strains (extension, curvature, distortion) and the generalised stresses (membrane forces, bending forces and shear forces). Thus, this constitutive law applies with a plate or shell finite element. This makes it possible to save, compared with a multi-layer approach, CPU time as well as memory. The advantage over multi-layer shells is even greater when one of the constituents of the plate behaves in a quasi-brittle manner (concrete, for example), since the global model makes it possible to avoid localisation problems. The constitutive law GLRC_DM models damage under membrane loading and under bending loading of reinforced-concrete plates, with the aid of “homogenised” parameters. This constitutive model therefore represents an evolution with respect to the model GLRC_DAMAGE, which treats damage only under bending loading. The structure of the damage model of GLRC_DM resembles that of GLRC_DAMAGE, and both are inspired by ENDO_ISOT_BETON. Unlike GLRC_DAMAGE, GLRC_DM does not make it possible to model a possible yielding, which makes it less suitable for simulating extreme loadings. Moreover, the constitutive behaviour GLRC_DM is isotropic before damage: the orthotropy brought by the steel reinforcement layers is neglected. One may consider using the constitutive behaviour GLRC_DM “alone” on a plate modelling in order to represent reinforced concrete, or else only in order to represent the concrete alone, associating it then with modellings of steel reinforcement grids, which makes it possible to represent the orthotropy and possibly the non-symmetry of the reinforcement layers. This latter choice also simplifies the parameterisation of this constitutive behaviour. 1 Introduction 1.1 Global models A plate constitutive model said to be global, or a structural-element model in general, means that the constitutive law is written directly in terms of a relation between the generalised stresses and the generalised strains. The global approach to modelling the behaviour of structures applies in particular to composite structures, for example reinforced concrete (see figure r7.01.32-fig-1), and represents an alternative to the so-called local or semi-global approaches, which are finer but more costly modellings (see and ). In the local approach one uses a fine modelling for each of the phases (steel, concrete) and their interactions (bond), and in the semi-global approach one exploits the slenderness of the structure to simplify the description of the kinematics, which leads to the PMF (multi-fibre beam) or multi-layer shell models. The interest of the global model lies in the fact that the corresponding finite element requires only one integration point through the thickness, and above all in the obtaining of a homogenised behaviour. This advantage is even more important in the analysis of reinforced concrete, since one bypasses the localisation problems encountered when modelling concrete without reinforcement. Obviously, a global model represents the local phenomena in a coarse manner and requires more validation before its application to industrial examples. Reinforced-concrete slab 1.2 Objectives of the law GLRC_DM The model GLRC_DM is capable of representing the damage of a reinforced-concrete plate, when the latter remains limited, that is, without reaching failure. It was inspired by the model GLRC_DAMAGE and is complementary to it. If GLRC_DAMAGE can also represent damage, this is possible only for bending loading, with no impact on the membrane behaviour. On this point GLRC_DM is more faithful to the physics, but unlike GLRC_DAMAGE it does not make it possible to take plasticity into account. Being simpler, GLRC_DM is also more efficient in terms of computation cost and numerical robustness. One aims at an identical behaviour in the directions \mathrm{Ox} and \mathrm{Oy} ; moreover the upper and lower reinforcement layers are assumed to be identical. 2 Formulation of the constitutive model The use of the theory of thin plates and shells makes it possible to describe efficiently the mechanical behaviour of reinforced-concrete structures, which are generally slender. In a first step of the construction of the model, the existence of a homogenised medium with the same mechanical behaviour as the reinforced-concrete structure of interest is assumed. For simplicity, it is assumed that this medium is isotropic and that the structural element studied is symmetric with respect to its middle surface. These assumptions are not indispensable for the formulation, but were made in order to simplify the approach. Moreover, their impact on the behaviour is estimated to be smaller than that of cracking, which is at the centre of interest of the model. It must be noted that the use of this model is associated with that of a plate element. It can be used only in the framework of DKT finite elements (supported modelling: DKTG), corresponding to the theory of Love-Kirchhoff , in which any transverse distortion through the thickness of the plate is neglected. 2.1 Free energy For a homogeneous isotropic continuous medium with linear elastic behaviour, the volumetric density of the free energy can be written as: {\Phi}_{e}(\varepsilon )=\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathrm{tr}{(\varepsilon )}^{2}+\mu \sum_{i=1}^{3}{{\tilde{\varepsilon}}_{i}}^{2} where \lambda ,\mu are the Lamé coefficients, \varepsilon the strain tensor and {\tilde{\varepsilon}}_{i} its eigenvalues. As for the model ENDO_ISOT_BETON, damage is introduced by a function \xi (.,{d}_{i}) , {d}_{i} being a damage variable. Thus, for a damageable medium, the free energy is written: {\Phi}_{\mathrm{ed}}(\varepsilon ,{d}_{j})=\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathrm{tr}{(\varepsilon )}^{2}\xi (\mathrm{tr}(\varepsilon ),{d}_{j})+\mu \sum_{i=1}^{3}{{\tilde{\varepsilon}}_{i}}^{2}\xi ({\tilde{\varepsilon}}_{i},{d}_{j}) with the function (x,d)\in {ℝ}^{2}\to \xi (x,d)\le 1 satisfying a priori \frac{\partial \xi }{\partial d}\le 0 in order to represent the loss of stiffness linked to damage, and \frac{\partial \xi }{\partial x}=0 \quad \mathrm{pour} \quad x\in \left]-\infty ,0\right[\cup \left]0,+\infty \right[ , the jump at 0 making it possible to represent the discontinuity of behaviour between tension and compression. In order to plot the maxima of the strains, one introduces \mathit{V14} , \mathit{V15} and \mathit{V16} : - V14 : TRAMAX : maximum tensile strain over time - V15 : COMMAX : maximum compressive strain over time - V16 : FLEMAX: maximum bending strain over time In order to assess the validity of the parameters, the following error analyses are proposed: - V17 : ERRCOM: error expressed as a percentage between the areas of the theoretical compression curve (defined by EPSI_C and FCJ ) and the approximate curve ( NYC, GAMMA_C ) between 0 and COMMAX - V18 : ERRFLE: error expressed as a percentage between the areas of the theoretical bending curve (reinforced-concrete section analysis) and the approximate curve ( MFY, GAMMA_F) between 0 and FLEMAX 2.9 Use of the model GLRC_DM in thermomechanical situations It is assumed that the temperature distribution is affine through the thickness: this is admissible for a plate in a stationary thermal situation. The thermal expansion coefficient is assumed to be that of the concrete, which is clearly predominant in the section: it is therefore used directly in the membrane and bending situations of the plate. It is also assumed that the material coefficients and parameters do not depend on the temperature in the range studied. This affine temperature distribution through the thickness therefore results in a membrane thermal strain and a thermal curvature change, whence a simple shift of the membrane strains and of the curvatures as a function of the wall temperatures of the plate. Thus, once this shift has been applied, there is no direct impact on the expression of the constitutive law nor on the analysis of the irreversible evolutions. Two tests verify the results obtained, cf. r7.01.32-verification . The model GLRC_DM can therefore be used in stationary thermomechanical situations without modification, within this set of assumptions. 3 Parameters of the law The damageable reinforced-concrete slab model GLRC_DM therefore needs parameters characteristic of elasticity, supplemented by 6 parameters in order to describe the damage constitutive behaviour: {k}_{0} , in order to define the elastic limit, \alpha in order to determine the participation of bending (see r7.01.32-contraintes-generalisees ), {\gamma}_{\mathrm{mt}} , {\gamma}_{\mathrm{mc}} and {\alpha}_{c} , {\gamma}_{f} in order to describe the non-linear response. All these parameters can be identified from monotonic pure uniaxial tension and bending tests. Some of them are replaced in the code_aster data set by more “meaningful” parameters, see below in paragraph r7.01.32-bilan-identification-parametres . It is possible to proceed either from simple analytical estimates (which give the orders of magnitude) or from a calibration on a response curve supplied by another constitutive model, possibly incorporating compromises. The procedure is described in the paragraphs below and a summary is given in paragraph r7.01.32-bilan-identification-parametres . 3.1 Identification of the linear-elastic constitutive parameters In this model it is assumed that the reinforced-concrete medium is homogenised and the user is left to choose (compute or measure) the parameters: {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m} (effective Young's modulus in membrane), {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f} (effective Young's modulus in bending), {\nu}_{m} (effective Poisson's ratio in membrane) and {\nu}_{f} (effective Poisson's ratio in bending). The following relations are applied in order to determine the Lamé coefficients {\lambda}_{m} , {\mu}_{m} and {\lambda}_{f} , {\mu}_{f} : \begin{array}{ccc}{\lambda}_{m}=\frac{{\nu}_{m}{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m}h}{(1+{\nu}_{m})(1-2{\nu}_{m})}& ,& {\mu}_{m}=\frac{{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m}h}{2(1+{\nu}_{m})}\\ {\lambda}_{f}=\frac{{\nu}_{f}{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}{h}^{3}}{12(1-{\nu}_{f}^{2})}& ,& {\mu}_{f}=\frac{{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}{h}^{3}}{24(1+{\nu}_{f})}\end{array} The relations above are not interchangeable by F↔M for the membrane and bending parameters, since in membrane the relations correspond to the general case (3D elasticity) and the plane-stress condition is treated within the formulation of the model, whereas for bending one has placed oneself from the outset in 2D elasticity with plane stress. In the elastic range one thus has: \begin{array}{}{N}_{\alpha \beta }=\frac{{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m}h}{1-{\nu}_{m}^{2}}({\nu}_{m}.\mathrm{tr}\epsilon .{\delta}_{\alpha \beta }+(1-{\nu}_{m}){\epsilon}_{\alpha \beta })\\ {M}_{\alpha \beta }=\frac{{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}{h}^{3}}{12(1-{\nu}_{f}^{2})}({\nu}_{f}.\mathrm{tr}\kappa .{\delta}_{\alpha \beta }+(1-{\nu}_{f}){\kappa}_{\alpha \beta })\end{array} \alpha and \beta being indices ranging from 1 to 2. By default {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m}={E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}=E and {\nu}_{m}={\nu}_{f}=\nu , where E and \nu are the elastic coefficients supplied in the command file under the keyword ELAS. On the other hand, since reinforced concrete is not a homogeneous material, the effective value of {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f} may differ from {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m} . Consequently, the user is left the possibility of introducing values {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f} and {\nu}_{f} (EF and NUF under the factor keyword GLRC_DM) different from E and \nu , which in that case serve only to describe the membrane elasticity. The plane-stress condition for the membrane {\sigma}_{zz}=0 is satisfied in the manner described in paragraph r7.01.32-seuils-evolution-endommagement . Note: In , one obtains a different relation between {\lambda}_{f} , {\nu}_{f} and {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f} on the one hand, and between {\lambda}_{m} , {\nu}_{m} and {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m} on the other hand. This difference is directly linked to the different taking into account, in membrane and in bending, of the plane-stress condition. More particularly, one defines {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f} and {\nu}_{f} through a pure bending test, where {\kappa}_{yy}=-{\nu}_{f}{\kappa}_{xx} , and {M}_{ij}=0 , except {M}_{xx}\ne 0 . One then uses the following equations in order to find the relation between {\lambda}_{f} , {\mu}_{f} and {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f} , {\nu}_{f} : {M}_{yy}=({\lambda}_{f}(1-{\nu}_{f})-2{\mu}_{f}{\nu}_{f}){\kappa}_{xx}=0 and {M}_{xx}=({\lambda}_{f}(1-{\nu}_{f})-2{\mu}_{f}){\kappa}_{xx}=\frac{{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}{h}^{3}}{12}{\kappa}_{xx} whence one obtains: {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}=\frac{12}{{h}^{3}}({\lambda}_{f}(1-{\nu}_{f})+2{\mu}_{f}) \text{et} {\lambda}_{f}(1-{\nu}_{f})-2{\mu}_{f}{\nu}_{f}=0 Solving , one has the relations expressed in . The identification of the elastic parameters {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m} , {\nu}_{m} , {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f} and {\nu}_{f} of the model from the characteristics of the concrete and of the steels rests on two loading cases: pure tension and pure bending. Consider the following characteristics for the concrete: Young's modulus {E}_{b} , Poisson's ratio {\nu}_{b} , slab thickness h , and for the steels: Young's modulus {E}_{a} , Poisson's ratio {\nu}_{a} , total cross-section per linear metre (for the two layers, assumed symmetric through the thickness and identical in both directions) {S}_{a} , relative position of a layer through the thickness {\chi }_{a}\in \left]0,1\right[ . One thus obtains from the uniaxial test in pure elastic tension : \begin{array}{}{N}_{xx}={E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m}h{\epsilon}_{xx}={E}_{a}{S}_{a}{\epsilon}_{xx}+\frac{{E}_{b}h}{1-{\nu}_{b}^{2}}({\epsilon}_{xx}+{\nu}_{b}{\epsilon}_{yy})\\ {N}_{yy}=0={E}_{a}{S}_{a}{\epsilon}_{yy}+\frac{{E}_{b}h}{1-{\nu}_{b}^{2}}({\epsilon}_{yy}+{\nu}_{b}{\epsilon}_{xx})\end{array} Whence (keywords E and NU): {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m}={E}_{a}\frac{{S}_{a}}{h}+{E}_{b}\cdot \frac{{E}_{b}h+{E}_{a}{S}_{a}}{{E}_{b}h+{E}_{a}{S}_{a}(1-{\nu}_{b}^{2})} One observes that this identification produces an error on the in-plane elastic shear stiffness of the slab, a case for which the steels do not contribute (they are grids of welded bars), which makes the homogenised constitutive behaviour orthotropic and not isotropic. Indeed, one obtains with the values : {G}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m}=\frac{{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m}}{2(1+{\nu}_{m})}=\frac{{E}_{b}}{2(1+{\nu}_{b})}\cdot \frac{{E}_{b}^{2}{h}^{2}+2{E}_{a}{E}_{b}h{S}_{a}+{E}_{a}^{2}{S}_{a}^{2}(1-{\nu}_{b}^{2})}{{E}_{b}^{2}{h}^{2}+{E}_{a}{E}_{b}h{S}_{a}(1-{\nu}_{b})}\ne \frac{{E}_{b}}{2(1+{\nu}_{b})} If one prefers to ensure primarily the identification on the case of in-plane elastic shear of the slab, and on the case of the response in the pure-tension direction (thus accepting the error on the orthogonal Poisson effect), one obtains: {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{m}={E}_{b}+\frac{{E}_{a}{S}_{a}(1-{\nu}_{b})}{h} Care will be taken that this rough identification (not thermodynamically admissible with respect to the pure-tension test) does not give unrealistic values of {\nu}_{m} . Next, one obtains from the uniaxial test in pure elastic bending : \begin{array}{}{M}_{xx}=\frac{{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}{h}^{3}}{12}{\kappa}_{xx}=\frac{1}{4}{E}_{a}{S}_{a}{h}^{2}{\chi }_{a}^{2}{\kappa}_{xx}+\frac{{E}_{b}{h}^{3}}{12(1-{\nu}_{b}^{2})}({\kappa}_{xx}+{\nu}_{b}{\kappa}_{yy})\\ {M}_{yy}=0=\frac{1}{4}{E}_{a}{S}_{a}{h}^{2}{\chi }_{a}^{2}{\kappa}_{yy}+\frac{{E}_{b}{h}^{3}}{12(1-{\nu}_{b}^{2})}({\kappa}_{yy}+{\nu}_{b}{\kappa}_{xx})\end{array} Whence (keywords EF and NUF): {E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}=\frac{3}{h}{E}_{a}{S}_{a}{\chi }_{a}^{2}+{E}_{b}\cdot \frac{{E}_{b}h+3{E}_{a}{S}_{a}{\chi }_{a}^{2}}{{E}_{b}h+3{E}_{a}{S}_{a}{\chi }_{a}^{2}(1-{\nu}_{b}^{2})} One also observes that this identification produces an error on the anticlastic elastic bending stiffness {M}_{xy} of the slab (coefficient {G}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}=\frac{{E}_{\mathrm{eq}}^{f}{h}^{3}}{24(1+{\nu}_{f})} instead of {G}_{b}^{f}=\frac{{E}_{b}{h}^{3}}{24(1+{\nu}_{b})} ), a case for which the steels do not contribute. 3.2 Identification of the damageable elastic constitutive parameters The way in which the linear-elasticity parameters are obtained having been presented in paragraph r7.01.32-parametres-elastique-lineaire , it is proposed to compute the damage parameters of the model from three tests: a pure-tension test, a pure-compression test and a monotonic uniaxial pure-bending test.
