r7.01.33 Elasto-plasticity–damage coupling r7.01.33 Elasto-plasticity–damage coupling Summary: This document presents a method for coupling an elasto-plastic model with a damage model, which is implemented within the framework of KIT_DDI. The method uses an approach of partitioning the model into three modules: elasto-plasticity, damage and coupler. It is particularly this modularity which represents the principal interest of the method. It makes it possible to use the same “coupler” module for couplings between different elasto-plasticity and damage models without intervening in the implementation of the latter. Exactly the same idea is used for the mechanical/creep couplings (see R7.01.19). For the moment, the implementation makes it possible to couple only the model GLRC_DM for the damage with the models VMIS_(ISOT/CINE)_LINE for the elasto-plasticity, and this only for DKTG modellings. 1 Introduction The document is organised in two main parts: the first presents the general method of the elasto-plasticity–damage couplings and the second describes the specific features of the various couplings, which are at present limited to the coupling between GLRC_DM and VMIS_(ISOT/CINE)_LINE for the “global” models. In the first part one considers in particular the following aspects: the issues of this type of coupling, the thermodynamic framework and the numerical implementation. In the second part one recalls what the global models () are for reinforced-concrete plates and shells and how the general method is applied in that framework. 2 Elasto-plasticity–damage models in general 2.1 Issues and difficulties In the modelling of the behaviour of solids, one observes that the most important non-linear phenomena to be taken into account, during a structural analysis under extreme loading, concern the presence and the evolution of the anelastic strain (plasticity) and the degradation of the stiffness (damage). The relative importance of these two phenomena can vary drastically from one material to another. Thus, most often one considers only plasticity when modelling metals while neglecting damage, whereas for a material of concrete type, damage is judged more important and plasticity is not taken into account. Nevertheless, often this simplification is not justifiable and one is led to model both phenomena, plasticity and damage, at the same time. For some time already the thermodynamic framework for the modelling of the two phenomena has been well established (e.g. see [bib1], [bib2]) and there exists no obstacle to extending it to elasto-plastic–damageable couplings. As regards the numerical solution of these models within the framework of the finite-element method (FEM), there exist very robust algorithms, notably for plasticity (e.g. see [bib13]) and also for damage (e.g. see [bib14]), provided that the localisation phenomenon does not become predominant. On the other hand, the numerical solution of a coupled model is much less obvious. The numerical difficulties concerning the solution algorithm of a coupled model intervene on two aspects essentially: - satisfaction of the (Kuhn–Tucker) conditions of the plasticity and damage thresholds, - construction of the tangent matrix. The first difficulty is due to the fact that the plastic and damageable internal variables act very differently on the stress level, which makes the system of equations difficult to solve. The second point is a simple consequence of the increased complexity of the coupled model with respect to the single-phenomenon models. Recently, one has proposed in [bib3] and [bib4] a solution algorithm for an elasto-plastic–damageable model based on the strict partitioning into a plastic part and a damageable part. It consists in introducing an additional iterative process in order to satisfy the plastic admissibility and the damageable admissibility simultaneously. This iterative process is driven by what one calls the damage strain, a variable which, unlike the plastic strain, is not a state variable, but rather represents a means of coupling between different models. Thus, in the model introduced in [bib3] the choice of the elasto-plastic model being free, one nevertheless had to modify the damage formulation, which in that case provided only for the modelling of non-softening behaviours. In [bib4] one demonstrated the interest of integrating this type of law within the framework of mixed finite elements. In this document one generalises the approach presented in [bib3] in order to be able to couple practically any elasto-plastic model with any damage model. The interest of such a platform in fact goes beyond the elasto-plastic–damageable coupling. 2.2 Thermodynamic framework In this part one recalls the usual approach for constructing damage and elasto-plasticity models, based on thermodynamics. The combination of the two types of model can be done in a fairly natural manner, provided that the coupling is made at the level of the computation of the stresses. The whole of the approach presented here is carried out under the assumption that the internal variables of damage and of plasticity are not coupled directly to one another. Moreover, one places oneself within the framework of small strains and without thermal phenomenon. 2.2.1 Plasticity The free energy \psi may be written as the sum of the elastic energy and of the so-called stored energy, due to plasticity: \psi (\varepsilon ,{\varepsilon}^{p},\alpha )={\psi}^{e}(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{p})+{\psi}^{p}(\alpha ) where \varepsilon is the total strain, {\varepsilon}^{p} the plastic strain and \alpha a vector of internal variables. The essential assumption that one makes in () is that the elastic energy depends only on the elastic strain, {\psi}^{e}={\psi}^{e}({\varepsilon}^{e}) , where {\varepsilon}^{e}=\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{p} . In the second step one defines the plastic dissipation rate and one ensures that it always remains positive, {D}^{p}=\sigma :\dot{\varepsilon}-\rho \dot{\psi}=(\sigma -\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{e}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}}):{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{e}+\sigma :{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}-A\mathrm{\ast }\dot{\alpha}\ge 0 where A=\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{p}}{\partial \alpha } are the thermodynamic forces associated with internal variables and the symbol \ast refers to the appropriate product operator between A and \dot{\alpha} . One assumes that the dissipation does not evolve, i.e. \dot{D}=0 , when the plastic variables do not evolve, i.e. {\dot{\epsilon}}^{p}=\dot{\alpha}=0 , which allows us to define the stress as: \sigma =\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{e}}{\partial {\epsilon}^{e}} In this document, one contents oneself with materials which have a linear and isotropic behaviour. In this case, the elastic contribution of the free energy is given by: \rho \psi ({\epsilon}^{e})=\frac{1}{2}{\epsilon}^{e}:{D}^{e}:{\epsilon}^{e} where {D}^{e} is the standard isotropic elasticity tensor. From the two preceding equations, one deduces the expression of the stress tensor: \sigma ={D}^{e}:{\epsilon}^{e} Another essential ingredient of an elasto-plastic model is the definition of the yield-threshold function, which depends on the stress tensor and on the thermodynamic forces associated with the internal variables. This function is negative when the strains are purely elastic and reaches zero when plastic flow is imminent: {\Phi}^{p}={\Phi}^{p}\left(\sigma ,A\right)\le 0 The complete characterisation of the general plasticity model requires the definition of the evolution laws of the internal variables, i.e. the variables associated with the dissipation phenomena. In our case, the internal variables are the plastic strain tensor and the set of internal variables \alpha . To establish the evolution laws of these internal variables one often uses the principle of maximum plastic dissipation. However this is not essential in our approach. One will make use of a more general writing: \begin{array}{c}{\dot{\epsilon}}^{p}={\dot{\gamma}}^{p}N={\dot{\gamma}}^{p}\frac{\partial \psi }{\partial \sigma }\\ \dot{\alpha}={\dot{\gamma}}^{p}H=-{\dot{\gamma}}^{p}\frac{\partial \psi }{\partial A}\end{array} \dot{\gamma} is the plastic multiplier, N is called the flow vector and H is the hardening modulus. Moreover every solution must satisfy the plastic admissibility conditions, which are: {\Phi}^{p}\le 0,\dot{\gamma}\ge 0,{\Phi}^{p}\dot{\gamma}=0 2.2.2 Damage For the damage models it is more difficult to have a construction as general as that of plasticity. Consequently one will treat a simple case but one that is fairly representative of the desired characteristics of the model. Thus, one defines the free energy as: \psi \left(\epsilon ,d\right)={\psi}^{e}\left(\epsilon \right)\zeta \left(d\right) where \zeta is the damage function and d the damage variable, which is a scalar but which may equally well be a tensor. Likewise, the function \zeta may in general depend on \epsilon , notably on the sign of its trace in order to distinguish behaviours that are typically very different in tension and in compression. By using (), one defines the damage dissipation as, {D}^{d}=\sigma :\dot{\epsilon}-\rho \dot{\psi}=\left(\sigma -\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial \epsilon }\right):\dot{\epsilon}-\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial d}\dot{d}\ge 0 The dissipation does not evolve, i.e. {\dot{D}}^{d}=0 , when the damage variable does not evolve, i.e. \dot{d}=0 , which allows us to define the stress as: \sigma =\rho \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial \epsilon }=\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{e}}{\partial \epsilon }\zeta \left(d\right)={D}^{e}\left(d\right):{\epsilon}^{e} where {D}^{e}(d) represents the standard isotropic elasticity tensor evolving as a function of the damage. By making the assumption of an isotropic damage, taking \zeta =1-d the stress becomes: \sigma =(1-d){D}^{e}:{\varepsilon}^{e} As for plasticity one introduces a damage threshold function: {\Phi}^{d}={\Phi}^{d}(\varepsilon ,Y)\le 0 where Y is the variable dual to d . This time, the threshold is a direct function of the total strain, \varepsilon , and one seeks to satisfy the damage admissibility conditions: {\Phi}^{d}\le 0,\dot{d}\ge 0,{\Phi}^{d}\dot{d}=0 One must also formulate the evolution law of d : \dot{d}=\dot{d}\left(Y\right) 2.2.3 Coupling Finally, one combines the formulations of damage and of plasticity in order to arrive at a coupled model. The free energy of the coupled model is therefore written as: \psi (\varepsilon ,{\varepsilon}^{p},\alpha ,d)={\psi}^{e}(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{p})\zeta (d)+{\psi}^{p}(\alpha ) The dissipation is written: D=\sigma :\dot{\varepsilon}-\rho \dot{\psi}=(\sigma -\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{e}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}}):{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{e}+\sigma :{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}-A\mathrm{\ast }\dot{\alpha}-\frac{\partial {\psi}^{d}}{\partial d}\dot{d}\ge 0 The stress tensor is: \sigma =\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{d}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}}=\rho \frac{\partial {\psi}^{e}}{\partial {\varepsilon}^{e}}\zeta (d)={D}^{e}(d):(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{p}) If the elasticity is linear isotropic and the damage is isotropic: \sigma =(1-d){D}^{e}:(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{p}) One then has two threshold functions: one for the plastic flow and the other for the damage: \begin{array}{c}{\Phi}^{p}={\Phi}^{p}(\sigma ,A)\le 0\\ {\Phi}^{d}={\Phi}^{d}({\varepsilon}^{e},Y)\le 0\end{array} The evolution laws of the damage variables are given by: \begin{array}{c}{\dot{\varepsilon}}^{p}={\dot{\gamma}}^{p}N={\dot{\gamma}}^{p}\frac{\partial \psi }{\partial \sigma }\\ \dot{\alpha}={\dot{\gamma}}^{p}H=-{\dot{\gamma}}^{p}\frac{\partial \psi }{\partial A}\\ \dot{d}=\dot{d}(Y)\end{array} The admissibility conditions are: \begin{array}{c}{\Phi}^{p}\le 0,\dot{\gamma}\ge 0,{\Phi}^{p}\dot{\gamma}=0\\ {\Phi}^{d}\le 0,\dot{d}\ge 0,{\Phi}^{d}\dot{d}=0\end{array} 2.3 Numerical integration 2.3.1 Reminder of the classical solution of non-linear problems by finite elements In the method proposed one adds an additional iterative process with respect to a classical computation by the FEM, which one recalls in this section. In a global solution of a structural problem one seeks the equilibrium state, defined by: {f}^{int}(u(t))={f}^{\mathit{ext}}(t) where {f}^{int} is the vector of the internal forces and {f}^{\mathit{ext}} the vector of the external forces (the loading). The first is a function of the displacement vector, the principal variable of the system, and the second a function of the parameter t (pseudo-time), defining the notion of trajectory both for the loading and for the evolution of the displacement field. Within the framework of the FEM the internal force is determined by: {f}^{int}(u)={\int}_{\Omega}{B}^{T}\sigma (\varepsilon )d\Omega where \Omega defines the domain considered, \varepsilon the strain tensor, \sigma the stress tensor and B is the classical matrix corresponding to the discretised operator of the symmetric gradient which makes it possible to pass from the strains to the displacements. As we have considered the small-strain assumption, the tensor \varepsilon is defined as: {\epsilon}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\partial {u}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}+\frac{\partial {u}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}}) By using the definition of B , one has: {\varepsilon}_{ij}={B}_{\mathit{ijk}}{u}_{k} after having discretised the displacement field by the FEM. When the behaviour of the material is non-linear, one most often has recourse to Newton's method to solve (). To do this, one is led to linearise (), which gives us: {f}^{int,(k+1)}={f}^{int,(k)}+\frac{\partial {f}^{int,(k)}}{\partial {u}^{(k)}}\Delta {u}^{(k)} where the index k represents the number of the current iteration. At convergence one must have: {f}^{int,(k)}\stackrel{k\to \infty }{\to }{f}^{\mathit{ext}}(t) In order to be able to compute the displacement correction from one iteration to the next, \Delta {u}^{(k)} , one must determine: K=\frac{\partial {f}^{int,(k)}}{\partial {u}^{(k)}}=\underset{\Omega}{\int}{B}^{T}{D}^{\mathit{epd}}Bd\Omega where {D}^{\mathit{epd}} is the consistent tangent modulus for the constitutive law used: {D}^{\mathit{epd}}=\frac{\partial \sigma (\varepsilon )}{\partial \varepsilon } The method detailed below is positioned at the level of a material point (or even at the Gauss point) and intervenes at the level of the computation of \sigma and {D}^{\mathit{epd}} from the strain \epsilon , given for each call of the global process of the Newton iterations. 2.3.2 Approach to the coupled problem In this document one does not detail the numerical integration in time for each of the models. One simply assumes that one knows how to do it, and this with an implicit (backward) Euler scheme. Let us say that, in an incremental solution by the finite-element method, for each Newton iteration of the global iterative process, one wishes to compute, for each Gauss point, the stresses {\sigma}_{n+1} and the internal variables {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{p} , {\alpha}_{n+1} and {d}_{n+1} from the values of the total strain, {\epsilon}_{n+1} , while assuming that one has converged at the previous instant and that one knows {\sigma}_{n} , {\epsilon}_{n}^{p} , {\alpha}_{n} and {d}_{n} . The indices n or n+1 indicate that the value of the variable corresponds to the instant {t}_{n} or {t}_{n+1} , respectively. Thus one assumes that the two models can be integrated in uncoupled mode and that one is therefore capable of writing: {\sigma}_{n+1}^{p}={\sigma}^{p}\left({\tilde{\epsilon}}_{n+1}\right) and {\sigma}_{n+1}^{d}={\sigma}^{d}\left({\tilde{\epsilon}}_{n+1}\right) The exponents d or p in {\sigma}^{d} and {\sigma}^{p} mean that the stress is computed with the damage model and with the plasticity model, respectively. \tilde{\epsilon} is a variable of strain type. In the algorithm presented in what follows one introduces an additional iterative process so that the stresses {\sigma}^{d} and {\sigma}^{p} converge towards a single value. It is similar to that proposed in [bib3] except that here the construction of the damage model is more general, which requires considering a variable other than the damage strain (used in [bib3]) on which one iterates. 2.3.3 Construction of the non-linear system With respect to a classical solution of the constitutive law, one must here make two stress values converge by introducing another unknown of strain type. This partitioned system is constructed more easily by introducing the following decomposition of the total strain, \epsilon ={\epsilon}^{e}+{\epsilon}^{p}+{\epsilon}^{d} where one has introduced the damage strain, which allows us to write the elasticity relation as: \sigma ={D}^{e}:\left(\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p}-{\epsilon}^{d}\right) or again: {\epsilon}^{d}\left(\sigma ,\epsilon ,{\epsilon}^{p}\right)=\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p}-{({D}^{e})}^{-1}:\sigma One can summarise the equations to be solved in three groups: Plasticity module {\sigma}_{n+1}^{p}={\sigma}^{p}{\left({\epsilon}_{n+1}-{\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d}\right)}_{e} {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{p}={\epsilon}^{p}\left({\epsilon}_{n+1}-{\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d}\right) The index e means that the elastoplastic law is computed with the elasticity operator {D}^{e} Damage module {\sigma}_{n+1}^{d}={\sigma}^{d}{\left({\epsilon}_{n+1}-{\epsilon}_{n+1}^{p}\right)}_{e} Coupling module {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d}={\epsilon}_{n+1}-{\epsilon}_{n+1}^{p}-{({D}^{e})}^{-1}:{\sigma}_{n+1}^{d} {\sigma}_{n+1}^{p}={\sigma}_{n+1}^{d} In [bib3] one chose {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d} as the additional unknown, which is not possible in our case, since {\sigma}^{d} is not a function of {\epsilon}^{d} but of {\bar{\epsilon}}^{\mathit{ed}}=\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p} , the variable which is finally used to drive the iterative processes described below. Moreover it is also equal to {\bar{\epsilon}}^{\mathit{ed}}={\epsilon}^{e}+{\epsilon}^{d}=\epsilon -{\epsilon}^{p} . 2.3.4 Solution algorithm To solve the non-linear system, defined in equations ( to ) by assigning them to the different modules (plasticity, damage and coupling), one applies the classical Newton method. In order to linearise the system, one must define the following derivatives: {D}^{\mathit{ep}}\left({\bar{\epsilon}}^{\mathit{ed}}\right)=\frac{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}^{p}}{\partial {\bar{\epsilon}}^{\mathit{ed}}} {D}^{d}\left({\bar{\epsilon}}^{\mathit{ed}}\right)=\frac{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}^{d}}{\partial {\bar{\epsilon}}^{\mathit{ed}}} \frac{\partial {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d}}{\partial {\bar{\epsilon}}^{\mathit{ed}}}=1-{\left({D}^{e}\right)}^{-1}{D}^{d}\left({\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed}}\right) The non-linear system (to ) is first reduced to the last of the equations, that is to say to {\sigma}_{n+1}^{p}={\sigma}_{n+1}^{d} , since one can express all the unknowns with respect to the value of {\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed}} . One can therefore define the residual as: {R}_{\sigma}^{(k)}={\sigma}^{p}\left({\epsilon}_{n+1}-{\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d,(k)}\right)-{\sigma}^{d}\left({\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)}\right) where the exponent k indicates the current iteration and where: {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d,(k)}={\epsilon}_{n+1}-{\epsilon}_{n+1}^{p,(k)}-{\left({D}^{e}\right)}^{-1}:{\sigma}^{d}\left({\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)}\right) By applying Newton's method, one computes the new approximation of {\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k+1)} as: {\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k+1)}={\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)}+\Delta {\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)} where \Delta {\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)}=-{\left(\frac{\partial {R}_{\sigma}^{(k)}}{\partial {\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed}}}\right)}^{-1}{R}_{\sigma}^{(k)} The corresponding tangent modulus can be expressed entirely by the uncoupled moduli (): \left(\frac{\partial {R}_{\sigma}^{(k)}}{\partial {\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed}}}\right)=-{D}^{\mathit{ep},(k)}\frac{\partial {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d,(k)}}{\partial {\bar{\epsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)}}-{D}^{d,(k)}=-\left({D}^{d,(k)}+{D}^{\mathit{ep},(k)}\left(1-{\left({D}^{e}\right)}^{-1}{D}^{d,(k)}\right)\right) One recalls here that the total strain {\epsilon}_{n+1} , coming from the global process of the Newton iterations, is constant for the local iterative process determining {\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed}} . The algorithm for the computation of the variables at iteration k+1 is carried out in the following manner: 1. Initialisation: {\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k=0)}={\varepsilon}_{n+1}-{\varepsilon}_{n}^{p} 1. Loop over the k=0,\mathrm{...},{N}_{max} 2. Computation of the increment: {\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k+1)}={\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)}+\Delta {\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)} where \Delta {\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)}={({D}^{d,(k)}+{D}^{\mathit{ep},(k)}(1-{({D}^{e})}^{-1}{D}^{d,(k)}))}^{-1}{R}_{\sigma}^{(k)} 1. {\sigma}_{n+1}^{d,(k+1)}={\sigma}^{d}{({\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k+1)})}_{e} 2. {\varepsilon}_{n+1}^{d,(k+1)}={\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k+1)}-{\varepsilon}_{n+1}^{\mathit{el},(k+1)} where {\varepsilon}_{n+1}^{\mathit{el},(k+1)}={({D}^{e})}^{-1}:{\sigma}^{d}({\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k+1)}) 3. {\sigma}_{n+1}^{p,(k+1)}={\sigma}^{p}{({\varepsilon}_{n+1}-{\varepsilon}_{n+1}^{d,(k+1)})}_{e} 4. {R}_{\sigma}^{(k+1)}={\sigma}_{n+1}^{p,(k+1)}-{\sigma}_{n+1}^{d,(k+1)} 5. If \mid \Delta {\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)}{R}_{\sigma}^{(k+1)}\mid >\mathit{tol} resume the loop at 1), otherwise END Note 1: the only places where the physical specificities of the coupled models are taken into account are points 3) and 5), where one calls the plasticity and damage modules, respectively. Note 2: the value of {\varepsilon}_{n+1} is considered constant in the process of equilibrating the stresses and, when {\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed}} varies, one in fact varies the value of {\varepsilon}_{n+1}^{p} . This plastic strain is in principle determined by the elasto-plasticity module as a function of {\varepsilon}_{n+1} (see ()). In reality, {\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed}} is considered here as a variable and its link with {\varepsilon}_{n+1}^{p} is restored only at the convergence of the iterative process. Thus: {\bar{\varepsilon}}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ed},(k)}\mathrm{\ne }{\varepsilon}_{n+1}-{\varepsilon}^{p}({\varepsilon}_{n+1}-{\varepsilon}_{n+1}^{d,(k)}) 2.3.5 Construction of the consistent tangent modulus Finally, in order to obtain an optimal performance in the global iterative process one must compute the consistent tangent modulus, once the process described above has converged, i.e. {\sigma}_{n+1}={\sigma}_{n+1}^{p}={\sigma}_{n+1}^{d} : {D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{epd}}=\frac{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}}{\partial {\varepsilon}_{n+1}} First one observes that if one differentiates () with respect to {\sigma}_{n+1}^{p} one can write: I={D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ep}}\left({D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{epd}}-\frac{\partial {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d}}{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}^{p}}\right) and that in the same manner, by differentiating () with respect to {\sigma}_{n+1}^{d} one obtains: I={D}_{n+1}^{d}\left({D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{epd}}-\frac{\partial {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{p}}{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}^{d}}\right) with, at the end of the iterative process {\sigma}_{n+1}={\sigma}_{n+1}^{p}={\sigma}_{n+1}^{d} , one finally obtains: \frac{\partial {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d}}{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}}={({D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{epd}})}^{-1}-{({D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{ep}})}^{-1} By then using {\epsilon}_{n+1}={\epsilon}_{n+1}^{e}+{\epsilon}_{n+1}^{p}+{\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d} and therefore that: \frac{\partial {\epsilon}_{n+1}}{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}}=\frac{\partial {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{e}}{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}}+\frac{\partial {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{p}}{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}}+\frac{\partial {\epsilon}_{n+1}^{d}}{\partial {\sigma}_{n+1}} one obtains the consistent tangent modulus directly as: {D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{epd}}={\left({\left({D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{epd}}\right)}^{-1}+{\left({D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{epd}}\right)}^{-1}+{\left({D}_{n+1}^{\mathit{epd}}\right)}^{-1}\right)}^{-1} 2.4 Limitations of the coupler There exist a few conditions to be satisfied for the use of this coupling method concerning aspects that are both physical and numerical: - Distinct internal variables: As specified in the introduction of the thermodynamic framework, the two coupled models must not share the same internal variables. The method is designed to be able to combine models representing uncoupled physical phenomena, which is judged to be the case in most of the target applications. - Existence of the consistent tangent moduli: For the approach to work, it is absolutely necessary that one have the consistent tangent moduli for the two modules, elasto-plastic and damageable. By “consistent tangent modulus” one means that it is the derivative, consistent with the time discretisation employed, of the stress tensor at the given instant with respect to the strain tensor at the same instant. - Non-singularity of the tangent moduli: One is obliged on several occasions to invert the tangent matrices of the individual modules. If the behaviour of a module has a flat non-linear slope (perfect elasto-plasticity for example) it is necessary to give it a non-zero value. This non-zero value must be chosen such that it is large enough for the algorithm to work and small enough for it to be consistent with the physical model studied. 3 Specific models 3.1 Reminder of the global models In this context, a plate constitutive model said to be global, or of a structural element in general, means that the constitutive law is written directly in terms of a relation between the generalised stresses and the generalised strains. The global approach to the modelling of the behaviour of structures applies in particular to composite structures, for example reinforced concrete (see Figure 1), and represents an alternative to the so-called local or semi-global approaches, which are finer but more costly modellings (see [bib6] and [bib7]). In the local approach one uses a fine modelling for each of the phases (steel, concrete) and their interactions (bond) and in the semi-global approach one exploits the slenderness of the structure in order to simplify the description of the kinematics, which leads to the PMF (Multi-Fibre Beam) models or to multi-layer shells. The interest of the global model lies in the fact that the corresponding finite element requires only one integration point through the thickness and above all in the obtaining of a homogenised behaviour. This advantage is even more important in the analysis of reinforced concrete, since one bypasses the localisation problems encountered when modelling concrete without reinforcement. Obviously, a global model represents the local phenomena in a coarse manner. Figure 3.1-a. Reinforced-concrete slab. 3.2 Implementation of the coupling GLRC_DM/ The most important assumption which is made in this particular coupling is that elasto-plasticity can be activated only by loading the plate in membrane. In other words, in pure bending the structure will never plastify. On the one hand, this simplification is justified by the target applications, in which the loadings are more important in membrane than in bending and in which one therefore does not expect dominant influences of bending. On the other hand, the assumption is imposed for technical reasons, because at present one does not have a “global” elasto-plastic model suitable for the coupling with a “global” damage model. The global models are formulated in terms of generalised stresses and strains, which imposes on us, in the coupler (see §2), to replace the stresses, \sigma , and the strains, \epsilon , by: \sigma \to \Sigma =\left(\begin{array}{c}{N}_{xx}\\ {N}_{yy}\\ {N}_{xy}\\ {M}_{xx}\\ {M}_{yy}\\ {M}_{xy}\end{array}\right) where the generalised strains, {\rm E} , are decomposed into membrane extensions ϵ and the curvatures \kappa while the generalised stresses are composed of the membrane forces N and of the bending moments M . It is important to note that in this framework one makes the thin-plate assumption in which the transverse distortion and the shear force are negligible. Below one recalls the Hencky–Mindlin kinematics (see [bib9] for the details) for shells and plates as well as the definition of the generalised stresses: (\begin{array}{}{U}_{1}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2,}z)\\ {U}_{2}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2,}z)\\ {U}_{z}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2,}z)\end{array})=\underset{\begin{array}{}\mathrm{cinématique}\mathrm{de}\mathrm{plaque}\\ {u}^{s}\in {V}_{s}\end{array}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{(\begin{array}{}{u}_{1}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2})\\ {u}_{2}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2})\\ {u}_{z}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2})\end{array})+z(\begin{array}{}{\theta}_{2}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2})\\ -{\theta}_{1}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2})\\ 0\end{array})}}+\underset{\begin{array}{}\mathrm{déplacement}\mathrm{complémentaire}\\ {u}^{c}\in {V}_{c}\end{array}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{(\begin{array}{}{u}_{1}^{c}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2,}z)\\ {u}_{2}^{c}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2,}z)\\ {u}_{z}^{c}({x}_{1,}{x}_{2,}z)\end{array})}} where U={({U}_{1}{U}_{2}{U}_{z})}^{T} is the displacement field in 3D, u={({u}_{1}{u}_{2}{u}_{z})}^{T} the displacement of the middle surface and {\theta}_{x} , {\theta}_{y} its rotations. Thus, the strain tensor, defined as: {\varepsilon}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\partial {U}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}+\frac{\partial {U}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}}),i,j=\mathrm{1..3} is also written as: \begin{array}{}{\varepsilon}_{11}=\underset{{\varepsilon}_{11}^{s}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{\epsilon}_{11}+z{\kappa}_{11}}}+{u}_{1,1}^{c}\\ {\varepsilon}_{22}=\underset{{\varepsilon}_{22}^{s}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{\epsilon}_{22}+z{\kappa}_{22}}}+{u}_{2,2}^{c}\\ {\varepsilon}_{12}=\underset{{\varepsilon}_{12}^{s}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{\epsilon}_{12}+z{\kappa}_{12}}}+\frac{1}{2}({u}_{2,1}^{c}+{u}_{1,2}^{c})\\ {\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{1z}}={\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{1z}}^{c}=\frac{1}{2}{u}_{3,1}^{c}\\ {\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{2z}}={\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{2z}}^{c}=\frac{1}{2}{u}_{3,2}^{c}\\ {\varepsilon}_{zz}={\varepsilon}_{zz}^{c}={u}_{3,z}^{c}\end{array} where \epsilon is the membrane-extension tensor, defined in the plane: {\epsilon}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\partial {u}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}+\frac{\partial {u}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}}),i,j=\mathrm{1..2} and \kappa the curvature-change tensor, defined in the plane: {\kappa}_{11}=\frac{\partial {\theta}_{2}}{\partial {x}_{1}} relations to which is added the plane-stress assumption {\sigma}_{zz}=0 , {\sigma}_{\mathrm{1z}}=0 , {\sigma}_{\mathrm{2z}}=0 which will determine the complementary displacement field {\mathrm{u}}^{c}\in {V}_{c} . In the theory used here, one introduces only two rotation components {\theta}_{x} and {\theta}_{y} , which implies that the curvature-change tensor is 2D and has only 3 independent components. Among the two coupled models, GLRC_DM is a global model and is therefore formulated directly in terms of \Sigma =\Sigma (E) , but the models VMIS_ISOT_LINE and VMIS_CINE_LINE are the classical 3D constitutive laws. Since one wishes above all that the elasto-plastic part be represented in membrane, one applies the constitutive law only to the relation N=N(\epsilon ) , then one assumes that the bending behaviour remains linear elastic. One therefore has: Damage : {\Sigma}^{d}(\epsilon ,\kappa )={\Sigma}_{\text{GLRC\_DM}}(\epsilon ,\kappa ) Elasto-plasticity : {\Sigma}^{p}(\epsilon ,\kappa )=(\begin{array}{c}{N}_{\mathit{VMIS}}(\epsilon )\\ {H}_{\mathit{ELAS}}:\kappa \end{array}) where {\Sigma}_{\text{GLRC\_DM}}(\epsilon ,\kappa ) represents the global constitutive law GLRC_DM, {N}_{\mathit{VMIS}}(\epsilon ) the von Mises law in plane stress and {H}_{\mathit{ELAS}} the elastic tensor acting on the curvature (see [bib9] for its exact form). These two modules, of damage and of elasto-plasticity, are then used in the coupler (see §2) by replacing {\sigma}^{p}\to {\Sigma}^{p} and {\sigma}^{d}\to {\Sigma}^{d} . 3.3 Internal variables The internal variables of the coupled model are stored in series: the first correspond to the damage model, which are followed by those of the elasto-plastic model. The coupler needs six (6) internal variables in order to store the tensor of strain type, {\bar{\varepsilon}}^{\mathit{ed}} , which drives the internal loop (see §2.3). In the case of the coupling GLRC_DM/ one adds four (4) of them because of the algorithm making it possible to satisfy the plane-stress condition. These four internal variables have the same meaning as those used for the DEBORST method (see [bib12]). For GLRC_DM/ one therefore has 24 internal variables: V1–V7: GLRC_DM; V8–V14: (one uses only V5 and V6 for VMIS_ISOT_LINE); V15–V20: strain tensor {\bar{\epsilon}}^{\text{ed}} ; V21–V24: DEBORST method. 3.4 Validation This model is validated by the tests SSNS106F,G (see [bib8]). 4 Bibliography 1. r7.01.35 Constitutive relations BETON_BURGER and BETON_AGEING for the creep of concrete r7.01.35 Constitutive relations BETON_BURGER and BETON_AGEING for the creep of concrete Summary: This document presents the constitutive models BETON_BURGER and BETON_AGEING, making it possible to represent the creep of concrete (basic and desiccation). These models draw heavily on the structure already set up in the model BETON_UMLV. These models are implemented under MFront and integrated directly into code_aster. 1 Introduction Within the framework of studies of the long-term behaviour of concrete structures, a predominant part of the strains measured on a structure concerns the delayed strains which appear in the concrete in the course of its life. One speaks of “shrinkage” when the strain is measured on a specimen not subjected to mechanical loading and of “creep” when the strain takes place under mechanical loading. The exchanges of water between the specimen and the environment influence the final strain considerably. This observation classically gives rise to further distinctions on the delayed strains. One then distinguishes the early-age shrinkages, the desiccation shrinkage, the basic creep and the desiccation creep. The classification of the delayed strains of a concrete structure is recalled below: - at early age without load: 1. the autogenous shrinkage (1 day – 1 year) 2. the thermal shrinkage (1 hour – 1 day) caused by a thermo-hydration reaction. - in the medium term without load: the desiccation shrinkage (a few months – a few years), depending on the dimensions of the structure, caused by drying, which results in an evaporation of part of the water not used in the hydration process. - in the long term under load: 1. the basic creep, which is the part of the creep of the concrete that one would observe during a test without exchange of water with the exterior. 2. the desiccation creep, in addition to the basic creep, is the part of the total creep directly linked to the departure of water affecting the concrete which undergoes a mechanical loading on the one hand and drying on the other. The models presented here, under the names BETON_BURGER (r7.01.35-description_beton_burger) and BETON_AGEING (r7.01.35-description_beton_ageing), are devoted to the modelling of the delayed strain associated with creep, basic and desiccation. 2 Description of the model BETON_BURGER 2.1 Hypotheses The law is written within the framework of small perturbations. The total strain tensor is decomposed into several terms relating to the processes considered. One admits that the total strain is written: \strain = \underbrace{\strain^e}_{\text{déf. élastique}} + \underbrace{\strain^{fp}}_{\text{fluage propre}} + \underbrace{\strain^{fdess}}_{\text{fluage de dessiccation}} + \underbrace{\strain^{re}}_{\text{retrait endogène}} + \underbrace{\strain^{rd}}_{\text{retrait de dessiccation}} + \underbrace{\strain^{th}}_{\text{déf. thermique}} In this document, one does not describe the taking into account of the various types of shrinkage (for that, see the documentation R7.01.12), nor of the thermal strain, so that it reduces to: \strain = \strain^e + \strain^{fp} + \strain^{fdess} In general, basic creep may be modelled by combining the elastic behaviour of the solid and the viscous behaviour of the fluid. For the law presented, basic creep is described as the combination of the elastic behaviour of the hydrates and of the aggregates and of the viscous behaviour of the water. In the case of the model BETON_BURGER, one makes the hypothesis that the basic creep may be decomposed into a process decoupling a spherical part and a deviatoric part. One then decomposes the tensors of the basic-creep strains and of the stresses as: \strain^{fp} = \underbrace{\varepsilon^{fp}_s\tensTwoUnit}_{\text{partie sphérique}} + \underbrace{\strain^{fp}_d}_{\text{partie déviatorique}} \quad \text{et} \quad \stress = \underbrace{\sigma_s\tensTwoUnit}_{\text{partie sphérique}} + \underbrace{\stress_d}_{\text{partie déviatorique}} The model BETON_BURGER assumes a total decoupling between the spherical and deviatoric components of the basic creep: the strains induced by the spherical stresses are purely spherical and the strains induced by the deviatoric stresses are purely deviatoric. On the other hand, the cumulative viscous strains have an effect on the viscous properties of the fluid, whatever their origin (spherical or deviatoric). In order to take account of the effect of the relative humidity h , the basic-creep strains are generated by the source term h\stress . 2.2 Elasticity The elasticity is linear isotropic: \stress = \tensFour{C}:\strain^e with \tensFour{C} the linear isotropic elasticity tensor, of Young's modulus \youngModulus and of Poisson's ratio \poissonCoef . 2.3 Basic creep In order to model the phenomenon of basic creep, the model proposed relies on simple rheological models (r7.01.35-schema_rheo) comprising in series an elastic body (described by the behaviour ELAS), a linear Voigt solid for the modelling of the reversible creep (recovery), and a Maxwell fluid with a non-linear viscosity in order to model the long-term creep. The spherical and deviatoric chains are equivalent in their construction. The Voigt stage has a strain limit governed by the elastic modulus. The particularity of the model rests on the choice of the non-linearity assigned to the viscosity of the Maxwell body. Rheological diagram distinguishing the spherical and deviatoric part of the stress tensor. 2.3.1 Description of the spherical part The spherical strain of basic creep is written as the sum of a reversible part and of an irreversible part: \varepsilon^{fp}_s = \varepsilon^{fp}_{s,r} + \varepsilon^{fp}_{s, i} The process of spherical creep strain is governed by the following equations: h\sigma_s = k_{s,r}\varepsilon^{fp}_{s,r} + \eta_{s,r}\dot{\varepsilon}^{fp}_{s,r} \quad \text{et} \quad h\sigma_s = \eta_{s,i}\dot{\varepsilon}^{fp}_{s,i} with: - k_{s,r} the bulk modulus associated with the reversible spherical basic creep, - \eta_{s,r} the viscosity of the Voigt stage associated with the reversible spherical basic creep, - \eta_{s,i} the non-linear spherical viscosity (see ) of the Maxwell fluid. 2.3.2 Description of the deviatoric part The deviatoric strain of basic creep is likewise written as the sum of a reversible part and of an irreversible part: \strain^{fp}_d = \strain^{fp}_{d,r} + \strain^{fp}_{d, i} The process of deviatoric creep strain is governed by the following equations: h\stress_d = k_{d,r}\strain^{fp}_{d,r} + \eta_{d,r}\dot{\tensTwo{\varepsilon}^{fp}_{d,r} \quad \text{et} \quad h\stress_d = \eta_{d,i}\dot{\tensTwo{\varepsilon}^{fp}_{d,i}}} with: - k_{d,r} the shear modulus associated with the reversible deviatoric basic creep, - \eta_{d,r} the viscosity of the Voigt stage associated with the reversible deviatoric basic creep, - \eta_{d,i} the non-linear deviatoric viscosity (see ) of the Maxwell fluid. 2.3.3 Description of the viscous non-linearity The non-linearity of the viscosity is interpreted according to as the result of a spherical consolidation of the specimen and of an entanglement or blocking of the displacements of the CSH sheets, constituents of the mortar. A “consolidation” coefficient is therefore introduced along the same idea in order to control the evolution of the viscosities. This additional coefficient acts on the evolution laws of the Maxwell bodies (spherical and deviatoric). It depends directly on the norm of the tensor of the cumulative irreversible delayed strains. This extension of the hypotheses set out by makes it possible to take the non-linearity into account for every type of path (with or without spherical loading). The explicit formulation of the Maxwell bodies is the following: \eta_{s,i}=\eta_{s,i}^0\exp\left(\frac{\|\strainCmp_{m,i}^{fp}\|}{\kappa}\right) \quad \text{et} \quad \eta_{d,i}= \eta_{d,i}^0\exp\left(\frac{\|\strainCmp_{m,i}^{fp}\|}{\kappa}\right) with: - \eta_{s,i}^0 the initial viscosity of the Maxwell fluid acting on the spherical part, - \eta_{d,i}^0 the initial viscosity of the Maxwell fluid acting on the deviatoric part, - \kappa the non-linearity coefficient, - \|\strainCmp_{m,i}^{fp}\| the irreversible equivalent strain, defined as the norm of the complete tensor (spherical and deviatoric) of irreversible creep strains, the maximum value reached in the course of the loading. Precisely, the construction of \|\strainCmp_{m,i}^{fp}\| follows the following logic: \|\strainCmp_{m,i}^{fp}\|=\max\left(\|\strainCmp_{m,i}^{fp}\|,\sqrt{\strain_{i}^{fp}:\strain_{i}^{fp}}\right) . 2.3.4 Restriction of the number of parameters of the model The equivalence of the deviatoric and spherical rheological chains makes it possible to obtain, by complying with the following expression, an apparent creep Poisson's ratio \poissonCoef that is constant: \frac{\eta_{s,i}^0}{\eta_{d,i}^0} = \frac{\eta_{s,r}}{\eta_{d,r}} = \frac{k_{r,s}}{k_{r,d}} = \frac{1+\poissonCoef}{1-2\poissonCoef} For the use of the model BETON_BURGER on uniaxial creep tests, one rarely has the radial strains of the specimens, which makes identification of the whole set of parameters of the model difficult. A first approximation consists in assuming the relation and thus limits the number of parameters to be determined to four, \eta_{s,i}^0, \eta_{s,r}, k_{r,s}, \poissonCoef , as regards the basic creep (at constant temperature) of the model BETON_BURGER. 2.3.5 Thermal activation of the basic-creep strains The experimental results of a basic-creep test in temperature show that the creep strain is thermally activated. For temperatures T below 55°C, it obeys an Arrhenius-type law: \strain^{fp}(T) = \strain^{fp}(T_0)\vartheta(T) \quad \text{avec} \quad \vartheta(T) = \exp\left(-\frac{E_{ac}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}-\frac{1}{T_0}\right)\right) with: - {T}_{0} the reference temperature, - {E}_{ac} the activation energy, - R the perfect-gas constant. In order to satisfy the relation while keeping a constant characteristic time, the stiffness of the springs and the viscosity of the dashpots are modified in the following manner: \frac{k_{s,r}(T)}{k_{s,r}(T_0)} = \frac{k_{d,r}(T)}{k_{d,r}(T_0)} = \frac{\eta_{s,r}(T)}{\eta_{s,r}(T_0)} = \frac{\eta_{d,r}(T)}{\eta_{d,r}(T_0)} = \frac{\eta_{s,i}^0(T)}{\eta_{s,i}^0(T_0)} = \frac{\eta_{d,i}^0(T)}{\eta_{d,i}^0(T_0)} = \frac{\kappa(T_0)}{\kappa(T)} = \frac{1}{\vartheta(T)} 2.4 Desiccation creep Following the experimental justifications presented in , desiccation creep is non-symmetric with respect to the variation of the relative humidity. r7.01.37 Dissipative Homogenised Reinforced Concrete (DHRC) constitutive model devoted to reinforced concrete plates r7.01.37 Dissipative Homogenised Reinforced Concrete (DHRC) constitutive model devoted to reinforced concrete plates Abstract : This documentation presents the theoretical formulation and numerical integration of the DHRC constitutive law, acronym for "dissipative homogenised reinforced concrete" used with modelling DKTG plates. It is one of models called "global" used to thin structures (beams, plates and shells). Nonlinear phenomena such as plasticity or damage, are directly related to the generalised strains (extension, curvature, distortion) and generalised stresses (membrane forces, bending and cutting edges). So, this constitutive law is applied with a finite element plate or shell. Compared to a multi-layered approach, CPU time and memory are saved. The advantage over multi-layer shells is even more important when the constituents of the plate behaves in a quasi-brittle manner (concrete, for example), as the global model avoids localisation issues. The DHRC constitutive law idealises both damage and irreversible deformation under combined membrane stress resultant and bending of reinforced concrete plates using "homogenised" parameters. This constitutive law represents an evolution of the GLRC_DM constitutive model which idealises only damage in membrane and bending situations. Unlike GLRC_DM, the DHRC constitutive model has a complete theoretical justification by using the theory of periodic homogenisation: it idealises the effects of steel-concrete slip in addition to the degradation of stiffness from the concrete diffuse cracking, the bending-membrane coupling in a consistent way and accounts for the orthotropy and possible asymmetries coming from steel reinforcement grids. The DHRC macroscopic constitutive law is not softening: this avoids solving problems throughout the structural analysis. The parameter setting of this constitutive law results of the particular characteristics of concrete and steel materials used, and the geometrical characteristics of the section, the thickness ratio of steel rebar, positions and directions, which are input data of a identification procedure from the responses of representative elementary volumes of the section of the reinforced concrete plate. The total user parameter number is 21 : 11 geometrical parameters and 10 material parameters. 1 Introduction 1.1 Global modelling Reinforced concrete is a heterogeneous material constituted of ribbed or plain steel rebar and concrete. The rebar have regular spacing on the two directions x and y in the plane. We consider moderate cycling or alternate loading conditions: the material is therefore considered as a continuum. A global constitutive plate model devoted to structural element generally means that the constitutive law is written directly in terms of the relationship between the generalised stresses and generalised strains. The overall approach of the structures behaviour modelling is particularly applicable to composite structures, such as reinforced concrete (see figure r7.01.37-fig-1-1), and this represents an alternative to the so-called local approaches or semi-global ones, which are finer but more expensive models (see and ). In the local approach a thin model is used for each phase (steel, concrete) and their interactions (adhesion). In the semi-global approach one exploits the slenderness of the structure to simplify the description of the kinematics, it leading to “PMF” models (multi-beam fiber) or multi-layer shells. The use of the theory of plates and thin shells can effectively describe the mechanical behaviour of reinforced concrete structures, which are usually slender; indeed we use this constitutive modelling in the context of Love-Kirchhoff's kinematics, see and . The interest of the overall model lies in the fact that the structural finite element requires only a unique point of integration in the element thickness and also in the use of a homogenised behaviour. This advantage is even more important in the analysis of reinforced concrete, since it bypasses the localisation problem encountered in the modelling of concrete without reinforcement. Obviously, a global model idealises local phenomena of a coarse manner and requires more validation prior to its application to industrial situations. Finally, it is impossible as soon as we consider the non-linear phase behaviour back locally to provide field values, except strain fields. This simplified modelling approach can be enhanced by an appropriate calibration of the overall parameters. Reinforced concrete slab 1.2 Objectives of the DHRC constitutive model The DHRC constitutive model, named for «dissipative homogenised reinforced concrete», is able to idealise the stiffness degradation of a reinforced concrete plate, for a quite moderate load range, i.e. without reaching the collapse, as the GLRC_DM constitutive model does, see r7.01.32, We can refer to the published papers , for extensive explanations; however this Code_Aster Reference document reuses the main parts of . Nevertheless, DHRC brings an important enhancement of the GLRC_DM model: (1) it is based on a full theoretical formulation from the local analysis, (2) it involves natively the membrane-bending coupling, (3) accounts for any type of rebar grids in the thickness (e.g. different upper and lower grids, or rebar with distinct sections on the two \mathrm{Ox} and \mathrm{Oy} directions), In that sense, DHRC constitutive model is more representative than GLRC_DM. The reference frame is constituted by the two directions x and y of steel rebar in the plane. The user can define these two local directions with the command, see u4.42.01, with respect to the global mesh reference frame: AFFE_CARA_ELEM(COQUE = _F(ANGL_REP = (\alpha ,\beta ) )) It is built by a periodic homogenisation approach using the averaging method and it couples concrete damage and periodic debonding between steel rebar and surrounding concrete. It leads to a better modelling of the energy dissipation during loading cycles. By construction, the DHRC model has comparable performance in terms of computational cost and numerical robustness with GLRC_DM model. A restricted number of geometric and material characteristics are needed from which the whole set of model parameters are identified through an automatic numeric procedure performed on a Representative Volume Elements (RVE) of the RC plate. As GLRC_DM model does, DHRC ones accounts for thermal strains, idealised in the plate thickness, see R3.11.01. 1.3 Notations A Cartesian orthonormal coordinate system is chosen so that covariant and contra-variant components are assimilated. Uppercase letters will refer generally to the macroscopic scale and lowercase ones to the microscopic scale. The simply contracted tensorial product will be noted by a simple dot “ . ” and the double one by two dots “ : ” or “ \text{}\otimes \text{} ”. - Tensor components will be given through subscripts relatively to the differential manifold used: Greek subscripts will set for integers ranging from 1 to 2 and Latin ones for integers ranging from 1 to 3. 2 Formulation of the constitutive law We consider a concrete panel reinforced by two steel grids located on one side and the other of the middle plane of the plate. The thickness H of the plate is considered to be small compared to its overall lateral dimensions {L}_{1} and {L}_{2} , see figure r7.01.37-fig-2-1, and the grids are composed with a periodic pattern of natural periodicity along {e}_{{x}_{1}} and {e}_{{x}_{2}} directions of the same length order as H . Moreover we consider that external loading and inertia forces spatial distributions are “smooth” with respect to the thickness H of the plate and restricted to the low frequencies range, as usual for seismic studies. Thus, it is possible to define a Reference Volume Element (RVE), denoted hereafter by \Omega , including both concrete and steel grids, whose lateral dimensions are {l}_{1} and {l}_{2} , see figure r7.01.37-fig-2-1. We assume that the ratio of the lateral dimensions {l}_{1} or {l}_{2} over the dimensions {L}_{1} or {L}_{2} of the whole plate is of the same length order as the ratio of the plate thickness H over its lateral dimensions. RVE \Omega definition from the actual RC plate geometry We are interested in deriving an overall macroscopic plate constitutive relation and the previous geometrical characteristics lead us to use a multi-scale analysis or a homogenisation technique, as it was already proposed in the literature for many decades. In the case where components are assumed to be linear elastic, this multi-scale approach has been justified by using an asymptotic expansion method on three-dimensional elasticity equations. It leads to the well-known bi-dimensional linear Love-Kirchhoff’s thin plate theory if the dimensionless size of heterogeneities is of the same order that the relative slenderness of the solid, . Both periodicity directions {e}_{{x}_{1}} and {e}_{{x}_{2}} ,corresponding to steel grid rebar directions, will be preferred directions for the sequel of this document. The chosen microscopic coordinate system will be the steel grid coordinate system (O,{e}_{{x}_{1}},{e}_{{x}_{2}},{e}_{{x}_{3}}) , where {e}_{{x}_{3}}={e}_{{X}_{3}} and O is the centre of the considered RVE. The plane {x}_{3}=0 is the mid-plane of the RVE. Upper and lower faces of the RVE are assumed to be free of charge, see . Given the fact that material considerations for the actual RC plate problem are complex, several simplifications have been proposed. As reported in Suquet’s work (Suquet, 1993), the essential properties of the macroscopic homogenised model are directly defined from average energetic quantities that are computed from microscopic corresponding ones in the RVE and from some optimisation arguments associated to local thermodynamic equilibrium – especially in the standard generalised materials context (Halphen & Nguyen, 1975). Therefore, it is believed that average quantities can catch with a reasonable good agreement the overall behaviour of an actual RC plate, even if the detail of microscopic phenomena is roughly idealised. The constitutive hypothesis about materials and their bond behaviours, needed to formulate the mathematical expression of the model are listed below with their justifications 2.1 Materials behaviour in RVE \Omega Hyp 1 . Steel is considered linear elastic, without irreversible plastic strains, as we do not consider ultimate states of the RC plate. We denote by {a}^{s} the corresponding elastic tensor. Hyp 2. Concrete is considered elastic and damageable, according to the following constitutive model \text{}\sigma ={a}^{c}(d):\text{}\varepsilon , d being a scalar damage variable idealising distributed cracking. The associated induced anisotropy is modelled through a suitable definition of {a}^{c}(d) . Concrete rigidity tensor {a}^{c}(d) is defined by its initial undamaged value {a}^{c}(0) , whose components are reduced by a decreasing convex damage function \xi (d) . We will give more details about the concrete constitutive model in r7.01.37-identification-approach. 2.2 Steel-concrete interface in RVE \Omega Hyp 3 . Concrete and steel rebar can slide one on the other beyond a given threshold. Hyp 4 . The bond status at steel-concrete interface is either sticking or sliding. Normal separation is not allowed. We do not consider any interface elastic energy associated to the sliding motion. Hyp 5 . The relative steel-concrete sliding, appearing after concrete damage and transmission of internal forces from concrete to steel rebar, can occur only in the two preferred directions {e}_{{x}_{1}} and {e}_{{x}_{2}} -- along longitudinal rebar. It can differ whether considering the bar of the upper grid or of the lower grid, thus allowing to take into account its consequence on the RC plate flexural behaviour. Let’s denote by {\Gamma}_{b} the generic steel-concrete interfaces along {e}_{{x}_{1}} or {e}_{{x}_{2}} . Hyp 6 . Steel rebar orthogonal to the sliding direction -- i.e. either perpendicular grid rebar or transversal rebar -- are considered to prevent relative sliding. As a consequence, steel-concrete sliding is periodical with a period equal to the spacing between two consecutive grid bars in the considered sliding direction. This defines the lateral dimensions of the RVE \Omega . 2.3 Non-uniform damage in RVE \Omega Hyp 7. In order to idealise the non-uniform damage distribution of concrete along the steel rebar, concrete domain in the RVE is in fact divided into two sub-domains associated respectively to sound concrete and damaged one. Therefore, we define a whole RVE partition into two sub-domains {\Omega}_{\mathrm{sd}} and {\Omega}_{\mathrm{dm}} , respectively. The {\Gamma}_{s} interface between these two sub-domains is assumed to be totally stuck. Actually, concrete of the plate is not damaged in a uniform way in its volume. In order to idealise this phenomenon, one should introduce a non-uniformly distributed damage variable d in the whole RVE. Nevertheless, according to the Suquet’s work (Suquet, 1987), this non-uniformity of the microscopic internal variable field leads to the necessity to consider an infinite number of macroscopic internal variables at each macroscopic material point. This issue prevents the practical use of the macroscopic standard generalised model that would result from the chosen microscopic ones. However, still according to (Suquet, 1987), it is possible to reduce this number of internal variables to a finite one if it can be demonstrated that these internal variables are uniform or piecewise uniform or more generally described by a vector space of finite dimension. The standard generalised character of the macroscopic model is obtained from the microscopic scale behaviours thanks to the usual properties of Caratheodory’s functions of Convex Analysis. Thus, if such a chosen set of internal variables can represent the actual material state in the RVE, with a sufficient approximation degree, it is possible to build a macroscopic standard generalised model with a finite number of macroscopic internal variables. In our study, in order to restrict the number of macroscopic internal variables, we decided to define only one microscopic internal variable d for damage, considered as piecewise uniformly distributed inside the whole RVE and two sets of materials representing two different states of damage in concrete located in sub-domains {\Omega}_{\mathrm{sd}} and {\Omega}_{\mathrm{dm}} . This distribution of microscopic damage allows in a simple way the representation of the “tension-stiffening” effect (Combescure et al., 2013). The values of microscopic and macroscopic internal variables d and D are then equated, for the sake of simplicity, without losing any generality, since the only matter is the actual value of the respective elastic stiffness tensors. Hyp 8 . In order to take into account the a priori non-uniform damage in the RVE thickness, two damage variables will be set up corresponding to the piecewise damage in the upper and lower halves of the RVE. d=\left\{ \begin{array}{}{d}_{1}\mathrm{~if~}{x}_{3}\ge 0\\ {d}_{2}\mathrm{~if~}{x}_{3} }}_{\Omega}=\frac{1}{\mid \Omega \mid }{\int}_{\text{}\cup {\Omega}_{i}^{\zeta}}\cdot ~dV stands for the average value of the considered field in the RVE. We can easily observe that the expressions in encompass the usual definition for homogeneous plate kinematics. We must now deal with the non-regular part {u}^{d} of the displacement field in the RVE. In the sequel 〚.〛 stands for the jump operator on the steel-concrete interface. So, we define the macroscopic sliding strain tensor {E}^{\mathrm{\eta \zeta }} as the average of sliding on each steel-concrete interface {\Gamma}_{b}^{\zeta} . First, we observe that the contribution of discontinuous displacement {u}^{d} to the macroscopic strain tensors vanishes, due to Hyp 4 and Hyp 10 (Andrieux et al., 1986): \frac{1}{∣\Omega ∣}{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{b}^{\zeta}}〚\mathbf{u}^{d}〛{\text{}\otimes ^{s} \mathbf{n} ~dS=0} where \mathbf{n} is the outward normal at the steel-concrete interface {\Gamma}_{b}^{\zeta} and \otimes ^{s} stands for the symmetrised dyadic tensor product. Extending the proposed definition by (Combescure et al., 2013), the components of {E}^{\mathrm{\eta \zeta }} are: {E}_{\mathrm{\alpha \alpha }}^{\eta \zeta }=\frac{1}{∣\Omega ∣}{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{b}^{\zeta}}(〚\mathbf{u}^{d}〛{.\mathbf{e}}_{{x}_{\alpha}}){.\mathbf{e}}_{{x}_{\alpha}}{\text{}\otimes ^{s}{\mathbf{e}}_{{x}_{\alpha}}~dS} Indeed, the only non-zero components of tensor {E}^{\mathrm{\eta \zeta }} are {E}_{\mathrm{\alpha \alpha }}^{\mathrm{\eta \zeta }} . Vector {E}^{\mathrm{\eta \zeta }} will then more conveniently be considered in the following as a first-order tensor of the plate mean surface, whose components are denoted by {E}_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{\eta \zeta }} . The macroscopic primal state variables associated to the DHRC proposed model are then: membrane strains E and bending strains K tensors, damage variables {D}^{\zeta} on upper and lower halves of the homogenised plate, sliding strain {E}^{\mathrm{\eta \zeta }} vectors on upper and lower grids. These variables will be used to define state functions, as the macroscopic free energy density W(E,K,{D}^{\zeta},{E}^{\eta \zeta }) . 3 Weak form of the auxiliary problems and homogenised model 3.1 Local auxiliary problems In order to determine the macroscopic constitutive relation, we have to establish the relation between microscopic fields and macroscopic ones, for various fixed values of internal state variables. Remark 8: Macroscopic threshold functions and flow rules are similar to their microscopic homonyms modulo a scaling factor. Indeed, dissipative phenomena at the microscopic scale are naturally similar to the one located at the macroscopic scale since the homogenisation process cannot create news dissipative sources (Suquet, 1987). According to the work of (Suquet, 1987), the considered microscopic internal damage and sliding variables being uniform or piecewise constant in the whole unit cell, one can affirm, thanks to the arguments of convex analysis, that the standard generalised properties of materials, at the microscopic scale, are transferred to the macroscopic homogenised model. Hence, the formerly presented model with its free energy density and pseudo-potentials of dissipation can be classified as a Standard Generalised model . Remark 9: Since microscopic and macroscopic threshold functions are similar, it is possible to choose enriched threshold functions for microscopic damage and sliding. This new choice will then immediately be translated at the macroscopic scale. However, the choice of very simple threshold functions, see Hyp 11, with one only threshold parameter restricts the number of parameters to identify. Therefore, it is expected that these simple threshold functions will be sufficient for practical applications . Remark 10: According to Remark 5, as tensor B vanishes if there is no damage, then {\Sigma}^{\mathrm{\eta \zeta }} vanishes too and the macroscopic bond sliding threshold cannot be reached before the macroscopic damage one . 4 Finite Element implementation The non-linear DHRC constitutive model formulated for plate structural element has been implemented for a DKT-CST plate finite element family (Batoz, 1982), see R3.07.03, allowing a rather efficient and versatile modelling of complex building geometries. We remark that the curvature tensor K has opposite components in the notations used by plates elements in Code_Aster , see R3.07.03: the sub-matrices {A}^{\mathrm{mf}} and {B}^{f\zeta } have to be multiplied by -1 . The numerical integration of DHRC constitutive model lies on direct implicit time discretisation method (Nguyen, 1977), (Simo & Taylor, 1985), which is included in the Newton’ method with an elastic predictor step followed by a “plastic” corrector step, at the global balance equations stage. At the beginning of each time step, trial generalised stresses are calculated by assuming a fully elastic response rate, with an elastic tensor evaluated for the previous damaged state. section the general approach carried out in order to identify DHRC parameters. The needed microscopic scale data: geometry and material characteristics, and the main steps of the proposed automated procedure are detailed. 4.2 Identification approach The main difficulty to be overcome hereafter is to ensure that with a limited number of auxiliary problems solutions, we will be able to identify DHRC parameters that: - cover the space of macroscopic states ( \mathbf{E} , \mathbf{K} , {D}^{\zeta} , {E}^{\eta \zeta } ), - have a generic dependency on macroscopic damage variable {D}^{\zeta} , from the sound state, distinguishing tensile and compressive regimes, - ensure continuity of stress resultants ( \mathbf{N} , \mathbf{M} , {\Sigma}^{\eta \zeta } ) at each regime change, - ensure the convexity of the macroscopic free energy density. We decided to perform some “snapshots” of microscopic states for a limited number of selected macroscopic ones, and to entrust the task of determining the parameters dependency to {D}^{\zeta} to a least squares method and an appropriate selected function of {D}^{\zeta} . We recall from (Combescure et al., 2013), that in one dimension, if the microscopic damage function, controlling the elastic stiffness degradation {a}^{c}(d) , is expressed as \xi (d)=(\alpha +\mathrm{\gamma d})/(\alpha +d) (which is decreasing convex for \gamma \le 1 ) then the macroscopic one-dimensional elastic tensor A follows the same dependency and is equal to \mathbf{A}={\mathbf{A}}^{0}({\alpha}_{A}+{\gamma}_{A}D)/({\alpha}_{A}+D) , with {\gamma}_{A}\le 1 , similarly for the other tensors \mathbf{B} and \mathbf{C} . This ensures the convexity of the resultant Helmholtz free energy function, provided that γ is not “excessively” negative. As shown in the previous section, from the solutions of a set of auxiliary elastic problems, we have to identify the components of three tensors \mathbf{A} , \mathbf{B} and \mathbf{C} with their macroscopic damage variable {D}^{\zeta} dependency. Two macroscopic threshold values for damage and sliding need also to be determined. Hyp.12 . According to the results obtained for the macroscopic one-dimensional case (Combescure et al., 2013), we assume the generic following dependency on {D}^{\zeta} variable of the macroscopic tensors components (the particular expression for tensor \mathbf{B} resulting from Remark 6): \frac{\alpha +\gamma {D}^{\zeta}}{\alpha +{D}^{\zeta}} Of course this compromise will have to be assessed by comparison of DHRC model results with available experimental data on actual RC structures and usual loading paths. 4.3 Microscopic material parameters in RVE \Omega According to assumptions Hyp 1, steel is considered as linear elastic (defined by its Young’s modulus {E}_{s} and Poisson’s ratio {\nu}_{s} ). r7.01.38 Iwan law for the cyclic behaviour of granular materials r7.01.38 Iwan law for the cyclic behaviour of granular materials Summary: The constitutive model of Iwan [ 1 ], [ 2 ] is a classical multi-mechanism elastoplastic model for the description of the cyclic deviatoric behaviour of materials and particularly of geomaterials. The hardening is linear kinematic for each mechanism and the flow rule considered is associated. By construction, the model automatically satisfies the Masing rules. The model allows an easy description of the behaviour via parameters obtained directly from the curves of variation of the secant shear modulus. The user must simply supply the parameters of a hyperbolic function describing the variation of the secant modulus as a function of the shear strain. It is implemented in the MFront environment, which facilitates the implementation and the maintainability of the model. 1 Theoretical formulation 1.1 1D view of the behaviour of the Iwan model A purely 1D description of the Iwan model consists of an arrangement in parallel or in series of Jenkin elements, each element being composed of a spring and of a perfectly plastic frictional slider (Coulomb criterion) in series (Figure 1). The arrangement of the elements and the parameters of the model determine the shape of the cyclic shear response. | | | | --- | --- | | Series-parallel model | Parallel-series model | | Figure 1.1-1: 1D rheological models of Iwan [3] | | 1.2 3D formulation of the Iwan model In the 3D description of the behaviour, each element is associated with a yield surface, defined from the deviatoric stress associated with each mechanism. One therefore passes from a 1D description of the shear behaviour to a 3D description of the deviatoric behaviour on the basis of the stress and strain invariants, defined in the following manner: \textrm{Pression moyenne:} \text{p}=\frac{\text{t}\text{r}(\text{σ})}{3} \textrm{Tenseur déviateur de contraintes:} \mathrm{S}=\sigma -p\mathrm{I} | Deviatoric stress: \text{q}={\mathrm{S}}_{\text{V}\text{M}}^{3\text{D}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}\text{S}:\text{S}} | | | --- | --- | \textrm{Déformation volumique:} {\epsilon}_{v}=\mathit{tr}\left(\epsilon \right) | Deviatoric strain: {\text{q}}_{\text{n}}={\left(\text{S}-{\text{X}}_{\text{n}}\right)}_{\text{V}\text{M}}^{3\text{D}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}(\text{S}-{\text{X}}_{\text{n}}):(\text{S}-{\text{X}}_{\text{n}})} | | | --- | --- | For an arrangement of series-parallel type, when the applied stress exceeds the limit stress {Y}_{n} of mechanism n , there is hardening of this mechanism and the associated stress remains equal to the limit stress, i.e. only a kinematic hardening is associated with each mechanism of the model. The model allows great flexibility in the description of the behaviour, in particular through the possibility of direct use of laboratory test data. The error associated with the description of the cyclic behaviour depends directly on the number of yield surfaces and on their arrangement. However, the greater the number of mechanisms, the more numerically expensive the system to be solved, despite the passage from a tensorial system to a scalar system (section 2). The model is based on the theory of multi-mechanism elastoplasticity. In a series-parallel description, it assumes an additive and independent decomposition of the strains on the hardening mechanisms: \epsilon =\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\epsilon}_{n} For each mechanism, the model considers an additive decomposition of the total strain tensor \text{ε} into an elastic part {\text{ε}}_{\text{n}}^{\text{e}} and a plastic part {\epsilon}_{n}^{p} : {\epsilon}_{n}={\epsilon}_{n}^{e}+{\epsilon}_{n}^{p} The stress–strain relation is written directly from the fourth-order elasticity tensor, C . The elasticity is therefore linear and the model does not make it possible to take into account the effect of confinement in the elastic constants. \sigma =C{\epsilon}^{e} The model describing only the deviatoric behaviour, the volumetric response is assumed linear elastic: {\epsilon}_{v}=\frac{p}{3K} where > is the bulk modulus. In what follows, the various ingredients necessary to describe the constitutive law in an elastoplastic framework are described, namely: - Yield surface \text{f} : defines the zone in the stress space inside which the behaviour is linear elastic ( \text{f} 0 ). - Flow law: rule defining the plastic strain increment, in a generic manner {\dot{\epsilon}}^{p}=\dot{\lambda}\Psi , where \dot{\lambda} is the plastic multiplier and \Psi the flow law. 1.2.1 Description of the yield surface The yield surface of each mechanism is written in the following way: {f}_{n}={q}_{n}-{Y}_{n} With {Y}_{n} a limit constant from which the mechanism > hardens. This value is chosen from a pure shear test, by associating with each hardening mechanism > a pair of values \left({\gamma}_{n},{\tau}_{n}\right) with \gamma =2{\epsilon}_{ij} , i\ne j . {Y}_{n} is therefore obtained directly from {\tau}_{n} by the following relation: {Y}_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}{\tau}_{n} The value of {q}_{n} is the deviatoric stress associated with mechanism n , defined in the following manner: | {\text{q}}_{\text{n}}={\left(\text{S}-{\text{X}}_{\text{n}}\right)}_{\text{V}\text{M}}^{3\text{D}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}(\text{S}-{\text{X}}_{\text{n}}):(\text{S}-{\text{X}}_{\text{n}})} | | | --- | --- | The tensor {\text{X}}_{\text{n}} represents the kinematic hardening of mechanism \text{n} . It is obtained from the expression defined by Prager: {X}_{n}={C}_{n}{\dot{\epsilon}}_{n}^{p} With {C}_{n} a parameter of the model determined from a monotonic shear test. Because {C}_{n} is constant, one considers the hardening to be linear. 1.2.2 Description of the flow law The plastic strain increments of each mechanism n are obtained from the plastic multiplier {\dot{\lambda}}_{n} and from the flow law {\Psi}_{n} : {\dot{\epsilon}}_{n}^{p}={\dot{\lambda}}_{n}{\Psi}_{n} The model assuming an associated flow, the flow law is obtained directly from the yield surface: {\Psi}_{n}=\frac{\partial {f}_{n}}{\partial \sigma }=\frac{3}{2}\frac{\left(S-{X}_{n}\right)}{{q}_{n}} The plastic multiplier associated with each mechanism is obtained from the consistency equation, i.e. {\dot{f}}_{n}=0 : {\dot{\lambda}}_{n}=\frac{\frac{\partial {f}_{n}}{\partial \sigma }:{C}_{n}:\dot{\epsilon}}{\frac{\partial {f}_{n}}{\partial \sigma }:{C}_{n}:{\Psi}_{n}-{C}_{n}\frac{\partial {f}_{n}}{\partial {X}_{n}}:{\Psi}_{n}} With: \frac{\partial {f}_{n}}{{\partial X}_{n}}=\frac{3}{2}\frac{\left(S-{X}_{n}\right)}{{q}_{n}} The computation of the plastic multiplier is set out in section 2. 1.2.3 Computation of the hardening parameters {C}_{n} The determination of the kinematic hardening parameters {C}_{n} is carried out from a stress path in pure shear ( \Delta p=0 ). Suppose the response known for this stress path from an initial state with zero deviatoric stress and zero plastic strain. In this case: \dot{\gamma}=\left(\frac{1}{2G}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{{C}_{n}}\right)\dot{\tau} From > pairs \left({\gamma}_{n},{\tau}_{n}\right) , one can estimate the value of {C}_{n} recursively with the following expression: \frac{1}{{C}_{n}}=\frac{{\gamma}_{k+1}-{\gamma}_{k}}{{\tau}_{k+1}-{\tau}_{k}}-\frac{1}{2G}-\sum_{m=1}^{k-1}\frac{1}{{C}_{m}} The computation of the kinematic hardening parameters {C}_{n} is carried out in the @InitLocalVars block of Mfront. 2 Numerical integration of the constitutive law The choice in MFront is directed towards the integration of the systems of differential equations written in the following manner: \dot{Y}=G\left(Y,t\right) Where G is an a priori non-linear function and assumed at least continuously differentiable. An implicit integration of theta-method type is chosen for the numerical integration of the non-linear system. In this case the system is written in the following manner: Y{|}_{t+\Delta t}=Y{|}_{t}+\Delta tG\left(\left\lbrace 1-\theta \right\rbrace Y{|}_{t}+\theta Y{|}_{t+\Delta t},t+\theta \Delta t\right) Or equivalently: F\left(\Delta Y\right)=\Delta Y-\Delta tG\left(\left\lbrace 1-\theta \right\rbrace Y{|}_{t}+\theta Y{|}_{t+\Delta t},t+\theta \Delta t\right)=0 The Newton–Raphson method is chosen for the computation of the zero of the function F\left(\Delta Y\right) . That is: F\left(\Delta Y\right)=F\left(\Delta {Y}^{-}\right)+{\left(\frac{dF}{d\Delta Y}\right)}_{\Delta Y=\Delta {Y}^{-}}\left(\Delta Y+\Delta {Y}^{-}\right) Where J=\frac{dF}{d\Delta Y} is the Jacobian matrix of the function F . The approximation \Delta {Y}^{+} is obtained by considering F\left(\Delta {Y}^{+}\right)=0 , that is: \Delta {Y}^{+}=\Delta {Y}^{-}-\left({J}^{-1}\left(\Delta {Y}^{-}\right)\right)F\left(\Delta {Y}^{-}\right) The difficulty of the Newton–Raphson method lies in the computation of the Jacobian matrix, the analytical computation of which is supplied in section 2.4. A purely implicit scheme is chosen for the integration of the equations ( \theta =1 ), in order to give physically satisfactory results. Following the approach presented in document [ 4 ], for a linear kinematic hardening it is possible to reduce the tensorial system to a scalar system, thanks to the collinearity between the plastic strain increment {\dot{\epsilon}}_{n}^{p} and the difference S-{X}_{n} in the absence of plastic strain, {S}_{n}^{e} . This can be written in the following manner for a multiple kinematic hardening: {S}_{n}^{e}={S}^{-}+\dot{S}-{X}_{n}^{-}={S}^{-}+2\mu {\dot{\epsilon}}_{n}^{e}-{X}_{n}^{-} Therefore: S-{X}_{n}={S}_{n}^{e}-{\dot{X}}_{n}={S}_{n}^{e}-{C}_{n}{\dot{\epsilon}}_{n}^{p} The plastic strain increment of mechanism > is therefore written: {\dot{\epsilon}}_{n}^{p}=\frac{3}{2}\frac{{\dot{\lambda}}_{n}}{{q}_{n}}\left({S}_{n}^{e}-{C}_{n}{\dot{\epsilon}}_{n}^{p}\right)=\frac{3}{2}\frac{{\dot{\lambda}}_{n}}{{q}_{n}^{e}}{S}_{n}^{e} With {q}_{n}^{e} the norm of {S}_{n}^{e} . By substituting {\dot{\epsilon}}_{n}^{p} into the expression (), one obtains: S-{X}_{n}={S}_{n}^{e}\left(1-\frac{\frac{3}{2}{C}_{n}\dot{{\lambda}_{n}}}{{q}_{n}^{e}}\right) By injecting the expression of S-{X}_{n} into the condition f=0 , one obtains: \left({q}_{n}^{e}-\frac{3}{2}{C}_{n}\dot{{\lambda}_{n}}\right)-{Y}_{n}=0 Insofar as {Y}_{n}>0 and {q}_{n}^{e}>0 , this equation admits the following solution for the plastic multiplier: \dot{{\lambda}_{n}}=\frac{{q}_{n}^{e}-{Y}_{n}}{\frac{3}{2}{C}_{n}} Therefore, necessarily: 0 0 ): \frac{\partial {f}_{\dot{{\lambda}_{n}}}}{\partial {\dot{\epsilon}}^{e}}=-\frac{4}{3}\frac{\mu}{{C}_{n}}{\Psi}_{n}:{I}_{4} On checking the values obtained for the numerical Jacobian (option @CompareToNumericalJacobian), it has been observed that for values of {f}_{\dot{{\lambda}_{n}}} close to zero (positive or negative), \frac{\partial {f}_{\dot{{\lambda}_{n}}}}{\partial {\dot{\epsilon}}^{e}} is equal to half of the expression obtained analytically. The treatment in this case is carried out by considering a critical value of the value of the yield surface of {10}^{-6} . 3 Implementation in code_aster The number of kinematic hardening surfaces of the model is fixed at twelve. The first eleven surfaces make it possible to cover the range of shear strains between {10}^{-5} and 2,0\times {10}^{-2} . One considers a linear elastic behaviour for strains smaller than {10}^{-5} and a maximum shear strain of 2,0\times {10}^{-2} . The interpolation values used are the following: | γ1=1.00000000e-05 | | --- | | γ2=2.15443469e-05 | | γ3=4.64158883e-05 | | γ4=1.00000000e-04 | | γ5=2.15443469e-04 | | γ6=4.64158883e-04 | | γ7=1.00000000e-03 | | γ8=2.15443469e-03 | | γ9=4.64158883e-03 | | γ10=1.00000000e-02 | | γ11=2.00000000e-02 | Beyond a shear strain of 2,0\times {10}^{-2} , the results of the model will be approximate because the last surface, positioned at a shear strain of 1,0\times {10}^{-1} , simply makes it possible to ensure that the model supplies a response between 2,0\times {10}^{-2} and 1,0\times {10}^{-1} . 3.1 Internal variables The following internal variables (StateVariable and AuxiliaryStateVariable in the MFront language) are available during an analysis with the constitutive law of Iwan: | Eel(1-6) | Elastic strain tensor | | --- | --- | | pp (7-18) | Vector of scalar plastic multipliers > | | X (19-91) | Vector of kinematic hardening tensors {\text{X}}_{\text{n}} | | fn(92-103) | Vector of values of the yield surface | 3.2 Description of the model under MFront The behaviour is defined in the file Iwan.mfront. | Parser/DSL | Implicit | | --- | --- | | Algorithm | NewtonRaphson | | | @Theta 1. @IterMax 50 @Epsilon 1.E-12 | | Internal variables (@StateVariable) | real pp[1:12] | | Auxiliary internal variables (@AuxiliaryStateVariable) | Stensor X[1:12] real fn[1:12] | | Command variables (@ExternalStateVariable) | none | | Modellings | '3D' 'AXIS' 'D_PLAN' | | Strains | 'PETIT' 'PETIT_REAC' 'GDEF_LOG' | 4 Features and verification Here is the list of the verification cases available: | ssnv205b | V6.04.205 | cyclic shear test controlled in strain. | | --- | --- | --- | | ssnv207b | V6.04.207 | cyclic shear controlled in strain with micro-unloading. | | COMP012 d | V6.07.112 | Cyclic shear test with the command CALC_ESSAI_GEOMECA | 5 Bibliography IWAN W.
