r7.01.40 Constitutive model LKR r7.01.40 Constitutive model LKR Summary: The constitutive model LKR is a thermomechanical extension of the elasto(visco)plastic model LETK [1] and [2]. Its development and its numerical integration are the outcome of the thesis work of S. Raude [3]. This document presents the main conceptual outlines of the model and the principal equations that govern its operation. The first paragraph introduces the main concepts of the model, essential to the understanding of the second paragraph, in which its principal equations taken from [3] are presented. The last paragraph returns briefly to the main outlines of the numerical integration of the model. 1 Physical framework and concepts of the LETK model The aim of this paragraph is not to describe exhaustively the approach undertaken by [1] and [2] in order to arrive at the development of the LETK model. The purpose is to return to certain points essential to the understanding of paragraphs § 2 and § 3. The reader is invited to refer to [1] and [2] for more details. The concepts presented in this paragraph were retained by [3] in the development of the LKR model. The model presented by [2] is an elasto(visco)plastic model with two mechanisms. The first mechanism, elastoplastic, is concerned with describing the instantaneous deviatoric behaviour of geomaterials. The second mechanism, viscoplastic, accounts for the effect of time on the deviatoric behaviour. The instantaneous deviatoric behaviour is characterised by uniaxial/triaxial compression tests and extension tests (among others). The conceptual framework retained for the development of the elastoplastic mechanism is based mainly on the analysis of the behaviour in triaxial compression. The response of geomaterials to this type of loading is divided into two phases (see Figure ). For relatively small strains, the strength of a specimen increases with its axial strain. This phase, termed pre-peak , ends when the material reaches its maximum strength. Beyond this peak, the strength decreases until a residual value is reached. The evolution of a material between its peak and residual strengths is termed post-peak . The pre-peak and post-peak behaviours are detailed in paragraph § 1.1. The effect of time on the deviatoric behaviour is characterised by creep tests, relaxation tests or triaxial compression tests at different loading rates. The conceptual framework retained for the development of the viscoplastic mechanism is based mainly on the analysis of the behaviour during a creep test. This point is detailed in paragraph § 1.2. Figure 1.1: Uniaxial compression test on Cox argillite [4]. 1.1 Elastoplastic mechanism The elastoplastic mechanism is concerned with reproducing the following phenomena [1]: - the elastic behaviour is non-linear for small strains; - the maximum strength depends on the confinement level; - the post-peak softening is governed by the progressive loss of cohesion and by the evolution of the dilatancy angle; - the residual state, or critical state, is characterised by a zero cohesion, a zero dilatancy and a purely frictional behaviour. 1.1.1 Pre-peak behaviour The pre-peak behaviour can be decomposed into several phases. By way of example, [2] and [5] distinguish six of them (see Figure ): 1. This phase, termed compaction, concerns the low stress levels. It is accompanied by a contraction of the specimen and accounts for the initial closure of the pre-existing cracks within the material. This phase is considerably reduced, or even non-existent, when a confining pressure is applied to the specimen. 1. This phase corresponds to the linear/elastic part of the stress–strain curve and rarely exceeds 40% of the maximum strength. The volumetric behaviour remains contracting but evolves more slowly than during the first phase. 1. This phase marks the initiation of cracking and of dilatancy. The propagation of the cracks that have been created nevertheless remains stable. The stress level corresponding to this phase is generally between 30% and 60% of the maximum strength. 2. For deviators between 50% and 60% of the maximum strength, a marked intensification of cracking is observed. An increase in the confining pressure has a stabilising effect on the development of these cracks. 3. The coalescence of the cracks begins. This phase corresponds to deviators between 70% and 90% of the maximum strength. Phases 3, 4 and 5 are not always the subject of such a distinction. Their characterisation and the deviator levels to which they correspond depend strongly on the confining pressure applied to the specimen. For low confinements, cracking will rapidly become unstable from the third phase onwards. At high confinement, this transition can be delayed until the end of the fifth phase. 1. This phase is associated with the unstable development of cracking and with a significant increase in dilatancy up to the maximum strength of the specimen. Figure 1.2: Phases characterising the mechanical and volumetric evolutions of a material during uniaxial or triaxial compression tests (from [5], taken up by [2]) In a simplified manner, three phases will be retained: 1. Phases 1 and 2 can constitute one and the same domain within which the behaviour is elastic. The upper limit of this phase corresponds to the elasticity limit of the material. 2. Phases 3, 4 and 5 can also constitute one and the same domain, which marks a transition in the volumetric behaviour (stable/unstable cracking). For low confinements, this transition takes place at low stress levels, close to the initial elasticity limit. For high confining pressures, this transition can take place at stress levels very close to the strength peak. 3. Phase 6 is associated with the unstable development of cracking. The upper limit of this phase coincides with the maximum strength of the material. This decomposition into three simplified phases makes it possible to define three thresholds in stress space (Figure ). The upper limits of domains 1 and 3 characterise mechanical thresholds: the initial elasticity limit and the maximum strength, also called the peak strength. The upper limit of phase 2 marks a transition in the volumetric behaviour (contractancy/dilatancy). This transition between contracting and dilating behaviours takes place for stress states called characteristic states [6] and [7]. The set of characteristic states obtained for triaxial compression tests at different confining pressures defines the characteristic threshold. Figure 1.3: Evolution thresholds in the pre-peak phase. Within the framework retained by [2], the pre-peak hardening is therefore expressed by a dilation of the elastic domain between the damage thresholds (or initial elasticity limit) and the peak threshold (or maximum strength) (Figure ). When the stress state lies between the initial elasticity limit and the characteristic threshold, the plastic volumetric behaviour is termed contracting. When the stress state lies between the characteristic threshold and the peak threshold, the plastic volumetric behaviour is termed dilating. The characteristic threshold is defined as the union of the initial elasticity limit (for low confinements) and of a threshold called the cleavage limit, with reference to the work carried out by [8] and [9] (higher confinements) (Figure ). 1.1.2 Post-peak behaviour The post-peak behaviour characterises the evolution of the material in the vicinity of and beyond the strength peak (between its maximum and residual strengths). Most cohesive materials exhibit a softening behaviour after having reached their peak strength. This domain accounts for a deterioration of the mechanical properties of the material and, in particular, a loss of cohesion. The post-peak behaviour depends strongly on the confinement [2]. An increase in the confining pressure tends to stabilise the drop in strength. This stabilisation is nevertheless progressive and a function of external parameters such as the loading rate, the temperature, the stress path, the pore pressure, etc. Several failure patterns, or modes of collapse [1], are observed as a function of the confining pressure. It is commonly accepted to distinguish three of them: - Low confinement: the specimen fails by cleavage ; the failure is brittle and explosive. This failure mode is termed diffuse bifurcation by [10] (Figure ); - Intermediate confinement: the formation of one or more shear structure(s) within the specimen controls the loss of strength (Figure ). As soon as these so-called induced structures [1] are created, the loss of strength is entirely controlled by the behaviour along these discontinuities up to the residual threshold (residual strength criterion, critical state of the material, purely frictional behaviour, zero cohesion and dilatancy). This failure mode is termed localised bifurcation by [10]; - High confinement: the behaviour becomes ductile. The specimen can deform substantially without loss of strength or of homogeneity. The volumetric behaviour can remain purely contracting. There is barrelling of the specimen (Figure ). The work carried out by [1] and [2] made it possible to bring out the existence of an intermediate state between the maximum and residual strengths of a material. This state coincides with a total loss of cohesion and a maximum of dilatancy, which correspond to the formation of one or more shear surface(s) (Figure ). The set of these intermediate states defines a threshold in stress space, called the intermediate threshold. [1] and [2] assume that the intermediate threshold coincides with the second part of the characteristic threshold introduced in paragraph § 1.1.1. These two thresholds must nevertheless not be confused. The characteristic threshold is a transition threshold in the pre-peak volumetric behaviour, whereas the intermediate threshold is a mechanical threshold through which the elastic domain hardens in the post-peak regime. The volumetric behaviour in the post-peak phase is always dilating, whatever the stress state. The evolution of the elasticity domain for the post-peak behaviour therefore takes place in two stages [2]: - A first transition between the peak and intermediate thresholds, during which the cohesion of the material will progressively vanish (quantity C in the Figure ) while the dilatancy will increase to reach its maximum on the intermediate threshold (quantity \psi in the in the Figure ). - A second transition between the intermediate and residual thresholds, during which the dilatancy decreases by progressive wear of the lips of the shear structures created at the intermediate threshold (Figure ). On the residual threshold, cohesion and dilatancy are zero; the behaviour is purely frictional (critical state) (quantity {\mathrm{\phi }}_{\mathit{rés}} in the Figure ). Figure 1.4: The various failure modes as a function of confinement [1] For low confinements, the transition between the peak threshold and the residual threshold takes place essentially by loss of cohesion. There is failure by cleavage or diffuse bifurcation (Figure ). The dilatancy only increases; no independent shear surface is created. For higher confinements, the tendency is reversed; the role of dilatancy becomes increasingly important (Figure ). 1.2 Figure 1.5: Evolution thresholds in the post-peak phase. Viscoplastic mechanism The effect of time on the behaviour of a material is expressed by various phenomena. Let us mention, for example: - Consolidation: decrease in volume with time following drainage of the material (hydromechanical phenomenon). - Swelling: increase in volume generated by chemical modifications of the structure of the rock. - Creep: delayed strains at constant loading. - Relaxation: release of the stresses at constant strain. - Ageing: degradation of the mechanical properties of the rock following a chemical alteration of its constituent minerals. - Healing: physicochemical phenomenon of recrystallisation allowing the rock to recover its mechanical properties. The delayed deviatoric behaviour of geomaterials can be characterised by various types of tests: - Triaxial compression tests at different loading rates: it is commonly accepted that the maximum strength of a material decreases with a decrease in the loading rate [2]. - Creep tests (Figure ): a deviator is held constant after a phase of isotropic confinement. The evolution of the axial strains as a function of time makes it possible to characterise the rate and the amplitude of the delayed effects. Three distinct regimes are generally brought out: a primary creep during which the creep rate only decreases with time; a secondary creep during which the creep rate is constant; a tertiary creep during which the creep rate increases rapidly. This last regime generally leads to the failure of the specimen. - Relaxation tests: the strain is held constant. The drop in stress with time also makes it possible to characterise the rate and the amplitude of the delayed effects. Figure 1.6: Results of creep tests carried out on Cox argillite [11], taken up by [12] (on the left), [13] taken up by [2] (on the right). Depending on the deviator level applied to a specimen, the three creep regimes presented above may or may not exist. For low deviator levels, creep stabilises rapidly (primary creep). For higher deviators, the long-term behaviour evolves in an unstable manner. The transition time between secondary and tertiary creeps depends on the applied stress level and on external parameters such as the temperature. An increase in the confining pressure stabilises the long-term behaviour. The identification of the stress states corresponding to the transition between stable and unstable long-term behaviours for different confining pressures makes it possible to define a threshold in stress space, called the maximum viscoplastic threshold. This threshold is also called the long-term strength threshold by [2], because the transition stress level between stable and unstable creeps also corresponds to the maximum strength that can be reached during a triaxial compression test at an infinitely slow loading rate. Figure 1.7: Evolution thresholds for the viscoplastic mechanism. The existence of this threshold is not unanimously accepted by the scientific community, because its determination remains difficult to define, in particular for materials with a slow creep kinetics. However, based on several studies listed by [2], the LETK model retains, as the long-term strength threshold, the threshold of initiation of extension cracks (unstable cracking), that is to say the envelope of the damage threshold and of the cleavage limit. The long-term strength threshold therefore coincides with the characteristic threshold defined in paragraph § 1.1.1. Here again, the role of these two thresholds must not be confused. The maximum viscoplastic threshold is a mechanical threshold through which the elasticity domain of the viscoplastic mechanism hardens, whereas the characteristic threshold is a transition threshold in the volumetric behaviour for both mechanisms. With these definitions, an unstable long-term behaviour necessarily corresponds to a dilating volumetric state. The threshold of initiation of the viscoplastic strains corresponds to the initial elasticity limit (damage threshold). The elastic domain of the viscoplastic mechanism therefore evolves between the initial elasticity limit (which is identical to that of the elastoplastic mechanism) and the long-term strength threshold. During a creep test, a deviator held constant between the initial elasticity limit and the maximum viscoplastic threshold corresponds to a stable creep (primary creep) and to a contracting volumetric behaviour. A deviator held constant between the maximum viscoplastic threshold and the peak threshold corresponds to an unstable long-term behaviour and to a dilating volumetric behaviour. 1.3 Anisotropy Because of their geological history and their mode of deposition/formation, certain geomaterials present one or more preferential orientations, which can have an influence on their instantaneous and/or delayed mechanical behaviour. The properties generally affected by this initial anisotropy are: Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, the shear modulus, the uniaxial compressive strength, the amplitude of the delayed strains, … Structural (or initial) anisotropy is among the physical phenomena taken into account by the LKR model (see § 2.2 and § 2.5). 1.4 Coupling between the two mechanisms As indicated in paragraph 1.2, the maximum strength reached during a triaxial compression test depends on the loading rate and therefore on time. Now the maximum strength is a notion carried solely by the plastic mechanism (peak threshold), which is independent of time. In order to be able to reproduce this kind of phenomenon, it is therefore necessary to couple the two mechanisms so as to introduce, in an implicit manner, the notion of time within the plastic mechanism. The coupling introduced by [2] operates at the level of the internal hardening variables of the two mechanisms. When the stress state lies above the maximum viscoplastic threshold, the hardening of the viscoplastic surface influences that of the plastic surface. The reader will refer to [2] for more details on this subject. The coupling between the two mechanisms will moreover be mentioned in paragraph 2.6, in which the expressions of the hardening variables of the two mechanisms are presented. 1.5 Remarks on the spherical behaviour The LETK constitutive model was initially developed in order to reproduce the behaviour of structures during underground excavations. The stress path followed at the wall of a gallery during an excavation is not spherical. The LETK model is therefore concerned essentially with reproducing the deviatoric behaviour of geomaterials. Along a purely spherical stress path, the modelled behaviour will therefore remain linear elastic . 2 Thermomechanical extension of the LETK model (LKR model) The aim of this paragraph is to present the developments made to the LETK constitutive model, whether on the mechanical part of the model or on the integration of the effects of temperature. This method consists in making the plastic and/or viscoplastic mechanisms dependent on the orientation of the loading, via the introduction of a microstructure tensor (fabric tensor) into the expressions of {F}^{p} and/or {F}^{\mathit{vp}} . In the LKR model, this dependence is introduced via the parameter {\sigma}_{c} , which represents the uniaxial compressive strength of the material. {\sigma}_{c} takes the following form: {\sigma}_{c}={\widehat{\sigma}}_{c}(1+{A}_{ij}{l}_{i}{l}_{j}+{b}_{1}{({A}_{ij}{l}_{i}{l}_{j})}^{2}+{b}_{2}{({A}_{ij}{l}_{i}{l}_{j})}^{3}+\mathrm{...}) Where {A}_{ij} is a second-order tensor that is a function of the fabric tensor of the material, {l}_{i} is a vector describing the orientation of the loading in the local frame of the material, {\widehat{\sigma}}_{c} and {b}_{i} are material parameters. The expression is generally simplified to order 2 (sufficient to reproduce the behaviour observed in the laboratory) and for transversely isotropic materials ( {A}_{ij} becomes a scalar {A}_{22}={A}_{33}=-0.5{A}_{11} , which is a material parameter). The three material parameters introduced by the expression are therefore {\widehat{\sigma}}_{c} (SIGMA_C), {b}_{1} (B_SIGC) and {A}_{11} (A_SIGC). A routine is specifically dedicated to the computation of {\sigma}_{c} . The components {l}_{i} have the expression: {l}_{i}=\frac{\sqrt{{\lbrace {\sigma}_{\mathit{iL}}^{l}\rbrace }^{2}+{\lbrace {\sigma}_{\mathit{iT}}^{l}\rbrace }^{2}+{\lbrace {\sigma}_{iN}^{l}\rbrace }^{2}}}{{\lbrace {\sigma}^{l}\rbrace }_{kk}^{2}} Where {\sigma}^{l} is the stress tensor in the local frame: {\sigma}_{l}={}^{T}\lbrace {P}_{33}^{\mathit{gl}}\rbrace \lbrace {\sigma}^{g}\rbrace \lbrace {P}_{33}^{\mathit{gl}}\rbrace With {P}_{33}^{\mathit{gl}} the transformation matrix from the global frame to the local frame and {\sigma}^{g} the stress tensor expressed in the global frame. 2.6 Coupling between the two mechanisms The plastic and viscoplastic mechanisms are coupled through their internal hardening variables. This coupling makes it possible, among other things, to reproduce the dependence of the maximum strength of geomaterials on the loading rate, and therefore on time. The coupling between the two mechanisms is triggered as soon as the stress state lies above the characteristic threshold [2]. The hardening of the viscoplastic surface influences that of the plastic surface. As long as the stress state is below the characteristic threshold, the increment of the hardening variable of the plastic mechanism, {\dot{\xi}}^{p} , coincides with the increment of equivalent plastic strain, or plastic distortion, {\dot{\gamma}}^{p} : {\dot{\xi}}^{p}={\dot{\gamma}}^{p}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{\dot{e}}^{p}:{\dot{e}}^{p}} When the stress state lies above the characteristic threshold, {\dot{\xi}}^{p} is the sum of the increment of plastic distortion {\dot{\gamma}}^{p} and of the increment of viscoplastic distortion, {\dot{\gamma}}^{\mathit{vp}} : {\dot{\xi}}^{p}={\dot{\gamma}}^{p}+{\dot{\gamma}}^{\mathit{vp}} The increment of the hardening variable of the viscoplastic mechanism is equal to the increment of viscoplastic distortion, whatever the stress state: {\dot{\xi}}^{\mathit{vp}}=\min\left\lbrace {\dot{\gamma}}^{\mathit{vp}};⟨{\xi}_{[5]}-{\xi}^{\mathit{vp}}⟩\right\rbrace 2.7 Flow rules It is commonly accepted that the direction of the (visco)plastic flows is derived from a function {g}^{(v)p} called the (visco)plastic potential. If this potential coincides with the function {F}^{(v)p} , the flow rule is said to be normal or associated , in the sense that it is associated with the (visco)plasticity criterion {F}^{(v)p} . A flow rule derived from a potential distinct from {F}^{(v)p} (more precisely such that \frac{\partial {g}^{(v)p}}{\partial \sigma } is not proportional to \frac{\partial {F}^{(v)p}}{\partial \sigma } is said to be non-associated . Materials obeying the normality rule are generally termed generalised standard materials. The notion of a standard material is “practical”, since it makes it possible to describe the plastic behaviour of a material from a single function [24]. Nevertheless, the hypotheses that underlie the theory of associated plasticity are not representative of the real behaviour of rocks, soils and concretes [25]. Two approaches are proposed. The first approach makes it possible to describe the evolution of the dilatancy angle for the pre-peak part of the plastic mechanism and for the viscoplastic mechanism. This approach is based on the notion of characteristic state. As long as the stress state is below the characteristic threshold, the dilatancy angle is negative and the (visco)plastic volumetric behaviour is contracting. When the stress state lies above the characteristic threshold, the dilatancy angle is positive and the (visco)plastic volumetric behaviour is dilating. The second approach makes it possible to describe the evolution of the dilatancy angle for the post-peak regime of the plastic mechanism. In the first approach, one must be able to determine the position of the stress state with respect to the characteristic threshold. r7.01.41 Constitutive law of porous media: GonfElas r7.01.41 Constitutive law of porous media: GonfElas Summary: The GonfElas model is a model initially proposed by D. Hoxan and F. Colin [ 1 ] to describe the swelling behaviour of certain types of clay. It is a non-linear elastic model depending on suction (this model must therefore be used in a THHM or HHM environment only). This model is inspired by the Barcelona model BBM (cf. R7.01.17) and corresponds to its elastic part. It is particularly suited to the study of the behaviour of compacted clay plugs (bentonite). This model is developed within the MFront framework. 1 Presentation of the model and notation This model is a constitutive law in rock mechanics making it possible to describe the behaviour of materials of the “swelling clay” type (bentonite). It is a non-linear elastic model relating the net stress to the swelling pressure, which itself depends on the suction (or capillary pressure). It can be used only within the framework of the THHM and HHM behaviours. This model rests on the following relation: d\tilde{\sigma}={K}_{s}(\mathit{Pc})d{\epsilon}_{V}+b\left(1+\frac{\mathit{Pc}}{A}\right){e}^{-{\beta}_{m}{\left(\frac{s}{A}\right)}^{2}}\mathit{dPc} with \tilde{\sigma} : net stress or effective stress. Here the net stress is chosen (cf. section 2.1). In the version of the model available here, neither the non-linearity of {K}_{s}(\mathit{Pc}) nor its dependence with respect to suction is taken into account. In the end, one simply has {K}_{s}(\mathit{Pc})={K}_{0} . With the following notation: {K}_{0} is the bulk modulus of the material b is the Biot coefficient A is a parameter with the dimension of a pressure {\beta}_{m} is a dimensionless parameter \mathit{Pc} is the capillary pressure The notion of swelling pressure {P}_{\mathit{gf}} , which will be used later, is also defined here. 2 Implementation of the model 2.1 Effective stresses and net stresses It is recalled that the THM formulation rests on the distinction between the effective stress \sigma' and the total stress \sigma , such that: d\sigma =d\sigma '+d\pi with \pi the hydraulic stress such that d\pi =-b(\mathit{dPg}-S\mathit{dPc}) where S is the liquid saturation and Pg the gas pressure. In the case of a net-stress formulation, one has: d\sigma =d\tilde{\sigma}+d\pi with \pi the hydraulic stress, which is then defined such that d\pi =-b(\mathit{dPg}) . It is this formulation that is retained for the law GonfElas, which differs from the other constitutive laws available in unsaturated THM. This allows this law to have notation consistent with that of the Barcelona law. 2.2 Programming of the law The law is programmed incrementally on the mean stress (applied to the net stresses), which gives: \Delta \tilde{{\sigma}_{m}}={K}_{0}\Delta {\epsilon}_{V}+b\Delta \mathit{PG} With: \tilde{{\sigma}_{m}}=\frac{1}{3}\mathit{Tr}(\tilde{\sigma}) and by introducing the swelling-pressure function in the saturated and unsaturated cases: \mathit{PG}(\mathit{Pc})=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}A\left(\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{{\beta}_{m}}}\right)\mathit{Erf}\left(\frac{\mathit{Pc}}{A}\sqrt{{\beta}_{m}}\right)+\frac{1}{2{\beta}_{m}}\left(\begin{array}{c}1-{e}^{-{\beta}_{m}{\left(\frac{\mathit{Pc}}{A}\right)}^{2}}\\ \phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\end{array}\right)& \text{si}S<1\\ \mathit{Pc}\text{si}S=1\hfill & \phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\end{array} with \mathit{Erf}(x)=\underset{0}{\overset{x}{\int}}{e}^{-{\mathrm{\chi }}^{2}}d\mathrm{\chi } . 2.3 Material data and identification The material parameters specific to the law and to be entered in DEFI_MATERIAU are: - BETAM: dimensionless material parameter corresponding to the {\beta}_{m} of the law above. - PREF: parameter with the dimension of a pressure corresponding to the A of the law above. The identification of {\beta}_{m} is carried out by seeking the swelling pressure. Let {P}_{\mathit{gf}}({\mathit{Pc}}_{0}) be the swelling pressure found by the model when a sample is re-saturated in a blocked-strain test, starting from a suction {\mathit{Pc}}_{0} . It is recalled that at saturation, \mathit{Pc}=0 , which implies that: {P}_{\mathit{gf}}({\mathit{Pc}}_{0})=\underset{{\mathit{Pc}}_{0}}{\overset{0}{\int}}b\left(1+\frac{\mathit{Pc}}{A}\right){e}^{-{\beta}_{m}{\left(\frac{s}{A}\right)}^{2}}\mathit{dPc} After integration one obtains: \frac{{P}_{\mathit{gf}}({\mathit{Pc}}_{0})}{A}=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{{\beta}_{m}}}\mathit{Erf}\left(\frac{{\mathit{Pc}}_{0}}{A}\sqrt{{\beta}_{m}}\right)+\frac{1}{2{\beta}_{m}}\left(\begin{array}{c}1-{e}^{-{\beta}_{m}{\left(\frac{{\mathit{Pc}}_{0}}{A}\right)}^{2}}\\ \phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\end{array}\right) The expected swelling pressure corresponds to the re-saturation path between the dry state ( {P}_{c}=\infty ) and the saturated state, that is {P}_{\mathit{gf}}={P}_{\mathit{gf}}(\infty ) . It is known that \mathrm{Erf}(\infty )=1 and therefore: \frac{{P}_{\mathit{gf}}}{A}=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{{\beta}_{m}}}+\frac{1}{2{\beta}_{m}} An identification of the coefficient {\beta}_{m} is deduced from this. 2.4 Output internal variables There are no output internal variables. 3 Bibliography 1. Gerard P., Charlier R., Barnichon J.D., Su K., Shao J-F, Duveau G., Giot R., Chavant C., Collin F., Numerical Modelling of Coupled Mechanics and Gas Transfer around Radioactive Waste in long term storage. Journal of Theoretical and Applied Mechanics, Sofia, 2008, vol. 38, N 1-2, pp.25-44. 4 Verification The constitutive law GonfElas is verified by the following test cases: | WTNV103 | 3D modelling of the unconstrained swelling of a clay | V7.31.103 | | --- | --- | --- | | WTNV136 | 3D modelling of the swelling of a clay | V7.31.136 | | WTNP119 | Plane modelling of the swelling of a clay | V7.32.119 | | WTNA110 | Axisymmetric modelling of the swelling of a clay | V7.33.110 |

r7.01.42 Homogeneous damage law ENDO_LOCA_EXP r7.01.42 Homogeneous damage law ENDO_LOCA_EXP Summary: This document describes the elastic brittle constitutive model ENDO_LOCA_EXP, available in local modelling only (as opposed to a non-local formulation of GRAD_VARI type). This implies restricting the use of the model to situations in which the damage is diffuse and not localised. The corresponding non-local version is supplied by the model ENDO_FISS_EXP R5.03.28. Although the damage is modelled there in an isotropic manner, the damage criterion is for its part well suited to the modelling of concrete, distinguishing in particular the states of tension and of compression, unlike the model ENDO_ISOT_BETON R7.01.04 for example. Moreover, a recovery of stiffness in compression is introduced in order to reflect the closure of the cracks. On the other hand, the model is a priori not suited to modelling the damage of concrete in compression. 1 Scope 1.1 Purposes The constitutive law ENDO_LOCA_EXP, available in the command STAT_NON_LINE, has the objective of describing the diffuse quasi-brittle damage of concrete under tensile mechanical loadings. The damage is described there in an isotropic manner. On the phenomenological level, the model aims more particularly to reflect: - the contrast between the elastic limits in tension and in compression, thus avoiding premature damage in compression under prestress, for example; - the specific shape of the damage surface in multiaxial tension, close to a Rankine criterion; - the impact on the stiffness of the closure of the cracks in the compression directions, which also reinforces the robustness of the simulations in the presence of surface-breaking cracks. In the presence of localised damage, one will prefer to it the non-local model ENDO_FISS_EXP, whose parameter definition is close to that of ENDO_LOCA_EXP. The interested reader will be able to find more detailed elements on the formulation of the law and its validation in the reference [Lorentz, 2020]. Given the proximity to the constitutive laws ENDO_ISOT_BETON and ENDO_FISS_EXP, the reader may also refer to the references [Badel et al., 2007], [Lorentz, 2017], R7.01.04 and R5.03.28. 1.2 Material parameters The constitutive law is based on six internal parameters (including the elastic constants), as will be seen in the presentation of the equations in the following chapter. However, in a diffuse-cracking regime in which a mean inter-crack distance emerges, one will be able to reformulate the parameters in terms of quantities more accessible to the engineer. Besides Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, one will supply the tensile and compressive strengths (the latter being less significant for the problems targeted), the fracture energy and a parameter to describe the shape of the softening response. Finally, the mean inter-crack distance will be fixed on the basis of the characteristics of the reinforcement, for example. The command DEFI_MATER_GC takes charge of the transformation of these engineering parameters into internal characteristics of the law and can therefore be substituted for the command DEFI_MATERIAU, but it requires in that case that the mean inter-crack distance also be supplied. 1.3 Internal variables The constitutive law ENDO_LOCA_EXP gives access to five internal variables. The degree of damage b , lying between 0 for a sound material and 1 for a fully damaged material, constitutes a priori the only true internal variable of the model. For reasons of numerical efficiency, one also keeps the state of the current time step, with the values 0=elastic, 1=damaging, 2=saturated. Finally, one also groups there three variables in order to facilitate the post-processing. The internal variables are grouped in the following table: | ENDO | V1 | Damage b | | --- | --- | --- | | INDIENDO | V2 | State of the current time step (0, 1 or 2) | | ENDORIGI | V3 | Loss of stiffness 1-B(b) | | ENERELAS | V4 | Volumetric elastic energy | | ENERDISS | V5 | Volumetric energy consumed | 2 Continuous model 2.1 Constitutive equations The stress–strain relation takes the following form, in which {⟨x⟩}_{-} and {⟨x⟩}_{+} denote respectively the negative and positive parts of a scalar or of a symmetric tensor: \sigma (\epsilon ,b)	ext{}=	ext{}B(b)\left[\lambda {⟨\mathit{tr}(\epsilon )⟩}_{+}+2\mu {⟨\epsilon ⟩}_{+}ight]	ext{}+	ext{}\left[\lambda {⟨\mathit{tr}(\epsilon )⟩}_{-}+2\mu {⟨\epsilon ⟩}_{-}ight] As for the stiffness function B(b) , it is equal to: B(b)	ext{}=	ext{} rac{1-b}{\left(1-bight)+ rac{\kappa}{2}b\left({m}_{0}+({D}_{1}-{m}_{0}){b}^{r-1}ight)} The evolution of the damage is governed by the following Kuhn–Tucker conditions: \dot{b}⩾0;Q(\epsilon )-\varphi (b)⩽0;\dot{b}\left[Q(\epsilon )-\varphi (b)ight]=0 The threshold function \varphi (b) has the expression: \varphi (b)={\left[(1-b)+ rac{\kappa}{2}b\left({m}_{0}+({D}_{1}-{m}_{0}){b}^{r-1}ight)ight]}^{2} As for the function of the strain Q(\epsilon ) , it is written: Q(\epsilon )={\epsilon}_{	ext{ }}^{2} In this expression, the pseudo-norm {\epsilon}_{	ext{ }} is the solution of the following scalar equation: {f}_{\sigma}\left( rac{\lambda \mathit{tr}(\epsilon )	ext{Id}+2\mu \epsilon }{{\epsilon}_{	ext{ }}}ight)=0 Finally, the initiation threshold has the expression: {f}_{\sigma}(\sigma )=\Vert  rac{\sigma}{{\sigma}_{0}}+\left({ eta}_{0}- rac{1}{3}ight)\mathrm{tr}\left( rac{\sigma}{{\sigma}_{0}}ight)	ext{Id}\Vert +\Vert \exp\left( rac{\sigma}{{\sigma}_{0}}ight)\Vert -{\gamma}_{0} The stiffness function B(b) which appears in the stress–strain relation measures the impact of the damage level on the residual stiffness (in tension). Its particular form, as well as that of the threshold \varphi (b) , is guided by consistency with the response of the law ENDO_FISS_EXP in a confined uniaxial tension test. It plays the same role as the more classical form (1-b) used in a number of models in the literature. 2.2 Elastic energy and tension–compression transition In order to take into account the recovery of stiffness in compression, the elasticity law is no longer linear, even though it remains hyperelastic ( i.e. it derives from an energy) in order to avoid any spurious production or consumption of energy. It is similar to the formulation adopted for the law ENDO_ISOT_BETON R7.01.04; it takes into account not only the sign of the principal strains but also that of the trace of the strains. On the practical level, it therefore requires the principal strains to be determined. Its value is supplied among the internal variables (ENERELAS). Its properties are studied in detail in [Badel et al., 2007]. One will retain that it is continuously differentiable, which ensures the continuity of the stress–strain relation. On the other hand, it is not twice continuously differentiable, which means that the stiffness presents a jump when the tension–compression transition is crossed. This may harm the convergence of the analysis; this is why one proposes to regularise this transition. The idea, set out in [Lorentz, 2017] and [Lorentz, 2020], consists in regularising the elastic energy. This has as a consequence on the stress–strain relation () that the positive and negative parts in it are approximated by infinitely differentiable functions: {⟨x⟩}_{-}\simeq 	ext{}{N}_{\gamma}(x);{⟨x⟩}_{+}\simeq 	ext{}x-{N}_{\gamma}(x) The approximation {N}_{\gamma} depends on a parameter \gamma >0 which tends to infinity in the absence of regularisation. It has the expression: {N}_{\gamma}(x)=\lbrace  egin{array}{cc}\left(x+ rac{1}{2\gamma }ight)\exp\left(-	ext{} rac{1}{\gamma x}ight)& 	ext{si}x<0\ 0& 	ext{si}x⩾0\end{array} 2.3 Parameters of the model One can list the parameters used in the constitutive equations. These are \lambda , \mu , {\sigma}_{0} , {\gamma}_{0} , { eta}_{0} , \kappa , {m}_{0} , {D}_{1} and r . One proposes to give their meaning and their expression, in order finally to list those which must be supplied by the user. Elasticity – The elastic characteristics, which appear in the expression of the strain energy, reduce classically to the Lamé coefficients \lambda and \mu or, equivalently, to Young's modulus E and Poisson's ratio 
u . One deduces from them in particular the confined stiffness {E}_{c}=\lambda +2\mu . Damage initiation threshold – The initiation threshold is defined via the function {f}_{\sigma} which depends on three parameters: {\sigma}_{0} , {\gamma}_{0} and { eta}_{0} . In practice, one fixes { eta}_{0} at 0.1 and one determines {\sigma}_{0} and {	au}_{0} as a function of the tensile strength {f}_{t} and the compressive strength {f}_{c} of the concrete, according to the methodology presented in [Lorentz, 2017]. These data then make it possible to compute Q\left(\epsilon ight) for any strain. In particular, one can determine the initiation stress in confined uniaxial tension {\sigma}_{c} by the solution of the following equation, in which n denotes the (arbitrary) direction of tension: {f}_{\sigma}\left(\left( rac{\lambda}{{E}_{c}}\mathit{Id}+ rac{2\mu }{{E}_{c}}n\otimes night){\sigma}_{c}ight)=0 One then has access to {w}_{c} , the strain energy when the initiation threshold is reached in confined uniaxial tension, via {w}_{c}={\sigma}_{c}^{2}/2{E}_{c} . - Damage energy – The fracture energy {G}_{F} measures the energy consumed per unit cracked surface. It is to be related to the mean distance L which separates two cracks in order to construct the volumetric energy k={G}_{F}/L consumed by the damage model; one chooses to normalise the latter via \kappa ={G}_{F}/\left(L{w}_{c}ight) . The two parameters {G}_{F} and L therefore appear in the damage model only through their ratio, even though both have their own physical meaning. - Shape factor – A last parameter, p⩾1 , influences the shape of the response in the damage phase (a response which is all the more curved in a diagram \sigma -\epsilon as p is large). The datum of p also limits the possible values for \kappa for questions of stability of the material point, which, indirectly, fixes an upper bound {L}_{c} on the inter-crack distance L via the following inequality: L	ext{}⩽	ext{}{L}_{c}= rac{{G}_{F}}{{w}_{c}} rac{3\pi }{4}{(p+2)}^{-	ext{} rac{3}{2}} - Regularisation of the tension–compression transition – The last parameter, \gamma , conditions the regularisation of the positive and negative part functions appearing in the stress–strain relation, as explained in § 2.2. Alternatively to supplying a value for \gamma , one may prefer to fix the proportion of the stiffness (without regularisation) which is recovered for a (compressive) strain of the order of {f}_{c}/E , a proportion which one denotes {ho}_{\gamma} . Finally, relying on the command DEFI_MATERIAU, one is led to supply the following nine parameters: E , 
u , {\sigma}_{\mathrm{c}} , {\sigma}_{0} , {\gamma}_{0} , { eta}_{0} , \kappa , p and \gamma . Default values are proposed: { eta}_{0}=0.1 and \gamma =0 (no regularisation). Alternatively, the command DEFI_MATER_GC makes it possible to supply these parameters in a more usual manner. One indeed supplies there the following ten parameters: E , 
u , {f}_{t} , {f}_{c} , {\gamma}_{0} , { eta}_{0} , {G}_{F} , L , p and {ho}_{\gamma} . Here too, two default values are proposed: { eta}_{0}=0.1 and {ho}_{\gamma}=0.95 (a regularisation judged reasonable). 3 Numerical integration 3.1 Discretised equations The discretisation in time of the constitutive equations is based on an implicit Euler scheme, that is to say that the various variables of the problem are expressed at the final time instant of the time step. The expression of the stress at the end of the time step thus obeys (), the strain and the damage also being expressed there at the end of the time step. There remains the delicate part, which consists in computing the evolution of the damage. Integrating the evolution equation of the damage is a non-linear scalar problem. It results from the time discretisation of the Kuhn–Tucker conditions (), indexing by n the quantities at the beginning of the time step and omitting any index for those at the end of the time step: b-{b}_{n}⩾0;Q(\epsilon )-\varphi (b)⩽0;(b-{b}_{n})\left[Q(\epsilon )-\varphi (b)ight]=0 It is then a matter of determining the value of b , \epsilon being known; this is what one calls the integration of the constitutive law. It must also be noted that the strain \epsilon corresponds to the mechanical part of the strains, that is to say the total strain from which one has removed the shrinkage strains, in particular the thermal strain (expansion). In the terminology specific to code Aster (Code_Aster), this is a law expressed in mechanical strain. 3.2 Solution of the algorithmic evolution equation In order to treat the alternative (), one takes up the method described in [Lorentz, 2020], where the existence and the uniqueness of the solution b have also been demonstrated. One begins by evaluating the function Q(\epsilon ) ; this involves the solution of the scalar equation (). The reader is referred to document R5.03.28 for the solution method, the function Q being equal, up to a factor, to the function \Gamma defined in that booklet. One then proceeds to an elastic trial by supposing that b={b}_{n} . If Q(\epsilon )-\varphi ({b}_{n})⩽0 , then this is the solution; this is the elastic regime. Otherwise, one examines the ultimate value b=1 . If Q(\epsilon )-\varphi (1)⩾0 , then this is the solution; this is the saturated regime. Finally, the last case, the damaging regime, the solution b is the root of the following equation, lying between {b}_{n} and 1: \varphi (b)-Q(\epsilon )=0 The left-hand side is increasing with b and of opposite sign at the two bounds. The solution is carried out by a Newton method with controlled bounds. The accuracy with which the two scalar equations are solved, that for evaluating Q(\epsilon ) and (), is fixed indirectly by the user, so that the error committed on the stress is less than the tensile limit {\sigma}_{c} multiplied by the parameter RESI_INTE_RELA of STAT_NON_LINE. One may refer to [Lorentz, 2020] for the computation of the accuracies expected for these two scalar equations. 3.3 Tangent matrix The tangent matrix is obtained by variation of the stress in () with respect to the strain. For that, one begins by denoting {E}_{+}(\epsilon ) and {E}_{-}(\epsilon ) the positive and negative parts of the elasticity operator: {E}_{+}(\epsilon )=\lambda {⟨\mathit{tr}(\epsilon )⟩}_{+}+2\mu {⟨\epsilon ⟩}_{+};{E}_{-}(\epsilon )=\lambda {⟨\mathit{tr}(\epsilon )⟩}_{-}+2\mu {⟨\epsilon ⟩}_{-} By differentiating (), one then has: \delta \sigma =\left[B(b) rac{{\mathit{dE}}_{+}}{d\epsilon }(\epsilon )+ rac{{\mathit{dE}}_{-}}{d\epsilon }(\epsilon )ight]:\delta \epsilon +{E}_{+}(\epsilon ) rac{\mathit{dB}}{\mathit{db}}\delta b In the elastic or saturated regime, the last term is zero (no variation of b ). In the damaging regime, the variation of b is obtained by differentiating equation (). This leads to: \delta b={\left( rac{d\varphi }{\mathit{db}}(b)ight)}^{-1} rac{\mathit{dQ}}{d\epsilon }:d\epsilon The delicate part then consists in differentiating \Gamma , {E}_{+} and {E}_{-} with respect to \epsilon . One refers for that to document R5.03.28, in which these operations are detailed. Although these quantities depend on the principal strains, one may note that the differentiation methodology which is implemented does without the derivative of the associated eigenvectors which, one recalls, are not defined when the eigenvalues are not distinct. 4 Piloting by elastic prediction This being a damage law, material instabilities may appear. r7.01.43 Elastoplastic constitutive law with a smoothed Mohr-Coulomb criterion r7.01.43 Elastoplastic constitutive law with a smoothed Mohr-Coulomb criterion Summary: This document presents the solution method of the non-associated elastoplastic constitutive law with a smoothed Mohr-Coulomb yield surface dedicated in particular to granular geomaterials, accessible via the MFront environment. The original Mohr-Coulomb criterion is a pyramid: the edges and the apex constitute difficulties for the solution algorithm, cf. R7.01.28. One adopts here the formulation in invariants and the smoothing (regularisation) solution proposed by Abbo and Sloan in [ 2 ], with a direct implicit time-integration method. It is implemented in the MFront environment, cf. [ 4 ], using the algorithm developed by [ 3 ] within the community http://www.opengeosys.org _. 1 Introduction This elastoplastic constitutive relation, dedicated in particular to granular geomaterials, such as sands, describes the following phenomenological aspects: cohesion, dilatancy and internal friction. This model is designed above all to treat monotonic loading paths, up to the failure of the structure, knowing that the absence of hardening causes losses of stability, cf. [ 5 ] , and also of controllability of the loading, and therefore solutions depending on the mesh. The original Mohr-Coulomb criterion is a pyramid characterised by the intersection of 6 planes in the space of the principal stresses; the major and minor principal stresses come into play but not the intermediate stress. It is not bounded in the direction of the spherical compressive stresses. The edges and the apex of the Mohr-Coulomb pyramid constitute difficulties for the solution algorithm, in particular because this requires a management of the evolution mechanisms dedicated to each face of the pyramid and also for the apex regime, cf. R7.01.28. These difficulties possibly cause a lack of robustness. One adopts here the smoothing (regularisation) solution of the criterion proposed by Abbo and Sloan in [ 2 ], and implemented in the MFront environment, cf. [ 4 ], using the algorithm developed by [ 3 ]. The MFront programming [ 4 ] has been modified in order to add a few specific features to it. At the apex of the Mohr-Coulomb pyramid, the smoothing consists of a hyperbolic approximation. The parameters of the constitutive relation, besides the elastic parameters, assumed here isotropic, are 5 in number: the cohesion c , the friction angle {\varphi}_{\mathit{pp}} (supplied in °), the dilatancy angle \psi supplied in °), which must be lower than or equal to the internal friction angle {\varphi}_{\mathit{pp}} , identical to the original Mohr-Coulomb model, and two parameters associated with the smoothing: the transition Lode angle {\theta}_{T} (supplied in °), and the tension cut-off {a}_{\mathit{tt}} . The plastic flow is assumed non-associated and perfect. If \psi ={\varphi}_{\mathit{pp}} , then the flow is associated and the consistent tangent matrix is then symmetric. One uses a direct implicit time-integration method ( MFront ). The internal variables are also 4 in number: norm of the deviatoric strains (equivalent plastic strain: the only true thermodynamic internal variable); volumetric plastic strain; volumetric density of dissipation; indicator of activation of the plasticity (1) or not (0). r7.01.44 CSSM constitutive model r7.01.44 CSSM constitutive model Summary: This document presents the formulation and the numerical integration of the elastoplastic constitutive model CSSM ("Critical State Soil Model"). The CSSM model is a combination of two models intended to represent respectively the monotonic and the drained cyclic behaviour of soils. The first component is based on the modified Cam-Clay model, which describes the phenomena of dilatancy or contractancy as well as confinement effects under monotonic and drained loadings. The second component is a multi-mechanism model of Iwan type, designed to represent the non-linear cyclic behaviour of soils at low strain levels. The CSSM constitutive model comprises a total of eleven parameters: two to describe the reversible (elastic) behaviour, five for the irreversible behaviour linked to the modified Cam-Clay component, and three for the irreversible behaviour linked to the Iwan component. A last parameter weights the contributions of the two components to the shear behaviour of the CSSM model. The constitutive equations are solved using a direct implicit time-integration method, implemented in the tool MFront. 1 Notations The notations and sign conventions used are those of continuum mechanics. A bold character represents a tensor of order two and an open-face character a tensor of order four. For a tensor of order two \boldsymbol{a} , its decomposition into deviatoric and volumetric parts, denoted respectively \boldsymbol{a}_d and a_v , is written as follows: \boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{a}_d + \frac{a_v}{3}\boldsymbol{I},\quad\text{avec}\quad a_v = \boldsymbol{I}:\boldsymbol{a},\quad \boldsymbol{I}:\boldsymbol{a}_d=0 where one denotes by \boldsymbol{I}=\boldsymbol{\delta} the identity tensor of order two. One also writes a_m=\cfrac{a_v}{3} . For a tensor of order two \boldsymbol{a} of the same nature as a strain, one denotes its von Mises equivalent norm by a_{eq}=\sqrt{\cfrac{2}{3}\boldsymbol{a}_d:\boldsymbol{a}_d} . For a tensor of order two \boldsymbol{A} of the same nature as a stress, it is written A_{eq}=\sqrt{\cfrac{3}{2}\boldsymbol{A}_d:\boldsymbol{A}_d} . The notations defined in r7.01.44-table_notations_latines and r7.01.44-table_notations_grecques will be progressively supplemented by other symbols in the course of the presentation of the CSSM model. | \mathbb{C} | Isotropic linear elasticity tensor | | --- | --- | | f, F_i | Plasticity criteria | | \boldsymbol{I} | Identity of order two operating on vectors | | \mathbb{I} | Identity of order four operating on symmetric second-order tensors | | \mathbb{J} | Projector onto the space of hydrostatic tensors of order two ( \mathbb{J}:\boldsymbol{a}=\cfrac{a_v}{3}\boldsymbol{I} ) | | \mathbb{K} | Projector onto the space of symmetric traceless tensors of order two ( \mathbb{K}:\boldsymbol{a}=(\mathbb{I}-\mathbb{J}):\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{a}_d ) | | \boldsymbol{\alpha}_i,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^p,\xi,\gamma | Internal variables | | --- | --- | | \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} | Total strain tensor | | \varepsilon_v | Total volumetric strain | | \dot{\lambda},\dot{\lambda}_i | Plastic multipliers associated respectively with the plasticity criteria f, F_i | | \boldsymbol{\sigma} | Stress tensor | | \sigma_{eq} | von Mises equivalent stress | | \sigma_m | Mean stress | | \psi | Energy potential (volumetric density) | 2 Formulation of the model The CSSM model is based on the association of constitutive equations similar to the modified Cam-Clay and Iwan models. On the triaxial compression tests, the CSSM model was calibrated "as well as possible" by adjusting the five parameters p_{c0},M,\beta,\omega and C , assuming the other parameters of r7.01.44-table_parametres_simules and considering three distinct cases which have already been the subject of previous comparisons: - \rho=0\leftrightarrow effect of component 2 of the model only on the shear behaviour. - \rho=1\leftrightarrow effect of component 1 of the model only. - \rho=0.1\leftrightarrow effect of the two components of the model. The last case corresponds to considering that the shear stiffness in component 1 \rho\mu ("static" stiffness) is ten times smaller than the total shear stiffness \mu ("dynamic" stiffness). This ratio of ten is not unreasonable, compared with the ratios observed between the dynamic and static moduli for soil materials. r7.01.44-comparaison_rho_0 confronts the predictions for the case where \rho=0 with the experimental data. It is clear that component 2 of the model on its own does not succeed in reproducing in a realistic manner the evolutions of the von Mises equivalent stress \sigma_{eq} and of the volumetric strain \varepsilon_v observed during the triaxial compression tests. On the other hand, component 2 offers a fairly precise representation of the normalised secant shear modulus \mu_{\mathrm{secant}}/\mu during shear tests. As for the reduced damping, the prediction progressively overestimates the experimental evolution with the increase of the distortion level \gamma . This prediction is very similar to that of the Iwan model but also of Hujeux r7.01.23. Comparison of the predictions in the case \rho=0 with the experimental data. r7.01.44-comparaison_rho_1 confronts the predictions for the case where \rho=1 with the experimental data. In this case, component 1 of the model appreciably improves the evolution of the von Mises equivalent stress during the triaxial compression tests. However, only the volumetric strain for the confinement p_{\mathrm{conf}}=200 kPa is correctly reproduced. For the confinement p_{\mathrm{conf}}=100 kPa, the prediction lacks dilatancy. As regards the shear tests, the predictions of the normalised secant shear modulus \mu_{\mathrm{secant}}/\mu and of the reduced damping are largely deteriorated compared with those obtained for the case \rho=0 . Comparison of the predictions in the case \rho=1 with the experimental data. r7.01.44-comparaison_rho_01 finally presents the predictions in the case where \rho=0.1 . This combination of components 1 and 2 of the model makes it possible: - To improve the observed evolution of the dilatancy for the confinement p_{\mathrm{conf}}=100 kPa during the triaxial compression tests, while keeping a correct representation of the von Mises equivalent stress. This representation is similar to that obtained with component 1 alone in the case where \rho=0 . - To obtain predictions close to those of component 2 for the shear tests when \rho=1 . In summary, the combination of the two components of the model makes it possible to take advantage of the best characteristics of each individual component, thus offering an improved representation for both types of test, monotonic and cyclic. Comparison of the predictions in the case \rho=0.1 with the experimental data. > Note: > The previous comparisons validate the relevance of the CSSM model on loadings with shear, with a calibration of the parameters p_{c0},M,\beta,\omega and C on the triaxial compression tests. Nevertheless, in order to evaluate more globally, and rigorously, the capabilities of the model, it will be necessary to compare it with isotropic compression tests. r7.01.45 Constitutive law RGI_BETON_BA r7.01.45 Constitutive law RGI_BETON_BA Summary: The model presented in this document is an enrichment of a model already effective in Code_Aster: RGI_BETON (cf. R7.01.30). It makes it possible to consider reinforcements distributed within a concrete mass without differentiating their mesh. The behaviours of the two materials are evaluated and homogenised in order to deduce from them the response of the reinforced-concrete material. Contents 1 Introduction The model presented in this document is a development of a model already effective in Code_Aster: RGI_BETON. This document therefore follows on from that one r7.01.30, since only the development will be described here. It makes it possible to consider reinforcements distributed within a concrete mass without differentiating their mesh. The behaviours of the two materials are evaluated independently and then homogenised in order to deduce from them the response of the reinforced-concrete material. 2 Constitutive law RGI_BETON_BA 2.1 Constitutive law of the homogenised reinforced concrete This law therefore makes it possible to consider the reinforced concrete as a single material and thus to avoid differentiating the mesh of the concrete from that of the reinforcements. The evaluation of its behaviour is obtained by combining the contribution of the reinforcement and of the concrete by a homogenised constitutive law. In the model presented here, taken from the work of , up to five reinforcement densities may be considered. These are defined according to an index r , with which are associated a direction \vec{{V}^{r}} , a surface density {\rho}^{r} , and other material parameters. The material then being defined as reinforced concrete, the parameters supplied in ELAS in order to approach the solution therefore correspond to those specific to the reinforced concrete. The response of this material being obtained from the contributions of the concrete and of the steel evaluated independently, it is therefore a matter of supplying to the model the parameters specific to the concrete alone. Considering {E}^{\mathit{be}} the modulus of the concrete alone and {E}^{r} the modulus of the reinforcement, the latter may be evaluated by the following formula, {E}^{\mathit{ELAS}}=(1-\rho^r ){E}^{\mathit{be}}+\rho^r {E}^{r} The concrete constitutive model with which this development is associated taking damage into account, it is therefore a matter of considering the impact of these reinforcements in undamaged zones and in damaged zones. These zones being able to coexist within one and the same element, the same is true of the response of the reinforcement. In order to ensure this differentiation, the contribution of the reinforcement is decomposed according to the undamaged or damaged zone considered, respectively {\sigma}_{ij}^{H} and {\sigma}_{ij}^{R} , and they are weighted so as to consider the local damage of the concrete. Thus, in the cracked zone the stress {\sigma}_{ij}^{R} is multiplied by the local damage of the concrete in the principal direction {D}_{i}^{t} , and in the undamaged zone the stress {\sigma}_{ij}^{H} is multiplied by its complement to 1. Finally, the global behaviour of the reinforced concrete is obtained by homogenising these stresses with that of the concrete matrix {\sigma}_{ij}^{m} such that, {\sigma}_{ij}=\left(1-\sum_{r=1}^{\mathit{Nr}}{\rho}^{r}\right){\sigma}_{ij}^{m}+\left(1-{D}_{ijkl}^{t}\right){\sigma}_{kl}^{H}+{D}_{ijkl}^{t}\bullet {\sigma}_{kl}^{R} 2.1.1 Contribution in the undamaged zone In this model, the participation of the reinforcement is limited to that of its axial direction. Its contributions {\sigma}_{i}^{H} and {\sigma}_{i}^{R} , respectively in the undamaged zone and in the cracked zone, are evaluated from this stress {\sigma}^{r} . In the undamaged zone, {\sigma}_{i}^{H} is such that, {\sigma}_{ij}^{H}=\sum_{r=1}^{\mathit{Nr}}{\rho}^{r}{\sigma}^{r}{(\vec{{V}^{r}}\otimes\vec{{V}^{r}})}_{ij} 2.1.2 Contributions in the damaged zone In the cracked zone, the orientation of the reinforcement may evolve if the normal to the crack is not aligned with it. This is the Dowell effect, also called the Goujon effect. In the model, and within the crack, only the part of the reinforcement is considered. In addition to the evolution of its direction, it is therefore also a matter of taking into account the impact of the damage on its contribution. First, the new direction of the reinforcement {\vec{D}}^{r} is evaluated. Crossing a crack of the concrete, it therefore lies between its initial direction \vec{{V}^{r}} and the principal direction of the crack {\vec{V}}^{I} . It should be noted that, this document detailing only the development relating to the homogenised reinforcements, the detail of the computation of {\vec{V}}^{I} is not presented here, and may be found in the document of the initial model (r7.01.36) The new direction may then be written such that, {\vec{D}}^{r}=\cos({\alpha}^{r})\vec{{V}_{r}}+\sin({\alpha}^{r})\cdot \frac{\vec{{g}_{I}^{r}}}{\Vert \vec{{g}_{I}^{r}}\Vert } With: - {\vec{g}}_{I}^{r} the displacement between the crack opening {w}_{I}^{\mathit{pl},t} and its projection onto the initial direction of the reinforcement \vec{{V}^{r}} such that, {\vec{g}}_{I}^{r}={w}_{I}^{\mathit{pl},t}\left(\vec{{V}^{I}}-\left(\vec{{V}^{r}}\cdot \vec{{V}^{I}}\right)\cdot {\vec{V}}^{r}\right) - {\alpha}^{r} the angle separating the initial reinforcement direction \vec{{V}^{r}} from its new direction {\vec{D}}^{r} , {\alpha}^{r}=2\arcsin{\left(\sqrt{\frac{{g}_{I}^{r}}{4{R}^{r}}}\right)}\le\arccos{\left(\vec{{V}^{I}}\cdot{\vec{V}}^{r}\right)} - {R}^{r} the radius of curvature obtained such that, {R}^{r}=\frac{\pi {D}_{r}^{\mathit{eq}}{\sigma}^{r}}{4{f}_{c}} If several reinforcements cross the same crack, the whole of their contributions is considered. These are weighted by the corresponding local damage, then summed and brought back into the local basis by means of the passage matrix P . The evaluation of these contributions is initiated by the definition of a first computation matrix R , and they are subsequently deduced from its symmetric part such that, R=\sum_{r}{\rho}^{r}{\sigma}^{r}{P}^{T}[{D}_{I}^{t}\left(\vec{{V}^{r}}\cdot \vec{{V}^{I}}\right){\vec{D}}_{I}^{r}];{P}^{T}[{D}_{\mathit{II}}^{t}\left(\vec{{V}^{r}}\cdot \vec{{V}^{\mathit{II}}}\right){\vec{D}}_{\mathit{II}}^{r}];{P}^{T}[{D}_{\mathit{III}}^{t}\left(\vec{{V}^{r}}\cdot \vec{{V}^{\mathit{III}}}\right){\vec{D}}_{\mathit{III}}^{r}] R=\sum_{r}{\rho}^{r}{\sigma}^{r}\left(\begin{array}{c}{P}^{T}[{D}_{I}^{t}\left(\vec{{V}^{r}}\cdot \vec{{V}^{I}}\right){\vec{D}}_{I}^{r}]\\ {P}^{T}[{D}_{\mathit{II}}^{t}\left(\vec{{V}^{r}}\cdot \vec{{V}^{\mathit{II}}}\right){\vec{D}}_{\mathit{II}}^{r}]\\ {P}^{T}[{D}_{\mathit{III}}^{t}\left(\vec{{V}^{r}}\cdot \vec{{V}^{\mathit{III}}}\right){\vec{D}}_{\mathit{III}}^{r}]\end{array}\right) {D}_{ijkl}^{t}\bullet {\sigma}_{kl}^{R}={\left[P\left[\frac{1}{2}\left[R+{R}^{T}\right]\right]{P}^{T}\right]}_{ij} Mechanisms ensuring the Dowel effect (a); Case of a more limited effect (b) It should be noted that this effect is made possible by the confinement zones developed between the reinforcements and the concrete, as in r7.01.45-dowel_effect (a). If the number of reinforcements is more limited, r7.01.45-dowel_effect (b), the impact of this Dowel effect is greatly reduced. Finally, it should be noted that in the case of elements of large size the representation of cracking is not often explicit. It is nevertheless possible, for these reinforced elements, and by considering an anchorage length of the steel and the maximum distance between two cracks, to obtain the number of localised cracks. 2.2 Constitutive law of the axial contribution of the reinforcement The contribution of the reinforcement is considered in its axial direction only. The constitutive law which defines it allows plasticity and relaxation to be taken into account. The strain of the reinforcement is decomposed according to its plastic part {\epsilon}^{r,\mathit{pl}} , and its elastic and permanent relaxation parts, {\epsilon}^{r,K} and {\epsilon}^{r,M} . Moreover, it is also possible to consider densities of active reinforcements by considering a value of initial prestress {\sigma}_{0}^{r} such that, {\sigma}^{r}-{\sigma}_{0}^{r}={E}^{r}({\epsilon}^{r}-{\epsilon}^{r,\mathit{pl}}-{\epsilon}^{r,M}-{\epsilon}^{r,K}) The plastic strain is evaluated by a criterion function making it possible to take into account the hardening of the reinforcement. Considering the hardening modulus and the elastic limit, respectively {H}^{r} and {f}_{y}^{r} , the criterion function is written, {f}^{r}={\sigma}^{r}-{H}^{r}{\epsilon}^{r,\mathit{pl}}-{f}_{y}^{r}\le 0 2.2.1 Relaxation As seen in the equation , the model makes it possible to consider a prestress. The present model having the purposes of a structural analysis, the relaxation phenomena must therefore be considered. These being strongly affected by the value of the initial tension as well as by the temperature, a relaxation model considering these effects has been implemented by . In the same way as the creep model implemented for the concrete [cf. Code_Aster document RGI_BETON], this is ensured by various coefficients affecting the instantaneous characteristics of the reinforcements considered. The model is composed of a first elastic part ensuring the instantaneous behaviour, followed by a Kelvin stage ensuring the share of the viscoelastic strains, and of a third level governing the share of permanent strain, ensured by a Maxwell element r7.01.45-shema_rheo. Idealised rheological diagram of the relaxation model taken from . 2.2.1.1 Maxwell stage The permanent part of the relaxation is evaluated in a manner analogous to that used by/in /r7.01.36 for the modelling of the permanent creep strains. It is evaluated as a function of the ratio of the elastic strain {\epsilon}^{r,\mathit{el}} divided by the product of the characteristic Maxwell time {\tau}^{r,M} , a material parameter, and the consolidation coefficient \mathit{Cc} , \frac{\partial {\epsilon}^{r,M}}{\partial t}=\frac{{\epsilon}^{r,\mathit{el}}}{{\tau}^{M}\mathit{Cc}} With \mathit{Cc} a function of the viscous strain reached at the current step, and of a coefficient k , the relaxation-amplitude coefficient, \mathit{Cc}=\frac{1}{k}\exp\left(\frac{1}{k}\frac{{\epsilon}^{r,M}}{{\epsilon}^{r,\mathit{el}}}\right) In this equation, k makes it possible to consider the non-linear impact of the temperature ( T ) and of the loading ratio ( M ) on the relaxation phenomenon, k={k}_{\mathit{ref}}{k}^{T}{k}^{M} With, - {k}_{\mathit{ref}} , a parameter expressing the relaxation capacity of the material, obtained by considering the parameters {\epsilon}_{\mathit{ref}}^{K} and {\sigma}_{\mathit{ref}} , respectively the reference potential of the relaxation and the loading ratio at which this potential was fixed, such that, {k}_{\mathit{ref}}=E\frac{{\epsilon}_{\mathit{ref}}^{K}}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ref}}} - {k}^{M} , making it possible to consider the non-linear amplification of the relaxation rate with the loading ratio, {k}^{M}=\frac{{\mu}^{\mathit{cr}}}{{\mu}^{\mathit{cr}}-\mu } \mu being the loading ratio defined as a function of the elastic limit {f}_{y} such that, \mu =\frac{\sigma}{{f}_{y}} and {\mu}^{\mathit{cr}} the critical loading ratio, expressing the non-linear tendency of the material to increase its relaxation rate with the increase of the loading ratio, a function of \chi the non-linear relaxation coefficient (defined such that the tendency is linear for \chi=1 and becomes non-linear for \chi>1 ), {\mu}^{\mathit{cr}}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\chi }{\chi-1} Non-linear amplification function {k}^{M} taken from - {k}^{T} , the coefficient governing the acceleration of the relaxation with the increase of the temperature, and ensuring the non-linear evolution for high loading levels, {k}^{T}=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\exp\left[{A}^{T}{(T-{T}_{\mathit{ref}})}^{{n}^{r}}\right]\phantom{1111}\mathit{si}\phantom{1}T>{T}_{\mathit{ref}}\\ \exp\left[-{A}^{T}{({T}_{\mathit{ref}}-T)}^{{n}^{r}}\right]\phantom{11}\mathit{si}\phantom{1}T⩽{T}_{\mathit{ref}}\end{array}\right\rbrace The non-linear evolution is governed by {A}^{T} , the thermal-activation coefficient, a function of the loading ratio, {A}^{T}={A}_{\mathit{ref}}^{T} \exp{\left(\gamma \cdot {\mu}^{\mathit{TM}}\right)} With {A}_{\mathit{ref}}^{T} the reference value for the thermal-activation coefficient, \gamma the coupling coefficient for the effect of the stresses on the activation energy, {\mu}^{\mathit{TM}} the loading ratio which may modify the thermal activation. Considering {\mu}^{\mathit{thr}} the minimum threshold of loading ratio for affecting the thermal-activation coefficient, fixed at 0.7 , {\mu}^{\mathit{TM}} is written such that, {\mu}^{\mathit{TM}}(t+\mathit{dt})=max({\mu}^{\mathit{TM}}(t),\mu (t+\mathit{dt}),{\mu}^{\mathit{thr}}) 2.2.1.2 Kelvin stage Concerning the viscoelastic behaviour, and as developed by , this is ensured by a Kelvin element. In the same way as the permanent strains, these are also affected by the temperature, \frac{\partial {\epsilon}^{K}}{\partial t}=\frac{1}{{\tau}^{r,K}}\left(\frac{{\epsilon}^{\mathit{el}}}{{\Psi}^{K}}-{\epsilon}^{K}\right) With {\tau}^{r,k} and {\Psi}^{k} respectively the characteristic time for the Kelvin strains and the rate of this relaxation with respect to the elastic strain, a function of reference values and of {k}^{T} , the thermal-activation multiplier coefficient defined in the equation , {\tau}^{r,K}=\frac{{\tau}_{\mathit{ref}}^{r,K}}{{k}^{T}} {\Psi}^{K}=\frac{{\Psi}_{\mathit{ref}}^{K}}{{k}^{T}} It should be noted that this part of the model has been validated at the scale of the laboratory structure and applied to a large-scale structure . 2.2.2 Steel-concrete bond In the version of the present model, the assumption of perfect bond is made between the two materials, steel and concrete. In this way, the total axial strain of the reinforcement is evaluated from its elongation, assumed to be determined from the strain matrix of the concrete \overline{\overline{\epsilon}} such that, {\epsilon}^{r}\approx {\epsilon}_{r}+\frac{1}{2}{\gamma}_{r}^{2} With {\epsilon}_{r} the axial strain of the reinforcement, {\epsilon}_{r}={(\vec{{V}^{r}})}^{t}\overline{\overline{\epsilon}}\vec{{V}^{r}} And {\gamma}_{r} the shear strain {\gamma}_{r}=\Vert \overline{\overline{\epsilon}}\vec{{V}^{r}}-{\epsilon}_{r}\vec{{V}^{r}}\Vert It should be noted that taking a slip at this interface into account is possible but is not implemented in this present model. Solution flowchart As said previously, the first consideration induced by these homogenised reinforcements is the assumption of perfect bond. By virtue of this fact, the final strain of the concrete is recovered and the stress in the reinforcement is deduced from it. The stress is subsequently subjected to a plasticity criterion. If the latter is active, the reinforcement has plasticised and an iteration is performed in order to re-evaluate the value of its stress, taking into account the plastic strain induced. Once the stress of the reinforcement has been obtained, it is the damage of the concrete that one will consider. This work of “modernisation” forms part of the development actions of the EDF-R&D project “Management of Radioactive Waste” (GDR2). The scope of use of the model NLH_CSRM is for the moment limited to isotropic mechanical behaviour. The taking into account of structural anisotropy and of the dependence of the hardenings on temperature — effective in the latest version of the model LKR — will be the subject of forthcoming submissions; likewise the dependence of the criteria on the third invariant of the stress deviator (Lode angle). The model NLH_CSRM lies within the thermodynamic framework of generalised standard materials with two irreversible mechanisms, - Plastic mechanism — instantaneous irreversible behaviour: hardening and/or softening, contractant or dilatant volumetric behaviour, influence of the mean stress on the brittle character of the response in compression, …; - Viscoplastic mechanism — delayed irreversible behaviour (of Perzyna type): primary, secondary and tertiary creep (failure). A coupling between these two mechanisms makes it possible — among other things — to represent the dependence of the maximum strength of certain geomaterials on the loading rate. These works of “modernisation” are motivated by the wish to increase the robustness and the efficiency of the model used to describe the behaviour of the Callovo-Oxfordian argillite — the host rock constituting the first geological barrier of Cigéo — in order to be able to envisage its use on 3D problems that are demanding in memory and in computation time. 2 Constitutive equations 2.1 Free energy The free energy is put in the following general form, > (2.1) with, > (2.2) is the strain tensor, is the plastic strain tensor, is the viscoplastic strain tensor, is the Hooke tensor — and are respectively the bulk and shear moduli, and are respectively the spherical and deviatoric projectors — and are state variables respectively associated with the plastic and viscoplastic mechanisms, and are homogeneous to hardening moduli [Pa]; they are material parameters of the model. 2.2 Thermodynamic forces The thermodynamic forces associated with the state variables , , , , and are respectively, > (2.3) 2.3 Plasticity and viscoplasticity criteria The evolution of the maximum strength of cohesive geomaterials as a function of the mean stress, , is generally non-linear.
