r7.01.47 Damage law ENDO_LOCA_TC r7.01.47 Damage law ENDO_LOCA_TC Summary: This document describes the isotropic quasi-brittle constitutive model ENDO_LOCA_TC. It takes up the fundamentals of the models ENDO_ISOT_BETON R7.01.04 and ENDO_LOCA_EXP R7.01.42 and enriches them by introducing: - a rationalised damage threshold with a view to optimising numerical robustness; - an effect of damage in compression, so as to bound the stresses there, without however seeking to model the post-peak phase. The threshold stress in compression tends in a monotonic manner towards a limit, the compressive strength. This document summarises the main information on the model for its use in code_aster, relying on the internal note . The user wishing to have more information on the model (complete description of the equations, mechanical or mathematical properties...) is invited to refer to this reference. 1 Introduction 1.1 History The development of the model ENDO_LOCA_TC results from a progressive approach which now extends over more than 25 years within EDF. It aims to build a hierarchy of models with an increasingly rich phenomenology, but without sacrificing numerical robustness. Figure r7.01.47-fig-tab_modeles indicates the phenomenological characteristics of some of these models. Characteristics of the numerically robust damage models of Code_Aster ENDO_LOCA_TC meets a need brought out in recent studies: to have available a model which is both numerically robust and able to account for the unilateral effect of damage on the initiation threshold and on the current stiffness (effect of damage different in compression and in tension) as well as for the bounded character of the stresses in tension and compression. ENDO_LOCA_TC is a robust local isotropic model without irreversible strains. 1.2 Requirements In order to preserve the balance between phenomenological richness and numerical robustness, a compromise proves necessary in modelling. It is guided by the following minimum expectations, which in fact constitute the requirements of the model ENDO_LOCA_TC. Phenomenological (physical) expectations: - (AP1) The stresses remain bounded whatever the strain loading path. - (AP2) The damage threshold differs according to the direction of loading in order to take account in particular of the contrast between tension and compression. - (AP3) In the tension domain, the stress threshold corresponds to a Rankine criterion, close to the experimental observations, see . - (AP4) Beyond a critical strain level in pure tension, the stress becomes zero. - (AP5) Even for strain paths whose tensile components become high, a stiffness in compression remains (unilateral effect of damage on the stiffness). - (AP6) In the current reversibility domain (elastic domain for a given mechanical state), any closed strain path leads to a closed stress path (elasticity) and neither produces nor consumes energy (hyperelasticity). - (AP7) A path of pure slip type (shear in strain, typical of the loadings in the neighbourhood of the reinforcement) leads to a response qualitatively distinct from a path in pure shear stress. Expectations guaranteeing numerical robustness: - (AR1) There exists a continuous response in stress whatever the continuous strain path. - (AR2) The process of numerical integration of the constitutive relation (for a given strain increment) admits a unique solution. - (AR3) A robust numerical method is available to determine this solution whatever the level of imposed strain. - (AR4) Only the damage process in tension results in a softening response. - (AR5) The reversibility domain in strain space is convex, in order to allow the implementation of a piloting technique adapted to damage (PRED_ELAS) Finally, one will prefer a model whose parameters remain limited in number and whose identification is deduced simply from the usual experimental measurements. 1.3 Field of use: local vs. non-local Damage of a material leads to a decrease of its resistance capacity in terms of stresses that can be supported : one speaks of softening or negative hardening. This physical characteristic is at the origin of the phenomenon of localisation of the damage and of the strain in bands of moderate thickness . In order to treat the localised case, specific models are required: these are the non-local constitutive models or else the cohesive models (CZM), which make it possible to describe the localised regime properly. A local model such as ENDO_LOCA_TC must be used in situations of diffuse damage which can appear thanks to the presence of reinforcement in the concrete or because of an imposed-strain loading such as in thermal analysis. The field of use of ENDO_LOCA_TC is therefore that of distributed cracks (or crack networks) for which one can build a mean behaviour per REV (Representative Elementary Volume). Conversely, one recommends not seeking to model the cracks individually by bands of localised damage one mesh cell thick. If such a result occurs during analyses under code_aster with a local model, its objectivity can be called into question. A non-local version of ENDO_LOCA_TC is under development which will make it possible to predict the cracking of concrete at the scale of the individual crack. 2 Phenomenology & Use 2.1 Phenomena covered and modelling choices The damage model ENDO_LOCA_TC is isotropic. It therefore accounts neither for an initial anisotropy – the initial elasticity is isotropic there, as is the damage threshold – nor for an induced anisotropy: the damage accumulates without keeping the memory of the loading directions which lead to its evolution, so that the current elasticity and damage threshold remain isotropic. This isotropic framework nevertheless makes it possible to distinguish tension vs. compression effects. Indeed, among the loading directions (the principal directions of the strains), it is possible to identify those corresponding to positive principal strains (respectively negative): the directions of tension (resp. compression). This distinction makes it possible to separate the elastic stress (that which one would observe under the same strain in the absence of damage) into two terms, one relating to tension and the other to compression, which will be affected differently by the damage in order to supply the stress actually undergone by the point considered. At fixed damage, the model is therefore non-linear elastic. The model accounts for two distinct contributions to the damage. A first, called tensile damage, is driven by the tensile strains and weights only the elastic tensile stress. For increasing tensile strains, this weighting coefficient (denoted A), initially equal to 1, remains so up to a certain tensile strength threshold, then decreases until it becomes zero (total ultimate damage) for a strain which is sufficiently high but finite, so that only the elastic compressive stress still contributes to the stress. This means that at ultimate tensile damage, the point no longer resists tensile loadings but only compressive ones. A second damage component is driven by the compressive strains (more precisely the elastic compressive stress). This is why it is called compressive damage, even if it affects not only the elastic compressive stress but also the tensile one (it therefore weights the whole elastic stress). For increasing compressive strains (in absolute value), this weighting coefficient (denoted C), initially equal to 1, remains so up to a certain threshold of loss of linearity in compression, then decreases and tends asymptotically towards 0 but without ever reaching the zero value. Its evolution as a function of the strain is such that the stresses remain bounded. But unlike tension, they continue to increase (no softening in compression), until they reach an ultimate value, the compressive strength limit. The model ENDO_LOCA_TC presents no dissipative mechanisms other than the tensile and compressive damages. In particular, it accounts for no irreversible strain. Finally, it is possible to take account of the influence on the mechanical response of other physical phenomena such as thermal effects or the hydric transfers within the concrete. On the one hand, the temperature can influence the characteristic parameters of the model. And on the other hand, the latter is expressed in mechanical strains, that is the strains of thermal or drying origin are subtracted from the total strain. 2.2 Parameters of the model In addition to the elastic parameters (Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio), the parameters of the model are five in number: - f_{t} the tensile strength with f_{t} > 0 - p a tensile hardening coefficient, with in practice p\in\left[-0.2,9\right] - \bar{\omega} the energy to failure in confined tension normalised by the elastic energy at the initiation of damage with \bar{\omega}> \frac{4}{3\pi}\left(p+2\right)^{3/2} - f_{c} the (mean) compressive strength with f_{c} > 2\,f_{t} - \sigma^{0} the initiation threshold stress in compression with 2\,f_{t} \leq \sigma^{0} \sigma^{0} Two new parameters are introduced: the compressive strength of the concrete f_{c} and the initiation threshold in compression \sigma^{0} . The graph of the function C for the set of values of r7.01.47-tab-para is presented in r7.01.47-fig-evol_C. Stiffness function C as a function of the compressive damage c. 3.2 Evolution of the tensile damage The strain relative to the tensile damage is defined by: \chi_{t}=\langle\frac{s_{3}}{f_{t}}\rangle_{+} \quad ; \quad s_{3}=\lambda_{3}\left(\tensTwo{ s}\right) f_{t} is a parameter of the law corresponding to the tensile limit of the concrete. s_{3}=\lambda_{3}\left(\tensTwo{ s}\right) denotes the maximum eigenvalue of the elastic stress tensor \tensTwo{ s} defined as the derivative of the elastic energy density (). \tensTwo{ s} =\frac{\partial w_{e}}{\partial \tensTwo{\varepsilon}}\left(\tensTwo{\varepsilon}\right)=s^{+}+s^{-} The strain measure \chi_{t} makes it possible to build the threshold function for the tensile damage, as well as the corresponding evolution equation. The equation governing the threshold function in tension is: g_{t}\left(\tensTwo{{\varepsilon}},a\right) = \chi_{t}\left(\tensTwo{{\varepsilon}}\right)^{2}-e\left(a\right)^{2} with e\left(a\right) the damage threshold defined by . The evolution law of the damage in tension is: g_{t}\left(\tensTwo{{\varepsilon}},a\right) \leq 0\quad ; \quad \dot{a}\geq0\quad ; \quad \dot{a}\,g_{t}\left(\tensTwo{{\varepsilon}},a\right) = 0 For an initially undamaged state, one has a\left(0\right)=0 3.3 Evolution of the compressive damage The evolution of the relative residual stiffness in compression C is governed by a mechanism similar to that of tension. The strain measure relative to the damage in compression is defined as follows: \chi_{c}=\langle-\,\frac{s_{1}^{-}}{\sigma^{0}}\rangle_{+} \quad ; \quad s_{1}^{-}=\lambda_{1}\left(\tensTwo{ s}^{-}\right) Where \sigma^{0}\geq 2\,f_{t} in order to guarantee certain properties of the model such as the absence of initiation of damage in tension in a compressive loading. \lambda_{1}\left(\tensTwo{ s}^{-}\right) is the smallest eigenvalue of the tensor \tensTwo{ s}^{-} defined in . The evolution of the damage is then governed by means of the following threshold function: g_{c}\left(\tensTwo{\varepsilon},c\right) = \chi_{c}\left(\tensTwo{\varepsilon}\right)-c The evolution law of the damage in compression is written: g_{c}\left(\tensTwo{\varepsilon},c\right) \leq 0\quad ; \quad \dot{c}\geq0\quad ; \quad \dot{c}\,g_{c}\left(\tensTwo{\varepsilon},c\right) = 0 For an initially undamaged state, one has c\left(0\right)=1 . Unlike the tensile damage measure a which evolves from 0 to 1, the compressive damage c evolves from 1 to +\infty . 4 Numerical implementation In general, the integration of a constitutive relation consists in determining the time history of the internal variables, here t\rightarrow a\left(t\right) and t\rightarrow c\left(t\right) , and of the stresses t\rightarrow \tensTwo{\sigma}\left(t\right) for a strain loading t\rightarrow \tensTwo{\varepsilon}\left(t\right) . Traditionally, this operation is carried out by proceeding to a discretisation in time of the differential equations which characterise the behaviour and then to the treatment of the (non-linear) algebraic systems which result from it. 4.1 Equations discretised in time For the discretisation in time of the constitutive relation ENDO_LOCA_TC, one adopts an implicit Euler scheme, of order 1. For a time step \left[t_{n},t_{n+1}\right] and any quantity (grandeur) X , one denotes X_{n}=X\left(t_{n}\right) , X_{n+1}=X\left(t_{n+1}\right) and \triangle X =X_{n+1}-X_{n} . The discretisation of the stress – strain relation via the scheme retained leads to: \tensTwo{\sigma}_{n+1}=C\left(c_{n+1}\right)\left[A\left(a_{n+1}\right)\tensTwo {s}_{n+1}^{+}+\tensTwo {s}_{n+1}^{-} \right] Where \tensTwo {s}_{n+1}^{+}=\frac{\partial w^{+}}{\partial \tensTwo{ \varepsilon}}\left(\tensTwo{ \varepsilon}_{n+1}\right) \quad ; \quad \tensTwo {s}_{n+1}^{-}=\frac{\partial w^{-}}{\partial \tensTwo{ \varepsilon}}\left(\tensTwo {\varepsilon}_{n+1}\right) The discretisation of the evolution equation in tension is written: g_{t}\left(\tensTwo{\varepsilon}_{n+1},a_{n+1}\right) \leq 0\quad ; \quad \triangle a\geq0\quad ; \quad \triangle a \,g_{t}\left(\tensTwo{\varepsilon}_{n+1},a_{n+1}\right) = 0 Finally, the evolution equation in compression is written after discretisation: g_{c}\left(\tensTwo{\varepsilon}_{n+1},c_{n+1}\right) \leq 0\quad ; \quad \triangle c\geq0\quad ; \quad \triangle c_{n+1}\, g_{c}\left(\tensTwo{\varepsilon}_{n+1},c_{n+1}\right) = 0 4.2 Solution of the algebraic system The integration of the behaviour consists in determining a_{n+1} and c_{n+1} knowing a_{n} , c_{n} , \varepsilon_{n} and \triangle \varepsilon and then in computing \sigma_{n+1} via . It is interesting to note that the decoupling between the evolution laws makes it possible to determine a_{n+1} and c_{n+1} independently. r7.01.48 Constitutive model MCC r7.01.48 Constitutive model MCC Summary: This document presents the formulation and the numerical integration of the modified Cam-Clay elastoplastic constitutive model within the framework of Generalised Standard Materials. This model is intended to represent qualitatively the phenomenology of granular soils, taking account of the effects of dilatancy/contractancy, of softening/hardening, as well as of the critical state. The parameters of the constitutive model are seven in total. Three define the isotropic non-linear elastic behaviour; three represent the initial reversibility domain. A combined kinematic-isotropic hardening carried by the volumetric plastic strain is driven by a last parameter. The constitutive equations are solved according to a variational principle for which the optimality conditions are equivalent to a system of non-linear equations governing the incremental evolution equations of the internal variables. These are solved by employing a direct implicit time-integration method in MFront. 1 Introduction Conceived in the nineteen-sixties to describe the behaviour of normally consolidated clays, the modified Cam-Clay constitutive model represents the essential phenomenology of granular soils under monotonic drained loadings: dilatancy or contractancy and softening or hardening, regimes driven by the evolution of the volumetric plastic strain, as well as the critical state. This internal variable is the only hardening variable of the model. By means of a state parameterisation in the plasticity criterion by the hardening variable, the modified Cam-Clay model falls within the framework of Generalised Standard Materials. Consequently, a solution of the constitutive equations based on a variational principle may be proposed, making it possible advantageously to ensure the existence and the uniqueness of the incremental evolution problem of the internal variables. The robustness of the numerical integration of the modified Cam-Clay model is thereby greatly strengthened for the analysis of geotechnical structures in Code_Aster. This document summarises the essential information on the presentation of the modified Cam-Clay model, as well as the solution of its constitutive equations in MFront. It updates the formulation and the numerical solution method of the model CAM_CLAY r7.01.14_, while remaining faithful to the elements of phenomenology predicted by the latter. 2 Formulation of the model The modified Cam-Clay model is formulated according to the usual construction of Generalised Standard Materials, from an energy potential and a plasticity criterion (or a dissipation potential). r7.01.49 Finite element for soil–pile interaction (3D_INTERF_POU) r7.01.49 Finite element for soil–pile interaction (3D_INTERF_POU) Summary: This document presents a finite element for interaction between a matrix and a reinforcement. The corresponding keyword for the modelling is 3D_INTERF_POU . 1 Introduction This model describes the interaction between a reinforcement and its surrounding matrix. Their kinematics are represented respectively by those of a two-node Timoshenko beam and of an eight-node hexahedral 3D element. The interaction domain considered (the interface) is a line coincident with the domain of the beam. The element 3D_INTERF_POU integrates there, at its Gauss points, a phenomenological law R7.01.50 returning the interaction forces between the matrix and the reinforcement as a function of their relative displacement, carried by three components. First, a general formulation is presented for the description of the interaction between a reinforcement and its matrix. Second, the formulation of the element 3D_INTERF_POU is detailed. 2 General formulation of a mixed matrix–reinforcement finite element 2.1 Formulation of the continuous problem Under certain conditions, a reinforced soil may be represented by a homogenised medium. The classical technique consists in defining a medium with anisotropic properties. The multiphase approach emerges as an alternative. The anisotropic medium is replaced by two superimposed phases in interaction. At each point of the medium, a matrix particle and a reinforcement particle are superimposed. Each particle has its own kinematics. The method extends to an arbitrary number of reinforcement phases, each describing a reinforcement direction. Let \dispVirt be an arbitrary virtual displacement field. It is composed of the kinematics of the matrix \dispVirt_s and of those of the reinforcement \dispVirt_p . The internal work \work{int} of the two-phase system comprises three contributions: those of the matrix \work{s} , of the reinforcement \work{p} and of the interaction forces \work{f} : \forall \dispVirt \, , \quad \work{int} = \work{s} + \work{p} + \work{f} From the point of view of a single phase, the interaction forces may be regarded as external. Application of the principle of virtual work to the two-phase system in rigid-body motion (zero work) shows that the work of the interface forces \vector{\tau} takes the form: \work{f} = \left( \transpose{\dispVirt_s} - \transpose{\dispVirt_p} \right) \vector{\tau} 2.2 Discretisation of the problem In the previous approach, the whole reinforced medium is homogenised. There is no longer an explicit description of the reinforcements. The approach proposed below, derived from the first, is limited to the representation of one (single) reinforcement and of the surrounding matrix. It describes the reinforcement explicitly. Taking advantage of the finite elements that already exist, the reinforcement and the matrix are represented separately by their own element. They are referred to below as "independent" elements and represent the internal works (eq. ) \work{int} = \work{p} and \work{int} = \work{s} respectively. As the interaction forces may be regarded as external from the point of view of a single phase, they may be treated by a distinct interaction (or interface) finite element. On this element, defined on the interface domain \domain_f , the internal work (eq. ) therefore reduces to: \work{int} = \work{f} Its evaluation requires the expression of the displacement of each of the phases at the interface. For consistency, the kinematics of each phase there correspond to the kinematics adopted in the corresponding independent element (matrix and reinforcement). The interpolation of the displacement at the interface is performed from the nodal displacements and the shape functions of each of the phases, such that: \begin{split}\begin{align} \disp_{pf} = & \discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}} \discVect{U_s} \\ \disp_{sf} = & \discMatr{\shapeFunc_{sf}} \discVect{U_p} \end{align}\end{split} where \discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}} and \discMatr{\shapeFunc_{sf}} are the projections of the interpolation functions of the reinforcement and of the matrix onto the interface, and \discVect{U_p} , \discVect{U_s} are respectively the displacements at the nodes of the phases. The virtual relative displacement at the interface may then be rewritten as follows (an isoparametric approach is used): \begin{split}\begin{align} \transpose{\dispVirt_r} & = \transpose{\dispVirt_{sf}} - \transpose{\dispVirt_{pf}} \\ & = \left\langle \begin{matrix} \transpose{\discVect{\delta U_s}} & \transpose{\discVect{\delta U_p}} \end{matrix} \right\rangle \discMatr{ \begin{matrix} \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{sf}}} \\ - \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}}} \end{matrix} } \end{align}\end{split} and \begin{split}\begin{align} \disp_r & = \disp_{sf} - \disp_{pf} \\ & = \discMatr{ \begin{matrix} \discMatr{\shapeFunc_{sf}} & - \discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}} \end{matrix} } \left\{ \begin{matrix} \discVect{U_s} \\ \discVect{U_p} \end{matrix} \right\} \end{align}\end{split} This leads to the expression for the work of the interface, such that: \begin{split}\work{f} = \int_{\domain_f}{} \left\langle \begin{matrix} \transpose{\discVect{\delta U_s}} & \transpose{\discVect{\delta U_p}} \end{matrix} \right\rangle \discMatr{ \begin{matrix} \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{sf}}} \\ - \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}}} \end{matrix} } \vector{\tau} \; d\domain\end{split} The interface forces are coupled in the vertical and horizontal directions. Simplification of the previous equation by the virtual displacement leads to the elementary force arising from the interface and applied to the two independent elements (reinforcement and matrix): \begin{split}\discVect{p_{f}} = \left\{ \begin{matrix} \discVect{p_{sf}} \\ \discVect{p_{pf}} \end{matrix} \right\} = \int_{\domain_f}{} \discMatr{ \begin{matrix} \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{sf}}} \\ - \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}}} \end{matrix} } \vector{\tau} \; d\domain\end{split} The tangent operator associated with the interface is derived from this expression. \begin{split}\begin{align} \frac{\partial \discVect{p_{f}}}{\partial \discVect{U}} & = \int_{\domain_f}{} \discMatr{ \begin{matrix} \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{sf}}} \\ - \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}}} \end{matrix} } \frac{\partial \vector{\tau} }{\partial \discVect{U}} \; d\domain = \int_{\domain_f}{} \discMatr{ \begin{matrix} \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{sf}}} \\ - \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}}} \end{matrix} } \frac{\partial \vector{\tau} }{\partial \disp_r} \discMatr{ \begin{matrix} \discMatr{\shapeFunc_{sf}} & - \discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}} \end{matrix} } \; d\domain \end{align}\end{split} because \frac{\partial \vector{\tau} }{\partial \discVect{U}} = \frac{\partial \vector{\tau} }{\partial \disp_r} \frac{\partial \disp_r}{\partial \discVect{U}} where \frac{\partial \vector{\tau} }{\partial \disp_r} is the tangent operator returned by the interface law. 3 Formulation of the element 3D_INTERF_POU In the case of the interaction element 3D_INTERF_POU , the discretisation adopted (and the associated kinematics) for the reinforcement is a two-node Timoshenko beam, whereas the discretisation adopted for the matrix is an eight-node hexahedral 3D element (hence no additional kinematic assumption relative to the usual 3D case). The corresponding modellings for the "independent" elements are respectively the modelling POU_D_T and the modelling 3D . A representation of the decomposition of the mesh of the element is given in figure r7.01.49-fig-decompo-elem. Decomposition of the mesh of the element 3D_INTERF_POU 3.1 Projection of the shape functions of the matrix and of the reinforcement onto the interface The projection of the shape functions of the matrix and of the reinforcement onto the interface is developed below. It is these functions that make it possible to compute the relative displacement between the two phases. The shape functions of the matrix and of the reinforcement at the interface must therefore be evaluated: \begin{split}\begin{align} \discMatr{\shapeFunc_f} & = \discMatr{ \left. \shapeFunc_s \right|_{\domain_f} } \\ \discMatr{\shapeFunc_{pf}} & = \discMatr{ \left. \shapeFunc_p \right|_{\domain_f} } \end{align}\end{split} where \discMatr{\shapeFunc_s} and \discMatr{\shapeFunc_p} are the shape functions of the matrix and of the reinforcement. The interaction domain \domain_f is one-dimensional and coincident with the line of the beam \domain_p . The shape functions of the reinforcement \discMatr{\shapeFunc_p} are therefore already expressed in the frame of the interface. The domain of the matrix \discMatr{\shapeFunc_s} , on the other hand, is three-dimensional. It is therefore necessary to find the equation of the interface in this domain. Consider the physical frame X \left( x_s, y_s, z_s \right) (fig. r7.01.49-fig-repere-phys) of the mesh cell of the matrix, of dimensions l_x , l_y and l_z . Physical frame of the element 3D_INTERF_POU And \Xi \left( \xi_s, \eta_s, \chi_s \right) its frame in the parametric space (fig. r7.01.49-fig-repere-std), of dimensions 2 , 2 , 2 . Parametric frame of the element 3D_INTERF_POU Let \Gamma_X \left( \gamma_x \right) be the physical frame of the interface, of dimension l_x , and \Gamma_\Xi \left( \gamma_{\Xi} \right) its parametric frame, of dimension 2 . Finally, let \gamma_X = \inverse{f} \left( x_s, y_s, z_s \right) be the equation of the interface in the physical frame. The aim is to determine its inverse \left( x_s, y_s, z_s \right) = f \left( \gamma_X \right) . From a practical point of view, one works in the parametric space \Xi \left( \xi_s,\eta_s, \chi_s \right) of the mesh cell of the matrix. One therefore seeks to express the inverse of the equation of the interface in this frame: \left( \xi_s, \eta_s, \chi_s \right) = g \left( \gamma_\Xi \right) . Finally, this indeed makes it possible to obtain \int_{\Gamma_X} \transpose{ \discMatr{\left. \shapeFunc_s^X \right|_{\Gamma_X}} } \, d\Gamma_X from the shape functions of the matrix expressed in its parametric frame \discMatr{\shapeFunc_s^{\Xi}} , such that: \begin{split}\begin{align} \int_{\Gamma_X} \transpose{ \discMatr{ \left. \shapeFunc_s^X \right|_{\Gamma_X} } } \, d\Gamma_X & = \int_{\Gamma_\Xi} \transpose{ \discMatr{ \left.\shapeFunc_s^\Xi \right|_{\Gamma_\Xi} } } \valeAbs{ \det \left( \discMatr{\jacobTransfor_{\Gamma_X \rightarrow \Gamma_\Xi}} \right) } \, d\Gamma_\Xi \\ & = \int_{\gamma_\Xi = -1}^{\gamma_\Xi=1} \transpose{\discMatr{\shapeFunc_s^\Xi \left( g \left( \gamma_\Xi \right) \right) }} \valeAbs{ \det \left( \discMatr{\jacobTransfor_{\Gamma_X \rightarrow \Gamma_\Xi}} \right) } \, d\gamma_\Xi \end{align}\end{split} 3.2 Jacobian of the transformation of the interface frame Let us determine the terms of the previous equation. We begin with the expression of the determinant \discMatr{\jacobTransfor_{\Gamma_X \rightarrow \Gamma_\Xi}} of the change of variable for the passage from the parent space of the interface to its parametric space. l_x is the length of the interface in the parent space. This frame extends over [0, l_x] . The parametric space extends over [-1, 1] . The boundary conditions \gamma_X \left( \gamma_\Xi = -1 \right) = 0 and \gamma_X \left( \gamma_\Xi = 1 \right) = l_x may be written, and one finds that: \begin{split}\left\{ \begin{align} \gamma_X & = \frac{L_f}{2}(\gamma_\Xi+1) \\ d\gamma_X & = \frac{\partial \gamma_X}{\partial \gamma_\Xi} d\gamma_\Xi = \frac{L_f}{2} d\gamma_\Xi \end{align} \right.\end{split} Hence the expression of the Jacobian of the transformation: \discMatr{\jacobTransfor_{\Gamma_X \rightarrow \Gamma_\Xi}} = \frac{\partial \Gamma_X}{\partial \Gamma_\Xi} = \frac{\partial \gamma_X}{\partial \gamma_\Xi} = \frac{l_x}{2} And finally one has: \valeAbs{ \det \left( \discMatr{\jacobTransfor_{\Gamma_X \rightarrow \Gamma_\Xi}} \right) } = \frac{l_x}{2} 3.3 Equation of the interface in the parametric frame g is the equation which associates with a point on the interface a point in the parametric space of the matrix \Xi \left( \xi_s,\eta_s, \chi_s \right) . \begin{split}\begin{align} g \; : \; & \Gamma_\Xi \; \longrightarrow \; \Xi \\ & \gamma_\Xi \; \longrightarrow \; \left\{ \begin{matrix} \xi_s \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right\} \end{align}\end{split} 3.4 Shape functions at the interface In the case of the element whose formulation is detailed here, the shape functions used for the interpolation of the relative displacements are the same as those used by the "independent" elements representing the contributions of the matrix and of the reinforcement. Note It is, however, entirely possible to choose other shape functions supported by the mesh cells. If one wished to develop a quadratic element, this is in practice what would have to be done, as in the case of the quadratic interface elements 3D_JOINT , for example. 3.4.1 Shape functions of the matrix The interpolation of the displacements of the matrix is written: \begin{split}\left\{ \begin{align} u & = \sum_{i=1}^{8} \shapeFunc_i U_i \\ v & = \sum_{i=1}^{8} \shapeFunc_i V_i \\ w & = \sum_{i=1}^{8} \shapeFunc_i W_i \\ \end{align} \right.\end{split} where \shapeFunc_i is the shape function of node i and U_i , V_i , W_i are the nodal displacements of the element. The previous system can be rewritten in matrix form, such that: \begin{aligned}\disp_s &= \discMatr{\shapeFunc_s} \discVect{U_s} \\ &= \left[\begin{matrix} \shapeFunc_1 & 0 & 0 & \shapeFunc_2 & 0 & 0 & ... & \shapeFunc_8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \shapeFunc_1 & 0 & 0 & \shapeFunc_2 & 0 & 0 & ... & \shapeFunc_8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \shapeFunc_1 & 0 & 0 & \shapeFunc_2 & 0 & 0 & ... & \shapeFunc_8 \end{matrix}\right] \left\{ \begin{matrix} u_1 \\ v_1 \\ w_1 \\ u_2 \\ v_2 \\ w_2 \\ \vdots \\ u_8 \\ v_8 \\ w_8 \end{matrix} \right\}\end{aligned} The expressions of the shape functions of the matrix in its parametric space \Xi \left( \xi_s,\eta_s, \chi_s \right) are given below. They are linear: \begin{split}\left\{ \begin{align} \shapeFunc_1^\Xi & = (1-\xi_s)(1-\eta_s)(1-\chi_s)/8 \\ \shapeFunc_2^\Xi & = (1+\xi_s)(1-\eta_s)(1-\chi_s)/8 \\ \shapeFunc_3^\Xi & = (1+\xi_s)(1+\eta_s)(1-\chi_s)/8 \\ \shapeFunc_4^\Xi & = (1-\xi_s)(1+\eta_s)(1-\chi_s)/8 \\ \shapeFunc_5^\Xi & = (1-\xi_s)(1-\eta_s)(1+\chi_s)/8 \\ \shapeFunc_6^\Xi & = (1+\xi_s)(1-\eta_s)(1+\chi_s)/8 \\ \shapeFunc_7^\Xi & = (1+\xi_s)(1+\eta_s)(1+\chi_s)/8 \\ \shapeFunc_8^\Xi & = (1-\xi_s)(1+\eta_s)(1+\chi_s)/8 \end{align} \right.\end{split} 3.4.2 Shape functions of the reinforcement Consider a straight beam in a three-dimensional space. The principal inertia frame is centred at G , the centre of gravity. The axis x is directed along the axis of the beam; y and z are the other two principal axes of inertia of the cross-section. The effects of torsion and of bending are decoupled in the local frame (translated from the principal inertia frame) whose origin is the centre of torsion C (also called the shear centre). The displacements in the plane of the cross-section ( v_c and w_c ) are expressed in this frame, whereas the axial displacements remain expressed in the principal inertia frame attached to the centre of gravity G R3.08.04. The reinforcement adopts a Timoshenko kinematic assumption. The generalised displacements \vector{U}_p are set as follows: \transpose{\vector{U}_p} \left( x \right) = \left\langle \begin{matrix} u_g & v_c & w_c & \theta_x & \mu_y & \psi_z \end{matrix} \right\rangle where u_g , v_c , w_c are the translations and \theta_x , \mu_y , \psi_z the rotations. These coefficients depend in particular on the elastic properties of the material of the beam and are therefore valid only in that range. 4 Conclusion A finite-element model of the interaction between matrix and reinforcement is proposed. The kinematics of the elements used together with the interaction element to represent the behaviours specific to the reinforcement and to the matrix must correspond to the kinematics adopted in the interaction element. The element carries unknowns corresponding to the degrees of freedom of the reinforcement (including rotations) and of the matrix. 5 Bibliography de Buhan, P., & Sudret, B. (2000). r7.01.50 Integration of the elastoplastic constitutive relation INTERF_POU_CINE for the 3D_INTERF_POU elements r7.01.50 Integration of the elastoplastic constitutive relation INTERF_POU_CINE for the 3D_INTERF_POU elements Summary: This document describes the integration of the elastoplastic constitutive relation INTERF_POU_CINE. This law concerns only the 3D_INTERF_POU elements R7.01.49. The integration method used is based on a direct implicit formulation. From the initial state, or from the previous analysis time instant, one computes the stress field resulting from a strain increment. One also computes the tangent operator. 1 Introduction The 3D_INTERF_POU element represents the interaction between a reinforcement and its surrounding matrix. Their kinematics are represented there respectively by those of a 2-node beam and of an 8-node hexahedral 3D element. The interaction domain considered (the interface) is a line coincident with the beam domain. The 3D_INTERF_POU element integrates there, at its Gauss points, a phenomenological law returning the interaction forces between the matrix and the reinforcement as a function of their relative displacement , carried by three components. This document describes the INTERF_POU_CINE law with kinematic hardening . The behaviour is uncoupled in the different directions in elasticity, but coupled in plasticity. 2 General notations and hypotheses in elastoplasticity 2.1 General notations The quantities evaluated at the previous time instant t are indexed {}_{n} . The quantities evaluated at the current time instant t+\Delta t are indexed {}_{n+1} . The increments are denoted by \Delta . For the computation of the derivatives, one will write: \dot{\eps} derivative of \eps with respect to time. | \sig = \transpose{\langle \begin{matrix} \sigt & \signx & \signy \end{matrix} \rangle} | vector of the interface forces. | | --- | --- | | \eps = \transpose{\langle \begin{matrix} \epst & \epsnx & \epsny \end{matrix} \rangle} | vector of the relative displacements. | | \Cel = \transpose{\langle \begin{matrix} k_t & k_n & k_n \end{matrix} \rangle} | vector of the elastic stiffnesses. | | k_n, k_t | elastic stiffnesses in the directions respectively normal and tangential to the reinforcement. | | \sigy = \transpose{\langle \begin{matrix} \sigyt & \sigyn & \sigyn \end{matrix} \rangle} | vector of the elastic limits. | | \sigyn, \sigyt | elastic limits in the directions respectively normal and tangential to the reinforcement. | | \rsig = \transpose{\langle \begin{matrix} \rsigt & \rsignx & \rsigny \end{matrix} \rangle} | vector of the recall interface forces (kinematic hardening). | | \ksi = \isigy \left( \sig - \rsig \right) | | | \Gpl = \transpose{\langle \begin{matrix} g_t & g_n & g_n \end{matrix} \rangle} | vector of the plastic stiffnesses. | | g_n, g_t | plastic stiffnesses in the directions respectively normal and tangential to the reinforcement. | | \lambda | plastic multiplier. | | t | time. | | \Delta | increment | 2.2 Hypotheses of elastoplasticity The hypotheses of elastoplasticity are recalled below: - decomposition of the strain into an elastic part and a plastic part: \dot{\eps} = \dot{\eps}^{el} + \dot{\eps}^{pl} - existence of an elastic domain governed by a linear elastic relation such that: \dot{\sig} = \Cel \dot{\eps}^{el} - existence of a yield surface bounding this elastic domain: f (\sig, \rsig) \leq 0 - existence of a flow rule giving the direction of plastic flow from a plastic potential : \dot{\eps}^{pl} = \dot{\lambda} \transpose{\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \sig}} - existence of a hardening function prescribing the evolution of the internal variables: \dot{\rsig} = - \dot{\lambda} \vector{h} \left(\sig, \rsig\right) - application of the Kuhn-Tucker complementarity conditions : \begin{array}{ccc} f \le 0 \quad \quad & \quad \quad \dot{\lambda} \ge 0 \quad \quad & \quad \quad \dot{\lambda} f = 0 \end{array} 3 General characteristics The yield surface is considered elliptical in the space of the interface forces (spherical in the normalised space). It is symmetric in the two directions normal to the reinforcement (fig. r7.01.50-fig-surface). Yield surface in the normalised space of the interface forces | Yield surface | f (\sig, \rsig) = \transpose{\ksi} \ksi - 1 = 0 | | --- | --- | | Flow rule (associated: \Phi = f ) | \dot{\eps}^{pl} = \dot{\lambda} \tdfds = 2 \dot{\lambda} \isigy \ksi | | Hardening function | \dot{\rsig} = \Gpl \dot{\eps}^{pl} = 2 \dot{\lambda} \Gpl \isigy \ksi | 4 Integration of the local constitutive behaviour 4.1 Formulation of the time-continuous problem The solution of a mechanical problem at the scale of the structure requires knowledge of the stress state at each of the Gauss points of the model. In the context of a non-linear constitutive behaviour at a Gauss point, a step of integration of this behaviour is necessary at that point. This step consists in updating the local variables ( \sig , \rsig , \eps^{pl} ) at \idp{t} , from their knowledge at \idn{t} and from the knowledge of \idp{\eps} , and consistently with the evolution equations of the variables given in the previous section r7-01-50-equations-evolution, \begin{split}\begin{align} \dot{\sig} & = \Cel \left( \dot{\eps} - \dot{\eps}^{pl} \right) \\ \dot{\eps}^{pl} & = 2 \dot{\lambda} \isigy \ksi \\ \dot{\rsig} & = 2 \dot{\lambda} \Gpl \isigy \ksi \end{align}\end{split} while respecting the Kuhn-Tucker complementarity conditions : \begin{split}\begin{align} f & \le 0 \\ \dot{\lambda} & \ge 0 \\ \dot{\lambda} f & = 0 \end{align}\end{split} 4.2 Time discretisation of the problem This time-continuous problem is transformed into a discrete constrained-optimisation problem by the application of an implicit Euler scheme . The non-linear evolution equations thus take the form: \begin{split}\begin{align} \sigp & = \Cel \left( \epsp - \epsp^{pl} \right) \\ \epsp^{pl} & = \epsn^{pl} + 2 \Dlamp \isigy \idp{\ksi} \\ \rsigp & = \rsign + 2 \Dlamp \Gpl \isigy \idp{\ksi} \end{align}\end{split} The Kuhn-Tucker conditions take the discrete form: \begin{split}\begin{align} f \left( \sigp, \rsigp \right) & \le 0 \\ \Dlamp & \ge 0 \\ \Dlamp f \left( \sigp, \rsigp \right) & = 0 \end{align}\end{split} In order to be solved algorithmically, these conditions are reformulated in the form of a two-step procedure : 1. elastic prediction , which freezes the plastic flow during the time step, followed, if the Kuhn-Tucker conditions are violated by the elastic prediction , by a 2. plastic correction , bringing back onto the yield surface the point representing the stress state The integration here is indeed carried out with respect to time t , but it is easier to reduce the problem to one in \lambda . Let us detail, by way of example, the computation of the expression for \epsp^{pl} . The application of the implicit Euler scheme to \eps^{pl} gives: \epsp^{pl} = \epsn^{pl} + \Dtp \idp{\dot{\eps}}^{pl} where \idp{\dot{\eps}}^{pl} = \idp{\dot{\lambda}} \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|} And the application of the scheme to \lambda gives: \begin{split}\begin{align} & \lamp = \lamn + \Dtp \idp{\dot{\lambda}} \\ \Leftrightarrow \quad & \idp{\dot{\lambda}} = \frac{\lamp - \lamn}{\Dtp} \\ \Leftrightarrow \quad & \idp{\dot{\lambda}} = \frac{\Dlamp}{\Dtp} \end{align}\end{split} Replacing \idp{\dot{\lambda}} by this last expression in the equation, we finally obtain: \begin{split}\begin{align} & \epsp^{pl} = \epsn^{pl} + \Dtp \frac{\Dlamp}{\Dtp} \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|} \\ \Leftrightarrow \quad & \boxed{\epsp^{pl} = \epsn^{pl} + \Dlamp \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|}} \end{align}\end{split} where \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|} = 2 \isigy \idp{\ksi} 4.3 Elastic prediction The elastic prediction step assumes the plastic flow to be frozen during the time step. Thus, all the quantities at the time step \idp{t} which relate to the plasticity state are considered equal to those of the previous time step \idn{t} . \begin{split}\left \lbrace \begin{align} \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{trial} & := \epsn^{pl} \\ \idp{\sig}^{trial} & := \Cel \left( \epsp - \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{trial} \right) \\ \idp{\rsig}^{trial} & := \idn{\rsig} \\ \idp{f}^{trial} & := f \left( \idp{\sig}^{trial}, \idp{\rsig}^{trial} \right) \end{align} \right.\end{split} If \idp{f}^{trial} \le 0 , then the system is in an elastic regime during the time step and the state \idp{} is fully determined: \begin{split}\left \lbrace \begin{align} \epsp^{pl} & = \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{trial} \\ \idp{\sig} & = \idp{\sig}^{trial} \\ \idp{\rsig} & = \idp{\rsig}^{trial} \\ \idp{f} & = \idp{f}^{trial} \\ \idp{\Dlam} & = 0 \end{align} \right.\end{split} Otherwise, if \idp{f}^{trial} \gt 0 , then the elastically predicted state violates the Kuhn-Tucker conditions . The system is in a plastic regime. The plastic-correction step will make it possible to bring the system back into a state compatible with the conditions. Determining the state in this regime requires the solution of the equation \idp{f} = 0 . 4.4 Plastic correction The plastic correction step assumes a plastic regime : \begin{split}\begin{align} f \left( \sigp, \rsigp \right) & = 0 \\ \Dlamp & \gt 0 \\ \Dlamp f \left( \sigp, \rsigp \right) & = 0 \end{align}\end{split} In order to solve the equation f \left( \sigp, \rsigp \right) = 0 , and thus to determine a plastic state compatible with the Kuhn-Tucker conditions , it is first necessary to express this equation solely from quantities known at the previous time instant \idn{} and from a single scalar unknown \Dlamp , the plastic multiplier expressed at the current time instant \idp{} : \begin{split}\begin{align} f \left( \sigp, \rsigp \right) & = f \left( \Dlamp \right) \\ & = \ksip^2 \cdot \vId - 1 \\ & = \left( \frac{\ksip^{trial}}{\vId + \vA \Dlamp} \right)^2 \cdot \vId - 1 \end{align}\end{split} where \ksip^{trial} = \isigy \left( \idp{\sig}^{trial} - \idp{\rsig}^{trial} \right) The equation f \left( \Dlamp \right) = 0 is non-linear. It is solved by means of a local Newton method , which requires linearising the equation about the current point \Dlamp : f \left( \Dlamp^{(k+1)} \right) = f \left( \Dlamp^{(k)} \right) + \idp{\left. \frac{d f}{d \left( \Dlam \right)} \right|}^{(k)} d \left( \Dlamp \right) = 0 where \begin{split}\boxed{ \left \lbrace \begin{align} f \left( \Dlamp^{(k)} \right) & = \left( \frac{\ksip^{trial}}{\vId + \vA \Dlamp^{(k)}} \right)^2 \cdot \vId - 1 \\ \frac{d f}{d \left( \Dlam \right)} & = - \frac{2 \vA {\ksip^{trial}}^2}{\left( \vId + \vA \Dlamp^{(k)} \right)^3} \cdot \vId \end{align} \right. }\end{split} The final state at \idp{t} is obtained from the converged state of the local Newton method : \begin{split}\left \lbrace \begin{align} \epsp^{pl} & = \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} \\ \sigp & = \sigp^{(k+1)} \\ \rsigp & = \rsigp^{(k+1)} \\ \Dlamp & = \Dlamp^{(k+1)} \end{align} \right.\end{split} The final stress state at \idp{t} at the Gauss point is finally returned to the finite element and, from there, by assembly, to the global Newton-Raphson loop (at the scale of the structure). The latter also requires the computation of the tangent matrix of the constitutive behaviour for the assembly of the global tangent matrix. This computation is presented in the following part. Let us detail the computation of \ksip : Let \begin{split}\begin{align} \sigp & = \Cel \left( \epsp - \eps^{pl} \right) \\ & = \Cel \left( \epsp - \epsn^{pl} - \left( \epsp^{pl} - \epsn^{pl} \right) \right) \\ & = \sigp^{trial} - \Cel \Delta \epsp^{pl} \end{align}\end{split} \dot{\lambda} \dot{f} = 0 and \begin{split}\begin{align} \rsigp & = \rsign + \Gpl \Delta \epsp^{pl} \\ & = \rsigp^{trial} + \Gpl \Delta \epsp^{pl} \end{align}\end{split} substituted into \begin{split}\begin{align} \ksip & = \isigy \left( \sigp - \rsigp \right) \\ & = \isigy \left( \sigp^{trial} - \rsigp^{trial} - \left( \Cel + \Gpl \right) \Delta \epsp^{pl} \right) \\ & = \ksip^{trial} - \isigy \left( \Cel + \Gpl \right) \Delta \epsp^{pl} \\ & = \ksip^{trial} - \underbrace{2 \sigy^{-2} \left( \Cel + \Gpl \right)}_{\vA} \ksip \Dlamp \end{align}\end{split} This expression is manipulated in order finally to obtain \ksip : \begin{split}\begin{align} & \ksip^{trial} = \left( \vId + \vA \Dlamp \right) \ksip \\ \Leftrightarrow \quad & \boxed{\ksip = \frac{\ksip^{trial}}{\vId + \vA \Dlamp}} \end{align}\end{split} 5 Computation of the tangent operator One seeks the expression of the consistent tangent matrix (or algorithmic tangent matrix) at the converged state \idp{}^{(k+1)} : \idp{\Ct}^{(k+1)} = \idp{\left. \frac{d \sig}{d \eps} \right|}^{(k+1)} One recalls that \begin{split}\left \lbrace \begin{align} d \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} & = d \idp{\left( \Dlam \right)}^{(k+1)} \idp{\left. \dfds \right|}^{(k+1)} \\ d \rsigp^{(k+1)} & = \Gpl d \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} \end{align} \right.\end{split} because d \epsn^{pl} = d \rsign = 0 (constant over the time step). One also recalls that \sigp^{(k+1)} = \Cel \left( \epsp - \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} \right) whence d \sigp^{(k+1)} = \Cel \left( d \epsp - d \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} \right) \\ The equation, through d \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} , depends on d \idp{\left( \Dlam \right)}^{(k+1)} , which is unknown. The consistency condition makes it possible to determine the value of d \idp{\left( \Dlam \right)}^{(k+1)} . This condition follows from the Kuhn-Tucker conditions and is written as follows: In plastic regime 1, this condition imposes that d \idp{f}^{(k+1)} = 0 . \begin{split}\begin{align} d f \left( \sigp^{(k+1)}, \rsigp^{(k+1)} \right) & = \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|}^{(k+1)} d \sigp^{(k+1)} + \idp{\left. \tdfdr \right|}^{(k+1)} d \rsigp^{(k+1)} \\ & = \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|}^{(k+1)} \Cel \left( d \epsp - d \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} \right) + \idp{\left. \tdfdr \right|}^{(k+1)} \Gpl d \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} \\ \end{align}\end{split} By replacing d \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} by its expression in the equation \idp{f}^{(k+1)} = 0 , d \idp{\left( \Dlam \right) }^{(k+1)} can be isolated: \begin{split}\begin{align} & \idp{f}^{(k+1)} = 0 \\ \Leftrightarrow \quad & d \idp{\left( \Dlam \right)}^{(k+1)} = \frac{ \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|}^{(k+1)} \Cel }{ \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|}^{(k+1)} \Cel \idp{\left. \dfds \right|}^{(k+1)} - \idp{\left. \tdfdr \right|}^{(k+1)} \Gpl \idp{\left. \dfdr \right|}^{(k+1)} } d \epsp \end{align}\end{split} Knowing that \dfdr = - \dfds , the expression can be simplified to d \idp{\left( \Dlam \right)}^{(k+1)} = \frac{ \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|}^{(k+1)} \Cel }{ \idp{\left. \tdfds \right|}^{(k+1)} \left( \Cel + \Gpl \right) \idp{\left. \dfds \right|}^{(k+1)} } d \epsp By replacing d \idp{\left( \Dlam \right) }^{(k+1)} by the previous expression in the equation, one obtains: \begin{split}\begin{align} d \sigp^{(k+1)} & = \Cel \left( d \epsp - d \idp{\eps^{pl}}^{(k+1)} \right) \\ & = \Cel \left( d \epsp - d \idp{\left( \Dlam \right)}^{(k+1)} \idp{\left. \dfds \right|}^{(k+1)} \right) \end{align}\end{split} And finally the consistent tangent matrix \Ct : In the elastic regime, the tangent matrix simply corresponds to the elastic matrix. 6 Bibliography Simo J.C., Hughes T.J.R., Computational Inelasticity, Mechanics and Materials, Interdisciplinary Applied Mathematics Vol. 7 , Edition Springer-Verlag, New York, 1998 Bertrand D., Grange S., Vulnerability assessment of civil engineering structures subjected to earthquakes and impacts, Course INSA Lyon, 2021.

When the crack lies along an axis of symmetry, one may represent only half of the model, and specify the symmetry of the loading by the keyword SYME in DEFI_FOND_FISS. By default, it is assumed that there is no symmetry. If the model exhibits a symmetry, CALC_G detects it automatically via the concept fond_fiss. Non-meshed crack (X-FEM method): In 2D as in 3D, the crack must be defined, for the mechanical analysis and for the post-processing, by means of the command DEFI_FISS_XFEM. The keyword FISSURE must be supplied in CALC_G_XFEM. If the crack is not meshed, it is not possible to take into account any symmetries of the model with respect to the crack lips. The calculation of G is carried out in post-processing, solely from the displacement field which is the solution of the analysis on the model considered. These faces appear in one or more mesh-cell groups and are described in the connectivities of the surface elements. The algorithm sorts these faces in order to retain only those having two vertices on \Gamma_0 . The steps of the algorithm are: 1. For each node of \Gamma_0 , extraction of the mesh cells belonging to the crack lips. 2. Filtering of the mesh cells in order to keep only those having two nodes on \Gamma_0 . 3. Retrieval of the type of the face (triangle or quadrilateral) and calculation of the equation of the tangent plane or planes. 4. r7.02.03 Energy release rate in non-linear thermoelasticity r7.02.03 Energy release rate in non-linear thermoelasticity Summary: The calculation of the energy release rate by the theta method in 2D or in 3D is presented for a non-linear thermoelastic problem. The non-linear elastic constitutive relation is described in R5.03.20. 1 Calculation of the energy release rate by the theta method in non-linear thermoelasticity 1.1 Constitutive relation A cracked solid is considered, occupying the domain \Omega of the space {R}^{2} or {R}^{3} . Let: - u be the displacement field, - T the temperature field, - f the field of body forces applied on \Omega , - g the field of surface forces applied on a part S of \partial \Omega , - U the field of displacements imposed on a part {S}_{d} of \partial \Omega . The behaviour of the solid is assumed non-linear elastic, such that the constitutive relation coincides with the elastoplastic Hencky–von Mises law (isotropic hardening) in the case of a loading which induces a radial and monotonic evolution at every point. This model is chosen in the commands CALC_G by means of the keyword RELATION='ELAS_VMIS_LINE' or 'ELAS_VMIS_TRAC' or 'ELAS_VMIS_PUIS' under the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT R5.03.20. One denotes by: - \varepsilon the strain tensor, - \varepsilon ° the tensor of the initial strains, - \sigma the stress tensor, - \sigma ° the tensor of the initial stresses, - \Psi (\varepsilon ,\varepsilon °,\sigma °,T) the free-energy density. \varepsilon is related to the displacement field u by: \varepsilon (u)=\frac{1}{2}({u}_{i,j}+{u}_{j,i}) The free-energy density \Psi (\varepsilon ,\varepsilon °,\sigma °,T) is a convex and differentiable function, known for a given state [R5.03.20éq3]. The constitutive relation of the material is written in the form: {\sigma}_{ij}=\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}_{ij}}(\varepsilon ,\varepsilon °,\sigma °,T) It derives from the free-energy potential. For this hyperelastic constitutive relation, a meaning can be given to the energy release rate within the framework of the global approach in fracture mechanics. This is not the case for a plastic constitutive relation. 1.2 Potential energy and equilibrium relations The spaces of kinematically admissible fields V and {V}_{0} are defined. \begin{array}{}V=\lbrace v\text{admissibles},v=U\text{sur}{S}_{d}\rbrace \\ {V}_{0}=\lbrace v\text{admissibles},v=O\text{sur}{S}_{d}\rbrace \end{array} With the assumptions of paragraph [§1.1] (with \varepsilon °=\sigma °=0 ), the equilibrium relations in weak form are: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}u\in V& \\ \underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{ij}{v}_{i,j}d\Omega =\underset{\Omega}{\int}{f}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Omega +\underset{\Omega}{\int}{g}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Gamma ,& \forall v\in {V}_{0}\end{array} They are obtained by minimising the global potential energy of the system: W(v)=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\Psi (\varepsilon (v),T)d\Omega =\underset{\Omega}{\int}{f}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Omega +\underset{\Omega}{\int}{g}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Gamma The demonstration is identical to that in linear elasticity [R7.02.01§1.2]. 1.3 Lagrangian expression of the energy release rate Let m be the unit normal to {\Gamma}_{0} lying in the plane tangent to \partial \Omega in \Omega . Let the field \theta be such that: \theta \in \Theta =\lbrace \mu \text{tels que}\mu .n=0\text{sur}\Omega \rbrace denoting by n the normal to \partial \Omega . The energy release rate G is the solution of the variational equation: {\int}_{{\Gamma}_{o}}G\theta \cdot m\text{dS}=G(\theta ),\forall \theta \in \Theta where G(\theta ) is defined by: \begin{array}{cc}G(\theta )& ={\int}_{\Omega}{\sigma}_{ij}{u}_{i,p}{\theta}_{p,j}-\Psi {\theta}_{k,k}-\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}{T}_{\text{,k}}{\theta}_{k}d\Omega \\ & +{\int}_{\Omega}({\sigma}_{ij}-\frac{1}{2}{\sigma}_{ij}^{°}){\varepsilon}_{ij,k}^{°}{\theta}_{k}-({\varepsilon}_{ij}-{\varepsilon}_{ij}^{\text{th}}-\frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon}_{ij}^{°}){\sigma}_{ij,k}{\theta}_{k}d\Omega \\ & +{\int}_{\Omega}{f}_{i}{u}_{i}{\theta}_{k,k}+{f}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}{u}_{i}d\Omega \\ & +{\int}_{S}{g}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}{u}_{i}+{g}_{i}{u}_{i}({\theta}_{k,k}-\frac{\partial \theta }{\partial {n}_{k}}{n}_{k})d\Gamma \\ & -{\int}_{{S}_{d}}{\sigma}_{ij}{n}_{j}{U}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}d\Gamma \end{array} The demonstration is identical to that of the calculation of G in linear elasticity R7.02.01. The expression is the same, so the post-processing is identical. 1.4 Implementation of G in non-linear thermoelasticity The types of elements and of loadings, and the necessary environment, are the same as for the implementation of G in linear thermoelasticity [R7.02.01 §2.4]. For the calculation of the various terms of G(\theta ) , at a given state, the free-energy density \Psi (\varepsilon ,T) , the strains \varepsilon and the stresses \sigma are recovered, computed for the non-linear constitutive relation. It is assumed that \varepsilon °=\sigma °=0 (a term identical in linear or non-linear thermoelasticity). The free-energy density is then written [R5.03.20 §1.5]: - in linear thermoelasticity: \Psi (\varepsilon ,T)=\frac{1}{2}K{({\varepsilon}_{kk}-3\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{réf}}))}^{2}+\frac{2\mu }{3}{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}^{2} with \begin{array}{}{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}^{2}=\frac{3}{2}{\varepsilon}_{ij}^{D}{\varepsilon}_{ij}^{D}=\frac{3}{2}({\varepsilon}_{ij}-\frac{1}{3}{\varepsilon}_{kk}{\delta}_{ij})({\varepsilon}_{ij}-\frac{1}{3}{\varepsilon}_{kk}{\delta}_{ij})\\ {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}^{2}=\frac{3}{2}({\varepsilon}_{ij}{\varepsilon}_{ij}-\frac{1}{3}{\varepsilon}_{kk}^{2})\end{array} - in non-linear thermoelasticity (2\mu {\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}\ge {\sigma}_{y}) : \Psi (\varepsilon ,T)=\frac{1}{2}K{({\varepsilon}_{kk}-3\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{réf}}))}^{2}+\frac{1}{6\mu }R{(p({\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}))}^{2}+{\int}_{0}^{p({\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}})}R(s)\text{ds} with R(p({\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}})) : hardening function. For a linear isotropic hardening (RELATION= ‘ELAS_VMIS_LINE’) one has: \begin{array}{}R(p)={\sigma}_{y}+p\frac{E{E}_{T}}{E-{E}_{T}}={\sigma}_{y}+ap\\ p=\frac{{\sigma}_{\text{eq}}-{\sigma}_{y}}{3\mu +a}\text{avec}a=\frac{E{E}_{T}}{E-{E}_{T}}\\ A(p)={\int}_{0}^{p}R(s)\text{ds}={\sigma}_{\text{yp}}+\frac{1}{2}a{p}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}{\sigma}_{y}p+\frac{p}{2}({\sigma}_{y}+ap)\\ A(p)=\frac{p}{2}({\sigma}_{y}+R(p))\end{array} The post-processing is then identical to the problem in linear elasticity, except for the thermal term: \text{THER}=-\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}{T}_{,k}{\theta}_{k} If the Lamé coefficients \lambda (T) and \mu (T) are independent of temperature, this term is zero. Otherwise, \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}(\varepsilon ,T) must be computed at a given time instant. For a linear isotropic hardening, one has: \begin{array}{cc}\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}& (\varepsilon ,T)=\left\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{dK}(T)}{\text{dT}}({\varepsilon}_{kk}-3\alpha (T-{T}_{\text{réf}}))-\mathrm{3K}(\alpha +\frac{d\alpha (T)}{\text{dT}}(T-{T}_{\text{réf}}))\right\\ & +\frac{R(p)}{6{\mu}^{2}}\left[2\mu \frac{\text{dR}(P)}{\text{dT}}-\frac{d\mu (T)}{\text{dT}}R(p)\right]+\frac{\text{dA}(p)}{\text{dT}}\end{array} with \begin{array}{c}\frac{\text{dR}(p)}{\text{dT}}=\frac{d{\sigma}_{y}(T)}{\text{dT}}+\frac{da(T)}{\text{dT}}p+a\frac{dp(T)}{\text{dT}}\\ \frac{da(T)}{\text{dT}}=\frac{1}{{(E-{E}_{T})}^{2}}(\frac{{\text{d E}}_{T}(T)}{\text{dT}}{E}^{2}-\frac{dE(T)}{\text{dT}}E{}_{T}{}^{2}\text{})\\ \frac{\mathrm{dp}(T)}{\text{dT}}=\frac{1}{{(3\mu +a)}^{2}}\left[({\sigma}_{y}-{\sigma}_{\text{eq}})(3\frac{d\mu (T)}{\text{dT}}+\frac{\text{dA}(T)}{\text{dT}})-(3\mu +a)\frac{d{\sigma}_{y}(T)}{\text{dT}}\right]\\ \frac{\text{dA}(p)}{\text{dT}}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{dp}(T)}{\text{dT}}({\sigma}_{y}+{R}_{p})+\frac{1}{2}p(\frac{d{\sigma}_{y}(T)}{\text{dT}}+\frac{\text{d Rp}(T)}{\text{dT}})\end{array} 1.5 Warning Warning! By definition, in the general case: \Psi (\varepsilon ,T)\ne \sigma :\varepsilon Although it is possible to carry out an elastoplastic analysis followed by the calculation of in non-linear elasticity, it must be clearly understood that this has no thermodynamic meaning and that it is normal for the result to depend on the field \theta . 2 Calculation of the energy release rate by the theta method in large transformations The constitutive relation of [§1] is extended to large displacements and large rotations, in so far as it derives from a potential (hyperelastic law). This functionality is triggered by the keyword DEFORMATION='GROT_GDEP' in the command CALC_G. 2.1 Constitutive relation One denotes by: - \mathrm{E} the Green–Lagrange strain tensor, - \mathrm{S} the second Piola–Kirchhoff stress tensor, - \Psi (E) the internal-energy density. The behaviour of the solid is assumed hyperelastic, namely: - E is related to the displacement field u measured with respect to the reference configuration {\Omega}_{0} by: {E}_{ij}(u)=\frac{1}{2}({u}_{i,j}+{u}_{j,i}+{u}_{k,i}{u}_{k,j}) - S is related to the Cauchy stress tensor by: {S}_{ij}=\det(F){F}_{\mathrm{ik}}^{\text{-1}}{T}_{kl}{F}_{\mathrm{jl}}^{\text{-1}} F being the gradient of the transformation which takes one from the reference configuration {\Omega}_{0} to the current configuration \Omega , related to the displacement by: {F}_{ij}=({\delta}_{ij}+{u}_{i,j}) The constitutive relation of a hyperelastic material is written in the form: {S}_{ij}=\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {E}_{ij}}=\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {E}_{jj}}={S}_{ji} This relation describes a non-linear elastic behaviour, analogous to that of [§1.1]. It offers the possibility of treating fracture-mechanics problems without incorporating plasticity into them. And in the case of a monotonic radial loading, it makes it possible to obtain strains and stresses of the structure similar to those which would be obtained if the material presented an isotropic hardening. The hyperelastic material has a reversible mechanical behaviour, that is any loading cycle generates no dissipation. This model is chosen in the command CALC_G U4.82.03 by means of the keyword: RELATION: 'ELAS' for a “linear” elastic relation, that is the relation between the strains and the stresses considered is linear, RELATION: 'ELAS_VMIS_LINE' or 'ELAS_VMIS_TRAC' or 'ELAS_VMIS_PUIS' for a “non-linear” elastic constitutive relation (Hencky–von Mises law with isotropic hardening). Such a constitutive relation makes it possible, strictly speaking, to take large strains and large rotations into account. However, one confines oneself to small strains in order to ensure the existence of a solution and in order to be identical to an elastoplastic behaviour under a monotonic radial loading [R5.03.20§2.1]. 2.2 Potential energy and equilibrium relations The loading considered reduces to a non-follower surface density R applied on a part {\Gamma}_{0} of the boundary of {\Omega}_{0} (dead-load assumption [R5.03.20 §2.2]). A space of kinematically admissible fields V is defined: V=\lbrace v\text{admissibles,}v=0\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{0}\rbrace The equilibrium relations in weak form are: \underset{{\Omega}_{0}}{\int}{F}_{\mathrm{ik}}{S}_{\mathrm{kj}}{v}_{i,j}d{\Omega}_{0}=\underset{\Gamma}{\int}{R}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Gamma They may be obtained by minimising the global potential energy of the system: W(v)=\underset{{\Omega}_{0}}{\int}\Psi (E(v))d\Omega -\underset{\Gamma}{\int}{R}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Gamma Indeed, if this functional is minimal for the displacement field u , then: \begin{array}{cc}\delta W& =\underset{{\Omega}_{0}}{\int}\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {E}_{ij}}\delta {E}_{ij}d\Omega -\underset{\Gamma}{\int}{R}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Gamma =0,\forall \delta v\in V\\ & =\underset{{\Omega}_{0}}{\int}{S}_{ij}\frac{1}{2}(\delta {v}_{i,j}+\delta {v}_{j,i}+\delta {v}_{p,i}{u}_{p,j}+{u}_{p,i}\delta {v}_{p,j})d\Omega -\underset{\Gamma}{\int}{R}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Gamma \\ & =\underset{{\Omega}_{0}}{\int}{S}_{ij}({\delta}_{\mathrm{ip}}+{u}_{p,i})\delta {v}_{p,i}d\Omega -\underset{\Gamma}{\int}{R}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Gamma \\ & =\underset{{\Omega}_{0}}{\int}{F}_{pi}{S}_{ij}\delta {v}_{p,j}d\Omega -\underset{\Gamma}{\int}{R}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Gamma \\ & =\underset{{\Omega}_{0}}{\int}{F}_{\mathrm{ik}}{S}_{\mathrm{kj}}\delta {v}_{i,j}d\Omega -\underset{\Gamma}{\int}{R}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Gamma =0\end{array} The equilibrium equations and the constitutive relation are thus recovered, having set: {S}_{ij}=\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {E}_{ij}} 2.3 Lagrangian expression of the energy release rate in non-linear thermoelasticity and in large transformations By definition, the energy release rate G is defined by the opposite of the derivative of the potential energy at equilibrium with respect to the domain \Omega [bib1]. It is computed by the theta method, which is a Lagrangian method of derivation of the potential energy [bib4] and [bib2]. Transformations {F}^{\eta}:M\to M+\eta \theta (M) of the domain are considered, taking {\Omega}_{0} to a domain {\Omega}_{0} which correspond to propagations of the crack. To these families of reference configurations thus defined {\Omega}_{\eta} there correspond families of deformed configurations in which the crack has propagated. The energy release rate G is then the opposite of the derivative of the potential energy W(u(\eta )) at equilibrium with respect to the initial evolution of the crack front: \eta G=-{(\frac{\text{d}W(u(\eta ))}{\text{d}\eta })}_{\eta =0} As in [bib4], . denotes the Lagrangian derivative in a virtual crack propagation of velocity \theta . Let \varphi (\eta ,M) be an arbitrary field ( \eta a positive real number and M belonging to the domain {\Omega}_{0} ); one will denote: \bar{\varphi}(\eta ,M)=\bar{\varphi}(\eta ,{F}^{\eta}M)\text{et}\dot{\varphi}={(\frac{\partial \bar{\varphi}}{\partial \eta })}_{\eta =0} The potential energy defined on {\Omega}_{\eta} is brought back onto {\Omega}_{0} , is assumed independent of \eta ; derivation with respect to the propagation parameter \eta is then straightforward, and the energy release rate in this propagation is the solution of the variational equation: {\int}_{{\Gamma}_{o}}G\theta \cdot m\text{dS}=G(\theta ),\forall \theta \in \Theta with: -G(\theta )={\int}_{{\Omega}_{o}}\stackrel{.}{\stackrel{}{(\Psi (E,T))}}+\Psi (E,T){\theta}_{k,k}\text{d}\Omega -{\int}_{\Gamma}{R}_{i}\dot{{u}_{i}}+{R}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}{u}_{i}+{R}_{i}{u}_{i}({\theta}_{k,k}-\frac{\partial \theta }{\partial {n}_{k}}{n}_{k})\text{d}\Gamma Now: \stackrel{.}{\stackrel{}{(\Psi (E,T))}}=\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {E}_{ij}}{\dot{E}}_{ij}+\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}\dot{T} In what follows, only the term \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {E}_{ij}}{\dot{E}}_{ij} will be considered, the thermal term being treated in the same way as in small displacements R7.02.01.
