r7.02.04 Beremin model r7.02.04 Beremin model Summary The foundations of the local-approach models of fracture, which make it possible to model brittle fracture, are first recalled. It is described how, with the Beremin model, the fracture probability of a structure is computed from knowledge of the mechanical fields acting on it. Placing oneself in the general case of a non-monotonic thermomechanical loading path, and assuming that certain parameters of the models do not depend on temperature, the general expression for the cumulative fracture probabilities is established. The Beremin model also makes it possible to include a plastic-strain correction. The industrial version of the Beremin model is briefly described. Finally, indications concerning the numerical implementation of the Beremin model are summarised. 1 Introduction The integrity of the structures of nuclear power plants, for all loading modes, normal or accidental, must be constantly ensured. In particular, for the most important structures such as the vessel or the primary circuit, the aim is to assess the mechanical strength, from the design stage, with respect to brittle and ductile fracture. From the point of view of continued operation, the aim is also to justify the mechanical strength of the structures in the presence of a crack when defects have been detected during an inspection. This approach makes it possible to establish a schedule for repair or replacement of the components. Furthermore, certain components cannot be inspected, in which case a demonstration of the mechanical integrity in the presence of hypothetical defects must be carried out. In this context, fracture mechanics provides the tools required for the analysis of cracked components. Its objective is to characterise the damage (crack, damage) in order to model each type of fracture, so as to be able to establish fracture criteria making it possible to judge the loading margins under normal or accidental operating conditions. From a physical point of view, a metallic structure subjected to thermomechanical loading is considered. This document is concerned only with the brittle fracture of a structure, that is, when the material fails suddenly by cleavage. The Beremin model is used. It relies on knowledge of the mechanical fields around the crack front in order to obtain a local fracture criterion representative of the physical mechanisms involved (instability of the cleavage microcracks). 1.1 Industrial context From an engineering point of view, the resistance of a material to the propagation of a crack is measured by means of the toughness. Depending on the temperature and the strain rate, certain steels (in particular the ferritic steels of PWR vessels, or carbon-manganese steel for secondary piping) exhibit characteristics which are either brittle or ductile. At low temperatures, these steels fail in a brittle manner by cleavage, sometimes exhibiting intergranular decohesion, whereas at higher temperatures ductile tearing appears. The transition between these two mechanisms is characterised by the brittle/ductile transition temperature. Resilience measurements make it possible to establish criteria, such as the transition temperature, in order to define the domain of use of the material. In the case of the ferritic steels of PWR vessels under normal operating conditions, the material is loaded in the ductile domain. However, during its operation, under the effect of neutron irradiation, the vessel will “age” and may become embrittled. Moreover, very exceptional accidental conditions, such as the cold thermal shock (Pressurized Thermal Shock, PTS) under pressure in the event of a loss of primary coolant (APRP), could cause the component to be loaded in the ductile-brittle transition domain. This is why it is important to determine the degree of embrittlement of the material by means of the ductile-brittle transition curve, and to know precisely the toughness of the material in the transition domain, in order to prevent all risks of sudden fracture. Concerning the piping of the secondary circuit, the C-Mn steels which are used in the various backup circuits (ASG, Emergency Feedwater of the Steam Generators, for example) are sensitive to (static) strain ageing, which induces a shift of their ductile-brittle transition towards high temperatures. In order to predict the brittle fracture of these components in the presence of static ageing, several earlier studies have been carried out, making it possible to model the mechanical constitutive behaviour of the material taking strain ageing into account (see , , ). These works have already shown that the cleavage fracture probability can be correctly described on the brittle shelf by a local approach to fracture such as that proposed by Beremin. 1.2 Value of the local approach To justify the mechanical integrity of nuclear-power-plant components, the global approach is used first. The global approach aims to describe the loading conditions of a cracked component leading to fracture by means of a single parameter which depends on the geometry and on the loading. The parameter most commonly used in the domain of cleavage fracture (linear elastic case) is the mode I stress intensity factor, {K}_{I} . Failure of the structure is obtained when this parameter reaches a critical value, the toughness {K}_{\mathit{Ic}} . The safety analysis compares the stress intensity factor with minimum values of the toughness of the steel, which are established by numerous mechanical tests and gathered in the form of an RCC-M Appendix Z.G. reference curve. Throughout the operating life of the vessel, it is verified that the toughness properties, deduced from exploitation of the surveillance programme, are higher than those provided by the reference curve, indexed on a conventional transition temperature RTNDT (Reference Temperature for Nil Ductility Transition) . The global approach is well validated and accepted, but it remains simple and conservative. It can therefore be too enveloping in certain particular cases, such as for example in the case of a “small-defect effect”, a “triaxiality effect”, a “warm pre-loading effect”, or in the case of non-proportional loading. This is why one may seek to use a finer local approach, which makes it possible to establish a link between the toughness of a material and the local fracture stress for a macroscopically homogeneous material. An additional reason for using the Beremin-type local-approach method is explained by the toughness values, which exhibit a large scatter in the ductile-brittle transition domain. By introducing a statistical model, this approach makes it possible to explain and quantify the scatter inherent in these tests, via knowledge of local metallurgical parameters . The industrial version of the Beremin model is, for its part, a deterministic approach which relies on the surface density of Weibull stress in order to characterise the stress field at the crack tip . 2 Brittle fracture 2.1 Mechanisms Brittle fracture is a sudden mode of fracture. It is generally associated with the phenomenon of cleavage. Cleavage is the complete decohesion of a crystal along one of its crystallographic planes. The theoretical local stress required for this separation of the crystal lattice {K}_{\mathit{Ic}} is very high, and is expressed as a function of the interplanar spacing and of the surface energy: {{\sigma}}_{c}=\sqrt{\frac{E{{\gamma}}_{s}}{{d}_{{hkl}}}} where E is Young's modulus, {{\gamma}}_{s} is the energy which corresponds to the creation of new surfaces and {d}_{{hkl}} is the interplanar spacing. However, the theoretical stress for separation of the atomic planes is never reached globally, but it can become so locally thanks to structures acting as stress amplifiers. In the case of steels, it is the numerous defects which play this role, whether they are due to plasticity at the crack tip (dislocations) or to the composition of the steel (inclusions, cracks) . Fracture of steels by cleavage generally distinguishes three successive phases: (1) nucleation, (2) propagation and (3) the crossing of the microstructural barriers (grain boundaries, bainite-packet boundaries). Nucleation corresponds to the development of a microcrack inside the sound metal; it is generally accepted that this stage requires a fairly small prior plastic strain, which produces a pile-up of dislocations and a stress singularity, and the reaching of a limit fracture stress {\sigma}_{c} (critical threshold). The phenomenon of nucleation of a microcrack can be explained by the various mechanisms of plasticity (Zener-Stroh, Cottrell, Smith, twinning) listed in . Once the nucleation stage has passed, a crack can propagate under a decreasing normal stress provided that an energy criterion of Griffith type is satisfied: {{\sigma}}_{c}=\sqrt{\frac{E \, W}{r}} with W which represents the fracture energy, and r the radius of a crack of circular shape. Unstable propagation of the cleavage cracks is obtained, at high speed, which can sometimes be slowed by a relaxation mechanism by glide of the dislocations (blunting of cleavage by emission of dislocations) . In order to be able to propagate in a polycrystal without being arrested by blunting, the crack must cross certain microstructural barriers (grain boundaries, interphases …) in order to lead to failure of the structure. At the microscopic level, the microstructural entity which controls fracture is not unique and depends strongly on the type of material. All three stages contribute to the description of brittle fracture. However, depending on the test temperature and the geometry of the specimen (notched or cracked), one of these stages is predominant and controls the triggering of brittle fracture. Consequently, within the framework of taking the cleavage mechanisms into account in a fracture model, only one of these three stages is used to define a fracture criterion . In the case of low-alloy steels at very low temperature ( T -160°C ) fracture is controlled by the propagation phase of the microcracks initiated on brittle second-phase particles (carbides, manganese sulphides, titanium nitrides) (, ). The amplification of the stresses results from the strain incompatibilities between these particles and the matrix. This amplification of the stresses at the head of the dislocation pile-up can cause: fracture of the brittle second-phase particle (figure r7.02.04-amorcageFissure) or, in the case of a weak particle/matrix interface, decohesion of the interface (figure r7.02.04-decohesion). Initiation of a microcrack on a brittle second-phase particle Decohesion of the interface Studies on the ferritic steels of vessels (16MND5) show that at low temperatures (negative temperatures), it is indeed the stage of propagation of the micro-defects (created during the initiation phase) into the surrounding ferritic matrix which constitutes the critical stage for propagating cleavage (see , and ). On the other hand, the origin of cleavage cannot be attributed solely to a single microstructural element (a chemical species). The influence of the microstructure of vessel steels is complex, since it can involve numerous parameters whose variation induces several consequences . Among these parameters, one thinks in particular of the grain size, the inclusion sizes and the distribution of defect sizes. One can therefore conclude that there exists a statistical aspect in terms of the population of defects leading to brittle fracture. For more details on the influence of the microstructure on brittle fracture in low-alloy steels of 16MND5 type, one may refer to the works , and . 2.2 Statistical aspect of brittle fracture Cleavage is a mode of fracture of a probabilistic nature, because the cleavage stress depends on the size distribution of the defects and the local mechanical fields depend on the local microstructure. Fracture initiates on the defect for which the critical stress is reached first. However, Ritchie, Knott and Rice (RKR model) postulate that fracture occurs only if the critical stress at the crack tip is reached over a characteristic distance which represents approximately the size of two grains. Thus cleavage fracture is conditioned by a characteristic distance and a critical defect size. The RKR model represents the first attempt to relate the resistance to brittle fracture, expressed by the toughness, to a local fracture criterion based on the nucleation mechanisms . This model opened the way towards probabilistic models. Subsequently, the works of Curry and Knott demonstrated that the characteristic distance of the RKR model must not be correlated with the grain size but with the distribution of the carbides and with their sizes. Thus, for a fixed grain size, at a given test temperature, the toughness of the material increases when the inter-particle distance decreases. These works made possible the introduction of the notion of statistics into the brittle-fracture models . However, in both models the scale effect and the scatter of the experimental measurements associated with the brittle fracture mode are not taken into account. In order to describe the scale effect and the scatter of the toughness measurements, statistical models were developed from the 1980s onwards. Among these models, the most commonly used are those of Beremin and of Wallin . These models rest on the weakest-link theory and on a Weibull statistic ( and ). The Beremin model enjoys strong recognition at the international level. The Beremin approach benefits from substantial feedback from experience, owing both to its maturity and to the number of researchers and engineers who have tested and modified it. The model makes it possible to take into account numerous effects (small defect, triaxiality, warm pre-loading) in complex loading situations. Numerous applications have been considered, both on specimens and on structures. 3 Description of the Beremin model In this section, the foundations of the Beremin model are first recalled. The assumptions linked to the definition of the potential cleavage sites are set out explicitly. The mechanism considered as critical is the propagation of a cleavage crack into the adjacent grain, itself considered as initiated by the mechanisms of plasticity. The fracture probability of these sites, which leads to the fracture probability of the structure, follows from this. The classical formulation of the Beremin model is extended to more general loadings by including a variant of plastic correction often used in this model . The Beremin model relies on knowledge of the local mechanical fields loading the structure considered. A structure subjected to a history of thermomechanical loadings from the time instant t=0 fixed arbitrarily is considered. The aim is to determine the cumulative fracture probability of this structure at any instant. By assumption, this structure consists (at least in part) of a steel liable to fail by cleavage at low temperature, exhibiting an elastoviscoplastic constitutive law, one of whose internal variables corresponds to the cumulative equivalent plastic strain: an example of a list of compatible laws is provided in the following paragraph. 3.1 Foundations 3.1.1 General assumptions The model considers a representative elementary volume {\Omega} of the material and rests on several fundamental assumptions summarised in : Assumption 1 It is assumed that the initiation of microcracks on the damage sites can occur only when plasticity is active (the cumulative plastic strain rate \dot{p}(u) at instant u must be positive \dot{p}(u)>0 ) and that their number no longer increases during the history of the loadings. - Let us emphasise that this active-plasticity condition, which will be the one considered throughout the remainder of the document, is different from the condition classically adopted ( p>0 ). These two conditions are equivalent in the case of a monotonic loading path. - For more general loading paths, this active-plasticity condition \dot{p}>0 leads on the contrary to much better results . Notes Assumption 2 It is noted that only the maximum principal stress {{\sigma}}_{I} is involved in the propagation of the defect, the defects then being considered as oriented perpendicularly to the principal direction. Assumption 3 The propagation of microcracks is controlled by a criterion of Griffith type. Assumption 4 Fracture will initiate from the most important defects in terms of size; only knowledge of the distribution of the latter is necessary. Assumption 5 The loaded structure can be considered as the juxtaposition of several volume elements {V}_{0} which are perfectly independent from the point of view of fracture. {V}_{0} must be as small as possible in order to verify statistical independence, but large enough for the probability of finding there a defect of sufficient size to be reasonable (in practice {V}_{0} includes a few grains). Assumption 6 The weakest-link theory is used, according to which the fracture of one of the elementary volumes {\delta}V entails the fracture of the whole of the structure. Assumption 7 A form of the defect distribution g is postulated for the positive stresses g({\sigma})={\alpha}'{{\sigma}}^{m-1} and g({\sigma})=0 \ \text{si} \ {\sigma} {V}_{0} ) and whose stress field is assumed homogeneous: 1-{p}_{r}(\delta V) = \prod_{\text{site}\in \delta V}(1-{p}_{r}(\text{site})) That is: {p}_{r}(\delta V) = 1-{ \left(1-{p}_{r}(\text{site}) \right)}^{\frac{\delta V}{{V}_{0}}} The survival probability of the structure (volume {\Omega} ) at the end of the loading is equal to the product of the survival probabilities of each of the elementary volumes {\delta}V (statistical independence). The survival probability of the structure then amounts to: 1-{P}_{r} = \prod_{\delta V\in \Omega }(1-{p}_{r}(\delta V)) = \prod_{\delta V\in \Omega }\left(1-{p}_{r}(\text{site})\right)^{\frac{\delta V}{{V}_{0}}} = \prod_{\delta V\in \Omega }\exp(\ln(1-{p}_{r}(\text{site}))\frac{\delta V}{{V}_{0}}) Given that {p}_{r}(\text{site}) remains small compared with unity, the previous expression can be simplified to give finally: {P}_{r} \approx 1-\prod_{{\delta}V\in {\Omega}} \exp \left(-{p}_{r}(\text{site})\frac{{\delta}V}{{V}_{0}} \right) = 1-\exp \left(-\underset{{\Omega}}{\int}{p}_{r}(\text{site})\frac{{\delta}V}{{V}_{0}} \right) That is: {P}_{r}=1-\exp\left(-x\right) \text{ avec } x=\underset{{\Omega}}{\int}{p}_{r}(\text{site})\frac{{\delta}V}{{V}_{0}} 3.3 Cumulative fracture probability of the sites The case of the radial and not necessarily monotonic loading path is considered here; the evolution of the mechanical fields in each element {\delta}V is characterised at every point by a history of maximum principal stress {{\sigma}_{I}(u)}_{0\le u\le t} . 3.3.1 Case in which the critical cleavage stress is independent of temperature The loading being radial, the direction of the maximum principal stress is assumed constant. Only the past times u for which plasticity is active ( \dot{p}(u)>0 ) are considered, since fracture is possible only at those instants (assumption 1). \left\lbrace u 0\right\rbrace denotes the set of these instants for the element {\delta}V considered. According to assumption (2), only the maximum principal stress {{\sigma}}_{I} is involved in the propagation of the defect. For the volume {\delta}V to be broken at instant t , it is necessary that: {{\sigma}}_{\text{Ic}}\le \underset{\left\lbrace u 0\right\rbrace }{\max}{{\sigma}}_{I}(u) Taking assumption (7) into account, the fracture probability of this volume {\delta}V can therefore be written: {p}_{r}(\text{site}) = \underset{0}{\overset{\underset{\left\lbrace u 0\right\rbrace }{\max}{{\sigma}}_{I}(u)}{\int}}g({\sigma}) \, d{\sigma} = {\left(\frac{\underset{\left\lbrace u 0\right\rbrace }{\max}{{\sigma}}_{I}(u)}{{{\sigma}}_{u}}\right)}^{m} By defining {{\sigma}}_{u}={\left(\frac{m}{{\alpha}'}\right)}^{\frac{1}{m}} as the cleavage stress (that is, the stress for which the cumulative fracture probability of the potential cleavage sites is equal to 1 ), the fracture probability of the structure can be written as: {P}_{r} = 1-\exp\left(-{\left(\frac{{{\sigma}}_{W}}{{{\sigma}}_{u}}\right)}^{m}\right) with {{\sigma}}_{W} being the Weibull stress at instant t defined by: {\sigma}_{W}(t)={\left[\underset{{\Omega}}{\int}{{\sigma}}_{I}^{m}\frac{{\delta}V}{{V}_{0}}\right]}^{\frac{1}{m}} \text{ avec } {\sigma}_{I}=\underset{\left\lbrace u 0\right\rbrace }{\max}{{\sigma}}_{I}(u) In this expression, the Weibull modulus m gives an idea of the scatter of the size of the defects liable to initiate brittle fracture. {{\sigma}}_{u} represents a mean fracture stress of a sample of volume {V}_{0} . In the case where, at every instant, the evolution of the mechanical fields in each element {\delta}V is assumed radial and monotonically increasing ( \dot{p}>0 ), the previous expression for the Weibull stress reduces to: {\sigma}_{W} = {\left[\underset{{\Omega}}{\int}{{\sigma}}_{I}^{m}\frac{{\delta}V}{{V}_{0}}\right]}^{\frac{1}{m}} 3.3.2 Case in which the critical cleavage stress is dependent on temperature Until now the parameters of the cleavage model have been considered independent of temperature. Application of the local approach to real study transients (for example, the simulations of warm pre-loading tests on 16MND5 steel with the Beremin model) requires modification of the initial formulation in order to be able to take into account loading paths comprising mechanical and thermal unloadings (see , and ) and also in order to be able to take into account the dependence of the cleavage stress on temperature. For this, it is assumed that the evolution of the mechanical fields in each element {\delta}V is radial and non-monotonic. This evolution is characterised by a history of maximum principal stress {{\sigma}}_{I}(u{)}_{0\le u\le t} as well as by a temperature history {\theta}{\left(u\right)}_{0\le u\le t} . For every instant u , it is assumed that, in the vicinity of each damage site, the “microscopic” normal stress satisfies: {\sigma}_{I\left(\text{micro}\right)}\left(u\right) = f{{\sigma}}_{I}\left(u\right) f being a localisation parameter depending only on the mean temperature {\theta}\left(u\right) in {\delta}V . For the damage site not to have failed, it is therefore necessary that: {{\sigma}}_{\mathit{Ic}}\ge {{\sigma}}_{I\left(\mathit{micro}\right)}(u) \text{ tel que } \dot{p}\left(u\right)>0 That is: {{\sigma}}_{\text{Ic}}\ge f{{\sigma}}_{I}(u) \text{ tel que } \dot{p}\left(u\right)>0 So that the cumulative fracture probability of a site amounts to: {p}_{r}\left(\text{site}\right) = {\left[\underset{\left[u 0\right]}{\max}\left\lbrace \frac{{{\sigma}}_{I}\left(u\right).f\left({\theta}\left(u\right)\right)}{{{\sigma}}_{u}}\right\rbrace \right]}^{m} Or again: {p}_{r}\left(\text{site}\right) = {\left[\underset{\left[u 0\right]}{\max}\left\lbrace \frac{{{\sigma}}_{I}\left(u\right)}{{{\sigma}}_{u}\left({\theta}\left(u\right)\right)}\right\rbrace \right]}^{m} With {{\sigma}}_{u}\left({\theta}\right) a function of temperature such that: {{\sigma}}_{u}\left({\theta}\right)=\frac{{{\sigma}}_{u}}{f\left({\theta}\right)} The introduction of the localisation parameter f therefore leads to an apparent dependence of the cleavage stress. In a general manner, the cumulative fracture probability of the structure is expressed by: {P}_{r} = 1-\exp\left(-{\int}_{{\Omega}}{\left[\underset{\left\lbrace u 0\right\rbrace }{\max}\left\lbrace \frac{{{\sigma}}_{I}\left(u\right)}{{{\sigma}}_{u}\left({\theta}\left(u\right)\right)}\right\rbrace \right]}^{m}\frac{{\delta}\text{V}}{{V}_{0}}\right) It is this latter formulation which is used to simulate the warm pre-loading tests and, more generally, the loading paths with unloading. Denoting by {{\sigma}}_{u}^{o} a value chosen arbitrarily, one can write: {P}_{r} = 1-\exp\left(-{\left(\frac{{{\sigma}}_{W}^{o}}{{{\sigma}}_{u}^{o}}\right)}^{m}\right) The Weibull stress {\sigma}_{w}^{o} then becomes: {{\sigma}}_{W}^{o} = {\left[{\int}_{{\Omega}}{(\tilde{{\sigma}}}_{I}^{o}{)}^{m}\frac{{\delta}V}{{V}_{0}}\right]}^{\frac{1}{m}} \text{ avec } {\tilde{{\sigma}}}_{I}^{o}=\underset{\left[u 0\right]}{\max}\left\lbrace \frac{{{\sigma}}_{u}^{o}{{\sigma}}_{I}\left(u\right)}{{{\sigma}}_{u}\left({\theta}\left(u\right)\right)}\right\rbrace 3.4 Plastic-strain correction Several works on fracture by cleavage show the beneficial effect of plastic strain on the resistance to cleavage. Several reasons are put forward by the authors, and in particular the apparent reduction of the micro-defects in the direction perpendicular to tension under large strains. It is also probable that a pre-strain at temperatures higher than that of cleavage may lead to a blunting of the micro-defects already present in the material. A correction of the largest principal stress {{\sigma}}_{I} which enters the computation of the Weibull stress has been proposed in the Beremin model. The principal stress is corrected by a factor depending on the plastic strain along the principal direction {{\varepsilon}}_{I}^{p} : {{\sigma}}_{I}^{\star}={{\sigma}}_{I}\exp\left(-\frac{{{\varepsilon}}_{I}^{p}}{k}\right) \text{ avec } 2 \le k \le 4 The new expression for the Weibull stress is: {{\sigma}}_{W} = {\left[\underset{{\Omega}}{\int}{({{\sigma}}_{I})}^{m}\exp\left(-\frac{{{\varepsilon}}_{I}^{p}m}{k}\right)\frac{{\delta}V}{{V}_{0}}\right]}^{\frac{1}{m}} The fracture probability of a site at a given instant t is now written: {p}_{r}(\text{site}) = \underset{\left\lbrace u 0\right\rbrace }{\max}\lbrace \frac{{{\sigma}}_{I}\left(u\right)}{{{\sigma}}_{u}\left({\theta}\left(u\right)\right)}.\exp{\left(-\frac{1}{2}{{\varepsilon}}_{I}^{p}\left(u\right)\right)\rbrace }^{m} For a monotonic loading path (constant and uniform temperature), the previous relation leads to the classical expression : {p}_{r}(\text{site}) = {\left[\frac{{{\sigma}}_{I}}{{{\sigma}}_{u}}\right]}^{m}\exp \left(-\frac{m}{2}{{\varepsilon}}_{I}^{p} \right) 3.5 Threshold stress As detailed in reference , several authors, including Bakker and Koers (1991), propose a probability distribution for the fracture stress based on a three-parameter Weibull distribution (Weibull, 1939; Mann et al., 1974). The formulation implies the introduction of a critical stress \sigma_{th} directly into the brittle-fracture probability P_r = 1-\exp\left(-\frac{1}{V_0}\int_\Omega \left(\frac{\sigma_I-\sigma_{th}}{\sigma_u}\right)^m\right)=1-\exp\left(-\left(\frac{\sigma^\star_w}{\sigma_u}\right)^m\right), \sigma_I\geq \sigma_{th} with a modified Weibull stress \sigma^\star_w For example, in the case TYPE_SEUIL = "REDUIT" POST_BEREMIN, one will have : In the case TYPE_SEUIL = "RESTREINT", one will have : \sigma^\star_w = \left(\frac{1}{V_0} \int_{\Omega_{th}} \sigma_I ^m dV \right)^\frac1m \ \text{avec} \ \Omega_{th} \text{ le volume où } \sigma_I > \sigma_{th} 3.6 Temporal maximum Reference proposes a variant of the Beremin model by offering the possibility of considering the instantaneous value instead of the temporal maximum over the whole history for the maximum principal stress. This consists in replacing, in the equations of paragraph 3.3, the quantity \underset{\left\lbrace u 0\right\rbrace }{\max}{{\sigma}}_{I}(u) by \sigma_I(t) 3.7 Active plasticity It is possible to deactivate the condition \dot{p}(u)>0 . In this case, integration of the stress field is carried out over the whole of the volume. This variant of the Beremin model is used in particular in the case of a three-parameter Weibull distribution . 3.8 Industrial version of the Beremin model This deterministic variation of the model is described in detail in references and . Its main lines are taken up here. The industrial version of the Beremin model considers that, in the most penalising case, the instability of brittle fracture originates from the interaction between the maximum principal stress \sigma_I and a distribution of initiation sites liable to initiate cleavage in the plane perpendicular to the most highly loaded defect. The combination of these two factors leads one to quantify the risk of sudden fracture by means of a surface density of Weibull stress, denoted \sigma_W^{2D} , defined as follows : \sigma_W^{2D} = \left[ \frac{1}{V_0} . \int_{A_p} \left _+^m dS \right]^{1/m} In the expression above, m is the material parameter linked to the distribution of the initiation sites, \sigma_{th} is the threshold stress (the minimum stress below which a site cannot initiate cleavage), and V_0 a normalisation constant usually fixed at 50 \mu m ^3 Finally, A_p corresponds to the zone of active plasticity in the plane perpendicular to the crack tip. In practice, for sufficiently high values of \sigma_{th} , this surface is included in the zone such that \sigma_I > \sigma_{th} and this active-plasticity condition is abandoned. In practice, computation of the volume integrand of the Weibull stress is identical in the case of the Beremin model and of its industrial version. Once the integrand has been computed over the volume, it is projected onto planes perpendicular to the crack front (illustration in the figure below). Planes of integration of \sigma_W^{2D} along a semi-elliptical front 4 Implementation 4.1 Computation of the fracture probability Advice on the use of this model is given in the documentation U2.05.08. Consider a domain {\Omega}_{c} of the structure studied, which may be the whole of the mesh studied, a mesh-cell group or a mesh cell. Following an elastoplastic thermomechanical analysis, the evolution of the fields of stress, of strain and of cumulative plastic strain in this domain is known. From the stress field at the tip of the crack (or of the notch), the aim is to determine the cumulative cleavage fracture probability of the structure (Beremin model) or the surface density of Weibull stress (industrial version of the Beremin model). Use of the model is made in post-processing by means of the macro-command POST_BEREMIN. Moreover, in the case of a filter on active plasticity or of any plastic correction, the constitutive law of the material must include an internal variable corresponding to the plastic indicator or to the cumulative equivalent plastic strain p . These are in particular the laws (non-exhaustive list): VMIS_ISOT_ , VMIS_ECMI_ , VMIS_ _CHAB, ROUSS_ , LEMAITRE, MONOCRISTAL. The corresponding numerical integration in code_aster is carried out in two stages: - {{\sigma}}_{I} is computed at each Gauss point - the filters requested by the user are applied (active plasticity, threshold stress, maximum of the stresses over the history) - by quadrature over each mesh cell, then by simple summation over the target domain {\Omega}_{c} , the Weibull stress and the associated fracture probability are deduced from it. The summation is weighted by a multiplicative coefficient which takes into account any symmetries and the type of modelling adopted (axisymmetric, 2D, 3D..). Care will be taken to define this coefficient (COEF_MULT) in accordance with the indications given in POST_BEREMIN. The first stage makes it possible to introduce a variant (keyword SIGM_ELMOY instead of SIGM_ELGA) leading to appreciably different results in the case of a cracked structure (presence of a gradient): in each mesh cell, {{\sigma}}_{I} is determined from the average, weighted by the Gauss weights over this mesh cell, of the stress field. 4.2 Parameters of the material The Beremin model requires knowledge of several parameters: the characteristic parameters of the material considered in the Weibull law, m and {\sigma}_{u} (possibly the threshold stress \sigma_th ) as well as the elementary volume of the elementary plastic zone {V}_{0} . The elementary volume {V}_{0} must be sufficiently large in order to comply with assumption (5). In the Weibull law, the parameters {V}_{0} and {{\sigma}}_{u} are not independent: it is the product {V}_{0}{{\sigma}}_{u}^{m} which enters the computation of the fracture probability. The identification of these parameters is not unique, but depends strongly on the computed stress fields. 4.3 Projection for the industrial version of the Beremin model The various stages making it possible to compute the surface density of Weibull stresses are presented below. 1. The integrand of the Weibull stress is computed over the volume specified by the user, as a function of the various filters or options requested (active plasticity, threshold stress, average per element, and maximum of the stress history). This stage is therefore identical for the Beremin model and for its industrial version. 2. The volume integrand is then projected onto the integration plane. For example, in the case of a formulation with a threshold stress, it is the quantity \left _+^m which is projected. 3. The surface integral is then computed in order to obtain \sigma_W^{2D} Thus, for each integration plane, it is necessary to compute a projector making it possible to pass from a field expressed at the Gauss points of the 3D model to a field expressed on the 2D mesh of the integration plane. To this end, the field expressed at the Gauss points is transformed into fields by cells on the dual mesh. Each cell of the 2D mesh is located by its centre, and one identifies to which 3D cell or cells this centre belongs (to within a numerical precision). These operations are carried out in medcoupling. Construction of this projector can be relatively slow, but it is carried out only once per plane. In the case of a sensitivity analysis with respect to the material parameters, it is therefore strongly recommended to supply all the material parameters in the same call to POST_BEREMIN. 5 Alternative approaches Among the local models introduced into code_aster (R7.02.06 and U2.05.08) which make it possible to describe brittle fracture by cleavage, there exists the Bordet model (see and R7.02.06). This model represents an extension of the Beremin model in which it is assumed that the microcracks created at the moment when the plasticity threshold is reached remain potentially active throughout the loading which follows. However, in steels, global fracture is mainly linked to newly created microcracks. The level of plastic strain reached at each instant must therefore be taken into account. This option is possible in the Beremin model via the plastic-correction option . The effect of plasticity on the micro-defects is taken into account in the Bordet model by considering that the cleavage probability is expressed as the product of the probabilities of nucleation and of propagation at the same instant. Among the other alternative approaches there is the Gp approach, which makes it possible to define a criterion for initiation of an already existing crack through the computation of the elastic energy-release rate. This approach is valid in linear elasticity as well as in non-linear elasticity. This option is valid both for a meshed crack (classical finite elements) and for a non-meshed crack (enriched finite elements: X-FEM method). It is available in 2D (modellings 'C_PLAN' and 'D_PLAN' for a meshed or non-meshed crack; modelling 'AXIS' for a meshed crack only) and in 3D, for linear or quadratic finite elements. All the classical thermomechanical loadings are taken into account: thermal loadings, body loadings (gravity, rotation, …), surface loadings (including on the lips of the crack). r7.02.06 Bordet model and Rice and Tracey model r7.02.06 Bordet model and Rice and Tracey model Summary The foundations of the local-approach models of fracture which make it possible to model brittle fracture (Bordet model) and ductile initiation (Rice and Tracey model) are recalled. In the case of the brittle-fracture model (Bordet), one describes how the fracture probability of a structure is computed from the knowledge of the mechanical fields loading it. Placing oneself in the general case of a non-monotonic thermomechanical loading path and assuming that certain parameters of the models do not depend on the temperature, one establishes the general expression for the cumulative fracture probabilities. The model leading to the cavity-growth law of Rice and Tracey is then presented, together with the ductile-initiation criterion relating to it. Finally, indications concerning the implementation of these models in code_aster are summarised. 1 Introduction One is interested here in a metallic structure loaded thermomechanically. One seeks to determine fracture criteria for this structure, representative of the two mechanisms encountered on certain steels: - at low temperature, certain metallic materials (such as reactor-vessel steel) may behave as brittle materials, fracturing suddenly by cleavage, - at higher temperature, ductile tearing appears. By contrast with the global approach, the Bordet and Rice–Tracey models presented here rely on knowledge of the mechanical fields in the most highly loaded zones in order to obtain a local fracture criterion representative of the physical mechanisms involved (instability of cleavage microcracks, or growth then coalescence of the porosity). The foundations of the Beremin model, which likewise makes it possible to model brittle fracture, are given in the documentation R7.02.04. Advice on the use of the Beremin and Bordet models is given in the documentation U2.05.08. 2 The Bordet model The Bordet model is presented briefly here. For further details, one may refer to [3], [4] or [5]. The Bordet model is based on the same foundations as that of Beremin. It defines a probability of fracture by local cleavage. However, in the Beremin model, one assumes the creation of microcracks at the moment when the plasticity threshold is reached, and these microcracks remain potentially active throughout the loading which follows. In steels, however, global fracture is mainly related to newly created microcracks. The level of plastic strain reached at each time instant must therefore be taken into account. This is already possible in the Beremin model via the plastic-correction option defined in the document U4.81.22. In the Bordet model, this is taken into account by considering that the probability of fracture by cleavage is the product of the probabilities of nucleation and of propagation at the same time instant. 2.1 Local cleavage-fracture probability of the Bordet model The local criterion is defined here as the statistical event of simultaneously fulfilling the conditions of nucleation and of propagation of the microcracks. In the model, nucleation and propagation of the microcracks are considered as independent events; nucleation denotes the fracture of a carbide leading to the formation of a microcrack, whereas propagation is defined as the local instability of cleavage driven solely by the local stresses. The local cleavage-fracture probability is then written: {P}_{\mathit{cliv}}={P}_{\mathit{nucl}}{P}_{\mathit{propa}} By plastic strain {\varepsilon}_{p} one means the equivalent plastic strain defined by: {\epsilon}_{p}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{\epsilon}_{p}:{\epsilon}_{p}} This definition is valid only for elastoplastic constitutive laws with a von Mises criterion. In code_aster , only constitutive laws of this type are therefore suited to this model. 2.1.1 Local nucleation probability With the definition given above, the probability of nucleation of a microcrack during an increment of plastic strain d{\epsilon}_{p} is proportional to the yield stress {\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p}) at the temperature T and the plastic strain rate {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{p} : {P}_{\mathit{nucl}}\propto {N}_{\mathit{unc}}({\epsilon}_{p}){\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p})d{\epsilon}_{p} This remains true so long as the number of microcracked carbides remains small compared with the number of sound carbides {N}_{\mathrm{unc}}({\varepsilon}_{p}) . The microcracking rate of the carbides is constant for a given plastic strain; the number of sound sites varies exponentially with {\varepsilon}_{p} . Denoting by {\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0} the yield stress at a reference temperature and plastic strain rate and by {\varepsilon}_{p,0} a reference plastic strain, the probability {P}_{\mathrm{nucl}} may be expressed as follows: {P}_{\mathit{nucl}}\propto \frac{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p})}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}}\exp\left(\frac{-{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p})}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}}\frac{{\epsilon}_{p}}{{\epsilon}_{p,0}}\right) If the plastic strain is small, and therefore if the cracking of carbides is fairly limited, i.e. \frac{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}{\epsilon}_{p,0}}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p})}\gg {\epsilon}_{p} , then the nucleation probability reduces to {P}_{\mathit{nucl}}\propto \frac{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p})}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}} . 2.1.2 Local propagation probability As in the Beremin model R4.02.04, the size density of the carbide microcracks is assumed to be distributed according to an inverse power law (with \alpha and \beta material parameters independent of the temperature and of the strain rates, and l the size of the microcrack): f(l)=\frac{\alpha}{{l}^{\beta}} The cracking of a carbide will propagate into the ferrite (by virtue of the propagation inertia alone, by a dynamic effect) only on condition that a sufficiently high local stress is present. An upper bound on the size of a nucleated ferritic microcrack {l}_{max}=l\left({\sigma}_{\mathit{th}}\right) is therefore introduced; it makes it possible to define the minimum local stress necessary for the propagation of the largest possible ferritic microcrack. The propagation probability is therefore written: {P}_{\mathit{propa}}({\sigma}_{I})={\int}_{{l}_{c}({\sigma}_{I})}^{{l}_{max}}f(l)\mathit{dl} With {\sigma}_{I} the maximum principal stress, {\sigma}_{\mathrm{th}} the threshold below which propagation cannot take place and {l}_{c} the critical size of the ferritic microcrack, obeying the Griffith relation for an elliptical microcrack: {l}_{c}\left(\sigma \right)=\frac{\pi E{\gamma}_{p}}{2\left(1-{\nu}^{2}\right){\sigma}^{2}} With E Young's modulus, \nu Poisson's ratio and {\gamma}_{p} the surface energy density. One finally obtains: \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}{P}_{\mathit{propa}}({\sigma}_{I})& =0& {\sigma}_{I}<{\sigma}_{\mathit{th}}\\ {P}_{\mathit{propa}}({\sigma}_{I})& =\left({\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{I}}{{\sigma}_{u}}\right)}^{m}-{\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{\mathit{th}}}{{\sigma}_{u}}\right)}^{m}\right)& {\sigma}_{I}⩾{\sigma}_{\mathit{th}}\end{array} With m a parameter independent of the temperature, like \alpha and \beta , and {\sigma}_{u} which may depend on it (if Young's modulus depends on it). As for the Beremin model, the effects of the orientation of the microcracks relative to the direction of the maximum principal stress are taken into account only via the parameter {\sigma}_{u} . 2.1.3 Local cleavage probability As stated previously, the local cleavage probability is assumed to be the product of the nucleation probability and the propagation probability; for this one considers that, during an infinitesimal increment of plastic strain, the active stress is constant. Whence, if {\sigma}_{I}⩾{\sigma}_{\mathit{th}} : \begin{array}{ccc}{P}_{\mathit{cliv}}\left({\sigma}_{I},d{\epsilon}_{p}\right)& \propto & {P}_{\mathit{nucl}}\left(d{\epsilon}_{p}\right).{P}_{\mathit{propa}}\left({\sigma}_{I}\right)\\ \text{}& \propto & \frac{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}\left(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p}\right)}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}}\exp\left(\frac{-{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}\left(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p}\right)}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}}\frac{{\epsilon}_{p}}{{\epsilon}_{p,0}}\right)\left({\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{I}\left({\epsilon}_{p}\right)}{{\sigma}_{u}}\right)}^{m}-{\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{\mathit{th}}}{{\sigma}_{u}}\right)}^{m}\right)d{\epsilon}_{p}\end{array} This equation does not indicate that the nucleated microcracks remain active during the increment of plastic strain, but rather that the propagation condition for each of these microcracks is determined by the value of the local stress field at the moment of creation. The probability that a ferritic microcrack is created and propagates over a plastic-strain interval \left[0,{\epsilon}_{p,u}\right] is then: {P}_{\mathit{cliv}}\left({\sigma}_{I},{\epsilon}_{p,u}\right)\propto {\int}_{0}^{{\epsilon}_{p,u}}\frac{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}\left(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p}\right)}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}}\exp\left(\frac{-{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}\left(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p}\right)}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}}\frac{{\epsilon}_{p}}{{\epsilon}_{p,0}}\right)\left({\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{I}\left({\epsilon}_{p}\right)}{{\sigma}_{u}}\right)}^{m}-{\left(\frac{{\sigma}_{\mathit{th}}}{{\sigma}_{u}}\right)}^{m}\right)d{\epsilon}_{p} This probability does indeed reduce to 0 if the stress remains below {\sigma}_{\mathrm{th}} throughout the loading path. 2.2 Global cleavage-fracture probability of Bordet The previous paragraph has made it possible to determine the local cleavage-fracture probability. Following the weakest-link principle, the global cleavage-fracture probability over {n}_{c} potential initiation sites is written: {P}_{\mathit{Bordet}}=1-\exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{{n}_{c}}{P}_{\mathit{cliv}}\left({\sigma}_{I,i},{\epsilon}_{p,u,i}\right)\right) This equation may be expressed as a function of the volume of the process zone by introducing an infinitesimal volume \mathrm{dV} over which the strains and the stresses are constant (in the numerical case, the Gauss point). In order to compare simply the Beremin and Bordet probabilities on a given example, one may define a Bordet stress of the same type as the Weibull stress: {\sigma}_{\mathit{Bordet}}={\left\lbrace {\int}_{{V}_{p}}\left({\int}_{0}^{{\epsilon}_{p,u}}\frac{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}\left(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p}\right)}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}}\left({\left({\sigma}_{I}\left({\epsilon}_{p},\mathit{dV}\right)\right)}^{m}-{\left({\sigma}_{\mathit{th}}\right)}^{m}\right)\exp\left(\frac{-{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}\left(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p}\right)}{{\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0}}\frac{{\epsilon}_{p}}{{\epsilon}_{p,0}}\right)d{\epsilon}_{p}\right)\frac{\mathit{dv}}{{V}_{0}}\right\rbrace }^{\frac{1}{m}} and the global cleavage-fracture probability is written with a Weibull distribution: {P}_{\mathrm{Bordet}}=1-\exp(-{(\frac{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{Bordet}}}{{\sigma}_{u}})}^{m}) If the number of microcracked carbides is small compared with the number of sound carbides, the exponential term is close to 1 and the Bordet stress is thereby simplified. 2.3 Discussion 2.3.1 Bordet or Beremin? The Bordet model is slightly more complex and finer than the Beremin model. One of its advantages is that it considers the maximum principal stress at each time instant, and not the maximum principal stress during the loading; consequently nothing prevents the Bordet probability from decreasing, unlike that of Beremin. Moreover, the Bordet model accounts for the fact that a region with a lower stress but a larger plastic strain may be more critical than a zone in which the stresses are higher but the level of plastic strain is lower. However, the Bordet model requires knowledge of additional material parameters, as will be described in the paragraph below. 2.3.2 Material parameters The usual Beremin model requires knowledge of three material parameters: the two shape parameters of the Weibull law, m and {\sigma}_{u} , as well as the elementary volume of the plastic zone {V}_{0} ; only the parameter {\sigma}_{u} depends on the temperature. To these three parameters, one may add the threshold plastic strain making it possible to define the plastic zone over which the integration is carried out. The first three parameters are formally retained by the Bordet model. Note: they are only formally retained; they may be different and require a calibration of the same type as that carried out for Beremin and presented in R7.02.09. Other parameters are added to them. The plasticity threshold {\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}(T,{\dot{\epsilon}}_{p}) is a function at least of the temperature and potentially of the plastic strain rate, and its reference value {\sigma}_{\mathit{ys},0} . The critical stress below which propagation of the ferritic microcracks cannot take place, {\sigma}_{\mathrm{th}} , independent of the loading conditions. In the complete version only (with the exponential term taken into account), a reference plastic strain {\varepsilon}_{p,0} whose identification method is not given and which seems fairly delicate. One will note that the author himself (cf. [8], [9]) seems to use, for certain studies and validation, the version of the model in which this parameter does not appear (for the user of code_aster, it is sufficient to specify PROBA_NUCL='NON') 2.4 Implementation in code_aster The computation of the Bordet probability and stress is carried out by the operator POST_BORDET. It requires a prior elastoplastic thermomechanical analysis via the operator STAT_NON_LINE. Advice on the use of this model is given in the documentation U2.05.08. In the version currently implemented, the temperature of the medium on which the analysis is carried out must be uniform (but may evolve in the course of time); this limitation does not seem prohibitive inasmuch as the plastic zone at the crack tip is as a rule fairly small. It is possible to carry out the analysis with or without the exponential term; if this term is requested, the material parameter {\varepsilon}_{p,0} must be supplied. In all cases, one computes at each time instant the quantities such as the maximum principal stress and the equivalent plastic strain. One determines the value of the parameters {\sigma}_{u}(T) and {\sigma}_{\mathit{ys}}(T,\dot{{\epsilon}_{p}}) as a function of the material data supplied by the user, then one computes the global Bordet stress by summation over the Gauss points of the elements of the mesh-cell group indicated by the user, and finally the global Bordet fracture probability over all the time instants up to the one requested. The analysis carried out is finally written as follows: {\sigma}_{\mathrm{Bordet}}={\left\lbrace \sum_{o\text{=1}}^{{n}_{\mathrm{inst}}}\sum_{\mathrm{el}\text{=1}}^{{n}_{\mathrm{elem}}}\sum_{\mathrm{pg}=1}^{{n}_{\mathrm{pg}}}(\begin{array}{}\frac{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{ys}}(T(o),{\dot{\bar{\varepsilon}}}_{p,\mathrm{el},\mathrm{pg}}(o))}{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{ys},0}}\\ \mathrm{Max}({\bar{\sigma}}_{1,\mathrm{el},\mathrm{pg}}^{m}(o)-{\sigma}_{\mathrm{th}}^{m},0)\\ \exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{\mathrm{ys}}(T(o),{\dot{\bar{\varepsilon}}}_{p,\mathrm{el},\mathrm{pg}}(o))}{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{ys},0}}\frac{{\bar{\varepsilon}}_{p,\mathrm{el},\mathrm{pg}}(o)}{{\varepsilon}_{p,0}})\\ \Delta {\varepsilon}_{p,\mathrm{el},\mathrm{pg}}(o)\frac{{V}_{\mathrm{el},\mathrm{pg}}}{{V}_{0}}\end{array})\right\rbrace }^{1/m} With {n}_{\mathrm{inst}} the number of time instants over which the analysis is carried out, {n}_{\mathrm{elem}} the number of elements contained in the mesh-cell group requested by the user and {n}_{\mathrm{pg}} the number of Gauss points of each of these elements. Moreover, for any scalar a , \bar{a}(o)=\frac{a(o)+a(o-1)}{2} , \dot{a}(o)=\frac{a(o)-a(o-1)}{t(o)-t(o-1)} and \Delta a(o)=a(o)-a(o-1) . The result is a table containing the global values of the Bordet stress and of the Bordet fracture probability. For the analysis to be correct, the user must supply the keyword COEF_MULT as recommended in the user's documentation of POST_BORDET. 3 The Rice and Tracey model One is now interested in the case of ductile initiation. Considering a volume element initially sound, the ductile tearing of this element results from the following elementary mechanisms: - nucleation of cavities caused by the decohesion of inclusions present in the material, - growth then coalescence of these cavities. 3.1 Isolated cavity in an infinite rigid-plastic matrix In an approach of analytical understanding, Rice and Tracey studied the behaviour of a cavity, initially spherical (surface {S}_{v} ), isolated in an infinite isotropic medium (volume V ), with rigid-plastic von Mises behaviour (yield stress {\sigma}_{0} ), incompressible, subjected at infinity to an arbitrary strain rate {\dot{\varepsilon}}^{\infty} (stress denoted {\sigma}^{\infty} at infinity). They show that the displacement-velocity field, solution of the mechanical problem posed, minimises the functional: Q(\dot{u})=\underset{V}{\int}\left[{s}_{ij}(\dot{\epsilon})-{s}_{ij}^{\infty}\right]{\dot{\epsilon}}_{ij}\text{dV}-{\sigma}_{ij}^{\infty}\underset{{S}_{v}}{\int}{n}_{i}{\dot{u}}_{j}\text{dS} 3.2 Approximate law of cavity growth By succeeding in minimising this functional in various situations, Rice and Tracey then showed the predominant influence of the triaxiality ratio \frac{{\sigma}_{m}^{\infty}}{{\sigma}_{\text{eq}}^{\infty}} ( with {\sigma}_{m}^{\infty} the trace and {\sigma}_{\text{eq}}^{\infty} the von Mises equivalent of the stress imposed on the volume element considered) on the cavity growth rate. They even exhibit a cavity-growth law which, although approximate, is very close to the results of the previous model. Thus, in each of the principal directions (K) associated with the strain rate {\dot{\epsilon}}^{\infty} , the elongation rate of a cavity amounts to: {\dot{R}}_{K}=\left\lbrace \mathrm{\chi }{\dot{\epsilon}}_{K}^{\infty}+{\dot{\epsilon}}_{\text{eq}}^{\infty}D\right\rbrace {R}_{K} For a principal direction K , the parameter {R}_{K} is the radius of the cavity, {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{K}^{\infty} the principal value of the strain rate imposed at infinity and {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{eq}}^{\infty} the von Mises equivalent value of the strain rate imposed at infinity. This relation, in which the coefficients \khi and D depend on the situation envisaged: - \khi =\frac{5}{3} for a linearly hardening matrix or a perfectly plastic matrix at low triaxiality ratio, or \khi =2 in the case of a perfectly plastic matrix at high triaxiality ratio, - D=\alpha \exp(\frac{3{\sigma}_{m}^{\infty}}{2{\sigma}_{0}}) for a perfectly plastic matrix or D=\frac{{\sigma}_{m}^{\infty}}{4{\sigma}_{{}^{\text{eq}}}^{\infty}} for a linearly hardening matrix. \alpha =0,283 is the value given by Rice and Tracey, whereas more precise computations (cf. [bib4]) have shown that this coefficient is higher ( \alpha =1,28 ). Mudry then proposed to apply these theoretical results to the case of reactor-vessel steel, i.e. : - behaviour intermediate between the extreme behaviour cases studied by Rice and Tracey, with non-zero but reasonable hardening, - cracked structures (high triaxiality ratio). He deduced from this the following approximate law, valid for sufficiently high triaxiality ratios (greater than 0.5): \dot{R}=\alpha {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{eq}}^{{p}^{\infty}}\exp(\frac{3{\sigma}_{m}^{\infty}}{2{\sigma}_{{}_{\text{eq}}}^{\infty}})R In which: - {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{eq}}^{\infty} has been replaced by {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{\text{eq}}^{{p}^{\infty}} (von Mises equivalent of the plastic part of the strain rate) in order to extend the Rice and Tracey law to the elastoplastic case, - the yield stress {\sigma}_{0} has been replaced by {\sigma}_{\text{eq}}^{\infty} in order to take account of the hardening of the matrix around the cavity. Experimental measurements of porosity growth for various triaxiality ratios have made it possible to validate this expression. These results show that, when the initial porosity ratio remains low, the exponential character of the relation between the cavity radius and the triaxiality ratio is indeed confirmed. On the other hand, the coefficient \alpha depends on the material considered as well as on the initial porosity fraction. 3.3 Ductile-initiation criterion {R}_{0} and R(t) denoting the radius of the cavities initially and at the time instant t considered, the ductile-initiation criterion adopted here is: \frac{R(t)}{{R}_{0}}={(\frac{R}{{R}_{0}})}_{c} The left-hand side of this expression results from the integration of the growth law, in accordance with the indications of the previous paragraph. Several arguments of principle may be raised against the direct use of this Rice and Tracey cavity-growth law as a ductile-initiation criterion. Thus: - the inclusions, and therefore the cavities, are not in reality isolated. Worse, they are often grouped in clusters, - the coalescence of the cavities doubtless results from interactions which, likewise, are not described in the model established, - in a cracked structure, the presence of gradients at the crack tip makes the previous analysis, which concerns an infinite medium subjected to homogeneous boundary conditions, less directly applicable. Nevertheless, by using the previous criterion, one hopes that this law remains realistic, on average, even in clusters or in zones of strong gradients (average over an element of dimensions comparable to that of the Beremin model). Furthermore, one makes the hypothesis that the critical size retained, generally recalibrated on given geometries (CT specimen, for example), represents the coalescence, which amounts to assuming that the coalescence does not depend too much on the nature of the mechanical loadings imposed on the volume element (triaxiality, shear, ...). Let us note finally that the Rice and Tracey model is only an approximate law, valid for high triaxiality ratios ( i.e . greater than 0.5). 3.4 Implementation in code_aster Consider a domain {\Omega}_{c} of the structure studied, which may be the whole of the mesh studied, a mesh-cell group or a mesh cell. Following an elastoplastic thermomechanical analysis, one knows the evolution of the stress, strain and plastic-strain fields in this domain and one wishes to determine the spatial and temporal variations of the cavity growth rate in this domain. To do this, one uses the keyword RICE_TRACEY of the command POST_ELEM. At each Gauss point of the domain {\Omega}_{c} , one identifies the stresses and strain rates computed at each time instant with the quantities applied to the infinite medium considered previously. The Rice and Tracey growth law is thus integrated step by step with the aid of the following approximate formula: \text{Log}(\frac{R({t}_{n})}{{R}_{0}})=\text{Log}(\frac{R({t}_{n-1})}{{R}_{0}})+0,283\text{signe}(\frac{{\sigma}_{m}({t}_{n})}{{\sigma}_{\text{eq}}({t}_{n})})\text{Exp}(1,5.\mid \frac{{\sigma}_{m}({t}_{n})}{{\sigma}_{\text{eq}}({t}_{n})}\mid )({\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}^{p}({t}_{n})-{\varepsilon}_{\text{eq}}^{p}({t}_{n-1})) One thus obtains at each time instant the values of the ratio \frac{R}{{R}_{0}} at each Gauss point of the domain {\Omega}_{c} , the sign of the triaxiality ratio making it possible to take account of evolutions both in tension and in compression. Two functionalities are then offered in code_aster : the maximum value and the mean value of the growth rate. 3.4.1 Search for the maximum value of the growth rate At each time instant, one seeks over the whole of the domain {\Omega}_{c} the Gauss point (and the volume of the associated sub-cell) maximising \frac{R}{{R}_{0}} . 3.4.2 Computation of the mean value of the growth rate By quadrature on each mesh cell and then averaging over the target domain {\Omega}_{c} , one deduces at each time instant the mean value of \frac{R}{{R}_{0}} over {\Omega}_{c} . As in the case of the Weibull model, a variant is introduced: the previous time integration is then carried out from the stress and the plastic strain averaged per mesh cell. 4 Bibliography 1. S.R BORDET, A.D. KARSTENSEN, .D.M. KNOWLES, C.S. WIESNER: “A new statistical local criterion for cleavage fracture in steel. Part I: model presentation”, Eng. Frac. Mech., Vol. 72, pp.435-452, 2005. 2. S.R BORDET, A.D. KARSTENSEN, .D.M. KNOWLES, C.S. WIESNER: “A new statistical local criterion for cleavage fracture in steel. Part II: application to an offshore structural steel”, Eng. Frac. Mech., Vol. 72, pp.453-474, 2005. 1. TANGUY, C. BOUCHET, S.R. BORDET, J. BESSON, A. PINEAU: “Toward a better understanding of the cleavage in RPV steels: Local mechanical conditions and evaluation of a nucleation enriched Weibull model and of the Beremin model over a large temperature range”, 9th European Mechanics of Materials Conference, Local approach to fracture, pp 129-134, Moret sur Loing, 2006.

r7.02.09 Identification of the Weibull model r7.02.09 Identification of the Weibull model Summary This document addresses the problem of identifying the parameters of the WEIBULL model on a sample of tests representative of the fracture behaviour of a brittle material (typically, a ferritic steel at low temperature). The linear-regression method and the maximum-likelihood method are the two methods retained. Their principle is set out in detail, together with the associated solution methods, both of which rely on an iterative procedure. Finally, their extension is shown to the case in which one of the two parameters of this model (the cleavage stress) depends on the temperature. > Contents 1 1 Introduction When they call upon the WEIBULL model (cf. POST_ELEM U4.81.22), studies of the modelling of the brittle fracture of steels generally require a prior identification of the parameters of this model. In order to avoid a laborious identification "by hand" of these parameters, which would require the POST_ELEM operation with the WEIBULL option to be relaunched iteratively, an automatic calibration procedure has been implemented in Code_Aster . In this document, the equations of the WEIBULL model are briefly recalled, then the identification problem posed is defined. The principle of the two solution methods retained (linear regression and maximum likelihood) is then described, including the case in which one of the two parameters of the model depends on the temperature. 2 2 Reminders 2.1 2.1 The WEIBULL model Consider a structure of elastoplastic constitutive behaviour subjected to a thermomechanical loading. It is assumed that the cumulative failure probability of this structure follows the following two-parameter WEIBULL law [bib1]: {P}_{f}({\sigma}_{w})=1-\exp\left[-{(\frac{{\sigma}_{w}}{{\sigma}_{u}})}^{m}\right] eq 2.1-1 an expression in which the WEIBULL modulus m>1 describes the tail of the statistical distribution of the sizes of the defects giving rise to cleavage, {\sigma}_{u} is the cleavage stress and {\sigma}_{w} is the WEIBULL stress, which depends on the history of the maximum principal stress field in the plastified zone of the structure. For example, in the case of a monotonic loading path, it is written: {\sigma}_{w}=\sqrt[m]{\sum_{p}{({\sigma}_{I}^{p})}^{m}\frac{{V}_{p}}{{V}_{0}}} . eq 2.1-2 The summation is carried over the volumes of material {V}_{p} which have plastified, {\sigma}_{I}^{p} denoting the maximum principal stress in each of these volumes ( {V}_{0} is a characteristic volume of the material). 2.2 2.2 Identification of the parameters In a very general manner, one considers an experimental database made up of tests of different kinds (type 1, 2, ..., n), each type of test being carried out {n}_{j} times, so that the total number of tests amounts to: N=\sum_{j=1}^{j=n}{n}_{j} . This experimental database could, for example, be made up of tests on notched axisymmetric specimens of different notch radii, carried out at different temperatures. Given the random nature of the fracture properties of the material considered, this database constitutes only a sample. The larger the number of these samples, the more representative it will be of the behaviour of the material considered. Among the various identification methods proposed in the literature (see for example [bib2]), two are retained: the linear-regression method, often used, and the maximum-likelihood method recommended by the "European Structural Integrity Society (ESIS)" [bib3]. Note : A systematic comparative study of the results given by these two methods [bib2] as a function of the number of samples drawn at random from a theoretical distribution has shown that the maximum-likelihood method leads to a better estimate of the parameters of the WEIBULL model. The linear-regression method nevertheless remaining very widely used, it has been incorporated into the developments. In both calibration methods retained, a first computation of the WEIBULL stresses is carried out with a given set of parameters (typically, m=20 , {s}_{u}=3000\text{MPa} ). These N tests are ranked by means of their WEIBULL stress reached at the moment of failure. One therefore has an increasing list of WEIBULL stresses ({\sigma}_{w}^{1}\text{,...,}{\sigma}_{w}^{i}\text{,...,}{\sigma}_{w}^{N}) , such that for each (i) , the number of specimens broken with a WEIBULL stress less than or equal to {\sigma}_{w}^{i} is {n}_{w}^{i} (in general {n}_{w}^{i}=i ). Among the various possible estimators of the cumulative failure probability {P}_{f}^{i} corresponding to {\sigma}_{w}^{i} [bib2], the one generally recommended is chosen: {P}_{f}^{i}=\frac{i}{N+1} . Note : In the particular case in which the WEIBULL stress depends on the temperature, the preceding ranking must be carried out temperature by temperature, each temperature corresponding to a different statistical law. The preceding estimator of the failure probability therefore becomes: {P}_{f}^{i}=\frac{i}{{N}_{T}+1} , if specimen (i) was broken at temperature T , for which there were {N}_{T} tests. The two calibration methods retained are valid so long as [eq 2.1-1] remains true. If the identification is carried out on results of non-isothermal tests whereas the cleavage stress is assumed to depend on the temperature, this condition is no longer satisfied (cf. POST_ELEM U4.81.22). In this particular case, one will therefore not be able to apply the developments that follow. 3 3 Linear-regression method 3.1 3.1.1 Principle The theory–experiment discrepancy is measured by the expression: \sum_{i}{(\text{LogLog}(\frac{1}{1-{P}_{f}^{i}})-\text{LogLog}(\frac{1}{1-{P}_{f}({\sigma}_{W}^{i})}))}^{2} eq 3.1.1-1 ("Log" denotes the natural logarithm). One wishes to minimise this discrepancy with respect to (m, {\sigma}_{u} ). 3.2 3.1.2 Solution The calibration method usually used relies on successive linear regressions: at iteration (k) , the values ( {m}_{k},{\sigma}_{u(k)} ) of the modulus and of the cleavage stress are known. It is therefore possible, with these values, to compute the WEIBULL stresses {\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i} at the various failure time instants by means of [eq 2.1-2]. These new WEIBULL stresses are then ranked by increasing amplitude and the new estimates of the failure probability {P}_{f(k)}^{i} at iteration (k) are deduced from them. For these fixed values of the WEIBULL stresses, the minimisation of [eq 3.1.1-1] reduces to a simple linear regression on the cloud of points ( \text{Log}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i}) , \text{LogLog}(\frac{1}{1-{P}_{f(k)}^{i}}) ), since if one plots \text{LogLog}(\frac{1}{1-{P}_{f}}) as a function of \text{Log}({\sigma}_{W}) , one obtains a straight line of slope m which intersects the abscissa axis at ( \text{Log}({\sigma}_{u}) ). The new values ( {m}_{k+1},{\sigma}_{u(k+1)} ) of these parameters are therefore given by (vanishing of the partial derivatives of [eq 3.1.1-1] with respect to each parameter): {m}_{k+1}=\frac{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i,j}{X}_{i(k)}{Y}_{j(k)}-\sum_{i}{Y}_{i(k)}{X}_{i(k)}}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i,j}{X}_{i(k)}{X}_{j(k)}-\sum_{i}{X}_{i(k{)}^{2}}} eq 3.1.2-1 {\sigma}_{u(k+1)}=\exp(\frac{1}{N}(\sum_{i}{X}_{i(k)}-\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i}{Y}_{i(k)})) , eq 3.1.2-2 with {X}_{i(k)}=\text{Log}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i}) and {Y}_{i(k)}=\text{LogLog}(\frac{1}{1-{P}_{f(k)}^{i}}) . These iterations are repeated so long as the difference between the sets of parameters obtained at iterations (k) and (k+1) is significant (typically, five iterations). The measure of this discrepancy is given by: \text{Max}\left[∣\frac{{m}_{k+1}-{m}_{k}}{{m}_{k}}∣,∣\frac{{\sigma}_{u(k+1)}-{\sigma}_{u(k)}}{{\sigma}_{u(k)}}∣\right] . Note : If m is fixed, {\sigma}_{u(k+1)} is still given by [eq 3.1.2-2]. On the other hand, if {\sigma}_{u} is fixed, {m}_{k+1} is no longer given by [eq 3.1.2-1] but: {m}_{k+1}=\frac{\sum_{i}{X}_{i(k)}{Y}_{i(k)}}{\sum_{i}{X}_{i(k{)}^{2}}-\log({\sigma}_{u})\sum_{i}{X}_{i(k)}} . 4 4 Maximum-likelihood method 4.1 4.1 Principle Let {p}_{f}({\sigma}_{w}) denote the probability density associated with the cumulative failure probability {P}_{f}({\sigma}_{w}) : {p}_{f}({\sigma}_{w})=\frac{m}{{\sigma}_{u}}{(\frac{{s}_{w}}{{\sigma}_{u}})}^{m-1}\exp\left[-{(\frac{{\sigma}_{w}}{{\sigma}_{u}})}^{m}\right] The quantity {p}_{f}({\sigma}_{w})d{\sigma}_{W} is equal to the probability of breaking a specimen subjected to a loading corresponding to a WEIBULL stress lying in the interval \left[{\sigma}_{W},{\sigma}_{W}+d{\sigma}_{W}\right] . The probability that all the specimens of the database have broken therefore amounts to: p(m,{\sigma}_{u})d{\sigma}_{w}=\prod_{i}{p}_{f}({\sigma}_{W}^{i})d{\sigma}_{w} , eq 4.1-1 p being the likelihood function. The maximum-likelihood method then consists in choosing the parameters of the WEIBULL model so that the likelihood function defined by [eq 4.1-1] (in practice rather its natural logarithm) is maximal. 4.2 4.2 Solution An iterative procedure is again used. Here again, at iteration (k) , ( {m}_{k},{\sigma}_{u(k)} ) as well as the {\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i} are known. For these fixed values of the WEIBULL stresses, the maximisation of \text{Log}(p) leads to a new pair ( {m}_{k+1},{\sigma}_{u(k+1)} ) given by: f({m}_{k+1})=\frac{N}{{m}_{k+1}}+\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}\text{Log}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i})-N\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i}{)}^{{m}_{k+1}}\text{Log}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}{({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i})}^{{m}_{k+1}}}=0 eq 4.2-1 {\sigma}_{(k+1)}=\sqrt[m_{k+1}]{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i}{)}^{{m}_{k+1}}} . eq 4.2-2 At each step, the solution of [eq 4.2-1] may be carried out by means of Newton's method, the gradient of f(m) being given by: \frac{\text{df}}{\text{dm}}(m)\text{=-}N\left(\frac{1}{{m}^{2}}+\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}({\sigma}_{W}^{i}{)}^{m}{\text{Log}}^{2}({\sigma}_{W}^{i})\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}({\sigma}_{W}^{i}{)}^{m}\right)-{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}({\sigma}_{W}^{i}{)}^{m}\text{Log}({\sigma}_{W}^{i})\right)}^{2}}{{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}({\sigma}_{W}^{i}{)}^{m}\right)}^{2}}\right) . Note : If m is fixed, {\sigma}_{u(k+1)} is given by [4.2-2]. On the other hand, if {\sigma}_{u} is fixed, {m}_{k+1} is no longer the solution of [4.2-1] but of: f({m}_{k+1})=\frac{N}{{m}_{k+1}}+\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}\text{Log}(\frac{{\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i}}{{\sigma}_{u}})(1-(\frac{{\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i}}{{\sigma}_{u}}{)}^{{m}_{k+1}})=0 . This equation may again be solved by means of Newton's method, the gradient now being given by: \frac{\text{df}}{\text{dm}}(m)\text{=-}\frac{N}{{m}^{2}}-\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}(\frac{{\sigma}_{W}^{i}}{{\sigma}_{u}}{)}^{m}{\text{Log}}^{2}(\frac{{\sigma}_{W}^{i}}{{\sigma}_{u}}) . 5 5 Dependence of the parameters on the temperature If one wishes to calibrate the two parameters independently, temperature by temperature, it is sufficient to split the test database into as many sub-databases by temperature and to apply the preceding methods to each of these sub-databases. If, on the other hand, one wishes only to make the cleavage stress {\sigma}_{u} vary with the temperature, one proceeds as follows. 5.1 5.1 Linear regression The estimation of the failure probabilities now being carried out temperature by temperature (cf. note of [§2.2]), it is sufficient to calibrate the cleavage stress on each cloud of points associated with the different temperatures (T). Equation [eq 3.1.2-2] therefore becomes: {\sigma}_{u(k+1)}=\exp(\frac{1}{{N}_{T}}(\sum_{i\in T}{X}_{i(k)}-\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i\in T}{Y}_{i(k)})) ( {N}_{T} denoting the number of tests for the sub-database corresponding to temperature (T)), the WEIBULL modulus being given by: {m}_{k+1}=\frac{\sum_{T}(\frac{1}{{N}_{T}}\sum_{i\in T,j\in T}{X}_{i(k)}{Y}_{j(k)})-\sum_{i}{Y}_{i(k)}{X}_{i(k)}}{\sum_{T}(\frac{1}{{N}_{T}}\sum_{i\in T,j\in T}{X}_{i(k)}{X}_{j(k)})-\sum_{i}{X}_{i(k{)}^{2}}} . 5.2 5.2 Maximum likelihood The cleavage stress is given for each temperature (T) considered by: {\sigma}_{u(k+1)}(T)=\sqrt[m_{k+1}]{\frac{1}{{N}_{T}}\sum_{i\in T}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i}(T){)}^{{m}_{k+1}}} , {m}_{k+1} being the solution of: f({m}_{k+1})=\frac{N}{{m}_{k+1}}+\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}\text{Log}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i})-\sum_{T}{N}_{T}\frac{\sum_{i\in T}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i}{)}^{{m}_{k+1}}\text{Log}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i})}{\sum_{i\in T}({\sigma}_{W(k)}^{i}{)}^{{m}_{k+1}}}=0 . 6 6 Conclusion The command RECA_WEIBULL of Code_Aster makes it possible to carry out the calibration of the parameters of the WEIBULL model U4.82.06. The user gives as input to this command the result concepts associated with the various non-linear analyses carried out. The possible dependence of the cleavage stress on the temperature is implicitly specified when different temperatures are associated with each of these result concepts (if all these temperatures are identical or if they are not specified, there is no dependence on the temperature of this parameter). The user may carry out this calibration by the maximum-likelihood method (METHODE: ‘MAXI_VRAI’) or that of linear regression (METHODE: ‘REGR_LIN’). The quantities determined by the command RECA_WEIBULL are reported in a table in which one finds the value of the identified parameters, the failure probabilities estimated from the experimental results, as well as the theoretical failure probabilities computed with the identified parameters. 7 7 Bibliography 1.
