r7.02.10 Simplified harmfulness analysis of a defect by the Kcp method, β correction r7.02.10 Simplified harmfulness analysis of a defect by the Kcp method, β correction Summary: The analysis method presented (Kcp method, β correction) is applied to the harmfulness analysis of a defect located under the cladding of pressurised-water reactor vessels, implemented by the command POST_KCP. The reference Kcp method is codified in the RSE-M and has the aim of evaluating, from a study carried out within the framework of linear elasticity and in which the defect is not explicitly meshed, the elastoplastic stress intensity factor (also described as "plastically corrected" in the context of the present methodology) at each of the various tips of the defect, that is to say at the tip of the defect located on the cladding side (named tip A) and at the tip of the defect located in the base metal (named tip B). To this end, one first computes the elastic stress intensity factor at the two tips of the defect, with the aid of the stresses at the nodes coming from the mechanical solution and of the residual stresses given by the user. Then, in a second stage, one computes the plastically corrected stress intensity factor from its elastic equivalent via the method known as the "β correction". At each time instant of the analysis and at each of the tips of the defect, the ratio obtained of the critical toughness to the plastically corrected stress intensity factor determines the instantaneous margin factor and then makes it possible to deduce from it the minimum margin factor with respect to fracture. The theoretical aspects of the method and of its software implementation are the subjects of the following paragraphs. 1 General description of the method 1.1 Principle of the analyses carried out In a first stage, from the processing of the stresses coming from the numerical analysis in linear elasticity on the sound mesh (without a meshed defect) on the one hand, and from the residual stresses supplied by the user on the other hand, the elastic stress intensity factor is computed on the basis of an analytical formula. This analytical formula corresponds to the method of influence coefficients for a semi-elliptical defect, which is codified in the RSE-M. In a second stage, the application of the method known as the "β correction" to the elastic stress intensity factor makes it possible to deduce the elastoplastic stress intensity factor (consequently also described as "plastically corrected"). 1.2 Domain of validity of the Kcp method, β correction The method proposed applies to an underclad defect located in the regular region of a ferritic-steel vessel clad on the internal wall with austenitic stainless steel, subjected either: - to a thermal transient applied on the internal surface, possibly combined with a limited pressure loading - to a pressure loading alone. The method known as the "β correction" correction is valid for an underclad defect whose tip located on the cladding side lies strictly at the interface between the cladding and the base metal. 2 Step no. 1: computation of the elastic stress intensity factor of the semi-elliptical defect 2.1 Definition of the defect The underclad defect of semi-elliptical shape is characterised by its radial depth (semi-axis of the ellipse), denoted a , and by its width, denoted {2b} . The whole of the characteristics of the defect is illustrated in figure 3.1-a. Semi-elliptical defect 2.2 Computation of the elastic stress intensity factor The elastic stress intensity factors (K1, K2 and K3) are computed from the following formula: {K} = \sqrt{(\pi a)} \left[ {\sum}_{j=0}^{4}{\sigma}_{j}{i}_{j}{\left(\frac{a+{t}_{r}}{t+{t}_{r}}\right)}^{j} \right] The values {i}_{0,1,2,3,4} are given in the RSE-M in paragraph VII.5.3.2. For homogeneity with the notations of the RSE-M, one denotes this time {t}_{r}={{ep}}_{{rev}} and t={{ep}}_{{mdb}} . The elastic stresses {\sigma}_{0},\cdots,{\sigma}_{4} used for the computation are the coefficients of the polynomial representation of the stress associated with the fracture mode of the defect, computed along the support segment in the base metal without a defect as a function of the variable u equal to 0 at the external wall of the cladding, and t+{t}_{r} at the opposite wall: \sigma (\frac{u}{L}) = {\sum}_{j=0}^{4}{\sigma}_{j}{(\frac{u}{t+{t}_{r}})}^{j} The values of the stresses {\sigma}_{0},\cdots,{\sigma}_{4} are obtained by an elastic finite-element analysis without a defect subjected to the applied loading. 2.3 Determination of the influence coefficients The values of the influence coefficients {i}_{0,1,2,3,4} for the three points of the defect A , B and C are given in tables VII.5.3.2a and b (RSE-M) in the case where the cladding and the plate have the same Young's modulus. Table VII.5.3.2c (RSE-M) supplies the values of these influence coefficients at the points A and C in the case where Young's modulus of the cladding {E}_{r} is equal to 0,7 \times E , where E is Young's modulus of the base metal. If the geometrical parameters of the defect differ from those for which the tables are established, the values of the influence coefficients are {i}_{0,1,2,3,4} determined with a "barycentric" interpolation on the variables x=\frac{a}{b} , y=\frac{a}{{t}_{r}} and z=\frac{{E}_{r}}{E} . 2.4 Change of frame In the linear elastic study, the frame considered for the vessel is the global Cartesian basis. Now, with a view to identifying the stress associated with each fracture mode, given the cylindrical geometry of the vessel and the two types of defect orientation studied, it is practical and appropriate to be able to place oneself in the cylindrical basis centred on the middle of the defect. Thus, a change of frame is carried out in POST_KCP before the application of the analytical formula described in §2.2. Case 1: Passage from the local Cartesian basis (in the section plane of the axisymmetric model) to the cylindrical basis. Cylindrical basis - Axisymmetric case One has: e_{x} = e_{r}, \quad e_{y} = e_{Z}, \quad e_{z} = -e_{\theta}. The change of basis for the stress tensor is written: \begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{rr} & \sigma_{r\theta} & \sigma_{rZ} \\ \sigma_{r\theta} & \sigma_{\theta\theta} & \sigma_{\theta Z} \\ \sigma_{rZ} & \sigma_{\theta Z} & \sigma_{ZZ} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{xx} & \sigma_{xy} & \sigma_{xz} \\ \sigma_{xy} & \sigma_{yy} & \sigma_{yz} \\ \sigma_{xz} & \sigma_{yz} & \sigma_{zz} \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned} \begin{split}\begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{rr} & \sigma_{r\theta} & \sigma_{rZ} \\ \sigma_{r\theta} & \sigma_{\theta\theta} & \sigma_{\theta Z} \\ \sigma_{rZ} & \sigma_{\theta Z} & \sigma_{ZZ} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{xx} & \sigma_{xy} & \sigma_{xz} \\ \sigma_{xy} & \sigma_{yy} & \sigma_{yz} \\ \sigma_{xz} & \sigma_{yz} & \sigma_{zz} \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\end{split} One finally obtains: \begin{cases} \sigma_{rr} = \sigma_{xx} \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{zz} \\ \sigma_{ZZ} = \sigma_{yy} \end{cases} \quad \text{et} \quad \begin{cases} \sigma_{r\theta} = -\sigma_{xz} \\ \sigma_{rZ} = \sigma_{xy} \\ \sigma_{\theta Z} = -\sigma_{yz} \end{cases} \begin{split}\begin{cases} \sigma_{rr} = \sigma_{xx} \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{zz} \\ \sigma_{ZZ} = \sigma_{yy} \end{cases} \quad \text{et} \quad \begin{cases} \sigma_{r\theta} = -\sigma_{xz} \\ \sigma_{rZ} = \sigma_{xy} \\ \sigma_{\theta Z} = -\sigma_{yz} \end{cases}\end{split} Cylindrical basis - 3D case. Case 2: Passage from the global Cartesian basis (3D model) to the cylindrical basis (assuming that the axes z and Z are collinear). One has: \begin{cases} e_r = \cos\theta e_X + \sin\theta e_Y \\ e_\theta = -\sin\theta e_X + \cos\theta e_Y \\ e_Z = e_Z \end{cases} \quad \text{d'où} \quad \begin{cases} e_X = \cos\theta e_r - \sin\theta e_\theta \\ e_Y = \sin\theta e_r + \cos\theta e_\theta \\ e_Z = e_Z \end{cases} \begin{split}\begin{cases} e_r = \cos\theta e_X + \sin\theta e_Y \\ e_\theta = -\sin\theta e_X + \cos\theta e_Y \\ e_Z = e_Z \end{cases} \quad \text{d'où} \quad \begin{cases} e_X = \cos\theta e_r - \sin\theta e_\theta \\ e_Y = \sin\theta e_r + \cos\theta e_\theta \\ e_Z = e_Z \end{cases}\end{split} The change of basis for the stress tensor is written: \begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{rr} & \sigma_{r\theta} & \sigma_{rZ} \\ \sigma_{r\theta} & \sigma_{\theta\theta} & \sigma_{\theta Z} \\ \sigma_{rZ} & \sigma_{\theta Z} & \sigma_{ZZ} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{XX} & \sigma_{XY} & \sigma_{XZ} \\ \sigma_{XY} & \sigma_{YY} & \sigma_{YZ} \\ \sigma_{XZ} & \sigma_{YZ} & \sigma_{ZZ} \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned} \begin{split}\begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{rr} & \sigma_{r\theta} & \sigma_{rZ} \\ \sigma_{r\theta} & \sigma_{\theta\theta} & \sigma_{\theta Z} \\ \sigma_{rZ} & \sigma_{\theta Z} & \sigma_{ZZ} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{XX} & \sigma_{XY} & \sigma_{XZ} \\ \sigma_{XY} & \sigma_{YY} & \sigma_{YZ} \\ \sigma_{XZ} & \sigma_{YZ} & \sigma_{ZZ} \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\end{split} One finally obtains: \begin{cases} \sigma_{rr} = \cos^2\theta \sigma_{XX} + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \sigma_{XY} + \sin^2\theta \sigma_{YY} \\ \sigma_{r\theta} = -\sin\theta\cos\theta \sigma_{XX} + (\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta) \sigma_{XY} + \sin\theta\cos\theta \sigma_{YY} \\ \sigma_{rZ} = \cos\theta \sigma_{XZ} + \sin\theta \sigma_{YZ} \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sin^2\theta \sigma_{XX} - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \sigma_{XY} + \cos^2\theta \sigma_{YY} \\ \sigma_{\theta Z} = -\sin\theta \sigma_{XZ} + \cos\theta \sigma_{YZ} \\ \sigma_{ZZ} = \sigma_{ZZ} \end{cases} \begin{split}\begin{cases} \sigma_{rr} = \cos^2\theta \sigma_{XX} + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \sigma_{XY} + \sin^2\theta \sigma_{YY} \\ \sigma_{r\theta} = -\sin\theta\cos\theta \sigma_{XX} + (\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta) \sigma_{XY} + \sin\theta\cos\theta \sigma_{YY} \\ \sigma_{rZ} = \cos\theta \sigma_{XZ} + \sin\theta \sigma_{YZ} \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sin^2\theta \sigma_{XX} - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \sigma_{XY} + \cos^2\theta \sigma_{YY} \\ \sigma_{\theta Z} = -\sin\theta \sigma_{XZ} + \cos\theta \sigma_{YZ} \\ \sigma_{ZZ} = \sigma_{ZZ} \end{cases}\end{split} Summary of the components Components used for the computation of the stress intensity factor of mode 1 (likewise mode 2 and mode 3 with the associated components) 1. \sigma_{yy} with an axisymmetric model, 2. \sigma_{zz} with a 3D model. Circumferential defect: \sigma_{zz} in the cylindrical basis, that is: 1. \sigma_{zz} with an axisymmetric model, 2. \sin^2\theta \sigma_{xx} - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \sigma_{xy} + \cos^2\theta \sigma_{yy} with a 3D model. Longitudinal defect: \sigma_{\theta\theta} in the cylindrical basis, that is: 3 Step no. 2: computation of the elastoplastic stress intensity factor by the Kcp method, β correction 3.1 Plastic correction factor over a loading phase considered in isolation The expression of the stress intensity factor corresponds to that of a semi-elliptical underclad defect under the assumption of a linear elastic constitutive behaviour of the cladding and of the base metal . The method known as the "β correction" is specific to underclad defects and applies only within the framework of an increasing loading phase considered in isolation. It consists in applying a corrective factor, denoted βA for the tip on the cladding side (respectively βB for the tip on the base-metal side), to the elastic stress intensity factor equivalent at tips A and B, in order to take account of the influence on the defect of the plastification phenomenon occurring at the tip on the cladding side and at the tip on the base-metal side. The radius of the plastic zone r_y is defined at point A by the formula: r_{yA} = \frac{1}{6 \pi} \left( \frac{K_{\text{eqA}}}{S_{yA}} \right)^2 where S_{yA} is the elastic limit of the cladding at A. In the increasing phase of K_{\text{eq}} , the factor K_{\text{cp}} is obtained by the expressions: - At point A : K_{\text{cpA}} = \beta_A \cdot K_{\text{eqA}} with: \beta_A = 1 + C_A \cdot \tanh\left( \frac{36 \cdot r_{yA}}{t_r} \right) - At point B : K_{\text{cpB}} = \begin{cases} \beta_B^{3D} \cdot K_{\text{eqB}}, & \text{pour les défauts semi-elliptiques} \\ \beta_B \cdot K_{\text{eqB}}, & \text{pour les défauts bandes} \end{cases} with: \beta_B^{3D} = \max\left( 1, \beta_B \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1 + 1.464 \cdot \left( \frac{h}{2c} \right)^{1.65}}{1 + 1.464 \cdot (\beta_B^2) \cdot \left( \frac{h}{2c} \right)^{1.65}}} \right) and: \beta_B = 1 + C_B \cdot \tanh\left( \frac{36 \cdot r_{yA}}{t_r} \right) - At point C : K_{\text{cpC}} = \beta_C \cdot K_{\text{eqC}} with: \beta_C = \beta_B The coefficients C_A and C_B are given in the following table: | | Longitudinal defect | Circumferential defect | | --- | --- | --- | | Tip A (interface) | C_A = 0.165 \ln(h) | C_A = 0.5 | | Tip B (base metal) | C_B = 0.465 (1 + h / 100) | C_B = 0.5 | With the depth h of the defect expressed in millimetres. 3.2 Plastic correction in the course of a transient In the course of a transient, the vessel generally passes through a succession of increasing loading phases and of unloading phases . Consequently, a transient lies outside the theoretical domain of application of the method known as the "β correction". However, the notion of plastic correction has been extended to the case of a real transient by retaining, at a given time instant, the maximum plastic correction obtained over all the preceding increasing loading phases. The principle of this extension is the same whether one considers the tip on the cladding side or the tip on the base-metal side. For the sake of simplicity, the explicit mention of the tip considered is omitted in the notations used in the remainder of this section. Determination of the plastic correction: At each new increasing loading phase, a plastic correction, denoted \Delta K , is re-evaluated as follows: \Delta K = K_{\beta} - K_{I} = (\beta - 1) \times K_{I} where: - K_{I} is the elastic stress intensity factor determined in §2. - \beta is the plastic correction factor described in §3.1. If this new plastic correction is greater than the preceding maximum plastic correction, denoted \Delta K_{\text{max}} , then \Delta K_{\text{max}} is updated. Expression of the plastic correction applied: The plastic correction finally applied, denoted K_{\text{cp}} , is written: K_{\text{cp}} = K_{I} + \Delta K_{\text{max}} Case of the unloading phases: During an unloading phase, the plastic correction applied consists in adding \Delta K_{\text{max}} (computed during the preceding increasing loading phases) to the elastic stress intensity factor K_{I} . Indeed, the absence of plastification during an unloading phase implies that the plastic correction corresponds only to the plastified residue of the preceding loading phases. Algorithm - One initialises K_{\text{max}} = 0 . - at the first time instant, one will be in an unloading phase by comparison with K_{I_{\text{last}}} , - no plastification at the first time instant. One initialises K_{I_{\text{last}}} to an arbitrarily high value: Loop over the time instants of the loading history : 1. If K_I(t_n) \leq K_{I_{\text{last}}} then (unloading phase): K_{\text{cp}}(t_n) = K_I(t_n) + \Delta K_{\text{max}} 2. Else (loading phase): - If \beta(t_n) \times K_I(t_n) > K_I(t_n) + \Delta K_{\text{max}} then : K_{\text{cp}}(t_n) = \beta(t_n) \times K_I(t_n) \Delta K_{\text{max}} = K_{\text{cp}}(t_n) - K_I(t_n) - Else : K_{\text{cp}}(t_n) = K_I(t_n) + \Delta K_{\text{max}} End If End If 1. One updates K_{I_{\text{last}}} = K_I(t_n) . End Loop The same algorithm described above is implemented for the plastic corrections of the stress intensity factors at the two tips A and B of the crack as the loading history proceeds. 4 Validation The command POST_KCP is validated by the test EPICU03 in comparison with the result of CUVE1D: - EPICU03 validates the case of a longitudinal then circumferential semi-elliptical defect in AXIS 5 Bibliographic references «CUVE1D Version 2 - Validation note» H-T26-2007-00833-FR «CUVE1D Version 2 - Reference note» H-T26-2007-00803-FR. «Analytical methods for computing the stress intensity factors and the J-integral» RSE-M -Edition 2010

r7.02.11 Cohesive constitutive laws: CZM_xxx_xxx and load piloting r7.02.11 Cohesive constitutive laws: CZM_xxx_xxx and load piloting Summary: The cohesive constitutive laws: - CZM_EXP_REG (Cohesive Zone Model EXPonential REGularised) - CZM_LIN_REG (Cohesive Zone Model LINear REGularised) - CZM_OUV_MIX (Cohesive Zone Model OPENing based on a MIXed formulation) - CZM_EXP_MIX (Cohesive Zone Model EXPonential based on a MIXed formulation) - CZM_TAC_MIX (Cohesive Zone Model TAlon-Curnier based on a MIXed formulation) - CZM_TRA_MIX (Cohesive Zone Model TRApezium based on a MIXed formulation) - CZM_FAT_MIX (Cohesive Zone Model FATigue based on a MIXed formulation) make it possible to model the opening of a crack while taking into account a cohesive force between its lips. A surface energy makes it possible to take into account the energy cost of the opening of the crack. The latter is represented by joint finite elements for the first two and by interface finite elements for the following ones. The cohesive law CZM_ELAS_MIX constitutes a simplified version of the previous models, since the response remains elastic, with or without contact, and possibly with normal or tangential adherence. It makes it possible, among other things, to test a data setup before moving on to the more advanced models. The constitutive law CZM_LAB_MIX (Cohesive Zone Model Liaison Acier-Béton based on a MIXed formulation) furthermore makes it possible to model the sliding of the steel reinforcement relative to the concrete within a structure. We present here the form of the energy and of the cohesive law which derives from it as a function of the displacement jump, as well as the internal variables of the model. The existence of potential instabilities during crack propagation may require piloting by elastic prediction, of which the elements specific to these laws are presented. 1 General remarks on the cohesive laws In brittle fracture, in order to remove the problem of infinite stresses at the crack tip, one can introduce cohesive forces which impose a stress initiation criterion (see (3)). The forces act between the particles on either side of the separation plane of the crack (see r7.02.11-fig-fissure). Historically, one of the first to propose this type of approach is Barenblatt (1) at the beginning of the nineteen-sixties. Based on this idea, numerous models have appeared in the literature under the name: “Cohesive zone models”, or CZM in English. For a bibliography one may refer to (5). Diagram of a crack One considers that the opening of the crack costs an energy proportional to its length. One calls it the surface energy, which one denotes \Psi . The displacement field at equilibrium \boldsymbol{u} is obtained by minimising the sum of the elastic energy \Phi of the surface energy \Psi and of the work of the external forces {W}^{ext} : \underset{\boldsymbol{u}}{\min}(\Phi+\Psi+{W}^{ext}) The discontinuity surface is discretised in 2D or 3D by joint finite elements (see R3.06.09) or by interface finite elements (in this case the problem reduces to a search for a saddle point, see R3.06.13). The displacement jump in the element \boldsymbol{\delta} is a linear function of the nodal displacements. The cohesive force 1 which acts on the lips of the crack is denoted \vec{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} ; it is defined by the derivative of the surface-energy density with respect to the displacement jump. One calls a cohesive law a relation between \vec{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} and the displacement jump \boldsymbol{\delta} . The material parameters of the model are: - the toughness, or critical surface-energy density, denoted G_c (keyword GC), which expresses the energy cost of cracking; - and the critical stress at fracture, denoted \sigma_C (keyword SIGC). In the cohesive laws CZM_xxx_REG which are presented in the following section, these parameters may depend on a temperature field. Furthermore, the laws CZM_xxx_REG depend on two dimensionless numerical parameters: PENA_ADHERENCE and PENA_CONTACT. The first controls the regularisation of the surface energy (or penalisation of the adherence), the second the penalisation of the contact. The laws CZM_xxx_MIX likewise depend on two numerical parameters, PENA_LAGR and RIGI_GLIS. The first is a penalisation coefficient of the Lagrangian and the second determines the sliding stiffness (only for the law CZM_OUV_MIX). The law dedicated to ductile fracture, CZM_TRA_MIX, has a trapezoidal shape. To define this shape one introduces two additional dimensionless parameters. They are positive and strictly less than 1, named COEF_EXTR, as in extrinsic 2, in order to determine the slope at the origin (infinite or not, at choice) and COEF_PLAS, as in plastic, in order to determine the end of the plastic plateau. We shall give a detailed definition of the parameters in the following sections. Note One adopts the following notations: \boldsymbol{n} denotes the normal to the cracking surface and \boldsymbol{t} and \boldsymbol{\tau} the sliding directions in the plane of the crack. For further information on the interface model ( _INTERFACE and _INTERFACE_S), the reader may refer to the documentation R3.06.13. 3.1 Elastic cohesive law CZM_ELAS_MIX The reader will find the details of the formulation and of the numerical implementation of this model in document (10). Only the principal results are supplied here, taking up the notations introduced in R3.06.13. The mechanical characteristics of the model are supplied in the command DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01 under the keyword CZM_ELAS. 3.1.1 Surface energy The surface energy \Psi , defined on a discontinuity \Gamma , depends quadratically on the displacement jump \boldsymbol{\delta} between the lips of the crack: \Psi (\boldsymbol{\delta})=\int_{\Gamma}\Pi(\boldsymbol{\delta})d\Gamma with the surface-energy density: \Pi(\boldsymbol{\delta})=\psi(\boldsymbol{\delta})+A_{n}(\delta_{n})+{A}_{t}(\delta_{t},\delta_{\tau}) The function \psi denotes the elastic energy density: \psi (\boldsymbol{\delta})=\frac{1}{2}{k}_{nt}\langle\delta_n\rangle_{+}^{2} +\frac{1}{2}{k}_{nc}\langle\delta_n\rangle_{-}^{2} +\frac{1}{2}{k}_{t}(\delta_{t}^{2}+\delta_{\tau}^{2}) where {k}_{nt} , {k}_{nc} and {k}_{t} denote respectively the normal stiffness modulus in tension, the normal stiffness modulus in compression, and the tangential stiffness modulus. In the command DEFI_MATERIAU/CZM_ELAS, they are supplied under the keywords RIGI_NOR_TRAC, RIGI_NOR_COMP and RIGI_TAN respectively. When {k}_{nt}={k}_{nc} , the stiffness is identical in tension and in compression and it may be supplied by a single keyword RIGI_NOR. The function {A}_{t} makes it possible to consider a tangential behaviour which is perfectly adherent or else elastic: \begin{split}A_{t}(\delta_{t},\delta_{\tau})= \left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} I_{\{0,0\}}((\delta_{t},\delta_{\tau})) & \text{en adhérence parfaite}\\ 0 & \text{en élasticité} \end{array} \right.\end{split} The choice between perfect adherence and elasticity for the tangential direction is fixed by the keyword ADHE_TAN of DEFI_MATERIAU ('PARFAITE' or 'ELAS'). Finally, the function {A}_{n} makes it possible to consider a normal behaviour which is perfectly adherent, with a unilateral contact condition (and elasticity in opening) or else elastic in opening and in closure: \begin{split}A_{n}(\delta_{n})= \left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} I_{\{0\}}(\delta_{n}) & \text{en adhérence parfaite}\\ I_{\mathbb{R}^+}(\delta_{n}) & \text{en contact unilatéral}\\ 0 & \text{en élasticité} \end{array} \right.\end{split} The choice between perfect adherence, unilateral contact and elasticity for the normal direction is fixed by the keyword ADHE_NOR of DEFI_MATERIAU ('PARFAITE', 'UNILATER' or 'ELAS'). 3.1.2 Stress vector The stress vector \vec{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} derives from the surface energy \Pi . But in the presence of adherence or contact conditions, the latter is not differentiable at every point. One then generalises the notion of derivative by that of subdifferential. Without entering into the details, the following relations between the stress vector and the displacement jump follow: - For the normal behaviour: \begin{split}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} \text{adhérence parfaite :} &\delta_n = 0 \text{ et } \vec{\sigma}_n \text{ quelconque} \\ \text{contact unilatéral :} &\delta_n = \frac{\langle \vec{\sigma_n} \rangle_+}{k_{nt}} \\ \text{élasticité :} &\delta_n = \frac{\langle \vec{\sigma_n} \rangle_+}{k_{nt}} + \frac{\langle \vec{\sigma_n} \rangle_-}{k_{nc}} \end{array} \right.\end{split} - And for the tangential behaviour: \begin{split}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} \text{adhérence parfaite :} &\delta_t = \delta_\tau = 0 \text{ et } \vec{\sigma}_t, \vec{\sigma}_\tau \text{ quelconques} \\ \text{élasticité :} &\delta_t = \frac{\vec{\sigma_t}}{k_{t}} \text{ et } \delta_\tau = \frac{\vec{\sigma_\tau}}{k_{t}} \end{array} \right.\end{split} 3.1.3 Augmented Lagrangian and integration of the constitutive relation In accordance with R3.06.13, the Lagrangian of the relaxed interface problem is augmented by a penalisation term where r denotes the augmentation coefficient. The value of r is fixed by the user under the keyword PENA_LAGR_ABSO, with as unit a stress per unit area ( J/{m}^{4} ). The integration of the mixed constitutive relation consists in solving the following algebraic system: \boldsymbol{\lambda} +r(⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧-\boldsymbol{\delta})\in\partial\Pi(\boldsymbol{\delta}) where \boldsymbol{\lambda} denotes the Lagrange multiplier (the augmented nodal cohesive force), ⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧ is the displacement jump computed from the nodal displacements and \boldsymbol{\delta} is the local displacement jump (at the integration points), the result of the integration process of the constitutive law. At this stage, \boldsymbol{\lambda} and ⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧ are known quantities and \boldsymbol{\delta} is the unknown of the system. Denoting \varphi \equiv \boldsymbol{\lambda} +r⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧ , the solution of the algebraic system is the following: - For the normal behaviour: \begin{split}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} \text{adhérence parfaite :} &\delta_n = 0 \\ \text{contact unilatéral :} &\delta_n = \frac{\langle \varphi_n \rangle_+}{k_{nt}+r} \\ \text{élasticité :} &\delta_n = \frac{\langle \varphi_n \rangle_+}{k_{nt}+r} + \frac{\langle \varphi_n \rangle_-}{k_{nc}+r} \end{array} \right.\end{split} - And for the tangential behaviour: \begin{split}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} \text{adhérence parfaite :} &\delta_t = \delta_\tau = 0 \\ \text{élasticité :} &\delta_t = \frac{\varphi_t}{k_{t}+r} \text{ et } \delta_\tau = \frac{\varphi_\tau}{k_{t}+r} \end{array} \right.\end{split} 3.1.4 Internal variables The interface behaviour being elastic, there are no internal variables strictly speaking. On the other hand, one supplies the local displacement jump \boldsymbol{\delta} for post-processing purposes. Its components (\delta_n, \delta_t, \delta_\tau) are stored in the array of internal variables (V1,V2,V3). 3.2 Cohesive laws for brittle fracture CZM_OUV_MIX , CZM_TAC_MIX and CZM_EXP_MIX 3.2.1 Surface energy The surface energy \Psi , defined on a discontinuity \Gamma , depends on the displacement jump between the lips of the crack \boldsymbol{\delta} and on \kappa , the threshold internal variable which governs the irreversibility of the cracking. The latter stores the greatest norm of the jump reached during the opening. Its evolution law between two successive loading increments - and + is written: \kappa^{+}=\max(\kappa^{-},\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{+}) The surface energy is defined in the following way: \Psi (\boldsymbol{\delta},\kappa)={\int}_{\Gamma}\Pi(\boldsymbol{\delta},\kappa)d\Gamma with the surface-energy density: \Pi(\boldsymbol{\delta},\kappa)=\psi(\max(\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|,\kappa))+{I}_{\mathbb{R}^+}(\delta_n) where {I}_{\mathbb{R}^+} the indicator function expresses the non-interpenetration condition of the lips of the crack, and \psi is the cohesive energy density defined in the following way: - CZM_TAC_MIX: \begin{split}\psi(\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|)= \left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} \frac{-{\sigma}_{c}^{2}}{4{G}_{c}}\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|+{\sigma}_{c}\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\| & \text{si }\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\| \le 2{G}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c}\\ {G}_{c}& \text{si }\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\| \ge 2{G}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c} \end{array} \right.\end{split} - CZM_OUV_MIX: \begin{split}\psi(\delta_n)= \left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} \frac{-{\sigma}_{c}^{2}}{4{G}_{c}}\delta_n+{\sigma}_{c}\delta_n & \text{si }\delta_n \le 2{G}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c}\\ {G}_{c}& \text{si }\delta_n \ge 2{G}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c} \end{array} \right. ,\quad \psi(\delta_T) = \frac{1}{2}C\delta_T^2,\, \quad{T=t} \text{ ou } \tau\end{split} - CZM_EXP_MIX: \begin{split}\psi(\delta_n)= \left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} -G_{c}\exp\left(-\delta_n\frac{\sigma_c}{G_c}\right)&\text{si }\delta_n\le 3.2G_c/\sigma_c\\ G_{c}&\text{si }\delta_n\ge 3.2{G}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c} \end{array} \right. ,\quad \psi(\delta_T) = \frac{1}{2}C\delta_T^2,\, \quad{T=t} \text{ ou } \tau\end{split} - C depends on a numerical parameter chosen by the user (see section 3.5). - For the laws CZM_OUV_MIX and CZM_EXP_MIX, the dissipation is controlled only by the normal opening; Of elastic-prediction type: PRED_ELAS (see R5.03.80), it makes it possible to follow dissipative solutions for which the loading is no longer necessarily monotonic. The aim of the exercise is to set oneself a piloting control equation which makes the cracking evolve progressively in order to follow the unstable parts of the global response. This makes it possible to obtain convergence more easily for analyses with sudden crack propagations. As a reminder, one considers that the loading (external forces and imposed displacements) decomposes into two terms, one known and the other of which only the direction is known; its intensity, which one denotes eta , becomes an unknown of the problem: \begin{split}\begin{array}{l} &F^{ext} = F^{ext}_{cst} + \eta F^{ext}_{pilo} \\ &U^{d} = U^{d}_{cst} + \eta U^{d}_{pilo} \end{array}\end{split} Furthermore, the cohesive law must supply the Taylor expansion of the criterion {F}_{el} . For further details on this technique, one may also refer to 5. Since one introduces a new unknown, one must “close” the system by introducing a new equation, which one calls the piloting equation. P(\Delta U_i) = \Delta\tau where \Delta U_i is the displacement increment over the current time step sought by the Newton method and where the quantity \Delta\tau makes it possible to control the fineness of the solution (of the piloting steps). This equation can be rewritten in order to obtain an equation in the piloting unknown \eta , the displacement increment itself being able to be put in the form of a “constant” part (with respect to the piloting) and of a piloted part: \Delta U_i = \Delta U_i^0 + \eta_i\Delta U_i^1 , which makes it possible to write: The reader is referred to reference [5] or the documentation R5.03.80 for further details. The issue of the piloting within the framework of the cohesive laws is to write a relevant piloting equation at the level of the law in order to control the dissipation progressively. This type of piloting is called “elastic prediction” (keyword PRED_ELAS). In what follows, one details the piloting equation for the two cases of the regularised laws and of the mixed laws. One now dispenses with the index linked to the time step. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, the quantities are expressed at their value at the end of the current time step. 4.1 Regularised laws One recalls that in the case of the regularised laws, the cohesive law relates the displacement jump to the cohesive stress and to the internal variable representing the dissipation, which may be the damage variable d or else the threshold variable denoted \kappa (or else r ), according to the manner in which the law is formulated. One writes the law schematically: \boldsymbol{\delta} \longrightarrow (\vec{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}, \kappa) For these laws, one controls the dissipation progressively by controlling the quantity called “threshold departure”, which is written: G_{el}(\boldsymbol{\delta}) = \|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|-\kappa^- = \sqrt{\langle\delta_n\rangle_+^2 + \delta_t^2} - \kappa^- At the level of the cohesive law, the unknown displacement jump in turn decomposes into a “constant” part and a piloted part: \boldsymbol{\delta}=\boldsymbol{\delta}^0 + \eta\boldsymbol{\delta}^1 . One therefore has \delta_n = \boldsymbol{\delta}\cdot\boldsymbol{n} = (\boldsymbol{\delta}^0\cdot\boldsymbol{n}) + \eta(\boldsymbol{\delta}^1\cdot\boldsymbol{n}) (likewise for the tangential component) and the controlled quantity can therefore be written as a function of the piloting unknown: G_{el}(\boldsymbol{\delta}) = \hat{G}_{el}(\eta) Here, one will impose that the controlled quantity, this “threshold departure”, correspond to a certain portion \Delta\tau of the previous threshold: \hat{G}_{el}(\eta) = \kappa^-\Delta\tau The threshold being able to become very large at the “broken” Gauss points, one limits the threshold departure to a certain fraction of a critical length associated with the cohesive element, denoted l_c (for example l_c = G_c/\sigma_c ), for these elements. One will therefore rather write: \hat{G}_{el}(\eta) = \max(l_c,\kappa^-)\Delta\tau which gives us our piloting equation at the level of the Gauss point. One will finally specify that one pilots so that the piloting equation is satisfied at at least one Gauss point, which amounts to defining the following global equation: F_{el}(\eta) = \max_{\text{pt Gauss}}\left(\frac{\hat{G}_{el}(\eta)}{\max(l_c,\kappa^-)}\right) = \Delta\tau 4.2 Laws with mixed formulation Unlike the regularised laws, the numerical integration of the laws based on interface elements with mixed formulation consists, at each Gauss point, in computing the displacement discontinuity boldsymbol{\delta} for given values of the cohesive forces \boldsymbol{t} (corresponding to the Lagrange multipliers of the augmented formulation and therefore sometimes denoted \boldsymbol{\lambda} ) and of the jumps across the element ⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧ of the global displacement, which are in both cases nodal quantities. One denotes the law schematically: (\boldsymbol{t}, ⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧, \kappa) \longrightarrow \boldsymbol{\delta} for it is indeed in this manner that one proceeds with the numerical integration. In this formulation, the condition \boldsymbol{\delta}=⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧ is thus satisfied only in the weak sense. Now, for a constitutive law defined in this way, one does not necessarily have uniqueness of the solution: one can find several values of the displacement discontinuity \boldsymbol{\delta} corresponding to a given cohesive force and displacement jump (r7.02.11-fig-pilotage_mix.a). One will therefore rather work with the pseudo-force \boldsymbol{s} = \boldsymbol{t} + r⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧ which brings in a penalisation parameter r , which amounts to performing a rotation of angle r and of centre (0, t_0) of the law in the space (⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧, \boldsymbol{t}) . One then indeed has uniqueness of the solution (see r7.02.11-fig-pilotage_mix.b). Law formulated on mixed interface elements: a. expressed from the cohesive force; b. expressed from the pseudo-force. The law in the pseudo-force variable is therefore written schematically in the following way: (\boldsymbol{s}, \kappa) = (\boldsymbol{t}+ r⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧, \kappa) \longrightarrow \boldsymbol{\delta} For further details on the mixed formulation, the reader is referred to the documentation R3.06.13. Within the framework of the piloting, one will control the dissipation during the loading by controlling the quantity “dissipated energy”, denoted g . The piloting equation is therefore: g=g(\boldsymbol{s}, \kappa) = g^- + \Delta\tau At the level of the cohesive law, the unknown cohesive forces and global displacement jumps in turn decompose into a “constant” part and a piloted part: \begin{split}\begin{array}{l} &t = t_{cst} + \eta t_{pilo} \\ &⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧ = ⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧_{cst} + \eta ⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧_{pilo} \end{array}\end{split} which is found again at the level of the pseudo-force: \boldsymbol{s} = \boldsymbol{s}_{cst} + \eta \boldsymbol{s}_{pilo} with boldsymbol{s}_{cst}=t_{cst}+⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧_{cst} and boldsymbol{s}_{pilo}=t_{pilo}+⟦\boldsymbol{u}⟧_{pilo} . The issue here is therefore to relate the controlled quantity g=g(\boldsymbol{s}, \kappa) to the piloted pseudo-force. This step obviously depends on the constitutive law considered. By way of example, one writes it explicitly for the exponential law CZM_EXP_MIX. The dissipated energy g is computed in post-processing in the constitutive law from the internal variable \kappa recording the greatest displacement discontinuity reached during the history of the loading. Here, one inverts the relation \kappa\longrightarrow g in order to obtain (the reader is referred to the formulation of the law for further details): \kappa_g = l_c\left(1-\sqrt{1-g}\right) where l_c is a critical length characteristic of the cohesive element, for example l_c = 3.2G_c/t_c ( t_c and G_c are the values of the initial critical cohesive stress and of the critical energy-release rate which are the material parameters of the law). One then determines the critical cohesive force t_g corresponding to this value of \kappa_g : t_g = t_c - \frac{t_c}{t_g}\kappa_g and finally the pseudo-force: s_g = t_g + r\kappa_g One can therefore rewrite the piloting equation as an equation in \eta : \hat G_{el} = s_{cst} + \eta s_{pilo} - s_g = s_{cst} + \eta s_{pilo}-rl_c+(t_c-r l_c)\sqrt{1-g} = 0 with g = g^- + \delta\tau the controlled quantity. One may note that the solutions of the piloting equation, once determined, can be modified in order to be made more non-dimensional and more “ \tau - independent”. For example, in the present case, one can multiply them by the quantity \Delta\tau / s_g . The meaning of the piloting increment \Delta \tau and what it imposes in terms of energy dissipation depends on the constitutive law. The normalisation choices adopted are the following: - CZM_OUV_MIX - Control of the increment of normalised dissipated energy (internal variable PCENERDI) \Delta \psi=\Delta \tau \times G_c - CZM_TAC_MIX - Control of the increment of normalised dissipated energy (internal variable PCENERDI) \Delta \psi=\Delta \tau \times G_c - CZM_EXP_MIX - Control of the increment of normalised dissipated energy (internal variable PCENERDI) \Delta \psi=\Delta \tau \times G_c - CZM_LAB_MIX - Control of the increment of the maximum displacement jump (internal variable SEUILDEP) \Delta \kappa = \Delta \tau \times \delta^c Finally, one will note that the solution of this global equation can be obtained by the method described in [ 5 ]. One dispenses with the vector notation, but and are indeed vectors of dimension 2 or 3 according to the space dimension. 5 Keywords 5.1 Laws CZM_xxx_REG The cohesive constitutive laws CZM_EXP_REG and CZM_LIN_REG are used in STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE. r7.02.12 eXtended Finite Element Method: General remarks r7.02.12 eXtended Finite Element Method: General remarks Summary: This document presents the X-FEM method (eXtended Finite Element Method), which makes it possible mainly to consider cracks which do not conform to the mesh in order to treat 2D and 3D crack problems. The crack is defined by the command DEFI_FISS_XFEM u4.82.08 and can be used for linear and non-linear static analyses. Other documents dedicated to specific problems are available: - frictional contact on the lips of the crack in small sliding with X-FEM r5.03.54, - frictional contact on the lips of the crack in large sliding with X-FEM r5.03.53, - crack propagation with X-FEM r7.02.13 1 Introduction Numerical simulation in fracture mechanics is essentially based on the use of the finite element method (FEM). Classically, for a crack-propagation problem, a first analysis is carried out on an initial mesh, then a new mesh is determined, taking into account the advance of the crack (according to the chosen propagation law). A new analysis follows from it, and the procedure is iterated for each propagation step. A major and immediate drawback is the necessity of remeshing at each propagation step. The remeshing process can easily be automated in 2D, and in certain cases in 3D, but a quality 3D remeshing proves costly in time (human supervision) and in money. Indeed, with an automatic mesher, a local refinement appropriate to the cracking zone often leads to an excessive number of elements everywhere else on the rest of the structure. A layer-by-layer refinement process is generally useful, such as the introduction of a torus at the crack front, an efficient solution (also facilitating the introduction of Barsoum elements) but requiring a costly human intervention; and all the more so as the geometrical shape of the crack is very complex (helical cracks for example). The problem becomes almost inconceivable in 3D multiple cracking. In addition to these practical difficulties, the projection of quantities (stresses, internal variables) from one mesh onto another poses fundamental theoretical problems (verification of the conservation equations of energy, of momentum, of mass). In parallel with the difficulties linked to propagation, methods with a mesh prove rather ineffective for parametric studies in which one is interested in the influence of the position and of the shape of the crack. The so-called “Meshless” methods have been proposed in order to free oneself from the constraints linked to the mesh. Meshless methods are based on a purely nodal discretisation, without connectivity, and the shape functions are constructed from the nodal configuration. Initially introduced at the end of the 1970s for problems without boundaries (Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics method in the field of astrophysics), Meshless methods were subsequently extended to mechanical problems and today come in various variants: MLS (Moving Least Square) methods, Diffuse Element Method (DEM), Element Free Galerkin (EFG), Reproducing Kernel Particle Method (RKPM), hp clouds, and many others. The common element of all these methods is the notion of Partition of Unity, which is a set of functions whose sum is equal to one at each point of the domain considered. The main drawback of these methods is that they require a greater numerical effort than those based on a mesh (CPU time in particular). In particular, the evaluation of the shape functions is far from being as trivial, the numerical integration schemes are generally richer and therefore more costly, and the resulting global system of equations has a larger bandwidth compared with an FEM. Even in the recent versions of Meshless methods combining physical and mathematical supports, the imposition of boundary conditions remains problematic. Other methods are based on a partition of unity within the framework of standard finite elements, where only the definition of the shape functions differs. This choice of partition of unity avoids the problems of integration of the stiffness, which is considerably expensive for Meshless methods (EFG, DEM, RKPM in particular). Moreover, the use of a partition of unity based on finite elements allows an easy implementation of Dirichlet-type boundary conditions (unlike techniques using a partition of unity based on least squares). These methods, which are first found in their meshed versions under the name of Partition of Unity Finite Element Method (PUFEM) or of Generalized Finite Element Method (GFEM), make it possible to enrich easily the space of the shape functions, thanks to the a priori knowledge of the properties of the solution of the problem. Combining the GFEM and the hp-cloud , Duarte et al. proposes a mixed partition of unity (finite elements and Shepard), which makes it possible to consider a non-meshed crack, with enriched shape functions. Even closer to the classical finite-element framework, the extended finite element method (X-FEM) has aroused one of the keenest interests if one refers to the evolution of the number of publications on this subject since its appearance and to the place reserved for it in international conferences. This method uses the partition of unity to enrich the basis of the shape functions in order to represent a jump of the displacement field at the lips of the crack, as well as the singularity at the crack front. Two enrichments are then introduced: an enrichment by a jump function which makes it possible to handle the discontinuity across the lips of the crack, and an enrichment by asymptotic functions, which allows a faithful representation of the physical phenomena taking place at the crack front. Historically, the precursor signs are due to Belytschko and Black, who apply the partition of unity to fracture mechanics by incorporating the analytical formulae of the asymptotic fields into the displacement approximation. The addition of the generalised Heaviside function makes it possible to write the enriched approximation of the displacement in its final form, an expression which gives birth to the extended finite element method. Compared with GFEM, it offers less dependence with respect to the knowledge of the form of the solutions, which offers greater flexibility. The field of application of X-FEM continues to widen, this approach having been used in very varied frameworks: Reissner-Mindlin plates, shells, fracture in 3D, multiple cracking, cohesive zones, modelling of holes and of bi-materials, incompressible formulations and large transformations, nucleation of cracks, cracking under contact, dynamic fracture, plasticity… Moreover, the use of the level set method coupled with X-FEM has greatly facilitated the treatment of cracks in 2D (, and ) and in 3D. Initially introduced within the framework of fluid mechanics in order to represent the evolution of interfaces, the level set method considers the interface as the zero iso-value of a distance function. This method proves particularly effective for the propagation of a crack in 3D, coupled with the use of the Fast Marching Method. This document is organised around 4 sections, of which this introduction serves as section r7.02.12-calcul-energetique-facteurs-intensite-contraintes. r7.02.12-representation-fissure is devoted to the use of the level set method for cracking. After a brief theoretical reminder, the computation of the level sets is specified; they prove practical for determining the position of the crack in 3D and of the crack front, and they make it possible to define a local basis at the crack front. r7.02.12-probleme-fissuration presents the cracking problem treated with X-FEM. At r7.02.12-enrichissement-approximation-deplacement one introduces the approximation of the displacement written in a basis of enriched shape functions. The addition of functions discontinuous across the interface leads to a subdivision procedure detailed at r7.02.12-sous-decoupage, prior to the phase of integration of the stiffness terms and of the right-hand side, the implementation of which is explained at r7.02.12-integration-rigidite. r7.02.12-calcul-energetique-facteurs-intensite-contraintes is concerned with the post-processing of the energy release rate and of the stress intensity factors in linear fracture mechanics. The G -theta method makes it possible to compute the local energy release rate. For this purpose, a theta field is introduced, representing a virtual extension of the crack. The local G is then the solution of a variational equation, using the J integral in the form of domain integrals. The choices of discretisations of G and of the theta field lead to a linear system, the solution of which yields the values of G along the crack front. The G-theta method also makes it possible to determine the stress intensity factors along the crack front. Instead of using the J integral, one uses the bilinear form of G , which leads to domain integrals mixing solution fields and analytical asymptotic fields (also called interaction integrals). Thus, in the same way as for G , the K are then solutions of a variational equation, using interaction integrals. The choices of discretisations of the K and of the theta field lead to a linear system, the solution of which yields the values of the K along the crack front. 2 Representation of the crack by “level sets” The “Level set” method was introduced within the framework of fluid mechanics in order to represent the evolution of interfaces. The main idea is to consider the interface as the zero iso-value of a distance function. Indeed, in order not to multiply the configurations of cutting of the enriched elements into integration sub-elements, one authorises only two situations of multiple cancellation along the edge of an enriched element. The first corresponds to the case where the level set is zero all along the edge (therefore zero at its two end nodes and at its mid-side node). The second is the situation where the level set is zero at one of the end nodes and at the mid-side node (see r7.02.12-fig-2-11). In all the other situations, the level set must vanish only once along an edge. It will then be easy to detect the cancellations of the level set along an edge in order to form the integration sub-elements. In order to reduce the problem to these situations, a readjustment is carried out when one is in one of the situations represented on the figure r7.02.12-fig-2-12. Multiple cancellation of the level set along an edge Complementary readjustment of the level sets In the two configurations of r7.02.12-fig-2-12 where one adjusts the level set of one of the end nodes to zero, it is the end of the edge which has the smallest level set in absolute value which is chosen to be adjusted. Also, when the adjustment to be carried out is judged too large, which reveals a significant curvature of the level set relative to the size of the element, an alarm message recommending the use of a finer mesh is issued. The criterion chosen is the following: the alarm message is issued as soon as: \mid \mathit{lsn}à\mathit{ajuster}\mid >0.01\ast \underset{\mathit{noeuds}\mathit{de}l'\mathit{élément}}{max}\mid \mathit{lsn}\mid This procedure is applied both for the tangent level set and for the normal level set. 2.2.5 Notion of true signed distance If the level sets are computed by analytical functions, the choice of the functions is not unique for a given crack geometry. Indeed, any function with positive values on one side and negative values on the other is valid. However, if one wishes the level set to represent the true signed distance, then the choice is unique. This notion is important subsequently when one defines the coordinates in the local basis at the crack front by means of the values of the level sets. One must therefore take care to give the exact formula of the distance to the crack (an expression which is not easy for complex crack geometries). One of the interests of the projection method is that it provides a field which is the true signed distance. One could therefore also envisage combining the two methods. The data of a simple analytical function would make it possible in a first stage to determine the zero iso-value; then to create a simplified mesh of this surface, which would serve as a support for the projection method. The drawback is to create a virtual 2D mesh of the crack which is disjoint from the real 3D mesh. Otherwise, one could also envisage an orthogonalisation phase which transforms an arbitrary level set into a true distance. Note: If the shape of the level-set represented is not regular enough (for example, possesses a sharp angle or a bifurcation), the definition of the distance by orthogonal projection onto the zero iso-value may be ambiguous r7.02.12-fig-2-13 . In the neighbourhood of the singularity, the projection onto the surface of the level-set is not possible: the gradient of the zero iso-value of the level-set is discontinuous, therefore the normal to the zero iso-value of the level-set does not exist. One then designates by “shadow zone” the region where the computation of the distance by orthogonal projection onto the zero iso-value is to be ruled out. In the “shadow zone”, one computes the distance by returning to its fundamental definition: the distance of a point M to the zero iso-value is the minimum length connecting the point M to a point of the zero iso-value. Let C be the point corresponding to the vertex of the right angle on the zero iso-value. For every point M in the “shadow zone” r7.02.12-fig-2-13 , C satisfies the minimum length, that is to say: d(M,\text{iso\_zero})=min(\parallel \vec{\mathit{MN}}\parallel ,N\in \text{{iso\_zero}})=\parallel \vec{\mathit{MC}}\parallel . Difficulty of the definition of a distance by orthogonal projection in the case of a singularity of the zero iso-value Moreover, let us note that the interpolation of the level-set regularises the singularity. As the non-regular level-set is interpolated by polynomial functions r7.02.12-approximation-level-sets , the discretised level-set becomes a regular function within the element. 2.2.6 Multiple cracking The level sets are defined for each crack by the operator DEFI_FISS_XFEM. The list of the cracks is necessary for the creation of the X-FEM finite elements (operator MODI_MODELE_XFEM). During this phase, “concatenated” fields are created. For example, one creates a global normal level set field for all the cracks. For each node (nodal fields) or each mesh cell (element fields), one goes and seeks the information associated with the closest crack. The “concatenated” nodal fields created are: - Normal level set, - Tangent level set, - Status of the nodes (see r7.02.12-enrichissement-statut-nœuds), - Local basis at the crack front (see r7.02.12-base-locale-fissure). - Those linked to the subdivision (see r7.02.12-sous-decoupage), The “concatenated” element fields created are: - Those linked to the data structures for contact (see document R5.03.54). As regards propagation r7.02.13, one can define several cracks on the model and one can give the list of the cracks which propagate: at each call of the operator PROPA_FISS, all the cracks given propagate. Restrictions: The cracks must be sufficiently spaced from one another (3 mesh cells without cracks must at least separate them). A fortiori , the cracks must not intersect either. Otherwise, the introduction of special enrichments is necessary. 2.3 Local basis at the crack front The gradients of the level sets can be used to define the local basis at the crack front. The gradients are determined thanks to the derivatives of the shape functions and of the nodal values of the level sets. \left \lbrace \begin{array}{}\nabla {\mathrm{lsn}}_{j}^{\mathrm{elt}}=\sum_{i}{\phi }_{i,j}{\mathrm{lsn}}_{i}\\ \nabla {\mathrm{lst}}_{j}^{\mathrm{elt}}=\sum_{i}{\phi }_{i,j}{\mathrm{lst}}_{i}\end{array}j=1,3 \right. where the {\phi }_{i,j} are the derivatives of the shape functions with respect to the direction j . One thus determines a field of gradients per element. The values are computed at the nodes of the elements, for each element independently of the others; then in order to compute the nodal value one averages over the values obtained by elements at the nodes. The local basis at the crack front \left\lbrace {e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}\right\rbrace is then computed at every point thanks to the nodal gradient fields: {e}_{1}=\frac{\sum_{i}{\varphi}_{i}\nabla {\mathit{lst}}_{i}}{\parallel \sum_{i}{\varphi}_{i}\nabla {\mathit{lst}}_{i}\parallel },{e}_{2}=\frac{\sum_{i}{\varphi}_{i}\nabla {\mathit{lsn}}_{i}}{\parallel \sum_{i}{\varphi}_{i}\nabla {\mathit{lsn}}_{i}\parallel },{e}_{3}={e}_{1}\times {e}_{2} where \nabla {\mathrm{lsn}}_{i} and \nabla {\mathrm{lst}}_{i} are the nodal values of the gradients. Local basis at the crack front In 2D one will have only: {e}_{1}=\frac{\sum_{i}{\phi }_{i}\nabla {\mathrm{lst}}_{i}}{\parallel \sum_{i}{\phi }_{i}\nabla {\mathrm{lst}}_{i}\parallel },{e}_{2}=\frac{\sum_{i}{\phi }_{i}\nabla {\mathrm{lsn}}_{i}}{\parallel \sum_{i}{\phi }_{i}\nabla {\mathrm{lsn}}_{i}\parallel } 2.4 Determination of the crack front The crack front is defined by the intersection of the zero iso-values of the two level sets. For the computation of the stress intensity factors (Stress Intensity Factors in English), it is practical to define points belonging to the crack front, which will serve as a basis for the interpolation of the SIFs (see r7.02.12-discretisations). The points chosen are the intersections of the faces of the elements with the curve \text{lsn}=0\cap \text{lst}=0 . These points will then be ordered so as to define a curvilinear abscissa along the crack front. 2.4.1 Search for the points of the crack front The search for the points of the crack front is carried out in the following manner. One restricts oneself to the elements where the normal level set changes sign and where all the nodes are of status “Crack-Tip” (this notion is defined at r7.02.12-enrichissement-statut-nœuds). Let a face of such an element; if this face is a quadrangle, one reduces it to two triangles. Let the triangle \mathit{ABC} Face of an element intersected by the crack front One seeks the point M solution of the following system: \left \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\text{lsn}(M)=0\\ \text{lst}(M)=0\end{array} \right. One writes the point M in the frame \left(A,\vec{\text{AB}},\vec{\text{AC}}\right) M=A+{\xi}_{1}\overrightarrow{\text{AB}}+{\xi}_{2}\overrightarrow{\text{AC}} The system is then written \left \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\left(1-{\xi}_{1}-{\xi}_{2}\right)\mathit{lsn}(A)+{\xi}_{1}\mathit{lsn}(B)+{\xi}_{2}\mathit{lsn}(C)=0\\ \left(1-{\xi}_{1}-{\xi}_{2}\right)\mathit{lst}(A)+{\xi}_{1}\mathit{lst}(B)+{\xi}_{2}\mathit{lst}(C)=0\end{array} \right. \mathrm{\iff }\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\xi}_{1}\\ {\xi}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace ={\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathit{lsn}(B)-\mathit{lsn}(A)& \mathit{lsn}(C)-\mathit{lsn}(A)\\ \mathit{lst}(B)-\mathit{lsn}(A)& \mathit{lst}(C)-\mathit{lsn}(A)\end{array}\right]}^{-1}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}-\mathit{lsn}(A)\\ -\mathit{lst}(A)\end{array}\right\rbrace The point M is retained provided that it belongs to the triangle \mathit{ABC} . In 2D, one uses the same procedure but directly on the mesh cells and not on the faces of the mesh cells (always triangles or else quadrangles cut into triangles). The search for the points of the crack front is accompanied by a strategy of elimination of the redundant points M . Indeed, if the face is not a face of the geometrical boundary of the structure, it is then common to two mesh cells of the list of the mesh cells of the front, and a point of the front can thus be detected (at least) twice. In order to check whether the new point M detected does not already belong to the list of the points P of the front, one proceeds to a characterisation of the point M according to whether it is situated on a vertex node of the face, an edge of the face or else inside the face. One then carries out a check according to the cases, via a loop on the points P of the same status as M : - if M is situated on a vertex node of number {N}^{M} and {N}^{M}={N}^{P} , - if M is situated on an edge characterised by the vertex numbers {N}_{1}^{M} and {N}_{2}^{M} and \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{N}_{1}^{M}+{N}_{2}^{M}={N}_{1}^{P}+{N}_{2}^{P}\\ {N}_{1}^{M}.{N}_{2}^{M}={N}_{1}^{P}.{N}_{2}^{P}\end{array}\right. , - if M is situated inside a face characterised by \mathit{NNF} vertices and \left \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\sum}_{i=1}^{\mathit{NNF}}{N}_{i}^{M}={\sum}_{i=1}^{\mathit{NNF}}{N}_{i}^{P}\\ {\prod}_{i=1}^{\mathit{NNF}}{N}_{i}^{M}={\prod}_{i=1}^{\mathit{NNF}}{N}_{i}^{P}\\ {\sum}_{i,j\in (1,\mathit{NNF}),i\ne j}{N}_{i}^{M}.{N}_{j}^{M}={\sum}_{i,j\in (1,\mathit{NNF}),i\ne j}{N}_{i}^{P}.{N}_{j}^{P}\end{array} \right. , then the point M is not retained. In the opposite case, it is added to the list of the points P of the front. In order to free oneself from the numerical errors which could cause a point M normally situated on a vertex node to be characterised as a point interior to the surface, a “fit to vertex” procedure is associated with the previous strategy. Thus, if M is detected as a point situated on an edge or inside a face, the following algorithm is used: - computation of the distance from each vertex node of the face to the point M , - each of these values is placed in the vector \mathit{Dist} which is then sorted from the smallest value to the largest, - if \mathit{Dist}(1) 2 : - If the pair of \mathit{IMA} has already been found (case of a duplicate pair): - set the second value of the pair to 0 in order to ignore this pair at the next iteration - go to the following mesh cell \mathit{IMA}+1 - If one is dealing with a new pair, the second index is the following point of the front: - \mathit{TABPT}(\mathit{IPT}+1)=\mathit{LISTPT}(2\times \mathit{IMA}+1) - set the second value of the pair to 0 in order to ignore this pair at the next iteration - If it is the second index of the pair which corresponds to the one sought: - If \mathit{IPT}>2 : - If the pair of \mathit{IMA} has already been found (case of a duplicate pair): - set the second value of the pair to 0 in order to ignore this pair at the next iteration - go to the following mesh cell \mathit{IMA}+1 - If one is dealing with a new pair, the first index is the following point of the front: - \mathit{TABPT}(\mathit{IPT}+1)=\mathit{LISTPT}(2\times \mathit{IMA}) - set the second value of the pair to 0 in order to ignore this pair at the next iteration - If one has not found any points to associate with \mathit{IPT} , it is therefore an end point (case of multiple fronts) - one checks that \mathit{IPT} is indeed a point of the list \mathit{PTEXTR} then one sets it to 0 in order to ignore it at the next iteration - one searches for a new end point in the list \mathit{PTEXTR} in order to begin the new crack front and one goes to the following mesh cell \mathit{IMA}+1 3 Cracking problem with X-FEM 3.1 General problem In this part, one recalls the equations of the general problem of a cracked structure. One considers a crack {\Gamma}_{c} in a domain \Omega \in {\Re }^{3} delimited by \partial \Omega of outward normal {n}_{\mathrm{ext}} . The lips of the crack are denoted {\Gamma}^{1} and {\Gamma}^{2} of outward normals {n}^{1} and {n}^{2} . The stress and displacement fields are denoted respectively \sigma and u . A quasi-static loading is imposed on the structure by means of a body-force density f , of a surface-force density t on {\Gamma}_{t} and of a surface-force density g on the lips. The solid is clamped on {\Gamma}_{u} . Notations of the general problem The strong form of the equilibrium equations and of the boundary conditions is written: \begin{array}{}\nabla \cdot \sigma =f\text{dans}\Omega \\ \sigma \cdot {n}_{\mathrm{ext}}=t\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{t}\\ \sigma \cdot {n}^{1}=g\text{sur}{\Gamma}^{1}\\ \sigma \cdot {n}^{2}=g\text{sur}{\Gamma}^{2}\\ u=0\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{u}\end{array} We place ourselves within the framework of small strains and small displacements, for which the strain-displacement relation is written: \varepsilon =\varepsilon (u)={\nabla}_{s}u where {\nabla}_{s} is the symmetric part of the gradient and \varepsilon the strain tensor. One considers a linear elastic material 1. The constitutive law of the solid \Omega is written: \sigma =C:\varepsilon \text{dans}\Omega where C is the Hooke tensor. The principle of virtual work is written: {\int}_{\Omega}\sigma (u):\epsilon (v)d\Omega ={\int}_{\Omega}f\cdot \mathrm{vd}\Omega +{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{t}}t\cdot \mathrm{vd\Gamma }+{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{c}}g\cdot \mathrm{vd\Gamma }\forall v\in {H}_{0}^{1}(\Omega ) where {H}_{0}^{1}(O) is the Sobolev space of the functions whose derivative is square-integrable, vanishing on \partial \Omega . 3.2 Enrichment of the displacement approximation The main idea is to enrich the basis of the interpolation functions thanks to the partition of unity. One recalls the classical finite-element approximation: {u}^{h}(x)=\sum_{i\in {N}_{n}(x)}{a}_{i}{\phi }_{i}(x) where the {a}_{i} are the displacement degrees of freedom at node i and {\phi }_{i} the shape functions associated with node i. {N}_{n}(x) is the set of the nodes whose support contains the point x . One identifies the support of a node i with the support of the shape functions associated with this node, that is to say with the set of points x such that {\phi }_{i}(x)\ne 0 . The enriched approximation is written: {u}^{h}(x)=\sum_{i\in {N}_{n}(x)}{a}_{i}{\varphi}_{i}(x)+\sum_{j\in {N}_{n}(x)\cap K}{b}_{j}{\varphi}_{j}(x){H}_{j}\left(\mathit{lsn}(x)\right)+\sum_{k\in {N}_{n}(x)\cap L}\sum_{\alpha =1}^{4}{c}_{k}^{\alpha}{\varphi}_{k}(x){F}^{\alpha}\left(\mathit{lsn}(x),\mathit{lst}(x)\right) This expression is composed of 3 terms. The 1st term is the classical continuous term. The 2nd and 3rd terms are enriched terms. Being at the heart of the X-FEM method, these terms are made explicit in the following paragraphs. 3.2.1 Enrichment with a domain-selection function (2nd term) Suppose that the interface {\Gamma}_{c} partitions the domain such that \Omega ={\Omega}_{+}\cup {\Omega}_{-} . If {\Gamma}_{c} is a crack, one partitions in the same manner the domain \Omega by virtually extending {\Gamma}_{c} . In order to represent the displacement jump across {\Gamma}_{c} , one introduces the domain-selection function or characteristic function of the domain {H}_{j}\left(x\right) defined by: \mathit{Si}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{x}_{j}\in {\Omega}_{+},\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{H}_{j}(x)=\left \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}0\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{si}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}x\in {\Omega}_{+}\\ -2\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{si}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}x\notin {\Omega}_{+}\end{array} \right. \mathit{Si}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{x}_{j}\in {\Omega}_{-},\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{H}_{j}(x)=\left \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}0\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{si}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}x\in {\Omega}_{-}\\ +2\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{si}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}x\notin {\Omega}_{-}\end{array} \right. By making use of the normal level set, the quantity {H}_{j}\left(\text{lsn}\left(x\right)\right) is equal to 0 if the point x and the node {x}_{j} are on the same side of the crack and \pm 2 otherwise. The coefficient “2” is introduced in order to have a simpler writing of the mean displacement jump along the interface. The {b}_{j} are the enriched degrees of freedom. K is the set of the nodes whose support is entirely cut by the crack (nodes represented by a circle on r7.02.12-fig-3-2). Note By abuse of language, one will also call the domain-selection functions “Heaviside” functions. But one will have to refer to the definition above, in order to represent the approximation of the discontinuity of the displacement field. On the left, the “circle” nodes are enriched by the Heaviside function and the “square” nodes by the singular functions (topological enrichment). On the right, the “square” nodes are enriched by the singular functions (geometrical enrichment). 3.2.2 Enrichment with a domain-selection function for a branching of cracks Suppose a branching of two discontinuities, which partitions the space into three domains such that \Omega ={\Omega}_{1}\cup {\Omega}_{2}\cup {\Omega}_{3} . If it is a branching of two cracks, one partitions in the same manner the domain \Omega by virtually extending the three crack branches. Partitioning of the domain by a crack junction For a simple branching, the generalisation of the domain-selection functions leads to the following writing: \begin{array}{c}{u}^{h}(x)=\sum_{i\in {N}_{n}(x)}{a}_{i}{\varphi}_{i}(x)+\sum_{j\in K\cap {\Omega}_{1}}{b}_{j,1}{\varphi}_{j}(x){\mathrm{\chi }}_{{\Omega}_{2}}+{b}_{j,2}{\varphi}_{j}(x){\mathrm{\chi }}_{{\Omega}_{3}}\\ +\sum_{j\in K\cap {\Omega}_{2}}{b}_{j,1}{\varphi}_{j}(x){\mathrm{\chi }}_{{\Omega}_{1}}+{b}_{j,2}{\varphi}_{j}(x){\mathrm{\chi }}_{{\Omega}_{3}}\\ +\sum_{j\in K\cap {\Omega}_{3}}{b}_{j,1}{\varphi}_{j}(x){\mathrm{\chi }}_{{\Omega}_{1}}+{b}_{j,2}{\varphi}_{j}(x){\mathrm{\chi }}_{{\Omega}_{2}}\end{array} Where {\mathrm{\chi }}_{{\Omega}_{i}} are domain-selection functions defined by: {\mathrm{\chi }}_{{\Omega}_{i}}(x)=\left \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}2\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{si}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}x\in {\Omega}_{i}\\ \phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}0\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}\text{si}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}x\notin {\Omega}_{i}\end{array} \right. However, the topological description of the three connected domains (Ω1, Ω2 and Ω3) is not trivial, given the only information provided by the level-sets. The level-sets make it possible to represent a scalar change of sign across a discontinuity. Whereas we wish to represent the partitioning of the space in the neighbourhood of the discontinuity. From an “elementary” point of view, we observe that the sign field of the level-sets read in vector form sticks approximately to the partitioning that we wish to carry out. This partitioning, thanks to the vectorisation of the scalar level-sets, then makes it possible to reuse advantageously the data structures of Code_Aster. However, the elementary partitioning alone is insufficient to represent the “domain dof” (χΩϕi). Note In fact, the “domain dof” corresponds to the collection of the partitions of the domain Ω over the whole support of the node i. On the support of each node, it is therefore indispensable to concatenate the elementary partitions corresponding to a given “domain dof”. This operation is not trivial since the sign fields evolve from one element to another (as the scalar sign fields are not extended onto all the elements, in order to localise on a few elements of interest the definition of a crack, also called the “near band” of enrichment). An algorithm dedicated to the concatenation of the elementary partitioning has been developed in order to solve this fundamental difficulty. Partitioning of a multi-cracked element by means of the “vectorised” sign field. For each domain, the first scalar component of the sign vector corresponds to the characterisation of the discontinuity of crack no. 1 and the second scalar component of the sign vector corresponds to the discontinuity of crack no. 2. This choice is well suited, given the conditioning problems detailed at r7.02.12-conditionnement-enrichissement . 2. In code_aster, one prefers to store the information of the Heaviside sign and that of the domain identifier at the Gauss point in the integration sub-elements. 3.2.3 Enrichment with the singular functions (3rd term) In order to represent the singularity at the crack front, one enriches the approximation with functions based on the asymptotic expansions of the displacement field in linear elastic fracture mechanics. These expressions have been determined for a plane crack in an infinite medium. \begin{array}{}{u}_{1}=\frac{1}{2\mu }\sqrt{\frac{r}{2\pi }}({K}_{1}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}(\kappa -\cos\theta )+{K}_{2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}(\kappa +2+\cos\theta ))\\ {u}_{2}=\frac{1}{2\mu }\sqrt{\frac{r}{2\pi }}({K}_{1}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}(\kappa -\cos\theta )+{K}_{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}(\kappa -2+\cos\theta ))\\ {u}_{3}=\frac{1}{2\mu }\sqrt{\frac{r}{2\pi }}{K}_{3}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\ \mu =\frac{E}{2(1+\nu )}\text{et}\kappa =3-4\nu \text{en}\text{déformations}\text{planes}.\end{array} The plane-stress assumption cannot be retained because no cracked plate is in a situation of plane stress in the neighbourhood of the singularity, when one places oneself at a finite distance from the skin of the shell. The basis making it possible to describe these fields comprises 4 functions: \left\lbrace \sqrt{r}\cos\frac{\theta}{2},\sqrt{r}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\theta ,\sqrt{r}\sin\frac{\theta}{2},\sqrt{r}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\theta \right\rbrace . As: \left \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\theta =-\sin\theta \sin\frac{\theta}{2}+\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\\ \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\theta =\sin\theta \cos\frac{\theta}{2}-\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\end{array} \right. one then chooses the following basis 2: F=\left\lbrace \sqrt{r}\sin\frac{\theta}{2},\sqrt{r}\cos\frac{\theta}{2},\sqrt{r}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\sin\theta ,\sqrt{r}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\sin\theta \right\rbrace . where (r,\theta ) are the polar coordinates in the local basis at the crack front (see r7.02.12-fig-2-14 and r7.02.12-fig-3-8). These coordinates can be expressed easily thanks to the level sets, since: r=\sqrt{\text{lsn}\mathrm{²}+\text{lst}\mathrm{²}},\theta =\arctan(\frac{\text{lsn}}{\text{lst}}),\theta \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right] In practice, one rather uses the computer function \text{atan2}(\text{lsn},\text{lst}) which returns the principal value of the argument of the complex number (\text{lst},\text{lsn}) expressed in radians in the interval \left[-\pi ,\pi \right] . For points situated exactly on the lower lip (\text{lsn}=0) , the function \text{atan2}(0,\text{lst}) gives an angle equal to \pi . In theory, \text{atan2}(-0,\text{lst}) makes it possible to obtain -\pi as expected, but this is not numerically always the case. In order to remedy this drawback, one rather uses the following expression for the angle \theta : \theta =H(\text{lsn})\mid \text{atan}2(\text{lsn},\text{lst})\mid ,\theta \in \left[-\pi ,\pi \right] where H(\text{lsn}) is the value of the Heaviside function. Thus, when one is on the lower lip, the value -\pi is indeed reached. Polar coordinates in the local basis One notes that only the 1st function of the basis is discontinuous across the crack. The other functions are added only in order to improve the precision. These functions are the Westergaard solutions, analytical asymptotic solutions of an elastic fracture problem in 2D. This basis is well suited to the 3D cases, at least for cracks whose front is fairly regular. These functions are said to be “singular” because their derivatives are singular at r=0 . A quadrangle with 8 nodes and its 3 contact facets 3.4.4.2 3D case In the 3D case, for a hexahedron, one can bound from above the maximum number of contact facets for a single crack by 18. One is indeed liable to reach this figure for an element which contains the crack front. During the recutting of the triangular facets in conformity with the \mathit{lst} , certain facets give rise to two facets (see ), which explains that one can have finally nearly 18 facets. Recutting of a triangular facet at the crack front 3.4.4.3 Multi-Heaviside case In the multi-cracked case, the maximum number of contact facets per crack is higher than the maximum number of contact facets for an element crossed by a single crack. Indeed, the sequential cutting generates more sub-elements for each new crack and therefore more contact facets because the latter rely on the sub-elements. In 3D, for a hexahedron, one fixes the maximum number of contact facets per crack at 30. A 3D element crossed by 4 cracks can therefore have a total of 30\ast 4=120 facets. In 2D, one fixes the maximum number of contact facets per crack at 7. A 2D element crossed by 4 cracks can therefore have a total of 4\ast 7=28 facets. 3.5 Integration of the stiffness 3.5.1 Integrand of the mechanical stiffness term The X-FEM approximation of the displacement field is written in vector form: \left\lbrace {u}^{h}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace {\varphi}_{i}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{\varphi}_{j}{H}_{j}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{\varphi}_{k}{F}^{1}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{\varphi}_{k}{F}^{2}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{\varphi}_{k}{F}^{3}\phantom{\rule{2em}{0ex}}{\varphi}_{k}{F}^{4}\right\rbrace \cdot \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{a}_{i}\\ {b}_{j}\\ {c}_{k}^{1}\\ {c}_{k}^{2}\\ {c}_{k}^{3}\\ {c}_{k}^{4}\end{array}\right\rbrace Or again: \left\lbrace {u}^{h}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace N\right\rbrace \cdot \left\lbrace u\right\rbrace where \left\lbrace N\right\rbrace is the vector of the enriched basis of the shape functions and \left\lbrace u\right\rbrace the vector of the nodal displacement dofs. Now the presence of monomials in 1/\sqrt{r} coming from the enrichment with the asymptotic fields leads to a very slow convergence of the precision of these schemes: a considerable number of Gauss points is then necessary in order to obtain an acceptable error. When the singularity is found on the boundary of the integration domain, well-chosen successive changes of variables make it possible to reduce the problem to the integration over a unit domain of a non-singular function, polynomial (or quasi-polynomial), on which a classical Gauss-Legendre integration proves effective and rapidly convergent. About ten Gauss points in each direction suffice to reach the limits of the numerical precision of a computer. When the singularity is not found on the boundary, one must cut the domain into sub-domains, in such a way that the singularity is found on the boundaries of the sub-domains. Despite very satisfactory results in terms of convergence of the relative integration error on each term, the implementation effort to be provided for the 3D structures seems to us considerable. All the more so as the difference at the level of the global errors (after solution) between a classical integration with a number of Gauss points that is fairly high but reasonable and a modified singular integration is not really significant. For the moment, one has put in place the same classical Gauss-Legendre scheme as the one which is used for the integration of the non-singular terms. 3.6 Integration of the surface right-hand sides 3.6.1 Integrand of the right-hand side of the surface forces The right-hand sides due to the surface forces are written in discretised manner: {\int}_{{\Gamma}^{t}}t\cdot {u}^{\ast }{\mathrm{d\Gamma }}^{t} the discretised surface {\Gamma}^{t} corresponds to the faces of the 3D elements. a possible subdivision for these 2D faces is the one corresponding to the trace of the subdivision of the 3D elements.
