An integration preserving the finite-element order of approximation would in fact be sufficient 4 Linear thermal analysis with X-FEM 4.1 Introduction The X-FEM method has been introduced into the linear thermal operator in order to be able to carry out chained thermo-mechanical analyses taking the crack into account in the thermal solution: the temperature field is then discontinuous across the crack if no thermal loading is applied on its lips (with a natural condition of zero flux). It is also possible to define a condition of thermal exchange between the lips of the crack by the data of an exchange coefficient. Note : The solution of the linear thermal problems with X-FEM relies on an algorithmics almost identical to that implemented for the solution of mechanical problems of cracked structures with X-FEM, detailed in r7.02.12-probleme-fissuration . In particular the procedures making it possible: - to enrich the approximation of the field of the nodal unknowns (status of the nodes, status of the mesh cells, cancellation of the degrees of freedom enriched wrongly); - to subdivide the elements crossed by a crack; - the procedures of integration of the matrices and of the elementary vectors on this subdivision ; are identical to those which have been previously detailed; they will therefore not be so in this part. 4.2 Restrictions The set of the modellings and of the types of loading available for the transient linear thermal algorithm in the case of classical models (non X-FEM) has not been integrally carried over for the thermal X-FEM finite elements. All these functionalities of course remain available on the non-enriched part of the model, and are documented in . Forthcoming developments will make it possible to complete progressively the list of the functionalities available to date. Type of problems treated Solution of linear thermal transients (independence with respect to temperature of the material parameters), for an isotropic material (scalar conductivity). The branching of cracks (multi-Heaviside) is excluded. Finite elements available For the moment, only the X-FEM elements of the 3D, axisymmetric and plane modellings have been introduced for the following linear support mesh cells: | modelling | support mesh cells of the principal elements | support mesh cells of the boundary elements | | --- | --- | --- | | 3D | TETRA4, HEXA8, PENTA6, PYRA5 | TRIA3, QUAD4 | | plane / axisymmetric | TRIA3, QUAD4 | SEG2 | There therefore do not exist lumped thermal X-FEM elements, and the mesh from which one defines the enriched model is obligatorily linear. Thermal loadings available on the enriched part of the model For the moment, the only loading available on the enriched part of the model is the condition of thermal exchange between the lips of the crack. No other boundary condition can be imposed on boundary thermal X-FEM elements, or on nodes belonging to thermal X-FEM elements. Likewise, no source term can be imposed on principal thermal X-FEM elements. The user must therefore make sure of applying his loadings sufficiently “far” from the crack, that is to say on non-enriched elements (or nodes whose support is formed only of non-enriched elements). 4.3 Problem treated In order not to weigh down the expression of the variational formulation, one considers the simplified problem of a cracked solid, constituted of a linear and isotropic material, of which a part of the boundary (sufficiently far from the crack) is subjected to an imposed temperature. The rest of the boundary (crack excluded) is subjected to a condition of zero flux. Finally, one imposes a condition of thermal exchange between the lips of the crack. One therefore considers a crack {\Gamma}^{c} in a domain \Omega \subset {ℝ}^{{n}_{\mathit{dim}}} , with {n}_{\mathit{dim}}=2\text{ou}3 . One denotes n the outward normal to its boundary \partial \Omega , {\Gamma}_{1}^{c} and {\Gamma}_{2}^{c} the lips of the crack of respective outward normals {n}_{1} and {n}_{2} , and {\Gamma}^{d} the part of \partial \Omega subjected to an imposed temperature (see Figure ). One denotes x the space variable, t the time, and T the temperature. The interval \left]{t}_{0},{t}_{f}\right] corresponds to the time interval considered for the solution of the problem. This method is also used for the computation of the stress intensity factors, by using the bilinear form of g but only in 2D. Because in order to be able to use it in 3D, one must know the local basis at the crack front in order to express the asymptotic fields as a function of the polar coordinates (r,\theta ) . Then, one presents the contribution of the level sets in classical finite elements, which has been to be able to construct a local basis at the crack front in 3D. As one has seen at r7.02.12-base-locale-fissure, the gradients of the level sets give a local basis at the crack front. Moreover, the polar coordinates in this local basis are expressed easily as a function of the level sets (see r7.02.12-fig-3-8). Thus thanks to the level sets, the G -theta method has been applicable to the computation of the stress intensity factors in 3D with classical finite elements. In this context, the crack is meshed, a classical analysis is carried out. In post-processing, one determines the two level set fields from the meshed crack and one deduces from them a discretisation of the crack front. The theta field is constructed from this discretised crack front, and the G -theta method is applied. The last point is the computation of the energy release rate and of the stress intensity factors, following an X-FEM analysis. In this case, the crack is not meshed, but the procedure followed is almost the same: the discretisation of the crack front is determined from the level sets, a theta field is constructed and the G -theta is applied. The only difference is situated at the level of the numerical integrations: with X-FEM, the numerical integrations require a subdivision of the elements to be integrated. In fact, one uses the subdivision carried out for the computation of the tangent matrices and of the right-hand sides. 5.1 G-theta method for the computation of G 5.1.1 Equilibrium relations In linear elasticity, one defines the free-energy density \Psi , in the absence of initial strains and stresses, by a positive definite quadratic form of the components of the strain tensor: \Psi (\varepsilon ,T)=\frac{1}{2}(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{\text{th}}):C:(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{\text{th}}) C is the Hooke tensor (tensor of the 4th order), and the two dots designate the tensor product contracted on two indices. The stress tensor \sigma derives from the potential \Psi in order to give the state law (or constitutive law of the material): \sigma =\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial \varepsilon }(\varepsilon ,T)=C:(\varepsilon -{\varepsilon}^{\text{th}}) The equilibrium relations in weak formulation are obtained by minimising the global potential energy of the system: W(v)=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\Psi (\varepsilon (v))d\Omega -\underset{\Omega}{\int}{f}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Omega -\underset{S}{\int}{g}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Gamma This functional being minimal for the displacement field u : \begin{array}{c}\delta W=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {\varepsilon}_{ij}}\delta {\varepsilon}_{ij}d\Omega -\underset{\Omega}{\int}{f}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Omega -\underset{S}{\int}{g}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Gamma \\ =\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{ij}\frac{1}{2}(\delta {v}_{i,j}+\delta {v}_{j,i})d\Omega -\underset{\Omega}{\int}{f}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Omega -\underset{S}{\int}{g}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Gamma \\ =\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{ij}\delta {v}_{i,j}d\Omega -\underset{\Omega}{\int}{f}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Omega -\underset{S}{\int}{g}_{i}\delta {v}_{i}d\Gamma =0\end{array} The equilibrium relations in weak formulation are therefore written in the following manner: Find u\in V such that \underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{ij}{v}_{\text{i,j}}d\Omega =\underset{\Omega}{\int}{f}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Omega +\underset{S}{\int}{g}_{i}{v}_{i}d\Gamma ,\forall v\in {V}_{0} 5.1.2 Lagrangian expression of the energy release rate By definition, the local energy release rate G is defined by the opposite of the derivative of the potential energy with respect to the domain: G=-\frac{\partial W}{\partial \Omega } The method of virtual extensions used here is a Lagrangian method of derivation of the potential energy. It consists in introducing transformations: {F}^{\eta}:P\in \Omega \to M=P+\eta \theta (P)\in {\Omega}^{\eta} which, to each material point P of the reference domain O , associate a spatial point M of the transformed domain {\Omega}^{\eta} . These transformations representing propagations of the crack, must modify only the position of the crack front {\Gamma}_{0} . The fields \theta must be tangent to the surface of the crack. Let n be the normal to the surface of the crack, the fields \theta must satisfy: {\theta}_{j}{n}_{j}=0\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{\text{cr}} Let m be the unit normal to the crack front, situated in the tangent plane of the crack. According to , the local energy release rate G is the solution of the following variational equation: \underset{{\Gamma}_{0}}{\int}G\theta \cdot m=G(\theta ),\forall \theta \in \theta where G(\theta ) is defined by the opposite of the derivative of the potential energy W(u(\eta )) at equilibrium with respect to the initial evolution of the crack front: G(\theta )=-{\frac{\text{dW}(u(\eta ))}{d\eta }\mid }_{\eta =0} (particle derivative) In order to derive the potential energy with respect to its support (in the neighbourhood of the reference support), one uses the Reynolds transport theorem: For a transformation {F}^{\eta} of class {C}^{1} and a function \varphi (tensor of order 0, 1 or 2) of class {C}^{1} , denoting \dot{\varphi} the Lagrangian derivative linked to the variation of domain, one has the following relation: {\frac{\partial}{\partial \eta }(\underset{\Omega}{\int}\varphi d\Omega )\mid }_{\eta =0}=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\dot{\varphi}+\varphi div{(\frac{\partial {F}^{\eta}}{\partial \eta })}_{\eta =0}d\Omega In fact, in practice, the transformation {F}^{\eta} is not always of class {C}^{1} because the field \theta is only piecewise {C}^{1} . Thus, \begin{array}{rcl}-G(\theta) & = & \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \eta} \left( \int_{\Omega} \Psi - f_i u_i \, d\Omega - \int_{S} g_i u_i \, d\Gamma\right) \right|_{\eta = 0} \\[6pt]& = & \int_{\Omega} \overbrace{\Psi - f_i u_i}^{\dot{\phantom{a}}} + (\Psi - f_i u_i)\,\operatorname{div}(\theta)\, d\Omega \\[6pt]& & - \int_{S} \overbrace{g_i u_i}^{\dot{\phantom{a}}} + g_i u_i \left( \operatorname{div}(\theta) - \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial n_k} n_k \right) d\Gamma\end{array} where: \Psi (\varepsilon ,T)=\frac{1}{2}\lambda {({\epsilon}_{ii})}^{2}+\mu {\varepsilon}_{ij}{\varepsilon}_{ij}-3K\alpha (T-{T}_{\mathrm{réf}}) \dot{\Psi}(\epsilon )=\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {\epsilon}_{ij}}{\dot{\epsilon}}_{ij}+\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}\dot{T}={\sigma}_{ij}{\dot{\epsilon}}_{ij}+\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}\dot{T} therefore: \begin{array}{c}-G(\theta )=\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{ij}{\dot{\varepsilon}}_{ij}+\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}\dot{T}-{\dot{f}}_{i}{u}_{i}-{f}_{i}{\dot{u}}_{i}+(\Psi -{f}_{i}{u}_{i}){\theta}_{k,k}d\Omega \\ -\underset{S}{\int}{\dot{g}}_{i}{u}_{i}-{g}_{i}{\dot{u}}_{i}+{g}_{i}{u}_{i}({\theta}_{k,k}-\frac{\partial \theta }{\partial {n}_{k}}{n}_{k})d\Gamma \end{array} Firstly, let us use the relation giving the Lagrangian derivative of a field \varphi as a function of its Eulerian derivative \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial \eta } : \dot{\varphi}=\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial \eta }+\nabla \varphi \cdot \theta According to this relation, the body force f being assumed independent of \eta , that is to say being the restriction to O of fields defined on {ℝ}^{3} , one can write that \frac{\partial {f}_{i}}{\partial \eta }=0 . As it is the same for g and T , one has the following relations: \begin{array}{c}\dot{T}={T}_{,k}{\theta}_{k}\\ {\dot{f}}_{i}={f}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}\\ {\dot{g}}_{i}={g}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}\end{array} Secondly, let us use the relation giving the Lagrangian derivative of the gradient of a field as a function of the gradient of the field and of the gradient of the derivative of the field: \dot{\nabla}\varphi =\nabla \dot{\varphi}-\nabla \varphi \cdot \nabla \theta that is in indicial notations, \stackrel{\cdot}{\overbrace{{\varphi}_{i,j}}} = {\dot{\varphi}}_{i,j} - {\varphi}_{i,p}{\theta}_{p,j} therefore {\dot{\varepsilon}}_{i,j}=\frac{1}{2}({\dot{u}}_{i,j}+{\dot{u}}_{j,i})-\frac{1}{2}({u}_{i,p}{\theta}_{p,j}+{u}_{j,p}{\theta}_{p,i}) One replaces the 2 expressions in the 1st and one obtains: \begin{array}{c}-G(\theta )=\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{ij}{\dot{u}}_{i,j}+\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}{T}_{,k}{\theta}_{k}-{\sigma}_{ij}{u}_{i,p}{\theta}_{p,j}-{f}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}{u}_{i}-{f}_{i}{\dot{u}}_{i}+(\Psi -{f}_{i}{u}_{i}){\theta}_{k,k}d\Omega \\ -\underset{S}{\int}{g}_{i,k}{\sigma}_{k}{u}_{i}-{g}_{i}{\dot{u}}_{i}+{g}_{i}{u}_{i}({\theta}_{k,k}-\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial {n}_{k}}{n}_{k})d\Gamma \end{array} One can eliminate the terms in \dot{u} by noting that the field \dot{u} is kinematically admissible and satisfies the equilibrium equation: \underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{ij}{\dot{u}}_{i,j}d\Omega =\underset{\Omega}{\int}{f}_{i}{\dot{u}}_{i}d\Omega +\underset{S}{\int}{g}_{i}{\dot{u}}_{i}d\Gamma Which gives the final expression of J(\theta ) : \begin{array}{c}G(\theta )=\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{ij}{u}_{i,p}{\theta}_{p,j}-\Psi {\theta}_{k,k}+\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}{T}_{,k}{\theta}_{k}d\Omega \\ +\underset{\Omega}{\int}{f}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}{u}_{i}+{f}_{i}{u}_{i}{\theta}_{k,k}d\Omega \\ +\underset{S}{\int}{g}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}{u}_{i}+{g}_{i}{u}_{i}({\theta}_{k,k}-\frac{\partial \theta }{\partial {n}_{k}}{n}_{k})d\Gamma \end{array} Note This form of the J integral does not use contour integrals but domain integrals. 5.1.3 Discretisations One denotes s the curvilinear abscissa at the crack front. The computation of the local value of G requires solving the following variational equation for several fields {\theta}^{i} : {\int}_{{\Gamma}_{0}}G(s){\theta}^{i}(s)\cdot m(s)\text{ds}=G({\theta}^{i})\forall i\in [1,P] The scalar field G(s) is discretised on a basis denoted {({p}_{j}(s))}_{1\le j\le N} : G(s)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}{G}_{j}{p}_{j}(s) Likewise, the fields {\theta}^{i} are discretised on a basis denoted {({q}_{k}(s))}_{1\le k\le M} . Let {\bar{\theta}}^{i} be the trace of the field {\theta}^{i} on the crack front {\Gamma}_{0} : {\bar{\theta}}^{i}(s)={\theta \mid }_{{\Gamma}_{0}}(s) and let {\theta}_{k}^{i} be the components of {\bar{\theta}}^{i}(s) in this basis: {\bar{\theta}}^{i}(s)=\sum_{k=1}^{M}{\theta}_{k}^{i}{q}_{k}(s) By injecting these expressions into the variational equation, one obtains: \underset{{\Gamma}_{0}}{\int}\sum_{j=1}^{N}{G}_{j}{p}_{j}(s)\sum_{k=1}^{M}({\theta}_{k}^{i}{q}_{k}(s))\cdot m(s)\mathit{ds}=G({\theta}^{i}),\forall i\in [1,P] The {G}_{j} can therefore be determined by solving the linear system with P equations and N unknowns: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\sum_{j=1}^{N}{a}_{ij}{G}_{j}={b}_{i},i=1,P\\ \quad\text{avec}\quad {a}_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{M}{\theta}_{k}^{i}\underset{{\Gamma}_{0}}{\int}{p}_{j}(s){q}_{k}(s)\cdot m(s)\mathit{ds}\\ \phantom{\mathit{avec}}{b}_{i}=G({\theta}^{i})\end{array}\right. This system has a solution if one chooses P independent fields {\theta}^{i} such that: P\ge N and if M\ge N . It can comprise more equations than unknowns, in which case it is solved in the least-squares sense. 5.2 G-theta method for the computation of KI, KII and KIII with the level sets This paragraph presents the contribution of the level sets for the computation of the stress intensity factors in 3D. It is based on the separation of the mixed modes thanks to the bilinear form of g . This bilinear form is used in Code_Aster for the computation by the G -theta method of {K}_{I} , {K}_{\mathit{II}} in 2D. 5.2.1 Bilinear form of g The computation of the stress intensity factors can also be done by the theta method, by defining a symmetric bilinear form g with: g(u,v)=\frac{1}{4}(G(u+v)-G(u-v)) Thus, let two displacement fields u and v , the computation of g(u,v) is carried out thanks to the expression of G given by the equation, in which the strains linked to u and v derive from the fields u and v , and the stresses linked to u and v are deduced by the constitutive law: \begin{array}{c}\varepsilon (u)={\nabla}_{s}u,\varepsilon (v)={\nabla}_{s}v\\ \sigma (u)=C:\varepsilon (u),\sigma (v)=C:\varepsilon (v)\end{array} Taking up the notations of , the classical term of J(\theta ) is: \begin{array}{c}\text{TCLA}=\sigma (u):(\nabla u\nabla \theta )-\Psi (\varepsilon (u))div\theta \\ =(\mathit{S2}-\mathit{S2}\text{TH})-\frac{1}{2}(\mathit{S1}-\mathit{S1}\text{TH})div\theta \end{array} One recalls that in elasticity, the free energy is expressed as a function of the Lamé coefficients \lambda and \mu : \begin{array}{c}\Psi =\frac{1}{2}\lambda {({\varepsilon}_{ii})}^{2}+\mu {\varepsilon}_{ij}{\varepsilon}_{ij}-{\Psi}^{\text{th}}\\ \phantom{\Psi}=\frac{1}{2}\left[(\lambda +2\mu )({\varepsilon}_{11}^{2}+{\varepsilon}_{22}^{2}+{\varepsilon}_{33}^{2})+2\lambda ({\varepsilon}_{11}{\varepsilon}_{22}+{\varepsilon}_{11}{\varepsilon}_{33}+{\varepsilon}_{22}{\varepsilon}_{33})+2\mu (2{\varepsilon}_{12}^{2}+2{\varepsilon}_{13}^{2}+2{\varepsilon}_{23}^{2})\right]-{\Psi}^{\text{th}}\end{array} with {\Psi}^{\text{th}}=\mathrm{3K}\alpha (T-{T}^{\text{ref}})\text{tr}\varepsilon For each term \mathrm{S1} and \mathrm{S2} , one will first write their usual expression, then afterwards, one will pass to the bilinear form. 5.2.1.1 Expression of S1 and S1TH One writes \mathrm{S1} with the following expression: \mathit{S1}=\mathit{C1}.S11+\mathit{C2}.S12+\mathit{C3}.S13 by setting: \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\mathit{C1}=\lambda +2\mu \\ \mathit{C2}=\lambda \\ \mathit{C3}=\mu \end{array}\right. and \begin{array}{c}S11={u}_{1,1}^{2}+{u}_{2,2}^{2}+{u}_{3,3}^{2}\\ S12=2({u}_{1,1}{u}_{2,2}+{u}_{1,1}{u}_{3,3}+{u}_{2,2}{u}_{3,3})\\ S13={({u}_{1,2}+{u}_{2,1})}^{2}+{({u}_{1,3}+{u}_{3,1})}^{2}+{({u}_{2,3}+{u}_{3,2})}^{2}\end{array} Let us now write the associated bilinear form. The free energy then depends on two fields u and v . The material coefficients \mathrm{C1} , \mathrm{C2} and \mathrm{C3} are obviously unchanged, and the new coefficients S11 , S12 and S13 have for expressions: \begin{array}{}S11={u}_{1,1}{v}_{1,1}+{u}_{2,2}{v}_{2,2}+{u}_{3,3}{v}_{3,3}\\ S12=({u}_{1,1}{v}_{2,2}+{u}_{2,2}{v}_{1,1})+({u}_{1,1}{v}_{3,3}+{u}_{3,3}{v}_{1,1})+({u}_{2,2}{u}_{3,3}+{u}_{3,3}{v}_{2,2})\\ S13=({u}_{1,2}+{u}_{2,1})({v}_{1,2}+{v}_{2,1})+({u}_{1,3}+{u}_{3,1})({v}_{1,3}+{v}_{3,1})+({u}_{2,3}+{u}_{3,2})({v}_{2,3}+{v}_{3,2})\end{array} The expression of the thermal part is: \text{SITH}=3K\alpha (({T}_{u}-{T}_{\text{réf}})\text{tr}\epsilon (v)+({T}_{v}-{T}_{\text{réf}})\text{tr}\epsilon (u)) For the computation of {K}_{i} , v is the asymptotic field in mode i, obtained for {T}_{v}={T}_{\text{réf}} , therefore the terms in ({T}_{v}-{T}_{\text{réf}}) simplify: \text{SITH}=3K\alpha (({T}_{u}-{T}_{\text{réf}})\text{tr}\epsilon (v)) 5.2.1.2 Expression of S2 and S2TH As for \mathrm{S1} , one writes \mathrm{S2} with the following expression: \mathit{S2}=\mathit{C1}.S21+\mathit{C2}.S22+\mathit{C3}.S23 The material coefficients \mathrm{C1} , \mathrm{C2} and \mathrm{C3} are those defined in the preceding paragraph. The coefficients S21 , S22 and S23 have for expressions: \begin{array}{c}\mathit{S21}=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\sum_{p=1}^{3}{u}_{k,k}{u}_{k,p}{\theta}_{p,k}\\ \mathit{S22}=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\sum_{l\mathrm{\ne }k}^{}\sum_{p=1}^{3}{u}_{l,l}{u}_{k,p}{\theta}_{p,k}\\ \mathit{S23}=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\sum_{l\mathrm{\ne }k}\sum_{\begin{array}{c}m\mathrm{\ne }k\\ m\mathrm{\ne }l\end{array}}\sum_{p=1}^{3}{u}_{l,m}{u}_{l,p}{\theta}_{p,m}+{u}_{l,m}{u}_{m,p}{\theta}_{p,l}\end{array} This writing makes it easy to pass to the associated bilinear form. It suffices to replace the terms {u}_{i,j}{u}_{k,l} by \frac{1}{2}({u}_{i,j}{v}_{k,l}+{u}_{k,l}{v}_{i,j}) . If one introduces the following notation: B({u}_{i,j},{v}_{k,l})=\frac{1}{2}({u}_{i,j}{v}_{k,l}+{u}_{k,l}{v}_{i,j}) then the new coefficients S21 , S22 and S23 have for expressions: \begin{array}{c}\mathit{S21}=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\sum_{p=1}^{3}B({u}_{k,k},{v}_{k,p}){\theta}_{p,k}\\ \mathit{S22}=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\sum_{l\mathrm{\ne }k}^{}\sum_{p=1}^{3}B({u}_{l,l},{v}_{k,p}){\theta}_{p,k}\\ \mathit{S23}=\sum_{k=1}^{3}\sum_{l\mathrm{\ne }k}\sum_{\begin{array}{c}m\mathrm{\ne }k\\ m\mathrm{\ne }l\end{array}}\sum_{p=1}^{3}B({u}_{l,m},{v}_{l,p}){\theta}_{p,m}+B({u}_{l,m},{v}_{m,p}){\theta}_{p,l}\end{array} The expression of the thermal part is: \mathit{S2}\text{TH}=\frac{\text{TH1}}{2}3K\alpha ({T}_{u}-{T}_{\text{ref}})(\frac{\partial {v}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}})+\frac{\text{TH1}}{2}3K\alpha ({T}_{v}-{T}_{\text{ref}})(\frac{\partial {u}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}}) where \text{TH1}=1 in D_PLAN, AXIS and in 3D and \text{TH1}=\frac{1-2\nu }{1-\nu } in C_PLAN. For the computation of \mathit{Ki} , v is the asymptotic field in mode i , obtained for {T}_{v}={T}_{\text{réf}} , therefore the terms in ({T}_{v}-{T}_{\text{réf}}) simplify: \mathit{S2}\text{TH}=\frac{\text{TH}1}{2}\mathrm{3K}\alpha ({T}_{u}-{T}_{\text{réf}})(\frac{\partial {v}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}\frac{\partial {\theta}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}}) 5.2.1.3 Surface term The additional term in the expression of G , due to the imposition of a surface force g on {\Gamma}_{c} of outward normal n is the following: \begin{array}{c}\text{TSUR}=(\nabla g\cdot \theta )u+g\cdot u(div\theta -n\frac{\partial \theta }{\partial n})\\ ={g}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}{u}_{i}+{g}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}({\theta}_{k,k}-{n}_{k}\frac{\partial \theta }{\partial {n}_{k}})\end{array} The term n\frac{\partial \theta }{\partial n} is zero because the gradient of the field \theta is orthogonal to n . There therefore remains: \begin{array}{c}\text{TSUR}=(\nabla g\cdot \theta )u+g\cdot udiv\theta \\ ={g}_{i,k}{\theta}_{k}{u}_{i}+{g}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}{\theta}_{k,k}\end{array} The associated bilinear form g(u,v) for the computation of G and of {K}_{I} , {K}_{\mathit{II}} and {K}_{\mathit{III}} is: \text{TSUR}(u,v)=\frac{1}{2}\left[((\nabla {g}_{u}\cdot \theta )v+{g}_{u}\cdot vdiv\theta )+((\nabla {g}_{v}\cdot \theta )u+{g}_{v}\cdot udiv\theta )\right] For the computation of {K}_{i} , v is the asymptotic field in mode i , obtained for {g}_{v}=0 , therefore the terms in {g}_{v} and \nabla {g}_{v} simplify: \text{TSUR}(u,v)=\frac{1}{2}\left[(\nabla {g}_{u}\cdot \theta )v+{g}_{u}\cdot vdiv\theta \right] 5.2.1.4 Thermal term The additional term in the expression of G , due to the temperature field T is the following: \begin{array}{ccc}\mathit{TTHE}=\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial T}{T}_{,k}{\theta}_{k}& =& \frac{1}{2}3K\alpha \text{tr}\varepsilon (v)(\frac{\partial {T}_{v}}{\partial x}{\theta}_{x}+\frac{\partial {T}_{v}}{\partial y}{\theta}_{y}\frac{\partial {T}_{v}}{\partial z}{\theta}_{z})\end{array} For the computation of {K}_{i} , v is the asymptotic field x}{\theta}_{x}+\frac{\partial {T}_{u}}{\partial y}{\theta}_{y}+\frac{\partial {T}_{u}}{\partial z}{\theta}_{z}) 5.2.2 Separation of the mixed modes The symmetric bilinear form g(u,v) has as an interesting property that of separating the three opening modes of the crack. Indeed, in the form g(u,v) , if the field on the left is the solution displacement field and if the term on the right is a field of singular displacements at the crack front {u}_{I}^{S} , {u}_{\text{II}}^{S} or {u}_{\text{III}}^{S} , the stress intensity factors are expressed in the following manner: {K}_{I}=\frac{E}{(1-{\nu}^{2})}g(u,{u}_{I}^{S}) {K}_{\text{II}}=\frac{E}{(1-{\nu}^{2})}g(u,{u}_{\text{II}}^{S}) {K}_{\text{III}}=2\mu g(u,{u}_{\text{III}}^{S}) Certain authors use the concept of interaction integrals, in place of the bilinear form of g . These two vocabularies designate in fact the same quantities. Indeed, denoting {I}^{u,{u}_{I}^{S}} the interaction integral between the solution field and the singular field in mode I , the expression of {K}_{I} in terms of interaction integral is: {K}_{I}=\frac{E}{2(1-{\nu}^{2})}{I}^{u,{u}_{I}^{S}} This expression for {K}_{I} is identical to the one given by the equation up to a multiplicative term. If one applies the method of virtual extensions to the bilinear form of g , the equivalent expression of the variational equation for the local {K}_{i} is: \begin{array}{c}\frac{(1-{\nu}^{2})}{E}\underset{{\Gamma}_{0}}{\int}{K}_{I}\theta \cdot m\text{ds}=g{(u,{u}_{I}^{S})}_{\theta},\forall \theta \in \Theta \\ \frac{(1-{\nu}^{2})}{E}\underset{{\Gamma}_{0}}{\int}{K}_{\text{II}}\theta \cdot m\text{ds}=g{(u,{u}_{\text{II}}^{S})}_{\theta},\forall \theta \in \Theta \\ \frac{1}{2\mu }\underset{{\Gamma}_{0}}{\int}{K}_{\text{III}}\theta \cdot m\text{ds}=g{(u,{u}_{\text{III}}^{S})}_{\theta},\forall \theta \in \Theta \end{array} One finds the analogue of these expressions written with interaction integrals in and . One recalls that the right-hand side of the equations is the bilinear form of g (see ) in which the term on the left u is the solution displacement field (coming from the solution of the problem by the finite element method) and the term on the right {u}_{i=I,\text{II},\text{III}}^{S} is the asymptotic field (in mode i=I,\text{II},\text{III} ) whose analytical expression is given by the equation. These analytical expressions are given in the local basis at the crack front ({e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}) arising from the gradients of the level sets, whereas the derivatives intervening in g{(u,{u}_{I,\text{II},\text{III}}^{S})}_{\theta} are taken with respect to the global frame ({E}_{1},{E}_{2},{E}_{3}) (see the expressions of the terms \mathit{S1} and \mathrm{S2} in the preceding paragraph). One must therefore proceed to a change of basis. Polar coordinates, local basis and global basis Let \text{DPODL} be the matrix of the derivatives of the polar coordinates in the local basis: \text{DPODL}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}& \frac{\partial r}{\partial y}& \frac{\partial r}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial \theta }{\partial x}& \frac{\partial \theta }{\partial y}& \frac{\partial \theta }{\partial z}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0\\ -\frac{\sin\theta }{r}& \frac{\cos\theta }{r}& 0\end{array}\right] Let u be an auxiliary field expressed as a function of the polar coordinates (r,\theta ) . The derivatives of u with respect to the variables (r,\theta ) are determined analytically. One writes them in matrix form: \text{DUDPO}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\frac{\partial {u}_{1}}{\partial r}& \frac{\partial {u}_{1}}{\partial \theta }\\ \frac{\partial {u}_{2}}{\partial r}& \frac{\partial {u}_{2}}{\partial \theta }\\ \frac{\partial {u}_{3}}{\partial r}& \frac{\partial {u}_{3}}{\partial \theta }\end{array}\right] Then, one writes the derivatives in the local basis ({e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}) : \text{DUDL}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{\partial {u}_{1}}{\partial x}& \frac{\partial {u}_{1}}{\partial y}& \frac{\partial {u}_{1}}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial {u}_{2}}{\partial x}& \frac{\partial {u}_{2}}{\partial y}& \frac{\partial {u}_{2}}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial {u}_{3}}{\partial x}& \frac{\partial {u}_{3}}{\partial y}& \frac{\partial {u}_{3}}{\partial z}\end{array}\right]=\text{DUDPO}.\text{DPODL}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\frac{\partial {u}_{1}}{\partial r}& \frac{\partial {u}_{1}}{\partial \theta }\\ \frac{\partial {u}_{2}}{\partial r}& \frac{\partial {u}_{2}}{\partial \theta }\\ \frac{\partial {u}_{3}}{\partial r}& \frac{\partial {u}_{3}}{\partial \theta }\end{array}\right].\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}& \frac{\partial r}{\partial y}& \frac{\partial r}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial \theta }{\partial x}& \frac{\partial \theta }{\partial y}& \frac{\partial \theta }{\partial z}\end{array}\right] It now remains to write the derivatives of u in the global basis ({E}_{1},{E}_{2},{E}_{3}) . For this purpose, one denotes R the matrix of the vectors of the global basis written in the local basis (passage matrix): {R}_{\alpha m}=({e}_{\alpha}\cdot {E}_{m}) Let i and j be global indices, the j th derivative of the i th component of u is then written: {u}_{i,j}={(\sum_{\alpha =1}^{3}{u}_{\alpha}{R}_{\alpha i})}_{,j}=\sum_{\alpha =1}^{3}({u}_{\alpha ,j}{R}_{\alpha i}+{u}_{\alpha}{R}_{\alpha i,j})=\sum_{\alpha =1}^{3}(\sum_{\beta =1}^{3}({u}_{\alpha ,\beta }{R}_{\beta j}){R}_{\alpha i}+{u}_{\alpha}{R}_{\alpha i,j}) In this expression, the terms {u}_{\alpha ,\beta } are the components of the matrix \text{DUDL} . The term {R}_{\mathrm{\alpha i},j} appears as the curvature of the local basis. It can be neglected if the curvature of the crack front is small. In practice, taking it into account hardly changes the results. 5.2.3 Discretisations As previously, one denotes s the curvilinear abscissa at the crack front. The computation of the local value of {K}_{I} , {K}_{\text{II}} and {K}_{\text{III}} requires solving the following variational equation for several fields {\theta}^{i} : \begin{array}{c}\frac{(1-{\nu}^{2})}{E}{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{0}}{K}_{I}(s){\theta}^{i}(s)\cdot m(s)\text{ds}=g{(u,{u}_{I}^{S})}_{{\theta}^{i}}\forall i\in [1,P]\\ \frac{(1-{\nu}^{2})}{E}{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{0}}{K}_{\text{II}}(s){\theta}^{i}(s)\cdot m(s)\text{ds}=g{(u,{u}_{\text{II}}^{S})}_{{\theta}^{i}}\forall i\in [1,P]\\ \frac{1}{2\mu }{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{0}}{K}_{\text{III}}(s){\theta}^{i}(s)\cdot m(s)\text{ds}=g{(u,{u}_{\text{III}}^{S})}_{{\theta}^{i}}\forall i\in [1,P]\end{array} The scalar fields {K}_{\text{I}}(s) , {K}_{\text{II}}(s) and {K}_{\text{III}}(s) are discretised on the basis denoted {({p}_{j}(s))}_{1\le j\le N} : \begin{array}{ccc}{K}_{I}(s)& =& \sum_{j=1}^{N}{K}_{Ij}{p}_{j}(s)\\ {K}_{\mathit{II}}(s)& =& \sum_{j=1}^{N}{K}_{\mathit{II}j}{p}_{j}(s)\\ {K}_{\mathit{III}}(s)& =& \sum_{j=1}^{N}{K}_{\mathit{III}j}{p}_{j}(s)\end{array} For the theta fields, the approximation is retained. As for G , by injecting the expressions of the discretisations into the variational equation, one obtains the linear system: \begin{array}{cccc}\underset{{\Gamma}_{0}}{\int}\sum_{j=1}^{N}{K}_{Ij}{p}_{j}(s)\sum_{k=1}^{M}({\theta}_{k}^{i}{q}_{k}(s))\cdot m(s)\mathit{ds}& =& g{(u,{u}_{I}^{S})}_{{\theta}^{i}},& \forall i\in [1,P]\\ \underset{{\Gamma}_{0}}{\int}\sum_{j=1}^{N}{K}_{\mathit{II}j}{p}_{j}(s)\sum_{k=1}^{M}({\theta}_{k}^{i}{q}_{k}(s))\cdot m(s)\mathit{ds}& =& g{(u,{u}_{\mathit{II}}^{S})}_{{\theta}^{i}},& \forall i\in [1,P]\\ \underset{{\Gamma}_{0}}{\int}\sum_{j=1}^{N}{K}_{\mathit{III}j}{p}_{j}(s)\sum_{k=1}^{M}({\theta}_{k}^{i}{q}_{k}(s))\cdot m(s)\mathit{ds}& =& g{(u,{u}_{\mathit{III}}^{S})}_{{\theta}^{i}},& \forall i\in [1,P]\end{array} 5.3 G-theta method with X-FEM Up to now, the G-theta method has been presented within the framework of the finite element method (FEM). In order to adapt the G-theta method to the X-FEM framework, there are very few modifications to be made. The only difference resides at the level of the numerical integrations, in order to compute the domain integrals. r7.02.13 Crack propagation algorithms with X-FEM r7.02.13 Crack propagation algorithms with X-FEM Summary: This document presents the crack propagation algorithms within the framework of the X-FEM R7.02.12 method. The crack is then represented by level-sets. The propagation of the crack therefore consists of updating the level-sets taking into account the advancement of the crack front. 1 Introduction A significant advantage of the X-FEM method being the possibility of studying several crack geometries on the same mesh, we can easily study the evolution of the crack over time. The operator PROPA_FISS U4.82.11 calculates the crack resulting from a fatigue propagation according to a local Paris law. From the data of a crack at a given time and the corresponding stress intensity coefficients (Operator CALC_G U4.82.03), the operator calculates the level-sets after advancement of the crack, then the data structure fiss_xfem is enriched in the same way as with the operator DEFI_FISS_XFEM U4.82.08. An introduction to the Level-sets method is given in R7.02.12. The crack propagation phase simply translates into the propagation of the level-sets Currently we can calculate the new level-sets after advancement by three different approaches: by updating the level-sets following a fast marching type method, by updating after a direct geometric calculation or by updating from a reconstructed propagated mesh (the crack mesh is reconstructed from the propagation data and the level-sets are calculated in a second step by distance to the mesh). The different stages of X-FEM crack propagation in Code_Aster change depending on the approach used. However, the step of calculating the crack front advancement speed is common to all methods (see [§ 2 ]). We define the level-sets reflecting the new crack geometry and we ensure that these keep definitions close to signed distance functions (cf. [§ 4 ]). The propagation of a level-set thus requires the following three successive steps (bib 2): - extension of the known speed on iso-zero towards the entire domain, - propagation of the level-set from this speed field, - resetting the level-set function in order to maintain a signed distance function. On the contrary, in the case where we use direct calculation, we immediately recalculate the new values of the two level-sets (cf. [§ 6 ]). 2 Computation of the propagation velocity field The first steps consist of calculating two velocity fields, normal and tangential, defining the dissociated evolution of the two level-sets. We place ourselves within the framework of mixed mode propagation. 2.1 Advance rate of the crack front The advancement of the crack front at each of its points evolves in the local basis according to a Paris law. Its direction can be determined by several criteria detailed in paragraph [§ 2.7]. It should be observed that, in this context, we take as the point of the crack front the physical points at the intersection between the crack front and the faces of the elements of the mesh, for which we know the speed and the angle of propagation, but that we also take the geometric points of the front which are the normal projection of the nodes of the mesh on the front itself [§ 2.2]. However, the propagation speed is calculated for these last points using linear interpolation [§ 2.2] and for each edge which forms the crack front the maximum speed is obtained at one of its two ends. We can therefore limit the search for the maximum speed to the points of intersection between the crack front and the faces of the mesh elements. Note : In the description above, the symbols t and \Delta t have been used to indicate time. However, the quantity described by these symbols is effectively the number of fatigue cycles which cause the crack to advance. In fact, if we look at the equation used above for the calculation of \Delta t , \Delta t is obtained by dividing between the distance of advance of the crack (for example: millimeters) and the speed of advance. The speed calculated using a propagation law (for example the Paris law) is given as an advance of the crack per fatigue cycle (for example: millimeters/cycle). We therefore deduce that \Delta t represents the number of fatigue cycles that must be applied to obtain the desired maximum progress. The link between the number of fatigue cycles and time is given by the frequency of application of the loading. This is true for all the equations used and we can say that all the quantities which are reduced to time ( t , \Delta t , …) in fact express a number of fatigue cycles. 4 Reinitialization and reorthogonalization of level-sets 4.1 Introduction During their evolution, the level-sets must imperatively keep a relatively close definition of signed distance functions. First of all, localizing the domain would not improve the robustness of the algorithm. In (bib 14), it is shown that small errors in the calculation of the propagation angle (which is always the case during numerical simulations) are amplified at points located far from the crack front (due to the linear interpolation used to create the velocity field {V}_{N} ). The iso-surfaces of the normal level-set are then no longer regular and this can lead to the failure of the level-set reset phases. The localisation of the domain thus makes it possible to reduce the level-set updating domain to a domain encompassing the crack front, which leads to a limitation of the amplification effect. However, the geometric method successfully handles non-regular iso-surfaces since it is based on explicit polynomial equations and not on differential equations. Furthermore, the geometric method does not use a process of reinitialization and reorthogonalization of the level-sets (which are calculated at each propagation step). For all these reasons, the location of the domain does not affect the robustness of the geometric method. Locating the domain when using the geometric method would also not necessarily reduce the calculation time necessary for updating the level-sets. It turns out that the calculation of the level-sets at each point of the domain is fast and that the time necessary for this calculation can be lower than the time necessary to select the points of the localised domain. The algorithm used for the selection of points belonging to the restricted domain is based on the calculation of the distance between a point M of the domain and its projected P on the crack front. As the point P must also be calculated for the calculation of the level-sets, the additional calculation cost for the selection algorithm is reduced to the cost of calculating the distance ∣∣\vec{\mathit{PM}}∣∣ and the complexity of the algorithm is O(n) . Even if the complexity of the algorithm for updating the level-sets by the geometric method is O(n) , it appears clear that the sum of the calculations carried out by the selection algorithm will be less than that carried out by the algorithm for updating the level-sets. This leads us to think at first glance that the localisation of the domain would be advantageous in terms of calculation time compared to the calculation of level-sets throughout the domain. However, the selection (based on the distance ∣∣\vec{\mathit{PM}}∣∣ ) of points inside the restricted domain is not sufficient. Indeed, for the calculation of the local basis at each point, it is a question of determining the gradient of the level-sets which requires the selection of the elements containing the selected points (the shape functions of the elements being used to calculate the gradients). Even if the selection algorithm does not necessarily change, the number of operations performed increases and this can make the calculation time of the selection higher than the calculation of level-sets by the geometric method throughout the domain. Note that, at the same time, the time to calculate the gradients of the level-sets is also higher if the location of the domain is not taken into account. Finally, the advantage of domain localisation in terms of calculation time strongly depends on the algorithms and implementations chosen and the number of points in the calculation domain. The localisation of the domain could thus be advantageous in the case of “very large” finite element mesh cells. In this case, limiting the updating of the level-sets to a group of nodes (fixed and defined by the user) defining the potential propagation surface of the crack can be a more efficient way to reduce the calculation time rather than the choice of a domain localisation algorithm for which a new restricted domain must be calculated at each propagation step in order to follow the movement of the crack front. 7 Mesh method for updating level-sets The most intuitive method for updating the level-set values at each crack propagation step is to use their signed distance property. This involves an explicit representation of the crack (crack lips and crack front) propagated in order to calculate the distances from the nodes to the crack. This method thus uses two distinct mesh cells (crack and structure) and only the crack mesh is modified during propagation. Updating the crack mesh at each propagation step concretely consists of creating a new row of surface mesh cells to represent the advancement of the crack and a new row of linear mesh cells to represent the new front. Once this mesh has been updated, we recalculate the new level-sets by direct calculation of the distance to the crack (orthogonal projection on the crack mesh). 7.1 Presentation of the method The mesh of the crack is carried out in Code_Aster by the PROPA_FISS command. The input data is the value of the propagation vector on the crack front, determined from the stress intensity factors and the Paris law. The principle of the mesh method is to calculate the nodes of the new front from the propagation speeds and the nodes of the current front. It comes down to the following three steps: - Calculation by linear interpolation of the propagation vector at each node of the discretised crack front. The propagation vector is orthogonal to the crack front: the direction of propagation at a node corresponds to the average of the normal vectors of the two linear elements sharing this node. This step gives the position of each propagated point. - Addition of a node at each of these points, creation of a new surface (addition of linear elements for the new crack front and quadrangle elements for the new surface) and meshing process of this created surface. - Specific treatment of edge nodes which, depending on the case, can “come out” of the structure. They are then moved to the borders of the structure. For 2D modelling, the method is even simpler. Only one linear element needs to be added at each propagation step and no edge point correction is necessary. 7.2 Algorithm The algorithm implemented for propagation by the mesh method is the following (as described in (bib 20) and in the figure). How to manage the separation of this crack front into two, or even several other pieces? Likewise, what about the merger of two independent crack fronts into one? These are the level-sets which determine the crack front and therefore the presence or not of several crack fronts. But in certain cases it is a question of making improvements to the previous methods so that they adapt to the separation of the crack front (modification of the creation of the crack mesh for the mesh method, continuity of the level-sets in the hole for the upwind method with use of an auxiliary grid). Depending on the methods used for managing the updating of the level-sets, the strategy implemented to account for the separation or merger of crack fronts differs. 8.1 Mesh method For the mesh method, a first option is to extend what is done in paragraph 7.2 to the framework of several crack fronts. The level-sets give information on the number and position of the ends of the crack fronts (intersection between the mesh of the structure and the iso-zero of the two level-sets). While retaining the nodes which constitute the ends already existing at time i-1 , the nodes constituting the new ends are selected (figure a.). Figure 8.1-1 : a. nodes determining the ends of the crack fronts (in blue: nodes selected for the already existing ends, in red: nodes selected for the new ends), b. repositioning of the selected nodes on the different fronts, c. calculation of propagated nodes and formation of new mesh cells. As in paragraph 7.2, a procedure for repositioning the nodes of the different fronts (figure b.) is carried out. All that remains is to calculate the propagated nodes and form the mesh cells (figure c.). Although this method works correctly, it has a disadvantage: the loss of nodes when two backgrounds are separated. The mesh cells can, moreover, deform significantly during the repositioning phase of the nodes outside the structure. This can in particular lead to poor discretisation of the out-of-plane propagation crack. To overcome these difficulties, the idea was to increase the number of nodes on each crack front. There remains the question of creating these nodes and the mesh. Noting that the mesh cells representing the crack are only used to make projections, it is possible to create a row of mesh cells for the advancement of cracks that does not conform to the previous row of mesh cells (figure). In this way, we can increase the number of nodes between two propagation steps without modifying the discretisation induced by the propagation speeds. The algorithm is therefore summarized as follows: search for the nodes closest to the ends of the background, repositioning on the edge, creation of new nodes on the current front positioned equidistant from each other, calculation of the nodes of the new front. As there are the same number of nodes between the two backgrounds, quadrangles respecting the surfaces of the background are created. r7.02.16 Gp method: an energy approach to the prediction of cleavage r7.02.16 Gp method: an energy approach to the prediction of cleavage Summary The parameter {G}_{p} makes it possible to define an initiation criterion valid in the cleavage domain (intragranular brittle fracture in the presence of plasticity). The foundations of this approach are first recalled: energy framework of the behaviour of structures, modelling of the crack by a notch, principle of minimisation of the energy and definition of the criterion. The link between the global approach and the local approach is discussed before then specifying the elements essential to the implementation of {G}_{p} in Code_Aster . 1 Introduction In this chapter one begins by introducing the limits of the classical approach in fracture mechanics (§ 1.1 ), then the objective and the value of the approach {G}_{p} are recalled (§ 1.2 ). Finally the foundations of this method are addressed in (§ 1.4 ). 1.1 Limits of the classical approach In fracture mechanics, the classical parameter making it possible to define an initiation criterion for an already existing crack 1 is the parameter G , the elastic energy-release rate. The parameter G is valid in linear elasticity as well as in non-linear elasticity. That is to say that the framework and the physical assumptions are well defined, and that the calculation formula G\theta is consistent with this framework. On the other hand, the relevance of the fracture criterion :math: G=\mathit{Gc} with respect to the experimental results is another question, not addressed in this document. In elastoplasticity, the parameter G is in general not valid. However, if the loading remains radial and monotonic, then G is valid. This assumption implies that the equations of plasticity are equivalent to the equations of Hencky (which are those of non-linear elasticity [:ref: R4.20.01 ]). Now, the cases of strictly proportional loadings are rather rare (indeed they do not exist when one is concerned with structures presenting geometric defects such as cracks). 1.2 Objective and value of Gp The objective of the method {G}_{p} is to define an initiation parameter valid in incremental plasticity. This theory assumes a decoupling of plasticity and cracking (the case of fracture by cleavage). Thus the use of {G}_{p} to predict cleavage will make it possible to reduce the conservatisms of the classical approach. Its definition calls upon the free energy as well as upon a few geometric parameters necessary for the definition of the crack, which is modelled by a notch. This parameter {G}_{p} has the unit of a surface energy density and is calculated in the zone adjacent to the notch front. The value of the method is threefold: {G}_{p} is a deterministic initiation criterion, in other words it makes it possible to assess whether or not there is initiation of a crack. This parameter is consistent with the elastic G [WAD 13, LOR 14], and it is valid in an elastoplastic framework under non-proportional loading and under unloading. Note: - {G}_{p} is not a criterion of stability or of instability of the defect. - {G}_{p} does not predict a propagation length. 1.3 History of the development of the Gp approach The development of this approach, which has its origins at the beginning of the 2000s, stems from the work of Lorentz, Wadier and Debryune [LOR00]. The crack is then modelled by a cut in the plane but the idea of introducing a notch is already mentioned there as a prospect and will rapidly be adopted. The modelling of the crack by a notch is presented in 2003 (CR) in [WAD 03d] and in 2004 (articles) in [LOR 04] and [WAD 04]. The approach has been presented many times at international conferences, presenting first its value for the vessel in loading/unloading situations [WAD 00], [WAD 01a], [WAD 01b], then showing the interpretations of experimental results illustrating the "small-defect" effect [WAD 03a] [WAD 03c] then the effect of warm pre-loading [WAD 03b] [WAD 05] [WAD 09]. A synthesis recalling the foundations of the Gp approach as well as the principal validation results is carried out in [WAD 13]. To this day it is the only article published in an international journal dedicated to the Gp approach. For this reason, it stands as the reference as regards the Gp approach. It should be noted that attempts to predict crack arrest by means of an approach of Gp type (G-delta) were carried out in the past [WAD 07a], but this path is no longer pursued at the present time. Since the principal actor of the method (Y. Wadier) went into inactivity, a new generation of engineers at EDF R&D has taken up the torch and continues to promote the Gp approach within the scientific community [GEN 16] [JUL 17]. Recently, the Gp approach has been extended to the configurations for which the zone around the defect tip is in compression [HAB 17]. 1.4 Foundations of the Gp approach The method {G}_{p} is set in the context of a global energy formulation of brittle fracture. The approach consists in determining whether a propagation of the defect (preserving the geometry of the defect root and with constant mechanical fields) makes it possible to decrease the total energy of the structure (minimisation principle). In order to achieve this, the cracking path is assumed known a priori . Under this assumption, the energy framework proposed by Francfort and Marigo [FRA 93, FRA 98] can be put into practice in order to predict the sudden initiation of cracks. However, this framework presents certain characteristics which limit its scope [LOR 08], notably undesirable scale effects and the incompatibility of the theory with loadings of imposed-force type. This is why two types of modifications have been introduced in order to resolve these difficulties, while preserving the form of the energies introduced. On the one hand, the crack is replaced by a notch whose radius becomes a parameter of the model. On the other hand, one examines whether the absence of propagation is a (global) minimum at fixed mechanical fields; one therefore carries out a global minimisation but in a single direction. The energy nature of the proposed formulation authorises the introduction of plastic mechanisms. The meaning of the term initiation is here different from the terminology used in fatigue, where initiation means the creation of a crack starting from a sound material. In fracture, one ought rather to say a criterion of "re-initiation", but the term initiation is commonly employed. 2 Modelling of defects in the form of a notch One places oneself in 2D modelling. Within the framework of the approach {G}_{p} , the real crack situated in the domain \Omega is not modelled by a surface of discontinuity of the displacement fields, but by a "notch" in the shape of a U (H1) , of thickness :math: D=2R , with R the radius of the notch root (see [Figure 2-a]). It is assumed that the notch may propagate without changing shape (H2) and without bifurcation (H3) , in mode I. Thus, the cracking paths are predefined and subject to a continuous evolution of the crack (i.e. no "dotted" cracks along the path). Figure 2-a – Modelling of the defect by a notch and representation of the virtual propagation zone C\left(\Delta a\right) in grey. One then defines a virtual propagation zone of the notch called C(\Delta a) , which corresponds to a damaged zone, of thickness D and of length \Delta a . The zone C\left(\Delta a\right) illustrated by [Figure 2-b] may be defined as the union of a rectangle {R}_{1} and of a half-disc {C}_{2} , from which the half-disc {C}_{1} is subtracted: C(\Delta a)=({R}_{1}\cup {C}_{2})-{C}_{1} The entities {R}_{1} , {C}_{1} and {C}_{2} are defined below, given a notch along the axis X and the coordinates ({X}_{0},{Y}_{0}) of the centre of the circular root of the notch [BAR 12]: {R}_{1}=(X,Y)\text{tels que}\lbrace \begin{array}{c}0⩽X-{X}_{0}⩽\Delta a\\ -R⩽Y-{Y}_{0}⩽R\end{array} {C}_{1}=(X,Y)\text{tels que}\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{(X-{X}_{0})}^{2}+{(Y-{Y}_{0})}^{2}⩽{R}^{2}\\ X-{X}_{0}⩾0\end{array} {C}_{2}=(X,Y)\text{tels que}\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{(X-{X}_{0}-\Delta a)}^{2}+{(Y-{Y}_{0})}^{2}⩽{R}^{2}\\ X-{X}_{0}-\Delta a⩾0\end{array} Figure 2-b – Geometric definition of the notch: the zone C\left(\Delta a\right) hatched, the rectangle {R}_{1} dotted, and the half-discs {C}_{1} and {C}_{2} . Note: the integral over C\left(\Delta a\right) of a constant w independent of space is written simply: {\int}_{\textcolor{#ff0000}{C(\Delta a)}}wd\Omega =w\times \Delta a\times D Strictly speaking, one is no longer in the context of fracture mechanics but in that of damage mechanics, considering a model of brutal damage (assumption H4) which is total (assumption H5) . The term brutal, as opposed to progressive, means that only two damage states are possible for the material: sound or damaged. The term total, as opposed to partial, indicates that the damaged material has zero residual stiffness. A two-valued damage field \mathrm{\chi } is thus defined on the domain \Omega , taking values in \left\lbrace 0,1\right\rbrace . By definition, \mathrm{\chi }=0 corresponds to the sound material, and \mathrm{\chi }=1 to the damaged material. A damage model makes it possible to fix a critical stress. As a reminder, one fixes the thickness of the zone over which the damage propagates: one considers only the evolutions of the damage which correspond to the growth of the notch C\left(\Delta a\right) , where \Delta a is the length over which the notch propagates, and D its thickness. One thus controls the energy dissipated during the advance of the damaged zone. One denotes \Omega \setminus C\left(\Delta a\right) the set constituted by the difference between the domain \Omega and the virtual propagation zone of the notch :math: C\left(\Delta a\right) . Then one has: \mathrm{\chi }(\Delta a)(x)=\lbrace \begin{array}{c}1\text{si}x\in C(\Delta a)\\ 0\text{si}x\in \Omega \setminus C\left(\Delta a\right)\end{array} Note: One could have distinguished the thickness of the pre-existing notch from that of the damaged zone C\left(\Delta a\right) . This would have led to a more complex model (with more parameters). For the sake of simplicity one therefore does not make this distinction. 3 Principle of energy minimisation 3.1 Energy formulation in the elastic framework An energy formulation characterises the response of a structure as a minimum of an energy with respect to the set of the variables which one has chosen in order to describe the mechanical state of the structure [LOR 08]. In the elastic case, the matter is to minimise the potential energy with respect to the displacement field. In order to take the dissipative phenomena into account, the approach {G}_{p} relies on the work of Francfort and Marigo [FRA 93, FRA 98] devoted to a model of brutal partial damage. Unlike the elastic case, the energy depends on two fields, the displacement field u and a damage field \mathrm{\chi } with values in \left\lbrace 0,1\right\rbrace , 0 corresponding to the sound material of volumetric free energy {\varphi}_{s} and 1 to the damaged material of volumetric free energy {\varphi}_{d} : {E}_{\mathit{tot}}\left(u,\mathrm{\chi }\right)=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\varphi (\epsilon (u),\mathrm{\chi })+{w}_{c}\mathrm{\chi };\varphi (\epsilon (u),\mathrm{\chi })=\mathrm{\chi }{\varphi}_{d}(\epsilon )+(1-\mathrm{\chi }){\varphi}_{s}(\epsilon ) where one restricts oneself to imposed displacements (the potential of the external forces {W}_{\mathit{ext}} is zero). The additional term {w}_{c}\mathrm{\chi } measures the energy to be supplied in order to pass from the sound state to the damaged state. After discretisation in time, Francfort and Marigo then postulate that the displacement field u and the damage field \mathrm{\chi } realise a minimum of the incremental potential energy: (u,\mathrm{\chi })=\underset{u,\mathrm{\chi }}{\mathit{argmin}}{E}_{\mathit{tot}}\left(u,\mathrm{\chi }\right) One subsequently considers the model of brutal damage presented by Francfort and Marigo, except that the residual stiffness is zero for a damaged state (model of brutal total damage). One then retains from the theory of Francfort and Marigo that, at a given displacement, the evolution of the damage is governed by the minimisation of the total energy with respect to \mathrm{\chi } . In this case, a total damage or external forces are no longer problematic. Thus, in the elastic framework, the evolution of the damage is obtained by the minimisation of the following total incremental potential energy: {E}_{\mathit{tot}}\left(u,\mathrm{\chi }\right)={\int}_{\Omega}\left[\left(1-\mathrm{\chi }\right){\Phi}_{\mathit{el}}+\mathrm{\chi }{w}_{C}\right]d\Omega -{W}_{\mathit{ext}}(u) where {\Phi}_{\mathit{el}} is the free-energy density, {\Phi}_{\mathit{el}}={\int}_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}[\sigma :{A}^{-1}:\sigma ]d\Omega with A the tangent matrix of the constitutive behaviour, and {w}_{c} the volumetric energy dissipated in the damage process at each material point. In this new approach, one may take loadings of imposed-force type: the potential of the external forces {W}_{\mathit{ext}} is not necessarily zero. 3.2 Modification of the form of the energy One of the limitations of the proposed damage model is that it does not distinguish tension from compression, on account of the form of the free-energy density, so that the restitution of a compressive energy contributes just as much to the propagation of the defect as a tensile energy [HAB 16]. One chooses to eliminate artificially the zones in compression from the integral (assumption H6) . To this end one considers a tension/compression dissymmetry in the formulation of the energy considered, relying on the method developed by Badel in [BAD 01]. Thus, placing oneself in the principal frame of the strains, one will adopt the following elastic energy: {\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}}({\epsilon}^{\mathit{el}})=\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathit{tr}{({\epsilon}^{\mathit{el}})}^{2}H(\mathit{tr}({\epsilon}^{\mathit{el}}))+\mu \sum_{i}{({\epsilon}_{i}^{\mathit{el}})}^{2}H({\epsilon}_{i}^{\mathit{el}}) where \lambda and \mu denote the Lamé coefficients which characterise the stiffness tensor. The eigenvalues of the elastic strain tensor are denoted {\epsilon}_{i}^{\mathit{el}} . H is the Heaviside function such that: H(x)=\lbrace \begin{array}{c}1\text{si}x⩾0\\ 0\text{si}x 0\text{}{E}_{\mathit{tot}}(u,{\epsilon}^{p},\alpha ,\mathrm{\chi }=0)⩽{E}_{\mathit{tot}}(u,{\epsilon}^{p},\alpha ,\mathrm{\chi }(\Delta a))\end{array} Thus, by expressing the second line thanks to equation (), one obtains after simplification that \forall \Delta a>0 , there is no initiation of the defect for as long as: {\int}_{\Omega}{\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}}(\epsilon (u)-{\epsilon}^{p})d\Omega ⩽{\int}_{\Omega}\left[\left(1-\mathrm{\chi }(\Delta a)\right){\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}}(\epsilon (u)-{\epsilon}^{p})+\mathrm{\chi }(\Delta a){w}_{C}\right]d\Omega In what follows, one will omit the argument of the adopted elastic energy in order to lighten the expression. By expanding on the one hand the integral on the left-hand side and on the right-hand side over the domains C\left(\Delta a\right) and \Omega \setminus C\left(\Delta a\right) , and by using on the other hand the definition of the damage field (), one arrives after simplification at: {\int}_{\textcolor{#ff0000}{\Omega \setminus C(\Delta a)}}{\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}}d\Omega +{\int}_{\textcolor{#ff0000}{C(\Delta a)}}{\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}}d\Omega ⩽{\int}_{\textcolor{#ff0000}{\Omega \setminus C(\Delta a)}}{\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}}d\Omega +{\int}_{\textcolor{#ff0000}{C(\Delta a)}}{w}_{C}d\Omega Now, according to () : {\int}_{\textcolor{#ff0000}{C(\Delta a)}}{w}_{C}d\Omega ={w}_{c}\times \Delta a\times D Inequality () is then expressed as below: \forall \Delta a>0\text{}\frac{{\int}_{\textcolor{#ff0000}{C(\Delta a)}}{\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}}d\Omega }{\Delta a}⩽{w}_{c}\times D One defines the left-hand term \tilde{{G}_{p}}(\Delta a) such that: \tilde{{G}_{p}}(\Delta a)=\frac{{\int}_{\textcolor{#ff0000}{C(\Delta a)}}{\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}}d\Omega }{\Delta a} And one defines the right-hand term {G}_{\mathit{pc}}={w}_{c}\times D as the fracture energy of the material. The non-initiation condition is then written: \forall \Delta a>0,\text{}\tilde{{G}_{p}}(\Delta a)⩽{G}_{\mathit{pc}} One then defines the parameter {G}_{p} as the maximum value of the function \tilde{{G}_{p}}(\Delta a) : {G}_{p}=\underset{\Delta a}{max}\tilde{{G}_{p}}(\Delta a) The non-re-initiation criterion is written {G}_{p}⩽{G}_{\mathit{pc}} . The initiation criterion may then be written {G}_{p}>{G}_{\mathit{pc}} . This criterion implies knowledge of two material parameters, {w}_{c} and D . For practical reasons, one prefers to choose D and {G}_{\mathrm{pc}} . These parameters therefore require an identification (see paragraph § 6.2 ). The parameter {G}_{p} is calculated as the maximum (with respect to \Delta a , the virtual propagation length) of the integral over the domain C\left(\Delta a\right) of the modified free energy {\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}} , divided by \Delta a . It is therefore a mean elastic energy density ( \mathrm{kJ}/{m}^{2} ). It is not here an energy-release rate because the energy considered for the minimisation is that of the current time instant, and it does not include the re-equilibration of the fields after propagation. In the manner of {K}_{J} (\mathit{MPa}.{m}^{1/2}) , defined from J in a way similar to the Irwin relation J=\frac{\left(1-{\nu}^{2}\right)}{E}{K}_{J}^{2} — valid in 2D plane strain and in 3D —, one may also define a parameter {K}_{{G}_{P}} (\mathit{MPa}.{m}^{1/2}) from {G}_{p} by means of this same relation: {G}_{p}=\frac{\left(1-{\nu}^{2}\right)}{E}{K}_{{G}_{P}}^{2} 5 Link between the global approach and the local approach Lorentz [LOR 08] and Wadier [WAD 07b] position the energy approach {G}_{p} with respect to the global and local approaches to fracture. More recent than the global approach in fracture mechanics, the local approach aims to predict the failure of a structure by relying on the microscopic mechanism of cleavage. It accounts for the scatter of the results by an intrinsically probabilistic modelling. The Beremin model, for example, defines the fracture probability and the Weibull stress {\sigma}_{w} at time t by: {P}_{R}(t)=1-\exp\left[-{\left(\frac{\underset{\tau \le t}{\max}{\sigma}_{w}(\tau )}{{\sigma}_{c}}\right)}^{m}\right];{\sigma}_{w}(\tau )={\left[\frac{1}{{V}_{0}}\underset{{\Omega}_{p}(\tau )}{\int}{\sigma}_{I}{(\tau )}^{m}d\Omega \right]}^{\frac{1}{m}} with {\sigma}_{I}(t) and {\Omega}_{p}(t) the maximum principal stress and the domain undergoing yielding at time respectively. {V}_{0} is a reference volume, {\sigma}_{c} the critical stress and m a dimensionless exponent. Thus, the expression of the fracture probability is based in particular on the weakest-link assumption, i.e. failure is associated with the initiation of the most penalising microscopic defect. For the sake of comparison between the two models, one may define a fracture probability of the approach {G}_{p} by the formula: {P}_{R}(t)=1-\exp\left[-a{\left(\frac{{G}_{p}}{{G}_{p0}}\right)}^{m/2}\right]\text{} where a and m are constants identified from the experimental results, and {G}_{p0} a constant such that {P}_{r} is equal to 5% when {G}_{p} is equal to the value identified for a fracture probability of 5%. The comparison between the two approaches brings out a certain number of links. The quantities involved in the initiation criterion (elastic energy or stress) are similar. These quantities are averaged over a zone situated in the neighbourhood of the notch root. Finally, one may be led to take the hydrostatic stress into account [WAD 07b]. The Beremin model allows the tension/compression distinction to be taken into account naturally thanks to the introduction of the maximum principal stress rather than that of the elastic energy. Conversely, the approach {G}_{p} offers a simpler transition towards the earlier approaches of the industrial domain. It makes it possible to link up with the classical global approach because it is founded, as that approach is, on energy principles: {G}_{p}=G notch in elasticity [LOR 14]. 6 Implementation in Code_Aster The mechanical analysis is carried out under the assumption of a thermo-elasto-plastic constitutive behaviour associated with a von Mises criterion with isotropic or linear kinematic hardening (VMIS_ISOT_TRAC, VMIS_ISOT_LINE, VMIS_CINE_LINE). One will specify what the calculation of {G}_{p} consists in and how the identification of the material parameters R=D/2 (radius of the notch) and {G}_{\mathit{pc}} (fracture limit) is carried out. The methodology of calculation and identification with Code_Aster is presented in U2.05.08. The plain user's documentation is in [U4.82.31]. 6.1 Calculation of Gp The calculation of {G}_{p} , carried out with the aid of the macro-command CALC_GP, is based on the use of POST_ELEM, which allows the calculation of the elastic energy over a mesh-cell group. The modellings (finite elements, small strains, etc.) and the loadings which may be used are those of the command POST_ELEM, keyword ENER_ELTR. More precisely, for each time instant provided for in the list of analysis time instants, the following two stages are to be carried out: 1/ First calculate the quantity \tilde{{G}_{p}}(\Delta a) for increasing values of \Delta a by: \tilde{{G}_{p}}(\Delta a)=\frac{{\int}_{\Omega}{\Phi}_{t}^{\mathit{el}}d\Omega }{\Delta a} In 2D one must therefore identify the elements of the zone C\left(\Delta a\right) by a mesh-cell group defined at mesh level as presented in [Figure 2-a], or by a geometric zone of Gauss points, then calculate the elastic energy over this zone and then divide it by \Delta a . In order to identify the elements of the zone C\left(\Delta a\right) one will proceed as follows: the elements of the first chip will constitute a first mesh-cell group, the elements of chips 1 and 2 will constitute a second group, the elements of the chips 1,2,3,\mathrm{...},i will constitute a i th group, etc. A sufficiently large number of chips must be provided in order to be able to find the maximum of \tilde{{G}_{p}}(\Delta a) , which is located most often at a distance of about 3R from the notch root. Figure 6.1-1- Definition of the chips in the mesh 2/ Next it is a matter of identifying the maximum of this function: {G}_{p}=\underset{\Delta a}{max}\tilde{{G}_{p}}(\Delta a) Examples and advice on use will be found in the document [:ref: U2.05.01 ], in the tests ssnp131 (see V6.03.131 and ssnv218 (see V6.04.218). 6.2 Identification of the parameters The energy model is based on the pair of material parameters ({G}_{\mathit{pc}},R) which must therefore be determined at each temperature. One notes that {G}_{\mathit{pc}} depends in reality on the notch radius [WAD 13]. One will see that the prediction of fracture does not depend on it. One assumes known, on the one hand, Young's modulus E and the critical stress {\sigma}_{c} of a material. On the other hand, one assumes that the toughness {K}_{\mathit{Jc}} is known, evaluated experimentally from a tensile test on a CT specimen, for example. Application of the "minimum with respect to the damage" at the scale of a material point in a state of simple tensile stress gives the relation between the volumetric energy dissipated by a material point which becomes damaged {w}_{c} and the critical stress [WAD 13] (assumption H11) : {w}_{c}=\frac{{\sigma}_{c}^{2}}{2E} One then obtains the following equation, which must be solved in order to identify the two parameters: {G}_{\mathit{pc}}(R)=\frac{{\sigma}_{c}^{2}}{E}R The left-hand side {G}_{\mathit{pc}}\left(R\right) is a non-linear function of R . The right-hand side is a linear function of R . Thus, in order to solve (25) one must calculate {G}_{\mathit{pc}} for various values of R as the figure [Figure 6.2-1] illustrates. Figure 6.2-1: identification of the pair ({G}_{\mathit{pc}},R) [WAD 13] For each notch of given radius R , the parameter {G}_{\mathit{pc}} is determined by simulation of a test on a specimen \mathit{CT} in the following manner: for each value of the loading, increasing from 0 up to a critical value, one calculates on the one hand the parameter {K}_{J} and on the other hand the parameter {G}_{p} . For the critical value of the loading corresponding to {K}_{J}={K}_{\mathit{Jc}} , one obtains {G}_{p}={G}_{\mathit{pc}} (Assumption H12) . Solving equation (25) for various values of R finally makes it possible to determine both the value of R and the value of {G}_{\mathit{pc}} at a given temperature. In the case of a steel, one finds values lying between 10 and 100 microns, which is representative of a real crack. 7 Bibliography The bibliography is deliberately exhaustive.
