r7.02.17 Determination of an equivalent crack from a damage field r7.02.17 Determination of an equivalent crack from a damage field Summary: The command POST_ENDO_FISS carries out a post-processing on a result coming from continuum mechanics. The aim is to find the curve which represents the crack from a representative field, and the crack opening. The field may be the damage or another scalar field. On input, the command uses a concept evol_noli or cham_gd, containing the field to be post-processed. The latter must be a field at the nodes. On output, the command returns the mesh of the crack, together with a table containing the coordinates of the nodes of the crack and the value of the opening on each node. The procedure applies to 2D studies. Contents 1 Introduction The estimation of crack opening is important in many industrial applications, for example the evaluation of the permeability in structures whose function is to guarantee leaktightness. The aim of POST_ENDO_FISS U4.86.01 is to extract the crack opening from an analysis coming from continuum mechanics. The command is used as a post-processing and therefore does not burden the analysis itself. The method used is capable of finding the cracking path from the map of a (scalar) field X which represents the cracking, and then of determining the opening on the crack. The evaluation of the crack opening is therefore decomposed into two steps: first the automatic search for the crack path, then the extraction of the opening. For the moment, the command applies to 2D studies. If damage models or other softening constitutive laws are used for the mechanical analysis, it is necessary, for a correct application of the command, that regularisation methods be employed: this will make it possible to obtain fields well distributed over several finite elements. Also, the regularisation methods will avoid any dependence of the results on the mesh. 2 Search for the cracking path 2.1 General points One assumes that the crack belongs to a certain mesh-cell group (GROUP_MA), on which the field X (damage, plastic strain) is defined. The crack is identified by a zone in which the values of this field are especially high, and normally greater than a certain value: damage greater than 0 , for example. In what follows, the procedure for searching for the cracking path is described. We exploit the fact that, in the plane orthogonal to the crack, the field X has a maximum on the crack itself. The procedure is step by step; a new point of the crack is found at each step. It can be described by the typical step , by its initiation and by the stopping criteria . 2.2 Typical step At each step, the search requires two points. The last point found {P}_{i} is the starting point and the vector \overrightarrow{{P}_{i-1}{P}_{i}} ( {P}_{i-1} being the last point but one found) gives the search direction . Figure 1: diagram of the typical step At each typical step, the following actions are carried out (see also the diagram of ) : 1. the position of the following point is first estimated ( prediction point {P}_{i}^{\mathit{pr}} ) at the distance a from the starting point in the search direction, a being the advance step; 2. the field X is projected onto a line orthogonal to the search direction and passing through the prediction point; 1. the projected field is smoothed by convolution ( eq ) in order to free oneself partly from the mesh (for example, if one relies on finite elements with linear interpolation, the projected field is piecewise linear); 2. the new point of the crack {P}_{i+1} is the one at which the smoothed field reaches its maximum value. The smoothing mentioned at point 3 is necessary: for example, if the field projected onto the orthogonal profile is piecewise linear, its maximum is necessarily located on the edge of an element. The smoothing is carried out by convolution: \overline{X}(s)=\frac{{}_{{l}_{\mathit{orth}}}\intX(\zeta )\Psi (\mid \zeta -s\mid )d\zeta }{{}_{{l}_{\mathit{orth}}}\int\Psi (\mid \zeta -s\mid )d\zeta } eq 2.2-1 where \overline{X} is the smoothed field, {l}_{\mathit{orth}} is the length of the line orthogonal to the search direction, s is the curvilinear abscissa on this line and \Psi is a Gaussian function: \Psi (\mid \zeta -s\mid )=\exp(-{(\frac{2(\zeta -s)}{{l}_{\mathit{reg}}})}^{2}) eq 2.2-2 An example of the fields X and \overline{X} as a function of the parameter {l}_{\mathit{reg}} is given in the . Figure 2: Smoothing of the field X projected onto the orthogonal line. An additional parameter is given by the number of points on the orthogonal line, {N}_{\mathit{orth}} . This determines the accuracy of the discrete convolution product, as well as the accuracy {\delta}_{\mathit{orth}}={l}_{\mathit{orth}}/{N}_{\mathit{orth}} (distance between the points). The discrete convolution is carried out by the function convolve of the Python library numpy . The functions X(s) and \Psi (s) are sampled on {l}_{\mathit{orth}} at the constant distance {\delta}_{\mathit{orth}} . Denoting by \mathrm{X} , \Psi the two sampled vectors, the point \overline{{X}_{j}} of the vector \overline{\mathrm{X}} which approximates by points the smoothed function \overline{X}(s) will be given by: \overline{{X}_{j}}=\frac{\sum_{i}{\Psi}_{i}{X}_{i+j}}{\sum_{i}{\Psi}_{i}} eq 2.2-3 2.3 Initialisation The aim of the initialisation is to obtain the first two points, in order to continue afterwards as described in the typical step. A diagram of the initialisation procedure is given in the : Figure 3: diagram of the initialisation procedure. In detail: 1. the field X is projected onto a circle of radius a and centred on the node 1 where the field at the nodes has its maximum on the chosen GROUP_MA; 2. the field X is smoothed on the circle via a discrete convolution product ( eq. ), the second point of the crack {P}_{2} is the point of the circle where \overline{X} is maximum; 3. one corrects the position of the point 1 by projection and smoothing of the field \overline{X} onto a line orthogonal to \overrightarrow{{P}_{2}1} and passing through {P}_{2} : the new point 3={P}_{1} is found; 4. two possible search directions are thus determined: \overrightarrow{{P}_{1}{P}_{2}} and \overrightarrow{{P}_{2}{P}_{1}} . 2.4 Stopping criteria The search for the cracking path is carried out in the two directions \overrightarrow{{P}_{1}{P}_{2}} and \overrightarrow{{P}_{2}{P}_{1}} until stopping, in one of the following cases: - the value of the field corresponding to the new point is lower than a threshold value, defined a priori. This value must be supplied among the parameters of the command under the operand BORNE_MIN of the factor keyword RECHERCHE. - the prediction point is outside the material. 2.5 Fields for the search for the cracking path The method described can be applied to any scalar fields which represent the cracking of the material. Typically, it is the damage d which can be used. It sometimes happens that the damage field is too “flat”, and that at failure it presents a plateau with d=1 . As there would not then be a well-defined maximum, the procedure described in paragraphs 2.2–2.3 might not give the desired results. One can then choose other relevant fields: a principal-strain component, an equivalent strain... An example of the choice of the relevant field is given by the test cases zzzz264b,c V1.01.264. 3 Crack opening The crack opening is found by the displacement difference \mathit{DN} in the direction normal to the cracking path, between two points {P}_{g},{P}_{d} on this normal. It is then necessary to determine: - the line normal to the cracking path (taking into account the fact that the crack is known in a discrete way by points), - the appearance of the displacements on this line, in particular the displacement component in the same direction, - the coordinates of the two points {P}_{g},{P}_{d} in order to carry out the displacement difference \mathit{DN} . The normal is determined on each node of the crack as the bisector of the angle formed by the two normals to the segments which have the node in common (see ). Once the normal n has been determined on a node of the cracking path, one carries out a change of frame on the displacement field, from the global frame to the frame (n,t) ( t is the tangent vector); in particular the component \mathit{DN} is computed. The points {P}_{g},{P}_{d} are those for which the following relation is satisfied: X\ge BORNE_MAX (BORNE_MAX is a parameter to be supplied as an operand under the keyword RECHERCHE). The projection of the field X\ge onto the line normal to the path is therefore necessary for the determination of {P}_{g},{P}_{d} (see ). Normally, for the damage laws, the value X=d=0.8 is sufficient to capture the displacement jump (see V1.01.264). Figure 4: mean normal to the cracking path for the computation of the crack opening. Figure 5: Projection of the displacement DN and of the field X onto the normal to the crack path (normalised values); determination of {P}_{g},{P}_{d} . 4 Features and validation 4.1 Advice on the use of the parameters In summary, for the search for the cracking path the necessary parameters are: - {l}_{\mathrm{orth}} (LONG_ORTH) - {l}_{\mathrm{reg}} (LONG_REG) - a (PAS) - {N}_{\mathit{orth}} (NB_POINT) - BORNE_MIN to be supplied under the factor keyword RECHERCHE. The recommended range of use is the following: - {l}_{\mathit{orth}} must be greater than or equal to the width of the damaged band; good results are already obtained by adopting twice this width; - {l}_{\mathrm{reg}} may lie in the interval 0.5\Delta \le {l}_{\mathit{reg}}\le 2\Delta , \Delta being the size of the finite elements in the damaged zones (a compromise between sufficient smoothing and the risk of losing too much information from the unsmoothed damage profile); - a depends on the curvature of the path and on how many points the user wishes in order to describe the crack; as an indication one may also take it in an interval 0.5\Delta \le a\le 2\Delta ; - the choice of {N}_{\mathrm{orth}} must guarantee at least 10 points per finite element; - BORNE_MIN is the value of the field for which the search is stopped in one direction; in the case of damage one takes values >0.5 in order to be sure that the crack is well formed. As regards the computation of the crack opening, the parameter BORNE_MAX must be lower than 0.8 if the field X is the damage. 4.2 Validation The command is validated by the test case zzzz264 V1.01.264. In modelling A one searches for a cracking path and one compares it with an analytical path. In modellings B and C, one searches for the cracking path and the opening on a mechanical result, obtained by using damage laws of Code_Aster . 5 Description of the versions of the document | Aster version | Author(s) Organisation(s) | Description of the modifications | | --- | --- | --- | | 11.2 | BOTTONI | Initial text |

r7.02.19 Cohesive elements with X-FEM r7.02.19 Cohesive elements with X-FEM Summary: This document presents the various cohesive elements available with the extended finite element method (X-FEM). Three types of cohesive law are available. The law introduced first is a regularised law, available for the linear elements, and a function of the displacement jump alone. Following the limitations of the latter, two mixed laws were introduced: one for the linear elements, the other for the quadratic elements. A crack-propagation procedure with cohesive elements is implemented. It is based on the linear mixed elements. The cohesive elements are implemented in Code_Aster in 2D and in 3D. They can be used with two types of discontinuity: the emerging interfaces (keyword TYPE_DISCONTINUITE='INTERFACE' in DEFI_FISS_XFEM) and the cohesive-type cracks (keyword TYPE_DISCONTINUITE='COHESIF'), which are used for propagation studies on an unknown path. The cohesive law is defined in STAT_NON_LINE, and the solution is carried out with the command STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03. For a propagation study on an unknown path, the cracked surface is updated by the command PROPA_FISS, and the directional criterion is computed by the command CALC_G. > Contents 1 Introduction Among the classical approaches of fracture mechanics, one counts the damage laws, for which the loss of mechanical strength is described by the degradation of the volumetric properties of the material, and two approaches which concentrate this degradation on a surface: Griffith's approach [bib1], and the cohesive-zone models (CZM). Griffith's model consists in carrying out a mechanical analysis on a cracked domain, the crack being free of stress, and in computing energy quantities (energy release rate G and stress intensity factors {K}_{I},{K}_{\mathit{II}} , see the documents R7.02.01 and R7.02.05) which trigger propagation if a threshold quantity {G}_{c} (which is a material property) is reached. > Despite this simplicity, this method has drawbacks for certain applications: - If the size of the crack-process zone becomes comparable to the characteristic lengths of the model (size of the structure, initial crack length...), the response of the structure exhibits a scale effect which Griffith's model fails to reproduce. This is generally the case for concrete and geomaterials, as well as for short cracks . - Griffith's propagation criterion being implicit, it is very difficult to determine the advance of the front as a curve G={G}_{c} . As explained by Fries [bib11], very empirical explicit criteria must be used instead. In the CZMs, cohesive forces {t}_{c} act between the crack lips. They obey a softening relation in the displacement jump ⟦u⟧ , so that they are equal to 0 when the crack is fully open (see fig.). Figure 1-1: Cohesive-zone model. In this context, the extended finite element method (XFEM) is a numerical technique which makes it possible to insert discontinuity surfaces through the elements [bib2], and therefore to free oneself from the constraint of meshing them. This is particularly useful for crack-propagation studies on an unknown path: the remeshing issues are avoided. Three types of cohesive law are available for the X-FEM elements: - the regularised cohesive laws (that is, with a finite initial stiffness) for linear finite elements CZM_LIN_REG and CZM_EXP_REG. These are the first laws introduced and the simplest, but they present convergence difficulties as soon as the adherent zone becomes large. - the mixed cohesive laws (that is, with an infinite initial stiffness) for quadratic finite elements CZM_OUV_MIX and CZM_TAC_MIX. They are more robust and more accurate, but reserved for quadratic elements. - the mixed cohesive law CZM_LIN_MIX, for linear finite elements. Propagation studies on an unknown path can be carried out only with the law CZM_LIN_MIX. In this document, we begin by writing the strong formulation of the problem and by presenting the cohesive-force/displacement-jump relations for the three cohesive laws (cf. [§2]). We then write the variational formulation of the problem (cf. [§3]). We explain the solution of the problem by a Newton–Raphson method (cf. [§4]), and present the linearisation of the variational formulation. We write the finite-element discretisation of the problem, giving the matrix expressions of the tangent matrix and of the right-hand side vectors (cf. [§5]). Finally, we detail the procedure for studying the propagation of cohesive cracks on an unknown path (cf. [§6]). 2 Strong formulation of the cohesive problem 2.1 Formulation of the equations of the general problem Let \Omega \subset {ℝ}^{d},d\in \lbrace 1,2brace denote the uncracked computational domain. Its boundary \partial \Omega is split into two parts {\Gamma}_{u} and {\Gamma}_{g} , on which displacements and a surface-force density t are imposed respectively (see fig.). We denote by \Gamma the potential cracking zone on which the cohesive law is defined, composed of an upper crack lip {\Gamma}^{+} and a lower lip {\Gamma}^{-} . If {u}^{i} is the displacement on {\Gamma}^{i} , then the displacement jump is introduced as ⟦u⟧\left(xight)={u}^{+}\left(xight)-{u}^{-}\left(xight) . As we can see in the figures, the regularised cohesive laws present three difficulties: 1. if the penalisation is too weak, the displacement jump along the inclusion is wrong: one observes an opening which is not physical (mark 1 in the fig.); 2. if, on the contrary, the penalisation is too high, spurious oscillations of the cohesive stress appear in the adherent zone (mark 2 in the fig.). Originally noticed in the context of contact for Code_Aster, and referred to as the “LBB condition”, it is treated in the documentation R5.03.54, §6. In a word, it comes from the fact that the discretisation space of the cohesive forces becomes too rich in comparison with that of the displacement, when the stiffness of the law becomes such that one approaches a Dirichlet condition; 3. a poor evaluation of the operating regime (adherent or dissipative) can occur as a consequence of these oscillations (mark 3 in the fig.). Unlike the case of frictional contact R5.03.52 or R5.03.54, there are neither fixed-point loops nor sign fields. The only operation to be carried out in addition to the Newton iterations is therefore the updating of the internal variable. - For a time step: - Newton iterations. Computation of the tangent matrix and of the right-hand side - End of the Newton iterations Updating of the internal variable \alpha One might legitimately wonder why the internal variable is not updated during the Newton iterations. In fact, since it is a parameter measuring irreversibility, and determined by a maximum over time, it must be updated only at each converged time step. Indeed, otherwise, if this parameter exceeds its equilibrium value during a Newton iteration, the Newton algorithm will then be unable to decrease it in order to find the equilibrium value. In the one-dimensional case, the Newton method is an iterative process making it possible to approach the zeros of a continuous and differentiable function. One reduces the problem to the solution of F(x)=0 . One constructs a sequence of points {x}^{k} by carrying out a Taylor expansion of F in the neighbourhood of {x}^{k} , which gives, to first order: F({x}^{k+1})\approx F({x}^{k})+{F}^{'}({x}^{k})({x}^{k+1}-{x}^{k}) Denoting by {\mathrm{\delta x}}^{k}={x}^{k+1}-{x}^{k} the increment between two successive iterations, the linearised equation at iteration k+1 is then the following: {F}^{'}({x}^{k}){\mathrm{\delta x}}^{k}=-F({x}^{k}) In the case of the finite element method, {F}^{'}({x}^{k}) corresponds to the tangent matrix, which can be computed at each iteration if necessary, {\mathrm{\delta x}}^{k} is the vector of the increments of the nodal unknowns, and F({x}^{k}) is the right-hand side. Thus, the cohesive law will naturally separate the adherent and open domains, which requires a formulation of the cohesive law that allows a faithful representation of adherent zones of large size. The problem was discussed in § 3 . An implicit updating of the propagation front can then be carried out, which is the originality of the method proposed here. For the propagation algorithms, we use a mixed cohesive law with linear elements CZM_LIN_MIX, which is introduced into the model by the command DEFI_CONTACT, with the keywords ZONE/RELATION. Suppose a structure presenting a cracked surface, described by a cohesive law, for which the cohesive front separating the effective cohesive zone from the potential cracking surface is known, that is the surface within which the crack will be able to propagate at the next loading step (see fig.). Carrying out one iteration of the propagation computation then comprises, in order, the following steps (see fig.): 1. carrying out the mechanical analysis at the next time step (command STAT_NON_LINE), 2. detection of the new cohesive front (command PROPA_FISS, operation DETECT_COHESIF), 3. determination of the propagation direction along this new front (command CALC_G), 4. construction of a new potential cracking zone beyond this front, from the directions determined in c), according to an extension of fixed length (command PROPA_FISS, operation PROPA_COHESIF), 5. updating of the model according to this new zone (command MODI_MODELE_XFEM), and if necessary, projection of the current cohesive state onto this new model (keyword ETAT_INIT/COHE in STAT_NON_LINE). This state will serve as the initial state for the mechanical analysis of step a) of the next iteration. Figure 6-a: Propagation of a crack on an unknown path: steps for carrying out a propagation step. 6.1 Description of a cohesive crack In order to be able to locate the cohesive front, one defines a discontinuity of type 'COHESIF' in DEFI_FISS_XFEM. Compared with a discontinuity of type 'INTERFACE', it must contain additional information in order to locate the cohesive front: the data structures relating to the description of a front (coordinates of the points, covariant basis...) and an additional level-set. Indeed, given that the position of the potential cracking surface is described with a normal level-set by [{\varphi}_{n}=0] , the cohesive front is classically located by an additional “tangent” level-set, as [{\varphi}_{n}=0]\cap [:ref: {\varphi}_{t}=0 ] (see fig.). For a detailed description of the use of level-sets with XFEM, see the documentation R7.02.12, §2. Figure 6.1-a: Description of the cohesive front by means of level-sets. Unlike the type 'FISSURE', the type 'COHESIF' has no pointwise singular enrichment, because of the regularity of the cohesive fields. The potential cracking zone therefore stops on the faces (in 3D) or the edges (in 2D, see fig.) of the elements. Figure 6.1-b: Characteristics of a crack of type COHESIF, at the output of a DETECT_COHESIF operation of PROPA_FISS Note: In fact, for the type COHESIF , the propagation front does not necessarily always coincide with the zero iso-value of the tangent level-set. Indeed, during the mechanical-analysis phases (step a of the fig.), the zero iso-value of the tangent level-set is used to locate the end of the potential cracking zone, and therefore of the enrichment (see fig.), whereas the propagation front always locates the cohesive front (from which the interface is actually open, see fig.). Figure 6.1-c: Characteristics of a crack of type COHESIF, at the output of a PROPA_COHESIF operation of PROPA_FISS Note – initialisation of the procedure: The initialisation of a propagation study (by step a of the fig.) is carried out by giving an initial potential cracking zone and an initial propagation front (see fig.). The latter may correspond to a corner of the structure, a simple line on a free edge, or a pre-existing crack tip (in the latter case, it must be meshed). The authors explain there that this is a reasonable assumption for concrete, since the experiments show that the cracking path, unlike the force/displacement response curve, is almost insensitive to the size of the cohesive zone. One could compute these stress intensity factors from an additional elastic analysis of a free crack — one removes the cohesive forces from the model — as in [bib6, bib7]. > One can nevertheless do without this additional step: for example, Moës and Belytschko [bib8] compute them directly from the result with cohesive forces. Note – choice of the basis 	heta for the decomposition of the modes: If the cohesive zone is of large size, it is distributed over a curved surface. The choice of the basis for the decomposition of the modes is then not obvious: one may choose: -either the basis at the crack front (figure, solution a), -or the basis at the point under consideration (fig., solution b), -or the basis linked to the polar coordinates at the crack front (fig., solution c). Whereas the first solution underestimates the bifurcation angle and the second overestimates it, the third solution c) is the one which produces the most balanced results, and therefore the one which has been implemented. In the detection phase described in § 6.3 , only the tangent level-set is updated (OPERATION='DETECT_COHESIF' in PROPA_FISS). In the phase of extension of the potential cracking surface detailed here (OPERATION='PROPA_COHESIF' in PROPA_FISS), the normal level-set is also updated, and the extension is carried out over a fixed length DA_MAX, which must be chosen much greater than \Delta l . The various methods for updating level-sets are listed in the documentation R7.02.13. Whereas the classical methods are based on a centred-difference discretisation of Hamilton–Jacobi equations (METHODE_PROPA='SIMPLEXE'/'UPWIND' in PROPA_FISS), simpler methods have appeared since (METHODE_PROPA='GEOMETRIQUE' in PROPA_FISS), for which the only remaining step is the updating proper. This technique takes advantage of the fact that the crack surface created at the previous instant is frozen: the problem of the propagation of a surface therefore reduces to the propagation of a front from which distances can be evaluated directly. Figure 6.5-a : Direct computation, plane by plane, of the new level-sets by the geometric propagation algorithm. r7.02.20 Computation of T-stress by extrapolation of displacement field r7.02.20 Computation of T-stress by extrapolation of displacement field Summary: The computation of T-stress is implemented for linear, homogeneous and elastic-isotropic materials with plane crack mesh (FEM only). The accuracy of T-stress results obtained by extrapolation of the displacement field method is clearly improved if the meshing elements are quadratic. It is also highly recommended to use “Barsoum” type elements in the crack tip (elements where the mid-side nodes are located at the quarter of edges). 1 Theory Based on isotropic-linear-elasticity theory, when an elastic cracked body is subjected to external forces (see Fig.1), the stress field in the vicinity of a crack tip can be expressed by the Williams’ expansion. The stresses near the crack-tip can be written according to equations 1-2, where {\sigma}_{ij} is the stress tensor, r represents the distance of element from crack tip, and \theta is the angle of element with respect to a polar axes located at the crack tip [:ref: 1 ]. {\sigma}_{\mathit{rr}}=\frac{{K}_{1}}{\sqrt{(2\pi r)}}(\frac{5}{4}\cos(\frac{\theta}{2})-\frac{1}{4}\cos(\frac{3\theta }{2}))+\frac{{K}_{2}}{\sqrt{(2\pi r)}}(\frac{-5}{4}\sin(\frac{\theta}{2})+\frac{3}{4}\sin(\frac{3\theta }{2}))+T{\cos}^{2}(\theta ) Equation 1 {\sigma}_{\theta \theta }=\frac{{K}_{1}}{\sqrt{(2\pi r)}}(\frac{3}{4}\cos(\frac{\theta}{2})+\frac{1}{4}\cos(\frac{3\theta }{2}))+\frac{{K}_{2}}{\sqrt{(2\pi r)}}(\frac{-3}{4}\sin(\frac{\theta}{2})+\frac{3}{4}\sin(\frac{3\theta }{2}))+T{\sin}^{2}(\theta ) Equation 2 | | | --- | | Fig.1 Stress in a polar coordinate system ahead of a crack in an infinite plate | The non-singular term is known as T-stress, and characterises the crack tip constraint; this is particularly useful in the assessment of the integrity of structures containing defects. A robust method for obtaining T-stress is via the displacement field along the crack faces. This method is based on the asymptotic development of the displacement field in the crack tip. For \theta =-\pi or theta =+pi the singular term of {\sigma}_{\mathit{rr}} vanished and hence near the crack tip, T-stress can be represented by: T={E}^{'}\frac{[{U}_{\theta =\pi }(r)]-[{U}_{\theta =\pi }(0)]}{r} where [U] is the displacement step between the crack lips and hence [{U}_{\theta =\pi }(0)] denotes displacement of crack tip; details of the method are given elsewhere [2]. {E}^{'} is defined for plane stress and plane strain conditions as: {E}^{'}=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}E\\ \frac{E}{1-{\mathrm{\upsilon }}^{2}}\end{array}\begin{array}{c}\mathit{Plane}\mathit{stress}\\ \mathit{Plane}\mathit{strain}\end{array}\right\rbrace Note: - It is also possible to compute T-stress according to the stress fields, but the values of the vector forced on the lips of crack are less accurate than displacements (resulting from a stress singularity in crack tip). - The user must take care to refine the mesh in the vicinity of crack tip so that enough points are available for extrapolation. - The method used here is theoretically less accurate than the integration integral method for computation of T-stress since the integral is taken over a domain of elements surrounding the crack and errors in local solution parameters have less effect on the evaluated quantities. However, in this method no special crack tip elements are required and the determination of node sets for the calculation of T-stress is simpler than in the J-integral approach. Thus it makes possible to obtain easily relatively reliable values of T-stress for any type of mesh strategy. The comparison of the different methods of calculating is always useful to estimate the accuracy of the results obtained. 2 Implementation of extrapolation method The extrapolation displacement method is implemented in the POST_T_Q operator which starts by computing the displacement field on the global structure. Since the definition of T-stress are only asymptotically true; extrapolation is restricted to the vicinity of the crack tip limited by a maximum distance \mathit{dmax} around the crack. \mathit{dmax} is a parameter of the ABSC_CURV_MAXI operator. In the case of a meshed crack ABSC_CURV_MAXI is optional. If \mathit{dmax} is not defined in the .comm file, by default it is automatically assigned in POST_T_Q operator as equal to three times the maximum size of the mesh elements connected to the nodes on the crack front. The general principle of T-stress computation is defined as follows: 1. Loop on the crack tip nodes 2. Extract the crack tip displacement, 3. Define the plane normal to crack and the crack tip, 4. Project the displacement field in \theta =+\pi and theta =-pi , 5. Calculate the difference of the displacement value, 6. The displacement difference is divided by r with material multiplicative factor will obtaine and then extrapolate into r=0 . If the solution is perfect, one should obtain a line. Actually, we obtain almost a line with a mesh of the type “Barsoum”. 3 Accuracy of suggested method The extrapolation displacement method was validated on the test case (SSS?) , for which analytical solutions are known [3]. This test case, as detailed in (T₁.odt), considers an elliptic crack in a three-dimensional body subject to a tensile load. A cube by size of (h=w=t=16) , containing a horizontal circular crack of radius c=a=1 is considered (see Fig.2). The value of far-field stress, \sigma , was prescribes as 1 MPa. Due to symmetry, only one quarter of the elliptical crack is considered. The crack is meshed with fine quadratic mesh type in the vicinity of crack tip. The results are compared with reference solution (see Fig.3). | | | --- | | Fig.2 Geometric configuration of the testcase shown in half symmetry [3] | | | | --- | | Fig.3 T-stress compression | 4 Conclusion The results obtained with extrapolation displacement method are in a good agreement, with less than 5% error compared to the analytical solution of T-stress. It should be noticed that the asymptotic relation of displacements is valid only for r tending towards 0. Therefore, it is necessary to take care not to choose too large a domain of extrapolation (distance \mathit{dmax} from operator POST_T_Q of about 4 to 5 elements). 5 Bibliography 1. r7.02.21 1 r7.02.21 Cohesive constitutive law 1 r7.02.21 Cohesive constitutive law 2 r7.02.21 dependent on the loading mixity: CZM_TURON Summary: The cohesive constitutive law CZM_TURON makes it possible to model the damage of a cracking interface such that the opening of the crack generates cohesive forces between the faces of the latter. It relates the cohesive forces, homogeneous to a stress, to the displacement discontinuity across the interface according to a bilinear law, which depends on the mixity ratio of the loading: an interface subjected to a mixed loading will damage earlier than in pure mode. This model was developed by the team of Turon of the University of Girona (Spain) [ 1 ]. It is for example used in the framework of the modelling of bonded joints in composite material in the blades of wind turbines. The law is supported by joint finite elements whose degrees of freedom are the displacement jumps across the interface (see R3.06.13). We present here the formulation of the cohesive law as well as the internal variables of the model. The existence of instabilities during crack propagation requires a control by the elastic prediction, whose elements specific to these laws are presented. 1 Generalities on the cohesive laws In brittle fracture, in order to remove the problem of infinite stresses at the crack tip, one can introduce cohesive forces that impose an initiation criterion in stress [ 2 ]. The forces are exerted between the particles on either side of the separation plane of the crack (see Figure ). Historically, one of the first to propose this type of approach is Barenblatt [ 3 ] at the beginning of the 1960s. Based on this idea, numerous models have appeared in the literature under the name: "Cohesive zone models" or CZM in English. For a more complete bibliography one may refer to [ 4 ]. Figure 1.1: Diagram of a crack It is considered that the opening of the crack costs an energy proportional to its length. It is called surface energy and is denoted \Psi . The displacement field at equilibrium u is obtained by minimising the sum of the elastic energy \Phi of the surface energy, and of the work of the external forces {W}^{\mathrm{ext.}} : \underset{u}{\min}(\Phi +\Psi +{W}^{\mathrm{ext}}) The displacement-jump vector in the element \Delta is a linear function of the nodal displacements. The cohesive force 1 that is exerted on the faces of the crack is denoted , it is defined by the derivative of the free surface-energy density with respect to the displacement-jump vector. A cohesive law is called a relation between \sigma and the displacement jump \Delta . In the system of coordinates linked to the interface, N denotes the direction normal to the interface and T=({T}_{1,}{T}_{2}) the subsystem of coordinates in the tangential plane of the interface. force per unit area, homogeneous to a stress. 2 Definition of the law CZM_TURON 2.1 Definitions Let us begin by introducing the parameters of the model. One has: - the critical surface-energy densities in pure normal mode and in pure tangential mode, denoted {G}_{c,N} (keyword GC_N) and {G}_{c,T} (keyword GC_T) which express the energy cost of cracking in each of the two modes; - the critical stresses at rupture denoted {\sigma}_{N}^{c} (keyword SIGM_C_N) and {\sigma}_{T}^{c} (keyword SIGM_C_T); - the initial stiffness of the interface K (keyword K); - the parameter of the Benzeggagh-Kenane criterion (keyword ETA_BK); - the dimensionless parameter C_RUPT which makes it possible to define a residual "post-rupture" stiffness (when the element is completely damaged and the cohesive stress is zero), as a fraction of the initial stiffness. It is equal to 0.001 by default and cannot exceed 0.1; - the parameter CRIT_INIT which makes it possible to choose the type of damage-initiation criterion, among 'YE' (elliptic criterion) or 'TURON' (Benzeggagh-Kenane type criterion). The material parameters proper, namely GC_N, GC_T, SIGM_C_N, SIGM_C_T, K and ETA_BK, are to be identified from standard quasi-static tests. For example, in the framework of the simulation of a bonded joint, the adhesive being modelled with the cohesive-zone model, the parameters will be identified by carrying out the following tests on "sandwich" specimens: - the DCB test ("Double Cantilever Beam"), which loads the joint in pure normal mode, makes it possible to identify the parameters GC_N and SIGM_C_N; - the ENF test ("End-notched flexure"), corresponding to 3-point bending, loads the joint in pure tangent mode and makes it possible to identify the parameters GC_T and SIGM_C_T; - the MMB test ("Mixed-mode bending") is a combination of the two previous tests and makes it possible to subject the joint to a mixed loading, the mixity ratio being in the hands of the experimenter, who can adjust the device. In addition to the previous tests, it is used to calibrate the parameter ETA_BK. As regards the parameter K , it is generally observed that it influences little the simulated global response and that it is therefore difficult to identify it by adjustment of the numerical and experimental curves. In practice, it is often assumed ad hoc . Note: > The following notations are adopted: for every vector x one denotes: > x={x}_{N}N+{x}_{{T}_{1}}{T}_{1}+{x}_{{T}_{2}}{T}_{2} > {x}_{T}={x}_{{T}_{1}}{T}_{1}+{x}_{{T}_{2}}{T}_{2} > ⟨x⟩=⟨{x}_{N}⟩N+{x}_{{T}_{1}}{T}_{1}+{x}_{{T}_{2}}{T}_{2} with ⟨{x}_{i}⟩=max({x}_{i},0) > \Vert x\Vert =\sqrt{x.x} and {\Vert x\Vert }_{+}=\sqrt{⟨x⟩.⟨x⟩} In particular, one will denote \lambda ={\Vert \Delta \Vert }_{+} the equivalent displacement of the cohesive element and {\lambda}_{T}=\Vert {\Delta}_{T}\Vert the norm of the tangential jump. Finally one calls: - {\Delta}^{0} the value that the equivalent jump must reach for the damage to initiate. It is therefore called the damage-initiation jump; - {\Delta}^{f} the value that the equivalent jump must reach for the element to break. It is therefore called the crack-propagation jump (but this name must not mislead the reader: modellings with a CZM law do not present a crack proper, for example directly meshed or else defined by level sets). The initial stiffness K makes it possible to regularise the free energy at 0. The present law is therefore a law of regularised type. Note that in the case where the interface is supposed to be infinitely stiff, for example when the interface models a cracking path in a brittle material, then the initial stiffness must be small enough for the energy to be well regularised, but this can in return generate a global softening of the structure that is not physical. In the framework of the modelling of an interface possessing a certain "compliance" that is physical (for example a layer of adhesive between two adherends that will deform elastically before starting to damage), this problem does not arise. It should be recalled that there must not be too great a difference in stiffness between the cohesive elements of type JOINT and the directly neighbouring elements (generally solid), at the risk of encountering conditioning problems of the stiffness matrix of the system, specific to this type of elements [ 5 ]. In practice, one can check that the parameter K and the quantity \frac{E}{{h}_{\mathit{elem}}} are of the same order of magnitude, E being the Young modulus of the adherend and {h}_{\mathit{elem}} being the size of the mesh cells adjacent to the joint elements. One can, to a certain extent, adapt the size of the adjacent mesh cells. But if the conditioning problems cannot be removed given too great a difference between the material properties of the cohesive interface and of the adherend, one will rather turn towards elements of type INTERFACE [ 5 , 6 ], on which certain CZM laws are available [ 7 ]. 2.2 Constitutive equations In this part one presents the surface energy \Psi as well as the stress vector which is derived from it. The formulation proposed ensures the irreversibility of the damage. 2.2.1 Free surface energy The free energy per unit area \Psi , defined on a discontinuity \Gamma , depends on the displacement-jump vector between the faces of the crack \Delta (denoted \Delta in order to lighten the writing) and on an internal variable that manages the irreversibility of the cracking. One first defines the variable v which stores the largest norm of the jump (equivalent displacement) reached during the opening. Its evolution law between two successive loading increments - and + is written: {v}^{+}=max({\lambda}_{+},{v}^{-}) One also defines the threshold variable denoted r which gives the minimum jump to be reached in order to (re)start damaging: {r}^{+}=max({\Delta}^{0,}{v}^{-}) Let us finally define the damage variable d , whose evolution law will be given in what follows. The element is sound when d=0 and completely damaged, broken, when d=1 . One notes that from the thermodynamic point of view, the variable d used here is the internal variable of the constitutive behaviour. On the other hand, from the point of view of the numerical implementation, the variable v will be used as internal variable, the other variables r and d being computed from v . The following free energy per unit area is given: \Psi (\Delta ,d)=(1-d){\Psi}^{0}(\Delta ) with {\Psi}^{0}(\Delta )=\frac{1}{2}{\Delta}_{i}{D}_{ij}^{0}{\Delta}_{j} for i,j=1,3 {\Psi}^{0} being a convex function in the space of the displacement jumps. The negative values of {\Delta}_{N} have no meaning because the interpenetration of the faces is made impossible by the contact. In order to prevent interpenetration after complete decohesion, the modification of the equation according to the following form is proposed: \Psi (\Delta ,d)=(1-d){\Psi}^{0}(\Delta )-d{\Psi}^{0}({\delta}_{Ni}⟨-{\Delta}_{N}⟩) where {\delta}_{ij} is the Kronecker symbol. 2.2.2 Expression of the stress The constitutive equations are obtained by differentiating the free energy with respect to the displacement jumps: {\tau}_{i}=\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial {\Delta}_{i}}=(1-d){D}_{ij}^{0}{\Delta}_{j}-d{D}_{ij}^{0}{\delta}_{\mathit{Nj}}⟨-{\Delta}_{N}⟩ where {D}_{ij}^{0}={\delta}_{ij}K is the initial stiffness tensor, with K the penalisation stiffness. Assuming that N\equiv 1 and that ({T}_{1,}{T}_{2})\equiv (2,3) , the equation can be written in vector form: \tau =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\tau}_{1}\\ {\tau}_{2}\\ {\tau}_{3}\end{array}\right\rbrace =(1-d)K\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\Delta}_{1}\\ {\Delta}_{2}\\ {\Delta}_{3}\end{array}\right\rbrace -dK\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}⟨-{\Delta}_{1}⟩\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace The energy dissipated during the evolution of the damage is denoted \Xi and is obtained by differentiating the free energy with respect to the internal damage variable: \Xi =-\frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial d}\dot{d} The constitutive model given in the equation is well evaluated if the damage variable d can be computed at each time instant of the strain process, which is possible by giving oneself an initiation criterion and an evolution law for the damage. 2.2.3 Evolution of the damage The evolution of the damage is formulated in the form of a threshold function in the space of the displacement jumps. It is written, at each time instant t : F({\lambda}^{t},{r}^{t}):={\lambda}^{t}-{r}^{t}\le 0 \forall t\ge 0 where {r}^{t} is the damage threshold at the current time instant. If one denotes {r}^{0} the initial damage threshold then one must have {r}^{t}\ge {r}^{0} at each time instant. The damage threshold can only increase. The damage initiates when the norm of the displacement jump \lambda exceeds the initial threshold :math: {r}^{0} , which is computed in particular from the material characteristics. In the present formulation, an equivalent expression easier to treat from the algorithmic point of view will be used: \overline{F}({\lambda}^{t},{r}^{t}):=G({\lambda}^{t})-G({r}^{t})\le 0 \forall t\ge 0 where G is a monotonic scalar function going from 0 to 1. The evolution of the threshold and of the damage are given by their increments: \dot{r}=\dot{\mu} \dot{d}=\dot{\mu}\frac{\partial \overline{F}(\lambda ,r)}{\partial \lambda }=\dot{\mu}\frac{\partial G(\lambda )}{\partial \lambda } the variable \mu being the Lagrange multiplier that makes it possible to define the loading–unloading conditions according to the Kuhn and Tucker relations: \dot{\mu}\ge 0 (a); \overline{F}({\lambda}^{t},{r}^{t})\le 0 (b); \dot{\mu}\overline{F}({\lambda}^{t},{r}^{t})=0 (c) For pedagogical reasons, the integration — very classical — of the Kuhn and Tucker relations will be carried out explicitly. For this purpose, the two "phases" are separated: Phase A (non-damaging) : As long as {\lambda}^{t} {r}^{t} otherwise (b) is no longer satisfied). Let us set aside the case where \dot{\mu}=0 corresponding to the case where \lambda does not evolve. Then \dot{\mu}>0 according to (a) and therefore r increases, at the same time as \lambda . Moreover, one can write that \dot{d}=\dot{r}\frac{\partial G(r)}{\partial r} whence the direct integration of d . The two phases can alternate according to the loading path, and one can therefore integrate the threshold variable r and the damage variable d in the following manner: {r}^{t}=max({r}^{0},{max}_{s}\lambda ) 0\le s\le t {d}^{t}=G({r}^{t}) In what follows one will denote {r}^{0}={\Delta}^{0} the damage threshold. The scalar function G defines the evolution of the damage variable. r7.02.22 Calculation of modified J-integral in presence of initial state r7.02.22 Calculation of modified J-integral in presence of initial state Summary: This document aims at describing the theoretical formulations and implementation to compute the modified J -integral in 3D and 2D via the macro_command POST_JMOD. The theoretical background of J -integral is presented in Section 1 . It is first introduced by the continuous mathematical description of the standard J in 2D [1]. This standard formulation without initial state is extended successively to the full 3D formulation [2] and the modified formulations to account for the presence of an initial strain field [3] and the non-proportional loading conditions [4]. In Section 2 , the domain integral formulations are detailed in discretised form adapted for the finite element method. The overall strategy for implementation of the macro_command POST_JMOD in code_aster , and general information regarding the supported element types, loads, and required mechanics fields are presented in Section 3 . Specific details of the procedures used in the identification of key terms such as the virtual crack extension field, the cracked surface advancement and the gradient of the deformation and strain energy terms are presented in Section 2 . Finally, an overview list of the test cases used to validate POST_JMOD is presented in Section 3 . The current development version of POST_JMOD is applicable for: - elastic and plastic material behaviours; - proportional/non-proportional and mixed mode loads; - initial strain (associated with an equilibrium residual stress); - Standard FEM with a meshed crack Table of Contents Table of Figures 1 Theoretical background 1.1 Standard J-integral formulation in 2D The J -integral [1] is widely used in fracture mechanics analyses to assess the structural integrity of industrial components. In its basic definition, the value of the J -integral is calculated along a small closed contour around the crack tip in a two-dimensional ( 2D ) problem for an elastic (linear or non-linear) material subjected to a proportional monotonic stress, as shown in Figure 1 .: For a 2D analysis, in the absence of the body forces and the crack face traction, under quasi-static conditions with a crack directed along the x1 -axis ( Figure 1 ), a path independent formulation of the standard J -integral definition is defined as ([1], [2],): where δij is the Kronecker coefficient, σij and ui are components of stress and displacement in the Cartesian coordinates, respectively. In Equation 1, Γ represents a curve surrounding the crack tip which begins at the lower face of the crack and ends at the upper one while ni represents the unit vector normal to Γ and d s represents the infinitesimal path length along Γ. The strain energy density W is defined at Gauss points as: Applying the divergence theorem, Equation 1 is transformed into a domain integral formulation as shown in [2]: where q is any smoothing function defined over the area A , which takes the values of unity at the crack-tip node, zero on the contour Γ, and varies from 0 to 1 within the ring of elements containing Γ. Physically, q represents the virtual crack extension. It should be noted that the J -integral approach in this macro_command is equivalent to the G-theta method used in the operator CALC_G of code_aster but with a different numerical implementation. Also, q- field plays a similar role as the theta-field in CALC_G. Only the u and q fields are evaluated on nodes, and the remaining parameters are evaluated at the Gauss points. 1.2 Extension of standard J-integral 3D Assuming planar crack surfaces, the standard J -integral formulation defined in Equation (1) in 2D can be extended to a three-dimensional ( 3D ) problem where a 2D formulation is defined locally on each plane Si perpendicular to the crack front line at each crack tip point for all the points along the crack front. Then, a local coordinate system ξ1ξ2ξ3 is introduced at arbitrary crack tip point Ni of the crack front ( Figure 2 ). The coordinate axes ξ1 and ξ2 lie in a plane Si normal to the crack front through Ni, ξ2 is perpendicular to the crack surface, and ξ3 is tangent to the crack front. According to the basic definition of J -integral in 2D , the local J- integral can be computed along a small contour around Ni in the ξ1ξ2 plane. For an arbitrary crack, the general 3D expression of J -integral to perform computations in the global coordinate system x1x2x3 can be expressed by Equation 4 at each local crack tip node Ni, as shown in [5]: In this equation Ac is the area increase in the cracked surface ( Figure 3 ) generated by the virtual crack extension q and V represents the volume ( Figure 4 ). Figure 4: Definition of the volume integration V around crack front. 1.3 Modified J-integral for initial strain under proportional loads For cases of initial strains, we define the “initial state” as the moment in time prior to the application of external loading to a cracked body. When initial strains are present, the total strain during mechanical loading εij is the sum of the mechanical strain εmij under load and the initial strain ε0ij at initial state, as shown in Equation 5: {\epsilon}_{ij}={\epsilon}_{ij}^{m}+{{\epsilon}_{ij}^{0}|}_{\mathit{initial}\mathit{state}} It is assumed that the initial strain ε0ij remains constant during subsequent deformation and the mechanical strain εmij is related to the applied stress through the material constitutive law. Note that ε0ij arises from a preliminary calculation of the initial state and more detail on the initial state is given in Section 1.1 . A 3-dimensional path independent J -integral (Equation 6) for this loading condition can be obtained under the conditions of proportional loading as shown in [2]: In this modified J -integral, W is defined as the mechanical strain energy density: Note that εmij is the sum of the elastic and inelastic strain obtained during loading of a cracked body, corrected for the inelastic strains at the initial state (Equation 11 in Section 1.5). The calculation procedure illustrated in Figure 6 of Section 1.5 shows that the initial state arises from a preliminary calculation step before the cracked body analysis (CBA) occurs. The initial strains at the initial state is effectively a constant field used in the post-processing of the results from the cracked body analysis. 1.4 Modified J-integral for initial strain under non-proportional loads Lei [3] proposed a more general modified J -integral formulation which covers both cases with the presence of initial strains and non-proportional stress occurring during applying mechanical load (after initial state) while accounting for initial strains. Following the method of Wilson and Yu [6], Equation 4 is modified as: with strain energy density W defined by Equation 7 and the total strain εij by Equation 5. Practically, the J values obtained on the first, second, or third contours are generally dropped because of the inaccurate stress, strain, and displacement rate at the vicinity of the crack tip (this may depend on the mesh refinement). As a general rule of thumb, it is best practice to have a sufficiently fine mesh around the crack tip for calculations. Moreover, the correction part in the right-hand side of Equation 8 can be also affected by the inaccurate near tip field data, resulting in an incorrect correction to the modified J . Note that the correction part of the modified J is evaluated using the volume integration. Therefore, any errors evaluated at the near-tip volume affect all the following calculations and force the path-independent modified J to approach an incorrect value; typically this occurs on the first or second domain. This source of error may lead to an underestimation of the modified J , and it is found that the error due to this may be significant at lower load levels (for small scale yielding conditions). However, this error reduces with increasing load level and almost disappears when the load exceeds approximately half of the yield stress-based limit. The specific reason for the error reduction at high load level is not fully identified but it is conjectured that the higher absolute J value at a high load level reduces the relative error [4]. In order to minimize the effect of the inaccurate near-tip data on the correction term of the modified J , a very small volume surrounding the considered points on crack front is excluded from the integration volume and Equation 8 can then be modified following the method in [4]: Here the volume V1 is limited by two volumes V and V’ . The size of V’ may be determined empirically by selecting the first three contours around crack front for a reasonably finely focused mesh (see Figure 5 below). It is noted that there is no specific requirement for the shape of the volumes V and V’ around the crack tip when performing this domain integral. The path-dependence leads to the non-validity of J -integral as a useful constant fracture mechanics parameter. Lei et al. [2] proposed the modification of Rice’s J -integral to correct the formulation to produce a path-independent J- integral to account for initial strains under proportional loads. Note that, generally speaking, a residual stress field can arise from internal strains, which could form due to non-uniform plastic deformation, non-uniform heat expansion, or local volume changes owing to phase transformations, etc. If the internal strain field produces an additional mechanical strain field (without external loading) residual stresses occur in the body. It is these such residual stress problems that can be considered as initial strain problems [2]. For this reason, only the initial strain state is treated in the modified J -integral calculation illustrated in Figure 6. Figure 6 shows an example process to evaluate the initial strains at the “initial state”. The first step may be a preliminary non-linear analysis of the problem to generate a residual stress field in the body, which features an associated initial strain field. A user would then, in the second step, perform a CBA under loading that includes the effects of the residual stresses in initial state. The modified J-integral computation would then occur in the third step, as a post-processing operation on the results output from the second step, using the initial strain field at the initial state evaluated in step 1. Figure 6- Example of the sequence of calculations that produce: the initial state, the CBA with initial state, modified J-integral calculation on the CBA. Example based on computations done within code_aster. From the user’s viewpoint, it is emphasized that only the initial strain state is required as an input, and not a distinction as to the type of strain. However, the user must be aware that they need to carefully assign the initial strain state depending on the specific engineering problems to be assessed. For example, thermal loading cases allow the initial strains to be evaluated directly, but more generally, the initial strains can be determined from the total and elastic strains at the initial state (Step 1). {\epsilon}_{ij}^{0}={\left({\epsilon}_{ij}^{\mathit{Total}}-{\epsilon}_{ij}^{e}\right)|}_{\mathit{initial}\mathit{state}}={{\epsilon}_{ij}^{p}|}_{\mathit{initial}\mathit{state}} (11) From the developer viewpoint, it is necessary to be aware that the CBA in step 2 generates total strains which include the effect of the initial strain field, as shown by Equation {{\epsilon}_{ij}^{\mathit{Total}}={\epsilon}_{ij}^{e}+{\epsilon}_{ij}^{p}+\epsilon }_{ij}^{0} Hence, when evaluating εmij (Equation 7) required for modified J-Integral calculations in step 3, it may be necessary to separate the initial strain from the total mechanical strain arising from the CBA in step 2. For this reason, the concept “initial state” was introduced earlier. All plastic strains before the initial state must be treated as initial strains in the post-processing calculation of step 3. Elastic strains, at the initial state, however, are recoverable and therefore contribute to the mechanical strain during step 2. The procedure to calculate J has only been developed with hexahedral elements in mind. However, for complex 3D cracks, it is possible to use the prism elements for the first ring around the crack front. It must be noted that one of the quadrangle surfaces of these prism elements should be located on one of the crack surfaces ( Figure 8 ). This restriction comes from the difficulty in determination of crack propagation direction and of the area increase of the cracked surface with irregular meshes. The user must take to ensure an appropriate mesh is utilised in the computation. Figure 8: Definition of the pentahedral element for J calculation. It should be emphasized that the same limit was observed in the J -integral development of Abaqus software [7]: “ The contour integral evaluation capability of ABAQUS assumes that the elements that lie within the domain used for the calculations are quadrilaterals in two-dimensional or shell models or bricks in continuum three-dimensional models. Triangles, tetrahedrals, or wedges should not be used in the mesh that is included in the contour integral regions ”. In code_aster , it is possible to calculate the J -integral using the command POST_JMOD U4.82.41. The virtual crack extension field of the crack q is calculated automatically in this command from the information provided by the user. The current development is valid for the 3D modelling and deals with the following conditions only: - both elastic and plastic behaviours of materials; - proportional, non-proportional and mixed mode loads; - initial strains (representing residual stress fields) It cannot deal with cases where there is pressure on the crack surfaces. 3.4 Required existing code_aster concepts For the calculation of the energy release rate, it is necessary to characterise beforehand the meshed crack via the concept of the FOND_FISS type with the command DEFI_FOND_FISS U4.82.01. Figure 14- Domain extraction step 1. All elements with at least one node connected to the crack front are extracted for each node along the crack front. The difference in element sets between neighbouring groups is then taken. Firstly, the nodes of the crack front are interrogated sequentially ( Figure 14 ). This allows the creation of the sub sets of elements that have at least one node contained within each of those crack front nodes. By comparing the first element set along the crack front with its neighbouring element set, the elements contained within both sets can be extracted. These elements correspond to the elements lying on the plane emanating from each crack front nodal position. Figure 15- Domain extraction step 2. The nodes within each element set is extracted for each crack front nodal position. The neighbouring node sets are compared to obtain the intersecting nodes. Then, the set of elements at the crack front nodal positions are interrogated sequentially ( Figure 15 ). This allows the extraction of the node sets corresponding to the element sets. The intersection between neighbouring nodal sets is used to extract the node set attached to the first contour of elements at each crack front nodal position. These nodes correspond to the nodes lying in the plane emanating from each crack front nodal position. Note that only local values of J are computed along the crack front. r7.04.02 Estimation of fatigue under random loading r7.04.02 Estimation of fatigue under random loading Summary: This note presents two stress-cycle counting methods which lead to an analytical expression for the mechanical damage produced by a random loading: - stress-peak counting method, - method of counting exceedances of a given level. The first method uses the signal, its first derivative and its second derivative. The second requires only knowledge of the signal and of its first derivative. Once the stress cycles are known by these methods, the mean damage over the duration of the signal is determined using the Wöhler method. 1 Introduction The assessment of damage is based on the use of endurance curves of the material, associating a stress variation of given amplitude with an allowable number of cycles defined by a fatigue curve. The fatigue curves of the material are established by subjecting specimens to sinusoidal loadings of constant amplitude from the start of the test until failure. In order to use these curves from a real loading, cycles must be identified in the stress history, which is done by cycle-counting methods. Many methods exist: document R7.04.01 presents two cycle-counting methods in the case of a deterministic real loading. However, many real mechanical loadings affecting nuclear components have a random character, which leads one to favour the use of statistical methods in order to assess the damage undergone by these structures. Some stress-cycle counting methods have been given a statistical interpretation: - stress-peak counting method - method of counting exceedances of a given level. The field of application of these two methods [bib1][bib2] is limited to random loadings that are ergodic (the analysis of a single sample is sufficient to characterise the parameters of the process) and Gaussian (the values of the measured signal are distributed according to a normal law). Furthermore, the evolution of the signal is treated as a random process characterised by its statistical parameters (spectral moments of order 0, 2 and 4) R7.10.01. In both cases, the statistical event to be taken into account is simple to define: - a stress peak is defined by a zero slope and a negative acceleration for a positive peak, a positive acceleration for a negative peak, - an exceedance of a stress level {S}_{0} is characterised by a signal value equal to {S}_{0} and by a positive slope. Once the stress cycles are known by these methods, one then proceeds to the computation of the number of cycles to failure from a fatigue curve. The Wöhler curves, which are established experimentally, have been approximated by various mathematical expressions characterising the different regions of these curves more or less correctly. Three mathematical expressions are available in Code_Aster : a discretised form and two analytical forms. Knowing the number of stress cycles (given by one of these two cycle-counting methods) and the elementary damage associated with them (determined by interpolation on the Wöhler curve of the material), one can compute a mean damage over the duration of the signal. 2 Assessment of the damage For a structure with no geometrical defect and subjected to a purely alternating stress, the number of cycles to failure is determined from an endurance diagram, also called a Wöhler curve or an S-N curve. The number of cycles to failure is determined by interpolation of the Wöhler curve of the material for a given alternating (one-dimensional) stress level (to each elementary cycle there corresponds a stress-amplitude level \mathrm{Ds}=\mid {s}_{\max}-{s}_{\min}\mid and an alternating stress {S}_{\text{alt}}=1/\mathrm{2Ds} ). The damage of an elementary cycle is equal to the inverse of the number of cycles to failure: D=\frac{1}{{N}_{r({S}_{\text{alt}})}} 2.1 Endurance diagram The endurance diagram, also called the Wöhler curve or the S-N curve (stress–number of cycles to failure curve), is obtained experimentally by subjecting specimens to cycles of periodic forces (generally sinusoidal) of normal amplitude \sigma and of constant frequencies, and by recording the number of cycles {N}_{r} at the end of which failure occurs R7.04.01. The various mathematical forms of the Wöhler curve are described in the document “Estimation of high-cycle fatigue”, R7.04.01, together with the way of introducing them into Code_Aster . 2.2 Elastoplastic concentration coefficient It may also be necessary to weight the stress value determined by the counting method by the elastoplastic concentration coefficient {K}_{e} . The elastoplastic concentration coefficient {K}_{e} (referred to in articles B3234.3 and B3234.5 of the RCC_M [bib4]) is defined as the ratio between the real strain amplitude and the strain amplitude determined by the elastic analysis. The value of the coefficient {K}_{e} is given in document R7.04.01. 3 Number of stress cycles 3.1 Reminders: spectral moments and irregularity factor The spectral moment of order i is the following quantity R7.10.01: {\lambda}_{i}=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{\mid \omega \mid }^{i}{G}_{\text{SS}}(\omega )d\omega where \omega is the angular frequency and {G}_{\text{SS}} the power spectral density, or PSD. In particular one has: {\lambda}_{0}={s}_{S}^{2}{\lambda}_{2}={s}_{{S}^{'}}^{2}{\lambda}_{4}={s}_{{S}^{''}}^{2} , which are the standard deviations of S and of its first derivatives. The irregularity factor describes the frequency content of the signal. Lying between 0 and 1, it tends towards 1 when the process is narrow-band, whereas it tends towards 0 for a broad-band process. Its expression is: I=\frac{{s}_{{S}^{'}}^{2}}{{s}_{{S}^{}}{s}_{{S}^{\text{''}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{{\lambda}_{2}^{2}}{{\lambda}_{0}{\lambda}_{4}}} These definitions are recalled because the evolution of the signal is treated as a random process characterised by its statistical parameters (spectral moments of order 0, 2 and 4). For the stress-peak counting method, the random signal is fully characterised by the three spectral moments of orders 0, 2 and 4. In the case of the level-exceedance counting method, the spectral moments of orders 0 and 2 are sufficient to characterise the random signal. In practice, these values are determined by the command POST_DYNA_ALEA U4.76.02, which performs statistical processing on a random loading. The definition of the various parameters is given in document R7.10.01. The operator for the computation of fatigue in the random domain, POST_FATI_ALEA U4.67.05, uses the values of the three spectral moments computed by POST_DYNA_ALEA and computes the mean damage and the standard deviation of the damage by the methods described in this document. 3.2 Stress-peak counting method The principle of this method consists in counting the local maxima (in absolute value) located on either side of the mean value of the stresses. The signal being stationary and Gaussian, centred with respect to its mean value, the distribution of the peaks is symmetric with respect to this mean. One is therefore interested in the distribution of the positive peaks . In the general case, the distribution of the peaks of positive amplitude S is written in the form: {P}_{\text{pic}}^{+}\left(S\right)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi }{s}_{S}\left(1+I\right)}\left[\sqrt{1-{I}^{2}}{e}^{\text{}\frac{{S}^{2}}{{\mathrm{2s}}_{S}^{2}\left(1-{I}^{2}\right)}}+\frac{\text{IS}}{{s}_{S}}{e}^{\text{}\frac{{S}^{2}}{{\mathrm{2s}}_{S}^{2}}}\underset{-\infty }{\overset{\alpha}{\int}}{e}^{\text{}\frac{-{t}^{2}}{2}}\text{dt}\right] \text{avec}\lbrace \begin{array}{c}I=\frac{{\sigma}_{{S}^{'}}^{2}}{{\sigma}_{S}{\sigma}_{{S}^{''}}}\\ \alpha =\frac{S}{{\sigma}_{S}}\frac{I}{\sqrt{1-{I}^{2}}}\end{array} This distribution of the positive peaks simplifies in the case of signals for which the irregularity factor equals I=0 or I=1 : - Broad-band signal: Gaussian law or normal law (I=0) {P}_{\text{pic}}^{+}\left(S\right)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi {\sigma}_{{S}^{2}}}}{e}^{-\frac{{S}^{2}}{2{\sigma}_{{S}^{2}}}} - Narrow-band signal: Rayleigh law (I=1) {P}_{\text{pic}}^{+}(S)=\frac{S}{{\sigma}_{{S}^{2}}}{e}^{-\frac{{S}^{2}}{2{\sigma}_{{S}^{2}}}} The stress-peak counting method associates with each peak of positive amplitude S a cycle of amplitude \Delta S=2S (one therefore has directly S=\text{Salt} ). The number of peaks of positive amplitude is written: {n}_{\text{pic}}^{+}(S)={P}_{\text{pic}}^{+}(S)\times {N}_{\text{pic}}^{+} where {N}_{\text{pic}}^{+}=\frac{1}{4}(1+I)\times \frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\sigma {S}^{''}}{{\sigma}_{{S}^{'}}} = mean number of positive peaks per unit time. Hence the number N of cycles to be taken into account is: N(S)=\frac{1+I}{4\pi }\frac{{\sigma}_{{S}^{''}}}{{\sigma}_{{S}^{'}}}{P}_{\text{pic}}^{+}(S) Note: One indeed observes that the expression for the number N of cycles to be taken into account depends only on {s}_{S} (for the computation of the irregularity factor I ), {\sigma}_{{S}^{'}} and {\sigma}_{{S}^{''}} . 3.3 Level-exceedance counting method This method requires the stress variations to be divided into amplitude classes. The number of cycles N(S) is obtained from the difference between the numbers of level exceedances with a positive slope between two successive classes, starting from the class of maximum amplitude. For a centred Gaussian process the expression for N(S) is: N(S)=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{{\sigma}_{{S}^{'}}}{{\sigma}_{S}^{}}{e}^{-\frac{{S}^{2}}{2{\sigma}_{S}^{2}}} Notes: The expression for the number N of cycles to be taken into account requires only knowledge of {\sigma}_{S} and {\sigma}_{{S}^{'}} (independence with respect to {\sigma}_{{S}^{''}} ). The irregularity coefficient I does not appear in this method. 4 Statistical estimation of the damage The mechanical damage is computed using Miner's linear cumulative rule. The damage D produced by N cycles of half-amplitude S is expressed by D=\frac{N}{\text{Nr}(S)} where \text{Nr}(S) is the allowable number of cycles determined by the endurance curve of the material. The mechanical damage is a random variable whose mean is determined. 4.1 Mean damage The mean damage is written in the form of the mathematical expectation: E(D)=T\underset{{S}_{\min}}{\overset{{S}_{\max}}{\int}}\frac{N(S)}{{N}_{r}(S)}\text{dS} where T is the duration of the signal The two counting methods proposed compute the number of cycles N(S) from stresses of positive amplitude, whence {S}_{\min}=0 (except when the Wöhler curve is given in the “current zone” form, in which case {S}_{\min}={S}_{l} with {S}_{l} the endurance limit of the material). Furthermore, the distribution laws used being continuous, {S}_{\max}=\infty . However, experience shows that the expression to be integrated decays rapidly, and one therefore takes {S}_{\max}=10{\sigma}_{S} , where {\sigma}_{S} is the standard deviation of the signal. The computation of E(D) is carried out by numerical integration, by the trapezoidal method, taking as the integration step \frac{{S}_{\max}-{S}_{\min}}{300.} . Note: In the case of the level-exceedance counting method and for a Wöhler curve expressed in the mathematical form proposed by Basquin, the mean damage per unit time has an analytical expression (this expression is not used in the command POST_FATI_ALEA). 5 Conclusion In the case of a Gaussian, ergodic and stationary loading, two cycle-counting methods admit a statistical interpretation and provide an analytical expression for the mean damage, involving only the formulation of the endurance curve of the material and the standard deviations of the signal and of its first and second derivatives. In Code_Aster , the computation of the damage under random loading is performed by the command POST_FATI_ALEA U4.67.05. The user may determine the damage by the stress-peak counting method (COMPTAGE = ‘PIC’) or by the method of counting exceedances of a given level (COMPTAGE = ‘NIVEAU’). Depending on the method adopted, the random signal must be introduced by giving the spectral moments of orders 0 and 2, or by giving the spectral moments of orders 0, 2 and 4 (keywords MOMENT_SPEC_0, MOMENT_SPEC_2 and MOMENT_SPEC_4). The values of the spectral moments may also be retrieved from a table created by POST_DYNA_ALEA U4.76.02 (keyword TABLE). The Wöhler curve of the material may be introduced in three distinct forms (in accordance with the command POST_FATIGUE U4.67.01 (computation of high-cycle damage) and the POSTDAM software). The quantity (grandeur) determined is the mean damage over the duration of the signal, which is stored in a table of type POST_FATI_ALEA. 6 Bibliography 1.
