r7.04.05 Computation and verification of reinforcement r7.04.05 Computation and verification of reinforcement Summary: The algorithm for computing the reinforcement densities of reinforced-concrete elements is presented, as implemented in the command CALC_FERRAILLAGE. To this end, the computation algorithm for the line elements 1D will first be presented, and then that for the surface elements 2D of plate type will be examined. The determination of the reinforcement of a section is carried out, according to the option chosen, to Eurocode 2 part 1-1 [bib2] ( CODIFICATION = 'EC2' ) or to BAEL91-99 ( CODIFICATION = 'BAEL' ). This document also presents, in the section Verification of the reinforcement, the reinforcement-verification method used in the operator VERI_FERRAILLAGE. 1 Computation of the reinforcement of beams and columns 1.1 Notation and equilibrium principles The internal forces of the 1D structural elements (beams/columns) are expressed in the local frame of the element, which will be defined here consistently with the documentation of CALC_FERRAILLAGE. Thus, the axis X coincides with the load-bearing axis of the element, while the axes Y and Z lie in the plane of the cross-section and parallel to its sides, in accordance with the figure below. Definition of the axes of a line element of beam/column type Using a beam of rectangular cross-section, one defines in the command file the two sides of the rectangle {l}_{y} and {l}_{z} , which then makes it possible to define the two principal axes of inertia of the section, namely the axes y and z . The forces expressed in the local frame of the element are therefore: - N for the axial force - {V}_{y} and {V}_{z} for the shear forces - {M}_{y} and {M}_{z} for the bending moments - {M}_{x} for the torsional moment It should be noted that the moments are expressed with respect to the centre of gravity of the unreinforced section (centre of the geometric section). Furthermore, one will say that the section is subjected to: - simple bending if only one bending moment ( {M}_{y} or {M}_{z} ) loads the section. - combined bending if a bending moment ( {M}_{y} or {M}_{z} ) and an axial force N act on the section. - biaxial combined bending if the section is subjected simultaneously to the two bending moments ({M}_{y},{M}_{z}) as well as to an axial force N . - pure compression or pure tension if only N acts on the section. The typical reinforcement field of a beam/column is defined as follows, at the cross-section of the element: - Four layers of longitudinal reinforcement: {A}_{s_y, \text{sup}} , {A}_{s_y, \text{inf}} , {A}_{s_z, \text{sup}} and {A}_{s_z, \text{inf}} usually expressed in {\text{cm}}^{2} These sections are carried by the two principal axes of inertia Y and Z of the section - a density/ratio of transverse reinforcement: \frac{{A}_{\text{sv}}}{s} usually expressed in {\text{cm}}^{2}/m To this end, the reinforcement computation is carried out in two stages: - computation of the longitudinal reinforcement: equilibrium in combined and/or biaxial bending, with respect to the axial compressive forces N , and to the two bending moments along the two axes of inertia of the beam, namely {M}_{y} and {M}_{z} . - computation of the transverse reinforcement: equilibrium under the shear forces {V}_{y} and {V}_{z} , and under the torsional moment {M}_{x} . It should then be noted, in accordance with the explanations which follow, that these forces may in certain cases induce additional tensile forces along the load-bearing axis X of the element, thus leading to additional longitudinal reinforcement. These equilibrium computations therefore rest on criteria linked to the design limit state retained, namely: - ULS: the criterion is that the ultimate strains of the compressed concrete and of the reinforcing steel are not exceeded. - Characteristic SLS: the criterion is that the limiting compressive stress of the concrete in compression and the limiting stress of the bending steel are not exceeded. - Quasi-permanent SLS: the criterion is that the maximum crack opening is not exceeded. 1.2 Design at the ULS 1.2.1 Computation of the longitudinal reinforcement in simple or combined bending 1.2.1.1 Definition of the computation hypotheses At the ULS, the principles of verification of the section and of computation of the reinforcement in combined bending with respect to the internal forces N , {M}_{y} and {M}_{z} , rest on the following three hypotheses: - The plane cross-sections remain plane after deformation (Euler-Bernoulli). Consequently, this implies that the strain diagram governing the section at equilibrium in combined bending is linear along - A limit threshold is imposed on the strains: - steel strain limited to {\strainCmp}_{\text{ud}} (pivot A) - compressive strain of the concrete limited to {\strainCmp}_{\text{cu2}} (pivot B), in the case of a partially tensioned/compressed section - compressive strain of the concrete limited to {\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}} (pivot C), in the case of a fully compressed section - The stress-strain diagrams of the steel and of the concrete are those given below: For the compressed concrete: Constitutive law of concrete in compression at the ULS The parameters below are therefore defined: - {f}_{\text{ck}} : characteristic value of the compressive strength of the concrete, which in practice is defined according to the concrete class in Eurocode 2. - {f}_{\text{cd}} : value of the compressive strength of the concrete retained for the ULS computation, namely {f}_{\text{cd}}=\frac{{\alpha}_{\text{cc}}{f}_{\text{ck}}}{{\gamma}_{c}} , with {\alpha}_{\text{cc}}=1 for EC2 and {\gamma}_{c} (safety factor) which depends on the type of ULS considered (1.5 in a persistent situation and 1.2 in an accidental situation). - {\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}} : strain reached for the maximum stress. It is equal to: - {\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}}=2\text{‰} if {f}_{\text{ck}}\le 50 \, \text{MPa} - {\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}}(\text{‰} )=2+0,085{({f}_{\text{ck}}-50)}^{0.53} if {f}_{\text{ck}} \gt 50 \, \text{MPa} - {\strainCmp}_{\text{cu2}} : ultimate strain of the concrete at failure. It is equal to: - {\strainCmp}_{\text{cu2}}=3.5\text{‰} if {f}_{\text{ck}}\le 50 \, \text{MPa} - {\strainCmp}_{\text{cu2}}(\text{‰} )=2.6+35 \, \left(90 - \frac{{f}_{\text{ck}}}{100}\right)^{4} if {f}_{\text{ck}} \gt 50 \, \text{MPa} - n : parameter for the definition of the parabolic branch of the constitutive law, which is equal to: - n=2 if {f}_{\text{ck}}\le 50 \, \text{MPa} - n=1.4 + 23.4 \, \left( 90- \frac{{f}_{\text{ck}}}{100} \right)^{4} if {f}_{\text{ck}} \gt 50 \, \text{MPa} Thus, for values of the concrete strains {\strainCmp}_{c}\le {\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}} , the stress in the concrete is then computed by the following formula: {\stressCmp}_{c} = {f}_{\text{cd}} \left( 1 - \left( 1- \frac{{\strainCmp}_{c}}{{\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}}} \right)^{n} \right) It is also possible to carry out the computation under the hypothesis of a “simplified rectangular diagram”: the concrete stress is then considered constant and equal to \eta{f}_{\text{cd}} over a depth equal to \lambda x (fraction “ \lambda ” of the compressed zone). This simplification is suggested and accepted by Eurocode 2 ( as long as the neutral axis remains inside the section ), since the error thus produced on the resultant {F}_{c} of the compressive forces in the concrete remains small. Simplified rectangular stress-strain diagram for the concrete. The values \lambda=0.8 and \eta=1 are to be retained for ordinary concretes ( {f}_{\text{ck}} \le 50\, \text{MPa} ). For values 50 \, \text{MPa} \lt {f}_{\text{ck}} \le 90\, \text{MPa} one has \lambda =0.8- \frac{{f}_{\text{ck}}-50}{400} and \eta =1- \frac{{f}_{\text{ck}}-50}{200} . For the reinforcing steel: The behaviour of the steel recommended by Eurocode 2 in terms of stress-strain is of bilinear type. It is also possible to adopt a perfectly plastic behaviour (diagram with a horizontal plateau in the following figure); the current version of the operator CALC_FERRAILLAGE makes it possible to choose between these two types of diagram by means of the keyword TYPE_DIAGRAMME . Stress-strain diagram for the bending steel. In the diagram presented above, the following parameters are identified: - The limiting stress of the elastic behaviour {f}_{\text{yk}} which depends on the type of steel used - The limiting stress of the elastic behaviour retained for the computation, namely {f}_{\text{yd}}=\frac{{f}_{\text{yk}}}{{\gamma}_{s}} , where {\gamma}_{s} is a safety factor. - The ultimate strain at failure {\strainCmp}_{\text{uk}} , which depends on the steel class used: - Class A: {\strainCmp}_{\text{uk}}=2,5 \, {\%} - Class B: {\strainCmp}_{\text{uk}}=5,0 \, {\%} - Class C: {\strainCmp}_{\text{uk}}=7,5 \, {\%} - The ultimate strain at failure retained for the computation, namely {\strainCmp}_{\text{ud}}=0,9 \, {\strainCmp}_{\text{uk}} . - The parameter k in the figure above (necessary only in the case of use of the inclined plateau) is defined by k= \left( \frac{{f}_{t}}{{f}_{y}}\right)_{k} , with {f}_{t} the ultimate stress at failure. The value of this parameter also varies as a function of the steel class (A, B or C) as indicated in the previous figure. - Young's modulus {E}_{s} of the steel (mean value and not characteristic). One then defines, among other things, the limit of the elastic behaviour in strain, namely {{\strainCmp}_{\text{yd}}= \frac{f{\text{yd}}}{/{E}_{s}}} . Apart from Young's modulus, it is indeed the design values (index d ) which are used in the design or verification computations. 1.2.1.2 Equilibrium principle and computation of the steel areas The hypotheses introduced in the previous paragraph are used to draw the diagram of the Figure which follows and are at the origin of the “three-pivot rule” used to design or verify a reinforced-concrete section. Design principle in combined bending at the ULS In the Figure above, one distinguishes: - A typical concrete section with a lower reinforcement {A}_{s, \text{inf}} and an upper reinforcement {A}_{s, \text{sup}} , of depth equal to h and an effective depth d , which represents the lever arm of the centre of gravity of the lower reinforcement relative to the upper fibre of the section ( in the case of a negative bending moment, it is then the lever arm of the centre of gravity of the upper reinforcement relative to the lower fibre of the section) . In practice, one can estimate that d=h-{c}_{\text{inf}} , such that {c}_{\text{inf}} represents the cover (to within half a reinforcement diameter) of the lower reinforcement, that is the distance from the centre of gravity of the lower reinforcement to the lower fibre of the section ( in the case of a negative bending moment, one then considers d = h-{c}_{\text{sup}} ) . - The plotting of the limit strain diagrams, in the form of straight lines in view of the Euler-Bernoulli hypothesis, passing through the three pivots A, B and C. Design at the ULS consists in placing oneself under failure conditions corresponding to the attainment of a limit strain relating either to the steel or to the concrete, so that the strain diagram passes through one of the three points A, B, C shown in the previous figure: - Pivot A corresponds to the failure of the lower steel ( in the case of a negative bending moment, it is then the upper steel) , that is when the tensioned steel reaches the limit strain {\strainCmp}_{\text{ud}} - Pivot B corresponds to the failure of the concrete at the upper fibre ( in the case of a negative bending moment, it is then the concrete at the lower fibre) , that is when the most compressed concrete reaches the limit strain {\strainCmp}_{\text{cu2}} - Pivot C corresponds to the attainment of the maximum strength {f}_{\text{cd}} of the concrete (in accordance with the constitutive law), that is for a strain equal to {\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}} . This pivot is used for the study of the fully compressed cases; its position relative to the depth of the section is obtained from the intersection of the diagram relating to the limit of the partially compressed case (neutral axis positioned at the lower fibre ( in the case of a negative bending moment, it is then the upper fibre ) of the cross-section (BC)) and of the case of pure compression ( {\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}} over the whole depth of the section). For this last case (pure compression), Eurocode 2 thus prefers to limit the concrete strains to {\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}} rather than {\strainCmp}_{\text{cu2}} . The points A, B, C are called “pivots” since one can sweep all the possible failure configurations of the section by pivoting about one of them. Indeed, from the definition of the three pivots and from the position of the neutral axis of the strain diagram, it is possible to define failure “domains”, as represented in the following figure: Domains of behaviour/equilibrium in combined bending at the ULS. Domain 1 : the strain diagram passes through pivot A, but the neutral axis lies outside the section and above the upper fibre, so that the whole section is in tension. Domain 2 : the strain diagram still passes through pivot A, but the neutral axis now lies inside the section. The section is thus partially compressed, so that failure occurs at the tensioned steel. Domain 3 : the strain diagram now passes through pivot B, and the neutral axis lies inside the section. The section is therefore still partially compressed, with failure at the upper fibre of the concrete. Domain 4 : this is a continuation of the hypotheses of the previous domain, but the strain of the lower steel becomes smaller than the limit of the elastic-plastic behaviour, namely {\strainCmp}_{\text{yd}}=\frac{{f}_{\text{yd}}}{{E}_{s}} . The tensioned steel falls into the elastic domain and therefore no longer works in an optimal manner in terms of strength. Domain 5 : the neutral axis is again outside the section, but below the lower fibre. The section is now fully compressed, so that the strain diagram passes through pivot C. Depending on the applied force resultant, the algorithm will then determine the optimal domain of behaviour for equilibrium; the upper and lower reinforcement areas are then computed from the equilibrium equations of the forces and of the moments, as will be set out in what follows. Consistently with the notation above, when M \gt 0 , the moment and the reduced moment are computed at the centre of gravity of the lower reinforcement, such that (the axial force N being positive in compression): {M}_{\text{inf}} = M + N \, \left( \frac{h}{2}-{c}_{\text{inf}} \right) and {\mu}_{\text{inf}} = \frac{{M}_{\text{inf}}}{b d^{2} \eta {f}_{\text{cd}}} In the same way when M \lt 0 , the moment and the reduced moment are computed at the centre of gravity of the upper reinforcement, such that: {M}_{\text{sup}} = - M + N \, \left( \frac{h}{2} - {c}_{\text{sup}} \right) and {\mu}_{\text{sup}} = \frac{{M}_{\text{sup}}}{b d^{2} \eta {f}_{\text{cd}}} In what follows, the case of positive bending is considered (the results of the case M \lt 0 are then obtained by symmetry). Principle of the three-pivot rule for a rectangular section (hxb) Considering a partially compressed section (that is, the neutral axis x=\alpha \times d of the strain diagram lies inside the section; concretely, this corresponds to domain 0 \le \alpha \le 1 ), in the absence of compression steel (that is {A}_{s, \text{sup}}=0 ) and with the notation of the figure, the resisting moment of the section expressed at the centre of gravity of the tensioned steel is provided exclusively by the compressed concrete, and is expressed as follows: {M}_{c} = \left( \alpha \lambda d b\times \eta {f}_{\text{cd}} \right) \times \left( d-\alpha \lambda \frac{d}{2} \right) = \left( bd^{2}\eta {f}_{\text{cd}} \right) \times \lambda \alpha \left( 1-0,5\lambda \alpha \right) Or again, as a reduced moment: {\mu}_{c} = \frac{{M}_{c}}{bd^{2}\eta {f}_{\text{cd}}} = \lambda \alpha ( 1-0,5\lambda \alpha ) Equilibrium of the moments then leads to: {\mu}_{c} = \lambda \alpha ( 1-0,5\lambda \alpha ) = {\mu}_{\text{inf}} The solution of this quadratic equation then makes it possible to determine the value of the neutral-axis depth coefficient \alpha . Depending on the value of this coefficient, one finds oneself in one of the five equilibrium domains stated previously in the documentation, namely: - Domain 1: \alpha \le 0 and \mu \le 0 - Domain 2: 0 \le \alpha \le {\alpha}_{\text{AB}} and 0 \le \mu \le {\mu}_{\text{AB}} , such that {\alpha}_{\text{AB}}=\frac{1}{1+ \frac{{\strainCmp}_{\text{ud}}}{{\strainCmp}_{\text{cu3}}}} and {\mu}_{\text{AB}}=\lambda {\alpha}_{\text{AB}}(1-0,5\lambda {\alpha}_{\text{AB}}) - Domain 3: {\alpha}_{\text{AB}} \le \alpha \le {\alpha}_{R} and {\mu}_{\text{AB}} \le \mu \le {\mu}_{R} , such that {\alpha}_{R}=\frac{1}{1+ \frac{{\strainCmp}_{\text{yd}}}{{\strainCmp}_{\text{cu3}}}} and {\mu}_{R}=\lambda {\alpha}_{R}(1-0,5\lambda {\alpha}_{R}) - Domain 4: {\alpha}_{R} \le \alpha \le {\alpha}_{\text{BC}} and {\mu}_{R} \le \mu \le {\mu}_{\text{BC}} , such that {\alpha}_{\text{BC}}=1 and {\mu}_{\text{BC}}=\lambda {\alpha}_{\text{BC}}(1-0,5\lambda {\alpha}_{\text{BC}}) - Domain 5: \alpha \ge {\alpha}_{\text{BC}} and \mu \ge {\mu}_{\text{BC}} Concretely, the previous quadratic equation admits an acceptable solution if one is in one of Domains 2, 3 or 4 (otherwise, that is if the equation is not solvable, the algorithm activates the keyword COND_ITER = VRAI). Knowing then the pivot (A or B) associated with the domain, one determines the strain diagram associated with equilibrium, and therefore the strain experienced at the centre of the tensioned steel {\strainCmp}_{s, \text{inf}} . As a function of the constitutive law associated with the steel, one determines the associated stress {\stressCmp}_{s, \text{inf}} (negative in tension). Writing the equilibrium of the axial forces then makes it possible to write: {F}_{c} + {A}_{s, \text{inf}} {\stressCmp}_{s, \text{inf}} = N such that {F}_{c}=\alpha \lambda b d \eta {f}_{\text{cd}} One then determines the steel area: {A}_{s, \text{inf}} = \frac{N-{F}_{c}}{{\stressCmp}_{s, \text{inf}}} If the equation leads to a negative value, then the algorithm activates the keyword COND_ITER = VRAI. For the cases where COND_ITER = VRAI, one must then sweep the five equilibrium domains, that is by iterating \alpha from -\infty to +\infty (and thus traversing the three Pivots A, B and C). On the basis of the two equilibrium equations (moments and forces), one determines for each value of alpha the pair (A_{s_s},A_{s_i}) associated. The algorithm will finally retain the configuration leading to a minimisation of the sum A_{s_s}+A_{s_i} , while ensuring that the two areas are positive. The case of biaxial bending or biaxial combined bending is more complex to solve. Indeed, the interaction diagram (limit strength surface) is in this case three-dimensional, in accordance with the figure below: 3D interaction diagram along the axes N , M_y , M_z in the case of a biaxial combined section An exact and rigorous design process (similar to the previous computations) would, given the three-dimensional nature of the internal forces, be complex to develop. One therefore opts for a simplified verification procedure. It will indeed be an iterative design method (and therefore not direct), based on the principle of verification of the Bresler inequality developed by Bresler, as presented in §5.8.9 of Eurocode 2. This method will thus make it possible to study separately, and in a perfectly decoupled manner, the two combined bendings loading the section, the first (N,M_y) along the principal axis of inertia Y and the second (N,M_z) along the second principal axis of inertia, Z . Once the reinforcements obtained at the end of the design computations with respect to these two combined bendings (namely the quadruplet \left(A_{s_y,\text{sup}}, A_{s_y,\text{inf}}, A_{s_z,\text{sup}}, A_{s_z,\text{inf}}\right) ) are known, the design method in biaxial bending then consists in verifying the following inequality {(\frac{{M}_{y}}{{M}_{R_y}})}^{a} + {(\frac{{M}_{z}}{{M}_{R_z}})}^{a} \le 1 Where the moments {M}_{R_y} and {M}_{R_z} are the resisting moments in combined bending, under the acting axial force N , of the section reinforced respectively along the axis Y (that is with the pair \left(A_{s_y,\text{sup}}, A_{s_y,\text{inf}}\right) ) and along the axis Z (that is with the pair \left(A_{s_z,\text{sup}}, A_{s_z,\text{inf}}\right) ). These resisting moments are deduced from the 2D interaction diagrams along Y and Z respectively. The exponent a is computed as a function of the ratio between the axial force N loading the section, and the maximum resisting axial force, namely {N}_{R}={A}_{c} {f}_{\text{cd}}+{A}_{s} {f}_{\text{yd}} . In practice, a will be computed by interpolation between the values given in the table of the figure below (as extracted from §5.8.9 of Eurocode 2); in particular, for \frac{N}{{N}_{R}} \lt 0.1 , one will take a=1 . Computation of the coefficient a for the Bresler method of EC2. | \frac{N}{{N}_{R}} | 0.1 | 0.7 | 1 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | a | 1 | 1.5 | 2 | Thus, as long as the Bresler inequality is not verified (that is if the sum of the left-hand side is greater than 1), the algorithm currently proposed will resume the computation of the resisting moments by increasing proportionally the four reinforcement areas as follows: {A}_{s_y, \text{sup}}[i+1] = {A}_{s_y, \text{sup}}[i] + {\rho}_{s_y, \text{sup}}[i] {A}_{s, \text{iter}}[i] {A}_{s_y, \text{inf}}[i+1] = {A}_{s_y, \text{inf}}[i] + {\rho}_{s_y, \text{inf}}[i] {A}_{s, \text{iter}}[i] {A}_{s_z, \text{sup}}[i+1] = {A}_{s_z, \text{sup}}[i] + {\rho}_{s_z, \text{sup}}[i] {A}_{s, \text{iter}}[i] {A}_{s_z, \text{inf}}[i+1] = {A}_{s_z, \text{inf}}[i] + {\rho}_{s_z, \text{inf}}[i] {A}_{s, \text{iter}}[i] such that: {\rho}_{s_y, \text{sup}}[i] = \frac{{A}_{s_y, \text{sup}}[i]}{{A}_{s, \text{TOT}}[i]} {\rho}_{s_y, \text{inf}}[i] = \frac{{A}_{s_y, \text{inf}}[i]}{{A}_{s, \text{TOT}}[i]} {\rho}_{s_z, \text{sup}}[i] = \frac{{A}_{s_z, \text{sup}}[i]}{{A}_{s, \text{TOT}}[i]} {\rho}_{s_z, \text{inf}}[i] = \frac{{A}_{s_z, \text{inf}}[i]}{{A}_{s, \text{TOT}}[i]} With {A}_{s, \text{TOT}}[i]={A}_{s_y, \text{sup}}[i]+{A}_{s_y, \text{inf}}[i]+{A}_{s_z, \text{sup}}[i]+{A}_{s_z, \text{inf}}[i] and {A}_{s, \text{iter}}[i] denotes an iteration area (currently taken by default equal to 10% of {A}_{s, \text{TOT}}[i] ). 1.2.3 Computation of the transverse reinforcement One begins by defining the transverse reinforcement ratio in accordance with the following expression: {\rho}_{w} = \frac{{A}_{\text{sw}}}{s{b}_{w}\sin(\alpha)} Where: - The quantities below are defined for what follows: - \lbrace \strainCmp_{c}, \stressCmp_{c} \rbrace respectively the strain and the stress experienced at the most compressed concrete fibre. In accordance with what precedes (linear stress diagram), one has {\stressCmp}_{c}={E}_{c}{\strainCmp}_{c} such that {\strainCmp}_{c} \gt 0 in compression. - \lbrace \strainCmp_{s}, \stressCmp_{s} \rbrace respectively the strain and the stress experienced at the tensioned steel, such that {\stressCmp}_{s}={E}_{s}{\strainCmp}_{s} and {\strainCmp}_{s} \lt 0 in tension. In accordance with the notation of the following figure, the resultant of the compressive stresses in the concrete is, for the partially compressed case: {F}_{c} = \frac{1}{2}{\stressCmp}_{c} b x = \frac{1}{2}{E}_{c}{\strainCmp}_{c} b x In accordance with the linearity of the stress diagram, and still in the case of a partially compressed section, this force is applied at a distance \frac{x}{3} from the most compressed fibre of the concrete, that is at a distance \left(d-\frac{x}{3}\right) from the principal longitudinal steel (or \left(d'-\frac{x}{3}\right) if the acting moment is negative). In a manner similar to the design at the ULS, one seeks to express the acting moment at the centre of gravity of the tensioned reinforcement, such that: {M}_{\text{inf}} = M + N \, \left(\frac{h}{2}-c\right) \text{ si } M \gt 0 and {M}_{\text{sup}} = -M + N \, \left(\frac{h}{2}-{c}^{\prime} \right) \text{ si } M \lt 0 One will henceforth continue with the case M \gt 0 (the other case is obtained by symmetry). From the linearity of the stress diagram, and setting x=\xi \, d , the relation between the stress in the tensioned steel and that at the compressed concrete is written: {\stressCmp}_{s} = \left( \frac{1-\xi}{\xi} \right) {\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c} where {\alpha}_{e}=\frac{{E}_{s}}{{E}_{c}} denotes the ratio between Young's modulus of the steel and that of the concrete (making it possible to obtain a homogenised section). The equilibrium of the moments is then written: {M}_{\text{inf}} = {F}_{c}\, {z}_{c} = \left( \frac{1}{2} b x {\stressCmp}_{c} \right) \left( d-\frac{x}{3} \right) One can define the reduced moment as follows: {\mu}_{\text{inf}} = \frac{{M}_{\text{inf}}}{b{d}^{2}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}} Where {\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} is the limiting stress that the compressed concrete can take at the characteristic SLS. The previous equilibrium is then rewritten as follows: {\mu}_{\text{inf}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \xi \left(1-\frac{\xi}{3}\right) \right) \frac{{\stressCmp}_{c}}{{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}} On the other hand, the equilibrium of the forces is written (considering only a lower steel): N = {F}_{c} + {F}_{s} = \frac{1}{2} b x {\stressCmp}_{c} + {A}_{s, \text{inf}} \, {\stressCmp}_{s, \text{inf}} In a manner similar to the pivot rule of the strain diagram at the ULS, the serviceability limit state of the section can be reached along similar pivots but on the stress diagram , either on the steel side for {\stressCmp}_{s}={\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}} , or on the compressed-concrete side for {\stressCmp}_{c}={\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} . By progressively increasing the value of \xi (neutral-axis depth coefficient such that \xi =\frac{x}{d}) the stress diagram begins by “pivoting” about the pivot relating to the limit of the tensioned steel ( {\stressCmp}_{s}={\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}} ), and then “pivots” about the pivot relating to the limit of the compressed concrete ( {\stressCmp}_{c}={\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} ). In this sense, the limit separating the two “pivoting” zones is obtained by saturating simultaneously the two stress-limitation criteria, namely by having both {\stressCmp}_{c}={\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} and {\stressCmp}_{s}={\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}} ; one then obtains: {\xi}_{1,2} = \frac{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}} {{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} + {\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}}} Referring then to the reduced-moment equation given above, one computes the limit reduced moment {\mu}_{\text{inf}}^{\prime} (or {\mu}_{\text{sup}}^{\prime} if M \lt 0 ), obtained for \xi =\xi_{1,2} , making it possible to recognise the pivot to be retained for a given pair (M,N) . Thus, in the case where M \gt 0 : - If {\mu}_{\text{inf}} \lt \mu^{\prime}_{\text{inf}} , it is the pivot relating to the tensioned steel which is retained, namely {\stressCmp}_{s}={\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}} . In this case, the relations given then make it possible to express the stress at the most compressed concrete fibre {\stressCmp}_{c} , as a function of {\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}} , {\alpha}_{e} and \xi . The equilibrium of the moments is then rewritten as follows: \frac{1}{2} \frac{{\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}}}{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}} \frac{{\xi}^{2}}{1-\xi} \left( 1-\frac{\xi}{3} \right) = {\mu}_{\text{inf}} The solution of this third-degree polynomial equation makes it possible to determine the neutral-axis depth coefficient \xi ; from there, the axial-force equilibrium equation then makes it possible to compute the principal steel area {A}_{s} . - If {\mu}_{\text{inf}} \gt \mu^{\prime}_{\text{inf}} , it is the pivot relating to the compressed concrete which is retained, namely {\stressCmp}_{c}={\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} . The equilibrium of the moments given previously is then rewritten as follows: {\mu}_{\text{inf}} = \frac{1}{2} \xi \left( 1-\frac{\xi}{3} \right) The solution of this second-degree polynomial equation makes it possible to determine the neutral-axis depth coefficient \xi ; from there, one determines the stress at the tensioned steel {\stressCmp}_{s} , as a function of {\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} , {\alpha}_{e} and \xi . The axial-force equilibrium equation then makes it possible to compute the principal steel area {A}_{s} . If the previous equilibrium leads to a negative value of {A}_{s} , or if one finds oneself in a fully tensioned or fully compressed case, then the algorithm activates the keyword COND_ITER = VRAI. For the cases where COND_ITER = VRAI, one must then sweep the various equilibrium domains, that is by iterating \xi from -\infty to +\infty . On the basis of the two equilibrium equations (moments and forces), one determines for each value of \xi the associated pair (A_{s_s},A_{s_i}) . The algorithm will finally retain the configuration leading to a minimisation of the sum A_{s_s}+A_{s_i} , while ensuring that the two areas are positive. Thus, still having \xi=\frac{x}{d} , \delta =\frac{d}{h} and \delta^{\prime}=\frac{d^{\prime}}{h} , one distinguishes the cases below: - for \xi \le 0 , the section is fully tensioned so that the stress diagram passes through the pivot relating to the principal tension steel ( {\stressCmp}_{s}=-{\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}} ), with: - {\stressCmp}_{c}=0 (the concrete has no strength and in particular {F}_{c}=0 ) - {\stressCmp}_{\text{sc}}=\frac{1-\delta^{\prime} - \xi \delta }{\delta -\xi \delta }{\stressCmp}_{s} ( {\stressCmp}_{\text{sc}} becomes negative, this being a state of tension, in accordance with what precedes). - for 0 \lt \xi \lt \frac{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}}{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}+{\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}}} , the section is partially compressed so that the stress diagram still passes through the pivot relating to the principal tension steel ( {\stressCmp}_{s}=-{\stressCmp}_{{s, \text{lim}}} ), with: - {\stressCmp}_{c}=\frac{\xi}{1-\xi}\frac{{\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}}}{{\alpha}_{e}} - {\stressCmp}_{\text{sc}}=\frac{1-\delta^{prime}-\xi \delta }{\delta -\xi \delta}{\stressCmp}_{s} - for \xi \gt \frac{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}}{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}+{\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}}} , the section is partially compressed so that the stress diagram now passes through the pivot relating to the most compressed concrete fibre ( {\stressCmp}_{c}={\stressCmp}_{{c, \text{lim}}} ), with: - {\stressCmp}_{s}=\frac{\xi -1}{\xi}{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} - {\stressCmp}_{\text{sc}}=\frac{\xi \delta-1+\delta^{prime}}{\xi \delta}{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} - for \xi=\frac{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}}{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}+{\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}}} , the criterion is reached simultaneously on the steel side and on the concrete side. The solution of the two equilibrium equations (forces and moments) will make it possible to determine the two unknowns of the problem, namely {A}_{s, \text{sup}} and {A}_{s, \text{inf}} . By continuity with the previous case ( \xi \gt \frac{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}}{{\alpha}_{e}{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}}+{\stressCmp}_{s,\text{lim}}} ), the stress diagram still passes through the pivot relating to the most compressed concrete fibre ( {\stressCmp}_{c}={\stressCmp}_{{c, \text{lim}}} ), with, in accordance with the notation of the figure: - \Delta\stressCmp={\stressCmp}_{{c, \text{lim}}}-{\stressCmp}_{{c}_{i}} - {\stressCmp}_{c}\left(y\right)={\stressCmp}_{{c}_{i}}+(\frac{\Delta\stressCmp }{h})y - \delta =\frac{d}{h} and \delta^{prime}=\frac{d^{\prime}}{h} - {\stressCmp}_{\text{sc}}={\alpha}_{e}({\stressCmp}_{{c}_{i}}+\Delta\stressCmp \cdot \delta^{prime}) - {\stressCmp}_{\text{sc}}={\alpha}_{e}({\stressCmp}_{{c}_{i}}+\Delta\stressCmp \cdot (1-\delta )) Setting X=\frac{\Delta\stressCmp}{{\stressCmp}_{{c, \text{lim}}}} , the forces taken by the concrete of the section are written as follows: - Resisting force: {F}_{c}=\frac{1}{2} b h \left(2-X\right){\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} - Resisting moment with respect to the centre of the section: {M}_{c}=\frac{1}{12}b{h}^{2}X{\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim}} The resisting axial force is then written as follows: {N}_{R} = {F}_{c} + {F}_{\text{sc}} + {F}_{s} = {F}_{c} + {A}_{s, \text{sup}}{\stressCmp}_{s, \text{sup}} + {A}_{s, \text{inf}}{\stressCmp}_{s, \text{inf}} And the resisting moment (computed at the centre of the section) is written as follows: {M}_{R} = {M}_{c} + {F}_{\text{sc}} \left( d^{\prime} - \frac{h}{2} \right) - {F}_{\text{sc}} \left( d-\frac{h}{2} \right) The solution of the two equilibrium equations (forces and moments) will make it possible to determine the two unknowns of the problem, namely {A}_{s, \text{sup}} and {A}_{s, \text{inf}} . 1.3.2 Computation of the longitudinal reinforcement in biaxial bending In this part, the section is subjected both to a bending moment along the axis Y and to another along the axis Z , as well as to an axial force (positive in compression). Similarly to the case at the ULS, an iterative design method will be applied, based on the principle of verification of the Bresler inequality developed by Bresler, as presented in §5.8.9 of Eurocode 2. This method will thus make it possible to study separately, and in a perfectly decoupled manner, the two combined bendings loading the section, the first (N, M_y) along the principal axis of inertia Y and the second (N, M_z) along the second principal axis of inertia, Z . Once the reinforcements obtained at the end of the design computations with respect to these two combined bendings (namely the quadruplet \left(A_{s_y,\text{sup}}, A_{s_y,\text{inf}}, A_{s_z,\text{sup}}, A_{s_z,\text{inf}}\right) ) are known, the design method in biaxial bending then consists in verifying the following inequality: \left( \frac{{M}_{y}}{{M}_{R_y}} \right)^{a} + \left( \frac{{M}_{z}}{{M}_{R_z}} \right)^{a} \le 1 where the moments {M}_{R_y} and {M}_{R_z} are the resisting moments in combined bending, under the acting axial force N , of the section reinforced respectively along the axis Y (that is with the pair \left(A_{s_y,\text{sup}}, A_{s_y,\text{inf}}\right) ) and along the axis Z (that is with the pair \left(A_{s_z,\text{sup}}, A_{s_z,\text{inf}}\right) ). These resisting moments are deduced from the 2D interaction diagrams along Y and Z respectively. The exponent a is computed as a function of the ratio between the axial force N loading the section, and the maximum resisting axial force, namely {N}_{R}={A}_{c} {f}_{c}+{A}_{s} {f}_{s} , such that: {f}_{c} = \left( {\stressCmp}_{c, \text{max}}^{\text{y, \text{sup}}} + {\stressCmp}_{c, \text{max}}^{\text{y, \text{inf}}} + {\stressCmp}_{c, \text{max}}^{\text{z, \text{sup}}} + {\stressCmp}_{c, \text{max}}^{\text{z, \text{inf}}} \right) and {f}_{s} = {\stressCmp}_{s,\text{max}} The remainder of the design process is similar to that set out at the ULS. 1.3.3 Computation of the transverse reinforcement One begins by defining the transverse reinforcement ratio in accordance with the following expression: {\rho}_{w} = \frac{{A}_{\text{sw}}}{s{b}_{w}\sin(\alpha)} where: - {A}_{\text{sw}} denotes the area of the total section (per reinforcement plane) of the transverse reinforcement. - s denotes the longitudinal spacing between the transverse reinforcement stirrups. - {b}_{w} denotes the smallest width of the tensioned zone of the cross-section of the element. - \alpha denotes the angle of inclination of the transverse reinforcement stirrups with respect to the longitudinal axis of the element. CALC_FERRAILLAGE offers the possibility of taking this additional tensile force into account; to this end, it is sufficient to take EPURE_CISA = 'OUI' . 1.4 Design at the Quasi-Permanent SLS 1.4.1 Computation of the longitudinal reinforcement in simple or combined bending The design computation of the reinforcement at the QP SLS (Quasi-Permanent Serviceability Limit State) is based on a reuse of the previous algorithm for the reinforcement computation at the (Characteristic) SLS, but by varying the two pivots of the limiting stresses so as to saturate one of the two criteria below: - Limitation of the compressive stress in the concrete to {\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim},\text{FL}} , in order to avoid the non-linear creep of the concrete - Limitation of the crack opening ( {w}_{k, \text{sup}}\le {w}_{\text{max}, \text{sup}} and {w}_{k, \text{inf}}\le {w}_{\text{max}, \text{inf}} ) Concretely, one proceeds by iteration by repeatedly taking up the computation set out in the previous section, considering: - {\stressCmp}_{{c, \text{lim}}} = {\stressCmp}_{c, \text{lim}, \text{FL}} - {\stressCmp}_{{s, \text{lim}}} = {k}_{\text{var}} \times {f}_{\text{yk}} - M={M}_{\text{qp}} and N={N}_{\text{qp}} where {\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim},\text{FL}} is defined by the user (EC2 recommends considering {\stressCmp}_{c,\text{lim},\text{FL}}={k}_{2}\times {f}_{\text{ck}} with a usual value of {k}_{2}=0,45 ). For the pivot at the tensioned steel, the algorithm will seek to iterate on the value of the coefficient {k}_{\text{var}} by starting with an initial value {k}_{\text{var}}={k}_{\text{var}}^{A}=1,0 . The deterministic design algorithm at the Characteristic SLS will then give: - The elastic stress diagram governing the section at equilibrium (including as information the depth of the neutral axis xAN ) - The upper steel area {A}_{s, \text{sup}} and lower steel area {A}_{s, \text{inf}} designing the section From there, the computation of the crack opening is based on the detailed method in §7.3.4 of EC2; in particular, the computation with respect to BAEL will also rest on the same theory (the operator CALC_FERRAILLAGE will return an alarm message): - At the upper fibre: {w}_{k, \text{sup}} = {s}_{\text{rmax}} \times \left( {\strainCmp}_{\text{sm}} - {\strainCmp}_{\text{cm}} \right) such that: {\strainCmp}_{\text{sm}} - {\strainCmp}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{{\stressCmp}_{s}-{k}_{t} \times \frac{{f}_{\text{ctm}}}{{\rho}_{\text{peff}}} \times \left( 1+{\alpha}_{e}\times {\rho}_{\text{peff}} \right) } {{E}_{s}} and {s}_{\text{rmax}} = \min \left \lbrace {k}_{3} \times c^{\prime} + {k}_{1}{k}_{2}{k}_{4} \times \left( \frac{{\varphi}_{\text{sup}}}{{\rho}_{\text{peff}}} \right) ; 1,3\times h \right \rbrace where: - {\stressCmp}_{s} represents the stress experienced at the upper steel - {k}_{t} represents a coefficient taking into account the duration of the applied loading. This method will thus make it possible to study separately, and in a perfectly decoupled manner, the two combined bendings loading the section, the first (N, M_y) along the principal axis of inertia Y and the second (N, M_z) along the second principal axis of inertia, Z . Beyond {l}_{c}=2,0 one considers that the placing of the reinforcement is very complicated and beyond {l}_{c}=3,0 one considers that the placing of the reinforcement is impossible. 2 Computation of the reinforcement of plates The computation of the reinforcement of plates can be carried out according to two distinct methods: the Capra-Maury method (which is a generalisation of the 1D computation to a finite number N of fictitious facets) or the Sandwich method (in accordance with Annex LL of EN-1992-2). 2.1 Capra and Maury method 2.1.1 Computation of the longitudinal reinforcement The principle of the Capra-Maury method consists in assimilating the study of a plate to an equivalent problem of beam reinforcement, by considering, by means of cuts, the successive equilibrium of the various facets obtained — each facet being loaded by a reduced 1D force resultant and consequently reinforced according to beam theory. In this sense, each facet is defined by its normal vector \vector{n}( \theta) making an angle \theta with the local axis x of the plate, and it is subjected to the forces obtained by writing the equilibrium of the corresponding prism and illustrated in the figure below. Corner equilibrium and passage from the 2D forces to the 1D forces One finds: N \left( \theta \right) = {N}_{xx} \cos^{2} \theta + 2 {N}_{xy} \cos \theta \, \sin \theta + {N}_{yy} \sin^{2} \theta M \left( \theta \right) = {M}_{xx} \cos^{2} \theta + 2 {M}_{xy} \cos \theta \, \sin \theta + {M}_{yy} \sin^{2} \theta T \left( \theta \right) = \frac{-1}{2} {N}_{xx} \sin 2\theta + {N}_{xy} \cos 2\theta + \frac{1}{2} {N}_{yy} \sin 2\theta {M}_{t}\left( \theta \right) = \frac{-1}{2} {M}_{xx} \sin 2\theta + {M}_{xy} \cos 2\theta + \frac{1}{2} {M}_{yy} \sin 2\theta Q\left( \theta \right) = - {Q}_{x} \cos \theta - {Q}_{y} \sin \theta Such that: - N\left( \theta \right) and M\left( \theta \right) load the fictitious beam in combined bending (FC) - T \left( \theta \right) and {M}_{t}\left( \theta \right) load the fictitious beam in membrane shear (CISA) - Q\left( \theta \right) loads the fictitious beam in out-of-plane shear (CISHP) As it is used in its current version, the classical Capra-Maury method would cover only the verification of the axial force N\left( \theta \right) and of the bending moment M\left( \theta \right) as membrane forces. The internal forces T\left( \theta \right) and {M}_{t}\left( \theta \right) are neglected. In this sense, for \theta ranging from 0 to 360°, one would reduce the problem to the design of a fictitious beam in combined bending, so that one will determine the upper steel area {A}_{s, \text{sup}}\left( \theta \right) and lower steel area {A}_{s, \text{inf}}\left( \theta \right) required for equilibrium, in accordance with the beam design principles set out previously. This reinforcement is “fictitious” and it is experienced through the projection of the reinforcement layers actually arranged in the plate, namely the projection of the steel areas along the axes x and y respectively, and along the upper and lower faces of the slab. Projection of the reinforcement layers and constitution of the fictitious reinforcement for the facet considered Thus, referring to the real reinforcement of the slab/wall, namely the quadruplet \left({A}_{s_x,s},{A}_{s_y,s},{A}_{s_x,i},{A}_{s_y,i}\text{ en } cm^{2} ml^{-1} \right) ( ml for linear metre ) one must verify, in accordance with the previous figure, the two inequalities below: For the upper face: {A}_{s_x,s} {\cos}^{2} \, \theta + {A}_{s_y,s} {\sin}^{2} \, \theta \ge {A}_{s, \text{sup}}(\theta) For the lower face: {A}_{s_x,i} {\cos}^{2} \, \theta + {A}_{s_y,i} {\sin}^{2} \, \theta \ge {A}_{s, \text{inf}}( \theta) In what follows one restricts oneself to a single face of the section (lower or upper), so that one seeks to minimise the sum {A}_{s_x}+{A}_{s_y} while verifying that the two terms remain of course positive. To this end, one proceeds by a graphical argument and one plots, in the orthonormal frame \left( A_{s_x}, A_{s_y} \right) , for each angle \theta considered, the straight line of equation: \left({d}_{\theta}\right) : {A}_{s_y} = \frac{{A}_{s}( \theta)}{{\sin}^{2} \, \theta} - {A}_{s_x} \cot^{2}( \theta) The set of straight lines thus plotted would bound a validation domain constructed by means of the intersections of these lines, and guaranteeing compliance with the inequalities given previously for each value of \theta considered — it being noted of course that one would have two distinct sets of lines: one for equilibrium in the upper layer and another for equilibrium in the lower layer. Knowing that for a given straight line, its domain of validity is the part of the frame situated above the line, the set of lines plotted would consequently constitute a convex polygon “open” upwards, whose vertices are none other than the intersections of the various lines ( d_{\theta} ). These latter points are therefore pairs of reinforcement (Ax; Ay)_i which are solutions of the global equilibrium of the upper/lower layer. In particular, in view of the convexity of the validation domain constructed, these points would lead to the minimum reinforcement (that is to the solutions giving the smallest sums Ax+Ay ) of the whole validity domain, and one will finally retain the point making it possible to minimise the distance d between its orthogonal projection onto the first bisector of the plane and the origin of the frame (see the figure below). Construction of the validation domain per layer (upper and lower) Concretely in the algorithm, one defines a discrete set of facets centred at the computation point, whose normal rotates in the plane tangent to the mid-surface. The angle \theta of the facets is discretised regularly from -90° to +90° , taking into account the symmetry of the equilibrium inequalities. 2.1.2 Taking out-of-plane shear into account (CISHP) This part concerns the taking up of the transverse shear forces of the facets, namely Q\left( \theta \right) with: The taking up of Q\left( \theta \right) by each of the fictitious beams corresponds to a classical study of the transverse shear force of a beam (§6.2 of EN-1992-1). This method divides the plate into three layers (hence its name): - The upper and lower layers (of respective thicknesses t_{\text{sup}} and t_{\text{inf}} ) resist the membrane internal forces (axial forces, bending moment, membrane shear and torsion). They therefore take up the forces {N}_{xx} , {N}_{yy} and {N}_{xy} as well as the forces {M}_{xx} , {M}_{yy} and {M}_{xy} . - The intermediate layer, or concrete core (of thickness t_{c} ), resists the out-of-plane shear. It therefore takes up the forces {Q}_{x} and {Q}_{y} . Presentation of the “Sandwich” model (division of the plate into three layers) Thus, the first step of the method is to determine, by means of an iterative computation, the optimal thicknesses of the two outer layers and then to deduce from them, by means of the membrane equilibrium equations, the membrane reinforcement (namely the quadruplet \left( {A}_{\text{x,\text{sup}}},{A}_{\text{y,\text{sup}}},{A}_{\text{x,\text{inf}}},{A}_{\text{y,\text{inf}}}\right) in cm^2.ml ). In a second step, the thickness of the intermediate layer can be deduced ( t_c = h–t_{\text{sup}}–t_{\text{inf}} ) and the transverse reinforcement (namely the pair \left( {A}_{\text{sv},x},{A}_{\text{sv},y}\right) in cm^2.ml.ml ) will be computed according to the classical rules for the shear design of beams as developed in §6.2 of EN-1992-1. 2.2.2 Determination of the membrane equilibrium One begins by computing the forces ‘experienced’ at the centres of gravity of the upper reinforcement layers ( \text{sup} ) and lower reinforcement layers ( \text{inf} ). By thus isolating this third layer from the two upper and lower layers, one confers on the Sandwich model an orthotropic mode of behaviour, which in itself is an important advantage with respect to the Capra-Maury method. For the computation of the transverse reinforcement at the intermediate layer, one applies a reasoning similar to the reinforcement of beams in shear. To this end, one should evaluate the equivalent principal shear force {V}_{\text{Ed}} and its direction \beta as follows: \begin{split}\left( \begin{array}{l} {n}_{c_{x}, \text{inf}}\\ {n}_{c_{xy}, \text{inf}} \end{array} \begin{array}{c} {n}_{c_{xy}, \text{inf}}\\ {n}_{c_{y}, \text{inf}} \end{array} \right)\end{split} and \tan\beta = \frac{{Q}_{y}}{{Q}_{x}} In the direction of the principal shear force, the plate element therefore behaves like a beam and one should then refer to a Ritter-Mörsch truss modelling, in the case where {V}_{\text{Ed}} is greater than the resisting shear force of the concrete alone {V}_{\text{Rd}, c} . The specifications and procedures of §6.2 of EN-1992-1 then apply. In particular, for the computation of the longitudinal reinforcement ratio {\rho}_{L} , one considers: {\rho}_{L} = {\rho}_{x} \, {\cos}^{2} \beta + {\rho}_{y} \, {\sin}^{2} \beta where {\rho}_{x}=\frac{{A}_{xy, \text{sup}}+{A}_{xy, \text{inf}}}{{t}_{c}} and {\rho}_{y}=\frac{{A}_{s_y, \text{sup}}+{A}_{s_y, \text{inf}}}{{t}_{c}} . At the cost of counting only the tensioned reinforcement. Reinforcement of the intermediate layer for the equivalent principal shear force Furthermore, for taking the prestress state into account (impact on the coefficients {\alpha}_{\text{cw}} and {\stressCmp}_{\text{cp}} ), one considers as the design axial force: {N}_{\text{Ed}} = {N}_{xx} \, {\cos}^{2} \beta + 2 \, {N}_{xy} \cos \beta \, \sin \beta + {N}_{yy} \, {\sin}^{2} \beta In the case where the computation shows that a transverse reinforcement is required ( {V}_{\text{Ed}} \gt {V}_{\text{Rd},c} ) then one computes, in accordance with the Eurocode, a design reinforcement {A}_{\text{sv0}} (in cm^{2}\,{ml}^{-1},{ml}^{-1} ) along the direction \beta and from there, one passes to the real transverse reinforcement so as to verify the inequality below: {A}_{\text{sv}, x} \, {\cos}^{2} \beta + {A}_{\text{sv}, y} \, {\sin}^{2} \beta \ge {A}_{\text{sv0}} This is a reasoning analogous to that introduced in Capra-Maury. Search for the optimal transverse reinforcement Thus the search for the reinforcement optimum consists in determining the point of the red straight line whose projection onto the first bisector of the plane \left( {A}_{\text{sv}, x}; {A}_{\text{sv}, y}\right) is the closest to the origin of the frame. Consequently, one will retain as the final solution: - If \beta =0 , then {A}_{\text{sv}, x} = {A}_{\text{sv0}} \text{ et } {A}_{\text{sv}, y}=0 - If \beta =\pm \frac{\pi}{2} , then {A}_{\text{sv}, x}=0 \text{ et } {A}_{\text{sv}, y}={{A}_{\text{sv0}}} - Otherwise: - if \left\vert \beta \right\vert \lt \frac{\pi}{4} , one takes {A}_{\text{sv}, x}=\frac{{A}_{\text{sv0}}}{{\cos}^{2} \beta } \text{ et } {A}_{\text{sv}, y}=0 - if \left\vert \beta \right\vert \gt \frac{\pi}{4} , one takes {A}_{\text{sv}, x}=0\text{ et }{A}_{\text{sv}, y}=\frac{{A}_{\text{sv}, 0}}{{\sin}^{2}\beta } - if \left\vert \beta \right\vert=\frac{\pi}{4} , one takes {A}_{\text{sv}, x}=\frac{{A}_{\text{sv},0}}{2{\cos}^{2}\beta } \text{ et }{A}_{\text{sv},y}=\frac{{A}_{\text{sv}, 0}}{{2\sin}^{2}\beta } Furthermore, in the case where the transverse reinforcement is required, one must add the additional tensile forces introduced: {D}_{\text{nxx}} = \frac{{Q}_{x}^{2}}{{V}_{\text{Ed}}} \, \cot\theta {D}_{\text{nyy}} = \frac{{Q}_{y}^{2}}{{V}_{\text{Ed}}} \, \cot\theta {D}_{\text{nxy}} = \frac{{Q}_{x} {Q}_{y}}{{V}_{\text{Ed}}} \cot\theta \theta being the angle of inclination of the compression strut in the Ritter-Mörsch truss for the shear reinforcement of the beam of direction \beta . 2.3 Taking the minimum reinforcement into account For the minimum percentage of longitudinal steel in the principal direction, and in accordance with the specifications of §9.3 of EC2, the specifications of the present documentation apply. No minimum threshold is required for the transverse reinforcement. When the reinforcement computation is carried out at the SLS-QP, it is possible to take into account the minimum reinforcement for crack control in Eurocode 2 and in the RCC-CW. In accordance with equation 7.1 of §7.3.2 of EC2 or with equation DCONC 4110-2 of §DCONC 4110 of the RCC-CW, this minimum reinforcement is such that: {A}_{s,\text{min}} \stressCmp_{s} = k_{c} k f_{\text{ct}, \text{eff}} \, A_{\text{ct}} where {A}_{s, text{min}} is the minimum quantity of reinforcement to be placed in the tensioned zones; {f}_{\text{ct}, \text{eff}} is the effective tensile strength of the concrete; {A}_{\text{ct}} is the area of concrete in tension; {\stressCmp}_{s} is the allowable stress in the steel; {k}_{c} and {k} are computed according to Eurocode 2. In particular, the parameter {k}_{c} depends on the axial force applied to the reinforced-concrete section. The minimum reinforcement can therefore depend on the forces applied to the structure. For simplicity, sigma_{s} is considered equal to the yield strength of the steel f_{\text{yk}} . The computation of the area of concrete in tension A_{\text{ct}} can be carried out by considering the effective depth of concrete in tension h_{c, \text{ef}} , which is, in accordance with Eurocode 2, §7.3.2: {h}_{c, \text{ef}} = \min \left\lbrace 2,5 \, (h-d); \frac{h-x}{3}, \frac{h}{2} \right \rbrace where h , d and x represent respectively the effective height, the effective depth and the depth of the neutral axis of the section. Extract from Eurocode 2 showing the effective depth of concrete in tension. For simplicity and conservatism, one considers {h}_{c, \text{ef}} = \frac{h}{2} . Furthermore, for the computation of the minimum reinforcement for crack control of walls and floors, it is possible to take the scale effect into account according to equation DN 2200-1 of § DN2200 of the RCC-CW. 2.4 Properties relating to the output reinforcement field The current version of the operator CALC_FERRAILLAGE also proposes the computation of the quantities below, at the end of the determination of the reinforcement field required by the element: 2.4.1 Computation of the volumetric reinforcement density At the end of the computations at ULS, SLS and SLSQP, the bending-steel areas {A}_{\text{XS}} , {A}_{\text{XI}} , {A}_{\text{YS}} , {A}_{\text{YI}} and the shear-steel areas {A}_{\text{sv}, x} and {A}_{\text{sv}, y} are used to compute the volumetric reinforcement density {\delta}_{\text{BA}} in kg.{m}^{-3} if they are expressed in {m}^{2}.m^{-1} for the bending steels and in {m}^{2}.m^{-2} for the shear steels according to the following formula where {\rho}_{\text{acier}} is the density of the steels in {kg}.{m}^{-3} . {\delta}_{\text{BA}} = \frac{ \left( {A}_{\text{XS}} + {A}_{\text{YS}} + {A}_{\text{XI}} + {A}_{\text{YI}} \right) + \left( {A}_{\text{SV},X} + {A}_{\text{SV}, Y} \right) \, h }{h} \times {\rho}_{\text{acier}} 2.4.2 Computation of the constructability complexity indicator A complexity indicator {I}_{c,i} intended to reflect the difficulty of placing the reinforcement on site is computed according to the following formula: {I}_{c,i} = \frac{ {\alpha}_{\text{reinf}} \, \frac{{\rho}_{i}}{{\rho}_{\text{critic}}} + {\alpha}_{\text{shear}} \, \frac{{A}_{\text{sw},i}}{{A}_{\text{sw}, \text{critic}}} + {\alpha}_{\text{stirrups}} \, \frac{{A}_{\text{sw},i}} {{A}_{\text{sw},\text{critic}}} \, \frac{{h}_{\text{eff},i}}{{l}_{\text{crit}}} } { {\alpha}_{\text{reinf}} + {\alpha}_{\text{shear}} + {\alpha}_{\text{stirrups}} } with: - {\alpha}_{\text{reinf}} is a weighting coefficient of the ratio of steel density per cubic metre of concrete; - {\rho}_{i} is the total volumetric steel density for the element i computed previously {\delta}_{\text{BA}} ; - {\rho}_{\text{critic}} is the critical volumetric steel density for the element i ; - {\alpha}_{\text{shear}} is a weighting coefficient of the ratio of shear-steel density; - {A}_{\text{sw},i} is the shear-steel density for the element i ; - {A}_{\text{sw}, \text{critic}} is the critical shear-reinforcement density; - {\alpha}_{\text{stirrups}} is a weighting coefficient of the ratio of the length of the shear-steel hairpin links; - {h}_{\text{eff},i}=h-c-c^{\prime} is the effective depth considered for the element i ; - {l}_{\text{crit}} is the critical length of the shear-steel hairpin links. {\alpha}_{\text{reinf}} , {\alpha}_{\text{shear}} and {\alpha}_{\text{stirrups}} have the default value 1 . The critical volumetric steel density {\rho}_{\text{critic}} has the default value 150 \,kg.m^{-3} , the critical shear-reinforcement density {A}_{\text{sw},\text{critic}} has the default value 60\,{cm}^{2}.m^{-2} and the critical length of the shear-steel hairpin links has the default value 1~m . With such values, one considers that the transition between constructable and unconstructable is given for values of {l}_{c} between 1,0 and 1,2 . Beyond {l}_{c}=2,0 one considers that the placing of the reinforcement is very complicated and beyond {l}_{c}=3,0 one considers that the placing of the reinforcement is impossible. 3 Verification of the reinforcement This section presents the method used for the verification of an existing reinforcement employed in the operator VERI_FERRAILLAGE and the macro-command POST_VERI_FERRAILLAGE. The objective is to verify whether the structure with an existing reinforcement (coming from a reinforcement drawing or from a reinforcement computation) supports a given load by providing a mechanical margin and/or a utilisation ratio of the maximum capacity of the structure under this load. The method used is inspired by that employed in the RunAéro tool. 3.1 Verification of the reinforcement of plates As for the reinforcement computation of plates, the verification is also based on the Capra-Maury algorithm. The various steps of the method employed are the following: 3.1.1 Loop over the facets One considers n facets pivoting about the axis normal to each finite element (as presented in the part r7.04.05-calcul-ferraillage-longitudinal). Each of the facets is defined by its normal vector \vector{n}(\theta) making an angle \theta with the local axis x of the plate. This makes it possible to assimilate the study of a plate to an equivalent problem of beams ( 1D ). 3.1.2 Projection of the reinforcement The upper and lower reinforcement along x and y of the plate will be projected onto the facet as follows, making it possible to obtain the reinforcement of the fictitious beam ( {A}_{s, \text{sup}}(\theta) and {A}_{s, \text{inf}}(\theta) ): {A}_{s, \text{sup}}(\theta) = {A}_{s_x, \text{sup}} \, {\cos}^{2}\theta + {A}_{s_y, \text{sup}} \, {\sin}^{2}\theta {A}_{s, \text{inf}}(\theta) = {A}_{s_x, \text{inf}} \, {\cos}^{2}\theta + {A}_{s_y, \text{inf}} \, {\sin}^{2}\theta It is important to note that the method employed for the computation of the margin does not take into account the transverse reinforcement for out-of-plane shear. 3.1.3 Interaction diagram In this step, the interaction diagram of each facet will be constructed. The interaction diagram of a reinforced-concrete section represents the set of points (N, M) corresponding to a limit state of the section. These points are then plotted on a 2D graph whose abscissa axis represents the axial force and whose ordinate axis represents the bending moment. Every point of the curve represents a unique combination of bending moment and axial force which the section can resist. The construction of this diagram is carried out by considering the strain diagrams or the relative stress diagrams over the depth of the section, passing through one of the three pivots A, B or C (see r7.04.05-calcul-ferraillage-1D for further information on the rule and the definition of the three pivots). Construction of the N-M interaction diagram at the ULS ULS : The procedure for constructing this diagram at the ULS consists in considering successively the strain diagrams pivoting about the three pivots A, B or C (see r7.04.05-equilibre-calcul-sections-acier for further information on the rule and the definition of the three pivots). For the computation of the points of the diagram, the parabola-rectangle law (see r7.04.05-loibetonelu) is used for the concrete, and the choice is free between an inclined or a horizontal plateau for the steel. By way of illustration, figure r7.04.05-diagrammeelu shows an example of an interaction diagram for a particular case where the upper and lower steel is symmetric (same quantity and same cover) and a diagram with a horizontal plateau is chosen for the steel. The construction of the diagram is carried out by dividing it into five domains as follows: Domain 1 : One begins with a vertical diagram passing through pivot A. Then, while maintaining pivot A for the lower steel, one rotates the strain until a zero strain on the upper part of the section. The neutral axis lies outside the section (above the upper fibre) and the whole section is in tension. The concrete does not work in this domain. In the example illustrated, the strain in the upper steel always remains greater than the strain corresponding to the elastic limit. With a horizontal plateau, this leads to the maximum stress f_{\text{yd}} equal to that of the lower steel. Because of the symmetry of the steel, this leads to a zero moment and to the same force over the whole of domain 1. This is why domain 1 in red does not appear on the interaction diagram. Domain 2 : Next, one continues to pivot about pivot A until pivot B is reached on the upper fibre of the section. In this domain, the neutral axis is now inside the section and the section is partially compressed. The part of the concrete in compression therefore works. Domain 3 : By fixing pivot B at the upper fibre, one moves the strain of the lower steel to the right until the strain corresponding to the elastic limit of the steel. The neutral axis is still inside the section and the section remains partially compressed. Domain 4 : Still fixing pivot B at the upper fibre, one continues to move the strain of the lower steel, which becomes elastic and then passes into compression. One stops when the strain of the lower fibre is zero. The neutral axis remains inside the section and the section passes from partially compressed to pure compression. Domain 5 : In this domain, one now pivots about pivot C until a uniform compression is reached over the whole section with a strain equal to pivot C ({\strainCmp}_{\text{c2}}) . This method makes it possible to obtain the upper part of the diagram, above the abscissa axis, corresponding to a tensioned lower section. Because of the symmetry of the problem, the lower part of the diagram is obtained by symmetry with respect to the abscissa axis. SLS : At the SLS, a homogenised steel-concrete section is considered, so that the stress diagram is systematically linear (see r7.04.05-dimensionnement-ELS). To this end, the construction of the interaction diagram at the SLS is carried out in a manner similar to the pivot rule of the strain diagram at the ULS, but applied to the stress diagram. Two pivots are considered at the SLS: pivot A, where the steel reaches its limit, and pivot B, where the concrete reaches its limit. In a similar manner, all the limit states are traversed, from uniform tension (pivot A) to uniform compression (pivot B). One begins by pivoting about pivot A for the lower steel until pivot B is reached on the upper fibre, then one pivots about B until uniform compression. As at the ULS, this method makes it possible to obtain the upper part of the diagram, above the abscissa axis, corresponding to a tensioned lower section. Because of the symmetry of the problem, the lower part of the diagram is obtained by symmetry with respect to the abscissa axis. The number of points of the diagram, often around 600 points, varies as a function of the geometric characteristics (in particular the ratio \frac{h}{d} ) and of the values of the pivots. 3.1.4 Projection of the forces The objective of this method is to assess the structural response by following a given loading path. This loading path can be defined by two types of loading: a reference loading C_0 , often made up of the permanent loads, and a study load C (the new loading to be assessed). These loadings (2D internal forces (N_{xx}, N_{yy}, N_{xy}, M_{xx}, M_{yy}, M_{xy}) ) will be projected onto the facet by means of equations and , which makes it possible to obtain the reduced 1D force resultant (N_0(\theta), M_0(\theta)) for the reference loading and the resultant (N(\theta), M(\theta)) for the study load. By placing these two points on the interaction diagram corresponding to the facet, one can determine a third point C_{\text{Rd}} as the intersection point of the half-line \left[ C_{0C} \right) with the diagram, as illustrated in figure r7.04.05-diagramme-calcul-marge. M-N interaction diagram for a facet and loading points. 3.1.5 Computation of the margin The margin is then computed, for each facet, according to the following formula: m(\theta) = 1 - \frac{C_{0} C}{C_{0} C_{\text{Rd}}} = 1 - \frac{\Vert(N (\theta), M(\theta)) - (N_0 (\theta), M_0(\theta))\Vert} {\Vert(N_{\text{Rd}} (\theta), M_{\text{Rd}} (\theta)) - (N_0 (\theta),M_0 (\theta))\Vert} The margin of the plate element is equal to the minimum of the margins over all the facets: \text{marge} = \min \left( m(\theta) ; 0 \le \theta \le 180° \right) A positive margin indicates that the loading point is inside the diagram, which means that the reinforcement is verified. The larger the margin, the lower the risk. A negative margin indicates that C_0 \, C is greater than C_0 \, C_{\text{Rd}} and that the element is not verified for the load studied. 3.1.6 State of the critical section The macro-command POST_VERI_FERRAILLAGE also makes it possible to compute the parameters related to the equilibrium state of the critical facet identified by the operator VERI_FERRAILLAGE. The equilibrium parameters of the critical section which are computed are the following: the compressed depth, the strain of the upper fibre of the concrete, the strain of the upper and lower steels, the compressive stress of the upper fibre of the concrete and the stresses in the upper and lower steels. For the equilibrium equations, one assumes a linear strain diagram in accordance with the Euler-Bernoulli hypotheses. Thus, the strain at any fibre of the section, situated at a distance z from the upper fibre of the concrete, depends on the depth of the neutral axis relative to the upper fibre of the concrete x and on the curvature \chi , by the relation: \strainCmp = - \chi(z-x) The constitutive laws of the concrete and of the steel make it possible to obtain, for each fibre, the corresponding stress. \stressCmp_{\text{béton}} = \stressCmp_{\text{béton}}(x,\chi) \stressCmp_{\text{acier}, \text{inf}} = \stressCmp_{\text{acier}, \text{inf}}(x,\chi) \stressCmp_{\text{acier}, \text{sup}} = \stressCmp_{\text{acier}, \text{sup}}(x,\chi) In order to find equilibrium, it is then enough to find the pair (x,\chi) making it possible to balance the resultant (N,M) considered. One then obtains a system of two equations in two unknowns: N = \iint_S \stressCmp_{\text{béton}}(x,\chi) \,dS + \stressCmp_{\text{acier}, \text{inf}} \, A_{\text{acier}, \text{inf}} + \stressCmp_{\text{acier}, \text{sup}} \, A_{\text{acier}, \text{sup}} M = \iint_S \stressCmp_{\text{béton}}(x,\chi) y \,dS + \stressCmp_{\text{acier}, \text{inf}} \, A_{\text{acier}, \text{inf}} \, y_{\text{inf}} + \stressCmp_{\text{acier}, \text{sup}} \, A_{\text{acier}, \text{sup}} \, y_{\text{sup}} where y represents the distance of the fibre considered from the centre of inertia of the section. At the SLS, the solution is obtained with a direct approach. However, at the ULS, the system of equations becomes non-linear. It is solved with the iterative Newton-Raphson method and the starting point of the iterations is the solution at the SLS. 4 Bibliographic references [bib1] Automatic computation of the optimal reinforcement of reinforced-concrete plates and shells. r7.04.10 Operator for the computation of wear r7.04.10 Operator for the computation of wear Summary: This note presents three wear laws which make it possible to evaluate the worn volume from the quantities coming from a dynamic analysis carried out with the operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.54.03 and the keyword CHOC. - Archard's law, - The KWU_EPRI law, - The EDF_MZ law. The wear coefficients required for these computations are supplied by the user or else specified in a database. From the worn volume and the geometry of the contact, it is possible to compute the wear depth for the moving body or its obstacle. An angular subdivision of the clearance pattern allows the operator to compute the quantities relating to wear by sectors. > Contents 1 Introduction The assessment of damage by wear requires a thorough knowledge of the bodies present during contact, of the loadings and of the kinematics. The investigations carried out at the Component Mechanics and Technology Department make it possible to supply coefficients for wear laws relating to wear configurations affecting the components of nuclear power plants. A transient analysis by modal recombination, by means of the operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.54.03, makes it possible to know the kinematics and the dynamics of the contact for line structures such as the control-rod clusters and the steam-generator tubes which impact and slide against their guides. In order to compute the wear power, the wear post-processing module of Code_Aster , (POST_USURE U4.67.03), uses, at an impact node, the result in generalised coordinates (tran_gene) coming from DYNA_VIBRA. It combines the normal forces and the sliding velocities according to the method defined in the following paragraph. From knowledge of the wear power, it is possible to recover the worn volumes by using one of the wear laws proposed in POST_USURE. The coefficients to be used are to be defined by the user or to be looked up in a database integrated into the operator. In a second stage, knowledge of the geometry of the internal structures of nuclear power plants makes it possible to compute the wear depths from the worn volumes. The operator POST_USURE makes it possible to subdivide the clearance pattern into sectors in order to assign several wear coefficients to one and the same impact zone, so as to take complex geometries into account. For example, edge contact leads to greater losses of material than conforming contact in the case of control-rod clusters. The table generated by POST_USURE gives the value of the worn volumes for several values of time. 2 Wear laws In its initial form, Archard's law [bib1] expresses, for an adhesive wear configuration, in sliding, a relation between the worn volume and quantities characteristic of the contact: V=\frac{k.\parallel {F}_{n}\parallel .L}{H} | where | V | : | worn volume, | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | k | : | dimensionless wear coefficient, | | | \parallel {F}_{n}\parallel | : | modulus of the normal contact force, assumed constant, | | | L | : | sliding length, | | | H | : | hardness. | The coefficient k is different for each of the bodies present. It depends on the geometric and thermodynamic conditions during contact. It has been shown that Archard's law can be extended to other mechanisms, with sliding dominant. Subject to a redefinition of certain parameters, the previous equation can be written: V=K.W | where | K | : | is equal to \frac{k}{H} , | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | W | : | is equal to \parallel {F}_{n}\parallel .L . | W has the dimension of a work. By convention, it is called the "wear work". In the case where the normal contact force varies in the course of time (for example, in an impact-sliding situation, \parallel {F}_{n}\parallel exhibits very strong variations of short duration during the impacts), the definition of W becomes: W=\underset{{t}_{0}}{\overset{{t}_{1}}{\int}}\parallel {F}_{n}\parallel \cdot \parallel {V}_{t}\parallel \cdot \mathrm{dt} | where | W | : | wear work, | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | \parallel {F}_{n}\parallel | : | modulus of the normal force in the course of the contact, | | | \parallel {V}_{t}\parallel | : | modulus of the sliding velocity in the course of the contact, | | | {t}_{0} | : | time instant of the start of the analysis, | | | {t}_{1} | : | time instant of the end of the analysis. | Henceforth, by analogy with the usual laws of mechanics, it is possible to define a "wear power" by setting: P=\parallel {F}_{n}\parallel \cdot \parallel {V}_{t}\parallel where P : wear power. In the case where a stationary regime is reached, the wear power is assumed constant in the course of time. In order to make sure of this stationarity, the interval [{t}_{0,}{t}_{1}] can be subdivided into several blocks in the operator POST_USURE U4.67.03. For each of these blocks, one should verify that the wear power evolves little (strictly speaking, the use of the wear laws below assumes that the wear power is constant). 2.1 Wear law 'ARCHARD' The law is of linear type [bib1]: V=K\cdot P\cdot t | where | V | : worn volume, | | --- | --- | --- | | | K | : wear coefficient, | | | P | : wear power, | | | t | : time interval. | The coefficient K is supplied by the user or is taken from a database (see [§3]). It is different for the two bodies present and depends on the geometric and thermodynamic conditions in the contact. The time interval t used for the computation of the wear does not correspond to the effective simulation time but to the time interval over which the user wishes to evaluate the wear. 2.2 Wear law 'KWU_EPRI' The approach of the model consists in determining a wear coefficient K , in the sense of Archard's law, by taking into account the particular conditions of the contact studied [bib2]. The normal forces {F}_{i}(N) are distributed into 5 classes, as are the sliding velocities {V}_{j}(m/s) . One obtains 25 classes whose identification is indicated as follows: For a given analysis, one determines the percentages obtained for each of the 25 classes. The processing is done by applying appropriate weighting factors for each class, which account for its particular contribution in the overall wear process. In the case of pure impacts (classes 1.1 to 1.5), the contribution of these classes is modelled by calling upon a weighting factor {m}_{{h}_{ij}} defined by: {m}_{{h}_{ij}}={k}_{1}\cdot k\cdot {(\frac{{F}_{i}}{c})}^{3} | where | {m}_{{h}_{ij}} | : | dimensionless factor of impact-hardening intensity | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | {k}_{1} | : | dimensional correction coefficient | | | k | : | experimental dimensionless constant | | | c | : | experimental dimensionless constant | | | {F}_{i} | : | mean value of the normal force for class ij | In the case of sliding (class 1.1 and classes 2.1 to 5.5), the contribution of these classes is modelled by calling upon a weighting factor {m}_{{w}_{ij}} defined by: {m}_{{w}_{ij}}={k}_{2}\cdot {F}_{i}\cdot {({V}_{j})}^{2} | where | {m}_{{w}_{ij}} | : | dimensionless factor of sliding-wear intensity | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | {k}_{2} | : | dimensional correction coefficient | | | {F}_{i} | : | mean value of the normal force for class ij | | | {V}_{j} | : | mean value of the sliding velocity for class ij | One must then compute the weighted percentages for each class of the two categories impact-hardening and sliding wear: {P}_{{h}_{ij}}={m}_{{h}_{ij}}\cdot {p}_{ij} {P}_{{w}_{ij}}={m}_{{w}_{ij}}\cdot {p}_{ij} where {p}_{ij} is the percentage of elements of the class ij . Which leads to an overall wear-intensity factor w=\frac{{(\sum{P}_{{w}_{ij}})}^{2}}{\sum{P}_{{h}_{ij}}+\sum{P}_{{w}_{ij}}} The overall intensity factor w is used as a correction factor of the wear coefficient in the sense of ARCHARD's law according to the expression: {K}_{\mathrm{KWU}}={k}_{r}\cdot w/{w}_{r} V={K}_{\mathrm{KWU}}\cdot P\cdot t | where {k}_{r} : | is the reference wear coefficient obtained experimentally for conventional test conditions in oscillating sliding, | | --- | --- | | and {w}_{r} | is the overall intensity factor evaluated for this same test. | 2.3 Wear law 'EDF_MZ' It is at present developed for the sole case of the control-rod clusters. Feedback from experience shows that the wear kinetics slows down with time t ; one way of taking the observations into account is to express the worn volume in the form: V=(\frac{{S}_{0}-S}{n})\cdot (1-{e}^{-\mathrm{nt}})+S\cdot t where {S}_{0} is the initial rate and S the asymptotic wear rate (see below), n is a parameter of the model. The values of n and of S are deduced from feedback from experience. Tests on simulators, of short duration compared with that of an operating cycle of a reactor, show that the initial wear rate {S}_{0} follows a law of the type: {S}_{0}=A\cdot {({P}_{0})}^{b} where {P}_{0} is the initial wear power A and b are coefficients determined by tests on simulators [bib4] Feedback from experience shows that the wear rate reaches an asymptotic value S . The previous relation, observed on a simulator, is assumed valid for all the instants of the wear phenomenon. This assumes a wear power P which makes it possible to reach S=A\cdot {(P)}^{b} , for the high values of the time t (typically, one or several operating cycles). The corresponding evolution of the worn volume as a function of time is of the form: The worn volume V computed by means of the operator POST_USURE is written: V=(\frac{A\cdot {({P}_{0})}^{b}-S}{n})\cdot (1-{e}^{\mathrm{nt}})+S\cdot t | where | V | : worn volume, | | --- | --- | --- | | | {P}_{0} | : wear power computed by Code_Aster ® , | | | A,b,S,n | : coefficients of the model defined above. | This model is described in detail by reference [bib4]. 3 Database The materials are identified by a letter followed by alphanumeric characters.
