It should be noted that reference [bib6] does not give a value of the wear coefficient for the mating components. 4 Relation between the worn volume and the wear depth From the wear power, the operator POST_USURE computes the worn volumes and then the wear depths. The geometric relations between the worn volumes and the worn depths depend on the type of contact. | Let: | {d}_{m} | : | worn depth of the moving tube, | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | {d}_{o} | : | worn depth of the obstacle, | | | {R}_{m} | : | outer radius of the moving tube, | | | {R}_{o} | : | inner radius of the obstacle, | | | l | : | width of the obstacle, | | | \theta | : | angle between moving body and obstacle, | | | {V}_{m} | : | worn volume of the moving tube, | | | {V}_{o} | : | worn volume of the obstacle. | 4.1 Situation ‘CLUSTER - BORE’ The keyword used is "GRAPPE_ALESAGE". The cluster is centred in a bore. The wear trace has a lune-shaped cross-section [bib6]. The worn volume is reduced to a worn area in a cross-section, multiplied by the worn height l The worn volumes are written [bib3]: \begin{array}{}\frac{{V}_{m}}{l}={r}^{2}(\beta -\sin(2\beta ))-{R}_{m}^{2}(\alpha -\sin(2\alpha ))\\ \frac{{V}_{o}}{l}={R}_{o}^{2}(\gamma -\sin(2\gamma ))-{r}^{2}(\beta -\sin(2\beta ))\\ {R}_{m}\sin(\alpha )=r\sin(\alpha )\\ r\sin(\beta )={R}_{o}\sin(\gamma )\end{array} The variables r,\alpha ,\beta and \gamma are intermediate computation variables defined in the figure below: A numerical solver integrated into Code_Aster® makes it possible to go from solving this system of coupled equations with 4 unknowns, r,\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma . The wear depths are then given by the following relations: \begin{array}{}{d}_{o}=r-{R}_{t}-(r\cos(\beta )-{R}_{t}\cos(\alpha ))\\ {d}_{m}={R}_{o}-r-({R}_{o}\cos(\gamma )-r\cos(\beta ))\end{array} 4.2 Situation ‘CLUSTER - SINGLE NOTCH’ The keyword used is "GRAPPE_1_ENCO". The guide card comprises a single notch. The worn volume is reduced to a worn area in a cross-section, multiplied by the worn height . The worn volumes are written [bib7]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}\frac{{V}_{m}}{l}={A}_{m}{d}_{m}^{3}+{B}_{m}{d}_{m}^{2}+{C}_{m}{d}_{m}+{D}_{m}\\ {V}_{o}=0,47\cdot h\cdot {R}_{o}\cdot {d}_{o}\cdot \pi \end{array} with [bib7]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{A}_{m}=-2,76\\ {B}_{m}=10,30\\ {C}_{m}=0,83\\ {D}_{m}=0\end{array} These coefficients are based on feedback from experience. They apply only to control-rod clusters whose characteristics are: - outer diameter of the cluster rodlet: 9.7 mm - inner diameter of the guide card: 10.5 mm A solver integrated into POST_USURE makes it possible to determine {d}_{m} as a function of {V}_{m} 4.3 Situation ‘CLUSTER - DOUBLE NOTCH’ The keyword used is "GRAPPE_2_ENCO". The guide card is formed of 2 diametrically opposite notches. The worn volume is reduced to a worn area in a cross-section, multiplied by a worn height l . The worn volumes are written [bib7]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}\frac{{V}_{m}}{l}={A}_{m}{d}_{{m}^{3}}+{B}_{m}{d}_{{m}^{2}}+{C}_{m}{d}_{m}+{D}_{m}\\ {V}_{o}=0,94\cdot h\cdot {R}_{o}\cdot {d}_{o}\cdot \pi \end{array} with [bib7]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{A}_{m}=-5,52\\ {B}_{m}=20,60\\ {C}_{m}=1,66\\ {D}_{m}=0\end{array} These coefficients are based on feedback from experience. They apply only to control-rod clusters whose characteristics are: - diameter of the rodlet: 9.7 mm - diameter of the card: 10.5 mm A solver integrated into POST_USURE makes it possible to determine {d}_{m} as a function of {V}_{m} 4.4 Situation ‘Steam-generator tube - Anti-vibration bar’ The keyword used is "TUBE_BAV". Case 1: The tube is presented vertically, the bar impacts perpendicularly to the tube, and one assumes that the bar does not wear. The wear depths are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{d}_{m}={(\frac{1}{2{R}_{m}})}^{1/3}\cdot {(\frac{3{V}_{m}}{41})}^{2/3}\\ {d}_{o}=0\end{array} Case 2: The bar is presented inclined (angle \theta ) with respect to the tube, the bar impacts perpendicularly to the tube, and one assumes that the bar does not wear. - if {d}_{m}<l\theta The wear depths are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{d}_{m}={(\frac{1}{2{R}_{m}})}^{1/5}\cdot {(\frac{15\cdot \theta \cdot {V}_{m}}{8})}^{2/5}\\ {d}_{o}=0\end{array} - if {d}_{m}\ge l\theta The relations between worn volume and wear depths are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{V}_{m}=\frac{8\sqrt{2{R}_{m}}}{15\theta }\cdot \left[{d}_{m}^{5/2}-{({d}_{m}-\theta l)}^{5/2}\right]\\ {d}_{o}=0\end{array} A solver integrated into POST_USURE makes it possible to determine {d}_{m} as a function of {V}_{m} Case 3: The tube is presented vertically, the bar impacts perpendicularly to the tube, and one takes into account the wear of the bar. \alpha is an unknown to be determined. The relations between worn volume and wear depths are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{d}_{m}=(\frac{{V}_{m}}{{V}_{m}+{V}_{o}}){(\frac{1}{2{R}_{m}})}^{1/3}{(\frac{3\cdot ({V}_{m}+{V}_{o})}{4\cdot l})}^{2/3}\\ \frac{{V}_{m}+{V}_{o}}{l}=\alpha \cdot {R}_{m}^{2}-{R}_{m}^{2}\sin(\alpha )\cos(\alpha )\\ {d}_{o}={R}_{t}(1-\cos(\alpha ))-{d}_{m}\end{array} A solver integrated into POST_USURE makes it possible to determine \alpha Case 4: The bar is presented inclined (angle \theta ) with respect to the tube, the bar impacts perpendicularly to the tube, and one takes into account the wear of the bar. \alpha is an unknown to be determined. - if ({d}_{m}+{d}_{o})<l\theta The relations between worn volume and wear depths are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{d}_{m}=(\frac{{V}_{m}}{{V}_{m}+{V}_{o}}){(\frac{1}{2{R}_{m}})}^{1/5}{(\frac{15\cdot \theta \cdot ({V}_{m}+{V}_{o})}{8})}^{2/5}\\ \frac{{V}_{m}+{V}_{o}}{l}=\alpha \cdot {R}_{m}^{2}-{R}_{m}^{2}\sin(\alpha )\cos(\alpha )\\ {d}_{o}={R}_{m}(1-\cos(\alpha ))-{d}_{m}+\frac{l}{2}\sin(\theta )\end{array} A solver integrated into POST_USURE makes it possible to determine \alpha - if ({d}_{m}+{d}_{o})\ge l\theta The relations between worn volume and wear depths are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{V}_{m}=\frac{8\cdot \sqrt{2{R}_{m}}}{15\cdot \theta \cdot (1+k)}\cdot \left[{(({d}_{m}+{d}_{o})\cdot (1+k))}^{5/2}-{(({d}_{m}+{d}_{o})\cdot (1+k)-l\theta )}^{5/2}\right]\\ \frac{{V}_{m}+{V}_{o}}{l}=\alpha \cdot {R}_{m}^{2}-{R}_{m}^{2}\sin(\alpha )\cos(\alpha )\\ {d}_{o}={R}_{m}\cdot (1-\cos(\alpha ))-{d}_{m}+\frac{l}{2}\sin(\theta )\end{array} where k is the ratio between the worn volumes of the bar and of the tube ( k=\frac{{V}_{o}}{{V}_{m}} ) A solver integrated into POST_USURE makes it possible to determine {d}_{m} as a function of {V}_{m} . Likewise, a solver makes it possible to determine \alpha . 4.5 Situation ‘Steam-generator tube - Bore’ The keyword used is "TUBE_ALESAGE". Case 1: The tube is perfectly centred in a bore animated by a pure orbital motion which wears uniformly over the whole of the periphery in contact with the obstacle. The worn depths are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{d}_{m}=\frac{{V}_{m}}{2\cdot \pi \cdot l\cdot {R}_{m}}\\ {d}_{o}=\frac{{V}_{o}}{2\cdot \pi \cdot l\cdot {R}_{o}}\end{array} Case 2: The tube is centred in a bore animated by an impact-sliding motion of elliptical type which leads to the formation of wear traces of cylindrical type, diametrically opposite on the tube and having a lune-shaped cross-section. The worn volumes are written [bib3]: \begin{array}{}\frac{{V}_{m}}{l}={r}^{2}(\beta -\sin(2\beta ))-{R}_{m}^{2}(\alpha -\sin(2\alpha ))\\ \frac{{V}_{o}}{l}={R}_{o}^{2}(\gamma -\sin(2\gamma ))-{r}^{2}(\beta -\sin(2\beta ))\\ {R}_{m}\sin(\alpha )=r\sin(\beta )\\ r\sin(\beta )={R}_{o}\sin(\gamma )\end{array} system of coupled equations with four unknowns to be determined: r,\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma \begin{array}{}{d}_{o}=r-{R}_{m}-(r\cos(\beta )-{R}_{m}\cos(\alpha ))\\ {d}_{m}={R}_{o}-r-({R}_{o}\cos(\gamma )-r\cos(\beta ))\end{array} These formulae have the same origin as those of paragraph [§4.1]. Case 3: The tube, animated by an impact-sliding motion, this time presents an inclination with respect to the support. One obtains two symmetric wear traces on the tube. \begin{array}{}\frac{{V}_{m}}{l}={r}^{2}(\beta -\sin(2\beta ))-{R}_{m}^{2}(\alpha -\sin(2\alpha ))\\ \frac{{V}_{o}}{l}={R}_{o}^{2}(\gamma -\sin(2\gamma ))-{r}^{2}(\beta -\sin(2\beta ))\\ {R}_{m}\sin(\alpha )=r\sin(\beta )\\ r\sin(\beta )={R}_{o}\sin(\gamma )\end{array} system of coupled equations with four unknowns to be determined: r,\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma \begin{array}{}{d}_{o}=r-{R}_{m}-(r\cos(\beta )-{R}_{m}\cos(\alpha ))+\frac{l}{2}\sin(\theta )\\ {d}_{m}={R}_{o}-r-({R}_{o}\cos(\gamma )-r\cos(\beta ))+\frac{l}{2}\sin(\theta )\end{array} These formulae have the same origin as those of paragraph [§4.1]. 4.6 Situation ‘Steam-generator tube - Trefoil’ The keyword used is "TUBE_3_ENCO". The tube is assumed perfectly centred with respect to its obstacle. The wear trace does not extend over the whole land. The wear of the obstacle is not taken into account. The relations between the worn volume and the wear depth are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{V}_{m}=\frac{l}{2}\left[{R}_{m}^{2}{\sin}^{-1}(\frac{x}{{R}_{m}})-{R}_{o}^{2}{\sin}^{-1}(\frac{x}{{R}_{o}})+x({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m})+{d}_{m}^{2}\mathrm{tg}\alpha \right]\\ {d}_{o}=0\end{array} with x=\sqrt{{R}_{m}^{2}-\frac{{({R}_{o}^{2}-{R}_{m}^{2}-{({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m})}^{2})}^{2}}{4{({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m})}^{2}}} A solver integrated into POST_USURE makes it possible to determine {d}_{m} as a function of {V}_{m} Case 2: The same assumptions as for case 1 except for the position of the tube with respect to the obstacle. One assumes this time that the tube presents an angle of inclination \theta . - if {d}_{m}<l\theta The relations between the worn volume and the wear depth are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{V}_{m}=\frac{{d}_{m}}{6\theta }\left[{R}_{m}^{2}{\sin}^{-1}(\frac{x}{{R}_{m}})-{R}_{o}^{2}{\sin}^{-1}(\frac{x}{{R}_{o}})+x({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m})+{d}_{m}^{2}\mathrm{tg}\alpha \right]\\ {d}_{o}=0\end{array} with x=\sqrt{{R}_{m}^{2}-\frac{{({R}_{o}^{2}-{R}_{m}^{2}-{({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m})}^{2})}^{2}}{4{({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m})}^{2}}} A solver integrated into POST_USURE makes it possible to determine {d}_{m} as a function of {V}_{m} - if {d}_{m}\ge l\theta The relations between worn volumes and wear depths are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{V}_{m}=\frac{l}{6}(\mathrm{V1}+\sqrt{\mathrm{V1}\cdot \mathrm{V2}}+\mathrm{V2})\\ {d}_{o}=0\end{array} with \mathrm{x1}=\sqrt{{R}_{m}^{2}-\frac{{({R}_{o}^{2}-{R}_{m}^{2}-{({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m})}^{2})}^{2}}{4{({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m})}^{2}}} \mathrm{V1}={R}_{m}^{2}{\sin}^{-1}(\frac{\mathrm{x1}}{{R}_{m}})-{R}_{o}^{2}{\sin}^{-1}(\frac{\mathrm{x1}}{{R}_{o}})+\mathrm{x1}({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m})+{d}_{m}^{2}\mathrm{tg}\alpha \mathrm{x2}=\sqrt{{R}_{m}^{2}-\frac{{({R}_{o}^{2}-{R}_{m}^{2}-{({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m}-l\cdot \theta )}^{2})}^{2}}{4{({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m}-l\cdot \theta )}^{2}}} \mathrm{V2}={R}_{m}^{2}{\sin}^{-1}(\frac{\mathrm{x2}}{{R}_{m}})-{R}_{o}^{2}{\sin}^{-1}(\frac{\mathrm{x2}}{{R}_{o}})+\mathrm{x2}({R}_{o}-{R}_{m}+{d}_{m}-l\cdot \theta )+{({d}_{m}-l\cdot \theta )}^{2}\cdot \text{tg}\alpha A solver integrated into POST_USURE makes it possible to determine {d}_{m} as a function of {V}_{m} . Following the rupture of a plugged tube, there may be contact between this tube and one of its neighbours. The wear of the two tubes by accommodation of the surfaces leads, at contact, to the creation of two plane surfaces. This statement is confirmed by tests carried out on a wear machine. The worn depths are written [bib3]: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{d}_{t}={(\frac{1}{2\cdot {R}_{m}})}^{}{(\frac{15\cdot \theta \cdot {V}_{m}}{8})}^{}\\ {d}_{o}={(\frac{1}{2\cdot {R}_{o}})}^{}{(\frac{15\cdot \theta \cdot {V}_{o}}{8})}^{}\end{array} 5 Subdivision of the clearance pattern into sectors The user has the possibility of defining a subdivision of the clearance pattern into angular sectors for which he or she gives a type of contact (GRAPPE_1_ENCO...), a wear coefficient and the start and end angles of the subdivision (these angles must be increasing between -180° and +180°). The wear power for each sector is then computed as the arithmetic mean, over the instants previously subdivided into blocks, of the product of the norms of the normal impact force and of the sliding velocity, taking into account only the contacts which take place in the angular sector concerned. From this power, it is possible to define a worn volume by multiplying the wear power of the sector by the wear coefficient of the sector and by an operating time given by the user. It is also possible to compute the wear depth for this sector, assuming that the angular extent of the defect does not exceed that of the sector in which it is detected. It is the keyword SECTEUR which makes it possible to define all of these modifications. It is not planned to verify the overall consistency of the computations carried out. In particular, a wear may be distributed over several sectors and in this case the computation of the wear depth no longer has any meaning. It is for the operator to make sure a posteriori of the validity of the results. A new analysis with another subdivision must possibly be carried out in order to obtain the value of the wear depth. This choice is not constraining because of the speed of the post-processing considered. The interest of carrying out these analyses in POURSUITE is obvious, taking into account what precedes. 6 Updating of the table The operator POST_USURE extrapolates the worn volume obtained in a few seconds of simulation to durations defined by the user (typically a few months, or even a few years). It returns a table which contains the worn volumes and the wear depths for all the sectors and all the instants defined by the user, accumulating them from the initial instant of the simulation. It is possible to give a table to be updated by using the keyword ETAT_INIT. This makes it possible to take into account the evolution of the geometries linked to wear: - From a clearance pattern, the user carries out a dynamic analysis. - He or she obtains worn volumes and wear depths at the output of POST_USURE. - He or she carries out a new dynamic analysis with the modified clearance pattern. - He or she deduces from it new quantities linked to wear and accumulates them in the result table of POST_USURE. By iterating the process a certain number of times [bib9], it is possible to take into account the evolution of the geometries as a function of wear and to deduce from it the impact of this phenomenon on the dynamics of the system studied. 7 Bibliography 1. r7.05.01 Mechanical stability criteria r7.05.01 Mechanical stability criteria Summary: This document presents the various mechanical stability criteria available in Code_Aster . They may be classified into two categories: - The stability criterion associated with conservative systems, which appears as the generalisation of the Euler criterion based on the analysis of the updated global stiffness matrix. - The stability criterion associated with dissipative systems, which must take into account the irreversibility constraints linked to the dissipation of energy. These criteria are used to distinguish, in quasi-static problems, the unstable numerical solutions arising from the equilibrium analysis carried out in the finite-element method (first derivative of the energy zero but second derivative negative) from the physical, stable solutions, for which the second derivative of the energy is positive. The criteria presented in this document are directly transposable to the framework of dynamics, but since they take into account neither the mass matrix nor the damping matrix, one cannot speak of a dynamic stability criterion in the classical sense (for example, of damping becoming negative or zero). These criteria are called within the operators STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, so that they can be evaluated at each step of the incremental quasi-static or non-linear dynamic transient solution. 1 Stability of a conservative system 1.1 Definition of the stability of a conservative system The equilibrium position of a conservative system is said to be stable if it is invariant under the effect of small perturbations. This amounts to verifying that the solution obtained does indeed lie at a local minimum of the potential energy or, put otherwise, to verifying that the Hill functional [bib19] is convex. Mathematically, this is expressed by the verification of the positivity of the second derivative of the potential energy Φ at the equilibrium point u . Consider a small perturbation of the equilibrium state ν, complying with the boundary conditions imposed on the structure. One must always recover the inequality: \phi (u)\le \phi (u+v) eq 1.1‑1 The principal cause of loss of stability for a conservative mechanical structure is buckling. One is therefore interested more particularly, in what follows, in this notion. Note: Other definitions of stability exist. One finds in particular stability in the sense of Rice, a criterion defined in 1975, which amounts to verifying the strict positivity of the eigenvalues of the acoustic tensor. However, one may have instability in the sense of Hill before instability in the sense of Rice. The criterion in the sense of Hill is therefore more conservative. That is why it is the one that is preferred. 1.2 General notion of buckling Buckling is an instability phenomenon [bib6]. Its appearance may be observed in particular on slender members of low flexural stiffness. Beyond a certain loading level, the structure undergoes a significant change of configuration (which may manifest itself by the sudden appearance of undulations, for example). Two types of buckling are distinguished: buckling by bifurcation and buckling by limit point ([bib1], [bib7], [bib8]). In order to describe the behaviour of these two types of buckling, one considers a structure whose parameter \mu is characteristic of the loading and whose parameter \delta is characteristic of the displacement. | | | --- | Figure 1.2-a : Buckling by bifurcation Between the point O and the point A , the structure admits a single family of curves (\mu ,\delta ) . It may, for example, be a matter of classical linear elasticity or of elastoplasticity, where, if the problem is well posed ( cf. [§ 1.3 ]), one has the classical result of existence and uniqueness of the solution. On the other hand, beyond the point A , several families of curves are solutions of the equilibrium problem. This loss of uniqueness is accompanied by an instability of the initial branch (called the fundamental branch). The secondary branch may be stable (curve \mathit{AB} ) or unstable (curve \mathit{AB}’ ). The load beyond which there is bifurcation is called the critical load {\mu}_{\mathit{cr}} . Buckling by bifurcation is characterised by the fact that the mode (or buckling direction), which initiates the secondary branch, does not generate any additional work in the applied loading: the buckling mode being orthogonal to it. An example of buckling by bifurcation with instability of the secondary branch is found in the case of a circular cylindrical shell under axial compression [bib10]. Examples of buckling by bifurcation with stability of the secondary branch are found in elastic beams in axial compression, circular rings in radial compression and rectangular plates in longitudinal compression. | | | --- | Figure 1.2-b : Buckling by limit point | | | --- | Figure 1.2-c : Buckling by limit point with snap-through On the figures [ Figure 1.2-b ] and [ Figure 1.2-c ], which illustrate buckling by limit point, the structure admits only a single family (\mu ,\delta ) of solution of the equilibrium equations. At the point A , there is a loss of stability of the solution with a total loss of rigidity in the case of figure [ Figure 1.2-b ] and with a snap-through phenomenon in the case of figure [ Figure 1.2-c ] (the solution becomes stable again after a discontinuity of displacement; case of a spherical cap under external pressure). The point A is then called the limit point. The problem therefore amounts in every case to seeking the load from which the fundamental equilibrium branch becomes unstable or of uncertain stability. This generally mobilises large displacements. One may finally have the case of collapse by plastic flow, which is akin to the limit point [ Figure 1.2-b ]. Code_Aster allows the search for linear buckling modes, described as the Euler method. It is sufficient to solve a generalised eigenvalue problem (by means of the operator CALC_MODES with the keyword TYPE_RESU=’MODE_FLAMB’). The two matrix arguments of the generalised problem are the stiffness matrix and the geometric stiffness matrix, arising from a prior linear elastic analysis (operator MECA_STATIQUE). In all cases where the non-linearities, whether geometric or behavioural, cannot be neglected, the Euler approach is no longer valid. We therefore propose an ad hoc criterion, which may be considered as a generalisation of the Euler criterion on an updated configuration. This criterion is constructed on the assembled tangent stiffness matrix, which is computed in the Newton-type algorithm in order to solve the non-linear quasi-static problems (operator STAT_NON_LINE) or the non-linear transient dynamic problems (operator DYNA_NON_LINE). This criterion, in the non-linear regime, makes it possible to treat rigorously the non-linear elastic constitutive relations. On the other hand, the laws that present a dissipative aspect are treated rigorously only if the loading, at every point of the structure, follows a monotonic evolution (this corresponds to the Hill assumption [bib4]). 1.3 Writing of the mechanical problem The objective of this chapter is to introduce the general formalism of structural analysis adapted to the non-linear mechanical problem that we wish to address. Let us take the example of a pressure applied to the structure. This pressure will be assumed constant during buckling: in other words, the pressure value does not change during the displacement. This assumption corresponds to two types of real problems. The first type is that in which the volume of the fluid imposing the pressure on the structure is very large compared with the volume variations generated by the displacement of the solid. The problems of reservoirs under internal pressure, in which the wall displacements are not negligible compared with the dimensions of the structure itself, therefore do not fall within this framework. The second case corresponds to the existence of a fluid source which makes it possible to maintain the pressure at a constant value. It is then no longer necessary to concern oneself with the amplitude of the displacement of the solid. The pressure value being taken as fixed, the variation of the normal over time is to be taken into account. This variation is due to the displacement field which modifies the surface of the structure. Likewise, if one reasons in terms of resultant and therefore of integral, the surface element may also change in area. Consequently, the resultant of the pressure forces will vary and it is appropriate to take this into account. It is however difficult to exhibit the existence of a potential. Moreover, we observe that the natural frequencies of the loaded structure are different from those of the initial structure for two reasons: 1. The natural circular frequency \omega is modified by the prestress p : this is the principal effect which is used, for example, to tune a violin. The tension of the string acts on the pitch of the corresponding note, therefore on its natural frequency. 2. A second effect is the variation of the frequency by modification of the geometry: the initial geometric stiffness matrix is replaced by the stiffness matrix on the current geometry: {K}_{0}+{K}^{L}+{K}^{Q} . Which has the effect of modifying the vibratory equations. The operator DYNA_NON_LINE makes it possible to carry out vibratory analyses on the current non-linear configuration (keyword MODE_VIBR), but without taking the prestress into account for the moment. 1.5 Implementation in the code Strictly speaking, in order to ensure the stability analysis of a non-linear quasi-static analysis, the ad hoc stability criterion must be used at each step of the incremental analysis. Any non-linear stability criterion must therefore be intrinsically as inexpensive as possible in CPU time and in memory space. Algorithmically speaking, it appears judicious to implant the call to the criterion inside the routine itself corresponding to the operator STAT_NON_LINE [bib15]. Indeed, the principle of a call at each step sits poorly with a call totally externalised from the incremental method of solution of the non-linear mechanical problem. 1.6 Euler criterion This criterion (cf. [§1.4.2.2]) requires only the solution of a linear static problem, then the construction and the assembly of the geometric stiffness matrix. The latter and the assembled stiffness matrix are then to be passed as the argument of a solver [bib12] for the eigenvalue problem [eq 1.4.2.2-2]. As output one therefore recovers the buckling modes and the corresponding critical loads. For further details, the user may usefully consult the document U2.08.04 [bib17]. 1.7 Non-linear criterion 1.7.1 Impact on the operator STAT_NON_LINE Let us begin by briefly recalling the operation of the incremental method of solution of non-linear structural problems [bib15]. 1.7.1.1 Algorithm of STAT_NON_LINE One will use the index i (as in "time instant") to denote the number of a load increment and the exponent n (as in "Newton") to denote the number of the current Newton iteration. The result of this analysis will therefore be a set of critical-load / buckling-mode pairs. The critical loads are scalars and the associated modes are displacement fields, which will enrich the result data structure of STAT_NON_LINE. 1.7.2 Particular features linked to the strain tensor In the code, it is appropriate to distinguish two broad families of description of the strains. On the one hand the linearised tensor corresponds to the case of small perturbations (argument PETIT of the keyword DEFORMATION), but also to the case of updated small perturbations (Lagrangian updated at each step of the incremental analysis: argument PETIT_REAC of the keyword DEFORMATION). The strain tensor is then written (as [eq 1.3-3]): > \varepsilon = rac{1}{2}(
abla \mathrm{u}+{
abla}^{T}\mathrm{u}) eq 1.7.2-1 The use of PETIT_REAC implies a solution of the equilibrium of the structure on its current geometry with a linearised strain tensor. One therefore computes the strain increment with respect to the position X , to the displacement \mathrm{u} and to the displacement increment \Delta u in the following way: > \Delta {\varepsilon}_{ij}= rac{1}{2}( rac{\partial \Delta {u}_{i}}{\partial {(X+u)}_{j}}+ rac{\partial \Delta {u}_{j}}{\partial {(X+u)}_{i}}) eq 1.7.2-2 On the other hand, the code proposes Green–Lagrange type strain tensors (GROT_GDEP) for the treatment of large displacements (and of finite rotations for certain structural elements) but under the assumption of small strains. The tensor used is the following classical tensor [eq 1.4.1-5]: > {\varepsilon}_{ij}(u)= rac{1}{2}({u}_{i,j}+{u}_{j,i}={u}_{k,i}{u}_{k,j}) eq 1.7.2-3 The keyword GROT_GDEP applies to beam, shell or 3D modellings. Finally, the most complete large-transformation modelling framework accessible in Code_Aster is derived from the theory of Simo and corresponds to the keyword SIMO_MIEHE. It takes into account the large rotations and the large strains since the constitutive law is written in large strains. For further details on the fundamental differences between the various types of strains, the documentation [bib16] of Code_Aster presents the SIMO_MIEHE modelling in detail. Code_Aster does not allow analyses in an Eulerian configuration: as with the Almansi tensor, for example. All the available strain tensors are of Lagrangian type. The fundamental difference, as regards the writing of the criterion, lies between the linearised strains (PETIT and PETIT_REAC) and the GROT_GDEP and SIMO_MIEHE strains. Indeed, Code_Aster needs, in order to carry out its search for equilibrium, the tangent matrix. The latter is written according to the equation ([§2.2.2.1] of the documentation on STAT_NON_LINE [bib15]): > {K}_{T}={Q}^{T}: rac{\partial \sigma }{\partial u}+ rac{\partial {Q}^{T}}{\partial u}:\sigma eq 1.7.2-4 Now, {Q}^{T}: rac{\partial \sigma }{\partial u} corresponds to the classical material-stiffness term and  rac{\partial {Q}^{T}}{\partial u}:\sigma corresponds to the geometric-stiffness term which is present only in large displacements. Thus the buckling criterion (formally assimilable to [eq 1.4.2.2-2]): (K+\lambda K(\sigma ))
u =0 is valid only in small strains, since the geometric-stiffness term is considered as negligible in the tangent matrix. One may then, with good reason, carry out a classical search for eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Euler-buckling type. On the other hand, in large transformation, the evaluation of this criterion by the same method is problematic for two reasons: on the one hand, in the tangent matrix, the geometric-stiffness term is already computed and, on the other hand, the matrix K(\sigma ) that it would possibly be necessary to add is obtained in Code_Aster in small strains. For these reasons, it is necessary to evaluate the criterion differently according to the type of strain tensor requested by the user. If one made the choice of an Eulerian description, the development of an updated Euler type criterion would be facilitated at the level of the computation of the term \mathrm{K}(\sigma ) , whatever the strain tensor. 1.7.2.1 In linearised strains: PETIT and PETIT_REAC As we have said previously, this case does not pose any major problem. It suffices to compute the geometric stiffness matrix and to carry out a classical search for modes and eigenvalues, of Euler type [eq 1.4.2.2-2]: > (K+\lambda K(\sigma ))
u =0 eq 1.7.2.1-1 K is the tangent matrix updated at the end of the time step. In this case, one may therefore indeed speak of an updated Euler type criterion. Since one is in small strains, the geometric stiffness matrix is proportional to the loading. Therefore, when one obtains the critical coefficient \lambda , it suffices to multiply it by the real load at the current time step in order to obtain the critical buckling load. The case \lambda =1 therefore corresponds to the loss of stability. Certain finite elements such as the DKT shells do not allow the computation of the geometric stiffness matrix, unlike elements of COQUE_3D type, for example. 1.7.2.2 In large displacements: GROT_GDEP and SIMO_MIEHE The classical method no longer applies in this case. Indeed, Code_Aster computes as the tangent matrix the material stiffness matrix plus the geometric stiffness matrix (and possibly the contribution due to follower pressures). One of the ways of then verifying buckling is to carry out a search for the eigenvalues of the tangent matrix alone. If one of the eigenvalues is negative, it is because the matrix has become singular and an instability has occurred between the moment when all its eigenvalues were positive and the moment when one of them has become negative. The problem to be treated is therefore slightly different since in the case of small strains (PETIT and PETIT_REAC), one has the following system to solve [eq 1.7.2.1-1]: , (K+\lambda I)
u =0 whereas in the case GROT_GDEP and SIMO_MIEHE one must solve: (\mathrm{K}+\lambda \mathrm{I})
u =0 eq 1.7.2.2-1 With \mathrm{I} which is the identity matrix and \lambda is, this time, of physical dimension equivalent to K , whereas in the case of small strains, the eigenvalue \lambda is dimensionless (whence its direct interpretation as a load multiplier coefficient). One of the defects inherent in this method compared with the more classical search explained above [§ 1.4.2 ] is that one can have buckling predictions only when one approaches “close” to the critical load, or even when one exceeds it. Far from this load, the first eigenvalue found has no real physical meaning since non-linearities may appear between the current step and the computed critical load. The ratio of critical coefficient to load at the time instant i is therefore different from that at the time instant i+1 whereas in small strains this ratio remains constant. Moreover, for all the time steps, all the eigenvalues and eigenvectors except the lowest have no physical meaning since, for an eigenvector–eigenvalue pair ({\mathrm{V}}_{i},{\lambda}_{i}) , one has: > (\mathrm{K}(\mathrm{u})+\mathrm{K}(\sigma )){\mathrm{V}}_{i}={\lambda}_{i}{\mathrm{V}}_{i} eq 1.7.2.2-2 This has a clear meaning only from the moment when {\lambda}_{i}	o 0 , in which case one recovers the critical load and the associated critical eigenvector. u =0 is not made dimensionless. There follows from this a greater difficulty of interpretation as regards knowing whether the value is “small” or not. In other words, when can one say that one is close to a bifurcation? In order to define a relevant interval of general use, so as to bound the neighbourhood of an instability, it would be of interest to make the eigenvalues dimensionless. 1.7.2.3 Case of mixed modellings Since Code_Aster makes it possible to assign several types of strains to the same structure, one must consider the case in which one uses several types of strain tensors in the same analysis. The differentiation of the various elementary matrices being of no use, it is appropriate to resolve to decide at the global level between one method or the other. One has chosen to extract the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the tangent matrix without adding geometric stiffness matrices. Everything proceeds as if the structure were in a Green–Lagrange type strain from the point of view of the criterion. Indeed, let us consider an arbitrary solid composed of two parts I and II. On part I, the strain tensor that has been adopted is the linearised tensor PETIT and on part II that of Green‑Lagrange. The tangent matrix arising from the assembly of the two sub-matrices becomes: > \left[ egin{array}{ccc}{\mathrm{K}}_{I}& 	ext{ }& 0\ 	ext{ }& 	ext{ }& 	ext{ }\ 0& 	ext{ }& {\mathrm{K}}_{\mathit{II}}+{\mathrm{K}}_{\mathit{II}}(\sigma )\end{array}ight] eq 1.7.2.3-1 The starred terms represent the nodes common to the two parts and are therefore a linear combination of the values of the two matrices. In this configuration, it appears that none of the solutions is satisfactory but that the least penalising is to carry out a search of “Green‑Lagrange type” [§ 1.7.2.2 ], that is to say to use (\mathrm{K}+\lambda \mathrm{I})
u =0 [eq 1.7.2.2-1]. This solution not being exact but nevertheless the only one capable of being carried out simply, it is planned to add an alarm message informing the user that the results obtained are not guaranteed owing to the juxtaposition of several types of strain tensors. 1.7.3 Improvement of the performance of the criterion During the incremental solution of a non-linear quasi-static problem, ideally and if one accepts that the discretisation in time is sufficiently fine, a stability analysis should be carried out at each computation step. At each step, this induces the solution of an eigenvalue problem, admittedly limited to the search for a few modes. The stability analysis therefore brings a significant CPU overhead, to a non-linear analysis that may already be long. The idea is to call the solution of an eigenvalue problem only when it is really necessary, therefore when the current configuration is “close” to an instability. If one can define this neighbourhood by a predefined interval, then one can call a Sturm test [bib12]. This test makes it possible to know whether there exists at least one eigenvalue on the search interval. If so, one will then be able to carry out the modal search. Otherwise, one continues the quasi-static incremental solution, without solving an eigenvalue problem. The cost of a Sturm test is notably lower than the cost of the search for the critical loads. The search interval for the Sturm test may either be given by the user, or have a default value in the code. In the case of an updated Euler criterion (case of small strains [§ 1.7.2.1 ]), where the problem to be solved is written: (\mathrm{K}+\lambda \mathrm{K}(\sigma ))
u =0 [eq 1.7.2.1-1], the search interval must be centred on the eigenvalue \lambda =1 (which corresponds to the value -1 for the algorithm of CALC_MODES, because it in fact solves a problem of the type: \mathrm{K}
u =\mu \mathrm{K}(\sigma )
u ). The bounds of the interval are the bounds of the load multiplier coefficient, therefore dimensionless quantities, which are a function of the safety coefficients and of the evaluation of the uncertainties for the given problem. The Sturm test is implemented in this framework. In the specific case adapted to the Green–Lagrange tensor [§ 1.7.2.2 ], where one solves: (\mathrm{K}+\lambda \mathrm{I})
u =0 [eq 1.7.2.2-1], the interval is centred on 0. Moreover, the bounds of the test interval are, unlike the previous case, not dimensionless [§ 1.7.2.2 ]. It is therefore more difficult to identify relevant and general values (for the case of the default values). The Sturm test is not currently implanted for this case. 1.8 Generalisation to dynamics We shall not address here the framework of the dynamic instability criteria (negative damping…). The point is merely to indicate that the non-linear criterion presented here may perfectly well be applied directly in non-linear dynamics. It will then detect any potential buckling of the structure, in the sense of the singularity of the updated global tangent stiffness matrix. In order to be exhaustive in terms of stability analysis on a non-linear dynamic study, the user should use two criteria: - a buckling criterion (criterion on the stiffness), - a dynamic criterion (criterion on the damping or on the global quadratic linearised problem [bib14], for example). For the moment, the buckling criterion on the stiffness (identical to that of STAT_NON_LINE) is alone available in DYNA_NON_LINE. The coupled fluid–structure modelling (u,p,f) R4.02.02, which is available in DYNA_NON_LINE, requires a few adaptations in the use of the non-linear stability criterion. Indeed, this coupled formulation generates a global assembled stiffness matrix that is intrinsically singular on all the fluid degrees of freedom, which makes it incompatible with the eigenvalue search method used for the stability analysis. One may however circumvent the problem by correcting the assembled problem (stiffness matrix and geometric stiffness matrix if need be) by means of the use of two specific keywords. The stability analysis then concerns the structural degrees of freedom alone. 1.9 Validation of the developments The validation test cases are: SSNL126 and SSLL105D. More precisely, the test cases SSNL126 treat the case of a beam clamped at one end and subjected to a compression at the other end. The modelling is three-dimensional, with an elastoplastic constitutive relation with linear isotropic hardening. Two kinematic representations are presented: - modelling a: linearised strains, - modelling b: Green–Lagrange strains. The test case SSLL105D is based on a beam problem in L , whose elastic buckling is studied. The finite elements are of beam type. 1.10 Extension of the buckling criterion to the treatment of elastoplastic behaviour Far from any exhaustiveness, we shall present here only the simplest approaches, with a view to their easy implantation in the code. When the structure operates in an elastoplastic regime, buckling is affected by the loss of strength due to plasticity [bib2]. The modification comes from the constitutive relation during the additional displacement \alpha {u}_{1} . The stress becomes, in incremental form: \Delta {\pi}_{1}=\Delta \pi +\alpha {C}_{T}[\Delta {\varepsilon}^{L}(u)+\Delta {\varepsilon}^{Q}(u,u)]+ rac{{\alpha}^{2}}{2}{C}_{T}\Delta {\varepsilon}^{Q}({u}_{1},{u}_{1}) 1.11-1 In this expression, the behaviour matrix is the tangent matrix {C}_{T} . The choice of this matrix is not immediate: indeed, the matrix depends on \alpha {\mathrm{u}}_{1} and is therefore not known so long as the mode is unknown. One may, for example, unload during buckling if the mode develops in one direction and load if it develops in the opposite direction. On the one hand, in the cases where a linearised approach is sufficient, one may apply an Euler type criterion ([bib13] and [bib18]), by a call to an operator for the solution of the generalised eigenvalue problem (CALC_MODES with the keyword TYPE_RESU=’MODE_FLAMB’). 1. On the other hand, for all the cases where it is indispensable to take the non-linearities into account, whether they are due to the constitutive relation or to the large transformations, the user may employ an adapted criterion, of generalised Euler type. The call of this criterion is made during the incremental solution of the quasi-static problem (operator STAT_NON_LINE [bib15]). At each time step, the criterion is based on the solution of an eigenvalue problem [bib13] on the updated global stiffness matrices. This criterion, which comes in two different forms, according to the strain tensor chosen, is based on a linearisation about the current computation step. It accepts any type of strain tensor, as well as any type of constitutive relation for which one is able to construct the global stiffness matrix, at each time instant. Moreover, the criterion chosen is perfectly rigorous in the case of non-linear elastic constitutive relations, and may be extended to the case of elastoplasticity associated with the Hill assumption [bib4]. 2 Stability of a dissipative system 2.1 Definition of the stability of a dissipative system When one is interested in dissipative phenomena (case of plastic or brittle materials...) one adds, in the expression of the total energy Φ , a term representing the dissipated part. r7.05.02 Static stability analysis of embankment slopes r7.05.02 Static stability analysis of embankment slopes Summary: The command CALC_STAB_PENTE makes it possible to analyse the static stability of embankment slopes modelled in 2D in hydraulic works such as dams, slopes and dykes around reservoirs, taking into account the pore pressure in the porous medium and possibly other types of mechanical loading. In general, in order to analyse the static stability of slopes according to the various professional regulations in the world, one uses the method of progressive reduction of the material properties ( SRM method – strengh reduction method ), or else the method based on the limit-equilibrium theory ( LEM method ). Both are available in CALC_STAB_PENTE, so that the command adapts to all circumstances of analysis under static conditions. In this document one presents in detail the algorithms implemented in CALC_STAB_PENTE. 1 Introduction 1.1 Definition of the stability of embankment slopes In a general way, the regulations on the design and the verification of embankment works require that the factor of safety (FS) associated with the static stability of the work does not exceed an imposed threshold. This factor of safety, whose definition may vary according to the category of the calculation methods used, measures in all cases the safety margin of the slope with respect to the failure state. Its value often depends on the geometry of the work, on the mechanical loadings applied and on the properties of the material. In practice, the factor of safety is verified once the static loadings to which the work is subjected have been taken into account. Failure of the slope occurs when the plasticised zone of the material forms a continuous surface linking two ends on the profile of the slope. One thus defines this zone as being the failure surface. Along the failure surface, the shear strength of the soil becomes insufficient to resist the tangential stresses[bib1]_. Several processes can lead to the failure of slopes[bib2]_: - Reduction of the shear resistance force , for example: - Increase of the pore pressure because of the infiltration of water into the work. - Appearance of cracks around the crest of the work. - Loss of strength of the clayey fill. - Increase of the shear stresses , for example: - Loading on the crest of the work. - Excavation at the toe of the slope. - Rapid drop of the upstream water level. The shape of the failure surface depends on the nature of the slope. For slopes made up of homogeneous and isotropic materials, the failure surface is probably circular, which leads to rotational slip. On the other hand, if the materials constituting the slope are heterogeneous or anisotropic, the surface will be non-circular, thus leading to stepped slip. Given the complexity of the failure mechanism and of the influencing factors, the practice in geotechnics is to employ mathematical tools (analytical or numerical) for the computation of the factor of safety. As a result, a great multitude of calculation methods developed during the past century. In the command CALC_STAB_PENTE two categories of the most popular methods are implemented, offering an effective tool for computing the factor of safety of slopes and visualising the failure surface. 1.2 Reminder of the functionalities of CALC_STAB_PENTE The command CALC_STAB_PENTE makes it possible to analyse the static stability of embankment slopes modelled in 2D by two categories of method: - SRM method : the method of progressive reduction of the parameters linked to the shear strength of the material (named the SRM method). This method was proposed by Griffiths et al. in 1999. - LEM method : a series of methods based on the limit-equilibrium theory (named the LEM method), including the simplified Bishop, Fellenius, Spencer and Morgenstern-Price procedures. The first ( SRM ) is based on a non-linear finite-element analysis, and proposes to approach the factor of safety by modelling the failure of the slope. It therefore requires more care when configuring the analysis. Nevertheless, by dividing the slope into rigid slices, the second method ( LEM ) is often numerically more efficient and is usually recommended by the design regulations for hydraulic works (despite the assumptions required on the interaction between the different slices). The functionalities of CALC_STAB_PENTE are explained in more detail in the document CALC_STAB_PENTE. 2 SRM method 2.1 General remarks on the SRM method The SRM method takes advantage of the accuracy of modelling by the finite-element method in order to analyse the stability of slopes without needing to assume the slip circles in advance. Indeed, by using a failure criterion of Mohr-Coulomb or Drucker-Prager type, the SRM method defines the factor of safety as being the ratio between the initial material parameters and the reduced parameters leading to the divergence of the non-linear analysis under the static loadings applied : \mathit{FS} = \frac{\cohesion}{{\cohesion}_{i}} = \frac{\tan(\anglFric )}{\tan({\anglFric }_{i})} = \frac{\tan(\anglDila )}{\tan({\anglDila }_{i})} where - \anglDila is the dilatancy angle of the material - \cohesion and \anglFric represent respectively the cohesion and the friction angle of the material constituting the embankment. Griffiths et al. show that the expression has the same physical meaning as the traditional definition by the ratio between the resistance force and the tangential force along the failure surface. As fig1-srm illustrates, the software treatment in the command CALC_STAB_PENTE of the SRM method is carried out in three stages: - Stage 1 : Treatment of the SRM zone. One identifies the materials existing in the SRM zone indicated, and one creates the mesh-cell groups in the SRM zone in order to reassign the field of the degraded materials. - Stage 2 : Creation of the field of the degraded materials. One then tests the convergence of the non-linear analysis and one refines the increment of the factor of safety until the analysis diverges and the desired accuracy is reached. - Stage 3 : Post-processing. If requested, one obtains as output the cumulative plastic strain field (V1 of the field VARI_NOEU) in order to visualise the failure surface. Diagram of the SRM method 2.2 Treatment of the SRM zone The command CALC_STAB_PENTE makes it possible to define the zone where the SRM algorithm applies. This functionality is particularly suitable when the model comprises several slopes and one wishes to check the stability of a slope which does not necessarily undergo the most significant failure risk. It should be noted that the SRM zone can be defined by mesh-cell groups distinct from those which are assigned in the input material field. In that case one identifies the materials in the SRM zone and one reassigns the mesh-cell groups by the overloading principle. As fig2-srm-mater illustrates, for each mesh-cell group in the SRM zone, one examines whether it has mesh cells in common with the mesh-cell groups assigned by the materials present in the aster object CHAM_MATER. Diagram of the generation of the degraded cham_mater in the SRM zone 2.3 Reduction of the strength properties of the materials The Mohr-Coulomb and Drucker-Prager failure criteria are authorised in CALC_STAB_PENTE. At the same time as the generation of the field of the degraded materials, one checks that there exists exactly one constitutive law among the two assigned to the SRM zone by the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT. According to the expression, the degraded properties are computed by: \tan({\anglFric}^{\prime}) = \frac{\tan(\anglFric)}{\mathit{FS}} \text{ et } {\cohesion^{\prime}} = \frac{\cohesion}{\mathit{FS}} One makes the assumption of the associated plastic flow law of the Mohr-Coulomb behaviour, that is {\anglFric}^{\prime}={\anglDila}^{\prime} . In the contrary case, the dilatancy angle will automatically take the value of the friction angle during the execution of the SRM algorithm. Apart from the Mohr-Coulomb criterion, it is also possible to employ the Drucker-Prager criterion, which improves the singularity problem caused by the vertices of the cone of the Mohr-Coulomb yield surface in the \pi plane. Instead of directly reducing the Drucker-Prager parameters ( {\alpha} and \yieldStress ), the command favours the phi-c strategy in order to avoid the conservatism of the result: \tan {\anglFric}^{\prime} = \frac{3{\alpha}}{2\mathit{FS}\sqrt{(2{\alpha}+1)(1-{\alpha})}} \text{ et } {\cohesion}^{\prime} = \frac{\yieldStress}{2\mathit{FS}\sqrt{(2{\alpha}+1)(1-{\alpha})}} \text{ et } \tan{ {\anglDila }^{\prime}} = \frac{\tan{\anglDila }}{\mathit{FS}} 2.4 Control of the convergence of the FS In order to accelerate the search for the factor of safety (FS), it is possible to control the iterative solution by configuring the parameters linked to the refinement of the increment {dP} (fig1-srm) according to the method indicated. The increment decreases each time the non-linear analysis diverges until the maximum residual is reached. Two laws of variation of the increment {dP} are available: 1. 'EXPONENTIELLE' : Exponential variation The increment of the factor of safety approaches the maximum residual in an exponential manner. At the n-th refinement, the increment is computed by: {p}_{n} = {p}_{0} \, {2}^{-n} until {p}_{N} ] one therefore adopts the EFWA as the optimisation algorithm. The EFWA simulates the explosion process of fireworks. In the space of the state variables depicted as the night sky, one explodes the fireworks at different places. Each explosion locally generates sparks in order to search for the optimum in the neighbouring space. Among these sparks, certain ones which present a high selective value (inversely proportional to the FS) are kept for the next explosion. The EFWA proceeds in three stages: 1. Random generation of the N initial fireworks The vector of the state variables comprises N+1 components, which are the abscissae of the end points of the failure surface, and N-1 which are the ordinates of the intermediate points, where N is the number of slices: X=\lbrace {x}_{0},{y}_{1}, \cdots ,{y}_{N-1},{x}_{N}\rbrace If one does not specify the initial state via the operand ETAT_INIT of CALC_STAB_PENTE, one randomly generates {N}_{\mathit{FA}} initial positions of the fireworks (uniform distribution law): {X}_{i} = \rand \left( {x}_{\min,i},{x}_{\max,i} \right ) One notes that \rand([i,j]) is a random-number generator in the interval [i,j] and where the limits of the degrees of freedom are determined by the algorithm described in section 3.4.2.2. If one supplies to ETAT_INIT the table output by CALC_STAB_PENTE, one adds it into the initial generation of the fireworks. 2. Generation of the ordinary and Gaussian sparks During the generation of the ordinary sparks from the explosion position i , the amplitude of the explosion is computed by: {A}_{i} = A \, \frac{\mathit{FS} \left({X}_{i} \right)-{\mathit{FS}}_{\min}+\varepsilon} {\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathit{FS}({X}_{i})-{\mathit{FS}}_{\min})+\varepsilon} where A is the value of the keyword A of CALC_STAB_PENTE denoting the total amplitude of the ordinary sparks, and \varepsilon=1.0 \times 10^-8 is a constant close to zero in order to avoid division by zero. By the equation one searches in a wider interval if the central position is of insufficient quality, and one concentrates on the space close to the minimum value of FS. According to the equation, the explosion amplitude will be very small around the surface minimising the FS in the current iteration, which restricts the local search capability. Therefore, one corrects the explosion amplitude by a lower limit which decreases during the iterations: A_{\textrm{min}}(N) = A_{\textrm{init}} - \frac{A_{\textrm{init}} - A_{\textrm{fina}}}{N_{\textrm{max}}}\sqrt{(2N_{\textrm{max}} - N)N} where N is the number of the current iteration and N_{\textrm{max}} is the maximum number of EFWA iterations defined in the keyword ITER_MAXI. By default the parameters A_{\textrm{init}} and A_{\textrm{fina}} are fixed at 100% and 10% of the width of the slices. It is also possible to define them manually via the keywords A_INIT and A_FINAL. The number of ordinary sparks of an explosion is computed by: {S}_{i} = M \, \frac{{\mathit{FS}}_{\max}-\mathit{FS}({X}_{i})+\varepsilon} {\sum_{i=1}^{N}({\mathit{FS}}_{\max}-\mathit{FS}({X}_{i}))+\varepsilon} where M is the value of the keyword M of CALC_STAB_PENTE denoting the total number of ordinary sparks. By the equation one generates more sparks if the central position is of good quality. In order to avoid the appearance of absurd numbers, one corrects: \widehat{S}_{i} = \left\lbrace \begin{array}{l} \round(aM) & \text{si } S_{i} bM \\ \round(S_{i}) & \text{sinon } \end{array} \right. One generates the ordinary sparks by arbitrarily modifying the degrees of freedom of the positions of the current generation: \widehat{X}_{i}^{k} = {X}_{i}^{k} + {\Delta}{X}^{k} \text{ avec } \Delta{X}^{k}={A}_{i}\rand{-1,1}) In order always to keep the diversity of the search for the optimum, one also generates the Gaussian sparks of quantity {M}_{g} . One selects in an arbitrary manner the firework positions, and one arbitrarily modifies the degrees of freedom: \widehat{X}_{i}^{k} = {X}_{i}^{k} + \left( {X}_{B}^{k}-{X}_{i}^{k} \right) e \text{ avec } e=N(\left\{0,1\right\}) where {X}_{B}^{k} is the position corresponding to the minimum FS of the current generation. If certain degrees of freedom are outside the limits determined by the algorithm described in section 3.4.2.2, one projects them into the admissible band: \widehat{X}_{i}^{k} = {X}_{\min,i}^{k} + \rand(\left\{0,1 \right\}) \, \left( {X}_{\max,i}^{k}-{X}_{\min,i}^{k} \right) Because the modification of a degree of freedom influences the admissible band of the intermediate points to its right, one also adjusts them so that the failure surface generated is kinematically admissible. Finally, in the case where the failure surface generated is so close to the slope profile that it is impossible to create the mesh-cell group of the slices, one evaluates the admissible band of the degrees of freedom by taking into account the size of the 2D elements around the slope profile or the imposed MARGE_PENTE, and one adjusts the parameters of the new surfaces by a recursive algorithm (ref. 3.4.2.2) by rechecking the admissible bands of the degrees of freedom which follow. 3. Selection of the sparks for the next generation The new generation of fireworks occurs through the roulette algorithm. The probability that an ordinary or Gaussian spark is kept in the next generation is: {p}_{i} = \frac{{\mathit{FS}}_{\max}-{\mathit{FS}}_{i}} {{\mathit{FS}}_{\max}-{\mathit{FS}}_{\min}} The diagram of the EFWA algorithm is represented in fig14-diag-EFWA. Diagram of the EFWA algorithm 3.4.2.2 Dynamic constraints on the state variables Illustration of the constraints on the state variables In order to ensure that the failure surface is always convex and kinematically admissible, one adopts the procedure proposed by Cheng et al. in order to determine the dynamic constraints on the state variables. In this procedure, the limits of the ordinates of the intermediate points depend on one or two preceding points (to the left). Let us take the example in fig15-cont-VarEtat: - Lower bound : - The failure surface making an angle of less than 45 degrees with the slope profile at the end point A, which determines the lower bound of the point C. - One extends the straight line AC up to the abscissa of the point D in order to determine the lower bound of the point D. - Upper bound : - One links CB and checks whether CB intersects the slope profile. If that is the case, one finds the intersection point of minimum ordinate J and links CJ in order to determine the upper bound D2 of the point D. Otherwise, D1 will be the upper bound of the point D. In order to ensure that the failure surface remains in the domain, one adjusts the lower bound to the bottom of the domain if it lies below the latter. 1. In CALC_STAB_PENTE one adopts a stochastic strategy which chooses a random number of surfaces at each EFWA iteration and generates / modifies the intermediate points in the reverse direction, that is from the active end (at the top) to the passive end (at the bottom). This makes it possible to increase the topological diversity of the potential surfaces, and therefore to accelerate the convergence of the EFWA. It also increases the probability of falling upon the exact solution of the critical surface thanks to the enlarged search space. 2. In a manner similar to the generation of the circular surfaces, a recursive algorithm applies to the verification of the consistency of the surfaces and to the automatic correction in the explosion phase of the EFWA. In the absence of the parameter MARGE_PENTE explicitly defined by the user, one recovers the size of the 2D elements around the slope profile by analysing the mesh and one ensures that the surface moves away from the slope by a distance greater than the vertical size of these elements at the edges. 3.5 Mesh adaptation Diagram of the stability analysis with mesh refinement The stability analysis via CALC_STAB_PENTE being based on the mesh, its fineness significantly influences the result of the factor of safety. As a result, CALC_STAB_PENTE automates the mesh refinement. However, the computation time increases all the more as the mesh is fine. As a result, as fig16-sensibilite-maillage shows, one isolates the mesh refinement at the moment of the search for the critical surface, given that the fineness of the mesh has a negligible influence on the location of the failure surface. In order to accelerate the creation of the slice groups, with the aid of the command MACR_ADAP_MAIL, one refines the mesh only on the contour of the slices until the maximum number of refinements is reached or until the stabilisation of FS. This process is driven by a proximity-indicator field expressed in the form of a Gaussian function of zero mean and of standard deviation \sigma : \mathit{val} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }\sigma }\exp\left(\frac{-{d}_{\min}^{2}}{2{\sigma}^{2}} \right) where {d}_{\min} is the minimum distance between a node of the mesh and the contour of the slices. One refines the mesh cells according to a criterion given by the value of \sigma , that is 68% of the mesh cells closest to the contour, and one unrefines the mesh cells according to the criterion of value 2 \,\sigma , that is 5% of the mesh cells furthest from the contour. One decreases the standard deviation in an exponential manner in order to control dynamically the refinement zone. Mesh-adaptation algorithm fig17-algo-adapt-maillage illustrates the mesh-adaptation algorithm and the result of the adapted mesh. 4 Validation and verification of the functionalities | ZZZZ135 | V1.01.135 | Software validation of the SRM methods in the command CALC_STAB_PENTE | | --- | --- | --- | | ZZZZ146 | V1.01.146 | Software validation of the LEM methods in the command CALC_STAB_PENTE | | SSNP507 | V6.03.507 | Stability analysis of an undrained clayey slope on a weak foundation | | SSNP006 | V6.03.006 | Stability analysis of a homogeneous slope by the Bishop method | | SSNP007 | V6.03.007 | Stability analysis of an undrained slope with a weak layer by the Morgenstern-Price method | | SSNP008 | V6.03.006 | Stability of a two-level slope with phreatic line and matric suction | | SSNP009 | V6.03.006 | Stability of a homogeneous slope with the suction evaluated by the water-retention curve | | SSNP010 | V6.03.006 | Stability of a slope subjected to the seismic inertial force | | SSNP011 | V6.03.006 | Computation of the critical acceleration coefficient of homogeneous and stratified slopes | 5 Bibliography Griffiths, D. r7.07.01 Calculation of the limit load by the Norton-Hoff-Friaâ method, constitutive behaviour NORTON_HOFF r7.07.01 Calculation of the limit load by the Norton-Hoff-Friaâ method, constitutive behaviour NORTON_HOFF Summary: Limit analysis makes it possible to determine the admissible loadings of a structure, of given fixed geometry, constituted of a material having a strength criterion. One considers the case of loadings constituted of the sum of a permanent load and of another parameterised by the load factor, whose extreme supportable value one seeks. After a reminder of the theoretical formulation, one presents the regularised kinematic approach applied to the Von Mises strength criterion (Norton-Hoff-Friaâ method) and implemented in Code_Aster . One may refer to [bib4] for the various possible regularisation methods proposed in the literature. One then sets out the calculation of the solutions of this non-linear problem and the post-processing providing an estimate of the limit load (a value from above in every case, and when there is no permanent loading, a value from below). > Contents 1 Theoretical formulation of limit analysis 1.1 Definition of the limit load One considers a solid occupying a bounded domain \Omega subjected to surface loadings \lambda F+{F}_{0} on the boundary {\Gamma}_{f} and to volume loadings \lambda f+{f}_{0} on \Omega . One distinguishes the loading (F,f) , parameterised by the positive real \lambda , and the “permanent” loading ({F}_{0},{f}_{0}) . The homogeneous Dirichlet conditions which are applied on the complementary boundary {\Gamma}_{u} of \partial \Omega (an imposed displacement or an initial anelastic strain – thermal, plastic… – have no effect on the domain of the admissible loads). One may find in [bib5] several other useful properties. The constitutive material of the solid possesses a strength criterion expressed by a scalar function of the stresses, negative for the admissible stresses. The criterion used for a material of the perfect elastoplastic type with a von Mises threshold and retained here is: g(\sigma )=J(\sigma )-{\sigma}_{y}=\sqrt{}.\sqrt{{\sigma}^{D}.{\sigma}^{D}}-{\sigma}_{y}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\sqrt{{({\sigma}_{1}-{\sigma}_{2})}^{2}+{({\sigma}_{2}-{\sigma}_{3})}^{2}+{({\sigma}_{1}-{\sigma}_{3})}^{2}}-{\sigma}_{y} | {\sigma}^{D} | is the deviator of the stress tensor, | | --- | --- | | {\sigma}_{y} | is the strength threshold in simple tension (like a yield limit), possibly variable according to the zones of the solid considered. | | {\sigma}_{i} | being the principal stresses of \sigma . | Given this strength criterion one seeks to calculate the limit value of \lambda , called the limit load {\lambda}_{\lim} , for which the structure can support the loadings {\lambda}_{\lim}F+{F}_{0} and {\lambda}_{\lim}f+{f}_{0} . Strictly speaking, the value {\lambda}_{\lim} denotes the limit of the supportable loadings, but for the materials obeying the Principle of Maximum Plastic Work, this value is the limit of the supported loadings. 1.2 Calculation of the limit load by a kinematic approach In yield design two approaches are possible: the static approach (in stress variables) and the kinematic approach (in velocity variables). These approaches provide bounds of the limit load: a lower bound for the static approach and an upper bound for the kinematic approach. When the two provide the same result, the limit load obtained is exact. The kinematic approach is the one used in Code_Aster by means of displacement finite elements . For the given loading , one defines the space of the kinematically admissible and normalised velocities by: {V}_{a}^{1}=\left\lbrace v\text{admissible,}v=0\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{u},L(v)={\int}_{\Omega}f.vd\Omega +{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{f}}F.v\text{ds}=1\right\rbrace This normalisation forces the work of the loading to be unity. The power of the “permanent” loading ({F}_{0},{f}_{0}) is denoted: {L}_{0}(v) . From the strength criterion in stresses g(\sigma ) , one defines: - the set of admissible stresses by: {G}_{(x)}=\left\lbrace \sigma (x),g(\sigma (x))\le 0\text{}\right\rbrace ( {G}_{(x)} is convex for the criterion g ) - the indicator function: {\Psi}_{G}(\sigma (x))=\lbrace \begin{array}{c}0,\text{si}\sigma (x)\in {G}_{(x)}\\ +\infty ,\text{si}\sigma (x)\notin {G}_{(x)}\end{array} - the support function: \pi (\varepsilon )=\underset{\sigma \in {\mathrm{IR}}^{6}}{\text{Sup}}\left[\sigma .\varepsilon -{\Psi}_{G}(\sigma )\right] The Sup in \pi (\varepsilon ) can be attained only if \sigma is chosen in {G}_{(x)} , such that: \sigma =\lambda {\varepsilon}^{D}+\mu \text{Id} (which ensures \sigma \text{//}{\varepsilon}^{D} ). The optimum corresponds to g(\bar{\sigma})=0\Rightarrow \bar{\lambda}={\sigma}_{y}\sqrt{}.{({\varepsilon}^{D}.{\varepsilon}^{D})}^{-1/2} Figure 1.2-a: Optimum \bar{\sigma} and graph of the function \pi (\varepsilon ) in 1D Hence the support function: \pi (\varepsilon (v))={\sigma}_{y}.\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\sqrt{\epsilon (v).\epsilon (v)}+\underset{\mu \in \text{IR}}{\text{Sup}}(\mu .divv)={\pi}_{R}(\varepsilon (v))+\underset{\mu \in \text{IR}}{\text{Sup}}(\mu .divv) One observes that the function \pi (\varepsilon ) , which is interpreted as the density of dissipatable power at the material point, is not differentiable at 0 . One does not treat to date in Code_Aster the possible internal surfaces of discontinuity within the solid \Omega [bib 4]. The kinematic approach is defined by means of the convex functional {S}_{e}(v) , positively homogeneous of degree one, for v\in {V}_{a}^{1} defined on the whole domain: \begin{array}{cc}{S}_{e}(v)& ={\int}_{\Omega}\pi (\varepsilon (v))d\Omega \end{array}-{L}_{0}(v) This functional is the integral over the domain of the support function \pi of the convex {G}_{(x)} , calculated at \varepsilon (v) and is interpreted as the maximum resisting power in the velocity field (the contribution of interface resistance on discontinuity surfaces is assumed zero). The support function \pi is positively homogeneous of degree 1, and therefore the functional {S}_{e}(v) is too as a consequence. With the Von Mises criterion the power functional {S}_{e}(v) is: {S}_{e}(v)={\int}_{\Omega}\left[{\sigma}_{y}.\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\sqrt{\varepsilon (v).\varepsilon (v)}+\underset{q\in \text{IR}}{\text{Sup}}(q.divv)\right]d\Omega -{\text{L}}_{0}(v) eq 1.2-1 where one observes that only the fields v belonging to C=\left\lbrace v\in {V}_{a}^{1},divv=0\text{dans}\Omega \right\rbrace provide finite values. The fields v must therefore satisfy the so-called incompressibility condition divv=\text{tr}\varepsilon (v)=0 . This is why one must use the quasi-incompressible elements for a limit-load calculation with the Von Mises criterion R3.06.08. The limit load {\lambda}_{\lim} given by the kinematic approach is: {\lambda}_{\lim}=\underset{\mathrm{v}\in {V}_{a}^{1}}{\text{Inf}}{S}_{e}\left(\mathrm{v}\right)=\underset{\begin{array}{c}\mathrm{v}\in {V}_{a}^{1}\\ L\left(v\right)>0\end{array}}{\text{Inf}}\frac{{S}_{e}\left(v\right)}{L\left(v\right)}=\underset{l>0}{\text{Sup}}\underset{\mathrm{v}\in {V}_{a}}{\text{Inf}}\left({S}_{e}\left(\mathrm{v}\right)-l\left(L\left(\mathrm{v}\right)-1\right)\right) where l is the Lagrange multiplier. At the optimum one obtains a solution u and the limit load {\lambda}_{\lim} (non-uniqueness of u but uniqueness of {\lambda}_{\lim} ). Thus, every loading {L}_{0}(v)+\lambda L(v) with 0\le \lambda \le {\lambda}_{\lim} is supportable. Beyond {\lambda}_{\lim} , the equilibrium problem has no solution. Note: There exist situations where, even if {L}_{0}(v) is not supportable alone, the combination {L}_{0}(v)+\lambda L(v) , for {\lambda}_{1}\le \lambda \le {\lambda}_{2} , becomes so over a certain interval, and not only for two collinear loadings. Note: The limit load calculated for a two-dimensional problem, in plane strain, is necessarily greater than that obtained for this problem modelled in plane stress. This result therefore provides an upper bound. If one wishes to treat a problem in plane stress, it is then necessary to carry out the kinematic approach on a three-dimensional modelling. 1.3 Regularisation of the kinematic approach by the Norton-Hoff-Friaâ method The numerical implementation of the kinematic approach requires the minimisation of the non-differentiable functional {S}_{e}(v) . Numerous regularisation techniques exist [bib4]. The Norton-Hoff-Friâa method is used here [bib2], [bib7]. It rests on precursor work by Casciaro in 1971. It consists in replacing the support function \pi (\varepsilon ) by the regularised and differentiable support function {\pi}^{\mathrm{NH}}(\varepsilon ) . It is adjustable by a regularisation parameter m ( 1\le m\le 2 ), whose limit value m\to {1}^{+} leads to convergence towards the support function \pi (\varepsilon ) : {\pi}^{\text{NH}}(\varepsilon )=\frac{{k}^{1-m}}{m}{(\pi (\varepsilon ))}^{m} eq 1.3-1 The scalar k in [eq 1.3-1] is homogeneous to a stress. One denotes the space of admissible velocities adapted to the viscous flow problem for the Norton-Hoff law of order m : {V}_{a}^{\mathrm{m1}}=\left\lbrace v\in {L}^{m}(\Omega ),\text{et}\varepsilon (v)\in {L}^{m}(\Omega ),v=0\text{sur}{\Gamma}_{u},L(v)=1\right\rbrace One defines on this space the regularised functional {S}_{e}^{m}(v) : {S}_{e}^{m}(v)={\int}_{\Omega}\frac{{k}^{1-m}}{m}\pi {(\varepsilon (v))}^{m}d\Omega -{L}_{0}(v) The minimisation problem \underset{v\in {V}_{a}^{\mathrm{m1}}}{\text{Inf}}\left[{S}_{e}^{m}(v)\right] is well posed thanks to the properties of the spaces {L}^{m}(O) and admits a unique solution {u}_{m} , for which the value attained by the is precisely {\lambda}_{m} . One denotes the space of the incompressible fields of {V}_{a}^{m1} by: \tilde{{V}_{a}^{m1}}=\left\lbrace v\in {V}_{a}^{m1}\text{tel}\text{que}divv=0\right\rbrace One then shows that this problem can also be written in the form of the search for the saddle-point ({\lambda}_{m},{u}_{m}) of the following Lagrangian: \underset{l\in \text{IR}}{\text{Max}}\left[\underset{\mathrm{v}\in \tilde{{V}_{a}^{m}}}{\text{Inf}}\phantom{\rule{0.5em}{0ex}}\left\lbrace {\int}_{\Omega}\frac{A\left(m\right)}{m}.{\left(\sqrt{\epsilon (\mathrm{v}).\epsilon (\mathrm{v})}\right)}^{m}d\Omega -{L}_{0}(\mathrm{v})-l\left(L(\mathrm{v})-1\right)\right\rbrace \right] eq 1.3-2 with: A(m)={k}^{1-m}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{m/2}.{\sigma}_{y}^{m}={\sigma}_{y}^{2-m}.{(3\mu )}^{m-1}.{(\frac{2}{3})}^{m/2} . One notes that A(m) is increasing with m (if E\ge {\sigma}_{y} , which is the case in practice) and homogeneous to a stress, and remains bounded when m\to {1}^{+} . If one chooses k={\sigma}_{y} , then A(m)={\sigma}_{y}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{m/2} and one recovers the incompressible elastic problem when m=2 , if one chooses a Young's modulus E={\sigma}_{y} . One therefore observes that this potential [eq 1.3-2] defines a constitutive law giving the stress tensor \sigma (u) by the Norton-Hoff constitutive relation, see [§2.1]. One thus constructs a decreasing sequence of {\lambda}_{m} and the limit load {\lambda}_{\lim} is the limit of this sequence when m\to {1}^{+} (that is n\to +\infty ): {\lambda}_{\lim}=\underset{m\to 1}{\lim}(\underset{v\in {V}_{a}^{\mathrm{m1}}}{\text{Inf}}\left[{S}_{e}^{m}(v)\right])=\underset{m\to 1}{\lim}({S}_{e}^{m}({u}_{m})) eq 1.3-3 For the proof one will refer to [bib4] and [bib7]. Note: If one amplifies the intensity of the loading L\to \beta L (whereas one does not consider a permanent loading {L}_{0}=0 ), the solutions depend on the factor \beta according to the following relations: {u}_{m}(\beta )={\beta}^{-1}{u}_{m}(1);{\sigma}^{D}({u}_{m}(\beta ))={\beta}^{1-m}{\sigma}^{D}({u}_{m}(1));{S}_{e}^{m}({u}_{m}(\beta ))={\beta}^{-m}{S}_{e}^{m}({u}_{m}(1)) . At convergence for m\to {1}^{+} , the conclusion given by the solution {u}_{m}(\beta ) is indeed the same as that given by {u}_{m}(1) , since {\lambda}_{\lim}(\beta )={\lambda}_{\lim}(1)/\beta . 2 Numerical aspects of the calculation of the limit load 2.1 Norton-Hoff constitutive relation The stress tensor \sigma (u) satisfies the Norton-Hoff constitutive relation. The stress deviator associated with the strain rate is: {\sigma}^{D}\left(\mathrm{u}\right)=A\left(m\right).{\left(\sqrt{{\epsilon}^{D}\left(\mathrm{u}\right).{\epsilon}^{D}\left(\mathrm{u}\right)}\right)}^{m-2}.{\epsilon}^{D}\left(\mathrm{u}\right) eq 2.1-1 with \text{tr}\varepsilon (u)=0 , and: A(m)={k}^{1-m}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{m/2}{\sigma}_{y}^{m} . This behaviour is integrated in the same way as the incremental elastoplastic Von Mises behaviours R5.03.02. Let us note however that, at an integration point, the calculation of the stress tensor as a function of the strain tensor is explicit, no iterative scheme being used. Moreover, no internal variable is necessary for the integration of this behaviour. In Code_Aster , the calculation of the limit load being independent of the elasticity coefficients , one chooses k={\sigma}_{y} , whence A(m)={\sigma}_{y}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{m/2} . One thus recovers the incompressible elastic problem when m=2 , for a Young's modulus E={\sigma}_{y} . Moreover, the sequence of the scalars m is deduced directly from the list of (fictitious) calculation time instants by: m=1+{10}^{1-t} , so that when the time instant increases, m tends towards 1, and the behaviour approaches a perfect rigid-plastic behaviour, see in one dimension the curves [fig. 2.1-a]. In practice, one chooses the sequence of the values of [tab. 2.1-a]. Fig. 2.1-a.
