The tangent operator, used in the option FULL_MECA of Newton's method, is written thanks to [eq 2.1-1]: {\begin{array}{c}\frac{d{\sigma}^{D}}{d{\varepsilon}^{D}}\end{array}\mid }_{\varepsilon (u)}=A(m){\parallel {\varepsilon}^{D}\parallel }^{m-2}(\text{Id}\otimes \text{Id}+(m-2){\parallel {\varepsilon}^{D}\parallel }^{-2}{\varepsilon}^{D}\otimes {\varepsilon}^{D}) eq 2.1-2 with {\varepsilon}^{D} , {\sigma}^{D} the vectors of the deviatoric strains and stresses written in the vector notations of WALPOLE-COWIN: {\varepsilon}^{D}=({\varepsilon}_{11}^{D},{\varepsilon}_{22}^{D},{\varepsilon}_{33}^{D},\sqrt{2}{\varepsilon}_{12}^{D},\sqrt{2}{\varepsilon}_{23}^{D},\sqrt{2}{\varepsilon}_{31}^{D}) {\sigma}^{D}=({\sigma}_{11}^{D},{\sigma}_{22}^{D},{\sigma}_{33}^{D},\sqrt{2}{\sigma}_{12}^{D},\sqrt{2}{\sigma}_{23}^{D},\sqrt{2}{\sigma}_{31}^{D}) 2.2 Piloting The problem is written in variational form in the following way on the space of incompressible fields. For a given m , therefore at a given time instant t , knowing the solution at the previous time instant (denoted {u}^{-},{\lambda}^{-} ), find (\Delta \lambda ,\Delta u)\in \mathrm{IR}\times \tilde{{V}_{a}} such that: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{\int}_{\Omega}\sigma ({u}^{-}+\Delta u).\varepsilon (v)d\Omega ={L}_{0}(v)+({\lambda}^{-}+\Delta \lambda )L(v)\forall v\in {\tilde{}V}_{0}\\ L(v)={\int}_{\Omega}f.vd\Omega +{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{f}}F.v\text{dS}=1\end{array} eq 2.2-1 - {L}_{0} is the permanent loading and L the loading piloted by the parameter \lambda , cf. [§1.1], - \tilde{{V}_{0}} is a space of functions discretised on the basis of incompressible finite elements, and is therefore defined by a vector (U) of degrees of freedom. This problem admits a unique solution for every 1\le m\le 2 (see [bib4]). For m=2 the problem is of incompressible linear elasticity type. The discretised problem at the time instant t (therefore for a value of m , cf. [tab. 2.1-a]) may be written (omitting the boundary conditions for simplicity): \lbrace \begin{array}{}{F}_{int}(\Delta U;{U}^{-};..)={F}_{0}^{\text{ext}}+\lambda {F}^{\text{ext}}\\ L({U}^{-}+\Delta U)=1\end{array} The search for \lambda ensuring the condition L(U)=1 is ensured by a piloting algorithm R5.03.80. Briefly, the principle is the following: by linearisation of the equations bearing on the internal forces, one obtains, for iteration n of Newton's algorithm, cf. R5.03.01: \underset{{K}_{T}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{\left[\frac{\partial {F}_{int}}{\partial U}(\Delta {U}^{n})\right]}}\left[\delta U\right]=\underset{{R}^{\text{cst}}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{\left[{F}_{0}^{\text{ext}}-{F}_{int}(\Delta {U}^{n})\right]}}+\lambda \underset{{R}^{\text{pilo}}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{\left[{F}^{\text{ext}}\right]}} eq 2.2-2 One can now express the corrections of displacements \delta U and of Lagrange multipliers \delta \lambda as a function of \lambda by means of the resolution of this linear system: \left[\delta U\right]=\left[\delta {U}^{\text{cst}}\right]+\lambda \left[\delta {U}^{\text{pilo}}\right]\text{où}\left[\delta {U}^{\text{cst}}\right]={K}_{{T}^{-1}}{R}^{\text{cst}}\text{et}\left[\delta {U}^{\text{pilo}}\right]={K}_{{T}^{-1}}{R}^{\text{pilo}} eq 2.2-3 One can substitute the displacement correction \delta U as a function of its expression [eq 2.2-2] into the control equation of the piloting of the system L(U)=1 ; there results a scalar equation in \Delta \lambda : L({U}^{-}+\Delta {U}^{n}+\delta {U}^{\text{cst}}+\lambda \delta {U}^{\text{pilo}})=1 that is {\int}_{\Omega}f.({U}^{-}+\Delta {U}^{n}+\delta {U}^{\text{cst}}+\lambda \delta {U}^{\text{pilo}})d\Omega +{\int}_{{\Gamma}_{f}}F.({U}^{-}+\Delta {U}^{n}+\delta {U}^{\text{cst}}+\lambda \delta {U}^{\text{pilo}})\text{dS}=1 eq 2.2-4 which in discretised form amounts to: \begin{array}{}\\ \sum_{e}{F}^{\text{ext}}.({U}^{-}+\Delta {U}^{n}+\delta {U}^{\text{cst}}+\lambda \delta {U}^{\text{pilo}})=1\end{array} which leads to: \lambda =\frac{1-\sum_{e}{F}^{\text{ext}}.({U}^{-}+\Delta {U}^{n}+\delta {U}^{\text{cst}})}{\sum_{e}{F}^{\text{ext}}.\delta {U}^{\text{pilo}}} eq 2.2-5 2.3 Post-processing of the calculation of the limit load Having obtained the solution ({\lambda}_{m},{u}_{m}) , for each time instant, therefore each given m , it remains to use the sequence of the {\lambda}_{m} in order to construct the approximation of the limit load. For this one exploits the properties [eq 1.3-2], [eq 1.3-3], the fact that A(m) is increasing and the property resulting from the minimisation [eq 1.3-2] (see [bib7]). From these last two, with 1\le r\le s , one deduces that for {u}_{r} and {u}_{s} respective solutions (also satisfying the incompressibility and normalisation condition) of [eq 1.3-2] for m=r and : ({\int}_{\Omega}A(r){(\varepsilon ({u}_{r}).\varepsilon ({u}_{r}))}^{r/2}d\Omega )\le ({\int}_{\Omega}A(s){(\varepsilon ({u}_{s}).\varepsilon ({u}_{s}))}^{s/2}d\Omega ) Associated with the property [eq 1.3-3], one draws for 1\le r\le s , denoting {\parallel \Omega \parallel }_{r}={\int}_{\Omega}A(r)d\Omega : {\int}_{\Omega}A(r)\sqrt{\varepsilon ({u}_{r}).\varepsilon ({u}_{r})}d\Omega \le {\parallel \Omega \parallel }_{r}^{1-\frac{1}{r}}{({\int}_{\Omega}A(r){(\varepsilon ({u}_{r}).\varepsilon ({u}_{r}))}^{r/2}d\Omega )}^{\frac{1}{r}}\le {\parallel \Omega \parallel }_{s}^{1-\frac{1}{s}}{({\int}_{\Omega}A(s){(\varepsilon ({u}_{s}).\varepsilon ({u}_{s}))}^{s/2}d\Omega )}^{\frac{1}{s}} eq 2.3-1 Indeed, this property results from the inclusion of the functional spaces {L}^{r}\supset {L}^{s} , for 1\le r\le s , that is also, where h(x) plays the role of a variable measure (conditioned by the strength limit {\sigma}_{y} ): {\parallel \Omega \parallel }_{r}^{-\frac{1}{r}}{({\int}_{\Omega}h(x){\mid f(x)\mid }^{r}d\Omega )}^{\frac{1}{r}}\le {\parallel \Omega \parallel }_{s}^{-\frac{1}{s}}{({\int}_{\Omega}h(x){\mid f(x)\mid }^{s}d\Omega )}^{\frac{1}{s}} One denotes the terms {\tilde{\lambda}}_{m} of the sequence below, which one calculates in practice by post-processing by means of {u}_{m} (the external power being unity: {\tilde{\lambda}}_{m}={\parallel \Omega \parallel }_{m}^{1-\frac{1}{m}}{({\int}_{\Omega}A(m){(\varepsilon ({u}_{m}).\varepsilon ({u}_{m}))}^{m/2}d\Omega )}^{\frac{1}{m}}\text{}-{L}_{0}({u}_{m}) eq 2.3-2 This sequence {\tilde{\lambda}}_{m} is therefore decreasing for m\to {1}^{+} and one shows [bib7] that it converges towards, which {\lambda}_{\lim} allows a good control. As one can bound from below (knowing that ) the first term of [eq 2.3-1]: {\lambda}_{\lim}\le {\int}_{\Omega}{\sigma}_{y}\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}\varepsilon ({u}_{m}).\varepsilon ({u}_{m})}d\Omega \text{}-{L}_{0}({u}_{m})\le {\tilde{\lambda}}_{m} one therefore calculates for each value of (therefore of the time instant t ) the limit load {\tilde{\lambda}}_{m} from above, also converging towards {\lambda}_{\lim} : {\lambda}_{\lim}\le {\hat{\lambda}}_{m}={\int}_{\Omega}{\sigma}_{y}\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}\varepsilon ({u}_{m}).\varepsilon ({u}_{m})}d\Omega \text{}-{L}_{0}({u}_{m}) eq 2.3-3 One judges the quality of the approximation of the limit load {\lambda}_{\lim} by comparison of the different values of {\tilde{\lambda}}_{m} which converge towards {\lambda}_{\lim} from above (as m\to {1}^{+} ). These terms are calculated by numerical integration at the Gauss points of the finite elements. Another interpretation of the interest that this sequence brings lies in the fact that it exploits directly the expression of the support function of the strength convex, that is the dissipatable power in the potential collapse modes, applied to the calculated incompressible and normalised solutions {u}_{m} . In the case where the permanent loading is zero: {L}_{0}=0 , one can easily exploit the stress field (almost statically admissible) calculated with the solution {u}_{m} and obtain a value by estimation of the limit load, which would necessarily be a true lower bound if equilibrium were satisfied exactly (see [bib4]). One therefore calculates the sequence {\underline{\lambda}}_{m} , which by contrast has no monotonicity properties: {\underline{\lambda}}_{m}={\int}_{\Omega}\frac{A(m)}{m}.{(\sqrt{\varepsilon ({u}_{m}).\varepsilon ({u}_{m})})}^{m}d\Omega .{(\underset{x\in \Omega }{\text{Sup}}(\frac{\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}{\sigma}^{D}({u}_{m}).{\sigma}^{D}({u}_{m})}}{{\sigma}_{y}}))}^{-1}\le {\hat{\lambda}}_{m} eq 2.3-4 This maximisation (of the function called the gauge of the strength convex) is calculated only at the Gauss points of the finite elements. Thus the value obtained, for each , lower than {\tilde{\lambda}}_{m} [bib4], can be considered only as an indication. By contrast, still in the case where the permanent loads are zero, it makes it possible, with the value from above {\tilde{\lambda}}_{m} , to provide a bracketing of the limit load of the discretised problem. 3 Functionalities and verification In order to carry out a calculation in Code_Aster in limit analysis with the Norton-Hoff-Friaâ regularisation method with the Von Mises strength criterion, one must: - define the 2D (plane or axisymmetric) or 3D model with the quasi-incompressible finite elements, modellings 3D_INCO_UPG, D_PLAN_INCO_UPG, or AXIS_INCO_UPG; - ensure the incompressibility condition: GONF=0 in AFFE_CHAR_MECA; - define only the material characteristic {s}_{y} , the limit load being independent of and \nu , - define the permanent loading and the one which is parameterised by \lambda ; - define the discretisation in time, (in practice between {t}_{min}=1 and {t}_{max}=2 to 5 ); - carry out a non-linear calculation with the constitutive relation NORTON_HOFF with the command STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03, and the piloting ANA_LIM. One may in practice use line search in order to improve the convergence, and the subdivision of the time step, - post-process the calculation in order to obtain the limit load with the command POST_ELEM U4.81.22. The use of these commands is detailed in the document U2.05.04. As regards the post-processing, the operator POST_ELEM then produces a table which gives for each time instant of the calculation, that is for increasingly weak regularisations, 2 parameters: - the parameter 'CHAR_LIMI_SUP' contains an upper bound of the limit load, by integration on each finite element and a sum over the set of the elements of the model: {\hat{\lambda}}_{m}={\int}_{\Omega}{\sigma}_{y}\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}\varepsilon ({u}_{m}).\varepsilon ({u}_{m})}d\Omega \text{}-{L}_{0}({u}_{m}) - and, in the absence of constant loading, (CHAR_CSTE ='NON'), the parameter 'CHAR_LIMI_ESTIMEE' contains an estimate of a lower bound {\underline{\lambda}}_{m} corresponding to: {\underline{\lambda}}_{m}={\int}_{\Omega}\frac{A(m)}{m}.{(\sqrt{\varepsilon ({u}_{m}).\varepsilon ({u}_{m})})}^{m}d\Omega .{(\underset{x\in \Omega }{\text{Sup}}(\frac{\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}{\sigma}^{D}({u}_{m}).{\sigma}^{D}({u}_{m})}}{{\sigma}_{y}}))}^{-1}\le {\hat{\lambda}}_{m} If a constant loading is present, (then it is imperative to enter CHAR_CSTE = 'OUI'), the parameter PUIS_CHAR_CSTE represents the power of the constant loading in the solution velocity field of the problem. Several verification tests are available, in particular the test SSNV124 V6.04.124. On this very simple problem, an analytical calculation makes it possible to obtain the exact limit load in the direction of the loading, as well as the estimates produced by the regularisation method. For more details one will refer to [bib4] and [bib5]. Furthermore complementary validations have been carried out within the framework of comparative studies, such as the European benchmark LISA [bib8, bib10]: on calculations of limit loads in 2D, 2D axisymmetric and 3D, the regularised kinematic method presented here makes it possible to gain a factor of 6 to 10 on the calculation time with respect to an incremental elastoplastic calculation, and makes it possible to obtain a bracketing of the limit load, unlike the methods of the other participants. 4 Bibliography 1. r7.10.01 Processing of random responses r7.10.01 Processing of random responses Summary: The introduction of a “stochastic approach to the seismic analysis” in order to solve a problem of vibratory mechanics under random excitation requires a particular post-processing. The command POST_DYNA_ALEA U4.76.02 makes it possible, from the power spectral density of a response cross-spectrum, to evaluate its standard deviation, its apparent frequency and the distribution of its peaks. It also makes it possible, as a first approach, to compute the Vanmarcke function, which is useful in the case of a seismic analysis. NB: This command also makes it possible to carry out the statistical estimates for any type of response cross-spectrum to a random excitation which is not necessarily seismic (for example: the effect of swell or of a turbulent flow). > Contents 1 Introduction For a structure subjected to a random excitation of swell, turbulent-flow or earthquake type..., the loading is not known in a deterministic manner, but is most often described by probabilistic or spectral information such as the power spectral density. For linear structures it is possible to use a stochastic computation method which makes it possible to determine the power spectral densities of the response to these random excitations. The operator POST_DYNA_ALEA has the function of carrying out the statistical analyses of the power spectral density of the response. It therefore supplies the probabilistic information on the response of the structure. The computations of statistical parameters are carried out on the basis of the computation of the spectral moments of the power spectral density considered. These statistical parameters are: the standard deviation, the apparent frequency, the peak factor according to the definition of Vanmarcke, the mean maximum and the irregularity factor. Note: The operator POST_DYNA_ALEA, designed initially for the seismic approach, after an analysis with the operator DYNA_ALEA_MODAL U4.56.06([bib1], [bib2]) , can also carry out the post-processings of the operator DYNA_SPEC_MODAL developed by the TTA department within the framework of the phasing-out of FLUSTRU. This operator carries out the computation of the response of a steam-generator tube structure uniformly excited by a transverse flow. 2 Spectrum - Cross-spectrum - Cross-spectral matrix 2.1 Signal processing - Conventions adopted 2.1.1 Introduction A signal can have two representations: a temporal representation of the form x=f(t) or a frequency representation of the form X=F(f) . These two representations are linked to one another by the Fourier transform. There exist, in the numerical domain and in the experimental domain, different ways of computing the spectral quantities relating to a temporal signal x(t) (dimensional representation or not, factor 1/2 or not for the Fourier transform). Now, if the various definitions of the PSD (cf. [§2.2.2] and [Appendix1]) from the Fourier transform of the signal change nothing in the computation carried out by CALC_INTE_SPEC U4.56.03, it is on the other hand important, in the computations carried out by the post-processing operator POST_DYNA_ALEA, that the data be consistent so that the results produced by this operator have the physical dimension of the original signal. It is also necessary to know, for a quantitative comparison between computation and experiment, what conventions are adopted for the computation of the spectral quantities. All of these conventions are recalled in [Appendix1] for each type of signal. Only the general formulae are given again here. 2.1.2 Fourier transform For the Fourier transform in frequency (f) of a signal (of unit u) , expressed in u/Hz, the following definition is adopted: X(f)=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}x(t){e}^{-2i\pi \text{ft}}\text{dt} The inverse transform is then expressed by: x(t)=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}X(f){e}^{+2i\pi \text{ft}}\text{df} One can also express the Fourier transform in circular frequency (\omega =2\pi f) , by the following definition: {X}^{p}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}x(t){e}^{-i\omega t}\text{dt} The inverse transform is expressed by: x(t)=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{X}^{p}(\omega ){e}^{+i\omega t}d\omega Which leads to the equivalence: {X}^{p}(\omega )={X}^{p}(2\pi f)=\frac{1}{2\pi }X(f) 2.2 Notion of power - Power spectral density 2.2.1 Power of a signal - Power spectrum of a signal Just as for the signal itself, the power of the signal can be expressed as a function of time or of frequency: - the instantaneous temporal power is simply called power: p(t)=x(t).\text{x }(t) where \text{x }(t) is the complex conjugate quantity of x(t) . - the frequency power is commonly called the power spectral density or spectrum: \underline{{S}_{xx}(f)=X(f).\text{X }(f)={\mid X(f)\mid }^{2}} This definition is possible only when the Fourier transform of the signal exists. One can then express the total energy of the signal by E=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{S}_{xx}(f)\text{df}=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{\mid X(f)\mid }^{2}\text{df} The expression for this PSD for the various types of signal is given in [Appendix1]. One will see later [§3.3] another definition — equivalent according to the Wiener-Khinchin theorem — but more general, of the power spectral density based on the statistical approach. 2.2.2 Interaction power - Interaction spectral density of two signals - Cross-spectrum - One also defines the instantaneous interaction power of two signals x(t)\text{et}y(t) : \begin{array}{}{p}_{xy}(t)=x(t).\text{y }(t)\text{et}{p}_{yx}(t)=\text{x }(t).y(t)\\ \text{reliées par}{p}_{xy}(t)={p}_{yx}\ast (t)\end{array} - If the two signals admit a Fourier transform X(f)\text{et}Y(f) , one can express the frequency interaction power or cross-spectrum by {S}_{\text{XY}}(f)=X(f).\text{Y }(f) - If the two signals are real then the interaction power {p}_{xy}(t)={p}_{yx}(t)=x(t).y(t) is real. But there is no reason for {S}_{\text{XY}}(f) also to be real; on the other hand {S}_{\text{XY}}(f) is complex with Hermitian symmetry, namely: even real part and odd imaginary part, or even modulus and odd phase - If X(f)=Y(f) , one then speaks of an auto-spectrum. 2.2.3 Cross-spectral matrix A cross-spectral matrix of order N is a complex N\times N matrix, each term of which depends on the frequency in the form of a function of f . The diagonal terms are the auto-spectra, the off-diagonal terms are the cross-spectra between the points considered (each row or column representing a point in the physical mesh or a mode in a modal analysis). The cross-spectra handled in practice being Hermitian, only the \frac{N(N+1)}{2} terms of the upper (or lower) triangle are sufficient to define the cross-spectral matrix completely. 2.3 Implementation in Code_Aster The cross-spectral matrices handled by the operator POST_DYNA_ALEA consist of complex functions of the frequency: {S}_{\text{XY}}(f) . These matrices are stored in tables of interspectre concept. 3 Reminders on the statistical laws [bib4] 3.1 Definitions t discrete parameter {({t}_{n})}_{n=\text{1,N}} or continuous (time or a space variable). X(t) random process. With each instant {t}_{n} is associated a random variable {X}_{n} , a random variable with realisation {x}_{n} . Then x(t)={({x}_{n}=x({t}_{n}))}_{n=1\text{,N}} is a realisation of the process X(t) , a process constituted of N a priori independent random variables. Each variable {X}_{n} is characterised by its cumulative distribution function {F}_{n}({\text{x,t}}_{n})=\text{Prob}({X}_{n}\le x) or by its probability density p({\text{x,t}}_{n})=\frac{\partial {F}_{n}}{\partial x}({\text{x,t}}_{n}) . The random process is also characterised by its moment functions ; the first two moments are of particular importance. These are the mathematical expectation or mean m(t) also denoted E\left[X(t)\right] and, for every pair ({t}_{1},{t}_{2}) , the autocorrelation function R({t}_{1},{t}_{2}) or {R}_{\text{XX}}({t}_{1},{t}_{2}) also denoted E\left[X({t}_{1})X({t}_{2})\right] . \begin{array}{}m(t)=E\left[X(t)\right]=\int\mathrm{xp}(x,t)\text{dx}\\ {R}_{\text{XX}}({t}_{1},{t}_{2})=E\left[X({t}_{1})X({t}_{2})\right]=\int\int{x}_{1}{x}_{2}p({x}_{1},{t}_{1};{x}_{2},{t}_{2}){\text{dx}}_{1}{\text{dx}}_{2}\end{array} One also defines a cross-correlation function for two processes X(t)\text{et}Y(t) . {R}_{\text{XY}}({t}_{1},{t}_{2})=E\left[X({t}_{1})Y({t}_{2})\right]=\int\int{x}_{1}{y}_{2}p({x}_{1},{t}_{1};{y}_{2},{t}_{2}){\text{dx}}_{1}{\text{dy}}_{2} The “spread” of the process is characterised by the variance : {\sigma}^{2}(t)=E\left[{(X(t)-\mu (t))}^{2}\right] For a zero-mean process ( \mu = 0.), the variance , which then characterises the “intensity of the phenomenon” (square of the standard deviation, or mean-square value), is equal to the autocorrelation function at time t={t}_{1}={t}_{2} : {\sigma}^{2}(t)=E\left[X(t)X(t)\right]={R}_{\text{XX}}(\text{t,t})=\int{x}^{2}p(x,t)\text{dx} 3.2 Assumptions in random dynamics Very classically, several assumptions are made within the framework of random dynamics. It is thus accepted that the processes studied are stationary, zero-mean and ergodic . 3.2.1 Stationary zero-mean processes - variance A process is said to be stationary if the whole of its “probabilistic characteristics” is invariant under a translation {t}_{0} of the parameter t . Which implies: \begin{array}{}\mu (t)=\text{Cte}\\ {R}_{\text{XX}}({t}_{1},{t}_{2})={R}_{\text{XX}}({t}_{2}-{t}_{1})={R}_{\text{XX}}(\tau )={R}_{\text{XX}}(-\tau )\end{array} For a zero-mean process {\sigma}^{2}={R}_{\text{XX}}(0) . 3.2.2 Ergodicity This notion comes from a reasoning of Gibbs (1839-1903) for which the observation time of a physical phenomenon can be considered as infinite compared with the time scale at the molecular level. The system then passes through all the possible states, remaining as long as possible, or passing most often, in the states which are the most probable, so that the temporal mean becomes equal to the statistical mean over the states , that is, the mathematical expectation. This extends to the correlation and cross-correlation functions. \begin{array}{}\mu =\underset{T\to +\infty }{\lim}\frac{1}{T}\underset{-T/2}{\overset{+T/2}{\int}}x(t)\text{dt}\\ {R}_{\text{XX}}(t)=\underset{T\to +\infty }{\lim}\frac{1}{T}\underset{-T/2}{\overset{+T/2}{\int}}x(t-\tau )x(t)\text{dt}\end{array} Note: For the remainder of the document it will be assumed that the random process is stationary and zero-mean. All of the developments carried out in Code_Aster satisfy these assumptions. 3.3 Power spectral density Within the framework of this statistical approach, one can give a very general definition of the power spectral density or PSD. The following definitions, expressed in frequency or in circular frequency, will be retained for Code_Aster : \begin{array}{}{S}_{\text{XX}}(f)=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{R}_{\text{XX}}(\tau ){e}^{-\mathrm{2i}\pi f\tau }d\tau ;{G}_{\text{XX}}(f)=\underset{0.}{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{R}_{\text{XX}}(\tau ){e}^{-\mathrm{2i}\pi f\tau }d\tau \\ {S}^{{p}_{\text{XX}}}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{R}_{\text{XX}}(\tau ){e}^{-i\omega \tau }d\tau ;{G}^{{p}_{\text{XX}}}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }\underset{0.}{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{R}_{\text{XX}}(\tau ){e}^{-i\omega \tau }d\tau \end{array} which lead to the following relations: \begin{array}{}{G}^{{p}_{\text{XX}}}(\omega )=\frac{1}{2\pi }{G}_{\text{XX}}(f)\\ {S}_{\text{XX}}(f)=2{G}_{\text{XX}}(f){S}_{\text{XX}}^{p}(\omega )=2{G}^{{p}_{\text{XX}}}(\omega )\end{array} One can show that {G}_{\text{XX}}(f) , which is equal to the Fourier transform of {R}_{\text{XX}}(t) , is real and positive. One will refer to [Appendix1], which contains all the conventions adopted in order to ensure the consistency of the results. 3.4 Spectral moments The following quantities are called spectral moments (which have been defined in circular frequency): {\lambda}_{i}=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{\mid \omega \mid }^{i}{S}^{{p}_{\text{XX}}}(\omega )d\omega =\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{\mid \omega \mid }^{i}{S}_{\text{XX}}(f)\text{df} One has in particular: {\lambda}_{0}={\sigma}^{2}{\lambda}_{2}={\sigma}_{\dot{X}\dot{X}}^{2}{\lambda}_{4}={\sigma}_{\ddot{X}\ddot{X}}^{2} which are the standard deviations of X and of its first derivatives. These moments are systematically computed up to order 4; by means of the keyword MOMENT it is possible to request the computation of the higher modes. In Code_Aster , the computation is carried out for a PSD expressed as a function of the frequency f . 4 Threshold-exceedance measures and reliability The classical methods make it possible to access only the maximum of the displacement (or of the acceleration) by an “adapted” summation of the maxima on each mode. The essential interest of the stochastic approach to random vibratory analysis lies in the statistical knowledge of the response of the structure, which can therefore be converted into statistical information on the reliability. In this respect, two modes of failure can be taken into consideration: - failure by threshold exceedance: this type of failure occurs when the response of the system exceeds a limit value. This amounts to seeking the probability that the values of the process remain below a threshold value during the observation duration T. The peak factor ( peak factor) makes it possible to estimate, in an approximate manner, the mean maximum, over an observation duration of the signal. - failure by fatigue or accumulation of damage. This second approach can also be treated from the first statistical elements computed in POST_DYNA_ALEA. It is carried out in the command POST_FATI_ALEA U4.67.05 R7.04.02. Within the framework of studies under seismic excitations, we are essentially interested in the problem of threshold exceedance. Hence, as a first step, the computation of a certain number of statistical parameters which make it possible to characterise the signal to be studied (spectral moments and Rice formulae [§4.1]); equipped with these characteristics one will then be able to estimate the threshold-exceedance probabilities by means of classical probability models [§4.2], as well as a reliability criterion (Vanmarcke law [§4.3]). 4.1 Spectral moments and characteristic parameters The spectral moments are defined by: {\lambda}_{i}=\underset{-\infty }{\overset{+\infty }{\int}}{\mid \omega \mid }^{i}{S}_{\text{XX}}(f)\text{df} The infinite set of these spectral moments characterises the cross-spectrum perfectly and thus makes it possible to establish a certain number of numerical results. In the particular case of a 1-dof oscillator or of a signal with a single peak, the first three spectral moments are sufficient to recover the auto-spectrum {S}_{\text{XX}} . This is the case which is retained in Code_Aster , since it is assumed that the values are distributed according to a GAUSS law. 4.1.1 Rice formulae For a random signal such as defined previously: stationary with zero mean (centred) and ergodic, it is furthermore assumed that the measured values are distributed according to a normal law, Gauss-type profile (cf. [§4.2.1]). The analysis of a stationary Gaussian random loading has the advantage of leading to simple analytical expressions — known under the name of Rice formulae — and of representing numerous real phenomena. The following statistical parameters are obtained from the various spectral moments linked to the various derivatives of X (cf. [§3.4]): - Standard deviation: {\sigma}_{X}=\sqrt{{\lambda}_{0}} Note: If only the positive part of the spectrum is supplied, Code_Aster multiplies the 1st spectral moment by 2 {\sigma}_{X}=\sqrt{{\mathrm{2\lambda }}_{0}} . An extremum (maximum or minimum) of amplitude X is defined by the probability of having a zero derivative \dot{X}=0 associated with an arbitrary second derivative \ddot{X} . - Mean number of extrema per second: {N}_{e}=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{{\sigma}_{\ddot{X}}}{{\sigma}_{\dot{X}}}=\frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{{\lambda}_{4}}{{\lambda}_{2}}} The exceedance of a level {X}_{0} is defined by the probability of having X={X}_{0} with an arbitrary slope \dot{X} : one therefore counts the passages through this level with positive and negative slopes. Taking into account the assumptions of Gaussian laws, the number of passages through {X}_{0} per second is expressed by: {N}_{{X}_{0}}=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{{\sigma}_{\dot{X}}}{{\sigma}_{X}}{e}^{-\frac{{X}_{0}^{2}}{2{\sigma}_{X}^{2}}} Which leads to the following expressions: - Number of exceedances of the level with positive slope per second: {N}_{{{X}_{0}}^{+}}=\frac{1}{2}{N}_{{X}_{0}} - Number of passages through zero ( {X}_{0} = 0) per second: {N}_{0}=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{{\sigma}_{\dot{X}}}{{\sigma}_{X}}=\frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{{\lambda}_{2}}{{\lambda}_{0}}} - Number of passages through zero with positive slope per second: {N}_{{0}^{+}}=\frac{1}{2}{N}_{0}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{{\lambda}_{2}}{{\lambda}_{0}}} {N}_{{0}^{+}} represents a mean statistical frequency of passage through zero with positive slope. In the case of a “simple” signal, that is, with a single peak , {N}_{{0}^{+}} , the number of passages through zero, can be assimilated to an apparent frequency also denoted {f}_{e} . In the much more general case of an arbitrary signal, the physical interpretation of the value {N}_{{0}^{+}} is more open to caution! The irregularity factor reflects the frequency appearance of the signal. Lying between 0 and 1, it tends towards 1 when the process is narrow-band; on the other hand it tends towards 0 for a broad-band process. Its expression is: I=\frac{{N}_{0}}{{N}_{e}}=\frac{{\sigma}_{\dot{X}}^{2}}{{\sigma}_{X}{\sigma}_{\ddot{X}}}=\sqrt{\frac{{\lambda}_{2}^{2}}{{\lambda}_{0}{\lambda}_{4}}} The three parameters — {N}_{0},{N}_{e},I — characterise the signal completely. One can, in particular, estimate the mean number of positive peaks per second: {N}_{{\text{pic}}^{+}}=1/4(1+I){N}_{e} . All of these parameters are computed and stored in a "printable" table on the RESULTAT file by means of the command IMPR_TABLE. 4.2 Distributions of the positive peaks One of the main items of knowledge of interest to the designers of structures, from its response estimated for a random excitation, is the determination of the threshold exceedances and in particular the probabilities of exceedance of certain critical thresholds. The Rice formulae (previous paragraph) make it possible to know the mean rate of the crossings of certain levels. The following approach makes it possible to give a probability law for the presence of such and such a peak. One is therefore interested in the positive maxima of the response. A maximum occurs when \dot{x}(t)=0\text{avec}\ddot{x}(t) 0\\ -j& \omega <0\\ 0& \omega =0\end{array} | H(\omega ) transforms X(t) into its Hilbert transform denoted \hat{X}(t) . The system with transfer function H(\omega ) produces a phase shift of +90° for the positive frequencies and of –90° for the negative frequencies. It follows from the convolution theorem that \hat{X}(t) can also be defined as the convolution of X(t) by the corresponding impulse response, that is h(t)=1/\pi t . \hat{X}(t) is likewise real; a second application of the Hilbert transform restores the initial signal, with a change of sign and stripped of its possible continuous component. Example : x(t)=A\cos\omega t\to \hat{x}(t)\text{=-}A\sin\omega t This property is the basis of the use of the Hilbert transform in order to define the envelope of a narrow-band process.

r7.10.02 Post-processing of modal analyses with shock r7.10.02 Post-processing of modal analyses with shock Summary: This document presents the principle of post-processing of transient analyses by modal recombination with shock non-linearities available in the operator POST_DYNA_MODA_T. Two post-processing options may be used. The first, usable for vibration–wear problems, determines mean and RMS values of displacements, shock forces and wear power dissipated at the supports with clearances; the second is applicable to the detailed analysis of the impacts occurring during transient loadings. The instantaneous maximum force, the duration of the shock time, the impulse exchanged and the velocity before impact are determined for each shock. 1 Introduction Numerical developments have been carried out in Code_Aster in order to allow the transient analysis of structures presenting vibrations with shock at certain points. In certain cases, friction forces may also appear and lead to a phenomenon of localised wear. Whether the damage is by pure impact or by impact–friction, the engineer wishes to access the quantities associated with this damage, which requires a specific post-processing downstream of the non-linear transient analysis. This post-processing information is also valuable when one wishes to validate the non-linear analysis module by comparing its results with what can be measured on a specific test rig. Test programmes (MASSIF and MULTICHOC) have been implemented for this purpose and were the first users of these post-processing features. The objective of this note is to specify the quantities to be analysed in vibrations with shock and their specific character. It is then a matter of determining the appropriate statistical treatments to apply to these signals in order to extract the most characteristic instantaneous or mean quantities. First, the treatments applied in the case of a problem with shock and friction will be seen (option 'USURE' of the command POST_DYNA_MODA_T). The following chapter will be devoted to the treatments applied in the case of a pure vibration–impact phenomenon, in which the quantities of each impact are analysed in more detail (option 'IMPACT' of the command POST_DYNA_MODA_T). 2 Quantities considered in vibrations with shocks The primary quantities considered in vibrations with shock are the same whether they come from experimental measurements or from the numerical analysis; they concern the shock forces and the displacements at the shock points. The experimental results nevertheless present an additional difficulty of analysis, due to the errors or biases introduced by the measurement systems. The two quantities mentioned above will be examined in turn. 2.1 Shock forces The first concern regarding structures vibrating with shocks is to know better the forces received by the structure during the shocks on its supports with clearances, or between the structures. These data are computed in time by the algorithm of DYNA_VIBRA; they are then archived with a step defined in this same operator. The shock data having a very significant frequency content, care will be taken to have sufficient archiving (do not exceed PAS_ARCH : 10 ). These forces, expressed in a local frame attached to the obstacle (\mathrm{Yloc},\mathrm{Zloc}) , are traditionally decomposed into a part normal to the obstacle ( \mathrm{Fn} in the figure below) and a tangential part ( \mathrm{Ft} ) if friction is taken into account between the structures. The shock conditions are such that the normal shock force has a constant sign, taken by convention as positive in Code_Aster . 2.2 Shock displacements The displacements of the structure at its supports with clearance are another important piece of computed information. Their analysis nevertheless poses fewer problems, because the spectral content is less rich. In the case of circular obstacles, or obstacles described in a polar manner, a polar description of the displacement may be of interest. 2.3 Secondary quantities 2.3.1 Shock time The contact time between the structure and the supports with clearances is an indirect quantity characteristic of the vibration motion with shock. It may be deduced in various ways, on a displacement criterion or on a criterion of positive reaction force. A notion of overall shock time, decomposed into elementary shock (or rebound), will be introduced in [§3.4]. 2.3.2 Computed quantities Other secondary quantities may be important in the analysis of the shock conditions; these are the impulse during the impact (integral of the force exchanged), the wear power , the maximum force during an impact, ... These quantities are specific to each post-processing and they will be specified in the two chapters that follow, for the post-processing option ' USURE ' and ' IMPACT ' . 3 Modal transient post-processing — option 'USURE' The characterisation of transient measurements is the aim of signal processing. It teaches us that a signal is entirely determined by the data of all its statistical moments. In practice it is out of the question to compute all the statistical moments; the post-processing is limited to the quantities classically computed in signal processing (simple mean, standard deviation and RMS value). They are characteristic of the signals that one wishes to analyse and compare. Similar signals must necessarily have these first statistical moments close to one another (the converse being false). The statistical quantities retained here are well suited to the analysis, the comparison or the classification of vibration signals under random excitation with shock non-linearities. The averaged quantities and their computation will therefore be examined, distinguishing the various quantities mentioned in the previous chapter: - the displacements, - the shock forces, - the determination of the contact and of the contact time. Other composite information may be computed from the previous ones, in particular the wear power. 3.1 Statistical treatment by blocks In order to analyse the stationarity of the signals and of the statistical treatments carried out on the signals, a splitting of the time signals into blocks is carried out. Thus the post-processing duration, defined between the initial time instant (INST_INIT) and the final time instant (INST_FIN), is split into a number of time blocks (NB_BLOC) of identical duration. The computation of the statistical values — mean, standard deviation, ... — is carried out for each of the blocks; a general value for the signal over the set of blocks is also computed. In the case of an analysis of the response of a structure to a random loading, this technique of computation by blocks makes it possible to make sure that the transient phase of the analysis is over and that the value announced is indeed stationary over an observation time associated with the duration of the analysis. 3.2 Statistical treatments applied to the shock displacements Consider the time signal \mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x(t) , of which an archiving is carried out at a certain frequency {F}_{\mathrm{acquis}} over N points. The starting data is therefore a vector \mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x(i) with N components. The mean displacement is defined in this case by: \overline{\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x}=\frac{\sum_{1}^{N}\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x(i)}{N} This mean value characterises the central value about which the displacement signal evolves. For the displacements, it will therefore make it possible to determine whether a centred configuration is observed (displacements with zero mean), or an off-centre one (non-zero mean). The variance of the displacement is by definition: \mathrm{var}(\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x)=\frac{\sum_{1}^{N}{(\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x(i)-\overline{\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x})}^{2}}{N} The standard deviation of the displacement is then: \sigma (\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x)=\sqrt{\mathrm{var}(\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x)} The standard deviation of a signal characterises its dispersion about its mean value. A small standard deviation will concern rather a signal with small variations of amplitude; a large standard deviation, larger variations. For a centred variable, that is with zero mean, the standard deviation is equal to the RMS mean of the signal (Root Mean Square). For an arbitrary variable, the RMS mean of the signal is defined by: \mathrm{RMS}(\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x)=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{1}^{N}\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x{(i)}^{2}}{N}} The absolute minimum and maximum of the signal are also an interesting and very simple piece of information to obtain, which determines the range of the signal. Figure 3.2-a: Example of a displacement signal and visualisation of the statistical quantities A polar representation of the set of signals \mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x and \mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}y is also interesting to analyse in the case of an obstacle of circular or similar geometry. Let us agree to call R the radial displacement and \theta the angular displacement, equivalents of \mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x and \mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}y in polar coordinates. By definition one has: R(i)=\sqrt{\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x{(i)}^{2}+\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}y{(i)}^{2}} \theta (i)=\mathrm{Arctg}(\frac{\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}y(i)}{\mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x(i)}) This representation makes it possible, among other things, to distinguish: - orbital motions with permanent contact (mean radial displacement of the order of the clearance and small standard deviation of the radial displacement), - pure-impact motions (large standard deviation of the radial displacement, small variation of the angular displacement), - other configurations: orbital motion with impacts ... Note: In the local frame chosen for the shock obstacles, the quantities called here \mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}x and \mathrm{Depl}\text{\_}y are in fact \mathrm{DYloc} and \mathrm{DZloc} , the axis \mathrm{Xloc} having been chosen by convention perpendicular to the plane of the obstacle. In summary , the post-processing option 'USURE' of the operator POST_DYNA_MODA_T will determine, for the local displacements \mathrm{DYloc},\mathrm{DYloc},\mathrm{DZloc} as well as for their polar decomposition R and \theta , the statistical quantities by blocks, with the principle stated above: - mean value, - RMS value, - standard deviation, - minimum value, - maximum value. 3.3 Statistics for the shock forces It is assumed that, as for the displacements, a discrete signal over N points is available: \mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}(i) . The signal obtained should be composed of time ranges where the shock force is zero (no contact) and of others where the shock force is significant (effective contact), which is the case in numerical analyses. In fact, for experimental signals, because of the dynamics of the measurement system, a noise level may be observed outside the shock period (cf. [Figure 3.3-a]). The statistical treatment must therefore be carried out only when the signal leaves the noise level. This requires the introduction of a detection threshold ( SEUIL_FORCE ) which, although superfluous in the numerical domain, has been reproduced in the post-processing of Code_Aster . Figure 3.3-a: Example of an experimental shock-force signal Let S\max be the value determining the maximum level of the noise considered; one will then compute: - The number of time instants in shock : \mathrm{Nchoc}=\mathrm{card}\left\lbrace i/\mid \mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}(i)\mid >S\max\right\rbrace - The mean shock force over the total time : \overline{\mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}}=\frac{1}{N}\cdot (\sum_{i/\mid \mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}(i)\mid >S\max}^{N}\mid \mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}(i)\mid ) - The mean shock force reduced to the shock time is: \mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}=\overline{\mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}}\cdot \frac{N}{\mathrm{Nchoc}} - The RMS mean of the shock force over the total time is computed as follows: \mathrm{RMS}(\mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc})={(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i/\mid \mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}(i)\mid >S\max}^{N}{\mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}(i)}^{2})}^{1/2} - The RMS mean reduced to the shock time is: \mathrm{RMS}(\mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc})=\mathrm{RMS}(\mathrm{Fx}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc})\cdot \frac{N}{\mathrm{Nchoc}} As for the displacement signals, one may also be interested in the absolute maximum or minimum of the force signal, thus determining its range. For the normal force, the minimum is always equal to zero, whereas the tangential force alternates. In summary , the post-processing option 'USURE' of the operator POST_DYNA_MODA_T will determine, for the normal and tangential shock forces, the statistical quantities by blocks, with the principle stated above: - mean value computed over the shock time or the total time, - RMS value computed over the shock time or the total time, - maximum value of the signal. 3.4 Statistics for the shock times The percentage of shock time is defined by: \text{\%}\mathrm{Tchoc}=\mathrm{Nchoc}/N If one looks at the information available on an experimental system, the shock-force signal is the most appropriate for determining the occurrence of a contact precisely. As mentioned above, one feels the need to introduce a maximum noise level, and to count the shock phases when the signal exceeds this threshold (SEUIL_FORCE). In the figure below, one can distinguish a notion of elementary shock , determined as a successive passage above and then below the threshold, and a more general notion of overall shock , gathering several elementary shocks separated by short time instants of return below the threshold. Figure 3.4-a A characteristic rest time \mathrm{Tr} ( DUREE_REPOS ) is therefore introduced; the end of an overall shock time occurs if the signal remains at rest for a time at least greater than \mathrm{Tr} . This notion of characteristic rest time \mathrm{Tr} is of course rather vague and will have to be determined by the user in the light of the transient results. It is nevertheless essential, because it alone makes it possible to gather a train of very closely spaced impacts constituting in fact a single contact phase. The notion of elementary shock time being defined, the statistical treatment of the shock time will consist in determining the following information: - number of elementary shocks : \mathrm{Nb}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}\text{\_}\mathrm{elem} - number of overall shocks : \mathrm{Nb}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}\text{\_}\mathrm{glob} - number of elementary shocks per overall shock : \frac{\mathrm{Nb}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}\text{\_}\mathrm{elem}}{\mathrm{Nb}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}\text{\_}\mathrm{glob}} - mean elementary shock time : {\bar{T}}_{\mathrm{choc}\text{\_}\mathrm{elem}}=\frac{\mathrm{Nchoc}\cdot \Deltat }{\mathrm{Nb}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}\text{\_}\mathrm{elem}} - mean overall shock time {\bar{T}}_{\mathrm{choc}\text{\_}\mathrm{glob}}=\frac{\mathrm{Nchoc}\cdot \Deltat }{\mathrm{Nb}\text{\_}\mathrm{choc}\text{\_}\mathrm{glob}} - maximum overall shock time , the largest overall shock time observed on the block analysed. In summary , the post-processing option 'USURE' of the operator POST_DYNA_MODA_T will determine, for the shock times, the statistical quantities by blocks, with the principle stated above: - mean value of the overall shock time, - maximum value of the overall shock time, - mean value of the elementary shock time, - the number of overall shocks per second, - the mean number of elementary shocks per overall shock. 3.5 Wear power The quantity generally computed in vibrations with shock and friction is the wear power defined by ARCHARD [bib1], which expresses the mean power developed by the friction forces during the motion. These forces are the driving force of wear by friction. The wear power in the case of discrete signals is computed as follows: \overline{{P}_{\mathrm{usure}}}=\frac{\sum_{i/\mid \mathrm{Fn}\mid >S\max}^{N}\mid \mathrm{Fn}(i)\cdot \mathrm{Vt}(i)\mid }{N} This power may, for example, be correlated with a wear or a removal of material by means of a wear coefficient {K}_{T} , by a relation of the type: V(T)={K}_{T}\ast {P}_{\mathrm{usure}}\ast T where V(T) is the volume removed during the duration T . Other, more sophisticated wear laws may be used in another post-processing operator: POST_USURE, described in R7.01.10. 3.6 Table data structure POST_DYNA associated with the option 'USURE' A structure of type table for the option USURE of the operator POST_DYNA_MODA_T gathers the results described previously. This table contains the names of the statistical-result sub-tables associated with the various quantities analysed: displacements, shock forces, shock counting and wear power. The access variables of this table are 10 in number: - for the displacement variables : DEPL_X, DEPL_Y, DEPL_Z, DEPL_RADIAL, DEPL_ANGULAIRE, which correspond respectively to the displacements in local X, Y and Z and to their cylindrical decomposition in the plane of the obstacle. - for the shock-force variables : FORCE_NORMALE, FORCE_TANG_1, FORCE_TANG_2, which correspond respectively to the forces normal and tangential to the obstacle, the first being in the plane of the obstacle, the second orthogonal to the plane of the obstacle. - for the shock-counting variables : STAT_CHOC. - for the wear-power variable : PUIS_USURE. The sub-tables associated with the 10 quantities above contain a certain number of access variables for each shock connection: - for the displacement variables : MOYEN, ECART_TYPE, RMS, MAXI, MINI, which correspond respectively to the mean value, the standard deviation, the RMS or effective value, and the maximum and minimum values of the corresponding displacement variable. - for the shock-force variables : MOYEN_T_TOTAL, MOYEN_T_CHOC, RMS_T_TOTAL, RMS_T_CHOC, MAXI, which correspond respectively to the mean value over the total time, the mean over the shock time, the RMS or effective value averaged over the total time, the RMS or effective value over the shock time, and the maximum value of the corresponding force variable. - for the shock-counting variables : NB_CHOC_S, NB_REBON_CHOC, T_CHOC_MOYEN, T_CHOC_MAXI, T_CHOC_MINI, T_REBON_MOYEN, %_T_CHOC, which correspond respectively to the values of the number of shocks per second, of the number of rebounds per shock, of the mean shock time, the maximum shock time, the minimum shock time, the mean rebound time and the percentage of shock time. - for the wear-power variable : PUIS_USURE, which corresponds to the wear power computed according to ARCHARD. 4 Modal transient post-processing — option 'IMPACT' 4.1 Current practice for post-processing core analyses Before the development of the post-processing in Code_Aster , SEPTEN used, for its design-verification needs, the code CLASH [bib2] developed by BELGONUCLEAIRE. This software computes the seismic response of a row of assemblies. This code supplies a set of detailed information for each shock point and for each impact. Each result consists of a table per shock point, an example of which is in Annex 1. This table contains the following information: - the time instant of the impact peak, - the maximum impact force reached, - the impulse exchanged, defined as the integral of the shock force over time, - the total duration of the shock, - the relative velocity before impact. These elements are particularly interesting for SEPTEN because, in addition to the very limited contractual information, they make it possible to know the number and the composition of the impacts, as well as essential physical quantities associated with them. The relative velocity before impact and the impulse are, for example, very valuable information in the specification of experimental tests of dynamic buckling of the assembly grids. 4.2 Computations for the post-processing of the impacts It is considered, as for the previous post-processing, that the impact conditions are determined as previously by the exceeding of a force threshold \mathrm{Smax} , and the overall shock and the elementary shock are distinguished in the same way by the notion of rest time. The computation carries out a loop over all the shock non-linearities and an identical treatment for each of them. Then, for each overall shock identified, the following quantities will be determined: - Shock start time: {T}_{\mathrm{début}}\text{tel que}{F}_{\mathrm{choc}}({T}_{\mathrm{début}})>{S}_{\max} - End time of the overall shock: {T}_{\mathrm{fin}}\text{tel que}{F}_{\mathrm{choc}}({T}_{\mathrm{fin}})\le {S}_{\max},{F}_{\mathrm{choc}}({T}_{\mathrm{fin}}-\Deltat )\ge {S}_{\max} \text{et}\forall t\in [{T}_{\mathrm{fin}},{T}_{\mathrm{fin}}+{T}_{\mathrm{repos}}]{F}_{\mathrm{choc}}(t)\le {S}_{\max} \text{où}\Deltat \text{est le pas de temps d'intégration} - Total duration of the shock: {T}_{\mathrm{choc}}={T}_{\mathrm{fin}}-{T}_{\mathrm{début}} - Maximum force during the shock: {F}_{\max}={\max}_{T\in [{T}_{\mathrm{début}},{T}_{\mathrm{fin}}]}({F}_{\mathrm{choc}}(t)) - The time instant of the maximum of the shock force, - The impulse exchanged during the shock: I=\underset{t={T}_{\mathrm{début}}}{\overset{{T}_{\mathrm{fin}}}{\int}}{F}_{\mathrm{choc}}(t)\cdot \mathrm{dt} - The relative normal velocity before impact: {V}_{\mathrm{choc}}=V({T}_{\mathrm{début}}-\Deltat ) - The number of elementary impacts accumulated in the overall shock: {N}_{\mathrm{impacts}\mathrm{élémentaires}}=\mathrm{card}\left\lbrace t\in [{t}_{\mathrm{début}},{T}_{\mathrm{fin}}]/{F}_{\mathrm{choc}}(t)>{S}_{\max}\text{et}{F}_{\mathrm{choc}}(t+\deltat )\le {S}_{\max}\right\rbrace In order to synthesise the information, one will in addition determine: - the absolute maximum of the shock force, on a given shock connection, for the duration of the analysis, The maximum shock force, in order to be determined more precisely, will not be obtained as the maximum in time over the set of shocks for each shock node (in order to avoid the bias of the archiving precision), but determined in the transient analysis over all the computation steps and archived in the result concept tran_gene . It is this information that will be used. - the mean value of the extrema of the shock force, as well as their standard deviation. - a histogram of the probability density of the maximum impact forces. This histogram will be relatively summary and will give, for {N}_{C} classes, the probability density of the maximum shock force. The classes will be defined as follows: {\mathrm{classe}}_{i={\mathrm{1..N}}_{C}}=\left\lbrace {F}_{\max}/\frac{i-1}{{N}_{C}}{F}_{\max}^{\mathrm{absolu}}\le {F}_{\max}\le \frac{i}{{N}_{C}}{F}_{\max}^{\mathrm{absolu}}\right\rbrace 4.3 Table data structure POST_IMPACT associated with the option 'IMPACT' 4.3.1 Table POST_IMPACT A data structure of type table for the option IMPACT of the operator POST_DYNA_MODA_T of Code_Aster is produced. The result structure will be a table indexed by the names of the shock connections, of type POST_IMPACT , containing the names of the tables that it contains. The content of each cell of this table is a table name stored as CHARACTER 24. Three types of table are contained: a table called IMPACT, a table called GLOBAL and a table called PROBA. It therefore has 3 parameters: IMPACT , GLOBAL and PROBA . The access variable corresponds to the name of the shock connection considered. 4.3.2 Table IMPACT The IMPACT table is of type TABL_IMPACT and has 6 access parameters: INST , F_MAX , T_CHOC , IMPULS , V_IMPACT , NB_IMPACT . The content of each cell of this table is a REAL 8 . 4.3.3 Table GLOBAL The GLOBAL table is of type TABL_FMAX and has 3 access parameters: - F_MAX_ABS , which gives access to the absolute maximum of the shock force over all the shocks observed, - F_MAX_MOY , which gives access to the mean value of the maxima of the shock force observed, - F_MAX_ETYP , which gives access to the standard deviation of the extrema of the shock forces. The content of each cell of this table is a REAL 8 . 4.3.4 Table PROBA The PROBA table is of type TABL_HISTO and has 3 access parameters: - DEBUT , which gives access to the minimum force value of class i , - FIN , which gives access to the maximum force value of class i , - PROBA , which gives access to the probability density of the maximum-force variable for class i . The content of each cell of this table is a REAL 8. 5 Conclusion This document has presented the post-processing methods applicable to transients with shock computed by modal synthesis on structures with clearance. Depending on the concerns, a post-processing oriented towards a diagnosis of the wear undergone by the components during the shocks may be carried out; a set of important statistical quantities is then determined. If the concern is rather the impacts and their level, another option allows a detailed analysis of each impact. These two features make it possible to synthesise the transient results obtained by time integration, to classify different numerical simulations by level of severity, or to compare, for validation purposes, computed and measured quantities. 6 Bibliography 1. r7.10.03 Post-processing of shaft-line analyses: Campbell diagram r7.10.03 Post-processing of shaft-line analyses: Campbell diagram Summary: This document presents the commands CALC_MODE_ROTATION and IMPR_DIAG_CAMPBELL, which make it possible to follow the modes of rotating machines as a function of the rotational speed, together with the instability zones of these modes. The definition of this tool is first recalled, then its flow chart is detailed. Finally, the main steps of the corresponding algorithm are set out, as it is designed and implemented in Code_Aster . 1 Purpose The purpose of this document is to describe the macro-commands required to plot the Campbell diagram in Code_Aster . The approach is based on that already developed in the ROTORINSA software [bib1]. The Campbell diagram is a graphical representation of the natural frequencies of a rotating system as a function of its rotational speed. The natural frequencies and the modes of a rotating system are obtained by solving the dynamic equilibrium equation of a system of rotating shafts, with no right-hand side and including the effects due to damping. > M\ddot{\delta}+C(\Omega )\dot{\delta}+K\delta =0 eq 1- 1-1 Where M is the mass matrix of the system, C(\Omega ) is a non-symmetric matrix, a function of the rotational speed, including the gyroscopic effect (skew-symmetric) and the damping characteristics of the bearings, and K is the stiffness matrix of the system. The data required to plot the Campbell diagram are therefore the natural frequencies, together with the corresponding modes, as a function of the rotational speed, in the form of a table. The step allowing the computation of these modes is already developed in Code_Aster (cf. R5.01.01). Two macro-commands are developed. The first macro-command, CALC_MODE_ROTATION, computes the frequencies and the modes on the complete system as a function of the rotational speeds. The second macro-command, IMPR_DIAG_CAMPBELL, classifies the modes into bending, torsion and tension/compression, normalises these modes, determines the sense of precession of the bending modes, sorts the frequencies according to various mode-tracking methods, then plots the Campbell diagram. 2 Flow chart Figure 2-a -a: Flow chart of the Campbell diagram The three mode-tracking methods are: - no sorting, - step-by-step sorting of the frequencies, - sorting by mode shape 3 Algorithm After the computation of the frequencies and of the complex modes of the system, the list ‘MODES’ of mode_meca_c is one of the input data of the macro. The algorithm is presented below: - Classification of the modes ‘MODES’ into bending, torsion and tension/compression: - Extraction of the bending modes - Normalises the bending modes - Extraction of the torsion modes - Normalises the torsion modes - Extraction of the tension/compression modes - Normalises the tension/compression modes - Extraction of the frequencies - Bending frequencies - Torsion frequencies - Tension/compression frequencies - Initialisation of the frequency-connection tables; the filling of these tables corresponds to the mode-tracking method ‘Pas de TRI’, following the order of the mode as it stands in the mode_meca_c concepts. - Computation of the direct or reverse sense of precession 1 for the bending modes at each rotational speed, carried out in two different ways according to the choice of the type of computation of the precession: - PREC_GOR: The identification of the precession is a function of the sign of the largest orbit in a mode (direct precession, reverse precession) - PREC_MOY: The identification of the precession is performed according to the sign of the sum of the signs of all the orbits - Filling of the precession-sense table SENS - Mode tracking: - If the type of mode tracking is TRI_PREC_MOD, that is, step-by-step sorting of the frequencies according to the sense of the precession. It requires the computation of the axes of the orbits and the evaluation of the sense in which the orbits are traversed. The identification of the precession is performed according to the sign of the largest orbit or the sign of the sum of the signs of all the orbits. The frequencies are then classified into two groups (direct precession and reverse precession). Within each group the frequencies are classified in increasing order for each rotational speed. Each curve of the Campbell diagram connects the points as a function of the rotational speed, respecting the classification order in each group (the i -th frequency of group p (speed {\Omega}_{p} ) with the i -th frequency of group p+1 (speed {\Omega}_{p+1} ), and so on). - Bending connection table updated - If the type of mode tracking is TRI_FORM_MOD, that is, sorting by mode shape. Sorting the frequencies according to the mode shape requires the computation of the MAC correlation matrix of the modes. The modes are then compared as follows: each mode (starting from the highest rotational speed) is compared with the other modes of the previous rotational speed by taking the maximum correlation. This comparison makes it possible to plot, for each mode, the curve of evolution of its frequency as a function of the rotational speed in order to build the Campbell diagram. - Bending connection table updated - Torsion connection table updated - Tension/compression connection table updated. - Plotting of the Campbell diagram - Plotting of the Campbell diagram of the bending modes - Plotting of the Campbell diagram of the torsion modes - Plotting of the Campbell diagram of the tension/compression modes. - Plotting of the straight lines of slopes S and determination of the intersection points (critical speeds). 3.1 Classification of the modes The rotation of the rotor takes place about the axis Z (this is the condition for correct use of IMPR_DIAG_CAMPBELL). After the computation of the modes in rotation at various speeds, the following results are obtained: - bending modes characterised by the translational displacements \mathit{DX} , \mathit{DY} and the rotational displacements \mathit{DRX} and \mathit{DRY} - torsion modes characterised by the rotational displacements \mathit{DRZ} - tension/compression modes characterised by the translational displacements \mathit{DZ} . As a first step, the modes are classified according to these three categories. For each mode, the following computations are performed: 1. Total norm \mathit{Ntot} \mathrm{Ntot}=\sqrt{\sum{\mid \mathrm{DX}\mid }^{2}+{\mid \mathrm{DY}\mid }^{2}+{\mid \mathrm{DZ}\mid }^{2}+{\mid \mathrm{DRX}\mid }^{2}+{\mid \mathrm{DRY}\mid }^{2}+{\mid \mathrm{DRZ}\mid }^{2}} 1. Bending ratio \mathit{Nflexion} \mathit{Nflexion}=\frac{\sqrt{\sum{\mid \mathit{DX}\mid }^{2}+{\mid \mathit{DY}\mid }^{2}+{\mid \mathit{DRX}\mid }^{2}+{\mid \mathit{DRY}\mid }^{2}}}{\mathit{Ntot}} 1. Torsion ratio \mathit{Ntorsion} \mathit{Ntorsion}=\frac{\sqrt{\sum{\mid \mathit{DRZ}\mid }^{2}}}{\mathit{Ntot}} 1. Tension/compression ratio \mathit{Nlongi} \mathit{Nlongi}=\frac{\sqrt{\sum{\mid \mathit{DZ}\mid }^{2}}}{\mathit{Ntot}} The modes are classified as follows: 1. For the bending modes: \mathit{Nflexion}>\mathit{Ntorsion}\mathit{et}\mathit{Nflexion}>\mathit{Nlongi} 1. For the torsion modes: \mathit{Ntorsion}>\mathit{Nflexion}\mathit{et}\mathit{Ntorsion}>\mathit{Nlongi} 1. For the tension/compression modes: \mathit{Nlongi}>\mathit{Nflexion}\mathit{et}\mathit{Nlongi}>\mathit{Ntorsion} If the system includes a foundation block (supporting member), mixed modes may exist (all three at once). In that case, the same method as above is applied. From the initial modal basis \mathit{MODES} , three modal bases are therefore extracted: 1. \mathit{MODEf} : containing the bending modes 2. \mathit{MODEt} : containing the torsion modes 3. \mathit{MODEl} : containing the tension/compression modes For the modal bases \mathit{MODEf} and \mathit{MODEl} , normalisation is performed with respect to the largest of the translational components (\mathit{DX},\mathit{DY},\mathit{DZ}) . For the modal basis \mathit{MODEf} , normalisation is performed with respect to the largest of the rotational components (\mathit{DRX},\mathit{DRY},\mathit{DRZ}) . Extraction and normalisation of the modes of the structure are performed by means of the operators EXTR_MODE and NORM_MODE, respectively. 3.2 Computation of the sense of precession for the bending modes 3.2.1 Concepts The modes in rotation are defined by the ellipses at each node. Figure 3.2-a: Ellipses defining the modes For a given mode and for each node, one has the translational displacements \mathit{DX} , \mathit{DY} with: \mathit{DX}=({X}_{R},{X}_{I}),{\mid \mathit{DX}\mid }^{2}={\mid {X}_{R}\mid }^{2}+{\mid {X}_{I}\mid }^{2} \mathrm{DY}=({Y}_{R},{Y}_{I}),{\mid \mathrm{DY}\mid }^{2}={\mid {Y}_{R}\mid }^{2}+{\mid {Y}_{I}\mid }^{2} 4 cases are possible: 1. If {\mid \mathit{DX}\mid }^{2}+{\mid \mathit{DY}\mid }^{2}\approx 0 there is no ellipse, then a=0,b=0,\alpha =0,S=0 2. If {\mid \mathit{DX}\mid }^{2}\approx 0 there is no ellipse, the trajectory is along the axis Y , then a=0,b=\mid \mathit{DY}\mid ,\alpha =0,S=0 3. If {\mid \mathit{DY}\mid }^{2}\approx 0 there is no ellipse, the trajectory is along the axis X , then a=\mid \mathit{DX}\mid ,b=0,\alpha =90°,S=0 4. If {\mid \mathit{DX}\mid }^{2}\mathrm{\ne }0 and {\mid \mathit{DY}\mid }^{2}\mathrm{\ne }0 then the precession S can be computed for each node. The displacements u along X and v along Y of this node will be of the following form: u={X}_{R}\cos(\omega t)-{X}_{I}\sin(\omega t) , v={Y}_{R}\cos(\omega t)-{Y}_{I}\sin(\omega t) 3.2.2 Determination of the sense of traversal During a period of vibration, the ellipse may be traversed in the positive or the negative sense (direct or reverse precession). 1. at \omega t=0 the axis of the rotor is at the point P 2. at \omega t=\frac{\pi}{2} the axis of the rotor is at the point Q The previous relations make it possible to compute the components of the vectors \overrightarrow{\mathit{OP}}=(\begin{array}{c}{X}_{R}\\ {Y}_{R}\\ 0\end{array}) and \overrightarrow{\mathit{OQ}}=(\begin{array}{c}-{X}_{I}\\ -{Y}_{I}\\ 0\end{array}) . The sign of the vector product \overrightarrow{\mathit{OP}\mathrm{\wedge }\mathit{OQ}}=(\begin{array}{c}0\\ 0\\ {Y}_{R}{X}_{I}-{Y}_{I}{X}_{R}\end{array}) indicates the sense of traversal, or precession (positive or negative). For each node, the results are available at maximum amplitude, i.e.: u:\mathit{XMAX}=\sum{X}_{R}^{2}+{X}_{I}^{2} and v:\mathit{YMAX}=\sum{Y}_{R}^{2}+{Y}_{I}^{2} For a mode, there are two ways of determining the sense of precession: - PREC_GOR: The identification of the precession is performed according to the sign of the largest orbit in a mode (direct precession, reverse precession). - PREC_MOY: The identification of the precession is performed according to the sign of the sum of the signs of all the orbits. On output, the table SENS is filled for the senses of precession of all the modes at all the rotational speeds. This table makes it possible to track the bending modes with the method TRI_PREC_MOD. It also makes it possible to determine the sense of precession on the Campbell diagram according to the colour code defined in the User's manual of the command IMPR_DIAG_CAMPBELL. 3.3 Computation of the MAC matrices between modal bases at two rotational speeds For the sorting of the modes by shape comparison, the correlation coefficients (MAC matrix) between the modes of the two rotational speeds of successive indices are computed. The operator MAC_MODES is used to - compute the MAC matrix between two successive bending modal bases. - compute the MAC matrix between two successive torsion modal bases. - compute the MAC matrix between two successive tension/compression modal bases. 3.4 Sorting according to the sense of the precession This is a mode-tracking method by step-by-step sorting of the frequencies with a check of the sense of precession. The modes are classified into two groups according to the sense of precession (direct-precession mode, reverse-precession mode). Tracking is then performed within each group according to the order of the modes. Tracking starts from the last rotational speed, of number \mathit{NBV} , and the last mode \mathit{NFREQf} of that speed (cf. [Figure 3.4-a]). Figure 3.4-a .4-a: Sorting according to the sense of precession 3.5 Sorting according to the mode shape (MAC) This mode-tracking method by shape comparison requires the computation of the MAC correlation matrix of the modes of two successive rotational speeds; see paragraph 3.3. Tracking starts from the last rotational speed, of number \mathit{NBV} . For each mode of a given rotational speed \mathit{IVI} , one looks for a mode of the previous rotational speed \mathit{IVI}-1 which gives the maximum correlation coefficient. The connection table is filled with the value of the number of the selected mode (cf. [Figure 3.5-a]). Figure 3.5-a: Sorting according to the mode shape This tracking is performed separately for the three categories of bending, torsion and tension/compression modes. Direct precession (respectively reverse) corresponds to the case in which the orbit of the rotor is described in the same sense as (respectively the sense opposite to) the rotation of the shaft. 4 References 1.
