r7.10.04 Post-processing according to the Roche method r7.10.04 Post-processing according to the Roche method Summary: The operator POST_ROCHE is a post-processing of purely linear elastic analyses, which uses the Roche method to evaluate the response of a piping line under an elastoplastic constitutive behaviour. 1 Introduction The Roche method makes it possible to evaluate the response relating to an elastoplastic constitutive behaviour of a pressurised piping line, from the results of linear elastic analyses to which abatement coefficients are applied. The mechanical loadings considered are: the inertial earthquake, the displacements imposed at the anchors, the thermal expansion and the weight. The objective of this approach is to reduce significantly the run times compared with a classical non-linear solution approach for the seismic analyses. The abatement coefficients are computed from spring-effect factors. The linear elastic response, reduced following the application of the abatement coefficients, is deemed to provide a conservative estimate of the non-linear response. The abatement coefficients are applicable only to the moments depending on the displacements, according to the CMS2 classification of the RCC-MRx; they are not applicable to the moments depending on the forces. Two variants of the macro-command POST_ROCHE are proposed: - The RCC-MRX variant, in accordance with the codification, for which the determination of the abatement coefficients of the moments coming from the linear elastic flexibility analyses of the piping lines follows the specifications of chapters RB 3651.1132 and RB 3651.1142 of the RCC-MRx (post-spectral Roche method), - The ASNR variant, in accordance with the validation file of the Roche method supplied to the ASNR in 2024. The output quantities (grandeurs), functions of the curvilinear abscissa, are: - the optimised monotonic and seismic abatement coefficients, - the components of the abated moment, and its norm, relative to the set of the loadings considered, - the abated equivalent stress, taking into account the abated moments and the non-abated moments, relative to the set of the loadings considered. The geometries concerned are: - the pipes of constant diameter and of variable diameter (reducers), - the single-run lines and the branched lines (including tees). 2 Input data The input data of the operator POST_ROCHE are: The data recovered from the results of the previous analyses: - the geometry of the piping line, - the field of characteristics of the beam elements, - the elastic characteristics of the material, - the flexibility coefficients of the elbows, The specific data: - the material field CHAM_MATER : it is the map of the materials assigned to the mesh-cell groups of the mesh by AFFE_MATERIAU, whose parameters of the Ramberg-Osgood curve ( K and n ) as well as other parameters in the case LIMITE_ADM=’OUI’, these data are supplied in DEFI_MATERIAU (keyword POST_ROCHE or POST_ROCHE_FO ); if POST_ROCHE_FO , declaration of a temperature field via the keyword AFFE_VARC of the operator AFFE_MATERIAU, - the tension curve of the material, a function defined under TRAC_EPSI describing the strain as a function of the stress, - the orientations of the local frames (in AFFE_CARA_ELEM, keyword ORIENTATION ) for the bent parts, making it possible to separate the in-plane and out-of-plane bending moments (see sdll157a), - the angles and radii of curvature of the elbows, - the internal pressure P imposed on the mesh-cell groups, - the list of the mechanical loadings among: non-seismic imposed displacements DINS, seismic differential displacements DDS, thermal expansion, self-weight, inertial spectral earthquake, - the results of the analyses for each mechanical loading: field by elements at the nodes of generalised forces ( EFGE_ELNO ). 3 Analysis stages In order to determine the reversibilities and the spring-effect factors, one uses a plastic constitutive law according to Ramberg-Osgood, previously fitted to the monotonic tension law. The projection of the linear elastic stress is carried out onto the real monotonic tension curve of the material. 3.1 Establishment of the curve according to Ramberg-Osgood, representative of the monotonic tension curve of the material A Ramberg-Osgood curve must previously be fitted to the real tension curve of the material. With the aim of minimising the exponent {1/n} , it is advised to determine it in the domain of small strains (plastic strain {\strainCmp}_{M,p} lower than 0.2%) (RB 3643.31). The Ramberg-Osgood curve is characterised by three parameters E , K and n . The strain is then written as a function of the stress: \strainCmp = \frac{\stressCmp}{E} + \varepsilon_{M,p}(\stressCmp) where E is Young's modulus and {\strainCmp}_{M,p} the plastic strain of the mean monotonic tension curve, defined by the power law: {\strainCmp}_{M,p} = K{ \left( \frac{\stressCmp}{E} \right)}^{1/n} The material parameters of this law are given by using the keyword POST_ROCHE (or POST_ROCHE_FO ) of left lbrace:ref:DEFI_MATERIAU right rbrace. K corresponds to the keyword RAMB_OSGO_FACT and n to RAMB_OSGO_EXPO . They are used in the computation of the spring-effect factors. Example of a Ramberg Osgood law 3.2 Recovery and classification of the moments One classifies the moments according to the curvilinear abscissa, for each segment. In the RCC-MRX variant, the combination of the moments is carried out in accordance with the RCC-MRx CMS2 (RB 3645.82), for the computation of the abated equivalent stress, formula CODE. Another combination is proposed for the computation of the abated moment and of the abated equivalent stress (RCC-MRX variant, formula REFE_ELAS, and ASNR variant). 3.2.1 Classification of the moments according to RCC-MRx CSM2 The moments depending on the forces (RB 3623.3) are due: - to the weight; they are denoted {M}_{\text{poids}} . - to the earthquake, quasi-static inertial part, if the second method of classification of the seismic moments CMS2 is applied; they are denoted {M}_{\text{SI}} . - to the applied mechanical loadings (including the pressure). The moments depending on the displacements (RB 3623.4) are due: - to the thermal expansions; they are denoted {m}_{\text{ther}} . - to the displacements imposed at the anchors (signed permanent imposed displacements DINS and unsigned seismic differential displacements DDS); they are denoted respectively {m}_{\text{DINS}} and {m}_{\text{S}} . - to the earthquake, inertial part complementary to the quasi-static part, if the 2nd method of classification of the seismic moments CMS2 is applied. They are denoted {m}_{\text{SI}} . 3.2.2 Combination of the moments for the computation of the abated equivalent stress according to RCC-MRx CMS2 (RB 3645.82) (RCC-MRX variant, formula CODE) The combination of the moments, for the computation of the abated equivalent stress, is the following, in accordance with the RCC-MRx: The moments {M}_{\text{SI}} are combined with the other moments “depending on the forces” by adding the absolute values and by assigning to each component the sign of the component of the moment due to the permanent mechanical loadings. The result is denoted M . M = {M}_\text{poids} + \sgn \left( {M}_\text{poids} \right) \vert {M}_{\text{SI}} \vert The moments {m}_{\text{S}} are combined with the other moments “depending on the displacements” by assigning to them, for each component, the sign of the sum of the latter. The result is denoted m . m = {m}_{\text{ther}} + {m}_{\text{DINS}} + \sgn \left( {M}_{\text{ther}}+{m}_{\text{DINS}} \right) \vert {m}_{S} \vert The signed moments are summed together and the absolute values of the unsigned moments are summed together; the sign of the sum of the signed moments is assigned to the sum of the absolute values of the unsigned moments. These two sums are then added. 3.3 Computation of the reference stresses The reference stress is computed for each section. One distinguishes the reference stress due to the imposed displacements and thermal expansions and the inertial seismic reference stress. For each of them, one value is determined for the computation of the abated moment (RCC-MRX variants) and the computation of the abated equivalent stress (RCC-MRX and ASNR variants), and another value is determined specifically for the computation of the abated moment (ASNR form). For the computation of the abated moment (RCC-MRX variant) and the computation of the abated equivalent stress (RCC-MRX and ASNR variants), the stress coefficient {B}_{2} , appearing in the formula of the reference stresses, is defined according to: - {B}_{2}=1 stress coefficient (RB 3680) for the segments of straight part (straight pipes, reducers, tee and branch connections), - {B}_{2}=\max \left( \frac{1.30}{{f}^{2/3}},1.0 \right) stress coefficient (RB 3680) for the elbows and the bends, with f={h}_{c}\frac{{R}_{c}}{{r}_{m}^{2}} where {r}_{m}=\frac{{D}_{e}-{h}_{c}}{2} . {R}_{c} is the radius of curvature, {D}_{e} and {h}_{c} correspond respectively to the outside diameter and to the thickness of the pipe, For the computation of the abated moment (ASNR form), the stress coefficient {B}_{2} , appearing in the formula of the reference stresses, is defined according to: - {B}_{2}=1 everywhere 3.3.1 Reference stresses due to the imposed displacements and to the thermal expansions The reference stress is computed in accordance with §RB 3643.31 (Combination according to the 2nd method of Classification of the Moments depending on the displacements CMS2): {\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}^{2} = {\left(0.79{B}_{2} \frac{{m}_{R}^{\prime}}{Z}\right)}^{2}+{\left(0.87\frac{{m}_{1}}{Z}\right)}^{2} where: - {m}_{R}^{\prime}=\sqrt{{m}_{2}^{2}+{m}_{3}^{2}} is the norm of the resulting bending moment due to the imposed displacements and to the thermal expansions (RB 3623.4), - {m}_{1} is the torsional moment due to the imposed displacements (RB 3623.4), - Z is the moment of inertia, which is written for circular beams Z=\frac{{I}_{y}}{R} , for the reducers one takes the minimum of the ratio over the pipe element Z=\min \left( \frac{{I}_{y}}{R} \right) . 3.3.2 Inertial seismic reference stresses The inertial seismic reference stress is computed in accordance with §RB 3643.31 (Combination according to the 2nd method of Classification of the Seismic Moments CMS2): {\stressCmp}_{\text{S2},\text{ref}}^{2} = {\left(0.79{B}_{2}\frac{{({M}_{\text{S2}})}_{R}^{\prime}}{Z}\right)}^{2} + {\left(0.87\frac{{M}_{S21}}{Z}\right)}^{2} where: - {({M}_{\text{S2}})}_{R}^{\prime} is the resulting inertial seismic bending moment (RB 3645.7 and RB 3645.82), - {M}_{S21} is the inertial seismic torsional moment (RB 3645.7 and RB 3645.82), - the index \text{S2} relates to the CMS2 combination, - {B}_{2} is defined as in r7.10.04-sections-contraintesReferences. 3.4 Computation of the local and total reversibilities The local reversibility is computed for each section and the total reversibility for each segment of the line. For each of them, one distinguishes the reversibilities due to the imposed displacements and thermal expansions and the inertial seismic reversibilities. For each of them, one value is determined for the computation of the abated moment (RCC-MRX forms) and the computation of the abated equivalent stress (RCC-MRX and ASNR variants), and another value is determined specifically for the computation of the abated moment (ASNR form). 3.4.1 Local reversibilities t and {t}_{S} The local reversibility is defined by the ratio of the elastic strain to the plastic strain, corresponding to the reference stress. At each cross-section, the local reversibility linked to the reference stresses due to the imposed displacements and thermal expansions is written: \frac{1}{t} = \frac{{\strainCmp}_{M,p}({\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}})}{\frac{{\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}}{E}} The local reversibility linked to the seismic reference stresses is written: \frac{1}{{t}_{S}} = \frac{{\strainCmp}_{M,p}({\stressCmp}_{\text{S2},\text{ref}})}{\frac{{\stressCmp}_{\text{S2},\text{ref}}}{E}} 3.4.2 Total reversibilities T and {T}_{S} The total reversibility is computed on each segment of the piping system presenting two fixed points. The total reversibility linked to the reference stresses due to the imposed displacements and thermal expansions is written: \frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{l}{\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}^{2}\, A \, ds = \int_{0}^{l}\frac{1}{t}{\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}^{2}\, A \, ds and the total reversibility linked to the seismic reference stresses is written: \frac{1}{{T}_{S}}\int_{0}^{l}{\stressCmp}_{\text{S2},\text{ref}}^{2}\, A \, ds = \int_{0}^{l}\frac{1}{{t}_{S}}{\stressCmp}_{\text{S2},\text{ref}}^{2}\, A \, ds where: - l is the length of the segment of the curvilinear abscissa, - A is the area of the cross-section along the curvilinear abscissa. 3.5 Computation of the spring-effect factors The spring-effect factor is computed for each section; their maxima are computed on each segment. One distinguishes the spring-effect factor due to the imposed displacements and thermal expansions and the inertial seismic spring-effect factor. For each of them, one value is determined for the computation of the abated moment (RCC-MRX variant) and the computation of the abated equivalent stress (RCC-MRX and ASNR variants), and another value is determined specifically for the computation of the abated moment (ASNR variant). 3.5.1 Monotonic spring-effect factor The monotonic spring-effect factor {r}_{M} quantifies the monotonic spring effect. It is computed on each smallest part of the piping system presenting two fixed points. This factor characterises the difference between the stresses and strains {\stressCmp}_{\text{élas}} and {\strainCmp}_{\text{élas}} computed by assuming an elastic constitutive behaviour and the true values \stressCmp and \strainCmp , related by the monotonic tension curve: {r}_{M} = -E \left( \frac{\strainCmp-{\strainCmp}_{\text{élas}}}{\stressCmp-{\stressCmp}_{\text{élas}}} \right) This factor {r}_{M} is: - zero when the spring effect is zero and the stress is purely secondary (the strain is that computed elastically) - infinite when the stress is purely primary (the stress is that computed elastically) There is a factor {r}_{M} at each piping cross-section: {r}_{M} = \max \left( \frac{T}{t}-1;0 \right) 3.5.2 Seismic spring-effect factor The seismic spring-effect factor {r}_{s} quantifies the seismic spring effect: {r}_{s} = \frac{{T}_{s}}{{t}_{s}}-1 3.6 Computation of the abatement coefficients for each segment The elastic stress is assumed to be the linear sum of the reference stress {\stressCmp}_{R} and of the pressure stress {\stressCmp}_{P} {\stressCmp}_{\text{élas}} = {\stressCmp}_{R}+{\stressCmp}_{P} For the monotonic case, one has {\stressCmp}_{R}={\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}} and for the seismic case, one has {\stressCmp}_{R}={\stressCmp}_{\text{S2},\text{ref}} . The abatement coefficients g and {g}_{S} relate the reference stress computed linearly to the “true” stress, coming from the projection of the elastic stress onto the monotonic tension curve along the straight line of slope -\frac{E}{r} . They are computed for each section of each piping segment (option SIGM_LIM ='NON' ). Depending on the monotonic or seismic cases, one has r={r}_{M} or r={r}_{S} respectively. Abatement of the linear elastic stress {\stressCmp}_{\text{élas}} onto the monotonic tension curve Two formulations of the abatement coefficient exist, according to the RCC-MRX and ASNR variants, respectively: - For the RCC-MRX variant: {g}_{\text{opti}} = \frac{\stressCmp -{\stressCmp}_{P}}{{\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}} - For the ASNR variant: {g}_{\text{opti}} = \frac\stressCmp{{\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}+{\stressCmp}_{P}} 3.6.1 Optimised monotonic abatement coefficient The optimised monotonic abatement coefficient {g}_{\text{opti}} is computed from the maximum of the monotonic spring-effect factor along the curvilinear abscissa {\underset{s}{\max}} \left( {r}_{M} \right) , depending on the segment. The true stress \stressCmp and the true strain \strainCmp are then solutions of the following system of equations: {\underset{s}{\max}} \left( {r}_{M} \right) = -E \left( \frac{ \strainCmp-\frac{{\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}}{E} - {\strainCmp}_{trac}({\stressCmp}_{P}) } {\stressCmp -{\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}-{\stressCmp}_{P}} \right) and \strainCmp={\strainCmp}_{trac}(\stressCmp) where {\stressCmp}_{P} corresponds to the stress induced by the internal pressure of the pipe, of expression: {\stressCmp}_{P} = 0,87 \, P \frac{{D}_{i}}{2{h}_{c}} with P the internal pressure, {D}_{i} the inside diameter and {h}_{c} the thickness of the pipe. The inequality {\stressCmp}_{P}<\stressCmp must be satisfied in order to guarantee the correct computation of {g}_{\text{opti}} . 3.6.2 Optimised seismic abatement coefficient The optimised seismic abatement coefficient {g}_{\text{Sopti}} is computed from the maximum of the seismic spring-effect factor along the curvilinear abscissa {\underset{s}{\max}} \left( {r}_{M} \right) , depending on the segment. The true stress \stressCmp and the true strain \strainCmp are then solutions of the following system of equations: {\underset{s}{\max}} \left( {r}_{M} \right) = -E \left( \frac{\strainCmp-\frac{{\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}}{E}-{\strainCmp}_{trac}({\stressCmp}_{P})} {\stressCmp-{\stressCmp}_{\text{ref}}-{\stressCmp}_{P}} \right) and \strainCmp={\strainCmp}_{trac}(\stressCmp) The inequality {\stressCmp}_{P}<\stressCmp must be satisfied in order to guarantee the correct computation of {g}_{\text{Sopti}} . 3.7 Computation of the abatement coefficients for each segment for the RCC-MRX variant The abatement coefficients are computed for each section of each piping segment (option SIGM_LIM ='OUI' ). In this case, one considers that the true stress is no longer an unknown of the system of two equations, but a constant depending on an allowable stress defined from the datum of the minimum rupture stress and of the minimum stress at 0.2% strain of the material; the abatement coefficient can then be computed directly without solution of the system, by an analytical formula codified in the RCC-MRx. 3.7.1 Computation of the true stress from an allowable stress The allowable stress {S}^{\star} is defined by: {S}^{\star} = \alpha \left \lbrace 0,426{({R}_{p0,2})}_{\text{min}}({\theta}_{m}) + 0,032{({R}_{m})}_{\text{min}}({\theta}_{m}) \right \rbrace where: - \alpha is a dimensionless coefficient greater than or equal to 1; it corresponds to the keyword COEF of the material POST_ROCHE - {({R}_{p0,2})}_{\text{min}}({\theta}_{m}) is the minimum conventional yield strength at 0.2% strain, for the mean temperature {\theta}_{m} in the thickness during the loading studied; it corresponds to the operand RP02_MIN of the material POST_ROCHE - {({R}_{m})}_{\text{min}}({\theta}_{m}) is the minimum tensile strength, for the mean temperature {\theta}_{m} in the thickness during the loading studied; it corresponds to the operand RM_MIN of the material POST_ROCHE The true stress \stressCmp is then defined by: \stressCmp = 2{S}^{\star} \frac{{({R}_{p0,2})}_{\text{moy}}({\theta}_{m})} {{({R}_{p0,2})}_{min}({\theta}_{m})} with: - {({R}_{p0,2})}_{\text{moy}}({\theta}_{m}) the mean conventional yield strength at 0.2% strain, for the mean temperature {\theta}_{m} in the thickness during the loading studied 3.7.2 Computation of the monotonic and seismic abatement coefficients According to the RCC-MRx codification (RB 3651.1132 and RB 3651.1142) the monotonic abatement coefficients {g}_{\text{RX}} and seismic abatement coefficients {g}_{\text{SRX}} are then the following: {g}_{\text{RX}} = \frac{(\stressCmp-{\stressCmp}_{P}) \left( 1+{\underset{s}{\max}} \left( {r}_{M} \right) \right )} { E \left \lbrace {\strainCmp}_{M,p}(\stressCmp)-{\strainCmp}_{M,p}({\stressCmp}_{P}) \right \rbrace + \left ( \stressCmp -{\stressCmp}_{P} \right) \left( 1+{\underset{s}{\max}} \left( {r}_{M} \right) \right) } and {g}_{\text{SRX}} = \frac{(\stressCmp -{\stressCmp}_{P}) \left( 1+{\underset{s}{\max}} \left( {r}_{S} \right) \right )} { E\left \lbrace {\strainCmp}_{M,p}(\stressCmp)-{\strainCmp}_{M,p}({\stressCmp}_{P}) \right \rbrace + \left ( \stressCmp -{\stressCmp}_{P} \right) \left( 1+{\underset{s}{\max}} \left( {r}_{S} \right) \right) } Note that these monotonic and seismic coefficients are computed from the maximum monotonic and seismic spring-effect factors along the curvilinear abscissae, respectively. In what follows, the processing is the same whatever the value of SIGM_LIM . {g}_{\text{RX}} will therefore correspond to {g}_{\text{opti}} and {g}_{\text{SRX}} to {g}_{\text{Sopti}} . 3.8 Computation of the abated moments (components and norm) The computation of the abated moments is not explicitly provided for in the RCC-MRX; it is nevertheless available in the RCC-MRX variant. It is available in the ASNR variant. The abated moments fall into two categories: permanent and seismic (or non-permanent). They are differentiated because the former are signed (relative) whereas the latter are unsigned (absolute). They are also added in absolute value, component by component, in order to form the complete abated moments (used for the computation of the abated equivalent stresses). 3.8.1 Abated permanent moments \begin{split}{M}_{\text{abat\_perm}, k} = &{M}_{\text{poids}, k} +{g}_{\text{opti}}{m}_{{\text{ther},k}} +{g}_{\text{opti}}{m}_{{\text{DINS},k}} \\\end{split} With k which is worth 1 torsion for the torsion, 2 for the bending in the plane of the elbow and 3 for the bending out of the plane of the elbow. The resultant is written {M}_{\text{abat\_perm}} = \sqrt{ {M}_{\text{abat\_perm},1}^{2} + {M}_{\text{abat\_perm},2}^{2} + {M}_{\text{abat\_perm},3}^{2} } These 4 values are supplied to the user in the principal output field. 3.8.2 Abated seismic moments {M}_{\text{abat\_sism}, k} = \left \lvert M_{SI,k} \right \rvert + {g}_{\text{opti}} \left \lvert m_{S,k} \right \rvert + {g}_{\text{Sopti}}\left \lvert m_{SI,k} \right \rvert The resultant is written in the same way: {M}_{\text{abat\_sism}} = \sqrt{ {M}_{\text{abat\_sism},1}^{2} + {M}_{\text{abat\_sism},2}^{2} + {M}_{\text{abat\_sism},3}^{2} } These 4 values are also supplied to the user in the principal output field. 3.8.3 Abated moments {M}_{\text{abat}, k} = \left \lvert {M}_{\text{abat\_perm}, k}\right \rvert + \left \lvert{M}_{\text{abat\_sism}, k}\right \rvert These three values are used in the computation of the abated equivalent stresses in the case VARIANTE = 'ASNR' as well as in the case SIGM_ABAT = 'REFE_ELAS' of VARIANTE = 'RCC_MRX' . 3.9 Computation of the equivalent abated stresses 3.9.1 Codified formula The codified formula corresponds to SIGM_ABAT = 'CODE' and is valid only for the RCC-MRX variant. 3.9.1.1 General case The optimised equivalent abated stress is obtained by combination of the moments obtained in §:ref:r7.10.04-sections-classementMomentsRCCMRX weighted by the abatement coefficients. One then uses the coefficients {g}_{\text{opti}} and {g}_{\text{Sopti}} in order to obtain the optimised equivalent stress (this value is not computed in the case RCCM_RX=’OUI’ ) \stressCmp_{\text{equi,opti}} = \sqrt{ \left( D_1 \frac{P \, D_i}{2 h_c} \right)^2 + \left( \left \langle \frac{D_2}{Z} ,\, \vert M \vert + g_{\text{opti}} \vert m \vert + g_{\text{Sopti}} \vert m_{\text{SI}} \vert \right \rangle \right)^2 } where: - \left \lvert M \right \rvert = \left(\begin{array}{c}\left \lvert {M}_{1} \right \rvert\\ \left \lvert {M}_{2} \right \rvert\\ \left \lvert {M}_{3} \right \rvert\end{array}\right) is the signed sum {M}_{\text{forc}} of the moments depending on the forces, including the contribution of the primary loadings (weight…), plus the absolute value of the quasi-static part of the inertial earthquake (pseudo-mode), assigned the sign of {M}_{\text{forc}} , - \left \lvert m \right \rvert = \left(\begin{array}{c}\left \lvert {m}_{1} \right \rvert\\ \left \lvert {m}_{2} \right \rvert\\ \left \lvert {m}_{3} \right \rvert\end{array}\right) is the signed sum {M}_{\text{depl}} of the moments depending on the displacements (thermal expansion, non-seismic imposed displacements), plus the absolute value of the unsigned moments due to the seismic differential displacements, assigned the sign of {M}_{\text{depl}} - \left \lvert {m}_{\text{SI}} \right \rvert = \left(\begin{array}{c}\left \lvert {{m}_{\text{SI}}}_{1} \right \rvert\\ \left \lvert {{m}_{\text{SI}}}_{2} \right \rvert\\ \left \lvert {{m}_{\text{SI}}}_{3} \right \rvert\end{array}\right) is the moment corresponding to the dynamic part of the inertial earthquake, classified as depending on the displacements, taken in absolute value, - P is the pressure imposed inside the pipe, - {D}_{i} and {h}_{c} correspond respectively to the inside diameter and to the thickness of the pipe, - Z is the moment of inertia (which is written for circular beams Z=\frac{{I}_{y}}{R} ), - {D}_{1} is the stress coefficient associated with the internal pressure, - {D}_{2}=\left(\begin{array}{c}{D}_{21}\\ {D}_{22}\\ {D}_{23}\end{array}\right) are the stress coefficients associated with the moments in torsion ( {D}_{21} ) and in bending ( {D}_{22} and {D}_{23} ), - \left \langle \cdot , \cdot \right \rangle is the scalar product. 3.9.1.2 Case of the straight pipes In the case of the straight pipes, one sets: - {D}_{1}=0 , - {D}_{21}=0,712 , - {D}_{22}={D}_{23}=0,429 \left( \frac{{D}_{e}}{{h}_{c}} \right)^{0,16} , where {D}_{e} is the outside diameter of the pipe. 3.9.1.3 Case of the reducers In the case of the reducers, one sets: - Z=\min \left( \frac{{I}_{y}}{R} \right) - {D}_{1}=0 , - {D}_{21}=0,712 , - {D}_{22}={D}_{23}=0,429 \left( \max \left( \frac{{D}_{e}}{{h}_{c}} \right) \right)^{0,16} , where \min \left( \frac{{I}_{y}}{R} \right) is the minimum of the ratio and \max \left( \frac{{D}_{e}}{{h}_{c}} \right) is the maximum of the ratio over the pipe element. 3.9.1.4 Case of the bent pipes and of the elbows In the case of the elbows, one sets: - {D}_{1}=0,87 , - {D}_{21}=0,712 , - {D}_{22}=\max \left( 1,07 \left(\frac{\pi}{{\psi}_{c}}\right)^{-0.4} \, {f}^{-2/3} \left( 1+0,142 \frac{P \, D_{i}} {2 \, {h}_{c} \, {S}_{y} \, {f}^{1,45}} \right)^{-1} , 1,02 \right ) , - {D}_{23}=\max \left( 0,809 \, {f}^{-0,44} \left( 1 + 0,142\frac{ P \, {D}_{i}}{2 \, {h}_{c} \, {S}_{y} \, {f}^{1,45}} \right)^{-1}, 1,02 \right) , - f={h}_{c}\frac{{R}_{c}}{{r}_{m}^{2}} where {r}_{m}=\frac{{D}_{e}-{h}_{c}}{2} , - {D}_{i} , {D}_{e} and {h}_{c} correspond respectively to the inside and outside diameters and to the thickness of the pipe. - {S}_{y} is the minimum conventional yield strength at 0.2% strain (given by the user), - {R}_{c} is the radius of curvature (given by the user), - {\psi}_{c} is the opening angle of the elbow (given by the user). 3.9.2 Modified formula Another formulation of the optimised equivalent abated stress is available, based on the formula of the reference elastic stress. It is selected by SIGM_ABAT = 'REFE_ELAS' . It is proposed as a choice in the RCC-MRX variant; it is integrated, with no possible choice, into the ASNR variant. \stressCmp_{\text{equi,opti}} = \left( D_1 \frac{P \, D_i}{2 \, h_c} \right) + \sqrt{ \left( 0,79 \, {B}_{2} \frac{{M}_{\text{abat},R}^{\prime}}{Z} \right)^2 + \left( 0,87 \, \frac{{M}_{\text{abat},1}}{Z} \right)^{2} } where {M}_{\text{abat},R}^{\prime} is the norm of the optimised abated bending moment: {M}_{\text{abat},R}^{\prime} = \sqrt{ {M}_{\text{abat},2}^{2} + {M}_{\text{abat},3}^{2} } Note that the cumulation of the pressure stress with the stress relative to the other loadings is algebraic, and not quadratic as in the RCC-MRX formula, for reasons of conservatism.

r7.20.01 Projection of a field onto a mesh r7.20.01 Projection of a field onto a mesh Summary: The command PROJ_CHAMP makes it possible to "project" fields (known on a mesh \mathit{ma1} ) onto another mesh \mathit{ma2} . This document describes the various projection methods accessible in this command. Paragraph [§ 6 ] gives a few elements of validation of these methods. 1 General points on the command PROJ_CHAMP The command PROJ_CHAMP makes it possible to project the fields at the nodes or the fields by element onto another mesh. For the fields at the nodes, 4 methods are available: METHODE: 'COLLOCATION' METHODE: 'NUAGE_DEG_0' METHODE: 'NUAGE_DEG_1' METHODE: 'COUPLAGE' The method 'COLLOCATION' uses the shape functions of the elements of the mesh \mathit{ma1} . It is detailed in paragraph [§ 2 ]. The 2 other methods use a smoothing of the values of the field in the neighbourhood of the point where one wants to project the field. These 2 methods are detailed in paragraph [§ 3 ]. Finally, the method 'COUPLAGE' is a variant of the method 'COLLOCATION'. It is developed specially for the fluid-structure coupling with Code_Saturne and must therefore normally not be used outside this framework. For the fields by element 'ELNO', one can use the method 'COLLOCATION'. The problem is the same as for a field at the nodes but the projected field is always continuous whereas the initial field is discontinuous. Moreover, if a node of the mesh \mathit{ma2} lies on the boundary of 2 elements of the mesh \mathit{ma1} , the projected value will be random: it will come from one or the other side of the boundary according to the numbering of the elements. This is why it is not advised to project the 'ELNO' fields. For the fields by element 'ELEM', one can still use the method 'COLLOCATION'. The value of the field (constant per element) is duplicated onto the nodes of the element and one is brought back to the case of the 'ELNO' fields. For the fields by element 'ELGA', a dedicated method ('ECLA_PG') is described in paragraph [§ 4 ] Whatever the method, the user has the possibility of projecting only a "piece" of field onto a "piece" of the mesh \mathit{ma2} . This possibility is offered by the factor keyword VIS_A_VIS. A piece of field is the restriction of the field to a set of nodes (or of mesh cells) of the mesh \mathit{ma1} . A piece of the mesh \mathit{ma2} is a subset of the nodes of \mathit{ma2} . In the remainder of the document, one will no longer speak of a subset of a mesh; one will proceed as if one were projecting the whole mesh \mathit{ma1} onto the whole mesh \mathit{ma2} . 2 Method 'COLLOCATION' Note on the vocabulary: The word "project" is sometimes ambiguous in this document. When one says "project" the field from \mathit{ma1} towards \mathit{ma2} , one seeks the field on \mathit{ma2} knowing that on \mathit{ma1} : the projection goes from 1 towards 2. For the method 'COLLOCATION', one must find for each node \mathit{n2} of \mathit{ma2} which is the point of \mathit{ma1} that occupies the same position as \mathit{n2} ; for this one projects the node \mathit{n2} onto the mesh \mathit{ma1} : the projection goes from 2 towards 1. 2.1 Algorithm implemented One loops over all the nodes of the mesh \mathit{ma2} : for each node ( \mathit{n2} ), one proceeds in 4 stages: 1. One seeks which is the mesh cell \mathit{m1} of \mathit{ma1} which geometrically "contains" the node n2, 2. One determines an approximate position of \mathit{n2} in \mathit{m1} (i.e. its coordinates in the reference element associated with the mesh cell \mathit{m1} ), 3. One "refines" the position computed previously by solving a non-linear problem in order to take into account the fact that the mesh cells are not linear (the Jacobian of the geometric transformation varies over the mesh cell). 4. One uses the shape functions of the mesh cell \mathit{m1} in order to determine the value of the field on \mathit{n2} knowing the value of the field on the nodes of \mathit{m1} . 2.1.1 Note The third stage shows that this method assumes that all the nodes of the mesh cell m1 know the field to be projected. For example, one would not know how to project a field which would carry different degrees of freedom on its "vertex" nodes and on its "edge-midpoint" nodes. The projection of such a field is on the other hand possible with the 2 other projection methods [§ 3 ]. 2.2 The difficulties encountered and their treatment 2.2.1 Stage 1 - One does not treat the possible curvature of the edges of the elements. For example, in the figure below (plane problem), the node \mathit{n2} will be declared to belong to the mesh cell \mathit{m1a} whereas it belongs to the mesh cell \mathit{m1b} . In reality, this problem is rare because, most often, the "curved" edges exist only on the boundary of the meshed domains (the internal facets are plane). - If the node \mathit{n2} is in reality "outside" the mesh \mathit{ma1} , one will assign to it the mesh cell \mathit{m1} closest to it. This behaviour makes it possible to project, without stopping in fatal error, a field onto a mesh whose boundary differs slightly from that of the initial mesh (which is always the case in practice). 2.2.2 Stages 2 and 3 In order to find the point of the reference element which gives, by the geometric transformation, the node \mathit{n2} , one must in general solve a non-linear problem, because it is only for the triangle with 3 nodes (in 2D) and for the tetrahedron with 4 nodes (in 3D) that the geometric transformation is linear. One assumes at first that the mesh cell is linear by forgetting its mid-side nodes and by cutting it arbitrarily into triangles or tetrahedra. In this "linearised" mesh cell one determines an approximate position of the point facing the node \mathit{n2} . Then one solves by a Newton algorithm the non-linear problem of the precise search for the point, starting from the approximation computed previously. Note: the non-linear problem is solved in two cases, 2D (projection of a 2D mesh onto another 2D mesh) or 3D (projection of a 3D mesh onto another 3D mesh), but not for the 2.5D cases (shells immersed in 3D space) or 1.5D (wire mesh in 2D), 2.2.3 Stage 4 One does not always use the true shape functions of the elements of the initial mesh. Indeed, in Code_Aster , it is the finite elements which choose their shape functions: a thermal triangle is not obliged to choose the same shape functions as a mechanical triangle. An element may also not need shape functions, or it may choose different functions according to the variables to be interpolated. The formulation of the element does not always bring out a reference element and an associated geometric transformation either. For all these reasons and so that the programming of PROJ_CHAMP is independent of the finite elements present in the model, one assigns to all the mesh cells of \mathit{ma1} the shape functions of the isoparametric elements 1D, 2D or 3D R3.01.01. 2.3 Details concerning stages 1 and 2 In terms of the software, stages 1 and 2 are carried out simultaneously. We shall discuss in succession the way of treating the following 3 problems: - treatment of a node \mathit{n2} found inside the boundary of the mesh \mathit{ma1} (the most frequent case), - treatment of a node \mathit{n2} outside the boundary of \mathit{ma1} , - treatment of the case of meshes of "shell" type (surfaces immersed in {\mathrm{ℝ}}^{3} ). 2.3.1 Node n2 "interior" In order to understand the treatment of an interior node, let us take the case of a 2D mesh cell QUAD8 ( \mathit{abcd} ). One begins by forgetting its mid-side nodes (and therefore their possible curvature) then one cuts it into 2 triangles ( \mathit{abc} and \mathit{acd} ). This cutting is arbitrary (it depends on the local numbering of the nodes of the QUAD8). Note that the other possible cutting (the other diagonal) would in general give another point in the reference element. \mathit{n2} belongs to the triangle \mathit{abc} . One seeks its barycentric coordinates in this triangle. These are the 3 numbers \mathit{xa},\mathit{xb},\mathit{xc} such that one can write: \mathit{n2}=\mathit{xa}\times a+\mathit{xb}\times b+\mathit{xc}\times c The point N2 of the reference element retained by the algorithm will be: \mathit{N2}=\mathit{xa}\times A+\mathit{xb}\times B+\mathit{xc}\times C For the volume mesh cells (hexahedra, pentahedra, pyramids and tetrahedra), one proceeds in the same way: one forgets the mid-side nodes and one cuts the non-tetrahedral mesh cells into tetrahedra. 2.3.2 Node n2 "exterior" A node \mathit{n2} is declared exterior to the mesh \mathit{ma1} if one has found no mesh cell for which it is interior. When this is observed, one searches for the mesh cell \mathit{m1} closest to \mathit{n2} . The distance computed is that which separates the node \mathit{n2} and the boundary of the mesh cell \mathit{m1} . Let us call \mathit{p2} the point of \mathit{m1} closest to \mathit{n2} . This point may be on a face of a volume element or on an edge or on a vertex. Example (in 2D): With the node B , one associates the point \mathit{pB} obtained here by orthogonal projection of B onto an edge of \mathit{T1} . With the node A , one associates the point \mathit{pA} of the triangle \mathit{T1} . One could just as well have associated with it the point pA of the triangle \mathit{T2} , but this would have changed nothing since the field to be projected is known at the nodes of the mesh. It is therefore continuous between the adjacent elements. Once one has found the point \mathit{p2} of the mesh cell \mathit{m1} which realises the minimum of the distance to \mathit{n2} , one is brought back to the previous problem: the point \mathit{N2} of the reference element which will be associated with \mathit{n2} will be the correspondent of \mathit{p2} by the procedure of paragraph [§ 2.3.1 ]. Notes: For a given triangle (or tetrahedron) T , there is only one point \mathit{p2} realising the minimum distance between \mathit{n2} and T because T is convex. This property would disappear if one took into account the curvature of the edges of the mesh cells. One sees there that the two simplifications of the implementation (forgetting the mid-side nodes and cutting the mesh cells into linear triangles) are linked to each other. An exterior point will always have a value interpolated between the values of the nodes of the mesh \mathit{ma1} and never extrapolated; which is not the case of the 2 methods NUAGE_DEG_0/1. 2.3.3 Case of the "shell" meshes When one seeks to project the nodes of a surface mesh onto another surface mesh, one falls in general systematically on the case of the "exterior" points above. Indeed, the inaccuracy on the coordinates of the nodes means that a node \mathit{n2} is never rigorously in the plane of the triangles of the mesh cells of \mathit{ma1} . It is therefore the procedure of [§ 2.3.2 ] which applies: For each node \mathit{n2} : - search for the triangle (or the tetrahedron) which realises the minimum distance to \mathit{n2} . Identification of the point \mathit{p2} which realises this distance, - computation of the point \mathit{n2} of the reference element which corresponds to \mathit{p2} by the procedure of [§3.3.1]. 3 Method 'NUAGE_DEG_0' or 'NUAGE_DEG_1' 3.1 Principle of the method These 2 methods are based on the same principle: one chooses a priori basis functions \mathit{Fi}(x,y,z) (here polynomials of degree 0 or 1). One seeks, in the vector space generated by these basis functions, the function F=\sum({\alpha}_{i}{F}_{i}) which realises the minimum distance (in the least-squares sense) to the "cloud" of the known points. Once this function has been found, one evaluates it at the point sought. In order to lighten the notations, one places oneself in 2D (but the analyses can be done in the same way in dimension 3 or more ...). The field to be projected is a set of pairs (\mathit{Xj},\mathit{Vj}) where \mathit{Xj}=(\mathit{xj},\mathit{yj}) is a node of the mesh \mathit{ma1} and \mathit{Vj} is a real (value of the field on this node). This field constitutes the cloud of the known points. Let a node \mathit{n2} (x,y) of the mesh \mathit{ma2} for which one wants to compute the value of the field ( V ). Choice of the basis functions: | NUAGE_DEG_0: | a single function: \mathit{F1}=1 | | --- | --- | | NUAGE_DEG_1: | 3 functions: \mathit{F1}=1 ; \mathit{F2}=x ; \mathit{F3}=y | In the remainder of this paragraph, one will choose NUAGE_DEG_1 so that the formulae do not degenerate too much. The function sought is F=\alpha 1\mathrm{F1}+\alpha 2\mathrm{F2}+\alpha 3\mathrm{F3} . One defines a sort of "distance" between F and the pairs (\mathit{Xj},\mathit{Vj}) : D=\sum(\mathit{wj}{(F({X}_{j})-{V}_{j})}^{2}) where the \mathit{wj} are the weights assigned to each pair (\mathit{Xj},\mathit{Vj}) . One wants to minimise D with respect to the 3 variables \alpha 1,\alpha 2,\alpha 3 . D is a quadratic function of \alpha 1,\alpha 2,\alpha 3 . Minimising D amounts to cancelling its derivatives and therefore to solving a linear system with 3 unknowns: \alpha 1,\alpha 2,\alpha 3 . When this problem is solved, one computes: V=\alpha 1+\alpha 2x+\alpha 3y 3.2 Choice of the weighting of the points of the cloud The whole trick of these methods lies in the (difficult) choice of the weights \mathit{wj} assigned to the points of the cloud. - one decides a priori that the weight of a point ( \mathit{Xj} ) depends only on the distance ( d ) separating this point from the node \mathit{n2} (isotropic weighting), - if \mathit{wj} is a constant, the problem no longer depends on the unknown node \mathit{n2} . The function F is unique (for all the nodes of \mathit{ma2} ): it is "the linear regression line" of the cloud, - if \mathit{wj}(d) is a function that decreases too little, the function F is too "smoothed": the local "accidents" are "smoothed out" by the large number of distant points taken into account, - if \mathit{wj}(d) is a function that decreases too much, one takes the risk of catching no point of the cloud. The numerical consequence is that the linear system to be solved becomes singular (and therefore insoluble). We have chosen to write w(d) as a decreasing exponential parameterised by 2 parameters: \mathit{dref} and \beta : w(d)={e}^{-{(d/\mathit{dref})}^{2\beta }} \mathit{dref} is a reference distance (depending on the node \mathit{n2} ). We shall see below how it is computed. \beta is a constant chosen in order to cancel more or less rapidly the weight of the points distant from \mathit{n2} . In the code, \beta has been chosen equal to 0.75. \mathit{dref} is the distance from which one wishes to see the weight of the points decrease rapidly. In the programming, \mathit{dref} is computed as the product of a distance \mathit{d1} by a coefficient \mathit{C1} . Today, we have chosen \mathit{C1}=0.45 . \mathit{d1} is defined as follows: - in 3D, \mathit{d1} is the radius of the smallest ball with centre \mathit{n2} which contains 4 non-coplanar points of the cloud, - in 2D, \mathit{d1} is the radius of the smallest ball with centre \mathit{n2} which contains 3 non-aligned points of the cloud. The problem is said to be 2D if all the nodes of the mesh \mathit{ma1} have the same coordinate z ; it is said to be 3D otherwise. 3.3 Current restriction of the programming The 2 projection methods NUAGE_DEG_0/1 are programmed only for real fields (and not for complex fields) 4 Method 'ECLA_PG' This method is dedicated to the projection of the fields at the Gauss points (ELGA). Let us illustrate this method on a 2D example. One assumes that the initial mesh is made up of 3 triangles (green) having 3 Gauss points (see the figure below). Each triangle is cut into as many sub-elements as there are Gauss points (here 3). The value carried by the Gauss point is assigned to the whole sub-element. A mesh cell of the final mesh (parallelogram) is drawn in light yellow. It has four Gauss points (small orange circles). The value of the projected field on each of these four Gauss points will be that of the sub-element facing the point. In our example, the 2 upper points belong to the same sub-element and they will carry the same value at the end of the projection. 5 Method 'COUPLAGE' This method is dedicated to the fluid-structure coupling with Code_Saturne for the fluid domain. It is based on the method 'COLLOCATION' taking into account specific features of the fluid-structure problems envisaged ( cf. [bib2]). One therefore seeks to project data from a fluid mesh onto a structure mesh, and conversely. The structure mesh is based on an FE discretisation, therefore with knowledge of the associated shape functions, whereas the fluid mesh is based on a finite-volume (FV) discretisation, therefore without shape functions a priori . The kinematic fields on the FV fluid domain are defined at the vertex nodes whereas their dual fields (forces) are constant per face and defined at the midpoints of the faces. Moreover, the structure mesh is very generally markedly coarser than the fluid mesh (which must be very refined at the wall in order to represent the boundary layer well). The first stage of pairing of the nodes of the fluid mesh onto the solid is done by a method of classical 'COLLOCATION' type. It must be pointed out that this method can be used only to generate the mesh-correspondence matrix data structure (CORRESP_2_MAILLA cf. documentation U4.72.05). This data structure will then be reused by the operators of exchange at the interfaces for the fluid-structure coupling: - ENV_CINE_YACS (in order to send the displacement and velocity fields to the fluid code, cf. documentation U7.06.11), - MODI_CHAR_YACS (in order to recover the fluid forces and to add them to the existing structural loading, cf. documentation U7.06.22). Apart from this limitation, the main difference with the method 'COLLOCATION' will be in the construction of the correspondence-matrix data structure (CORRESP_2_MAILLA cf. documentation U4.72.05) at the output of PROJ_CHAMP. Indeed, one will seek to respect as well as possible the conservation of energy at the interface, therefore the conservation of the work of the discretised forces during the passage from fluid to solid ( cf. [bib2]). Obviously, this result is valid only under particular assumptions: - fluid force fields constant per element, - fluid mesh finer than the solid mesh, - pairing method of 'COLLOCATION' type of Code_Aster . In practice, for any coupled fluid-structure problem, one will have to use the method 'COUPLAGE' twice in order to compute two mesh-correspondence data structures. Indeed, one must manage separately the projection of the kinematic fields, which is based on fluid fields defined at the vertex nodes of the fluid mesh, from that of the forces, which are defined at the midpoints of the fluid faces. In each of these two cases, the corresponding fluid mesh will be either the mesh of the vertex nodes, or that of the face-midpoint nodes. The projection method is then the same and the structure mesh is, for its part, unique. All the fluid fields (displacements, velocities and forces at the interface) will be considered by Code_Aster as classical fields at the nodes. 6 Elements of validation for the projection of the fields at the nodes In order to validate the 3 proposed methods, we shall treat the example of the projection of a "one-dimensional" temperature field T=T(x) . The field to be projected is equal to: T(x)=\sin(\mathrm{3x})+\mathrm{Heavyside}(x-1) This field is assigned to the nodes of a rather coarse linear mesh \mathit{ma1} (14 mesh cells) of the segment [0,2] . This field has the property of being discontinuous (in theory) at the point x=1 . Because of the discretisation on the mesh \mathit{ma1} , the field seems only to vary very abruptly between the 2 points x=0.99 and x=1.01 . One projects this field onto a very fine mesh \mathit{ma2} of the same segment (300 elements of length 2/300 ). 6.1 Method: 'COLLOCATION' Collocation One notes that with this method, the projected field holds no surprise: the value obtained by projection is always the linear interpolate between the 2 nodes of \mathit{ma1} where the field is known. 6.1.1 Quadratic initial mesh If one redoes the same analysis by replacing the linear mesh \mathit{ma1} by a quadratic mesh (containing about 2 times fewer mesh cells), one finds: Collocation One notes that the interpolation of the field is now parabolic between the nodes of \mathit{ma1} . One therefore approaches better the shape of the initial function. 6.2 Method: 'NUAGE_DEG_0' One notes that with this method, the projected field appears as a succession of small horizontal "plateaux" connected to one another. This staircase aspect is linked to the parameters ( \beta and \mathit{C1} ) chosen as hard-coded in the code for the form of the exponential decrease of the weight of the points. One also sees that the discontinuity of the initial field is very strongly smoothed out. 6.2.1 Influence of the form of the decreasing exponentials In the following figure, we have modified a parameter of the decreasing exponential of the method 'NUAGE_DEG_0': the parameter \mathit{dref} (or \mathit{C1} , which amounts to the same thing) has been multiplied by 0.5 or 2 relative to the value retained by the code. One notes that the choice of \mathit{dref} influences the result a great deal. If it is too large, one no longer sees the discontinuity. If it is too small, the staircase form becomes more marked. 6.3 Method: 'NUAGE_DEG_1' One notes that with this method, the projected field is correct in the 2 regular zones ( x 1.01 ). On the other hand the discontinuity of the field between these 2 values is strongly exaggerated. This example illustrates well the ability of this method to extrapolate the values of the initial points (because of the estimation of the gradient of the field). In the 2 regular parts, the projected field is fairly close to that obtained with the method 'COLLOCATION'. One simply notes that the method 'NUAGE_DEG_1' rounds the corners a little 6.3.1 Influence of the form of the decreasing exponentials In the following figure, we have modified a parameter of the decreasing exponential of the method 'NUAGE_DEG_1': the parameter \mathit{dref} (or \mathit{C1} , which amounts to the same thing) has been multiplied by 0.5 or 2 relative to the value retained by the code. Here again, one notes that the choice of \mathit{dref} is crucial for the result: too large, the discontinuity is smoothed out; too small, the discontinuity is exaggerated. 6.4 Choice of the best projection method for the fields at the nodes In view of the few preceding curves, it seems clear that the method 'COLLOCATION' is in general preferable to the methods NUAGE_DEG_0/1. This method is "natural" within the framework of the finite elements and it depends on no numerical adjustment coefficient. The methods NUAGE_DEG_0/1 must be reserved, in our opinion, for somewhat special uses: - case of a "non-existent" mesh \mathit{ma1} : one has available only the nodes but not the mesh cells (for example, the "nodes" of \mathit{ma1} are in fact measurement sensors), - case of a field (result of an analysis or obtained by measurements) which one wants to smooth deliberately. But in this case, the 2 numerical parameters ( \mathit{C1} and \beta ) would have to be accessible to the user, which is not the case today. 7 Bibliography 1. FARHAT: «Matching computations : a parallel approach.» Computers & Structures, vol. 54 (4), p. 779-785, 1995.

r7.20.02 Extrapolation of measurements onto a numerical model in dynamics r7.20.02 Extrapolation of measurements onto a numerical model in dynamics Summary: A procedure for extrapolating results of experimental measurements in dynamics (displacements, velocities, accelerations, strains, stresses) onto a numerical model is presented. Based on a representation of the structure on a previously chosen projection basis, it consists in the solution of the inverse problem defined by the identification of the generalised coordinates relative to the projection basis. The solution proposed uses a minimisation, in the least-squares sense, using the LU decomposition or the singular value decomposition (SVD), of a functional possibly regularised by the addition of a criterion of proximity to a solution known a priori. In the case of a temporal identification, an explicit formulation of the a priori information is proposed. > Contents 1 Problem statement One wishes to estimate numerically the behaviour at every point of a structure from the measurements carried out at a few points of the structure. Given the costs and the constraints of accessibility, the experimental measurements are generally limited in number and located at places which are not necessarily the most highly loaded. Thus, in dynamics, knowledge of the stress-concentration zones and of the local values of the stresses is crucial in order to check the mechanical integrity of the equipment. One is then led to extrapolate results of localised measurements over the whole of the numerical mesh of the structure. The extrapolation procedure proposed is based on a representation of the structure on a judiciously chosen projection basis (eigenmodes, static response, ...). It consists in the determination of the generalised coordinates relative to this projection basis. The solution proposed uses a minimisation, in the least-squares sense, by LU or singular value decomposition (SVD), of a functional possibly regularised by the addition of a criterion of proximity to a solution known a priori. In the case of a temporal identification, an explicit formulation of the a priori information is proposed. 2 Notations q,\dot{q},\ddot{q} : vectors of the displacements, velocities and accelerations in the physical frame \eta ,\dot{\eta},\ddot{\eta} : vectors of the generalised displacements, velocities and accelerations F : matrix formed of the projection-basis vectors (displacements) {\Phi}_{\epsilon} : matrix formed of the projection-basis vectors (strains) {\Phi}_{\sigma} : matrix formed of the projection-basis vectors (stresses) \bar{\Phi} : matrix of the basis vectors (displacements), restricted to the measured degrees of freedom {\bar{\Phi}}_{\epsilon} : matrix of the basis vectors (strains), restricted to the measured degrees of freedom {\bar{\Phi}}_{\sigma} : matrix of the basis vectors (stresses), restricted to the measured degrees of freedom I : identity matrix {N}_{\text{num}} : number of projection-basis vectors, {N}_{\exp} : number of measured degrees of freedom t : time variable, \omega : angular-frequency variable \text{TF} : Fourier transform, {\text{TF}}^{-1} : inverse Fourier transform A+: pseudo-inverse of the matrix A 3 Extrapolation procedure The procedure which one wishes to put in place in order to extrapolate results of vibratory measurements onto a numerical model is broken down into 4 stages[bib1] : This procedure relies on the notion of projection of a field into a space of dimension lower than the dimension of the space of the numerical model, and then extrapolation onto the space of the numerical model. The fact of projecting the field into a space of reduced dimension necessarily generates a loss of information during the extrapolation. One therefore sees here the importance of the choice of the projection basis. This basis may be formed of a modal response and/or of a static response. It is assumed here that the numerical model is linear. 4 Relations between the physical quantities and the generalised quantities One assumes that the intrinsic behaviour of the structure is represented in a space spanned by the {N}_{\text{num}} projection-basis vectors. The Rayleigh-Ritz transformation establishes the relation between the degrees of freedom of the structure in the physical frame and its generalised coordinates: q=\Phi \eta In this formulation, the matrix of the basis vectors contains all the spatial information; the generalised coordinates, for their part, depend: - on the time, in the case of a time-response analysis: q(M,t)=\Phi (M)\eta (t) - on the angular frequency, in the case of a harmonic-response analysis: q(M,\omega )=\Phi (M)\eta (\omega ) One may therefore deduce very simply the following relations: | | Harmonic response | Time response | | --- | --- | --- | | Displacement | q(M,\omega )=\Phi (M)\eta (\omega ) | q(M,t)=\Phi (M)\eta (t) | | Velocity | \dot{q}(M,w)=j\omega \Phi (M)\eta (\omega ) | \dot{q}(M,t)=\Phi (M)\dot{\eta}(t) | | Acceleration | \ddot{q}(M,w)=-{\omega}^{2}\Phi (M)\eta (\omega ) | \ddot{q}(M,t)=\Phi (M)\ddot{\eta}(t) | | Strains | \epsilon (M,\omega )={\Phi}_{\epsilon}(M)\eta (\omega ) | \epsilon (M,t)={\Phi}_{\epsilon}(M)\eta (t) | | Stresses | \sigma (M,\omega )={\Phi}_{\sigma}(M)\eta (\omega ) | \sigma (M,t)={\Phi}_{\sigma}(M)\eta (t) | All these formulations therefore present an equivalent form: in the remainder of the document, we shall treat essentially the case of the time displacement, but the results obtained may be transposed to all the other quantities: velocity, acceleration, strain and stress. Likewise, the relations established as a function of time are applicable in the spectral domain: \begin{array}{}\mathrm{TF}(q(M,t))=\Phi (M)\text{TF}(\eta (t))=\Phi (M)\eta (\omega )\\ {\text{TF}}^{-1}(q(M,\omega ))=\Phi (M){\text{TF}}^{-1}(\eta (\omega ))=\Phi (M)\eta (t)\end{array} 5 Computation of the generalised coordinates 5.1 Formulation of the problem The computation of the generalised coordinates \eta is carried out on the matrix of the displacements (respectively velocities, accelerations, strains, stresses) restricted to the measured degrees of freedom, by solution of the matrix system: {q}_{\exp}=\bar{\Phi}\eta The dimensions of the matrix \bar{\Phi} to be "inverted" are ( {N}_{\exp},{N}_{\text{num}} ). One sees here that the computation of the generalised coordinates is carried out in a restricted space: the dimension of the space spanned by the basis vectors is lower than the dimension of the numerical model; one exploits only the information at the measured degrees of freedom. 5.2 Determination of a quasi-solution For the solution of the inverse problem, 3 cases may arise: - {N}_{\exp}={N}_{\text{num}} : the number of measured degrees of freedom is equal to the number of projection-basis vectors whose generalised coordinates one wishes to identify. In this case, there exists a unique solution to the inversion problem: \eta ={\bar{\Phi}}^{-1}{q}_{\exp} - {N}_{\exp}>{N}_{\text{num}} : the number of measured degrees of freedom is greater than the number of projection-basis vectors of the numerical model whose generalised coordinates one wishes to identify. In this case, there exists no exact solution to the inversion problem. A quasi-solution may nevertheless be defined, which minimises the distance: \mid {q}_{\exp}-\bar{\Phi}\eta \mid . The formula \eta ={\left[{\bar{\Phi}}^{T}\bar{\Phi}\right]}^{+}{\bar{\Phi}}^{T}{q}_{\exp} then supplies the (unique) solution in the least-squares sense. In this expression, the matrix {\left[{\bar{\Phi}}^{T}\bar{\Phi}\right]}^{+}{\bar{\Phi}}^{T} denotes the generalised inverse matrix of \bar{\Phi} . The computation of the pseudo-inverse may be carried out using the LU decomposition or the singular value decomposition (SVD). - {N}_{\exp}<{N}_{\text{num}} : the number of measured degrees of freedom is less than the number of projection-basis vectors whose generalised coordinates one wishes to identify (which corresponds to the most common case). In this case, there exists an infinity of solutions to the inversion problem and the objective is to determine an acceptable solution by introducing an additional condition (minimum norm of the solution, or application of methods known as "regularisation methods"). 5.3 Determination of a regularised inverse solution 5.3.1 Principles of the regularisation methods The aim of the regularisation methods [bib4], [bib5] is to propose an approximate solution which is stable with respect to the variations of the input data. One no longer seeks to solve the minimisation equation resulting from the formulation: {q}_{\exp}=\bar{\Phi}\eta , but to determine an approximate (or regularised) solution meeting two requirements: - it satisfies a proximity condition: one seeks {\eta}_{\delta} such that \mid {q}_{\exp}-{\Phi}_{\text{num}}{\eta}_{\delta}\mid <\delta , - it meets an additional condition known as "a priori information". The regularisation methods therefore consist in completing the statement of the problem by introducing a priori information in order to extract, from the family of solutions which are compatible with the experimental data, the one which corresponds best to the problem. This is done by merging, in a single criterion, a measure of the fidelity of the solution with respect to the experimental data and a measure of its fidelity to the a priori information [bib2]. An approach which may easily be implemented in finite dimension is regularisation by optimisation. To be compared with Tikhonov's regularisation method [bib3], it consists in considering an a priori solution {\eta}_{\text{priori}} of the minimisation problem and in seeking the solution of the approximate system which is closest to this solution. One then seeks to minimise the following functional: {\mid {q}_{\exp}-\bar{\Phi}\eta \mid }^{2}+a{\mid \eta -{\eta}_{\text{priori}}\mid }^{2} The parameter a determines the weight assigned to the a priori information. The solution of the minimisation equation is given by: \eta ={\left[{\bar{\Phi}}^{T}\bar{\Phi}+aI\right]}^{-1}({\bar{\Phi}}^{T}{q}_{\exp}+a{\eta}_{\text{priori}}) or, by bringing out explicitly the deviation from the a priori solution: \eta ={\eta}_{\text{priori}}+{\left[{\bar{\Phi}}^{T}\bar{\Phi}+aI\right]}^{-1}{\bar{\Phi}}^{T}({q}_{\exp}-\bar{\Phi}{\eta}_{\text{priori}}) If one sets {\eta}_{\text{priori}}=0 , this formulation consists in seeking the solution known as of "minimum norm" (or Tikhonov of order 0). The addition of the regularising term linked to the matrix aI has the role of shifting the spectrum of {\bar{\Phi}}^{T}\bar{\Phi} in order to ensure the matrix-inversion stage. This analysis procedure therefore makes it possible to implement a better-conditioned computation procedure, which softens the effects of the noise and which supplies a physically acceptable solution. Furthermore, the choice of the values of the matrix aI results from a compromise between the stability of the sought solution and the confidence which one may place in the a priori solution. 5.3.2 Choice of the a priori information In the case of the regularisation methods, the choice of the a priori information constitutes a key stage which determines the representativeness of the final results. This choice may rely on a physical knowledge of the solution or on a knowledge of its evolution as a function of the parameter retained. We provide, in what follows, an example applied to the determination by minimisation of a time variable [bib1]. The minimisation of a variable as a function of time may be carried out at each time step independently of the preceding time step. The introduction of a priori information nevertheless makes it possible to enrich the functional by assuming a slow evolution of the variables determined: {\eta}_{\text{priori}}(t)=\eta (t-\text{dt}) This assumption is acceptable only when the sampling step is sufficiently small. Indeed, the solution at a given time instant is approximated by (Taylor expansion): \eta (t)=\eta (t-\text{dt})+\text{dt}\dot{\eta}(t-\text{dt})+o(\text{dt}) The maximum response frequency of the structure is determined by the angular frequency of the mode of highest order {\omega}_{\max} taken in the modelling. One therefore has: \mid \frac{\eta (t)-\eta (t-\text{dt})}{\eta (t-\text{dt})}\mid <{\omega}_{\max}\text{dt}+\mid o(\text{dt})\mid In order that the corrective term be small (and therefore that the a priori information constitute a first-order approximation of the sought solution), the sampling step must satisfy: \text{dt}\text{<<}\frac{1}{{\omega}_{\max}} At the initial time instant (t=0), given that one has no information on the a priori solution, the analysis is carried out by seeking the minimum-norm solution. In order to avoid propagating the error which results from this, it may be necessary to assign a low confidence to the a priori information over the first time steps (by means of the parameter ) and to exploit the results only from the time instant at which one may consider that the errors have been sufficiently attenuated. If need be, complementary studies will be carried out in order to determine the optimal parameters for use of the feature developed in Code_Aster . In the frequency domain, numerous possibilities are offered for determining the a priori information. They rely either on a physical knowledge of the solution (experimental highlighting of resonances or of forced responses), or on a formulation of the generalised displacements as a function of the frequency (type: gain functions), in which case the minimisation finally leads to characterising the dynamic loadings. 6 Implementation in Code_Aster The projection basis is constituted either of the dynamic modes computed by the command CALC_MODES U4.52.02 stored in a concept of type mode_meca, or of the dynamic modes and the static modes computed by the command DEFI_BASE_MODALE U4.64.02 stored in a concept of type base_modale. The phase of computation of the generalised coordinates is treated by the command PROJ_MESU_MODAL U4.73.01. The data are gathered there under 4 factor keywords. The data relating to the numerical model (projection basis) are gathered under the factor keyword MODELE_CALCUL. One specifies there the numerical model and the projection basis. The data relating to the measurements are gathered under the factor keyword MODELE_MESURE. One specifies there in particular the model associated with the structure and the measurement read by the command LIRE_RESU. The possible manual spatial association of the nodes is given under the factor keyword CORR_MANU. The data concerning the solution of the inverse problem are gathered under the factor keyword RESOLUTION. One specifies there the decomposition method employed (LU, SVD) and the taking into account of the regularisation term. The restitution of the results in the physical basis may then be carried out by the command REST_GENE_PHYS U4.63.31. 7 Bibliography 1. u0.00.01 Reading guide to the User documentation Reading guide to the User documentation > Summary. This document aims to offer help for a first access to the content of the User documentation. 1 Documentation of Code_Aster: organisation and access 1.1 A logical breakdown into Manuals: the ARDUV The technical documentation of Code_Aster comprises: - five manuals, - a set of other documentary items which complement the basic technical documentation above. | User's manual | U | Instructions for use of the commands, user data structures, examples of use | | --- | --- | --- | | Reference manual | R | Formulation of the modelled phenomena, analysis methods, numerical algorithms | | Programmer's manual (Descriptif informatique) | D | Data structures, algorithms, the architecture, environment | | Validation manual | V | Elementary test sheets in all areas of modelling | | Administration manual | A | Quality plan, development and maintenance procedures, service commitments, versioning | Other documentary items exist (the newsletters, the presentation brochure of the code, various talks, the presentations at the annual day …) and are all accessible on the website https://www.code-aster.org. The basic manuals for the user of Code_Aster are the User's manual, the Reference manual and the Validation manual. The User's manual frequently refers to the Reference manual. The Programmer's manual (Descriptif informatique) is reserved for developers; in principle it does not concern users. The same is true of the Administration manual. One major exception for the latter: the user has access to the Quality sheets and the Quality follow-up sheets, which indicate, for the production versions (version d'exploitation) and the development versions of the code, what the changes are, which identified errors have been corrected or not, and the workarounds. The manual is subdivided into ten named parts (numbered from 0 to 9), the parts into booklets which are likewise named (00 to 99), and the booklets into documents (00 to 99). 1.1.1 The document key A document is located in the document space of the manuals by a document key: Manual_Part.Booklet_number.Document_number Example of a document key: U1.02.00 Naturally, a document is referred to by its document key. For convenience, two classes of documents are also designated by the Aster function which they document: - the documents of the instructions for use of the commands (User's manual), designated by the name of the command documented, - the documents describing the elementary test cases dedicated to validation of the code (Validation manual), designated by the test-case code . Examples : U4.43.01 documents the command DEFI_MATERIAU; one calls it the document DEFI_MATERIAU. V7.90.04 documents the thermomechanical test case HNSV100: Thermoplasticity in simple tension; one calls it the document HNSV100. Documentary items other than those contained in the manuals are not assigned the key just described. 1.1.2 Which version of the code does the document apply to? Each technical document of the manuals carries in its header a certain amount of bibliographic particulars (the title of the document, the name of the person responsible, the key, the summary, the version of the code). Among these, three deserve particular attention because they relate to the Quality Assurance of the code and to the updating of the documents: - the version of the code concerned by the document, - the revision index of the document, - the date, which corresponds to the publication date of the revision of the document concerned. At the top right of the page header of the document there is an indicator which specifies the version of Code_Aster to which the document applies. This indicator may take two kinds of value: - "Development version" if the document is in the current production cycle, linked to the development version of Code_Aster. The document visible to the reader is then the latest published state, which replaces any earlier states attached to this version. - A version number, "10" for example, when the document is attached to a production version (version d'exploitation) of Code_Aster. This number is then the major version number of Code_Aster. The documentation applies to the production sub-index then in force ("10.6" for example). There are always at least 2 versions of the code available: - The so-called production version (version d'exploitation), validated and qualified, which must be used for studies under quality assurance. - The development version, not yet validated or qualified. The user of Code_Aster must at all times know which are officially the production version (version d'exploitation) and the development version. These versions change every 2 years (increment of the version number). Each time a version and production or development sub-versions are brought into service, a Quality sheet and Quality follow-up sheets are brought into service. These documents list, for a given version or sub-version, the qualified areas (features) and the notes and the restrictions on the qualified areas. These sheets (which are documents from the Administration file) are available as A documents. 1.2 Accessing the User documentation of Code_Aster The technical User documentation of Code_Aster is a subset of its general documentation. 1.2.1 It is entirely electronic documentation The documentation is published on the website of the code at: https://www.code-aster.org/ Every night, an automatic process publishes on this site the documents which have been published in the document-management application a-ged during the previous day. In practice, the updates mainly concern the development version, whose documentation changes at the pace of the new developments integrated into the code each week. 1.3 General presentation of the User documentary resources In practice the ordinary user will draw documentary resources from 3 manuals , in this order: - Manual U , whose structure the user must keep clearly in mind | Documented features | Manual parts | | --- | --- | | Instructions for use of the commands | U4: basic commands U7: commands for data exchange with other software | | Characteristics of the modellings | U3 | | User's guide to the modellings | U2 | | Access to the code | U1 | - Manual R : the finite elements, the formulation of the modellings of the phenomena - Manual V : the validation test cases 2 Getting started It is obviously out of the question to read the whole User's manual exhaustively. In May 2011, it comprised 338 documents (of which 242 concern the use of the commands proper) representing thousands of physical pages. Many documents probably do not concern the user at the time of a first modelling and a first analysis; it is nevertheless absolutely necessary to consult the documents describing the features which implement this first modelling. This is for two reasons: - to avoid errors in use, - but also to be aware of the capabilities of Code_Aster close to those being sought (workarounds) which might perhaps prove useful. It is therefore advisable to consult the User documentation following the approach proposed below. 2.1 Can Code_Aster deal with the subject of my problem? Four documents claim to answer this question. They are presented from the most concise to the most complete. 2.1.1 For a quick answer Consult the pages of the brochure presenting the modelling areas of the code, on the website, Product section, where the physical phenomena which can be modelled by the code are described concisely. 2.1.2 For a more thorough answer Consult the document U1.02.00 Introduction to Code_Aster , in particular chapters 1.3 (Phenomena, modellings, finite elements and constitutive behaviours) and 1.4 (Several analysis methods), where the phenomena which can be modelled by the code are described concisely. 2.1.3 For a more up-to-date answer (taking the latest developments into account) Consult the slides of the latest presentation of the new features of the code at the annual users' day of Code_Aster , as of the publication date of this document: Product section of the website. 2.1.4 For a still more developed answer ... Here one enters an area of questioning where the answer can no longer be given directly by items present on the documentary server. For example, the answer may be YES and consist of subtleties of modelling or roundabout modelling paths. In any event, it is addressed to users who are already experienced. The AOM service ( A id to the O ptimisation of M odelling) of the Experience Feedback (REX) makes it possible to submit to the Aster Development Team (EDA) a particular modelling problem to be carried out with Aster resources. A person from the EDA is then assigned to help the requester carry out the modelling. 2.2 Has Code_Aster already dealt with a problem comparable (similar) to mine? Two paths are proposed: the path of the elementary test cases, and the path of the industrial applications. 2.2.1 The elementary test cases The test-case base associated with Code_Aster is supplied with the local installations or can be consulted on the centralised server. These tests serve three purposes: - verification of the programmed models by comparison with reference solutions (analytical or computed); - computer verification of Code_Aster: exhaustive coverage of the software paths, verification of non-regression of operation when porting to different system solutions. - the educational presentation of simple implementations: small studies which are quickly understood on reading the command files and the associated validation documents (V). It is this third function of the test cases that is discussed here. The user will look to see whether an elementary test case deals with a problem similar to the user's own: documentary server, heading VALIDATION / Test cases by name ; the list of the documentation of the test-case names (classified by area of application) is displayed, together with their titles; or else the Use/Examples section of the site. 2.2.2 The industrial studies A certain number of industrial studies (applications), carried out using Code_Aster , have been presented at the annual users' day. These documented studies are available on the site, under Product/Applications. There one finds the collection of Study sheets from the periodical ASTER échos since its creation (10/91, 39 issues published as of 01/2003) and a collection of industrial studies in all the modelling areas of the code, presented on the occasion of the annual days of Code_Aster . 3 First use of code_aster Consult the document U1.01.04 describing the graphical access interface astk . The simplest way to carry out an analysis with code_aster is to start from a similar example, which is often found among the elementary test cases described in the Validation manual. The command files associated with the test cases described in the validation documentation are located in the astest directory of the version used. On the centralised computing server of EDF R&D, they are in /aster/vx/STAx/astest where x is the number of the production version (version d'exploitation). This way of proceeding by analogy, generally well appreciated by the community of mechanical engineers, must not completely replace a constructive approach. Very often many possibilities are available for doing the same work, and they are more or less well suited to each case. One must therefore get into the habit of consulting this validation manual for every new need. 3.1 The main principles and the key stages of an analysis A reading path is set out below, inspired by the major compulsory stages of a mechanical study with code_aster. In this approach, three documents are proposed for reading. 3.1.1 The main principles of code_aster Consult the document U1.03.00 The main principles of code_aster, which briefly presents the operating principles and the main rules of use. 3.1.2 Simple example of use of code_aster Consult the document U1.05.00 Simple example of use of code_aster: the "essential" commands, for an analysis of a thin cylindrical tank under hydrostatic pressure, axisymmetric modelling. 3.2 The mesh The structure of the Aster mesh file is described in the document U3.01.00 Description of the code_aster mesh file. If the initial mesh comes from a mesher external to Aster , for example GMSH, GIBI or I-DEAS, the Aster interfaces and commands which create, from the objects produced by these pre-processors, objects of the Aster mesh (which are not a copy of the initial objects; their meaning may change, and new objects may be created) are described in the documents: U3.02.01 Interface of the GMSH mesh file with Aster, U3.03.01 Interface of the I-DEAS mesh file with Aster, U3.04.01 Interface of the GIBI mesh file with Aster, U7.01.01 Procedure PRE_IDEAS, U7.01.11 Procedure PRE_GIBI, U7.01.31 Procedure PRE_GMSH, The mesh format recommended when using code_aster is the MED format (Data Exchange Model). It is the default format when reading meshes and writing results. 3.3 The commands The descriptions of the commands of Code_Aster are contained in parts U4 and U7 of the User's manual. It is certainly to these 2 parts of the manual that the Aster user will turn most often.
