It would indeed be unfortunate to stop with a fatal error after a long solution because of a keyword forgotten in a post-processing command. This also means that all the stages of the command set are built and kept in memory. If several thousand stages are reached, this can become very memory-consuming and this mode is then no longer recommended. The step-by-step mode builds a stage only after having executed the previous one. It therefore detects only the semantic errors of the current command and has the disadvantage described above. It does however make it possible to exploit a computed result (in a concept) in the command file in order, for example, to place conditional instructions there. In this mode, the executed stage is immediately released from memory. The memory used is then independent of the number of stages to be executed. Here is an example of a loop with a stopping criterion on the value of a computed quantity (grandeur), stored in the concept of type table: RELV[k]. If, for example, a mandatory keyword is missing in the call to POST_RELEVE_T, this will be detected only after the complete execution of the first MECA_STATIQUE. On the other hand, the step-by-step mode makes possible here the assignment of the variable SYY, since the concept RELV[k] has been completely computed at the moment when the supervisor executes this line. DEBUT(PAR_LOT='NON') RESU=[None] 10 RELV=[None] 10 for k in range(1,10): RESU[k]=MECA_STATIQUE( ... ) RELV[k]=POST_RELEVE_T( ... ) SYY=RELV[k]['VMIS',4] if SYY Note. EFICAS can generate and re-read only command sets containing exclusively ASTER commands, without other python instructions; this independently of the PAR_LOT mode chosen. 2.3 The construction of the stages During the construction of each ETAPE object, its semantic consistency with the catalogue of the command to which it refers is checked. Any error detected is recorded in a report which, in global execution mode, is delivered after the analysis of the whole command file. Examples of semantic checks: - compliance with the number of arguments of the keywords, - compliance with the argument type, - membership of an argument in a list of possible values, - correctness of the spelling of a keyword or of a factor keyword, - compliance with the rules of exclusion or of implication between keywords, - presence of the mandatory keywords. At this stage, if the command is an operator and produces a concept, the latter is typed. The supervisor checks that a concept of the same name has not already been defined or, if it is reused, that the command authorises it. 2.4 The processing of macro-commands A macro-command, as seen by the user, is an ordinary command. In fact, it does not call a high-level Fortran routine directly but generates other commands. Two types of macro-command exist: - the macros in Python, - the supervisor macros: these are the special commands (DEBUT, FORMULE, INCLUDE, INCLUDE_MATERIAU, POURSUITE) which require processing at the level of their construction. In the same way as the JDC itself, the call to a macro-command produces a parent object (of type MACRO-ETAPE) which contains child objects: the stages generated by the macro, or even other macros. A macro-command of the JDC is first processed like the other commands (syntactic verification, construction of the macro stage). It is then “built” by application of the python Build method to the JDC object. After its construction, the stages of the commands produced by the macro are substituted for the stage of the macro itself, for later execution. It is important to note that the construction phase of the macro-commands takes place just before their execution, and not during the global pass over the command file in PAR_LOT='OUI' mode. This has two consequences: - EFICAS analyses the syntax of the macro-command itself, but not that of its sub-commands. - One can on the other hand exploit, in the programming of the macros, previously computed data brought back into the python namespace, without having to impose PAR_LOT='NON' mode on the user of the macro. 2.5 The start-up procedures The start-up procedures available are: DEBUT (cf. U4.11.01 and POURSUITE U4.11.03) At least one of these two procedures must mandatorily be present in the command file. No other Aster command must precede them. If this is the case, or if neither is present, execution will be stopped as soon as the JDC is created. It is these procedures which contain the information on the execution mode (PAR_LOT='OUI' or 'NON') which conditions the execution mode of the commands which follow. They are supervisor macro-commands which, on their construction, call the Fortran routines making it possible to initialise the analysis by the following tasks: - "connection" of the logical units of the standard files, - opening of the databases, - reading of the element catalogue. The first task consists in matching the logical-unit numbers of standard input/output files (message, error, result). The second task consists in defining and opening the databases (direct-access file used by the memory manager) in accordance with the user's instructions; the user can redefine parameters of these files (see documents U4.11.01 and U4.11.03 on the start-up procedures). The JEVEUX initialisation routines are called for this purpose (see document D6.02.01, the Memory manager, JEVEUX). The sequence of commands to be executed ends mandatorily with the FIN command. The text which follows FIN must be commented out (that is, begin with #). For an included file, it is the RETOUR command which marks the end of the instructions that ASTER must take into account. > Note. In interactive mode, commands entered by hand, do not put a FIN command and pass the –interact argument on the job-submission command line. 2.6 Links with EFICAS The kernel of the supervisor is common with Eficas, the editor of Aster command files. When a command file is edited, the latter carries out the syntactic analysis and the consistency checks of the concepts by construction of the JDC and of its ETAPE objects. Eficas does not of course carry out the macro-command construction task, which would require the source code of Aster . 3 The command language 3.1 Python and the command language A command file for Code_Aster is composed exclusively of Python instructions. The first of the constraints is therefore to comply with the rules of this language. One may read the Python tutorial (www.python.org) or the many introductory books on Python for more detail, but this is not necessary for the use of Aster. A command file may contain python instructions of two kinds: Aster commands and … any other python instruction. Indeed, a command file is a python program in its own right and one can in particular place in it control structures (loops), tests (if), numerical computations, and calls to pre- and post-processing functions. In the context of a “classical” use of the code, where the command file contains exclusively Aster commands, the two rules specific to Python to be remembered are: - No indentation on the first line of the declaration of an instruction. mail = LIRE_MAILLAGE ( ) Neither a blank nor a tabulation must be placed before the character string mail. - The arguments of the functions, in other words the keywords of the commands, are separated by commas; they consist of a keyword, the “=” sign, and the content of the keyword. Important: The EFICAS editor makes it possible to produce only command files of this type: containing exclusively ASTER commands, without any other Python instruction. Using EFICAS essentially guarantees three things: - the file produced will have a correct python syntax, - the commands produced will be consistent with the command catalogue, - the produced concepts will be correctly chained (no use of a concept without its having been created by a previous command). The user having composed his command file in this way will be safe from a stop at execution on the grounds of a syntax problem. 3.2 Notion of concept Definition: the Aster data structures which the user can handle and name are called concepts . These concepts are typed at the time of their creation and can be used only as an input argument of the corresponding type in a later command. The notion of concept therefore allows the user to handle objects symbolically and independently of their internal representation (which he may not know). Moreover, the python object designated by the name of the concept contains no information other than its type and its class in the python sense (cf. doc D). Its name, transmitted by the supervisor to FORTRAN, allows Aster to find the corresponding data structure in the global database. But it is not possible to have visibility of the data structure from the command file. For example, the following instructions do not make it possible to print the data structure of type maillage and of name mail: mail=LIRE_MAILLAGE ( ) print mail but generate the following message: There is an exception to this rule: the tables. Indeed, a programming device makes it possible to recover simply the information contained in a TABLE data structure by handling the latter as a two-entry array: pour imprimer une valeur: print resu[ ‘DX’ , 1] pour l’affecter à une variable: valeur = resu[ ‘DX’ , 1] This of course assumes that the data structure resu, of type TABLE, has already been computed at the moment when this instruction is encountered: therefore in step-by-step execution mode (PAR_LOT='NON'). Lexical note: Concept names must not exceed 8 characters. Alphanumeric characters are allowed (lower-case and upper-case letters, and digits not placed in first position) as well as the underscore ‘_’. Case is important: the concepts “MAIL” and “Mail” may be used in the same command file and will be regarded as different … this is however not recommended for the readability of the file! 3.3 Possible operations The structure of the command language takes the form of a linear sequence of instructions. Apart from python instructions other than Aster commands, which are not at issue for the moment, three kinds of instructions (or of commands) are available: - the operator, which carries out an action and which supplies a produced concept of a predefined type that can be used by the following instructions in the command set, - the procedure, which carries out an action but does not supply a concept, - the macro-command, which generates a sequence of instructions of the two previous types and which can produce zero, one or several concepts. Typically, an operator will be an assignment or solution command, and a procedure will be a print command (to a file). From the syntactic point of view an operator takes the form: nomconcept = opérateur( arguments . . . ) Whereas a procedure takes the form: procédure( arguments . . . ) The syntax of an operator or of a procedure is described in the following paragraph. 3.4 Rules on the concept produced by an operator 3.4.1 Basic principle At each execution of an operator, the latter supplies a new produced concept of the type predefined in the command catalogue. The concepts appearing as an input argument of the commands are not modified. 3.4.2 Produced concept and reused concept A reused concept is a concept which, having been produced by an operator, is modified by a new occurrence of this operator or by another operator. The use of a reused concept is possible, as an exception to the Basic Principle, only under two conditions: - authorisation given, by the catalogue and the programming of the command, to use reusable concepts for the operator: the reentrant attribute of the catalogue is equal to ‘o’ or ‘f’, - an explicit request by the user for the reuse of a produced concept, by the attribute reuse=nom_du_concept in the arguments of the commands which allow it. 3.4.3 Checks carried out by the supervisor on the produced concepts - Produced concept complying with the basic principle: The supervisor checks that the name of the produced concept is not already assigned by one of the previous commands, in particular by a command of a previous execution in the case of a POURSUITE or of an INCLUDE. - Concept used in reuse: The supervisor checks that: - the name of the produced concept is indeed already assigned. - the operator is indeed authorised to accept reused concepts, - the type of the concept complies with the type of concept produced by the operator. Commented examples: DEBUT ( ) concept=opérateur ( ) # (1) est correct : on défini le concept, concept=opérateur ( ) # (2) est incorrect : on essaie de redéfinir le # concept mais sans le dire, concept=opérateur (reuse = concept ) # (3) est correct, si l'opérateur accepte des # concepts existants et si le type est # cohérent; c’est incorrect si l'opérateur # ne les accepte pas. FIN ( ) In fact a concept can be created only once: which means appearing to the left of the = (equals) sign without reuse being used in the arguments of the command. In the case of a reuse, specifying the name of the concept again after the reuse attribute is redundant; all the more so since the supervisor checks that the two concept names are identical. > Note. A concept can be destroyed, and therefore its name reused afterwards. 3.5 Body of a command 3.5.1 Introduction The body of a command contains the "variable" part of the command. The declarations are separated by commas and, apart from the reuse attribute mentioned above, they are all of the form: [keyword] = [argument] The keyword is necessarily a keyword of the current command, declared in the catalogue of the latter. 3.5.2 Keyword A keyword is a formal identifier; it is the name of the attribute receiving the argument. Example: MATRICE = ... Syntactic notes: - the order of appearance of the keywords is free; it is not imposed by the order of declaration in the catalogues, - the keywords cannot exceed 16 characters (but only the first 10 characters are significant). There are two types of keywords: the simple keywords and the factor keywords, which differ by the nature of their arguments. 3.5.3 Argument of a simple keyword 3.5.3.1 The type of the arguments The basic types recognised by the supervisor are: - the integers, - the reals, - the complexes, - the texts, - the logicals, - the concepts, - as well as the lists of these basic types. The integers and the reals correspond exactly to the equivalent types in python. - Optional simple keyword expecting a real: Catalogue : VALE = SIMP( statut=’f’ , typ = ‘R’ ) , Fichier de commandes : VALE = 10. , - Optional simple keyword expecting an integer: Catalogue : INFO = SIMP( statut=’f’ , typ = ‘I’ ) , Fichier de commandes : INFO = 1 , The representation of the complex type is a python "tuple" containing a character string indicating the mode of representation of the complex number (real and imaginary parts, or modulus and phase) then the numerical values. Catalogue : VALE_C = SIMP( statut=’f’ , typ = ‘C’ ) , Fichier de commandes : VALE_C = ( ‘RI’ , 0.732 , -0.732 ) , Fichier de commandes : VALE_C = ( ‘MP’ , 1. , -45. ) , The two notations are strictly equivalent. In ‘MP’ notation, the phase is in degrees. The text type is declared between single quotes. Case is respected. However, when a keyword must take a value from a list predefined in the catalogue, usage has it that this value is today always in capitals. Catalogue : TOUT =SIMP( typ=‘TXM’,into=(‘OUI’,’NON’)) , Fichier de commandes : TOUT = ‘OUI’ , Case is important and, in the context above, the following command line will fail: Fichier de commandes : TOUT = ‘oui’ , The logical type is not used today in the command catalogue. The concept is declared simply by its name, without quotes or double quotes. 3.5.3.2 Notion of list Caution : The word “list” is here a misuse of language. It is not the python “list” type but rather tuples, in the python sense: the various items are declared between an opening parenthesis and a closing parenthesis; they are separated by commas. Lists are homogeneous lists, that is to say lists whose elements are of the same basic type. Any basic type can be used in a list. Examples of lists: | list of integers | (1, 2, 3, 4), | | --- | --- | | list of text | ( 'ceci', 'est', 'une', 'liste', 'de', 'texte'), | | list of concepts | ( resu1, resu2, resu3 ), | Ease of use: It is accepted that a list reduced to a single element may be described without parentheses. Example of an erroneous list: Heterogeneous list of an integer and a real (1, 3, 4.) 3.5.4 Factor keyword Some information cannot be given globally (all at once in the command); it is therefore important to provide for the repetition of certain keywords, in order to be able to assign different arguments to them. The factor keyword offers this possibility; under a factor keyword, one will therefore find a set of (simple) keywords, which can be used at each occurrence of the factor keyword. This also makes it possible to improve the readability of the command file by grouping keywords which share a common meaning: for example the various parameters of one and the same material. Unlike the simple keyword, the factor keyword can receive only a single type of object: the supervisor object “_F”, or a list of the latter. Either the factor keyword has only one occurrence, and one can write for example, at choice: IMPRESSION = _F( RESULTAT = resu, UNITE = 6), ou IMPRESSION = ( _F( RESULTAT = resu, UNITE = 6), ), In the first case, the factor keyword IMPRESSION receives an _F object; in the other, it receives a singleton. Watch the comma; in python, a one-element tuple is written: (element,) Or the factor keyword has several occurrences, two in this example: IMPRESSION = ( _F( RESULTAT = resu1, UNITE = 6), _F( RESULTAT = resu2, UNITE = 7) ), The number of occurrences (minimum and/or maximum) expected of a factor keyword is defined in the command catalogue. Notion of default value It is possible to have default values assigned by the supervisor. These values are defined in the command catalogue and not in the FORTRAN. There is no distinction, from the point of view of the routine associated with the command, between a value supplied by the user and a default value introduced by the supervisor. This appears when the user commands are printed by the supervisor in the message file: all the default values appear in the command text, if they have not been supplied by the user. Reminder : a default value cannot be given to a concept. 4 Definition of values and evaluation of expressions It is possible to assign values to python variables in order to use them as arguments of simple keywords: these variables are called parameters in EFICAS. They can contain integer, real or complex values, texts, or lists of these types. Example: young = 2.E+11 mat = DEFI_MATERIAU ( ELAS = _F( E = young , NU = 0.3 ) ) At the end of execution, the python context is saved with the database. Thus, in the restart which will follow, the parameters will still be present, with their predefined values, just like the ASTER concepts. It is possible to carry out operations in python on the arguments of simple keywords: Pisur2 = pi/2. mat = MA_COMMANDE ( VALE = Pisur2 ) or: var = ’ world’ mat = MA_COMMANDE ( VALE = pi/2. , VALE2 = Pisur2+cos(30.) , TEXTE = ‘hello’+var ) 5 Use of python in the command files It is not necessary to know the python language in order to use Code_Aster . Indeed, subject to a few basic rules to be respected concerning indentation and parenthesisation, only knowledge of the command language described in the command catalogues is necessary. And furthermore, EFICAS makes it possible to do without referring to the catalogue or to the “syntax” paragraph of the commands, by proposing graphically the keywords to be filled in. However, the advanced user will be able to put to good use the power of the PYTHON language in his command file, since the latter is already written in this language. The four main uses can be: the writing of customised macro-commands, the use of general python instructions, the import of useful python modules, and the recovery of information from the Code_Aster data structures into PYTHON variables. > Note. If one wants to use accented French characters in the command file or the imported modules, the following instruction must be placed on the first or second line of the file: – – coding: iso–8859–1 – – In python 2.3, the absence of this line causes a warning which will become an error in python 2.4; in ASTER, it is systematically an error. 5.1 Customised macro-commands See document D5.01.02: “Introducing a new macro-command”. Customised macro-commands are very easy to program. They can serve to capitalise recurring analysis schemes and thus constitute a trade tool. It is strongly recommended to take the existing macro-commands as an example: the Macro package in the bibpyt directory. 5.2 General PYTHON instructions and useful modules Advanced users can derive great benefit from the use of loops (for), of tests (if), of exceptions (try, except) and, in general, from all the power of the PYTHON language directly in their command file. The list of uses is impossible to draw up exhaustively. Many examples are present in the test cases of the test database. One can for example carry out mesh adaptation by placing the analysis/remeshing sequence in a loop, or establish a stopping criterion for the iterations by a test on a computed value. Consult the following paragraph devoted to the “particularised” Aster exceptions. In a loop, if one recreates an already existing concept, one must remember to destroy it beforehand by the DETRUIRE command. The other miscellaneous python features of interest to the Code_Aster user can be: - reading and writing to a file, - numerical computation (for example using Numerical Python), - the call, via the os module, to the script language, and in particular the launching of a third-party code (os.system) - the handling of character strings - the call to graphical modules (grace, gnuplot) 5.3 PYTHON exceptions of the aster module The Python exception mechanism is very useful; it allows, for example, one to “try” a command and then regain control if the latter “crashes” by raising a particular exception: try: bloc d’instructions except ErreurIdentifiée, message: bloc d’instructions exécuté si ErreurIdentifiée se produit… In the command file, this mechanism can be used with any exception of the standard Python modules. One also has exceptions specific to Code_Aster (to the aster module), divided into two categories: the exceptions associated with errors, and that associated with errors. 5.3.1 Interception of errors In the event of an error, the error is identified by one of these exceptions: | aster.NonConvergenceError | in the event of non-convergence of the analysis, | | --- | --- | | aster.EchecComportementError | problem during the integration of the constitutive law, | | aster.BandeFrequenceVideError | no mode found in the frequency band, | | aster.MatriceSinguliereError | singular matrix, | | aster.TraitementContactError | problem during the treatment of contact, | | aster.MatriceContactSinguliereError | singular contact matrix, | | aster.ArretCPUError | stop for lack of CPU time. | All these exceptions derive from the general exception which is aster.error. This means that except aster.error intercepts all the exceptions cited above. It is nevertheless always preferable to specify which error one expects! Example of use: try: resu = STAT_NON_LINE(...) except aster.NonConvergenceError, message: print ‘Arrêt pour cette raison: %s’ % str(message) # On sait qu’il faut beaucoup plus d’itérations pour converger print "On continue en augmentant le nombre d’itérations." resu = STAT_NON_LINE(reuse = resu, ..., CONVERGENCE=_F(ITER_GLOB_MAXI=400,),) except aster.error, message: print "Une autre erreur s’est produite: %s" % str(message) print "Stop" from Utilitai.Utmess import UTMESS UTMESS(‘F’, ‘Exemple’, ‘Erreur inattendue’) 5.3.2 Interception of fatal errors In the event of a fatal error, the behaviour can be modified by the user. By default, the code stops with an error; the error traceback (call of the fortran routines) can be seen in the output file. If one so wishes, the code can raise the aster.FatalError exception, and in this case (as for an error), if the exception is intercepted by an except, the user regains control; otherwise the code stops (no fortran error traceback). This choice is determined in the DEBUT/POURSUITE commands, factor keyword ERREUR (cf. [U4.11.01] and U4.11.03), and at any time by the aster.onFatalError method. The latter, called without argument, returns the current behaviour in the event of a fatal error: comport = aster.onFatalError() print "Comportement courant en cas d’erreur fatale : %s” % comport and makes it possible to define the behaviour that one wishes: aster.onFatalError(‘EXCEPTION’) # on lève l’exception FatalError or aster.onFatalError(‘ABORT’) # on s’arrête avec remontée d’erreur. 5.3.3 Validity of concepts when an exception is raised When an exception is raised and intercepted (by except), the concept produced by the command in which the error occurred is returned as it stands, the command not having finished normally. In some cases, in particular after a fatal error, it may be that the produced concept is not usable; then use DETRUIRE to delete it. Likewise, if one wishes to reuse the name of the concept in order to create a new one, one must DETRUIRE the one obtained in the try. In the event of errors raised in STAT/DYNA_NON_LINE, the concept is generally valid, and can be reused (keyword reuse) in order to continue the analysis with another strategy (as in the example cited previously). Finally, before control is returned to the user, the objects of the volatile database are deleted by a call to JEDETV, and the Jeveux mark is reset to 1 (with JEDEMA) in order to release the objects brought back into memory. 5.3.4 Precautions in the use of exceptions The two exceptions aster.error and aster.FatalError are independent (neither derives from the other), which means that if one wishes to regain control in the event of an error and of an error: - the raising of an exception in the event of an error must be activated with aster.FatalError(‘EXCEPTION’), or in DEBUT/POURSUITE. - the two exceptions must be intercepted: except (aster.FatalError, aster.error), message: … It is not recommended to use “except:” without specifying which exception one expects (this is a general rule in Python, independently of the Aster exceptions). Indeed, the processing carried out under the except has little chance of being valid in every error case. Likewise, as in the example given above, it is preferable to use the particularised exceptions NonConvergenceError, ArretCPUError, … rather than the higher-level exception aster.error; always with the idea of knowing exactly what has occurred. 5.4 Recovery of computed values in PYTHON variables Exploiting the PYTHON language in one's command file is of interest only if one can conditionally launch actions according to what the code has computed. Certain bridges exist between python and the data structures computed by the code and present in the JEVEUX memory. Others remain to be programmed; this is an evolving area and future developments are expected. It is essential to understand that recovering computed data requires that the instructions leading to their being obtained have indeed been executed beforehand. In other words, it is essential to execute the code in PAR_LOT='NON' mode (keyword of the DEBUT command). Indeed, in this case, there is no global analysis of the command file, but each instruction is executed sequentially. When one arrives at an instruction, all the concepts preceding it have therefore already been computed. Here are a few methods of access to the data structures. The list is not exhaustive; refer to the documentation U1.03.02. | Data structure | Method | Python type returned | Information returned | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | listr8 | LIST_VALEURS | list | List of the values | | maillage | LIST_GROUP_NO | list | List of the node groups | | | LIST_GROUP_MA | list | List of the mesh-cell groups | | table | […] | real | Content of the table | | fonction | LISTE_VALEURS | list | List of the values | | résultat | LIST_CHAMPS | list | List of the computed fields | | | LIST_NOM_CMP | list | List of the components | | | LIST_VARI_ACCES | list | List of the access variables | | | LIST_PARA | list | List of the parameters | | cham_no | EXTR_COMP | post_comp_cham_no | Content of the field in a table | | cham_elem | EXTR_COMP | post_comp_cham_el | Content of the field in a table | | Any JEVEUX object | getvectjev | list | List of the objects of the jeveux vector | 5.5 Example of dynamic construction of factor keywords In the case of a factor keyword that is very repetitive to write, the user may want to compose its content by script, in a list or a dictionary, which he will then supply to the factor keyword. The example below shows three ways of writing one and the same factor keyword. DEBUT(PAR_LOT='NON') ooo=[ _F(JUSQU_A=1.,PAS=0.1), _F(JUSQU_A=2.,PAS=0.1), _F(JUSQU_A=3.,PAS=0.1)] ppp=[_F(JUSQU_A=float(i),PAS=0.1) for i in range(1,4)] qqq=[{'JUSQU_A':float(i),'PAS':0.1} for i in range(1,4)] rrr=[_F( args) for args in qqq] li1=DEFI_LIST_REEL( DEBUT=0., INTERVALLE=ooo / or INTERVALLE=ppp / or INTERVALLE=rrr ) FIN()

u1.03.02 Python methods for accessing Aster objects Python methods for accessing Aster objects > Summary. This document presents the Python methods for accessing the information contained in Aster data structures. This information can be processed by Python programming, or used for the conditional chaining of the subsequent commands. 1 Introduction and precautions for use In Code_Aster , most commands are programmed in Fortran. The data structures produced are accessible only through the JEVEUX memory manager, itself written in Fortran. In a standard run of the code, only the names of the concepts (and not the objects that themselves carry the computed information) are passed up to the supervisor, from command to command, by means of the keywords. In a use of Python more advanced than the simple declaration of Code_Aster commands, the command file written in Python can use the content of the data structures specific to Code_Aster . Indeed, Python can be used in command files to create macro-commands and operations such as loops (for, while,…), tests (if,…), executions of external commands (via the os module), etc. The page "Use / Examples / Examples of the use of Python in Aster" of the website www.code‑aster.org brings together a certain number of application cases. It is then of interest to the user to recover the product of the Fortran computations in the Python space, that is, in the command file. Several Python methods have been developed in order to access the content of other data structures. To recover computed data (in the JEVEUX memory), it is absolutely necessary that the instructions leading to their production have indeed been executed beforehand. In other words, the code must be run in PAR_LOT='NON' mode (keyword of the command DEBUT or POURSUITE). In this case, indeed, there is no global analysis of the command file; each instruction is executed sequentially. When an instruction is reached, all the concepts preceding it have therefore already been computed. DEBUT ( PAR_LOT = ‘NON’) It must then be noted that the command file thus produced is not readable by EFICAS, which tolerates only files composed exclusively of commands specific to Code_Aster. Only the simple variables (reals, integers, strings) defined in declarative mode a=’\mathit{toto}’ or in algebraic mode n=3+4 are readable by EFICAS. The information read back from the JEVEUX memory, the product of a prior analysis, can be exploited for example in order to (non-exhaustive list): - Chain other commands conditionally (execution of a while loop until a computed value of a limit stress is obtained) - Handle in Python the content of a table or of a fonction, for the purposes of computation - Recover the attributes of a mesh: list of the node groups and of the mesh-cell groups, coordinates. 2 Tables Data structures of type table are produced in Aster by creation (CREA_TABLE), by reading from a file (LIRE_TABLE), or by recovery from another concept (RECU_TABLE). Functionally they are tables of heterogeneous data (integers, reals, character strings) whose columns are identified by label names. They are convenient structures whose use is widespread in the code. For example, most post-processing commands produce tables: in order to extract stresses at given geometric locations, in order to produce computed macroscopic quantities (grandeurs) (post-processing in fracture mechanics). Take for example the following table tab1, coming from an Aster analysis: | NOEUD | NUME_ORDRE | DX | | --- | --- | --- | | \mathit{N2} | 14 | 0.93 | | \mathit{N2} | 15 | 1.16 | | \mathit{N1} | 3 | 0.70 | | \mathit{N1} | 2 | 0.46 | | \mathit{N1} | 1 | 0.23 | Table 2-1 It could also have been created directly as an Aster concept of type table by: tab1=CREA_TABLE(LISTE = ( _F( PARA=’NOEUD’, LISTE_K=(‘N2’,’N2’,’N1’,’N1’,’N1’),), _F( PARA=’NUME_ORDRE’, LISTE_I=(14,15,3,2,1),), _F( PARA=’DX’, LISTE_R=(0.93,1.16,0.70,0.46,0.23),),) Any value in the table can be recovered directly when its access key (column label name) and the row number are known: >>> print tab1[’DX’,3] 0.70 It is also possible to recover the whole of the table in the Python environment through a dedicated class, produced by the EXTR_TABLE method, attached to the class of the ASTER concept: tab2 = tab1.EXTR_TABLE() tab2 is a Python object, an instance of the class Table of the module Utilitai.Table. It can be handled with the methods associated with this class; one can call help(Table) to find out the methods of this class. The table tab2 could also have been defined directly by a dictionary: From Utilitai.Table import Table listdic = [ {'NOEUD': 'N2' ,'NUME_ORDRE': 14,'DX': 0.93, }, {'NOEUD': 'N2' ,'NUME_ORDRE': 15,'DX': 1. 16,}, {'NOEUD': 'N1' ,'NUME_ORDRE': 3 ,'DX': 0.70, }, {'NOEUD': 'N1' ,'NUME_ORDRE': 2 ,'DX': 0.46, }, {'NOEUD': 'N1' ,'NUME_ORDRE': 1 ,'DX': 0.23, }, ] listpara=['NOEUD','NUME_ORDRE','DX'] listtype=['K8','I','R'] tab2=Table(listdic,listpara,listtype) The operations possible on tab2 are described below. 2.1 Printout >>> tab2 ---------------------------------------------- NOEUD NUME_ORDRE DX N2 14 9.30000E-01 N2 15 1.16000E+00 N1 3 7.00000E-01 N1 2 4.60000E-01 N1 1 2.30000E-01 Also possible: >>> print tab2 Display of a single parameter: >>> t.DX ---------------------------------------------- DX 9.30000E-01 1.16000E+00 7.00000E-01 4.60000E-01 2.30000E-01 The IMPR_TABLE command uses the printout capabilities offered by this class. The interested reader may read the Python programming of this macro-command. In particular, the possibility of printing cross tables. 2.2 Creation or printout of a sub-table extracted by a filter Extraction according to a single criterion: >>> print tab2.NUME_ORDRE >> print (t.NUME_ORDRE =0.3) ---------------------------------------------- NOEUD NUME_ORDRE DX N1 3 7.00000E-01 N1 2 4.60000E-01 Extraction according to two criteria with the logical combination «|» / OR: >>> print (t.NUME_ORDRE >> t['DX','NUME_ORDRE'] ---------------------------------------------- DX NUME_ORDRE 9.30000E-01 14 1.16000E+00 15 7.00000E-01 3 4.60000E-01 2 2.30000E-01 1 Extraction according to an equality criterion (here with the value of the criterion itself deduced from the table) >>> t.DX == max(t.DX) ---------------------------------------------- NOEUD NUME_ORDRE DX N2 15 1.16000E+00 2.3 Sorting Sorting of the whole table according to a label: >>> t.sort('NUME_ORDRE') >>> t ---------------------------------------------- NOEUD NUME_ORDRE DX N1 1 2.30000E-01 N1 2 4.60000E-01 N1 3 7.00000E-01 N2 14 9.30000E-01 N2 15 1.16000E+00 To sort according to several labels, the order of precedence being the order in which the labels are declared, the labels must be supplied in the form of a list or of a tuple: >>> t.sort(['NUME_ORDRE',’DX’]) A second argument, ordre, equal to 'CROISSANT' or 'DECROISSANT', makes it possible to specify the sort order: >>> t.sort(['NUME_ORDRE',’DX’],'DECROISSANT') 2.4 Access to the values The content of the table is accessible through the values() method, which produces a dictionary whose keys are the access parameters of the table and whose values are the columns: >>> tab2.values() {'NOEUD': [:ref: 'N1', 'N1', 'N1', 'N2', 'N2' ], 'NUME_ORDRE': [:ref: 1, 2, 3, 14, 15 ], 'DX': [:ref: 0.23, 0.46, 0.70, 0.93, 1.156 ]} The parameters are given by the attribute para (same as tab2.values().keys()) >>> tab2.para ['NOEUD', 'NUME_ORDRE', 'DX'] 3 Access methods on concepts 3.1 Access to the content of a list SD lst = listr8 .Valeurs() lst is a Python list that contains the values of the Aster list: lst = 0., 1.1, 2.3, ... 3.2 Access to the content of a fonction SD or of a nappe SD lst1, lst2 , (lst3) = [fonction / nappe] .Valeurs() lst1 and lst2 are two Python lists that contain the abscissae and the ordinates. If the function is complex, a third list is obtained, and lst2 and lst3 will contain the lists of the real and imaginary parts. lst1 = [fonction] .Absc() lst1 is the list of the abscissae, that is, also the first list returned by Valeurs(). lst2 = [fonction] .Ordo() lst2 is the list of the ordinates, that is, also the second list returned by Valeurs(). dico1 = [fonction] .Parametres() returns a dictionary containing the parameters of the function; the JEVEUX type (FONCTION, FONC_C, NAPPE) is not returned, so the dictionary can be supplied to CALC_FONC_INTERP as it stands (see efica02a). 3.3 Evaluation of a fonction SD or of a formule Functions and formulae can be evaluated simply in the Python namespace, that is, in the command file, as follows: FONC1=FORMULE( VALE='(Y 2)+ X’, NOM_PARA=('X','Y',)), ); >>> print FONC1(1.,2.) 5. or with a function: FONC2=DEFI_FONCTION( NOM_PARA='X', VALE=(0., 0., 1., 4.,) ) >>> print FONC2(0.5) 2. In the case of functions, it should be noted that a relative tolerance of 1.e-6 is applied when the value of the parameter lies very close to the bounds, so as to avoid an error due to a forbidden extension, to within rounding. 3.4 Access to the content of a maillage SD Two methods make it possible to recover the list of the mesh-cell groups and of the node groups of a data structure of type maillage: [ (tuple), …] = [maillage] .LIST_GROUP_MA() returns a list of tuples, each containing the name of each mesh-cell group, the number of mesh cells it contains, and the highest dimension (0, 1, 2 or 3) of its mesh cells: tuple = (‘GMA’, number of mesh cells, mesh-cell dim.) [ (tuple), ...] =[maillage] .LIST_GROUP_NO() returns the list of the node groups in the form: tuple = (name of the group_no, number of nodes of the group_no) 3.5 Access to the content of an SD matr_asse_ Let matr be a data structure matr_asse_depl_r. A numpy array of the full matrix is recovered by: array = matr.EXTR_MATR() To recover the matrix with sparse storage, one does: data, lines, cols, dim = matr.EXTR_MATR(sparse=True) One has: array has dimension (dim, dim) number of non-zero terms: len(data) = len(lines) = len(cols) data[k] = array[ lines[k], cols[k] ] Likewise, for matrgene, a data structure matr_asse_gene_r, for example, produced by the operator PROJ_MATR_BASE. A numpy array of the full matrix is recovered by: array = matrgene.EXTR_MATR_GENE() 3.6 Access to the keys of a resultat SD If EVOL is a resultat data structure, then: | dico = EVOL.LIST_CHAMPS() | is a dictionary whose keys are the names of the fields, which index the list of the computed order numbers. | | --- | --- | Table 3.6-1 Example: | >>> print dico['DEPL'] 0,1,2 | (the field DEPL is computed at order numbers 0, 1 and 2) | | --- | --- | | >>> print dico['SIEF_ELNO'] [] | (the field is not computed) | Table 3.6-2 | dico = EVOL.LIST_VARI_ACCES() | is a dictionary whose keys are the access variables, which index their own values. | | --- | --- | Table 3.6-3 Example: | >>> print dico['NUME_ORDRE'] 0,1,2 | (the order numbers of the result EVOL are: 0, 1 and 2) | | --- | --- | | >>> print dico['INST'] 0., 2., 4. | (the computed time instants of the result EVOL are: 0.s, 2.s and 4.s) | Table 3.6-4 | dico = EVOL.LIST_PARA() | is a dictionary whose keys are the parameters of the analysis, which index the lists (of cardinality equal to the number of computed order numbers) of their values. | | --- | --- | Table 3.6-5 Example: | >>> print dico['MODELE'] [‘MO’,’MO’,’MO’] | (name of the reference model concept for each order number) | | --- | --- | | >>> print dico['ITER_GLOB'] 4,2,3 | (number of convergence iterations for each order number) | Table 3.6-6 3.7 Access to the content of a tran_gene SD If trangene is a tran_gene data structure, for example produced by the operator DYNA_VIBRA, then: | trangene.FORCE_AXIALE(inoli=-1) | 1D matrix of type « numpy array » containing the evolution of the axial force at the archived time instants, with inoli being the index of the non-linearity; by default, inoli= -1 (first non-linearity). | | --- | --- | | trangene.FORCE_NORMALE(inoli=-1) | 1D matrix of type « numpy array » containing the evolution of the normal force at the archived time instants, with inoli being the index of the non-linearity; by default, inoli= -1 (first non-linearity). | | trangene.FORCE_RELATION(inoli=-1) | 1D matrix of type « numpy array » containing the evolution of the force of the non-linear relation in displacement or velocity at the archived time instants, with inoli being the index of the non-linearity; by default, inoli= -1 (first non-linearity). | | trangene.INFO_NONL() | List of the information on the non-linearities, including the index and the title of the non-linearities. | | trangene.LIST_ARCH() | List of the archived time instants. | | trangene.VARI_INTERNE(inoli=-1) | 2D matrix of type « numpy array » of all the internal variables of the non-linearity given by the index | Table 3.7-1 3.8 Access to the content of a melasflu SD This Python method makes it possible to extract the list of fluid velocities for which the computation of the fluid-elastic coupling parameters has been carried out. | >>> base = CALC_FLUI_STRU (...) | | | --- | --- | | >>> print base.VITE_FLUI() 1., 1.5, 2.5, 3. | List of fluid velocities for which the coupling coefficients have been computed. | 3.9 Retrieval in Python of fields by element and fields at the nodes (EXTR_COMP) The EXTR_COMP method, applied to a field, makes it possible to retrieve the content of the field in Python. 3.9.1 Arguments of the EXTR_COMP command The command has 3 arguments: ch1 = CHAMP.EXTR_COMP(comp=' ',lgma=[],topo=0), for fields at the nodes, ch1 = CHAMP.EXTR_COMP(comp,lgma,topo=0), for fields by element, | comp | component of the field on the list lgma. For fields at the nodes, if comp is left at its default, all the components are returned. The result of the command is modified (see below). | | --- | --- | | lgma | list of mesh-cell groups; if empty, all the group_ma are taken (equivalent to TOUT='OUI' in the Aster commands. | | topo | topology information is returned if >0 (optional, default = 0). | Table 3.9.1-1 Note: for fields at the nodes, the command can be launched as follows: ch1=CHAMP.EXTR_COMP(topo=1). In this case, all the components are returned for all the topological entities of the field CHAMP. 3.9.2 Example of use Starting from the result U: 1. A field (node or elXX) corresponding to a time instant is created with CREA_CHAMP. 1. The component is extracted by the EXTR_COMP method (declared for the cham_elem and the cham_no), which creates a new type of Python object: post_comp_cham_el and post_comp_cham_no, whose attributes are described below. All the components can be extracted at once by not specifying the component (for fields at the nodes only). U = STAT_NON_LINE( ... ) U104 = CREA_CHAMP( TYPE_CHAM = 'NOEU_DEPL_R', OPERATION = 'EXTR', RESULTAT = U, NOM_CHAM = 'DEPL', NUME_ORDRE = 104, ) U104NP = U104.EXTR_COMP('DX',['S_SUP',]) print U104NP.valeurs V104 = CREA_CHAMP( TYPE_CHAM = 'ELGA_VARI_R', OPERATION = 'EXTR', RESULTAT = U, NOM_CHAM = 'VARI_ELGA', NUME_ORDRE = 104, ) V104NP = V104.EXTR_COMP('V22',[],1) print V104NP.valeurs print V104NP.maille print V104NP.point print V104NP.sous_point 3.9.3 Results of the EXTR_COMP command ch1.valeurs: Numeric.array containing the values - For fields by element, if the topology has been requested (topo>0): - ch1.maille: mesh-cell numbers - ch1.point: number of the point in the mesh cell - ch1.sous_point: number of the sub-point in the mesh cell - For fields at the nodes, if the topology has been requested (topo>0): - ch1.noeud: node numbers - ch1.comp: if all the components of the field have been requested (comp = ' ', the default value), the component associated with the value. 4 Method for accessing an arbitrary data structure Any vector or any collection present in memory can be recovered, provided that the data structure is known. Two methods are possible (and equivalent): by using the catalogue of the data structure, or directly the JEVEUX name of the object. In the first case, one uses the "property" sdj of the concept, which makes it possible to navigate in the data structure (see the example below). 4.1 Access to a data structure of vector type The getvectjev method gives access to a data structure of vector type. It is always applied to the "aster" object, and takes as argument the complete character string (including spaces) that defines the name of the object, contained in the data structure, that one wants to access. This name can be determined by means of the Aster command IMPR_CO(CONCEPT=_F(NOM=nom)). Example: recover the coordinates of the nodes of a mesh named MA: res = aster.getvectjev("MA .COORDO .VALE ") The equivalent syntax, using the data-structure catalogue, is: res = MA.sdj.COORDO.VALE.get() A Python list containing the values of the vector is obtained. 4.2 Access to a data structure of collection type In a similar way, the getcolljev method allows collections to be consulted from Python. It returns a dictionary whose keys are the names of the objects in the case of a named collection, and the index numbers otherwise. Example: recover the information concerning the connectivity of the elements of the mesh MA: res = aster.getcolljev("MA .CONNEX ") The equivalent syntax, using the data-structure catalogue, is: res = MA.sdj.CONNEX.get() A dictionary resembling the following is obtained: {3: (2, 1, 5), 2: (6, 9, 10, 7, 11, 12, 13, 8), 1: (1, 6, 7, 2, 3, 8, 5)}

u1.03.03 Performance indicators of a run (time/memory) Performance indicators of a run (time/memory) 1 Purpose During a simulation with Code_Aster , default displays record , in the message and result files (.mess/.resu), certain sizing characteristics of the run (RAM consumption, CPU time, system time and user time...). This document details the displays of these performance indicators. Some advice is also formulated to help the user take advantage of these diagnostics . One must, however, be well aware that there is no universal recipe for optimising the overall performance of a run. It depends on the type of study, on the software and hardware aspects of the machine, and even on its load! The default settings and the displays/alarms of the code provide a balanced and instrumented mode of operation . But, to be sure of having made the best use of the capabilities of one's machine, the user must remain attentive to the points described in this document as well as to the advice given in the command documentation. This document takes up many points from the User documentation on the keyword SOLVEUR U4.50.01, U2.08.06 and on parallelism U2.08.03. 2 General points During a Code_Aster simulation, default displays record in the message and result files (.mess/.resu) certain sizing characteristics of the run . In particular, for each Aster operator, one finds: - The characteristics of the linear systems to be built and solved (number of nodes, of equations and of Lagrange multipliers, matrix size...), - The minimum JEVEUX memories (in order to switch to Out-Of-Core [1]_) and the optimum memory (in order to switch to In-Core), - The memory outside JEVEUX required by certain external products (for example MUMPS), - The CPU, system and "user" (elapsed) times , - The breakdown of the times consumed according to the stages of the analysis (elementary computation, assembly, solution of the linear system). This last description of the times consumed can be presented at different levels of detail (summary printout, detailed printout, and printout detailed by analysis increment) via the parameter MESURE_TEMPS/NIVE_DETAIL of the commands DEBUT/POURSUITE. In parallel mode, the mean value, over all the processors, of the times consumed is added, as well as their standard deviation. 3 Characteristics of the linear system A large number of operators (STAT/DYNA/THER_NON_LINE, CALC_MODES, ...) require the construction and the solution of linear systems. To solve these systems of equations, particular algorithms called " linear solvers " are used. These linear solvers are in fact ubiquitous in the course of the Code_Aster operators, because they are often employed by the numerical algorithms: nonlinear scheme, time integration, modal analysis, etc. They consume most of the CPU time and of the memory. Total number of nodes (N T ) = physical (N p ) + Lagranges (N L ) By default (INFO=1), each command records, when building its first linear system, its characteristics: size N , number of non-zero terms \mathit{NNZ} ... Number of late nodes (Lagranges): N L Size of the system (here in isoparametric 2D): N=2N P +N L --- TOTAL NUMBER OF NODES : 1705 OF WHICH : 1364 "LAGRANGE" NODES --- TOTAL NUMBER OF EQUATIONS : 2046 --- SIZE OF THE MORSE PROFILE OF THE UPPER TRIANGULAR PART (SCR FORMAT): 26652 --- HENCE THE SIZE OF THE MATRIX IS: --- IN SYMMETRIC NNZ = 26652 Number of non-zero terms of the matrix ('Number of Non Zero terms') in its sparse storage. Here, one therefore has on average about 26652/2046≈13 non-zero terms per row/column. --- IN NON-SYMMETRIC NNZ= 51016 At this stage of the run, it is not yet known whether the matrix is symmetric or not. Both possible storage sizes are therefore mentioned: - upper triangular part - The same + lower triangular part minus the diagonal. Figure 3-a : Characteristics of the linear system being assembled in a typical Aster command STAT_NON_LINE or THER_LINEAIRE (extract from the .mess ). The size of the system , the proportion of Lagrange multipliers and the fill of the matrix give indirect information on the memory/CPU consumption of the run and on possible difficulties in the solution. Broadly speaking, the algorithmic complexity of the construction of the linear system is of order \mathit{NNZ} , whereas that of its solution is of order {N}^{\alpha}.\mathit{NNZ} (with 1 Note. The total volume recovered and the number of occurrences of this mechanism are summarised at the end of the message file (see §5.1). 4.2 Overall times consumed At the end of the message file, the sum of the consumptions of CPU, CPU+SYST and SYST, and the remainder of unused time (between the time stated by the user in Astk and the CPU+SYST time), are systematically recorded. A priori, any significant drift in the SYSTEM time must raise questions (see §6.2). (IN SECONDS) TOTAL CPU TIME .............. 2160.55 TOTAL USER CPU TIME ......... 2099.33 TOTAL SYSTEM CPU TIME ...... 61.22 REMAINING CPU TIME ............ 439.45 Figure 4.2-a : Overall time consumption of a run (extract from a .mess ). 4.3 Special case of DYNA/STAT_NON_LINE In these nonlinear dynamics/statics commands, one records as standard (INFO=1), for each time step or analysis increment , in addition to the table of decrease of the residuals (the level of detail is managed by the keyword AFFICHAGE of the commands): - The stored fields (selected by the keyword ARCHIVAGE), - The breakdown of the CPU times consumed and, where applicable, the associated number of iterations (e.g. Newton process), - Dedicated display blocks (e.g. discrete contact). The archiving of the fields can be costly in time (especially in parallel) and in memory . It is therefore of interest to analyse the list of archived fields so as, if need be, to limit them. ARCHIVING OF THE FIELDS: Archived fields To be limited (especially in parallel) STORED FIELD : CONT_NOEU TIME INSTANT : 5.00000E+02 ORDER NUMBER : 50 STORED FIELD : DEPL TIME INSTANT : 5.00000E+02 ORDER NUMBER : 50 STORED FIELD : SIEF_ELGA TIME INSTANT : 5.00000E+02 ORDER NUMBER : 50 STORED FIELD : VARI_ELGA TIME INSTANT : 5.00000E+02 ORDER NUMBER : 50 STORED FIELD : VITE TIME INSTANT : 5.00000E+02 ORDER NUMBER : 50 CPU time/iteration breakdown STORED FIELD : ACCE TIME INSTANT : 5.00000E+02 ORDER NUMBER : 50 CPU TIME CONSUMED IN THIS TIME STEP : 0 s TIME PER NEWTON ITERATION : 0 s - NO. NEWT.: 2 ARCHIVING TIME : 0 s Only these parts can benefit from parallelism NUMBERING CREATION TIME : 0 s - NO. NUME.: 0 MATRIX FACTORISATION TIME : 0 s - NO. FACT.: 0 CONSTITUTIVE BEHAVIOUR INTEGRATION TIME : 0 s - NO. INTE.: 3 SOLUTION TIME K.U = F : 0 s - NO. RESO.: 2 CONTACT SOLUTION TIME : 0 s - NO. ITER.: 2 OTHER OPERATIONS TIME : 0 s Dedicated display block (contact...) DISCRETE CONTACT: NUMBER OF CONTACT ITERATIONS : 2 NUMBER OF GEOM. UPDATE ITERATIONS : 2 FINAL NUMBER OF CONTACT LINKS : 0 TOTAL PAIRING TIME : 0 s TOTAL SOLUTION TIME : 0 s Figure 4.3-a : Display at each time step of DYNA/STAT_NON_LINE with INFO=1 in sequential mode (extract from a .mess ). At the end of the operator, the overall statistics over the whole transient are summarised . These CPU times are found again in the overall end-of-operator statistic mentioned in the previous paragraph. Their granularity is, however, finer and adapted to the different stages of the operator. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- STATISTICS ON THE TRANSIENT --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- NUMBER OF TIME STEPS : 100 NUMBER OF NEWTON ITERATIONS : 200 NUMBER OF CONTACT ITERATIONS (ALGO) : 456 NUMBER OF CONTACT ITERATIONS (GEOM) : 200 NUMBER OF NUMBERING CREATIONS : 1 NUMBER OF MATRIX FACTORISATIONS : 2 NUMBER OF CONSTITUTIVE BEHAVIOUR INTEGRATIONS : 201 NUMBER OF SOLUTIONS K.U = F : 200 TIME FOR NUMBERING CREATION : 10 s TIME FOR MATRIX FACTORISATION : 100 s TIME FOR CONSTITUTIVE BEHAVIOUR INTEGRATION : 3 m 8 s TIME FOR SOLUTION K.U = F : 9 s TIME FOR CONTACT (PAIRING) : 17 s TIME FOR CONTACT (ALGORITHM) : 2 m 30 s --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Figure 4.3-b : Overall statistics at the end of DYNA/STAT_NON_LINE with INFO=1 (extract from a .mess ). 5 RAM consumption At any given moment, the RAM used by Code_Aster may be the sum of three components. - The memory allocated directly by the sources of the code. This is mainly that allocated by the JEVEUX package D6.02.01 in order to manage all the F77 data structures of the code. This package also makes it possible to unload these objects to disk (Out-Of-Core functionality). Depending on the size of the problem, that of the RAM and the programmer's recommendations, JEVEUX performs more or less pronounced exchanges of data between the disk and the RAM. - The memory used by external software called upon by the Aster run (MUMPS/PETSc, METIS/SCOTCH, HOMARD, MISS3D...). Most external software operates In-Core. That is to say that it does not directly manage possible memory overflows and that it delegates this task to the operating system. Others, such as the linear solver MUMPS, are potentially OOC and they themselves explicitly manage the unloading to disk of certain large objects (see keyword SOLVEUR/GESTION_MEMOIRE [U4.50.01]). - The memory required by the system (loading of part of the executable, network layer in parallel...) and by the supervisor and the Python libraries. When a Code_Aster operator requiring the construction and the solution of linear systems is used (for example STAT_NON_LINE or CALC_MODES), the memory limits are often imposed by the linear solver (see U4.50.01[U2.08.03]). When internal solvers are involved (LDLT, MULT_FRONT, GCPC), their RAM consumption appears in the JEVEUX displays. On the other hand, when an external product is used (MUMPS or PETSC), its own consumption must then be taken into account (which to a large extent replaces that of JEVEUX). Solution via MUMPS usol Course of the run Construction of the linear system Ku=F RAM consumption MUMPS memory JEVEUX memory Figure 5-a: Diagram of the evolution of the RAM consumption during a standard linear mechanics run. 5.1 Memory calibration of a run It is often useful to calibrate an Aster run at the RAM level. This can, for example, make it possible to optimise its placement in a batch class (sequential or parallel) or simply to avoid its abrupt stop due to a memory fault. To do this, one can proceed as follows: - Step no. 1 : identify, in the course of the run, the operator which seems the most sizing in terms of problem size (it is often the STAT/DYNA_NON_LINE or the CALC_MODES... dealing with the largest model). - Step no. 2: if this is not the case, set the SOLVEUR block of this operator with METHODE='MUMPS' and GESTION_MEMOIRE='EVAL'. At the end of the calibration, remember if necessary to restore the previous setting. - Step no. 3: launch the run as it stands with memory and time parameters that are modest compared with the usual consumption of this type of run. Indeed, with this option, Code_Aster will only build the first linear system of the operator and pass it to MUMPS for analysis. The latter will not carry out its most costly stage (in time and especially in memory), that of numerical factorisation. Once this analysis is complete, the MUMPS memory estimates ( {\mathit{MUE}}_{\mathit{IC}} and {\mathit{MUE}}_{\mathit{OOC}} ), together with that of JEVEUX ( {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{OOC}} ), are recorded in the message file (see figure 5.1-a). The run then stops in FATAL ERROR so as to make it possible to move on to the next step as quickly as possible. - Size of the linear system: 500000 - Minimum RAM consumed by Code_Aster : 200 MB - Estimate of the Mumps memory with GESTION_MEMOIRE='IN_CORE' :3500 MB - Estimate of the Mumps memory with GESTION_MEMOIRE='OUT_OF_CORE' : 500 MB - Estimate of the disk space for Mumps with GESTION_MEMOIRE='OUT_OF_CORE':2000 MB ===> For this run, a quantity of RAM of at least the following is therefore required - 3500 MB if GESTION_MEMOIRE='IN_CORE', - 500 MB if GESTION_MEMOIRE='OUT_OF_CORE'. If in doubt, use GESTION_MEMOIRE='AUTO'. Figure 5.1-a : Display in the message file in mode ' EVAL. - Step no. 4 : use of the memory estimates proper. To relaunch the run with the linear solver MUMPS, one has direct access to the "minimum" values of the RAM that are indispensable for the run. Two cases are distinguished according to the memory management mode chosen for MUMPS: In-Core (value max({\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{OOC}},{\mathit{MUE}}_{\mathit{IC}}) if GESTION_MEMOIRE='IN_CORE') or Out-Of-Core (value max({\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{OOC}},{\mathit{MUE}}_{\mathit{OOC}}) if GESTION_MEMOIRE='OUT_OF_CORE'). Depending on the machine/the batch classes available, the complete run must therefore be relaunched, also modifying if necessary this parameter of the SOLVEUR block. These estimates are established for a given computer and numerical configuration: hardware platform, libraries, number of MPI processes, renumberer, pre-processings... - Step no. 4bis : on the other hand, if one wishes to relaunch the run while changing linear solver or one of the numerical parameters, it is more difficult to deduce the appropriate memory estimate from them. The range of combinations and the variability of the possibilities are too great. A few empirical rules can nevertheless be proposed (in sequential mode). Roughly, if instead of METHODE='MUMPS' one chooses 'MULT_FRONT', the memory estimate should remain valid (with RENUM='METIS', the default value). With 'LDLT', this figure must be significantly revised upwards. With 'PETSC'/'GCPC'+'LDLT_SP', it can probably be reduced to max({\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{OOC}},{\mathit{MUE}}_{\text{IC/OOC}}/2) . With 'PETSC'/'GCPC'+'LDLT_INC' it can probably be reduced to a factor times {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{OOC}} according to the fill level of the preconditioner (keyword NIVE_REMPLISAGE, see [R6.01.02]). - Step no. 5: relaunch the complete run, modifying if necessary the setting of the SOLVEUR block and setting Astk with the value deduced at step no. 4 ("Total memory (MB)" menu of figure 5.2-b). > Note. This procedure for the memory calibration of a study has only been available since the introduction of the keyword SOLVEUR/GESTION_MEMOIRE (from version v11.2 of Code_Aster). For older versions, if the run has already been launched (and if a usable message file is available), one can, at a minimum, cautiously take as the optimum estimate of the memory required the largest value, over all the processors, of the Vmpeak of the last operator. Otherwise, one must proceed as mentioned in the earlier versions of this document: - Step no. 1 : as above. - Step no. 2 : set the SOLVEUR block with METHODE='MUMPS','OUT_OF_CORE'='OUI' and INFO=2. - Step no. 3 : launch the run while limiting the time consumption (for example, with few time steps or little eigenmode searching). - Step no. 4 : according to the memory management mode of MUMPS required (IC or OOC), take the maximum of the MUMPS estimate and of the JEVEUX consumption. 5.2 JEVEUX memory consumption Information for quantifying the memory consumption of JEVEUX is recorded at the end of each Aster operator (see figure 5.2-a). Broadly speaking, it can be explained as follows: - {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{OOC}} gives the minimum size ('Minimum') that JEVEUX needs in order to operate up to this operator . It will then be completely Out-Of-Core (OOC). Below this value, the run is not possible (in the configuration adopted). - {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{IC}} gives a lower bound ('Optimum'), up to this operator, of the JEVEUX memory required in order to operate completely In-Core (IC): {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{IC}}^{'} . With at least this value of RAM set in Astk (see {\mathit{MEM}}_{\mathit{ASTK}} ), the run will proceed in an optimal manner: there is no risk of a crash due to a lack of memory, and access to the purely Aster data structures is little slowed by unloading to disk. These two figures are necessarily lower than the total value of RAM devoted to the run (set in Astk ), denoted {\mathit{MEM}}_{\mathit{ASTK}} . If there has been no global release mechanism (see the paragraph below), {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{IC}} truly represents the JEVEUX memory required in order to operate in IC. Otherwise, this latter estimate must be close to the sum 11_ {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{IC}}^{'}={\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{IC}}+. "the average gain provided by each release". It is therefore pointless (if no external product is used) to set the run with a value much higher than {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{IC}}^{'} . When setting up the run, a compromise must therefore be struck between its speed and its memory consumption . By ranking the memory consumption of all the commands, one can identify the one which sizes the run. For a fixed run configuration (number of processors), the larger the memory space reserved for JEVEUX, the more the run will be In-Core (IC) and therefore the faster it will be. One can also, according to the constraints of the batch queues, split one's run into different POURSUITE so as to mix them and thus optimise the "run time/memory" settings. Figure 5.2-c : Meaning of the displays linked to JEVEUX in the message file. During the run, JEVEUX can unload a large part of the objects from RAM to disk . This mechanism is either: - Automatic (there is no longer enough RAM space to create an object or to bring it back), - Managed by the programmer (for example, a call to this release mechanism just before handing over to MUMPS). The statistics concerning this mechanism are summarised at the end of the message file (see §5.2-d) for all of the commands. Obviously, the more this mechanism intervenes (and on large volumes of memory released), the more the run is slowed down (system and elapsed times which grow, and a stable CPU time). This phenomenon may be accentuated in parallel mode (simultaneous memory contention) depending on the distribution of the processors over the compute nodes and depending on the characteristics of the machine. Its consumption (In-Core and Out-Of-Core) can be recorded in two ways: - By a pre-computation that is very fast and inexpensive in memory via the mode GESTION_MEMOIRE='EVAL' (see §5.1). But these are only estimates (values {\mathit{ME}}_{\mathit{IC}} and {\mathit{ME}}_{\mathit{OOC}} of figure 5.1-a). They can therefore be a little pessimistic (especially in Out-Of-Core and/or in parallel). In parallel mode, only the estimates of the most demanding MPI process are recorded. - By the standard run (limited if possible to a few time steps or to a few eigenmodes) by adding the keyword INFO=2 in the command assumed to be the most costly. One then summarises in the message file (see 5.3-a) not only the previous memory estimates {\mathit{ME}}_{\mathit{IC}} and {\mathit{ME}}_{\mathit{OOC}} (columns 'ESTIM IN-CORE' and 'ESTIM OUT-OF-CORE'), but also the actual consumption of the mode chosen {\mathit{MR}}_{\text{IC/OOC}} (here in OOC mode, because of the display 'RESOL OUT-OF-CORE'). Besides this RAM consumption information, it also summarises items linked to the type of problem, to its numerical difficulty (errors) and to its parallel distribution (load balance).
