Broadly speaking, VmPeak indicates the peak memory size caused by all the active executables of the Aster job. Care must be taken that this figure remains lower than the physical memory available to the job. Otherwise the system will, up to a certain point, "swap", and this will slow the run down. At the level of the JEVEUX package this will result in more unloadings (see §4.1.2 and §5.2) and, at the level of the external products, in a growing ELAPS/USER gap (recorded at the end of the command, see §4.1.1). Notes if SOLVEUR='MUMPS' : - Since the introduction of the keyword SOLVEUR/GESTION_MEMOIRE (from version v11.2 of Code_Aster), the solver is allowed to "spread out" in memory, in addition to the JEVEUX/Python/library allocations, until it occupies the maximum size allocated. This allows the product to be faster and less exacting about its memory requirements in terms of pivoting. On the other hand, as a corollary of this strategy of optimum occupation of the memory resources, the VmPeak displayed in the message file becomes dependent on the memory allocated to the run (MEMASTK or the bound of the batch class). It therefore cannot be used, as previously, to calibrate the minimum memory consumption of the study. To do this, the strategy detailed in §5.1 should rather be applied 6 Some advice for optimising performance Here some advice is formulated to help the user take advantage of the diagnostics recorded in the message file. One must, however, be well aware that there is no universal recipe for optimising the overall performance of a run. It depends on the type of study, on the software and hardware aspects of the machine, and even on its load! The default settings and the displays/alarms of the code provide a balanced and instrumented mode of operation . But, to be sure of having made the best use of the capabilities of one's machine, the user must remain attentive to the points described in this document as well as to the advice which abounds in the command documentation. Listed below, and in a non-exhaustive manner, are several questions which it is useful to ask oneself when seeking to optimise the performance of one's run. Of course, some questions (and answers) are cumulative and can therefore apply simultaneously. 6.1 Concerning the characteristics of the problem In view of the points of §3, two empirical rules can be formulated: - The more the size of the problem ( N ) and/or the fill of the matrix ( \mathit{NNZ} ) increase, the more costly (CPU/RAM) the construction, and especially the solution, of the linear system will be. - An increase in the proportion of Lagrange multipliers ( {N}_{L}/N ) can make the solution of the linear system more difficult (execution time, quality of the solution). - The size of the problem sizes the maximum number of processors which it is relevant to devote to its parallel run: a granularity of at least 20.103 degrees of freedom per MPI process is required. 6.2 Concerning the times consumed To reduce the CPU times, the Aster user has various tools available: - If most of the costs concern the elementary computations/assemblies and/or the solutions of linear systems (see §4.1), it is recommended to use Aster in parallel mode. It is then preferable to use the linear solver MUMPS in distributed MPI mode or the MULT_FRONT solver in OpenMP. The first strategy also makes it possible to bring down the RAM consumption per processor. - If the linear solver MUMPS is already being used , one can deactivate its OOC 12_ functionalities (GESTION_MEMOIRE='IN_CORE') and the improvement of the quality of the solution (RESI_RELA=-1.d0). If the matrix is well conditioned and/or non-symmetric, one can also try relaxation parameters of the linear solver (FILTRAGE_MATRICE, MIXER_PRECISION, SYME). - If one is carrying out a nonlinear analysis , one can test various relaxation parameters of the nonlinear solver (REAC_INCR, REAC_ITER, SYME). - If one is carrying out a modal analysis , the use of the IRAM method is recommended (METHODE='SORENSEN'), together with the splitting of the spectrum sought into several frequency bands ( via the operator CALC_MODES with OPTION='BANDE' split into several sub-bands). - In general, the more the mode of operation of JEVEUX (and of MUMPS) is in IC (see §5.1), the faster the run. These gains are not, however, very large compared with those provided by parallelism and by the choice of a suitable linear solver (together with its settings). For each stage of the analysis, one should normally have a low system time (SYST) and a cumulative total "CPU time + system time" (CPU+SYST) very close to the real waiting time (ELAPS). If this is not the case, two classic situations may arise: - The USER+SYS time is much greater than the ELAPS time . The run is certainly using the OpenMP parallelism of the parallel strategies 1c or 2a described in the U2 document on parallelism and in §2.2 of document U4.50.01. This situation is not worrying (and is even intended); the main point is that the turnaround time of the run should be as low as possible! - The ELAPS time is much greater than the CPU time and/or the SYS time is large. The run is probably suffering from memory contention (system swap, RAM/disk I/O...). - Line of enquiry no. 1: This extra cost may come from the global unloadings of JEVEUX . To confirm this, it is enough to go and read, at the end of the .mess, the statistics concerning dynamic allocation (see §5.2) or the time consumption of the various unloadings (see §4.1). The more calls there have been to the release mechanisms and/or the more large objects have been released, the more the SYST and ELAPS times will deteriorate. One solution is then to increase the memory size devoted to JEVEUX . - Line of enquiry no. 2: As a corollary of the previous observation, MPI parallel mode tends to increase tenfold the extra costs due to unloadings. Indeed, the distribution of the data induced by parallelism will reduce the size of the JEVEUX objects (if SOLVEUR/MATR_DISTRIBUEE is activated) and thus limit the impact of the unloadings. Conversely , these are liable to take place at the same time and on contiguous processors. A palliative solution may then consist in "wasting" processors, by interleaving the active MPI processors with sleeping processors (for example, the ncpus value of Astk initialised to 2). - Line of enquiry no. 3: If the linear solver MUMPS is used in OOC, the problem may come from a large number of forward/back substitutions by the product (see stage 1.4 of §4.1). They can be limited by switching off the automatic refinement option (RESI_RELA=-1.d0) or by returning to IC mode (if the memory resources allow it). 6.3 Concerning the RAM consumed - If the consumptions {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{IC}} and {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{OOC}} are close (a few tens of percent), this means that JEVEUX has often had to operate in OOC mode. There have probably been numerous memory unloadings (see §4.1/5.2). The computation time may suffer as a result (especially in parallel). One should try to add memory or to increase the number of processors (if the MATR_DISTRIBUEE option is activated). - The run is often sized in memory , by the maximum, over the most demanding operator, of the JEVEUX minimum value ( {\mathit{JE}}_{\mathit{OOC}} ) and the value used by the linear solver MUMPS (if it is used). To reduce this figure one can act on several factors: - If MUMPS is used and the latter is predominant (this is often the case): use more processors in MPI (parameters mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnoeud of Astk ), switch to OOC (keyword SOLVEUR/GESTION_MEMOIRE). If the matrix is well conditioned and/or non-symmetric, one can also try relaxation parameters of the linear solver (FILTRAGE_MATRICE, MIXER_PRECISION, SYME). - If MUMPS is used and the latter is not predominant: use the distribution of JEVEUX objects of the option MATR_DISTRIBUEE in parallel mode. - If another linear solver is used: use MUMPS in parallel, or even GCPC/PETSC (in sequential/parallel mode). 6.4 Concerning parallelism - If most of the costs concern the elementary computations/assemblies and/or the solutions of linear systems (see §4.1), it is recommended to use Aster in parallel mode. It is then preferable to use the linear solver MUMPS in distributed MPI mode (see the U2 document on parallelism or U4.50.01) or the MULT_FRONT solver in OpenMP. - It is preferable to limit the parallelism of the run solely to the few operators that are costly (in time/memory): STAT/DYNA_NON_LINE, CALC_MODES ... And therefore, if possible, to split the run into a succession of sequential pre/post-processings and of parallel analyses. During long runs (a few days), this strategy furthermore makes it possible to protect oneself better against possible stops in error, by saving the database associated with each major stage of the run. - It is useful, beforehand, to validate one's parallel run by comparing a few iterations in sequential mode and in parallel mode. Moreover, this approach also makes it possible to calibrate the maximum gains attainable (theoretical speed-ups) and thus to avoid "wasting too many processors". Thus, if f denotes the parallel portion of the code (determined for example via a prior sequential run), then the maximum theoretical speed-up {\mathrm{S}}_{\mathrm{p}} accessible on p processors is calculated according to Amdahl's formula: {\mathrm{S}}_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{1}{1-\mathrm{f}+\mathrm{f}/\mathrm{p}} . For example, if the default distributed parallelism is used (scenarios 1b+2b, see the U2 document on parallelism) and stages 1.3/1.4 and 2. (see §4.1) represent 90% of the sequential time ( f=0.90 ), the theoretical speed-up is bounded by the value {\mathrm{S}}_{\infty}=\frac{1}{1-0.9+0.9/\infty }=10 ! And this, whatever the number of MPI processes allocated. - In order to optimise one's parallel run, one must watch for possible load imbalances in the data flow (CPU and memory) and limit the extra costs due to memory unloadings (JEVEUX and MUMPS OOC) (see §4.1) and to the archiving of fields (see §4.3). In order to gain run time, one must also rule out any procedure for compaction of the memory (command FIN, keyword RETASSAGE), which is counter-productive in parallel. - Resorting to the MPI parallelism of MUMPS makes it possible to gain in CPU time (on the parallelised stages) and in RAM: thanks to the data distribution of JEVEUX (if the option MATR_DISTRIBUEE is activated) and, above all, thanks to that of the MUMPS objects. - A few empirical figures: it is recommended to allocate at least 20,000 degrees of freedom per MPI process; a standard thermomechanical analysis generally benefits, on 32 processors, from a gain of the order of ten in elapsed time and from a factor of 4 in RAM.

u1.04.00 Methods for launching a code_aster run Methods for launching a code_aster run > Summary. This document presents the different ways of launching a study on code_aster, such as AsterStudy, astk, run_aster, run_ctest and run_sbatch. All the methods are described in terms of their operating logic, their advantages and their disadvantages. More precisely, we describe their graphical interfaces or their command-line approaches, and we explain how the user can launch a study according to his or her needs. Note: Note that some methods are already contained in other methods. For example, AsterStudy uses the command run_aster or run_sbatch. Likewise, astk uses the low-level command as_run to launch a run. It is not recommended to use as_run directly, which is why we shall not give any details of this command here. 1 General notions Here are a few definitions and pieces of information which will be used in the following sections: 1.1 Server There are two types of server used in the context of the execution of code_aster: - Compute server: machine on which the services required for the execution of the analyses are installed. One can access it in order to launch analyses, consult the results and handle the files required for execution. - File server: machine used only to store and access the files required for the analyses, with no possibility of direct execution on it. In the remainder of this document, we shall distinguish two categories of server according to their location relative to the user: - Local server: this is the machine on which the user works directly. By default, this machine can be used as a file server, because its connection information is already known. However, if one wishes to execute analyses on it (for example if a version of code_aster is installed there), it is necessary to declare it explicitly as a compute server. - Remote server: any machine other than that of the user, accessible via the network, can be declared as a compute server or a file server, according to requirements. 1.2 salome_meca container This is a self-contained software environment, containing the main program as well as its dependencies. It makes it possible to run an application without having to install it directly on the host system. The name of the container image is constructed in the following manner: salome_meca- - - - - .sif The latest images are built on the basis of salome_meca 2024. The reference image is: salome_meca-edf-2024.1.0-1-20240327-scibian-11 (see historique_des_images _ for more details.) 1.2.0.1 How to install the container? There are two ways: 1. Open the Packages application and search for salome-meca (see the figure opposite). Select the package salome-meca or scibian11 container for salome-meca-2024 , tick the box and click on Apply the changes. 1. Download the image locally (often into the directory {HOME}/containers/ ) from a terminal. Enter the command line: wget -c https://minio.retd.edf.fr/codeaster/sif/stable/salome_meca-edf-2024.1.0-1-20240327-scibian-11.sif Then, launch the installation script: singularity run --app install salome_meca-edf-2024.1.0-1-20240327-scibian-11.sif For more information, please visit Prise en main rapide _. 1.2.0.2 How to access the container? There can be two cases, according to how the container was installed: 1. When the Packages application was used: On a Scibian machine, the Packages application has installed various files, of which the most important are /usr/bin/salome-meca-2024 and /usr/bin/salome-meca-2024-container-shell . The first allows us to access the salome_meca container, in which one will be able to use asterStudy and astk. The second allows us to access the bash of the container in order to execute the command lines run_aster/run_ctest and/or as_run. 1. When the container image was downloaded: One goes into the directory containing the container and starts the execution of salome_meca with: ./salome_meca-edf-2024.1.0-1-20240327-scibian-11 One can add the installation path to the PATH by putting: export PATH= {HOME}/containers: {PATH} in the file ~/.bashrc . One will then be able to execute salome_meca-edf-2024.1.0-1-20240327-scibian-11 directly from anywhere (and without ./ in front). One can simplify the execution further by creating a link in the terminal with: ln -s {HOME}/containers/salome_meca-edf-2024.1.0-1-20240327-scibian-11 ct Then, one can launch the container by doing: ct In addition, here are a few launching options: ct --shell # démarre bash (seul .bashrc est chargé). ct --help # affiche l'aide d'utilisation du script de démarrage. ct shell # démarre salome shell (charge l’environnement SALOME). ct -- shell --help # affiche l’aide de salome shell (pas du script de lancement). 1.3 ASTK profile A profile is a file (extension .astk) which contains all the information relating to a study: the location of the files of the study, as input data and as results, the type associated with each file, the parameters for submission of the run (memory, time, compute machine, batch/interactive, etc.). As its name indicates, it is inherent to the astk interface. Consequently, it also contains parameters concerning the interface itself, so as to resume a study in exactly the same state in which it had been left. It is saved at the user's request and at each launching of a run. 1.4 EXPORT file This file (extension .export) is a simplified representation of the astk profile: it contains only the information on the files and the parameters required for the run (and no information on the astk graphical interface). The syntax of this file is the same for all the tools which launch code_aster from the command line. Note: Note that all the tools for launching code_aster need, in one way or another, the .export file (see documentation D1.02.05). 1.4.0.1 Example of a .export file Here is an extract: P actions make_etude P time_limit 60 P memory_limit 512 P ncpus 1 P mpi_nbcpu 1 P mpi_nbnoeud 1 P version stable F comm fichier.comm D 1 F datg fichier.datg D 16 F mmed fichier.mmed D 20 F resu fichier.resu R 8 F mess fichier.mess R 6 This example illustrates the indispensable parameters to be defined: - actions make_etude : in order to launch a run - time_limit : time in seconds of the submitted job - memory_limit : memory in MB for the run - ncpus : number of processors for OpenMP parallelism - mpi_nbcpu : total number of processors for MPI parallelism - mpi_nbnoeud : number of nodes for MPI parallelism - version: a version of code_aster: stable, dev, etc. For more information and the other optional parameters, visit document D1.02.05. Note that the data files required in order to run the test are described in the form: F/R type chemin D/R/C numéro_unité_logique Here, F/R means that the user has the possibility of declaring the nature of the object pointed to by the path: file (F) or directory (R). In addition, the user also has the possibility of saying whether the object consists of input data (D), of results (R) or is compressed (C). The logical unit number makes it possible to identify each of the files (it can be used in the command file to designate the input or output files). 1.4.0.2 List of types for a study | TYPE | DESCRIPTION | LOGICAL UNIT | | --- | --- | --- | | comm | code_aster command files (including the restart files) | 1 | | mail | mesh file in code_aster format | 20 | | mmed | mesh in MED format | 20 | | mess | file of the messages of the execution | 6 | | resu | result file (printout of the tests, printout in code_aster format) | 8 | | rmed | result file in MED format | 80 | | base | directory containing the database of the run | 0 | 1.4.0.3 How to add Python files and/or directories? We deal with the case in which the user has a Python file .py with functions which are called in the command file. First of all, it should be noted that performing this action is possible with as_run, run_aster and astk. Up to version 2024, AsterStudy does not include this functionality. If the user uses the methods as_run, run_aster or astk, the following line should be added to the .export file: F nom chemin_du_fichier D 0 If the user needs to add a folder with various files, the following line should be added: R nom chemin_du_dossier D 0 # ou R repe chemin_du_dossier D 0 However, when astk is used, there are a few notes to consider when calling the functions. For more information, please read Example of importing folders. 1.4.0.4 How to add a development version? There is the possibility of adding new versions of code_aster (for example a development version) in astk and asterStudy (based on as_run). To do this, one adds the following line to the file HOME/.astkrc/prefs : vers : DEV: HOME/dev/codeaster/install/mpi/share/aster On the remote servers of EDF R&D, the installation path is different: vers : DEV:/scratch/users/ USER/dev/codeaster/install/mpi/share/aster 2 Use of the AsterStudy interface 2.1 How to access it? One must first launch the salome_meca container, then click on View/AsterStudy or directly on the tool icon in the toolbar. 2.2 How to launch a run? In a very simplified manner, one should first define the different stages to be carried out in the CaseView tab (via Operations/Add stage ). There is also the possibility of importing a test case by clicking Operations/Import Testcase . For more detailed information, visit the code_aster - salome_meca training. Once this step has been completed, one goes to the History View tab in order to provide the simulation parameters. Finally, one selects the CurrentCase and one clicks on the Run button (see the figure below). Note: In AsterStudy we have the possibility of choosing the machine on which to execute (e.g. local, cronos, gaia) as well as the code_aster version available on each machine (e.g. stable, dev, etc.). 2.2.0.1 Run properties In the Run properties window of the History View tab, we can provide salome_meca with the launching parameters. 2.2.1 Basic - Memory: equivalent to memory_limit of the export file. Memory in MB for the aster run - Time: equivalent to time_limit. Time of the submitted job - Run servers: the local or remote server available - Version of code_aster: the versions installed on the selected server - Number of MPI CPU: equivalent to mpi_nbcpu. Total number of processors for MPI parallelism. 2.2.2 Advanced Among the most used options: - Run mode: interactive or console - Number of MPI nodes: equivalent to mpi_nbnoeud. Number of nodes for MPI parallelism - Number of threads: Number of threads for OpenMP parallelism. 2.3 Retrieval of the results 2.3.0.1 In the event of success If the simulation finishes without a major problem, AsterStudy will copy the various result files from the /tmp folder and paste them into the location given beforehand. In addition, it will create a folder named _Files in which one will be able to find the logs, the messages, etc., of each RunCase. 2.3.0.2 In the event of failure When an error occurs during a run, it is possible to retrieve the computation files already created (.rmed, .txt, logs, etc.). On a local machine, this directory is normally found at the location /tmp (or /local00/tmp/ ). On the cronos and gaia servers, access to the directory is restricted. By construction, even in the event of a fatal error, AsterStudy will copy the intermediate results into the directory specified by the user. If the user wishes to analyse the cause of the error, he or she can consult the logs which are located in the /logs directory on the tree of the study that was launched, or in the /tmp directory. Note: The tmp file is located at /local00/tmp/ because that is the default path. To modify it, one would need to change the file HOME/.astkrc/config_servers. 3 Use of the Astk interface Astk is the graphical interface which makes it possible to organise code_aster analyses: prepare the data, organise the files, access the pre- and post-processing tools, launch and follow the progress of the analyses. Astk also makes it possible to choose the version of code_aster to be used from among those available (stable, testing, etc.). 3.1 How to access it? There are two ways of opening Astk: - In the salome_meca container, one must click on Tools/Plugins/code_aster/Run astk . - From the command line, one must execute, in the salome terminal: Astk Note: For more information on access to the salome_meca terminal, consult General notions. 3.2 Configuration The first time the user launches the interface, he or she has a default configuration which was defined at installation. The configuration is then stored in the directory HOME/.astkrc. If the user wants to return to the original configuration, he or she must delete this directory and relaunch Astk. In the following paragraphs, only the Servers menu is detailed. 3.2.0.1 Servers One accesses the servers window by clicking on Configuration/Servers . The first button makes it possible to switch from one server to another and to add a "New server". The fields are: - Full name or IP address: this is the name of the server on the network; one can give its full name with the domain name (for example: linux.labo.univ.fr) or its IP address (for example: 156.98.254.36). - The "local machine" box indicates that Astk must not use ssh to contact this machine. - Server state: one can set to "off" a server which is temporarily inaccessible. - Login: identifier with which one connects to the server. - HOME directory: default directory when one browses on this machine. - Services directory: directory where the services are installed on this server (give the installation path, for example: /opt/aster); leave empty for a file server. - Configuration download mode: none (for a file server), manual (one must click on the "Download now" button in order to retrieve the Aster configuration of the server), automatic (Astk queries the server at start-up every 30 days). - Last download: date of the last update of the configuration information. - Terminal: command for opening a terminal on the server. This makes it possible to open a command window on the server when one uses the bsf. - Editor: text editor (for example, nedit). The installation procedure chooses an editor from among (and in this order): nedit, gedit, xemacs, emacs, xedit, vi. Note: - Whenever one defines a command to be executed (terminal, editor, etc.), it is advisable to give the absolute path (from the root) so that the command is not left unfound if the PATH variable is incorrect. - For users who have access to the EDF R&D servers, the information in the Configuration/Servers tab will need to be updated by clicking on the Refresh now button. 3.3 How to get a run launched? In this paragraph and the following ones, a general description is given of how to use Astk in order to carry out a study. Suppose that one wants to launch the study of the test case forma00a , for which the items available are: - The Aster command file: forma00a.comm - The description of the geometry produced with Salomé: forma00a.datg - The mesh built by Salomé: forma00a.mmed - The file containing the execution messages: forma00a.mess In the example, all the files are placed in the directory HOME/. The files of this example are available in the astest directory of your version of code_aster . Note: In the case of a study with several command files, all the files must be of type "comm", associated with logical unit 1, and it is the order of appearance in the profile which determines the order of execution. 3.3.0.1 Creation of the profile One launches the interface, which opens onto a blank profile; or else, if Astk is already launched, one chooses File/New in the menu in order to create a new empty profile. One goes to the STUDY tab. 3.3.0.2 Selection of the files - Definition of a base path In the STUDY tab, one chooses a base path in order to simplify access to the files. One clicks on the icon , and one chooses the directory HOME/. - Addition of existing files One adds the command file by clicking on ; the file selection opens directly in the base path which has just been defined. All that remains is to select the file so that it appears in the list. - Addition of files which do not yet exist Unless an execution has already taken place, the result files do not yet exist, so one cannot add them by browsing the tree. - by inserting an empty line: by clicking on the new-file button , a line is added to the list. For example, one can choose the type "mess" in the list in order to print the messages during execution. Then, one indicates the path HOME/forma00a.mess or forma00a.mess or ./forma00a.mess (since it is possible to indicate the name of the file in absolute form, or relative to the base path). Finally, one fills in the logical unit number (equal to 6 by default), one ticks the "R" box (result) and one unticks "D". - with "Default value": This function uses the name of the Astk profile in order to build the default values. The profile must therefore be saved, if this has not yet been done. One chooses Save as in the File menu, one goes with the browser into the reference directory, and in the Selection line one writes, for example, forma00a (the extension .astk is added automatically). One inserts an empty line and one chooses the file type "mess", then one right-clicks in the file-name box and one chooses "Default value": Astk builds a file name from the base path, the profile name (with the extension removed) and the type "mess", that is HOME/forma00a.mess. The "R" box has been ticked, and the logical unit number has been set to 6. - Delete a file To delete a line from the list of files, it is enough to select it by clicking in the area where the name of the file is indicated, and to click on the icon . It should be noted that only the reference to this file in the Astk profile is forgotten; the file itself is not deleted. 3.3.0.3 Launching of the run The data and result files having been selected, one adjusts the parameters of the run, and one clicks on the "Launch" button. One takes care to tick the box which is located just next to STUDY, in order to indicate that one wishes to use the contents of this tab; otherwise the interface replies "Nothing to launch!". If the profile has not yet been saved, the interface asks one to choose a location and a name for this profile. Astk calls as_run in order to execute the run, and transmits to the job monitor (asjob) the job number (process number in interactive mode) and other information which will make it possible to follow the progress of the run. The initial state of the run is PEND (pending); when the run starts, it becomes RUN, then ENDED when it is finished (other states are possible in batch). The "Refresh" button calls the service which refreshes the state of the runs in progress. When the run is finished, one can consult the result of the job by double-clicking on the job, or via Edit/Output file . Figure 5.3-1: Job monitoring window 3.3.0.4 Consultation of the results One can consult the result files simply by double-clicking on their name, which opens a text editor for the "mess" and "resu" files. Note: - The directory which is to receive a result file does not exist; it is created automatically if the permissions are sufficient. - If the copying of result files fails (problem of permissions, of quota, of remote connection...), they are copied into a temporary directory on the execution machine. An alarm _COPY_RESULTS indicates the path where one must go to fetch the results. 3.4 Retrieval of the results 3.4.0.1 In the event of success If the simulation finishes without a major problem, Astk will copy the various result files from the /tmp folder and paste them into the location indicated previously. 3.4.0.2 In the event of failure In the same way as for AsterStudy, when an error occurs during a run, it is possible to retrieve the log files of the terminal, which will contain additional information (in order to analyse the cause of the error) according to the verbose option chosen. In that case, there are two directories to be taken into account: the flasheur and the tmp. On a local machine, the flasheur directory is normally found at the location HOME/flasheur/ , whereas the temporary directory tmp is located at /local00/tmp/ . On the cronos and gaia servers, users have access only to the flasheur directory (also located at HOME/flasheur/ ), access to the tmp directory being restricted. An important distinction to note: the files in flasheur and tmp can vary according to the number of nodes or of processors used. For example, if two nodes are involved in the run, the information in the tmp directory can be duplicated and less well structured, which can complicate their analysis. Note: The tmp file is located at /local00/tmp/ because that is the default path. To modify it, one would need to change the file HOME/.astkrc/config_servers. 4 Use of the commands run_aster, run_sbatch and run_ctest Unlike astk and as_run, which make it possible to address different versions of code_aster, run_aster and run_sbatch launch only their own version. There is therefore one run_aster script (and one run_sbatch) per version. Using run_aster is the recommended method for launching a code_aster run on the local server, and run_sbatch is the best option on the remote servers. 4.1 How to launch a run? 4.1.0.1 The run_aster command 4.1.1 On the local server Locally, only run_aster is accessible (run_sbatch is not available, because there is in general no batch manager). In order to launch the executables on the local server, one must first place oneself in the terminal of the container. Once inside, in order to launch the study of a single run, one must execute: run_aster [options] file[.export|.py] Here, run_aster is an alias to /opt/salome_meca/V /tools/code_aster /bin/run_aster . It is enough to choose the run_aster script of the version which one wishes to execute. For developers, the path of the executable will frequently be HOME/dev/codeaster/install/mpi/bin/run_aster . It is possible to retrieve the information from the terminal during compilation by doing: run_aster [options] file[.export|.py] > path_to_output_file If needed, it is possible to display the help for run_aster by doing: run_aster --help 4.1.2 On the remote servers First of all, one must connect to the remote server via ssh: ssh NNI@ssh.hpc.edf.fr On the servers of EDF R&D, it is mandatory to launch the analyses on the compute nodes in batch (and therefore with run_sbatch) and not on the front-end. Note: run_aster executes directly, so it must not be used on the front-end. 4.1.2.1 The run_sbatch command This command is used to execute code_aster on the remote server. The simplest way of doing so is the following: run_sbatch --wckey= SBATCH_WCKEY [options] file[.export|.py] Here run_sbatch is an alias for the executable /aster/install/ /bin/run_sbatch . It is enough to choose the run_sbatch script of the version which one wishes to execute. In this context, the key SBATCH_WCKEY is to be requested from your project manager. To find out more about the other launching options, the command available is: run_sbatch --help A recommended option is "--dry-run", which makes it possible to create and to read the submission script. This allows users to validate the parameters of the run before launching it. Here is an extract of what one might read: #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=myfile # number of nodes #SBATCH --nodes=1 # number of MPI processes #SBATCH --ntasks=1 # number of threads per MPI process #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1 --threads-per-core=1 # max walltime #SBATCH --time="01:00:00" # memory in MB #SBATCH --mem=11596M # add --exclusive if several nodes, define --partition=... #SBATCH 4.1.2.2 The run_ctest command This command is used to launch one or more test cases. 4.1.3 On the local server One must execute: run_ctest --testlist=file[.txt] --resutest=folder [options] By similarity, here run_ctest is an alias for the executable /opt/salome_meca/V /tools/code_aster /bin/run_ctest (which can change according to the version installed). For developers, the path of the executable will frequently be HOME/dev/codeaster/install/mpi/bin/run_ctest . Note: Locally, the command run_ctest executes in a linear manner the computation of the test cases whose name is in the file file.txt (one test case after another). On a remote server, run_ctest executes the analyses in parallel (one job for each test case). In this example, the file file.txt contains the names of the export files to be executed. For example: sdls118a sdls118b sdls118c sdls118d sdls118e sdnx100g Finally, the resutest option makes it possible to change the directory of the results of the test cases. For more details on the other options available, one must execute in the terminal: run_ctest --help 4.1.4 On the remote servers In a manner very similar to the case of the local server, one executes run_ctest by means of this command line: run_ctest --wckey= SBATCH_WCKEY --testlist=file[.txt] --resutest=folder [options] --sbatch where one indicates the WCKEY key and the sbatch option, in order to launch the different test cases in different jobs with slurm. 5 Example: Using Python modules in an export file Suppose that the tree of our project is: project ├── mesh_file.mmed ├── command_file.comm ├── export_file.export ├── src │ ├── __init__.py │ └── python_file.py The export file, which contains the information for the execution of the study, has the form: P actions make_etude P time_limit 60 P memory_limit 512 P ncpus 1 P mpi_nbcpu 1 P mpi_nbnoeud 1 P version stable F comm command_file.comm D 1 F mmed mesh_file.mmed D 20 To this export file, a line should be added in order to indicate the path of the folder to be taken into account during the run. Depending on the case, this line may be: - When run_aster is used: R nom chemin_du_src D 0 - When astk is used: R repe chemin_du_src D 0 The difference between these two cases is due to the fact that astk, up to version 17.2 of code_aster, restricts the type nom to files. The type to be used is then repe . As a result of this, one must also adapt the way of calling the functions in the files of the src folder of our example. 5.1 Calling functions with run_aster The way of importing, into the file command_file.comm, the functions contained in python_file.py is the following: from src.python_file import my_function Assuming that the file python_file.py contains: def my_function(): pass 5.2 Calling functions with astk It should be noted that when a folder is imported with repe , astk will copy the files of the folder into a folder named REPE_IN in the temporary directory. This operation means that the Python modules must no longer be imported from src , but from REPE_IN . In the command file, the way of importing the functions becomes: from REPE_IN.python_file import my_function Note: astk does not allow more than one repe folder. Whereas with run_aster, which is the recommended solution, it is possible to have several.

u1.05.00 A simple example of use A simple example of use > Summary. This document describes a very simple example of use of Code_Aster . The data-setup files are those of the test case FORMA00, available in the test-case base of Code_Aster: | Salomé script for generating the CAD and the mesh | forma00.datg | | --- | --- | | Code_Aster command file | forma00.comm | On the basis of this simple analysis of a thin tank under hydrostatic pressure, modelled as axisymmetric, the "essential" commands are commented on. 1 Modelling a mechanical problem with Code_Aster The problem to be modelled is a thin cylindrical tank of constant thickness (thickness 0.1m , internal radius R=1m , height L=4m ) subjected to an internal pressure varying with the height, corresponding to a hydrostatic pressure. Given the symmetries of the geometry and of the loading, a two-dimensional axisymmetric modelling is chosen. It is therefore sufficient to represent a vertical slice of this cylinder (in the plane XY ). The two stages to be planned are: - creation of the mesh - writing of the command file 2 Building the mesh: what to plan for? Whatever meshing software is used, one must plan, from the creation of the mesh, to name the topological zones which will be used in the analysis to assign elementary characteristics, boundary conditions, loadings, materials... Indeed, although it is possible to use node numbers and mesh-cell numbers directly in the command file, it is preferable to use named entities (node groups, mesh-cell groups). This makes it possible to have a command file independent of the degree of refinement of the mesh, and of any renumbering of the nodes or of the elements. In practice, these entities are groups: - node groups (possibly containing a single node, as with the points A , B , C , D in the example), - mesh-cell groups corresponding to subdomains of the mesh, or else mesh cells used to apply the loadings: here, for example, the mesh-cell group LDA contains linear mesh cells (skin mesh cells) which will be used to apply the pressure. The simple script generating the geometry (a rectangle) and the mesh can be read in the file forma00.datg. 3 How to write the command file? 3.1 Starting from nothing? When one wants to model a new thermomechanical problem, one does not in general start from a blank sheet: it is useful to take inspiration from a command file of a modelling close to the one to be treated. How are these files obtained? The sources are various: - the test base of Code_Aster , together with its documentation, is often an important help, because it covers a large part of the features of the code (these tests can be found in the astest directory of the code installation), - training courses make it possible to learn in depth the whole set of commands relating to types of modelling: linear statics, thermal analysis, dynamics, thermoplasticity, post-processing… In particular, the practical work of the training courses consists of tests: FORMA . The associated validation documents (V) contain the titles and the solutions of this practical work. Writing this command file will be made much easier by using the command-file editor EFICAS. 3.2 A few essential commands We shall now detail the commands needed to carry out the analysis under consideration. | Command file | Explanations | | --- | --- | | # Thin cylinder under hydrostatic pressure | Comments are preceded by the # sign, | | DEBUT ( ) ; | Compulsory command in order to begin. | | mail = LIRE_MAILLAGE ( FORMAT='MED' ) ; | Reading of the mesh in MED format in the file associated by default with the mesh: logical unit 20. Creation of the concept mail containing the mesh in Aster format | | # Definition of the model | | | modl=AFFE_MODELE(MAILLAGE=mail, AFFE=_F(TOUT='OUI', PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='AXIS',),); | A model is a concept, here named modl, containing the types of finite element useful to the analysis. Axisymmetric mechanical finite elements are assigned to all the mesh cells of the mesh. Note: one and the same command may continue over several lines | | # Definition of the material | | | acier=DEFI_MATERIAU(ELAS=_F(E=210000000000.0, NU=0.3,),); | Definition of a particular material, which we have chosen to name acier here, and of its characteristics: Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio for the case of an elastic material. | | # Assignment of the material to the mesh | | | chmat=AFFE_MATERIAU(MAILLAGE=mail, AFFE=_F(TOUT='OUI', MATER=acier,),); | Assignment of the material acier to the mesh mail. Here the material is the same for the whole mesh. One could of course assign different materials to particular mesh-cell groups. | | # Definition of the boundary conditions | | | clim=AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=modl, FACE_IMPO=_F(GROUP_MA='LAB', DY=0,),); | Boundary conditions may apply to nodes, node groups, mesh cells or mesh-cell groups. Here the nodes of the mesh-cell group LAB (boundary mesh cells) are assigned the following condition: \mathrm{DY}=0 which means: "displacement along y " zero for all the nodes of the group LAB | | # Definition and assignment of the loading: pressure as a function of y | | | f_y=DEFI_FONCTION(NOM_PARA='Y', VALE=(0.0,200000.0, 4.0,0.0,),); | Functions are defined point by point (affine variation between two points by default). Here, the pressure varies between: 200000\mathit{Pa} for y=0 and 0 for y=L | | charg=AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F(MODELE=modl, PRES_REP= _F(GROUP_MA=('LFA','LDF',), PRES=f_y,),); | Assignment of the pressure (a function of y ) on the edge made up of the mesh-cell groups LFA and LDF | | # Solution | | | res1=MECA_STATIQUE(MODELE=modl, CHAM_MATER=chmat, EXCIT=(_F(CHARGE=charg,), _F(CHARGE=clim,),),); | Global command for the solution of static problems in linear thermoelasticity. Association with the model, the material field(s) and the loading(s) previously defined. res1 is the name of the result concept produced by the command. It contains in particular the computed displacement field. | | # Computation of the stresses | | | res1=CALC_CHAMP(reuse =res1, RESULTAT=res1, CONTRAINTE='SIGM_ELNO',); | reuse=res1 means that one "enriches" the concept. res1: the stress field will be stored in addition to the displacement field already present in the concept. The name 'SIGM_ELNO' means "stresses computed at the nodes of each element from the displacements" | | # Printout of the results | | | IMPR_RESU(FORMAT='MED', RESU=_F(RESULTAT=res1,),); | Printout of the results in MED format: displacements/stresses over the whole mesh | | IMPR_RESU(RESU=_F(RESULTAT=res1, GROUP_NO='A',),); | Printout of the results in text format for the single node group "A". | | FIN(); | Compulsory command to close an execution | 4 What does the result file contain? u2.01.02 User's guide to boundary conditions treated by elimination u2.01.02 User's guide to boundary conditions treated by elimination > Summary. The treatment of Dirichlet boundary conditions by elimination (AFFE_CHAR_CINE) does not offer the same generality as treatment by dualisation (AFFE_CHAR_MECA, for example). This treatment is to be used when one seeks to improve the execution time of a run, or when one wishes to work with positive-definite matrices. Note that the boundary conditions available in AFFE_CHAR_ ( = MECA/THER/ACOU) cannot all be eliminated and treated by AFFE_CHAR_CINE. This document shows how to use the "kinematic loads" in Aster command sets. There are 3 cases (from the simplest to the most complicated): - One uses a "global" analysis command (THER_LINEAIRE, STAT_NON_LINE, …). In this case, the kinematic loads are used like the other loads. - One wishes to carry out an eigenmode analysis. An argument must then be added in the command ASSE_MATRICE. - One wishes to carry out a "step-by-step" analysis and to solve the linear systems with the commands FACTORISER and RESOUDRE. In this case, the command CALC_CHAR_CINE must be used. 1 Principle of elimination One seeks to solve in {ℝ}^{n} the following constrained minimisation problem (Pb1): \underset{u\in {U}_{G}}{\min}(\frac{1}{2}{u}^{T}Ku-{u}^{T}f) with {U}_{G}=\left\lbrace u\in {ℝ}^{n},{u\mid }_{G}={u}_{0}\right\rbrace where - {u}_{0}\in {ℝ}^{p} is known ( 1\le p\le n ) - G is the subset of N=\lbrace 1,\mathrm{...},n\rbrace , of cardinality p : G={g}_{1}\mathrm{...}{g}_{p} - {u\mid }_{G} is the projection of u onto the subspace spanned by {\lbrace {u}_{i}\rbrace }_{i\in G} - where {({u}_{i})}_{j}={\delta}_{ij},\forall j\in N - K is a symmetric matrix n\times n , - f\in {ℝ}^{n} is given. The constraint {u\mid }_{G}={u}_{0} represents boundary conditions of Dirichlet type, homogeneous or not. If one denotes by L={C}_{N}G the complement of G in N , one can, with the help of the {u}_{i} defined above, decompose {ℝ}^{n} into the direct sum of {V}_{G} = vector space spanned by {\lbrace {u}_{i}\rbrace }_{i\in G} and of {V}_{L} = vector space spanned by {\lbrace {u}_{i}\rbrace }_{i\in L} ; Hence we have {ℝ}^{n}={V}_{G}\oplus {V}_{L} and one writes u={u}_{G}\oplus {u}_{K} where {u}_{G}={u\mid }_{G} and {u}_{L}={u\mid }_{L} or again, in vector notation, u=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{u}_{G}\\ {u}_{L}\end{array}\right\rbrace The problem (Pb1) can therefore be written in the form of the problem (Pb2): \lbrace \begin{array}{}\min(\frac{1}{2}{u}_{G}^{T}{K}_{\text{GG}}{u}_{G}+\frac{1}{2}{u}_{L}^{T}{K}_{\text{LL}}{u}_{L}+{u}_{L}^{T}{K}_{\mathrm{LG}}{u}_{G}-{u}_{L}^{T}{f}_{L}-{u}_{G}^{T}{f}_{G})\\ {u}_{G}\in {V}_{G}\\ {u}_{L}\in {V}_{L}\\ {u}_{G}={u}_{0}\end{array} Which amounts to writing: (\text{Pb1})\iff (\text{Pb2}) \lbrace \begin{array}{}\min(\frac{1}{2}{u}_{L}^{T}{K}_{\text{LL}}{u}_{L}+{u}_{L}^{T}{K}_{\mathrm{LG}}{u}_{0}-{u}_{L}^{T}{f}_{L})\\ {u}_{L}\in {V}_{L}\\ u={u}_{0}\oplus {u}_{L}\end{array} One has then eliminated {u}_{G} from the minimisation problem. We shall now look for the matrix problem associated with (Pb3). One looks for {u}_{L} minimising \frac{1}{2}{u}_{L}^{T}{K}_{\text{LL}}{u}_{L}+{u}_{L}^{T}{K}_{\mathrm{LG}}{u}_{0}-{u}_{L}^{T}{f}_{L} which amounts to solving the following matrix problem: {K}_{\text{LL}}{u}_{L}={F}_{L}-{K}_{\mathrm{LG}}{u}_{0} One may therefore write: (\text{Pb1})\iff (\text{Pb2})\iff (\text{Pb3})\iff \left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{\text{LL}}& 0\\ 0& {I}_{G}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{}{u}_{L}\\ {u}_{G}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{}{f}_{L}-{K}_{\mathrm{LG}}{u}_{0}\\ {u}_{0}\end{array}\right] , that is K'\left[\begin{array}{}{u}_{L}\\ {u}_{G}\end{array}\right]=f' 2 Treatment in Aster 2.1 The kinematic loads A kinematic load (Aster type: char_cine_ [ = meca/ther/acou]) makes it possible to characterise the set G of the imposed degrees of freedom and the {({u}_{0})}_{i} for i\in G , which are the values assigned to these degrees of freedom. The definition of a kinematic load is made by means of the operator AFFE_CHAR_CINE for the (u0)i which are constant, or functions of the geometry or of time. 2.2 The kinematic vectors The kinematic vector is a cham_no_ which represents the vector \left[\begin{array}{}0\\ {u}_{0}\end{array}\right] . To each kinematic load there corresponds a kinematic vector. This operation is carried out by the operator CALC_CHAR_CINE. 2.3 Computation of K' K' is computed directly at assembly time by the operator ASSE_MATRICE, provided of course that a list of kinematic loads is supplied as an argument. The data structure MATR_ASSE_ has been modified so as to be able to store K' when this is necessary. 2.4 Computation of f' After the operator FACTORISER, the produced concept of type matr_asse_ contains the factorised form of K' and the unchanged matrix KLG. The computation of f' is carried out at solution time: the kinematic vector corresponding to \left[\begin{array}{}0\\ {u}_{0}\end{array}\right] must be supplied to the operator RESOUDRE as an argument, by means of the keyword CHAM_CINE. This operator then computes f' before solving \text{fact}(K')\left[\begin{array}{}{u}_{L}\\ {u}_{G}\end{array}\right]=f' . 3 Examples of command files 3.1 Mechanical analysis with a global command (STAT_NON_LINE) DEPIMP = AFFE_CHAR_CINE ( MODELE=MOD, MECA_IMPO=_F( GROUP_MA = 'LCD1', DY = -2.0)) RESU=STAT_NON_LINE( MODELE=MOD, CHAM_MATER=CHMAT, EXCIT= _F( CHARGE = DEPIMP , FONC_MULT = FONC), ...) 3.2 Kinematic loads for an eigenmode analysis CHARCINE = AFFE_CHAR_CINE (MODELE=MODEL, MECA_IMPO=_F(GROUP_MA='GM2', DX=0.0, DY=0.0)) KASS= ASSE_MATRICE (MATR_ELEM=KELEM, NUME_DDL=NUME, CHAR_CINE=CHARCINE ,); MASS= ASSE_MATRICE (MATR_ELEM=MELEM, NUME_DDL=NUME, CHAR_CINE=CHARCINE ,); computation of the eigenmodes of the structure MODES=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=KASS, MATR_MASS=MASS, CALC_FREQ=_F( NMAX_FREQ=10 )) 3.3 "Step-by-step" analysis using the commands FACTORISER and RESOUDRE CHCINE=AFFE_CHAR_CINE ( MODELE=MO, MECA_IMPO=( _F( GROUP_NO = 'SUPY', DY = 0.), _F( GROUP_NO = 'CHARGE', DX = -1.))) MEL=CALC_MATR_ELEM( MODELE=MO, CHAM_MATER=CHMAT, OPTION='RIGI_MECA') NU=NUME_DDL( MATR_RIGI=MEL ) MATAS= ASSE_MATRICE ( MATR_ELEM=MEL, NUME_DDL=NU, CHAR_CINE=CHCINE ) SCMBRE=CREA_CHAMP( ... ) VCINE=CALC_CHAR_CINE ( NUME_DDL=NU, CHAR_CINE=CHCINE ) MATAS=FACTORISER(reuse=MATAS, MATR_ASSE=MATAS ) DEP= RESOUDRE (MATR=MATAS, CHAM_NO=SCMBRE, CHAM_CINE=VCINE )

u2.01.05 Stresses, internal forces, forces and strains u2.01.05 Stresses, internal forces, forces and strains > Summary. This document defines the quantities which characterise the stresses, the forces and the strains inside a structure in a finite-element analysis in displacement, and how this is expressed. The expression of these quantities is given for the finite elements of mechanics: 2D or 3D continuum, shells and beams. 1 Statics 1.1 Stresses Cauchy's postulate is that the contact forces exerted at a point by one part of a continuum on another depend only on the normal to the surface at that point which separates the parts. In accordance with this postulate, one calls stress vector, for non-micropolar media, 	ext{F}\left(	ext{n}ight) the vector which characterises the contact forces exerted through a surface element \mathit{dS} of normal 	ext{n} on a part of a continuum [bib1]_. One then shows [bib3]_ that the dependence, at a fixed point, of 	ext{F} with respect to the normal 	ext{n} is linear, and that there exists a tensor, which one calls the stress tensor \sigma , such that: 	ext{F}\left(	ext{n}ight)=\sigma 	ext{n} The unit of stress in the International System is the 	ext{N}.{	ext{m}}^{-2}\equiv 	ext{Pa} . For the structure as a whole, the "stress state" is characterised by a field of the stress tensor, which is more simply called the stress field. 1.2 Internal force As regards beam or shell structures, unlike the continuum case, it must be noted that: - only the normal directions 	ext{n} of the cuts along the space tangent to the manifold are possible, - the characteristic quantities are obtained by integration, through the cross-section or the thickness, of the quantities defined for continua. 1.2.1 Case of discrete elements Discrete elements are finite elements which may have no physical dimension. They are represented by their stiffness matrix. The internal forces are obtained by multiplying this matrix by the displacement vector: ( egin{array}{c}F\ M\end{array})=\left[kight].( egin{array}{c}D\ R\end{array}) 1.2.2 Case of beams One calls internal force the reduction elements \left(F,Might) at P , the geometric centre of inertia of the cross-section \Sigma , of the resultant wrench of the contact forces exerted on the cross-section [bib2]_. With the previous notation:  egin{array}{ccc}F& ={\int}_{\Sigma}	ext{F}(	au )	ext{ds}& (N)\ {M}_{p}& ={\int}_{\Sigma}	ext{PM}\wedge 	ext{F}(	au )	ext{ds}& (N.m)\end{array} The force F is decomposed into a normal force N and shear forces T in the plane of the cross-section, while the moment M acting at the point P is decomposed into a torsional moment and bending moments at the point P . The fuel-assembly skeleton elements (R3.08.08) also carry the grid moments {M}_{g} , of a formulation equivalent to M . For beams whose cross-section is not regarded as rigid, these reduction elements are not sufficient: for example, for beams which take the warping of the cross-sections into account, one is led to consider an additional internal-force quantity due to warping (the bimoment). Multi-fibre beams (with a local 1D constitutive behaviour, relating stresses to strains at a certain number of points of the cross-section) and pipes (local constitutive behaviour in plane stress) supply both the reduction elements of the beams and a stress field for each fibre or sector. 1.2.3 Case of shells Let P be a point of a surface medium S of thickness h , let \mathrm{dl} be an element of length on S , and let n be the normal orienting the shell at that point. Let \left(F,Might) be the reduction elements at that point of a wrench resulting from the forces exerted through a surface element \mathrm{dS}=h\mathrm{dl} of normal n tangent to S on a part of S . The displacement fields u(x) are expressed from their nodal values, which form a vector q , and from the shape functions {\Phi}_{i}(x) by: u\left(xight)=\sum_{i}{q}_{i}{\Phi}_{i}\left(xight) In these conditions: w\left(uight)=\sum_{i}{q}_{i}{F}_{i} - The notion of node here is very general and means, in fact, carrier of a degree of freedom (whether of Lagrange or of Hermite type). - The notion of displacement is also very general, and includes the notion of generalised displacement, comprising translations and rotations. > Notes. 1.4 Representation of the fields There are several ways of representing the fields in a finite-element modelling: - for fields continuous over the whole domain, the values at the nodes are used (CHAM_NO of Code_Aster ) u\left(xight)=\sum_{i}{u}_{i}{\Phi}_{i}\left(xight) one then speaks of displacements at the nodes, of stresses at the nodes or of internal forces at the nodes, > Note. The stress or internal-force fields are generally computed at the Gauss points; if they are represented continuously, it is solely for visualisation purposes. For the other fields, the values at certain characteristic points of the finite elements (Gauss points or nodes) are used. One then speaks of stresses per finite element at the nodes, or of internal forces per finite element at the nodes, or again of stresses at the Gauss points or of internal forces at the Gauss points. > Note. Axisymmetric modellings For axisymmetric modellings, the axis of revolution is the Y axis of the mesh. The whole solid is meshed in X\ge 0 . The \mathit{Ox} axis therefore denotes the radial direction. The components of the computed fields will therefore be: X for the radial direction, Y for the axial direction, Z for the orthoradial (circumferential) direction. 1.5 Quantities associated in Code_Aster 1.5.1 SIEF_R The quantity SIEF_R represents the "stress state" of the structure; it therefore contains, at least, the components: - of the stress fields of continua (in the global frame): SIXX, SIYY, SIZZ, SIXY, SIXZ, SIYZ - of the internal-force fields of a beam and of a discrete element (in the "user" frame attached to the beam or to the discrete element): N, VY, VZ, MT, MFY, MFZ, MGX, MGY, MGZ - for beams with warping, the bimoment must be added (necessarily in the "user" frame attached to the fibre): BX - of the shell internal-force fields (necessarily in the "user" frame attached to the surface): NXX, NYY, NXY, MXX, MYY, MXY, QX, QY In addition, it is sometimes convenient to be able to use directly the internal-force fields of a beam and of a discrete element in the global frame: FX, FY, FZ, MX, MY, MZ It is also useful to represent the components of a stress field on the beam or shell finite elements in the "user" frame. To that end, the same components as in the global frame will be used, although confusion is possible. 1.5.2 FORC_F and FORC_R These quantities represent the forces applied to the structure on an interface. For: - a continuum, it is therefore a force vector, - a beam, a wrench of forces, - a shell, a wrench of forces. This quantity must therefore have the following components: - for a continuum: FX, FY, FZ - and, in addition, for the beams and the shells: MX, MY, MZ 1.5.3 DEPL_R Given that: - a field can be attached to only one quantity, - mixed finite-element methods (mixing unknowns of displacement type and unknowns of nodal-force type) are not excluded, - the dualisation of the boundary conditions leads to having, as unknown, a vector containing Lagrange variables which are nodal forces in the sense made precise above, - it is necessary to be able to carry out any kind of linear combination on the nodal forces, - the numbering of the unknowns must be the same as that of the right-hand sides, the nodal forces (dual, in the sense of the energy W , of the nodal displacements) necessarily have the same components as the displacements, namely: DX, DY, DZ, DRX, DRY, DRZ, DRGX, DRGY, DRGZ plus, for beams with warping, the degree of freedom associated with the bimoment: GRX. 1.6 Calculation options 1.6.1 Computation of the stress state 1.6.1.1 Field SIEF_ELGA This is the field representing the stress state and making it possible to continue analyses (geometric stiffness, nodal forces, etc.). This is a field on the nodes of the mesh, in which the value at a node is obtained from the stresses computed on the finite elements meeting at that node; their values therefore change when the mesh changes. In the absence of a distributed loading, equilibrium requires them to vanish at an interior node, whereas they correspond to the reaction on the supports where a kinematic relation is imposed (the case of an imposed displacement). In the case of shells, the components DX, DY and DZ give the FORC_NODA (of the dimension of a force) in the global frame of the mesh. These components are built from the normal forces and the shear forces in the shell. The components DRX, DRY and DRZ give the FORC_NODA (of the dimension of a moment) in the global frame of the mesh, built from the bending moments in the shell. 2 Kinematics 2.1 Strains 2.1.1 Continuum In this case, the displacements of the structure are represented by a vector field u with three components in general. The strain (under the small-perturbation hypothesis) is defined by the strain tensor \varepsilon by (options EPSI_ELGA and EPSI_ELNO): {\varepsilon}_{ij}(u)= rac{1}{2}({u}_{i,j}+{u}_{j,i}) One may wish to compute the "mechanical" strain, that is by subtracting the thermal expansions (options EPME_ELGA and EPME_ELNO): {\epsilon}_{ij}^{m}\left(uight)= rac{1}{2}\left({u}_{i,j}+{u}_{j,i}ight)-{\epsilon}^{	ext{th}} For non-linear analyses, it is sometimes useful to know the plastic strain (options EPSP_ELGA and EPSP_ELNO), denoted {\epsilon}^{\mathit{pl}} . In the case of large displacements, the Green-Lagrange strains are (options EPSG_ELGA and EPSG_ELNO): {E}_{ij}(u)= rac{1}{2}({u}_{i,j}+{u}_{j,i}+{u}_{k,i}{u}_{k,j}) From which one may wish to subtract the thermal strains (options EPMG_ELGA and EPMG_ELNO): {E}_{ij}^{m}(u)= rac{1}{2}({u}_{i,j}+{u}_{j,i}+{u}_{k,i}{u}_{k,j})-{\varepsilon}^{	ext{th}} For the plane-strain hypothesis (D_PLAN), it is important to note that the plane-strain condition is written on the total strain: {\epsilon}_{33}\left(uight)=0 If one writes the total strain as the sum of a purely mechanical strain and of the strain coming from the command variables (such as the thermal-expansion strain): {\epsilon}_{33}\left(uight)={\epsilon}_{33}^{m}+{\epsilon}_{33}^{\mathit{th}}=0 Then it follows naturally that, in plane strain, the out-of-plane mechanical strain is not zero in the presence of a thermal expansion. {\epsilon}_{33}^{m}\left(uight)
e 0 2.1.2 Case of beams In the traditional beam theories, each point P of the beam represents a cross-section. It is therefore the reduction elements of the displacement wrench (T(s),\Omega (s)) of the cross-section, assumed rigid, which characterise the displacement of the point P at the curvilinear abscissa s . T is the translation of the centre of inertia of the cross-section, \Omega (s) the rotation vector of the cross-section at that point. Application of the theorem of virtual work (cf.[bib2]_) naturally leads to defining, as the strain, the wrench (\varepsilon ,\chi ) obtained by differentiation of (T(s),\Omega (s)) with respect to the curvilinear abscissa s :  egin{array}{}\varepsilon = rac{\mathrm{dT}}{	ext{ds}}+	au \wedge \Omega \ \chi = rac{d\Omega }{	ext{ds}}\end{array} Let us then set:  egin{array}{}\varepsilon ={\varepsilon}_{L}	au +{\gamma}_{T}\ \chi ={\gamma}_{t}	au +	ext{K}\end{array} {\varepsilon}_{L} is the longitudinal strain, {\gamma}_{T} is the vector of the distortion strains (zero under the Navier-Bernoulli hypothesis), {\gamma}_{t} is the torsional strain of the cross-section, 	ext{K} is the bending strain. > Note. For beam modellings which take warping into account, the kinematics is more complicated to describe, but they nevertheless lead to notions close to those presented above. 2.1.3 Case of shells We shall restrict ourselves here to the case of plates. Indeed, in the general case of shells: - the spatial derivatives use mathematical notions too complicated for the scope of this document, R3.07.04, - shells are very often modelled by assembled plate finite elements. In this case, only the material normals are assumed rigid. The displacement of these normals is therefore represented by the reduction elements of a wrench (T,\Omega ) . T is the translation of the point lying on the mid-surface, \Omega the rotation vector of the normal at that point. It is clear that the normal component of \Omega is zero (in the case of non-micropolar media). One introduces the vector 	ext{I} in the tangent plane, defined by: 	ext{I}=\Omega \wedge 	ext{n} where n is the normal vector orienting the surface. Let the decomposition be: T=w	ext{n}+{	ext{u}}_{T} {	ext{u}}_{T} is the tangential displacement, w is the deflection. In the same way as for the beams, application of the theorem of virtual work (cf.[bib2]_) leads to defining, as the strain, the set formed by the tensors E and K and the vector \gamma , all these quantities being defined in the tangent plane by:  egin{array}{ccc}{E}_{\alpha  eta }& =&  rac{1}{2}({u}_{\alpha , eta }+{u}_{ eta ,\alpha })\ {K}_{\alpha  eta }& =&  rac{1}{2}({l}_{\alpha , eta }+{l}_{ eta ,\alpha })\ {\gamma}_{\alpha}& =& {l}_{\alpha}+{w}_{,\alpha }\end{array} The strain is therefore defined by 7 real numbers. {E}_{\alpha  eta } are the membrane strains, {K}_{\alpha  eta } are the inverses of the curvatures of the deformed mid-surface, {\gamma}_{\alpha} is the distortion-strain vector. > Note. Here again, there is no universal convention, and the disparity of the conventions is even greater than for the internal-force tensors. Link with the three-dimensional strain field In these conditions, one has:  egin{array}{cc}{\varepsilon}_{\alpha  eta }& ={E}_{\alpha  eta }+{x}_{3}{K}_{\alpha  eta }\ {\varepsilon}_{\alpha 3}&
