CANO: "Identification of the material parameters of 16MND5 associated with the thermal, metallurgical and mechanical models", EDF/R&D internal note H-T64-2008-03224, Issued during 2009. 2 General points on welding 2.1 What is welding? The welding of two metal parts is the obtaining of continuity by local fusion or diffusion, thanks to a supply of heat and possibly of a supply of metal. Many welding processes can therefore be described physically as a brief passage to very high temperature of a small quantity of metal, followed by free or forced cooling , most often by conduction in the bulk of the welded parts and in the elements of the workstation. Over time, this temperature evolution determines the final metallurgical structure of the welded joint, sometimes different from the base metal. 2.2 Phenomena involved during welding From a mechanical point of view, the highly localised thermal gradients involved during the welding of two materials generate local expansions and contractions, with the consequence that incompatible strain and stress fields appear, which remain after return to ambient temperature. For certain materials, the thermal history associated with the welding operation generates changes of microstructure in the solid state which influence the residual stress state and the distortions of the welded joint. These changes of microstructure occur when the temperature reaches a threshold called the transformation start temperature. These transformations stop when the temperature exceeds the transformation finish temperature. One can then distinguish two types of stress: the stresses of thermal origin generated throughout the duration of the welding process, and the stresses of metallurgical origin (possibly) generated during the duration of the transformations. Consequently, a numerical simulation of welding must take into account the phenomena coupled with one another: thermal, possibly metallurgical, and finally mechanical. 2.3 Review of the various interactions 2.3.1 Thermal–metallurgical interaction - Thermal => Metallurgical direction : the thermophysical properties (conductivity, heat capacity, diffusivity…) depend on the phases present. - Metallurgical => Thermal direction : the metallurgical transformations are accompanied by latent-heat effects which modify the temperature distributions. 2.3.2 Thermal–mechanical interaction - Thermal => Mechanical direction : this influence results, on the one hand, from the variations of the mechanical characteristics with temperature and, on the other hand, from the expansions and contractions of thermal origin. - Mechanical => Thermal direction : the evolution of the irreversible strain, as well as of the internal hardening variables, leads to a dissipation of energy in the form of heat. However, this temperature rise of mechanical origin is often negligible in comparison with that coming from the heat input delivered by the welding process, given the relatively small strains and strain rates which are involved. This assumption is no longer valid in the case of processes involving strong dissipations, for example friction welding. 2.3.3 Metallurgical–mechanical interaction - Metallurgical => Mechanical direction : the influence of the metallurgical history on the mechanical history results mainly from four factors. The first lies in the expansions and contractions caused by the metallurgical transformations. The second factor is the transformation-plasticity phenomenon. The third is the hardening-recovery phenomenon. Finally, the last factor corresponds to the particular behaviour linked to the multiphase nature of the material. - Mechanical => Metallurgical direction : the application of a stress modifies the energy stored in the material and the atomic structure of the lattice. The presence of a mechanical loading can therefore play a role in the metallurgical transformations. 2.4 What is meant by fusion zone, HAZ, tempered zone? When one speaks of welding, the study engineer will often hear of fusion zone, of HAZ and of tempered zone, which correspond to three distinct zones in a welded component. That is why we give below a very general definition of these zones. - The fusion zone (F.Z.) : this is the zone where the temperature is higher than the solidus of the steel considered , or of the filler metal. The composition of the molten metal results from the chemistry of the filler metal, from the chemistry of the base metal and from the interactions with the environment. This zone is separated from the heat-affected zone (HAZ) by the fusion line, which characterises the set of points that have reached the solidus temperature. - The heat-affected zone (HAZ) : in a very general way, this is the solid zone of the welded assembly where the constitutive behaviour of the material is strongly influenced by the temperature field due to welding. The term HAZ has a very particular meaning when the material of the base metal or of the filler metal undergoes structural transformations: it is the zone where the transformation takes place. This H.A.Z. itself breaks down into three main parts: the zone where the transformation is complete, the zone where the transformation is partial, and finally the tempered zone (T.Z.) , where the maximum temperature reached is slightly lower than the transformation start temperature but where the constitutive behaviour of the material is slightly modified relative to that of the base metal. - The zone not affected thermally : in a very general way, this is the solid zone of the welded assembly where the constitutive behaviour of the material is little influenced by the temperature field . For materials undergoing structural transformations, this is the part of the welded assembly where the maximum temperature reached is well below the transformation start temperature and where the welding operation does not generate any modification of the metallurgical and mechanical characteristics of the base metal. 2.5 Why is it important to simulate the welding process? The evolution of the welding processes applied to steels has made it possible today to achieve good reproducibility of the operation and good quality of the welded assemblies. Welds nevertheless constitute the weak points of structures. The strain and stress fields induced by the welding operation have a determining role in the quality and the mechanical strength of the welded component; the residual stresses induced by welding accentuate all the risks of damage by fatigue, by creep, by corrosion and by brittle fracture… That is why it is important to have robust and reliable tools in order to simulate this process. 3 Numerical simulation of welding Everything that is written hereafter can be implemented in two study situations: - When one simulates, obviously, the welding of two parts; - But also when one simulates the deposition of a cladding on a part. One can apply the same methodology as that adopted for a welding operation. 3.1 Visual representation of a welding operation - Reality : one has two parts A and B which one wishes to weld in order to obtain a part AB, using a suitable welding process (for example by heat input). The two parts are never welded in a single operation, but in successive passes, the first pass being called the root pass. - The numerical representation : the first root pass is never modelled. One therefore assumes that, initially, the two parts A and B form a single block. Later, we shall see that several methods exist for activating the passes. Most often (this is the configuration presented in the drawing below), one chooses to represent all the passes in the initial model and one activates them progressively. | Reality | The numerical representation | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | The welder | | | | | The heat source supplied by the welding process, with filler metal here | | | | | The two parts to be welded | | The initial part to be modelled, with here all the passes represented initially in the model | | | 1st pass = root pass | | | | | 2nd pass | | Activation of the 1st pass to be simulated | | | 3rd pass | | Activation of the 2nd pass to be simulated | | | 4th pass | | Activation of the 3rd pass to be simulated | | | 5th pass | | Activation of the 4th pass to be simulated | | | 6th pass Welded part AB | | 5th pass Simulated part AB | 3.2 What does one seek to compute? The final aim of the simulation is to determine the residual stress and strain fields. To do this, it is necessary to couple or to chain thermal, possibly metallurgical, and finally mechanical analyses. 3.3 What are the main difficulties of the simulation? The main difficulties, questions and methodological choices which the engineer will face can be summarised in six points: - 2D or 3D representation of the structure studied? - Which mesh to adopt? - How to take the heat input into account? - How to handle the addition of material, in the thermal analysis and in the mechanical analysis? - Which mechanical constitutive model (for the metallurgical transformations, a single model exists in Code_Aster )? - Which physical data? Note : The choices which will finally be adopted for the simulation depend greatly on the experimental data in the possession of the engineer. These data include: - Material data. As in any simulation, it is important to have material data in order to identify as cleanly as possible the constitutive laws (thermal, metallurgical and mechanical). Welding involving very high temperatures (up to melting of the material), one must have available, if possible, on the one hand parameters between 20°C and the melting temperature, and on the other hand tests making it possible to characterise the viscous phenomena. - Data on the welding conditions. Among the numerous uncertainties on the input data which come into play during the numerical simulation of a welding operation or of the deposition of a cladding, the indeterminacy of the heat input is the most penalising. Indeed, even when the welding is automated and the welding parameters are well known, the modelling of the heat input remains difficult in any case, and a calibration is almost always necessary (on temperature measurements or on macrographs of fusion zones) if a predictive numerical simulation is aimed at . In section 3, and for each of these points, we shall present the various possible methodologies and, sometimes, the recommended choices. 3.4 The specific features of Code_Aster 3.4.1 Which couplings are considered? In Code_Aster , it is currently possible to take into account the essential phenomena, but in a decoupled way, by means of chained thermal, then metallurgical (possibly), and finally mechanical analyses. The possible metallurgical analysis is thus carried out as post-processing of the thermal analysis, without taking into account the influence of the metallurgy on the thermal analysis (difference in thermophysical properties according to the phases, and latent heats of transformation). Likewise, the mechanical analysis is decoupled from the thermal and metallurgical analyses: the influence of the intrinsic dissipation on the thermal fields is neglected, as is the influence of the stress state on the metallurgical transformations. To summarise, here are the interactions taken (OUI) or not (NON) into consideration: - Influence of the thermal analysis on the metallurgy: OUI - Influence of the metallurgy on the thermal analysis: NON - Influence of the thermal analysis on the mechanical analysis: OUI - Influence of the mechanical analysis on the thermal analysis: NON - Influence of the metallurgy on the mechanical analysis: OUI - Influence of the mechanical analysis on the metallurgy: NON 3.4.2 Typical layout of a Code_Aster command file To summarise, here are the main stages of an analysis of a welding operation in Code_Aster : | 1 | A thermal analysis is carried out, which makes it possible to obtain the temperature field at each node of the mesh. | | --- | --- | | 2 | If the material considered undergoes metallurgical transformations: one carries out, as post-processing of the thermal analysis, the metallurgical analysis, which makes it possible to obtain the proportion of the various metallurgical phases (and possibly the associated hardness) at each node of the mesh. | | 3 | From the temperature field and possibly from the metallurgical phases, one carries out the mechanical analysis by choosing a constitutive model which possibly takes into account the various possible effects of the metallurgical transformations. One thus obtains the stress, strain and internal-variable fields at each Gauss point. | 3.4.3 Restrictions of Code_Aster [5] - Thermal analysis - The solution of the heat equation in a moving frame by the command THER_NON_LINE_MO U4.53.03 (useful for calibrating the heat source of an unsteady 3D thermal analysis) is available only in the case of a rectilinear path of the heat source, and not in the case of an axisymmetric path, as during the welding of cylindrical pipes for example. - It is currently impossible to define a function of more than two variables with Code_Aster , whereas the "classical" heat sources (Gaussian, double ellipsoid, CIN source) are volume or surface flux densities, functions of space and of time. If the source is a function of time (at a minimum, except if the analysis is carried out in a moving frame), only a single space parameter remains available. - Metallurgical analysis - The tempering phenomenon (which has in particular, as a consequence, a decrease in the yield stress) of the as-quenched phases is not taken into account. One can possibly work around this problem. If the number of phases formed on cooling makes it possible to leave metallurgical internal variables "free", one can then assign to these internal variables proportions of tempered phases and model the tempering kinetics by introducing a fictitious TRC. - Mechanical analysis - It would be of interest to develop, for a material comprising only a single metallurgical phase, the models equivalent to META_XXX_XXX (several phases). This currently forces one to carry out a dummy metallurgical analysis in order to benefit from these laws. This can pose, in 3D, significant problems of analysis time and of memory capacity, if for example one uses a model with kinematic hardening (one stores a tensor as an internal variable for each computation step and for each phase). 4 Methodology for the simulation The feedback cited in this part comes essentially from the following three studies: - A bevelled 316L pipe welded by the TIG process [2], with filler metal, in thirteen passes (CEA/EDF/FRAMATOME sheet 3488); the first 2 passes of this example constitute a Code_Aster test case V7.42.100; - A bevelled 316L plate welded by the TIG process [4], with filler metal, in two welding passes (CEA/EDF sheet 2425); the various command files attached to this study are stored in the Code_Aster study database (SERVICE/BDD Etudes); - An unbevelled 316L plate, with creation of a fusion line by the TIG process [3], but without filler metal (INSA Lyon thesis of L. Depradeux, defended in 2004). For simplicity, we shall subsequently name them sheet 3488, sheet 2425 and thesis L.D. 2004. 4.1 Type of modelling: 2D or 3D? In all rigour, the welding process is strictly three-dimensional, the input of heat and possibly of material being mobile and often of constant speed. The temperature and mechanical fields generated are therefore three-dimensional and transient. It is therefore preferable to carry out a three-dimensional transient analysis. However, this choice not always being possible because of the complexity, the analysis time and the memory capacity required by 3D analyses, one often resorts to a 2D modelling in the numerical simulation of welding (in particular for multipass welding with a large number of passes). Case of a 2D modelling - In the majority of cases, the 2D simulations consider a transverse section, perpendicular to the advance of the welding torch. These simulations are carried out under the plane-strain assumption; - 2D axisymmetric analyses are also adopted for the case of the welding of cylindrical pipes. - The weak point of the two preceding modellings is that one neglects the effect of the welding speed and that one assumes that the bead (or the heat) is deposited simultaneously over the whole length of the part to be welded. - Other, less classical, choices are also possible: one can choose, for example, to mesh a longitudinal section (in the welding direction) or else, if one considers that the temperatures are constant through the thickness, one can choose to mesh the mid-plane of the plate. These simulations are then carried out under the plane-stress assumption. Feedback - Sheet 3488: The analysis of the bevelled tube is carried out as axisymmetric. Comparisons between this 2D axisymmetric approach and a 3D approach have been carried out in [1] and show the good representativeness of the 2D approach, even if the latter does not take speed effects into account. - Thesis L.D. 2004: On the unbevelled plate, several modellings are tested: - Full 3D thermomechanical analysis; - 2D plane-strain analysis, in which one models a section perpendicular to the advance of the torch; - 2D plane-stress analysis, in which one models the mid-plane of the plate. One observes, in this case , that the 2D plane-strain analysis does not reproduce well the results obtained on the 3D analysis, in terms of displacements and of residual stresses, except for the latter in the central zone of the plate. As for the 2D plane-stress analysis, it gives residual-stress results very close to those of the 3D analysis. 4.2 The mesh General advice - As with any numerical study, it is always difficult to give precise values for the mesh density; this depends greatly on the physical problem considered. In the case of welding, the mesh must be sufficiently fine around the heat source (weld beads and fusion zone) in order to capture correctly the strong thermal and mechanical gradients in this zone. - In the case of a quasi-steady thermal modelling in a moving frame (cf. § 3.3.2), the speed of the analyses allows a higher mesh density, in particular around the source. - In the case of welding on steels with metallurgical phase transformations, it is necessary to mesh the HAZ sufficiently finely. This is all the more important as the stress maximum is generally reached at the periphery of the HAZ, in the partially austenitised zone. The mesh density in this zone is therefore essential. Welding simulations on a steel which presents phase transformations therefore require, a priori, meshes that are larger in number of elements than welding simulations on steels without transformations (for an identical study). - For 3D mechanical analyses, it is very important to coarsen the mechanical mesh as much as possible as one moves away from the welded zone. Indeed, the strong non-linearity of the problem (and the analysis times that go with it) and the transient aspect (requiring numerous time steps) limit in practice the number of nodes of the model. - As for any problem, it is necessary to plan, from the meshing stage, the groups intended to receive the thermal and mechanical boundary conditions (path of the source, exchange surface…), as well as the zones intended for post-processing. This is all the more true for the thermal mesh, where the loading (heat source) and the boundary conditions (convection and radiation) move as the beads are deposited. - For the fusion zone, it is often difficult to represent it because, in the absence of a macrograph, its shape is unknown. Feedback - Sheet 3488: The weld beads can be represented geometrically and meshed in a more or less complex way. There are 3 possible choices, going from the most complicated to the simplest: - One can choose to respect both the volume and the shape of the pass. The shape of the beads being curved, one will have to mesh surfaces with curved edges, and therefore use finite elements of degree at least 2; - One respects only the volume of the pass; - One respects the volume of the pass as well as possible. Comparisons have been made in [2] with these three possibilities. It turns out that the results of the mechanical analyses differ very little from one mesh to another (for an equivalent thermal analysis). In conclusion, a curved mesh brings nothing significant in terms of results compared with a polygonal mesh. It is important, on the other hand, to respect approximately the volume of the deposited beads. 4.3 Thermal analysis The critical point for the thermal part concerns the modelling of the heat input. 4.3.1 Introduction In Code_Aster , the computation of the thermal evolution is carried out by the non-linear solution of the heat equation (operator THER_NON_LINE R5.02.02) in the volume of the part, given an initial condition and thermal boundary conditions on the boundaries. The solution is transient; the heat source moves over the mesh. The diffusion of heat is treated by an enthalpic formulation, which is the integral of the specific heat with respect to temperature \beta (T)=\underset{0}{\overset{T}{\int}}\rho {C}_{p}(u)\mathrm{du} . One can therefore supply either the conductivity and the specific heat \rho {C}_{p} as a function of temperature, or, and this is preferable (cf. the note below), the conductivity and the enthalpy as a function of temperature. Note on the choice of an enthalpic formulation - At the melting temperature, the heat capacity (which is the energy to be supplied in order to raise the temperature of the body) undergoes a discontinuity which is expressed by the latent heat of fusion, which represents the energy to be supplied in order to pass the phase-change temperature. In the case of a mixture of constituents (this is the case of alloys), melting is spread between the liquidus and solidus temperatures \mathrm{Tl} and \mathrm{Ts} . An "enthalpic" formulation of the heat equation is useful for taking into account the latent-heat phenomena of phase changes. Indeed, this formulation avoids "missing" the transformation, which risks happening for the capacity formulation if the time steps are not sufficiently small. 4.3.2 Handling of the addition of material (the weld beads) Description of the various methods Several methods exist for taking into account, in the transient thermal model, the successive addition of material during the various welding passes: - The first method consists in considering only a single model (in the Code_Aster sense, defined by the command AFFE_MODELE) containing all the passes, and in artificially "deactivating" the beads not yet deposited by imposing on them a zero thermal conductivity ( {10}^{-5}W/m°C in practice). - The second method consists in nesting the thermal models (in the Code_Aster sense): a global mesh of all the beads is used, but the thermal model is assigned only on the part of the mesh corresponding to the metal already deposited (during the AFFE_MODELE stage). The beads not yet deposited are not included in the model. In this case, it is necessary to have as many thermal models as there are deposited beads. The various models are nested in one another, that is to say that thermal model I contains the passes from 1 to I and thermal model I+1 contains the passes from 1 to I and pass I+1 . This method is cleaner than the previous one, in so far as the elements not deposited do not disturb the analysis of the pass in progress, since they are not included in the model. On the other hand, this poses a problem when chaining the thermal analyses, the temperature fields of model I not being defined at all the nodes of the model corresponding to the next pass I+1 . One must therefore carry out an extension of the computed fields from one model to the other. To do this, one proceeds in 4 stages: - One begins by creating a temperature field at ambient temperature ( \mathrm{T20} ) over the whole mesh by the command CREA_CHAMP (operation 'AFFE'), - One extends the first temperature field computed at pass I (sequence number 1) by completing it with \mathrm{T20} on the new mesh cells (CREA_CHAMP, operations 'EXTR' then 'ASSE'), - One stores this field in a new data structure of type evol_ther by the command CREA_RESU, ⇒ one loops over the remaining sequence numbers and one repeats operations 2 and 3 for each sequence number, enriching the data structure created at stage 3 (keyword reuse of CREA_RESU). - Finally, the third method consists, on a single thermal model (in the Code_Aster sense), in duplicating the nodes at the interface of each bead, which must be planned for at the mesh-construction stage. When assigning the thermal loading (AFFE_CHAR_THER), one assigns only the part of the model which corresponds to the metal already present. Thus, the beads not deposited do not see the loading, and the duplication of the nodes prevents heat transfer at the interface of the beads not deposited (a temperature equal to ambient is applied in the beads not yet deposited). When a new bead is added, one reconnects the corresponding nodes by applying equality of the temperatures at the duplicated nodes, by the command LIAISON_GROUP. This method is certainly the most reliable, but construction of the mesh becomes tedious if the number of passes is large. Feedback - The advantage of the first method (a single model and an almost zero conductivity for the bead not yet deposited) is its simplicity of implementation. On the other hand, it can lead to numerical oscillations of the temperature, due to the discontinuity of the conductivity at the interfaces between the beads, as observed in sheet 3488 [2]. Nevertheless, this method is often chosen because of its simplicity. - The three methods have been tested on plate 2425 [4] and compared with experimental temperature measurements. The three analyses lead to results that are essentially identical at the measurement points. 4.3.3 Modelling of the heat source A truly complete modelling of the thermal problem would require taking into account the electro-thermo-fluid heat transfers in the electric arc, with account taken of the electromagnetic phenomena, and the modelling of the convective movements in the weld pool, in interaction with the shielding plasma, and the heat transfers in the solid part. Although an abundant literature exists concerning the taking into account of the modelling of the arc and of the weld pool in the simulation, we shall subsequently place ourselves in the perspective of modelling with an industrial analysis code, which does not make it possible to model the phenomena present in the arc and in the weld pool. These are replaced by the definition of a heat source of suitable shape. Only heat conduction is therefore modelled, which is why no further allusion will be made to the modelling of the arc and of the pool. Description of the two possible methods - The first method consists in imposing temperature cycles on the material which one deposits. These imposed temperatures can be applied either on the deposited bead alone, or on the whole formed by the deposited bead plus the fusion zone. - For simplicity, the imposed-temperature function {T}^{\mathrm{imp}} is chosen, most often, constant in space but variable in time, that is {T}^{\mathrm{imp}}={T}^{\mathrm{imp}}(x,y,z;t)={T}^{\mathrm{imp}}(t) ; - Moreover, one often imposes this temperature only on the deposited bead: indeed, the shapes and sizes of the fusion zones are rarely known, and even if they are, this makes construction of the mesh tedious, especially if the number of beads is high; - The temperature method is recommended in the case of 2D modellings, or when no data are available on the welding parameters. The function {T}^{\mathrm{imp}}(t) often has the following form: {T}^{\mathrm{imp}}(t)=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\frac{{T}^{\max}}{{t}_{1}}t+{T}^{\mathrm{ini}}& \text{si}t\le {t}_{1}\\ {T}^{\max}& \text{si}{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}\\ \text{éventuellement,}\frac{-({T}^{\max}-{T}^{\min})}{{t}_{3}-{t}_{2}}(t-{t}_{2})+{T}^{\max}& \text{si}{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{3}\end{array} One prescribes a rise from the initial temperature {T}^{\mathrm{ini}} to the melting temperature, or to a possibly higher temperature {T}^{\max} , of duration {t}_{1} (the prescribed temperature rise can be linear or non-linear, exponential for example), then a hold at this temperature for a duration ( {t}_{2}-{t}_{1} ), and finally, possibly, one can prescribe the start of cooling down to the temperature {T}^{\min} . The parameters ({t}_{1,}{t}_{2,}{t}_{3,}{T}^{\min}) can be identified if temperature measurements exist; - The remainder of the cooling takes place with exchanges by convection and radiation. - The second method consists in imposing a surface ( J/{\mathrm{sm}}^{2} ) or volume ( J/{\mathrm{sm}}^{3} ) heat flux on the modelled weld bead. - It is used preferentially when the welding energy delivered is known: this is the case for arc welding, for which one can estimate the power delivered, UI (with U the voltage and I the current). Of this delivered power, only a fraction \eta \mathrm{UI} actually penetrates the part and contributes to the heating and the melting of the materials. For the TIG process, for example, the parameter \eta is of the order of 0.6 to 0.9; - It is then possible to distribute this power, over the surface or through the volume (or both), on the mesh. The distribution of this heat flux can be extremely simple (constant in space in the deposited metal), or more elaborate (double-ellipsoid model with a Gaussian distribution, developed by J. Goldak). Calibration of the parameters of the heat source adopted requires temperature measurements. Subsequently, we detail the procedure to follow in the case of a modelling by heat flux, distinguishing the 3D and 2D simulations. One assumes that temperature data are available. Case of a 3D modelling with heat flux - We give below a few possible forms for the spatial representation of the volume or surface fluxes: - Example of a volume flux, constant along y and z and variable in the welding direction, here x . {Q}^{V}={Q}^{V}(x,y,z;t)={Q}^{V}(x;t)=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\frac{{Q}^{\max}}{L/2}x& \text{si}0\le x\le \frac{L}{2}\\ \frac{-{Q}^{\max}}{L/2}(x-L)& \text{si}\frac{L}{2}\le x\le L\end{array} - Example of a cylindrical surface flux {Q}^{S}={Q}^{S}(x,y;t) , with circular base of radius R and maximum intensity {Q}^{\max} . - When temperature measurements are available, the parameters of this heat input (sizes, values of the maximum power injected) can be calibrated so as to reproduce as well as possible, by analysis, the measured thermal cycles. - This calibration stage can be carried out easily and with short analysis times by means of a quasi-steady analysis in a moving frame (THER_NON_LINE_MO). This assumes that the path of the source is rectilinear and uniform, at constant speed. In this case, one assumes that a steady regime is established, and the heat equation written in this frame becomes independent of time. One therefore obtains the temperature field in this frame (a function of space only). One can possibly recover the time dimension by a change of variable ( X=x–\mathrm{V.t} ). One can therefore rapidly (a single time step) identify the parameters of the source, which are then reused in the case of the transient analysis. - Once the identification has been carried out, and if the power of the welding process is known, one will be able to deduce from it the value of the parameter \eta in the net power (in order to check the consistency of the value obtained with respect to the process). Indeed, the integral of the volume (respectively surface) density of heat flux over the chosen volume (respectively the chosen surface) must be equal to the net power, that is \underset{V}{\int}{Q}^{V}(x,y,z;t)\mathrm{dv}=\eta \mathrm{UI}\text{et}\underset{S}{\int}{Q}^{S}(x,y,z;t)\mathrm{ds}=\eta \mathrm{UI} In the two examples presented above, this gives: - Example of the volume flux: S\underset{0}{\overset{L}{\int}}{Q}^{V}(x;t)\mathrm{dx}=S\ast \frac{L}{2}\ast {Q}^{\max}=\eta \mathrm{UI} where S is the surface of the deposited bead perpendicular to the welding direction. - Example of the surface flux: \underset{S}{\int}{Q}^{S}(x,y,z;t)\mathrm{ds}=\pi \ast {R}^{2}\ast {Q}^{\max}=\eta \mathrm{UI} . - The heat flux having been identified spatially, one must now implement the displacement of this source over the mesh for the transient thermal analysis. One thus defines a function of the welding direction, here x , and of time, by the operator DEFI_NAPPE: a flux as a function of time is applied successively on the mesh cells located under the path of the welding torch, considering a rise to the maximum value, followed by a descent to zero. The descent of the flux on one mesh cell corresponds to the rise of the flux on the next adjacent mesh cell. Thus the sources are "switched on" successively along the welding axis during the passage of the torch, which corresponds to a heat source of constant intensity travelling in space along the welding axis. Case of a 2D modelling with heat flux - In the case of a 2D modelling, the approach is different, because one must choose a flux (volume or surface) which varies in time, in order to take into account, in the 2D analysis, the approach and the moving away of the torch. For the spatial distribution of this flux, one often chooses a flux that is constant in space. An example of a surface flux is given below: {Q}_{r}={Q}_{r}(x,y,z;t)={Q}_{r}(x;t)=\lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\frac{{Q}^{\max}}{{t}_{1}}t& \text{si}t\le {t}_{1}\\ {Q}^{\max}& \text{si}{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}\\ -{Q}^{\max}\frac{(t-{t}_{2})}{({t}_{3}-{t}_{2})}& \text{si}{t}_{2}\le t\le {t}_{3}\end{array} - Here again, one will have to identify, from temperature measurements, the parameters of the chosen flux (in our example, the time instants {t}_{1} , {t}_{2} and {t}_{3} , as well as the value {Q}^{\max} ). - If one knows the power delivered by the process, one can also deduce from it the parameter \eta . This gives, for our example: \underset{t}{\int}\left\lbrace \underset{S}{\int}{Q}_{r}(t)\mathrm{ds}\right\rbrace =S\underset{t}{\int}{Q}_{r}(t)\mathrm{dt}=\frac{\eta \mathrm{UI}}{V}\iff \underset{t}{\int}{Q}_{r}(t)\mathrm{dt}=\frac{\eta \mathrm{UI}}{\mathrm{SV}} which gives: \underset{t}{\int}{Q}_{r}(t)\mathrm{dt}={Q}^{\max}\ast \frac{1}{2}({t}_{3}+{t}_{2}-{t}_{1})=\frac{\eta \mathrm{UI}}{\mathrm{SV}} where V is the known welding speed and S the known surface of the deposited bead. In order to refine the identification of the parameters of the source, one can use the parameter eta found by a quasi-steady 3D analysis in a moving frame. Feedback - INSA thesis L.D. 2004: - For the transient 3D modelling of the plate, several forms of surface flux were tested: triangular in the welding direction, cylindrical with a circular base, and Gaussian. For these three fluxes, the temperature distribution proved to be approximately identical. - For the 2D modelling (plane strain), three representations were tested: imposed temperature, surface flux and volume flux, with identification of the parameters on measurements. Only the modelling with imposed temperature led to melting of the deposited metal. With a volume flux, the fusion zone was not reproduced. - Sheet 3488: The imposed-temperature approach was used on the axisymmetric analysis of the tube. The results of this simulation show that the analyses overestimate the fusion zone and the maxima of the thermal cycles. The imposed-temperature approach is therefore too energetic, and it is the flux approach which is recommended for this study. 4.3.4 Thermal boundary conditions with the environment The thermal boundary conditions are modelled by convective and radiative exchanges of the welded part with the environment, which are written: -\lambda \frac{\partial T}{\partial n}=h(T-{T}_{\mathrm{air}})+\varepsilon \sigma ({T}^{4}-{T}_{\mathrm{air}}^{4}) where n is the outward normal, h the convective exchange coefficient, \sigma the Stefan–Boltzmann constant and \varepsilon the emissivity of the material. Notes - In the case of the welding of relatively thick parts, the values taken for the exchange coefficient and the emissivity often have only a secondary influence on the thermal analyses: indeed, the heat flux exchanged with the ambient air during heating and on cooling is very small compared with the heat flux by conduction in the part coming from the heat input. - In the immediate vicinity of the source, the flux emitted by radiation is not negligible in reality, but the corresponding unknowns can be integrated into the definition of the size and of the distribution of the heat source. - The thermal problem therefore reduces, most often, to a purely conductive problem, and not taking the radiative and convective exchanges with the environment into account is not essential. 4.3.5 Thermophysical characteristics The thermophysical properties appearing in the heat equation are functions of temperature. They are the thermal conductivity \lambda (T) and the specific heat \rho {C}_{p} , or the enthalpy. Notes - As regards the thermal conductivity, it is sometimes customary to increase it artificially for temperatures higher than the melting temperature, so as to "take into account" the convective phenomena inside the pool and to homogenise the temperature of the latter. In the literature, the conductivity is thus increased by a factor of 2, 10 or 100 according to the authors (this is what is done for tube 3488, with a factor of 100). In practice, it is often reasonable to take a conductivity that is constant from the melting temperature onwards, and one considers that it is not necessary to increase it artificially, given that the unknowns concerning the weld pool (convective phenomena, and so on) are included in the definition of an ad hoc heat source. - During welding, the latent heat of fusion (cf. the note of paragraph 3.3.1) is small compared with the heat input coming from the process, and it is not necessarily useful to take it into account. Moreover, this latent heat of fusion can also be included implicitly in the definition of the heat input. 4.4 Metallurgical analysis The critical point for the metallurgical part concerns, essentially, the knowledge of experimental data, in order to identify the metallurgical constitutive models correctly. 4.4.1 Introduction In this part, one is interested only in steel-type material, in particular 16MND5, which can comprise five different metallurgical phases: ferrite, pearlite, bainite and martensite, called the cold phase or \alpha , and austenite, called the hot phase or \gamma . When one heats a material, the \alpha phases transform into the \gamma phase. When one cools the material, the austenite transforms, according to the cooling rate, into ferrite and/or pearlite and/or bainite and/or martensite. One must therefore define, for heating, the kinetics of the transformation \alpha \to \gamma and, for cooling, the nature and the kinetics of the possible transformations \gamma \to \alpha . The metallurgical phases present therefore depend on the temperature and on the temperature rate. The computation of these phases is carried out as post-processing of a mechanical analysis, by the command CALC_META. One must specify in this command the initial metallurgical state. 4.4.2 Constitutive models on heating and on cooling Currently in Code_Aster , for steel-type materials, there exists only a single constitutive model making it possible to compute, at each time step, the proportions of the various phases. Nevertheless, this model is different on heating and on cooling. The detailed expression of the kinetics on heating and on cooling will be found in R4.04.01. 4.4.3 Thermal => Metallurgical interaction As we have already specified previously, there is no coupling between the thermal and metallurgical analyses. Now, the thermophysical properties (conductivity, specific heat or enthalpy) of the material point depend on the proportions of the various phases present: if this is in general not too detrimental with respect to the mechanical predictions, it can be so for a fine prediction of the final metallurgy (but this is not, in general, the objective of a numerical simulation of welding). 4.5 Mechanical analysis The critical points for the mechanical part concern the choice of the constitutive law and the identification of the parameters of this law. 4.5.1 Principle of the mechanical analysis The mechanical analysis is carried out by solution of the equilibrium equations (operator STAT_NON_LINE), taking into account the dependence of the mechanical properties with respect to temperature and, possibly, to the proportions of the metallurgical phases. 4.5.2 Handling of the addition of material (the weld beads) In mechanics, two methods exist for handling the addition of material, equivalent in principle to those of the thermal analysis. - One can consider a single mechanical model comprising all the beads, in which the nodes at the interface between beads are duplicated. When a new bead is added, one assigns interface conditions bearing on the displacement increment (LIAISON_DDL). Just as in the thermal analysis, this method is certainly the most reliable, but construction of the mesh becomes tedious if the number of passes is high. There is no recent feedback on this method. - The method most commonly used in mechanics is that in which one has a single mechanical model for all the passes, the elements not yet present being artificially deactivated by assignment of a "quasi-zero" Young's modulus ( E={10}^{-11}.E(20°C) in practice). The value of Young's modulus to assign in the metal not deposited results from a compromise: if the value is too high, stresses will be generated in the metal not yet deposited, but if it is too low, this can lead to convergence problems. 4.5.3 Constitutive law In Code_Aster , various constitutive laws exist for describing the non-linear behaviour of a material (isotropic, kinematic or mixed hardening, viscous effect, …). The user will find in document U4.51.11 the inventory of these models. Given that these models are not specific to welding simulations alone, we shall not describe them. Note Nevertheless, we can cite the mechanical models with the effect of the structural transformations, which have been developed for steels such as 16MND5, and especially within the framework of welding activities. These models, which are described in detail in documents R4.04.02 and R4.04.03, make it possible to model the following phenomena: plastic behaviour or viscous behaviour, linear or non-linear isotropic hardening or linear kinematic hardening, transformation plasticity, recovery of hardening of metallurgical origin, recovery of hardening of viscous origin. One can carry out an analysis in small strains but also in large strains, either with the option PETIT_REAC or with the option SIMO_MIEHE (the models with kinematic hardening do not exist with SIMO_MIEHE). The two important questions concerning the choice of the constitutive law are: - Must one take into account the viscous effects, because of the high temperatures generated during welding? - Which type of hardening must one consider (isotropic, kinematic or mixed)? This question is important in welding, because this process involves tension and compression cycles. The viscous effects are often neglected, essentially because of the lack of experimental data. A plastic model can then be sufficient if its identification is carried out from tests in which the loading rate is close to that encountered in the structure studied [6]. Otherwise, it is preferable to take a viscous model, especially if one wishes to simulate a loading of stress-relief type. As regards the type of hardening, it has been observed in [3], [4] and [6] that a model with isotropic hardening generally leads to a very high final stress level (compared with measurements). The final maximum stress level will be all the higher as the tension–compression plastic cycles are numerous. That is why, the higher the number of passes modelled, the higher will be the residual stresses predicted by a modelling with isotropic hardening. One can attenuate this result by using isotropic hardening with recovery of viscous origin, which compensates the effect of the isotropic hardening. Conversely, a model with kinematic hardening tends to underestimate the residual stresses. The real behaviour of the material is often a combination of the two hardenings. 4.5.4 Note on large strains Taking large strains into account is in general not indispensable for a welding simulation on thick structures. On the other hand, if the structures are thin (large distortions), it is necessary to take them into account. In Code_Aster , two possibilities exist for taking large strains into account in the operator STAT_NON_LINE: - The option PETIT_REAC, suited when the rotations are small; - The option SIMO_MIEHE, for an exact formulation of large strains, but restricted to models with isotropic hardening. 4.5.5 Boundary conditions Feedback - Sheet 3488: The axisymmetric modelling of welding on the tube implicitly, and wrongly, assumes that welding takes place simultaneously over the whole circumference of the tube, and therefore that the temperature rises everywhere in the bevel. In reality, the heat source advances towards a part of the structure which has remained cold, which necessarily restrains the welded zone. The part, at the location of the heat source, cannot therefore expand freely. This self-restraint effect must fade when the heat diffuses, and disappear during the cooling phase. To remedy this problem, one can impose an axial restraint on the tube, only during the heating phase. One thus prevents the tube from expanding freely on heating; on the other hand, it is free to deform on cooling. 4.6 Analysis time One observes (in version STA9), through the various welding studies carried out in recent years, that most of the analysis time is consumed in the mechanical analysis. To give an order of magnitude, we give two examples below: - Test case HTNA100A, which considers a bevelled tube welded in two passes by the TIG process (the so-called sheet 3488): - Number of nodes = 3632 - Modelling: axisymmetric - CPU time of the thermal analysis = 307 s - CPU time of the metallurgical analysis = 25 s - CPU time of the mechanical analysis = 5169 s - Study on a bevelled plate welded in two passes by the TIG process (the so-called sheet 2425) - Number of nodes = 11600 - Modelling: 3D - CPU time of the thermal analysis = 951 s - CPU time of the mechanical analysis = 64601 s Notes - The possible metallurgical analysis costs nothing in analysis time, because it consists only in integrating the constitutive models; there are no equilibrium equations to solve. - The mechanical time could certainly be improved if one considered (during the solution of the mechanical equilibrium equations by the operator STAT_NON_LINE), in the prediction phase, the dependence of Young's modulus, and perhaps of the coefficient of thermal expansion, with respect to temperature. Currently, only the thermal strain (in fact its derivative) is taken into account in the right-hand side. - The mechanical part being a strongly non-linear problem, it is often necessary to use line search in the STAT_NON_LINE module in order to facilitate convergence. Moreover, a time-step subdivision adapted to the evolution of the temperatures makes it possible to facilitate convergence.

u2.03.06 Carrying out a civil-engineering study with prestressing cables u2.03.06 Carrying out a civil-engineering study with prestressing cables > Summary. The aim of this document is to give advice for carrying out studies of reinforced concrete with prestressing cables, using the dedicated features (DEFI_CABLE_BP/CALC_PRECONT). It gives information on the precautions for meshing, on the ways of applying the prestress, and on the possibilities of phasing. 1 Introduction Civil-engineering studies are often fairly complex to carry out, in so far as they involve \mathrm{3D} modellings, shells, bars and several materials. This document tries to pool the experience acquired on the subject by giving methodological advice for the mesh and for the modelling stage, as regards prestressed structures. The numerical implementation of the tension requires a few usual precautions, in particular in the case of non-linear analyses, since the chronology of the loadings can affect the results. In this document, we see how to set up the commands in order to reproduce a few examples of situations that can be envisaged in reality. For a more visual presentation, the materials of the training course "Code_Aster/salome_meca Module 4: Civil engineering" can also be consulted ( 02-Modeling of the prestressed reinforced structures _) and an application in the form of practical work, accessible via the test FORMA42. 2 Preliminary note In Code_Aster , two types of modelling exist for describing prestress. - The first method is suited to describing bonded prestress . In this case, the prestressing cables are represented by 1D elements with the modelling BARRE. The prestress can be applied easily via the operators DEFI_CABLE_BP and AFFE_CHAR_MECA, which make it possible to estimate the initial tension profile (N), variable along the cable, according to the regulatory formulae (BPEL or ETCC), and to transform it into a loading. - The second method (less proven) is suited to describing unbonded prestress (typically the TGG). In this case, the prestressing cables are represented by \mathrm{1D} elements with the modelling CABLE_GAINE. Tensioning of the cable is obtained by simulating the process of tensioning the cable via the operator CALC_PRECONT, assuming that the cables slide with a friction of Coulomb-law type. 3 First stage: the mesh To carry out an analysis on a prestressed reinforced-concrete structure, it is necessary to mesh the concrete, the reinforcements and the prestressing cables. - The mesh of the concrete can be produced with any volume element in \mathrm{3D} or in \mathrm{2D} . In 3D , the elements can be linear or quadratic. If a shell-type modelling is chosen, the elements will be linear. - The reinforcements can be represented: - either individually; in this case, they will necessarily be meshed with \mathit{SEG2} (linear elements) whose nodes are common with those of the concrete. One must therefore think of this when meshing the concrete. Moreover, one must be careful if the concrete is meshed with quadratic elements, so as to match properly all the concrete nodes located along the reinforcement with a steel node: in other words, if the concrete is meshed with quadratic elements, at the place where a reinforcement must pass, one must define 2 steel \mathit{SEG2} for one concrete mesh cell; - or in a distributed manner, in the form of a surface whose nodes are the same as the nodes of the concrete. The mesh cells may equally well be triangles or quadrangles, linear or quadratic. One must therefore take care to identify this surface at the time of meshing the concrete, and to duplicate the mesh cells in order to define the steel layer (via Transformation → Duplication Nodes/Elements in salome_meca ). If there are several layers of reinforcement, these elements will have to be duplicated as many times as necessary. - The prestressing cables must be meshed with one-dimensional elements. If the modelling BARRE is used, these elements will be \mathit{SEG}2 ; if the modelling CABLE_GAINE is used, these elements will be \mathit{SEG}3 . Whatever the modelling, it is not necessary to make the nodes of the cable coincide with the concrete nodes: the command DEFI_CABLE_BP indeed makes it possible to create the kinematic relations which will link the nodes of the cable with the nodes of the concrete of the surrounding mesh cell. One must, on the other hand, take care to have a similar level of discretisation for the concrete and the steel, so as to have, as far as possible, one steel node in each concrete mesh cell (so that all the elements see the cable) and to avoid having several steel nodes in one concrete mesh cell (in order to avoid weighing the problem down with unnecessary Lagrange multipliers). The anchorage nodes having to be defined for each cable, it is necessary to have created node groups for each end of the cables. 4 Second stage: data setup of the problem The various stages of the data setup of a typical prestressed-concrete problem in Code_Aster are detailed here, for the two types of modelling. For each stage, the possible questions to be asked and the information which must be supplied are specified. In the case of the modelling BARRE, an example of application is proposed in the appendix, where the various variants for the solution stage are given. 4.1 Reading and possible enrichments of the mesh - Check that the anchorage nodes are indeed accessible (individually) through a GROUP_NO. - Create any node groups or mesh-cell groups for post-processing. If one wishes to post-process the tensions in prestressing cables, one must remember to order the nodes of the corresponding node group (option 'SEGM_DROI_ORDO' or 'NOEUD_ORDO' in DEFI_GROUP/CREA_GROUP_NO). - Orient correctly the mesh-cell groups on which loadings of pressure or flux type are imposed (command ORIE_PEAU_3D (2D)). 4.2 Assignment of a model - For the reinforcements In the case of a 3D modelling, the reinforcements will be modelled by BARRE elements if they have been represented by line elements, or by GRILLE_MEMBRANE or MEMBRANE elements if they have been represented by surface elements. In the case of a plate-type modelling (DKT, Q4GG), one must use the modelling GRILLE_EXCENTREE. - For the prestressing cables For bonded cables, the model BARRE (based on \mathit{SEG}2 ) will be used. For unbonded cables, the model CABLE_GAINE (based on \mathit{SEG}3 ) will be used. 4.3 Characteristics of the structural elements In AFFE_CARA_ELEM, define: - for the passive reinforcements, either their cross-section (BARRE), or the cross-section and the orientation of the layer (GRILLE) - for the prestressing cables, define the cross-section (BARRE). 4.4 Definition of the materials Various types of law are available, according to the phenomena which one wishes to take into account (elasticity, damage, creep, …). Summary tables giving the main characteristics of each of them are available in u2.03.07. The choice of the law determines the keywords to be entered under DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01. In the presence of cables, and in order to be able to use DEFI_CABLE_BP, one must also have entered, in addition to the parameters linked to the constitutive law used, and according to the regulation used (BPEL or ETCC): - for the concrete, either the keyword BPEL_BETON, entering if necessary the losses by creep PERT_FLUA and the losses due to shrinkage PERT_RETR, or the keyword ETCC_BETON(); - for the steel of the prestressing cables, either the keyword BPEL_ACIER, entering the rupture stress F_PRG, the friction coefficient on the straight part FROT_LINE and on the curved part FROT_COURB, the relaxation coefficient MU0_RELAX, and the relaxation of the steel at 1000 hours RELAX_1000, or the keyword ETCC_ACIER. In this case, the data to be supplied are the rupture stress F_PRG, the friction coefficient COEF_FROT, the in-line loss coefficient PERT_LIGNE, and the relaxation of the steel at 1000 hours RELAX_1000. All these parameters are optional. Notes: 1. The parameter F_PRG does not come into play in a possible non-linear analysis with plasticity of the cables; it serves only to compute the loss by relaxation. In order to allow an analysis with yielding, the yield stress must be declared with the constitutive law chosen. 2. The command DEFI_CABLE_BP cannot consider the case in which the elastic characteristics of the concrete crossed by the cable may vary with temperature. 3. The command DEFI_CABLE_BP can support the case in which a cable crosses several concrete materials. All the concretes must however have the same properties with respect to the BPEL or ETCC, that is to say the same properties under the keyword BPEL_BETON or ETCC_BETON. Case of unbonded cables: When the modelling CABLE_GAINE is used, the user must also enter the friction law which is to be used, via the keyword CABLE_GAINE_FROT. The choice is logically of type 'FROTTANT', which implies entering the friction coefficients on the straight line and on the curve. The user also has, however, the possibility of choosing the option 'ADHERENT', in order to make comparisons easily between the two behaviours (results equivalent to the modelling BARRE), or the option 'GLISSANT', which makes it possible to avoid the possible convergence difficulties linked to friction. 4.5 Definition of the cables The stage of definition of the cables goes through the command DEFI_CABLE_BP. This makes it possible to define what the tension in the cables must be according to the rules of the BPEL/ETCC, as a function of the initial tension, of the anchorage draw-in (which applies only for the active anchorages), of the relaxation of the steel and of the delayed strains of the concrete (creep and shrinkage). Let us note that a single DEFI_CABLE_BP can group several cables, provided that they have the same input parameters for the computation of the tension, and that one wishes to tension all these cables simultaneously. This is in general preferable from the point of view of performance. In order to facilitate the data setup and to avoid resorting to Python macros, it is possible to define the cables via a table defined in an external file (cf. SSNV229A). If the user has chosen to model unbonded cables (FROTTANT or GLISSANT), one should specify in DEFI_CABLE_BP, ADHERENT='NON'. The punching created by the anchorages can sometimes give rise to numerical modelling difficulties. The origin of this problem is linked to the incompatibility of the loading mode (a point force created by the anchorage) with respect to the mesh of the concrete ( \mathrm{2D} or \mathrm{3D} ). To avoid this problem, the keyword CONE under DEFI_CABLE_BP makes it possible to define a volume representing the dispersion cone placed at the end of the cables, and thus to distribute the punching force over a volume of the concrete, and no longer over one or a few nodes. The geometry of this volume corresponds to a cylinder whose dimensions (length and radius) should ideally correspond to the dispersion cone actually employed. It must be noted, however, that if the mesh of the concrete in this region is not sufficiently fine, the volume of the cone will not include any additional nodes and the problem will not be modified. Overlap of the cones is also not possible. The option CONE cannot be activated in the case of unbonded cables. Notes: 1. Each cable end can be declared as being "active" or "passive". If a cable has no active end, no tension is then applied. 2. Use of the option CONE requires particular attention as to the way of imposing the boundary conditions, on pain of seeing redundant kinematic conditions appear which prevent solution of the problem. 4.6 Definition of the loadings 4.6.1 Case of bonded cables Two variants exist for carrying out the tensioning. The first method consists in applying the prestress directly, in the form of an initial tension in the cables, as a loading with STAT_NON_LINE. The loading is instantaneous. Its drawback is that the tension which results from equilibrium is generally lower than that requested by the user, because of the elastic strain of the concrete under the effect of the prestress. The second method is an improvement on the first and is based on the macro-command CALC_PRECONT, which encompasses a certain number of manipulations of the model in order to ensure the tensioning (cf. R7.01.02). By using this operator, the tension at equilibrium is exactly that requested (that is to say, that computed by the regulatory formulae); it also allows the successive tensioning of the cables, in order to recreate the phasing of the prestressing of the structure. Finally, the last advantage of this method is the possibility of applying the cable tension gradually, which may be necessary for behaviours of non-linear type, in particular in the event of cracking of the concrete during the prestressing stage. Basic method: STAT_NON_LINE In addition to the boundary conditions and the various loadings, it is sufficient to create a loading linked to the cables via the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA, including the loadings linked to the tension and those linked to the kinematic relations between the steel and the concrete, that is: CHCAB=AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=MO,RELA_CINE_BP=_F(CABLE_BP=CAB_BP3, SIGM_BPEL='OUI',RELA_CINE='OUI',),). However, if the user envisages chaining several STAT_NON_LINE, this loading will have to be duplicated, including only the kinematic relations (SIGM_BPEL='NON', RELA_CINE='OUI'). This loading will be used from the second call to STAT_NON_LINE onwards. Recommended method: CALC_PRECONT In addition to the boundary conditions and the various loadings, one must define the loadings linked to the cables, which must include only the kinematic relations, that is: CHCAB=AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=MO,RELA_CINE_BP=_F(CABLE_BP=CAB_BP3, SIGM_BPEL='NON',RELA_CINE='OUI',),). These loadings will be used: - for any analysis with STAT_NON_LINE during the stages prior to tensioning (for example, if one simulates a creep stage) - for the stages subsequent to tensioning (otherwise the analysis stops in fatal error because of a matrix which cannot be factorised), whether the analysis is done with STAT_NON_LINE or with CALC_PRECONT. One must therefore remember to define as many loadings as there are different tensioning stages. 4.6.2 Case of unbonded cables The instructions are the same as for the bonded case with CALC_PRECONT. On the other hand, one must also plan to create additional loadings making it possible to block the sliding at the anchorage nodes of the cables once they have been tensioned. That is: CGLIS =AFFE_CHAR_MECA( MODELE=MO, > DDL_IMPO=( _F(GROUP_NO=('PC1D','PC1F'), > GLIS=0.0,),) Version 15.2.5 5 Solution of the mechanical problem The last stage consists in solving the mechanical problem. It proceeds differently according to the method employed and to whether phasing is taken into account. This chapter details how to proceed for each of the choices, specifying the loadings to be included (keyword EXCIT) when calling CALC_PRECONT or STAT_NON_LINE. 5.1 Bonded cables tensioned with CALC_PRECONT Three cases are possible: | 1 | The user wishes to tension simultaneously all the prestressing cables, as well as an instantaneous loading, without any other loadings beforehand. In this case, it is sufficient to call the macro-command CALC_PRECONT only once. The loading is composed of the boundary conditions and of any instantaneous loadings (no loading concerning the cables). Under the keyword CABLE_BP, one will include all the DEFI_CABLE_BP concepts (see scenario 3 in the appendix). | | --- | --- | | 2 | The user wishes to carry out analyses before the tensioning of the cables. In this case, one should: either deactivate the cables in the model by assigning them the constitutive law RELATION='SANS' under the keyword COMPORTEMENT of STAT_NON_LINE. In this case, the stiffness of the cables is zero. It is also indispensable to add to the loadings the kinematic relations linking cable and concrete (loading obtained by writing AFFE_CHAR_MECA(RELA_CINE_BP=_F(RELA_CINE='OUI'))) (see scenarios 1 and 3 in the appendix). or not include the cables in the model used to carry out the analyses before the tensioning of the cables (which is more tedious, since one must work with 2 models). | | 3 | The user wishes to tension the cables successively. In this case, CALC_PRECONT must be called as many times as necessary. CABLE_BP will contain the DEFI_CABLE_BP concepts associated with the cables which one is in the process of tensioning during this call to CALC_PRECONT. CABLE_BP_INACTIF will contain those which one wishes to tension later. In this way, it is the macro-command which takes care of assigning a constitutive law SANS to these cables and of including the kinematic relations associated with these same cables. For the loading, the boundary conditions must be included systematically, as well as any instantaneous loadings. From the second call to CALC_PRECONT onwards, one should in addition include the kinematic relations linked to the cables already tensioned at the previous stages (see scenario 1 in the Appendix). | In every case, for the STAT_NON_LINE which follow the tensioning of the cables, it is important not to forget the whole set of kinematic relations linked to the cables. 5.2 Bonded cables tensioned with STAT_NON_LINE If the user does not wish to use CALC_PRECONT in order to tension the prestressing cables, it is possible to resort to the former method of tensioning the cables, despite its drawbacks R7.01.02. Tensioning is carried out simply by including in the loads the concept AFFE_CHAR_MECA defined by RELA_CINE_BP = F(RELA_CINE = 'OUI', SIGM_BPEL='OUI'). At the end of this analysis, the tension in the cables is no longer equal to that prescribed by the BPEL. Nevertheless, it is possible to determine a multiplicative coefficient (of the order of ten percent) to be applied to the initial tensions applied to the cables (at the level of the declaration of the operator DEFI_CABLE_BP), making it possible to compensate globally for the losses by instantaneous strain of the structure. Once the command file has been modified by these correction coefficients, the modelling of the prestressing cables is complete. Warning: in the case of a chaining of STAT_NON_LINE, one should, from the second call onwards, include in the loading only the kinematic relations and not the tension in the cables, on pain of adding this tension at each analysis (see scenario 2 in the appendix). This therefore requires creating a second AFFE_CHAR_MECA with the operand RELA_CINE_BP = F(RELA_CINE = 'OUI', SIGM_BPEL='NON') (cf. scenario 2 in the Appendix). 5.3 Unbonded cables tensioned with CALC_PRECONT The instructions are identical to the case of bonded cables. Two specific points should nevertheless be noted. 1. The constitutive law for the cable is no longer simply elastic, but: - RELATION = 'KIT_CG', RELATION_KIT =('ELAS','CABLE_GAINE_FROT'), 'ELAS' may be replaced by 'SANS' when the cable must not take part in the analysis. - Once the cables have been tensioned, the loading which blocks the sliding of the anchorage nodes must be added (cf. § 4.6.2). It is recommended to rely on the test case SSNV164D. 6 Particular cases: relaxation of the cables and rupture of the cables 6.1 Relaxation of the cables To model the relaxation of the cables, two options are possible, but only in the case of bonded cables (modelling BARRE and not CABLE_GAINE): use the regulatory formulae, or use a viscoelastic law for the cables. - When the regulatory formulae (BPEL or ETCC) are used, the losses by relaxation are computed at a given date. This is therefore to be used with caution when a non-linear analysis is carried out. - For relaxation, the ETCC formula requires knowledge of the state of tension in the cable after the instantaneous losses have been taken into account: the analysis must therefore be done in 2 stages. Refer to the test case SSNV229B for an example. The user also has the possibility of using a simplified version: this is the option TYPE_RELAXATION='ETCC_DIRECT' (as opposed to TYPE_RELAXATION='ETCC_REPRISE'). The test SSNV229A implements this option. - For a fully non-linear analysis, it is sufficient to assign to the prestressing cable (modelling BARRE) the constitutive law RELAX_ACIER (cf. R5.03.09 and test SSNL143 for further details). 6.2 Rupture of the cables To simulate the rupture of a bonded cable, one must take care that the mesh is sufficiently refined for there indeed to be only one cable per concrete mesh cell. If one assumes that the tension is zero throughout the cable, it is sufficient to call CALC_PRECONT again, having defined a new DEFI_CABLE_BP with the cable or cables concerned and having defined a zero tension. If one assumes that the cable is re-anchored, then it is possible to enter the profile of one's choice. The proposed sequence is as follows: - carrying out the initial tensioning analysis - recovery of the tension in the cable(s) concerned: CALC_CHAMP/POST_RELEVE_T - modification of the tensions in the table by means of a formula defined by the user - creation of the concept DEFI_CABLE_BP by defining the cable by means of the factor keyword MODI_CABLE_RUPT - new application of the prestress by means of CALC_PRECONT. The test SSNV229C provides an example. Warning: given the modelling assumptions, the responses obtained are rather qualitative and must not be examined in a very local manner. 7 Post-processing For the bonded cases, it is possible to recover the tension profile in the cable computed according to the regulatory formulae, via the command: TAB_1_I=RECU_TABLE(CO=CAB_BP, NOM_TABLE='CABLE_BP',) After tensioning of the cables, it is of course possible to plot the tension profile at several time instants, by means of the commands POST_RELEVE_T/RECU_FONCTION/IMPR_FONCTION. An example is present in the test FORMA42. 8 List of the verification/validation test cases | Test name | Type of structure | Type of validation | | --- | --- | --- | | | | | | SSNV137/ ZZZZ305 | 3D beam subjected to bending-compression by a prestressing cable | DEFI_CABLE_BP (BPEL) + STAT_NON_LINE in 3D | | ZZZZ344 | 3D cylinder with 1 cable | Computation of the angular deviations in DEFI_CABLE_BP | | SSNV229 | 3D cylinder with 10 prestressing cables | Validation of the ETCC formulae | | SSLV115 | 3D prestressed-concrete element (BARRE or CABLE_GAINE for the cable) | Verification of the gravity analyses + validation of CALC_PRECONT in 3D | | SSNV164/ FORMA42 | 3D double beam with 5 prestressing cables | Validation of the prestressing phasing (comparison with CASTEM) + option CONE (SSNV164B) | | ZZZZ347 | Half-ring in 3D with one prestressing cable | Validation of the CABLE_GAINE elements for describing cables with friction. | | | | | | ZZZZ111 | Half-cylinder with 4 prestressing cables | Validation of DEFI_CABLE_BP with shell elements (DKT and Q4GG) | | SSNP108 | Plate with 1 prestressing cable (compression) | Validation of the equilibrium analysis with STAT_NON_LINE with the shells | | SSNP109 | Beam subjected to bending-compression by a prestressing cable (DKT) | Validation of the equilibrium analysis with STAT_NON_LINE | | SSLS137 | Plate with 1 prestressing cable (bending) | Validation of CALC_PRECONT with the shells | | | | | | ARCAD01 | Current portion of a containment | Test used for the industry-specific tool ARCADE | 9 Appendix Here is a commented application example, taken from the training practical work FORMA42 available in the list of test cases V6.04.165. u2.03.07 Overview of the tools available for carrying out structural analyses of civil-engineering concrete u2.03.07 Overview of the tools available for carrying out structural analyses of civil-engineering concrete > Summary. The aim of this document is to provide an overview of the modelling possibilities open to the user according to the type of analysis he or she wishes to carry out in civil engineering. Several choices are always possible, and the purpose of this document is not to take the place of the engineer's own analysis, but rather to make it easier to choose the modelling options, according to the tools available, and to direct the user towards more specific documents. 1 Introduction Behind the words “civil-engineering analysis” lie both analyses of structures whose dimensions and characteristics are very varied (specimen, beam, building, ...) but, above all, analyses whose purpose or the information sought are very different: design of a structure, prediction of long-term ageing, study of the cracking risk, verification of the seismic resistance of a structure, reassessment of the margins. It is up to the modeller to find the best compromise between the complexity, the cost of the study and the accuracy or the representativeness of the results sought, by correctly choosing the type of analysis, the finite-element modelling and the constitutive models, given that a wide choice is available in Code_Aster. 1.1 The type of analysis to be carried out The choice of the operators is made according to the type of phenomenon modelled (thermal, hydraulic, mechanical...) and the type of information sought (local or global information, steady state or study of the transient, ...), the type of loading (static, dynamic), and the non-linearities to be modelled (constitutive behaviour, large strains, loading, ...). The choice must be made from among the following operators: - a linear thermal analysis (THER_LINEAIRE) R5.02.01 in order to estimate the temperature of the concrete in the linear cases; - a non-linear thermal analysis (THER_NON_LINE R5.02.02), when the properties or the boundary conditions are not linear, but also in order to model the thermo-hydration of the concrete or the evolution of drying (under the effect of the moisture gradient); - a linear static analysis (MECA_STATIQUE U4.51.01) in the cases where the concrete is considered elastic and in the absence of any non-linearity; - a non-linear static analysis (STAT_NON_LINE, R5.03.01), as soon as one wants to take into account non-linearities of constitutive behaviour (creep, damage, ...) or of loading (prestress, contact, ...); - a thermomechanical analysis, by chaining a thermal analysis (linear or not) solved with THER_LINEAIRE or THER_NON_LINE and a static analysis (linear or not) solved with MECA_STATIQUE or STAT_NON_LINE; - a coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical analysis of porous-medium type, accessible via STAT_NON_LINE, in particular in order to study the exchanges of water or of gas through a concrete wall (cf. R7.01.10 and R7.01.11); - a vibratory dynamics analysis with the operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03, which may be of transient or harmonic type, on a physical basis or on a modal basis, with the possibility of taking into account certain localised non-linearities of shock or friction type. The operator DYNA_LINE U4.53.05 is also available and makes it possible to call on the same features as DYNA_VIBRA without having to concern oneself with the matrix-assembly stages. Moreover, with DYNA_LINE, the construction of a relevant projection basis for the solution of the problem on a generalised basis is carried out automatically by the operator from the information supplied. - an analysis of spectral-method type by modal synthesis COMB_SISM_MODAL R4.05.03, in order to compute the dynamic response to single or multiple imposed motions and to design a structure; - a direct transient dynamic analysis with DYNA_NON_LINE R5.05.05 if one wants to model localised non-linearities of friction type, or large displacements, or non-linear constitutive behaviours; - an analysis of fluid flow in a cracked concrete structure (in 2D), with MACR_ECREVISSE U7.03.41. Finally, note that Code_Aster makes it possible to carry out a deterministic analysis, but that procedures have been put in place to make it fairly easy to carry out mechanico-probabilistic analyses (cf. U2.08.05). 1.2 The type of modelling to use It is possible to use: - 3D solid elements R3.01.00 or 2D surface elements, when this is possible, by making use of simplifying assumptions such as plane strain, plane stress or axisymmetry; - plate-type elements (thin for the DKT, DST, Q4G R3.07.03 or thick for the Q4GG R3.07.09), membrane-type elements (GRILLE_MEMBRANE, GRILLE_EXCENTREE, MEMBRANE, R3.08.07) or solid shell elements (COQUE_3D R3.07.04, ... - line elements by means of a straight Euler beam element (POU_D_E), or Timoshenko-type beams, straight (POU_D_T) (cf. R3.08.01), multifibre beams in small or in large displacements (POU_D_EM R3.08.08, POU_D_TGM R3.08.09). These modellings can of course be used on their own or combined. To help the user make a choice (in particular as regards the use of structural elements), the reader may refer to the document U2.02.01 or to the document U2.06.10. Furthermore, the chapter U2.03.07-modele-meca of this document details how to represent the reinforcement and the prestressing cables, according to the choice made for representing the concrete. 1.3 The constitutive law This is to be chosen according to the phenomena that it is necessary to take into account, while being aware of their limitations, of the difficulty of identifying realistic material parameters when one starts to seek very fine information, of the robustness of the law and of the impacts in terms of run time, ... The characteristics of the main laws available are summarised in this document in order to make the user's choice easier.
