R7.01.12. It is solved via the operator THER_NON_LINE, and the constitutive behaviour 'THER_HYDR'. The model must contain only the concrete, modelled by means of solid or surface elements, preferably linear. The recommended modellings are 3D_DIAG, PLAN_DIAG and AXIS_DIAG (but 3D, PLAN or AXIS are also possible). Sufficiently small time steps must be used at early age (of the order of an hour up to the peak of thermal heating, then the time steps may be increased progressively) in order to obtain a solution of good quality, because an explicit discretisation of the heat source is used. The temperature and the hydration may then be taken into account in the mechanical analysis in the form of command variables (TEMP and HYDR). In this case, it is recommended to solve the thermal problem with linear elements. An example of the solution of such a problem is treated in the test case FORMA41. Note : It is possible not to solve the thermo-hydration problem, and to define a hydration field analytically by means of the commands CREA_CHAM and CREA_RESU (In this case, the heating due to the thermo-hydration reaction is neglected). Thus one commonly uses the following formula, coming from an LCPC calibration: h=\frac{t}{b+t} , with b=1684800\mathit{s.} , if t is the time expressed in seconds. (cf. test SSLA103 for an example of data setup). 4 Possible choices for the drying analyses It is possible to model the drying of the concrete under the effect of the moisture gradient (a simplifying assumption which makes it possible to model only drying by diffusion and not by advection, for example) with the operator SECH_NON_LINE 1, (cf. R7.01.12). The model must contain only the concrete, modelled by means of solid or surface elements, preferably linear (especially if one continues with a mechanical analysis), combined with lumped elements, that is to say with 3D_DIAG, PLAN_DIAG or AXIS_DIAG (but 3D, PLAN or AXIS are also possible if the temperatures do not vary abruptly). Five laws are available to represent the evolution of the diffusion coefficient D as a function of the water concentration (variable SECH expressed in l/m^3 for an analysis in SI units) and possibly of the temperature. The expressions of each of them are given in U4.43.01 or R7.01.12. - SECH_MENSI, in which D is a function of the water concentration; - SECH_GRANGER, which is equivalent to SECH_MENSI but which takes thermal activation into account (that is to say the acceleration of drying when the temperature increases); - SECH_BAZANT, in which D is a function of the humidity (related to the water concentration by the sorption function); - SECH_RFT, which corresponds to the Richards–Fick model in temperature and which models the permeation of water in liquid form and the diffusion of vapour in the gaseous mixture. - SECH_NAPPE, which makes it possible to define an arbitrary evolution for D in the form of a nappe that is a function of the water concentration and of the temperature. The drying may then be taken into account in the mechanical analysis in the form of a command variable SECH, which corresponds to the water concentration in the concrete. R7.01.10 and U2.04.05. > The identification of the material parameters is carried out from a mass-loss curve. An example is given for the law SECH_GRANGER in the test TTNV101. Previously, one had to use THER_NON_LINE 5 Possible modellings for the mechanical analyses (static or dynamic) A wide choice of modellings, but also of constitutive laws, is available in Code_Aster for the mechanical analyses. It is up to the user to define the most efficient strategy according to the characteristics of the structure studied (containment, tank, slab, beam...), the loadings applied (thermal, symmetric, 3D...), the information sought (global behaviour, limit load, cracking, creep, ...) but also the speed of execution expected (complexity of implementation, difficulty of convergence, run time, ...). In this chapter we are concerned with the modellings that are accessible; the following one concentrates on the constitutive laws. The aim of this chapter is not to give advice on the choice of the most suitable modelling, but to give a synthetic view of what it is possible to do in order to make the engineer's choice easier. More precisely, given that, in order to model the concrete alone, all types of element are usable. Here we only summarise the possible combinations — or at any rate those classically used — for representing concrete containing steels. In what follows, the entry point of each paragraph corresponds to the choice that is made for describing the concrete: solid, surface, or by means of structural elements. For the practical details, on carrying out analyses with the prestressing cables, and in particular the use of the operators DEFI_CABLE_BP and CALC_PRECONT, the reader is invited to consult the document U2.03.06. 5.1 Modelling of the concrete by 3D solid elements The modellings and elements possible for the concrete are: - the modellings 3D or 3D_SI in the general case, it being known that all the 3D isoparametric elements (hexahedron, tetrahedron, pentahedron, pyramid...) are usable in linear or in quadratic form for the 3D modelling, whereas the 3D_SI modelling allows the use only of hexahedral elements (linear or quadratic) and of quadratic tetrahedra. The quadratic elements are more costly but give results of better quality. The use of under-integration nevertheless makes it possible to reduce the run times. In the case of a chained thermomechanical analysis, it is recommended to use under-integrated quadratic elements (cf. u2.01.10). Note that, in the case of a local damage analysis, one may prefer the use of a linear mesh in order to limit the phenomenon of localisation of the damage. - the modelling 3D_GRAD_VARI if one wants to use a non-local damage model with damage gradient (cf. R5.04.01). In this case, the elements must be quadratic. The main characteristics of these laws are indicated in order to make it easy to identify the law best suited to the problem considered, but it is strongly recommended to refer to the reference documentation before any use. 6.1.1 Modelling of the delayed strains | | BETON_GRANGER_V [R7.01.01] | BETON_GRANGER [R7.01.01] | BETON_UMLV [R7.01.06] | BETON_BURGER [R7.01.35] | FLUA_PORO_BETON 1 [R7.01.30] | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Basic creep | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | | Desiccation creep | no | no | yes | yes | yes | | Thermal expansion / Autogenous shrinkage / Desiccation shrinkage | no | no | yes | yes | yes | | Thermal activation | yes | no | no | yes | yes | | Influence of “ageing” (hydration, polymerisation, ...) | yes | no | no | no | no | | Influence of the age of the concrete at the time of loading | no | no | no | no | no | | Influence of the water content | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | Several generations of models are available in Code_Aster , but all the models have the objective of describing properly the long-term creep: they do not seek to reproduce precisely what happens at early age, where the couplings between the phenomena are, it seems, more important. The most advanced EDF R&D model today is the BETON_BURGER model. One may note that: - the BETON_GRANGER model leads to a fairly rapid saturation of the creep strains; - the BETON_UMLV model assumes that the delayed strains evolve in a linear manner in the long term, which generally leads to overestimating them substantially. Moreover, the apparent Poisson's ratio is not controlled, and may evolve in an abnormal manner, including becoming negative. - the BETON_BURGER model makes it possible to describe the whole set of behaviours and in particular to recover a logarithmic evolution as a function of time, which seems to be a very commonly observed phenomenon. On the other hand, it has the drawback of not being linear as a function of the stress; - the FLUA_PORO_BETON model comes from the work of the LMDC and of the CIH on the behaviour of dams. It is based on a poromechanical formulation and resembles BETON_BURGER closely in the theory. It belongs to a set of models that can be coupled: Creep + Damage + RAG/RSI. Note: > At present, no regulatory creep law is available in the code. However, if the creep strain to be modelled is limited to a spherical strain ( {\epsilon}_{\mathit{fl}}=C\times {I}_{d} ), it is possible to model it by using a command variable. If it is proportional to the imposed strain, it is possible to use a variable Young's modulus. 6.1.2 Modelling of the damage/cracking of the concrete To describe the degradation of the behaviour, there exist several categories of model. In Code_Aster , three types are available: - softening plasticity models, which introduce irreversible strains, - damage models, which make it possible to represent a reduction in the stiffness of the material (irreversible or not in the case of “reclosure” of the cracks), - cohesive-zone models, which make it possible to represent the cracks explicitly, but on condition that the user has introduced a priori into the mesh the potential cracking paths by means of interface elements. Recall that, as soon as the model is softening (that is to say that the stress decreases beyond a certain level of strain), the results are valid only if there is no localisation of the damage or of the plasticity (in other words so long as the degradation remains diffuse). Indeed, if no specific treatment is carried out, as soon as there is localisation, the solution obtained becomes strongly dependent on the mesh, both on the size (the smaller the mesh cells, the easier it is to break them) and on the orientation of the mesh cells (the way in which the structure is meshed orients the direction of propagation of the damage). Certain models put in place an energy regularisation which consists in adjusting the dissipated volumetric energy as a function of the mesh-cell size, under the assumption of at most one crack per mesh cell): this technique makes it possible only to limit the dependence on the mesh-cell size but does not act on the dependence on the orientation of the mesh. The non-local modelling GRAD_VARI (which brings in the damage gradient) makes it possible, for its part, to regularise the problem by “spreading” the damaged zone over several mesh cells. However, this implies having meshes that are sufficiently fine (ideally 5 mesh cells in the characteristic length) in order to obtain a solution independent of the mesh and predictive of the cracking pattern. The cohesive-zone models, for their part, oblige the user to postulate the potential cracking paths. Let us also point out that the cracking models are models that are always complicated to implement, and that raise problems of robustness (even if the models generally manage to reach the stress peak without too much difficulty). They are therefore to be used only when it is necessary, or to be interpreted with caution (especially on the post-peak stages). For all these questions of robustness, one should refer to the documents U2.05.06 and U2.05.07 in order to obtain advice on how to carry out an analysis. It has a major drawback, which is that, because of the shape of the criterion, it is possible, in two- or three-dimensional loading configurations, to exceed the limit tensile stress. It should be withdrawn in the near future. 6.1.3 Description of the damage/cracking of reinforced concrete The following table summarises in the same way the characteristics of the laws making it possible to describe the damage of reinforced concrete via so-called global laws, that is to say describing the constitutive behaviour of the concrete and of the steels simultaneously. In this case, it is sufficient that the steel mesh cells and the concrete mesh cells rest on the same nodes. If the meshes are not compatible, then one must create kinematic relations between the nodes of the two materials (which of course makes the analyses heavier). These kinematic relations are generated automatically by the operator DEFI_CABLE_BP for a 1D mesh in a 3D mesh. For a 2D mesh embedded in a 3D mesh, it is possible to use AFFE_CHAR_MECA/LIAISON_PROJ in order to generate these relations. Nevertheless, it may happen that one wishes to take this phenomenon into account, for example in order to simulate a situation in which the bond between the steel and the concrete is very degraded, or because one wishes to seek local information such as crack spacings and crack openings. Models are therefore available in Code_Aster , but let us point out that the characterisation of the steel–concrete bond, and consequently the identification of the parameters of the constitutive laws, remain difficult to obtain. - For a modelling in AXIS or D_PLAN, the steel and the concrete may be meshed explicitly and connected by a joint element (modelling AXIS_JOINT or PLAN_JOINT, U3.13.14), to which the constitutive law JOINT_BA R7.01.21 is assigned. However, let us point out that this is a very rich model but complicated to implement, and that it may present results that are not very physical for large slips (significant recovery of stiffness) (cf. test SSNA112). - For a modelling of the concrete in 3D, and a representation of the steels, either in 3D or in the form of a MEMBRANE, it is possible to describe the steel–concrete bond by means of interface elements placed between the 2 materials (modelling 3D_INTERFACE U3.13.14) to which the constitutive law CZM_LAB_MIX is assigned (cf. R7.02.11 and test SSNS110). Finally, let us point out that it is possible to represent frictional cables in 1D , by means of the modelling CABLE_GAINE R3.08.10 and of the constitutive law CABLE_GAINE_FROT. The friction model is of Coulomb type (cf. test ZZZZ347E). Here we merely list the various operators existing in code_aster in order to have access to the main features. Thus, it is possible to compute the reinforcement of a structure for a load case by means of the operator CALC_FERRAILLAGE U4.81.42. The method used is that of Capra and Maury R7.04.05 and it is applicable for plate and shell elements but also for beams. It is possible to use either the rules of BAEL91, or those of EUROCODE 2. In order to study several loading combinations, it is possible to use the command COMBINAISON_FERRAILLAGE U4.81.44. Since version 17, it is also possible to check an existing reinforcement layout under a given load thanks to the command VERI_FERRAILLAGE U4.81.46. 8 Miscellaneous 8.1 Modelling of the soil–structure interaction and of the structure–soil–structure interaction Taking into account the soil–structure interaction (SSI) and the structure–soil–structure interaction (I3S) amounts to considering the energy dissipated in the soil and the coupling effects between the soil and nearby buildings under dynamic loadings (earthquake). In statics, it makes it possible to have boundary conditions that are more realistic than a perfect clamping. Several methods exist for modelling the interaction between the structure(s) studied and the soil. - Model the soil explicitly with isoparametric elements (note that, in Code_Aster , only the elastoplastic constitutive model known as “Hujeux” R7.01.23 is capable of taking a cyclic loading into account. It makes it possible to consider the behaviour of granular geomaterials, sandy clays that are normally consolidated or over-consolidated, gravels, ....). In statics, one can simply model the soil as elastic or with a Mohr-Coulomb law R7.01.28. - Use soil springs for regulatory SSI analyses, in order to take into account the uplift and the reduction in the number of modes of a foundation (cf. U2.06.08). - Use MISS3D (cf. U2.06.07 for the classical cases (elastic domain) and U3.06.21 for the more complex cases when taking into account the spatial variability in the seismic analyses U2.06.12). > It should be noted that MISS3D makes it possible to model both rigid and flexible foundations, heterogeneous soils — with a particular extension to stratified soils (no account taken of the dip) — and rafts of arbitrary shape, and thus to allow dynamic-interaction analyses with one or more arbitrary structures (I3S). > The Code_Aster –MISS3D chaining is based on a coupling of BEM-FEM type which makes it possible to take the SSI and the I3S into account in the dynamic analyses in seismic analysis. Nevertheless, the solution being in frequency, only linear problems could be treated until now with this approach. - Use MISS3D for the complex cases. A new Laplace-time method, which also goes through the computation of the soil impedances with MISS3D, then makes it possible to carry out non-linear transient analyses (with the use of DYNA_NON_LINE). Accordingly, certain macros have been developed to help the users carry out this stage, and even trade-specific tools under salome_meca. These are: - DEFI_GLRC U4.42.06 for the global laws GLRC_DM and GLRC_DAMAGE, which makes it possible to obtain the properties of the homogenised concrete from the physical and geometric characteristics of the reinforced concrete; - DEFI_MATER_GC U4.42.07 for (i) the laws of MAZARS or MAZARS_UNIL by using the rules coming from BAEL91, from Eurocode 2 or by supplying classical material characteristics (ii) for the laws ENDO_FISS_EXP, ENDO_LOCA_EXP or ENDO_LOCA_TC; - the trade-specific tool ARCADE [SU1.18.01] under salome_meca which makes it possible to identify the parameters of the creep law BETON_BURGER_FP and even to recalibrate them in the case of containment buildings; - the trade-specific tool for identification of the parameters of the reinforced-concrete law DHRC[SU1.10.01]. Let us point out that the use of this tool can also make it possible to give the realistic linear response for arbitrary reinforced-concrete plate sections in bending and in membrane, to check the homogenised properties or to quantify the bending–membrane coupling effects, for example. Also to be noted, in a closely related area, the existence of the command CALC_ESSAI_GEOMECA U4.90.21, which makes it possible to check the relevance of the parameters of identified soil laws by obtaining the response at a material point for various tests such as monotonic or cyclic triaxial tests, drained or undrained, oedometer tests, etc. The reference documentation remains, in any event, an indispensable source of information, it being known that, in addition, for certain laws, there exist internally at EDF Model Identity Sheets which set out the identification techniques. 8.3 Pre- / post-processing 8.3.1 Checking the data setup One often needs to check the data setup, in order to be sure for example of having assigned the right geometric characteristics to structural elements, of having oriented them correctly, that the assigned material fields have indeed been assigned to the right mesh-cell groups, ... Visualisation tools can be useful to help with the checking of the data setup. It is sufficient for this to print, via the command IMPR_CONCEPT (cf. [ref:U4.91.04 ] ) a certain number of concepts, such as CARA_ELEM in order to visualise the local frame, CHAM_MATER, in order to see the various materials, the loadings. The command is as follows: IMPR_RESU( FORMAT='MED', CONCEPT=(_F( CHAM_MATER = CHMAT), _F( CARA_ELEM = CARELE), _F( CHARGE = CHAR1),),); The rendering is visible in the two following figures: Example of visualisation of the orientation of the local frame Example of visualisation under Salomé of the material assignments 8.3.2 Post-processing For post-processing, numerous possibilities are offered to the user, which cannot be detailed. Let us simply mention a few options specific to civil engineering: - Thanks to the operator CALC_CHAMP U4.81.04, numerous options are available depending on the modelling or the constitutive law used, among which one may mention: - isolate the strains related to basic creep EPFP_XXXX or to desiccation EPFD_XXXX; - isolate the thermal strains, the autogenous or desiccation shrinkage EPVC_XXXX; - compute stresses projected onto the skin of a volume (for example onto the faces of a hydraulic structure) SIRO_ELEM; - compute the dissipated energies DISS_XXXX, ECIN_ELEM,.. - Visualise the stress or strain fields in the multifibre beams (POU_D_EM) and the multilayer shells (DKT) by using the command IMPR_RESU, cf. [ref:SV1.01.01 ]. Example of visualisation at the sub-points - Visualise the internal forces and moments for the structural elements, cf. U7.05.21 §6 Example of visualisation of the shear forces on beams - Extract forces or strains at an arbitrary point of a shell thanks to the operator POST_COQUE U4.81.23. - Plot the cracking path and compute the crack opening ( 2D only) from a non-local damage analysis (GRAD_VARI) thanks to the operator POST_ENDO_FISS U4.86.01. - Construction of a fragility curve with POST_DYNA_ALEA, U4.84.04 and U2.08.05. R means that it is a regulatory or quasi-equivalent model, I: means that it is a model that is relatively robust and qualified for our applications, E: means that it is a model dedicated to expert assessments, either because it is not very robust (difficulty of convergence), or because it is complex to implement, or because it is not yet fully validated. 9 What Code_Aster cannot do No model is available in a direct manner in Code_Aster for representing: - the damage of the concrete at high temperature (no damage of thermal origin), - the Transient Thermal Creep (irreversible strain which occurs when the concrete is heated above 100°C while it is subjected to a compressive loading), - the carbonation of the concrete, - the cracking of the concrete at early age, - taking thermal radiation into account in the analyses (one can however use the SYRTHES code), - the hydration–drying coupling, - a creep model adapted specifically to early age or to temperatures above 80°C. - taking drying and hydration into account for the structural elements. 10 Resources for training To finish, here is a non-exhaustive list of means of training yourself in code_aster for civil engineering. - Face-to-face training courses: - the ITECH Code_aster training course for civil engineering (once a year). The materials presented during this training course are accessible on the site code-aster.org, in the Training tab. - the Civil Master training workshops (on request) - Practical exercises to put into practice a certain number of notions, capitalised in the form of code_aster test cases: - FORMA40: to set up a first modelling of reinforced concrete, in 3D or with DKT elements - FORMA41: to set up a chained thermo-hydration analysis, then drying, then mechanical - FORMA42: to set up the modelling of prestressed concrete (in 3D) - FORMA43: to set up a modelling of reinforced concrete with a multifibre beam model - The code_aster documents of type U2, which are very numerous and give practical advice on very varied subjects. - Internally at EDF, do not hesitate to join the Civil-Engineering Structural Analysis community (Teams). There you will find: - in the Training channel, links to training videos for code_aster or salome ; - in the Civil Master development and monitoring channel, the documentation but also videos making it possible to discover the tool as well as examples of studies. - Still internally, do not forget Wiking! One possible entry point is the page https://prod-inge-wiki.edf.fr/wiki/Code_Aster#Formations_et_documents_officiels or https://prod-inge-wiki.edf.fr/wiki/Calcul_de_structure_en_G%C3%A9nie_Civil

u2.03.08 Carrying out a civil-engineering study with prestressing cables in fast dynamics via the macro-command CALC_EUROPLEXUS u2.03.08 Carrying out a civil-engineering study with prestressing cables in fast dynamics via the macro-command CALC_EUROPLEXUS > Summary. The aim of this document is to give advice for carrying out civil-engineering studies in fast dynamics with prestressing cables and the concrete modelled as a shell (Q4GG element). The fast-dynamics analyses are carried out with Europlexus via the macro-command CALC_EUROPLEXUS. The prestressing cables may be of three types: bonded, sliding or frictional. One recalls the three types of cable modelling available in Europlexus and one illustrates their use on the example of a prestressed containment subjected to an impact. The four stages for the solution of the problem will be presented: creation of the mesh, data setup in Code_Aster , solution of the numerical problem and post-processing. 1 Introduction In the context of the study of the resistance of civil-engineering buildings, the numerical simulations aim to gain a better understanding of their non-linear behaviour. This document presents the tools available in Code_Aster in order to model slender reinforced-concrete structures (Q4GG shell modelling) with prestressing cables and to carry out a fast-dynamics analysis calling on the Europlexus software. For more technical details on the data setup of an impact analysis with the law GLRC_DAMAGE, one may consult reference [8]. The aim of this document is to provide the user with advice on the data setup of the study with prestressing cables which may be of bonded, sliding or frictional type. 2 The EUROPLEXUS software The Europlexus software [1] is a simulation software dedicated to the fast-dynamics analysis of structures and fluids. EDF co-develops this code in partnership with the owners: the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA) and the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission located at Ispra (Italy). The Europlexus software is based on a discretisation of space by means of finite elements. The time integration is carried out by means of a conditionally stable explicit scheme. The solution algorithm is non-linear both at the geometric level (large displacements, large strains) and at the material level (non-linear constitutive laws). The Europlexus code can be called by the Code_Aster software via the macro-command CALC_EUROPLEXUS, which makes it possible to drive the execution of a Europlexus study from a Code_Aster command file. The command CALC_EUROPLEXUS thus makes it possible to define and execute a Europlexus study while remaining entirely within the Code_Aster environment. The solution is carried out in the background by Europlexus , without the user having to worry about the preparation of the Europlexus input files. CALC_EUROPLEXUS takes the Aster concepts as arguments, builds the Europlexus command file, launches and drives the execution of Europlexus , then rebuilds, from a Europlexus result file in MED format, an Aster result concept which can then be analysed with Aster in post-processing. The scope of application of the command CALC_EUROPLEXUS is detailed in the documentation U7.03.10. 3 Type of modelling of the prestressing cables 3.1 Introduction In Code_Aster and Europlexus , the prestressing cables are modelled by 1D elements (bar with 2 nodes). In Code_Aster , there also exists a CABLE-GAINE element using 3 nodes. Their tensioning consists in applying a non-zero tension in these cables. One distinguishes three cable modellings [5] and [6]: - bonded cables, - sliding cables, - frictional cables. The difference between these three types of cable rests on their connection with the concrete that surrounds them (see [2] for the theoretical aspects and the validation). 3.2 Bonded cables A bonded cable is a cable entirely linked to the concrete by kinematic relations. All the displacements of the nodes of the cables are therefore constrained by the displacements of the nodes of the concrete. This modelling corresponds to the technology of prestressing with bond. In this case, the cables or strands are placed in metal or plastic ducts, are tensioned, then the ducts are grouted with cement grout so as to ensure the bonding between the cables and the concrete. 3.3 Sliding cables A sliding cable is a cable which can move freely along its trajectory (and only in this direction) relative to the concrete in which it is embedded. A sliding cable is therefore kinematically linked to the concrete only along the two directions orthogonal to its trajectory at each of its nodes. In order for the cable to move along its trajectory in the case of large strains and large slips, these kinematic relations must be recomputed at each time step. One must both recompute the projection of the cable nodes onto the concrete and the trajectory of the cable in order to obtain the new tangent. The figure illustrates this procedure. Figure 3.3-a : Sliding of the cable along its duct This modelling corresponds to the technology of prestressing without bond: this is the case, for example, of greased sheathed strands (TGG). In these cases, the cables or strands are placed in ducts filled with grease. 3.4 Frictional cables A frictional cable is an intermediate case between a bonded cable and a sliding cable. The nodes of the cable can move relative to the concrete in which it is embedded according to a friction law in the direction of the trajectory of the cable. The friction law used in Code_Aster and Europlexus is a Coulomb law in which a friction threshold separates the bonded zone and the sliding zone (). The threshold of the law is defined by the linear (straight) and curved (curvilinear) friction coefficients (cf. 4.2.4). Figure 3.4-a : Friction model In this figure Flim denotes the threshold force of the law and dVr is the relative velocity of the cables with respect to the concrete. This modelling may be used to reproduce the tension profiles of the BPEL [3] or ETCC [4] standards. From a practical point of view, frictional spring-type elements, called discrete elements in Code_Aster , must be defined in the model in order to take into account the friction constitutive law linking the nodes of the cable and the nodes of the concrete (). Figure 3.4-b : Modelling of the frictional concrete–steel connections 4 Typical study of a prestressed containment 4.1 First stage: Creation of the mesh 4.1.1 Concrete structure The containment modelled for the typical study consists of a cylindrical barrel surmounted by a dome. The reinforced-concrete wall is meshed with 4-node surface elements (QUA4). The passive reinforcement is modelled via the homogenised reinforced-concrete constitutive law GLRC_DAMAGE; it is therefore not meshed. One can define a limited zone for taking into account the non-linear behaviour of the material. The ribs, located on either side of the containment for \theta =0° and \theta =180° , are reinforced zones in which the horizontal prestressing cables are anchored. They are modelled by shell elements () representing the extra thicknesses of concrete. The mesh-cell groups allowing the assignment of the materials and of the loading are defined. Figure 4.1.1-a: Mesh of the concrete structure of the containment | Figure 4.1.1-b: Close-up view of the anchorage theta =0° | Figure 4.1.1-c: View of the cylinder of the containment and of the frame | | --- | --- | Note One will take care to produce a regular mesh with a uniform mesh-cell size. The minimum mesh-cell size is taken into account in the computation of the time step for the explicit solution scheme. The stability of the scheme is therefore conditioned by the mesh. Moreover, in the case of the use of a non-linear constitutive law, the presence of local refinements can lead to a localisation of the stresses and to unrealistic damage. 4.1.2 Prestressing cables Each cable is meshed by two-node segment elements. The choice of mesh-cell size must be close to the mesh-cell size chosen for the plate elements. One thus ensures that there is not a large number of cable nodes in one and the same concrete mesh cell, which would lead to a model with numerous kinematic relations leading to a significant run time. Conversely, if the prestressing cables are not meshed finely enough, the prestressing forces are poorly distributed and certain cable segments may “come out” of the concrete mesh during the loading. It is not necessary to make the nodes of the cable coincide with the nodes of the concrete. The segment of the cables is not necessarily in the plane of the shell modelling the concrete, because the thickness of the shell will be taken into account in the pairing of the nodes of the cables and of the concrete. One must therefore ensure that the position of the nodes of the cable is indeed at a distance less than half the thickness of the corresponding concrete plate. For each cable, one must define the anchorage nodes, which are the two ends of the cable. One must create a node group (containing a single node) for each of these anchorage nodes. In this study, one distinguishes three groups of cables: vertical cables, horizontal cables and those of the dome. For the vertical cables and those of the dome, one can easily identify the ends in the figure. For the horizontal cables, a close-up view of the anchorage at the ends is proposed: the two terminations of the cables cross but are disconnected. The horizontal cables may be anchored on one of the two anchorage zones. It is advisable to alternate the horizontal cables anchored in the zones \theta =0° and \theta =180° , in order to obtain a uniform prestress of the containment. This advice is particularly necessary in the case where friction is considered during prestressing, because the tension is not uniform along the cable during prestressing. Figure 4.1.2-a : Mesh of the prestressing cables Figure 4.1.2-b : Close-up view of the anchorage of the horizontal cables Specific case of the frictional cables For the case of the frictional cables, discrete elements must be built in the mesh all along the cables. To do this, one duplicates each cable node in the Salomé mesh-generation script, except the ends, and one creates a SEG2 mesh cell of zero length. One can create a single mesh-cell group DISFROT grouping all the discrete elements created. 4.2 Second stage: Data setup of the problem 4.2.1 Reading and enrichments of the mesh One must first check that the anchorage nodes are indeed accessible (individually) by a GROUP_NO. One must also orient correctly the mesh-cell groups on which one imposes loadings of pressure or flux type (command ORIE_NORM_COQUE). Specific case of the frictional cables One must make sure that one has built a group of discrete mesh cells along the cables without including the ends. 4.2.2 Assignment of a model The components modelled are: 1. the prestressing cables modelled by BARRE elements (supported by SEG2), 2. the concrete modelled by Q4GG shells (these are the only shell elements accepted by the macro-command CALC_EUROPLEXUS). 3. Specific case of the frictional cables The discrete elements representing the friction between the cables and the concrete are modelled by DIS_T elements. | MODELE=AFFE_MODELE( MAILLAGE=MAIL, AFFE=(_F( GROUP_MA = l_beton, PHENOMENE = 'MECANIQUE', MODELISATION = 'Q4GG'), _F( GROUP_MA = l_cables, PHENOMENE = 'MECANIQUE', MODELISATION = 'BARRE'), _F( GROUP_MA = 'DISFROT', PHENOMENE = 'MECANIQUE', MODELISATION = 'DIS_T'),) ) | ← Modelling to be added for the case of the frictional cables | | --- | --- | 4.2.3 Characteristics of the structural elements The characteristics expected for the structural elements are: 1. the cross-section of the prestressing cables, 2. the thickness of the concrete shells (if necessary, the orientation of the shells is specified). 1. Specific case of the frictional cables The elementary stiffnesses of the discrete elements must be defined. These stiffnesses are necessary for the prestressing analysis carried out in Code_Aster . One chooses high stiffness values so that the “double” nodes remain tied to the nodes of the cable. However, these stiffnesses are not useful for the Europlexus part. The CARA_ELEM concept for the CALC_PRECONT command is: | CARAELE=AFFE_CARA_ELEM(MODELE=MODELE, COQUE =(_F( GROUP_MA = l_beton, EPAIS = ECYL, VECTEUR=(0.,0.,1.),) ...) This makes it possible to define what the tension in the cables must be according to the rules of the BPEL, as a function of the initial tension, of the anchorage draw-in (which applies only for the active anchorages), of the relaxation of the steel and of the delayed strains of the concrete (creep and shrinkage). Let us point out that a single DEFI_CABLE_BP can group several cables provided that they have the same input parameters for the computation of the tension, and that one wishes to tension all these cables simultaneously. The type of cable is selected under TYPE_EPX with the choice: 'ADHE', 'GLIS', 'FROT'. | CINE_CAB = AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=MODELE, RELA_CINE_BP=_F( CABLE_BP =L_CAB, RELA_CINE=’OUI’, SIGM_BPEL='NON', TYPE_EPX = type_epx)) | ← Keyword to be added in order to specify the type of cable | | --- | --- | This loading is necessary for any analysis with STAT_NON_LINE or CALC_EUROPLEXUS on the model containing the prestressing cables (otherwise a fatal error because the matrix cannot be factorised). However, the tangent is an approximation of the trajectory of the cable at the node considered. Thus, when the cable node slides, it moves away by a small distance from the trajectory and always towards the outside of it. At each time step this deviation is all the greater as the displacement is large. With the repetition of the time steps, the nodes may end up moving away in a non-negligible manner from the theoretical trajectory of the cable. In these cases, the analysis will stop with a message indicating that a cable node has left the thickness of the concrete mesh cell in which it should be included. In this case, one can use a smaller time step in order to remedy the problem. 4.4 Fourth stage: Post-processing Once the analysis has been executed by Europlexus, the results are stored in the evol_noli concept returned by the macro-command CALC_EUROPLEXUS. u2.03.09 Overview of the constitutive models for soils and rocks, and for joints u2.03.09 Overview of the constitutive models for soils and rocks, and for joints > Summary. The aim of this document is to provide an overall view of the modelling possibilities open to the user for the constitutive behaviour of soils and rocks, to which the constitutive behaviour of joints has also been added in order to describe the interfaces between geomaterial media. Different choices are always possible, and the aim of this document is not to take the place of the engineer's analysis, but rather to make it easier to choose the modelling options, according to the needs and the tools available, and to direct the user towards more specific documents. 1 Introduction 1.1 General points on the constitutive behaviour of soils and rocks, and of joints The modelling of the constitutive behaviour of the soils and rocks which make up many geotechnical structures seeks to represent complex phenomenologies, in particular non-linear ones, according to the objectives of the study being carried out. One may, for example, be concerned with assessing the bearing capacity of a foundation, the rise in water pressures, seismically induced settlements, the evolution of a slip zone, the margin available before the onset of liquefaction, the long-term stability of an underground structure, the amplification of waves in a sedimentary basin... The mechanical constitutive behaviour of geomaterials is characterised by: - an asymmetry between tensile states and compressive states; - irreversible evolutions, to be described by internal history variables; - a consolidation , for a spherical stress path, which exhibits a strong non-linearity; - a “critical state” curve, which is a material datum, in the {\log}_{10}p'–e plane ( confining pressure , also called mean effective stress p'=\frac{1}{3}\text{tr}(\sigma ') – void ratio e , which is linked directly to the density index {D}_{r} ) where the soil, when it undergoes pure shear, no longer shows any evolution of the volumetric strains (one has \dot{{\varepsilon}_{p}^{v}}=0 ); and a strength plateau is reached in the confining pressure – deviatoric stresses plane p'–q . For a cohesionless soil, the “critical state” curve is rather straight in the {\log}_{10}p'–e plane, whereas it is curved for a clayey soil. At the initial state of the soil, in the {\log}_{10}p'–e plane, the domain to the left of the “critical state” curve characterises dilatant situations, whereas to the right one has contractancy; - a dilatancy , that is, a coupling between volumetric behaviour and deviatoric behaviour, which varies during the evolution of the degradation of the soil and also with the evolution of the pore pressures, which act on p' . The name of Roscoe is associated with this phenomenology. The dilatancy phase generally follows a prior phase of contractancy ; these two phases are separated by a “characteristic state” curve in the p'–q plane (where one has \dot{{\varepsilon}_{p}^{v}}=0 ), dependent on the consolidation state, cf. for example [bib28]_. The dilatancy angle \psi characterises the slope of this curve, which always lies below the “critical state” curve, or is superimposed on it; - a strength depending on the loading history, increasing or decreasing (positive or negative hardening), associated with residual strains. A dilatant soil may see its strength decrease ( softening ) after a stage of positive hardening, whereas a contracting soil may undergo positive hardening up to failure, described by the “critical state” curve drawn in the confining pressure – deviatoric stresses plane p'–q . The internal friction angle {\phi }_{\mathrm{pp}} characterises the slope of this “critical state” curve in the p'–q plane. At the critical state, an evolution of the distortion occurs without any increase in the volumetric strain. In the case of a clay, these situations are associated with the value of the degree of consolidation of the soil (called OCR for “Over-Consolidation Ratio”, equal to the ratio between the greatest vertical effective stress reached during the loading process and the in-situ vertical effective stress), whereas for a sand, the initial state in the {\log}_{10}p'–e plane defines the softening and dilatant character, or the contractant and non-softening character, of the constitutive behaviour; - an initial cohesion (that is, a strength under deviatoric loading) for clays, almost zero for dry sands, even though the latter, once saturated, exhibit a certain cohesion; the cohesion of rocks is generally much higher; - this phenomenology therefore reflects a common characteristic: the dependence of the constitutive behaviour on the state of the material in the {\log}_{10}p'–e plane; - the elastic characteristics also depend on the initial void ratio {e}_{0} and on the confining pressure: this characterises a non-linear elasticity law. The elasticity modulus is therefore higher at depth than at the surface. In practice, even if the elasticity domain is very small, it is useful to represent this reduction of the elasticity modulus which occurs from the very beginning of the loading process. Poisson's ratio (under the isotropic assumption) is in general evaluated by means of the compressibility coefficient, which is more readily available. One sometimes needs to take into account a certain anisotropy induced by the stratification; - hysteresis loops under cyclic loading, whose shape also depends on the confining pressure and on the plasticity index {I}_{p} , which is measured in the laboratory; - in particular, a cohesionless material (sand...) under strain-controlled deviatoric cyclic loading densifies progressively (contractancy), especially if it is loose in the initial state (low value of {D}_{r} ); on the other hand, if the material is dense ( overconsolidated ) it undergoes a damage phase (dilatancy) after the peak has been reached, followed by failure (critical state). If the amplitude of these cycles is large, one may observe the absence of a stabilisation of the cyclic response: one no longer has shakedown but the onset of ratcheting; - tangent and secant stiffnesses depending on the loading history; - an influence of the loading rate: an equivalent viscosity may make it possible to represent this effect, even if it is difficult to quantify for sands; this characteristic is important for clays and rocks; all the behavioural properties cited above may depend on the loading rate; - and finally a strong spatial variability of the mechanical properties , characteristic of a natural material. To these common characteristics, the principal differences between a soil and a rock should be defined: - a soil is characterised by a generally porous medium having an unconsolidated behaviour, that is, deformable enough that it can be “worked”; the constitutive law of a soil will be concerned mainly with characterising its plastic flow and its strength under cyclic loading; a soil may be described by a granular-type porous continuous medium: the plastic flow and the long-term behaviour are intimately linked to the question of the variations in pore pressures of the fluid present in the porosity; - a rock is characterised by a cohesion much higher than that of a soil, and a stiff behaviour exhibiting a certain hardness; the constitutive law of a rock will be concerned mainly with characterising instantaneous and delayed cracking , as well as fatigue failure. The damage state of the rock, at the scale of a rock mass, is quantified by the RQD factor (Rock Quality Designation). It is important to take into account the discontinuous character of a rock mass at the scale of the structure, that is, to incorporate into the modelling the possible fractures which exceed the limits of what the constitutive law can represent. A joint model may prove relevant. The porosity of a rock is generally much lower than that of a soil, so hydromechanical coupling in rocks plays a role mainly in the long term. The interfaces of media made up of geomaterials are in general also characterised by complex behaviours: one cannot always be satisfied with a perfect modelling by simple continuity of the displacements, equivalent to continuity of the stress vector at the interface. A joint model is therefore defined. One finds the phenomena of cohesion and of dilatancy as in soils and, in addition, the unilateral character of failure. Hydromechanical coupling plays an essential role in certain types of application. The various constitutive models attempt to represent all or part of these characteristics. The parameters of the constitutive models are identified from laboratory tests: - simple shear, triaxial (consolidation at various confinement values, in a drained or undrained situation), torsion, isotropic compression, oedometer (drained cylindrical specimen subjected to a monotonic uniaxial compression, and to prevented lateral displacements: obtaining a consolidation curve); - these tests may be monotonic or cyclic, drained or undrained, strain-controlled or stress-controlled; - resonant column: obtaining the elastic moduli; - creep, failure, and relaxation for rocks; whose results must sometimes be corrected in order to reflect the real stress path in place, and from in-situ tests, at various depths in the soil. These tests are supplemented by geological analyses and site investigations: - SPT ( standard penetration test ), a test carried out by driving a tube, which does not provide a direct measurement of a physical parameter; - CPT (penetrometers), a monotonic static cone test driven at constant speed, which does not provide a direct measurement of a physical parameter; - pressuremeter: obtaining the elastic moduli, the strength and the creep moduli; one thus considers, for example, the “Ménard” pressuremeter test carried out by applying an increasing controlled pressure in a vertical cylindrical borehole. - CPTU (with measurement of the pore pressure); - shear-wave velocity {V}_{s} at low strain level ( cross-hole , SASW); - flat-jack test in order to assess the initial stress state in a rock mass. These tests produce relations between the number of cycles and the CSR (cyclic stress ratio equal to \tau /\sigma {'}_{v} ), the overconsolidation state (OCR, linked to the plasticity index {I}_{p} ), the CRR (cyclic resistance ratio), and the cyclic degradation curves G-\gamma . The elastic behaviour domain of soils is limited to very small strains: \varepsilon Note 1. A distinction will be made between verification and validation: verification is understood in the sense of the equations modelled and expressed in the software, whereas validation denotes the comparison of the results of the model in the software against reference experimental measurements, in situations representative of the intended applications. > Note 2. The link should be made between the parameters of the constitutive models resulting from the experimental measurements and the parameters of interest measured in situ for the engineer, such as “the plasticity index”, “the void ratio”, the cyclic resistance to liquefaction (CSR), the cone resistance (CPT)... The tests must be carried out with various density indices {D}_{r} (associated with the void ratio {e}_{0} ) and various confining pressures (in particular in order to identify the critical state properly) and under drained and undrained conditions. 2.2.1 General physical parameters A first class of general physical parameters characterises the material: - dry soil density {\rho}_{s} , - saturated soil density, - initial porosity {\varphi}_{0} , - void ratio {e}_{0}=\frac{{\varphi}_{0}}{1-{\varphi}_{0}} or density index {D}_{r} , - particle-size curve, - initial degree of saturation {S}_{0} , - plasticity index {I}_{p} , linked to the internal friction angle {\phi }_{\mathrm{pp}} and to the Atterberg limits, - permeability to the liquid and/or to the gas. 2.2.2 Elastic parameters The second step consists in the identification of the elastic parameters supplied to code_aster (drained bulk modulus {K}_{0} , shear modulus {G}_{0} in the drained situation), which are highly dependent on the confining pressure {P}_{\mathrm{réf}} or mean stress (via the void ratio). The datum of the coefficient of earth pressure at rest {k}_{0} helps to establish the initial elasticity of the material in place. One recalls that Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio are expressed by: {E}_{0}=\frac{9{K}_{0}{G}_{0}}{3{K}_{0}+{G}_{0}} and {\nu}_{0}=\frac{3{K}_{0}-2{G}_{0}}{6{K}_{0}+2{G}_{0}} The expressions in the drained situation involve the Biot coefficient and distinguish the drained compressibility of the porous medium from the compressibility of the solid grains {K}_{s} : \frac{1}{{K}_{s}}=\frac{1-b}{{K}_{0}} For a soil made up of grains (sands, gravels), it may be necessary to supply a parameter describing the non-linear dependence between the stiffness and the applied stress. Remarks: - comparing numerical predictions with a measurement carried out in situ on the structure, for low-level loadings (in geophysics: use of ambient noise, for example), constitutes a relevant approach for an analysis of an existing structure. - it is, however, difficult to assess the initial anisotropic characteristics, linked to the geological formation of the soils in place. The tests carried out in situ are performed, for example, by means of a pressuremeter (radial expansion) or of dynamic penetrometers. 2.2.3 Non-linear constitutive parameters The following steps consist in the identification of the parameters associated with the description of the cohesion, of the strength (failure criterion) and of the hardening, and of the contractancy and dilatancy domains, which depend on the consolidation (“normally consolidated” case, “overconsolidated” case). In particular, one recalls that the dilatancy angle \psi is less than or equal to the internal friction angle {\phi }_{\mathrm{pp}} . It will be noted that the natural equilibrium of a slope made up of a non-cohesive material, whether saturated or dry, requires that the friction angle {\phi }_{\mathrm{pp}} be greater than that of the slope. Under cyclic conditions, one seeks to identify the degradation curves G-\gamma , D-\gamma and the CSR. code_aster proposes a specific command to assist with the identification of the constitutive parameters of soils: CALC_ESSAI_GEOMECA, cf. U4.90.21. It makes it possible to simulate, for a material point, various loading paths characteristic of the usual geomechanical laboratory tests, monotonic/cyclic, drained/undrained, and to post-process the results obtained: - monotonic drained triaxial test, strain-controlled; - monotonic undrained triaxial test, strain-controlled; - drained cyclic shear test, strain-controlled; - undrained cyclic triaxial test, force-controlled; - alternated drained cyclic triaxial test, strain-controlled; - undrained cyclic triaxial test, strain-controlled; - drained cyclic oedometer test, force-controlled; - drained cyclic isotropic compression test, force-controlled. For its use, one should choose the behaviour, the necessary material parameters, and the loading data of the test considered. For the strain-controlled tests, it is advisable to supply strains of logarithmic type (GDEF_LOG) or Hencky strains, because in many tests the strains leave the framework of small transformations. This large-strain formulation allows the direct extension of the use of the elastoplastic constitutive relations developed within the framework of small transformations. 2.3 Phenomenology and modellings of the constitutive behaviour of rocks Rocks are essentially classified according to their level of strength in unconfined compression (Unconfined Compressive Strength: UCS), itself associated with their geological history (formation) and with the porosity. One cannot always be satisfied with a perfect modelling by simple continuity of the displacements, equivalent to continuity of the stress vector at the interface, supplemented, for a porous medium, by the continuity of the pore pressures. The joint appears as a discontinuity, rough, possibly reinforced by a filling material. code_aster has particular joint finite elements for studies in pure mechanics in 2D and in 3D (XXX_JOINT). Particular joint finite elements for coupled hydromechanical studies (XXX_JOINT_HYME in 2D and in 3D, and XXX_JHMS only in 2D) are also available: see R3.06.09 and R7.02.15: they represent the displacement and the fluid pressure in the joint, in particular a fluid flow inside it (cubic law, see R7.01.25). The introduction of the fluid into the joint modifies the normal mechanical stress. The joint (or crack) finite elements for coupled hydromechanical studies (saturated medium) in 2D, with a 1D support, see R7.02.15, (PLAN_JHMS, AXIS_JHMS), aim to model the displacement discontinuity across the joint and the Darcy flow along the joint. The pressure field is considered to be continuous across the interface, whereas flux discontinuities are allowed across the interface (unlike the XXX_JOINT_HYME finite elements), and a cubic law describes the volume flux as a function of the pressure gradient along the interface: the intrinsic permeability is therefore cubic as a function of the joint opening (discontinuity of the normal displacement). The parameters for modelling the hydraulic behaviour of the joint (permeability, porosity, Biot modulus, fluid viscosity...) are those of porous media, cf. R7.01.11. One may thus take into account the propagation of uplift pressures at a concrete–rock interface, and a fluid flow within a crack in a porous medium. u2.03.10 User's guide to the modelling of junctions between reinforced-concrete civil-engineering structural elements u2.03.10 User's guide to the modelling of junctions between reinforced-concrete civil-engineering structural elements > Summary. The purpose of this document is to give advice for carrying out studies of reinforced-concrete structures comprising walls, slabs and rafts, using the dedicated features (in particular the kinematic relations, a non-linear constitutive model of a junction). It gives information on the meshing methodology, on the implementation of the kinematic relations, and on the parameterisation of the constitutive models. The non-linear constitutive behaviour, which makes it possible to model a bending junction between a wall and a floor or a raft and is assigned on a discrete element (hinges), of type DIS_TR on SEG2 mesh cells, with two nodes, accessible via the keyword JONC_ENDO_PLAS, see §13 R5.03.17. 1 Introduction To carry out an analysis on a reinforced-concrete structure made up of walls, slabs and rafts, one may adopt, according to the stakes and the computational performance aimed at, a: - modelling with solid finite elements in the domain occupied by the concrete (formwork geometry), with the reinforcing steels also modelled as solid finite elements: this choice must be reserved for local analyses; - modelling with solid finite elements in the domain occupied by the concrete (formwork geometry), with the steels of the reinforcement layers modelled by grid membranes, placed on the mid-plane of the reinforcement layers. This situation is that, for example, of a raft or of thick floors; - modelling with plate finite elements known as “generalised”, which will carry a constitutive law expressed directly in generalised forces (bending and membrane), representing the constitutive behaviour of the reinforced concrete homogenised over the section. This situation is that, for example, of structural assemblies based on walls and floors. This modelling uses the geometry of the mid-planes of the walls, the slabs, the rafts... It is also necessary to model the reinforced-concrete junctions connecting a wall and a floor or a raft. These junctions have dimensions identical or close to that of the thickness of the structural elements connected: they are therefore essentially three-dimensional in the geometric part of the connection (the “core”). One can distinguish junctions between 2, 3 or 4 structural elements, of cross, T or L shape. Various codified construction provisions govern the reinforcement of these junctions. According to the design choices, one may consider a good continuity of transmission of the bending moments between the connected structural elements when the reinforcement is continuous through the junction. On the contrary, if the reinforcement is discontinuous, the possible cracking of the concrete modifies the constitutive behaviour of the connection: a perfect built-in fixity is not always representative. The choices made for the concreting also have an influence: one may have the case of a floor concreted at the same time as the wall, or on the contrary the case of a floor with a precast slab receiving, by concreting, a complementary compression slab. The construction sequence, with shoring present under the precast slabs, also contributes to the loading of the junction (dead weight of the concrete and of the additional loads during the pouring of the floor). Often the wall extending above the floor, continuing the wall of the lower lift, is not cast and the reinforcement is left waiting. Figure 1-a : Cross-section view of a reinforced-concrete junction connecting a wall and a floor and of its reinforcement: on the left: solution with L-bars; on the right: U-bar solution. With the reinforcement solution on the left, the L-bar ensures a good fixity including in a situation of cracking of the concrete; with the reinforcement solution on the right, the U-bar allows, after cracking of the junction, much larger differential rotations of the floor relative to the wall. The kinematics imposed on the boundaries of the junction core by the connected structural elements is nevertheless (to first order) controlled by that suited to the current zones of these structural elements of walls, slabs, rafts… The kinematics of the junction core itself can be represented with sufficient accuracy by simple strains in the transverse plane. Figure 1-b : Cross-section view of a reinforced-concrete junction connecting a wall and a floor: kinematics of the junction core. In this respect, wall–floor junctions behave differently from beam–column joints, which often exhibit cross-shaped cracking within the core. 2 First stage: the mesh The various stages of the data setup of a typical reinforced-concrete structural problem in Code_Aster are detailed here, for the two types of modelling. For each phase, the questions which may have to be asked and the information which must be supplied are specified. 2.1 Mesh for a model with plate finite elements This choice of mesh offers the advantage of simplicity; however it contains an arbitrary element, because one often uses the coordinates of the formwork planes and not the exact position of the mid-surfaces of the walls and of the floors. This has in addition the drawback of counting twice the volume which lies at the intersection of the two planes (thus in the modelling the mass will be counted twice and the spans will be exaggerated). It is accepted that two planes meshed with surface mesh cells (floor and wall) intersect along a straight line which belongs to the mesh of the structure. In order to model more precisely the junction between plane structural elements, it is therefore proposed to provide for the mesh of the “core” volume of the junction, in the form of a parallelepiped with transverse dimensions identical to the true thicknesses of the connected plane structural elements. On this volume a mesh will be produced as a single band of 8-node hexahedral mesh cells HEXA8. The transverse boundary planes between these mesh cells will contain the end nodes of the plane mesh cells of the geometry of the plane structural elements. Figure 2.1-a : Implementation of the discrete non-linear model in bending of a junction between two walls and two floors (current situation). On the left: cross-section view (plane (x,y) ); on the right: perspective view. 2.2 Mesh for a mixed model with solid and plate finite elements 3 Second stage: the data setup of the problem 3.1 Reading and possible enrichments of the mesh Figure 3.1-a : Cross-section view of a junction and its mesh. 3.2 Assignment of a model 3.2.1 Model with plate finite elements and with a cross junction 3.3 Characteristics of the structural elements 3.4 Choice of the constitutive law of the materials The choice of the constitutive law of the materials, either taken individually (concrete and steel), or after homogenisation for the reinforced concrete, determines the keywords to be filled in under DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01. The general survey U2.03.07 may be consulted. 3.4.1 Definition of the non-linear constitutive behaviour of a junction The constitutive behaviour JONC_ENDO_PLAS [R5.03.17] is used to model, on discrete elements (hinges), of type DIS_TR on SEG2 mesh cells, with two nodes, the non-linear constitutive behaviour of an out-of-plane bending connection. The non-linear relation is expressed in the plane of moment M – relative rotation \theta along the local axis \mathrm{Oz} . The phenomenology represented comprises: elasticity, then damage weakening the elastic stiffness, and kinematic hardening (irreversible strains). The paths in “positive” rotation and in “negative” rotation are distinguished, for which the degradation can occur in a non-symmetric manner according to the characteristics of the sections. Figure 3.4.1-a : Bending phenomenology of a reinforced-concrete walls–floors junction: crack opening and extension of the reinforcement according to the sense of the bending applied. 3.5 Definition of the characteristics of the materials 3.5.1 Definition of the parameters of the non-linear constitutive law of a junction There are eight of them (positive real numbers, all compulsory, cf. U4.43.01): - KE: elastic rotational stiffness {K}_{e}>0 ; - KP: plastic hardening slope {K}_{p}\le {K}_{e} ; - KDP: tangent stiffness {K}_{d}^{+}\in \left[{K}_{e},{K}_{p}\right] in the damaging phase for positive bending, - KDM: tangent stiffness {K}_{d}^{-}\in \left[{K}_{e},{K}_{p}\right] in the damaging phase for negative bending, - RDP: damage-threshold rotation {\theta}_{d}^{+}>0 in positive bending, - RDM: damage-threshold rotation {\theta}_{d}^{-}<0 in negative bending, - MYP: plasticity threshold {M}_{y}^{+} in positive bending, - MYM: plasticity threshold {M}_{y}^{-}\le {K}_{e}{\theta}_{d}^{-} in negative bending. Figure 3.5.1-a : Coxxxxxre 3.6 Definition of the kinematic relations In many situations, the design of the mesh of the structure and the assignment of the finite elements mean that kinematic continuity over all the degrees of freedom on the nodes common to the interfaces between structural elements is ensured automatically. The kinematic constraint equations are written in the local coordinate system of the discrete element: translation and rotation. 3.6.1 Definition of the local coordinate system It is recalled that Code_Aster uses a global coordinate system: that of the mesh of the whole structure. And every structural element has a local coordinate system, assigned automatically by Code_Aster by default, or else chosen by the user by means of the operator AFFE_CARA_ELEM / keyword ORIENTATION, cf. U4.42.01. 3.6.2 Simple perfect connection by relations on the degrees of freedom The straight line which belongs to the mesh of the structure and which supports the boundary between the plane of the floor and that of the wall, or between those of two walls, is duplicated: it is the support of pairs of nodes facing each other. The mesh must therefore have been built with nodes facing each other. The connection between the two plates is made by rigid-body relations: translation and rotations. The keyword LIAISON_COQUE of the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA U4.44.01 makes it possible to represent the connection between the two plates, by specifying the mesh-cell group or node group of the edge of the first plate, then the mesh-cell group or node group of the edge of the second plate. 3.6.3 Connection with releases of relations on the degrees of freedom The Release Tool of Salomé_Méca [SV1.05.01] makes it possible to build easily conditions of release of the connection between the degrees of freedom at the boundary between the plane of the floor and that of the wall, or between those of two walls. It uses a mesh and a Code_Aster model. One chooses the mesh-cell group or node group supporting the connection to be released. There are three possible options: - node–node release; - node–plane release; - plane–plane release; The degrees of freedom are in the global coordinate system of the mesh: DX, DY, DZ, DRX, DRY, DRZ. u2.03.11 Recommendations for the modelling of “SCS”, Steel Concrete Structures u2.03.11 Recommendations for the modelling of “SCS”, Steel Concrete Structures > Summary. The aim of this document is to provide recommendations for the modelling of “Steel Concrete Structures”. This document addresses the modelling of walls, of floors and of the junctions between the various structural elements. Different approaches are possible and the aim of this document is not to take the place of the engineer's analysis, but to allow the engineer to choose the modelling options while warning of certain modellings which can lead to “unrealistic” results. This document also addresses the constitutive laws and the post-processing. 1 Contents

u2.04.01 Advice on the use of STAT_NON_LINE u2.04.01 Advice on the use of STAT_NON_LINE > Summary. The aim of this note is to give some advice to a user wishing to carry out non-linear analyses with Code_Aster using the operator STAT_NON_LINE [U4.51.03]. General advice is given first. The remedies to be implemented for the main types of problem encountered are then specified. The problems in question are of the non-convergence type, or failure of an algorithm. Reference is also made to the documentation specific to each problem. 1 Introduction The purpose of this document is to help the user solve a quasi-static problem of mechanical or thermo-hydro-mechanical evolution of a structure in the non-linear regime, via the operator STAT_NON_LINE. A detailed presentation of the algorithm of this operator is given in its theoretical documentation R5.03.01. The 3 main types of non-linearity are the following: - non-linearity linked to the constitutive behaviour of the material (for example plastic); - non-linearity linked to the geometry (for example in large displacements); - non-linearity linked to frictional contact. In the 2nd part of this document, the main tools available to help the convergence of the analyses and to improve the quality of the results are set out in detail. The following parts are devoted to advice on use. In the 3rd part, general advice is given, common to the 3 types of non-linearity. In the 4th, 5th and 6th parts, advice dedicated to each of the 3 types of non-linearity is given: material, then geometric, and finally frictional contact. This advice refers to the tools mentioned in the 2nd part. 2 Tools to help convergence In the event of problems, several tools are available: - subdivision of the time step, - changing the matrices, - piloting, - line search, - changing the finite-element formulation. 2.1 Subdivision of the time step In general, the smaller the time step, the less non-linear the problem, and therefore the easier it is to solve. Subdivision of the time step is therefore an essential tool which makes it possible to get past the most common difficulties. Subdivision is activated by default in DEFI_LIST_INST U4.34.03. It is advisable always to activate it. Moreover, the smaller the time step, the smaller the time-discretisation error. 2.2 A judicious choice of the matrices In Newton's algorithm, it is possible to use different matrices in prediction and in correction and to update them more or less often. These choices are specified in STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword NEWTON U4.51.03. The most versatile and robust choice is to use the tangent matrix updated at each Newton iteration and to choose an elastic prediction. PREDICTION='ELASTIQUE' MATRICE='TANGENTE' (by default) REAC_ITER=1 REAC_INCR=1 (by default) In the event of a convergence problem in getting past a delicate time instant, it may be useful to switch from the tangent matrix to the unloading matrix if the time step becomes too small (that is, when the time step in question has been subdivided many times in succession). The value of the time step below which the unloading matrix is taken is given by the keyword PAS_MINI_ELAS. The update frequency of the unloading matrix is defined by REAC_ITER_ELAS. For a precise definition of the unloading matrix, see the factor keyword NEWTON of U4.51.03. 2.3 Piloting Piloting of the loading is a continuation method for Newton's method. Piloting makes it possible in particular to compute the response of a structure which would present instabilities, of geometric origin (buckling) as well as of material origin (softening). Its use is limited to simulations for which time does not play a physical role, which excludes a priori dynamic, or viscous, or thermo-mechanical problems. 2.4 Line search Newton's method supplies an increment of the unknowns, but this increment is valid only in a neighbourhood of the initialisation. The idea of the line search is to use the direction of the increment, while controlling the length of the advance in that direction. The advance step is then chosen by minimisation of a functional. This makes it possible in particular to avoid certain divergences of Newton's algorithm. However, activating the line search is “expensive”. It is recommended to activate it only when needed. In certain situations, the choice of partitioner can have an influence on the line search. It is therefore advisable either to increase ITER_GLOB_MAXI or to change partitioner. The SCOTCH partitioner tends to behave better than the METIS partitioner in certain cases (test case ssns115b). 2.5 A judicious choice of the finite-element formulation Not all finite elements are equal. Some elements behave better than others in certain situations U2.01.10. The choice of the finite elements is made in the operator AFFE_MODELE. 3 Advice common to the 3 types of non-linearity In this part, general advice is given on the solution of non-linear problems. 3.1 Management of the list of time instants The management of the list of time instants is specified via the operator DEFI_LIST_INST U4.34.03. By default, subdivision of the list of time instants is activated in the event of an error (in the contact, the constitutive law, the piloting, the factorisation...). It is also possible to trigger the subdivision of the time step when the increment of a quantity exceeds a fixed threshold (DELTA_GRANDEUR). This makes it possible, for example, to ensure that an internal variable does not vary too much over a time step. Another possible cause of subdivision is a failure of the residual to decrease during the Newton iterations (DIVE_RESI). This makes it possible to subdivide in the event of a problem without waiting until the end of the number of Newton iterations allowed. The so-called manual management of the list of time instants is the classical management: the analysis follows the list of time instants supplied by the user (with the possibility of subdivision). It is also possible to opt for an automatic management of the list of time instants. In this case, the user gives only a few passage time instants (time instants at which the loading changes, for example, or post-processing time instants). According to a first feedback of experience, automatic management of the time step [bib1]: - is of real interest if the user has no a priori knowledge of the time discretisation, - often makes it possible to save a considerable amount of time for “weakly” non-linear studies, that is studies which converge without advanced techniques (piloting, line search), - often fails for “strongly” non-linear studies if it is used alone; it appears necessary to combine it with another technique, such as the line search. This operator also makes it possible to extract from a previous analysis the list of the time instants actually computed and to refine it by a factor of 2. It is then possible to re-launch the same analysis with this new list, twice as fine, in order to control the error due to the time discretisation. 3.2 Management of the loadings The application of a loading in force, or in non-zero imposed displacement, is usually done gradually (by load stages). To this end, it is possible to define a loading of function type (of time), or else to multiply the loading by a ramp-type function (with FONC_MULT under the keyword EXCIT of STAT_NON_LINE), except in the case of piloting. The loads used for the boundary conditions (of zero imposed-displacement type) or for the contact are applied directly and do not require the definition of a function for a gradual application. 3.3 Management of the convergence of the global non-linear algorithm By default, the global non-linear solution algorithm is based on the Newton–Raphson method. The parameterisation of the convergence of Newton's algorithm is done under the factor keyword CONVERGENCE of STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03. The convergence of Newton's algorithm is characterised by the specification of a threshold value of the residual. When the value of the residual is below this threshold, the algorithm has converged. By default, it is the relative residual which is taken into account. The threshold is then given by the keyword RESI_GLOB_RELA ( 10^{-6} by default). It is strongly inadvisable to modify this convergence threshold . When the imposed loading is zero (in the case of total unloading, for example), the relative residual does not work and an attempt is made to switch automatically to an absolute convergence criterion (RESI_GLOB_MAXI). This operation is transparent to the user. In general it is inadvisable to fill in RESI_GLOB_MAXI. When these convergence criteria are not sufficient, it is possible to use finer criteria: a criterion which reasons component by component (RESI_COMP_RELA) or a criterion which reasons from a reference value for each quantity (RESI_REFE_RELA). 3.4 Management of archiving The question of archiving the fields computed implicitly is a less important question than in explicit dynamics, where the number of time steps is generally very high. Depending on the storage size available, and the number of fields one wishes to store, it is possible to estimate the number of time steps that can be stored. By default, all the time steps are archived, including the computation time instants newly created by automatic re-cutting of the time step. As this number cannot be determined in advance, it is advisable to archive only the time instants of the initial list of time instants. If this list still contains too many time instants, it is advisable to create a 2nd, reduced list, specific to archiving. If the initial list of time instants contains many time instants and automatic subdivision of the time step is not activated (which is not advisable), archiving can also be limited by an archiving frequency. It is also possible to reduce the bulk of the resultat data structure by extracting certain fields (operator EXTR_RESU). 3.5 Observation and monitoring of certain quantities It is possible to store in a table certain components of the fields computed on parts of the model at time instants of a list (known as the observation list) generally finer than the list of archived time instants. This feature can be activated in STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword OBSERVATION. This makes it possible to reduce the archiving requirements considerably. However, caution is required in the use of observation. Indeed, this feature was designed for a few points in the structure and it is not advisable to make several thousand observations at each time step, for performance reasons. It is also possible to follow the evolution of certain components of the computed fields during the Newton iterations and to display them in the convergence table. This feature can be activated in STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword SUIVI_DDL. 3.6 Display of information and performance A great deal of information is displayed by default in the message and result files (.mess and .resu). An essential piece of information is the convergence table displayed at each computation time instant. This table is very useful and makes it possible in particular to identify certain convergence anomalies. The operator STAT_NON_LINE displays the size of the matrix (number of equations of the system). Depending on the size of the matrix, the use of an iterative solver (such as PETSC) will allow a gain in time. For information, an iterative solver is considered to be faster than a direct solver (the default) from about 200000 equations in 3D. The counterpart of the use of an iterative solver is that robustness is not guaranteed. It should be noted that the use of PETSC requires an MPI version of Code_Aster (even if only one processor is used). The use of parallelism can also be effective if the time spent in STAT_NON_LINE is predominant with respect to the total time of the run. For this, it is sufficient to choose a suitable solver (example: MUMPS, PETSC), an MPI version of Code_Aster and to specify the number of processes in Astk. A great deal of advice on parallelism is given in the document U2.08.06. Finer information on the times spent in each part of the solution is also displayed, and can serve to parameterise the run better (time, memory, number of processors...).
