For this, the reader is referred to the documentation U1.03.03. 4 Material non-linearity This part deals with the problems most frequently encountered when using non-linear constitutive laws. 4.1 Parameters linked to the solution of the constitutive behaviour Most of the constitutive laws of Code_Aster are integrated analytically. In the event of an error in the integration of the constitutive law, there is therefore no numerical parameter on which one can act. The usual solution consists in re-cutting the global time step (or in choosing a finer list of time instants). Certain constitutive laws are solved locally via an iterative numerical method, for which the user can choose the maximum residual allowed and the maximum number of local iterations. Most of the time, the default parameters (RESI_INTE_RELA = {10}^{-6} and ITER_INTE_MAXI = 20) are sufficient. In the event of an error in the integration of the law, one can, as previously, subdivide the time step, but also allow additional local iterations (ITER_INTE_MAXI). For example, for MONOCRISTAL, it is common to allow 100 or 200 local iterations. The choice of the residual is more delicate. Indeed, it is important that the constitutive behaviour be integrated correctly. This means that it is imperative not to increase the residual beyond the default value ( {10}^{-4} for example), except for the constitutive behaviours integrated by an explicit algorithm. On the other hand, it is sometimes advisable to tighten the residual (for example RESI_INTE_RELA = {10}^{-10} ). In fact, depending on the way in which the constitutive behaviour is implemented, the residual does not have the same physical meaning (stress, strain...). One must then refer to the reference documentation of the constitutive law in question. 4.2 Management of plastic incompressibility If the material is incompressible ( \nu >0.45 ) or in the case of large plastic strains, oscillations in the stresses or in the trace of the stresses may appear. Certain special finite elements, such as the under-integrated elements or the mixed elements, make it possible to treat these problems U2.01.10. If the use of under-integrated elements does not settle the problem, then the use of the 2-field mixed formulation (displacement and pressure) in small strains, and of the 3-field mixed formulation in large strains, is advised. Note that the latter works only on quadratic meshes. 4.3 Unloading In the case of unloading, convergence problems of Newton's algorithm may be encountered. It is advisable to use the elastic prediction (in STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword NEWTON). It is also useful to activate the subdivision of the time step in the event of a singular matrix (this is automatic in version 11, but it must be activated by hand in the previous versions via STOP_SINGULIER = 'DECOUPE' in STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword SOLVEUR). 4.4 Plane stresses The treatment of the plane-stress condition is carried out in the general framework by the Deborst method. It is advisable to update the tangent matrix often (every one to three Newton iterations). In certain cases, convergence is reached for Newton's algorithm, but not for the verification of the plane-stress state, which leads to additional iterations, or even to an excessive re-cutting of the time step. It is then advisable to activate an additional loop in order to satisfy the plane stresses better during the Newton iterations: ITER_CPLAN_MAXI must be chosen at least equal to 5 U4.51.11. 4.5 Damage (softening problems) For the treatment of damage problems, a great deal of advice is given in U2.05.06. In general, it is advisable to use piloting, possibly together with the mixed line search. For certain constitutive laws (ENDO_FRAGILE and ENDO_ISOT_BETON), the IMPLEX method is proposed as an alternative to Newton's method. This method is activated in STAT_NON_LINE under the keyword NEWTON. This method is based on an explicit extrapolation of the internal variables in order to determine the displacements from which the constitutive behaviour is integrated implicitly. The vanishing of equilibrium is not verified. Because of this, it introduces an approximation of the solution but makes it possible to guarantee the robustness of the analysis. An error control and an optimisation of the time steps are possible via the operator DEFI_LIST_INST, by choosing an automatic management of the time step and a mode of computation of the time steps specific to IMPLEX. From a practical point of view, the method imposes an update of the matrix at each increment and a single iteration. Before any use of the IMPLEX method, the document R5.03.81 must imperatively be consulted. 4.6 Thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) THM problems involve quite particular notions. It is advisable to consult the documentation U2.04.05. Some general advice for the solution is given here. The initialisation of the fields is a delicate stage to which close attention must be paid (ETAT_INIT). It is necessary to use the updated tangent matrix. In the event of a convergence problem, it can be very useful to activate the line search (mixed, preferably). The line search does not, however, systematically improve convergence; it must therefore be handled with caution, inasmuch as it can increase the CPU cost. 5 Geometric non-linearity This part deals with the problems most frequently encountered during analyses with geometric non-linearities. 5.1 Buckling The operator STAT_NON_LINE makes it possible to compute a stability criterion via the keyword CRIT_STAB=_F (TYPE='FLAMBEMENT'). The user's guide for buckling U2.08.04 gives a great deal of advice on setting up a stability analysis. Some general advice is given here. In general, the stability analysis is conducted on updated stiffness matrices. In practice, the calls to CRIT_STAB must be limited for reasons of computation cost, by limiting the time instants on which the stability analysis is carried out. In addition, it is judicious to use CRIT_STAB only on the time intervals where the possibility of instabilities is suspected. The time step should also be refined properly on the approach to this zone. By default, 3 critical loads are computed (NB_FREQ). Often the first one may suffice. One particular point linked to instability is the choice of the piloting technique of the algorithm. Indeed, classical piloting in force is not suitable. On the approach to a limit point, the load increment must be reduced and the maximum number of iterations increased. It is also advisable to use arc-length piloting. 5.2 Large strains The keyword DEFORMATION under COMPORTEMENT makes it possible to define the assumptions used for the computation of the strains. By default, small displacements and small strains are considered (DEFORMATION = 'PETIT'). This means that one remains within the small-perturbation hypothesis: small displacements, small rotations, small strains (lower than about 5%). When this hypothesis is no longer verified, the strain model must be changed. For slender structures (shells, plates, beams), it frequently happens that one is in large displacements and large rotations but small strains. One then uses DEFORMATION = 'GROT_GDEP'. The treatment of large strains differs according to the type of element and the constitutive law. The large-strain model of Simo and Miehe (DEFORMATION = 'SIMO_MIEHE') is advised for the constitutive relations VMIS_ISOT_LINE, VMIS_ISOT_TRAC, ROUSSELIER and all the constitutive behaviours with isotropic hardening only, associated with a material undergoing metallurgical phase changes (relations META_X_IL_XXX_XXX and META_X_INL_XXX_XXX). For the other constitutive laws, the large-strain model of Miehe and Apel (DEFORMATION = 'GDEF_LOG') is advised, theoretically applicable to any constitutive law for the 3D and 2D modellings. More detailed explanations are to be found in the user's guide for the non-linear constitutive behaviours U4.51.11, in the paragraph DEFORMATION. 6 Frictional-contact non-linearity The definition of the frictional-contact load is the subject of a specific operator: DEFI_CONTACT U4.44.11. Besides the choice of the entities in contact, this operator makes it possible to choose the type of formulation of the contact problem (discrete or continuous), parameters for the pairing operation and parameters for the solution phase. A great deal of advice on data setup is available in the document U2.04.04, in particular on the choice of the master and slave surfaces. Taking the contact conditions into account, with or without friction, leads to non-linear problems, which can be a source of difficulties in the solution of STAT_NON_LINE. One of the first difficulties is the blocking of the rigid-body modes. Indeed, the frictional-contact conditions do not take part in the blocking of the rigid modes. The rigid modes must therefore be blocked without taking the contact conditions into account (apart from rare exceptions). A poor blocking of the rigid-body modes leads to the appearance of zero pivots during the factorisation of the matrix. Advice is given in the documentation U2.04.04. Caution: certain contact formulations require a particular solver. In particular, in the discrete formulation, the CONTRAINTE method requires a direct solver (MULT_FRONT or MUMPS). In general, the use of the line search with contact is not advised. In the event of coupling with other non-linearities, it is advisable to make sure that each non-linearity taken separately converges. If problems appear only when the non-linearities are coupled, it is advisable to work with the updated tangent matrix and an elastic prediction. A comparative benchmark between Code_Aster and other commercial software packages was carried out in 2010 on 5 frictional-contact problems [2]. This benchmark made it possible in particular to bring to light oscillations of the contact pressure for the continuous formulation in the case of incompatible meshes, a defect from which the commercial software packages used also suffer. It is then recommended to extract the contact pressures from the stresses on the boundary, or else to use compatible meshes. 7 Bibliography [1] S. Geniaut, First feedback on the automatic management of the time step in STAT_NON_LINE, CR-AMA-09.268, 2009 [2] T. De Soza, Review of the “Contact/Friction” work package in 2010 (MNAM project), CR-AMA-11.049, 2011

u2.04.02 Advice on the implementation of non-linear analyses u2.04.02 Advice on the implementation of non-linear analyses > Summary. The aim of this document is to give advice to a user wishing to carry out non-linear analyses with Code_Aster . The user of linear analyses will also find useful information and advice in it. The following aspects will be addressed: - mesh and modelling, - loadings and boundary conditions, - materials and constitutive laws, - non-linear solution, - memory/time management and optimisation, - error control and quality. This document does not deal with questions specific to dynamics. 1 Mesh and modelling The choice of the finite elements has a direct influence on the solution. By choice, one means the choice of the degree of the finite-element approximation as well as the choice of a formulation. The degree of the approximation being generally linked to the degree of the mesh cells, the following paragraphs deal with the choice of the degree of the mesh and the choice of a finite-element formulation, with a particular point for incompressibility problems. 1.1 General points on the choice of the degree of the mesh and the choice of the finite elements In general, the use of a linear mesh is advised in thermal analysis and the use of a quadratic mesh is advised in mechanics. The command CREA_MAILLAGE (LINE_QUAD and QUAD_LINE) makes it possible to pass from a linear mesh to a quadratic mesh and vice versa, but it does not make it possible to generate quadratic elements with curved edges. It is moreover preferable to generate the quadratic elements directly with the meshing tool (the meshing module of Salome-Meca, for example). For fracture mechanics, the use of Barsoum elements at the crack tip improves the quality of the result (command MODI_MAILLAGE / NOEUD_QUART). The choice of the finite elements is made in the command AFFE_MODELE. In thermal analysis, it is advisable to use lumped elements (_DIAG). In mechanics, the finite elements classically used are the isoparametric elements (3D, D_PLAN, C_PLAN, AXIS). However, these elements are ill-suited to quasi-incompressible problems. The choice of a formulation answering this problem is the subject of the following paragraph. For more details, see u2.01.10 1.2 Choice of a formulation to treat quasi-incompressible problems A problem is quasi-incompressible if the Poisson's ratio is close to 0.5 ( \nu >0,45 ) or if the plastic strain rate is high. This results in an oscillation of the trace of the stresses. There are 6 formulations for treating this problem in Code_Aster , the choice of which depends on the type of mesh cells, on the strain model and on the quality/computation-cost ratio. The possible formulations are: - in small strains: _SI, _INCO_UP, _INCO_UPG, INCO_UPO - in large strains: _INCO_UP, _INCO_UPG. All the formulations are compatible with the modellings 3D, D_PLAN and AXIS, but in plane stresses (C_PLAN) only the under-integrated formulation (_SI) is possible. The table below presents the compatibility between quasi-incompressible formulation and type of mesh cell (limited to the main 3D mesh cells). | | _SI | _INCO_UP | _INCO_UPG | _INCO_UPO | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | HEXA20 | X | X | X | | | PENTA15 | | X | X | | | PYRAM13 | | | | | | TETRA10 | X | X | X | | | HEXA8 | X | | | X | | PENTA6 | | | | X | | PYRAM5 | | | | X | | TETRA4 | | X | | X | In the general case, it is therefore necessary to mix different formulations in order to cover all the types of mesh cell (for example, as no formulation handles the PYRAM13 mesh cells, an isoparametric modelling must also be assigned). In the case where one remains in small strains, it is advisable to use a mixture of formulations (the mesh being able to contain several types of mesh cell): | | quality | cost | | --- | --- | --- | | MODELISATION=('3D', '3D_INCO_UPG', '3D_INCO_UPO') | +++ | +++ | | MODELISATION=('3D', '3D_INCO_UP' , '3D_INCO_UPO') | ++ | ++ | | MODELISATION=('3D', '3D_SI' , '3D_INCO_UPO') | | | For more details, see u2.01.10 2 Loadings, boundary conditions, initial conditions 2.1 Core of the problem The loadings and boundary conditions are important for a good modelling. Their influence on the results is most of the time direct, so that their application can be checked by a simple preliminary analysis, for example by means of MECA_STATIQUE, or by visualising the boundary conditions via the keyword CONCEPT of IMPR_RESU in MED format. As regards the boundary conditions, it is often a matter of introducing the minimum of them in order to block the rigid-body displacements, and thus to avoid having floating bodies in the structure, which would cause a zero pivot or a singular matrix during the solution. Certain boundary conditions are non-linear, for example unilateral contact. Their verification therefore cannot be done by means of a first linear analysis (MECA_STATIQUE): the various objects in contact must not have a rigid-body motion u2.04.04. If this is the case, zero pivots can be avoided by adding discrete elements (springs) of low stiffness. The loadings (other than the blockings) may consist either of imposed-displacement conditions, or of imposed forces, or of an imposed initial-field type. In every case, it is important to represent reality well. The conditions of symmetry or of antisymmetry may usefully be used [1]. In general, a condition of imposed-displacement type does not give the same results as a condition of imposed-force type: an imposed displacement on a part of the boundary imposes that the (imposed) displacement be constant in space on that part, and therefore brings stiffness, or even singularities. Take the example of the punch indentation of a solid mass: the imposed displacement on the edge of the punch induces stress singularities of the same nature as those encountered at the tip of a crack. Figure 2.1-1: Example of a force–displacement curve Figure 2.1-2: punch indentation with imposed displacement Moreover, for non-linear analyses, the conduct of the analysis is not the same: in the event of softening or of a limit load, the imposed-force loading may be inadmissible (beyond the limit load). Take for example the punch indentation (see and ): the response in terms of the resultant force on the punch as a function of the displacement shows that the closer the imposed force gets to the limit load, the more difficult the convergence will be, until it becomes impossible beyond the limit load. If the correct modelling requires an imposed force to be applied, the problem can be solved via the piloting of the imposed force with respect to the displacement of a point or of a set of points (continuation method or arc-length method) (see r5.03.80 r5.03.80). The user's guides relating to the application of the loadings and boundary conditions are u4.44.01 u4.44.01 u4.44.01 and :ref: u4.44.03 u4.44.03 u4.44.03. 2.2 Precautions for the application of the loadings It is useful, for the application of the loadings, to go through the various keywords of u4.44.01 u4.44.01. Beware of the vocabulary: in particular, the loadings of type FORCE_FACE, PRES_REP, FORCE_CONTOUR, FORCE_ARETE, FORCE_INTERNE, FORCE_COQUE, FORCE_TUYAU correspond to distributed forces (line, surface, volume) and are expressed in units of stress (for example \mathit{Pa} in SI units). Only the FORCE_NODALE are expressed in units of force ( N ), and the distributed forces of beams (FORCE_POUTRE) in units of force divided by a length. As regards the pressures (PRES_REP, FORCE_COQUE/PRES), the pressure applied is positive in the direction opposite to the normal to the element. It is strongly advisable to reorient these normals via the operator MODI_MAILLAGE, keywords ORIE_PEAU_ , ORIE_NORM_COQUE. For 2D and 3D continuous media, the use of point forces (FORCE_NODALE) is to be avoided, because it always leads to singularities. The application of loads which are a function of time can be carried out in two ways: - either by defining constant loads, then by applying a multiplying coefficient which is a function of time to these loads during the solution (keyword FONC_MULT under EXCIT in STAT_NON_LINE), - or by defining directly loads which are a function of time via AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F. In the case where the loadings are of imposed-displacement type, they can be introduced either by AFFE_CHAR_MECA(_F), or by AFFE_CHAR_CINE(_F). The use of this latter command allows a saving in computation time which can be appreciable in non-linear analysis (because it does not add Lagrange multipliers, so there are fewer equations to solve). The command variables are not part of the commands AFFE_CHAR_MECA(_F). They are nevertheless, in many modellings, comparable to loadings: for example thermal expansion can by itself generate states of stress and of strain leading to non-linearities of the constitutive behaviour. The command variables are applied via AFFE_MATERIAU. A modelling precaution concerning these command variables must however be pointed out here: indeed, as soon as the analysis is incremental, STAT_NON_LINE uses at each time step the increment of the command variable in order to compute the corresponding strains (cf. for example r5.03.02). In general, it is preferable that at the initial time instant the structure be unstressed and unstrained. If this is not the case, a preliminary time instant must be added at which the structure is at rest; see for example the test FORMA30 v7.20.101. If stresses due to the command variables are detected at the initial time instant, the following alarm is obtained: : -> The initial command variables induce incompatible stresses: the initial state (before the first computation time instant) is such that the command variables (temperature, hydration, drying...) lead to unbalanced stresses. -> Risk & Advice: in the case of an incremental solution, only the variation of the command variables between the previous time instant and the current time instant is considered. Possible incompatible stresses due to these initial command variables are therefore not taken into account. To take these stresses into account you can: - start from an earlier fictitious time instant at which all the command variables are zero or equal to the reference values - choose suitable reference values For more information, see the documentation of STAT_NON_LINE (U4.51.03) keyword EXCIT, and the test FORMA30 (V7.20.101). 2.3 The various types of boundary condition The simplest boundary conditions serve mainly to introduce symmetry conditions, on the one hand, and to prevent rigid-body motions, on the other. When they are of imposed degree-of-freedom type, one can use either AFFE_CHAR_MECA or (in order to optimise the computation time) AFFE_CHAR_CINE u2.01.02. A methodological piece of advice: it is always preferable to apply the boundary conditions on mesh-cell groups rather than on node groups or on lists of nodes or of mesh cells. Indeed, the mesh-cell groups correspond to geometric zones, and are preserved during a refinement of the mesh (manual or by means of Homard), whereas the node groups are modified. This is why in AFFE_CHAR_MECA the keywords DDL_IMPO, FACE_IMPO, LIAISON_UNIF, as well as all the keywords of AFFE_CHAR_CINE, include the keyword GROUP_MA, which is therefore to be preferred. It is sometimes necessary to impose linear relations between degrees of freedom. The keywords LIAISON_ of AFFE_CHAR_MECA make it possible to introduce this type of relation. The elementary relations can be defined by means of LIAISON_DDL, but this becomes tedious if the equations to be written are numerous. Higher-level features are available, for example: - LIAISON_SOLIDE to rigidify a part of the structure, (in small strains and small displacements only) r3.03.02; - LIAISON_UNIF to ensure that a part of the boundary will keep the same displacement (unknown a priori); u4.44.01 u4.44.01 - LIAISON_MAIL, LIAISON_GROUP to connect two edges, - and other keywords specific to AFFE_CHAR_MECA. In addition it is possible to connect (in the energy sense) modellings of different natures, via LIAISON_ELEM and several options (in small strains and small displacements only) - '2D_POU','3D_POU', beams or discrete elements with 2D or 3D elements r3.03.03; - 'COQ_TUYAU','3D_TUYAU', pipe elements with plates and shells, 3D; - 'COQ_POU', beams or discrete elements with plates and shells r3.03.06. Note : in certain cases, the boundary conditions or the loadings of imposed-displacement type are not suitable because they bring too much local stiffness. It may be of interest to replace these conditions by a relation between the part of the boundary concerned and a discrete element, on which the imposed-displacement conditions or a resultant wrench of imposed forces will be applied. This means that the displacements of the boundary will be equal on average to the displacement of the discrete element, without introducing parasitic stresses. On the other hand, this procedure introduces additional degrees of freedom (Lagrange multipliers), so the solution of the linear systems can be more costly. Unilateral contact, with or without friction, is a particular type of boundary condition. It is strongly non-linear, and its treatment in STAT_NON_LINE / DYNA_NON_LINE requires additional iterations in order to obtain convergence. It is strongly advisable to consult the document u2.04.04 u2.04.04 u2.04.04 in order to model these phenomena correctly. 2.4 The initial conditions In AFFE_CHAR_MECA, it is possible to define loadings of mean strains or of mean stresses, globally uniform (keywords PRE_EPSI, PRE_SIGM). These loadings must not be confused with the initial strains and stresses used in non-linear analysis, because these quantities do not intervene directly in the expression of the constitutive law, but only on the right-hand side. The initial fields of stresses, displacements and internal variables are to be supplied directly in STAT_NON_LINE (keyword ETAT_INIT). In order to build these fields, it may be useful to consult the document u2.01.09. 3 Materials and constitutive behaviours 3.1 Choice of the constitutive law The choice of the constitutive law depends of course on the material being modelled, but also on the phenomena to be treated: for example, one and the same steel will be elastoplastic at low temperature, and viscoplastic at high temperature. The values of the parameters of these laws (in DEFI_MATERIAU) are often identified over a range of strain, of rate and of temperature which is quite specific. - For the elastoplastic constitutive behaviours, see u2.04.03 - For the laws with damage (the case of concrete, for example), see u2.05.06 u2.05.06 - For metallurgy, see u2.03.04 - For porous media in THM, see u2.04.05 and r7.01.11 - For the use of CZM elements, see u2.05.07 u2.05.07 3.2 Keywords of COMPORTEMENT 3.2.1 DEFORMATION This keyword makes it possible to define the assumptions used for the computation of the strains: by default, small displacements and small strains are considered. The type of strain used can have a great influence on the analysis as soon as a strain component exceeds a few % (typically 5%). - PETIT : small strains, small displacements. Linearity of the strain operator. GROT_GDEP v6.02.134 v6.02.134). As regards hyperelastic laws of the ELAS_VMIS type, they are not suited to large strains (loss of existence of the solution, see §2.1 of r5.03.20). One must use either a large-strain model with VMIS_ISOT, or the constitutive behaviour ELAS_HYPER. GDEF_LOG u4.51.11 u4.51.11). The stress–strain relation being hypoelastic, this formulation is limited to small elastic strains (but large plastic strains). - SIMO_MIEHE : large-strain model of the constitutive laws based on a Von Mises criterion with isotropic hardening, and all the constitutive behaviours with isotropic hardening associated with a material undergoing metallurgical phase changes. The elastic stress–strain relation is hyperelastic, which makes it possible to treat large elastic strains (provided that this makes sense for the material used). - other formulations exist, see u4.51.11 u4.51.11. 3.2.2 ALGO_INTE, ITER_INTE_MAXI, RESI_INTE_RELA, ITER_INTE_PAS Makes it possible to specify the type of integration scheme used to solve the non-linear equation or system of equations formed by the constitutive equations of the constitutive models with internal variables. A default solution method is provided for each constitutive behaviour. However, it is possible to modify the default solution method for a certain number of constitutive behaviours (see u4.51.11). In the case of an iterative solution (that is if ALGO_INTE is not ANALYTIQUE), the keywords ITER_INTE_MAXI and RESI_INTE_RELA define the maximum number of iterations and the relative residual for integrating the constitutive behaviour. If this integration fails, it is possible to subdivide the time step, either locally (keyword ITER_INTE_PAS) or globally (command DEFI_LIST_INST). The default value of ITER_INTE_MAXI is 20. This may be insufficient for certain constitutive behaviours (MONOCRISTAL, for example). Do not hesitate in this case to increase this parameter (100, for example). On the other hand it is strongly inadvisable to increase RESI_INTE_RELA ( {10}^{-6} by default), otherwise unconverged solutions will be obtained. Local subdivision of the time step is a means of improving the robustness of the local integration; on the other hand it does not make it possible to supply a consistent tangent matrix (loss of the quadratic convergence of the global problem). 3.2.3 POST_ITER='CRIT_RUPT' Definition of a failure criterion in critical stress, in post-processing of the Newton iterations, at each time step. If the largest mean principal stress in an element exceeds a given threshold {\sigma}_{c} , Young's modulus is divided at the following time step by a coefficient. These two coefficients are defined under the keyword CRIT_RUPT of the operator DEFI_MATERIAU. 3.2.4 RESI_RADI_RELA Measure of the error due to the discretisation in time, linked directly to the rotation of the normal to the yield surface. The angle between the normal to the plasticity criterion at the beginning of the time step and the normal to the plasticity criterion computed at the end of the time step is calculated. The time step is cut ( via DEFI_LIST_INST) if the error is greater than the tolerance defined by the user. This criterion is operational for the elastoplastic Von Mises constitutive behaviours with isotropic, linear kinematic and mixed hardening, and for the elasto-visco-plastic Chaboche constitutive behaviours. 4 Non-linear solution The 3 main types of non-linearity in Code_Aster are the following: - non-linearity linked to the constitutive behaviour of the material (for example plastic); - non-linearity linked to the geometry (for example in large displacements); - non-linearity linked to frictional contact. The general advice on the solution of non-linear problems is the subject of a specific document, the reading of which is strongly recommended: u2.04.01 u2.04.01 u2.04.01. Before any non-linear analysis, it is essential to make sure that the analysis works correctly in linear elasticity. The non-linearities can then be added one after another. The major advice on the time discretisation and the numerical parameters of the non-linear solution is recalled briefly in the following paragraphs. 4.1 Non-linearity and time discretisation The solution of a non-linear problem generally requires the external loading to be applied progressively, by load increment. Thus time (or pseudo-time in quasi-statics) is discretised into time steps and to each time step there corresponds a load increment (see § 2.2). The smaller the time step, the less non-linear the problem and therefore the easier it is to solve. In order to allow the subdivision of the time step in the event of a failure of convergence, it is essential to use the command DEFI_LIST_INST (for more details on the management of the list of time instants, see paragraph §3.1 of the document u2.04.01) In order to check the consistency of the data (system of units, boundary conditions, elementary characteristics, effect of the command variables), it is always useful to carry out a first linear elastic analysis (STAT_NON_LINE/RELATION='ELAS', or MECA_STATIQUE), before any non-linear study, and then to add the non-linearities one after another. 4.2 Numerical parameters for the non-linear solution algorithm By default, the non-linear solution algorithm is based on the Newton–Raphson method (STAT_NON_LINE / METHODE='NEWTON'). It is advisable to use a tangent matrix updated at each Newton iteration: REAC_ITER=1, in order to facilitate the convergence of the algorithm (see paragraph §2.2 of the document u2.04.01). It is strongly recommended not to relax the convergence criterion of Newton's method (RESI_GLOB_RELA= 10^{-6} by default). Other convergence criteria are also available (see paragraph §3.3 of the document u2.04.01). Notes: - For softening problems, Code_Aster offers the possibility of using a method alternative to the Newton–Raphson method: this is the IMPLEX method, which is a robust but approximate method (see paragraph §4.5 of the document u2.04.01). - For an optimisation of the computation time, Code_Aster offers the possibility of using an inexact Newton method (provided that the linear solver chosen is an iterative solver): this is the NEWTON_KRYLOV method. 5 Memory/time management and optimisation Before speaking of optimisation, the first question which arises is how to choose the execution parameters in Astk: total memory and time, so that the first launching of the run finishes correctly. Then, once the run has gone through a first time, it will always be possible to try to optimise it according to the information recovered from the 1st run. 5.1 First execution of a run Knowledge of the size of the memory available is necessary. The answer depends of course on the execution machine: centralised server, local machine.... On a local machine, it is always possible to allow the maximum memory available, whereas on the centralised server it may be opportune not to request too much memory, otherwise one has to wait for the associated job class to become free. Estimate of the memory required : in quasi-statics, the total memory is generally a function of the size of the linear system or systems to be solved. For the isoparametric finite elements, it is fairly easy to estimate the global size of these systems. The number of degrees of freedom can be estimated by the relation: (number of nodes of the mesh) x (dimension of the problem (2 or 3)) This relation does not take into account the degrees of freedom relating to the dualised boundary conditions. But in general this share is small. If the finite elements are not isoparametric (mixed formulations, for example), this estimate is more delicate. In any event, the size of the linear systems is displayed at each solution in the .mess file: total number of equations, or the matrix is of size n equations. It is important to know this number (although on its own it is not always a totally reliable indicator, because the memory and the time required to solve a linear system depend on many other parameters: bandwidth, number of non-zero terms in the matrix, renumberer... but that would take us too far). Therefore, if one does not know how to estimate the size of the linear system, it is useful to launch the study a first time in degraded mode : reading of the mesh, assignment of the finite elements, of the material, and solution (MECA_STATIQUE or STAT_NON_LINE) with the direct solver MUMPS. Launch the simplified study in interactive mode with interactive monitoring, then stop the run once the information on the size of the system is known. In the ideal case 1, one must have about 30 GB available in order to get through a run with one million degrees of freedom (the case of the cube meshed with HEXA8, one face of which is clamped by dualisation), the minimum memory 2 being 9 GB. The table below gives orders of magnitude of the “ideal” (or optimal) memory and of the minimum memory for solving a system of a given size (with the direct solver MUMPS). | Number of degrees of freedom | Minimum memory | “Ideal” memory | | --- | --- | --- | | 200000 | 1 GB | 4 GB | | 400000 | 2.5 GB | 9 GB | | 600000 | 4 GB | 15 GB | | 800000 | 6 GB | 23 GB | | 1000000 | 9 GB | 31 GB | Once the memory required has been estimated, the complete run can be launched with the direct solver MUMPS. Following this 1st run, it is very useful to look at: - In the .mess file, the total memory (JEVEUX + python + external libraries) used by the run: this information is displayed at the end of the file: see MAXIMUM DE MEMOIRE UTILISEE PAR LE PROCESSUS; - In the .resu file: the solution time (MECA_STATIQUE / STAT_NON_LINE) relative to the total time of the run. 5.2 Optimisation of a run The optimisation of a run on the aspects of time and memory is an interesting operation but a somewhat delicate one, because there is no miracle recipe. Moreover it is not always easy to distinguish between optimisation of the memory and optimisation of the computation time, so in the following paragraphs some lines of optimisation are given “in the broad sense” and the reader is referred to the appropriate documents. Parallelism The use of parallelism is certainly the easiest and safest solution for reducing the computation time (and sometimes also the memory required). Parallelism consists in executing operations on several processors at the same time. Setting up parallelism is effective only if the time spent in STAT_NON_LINE is predominant with respect to the total time of the run. For this, it is sufficient to choose a suitable solver (example: MUMPS, PETSC), an MPI version of Code_Aster and to specify the number of processors in Astk (Options/mpi_nbcpu menu). On the centralised server aster4, it is advisable to begin by choosing mpi_nbcpu=2, to observe the gain in time, then to start again with mpi_nbcpu=4, then possibly mpi_nbcpu=8. It is possible to choose mpi_nbcpu=16, but one risks waiting a long time before all these processors are available, and therefore before the run starts (it all depends on the machine load!). A great deal of advice on parallelism is given in the document u2.08.06. Finer information on the times spent in each part of the solution is also displayed, and can serve to parameterise the run better (time, memory, number of processors...). For this, the reader is referred to the documentation u1.03.03. The linear solver Depending on the size of the matrix, the use of an iterative solver (such as PETSC) in place of a direct solver will allow a gain in time. For information, an iterative solver is considered to be faster than a direct solver (the default) from about 200000 equations in 3D. But this depends on the type of structure 3. The counterpart of the use of an iterative solver is that robustness is not guaranteed. It should be noted that the use of PETSC requires an MPI version of Code_Aster (even if only one processor is used). From a certain problem size (a few million degrees of freedom), the use of a direct solver becomes impossible and it is essential to use an iterative solver. In the event of failure of the solution by an iterative solver, the levers for action are the choice of another preconditioner (simple-precision direct preconditioner LDLT_SP by default, incomplete preconditioner LDLT_INC, …), and the choice of another iterative algorithm (GMRES by default, CG, CR, …). A great deal of advice on the choice of the solver is given in u2.08.03. Management of the global database In the event of the memory limit being exceeded, one can act on the archiving of the results. Archiving (factor keyword ARCHIVAGE of STAT_NON_LINE) makes it possible to reduce appreciably the size of the databases by selecting the time instants saved. By default, everything is archived (even the time instants coming from the subdivision of the time step). During the phase of setting up a study, this can prove useful, but too costly in memory. The observation and the monitoring of certain quantities can answer the archiving need in an effective manner (see §3.4 of u2.04.01). Once the study has been set up, archiving can be restricted to a limited number of time steps (post-processing time instants, for example). In order to reduce the bulk of the resultat data structure, it is possible to choose a posteriori the fields to be archived, either by indicating the fields to be kept, or by indicating the fields to be excluded (command EXTR_RESU). The extraction can also be done on a part of the mesh or of the model. The command DETRUIRE can also be used to destroy a concept. Following these extraction or deletion operations, RETASSAGE='OUI' must be specified in the command FIN in order actually to recover the disk space associated with the global database. To reduce the size of the result files in MED format (.rmed): use IMPR_RESU/RESTREINT. With a view to a restart, one can in certain cases replace the database by the printout of MED fields. The “restart” will then begin with the commands DEBUT then LIRE_RESU. Ideal meaning here IN_CORE memory management Minimum meaning here for an OUT_OF_CORE management A cube penalises the direct solver, whereas a thin or slender structure gives an advantage to the direct solver 6 Quality control In general, the overall quality of a study depends on several factors. Among the causes which can impair the quality of a study, one can distinguish in particular: - the uncertainties on the data, - the modelling choices (passage from the physics to the numerical model), - the discretisation errors, once the data have been established and the modelling chosen. 6.1 Uncertainties on the data On this point the uncertainties can be multiple, because they can concern each of the following aspects. - The material data: once the constitutive law has been chosen, and its parameters correctly identified on appropriate characterisation tests, an uncertainty may remain on the values of the parameters of this law, due to the variability of the materials. - The exact geometry of the structure to be modelled may contain uncertainties: the real dimensions are not those planned at the design stage, or else the degradation of the shape of a part leads to a poorly controlled geometry (quite apart from any aspect of discretisation). - The loadings (including thermal ones, or those due to other command variables: irradiation, hydration, drying, etc.) and the boundary conditions may present numerous uncertainties. - The initial conditions, in particular those due to manufacture (residual stresses, initial hardening). For each of the uncertain parameters mentioned above, it will sometimes be necessary to carry out a sensitivity analysis: - either the user carries out a few simulations for extreme values of the uncertain parameters, which is sufficient in the case of a monotonic variation of the result with these parameters (but this is not always the case: for example the dependence of the stresses on the extreme values of temperature, with material coefficients which are a function of them, is not trivial.) Let us point out in this connection the possibility of carrying out parametric analyses very simply with Code_Aster (cf. u2.08.07) - or, in the case of highly variable parameters, the user carries out a mechanical reliability analysis, with OpenTurns ( http://www.openturns.org) coupled to Code_Aster , in the Salome-Meca platform sv1.04.01). 6.2 Modelling choices and verification of the data Even if the data are reliable, the quality of the results also depends on choices made by the user relating to the simulation to be carried out. The preceding paragraphs describe these choices. Let us recall a few general pieces of advice: - Beyond the mesh, it may be useful to check the data of the analysis, for example to visualise the boundary conditions and loadings (sense and place of application), the assignments of the materials, and the elementary characteristics (orientation of the beams, thicknesses, sections). For this, use IMPR_RESU/CONCEPT. - Other checks can be carried out directly in the command file; for example, to check the consistency of the system of units, the boundary conditions and the elementary characteristics, it is always useful to carry out a first elastic analysis, before any non-linear study. - In order to check the material data, it may be useful to carry out, with the Code_Aster data setup, a test simpler than the study, for example on a material point (SIMU_POINT_MAT). Does one recover the tension–compression curve? - The computation of the mass (or of the volume) of the structure is also among the checks which are simple but sometimes useful. 6.3 Controlling the errors due to the spatial discretisation On this point, a few general remarks are recalled here, but reading u2.08.01 is more than advisable. Independently of any wish to carry out mesh adaptation, it is advisable to check the initial mesh with the command MACR_INFO_MAIL u7.03.02 u7.03.02. This command makes it possible to carry out, at low cost, the following checks: - check the agreement of the mesh with the initial geometry (in dimension, in volume); - list the GROUP_MA and GROUP_NO, for a good modelling of the boundary conditions; - diagnose possible problems (connectivity, holes, interpenetration of mesh cells); - supply quality criteria for the mesh cells (evaluated mesh cell by mesh cell). In order to control more easily the effect of the quality of the mesh, an automatic mesh-adaptation strategy is operational: it relies on the mesh-adaptation software Homard, which can be called directly from the Code_Aster command file or in the Salome-Meca platform, and uses either error indicators making it possible to drive the adaptation, or the values of a field, or the jump of a field from one element to another. Several motivations appear for adapting a mesh: - The mesh is very complicated to produce: one starts from a simple version and entrusts to an automatic process the task of refining it. - One wants to make sure of the convergence of the numerical solution: rather than producing by hand meshes which are finer and finer, one lets the software itself look for the places where the mesh ought to be refined in order to increase the accuracy of the result. - The conditions of the analysis change in the course of its progress: the zones which must be meshed finely move. If one meshes finely everywhere from the start, the mesh is too large. By adapting as one goes along (refinement – coarsening), the mesh will be fine only at the places where this is necessary: its size will be reduced and the quality of the solution will be good. The zones to be refined can be located: - Either with an error indicator. Note that the simplest ones (ZZ1, of Zhu-Zienkiewicz type) are very robust, available in 2D and 3D, and even if they do not supply the best upper bounds of the error, their variations are sufficient to drive the adaptation. The estimators in quantity of interest are more relevant for supplying a bound on the error committed. - Or with a relevant field (strain, internal variable). Caution: in plasticity, the Von Mises stress is not always one. One can use: - either the extreme values of this field (for example asking to refine the 5% of elements which have the highest value), - or drive the adaptation by the jump of the values of this field at the boundary between two finite elements. - Or by boxes (uniform refinement in geometric zones). For more information, see u2.08.01 6.4 Time-discretisation errors For most of the non-linearities (constitutive behaviour, contact, large strains) the time discretisation influences the result. Convergence results exist (fortunately) in all the classical cases (elasto-visco-plasticity, contact), but it nevertheless remains to make sure that, for a chosen time step, the solution is sufficiently close to the solution which is continuous in time. The simplest solution is similar to uniform refinement for mesh adaptation: it consists in refining the time step uniformly over the whole transient and re-launching STAT_NON_LINE. This can be automated thanks to a feature of DEFI_LIST_INST (see u2.04.01 and :ref: u4.34.03). Another criterion for controlling the time step is subdivision as a function of a quantity of interest: DEFI_LIST_INST / DELTA_GRANDEUR indeed makes it possible to re-cut the time step if the maximum variation of a given quantity (for example a plastic-strain component) is greater than a threshold supplied. In addition, for the elastoplastic constitutive behaviours, it is possible to estimate directly the error due to the discretisation in time, in a manner analogous to RESI_RADI_RELA (cf. 3.2.4). If this criterion was not taken into account during the analysis, it is possible to compute it in post-processing, in CALC_CHAMP: the component ERR_RADI of the option DERA_ELGA contains the error estimate at each time instant and at each integration point. 7 References [1] “Mechanics of structures”, p.658, F.Voldoire; Y.Bamberger, Presses de l'ENPC 2008.

u2.04.03 Choice of the elasto-(visco)-plastic constitutive behaviour u2.04.03 Choice of the elasto-(visco)-plastic constitutive behaviour > Summary. The aim of this note is to give advice to a user wishing to carry out analyses with non-linear constitutive behaviours of elastoplastic or elastoviscoplastic type, in order to choose a law suited to the modellings envisaged. The materials concerned are mainly metals. For the other types of material, the first paragraph refers to the appropriate references. The specific features and capabilities of the elastoviscoplastic laws are described. A description is then given of the particularities of the different types of hardening, which makes it possible to put forward a few recommendations. Some general advice is given on the identification of the parameters of the laws. The effects of viscosity and of temperature are also addressed. Finally, some elements are given for checking the validity of the choices made concerning the constitutive behaviour and its parameters. 1 Introduction 1.1 Choice of the type of constitutive law The choice of the constitutive law is of course a function of the material that one is modelling, but also of the phenomena to be treated: for example, the same steel will be elastoplastic at low temperature, and viscoplastic at high temperature. This document gives some pointers for making proper use of the elasto-(visco)-plastic constitutive behaviours (mainly for metals). For other types of constitutive behaviour, reading the following documents is recommended: - For the laws with damage (the case of concrete, for example), see u2.05.06 u2.05.06 - For metallurgy, see u2.03.04 - For porous media in THM, see u2.04.05 and r7.01.11 - For the use of the CZM elements, see u2.05.07 u2.05.07 - For the laws specific to the discrete elements, see r5.03.17 - For the laws specific to the 1D elements, see r5.03.09 - For the hyperelastic laws (of Mooney-Rivlin type) see r5.03.19 - For the constitutive laws specific to fuel rods and to metals under irradiation, see r5.03.08 and :ref: r5.03.23 - For the crystal-plasticity laws, see r5.03.11 r5.03.11 1.2 Which elastoplastic laws to choose: what are their capabilities? This document provides elements for choosing the constitutive laws, according to their capabilities, and the phenomena to be modelled. Advice for the identification of the parameters will be given, with emphasis on the domain of validity of the models: the parameters are identified for quite specific strains, rates and temperatures, which must correspond to the studies envisaged. Moreover, if the modellings envisaged require it, it may be necessary to carry out the identifications in the large-strain domain. Suitable formalisms may be used for this purpose: - SIMO_MIEHE for the Von Mises constitutive behaviours with isotropic hardening, the laws with the effect of the metallurgical phases, the Rousselier law, - GDEF_LOG for most of the constitutive behaviours, - GROT_GDEP for the hyperelastic laws of MOONEY-RIVLIN type. 2 Specific features and capabilities of the elastoviscoplastic laws The elasto-(visco)-plastic constitutive laws available in Code_Aster (for the 2D and 3D modellings), and their specific features, are detailed here. 2.1 The available elastoplastic laws Apart from linear elasticity (ELAS), the available elastoplastic models are (cf. u4.51.11 u4.51.11): | Von Mises elastoplasticity with isotropic hardening: VMIS_ISOT_TRAC, VMIS_ISOT_PUIS, VMIS_ISOT_LINE cf. r5.03.02 | | --- | | Von Mises elastoplasticity with linear kinematic hardening (alone or combined with the isotropic hardening): VMIS_CINE_LINE, cf r5.03.02 r5.03.02 VMIS_ECMI_TRAC, VMIS_ECMI_LINE cf. r5.03.16 | | Elastoplasticity with non-linear kinematic hardening (laws of J.L. Chaboche) VMIS_CIN1_CHAB, VMIS_CIN2_CHAB, VMIS_CIN2_MEMO cf. r5.03.04 | | Elastoplasticity with a semi-discrete internal variable for cyclic loadings VISC_TAHERI cf. r5.03.05 r5.03.05 | | Von Mises elastoplasticity with isotropic hardening of Johnson-Cook (high rates) VMIS_JOHN_COOK cf r5.03.02 r5.03.02 | | Non-linear elasticity (Hencky laws) ELAS_VMIS_LINE, ELAS_VMIS_TRAC, ELAS_VMIS_PUIS cf. r5.03.20 | 2.2 The available elastoviscoplastic laws The available elastoviscoplastic constitutive behaviours are: | Elastoviscoplasticity with isotropic hardening LEMAITRE cf. r5.03.08 VISC_ENDO_LEMA, VENDOCHAB cf. r5.03.15 r5.03.15 HAYHURST cf. r5.03.13 r5.03.13 | | --- | | Elastoviscoplasticity with non-linear kinematic hardening (laws of J.L. Chaboche) VISC_CIN1_CHAB, VISC_CIN2_CHAB, VISC_CIN2_MEMO cf. r5.03.04 VISCOCHAB cf. r5.03.12 VISC_TAHERI cf. r5.03.05 r5.03.05 | | Viscosity law as a hyperbolic sine and isotropic hardening VISC_ISOT_LINE, VISC_ISOT_TRAC cf. r5.03.21 | 2.3 The choice of the type of hardening 2.3.1 Isotropic hardening The elastoplastic laws with isotropic hardening make it possible to model an increase in the size of the elastic domain with the plastic strain that is identical in all directions. Although certain materials may correspond to this type of law, for most metals, which exhibit strong kinematic hardening, these laws are suited to modellings in which the global loadings are monotonic, or possibly with unloadings of small amplitude, so as to remain in the elastic regime. This is a necessary condition for the response of the model to conform to reality (a complete model, with non-linear kinematic and isotropic hardenings, would in this case give the same result). But it is not a sufficient condition: there may exist structures in which a global monotonic loading produces local unloadings. The validity of the approach with an isotropic hardening can be checked a posteriori: it is sufficient that, at every point, no unloading has given rise to an entry into plasticity. This check is detailed in § 5.2 To define the parameters of a law with isotropic hardening, the constitutive behaviour must be identified on a tensile curve, checking that the identification is indeed carried out over the range of strains likely to be encountered during the structural analysis envisaged. The different types of hardening proposed (curve, power law) generally make it possible to reproduce the tensile test well (see :ref: r5.03.02 and the training documents: 15-Constitutive laws _ _). 1. Evolution of the 3D elastic domain b) Evolution of the elastic domain in 1D Figure 2.3.1-a . Von Mises criterion, isotropic hardening In certain cases (fracture mechanics), it is necessary to approximate the elastoplastic constitutive behaviour by an equivalent non-linear elastic constitutive behaviour: these are the Hencky laws ( ELAS_VMIS_LINE, ELAS_VMIS_TRAC, ELAS_VMIS_PUIS ). Here again, these laws are valid only with a monotonic loading, and this time without any unloading, because they do not make it possible to model the plastic strain. A very simplified way of using an isotropic hardening is to consider that it is linear (VMIS_ISOT_LINE). This may be valid over one range of strains, and not valid over another. Let us take for example tensile curves of a stainless steel: Figure 2.3.1-b . Tensile curves up to 20% strain Figure 2.3.1-c . Tensile curves up to 3% strain It can be seen from the figure that it is possible to model the tensile curve by a linear hardening, in large strains, if one is not interested with any precision in the small strains (lower than 1%). In the opposite case (figure ), it seems quite tricky to construct a linear hardening that is valid right from the entry into plasticity. Moreover, this type of hardening (like all the models with linear hardening) risks overestimating the stresses in the case of large strains (or underestimating the strains at imposed stress), because nothing limits the hardening curve. A remedy for this difficulty is described in paragraph 5.1. By using the constitutive behaviour VMIS_ISOT_TRAC, the risks are smaller: the tensile curve is defined by a function DEFI_FONCTION, and the maximum value of the abscissa (strain) makes it possible to define the domain of validity and thus to avoid exceeding this value in the structural analysis (take care to leave the default value PROL_DROITE='EXCLU' in DEFI_FONCTION). 2.3.2 Linear kinematic hardening The elastoplastic laws with linear kinematic hardening are suited to modellings in which the global loadings contain a few unloadings, and for which the approximation of the hardening curve by a straight line is acceptable . They make it possible to represent, in a very simplified way, the Bauschinger effect, which is present for most metals. Let us examine the law VMIS_CINE_LINE: 1. Evolution of the 3D elastic domain (section) b) Evolution of the elastic domain in 1D Figure 2.3.2-a . Von Mises criterion, kinematic hardening Advantage : - The interest of this model lies in its simplicity; it makes it possible in particular to test rapidly the effect of the kinematic hardening, because the identification and the solution are very rapid. Limitations : 1. This model presents no isotropic hardening. 2. The approximation of the real tension–compression curve is often poor (cf. previous paragraph) 3. This model (like all the models with linear hardening) risks overestimating the stresses in the case of large strains (or underestimating the strains at imposed stress), because nothing limits the hardening curve. 4. Finally, if the loading comprises cycles, this model tends very quickly towards a stabilised cycle (in the uniaxial case, it is reached in a single cycle), which does not correspond to reality. To remove the first limitation, it is possible to combine the linear kinematic hardening with an isotropic hardening: these are the models VMIS_ECMI_LINE (which nevertheless presents the 3 other drawbacks), VMIS_ECMI_TRAC (which also makes it possible to answer the second limitation). Great care must be taken when identifying VMIS_ECMI_TRAC (cf. r5.03.16 r5.03.16): indeed, the share of kinematic hardening, over the strain range studied, must remain smaller than the share of isotropic hardening; otherwise a negative isotropic hardening may be obtained. 2.3.3 Non-linear kinematic hardening: laws of J.L. Chaboche These laws make it possible at the same time to represent the Bauschinger effect (kinematic hardening), its non-linear evolution, and the isotropic hardening, as well as other phenomena (memory effect of the maximum plastic strain, recovery). In their simplest form ( VMIS_CIN1_CHAB ) they lead to a particular form of the hardening curve, with a determined asymptote. The idea underlying these models is to reproduce the tension–compression cycles well, in size and in shape. To improve the description of the real curves, several independent kinematic variables can be introduced, each having a specific role in representing a given strain level. In Code_Aster, one has limited oneself to two kinematic variables ( VMIS_CIN2_CHAB ). Their identification is more complex than for the previous models: the number of parameters increases, and at a minimum a cyclic test (tension–compression over several cycles) is required in order to identify them correctly. Moreover, tests at several strain levels are often necessary (and difficult to represent completely). Here again it is indispensable to target properly the range of strain expected in the studies, so that the parameters are adjusted to that strain level. If parameters coming from an earlier identification are used, one must at a minimum check (via SIMU_POINT_MAT, for example, on a modelling of the tension–compression test) the response of the model for these parameters. To illustrate the advantage of using a non-linear kinematic hardening beyond a few loading cycles, let us consider an example of tension–compression cycles at imposed strain: This curve is in fact a numerical curve (simulated with VMIS_CIN2_CHAB) but it correctly reproduces the experimental curves for the stainless steel considered. It will serve as a reference for the illustrations below. The approximation of this curve by a linear kinematic hardening (with an isotropic component, adjusted on the first tensile curve) shows that the response is very far from it: The representation of the very first cycles can be improved by choosing VMIS_ECMI_TRAC, and by readjusting the values of the Prager coefficient. It is found that, although the first 2 cycles are well represented, the model VMIS_ECMI_TRAC tends towards a stabilised state with a stress amplitude very much higher than the real curve. If the cycles are continued, this model would moreover tend towards an adapted cycle, of amplitude 1600\mathit{MPa} ! If the modelling aims to predict a progressive-strain phenomenon, the use of such models is delicate: indeed, they lead to a constant ratcheting at a non-zero mean stress, of a value very much higher than the experimental ratcheting (unless the parameters are chosen so that one of the kinematic hardenings is linear, in which case a stabilised accommodated cycle is recovered (too) rapidly). It is preferable in these situations to use the TAHERI model. If the situation studied involves a pre-hardening, it may be useful to identify the model VMIS_CIN2_MEMO on cyclic tests with pre-hardening. (see for example v6.08.105 v6.08.105). Other aspects can be taken into account, in particular the over-hardening due to non-proportional cyclic loadings. This is modelled in VMIS_CIN2_CHAB (without memory effect) or VMIS_CIN2_MEMO (with memory effect) via the parameters DELTA1, DELTA2. 2.3.4 Conclusions on the choice of the type of elastoplastic hardening The previous paragraphs show that this choice is essential: - for a monotonic loading, the tensile curve should be well approximated over the target strain range, and it should be checked that the structural analysis remains within this interval - to model one or two loading–unloading cycles, a model with linear kinematic hardening may be used, provided that the response is carefully checked at one or several points. - To simulate several loading cycles, a model of Chaboche (or Taheri) type is necessary. 2.4 Influence of the rate For purely elastoplastic materials, the time used in the simulations is a mere parameter of the loading (even if it has a physical meaning in the thermo-mechanical cases) and has no direct influence on the constitutive laws. But it is necessary to take it into account in the constitutive behaviour in the following cases: - high loading rate: elastoplastic law of Johnson-Cook - viscosity: elastoviscoplastic laws. 2.4.1 Johnson-Cook law This law makes it possible to take the strain rate and the temperature directly into account in the evolution of the isotropic hardening (cf. r5.03.02 page 11). It makes it possible to treat impact problems, and to implement the thermo-mechanical coupling (see for example :ref: v7.20.105 v7.20.105). 2.4.2 Elastoviscoplasticity with isotropic hardening The elastoviscoplastic model of Lemaître makes it possible to take into account secondary creep (at constant rate – for certain particular values of the parameters it can reduce to a Norton constitutive relation) and primary creep. (cf. r5.03.08 ). The loading surface remains isotropic (no kinematic hardening). Creep tests, relaxation tests, or tensile tests at different strain rates are necessary for the identification of the parameters. Here again, it must be checked that the values thus obtained are valid for the studies envisaged, that is to say that the strain rates encountered in the studies do indeed lie in the range of those that were used for the identification. Where one wishes to go further, that is to say to model tertiary creep (taking large strains into account is often necessary), the following models may be used, which incorporate a creep damage: - VISC_ENDO_LEMA, VENDOCHAB cf. r5.03.15 r5.03.15 - HAYHURST cf. r5.03.13 r5.03.13 2.4.3 Elastoviscoplasticity with non-linear kinematic hardening The following constitutive behaviours make it possible to take kinematic hardening into account: - VISC_CIN1_CHAB, VISC_CIN2_CHAB, VISC_CIN2_MEMO cf. r5.03.04 These laws are extensions of the elastoplastic laws of J.L. Chaboche to the viscoplastic case. The various components of the Chaboche laws described previously are present, and the viscosity must in addition be included (of Lemaître type, that is to say making it possible to reproduce primary and secondary creep). This means that their identification will have to take the strain rate into account (for example on the cyclic tests). Other phenomena can be represented (the hardening linked to the non-proportionality of the loading, the recovery of hardening), by the following model: - VISCOCHAB cf. r5.03.12 The complete identification of this model requires a large number of different tests: cyclic tests at different rates and at different strain levels, with pre-hardening, tension–torsion tests, relaxation tests. 2.4.4 Viscosity law as a hyperbolic sine and isotropic hardening Another form of viscosity law is proposed in the following models: - VISC_ISOT_LINE, VISC_ISOT_TRAC cf. r5.03.21 They have isotropic hardening, and require the use of SIMO_MIEHE. 3 Identifying the parameters: which tests are necessary? The identification of the parameters of the models quickly becomes difficult to carry out manually, except for the simplest models ( VMIS_CINE_LINE, VMIS_ISOT_LINE, VMIS_ISOT_TRAC ). One therefore resorts to an optimisation procedure, available in the command MACR_RECAL u4.73.02 u4.73.02. There are several advantages in using this command: - the simulation that makes it possible to find the numerical curves (which will be compared with the experimental curves) is a classical Code_Aster command file, which can be launched on its own, and which represents any analysis (not necessarily on a material point); - the recalibrated coefficients are directly usable in the studies, since they are parameters of the simulation file; - numerous algorithms are available, as well as analysis modes making it possible to use multi-processor architectures if necessary. Details of the algorithms used may be consulted in the document r4.03.06 r4.03.06. But the tools do not do everything! Indeed, before seeking to identify the parameters of a model, several questions must be asked: - is the number of tests available sufficient with respect to the number of parameters to be recalibrated; - do the tests bring out the physical phenomena simulated by the constitutive law (already mentioned previously): loading–unloading, cycles, memory effects, recovery, non-radiality, high rate, viscosity, …); - can these effects be separated, so as to identify the parameters successively, which will lighten the optimisation task and make it possible to grasp the results better. To go further into the detail of the identification, documents specific to the different constitutive behaviours remain to be written; as regards the cyclic elastoviscoplastic constitutive behaviours, a more detailed user's guide is in the course of being written, drawn from EDF/R&D work [ 4 ] and [ 5 ]. Moreover, a fairly general methodology is proposed in [ 1 ] page 617 and [ 3 ]. 4 The anisothermal simulations During anisothermal simulations, the variation of the parameters with temperature must most of the time be taken into account. Care must therefore be taken that these parameters are properly identified. In this paragraph, a few classical errors induced by the interpolation or the extrapolation of the values as a function of the temperature are illustrated. The tests are carried out with the laws VMIS_ISOT_TRAC and VMIS_CIN1_CHAB. The conclusions retained are not, however, exclusive to one particular law. 4.1 Dangers of extrapolation: To carry out a thermo-mechanical study with a constitutive law whose coefficients depend on the temperature, the user may wish to extrapolate the curves in order to carry out the study at a given temperature. This is strongly discouraged. An example: In the case of an isotropic hardening, it is common to use experimental tensile curves for a few temperatures, varying for example between 20° and 350° . The tensile curves are entered in the command file for different temperatures with the command ‘DEFI_NAPPE’. Suppose that the extensions have been defined by PROL_DROITE='LINEAIRE' and PROL_GAUCHE='LINEAIRE'. Suppose that the user wishes to carry out an analysis at a temperature which exceeds the maximum temperature at which the identifications of the tensile curves were made, say 1000°C for example (this is a deliberately exaggerated example, but it makes it possible to illustrate the point). The material coefficients of the law would thereby be obtained at 1000°C by extrapolation. This can lead to aberrant results ( Figure 4.1-a ): the tensile curve obtained at the extrapolated temperature of 1000°C presents a concavity and a hardening slope that contradict the other curves and reality. To avoid this kind of error, any extrapolation with respect to the temperature must be avoided. Figure 4.1-a . Tensile curves as a function of temperature – result at 1000°C 4.2 Error in the interpolation of the temperature This example brings out a possible error in the interpolation of the temperature, generally due to a non-monotonic evolution of the material coefficients with temperature. It is sufficient that a single one of the coefficients does not evolve in a monotonic manner for the interpolation between two tensile curves to lead to a curve which does not lie between the two extremes. To exhibit this kind of error, with a constitutive law of type ‘VMIS_CIN1_CHAB’, the following test was set up: Suppose that three tensile curves identified experimentally at 3 different temperatures are known: 20° , 100° and 200°C . One seeks to identify the parameters of the law ‘VMIS_CIN1_CHAB’ at these three temperatures. In order to understand the point, let us briefly recall the form of the hardening of the law ‘VMIS_CIN1_CHAB’: - Criterion: {(\sigma -C\alpha )}_{\text{eq}}-R(p)\le 0 - kinematic hardening: \dot{\alpha}=\dot{{\varepsilon}^{p}}-\gamma \alpha \dot{p} - isotropic hardening: R(p)={R}_{\infty}+({R}_{0}-{R}_{\infty}){e}^{-\text{bp}} Suppose that the results of 3 identifications at three different temperatures are: - at T=20° ; the identified material parameters are: {C}_{1} , {\gamma}_{1} , {R}_{0} , non-zero, and {R}_{\infty}\mathrm{\simeq }{R}_{0} b\mathrm{\simeq }0 , (that is, an almost purely kinematic constitutive behaviour); - at T=100° ; the identified material coefficients are: {C}_{2}\mathrm{\simeq }0 , {R}_{0} , {R}_{\infty} , {b}_{2} , non-zero, (that is, an almost purely isotropic constitutive behaviour) - at T=200° ; the material coefficients are: {C}_{3} , {\gamma}_{3} , {R}_{0} , non-zero, {R}_{\infty}\mathrm{\simeq }{R}_{0} , {b}_{3}\mathrm{\simeq }0 , (that is, once again a purely kinematic constitutive behaviour). Each of these identifications is sufficiently accurate, and makes it possible to recover, for each temperature, numerical curves very close to the experimental curves. The simulation of the tensile curve at the temperature of 50°C is shown in the figure ) It is found that the curve obtained by interpolation at 50°C is erroneous: Figure 4.2-a . Tensile curves as a function of temperature – result at 50° This comes from the fact that the identifications were carried out independently, without checking the consistency of the results. The variations of each coefficient with temperature are enormous: for example | Temperature °C | C | b | | --- | --- | --- | | 20 | {C}_{1} | \mathrm{\simeq }0 | | | \mathrm{\simeq }0 | {b}_{2} | | | {C}_{3} | \mathrm{\simeq }0 | This example is of course extreme, but it makes it possible to put forward a recommendation: - either check the monotonic evolution of the material parameters as a function of temperature, and carry out the identification again for the suspect values, - or, if possible, carry out the identification in one go for all the temperatures. 5 The domain of validity Several checks are possible in order to verify that the constitutive law chosen, and the values of the parameters used, are valid for the simulation. In addition to the advice given previously, so as to choose the constitutive law properly according to what one wants to model, certain additional checks can be carried out with the aid of specific tools. 5.1 Validity of the parameters over the strain and rate range. The parameters of the chosen model having been identified over a certain strain range, it is important to check that, in the studies using these parameters, these strains do indeed remain within the identification interval. The tensile curves defined by DEFI_FONCTION incorporate a "safeguard": the maximum value of the abscissa ( EPSI ) cannot be exceeded in the study. But if this should nevertheless occur, instead of defining a constant extension (or worse: a linear one) the identification should be taken up again in order to define additional points on the tensile curve. Linear hardenings ( ECRO_LINE ), or those defined by an analytical function ( ECRO_PUIS , VMIS_CINx _CHAB , etc.), are much more dangerous. Nothing will prevent the studies from greatly exceeding the strain level of the identification. This is why a safeguard ought to be put in place in a future version. In any event, it is relatively easy, in the post-processing of a study, to compute ( CALC_CHAMP ) the norm of the strain field ( EPEQ_ELGA ) and to extract its maximum from it ( POST_ELEM / MINMAX , or graphical post-processing in SALOME_MECA ). If the study leads one to use a large-strain formalism, the identification must use it as well. As regards the strain rate, a check is again necessary here. Its automatic computation ought to be proposed in a future version. 5.2 Unloading: validity of the isotropic hardening (and of the Hencky laws) How can one check that the unloadings are small enough for the analysis with an isotropic hardening to be valid? There exists in CALC_CHAMP an unloading indicator DERA_ELGA (cf. u4.81.04 u4.81.04). - The components DCHA_V, DCHA_T indicate whether there exist unloadings on the stresses (either on the Von Mises stress, or on the total tensor), thus invalidating the analysis with a non-linear elastic law. - The component IND_DCHA supplies an indicator which indicates whether there is a risk of entering plasticity on unloading, thus invalidating the analysis with isotropic hardening. For further details of their computation, see r4.20.01 ). 5.3 Radiality: effects of non-proportionality In the case of strongly non-proportional cyclic loadings, the over-hardening effect may be ignored by the constitutive behaviour chosen. By using, in CALC_CHAMP, the indicator of unloading and of radiality of the loading, DERA_ELGA (cf. u4.81.04), the component ERR_RADI measures the error committed through the rotation of the normal to the loading surface. If this value is large, a model making it possible to take this effect into account must then be used (for example VISCOCHAB). 6 References 1. J. LEMAITRE, J.L.
