u2.04.04 User's guide to contact in code_aster u2.04.04 User's guide to contact in code_aster > Summary. This document describes the procedure to be followed in order to take frictional-contact conditions into account in non-linear studies. The concern is surface contact between deformable solids, or between a deformable solid and a rigid solid. First, what it means to take frictional contact into account in structural mechanics is recalled, then the broad outline of a contact problem in code_aster is drawn: pairing and solution. Contact is defined with the command DEFI_CONTACT, while the solution is carried out with the commands STAT_NON_LINE or DYNA_NON_LINE. Recommendations are given for the parameterisation of the pairing and for the choice of the solution methods in these operators. Finally, various methodologies are mentioned (contact with a rigid surface, recovering a contact pressure in post-processing, large strains and contact, rigid-body motions blocked by contact, …). They make it possible to overcome the difficulties frequently encountered in studies. In this section, alternative modellings of the frictional-contact phenomenon by joint elements or by discrete elements (through the constitutive law) are also discussed. Table of Contents 1 Introduction 1.1 Purpose of this document To say that two solid bodies placed in contact do not interpenetrate, but that on the contrary a reciprocal force is exerted by one on the other and that this force disappears when the bodies are no longer touching, is common sense. It is the most succinct definition that one can give of the “contact” problem: yet enforcing these conditions in a structural analysis code such as Code_Aster requires a great deal of effort. Solving the contact problem amounts, in the end, to imposing an inequality boundary condition on certain displacement degrees of freedom (negative or zero gap) and to finding an additional unknown, which is the reciprocal force exerted between the two bodies. The difficulty comes from the strong non-linearity induced by this “pseudo-boundary condition”. Indeed, the condition to be imposed on the displacements (in order to prevent any interpenetration) itself depends on the displacements (which will determine at which point the surfaces come into contact). The non-linearity due to taking contact into account is separated in Code_Aster into two points: - contact(-friction) non-linearity: it follows from the contact(-friction) conditions, which are not differentiable. To solve the problem, two main families of solution are available: the DISCRETE formulation and the CONTINUE formulation. The first family is suited to problems with a small number of contact unknowns and allows short computation times, whereas the second is suited to problems which require the other mechanical non-linearities to be taken into account together with frictional contact (plasticity and large transformations). - geometric non-linearity: it follows from the large relative sliding liable to occur between the surfaces in contact (the effective final contact surfaces being unknown a priori ). Use is made here of a fixed-point or Newton algorithm coupled with a geometric search. In Code_Aster , in the presence of contact, the user must at least identify the potential contact surfaces. The solution technique then rests on two fundamental stages: - Pairing phase: it makes it possible to treat the geometric non-linearity as a sequence of small-sliding problems (in which the problem is geometrically linear). The technique for determining the effective contact surfaces, and advice on the parameter setting of this phase, are given in section 2. - Solution phase: it makes it possible to solve the constrained optimisation problem linked to the contact non-linearity and, possibly, to friction. The various optimisation algorithms available are presented in section 3. A path is given there for choosing an algorithm suited to one's study. It is essential to have understood that frictional contact is a non-linearity in its own right, on the same footing as the material non-linearities (non-linear constitutive law) and the kinematic non-linearities (large displacements, large rotations). It therefore requires both a knowledge of the bases of contact theory and an understanding of its treatment in Code_Aster , in order to make the right modelling choices (mesh and data setup). This document is here to assist the user in these choices. 1.2 A question of vocabulary In order to make the reading easier, some of the terms used abundantly in this document are given here. When one speaks of contact mechanics, two characteristic quantities are used: - the gap, often denoted g or d . It characterises the signed distance between two contact surfaces; - the contact force density p . This is the reciprocal force exerted by one solid on the other when the gap is closed (zero). It is carried by the normal to the contact surfaces. The term contact pressure will also be used, loosely. - Master and slave zones: this is a boundary of a solid on which the frictional-contact conditions will be imposed. Contact is defined by a “pair of solids”. In each pair, the master–slave role is crucial for the proper running of an analysis. - Incompatible meshes: these are the cases in which the master mesh cell does not coincide with the slave mesh cell. These cases are extremely difficult to handle. The best method for these cases is the MORTAR methods known as LAC, usable in the continuous formulation only. One will also speak of strong or weak mesh incompatibilities. There is no rigorous criterion for declaring a strong or a weak incompatibility. Engineering judgement is left to decide according to the case to be treated. An example of strong and of weak incompatibility is nevertheless illustrated in the figure below. Strong incompatibilities Figure 1.2-1: Examples of mesh incompatibilities - Contact states: this is the pair (gap–pressure) characterising a contact element. There are 2 possible contact states: contact (zero gap, non-zero pressure) and separation (non-zero gap, zero pressure). The two situations are mutually exclusive. Each state can have variants: grazing contact (gap almost zero, non-zero but low pressure), firm contact (zero gap and high contact pressure), grazing separation (the opposite of grazing contact), firm separation (the opposite of firm contact). - Cycling: this is a frequent case of non-convergence in contact analyses. The cycling situation is when a contact point or a contact mesh cell has difficulty in stabilising its status (contact/no contact, sticking/sliding, forward sliding/backward sliding). - Hertz–Signorini–Moreau contact laws: as with any constitutive law, the interfaces between solids have their own mathematical formalisms. The contact laws derive from a formalism of non-smooth mechanics (just as, for example, the problems of fracture mechanics or of cohesion): the absence of a differentiable energy from which a force–displacement relation can readily be written. - LAC or Mortar LAC: Local Average Contact, a method suited to incompatible meshes. - Oscillating contact pressures: in the case of incompatible meshes, it can happen that the contact pressures have an oscillating character. One notices it through a strong scatter of the contact-pressure values. These quantities are described in detail in the reference document R5.03.50. In the presence of friction, one introduces in addition: - the sliding direction \overrightarrow{t} - the friction force density \tau , carried by -\vec{t} . In Code_Aster , a Coulomb friction criterion is used; the friction conditions are described in R5.03.50. 1.3 Alternative modellings of frictional contact Although the way of treating the frictional-contact phenomenon described in the introduction and in the bulk of this document is the most widespread, it is not the only one. Code_Aster thus proposes two alternative modellings of the mechanical interactions: - (hydro-)mechanical joint elements (modellings _JOINT ) for the representation of the opening of a crack under the pressure of a fluid and of the friction between the faces of the closed crack - discrete shock elements (modellings _DIS_T ) for the representation of a point contact by springs, with possible account taken of friction These two other modellings both rely on finite elements and therefore on specific constitutive laws (JOINT_MECA_FROT for the joint elements and DIS_CHOC for the discrete elements). Further details on these elements are given in § 4.10 and § 4.11. Finally, it will be noted that it is possible to model contact on the edges of a crack represented with the X-FEM method. The reader is referred to the user's guide U2.05.02 for further information. 2 Pairing 2.1 Notion of contact zones and contact surfaces It is always for the user to define the potential contact surfaces: there is no automatic mechanism in Code_Aster for detecting the possible interpenetrations in a structure. The user therefore supplies, in the command file, a list of pairs of contact surfaces. Each pair contains a surface said to be “master” and a surface said to be “slave”. Such a pair is called a “contact zone ”. MAIT_ESCL pairing case: The contact conditions will be imposed zone by zone. Enforcing the contact consists in preventing the slave nodes from penetrating inside the master surfaces (the converse, on the other hand, is possible). In the example below ( cf. ), the structure studied is made up of three solids; three potential contact zones have been defined, symbolised by the red ellipses. As their name indicates, these contact zones determine parts of the structure in which bodies are liable to come into contact. This means that the frictional-contact conditions are enforced there, the effective activation of contact depending in the end on the imposed loading. There is no restriction on the number of contact zones. The zones must however be separated, that is to say that the intersection of two distinct zones must be empty 1 . Furthermore, within a zone, the master and slave surfaces of one and the same zone must also have a zero intersection: if this is not the case, the analysis is stopped. When a node is necessarily common to the master and slave surfaces, because of a meshing constraint for example, see § 2.3.4 for a solution. In the case where a continuous formulation is used ( cf. 3.1.3), the slave surfaces must imperatively be pairwise disjoint. One should not hesitate to describe wide contact zones in order to avoid any interpenetration. It is the number of nodes of the slave surface that is decisive in the computation cost. The master surface may, for its part, be as large as one wishes. It is imperative that the nodes of the contact surfaces (master and slave) all carry displacement degrees of freedom (DX, DY and possibly DZ), that is to say that they belong to mesh cells of the model . An error message stops the user if this is not the case. See § 4.6 for the modelling of a contact with a rigid surface. Figure 2.1-1: Definition of three contact zones MORTAR pairing case: When one has analyses with incompatible meshes and one needs to estimate the contact states precisely, it is recommended to use the MORTAR LAC method. This method makes it possible to carry out contact analyses on intersecting pairs, SURFACE ESCL on SURFACE MAIT, unlike the MAIT_ESCL pairing method, which associates NOEUDS with SEGMENTS. To do this, there is a necessary stage which consists in pre-processing the mesh before the use of DEFI_CONTACT: CREA_MAILLAGE/DECOUPE_LAC. This stage prepares the slave contact surface for an integration of the contact terms of MORTAR type on the intersected mesh cells. This method, because it uses a surface-to-surface approach, respects the master/slave and slave/master interpenetration conditions better. As for the MAIT_ESCL method, the user must define the potential contact zones pair by pair. There is no restriction on the number of contact zones. Two distinct zones may have common nodes but not common mesh cells, because the contact condition is imposed on the mesh cells. Furthermore, within a zone, the master and slave surfaces of one and the same zone must also have a zero intersection. The kinematic contact quantities for the MORTAR method are geometric fields per element. 2.2 Choice of the master and slave surfaces As has just been said, each contact zone is made up of a master surface and a slave surface. In the present state, one cannot do self-contact in Code_Aster (except in the rare cases where one can predict the future contact zone and thus define a slave and a master). The need to differentiate the two surfaces comes from the technique adopted in the computation of the gap. This computation is carried out in a phase that is called pairing . In the case of the MAIT_ESCL pairing, the gap is defined at every point of the slave surface (for the discrete methods these are the nodes, for the continuous methods the integration points) as the minimum distance to the master surface. This dissymmetry implies a choice which can a priori prove difficult (how is one to decide?). The points which must prevail in this choice are given in the following paragraphs. In the case of the MORTAR pairing, the gap is defined by the intersected slave-surface–master-surface patch. These surfaces are entered in the operator DEFI_CONTACT under the factor keyword ZONE. 2.2.1 Case in which a surface must be chosen as master (GROUP_MA_MAIT) When one of these conditions is met: - one of the two surfaces is rigid (a); - one of the two surfaces covers the other (b); - one of the two surfaces has an apparent stiffness which is large compared with the other (“apparent” in the sense that one is not speaking of Young's moduli but of stiffnesses in {\mathit{N.m}}^{-1} ) (c); - one of the two surfaces is meshed much more coarsely than the other (d); then this surface must be chosen as the master surface. 2.2.2 Case in which a surface must be chosen as slave (GROUP_MA_ESCL) When one of these conditions is met: - one of the two surfaces is curved (a); - one of the two surfaces is smaller than the other (b); - one of the two surfaces has an apparent stiffness which is small compared with the other (c); - one of the two surfaces is meshed much more finely than the other (d); then this surface must be chosen as the slave surface. 2.2.3 General case When studying complex structures, it happens that the rules given in § 2.2.1 and § 2.2.2 are difficult to apply. For example, when a solid is almost rigid (with respect to the other solid) and is curved, rule (a) does not make it possible to decide: should the curved character or the rigid character be given priority? In these situations, “engineering judgement” must prevail. In our example, if the two solids undergo small sliding, the curved character of the rigid solid will have little influence and one will therefore choose the latter as the master surface. When convergence problems are encountered (especially in plasticity), it is very likely that the choices of the master and slave sides are not judicious. In this case, change the role of the surfaces. Figure 2.2.3-1: Choice of master and slave surfaces according to different situations 2.2.4 Orientation of the normals It is essential always to orient the normals of the contact surfaces so that they are outward . This can be done with the operator MODI_MAILLAGE. According to whether the surface to be oriented is a skin mesh cell of a solid element, a shell or a beam, one will use respectively the keywords ORIE_PEAU_2D or ORIE_PEAU_3D, ORIE_NORM_COQUE, ORIE_LIGNE. In the case of ORIE_LIGNE, the tangent is oriented, so as to be able to produce the normal systematically by a vector product. By default (keyword VERI_NORM of DEFI_CONTACT), the correct orientation of the normals is checked and the user is stopped if need be. 2.2.5 Fineness and degree of the mesh of curved surfaces When the contact surfaces are curved, the proper continuity of the normal to the facets must be guaranteed. For this, one can either: - mesh finely with linear elements and use the smoothing option ( cf. § 2.3.2) - mesh with quadratic elements For the quadratic mesh to retain its interest, the mid-side nodes must have been placed on the geometry in the mesher, and the operator CREA_MAILLAGE/LINE_QUAD of Code_Aster must not have been used. Discrete formulation case: In the case of quadratic contact surfaces, in the discrete formulation the contact surfaces must not be made up of 8-node quadrangular mesh cells (QUAD8), and the 9-node mesh cells (QUAD9) will therefore be preferred. The HEXA20 will then be transformed into HEXA27 and the PENTA15 into PENTA18 (with the operator CREA_MAILLAGE). At the present time, mixed meshes made up of both HEXA20 and PENTA15 cannot be transformed by CREA_MAILLAGE. If, however, the use of HEXA20 elements proves mandatory, the linear relations written automatically on this occasion may be liable to conflict with boundary conditions (in particular of symmetry); this is why it may be necessary to impose the boundary conditions only on the vertex nodes of the QUAD8 mesh cells concerned (the operator DEFI_GROUP can be used for the creation of the ad hoc node group). Continuous formulation case: In the continuous formulation (ALGO_CONT='STANDARD'), for curved boundary mesh cells, the use of QUAD8 or TRIA6 elements can lead to violations of the contact law : the latter is satisfied on average. One then observes slightly positive or slightly negative gaps in the presence of contact, which can disturb the results close to the contact zone or the analyses restarted with an initial state. For this reason it is advisable to use HEXA27 or PENTA18 elements (with QUAD9 faces) or else linear elements. When, at the end of an analysis, one notices a high rate of interpenetration of the master nodes inside the slave surfaces (which is possible, unlike the converse), this generally means that the mesh of one or both surfaces is too coarse, or that there is too great a difference in fineness between the two meshes of the surfaces. One can then either refine, or swap master and slave. If a surface is rigid (and therefore master), a coarse mesh is sufficient, except of course in the curved zones. Finally, in the particular case of a cylinder-on-cylinder or sphere-on-sphere contact, care must be taken to mesh each surface sufficiently in order to avoid leaving too much void between them. Indeed, in Code_Aster , for the moment neither node repositioning nor projections onto splines passing through the master surface are carried out; a mesh that is too coarse will then cause a strong oscillation of the contact pressure (detection of contact on every other node). In the case where there are oscillations in the contact pressures due to a strongly incompatible mesh in the contact zone, the method ALGO_CONT='LAC' must be preferred. 2.2.6 Sharp corners The pairing algorithms work less well in the presence of sharp corners, which is why one will avoid having them as far as possible in the mesh of the master and slave surfaces. For example, one will prefer to model a fillet rather than a sharp corner. If a sharp corner is indispensable, the surface which carries it will be chosen as slave. 2.2.7 Mesh quality The quality of the surface elements which make up the master contact surface has a direct impact on the quality of the pairing. Indeed, distorted mesh cells, for example, can harm the accuracy of the projections despite the robustness of the algorithm: the uniqueness of the projection is no longer guaranteed. For these reasons, it is recommended to check the quality of the meshes produced and, if necessary, to correct their defects. In Code_Aster , the command MACR_INFO_MAIL makes it possible to display the distribution of the elements as a function of their quality. 2.3 Control of the pairing 2.3.1 Choice of the type of pairing In Code_Aster , three types of pairing are available: - “master–slave” (by default): this is the most generic; it makes it possible to prevent the nodes of the slave surface from penetrating the mesh cells of the master surface by means of orthogonal projections of a node onto a mesh cell. It is available for the discrete formulation and the continuous formulation ( ALGO_CONT='STANDARD' ). - “nodal”: it makes it possible to prevent the slave nodes from penetrating the master nodes along a direction (given by the slave normal). This is a pairing reserved for compatible meshes of the contact surfaces, for analyses in small sliding. It is not available in the continuous formulation ( cf. § 3.1.3). - “MORTAR” (by default): this is the one of highest quality; it makes it possible to impose the contact conditions on average on the intersected mesh cells. With this method, interpenetration accuracies lower than 1.E-10% are reached. It is available only for the continuous formulation ( ALGO_CONT='LAC' ). 2.3.2 Smoothing of the normals As its name indicates, this option makes it possible to smooth the normals. It is particularly useful in the case of curved surfaces meshed with linear elements. This process is based on the average of the normals at the nodes, then on their interpolation from the shape functions and the averaged normals; it makes it possible to ensure the continuity of the normal at the nodes. The normal is then no longer the geometric normal; one will therefore take the precaution (advisable in any case) of checking the results visually carefully. A check of the faceting of the surfaces is carried out automatically at the end of the time step. It emits an information message when the faceting becomes too great, and it is then advisable to activate the smoothing. 2.3.3 Choice of the normals: case of a formulation other than the LAC method It is advisable always to leave the default values: NORMALE='MAIT', VECT_MAIT='AUTO'. That is to say that the non-penetration relation is written from the master normal, determined from the mesh. However, there exist a few rare situations in which one may wish to impose the choice of the normal: these are essentially the treatment of beam–beam contact (in 2D only) and the case in which the master surface is a mesh cell of type POI1. The reader is referred to §3.1.6 of U4.44.11 for further details. 2.3.4 Exclusion of slave nodes from the pairing: case of a formulation other than the LAC method The keyword SANS_GROUP_NO/SANS_NOEUD is used to exclude slave nodes from the pairing. There may be several reasons for this: - the master and slave surfaces have a non-empty intersection (crack front, blocking of rigid-body motions); the common nodes do not need to be treated by the contact, and they must therefore be excluded. - there already exist, on the slave nodes considered, linear relations (boundary conditions, blocking of rigid-body motions); if these interfere with the contact direction (respectively the friction direction), it is generally advisable to give priority to the boundary conditions and therefore not to solve the contact on these nodes. A fatal error is emitted when there exist nodes common to the master and slave surfaces and these have not been excluded. 2.4 Understanding the geometric non-linearity As has been explained, the geometric non-linearity follows from the fact that frictional-contact conditions must be applied on a geometric configuration which is not known. In this section, a short digression is made in order to explain the approach adopted to overcome this difficulty. 2.4.1 Small-sliding hypothesis The pairing phase is a phase prior to the formulation of the contact conditions to be solved. In practice, this means: - for the discrete methods, the construction of a matrix A (for Pairing) such that, multiplied by the displacement increment \delta u from the paired configuration, it gives the (linearised) gap increment. - for the continuous method, the association between a contact point and its projection in the parametric space of the paired master mesh cell. It is by updating the coordinates of the master mesh cell with the displacement \delta u that one obtains the new (linearised) coordinates of the projection. Just as for the equilibrium conditions, the contact conditions are expressed on the deformed configuration (or final configuration). This configuration is not known a priori . The hypothesis of small relative sliding of the surfaces in contact is the analogue of the small-perturbation hypothesis (for the writing of the equilibrium relations). It consists in saying that the final configuration of the surfaces in contact differs little from the initial configuration, which therefore makes it possible to carry out the pairing once and for all at the beginning of the analysis, on the initial configuration. Then to use the conditions established on this configuration for the whole analysis. Such a problem is then geometrically linear: only the frictional-contact non-linearity remains; it is treated with suitable algorithms ( cf. section 3). 2.4.2 General case To treat problems of large relative sliding of the surfaces in contact, two possibilities exist: the use of a fixed-point loop in order to come back to the small-sliding cases, or else, for the continuous formulation (§ 3.1.3), the simultaneous solution within Newton's algorithm. 2.4.2.1 Fixed-point loop (ALGO_RESO_GEOM='POINT_FIXE') The approach adopted is very similar to the solution of a non-linear problem by Newton's method. A geometrically non-linear problem is transformed into a sequence of geometrically linear problems . For this, a sequence of problems will be solved under the small-sliding hypothesis. That is to say that a pairing is carried out (on a balanced initial configuration) and a Newton solution (with solution of the contact, as will be explained in section 3). This gives a new configuration; if this configuration is “close” to the initial configuration then one has converged (it was therefore the final configuration), otherwise one loops: a pairing is done again, then a solution … and so on until the final configuration is found ( cf. ). The difficulty lies in the characterisation of the convergence of this fixed-point process. What are two “close” configurations? In Code_Aster , these are two configurations whose “mechanical” displacement vector for passing from one to the other (that is to say the displacement increment obtained by Newton, restricted to the degrees of freedom DX, DY, DZ) has an infinity norm which is small compared with the infinity norm of the previous displacement vector. This implies that one therefore always performs at least two geometry iterations with this criterion (in order to give oneself an initial displacement vector). The reader is referred to paragraph 3.7 of R5.03.50 for the exact expression of the infinity norm. 2.4.2.2 Generalised Newton algorithm (ALGO_RESO_GEOM='NEWTON') The continuous formulation (§ 3.1.3) offers the possibility of treating the geometric non-linearity directly within Newton's algorithm. For this, a pairing is carried out at each iteration and the geometric terms of the tangent matrix are themselves also updated. The geometric convergence criterion thus becomes an additional criterion of Newton's algorithm: the displacement increment must tend towards zero. 2.4.3 Convergence of the geometry loop 2.4.3.1 Linearisation of the normal The pairing supplies two pieces of information: - the gap on the paired configuration, - the coordinates of the potential contact point on the master surface. Whether a discrete or a continuous contact method is used, the principle of virtual power must be differentiated (linearised), in particular the contact terms. The fixed-point hypothesis leads one also to make the hypothesis of a small variation of the normal during the Newton iterations (of a time step). This hypothesis is consistent with the small-sliding hypothesis. The “gap” operator is thus linearised more easily. It remains in particular constant during a geometry iteration. This also has another implication: the geometric convergence towards the final configuration in fixed-point mode can sometimes be very slow. Conversely, the solution by a generalised Newton method, possible only in the continuous formulation (§ 3.1.3), presents a much faster convergence but can prove less robust. This is why it is not the default setting. To activate it, the keyword ALGO_RESO_GEOM will be used. 2.4.3.2 Geometric convergence criterion It has been seen above that the convergence of the geometry loop is done on a geometric criterion: the difference of the displacement vectors between two successive geometric configurations is relatively small. The displacement vectors are evaluated only on the contact zone. For the particular case of the generalised Newton algorithm in the continuous formulation, the criterion applies directly to the Newton displacement increment. For the solution by a fixed-point loop, “small” corresponds by default to less than 1% of the displacement since the beginning of the time step, whereas with the generalised Newton algorithm it is 0.0001% (the latter benefiting, in favourable cases, from a better convergence, it is possible to require a tighter criterion). When, following an analysis, one observes an interpenetration of the slave nodes into the master surface, the only explanation 2 2.2.5 is a failure to satisfy the geometric criterion. One must then not hesitate to tighten the criterion . For this, the keyword RESI_GEOM=0.005 is used so as to lower the threshold to around 0.5%, for example. Sometimes the geometric convergence is simply slow; in this case it is enough to increase the maximum number of iterations tolerated: ITER_GEOM_MAXI=20, for example. In certain situations, however much one varies the value of the criterion or the number of iterations, the analysis does not converge: it cycles. Several possibilities are then open to the user: - the most common explanation is a poor discretisation of the contact surfaces (that is to say a mesh that is too coarse, a difference in fineness between the two surfaces, or a poor choice of the master and slave surfaces). The reader is then referred to § 2.2. - when the contact surfaces are curved and meshed relatively coarsely, the explanation may come from too great a discontinuity of the normal (faceting). Activating the smoothing then very often makes convergence easier ( cf. § 2.3.2). This must not, however, prevent the user from reviewing the mesh. - if the case is truly pathological, one must oneself force the number of updates by using REAC_GEOM='CONTROLE' and NB_ITER_GEOM=n. After n geometry iterations, the analysis will pass to the following time step whatever the value of the geometric criterion, but it will emit an alarm when the criterion is not satisfied to within less than 1% (for n\ge 2 ).
