u2.04.07 1 u2.04.07 Use of transient solution methods for strongly non-linear quasi-static problems 1 u2.04.07 Use of transient solution methods for strongly non-linear quasi-static problems > Summary. This document presents the use of transient solution methods (implicit or explicit) for the numerical simulation of quasi-static problems presenting strong material non-linearities. The only aim is to obtain solutions in which the dynamic effects are negligible. These solution methods (based on the use of DYNA_NON_LINE) are designed as an alternative to the usual quasi-static approaches of Code_Aster (based on STAT_NON_LINE) when the latter prove unable to converge in an acceptable time. This may be the case for applications involving damaging materials. The methods that are the subject of this document are of two types: 1. implicit transient solution, 2. explicit pseudo-dynamic solution. The choice will depend on the nature of the problem to be treated, in particular in connection with the time scale considered. The use of these strategies being more delicate than the quasi-static approach, they are to be reserved for the most problematic cases. Reading documentation U2.06.13 constitutes a strongly recommended prerequisite: the general advice on the use of DYNA_NON_LINE remains relevant. 2 u2.04.07 Table of contents 1 Introduction Many problems in mechanics require taking into account, at the material level, damaging constitutive behaviours: reinforced-concrete structures, soil models… The constitutive relation may then present softening, and the known implicit quasi-static solution methods have difficulty in converging (the tangent stiffness operator becomes singular). In certain cases, even resorting to very high-performance strategies such as mixed line search or piloting is insufficient. In order to be able to overcome these limitations, there exist alternative strategies which are based on methods inspired by the tools of direct transient analysis [bib1]. It is stated clearly that there is no question here of wanting to simulate a dynamic response of vibratory type or with wave propagation: the aim is to obtain slowly evolving solutions, and therefore solutions consistent with the quasi-staticity hypothesis. The usual dynamic methods must therefore be adapted to this framework, and the solution thus obtained will have to satisfy the hypotheses of a sufficiently slow evolution. Finally, it should be kept well in mind that these transient approaches, because of their specific features, must be used as a last resort, when all the remedies available in STAT_NON_LINE have failed. The prerequisite for the use of the methods presented in this documentation is therefore to have already developed and exhaustively tested the options available in STAT_NON_LINE for the application considered. It goes without saying that a good knowledge of STAT_NON_LINE and of DYNA_NON_LINE is also strongly recommended, as is reading the corresponding documentations: R5.03.01, R5.05.05 and above all U2.06.13. In particular, the general advice on the use of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE given in documentation U2.06.13 remains valid, and it therefore constitutes an indispensable prerequisite for the proper implementation of the methods that are the subject of this documentation. 2 Features available in quasi-statics and absent in transient analysis The problem of damaging laws, in the local version, will mainly be addressed here. Indeed, non-local approaches, such as GRAD_VARI, are not available in dynamics. Particular care must therefore be taken to define for oneself a suitable minimum mesh-cell size so as not to observe excessive localisation phenomena. Next, methods of line-search type (mixed or otherwise) are not authorised in dynamics. This lack must be put into perspective, knowing that attempts to apply these methods to studies of reinforced-concrete structures in dynamics have not brought out any significant contribution to convergence, unlike what is observed in quasi-statics. Let us note, nevertheless, that no theoretical argument would forbid the use of these methods in dynamics. Finally, the piloting techniques available in STAT_NON_LINE (arc length, for example) are forbidden in dynamics because they then have no meaning. 3 Passing from a quasi-static analysis to a transient analysis Far from being limited to replacing the term STAT_NON_LINE by DYNA_NON_LINE in a command file (and to defining the densities, at a minimum …), the passage from the quasi-static to the transient must be accompanied by a certain number of indispensable precautions, on pain of strongly degrading the quality of the numerical solution obtained. These adaptations, described in detail in documentation U2.06.13, concern: - the regularisation in time of the boundary conditions, - the definition of initial conditions which do not introduce numerical oscillations. In addition to these general aspects, the user will have to pay attention to other, more specific adaptations. - Definition of the densities: from the physical point of view, the density must of course be defined at every point of the model. If the model comprises discrete elements, a discrete mass will have to be attached to them. The assembled mass operator must be invertible. The devices sometimes employed in quasi-statics, such as stiffenings on zones of the model (anchorages…) with materials having very large Young's moduli (or very large point stiffnesses), are to be handled with caution. Indeed, these very stiff zones will generate high-frequency disturbances in dynamics. Moreover, with an explicit time scheme, these very stiff zones risk causing the value of the critical time step to drop ( cf. R5.05.05). - Definition of the mesh-cell sizes and of the time steps: as a preliminary to the transient analysis, it is strongly recommended to carry out a modal analysis (with CALC_MODES) in order to obtain modal information which will make it possible to qualify the quality of the model in dynamics and to adjust certain parameters. The objective not being to go into the details of modal analysis, a few rules can nevertheless be recalled. Low-frequency solutions are sought, so only the first modes are relevant. Their proper representation can give indications of the mesh-cell sizes to be employed, in addition to the considerations already taken into account for the previous quasi-static analyses. Roughly, about ten mesh cells per smallest wavelength is sufficient. The modal analysis will also make it possible to check that the model is free of problems such as contributions to the inertia or to the stiffness that are not defined. Finally, the modal analysis is indispensable for the use of modal damping in DYNA_NON_LINE or for recalibrating the Rayleigh damping, as will be seen in what follows. - Definition of the damping: the user will also have to consider the question of the damping intrinsic to the model that he wants to use. In DYNA_NON_LINE, apart from the discrete elements, a global damping of Rayleigh or modal type can be introduced. Since one is seeking to simulate slow evolutions, one may be tempted to use damping values higher than for the classical dynamic analyses. A compromise nevertheless remains to be found, case by case, between a problem that is insufficiently damped (which will present oscillations) and a problem that is too heavily damped (critical or even super-critical damping). It is therefore advised to begin by implementing a "realistic" damping (therefore of a value identical to what is encountered in transient dynamics). Then, if this damping is judged insufficient, to increase it progressively. On various applications [bib1], it has been possible to observe that a damping of Rayleigh type, recalibrated on an equivalent modal damping of the order of 20%, or even 30%, was suitable. 4 Numerical implementation This chapter will address the choices to be favoured at the level of the numerical methods of DYNA_NON_LINE [bib2]. In a general manner, it is advised to follow the following logic: 1. once the possibilities of quasi-static solution through STAT_NON_LINE have been exhausted (including line search and piloting), 2. begin the dynamic approaches with an implicit solution, 3. in the event of failure of the transient implicit strategies (including by combining different dampings such as Rayleigh and a scheme of HHT type [bib2] and [bib3]), one switches to explicit (having first checked that the global damping does not depend on the stiffness matrix). For each transient approach, one should begin with as little damping as possible and therefore, in particular, with non-dissipative time schemes (such as Newmark or the central differences [bib4]). 4.1 Discretisation in time Unlike the quasi-static case, time has a physical meaning. Its discretisation is all the more sensitive for that. A few rules can be stated: - the evolution of the imposed loadings must be sampled sufficiently finely (between 5 and 10 time steps per shortest period of the signals considered), - the modal behaviour of the structure must be well represented (as above, one must have between 5 and 10 time steps per lowest period of the modes considered). Given the low-frequency character of the problems that one wants to address here, these two rules are in general not very penalising. Nevertheless, compared with the time steps of the previous quasi-static analyses, the dynamic time steps can be quite markedly smaller. In the explicit case, the Courant condition must in addition be respected (CFL cf. [bib5], [bib2] and R05.05.05), on pain of numerical divergence. For an integration scheme of central-difference type, the critical time step is equal to 2/\omega , where \omega is the highest natural angular frequency of the system. This angular frequency can be computed with CALC_MODES by choosing the option 'PLUS_GRANDE'. For further details, the reader may refer to documentation U2.06.13. For most structures, the Courant condition is very penalising: the wave speed often being of the order of a few thousand m / s, one arrives at time steps of less than 10-5 s. 4.2 Choice of the time-integration schemes The implicit schemes can be classified in two categories (the schemes of order 1 and/or in velocity, which are more specifically suited to very irregular problems, are deliberately set aside): - average acceleration (NEWMARK [bib4]), of order 2, which brings no numerical dissipation: to be used first, - complete HHT (MODI_EQUI = 'OUI' [bib3]), which remains of order 2, unlike the case of the modified average acceleration (MODI_EQUI = 'NON', the default option). This scheme is specifically developed in order to introduce a high-frequency numerical damping and therefore not to disturb the low-frequency physical response. The damping is controlled directly by the parameter ALPHA of the scheme. If high-frequency oscillations are observed in the numerical solution (roughly, oscillations whose period is of the order of a few time steps), the complete HHT scheme can be chosen, to begin with a value of the order of –0.1 for the parameter ALPHA. A value of –0.3 constitutes an upper limit that is still usable. If more damping is desired in the medium-frequency range, then the modified average-acceleration scheme can be employed. In the explicit case, two schemes are available: - central differences (DIFF_CENT [bib4]), which is non-dissipative, - Tchamwa-Wielgosz (TCHAMWA [bib6]), which is dissipative, in a manner comparable to HHT. Here again, it is recommended to begin by using a non-dissipative scheme. 4.3 Damping models The order of introduction and of use of the dissipation in the discretised model is the following: 1. intrinsic dissipation linked to the non-linear constitutive relations and to the links (friction), 2. global dissipation of structural-damping type (Rayleigh or modal), 3. numerical dissipation of the time scheme. Ideally, the first category ought to be sufficient, but in practice, for reasons of simplification of the model, it is often indispensable to add structural damping, the damping of the scheme being the last resort. Only the use of structural damping, in the Rayleigh sense, and that linked to the scheme will be addressed here. Let us simply recall that the more the sources of dissipation are multiplied, the more arduous their control and their physical interpretation will be. 4.3.1 Rayleigh damping This model makes it possible to define the global damping matrix C as being a linear combination of the stiffness and mass matrices (in order to have a damping matrix that is diagonal on the basis of the usual dynamic modes): C=\alpha K+\beta M Documentation U2.06.13 presents it in detail. The Rayleigh damping coefficients are defined, at the level of the characteristics of the material (command DEFI_MATERIAU), by the parameters AMOR_ALPHA and AMOR_BETA. The values to be imposed in order to obtain the desired damping x in the interval of the natural frequencies f1 and f2 are deduced from the following equations: Equation 1: Equation 2: Where f1 and f2 are the two natural frequencies bounding the interval of study considered. Within the framework of this document, low-frequency solutions are sought, so the frequencies f1 and f2 will be associated with the first frequencies of the model, whose modes are consistent with the imposed loading. 4.3.2 Damping due to the time scheme [bib2] Documentations R05.05.05 and U2.06.13 present this aspect. Here one will confine oneself to recalling the broad trends. To summarise, it can be recalled that, among the implicit schemes: - the average-acceleration scheme does not dissipate, - only the complete HHT scheme does not disturb the low-frequency domain, - for one and the same value of the parameter ALPHA, the modified average acceleration introduces much more dissipation than the HHT scheme. In order to highlight the influence of the high-frequency damping of the implicit schemes, documentation U2.06.13 presents examples of applications. Finally, as regards the explicit schemes, the shape of the damping of the Tchamwa scheme is qualitatively close to that of the modified average acceleration. 4.4 Adaptation of the explicit methods The conditional stability of the explicit schemes makes them very poorly suited to the simulation of slow phenomena. The explicit solution methods are not used here to capture rapid phenomena such as wave propagation; their use must rather be perceived as a particular solver that one adapts for slow problems. In order to be able to increase the critical time step [bib2], the density of the structure can be increased (which lowers the wave speed in proportion to its square root): This must however be done progressively. Indeed, two risks exist: - if the time step becomes too large, the computed solution may miss certain phenomena, such as the appearance of shear bands, and go so far as to bifurcate towards a branch very different from the expected response, - the increase in the density may be limited by the poor conditioning of the mass matrix. As an indication, the maximum time step in the explicit case (and therefore the maximum density) may be of the same order of magnitude as the time step necessary for the implicit transient analysis; in any case, it must remain smaller than the quasi-static time step. These are rough trends, which do not dispense with a parametric study on the explicit time step. If the model presents strong heterogeneities of stiffness (definition of several materials), it may be relevant to modify the densities separately, so as to have a Courant condition that is relatively homogeneous between the zones having different materials. Important note If displacement boundary conditions which evolve in the course of time are imposed, account must be taken of the fact that these conditions are in fact imposed in acceleration in the explicit case (because that is the primal unknown). This means that one must enter into DYNA_NON_LINE the second derivative of the displacement signal that one wants to impose. This evolution of the imposed displacement must therefore be differentiable at least twice with respect to time… Finally, it is recommended to use a diagonal (lumped) mass matrix, which is obtained by the keyword MASS_DIAG = 'OUI' of DYNA_NON_LINE. This computation option not being available for all the finite elements, the user may be obliged to use the consistent mass, should the occasion arise, as in the implicit case. 5 Quality control of the computed solutions 5.1 Quantities of interest coming from the quasi-static case As for the quasi-static analyses, the quantities relevant to post-processing can be classified in two categories [bib1]: 1. evolutions of force / displacement type: quantities making it possible to interpret the global response of the structure, 2. isovalues of fields such as the damage or the cumulative plastic strain. 5.2 Complementary dynamic quantities to be analysed In addition to these analyses, for the dynamic analyses it is indispensable to check that the slow-evolution hypothesis is respected. To this end, one must make sure that the inertia forces remain small compared with the other forces in the system (external and internal forces). A simple means of having an evaluation of the evolution of the inertia forces in the course of the analysis consists in observing the acceleration field in the course of time. A first simple criterion can be based on an (infinite) norm of the acceleration at each time instant. In the event of a notable and lasting increase in the acceleration (for example beyond 1 m/s2 over several successive time steps), this means that dynamic phenomena (therefore not taken into account by a quasi-static solution) are occurring: - if one is within a physical framework, and therefore with a realistic density, the computed solution is then subjected to non-negligible dynamic phenomena; - if one is within an explicit framework in which the density has been multiplied in order to increase the critical time step, then the inertia effects observed are the sign that the solution method is not suited. It is then imperative to modify the parameters, such as lowering the density, or modifying the damping… In the first case, one can attempt to relaunch an analysis with a slightly finer time step and possibly a slightly higher Rayleigh damping, or even with a scheme of HHT type. If, even with all these modifications, the solution still presents inertia effects, then any quasi-static approach is unsuitable. 5.3 Examples of analysis On the graph below (a small reinforced-concrete structure), a case is presented in which the acceleration is going to become non-negligible, from 6 s onwards. The maximum value remains lower than 0.4 m/s2 and we are in a case with a realistic density. Moreover, the acceleration is going to become small again after 10 s: from all of this one can conclude that the analysis remains compatible with the slow-evolution hypothesis. On the following graph, the influence of the damping (due to Rayleigh and to the scheme) on the maximum acceleration can be quantified. Overall, on this example, the use of a scheme of HHT type with a Rayleigh damping set to an equivalent modal value of 20% is well suited (black curve). On the other hand, the average-acceleration scheme (Newmark) will make it possible to control the acceleration only if it is coupled with a very large Rayleigh damping: 50% equivalent modal damping. The computed solution then risks being too dissipative. On the following figure, one can judge the influence of a parameter of the discretisation: the time step, in terms of control of the maximum acceleration. The value of 10-3 s for the time step is not well chosen, and it is then preferable to divide the time step by two. To analyse this behaviour, it is indispensable to carry out a parametric study on the time step. In the case of an explicit solution (on an example very different from the previous ones: excavation of a circular gallery [bib1]), different time schemes are compared: the central differences (therefore without induced damping) and the Tchamwa scheme for two values of the parameter PHI. The larger this parameter, the more high-frequency damping is introduced, and this damping becomes zero for PHI=1. In addition to the previous curves, it is instructive to visualise a few isovalues of the acceleration norm (for the same example of excavation in the explicit case): On the left-hand figure, one is in a phase of low acceleration (the non-linearity linked to the deconfinement rate is still weak). The appearance of the acceleration field is fairly random: no "pattern" betraying a real dynamic phenomenon can be perceived. On the right-hand figure, the non-linearity is established and a very different distribution of acceleration is observed: the appearance of shear bands can be seen taking shape around the periphery of the excavation. But even in this case, the maximum values of acceleration remain very small (including when the factor of increase of the density is taken into account). The solution obtained explicitly is therefore relevant in the sense of a slow evolution. 6 Optimisation of performance In most cases it is recommended to carry out the analysis in quasi-statics when the non-linearities are moderate and then, as soon as the number of iterations to convergence for equilibrium increases significantly, to switch to dynamics (implicit, then explicit if need be). More precisely, it is advised to switch before the appearance of strong non-linearities, so that the dynamic analysis is initiated on an evolution that is still fairly "regular". In quasi-statics, it is not rare to have to carry out more than 10 iterations in order to obtain convergence in the sense of the equilibrium residual. In implicit dynamics this value of 10 iterations constitutes, in general, a good starting value for the parameter ITER_GLOB_MAXI of CONVERGENCE. If one cannot converge in fewer than 10 to 20 iterations, it is then preferable to decrease the time step rather than to increase the maximum number of iterations allowed. In the explicit case, there are no iterations for equilibrium, so the computation cost of each time step will therefore be constant, whatever the level of non-linearity (apart, possibly, from the local check of the constitutive behaviour). In the case of a quasi-static analysis in which the non-linearity increases with time, a crossover point can therefore be found, at the level of the CPU time, beyond which the efficiency of the explicit methods (or even of the implicit methods, depending on the cases) becomes greater than that of continuing in quasi-statics. The gain brought by a larger time step in quasi-statics is cancelled out by the necessity of carrying out more and more iterations at each step. Likewise, the computation cost in the explicit case remaining constant, one can also evaluate fairly precisely the total computation time necessary for the solution of the complete case, whereas in quasi-statics, the number of iterations at each step being highly variable and also being liable to entail an unknown number of subdivisions of the step, the total computation time is sometimes very difficult to predict. The use, even as a matter of routine, of the explicit methods therefore seems very attractive in view of the CPU time, which remains under control. This optimism must however be tempered by keeping well in mind that one is depriving oneself of the safeguard constituted by the precise check of equilibrium and that, consequently, the quality of the explicit solution obtained must be analysed with greater care. The explicit algorithm will not diverge (if the Courant condition is respected), but the solution obtained is not guaranteed by an equilibrium-verification criterion. In particular, a parametric study on the time step is indispensable, because the appearance of the solution can vary strongly when this step becomes too large. This obligation to check the explicit solution is all the greater in that one is furthermore seeking to verify the fundamental hypothesis of slow evolution. 7 Conclusion This document presents the use of transient dynamic methods for the simulation of slow and strongly non-linear evolutions [bib1]. The dynamic operators thus employed for the solution can be seen as particular solvers making it possible, in certain cases, to obtain solutions for which the quasi-static algorithmics available in Code_Aster (around the operator STAT_NON_LINE) shows great difficulties of convergence (in the sense of the verification of equilibrium). These dynamic methods are to be used as a last resort, because mastering them is more delicate than in the quasi-static framework. This is even more marked with the explicit methods, since the quality of the solution is not guaranteed by a precise verification of equilibrium at each time instant. The first stage is the adaptation of the model to the dynamic methods. It is mainly a matter of making sure of the proper regularity of the imposed conditions and of the correct definition of the density and of the global damping (Rayleigh). The piloting methods, the non-local approaches and the line search cannot be used in dynamics. Moreover, it is necessary to introduce a global damping model (Rayleigh or modal) whose level is higher than in classical dynamics (commonly 20% equivalent modal damping). Next, it is recommended to begin by using an implicit transient method (DYNA_NON_LINE with a time scheme of NEWMARK type, or HHT). From the point of view of the optimisation of the computation time, it is recommended to carry out all the weakly non-linear phases in quasi-statics and to switch to transient analysis (implicit to begin with) only upon the appearance of notable non-linearities (this may take the form of a clear increase in the number of iterations to convergence, or even of a subdivision of the time step). In the event of failure, including with a complete HHT scheme and a relatively strong structural damping (up to about 30% equivalent modal damping), the user can switch to explicit. Further adaptations must then be made, such as increasing the density in order to obtain a sufficiently large critical time step, and modifying the damping. In all the dynamic cases, it is indispensable to analyse the evolution of the acceleration in the course of time, in order to make sure of the validity of the slow-evolution hypothesis. The inertia effects must remain small. 8 Bibliography [1] N. Greffet, Assessment of transient methods for excavation analyses , Note EDF R&D H-T62-2007-02878-FR, 2008. [2] N. u2.05.00 Methodological guide on the approaches in fracture mechanics u2.05.00 Methodological guide on the approaches in fracture mechanics Summary: This note constitutes a methodological guide for the use of fracture mechanics with Code_Aster . It provides an overall view of the approaches in fracture mechanics existing or planned in Code_Aster and constitutes a signpost towards the dedicated notes and documentations. 1 Glossary Acronyms - SENT : Single Edge Notched Tension: tensile specimen with a lateral notch - SENB : Single Edge Notched Bending : three-point bending specimen with a lateral notch - CT : Compact Tension specimen for the measurement of the toughness and of the resistance to ductile tearing - AE : axisymmetric notched specimen - LCF: cycle of a warm preloading of Loading Cooling Fracture type - LUCF : cycle of a warm preloading of Loading Unloading Cooling Fracture type - DSR : defect under cladding - DDR : defect in the cladding Definitions - Initiation/Propagation of a crack: According to the reference or the discipline, there may be a dispute over these definitions. For example, in fatigue, the word initiation is more commonly employed to designate the appearance of the crack in a sound material. Whereas in fracture mechanics, one evaluates the initiation of an existing crack. In fatigue, one implies the propagation under cyclic loading. Whereas in fracture mechanics, one employs the word propagation to designate a tear under monotonic loading. In order to remove any ambiguity, one employs in this document the word initiation to designate the stability aspect of an existing crack; will it propagate or not? One also employs the word propagation to designate the evolution of the crack front under monotonic loading: - if rapid evolution - unstable propagation: cleavage - if progressive evolution - stable propagation: ductile tearing - {K}_{I} , {K}_{\mathit{II}} and {K}_{\mathit{III}} , the stress intensity factors of modes I , \mathit{II} and \mathit{III} , respectively, valid in linear thermo-elastic mechanics, supplying the characteristics of the stress fields in the vicinity of the crack tip - G , energy release rate , due to Griffith, valid in linear or non-linear elasticity. A link (Irwin formulae) exists between the factors {K}_{I} , {K}_{\mathit{II}} , {K}_{\mathit{III}} and G in linear elasticity. For example, in plane strain: G=\frac{1-{\nu }^{2}}{E}({K}_{I}^{2}+{K}_{\text{II}}^{2})+\frac{1+\nu }{E}{K}_{\text{III}}^{2} - {G}_{\mathit{ENL}} , energy release rate in the post-processing of a non-linear thermoelastic analysis - J , contour integral , due to Rice, equivalent to G in plane linear elasticity, characterises the energy release rate of a structure containing a crack during the advance of the latter. This integral is independent of the contour when the material is elastic - {J}_{\mathit{MOD}} , contour integral J modified to take account of the initial stresses, valid under a non-proportional loading. - The toughness of a material is its ability to resist the propagation of a crack; it is defined by the stress intensity factor {K}_{\mathit{IC}} or, when the plasticity is confined at the crack tip, by the Rice–Cherepanov integral ( {J}_{\mathit{IC}} ). {G}_{\mathit{IC}} is the critical energy release rate. {K}_{\mathit{IC}} and {G}_{\mathit{IC}} characterise the criteria of resistance of the material to the propagation of cracks - In plane elasticity, there exists an equivalence between the propagation criteria: - G 0\\ \chi ({K}_{\mathit{plas}}(u)-{K}_{\mathit{elas}}(u))\end{array}\right]\right\} - and \chi =\left\{\begin{array}{ccc}1& \mathit{si}max({K}_{\mathit{plas}})\ge max({K}_{\mathit{elas}})& :\mathit{cas}\mathit{DSR}\\ -1& \mathit{sinon}& :\mathit{cas}\mathit{DDR}\end{array}\right\} - Regulatory margin factor : it is defined as: - {\mathit{FM}}_{\mathit{ASN}}=\left\{\begin{array}{ccc}\mathit{FM}& \mathit{si}max({K}_{\mathit{plas}})\ge max({K}_{\mathit{elas}})& :\mathit{cas}\mathit{DSR}\\ \frac{{K}_{\mathit{IC}}}{{K}_{\mathit{elas}}}& \mathit{sinon}& :\mathit{cas}\mathit{DDR}\end{array}\right\} 2 Introduction This methodological guide constitutes an aid to facilitate the understanding of a study of the harmfulness of generic or exceptional defects revealed on metallic structures. The main aim of this document is to inform the fracture-mechanics engineer about the approaches available in Code_Aster for solving a given problem. This document refers to the documents of type U2 in the documentation base of Code_Aster ; it does not recall the formulations detailed in the reference documents R, nor the means of using these functionalities, which are sufficiently explained in the user's documents U4 or U2, but it delimits the field of application of each approach. Thus, one proposes to recall the various approaches available and to define briefly their field of application. The field of validity of these approaches may be linked either to the definition of the model (brittle fracture, ductile fracture, …), or to the degree of maturity of the approach as regards its industrial implementation (heaviness of the analyses, developments still necessary, material parameters not available…). However, we cannot describe all the types of study possible or carried out in fracture mechanics. The user will choose the approach according to the requirements and conditions of his or her study. References to a few study notes whose aim was to validate these approaches or to apply them to industrial cases are also given. The approaches on initiation and stability are dominant in this document, to the detriment of those which treat tearing. The methods of propagation under monotonic loading for simulating ductile tearing remain to be developed in Code_Aster. 3 Brief overview of fracture mechanics Any metallic component subjected to mechanical, thermal, hydraulic or chemical loadings is exposed to cracking. The defect or the crack comes from manufacture (welding) or from a process of damage of the material in the course of operation (fatigue, creep, stress-corrosion, ...). As soon as the cracks become of a size large enough for the volume which surrounds them to satisfy the continuity assumptions of continuum mechanics, the mechanical study must be carried out in the field of fracture mechanics. The studies must then estimate the degree of harmfulness of these cracks: are they harmless, and will their presence therefore be tolerated for a more or less long time without risks, or on the contrary are they harmful, which makes it necessary to repair or replace the component? 3.1 Initiation / Propagation On certain types of component, degradation mechanisms such as creep, stress-corrosion or fatigue are at the origin of the creation of cracks which may then give rise to sudden fracture. Fracture mechanics makes it possible to predict the harmfulness of an existing crack : the kinetics of propagation of defects and their critical sizes. In the case where the propagation phase would be very rapid, the final fracture is said to be sudden or unstable; in the contrary case, the fracture is stable, which characterises for example ductile tearing. Propagation may lead to a total fracture or to an arrest of the crack. 3.2 Brittle fracture (cleavage) / Ductile fracture (tearing) The temperature and the strain rate of a material are two parameters which characterise its state: brittle or ductile. Certain metallic materials are brittle below a temperature called the brittle/ductile transition temperature (cf. schematic figure Figure 3.2-a ), and in particular the ferritic steels (low-alloy steels and carbon-manganese steels). Structures are generally designed in such a way that the nominal stress undergone does not exceed the yield stress of the material, which protects them from irreversible strains. A fracture of brittle type may then occur on a pre-existing crack or on a crack created by fatigue, at low temperature and/or at high strain rates. Ductile fracture (tearing) A material is ductile when it deforms plastically before fracturing; the plasticity is generalised. This plastic deformation may lead to the appearance of a crack which becomes critical when it propagates. After initiation, the growth of the crack is in general slow and stable (according to the characteristics of the applied loading). Ductile fracture concerns materials such as copper, lead, mild steels at ambient temperature, and austenitic stainless steels. The fracture mechanism comprises three phases: the generation of microscopic voids around preferential sites, the growth and the coalescence of the cavities leading to fracture. The fracture surface is in this case of a dull and rough appearance. Brittle fracture (cleavage) Brittle fracture occurs without notable local plastification. After initiation, the propagation of the crack is rapid (the tests reveal speeds of a few hundred m\mathrm{/}s ) and most often unstable (with arrest or sudden fracture of the component according to the case). It characterises brittle materials such as glass, ceramics and irradiated steels or steels at low temperature. Resilience characterises the capacity of the material to store energy when it deforms in an elastic manner. The brittle material fractures under the effect of a low energy. The greater the energy which must be supplied in order to deform it, the tougher the material is. The resilience tests are carried out on specimens of Charpy type and the toughness tests are carried out most often on specimens of type \mathit{CT} . In the case of a brittle material — unlike the ductile material — the plasticity remains confined at the crack tip; this type of phenomenon is known under the term “cleavage”: the propagation of the crack takes place by separation of atomic planes and the fracture surface is made up of planes of a bright appearance. To a brittle material there corresponds a low toughness. The toughness at initiation {K}_{\mathrm{1c}} is not an intrinsic datum of the material; it depends on the geometry and on the level of triaxiality. Figure 3.2-a. Brittle – ductile transition curve 4 Summary or mini user's guide to the approaches The following table and flowchart aim to give the user, in a rapid manner, an indication of the field of application of a given approach. In other words, would it be valid for representing initiation in brittle or ductile fracture? Would it be valid for simulating propagation in brittle or in ductile fracture? This table allows a brief reading of the document, helping one to ask the questions which will direct the reader according to the conditions of his or her study towards the approaches described in the document. These approaches exist or are in the course of development in Code_Aster . For the sake of readability, the table and the flowchart contain the minimum of information, and do not mention the particularities of the studies, the maturity of the approaches, the advantages and the disadvantages of the approaches. User flowchart 5 Panorama of the approaches in fracture mechanics The global approach has been known for a long time, but it has a limited domain of validity. The local approach has a more extended validity, but it is within the reach only of experienced mechanicians. The local approaches make it possible to apprehend and to understand phenomena which are all the more complex in that they can reduce the degree of conservatism of the codified approaches based on the global approaches. The theory of brittle fracture rests on fracture criteria of “global approach” established in a macroscopic manner and it does not address the problems of constitutive behaviour, because the material is often considered elastoplastic with confined plasticity. The purely macroscopic approach to brittle fracture is no longer valid when the material is strongly plastified, because it is no longer possible to represent the crack as a surface of discontinuity of the displacements and of the stresses. The dissipation is concentrated at the crack tip and it is difficult to separate the plastic dissipation from the fracture dissipation. In ductile fracture, a “local approach” based on a mechanical procedure is often necessary. When an approach becomes generic and applicable over a fairly wide range of situations, it also becomes complex. 5.1 Classical approach Linear elastic fracture mechanics rests on the stress intensity factor, which characterises the stress and strain fields in the neighbourhood of a crack. In plasticity, classical fracture mechanics possesses rigorous bases only by analogy with non-linear elastic constitutive behaviours (in the case of non-proportional loadings and isotropy), for which the contour integral J or the energy release rate is the fundamental parameter. In linear or non-linear elasticity (cf. § 7.1 and § 7.2 ), three parameters can be computed: - J , the Rice integral: contour integral – the experimental computation of J is obtained by the area under the force–opening curve of the specimens ( \mathit{CT} or \mathit{SENB} in general). This parameter is available in Code_Aster (cf. [65]) - G , the energy release rate: domain integral suited to computation by finite elements (cf. [57], [58]), - K , the stress intensity coefficients corresponding to the 3 modes, associated with the singular fields at the crack tip. The latter have a meaning only in linear elasticity (cf. [60], [62]). In elastoplasticity, this parameter is strictly valid only when elastoplasticity can be assimilated to non-linear elasticity, that is to say for a radial monotonic loading . However, a modified form of the contour integral, {J}_{\mathit{MOD}} , has been proposed, which is valid for non-proportional stress conditions (cf. [18], [47], [65]). The expression of the modified integral ( {J}_{\mathit{MOD}} ) reduces to the classical integral, J . The classical approach presents several limitations when it is applied outside its domain of validity (“small-defect effect”, “triaxiality effect”, “warm-preloading effect”, …) or in the case of non-proportional loading, which has led to the developments of new global or energy approaches or of local approaches. It turns out that in certain particular cases {J}_{\mathrm{1C}} or {K}_{\mathrm{1C}} may depend on the geometry and are not intrinsic to the material. Small-defect effect: It turns out that the toughness, which is supposed to be intrinsic to the material, seems to depend on the size of the defect, or more exactly on the ratio of the size of the defect to the size of the ligament (in fact, it is the level of triaxiality affecting the neighbourhood of the defect which is responsible for this effect). The toughness in the case of a small defect is greater than that of a large defect. Geometry effect: The geometry of the medium ‘specimen or structure’ influences the nature of the fracture, in particular in the transition zone. At a given temperature, for the same material and at equivalent loading, a \mathit{CT} specimen fractures in a brittle manner whereas a cracked pipe fractures in a ductile manner. For homothetic notched \mathit{AE} specimens, the scatter and the mean value of the diametral strain at fracture decrease when the diameter of the specimen increases. The smaller a\mathrm{/}w is, the higher the apparent value of {J}_{\mathrm{1C}} is. “Mismatch” effect: In the presence of two materials, the classical approach is valid when the plasticity remains confined in a homogeneous zone. When the plastification domain covers two materials, the classical approach is no longer valid. Triaxiality effect “constraint effect”: In order to be able to use the classical approach in elastoplasticity, one must assume that the loading is proportional, which is often far from being the case for real structures. The loading and the geometry influence the type of stress field at the crack tip in a structure. The stress field at the crack tip may become complex compared with the usual conditions of proportional loading adopted on a specimen. Warm-preloading effect: Warm-preloading effect or “WPS: Warm Pre-Stressing”: following a rise in temperature, the material passes from the brittle domain to the ductile domain, and a mechanical loading is then applied (warm preloading). After cooling of the specimen and a toughness-measurement test, one finds a value of the toughness greater than that of the material tested without the preloading. The warm preloading has a beneficial effect induced by the blunting of the crack and the appearance of residual stresses. Non-proportional loading effect: Several situations induce a non-proportional loading at the crack point, which makes the classical approach invalid: - unloading problem following a thermal shock, although in certain cases the Beta correction can be applied in order to assume that the constitutive behaviour after unloading is elastic (cf. [75]), - problem of non-monotonic or non-proportional loading, following a propagation, a thermal transient, the presence of residual stresses or a mixed mode. If the loading is arbitrary, one may use a local approach (Beremin (cf. [59]) or Bordet (cf. [61]) or an energy approach (cf. [64]) in the case of cleavage, or Rousselier and GTN for tearing (cf. [67], [68] and [87) which do not need the assumption of proportional loading. 5.2 Two-parameter approach This approach is developed in order to respond to the dependence of the toughness on the triaxiality. It rests on the extension of the expression of the fields at the crack tip with higher-order terms. More complex than the classical approach, it enriches it by the introduction of a second parameter which takes account of the triaxiality, of the stability and of the plasticity zone. It loses its validity when the loading is no longer proportional: loading followed by an unloading, propagation of cracks, residual stresses, mixed mode ... or when the material is viscous or subjected to a thermal transient. This approach requires the setting up of a very large number of tests in order to construct the locus of fracture (cf. § 7.13 ). The global two-parameter approach is not developed in Code_Aster (cf. [50]). 5.3 Energy approach In an elastic or non-linear elastic framework, the energy approach leads to the computation of the parameter G , energy release rate. In the case of a confined plasticity, it has given rise to the development of the \mathit{Gp} approach (cf . [64], [73]), which is an energy approach avoiding the Rice paradox by the use of a notch (cf. § 7.4 ). It is possible to estimate the energy release rate, thanks to the use of contour integral methods (cf. [18], [47], [65]). In the case of a ductile material or of extended plasticity, it is declined as the computation of the parameter \mathit{Gtp} (cf. [37]), which is now withdrawn from Code_Aster. This approach has been applied within the framework of the European project VOCALIST on the small-defect-effect case and within the framework of the European project SMILE on the warm-preloading WPS case. It is possible to employ this approach in the cases of non-proportional loadings. 5.4 Local approach to fracture The description of fracture passes through a local modelling of the damage. Fracture is characterised by an intrinsic variable of the material. It allows the definition of a local fracture criterion based on material and geometric considerations at the level of the crack tip. In brittle fracture: In this case, it is sufficient to analyse the harmfulness of the defect at initiation. The models are in general criteria in the post-processing of an analysis. For brittle fracture or cleavage, the model most used is the Beremin model (cf. [8], , [59], [69]), based on the weakest-link theory, with a Weibull stress and a statistical law of distribution of micro-defects (cf. § 7.5 ). This model also makes it possible to account for the scale effect, that is to say the variation of the risk of fracture with respect to the size of the specimen. The users of the Beremin approach recommend the use of a crack or, more recently, of a notch, with a mesh-cell size of 50\mu m as has long been accepted. Indeed, the notch has a morphology better suited than the crack for capturing the fields in elastoplasticity. The advantage of the Beremin approach is that it is widely tested. The account taken of the triaxiality is intrinsic to the method. The local approach of Bordet (cf. § 7.6 ), introduced recently into Code_Aster (cf. [61], [70], [85]) is an extension of Beremin. It furthermore allows an improved treatment in the case of warm preloading thanks to the account taken of the active plasticity. Whereas the active plasticity is taken into account in modified Beremin, the Bordet model furthermore makes it possible to take into account the effect of the plasticity on the micro-defects at the origin of cleavage. In ductile fracture: The models for ductile tearing raise several difficulties. The determination of the material parameters is not standardised and is carried out case by case. The approaches proposed in the literature are classified into 3 families: - The uncoupled models : the damage of the material does not affect its global constitutive behaviour. The fracture of the structure occurs when the damage reaches a critical value which is supposed to be intrinsic to the material. These models are used to analyse the initiation of the crack. - The coupled models : based on damageable elastoplastic potentials or on micro-mechanical approaches. The constitutive behaviour of the material and the damage are linked. The fracture of the structure is described implicitly by the softening of the global response of the structure. - The semi-coupled models : models intermediate between the two preceding families. The global constitutive behaviour is not affected by the damage but there is a local coupling of the damage with the constitutive behaviour. The fracture of the structure takes place when the local softening is reached. The uncoupled model of Rice & Tracey (cf. [61] and § 7.12 ), or the coupled model of Gurson [87] and of Rousselier (cf. [67] and § 7.10 ) are intended for ductile fracture. The limitations relating to these approaches come from the difficulty of identification of the parameters and of the transferability from specimen to structure. 5.5 Alternative approach - CZM This is an approach widely developed in the literature which is global as regards the minimisation of the energy and local through the fine description of the residual forces at the crack tip. It makes it possible to predict in a robust manner the kinetics of propagation (cf. [81], [51]). The ambition of these cracking models is to represent the evolution of the damage and/or fracture surfaces of a solid in 2D or in 3D, sound or partially cracked, subjected to a wide range of loadings (mixed mode, cyclic of any amplitude, thermal, ...). The characterisation of the material parameters, in particular the critical stress, is a primordial step for the proper use of these elements. It is an approach which makes it possible to predict initiation and propagation along a path known a priori (cf. 7.9 ). However, the size of the crack at initiation is not precise because it is dependent on the size of the cohesive element in the mesh. It is less influential on the expected result in the analysis of the propagation. Table 5.5-1. In every case, a precise computation of the mechanical fields at the tip of the crack/notch is primordial. To do this, it is widely recommended to mesh finely at the crack tip or to use quadratic elements with Barsoum elements at the crack tip if the analysis is elastic, and to employ under-integrated elements or incompressible elements if the analysis is elastoplastic. It is known that a radiating mesh at the crack tip leads to a quality of the solution in terms of energy release rate superior to that obtained with other types of mesh and at a lower cost in terms of performance in computation time. Crack meshes are widely used in the business tools when one must use the classical approaches of the computations of G , energy release rate. Cracks are distinctly easier to model than notches on 3D meshes. When one is interested in a global result obtained on a \mathit{CT} or \mathit{AE} specimen, the defect may be represented by a crack or a notch. On the other hand, in order to know precisely the mechanical fields around the tip of the defect, it is recommended to mesh a notch. Indeed, the notch makes it possible to smooth the singular mechanical fields at the crack tip and to reduce the zone in which the stresses are disturbed. The meshing of a notch in 3D is tedious. As the analyses with \mathit{Gp} require meshes of notches with slices, on which this method rests, Gibi scripts have been developed for this purpose. The definition of the cracked block defined with Gibi, some twenty years ago, is inherent in the presence of a torus around the crack tip with a radiating mesh. The specification of the meshes is complicated for the contour integrals, {J}_{\mathit{MOD}} , because they must satisfy specific mathematical criteria [1]. Moreover, the elements which define a contour must be extracted. Inevitably, this still impacts the time of creation of a mesh and the post-processing time. Under development: - A procedure for insertion of a crack with a radiating mesh into a sound structure with Salomé. - A procedure for insertion of a crack with a free mesh with the tool Zcracks. - A library of meshes of cracked specimens in 3D is planned in Salomé-Meca. The parametric mesh of a \mathit{CT} specimen in 3D is already available (as an overload) in the form of a plug-in. 6.1.2 XFEM This method makes it possible to avoid meshing the crack. It is based on the definition and the enrichment of the model by level-sets (cf. [82]). The implementation of an analysis with XFEM is recalled in the document [80]. The criteria and the refinement method for the analyses as well as a synthesis of the developments and applications are the subject of the references [55] and [56]. This method is operational at the present time on elastic structures. The extension of the validation of its domain to plasticity is in the course of development. 6.2 Evaluating the risk of initiation: Will the crack propagate? 6.2.1 In thermoelasticity In linear thermoelasticity , the classical global approaches are applicable: - Computation of the energy release rate G (cf. [71], [57]), - Estimation of the energy release rate {J}_{\mathit{MOD}} (cf. [18], [47], [65]), - Computation of the stress intensity factors K (cf. [60], [72]), - Comparison of the stress intensity factor with the toughness or of the energy release rate with the critical energy, In non-linear thermoelasticity , the classical global approaches are applicable only in the case of a radial and proportional loading. They are based on the computation of the energy release rate {G}_{\text{ENL}} in the post-processing of a non-linear thermo-elastic analysis (cf. [71], [58]). A method for the case of non-proportional loading has been proposed, which is {J}_{\mathit{MOD}} (cf. [18], [47], [65]). In brittle fracture , computation of {G}_{\text{ENL}} in comparison with {G}_{\text{c}} or computation of {K}_{G} from {G}_{\text{ENL}} and comparison with the toughness of the material {K}_{\mathrm{1C}} . Estimation of the probability of fracture via the “Master Curve” (cf.[[25]]), In ductile fracture , {G}_{\text{ENL}} is compared with {J}_{0,2} in order to study the risk of initiation of tearing, These approaches are applicable in a well-defined domain of validity (non-linear elasticity, hence proportional loading, and when the crack is sufficiently large), outside which we observe effects : - non-proportional loading following: - an unloading, - a propagation, - a thermal transient, - a presence of residual stresses, - a “constraint effect” or triaxiality effect - Mismatch effect (2 materials) - “Small defect” effect - Warm-preloading effect or “WPS” 6.2.2 In elastoplasticity - brittle fracture For a medium in which the plasticity remains confined, the medium remaining elastic in its entirety, the global and local approaches of fracture mechanics or energy approaches make it possible to apply the criteria of fracture mechanics. However, according to the material parameters which one has available, the time which one can devote to the carrying out of the study, the availability of an adequate mesh or the capacity to produce it are arguments which argue for one approach or for another (cf. Table 6.2.2-1 ): - Energy approach \mathit{Gp} (cf. [73]): The advantage of the \mathit{Gp} approach is that it is deterministic and comes close to the classical engineer's approach J . A relation between the two parameters \mathit{Gpc} , the critical value of \mathit{Gp} and the radius of the notch has been able to be established, which facilitates the data setup of the parameters. The account taken of the triaxiality is direct with this approach. Let us note that there remain points to be improved in the \mathit{Gp} approach in order to make it still more accessible to the engineer: - Although the energy approach \mathit{Gp} comes close to the global approach by virtue of its foundation on energy principles, it depends on the radius of the notch in the case of non-proportional/non- monotonic loadings and therefore on the thickness of the sliced zone. - The meshing of the slices is not easily achievable, and is obligatory in 3D. One must in addition master mesh-refinement techniques in order to avoid the stretching of the mesh cells at the notch tip causing stress concentrations. - One assumes that the \mathit{Gp} approach is valid for all non-proportional loadings. The analyses carried out under these conditions cannot be validated without accompanying them with large test campaigns. - Local approach of Beremin: This approach has the advantage of being widely used. However, it is a probabilistic approach, so the results are difficult to interpret and it is not recommended in the upper part of the transition zone. The material parameters must be finely identified in dependence on the temperature. - Local approach of Bordet: This approach requires a large number of parameters which are not obvious to identify. The macro POST_BORDET is developed in Code_Aster. - Approach based on the critical stress (Hajjaj [9], Ritchie, Knott, Rice [15], Dahl [12]): Approach developed for the treatment of crack arrest in viscoplasticity. The fracture criterion is a comparison between the maximum principal stress and the critical stress. This approach makes it possible to simulate the advance of the crack by cancelling the stiffness of the elements at the crack tip, when the criterion is reached. - Approach with cohesive elements (cf. [63], [72]). This approach has been compared with the classical approach in the note cited in [21]; it is not often used in brittle fracture for lack of material parameters. However, the identification of these parameters (only 2) can be done by comparison with other models or with the experimental results. It is an approach which makes it possible to predict cleavage on a known path. - Two-parameter approach K-T in brittle fracture and J-Q in ductile fracture, which makes it possible to take account of the triaxiality effect in a qualitative manner (cf. [50], [29]). These approaches are not yet developed in Code_Aster . - Damage laws in quasi-static conditions may be used in brittle fracture (cf. [84]). However, they are rather used for the simulation of the cracking of geomaterials, which does not prevent their use for the simulation of the damage of metallic materials with the appropriate material parameters and regularisation. The determination of the material parameters is not standardised and is carried out case by case. Same remark as for brittle fracture: according to the material parameters which one has available, the time which one can devote to the carrying out of the study, the availability of an adequate mesh or the capacity to produce it are arguments which argue for one approach or for another (cf. Table 6.2.3-1 ): - Energy approach \mathit{Gtp} : This approach is based on the computation of the total energy in the post- processing of an elastoplastic analysis with the operator CALC_G (cf. [71]). This approach was used some ten years ago and showed an advantage with respect to the classical approach J-\Delta a , by virtue of its applicability in the case of complex loadings. Its weak point lies in the definition of the criterion, which encompasses fracture and plasticity, which may overestimate the energy linked to fracture. It has been compared recently with the \mathit{CZM} on a study of crack initiation in an elastoplastic medium (cf. [21]). This approach is now withdrawn from Code_Aster. - Uncoupled local approach – Rice and Tracey: This is a simple ductile-initiation criterion because it rests on an analytical formula as a function of the stresses and strain rates at each computation instant. The advantage of this approach is that it is simple and widely used. Its use must remain limited to preliminary analyses (cf. [61]) - Coupled local approach of Rousselier: ROUSS_PR, ROUSS_VISC (cf. [68]) and ROUSSELIER model in large strains (cf.[67]) and of GTN [87]. These models present several difficulties of numerical implementation: identification of the parameters, mesh adaptation around the crack, adaptation of the boundary conditions, non-convergence of the constitutive law. Recommendations which help to overcome these difficulties (incompressible elements – large strains – mesh adaptation in order to take account of the unloading) must facilitate convergence. - Two-parameter approach (cf. [50]): The J-Q approach is promising because it will allow an application in the three domains, brittle, ductile and transition, and it makes it possible to represent the branching of cracks. It nevertheless remains applicable only within a framework of proportional loading. This approach is not available in Code_Aster . - The cohesive models (cf. [81], [63]). The account taken of the triaxiality has proved necessary for their good representativeness in 3D. Table 6.2.3-1. Table 6.2.4-1 ): - The Rousselier/Beremin chaining is implemented in the study on the passage from resilience to toughness (cf. [31]). This coupling is carried out with a representation of the defect by a notch. The simulation of the ductile propagation remains to be determined, the \mathit{Gtp} approach seeming legitimate since it is based on a notch. The coupling capability must still be verified. - The chaining J-\mathit{Gfr} /Le Corre: J-\mathit{Gfr} for the ductile propagation and Le-Corre for the prediction of the nature of the initiation. The Le-Corre model proposed at the CEA (cf. 7.7 ) uses the notion of threshold stress, coupled with a threshold-volume value. This model is based on the computation of J , and therefore can predict initiation only in the case of monotonic/proportional loadings (cf. [48], [85]). This model is not available in Code_Aster . Will it arrest? 6.3.1 Cleavage In brittle fracture, among the approaches cited in § 6.2.2 : - The CZM approach can evaluate the advance of the crack, along a path known a priori. It has also been used within the framework of the Vessel project to simulate the crack arrest of a defect under cladding (cf. [55]). - Approach based on the critical stress (Hajjaj [9], Ritchie, Knott, Rice [15], Dahl [12]): Approach developed for the treatment of crack arrest in viscoplasticity. The fracture criterion is a comparison between the maximum principal stress and the critical stress. This approach makes it possible to simulate the advance of the crack by cancelling the stiffness of the elements at the crack tip, when the criterion is reached. The thesis work of S. Cuvilliez (cf. [54]) aims to achieve a transition between a damage model and the cohesive elements in concrete. It is the only reference for a model of prediction of the cracking path by cleavage. 6.3.2 Tearing In the case of extended plasticity in ductile fracture, the evaluation of the risk of propagation does not come within the framework of the Griffith theory; other approaches exist, based in most cases on notions of critical stresses and energies. Likewise, we do not have tools allowing the simulation of ductile propagation in a transition zone: ductile propagation followed by cleavage. Several avenues are conceivable but remain to be consolidated: - The \mathit{Gtp} approach for the simulation of the propagation along a known path by excavation of slices. A single application exists at present (cf.[37]). - The J-\mathit{Gfr} approach of the CEA, along a known path. - The \mathit{CZM} approach, along a known path (cf. [32]). - The Gurson or Rousselier model can predict the cracking path. This model poses a problem of dependence on the mesh or on the regularisation parameters (cf.[30]). overview of the various approaches which exist in fracture mechanics, a procedure for carrying out a study in fracture mechanics is proposed, making it possible to direct the user at each stage towards the choice which is the most adequate for the case treated, with reference to the documents of Code_Aster . As one cannot be exhaustive with respect to all the particularities and difficulties encountered during a study in fracture mechanics, one proposes a signpost towards the dedicated notes and documentations in order to go more deeply into each subject. In each of the cases, one tries to specify the limitations of the approaches or of the modellings. For a rapid and occasional reading, one adds tables which make it possible to target certain key information. The approaches on stability and initiation are dominant in this document, to the detriment of those which treat tearing. The classical approach is limited to non-linear elasticity. Advice on use is given. It is advisable to have read the general methodological guide on fracture mechanics, which lists the various approaches available U2.05.00. 1 General points The classical approach is the historical approach for fracture mechanics. It was initially developed within the framework of linear elasticity, then extended to non-linear elasticity. 1.1 Linear elastic fracture mechanics in quasi-statics This paragraph recalls the characteristic parameters in linear elastic fracture mechanics. 1.1.1 Stress intensity factors The stress intensity factors characterise the singularity of the stresses at the crack tip. Their general expression is of the form: K=\underset{r	o 0}{\lim}\sigma (r)\sqrt{r} . Three stress intensity factors are defined, associated with the three opening modes of the crack. In linear elasticity, the stress intensity factors make it possible to decompose the displacement field \mathrm{u} into a singular part and a regular part [1] [6]: u={u}_{R}+{K}_{I}{u}_{S}^{I}+{K}_{\mathit{II}}{u}_{S}^{\mathit{II}}+{K}_{\mathit{III}}{u}_{S}^{\mathit{III}} . 1.1.2 Energy release rate One considers a cracked elastic solid occupying the domain \Omega . Let: \mathrm{u} the displacement field, T the temperature field, \mathrm{f} the field of body forces applied on \Omega , \mathrm{g} the field of surface forces applied on a part S of \partial \Omega , U the field of imposed displacements on a part {S}_{d} of \partial \Omega . \sigma the stress tensor, \varepsilon the strain tensor, {\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{th}} the tensor of strains of thermal origin, \psi (\varepsilon ,T) the free-energy density. The energy release rate G corresponds to the energetic approach to Griffith fracture [5]. It is defined by the opposite of the derivative of the potential energy at equilibrium W(u) with respect to the domain \Omega : G= rac{-\partial W(u)}{\partial \Omega } with: W(\mathrm{u})=\underset{\Omega}{\int}\psi (\varepsilon (\mathrm{u}),T)d\Omega -\underset{\Omega}{\int}\mathrm{f}\mathrm{u}d\Omega -\underset{S}{\int}\mathrm{g}\mathrm{u}d\Gamma One recalls that the energy release rate is equivalent to the Rice integral in linear elasticity [4]. One recalls that the calculation of the energy release rate is possible in the following cases: - linear thermoelasticity, - non-linear thermoelasticity (hyperelasticity), - thermo-elastoplasticity (von Mises criterion with isotropic or kinematic hardening). The calculation of the stress intensity factors is for its part possible only in linear thermoelasticity under the small-strain assumption. In these situations, there is therefore no reason to choose a different constitutive relation between the mechanical analysis and the post-processing. In this case, one must therefore not supply COMPORTEMENT under CALC_G. If COMPORTEMENT is not present under CALC_G, then the post-processing will be executed with the constitutive relation of the mechanical analysis. The factor keyword COMPORTEMENT under CALC_G is used only in the very particular cases in which one wishes to carry out the post-processing with a constitutive law different from that which was used for the mechanical analysis.
