In Table 1 one finds the advantages of the models \mathrm{EJ} and \mathrm{ED} in the model \mathrm{EI} without having their limits: non-regularised law, linear or non-linear material constitutive behaviour, jump \mathrm{P1} and a numerical parameter which does not influence the results of the analysis, whereas this is the case with that of the \mathrm{EJ} . 2.3 Cohesive laws The cohesive laws are a relation between the stress vector and the displacement jump at each Gauss point. All these laws are non-linear and must be used with the non-linear operators STAT/DYNA_NON_LINE (consequently they are not suited to MECA_STATIQUE). For the preceding models the cohesive laws are named: > EJ : CZM_LIN_REG , CZM_EXP_REG > ED : CZM_EXP > EI : CZM_OUV_MIX , CZM_TAC_MIX, CZM_EXP_MIX CZM_FAT_MIX, CZM_TRA_MIX, CZM_LAB_MIX One gives an example, in opening mode (Figure 2.3), of the relation between the normal component of the stress vector {\sigma}_{n} and the normal jump {\delta}_{n} . The internal threshold variable \kappa makes it possible to handle the irreversibility of the cracking. The mechanical parameters of the law are the critical initiation stress {\sigma}_{c} and the critical energy release rate {G}_{c} . The ratio of these two parameters defines a critical jump {\delta}_{c}={\mathrm{2G}}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c} beyond which the stress vanishes. Figure 2.3 : Normal component of the stress vector as a function of the normal jump for the law CZM_OUV_MIX (threshold \kappa zero on the left and positive on the right). The principal differences between the CZM laws concern the initiation phase and the shape of the post-peak law. The REG laws take account of the contact/adhesion part in a penalised manner, whereas the others carry out these phases in a perfect manner (infinite slope at the origin, see Figure 2.3). Note that the regularisation of the cohesive laws has an influence on the results of the analysis (see part 15). Furthermore, the EXP laws (except CZM_EXP_MIX, whose law has been truncated deliberately) have an exponentially decreasing behaviour which tends asymptotically towards zero with the opening of the lips. Formally, these do not make it possible to define a crack tip; one will prefer to them the other laws with linear decrease, which supply explicitly the position of the crack tip (critical fracture jump, see Figure 2.3). In a general manner, during the crack-propagation phase, the shape of the cohesive law (linear or exponential) has little influence on the cracking; on the other hand it may have a role in the initiation phase. For more details on these laws see R7.02.11. 2.4 Definition of the local frame of the crack For the integration of the cohesive law, which involves a displacement jump, a function of the nodal displacements expressed in the global frame, it is necessary to know a local frame (n,\mathrm{t1},\mathrm{t2}) of the element. For the EI and the EJ two different methods have been adopted, each having its advantages but also its limitations. For the \mathrm{EI} : the user supplies the information necessary to define the local frame (in 2D, one angle of rotation is sufficient; in 3D one must know the three nautical angles). This is relatively simple for a rectilinear or plane crack. It becomes much more complex when this is no longer the case. On the other hand this method makes it possible to impose a single local frame on all the elements of a given plane crack and thus authorises a consistent visualisation of the displacement jumps in mode \mathrm{II} and \mathrm{III} . We shall see that this is not the case for the \mathrm{EJ} and \mathrm{ED} . For a mesh-cell group of interface FISS in a given plane, the user supplies the characteristics of the EI in the following manner (nautical angles (a,b,c) in degrees): ORIEN_FI=AFFE_CARA_ELEM( > MODELE=MO, > MASSIF=( _F(GROUP_MA='FISS',ANGL_REP=(a, b ,c)), )); then CARA_ELEM = ORIEN_FI in STAT_NON_LINE. In 2D it is easy to know the angle between the normal of the local frame n and the vector X of the global frame. This angle is the first nautical angle; the other two are set to zero. In 3D it is a little more difficult. In order to help the user one supplies a few examples of nautical angles with the definition of the local frame (n,\mathrm{t1},\mathrm{t2}) in the global frame (X,Y,Z) . > (0,0,0):(n,\mathrm{t1},\mathrm{t2})=(X,Y,Z) > (90,0,0):(n,\mathrm{t1},\mathrm{t2})=(Y,-X,Z) > (-90,0,-90):(n,\mathrm{t1},\mathrm{t2})=(-Y,-Z,X) > (0,-90,-90):(n,\mathrm{t1},\mathrm{t2})=(Z,X,Y) For the \mathrm{EJ} and the \mathrm{ED} : the computation of the local frame is carried out (hard-coded) from the geometric coordinates of the element. No information is given by the user; the account taken of non-rectilinear or non-plane cracks is therefore immediate. In return, for a plane crack, the elements all have the same normal but tangent vectors (\mathrm{t1},\mathrm{t2}) which differ from one element to another. This of course has no effect on the validity of the analyses, but on the other hand it prevents a clean visualisation of the components of the jump in mode \mathrm{II} or \mathrm{III} . 3 Advice on the mesh After a few general points on the various types of finite elements, one supplies advice on the production of the mesh as well as on its characteristics in order to model the cohesive crack correctly in various configurations. 3.1 General points In a general manner, the cohesive models make it possible to represent a crack on a path \Gamma given a priori . These models account for the evolution but not for the direction of the propagation. It is therefore necessary to produce a mesh compatible with the potential crack path. This consists in placing cohesive elements along this path. Figure 3.1-a : 3D diagram of an element \mathrm{EI} or \mathrm{EJ} inserted between two tetrahedra. For the surface models ( \mathrm{EJ} and \mathrm{EI} ), in 2D the crack lips correspond to the long sides of the cohesive elements (degenerate quadrangles); in 3D the lips are defined by the triangular faces (for the degenerate pentahedra) or rectangular faces (for the degenerate hexahedra). For the element with internal discontinuity \mathrm{ED} , the crack passes through the centre of the element and is parallel to the two opposite sides. The models \mathrm{EJ} and \mathrm{ED} have a linear interpolation of the displacements; they are compatible with a linear volume mesh \mathrm{Q1} or \mathrm{P1} . The \mathrm{EI} has a quadratic interpolation of the displacements and is compatible with quadratic volume mesh cells \mathrm{Q2} or \mathrm{P2} . > \mathrm{EI} \mathrm{EJ} \mathrm{ED} Figure 3.1-b : 2D diagram of the cohesive elements 3.2 Creation of the mesh One gives in this part the tools available in Code_Aster in order to guarantee the proper production of a mesh with a cohesive crack, then one supplies advice for the meshers GMSH and Salomé. 3.2.1 Code_Aster tools The mesh cells of the cohesive elements \mathrm{EI} and \mathrm{EJ} are surface mesh cells; their orientation is defined by a local frame, and it is therefore necessary that their local connectivity be defined a priori . This is also the case for the \mathrm{ED} , which are volume elements since they are crossed by a surface discontinuity. Two techniques are available in Code_Aster for carrying out this task. The first, once the mesh has been produced, consists in checking that they have an ad hoc local numbering (orientation). The second consists in producing the mesh of the cohesive elements from two facing node groups (automatic creation). Notes : - The thickness of the elements \mathrm{EJ} and \mathrm{EI} has no influence on the solution. The latter may however modify the dimensions of the structure; the user must produce the mesh accordingly. When this is possible one advises producing mesh cells of zero thickness. - For the post-processing in 2D a small thickness may however facilitate the visualisation of the variables at the Gauss points (this problem does not arise in 3D because one visualises a surface). - On the other hand, the \mathrm{ED} necessarily have a non-zero thickness. One recommends choosing a size of the same order of magnitude as that of the surrounding non-cohesive elements. Orientation The keyword ORIE_FISSURE (command MODI_MAILLAGE) makes it possible to ensure the correct local numbering of the mesh cells and to renumber them correctly if necessary. For more details on the use of this procedure see U4.23.04. One advises using this command systematically; it works in 2D and in 3D (provided that the thickness of the mesh cells is non-zero) and whatever the type of cohesive elements (linear or quadratic). One gives an example of use for the cohesive layer 'JOINT': MA=MODI_MAILLAGE(reuse =MA, MAILLAGE=MA, ORIE_FISSURE =_F(GROUP_MA='JOINT'),) Automatic creation Another possibility: CREA_FISS allows the creation of cohesive mesh cells from two node groups (facing one another or coincident two by two). Certain precautions are necessary for the use of this command; it is therefore advised to read the documentation of CREA_MAILLAGE U4.23.02. This functionality is available in 2D (the 3D equivalent is possible with a Salomé Python script, see 12 below); here is an example from the node groups GN1 and GN2. MA = CREA_MAILLAGE( MAILLAGE = MA_INI, CREA_FISS = ( _F(NOM='JOINT', GROUP_NO_1='GN1', GROUP_NO_2='GN2', PREF_MAILLE='MJ'), )) Notes : - Once the command CREA_FISS has been carried out, it is not necessary to run ORIE_FISSURE if one produces a linear mesh. - If one wishes to use this procedure with the interface elements (hence a quadratic mesh), one must first carry out the preceding procedure on a linear mesh, then switch to quadratic ( LINE_QUAD/TOUT='OUI') and finally run ORIE_FISSURE again on the cohesive layer, because the command LINE_QUAD may have modified the local numbering. Finally, tools are under development in order to facilitate the creation of cohesive mesh cells. In particular in Salomé version 5 (see 12). 3.2.2 Advice for GMSH With the free mesher GMSH, it is fairly easy to build a layer of cohesive finite elements intended to be joint or interface elements, whatever the nature of the volume mesh. It is sufficient to use the command “Extrude” and to take a few precautions. In 2D: one extrudes a line n of an edge of the domain, of a thickness ep (small but non-zero) in the direction -Y, and one specifies that one wishes only one layer of elements with the keyword “Layers”; finally one adds “Recombine” so that the mesher creates quadrangles (triangles by default). > ep=0.001 > NbCouche = 1; > JOINT[]=Extrude Line {n, {0,-ep,0}} > { > Layers{NbCouche,1}; Recombine; > };; One may then define a “Physical Line” of the new line created, or a “Physical Surface” of the surface created, in the following manner: > Physical Line(a) = {JOINT[0]}; > Physical Surface(b) = {JOINT[1]}; The first may serve for example for the application of symmetry boundary conditions; the second corresponds to the layer of cohesive elements. If one wishes to include the crack inside a domain, one proceeds as previously, then one extrudes the new line JOINT[0] in order to create the second part of the volume. In 3D : one proceeds in the same manner with the extrusion of a boundary surface of the domain; “Recombine” makes it possible to create hexahedra if the trace of the mesh on the extruded surface comprises quadrangles, and pentahedra if the latter comprises triangles. Finally, the “physical” entities created in the .geo are used in the .comm command file in the usual way: > Physical Line(i) corresponds to 'GMi' if the mesh is in .msh format > Physical Surface(j) corresponds to 'GMj' if the mesh is in .msh format > Physical Line(k) corresponds to 'G_1D_k' if the mesh is in .med format > Physical Volume(l) corresponds to 'G_3D_l' if the mesh is in .med format Warning : There exists a bug in GMSH 2.3 for the 3D extrusion with the meshing algorithm 'Tetgen+Delaunay'. This algorithm is the one proposed by default; it is therefore necessary to modify it in the menu Option/mesh/General and to choose 3D algorithm='Netgen'. This bug is listed on the GMSH web site and should be corrected in future versions. Notes : - The mesh cells created by GMSH are topologically correct but the local numbering of the nodes is not necessarily properly carried out. In Code_Aster the latter must be defined in a specific manner in order to distinguish the orientation of the cohesive elements. After reading the mesh in .msh or .med format it is therefore necessary to pass through a MODI_MAILLAGE with the command ORIE_FISSURE , which carries out this renumbering operation of the cohesive elements automatically (see part 10 ). - Note that the extrusions mentioned above are also easily achievable in an interactive manner with the mouse. Once the .geo has been generated automatically, one must however add “ Recombine ” in order to create quadrangles in 2D or hexahedra/pentahedra in 3D. 3.2.3 Advice for Salomé In Salomé, it is possible to extrude a layer of surface elements from an edge of the domain. This makes it possible to create cohesive mesh cells whose connectivity one will change if necessary by means of the command ORIE_FISSURE (see part 10). Work is in progress in order to produce the mesh of cohesive elements between two volumes or along a surface layer in a volume. The Python command DoubleNodeGroups 1 makes it possible to duplicate the nodes of a surface mesh-cell group or of a given node group (see the reference manual of the MESH module). The weaving of the cohesive elements between these two node groups may then be carried out in 2D in the command file by means of the keyword CREA_FISS (see part 10) or from a Python script 2 in 3D. Note : Whatever the technique adopted for meshing the potential crack path, it is necessary that the latter cross the structure from one side to the other. Indeed, there do not exist cohesive finite elements intended to model a crack tip (a triangle, for example) which cannot propagate. This would moreover not really make sense, since it is contrary to the logic of the modelling of a potential path. 3.2.4 Case of advanced geometric configurations When one employs the interface finite elements (EI), the presence of two families of degrees of freedom, the displacements and the (augmented) cohesive forces, complicates the handling of advanced geometric configurations. This expression refers to situations in which several interfaces cross one another, emerge onto one another, emerge onto a kinematic boundary condition, or else present a boundary in the volume and not on an edge of the structure. Advice on the manner of meshing such configurations has been given in the note [bib9]. One observes there that it is indeed the nodes which carry the degrees of freedom corresponding to the cohesive forces that require particular care. 3.3 Modelling of the cohesive zone A CZM crack is defined by three zones: the first corresponds to a stress-free crack, the second, called the cohesive zone, in which the cohesion forces are non-zero, and finally a sound zone (or potential cracking zone) in which the initiation stress has not been reached (see Figure 3.3). The cohesive zone makes it possible to achieve a progressive transition from the sound material to a true crack. The size of the latter is linked to the characteristic length {G}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c} of the cohesive model; it adapts in order to remove the singularity of the stresses at the crack tip. The smaller this length, the more the size of the cohesive zone will be reduced. In the limit, if it tends towards zero, the cohesive zone disappears and one finds oneself in the case of classical fracture mechanics, with the theoretical possibility of having infinite stresses at the crack tip. Formally, this amounts to taking an infinite fracture stress {\sigma}_{c} . One emphasises here the importance, both from the mechanical point of view and from the numerical point of view, of simulating this cohesive zone correctly. In a general manner and whatever the type of analysis, one advises meshing this zone sufficiently so that it is composed of at least four or five cohesive finite elements. This makes it possible to represent finely the evolution of the crack from a mechanical point of view, but also to avoid numerical convergence problems linked to too coarse a discretisation of this zone of strong stress gradient. Figure 3.3 : Diagram of the cohesive crack. In the literature [bib7] there exists an estimate of the size of the cohesive zone {S}_{\mathrm{zc}} for a crack in an infinite elastic material: > {S}_{\mathrm{zc}}\simeq \frac{E}{1-{\nu}^{2}}\frac{{G}_{c}}{{\sigma}_{c}^{2}} with E Young's modulus, \nu Poisson's ratio. This value is given as an indication in order to estimate the size of the cohesive zone; however the latter may vary with various parameters of the mechanical problem. 3.4 Definition of a cohesive pre-crack In most cases, one places the cohesive elements in a cracking plane or in the extension of an existing crack. The latter is in general represented by a free surface. However, in certain cases, it may be useful to place cohesive mesh cells on an initial crack. These may for example serve as contact elements (small strains) or serve to define initial crack fronts, plane or semi-elliptical for example. In order to define an initial crack, it is necessary to build a mesh with two contiguous zones of cohesive elements, one for the pre-crack and the other for the potential crack. The idea then consists in imposing the internal variables of the pre-crack in such a way that they correspond to a stress-free zone, and in not modifying those of the potential crack (i.e. imposing them at 0). To do this, one uses the commands CREA_CHAMP in order to build a field of internal variables at the Gauss points. The latter is then used as the initial state on input to STAT_NON_LINE with the command ETAT_INIT. Note that it is necessary to define all the internal variables of the structure, including those of the volume part. In the case of an elastic material this operation is trivial; in the non-linear case it is not feasible to know them easily, unless one imposes them as zero, which is not necessarily realistic. Note : It is not possible to define an initial crack by imposing the material parameters {\sigma}_{c} and {G}_{c} as zero. 3.5 Multi-cracking It is possible to model several cracks with all the types of cohesive elements, provided that the mesh is produced accordingly. With the ED element one may for example place layers of elements in order to take account of a network of parallel cracks (see example [bib5]). For the EJ and EI elements the test of the plate with a hole (ssnp133 V6.03.133) makes it possible to model the simultaneous advance of two cracks. However, with this type of approach one advises against placing cohesive elements everywhere (i.e. on each edge of the mesh). Besides the difficulty of producing such a mesh, numerous works in the literature show that the results for the cracking path depend strongly on the mesh. Furthermore, for the EJ, the regularisation of the cohesive law may also contribute to the variability of the results and play a harmful role in the quality of the solution. Finally, this raises the non-trivial question of the conditions to be satisfied at the intersection of two cracks. No particular treatment is carried out for the models presented here. Available only in version 5 of Salomé A prototype in the course of validation is available from the author of this document 4 Advice on use The cohesive models cover a fairly wide spectrum of use in the field of fracture mechanics. One begins the advice on use with general points concerning the use of the parameters and the loadings, valid whatever the type of simulation. One continues by giving specific advice for the analyses in brittle fracture (linear or non-linear material), the fatigue analyses and the dynamic analyses. Subsequently one emphasises the importance of relying on numerical tools in order to improve the convergence of the analyses. Finally one ends with advice for the post-processing of the results. 4.1 General points 4.1.1 Mechanical parameters The mechanical parameters of the law are the critical initiation stress {\sigma}_{c} and the critical energy release rate {G}_{c} . On Figure 2.3 on the left, the stress {\sigma}_{c} corresponds to the peak of the law; the density {G}_{c} is linked to the area under the triangle. The user defines a material and (non-zero) values of these parameters under the keyword RUPT_FRAG. In the case of a thermal loading it is possible to make the latter depend on the temperature. One uses in this case the keyword RUPT_FRAG_FO; see the example in the test SDNS105a. The ratio of these two parameters defines a critical jump {\delta}_{c}={\mathrm{2G}}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c} beyond which the stress vanishes for the laws CZM_LIN_REG, CZM_OUV_MIX, CZM_TAC_MIX. For the two laws CZM_EXP_REG and CZM_EXP the stress tends asymptotically towards zero. For the law CZM_EXP_MIX, a critical jump is defined at {\delta}_{c}={\mathrm{3.2G}}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c} . This jump corresponds to an error of 1% on the critical energy release rate. For the fatigue law CZM_FAT_MIX, the value of the jump beyond which the stress remains zero depends on the loading. For the ductile law CZM_TRA_MIX the shape parameters supplied by the user influence this critical jump. For more details see the documentation R7.02.11. Note : When one imposes symmetry conditions on the crack lips it may be necessary to divide the value of {G}_{c} by two; see part 16. 4.1.2 Numerical parameters Elements with internal discontinuity : there is no numerical parameter to be supplied for this model. Joint element : this model has two numerical parameters intended to penalise the adhesion PENA_ADHERENCE and the contact PENA_CONTACT. One replaces the infinitely rigid parts (contact and adhesion) by strongly rigid elastic contributions (see doc R7.02.11). By default PENA_CONTACT is equal to 1 and leads to a penalisation identical to that of the adhesion; this is the value that one recommends. The parameter PENA_ADHERENCE corresponds to a percentage of the internal length of the cohesive law; it must be non-zero and less than 1. The smaller the value, the greater the penalisation slope. The results of the analyses depend strongly on the value of this parameter. In a general manner, one observes: - Oscillations (local snap-backs) in the global response of the structure, linked to the successive opening of the joints. But also oscillations of the stress profile along the crack, all the more marked as the stiffness of the joint is high. - An important influence of the parameter on the quality of the solution in stress. For fairly low values of PENA_ADHERENCE the error is reasonable; for higher values this may lead to very large discrepancies. - The convergence of the global Newton algorithm is all the more difficult as the penalisation is high. One therefore observes antagonistic effects of the penalisation parameter, which imply making a compromise between convergence of the analysis and accuracy of the solution. It is therefore difficult to recommend a general rule supplying the right value of this parameter. One therefore advises, before carrying out a numerical simulation, performing a sensitivity test with respect to this parameter. In every case, the initial stiffness of the joint elements must be greater than the stiffness of the neighbouring volume elements. Interface element: this model has a numerical parameter PENA_LAGR which corresponds to the penalisation of the augmented Lagrangian (see R3.06.13). The results of the analysis do not depend on the value of this parameter. One advises taking the default value (100). This value must be strictly greater than 1 in order to ensure the uniqueness of the solution during the integration of the cohesive law. Furthermore the laws CZM_OUV_MIX and CZM_TRA_MIX, intended for opening in mode I only, have a parameter named RIGI_GLIS which makes it possible to impose a non-zero stiffness in sliding and thus to avoid the problems of zero pivot at the fracture of the elements. One advises using the default value of 10. The solution is not affected by this parameter provided that the sliding modes are not activated. 4.1.3 Loadings and boundary conditions All the types of mechanical and thermal loadings may a priori be applied on a structure comprising cohesive elements: imposed displacements, surface forces, body forces, temperature fields coming from a prior thermal analysis. In order to achieve a saving in run time, taking account of the symmetries of the problem, it is often useful to simulate a half-structure. Symmetry conditions on the lips of the cohesive crack (i.e. the faces of the cohesive elements), leading to an opening in pure mode I, may be envisaged in two different ways: - The first consists in blocking the normal displacements of the faces of the cohesive elements which are not connected to the volume. These then coincide with the axis of symmetry of the structure. In this case, a precaution is to be taken on the value of the critical surface-energy density entered by the user. Since one models only one crack lip, one must, for a given material value of {G}_{c} , supply G_C = {G}_{c}/2 in the command file. In other words, it costs twice less energy to open a half-crack. - The second consists in making the crack open entirely. On the crack lips one imposes displacements that are symmetrical with respect to an axis passing between them (command AFFE_CHAR_MECA/LIAISON_GROUP). This type of modelling makes it possible to take the crack into account as a whole and does not require dividing {G}_{c} by two. On the other hand this poses a problem for the energy balance, since one models a half-structure (hence a volume energy half as large) with a complete crack. This method is therefore to be used with a great deal of caution; one rather advises adopting the preceding one. 4.1.4 Convergence criterion The convergence criterion of the Newton algorithm RESI_REFE_RELA makes it possible to build a reference nodal force, which serves to estimate the (approximate) vanishing of the residual (see R5.03.01). It makes it possible to improve the convergence in the case where the residuals are heterogeneous, that is to say when one treats degrees of freedom of different nature. This is the case of the mixed model EI, for which one recommends the use of this criterion. With the cohesive models, the force is defined from a stress and from its dual, a displacement. In order to use this criterion one therefore supplies a reference stress and a reference displacement: SIGM_REFE and DEPL_REFE. In order to choose these values, one proposes those coming from the cohesive law: the initiation stress {\sigma}_{c} for the first, and the characteristic length {G}_{c}/{\sigma}_{c} for the second. With the models EJ and ED it is not possible (and a priori not useful) to use this type of residual. 4.1.5 Linear solver The method of solution of the global linear system MUMPS is indispensable for the mixed elements having degrees of freedom of Lagrange type. It is therefore necessary to use it with the EI. Its principal interest lies in its ability to pivot rows and/or columns of the matrix during the factorisation in the event of a small pivot. The other finite-element models EJ and ED do not have this restriction; they may be used with the default method (multifrontal). Furthermore, the tangent matrix of the cohesive laws is symmetric; the use of the keyword SYME='OUI', intended to symmetrise the latter, is not necessary. 4.2 A linear interface in order to validate one's data setup In the same way as one recommends carrying out a linear elastic analysis prior to a plastic analysis, it is preferable to begin a cracking analysis by employing a linear cohesive constitutive relation. The model CZM_ELAS_MIX has been introduced with this aim; see U4.51.11. This makes it possible to validate one's data setup (orientation of the interfaces, numbering of the degrees of freedom, assignment of the characteristics and of the loadings, etc.) in a framework simple enough for the mechanical intuition (or the failure of the analysis) to suffice to detect possible aberrant results. Caution, however: this constitutive relation is available only with the interface elements (EI). This interface model is elastic, with a stiffness in the normal direction and another in the two tangent directions. They are defined via DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01 under the factor keyword CZM_ELAS. It is also possible to consider limit behaviours via perfect normal and/or tangential adhesion conditions, still under the same factor keyword (in this case, the stiffnesses no longer play any role, since the displacement jump in the normal or tangent direction is forced to zero). Typically, with perfect adhesion conditions (normal and tangential), the response of the structure must be very close to that which it would have without an interface (very close but not necessarily equal, because of the mixed formulation used with the EI element). Finally, a last adhesion condition is proposed: it consists of contact conditions in closure, together with an elastic stiffness in opening. The analysis becomes more complex because the problem is no longer linear. But this makes it possible to ensure that the zones where the interface opens and those where it remains closed are indeed in conformity with intuition. 4.3 Analyses in brittle fracture Possible models : EJ, EI, Recommended model : EI The cohesive models are suited to modelling brittle fracture in a linear material (all of them) or a non-linear material (EJ and EI only). One gives here a few pieces of advice specific to this type of simulation. Numerical tools make it possible to guarantee a good robustness of the solution algorithms; one also supplies advice on their use. 4.3.1 Linear material For a linear elastic material, there are no specific precautions of implementation other than the preceding general points (part 15) and those on the mesh (part 9). For the robustness of the analyses, the use of the piloting of the loading is essential. One devotes a part below to advice on the use of this method. 4.3.2 Non-linear material The cohesive models EJ and EI may interact with a surrounding non-linear material, a priori whatever it may be. The simulations that may be envisaged remain in the domain of brittle fracture in the presence of plasticity, the latter being confined to the neighbourhood of the crack tip. No specific numerical treatment is necessary for this type of analysis, other than the usual precautions on the fineness of the mesh (see part 9) in order to capture the cohesive zone but also the plastic band along the crack lips. The convergence of the Newton–Raphson algorithm is slowed (more Newton iterations for a given load step) and the run time is increased, but this remains entirely reasonable and does not hinder the robustness of the cohesive models in this field of application. From a mechanical point of view, the plastification of the material and the cracking are two phenomena which interact. Thus, particular attention will have to be paid to the choice of the ratio of the initiation stress of the cohesive law and of the yield stress of the material. Depending on the values of these parameters, one may find oneself either in the case where the cracking occurs without development of the plasticity, or in the opposite case where the stress in the material reaches the plastic threshold and evolves without exceeding the initiation stress, or finally in the case where plasticity and cracking evolve jointly. In this last case, one observes a plastic zone which initiates at the crack tip and which evolves with the propagation of the latter. Furthermore, a few analyses with viscoplastic materials have been carried out by way of illustration; the limited feedback of experience in this field does not allow us to supply specific advice. 4.3.3 Numerical tools Line search It is possible to use the line search with the cohesive models. This may occasionally improve the convergence of the analyses. This method is however not the best suited to getting past the instabilities linked to the sudden propagation of a crack in quasi-statics. In this case, one will prefer to it the piloting of the loading. Piloting of the loading The piloting of the loading, available for all the cohesive models, makes it possible to ensure the convergence of the Newton–Raphson algorithm in quasi-statics despite an instability in the global response of the structure (sudden propagation of a crack, for example). This method is valid for the softening laws which may lead to this type of response, and in particular for the cohesive laws. The idea consists in authorising the release of the loading in order to restore part of the potential energy and to make the cracking advance progressively by controlling locally the damage of the cohesive zones. The user supplies the direction of the loading (displacement or surface force) from an AFFE_CHAR_MECA; it is multiplied by the scalar piloting parameter \eta , a new unknown of the problem which gives its intensity. This last parameter replaces the multiplicative function of the loading FONC_MULT. During the solution of the mechanical problem, one adds a supplementary equation (control of the piloting) which closes the system. For more details on this technique, the reader may refer to the general documentation R5.03.80 and to the documentations specific to the piloting for the cohesive models R7.02.11 and R7.02.14. This numerical tool is particularly important for ensuring the convergence of the algorithm. It is often necessary, including when the global response does not admit a snap-back. Indeed, in certain configurations, local snap-backs, linked to a sudden opening at the element level, may occur. All the cohesive laws may be piloted by elastic prediction (PRED_ELAS); the ratio of the time step \Delta t to the coefficient COEF_MULT makes it possible to manage the evolution of the cracking. At the level of the constitutive law this amounts to controlling the exit from the threshold. The higher this ratio, the more rapidly one wishes to get past the instability, and therefore the higher \eta will be. In the command STAT_NON_LINE, one chooses to pilot the load TRACTION (supplied in the classical way) in the following manner: EXCIT = _F(CHARGE = TRACTION , TYPE_CHARGE = 'FIXE_PILO'), On ajoute ensuite les données propres au pilotage : PILOTAGE = _F( SELECTION = 'RESIDU', TYPE = 'PRED_ELAS', GROUP_MA = 'JOINT', COEF_MULT = c_mult_pilo, ), Notes and advice: - One advises defining the direction of the piloted loading by a unit vector. Thus, the piloting parameter \eta will correspond exactly to its intensity. - One advises the user to begin by choosing a ratio of \Delta t to COEF_MULT equal to 0.05. In this way, one seeks to damage by 5% the most highly loaded Gauss point. - If the algorithm does not converge despite the piloting, one advises reducing the preceding ratio: automatic or manual subdivision of the step and/or increase of COEF_MULT . The smaller the ratio, the slower the cracking, and conversely. - It is sometimes necessary to break the symmetry of the problem in order to avoid the piloting oscillating between two values of \eta if these supply an identical cracking state. For this, one advises carrying out a first non-linear analysis with a very small non-piloted load step. One thus remains in the linear domain of the response and the analysis converges rapidly. - Another way of avoiding the oscillations of the value of the piloting consists in supplying an ETA_PILO_R_MIN equal to zero in order to authorise only positive values of the piloting parameter. - It is necessary to pilot finely (small exit from the criterion) the first piloted load steps in order to capture correctly the peak value of the global response. - If the piloting is used in a situation in which one could do without it, the solution is not modified. The only difference is that one does not directly control the intensity of the load. - It is not possible to pilot thermal loadings. 4.4 Analyses in ductile fracture Possible models : EI The law CZM_TRA_MIX was introduced in version 10.4 in order to seek to model ductile fracture. The use of the latter must be confined to an upstream research framework. Indeed, it is in the course of validation and will certainly be led to evolve. The law for ductile fracture is inspired by the laws classically proposed in the literature. In addition to the parameters of critical stress and of critical energy density, one adds two parameters linked to the shape of the law (COEF_EXTR and COEF_PLAS). The latter is chosen trapezoidal. Sensitivity analyses with respect to the parameters, as well as tests on CT specimens (SSNP151) and AE specimens (SSNA120), have been carried out. The first conclusions show that this model makes it possible to reproduce correctly the global response and the propagation kinetics observed with a model of Gurson type (Rousselier) on a 2D CT specimen (SSNP151a). One notes however that the fitting of the parameters of the law in order to approach the fine analysis of the local approach remains difficult. On the other hand the gain in run time and in robustness is significant. When one moves to a 3D CT specimen (SSNP151b) the results are less conclusive beyond a certain loading level. It seems that this is due in part to the poor account taken of the volume effects in the cohesive model, and in particular the confinement effect. Work is in progress in order to try to take account of the influence of the triaxiality. Other limits are also to be emphasised: as for the other cohesive models, the crack path must be known a priori . The cracking can take place only in mode I (it is however conceivable to introduce the sliding modes if this proves judicious). Finally, large crack openings are not taken into account; one may however use large strains in the surrounding material. No specific numerical treatment is necessary for this type of analysis, other than the usual precautions on the fineness of the mesh (see part 9) in order to capture the cohesive zone but also the plastic band along the crack lips. The convergence of the Newton–Raphson algorithm is slowed (more Newton iterations for a given load step) and the run time is increased, but this remains entirely reasonable and does not hinder the robustness of the cohesive models in this field of application. From a mechanical point of view, the plastification of the material and the cracking are two phenomena which interact. Thus, particular attention will have to be paid to the choice of the ratio of the initiation stress of the cohesive law and of the yield stress of the material. Depending on the values of these parameters, one may find oneself either in the case where the cracking occurs without development of the plasticity, or in the opposite case where the stress in the material reaches the plastic threshold and evolves without exceeding the initiation stress, or finally in the case where plasticity and cracking evolve jointly. In this last case, one observes a plastic zone which initiates at the crack tip and which evolves with the propagation of the latter. 4.4.1 Numerical tools Line search It is possible to use the line search. This may occasionally improve the convergence of the analyses. Piloting of the loading One considers that the cracks propagate in a progressive manner in the ductile fracture mode. The piloting of the loading is therefore not developed for this type of law. 4.5 Analyses in fatigue Possible model : \mathrm{EI} The law available for treating the phenomenon of fatigue in mode I is CZM_FAT_MIX (see doc R7.02.11), usable with the interface elements. One may carry out analyses in 2D or 3D whatever the material and for all types of mechanical loadings (of constant or variable amplitude), or thermal loadings. One may also refer to the tests SSNP118JKL and SSNP139B and to part 25. In order to account for fatigue with this law, it is necessary to go through all the cycles of the loading. One readily understands that it is not feasible to simulate a large number of cycles. Nevertheless, the first results bring out a certain number of phenomena observed in fatigue (see report [bib3]). For an elastic material: - One succeeds in reproducing evolution laws of Paris type, whose coefficients one identifies a posteriori , - One notes the weak influence of an overload on the advance, - One observes the absence of a sequence effect at variable amplitude, - One simulates realistic evolutions of a 3D crack front. In the presence of plasticity several effects observed experimentally are reproduced: - One brings out the overload effect, which leads to the slowing of the propagation due to the compression induced by the increase of the plastic zone, - the slowing is all the more pronounced as the overload is large, - the increase of the load ratio contributes to reducing the delay at a fixed overload ratio and load amplitude. Furthermore, work on the cycle jump is envisaged. It will make it possible, by extrapolation, to simulate a large number of cycles. Advice on the discretisation of the loading: - When discretising the cyclic loading a few precautions are to be taken in order to optimise the run time. The risk is of carrying out at each cycle an automatic subdivision of the step which may become very costly in CPU time. The feedback of experience allows us to advise the user to carry out about 4 loading increments per cycle when the material is elastic and to double this value when the latter has a non-linear constitutive behaviour. This rule is not necessarily valid in all situations and will have to be adapted case by case in order to optimise the time spent in each cycle. Advice on the definition of the cyclic function: For the construction of the multiplicative function of the loading one may use DEFI_FONCTION or Python in the command file. One proposes below an example of a sawtooth function of variable amplitude. The odd time instants are the ends of the loading ramp (maximum amplitude) and the even time instants are the ends of the unloading (minimum amplitude). In this way, one finishes the i th cycle at the time instant \mathrm{2i} . In the example below the loading varies From val_inf to val_sup in the course of cycles 1 to nb_cy_1, From val_inf to val_surch in the course of cycles nb_cy_1+1 to nb_cy_2, From val_inf to val_sup in the course of cycles nb_cy_2+1 and nb_cy_3 Example of a cyclic function f of variable amplitude: > f = [] > for i in xrange(nb_cy_1) : > f.extend((2 i,val_inf,2 i+1,val_sup)) > for i in range(nb_cy_1,nb_cy_2) : > f.extend((2 i,val_inf,2 i+1,val_surch)) > for i in range(nb_cy_2,nb_cy_3) : > f.extend((2 i,val_inf,2 i+1,val_sup)) The definition of the function concept in Code_Aster is then carried out in the usual way: > FCT_FAT = DEFI_FONCTION( > NOM_PARA = 'INST', > PROL_GAUCHE='LINEAIRE', > VALE = f, > ) Advice on the storage of the data In order to avoid too large a storage of the databases, one advises keeping only the values of the fields at the peak of each cycle by means of the keyword ARCHIVAGE of STAT_NON_LINE . To do this, it is of course necessary to carry out a discretisation of the loading which passes through the peaks. 4.6 Analyses in dynamics Possible models : \mathrm{EJ} , \mathrm{EI} (in the course of validation), Recommended model : \mathrm{EJ} Taking the dynamic aspects into account introduces an additional complexity into the modelling. Besides the usual precautions in quasi-statics (sufficient mesh refinement in order to discretise the cohesive zone, relatively small for the characteristics of steels (of the order of 1 mm)), the dynamic regime imposes supplementary rules. One proposes the following few practical pieces of advice, resting on the feedback of experience. One may also refer to the report [bib1]. - The integration scheme first of all: the Newmark scheme known as “average acceleration” ( d=1/2 , a=1/4 ), unconditionally stable and non-dissipative in a linear medium, seems the best suited (no numerical dissipation detected in the presence of cohesive zones). Very few tests have been tried with other schemes (explicit, Wilson, etc.) but they have led to convergence problems. A thesis is in progress (D. Doyen) in order to optimise schemes in the presence of shocks. - As regards the time discretisation, everything depends on the phenomena that one seeks to simulate. In order to capture finely the reflections of the waves on the cohesive zone (causing a perturbation of the kinematics of the crack), one must (still for the usual characteristics of steels) consider time steps less than or equal to {10}^{-8}s . If a coarser tracking of the kinematics is sufficient and the important phenomenon is the initiation and the arrest, then steps of the order of {10}^{-7}\le \Delta t\le {10}^{-5}s are sufficient. Above that, convergence problems appear ( \Delta t\approx {10}^{-6}s seems to be a good compromise). - Very particular attention must be paid to the passage from a stable phase to an unstable phase (more precisely a phase in which the cohesive zone extends in a progressive manner, then in which it propagates in a sudden manner). In this case, one must adapt the time steps in order to capture the instant at which the cohesive zone accelerates, on pain of completely smoothing out “the dynamic effect”. The use of the piloting of the loading in quasi-statics, associated with the observation of the snap-back of the global response, may supply information on this critical instant. - The small parameter PENA_ADHERENCE representing the stiffness of the joint before decohesion (regularisation parameter) must be taken less than {10}^{-4} . Indeed, below this value the results are no longer sensitive to this parameter. In a general manner, the feedback of experience is limited in this field of application. The use of these models in dynamics remains, for the moment, intended for specialists. 4.7 Post-processing of the cracking and command POST_CZM_FISS Visualisation of the cracking for the \mathrm{EJ} and \mathrm{EI} In order to visualise a cohesive crack, several solutions are possible: - The internal variable at the Gauss point (VARI_ELGA) \mathrm{V3} is a cracking indicator which makes it possible to know whether the Gauss point is sound ( \mathrm{V3}=0 ), damaged ( \mathrm{V3}=1 ) or broken ( \mathrm{V3}=2 ). See the example in Figure 4.5. - The variable \mathrm{V4} varies continuously from 0 (sound) to 1 (broken); it corresponds to the percentage of dissipated surface energy and may be interpreted as a damage indicator. See the example in Figure 4.5. - One may also visualise the values of the displacement jump in the three fracture modes I, II and III respectively from the internal variables \mathrm{V7} , \mathrm{V8} and \mathrm{V9} . - A dissipation indicator \mathrm{V2} makes it possible to know whether the Gauss point dissipates energy or is unloading (the values taken by this internal variable depend on the cohesive law; see doc R7.02.11). - Finally one may visualise the components of the cohesive force in the three fracture modes I , \mathrm{II} and \mathrm{III} respectively from the stress vector at the Gauss point SIEF_ELGA: SIGN, SITX and SITY. The sign of SIGN makes it possible to know whether the point is in contact or not. Caution: for the \mathrm{EJ} the visualisation of the tangential jumps in mode \mathrm{II} and \mathrm{III} (respectively \mathrm{V8} and \mathrm{V9} ) has no meaning, given that the tangential vectors of the local frame are independent from one element to another (see on this subject part 7). Figure 4.5 : Evolution of the fracture in mixed mode in a 3D beam; visualisation of the cracking plane. Internal variable \mathrm{V4} at the top (1 in black, 0 in white) and \mathrm{V3} at the bottom (0 in blue, 1 in green, 2 in red). Visualisation of the cracking for the ED For the \mathrm{ED} the internal variables are not the same; the percentage of dissipated energy is stored in \mathrm{V5} and the dissipation indicator in the variable \mathrm{V4} . One also stores the normal and tangential stresses in \mathrm{V6} and V7 as well as the normal and tangential displacement jumps in \mathrm{V1} and \mathrm{V2} . POST_CZM_FISS : computation of the length of cohesive cracks in 2D This command makes it possible to know, at each time instant, the size of the cohesive crack as well as the size of the cohesive zone from the coordinates of a point POINT_ORIG and of a direction vector VECT_TANG given by the user. The latter must also supply the result of the non-linear analysis evol_noli as well as the cohesive mesh-cell group grma on which he or she wishes to carry out the post-processing. The syntax is as follows: table_sdaster = POST_CZM_FISS(RESULTAT = evol_noli, GROUP_MA = grma, POINT_ORIG = (R,R), VECT_TANG =(R,R)) This command is usable for the modellings PLAN_JOINT, PLAN_INTERFACE, AXIS_JOINT and AXIS_INTERFACE and the cohesive laws CZM_OUV_MIX, CZM_TAC_MIX, CZM_LIN_REG, CZM_EXP_REG. The crack lengths are evaluated from the geometric position of the Gauss points and from the internal variable V3 of the cohesive laws, which makes it possible to know the state of the point (sound, damaged, broken). One will refer to the U4 documentation of POST_CZM_FISS for more information. An example of use is proposed in the tests ssnp139a and ssnp139c. Computation of the crack length in 3D It is conceivable to extend the macro-command above to 3D, but this is not planned in the short term. 5 Carrying out a CZM analysis The cohesive models presented here have been the subject of a certain number of analyses in various mechanical problems, most often on target structures (specimens). Let us cite a few examples: - Initiation and propagation of a crack in an elastic or elastoplastic beam in brittle fracture, - propagation of a crack under cyclic loading in an elastoplastic beam in order to model fatigue as well as the overload effect. - Propagation of a plane 3D crack in brittle fracture or fatigue, tracking of the crack front. - Modelling of the dynamic propagation of a crack in a bimaterial. - Cracking and sudden propagation of two cracks across a plate with a hole (quasi-static analyses with piloting). - Pull-out of a rigid reinforcement. u2.05.08 Carrying out an analysis for the prediction of cleavage fracture u2.05.08 Carrying out an analysis for the prediction of cleavage fracture Summary: This document is intended to supply the information necessary to a user wishing to simulate a fracture by cleavage. The definition of cleavage is first recalled. One then presents in turn the models available for predicting this type of fracture, and methodological and implementation advice. The models described here are, in turn: Beremin, Bordet, Gp and Le Corre. 1 Introduction Elastic fracture mechanics, based on the classical criteria of energy release rate, of contour integral J and of stress intensity factor K , does not, in the general case, make it possible to treat problems in which plasticity plays an important role. In this case, other approaches must be put in place. In the case of proportional monotonic loading, the two-parameter approaches, such as the approaches (J,Q) or (K,T) ([1]), are generally satisfactory. Unfortunately, the domain of validity of these approaches is limited to proportional loadings. This is why elastoplastic fracture mechanics, which must make it possible to extend the validity of fracture mechanics, is being developed. The cleavage mechanism (with confined plasticity) falls particularly within its scope. The objective of this document is to supply methodological assistance for the use of the models of elastoplastic fracture mechanics within the framework of the prediction of cleavage. It in no way dispenses one from reading the Reference and User documents relating to the models and commands in question here. The phenomenon of cleavage is first explained briefly. The four available models (Beremin, Bordet, {G}_{P} and Le Corre) are described in turn, with assistance for their respective use. These models being of the post-processing type of a thermo-mechanical analysis, it is appropriate that this analysis be as reliable as possible, and therefore that the precautions recalled here be taken. 2 Brief general points on cleavage This paragraph is in particular inspired by [2], to which one may refer for more details, microstructural ones in particular. Cleavage is a fracture mode whose principal mechanism is the separation of the atomic planes, practically without strain. It is the principal mechanism of brittle fracture in metals, in particular in the case of the low crystal symmetries such as the body-centred cubic or the hexagonal ones. This fracture mode being in competition with plastic strain, it is facilitated by a low temperature (the deformation mechanisms are then less activated). This leads to the existence of a brittle (at low temperature)–ductile (at higher temperature) transition. Among the models which are defined here, the two deterministic methods are at present tested in the case of the transition zone in order to predict the risk of cleavage. This use nevertheless requires precautions; to our knowledge, no method can to this day be considered reliable for predicting the risk of cleavage in the transition zone. The morphology of the cleavage fracture surfaces corresponds to a transgranular propagation. It can easily be observed by microscopy, as in the Figure. It is frequently characterised by the presence of lines parallel to the direction of propagation, which one calls rivers. Figure 2-1: Microscopic fracture appearance of cleavage Fracture by cleavage, like the other modes of fracture by cracking, distinguishes in theory two mechanisms: initiation and propagation. Initiation corresponds to the development of a microcrack inside the sound metal; it is generally accepted that this stage requires a fairly small prior plastic strain, which gives rise to a pile-up of dislocations and a singularity of the stresses, and the reaching of a limit fracture stress, henceforth denoted {\sigma}_{c} . The propagation of the cleavage cracks is unstable, of high speed (of the order of 40% of the speed of sound in the metal), and must satisfy an energy criterion of Griffith type [3]. Cleavage not being accompanied by large strains, it does not require a large energy, unlike ductile fracture. This is why the Charpy test, measuring the resilience (energy necessary for fracture by impact of a standardised specimen), makes it possible to distinguish these two types of fracture for one and the same material (see the Figure). At low temperature, the energy necessary for fracture is low: the fracture mode is cleavage. At high temperature, the energy necessary for fracture is high: fracture takes place by tearing. The limit temperature between these two phenomena is called the transition temperature; there exist several definitions of it, including those based on a given energy level (one speaks for example of {T}_{\mathrm{k65}} , which would be equal here to about -20°C ). The irradiation of metals induces an increase of the yield stress and makes the pile-up of dislocations more difficult, and in fine favours cleavage: the transition temperature of an irradiated material is higher than that of the same non-irradiated material. In the transition zone, that is to say the temperature range close to this transition temperature, fracture may occur by cleavage, by tearing, or by a tearing over a finite length followed by cleavage. The prediction of cleavage in the transition zone remains in the domain of research: even if methodologies are proposed here, they still require validation and must not be seen as “turnkey” methods. Figure 2-2: Brittle–ductile transition curve from the Charpy test 3 Methodology of an analysis with the Gp energy model The energy model {G}_{P} is developed at EDF R&D. It is deterministic and therefore makes it possible to write a criterion that is simple to interpret. It makes it possible to treat all types of loading and takes account of numerous effects (small defect, triaxiality, warm preloading), and studies in order to validate it in the ductile–brittle transition are in progress. 3.1 Theoretical framework The energy model {G}_{P} is initially based on the variational approach to fracture proposed by Francfort and Marigo [4]. It makes it possible to define an initiation criterion valid in the cleavage domain whatever the type of loading. It is characterised by the representation of the crack by a notch, the principle of minimisation of the energy, and it postulates that initiation can be described by an energy criterion. It makes it possible in particular to take account of the small-defect effects, of triaxiality, and of the effects of warm preloading (which are however underestimated). For more details, one may refer to [5] or R7.02.16. One specifies here the elements essential to the use of this approach in code_aster, within the framework of cleavage and of the transition zone. 3.2 Necessary mesh In every case, the mesh must comprise a defect (crack) represented by a notch (crack whose front is not a tip but a semicircle) of initial radius {R}_{0} . This radius is a parameter to be identified. Its identification is described further on. In the case of proportional loading, one may use any radius that is sufficiently small. 3.2.1 In 2D In 2D, the user has the choice between two types of mesh. In the first case, the mesh must comprise specific analysis zones called chips, each chip being defined by a mesh-cell group. An example of a mesh with chips is presented in the Figure. The size of the chips must be supplied by the user. One advises using a chip thickness (mesh-cell size {t}_{e} ) at most equal to one fifth of the initial notch radius {R}_{0} . Figure 3-1- Classical mesh with definition of the chips. The user may however use in 2D an arbitrary mesh (with representation of the defect by a notch) sufficiently refined in the zone close to the notch. The chips are then defined automatically with user parameters. An example of a refined mesh usable for the method is presented in the Figure. Figure 3-2- Free mesh without definition of the chips. Finally, a user who does not have a specific dedicated 2D mesh may also use the command RAFF_GP in order to obtain a mesh that is sufficiently fine and regular in the zone of interest of the notch (the chips). The notch must nevertheless be represented geometrically, and the mesh sufficiently regular in the chip zone, with “clean” mesh cells (weakly distorted). 3.2.2 In 3D One of the principal difficulties of the use of this approach in 3D is due to the fact that it requires one to have produced a mesh defining the analysis zones known as chips and slice (see the Figure). This zone must be meshed with hexahedra. One advises using a chip thickness (mesh-cell size {t}_{e} ) at most equal to one fifth of the initial notch radius {R}_{0} : {t}_{e}\le \frac{{R}_{0}}{5} The notion of slice corresponds to an angular sector in the direction of propagation of the notch (see the Figure). In the case of a semi-elliptical front, it is advised to produce a mesh containing at least 16 slices along the notch front, or even 32 or 64 if it is elongated. The meshes are preferably quadratic, which makes it possible, for a given number of nodes, to have a more accurate analysis and to capture the stress gradients better. Figure 3-3: Definition of the chips: set of mesh cells of shape equivalent to the notch front. Figure 3-4: Definition of the slice zone As for the two-dimensional case with definition of the chips in the mesh, the chips of the various slices must be defined by mesh-cell groups. The chip mesh-cell groups must furthermore be arranged in a list of mesh-cell groups arranged slice by slice in the following manner (for p slices of n chips): tranche_1_copeau_1, tranche_1_copeau_2, ..., tranche_1_copeau_n, tranche_2_copeau_1, ..., tranche_p_copeau_n. 3.3 Identification of the parameters The energy model is based on two parameters: the initial notch radius {R}_{0} and the critical parameter {G}_{\mathrm{pc}} . These two parameters are to be identified from a test on a CT specimen. One assumes known, for the material considered: - Young's modulus E , - the critical stress {\sigma}_{c} , - the surface energy {G}_{C} . The parameter {G}_{\mathit{PC}} is determined by simulation of a test on a \mathit{CT} specimen in which the crack is represented by a notch of given radius R . This parameter corresponds to the maximum spatial value (over all the chips of all the slices) of the parameter {G}_{P} when the loading is such that G={G}_{C} . The identification procedure is as follows: - mesh with definition of the chips in 3D, with or without definition of the chips in 2D - carrying out of the elastoplastic mechanical analysis; it is advised to use under-integrated elements (D_PLAN_SI, 3D_SI, etc.) in order to reduce the effects of incompressibility - first post-processing: computation of the energy release rate by the operator CALC_G - post-processing of {G}_{P} via the command CALC_GP The syntax of the command CALC_GP is as follows (one takes here the 2D case with a mesh comprising the chip mesh-cell groups): tab [table] = CALC_GP( #Result of the mechanical analysis to be post-processed and time instants of post-processing > RESULTAT = resumeca, > LIST_INST = instants, #Abbreviated output table requested > GPMAX = CO('TABGPMAX') #Definition of the analysis zones (chips) > TRANCHE_2D =_F( > ZONE_MAIL = 'OUI', > GROUP_MA = l_group, > TAILLE = l_taille, > ) One obtains as output 2 tables: tab and tabgpmax. Here is their detailed content. tab contains the values of {G}_{P} at every time instant and place of analysis: INSTANT ZONE ENER_ELAS DELTAL GP MAX_INST #Time instant Chip Elastic energy Distance to the tip Value of GP Indicator 1.00000E+00 CO_1 0,004428 2E-02 2.21402E-01 0 1.00000E+00 CO_2 0,009678 4E-02 2.41955E-01 1 3.00000E+00 CO_1 0,007208 2E-02 3.60683E-01 0 3.00000E+00 CO_2 0,015359 4E-02 3.83966E-01 1 tabgpmax contains the same following information, but only when MAX_INST=1: INSTANT ZONE ENER_ELAS DELTAL GP MAX_INST #Time instant Chip Elastic energy Distance to the tip Value of GP Indicator 1.00000E+00 CO_2 0,009678 4E-02 2.41955E-01 1 3.00000E+00 CO_2 0,015359 4E-02 3.83966E-01 1 If G={G}_{C} at time instant 3, one then has {G}_{\mathit{PC}}\left(R\right)=0,38396 Up to this point, the analysis has been carried out for a given value of the notch radius R . Now, the value obtained for {G}_{\mathit{PC}} depends on the notch radius chosen. In absolute terms, one must therefore repeat the operation for different notch radii, then plot the dependence {G}_{\mathit{PC}}\left(R\right) . One then adds to it the straight line of slope \frac{{\sigma}_{c}^{2}}{E} ; the parameters to be chosen ({G}_{\mathrm{PC}},{R}_{0}) correspond to the point of intersection of the two curves (see the Figure). However, if the subsequent study to be carried out falls within the framework of a monotonic proportional loading, it is possible to choose arbitrarily the notch radius for the identification of {G}_{\mathrm{PC}} (the radius must however be chosen sufficiently small), and to carry out the study with this same radius and this same parameter {G}_{\mathrm{PC}} ; in the past, numerous studies under proportional loading have been carried out with a notch radius chosen arbitrarily between 50 and 100\mu m . Figure 3-5: Identification curve of the parameters of the energy model The identification procedure presented here is valid for a given temperature. Strictly speaking, one would have to identify the pair of parameters ({G}_{\mathrm{PC}},{R}_{0}) for several temperatures in the range of interest of the analysis. However, even if the temperature of the component evolves in the course of time, one readily understands that it is not possible to make the notch radius evolve in the course of the analysis. This is why the global identification must be carried out at a temperature close to the temperature of future interest (that at which one wishes to carry out the prediction of cleavage); if other temperatures are necessary, one will keep the radius {R}_{0} initially identified and one will identify afresh only the critical value {G}_{\mathrm{PC}} . 3.4 Prediction of the cleavage of a structure The energy model has been validated for numerous situations in the cleavage zone, but still requires validation tests in the transition zone (see the Figure for the definition of the cleavage or transition zones). The first question to be asked is the following: shall I carry out the mechanical analysis (the one to which I am going to apply my cleavage criterion) in large or small strains? This choice must be carried over to the identification procedure defined above: the mechanical identification analysis on the CT specimen must be conducted with the same type of strains and the same radius as the study on the structure. The methodology to be followed is as follows: - identify the parameters of the approach {G}_{\mathrm{PC}} and {R}_{0} on a CT specimen (with a notch, of course). - produce a mesh of the structure of notch type with chips, as defined in paragraph 3.2, with the notch radius {R}_{0} . - conduct the mechanical simulation of the structure with the same type of strain as that of the identification, preferably with an under-integrated formulation (D_PLAN_SI, 3D_SI, etc.) - post-process with the operator CALC_GP. Initiation will take place when {G}_{P} reaches, inside the chip zone (wherever that may be), the value {G}_{\mathrm{PC}} ; the critical value is generally reached at a non-zero distance from the crack front. 4 Methodology for the prediction of cleavage with the Beremin model or its industrial version The Beremin model has a high international recognition. It makes it possible to take account of numerous effects (small defect, triaxiality, warm preloading) in situations of complex loading. It is a probabilistic model. The industrial version of the Beremin model is a deterministic approach which relies on the surface density of Weibull stress [12] [14]. 4.1 Theoretical framework The Beremin model is based on the existence of a mechanical cleavage stress. Starting from this point, an estimate of the probability that a damage site (micro-defect) reaches the cleavage stress is established. By using a weakest-link assumption (if one site breaks, the entire structure breaks), it is then possible to determine the probability of complete fracture of the structure from the stress fields (and of plasticity within it). The industrial version of the Beremin model considers that, in the most penalising case, the instability of brittle fracture comes from the interaction between the maximum principal stress \sigma_I and a distribution of initiation sites liable to initiate cleavage in the plane perpendicular to the most highly loaded defect. The combination of these two factors leads one to quantify the risk of sudden fracture by means of a surface density of Weibull stress, denoted \sigma_W^{2D} . It is a deterministic approach. For more details, one may refer to R7.02.04, [6] or [14]. One specifies here the elements essential to the use of these two approaches (Beremin model and its industrial version), within the framework of cleavage and of the transition zone. 4.2 Mesh and modelling This model being based on the distribution of the stresses in a neighbourhood of the defect, it is necessary to take precautions in the choice of the mesh and of the finite elements at the crack tip. The use of elements with a gradient of internal variables (GRAD_INCO or GRAD_VARI) is the available approach giving the most accurate stress field at the crack tip. In practice, within the framework of an industrial approach, it is rather recommended to use the same modelling assumptions for the reference specimen and the target structure [13]. The mesh-cell size perpendicularly to the crack front must be sufficiently fine to capture the stress field close to the defect, of the order of 50 \mu m or less. Indeed, the distance from the crack tip at which the maximum of the stresses \sigma_I is reached is approximately \frac{2K_I^2}{E \sigma_Y} , which corresponds to a few tens of micrometres for a low-alloy steel. The mesh-cell size must be identical between the mesh of the geometry of interest and the mesh of the reference geometry. In order to be able to mesh components of large size, one advises choosing mesh cells of the order of 50 \mu m , as was recommended in the historical studies on the Beremin model [6]. The analysis formalism may be that of the small perturbations or of the large transformations (large displacements accompanied by large strains). Once again, it is appropriate to adopt a formalism that is consistent between the simulation on the reference geometry and the simulation on the geometry of interest. 4.3 Identification of the parameters Several material parameters enter into the definition of the Beremin model: {V}_{0} , m and potentially {\sigma}_{u} and {\sigma}_{th} . In practice, the exponent m expresses the scatter of the defects liable to initiate brittle fracture and {\sigma}_{u} may be likened to the critical fracture stress of an elementary volume {V}_{0} . The threshold stress {\sigma}_{th} corresponds to the stress below which fracture by cleavage may be excluded. The three parameters {\sigma}_{u} , {\sigma}_{th} and m are characteristic of the material considered. The elementary volume {V}_{0} must be large enough to encompass about ten grains and small enough for the stress field to be quasi-homogeneous. One uses the same value of {V}_{0} in the analyses D_PLAN_SI, AXIS, 3D_SI, etc. because the type of modelling (that is to say the manner in which the plastified volume is computed) is already defined by the operand COEF_MULT in POST_BEREMIN. The identification of these parameters is not unique, but depends on the choice made for the modelling. In the same way, the parameters must be identified on an analysis presenting the same characteristics as the prediction analysis (same definition of the Weibull stress). An example of such an identification in an industrial framework is for example presented in [13]: - Identification of the parameters entering into the computation of the Weibull stress with the Beremin model - Application of the industrial version of the Beremin model with the same set of material parameters 4.4 Prediction of the cleavage of a structure Once the parameters have been identified, the analysis is conducted with the same recommendations as for the identification and with the same type of modelling (mesh-cell size at the crack tip, type of finite elements, options for the computation of the Weibull stress). With the probabilistic Beremin model, it is possible, for a given loading level, to know the probability of fracture by cleavage of the structure. One will note that, in the procedures for determining the risks of cleavage, one generally seeks the loadings leading to fracture probabilities of 5%, 50% and 95%. The industrial version of the Beremin model is deterministic [12]. If at every point of the crack front the loading of the structure is lower than the maximum loading seen by a hypothetical CT specimen presenting an envelope toughness of the material considered, then the structure will not be able to fracture suddenly. In practice, one determines a curve K_J \ - \sigma_W^{2D} on a reference CT specimen. The local loading of an arbitrary structure, denoted K_J ^{CT} , is obtained for the same surface density of Weibull stress \sigma_W^{2D} as the reference CT specimen. One multiplies this figure by the total volume of the component, and one obtains the parameter {V}_{\mathrm{th}} . The identification of the parameters is summarised as follows: - on tensile tests on AE specimens at low temperature, determine the mean stress at fracture {\sigma}_{\mathrm{moy}} ; - deduce from it the parameter {\sigma}_{\mathit{LC}}=1.2\mathit{Min}({\sigma}_{\mathit{moy}}) ; - carry out a simulation, in 2D small strains, of tension on a CT specimen whose J at fracture is known; - determine the defect opening when the J at fracture is reached ( J computed by CALC_G); - carry out a simulation, in 2D large strains, of the same test on the CT specimen; - determine the loading level for which the opening of the defect equals the opening at fracture obtained in small strains; - at this loading level, use the command POST_ELEM in order to know the volume of material over which the maximum principal stress exceeds the stress {\sigma}_{\mathrm{LC}} : this volume is equal to {V}_{\mathrm{th}} (caution with the symmetries: a multiplicative factor must be added in order to account for the symmetries). 6.4 Prediction of the cleavage of a structure As for the other models, one must use the same type of simulation as that carried out for the identification of the parameters (crack or fine notch). One then carries out two thermo-mechanical analyses of the structure: one in small strains, the other in large strains. The analysis in small strains makes it possible to know the initiation loading, which is such that the integral J reaches the J at fracture (in general, the CEA uses the parameter {J}_{0.2} , corresponding to the value of J for an initiation of \mathrm{0.2mm} on a CT specimen). At this loading level, one determines the opening of the defect. The analysis in large strains makes it possible to know the nature of the initiation; one places oneself at a loading level such that the opening in large strains is equal to the opening in small strains when the J at fracture is reached. At this loading level, one determines the volume of material {V}_{\mathrm{LC}} over which the maximum principal stress exceeds {\sigma}_{\mathrm{LC}} : {V}_{\mathrm{LC}}=\frac{\sum_{i}({V}_{i}\vee {\sigma}_{i}\ge {\sigma}_{\mathrm{LC}})}{{V}_{\mathrm{total}}} However, the parameter {V}_{\mathrm{th}} has been identified on 2D tests. Furthermore, one suspects that if the crack front has an infinite length, the exceedance volume {V}_{\mathrm{LC}} will likewise tend towards infinity. This is why the volume {V}_{\mathrm{LC}} must be divided by the length of the crack front {L}_{\mathrm{front}} . If \frac{{V}_{\mathrm{LC}}}{{L}_{\mathrm{front}}} {V}_{\mathrm{th}} , then the risk of cleavage is non-zero and increases with {V}_{\mathrm{LC}} . There exists an expression of the probability of cleavage as a function of {V}_{\mathrm{LC}} , but it has not been sufficiently validated up to the present for us to mention it here. It is however described in [11]. 6.5 Precautions and limits of this approach From our point of view, this approach presents a few limits and precautions which are mentioned briefly here. First of all, the limit initiation loading is defined by the integral J ; the latter being rigorously computable only in elasticity (linear or not), the initiation loading cannot theoretically be determined when one leaves elasticity. However, in the case of monotonic proportional loading, the elastoplastic analysis may be considered as non-linear elastic, and the computation of J is valid. Be that as it may, the method does not make it possible to predict the moment of initiation for an arbitrary loading. Furthermore, in order to use the model completely, it is appropriate to carry out an analysis in small strains and an analysis in large strains, and to establish a link from the defect openings in the two cases. This type of analogy, although common, is not entirely satisfactory. These first two remarks could be got round by using another criterion for determining the initiation loading, computable in large strains and valid for an arbitrary loading. Unfortunately, this is not possible for the moment. At the level of the type of initiation itself, the criterion is based on a volume of exceedance of a critical value of stress in the zone close to the defect. Now, in the zones close to the defect, and even more so when the latter is modelled by a crack, the computation of the stresses is difficult because of the singularities generated and of the problems of incompressibility. It is therefore appropriate to visualise the stresses (in particular the hydrostatic ones, not the equivalent ones) at the defect front and to make sure that their distribution is physical. A common practice is to take the average of the stresses per element and to use it for the computation of the volume; one will recall that the average of two wrong results is not necessarily right. 7 Conclusion In code_aster, the prediction of cleavage may be carried out with four models; three of them (Beremin, Bordet, Le Corre) are based on a stress criterion (approach known as local), the last one ( {G}_{P} ) being based on the elastic energy (approach known as energy). Their respective domains of validity make it possible to cover the situations of complex loading, in particular the cases of non-proportional loading. The analyses in the ductile/brittle transition zone pose more difficulty, and still deserve fairly extensive validation. The principal piece of advice is to ensure that the thermo-mechanical analysis proceeds as well as possible. If the mechanical fields are computed in too approximate a manner, the quality of the predictions will be affected. The second piece of advice is to compare the predictions of several of the approaches and, as for all numerical simulations, to take a critical look at the results obtained. 8 Bibliography 1. u2.06.01 Carrying out an eigenmode analysis of a structure u2.06.01 Carrying out an eigenmode analysis of a structure Summary This document presents an overall view of the various approaches available in Code_Aster for computing the vibration eigenmodes of a mechanical structure. These approaches are described starting from the simplest to implement, for standard studies, and going progressively towards more elaborate implementations for advanced studies. The necessary sequences of the Code_Aster operators are presented, without going into the detail of each operator. 1 Reminders: formulation of the problem One considers a mechanical structure represented, within the framework of a finite-element modelling, by its stiffness matrix K , mass matrix M and possibly damping matrix C . The equation governing the evolution of the structure is written M\ddot{x}+C\dot{x}+Kx=0 . One wants to characterise the free vibrations of the mechanical structure, defined by eigenfrequencies {f}_{i}=\frac{{\omega}_{i}}{2\pi } ( {\omega}_{i} : natural angular frequency of mode no. i ) and the associated mode shapes {x}_{i} (and the modal dampings {\zeta}_{i} if the model contains damping).
