In the absence of damping (the simplest and most frequent case), the modal analysis consists in finding the pairs \left\lbrace {\omega}_{i},{x}_{i}\right\rbrace such that (K-{\omega}_{i}^{2}M){x}_{i}=0 . 2 Data setup of the problem The data setup for an analysis of vibration eigenmodes is classical and common to most mechanical analyses in Code_Aster : - reading of the mesh (operator LIRE_MAILLAGE), - assignment of the model characteristics: a beam-type or 3D or …? model (AFFE_MODELE), - definition and assignment of the materials (DEFI_MATERIAU and AFFE_MATERIAU) and/or assignment of the characteristics of the structural elements (AFFE_CARA_ELEM), - possible imposition of boundary conditions (stage absent if the structure is completely free). The particularity of the modal analysis in Code_Aster at present is that, in general, the displacement boundary conditions, if there are any, must be imposed by dualisation (AFFE_CHAR_MECA, factor keyword DDL_IMPO – the most common – or FACE_IMPO or ARETE_IMPO) rather than by kinematic loads (AFFE_CHAR_CINE). The figure outlines the data setup of a modal analysis problem. Figure 2-a : Data setup of a modal analysis problem. Notes: - For a modal analysis, no excitation is necessary, unless one wants to take into account the geometric-stiffness effect brought by a static loading (advanced study). Where applicable, paragraph 3.2.2.3 indicates the procedure to be adopted (advanced study). - For a simple study, the structure is not prestressed: any displacement boundary conditions are generally zero. If one wants to take into account the prestress generated by non-zero displacements, one must there too adopt the procedure indicated in paragraph 3.2.2.3 . 3 Analysis of the vibration eigenmodes of a structure From the input data seen in the previous paragraph, the various possibilities offered by Code_Aster for computing the eigenmodes of a structure are presented here, going from the simplest to implement to more complicated sequences. 3.1 The simplest studies For simple studies (one considers here a structure modelled without damping, without prestress, without fluid–structure interaction, without gyroscopy, without mixed modelling (i.e. all the finite elements are of the same dimension: volume, or else surface, or else line)), the most ergonomic solution is to use the modal analysis wizard available in the Aster module of the Salomé-Méca software. Figure 3.1-a: Location of the modal analysis wizard in Salomé-Méca. The wizard simply asks the user to supply the mesh, to enter the data on the materials and any boundary conditions. And finally the eigenmode search criterion (for example: the first N modes? or the modes over a given frequency band? or the modes around a target frequency?). The wizard then automatically generates the Code_Aster command file, visible in the tree of the study, which the user can open and edit (with the Eficas graphical interface or a text editor) if, for example, the user wishes to modify certain parameters or options. Finally, execution of the analysis automatically generates a message file (extension .mess) containing the detail of all the analyses, as well as a result file (in MED format) containing the eigenmodes. One can open this file in the ParaViS module in order to visualise the deformed shapes (paragraph 5.1). | Figure 3.1-b: Command file generated by the wizard. | Figure 3.1-c: Result file generated by the wizard. | | --- | --- | 3.2 More advanced features 3.2.1 Sequence of the Code_Aster commands From the input data, one proceeds as follows: - computation of the assembled matrices (operator ASSEMBLAGE with the options 'RIGI_MECA' and 'MASS_MECA'; other options exist for computing more specific matrices, for example the geometric stiffness, the damping, the gyroscopy, etc.); - computation of the eigenmodes: operator CALC_MODES, with the keyword OPTION and the factor keyword CALC_FREQ used to specify the search criterion. OPTION='BANDE' or 'PLUS_PETITE' or 'CENTRE' or 'TOUT' is to be preferred for its CPU performance if one is seeking a relatively large number of modes (up to 50 to 80; beyond that, it is recommended to split the search into several sub-bands, cf. paragraph 3.2.4.1), in particular with the search option on a given band (OPTION='BANDE') for better robustness. On the contrary, OPTION='PROCHE' or 'SEPARE' or 'AJUSTE', which is more costly, is rather to be used to compute a few modes with a very good quality, for example if one wants to refine first estimates of eigenmodes (cf. paragraph 3.2.3). As a first step, it is advisable to leave the default parameters of these operators, and to specify only the search criterion for the eigenfrequencies (by default, the first 10 modes). Figure 3.2-a : Computation of the modes by way of the assembled matrices. Example: computation of the eigenmodes over the band [\mathrm{20 };300]\mathit{Hz} : ASSEMBLAGE( MODELE = modele, CHAM_MATER = ch_mat, CARA_ELEM = cara_el, CHARGE = c_limite, NUME_DDL = CO("numerota"), # creation of a numbering of the degrees of freedom MATR_ASSE =( _F( MATRICE= CO("matr_k"), OPTION= 'RIGI_MECA'), _F( MATRICE= CO("matr_m"), OPTION= 'MASS_MECA'), ) ) modes = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, OPTION = 'BANDE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = (20., 300.) ) ) 3.2.2 Usefulness of an intermediate computation of the assembled matrices: a few examples 3.2.2.1 Prior counting of the eigenfrequencies Before the analysis proper of the eigenmodes, it is strongly recommended to carry out a count of the eigenmodes contained in one or more given frequency bands (in the standard case of real modes; if the modes to be computed are complex, it will be a count around a point of the complex plane). This count is much faster than the analysis proper of the eigenmodes. A priori knowledge of the number of eigenfrequencies contained in the search band has a twofold usefulness, of verification and of optimisation of the CPU performance of the modal analysis: - verification: one can check that the number of eigenmodes computed by the modal solver is indeed equal to the number of eigenmodes counted a priori ; - CPU optimisation: if the number of eigenfrequencies counted over the search frequency band is too high (a threshold lying between 50 and 80 is commonly observed), the user will be able to split the search band into several sub-bands, by means of the operator CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' split into sub-bands (cf. paragraph 3.2.4.1). The counting of the eigenmodes is carried out by the operator INFO_MODE. As a first approach, the user can simply supply: - in the standard case of real modes: the matrices of the structure with the keywords MATR_ as well as its search band(s) with the keyword FREQ; - in the case of complex modes (structures with damping, for example): one must specify TYPE_MODE='COMPLEXE' and supply the search disc in the complex plane by RAYON_CONTOUR (and possibly CENTRE_CONTOUR) in place of FREQ. 3.2.2.2 Structures with hysteretic damping One must explicitly compute the assembled total stiffness matrix including the hysteretic contribution (complex matrix). The sequence of the operators is as follows: - computation of the assembled hysteretic stiffness matrix (computed from the elastic stiffness matrix) and of the mass matrix (ASSEMBLAGE with the options 'RIGI_MECA_HYST' and 'MASS_MECA' respectively); - modal analysis with, as input, the hysteretic stiffness matrix (complex) and the mass matrix (CALC_MODES). One will refer to the documentation U2.06.03 for more information on taking hysteretic damping into account in Code_Aster . 3.2.2.3 Taking prestresses into account Taking prestresses into account (non-zero boundary conditions, static external loadings, ...) requires the assembled mechanical and geometric stiffness matrices to be computed. One can then combine them to form the assembled total stiffness matrix, which is the one used for the modal analysis. The sequence of the operators is as follows, in a relatively simple case of static external loading: - definition of the external loading (operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA, with for example the keyword FORCE_NODALE), - computation of the stress field associated with this loading (operator MECA_STATIQUE or STAT_NON_LINE or MACRO_ELAS_MULT to compute the static response, then CREA_CHAMP with the keyword OPERATION='EXTR' to recover the stress field), - computation of the assembled matrices of mechanical stiffness, geometric stiffness associated with the stress field, and mass (ASSEMBLAGE), - combination of the mechanical stiffness and geometric stiffness matrices to form the total stiffness matrix (COMB_MATR_ASSE), - modal analysis with, as input, the total stiffness matrix and the mass matrix (CALC_MODES). Example: The test case SDLL101 presents an example of an analysis of the modes of a beam subjected to static forces. 3.2.2.4 Taking gyroscopy into account (rotating machines) In addition to the other assembled matrices (stiffness, mass and possibly damping other than gyroscopic), one must compute the gyroscopic damping matrix with the option 'MECA_GYRO'. The operator CALC_MODE_ROTATION then makes it possible to compute the eigenmodes of the structure for various rotational speeds defined by the user under the keyword VITE_ROTA. One can then plot the Campbell diagram (evolution of the eigenfrequencies as a function of the rotational speed) of the rotating structure by means of the operator IMPR_DIAG_CAMPBELL. Note: The operator CALC_MODE_ROTATION is in reality a macro-command calling CALC_MODES: if need be, the user can therefore carry out the various elementary stages of CALC_MODE_ROTATION “by hand”, but in a much less ergonomic manner . The test case SDLL129 illustrates the procedure in the case of a rotor with bearings whose characteristics depend on the rotational speed. 3.2.2.5 Use of the modes for a dynamic analysis on a modal basis Here too one must have access to the assembled matrices: their projection onto a modal basis supplies the generalised matrices usable for a dynamic analysis, with CPU performance much better than the direct use of the assembled matrices. This model-reduction method is described in the reference documentation R5.06.01 and the user's documentation U2.06.04. 3.2.3 Improving the quality of the eigenmodes Attention is drawn to the fact that the quality of a modal analysis depends above all on the quality of the input data and of the physical modelling . One may in particular mention: - the choice of the boundary conditions: are they representative of reality? Their influence on the result of the analysis is strong; - the fineness of the mesh: a mesh-convergence study is necessary, as for any numerical study; - the choice of the modelling: by structural elements (beam, shell, …) or in 3D? For example, for a slender structure, a beam modelling will generally be better than a 3D modelling even with a good mesh fineness. If the input data and the modelling are fixed, it is possible to improve the “computational” quality of the result by means of the keyword AMELIORATION='OUI', which automatically carries out a chaining of two modal analyses: the first, which gives a first estimate of the eigenmodes (eigenfrequencies, mode shapes, …) with the search criterion requested by the user (for example with CALC_FREQ / OPTION='BANDE' or 'PLUS_PETITE', which use the subspace method), the second by the inverse iteration method (CALC_FREQ / OPTION='PROCHE'), which refines the estimate of the previous analysis. Note 1: The first estimate is generally already good and satisfactory. For more complicated models, it is nevertheless advisable to carry out this improvement. Note 2: this automatic feature is limited to the cases where the structure is represented by real symmetric matrices, and does not comprise multiple modes or several rigid-body modes. For the other cases, or if for example one wants to improve only certain modes among all those computed, one can of course carry out the sequence of the analyses manually. The sequence of the commands is then as follows: Figure 3.2-b : Improvement of the quality of the eigenmodes (done manually). Example: The first mode analysis over the band [0; 2000] Hz with the command below: mode1 = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = k_asse, MATR_MASS = m_asse, OPTION = 'BANDE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ= (0., 2000.) ), ) gives the following results, visible in the MESSAGE file: THE COMPUTED LOWER AND UPPER FREQUENCIES ARE: FREQ_INF : 4.65661E+01 FREQ_SUP : 1.60171E+03 MODAL ANALYSIS: SIMULTANEOUS ITERATION METHOD SORENSEN METHOD NUMBER FREQUENCY (HZ) ERROR NORM 1 4.65661E+01 1.82405E-07 2 2.91827E+02 3.47786E-09 3 8.17182E+02 9.83625E-11 4 1.60171E+03 4.31692E-11 MEAN ERROR NORM: 0.46506E-07 A POSTERIORI VERIFICATION OF THE MODES IN THE INTERVAL ( 4.64496E+01, 1.60571E+03) THERE ARE INDEED 4 FREQUENCY(IES) One can then refine, for example, the first two eigenmodes, by launching the second analysis from the eigenfrequencies previously computed: mode2 = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = k_asse, MATR_MASS = m_asse, OPTION = 'PROCHE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = ( 46.6, 291.8 ) ), ) which gives MODAL ANALYSIS: INVERSE ITERATION METHOD INVERSE NUMBER FREQUENCY (HZ) DAMPING NB_ITER PRECISION ERROR NORM 1 4.65661E+01 0.00000E+00 3 3.33067E-16 3.99228E-08 2 2.91827E+02 0.00000E+00 3 2.22045E-16 1.23003E-09 One observes that the error norm is slightly improved (admittedly weakly, but this is a very simple case). Note: One can also automate the retrieval of the eigenfrequencies coming from the first estimate in order to feed the second analysis, thanks to the Python language: retrieval of the list of the estimated eigenfrequencies in the Python variable f_estimation: f_estimation = mode1.LIST_VARI_ACCES()['FREQ'] mode2 = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = k_asse, MATR_MASS = m_asse, OPTION = 'PROCHE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = f_estimation ), ) 3.2.4 Optimisation of the CPU performance 3.2.4.1 Splitting of the search frequency band If one is seeking many eigenmodes (either because the search band is very wide, or because the modal density is high), the performance of the modal analysis will be better by splitting the global search band \left[{f}_{min};{f}_{max}\right] into several ( n ) sub-bands: \left[{f}_{min};{f}_{2}\right] , \left[{f}_{2};{f}_{3}\right] , …, \left[{f}_{n};{f}_{max}\right] . This is done by means of the operator CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' and by specifying the frequency splitting with the keyword FREQ=(fmin,f2,...,fn,fmax). In order to define the sub-bands, the user can rely on the a priori count of the eigenfrequencies supplied by the operator INFO_MODE, which can itself also operate by sub-bands. Figure 3.2-c : Computation of the eigenmodes by splitting into sub-bands. Example: identical to paragraph 3.2.1, splitting the band [\mathrm{20 };300]\mathit{Hz} into three sub-bands: ASSEMBLAGE( MODELE = modele, CHAM_MATER = ch_mat, CARA_ELEM = cara_el, CHARGE = c_limite, NUME_DDL = CO("numerota"), # creation of a numbering of the degrees of freedom MATR_ASSE =( _F( MATRICE= CO("matr_k"), OPTION= 'RIGI_MECA'), _F( MATRICE= CO("matr_m"), OPTION= 'MASS_MECA'), ) ); nb_modes = INFO_MODE( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, FREQ = (20.,300.), ); modes = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = (20., 100., 200., 300.) ) ); Notes: - There is a gain in CPU performance even when the sub-bands are treated sequentially (which is the case by default). The implementation of parallelism (cf. the following paragraph) makes it possible to improve the performance still further. - For optimum performance, it is advisable to have sub-bands that are as balanced as possible (that is, with a number of modes sought per sub-band that is relatively uniform). 3.2.4.2 Parallelism For the modal analysis, parallelism can be implemented at two levels: - parallelisation of the modal analyses carried out on each sub-band, in the operators INFO_MODE and CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' split into several sub-bands; - parallelism at the level of the linear solver MUMPS, in the operator CALC_MODES when it is used with OPTION='BANDE' or 'PLUS_PETITE' or 'CENTRE' or 'TOUT'. In order to implement parallelism, one must: - have a version of Code_Aster built with a parallel compiler (for example: OpenMPI, …). On the centralised Aster4 server, parallel versions already exist: STAxx_impi; - select in ASTK a parallel version of Code_Aster ; Figure 3.2-d : Selection in ASTK of a parallel version of Code_Aster (example on the centralised Aster4 server). - specify in ASTK the number of processors and of compute nodes to be used; one must use at least as many processors as there are non-empty frequency sub-bands, and it is advisable to use a number of processors that is a multiple of the number of non-empty sub-bands (for example: if there are 5 non-empty sub-bands, use 10 or 15 or … processors); Figure 3.2-e : Declaration in ASTK of the number of processors and compute nodes to be used. - In the Code_Aster command file: - in order to use the basic mode (parallelisation of the sub-bands only) with INFO_MODE or CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' split into several sub-bands, there is nothing to do: the default keywords activate the parallelisation of the sub-bands; - in order to use the advanced mode (parallelisation of the sub-bands for INFO_MODE and CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' split into several sub-bands, and of the linear solver for all the modal operators): use the linear solver MUMPS (factor keyword SOLVEUR, operand METHODE='MUMPS'; it is also recommended to set the operands RENUM='QAMD' and GESTION_MEMOIRE='IN_CORE'). Example: identical to paragraph 3.2.4.1, parallelising both the analyses on the sub-bands and the linear solver: modes = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = (20., 100., 200., 300.) ), NIVEAU_PARALLELISME = 'COMPLET', SOLVEUR =_F( METHODE = 'MUMPS', RENUM = 'QAMD', GESTION_MEMOIRE = 'IN_CORE' ), ); Note: For optimum performance, it is advisable to have sub-bands that are as balanced as possible (i.e.: with a number of modes sought per sub-band that is relatively uniform). The implementation of parallelism is presented in more detail in the generic documentation U2.08.06 and the user's guides of INFO_MODE U4.52.01 and of CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' split into several sub-bands U4.52.02. 3.2.4.3 Model reduction: analysis by substructuring When the numerical model comprises a high number of degrees of freedom or when the structure studied is an assembly of components meshed separately, one can use model-reduction methods by substructuring, which rely on a geometric partitioning of the global structure. On large models, these methods present better CPU performance than a direct analysis. - Dynamic substructuring This method has a very general field of application. The documentation U2.07.05 details its implementation. - Cyclic substructuring This method has a much more restrictive field of application than the previous one: it makes it possible to treat only structures with cyclic repetitivity (for example: a bladed wheel, …). The test case SDLV301 gives an example of implementation. 4 Parameters contained in a modal analysis result Execution of the modal analysis operator is accompanied by the automatic printout of certain parameters in the RESULTAT file: THE NUMBER OF DEGREES OF FREEDOM TOTAL IS: 234 OF LAGRANGE IS: 120 THE NUMBER OF ACTIVE DEGREES OF FREEDOM IS: 54 THE OPTION CHOSEN IS: CENTRE THE VALUE OF THE FREQUENCY SHIFT IS : 5.00000E+01 INFORMATION ON THE REQUESTED ANALYSIS: NUMBER OF MODES SOUGHT : 1 THE DIMENSION OF THE REDUCED SPACE IS : 0 IT IS LOWER THAN THE NUMBER OF MODES, IT IS TAKEN EQUAL TO 4 = SORENSEN METHOD (ARPACK CODE) = = VERSION : 2.4 = = DATE : 07/31/96 = NUMBER OF RESTARTS = 2 NUMBER OF OP X PRODUCTS = 7 NUMBER OF B X PRODUCTS = 20 NUMBER OF REORTHOGONALISATIONS (STEP 1) = 6 NUMBER OF REORTHOGONALISATIONS (STEP 2) = 0 NUMBER OF RESTARTS DUE TO A ZERO V0 = 0 THE COMPUTED LOWER AND UPPER FREQUENCIES ARE: FREQ_INF : 5.22037E+01 FREQ_SUP : 5.22037E+01 MODAL ANALYSIS: SIMULTANEOUS ITERATION METHOD eigenfrequencies SORENSEN METHOD NUMBER FREQUENCY (HZ) ERROR NORM 2 5.22037E+01 7.02498E-10 3 6.74211E+01 9.12843E-10 position of the mode in the global spectrum MEAN ERROR NORM: 0.80767E-09 A POSTERIORI VERIFICATION OF THE MODES IN THE INTERVAL ( 5.20730E+01, 5.23340E+01) THERE ARE INDEED 1 FREQUENCY(IES) If the computed modes are complex, there is in addition a column giving the modal dampings: THE NUMBER OF DEGREES OF FREEDOM TOTAL IS: 74 OF LAGRANGE IS: 44 THE NUMBER OF ACTIVE DEGREES OF FREEDOM IS: 8 INFORMATION ON THE REQUESTED ANALYSIS: NUMBER OF MODES SOUGHT : 5 the problem treated being quadratic, the search space is doubled QZ method in CALC_MODES: One finds a number of eigenvalues 17 different from the number of active physical degrees of freedom 8! your problem is strongly damped. real eigenvalue(s) : 14 complex eigenvalue(s) with conjugate : 10 complex eigenvalue(s) without conjugate : 0 MODAL ANALYSIS: GLOBAL METHOD OF QR TYPE eigenfrequencies (damped) ALGORITHM QZ_SIMPLE NUMBER FREQUENCY (HZ) DAMPING ERROR NORM 1 5.52718E+00 8.68241E-03 4.00918E-13 2 1.08852E+01 1.71010E-02 7.31808E-14 3 1.59105E+01 2.50000E-02 5.40182E-14 4 2.04500E+01 3.21394E-02 4.03817E-14 5 2.43661E+01 3.83022E-02 3.48265E-14 modal dampings MEAN ERROR NORM: 0.12067E-12 Warning: for the moment, there is no STURM-type verification (counting of the correct number of computed eigenvalues) when one is in the complex plane: generalised modal problem with complex MATR_RIGI, or generalised modal problem with non-symmetric matrix(ices), or quadratic modal problem (presence of the keyword MATR_AMOR). A POSTERIORI VERIFICATION OF THE MODES Furthermore, the computer data structure produced during a modal analysis may contain the following parameters: | Parameter name in Code_Aster | Definition | | --- | --- | | FREQ | Eigenfrequency (damped, where applicable) | | AMOR_GENE | Generalised modal damping | | AMOR_REDUIT | Reduced modal damping | | FACT_PARTICI_D ( = X or Y or Z) | Participation factor of the mode in the direction D | | MASS_EFFE_D ( = X or Y or Z) | Effective modal mass in the direction D | | MASS_EFFE_UN_D ( = X or Y or Z) | Unit effective modal mass in the direction D | | MASS_GENE | Generalised mass of the mode | | OMEGA2 | Square of the natural angular frequency (damped, where applicable) | | RIGI_GENE | Generalised stiffness of the mode | Table 4.1 : list of the modal parameters. These parameters are defined mathematically in the reference documentation R5.01.03. The user has access to them by printing the content of the data structure with the operator IMPR_RESU in FORMAT='RESULTAT' with the option TOUT_PARA='OUI'. 5 Post-processing of the eigenmodes 5.1 Visualisation The mode shapes computed by one of the methods described previously can be exported in various formats in order to be visualised in mechanical-analysis platforms: MED format for the Salomé platform, UNV format, … The user can thus characterise graphically the modes computed: bending mode? mode in a given plane? local mode? etc. Example: printout in MED format. modes = CALC_MODES (...) # calcul modal IMPR_RESU( FORMAT = 'MED', RESU=_F( RESULTAT = modes ) ) One can then open the file created in the Salomé platform in order to visualise the mode shape, animate it, … Figure 5.1-a : Visualisation of a mode in Salomé (ParaViS module): here the bending mode of order 2 of a beam. 5.2 Normalisation of the modes The mode shapes are defined up to a multiplicative factor (cf. formulation of the modal problem in paragraph 1). By default, the modes computed by the operator CALC_MODES are normalised so that the largest physical component is equal to 1. The user can modify this normalisation, either directly in the operator CALC_MODES by means of the factor keyword NORM_MODE, or later by means of the operator NORM_MODE U4.52.11. In both cases, the code also computes or updates the following modal parameters, which depend on the normalisation chosen: FACT_PARTICI_D , MASS_GENE and RIGI_GENE. It also enriches the data structure with the parameters MASS_EFFE_UN_D and INER_EFFE_UN_D (which are themselves independent of the normalisation). These parameters (defined in paragraph 4) can be useful in particular for eliminating from a modal basis certain unwanted modes (cf. paragraph 5.3). Example: normalisation with respect to the mass. First possibility: modes = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, OPTION = 'BANDE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = (20., 300.) ), NORM_MODE =_F( NORME = 'MASS_GENE' ) ) Second possibility: modes = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, OPTION = 'BANDE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = (20., 300.) ), ) modes = NORM_MODE( reuse = modes, MODE = modes, NORME = 'MASS_GENE' ) 5.3 Filtering of the modes according to a criterion With a view to a transient-response analysis, for example, the user can choose to keep in the projection modal basis only certain modes judged important in the dynamic response or fulfilling a given criterion. This can be done either directly in CALC_MODES with the factor keywords FILTRE_MODE and IMPRESSION, or by means of the operator EXTR_MODE U4.52.12. One can thus filter the modes according to various options: from their number in the global spectrum, from their generalised mass, etc. Example 1: elimination of the modes whose unit effective mass is lower than 5%, and display in the RESULTAT file of the cumulation of the unit effective masses of the modes retained. First possibility: modes = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, OPTION = 'BANDE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = (20., 300.) ), NORM_MODE =_F( NORME = 'MASS_GENE' ), FILTRE_MODE =_F( CRIT_EXTR = 'MASS_EFFE_UN', SEUIL = 0.05 ), IMPRESSION =_F( CRIT_EXTR = 'MASS_EFFE_UN', CUMUL = 'OUI'), ) Second possibility: modes = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, OPTION = 'BANDE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = (20., 300.) ), NORM_MODE =_F( NORME = 'MASS_GENE' ), ) modes_f = EXTR_MODE( FILTRE_MODE =_F( MODE = modes, CRIT_EXTR = 'MASS_EFFE_UN', SEUIL = 0.05 ), IMPRESSION =_F( CRIT_EXTR = 'MASS_EFFE_UN', CUMUL = 'OUI'), ); Example 2: elimination of the modes whose unit effective rotational inertia is lower than 5%, and display in the RESULTAT file of the cumulation of the unit effective masses of the modes retained. First possibility: modes = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, OPTION = 'BANDE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = (20., 300.) ), NORM_MODE =_F( NORME = 'MASS_GENE' ), FILTRE_MODE =_F( CRIT_EXTR = 'INER_EFFE_UN', SEUIL = 0.05 ), IMPRESSION =_F( CRIT_EXTR = 'INER_EFFE_UN', CUMUL = 'OUI'), ) Second possibility: modes = CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI = matr_k, MATR_MASS = matr_m, OPTION = 'BANDE', CALC_FREQ =_F( FREQ = (20., 300.) ), NORM_MODE =_F( NORME = 'MASS_GENE' ), ) modes_f = EXTR_MODE( FILTRE_MODE =_F( MODE = modes, CRIT_EXTR = 'INER_EFFE_UN', SEUIL = 0.05 ), IMPRESSION =_F( CRIT_EXTR = 'INER_EFFE_UN', CUMUL = 'OUI'), ); Note: - The operator EXTR_MODE makes it possible to filter with a threshold applied to one or more given directions (keyword SEUIL_X for example for the direction DX), which is not possible directly in CALC_MODES at present. 5.4 Filtering of the modes according to a "local" criterion It is sometimes necessary to be able to filter the modes with respect to a criterion computed on the basis of only part of the model. For this one has the operator POST_MODE. Example: selection of modes on the basis of a local unit effective-mass criterion One computes (in an approximate manner) the effective mass and inertia criteria, unit and non-unit, on the desired part of the model: table_crit = POST_MODE( MODE=modes, GROUP_MA=("BATIMENT2",), CARA_ELEM=caraelem, MATR_MASS=masse, ) One modifies the table created by filtering on the chosen criterion, here local unit effective masses along X greater than 5%: table_crit = CALC_TABLE(reuse=table_crit, TABLE=table_crit, ACTION=_F(OPERATION="FILTRE", NOM_PARA="MASS_EFFE_UN_DX", CRIT_COMP="GT", VALE=0.05), ) One can then recover the list of the selected modes and build a mode_meca object containing only these modes. Retrieval of the list of the numbers of the selected modes: liste_modes = table_crit.EXTR_TABLE().values()["NUME_MODE"] Extraction of the selected modes: EXTR = EXTR_MODE(FILTRE_MODE=_F(MODE=modes, NUME_MODE=liste_modes))

u2.06.03 User's guide for the modelling of mechanical damping u2.06.03 User's guide for the modelling of mechanical damping Linear and non-linear dynamic analyses, for the study of the vibratory response with a force excitation or an imposed motion, or for the complex modal analysis, require mechanical damping characteristics to be added to the stiffness and mass characteristics. Several classical modellings are available, applicable to all the types of finite elements available. These modellings are available directly through the operators. - the viscous damping model, - the hysteretic damping model (also called "structural damping") for the harmonic analysis and the eigenmode analysis. For finer analyses, it is also possible to model materials possessing a realistic viscoelastic constitutive behaviour, whose constitutive behaviour is described by a set of internal variables. For analyses using a modal basis of real eigenmodes, it is possible to introduce modal damping coefficients. These coefficients may come equally well from tests carried out on site as from a modal analysis taking into account any one of the types of damping proposed. 1 Viscous damping model The viscous damping model is the most commonly used. It corresponds to the modelling of a dissipated energy proportional to the vibratory velocity: {E}_{d}=\frac{1}{2}{v}^{T}\text{Cv}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{T}\text{Cu} where C is the viscous damping matrix, with real coefficients. It leads to the classical equations of structural dynamics: \text{Mu}+\text{Cu}+\text{Ku}=f(t) with K the stiffness matrix and M the mass matrix. 1.1 “Global” proportional viscous damping, or Rayleigh damping This modelling, easy to implement, corresponds to a linear combination of the mass and stiffness matrices: C=\alpha K+\beta M It is currently available, using the operators DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01 §3.1 and ASSEMBLAGE(OPTION='AMOR_MECA') U4.61.21. One can also use COMB_MATR_ASSE U4.72.01, after having assembled the stiffness and mass matrices with real coefficients. The option SANS_CMP='LAGR' must be used when combining the matrices in order to preserve the boundary conditions of the system (imposed by Lagrange relations in the stiffness matrix). This approach allows the validation of solution algorithms, It is not realistic for industrial studies, because it does not make it possible to represent the heterogeneity of the structure with respect to damping (dissipation at the supports or at the assemblies). Moreover, the global identification of the coefficients \alpha and \beta is possible, in experimental modal analysis, only for two distinct eigenfrequencies \left[{f}_{1},{f}_{2}\right] ; it gives, for the eigenfrequencies \omega \notin \left[{\omega}_{1},{\omega}_{2}\right] with \omega =2\pi f , an evolution law of the reduced damping of the form (see R5.05.04): 2\xi =\alpha \omega +\frac{\beta}{\omega} For the discrete elements, the Rayleigh damping parameters not being definable in the operator AFFE_CARA_ELEM, if one wishes to take into account the contribution of these elements in the global Rayleigh damping matrix, one must necessarily go through the assembly method for this matrix with the operator COMB_MATR_ASSE. Without proceeding in this way, the global damping matrix will take into account only the contribution of the volume, surface or beam-type elements. If one uses the operator DYNA_NON_LINE, the Rayleigh damping therefore does not take into account the contribution of the discrete elements. 1.2 Viscous damping proportional to the elements of the model 1.2.1 Damping characteristics It is possible to build a damping matrix from each element of the model, as for the stiffness and the mass. Several features can be used: - the assignment of discrete elements, on POI1 or SEG2 mesh cells, by the operator AFFE_CARA_ELEM U4.42.01. This makes it possible to define, with several possible modes of description, a damping matrix for each degree of freedom. - the definition of a damping characteristic for any elastic material by the operator DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01 by supplying the keywords AMOR_ALPHA This material is then assigned to the mesh cells concerned. 1.2.2 Computation of the damping matrices For all types of finite elements (continuum, structural or discrete), it is possible to compute the real elementary matrices corresponding to the analysis option AMOR_MECA , after having computed the elementary matrices corresponding to the analysis options RIGI_MECA and MASS_MECA or MASS_MECA_DIAG ; the elementary matrices are then of the form: - when the material i , with proportional viscous damping characteristics ({\alpha}_{i},{\beta}_{i}) , is assigned to an element C_{elem} = \alpha_{i} K_{elem} + \beta_{i} M_{elem} - for a discrete element C_{elem} = A_{elem} . When the discrete element is of type DIS_CHOC (thus defined with a penalisation stiffness), it is also possible to assign to it a damping which will be taken into account only when there is contact R5.03.17. This operation is possible with the command CALC_MATR_ELEM U4.61.01 with the option AMOR_MECA . The assembly of all the elementary damping matrices is obtained with the usual operator ASSE_MATRICE U4.61.22. Note that one must use the same numberings and the same storage mode as for the stiffness and mass matrices (operator NUME_DDL U4.61.11). One may also recall that the use of the macro-command ASSEMBLAGE U4.61.21 makes it possible to gather these stages advantageously. One notes that the damping matrix obtained may be non-proportional: C\ne \alpha K+\beta M 1.2.3 Use of the viscous damping matrix The matrix C is: - usable for the direct linear dynamic analysis (keyword MATR_AMOR) with the linear dynamic response operators. - indispensable for the complex modal analysis with the eigenvalue search operator. For analyses on a modal basis, one must project this matrix into the subspace defined by a set \Phi of real eigenmodes. This operation is possible with the operator PROJ_MATR_BASE U4.63.12. Note that in the general case ( C non-proportional), the projected matrix is not diagonal. It nevertheless remains usable (keyword AMOR_GENE) for the computation of the dynamic response to a force or to an imposed motion in the modal space, with the linear dynamic response operator: - Transient, Harmonic: DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 - Complex modal analysis: CALC_MODES U4.52.02 1.2.4 Use of viscous modal damping For analyses on a modal basis of real eigenmodes, the dynamic differential equation in generalised coordinates: {\ddot{q}}_{i}+2{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}{\dot{q}}_{i}+{\omega}_{i}^{2}{q}_{i}=\frac{{\Phi}_{i}^{T}}{{\mu}_{i}}f(t) brings out a modal damping coefficient {\xi}_{i} expressed as a fraction of the critical damping and the generalised mass of the mode {\mu}_{i} , which depends on the manner of normalisation of the eigenmode. In the case of a strictly proportional damping matrix C , the coefficients {\xi}_{i} are deduced from the diagonal terms of the generalised damping matrix {\Phi}^{T}C\Phi by: 2{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}=\frac{{\Phi}_{i}^{T}C{\Phi}_{i}}{{\Phi}_{i}^{T}M{\Phi}_{i}} and in the case of eigenmodes normalised to unit modal mass 2{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i}={\Phi}_{i}^{T}C{\Phi}_{i} One can use this relation in the case of a non-proportional damping matrix C , by applying the Basile hypothesis, which is acceptable for weak dampings (in particular if there is no dominant localised damping) and for real eigenmodes that are sufficiently decoupled. The modal damping coefficients can be supplied by command (keyword AMOR_REDUIT) to two operators for: - Transient analysis in the modal space: DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 - Transient analysis in the physical space: DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 - Seismic analysis by oscillator spectrum: COMB_SISM_MODAL U4.84.01 Note that there is no tool for the automatic extraction of these coefficients from the generalised damping matrix {\Phi}^{T}C\Phi , a concept produced by the operator PROJ_MATR_BASE U4.63.12. 2 Hysteretic damping model The hysteretic damping model can be used to treat the harmonic responses of structures with viscoelastic materials. The hysteretic damping coefficient \eta is determined from a test under harmonic cyclic loading at the angular frequency \omega for which one obtains a stress–strain relation which makes it possible to define: - the energy dissipated per cycle in the form: {E}_{d}={\int}_{\text{cycle}}\sigma d\varepsilon - the complex Young's modulus {E}^{\text{ }} from the stress–strain relation: \sigma ={\sigma}_{0}{e}^{j\omega t} and \varepsilon ={\varepsilon}_{0}{e}^{j(\omega t-\varphi )} with the amplitudes: {\sigma}_{0} and {\varepsilon}_{0} , the phase: \varphi \text{E }=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}=(\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{\varepsilon}_{0}}){e}^{j\varphi }=(\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{\varepsilon}_{0}})(\cos\varphi +j\sin\varphi ) where E\text{ }={E}_{1}+j{E}_{2}={E}_{1}(1+j\eta ) with: - real part: {E}_{1}=(\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{\varepsilon}_{0}})(\cos\varphi ) - imaginary part: {E}_{2}=(\frac{{\sigma}_{0}}{{\varepsilon}_{0}})(\sin\varphi ) - dissipation factor: \eta =\frac{{E}_{1}}{{E}_{2}}=\tan\varphi This leads to the equations of structural dynamics: M\ddot{u}+ K (1+j.\eta) u=f(\Omega ) with K the real elastic stiffness matrix, M the mass matrix and \eta the hysteretic damping coefficient. Note that one often speaks of a complex stiffness matrix. This model is a simplified version of the standard viscoelastic model, and has several drawbacks: - The model obtained cannot be transposed into the time domain, since this model would not be causal, - This model does not present a dependence of the damping on frequency, unlike the standard viscoelastic model It nevertheless constitutes a good approximation for the computation of harmonic responses in a reasonably narrow frequency band, and also has the advantage of being simple to implement. 2.1 “Global” hysteretic damping This modelling, easy to implement, corresponds to: (-M{\omega}^{2}+j.\eta K+K)u=f(\Omega ) It is currently available, using the operator COMB_MATR_ASSE U4.72.01, after having assembled the stiffness matrix with real coefficients, but it is of little use: - validation of solution algorithms, - useless for industrial studies, because it does not make it possible to represent the heterogeneity of the structure with respect to damping (dissipation localised in particular zones of the structure treated with viscoelastic materials). 2.2 Hysteretic damping of the elements of the model 2.2.1 Damping characteristics It is possible to build a complex stiffness matrix from each element of the model, as for the real stiffness and the mass. Two features can be used: - the assignment of discrete elements, on POI1 or SEG2 mesh cells, by the operator AFFE_CARA_ELEM U4.42.01. This makes it possible to define, with several possible modes of description, a real stiffness matrix for each degree of freedom and a hysteretic damping coefficient to be applied to this matrix AMOR_HYST . - the definition of a damping characteristic for any elastic material by the operator DEFI_MATERIAU U4.43.01 by the keyword AMOR_HYST . This material is then assigned to the mesh cells concerned. In the case where certain materials would not be considered as affected by hysteretic damping, it is necessary to assign to them a zero hysteretic damping. 2.2.2 Computation of the damping matrices For all types of finite elements (continuum, structural or discrete), it is possible to compute the complex elementary matrices corresponding to the analysis option RIGI_MECA_HYST , after having computed the elementary matrices corresponding to the analysis options RIGI_MECA . Each elementary matrix is then of the form: - when the material i , with hysteretic damping characteristics {\eta}_{i} , is assigned to the element {k}_{elem}^{ } = {k}_{elem} (1 + j.{\eta}_{i}) - for a discrete element defined by a stiffness matrix K and a hysteretic damping coefficient \eta {k}_{elem}^{ } = {k}_{discret} (1 + j.{\eta}) This operation is possible with the operator CALC_MATR_ELEM U4.61.01 option RIGI_MECA_HYST . The assembly of the complex stiffness matrix K\ast , from the elementary matrices, is obtained with the usual operator ASSE_MATRICE U4.61.22. Note that one must use the same numbering and the same storage mode as for the mass matrix (operator NUME_DDL U4.61.11). The loading used for the computation of the real stiffness matrix (option RIGI_MECA ) must be supplied by the keyword CHARGE for the computation of the complex elementary stiffness matrix. 2.2.3 Use of the complex stiffness matrix The complex stiffness matrix K\ast can be used for the direct linear dynamic analysis (keyword MATR_RIGI) with the linear dynamic response operator DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03. In the case where the model to be taken into account for the harmonic analysis is of large size, it may be of interest to resort to model-reduction methods. An efficient approach for strongly dissipative models is available in the documentation U2.06.04. The search for eigenvalues can be done only with certain settings of the eigenvalue search operator CALC_MODES U4.52.02. The reference documentation R5.01.02 specifies the types of problems that one can treat and the possible settings. This search leads to complex eigenmodes, which therefore cannot be used for analyses in the time domain. Nevertheless, in the cases where the damping introduced remains weak, it is possible to compute the real modes associated with the associated non-dissipative model, and to assign to them the damping ratios computed by the complex-mode analysis in order to build a reduced model on a modal basis. This system can then be used to carry out a transient analysis in the modal space with DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03. 3 Viscoelastic damping model with internal variables The viscoelastic damping model with an internal variable can be used to treat the harmonic and transient responses of structures with viscoelastic materials. This model relies on the existence of a constitutive law making it possible to determine the stress state as a function of the history of the strains: \sigma ={E}_{\infty}\varepsilon (t)-{\int}_{0}^{t}{E}_{v}(t-\tau )\frac{\partial \varepsilon (\tau )}{\partial \xi }d\tau where {E}_{\infty} represents the high-frequency Young's modulus, and {E}_{v} the relaxation modulus. This modulus can be represented in the time domain by a Prony series {E}_{v}(t)={E}_{r}+{\sum}_{k=1}^{N}{E}_{k}\exp(-t/{\tau}_{k}) , or by a sum of first-order rational fractions in the frequency domain. {E}_{v}(s)={E}_{r}+{\sum}_{k=1}^{N}\frac{{\omega}_{k}{E}_{k}}{s+{\omega}_{k}} . In order to take these constitutive laws into account, one introduces internal variables which make it possible to build an equivalent linear model of order two, compatible with Code_Aster . These variables provide the link between the physical degrees of freedom affected by the presence of a viscoelastic material and the quantities (grandeurs) defining the constitutive behaviour. Thus, one introduces as many vectors {q}_{\mathrm{vk}} as there are internal parameters. These variables are governed by the time-evolution equations {\tau}_{k}\dot{{q}_{\mathrm{vk}}}+{q}_{\mathrm{vk}}-q=0 that is, in the frequency domain s{q}_{\mathrm{vk}}+{\omega}_{k}({q}_{\mathrm{vk}}-q)=0 One can illustrate the relations describing this constitutive behaviour by considering a mass–“spring” system for which the spring possesses a constitutive behaviour which can be represented by N internal variables: Figure 1: Representation of a “1 degree of freedom” system with internal states. The equilibrium equations for this system are written \lbrace \begin{array}{}\text{}M\ddot{q}+{K}_{0}q+{\sum}_{k=1}^{N}{K}_{k}(q-{q}_{\mathrm{vk}})=0\text{}\\ \text{}\\ \text{}{C}_{k}\dot{{q}_{\mathrm{vk}}}+{K}_{k}({q}_{\mathrm{vk}}-q)=0\text{}\forall k\in [1,N]\end{array} The dynamic system for this oscillator can therefore be put in the classical form of a model of order 2 \left[\begin{array}{cccc}M& 0& \text{...}& 0\\ 0& 0& \ddots & ⋮\\ ⋮& \ddots & 0& ⋮\\ 0& \mathrm{...}& \mathrm{...}& 0\end{array}\right]\ddot{\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}q\\ {q}_{\mathrm{v1}}\\ {q}_{\mathrm{vk}}\\ {q}_{\mathrm{vN}}\end{array}\right\rbrace }+\left[\begin{array}{cccc}0& 0& \text{...}& 0\\ 0& {C}_{1}& \ddots & ⋮\\ ⋮& \ddots & {C}_{k}& 0\\ 0& \mathrm{...}& 0& {C}_{N}\end{array}\right]\dot{\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}q\\ {q}_{\mathrm{v1}}\\ {q}_{\mathrm{vk}}\\ {q}_{\mathrm{vN}}\end{array}\right\rbrace }+\left[\begin{array}{cccc}{K}_{0}+{\sum}_{k=1}^{N}{K}_{k}& -{K}_{1}& -{K}_{k}& -{K}_{N}\\ -{K}_{1}& {K}_{1}& 0& 0\\ -{K}_{k}& 0& {K}_{k}& 0\\ -{K}_{N}& 0& 0& {K}_{n}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}q\\ {q}_{\mathrm{v1}}\\ {q}_{\mathrm{vk}}\\ {q}_{\mathrm{vN}}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}f\\ 0\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right\rbrace As it stands, Code_Aster does not make it possible to take such constitutive laws into account for linear dynamic analyses. The solution adopted to solve this problem consists in building a reduction basis adapted to the problem. This reduction basis is built around eigenmodes and the static responses of the structure to the viscoelastic forces generated by the modes. Under these conditions, one has [T]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{\Phi}_{l}& {\Phi}_{e}& {T}_{p}\\ {\Phi}_{\mathrm{lv1}}& 0& {T}_{\mathrm{v1}}\\ {\Phi}_{\mathrm{lvk}}& 0& {T}_{\mathrm{kv}}\\ {\Phi}_{\mathrm{lvN}}& 0& {T}_{\mathrm{vN}}\end{array}\right] The sub-matrices T are built from the static problem \left[\begin{array}{cccc}{K}_{0}+{\sum}_{k=1}^{N}{K}_{k}& -{K}_{1}& -{K}_{k}& -{K}_{N}\\ -{K}_{1}& {K}_{1}& 0& 0\\ -{K}_{k}& 0& {K}_{k}& 0\\ -{K}_{N}& 0& 0& {K}_{n}\end{array}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}{T}_{p}\\ {T}_{\mathrm{v1}}\\ {T}_{\mathrm{vk}}\\ {T}_{\mathrm{vN}}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}0\\ {F}_{\mathrm{v1}}\\ {F}_{\mathrm{vk}}\\ {F}_{\mathrm{vN}}\end{array}\right\rbrace with the loading defined by \left\lbrace \begin{array}{}0\\ {F}_{\mathrm{v1}}\\ {F}_{\mathrm{vk}}\\ {F}_{\mathrm{vN}}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left[\begin{array}{cccc}0& 0& \text{...}& 0\\ 0& {C}_{1}& \ddots & ⋮\\ ⋮& \ddots & {C}_{k}& 0\\ 0& \mathrm{...}& 0& {C}_{N}\end{array}\right]\dot{\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}\Phi \\ {\Phi}_{\mathrm{v1}}\\ {\Phi}_{\mathrm{vk}}\\ {\Phi}_{\mathrm{vN}}\end{array}\right\rbrace } One can then solve the problem projected onto the basis T , a problem which takes into account the overall viscoelastic constitutive behaviour defined for the materials. The details for the implementation of these techniques in Code_Aster are detailed in the documentation on the construction of reduced models for dynamics U2.06.04. This approach is for the moment reserved for experienced users, since model reduction in the presence of internal states can lead to singular behaviours. On the other hand, the method proposed for the reduction is not necessarily sufficient, and it is sometimes necessary to enrich the basis thus constructed in order to build a reasonable model. The search for eigenvalues can be done only with certain settings of the eigenvalue search operator CALC_MODES U4.52.02. The reference documentation R5.01.02 specifies the types of problems that one can treat and the possible settings. However, for the computation of the eigenmodes of the reduced model, it is recommended to use the full solver (METHODE='QZ') by searching for all the eigenvalues (OPTION='TOUT'), since otherwise it is not possible to access the real eigenvalues, representing the relaxation, which are important components of the constitutive behaviour of this type of material.

u2.06.04 User's guide for the construction of reduced models in dynamics u2.06.04 User's guide for the construction of reduced models in dynamics Summary: The models used for response analyses in linear dynamics are increasingly large. In order to improve analysis times significantly, it is possible to build a subspace of reduced dimension which makes it possible to project the complete problem, and thus to speed up the various response analyses. These reduced-component models can also be used in substructuring approaches, and in certain non-linear analyses (shocks, non-linear constitutive behaviour). A methodology is also proposed which makes it possible to “condense” the internal variables for a linear dynamic analysis. This manual sets out to help users in the construction of reduced models in dynamics and proposes a framework for assessing the quality of the reduced models built. One stresses the importance of the process of orthogonalisation of the projection bases (operator DEFI_BASE_MODALE , keyword ORTHO_BASE ) which makes it possible to eliminate vectors that are too collinear, coming from the concatenation of several families of vectors. A family containing nearly collinear vectors will lead, in the worst case, to singular projected matrices and to an ill-posed problem. 1 Introduction The size of the models used for response analyses in linear dynamics is increasingly large, and the requirements on the accuracy of the results lead one to carry out finer and more costly analyses. In order to improve significantly the analysis times of the responses of these systems to the various excitations, it is of interest to build a subspace of reduced dimension which makes it possible to project the complete problem, and thus to speed up the various response analyses. These reduced-component models can be used either alone, or in substructuring approaches, for linear analyses but also for certain non-linear analyses, such as the presence of shocks. This approach is also particularly of interest when one must take into account the internal dissipation devices specific to each structure. The method proposed for enriching an initial subspace, built on the basis of the eigenmodes of the system, relies on residual methods ([bib1]_, [bib2]_). This method makes it possible, from an approximate solution of the solution, to build vectors making it possible to improve the prediction for a given problem. This method, which is iterative, gives very good results with a limited number of iterations (in general, two iterations are enough). The first iteration is in general carried out by computing the terms classically called “static corrections”, or “static modes”. This point is developed in the first section of this document. This technique is particularly suited to model reduction in the presence of few external forces, even if they present a spatial distribution (fluctuating pressure, gravity, etc.). This approach also makes it possible to treat shock problems efficiently by adopting a penalisation method (provided that one is interested in the phenomena “far” from the shock zone). Important indications are also given in this part for controlling the quality of the reduced models built with this approach. In the second part, the particular cases of reduced models of Craig&Bampton or McNeal type, used for dynamic substructuring approaches, will be discussed. These two methods can be seen as the generalisation of the enrichments by static corrections. Techniques making it possible to limit the size of these models will also be presented, in particular for the representation of interface behaviours. In the third part, the concepts presented are extended to the cases of structures presenting internal forces such as in the damped cases. The viscous, hysteretic and viscoelastic damping models will mainly be discussed. The first two approaches are indeed those usually retained for studies in dynamics. The case of the damping associated with a viscoelastic constitutive law is of interest since this law introduces internal variables which are not present in the initial constitutive law of the material, but which can be taken into account by means of the reduction. The particular case of the Rayleigh damping model, used frequently for seismic analyses, is not presented, since in these particular cases the eigenmodes of the system also diagonalise the matrices associated with the dissipation, and the basis thus built does not require any particular enrichment, apart from those associated with the external forces. In the fourth part, with the aid of a study entered in the Code_Aster database (study no. 3185: Analysis of the complex modes of a sandwich plate including a viscoelastic material), the various techniques presented are shown. These examples also make it possible to present the implementation of the methods in Code_Aster . 2 Model reduction: principle of the static correction In this part, the principles of the model-reduction methods suited to the cases of non-dissipative structures are presented. These principles will then be extended to the cases of dissipative structures. One begins by recalling the relations of dynamics associated with the finite-element modelling of the structure. The eigenvalue problem that one wishes to solve is then introduced. The assumptions associated with model reduction are then introduced, and a method for building a basis generating a suitable subspace is then proposed. One is then interested in the optimum reduction of this basis, and in its subsequent enrichment from a method of iteration on the residuals. 2.1 Description and notation Let us consider the finite-element (F.E.) model of a linear structure, presenting internal dissipation mechanisms, subjected to external forces, which may equally well be known a priori (loadings) as having to be evaluated as one goes along (shock forces, contact, etc.). In the time domain, the equilibrium relation is written \left[{K}_{e}q(t)+{D}_{v}\dot{q}(t)+M\ddot{q}(t)\right]=Bu(t) where {K}_{e} is the stiffness matrix of the structure, {D}_{v} the matrix associated with the viscous dissipation, and M the mass matrix. One furthermore denotes by q the vector of the degrees of freedom. The external-force term is defined by the product of a force-localisation matrix B and of a vector u specifying the time evolution of the excitation. This writing makes it possible to separate the spatial and temporal components of a force often denoted f(t) . One will therefore have, in this case, f(t)=\mathit{Bu}(t) In the presence of shocks, one will for example be able to separate the terms linked to the loadings and those linked to the shocks: f(t)={B}_{\mathit{eff.}\mathit{ext.}}{u}_{\mathit{eff.}\mathit{ext.}}(t)+{B}_{\mathit{chocs}}{u}_{\mathit{chocs}}(t) {B}_{\mathit{chocs}} is the term which localises the shock degrees of freedom, and {u}_{\mathit{choc}}(t) determines the evolution of the force. In the simple case of a shock at the level of the degree of freedom {q}_{c} treated by penalisation, one will for example write - {u}_{\mathit{choc}}(t)=0 if there is no contact - {u}_{\mathit{choc}}(t)=k{q}_{c}(t) if there is contact Concerning damping, the two models classically considered in these problems are viscous damping and hysteretic damping. Viscoelastic damping is also introduced, which it is of interest to treat within the framework of model-reduction methods. Under these conditions, the equilibrium equation in the Laplace domain can be put in the form \left[\left({K}_{e}+j{K}_{h}+{K}_{v}(s)\right)+s{D}_{v}+{s}^{2}M\right]q(s)=Bu(s) {K}_{h} is the matrix representing the hysteretic constitutive behaviour, {K}_{v} the matrix representing the viscoelastic constitutive behaviour. For these two damping models, the modelling adopted is meaningful only in the Laplace domain. Hysteretic damping, as it is introduced, is not causal. Nevertheless, by removing this term, one recovers the standard equations associated with the viscous and viscoelastic problem, valid even for s=0 . 2.2 Model reduction and static correction The construction of a reduced model can be envisaged in order to solve problems of different natures, whether it is the computation of the time or harmonic response of a structure to an excitation by the use of a single reduced model, or the computation of eigenmodes and of eigenvalues by a substructuring approach (coupling of reduced models), or by dynamic condensation (reduction of all or part of a structure). The response-analysis problems are put in the form :eq: eq-1 or :eq: eq-4 according to whether one considers a time or harmonic loading. The associated eigenvalue problem, considering the various types of damping, is put in the form \left[({K}_{e}+j{K}_{h}+{K}_{v}({\lambda}_{0}))+{\lambda}_{0}{D}_{v}+{\lambda}_{0}^{2}M\right]\psi =0 where the {\lambda}_{0} are the complex eigenvalues, and \psi the complex modes. In the case of the non-dissipative model, the eigenmodes \phi and the natural angular frequencies {\omega}_{0} satisfy \left[{K}_{e}-{\omega}_{0}^{2}M\right]\phi =0 The tools making it possible to solve the complete problem, with the exception of the viscoelastic case, are available in Code_Aster , by means of the command CALC_MODES. However, the complex matrix {\mathrm{jK}}_{h} is symmetric, and non-Hermitian. Because of this, the algebraic properties of the matrices considered in the dissipative problem do not make it possible to implement the most efficient algorithms. For further details on the eigenvalue search algorithms, one may refer to [bib1]_, [bib4]_, [bib5]_. 2.3 Model-reduction assumption The solution of the problem on the basis of the complete model presented in relation :eq: eq-5 is therefore not envisageable for models of industrial size. In order to get round this difficulty, it is proposed to build a reduced model possessing the same spectral properties as the complete problem. One therefore postulates the existence of a reduction basis {T}_{r} which allows a reasonable representation of the behaviour of the structure over the frequency band of interest. Under these conditions, one therefore has q\approx {T}_{r}{q}_{r} The terms {q}_{r} of the linear combination correspond to the generalised amplitudes of the complete problem projected onto the basis {T}_{r} . These amplitudes therefore satisfy, in the general case: - for the time responses: \left[{T}_{r}^{T}{K}_{e}{T}_{r}\right]{q}_{r}(t)+\left[{T}_{r}^{T}{D}_{v}{T}_{r}\right]\dot{{q}_{r}}(t)+\left[{T}_{r}^{T}M{T}_{r}\right]\ddot{{q}_{r}}(t)={T}_{r}^{T}Bu(t) - for the harmonic responses: {T}_{r}^{T}\left[({K}_{e}+j{K}_{h}+{K}_{v}(s))+s{D}_{v}+{s}^{2}M\right]{T}_{r}{q}_{r}(s)={T}_{r}^{T}Bu(s) The problem thus reduced must retain the same spectral characteristics. It is therefore natural to build {T}_{r} on the basis of the eigenmodes {\phi }_{0} of the associated conservative system. However, the eigenmodes are sufficient to represent the response of the system correctly only if one considers a very large number of them. In practice, the computation of a large number of modes is unrealistic for industrial problems of large size. One must therefore enrich the projection basis in order to improve the representativeness of {T}_{r} . 2.4 Definition of the static correction In order to compute efficiently the response of a structure to an external excitation, one generally chooses to project the system onto a basis made up of the modes whose eigenfrequencies lie in the frequency band of interest of the problem. This band in general includes the modes of the lowest frequencies, but not necessarily. Now, in order to ensure a good representation of the response, it is often necessary to take into account a much larger number of modes than those present in the frequency band. Let us consider the conservative system associated with relation :eq: eq-6 . By decomposing the response of this system on the modal basis, one obtains, using abusively the notation \infty to designate the size of the problem, q(s)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}Bu(s)}{{s}^{2}+{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}} If one considers only the first N modes of the structure, one obtains an approximate truncated solution whose validity decreases very rapidly with the number of modes: q(s)\approx \sum_{k=1}^{N<\infty }\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}Bu(s)}{{s}^{2}+{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}} In order to limit the truncation effects, one chooses a number of modes sufficient to represent the dynamic behaviour, and one completes this mode basis by including the quasi-static effects of the modes truncated in the frequency band of interest. In general, one considers modes up to 1.5 times the maximum frequency of interest of the problem (semi-empirical rule known as “Hurty’s” [bib7]_). Under these conditions, the eigenfrequencies of the modes outside the band are higher than the maximum frequency of interest, and one then assumes {s}^{2}\ll {\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2} and one can therefore write, separating the terms of :eq: eq-10 according to whether they belong to the frequency band of interest q(s)\approx \sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}Bu(s)}{{s}^{2}+{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}}+\sum_{k=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}Bu(s)}{{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}} The reduction basis associated with this model is therefore composed of the first N eigenmodes, but also of the various quasi-static contributions {T}_{s} {T}_{s}=\sum_{k=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}B}{{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}} In order to compute {T}_{s} efficiently, one can write the static solution {q}_{s} of the problem for the whole of the loading B by using the spectral decomposition of {K}_{e}^{-1} 1 . It then follows that {q}_{s}=({K}_{e}^{-1})B=(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}}{{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}})B Under these conditions, one can rewrite relation () by using this static response, and one obtains q(s)\approx \sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}Bu(s)}{{s}^{2}+{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}}+{K}_{e}^{-1}Bu(s)-\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}Bu(s)}{{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}} That is q(s)\approx \sum_{k=1}^{N}\left[{\phi }_{k}(\frac{{\phi }_{k}^{T}}{{s}^{2}+{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}}-\frac{{\phi }_{k}^{T}}{{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}})Bu(s)\right]+{K}_{e}^{-1}Bu(s) According to relation :eq: eq-16 , one can therefore build an efficient projection basis for computing the response of the dynamic problem. This basis {T}_{r} is therefore built around the first N eigenmodes of the structure, and the static response of the structure to unit forces or to unit accelerations, applied in the same way as the forces for which one seeks the response (cf. u2.06.04-prise-compte-efforts-exterieurs-chocs-comportements-non-lineaires for the corresponding operators). One therefore has: {T}_{r}=\left[{\phi }_{1}\mathrm{...}{\phi }_{N}{K}_{e}^{-1}B\right] The projection basis thus built constitutes a very good subspace for the search for the dynamic response of the structure. On the other hand, for its practical use, it is recommended to orthogonalise the family of vectors obtained by relation :eq: eq-17 . NB: Inertial correction Of more modest interest, one can define, in an analogous way, a low-frequency correction, if the analysis band of interest does not include the first modes of the structure. Relation :eq: eq-10 can be decomposed in the following manner: q(s)\approx \sum_{k=1}^{M}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}Bu(s)}{{s}^{2}}+\sum_{k=M+1}^{N}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}Bu(s)}{{s}^{2}+{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}}+\sum_{k=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}Bu(s)}{{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}} The first term corresponds to the spectral decomposition of {M}^{-1} , and one can therefore enrich the projection basis according to the same principle, and build {T}_{r}=\left[{M}^{-1}B{\phi }_{1}\mathrm{...}{\phi }_{N}{K}_{e}^{-1}B\right] 2.5 Test cases illustrating the use of static corrections Many test cases of code_aster already use the principles of the static correction. One may furthermore note that this correction can be applied at different time instants in the study: - either it is integrated directly into the reduction basis, in accordance with the presentation which has just been given (static correction a priori ), - or it is superimposed after the analysis on the dynamic response of the structure on the basis of the eigenmodes alone (static correction a posteriori ). These two approaches are equivalent and of course supply the same results. One will choose one or the other for reasons of simplicity. One generally chooses the first approach for harmonic (or frequency) analyses, whereas the second is preferred in the case of transient (or time) response analyses. One may cite, among the test cases presenting the use of the static correction, the following studies, all relating to a seismic analysis: —Static correction a priori, by addition of static modes with an imposed force or with an imposed acceleration to the basis of the eigenmodes (constitution of a Ritz basis), or static correction a posteriori via the pseudo-mode (static mode with imposed acceleration) in a transient seismic analysis on a modal basis: - v2.01.103 SDLD103 – Transient seismic response of a 3-mass and 4-spring multi-supported system with static correction - v2.01.105 SDLD105 – Transient response of a mass-spring system to a single-support earthquake with static correction —Static correction a posteriori via the pseudo-mode (static mode with imposed acceleration) in a spectral seismic analysis: - v2.01.030 SDLD30 – Spectral seismic response of a 2-mass and 3-spring multi-supported system - v2.01.301 SDLD301 – Spectral seismic response of a 2-mass and 3-spring multi-supported system (correlated or uncorrelated excitations) - v2.02.023 SDLL23 – Clamped-free beam subjected to an earthquake (spectral response) - v2.02.112 SDLL112 – Seismic analysis of a multi-supported beam (spectral response) 2.6 Indications for the a posteriori control of the quality of the reduced model One of the principles making it possible to validate the quality of a reduced model consists in estimating, a posteriori, the deviation from equilibrium which may exist after the analysis. 2.6.1 General case for an analysis on a reduced model In order to characterise this deviation from equilibrium, one uses the principle of the force residual. This force residual {F}_{r} is computed - for the time responses: \left[{K}_{e}{T}_{r}\right]{q}_{r}(t)+\left[{D}_{v}{T}_{r}\right]\dot{{q}_{r}}(t)+\left[M{T}_{r}\right]\ddot{{q}_{r}}(t)-Bu(t)={F}_{r}(t) - for the harmonic responses: \left[({K}_{e}+j{K}_{h}+{K}_{v}(s))+s{D}_{v}+{s}^{2}M\right]{T}_{r}{q}_{r}(s)-Bu(s)={F}_{r}(s) One can also adopt the same procedure for the computation of the complex eigenmodes, detailed in u2.06.04-iterations-residus . If the solution obtained is exact, then the residual {F}_{r} is zero, by definition. Otherwise, one can build a measure of the deviation from equilibrium from the static response of the structure to this loading. One denotes by {R}_{r} the displacement residual associated with each complex mode computed. By definition, one has {K}_{e}{R}_{r}={F}_{r} A measure of the deviation from equilibrium is given by the elastic potential energy of the structure, that is {E}_{r}=\frac{1}{2}{∥{R}_{r}^{T}{K}_{e}{R}_{r}∥}^{2} 2.6.2 Particular case of the computation of the modes of a generalised model The same principle can be implemented, but in a slightly more precise way, so as to bring out particular deviations from the various equilibria. Indeed, in the case of an analysis by substructuring with the use of interface modes, it is important to be able to determine more precisely the origin of an inaccurate analysis. The sources of inaccuracy are: - the poor representation of the displacements at the interfaces, for each substructure, - the dynamic behaviour of the internal parts, for each substructure, - the differential displacements (separation) which may appear at the interfaces between the substructures. The command CALC_CORR_SSD u4.52.16 makes it possible, on the basis of the computations of the works associated with these various forces, to build correction terms making it possible to improve separately the interface behaviours, and the internal dynamic behaviours of each of the substructures. The details of this approach are given in the reference documentation on dynamic substructuring r4.06.02 One has {\phi }^{T}{K}_{e}\phi ={\Omega}^{2} . If {\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}\ne 0\forall k , then {({\phi }^{T}{K}_{e}\phi )}^{-1}={\Omega}^{-2} , whence {K}_{e}^{-1}=\phi {\Omega}^{-2}{\phi }^{T}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{{\phi }_{k}{\phi }_{k}^{T}}{{\omega}_{\mathrm{0k}}^{2}} . 3 Taking external forces, shocks and non-linear constitutive behaviours into account The first application of the reduction methods concerns the transient analysis of a structure in the presence of external forces, shocks or non-linear constitutive behaviours. The reduction basis suited to such an analysis is directly the one described in relation :eq: eq-17 . This basis therefore contains both eigenmodes and static deformed shapes (corrections). The family resulting from the concatenation of the two sub-families must then be orthogonalised (or orthonormalised) in order to define a basis. - The eigenmodes of interest are computed by the operator CALC_MODES u4.52.02. - The static-correction terms can be computed: - with MECA_STATIQUE u4.51.01, or with MACRO_ELAS_MULT u4.41.02, in the case of multiple loadings (several different excitations, shock nodes / directions, etc.); - or with MODE_STATIQUE u4.52.14, keywords PSEUDO_MODE (imposed acceleration) or FORCE_NODALE (imposed force). - These various families of vectors must then be concatenated. This operation is carried out by means of the command DEFI_BASE_MODALE u4.64.02, using the keyword “RITZ”. In the case of non-linear viscoelastic constitutive behaviour dis_visc or non-linear dis_ecro_trac, there is no finite element between the nodes concerned (only a constitutive relation). When computing the reduced modal basis, it may be judicious to define an element with an elastic stiffness corresponding to the tangent to the constitutive behaviour of the device r5.03.17. The family thus built can then be orthogonalised, either by the use of the keyword “ORTHO” in the same command DEFI_BASE_MODALE, or by the use of a new occurrence of the command DEFI_BASE_MODALE, with the use of the keyword “ORTHO_BASE”. Orthonormalisation can be obtained by normalisation of the orthogonal family, by use of the command NORM_MODE u4.52.11. The orthogonalisation process is above all important for eliminating vectors that are too collinear, coming from the concatenation of several families of vectors. A family containing nearly collinear vectors will lead, in the worst case, to singular projected matrices and to an ill-posed problem. An alternative to the use of DEFI_BASE_MODALE consists in projecting the mass and stiffness matrices of the problem onto the complete family of vectors, and in computing the modes of the problem thus reduced. The user then selects the vectors of interest in order to build the final projection basis. This approach, more complex to implement, makes it possible to adjust the projection basis to the analysis as well as possible, but is to be reserved for experienced users. NB: Note on the number of eigenmodes to be taken into account In the case of a problem with a known external loading, it is classically recommended to use a family of eigenmodes whose highest eigenfrequency is of the order of 1.5 to 2 times the frequency of interest of the analysis. If this frequency is not known a priori, it can be estimated on the basis of the Fourier transforms of the excitation carried out for example with CALC_FONCTION u4.32.04. On the other hand, in the case of a problem involving shocks, it is difficult to carry out a priori an estimate of the maximum frequency of interest. A classical rule consists in looking, for one and the same initial loading, at the evolution of the “shock times” (duration during which the structure is in contact with the obstacle). The convergence of the shock times generally indicates a good representativeness of the basis retained for the analysis. The use of static corrections for the computation of the response of a structure in the presence of shocks is illustrated in the test case SDNL301 v5.02.301 4 Model reduction for dynamic substructuring. When one wishes to solve a large-size problem in structural dynamics, one generally proceeds by decomposing the main structure into various substructures. One then builds a reduced model of each substructure, on the basis of its eigenmodes. These reduced models are then assembled, in order to build a global reduced model of the complete structure. A few elements on the construction of bases suited to the solution of the problem by dynamic substructuring are recalled in this section. The complete presentations of these approaches, including in particular the aspects of implementation in code_aster, are available in the documents r4.06.02 (classical dynamic substructuring) and r4.06.03 (cyclic dynamic substructuring). One may also refer to the references [bib6]_ to [bib9]_. 4.1 Classical methods: Craig&Bampton and MacNeal&Rubin. In the same way as for the reduction of a single model, the reduction for dynamic substructuring must take two aspects into account: - retaining the spectral properties of the problem in the frequency band of interest; - correctly taking into account the quasi-static effects of the external forces applied to each substructure. The first constraint is satisfied by choosing a number of modes sufficient for the substructure considered, so that the Hurty criterion is verified. The second constraint is verified by considering that the external forces applied to a given substructure are: - real external forces, applied in the interior of the domain of the substructure considered, - the forces applied to the substructure of interest by the adjacent substructures. The two reduction bases classically retained for the construction of a reduced model for substructuring are the bases known as “Craig&Bampton”, and “MacNeal&Rubin” (see [bib8]_ for more details on the formulations). The basis of “Craig&Bampton” type is built from: - the eigenmodes of the substructure, clamped at the interfaces with the adjacent substructures, - the static liftings of the substructure for unit displacements imposed successively on the degrees of freedom of the interfaces with the adjacent substructures, - any inertial unloading modes, if the complete structure possesses rigid-body modes, or may be subjected to large interface accelerations (the case of an earthquake, for example), The basis of “MacNeal&Rubin” type is built from: - the eigenmodes of the substructure, free at the interfaces with the adjacent substructures, - the rigid-body modes, if the substructure is free when the interfaces with the other substructures are left free. - the static displacements of the substructure for unit forces imposed successively on the degrees of freedom of the interfaces with the adjacent substructures. In the case where the substructure presents rigid-body modes, one must regularise the computation of the static displacements, by a technique of shifting the spectrum by addition of mass to the stiffness matrix, or of computation of the self-equilibrated loads (see [bib6]_, for example) To fix the ideas, by partitioning the mass and stiffness matrices as a function of the interface degrees of freedom (indexed i ), and of the complementary degrees of freedom (indexed c), the complete reduction basis for “Craig&Bampton” is given by T_{C\&B} = \left[\begin{array}{ccc} \phi_{\mathrm{cF}} & -K_{\mathrm{cc}}^{-1}K_{\mathrm{ci}} & K_{\mathrm{cc}}^{-1}M_{\mathrm{cc}}\phi_{\mathrm{cR}} \\ 0 & I_{d} & 0 \end{array}\right] and the “MacNeal&Rubin” basis by T_{\mathrm{Mc\&R}} = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc} \phi_{\mathrm{cR}} & \phi_{\mathrm{cL}} & q_{\mathrm{cS}} \\ \phi_{\mathrm{iR}} & \phi_{\mathrm{iL}} & q_{\mathrm{iS}} \end{array} \right] The last vectors correspond to the computation of the displacement response of the structure to unit loadings imposed at the interface (in the absence of rigid-body modes for the substructure) \left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{\mathrm{cc}}& {K}_{\mathrm{ci}}\\ {K}_{\mathrm{ic}}& {K}_{ii}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}{q}_{\mathrm{cS}}\\ {q}_{\mathrm{iS}}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ {I}_{d}\end{array}\right] {\phi }_{\mathrm{cF}} are the modes of the structure with fixed interfaces, {\phi }_{L} the free modes and {\phi }_{R} the rigid-body modes of the substructure free at the interfaces. These two approaches are directly available in Code_Aster by combining the results of the dedicated operators: - DEFI_BASE_MODALE u4.64.02 - DEFI_INTERF_DYNA u4.64.01 - DEFI_BASE_MODALE u4.64.02 - MACR_ELEM_DYNA u4.65.01 - DEFI_MODELE_GENE u4.65.02 4.2 Use of interface modes. Nevertheless, in the case of a component presenting extended interfaces, the models thus reduced remain of large size. Furthermore, the projection of the mass and stiffness matrices onto these projection bases causes the sparse character of the original assembled matrices to be lost. Under these conditions, it is not always of interest to build a reduced model, as for the computation of a harmonic response, for example. On the other hand, when the number of analyses carried out around the model increases, the reduction becomes of interest, especially when one can further reduce the size of the problem. Indeed, if one remains within the framework of low-frequency dynamics, the whole set of constraint modes (or attachment modes) is not necessary in order to represent the dynamics of the problem. The wavelength of the phenomena which must pass across the interface is limited by that of the phenomena which one can find in the domains. One can therefore operate a judicious selection among the constraint modes (or attachment modes). Methods for the construction of these modes, called here “interface modes”, have been proposed in particular by Craig & Chang (see [bib10]_) for the substructuring approach, then by Bourquin and D’Hennezel (see [bib11]_) with a view to domain decomposition. The method proposed by Craig & Chang has the advantage of simplicity, and has been retained for the construction of the reduced models in code_aster with the operator DEFI_MODELE_GENE u4.65.02 (OPTION = ’REDUIT’). This method simply consists in projecting the mass and stiffness matrices of the substructure model onto the basis of the constraint modes (or attachment modes) and in solving the associated eigenvalue problem: {T}^{T}(K-{\omega}_{r}^{2}M)T{\phi }_{r}=0 with T=\left[\begin{array}{c}-{K}_{\mathrm{cc}}^{-1}{K}_{\mathrm{ci}}\\ {I}_{d}\end{array}\right] The interface modes {\phi }_{r} are classified with respect to their natural angular frequencies, and a truncation is carried out in order to select only the lowest-frequency components. The constraint modes (or attachment modes) are then advantageously replaced by the vectors T{\phi }_{r} in the projection basis. The gain is achieved both on the size of the matrix (which can be appreciably reduced if the interface is of large size), and on its topology, since, by construction, the projection of the mass and stiffness matrices of the system onto this new basis leads to diagonal matrices.
