In Table 4, the various possible modelling strategies are summarised. In order to choose the constitutive model suited to our problem, it is necessary to answer the following questions: - what is the maximum loading level that one wants to apply to the structure (damage level) and what is the robustness of the constitutive model of the concrete? - low damage: little risk of non-convergence; - high damage: risks of non-convergence becoming high; - which mechanical phenomena does one want to represent? - damage of the concrete (tension / compression); - damage of the concrete and plasticity of the steels and of the concrete. The advantages and disadvantages associated with each type of constitutive model are presented below. These questions are answered for each type of model. 4.5.2 Model ENDO_ISOT_BETON Advantages: - it is a simple 3D constitutive model of concrete, - the identification of the parameters is immediate. Disadvantages: - one represents the damage of the concrete in tension only, - one finds significant non-convergence problems when the damage becomes high. Note The model ENDO_ISOT_BETON used in plane stress via the Deborst method for multilayer shells is in principle more robust than its three-dimensional version. In practice, however, one observes convergence problems when the damage becomes too high in the structure. 4.5.3 Model ENDO_ORTH_BETON Advantages: - it is a 3D model making it possible to represent finely the damage of the concrete in tension and in compression. Disadvantages: - one finds significant non-convergence problems when the damage becomes high, - the determination of the parameters requires a relatively complex preliminary calibration. Note The model ENDO_ORTH_BETON used in plane stress via the Deborst method for multilayer shells is in principle more robust than its three-dimensional version. In practice, however, one observes convergence problems when the damage becomes too high in the structure. 4.5.4 Model MAZARS_UNIL R7.01.08 Advantages: - In 1D (used with the multifibre beams R5.03.09): ◦ as the model is written in 1D, the non-convergence problems are reduced in an important manner; ◦ it makes it possible to represent finely the mechanical phenomena in the longitudinal direction (tension–compression and bending); the model is capable of accounting for the phenomenon of closure of the cracks. - In 2D, 3D, C_PLAN: ◦ makes it possible to represent the shear phenomena, and makes it possible to translate the phenomenon of closure of the cracks (restoration of stiffness). 4.5.5 Model GLRC_DM R7.01.32 Number of parameters: steel: 3, concrete: 8, geometry: 5, method: 2. But these parameters are supplied in Code_Aster from "engineer" data and from assumptions on the post-elastic strain range. Advantages: - the softening behaviour of the concrete is no longer modelled. As a result, one avoids most of the non-convergence problems; - likewise, as one homogenises the behaviour of the concrete and of the steel, one avoids the localisation problems; - the model GLRC_DM + plasticity makes it possible to model the residual strains (in membrane only). Disadvantages: - the identification of the parameters requires a recalibration exercise by comparison with a more accurate model of ENDO_ISOT_BETON type. - Steel reinforcement layers necessarily identical in x–y, upper–lower. - no bending–membrane coupling 4.5.6 Model DHRC R7.01.37 Number of parameters: steel: 3, concrete: 10, steel–concrete slip: 1, geometry: 11. Advantages: - Arbitrary steel reinforcement layers, - Native anisotropy, - Steel–concrete slip consecutive to damage, hence a contribution to the dissipation and modelling of the "tension-stiffening effect" phenomenon, - native bending–membrane coupling - Tool for automated identification by numerical FE homogenisation of parameters in Salomé_Méca from "engineer" data. Disadvantages: - CPU: more costly than GLRC_DM: 30 to 100%, - avenues for improvement are expected on the tests for characterising the steel–concrete connection: at this stage of the state of the art, this restriction weakens the predictive capability of this modelling; - Industrialisation and validation on representative structures (experimental campaigns) still to be completed. Table 4 : summary of the choice of the modelling and of the associated constitutive model. 5 Data setup of the problem 5.1 Mesh 5.1.1 General advice The discretisation of the mesh must be suited to the wavelength of the phenomena that one wishes to represent. A cut-off frequency and therefore an element size can be established by means of a prior modal analysis of the structure. In many studies, the non-linear analyses are carried out following a linear study. In this case it is necessary to adapt the linear mesh by refining the zones that become non-linear, and also the zones where high levels of bending moment are liable to occur. In order to remesh, one may use the software HOMARD by means of the macro-command MACR_ADAP_MAIL U7.03.01. It is in particular possible to remesh part of a mesh by simply indicating the mesh-cell group that one wants to refine. It is strongly advised to carry out a study of the sensitivity of the results to the mesh. In practice, it is advised, when creating the mesh, to provide for several mesh refinements. 5.1.2 Local solid modelling and multilayer shell It is advised to make the steel and concrete nodes coincide in order to reduce the size of the problem. The elements BARRE, GRILLE_MEMBRANE or GRILLE_EXCENTRE representing the reinforcement bars must have their nodes coincident with those of the solid or shell elements of the concrete (cf. § 3.2.3 and 3.3.3). Concerning the modelling of the connections, one should refer to § 3.6. 5.2 Initial conditions The preloading of the reinforced-concrete structure (self-weight and other static loadings…) is necessary in the case of the use of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE. It is done by means of the operator STAT_NON_LINE by imposing only the loading due to the self-weight and to the other loadings. The dynamic loading is applied in continuation of the static self-weight analysis, while retaining this latter loading. Furthermore, one may possibly take into account the construction sequence of the structure. Taking this sequence into account makes it possible to simulate a pre-cracking appearing during construction. Moreover it may be necessary, even in linear elasticity, in order to represent a state of non-zero initial stresses in the structure (obtained during construction by modification of the static redundancies). These methods are currently little used for the analysis of civil-engineering works. It is nevertheless recommended to make use of the work carried out on the problem of excavation U2.04.06 and of the layered construction of an embankment (U2.04.07). 5.3 Boundary conditions The boundary conditions are to be defined in the classical manner, as in any study. The seismic analysis of a civil-engineering work resting on a flexible foundation may nevertheless require the soil–structure interaction (ISS) to be taken into account. One should refer to U2.06.07 for the description of the methods for taking the ISS into account. One may in particular represent the ISS by means of foundation impedances recalibrated about a linear behaviour of the structure founded on the soil. 5.4 Seismic loading This paragraph takes up the elements detailed in U2.06.09. It is recalled that the structure is said to be single-supported if all the supports on which the structure rests are subjected to the same excitation. The structure is said to be multi-supported if there exist at least two supports that are not subjected to an identical seismic excitation. 5.4.1 Single support In this case, there are no stresses induced by the differential displacements of the anchorages. One therefore uses a relative-displacement approach and one applies either the accelerogram (case 1) or the displacement (case 2) to the structure (operator CALC_CHAR_SEISME, U4.63.01). 1st case One has the seismic signal a(t), acceleration as a function of time in the three directions X , Y and Z – Use of CALC_CHAR_SEISME. The construction of the "loading" concept used by AFFE_CHAR_MECA proceeds as follows: - assembly of the assembled mass matrix {M}_{\mathrm{ass}} : operator ASSEMBLAGE; - construction of the assembled vectors ( {V}_{{\mathrm{ass}}_{X}} , {V}_{{\mathrm{ass}}_{Y}} and {V}_{{\mathrm{ass}}_{Z}} ), serving as the basis of the loading (1 per direction of the earthquake): operator CALC_CHAR_SEISME with the keyword MONO_APPUI =’OUI’; - construction of the "loading" concept (1 per direction of the earthquake): operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA with the keyword VECT_ASSE. This case is the most common in studies of civil-engineering works under earthquake loading. 2nd case One has the seismic signal d(t) , displacement as a function of time in the three directions X , Y and Z . The construction of the "loading" concept used by AFFE_CHAR_MECA is immediate: operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA with the keyword DDL_IMPO. 5.4.2 Multi-support In this case, the differential displacements of the anchorages induce secondary stresses. It is no longer possible to use a relative-displacement approach. One must therefore carry out the solution in the absolute frame. The loading must be imposed in the form of displacements at the anchorages of the structure. Relative to the single-support analysis, the 1st method proposed is no longer suited. The use of CALC_CHAR_SEISME in multi-support and in transient non-linear analysis (DYNA_NON_LINE) supplies results whose validity is not guaranteed, because CALC_CHAR_SEISME operates by elastostatic recovery (static modes). 1st case One has the seismic signal a(t) , acceleration as a function of time in the three directions X , Y and Z – Use of the Fourier transforms. It is necessary to construct d(t) , displacement as a function of time, from a(t) . The method proposed consists in using the Fourier transforms in order to integrate the signal: - computation of the acceleration a(\omega ) as a function of the angular frequency: carrying out a Fourier transform of a(t) in each direction; - computation of the displacement d(\omega ) as a function of the angular frequency: multiplication of a(\omega ) by {\omega}^{2} ; - computation of the displacement d(t) as a function of time: carrying out an inverse Fourier transform of d(\omega ) ; - construction of the "loading" concept used by AFFE_CHAR_MECA: operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA with the keyword DDL_IMPO. Note One should refer to [14] for the precautions to be taken in carrying out the Fourier transforms: checking of the causality principle (return to zero of the signal in order to perform the FFT) and absence of drift of the displacements. 2nd case: One has the seismic signal d(t) , displacement as a function of time in the three directions X , Y and Z . The construction of the "load" concept used by AFFE_CHAR_MECA is immediate: operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA with the keyword DDL_IMPO. 5.4.3 General precautions on the time signal The time evolution as a function of time a(t) or d(t) used as input to the analysis must be as regular as possible. The time step that defines the sampling must therefore be sufficiently fine. If one calls {f}_{\max} the maximum frequency of the spectrum of the signal, one must have a sampling frequency at least 5 to 10 times greater than {f}_{\max} . Initially, the structure being considered as subjected only to the permanent loadings (weight, ...), it is better to have a displacement, a velocity and an acceleration induced by the earthquake imposed as zero at the supports. If one does not respect these conditions, one risks observing initial oscillations of the response. In practice, in order to respect this, it is sufficient that the seismic signal imposed at the supports in displacement be zero over at least the first two time steps. It will therefore be appropriate to add manually zero values at the beginning of the loading files. At the end of the analysis, it is recommended also to return to imposed zero displacement conditions over a certain period. This makes it possible to ensure the return to rest of the structure. This is indispensable (causality condition) if one wants to carry out a correct spectral analysis by FFT of the responses. Note The ASN guide [15] recommends using a set of N accelerograms ( N=5 minimum) representative of the design seismic motion for the design of civil-engineering works. One therefore carries out N non-linear transient analyses in order to analyse the variability of the results as a function of the accelerograms used. One defines the quantity to be retained for the design as a function of the number of accelerograms used, of the mean and of the standard deviation of the absolute values of the results (one uses for this a confidence-interval estimator of Student–Fisher type, [15] , of the type mean of the non-linear transient responses + k.sigma, with k depending on the number N of realisations (5, 10…).). Certain quantities of interest are more sensitive than others to the variabilities; moreover the non-linearities may be localised and large parts of the structure may remain in the linear regime. One notes that within the linear framework, the ASN guide [15] recommends using a simple average of the transient responses. 5.5 Damping 5.5.1 Definition It is recommended to use Rayleigh damping R5.05.04 and R5.05.05 in the direct transient solution by means of DYNA_NON_LINE. The elementary damping matrix {C}_{\mathrm{elem}} is expressed as a linear combination of the elementary mass matrices {M}_{\mathrm{elem}} and stiffness matrices {K}_{\mathrm{elem}} : {C}_{\mathrm{elem}}=\alpha {K}_{\mathrm{elem}}+\beta {M}_{\mathrm{elem}} with \alpha and \beta the Rayleigh coefficients. The part \beta {M}_{\mathrm{elem}} corresponds to the low-frequency damping and the part \alpha {K}_{\mathrm{elem}} to the high-frequency damping (Figure 5.5.1-a). The damping ratio {\zeta}_{n} for the nth mode of the system considered is defined by: {\zeta}_{n}=\frac{\alpha {\omega}_{n}}{2}+\frac{\beta}{2{\omega}_{n}} with the angular frequency {\omega}_{n} associated with the nth mode. This Rayleigh damping is calibrated on two modes and damping ratios ({\omega}_{1,}{\zeta}_{1}) and ({\omega}_{2,}{\zeta}_{2}) relevant for the analysis of the structure studied. When one knows the values of the dampings for these two frequencies, one can compute \alpha and \beta : \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}\alpha & =& 2\frac{{\omega}_{1}}{{\omega}_{1}^{2}-{\omega}_{2}^{2}}{\zeta}_{1}-2\frac{{\omega}_{2}}{{\omega}_{1}^{2}-{\omega}_{2}^{2}}{\zeta}_{2}\\ \beta & =& 2\frac{{\omega}_{1}{\omega}_{2}^{2}}{{\omega}_{2}^{2}-{\omega}_{1}^{2}}{\zeta}_{1}-2\frac{{\omega}_{1}^{2}{\omega}_{2}}{{\omega}_{2}^{2}-{\omega}_{1}^{2}}{\zeta}_{2}\end{array} In practice, one often considers the case where the two dampings are equal {\zeta}_{1}={\zeta}_{2}=\zeta , and one then obtains the formulae to be used for the computation of \alpha and \beta : \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}\alpha & =& \frac{2}{{\omega}_{1}+{\omega}_{2}}\zeta \\ \beta & =& 2\frac{{\omega}_{1}{\omega}_{2}}{{\omega}_{1}+{\omega}_{2}}\zeta \end{array} It is then appropriate to enter the values \alpha and \beta by means of the command DEFI_MATERIAU, keywords AMOR_ALPHA/AMOR_BETA. Figure 5.5.1-a presents the graphical description of Rayleigh damping for two frequencies ({f}_{1,}\zeta ) and ({f}_{2,}\zeta ) between which the damping is relatively uniform. | | | --- | | Figure 5.5.1-a : description of Rayleigh damping. | 5.5.2 Non-linear case For the computation of {C}_{\mathrm{elem}} , one takes the stiffness matrix used in Newton's method (RIGI_MECA). If one uses the updated tangent matrix {K}_{\mathrm{elem}}^{\tan} in DYNA_NON_LINE (NEWTON=_F(MATRICE='TANGENTE', REAC_ITER=1,),), the damping matrix is then defined by: {C}_{\mathrm{elem}}=\alpha {K}_{\mathrm{elem}}^{\tan}+\beta {M}_{\mathrm{elem}} The damping matrix C then does not remain constant during the analysis. Indeed, when the structure becomes strongly damaged, {K}^{\tan} decreases and may even become negative. As a result, the interpretation of the effect of proportional damping in the non-linear regime is delicate (variation of the dissipation introduced over time). The user sets the damping parameters over the range in which the structure is elastic. 5.5.3 Other advice in the non-linear regime In the non-linear regime, part of the dissipative phenomena are modelled by means of the non-linear constitutive models of concrete and of steel. However, other dissipative phenomena are not modelled by the constitutive behaviours of the materials, which nevertheless dissipate the energy supplied by the excitation throughout the transient and at every material point. One therefore introduces, as in a linear elastic analysis, a conventional viscous damping matrix in the analysis in order to represent these phenomena, cf. [33]. One may choose with Code_Aster a damping matrix of Rayleigh type or a modal damping matrix, cf. u2.06.03. It is recommended to use a maximum damping value of 2% on the first mode, and of 5% at most for the cut-off frequency, in order to comply with the prescriptions of the ASN guide [15]). This value is much lower than that of 5 to 7% used in the linear regime for design analyses. It leads in general to overestimating the peaks of the floor spectra, including when the loading exceeds the design earthquake several times over, cf. [18]. It should be noted that in multi-support (cf. 5.4.2) the solution of the problem is carried out in the absolute frame ( {U}_{\mathrm{absolu}}={U}_{\mathrm{relatif}}+{U}_{\mathrm{entraînement}} ). In this case, it is indispensable not to introduce damping on the part corresponding to the entrainment velocity. The damping matrix must be taken proportional to the stiffness matrix only ( {C}_{\mathrm{elem}}=\alpha {K}_{\mathrm{elem}} in the method recommended by the ASN [15]). The choice of the modal damping matrix, by specifying a zero damping value on the rigid modes, is also suitable. Another possibility consists in clamping one of the supports and in describing the motion of the other supports relative to it (this amounts to cancelling the entrainment motion). In this case, one may use a classical Rayleigh damping. For the discrete elements DIS_T or DIS_TR U3.11.02, one defines directly the damping matrix for each degree of freedom in AFFE_CARA_ELEM (keyword DISCRET U4.42.01). This remark is important in the case where one models added masses by means of discrete elements. It is then indispensable to associate a damping matrix with them, otherwise these added masses are not damped. It is important to produce the balance of the energies during the transient over the whole of the system: by means of the keyword ENERGIE of DYNA_NON_LINE. This makes it possible to check the distribution of the kinetic energy, of the strain energy, of that supplied to the structure by the loading at each time instant, of that dissipated in viscous form, of that (called hysteretic) dissipated by the non-linear constitutive models. The remainder of the balance is to be assigned to the time-integration scheme, if the latter is dissipative. When one uses an explicit time-integration scheme (DIFF_CENT or TCHAMWA), it is imperative to use a damping proportional to the mass matrix only. The use of a complete Rayleigh damping leads to a drop in the stability time step and therefore to a very significant increase in the computation time. 6 Analyses prior to the non-linear transient dynamic analysis Before carrying out the non-linear transient analysis, it is advised to proceed step by step by increasing the "difficulties". This makes it possible to validate independently the various elements of the modelling. 6.1 Analysis of the mass It is advised, after having carried out the finite-element modelling, to compute the mass of the structure in order to ensure that the geometric and material characteristics (densities) are correct. This is all the more important as the structure is complex and as the number of different materials is high. One uses the operator POST_ELEM U4.81.22 and the keyword MASSE_INER. 6.2 Modal analysis It is recommended, before carrying out a transient analysis, to carry out a modal analysis of the structure. This makes it possible to check the quality of the modelling (global stiffness, boundary conditions). If, moreover, one has the first natural frequencies measured experimentally, one will be able to compare the finite-element modelling with the real structure and possibly recalibrate the finite-element modelling. The computation of the eigenmodes of a structure is not detailed in this document. For this, one should refer among others to U4.52.02 (operator CALC_MODES). It is nevertheless recalled that, for the seismic analysis of a linear structure, one must at least retain all the modes whose natural frequencies are lower than the cut-off frequency of the seismic spectrum (generally of the order of 33\mathrm{Hz} , beyond which there is no significant dynamic amplification). In practice, one often contents oneself with retaining only the modes that contribute significantly to the response. One then retains only the modes whose unit effective mass in one direction is greater than 1‰. A second selection criterion consists in also ensuring that, for all of these retained modes, the cumulative unit effective mass in each direction is little different from the total mass of the structure. An acceptability threshold of 95% is commonly accepted for the spectral method; a threshold of 90% is indicated for the transient method. If this second criterion is not satisfied with the modes lower than 33\mathit{Hz} , one extends the modal basis beyond this frequency until this threshold is reached. The sum of the effective modal masses is in fact equal to the total mass that works on the modal basis chosen. In other words, this total working mass is equal to the total mass minus the mass contributions that are carried by clamped degrees of freedom (which therefore do not work on the modal basis). Thus, for example, on a single-degree-of-freedom mass–spring system with a mass {M}_{1} at the top and another mass {M}_{2} at the level of the raft, the working mass will be equal to {M}_{1} and the total mass to {M}_{1}+{M}_{2} . Consequently, the unit effective modal mass for the single mode of the system will be equal to . The total cumulative value will therefore have the same value and, depending on the ratio of {M}_{1} and {M}_{2} , one will therefore not necessarily be able to reach 90% of the total mass {M}_{1}+{M}_{2} , even by considering all the modes (one has only a single mode in this example). In practice, the finer and more realistic the FE model is, the smaller the difference between the working mass and the total mass will be. One must therefore pay attention to the particular cases where a non-negligible part of the mass is concentrated in this zone of blocked degrees of freedom. Indeed, if this is the case, the dynamic modes computed will never make this zone work and therefore the cumulative effective modal mass will never be able to reach 100% of the total mass (which takes into account the mass at the level of the blocked degrees of freedom). One will therefore tend to take too many modes, which is conservative, but at the expense of the CPU time. In order to control this, one must compute the total mass excluding the blocked degrees of freedom: one can do this with POST_ELEM by specifying a GROUP_MA that would contain the whole building except the blocked surface. Then, it will suffice to apply a rule of three between the cumulative effective mass and the ratio between the total mass and the total mass on the blocked degrees of freedom. Example: \text{Cumul\_corrigé\_unitaire}=\text{Cumul\_unitaire}\times \text{Mtot / Mtot\_sans\_DDL\_bloqués} With meshes of solid elements, the underestimation of the cumulative value is small and will decrease as one refines further. With surface meshes of a raft or, worse, with a point mass at the raft, the underestimation may become significant. In the field of reinforced-concrete structures, one generally finds that the modellings have a global stiffness higher than that measured experimentally. The first natural frequency computed may overestimate the measured frequency by more than 20%. Various phenomena may be put forward in order to explain this difference: - boundary conditions (clamping on the shaking table for a mock-up), the soil–structure interaction (interface dynamic stiffness) and connections (slab–wall built-in connection) that are imperfect under the experimental conditions; - a significant heterogeneity of the concrete material and a possible debonding between the reinforcement bars and the concrete under the experimental conditions, leading to variations of Young's modulus in the structure; - initial geometric imperfections. In order to recalibrate the natural frequencies, several methods are generally used: - the reduction of Young's modulus of the concrete (the reduction relative to the experimental value of Young's modulus possibly reaching more than 20%). This artificial recalibration leads to a decrease in all of the following natural frequencies. The following modes are therefore poorly represented by the modelling; - the modification of the boundary conditions. Taking into account non-perfect clampings between the structure and the support frame or between the various structural elements (wall–floor connection, for example). These more or less conventional modifications are not very satisfactory. The impossibility of modelling properly the eigenmodes of a reinforced-concrete structure has important consequences for the ability of a numerical seismic simulation to predict design margins. 6.3 Linear elastic transient dynamic analysis It is recommended, before carrying out a non-linear transient analysis, to carry out a linear elastic transient analysis. For this, it is sufficient, starting from the command file of the non-linear transient analysis DYNA_NON_LINE, to define elastic materials: COMPORTEMENT (RELATION = ’ELAS’). This makes it possible to see, for example, whether the damping introduced is indeed taken into account for all the finite elements of the modelling. 6.4 Other analyses 6.4.1 Push-over analysis (monotonic non-linear quasi-static) This consists in applying to the structure a monotonically increasing displacement in order to load it in a manner equivalent to a seismic loading (push-over or progressive pushover). This loading corresponds to a distributed inertia force, corresponding to the mass distribution of a chosen vibratory mode, often the fundamental mode. One may also choose to take, in place of this mode, the static solution under the action of a uniform entrainment acceleration in the structure, in the direction of the seismic motion. One loads the structure until the creation of the cracks and the plastification of the reinforcement bars which, at the extreme, may lead to the ruin of the structure. This loading case constitutes a sort of envelope curve of the cyclic static non-linear response (Figure 6.4.2-a). The main advantage of this analysis is to analyse the behaviour of the structure for high levels of non-linearity (damage), which makes it possible to apprehend a certain redistribution of the forces, the ductility of the structure – its capacity to dissipate mechanical energy. One may also highlight possible convergence problems in the concrete constitutive model used. The computational effort is therefore much smaller than for a true non-linear transient dynamic analysis. This analysis requires, on the other hand, that one be able to define a relevant push-over type loading. Moreover, its implementation may be costly in time. Once the non-linear static analysis has been carried out, one represents on a diagram the dependence of a characteristic displacement at a given control point (for example the displacement of the centre of gravity of the roof of the building) as a function of a characteristic force (for example the global shear force at the base), in the direction of the earthquake. One then considers this response as being that of an equivalent non-linear single-degree-of-freedom oscillator. One first converts the characteristic displacement into a spectral displacement for the mode considered at the given control point. Then one converts the global force at the base into a spectral pseudo-acceleration, by means of the effective modal mass of the chosen mode. This conversion of the capacity curve produces a capacity spectrum , which one often agrees to smooth in the form of perfect elastoplasticity, with a plateau. One may therefore then compare this capacity spectrum with the response spectrum of the seismic signal, represented in the form of a demand curve in the form of a pseudo-acceleration–displacement diagram obtained from the seismic response spectrum. The response spectrum is plotted for a value of reduced damping compatible with the strain level reached in the non-linear regime. The comparison then makes it possible to determine the performance point of the structure studied by intersections of the capacity and demand curves, for the value of the reference angular frequency at this performance point; the latter is thus established in an iterative manner. Of course this method, which assumes that the mode studied is predominant, completely neglects the combination due to the coupling of the dynamic modes of the structure, their variation during the damage, the effects of cycling and of unloading… Moreover, the result of this method depends on the choice of the control point in the structure, which affects the capacity spectrum. There exists no criterion making it possible to estimate the error committed by this simplified method. 6.4.2 Cyclic static analysis One may carry out a cyclic static non-linear analysis by applying at the supports of the structure the imposed displacement coming from the seismic signal (Figure 6.4.2-a). The main advantage of this analysis is to analyse the behaviour of the structure for levels of non-linearity (damage) close to those encountered within the framework of the non-linear dynamic analysis, and to highlight possible convergence problems in the concrete models used. This analysis requires that one have this time evolution in displacement (cf. § 5.4). Moreover, its implementation may be costly in time. | | | --- | Figure 6.4.2-a : monotonic non-linear static response (push-over) and cyclic non-linear static response. 7 Solution of the non-linear transient dynamic analysis 7.1 Introduction In this chapter, one places oneself within the framework of an analysis in small perturbations, without impact. The only non-linearities are of material origin. This corresponds to the most frequent civil-engineering studies. One could nevertheless model geometric non-linearities (large displacements, large strains) or frictional contact. All of the keywords cited in this chapter are attached to the operator DYNA_NON_LINE. One should refer to U4.53.01 and U4.51.03 for more details. 7.2 Help with the convergence of the analysis 7.2.1 Time evolution of the loading The command DEFI_LIST_INST makes it possible to carry out an automatic subdivision of the time step when Newton's algorithm does not converge. Furthermore, it is recalled that it is necessary, for a given analysis, to test several time steps in order to analyse the stability of the results as a function of the time step chosen (cf. § 2.3). 7.2.2 Convergence criteria The keyword CONVERGENCE makes it possible to define the value of the relative residual on the equilibrium (RESI_GLOB_RELA). By default, this is {10}^{-6} . In order to facilitate the convergence of the analysis, one may relax this convergence criterion. One must nevertheless do so with caution, the use of too large a convergence criterion being liable to lead to results far from the real solution. It is advised not to use a RESI_GLOB_RELA greater than {10}^{-4} . There furthermore exists an absolute residual on the equilibrium (RESI_GLOB_MAXI). Initially, this criterion is used when the loading and the support reactions become zero (for example in the case of a total unloading). In this case, one passes automatically from the relative criterion to the absolute criterion. When one uses a damage constitutive model, one observes in certain cases a divergence of the absolute residual whereas the relative residual remains small. This is why it is advised, during the analyses, to check that RESI_GLOB_MAXI remains small. If it reaches high values, it is recommended to repeat the analysis by imposing a maximum value on the global residual by defining a RESI_GLOB_MAXI for the analysis. It is advised to use the default value of {10}^{-6} . Under ITER_GLOB_MAXI, one may modify the maximum number of iterations performed in order to solve the global problem at each time instant (10 by default). If one sees that, during the Newton iterations, the convergence of the constitutive model is slow, one may increase the value of this parameter. Under ITER_GLOB_ELAS, one may modify the maximum number of iterations performed with the unloading matrix when one uses the keyword PAS_MINI_ELAS of the factor keyword NEWTON (see § 7.2.3) in order to solve the global problem at each time instant (25 by default). 7.2.3 Newton's algorithm The keyword NEWTON makes it possible to specify the matrix used for the global iterations of Newton's method (Figure 7.2.3-a). One may use either the elastic matrix (MATRICE=’ELASTIQUE’), or the tangent matrix (MATRICE=’TANGENTE’). Moreover, in this latter case one may pass automatically from the tangent matrix to the unloading matrix when the time step is, or becomes (through the subdivision), smaller than a minimum step (PAS_MINI_ELAS). For the damage models the unloading matrix is identified with the secant matrix (Figure 7.2.3-a). This option may be useful when the automatic subdivision of the time step is not sufficient to make an analysis converge. For the damage models (concrete), the tangent matrix may become singular and it may be preferable to use the unloading matrix in order to converge. | | | --- | | Figure 7.2.3-a : schematic description of the solution operators of Newton's method in Code_Aster (for a damage constitutive model). | As a first step, it is recommended to use the tangent matrix. In order to optimise the convergence, it is strongly advised to update this tangent matrix as often as possible, the best strategy being, if the size of the problem allows it, to update it at every iteration (MATRICE=’TANGENTE’, REAC_ITER= 1, U4.51.03). This is all the more advised if one has a modelling using the De Borst method (cf. 4.2). If convergence problems appear (singular tangent matrix), one may choose to switch to the unloading matrix (activation of the keyword PAS_MINI_ELAS). As the convergence with the unloading matrix is slower than that with the tangent matrix, the keyword ITER_GLOB_ELAS (cf. § 7.2.2) makes it possible to define a maximum number of iterations specific to the use of the unloading matrix. For the damage constitutive models, the unloading matrix (which corresponds to the secant matrix) depends on the strain state reached. It is therefore necessary to update this matrix by means of the keyword REAC_ITER_ELAS. In the case where the convergence problems persist, it may be of interest to carry out an analysis with the elastic matrix in order to see how the Newton iterations proceed in this case. Note The line search theoretically makes it possible to improve the convergence of Newton's method R5.03.01. However, it is not operational with the operator DYNA_NON_LINE. 7.2.4 Material non-linearities The keyword COMPORTEMENT makes it possible to define the non-linear constitutive models implemented in DYNA_NON_LINE. In the event of non-convergence of the analysis, one may be led to modify the parameters associated with the De Borst algorithm (cf. § 4.2, for a multilayer-shell analysis). 7.2.5 Time-integration scheme DYNA_NON_LINE has various implicit time schemes (NEWMARK and HHT) and explicit ones (DIFF_CENT and TCHAMWA) described briefly in § 2.2. In seismic studies, it is recommended to use the implicit average-acceleration method, because it does not introduce artificial numerical damping: SCHEMA_TEMPS=_F(SCHEMA='NEWMARK', FORMULATION='DEPLACEMENT', ALPHA=0.25, DELTA=0.5,). If one observes parasitic high-frequency oscillations in the response of the structure, it is advised to use an HHT scheme, which makes it possible to introduce a significant numerical damping for the high frequencies with almost no impact on the low frequencies: SCHEMA_TEMPS=_F(SCHEMA='HHT', FORMULATION='DEPLACEMENT', ALPHA= alph, MODI_EQUI=‘OUI’,). By default, it is advised to take ALPHA= -0.3. One will note that the numerical damping is proportional to the time step, cf. R5.05.05; the introduction of a time-step subdivision therefore reduces the numerical damping. In the event of persistent non-convergence and if all the other methods of help with convergence have been tested, one may try to continue the analysis by using the explicit central-difference scheme: SCHEMA_TEMPS=_F(SCHEMA='DIFF_CENT', FORMULATION='ACCELERATION',). It is nevertheless recommended to opt for this explicit scheme with the greatest caution. Indeed, such an analysis has important specific features, in particular as regards the time step of the analysis, which must satisfy the CFL condition [5] of time is in general of the order of 10-5 to 10-6 second. This analysis strategy will be more relevant when Code_Aster has a method for switching from an implicit time scheme to an explicit one (and the converse). This method will in due course make it possible to change time-integration scheme during the solution of a non-linear transient dynamic problem. When the structure is in a phase of relatively regular evolution one uses an implicit scheme, which makes it possible to have relatively large time steps. Then, during the phases strongly disturbed by the damage of the concrete, one switches to an explicit scheme which could make it possible to get past the difficulties (snap-back). One may then switch back to an implicit scheme if the remainder of the response becomes more regular again. 7.3 Chaining of the analyses Starting from the static solution under self-weight, one carries out the seismic analyses one after another. The final state of the preceding analysis (n) serves as the initial state of the following analysis (n+1) : ETAT_INIT=_F( CRITERE= 'RELATIF', EVOL_NOLI = chargement de pesanteur,). Before continuing the analysis n+1 , it is necessary to check that the initial state supplied by analysis n does indeed correspond to the structure at rest: the acceleration field must be very small throughout the structure. When the seismic loading applied ends with a weak phase that does indeed allow the structure to return to rest (signal not truncated), one may chain the analyses directly. Otherwise, in order to make the acceleration field zero throughout the structure at the end of analysis n (elimination of a parasitic acceleration field), it is advised to bring the structure back to the complete state of rest by applying to the structure a high fictitious damping over a small time interval (a few tenths of a second, for example). For this, it is necessary to create fictitious materials possessing a high elementary damping. Following the seismic analysis, one carries out another dynamic analysis (DYNA_NON_LINE) with the static loading only and using the materials with high damping. At the end of this analysis the acceleration field is necessarily quasi-zero and one may use it as the initial state of the following analysis (n+1) . 8 Post-processing 8.1 Analysis of the global behaviour of the structure 8.1.1 Maximum displacements and forces The analysis of the evolution of the displacements and of the reactions at the supports (shear forces, normal forces and global bending moments) supplies important elements for apprehending the global behaviour of a structure. Notes It is practical to use the keyword OBSERVATION in order to save all of the results for a given point and not for the whole structure. 8.1.2 Determination of the oscillator spectrum The determination of the oscillator spectrum of an accelerogram a(t) is available via the operator CALC_FONCTION[U6.62.04] with the keyword SPEC_OSCI: it is obtained by numerical integration of Duhamel's equation by the method of Nigam R5.05.01. This command supplies the absolute pseudo-acceleration spectrum and, on request, the pseudo-velocity spectrum or the relative displacement spectrum. In general, the user must always check that the frequency range used for the computation of the oscillator spectrum is consistent with the frequency content of the input signal. This is all the more crucial if one seeks to obtain, for example, the asymptotic value of the pseudo-acceleration. In certain cases, the default frequency list of the keyword SPEC_OSCI may be too restrictive. 8.1.3 Natural frequencies The analysis of the evolution of the natural frequencies of a structure during loading makes it possible to have a good indication of its state of damage. The cracking phenomena decrease the global stiffness of the structure and one observes a drop in frequency. If one determines the natural frequencies and the damping of the damaged structure, one may then carry out a spectral seismic response analysis on it. The determination of the natural frequencies of the damaged structure is possible by means of the keyword MODE_VIBR of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE U4.53.01. This is a method making it possible to carry out a vibratory modal analysis (natural frequencies and associated modes) on the global stiffness and mass matrices of DYNA_NON_LINE. As one must compute the natural frequencies of the structure for a damaged elastic stiffness matrix, it is necessary to have returned the structure to rest before carrying out the computation of the natural frequencies by the operator MODE_VIBR. One should refer to the test case SDNV106 V5.03.106 for more details. Another possibility consists in carrying out, after the seismic loading and after the return of the structure to rest, a "white noise" type loading at a low level of excitation by means of Code_Aster . One then carries out a Fourier analysis of the response obtained in order to determine the natural frequencies of the damaged structure. 8.1.4 Balance of dissipated energies The computation of the energies over all or part of the structure is done by the operator POST_ELEM u4.81.22: the kinetic energy, the elastic strain energy, the total strain energy, the work of the external forces, the dissipation energy for the plate elements of the DKTG family with the global reinforced-concrete constitutive laws GLRC_DM and DHRC. However, the viscous damping energy is not currently computed, nor the strain energy for softening laws such as ENDO_ISOT_BETON. Moreover, the computation of the work of the external forces is carried out from part of the nodal forces and does not take into account the inertia or damping forces. The energy balance is therefore to be carried out with caution. One may also, with the keyword ENERGIE of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE, compute the energy balance over the whole structure, including the viscous damping energy. It is stored in the table of name PARA_CALC. It is extracted with the command RECU_TABLE U4.71.02. 8.2 Analysis of the local behaviour of the structure 8.2.1 Introduction The options for computing fields cited in this chapter are defined in CALC_CHAMP U4.81.04. Concrete The analysis of the contour maps of damage makes it possible to apprehend the local behaviour of a structure. One may determine the maximum levels of stress and of cracking reached at certain points of the structure. Note If one observes that only a few finite elements are very strongly damaged, it may be a phenomenon of localisation of the damage due to the softening constitutive model used. This phenomenon leads to a mesh dependence of the response. In order to determine whether there is localisation or not, it is recommended to repeat the analysis by remeshing more finely the suspect zone. If one observes that the damage again takes place on a single band of mesh cells (reduction of the damaged zone), it is because one has localisation. It should be noted that the models for delocalisation of the constitutive laws by regularisation of the strain are not yet currently available in non-linear dynamics in Code_Aster (cf. § 4.4.4 ). Reinforcement The analysis of the contour maps of the cumulative plastic strains in the reinforcement bars makes it possible to determine the level of plastification reached in the steels. 8.2.2 Local modelling (solid elements) There is no specific feature related to the post-processing in this case. It is therefore not detailed here. Concrete One computes directly the stresses at the nodes by element SIGM_ELNO. Reinforcement Likewise, the membrane grid elements (GRILLE_MEMBRANE) or the bar elements (BARRE) are post-processed by computing the associated stresses SIGM_ELNO. Note Under HPP, one computes directly the strains at the nodes by element EPSI_ELNO from the displacements. 8.2.3 Multilayer plate and shell elements Concrete For the multilayer shells, one post-processes the stresses by element at the nodes (SIGM_ELNO) from the stresses at the integration points of each layer (SIEF_ELGA) computed during a non-linear analysis. If one wishes to obtain these stresses in a particular layer and position, one must use the operator POST_CHAMP. These stresses are computed in the local frame of the shell defined by the user in the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM. One may post-process in the same manner the internal variables (VARI_ELNO). Reinforcement The offset grid elements (GRILLE_EXCENTRE) or the bar elements (BARRE) are post-processed simply by computing the associated stresses SIGM_ELNO. 8.2.4 Multifibre beam elements For the multifibre beams, one does not currently have an option for computing the stresses in the fibres directly in CALC_CHAMP. One may nevertheless recover the stresses in the fibres by using the operands for localisation of a field in the operator RECU_FONCTION: / NOEUD = no, [noeud] / GROUP_NO = grno, [gr_noeud] / MAILLE = ma, [maille] / GROUP_MA = grma, [gr_maille] / POINT = nupoint,[I] / SOUS_POINT = nusp, [I] The integer nupoint specifies the number of the Gauss point whose value one wants to recover (case of the cham_elem "at the GAUSS points"). The integer nusp specifies the number of the sub-point, that is to say of the fibre, on which one reads the stresses (cf. the mesh of the cross-section § 3.4). One may thus analyse the stresses and the strains in the concrete fibres and in the steel fibres. 8.2.5 "Global" plate and shell elements In this modelling, one does not have directly the stresses and the strains through the thickness of the shell. It is nevertheless possible to reconstruct the strain field (but not the stress field) for a given through-thickness position from the fields of generalised forces and strains. As the strain field is considered linear in the section, one has: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\varepsilon}_{x}(z)={\varepsilon}_{x}^{\mathrm{tot}}+z{\kappa}_{x}^{\mathrm{tot}}\\ {\varepsilon}_{y}(z)={\varepsilon}_{y}^{\mathrm{tot}}+z{\kappa}_{y}^{\mathrm{tot}}\end{array} with {\varepsilon}_{x}^{\mathrm{tot}} , {\varepsilon}_{y}^{\mathrm{tot}} , {\kappa}_{x}^{\mathrm{tot}} and {\kappa}_{y}^{\mathrm{tot}} the generalised strains and {\varepsilon}_{x}(z) and {\varepsilon}_{y}(z) the strains through the thickness of the global shell. 8.2.6 Discrete elements carrying linear or non-linear constitutive laws In this modelling, one has directly the displacements (or even rotations) of the end nodes of the discrete elements, but also the forces passing through them. Moreover, in the case of a non-linear constitutive law, cf. R5.03.17, one has access to the values of various internal variables useful for analysing the detailed functioning (anelastic contribution, energy dissipated, etc). 9 Test cases and existing studies 9.1 Code_Aster test cases 9.1.1 Time schemes Average-acceleration scheme (§ 2.2 ) - SDND102B and SDND102C - Seismic response of a non-linear multi-supported mass–spring system. - SDNL130 - Seismic response of a reinforced-concrete beam (rectangular cross-section) with non-linear behaviour. Computation of the stresses through the thickness of a multilayer shell (SIGM_ELNO, § 8.2.3 ) - SSLS115 - Composite square plate under uniform pressure. - SSLS118 - Supported square plate subjected to a sinusoidal pressure. Computation of the stresses in a fibre of a multifibre beam (TEST_RESU or RECU_FONCTION with SOUS_POINT, § 8.2.4 ) - SSNL120 - Cyclic response of the constitutive law of concrete (TEST_RESU). - SSNL127E - Tension test with the model CORR_ACIER (RECU_FONCTION). 9.2 Examples of studies carried out 9.2.1 Floor of P4 type Description of the test [2] Tests were carried out at the CEA / EMSI (Saclay) in order to characterise the non-linear behaviour of the floors of the BAS-BL 1300 MWe building subjected to a vertical earthquake. The mock-up designed was dimensioned so as to be representative of a real floor. The tests were carried out on the Azalée shaking table of the CEA at Saclay. The experimental programme consists of 9 runs of increasing acceleration levels. One studies the non-linear behaviour of the main slab in bending. Modelling carried out [25] , [26] One adopts a multilayer DKT plate modelling for the concrete and a modelling of GRILLE type for the reinforcement bars of the reinforcement. The model ENDO_ISOT_BETON is used in plane stress thanks to the De Borst approach. Starting from the static solution under self-weight, one carries out the seismic analyses chained one after another. The final state of the preceding analysis serves as the initial state of the following analysis. One analyses the damage undergone by the reinforced-concrete slab for the acceleration levels reached. The comparison with the experimental results shows that the modelling carried out makes it possible to represent correctly the non-linear behaviour of the slab, in particular the state of cracking at the end of the loadings. The comparison of the time responses of the vertical displacements at the centre of the slab is very satisfactory. The residual deflection of the cracked slab under self-weight at the end of the highest loadings studied is well determined by the analysis. 9.2.2 SAFE shear walls – T5 Description of the test [27] The SAFE programme (Reinforced Structures of Low Slenderness, CCR-ISPRA, 1998) concerns a series of 13 pseudo-dynamic tests on shear walls. Unlike a dynamic test on a shaking table, the pseudo-dynamic method is a hybrid numerical/experimental method that combines the computation of the displacement of the structure (here one degree of freedom of horizontal translation) and the measurement of the force used by a control system to impose this displacement. The differences between each series of tests are essentially linked to the proportion of reinforcement of the walls, to the initial frequency of the test (from which one determines the mass to be applied at the top of the wall) and to the mean vertical load that one seeks to keep constant during the test. Each series generally comprises at least 3 tests, carried out by varying the intensity of the reference accelerogram. Modellings carried out [11] , [23] , [24] Two modelling approaches were carried out: 3D representation by solid finite elements (HEXA), and multilayer shells (DKT). 3 studies were conducted: monotonic static (push-over), alternating static and transient dynamic (DYNA_NON_LINE). The study with a local modelling (concrete represented by means of solid elements) shows that one rapidly encounters enormous numerical difficulties both in statics and in non-linear dynamics. The constitutive models implemented are not very robust for this type of problem. The global modelling makes it possible to represent in a satisfactory manner the behaviour of the wall for the lowest loading level (static push-over, alternating static, seismic dynamic). One does not encounter numerical difficulties. The model GLRC_DM makes it possible to supply the static envelope of the experimental cycles (push-over). In dynamics, the comparison of the time responses of the displacements at the top of the wall is very satisfactory. However, the irreversible strains are not modelled in this study. This is why this study is currently being continued with the model GLRC_DM coupled to membrane elastoplasticity. 9.2.3 CAMUS 2000 mock-up Description of the test [4] The CAMUS 2000 mock-up is a structure at 1/3 scale made up of two walls and five reinforced-concrete floors. The base of the structure is very strongly reinforced in order to ensure the anchorage to the shaking table. The total height of the mock-up is 5,10m . Lateral strengthening systems are added to the structure in order to increase its strength. Additional masses are placed on the floors in order to represent the required state of stress at the foot of the structure. The total mass of the mock-up is 36 tonnes. The test programme consists of 3 seismic runs of increasing excitation levels. The loading is bidirectional horizontal. Modellings carried out [4] The analyses were carried out by means of the multifibre-beam modelling (POU_D_EM) and of the constitutive model LABORD_1D for the concrete. The results obtained by the analysis in terms of global quantities (displacements, generalised forces, …) are relatively close to those obtained experimentally. The comparison of the in-plane bending moments for the first storey of the right-hand wall and for the various loading levels shows that one has a good agreement between the analysis and the test. The multifibre-beam modelling of Code_Aster implemented is suited to simulating this type of simple structure under seismic loading. 10 Conclusions The methodology for carrying out a civil-engineering study under seismic loading is presented. One places oneself within the framework of non-linear transient dynamics (operator DYNA_NON_LINE). Various types of finite-element modelling are available in order to represent the reinforced-concrete structural elements (beam, column, slab, wall, …). One may use a local representation, a semi-global one (multilayer shell, multifibre beam) and a global shell. Non-linear constitutive models are furthermore available for the concrete (ENDO_ISOT_BETON, ENDO_ORTH_BETON, MAZARS_UNIL, GLRC_DM and GLRC_DM coupled to plasticity) and for the steel (VMIS_ISOT_LINE, VMIS_CINE_LINE), suited to seismic applications. The implementation of a non-linear seismic study is presented (data setup of the problem, preliminary analyses to be carried out before the non-linear dynamic analysis, advice in order to improve the convergence of the analyses and post-processings available). This document provides the user, for each stage of his or her analysis, with methodological advice and rules of good practice to be followed. 11 Bibliography 1. Badel P.
