u2.06.11 Analysis of the seismic resistance of large metal tanks u2.06.11 Analysis of the seismic resistance of large metal tanks Summary: The aim of this document is to describe the different steps to be implemented in Code_Aster in order to carry out the numerical simulation of the seismic resistance of large metal tanks. These thin metal structures can then present two preferred failure modes: failure of the anchorages or buckling of the shell courses. The first approach is based on a regulatory method of push-over type. One can, in addition, use a non-linear stability criterion ( cf. documentation U2.08.04 and test cases SSLL105 and SSNL126). The second approach is direct transient modelling with the fluid domain fully taken into account through a coupled fluid-structure approach in large displacements (a modelling similar to that of test case FDNV100). One can also couple this transient analysis to a non-linear stability analysis, as test case FDNV100 also shows. 1 Introduction This documentation presents the different numerical methodologies developed in order to simulate and analyse the seismic resistance of large metal tanks. The aim here is therefore to present the implementation and the chaining of various operators of Code_Aster in order to carry through the study of this type of component, according to different modelling hypotheses which are mainly dictated by regulatory considerations. These tanks, which are thin metal structures, can present two preferred failure modes: failure of the anchorages or buckling of the shell courses. The first methodology is based on a regulatory method of push-over type ([bib1], [bib2], [bib3], [bib4]). The tank is subjected to an imposed internal pressure, spatially variable and increasing. The solution is obtained in quasi-statics and the fluid domain is not modelled directly: its influence on the wall is transcribed by a particular imposed pressure field. The non-linearities are of geometric and constitutive type (plasticity). In the course of the incremental analysis, this pressure is increased until the ultimate load is obtained, which corresponds to the buckling of the structure (one can use the keyword CRIT_STAB of STAT_NON_LINE for a non-linear stability analysis). In order to model the anchorages more finely, one can introduce the uplift at the bolted anchorages with the ground [bib5]. One can also increase the mechanical resistance to buckling by adding a carbon-fibre reinforcement on the shell courses. Its modelling is presented in this document. The second approach is direct transient modelling with the fluid domain fully taken into account through a coupled fluid-structure approach in large displacements [bib6]. This modelling, finer than the previous one, complements the regulatory approaches, in particular by making it possible to identify more clearly the limits of their domain of validity, mainly with respect to the large global non-linearities such as the large displacements. However, the practical use of these transient approaches is limited by the extra computational cost which they induce (a ratio of the order of 10). It is possible to combine the transient approach with a non-linear stability analysis via the use of the keyword CRIT_STAB of DYNA_NON_LINE. Unlike the quasi-static analyses, the particular features of the fluid-structure model require a specific treatment in CRIT_STAB, which will be detailed in this document. 2 Presentation of the problem 2.1 Geometry of the structure The problem, in the case of a typical tank, can be represented geometrically as follows [bib2]: | | | --- | | Figure 2.1 -a: Schematic representation of a real tank | The tank presented is composed of 8 cylindrical shell courses of about 2m in height each, which are welded together to form the cylindrical wall of the tank. The thickness, constant on each shell course, decreases as one passes from one shell course to the one above it. This particular arrangement makes it possible to optimise the thickness of the shell courses, as a function of the hydrostatic pressure exerted by the contained fluid, which varies linearly with the depth. Given the very small thicknesses of the shell courses (about 4 to 5\mathrm{mm} ), one chooses to model the metal walls by volumetric thin shells (COQUE_3D). These finite elements have as their geometric support a 9-node quadrilateral. Some mesh generators do not know how to generate this type of finite element but offer meshes with more classical 8-node quadrilaterals. The mid-side nodes are therefore defined in Code_Aster by the following command: MAILLA2=CREA_MAILLAGE(MAILLAGE=MAILLA01, MODI_MAILLE=_F(GROUP_MA='RESERVOIR', OPTION='QUAD8_9', PREF_NOEUD='NSQ', PREF_NUME=1,),); One then makes sure that the normals are correctly oriented: MAILLA2 = MODI_MAILLAGE( reuse = MAILLA2 , MAILLAGE = MAILLA2 , ORIE_NORM_COQUE = _F( GROUP_MA = ( 'VIROLE', 'TFC2' ) , VECT_NORM = (0.,-1.,0.) , GROUP_NO = 'OY' , ) , MODELE = MODELE0 , INFO = 2 , ) One can then define the final model MODELE based on the volumetric shells. The geometric characteristics specific to the structural finite elements employed (COQUE_3D) are defined. Shell course by shell course, the thicknesses and the orientation of the local frames are given. One must be particularly careful about the consistency between the axes of the frames and the material characteristics when one is in an orthotropic case (the case of the reinforcement). Likewise for this reinforcement, one can use the offset in order to take into account its real arrangement on the outside of the metal shell course (its middle surface therefore cannot be confused with that of the shell course supporting it): CARAELEM = AFFE_CARA_ELEM ( MODELE = MODELE , COQUE = ( _F ( GROUP_MA = ( 'SURF0' , ) , EPAIS = 7.13E-3 , ANGL_REP = ( 0. , 90. ) , A_CIS = 0.8333 , COEF_RIGI_DRZ = 1.E-05 , EXCENTREMENT = 0. , INER_ROTA = 'OUI' , MODI_METRIQUE = 'OUI' , ) , … _F ( GROUP_MA = ( 'ANNEAU' , ) , EPAIS = 1.E-2 , ANGL_REP = ( 0. , 0. ) , A_CIS = 0.8333 , COEF_RIGI_DRZ = 1.E-05 , EXCENTREMENT = 0. , INER_ROTA = 'OUI' , MODI_METRIQUE = 'OUI' , ) , _F ( GROUP_MA = ( 'TFC2' , ) , EPAIS = ( 1. 1.72E-3 ) , ANGL_REP = ( 0. , 90. ) , A_CIS = 0.8333 , EXCENTREMENT = -4.425E-3 , INER_ROTA = 'OUI' , MODI_METRIQUE = 'OUI' ,),),) 2.2 Materials employed The platework is in austenitic stainless steel A240 type 304L and the bolting will be taken into account as being in steel A42. For steel A240, different elastoplastic laws with non-linear isotropic hardening (in the form of tensile curves) are proposed. The definition of the hardening from tensile curves, without information on the unloading, is well suited to applications in which the loading is monotonically increasing, which is what will be assumed in the present case ( cf. § 3.1 ): A5=DEFI_FONCTION(NOM_PARA='EPSI', VALE=( 0.00097 , 191820000. , 0.00116 , 221740000. , 0.00138 , 247020000. , 0.00167 , 267090000. , 0.00207 , 285920000. , 0.0029 , 304530000. , 0.00365 , 314300000. , 0.00468 , 322090000. ) , PROL_DROITE='LINEAIRE', PROL_GAUCHE='LINEAIRE',); # MAA240 = DEFI_MATERIAU ( ELAS = _F ( E = 1.98E11 , NU = 0.3 , RHO = 7900. , ) , TRACTION = _F ( SIGM = A5 , ) , ) This constitutive relation is of type 'VMIS_ISOT_TRAC' in the non-linear solution operator employed. The plastic behaviour of grade A42 will not be taken into account to begin with. Indeed, the elastic limit is higher than for the 304L and the parts made of this material are more massive, which leads to lower stress levels. The hypothesis of a purely isotropic elastic constitutive behaviour is therefore admissible for the corresponding material, named MAA42. In the case where a reinforcement in carbon-fibre fabric (TFC) is added, it is modelled by an orthotropic elastic material (the plasticity threshold is never reached for the loadings considered): MATFC = DEFI_MATERIAU ( ELAS_ORTH = _F ( E_L = 1.E10 , E_T = 1.E12 , G_LT = 3.E9 , NU_LT = 0.3 , RHO = 2500. , ) , ) 3 Quasi-static push-over approach 3.1 Imposed loadings The imposed loading is of regulatory origin (EC-8), and quasi-static [bib1]. The effects of an earthquake on the structure are represented by a variable pressure field imposed on the inner face of the shell courses. The value at each point is a function of the current coordinate and increases linearly with time. This monotonic evolution in time is characteristic of the methods known as push-over, in the sense of EC-8, whose objective is to simulate by a quasi-static analysis the response to a seismic loading, and therefore of a physically transient dynamic nature. The dynamic effects, such as the inertia and the forces generated by the sloshing fluid, are replaced by this imposed pressure distribution. The problem to be treated involves only a modelling of the structure, without modelling of the fluid domain. The push-over methods have of course been constructed and justified by making strong hypotheses of linearisation of the problem (small displacements, elastic constitutive behaviour, Euler buckling…). The definitions of the imposed pressure fields are given below [bib2]: ---------------------------------------------------------------------- DEFINITION OF THE PRESSURE FIELDS (PA) # PH(Z) : HYDROSTATIC PRESSURE PIF(Z,TETA) : FLEXIBLE IMPULSIVE PRESSURE PIR(Z,TETA) : RIGID IMPULSIVE PRESSURE PV(Z) : VERTICAL PRESSURE # PIF(Z,TETA) = PIF(Z) COS(TETA) PIR(Z,TETA) = PIR(Z) COS(TETA) # #P(Z,TETA)=PH(Z)+INSTANT ( PIF(Z,TETA) + PIR(Z,TETA) +/- 0.4 PV(Z) ) ---------------------------------------------------------------------- PHZ = DEFI_FONCTION ( NOM_PARA = 'Z' , … VERIF = 'CROISSANT' , ) PIFZ = DEFI_FONCTION ( NOM_PARA = 'Z' , … VERIF = 'CROISSANT' , ) PIRZ = DEFI_FONCTION ( NOM_PARA = 'Z' , … VERIF = 'CROISSANT' , ) PVZ = DEFI_FONCTION ( NOM_PARA = 'Z' , … VERIF = 'CROISSANT' , ) ---------------------------------------------------------------------- P(X,Y,Z) : TOTAL PRESSURE #P(Z,TETA)=PH(Z)+INSTANT ( PIF(Z,TETA) + PIR(Z,TETA) +/- 0.4 PV(Z) ) ---------------------------------------------------------------------- COSTE=FORMULE(NOM_PARA=('X','Y'),VALE='X/SQRT((X X)+(Y Y))') PH=FORMULE(NOM_PARA=('X','Y','Z'),VALE='PHZ(Z)') PIF=FORMULE(NOM_PARA=('X','Y','Z'),VALE='PIFZ(Z) COSTE(X,Y)') PIR=FORMULE(NOM_PARA=('X','Y','Z'),VALE='PIRZ(Z) COSTE(X,Y)') PV=FORMULE(NOM_PARA=('X','Y','Z'),VALE='PVZ(Z)') PS1=FORMULE(NOM_PARA=('X','Y','Z'), VALE='PIF(X,Y,Z)+PIR(X,Y,Z)+(0.4 PV(X,Y,Z))') PS2=FORMULE(NOM_PARA=('X','Y','Z') VALE='PIF(X,Y,Z)+PIR(X,Y,Z)-(0.4 PV(X,Y,Z))') One can then define the corresponding mechanical loadings (gravity and follower pressures): PESA = AFFE_CHAR_MECA( MODELE = MODELE , PESANTEUR=_F(GRAVITE=9.81, DIRECTION=(0.0,0.0,-1.0),),); # PRESPH = AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F( MODELE = MODELE , FORCE_COQUE = _F ( GROUP_MA = 'VIROLE',),PRES = PH, PLAN = 'INF',),) # PRESPS1 = AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F( MODELE = MODELE , FORCE_COQUE = _F ( GROUP_MA = 'VIROLE' , ) , PRES = PS1 , PLAN = 'INF' , ) , ) # PRESPS2 = AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F( MODELE = MODELE , FORCE_COQUE = _F ( GROUP_MA = ( 'VIROLE' , ) , PRES = PS2 , PLAN = 'INF' , ) , ) These pressure fields are multiplied by a linearly increasing function of time: FONCMUL = DEFI_FONCTION( NOM_PARA = 'INST' , = ( 0. , 0. , 3. , 3. ) , ) The connection with the ground is considered here as being complete (node group 'BASE'). The symmetry conditions are also defined (node group 'SYMETRIE'), since only a half-tank is meshed: CONDLIM = AFFE_CHAR_MECA( MODELE = MODELE , DDL_IMPO = ( _F ( GROUP_NO = 'BASE' , DX = 0., DY = 0., DZ = 0., DRX = 0., DRY = 0., DRZ = 0.,) , _F ( GROUP_NO = 'SYMETRIE' , DY = 0., DRX = 0., DRZ = 0.,),) , ) 3.2 Monotonic non-linear quasi-static solution method One wants to solve a non-linear quasi-static evolution problem. The operator STAT_NON_LINE will therefore be used (U4.51.03, R5.03.01). The imposed loading will be built with the pressure PRESPS1, for example: RESU = STAT_NON_LINE( MODELE = MODELE , CHAM_MATER = CHMAT , CARA_ELEM = CARAELEM , EXCIT = ( _F ( CHARGE = CONDLIM , TYPE_CHARGE = 'FIXE_CSTE' , ) , _F ( CHARGE = PESA , TYPE_CHARGE = 'FIXE_CSTE' , ) , _F ( CHARGE = PRESPH , FONC_MULT = FONCMUL , TYPE_CHARGE = 'SUIV' , ) , _F ( CHARGE = PRESPS1 , FONC_MULT = FONCMUL , TYPE_CHARGE = 'SUIV' , ) , ) , COMPORTEMENT = ( _F ( RELATION = 'ELAS' , COQUE_NCOU = 1 , DEFORMATION = 'GROT_GDEP' , GROUP_MA = ( 'SURF2' , 'ANNEAU' , 'TFC2' ) , ) , _F ( RELATION = 'VMIS_ISOT_TRAC' , COQUE_NCOU = 1, DEFORMATION = 'GROT_GDEP' , GROUP_MA = ( 'SURF0' , 'SURF1' , ) , ) , ) , INCREMENT = _F ( LIST_INST = L_INST1 , ) , ) 3.3 Notes on the analyses and the post-processings In the example presented above a Newton algorithm is used: one solves with the global tangent operator (stiffness) updated at each iteration. In the case where the problem is well posed (sufficiently “regular”), it is known that this type of algorithm offers the best convergence. Therefore, in the present case, as long as the global tangent operator is “well” defined (far from being singular), the analysis will proceed well with rapid convergence. When the imposed load level approaches the ultimate load, the structure will then become unstable in the sense of buckling R7.05.01, which is reflected by the tendency of the global tangent operator to become singular. The loss of stability by a limit point is in fact the loss of uniqueness of the solution, and hence the singularity of the solution operator. In the neighbourhood of the limit point the Newton algorithm will converge less well, whence the need to impose smaller time increments and an increase in the number of iterations on the equilibrium residual. In a general manner, the closer one gets to the ultimate load, the smaller the time step will have to be. Despite this, the risks of the analysis stopping on non-convergence are high, whence the obligation to carry out the analysis over several successive restarts. It is nevertheless possible to improve this convergence by changing algorithm in the course of the analysis and switching to a quasi-Newton method. To do this, it is sufficient to solve on the tangent operator which one updates only at each step (between two iterations one keeps the same one), and if this is insufficient, one can then solve with the elastic operator which, for its part, cannot become singular. This choice reinforces the robustness of the algorithm in terms of convergence, but it increases, sometimes considerably, the number of iterations (and/or of steps) necessary to obtain the solution. For this type of study one can distinguish two types of quantities of interest for the post-processing. On the one hand a quantity able to reflect the buckling of the structure and therefore to bring out the ultimate load. For this one can plot the pressure level (multiplier coefficient) as a function of the displacement of a point located at the top of the tank (at the end of the generatrix most subjected to compression). On the other hand a more local indicator of the appearance of plasticity: the iso-value of the cumulative plastic strain, at each time instant of the analysis. These two post-processings present no particular difficulty in Code_Aster . The finite-element models implemented comprised between 55000 and 110000 degrees of freedom. These models were based on a simplified representation of the anchorages: the geometry of the reinforcements and gussets is finely meshed, but the bolting is not present and it is replaced by a clamped boundary condition on all the nodes at elevation 0m . A more realistic modelling of the anchorages, with lift-off, would therefore have led to a global problem size that was appreciably larger. The analysis methodology presented here, whose objective is to study the quasi-static buckling response R7.05.01 of a tank, is very close to the framework of the user's guide for the buckling analysis U2.08.04. This documentation presents the linear stability analyses (in the Euler sense) and the setting up of a non-linear analysis of push-over type in order to obtain the ultimate load. 3.4 Fine modelling of the anchorages: uplift The type of tanks studied here are bolted to the ground [bib5]. These bolts (or tie rods) pass through reinforced flanges welded at the base of the shell course. For a faster run, the method implemented is presented below on a simplified mesh, but with realistic anchorages: the tank is fixed to the ground by 18 tie rods. In Code_Aster , several modellings of contact are available. The modelling of the geometry of the contact zone can be surfacic (3D problem), lineic (2D problem) or made up of discrete elements (keywords DIS_CHOC in STAT_NON_LINE and DIS_CONTACT for the material law). The contact itself can be treated either in a nodal manner by penalisation or by the Lagrangian method, with active constraints or not, or in a continuous manner by the augmented Lagrangian method. The simplest method, in this study configuration, is that of penalisation, which in this case also has the advantage of being able to take into account the role of the sealing joint without having to mesh it separately. For a quasi-static analysis, penalisation is not numerically problematic, as it is in dynamics where this technique can generate high-frequency disturbances (linked to the penalisation stiffness). Moreover, for structural finite elements, one can adjust the penalisation stiffness so as to approximate as well as possible the contact stiffness of the part which is in reality massive. The other methods are however more rigorous because they do not generate interpenetration. For the study of the lift-off of the tank, a penalisation method will therefore be used, which presents the best ratio of modelling quality to computational cost on this particular case. Given the option taken of forcing all the nodes to be able to move only vertically, one can take advantage of this complete pairing in order to be content with using discrete elements for the contact. Indeed, it is not necessary to carry out re-pairing, and therefore the general surfacic master-slave modellings of the contact zones are unnecessarily heavy. A carpet of discrete contact elements will therefore be placed under the lower hoop. There will then be one discrete element (DIS_T on a SEG2 mesh cell) under each node at elevation 0. If the computed solution proves too far from the experimental reference solution, it will be necessary to quantify the influence of the condition of purely vertical displacement. It will be sufficient to re-run analyses without this kinematic hypothesis, with, if the horizontal displacements are large, a contact-management method with re-pairing of the nodes of the surfaces concerned. Notes Strictly speaking, every node of the base shell course ought to be provided with a discrete contact element. However, if finite elements of type COQUE_3D are used for the hoops, one cannot place a contact element at the nodes at the centre of the finite elements. Indeed, this node has the particular feature of carrying only degrees of freedom of rotation type. The contact condition, which bears on the displacement normal to the face, therefore cannot be expressed at these nodes. The contact elements, as well as the kinematic condition of vertical displacement of the base nodes, must therefore be carried only by the vertex nodes or the mid-side nodes of the edges. The modelling of contact by discrete elements makes it possible, in Code_Aster , to define directly the preload of these elements. One can thus represent the prestress of the tie rods, without having to pre-deform these elements, as one would have to do if one had chosen another modelling of the contact based on the facing surfaces. Below, the position of the penalised discrete contact elements (in light grey) and of the 9 springs modelling the tie rods (in black) is presented. The reinforcement at the base of the shell course is indicated by dashed lines: | | | --- | | Figure 3.4 -a: Arrangement of the discrete elements for the connection with the slab | These discrete elements for the anchorages are grouped into 2 mesh-cell groups: - RESSC: contact elements in light grey (one SEG2 element per node of the lower flange, that is 57 SEG2), - RESS: tie rods in black (9 springs as SEG2 elements). An additional material (MATRES) is therefore introduced which corresponds to the contact elements and which makes it possible to take into account the prestress by the tightening of the nuts on the tie rods (one also defines the distance associated with the height between flanges with DIST_1 and DIST_2): Eboulon = 2.E11 ; Dboulon = 0.026 ; Sboulon = 3.14159 Dboulon Dboulon / 4 ; kressort = Eboulon Sboulon ; kpenal = kressort 100. MATRES = DEFI_MATERIAU( DIS_CONTACT = _F( RIGI_NOR = kpenal , DIST_1 = 0.05, DIST_2 = 0.05,) , ); The material assignment is completed with these discrete elements on the mesh-cell group RESSC: CHMAT = AFFE_MATERIAU( MAILLAGE = MAILLA2 , AFFE = ( _F ( GROUP_MA = 'VIROLE' , ) , MATER = MAA240 , ) , _F ( GROUP_MA = ( 'ANNET' , ) , MATER = MABID , ) , _F ( GROUP_MA = ( 'ANNEA' , ) , MATER = MAA240 , ) , _F ( GROUP_MA = ( 'RESSC' , ) , MATER = MATRES , ) , ) , ) The elementary characteristics of the new discrete elements are defined as follows: CARAELEM = AFFE_CARA_ELEM( MODELE = MODELE , DISCRET = (_F( GROUP_MA = 'RESSC' , REPERE = 'LOCAL', CARA = 'K_T_D_L', VALE = ( 10. , 0.0 , 0.0 ,) ,) , _F( GROUP_MA = 'RESS' , REPERE = 'LOCAL', CARA = 'K_T_D_L', VALE = ( kressort , 0., 0.,),),),) The springs which model the tie rods (GROUP_MA RESS) do indeed have the equivalent stiffness kressort. It remains to modify the displacement boundary conditions for the anchorages: only the displacements along the vertical of the nodes of the lower face of the lower flange are authorised (nodes initially in contact with the ground). The operator STAT_NON_LINE(U4.51.03, R5.03.01) also sees its arguments affected by the introduction of the uplift at the base (keyword DIS_CHOC for the mesh-cell group RESSC): RESU = STAT_NON_LINE( MODELE = MODELE , _MATER = CHMAT , … COMP_INCR = ( _F( RELATION = 'ELAS' , DEFORMATION = 'GROT_GDEP' , GROUP_MA = 'ANNEAU' , ) , _F( RELATION = 'ELAS' , GROUP_MA = 'RESS' , ) , _F( RELATION = 'DIS_CHOC' , GROUP_MA = 'RESSC' , ) , _F( RELATION = 'VMIS_ISOT_TRAC' , DEFORMATION = 'GROT_GDEP' , GROUP_MA = ( 'SURF0' , 'ANNEA' , 'SURF1' , 'SURF2' ) , ) , ) , … ); The rest of the command file is unchanged. 3.5 Use of the non-linear stability criterion One can also use a stability criterion based on the tangent matrix: there is an instability if the tangent stiffness matrix becomes singular, that is if at least one of its eigenvalues vanishes. One then solves the following eigenvalue problem, written in large displacements (Lagrangian formulation with the Green-Lagrange strain tensor) R7.05.01: ({K}_{T}+\lambda {I}_{d})x=0\mathrm{\iff }{K}_{T}x=\lambda {I}_{d}x with: | {K}_{T}=K+{K}^{L}(\underline{u})+{K}^{Q}(\underline{u})+K(\pi ) | Tangent stiffness matrix | | --- | --- | | {K}^{L}(\underline{u}) | Part of the matrix {K}_{T} linear in \underline{u} | | {K}^{Q}(\underline{u}) | Part of the matrix {K}_{T} quadratic in \underline{u} | | K(\pi ) | Geometric stiffness matrix | | \pi | Piola-Kirchhoff tensor \mathrm{II} | | {I}_{d} | Identity matrix | | \lambda | Eigenvalue | Documentation R7.05.01 presents these stability analyses in more detail. Documentation U2.08.04 presents their use. Notes When the displacements are small, one simply has K(\pi )=K(\sigma )={K}_{G} and the matrices {K}^{L} and {K}^{Q} can be neglected. The linear analysis in the Euler sense in Code_Aster does not make it possible to take into account the follower character of the pressure field: one must necessarily switch to the approach presented here and based on a non-linear solution. If one wants to make use of the stability criterion, it is sufficient to add the following line among the arguments of STAT_NON_LINE(U4.51.03, R5.03.01): CRIT_STAB=_F(NMAX_CHAR_CRIT=1,), One then looks for the first eigenvalue of the global tangent operator of the system. If in the course of the analysis one observes that this eigenvalue decreases, or even changes sign, this means that one has approached the first critical load and that one has then even gone past it. The number of eigenvalues to be determined can be imposed by the keyword NMAX_CHAR_CRIT (3 by default). It is also possible, by using the command CHAR_CRIT, to choose the band in which these eigenvalues are to be sought (from –10 to 10 by default). Note The indication of a frequency band is useful above all for analyses in small perturbations, where a Sturm test is carried out for the frequency band supplied. One can thus save time by computing the eigenvalues only if there are some in the band indicated. The Sturm test is not done in large strains and the eigenvalues are computed at each time step. The buckling mode as well as the eigenvalues determined (critical load coefficient) can be recovered by using the command IMPR_RESU: IMPR_RESU( MODELE = MODELE ,FORMAT = 'RESULTAT' ,RESU=(_F(RESULTAT=RESU, NOM_PARA='CHAR_CRIT',’MODE_FLAMB’,),),) Test case SSLL105 V3.01.105 offers an example of the use of this stability criterion for a linear case and test case SSNL126 V6.02.126 for a non-linear case (elastoplastic beam). 3.6 Piloting of the loading In order to facilitate the convergence of the incremental analysis when one is close to the ultimate load level, or in order to be able to go past this critical point, it can be judicious to no longer place oneself under imposed loading and to favour a displacement piloting or an arc-length piloting (its use for the post-critical regime is briefly recalled in documentation U2.08.04). Piloting cannot be used with contact U4.51.03. 4 Coupled transient approach 4.1 Reference problem One leaves here the regulatory framework and one is going to exploit all the modelling possibilities offered by Code_Aster . The model of the tank itself remains unchanged (elastoplastic volumetric shells). On the other hand, the fluid domain will be represented by a solid mesh. Moreover, the solution will be carried out in transient dynamics with the operator DYNA_NON_LINE (U4.53.01 , R5.05.05), the external loading being of seismic type. The fluid domain is modelled in linear acoustics (barotropic, compressible, non-viscous and with a free surface). The coupled fluid-structure problem is solved in Code_Aster by a symmetric formulation (u,p,\varphi ) (R4.02.02, [bib7]), in an updated Lagrangian formulation. The loading is of the type of an accelerogram imposed at the base of the tank. The discretised problem then appears as follows [bib6]: | | | --- | | Figure 4.1 -a: Complete mesh with the fluid domain and the structure | 4.2 Coupled fluid-structure modelling in Code_Aster In order to be able to carry out a coupled analysis by the formulation (u,p,\varphi ) [bib7] in Code_Aster , with free surfaces and slip at the interface (no adhesion between the non-viscous fluid and the inner wall of the tank), a certain construction of the mesh and of the corresponding models must be respected. One must therefore define the fluid mesh, the structure mesh and the fluid-structure interface. In the mesh generator one therefore generates two distinct meshes (different mesh cells but common nodes) for the fluid domain and the structure. For practical reasons, it can be simpler to generate the distinct mesh cells separately, therefore with duplicated nodes, and then to eliminate these duplicate nodes so as to have only single nodes. Then, in Code_Aster , the support mesh of the interface will be generated as follows, from the mesh-cell groups SURF0, SURF1 and SURF2 which are the shell courses of the tank: MAILLA01=CREA_MAILLAGE(MAILLAGE=MAILLA1, CREA_GROUP_MA=_F(NOM='IFLUSTRU', GROUP_MA=('SURF0','SURF1','SURF2',), PREF_MAILLE='I',),); One therefore creates a new mesh-cell group IFLUSTRU. The nodes of this mesh coincide with those of the structure, but the mesh cells are different. Notes The structure is meshed with COQUE_3D finite elements, whose geometric support is a 9-node quadrilateral. The central node has the particular feature of carrying only rotation degrees of freedom. If one wants to couple such a finite element with a solid fluid finite element, one therefore cannot write a kinematic coupling condition for this central node, since it does not have a translation degree of freedom, unlike the corresponding node which comes from the fluid domain and which, for its part, carries only translation degrees of freedom. To get round this problem, the fluid-structure coupling will be written only on the nodes of the shell mesh which carry the translation degrees of freedom: the vertex nodes and the mid-side nodes of the edges of the finite elements. One must therefore have in Code_Aster the structure mesh comprising only 8-node quadrilateral finite elements (these are indeed the vertex nodes and the mid-side nodes of the edges), on which the interface is defined. The structure mesh for the COQUE_3D is defined only afterwards, from this mesh, by adding the central nodes. The fluid mesh, in order to be conforming with the interface, will for its part be composed of 20-node parallelepipeds. Moreover, even if one used a structure mesh with shell finite elements whose geometric support was a 9-node quadrilateral, and where all the nodes, even the central one, carried translation degrees of freedom, the fluid-structure coupling could pose a problem. Indeed, the conforming solid fluid mesh would have to be built with 27-node parallelepiped solid finite elements. However, some mesh generators do not offer this type of complete finite element, which is rather little used in structural analysis, unlike the classical quadratic finite elements that are the 20-node parallelepipeds. It is imperative that the outward normal to the fluid domain always be oriented in the same direction. It is strongly advised to keep the convention of orientation from the structure towards the fluid for all the modellings of the fluid-structure interface, in particular FLUI_STRU. Once the interface has been defined, which is therefore meshed with 8-node quadrilateral finite elements (which are equivalent to the faces of the solid finite elements employed for the fluid domain: 20-node parallelepiped finite elements), one can therefore carry out the modification of the structure mesh (mesh-cell group RESERVOI) into 9-node finite elements, the geometric support of the COQUE_3D: MAILLA2=CREA_MAILLAGE(MAILLAGE=MAILLA01, MODI_MAILLE=_F(GROUP_MA='RESERVOIR', OPTION='QUAD8_9', PREF_NOEUD='NSQ', PREF_NUME=1,),); One can then define the models necessary for the coupled analysis: MODELE=AFFE_MODELE(MAILLAGE=MAILLA2, INFO=1, VERIF='MAILLE', AFFE=(_F(GROUP_MA='SURFLIBR', PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='2D_FLUI_PESA',), _F(GROUP_MA=('FLUID0','FOND','PLANCENT',), PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='3D_FLUIDE',), _F(GROUP_MA='IFLUSTRU', PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='FLUI_STRU',), _F(GROUP_MA='RESERVOI', PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='COQUE_3D',),),); The mesh-cell group SURFLIBR (boundary mesh cells of the fluid domain, located on its upper face) carries a free-surface model R4.02.04: 2D_FLUID_PESA. The mesh-cell groups FLUID0 (solid fluid domain), FOND (boundary mesh cells of FLUID0 defining the bottom) and PLANCENT (boundary mesh cells of FLUID0 defining the plane of symmetry) define the total fluid domain: 3D_FLUIDE. The fluid-structure interface (FLUI_STRU) is carried by the mesh-cell group IFLUSTRU. Finally, the mesh of the tank (RESERVOI) is the support of the structural model in volumetric shells (COQUE_3D). The compressible fluid material is also defined: EAU=DEFI_MATERIAU(FLUIDE=_F(RHO=1000.0, CELE_R=1500.0,),); which will be assigned to the fluid domain (solid model and its boundaries) as well as to the interface IFLUSTRU and to the free surface SURFLIBR: CHMAT=AFFE_MATERIAU(MAILLAGE=MAILLA2, AFFE=(_F(GROUP_MA=('FLUID0','FOND','PLANCENT','IFLUSTRU','SURFLIBR',), MATER=EAU,), … ); 4.3 Boundary conditions The kinematic boundary conditions bear on the clamping at the base of the tank (SYMETRI2), on the generatrices in the vertical plane of symmetry (SYMETRIE) and on the non-penetration (zero normal velocity) at the bottom of the fluid domain (FOND), as well as in its vertical plane of symmetry (PLANCENT). CONDLIM=AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=MODELE, DDL_IMPO=(_F(GROUP_NO='SYMETRI2', DX=0.0, DY=0.0, DZ=0.0, DRX=0.0, DRY=0.0, DRZ =0.0,), _F(GROUP_NO='SYMETRIE', DY=0.0, DRX=0.0, DRZ=0.0,),), VITE_FACE=_F(GROUP_MA=('FOND','PLANCENT',), VNOR=0.0,),); The effects of gravity are taken into account: PESA=AFFE_CHAR_MECA( MODELE=MODELE, > PESANTEUR=_F( GRAVITE=9.81, > DIRECTION=(0.0,0.0,-1.0),),); However this command is insufficient because, in the modelling (u,p,\varphi ) [bib7], the effects of gravity in the fluid domain cannot be taken into account. If nothing more were done, gravity would therefore truly be imposed only on the structure. In order to approximate the effects of the gravity of the fluid on the wall, an equivalent hydrostatic pressure will be imposed (but one which cannot take into account the variation in the height of the fluid in the course of the analysis when the sloshing begins): PHZ=DEFI_FONCTION(NOM_PARA='Z', … VERIF='CROISSANT',); # PH = FORMULE(NOM_PARA=('X','Y','Z'),VALE='PHZ(Z)',), # PRESSHYD=AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F(MODELE=MODELE, FORCE_COQUE=_F(GROUP_MA='VIROLE', PRES= PH , PLAN='INF',),); The earthquake is imposed as an accelerogram (function GASDM_X1) imposed at the base along the direction X . It is therefore a loading of classical single-support type: ACCELERX=CALC_FONCTION(COMB=(_F(FONCTION=GASDM_X1, COEF=0.5,),),); # MULT_X=CALC_CHAR_SEISME(MATR_MASS=MATMAS, DIRECTION=(1.0,0.0,0.0,), _APPUI='OUI',); # CHARG_SE=AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=MODELE, VECT_ASSE=MULT_X,); The mass matrix used (MATMAS) is the mass matrix of the total coupled system. 4.4 Initial conditions The initial state of the transient analysis must correspond to the equilibrium of the total system when it is not subjected to the earthquake. This static equilibrium state therefore corresponds to the gravity loading and to the hydrostatic effects. If one started the dynamic analysis with an initial state which did not respect this equilibrium, then this would generate oscillations of the transient solution, since it would not initially be at equilibrium (the seismic level then being however zero). One can attenuate these oscillations by adding a “large” structural damping and by waiting for the solution to stabilise before imposing the earthquake, but this technique is rather inelegant… In order to compute this statically equilibrated initial state, one can therefore solve a static equilibrium problem (which one assumes in addition to be linear) under the action of the gravity and hydrostatic forces. To do this, one computes and assembles beforehand the global matrices K and M with the hydrostatic loading and the gravity: ASSEMBLAGE( MODELE = MODELE, CHAM_MATER=CHMAT, CARA_ELEM=CARAELEM, CHARGE = (CONDLIM,PESA,PRESSHYD,), NUME_DDL = CO('NUMSTA'), SOLVEUR=_F(METHODE='MULT_FRONT',RENUM='METIS'), MATR_ASSE=( _F( MATRICE= CO('RIGSTA'), OPTION= 'RIGI_MECA'), _F( MATRICE= CO('MASSTA'), OPTION= 'MASS_MECA'), ),); The assembled stiffness matrix being singular because of the fluid domain (the formulation (u, p,) makes this matrix singular at zero frequency [bib8]), one slightly modifies the problem by considering the stiffness matrix {K}_{\mathrm{cor}}=K+\varepsilon M \varepsilon \ll 1 which is no longer singular (it is named RIGICOMB). One can, for example, take \varepsilon =0,001 as below: RIGICOMB = COMB_MATR_ASSE(COMB_R=(_F( MATR_ASSE= RIGSTA, COEF_R= 1.), _F( MATR_ASSE= MASSTA, COEF_R= -0.001),); One then assembles the loading vector F_0 (right-hand side): E_0 = CALC_VECT_ELEM(CARA_ELEM=CARAELEM, CHAM_MATER=CHMAT, OPTION='CHAR_MECA',CHARGE=(CONDLIM, PESA,PRESSHYD,),); F_0 = ASSE_VECTEUR(VECT_ELEM= E_0, NUME_DDL= NUMSTA ); One can then solve the linear statics problem {K}_{\mathrm{cor}}\underline{U}=\underline{{F}_{0}} , using, for example, a factorisation of type {\mathrm{LDL}}^{T} : RIGICOMB = FACTORISER(reuse=RIGICOMB, MATR_ASSE= RIGICOMB, STOP_SINGULIER= 'NON'); DEP0 = RESOUDRE(MATR_FACT= RIGICOMB, CHAM_NO=F_0); The solution field DEP0 will therefore be the initial state of the transient dynamic analysis which follows. 4.5 Transient solution The operator DYNA_NON_LINE (U4.53.01 , R5.05.05) is used as follows: RESU=DYNA_NON_LINE(MODELE=MODELE, CHAM_MATER=CHMAT, CARA_ELEM=CARAELEM, EXCIT=(_F(CHARGE=CONDLIM,), _F(CHARGE=PESA,), _F(CHARGE=PRESSHYD, FONC_MULT=FONCMUL0, TYPE_CHARGE='SUIV',), _F(CHARGE=CHARG_SE, FONC_MULT=ACCELERX,),), COMPORTEMENT=(_F(RELATION='ELAS', DEFORMATION='PETIT_REAC', GROUP_MA=('FLUID0','FOND','PLANCENT', 'IFLUSTRU','SURFLIBR',),), _F(RELATION='ELAS', DEFORMATION='PETIT_REAC', GROUP_MA='ANNEAU',), _F(RELATION='VMIS_ISOT_TRAC', DEFORMATION='PETIT_REAC', GROUP_MA=('SURF0','SURF1', 'SURF2','SURF3',),),), ETAT_INIT=_F(INST_ETAT_INIT=0.0, DEPL=DEP0,), INCREMENT=_F(LIST_INST=LINST,), SCHEMA_TEMPS=_F(SCHEMA='HHT', ALPHA=-0.1, FORMULATION='DEPLACEMENT',), NEWTON=_F(REAC_INCR=1, MATRICE='TANGENTE',REAC_ITER=1,), SOLVEUR=_F(STOP_SINGULIER='NON',), CONVERGENCE=_F(RESI_GLOB_RELA=1.e-05, ITER_GLOB_MAXI=20, ARRET='OUI',), ARCHIVAGE=_F(LIST_INST=LARCH),); The solution is carried out in updated Lagrangian (option DEFORMATION='PETIT_REAC') because the fluid domain is in small perturbations on each step. One must therefore check that the time step is small enough for this hypothesis to be verified. A time-integration scheme of modified average-acceleration type is used (SCHEMA='HHT', ALPHA=-0.1) with numerical damping in order to stabilise the solution and to facilitate convergence. Test case FDNV100 V8.03.100 presents the analysis of a rectangular vessel full of water with a flexible wall. The modelling implemented is very close to that used here for the large tanks. 4.6 Use of the non-linear stability criterion One can also use a stability criterion just as in quasi-statics. The presence of the fluid however requires a few specific options. Indeed, the global assembled stiffness matrix of the coupled fluid-structure problem is intrinsically singular (cf. documentation R4.02.02) at the level of the fluid degrees of freedom. These degrees of freedom must therefore be excluded from the stability analysis, but the stiffness matrix must also be modified (as well as the geometric stiffness matrix when it is used). To do this, the following keywords must be supplied, under CRIT_STAB: - MODI_RIGI = 'OUI', - DDL_EXCLUS=('PHI','PRES','DH',). The list of excluded degrees of freedom must include all the types of degrees of freedom linked to the fluid model: in the example of test case FDNV100 one therefore has the potential PHI, the pressure PRES and the vertical displacement at the free surface DH. If this treatment is not carried out, then the call to CRIT_STAB will abort because of a singular matrix and no shift strategy could overcome this. In quasi-statics, this problem does not arise because the coupled fluid-structure modelling then has no meaning. 5 Bibliography 1. Goubet: Seismic design / verification of large flat-bottom tanks . u2.06.13 General advice on the use of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE u2.06.13 General advice on the use of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE Summary: This document presents the use of transient solution methods (implicit or explicit) for the numerical simulation of non-linear dynamic problems on the physical basis. The general-purpose reference operator for this type of analysis is called DYNA_NON_LINE and its correct use will be made easier by respecting a few rules of good practice described in this document. This advice on use covers: - the correct definition of the model in the dynamic sense (including the initial conditions and the boundary conditions), - the definition of the discretisation, including the choice of the time scheme (R5.05.05, and also see u2.06.13-Bibliographie), - the choice of the damping models, - a few pieces of advice on post-processing. Given the great diversity of non-linear problems, the user will find it very useful to complete this reading with other, more specific references: - U2.06.03: on the modelling of damping, - U2.06.05: for soil-structure interaction (linear and non-linear), - U2.06.09: for single- and multi-support excitation in the seismic analysis of equipment in particular, - U2.06.10: on the specific features of civil-engineering studies under seismic loading, - U2.06.11: for the use of coupled fluid-structure models with DYNA_NON_LINE, - U2.04.07: use of DYNA_NON_LINE to solve problems in slow evolution which are strongly non-linear and which have difficulty converging with STAT_NON_LINE (see the bibliography), - U2.07.04: for the non-linear transient dynamics of a model partially reduced by dynamic condensation with DYNA_NON_LINE, - U2.06.32: for the modelling of rotating machines. Reading documentation U2.04.01, which gives advice on the use of the operator STAT_NON_LINE, is also strongly recommended, because the present document will mainly go deeper into the specific features linked to dynamics. All the aspects common to STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE which are detailed in documentation U2.04.01, such as the choice of the parameters of the Newton algorithm, remain valid in dynamics and are therefore not repeated here. 1 Introduction In order to have as fine an evaluation as possible of the response of a mechanical system to a given set of loadings, it can prove indispensable to take into account the non-linearities and the dynamic phenomena. Usually, one can distinguish two lines of evolution of the numerical methods in order to arrive at this: - on the one hand, the classical linear dynamic analyses (often on a modal basis) are called into question by the possible appearance of non-linearities (material, contact/friction or large transformations) which require the use of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE (the operator DYNA_VIBRA in transient analysis on a modal basis accepts only local non-linearities, for example of shock-node type), - on the other hand, one may question the validity and the limits of application of the non-linear quasi-static approaches (operator STAT_NON_LINE), when the evolution of the solution can be subjected to transient phenomena whose time scale becomes small compared with the natural characteristics of the structure. In the first case, the user therefore starts from a model which is relevant for linear dynamics and which must be enriched correctly for the taking into account of the non-linearities. In the second case, it is rather the reverse: the user starts from a model which is relevant in non-linear quasi-statics and which it is appropriate to adapt to dynamics. This documentation will attempt to guide users who are potentially faced with these two situations. Given the very great variety of problems liable to be addressed, the rules proposed here are necessarily fairly general and it is highly probable that case-by-case adjustments for specific problems will be indispensable. It is totally illusory to think that, even if all the specifications of this document are respected, the non-linear analysis will proceed without any surprise… The work of expert assessment remains unavoidable! As a preliminary to reading this documentation it is strongly recommended to have read the reference documentations of the operators STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE : R5.03.01 and R5.05.05. Indeed, the theoretical aspects will be little detailed here because they are already addressed in these two reference documents. This documentation is completed by other, more specific references: 1. U2.06.03: on the modelling of damping, 2. U2.06.05: for soil-structure interaction (linear and non-linear), 3. U2.06.09: for single- and multi-support excitation in the seismic analysis of equipment in particular, 4. U2.06.10: on the specific features of civil-engineering studies under seismic loading, 5. U2.06.11: for the use of coupled fluid-structure models with DYNA_NON_LINE , 6. U2.04.07: use of DYNA_NON_LINE to solve problems in slow evolution which are strongly non-linear and which have difficulty converging with STAT_NON_LINE (see the bibliography), 7. U2.07.04: for the non-linear transient dynamics of a model partially reduced by dynamic condensation with DYNA_NON_LINE , 8. U2.06.32: for the modelling of rotating machines. Reading documentation U2.04.01, which gives advice on the use of the operator STAT_NON_LINE , is also strongly recommended, because the present document will mainly go deeper into the specific features linked to dynamics. All the aspects common to STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE which are detailed in documentation U2.04.01, such as the choice of the parameters of the Newton algorithm, remain valid in dynamics and are therefore not repeated here. 2 Definition of a problem suited to transient dynamics In this chapter, advice will be proposed for the setting up of the modelling of a problem in mechanics whose non-linear transient numerical simulation one wishes to carry out with Code_Aster . The following chapter will deal with the discretisation in space and in time, whereas in this chapter only the continuous model will be addressed. The non-linearities in transient dynamics with DYNA_NON_LINE are: the large displacements and the large transformations, the non-linear constitutive relations (plasticity, damage, viscoplasticity...), the interface non-linearities: frictional contact, collisions... 2.1 Model The first step is the definition of a model consistent with the hypothesis of transient evolution. Thus, since any mechanical system must not have a mode with zero kinetic energy, one should make sure that the density is defined at every point of the continuous model. Likewise, if one wants to introduce discrete elements in order to simulate solid bodies, one must associate a mass with them. Likewise, for finite elements of shell or plate type, the user may have to make sure that all the degrees of freedom, in particular the rotations, have an associated mass term. In order to check this condition, it is advised to specify the option INER_ROTA='OUI' when calling the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM for all the COQUE models. Certain modellings which have no mass matrix (this computation has not been programmed) cannot be used directly with DYNA_NON_LINE, such as the non-local models. This difficulty can be got round by superimposing on them a classical model making it possible to represent the kinetic energy (mass matrix): the two models being supported by the same nodes. The use of certain devices which are current in quasi-statics, such as very stiff zones (a fictitious material having a very large Young's modulus) in order to take into account reinforcements which one does not wish to represent finely from the geometric point of view, for example, can generate disturbances in dynamics. Indeed, this very stiff material can generate high-frequency oscillations and wave propagations whose speed is non-physical. Moreover, with an explicit time scheme, these very stiff zones risk causing the value of the critical time step to drop (CFL stability condition, cf. R5.05.05). In addition to the inertial contribution, the system will have a dissipative contribution, and therefore a damping one. In the non-linear regime, dissipation can be due to the constitutive relation (plasticity…), to friction in the links… Usually, the lack of detailed knowledge of all the dissipative mechanisms in the system is compensated by a simplified representation which makes it possible to define a global damping. In Code_Aster , one has available two models of global viscous damping (which one can associate in the modelling with dampers on discrete elements, cf. command AFFE_CARA_ELEM (factor keyword DISCRET or DISCRET_2D, etc...): the Rayleigh model and modal damping. In practice, in both cases, it is indispensable to have carried out a prior modal analysis. Indeed, the modal damping is defined on the modes, which are then arguments of DYNA_NON_LINE. For Rayleigh damping, the only way of grasping its physical meaning simply is to recalibrate it on values of modal damping (which can come from experimental results). Rayleigh damping will be returned to in more detail in the following chapter, u2.06.13-Discretisation_du_probleme_continu. In a general manner, one must keep in mind that all the global damping models were designed for the linear cases and that they then serve to take into account certain dissipative phenomena such as friction or imperfect links. Therefore, if one adds to the model the taking into account of these non-linearities, while keeping the global damping values recalibrated on a linear approach, this can lead to having too much dissipation in the non-linear system, in particular at low frequencies. Ideally, the taking into account of all the non-linearities, associated with a fine discretisation of the system, ought to make it possible not to have to use in addition a blanket global damping. In reality, one is obliged to neglect certain non-linear aspects for reasons of CPU cost and/or of lack of knowledge of the mechanisms brought into play, and in this case the global damping has its role to play. Documentation U2.06.03 presents its use in more detail. 2.2 Boundary conditions and excitations The first decision to be taken in order to solve the transient is the choice of the configuration frame (the displacement field): the general case is a Galilean frame (absolute frame). In frequent cases where the system is driven in a rigid translation motion, one will be able to solve the transient in the relative frame. The analysis will be carried out with a fixed base; see u2.06.13-Mono_appui. If the system is loaded by various supports excited differently, one is in the case u2.06.13-Multi_appuis and one will have to solve the transient in the absolute frame (unless the constitutive behaviour is entirely linear elastic under the small-perturbation hypothesis, HPP). In quasi-statics, it is current to impose boundary conditions whose evolutions in time are simple functions to define, such as ramps or continuous functions which are piecewise affine. It is frequent that in dynamics the excitations are described by the product of a function of space and of a ramp or a function of time (or a signal in time). The factor keyword EXCIT will thus be used. It is recommended to define this signal in time so that it starts and finishes at zero. It can also be useful for the list of time instants chosen for the transient with DYNA_NON_LINE to last longer than the imposed signal, so as to let the system under study return to rest through the effect of the damping which has been chosen. In dynamics, if one wants to avoid parasitic oscillations of the solution, one must absolutely impose quantities which are sufficiently regular in time: therefore at least continuously differentiable, piecewise. In order to arrive at this simply, one can choose to define for oneself polynomial functions of time in place of the affine functions. Possible irregularities in the imposed loadings can be partially compensated by the use of a suitable damping model (or in particular thanks to a dissipative time-integration scheme of HHT type; see u2.06.13-Schema_integration_temps). Nevertheless, excessive oscillations in the non-linear regime can irremediably compromise the rest of the analyses, because the solution (including the internal variables) depends on its history. On the diagram u2.06.13-lissage a possible regularisation of an affine curve (in dashed lines) by a curve suited to the dynamic analysis is shown. One can note the necessity, on this example, of having to make the dynamic evolution start at a negative time, if one wants to keep comparable values for the positive time instants (outside the regularisation zones). Smoothing of an imposed evolution in order to adapt it to a transient analysis In all the cases where one can compute the spectrum of the imposed signals, the Shannon rule for defining the sampling is not strict enough for the non-linear analyses. In practice, it is advised to have between 4 and 10 time steps over the shortest period of all the imposed signals. Any insufficient discretisation in time risks being reflected by high-frequency over-oscillations of the solution. There then exists a palliative for this in choosing certain time schemes, but at the risk of introducing too much damping into the system. 2.2.1 Single support Loadings of single-support type (driving by a rigid translation motion), which are currently employed in seismic analyses, are characterised by particular features which it is appropriate to recall here. First of all, the solution, under the single-support hypothesis, is carried out natively in the relative frame linked to the support (basemat...). In post-processing, one must therefore recombine with the driving motion in order to obtain the absolute kinematic fields. For the acceleration, this is in general immediate because the driving acceleration is the known input datum in the form of the accelerograms employed. On the other hand, in order to reconstruct the absolute displacement, one must have available the driving displacement. In the classical case where one has available only accelerograms, one is obliged to integrate twice in time in order to compute the corresponding displacement (this integration can be done with the operator CALC_FONCTION, keyword INTEGRE). The user must then be very attentive to the problems of the numerical integration of sampled signals, such as integration constants which can induce a drift or oscillations at very low frequency. The operator CALC_FONCTION has options for correcting these drifts (keyword CORR_DEPL and CORR_ACCE ), but it is very strongly recommended to check carefully the quality of the final integrated result because, in certain cases, these corrections are insufficient, including the correction by high-pass filtering of CALC_FONCTION (with CORR_ACCE , METHODE = 'FILTRAGE' ). A complementary specific correction is then indispensable. Going through the FFT in order to carry out the integration in frequency can then constitute a good alternative, making it possible to arrive at integrated signals which are more correct or at least easier to correct (just a shift by a constant, for example, but without drift). 2.2.2 Multiple supports Among the types of loading which can require an adaptation to DYNA_NON_LINE, one can mention the case of multiple supports (in imposed accelerations on the supports) for seismic studies. This method, originally developed for transient analyses under the linear hypothesis, relies on the definition of elastic static modes at the supports. In the non-linear regime, as long as these modes remain relevant, that is to say that the non-linearities are weak enough not to require their updating, the usual multi-support approach remains acceptable. On the other hand, in the general case, one must call into question the use of elastic static modes computed initially. In this case, in order to avoid their use, the multi-support loading must be taken into account by imposing at the supports the displacements corresponding to the integration of the accelerograms which are input data of the usual linear multi-support method. The method is then rigorous, whatever the type of non-linearity, but the integration of the accelerograms must be carried out with care, so as not to arrive at incorrect signals. Apart from the sampling, it is indispensable, among other things, to check the absence of drift of the signal (a correction can be done with the option CORR_ACCE of CALC_FONCTION). In Code_Aster , one can carry out this integration easily by making use of the FFT which is available in CALC_FONCTION. It is also the occasion to analyse the frequency content of the signal. One then has the relation, in the frequency domain: U=-A/{\omega}^{2} . One can also make use of the option INTEGRE of CALC_FONCTION. For more information on the implementation of loadings of single- or multi-support type, reading documentations U2.06.09 and U2.06.10 is entirely appropriate. 2.2.3 Contact and collisions The loadings coming from contact by penalisation can also disturb the solution by high-frequency oscillations, which are linked to the value of the penalisation coefficient. These artefacts can be reduced with the use of a time-integration scheme which is dissipative at high frequencies. One can also provide oneself with a list of analysis time instants which manages the difficulties by subdivision, cf. the command DEFI_LIST_INST with the factor keyword ECHEC= _F(EVENEMENT = 'DELTA_GRANDEUR', ...) , of “event-driven” type, by testing whether the increment of a component of a field (of velocity, for example, at the contact point) exceeds a fixed threshold. If one wants to use an explicit time-integration scheme, too large a penalisation coefficient will lead to a drop in the critical time step. Compared with statics, it can prove obligatory to lower the penalisation coefficient, with the drawback of increasing the interpenetration of the solids during contact. One may consult the test cases: sdnv100, impact of a beam on a rigid wall V5.03.100, sdnv105, rocking of a block on a table V5.03.105, sdnv301, Hertzian collision of two elastic spheres V5.03.301. Note For the explicit time schemes ():ref:u2.06.13-Schema_integration_temps), if one imposes displacement boundary conditions which evolve in the course of time, one must take into account the fact that these conditions are in fact imposed in acceleration in the explicit case (because it is the primal unknown). This means that one must enter into DYNA_NON_LINE the second derivative of the displacement signal that one wants to impose. This evolution of the imposed displacement must therefore be differentiable at least twice in time 2.3 Initial conditions In the same logic as for the boundary conditions, it is recommended to avoid singular initial conditions, such as those which can be generated by imposed loadings having evolutions in time of Dirac or Heaviside type. Regular conditions will be favoured, therefore with derivatives (first and if possible second) in time which are zero at {t}_{0} . If one wants to start from a prestressed (non-virgin) state, it is entirely possible and recommended to chain a dynamic analysis onto a quasi-static analysis. In this case, the initial state (factor keyword ETAT_INIT) must then be perfectly equilibrated (displacements, stresses, internal variables, forces applied at this time instant) and, subject to regularity in the conditions imposed at the moment of the passage from statics to dynamics, the dynamic excitation having to start with a zero signal, the transient solution must not present non-physical oscillations. This method of chaining from quasi-statics to dynamics allows the easy taking into account of all the preloads, such as for example gravity. For example, in a release simulation, with a non-zero imposed initial displacement, one must then supply the stresses and internal variables corresponding to this time instant. If one had wanted to take this prestressed initial state into account with only a dynamic solution, it would have been necessary to introduce a strong initial damping and to wait until the oscillations had dissipated in order to have the prestressed static state. One can then continue the analysis with the physical damping. One is obliged to proceed in this way when one uses an analysis code which does not treat non-linear quasi-statics ( cf. Europlexus, see [bib2]_). In certain situations, one must chain a simulation in statics, with blocked boundary conditions, and then in dynamics under the action of a field of incident waves with absorbing and released boundary conditions. One will consult U2.04.08. During the initialisation of the integration scheme for the non-linear transient analysis, one therefore seeks to invert the mass matrix. If it is singular, then a message warns the user and the initial acceleration is arbitrarily set to zero. One can then fear the presence of parasitic oscillations at the beginning of the transient; one can reduce them by adopting a smaller time step right at the beginning of the transient. In a general manner the non-invertibility of the mass matrix must lead the user to check the model, unless it is intentional. During restarts, two aspects are sensitive. On the one hand, it is better to avoid having too sudden variations of the time step: the consistency of the solution at the passage of the restart would be affected by it. A strong change of time step can be seen as a filter. A large time step constitutes a low-pass filter of a solution initially computed with a fine time step. On the other hand, if one wants to change the type of time scheme, certain rules are to be respected. If one wants to pass from an implicit time-integration method (quasi-static or dynamic) to an explicit scheme, the restart will be mathematically valid because the initial state will be equilibrated (to within the residual). On the other hand, the direct reverse switch introduces an error because the initial state, coming from an explicit analysis, will not respect equilibrium in the implicit sense. Indeed, this operator will seek to recheck equilibrium: one solves the equilibrium by inverting the mass matrix, which gives the initial acceleration. If this field is non-zero, this reflects the failure to verify, in the static sense, the equilibrium, at the initial time instant. In practice, this inaccuracy can generate oscillations of the solution (overshooting phenomenon). In a more subtle manner, the switch from the \theta -scheme to a second-order scheme such as the complete average acceleration NEWMARK or HHT will introduce a small error on the acceleration terms, which can disturb the numerical solution. If, despite everything, one wants to make these switches which induce errors, one can minimise the inaccuracies by choosing to make these switches during phases in which the excitation, and therefore the solution, evolves little. In summary: | Origin | Destination | Possible | | --- | --- | --- | | STAT_NON_LINE | DYNA_NON_LINE | yes | | DYNA_NON_LINE with an implicit time scheme | DYNA_NON_LINE | yes | | DYNA_NON_LINE with an explicit time scheme | DYNA_NON_LINE with an explicit time scheme | yes | | DYNA_NON_LINE with an explicit time scheme | DYNA_NON_LINE with an implicit time scheme | no | 3 Discretisation of the continuous problem In addition to the advice previously given for the continuous model, this chapter will list the most important aspects to be respected in order to obtain a discretised model suited to DYNA_NON_LINE. 3.1 Mesh As a preliminary to the transient analysis, it is strongly recommended to carry out a modal analysis (with CALC_MODES), in order to obtain modal information which will make it possible to qualify the quality of the model in dynamics and to adjust certain parameters. The objective not being to go into the details of modal analysis, a few rules can nevertheless be recalled. In general, one can define for oneself a cut-off frequency for the problem to be studied, and therefore an associated modal truncation. The proper representation of all the modes of this truncated basis can give indications of the mesh-cell sizes to be employed, in addition to the considerations already taken into account for the quasi-static analyses. Roughly, about ten mesh cells per smallest wavelength is sufficient (to be adjusted according to the richness of the finite elements, of course). The modal analysis will also make it possible to check that the model is free of problems such as contributions to the inertia or to the stiffness that are not defined. Finally, it is indispensable for the use of modal damping in DYNA_NON_LINE or for recalibrating the Rayleigh damping, as will be seen in what follows ( cf. u2.06.13-Mod_lisation_de_l_amortissement). In a manner much more marked than for the quasi-static analyses, the dynamic solution will cope rather badly with meshes presenting sudden variations in finite-element sizes. Indeed, these zones can be likened to interfaces which will disturb the propagation of the waves. One can then see reflected waves appear which are superimposed on the “physical” wave trains. Likewise, if one wants a good representation of the waves, the mesh must be fine over the whole path of the waves: one cannot be content with refining only in certain non-linear zones. If a wave leaves a finely meshed zone in order to go towards a more coarsely meshed zone, it will undergo a filter and the wave reflected by the opposite boundary risks being strongly disturbed, or even disappearing. If one is interested only in short durations, therefore before any return of a wave onto the finely meshed zone, then this error on the reflected wave is not penalising. On the other hand, if one wants to compute solutions over longer durations, the error committed may be non-negligible. Finally, unlike the quasi-static case, time has a physical meaning and the time scales that one wants to analyse are strongly coupled to the spatial scales of the discretised problem. Thus, the time step is linked to the mesh-cell size, which one can perceive immediately with the notion of the CFL stability condition for the explicit schemes. 3.2 Time-integration scheme Time having a physical meaning in dynamics, the quality of its discretisation is all the more sensitive for that. An integration scheme has the role of expressing by an approximate expression two relations between the quantities ( DEPL , VITE , ACCE ) at the previous time instant and those at the following time instant. The equations of motion constitute the third set of equations which makes it possible to close the system to be solved. According to the principal quantity ( DEPL , VITE , ACCE ) which one chooses as the driver in order to express these equations, one adopts a type of FORMULATION : DEPLACEMENT , VITESSE , ACCELERATION . A few rules can be stated for the choice of the time step: - the evolution of the imposed loadings must be sampled sufficiently finely (between 5 and 10 time steps per shortest period of the signals considered), - the modal behaviour of the structure must be well represented (as above, one must have between 5 and 10 time steps per lowest period of the modes considered up to the cut-off frequency); in particular, the frequency distortion caused by the time-integration scheme must be limited: the choice of taking between 5 and 10 time steps per lowest period of the modes considered up to the cut-off frequency ensures a frequency distortion of less than one per cent. Given the low-frequency character, or at best medium-frequency character, of most of the problems that one can address here, these two rules are, in general, not very penalising. The choice of the time-integration scheme and of its parameters is made with the factor keyword: SCHEMA_TEMPS =_F(…) . Test cases SDLD31 V2.01.031 and SDLD32 V2.01.032 offer a comparison of the time-integration schemes proposed in DYNA_NON_LINE and in DYNA_VIBRA on simple linear systems under harmonic excitation. 3.2.1 Explicit integration scheme With an explicit integration scheme, conditionally stable, dedicated to problems of “fast dynamics” in the presence of transients with a “high-frequency” content, one must in addition respect the Courant stability condition (known as “CFL”, cf. R5.05.05 and u2.06.13-Bibliographie) on pain of numerical divergence (“explosion” of the kinetic energy). In Code_Aster , these schemes are treated in FORMULATION ='ACCELERATION' (one wants to solve by inverting the mass matrix). The mass matrix, which must be invertible, is preferentially chosen in diagonal form ( lumped ) for reasons of performance; this is obtained by the keyword: MASS_DIAG = 'OUI' . The lumped mass matrix makes it possible to correct part of the frequency drift over long durations coming from the error in time induced by the integration scheme. For the structural finite elements, for example DKT/DKTG/DST, it is necessary to specify in AFFE_CARA_ELEM, under the factor keyword COQUE , the simple keyword INER_ROTA = 'OUI' , so as to have non-zero inertia terms over the whole diagonal of the mass matrix, even if they are small, R3.07.03. However, this option not being available for all the finite elements, nor with all the discrete elements, one must then solve with the consistent mass matrix, as in the implicit case. For the finite elements of HM modelling, the mass matrix has zero terms for certain specific degrees of freedom, for example the pressure. In this case too, one must solve with the consistent mass matrix, to which one adds a small contribution of the stiffness matrix with the keyword COEF_MASS_SHIFT . Two explicit schemes are available: - central differences ( DIFF_CENT ), which is non-dissipative, - Tchamwa-Wielgosz ( TCHAMWA ), which is dissipative, in a manner comparable to HHT. It is recommended to begin by using a non-dissipative scheme. The automatic computation of the Courant condition on a modal basis is exact and will always be valid whatever the type of finite element used. For the explicit integration scheme of central differences DIFF_CENT , the critical time step is worth 2/{\omega}_{max} where {\omega}_{max} is the highest natural angular frequency of the discretised system. The presence of shock stiffnesses associated with the penalised modelling of frictional or frictionless contact significantly increases this highest natural angular frequency. In the presence of physical damping (reduced damping coefficient \xi ) the critical time step has the expression: 2 \left(\sqrt{1+\xi^2}-\xi\right)/{\omega}_{max} . One can compute this angular frequency with CALC_MODES by choosing the option 'PLUS_GRANDE' (or with the option PLUS_PETITE by inverting the roles of the mass matrix and of the stiffness matrix). For the TCHAMWA scheme of dissipative explicit integration of Tchamwa-Wielgosz (see [bib11]_), the critical time step is slightly smaller than that of the DIFF_CENT scheme and decreases when one increases the numerical damping linked to the scheme (parameter PHI , whose default value is 1.05 ). The Courant stability condition can also be approximated, at least on models with solid finite elements, by \Delta t={l}_{\min}/c where {l}_{\min} is the smallest length of the discretised model and c the speed of the tension waves at the point considered. The operator DYNA_NON_LINE makes use of this formula in order to give an approximation of the Courant stability condition. There are however certain limitations: 1. one does not know how to compute automatically the Courant stability condition associated with the presence of discrete springs (it is not programmed), 2. one does not correct the formula for the structural finite elements (shells, plates and beams). There can therefore exist cases where the value returned is not a lower bound of the true Courant condition. Therefore, in the event of divergence, it is appropriate to reduce the time step. Moreover, the computation of the Courant stability condition is not updated and is done only at the beginning of the analysis, being based on the speed of the elastic waves for the initial state. If the elastic modulus decreases (damage), the initial Courant stability condition can become too severe. There is no risk of divergence (except for materials whose elastic modulus could increase), but the CPU time could be reduced a little by updating the Courant stability condition (as is done in the codes dedicated to fast dynamics, such as Europlexus [bib2]_). For most structures, the Courant stability condition is very penalising: the wave speed often being of the order of a few thousand m/s , one arrives at time steps of less than {10}^{-5}s , for finite-element dimensions chosen for usual structures. This therefore imposes a very high total number of time instants in order to describe the transient, and therefore produces a considerable volume of results. If one solves the problem on a reduced modal basis (factor keyword PROJ_MODAL =_F() ), then the drawback of the very small critical time step for an explicit scheme disappears. Indeed, the limiting time step will be directly proportional to the smallest natural period of the truncated modal basis. One has the relation: \Delta t=2/\omega where \omega is the highest natural angular frequency of the system. The more the modal basis is truncated, the larger the associated critical time step will be. Moreover, the computation of the Courant condition is then immediate because one knows explicitly all the angular frequencies of the basis, and therefore the highest one in particular. With an explicit scheme, it is recommended to place oneself slightly below the Courant condition: between 0.5 and 0.7 times the Courant stability condition. There will be no subdivision of the time step on account of non-convergence at the scale of the global equilibrium: the user remains the sole master of the time step throughout the analysis. On the other hand, via the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT, cf. U4.51.11, the user indicates the requirements for the integration of the non-linear constitutive law, which can lead to the automatic subdivision defined in the command DEFI_LIST_INST. - if one imposes displacement boundary conditions which evolve in the course of time, one must take into account the fact that these conditions are in fact imposed in acceleration in the explicit case (because it is the primal unknown). This means that one must enter into DYNA_NON_LINE the second derivative of the displacement signal that one wants to impose. This evolution of the imposed displacement must therefore be differentiable at least twice in time - The use of quadratic finite elements is not recommended in the explicit case: indeed, parasitic oscillations can appear on the solution fields (displacement or stresses). This phenomenon can also be amplified by the joint use of the consistent mass matrix - For the verification of the plane-stress hypothesis, if one uses the de Borst method, the associated global iterative process is then blocked at the first iteration (unlike the implicit case). This can lead to a slight inaccuracy of the results, tempered by the fact that, the time step being in any case very small, the non-planarity of the stresses can only be very moderate. However, it is entirely possible to use the local version of the de Borst algorithm by means of the keyword ITER_CPLAN_MAXI under the factor keyword COMPORTEMENT , cf. Non-linear constitutive behaviours. Indeed, these local iterations do take place in the explicit case, with an associated extra computational cost. Notes 3.2.2 Implicit integration scheme With an implicit integration scheme, which makes it possible to respect as well as possible the non-linear dynamic equilibrium conditions, dedicated to problems of “slow dynamics” in the presence of transients with a “low-frequency” content, in a phase of setting up the transient simulation, it is recommended to make a comparison of the results obtained for two choices of values of the time step. In the implicit case, the schemes proposed are unconditionally stable, but this does not mean that one can take an arbitrary time step! Too large a step will not lead to a divergence, but the error on the solution, such as the frequency distortion, will obviously be large. These schemes are accessible in FORMULATION="DEPLACEMENT" , FORMULATION ="VITESSE" , FORMULATION ="ACCELERATION" . The FORMULATION ="DEPLACEMENT" is entirely natural and is favoured in the case of material non-linearities, because the internal forces result from the treatment of the constitutive relation expressed from the strains, themselves obtained with the displacement field. It is not possible to use a lumped mass matrix with these schemes. It is recommended to ensure a uniform and regular sampling of the time step as far as possible. However, in the presence of constitutive non-linearities, it is neither possible nor desirable to avoid the temporal resubdivision in the event of non-convergence of the Newton algorithm, driven by the step-subdivision directives which one will have defined in the command DEFI_LIST_INST. One can classify the implicit schemes in two categories: - average acceleration ( NEWMARK ), of order 2 and which brings no numerical dissipation: to be used first, - complete HHT ( MODI_EQUI = 'OUI' , the default option), which remains of order 2, unlike the case of the modified average acceleration. If one desires more damping in the medium-frequency range, then the modified average-acceleration scheme can be employed with MODI_EQUI = 'NON' , and the scheme becomes of order 1. The complete HHT scheme ( MODI_EQUI = 'OUI' ) is specifically developed in order to introduce a high-frequency numerical damping and therefore not to disturb the low-frequency physical response. The damping is driven directly by the parameter ALPHA of the scheme, If one observes high-frequency oscillations in the numerical solution (roughly, oscillations whose period is of the order of a few time steps), one will prefer to choose the complete HHT scheme, beginning with a value of the order of –0,1 for the parameter ALPHA . A value of –0,3 constitutes an upper limit that is still usable. It is strongly recommended to carry out a parametric study on the value of the parameter ALPHA in order to choose the value closest to zero which makes it possible to obtain a correct solution without numerical over-damping. One will refer to paragraph §5.4 of R5.05.05. The implicit schemes are to be used, as a priority, with a formulation in displacements: FORMULATION = 'DEPLACEMENT' . 3.2.3 Summary for the choice of the integration scheme The following table summarises the essential points. | name | NEWMARK | HHT | DIFF_CENT | TCHAMWA | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | type | implicit | implicit | explicit | explicit | | | applications | simulations of “long duration” for low-frequency excitations | likewise | short-duration simulations | likewise | | | FORMULATION | "DEPLACEMENT" | "DEPLACEMENT" | "ACCELERATION" | "ACCELERATION" | | | mass matrix | consistent | consistent | diagonal preferentially | diagonal preferentially | | | stability | unconditional | unconditional | conditional | conditional | | | order | order 2 except if \gamma \neq 1/2 | order 2 | order 2 | order 1 | | | numerical dissipation | no if \gamma=1/2 and \beta=1/4 | yes at HF if \alpha 1 | | | frequency distortion | in -{(\omega_{max} \Delta t)}^2 | in -(\omega_{max} \Delta t)^2 | in +(\omega_{max} \Delta t)^2 | | | | amplitude error | in \omicron (\Delta t )^2 | | in \omicron (\Delta t )^4 | | | | choice of the time step | limit the frequency distortion | limit the frequency distortion | guarantee stability | guarantee stability | | To finish, it should be pointed out that the analytical results on the characteristics (convergence, frequency distortion, error, numerical damping, overshooting…) of the time schemes are obtained for a linear framework. Demonstrations in the non-linear regime are very rare and are confined to particular cases. In practice, certain characteristics of the schemes can deteriorate in the non-linear regime.
