This can explain why it is not necessarily indispensable to use the scheme which, in the linear regime, will have exceptional performance (order 4…), but that it is better to favour simpler and more robust schemes, in particular with high-frequency numerical dissipation. Likewise, in the non-linear regime, the precise evaluation of the Courant stability condition of an explicit scheme requires an updating of its computation. Indeed, the Courant stability condition computed initially may not be conservative (for example if certain finite elements see their size decrease, or if shocks occur, with a modelling by penalisation). This computation is not updated and, in the event of divergence, it is recommended to reduce the time step and to re-run the analysis. The results of linear analysis on the schemes nevertheless constitute a solid basis for their analysis ( cf. R5.05.05 and u2.06.13-Bibliographie), while knowing that the non-linearities can disturb the behaviour of the schemes. The time step to be imposed can judiciously be bounded: - from above, by the time step to be respected in order to discretise well the evolutions of the imposed loadings and in order to represent well the highest natural frequency of the system which one wants to take into account, - from below, by the Courant stability condition, in the sense that it has of the shortest time for which a piece of information can pass from one node of the mesh cell to another. Between these bounds, it is indispensable to carry out a parametric study in order to make sure of the proper convergence of the numerical solution. The lower bound gives crucial information as to the maximum subdivisions of the time step which must be authorised when the algorithm does not converge. Letting the time step subdivide until it goes markedly below the Courant stability condition may be of no use, because the computed solution then risks undergoing a numerical pollution which will not facilitate convergence. Still in connection with the iterations for the verification of equilibrium at each step, one can note that, in most cases, if the time step is sufficiently fine, the maximum number of iterations to convergence remains moderate: often of the order of 10, whereas in quasi-statics one can currently exceed these values. Therefore, the idea consists in saying that the time step is of a good order of magnitude if the number of iterations to convergence remains moderate. If this number increases, one can attempt to reduce the step slightly, while always respecting the bounds defined above. There nevertheless exist cases where one can, at certain points, need to authorise more iterations during a few steps. To finish, if one is obliged to change time scheme in order to use a dissipative scheme, such as HHT, it is indispensable to carry out a parametric study on this damping. Indeed, the risk of introducing too great a dissipation is not negligible, especially with the modified average-acceleration scheme. The following paragraph will return to this point. 3.3 Initial conditions Regular initial conditions will be favoured: displacements and velocities differentiable at t=t_0 , a state of stresses in equilibrium at t=t_0 , for example resulting from a quasi-static analysis with STAT_NON_LINE. Indeed, many time schemes evaluate a predictor of the initial acceleration from the initial state, by inverting the mass matrix (if this can be done): if this initial acceleration is excessive, the disturbance can propagate over the transient, especially if the damping is weak, and generate parasitic oscillations of the solution (“overshooting”). If the mass matrix is not invertible, see section u2.06.13-Modification_de_la_matrice_de_masse. 3.4 Modelling of the damping The order of introduction and of use of the dissipation in a modelling of a structure discretised by finite elements is the following: 1. intrinsic dissipation linked to the irreversible non-linear constitutive relations of the constituent materials assigned to the support mesh cells of the finite elements, cf. factor keyword COMPORTEMENT=_F(RELATION='...') cf. Non-linear constitutive behaviours. These constitutive models can dissipate energy in the course of cycles in strain-stress (for example in elastoplasticity) and/or in strain-rate–stress (for example in non-linear viscoelasticity, in viscoplasticity), 2. intrinsic dissipation linked to the irreversible non-linear constitutive relations of the links on interfaces (collision, friction...): cf. factor keyword COMPORTEMENT with, as relations: DIS_CHOC , DIS_CONTACT , CHOC_ENDO , CHOC_ENDO_PENA , with the help of the parameters AMOR_NOR and AMOR_TAN of the corresponding materials, cf. R5.03.17 and AFFE_CARA_ELEM, which dissipate energy in the course of cycles in displacement-jump–force (for example in elastoplasticity) and/or in displacement-jump-rate–force. Damping forces proportional to the velocity on these interfaces are added to the equations of motion, as a function of the state of activation or otherwise of the frictional contact, without going through a contribution to the damping matrix, 3. dissipation linked to the linear viscous damping assigned to discrete elements, cf. command AFFE_CARA_ELEM (factor keyword DISCRET or DISCRET_2D , keyword CARA = ’A_T_D_N’ , etc...), 4. global dissipation of structural-damping type (Rayleigh or modal, also called Wilson & Penzien, which one can use simultaneously), 5. dissipation linked to the absorbing boundaries (Sommerfeld condition modelled with paraxial finite elements of order 0) of an elastic domain or of a perfect fluid domain ( 3D_ABSO , D_PLAN_ABSO , 3D_FLUI_ABSO , FLUI_ABSO , 2D_FLUI_ABSO , AXIS_FLUI_ABSO ), cf. R4.02.05, 6. numerical dissipation brought by the time scheme. Ideally, the first categories ought to be sufficient, but in practice, for reasons of simplification of the modelling, it is often indispensable to add structural damping, the damping brought by the time scheme being the last resort. Only the use of structural damping and that linked to the time-integration scheme will be addressed here (for more information on this point, the reader may refer to documentation U2.06.03). The global dissipation of structural-damping type is taken into account by modal damping or by Rayleigh damping. The transient solution with DYNA_NON_LINE uses: - the global damping matrix assembling by summation all the contributions: the global Rayleigh damping, the linear viscous damping assigned to discrete elements, the finite elements of absorbing boundaries (paraxial of order 0), solid and fluid, the constant matrix defined for the condensed substructures (dynamic macro-elements), and the matrix which DYNA_NON_LINE assembles from an elementary damping matrix built outside the operator in order to be able to add (accumulate) possibly a damping of another nature, for example IMPE_MECA in the U-P formulation of perfect-fluid–structure interaction. It is the purpose of the optional keyword MATR_ELEM_AMOR to supply it to DYNA_NON_LINE . See test case zzzz420a, - the vector of viscous forces assembling all the contributions: modal damping. It is possible to use at the same time the global Rayleigh damping, as well as the modal damping and also the numerical damping of the time scheme. In these cases of combinations of several sources of damping (without counting the material dissipation due to the constitutive relation chosen or the frictional contact), the user must check the global consistency of the dissipation and therefore not risk counting the damping several times on one and the same zone. For example, if one wishes to combine global damping (Rayleigh or modal) and material dissipation, in general the regulations impose lowering the value of the global damping compared with a purely elastic analysis. One will note, cf. R4.02.05, that one must not employ paraxial finite elements in the case MULTI_APPUI . Another example: the case of a building on seismic isolation bearings. If one wants to represent the dissipation of the bearings by a local model (non-linear law or dampers) and the damping of the building by modal damping, one will have to check that one does not introduce modal damping on the modes which mainly work the bearings, such as the horizontal rigid-body modes (two translations and the rotation about the vertical axis). Let us finally recall that the more one multiplies the sources of dissipation, the more arduous their control and their physical interpretation will be. 3.4.1 Structural damping In non-linear transient dynamics, Code_Aster offers two types of modellings of this type: 1. modal damping (of Wilson & Penzien), defined in a uniform manner over the whole of the finite-element model, after having established a reduced modal basis over a given representative frequency band, intervening in the form of assembled viscous forces, linear in the velocity vector, 2. global Rayleigh damping, defined according to the assignment of the materials on the mesh, intervening in the form of an assembled matrix carrying out the linear relation between the viscous forces and the velocity vector. For a linear system with two degrees of freedom these two modellings give the same viscous forces if the calibration of the Rayleigh damping is carried out on the two natural frequencies. In the other cases, the viscous forces differ. If one solves the equations of motion in the driven frame, considering a rigid translation driving motion, the driving inertia forces being defined with the command [:ref:CALC_CHAR_SEISME ] (MONO_APPUI= 'OUI'), then the damping is built with the relative velocity vector. One recalls that in non-linear dynamics, cf. R5.05.05, if the motions imposed at the supports are not a rigid-body motion (case MULTI_APPUI ), then one must solve the equations of motion in the absolute (Galilean) frame. 3.4.1.1 Modal damping As regards modal damping, the respect of the three basic rules is insisted upon: - check that the associated modal basis ( MODE_MECA ) is sufficiently complete (containing at a minimum the whole spectrum of the excitation) so as not to have an absence of damping along certain response modes of the structure, - check that all the values of modal damping coefficients ( AMOR_REDUIT / LIST_AMOR ) are indeed positive for all the modes retained ( MODE_MECA ), because any negative value risks leading to a dynamic instability, - the modal damping being treated in an explicit manner in DYNA_NON_LINE (the viscous forces being expressed with the velocities obtained at the previous step), it may be necessary to reduce the time step so that the time integration remains stable, even with a time scheme which is implicit and unconditionally stable. Indeed, one does not compute the assembled damping matrix because it would be full and therefore expensive. This modal basis, serving to define the modal dampings, must imperatively have the same numbering profile as that of the matrices of the dynamic system used during the computation of the response proper. Before use of the modal dampings of the modal basis in the computation of the response, this rule therefore requires, if need be, transforming beforehand this initial modal basis into a new modal basis, whose definition of the boundary conditions is identical to that relating to the computation of the response with DYNA_NON_LINE , thus ensuring the same number and the same position of the Lagrange multipliers of dualisation. This is in particular the case when non-zero imposed displacements are applied for the computation of the response. Test case zzzz113a details the corresponding procedure. If the structure studied is made up of several substructures or subdomains, composed of specific materials, whose reduced damping coefficients differ, one practice consists in the following evaluation of an equivalent modal damping coefficient (for a given mode) according to the rule of RCC-G 1988, ETC-C 2012 (section 1.A.5.4). This modelling is accessible, cf. CALC_AMOR_MODAL (AMOR_INTERNE=_F(...), AMOR_SOL=_F(...),...). One will take care not to have provided for dampers on discrete elements, at the risk of damping twice! 3.4.1.2 Rayleigh damping This modelling uses a global viscous damping matrix {\bf C} as being the assembly, on the finite-element model, of a linear combination of the stiffness and mass matrices. This global damping matrix is diagonalised on the basis of the natural eigenmodes only if the calibration of the Rayleigh parameters is identical throughout the finite-element model. The Rayleigh damping parameters are supplied by the factor keyword ’ELAS’ in the operator DEFI_MATERIAU. {\bf C} = \alpha {\bf K} + \beta {\bf M} Three identification cases are presented here in order to illustrate the effects induced by this modelling: - damping proportional to the inertia characteristics: \alpha =0 \beta ={\beta}_{i} . This case has been very much used in transient solution in the ACCELERATION formulation: if the mass matrix is diagonal, that of the damping still is, and the gain in memory space is obvious. The coefficient \beta can be identified with the experimental reduced damping {\xi}_{i} of the eigenmode ({\rho}_{i},{\omega}_{i}) which participates the most in the response, whence {\beta}_{i}=2{\xi}_{i}{\omega}_{i} . For any other angular frequency one obtains a reduced modal damping \xi ={\beta}_{i}\frac{{\omega}_{i}}{\omega} . The responses on the modes of high order \omega \gg {\omega}_{i} will be very little damped and those on the low-frequency modes \omega <{\omega}_{i} will be too heavily damped. Appearance of the damping proportional to the mass This damping proportional to the mass is the only Rayleigh damping which is easily usable with an explicit integration scheme. It is illustrated on figure u2.06.13-amorPropMass. Indeed, one can show that the introduction of a term proportional to the stiffness leads to a drop in the critical time step (CFL condition). - damping proportional to the stiffness characteristics: \alpha ={\alpha}_{j} \beta =0 . The coefficient can be identified, as previously, from the modal damping {\xi}_{j} associated with the mode ({\rho}_{j},{\omega}_{j}) , whence {\alpha}_{j}=2\frac{{\xi}_{j}}{{\omega}_{j}} . For any other angular frequency one obtains a reduced modal damping \xi ={\alpha}_{j}\frac{\omega}{{\omega}_{j}} . The responses on the high modes \omega \gg {\omega}_{j} are therefore very heavily damped. It is illustrated on figure u2.06.13-amorPropRigi Appearance of the damping proportional to the stiffness - complete proportional damping: \alpha ={\alpha}_{j} \beta ={\beta}_{i} . From an identification on two different natural frequencies ({\rho}_{i},{\omega}_{i}) and ({\rho}_{j},{\omega}_{j}) , one will obtain for any other angular frequency a reduced modal damping \xi ={\alpha}_{j}\frac{\omega}{{\omega}_{j}}+{\beta}_{i}\frac{{\omega}_{i}}{\omega} . In the interval [{\omega}_{i},{\omega}_{j}] the variation of the reduced damping is small and outside it one finds again the combination of the previous drawbacks: the responses on the modes outside the interval are too heavily damped. Appearance of the complete Rayleigh damping The complete Rayleigh damping illustrated on figure u2.06.13-amorPropComplet makes it possible to have a damping value that is almost constant over a given frequency plateau, always greater than \sqrt{\alpha \beta} , which makes it possible to control its effect over a frequency range defined consistently with the problem considered. However, when the stiffness is damaged, the transient dynamic responses present a central frequency which decreases. The Rayleigh damping perceived is then slightly stronger at low frequencies and weaker at high frequencies. Application to the structure The global viscous Rayleigh damping coefficients are defined, at the level of the characteristics of the material (command DEFI_MATERIAU), by the parameters AMOR_ALPHA and AMOR_BETA in the factor keyword ELAS. There is no specific keyword in DYNA_NON_LINE for activating the taking into account of this damping: if one does not want to use it, one must remove all the occurrences of the keywords AMOR_ALPHA and AMOR_BETA from all the materials of the finite-element model studied. The values to be imposed in order to obtain the desired damping \xi in the interval of the natural frequencies {f}_{1} and {f}_{2} are deduced from the following equations: \alpha =\frac{\xi}{\pi ({f}_{1}+{f}_{2})} \beta =\frac{4\pi \xi {f}_{1}{f}_{2}}{{f}_{1}+{f}_{2}} where {f}_{1} and {f}_{2} are the two natural frequencies bounding the interval of study considered. In the framework of this document, low-frequency solutions are sought, so the frequencies {f}_{1} and {f}_{2} will be associated with the first frequencies of the model, whose modes are consistent with the imposed loading. To give orders of magnitude, the modal damping for steel structures is generally of the order of a few %, whereas for concrete structures, of civil-engineering type, one can go up to 5, or even 7 % of damping, for analyses which are globally linear, intended to represent dissipations of energy coming from diffuse degradations or cracking. For the discrete elements, the Rayleigh damping parameters not being definable in the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM, if one uses the operator DYNA_NON_LINE, the Rayleigh damping therefore does not take into account the contribution of the discrete elements. On the other hand, the global damping matrix assembled for the solution will take into account their contribution and that of the Rayleigh damping coming from the finite elements (volumetric, surfacic or of beam type...). In the case of models coupled in hydromechanics, THM, for the analysis of geomechanical works (earth dams, soil columns...), cf. U2.04.05, DYNA_NON_LINE cannot build the Rayleigh damping matrix directly. See U2.04.05 and U2.04.08. An example of a non-linear dynamic analysis on a hydromechanical problem of a soil column is provided by test case wdnp101a. This difficulty can be got round by superimposing a classical mechanical model on the same mesh, making it possible to represent the kinetic energy (mass matrix) and the elastic energy (stiffness matrix), the two models being supported by the same nodes. Then by building the elementary damping matrix with the desired parameters \alpha ={\alpha}_{j} \beta ={\beta}_{i} , using the command CALC_MATR_ELEM with OPTION='AMOR_MECA' by giving the elementary mass and stiffness matrices ( MASS_MECA and RIGI_MECA ), then by specifying the concept obtained in DYNA_NON_LINE with the keyword MATR_ELEM_AMOR . The command DYNA_NON_LINE offers a variant of the Rayleigh damping using the tangent stiffness matrix instead of the initial elastic stiffness matrix. This is the purpose of the optional keyword: AMOR_RAYL_RIGI=("TANGENTE"/ "ELASTIQUE") . The default value being ELASTIQUE . One will then have a Rayleigh damping matrix which is fixed throughout the analysis, resulting from the chosen values of the material characteristics (parameters AMOR_ALPHA and AMOR_BETA ). Of course, the total assembled damping matrix can nevertheless be variable in the presence of other sources of damping, such as what comes from the relations on interfaces: DIS_CHOC , DIS_CONTACT , CHOC_ENDO , CHOC_ENDO_PENA ... With the value TANGENTE of the keyword AMOR_RAYL_RIGI , the updated stiffness matrix will be the same as that which is used for the computation of the internal forces. The choice of the Rayleigh damping with the TANGENTE matrix (built with the parameters AMOR_ALPHA and AMOR_BETA of the materials) introduces a non-linearity on the damping forces and this can generate additional time-step cuttings compared with the computation of the damping with the ELASTIQUE stiffness matrix. Indeed, the parasitic high-frequency disturbances are then less damped than with the latter. If in addition the material has an irreversible non-linear constitutive behaviour with softening damage, then the TANGENTE stiffness matrix can have negative eigenvalues, and therefore produce, if one chooses it in order to build the Rayleigh damping matrix, flutter instabilities at parasitic high frequencies. If the model contains command variables (temperature, irradiation, etc.) then the elastic stiffness matrix is not constant in the course of time, and one must then adopt the updated TANGENTE stiffness matrix in order to build the Rayleigh damping. For the joint finite elements, one notes that the elastic stiffness matrix does not exist; only the updated TANGENTE stiffness matrix is available. 3.4.2 Damping due to the time scheme Documentation R5.05.05 and above all note [bib6]_ present this aspect. One will confine oneself here to recalling the main trends. On a linear system with one degree of freedom (mass-spring, of natural angular frequency \omega ), one can obtain the following characterisation of the damping induced by the implicit scheme (average acceleration, modified average acceleration and complete HHT), as a function of the time step and for different values of the parameter ALPHA . One has an illustration of it on figure u2.06.13-amorNumerique. Comparison of the damping due to the time scheme One does indeed find that only the average-acceleration scheme does not dissipate. When one compares the two other schemes, one can note that: - only the complete HHT scheme does not disturb the low-frequency domain, - for one and the same value of the parameter ALPHA the modified average acceleration introduces much more dissipation than the HHT scheme. Finally, it should be noted that the value of the equivalent damping depends on the angular frequency \omega , and will therefore depend on the finite element considered. On a complex problem, the damping due to the scheme will therefore not be homogeneous: the “stiffer” the finite element, the more damping it will see. Likewise, if one reduces the time step, the damping will decrease. In order to bring out the influence of the high-frequency damping of the implicit schemes, a few evolutions of the solution acceleration of a simple linear problem of piping under earthquake will be presented. On the graph u2.06.13-amorNumeriqueZoom, one has zoomed in on part of the acceleration response in order to compare different methods of solution of the transient problem. The reference solution in green dashed lines is obtained by an analysis on a modal basis ( DYNA_VIBRA ). The truncation of the modal basis naturally filters any high-frequency disturbance. Local comparison of the behaviour of the time schemes This reference solution is compared with an analysis with the modified average-acceleration scheme (red curve) which oscillates strongly despite the adjustment of the parameter ALPHA. Finally, the response obtained with a complete HHT scheme (black curve) is plotted, which gives a result very close to the reference solution: the high-frequency disturbances (linked to the time step) are strongly attenuated. On the graph u2.06.13-amorNumeriqueComplet, the response curves are observed over a larger time interval. This makes it possible to grasp the influence of the scheme on the “physical” response: therefore low or medium frequency. The different responses correspond to different integration schemes and values of the time step. The reference solution (the problem being linear) is obtained by modal superposition (curve in thick brown dash-dot lines, named “modal cut-off 100\mathit{Hz} ” and obtained with DYNA_VIBRA ). Global comparison of the behaviour of the time schemes One observes that: - the non-dissipative solution ( HHT with ALPHA=0 , therefore a scheme of average-acceleration type) with a “large” time step overestimates the amplitude and introduces a phase shift, - the solutions obtained with schemes of modified average-acceleration type ( MODI_EQUI='NON' ), whatever the time step, have too strong a dissipation, - the solutions obtained with the complete HHT scheme ( MODI_EQUI='OUI' ) with a fine time step make it possible to recover the reference solution well. To conclude on this part, given the appearances of the Rayleigh damping, as well as that due to the scheme, one can build a total damping which is relatively varied. In order to choose in an optimal manner the value of the parameter ALPHA of the HHT scheme, it is indispensable to carry out a parametric study, in order to find the value closest to zero suited to the problem considered (one can advise beginning with a value of -0.1, for example). In order to validate this choice, one can rely on the two types of analysis presented above: control of the oscillations at high frequencies on the accelerations ( cf. figure) and absence of numerical over-damping on the displacement response ( cf. figure). On this last aspect, one can compare with the displacement response obtained with a non-dissipative scheme of NEWMARK type. With the complete HHT scheme, the damping at low and medium frequency being weak, one should not neglect to introduce into the model an ad hoc modelling of the real damping (global and/or due to the non-linearities). The appearance of the damping brought by the Tchamwa scheme is qualitatively close to that of the modified average acceleration. 3.5 Modification of the mass matrix In certain specific cases, such as the analyses on mixed hydromechanical models (HM or THM, cf. U2.04.05) or fluid-structure models, cf. R4.02.02 and U2.04.08, the cases having a very poor conditioning of the mass matrix, it can be useful to modify the mass matrix in order to make it invertible. This is also useful in order to establish an initialisation of the acceleration at the start of the time-integration scheme which reduces the overshooting. It is even indispensable, if this is not the case, for the explicit time schemes. This modification of the mass matrix can be done with the keyword COEF_MASS_SHIFT ( cf. documentation R5.05.05) in the keyword SCHEMA_TEMPS . This makes it possible to introduce a “shift” (or offset) of the mass matrix M which becomes: {\bf M} '={\bf M} +\mathrm{coef.} {\bf K} . This positive coefficient mathrm{coef.} has as its dimensions the inverse of an angular frequency squared. This offset of the mass matrix does not modify the modes. This functionality also makes it possible to improve the convergence of the implicit analyses or to increase the value of the critical time step in the explicit case. It must however be pointed out that this amounts to disturbing the mechanical system, in particular by shifting the natural frequencies of the system downwards (and by decreasing the wave speed): the error exceeds 5% on the natural frequencies as soon as they are above (\sqrt{\mathrm{coef.}})^{-1} . For example, an original natural angular frequency \omega then becomes \omega ' such that: \omega {'}^{2}=\frac{{\omega}^{2}}{1+\mathit{coef}.{\omega}^{2}} . One observes from this expression that \omega ' tends towards a maximum value {\mathit{coef}}^{-0.5} : the modified system therefore introduces a cut-off frequency driven by the value of the “shift” coefficient. Thus, for example, for a value which is a maximum in practice for \mathrm{coef}={10}^{-6} , the maximum corrected natural angular frequency of the system \omega ' is worth 1000r{\mathrm{d.s}}^{-1} , and a value for an original natural frequency of 30\mathrm{Hz} is corrected by this method to 29,481\mathit{Hz} . The natural frequencies situated below the new cut-off frequency are therefore slightly altered. In practice, it is appropriate not to use too large a value of the “shift”, unless one confines oneself to the computation of solutions at very low frequency, or even of quasi-static type. In this last case, the non-linear transient algorithm can then be seen as a regularised solver for the quasi-static problem, which can be useful when the classical static solution does not converge. In the same line of thought of using a transient solver in order to obtain a static response whose convergence with a usual implicit method is very difficult, one can also increase strongly the mass of the system (for example by acting on the density) and use an explicit time scheme with a strong structural damping. In this case one combines the convergence capability of the explicit method with a critical stability time step which is not too small, because of the increase in the mass (this stability time step will increase as the square root of the coefficient of increase of the total mass: if one multiplies the total mass by 100, the limiting time step will be multiplied by 10 because the wave speed will be ten times smaller). This type of method has already been used for delicate cases such as the simulation of the excavation of underground galleries, where the surrounding soil can become unstable. 3.6 Instability and updated modal analysis In the course of the solution of the transient problem it is possible to use tools of eigenvalue analysis on the updated global operators. One can carry out two types of analysis. On the one hand, the computation of the natural frequencies and of the vibratory modes with the updated stiffness matrix. This corresponds to the factor keyword MODE_VIBR (this option needing implicitly the mass matrix, it is not available in STAT_NON_LINE). The stiffness matrix can then be the elastic, secant or tangent stiffness, to be chosen with the keyword MATR_RIGI . Thanks to this factor keyword one can follow the influence of the non-linearities on the vibratory behaviour of a structure. An example of application would be the case of reinforced-concrete structures for which the damage causes the natural frequencies to decrease (with the tangent or secant stiffness). With an elastoplastic structure, having chosen the tangent stiffness for this purpose, one observes a drop in the natural frequencies during the regimes comprising a plastic excursion, whereas one recovers the initial natural frequencies during the elastic regimes. The graph u2.06.13-instabiliteChoixMatr presents the possible choices for the stiffness matrix (for a damaging material): Schematic representation of the stiffness operators On the other hand, one can, thanks to the factor keyword CRIT_STAB=_F(TYPE='FLAMBEMENT') , carry out a stability analysis of the stiffness operator. In the case of small perturbations and where one knows how to compute the geometric stiffness, then this option amounts to a buckling analysis in the Euler sense on the updated stiffness matrix. In the other cases, when one does not know how to compute the geometric stiffness, then one switches to the search for the singularity of the stiffness operator alone. In every case one obtains eigenvalues which will evolve in the course of the analysis. In the case of Euler buckling, the eigenvalue is directly the multiplier coefficient of the loading which makes it possible to obtain the critical load. In the second case, the interpretation is less easy (the eigenvalues are not dimensionless). If one observes that an eigenvalue changes sign, this means that the computed solution has passed a bifurcation and therefore that one has lost the uniqueness of the solution. In every case, these are stability analyses in the “static” sense and, moreover, this option is available in STAT_NON_LINE . At present, there exists no operator making it possible to carry out a stability analysis in the dynamic sense (flutter, divergence): therefore, for example, by computing the damping of the system in order to detect when it becomes negative. As these operations require a certain CPU cost (comparable to a call to CALC_MODES on the first few frequencies, with the keyword NMAX_FREQ , at each time instant requested), the possibility has been introduced of computing these eigenvalues only for the list of archiving time instants if it exists. In order to reduce the CPU time still further, it is also possible to carry out several restarts and to request the computation of the eigenvalues only over certain time intervals or particular time instants. One can also recover the eigenmodes (respectively buckling modes) associated with the execution of the keyword MODE_VIBR . The resultat concept produced by DYNA_NON_LINE is then enriched with a table_container. which bears the name 'ANALYSE_MODALE' . In order to recover it in the result concept produced by DYNA_NON_LINE , one calls the command RECU_TABLE. In this table, one will be able to recover the values of the parameters: time instant of the analysis considered, mode number, frequency (respectively critical load). One will then be able to print with IMPR_TABLE this table, filtering according to these parameters. By using the command EXTR_TABLE, specifying a TYPE_RESU='MODE_MECA' , filtering according to the desired parameters, one obtains a result concept, whose name one has chosen, containing the displacement fields of the modes computed, which one will then be able to visualise. One may consult test case sdnv106 V5.03.06. 3.7 Archiving and post-processing The number of time steps being liable to be very large, it is strongly recommended to use the archiving functionalities on a coarser list of time instants (factor keyword ARCHIVAGE of DYNA_NON_LINE ) on pain of having enormous databases and output files. The archiving step can range from a few steps in an implicit scheme to 10 to 100 steps in an explicit scheme. Be careful however of the risk of missing possible extreme values in the analysis of the quantities of interest of the computed solution. In addition, if one needs to follow precisely in the course of time the evolution of a few quantities of interest on a few GROUP_NO , there exists the observation (factor keyword OBSERVATION of DYNA_NON_LINE ) which complements the archiving. As one has been able to see in paragraph § u2.06.13-Amortissement_du_au_schema_en_temps, if one wants to analyse the responses in velocity or in accelerations in the course of time, one can obtain fairly rough curves. These high-frequency oscillations can be the sign of an insufficient discretisation in time (or of too great an irregularity in time) of the problem. It is also possible, by using a dissipative time scheme of complete HHT type, to smooth these disturbances. A compromise remains to be found between this smoothing and too strong a dissipation of the response. In a general manner, one must fully take in that the instantaneous values of the least smoothed quantities, such as the acceleration, are to be handled with caution. It is better to seek to carry out one's analysis on integrated quantities which are more physically relevant in dynamics, such as the energy. In addition, all the analysis methods coming from quasi-statics for quantifying the quality of a result (including the different norms of the equilibrium residual) are available and relevant with DYNA_NON_LINE . Finally, one can also recall that if one wishes to carry out frequency analyses, one should take care to respect the domain of validity of the FFT, for example the causality of the signal to be treated. For this, this signal in time must start and finish at zero, with zero derivatives. Without respect for these basic hypotheses, the user risks obtaining inaccurate frequency results. 3.8 Energy balance For any transient analysis, it is very useful to be able to have available the global energy balance, over the duration of the transient, which makes it possible to analyse the response of the system, in particular the contribution of the dissipation of energy by damping, and also to check the quality of the numerical solution. Documentation R4.09.01 presents all the energy functionalities available with the factor keyword ENERGIE=_F(CALCUL='OUI') of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE . One will use for this the factor keyword ENERGIE=_F() . It produces the table of name PARA_CALC . The energy balance can be extracted from this table with the help of the command RECU_TABLE and then printed with IMPR_TABLE. One will find in the energy-balance table, in the course of the transient, the quantities accumulated at each time instant: - ENER_CIN , for the kinetic energy, always positive or zero, - ENER_TOT , for the accumulated work of deformation (sum of the stored energy and of the energy dissipated by the irreversible constitutive models, including the case of the absorbing boundaries), - TRAV_AMOR , for the accumulated work of the damping forces coming from the assembled damping matrix (Rayleigh, discrete elements) or from modal damping, - TRAV_LIAI , for the accumulated work including the case of the internal forces of the interface materials ( DIS_CONTACT and DIS_CHOC , CHOC_ENDO , CHOC_ENDO_PENA , JOINT_MECA_FROT ), cf. R4.09.01, § 1.3.2, - TRAV_EXT , for the accumulated work including the excitation forces on the right-hand side (and the driving inertia forces). The remainder corresponds to the work dissipated by the numerical integration scheme. 3.9 Functionalities available in STAT_NON_LINE and not in DYNA_NON_LINE Methods of line-search type (mixed or otherwise) are not authorised in dynamics. However, this lack is to be put into perspective, knowing that attempts to apply these methods to studies of reinforced-concrete structures in dynamics have not brought out any significant contribution to convergence, unlike what is observed in quasi-statics. Let us note, nevertheless, that no theoretical argument would forbid the use of these methods in dynamics. Finally, the piloting techniques available in STAT_NON_LINE (arc length, for example) are forbidden in dynamics because they then have no meaning: time has, in dynamics, a physical meaning. 4 Specific features of coupled fluid-structure problems It is possible to use a coupled vibro-acoustic model in DYNA_NON_LINE . This model is based on an approach (u,p,\varphi ) with the following hypotheses: - the fluid is of linear acoustic type, - the structure must be considered as being in small perturbations or in updated Lagrangian. One can also take into account the free surfaces subjected to gravity (sloshing waves). Documentation U2.06.11 presents in detail the implementation of a non-linear coupled fluid-structure model for a tank analysis. Note [bib5]_ analyses the domain of application of the coupled fluid-structure model. 5 Optimisation of the performance In quasi-statics, it is not rare to have to carry out more than 10 iterations in order to have convergence in the sense of the equilibrium residual. In implicit dynamics this value of 10 iterations constitutes, in general, a good starting value for the parameter ITER_GLOB_MAXI of the factor keyword CONVERGENCE in DYNA_NON_LINE . If one cannot converge in fewer than 10 to 20 iterations, it is then preferable to reduce the time step rather than to increase the maximum number of iterations authorised. In the explicit case, there are no iterations for equilibrium, so the computational cost of each time step will therefore be constant, whatever the level of non-linearity (apart, possibly, from the local check of the constitutive behaviour). The use, even current, of the explicit integration schemes therefore seems very attractive in view of the CPU time, which remains under control. One must however temper this optimism by keeping well in mind that one deprives oneself of the safeguard which is the precise verification of equilibrium and that, consequently, the quality of the explicit solution obtained must be analysed with more precautions. The explicit algorithm will not diverge (if one respects the Courant stability condition), but the solution obtained is not guaranteed by an equilibrium-verification criterion. In particular a parametric study on the time step is indispensable because the appearance of the solution can vary strongly as the transient proceeds. Moreover, code_aster is not a code optimised for explicit analyses and its performance in the explicit case is modest, compared with specialised codes such as Europlexus [bib2]_. 5.1 Model reduction and dynamic condensation by substructuring One solution for reducing the computation time is to project the problem onto a reduced basis (modal basis or Ritz basis). One then greatly reduces the number of degrees of freedom and this type of approach is available in DYNA_NON_LINE (the solution also gains by being explicit because the Courant stability condition on a reduced modal basis is not very penalising, since this basis has a low cut-off frequency). To summarise, this type of approach is particularly suited to problems in which the non-linearities remain moderate and localised. As soon as the non-linearities become strong, one can question the updating of the initial reduced basis, which loses its consistency with the current solution. The extra computational cost due to the recomputation of the basis and to the reprojections then reduces the interest of this type of method. The factor keyword PROJ_MODAL makes it possible to carry out this type of analysis with an explicit integration scheme, the degrees of freedom being generalised. An example of an analysis is provided by test case SDNV107a V5.03.107. Another example of a non-linear dynamic analysis on a hydromechanical problem of a soil column is provided by test case WDNP101a V5.03.107. It is also recommended to use this reduction/condensation approach in a “mixed” manner, for “low-frequency” problems, where the model is made up of several subdomains, by condensing the solution of the subdomains of linear constitutive behaviour onto the degrees of freedom of their interfaces with subdomains of non-linear constitutive behaviour, these being treated with finite elements. Each of these linear subdomains is condensed onto a dynamic macro-element MACR_ELEM_DYNA U4.65.01 defined on each interface. By means of the operator - U4.63.33, after solution of the global “mixed” problem, one can reconstitute the fields in each subdomain. An example of a non-linear dynamic analysis by reduction/condensation is provided by test case FORMA12g V2.08.012 with an implicit integration scheme. The methodology is presented in detail in U2.07.04. 5.2 Parallelism Parallelism can bring a gain which is all the more notable when the system to be solved comprises a large number of degrees of freedom and the number of time steps is small. Indeed, the solution algorithm imposes significant communications at each step (one is not in a strategy of multi-domain type in time and in space). In practice, on problems comprising a few hundreds of thousands of degrees of freedom, the speed-up remains good up to 16 to 32 processors. In most cases, the iterative solver PETSC will bring a gain compared with the solver MUMPS . In addition to the parallelism at solver level, the parallelism of the elementary steps (solution of the constitutive behaviour at the Gauss points) will bring an important additional gain if the constitutive integration is costly. In every case, it is very useful to consult in the message file .mess the CPU-time measurements per step, which makes it possible to identify the most costly steps of the transient solution in order to adapt the parallelism accordingly. Documentation U2.08.06 gives all the details for the use of parallelism. 6 Conclusion This document presents a few general rules in order to facilitate the use of transient dynamic methods for the simulation of non-linear systems: see [bib3]_, [bib6]_, [bib8]_. The first step is the adaptation of the model to the methods of dynamic analysis. It is mainly a matter of making sure of the proper regularity of the imposed conditions, of the proper sampling of the excitations, of the correct definition of the density and of the global damping (Rayleigh, modal); it is recommended to begin with a linear transient analysis. Next, it is recommended to begin by using an implicit scheme ( DYNA_NON_LINE with a time scheme of type NEWMARK for the relatively regular problems or HHT , and THETA_SCHEMA for the problems with collisions). Indeed, the implicit time schemes are the most efficient and the most general-purpose in Code_Aster in so-called “slow” dynamics. Finally, for certain applications such as fast dynamics, the analysis on a modal basis or certain cases of analyses in slow evolution ( cf. U2.04.07), the user has the possibility of using explicit time schemes. The CPU-time performance of Code_Aster in the explicit case is fairly poor, if one compares it with a dedicated code such as Europlexus [bib2]_. Moreover, not all the functionalities available in the implicit case are available in the explicit case (as, for example, for contact, where only penalisation is authorised). In order to qualify the quality of the numerical solution obtained, it is indispensable to carry out certain parametric studies: - as for the quasi-static analyses, by acting on the spatial discretisation, - by testing different parameter settings of the damping, - by testing different time steps, - by testing different time schemes, first non-dissipative and, if need be, with numerical dissipation at high frequencies. In order to validate this choice of parameters, it is relevant to analyse the responses in displacements and in accelerations, as well as to make use of the energy-balance functionalities. 7 Bibliography 1. u2.06.14 Advice on carrying out Fluid-Structure Interaction analyses u2.06.14 Advice on carrying out Fluid-Structure Interaction analyses Summary This document presents an overall view of the different approaches available in Code_Aster for modelling the effects of fluid-structure interaction in the vibratory analyses of structures. It also recapitulates a number of practical pieces of advice and of precautions to be taken when carrying out Fluid-Structure Interaction analyses. 1 The fluid forces acting on a vibrating structure There exist two families of fluid forces which can act on a vibrating structure in a fluid medium: 1. The fluid-elastic forces : these are forces which depend on the motion of the structure; on its displacement, its velocity and its acceleration. Because of this, it is appropriate to take these fluid-elastic coupling effects into account by adding coefficients to the structural stiffness, mass and damping matrices. 2. The forces independent of the motion of the structure. These are the forces which act in the cases of turbulent or two-phase flows. In this document the different operators of Code_Aster are presented which make it possible to model each of the two types of fluid forces in the framework of the vibratory analyses of structures. 2 Modelling of the fluid-elastic forces In Code_Aster , there exist two different methods for modelling the fluid-elastic forces which represent the fluid-structure coupling forces. The difference between the two methods concerns the nature and the complexity of the physical phenomena that the user wishes to consider and, consequently, the hypotheses adopted when computing the coupling forces. The first method consists in computing added matrices representing the fluid-structure coupling with a potential approach. One makes the hypothesis that the structure undergoes only small strains and that the fluid which surrounds it is perfect ; the effect of shear in the fluid is then considered negligible. For the computation of the added mass, the fluid is considered unsteady. As for the added stiffness and the added damping, these can be computed only in the presence of a flow. In this case, one makes the hypothesis that the flow is potential ; one then neglects any effect linked to the physics of the rotational parts of the flow, which can be important in configurations with separation or at turbulent velocities. The second method for modelling the coupling forces consists in determining the fluid-elastic transfer matrix, particular to a predefined configuration; a “configuration” being the whole set: the structure and its geometry on the one hand and the flow and its properties on the other. The configurations which can be modelled with this method are: 1. Tube bundle under transverse flow 2. Rod under flow through an annular confinement (control-rod cluster) 3. Tube bundle under axial flow 4. Flow between two coaxial shells Despite its sometimes restrictive hypotheses, the potential method nevertheless remains the most generic from the point of view of its applicability, independent of the configuration of the study. The user is advised to employ the second method only in the case where the case under study corresponds to one of the four configurations currently available. 2.1 The “potential” approach for computing the modal basis of a coupled system In this approach, the computation method consists in determining, first, added fluid mass, stiffness and damping matrices with the help of the operator CALC_MATR_AJOU or the macro-command MACRO_MATR_AJOU. These two operators give as a result added matrices, projected onto the modal basis of the structure in vacuum. To determine the modal basis of the “wetted” structure, it is sufficient to combine the structural matrices with the generalised added matrices with the help of the operator COMB_MATR_ASSE. It will then be necessary to recompute the eigenmodes with CALC_MODES. The modes of the coupled system must finally be restored onto the physical basis of the structure with the help of the operator REST_GENE_PHYS. The steps of the analysis are detailed in the following diagram: Figure 2.1-a : Diagram of the computation of the modal basis of a wetted structure by the potential approach 2.2 The “predefined configuration” approach for computing the modal basis of a coupled system The data-setup and computation method for this second approach is different from that of the potential approach. Indeed, the physical phenomena which are modelled here are more complex and the results depend on an additional parameter, the flow velocity. The computation of a modal basis of the coupled system is therefore established for a range of velocities. One therefore obtains with this approach, not a traditional dynamic modal basis (mode_meca), but a fluid-elastic modal basis, which will be called melasflu in Code_Aster . To compute the fluid-elastic basis of a coupled system, the user must first call the operator DEFI_FLUI_STRU in order to supply the type of configuration of the study as well as all the characteristics which are associated with it. These characteristics differ according to the configuration but they generally concern the geometry of the structure, the properties of the fluid and of its flow. 2.2.1 Special case of a tube bundle under transverse flow In the case of the configuration of a tube bundle under transverse flow (FAISCEAU_TRANS), it is possible to compute, by means of the operator FONC_FLUI_STRU, the inertial distribution of the fluid all along the structure. The user can therefore use this information to enrich the structural matrices before carrying out the first modal analysis of the structure. In practice, after the call to FONC_FLUI_STRU, the user must create a fluid-structure hybrid material by using the option ELAS_FLUI of DEFI_MATERIAU and assign it to all the finite elements of the structure under transverse flow (AFFE_MATERIAU). The elementary mass and stiffness matrices can then be computed with the options MASS_FLUI_STRU and RIGI_FLUI_STRU of CALC_MATR_ELEM. After assembly of the elementary matrices, the user will be able to compute the modal basis of the wetted structure, for example with the operator CALC_MODES. It is important to note that this taking into account, upstream, of the inertial effect of the fluid is possible only in the case of a tube bundle under transverse flow. It makes it possible subsequently to carry out the whole of the dynamic analysis on a projection basis which corresponds to the modal basis of the wetted structure. 2.2.2 Case of the other configurations For the three other configurations, the reference modal basis is determined from the mechanical properties of the structure (purely structural mass and stiffness matrices), without any taking into account at this level of the effects linked to the presence of the fluid. Once the configuration of the study and the reference projection basis are well defined, the study of the coupled system can continue with a call to the operator CALC_FLUI_STRU. This operator recovers, in addition to the configuration of the study and the projection basis, a list of the velocities which represent the range of flow velocities over which the user wishes to study the dynamic behaviour of the structure. In the concept resulting from CALC_FLUI_STRU, the user has available, for each flow velocity, a basis modified by the taking into account of all the coefficients of the fluid-elastic coupling. The steps of the analysis for the four configurations are detailed in the following two diagrams: Figure 2.2.2-a : Diagram of the computation of the modal basis of a tube bundle under transverse flow Figure 2.2.2-b : Diagram of the computation of the modal basis of the structures in one of the 3 configurations: tube bundle under axial flow, control-rod cluster, and flow between 2 coaxial shells. 2.3 Vibratory analyses following the obtaining of the modal basis of the coupled system The modelling of the fluid-elastic forces is practically finished with the obtaining of a dynamic modal basis of the structure taking the coupling effects into account. To continue the study, the user can freely make use of the computed modal basis in order to analyse the behaviour of the coupled fluid-structure system. Transient analyses In the case where the modelling of the fluid-elastic coupling has been carried out according to the second method, that is to say on the basis of a configuration predefined in the operator DEFI_FLUI_STRU, the user must call the operator MODI_BASE_MODALE in order to extract from the melasflu basis a modal basis of type mode_meca for a single flow velocity. The modal basis will then be usable in all the transient-dynamics operators. In the case where added coefficients have been computed according to the potential method, the user can make direct use of the modal basis obtained by restoration onto the physical basis of the basis of generalised modes (result of the call to REST_GENE_PHYS, see ). There currently exists only one time-integration scheme which accepts modal bases of type melasflu , it is the ITMI method of the operator DYNA_VIBRA . Spectral analyses To carry out a spectral dynamic analysis of the coupled system, the user is on the other hand not obliged to extract a mode_meca basis from the wetted melasflu basis. The operator DYNA_SPEC_MODAL, which makes it possible to carry out the spectral analyses, is indeed compatible with modal bases of type melasflu. 3 Modelling of the forces independent of the motion of the structure In Code_Aster , it is possible to model several types of fluid forces which can act on a structure without however depending on its motion. Physically, these forces are directly linked to fluctuations in the pressure along the structure, observed in the turbulent regimes of the flow. It is important to note that most of the models of the turbulent forces which are predefined in Code_Aster apply only to well-defined configurations. These are indeed the same configurations which are available in the operator DEFI_FLUI_STRU (see paragraph 2.2 ). The definition of the model of the turbulent forces is done by means of the operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB. The different types of turbulence spectra which are available are presented in the following table. The type of structure-flow configuration which is generally associated with each model is also specified: | SPECTRUM MODEL | MEANING | CONFIGURATION | | --- | --- | --- | | SPEC_LONG_CORR_[1-4] | Turbulence of the long corr elation-length type for transverse flows | Tube bundle under transverse flow | | SPEC_CORR_CONV_[1/2] | Turbulence of boundary-layer conv ection type for parallel flows | Plate under parallel flow (Corcos) Tube bundle under axial flow (Au Yang) | | SPEC_CORR_CONV_3 | Turbulence spectrum defined from an analytical function | General configuration | | SPEC_FONC_FORME | Turbulence spectrum identified by its decomposition onto a family of shape func tions Predefined model: GRAPPE_1 | General configuration : Control-rod cluster | | SPEC_EXCI_POINT | Turbulence spectrum with exci tation of point force or moment type Predefined model: GRAPPE_2 | General configuration : Control-rod cluster | Table 3-1 : Details of the turbulence-spectrum models available in the operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB The operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB produces a spectre_sdaster concept which contains all the information necessary for the definition of the turbulent excitation spectrum according to the model chosen. For example, for spectra of correlation-length type (SPEC_LONG_CORR_[1-4]), the user must always supply the transverse velocity profile of the flow, a correlation length, and the coefficients of a pressure-spectrum model. The user can refer to the documentation of the operator DEFI_SPEC_TURB (U4.44.31) for more details on each turbulence model and its input parameters. It is important for the user to know that the “spectrum” obtained downstream of DEFI_SPEC_TURB is not really “computed” at this stage. One nevertheless has available, in the spectre_sdaster concept, the information on the spectrum making it possible to project it onto the modal basis of the wetted structure by using the operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE. The operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE takes care of computing the acceptance integrals corresponding to the spectrum and to the modal basis of the structure. It produces a matrix of inter-spectra of generalised excitations. In addition to the turbulence-spectrum model (spectre_sdaster) and the modal projection basis, the user must supply, in the operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE, information concerning the (frequency) discretisation of the spectrum by using the mandatory keywords FREQ_INIT, FREQ_FIN and NB_POIN. If the modal projection basis is of type melas_flu, it is mandatory at this stage to specify the fluid flow velocity. This makes it possible to extract, internally in the operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE, the projection basis which corresponds to the requested velocity. The user also has the option of computing only the auto-spectra of generalised excitations, that is to say only the diagonal terms of the generalised inter-spectrum matrix (OPTION='DIAG'). Finally, it is also possible to carry out the projection of the turbulent excitation onto part of the mesh. The interspectre concept produced by the operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE is then usable in all the operators of Code_Aster in order to take into account the effect of the turbulence in a vibratory analysis of the structure. The user can choose one of the two equivalent approaches in order to analyse the vibratory level of the wetted structure under turbulent excitation: the spectral approach and the temporal approach. The precautions to be followed in the implementation of each of the two approaches are specified in what follows. Figure 3-a : Diagram of the computation of the vibratory dynamics of a wetted structure with the forces of turbulence taken into account, with the two approaches: spectral and temporal 4 Vibratory analysis of a wetted structure: spectral approach From the modal basis of the wetted structure and the inter-spectrum of modal excitation computed in PROJ_SPEC_BASE, the user can proceed directly to the computation of an inter-spectrum of generalised displacements by means of the operator DYNA_SPEC_MODAL. Here the user also has the obligation to supply the flow velocity if the modal basis is of type melas_flu, and can choose to compute the whole inter-spectral matrix of the generalised displacements or else only the diagonal terms (the auto-spectra). To restore the generalised results onto the physical basis, the user must then call the operator REST_SPEC_PHYS. It will then be possible, for example, to compute a displacement inter-spectrum on one or several nodes, for the components of interest ( \mathit{DX} , \mathit{DY} , \mathit{DRX} , etc.). If the aim is to compute the RMS values, the resulting inter-spectra are to be post-processed by the operator POST_DYNA_ALEA. 5 Vibratory analysis of a wetted structure: temporal approach In certain cases, it is of interest to study the vibratory behaviour of a structure under flow by a transient analysis. The idea is to generate, from the inter-spectral matrix of generalised excitation (obtained by PROJ_SPEC_PHYS), a temporal excitation which has the same frequency signature as the original spectrum. This can be done by means of the operator GENE_FONC_ALEA, which makes it possible to generate temporal excitation functions from an inter-spectral matrix (interspectre concept). Three points of very great importance are to be taken into account when passing from the spectral domain to the temporal domain. They concern the relations which link: 1. The frequency samplings of the operator PROJ_SPEC_BASE and of GENE_FONC_ALEA. 2. The frequency sampling to the total duration of the temporal excitation. 3. The temporal sampling of the excitation to the cut-off (maximum) frequency of the spectrum. The user interested in carrying out a transient analysis should carefully choose the frequency discretisation of the turbulence spectrum when calling PROJ_SPEC_BASE (keywords FREQ_INIT, FREQ_FIN and NB_POIN). In addition, the input parameters of the operator GENE_FONC_ALEA must be consistent with those of PROJ_SPEC_BASE. In PROJ_SPEC_BASE, the spectrum is discretised with NB_POIN points between FREQ_INIT and FREQ_FIN. In the operator GENE_FONC_ALEA, the spectrum is re-sampled with a new NB_POIN, different from that of PROJ_SPEC_BASE. If the option INTERP='OUI' is used in GENE_FONC_ALEA, the spectrum is interpolated for frequencies lying between f = 0 Hz and f = FREQ_FIN. FREQ_FIN is deduced automatically from the maximum frequency in the original spectrum. It is therefore equal to the FREQ_FIN of PROJ_SPEC_BASE. If the option INTERP='NON' is used, the maximum frequency is recomputed. It is a function of the value of the keyword NB_POIN in GENE_FONC_ALEA. The user must in every case supply two different values for the keyword NB_POIN in PROJ_SPEC_BASE and GENE_FONC_ALEA. The minimum value of NB_POIN to be supplied in GENE_FONC_ALEA (GFA) can be computed as follows: > {{\mathit{NB}}_{\mathit{POIN}}}^{\mathit{GFA}}\ge \frac{({{\mathit{NB}}_{\mathit{POIN}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}-1)\times {{\mathit{FREQ}}_{\mathit{FIN}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}}{{{\mathit{FREQ}}_{\mathit{FIN}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}-{{\mathit{FREQ}}_{\mathit{INIT}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}}+1 (1) For example, if the turbulence spectrum is discretised in PROJ_SPEC_BASE at 2048 points between 25,5 and 45,5\mathit{Hz} , at least: \frac{2047\times 45,5}{45,5-25,5}+1=4657 points will be needed in GENE_FONC_ALEA in order not to lose information on the excitation spectrum even before the generation of the temporal excitation function. 5.1 Practical advice on use It is strongly advised to call GENE_FONC_ALEA with the option INTERP='NON' and to choose an NB_POIN well above the recommended minimum value. With the option INTERP='NON', the total duration of the temporal excitation can be computed as the inverse of the frequency step in the spectrum of PROJ_SPEC_BASE; it is equal to: > {t}_{max}=\frac{1}{\delta f}=\frac{{{\mathit{NB}}_{\mathit{POIN}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}-1}{{{\mathit{FREQ}}_{\mathit{FIN}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}-{{\mathit{FREQ}}_{\mathit{INIT}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}} (2) In the previous example, the duration of the excitation is equal to {t}_{max}=102,35s . The temporal sampling of the excitation can be computed from the maximum frequency of the excitation spectrum: > \delta t=\frac{1}{2\times {{\mathit{FREQ}}_{\mathit{MAX}}}^{\mathit{GFA}}} In the case where the option INTERP='NON' is used in GENE_FONC_ALEA, the maximum frequency of the spectrum used for the generation of the temporal excitation is given by the formula: > {{\mathit{FREQ}}_{\mathit{MAX}}}^{\mathit{GFA}}=\delta f\times {{\mathit{NB}}_{\mathit{POIN}}}^{\mathit{GFA}} It follows that: > \delta t=\frac{{t}_{max}}{2\times {{\mathit{NB}}_{\mathit{POIN}}}^{\mathit{GFA}}} (3) In practice, the user who wishes to carry out a transient analysis generally has an idea of the time-integration step and of the total duration of the vibratory analysis. The choice of the different parameters is made in the following order: 1. From the total duration of the desired transient simulation, the user must choose the number of points of the frequency discretisation (NB_POIN) in PROJ_SPEC_BASE according to equation (2). 2. Next, from the total duration of the excitation and the integration step, the user can compute, using equation (3), the number of sampling points (NB_POIN) to be chosen in the operator GENE_FONC_ALEA. One must therefore choose a number equal to or greater than this value, 3. Finally, the user must check that the value of NB_POIN of GENE_FONC_ALEA satisfies the condition in equation (1), To illustrate the practical application of these 3 steps, an example case is considered in which the turbulence spectrum is defined between 1,0 and 384,832\mathit{Hz} (keywords FREQ_INIT and FREQ_FIN of PROJ_SPEC_BASE). In addition, it is assumed that the transient vibratory analysis is to be carried out over a duration greater than 10s and with a minimum integration step of {10}^{-4}s . According to equation (2), {{\mathit{NB}}_{\mathit{POIN}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}={t}_{max}({{\mathit{FREQ}}_{\mathit{FIN}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}-{{\mathit{FREQ}}_{\mathit{INIT}}}^{\mathit{PSB}})+1=3839,32 An admissible value (a power of 2) is then {{\mathit{NB}}_{\mathit{POIN}}}^{\mathit{PSB}}=4096 , which gives a total duration of the excitation {t}_{max}=10,6687s The frequency sampling (NB_POIN) to be chosen in GENE_FONC_ALEA is then computed according to equation (3): {{\mathit{NB}}_{\mathit{POIN}}}^{\mathit{GFA}}=53343,65 An admissible value is then {{\mathit{NB}}_{\mathit{POIN}}}^{\mathit{GFA}}=65536 (a power of 2, and it satisfies equation (1)). This choice in GENE_FONC_ALEA with the option INTERP='NON' leads to a temporal sampling of the resulting excitation of: \delta t=8,139\times {10}^{-5}s . This is compatible with the integration time step wanted by the user ( {10}^{-4}s ).

u2.06.31 User's guide for the modelling of gyroscopy u2.06.31 User's guide for the modelling of gyroscopy Summary: Modal analyses, or linear and non-linear dynamic analyses, of shaft lines require the notion of gyroscopic damping to be included. The analysis of a rotational-speed transient (run-up or slowdown) requires, for its part, the notion of gyroscopic stiffness to be included. Dedicated rotating-machinery codes use a preferential axis for the modelling of rotors ( Y for ROTORINSA, Z for CADYRO, etc.). In Code_Aster , it is possible, provided a few precautions are taken in the data setup, to model a rotor with any axis of rotation. Once the axis of rotation has been chosen, the positive sense along this axis is defined as the usual anticlockwise sense of rotation. This user's guide is an aid to the use of the gyroscopic damping and stiffness functionalities. It should enable the user to carry through a consistent and correct rotating-machinery analysis, whatever the axis of rotation of the shaft line. 1 Gyroscopic damping and stiffness 1.1 Characteristics of gyroscopy The modellings currently available in Code_Aster for rotating machinery involve structural elements of beam type (for the rotors) and discrete elements (for the discs, the bearings, the supports, etc.). The computations of the kinetic energy of the Timoshenko beam element (considering the bending strains) or of the discrete element bring out the gyroscopic-effect terms. For a rotating system, the classical equation of structural dynamics depends on the rotational speeds as follows: > M\ddot{\delta}+{C}_{\mathit{gyro}}(\Omega )\dot{\delta}+(K+{K}_{\mathit{gyro}}(\dot{\Omega}))\delta =0 Where M and K are the classical stiffness and mass matrices of the rotating mechanical system. {C}_{\mathit{gyro}}(\Omega ) is a non-symmetric matrix, a function of the rotational speed \Omega , including the gyroscopic-damping characteristics. This gyroscopic-damping matrix is antisymmetric, and its contribution is proportional to the angular velocity. {K}_{\mathit{gyro}}(\dot{\Omega}) is a non-symmetric matrix, a function of the rotational acceleration (\dot{\Omega}) , including the gyroscopic-stiffness characteristics. This gyroscopic-stiffness matrix is full. Its contribution is proportional to the angular acceleration and is therefore zero in the case of a constant rotational speed. The gyroscopic-stiffness matrix is meaningful only for a speed transient. Gyroscopic damping and stiffness are currently available in Code_Aster for straight beams (Timoshenko elements POU_D_T and Euler elements POU_D_E) of constant or variable cross-section and of circular shape, as well as for discrete elements. The assumptions retained for the beams are: - Timoshenko assumption: transverse shear and all the inertia terms are taken into account. This assumption is to be used for low slenderness ratios (POU_D_T elements). - Euler assumption: transverse shear is neglected. This assumption holds for high slenderness ratios (POU_D_E elements). The spin speed (along the axis of the beam) may be constant or variable (case of a rotational-speed transient: run-up or slowdown). The discs are cylinders of revolution whose axis coincides with the axis of the beam. These discs are assumed to be non-deformable and are modelled by discrete elements. The material is homogeneous and isotropic. Finally, and for further details, the reader may refer to the reference documentation of gyroscopic damping and stiffness in Code_Aster R5.05.07. 1.2 Computation of the gyroscopic matrices It is possible to build the gyroscopic damping and stiffness matrices from each element of the model, as for the stiffness and the mass. For structural finite elements of beam type or for discrete elements, it is possible to compute the real elementary matrices corresponding to the analysis options 'MECA_GYRO' and 'RIGI_GYRO'. These operations are called as follows: AMGYELEM [ matr_elem_DEPL_R ] = CALC_MATR_ELEM ( / ♦ OPTION: 'MECA_GYRO' ♦ MODELE: mo [modele] ♦ CHAM_MATER: chmat [cham_mater] ◊ CARA_ELEM: cara [cara_elem] ) RIGYELEM [ matr_elem_DEPL_R ] = CALC_MATR_ELEM ( / ♦ OPTION: 'RIGI_GYRO' ♦ MODELE: mo [modele] ♦ CHAM_MATER: chmat [cham_mater] ◊ CARA_ELEM: cara [cara_elem] ) The assembly of the elementary gyroscopic matrices is obtained with the usual operator ASSE_MATRICE U4.61.22. AMGYASS=ASSE_MATRICE(MATR_ELEM=AMGYELEM, NUME_DDL=NUMEDDL,) RIGYASS=ASSE_MATRICE(MATR_ELEM=RIGYELEM, NUME_DDL=NUMEDDL,) It will be noted that one must use the same numberings and the same storage mode as for the stiffness and mass matrices (operator NUME_DDL U4.61.11). One can also carry out this operation at the same time as the construction of the other matrices (mass, stiffness, damping, ...) by means of the macro-command ASSEMBLAGE ASSEMBLAGE( MODELE=MODELE, CHAM_MATER=CHMAT, CARA_ELEM=CARELEM, CHARGE=BLOQUAGE, NUME_DDL=CO('NUMEDDL'), MATR_ASSE=(_F(MATRICE=CO('RIGIDITE'), OPTION='RIGI_MECA',), _F(MATRICE=CO('MASSE'), OPTION='MASS_MECA',), _F(MATRICE=CO('AMOR'), OPTION='AMOR_MECA',), _F(MATRICE=CO('AMGY'), OPTION='MECA_GYRO',), _F(MATRICE=CO('RIGY'), OPTION='RIGI_GYRO',),),) 1.3 Use of the gyroscopic matrices The computed gyroscopic damping and stiffness matrices {C}_{\mathit{gyro}} and {K}_{\mathit{gyro}} are unitary and must therefore be multiplied by the angular velocity and the angular acceleration respectively in order to obtain the gyroscopic effect of a given rotational speed. The gyroscopic-damping matrix is generally combined, after assembly, with the classical damping matrix by the operator COMB_MATR_ASSE as follows: OM=124.14 pi/30. # Rotational speed in revolutions/min converted to rad/s GYOM=COMB_MATR_ASSE(COMB_R=(_F(MATR_ASSE=AMGY, COEF_R=OM,), _F(MATR_ASSE=AMOR, COEF_R=1.,),)) where AMGY and AMOR are the assembled gyroscopic and viscous damping matrices. The gyroscopic matrices can be used for the direct linear dynamic analysis with the linear dynamic response operators: - linear transient on a physical basis DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 (cf. modelling A in V2.02.126) - linear transient on a modal basis DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 (cf. modelling B in V2.02.126) - harmonic DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 (cf. modelling C in [V2,02,126]) - DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 (cf. modelling C in [V2,02,126]) In the case of a rotational-speed transient treated on a modal basis, the two assembled gyroscopic matrices are combined with the classical damping and stiffness matrices in a manner completely transparent to the user. To this end, it is sufficient to supply in DYNA_VIBRA the parameters defining this speed transient (imposed angular-velocity and angular-acceleration laws and assembled gyroscopic matrices, cf. U4.53.03 and U2.06.32). These matrices are indispensable for the complex modal analysis of a rotating system with the eigenvalue-search operator: - CALC_MODES U4.52.02 For systems with a reduced number of degrees of freedom, a direct modal analysis can be carried out with the operator cited above and with one or other of the solution algorithms (here the 'SORENSEN' algorithm, for example): MODEG=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=RIGIDITE, MATR_MASS=MASSE, MATR_AMOR=GYOM, OPTION='CENTRE', CALC_FREQ=_F(FREQ=1., NMAX_FREQ=16), SOLVEUR_MODAL=_F(METHODE='SORENSEN'), VERI_MODE=_F(SEUIL=1.E-3), ) For a robust quadratic modal analysis (analysis of damped modes), one can use a two-step strategy. The QZ method is a reliable method for a quadratic modal analysis. However, it is costly. It is therefore to be restricted to systems with a small number of degrees of freedom (a few thousand degrees of freedom) or to problems reduced by modal truncation. One must proceed with a two-stage analysis: - 1a - compute a reduced undamped modal basis: MODES=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=RIGIDITE, MATR_MASS=MASSE, OPTION='BANDE', CALC_FREQ=_F(FREQ=(3.,3000.)) ); - 1b - project the mass, stiffness and total damping matrices GYOM onto this basis (modal truncation): PROJ_BASE(BASE=MODES, PROFIL='PLEIN', MATR_ASSE_GENE=(_F(MATRICE=CO('MAGE'), MATR_ASSE=MASSE,), _F(MATRICE=CO('RIGE'), MATR_ASSE=RIGIDITE,), _F(MATRICE=CO('OMGE'), MATR_ASSE=GYOM,),), ); - 2 - carry out a modal analysis on the generalised matrices obtained by projection: MOD2ETAG=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=RIGE, MATR_MASS=MAGE, MATR_AMOR=OMGE, OPTION='TOUT', SOLVEUR_MODAL=_F(METHODE='QZ'), ); One is therefore led to project the antisymmetric and non-symmetric matrices {C}_{\mathit{gyro}} and {K}_{\mathit{gyro}} into the subspace defined by a set of real eigenmodes. This operation is possible with the operator PROJ_MATR_BASE U4.63.12. Note that, in the general case, the projected matrices are not symmetric. They nevertheless remain usable for the computation of the dynamic response to a force or to an imposed motion in the modal space, with the linear dynamic response operator: - linear transient on a modal basis DYNA_VIBRA U4.53.03 (cf. modelling B in [V2,02,126]) 2 Example of a shaft-line analysis with the axis along X In this section, we give a concrete example of a shaft line modelled in two different ways (axis of rotation X on the one hand and an arbitrary axis on the other). We rely here on the example, documented in V6.02.126, of a simple rotor model. It is guided by 2 bearings (respectively the first and the last node of the rotor), and supports 3 discs (cf. figure below). Figure 2-a: Rotor model with 3 discs and 2 bearings taken from [bib1] We consider two modellings for this test case. In the first, the axis of rotation is along X ; in the second, it is along an arbitrary axis defined by its nautical angles (\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma ) . The steps of reading the mesh and of assigning models and material being identical for the two modellings (apart from the meshing of the shafts along the desired axis of rotation), we focus on the step which distinguishes them, namely the assignment of the elementary characteristics by the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM . The data setup of the discrete elements is done so as to supply the stiffness and damping characteristics (for the bearings) and the mass and inertias (for the discs) directly in the global coordinate system (keyword REPERE, by default REPERE = 'GLOBAL'). CARELEM=AFFE_CARA_ELEM(MODELE=MODELE, POUTRE= _F(GROUP_MA='ROTOR', SECTION='CERCLE', CARA='R', VALE=.05,), DISCRET=(_F(CARA='K_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='PALIER_A', REPERE='GLOBAL', VALE=(0.,5.E7,7.E7,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='K_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='PALIER_E', REPERE='GLOBAL', VALE=(0.,5.E7,7.E7,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='A_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='PALIER_A', REPERE='GLOBAL', VALE=(0.,5000.,7000.,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='A_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='PALIER_E', REPERE='GLOBAL', VALE=(0.,5000.,7000.,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='M_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='DISQ1', > REPERE='GLOBAL', VALE=(14.58,0.1232,0.0646,0.0646,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='M_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='DISQ2', > REPERE='GLOBAL', VALE=(45.94,0.9763,0.4977,0.4977,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='M_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='DISQ3', > REPERE='GLOBAL', VALE=(55.13,1.1716,0.6023,0.6023,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,),), ),); 3 Example of a shaft-line analysis with an arbitrary axis Below is an example of the data setup of the same shaft line oriented along an arbitrary axis of rotation defined by its nautical angles 1 (\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma ) . The mesh of the rotor is built along this axis and the assignment of the elementary characteristics of the corresponding beam-type elements is done directly in the global coordinate system. As, by default, the values of the matrices of the discrete elements are expressed in the global coordinate system, one specifies REPERE = 'LOCAL' in the assignment and one defines the local coordinate system with respect to the global coordinate system by the keyword ORIENTATION [U4,42,01]. CARELEM=AFFE_CARA_ELEM(MODELE=MODELE, POUTRE= _F(GROUP_MA='ROTOR', SECTION='CERCLE', CARA='R', VALE=.05,), DISCRET=(_F(CARA='K_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='PALIER_A', REPERE='LOCAL', VALE=(0.,5.E7,7.E7,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='K_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='PALIER_E', REPERE='LOCAL', VALE=(0.,5.E7,7.E7,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='A_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='PALIER_A', REPERE='LOCAL', VALE=(0.,5000.,7000.,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='A_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='PALIER_E', REPERE='LOCAL', VALE=(0.,5000.,7000.,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='M_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='DISQ1', > REPERE='LOCAL', VALE=(14.58,0.1232,0.0646,0.0646,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='M_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='DISQ2', > REPERE='LOCAL', VALE=(45.94,0.9763,0.4977,0.4977,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,),), _F(CARA='M_TR_D_N', GROUP_MA='DISQ3', > REPERE='LOCAL', VALE=(55.13,1.1716,0.6023,0.6023,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,),), ), ORIENTATION=_F(GROUP_MA=('DISQ1','DISQ2','DISQ3','PALIER_A','PALIER_E'), CARA='ANGL_NAUT', VALE=(α,β,γ),),); These are the angles which make it possible to pass from the global coordinate system in which the node coordinates are defined to the local coordinate system. For example: the nautical angles which allow the passage from the axis of rotation X to the axis of rotation Z are (\alpha =0,\beta =-\pi /2,\gamma =0) ; the nautical angles which allow the passage from the axis of rotation X to the axis of rotation Y are (\alpha =\pi /2,\beta =0,\gamma =0) . 4 Bibliographical references 1. LALANNE, G. FERRARIS, "Rotordynamics Prediction in Engineering", Second Edition, Wiley, 2001. - ROTORINSA, finite-element software intended to predict the dynamic behaviour of rotors in bending, LaMCoS UMR5259, INSA-Lyon.
