u2.06.41 Validation of a dynamic model by analysis–test correlation u2.06.41 Validation of a dynamic model by analysis–test correlation Summary This documentation is intended to describe the principal tools for assisting the validation of models in structural dynamics by analysis–test correlation. In particular, one describes: - how to import data coming from measurements, - validation by the MAC criterion, - validation by comparison of computed/simulated FRFs 1 Introduction In order to evaluate the predictive capability of a numerical model in structural dynamics, it can be useful, or even indispensable, to validate it against data measured in situ . The most classical manner is the comparison of the eigenmodes (frequencies and shapes) computed and identified experimentally, two by two. The eigenmodes reflect the global behaviour of the structure, and are often used as the sole validation tool. The principal difficulty in this case is to be capable of pairing the numerical and experimental modes two by two. The objective of this documentation is to describe the methods and tools usable in Code_Aster for comparing the data of the analysis and of the measurement. Section 2 deals with the importation of data coming from measurement software into Code_Aster . In section 3 , the use of one of the principal criteria for model validation is detailed: the MAC matrix. In section 4 , other means proposed in the Code_Aster environment for validation (comparison of FRFs and of shapes) are addressed. 2 Importing measured data into Code_Aster 2.1 Which data to import? The measured data come from a signal-acquisition and processing software. Among them one may cite: - LMS TestLab, - Me'Scope, - B&K Pulse, - Labview, - … Most of these software packages make it possible to export data in the universal format, developed by the IDEAS software (extension .unv), data which can be read back into Code_Aster by LIRE_RESU(FORMAT='IDEAS'). These files generally contain the information relating to the mesh of the structure and to the experimental data. The unv files are ascii files. Each set of data is called a “dataset”, and is framed in the file by two “-1”. The number which follows the first occurrence “-1” corresponds to the type of dataset. Each dataset is composed of several lines (record), and each line contains data arranged in columns (field) In the example below, a few lines of a dataset 55 are presented, which describes a basis of eigenmodes. -1 55 %VALEURS AUX NOEUDS ASTER 7.03.29 CONCEPT MODINTS1 CALC - CHAMP AUX NOEUDS DE NOM SYMBOLIQUE CHAMP AUX NOEUDS DE NOM SYMBOLIQUE DEPL - DX DY DZ DRX DRY DRZ ASTER 7.03.29 CONCEPT MODINTS1 CALCULE LE 22/11/2004 A 19:24:57 DE TYPE CHAMP AUX NOEUDS DE NOM SYMBOLIQUE DEPL NUMERO D'ORDRE: 1 NUME_MODE: 1 FREQ: 2.66902E-01 1 2 3 8 2 6 2 4 1 1 2.18331e+01 1.00000e+00 3.74657e-03 1011 % NOEUD NO1011 -1.37933E-001 7.39432E-007 3.38287E-001 0.00000E+000 0.00000E+000 0.00000E+000 1001 % NOEUD NO1001 -1.37933E-001-2.80459E-009 1.72767E-001 0.00000E+000 0.00000E+000 0.00000E+000 -1 2.1.1 The mesh Several data sets are used by the measurement software to describe a mesh. The one presented here is the format used by LMS to export simple meshes, composed only of nodes and of lines connecting them. The nodes are described by the data set 2411, and the connectivities by the data set 82 (example below). -1 2411 1 0 0 8 0.000000000000000e+000 0.000000000000000e+000 0.000000000000000e+000 2 0 0 8 0.000000000000000e+000 1.199999973177910e-001 0.000000000000000e+000 3 0 0 8 0.000000000000000e+000 3.300000131130219e-001 0.000000000000000e+000 -1 -1 82 1 30 8 LDN 1 2 3 0 0 0 0 -1 The importation of the mesh is done in Code_Aster with PRE_IDEAS. The description of the data sets 2411 and 82 is detailed in appendix 5.1 . 2.1.2 The raw time data, and FRFs It is possible to import the raw time data, or FRFs, into Code_Aster , in order to compare them with simulated data. These data are stored in the unv files under the data set 58. An example of this type of data set is given below: -1 58 FRF (H1-estimator) response / load 95-Oct-12 11:52:48 Alternate/identified FRF" NONE 0 4 0 139 NONE 1011 3 NONE 12 -3 5 3124 1 4.00390e+000 1.95312e-002 0.00000e+000 18 0 0 0 Frequency Hz 12 1 0 0 Channel 3(3) m/s2 13 0 1 0 Channel 1(1) N 0 0 0 0 Unknown NONE -1.33781e-001-5.07456e-003-1.31790e-001-5.19607e-003-1.29762e-001-5.32069e-003 -1.27699e-001-5.44850e-003-1.25597e-001-5.57962e-003-1.23458e-001-5.71414e-003 -1.21279e-001-5.85217e-003-1.19060e-001-5.99383e-003-1.16800e-001-6.13924e-003 -1.14497e-001-6.28851e-003-1.12151e-001-6.44177e-003-1.09760e-001-6.59917e-003 -1.07324e-001-6.76083e-003-1.04841e-001-6.92691e-003-1.02310e-001-7.09754e-003 The headers describe the type of data. Here, it is an “acceleration/force” FRF, on the degree of freedom 1011:+Z with respect to the reference 12:-Z . For further details, see the reference documentation of the data set 58 in appendix 5.2 . The use of LIRE_RESU in this case poses no particular problems, and is described in the test case sdls112a. Note: - the data structures created (in time or in frequency) are filled only for the degrees of freedom corresponding to the data read. This can produce incomplete data structures, unlike the \mathit{data}\mathit{set}55 in which all the degrees of freedom have a defined value, - the data structure defined uses a local coordinate system, with the components D1, D2 and D3, whose orientations are given in the components D1X, D1Y, D1Z, D2X, D2Y... It is not possible to display the result in Salomé. - For further details, see the documentation of LIRE_RESU. 2.1.3 The bases of identified modes The identified modes are stored in the \mathit{dataset}55 , which is dedicated to the fields at the nodes. In the \mathit{dataset}58 , each block corresponds to a function on a node (equivalent to a function in Aster), whereas in the \mathit{dataset}55 , each block corresponds to a field at the nodes (a cham_no in Aster). -1 55 %VALEURS AUX NOEUDS ASTER 7.03.29 CONCEPT MODINTS1 CALC - CHAMP AUX NOEUDS DE NOM SYMBOLIQUE CHAMP AUX NOEUDS DE NOM SYMBOLIQUE DEPL - DX DY DZ DRX DRY DRZ ASTER 7.03.29 CONCEPT MODINTS1 CALCULE LE 22/11/2004 A 19:24:57 DE TYPE CHAMP AUX NOEUDS DE NOM SYMBOLIQUE DEPL NUMERO D'ORDRE: 1 NUME_MODE: 1 FREQ: 2.18331E+01 1 2 2 8 2 3 2 4 1 1 2.18331e+01 1.00000e+00 3.74657e-03 1011 % NOEUD NO1011 -1.37933E-001 7.39432E-007 3.38287E-001 1001 % NOEUD NO1001 -1.37933E-001-2.80459E-009 1.72767E-001 -1 The detailed documentation of the data set is given in appendix 5.3 . It is important to understand certain characteristics of this storage, because the data must be recalled when calling LIRE_RESU. In particular: - Record 6 (1,2,2,8,2,3) : - 1 : domain of structural mechanics, - 2 : one describes an eigenmode (“normal mode”) - 2 : 3 degrees of freedom per node, - 8 : displacement field, - 2 : real field (5 for complex), - 6 : number of columns of values - Record 7 (2,4,1,1) : - 2,4: specific to the eigenmodes, - 1 : load case (1 by default), - 1, number of the mode - Record 8: 2.18331e+011.00000e+003.74657e-030.00000e+00 - 2.18331e+01 : natural frequency, - 1.00000e+00 : modal mass, - 3.74657e-03 : modal damping The value of these lines is given in LIRE_RESU, as the example below shows. This makes it possible in particular for Aster to differentiate, in a unv file, the classical eigenmodes from the static residuals which are often computed by the software used. MODMES=LIRE_RESU(TYPE_RESU='MODE_MECA', FORMAT='IDEAS', MODELE=MODEXP, UNITE=21, NOM_CHAM='DEPL', MATR_RIGI =KASSEXP, MATR_MASS =MASSEXP, FORMAT_IDEAS=_F(NOM_CHAM='DEPL', NUME_DATASET=55, RECORD_6=(1,2,2,8,2,3,), POSI_ORDRE=(7,4,), POSI_NUME_MODE=(7,4), POSI_FREQ=(8,1,), POSI_MASS_GENE=(8,2), POSI_AMOR_GENE=(8,3), NOM_CMP=('DX','DY','DZ'),), TOUT_ORDRE='OUI',); 2.2 Creation of an experimental model in Code_Aster The handling of experimental data in Code_Aster requires the adequate data structures to be created, with the formalism of the code. One must therefore reproduce all the steps of the creation of the model, up to the assembly of the matrices which are used in LIRE_RESU (keywords MATR_RIGI and MATR_MASS in the example above). 2.2.1 General case In the general case, the nodes are all connected to one another by linear SEG2 elements. The commands to be chained are the following: - importation and reading of the mesh with PRE_IDEAS and LIRE_MAILLAGE, - assignment of a mechanical modelling of type DIS_T; one could use a DIS_TR modelling in the case where the field to be read had 6 degrees of freedom per node (for example, if one is capable of measuring the rotational degrees of freedom), - assignment of arbitrary geometric characteristics in mass and stiffness on the nodes and segments with AFFE_CARA_ELEM, - assembly of the matrices with ASSEMBLAGE, - reading of the data with LIRE_RESU. Example: test case sdls112a, slightly modified so as not to take the orphan nodes into account. PRE_IDEAS(UNITE_IDEAS=32,UNITE_MAILLAGE=22); MAYAEXP=LIRE_MAILLAGE(UNITE=22); MAYAEXP=DEFI_GROUP(reuse =MAYAEXP, MAILLAGE=MAYAEXP, CREA_GROUP_MA=_F(NOM='ALL_EXP',TOUT='OUI',), CREA_GROUP_NO=_F(GROUP_MA='ALL_EXP',),); MODEXP=AFFE_MODELE(MAILLAGE=MAYAEXP, AFFE=_F(GROUP_MA='ALL_EXP', PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='DIS_T',),); CHCAREXP=AFFE_CARA_ELEM(MODELE=MODEXP, DISCRET=(_F(GROUP_MA='ALL_EXP', CARA='K_T_D_L', VALE=(1.0,1.0,1.0,),), _F(GROUP_MA='ALL_EXP', REPERE='GLOBAL', CARA='M_T_D_L', VALE=(1.0,),),),); ASSEMBLAGE( MODELE=MODEXP, CARA_ELEM=CHCAREXP, NUME_DDL=CO('NUMEXP'), MATR_ASSE=(_F(MATRICE=CO('KASSEXP'), OPTION='RIGI_MECA',), _F(MATRICE=CO('MASSEXP'), OPTION='MASS_MECA',),),); MODMES=LIRE_RESU(TYPE_RESU='MODE_MECA', FORMAT='IDEAS', MODELE=MODEXP, UNITE=32, NOM_CHAM='DEPL', MATR_RIGI =KASSEXP, MATR_MASS =MASSEXP, FORMAT_IDEAS=_F(NOM_CHAM='DEPL', NUME_DATASET=55, RECORD_6=(1,2,2,8,2,3), POSI_ORDRE=(7,4,), POSI_NUME_MODE=(7,4), POSI_FREQ=(8,1,), POSI_MASS_GENE=(8,2), POSI_AMOR_GENE=(8,3), NOM_CMP=('DX','DY','DZ'),), TOUT_ORDRE='OUI',); A few pieces of advice and pitfalls to be avoided: - The order of the components (keyword NOM_CMP) in LIRE_RESU is not compulsory; it is possible to carry out a simple change of coordinate system (the same for all the nodes) by choosing judiciously the order of the components. - Beware of the keyword RECORD_6; it can vary; this is in particular the case when the unv file has been created by Code_Aster itself. Indeed, it can happen that the data are printed on 6 columns, in the case where the user has printed the data on a DIS_TR modelling. The last 3 columns contain the rotational degrees of freedom. This is the case in the test case sdls112a. One can read back only the first three if the experimental model has only 3 degrees of freedom per node. - It is possible to read data coming from strain gauges. In this case, - NOM_CHAM='EPSI_NOEU', - NOM_CMP=('EPXX','EPYY'...) to be chosen according to the coordinate system used. - In order to compare these data with numerical data, one will be able to use the macro-command OBSERVATION. 2.2.2 Case of the orphan nodes It is not advisable to use orphan nodes in the mesh, because the associated fields are difficult to visualise in Salomé. One can nevertheless read experimental data on these nodes, provided that one applies to them a specific modelling of point type (POI1). The case is treated in the test case sdls112a. MAYAEXP=CREA_MAILLAGE(MAILLAGE=MAYAtmp, CREA_POI1=_F(TOUT='OUI',NOM_GROUP_MA='NOEU'),) MODEXP=AFFE_MODELE(MAILLAGE=MAYAEXP, AFFE=_F(GROUP_MA='NOEU', PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='DIS_T',),); CHCAREXP=AFFE_CARA_ELEM(MODELE=MODEXP, DISCRET=(_F(GROUP_MA='NOEU', REPERE='GLOBAL', CARA='K_T_D_N', VALE=(1.0,1.0,1.0,),), _F(GROUP_MA='NOEU', REPERE='GLOBAL', CARA='M_T_D_N', VALE=(1.0,),),),); 3 Model validation by the MAC criterion 3.1 What is the MAC? The MAC, Modal Assurance Criterion, is a criterion lying between 0 and 1 giving the collinearity between two modes with respect to a given norm. {\mathit{MAC}}_{ij}=\frac{{({\Phi}_{i}^{H}W{\Phi}_{j})}^{2}}{({\Phi}_{i}^{H}W{\Phi}_{i})({\Phi}_{j}^{H}W{\Phi}_{j})} The use of the weighting matrices ( W in the formula) is optional. When one knows them, one can use the mass or stiffness matrices of the model. This is the case when one handles numerical data, because the matrices have been assembled on the model. It makes it possible to check the orthogonality of the eigenmodes with respect to the mass and stiffness matrices: - {\mathit{MAC}}_{ij}=1\mathit{si}i=j - {\mathit{MAC}}_{ij}=0\mathit{sinon} But when one handles experimental data, one does not know the matrices condensed on this model. One can manufacture them by Guyan condensation from the numerical model, but, the latter not being updated, one risks making an error. One can, more simply, compute the MAC without a weighting matrix, and look at the collinearity of the modes in the norm {L}_{2} . - If the objective is to check the orthogonality of the basis, one can consider, as a first approximation, that the MAC without a weighting matrix is fairly similar to the MAC weighted by the mass matrix, - If the objective is to compare two bases of modes with each other, then the choice of this norm is equivalent to the others: the MAC will be equal to 1 if the modes are collinear (hence if they “look alike”) and 0 otherwise. NB: the use of the MAC on experimental modes makes it possible in particular to check the capability of the sensors to separate the modes. Indeed, the more sensors one has, the more the modes “will look different” as seen from them. The MAC of two different modes correctly identified will therefore be close to 0. If one has a single sensor, then the MAC between two modes will always be equal to 1: the modes are not separable. 3.2 Projection of fields 3.2.1 Projection of the numerical data onto the experimental model with PROJ_CHAMP The modes are comparable only if they are defined on the same model. One therefore projects the numerical modal basis, computed with Code_Aster , onto the experimental model, with the command PROJ_CHAMP. Image 3.2-1 : projection of data. Notes: - Important note: one must specify, in PROJ_CHAMP, the name of the NUME_DDL of the experimental model, so that the numberings of the experimental modes and of the projected numerical modes are the same. - If the NUME_DDL is not the same, one will not be able to compute a MAC criterion. - In PROJ_CHAMP, it is necessary to specify the dimension onto which one projects: by default, one will associate the nodes of the experimental model with 3D elements of the numerical model. - If the numerical model is constituted of plate elements, one must specify it with CAS='2.5D', - If the numerical model is composed of 3D and 2D elements, then it is not possible to specify several types of projection. One solution proposed is to assign a plate modelling (DKT for example) to the skin elements which cover the 3D elements and to place oneself in the case '2.5D'. - The operator OBSERVATION makes it possible to carry out the same operation, with additional options: - use of local coordinate systems sensor by sensor, - removal of the measured data from the result data structure (for the cases where the measurement had been made with uniaxial sensors), - creation of a mixed data structure comprising accelerometric and extensometric data, in order to reproduce an accelerometer + strain-gauge measurement, - simulation of a “virtual gauge”. - The description of this operator is proposed in the following paragraph. 3.2.2 Use of the macro-command OBSERVATION for the projection of the data It is proposed to give a practical example of the use of the macro-command on the following case: Image 3.2-2 : measurement of the vibrations of a blade using a strain gauge and an accelerometer. One assumes that the vibrations of the bladed wheel represented on the mesh below have been measured by placing a strain gauge at the root of each blade and an accelerometer at the tip. The identified eigenmodes are exported in unv format without passing to the global coordinate system . The vibrations at the tip having been measured in only one direction, one will have a line of the form: 2 4 1 1 2.18331e+01 1.00000e+00 3.74657e-03 1 % NOEUD NO1 0.00000e+00 0.00000e+00 7.39432e-01 -1 On the node \mathit{N01} , only the local component \mathit{DZ} has been measured. The directions not measured are set to 0. It is not possible, in a data set 55, to distinguish between unmeasured data and zero measurements. In order to compare the experimental data and the reduced numerical eigenmodes, two operations are necessary: - on the experimental data, one filters the modes so as to eliminate the unmeasured data, keeping only one direction for the strain gauge and the accelerometer - one uses OBSERVATION without projection (PROJECTION='NON'), because one is only filtering the data, OBSMXT = OBSERVATION( RESULTAT = MESURE, MODELE_1 = MODMESUR, MODELE_2 = MODMESUR, PROJECTION = 'NON', TOUT_ORDRE = 'OUI', NOM_CHAM = ('DEPL','EPSI_NOEU',), FILTRE =( _F( GROUP_NO = 'P1', NOM_CHAM = 'EPSI_NOEU', DDL_ACTIF = ('EPXX',),), _F( GROUP_NO = 'P2', NOM_CHAM = 'DEPL', DDL_ACTIF = ('DZ',),), ),); - on the numerical data, one projects the eigenmodes onto the experimental model: - one uses PROJECTION='OUI', - one computes the mean strain for the node group in red on the figure before carrying out the projection: this surface corresponds to the surface actually measured by the strain gauge, - one carries out the changes of coordinate system, using the option 'NORMALE': one computes the normal to the numerical mesh in order to define the axis Z of the local coordinate system (the second axis is defined with the keyword VECT_Y); here, one could also have used the option 'CYNLINDRIQUE'. - one filters the components corresponding to the measured data. OBSJAU = OBSERVATION( RESULTAT = CALCUL, MODELE_1 = MODNUME, MODELE_2 = MODMESUR, PROJECTION = 'OUI', TOUT_ORDRE = 'OUI', NOM_CHAM = 'EPSI_NOEU', EPSI_MOYENNE = _F( GROUP_MA='SURF1',SEUIL_VARI=(0.1,), MASQUE=('EPYY','EPZZ','EPXY', 'EPXZ','EPYZ'),), MODI_REPERE = _F( GROUP_NO = ('P1',P2'), REPERE = 'NORMALE', VECT_Y = (0.,1.,0.)),), FILTRE =( _F( GROUP_NO = 'P1', NOM_CHAM = 'EPSI_NOEU', DDL_ACTIF = ('EPXX'),), _F( GROUP_NO = 'P2', NOM_CHAM = 'DEPL', DDL_ACTIF = ('DZ',),),),); 3.3 Computation of the MAC between two bases of modes The computation of the MAC can be carried out with the operator MAC_MODES, which computes the MAC matrix between all the modes of two bases. The data structure produced is a table, which one prints with INFO=2 in MAC_MODES. The keyword MATR_ASSE makes it possible to use a weighting matrix. The printed table has the following form: ASTER 11.01.03 CONCEPT MAC_ET CALCULE LE 15/02/2012 A 14:18:54 DE TYPE TABLE_SDASTER MAC ! NUME_MODE_1 ! 1 2 3 4 5 NUME_MODE_2 1 ! 1.00000E+00 2.17692E-14 7.49505E-16 5.23742E-22 1.66188E-21 2 ! 2.17692E-14 1.00000E+00 4.21440E-13 9.40269E-19 1.12652E-19 3 ! 7.49505E-16 4.21440E-13 1.00000E+00 7.24387E-18 1.28403E-17 4 ! 5.23742E-22 9.40269E-19 7.24387E-18 1.00000E+00 2.11012E-13 5 ! 1.66188E-21 1.12652E-19 1.28403E-17 2.11012E-13 1.00000E+00 One can visualise the MAC produced in excel, or use the macro-command CALC_ESSAI, which offers a 2D visualisation. To this end, launch the macro-command without keywords at the end of the analysis, and position oneself on the “model expansion” tab. Image 3.3-1 : Image 3.3-1: CALC_ESSAI: model expansion. In the lower frame, choose the two bases of modes to be compared (if only one of the two bases is selected, one will compute a MAC of the basis with itself), and click on MAC. If the bases chosen are not defined on the same model, the MAC button is greyed out. The MAC matrix which appears is the following: Image 3.3-2 : MAC between two bases of modes visualised under CALC_ESSAI. By passing the mouse over the cells, one sees at the bottom the frequencies of the modes concerned and the value of the MAC for the latter. NB: in appendix 5.4 , a script is proposed which uses the python matplotlib library, making it possible to create 3D MAC diagrams which are more easily interpretable than the one implemented by default in CALC_ESSAI. In the longer term, the feasibility of integrating the 3D MAC by default into the operator is being studied. 4 Other validation methods 4.1 Validation by visual comparison of modal shapes This mode of validation is the most direct. It can be done by printing the modal shapes in Salomé in the classical manner. NB: in CALC_ESSAI, in the “Model expansion” tab, it is possible to select one or two bases (opposite “Result 1” and “Result 2”) and to visualise them in GMSH by clicking on “Shapes”. It is not currently possible to visualise the shapes in Salomé; this development is to be carried out in 2012 (by adding the possibility of superimposing the shapes). 4.2 Validation by comparison of FRFs A procedure is proposed in CALC_ESSAI making it possible to compare an FRF coming from the measurement with an FRF simulated by hammer impact. This validation method is different, because the comparison is done at one measurement point at a time, but over an extended frequency band. u2.07.01 User's guide to the FOURIER modelling u2.07.01 User's guide to the FOURIER modelling 1 Purpose Fourier analysis is intended to compute the response of structures of axisymmetric geometry subjected to non-axisymmetric loadings decomposed into Fourier series. Limitations: - the decomposition of the loading into Fourier series is assumed to have been carried out by the user, - the Aster implementation concerns only isotropic or orthotropic materials, - in thermal analysis, there is no global command making it possible to solve a problem over several harmonics. The analysis must be carried out harmonic by harmonic. 2 Notation All the fields considered (forces, displacements, strains, stresses, fluxes) are expressed in cylindrical coordinates with the following convention on the order of the components: | radial component along r axial component along z tangential (or circumferential) component along \theta Example: ({u}_{r},{u}_{z},{u}_{\theta}) ({f}_{r},{f}_{z},{f}_{\theta}) | | | --- | --- | The mesh is located in the plane (r,z) , the rotational symmetry being about the axis \mathrm{Oz} . The triad (r,z,\theta ) is oriented in the right-handed sense. 3 Modelling, loadings To assign the Fourier axisymmetric finite elements on the mesh, one uses the operator AFFE_MODELE in the following way: mo = AFFE_MODELE ( MAILLAGE = ma, AFFE= _F ( TOUT= 'OUI', PHENOMENE= 'MECANIQUE'ou'THERMIQUE', MODELISATION= 'AXIS_FOURIER' ) ); The decomposition of the loading into Fourier series must have been carried out beforehand by the user namely f=\sum_{l=0}^{N}\left[(\begin{array}{ccc}\cos l\theta & & 0\\ & \cos l\theta & \\ 0& & -\sin l\theta \end{array}){F}_{l}^{s}(r,z)+(\begin{array}{ccc}\sin l\theta & & 0\\ & \sin l\theta & \\ 0& & \cos l\theta \end{array}){F}_{l}^{a}(r,z)\right] with {F}_{l}^{s(a)}=({f}_{rl}^{\mathrm{ss}(a)},{f}_{zl}^{s(a)},{f}_{\theta l}^{s(a)}) The loads {F}_{l}^{s} and {F}_{l}^{a} are introduced harmonic by harmonic and type by type by the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA. One does not specify the mode or the type at this level. Example: one assumes a distributed-pressure loading, symmetric mode 1, and pure torsion (antisymmetric mode 0). One will write: ch1sym = AFFE_CHAR_MECA(Modele = mo, PRES_REP = _F( GROUP_MA = 'grma', PRES = p)) ch0anti = AFFE_CHAR_MECA(Modele = mo, FORCE_NODALE = _F( FZ = f, NOEUD = 'N1)) Dirichlet boundary conditions will be introduced in a separate load: chdir = AFFE_CHAR_MECA(Modele= mo, DDL_IMPO = _F(GROUP_NO = 'grno', DX = 0., DY = 0., DZ = 0.,)) The loadings admissible for the Fourier elements are: in elasticity: | Elements | Nature of the loading | Keyword AFFE_CHAR_MECA | | --- | --- | --- | | TRIA3 - TRIA6 QUAD4 - QUAD8 - QUAD9 | Body forces Rotation Gravity Point forces | FORCE_INTERNE ROTATION PESANTEUR FORCE_NODALE | | SEG2 - SEG3 | Pressure Surface forces | PRES_REP FORCE_CONTOUR | in thermal analysis: | Elements | Nature of the loading | Keyword AFFE_CHAR_THER | | --- | --- | --- | | Surface | Heat source | SOURCE | | Edge | Imposed normal flux Exchange | FLUX_REP ECHANGE | 3.1 Particular case of gravity One considers the cylinder below, whose hatched part corresponds to the meshed part on which one carries out a Fourier axisymmetric analysis (plane \mathrm{rZ} ). This cylinder is subjected to its self-weight P directed along the axis -\text{OX} . r \theta The loading to be applied here is \overrightarrow{P}=({P}_{r},{P}_{z},{P}_{\theta}) \theta =0 \theta With {P}_{r}=-g\cos\theta {P}_{z}=0 {P}_{\theta}=g\sin\theta \theta =\frac{3}{2}\pi One checks that, for every value of \theta , one does indeed have a loading r of amplitude g>0 directed downwards. The required loading is therefore g(-1,0,-1) according to the Fourier-mode decomposition (symmetric harmonic and cosine series expansion for the radial component). \theta =\pi \theta Warning: the direction is under the assumption that P is directed along the axis -\text{OX} . For another orientation of P , the analysis must be adapted. r X(r) Y(Z) Z(\theta ) \overrightarrow{P} Nevertheless, since the direction vector of the loading is normalised in AFFE_CHAR_MECA, one must multiply by this norm in order to obtain the required loading. The loading to be introduced in AFFE_CHAR_MECA under the keyword PESANTEUR is therefore \sqrt{2}g(-1,0,-1) . In MACRO_ELAS_MULT, this loading will be assigned to symmetric harmonic 1 (cosine series expansion for the radial component). 4 Solution with Aster Once the loading has been decomposed into Fourier harmonics, the harmonics being decoupled from one another (for a different Fourier number), one must assemble and solve as many linear systems as there are harmonics. Moreover, the material being assumed non-anisotropic, for one and the same harmonic number the symmetric and antisymmetric modes are decoupled. One must therefore carry out as many solutions (with the corresponding load) as there are different (harmonic, mode) pairs. The implementation in Code_Aster differs according to whether the phenomenon is thermal or mechanical. 4.1 Thermal analysis In thermal analysis, there is no global command making it possible to compute several harmonics directly. One must therefore proceed harmonic by harmonic. Moreover, the analyses of the elementary matrices and right-hand sides can be carried out only with the commands CALC_MATR_ELEM and CALC_VECT_ELEM (and not with the command THER_LINEAIRE). The Fourier mode is to be introduced in CALC_MATR_ELEM by the simple keyword MODE_FOURIER. The type of the harmonic is not required, the matrices (and vectors) being independent of the type. The type is taken into account only at the Fourier recombination. It is important to assemble the matrices and vectors corresponding to the different harmonics with the same numbering, so as to be able to recombine the result fields. The operator NUME_DDL, which builds the numbering, is therefore used once for the first harmonic, the numbering thus created being reused for all the other harmonics. This is possible if one has separated the Dirichlet loads from the loadings proper (see example [§6.1]). 4.2 Mechanics The command making it possible to treat several harmonics is MACRO_ELAS_MULT U4.51.02. In this macro, the harmonics are considered as load cases and one therefore carries out as many solutions as there are harmonics. As in thermal analysis, one must separate the Dirichlet loads, which must be identical for all the harmonics, from the loadings proper, which may vary. One obtains a RESULTAT data structure containing all the fields corresponding to the computed harmonics (see example [§6.2]). 5 Post-processing 5.1 Thermal analysis The analysis of the fluxes is carried out by the operator CALC_CHAM_ELEM, specifying the number of the harmonic by the simple keyword MODE_FOURIER. The flux-analysis options remain the standard options: FLUX_ELNO to compute the fluxes at the nodes per element FLUX_ELGA to compute the fluxes at the Gauss points The order of the components of the flux vector is ({\phi }_{r},{\phi }_{z},{\phi }_{\theta}) . The Fourier recombination on the temperatures is carried out from the operator CREA_CHAMP U4.72.04. It makes it possible to obtain the temperatures in different angular sections introduced by the user. The Fourier recombination on the fluxes is carried out in CREA_CHAMP U4.72.04 on the same principle. 5.2 Mechanics The analysis of the strains and of the stresses is carried out by the operator CALC_CHAMP. The analysis options remain the standard options: EPSI_ELNO to compute the strains at the nodes per element SIEF_ELGA to compute the stresses at the Gauss points SIGM_ELNO to compute the stresses at the nodes per element SIEQ_ELGA to compute the equivalent stresses at the Gauss points SIEQ_ELNO to compute the equivalent stresses at the nodes per element (for these last 2 options, one must have computed SIEF_ELGA beforehand) The order of the components of the strain tensor (resp. stresses) is: ({\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{rr}},{\varepsilon}_{zz},{\varepsilon}_{\theta \theta },{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{rz}},{\varepsilon}_{r\theta },{\varepsilon}_{z\theta }) (\text{resp.}{\sigma}_{\mathrm{rr}},{\sigma}_{zz},{\sigma}_{\theta \theta },{\sigma}_{\mathrm{rz}},{\sigma}_{r\theta },{\sigma}_{z\theta }) The Fourier recombination is carried out by the operator COMB_FOURIER U4.83.31, which makes it possible to recombine all the harmonics of the field or fields present in the RESULTAT data structure. This recombination can be carried out on a list of angles. The analysis of the equivalent stresses (von Mises, Tresca) is carried out by the operator CALC_CHAMP with the usual options SIEQ_ELGA and SIEQ_ELNO. It must be carried out after the Fourier recombination on the stresses SIGM_ELGA. 6 Examples 6.1 Thermal analysis: analysis on 2 harmonics Voir le cas test TPLV100 [:external:ref: V4.04.100 ]. 6.2 Mechanics: analysis and Fourier recombination on 2 harmonics Voir le cas test SSLV109 [:external:ref: V3.04.109 ].

u2.07.02 User's guide to static substructuring u2.07.02 User's guide to static substructuring Summary This document is an introduction to the use of static substructuring. Relying on a detailed example, the test case SSLP100B: - one will read paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4; - one will refer to the description of the specific commands: - MACR_ELEM_STAT u4.44.01 - DEFI_MAILLAGE u4.12.04 and, - DEPL_INTERNE u4.65.01, - one will return to the detailed comments on the command file (cf. u2.07.02-quelques-commentaires-fichier-commande). 1 General points The static substructuring implemented in Aster can be used in linear mechanics and in non-linear mechanics on linear parts of a model . It can be carried out a priori at several levels : a substructure can contain other substructures of lower level. All the types of elements of the phenomenon "MECANIQUE" are accepted, as are all the loadings supported by these elements. Substructuring is currently implemented within the framework of the ordinary commands [U4.4‑] and [U4.5-]. It is not, however, implemented within the framework of the global commands: MECA_STATIQUE, CALC_CHAMP, POST_ELEM, ... An exception exists: the commands STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE accept static macro-elements (see u2.07.02-utilisation-macro-elements). Static substructuring consists in "condensing" statically the problem to be treated: one eliminates a certain number of unknowns (internal ones). There then remain the so-called "external" unknowns, fewer in number. It is a method which reduces the size of the problem. One may therefore expect gains in CPU time and in disk occupancy. This static condensation applies naturally to the stiffness and mass matrices and to the right-hand sides representing the various loadings. In this case, the condensation method can be interpreted algebraically as a solution of the linear system by the "elimination" method. The solution of a linear statics problem is therefore not modified by the substructuring. On the other hand, it is possible to condense the mass matrix statically (Guyan condensation), but in that case the search for the eigenmodes of the condensed structure is altered by the substructuring method (see for example IMBERT [bib1]_). Other substructuring methods exist for dynamics problems in Aster [U4.55]. The theoretical principles of static substructuring are well explained in the book by IMBERT [bib1]_ and the PERMAS manuals [bib2]_. The use of static substructuring in the non-linear regime is dealt with in a first, separate chapter. In the remainder of this document, these theoretical principles will be assumed known and one will be concerned only with the "user" aspects. For this purpose, one will make much use of an example: the test case SSLP100 of the Aster validation manual. Through this test case, we have tried to illustrate a large number of capabilities of the software, by deliberately complicating the test: - substructuring at several levels (2), - use of one macro-element to generate several substructures by successive rotations, - boundary conditions and loadings at several levels, - mixture of substructures and ordinary finite elements, - "follower" loading or not. The command file of this test case, whose lines have been numbered, is given in the appendix to this document. When one wishes to refer to line n of this file, one will write {line n}. 2 Use of macro-elements in STAT_NON_LINE (or DYNA_NON_LINE) One can carry out a non-linear analysis with STAT_NON_LINE u4.51.03 on a model containing macro-elements. The interest of this type of analysis is a possible gain in performance (memory and/or CPU). For the analysis with macro-elements to be more economical, the model must possess large linear elastic zones (possibly repetitive). These elastic zones (which one will condense into macro-elements) must also have a boundary as small as possible. A favourable situation will be, for example, the case of a fully elastic structure with a small zone of confined plasticity (cf. u2.07.02-fig-structure-elastique). Fully elastic structure with a small zone of confined plasticity One will then condense the whole of the elastic part onto the interface nodes alone, with the zone of potential plasticity. The use of macro-elements in STAT_NON_LINE (see test cases SSLP100C and D) is subject to the following requirements: 1. each macro-element must be linear elastic; its temperature must not vary with time, 2. there can be no contact with macro-elements, 3. the loadings assigned to the macro-elements are "constant" (not multiplied by "FONC_MULT"), 4. the macro-elements must not undergo large rotations, 5. the "line search" is not possible. Once the analysis has been carried out with STAT_NON_LINE, the usual post-processing (CALC_CHAMP, POST_ELEM) will have an effect only on the ordinary finite elements of the model (the macro-elements are ignored). If one wishes to examine, for example, the state of stress inside a macro-element, one must use the basic commands: CREA_CHAMP/EXTR, DEPL_INTERNE, … (see §4.3 and §4.4). 3 Presentation of the test case SSLP100B used as an example It is a plane structure subjected to the following boundary conditions: | on the side [\mathit{GH}] : | u+v=0 | (sliding support) | | --- | --- | --- | | nodes \mathit{B1} , \mathit{B2} , \mathit{B3} : | u=v=0 | | | node J : | u=2.0 | | | load case 1: chf1: distributed pressure on \mathit{ADFH} p=10.0 | | | | load case 2: chf2: point forces on the nodes \mathit{F1} , \mathit{F2} , \mathit{F3} , \mathit{F4} and \mathit{P1} : \mathit{Fy}=-20.0 | | | 4 Treatment of the test case by the substructuring method - the initial mesh contains only the mesh cells (and the nodes) of the polygon \mathit{IJBCDA} , - one defines a macro-element (S_1) corresponding to the polygon \mathit{ABCD} , - the macro-element (S_1) is repeated twice by rotation about 0 , - one then obtains the macro-element (S_123) corresponding to the polygon \mathit{ABCEGHFD} , - the final model (on which one carries out the solution) is obtained by adding to the macro-element (S_123) the finite elements of the quadrilateral \mathit{IJBA} . 5 General organisation of the analyses and definitions 5.1 Construction of the global model The principle of the implementation of static substructuring in Code_Aster is that of an ascending approach: a model having been defined, one condenses it (operator MACR_ELEM_STAT) onto some of its nodes. One then obtains a macro-element which, functionally, closely resembles a new, "larger" finite element. This macro-element can then be integrated into a model of higher level (operators DEFI_MAILLAGE and AFFE_MODELE). This new model can then be condensed in its turn, and so on, with no a priori limitation on the number of levels. Definition : - the nodes onto which a macro-element is condensed are said to be " external " (the others are " internal "), - level : this is a notion useful for understanding the command text; every level describes the structuring relations between the different models and the different macro-elements. For us, it is an integer. The condensation operation increases the level by +1 : a model of level n gives, by condensation, a macro-element of level n+1 which will be integrated into a model of level n+1 , - the operator MACR_ELEM_STAT is the only operator making it possible to create a macro-element in static substructuring, - the operator DEFI_MAILLAGE is the only operator using the macro-elements in static substructuring. For our example: - MO_1 {line 22} is the model of lowest level (-2), - S_1 {lines 45, 59} is the macro-element of intermediate level (-1), - MA_123 and MO_123 {lines 68, 87} represent the mesh and the model of intermediate level (-1), - S_123 {line 104} is the macro-element of highest level (0), - MAG0, MAG and MOG {lines 120, 125, 129} represent meshes and a model of highest level (0): the distinction between the meshes MAG0 and MAG will be explained at u2.07.02-operateur-defi-maillage-ligne-120 and u2.07.02-operateur-asse-maillage-ligne-125. The structuring of the highest-level model MOG can be presented graphically by a tree , the distinction between macro-element and substructure being explained in the following paragraph. 5.2 Macro-element and substructure One calls macro-element the result of the operator MACR_ELEM_STAT: it is a model condensed onto its external nodes. One calls substructure an occurrence of a macro-element in a model of the same level. A substructure is a macro-element placed in position in physical space. The position of a substructure is given by the coordinates of the nodes of the super mesh cell associated with it. One and the same macro-element can give rise to several substructures by defining several positions: in our example, the macro-element S_1 generates 3 substructures S_1, S_2 and S_3 by appropriate rotations. A substructure is in some sense a new "finite element". The macro-element is the "type" of this element: one assigns a macro-element on a super mesh cell in order to form a substructure. One calls super mesh cell the geometrical support of a substructure. It is a named object included in a mesh . A super mesh cell, like an ordinary mesh cell, is only an ordered list of node names. Like an ordinary finite element, a substructure possesses: - an "elementary" stiffness matrix (and/or of mass, of damping, …), - "elementary" loading vectors, - a support mesh cell (one will speak of a super mesh cell), - nodes carrying degrees of freedom. Unlike an ordinary finite element, a substructure has several limitations: - the support mesh cell is not a simple type: TRIA3, …, HEXA20: certain post-processing is therefore not possible, - it has no type_élément, no shape functions, … - the only analysis options available are RIGI_MECA, MASS_MECA and CHAR_MECA, - the nodes may be LAGRANGE nodes coming from the dualisation of the internal kinematic conditions. Identification of the substructures and of the macro-elements: The macro-elements are concepts named by the user. The substructures (like the ordinary finite elements) are identified by the name of the super mesh cells which support them. In our example: - S_1 and S_123 are the two macro-elements defined by the user {lines 45 and 104}, - S_1, S_2, S_3, S_123 are the names of the super mesh cells (and therefore of the substructures) which the user gives when constructing the meshes MA_123 and MAG0. Note: There is no possible confusion (on the part of the program) between a substructure and a macro-element of the same name (here S_1 and S_123, although this does not make the command file easier to read!). 5.3 Descent into the substructures The ascending approach, which we have just detailed, makes it possible to construct the global, or final, model (mog) on which one carries out the solution: | CALC_MATR_ELEM | | | --- | --- | | CALC_VECT_ELEM | | | ASSE_MATRICE | {lines 151-184} | | … | | | RESOUDRE | | This solution has as its result the displacement field of the nodes of the global model. These nodes are: - the nodes of the ordinary finite elements of the model (here the quadrilateral IJBA), - the external nodes of the substructures of the model: (here a single substructure: S_123). To recover the displacement field on the internal nodes of the substructures, one must then " descend " the tree of the substructures by means of the operator DEPL_INTERNE. This operator computes the displacement field on all the nodes of the substructure from the data of the displacement field on its external nodes. For our example and for load case 1: | U1S_123 | {line 193} | is the displacement on the substructure | S_123 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | U1S_1 | {line 197} | is the displacement on the substructure | S_1 | | U1S_2 | {line 199} | is the displacement on the substructure | S_2 | | U1S_3 | {line 201} | is the displacement on the substructure | S_3 | 5.4 Post-processing The usual post-processing: analysis of the strains, of the stresses, … can be carried out only by the ordinary finite elements, which alone know the notion of interpolation function. One will therefore be able to compute the stresses at a given point of the structure only with the model containing the ordinary finite element containing that point. Before that, it will have been necessary to compute the displacement field on this model: Example: - to compute the stresses on the quadrilateral IJBA one will use the model: MOG and the displacements: U1 - to compute the stresses on the polygon DCEF one will use the model: MO_1 and the displacements: U1S_2 Note One must use CALC_CHAMP, but to do so one is obliged to create an evol_elas data structure by the command CREA_RESU. 6 Some comments on the command file The few comments which follow are intended to illustrate the commands which come into play in static substructuring. Understanding these comments obviously assumes prior reading of the user's guides of the commands concerned: - MACR_ELEM_STAT u4.44.01 - DEFI_MAILLAGE u4.12.04 - DEPL_INTERNE u4.65.01 Commands specific to static substructuring: - AFFE_MODELE[U4.22.01] - CAL_VECT_ELEM[U4.41.02] Commands modified for static substructuring: - ASSE_MAILLAGE u4.12.02 - DEFI_GROUP u4.12.03 Commands useful for static substructuring: 6.1 Operator AFFE_MODELE {line 22} Since one wishes to build a macro-element from the polygon ABCD and the mesh ma contains all the elements of IJBCDA, one cannot use the assignment: TOUT : 'OUI'. One must assign only the mesh-cell group ABCD (grsd2) and not forget to assign the elements of the edge AD (grma14) because of the pressure loading. 6.2 Operator MACR_ELEM_STAT {lines 45-59} - The example illustrates the fact that one can define the macro-element in several successive stages (use of the operator MACR_ELEM_STAT 3 times: {lines 45, 50 and 56} with the enrichment symbol &). > At the first call, one truly defines the macro-element: - its "volume": the model mo_1 - its external nodes {line 48} - the material field and the kinematic conditions applied to it {line 47}. > At the next 2 calls {lines 50 and 56}, one enriches the data structure of the macro-element: - computation of the condensed stiffness matrix {line 52} - computation of two "load cases" {lines 53 and 58}. > This possibility of enriching the macro-element makes it possible to "repair an omission" without starting again from scratch: - addition of a new load case, - computation of the condensed mass for a Guyan method. - Definition of load case 1: CHF1 {line 53} > This load case is a follower one (SUIV = 'OUI') because the pressure is a loading which always acts along the normal to the edge. > Having specified the load CHBL_1 serves no purpose here, because the kinematic conditions are zero DX = 0.0 DY = 0.0 {line 29}. 6.3 Operator DEFI_MAILLAGE {lines 68, 84} - {line 70}: one defines a substructure (and the support super mesh cell) by giving it the same name as the macro-element assigned to it. This is why the displacement field is recovered in the "local" frame of the macro-element S_1 (rotation of -45°).
