u2.07.03 Carrying out a structural-modification study from measured data u2.07.03 Carrying out a structural-modification study from measured data Summary: The purpose of this document is the description of the setting up of a structural-modification study from measured data. The method used is based on the substructuring technique. The first substructure (initial structure) is obtained from the eigenmodes identified experimentally and the second substructure (modification introduced) is modelled numerically by finite elements. 1 Context The detection of too high a vibration level on a given piece of equipment often leads to a stoppage of the use of the equipment in question, in order to avoid its failure. Thus, the putting in place of a specific solution to limit this phenomenon must be provided quickly in order to allow the installation to operate properly. Two strategies may be envisaged. If the problem is generic, the development of a predictive model updated from the measured information is the most reliable solution, but the updating is a tedious step, and does not make it possible to adapt the analysis to the specificity of each structure. If the problem is specific to a particular piece of equipment, one wishes to be able, without the model-updating step, to predict the effects of a modification on the modal characteristics of the structure. The technique presented here falls within this second strategy. In the majority of cases, one tries to shift the natural frequencies of the structure so that they do not lie in the excitation frequency band of the equipment concerned. The solution commonly used consists in adding a mass or a stiffness at a place in the structure chosen beforehand. The method for estimating the results of a structural modification described in this document was proposed by M. Corus within the framework of his thesis work [1]. It uses jointly the results of experimental measurements carried out on the initial structure and a numerical model of the modification. One presents the chaining of the different operators. The optimisation of the location and the mechanical characterisation of the modification are left to the user. Two ways of proceeding are presented in this document: in section 3, the method initially developed reproduces exactly the method proposed by M. Corus in his thesis: the structure is described on a modal basis, in generalised coordinates, and the modification on a physical basis. This technique is used in the test cases sdll137a and sdll137b. In section 4, the structure and the modification are described by their modal basis. This technique, simpler to set up, was developed subsequently for carrying out a modification study on piping. This technique is used in the test case sdll137e, on the same example; another major advantage of the proposed implementation is that the numerical models of the structure and of the modification do not need to have coincident nodes for the assembly. For information, the test cases sdll137c and sdll137d are identical to versions a and b, but use the macro-command CALC_ESSAI for carrying out the analysis. 2 Theoretical reminder This structural-modification technique is based on the substructuring method. The first substructure corresponds to the initial structure and the second substructure corresponds to the modification introduced. The initial structure is modelled from its eigenmodes identified experimentally. Except in a very particular case, the measurement points are not located at the interface between the initial structure and the modification to be introduced. Before carrying out the coupling between these two substructures, it is therefore necessary to go through an intermediate step which consists in condensing the measured information at the interfaces. The different models which come into play during this analysis are: the "measurement" model, the "support" model and the "modification" model. We shall describe these different models below. To simplify the presentation, we adopt the following notation: - the index \mathit{mes} relates to the measurement points, - the index int relates to the interface nodes, - the exponent "+" indicates the generalised inverse of a matrix, - L : localisation matrix (observability matrix), - y : displacement field, - \Phi : matrix made up of the expansion-basis vectors defined on the support model, - {\eta}_{\sup} : generalised coordinates associated with the expansion basis \Phi - \psi : identified modal matrix (eigenmode shapes) on the initial structure, - {\eta}_{\mathrm{test}} : generalised coordinates associated with \psi 2.1 The "measurement" model We call "measurement" model the modal model of the initial structure obtained from the measured information. On this model is defined a mesh made up of the measurement points. A measured displacement field can be projected onto a basis composed of the identified eigenmodes, namely: > {y}_{\mathrm{mes}}=\psi {\eta}_{\mathrm{test}} (1) One restricts oneself to the case of lightly damped structures (for which the damping can be modelled mode by mode), for which the modal model of the initial structure is written: \left\lbrace -{\omega}^{2}[\mathrm{Id}]+j\omega [{\beta}_{\mathrm{test}}]+[{\Omega}_{\mathrm{test}}^{2}]\right\rbrace {\eta}_{\mathrm{test}}={f}_{{\eta}_{\mathrm{test}}} (2) Where: | [\mathrm{Id}] | :60: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | identity matrix | | --- | --- | --- | | [{\Omega}_{\mathrm{test}}^{2}] | :60: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | spectral matrix (diagonal matrix whose diagonal terms are the natural angular frequencies squared) | | [{\beta}_{\mathrm{test}}] | :60: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | matrix of the generalised dampings | | {f}_{{\eta}_{\mathrm{test}}} | :60: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | modal loading | | \omega | :60: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | excitation angular frequency | 2.2 The "support" model We call "support" model the simplified numerical model of the initial structure. This model must include the interfaces between the initial structure and the modification. It is used for the expansion and the condensation of the measured information at the interfaces. The expansion consists in finding a field defined on this support model, whose restriction to the measurement points is as close as possible to the field measured experimentally. This field is obtained by minimising the distance between the measured information and the information estimated on the support model. The estimated displacement field {\tilde{y}}_{\mathrm{mes}} at the measurement points is given by the following relation: {\tilde{y}}_{\mathrm{mes}}={L}_{\mathrm{mes}}\Phi {\eta}_{\sup} (3) The estimated field {\tilde{y}}_{\mathrm{mes}} is of the same type as the measured field {y}_{\mathrm{mes}} . The generalised coordinates {\eta}_{\sup} , unknown, are obtained by minimising the distance between the measured field and the estimated field. By using the least-squares technique, one obtains: {\eta}_{\sup}={({L}_{\mathrm{mes}}\Phi )}^{+}{y}_{\mathrm{mes}} (4) One can thus estimate the field \tilde{y} defined at the nodes of the support model, consistent with the field measured experimentally. \tilde{y}=\Phi {\eta}_{\sup}=\Phi {({L}_{\mathrm{mes}}\Phi )}^{+}{y}_{\mathrm{mes}} (5) The restriction of this field to the interface degrees of freedom is: {\tilde{y}}_{int}={L}_{int}\tilde{y}={L}_{int}\Phi {({L}_{\mathrm{mes}}\Phi )}^{+}{y}_{\mathrm{mes}}={T}_{\mathrm{It}}{y}_{\mathrm{mes}} (6) {T}_{\mathrm{it}} can be defined as being the passage matrix between the measurement points and the interface between the initial structure and the modification. By replacing the measured field {y}_{\mathrm{mes}} by its expression (1), one obtains: {\tilde{y}}_{int}={T}_{\mathrm{It}}{y}_{int}={T}_{\mathrm{It}}\Psi {\eta}_{\mathrm{test}} (7) That is: {\eta}_{\mathrm{test}}={({T}_{\mathrm{It}}\Psi )}^{+}{\tilde{y}}_{int} (8) If one writes: B={({T}_{\mathrm{It}}\Psi )}^{+} , one obtains: {\eta}_{\mathrm{test}}=B{\tilde{y}}_{int} (9) By multiplying equation (2) on the left by {B}^{T} , and by replacing {\eta}_{\mathrm{test}} by its expression (9), the dynamic stiffness {\hat{Z}}_{\mathrm{test}} of the initial structure is given by the following relation: \left\lbrace -{\omega}^{2}{B}^{T}B+j\omega {B}^{T}[{\beta}_{\mathrm{test}}]B+{B}^{T}[{\Omega}_{\mathrm{test}}^{2}]B\right\rbrace {\tilde{y}}_{int}={\hat{Z}}_{\mathrm{test}}{\tilde{y}}_{int}={f}_{int}^{I} (10) With: {f}_{int}^{I} : force applied at the interface 2.3 The "modification" model We call "modification" model the numerical model of the modification introduced into the initial structure. If one denotes {Z}_{x} its dynamic stiffness, by partitioning the unknowns into internal degrees of freedom {y}_{i} and external degrees of freedom {y}_{e} (which are composed of interface degrees of freedom), the model of the modification can be rewritten in the following way: {Z}_{x}q=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{Z}_{ii}& {Z}_{\mathrm{ie}}\\ {Z}_{\mathrm{ei}}& {Z}_{\mathrm{ee}}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}{y}_{i}\\ {y}_{e}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}{f}_{i}^{M}\\ {f}_{e}^{M}+{f}_{\mathrm{eext}}^{M}\end{array}\right] (11) The index i relates to the internal degrees of freedom, the index e relates to the external degrees of freedom and {f}_{\mathrm{eext}}^{M} denotes the external force applied to the external degrees of freedom. 2.4 Coupling of the two substructures The dynamic stiffness of the coupled model is obtained by considering the continuity of the displacements at the interfaces: {\tilde{y}}_{int}={y}_{e} (12) and the equilibrium of the forces at the interfaces: {f}_{int}^{I}+{f}_{e}^{M}=0 (13) That is: \left[\begin{array}{cc}{Z}_{ii}& {Z}_{\mathrm{ie}}\\ {Z}_{\mathrm{ei}}& {Z}_{\mathrm{ee}}+{\hat{Z}}_{\mathrm{test}}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}{y}_{i}\\ {y}_{e}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}{f}_{i}^{M}\\ {f}_{\mathrm{eext}}^{M}\end{array}\right] (14) The solution of this system makes it possible to compute the behaviour of the modified structure. Note: in section 4, the compatibility equations at the interface are written on a modal basis, that is to say that equations (12) and (13) are not satisfied exactly: they are projected onto the subspace made up of the basis of the extended modes of the structure: {\Phi}^{T}{\tilde{y}}_{int}={\Phi}^{T}{y}_{e} (15) {\Phi}^{T}{f}_{int}^{I}+{\Phi}^{T}{f}_{e}^{M}=0 (16) Since there are in general more interface degrees of freedom than eigenmodes used, relations (15) and (16) cannot be ensured exactly. 2.5 Back-projection of the field onto the measurement points One can evaluate the field at the points where the measurement was carried out, by back-projection of the field at the interfaces obtained on the coupled model. By exploiting relations (1), (9) and (12), the field at the measurement points is written: {y}_{\mathrm{mes}}=\Psi {\eta}_{\mathrm{test}}=\Psi B{\tilde{y}}_{int}=\Psi B{y}_{e} (17) 2.6 Checking the quality of the expansion basis The quality of the results depends of course on the uncertainty in the measurement, but also on the capacity of the expansion basis to represent the behaviour of the real structure and the transmission of the information at the interface. The physical sense of the user comes into the choice of this expansion basis. It is difficult to know a priori the size of the expansion basis making it possible to obtain the best estimate of the coupled behaviour. The quality of the expansion basis can be measured by re-estimating the field at the interface by static expansion on the initial model from the field coming from the coupled model. This indicator does not make it possible to estimate directly the quality of the results obtained on the coupled model, but it indicates the relevance of the reconstruction of the field at the interface. 3 Setting up the structural-modification analysis, example of the test cases sdll137a and sdll137b The input data of the analysis are: - the eigenmodes (frequencies, mode shapes, generalised masses) identified on the initial structure, - the simplified finite-element model of the initial structure ("support" model), - the finite-element model of the proposed modification ("modification" model). In this section, the method described reproduces exactly that proposed by M. Corus in his thesis. To illustrate the presentation, we take as an example the test case sdll137 V2.02.137. We present only the main steps of the modelling. 3.1 The "measurement" model The "measurement" model makes it possible to define the location of the measurement points. The nodes of the mesh can be linked together by discrete elements, for example, in order to facilitate the visualisation of the measured information. The mechanical characteristics which one assigns to this model do not influence the results; they allow the model to accommodate the identified eigenmodes. This is expressed at the Aster level in the following way: Reading of the sensor mesh (measurement points): MAILEXP=LIRE_MAILLAGE(UNITE=22); MODLEXP=AFFE_MODELE(MAILLAGE=MAILEXP, AFFE=_F(TOUT='OUI', PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='DIS_TR',),); Reading of the identified eigenmodes: MODMESU=LIRE_RESU(TYPE_RESU='MODE_MECA', FORMAT='IDEAS', MODELE=MODLEXP, UNITE=21, NOM_CHAM='DEPL', MATR_RIGI =KASSEXP, MATR_MASS =MASSEXP, FORMAT_IDEAS=_F(NOM_CHAM='DEPL', NUME_DATASET=55, RECORD_6=(1,2,3,8,2,6,), POSI_ORDRE=(7,4,), POSI_NUME_MODE=(7,4), POSI_FREQ=(8,1,), POSI_MASS_GENE=(8,2), POSI_AMOR_GENE=(8,3), NOM_CMP=('DX','DY','DZ', 'DRX','DRY','DRZ'),), TOUT_ORDRE='OUI',); One can possibly carry out a selection on the identified modes in order to keep only the eigenmodes most worthwhile to exploit. MODEIDE=EXTR_MODE(FILTRE_MODE=_F(MODE=MODMESU, NUME_MODE=(1,2,3,4,5,),),); 3.2 The "support" model The "support" model is used for the expansion of the measurement onto the interface degrees of freedom. It must contain the interface nodes between the initial structure and the modification. On this model is defined an expansion basis which makes it possible to pass from the sensor degrees of freedom to the interface degrees of freedom. This expansion basis can be composed of eigenmodes, or of static responses, or of eigenmodes of the support model condensed onto the interface degrees of freedom and the sensor degrees of freedom[1]. The quality of the results depends on the ability of this basis to reproduce the real behaviour of the structure. The geometrical and mechanical characteristics assigned to this model are not necessarily the exact (updated) mechanical characteristics of the real structure, but they must be as close as possible to the physical reality. Indeed, the closer the model is to reality, the better the results of the expansion will be. Reading of the mesh of the "support" model: MAILSUP=LIRE_MAILLAGE(UNITE=20); MODLSUP=AFFE_MODELE(MAILLAGE=MAILSUP, AFFE=(_F(GROUP_MA=('POUTRE','VISUAL',), PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='POU_D_E',),),) Definition of the expansion-basis vectors: MODESUP=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=KASSUP, MATR_MASS=MASSUP, OPTION='PLUS_PETITE', CALC_FREQ=_F(NMAX_FREQ=20, SEUIL_FREQ=1.E-4,), VERI_MODE=_F(SEUIL=1.E-05, STOP_ERREUR='OUI',), ); MODSTSUP=MODE_STATIQUE(MATR_RIGI=KASSUP, FORCE_NODALE=(_F(GROUP_NO='CAPTEUR', AVEC_CMP=('DY','DZ',),),),); BASEMO=DEFI_BASE_MODALE(RITZ=(_F(MODE_MECA=MODESUP,NMAX_MODE=0,), _F(MODE_STAT=MODSTSUP,NMAX_MODE=8,),), NUME_REF=NUMSUP,); Expansion of the measured information onto the support model: PROJ=PROJ_MESU_MODAL(MODELE_CALCUL=_F(MODELE=MODLSUP, BASE=BASEMO,), MODELE_MESURE=_F(MODELE=MODLEXP, MESURE=MODEIDE, NOM_CHAM='DEPL',), RESOLUTION=_F(METHODE='SVD', EPS=1.E-5),); Condensation of the measurement onto the interface degrees of freedom (here the interface degrees of freedom are chosen as being the "external" degrees of freedom of the macro-element): SSEXP = MACR_ELEM_STAT(DEFINITION=_F(MODELE=MODLSUP, PROJ_MESU=PROJ, MODE_MESURE=MODEIDE, CARA_ELEM =CHCARSUP, CHAM_MATER=CHMATSUP,), EXTERIEUR=_F(GROUP_NO = ('EXTERNE',),), RIGI_MECA=_F(), MASS_MECA=_F(),); Creation of the «super mesh cell» comprising the interface nodes: MAILCOND=DEFI_MAILLAGE(DEFI_SUPER_MAILLE=_F(MACR_ELEM_STAT = SSEXP, SUPER_MAILLE='SUMAIL',), DEFI_NOEUD=_F( TOUT = 'OUI', INDEX = (1,0,1,8,),),); 3.3 Coupling of the measurement and of the modification Before carrying out the coupling of the substructures, one must make sure that the meshes of the different substructures are consistent (meshes expressed in the same coordinate system, …). The coupling consists in assembling the two models (initial structure condensed at the interface nodes, and modification) into a single model. The principle is identical to that of substructuring. Reading of the mesh of the modification: MAILX=LIRE_MAILLAGE(UNITE=24); Assembly of the two meshes (super mesh cell + modification): MAILCPL=ASSE_MAILLAGE(MAILLAGE_1=MAILCOND, MAILLAGE_2=MAILX, OPERATION='SOUS_STR',); MODLCPL=AFFE_MODELE(MAILLAGE=MAILCPL, AFFE=(_F(GROUP_MA=('POUTRE',), PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='POU_D_E',),), AFFE_SOUS_STRUC=_F(SUPER_MAILLE = 'SUMAIL', PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE',),); 3.4 Analysis on the coupled model After creation and assembly of the elementary matrices (here, the assembled matrices are KASCPL and MASCPL), one can carry out a modal analysis on the coupled model in order to evaluate the effect of the modification on the first natural frequencies of the modified structure. MODECPL=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=KASCPL, MATR_MASS=MASCPL, OPTION='PLUS_PETITE', CALC_FREQ=_F(NMAX_FREQ=2, SEUIL_FREQ=1.E-4,), VERI_MODE=_F(SEUIL=1.E-05, STOP_ERREUR='OUI',), ); 3.5 Back-projection onto the measurement model This is a post-processing which consists in going back up to the initial measurement points. This makes it possible to appreciate the effect of the modification introduced with respect to the initial measurement. MODERETR=DEPL_INTERNE(DEPL_GLOBAL=MODECPL,SUPER_MAILLE='SUMAIL') 3.6 Checking the quality of the expansion basis It is always of interest to check the quality of the expansion of the measurement. One can check it by using an indicator which reports two different estimates of the field at the interface of the coupled model. It consists in comparing the field at the interface by static expansion on the support model from the field coming from the coupled model, and the field at the interface of the coupled model. In order to be able to make this comparison, one can create a fictitious model containing only the interface. The idea consists in extracting the fields at the interfaces in order to be able to compare them by carrying out a MAC (Modal Assurance Criterion) computation. Reading of the mesh of the interface: MAILINT=LIRE_MAILLAGE(UNITE=26); MODLINT=AFFE_MODELE(MAILLAGE=MAILINT, AFFE=_F(GROUP_MA='VISUAL', PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='DIS_TR',),); Computation of the static response on the support model: MODSTINT=MODE_STATIQUE(MATR_RIGI=KASSUP, FORCE_NODALE=(_F(GROUP_NO='CAPTEUR', AVEC_CMP=('DY','DZ',),),),); Definition of the basis for the static expansion: BASEINT=DEFI_BASE_MODALE(RITZ=(_F(MODE_MECA=MODESUP,NMAX_MODE=0,), _F(MODE_STAT=MODSTINT,NMAX_MODE=4,),), NUME_REF=NUMSUP,); Static expansion of the field at the measurement points obtained during the solution at the global level: PROJMS=PROJ_MESU_MODAL(MODELE_CALCUL=_F(MODELE=MODLSUP, BASE=BASEINT,), MODELE_MESURE=_F(MODELE=MODLEXP, MESURE=MODERETR, NOM_CHAM='DEPL',), RESOLUTION=_F(METHODE='SVD', EPS=1.E-5),); DEPLPR=REST_GENE_PHYS(RESU_GENE=PROJMS, TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', NOM_CHAM='DEPL'); Field at the interfaces obtained by static expansion: DEPLINT=PROJ_CHAMP(METHODE='ELEM', RESULTAT=DEPLPR, MODELE_1=MODLSUP, MODELE_2=MODLINT, NOM_CHAM='DEPL', TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', NUME_DDL=NUMINT,); Field at the interfaces obtained during the solution at the global level: DEPLXINT=PROJ_CHAMP(METHODE='ELEM', RESULTAT=MODECPL, MODELE_1=MODLCPL, MODELE_2=MODLINT, NOM_CHAM='DEPL', TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', NUME_DDL=NUMINT,); The expansion basis is acceptable if the two fields defined at the interfaces are very close. The distance between the two fields can be measured by computing the scalar product between these two vectors by a MAC (Modal Assurance Criterion) computation. MACINT=MAC_MODES(BASE_1=DEPLINT, BASE_2=DEPLXINT, INFO =2,); This MAC matrix must be as close as possible to the identity matrix. A MAC matrix very different from the identity matrix indicates that the expansion basis chosen does not make it possible to reconstruct the information at the interfaces well. In this case, it is advisable to choose another basis for the expansion of the measurement. One can also evaluate the distance between the two vectors by computing the energy criterion IERI (Interface Regularity Energy Indicator). This criterion brings in the mass matrix or else the stiffness matrix of the structure. IERIK = MAC_MODES(BASE_1=DEPLINT, BASE_2=DEPLXINT, MATR_ASSE=KASMAC, IERI=’OUI’, INFO =2,); IERIM = MAC_MODES(BASE_1=DEPLINT, BASE_2=DEPLXINT, MATR_ASSE=MASMAC, IERI=’OUI’, INFO =2,); 4 Setting up the structural-modification analysis, example of the test case sdll137e The method presented here differs slightly from that proposed in the preceding section. Here, the two structures are described by their modal basis, whereas in section 3 the modification is described by its physical coordinates (finite-element model). The setting up of this method is much simpler, because it relies largely on the substructuring techniques described in the following documentation: - reference documentation on substructuring R4.06.02 - user's documentation for setting up a dynamic substructuring analysis: U2.07.05. Another (essential) advantage of this methodology is that the numerical models of the structure and of the modification do not need to have coincident nodes. The assembly of the two substructures is done by using the mesh-projection operators at the interface (techniques identical to what is done for the option LIAISON_MAIL of AFFE_CHAR_MECA and in PROJ_CHAMP). One does not present here the details of the setting up of an analysis by substructuring, but one presents the specific features of this test case, adapted to the case where the model of the base structure is not updated. 4.1 Experimental model of the structure One creates an experimental model on the mesh on which the measurement was carried out, and by importing the basis of modes identified via a modal-identification software. The reading of the modes is done with LIRE_RESU. The detail of the method is given in section 3, and in the document U2.07.06. MODMtmp=LIRE_RESU(TYPE_RESU='MODE_MECA', FORMAT='IDEAS', MODELE=MODLEXP, UNITE=21, NOM_CHAM='DEPL', FORMAT_IDEAS=_F(NOM_CHAM='DEPL', NUME_DATASET=55, RECORD_6=(1,2,3,8,2,6,), POSI_ORDRE=(7,4,), POSI_NUME_MODE=(7,4,), POSI_MASS_GENE=(8,2,), POSI_AMOR_GENE=(8,3,), POSI_FREQ=(8,1,), NOM_CMP=('DX','DY','DZ','DRX','DRY','DRZ',),), MATR_A=KASSEXP, MATR_B=MASSEXP, TOUT_ORDRE='OUI',); 4.2 Support model The support model is a finite-element model of the same structure, not updated. This means, for example, that its natural frequencies do not correspond at all to the natural frequencies of the real structure. MAILSUP=LIRE_MAILLAGE(UNITE=20,); MAILSUP=DEFI_GROUP(reuse=MAILSUP,MAILLAGE=MAILSUP, CREA_GROUP_NO=_F(NOM='CAPT2', DIFFE=('CAPTEUR','EXTERNE'),),); MODLSUP=AFFE_MODELE(MAILLAGE=MAILSUP, AFFE=_F(GROUP_MA=('SIMPLE','VISUAL',), PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', MODELISATION='POU_D_E',),); MATSUP=DEFI_MATERIAU(ELAS=_F(E=2.1E11, NU=0.3, RHO=7800.,),); MATDBL=DEFI_MATERIAU(ELAS=_F(E=4.2E11, NU=0.3, RHO=15600.,),); 'SIMPLE' : group that does not carry the modification. 'VISUAL' : group supporting the modification CHMATSUP=AFFE_MATERIAU(MAILLAGE=MAILSUP, MODELE=MODLSUP, AFFE=(_F(GROUP_MA='SIMPLE', MATER=MATSUP,), _F(GROUP_MA='VISUAL', MATER=MATDBL,),),); CHCARSUP=AFFE_CARA_ELEM(MODELE=MODLSUP, POUTRE=_F(GROUP_MA='POUTRE', SECTION='RECTANGLE', CARA=('HY','HZ',), VALE=(9E-3,38E-3,),), ORIENTATION=_F(GROUP_MA='POUTRE', CARA='VECT_Y', VALE=(0.,0.,1.,),),); CONDLSUP=AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=MODLSUP, DDL_IMPO=(_F(GROUP_NO='FIXE', LIAISON='ENCASTRE'))); ASSEMBLAGE(MODELE=MODLSUP, CHAM_MATER=CHMATSUP, CARA_ELEM=CHCARSUP, CHARGE=CONDLSUP, NUME_DDL=CO('NUMSUP'), MATR_ASSE=(_F(MATRICE=CO('KASSUP'), OPTION='RIGI_MECA',), _F(MATRICE=CO('MASSUP'), OPTION='MASS_MECA',),),); BAMO=MODE_STATIQUE(MATR_RIGI=KASSUP, MATR_MASS=MASSUP, FORCE_NODALE=(_F(GROUP_NO=('CAPT2','EXTERNE'), AVEC_CMP=('DY','DZ',),),),); NB: in the method proposed above, one computes the static responses corresponding to the degrees of freedom of the sensors. Provided that the mesh is sufficiently fine, there always exist nodes of the support mesh «close» to the position of the sensors. IF this is not the case, a method is proposed in the test case sdlll137e, using an external python routine (called calc_modestat_capteurs), to compute the static responses corresponding rigorously to the position of the sensors. This method «looks for» the nodes close to the sensor, and computes the corresponding static response by a weighted sum of the responses on these nodes. 4.3 Expansion of the experimental modes The experimental modes identified on the structure and imported onto the model in section 4.1 are interpolated onto the support model via the expansion methods presented in section 2. The expansion basis is composed of the static responses computed previously (the basis BAMO), re-orthonormalised via the following operations: PROJ_BASE( BASE=BAMO, STOCKAGE='PLEIN', MATR_ASSE_GENE=(_F(MATRICE=CO('KPROJ'), MATR_ASSE=KASSUP,), _F(MATRICE=CO('MPROJ'), MATR_ASSE=MASSUP,),),); nbmod_expans = 5 MODGENE=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=KPROJ, MATR_MASS=MPROJ, > OPTION='PLUS_PETITE', CALC_FREQ=_F(NMAX_FREQ=nbmod_expans,), VERI_MODE=_F(STOP_ERREUR='NON'), ); MODREPHY=REST_GENE_PHYS(RESU_GENE=MODGENE,NOM_CHAM='DEPL') The modes of MODREPHY generate the same subspace as BAMO, but its components are classified by increasing natural frequencies. By choosing the parameter nbmod_expans well, one can control the regularity of the extended-mode basis generated. The choice of this parameter is decisive for the quality of the analysis, and several methods are proposed, notably in the thesis of M. Corus, for choosing the best compromise. The expansion is done in the following two steps: extended modal basis for the structure tmp=PROJ_MESU_MODAL(MODELE_CALCUL=_F(MODELE=MODLSUP, BASE=MODREPHY,), MODELE_MESURE=_F(MODELE=MODLEXP, MESURE=MODMESU,),); extended modal basis for the structure MODEET=REST_GENE_PHYS(RESU_GENE=tmp) 4.4 Creation of the macro-element associated with the structure The extended-mode basis in the following commands is BAMOSTRU. The macro-element is built by giving to MACR_ELEM_DYNA: - this basis of mode shapes, - the modal characteristics identified on the measurement model (called here freq, amor and mass) INTSTRU=DEFI_INTERF_DYNA(NUME_DDL=NUMSUP, INTERFACE=_F(NOM = 'INTSTRU', TYPE = 'MNEAL', GROUP_NO = 'EXTERNE')) BAMOSTRU=DEFI_BASE_MODALE(RITZ=_F( MODE_MECA = MODEET), NUME_REF=NUMSUP, INTERF_DYNA=INTSTRU) freq = MODMESU.LIST_PARA()['FREQ'] amor = MODMESU.LIST_PARA()['AMOR_REDUIT'] mass = MODMESU.LIST_PARA()['MASS_GENE'] MACELSTR=MACR_ELEM_DYNA( BASE_MODALE=BAMOSTRU, MODELE_MESURE=_F(FREQ=freq, MASS_GENE=mass, AMOR_REDUIT=amor,)); 4.5 Modification model The model of the modification is entirely numerical (in general much simpler; the updating step is not necessary). In the test case sdll137e, one proposes to create the macro-element which describes it simply with the macro-command CREA_ELEM_SSD. MACELMOD = CREA_ELEM_SSD( MODELE = MODMODI, CHARGE = CONDMODI, CHAM_MATER = CHMAMODI, CARA_ELEM = CARAMODI, INTERFACE = _F( NOM = 'INTMODI', TYPE = 'CRAIGB', GROUP_NO = 'EXTERNE'), BASE_MODALE = _F( TYPE = 'RITZ', TYPE_MODE = 'STATIQUE', ), CALC_FREQ = _F(OPTION='SANS'),); 4.6 Assembly of the substructures, and computation of the natural frequencies of the modified structure The assembly is likewise done simply by using the macro-command ASSE_ELEM_SSD. ASSE_ELEM_SSD(RESU_ASSE_SSD = _F( MODELE = CO('MODEGE'), NUME_DDL_GENE = CO('NUMEGE'), RIGI_GENE = CO('RIGGEN'), MASS_GENE = CO('MASGEN'), ), SOUS_STRUC = (_F(NOM = 'MODIF', MACR_ELEM_DYNA = MACELMOD,), _F(NOM = 'STRUCT', MACR_ELEM_DYNA = MACELSTR,),), LIAISON=_F( SOUS_STRUC_2='STRUCT', INTERFACE_2='INTSTRU', SOUS_STRUC_1='MODIF', INTERFACE_1='INTMODI', GROUP_MA_MAIT_2='toto', OPTION='REDUIT'), VERIF = _F( STOP_ERREUR = 'OUI', PRECISION = 1.E-6, CRITERE = 'RELATIF'), METHODE = 'ELIMINE', ), Note: the use of the keyword GROUP_MA_MAIT_2 makes it possible to declare the direction of the master–slave relation for the projections of nodes from one substructure onto the other. It is not necessary to specify the mesh-cell group used, because, with the option REDUIT, the code uses by default the group which was declared in the definition of the interface in DEFI_INTERF_DYNA. Computation of the natural frequencies of the assembled structure: RESGEN=CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI=RIGGEN, MATR_MASS=MASGEN, OPTION = 'BANDE', CALC_FREQ=_F( FREQ = (1.0, 1000.0),), SOLVEUR_MODAL=_F( DIM_SOUS_ESPACE=10,), VERI_MODE=_F( STOP_ERREUR='NON', STURM='NON',), SOLVEUR=_F( METHODE='MUMPS'), ); FREQ=RECU_TABLE(CO=RESGEN,NOM_PARA='FREQ') It should be noted that here, unlike the other test cases, no method of checking the quality of the analysis is proposed by back-projection onto the sensors of the structure. One could envisage adding this procedure. The results of the test case are essentially equal to those obtained for sdll137a and b. 5 Conclusion The structural-modification analysis procedure presented here is based on the joint exploitation of the measured data and of the numerical model of the modification. It uses the principle of substructuring for the coupling of the two models. This technique must not be used as a black box. The user must intervene in the choice of the expansion basis so that it is as relevant as possible. The user must also find the modification best suited to the constraint imposed by the environment in which the initial structure is located. One can never insist enough on the importance of carrying out the experimental measurement. Indeed, the uncertainties in the experimental data are propagated throughout the analysis and can lead to a significant error in the final results. It is strongly recommended that the person who carries out the measurement be the same as the one who sets up the numerical modelling. That person is the best able to exploit the measured data, and the best placed to carry out the coupling between the measurement and the analysis. 6 Bibliography 1. CORUS, Thesis ECP no. 2003-23, Improvement of structural-modification methods by use of model-expansion and model-reduction techniques. 2. Validation manual (V2.02.137): SDLL137 – Structural modification of a beam. 1. GROULT, Thesis ECP no. 2008-14, Extension of a structural-modification method for the design of dissipative devices incorporating viscoelastic materials.

u2.07.04 Dynamic condensation of a model by static substructuring u2.07.04 Dynamic condensation of a model by static substructuring Summary: This document describes a way of using Code_Aster to allow the transient analysis by the non-linear transient dynamics operator DYNA_NON_LINE on a model reduced strictly to non-linear subdomains, the linear subdomains being taken into account once and for all by dynamic condensation by means of static macro-elements on the interfaces. The condensation method acts on all the interface degrees of freedom common to the condensed subdomains and to the subdomains computed by non-linear finite-element analysis. A complete general method requires the computation of all the constrained static interface modes, each associated with a response to a unit imposed displacement for each interface degree of freedom. An alternative method makes it possible to use a reduced basis of interface modes, fewer in number but representative of the displacements of all the interface degrees of freedom, in the expected frequency range. 1 Introduction The objective of the dynamic condensation of a model by static substructuring is to reduce the total number of degrees of freedom of a model made up of several subdomains, by condensing the solution of the subdomains of linear constitutive behaviour onto the degrees of freedom of their interfaces with subdomains of non-linear constitutive behaviour, treated with finite elements. The idea is then to represent each of these subdomains by a macro-element of static type, so as to be able to use it in a «mixed» reduced model also comprising finite elements for the non-condensed parts of non-linear constitutive behaviour, in order to proceed to non-linear analyses by means of the non-linear analysis operators STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03 or DYNA_NON_LINE U4.53.01. In the condensation of each linear subdomain, one also wishes to integrate the contribution of the inertia forces, hence the dynamic part of its behaviour obtained by modal analysis, and for this one will therefore use dynamic macro-elements in the same way as the static macro-elements required in static substructuring. This approach is known in the literature under the name: «System Equivalent Reduction-Expansion Process». In the linear regime, it preserves the natural angular frequencies of the initial system in the expected frequency range. The principle of this condensation and its application is described in the documents [bib1, bib2, bib5]. 2 Classical condensation problem and principle of the method Figure 2.1: Subdomains of the classical condensation problem. In figure 2.1 above are shown schematically the possible subdomains that one may encounter within the framework of a classical condensation problem by static substructuring: - the subdomains of type {E}_{1}^{l} : subdomains of a structure of constant linear constitutive behaviour, condensed and modelled by a dynamic macro-element, - the subdomains of type {E}_{2}^{\mathrm{nl}} : subdomains of a structure of potentially non-linear constitutive behaviour, not condensed and modelled by finite elements, - the subdomains of type {E}_{3}^{\mathrm{impé}} : soil subdomain represented by a macro-element coming from the conversion of a complex soil-impedance matrix. The basic principle of condensation by macro-element consists, for each subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} , in partitioning the degrees of freedom j of their interfaces denoted \Sigma with the subdomains of type {E}_{2}^{\mathrm{nl}} , as well as their other degrees of freedom i , said to be «internal». The stiffness matrices [K] and mass matrices [M] are thus decomposed on these degrees of freedom: [K]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{K}_{ii}& {K}_{ij}\\ {K}_{ji}& {K}_{jj}\end{array}\right] [M]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{M}_{ii}& {M}_{ij}\\ {M}_{ji}& {M}_{jj}\end{array}\right] The principle of static substructuring amounts, for the matrix [K] for example, to condensing it only onto the degrees of freedom j of the interfaces \Sigma by correcting the initial term {K}_{jj} by a complementary term called the «Schur complement», according to the principle of the so-called Guyan condensation [bib3]: {\bar{K}}_{jj}={K}_{jj}-{K}_{ji}{({K}_{ii})}^{-1}{K}_{ij}={\Psi}^{T}.[K].\Psi The computation of the new term {\bar{K}}_{jj} amounts to a projection of the matrix [K] onto a basis of static modes \Psi of «constrained» type, obtained by the static response to unit displacements imposed at each degree of freedom j of the interfaces \Sigma : \Psi =\left[\begin{array}{}[{\Psi}_{ij}]\\ \mathrm{Id}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{}[-{K}_{ii}^{-1}{K}_{ij}]\\ \mathrm{Id}\end{array}\right] The condensation onto the degrees of freedom j of the interfaces \Sigma of the mass matrix [M] and of the loads of the subdomains of type {E}_{1}^{l} will be carried out in an analogous way by the matrix product of the matrix and of the loading vectors onto the basis of static modes \Psi . One then observes that the terms {\Psi}^{T}.[K].\Psi and {\Psi}^{T}.[M].\Psi can be obtained directly for each subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} by means of the operator for computing a dynamic macro-element MACR_ELEM_DYNA U4.65.01 defined on the interface \Sigma , and that the load terms, applied on the subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} , are obtained by the projection {\Psi}^{T}.F by means of the operator PROJ_VECT_BASE U4.63.13. 3 Methods of dynamic condensation by a complete or reduced basis of motions on the interfaces One extends the preceding approach by including the condensation of the dynamic behaviour of the subdomains of type {E}_{1}^{l} with the aid of a reduced modal representation of eigenmodes fixed on the interface \Sigma , chosen so as to be representative of the dynamics in a certain frequency range. Depending on the way of computing the modes representing the motions of the interfaces, two condensation methods are proposed. 3.1 The method of computation by a complete basis of motions at the interface The motion U of an arbitrary point of a subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} is expressed from the decomposition onto the static modes \Psi and onto a complement brought by the dynamic part of the motion expressed by eigenmodes \Phi , fixed on the interface \Sigma : U=\sum\Psi {q}_{\Sigma}+\Phi q With the complete-basis method, on the interface \Sigma , the eigenmodes \Phi have a zero contribution and the static modes \Psi have a unit value, and therefore the displacement {U}_{\Sigma} of a point of the interface is expressed: U={X}_{\Sigma}={q}_{\Sigma} In this case, the physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma coincide with the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} associated with the static modes \Psi . As regards the generalised coordinates q associated with the eigenmodes \Phi of the subdomains of type {E}_{1}^{l} , which are zero on the interface, their solution will be decoupled from that of the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} . In the assembly of the matrices of the condensed problem, the terms of projection onto the eigenmodes {\Phi}^{T}.[K].\Phi and {\Phi}^{T}.[M].\Phi will be juxtaposed. In order to be able to «mix» physical degrees of freedom with generalised coordinates, one uses the device, transparent to the user, of passing the latter off as additional physical degrees of freedom taken from among the internal degrees of freedom of a subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} . This alias is active in the model in which the domains of type {E}_{1}^{l} are condensed by macro-elements, but in order to have the true displacement of the degrees of freedom internal to these domains, it is obtained in post-processing after solution of the assembled global problem by means of the operator REST_COND_TRAN U4.63.33, by applying the initial relation: U=\sum\Psi {q}_{\Sigma}+\Phi q It is necessary to retain a number of eigenmodes \Phi which is an exact multiple of the maximum number of components of the condensed domain ( 3 for solid mechanical finite elements, 6 for plates and shells, ...) in order to make the generalised coordinates q correspond exactly to components of additional interface nodes. At the level of the assembly of the degrees of freedom of a subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} , the initial storage represented in figure 3.1-a comprises terms both on internal degrees of freedom and on the interface degrees of freedom, with a fill profile that is not full. Figure 3.1-a: Initial assembly of the degrees of freedom of the subdomains E1 before condensation. After condensation by the complete method, most of the internal degrees of freedom disappear, but a very small part is devoted to representing the generalised coordinates associated with the eigenmodes, and the terms of the static macro-element are added to the interface degrees of freedom, with a full fill profile this time. The resulting storage is represented in figure 3.1-b below. Figure 3.1-b: Assembly of the degrees of freedom of the subdomains {E}_{1}^{l} with the complete method. The assembly of the terms of the static macro-element is carried out by simple summation on the interface degrees of freedom and does not in general require an additional connection on the interface when one takes into account all the constrained static modes of the interface. It is not so in the particular case where one decides to carry out a condensation on a single interface node: there, one must add a rigid-body connection relation on the interface degrees of freedom. In the case of the presence of a subdomain of type {E}_{3}^{\mathrm{impé}} , the post-processing by REST_COND_TRAN is unnecessary, because the displacement has no component on dynamic modes and the displacement at the interface is obtained definitively as soon as the global problem is solved. 3.2 The method of computation by modal reduction at the interface With the modal-reduction method, the motion U of an arbitrary point of a subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} is still expressed from the decomposition onto the static modes \Psi and onto a complement brought by the dynamic part of the motion expressed by eigenmodes \Phi : U=\sum\Psi {q}_{\Sigma}+\Phi q But this time, on the interface \Sigma , the eigenmodes \Phi have a non-zero contribution, because the static modes \Psi chosen do not have a unit value on each node and are in number generally much smaller than the number of physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma which, in this case, do not coincide with the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} associated with the static modes \Psi . One must therefore distinguish, in the assembly and the solution, the terms associated with the physical degrees of freedom and those associated with the generalised coordinates. In the same way as for the generalised coordinates q associated with the eigenmodes \Phi , one uses the device, transparent to the user, of passing the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} associated with the static modes \Psi off as additional physical degrees of freedom, also taken from among degrees of freedom internal to a subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} . But this time, the solution of the physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma will not be decoupled from that of the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} . In the assembly of the matrices of the condensed problem, the terms of projection onto the eigenmodes {\Phi}^{T}.[K].\Phi and {\Phi}^{T}.[M].\Phi will be juxtaposed. But one will then have to add a connection, and therefore Lagrange degrees of freedom, between the physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma and the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} . This connection is expressed by the relation: {X}_{\Sigma}=\sum\Psi {q}_{\Sigma} This relation will be expressed by the repeatable keyword LIAISON_INTERF of the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA U4.44.01, which makes it possible to connect each subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} to a subdomain of type {E}_{2}^{\mathrm{nl}} (cf. figure 2.1) by generating a particular case of LIAISON_DDL with the coefficients of the preceding linear relation. Then, in order to have the true displacement of the degrees of freedom internal to the subdomains of type {E}_{1}^{l} , one proceeds in the same way in post-processing after solution of the «mixed» global problem by means of the operator REST_COND_TRAN U4.63.33, by applying the initial relation: U=\sum\Psi {q}_{\Sigma}+\Phi q Note : Here too, it is necessary to retain a number of eigenmodes \Phi and a number of static modes \Psi , both exact multiples of the maximum number of components of the condensed domain ( 3 for solid mechanical finite elements, 6 for plates and shells, ...) in order to make the generalised coordinates correspond exactly to components of additional interface nodes. After condensation by the modal-reduction method, most of the internal degrees of freedom disappear, but a very small part is devoted to representing the generalised coordinates associated with the eigenmodes, and another small part is devoted to the generalised coordinates associated with the interface eigenmodes. This time, the terms of the static macro-element are not added to the interface degrees of freedom, which then retain a fill profile that is not full. But one then obtains a quadrangular block of Lagrange degrees of freedom between the physical degrees of freedom {X}_{\Sigma} of the interface \Sigma and the generalised coordinates {q}_{\Sigma} . The resulting storage is represented in figure 3.2 below. Figure 3.2: Storage of the degrees of freedom of the subdomains {E}_{1}^{l} with the modal-reduction method. One will note that there is no imposed choice of computation for the reduction basis of static interface modes \Psi . One possible choice will be that used in soil–structure interaction [bib4], by considering the restriction to the interface \Sigma of a basis of eigenmodes of the subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} on a bed of springs representative of the stiffness of the adjacent subdomains of type {E}_{2}^{\mathrm{nl}} or {E}_{3}^{\mathrm{impé}} , cf. [U2.06.07, §11,5]. 3.3 Validation of the use of the dynamic condensation methods A good approach to validating the dynamic condensation model – before carrying out the non-linear analysis – consists in the comparison of the modal analysis on the first modes between the complete initial model, not reduced, containing all the subdomains, and the final «mixed» reduced model containing the condensed subdomains in the form of dynamic macro-elements as well as the model of subdomains of type {E}_{2}^{\mathrm{nl}} treated in the linear regime. 3.4 Respective advantages of using the dynamic condensation methods The dynamic condensation method makes it possible in general, compared with the non-condensed model, to reduce the size of the matrix systems and of the total number of degrees of freedom, and to obtain gains in terms of memory and performance for the factorisation and the solution. For the complete method, because of the full storage of the terms of the interface modes, this method is of interest in the factorisation operations, especially if the number of interface degrees of freedom hardly exceeds 1/10 of the total number of degrees of freedom before condensation. On the other hand, this method requires the computation of the interface modes for all the degrees of freedom and can be prohibitive in memory for this computation if the total number of degrees of freedom before condensation is greater than 100000 and if the number of interface modes is of the order of 10000. The condensation method with modal reduction is then of interest if one reduces the number of interface modes to less than 1/10 of the number of interface degrees of freedom, that is, to less than 1000. While knowing that, in terms of performance: - one adds equations linked to the Lagrange degrees of freedom relating to the relations between the degrees of freedom and the reduced interface modes, which is liable to penalise the solution, - one obtains a gain on the factorisation of the system, because its size will decrease, as well as on the recovery onto the physical basis of each subdomain, in the ratio of the number of degrees of freedom to the number of reduced interface modes. The complete method seems efficient and sufficient for a total number of degrees of freedom before condensation lying between about 5000 and 50000. The method with modal reduction becomes of interest beyond 50000 degrees of freedom before condensation. 4 Summary of the analysis of the «mixed» reduced model with dynamic condensation The analysis with dynamic condensation requires one to go through the following steps of chaining the commands of Code_Aster : - Classical initial instructions: definition of the complete finite-element mesh of the whole structure and of the mesh-cell groups, in particular the mesh-cell groups and node groups of the interfaces \Sigma , and of the subdomain of type {E}_{2}^{\mathrm{nl}} , definition of the materials, assignment of the materials to the mesh-cell groups. And for each subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} which will be condensed: - Definition of the model and assignment of the finite elements to the model, assignment of the materials to the elements, assignment of the elementary characteristics, - Computation of the eigenmodes on a basis fixed on the interface \Sigma by the command CALC_MODES U4.52.02, with the original boundary conditions of this subdomain, - Definition of the dynamic interface of type CRAIGB on the node group of the interface \Sigma by the command DEFI_INTERF_DYNA U4.64.01, - Computation of the static modes of the dynamic interface defined previously with MODE_STATIQUE U4.52.14 in the case of the choice of a complete basis, or by CALC_MODES in the case of the choice of a reduced basis, with the appropriate conditions, - Definition of a modal basis by the command DEFI_BASE_MODALE [U4.64.02] with the RITZ option, integrating the static modes of the dynamic interface defined previously in order to complete the basis of the eigenmodes on the interface (keywords MODE_INTF and INTERF_DYNA to designate the dynamic interface), - Computation of the assembled loading vectors (forces, imposed displacements...) of the subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} and projection of these onto the complete RITZ basis, with the associated numbering of the degrees of freedom, - Assembly of the dynamic macro-element of the subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} on the interface \Sigma by the command MACR_ELEM_DYNA U4.65.01, from the RITZ basis defined previously, integrating therein the projected load vectors, or of a dynamic macro-element of a subdomain of type {E}_{3}^{\mathrm{impé}} by converting a soil impedance on the interface \Sigma , cf. the command LIRE_IMPE_MISS U7.02.32 and the keyword MATR_IMPE of the command MACR_ELEM_DYNA U4.65.01. Then, for the dynamic analysis of the «mixed» reduced model with the non-linear subdomains: - Definition and assembly to the initial mesh by DEFI_MAILLAGE [U4.23.01] and ASSE_MAILLAGE [U4.23.03] of super mesh cells each corresponding to a dynamic macro-element of the subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} in order to create a new «mixed» reduced mesh. The nodes of these super mesh cells will carry the degrees of freedom of the condensed subdomain, - Definition of a «mixed» reduced model assigned to the new «mixed» reduced mesh, integrating the non-condensed subdomain in finite elements of type {E}_{2}^{\mathrm{nl}} as well as the assignments of the super mesh cells by the keyword AFFE_SOUS_STRUC of the operator AFFE_MODELE U4.41.01, - Definition of the specific loads of the model by the keywords LIAISON_SOLIDE or LIAISON_INTERF of the operator AFFE_CHAR_MECA U4.44.01, - Call to the non-linear analysis operator STAT_NON_LINE U4.51.03 or DYNA_NON_LINE U4.53.01 on the «mixed» reduced model, including the material field defined on the subdomain of type {E}_{2}^{\mathrm{nl}} assigned to the «mixed» reduced mesh, the preceding specific loads by the keyword EXCIT, as well as the loading vectors defined on the subdomains which have been condensed and projected onto the macro-elements, via the keyword SOUS_STRUC, - Finally, one can validate the final «mixed» reduced model, under a fully linear assumption, containing the condensed subdomains in the form of macro-elements, by comparison of natural frequencies with the modal analysis on the first modes of the complete initial model, not reduced, containing all the subdomains, by using the keyword MODE_VIBR of the operator DYNA_NON_LINE. Then, for each subdomain of type {E}_{1}^{l} apart from those of a soil impedance: - Recovery onto the physical basis on the model of the subdomain on which the macro-element of the subdomain was built, by the operator REST_COND_TRAN U4.63.33. The command files miss06b.comm and sdnv107b.comm illustrate this type of analysis. 5 Bibliography 1. O.NICOLAS: Specification of the development of the translation MACR_ELEM_STAT / MACR_ELEM_DYNA. Report EDF/AMA-05.149. 2. Report EDF/AMA-07-165. 3. Aster document U2.07.02: User's guide to static substructuring. 4. u2.07.05 Setting up an analysis by dynamic substructuring u2.07.05 Setting up an analysis by dynamic substructuring Summary: The purpose of this document is to help users and to give them advice for carrying out a study involving the dynamic substructuring technique. One first presents the general approach for setting up the technique. One then describes the sequences of operations required in order to obtain usable results. The presentation is illustrated by three examples treating a modal analysis, a transient-response analysis and a harmonic-response analysis. 1 What does dynamic substructuring consist of? Dynamic substructuring consists in partitioning the structure into several substructures in order to reduce the size of the numerical model and to be able to study each substructure independently. The overall model is then obtained by assembling the models of the different substructures. Each substructure is projected onto a judiciously chosen basis of vectors. This projection makes it possible to reduce the size of the model of each substructure and consequently the size of the model of the assembled structure. 2 Why use dynamic substructuring? The growing complexity of mechanical structures makes it difficult to estimate their dynamic behaviour under an imposed loading. The numerical modelling of the complete structure would require a significant investment, both in terms of memory space and of analysis cost. In addition to the reduction in the size of the model, the dynamic substructuring technique makes the modelling of the global structure much more modular. 3 A short reminder of the methodology One recalls here only the fundamental principles of the technique. For more detail, the reader is invited to consult the reference document R4.06.02. Projecting the substructure onto a reduced basis necessarily introduces an approximation into the results obtained. The role of the modeller is to choose a basis rich enough to be able to capture the dynamic behaviour of the substructure. The quality of the results depends on the choice of this projection basis. The techniques most used for the choice of this basis are the Craig-Bampton technique and the Mac Neal technique. To these two techniques is added the use of interface modes, which is a variant of these two techniques in which one carries out a condensation of the connection degrees of freedom. - The Craig-Bampton technique consists in choosing, as projection basis, normal modes and constraint modes. The normal modes are eigenmodes of the substructure in which one fixes all the nodes of the interfaces with the adjacent substructures. A constraint mode is defined by the static deflected shape obtained by imposing a unit displacement on one connection degree of freedom, the other connection degrees of freedom being fixed. The projection basis contains normal modes and all the constraint modes associated with all the connection degrees of freedom. - The Mac Neal technique consists in choosing, as projection basis, normal modes and attachment modes. In this case, the normal modes are eigenmodes of the substructure with a free interface. An attachment mode is defined by the static deflected shape obtained by imposing a unit force on one connection degree of freedom, the other connection degrees of freedom being free. The projection basis contains normal modes and all the attachment modes associated with all the connection degrees of freedom. - Use of interface modes: one can observe that the dimension of the projection basis can become very large if the number of connection degrees of freedom is large. One then defines the notion of interface mode, which consists in carrying out a condensation of the behaviour of the structure onto the interface degrees of freedom and in solving the associated eigenvalue problem. This makes it possible to express the behaviour of the structure reduced to the interface. One limits oneself to keeping, as basis vectors, the first modes computed, in addition to the normal modes. Indeed, if one remains within the framework of low-frequency dynamics, the whole set of constraint modes (or attachment modes) is not necessary to represent the dynamics of the problem. Nevertheless, it is recommended to check a posteriori the relevance of the basis chosen, by verifying for example the continuity of the displacements at the interfaces. One can list below the different steps of the approach: - For each substructure: - Computation of the projection basis: normal modes and connection modes or interface modes - Computation of the generalised matrices of the substructure: projection of the mass and stiffness matrices of the substructure onto the reduced basis - Assembly of the substructures by the formulation of the continuity of the displacement at the interfaces and the vanishing of the work of the connection forces. One thus obtains a generalised model of the assembled structure - Computation of the response in generalised coordinates - Recovery of the results onto the physical basis - checking of the results obtained - post-processing (stress analysis, energy analysis, ...) 4 Setting up in Code_Aster 4.1 Notion of dynamic macro-element A dynamic macro-element is a reduced (generalised) model of a substructure. It comprises: - the projection of the model (mass and stiffness matrices) of the substructure onto the reduced basis, - the information on the interfaces where the adjacent substructures will be connected and the connection matrices associated with these interfaces. Normally, one builds as many dynamic macro-elements as there are substructures. In the case where one is in the presence of substructures which differ only by their position in space, a single macro-element is sufficient. One then applies a rotation and/or a translation of the macro-element at assembly. 4.2 The course of a study - For each substructure: creation of the dynamic macro-element - Computation and assembly of the mass and stiffness matrices and of the loading of the substructure: (CALC_MATR_ELEM, ASSE_MATRICE, CALC_VECT_ELEM, ASSE_VECTEUR) - Computation of the projection-basis vectors: normal modes, static modes, interface modes (CALC_MODES, MODE_STATIQUE, DEFI_BASE_MODALE) - Definition of the interfaces (DEFI_INTERF_DYNA) - Projection of the matrices of the substructure onto the basis vectors (MACR_ELEM_DYNA) The chaining of these operations can be carried out with a single call to the operator CREA_ELEM_SSD. This operator makes it possible to create a dynamic macro-element by supplying only the information on the model and the interfaces. It computes the projection-basis vectors (normal modes and connection modes), defines the interfaces and projects the stiffness and mass matrices onto the computed basis. It chains the following operators: CALC_MATR_ELEM, ASSE_MATRICE, CALC_MODES, MODE_STATIQUE, DEFI_INTERF_DYNA, DEFI_BASE_MODALE, MACR_ELEM_DYNA. - Assembly of the different substructures - Definition of the generalised model of the assembled structure: connection between substructures and numbering of the degrees of freedom of the system (DEFI_MODELE_GENE, NUME_DDL_GENE) - Assembly of the generalised matrices of the substructures (ASSE_MATR_GENE, ASSE_VECT_GENE) These operations of assembly of dynamic macro-elements can be carried out by using the operator ASSE_ELEM_SSD. It defines the generalised model and assembles the generalised matrices of the different substructures. It chains the following operators: DEFI_MODELE_GENE, NUME_DDL_GENE, ASSE_MATR_GENE. - Computation of the response on the generalised model (CALC_MODES, DYNA_VIBRA) - Recovery of the results in physical coordinates of the substructure or on a skeleton mesh (REST_SOUS_STRUCT) - A posteriori checking of the results by verifying the continuity of the displacement field at the interfaces (POST_RELEVE_T, TEST_TABLE) and the vanishing of the work of the connection forces (CALC_CORR_SSD) 4.3 Practical advice - For the standard cases: use the operator CREA_ELEM_SSD for the creation of the dynamic macro-element and the operator ASSE_ELEM_SSD for the assembly of the macro-elements. This makes the writing of the command file significantly easier. - For the non-standard cases (particular projection basis), it is sometimes necessary to go back to the elementary operators. The current limitations of CREA_ELEM_SSD and ASSE_ELEM_SSD are: - conservative structure (without damping) - projection basis: normal modes + connection modes (Craig-Bampton, Mac Neal, the first n interface modes) - All the components of the degrees of freedom of the interface nodes are considered for the computation of the connection modes (the keyword MASQUE, which makes it possible to select the active components of the interface nodes, is not active for CREA_ELEM_SSD) - The normal modes are computed by using the operator CALC_MODES; the options on the dimension of the mode-search subspace are those taken by default by this operator. - If one is in the presence of a point interface or of an interface with a small number of degrees of freedom, the use of the classical methods (Craig-Bampton or Mac Neal) is recommended. - The interface modes are appropriate for distributed (non-point) interfaces. The quality of the results depends on the number of interface modes taken into account in the projection basis. An a posteriori check of the results is always indicated. This check can be done by verifying the continuity of the displacement field at the interfaces and/or the vanishing of the work of the connection forces. One must increase the number of interface modes if one observes a separation at the interfaces or if the work of the connection forces is not negligible. - Choose carefully the normal modes which serve as projection-basis vectors. The subspace generated by these basis vectors must contain at least the deflected shape of the substructure after assembly. One cannot, for example, observe the torsion of the substructure if one does not put a torsion shape among the basis vectors. - For an interface of Mac Neal type, one must make sure that the substructure is held somewhere in order to avoid rigid-body motion. 5 Some examples of analysis One presents three cases to illustrate the setting up of the technique. The first case corresponds to a standard modal analysis with use of the operators CREA_ELEM_SSD and ASSE_ELEM_SSD. The second case corresponds to a transient-response analysis. One carries out a double projection. The first projection is executed at the creation of the dynamic macro-element and the second projection is carried out on the generalised model of the assembled structure for the response analysis. The third case corresponds to a harmonic-response analysis on a dissipative structure. One describes the chaining of the elementary operators required for the creation of the dynamic macro-elements and the assembly of the generalised matrices of the substructures. 5.1 An example of a modal analysis It is modelling e of the test case SDLS106 V2.03.106. In this test case, one wishes to compute the eigenmodes of a structure composed of two substructures defined in two different frames. The association of these two substructures is intended to produce a plate in a condition of simple support on its edges. One can sketch it as follows: | Sous-structure 1 | Sous-structure 2 | | --- | --- | | | | The assembled structure is a rectangular plate supported on its edges. To arrive at this assembled structure, one carries out a rotation and a translation of substructure 2. Indeed, the two substructures must be expressed in the same frame. Rotation of -90 degrees about DZ + Translation along DY One is going to present the steps for the creation of the dynamic macro-element of substructure 1; the dynamic macro-element of substructure 2 is created in an analogous way. Definition of the boundary conditions of substructure 1: One wishes to use a basis of Craig-Bampton type, so one must clamp the degrees of freedom of the interface, which are here associated with the node group GAUCHE. The other conditions correspond to the boundary conditions of the substructure. CHARGE_1=AFFE_CHAR_MECA( MODELE=MODELE1,DDL_IMPO=( _F( GROUP_NO = 'BLOQUE', DX = 0.0, DY = 0.0, DZ = 0.0), _F( GROUP_NO = 'GAUCHE', DX = 0.0, DY = 0.0, DZ = 0.0, DRX = 0.0, DRY = 0.0, DRZ = 0.0) , _F( GROUP_NO = 'BAS', DX = 0.0, DY = 0.0, DZ = 0.0), _F( GROUP_NO = 'HAUT', DX = 0.0, DY = 0.0, DZ = 0.0))) - Creation of the dynamic macro-element: One uses the operator CREA_ELEM_SSD for the creation of the dynamic macro-element, One has here a distributed interface; one wishes to use interface modes as connection modes. Under the factor keyword BASE_MODALE, one chooses a basis of type RITZ and one enters the number of interface modes to be used. The factor keyword CALC_FREQ gives the numbers of normal modes to be used. MACEL1 = CREA_ELEM_SSD( MODELE = MODELE1, CHARGE = CHARGE_1, CHAM_MATER = CHAMAT1, CARA_ELEM = PARAM1, INTERFACE = _F( NOM = 'GAUCHE', TYPE = 'CRAIGB', GROUP_NO = 'GAUCHE'), BASE_MODALE = _F( TYPE = 'RITZ' , NMAX_MODE_INTF = 20, ), CALC_FREQ = _F(NMAX_FREQ = 6,), ) One creates in the same way the dynamic macro-element of substructure 2. - Assembly of the different substructures: One carries out the assembly of the substructures by using the operator ASSE_ELEM_SSD The factor keyword RESU_ASSE_SSD makes it possible to assign a name to the result concepts (model, numbering of the generalised degrees of freedom, generalised matrices). The factor keyword SOUS-STRUCT makes it possible to name the different substructures. It is in this factor keyword that one assigns the possible rotation and translation of the macro-element (one first carries out the rotation ANGL_NAUT and then the translation TRANS). The keyword LIAISON makes it possible to define the interfaces between substructures. In the case where one uses interface modes as connection modes, one must specify REDUIT under the keyword OPTION. The mesh-cell group GROUP_MA_MAIT_ drives the displacement field at the interface. If the interfaces are not compatible (the nodes are not facing one another), it is advisable to choose as master mesh cell the finest mesh cell. Otherwise, by default, the mesh cells of substructure 1 are defined as master. The choice ELIMINE under the keyword METHODE means that one numbers the generalised degrees of freedom by taking the connection equations into account by the constraint-elimination method. ASSE_ELEM_SSD( RESU_ASSE_SSD = _F( MODELE = CO('MODEGE'), NUME_DDL_GENE = CO('NUMEGE'), RIGI_GENE = CO('RIGGEN'), MASS_GENE = CO('MASGEN'), ), SOUS_STRUC = ( _F(NOM = 'CARRE1', MACR_ELEM_DYNA = MACEL1,), _F(NOM = 'CARRE2', MACR_ELEM_DYNA = MACEL2, ANGL_NAUT = (-90.,0.,0.),), TRANS = (0.,0.5,0.), ), LIAISON = ( _F(SOUS_STRUC_1 = 'CARRE1', INTERFACE_1 = 'GAUCHE', GROUP_MA_MAIT_1 = 'CALCUL', OPTION = 'REDUIT', SOUS_STRUC_2 = 'CARRE2', INTERFACE_2 = 'BLOQUE',), ), VERIF = _F( STOP_ERREUR = 'OUI', PRECISION = 1.E-6, CRITERE = 'RELATIF'), METHODE = 'ELIMINE', ), - Computation of the eigenmodes of the assembled structure: One carries out the modal analysis on the assembled generalised matrices. The modal shapes obtained are expressed in generalised coordinates. RESGEN=CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI=RIGGEN, MATR_MASS=MASGEN, OPTION = 'PLUS_PETITE', CALC_FREQ=_F( NMAX_FREQ=10,), SOLVEUR_MODAL=_F( METHODE='SORENSEN',), VERI_MODE=_F(PREC_SHIFT=5.0E-3, STOP_ERREUR='NON', STURM='NON', SEUIL=9.9999999999999995E-01), STOP_BANDE_VIDE='NON', ) - Recovery onto the physical basis: For the exploitation of the results, it is necessary to recover them onto the physical basis. MODCOT1=REST_SOUS_STRUC(RESU_GENE=RESGEN, TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', SOUS_STRUC='CARRE1',); MODCOT2=REST_SOUS_STRUC(RESU_GENE=RESGEN, TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', SOUS_STRUC='CARRE2',); - Checking of the quality of the results: The quality of the results obtained can be checked by verifying the continuity of the displacements at the interface. This makes it possible to validate the number of interface modes chosen. In this test case, one compares the displacement of node N9 of substructure 1 with that of node N70 of substructure 2. These two nodes are facing one another. T1_DZ=POST_RELEVE_T(ACTION=_F(INTITULE='CARRE1', NOEUD=('N9'), RESULTAT=MODCOT1, NOM_CHAM='DEPL', TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', NOM_CMP='DZ', OPERATION='EXTRACTION', ),); T2_DZ=POST_RELEVE_T(ACTION=_F(INTITULE='CARRE2', NOEUD=('N70'), RESULTAT=MODCOT2, NOM_CHAM='DEPL', TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', NOM_CMP='DZ', OPERATION='EXTRACTION', ),); F_DZ=FORMULE(NOM_PARA=('DZ_C1', 'DZ_C2',), VALE='abs (DZ_C1 - DZ_C2)') TC_DZ=CALC_TABLE(TABLE=T1_DZ, ACTION=(_F(OPERATION='RENOMME', NOM_PARA=('DZ', 'DZ_C1'),), _F(OPERATION='COMB', TABLE=T2_DZ, NOM_PARA=('NUME_ORDRE',),), _F(OPERATION='RENOMME', NOM_PARA=('DZ', 'DZ_C2'),), _F(OPERATION='OPER', NOM_PARA='ECART', FORMULE=F_DZ), ), TITRE='Comparaison DZ ssd 1 / ssd 2') TEST_TABLE( TABLE = TC_DZ, NOM_PARA = 'ECART', TYPE_TEST = 'SOMM', VALE = 0., CRITERE = 'ABSOLU', PRECISION = 3.E-3, REFERENCE = 'ANALYTIQUE',) One computes here the sum of the absolute values of the differences. The keyword PRECISION makes it possible to define the maximum difference tolerated. One can also verify the vanishing of the work of the connection forces by using the operator CALC_CORR_SSD. This run is quite a heavy consumer of CPU time. CALC_ENR=CALC_CORR_SSD(MODELE_GENE=MODEGE, RESU_GENE=RESGEN, SHIFT=1., UNITE=6) A summary of the results obtained is deposited, by default, in the message file. One can enrich the basis if one observes that the work of the connection forces is not negligible. One can take as a model modelling a of the test case SDLS122 V2.03.122 for the setting up of this enrichment of the projection basis. 5.2 An example of a transient-response analysis It is modelling e of the test case SDLD102 V2.01.102. The substructures are composed of discrete elements. The first substructure is loaded by a point force. One uses the same model and the same mesh for the definition of the two substructures. The complete structure is obtained by assembling the two substructures. Definition of the boundary conditions of the substructure: One wishes to use a basis of classical Craig-Bampton type; the node at the interface must be fixed (node \mathit{N3} for substructure 1 and node \mathit{N1} for substructure 2). CHARGE_L=AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=MODELE, DDL_IMPO=( _F(NOEUD='N2', DY=0., DZ=0., DRX=0., DRY=0., DRZ=0.,), _F(NOEUD='N1', DX=0.,), _F(NOEUD='N3', DX=0.,) ,),); - Creation of the dynamic macro-elements: One applies the loading \text{FX} on this substructure 1; one must then enter a numbering for the degrees of freedom of the substructure. This numbering will be used subsequently when defining the loading on the assembled model. MACEL1 = CREA_ELEM_SSD( MODELE=MODELE, CARA_ELEM=PARAM, CHARGE=CHARGE_L, CHAM_MATER = CHAMAT, NUME_DDL=CO('NUMDDL_L') , INTERFACE=_F(NOM='DROITE', TYPE='CRAIGB' , NOEUD='N3',), BASE_MODALE = _F( TYPE = 'CLASSIQUE' ,), CALC_FREQ = _F(NMAX_FREQ = 1,), ) Creation of the dynamic macro-element of substructure 2: MACEL2 = CREA_ELEM_SSD( MODELE=MODELE, CARA_ELEM=PARAM, CHARGE=CHARGE_L, CHAM_MATER = CHAMAT, INTERFACE=_F(NOM='GAUCHE', TYPE='CRAIGB' , NOEUD='N1',), BASE_MODALE = _F( TYPE = 'CLASSIQUE' ,), CALC_FREQ = _F(NMAX_FREQ = 1,), ) - Assembly of the different substructures: ASSE_ELEM_SSD( RESU_ASSE_SSD = _F( MODELE = CO('MODEGE'), NUME_DDL_GENE = CO('NUMEGE'), RIGI_GENE = CO('RIGGEN'), MASS_GENE = CO('MASGEN'), ), SOUS_STRUC=(_F(NOM='COTE1', MACR_ELEM_DYNA=MACEL1,), _F(NOM='COTE2', MACR_ELEM_DYNA=MACEL2, TRANS=(0.2,0.,0.),),), LIAISON=_F(SOUS_STRUC_1='COTE1', INTERFACE_1='DROITE', SOUS_STRUC_2='COTE2', INTERFACE_2='GAUCHE',), VERIF=_F(STOP_ERREUR='OUI', PRECISION=1.E-6, CRITERE='RELATIF',), ); - Computation of the transient response of the assembled structure: Definition and assembly of the loading vector: CHARTRAN=AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=MODELE, FORCE_NODALE=_F(NOEUD='N2', FX=1.,),); V_ELEM=CALC_VECT_ELEM(OPTION='CHAR_MECA', CHARGE=CHARTRAN,); The loading must be expressed in the same numbering as the projection vectors (numbering of the degrees of freedom of substructure 1). V_ASSE=ASSE_VECTEUR(VECT_ELEM=V_ELEM, NUME_DDL=NUMDDL_L ,); Assembly of the loading vector on the generalised model (loading applied on the substructure COTE1): FGEN=ASSE_VECT_GENE(NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEGE, CHAR_SOUS_STRUC=_F( SOUS_STRUC='COTE1' , VECT_ASSE=V_ASSE,),); Definition of the projection basis for the transient-response analysis (in the majority of cases, the basis is composed of eigenmodes of the system): RESGEN=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=RIGGEN, MATR_MASS=MASGEN, OPTION='PLUS_PETITE', CALC_FREQ=_F(NMAX_FREQ=3,), TITRE='CALCUL DES MODES PROPRES DE LA STRUCTURE GLOBALE', ); Numbering of the degrees of freedom of the analysis basis: NUMEMODE=NUME_DDL_GENE(BASE=RESGEN, STOCKAGE='DIAG',); Projection of the assembled matrices onto the analysis basis: MASPRO=PROJ_MATR_BASE(BASE=RESGEN, NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEMODE, MATR_ASSE_GENE=MASGEN,); RIGPRO=PROJ_MATR_BASE(BASE=RESGEN, NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEMODE, MATR_ASSE_GENE=RIGGEN,); Projection of the loading onto the analysis basis: VECPRO=PROJ_VECT_BASE(BASE=RESGEN, NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEMODE, VECT_ASSE_GENE=FGEN,); By default, the displacement and the velocity are zero at the initial time instant. One shows below how to enter the initial condition of the system. One creates the field on the mesh of the substructure with the same numbering as that of the macro-element. CHAMP_0 = CREA_CHAMP( OPERATION='AFFE', TYPE_CHAM='NOEU_DEPL_R', MAILLAGE=MAILLA, NUME_DDL=NUMDDL_L , AFFE=_F( TOUT = 'OUI', NOM_CMP = ( 'DX', 'DY','DZ','DRX','DRY','DRZ', ), VALE = (0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,0.,)) ) Projection of the field onto the assembled generalised model: VGEN_0=ASSE_VECT_GENE(NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEGE, CHAR_SOUS_STRUC=_F(SOUS_STRUC='COTE1', VECT_ASSE=CHAMP_0,) ,); Second projection of the field onto the response-analysis basis: DEPINI=PROJ_VECT_BASE( BASE=RESGEN , VECT_ASSE_GENE= VGEN_0 , NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEMODE, TYPE_VECT='DEPL') VITINI=PROJ_VECT_BASE( BASE=RESGEN , VECT_ASSE_GENE= VGEN_0 , NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEMODE, TYPE_VECT='VITE') The transient-response analysis can be carried out by using the command DYNA_VIBRA. One uses the solution technique by projection onto an analysis basis. Computation of the transient response on the projected assembled model: TRANGEN1=DYNA_VIBRA( TYPE_CALCUL='TRAN' , BASE_CALCUL='GENE' , SCHEMA_TEMPS=_F(SCHEMA='EULER',), MATR_MASS=MASPRO, MATR_RIGI=RIGPRO, INCREMENT=_F(INST_INIT=0., INST_FIN=82., PAS=0.01,), ETAT_INIT=_F( DEPL = DEPINI, VITE = VITINI,), ARCHIVAGE=_F(PAS_ARCH=10,), EXCIT=_F(VECT_ASSE=VECPRO, COEF_MULT=1.,),); - Recovery onto the physical basis: One can recover the results directly on the substructure or on a visualisation mesh called a skeleton mesh, which must be defined beforehand. Creation of the visualisation mesh: SQUEL=DEFI_SQUELETTE(MODELE_GENE=MODEGE, SOUS_STRUC=(_F(NOM='COTE1', GROUP_MA='RESSORT' ), _F(NOM='COTE2', GROUP_MA='RESSORT' ),),); Recovery of the analysis basis onto the visualisation mesh: MODGLO=REST_SOUS_STRUC(RESU_GENE=RESGEN, TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', SQUELETTE=SQUEL,); Recovery of the response onto the visualisation mesh (for a solution with double projection, do not forget to specify the recovery of the analysis basis onto the substructure or onto the skeleton): TRAN1=REST_GENE_PHYS(RESU_GENE=TRANGEN1, MODE_MECA=MODGLO , LIST_INST=LIST_R, INTERPOL='LIN', TOUT_CHAM='OUI', NOEUD='NO3',); One therefore recalls that, for a time-response analysis, one carries out a double projection. A first projection of the substructure onto the basis composed of normal modes and connection modes, and a second projection of the reduced assembled model onto the response-analysis basis. 5.3 An example of a harmonic-response analysis In the majority of cases, a harmonic-response analysis is carried out on a dissipative model. The operators CREA_ELEM_SSD and ASSE_ELEM_SSD treat only conservative structures. One details in this example the underlying elementary operations, required for carrying out a harmonic-response analysis by dynamic substructuring. The test case SHLV301A is used to illustrate the presentation. It is a bar of rectangular cross-section modelled with quadratic solid elements. One applies a sinusoidal pressure on a lateral face of the bar. The assembled structure: Definition and assignment of the material: MAT=DEFI_MATERIAU( ELAS=_F( RHO = 7.8E03, NU = 0.3, E = 2.1E11, AMOR_ALPHA = 1.6E-5, AMOR_BETA = 16.)) CHMAT=AFFE_MATERIAU( MAILLAGE=MAYA, AFFE=_F( TOUT = 'OUI', MATER = MAT)) Description of the loading: PRESSION=AFFE_CHAR_MECA( MODELE=POVOL, PRES_REP=_F( GROUP_MA = 'PRESSION', PRES = 50.E4)) Description of the boundary conditions (one wishes to use a projection basis of Mac Neal type: the nodes of the interface are free): FIXAT1=AFFE_CHAR_MECA( MODELE=POVOL, DDL_IMPO=( _F( GROUP_NO = 'COND1', DY = 0.), _F( GROUP_NO = 'CONDZG', DZ = 0.), _F( NOEUD = 'N26', DX = 0.), _F( GROUP_NO = 'DROITE', DX = 0.))) - Creation of the dynamic macro-elements: Creation of the elementary matrices of substructure 1: K_ELEM1=CALC_MATR_ELEM( MODELE=POVOL, CHAM_MATER=CHMAT, OPTION='RIGI_MECA', CHARGE=( FIXAT1, ) ) M_ELEM1=CALC_MATR_ELEM( MODELE=POVOL, CHAM_MATER=CHMAT, OPTION='MASS_MECA', CHARGE=( FIXAT1, ) ) A_ELEM1=CALC_MATR_ELEM( MODELE=POVOL, CHAM_MATER=CHMAT, OPTION='AMOR_MECA', RIGI_MECA=K_ELEM1, MASS_MECA=M_ELEM1, CHARGE=( FIXAT1, ) ) Creation of the elementary vector of the loading for substructure 1: V_ELEM1=CALC_VECT_ELEM( OPTION='CHAR_MECA', CHARGE=PRESSION ) Assembly of the elementary matrices and vector: NUM1=NUME_DDL( MATR_RIGI=K_ELEM1) K_ASSE1=ASSE_MATRICE( MATR_ELEM=K_ELEM1, NUME_DDL=NUM1) M_ASSE1=ASSE_MATRICE( MATR_ELEM=M_ELEM1, NUME_DDL=NUM1) A_ASSE1=ASSE_MATRICE( MATR_ELEM=A_ELEM1, NUME_DDL=NUM1) V_ASSE1=ASSE_VECTEUR( VECT_ELEM=V_ELEM1, NUME_DDL=NUM1) Computation of the normal modes: MODES1=CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI=K_ASSE1, MATR_MASS=M_ASSE1, CALC_FREQ=_F( NMAX_FREQ = 20) ) Definition of the interface for a basis of Mac Neal type: INTERF1=DEFI_INTERF_DYNA( NUME_DDL=NUM1, INTERFACE=_F( NOM = 'DROITE', TYPE = 'MNEAL' , GROUP_NO = 'DROITE'), INFO=2) Definition of the projection basis: BAMO1=DEFI_BASE_MODALE( CLASSIQUE=_F( INTERF_DYNA = INTERF1, MODE_MECA = MODES1, NMAX_MODE = 20), INFO=2) Creation of the dynamic macro-element: One specifies that one wishes to take the damping into account by entering the damping matrix to be projected.
