MACRO1=MACR_ELEM_DYNA( BASE_MODALE=BAMO1, MATR_AMOR=A_ASSE1 ) One builds in the same way the dynamic macro-element of substructure 2. - Assembly of the different substructures: Definition of the generalised model: one assigns a name to each substructure and one specifies the interfaces between the different substructures MODEGE=DEFI_MODELE_GENE( SOUS_STRUC=( _F( NOM = 'COTE1', MACR_ELEM_DYNA = MACRO1, TRANS = (0., 0., 0.,), ANGL_NAUT = (0., 0., 0.,),), _F( NOM = 'COTE2', TRANS = (1., 0., 0.,), ANGL_NAUT = (0., 0., 0.,), MACR_ELEM_DYNA = MACRO2)), LIAISON=_F( SOUS_STRUC_1 = 'COTE1', SOUS_STRUC_2 = 'COTE2', INTERFACE_1 = 'DROITE', INTERFACE_2 = 'GAUCHE')) Definition of a numbering of the degrees of freedom of the assembled generalised system: NUMEGE=NUME_DDL_GENE( MODELE_GENE=MODEGE) Assembly of the generalised matrices of the different substructures: RIGGEN=ASSE_MATR_GENE( NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEGE, OPTION='RIGI_GENE' ) MASGEN=ASSE_MATR_GENE( NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEGE, OPTION='MASS_GENE' ) AMOGEN=ASSE_MATR_GENE( NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEGE, OPTION='AMOR_GENE' ) Assembly of the generalised loading vector: VECTGEN=ASSE_VECT_GENE( NUME_DDL_GENE=NUMEGE, CHAR_SOUS_STRUC=( _F( SOUS_STRUC = 'COTE1', VECT_ASSE = V_ASSE1), _F( SOUS_STRUC = 'COTE2', VECT_ASSE = V_ASSE2))) - Computation of the harmonic response of the assembled structure: DYNGEN=DYNA_VIBRA( TYPE_CALCUL='HARM' , BASE_CALCUL='GENE' , MATR_MASS=MASGEN, MATR_RIGI=RIGGEN, MATR_AMOR=AMOGEN, SOLVEUR=_F( METHODE='LDLT', ), FREQ=F, TOUT_CHAM='OUI', EXCIT=_F( VECT_ASSE = VECTGEN, COEF_MULT = 1.)) - Recovery onto the physical basis: One carries out here a recovery onto substructure 1 (COTE1): DYNHAR1=REST_SOUS_STRUC( RESU_GENE=DYNGEN, SOUS_STRUC='COTE1' ) One therefore recalls that, for a harmonic-response analysis, as for the modal analysis, one carries out the analysis directly on the generalised model of the assembled structure without doing a second projection onto an analysis basis.

u2.07.07 Setting up an analysis by dynamic substructuring in the presence of IFS u2.07.07 Setting up an analysis by dynamic substructuring in the presence of IFS Summary: The purpose of this document is to help users and to give them advice for carrying out a study involving the dynamic substructuring technique in the presence of fluid–structure interaction (IFS). The latter must be modelled in a displacement–pressure formulation (called U_P in code_aster) and in 3D. See the documents U3.14.02 and R4.02.02 for any further detail. One first presents the general approach for setting up the technique. One then describes the sequences of operations required in order to obtain usable results. The presentation is illustrated by an example treating a modal analysis. Reading the document U2.07.05 «Setting up an analysis by dynamic substructuring» is a prerequisite to reading the present document, which takes up many of its elements. 1 What does dynamic substructuring consist of? Dynamic substructuring consists in partitioning a part into several substructures in order to reduce the size of the numerical model and to be able to study each substructure independently. The overall model is then obtained by assembling the models of the different substructures. Each substructure is projected onto a judiciously chosen basis of vectors. This projection makes it possible to reduce the size of the model of each substructure and consequently the size of the model of the assembled structure. 2 Why use dynamic substructuring? The growing complexity of mechanical structures makes it difficult to estimate their dynamic behaviour under an imposed loading. The numerical modelling of the complete structure would require a significant cost, both in terms of memory space and of analysis cost. In addition to the reduction in the size of the model, the dynamic substructuring technique makes the modelling of the global structure much more modular. 3 Presentation of the methodology 3.1 General principle For a complete presentation of dynamic substructuring, the reader is invited to consult the reference document R4.06.02. By way of preamble, it is necessary to recall that projecting the substructure onto a reduced basis necessarily introduces an approximation into the results obtained. The role of the modeller is to choose a basis rich enough to be able to capture the dynamic behaviour of the substructure. The quality of the results depends on the choice of this projection basis. We concentrate here on the use of interface modes. This consists in carrying out a condensation of the behaviour of the structure onto the interface degrees of freedom and in solving the associated eigenvalue problem. The methodology proposed here differs from the general approach (see U2.07.05) by the fact that the interface modes mentioned here are defined in advance. This constitutes a limitation of the approach : the interface modes have been defined on the assumption that the methodology would be applied to piping, or at least to structures of shapes close to that of a pipe. The principle of the methodology is the following: - one computes, for each substructure, a set of modes with fixed interfaces; - for each interface, one gives oneself a well-defined set of modes, which describe its kinematics. These modes have been chosen in advance so as to be able to represent well the strains of a section of a pipe filled with fluid. - for each substructure, one computes its response under the effect of each of the interface modes. These modes come to complete the modes with fixed interfaces. One then determines the response of the global structure with the aid of the modes thus constructed for each of the substructures. A mathematical description is proposed in section 5. 3.2 Illustration on a simple structure To illustrate the procedure graphically, one proposes the following visualisations, which illustrate the case of a straight beam of square cross-section, clamped on its left-hand side and cut into 2 substructures denoted SD1 and SD2(). Figure 3.2-1: Beam divided into 2 substructures We present the fixed-interface modes of the substructure SD1. On the left-hand part the clamping linked to the modelled problem is applied, and on the right-hand part the clamping linked to the fixing of the interface is applied. This constitutes the 1st group of modes onto which one will reduce the behaviour of the substructure SD1. One does the same on the substructure SD2. | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | mode 1 horizontal | mode 1 vertical | mode 2 horizontal | mode 2 vertical | Figure 3.2-2: Fixed-interface modes We present the effect of the chosen interface modes on the substructure SD1. These modes have been defined in advance and one sees that they are composed of: - 3 unit displacements along the axes X, Y and Z 1; - 3 unit rotations along the axes X, Y and Z; - 1 swelling in the plane of the interface. The same construction is carried out on the substructure SD2. | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | vertical displacement | horizontal displacement | axial displacement | | | | | | axial rotation | vertical rotation | horizontal rotation | | | | | | | swelling | | Figure 3.2-3: Effect of the interface modes on a substructure It is then by mixing the local modes and the interface modes of the 2 substructures that one will construct the response of the global structure. It is important to emphasise that the number of interface modes is fixed (in this instance by the developer of this methodology), whereas the number of local modes is in the hands of the user. We propose below recommendations on the number of local modes to be retained. 3.3 Extension to the case of IFS The preceding example illustrates the methodology on a purely structural case. The extension to taking the interaction with a fluid into account is natural in this methodology. It proceeds essentially by recourse to the U_P formulation of the problem and by the definition of additional interface modes. Thus, the steps are modified as follows: - the local modes become modes with the interface fixed in displacement and in pressure, and they naturally comprise a structural part and a fluid part; - the interface modes are composed of structural modes identical to those presented in the preceding section, to which are added the fluid modes: 1 mode with constant pressure on the interface, 2 modes with a linear pressure variation along the X axis and along the Y axis of the interface, respectively. These are axes local to the interface. 4 Practical implementation 4.1 Prerequisites in terms of modelling and mesh We now turn to the implementation in code_aster of a modal analysis by dynamic substructuring with IFS taken into account. To do so, one defines the model problem of a lyre shown. It is a metal pipe in which water flows. The lyre is clamped at each of its ends, i.e. the displacement of the structure and the pressure of the fluid are fixed at 0. One seeks to determine the eigenmodes of this component. Figure 4.1-1: Model problem of a lyre A section of the lyre is shown: one sees in yellow the structural elements and in blue the fluid elements. The figure recalls the components of the degrees of freedom of each of the parts of the model. One observes that the nodes shared by the structure and by the fluid carry displacement and pressure degrees of freedom. One recalls that the mesh must be composed of 3D finite elements and that a fluid–structure modelling U_P must be assigned to it. Figure 4.1-2: Section of the lyre We are going to use dynamic substructuring to carry this simulation through. To do so, one must begin by cutting the global structure into 2 substructures. We must therefore produce 2 meshes, shown in the figure. The gap between the 2 substructures is purely artificial in this visualisation and is intended only to make the separation into 2 parts visible. For the simulation to be able to be carried out, it is obligatory that an interface surface be created. That is to say that, on the cut between the 2 substructures, a surface must be created and it must bear the same name for each of them . This is a means of identifying the interfaces in the case where one has more than 2 substructures. On the other hand, it is interesting to note that the meshes of 2 interface surfaces do not need to be conforming , i.e. their nodes do not need to be coincident. Figure 4.1-3: Cutting into 2 substructures 4.2 Course of the study At the beginning of the command file, import the necessary objects from the dynamic_substructuring module: | from code_aster.Applications.dynamic_substructuring import SubStructure, Structure, Interface | | --- | Once the meshes have been read into code_aster and the models assigned, the solution steps are the following. For each substructure: determination of the fixed-interface modes - Make sure that the displacements and the pressure are fixed at 0 on the interface (AFFE_CHAR_MECA – do not use AFFE_CHAR_CINE) - Computation and assembly of the mass and stiffness matrices of the substructure (ASSEMBLAGE): for example MASS1, MASS2, RAID1, RAID2 - Computation of the fixed-interface modes (CALC_MODES): for example MODES1, MODES2 Next, the definition of the substructures, of the interface between them and the computation of the global response is carried out as follows, with the aid of Python commands: | # definition of the substructures subS1 = SubStructure(RAID1, MASS1, MODES1) subS2 = SubStructure(RAID2, MASS2, MODES2) # definition of the interface from its name (here 'Interface') interface = Interface(subS1, subS2, 'Interface') # computation of the values of the degrees of freedom at the interface interface.computeInterfaceDofs('IFS') # computation of the interface modes ResuS_Tuyau1 = subS1.computeInterfaceModes() ResuS_Tuyau2 = subS2.computeInterfaceModes() # construction of the global structure myStructure = Structure([subS1, subS2],[interface]) # computation of the global modes (here 6) omega, resuSub = myStructure.computeGlobalModes(nmodes=6) | | --- | On exit from the call to the method computeGlobalModes of the object myStructure, the user obtains 2 outputs: - omega: this is a list which contains the natural frequencies of the global structure - resuSub: this is a list of code_aster result data structures of type MODE_MECA. These are the modes of the global structure projected respectively onto the first and the second substructure (in the order of the definition of the global structure, here [subS1, subS2]). 4.3 Practical advice - It is advisable to place the interface between 2 substructures in zones of moderate strain. In the case of piping, this means keeping away from the elbows, which are the zones where the strains will be the largest and the least regular. - It is advisable to compute the fixed-interface modes up to a frequency of at least 2 to 3 times the frequency sought on the global structure. - If one wishes to model 3 substructures SD1, SD2 and SD3 separated respectively by the interfaces Int12 and Int23 as in the figure, the global structure will be defined as follows: | # construction of the global structure myStructure = Structure([SD1, SD2, SD3],[Int12, Int23]) | | --- | Figure 4.3-1: Case of 3 substructures and 2 interfaces - If one wishes to model 3 substructures SD1, SD2 and SD3 separated respectively by the interfaces Int12, Int23 and Int31 as in the figure, the global structure will be defined as follows: | # construction of the global structure myStructure = Structure([SD1, SD2, SD3],[Int12, Int23, Int31]) | | --- | Figure 4.3-2: Case of 3 substructures and 3 interfaces 5 Theoretical elements One presents in this section the theoretical foundations of the approach. 5.1 Preliminary 5.1.1 General expression of the problem One begins by recalling the formulation of a linear dynamics problem in the form of the minimisation of the Hamiltonian: \underset{\mathit{𝑥}}{min}\underset{{\mathit{𝑡}}_{1}}{\overset{{\mathit{𝑡}}_{2}}{\int}}\left({\mathit{𝑥}}^{\mathit{𝑇}}\mathit{𝐾𝑥}-{\dot{\mathit{𝑥}}}^{\mathit{𝑇}}\mathit{𝑀}\dot{\mathit{𝑥}}\right)\mathit{𝑑𝑡} With a few algebraic manipulations, one can obtain the expression of the modal analysis which matters to us: \mathit{𝐾𝑥}-{\mathit{𝜔}}^{2}\mathit{𝑀𝑥}=0 5.1.2 Modes and generalised unknowns One also recalls that one denotes as follows the rectangular matrix of the {n}_{m} modes: \Phi =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{\Phi}_{1}& \text{...}& {\Phi}_{{n}_{m}}\end{array}\right] Each vector {\Phi}_{i} being of length {n}_{\text{eq}} , the matrix \Phi is of dimension {n}_{\text{eq}}\times {n}_{m} . One finally recalls the relation between a vector of unknowns in physical space x and a vector of generalised unknowns \eta : x=\Phi \eta ={\eta}_{1}{\Phi}_{1}+{\eta}_{2}{\Phi}_{2}+\text{...}+{\eta}_{{n}_{m}}{\Phi}_{{n}_{m}} 5.1.3 Constrained problem The last point presented concerns the solution of a dynamics problem under constraints. The latter is expressed in the general form: \mathit{Bx}=0 In the present case, the matrix B is a rectangular matrix whose number of rows is equal to the number of constraints applied to the unknowns. The constrained problem is expressed as follows: \underset{\mathit{𝐵𝑥}=0}{min}\underset{{\mathit{𝑡}}_{1}}{\overset{{\mathit{𝑡}}_{2}}{\int}}\left({\mathit{𝑥}}^{\mathit{𝑇}}\mathit{𝐾𝑥}-{\dot{\mathit{𝑥}}}^{\mathit{𝑇}}\mathit{𝑀}\dot{\mathit{𝑥}}\right)\mathit{𝑑𝑡} One assumes that one knows how to construct a basis of dimension {n}_{\mathit{ker}} of the kernel of the constraint matrix. One denotes it: \Psi =\left[{\Psi}_{1}\mathrm{...}{\Psi}_{{n}_{\mathit{ker}}}\right] Since the solutions sought satisfy the constraints \mathit{Bx}=0 , they do indeed belong to the kernel of B . One can therefore write them on this basis: x=\Psi \eta By injecting this expression into the minimisation problem, one observes that one can then relax the constraint and write the problem in the form: \underset{\eta}{min}\underset{{\mathit{𝑡}}_{1}}{\overset{{\mathit{𝑡}}_{2}}{\int}}\left({\eta}^{\mathit{𝑇}}\left[{\Psi}^{\mathit{𝑇}}\mathit{𝐾}\Psi \right]\eta -{\dot{\eta}}^{\mathit{𝑇}}\left[{\Psi}^{\mathit{𝑇}}\mathit{𝑀}\Psi \right]\dot{\eta}\right)\mathit{𝑑𝑡} The problem is therefore solvable with the aid of the classical techniques (minimisation without constraints). 5.2 Implementation One considers a structure cut into 2 substructures. For each of them, the following have been determined: - the mass matrices {M}_{1} {M}_{2} and the stiffness matrices {K}_{1} {K}_{2} , of respective dimensions {n}_{{\text{eq}}_{1}}\times {n}_{{\text{eq}}_{1}} and {n}_{{\text{eq}}_{2}}\times {n}_{{\text{eq}}_{2}} - the matrices of the fixed-interface modes {\Phi}_{1} and {\Phi}_{2} of respective dimensions {n}_{{\mathit{eq}}_{1}}\times {n}_{{m}_{1}} and {n}_{{\mathit{eq}}_{2}}\times {n}_{{m}_{2}} . They are linked respectively to the generalised unknowns {\eta}_{1} and {\eta}_{2} . - the matrices of the interface modes \overline{{\Phi}_{1}} and \overline{{\Phi}_{2}} of respective dimensions {n}_{{\mathit{eq}}_{1}}\times {n}_{i} and {n}_{{\mathit{eq}}_{2}}\times {n}_{i} . They are linked respectively to the generalised unknowns \overline{{\eta}_{1}} and \overline{{\eta}_{2}} . On the basis of these definitions, one can write the link between the physical and generalised degrees of freedom of each of the substructures: {\mathit{𝑥}}_{1}=\left[{\Phi}_{1}{\overline{\Phi}}_{1}\right]\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}_{1}\\ {\overline{\eta}}_{1}\end{array}\right\rbrace Denoting \tilde{{\Phi}_{i}}=\left[{\Phi}_{i}{\overline{\Phi}}_{i}\right] and \tilde{{\eta}_{i}}=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}_{i}\\ {\overline{\eta}}_{i}\end{array}\right\rbrace , one can write the preceding relation in the form: {\mathit{𝑥}}_{1}={\tilde{\Phi}}_{1}{\tilde{\eta}}_{1} For each substructure, one can then compute the mass and stiffness matrices projected onto the fixed-interface modes and the interface modes: {\tilde{\mathit{𝐾}}}_{1}={\tilde{\Phi}}_{1}^{T}{\mathit{𝐾}}_{1}{\tilde{\Phi}}_{1} One next constructs the global matrices which bear on the 2 substructures: {\mathit{𝐾}}_{\mathit{𝑔}}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}{\tilde{\mathit{𝐾}}}_{1}& 0\\ 0& {\tilde{\mathit{𝐾}}}_{2}\end{array}\right] The generalised degrees of freedom are constructed in the same way: {\eta}_{g}=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\tilde{\eta}}_{1}\\ {\tilde{\eta}}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}_{1}\\ {\overline{\eta}}_{1}\end{array}\right\rbrace \\ \left\lbrace \begin{array}{c}{\eta}_{2}\\ {\overline{\eta}}_{2}\end{array}\right\rbrace \end{array}\right\rbrace One recalls that the {\eta}_{i} are the generalised unknowns associated with the fixed-interface modes and the \overline{{\eta}_{i}} those associated with the interface modes. Therefore, to ensure the continuity of the displacements in physical space across the interface, one must impose: \overline{{\eta}_{1}}=\overline{{\eta}_{2}} This can be expressed simply with the aid of a constraint matrix in the form: B{\eta}_{g}=0 with: | | 17 | | --- | --- | The global problem can then be expressed in the form: \underset{\mathit{𝐵}{\eta}_{g}=0}{min}\underset{{t}_{1}}{\overset{{t}_{2}}{\int}}\left({\eta}_{g}^{\mathit{𝑇}}{\mathit{𝐾}}_{g}{\eta}_{g}-{\dot{\eta}}_{g}^{\mathit{𝑇}}{\mathit{𝑀}}_{g}{\dot{\eta}}_{g}\right)\mathit{𝑑𝑡} By computing the kernel of B , the problem above is solvable as presented in section 5.1.3. One will find examples of implementation in the tests sdlv102 and sdlv103.

u2.08.01 Mesh adaptation strategies with HOMARD u2.08.01 Mesh adaptation strategies with HOMARD Summary: This document aims to describe all the tools of Code_Aster related to mesh adaptation. It constitutes a methodological guide to the good practices to be put in place in order to conduct a study of quality as regards the mesh. Examples of use illustrate the possibilities and the implementation of remeshing strategies. 1 Introduction Mesh adaptation provides the user with assistance in supplying analyses that are as reliable as possible with respect to the discretisation errors due to the finite-element method employed. Several motivations appear for adapting a mesh: - the mesh is very complicated to produce: one starts from a simple version and one entrusts an automatic process with the task of refining it. - one wants to make sure of the convergence of the numerical solution: rather than producing by hand meshes that are finer and finer, one lets the software itself look for the places where the mesh ought to be refined in order to increase the accuracy of the result. - the conditions of the analysis change in the course of its progress: the zones which must be finely meshed move. If one meshes finely everywhere from the outset, the mesh is too large. By adapting progressively, the mesh will be fine only at the necessary places: its size will be reduced and the quality of the solution will be good. Whatever software is used, the principle of mesh adaptation remains the same. On the starting mesh, one carries out the standard analysis. From an analysis of the numerical solution obtained, one estimates the error which has been committed with respect to the real solution. This estimate is represented by a value of the error indicator in each element of the analysis. From there, the reasoning is simple: the mesh cells where the error indicator is high ought to be smaller; conversely, the mesh cells where the error indicator is low could be larger. With this information, one feeds the adaptation software, which will modify the mesh accordingly. On the new mesh, one will then start the analysis again. Schematically, an iteration of mesh adaptation appears as in the figure below. The software computes the numerical solution on mesh no. k, then deduces from it the values of the error indicator over the whole mesh. From the knowledge of mesh no. k and of indicator no. k, the mesh-adaptation software, HOMARD for Code_Aster , creates the new mesh no. (k+1). Figure 1-a : Iteration of mesh adaptation For a static analysis, this amounts to seeking to improve the solution by a succession of analyses on different meshes. For a transient analysis in time, the analysis is suspended at a given time instant; the mesh is adapted; the analysis resumes on the new mesh. With Code_Aster , this adaptation is carried out by a call to an external program, specialised in this task, HOMARD. The aim of this document is to provide as complete an entry point as possible for the user wishing to implement this kind of technique in his analyses. The plan of the document is then as follows: - How HOMARD works; - A focus on the error indicators; - A set of pieces of advice on the "good practices" to be implemented (which points deserve attention during use?); - A few examples illustrate the use of these techniques and the advice given previously (how does one do it in practice?). 2 How does HOMARD work? HOMARD is a software package developed by EDF R&D. A presentation of it can be found on its Web site [bib1] and in its own documentation [bib2]. 2.1 The scope of use of HOMARD The command of Code_Aster which makes it possible to access these functions is MACR_ADAP_MAIL. It is documented in [bib3]. HOMARD can handle meshes in 2 or 3 dimensions, of degree 1 or degree 2, and comprising the following elements: - point mesh cells - segments - triangles - quadrangles - tetrahedra - hexahedra These elements may be present simultaneously. For example, HOMARD will know how to adapt a mesh comprising triangles and quadrangles. The nodes accepted are obviously the nodes which are the vertices of the mesh cells, which corresponds to the classical description "in degree 1". If the mesh cells are described "in degree 2", that is to say with the presence of nodes in the middle of the edges, these complementary nodes are managed. On the other hand, there cannot be coexistence of mesh cells described in degree 1 and of mesh cells described in degree 2. Finally, HOMARD can take into account isolated nodes, which would not belong to any mesh-cell definition: they will come out of the adaptation process unchanged. A particular case: the pentahedra. At the date of writing of this document, HOMARD can handle meshes comprising pentahedra but only in order to carry out uniform refinement. Free refinement will be available at the end of 2011. 2.2 A word on the modes of cutting of the elements It is interesting here to know the mode of cutting of the mesh cells in HOMARD so as not to be possibly surprised by the new mesh. We shall give only an example in 2D; for 3D, the reader will consult the HOMARD Web site [bib1]. Among the various techniques possible for adapting a mesh, HOMARD uses refinement and unrefinement by cutting of the mesh cells. The standard cutting is that which applies to any mesh cell at the heart of a zone to be refined: a triangle is cut into four triangles (Figure 2.2-a) and a quadrangle is cut into four quadrangles (Figure 2.2-b). In 3 dimensions, a tetrahedron is cut into eight tetrahedra, a hexahedron into eight hexahedra, a pentahedron into eight pentahedra. Each cutting rests on the mid-points of the edges bordering the mesh cell. Figure 2.2-a : Standard cutting of the triangles Figure 2.2-b: Standard cutting of the quadrangles How does HOMARD manage conformity? Let us start from a situation such as that of Figure 2.2-c, representing a two-dimensional mesh formed of quadrangles and of triangles. The error indicator will have requested a refinement on the hatched zones. Figure 2.2-c: Example of a refinement request The strict application of the principle of cutting of the mesh cells designated by the error indicator produces the mesh of Figure 2.2-d: Figure 2.2-d: Example of a raw non-conforming refinement In order to manage conformity, the rule is as follows: - If an uncut mesh cell finds itself attacked on at least two sides, it is likewise cut into four; - If a mesh cell finds itself attacked on a single side: - if it is a triangle, it is cut into two, - if it is a quadrangle, it is cut into three triangles Which gives, for our example: Figure 2.2-e: Final enforcement of conformity Comment concerning the quality of the meshes resulting from the cutting: In the course of the standard cutting, the triangles produced are rigorously identical to the starting triangles. There is a perfect homothety and therefore identity of the mesh qualities. For the quadrangles, the situation is not so simple. If the quadrangle is a parallelogram, the quadrangles produced are likewise homothetic. This is therefore the case for a square or a rectangle. The mesh quality then remains the same. On the other hand, as soon as the quadrangle is arbitrary, the 4 children never resemble the parent: the quality changes. For the cuttings of final enforcement of conformity, it is blatant that they modify the quality of the mesh cells. An equilateral triangle will have two flattened children; a regular tetrahedron will have slender children. Conversely a flattened triangle cut along its long side will have two fairly regular children, and so on. We therefore have favourable situations and others which are less so. If we do nothing, we shall run the risk of seeing the quality of the mesh deteriorate. Let us indeed imagine the case of a zone in which the refinement indications would lead to subdividing a conformity triangle. After a few adaptations, the quality of the mesh would be completely degraded. HOMARD manages these difficulties by a special algorithm which guarantees that the angles do not flatten out over the course of the iterations. We thus limit the modifications of the quality level of the mesh: the quality of the mesh, at any level of adaptation, remains comparable to the quality of the starting mesh. We refer the reader to [bib2] for a fine description of this analysis of mesh quality, illustrated by typical cases. 2.3 The different modes of adaptation There exist several choices for driving an adaptation through the command MACR_ADAP_MAIL documented in [bib3]. 1. In the first place, one finds the modes of adaptation which are driven by a field or the derivative of this field, for example an error indicator (keywords 'RAFFINEMENT', 'DERAFFINEMENT' and 'RAFF_DERA'). This field may be expressed on the nodes or the elements. In other words, the decision to (un)refine a mesh cell is taken as a function of the value of this field computed beforehand on this mesh cell or of the jump of this field from one mesh cell to its neighbours. The choice of the refinement or unrefinement thresholds is made in three forms: - an absolute threshold value of this field (keyword 'CRIT_RAF_ABS'): one will refine all the mesh cells where the value of the field is greater than this threshold value. - a relative value of the field (keyword 'CRIT_RAF_REL'): one will refine the mesh cells where the value of the field is greater than x% of the maximum value. - a fraction of elements (keyword 'CRIT_RAF_PE'): one will refine the x% of mesh cells where the value of the field is the largest. Note: When one applies an unrefinement option, one only goes back on previous refinements. This option must be understood as un-refinement. In particular, one will never be able to obtain a mesh coarser than the initial mesh. If the driving field is defined on the nodes, HOMARD will cut in two all the edges whose nodes have field values greater than the criterion requested. Depending on the types of problem, one or the other of the strategies is preferable; it is the know-how proper to each discipline which makes it possible to define good practices. One must nevertheless be careful and not request too much refinement when one works with conforming meshes. Indeed, the threshold will trigger the compulsory refinement of the designated mesh cells. But in order to ensure conformity, there will necessarily be additional refinements in order to connect the zones of different levels. In the end, one will always have more mesh cells cut than those which had been requested initially. Experience has shown us that it is more effective for the accuracy of the solution to chain 3 successive refinements, requesting the refinement of 1% of the mesh cells, rather than to carry out only a single refinement requesting 5%. 1. In the second place, one may decide to refine the mesh in geometrical zones defined by boxes (keyword 'RAFF_DERA_ZONE'). All the mesh cells of which one of the nodes is present in one of these boxes will be refined. This makes it possible to carry out refinements a priori , without having carried out an analysis. The zones are rectangles or circles in 2D, parallelepipeds or spheres in 3D. It is possible to define several boxes, overlapping or not. 1. Finally, one may activate a uniform adaptation of a mesh (keywords 'RAFFINEMENT_UNIFORME' and 'DERAFFINEMENT_UNIFORME'). In other words, all the mesh cells of the mesh are treated in the same manner, without taking into account a field serving as a criterion for (un)refining. Note: The characteristics of the mesh cells are preserved: a mesh cell which is cut transmits to its daughters its properties of orientation or of belonging to subdomains. This is in particular true for the boundary mesh cells which serve to apply the loadings: the group which defines them is restored and it is unnecessary to reorient them 2.4 Other possible options The various options which may be activated in MACR_ADAP_MAIL: - HOMARD updates real fields from the old mesh onto the new mesh when they are defined on the nodes (keyword MAJ_CHAM). This makes it possible, in the course of a transient analysis, to restart from the solution previously computed but expressed on the new mesh. In general, it is moreover recommended to update the fields via HOMARD rather than to project them afterwards from one mesh onto the other in the analysis software. Indeed, HOMARD stores the parentage of all the nodes and mesh cells: it will therefore carry out only the strictly necessary computations and only by analytical formulae. At present, one cannot update fields at the Gauss points (such as the internal variables, for example). - HOMARD possesses mesh-analysis functions: connectivity (the software reports the number of disjoint blocks which form the global mesh), size (computation of the sizes of the various 1D, 2D or 3D subdomains), quality (determination of the quality of the 2D or 3D elements, extreme values and distribution), interpenetration (check of the non-overlapping of elements). These functions can be activated in the course of an adaptation. They can also be used outside any adaptation in order to check a mesh. They help the user to check that his mesh is correct and to locate errors in its production. One can find these functionalities on the quality of the mesh in the command MACR_INFO_MAIL [bib4]. - The user has the possibility of carrying out boundary tracking (keywords MAILLAGE_FRONTIERE and/or FRONTIERE_ANALYTIQUE). If one of the boundaries of the computational domain is curved and a mesh cell touching this boundary is refined, HOMARD will know how to place the new nodes on the "true" boundary. This option makes it possible to "smooth out", progressively with the cutting, the geometrical singularities (see the example of the rotor in paragraph 6). - When one adapts a mesh of degree 2 by the command MACR_ADAP_MAIL, one produces as output the new mesh in degree 2. Optionally (keyword MAILLAGE_NP1_ANNEXE), one will also produce the same mesh in degree 1. This option is of interest during a thermomechanical analysis in which one recommends a linear mesh in thermal analysis and a quadratic one in mechanics. - The keywords NIVE_MAX and NIVE_MIN make it possible to control the maximum level of refinement, respectively of unrefinement, of a mesh cell in the course of the adaptation process. - The keyword DIAM_MIN makes it possible to control the minimum size of a mesh cell in the course of the adaptation process. 3 The different criteria of refinement/unrefinement One saw in paragraph 2.3 that one can locate the zones to be refined: - either with an error indicator; - or with a field (or its derivative) which one considers as a measure of the error (temperature, stress, strain, …). This field may be expressed on the nodes or on the mesh cells (at the Gauss points, at the nodes per element or constant per element). If the criterion is expressed at the Gauss points or at the nodes per element, then HOMARD chooses the maximum of the value in the mesh cell considered; - or by boxes. For the error indicators, several choices are offered to the user. This is the subject of the following paragraphs. 3.1 The error indicators 3.1.1 What is an error indicator? It is important here to recall the definition of what is meant by error indicator (or error estimator) so that the user is well aware of what one can, or cannot, make this indicator say. A function e is an a posteriori error indicator if it satisfies the inequality: \parallel u-{u}^{h}\parallel \le e(h,{u}^{h},d) where u is the displacement field of the exact solution, {u}^{h} the displacement field of the finite-element solution, \parallel \cdot \parallel a norm on the displacement fields, h the size of the elements and d data of the problem. Moreover if e(h,d,{u}^{h}) can be localised in the form: e(h,{u}^{h},d)={(\sum_{E}{e}_{E}({u}^{h},d{)}^{2})}^{\frac{1}{2}} then the quantities {e}_{E}({u}^{h},d) are called local error indicators. For the two types of error indicator (hence two different functions e) present in Code_Aster , the norm \parallel \cdot \parallel is an energy norm. 3.1.2 What must be retained These error indicators lead to the estimation of a global error. The choice of a global accuracy founded on the energy norm is often delicate to interpret, because there is no direct quantitative link with an error on local mechanical quantities (stresses at a point or on a line, maximum of the stresses, etc.) and the error in displacement. In other words, X% of the error indicator in a mesh cell does not mean that there is X% of error on the stress or the strain. Used alone, that is to say without the objective of carrying out mesh adaptation, the indicator does not make it possible to quantify the quality of the initial mesh, except possibly to locate the problem zones, such as the geometrical singularities or the strong gradients. 3.1.3 Scope of use The error indicators used in Code_Aster are a posteriori indicators and are therefore computed in post-processing of Code_Aster by the command CALC_ERREUR. They are fields constant per element (hence one value per finite element). Their domain of use is delimited by the following constraints (one will refer to the reference documents given in the paragraph for more details): - the errors taken into account are the errors of spatial discretisation (hence the size of the elements employed); in particular, the errors of temporal discretisation (or pseudo-temporal in the case of non-linear materials) lie outside this scope; - the physical phenomena are limited to mechanics (linear or non-linear) and to thermal analysis (likewise); - in mechanics as in thermal analysis, the constitutive behaviour may be linear or non-linear (except for the Zhu-Zienkiewicz error estimator in mechanics, which treats only linear constitutive behaviour), it being known that the theoretical results of the error indicators are obtained in the linear domain (their use in the non-linear domain is therefore not based on theoretical results but on an empirical observation of their interest); - the elements used may be arbitrary for the use of the error indicators (except for the Zhu-Zienkiewicz error estimator in mechanics, which treats only the 2D elements; the estimator \mathrm{ZZ2} accepts only meshes composed either of triangles or of quadrangles); These elements may be linear or quadratic. 3.1.4 Error estimator in mechanics There exist two types of estimator for mechanics: - The Zhu-Zienkiewicz error estimator [bib5], which is computed directly in the operator CALC_ERREUR with the options 'ERZ1_ELEM' for the estimator \mathrm{ZZ1} and 'ERZ2_ELEM' for the estimator \mathrm{ZZ2} . This field comprises three components per element E : - 'ERREST': the absolute total error {e}_{E} ; - 'NUEST': the relative total error {e}_{{E}_{\text{REL}}}=100\times \frac{{e}_{E}}{\sqrt{{e}_{E}^{2}+{\mathrm{\parallel }{\sigma}_{h}\mathrm{\parallel }}_{E}^{2}}} ; - 'SIGCAL': the energy norm of the computed solution {\parallel {\sigma}_{h}\parallel }_{E} . - The residual error estimator [bib6], which is likewise computed in the operator CALC_ERREUR with the options 'ERME_ELEM' for the computation in the element and 'ERME_ELNO' for the computation at the nodes per element. This field comprises eight components per element E : - 'ERREST': the absolute total error {e}_{E} ; - 'TERMRE': the absolute error of the residual of equilibrium; - 'TERMSA': the absolute error of the stress jumps between two mesh cells; - 'TERMNO': the absolute error of the jumps between the normal stress and the Neumann force; - 'NUEST': the relative total error; - 'TERMR2': the relative error of the residual of equilibrium; - 'TERMS2': the relative error of the stress jumps between two mesh cells; - 'TERMN2': the relative error of the jumps between the normal stress and the Neumann force; - 'SIGCAL': the energy norm of the computed solution; For these two types of error estimator, the user also has access to printouts in the result file comprising the same information at the global level. A few pieces of advice for a good use of the option ERME_ELEM: - In order properly to carry out the computation of the residual indicator (within the theoretical limits of the formula developed in the elliptic framework with a regular boundary …), one must compute it over the whole model (CALC_ERREUR ( TOUT = 'OUI' (default value))). It should be noted that the model is not necessarily defined over the whole geometry. - One takes into account only loadings of the type: PESANTEUR, ROTATION, FORCE_INTERNE, PRES_REP, FORCE_FACE, FORCE_ARETE. Only the last three may be variable. For the other types of loading, execution stops in fatal error. - It is advised to use finite elements of order 2 in the case of body forces, otherwise this term is very poorly computed since DIV(SIGMA) is almost zero! - In order to take into account the error relative to a zero boundary condition of Neumann type, one must impose it as a function via an AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F. Via a constant, it will not be taken into account. - In 2D, it takes into account the errors on (and between) the isoparametric elements SEG2/3, TRIA3/6/7, QUAD4/8/9. In 3D, likewise with FACE3/4/6/8/9, TETRA4/10, PENTA6/13/15 and HEXA8/20/27. Only the error on the structural elements (shell, plate, beam...) and the PYRAM are not taken into account. - On the other hand, one must take care not to insert segments between two quadrangles or two triangles (resp. quadrangle or triangle between two hexahedra), otherwise one cannot compute the jump term relative to this neighbourhood. 3.1.5 Error estimator in thermal analysis There exists a single error indicator in thermal analysis [bib7], which is of residual type. It is computed in the operator CALC_ERREUR, by the options 'ERTH_ELEM' for the computation per element and 'ERTH_ELNO' for the computation per element at the nodes. For the option 'ERTH_ELEM', one must obligatorily compute the flux per element at the nodes 'FLUX_ELNO'. The estimator supplies the following components: - ERTABS: total absolute error - ERTREL: total relative error - TERMNO: normalisation term for the relative total error - TERMVO: absolute error of the residual of equilibrium (volume term) - TERMV2: relative error of the residual of equilibrium (volume term) - TERMV1: normalisation term for the volume error - TERMSA: absolute error of the jumps of the heat flux between two mesh cells - TERMS2: relative error of the jumps of the heat flux between two mesh cells - TERMS1: normalisation term for the relative error in jump - TERMFL: absolute error on the boundary conditions of imposed-flux type - TERMF2: relative error on the boundary conditions of imposed-flux type - TERMF1: normalisation term on the relative error on the flux - TERMEC: absolute error on the boundary conditions of exchange type - TERME2: relative error on the boundary conditions of exchange type - TERME1: normalisation term on the relative error on the exchanges A few pieces of advice for a good use: - particular overloading rules concerning the loadings (generation of an alarm in the event of non-compliance); - computation over the whole mesh associated with the model (generation of an error in the event of non-compliance) between two time steps, contiguous or not (generation of an alarm in the event of non-compliance); - all the 2D-plane/axisymmetric and 3D elements are treated (except PYRAM: generation of an alarm ); - all the boundary conditions except ECHANGE_PAROI, FLUX_NL and RAYO are taken into account (generation of an alarm in the event of use of ECHANGE_PAROI, FLUX_NL or RAYO); - the mesh tolerates "rough drafts" but needs to be somewhat "cleaned up" (no SEG/FACE inserted in surfaces/volumes, problem of symmetrisation, of double points: generation of an alarm or of an error ). 3.2 The error estimators in quantity of interest 3.2.1 Warning Unlike the classical error indicators above, the error indicators said to be in quantity of interest make it possible to access a local error on physical quantities (stress, displacement), and therefore in the unit of this quantity. Their use is more delicate and doubtless calls for a rapid reading of the documentation [bib9] and a more attentive reading of the recommendations given for the use of CALC_ERREUR. Moreover, their development being very recent, there is little feedback of experience on their use. What follows is therefore taken entirely from the reference documentation and from a report [bib10]. 3.2.2 What do these indicators compute? These error indicators make it possible to estimate, in a subregion of the mesh, a physical quantity, for example: A mean of displacement (the component x for example) in this subregion, expressed mathematically by the equation Q(u)=\frac{1}{\mid \Omega \mid }\underset{\Omega}{\int}{u}_{x}d\omega . A mean of stresses (for example the component xx ) Q(u)=\frac{1}{\mid \Omega \mid }\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{xx}d\omega . Once the quantity of interest has been chosen, the indicator estimates the quantity {\varepsilon}^{Q}=Q(u)-Q({u}^{h}) . It is here that the difficulty for the user arises, because this quantity of interest must be expressed in terms of a loading known in AFFE_CHER_MECA. For example, for the quantity of interest as a mean of the displacement, it is equivalent to a body loading: Q(u)=\frac{1}{\mid \Omega \mid }\underset{\Omega}{\int}{u}_{x}d\Omega =\frac{1}{\mid \Omega \mid }\underset{\Omega}{\int}fud\Omega with \overrightarrow{f}=(1,0,0) By choosing the vector \overrightarrow{f} correctly, one accesses each component of the displacement and possibly linear combinations of the components. This loading is accessible by the keyword 'FORCE_INTERNE' in 'AFFE_CHAR_MECA'. In the same way, for the quantity of interest as a mean of the stress, it is equivalent to an initial-strain loading: Q(u)=\frac{1}{\mid \Omega \mid }\underset{\Omega}{\int}{\sigma}_{xx}d\Omega =\frac{1}{\mid \Omega \mid }\underset{\Omega}{\int}A:\sigma (u)d\Omega =\frac{1}{\mid \Omega \mid }\underset{\Omega}{\int}A:K:\varepsilon (u)d\Omega One controls the choice of the component of the stress tensor by the choice of the components of the tensor A . This loading is accessible by the keyword 'PRE_EPSI' in 'AFFE_CHAR_MECA'. These two quantities are fairly simple to implement because they are represented by a loading existing in Code_Aster . For more complicated quantities (functions of the stress tensor, for example) and possibly non-linear ones, it is very difficult to express them as a function of known loadings. This is the main difficulty to be overcome in order to program new quantities of interest. 3.2.3 Scope of use These quantities of interest are computed from the classical error indicators presented in § 3.1 and only for mechanics. Their domain of use is therefore identical to that of the mechanical indicator chosen in order to compute them. One recalls, again, that the quantity of interest chosen depends on the degree of development of the loadings in AFFE_CHAR_MECA. 3.2.4 The different options in CALC_ERREUR The different options possible in CALC_ERREUR are: - 'QIZ1_ELEM' (respectively 'QIZ2_ELEM'): error estimator in quantity of interest based on the Zhu-Zienkiewicz method. One must compute beforehand the option 'ERZ1_ELEM' or 'ERZ2_ELEM'. - 'QIRE_ELEM' (per element) or 'QIRE_ELNO' (per element at the nodes): error estimator in quantity of interest based on the residuals in mechanics. One must compute beforehand the option 'ERME_ELEM'. Advice on use: The domain of use of the options 'QIZ1_ELEM' and 'QIZ2_ELEM' is the same as for the options 'ERZ1_ELEM' and 'ERZ2_ELEM', and that of the option 'QIRE_ELEM' is the same as that of the option 'ERME_ELEM' in mechanics. To date, only two quantities of interest are available: mean of a component of the displacement and mean of a component of the stress tensor. The computation of the quantity of interest passes through the solution of an elastic analysis (command MECA_STATIQUE) whose loading is, on the one hand, the same as that of the main problem on the Dirichlet conditions (hence in imposed displacement), and, on the other hand, that representing the quantity of interest chosen ('FORCE_INTERNE' or 'PRE_EPSI'). We give below an example of a command file. SOLUTION OF THE PROBLEM CHARG=AFFE_CHAR_MECA( MODELE=MO, FACE_IMPO=(_F(GROUP_MA='GRMA1',DY=0.0,), _F(GROUP_MA='GRMA2', DY=0.91333,),), FORCE_CONTOUR=(_F(GROUP_MA='GRMA3', FX=1.0,), _F(GROUP_MA='GRMA4', FX=-2.0,),),); RESU=MECA_STATIQUE( MODELE=MO, CHAM_MATER=CM, EXCIT=_F(CHARGE=CHARG,),); RESU=CALC_ERREUR(reuse =RESU, RESULTAT=RESU, TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', OPTION=('SIGM_ELNO','ERME_ELEM',),); COMPUTATION OF THE QUANTITY OF INTEREST AS A MEAN OF STRESS ON THE MESH-CELL GROUP GRMAQI CHARQ=AFFE_CHAR_MECA( MODELE=MO, FACE_IMPO=(_F(GROUP_MA='GRMA1',DY=0.0,), _F(GROUP_MA='GRMA2',DY=0.91333,),), FORCE_INTERNE=_F(GROUP_MA='GRMAQI',FX=1.0,),); RESUQ=MECA_STATIQUE(MODELE=MO, CHAM_MATER=CM, EXCIT=_F(CHARGE=CHARQ,),); RESUQ=CALC_ERREUR(reuse =RESUQ, RESULTAT=RESUQ, TOUT_ORDRE='OUI', OPTION=('SIGM_ELNO','ERME_ELEM',),); COMPUTATION OF THE ERROR ESTIMATOR IN QUANTITY OF INTEREST RESU=CALC_ERREUR(reuse =RESU, RESULTAT=RESU, OPTION=('QIRE_ELEM'), RESU_DUAL=RESUQ,); 3.3 Detection of singularities Another possible field (only in mechanics) which may serve as a criterion for refining the mesh is the use of the option 'SING_ELEM' (field constant per element) or 'SING_ELNO' (fields per element at the nodes) in CALC_ERREUR. This field is computed from the error indicators and it aims to improve the treatment of the singularities in the mesh-adaptation strategies. The reader will find in [bib8] a theoretical description of the methods employed. In practice the error indicators are high in the singular zones, so that rapidly only the singular zones are refined. This therefore masks the other sensitive zones (zones with a strong gradient) which one would wish to refine. This field, constant per element, comprises two components: - 'DEGRE', which indicates the level of singularity of a mesh cell. In practice, this component is equal to the degree of interpolation of the finite elements chosen if the finite element is connected to no singularity, and is equal to the order of the singularity if the finite element is connected to a node considered by the method as singular (for example, for an element neighbouring the tip of a crack, this value is equal to 0.5). This value cannot be greater than the degree of interpolation, hence 1 or 2. - 'RAPPORT', which corresponds to the map of modification of the size of the finite elements in the event of remeshing for a given global error. This component is equal to the ratio between the current size and the new size of the finite element. - 'TAILLE', which corresponds to the size map of the finite elements in the event of remeshing for a given global error. Advice on use: The computation of this option requires, beforehand, the computation of an error indicator (it is the absolute component which is used, and this is hard-coded in Code_Aster) and of the total strain energy. In the case where one of these options is not computed, an alarm message is emitted and the option 'SING_ELEM' is not computed. For the total strain energy, one uses 'ETOT_ELEM' with STAT_NON_LINE or 'EPOT_ELEM' with MECA_STATIQUE. The user must also fill in the keyword 'PREC_ERR' (a fatal message is emitted in the event of absence), which makes it possible to compute the accuracy wished for on the global error in order to determine the map of size modification. The value of 'PREC_ERR' lies strictly between 0 and 1, and a fatal message is emitted if this condition is not satisfied. The scope of use is the same (but more reduced) as that of the error indicator chosen, namely: - For the residual indicator: finite elements of continuous media in 2D (triangles and quadrangles) or 3D (only the tetrahedra) for an elastoplastic constitutive behaviour, - For the Zhu-Zienkiewicz indicator: finite elements of continuous media in 2D (triangles and quadrangles) for an elastic constitutive behaviour. Strictly speaking, the computation of the order of the singularity is obtained from the theoretical energy at the crack tip, an equation valid only in elasticity. The use of this option in elastoplasticity must therefore be handled with caution. 4 Advice and good practice 4.1 On the initial mesh Independently of any wish to carry out mesh adaptation, we advise checking the initial mesh with the command MACR_INFO_MAIL [bib4]. This command makes it possible to carry out, at little cost, the following checks: - check the agreement of the mesh with the initial geometry (in mass, in dimension, in area and in volume); - list the GROUP_MA and the GROUP_NO, for a good modelling of the boundary conditions; - diagnose possible problems (symmetrisation or connectivity, rough-draft elements, poor taking into account of boundary conditions, interpenetration of mesh cells); - evaluate the quality of the mesh by the following criterion q (evaluated mesh cell by mesh cell): - for the triangles: q=\alpha \times \frac{h}{r} , where h is the length of the longest side, r the radius of the inscribed circle and a a normalisation coefficient such that q is equal to 1 for an equilateral triangle, - for the quadrangles: q=\alpha \times \frac{h\times k}{S} , where h is the maximum of the lengths of the sides and of the diagonals, k the root-mean-square of the lengths of the sides, S the minimum of the areas of the four internal triangles and a a normalisation coefficient such that q is equal to 1 for a square, - for the tetrahedra: q=\alpha \times \frac{h}{r} , where h is the length of the longest side, r the radius of the inscribed sphere and a a normalisation coefficient such that q is equal to 1 for an equilateral tetrahedron, - for the hexahedra: q=\alpha \times (\text{qualité du pire des 24 tétraèdres inscrits}) , where a is a normalisation coefficient such that q is equal to 1 for a cube. Advice: An empirical criterion may be proposed: for example, at least 50% of the mesh cells with a quality < 1.5, at least 90% of the mesh cells with a quality < 2.0, no mesh cells with a quality above 10. 4.2 On HOMARD After cutting of the mesh cells, the mesh-cell groups are updated; on the other hand the node groups are left unchanged. One must make it a rule to impose boundary conditions on mesh-cell groups and not on node groups; one must therefore proscribe (but this is a rule of common sense) the direct use of mesh-cell or node numbers during the assignments, and prefer to it the notion of mesh-cell group. One recalls that adaptation by HOMARD accepts all types of element, of degree 1 or 2, in a conforming mesh, in zones which are connected or not, of the same dimension or not, except the pyramids and the pentahedra (for uniform refinement). On the other hand, for mesh analysis, HOMARD handles the pentahedra. 4.3 On the adaptation strategy The chaining "thermomechanical operators / MACR_ADAP_MAIL option 'RAFFINEMENT_UNIFORME'" (i.e. without error indicator) makes it possible to make a mesh converge cleanly, automatically and easily. One must however beware of the number of degrees of freedom generated! This constitutes an easy solution, rapid and robust, but rapidly extremely costly (rather to be reserved for evaluating whether there are large discretisation errors, or for small studies). The chaining "thermomechanical operators / MACR_ADAP_MAIL option 'RAFFINEMENT'" (i.e. with a field driving the adaptation) makes it possible to make the mesh converge in the most optimal manner possible (taking into account the tools available). This method demands more effort than the previous one, but the number of degrees of freedom generated is proportionally much smaller. The chaining "thermomechanical operators / MACR_ADAP_MAIL" can be carried out effectively in a Python loop (loop of "for" type), possibly with an exit test (loop of "while" type). The quality of the mesh cells is little affected by the refinement / unrefinement process. Taking into account the choices made in HOMARD®, it may even improve in 3D! MACR_ADAP_MAIL does not have a regularisation process; hence a poor initial mesh will probably produce a poor adapted mesh! Linear elements are not recommended in mechanics. Good practice is rather: lumped P1 in thermal analysis (PLAN_DIAG, AXIS_DIAG, 3D_DIAG) and P2 (possibly under-integrated) in mechanics, [bib14]. The choice of the type of finite elements takes precedence over the quality of the mesh cells on which the elements rest (Cf. the example of the beam below). 4.4 On the classical error indicators Choice of the error indicator in mechanics: the user has the choice between \mathrm{ZZ1} (first version of the Zhu-Zienkiewicz indicator), \mathrm{ZZ2} (second version of the Zhu-Zienkiewicz indicator), and the residual indicator. The first two have a fairly reduced domain of application (linear 2D for \mathrm{ZZ1} and \mathrm{ZZ2} , a single type of finite element in the whole mesh for \mathrm{ZZ2} ): for a "standard" use, one will prefer the residual indicator. The type of indicator and its mode of normalisation may have an effect on the adapted mesh. For example, in mechanics, {e}_{{E}_{\text{REL}}}=100\times \frac{{e}_{E}}{\sqrt{{e}_{E}^{2}+{\parallel {\sigma}_{h}\parallel }_{E}^{2}}} . This way of normalising may be dangerous: if there are zones where the stress norm is low, the error will approach 100% in this zone; if there are zones where the stress norm is very high (singularities, for example), the error will be low in this zone. This is obviously not the result sought. One must therefore use preferentially the absolute indicator, unless one knows precisely what one is doing. For indicators of residual type, one can also "juggle" with the components of the thermal indicator and with the boundary conditions, "fictitious" or not, in order to steer the construction of a mesh which is refined or unrefined by zones. In the event of the presence of singularities, it is advised to select the number of elements on which the refinement bears by a fraction of elements to be refined, 'CRIT_RAFF_PE' (and not by the quantum of elements presenting an error greater than a fraction of the total error, 'CRIT_RAFF_REL'). Indeed, in the case of a singularity, by using 'CRIT_RAFF_REL', after one or two iterations of adaptation, only the elements touching the singularity will be refined. By using 'CRIT_RAFF_PE', other zones will be able to continue to be refined. Finally the criterion 'CRIT_RAFF_ABS' (choice by a fixed error barrier) is to be reserved for the cases in which the user knows the problem envisaged very well. As a "simple post-processing" of the thermomechanical problem, the indicator unfortunately cannot supply a more reliable diagnosis in the zones where the solution of the initial problem comes to grief. It is therefore preferable to begin an adaptation process with a mesh already somewhat refined "by hand". In thermomechanics, different mesh-adaptation strategies are offered to the user: - adapt the mesh according to a thermal criterion only, - adapt the mesh according to a mechanical criterion only, - adapt jointly or separately (i.e. with one or two adaptation loops); in short, chain or couple the first two strategies. Good practice during such a thermomechanical analysis leads one to use two meshes and to interpolate the thermal field {P}_{1} onto the mechanical mesh {P}_{2} (via the operator PROJ_CHAMP). If one wishes to work with only a single mesh, one may apply one of the strategies via the option MAJ_CHAM of MACR_ADAP_MAIL. This makes it possible, while adapting the mesh according to a criterion, to update the complementary field on the new adapted mesh. In thermal analysis, in order to carry out a mesh adaptation based on the indicator ERTH_ELEM in the course of a transient, one must not forget to start the computation of the following time step with the old EVOL_THER updated onto the new mesh. 5 Examples of use 5.1 Introduction In what follows, we present five examples of mesh adaptation. These examples have different pedagogical objectives. The first example, which is the most recent, comes from a study carried out at the R&D of EDF on an HP rotor. The following three examples remain more academic but aim to show a particular aspect of the adaptation process. Finally the last example illustrates the mode of cutting chosen by HOMARD (it is a particular situation encountered by a user who was surprised by the final mesh). Pedagogical objective of each of the examples HP rotor: show the necessity of taking boundary tracking into account during the adaptation Beam in bending in elasticity: Know how to interpret the results of the command MACR_INFO_MAIL in the .mess file Illustrate the interest of a free refinement with respect to a uniform refinement Use the error indicators in mechanics and choose the right component (absolute or relative) Cylinder head in thermal analysis: Use the error indicators in thermal analysis and observe the zones refined according to the component of the indicator chosen Very simplified representation of the expanded tubesheet (thermoplastic analysis): Show the interest of a free adaptation with respect to a uniform adaptation as regards the computation times In thermal analysis, give the Python command file making it possible to carry out mesh adaptation in a transient Localisation band in a plate: understand the mode of cutting chosen by HOMARD Note : When one carries out mesh adaptation, it is useful to have a few notions of the Python language in order to spare oneself the repetition of the commands. One will find, in the test case ZZZZ121a.comm, an example of a Python loop. 5.2 Study on the HP rotor Context: This study was carried out in the AMA department in 2006 within the framework of the Project Lifetime of the Steam Turbines of the nuclear fleet. Very briefly, the point is to locate the zones of maximum stress encountered on the HP rotor (figure 5.2-a) of a turbine and to evaluate numerically the stress level, in order to check whether there exists a risk of crack initiation by stress-corrosion cracking. In order to reach a conclusion on the risk of cracking by SCC, several modellings were carried out, one of them a 2D axisymmetric modelling of the complete rotor with an aspect concerning the quality of the mesh. The reader is referred to the document [bib12] for further information on this study; our objective here is to point out only the mesh aspect. Approach of the study: This study is concerned with the maximum stresses obtained numerically, in order to compare them with threshold stresses coming from experimental tests. The analysis of the Von Mises stresses is required in the first place, because this type of stress is always an upper bound with respect to the relevant components of the stress tensor. Thus, when the Von Mises stresses are lower than the threshold stresses, one considers that the risk of cracking by SCC is unlikely in the absence of impurities. However, when the Von Mises stresses are higher than the threshold of cracking by SCC, it becomes necessary to analyse more finely the maximum values of the stress tensor, as well as the principal stresses, in order to evaluate the margins with respect to the risk of cracking by SCC. Modelling: The constitutive behaviour of the material is elastic. The loading is of centrifugal-force type due to the rotation. The analysis is carried out with the command STAT_NON_LINE. The initial mesh is free and very fine in the zones of curvature, in order to obtain stress values that are as reliable as possible. The elements are quadrilaterals of degree two. The mesh comprises 71037 elements and 217198 nodes. Result: One looks here at the zones where the Von Mises stress is maximum. The zone most heavily loaded in stress is situated near the coupling on the forward-bearing side, in the zone of curvature of the groove between the coupling and the rest of the rotor (zone A). The other zones loaded in stress are situated at the junction of the blade attachments on the rotor (zones B and C, for example). Blades Figure 5.2-a: partial view of the rotor and of the blades Mesh adaptation: In order to validate the stress level obtained in the most heavily loaded zone (zone A) and in two of the rotor/blade junction zones (zones B and C), a mesh adaptation is carried out with the absolute term of the residual error indicator and a criterion in percentage of finite element. Two results are presented in what follows: - one without boundary tracking: cutting of 5% of the elements whose error is the greatest, - and the other with boundary tracking: cutting of 2% of the elements. The mesh of the boundary makes it possible, by its fine discretisation, to define very precisely the curved zones of the geometry. This phenomenon is associated with a lack of discretisation of this curved zone, which creates a geometrical discontinuity. Without boundary tracking, the remeshing does not make it possible to correct this problem and even accentuates the geometrical discontinuity, which has the effect of increasing the stress. With boundary tracking, one notes that: - The stress at the level of zone A does not evolve. This constancy is to be linked to the reduction in the number of mesh cells taken into account in the course of the refinement. Indeed, the results obtained around zone A not forming part of the 2% of mesh cells presenting the largest error, no refinement is carried out in this zone and the stress then remains constant. The value to be taken into account for the maximum stress is therefore that presented in table 6.1-a. - Boundary tracking makes it possible to stabilise the Von Mises stresses in zones B and C. Conclusion: This analysis shows two important lessons. Firstly, it is risky to trust, without a critical look, the results of an analysis carried out on a single mesh. One sees here that, with the initial mesh, although fairly fine to the eye, the values obtained are far from being definitive. By modifying the mesh, they evolve until they stabilise. One must not deprive oneself of these additional analyses, all the more so as setting them up is simple and carrying them out is automated. Next, one notes the interest of carrying out boundary tracking if the geometry presents curved zones. 5.3 Beam in bending in elasticity This example was used during training courses. The loading is applied in 2 steps: - the first consists of a purely mechanical loading (pressure on the zone with arrows on the diagram), with a loading phase followed by an unloading phase; - the second consists of a transient thermal loading (exchange condition on the lower and upper parts of the structure). Remeshing strategy and list of time instants: The loading is discretised according to a list of time instants; the question then arises: what strategy should one adopt with respect to remeshing? Indeed, depending on the case treated, one can: - remesh at each computational step: the mesh is then adapted to each computational step individually. One must then project the fields from one mesh onto the other; - remesh only once, at the end of the analysis, and start the analysis again from the beginning with the new mesh. The first strategy is to be adopted in the case where the refinement zones evolve a great deal; we shall see an example of it in the following thermal analysis; the second may be adopted in the case where the refinement zones evolve little, as in this mechanical case, where the point is to follow the growth of a plastic zone. Mechanical analysis: For the mechanical analysis, one therefore adopts the following strategy: - computation of the whole list of time instants; - remeshing; - repetition of (1 & 2) until a satisfactory result is obtained. u2.08.03 User's guide for the linear solvers u2.08.03 User's guide for the linear solvers 1 Purpose The linear solvers are in fact omnipresent in the course of the operators of Code_Aster , because they are often buried in the deepest part of other numerical algorithms: non-linear scheme, integration in time, modal analysis, etc. They often consume the major part of the CPU time and of the memory. The choice and the complete parameter setting of the required linear solver are carried out via the factor keyword SOLVEUR. It is present in most of the analysis commands (STAT_NON_LINE, THER_LINEAIRE, CALC_MODES, etc.). This user's guide is complementary to the User documentation of the keyword SOLVEUR[U4.50.01]. It aims to be an intermediate link between the "simple" keyword documentation and the theoretical documentation (each solver is backed by a Reference documentation). The first part of this note gives an overall view of the different linear solvers available, of their scope of use and of their average performances in terms of robustness and of CPU/memory consumptions. The following chapter groups together a few pieces of advice for making the best use of the parameters of SOLVEUR according to the case in hand: the size of the system, its numerical properties, the CPU and memory consumptions... To finish, certain parameters of SOLVEUR are detailed in order to help the user in an advanced use of this functionality of the code. The related issues of improvement of the performances (RAM/CPU) of an analysis and of the use of parallelism are also briefly addressed. They are the subject of specific guides, respectively U1.03.03 and U2.08.06. 2 The different linear solvers available These linear solvers are in fact omnipresent in the course of the operators of Code_Aster , because they are often buried in the deepest part of other numerical algorithms: non-linear scheme, integration in time, modal analysis, etc. They often consume the major part of the CPU time and of the memory. The choice and the complete parameter setting of the required linear solver are carried out via the factor keyword SOLVEUR. It is present in most of the analysis commands (STAT_NON_LINE, THER_LINEAIRE, CALC_MODES...). This keyword makes it possible to choose between the two classes of solver: the direct ones and the iterative ones. Concerning the direct ones, one has the classical algorithm of "Gauss" (SOLVEUR/METHODE='LDLT'), a multifrontal factorisation ('MULT_FRONT') and an external one ('MUMPS'). For the iterative ones, it is possible to call a conjugate gradient ('GCPC') or certain tools of the public library PETSc ('PETSC'). Only MULT_FRONT, MUMPS and PETSC are parallelised . The first in OpenMP, the other two in MPI and in OpenMP (hybrid parallelism). But all the solvers are compatible with a parallel treatment ( via MPI) of the elementary computations and of the assemblies. And this, whether these treatments are initiated just before the use of the linear solver proper, or in another operator (for example of pre/post-processing). Let us detail a little the functioning of each of them: | Direct solvers | | | --- | --- | | /'MUMPS' | Direct solver of multifrontal type with pivoting. This solver is obtained by calling the external product MUMPS , developed by CERFACS/IRIT/INRIA/CNRS (cf. Copyright §4). The matrix storage outside the solver is MORSE. On entry to the solver, one carries out the conversion to the internal format of MUMPS: i , j , {K}_{ij} , centralised or distributed. For Code_Aster , its principal interest lies in its capacity to pivot rows and/or columns of the matrix during the factorisation in the event of a small pivot. This possibility is useful (indeed indispensable) for the models leading to matrices which are not positive definite (apart from the boundary conditions); for example, the 'mixed' elements having degrees of freedom of 'Lagrange' type (incompressible elements...). This method is parallelised in distributed memory (MPI) and in shared memory (OpenMP). It can be executed on several processors ( via the Astk interface, menu Options/Options de lancement/ncpus&mpi_nbcpu&mpi_nbnoeud). In MPI parallel (mpi_nbcpu&mpi_nbnoeud) , MUMPS naturally distributes its data (matrix, factorised form...) among the cores of the different computation nodes allocated. This greatly accelerates the analyses and makes it possible to reduce the memory occupation necessary, per MPI process, in order to launch the analysis. This RAM consumption can be reduced still further via the parameters GESTION_MEMOIRE or RENUM of MUMPS. In terms of memory, the bottleneck may then lie at the level of the JEVEUX space. In order to reduce the latter, one can distribute the Aster matrix (MATR_ASSE) via the option MATR_DISTRIBUEE. MUMPS also relies on a second level of nested parallelism within the MPI parallelism ( hybrid parallelism ), based on OpenMP. This second level of parallelism is activated mainly in the calls to the underlying mathematical libraries (BLAS, LAPACK). Unlike MPI, it is a shared-memory parallelism and is therefore limited to the cores of a single computation node (ncpus). In order to accelerate large studies (N at least > 2.106 degrees of freedom) one can in addition activate acceleration/compression options of MUMPS (from v5.1.0 onwards) via the keywords ACCELERATION/LOW_RANK_SEUIL. | | | | | /'MULT_FRONT' | Direct solver of multifrontal type developed internally at EDF R&D . The matrix storage is MORSE (or 'CSC' for 'Compressed Sparse Column') and therefore rules out any pivoting. This method is parallelised in shared memory (OpenMP) and can be executed on several processors ( via the Astk interface, menu Options/Options de lancement/ncpus). The initial matrix is stored in a single JEVEUX object and its factorised form is distributed over several, so it can be offloaded partially and automatically to disk. | | /'LDLT' | Direct solver with Crout factorisation by blocks (without pivoting) developed internally at EDF R&D . The matrix storage outside the solver is MORSE. On entry to the solver, one carries out the conversion to the internal format of LDLT: 'skyline' ('SKYLINE'). One has a completely parameterisable paging of the memory (the matrix is decomposed into blocks managed independently in memory and offloaded to disk as one goes along), which makes it possible to treat large cases but which is paid for by costly disk accesses. Moreover, this solver makes it possible to factorise the matrix only partially. This possibility is 'historical'. It makes it possible to factorise the matrix in several 'goes' (several jobs), or even to modify on the fly the last rows of this factorised form. Today, one does not really see the interest of this functionality except for certain methods (said to be discrete) of frictional contact, in which one has deliberately placed, in the last rows of the matrix, the terms concerning the nodes liable to be in contact. Thus, as the pairing iterations proceed and the relations between these nodes change, one erases and then recomputes only these last contributions of the factorised form. It is a typical example in which the clever use of a fairly crude algorithm can bring major gains (in time). | | | | | Iterative solvers | | | /'GCPC' | Iterative solver of conjugate-gradient type with preconditioning \mathit{ILU}(k) or based on a single-precision factorised form ( via MUMPS). The storage of the matrix is then MORSE. With the incomplete Cholesky, the initial matrix and its incomplete factorised form are each stored in a single JEVEUX object. With the single-precision factorised form, the preconditioner is much more costly (in CPU/RAM), but it is carried out in single precision and its computation can be shared over several resolutions (problem of multiple right-hand sides type, e.g. STAT_NON_LINE). | | | | | /'PETSC' | Iterative solvers coming from the external library PETSc (Argonne Laboratory). The matrix storage outside the solver is MORSE. On entry to the solver, one carries out the conversion to the internal format of PETSc: 'CSR' for 'Compressed Sparse Row'. PETSc allocates blocks of contiguous rows per processor. This method is parallelised in distributed memory (MPI) and can be executed on several processors ( via the Astk interface, menu Options/Options de lancement/mpi_nbcpu&mpi_nbnoeud). When PETSc uses a preconditioner based on MUMPS (PRECOND='LDLT_SP'), it also benefits from the potentially hybrid parallelism of the direct solver. But the best accelerations of PETSc occur rather by favouring the first level of parallelism, MPI.
