The latter is therefore inaccessible to users (without a software overload). Among these, one finds certain resolutions of the discrete methods of frictional contact (reserved for LDLT), the searches for rigid-body modes in modal analysis, the computations of interface modes (reserved for MUMPS or for LDLT)... Each time, functional reasons or reasons of performance explain this not very transparent choice. OOC stands for 'Out-Of-Core'. That is to say that one is going to free RAM by offloading part of the objects to disk. This makes it possible to supplement the system swap and to treat much larger problems. Depending on the algorithmics, these additional disk accesses may be penalising. The opposite mode of management is "In-Core" (IC). All the computer objects remain in RAM. This limits the size of the problems accessible (to within the system swap) but favours speed. 3 A few pieces of advice on use If one wishes 2 to change linear solver or to adapt its parameter setting, several questions must be addressed: What is the type of problem which one wishes to solve? What are the numerical properties of the linear systems encountered? etc. One lists below, and in a non-exhaustive manner, several questions which it is interesting to ask oneself when one seeks to optimise the linear-solver aspects. Of course, certain questions (and answers) are cumulative and may therefore apply simultaneously. In brief: The default method remains the internal multifrontal solver MULT_FRONT . But in order to benefit fully from the CPU and RAM gains which parallelism provides, or in order to solve a problem which is numerically often difficult (X-FEM, incompressibility, THM), one recommends the use of the external product MUMPS . The larger the problem, the more one advises the use of MPI parallelism and of the acceleration/compression techniques (ACCELERATION/LOW_RANK_SEUIL). If, in spite of everything, on a given computer platform, the problem does not fit into memory, recourse to the iterative solvers of PETSC may be a solution (if their functional scopes permit it). Let us note that by default they use MUMPS "under the bonnet" as a preconditioner (option PRE_COND='LDLT_SP'). In order to go further in the savings of memory space , one can also degrade the preconditioning (the analysis will probably be longer) by choosing one of the other preconditioners of PETSC ('LDLT_INC'...). In non-linear analysis, in order to gain time , one can also play on several relaxation parameters (SYME in the non-symmetric case) or of interactions between "non-linear solver/linear solver" (REAC_PRECOND, NEWTON_KRYLOV..). For well-conditioned non-linear problems (thermal...), recourse to a "relaxed" MUMPS (MIXER_PRECISION/FILTRAGE_MATRICE) can bring very significant memory gains. Likewise, in linear as in non-linear analysis, with PETSC without preconditioner (PRE_COND='SANS'). For more details and more advice on the use of the linear solvers, one may consult the user's guide U4.50.01 and the associated reference documentations [R6...]. The related issues of improvement of the performances (RAM/CPU) of an analysis and of the use of parallelism are also the subject of detailed guides: U1.03.03 and U2.08.06. What is the type of problem to be solved? - Resolution of numerous systems with the same matrix (problem of multiple right-hand sides type 3) ⇒ solvers MULT_FRONT or MUMPS (if possible by deactivating RESI_RELA and with GESTION_MEMOIRE='IN_CORE'). - Standard parametric analysis in linear ⇒ a first trial with MUMPS, leaving the parameters at their default values, then all the other runs by switching off RESI_RELA or with POSTTRAITEMENTS='MINI'. - Parametric analysis in non-linear with a well-conditioned matrix ⇒ a first trial with MUMPS, playing on the relaxation parameters (FILTRAGE_MATRICE/MIXER_PRECISION, or SYME if one is in the non-symmetric case). Then, if an optimised operating point (CPU/RAM consumptions) has been found, use it for all the other runs. One can also try MUMPS but, this time, as a single-precision preconditioner of PETSC/GCPC (LDLT_SP). The interest is then to update it only periodically (REAC_PRECOND). What are its numerical properties? - Well-conditioned linear system 4 ( 5.10 6 degrees of freedom )? - Robust solver ⇒ solver MUMPS with the previous memory optimisations and the low-rank compressions (ACCELERATION/LOW_RANK_SEUIL). - Solvers of "last resort" ⇒ iterative solvers (with a low level of preconditioning). How can one optimise the global performances of my analysis? - User's guide U1.03.03. How can one carry out, calibrate and optimise a parallel analysis? - User's guide U2.08.06. Or if, quite simply, one must play on this parameter because the analysis does not fit on the software platform chosen, or does so with consumptions in time and in memory incompatible with the constraints of the study. This is the case, for example, in a thermomechanical chaining when the material characteristics do not depend on the temperature or, in non-linear analysis, when one updates the tangent matrix only infrequently. Either the typology of the analysis provides this information (one knows, for example, that this is often the case for thermal analysis), or one obtains it otherwise (for example, by carrying out a preliminary test with MUMPS and by activating the keyword RESI_RELA+INFO=2). Convex non-linear analyses, a prospective analysis, or an analysis the quality of whose mechanical solutions of interest is mastered by other means. 4 Recommendations on the external products In order to solve the numerous linear systems which it produces, Code_Aster can rely on external products. This section documents the use of these products within the framework of Code_Aster , referring to a classical use and installation. Figure 5.1.1._ Example of the gains in time provided by the MPI parallelism of Code_Aster v13.0, and by the hybrid parallelism, MPI+OpenMP (+ low-rank compressions, cf. U4.50.01), of Code_Aster v13.1. Comparisons carried out on the performance test cases perf008d and perf009d and on the centralised machine Aster5. One can gain in time (with MPI parallelism and with OpenMP parallelism) as well as in memory (only via MPI). These gains vary according to the functionalities called upon, their parameter settings, the data set and the software platform used: cf. figure 5.1.1. In Code_Aster, by default, the analysis is sequential. But one can activate different parallelisation strategies . These depend on the computational step considered and on the parameter setting chosen. They are often cumulative, or can be chained. - One has three broad classes of problem which can be parallelised, the second being the most common: - either the simulation can be organised as several independent sub-analyses (cf. §5.2), - or this is not the case, but: - it remains dominated by linear or non-linear analyses (operators STAT/DYNA/THER_NON_LINE, MECA_STATIQUE... cf. §5.3), - it remains dominated by modal analyses which can be divided into frequency sub-bands (INFO_MODE/CALC_MODES+'BANDE', cf. §5.4). In order to have an estimate of the time spent by an operator , and therefore of the predominant steps of an analysis, one can activate the keyword MESURE_TEMPS of the commands DEBUT/POURSUITE (cf. U1.03.03) on a typical study (possibly shortened or watered down). In every case, one will advise dividing the largest analyses into different steps , in order to separate those which are purely computational [6]_ , from those concerning displays , post-processings and manipulations of fields [7]_ . 5.2 Independent analyses When the simulation can be organised as different independent Aster sub-analyses (cf. figure 5.2.1) , the Astk tool [U1.04.00] offers a suitable functionality (cf. U2.08.07). The latter distributes these sub-analyses over different machine resources and retrieves their results. It is a completely "computer-science" parallel scheme. The limit being, for the moment, that all these unit analyses must each be able to run sequentially on the machine chosen (which can sometimes pose problems of memory resources, cf. U4.50.01). Figure 5.2.1._: Parallelism of the independent analyses. 5.3 Parallelisation of linear systems - When this simulation cannot be decomposed into similar and independent Aster sub-analyses, but nevertheless remains dominated by linear or non-linear analyses (operators STAT/DYNA/THER_NON_LINE, MECA_STATIQUE... cf. §5.3), one can organise a specific parallel scheme. It is founded on the distribution of the tasks and of the data structures involved in the manipulations of linear systems . For it is these steps of construction and of resolution of linear systems which are often the most demanding in computation time and in memory resources. They are present in most of the operators, because they are buried in the deepest part of other, "more application-oriented", algorithms: non-linear solver, modal and vibratory analysis, time-stepping scheme... The first step of the parallel scheme concerns the distribution of the finite elements of the model over all the MPI processes. Each MPI process will therefore manage only the treatments and the data associated with the elements for which it is responsible. The construction of the linear systems in Code_Aster (elementary computations, assemblies) is then accelerated. One often speaks of " parallelism in space ". It is a parallel scheme of a rather "computer-science" kind. Once these portions of linear system have been built (cf. figure 5.3.1), two cases arise: - either the following treatment is naturally sequential , and therefore all the MPI processes must have access to the global information. To this end one gathers these pieces of linear systems together, and the following step will therefore be neither accelerated nor see its memory consumptions fall. It is most often the end of an operator, a post-processing, or a linear solver which is not parallelised in MPI (MULT_FRONT, LDLT, GCPC). - or the following treatment accepts MPI parallelism ; this is then mainly the HPC linear solvers MUMPS and PETSC. The parallel flow of data built upstream is then transmitted to them (after a few adaptations). These packages of linear algebra then reorganise, internally, their own parallel schemes (with a more algebraic view). One then speaks of a parallel scheme of a rather "numerical" kind. This combination of "computer-science parallelism", at the level of the assembly of the linear system, and of "numerical parallelism", at the level of its resolution, the two of them via MPI, is the most common combination. Figure 5.3.1._ Organisation of the MPI parallel scheme for the construction and the resolution of linear systems. Notes: - Let us note that, at the end of the cycle "construction of a linear system – resolution of that system", whatever scenario is implemented (sequential linear solver or MPI-parallel linear solver), the solution vector is then transmitted, in its entirety, to all the MPI processes. The cycle can thus continue whatever the following configuration. Moreover, one can superimpose upon this MPI parallelism, or substitute for it, (it works on all platforms) another level of parallelism, managed this time by the OpenMP language . The latter is however limited to the fractions of a machine which physically share the same memory (multi-core PC, or nodes of a computation server). It does not make it possible to lower the memory consumptions, but on the other hand it accelerates certain types of computation, and does so with a finer granularity than that of MPI: it provides a better acceleration even if the flow of data/treatments is not very large. It is a parallel scheme of "computer-science" kind, which intervenes mainly in the basic operations of linear-algebra algorithms ( via , for example, the BLAS library and certain steps of the MUMPS solver). This parallelism may: - either be cumulated with the MPI parallelism of MUMPS, by accelerating the computations within each MPI process. One then obtains a hybrid parallel scheme with 2 levels. - or be substituted for the MPI parallelism, by accelerating the resolution of the linear system with MULT_FRONT. 5.4 Distribution of modal analyses - When the simulation cannot be decomposed into independent Aster analyses, but nevertheless remains dominated by generalised modal analyses (operators INFO_MODE and CALC_MODES), one can organise a specific parallel scheme (cf. 5.4.1). Fig ure 5.4.1._ Organisation of the MPI parallel scheme for the distribution of the modal analyses and for the resolutions of the associated linear systems. It is founded on the distribution of independent modal analyses : each one being in charge of a frequency sub-band. This parallel scheme, of a purely "computer-science" kind, provides gains in time only (unless one cumulates it with MUMPS). It can however be mixed with the previous parallel schemes: - chaining between different operators: MPI parallelism of the construction of linear matrices (in, for example, CALC_MATR_ELEM) and modal resolution in CALC_MODES. - cumulation , within CALC_MODES, by activating the MPI parallelism (or even the OpenMP parallelism) of the direct solver MUMPS. One then obtains a hybrid parallel scheme with 2 or 3 levels. Possibly of different types (category no. 2 or no. 3 cited previously) and which will gain by being carried out in parallel. Which will often be faster sequentially, because of the risks of congestion during memory accesses. 6 Performance indicators of an analysis For further information one may consult the user's guide U1.03.03: 'Performance indicator of an analysis (time/memory)'. During a Code_Aster simulation, default displays trace, in the message file (.mess), certain dimensioning characteristics of the analysis. One finds in particular, for each Aster operator: - The characteristics of the analysis (number of nodes, of equations, of Lagranges, size of the matrix...), - The JEVEUX floor memory (in order to pass into Out-Of-Core) and the optimal memory (in order to pass into In-Core), - The memory required by certain external products (e.g. MUMPS), - The CPU times, system times and "user" (elapsed) times, - The breakdown of the times consumed according to the steps of the analysis (elementary computation, assembly, resolution of the linear system, offloading to disk). This last description of the times consumed can be set out at different levels of detail (synthetic printout, detailed printout, and printout detailed per computational increment) via the parameter MESURE_TEMPS/NIVE_DETAIL of the commands DEBUT/POURSUITE. In parallel mode, one adds the mean value, over all the processors, of the times consumed, as well as their standard deviation. 7 Complementary information on the keywords The meaning of the different parameters of the keyword SOLVEUR is the subject of the User documentation U4.50.01. The different cases of detection of singularity, and the associated advice. 7.2 MUMPS solver (METHODE='MUMPS') 7.2.1 General points The MUMPS solver , currently developed by CNRS/INPT-IRIT/INRIA/CERFACS , is a direct solver of multifrontal type, parallelised (in MPI) and robust, because it makes it possible to pivot the rows and columns of the matrix during the numerical factorisation. MUMPS supplies an estimate of the quality of the solution \text{u} (cf. keyword RESI_RELA) of the matrix problem \text{K}\text{u}=\text{f} via the notions of relative forward error ('relative forward error') and of backward error ('backward error'). This 'backward error', \eta (\text{K},\text{f}) , measures the behaviour of the resolution algorithm (when all goes well, this real number is close to machine precision, that is 10-15 in double precision). MUMPS also computes an estimate of the conditioning of the matrix, \kappa (\text{K}) , which reflects the good behaviour of the problem to be solved (a real number lying between 104 for a well-conditioned problem and 1020 for a very poorly conditioned one). The product of the two is an upper bound on the relative error in the solution ('relative forward error'): \frac{\parallel \delta u\parallel }{\parallel u\parallel } {\mathrm{K}}_{0}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{K}& \mathrm{blocage}\\ \mathrm{blocage}& 0\end{array}\right]\begin{array}{c}\mathrm{u}\\ \mathrm{lagr}\end{array} but with its doubly dualised form {\mathrm{K}}_{2} > {K}_{2}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}K& \mathrm{blocage}& \mathrm{blocage}\\ \mathrm{blocage}& -1& 1\\ \mathrm{blocage}& 1& -1\end{array}\right]\begin{array}{}u\\ {\mathrm{lagr}}_{1}\\ {\mathrm{lagr}}_{2}\end{array} Whence an overhead in memory and in computation. Since MUMPS has pivoting capabilities, this choice of dualisation of the boundary conditions can be called into question. By initialising this keyword to 'OUI', one no longer takes into account more than one Lagrange, the other being a spectator [12]_ . Whence a working matrix {\mathrm{K}}_{1} , simply dualised > {K}_{1}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}K& \mathrm{blocage}& 0\\ \mathrm{blocage}& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& -1\end{array}\right]\begin{array}{}u\\ {\mathrm{lagr}}_{1}\\ {\mathrm{lagr}}_{2}\end{array} which is smaller, because the off-diagonal terms of the rows and of the columns associated with these spectator Lagranges are then initialised to zero. Conversely , with the value 'NON', MUMPS receives the usual dualised matrices. For problems comprising numerous Lagranges (up to 20% of the total number of unknowns) , activating this parameter often pays (smaller matrix). But when this number explodes (>20%) , the process may be counterproductive. The gains achieved on the matrix are cancelled out by the size of the factorised form and, above all, by the number of delayed pivots which MUMPS must carry out. Imposing ELIM_LAGR2='NON' may then be very advantageous (for example: a gain of 40% in CPU time on the test case mac3c01). One also switches off this parameter temporarily when one wishes to compute the determinant of the matrix , because otherwise its value is falsified by these modifications of the blocking terms. The user is warned of this automatic modification of the parameter setting by a dedicated message (visible only with INFO=2). 7.2.5 Parameter RESI_RELA Default value = -1.d0 in non-linear and in modal analysis, 1.d-6 in linear analysis. This parameter is deactivated by a negative value. By specifying a strictly positive value for this keyword (e.g. 10-6), the user indicates that he wishes to test the validity of the solution of each linear system solved by MUMPS against this value. This cautious approach is advised when the solution is not itself corrected by another algorithmic process (Newton algorithm, detection of singularity…), in short in the linear operators THER_LINEAIRE and MECA_STATIQUE. In non-linear analysis, the singularity-detection criterion and the Newton correction are sufficient safeguards. One can therefore switch off this control process (this is what is done by default via the value -1). In modal analysis, this detection of singularity is an algorithmic tool for capturing the eigenmodes. This detection is the subject of a dedicated parameter setting, proper to each method. If the relative error in the solution estimated by MUMPS is greater than resi, the code stops in ERREUR_FATALE, stating the nature of the problem and the values incriminated. Activating this keyword also initiates an iterative-refinement process, whose objective is to improve the solution obtained. This post-processing benefits from a particular parameter setting (keyword POSTTRAITEMENTS). It is the solution resulting from this iterative improvement process which is tested by RESI_RELA. Note: - This control process implies the estimation of the matrix conditioning and a few forward-backward substitutions of the iterative-refinement post-processing. It may therefore be fairly costly, notably in OOC, because of the RAM/disk I/O during the forward-backward substitutions (up to 40%). When sufficient safeguards have been put in place, one can switch it off by initialising resi to a negative value. 7.2.6 Parameters for optimising the memory management (MUMPS and/or JEVEUX) In general, a large part of the computation times and of the RAM peaks of a Code_Aster simulation is attributable to the linear solvers. The linear solver MUMPS is no exception, but the richness of its internal parameter setting and its close coupling with Code_Aster leave the user a certain flexibility. In particular as regards the management of the RAM consumption. In fact, during a memory peak occurring for the resolution of a linear system via MUMPS, the RAM may be decomposed into 5 parts: - The JEVEUX objects other than the matrix, - The JEVEUX objects associated with the matrix (generally the data structures MATR_ASSE and NUME_DDL), - The MUMPS objects used to store the matrix, - The MUMPS objects used to store the factorised form, - The auxiliary MUMPS objects (pointers, vectors, communication buffers...). Roughly speaking, part 4 is the most bulky. In particular, it is much larger than parts 2 and 3 (a factor of at least 30, due to the fill-in phenomenon, cf. R6.02.03). The latter are equivalent in size, but one of them occupies the space allotted to JEVEUX, while the other lives in the complementary space allocated to the job by the task manager. As for the other two parts, 1 and 5, they often play only a marginal role [13]_ . In order to reduce these memory consumptions, the Aster user has several levers (cumulative, most of the time): - Centralised parallel analysis on n cores (part 4 divided by n ) or distributed (parts 3 and 4 divided by n ). - Distributed parallel analysis + MATR_DISTRIBUEE (limited scope of use): parts 3 and 4 divided by n , part 2 divided by a little less than n . - Activation of the OOC of MUMPS (keyword GESTION_MEMOIRE='OUT-OF-CORE'): part 4 is reduced by 2/3. It being understood that, before each call to the 'analysis + numerical factorisation' cycle of MUMPS, one systematically offloads to disk the largest JEVEUX objects of part 2. Advice: In view of the preceding points, an obvious tactic consists in running the analysis in distributed parallel mode (the default value) rather than sequentially. Centralised parallel mode bringing nothing from this point of view [14]_ , it is not to be considered. If, however, one remains tied to a particular mode, here is the advice associated with each: - In sequential mode: the principal gains will come from activating GESTION_MEMOIRE='OUT_OF_CORE' (on problems of reasonable size). - In distributed parallel mode: beyond about ten processors, OUT_OF_CORE no longer provides much gain. MATR_DISTRIBUEE can then help in certain situations. If these strategies do not bring sufficient gains, one can also try, in non-linear analysis (at the price of possible losses of accuracy and/or of time), to relax the resolution of the linear system (FILTRAGE_MATRICE, MIXER_PRECISION), or even that of the encompassing process (elastic tangent matrix, reduction of the projection space in modal analysis...). If the matrix is well conditioned and if one does not need to detect the singularities of the problem (hence not a modal analysis, not buckling...), one can also try an iterative solver (GCPC/PETSC+LDLT_SP). | Solution | Gain in RAM | Overhead in time | Loss of accuracy | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Parallelism | +++ | On the contrary, a gain in time | None | | GESTION_MEMOIRE= 'OUT_OF_CORE' | ++ | Low, except if there are numerous forward-backward substitutions | None | | MATR_DISTRIBUEE (limited scope) | | None | None | | Relaxation of the resolutions FILTRAGE_MATRICE, MIXER_PRECISION (limited scope) | ++ | Variable | Variable. Overview of the different solutions making it possible to optimise the memory during an analysis with MUMPS . Keyword GESTION_MEMOIRE =' OUT_OF_CORE' In order to activate or deactivate the OOC capabilities of MUMPS, which will then offload entirely to disk the real part of the blocks of the factorised form managed by each processor. This functionality can of course be cumulated with parallelism, whence a greater variety of modes of operation, so as to adapt to the contingencies of execution. OOC, just like parallelism, contributes to reducing the RAM required per processor. But of course (somewhat) to the detriment of CPU time: the price to be paid for the I/O in the one case, for the MPI communications in the other. Warning: During a parallel analysis, if the number of processors is large, the size of the MUMPS objects which can be offloaded to disk becomes small. Passing into OOC may then prove counterproductive (a small gain in RAM and an overhead in time) with respect to the IC mode, which is the default parameter setting. This phenomenon occurs all the earlier as the size of the problem is small, and it is all the more noticeable as one carries out many forward-backward substitutions [15]_ in the solver. Roughly [16]_ , below 50.103 degrees of freedom per processor, and if one has enough RAM (3 or 4 GB) per processor, one can doubtless switch to IC. Notes: - For the moment, during an execution of MUMPS in OOC, only the vectors of real numbers containing the factorised form are (entirely) offloaded to disk. The vectors of integers accompanying this data structure (of equally important size) do not yet benefit from this mechanism. On the other hand, this offloading takes place only after the analysis phase of MUMPS. In short, on very large cases (several million degrees of freedom), even with this OOC, memory contingencies may prevent the analysis. One exits, in principle, with a documented ERREUR_FATALE. - In MUMPS, so as to optimise the memory occupation, most of the integers are coded in INTEGER 4 . Only the integers corresponding to a memory address are transcribed into INTEGER 8 . This makes it possible to address problems of larger size, on 64-bit architectures. this coexistence of short and long integers, in order to optimise the memory space, has been extended to certain large JEVEUX objects. - When Code_Aster has finished assembling the working matrix, before "handing over" to MUMPS, it offloads to disk the largest JEVEUX objects linked to the resolution of the linear system ( SMDI/HC, DEEQ, NUEAQ, VALM. ..). And this in order to leave as much RAM as possible for MUMPS. In GESTION_MEMOIRE='AUTO' mode, if this memory space is not sufficient for MUMPS to operate in IC, one completes this partial release of JEVEUX objects by a general release of all the releasable objects (that is to say, those not open for reading/writing). This operation can provide large gains when one is "dragging" in memory many peripheral JEVEUX objects (projection of fields, a long transient...). On the other hand, this massive offloading can waste time. In particular in parallel mode, because of congestion of the accesses between cores and RAM. Keyword MATR_DISTRIBUEE This parameter can be used in the operators MECA_STATIQUE, STAT_NON_LINE, DYNA_NON_LINE, THER_LINEAIRE and THER_NON_LINE with AFFE_CHAR_MECA or AFFE_CHAR_CINE . It is active only in distributed parallel ( AFFE_MODELE/ DISTRIBUTION/ METHODE equal to something other than CENTRALISE ) . This functionality can of course be cumulated with GESTION_MEMOIRE='OUT_OF_CORE', whence a greater variety of modes of operation, so as to adapt to the contingencies of execution. In parallel mode, when one distributes the JEVEUX data upstream of MUMPS, one does not necessarily recut the data structures concerned. With the option MATR_DISTRIBUEE='NON', all the distributed objects are allocated and initialised to the same size (the same value as in sequential mode). On the other hand, each processor will modify only the parts of the JEVEUX objects for which it is responsible. This scenario is particularly well suited to the distributed parallel mode of MUMPS (the default mode), because this product gathers these incomplete data flows together internally. Parallelism then makes it possible, besides the gains in computation time, to reduce the memory space required by the MUMPS resolution, but not that necessary for the construction of the problem in JEVEUX. This is not a problem so long as the RAM space for JEVEUX remains very much smaller than that required by MUMPS. Since JEVEUX stores mainly the matrix, and MUMPS its factorised form (generally tens of times larger), the RAM bottleneck of the analysis is theoretically on MUMPS. But as soon as one uses a few tens of processors in MPI and/or one activates OOC, since MUMPS distributes this factorised form per processor and offloads these pieces to disk, the "ball is back in JEVEUX's court". Whence the option MATR_DISTRIBUEE, which resizes the matrix down to just the non-zero terms for which the processor is responsible. The JEVEUX space required then decreases with the number of processors, and falls below the RAM necessary for MUMPS. The results of figure 7.2-1 illustrate this gain in parallel on two studies: an RIS pump and the Epicure vessel. Figure 7.2-1: Evolution of the RAM consumptions (in GB) as a function of the number of processors, for Code_Aster v11.0 ( JEVEUX standard, MATR_DISTRIBUE='NON' , and distributed, resp. 'OUI' ) and for MUMPS OOC. Analyses carried out on an RIS pump (perf009) and on the vessel of the Epicure study (perf011). Notes: - One treats here the data resulting from an elementary computation (RESU_ELEM and CHAM_ELEM) or from a matrix assembly (MATR_ASSE). The assembled vectors (CHAM_NO) are not distributed, because the memory gains induced would be small and, on the other hand, since they intervene in the evaluation of numerous algorithmic criteria, that would imply too many additional communications. - In MATR_DISTRIBUE mode, in order to make the junction between the piece of MATR_ASSE local to the processor and the global MATR_ASSE (which one does not build), one adds an indirection vector in the form of a local NUME_DDL. 7.2.7 Parameters for reducing the run time via different acceleration/compression techniques Mots-clés ACCELERATION et LOW_RANK_SEUIL These two keywords activate and drive acceleration/compression techniques of MUMPS . These can significantly reduce the run time of large studies, and this without restriction of the scope of use, and with potentially little or no impact on the accuracy, the robustness and the global behaviour of the simulation. They are generally of interest only on problems of large size (N at least > 2.106 degrees of freedom) . The gains observed on a few performance test cases and Aster studies vary from 20% to 80% (examples in figures 7.2-2/7.2-3). They increase with the size of the problem and with its massive character, and they are complementary to those provided by parallelism and by the renumberer. One completes here the description of these functionalities given in the document U4.50.01. When one has chosen an acceleration based on 'low-rank' compressions (values 'LR' and 'LR+' of the keyword ACCELERATION), one must define the rate of these compressions. This rate is given by the keyword LOW_RANK_SEUIL. It drives the truncation criterion of the numerical compression algorithm [17]_ . Roughly , the larger this figure is, for example 10-12 or 10-9, the greater the compression will be, and therefore the more interesting the gains in time can be. However, if this value is too large (for example >10-9), the factorised matrix may be too approximate, and the solution vector may thus prove too inaccurate! In a non-linear process this is not always so serious, because the encompassing Newton algorithm can correct the aim! On the other hand, in linear analysis, or in order to treat numerically difficult problems (incompressible finite elements, X-FEM...), one must then make sure that the resolution does indeed include the corrective post-processing procedure (cf. iterative refinement, keyword POSTTRAITEMENTS). As it happens, in this situation, or when one seeks to strike a compromise between performance and accuracy, the value POSTTRAITEMENTS='MINI' (+ RESI_RELA 0). To be exhaustive, let us note that the real value of this keyword may also be zero — the compression is then carried out to within machine precision — or become negative — the compression then uses the relative threshold > ∥\mathrm{K}∥\times \mid \text{lr\_seuil}\mid The first value makes it possible to benefit from a little compression with no impact on the accuracy (for functional tests or for expert assessments). One plots, as a function of the number of MPI processes activated, the elapsed times consumed by the whole step of resolution of the linear system in Code_Aster v13.1, its peak RAM, and the acceleration factor provided by BLR. u2.08.04 User's guide to the analysis of critical loads and of Euler buckling modes, and to buckling analysis u2.08.04 User's guide to the analysis of critical loads and of Euler buckling modes, and to buckling analysis Summary: The aim of this documentation is to present a methodological guide for the analysis of critical loads and of Euler buckling modes on the one hand, and for the non-linear buckling analysis (instabilities) of a structure on the other. It deals mainly with the two functionalities of Code_Aster : - the linear buckling analysis, known as the Euler analysis, through CALC_MODES (with the keyword TYPE_RESU=‘MODE_FLAMB’), - the analysis of the quasi-static evolution (operator STAT_NON_LINE) of the structure, which presents geometric and constitutive non-linearities, for which one seeks the instabilities (option CRIT_STAB), a limit point, or even the post-critical response. The first step is, generally, an Euler buckling analysis, which will make it possible to know the buckling modes and the corresponding critical loads. From the designer's point of view, knowledge of the first mode and of its critical load is often sufficient, in order to define an operating margin with respect to the imposed loading: the multiplier coefficient between the imposed loading and the lowest critical load gives the safety margin. Notes - Knowledge of the first Euler buckling mode can also serve as an indication for optimising the management of the incremental non-linear analysis carried out afterwards. Indeed, as the critical load is approached, one can then decide to modify the piloting or to reduce the time step, or even to increase the number of iterations for checking equilibrium in the residual method, at each load step. - The shape of the Euler buckling mode can also be used to impose an initial geometric imperfection on the structure, in order to ensure, among other things, that the incremental non-linear buckling analysis will indeed bifurcate onto this mode. The Euler analysis being linear by definition, it does not make it possible to take into account inelastic constitutive relations, unilateral contact or the follower character of the forces applied. It is then necessary to carry out an incremental non-linear analysis, which in quasi-statics will rely on the STAT_NON_LINE command of Code_Aster . This is the classical incremental method by equilibrium residual. The particular points of its use will be dealt with later, in particular the use of the non-linear stability analysis with the keyword CRIT_STAB (which is also available in DYNA_NON_LINE for dynamic studies). A table of the test cases available for this type of simulation will be found in § u2.08.04-_tude_non_lin_aire_quasi-statique_de_la_structure of this document. 1 Euler buckling analysis The analysis of the buckling modes in the sense of Euler [bib5] is carried out by the operator for solving eigenvalue problems CALC_MODES (with the keyword TYPE_RESU = 'MODE_FLAMB'). In the context of buckling, one has the following typical syntax: MODP1 = CALC_MODES ( MATR_RIGI = RAMEP1 , MATR_RIGI_GEOM = RAGEP1 , TYPE_RESU = 'MODE_FLAMB' , OPTION = 'BANDE' , CALC_CHAR_CRIT = _F( CHAR_CRIT = ( -2.4 ,-2.2 , ) ,), SOLVEUR_MODAL=_F( METHODE= 'SORENSEN', DIM_SOUS_ESPACE = 80 , NMAX_ITER_SOREN = 80 , ) , ) The argument of the keyword MATR_RIGI must be the so-called material stiffness matrix, whereas the keyword MATR_RIGI_GEOM expects the geometric stiffness matrix. As a reminder, the buckling modes are the eigenmodes of the following eigenvalue problem: (K+\mu {K}_{g})x=0\iff Kx=\lambda {K}_{g}x with: | K | :31: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | stiffness matrix | | --- | --- | --- | | {K}_{g} | :31: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | geometric stiffness matrix | | \lambda | :31: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | eigenvalue ( \lambda =-\mu with \mu the multiplier coefficient of the loading) | Note: It is indeed the critical load coefficient \mu and not \lambda which is stored in the result concept. The material (or elastic) stiffness is computed with the option 'RIGI_MECA’ of CALC_MATR_ELEM. The geometric stiffness is computed from the stress field which is the solution of the linear problem (option 'RIGI_GEOM’ of CALC_MATR_ELEM). One must therefore have carried out a linear static analysis before using CALC_MODES for buckling. If the loading is composed of a fixed part (not piloted) and of a variable part, the multiplier coefficient of the loading must, of course, apply only to the variable part. The contribution of the other part of the loading is found in the first member. Let us denote by {f}_{c} the fixed loading and by {f}_{v} the piloted loading (proportional to \mu ). The eigenvalue problem becomes: (K+{K}_{g}({f}_{c}+\mu {f}_{v}))x=0\iff (K+{K}_{g}({f}_{c}))x=\lambda {K}_{g}({f}_{v})x with: | K | :52: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | material stiffness matrix | | --- | --- | --- | | {K}_{g}({f}_{c}) | :52: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | geometric stiffness matrix for the non-piloted loading | | {K}_{g}({f}_{v}) | :52: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | geometric stiffness matrix for the variable loading | | \lambda | :52: (INFO/1) Unexpected possible title overline or transition. Treating it as ordinary text because it's so short.: | eigenvalue \lambda =-\mu | In this case, one must therefore solve two prior linear elastic problems, in order to be able to compute the two different geometric stiffness matrices. In order to be exhaustive, the presentation will concern a structure subjected to imposed displacements as well as to forces, which will be the combination of a fixed loading and of a variable loading that one will pilot with an increasing coefficient which may lead to buckling. 1.1 Step 1: Preliminary linear analysis (analyses) One will use MECA_STATIQUE. The structure, meshed with shell-type elements (solid-shell type elements [bib3]), is subjected to Dirichlet (CONDLIM) and Neumann boundary conditions. The latter are decomposed into: - PESA: gravity field, - PRESPH: imposed non-piloted pressure field, - PRESPS1: imposed variable pressure field. For the buckling analysis, one must separate the constant forces from those which are variable (piloted by a coefficient). One will therefore carry out two linear static analyses. The first will be the case of the structure subjected to the imposed displacements and to the constant forces, the second will see the structure subjected to the imposed displacements and to the variable forces. Piloted loading: RESC11P1 = MECA_STATIQUE ( MODELE = MODELE , CHAM_MATER = CHMAT , CARA_ELEM = CARAELEM , EXCIT = ( _F( CHARGE = CONDLIM , ) , _F( CHARGE = PRESPS1 , ) , ) , OPTION = 'SIEF_ELGA' , ) Non-piloted loading: RESC12P1 = MECA_STATIQUE ( MODELE = MODELE , CHAM_MATER = CHMAT , CARA_ELEM = CARAELEM, EXCIT = ( _F( CHARGE = CONDLIM , ) , _F( CHARGE = PESA , ) , _F( CHARGE = PRESPH , ) , ) , OPTION = 'SIEF_ELGA' , ) One will use the stress field to compute the associated geometric stiffness matrices, for the two loadings: SIGC11P1 = CREA_CHAMP ( TYPE_CHAM = 'ELGA_SIEF_R' , OPERATION = 'EXTR' , RESULTAT = RESC11P1 , NOM_CHAM = 'SIEF_ELGA' , TYPE_MAXI = 'MINI' , TYPE_RESU = 'VALE' , ) # REGC11P1 = CALC_MATR_ELEM ( OPTION = 'RIGI_GEOM' , MODELE = MODELE , CARA_ELEM = CARAELEM , SIEF_ELGA = SIGC11P1 , ) REGC11P1 is therefore the geometric stiffness matrix associated with the variable loading case (PRESPS1). One likewise computes the geometric stiffness matrix for the constant loading (PESA and PRESPH), from RESC12P1: SIGC12P1 = CREA_CHAMP ( TYPE_CHAM = 'ELGA_SIEF_R' , OPERATION = 'EXTR' , RESULTAT = RESC12P1 , NOM_CHAM = 'SIEF_ELGA' , TYPE_MAXI = 'MINI' , TYPE_RESU = 'VALE' , ) # REGC12P1 = CALC_MATR_ELEM ( OPTION = 'RIGI_GEOM' , MODELE = MODELE , CARA_ELEM = CARAELEM , SIEF_ELGA = SIGC12P1 , ) It remains to compute the material stiffness matrix for the total loading: REMEP1 = CALC_MATR_ELEM ( OPTION = 'RIGI_MECA' , MODELE = MODELE , CHAM_MATER = CHMAT , CARA_ELEM = CARAELEM , CHARGE = ( CONDLIM , PESA , PRESPH , PRESPS1 , ) , ) All the elementary matrices have been computed; the next step is therefore their assembly: NUP1 = NUME_DDL ( MATR_RIGI = REMEP1 , ) # RAMC1P1 = ASSE_MATRICE ( MATR_ELEM = REMEP1 , NUME_DDL = NUP1 , ) # RAGEP1 = ASSE_MATRICE ( MATR_ELEM = REGC11P1 , NUME_DDL = NUP1 , ) # RAGC12P1 = ASSE_MATRICE ( MATR_ELEM = REGC12P1 , NUME_DDL = NUP1 , ) One then sums the material stiffness matrix (RAMC1P1) and the geometric stiffness matrix (RAGC12P1) corresponding to the constant loading case: RAMEP1 = COMB_MATR_ASSE ( COMB_R = ( _F( MATR_ASSE = RAMC1P1 , COEF_R = 1.0 , ) , _F( MATR_ASSE = RAGC12P1 , COEF_R = 1.0 , ) , ) , ) The two matrices required for the analysis of the buckling modes are therefore constructed. 1.2 Step 2: Analysis of the Euler modes It can be useful to carry out STURM tests (operator INFO_MODE) on the search interval over which one wants to find the buckling cases. This will make it possible to optimise the size of the interval and to check the correct progress of the subsequent modal analysis, since one will know in advance the number of existing modes. The syntax is: INFO_MODE ( MATR_RIGI = RAMEP1 , MATR_RIGI_GEOM = RAGEP1 , TYPE_MODE = 'MODE_FLAMB' , CHAR_CRIT = (-2.4 ,-2.2) ) Once the search interval for the critical buckling load has been chosen, one can then implement CALC_MODES as follows: MODP1 = CALC_MODES ( MATR_RIGI = RAMEP1 , MATR_RIGI_GEOM = RAGEP1 , TYPE_RESU = 'MODE_FLAMB' , OPTION = 'BANDE' , CALC_ CHAR_CRIT =_F( CHAR_CRIT = ( -2.4 ,-2.2 , ) , ), SOLVEUR_MODAL=_F( DIM_SOUS_ESPACE = 80 , NMAX_ITER_SOREN = 80 , ) , ) Note If the algorithm does not converge or if the number of modes is not that predicted by INFO_MODE, it may be useful to increase the values of DIM_SOUS_ESPACE and NMAX_ITER_SOREN. One normalises the modes [bib6], using only the translational degrees of freedom: MODP1 = NORM_MODE ( reuse = MODP1 MODE = MODP1 , NORME = 'TRAN' , ) The modes can then be post-processed. Notes - It is indispensable to check that the geometric stiffness of the chosen model is indeed an option available in Code_Aster. - A finer discretisation normally leads to a decrease in the critical loads. - The discretisation must be able to capture the buckling modes, bearing in mind that these modes may generate localised strains (folds). The prior analysis of the dynamic modes can constitute a first indication of the quality of the mesh, although these modes may be very different from the buckling modes. - The critical loads of the various modes are proportional to Young's modulus E . - With this method, one cannot take into account the follower character of the forces. Indeed, the geometric stiffness analysis carried out with the option RIGI_GEOM of CALC_MATR_ELEM is based on the assumption that all the forces imposed on the mechanical problem are of dead-force type. If one wants to take into account the follower character of certain loads, one must necessarily use the non-linear operators STAT_NON_LINE or DYNA_NON_LINE , with the keyword CRIT_STAB, as will be seen in the remainder of this document. 2 Quasi-static non-linear study of the structure This step is justified if the structure presents strong non-linearities, which the Euler buckling analysis cannot take into account. The operator for solving non-linear problems in quasi-statics is called STAT_NON_LINE [bib7]. These non-linearities may be linked to the material, which may have an elastoplastic constitutive behaviour [bib8], as in the example which follows. Taking contact into account, or even friction, is another source of non-linearities. One may also cite the case of follower loadings, such as pressure ([bib1] and [bib2] for solid-shell type elements), which require a non-linear approach in Code_Aster . One can distinguish two types of non-linear stability analysis, which may be combined. On the one hand, the generalisation of the Euler buckling analysis presented previously: one will follow the loading path in order to reach limit points or critical loads with the associated modes in the course of the incremental non-linear analysis. This takes the form of a stability analysis on the updated stiffness matrices. This type of analysis is often carried out on a structure without an initial imperfection. On the other hand, one can take into account imperfections introduced on the perfect model (by inserting initial geometric imperfections), in order to “force” the bifurcation of the solution branch and to follow the stable branch in order to analyse the post-critical response. The piloting of the quasi-static loading path must be treated in an appropriate manner (operator STAT_NON_LINE, cf. U4.51.03). Obviously, this following of the post-critical solution can be initiated by the eigenvalue analysis of the updated stiffness matrices, in particular in order to detect the bifurcation properly and to define the imperfection then introduced on the basis of the buckling mode observed. 2.1 Stability analysis on updated stiffness matrices Whether in quasi-statics (operator STAT_NON_LINE) or in dynamics (operator DYNA_NON_LINE), Code_Aster makes it possible to carry out incremental stability analyses in the sense of buckling on the current stiffness matrices. These analysis steps are managed by the factor keyword CRIT_STAB with the option TYPE = 'FLAMBEMENT' ( cf. U4.51.03 and U4.53.01). Notes for the stability analysis In Code_Aster , one restricts oneself today to the case where the updated stiffness matrix is symmetric, because one calls the modal solver of SORENSEN type, cf. U4.52.02. One therefore treats bifurcations of the equilibrium branches, that is to say a loss of uniqueness. This therefore restricts the families of constitutive models that one can treat (the so-called “associated” flow rule), as well as to cases of follower loadings such that a potential exists: for example for a closed enclosure under pressure. For a follower loading which removes the conservative character of the system and therefore leads to a non-symmetric stiffness matrix, the instability becomes dynamic. Notes for the non-linear transient dynamic analysis The stability analysis of trajectories is based on the study of the linearised system of the equations of motion and of the associated eigenvalue problem. Dynamic instability can occur if one exhibits a complex eigenvalue: with a strictly positive real part and with no imaginary part: the system is said to be unstable by divergence , the trajectory then having a non-oscillatory exponentially growing evolution; complex with a strictly positive real part: the system is said to be unstable by flutter , the trajectory then having an exponentially growing and oscillatory evolution. This is, for example, the case of the squeal produced by one solid sliding and rubbing on another; for irreversible constitutive laws with a non-associated flow rule, the loss of hyperbolicity may occur at the appearance of a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues with a negative imaginary part linked to the non-symmetry of the tangent tensor: this is a flutter instability. If the eigenvalues become negative, it is a divergence instability. In fluid–structure interaction, one also identifies these two types of instability: a flutter instability when the damping of the system vanishes and then becomes negative — a fluid flow is necessary for this — a buckling instability when a natural circular frequency of the system vanishes. The option CRIT_STAB acts in non-linear transient dynamics in Code_Aster as for the quasi-static case: one always carries out a stability analysis (therefore based only on the study of the symmetric stiffness matrices), not a dynamic instability analysis (damping becoming negative). With the coupled fluid–structure modelling (u,p,\phi ) R4.02.02, one must modify the assembled stiffness matrix (as well as the geometric stiffness when it is used). To do this, one must supply the following keywords, under CRIT_STAB: - MODI_RIGI = 'OUI', - DDL_EXCLUS=('PHI','PRES','DH',). The list of excluded degrees of freedom must include all the types of degrees of freedom linked to the fluid model: in the example of the test case FDNV100 one therefore has the potential PHI , the pressure PRES and the vertical displacement at the free surface DH . If one does not carry out this treatment, then the call to CRIT_STAB will fail because of a singular matrix and no shift strategy could overcome this. In quasi-statics, this problem does not arise because the coupled fluid–structure modelling then has no meaning. This keyword makes it possible to trigger, at the end of each time increment, the analysis of a stability criterion. This criterion is useful for detecting, in the course of the loading, the point from which one loses stability (by buckling, for example). This criterion is computed in the following way: at the end of a time step, in small perturbations, one solves det\left({K}^{T}+\mu .{K}^{g}\right)=0 . {K}^{T} is the consistent tangent matrix at this time instant. {K}^{g} is the geometric stiffness matrix, computed from the stress field at this time instant, and \mu the critical load coefficient. In practice, the loading is unstable if |\mu | ECHEC=_F(EVENEMENT='INSTABILITE',ACTION='ARRET',), Which means that, in the event of an instability-type event, the action triggered will be the stop. Under CRIT_STAB, the following optional options make it possible to control this stopping criterion: - PREC_INSTAB to define the (dimensionless) precision of the stopping criterion, - SIGNE to specify the critical values to be considered. The second keyword is used only when the geometric stiffness matrix is used. By default one considers the solution as being unstable if the critical load comes to lie between 1 and -1, but one can, if necessary, take into account only the positive or the negative part of this interval. Without a geometric stiffness matrix, the instability will be detected when an eigenvalue of the global assembled stiffness matrix either: - tends towards 0 (with a relative precision given by PREC_INSTAB), - changes sign. For example, in the case of a tank filled with water under earthquake, one can start the incremental or transient analysis with a critical load equal to 0.8 (analysis with geometric stiffness): which means that the tank would buckle if one imposed a depressurisation equal to 0.8 times the imposed hydrostatic pressure (the positive value of the critical load corresponds to a reversal of the direction of the loading considered). Therefore, if one specifies nothing, the analysis would be considered unstable and would stop. Since, in this case, one makes the assumption that there will be no depressurisation (for example by draining), one then excludes the interval [0,1] from the stability analysis. The problem will therefore become unstable if the critical load reaches the interval [-1,0] . For analyses with monotonic evolution this type of reasoning is readily conceived, which is indeed the case for the static part of the loading, but for the dynamic part, the loading being cyclic, and unless one has specific information, it is safer and more conservative to keep the default option and therefore to consider the structure unstable if the critical load becomes less than 1 in absolute value. Upon a stop on instability, the analysis will stop by closing the database cleanly: the user will be able to exploit it in restart. 2.2 Following of an unstable solution For the study of a structure which is potentially unstable or liable to encounter a limit point , and which therefore risks encountering a bifurcation in solution in the course of the evolution of the loading, it is often useful to be able to choose a particular solution branch (often the physical solution when it is defined a priori without ambiguities). To this end, the user may have to introduce an initial imperfection which will “force” the structure to bifurcate onto the particular solution branch. Several methods exist for defining this imperfection. - One of the most suitable is to pre-deform the structure slightly according to the shape of the buckling mode corresponding to the branch that one wants to follow. The amplitude of this pre-deformation must be small, for example less than 1/10th of the thickness for a thin structure. The ideal is to find the minimal imperfection which is compatible with a satisfactory performance of the equilibrium residual algorithm. Indeed, too small an imperfection can lead to a difficulty of convergence of the residual, mainly in the case of force piloting. This initial imperfection can very judiciously be constructed from the instability mode computed with the option CRIT_STAB of STAT_NON_LINE / DYNA_NON_LINE ( cf. previous paragraph). This mode then takes into account all the non-linearities introduced in the complete model. The more economical alternative is to use the Euler buckling mode, but this corresponds to the linear case. - The geometric imperfection can also be defined by experimental measurements of the real part, whose geometry cannot be perfect. - The imperfection can also take the form of a perturbation of the loading (misalignment, addition of a localised loading, ...) or of the mechanical characteristics of the material (local weakening of Young's modulus, for example). It may nevertheless then be more difficult to adapt the imperfection to the desired buckling mode, especially if the structure presents relatively close modes. Note In certain cases, even on the unperturbed problem, the loading is such that it causes the desired bifurcation. One of the other particular points, linked to the instability, is the choice of the piloting technique of the STAT_NON_LINE algorithm, cf. U4.51.03. Indeed, classical force piloting is no longer suitable because it cannot capture an unstable solution branch. Likewise, as a limit point is approached, convergence with force piloting will become more and more difficult, the tangent stiffness matrix becoming singular. It is then necessary to reduce the load increment and to increase the maximum number of iterations in order to continue the analysis. One can also make use of the possibility of stopping cleanly in the event of instability ( cf. previous paragraph) in order to manage, in restart, the bifurcation onto the chosen solution branch by initiating the continuation of the analysis with a perturbation along this instability mode. There exist piloting techniques [bib9] which make it possible to get round these numerical difficulties. Among the methods proposed by Code_Aster , the so-called arc-length method [bib12] (option TYPE=’LONG_ARC’ of the keyword PILOTAGE in STAT_NON_LINE), which is the most suitable for buckling-type instabilities, in the case of possible “gentle” snap-backs [bib13]. For more brutal snap-backs (snap-through), M.A. Crisfield proposes a variant [bib13], not available in Code_Aster . Other methods exist, such as that of E. Riks [bib14] (also not available in Code_Aster ), which also treats the dynamic case. If one only wants to obtain the limit point , including with good precision, loading piloting may suffice, provided that one manages well the parameters of the load-increment step (remember to use the command DEFI_LIST_INST) and of the maximum number of iterations allowed (ITER_GLOB_MAXI of CONVERGENCE). It may also be useful, as the limit point is approached, no longer to use the updated tangent matrix for the solver, since it is quasi-singular. One can then be content not to update this matrix at each analysis (parameters REAC_INCR and REAC_ITER) or, in the worst case, adopt the basic elastic matrix (PREDICTION=’ELASTIQUE’ and MATRICE=’ELASTIQUE’ of the keyword NEWTON). Here is an example of the use of STAT_NON_LINE for an elastoplastic analysis in large displacements ([bib4] for the elements used, which are of solid-shell type), with force piloting: RESU = STAT_NON_LINE ( ... EXCIT = ( _F( CHARGE = CONDLIM , TYPE_CHARGE = 'FIXE_CSTE' , ) , _F( CHARGE = PESA , TYPE_CHARGE = 'FIXE_CSTE' , ) , _F( CHARGE = PRESPH , FONC_MULT = FONCMUL2 , TYPE_CHARGE = 'SUIV' , ) , _F( CHARGE = PRESPS1 , FONC_MULT = FONCMUL , TYPE_CHARGE = 'SUIV' , ) , ) , ... ) Notes - One uses the tangent matrix updated at each analysis, allowing the cutting of the load step. - The imposed pressures are follower forces (TYPE_CHARGE='SUIV'). - In the case of a modelling with solid elements, the strain tensor recommended in large displacements is ‘SIMO_MIEHE’. If one wants to replace force piloting by an arc-length method, it is sufficient to add: RESU = STAT_NON_LINE ( ... PILOTAGE = _F( GROUP_NO = 'G' , TYPE = 'LONG_ARC' , NOM_CMP = ( 'DY' , ) , COEF_MULT = 7. ) , ...) Notes - In Code_Aster, one cannot pilot follower forces. - For arc-length piloting, it is, in general, recommended that GROUP_NO contain the whole structure. To finish, let us cite two articles by Crisfield which give a good general view of the problems and methods linked to non-linear analyses which may present various types of instability ([bib15] and [bib11]). The documentation U2.06.11 shows an example of the use of CRIT_STAB for the study of the behaviour of a metallic tank. 2.3 Test cases of Euler buckling and of buckling Here are some test cases of u2.08.05 Propagation of uncertainties and computation of fragility curves u2.08.05 Propagation of uncertainties and computation of fragility curves Summary: This document gives the elements for the implementation of numerical Monte Carlo simulations via the distribution of analyses with Code_Aster. The five main ingredients are: - the creation of the design of experiments: drawing of the random variables of the \mathit{Ns} study cases; - the putting into Code_Aster format for the launching of \mathit{Ns} mechanical studies (.distr file); - the Code_Aster analyses; - the reading of the analysis results and the writing into a single file; - the statistical post-processing: computation of classical statistical estimators such as the mean, the standard deviation, etc.; the estimation of the parameters of a log-normal fragility curve (POST_DYNA_ALEA); other post-processings ... 1 Introduction The numerical Monte Carlo method consists in carrying out \mathit{Ns} numerical simulations of the mechanical model in order to evaluate the statistical quantities of the analysis results. The 3 main steps of a propagation of uncertainties by Monte Carlo simulation are: - The modelling of the uncertainties: generation of a sample of \text{Ns} realisations of the random data at the input of the mechanical model (random parameters and stochastic process), - The propagation of the uncertainties: computation of the \text{Ns} result quantities corresponding to these data, - The computation of the statistical estimators of the quantities sought: mean, standard deviation, fractiles …; evaluation of seismic fragility curves. In the context of a mechanical study with Code_Aster, one can call upon the functionalities for the distribution of parametric studies in order to carry out such a probabilistic analysis. Indeed, in the usual case where the \mathit{Ns} draws and mechanical simulations are independent, one can beforehand establish a design of experiments of the study cases to be launched. One then launches the \mathit{Ns} corresponding studies, and the statistical quantities are computed in post-processing of the results. The procedure and its implementation with Code_Aster are described in this document. 2 Monte Carlo simulation with Code_Aster In the context of the Monte Carlo simulation, the modelling of the uncertainties proceeds by the generation of random variables and possibly of stochastic processes. In what follows, one assumes that the user has chosen laws which characterise well the m uncertain parameters. To do this, one may resort to test results, expert judgement or else the principle of maximum entropy (see R4.03.05). Very often, one can assume that the different sources of uncertainty are independent. One can then carry out random draws according to the m marginal laws of the random variables. In certain cases, one can also include more complex (non-scalar) quantities such as random matrices or else stochastic processes. One also speaks of a design of experiments to designate the drawing method and the sample which results from it. In Code_Aster, the Monte Carlo simulation according to a design of experiments is possible with the help of the distributed-analyses option U2.08.07. 2.1 Carrying out the design of experiments All the methods whose draws are independent can be implemented via the distribution of the analyses with Code_Aster . In particular, one can call upon random draws according to the Latin hypercube method (Latin Hypercube Sampling – LHS) or quasi Monte Carlo (quasi-random sequences such as the Sobol sequence, …) [bib4, bib5]. - Random variables: the uncertainties on the parameters of the finite-element model (material parameters, values of a clearance, of an elastic stop stiffness, of a Young's modulus, etc.). - Random matrices: in structural dynamics on a modal basis, the random variables may be the values of the generalised mass, stiffness and damping matrices of the finite-element model. In this approach, one draws these random matrices with the help of the operator GENE_MATR_ALEA U4.36.06. In this approach, one models both the model uncertainties and the modelling uncertainties by a probabilistic approach known as “non-parametric”. - Random excitations: the operator GENE_FONC_ALEA makes it possible to generate stationary random signals from the power spectral density. The operator GENE_ACCE_SEISME makes it possible to generate seismic signals which are non-stationary in amplitude and in frequency content. In other cases, one may have available a database containing signals which model a random physical phenomenon. This may be the case in seismic analysis, where a set of accelerograms measured in situ may be supplied by seismologists. There exist two possibilities for carrying out the design of experiments: 1) either one creates the sample of the parameter sets beforehand according to the desired drawing method and one stores it in a data file; for this one can use a dedicated software such as OpenTURNS or else the dedicated toolboxes of Python and Matlab 2) or one uses one of the operators of Code_Aster to generate a realisation of a stochastic process or of a random matrix. In the case of a transient dynamic analysis, one can thus use random time-dependent loadings generated by Code_Aster . One can of course use the two options jointly. Note : If, in the context of a seismic analysis, one has available a sample of \mathit{Ns} accelerograms, one can reduce oneself, for the design of experiments, to a discrete random variable taking values from 1 to \mathit{Ns} . Each integer designates one of the realisations of the random process (that is to say an accelerogram). Drawing by Latin hypercube then consists in running through the integers from 1 to \mathit{Ns} . Warning : The commands GENE_MATR_ALEA and GENE_FONC_ALEA generate the same sequence of random variables within one and the same execution of Code_Aster. Thus, from one execution to another, a strictly identical command file (the same calls to the commands in the same order with the same arguments) will supply exactly the same results. This is due to the fact that the random-variable generator used by Code_Aster is always initialised to the same value. If one wishes to generate different results from one execution to another, then one must use the keyword INIT_ALEA. On the other hand, GENE_ACCE_SEISME generates independent random seismic signals. 2.2 Definition and launching of the distributed studies with Code_Aster One must, in the astk window: | 1 | define the nominal deterministic study (.comm file, mesh, etc.) | | --- | --- | | 2 | define, in the .comm, the nominal values of the (uncertain) parameters which will then be modified according to the design of experiments | | 3 | define, still in the .comm, the variable or variables of interest and write these variables in a result file (in python format) | | 4 | define an output directory (type repe) in which these results will be written | | 5 | define the design of experiments in the .distr (parameter sets for the studies to be launched) | | 6 | go to the “Option” tab, choose distrib = yes (cf. U1.04.00 §8) | | 7 | in the “Option” tab, choose classe = distr if the analyses are on the centralised server | | 8 | if useful, add a file of type hostfile defining the machines available (cf. U1.04.00 §9) | For more detail, one can consult the tutorial U2.08.07. 2.3 Recovering the results of the analyses in a file The results of the analyses distributed with Code_Aster are written in output files which one finds in the \mathit{Ns} directories named {\mathit{CALC}}_{i} , i=1,\mathit{Ns} (cf. U2.08.07). In order to proceed to the post-processing with a statistics software (such as OpenTURNS or else the dedicated toolboxes of Python and Matlab, R), one must gather the sample of outputs in a single results file. This can be done very easily via a python script. 3 Statistical post-processings 3.1 Computation of the statistical quantities In the context of an approach by Monte Carlo simulation, one is interested not only in a deterministic analysis result, but one wishes to evaluate the mean, the median, the standard deviation, the fractile and other statistics describing the output variable. This makes it possible in particular to associate confidence intervals with the analysis results. After having recovered the sample of the outputs, one can call upon the preferred software (such as OpenTURNS, the dedicated toolboxes of Python and Matlab, R) to carry out these statistical post-processings. Furthermore, log-normal fragility curves can be evaluated with the help of the operator POST_DYNA_ALEA of Code_Aster . This is described in more detail in the following paragraph. 3.2 Computation of fragility curves 3.2.1 Definitions Fragility curves give the conditional probability of failure of a structure or of a component as a function of the level of seismic excitation. The modelling and the propagation of the uncertainties described above also allow the determination of the fragility curves. It is sufficient to introduce a failure criterion and to check at each Monte Carlo analysis whether failure is reached or not. The main ingredients for the establishment of fragility curves by numerical simulation are the following: - Determination of the seismic excitation to be considered (database of accelerograms), - Definition of failure criteria, - Modelling of the uncertainties and propagation by numerical simulation (Monte Carlo) - Estimation of the parameters (median and logarithmic standard deviation) of the log-normal fragility curve. The fragility curve of a component can be defined from the notion of “capacity”. The capacity of a component is the value of the parameter representative of the seismic action from which the component fails. The usual approach consists in modelling the capacity by a random variable following a log-normal law, such that A={A}_{m}\varepsilon , where {A}_{m} is the median capacity and \varepsilon denotes a log-normal random variable of unit median and of logarithmic standard deviation \beta . Also, the capacity A of a component (and {A}_{m} and thus its fragility curve) is characterised by two parameters, which are the median (“median capacity”) and the standard deviation \beta . Thus, the probability of failure for a given acceleration level a can be written [bib3, bib2]: log-normal law {P}_{f}(a)=\underset{0}{\overset{a}{\int}}\underset{}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{p(x)}}\text{dx}=\Phi (\frac{\ln(a/{A}_{m})}{\beta}) where \Phi (.) denotes the cumulative distribution function of a centred reduced Gaussian random variable. The use of the log-normal model has the advantage of requiring a reduced number of simulations compared with a direct computation of the failure probabilities. Indeed, in a direct computation, without an a priori assumption on the law, one must determine probabilities of rare events (the probabilities in the tail of the distribution), which requires a very large number of Monte Carlo simulations. In what follows, we present two methods, estimation by maximum likelihood and linear regression, for evaluating these two parameters. If the damage or the failure of a structure are characterised by a continuous variable of interest Y , accompanied by a threshold {Y}_{s} , one can express the probability of failure (of the damage level) for an earthquake of level a as {P}_{f}(a)=P(Y>{Y}_{s}\mid a) Classical damage variables Y for a concrete structure are the drift (differential displacement between two storeys of a building) or else the drop in the first natural frequencies. The notations introduced here will be used for the evaluation of a fragility curve by linear regression (§3.2.2). 3.2.2 Evaluation of the parameters by maximum likelihood In what follows, one considers that the peak acceleration has been chosen to characterise the level of seismic excitation and therefore the capacity. The procedure followed then consists in modelling the result of the numerical experiments by a Bernoulli random variable X . Indeed, for each numerical simulation i , one has two possible outcomes: either one has reached the critical level and one has failure ( {x}_{i}=1 ) or one does not have failure ( {x}_{i}=0 ). Likewise, for each simulation, one can determine the value of the peak acceleration {a}_{i} . The estimation of the parameters of a fragility curve can be done by the maximum-likelihood method. The likelihood function to be maximised for this problem is written: L=\underset{i=1}{\overset{N}{\Pi}}({P}_{f\mid a}({a}_{i})){}^{{x}_{i}}{(1-{P}_{f\mid a}({a}_{i}))}^{1-{x}_{i}} In this expression, the realisation {x}_{i} of X therefore takes the value 1 if one has failure or 0 if there is no failure for the loading (the peak acceleration) {a}_{i} . These events occur with the probability {P}_{f\mid a} given by expression (1). The estimates of the parameters \beta and {A}_{m} are those which minimise -\ln(L) : ({\beta}_{C}^{e},{A}_{m}^{e})=\text{arg}\underset{\beta ,{A}_{m}}{\min}\left[-\ln(L)\right] . This step can be implemented in post-processing of the analysis results. In the Code_Aster command file, one must, for each simulation, check whether one has failure or not. By way of example, if the failure criterion consists of an allowable stress, one checks whether the maximum stress computed exceeds this stress. Then one has the results of the simulations written, with the help of CREA_TABLE, in a results table. This table must contain two columns, PARA_NOCI and DEFA, which give respectively the value {a}_{i} (the PGA value or any other indicator) and the value {x}_{i} ( 1 or 0 ). TAB1=CREA_TABLE(LISTE=( _F(PARA='PARA_NOCI',LISTE_R = PGA,), _F(PARA='DEFA',LISTE_I =xi ,), ),); Note : If one supplies a column DEMANDE instead of DEFA, then this column must contain the values of the seismic demand (variable of interest describing the failure or the damage, for example a stress or a maximum displacement). TAB2=CREA_TABLE(LISTE=( _F(PARA='PARA_NOCI',LISTE_R = PGA,), _F(PARA='DEMANDE',LISTE_I =demande ,), ),); The keyword SEUIL must then be supplied in POST_DYNA_ALEA in order to determine the sequence of the {x}_{i} . The operator POST_DYNA_ALEA U4.84.04 makes it possible to estimate the parameters of the log-normal fragility curve from the table TAB1 via the keyword FRAGILITE: TAB_POST=POST_DYNA_ALEA( FRAGILITE=(_F(TABL_RESU=TAB1, AM_INI =0.3 , BETA_INI=0.1 , METHODE= 'EMV', FRACTILE = (0.0,0.05,0.5,0.95,1.0), NB_TIRAGE =Ns, ),), TITRE = 'courbe 1', INFO=2,); One gives initial values of the parameters {A}_{m} and \beta to be estimated (starting point for the optimisation algorithm) via AM_INI and BETA_INI. If one supplies the keyword FRACTILE, one also determines the fractiles (confidence intervals) of the fragility curve by a resampling method (known as the “bootstrap” method). Resampling consists in drawing new samples from the values of the original sample. These draws are carried out with replacement; see [bib1] for more details. Then, one determines the parameters of the fragility curve for each “bootstrap” sample, which gives a sample of fragility curves. One then determines the fractiles for the sample of fragility curves obtained. In general, one draws as many “bootstrap” samples as one has values in the original sample. It is nevertheless possible to work with a smaller number of draws by supplying NB_TIRAGE (by default the number of draws corresponds to the size of the original sample, here \mathit{Ns} ). In the example above, one therefore determines the envelope curves (fractiles 1.0 and 0.0 ) as well as the median (0.5) and the fractiles at 0.05 and 0.95 . In the graph below, one gives an example of a fragility curve for {A}_{m}=0.68 and \beta =0.25 : Figure 3.2.2-a: Conditional probability of failure as a function of the PGA 3.2.3 Evaluation by linear regression Regression is a very widespread method for determining the parameters of a log-normal fragility curve. It is practised above all in the United States in order to evaluate the fragility of civil structures such as roads, engineering structures and public buildings. In this approach, one relates the variable of interest Y (the drift, for example) to the value of the seismic indicator a (for example the PGA) via a relation of the type: Y=b{a}^{c}\eta In the expression above, \eta is a log-normal random variable which one can define from the centred reduced normal variable U : \eta =\exp(\beta U) , and the variables b and c are the parameters of the model. These latter are obtained by a linear regression with the help of the following expression: \ln(Y)=\ln(b)+c\ln(a)+ϵ where \epsilon is a centred normal (Gaussian) random variable of standard deviation \sigma such that ϵ=\sigma U . With these notations, the probability of failure is written as a conditional probability, as a function of the seismic level a and for a threshold {Y}_{s} : {P}_{f}(a)=P(Y>{Y}_{s}\mid a)=1-P(Y<{Y}_{s}\mid a) . Taking into account the log-normal expression of the variable Y , one obtains the analytical expression of the fragility curve: {P}_{f}(a)=\Phi \left(\frac{\ln(b{a}^{c}/{Y}_{s})}{\sigma}\right) With the help of the regression line, one can express the median threshold {Y}_{s} from the median capacity as {Y}_{s}=b{a}_{s}^{c}\eta . If one considers a “best-estimate” critical threshold which one identifies with the median value in the uncertainty procedure, one can write {A}_{m}={a}_{s} . One thus arrives at the expression of the log-normal fragility curve: {P}_{f}(a)=\Phi \left(\frac{\ln(a/{A}_{m})}{\beta}\right) where \beta =\sigma /c with the standard deviation of the regression error \sigma . In practice, the value of the median capacity can be deduced directly from the regression curve and is expressed from the parameters of the latter as {A}_{m}=\exp\left[\frac{\ln({Y}_{s}/b)}{c}\right] It is important to emphasise that this model makes it possible to take into account the heteroscedastic behaviour (the variance of Y depends on the parameters of the model and is not constant). The operator POST_DYNA_ALEA U4.84.04 makes it possible to estimate the parameters of the log-normal fragility curve by regression from the table TAB2 of §3.2.2 via the keyword FRAGILITE: TAB_POST=POST_DYNA_ALEA( FRAGILITE=(_F(TABL_RESU=TAB2, METHODE= 'REGRESSION', SEUIL=0.05, ),), TITRE = 'courbe 2', INFO=2,); Experience shows that the dispersion (variability) of Y increases with the seismic level. On the other hand, unlike the maximum-likelihood method, the logarithmic standard deviation does not depend on the threshold. u2.08.06 User's guide to parallelism u2.08.06 User's guide to parallelism Summary: Any Code_Aster simulation can benefit from the performance gains that parallelism provides (HPC 1 in English). These gains can be of two kinds: on the analysis time and on the RAM/disk space required (per core allocated). Well understood and well used, the impact of HPC on studies can be major in terms of: - Feasibility: unblocking a critical situation (model too fine, simulation too slow…); - Productivity: its accelerations of up to X10 or even X100 [2]_ contribute to smoothing and to securing the conduct of the simulations; - Predictivity: allowing finer models, more complex and better validated simulations (recalibration, sensitivity, parametric…); - Forward-looking studies: allowing oneself completely different studies. Code_Aster proposes different parallel strategies in order to adapt to the study and to the computing platform. Some are oriented rather towards computer-science aspects (distribution of complete analyses or of independent modal/MISS3D analyses, construction of linear systems, basic linear-algebra operations), others are more algorithmic (HPC linear solvers MUMPS and PETSc). This document briefly describes the organisation of parallelism in the code. It then recalls a few fundamentals in order to help the user take advantage of these parallel strategies. One then details their implementations, their scopes of use and their potential gains. The chainings/combinations of different strategies (often natural and parameterised by default) are also addressed. The user in a hurry can go straight to chapter 2 (“Parallelism in a few clicks!”). It summarises the operating procedure for implementing the parallel strategy recommended by default. Note: To use Code_Aster in parallel, (at least) three cases may arise: - One has access to the centralised Aster machine and one wishes to use the Astk access interface, - One carries out analyses on a cluster or on a multi-core machine with Astk, - The same as the previous case but without Astk. ‘High Performance Computing’. .. [2] Compared with the sequential strategies of the old versions of code_aster ( Example: Thus, an analysis comprising a finite-element model leading to linear systems of size N=10^6 can be, for example, parallelised over 8 MPI; each MPI process itself calling 6 OpenMP threads. Therefore, in total, the analysis requires 8 x 6 = 48 cores, that is, with nodes of 24 cores, 2 nodes. Whence the following Astk parameterisation for a proportionate use of the machine resources and an efficient activation of the two possible levels of parallelism (MUMPS/PETSc+ BLAS): ncpus=6, mpi_nbcpu=8 and mpi_nbnœud=2.
