Figure 1. 2b ._ Two levels of parallelism nested in the constructions and the solutions of the linear systems (MPI and OpenMP). In the third case , one distributes the modal analyses over several nodes (cf. §4.4), reserving several blocks of MPI processes. Each one will treat a frequency sub-band. Then, by using the linear solver MUMPS, one can add a second MPI level of parallelisation within each of these blocks (cf. previous case). One can possibly add a third level by activating OpenMP threads within each MPI process of the solution (cf. §4.3 and figures 1.3a/b). Note that the efficiency of this strategy requires frequency bands that are fairly well balanced. To calibrate these bands, it is advisable to use beforehand the operator INFO_MODE [U4.52.01]. It too benefits from a very efficient two-level MPI parallelism. Figure 1. 3a ._ Examples of the benefit of HPC on portions of industrial studies in dynamics: (on the left) acceleration X40 for the vibration diagnostics on 3D GTA models (N=2.5M degrees of freedom, 80 modes) and (on the right) X4000 on the Fluid–Structure Interaction analyses on a PTR tank (N=50000 degrees of freedom, 6100 modes). > Example: Thus an analysis on four sub-bands, each comprising about a hundred eigenmodes of size N=10^6, can be parallelised over 4 x 8 =32 MPI (4 for the sub-bands and 8 for each MUMPS call within these sub-bands). Each MPI process being able to call itself 6 OpenMP threads. Therefore, in total, the analysis requires 32x 6 = 192 cores, that is, on nodes of 24 cores, 8 nodes. Whence the following Astk parameterisation for a proportionate use of the machine resources and an efficient activation of the three possible levels of parallelism (CALC_MODES+ MUMPS+ BLAS): ncpus=6, mpi_nbcpu=32 and mpi_nbnœud=8. Figure 1. 3b ._ Up to three levels of parallelism nested in the modal analyses (MPI, MPI and OpenMP). In the fourth case , if the CALC_MISS analyses are independent (option FICHIER_TEMPS), one can already distribute them over several nodes, reserving several MPI processes per node. Each one will treat a series of frequencies. One will not take all the cores of a node, in order to leave enough RAM for the MISS3D analysis. Then, in order to make the best use of these unoccupied cores, it is then advisable to add a second level of parallelism by activating OpenMP threads within each MISS3D MPI process (cf. §4.5 and figures 1.4a/b). If these CALC_MISS analyses are, on the other hand, not independent (option other than FICHIER_TEMPS), one will use only one node of the cluster and one will activate only the second level of parallelism via OpenMP. Figure 1. 4a ._ Examples of the benefit of HPC on portions of industrial studies with MISS3D: acceleration X17 for the seismic reassessments of the Kashiwaski-Kariwa benchmark (14000 interface nodes, 100 frequencies). > Example: Thus, for an analysis of 160 frequencies parallelised over 8 MPI , each MPI process will treat twenty frequencies and each of them will itself be able to be parallelised over 6 OpenMP threads. Therefore, in total, the analysis requires 8 x 6 = 48 cores, that is, on nodes of 24 cores, 2 nodes. Whence the following Astk parameterisation for a proportionate use of the machine resources and an efficient activation of the two possible levels of parallelism (CALC_MISS+ OpenMP thread): ncpus=6, mpi_nbcpu=8 and mpi_nbnœud=2. Figure 1. 4b ._ Up to two levels of parallelism nested in the Code_Aster–MISS3D couplings (MPI and OpenMP). Note: - Other algorithmic portions of the code can benefit from parallelism (basic linear-algebra operations, pairing steps of certain contact algorithms…). This parallelism is in general automatic and not directly parameterisable. It accompanies the 4 parallelism strategies detailed previously. 1.3 In practice via Astk For the effective implementation of cases no. 2, 3 and no. 4 , one must pre-select a parallel version of Code_Aster (denoted _mpi), then specify the number of cores retained (Options menu of Astk) via the following fields: - (optional) ncpus=k , number of threads allocated in OpenMP per MPI process; generally used in addition to MPI; value parameterised by default if one does not fill in the field and it remains empty. - mpi_nbcpu=m , number of MPI processes allocated in total (sum over all the nodes). - mpi_nbnœud=p , number of nodes over which these m x k parallel tasks will be distributed. One advises in general not to allocate all the cores of a node in MPI alone . This can have the effect of slowing down the simulation because, even if part of the analyses is accelerated as a result of its distribution over more cores, since these share certain memory resources (caches, bus), the accesses to the data are, for their part, slowed down. To use more efficiently and at 100% all the resources allocated, one rather advises mixing and balancing the MPI and OpenMP parallelisms (hybrid parallelism on 2 levels). To remain efficient , one must of course take care not to exceed the physical capacities of the platforms : - no more OpenMP threads (ncpus) than cores sharing a physical memory (24 on Aster5 and 28 on EOLE); - no more MPI processes (mpi_nbcpu), possibly multiplied by the previous number of threads, than physical cores available: per node (24 on Aster5 and 28 on EOLE) and in total (size of the machine); - respect the constraints of the batch manager and, in particular, the maximum resources allocatable by a single user. Figure 1. 5 ._ Astk parameters dedicated to parallelism. The chapters of this document detail all these elements. Once these have been fixed, one can launch one's analysis as one would do in sequential mode (on the centralised machine, in batch mode only). Except that, with parallelism, one can of course reduce the specifications in time and in memory of the analysis entered in Astk (cf. U1.03.03). Notes: - For the MPI parallelism alone of the steps of manipulation of linear systems (second case) it is not useful to allocate too many processes. In general, the granularity of 1 MPI process per 30 or 50 000 degrees of freedom is amply sufficient. If one wishes to continue to accelerate the analysis, one can initiate a second level of parallelism and reduce this granularity to a few thousand degrees of freedom per thread. For example, a model comprising 0.6M degrees of freedom will very probably be able to benefit from an efficient parallelism by allocating 12 MPI x 5 OpenMP threads = 60 cores. - For INFO_MODE or CALC_MODES (third case), one begins by distributing the sub-bands, then one takes into account the possible parallelism of the linear solver (if use of MUMPS ). For example, for a modal analysis comprising 8 sub-bands, one can set mpi_nbcpu=32 . Each of the sub-bands will then use MUMPS on 4 MPI processes. And on each of these independent solutions one can request the previous parallel scheme. That is, potentially, three nested levels of parallelism. Figure 1. 6 ._ Astk parameters devoted to the resources in time and in RAM allocated (for each MPI process). For example, to accelerate the constructions/solutions of linear systems (case no. 2 of the previous paragraph), the fact of distributing the analysis over 12 MPI processes (mpi_nbcpu) generally makes it possible to reduce by at least: - a factor of X2 the RAM peak (per MPI process, cf. field 'Total memory' of Astk, figure 1.6), - a factor of X4 the execution time (the so-called 'elapsed' time, or “effective” waiting time for the return of the run, cf. field 'Time' of Astk, figure 1.6). And if one adds an additional level of parallelism via 4 or 6 OpenMP threads (ncpus) one can still gain: - a factor of X2 in execution time. Possibly of different types (category no. 2 or no. 3 cited previously) and which will gain by being carried out in parallel. Which will often be faster in sequential mode because of the risks of congestion during memory accesses. 2 General points Any simulation Code_Aster can benefit from the performance gains that parallelism provides. Provided that it carries out elementary computations/assemblies, solutions of linear systems, large modal analyses or independent/similar simulations. The gains can be of two kinds: on the analysis time and on the RAM/disk space required (per MPI process). Like most general-purpose codes in structural mechanics, Code_Aster proposes different strategies in order to adapt to the study and to the computing platform. Once parameterised, most of them chain together and couple automatically. The following paragraphs give an overview of them. 2.1 Computer-science parallelisms - 1a/Launching of batches of independent/similar analyses (parametric analyses, tests...). Tool: shell scripting. Gain : in elapsed time. Launching: standard via Astk [U2.08.07]. Chaining : none. Combination : possible with the other parallel schemes but only in advanced use (overloading of sources). - 1b/Distribution of the elementary computations and of the assemblies , matrix and vector, in the pre/post-processings and in the constructions of linear systems. Parallelism in distributed memory. Tool: MPI language. Gain : in elapsed time, or even in RAM peak with MUMPS+MATR_DISTRIBUEE. Launching: standard via Astk (mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud). Chaining : useful with 2b or 2c; possible but of little use with 1c or 1d alone; possible but useless with 2a. Combination : none. - 1c/Distribution of the basic linear-algebra computations (sub-steps of MUMPS, BLAS library) . Parallelism in shared memory activated only with the MUMPS package (cf. 2b) . Tool: OpenMP language. Gain : in elapsed time (but increase in the CPU time). Launching: standard via Astk (ncpus). Chaining : possible but of little use with 1b alone. Combination : counter-productive with 2a, useful with 2b, possible but of little use with 2c or 1d. - 1d/Distribution of the modal analyses (resp. of the modal calibrations) in the operator CALC_MODES (resp. INFO_MODE ). Parallelism in distributed memory (without memory gain, acceleration only). Tool: MPI language. Gain : in elapsed time (but increase in the RAM peak, to be offset by the combination with 2b). Launching: standard via Astk (mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud). Chaining : possible but of little use with 1b alone. Combination : useful with 2b (or even 2b/1c); possible but of little use with 2a; impossible with 2c. - 1e/Distribution of the MISS3D analyses in the operator CALC_MISS . Parallelism in distributed memory (if OPTION=FICHIER_TEMPS) and/or shared memory (without memory gain, acceleration only). Tool: MPI and OpenMP languages. Gain : in elapsed time. Launching: standard via Astk (ncpus, mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud). Chaining : none. Combination : with FICHIER_TEMPS two possible levels of parallelism, MPI x OpenMP. - 1f/Other distributions of analyses: certain steps of the frictional-contact algorithm, operator REST_SPEC_TEMP. Parallelism in distributed memory (without memory gain, acceleration only). Tool: MPI language. Gain : in elapsed time. Launching: standard via Astk (mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud). Combination : possible but of little use with 1b (OpenMP). 2.2 Numerical parallelisms - 2a/Direct solver MULT_FRONT ; parallelism in shared memory. Tool: OpenMP language. Gain : in elapsed time (but increase in the CPU time). Launching: standard via Astk (ncpus). Chaining : possible but of little use with 1b, 2b or 2c. Combination : counter-productive with 1c, possible but of little use with 1d. - 2b/ MUMPS package (either as a direct solver, via METHODE='MUMPS', or as a preconditioner of PETSC/GCPC via PRE_COND='LDLT_SP'). Parallelism in distributed memory. Tool: MPI language. Gain : in elapsed time and in RAM peak. Launching: standard via Astk (mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud). Chaining : useful with 1b or 2c, possible but of little use with 2a. Combination : useful with 1c or 1d. - 2c/ Iterative solver PETSC (with possibly MUMPS as a preconditioner, cf. PRECOND='LDLT_SP'); parallelism in distributed memory. Tool: MPI language. Gain : in elapsed time and in RAM peak. Launching: standard via Astk (mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud). Chaining : useful with 1b or 2b, possible but useless with 2a. Combination : possible but of little use with 1c, out of scope with 1d. The parallel schemes 1b+2b/1c or 1b+2b+2c are the most widely adopted. They support an “industrial” and “general-public” use. These general-purpose and reliable parallelisms provide notable gains in CPU and in RAM peak per core. Their parameterisation is simple, their implementation facilitated via Astk (cf. §1). For a standard use, the user no longer has to worry about the fine implementation of the parallelism . By filling in the dedicated menus of Astk [5]_ , one fixes the number of cores required (for MPI and/or OpenMP) as well as the number of nodes over which they are distributed. 2.3 Parallelisation of linear systems Once these portions of linear system have been constructed (parallel scheme 1b), two cases arise: - either the following treatment is naturally sequential and therefore all the MPI processes must have access to the global information. To this end one gathers these pieces of linear systems and therefore the following step will be neither accelerated, nor will it see its memory consumptions fall. It is most often the end of an operator, a post-processing or a linear solver not parallelised in MPI (strategy 1b+2a). - or the following treatment accepts MPI parallelism ; it is then mainly the HPC linear solvers MUMPS (1b+2b), PETSC (1b+2c) or both at once (1b+2b+2c). The parallel flow of data constructed upstream is then transmitted to them (after a few adaptations). These linear-algebra packages then reorganise, internally, their own parallel schemes (with a more algebraic view). One then speaks of a parallel scheme of rather “numerical” order. This combination of “computer-science parallelism”, at the level of the assembly of the linear system, and of “numerical parallelism”, at the level of its solution, the two via MPI, is the most common combination. Notes: - Let us note that at the end of the cycle “construction of the linear system – solution of it”, whatever the scenario implemented (sequential or MPI-parallel linear solver), the solution vector is then transmitted, in full, to all the MPI processes. The cycle can thus continue whatever the following configuration. In addition, one can superimpose on, or substitute for, this MPI parallelism (which works on all platforms) another level of parallelism managed this time by the OpenMP language . This is however limited to the fractions of the machine which physically share the same memory (multi-core PC or nodes of a computing server). It does not make it possible to lower the memory consumptions but, on the other hand, it accelerates certain types of computation, and this with a finer granularity than that of MPI: it provides a better acceleration even if the flow of data/treatments is not very large. It is a parallel scheme of “computer-science” order which intervenes mainly in the basic operations of linear-algebra algorithms ( via , for example, the BLAS library). This parallelism can be: - either complementary to the MPI parallelism by accelerating the computations within each MPI process (in the linear-system solution part with MUMPS, strategy known as “2b/1c”). - or a substitute for the MPI parallelism by accelerating the solution of the linear system with MULT_FRONT (strategy 2a). Figure 2.3.1._ Organisation of the MPI parallel scheme of construction and of solution of the linear systems. 2.4 Distribution of modal analyses - When the simulation cannot be decomposed into independent Aster analyses, but it remains nevertheless dominated by generalised modal analyses (operators INFO_MODE and CALC_MODES), one can organise a specific parallel scheme. It is founded on the distribution of independent modal analyses : each one being in charge of a frequency sub-band. This parallel scheme of purely “computer-science” order provides only gains in time. It can however coexist with the previous parallel schemes: - chaining with the MPI parallelism of construction of the linear systems (in, for example, CALC_MATR_ELEM, strategy 1b+1d), - combination with the MPI (or even OpenMP) parallelism in the solutions of linear systems (if MUMPS is used, strategy with 2 levels of parallelism, 1d/2b, or even three, 1d/2b/1c). Figure 2.4.1._ Organisation of the MPI parallel scheme for the distribution of the modal analyses and for the solutions of the associated linear systems. Notes: - Between each command, the user can even change the distribution of the mesh cells among the processors. It is sufficient to use the command MODI_MODELE. This mechanism remains licit when one chains different analyses ( POURSUITE mode). The rule being of course that this new distribution persists, for the model concerned, until the possible next MODI_MODELE and that this distribution must remain compatible with the parallel parameter setting of the analysis (number of nodes/processors...). - In any case, any parallel Aster analysis must respect the following paradigms : at the end of a computation operator [6]_ , the global databases of each processor are identical [7]_ and the current MPI communicator is the standard communicator ( MPI_COMM_WORLD ). All the other possible MPI sub-communicators must be destroyed. Because one does not know whether the operator which follows in the command file has provided for an incomplete data flow. One must therefore organise the appropriate communications in order to complete the fields which may be incomplete. Options menus + ncpus/mpi_nbcpus/mpi_nbnœud. This is not the case for printout operators (for example, IMPR_RESU) or for closing an analysis (FIN/POURSUITE). And very close to the database generated in sequential mode. 3 Some preliminary advice One formulates here some advice to help the user take advantage of the parallel computation strategies of the code . But one must be well aware that, before anything else, one must first optimise and validate one's sequential analysis, taking into account the advice which abounds in the command documentations. To do this, one uses, if possible, a coarser mesh and/or one activates only a few time steps. The default parameter setting and the displays/alarms of the code propose a balanced and instrumented mode of operation . One lists below, and in a non-exhaustive manner, several questions which it is interesting to ask oneself when one seeks to parallelise one's analysis. Of course, certain questions (and answers) are cumulative and can therefore apply simultaneously. 3.1 Preamble It is interesting to validate , beforehand, one's parallel analysis by comparing a few iterations in sequential mode and in parallel mode. This procedure also makes it possible to calibrate the maximum gains attainable (theoretical speed-ups) and therefore to avoid “wasting processors” too much. Thus, if one denotes by f the parallel portion of the code (determined for example via a prior sequential run), then the maximum theoretical speed-up S p accessible on p processors is computed according to Amdahl's formula: {S}_{p}=\frac{1}{1-f+\frac{f}{p}} For example, if one uses the distributed MUMPS parallelism by default (scenario 1b+2b) and the steps of construction/solution of the linear system represent 90% of the sequential time ( f =0.90), the theoretical speed-up is bounded by the value {\mathrm{S}}_{\infty}=\frac{1}{1-0.9+0.9/\infty }=10 ! And this, whatever the number of MPI processes allocated. It is interesting to evaluate the main items of consumption (time/RAM): in quasi-static mechanics, these are generally the steps of elementary computations/assemblies , of solution of the linear system and the frictional-contact algorithms. But their proportions depend greatly on the case (characteristics of the contact, size of the problem, complexity of the material laws...). If the elementary computations are important, one must parallelise them via scenario 1b (default scenario). If, on the contrary, the linear systems concentrate the essential part of the costs, scenarios 2b or 2c may suffice. On the other hand, if it is the frictional contact which sizes the analysis, one must seek to optimise its parameter setting and/or parallelise its internal linear solver (cf. GCP+MUMPS method). In dynamics, if one carries out an analysis by projection onto a modal basis, it may be this last step which proves the most costly. To gain time, one can then use the operator CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' cut into several sub-bands, in sequential mode and, above all, in parallel (scenario 1d). This operator exhibits a distribution of quasi-independent tasks which leads to good speed-ups. To optimise one's parallel analysis, one must watch for possible load imbalances of the data flow (CPU and memory) and limit the extra costs due to memory off-loading (JEVEUX and MUMPS OOC) and to the archiving of fields . On this subject, one may consult the documentation U1.03.03 “Performance indicator of an analysis (time/memory)”. It indicates the procedure to follow in order to establish the right diagnoses and it proposes solutions. For CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' cut into several sub-bands, respecting a good load balance is crucial for the efficiency of the parallel analysis : all the sub-bands must comprise a similar number of modes. One therefore advises proceeding in three steps: - Prior calibration of the spectral zone by calls to INFO_MODE (if possible in parallel), - Examination of the results, - Launching in POURSUITE mode of the CALC_MODES analysis, with the option 'BANDE' cut into several parallelised sub-bands. For more details one may consult the user's documentation of the operator [U4.52.02]. 3.2 Some empirical figures One advises allocating at least 30 to 50.103 degrees of freedom per MPI process (scenarios 1b, 2b or 2c). This granularity can go down to a few thousand degrees of freedom per OpenMP thread while remaining efficient (scenarios 1c or 2a). A standard thermo-mechanical analysis generally benefits, on 32 processors, from a gain of the order of ten in elapsed time and from a factor of 4 in RAM peak (per core). For CALC_MODES, one advises decomposing one's analysis into sub-bands of a few tens of modes (for example 60) and, then, providing for 2, 4 or even 8 MUMPS processes per sub-band. One must of course make do with the number of processors available and the memory peak required by the problem [8]_ . One can obtain gains of a factor of 30, in elapsed time, on about a hundred processors. The gains in memory are more modest (a few tens of percent). The modal calibration step via INFO_MODE costs practically nothing in parallel: a few minutes, at most, for problems of the order of a million unknowns, parallelised over about a hundred processors. The gains in time are of a factor of X70 on about a hundred processors and up to x2 in RAM peak. 3.3 Independent analyses When the simulation that one wishes to carry out decomposes naturally (parametric study, sensitivity analysis...) or artificially (particular thermo-mechanical chaining...), into similar but independent analyses, one can gain a great deal in analysis time thanks to the numerical parallelism 1a. 3.4 Gain in RAM When the dimensioning memory factor concerns the solution of linear systems (which is often the case), the combination of the computer-science parallelisms 1b (elementary computations/assemblies) and the numerical parallelisms 2b (distributed linear solver MUMPS) is entirely indicated [9]_ (or even 1b+2b/1c). Once one has distributed one's Code_Aster +MUMPS/PETSC analysis over enough processors, the RAM consumptions of JEVEUX can become predominant (compared with those of MUMPS, which one has spread over the processors). To re-establish the right hierarchy (the external solver must bear the peak RAM consumption!) one must activate, in addition, the option SOLVEUR/MATR_DISTRIBUEE U4.50.01. To solve frontier problems of very large sizes (> 5M degrees of freedom), one can also try the iterative solvers of PETSC (parallel strategy 2c or 2b+2c). 3.5 Gain in time If the essential part of the costs concerns only the solutions of linear systems of small size (N 5%) or these prove fairly large, it is essential to extend the parallel scope by activating the distribution of the elementary computations/assemblies (1b) and by switching to distributed MUMPS (default value). On frontier problems of large sizes (N>3M degrees of freedom), once the right numerical parameters have been selected [10]_ (preconditioner, relaxation... cf. U4.50.01), the parallel iterative solvers (2c) can provide very appreciable gains in time compared with the generic direct solvers (2a/2b). Especially if the solutions are relaxed [11]_ because, subsequently, they are corrected by an encompassing process (Newton algorithm of THER/STAT_NON_LINE...). For large modal problems (in problem size and/or in number of modes), one must of course think of using CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' cut into several sub-bands [12]_ . Distributing the linear solver MUMPS over more processes makes it possible to reduce the memory peak. Other levers: Out-Of-Core operation and change of renumberer. To lower the memory consumptions of MUMPS one can also act on other parameters: OOC, use as a preconditioner or relaxation of the solutions [U4.50.01]. There is, however, no universal rule; all the parameters must be adjusted case by case. That is to say that one is going to be less demanding as regards the quality of the solution. This can take the form of a mediocre stopping criterion, the computation of a crude preconditioner and its sharing during several solutions of the linear system... The functionalities of the non-linear and linear solvers of Code_Aster make it easy to implement this type of scenario. Balanced via prior modal calibrations carried out with INFO_MODE. If possible in parallel. 4 Computer-science parallelisms 4.1 Batches of independent analyses 4.1.1 Description Use: for the general user via Astk . Scope of use: independent analyses (parametric, sensitivity study...). Number of cores recommended: limit of the machine/batch manager . Gain: in CPU time. Speed-up: proportional to the number of independent cases. Type of parallelism: computer-science via shell scripts. Scenario: 1a of §3. Combination with all the other parallelism strategies is licit but addressed to advanced users (outside the scope of Astk ). 4.1.2 Implementation The tool Astk makes it possible to carry out a whole series of similar but independent analyses (in sequential mode and above all in MPI parallel). One can use an official version of the code or a private overload built beforehand. The command files setting out the analyses are constructed dynamically from a “model” command file and from a “dictionary”-type mechanism: different parameter sets for each study (keyword VALE of the .distr file), variable blocks of Aster /Python commands (PRE/POST_CALCUL)... The launching of these parallel batches is carried out with the usual submission parameters of Astk . One can even reparameterise the hardware configuration of the analysis (list of the nodes, number of cores, total RAM per node...) via a classical .hostfile file. For more information on the implementation of this parallelism, one may consult the documentations U1.04.00/[U2.08.07]. Notes: - Before launching such a batch of analyses, it is preferable to optimise beforehand, on a typical study, the various dimensioning parameters: memory management JEVEUX , non-linear/modal/linear solver aspects, keyword ARCHIVAGE, frictional-contact algorithm... (cf. documentations U1.03.03, U4.50.01...). - One can easily bring a machine down by launching too many analyses with respect to the resources available. It is advisable to proceed by stages and to enquire as to the possibilities of use of shared computing resources (batch class, large priority jobs...). 4.2 Elementary computations and assemblies 4.2.1 Description Use: for the general user via Astk . Scope of use: analyses comprising costly elementary computations/assemblies (non-linear mechanics). Activated by default as soon as the number of MPI processes >1. Number of cores recommended: alone, between 4 and 8. Chained with the distributed parallelism of MUMPS or of PETSC (default value), typically 16, 32 or even 64. Gain: in time or even in memory with the linear solver MUMPS/PETSC (if MATR_DISTRIBUEE). Speed-up: Gains variable according to the cases (parallel efficiency [13]_ >50%). One needs a fairly large granularity for this parallelism to remain efficient: 30 or 50.103 degrees of freedom per MPI process. Type of parallelism: computer-science via the MPI language (mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud). Scenario: 1b of §2. Natively designed to chain to the numerical parallelisms 2b or 2c. Chaining possible with 1c, possible but of little use with 1d or 2a. No combination possible. 4.2.2 Implementation The implementation of this parallel scheme is carried out transparently for the user. Via Astk, it is initialised by default as soon as one has selected a parallel version of Code_Aster (denoted _mpi) as well as a number of MPI processes at least equal to 2. Thus on the centralised Aster server, one must parameterise the following fields in the Options menu : - mpi_nbcpu=m , number of MPI processes allocated. - mpi_nbnœud=p , number of nodes over which these MPI processes will be distributed. For example, on the centralised machine Aster5, the nodes are composed of 24 cores. To allocate 32 MPI processes at a rate of 8 processes per node, one must therefore set mpi_nbcpu to 32 and mpi_nbnœud to 4. One advises, in general, not to allocate all the cores of a node in MPI alone . This can have the effect of slowing down the simulation because, even if part of the analyses is accelerated as a result of its distribution over more cores, since these share certain memory resources, the accesses to the data are, for their part, slowed down. To use more efficiently and at 100% all the resources allocated, one rather advises mixing MPI parallelism and OpenMP (cf. scenarios 1b+2b/1c or 1b+2b/1c+2c). Once this number of MPI processes has been fixed, one can launch one's analysis (in batch on the centralised machine) with the same parameter setting as in sequential mode. If this parallel scheme is chained with the numerical parallelism of MUMPS or that of PETSC (or both, cf. scenarios 2b and 2c), one can reduce one's RAM peak by activating the option MATR_DISTRIBUEE. As soon as several MPI processes are activated , the assignment of the model in the Aster command file (operator AFFE_MODELE) distributes its mesh cells among the processors . Code_Aster being a finite-element code, this is a natural distribution of the data (and of the associated tasks). Subsequently, the Aster steps of elementary computations and of assemblies (matrix and vector) will be based on this distribution in order to “drain” the data/treatment flows local to each processor. Each processor will carry out only the analyses associated with the mesh-cell group for which it is responsible. This mesh-cell/processor distribution comes in different forms and it is parameterisable in the operators AFFE_MODELE [U4.41.01]/MODI_MODELE [U4.41.02] via the values of the keyword DISTRIBUTION/METHODE=: - 'CENTRALISE': The mesh cells are not distributed (as in sequential mode). Each processor knows all the mesh cells of the model. Parallelism 1b is therefore not implemented. This mode of use is useful for non-regression tests and for certain studies where parallelism 1b brings little or is even counter-productive (for example if one must gather the elementary data in order to feed a non-distributed linear system and the MPI communications required are too slow). In all the cases where the elementary computations represent a small part of the total time (for example in linear elasticity), this option may be sufficient. - 'GROUP_ELEM' /' MAIL_DISPERSE' /'MAIL_CONTIGU' /'SOUS_DOMAINE' (default) /'SOUS_DOM.OLD': the mesh cells are distributed on the basis of different criteria: by type, by cyclic distribution, by packets of the same size or according to sub-domain strategies. In the last two scenarios, the distribution is carried out via the partitioners METIS (default) or SCOTCH (cf. keyword PARTITIONNEUR). These must therefore be installed and linked to the version of Code_Aster used. This is obviously done by default on the centralised machine. Notes: - Between each command, the user can even change the distribution of the mesh cells among the processors. It is sufficient to use the command MODI_MODELE. This mechanism remains licit when one chains different analyses ( POURSUITE mode). The rule being of course that this new distribution must remain compatible with the parallel parameter setting of the analysis (number of nodes/processors...). - Only MPI parallelism makes it possible to accelerate this step of the analysis. Now if one allocates too many MPI, the linear-system solution step risks being slowed down or being blocked for lack of memory. To remedy this problem, one can, with the linear solver MUMPS (cf. keyword SOLVEUR/REDUCTION_MPI), reduce the number of MPI processes used only in MUMPS. The unoccupied cores are then entrusted to the other level of parallelism, OpenMP. The overall memory consumption of the analysis is thus reduced, and this without slowing down the solutions of the linear system. One thus greatly accelerates the elementary-computation/assembly step without affecting either the memory cost or the time cost of the solution step. 4.2.3 Distributed data structures The distribution of the data implied by this type of numerical parallelism does not necessarily reduce the JEVEUX memory consumptions . For reasons of readability/maintainability, the usual Code_Aster objects are initialised with the same size as in sequential mode. Each MPI process merely “contents itself” with filling them partially with the data produced by the mesh cells for which the processor is responsible. It is then up to the parallel linear solver used in the remainder of the operator (MUMPS, PETSC or both) to assemble these incomplete and distributed data. One therefore does not generally resize these data structures; they contain many zero values. This strategy is tenable only so long as the main JEVEUX objects involved in the elementary computations/assemblies (CHAM_ELEM, RESU_ELEM, MATR_ASSE and CHAM_NO) do not size the memory constraints of the analysis (cf. §5 of U1.03.03). Normally their memory occupation is negligible compared with that of the linear solver. But when the latter (for example MUMPS) is itself Out-Of-Core [14]_ and parallelised in MPI (with the distribution of the data among processors that this implies), this hierarchy is no longer necessarily respected. Whence the introduction of an option (keyword MATR_DISTRIBUEE, cf. U4.50.01) making it possible truly to resize, as tightly as possible, the block of the Aster matrix proper to each MPI process. Note: - In distributed mode, each MPI process manipulates only incomplete matrices (resized or not). On the other hand, in order to avoid numerous MPI communications (during the evaluation of the stopping criteria, residual computations...), this scenario has not been retained for the right-hand-side vectors. Their constructions are indeed parallelised, but, at the end of the assembly, the partial contributions of each process are gathered. Thus, every MPI process knows in full the vectors (CHAM_NO) involved in the analysis. 4.3 Distribution of the basic linear-algebra computations 4.3.1 Description Use: for the general user via Astk. Scope of use: analyses comprising solutions of linear systems via MUMPS (use as a direct solver or as a preconditioner of PETSC/GCPC). Number of cores recommended: on Aster5, between 2 and 12. No more than the number of physical cores sharing the same physical memory. Gain: in elapsed time (but increase in the CPU time). Speed-up: Gains variable according to the cases (parallel efficiency [15]_ >50%). A low granularity is sufficient for this parallelism to remain efficient: 10.103 degrees of freedom per OpenMP thread. Type of parallelism: computer-science via the OpenMP language (ncpus). Scenario: 1c of §2. A classical use consists in taking advantage of a hybrid MPI+OpenMP parallelism in order to accentuate the performances of MUMPS and to take advantage of 100% of the machine resources (2b/1c or (2b/1c)+2c). Combination counter-productive with 2a, useful with 2b, possible but of little use with 2c (alone) or 1d. 4.3.2 Implementation The implementation of this parallel scheme is carried out transparently for the user. Via Astk, it is initialised by default as soon as one has selected a parallel version of Code_Aster (denoted _mpi) as well as a number of OpenMP threads at least equal to 2. Thus on the centralised Aster server, one must parameterise the following fields in the Options menu : - ncpus=k , number of OpenMP threads allocated (per MPI process if mpi_nbcpu>1). This parallel scheme is generally used in conjunction with the MPI parallelism of MUMPS. Because one advises, in general, not to allocate all the cores of a node in MPI alone . This can have the effect of slowing down the simulation because, even if part of the analyses is accelerated as a result of its distribution over more cores, since these share certain memory resources, the accesses to the data are, for their part, slowed down. To use more efficiently and at 100% all the resources allocated, one rather advises mixing MPI and OpenMP parallelism (cf. scenarios 2b/1c or (2b/1c)+2c). In this type of hybrid parallelism (MPI/OpenMP), the tool Astk [U1.04.00] automatically completes the number of threads according to the machine resources, as soon as the ncpus field is left empty. For example, on the centralised machine Aster5 , the nodes are composed of 24 cores. If one wishes to organise a hybrid parallelism of 12 MPI x 4 OpenMP, it is sufficient to set mpi_nbcpu to 12, mpi_nbnœud to 2 and ncpus= (or 4 explicitly). Note: - The implementation of this parallelism depends on the computing context (hardware, software) and on the linear-algebra libraries used. On the centralised Aster machine, one uses the threaded MKL BLAS. 4.4 Modal analyses of INFO_MODE/CALC_MODES 4.4.1 Description Use: for the general user via Astk. Scope of use: analyses comprising costly searches for eigenmodes. Number of cores recommended: several tens (for example, number of frequency sub-bands x 2, 4 or 8). Gain: in elapsed time or even in RAM (thanks to the second level of parallelism). Speed-up: Gains variable according to the cases: efficiency of the order of 70% on the first level of parallelism (on the frequency sub-bands) complemented by the possible parallelism of the second level (if SOLVEUR=MUMPS, complementary efficiency of the order of 20%). Type of parallelism: computer-science via the MPI language (mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud). Scenario: 1d of §2. Natively designed to couple to the parallelism 2b (or even 2b/1c). Chaining possible but of little use with 1b. Combination possible but of little use with 2a and impossible with 2c (out of scope). 4.4.2 Implementation The use of CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' cut into several sub-bands is to be favoured when one treats modal problems of medium or large sizes (>0.5M degrees of freedom) and/or when one seeks a good part of their spectra (> 50 modes). One then cuts the analysis into several frequency sub-bands. On each of these sub-bands, a modal solver carries out the associated mode search. To do this, this modal solver uses a linear solver intensively. These two computation bricks (modal solver and linear solver) are the dimensioning steps of the analysis in terms of memory and time consumption. It is on them that one must place the emphasis if one wants to reduce significantly the analysis costs of this operator (cf. figures 1.3a/b). Now, the organisation of the modal analysis over distinct sub-bands offers here an ideal framework for parallelism: distribution of large, almost independent analyses . Its parallelism makes it possible to gain a great deal in time but at the price of an extra cost in memory [16]_ . If one has available a sufficient number of processors (> the number of non-empty sub-bands), one can then engage a second level of parallelism via the linear solver (if one has chosen METHODE='MUMPS'). This will make it possible to continue to gain in time but, above all, it will make it possible to compensate for the memory extra cost of the first level or even to reduce notably the sequential memory peak. For an optimal use of CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' cut into several parallelised sub-bands, it is therefore advisable to: - Construct relatively balanced computation sub-bands . To do this, one can therefore, beforehand, calibrate the spectrum studied via a call to INFO_MODE U4.52.01 (if possible in parallel). Then launch the CALC_MODES analysis with the option 'BANDE' cut into several sub-bands parallelised according to the number of sub-bands chosen and the number of processors available. - Take sub-bands of between 50 and 100 modes . - Select a number of processors which is a multiple of the number of (non-empty) sub-bands. One thus reduces the load imbalances which harm the performances. For more details one may consult the user's documentation of the operator [U4.52.02]. 4.5 MISS3D analyses via CALC_MISS 4.5.1 Description Use: for the general user via Astk. Scope of use: analyses comprising MISS3D analyses. Number of cores recommended: with the option FICHIER_TEMPS, several tens (for example, number of frequencies x4 or X8); other option, up to 24 cores. Gain: in elapsed time. Speed-up: Gains variable according to the cases: efficiency of the order of 100% on the first level of parallelism (in MPI on the frequencies if FICHIER_TEMPS) complemented by the possible parallelism of the second level (in OpenMP). Type of parallelism: computer-science via the MPI language (mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud) if FICHIER_TEMPS, possibly complemented by an OpenMP parallelism (all the other options of CALC_MISS, ncpus). Scenario: 1e of §2. 4.5.2 Implementation If the CALC_MISS analyses are independent (option FICHIER_TEMPS), one can already distribute them over several nodes, reserving several MPI processes per node. Each one will treat a series of frequencies. One will not take all the cores of a node, in order to leave enough RAM for the MISS3D analysis. Then, in order to make the best use of these unoccupied cores, it is then advisable to add a second level of parallelism by activating OpenMP threads within each MISS3D MPI process (cf. figures 1.4a/b). If these CALC_MISS analyses are, on the other hand, not independent (option other than FICHIER_TEMPS), one will use only one node of the cluster and one will activate only the second level of parallelism via OpenMP. For more details one may consult the user's documentation of the operator [U2.06.07]. 4.6 Other distributions of analyses 4.6.1 Description Use: for the general user via Astk. Scope of use: analyses comprising frictional contact, calls to REST_SPEC_TEMP [U4.63.34], CALC_CHAMP [U4.81.04] (options REAC/FORC_NODA and _NOEU)... Number of cores recommended: no specific parameter setting (default parallel mode); keep the same MPI parallel parameter setting as for the parallelism of MUMPS: at least 50000 or 100000 degrees of freedom per MPI process. Except for the “parallelism in time” of CALC_CHAMP, which is efficient as soon as one reserves at least a dozen time steps per MPI process. Provided that the unit analysis of a single time step proves fairly costly. Gain: in elapsed time. Speed-up: Fairly large gain if the size above is respected: efficiency >50%. Type of parallelism: computer-science via the MPI language (mpi_nbcpu/mpi_nbnœud). Scenario: 1f of §2. 4.6.2 Implementation Implementation identical to that of MUMPS (cf. §5.5.2), except for CALC_CHAMP [U4.81.04], for which one must activate a specific keyword (PARALLELISME_TEMPS=’OUI’). One gains at least a factor of 2 (on the times consumed by the parallelised steps) by quadrupling the number of processors. Out-Of-Core (OOC) is a memory-management mode which consists in off-loading onto disk certain objects allocated by the code in order to free RAM. The OOC strategy makes it possible to treat larger problems but these disk accesses slow down the analysis. Conversely, In-Core (IC) mode consists in keeping the objects in RAM. This limits the size of the problems accessible but favours speed. One gains at least a factor of 2 (on the times consumed by the parallelised steps) by quadrupling the number of processors. Because of the MPI buffers required by the communications of eigenvectors at the end of MODE_ITER_SIMULT. 5 Numerical parallelisms 5.1 Direct solver MULT_FRONT 5.1.1 Description Use: for the general user via Astk . Scope of use: analyses comprising costly solutions of linear systems (in general STAT/DYNA_NON_LINE, MECA_STATIQUE...). Number of cores recommended: 2 or 4. Gain: in elapsed time. Speed-up: Gains variable according to the cases (parallel efficiency ≈50%). One needs a good granularity for this parallelism to remain efficient: at least 50.103 degrees of freedom per core. Type of parallelism: numerical via the OpenMP language (ncpus). Scenario: 2a of §2. Chaining possible but of little use with 1b, 2b or 2c. Combination counter-productive with 1c, possible but of little use with 1d. 5.1.2 Implementation This multifrontal method developed in-house (cf. R6.02.02 or U4.50.01 §3.5) is used via the keyword SOLVEUR/METHODE='MULT_FRONT'. It is the linear solver (historical and self-contained) recommended by default in sequential mode on models of small or medium size ( 50%). One needs a medium granularity for this parallelism to remain efficient: 50.103 degrees of freedom per MPI process. Type of parallelism: numerical via the MPI language. Scenario: 2c of §3. Natively designed to chain to the parallelisms 1b or 2b; chaining possible but of little use with 2a. Combination possible but of little use with 1c, out of scope with 1d. 5.3.2 Implementation This library of iterative solvers (cf. R6.01.02 or U4.50.01 §3.9) is used via the keyword SOLVEUR/METHODE='PETSC'. This type of linear solver is recommended for treating either frontier problems of very large size (>5M degrees of freedom), or, in non-linear analysis, for taking full advantage of the sharing of the preconditioner between different Newton steps . The implementation of this parallelism is carried out as for the MUMPS package (cf. §5.2). Note: - Unlike the direct parallel solvers (MUMPS, MULT_FRONT), the iterative ones are not universal (they cannot be used in modal analysis) and not always robust. They can be very competitive (in time and above all in memory), but one must find the operating point (algorithm, preconditioner...) suited to the problem. However, on this last point, the generalised use (and parameterised by default) of MUMPS in single precision as a preconditioner (PRE_COND='LDLT_SP') has considerably improved matters.

u2.08.07 Parametric analyses - Distribution of analyses u2.08.07 Parametric analyses - Distribution of analyses Summary: Certain studies lead one to carry out a more or less large number of analyses (sometimes several thousand), corresponding to the variations of the parameters. The use of standard analyses, consisting in modifying or creating the command file for each of the parameter sets, is tedious, difficult to manage and a source of error. The method presented in this document makes it possible to facilitate the implementation of such parametric studies by carrying out a minimum of interventions. From the standard study and a file containing the parameter set, the analyses are derived and executed automatically. The parametric analyses being independent of one another, it is possible to use the machine resources available by submitting the analyses in parallel. 1 General points 1.1 Presentation A parametric study is a standard study (ETUDE tab) in which one wishes to vary one or several parameters, such as for example: - Material parameters : Young's modulus, elastic limit,... - Geometric parameters : thickness of the shell, cross-section of a beam,... - Loading parameters : pressure, orientation of a force, ... - ... If one carries out these analyses as a standard analysis, the number of analyses to be carried out can become very large, several thousand analyses, and their implementation becomes very tedious. The aim of this document is to describe the methodology to be implemented in Code_Aster in order to carry out this type of study with the minimum of intervention. Overall, a parametric study is the data of a nominal study (command file common to each parameter) and of a parameter set: Code_Aster will derive the nominal study into several studies according to the parameters supplied, then will execute each derivation taking into account the machine resources available. Figure 1.1-а: Derived studies 1.2 Purpose of the tutorial The aim of the tutorial is to supply the user with as much information as possible to allow him or her to implement parametric studies. This document answers the following questions: - How to prepare a parametric study (files,...), - How to launch a parametric study (directories, options,...), - How to generate and re-read a database, - How to use the analysis resources available (distribution of the analyses,...), - How to recover the results of the parametric study (command file, results directory). In the last paragraph one presents a detailed example of a parametric study. In this document, one assumes that the user is familiar with standard Code_Aster analyses. Otherwise he or she is invited to consult the following documents U1.04.00, ... and to begin by carrying out a classical study. 2 Mode of operation of the parametric analyses 2.1 Principle The implementation of parametric studies in Code_Aster is relatively simple. Nevertheless it is important that: - your standard study runs without problem before undertaking this type of analysis. - you have properly defined beforehand the parameters that you wish to vary: - their names, - their values, - the analysis scenarios to be executed. In the case of a standard study you have at least: - As input: - a command file (.comm) - the necessary data files (.mail, .med,...) - the parameters (time and memory) - As output: - a message file (.mess) - a result file (.resu, .med,...) To carry out a parametric study you need in addition: - As input: - a file describing the parameter set (.distr) - a results directory (.repe) - an Astk option distrib=oui. Depending on the server, one may need to specify the batch class in which the analyses will be submitted. - the parameters (time/memory) are the same for all the analyses; those of the master job can be fixed independently of the study by the plugin mechanism (cf. U1.04.00). - As output: - a results directory (.repe) In the following paragraphs we take up all these points in detail. In the following table we have summarised the obligatory and optional elements that one finds in the case of a parametric study. | Elements | Standard studies | Parametric studies | Comments | § | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Command file | c | c | Defines the command set Use of the parameters | | | Mesh file | c | c | Definition of the mesh | | | distr | x | p | Definition of the parameters and of the analysis scenarios: value of the parameters, either explicitly or in a computed manner | 2.2.1 | | .mess | c | x | Message file | | | .resu | c | x | Result file in aster format | | | .rmed,... | c | p | Result file in med format | | | repe_out | c | p | Results directory | | | hostfile | x | p | Makes it possible to launch parallel analyses | 2.4 | | astk | c | p | Launch options distrib = oui | 2.3 | | base | c | p | The databases are stored in the repe_out | 2.4 | | poursuite | c | c | | 2.4 | | x : no file c: classical file p: parametric file | | | | | Table 2.1-1: Summary of the obligatory and optional elements in a parametric study 2.2 Implementation The actions to be undertaken in order to implement a parametric analysis are the following: 1. Writing of a parameter set, 2. Use of the parameters in the command file, 3. Under Astk, ETUDE tab: definition of the results directory and addition of the parameter set, 4. Under Astk, OUTILS menu: definition of the type of analysis 2.2.1 Writing of a parameter set The description, in the python language, of the parameter set is carried out in the '.distr' file, in which one finds - the list of the parameters, - the values that these parameters will take successively (analysis scenarios). Example: # young, temp_impo : nom des variables # la variable young aura comme valeur 2.1E11 et 7.E10 # la variable temp_impo aura comme valeur 100 et 273 VALE=( _F(young=2.1E11, temp_impo = 100.),# scénario de calcul n°1 _F(young=7.0E10, temp_impo = 273.), # scénario de calcul n°2 ) Figure 2.2.1-а: Example of an explicit ''distr'' file In this example, one has two analysis scenarios (no. 1 and no. 2) with the parameters young and temp_impo, which will take successively as value (2.1E11,100) and (7.0E10,273) . At this stage, although the name of the parameters is sufficiently explicit, nothing makes it possible to say how they will be used. For the parameter young, this suggests that it will be used during the definition of the material, but nothing for the moment makes it possible to assert this. From the point of view of the python language, the '.distr' file contains a list of dictionaries named VALE (each dictionary corresponding to an analysis). One uses _F as in the command file to define these dictionaries. The definition of the parameters of the analysis scenarios can be given explicitly or in a computed manner. Note In the previous example, the definition of the parameters and the analysis scenarios are given explicitly. It is possible to call upon the functionalities of the python language in order to define them automatically; a practical example is presented in § 3.2.2 ). The name of the parameters is defined by the user; it is advisable to use explicit names. 2.2.2 Use of the parameters in the command file In paragraph § 2.2.1 , one has defined the parameter set (name, values and analysis scenarios); the aim now is to use these parameters in the command file, at the desired place. The taking into account of these parameters in the command file is carried out in two stages: 1. declaration of the python variables: the parameters 2. use of these variables in the command file. - Declaration of the parameters (python variables) Before any use in a command or in any expression, it is obligatory that the parameters be known. The aim is not to initialise them once again, but simply to declare them as python variables. Example: in the previous .distr file, one has defined the parameters young and temp_impo. One will therefore find in the command file the following lines: DEBUT() ... young = 0. temp_impo = 0. ... FIN() Figure 2.2.2-а: Declaration of the parameters Notes: The values assigned in the command file will not be used; they will be replaced automatically by those defined in the 'distr' file, for each of the analysis scenarios. Avoid choosing a parameter name identical to a keyword of Code_Aster. The substitution being made by the regular expression '^( )nom = ', there could be confusion. The case being significant, using names in lower case makes it possible to avoid this pitfall. - Use of the parameters The use of the parameters in the command file is carried out in the classical manner, within the commands, the mathematical expressions, ... Example: DEBUT() ... young=0. temp_impo=0. ... mat=DEFI_MATERIAU(ELAS=_F(E=young,...)) ... t0 = AFFE_CHAR_CINE=(THER_IMPO=_F(TEMP=temp_impo, GROUP_NO='CHAUD',..) ... FIN() Figure 2.2.2-б : Command file 2.2.3 Type of the parameters The type of the parameters may be arbitrary. Then, one must bear in mind that the replacement is textual at the time of the instantiation of the command set for a given parameter set. Example: Let the parameter set be: VALE=(_F( young = 2.1e11, indice = 4, nomp = "'INST'", objf = 'FON1',),...) and the header of the command set: young = 2.e11indice = 0nomp = 'X'objf = FON0... The command set derived for the parameter set will be: young = 2.1e11indice = 4nomp = 'INST'objf = FON1... The difference is visible for the last two parameters, where one sees that one has used the text of the character string of nomp and objf (and not the representation of the latter, so a pair of quotation marks has disappeared). This makes it possible to parameterise the use of concepts. Here, one uses the function FON1 as the parameter objf. 2.2.4 Parameters of file type In the cases where the variable parameter is a file (for example in order to read a different mesh), it is a matter of making variable the name of this file (text string or else file number) and of using DEFI_FICHIER. Example which mixes a file name in the form of a character string and the same thing using a mesh number: Let the parameter set be: VALE=( _F( fname = "'/tmp/maillage_01.mmed'", indice = 1,), _F( fname = "'/tmp/maillage_02.mmed'", indice = 2,),...) and the command file: fname = 'nom_de_fichier_med'indice = 0# using the file name DEFI_FICHIER(ACTION='ASSOCIER', UNITE=20, FICHIER=fname)meshA = LIRE_MAILLAGE(FORMAT='MED', UNITE=20)# using a file index (one constructs the name# of the file from the index over 2 characters# with leading zeros)filename = '/tmp/maillage_{i:0>2}.mmed'.format(i=indice)DEFI_FICHIER(ACTION='ASSOCIER', UNITE=21, FICHIER=filename)meshB = LIRE_MAILLAGE(FORMAT='MED', UNITE=21) 2.3 Launching of the studies: Astk The launching of the parametric studies is managed directly by Astk. This launching is identical to that of a classical study subject to the addition of complementary information such as: - addition in the study profile of a line to take into account the 'distr' file - addition in the study profile of a line to define the results directory of type 'repe' - initialisation, in the option menu, of the parameter distrib to 'OUI'. Figure 2.3-а : Definition of the parameter set, directory (astk) Figure 2.3-б: option distrib (Astk) Notes It is possible, as for all Code_Aster analyses, to launch the parametric studies in command-line mode with as_run. For this, it is necessary to have available beforehand the .export file: > as_run --serv nom_etude.export 2.3.1 Management of the analyses and of the results The analysis directory is the same as that of the results: it is defined in the study profile under the type 'repe'. After the execution of the parametric analyses, one finds in this directory as many calc_i directories as analyses launched. One also finds a flash directory. The detail of each of these directories is presented below. 2.3.1.1 Management of the analyses The command files corresponding to each of the scenarios are derived automatically from the nominal command file and from the parameter set. These files are stored in the calc_i directories. The output files (message and error) of each analysis are stored in a single directory, the flash directory. All the information concerning the progress of each execution is found in this directory. 2.3.1.2 Management of the results As for a classical analysis, the user has the possibility of generating output files (tables, graphs, ...). He or she will have to define them in the standard command file. These outputs will be common to all the analysis scenarios. For example, suppose that the user wants to print a table in the file of logical unit 38 and a result in med format in the file of logical unit 39. He or she will have to define, in the nominal command file, the name of each of the output files so that they can be stored in the directory REPE_OUT produced automatically by Code_Aster. The extract from the command file below illustrates this definition: DEFI_FICHIER(UNITE=38,FICHIER='./REPE_OUT/table.out') IMPR_TABLE(TABLE=SIYY,UNITE=38,NOM_PARA=('NOEUD','SIYY')); DEFI_FICHIER(UNITE=39,FICHIER='./REPE_OUT/poutre.rmed') IMPR_RESU(FORMAT='MED',UNITE=39,RESU=_F(RESULTAT=depl)) Figure 2.3.1.2-а : definition of the output files and of their logical units Notes: In the case of a parametric study the files .mess and .resu are not created. However, consultation of the files of the flash directory makes it possible to gather the information ordinarily issued in the .mess . 2.3.1.3 Directory tree The figure below presents the location of the files and directories of 2 analysis scenarios. 2.4 Complementary functionalities 2.4.1 Generating a database As for a standard study, it is possible to generate a database. To do this, it is sufficient to add in the study profile an entry of type 'base' with as name that of the repe directory. One will find, for each of the analysis scenarios, the corresponding database stored in the directory calc_i/base. Figure 2.4.1-а: Example of a study profile for generating a database per analysis 2.4.2 Carrying out a restart As for a standard study, it is possible to exploit a database. To do this, it is sufficient to add in the study profile an entry of type 'base' with as name that of the repe directory in which each database to be read is present in the directory calc_i/base. Figure 2.4.2-а: Example of a study profile for exploiting the database associated with each analysis 2.4.3 Directory tree One presents the directory tree in the presence of a reading of a database for each of the 5 analyses. One will note the presence of a hostfile file, which will be the subject of the following paragraph. 2.4.4 Distribution of analyses In the case of parametric studies, the analyses are independent of one another. It is therefore possible to use the machine resources available at the time of the distribution of the analyses. One must therefore create a file of type 'hostfile' defining the machine resources. In it one defines: - the name of the node on which the jobs will be submitted, - the maximum number of jobs to be submitted at the same time, - the total memory allocated. Note: On a shared server, it is advisable to use the file defined by the administrator and therefore not to redefine one's own resources file. If the hostfile file is not present in the study profile, it is the file batch_distrib_hostfile present in the directory etc/codeaster which will be used by default. - For example on the centralised server, the resources are managed by the batch software. In this case, the hostfile file simply declares the number of analyses which will be submitted at the same time. Here one can submit up to 32 analyses on each front-end node (the memory is indicated as infinite , that is to say that one leaves the batch software to manage it): [:ref: ataster1 ] cpu=32 mem=9999999 [:ref: ataster2 ] cpu=32 mem=9999999 Figure 2.4.4-a : Example of a hostfile file with a batch server For your resources file to be taken into account, it is sufficient to add it in your study profile, specifying the type 'hostfile'. In the case of the use of a set of machines available interactively, the hostfile file could look like: # nom du nœud [:ref: machine1 ] # nombre de CPU disponible cpu=4 # mémoire totale de la machine en Mo mem=4000 # nom du nœud [:ref: machine2 ] # nombre de CPU disponible cpu=8 # mémoire totale de la machineen Mo mem=4000 Figure 2.4.4-b : Example of an interactive hostfile file One will be able to have up to 12 analyses executed simultaneously, according to the memory available, distributed over the two machines. If each analysis requires 2 GB of memory, there will be at most two analyses per machine so as not to exceed the total amount of memory available. 2.4.5 Pre/post-processings common to all the analyses One has 4 keywords in the “distr” file: PRE_CALCUL, UNITE_PRE_CALCUL, POST_CALCUL, UNITE_POST_CALCUL. PRE_CALCUL (resp. POST_CALCUL) defines a text (a set of Aster commands) which will be included just after DEBUT (resp. just before FIN). UNITE_PRE_CALCUL (resp. UNITE_POST_CALCUL) offers the same functioning except that one supplies a logical-unit number. This modification is made for all the files of type “comm” present in the profile. This possibility is used in particular by the recalibration command MACR_RECAL in order to add a post-processing to each slave analysis. 3 Examples of application 3.1 Presentation The example chosen to present the implementation of parametric studies is presented in the figure below. It is a beam clamped at one end and subjected to a distributed pressure at the other end. The aim of this parametric study is to determine the evolution of the von Mises equivalent stress along the upper line of the beam as a function of the orientation \alpha . The data files are those of the test case distr01a. The analyses will be carried out every 22.5° , for an angle \alpha varying from 0° to 90° . The number of analysis scenarios to be carried out is therefore 5. In the table below we present the values that the parameters \mathit{FX} and \mathit{FY} will take successively. | Scenario no. | Angle \alpha | \mathit{FX}=P.\cos(a) | \mathit{FY}=P.\sin(a) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | 0.0° | {10}^{6} | 0. | | 2 | 22.5° | 9.23879\times {10}^{5} | -3.82683\times {10}^{5} | | 3 | 45.0° | 7.07106\times {10}^{5} | -7.07106\times {10}^{5} | | 4 | 67.5° | 3.82683\times {10}^{5} | -9.23879\times {10}^{5} | | 5 | 90.0° | 0. | -{10}^{6} | Table 3.1-1: Values of the parameters The command file of the nominal study is distr01a.comm. In the remainder of this presentation, we shall detail the implementation of this type of analysis, namely: - the generation of the 'distr' file - the use of the parameters in the command file. 3.2 Definition of the parameter set and of the analysis cases It is possible to define the parameters in the '.distr' file in two ways: - Explicitly: in this case the user supplies all the values that the parameters can take. - Computed: in this case the user resorts to python programming - to compute these parameters automatically, in conditional form or not, - to define these analysis scenarios automatically, for example by sweeping all the possible combinations of parameters or by choosing the min/mean/max values of the parameters. 3.2.1 Explicit 'distr' file In this case, one writes explicitly the values of the parameters in the 'distr' file. In the case of the example, it appears in the following form (file distr01a.50 of the test case): VALE=( _F(F_Norm=1.E6, F_Tang=0.), # cas de calcul n°1 _F(F_Norm=9.23879E5,F_Tang=-3.82683E5), # cas de calcul n°2 _F(F_Norm=7.07106E5,F_Tang=-7.07106E5), # cas de calcul n°3 _F(F_Norm=3.82683E5,F_Tang=-9.23879E5), # cas de calcul n°4 _F(F_Norm=0., F_Tang=-1.E6), # cas de calcul n°5 ) Figure 3.2.1-а : Explicit 'distr' file 3.2.2 Computed 'distr' file In this case, the writing of the 'distr' file is less simple; one calls upon the programming of the python language. For this example, it appears in the following form (file distr01a.51 of the test case): from math import pi, cos, sin import numpy VALE = [] n = 5 list_theta = numpy.arange(n) 22.5 pi / 180. P = 1.e6 for a in list_theta: VALE.append(_F(F_Norm = P cos(a), F_Tang = P sin(a),)) Figure 3.2.2-а : Computed 'distr' file 3.3 Use of the parameters in the command file It is sufficient to reference, in the nominal command file, the names of the parameters present in the 'distr' file. DEBUT() # Initialisation (ici apparaitront les valeurs des paramètres) F_Norm=0. F_Tang=0. ... CHAR=AFFE_CHAR_MECA(MODELE=MODE, FORCE_CONTOUR=_F(GROUP_MA = 'Press', FX = F_Norm, FY = F_Tang),) 3.4 Post-processings The file distr01a.11 gives an example of post-processing with re-reading of all the result files, merging of the results in a single table, printing of a curve with all the evolutions of the stress ... 4 Advice on use Here is some advice: - The standard study must be valid before being derived over the parameter set. It must run without error. - Before being derived over the parameter set, it is also important to optimise the analyses by reducing the execution time, ... - Check that the parameter file 'distr' is correct. - Beware of the disk space: if the number of analyses and their size are large, the saving of the databases can take up a great deal of space. - Check the definition of the variables in the command file: is it correct? - Test the correct functioning of your parametric study by using a 'distr' file which defines only a single parameter set. 5 Questions/Answers | Questions | Answers | | --- | --- | | Where does one define the parameters? | In the file: .distr: one defines there their names and their values .comm: one defines there the python variable name | | Where does one define the analysis scenarios? | In the 'distr' file: VALE(_F(...)_F(...)) | | What must one do under Astk? | At a minimum: define a line for the 'distr' file define a line for the 'repe' directory define the launch option distrib=oui | | Where are the results found? | In the repe directory | | I cannot find my results! | Have you created in the command file the following command: DEFI_FICHIER(UNITE=numero_unite_logique, FICHIER='.REPE_OUT/nom_fichier') | | I cannot find a .mess and .resu file | These files do not exist; on the other hand you can consult, in the directory repe/flash, the files describing the execution of each of the scenarios. | | My analyses do not work? | Analyse the messages possibly issued on the screen; consult the output and error files present in the flash directory |

u2.08.09 1 u2.08.09 Mesh adaptation in the non-linear regime Illustration 2: Time marching with mesh adaptation 1 u2.08.09 Mesh adaptation in the non-linear regime Summary: This document presents the methodology for carrying out a non-linear study with mesh adaptation. This adaptation of the mesh in the course of the transient is obtained with the help of the HOMARD software, called via the command MACR_ADAP_MAIL U7.03.01. An example illustrates the possibilities and the implementation of remeshing strategies. 1 Introduction Mesh adaptation provides assistance to the user in supplying analyses which are as reliable as possible with respect to the discretisation errors induced by the finite-element solution method. We shall not detail in this document the principle of adaptation, and we refer the reader to the document U2.08.01. We merely recall a few elements. Schematically, an iteration of mesh adaptation appears as in the figure below. The software computes the numerical solution on mesh number k , then deduces from it the values of the error indicator over the whole mesh. From the knowledge of mesh number k and of indicator number k , the mesh-adaptation software HOMARD creates the new mesh number k+1 . Illustration 1: Iteration of mesh adaptation For a static analysis, this amounts to seeking to improve the solution by a succession of analyses on different meshes. For a transient analysis in time, the analysis is suspended at a given time instant; the mesh is adapted; the analysis resumes on the new mesh. It is this case that we tackle here. Indeed, in the case of the solution of a non-linear transient, restarting the analysis is not necessarily a straightforward matter. The aim of this document is to help the user to implement this type of modelling. 2 Adaptation in the non-linear regime In this part, one describes the typical problem that one seeks to solve, as well as the essential difficulties that it presents. 2.1 Problem considered The typical problem of interest is a transient involving a model with a non-linear constitutive law. One wishes to adapt the support mesh in the course of the solution according to the diagram of the figure . The principle is the following: - one solves the transient over one or several time steps - one adapts the mesh on the basis of the computation of an error indicator - one resumes the transient In fact, this diagram conceals a large part of the complexity of the problem. Let us take the example of the use of an elastoplastic von Mises constitutive law with isotropic hardening. At each time step, one stores the state of the analysis domain \Omega , given by the displacement field, the stress field and the field of internal variables (u,\sigma ,\alpha ) . It is this triplet, carried by the mesh M , which completely determines the equilibrium of \Omega . Now, in the case of the use of mesh adaptation, the mesh becomes an evolving element. If one assumes that the mesh is adapted at each time step, one must also transfer the triplet (u,\sigma ,\alpha ) from one mesh to the other. This is the projection phase. Unfortunately, once the projection has been carried out, nothing ensures that the new triplet ensures the equilibrium of the domain on the new mesh. One must for this purpose correct the new triplet. This is the rebalancing phase. 2.2 Rebalancing phase In what follows, one will use the following assumptions: - use of an elastoplastic von Mises constitutive law with isotropic hardening - adaptation of the mesh at each loading step One sets the following notations: - {M}_{i} denotes the mesh at loading step i - ({u}_{i},{\sigma}_{i},{\alpha}_{i}) denote the triplet displacement field, stress field and field of internal variables at loading step i - {(x)}_{{M}_{i}} denotes the quantity x carried by the mesh {M}_{i} One now details the analysis process. One starts from a balanced state {({u}_{i},{\sigma}_{i},{\alpha}_{i})}_{{M}_{i}} carried by the mesh {M}_{i} at loading step i . One proceeds to the solution of the problem at loading step i+1 . One obtains the balanced state {({u}_{i+1},{\sigma}_{i+1},{\alpha}_{i+1})}_{{M}_{i}} . On the basis of the computation of an error indicator, one produces a new mesh {M}_{i+1} . To continue the analysis, one must project the balanced state {({u}_{i+1},{\sigma}_{i+1},{\alpha}_{i+1})}_{{M}_{i}} onto the new mesh {M}_{i+1} . We shall detail this projection later. One then obtains the state {({u}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}},{\sigma}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}},{\alpha}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}})}_{{M}_{i+1}} but which is not necessarily balanced. Indeed, the projection phase can induce perturbations on each of the 3 fields and remove their consistency. It is therefore a matter of rebalancing the mechanical state at time instant i+1 of the domain \Omega discretised by {M}_{i+1} . To do this, one refers to the documentation R5.03.01 “Quasi-static non-linear algorithm” and, not taking into account the command variables, one finds that the system which one solves at the first iteration of each time step is the following: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{K}_{i}.\Delta {u}_{i+1}^{0}+{B}^{T}.\Delta {\lambda}_{i+1}^{0}={L}_{i+1}^{\text{méca}}-{Q}_{i}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i}\\ B.\Delta {u}_{i+1}^{0}={u}_{i+1}^{d}-B.{u}_{i}\end{array} The right-hand sides {L}_{i+1}^{\text{méca}}-{Q}_{i}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i} and {\mathrm{u}}_{i+1}^{d}-\mathrm{B}.{\mathrm{u}}_{i} measure respectively: - the deviation from equilibrium between the loading and a mechanical stress state - the deviation from the verification of the boundary conditions The solution of the underlying non-linear system leads to the cancellation of these deviations and to the production of a balanced mechanical state. This is exactly what one seeks to do, not starting from the mechanical state of the previous time instant {({u}_{i},{\sigma}_{i},{\alpha}_{i})}_{{M}_{i}} as in () but from the projected mechanical state {({u}_{i+1}^{\mathit{proj}},{\sigma}_{i+1}^{\mathit{proj}},{\alpha}_{i+1}^{\mathit{proj}})}_{{M}_{i+1}} . If one transposes it to the case of interest, the system to be solved is therefore the following: \lbrace \begin{array}{}{K}_{i}.\Delta {u}_{i+1}^{0}+{B}^{T}.\Delta {\lambda}_{i+1}^{0}={L}_{i+1}^{\text{méca}}-{Q}_{i+1}^{T}.{\sigma}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}}\\ B.\Delta {u}_{i+1}^{0}={u}_{i+1}^{d}-B.{u}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}}\end{array} From the point of view of the modelling, this therefore amounts to relaunching the solution of loading step i+1 using as initial state the projected mechanical state {({u}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}},{\sigma}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}},{\alpha}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}})}_{{M}_{i+1}} . The use of the projected mechanical state {({u}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}},{\sigma}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}},{\alpha}_{i+1}^{\mathrm{proj}})}_{{M}_{i+1}} as initial state is essential. It first makes it possible to start from a starting point as close as possible to the arrival point and therefore to increase the chances of seeing the Newton method converge. But there is a much more important reason. In the context of the use of irreversible constitutive laws, the internal variables, such as the cumulative plastic strain, carry the mechanical history of each point of the structure. One must start from a state of internal variables as faithful as possible to the real state of the structure in order to represent its mechanical history properly. This leads us to a new observation: it is essential to produce a projected mechanical state {({u}_{i+1}^{\mathit{proj}},{\sigma}_{i+1}^{\mathit{proj}},{\alpha}_{i+1}^{\mathit{proj}})}_{{M}_{i+1}} which is as faithful as possible. This is what we shall now address. 2.3 Projection The projection of the fields is carried out with the operator PROJ_CHAMP; for any information on its syntax and its complete functionalities, the reader is referred to U4.72.05. We are interested in the projection of the mechanical state, which is composed of 3 fields. We shall examine the projection of each of these fields. 2.3.1 Projection of the displacement field The displacement field DEPL is a continuous field at the nodes. Its projection poses no particular problem. The collocation method, which is used by default for this type of field, is perfectly suited. 2.3.2 Projection of the stress field The stress (and/or force) field SIEF_ELGA is natively computed at the integration points. In order to minimise the perturbation induced by the projection, it is preferable to exploit directly the field at the integration point. This is the method that the projection operator will choose automatically for this field. It is possible to carry out the projection using a field by element at the nodes or a field at the nodes. This implies additional manipulations which are fairly technical. This approach is not recommended. 2.3.3 Projection of the field of internal variables The field of internal variables VARI_ELGA is natively computed at the integration points. In order to minimise the perturbation induced by the projection, it is preferable to exploit directly the field at the integration point. This is the method that the projection operator will choose automatically for this field. As for the stress field, it is possible to use a field by element at the nodes or a field at the nodes, but this poses more of a problem. Indeed, if one considers the case of von Mises plasticity, the cumulative plastic strain p must always be positive, p\ge 0 . Consider the figure . It represents a SEG2 element with 2 nodes \mathit{N1} and \mathit{N2} and with 2 integration points \mathit{PG1} and \mathit{PG2} . This element carries a field at its integration points of value \mathit{VG1} and \mathit{VG2} , which are both positive. Now, following the extrapolation to the vertices, one observes that the value \mathit{VN1} at the vertex \mathit{N1} indeed remains positive whereas the value \mathit{VN2} at the vertex \mathit{N2} becomes negative. In order to be used as an initial value, the cumulative plastic strain p must be positive or zero; the value \mathit{VN2} will therefore be set to zero.
