The chaining of commands is the following: - Edit/Set Operations, - select G0 as the graph to be copied, S0 as the curve to be copied and G0 as the destination graph and “copy” as the operation to be carried out, finally “accept”, - one must now modify column Y of the set S1; this is done by opening the command console: Window/Commands, and typing “s1.y = s0.y^2” in order to obtain the previous curve squared (Cf. [§5.4] of the User's Guide for a complete list of the operations allowed). | | | | --- | --- | 2.3.2 creation in the console One opens the command console straight away: Window/Commands. - One first creates the curve by specifying the number of points (identical to the number of points of the set S0) “s1 length s0.length”, - then one duplicates the abscissae “s1.x = s0.x”, - finally one defines the ordinates “s1.y = s0.y^2” 3 Organisation of Grace into graphs and curves 3.1 General points For Grace, a graph is a plot which can contain several curves; a Grace “project” (which can be saved in a file bearing the extension “agr) can contain several graphs. The graphs are named G0, G1,... The curves are named S0, S1,... 3.2 Management of the graphs The user can manage the graphs in each graph-selection list (for example in the menus Edit/Arrange Graphs, Edit/Set Operations, Edit/Overlay Graphs, Plot/Graph Appearance as in the illustration below, or Data/Import/Ascii). In the zone below “Graph”, one finds a list of graphs (here, the project comprises two graphs, the first comprising three curves, the second comprising a single curve). One will note the “(-)” in front of the first graph, which means that the first graph is “hidden” (hidden, i.e. not displayed), whereas the (+) in front of the second means that it is displayed (showed). The graph or graphs highlighted are the graph or graphs concerned by the action in progress: here, the modification of the graph concerns G0 (even if it is hidden!). Likewise, on import of a curve: the curve that the user is preparing to import will go into the graph G0 (as previously, this graph being hidden, the imported curve will not be displayed). In certain menus (Plot/Graph Appearance for example), it is possible to select several graphs (in the usual way: Ctrl + left click for a selection of graphs “one by one”, or Shift + left click on the first and last element of a contiguous list, or left click + movement of the mouse over a list....), whereas other menus (Data/Import/Ascii for example) allow only a single graph to be selected. An important (and not very intuitive) command is the right click on the list of graphs, which opens a menu comprising the following commands: - focus to: in order to define the active graph (useful if several graphs are displayed: the active graph is the one which receives the actions when the user uses the icons; likewise, in order to manage the curves of a graph, the graph must be the active graph); - hide: hides the graph; - show: displays the graph; - duplicate: duplicates the graph and all its curves; - kill: destroys the graph; - swap: exchanges two graphs (two graphs must be highlighted); - create new: creates a new (empty) graph. In summary, in order to create a new graph, one must open the list of graphs (by using for example Plot/Graph Appearance), right-click on the list of graphs and choose “Create New”). One will note that there exists no menu making it possible to carry out this action directly. 3.3 Management of the curves The principle of management of the curves is roughly the same as that concerning the graphs. Grace displays the list of curves (of the active graph: warning, once again, the active graph is not necessarily visible!) in the menus which manipulate the curves: Edit/Data Sets, Edit/Set Operations, Data/Data set operations, Plot/Set Appearance as in the following illustration: The active graph is here G0 (it is recalled as a prefix of the curves in the list); it possesses three curves (one will note the mention, in brackets, after the name of the curves, of the dimension — here 2 for X and Y — and of the length — here, the curves all have 150 points —). In the list of curves, a right click opens a menu: - hide: hides the curve; - show: displays the curve; - bring to front: puts the curve in the foreground; - send to back: puts the curve in the background; - duplicate: duplicates the curve; - kill: deletes the curve; - kill data: deletes the data but not the curve, i.e. all the formatting is retained, which can be very practical if the user has two identical graphs to produce from different data: it is sufficient to create a graph, then to remove all the data with “kill data”, and to import the second series of data: the two graphs will have exactly the same appearance; - swap: exchanges the position of the two curves - edit: edits the data; - create new: creates a new curve; - pack all sets: ? - selector operations: a sort of preference menu for the display of this list of curves. Note: All the previous operations on the curves are done inside one and the same graph. In the case where the user would need to copy a curve from one graph onto another, one must use the menu Edit/Set Operations. 4 Formatting of the graphs and of the curves 4.1 Arrangement of graphs on a page Grace makes it possible to display several graphs on a page. The menu which manages this function is Edit/Arrange Graphs: The choices above indicate that a matrix of (2x2) graphs is to be plotted (plus options concerning the numbering order of the graphs and the various margins), which makes it possible to obtain a page of the form: 4.2 Formatting of the graphs The menu Plot/Graph Appearance makes it possible to define the formatting of the graphs, i.e. all the formatting common to all the curves of the graph, apart from the definition of the axes, which is accessible via Plot/Axis Properties. One confines oneself here to a summary description; for more advanced functions, the simplest is no doubt to go through the tabs of the dialogue window of Plot/Graph Appearance directly. In order to give a title to a graph, the text of the title is to be put in the Main tab, the character size being adjustable in the Title tab. The decision to display a legend or not is given in the Main tab, the position of the legend box being defined in the Leg. Box tab, the size of the characters used being specified in the Legend tab. The legend text, defined curve by curve, will be seen further on. For the axes (hence the menu Plot/Axis Properties), one also confines oneself to the most common commands. First of all one must note, in the dialogue box opened by Plot/Axis Properties, the drop-down menu which makes it possible to define the axis that one is in the process of modifying (X axis, Y axis,...). In this box one can choose the start and end values of the axis (via the Start and End fields), as well as the type of scale (linear, algorithmic, etc). One can give a title (label) to the axes in the Main tab, the character size as well as their orientation being defined in the 'Axis label & bar' tab. | | | --- | | | The major ticks (Major spacing, which are provided with a value indication) and the minor ones (minor ticks, which are only a stroke) are also defined in the Main tab; it is to be noted that the definition of the major ticks is done in the unit of the axes (for example put 10 for an axis going from 0 to 100 in order to number by steps of 10) whereas the minor ones are in number of subdivisions between each major tick (for example put 9 in order to graduate the previous subdivisions of 10 every 1, or 1 in order to graduate every 5): see the following illustrations. The way of writing the value corresponding to each major tick is defined in Tick labels, the way of drawing the major and the minor ticks being indicated in Tick marks. 4.3 Formatting of the curves The formatting of the curves is controlled from the menu Plot/Set Appearance. In the dialogue box opened by this menu, there is first of all a list of the curves contained in the current graph, which makes it possible to select the curve whose properties one is editing. In order to attach a legend to a curve, one must define the text of the legend in the Main tab (Legend, String). One will note that it is possible to produce complex legends. One can choose the line style, its colour and its thickness as well as the symbols used to materialise each point in the Main tab (Line Properties and Symbol Properties). More precise definitions can be added in the Line and Symbols tabs respectively. | | | --- | | | 5 Use of the toolbar The toolbar is displayed vertically at the top left of the Grace window: - The magnifying glass makes it possible to zoom by defining a zone with the mouse; - The “AS” icon (for autoscale) makes it possible to redefine the framing (zoom) automatically. - The buttons “Z” and “z” serve to zoom out and zoom in respectively. - The arrows serve to move the plotted zone. - AutoT: automatic definition of the ticks from the curve closest to the point clicked. - AutoO: automatic framing from the curve closest to the point clicked - ZX, ZY: like the magnifying glass but in a single direction (X or Y) - AX, AY: automatic framing in a single direction (X or Y) The other buttons concern the management of the stack of graphs and will not be explained here. 6 Tips and tricks 6.1 Extended characters, in particular the Greek alphabet It is possible to use fonts other than the standard font in any text zone (curve legend, axis label, etc...). In particular, it is possible to use the “Symbol” font in order to insert Greek characters. For this, if in the “String” field of the legend one puts the following string “test f{Symbol} test f{Arial} test”, like this: one obtains a legend which looks like this (the command f{x} changing the font) One will find in the User's Guide in paragraph 7.1 the various commands making it possible to control the formatting of the text zones (in particular the fonts, the size, the colour, etc) and in paragraph [§6.1] the mechanism for defining the various fonts usable by Grace. 6.2 Point or comma? By default, Grace relies on the user environment in order to know whether it must represent the decimal figures with a point or a comma. On most recent systems, in France, it will therefore use the comma. If it is necessary to print curves with points, under linux, one must carry out the following operation: before launching Grace, do “export LC_NUMERIC=POSIX” or “setenv LC_NUMERIC POSIX” depending on the shell used. 6.3 Batch It is possible to do without the graphical interface, in particular for repetitive tasks; one will find examples of the use of the batch mode in the tutorial: http://plasma-gate.weizmann.ac.il/Grace/doc/Tutorial.html

u2.51.02 Plotting curves with Code_Aster u2.51.02 Plotting curves with Code_Aster Summary: This document explains how, starting from an analysis result, one can produce tables or functions, extract the values of these tables or functions, manipulate them, and finally, as a last step, use the print commands in order to plot curves. If you have a function or a table and you simply wish to represent it in the form of a curve, go directly to paragraph [§ 4 ], and consult the documentations of the commands IMPR_FONCTION U4.33.01 and IMPR_TABLE U4.91.03. Preliminary note The post-processing must be carried out in POURSUITE and not in continuation of the analysis. There are several reasons for this: 1. in the event of an error , one does not lose the hours of the run which made it possible to reach the result , 2. one can carry out numerous post-processings directly by launching Stanley on the result database of the analysis (see astk U1.04.00 or STANLEY U4.81.31), 3. in order to simplify the post-processing, one can use the possibilities offered by Python, which require being in PAR_LOT='NON' in POURSUITE, which prevents the use of eficas for this type of post-processing, whereas it is simpler to use eficas to build the main data set. 1 Extracting the data with the help of the Aster commands One assumes that the user has an analysis result obtained from, for example, the command CALC_MODES for an eigenmode analysis, STAT_NON_LINE for a non-linear static analysis, or DYNA_NON_LINE for a non-linear dynamic analysis… One has in every case a result concept which will be, for example, of type mode_meca, mode_flamb, dyna_trans, tran_gene, evol_elas, evol_noli, evol_ther, etc. depending on the command used and which contains fields of values that one wishes to represent in the form of curves. 1.1 Producing a function or a table Reminder A function is composed of two lists of values, abscissae and ordinates; the abscissae are necessarily monotonic. A table is an agglomeration of values not necessarily of the same type, which one accesses via a parameter, “column name”. In the use of tables which interests us here, one will generally produce columns of real numbers; their variation is arbitrary. For further details on what a table is, one may consult the documentation of IMPR_TABLE U4.91.03. The values can be extracted by using the following commands: - RECU_FONCTION U4.32.03: produces a function from a result, from a field, from a table… Example: time evolution of a component of a field at a particular point. - POST_RELEVE_T U4.81.21: produces a table from a result or from a field. One can extract a quantity associated with the components of a field (a component, an invariant…) at certain particular points or along a path which is not necessarily straight. - MACR_LIGN_COUPE U4.81.13: produces a table from a result or from a field along a cutting line (straight line composed of regular segments). - RECU_TABLE U4.71.02: produces a table from the values of one or more parameters of a result. For example: the evolution of the piloting parameter in the course of an analysis. One can also extract a table from a few particular data structures. - CREA_CHAMP U4.72.04: makes it possible to extract a field from a result data structure. This can be useful when a command does not know how to treat certain results. One can for example then recover a function via RECU_FONCTION/CHAM_GD. 1.2 Treating data blocks A data block is simply an array of values with N rows and P columns. In certain cases, one has one or more files each composed of one or more data blocks, separated by lines of text. In order to build functions from such files, one can use LIRE_FONCTION U4.32.02. For example, one carries out a parametric study; each analysis produces an array which comes to enrich a result file; the file may also have been built by a single analysis or else manually, it hardly matters. Such a file could look like this: AVEC PARA=1.23 INST COOR_X DY 1.00000E+00 1.00000E+01 -3.02717E-2 1.20000E+00 1.00000E+01 -8.14498E-2 1.40000E+00 1.00000E+01 -7.97278E-2 1.60000E+00 1.00000E+01 -3.86827E-2 1.80000E+00 1.00000E+01 -8.48309E-2 2.00000E+00 1.00000E+01 -9.37561E-2 2.20000E+00 1.00000E+01 7.18293E-2 2.40000E+00 1.00000E+01 6.05322E-2 AVEC PARA=1.98 INST COOR_X COOR_Y DX DY 1.00000E+00 1.00000E+01 0.00000E+00 -3.02717E-2 2.07127E-01 1.10000E+00 1.00000E+01 0.00000E+00 -8.14498E-2 4.14928E-01 1.20000E+00 1.00000E+01 0.00000E+00 -7.97278E-2 7.92728E-01 1.80000E+00 1.00000E+01 0.00000E+00 -7.86827E-2 6.88227E-01 2.45000E+00 1.00000E+01 0.00000E+00 8.48309E-2 3.43029E-01 One has several blocks which do not necessarily have the same number of columns. Suppose that one wishes to compare the displacement DY obtained with the two values of PARA; one will use for example: fDY1=LIRE_FONCTION( TYPE='FONCTION', INDIC_PARA=(1,1,), # the abscissae are taken in block 1, column 1 INDIC_RESU=(1,3,), # the ordinates are taken in block 1, column 3 UNITE=38, NOM_PARA='INST', NOM_RESU='DY',) fDY2=LIRE_FONCTION( TYPE='FONCTION', INDIC_PARA=(2,1,), # the abscissae are taken in block 2, column 1 INDIC_RESU=(2,5,), # the abscissae are taken in block 2, column 5 UNITE=38, NOM_PARA='INST', NOM_RESU='DY',) classical plotting of two functions with IMPR_FONCTION: IMPR_FONCTION(FORMAT='XMGRACE', UNITE=29, COURBE=(_F(FONCTION=fDY1, LEGENDE='PARA=1.23',), _F(FONCTION=fDY2, LEGENDE='PARA=1.98',),), TITRE='DY=f(t)',) 2 Transforming the values of a table or of a function into Python objects Note The processings in Python which are used from now on require being in PAR_LOT='NON' in POURSUITE (or DEBUT). The object here is to recover the values of a table or of a function in a Python object in order to manipulate them afterwards. Note that it is sometimes practical to produce a function from the data of a table, possibly filtering certain rows of the table; this is a use of RECU_FONCTION U4.32.03, which we shall not address here. On objects of type function, one has the methods: 1. Valeurs, in order to recover the abscissae and the ordinates in 2 Python lists of reals. With the data of the previous paragraph: One obtains: [1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.8, 2.45] [0.207127, 0.414928, 0.792728, 0.688227, 0.343029] 1. Absc and Ordo make it possible to recover the abscissae and the ordinates separately. One can access the content of a cell of a table with [ parameter_name , row_number ]: -8.14498E-2 One can also transform the (JEVEUX) table object into an instance of the Python class Table. The document U1.03.02 details the Python methods available on objects of type Table. For the extraction of the values, one has in particular a method values() which returns a dictionary whose keys are the parameter names (e.g. ‘DY’) and the values the lists of the values of the table. Warning The Python lists are indexed from 0 to n-1 (for n elements); the equivalent of tab[‘DY’, 2] is therefore tabpy[‘DY’][1]! For the plotting of curves from lists of Python reals, see [§ 4 ]. 3 Manipulating the values in Python A few examples are given here of the manipulation of the values obtained previously in the form of lists or of Numeric arrays. Numeric is an optional Python module (that is to say not included in the Python distribution supplied on www.python.org) but indispensable in order to use Code_Aster ; one can therefore do import Numeric on all Code_Aster installations. 3.1 With Python lists Python lists are easily manipulated by using loops. Let us take the example of the guide U2.51.01 for –10. ] for each post-processing node... for point in lgrno: unit = 29 the files DEPL_point0i.dat will be copied into Resultats/courbes/ DEFI_FICHIER(UNITE=unit, FICHIER=‘./REPE_OUT/DEPL_’+point+’.dat’) tab=POST_RELEVE_T( ACTION=_F(INTITULE = 'VonMises', RESULTAT = resM, NOM_CHAM = 'SIEQ_ELNO', NOM_CMP = 'VMIS', TOUT_ORDRE = 'OUI', GROUP_NO = point, OPERATION = 'EXTRACTION',),) IMPR_TABLE( UNITE = unit, TABLE = tab, FORMAT = 'XMGRACE', NOM_PARA = ('INST', 'VMIS'),) one “releases” the unit in order to reuse it for the following curve DEFI_FICHIER(UNITE=unit, ACTION=‘LIBERER’) 5 A few useful tips A few manipulations of the data of the tables in Python are proposed here, which recur when one wishes to go further in the generation of curves from Code_Aster . Extract from the table coming from POST_RELEVE_T the list of the post-processing nodes: When one post-processes a quantity on a node group (with more than one node) for several time instants, the nodes appear for each time instant; it is therefore necessary to extract the list of these nodes without repetition. | tabpy = tab.EXTR_TABLE() | Creation of the Python Table object | | --- | --- | | tno = tabpy.NOEUD.values() | One extracts the values of the column NOEUD | | lno = list(set([i.strip() for i in tno])) | | | | Efficient method for eliminating the | | | duplicates, using set | | lno.sort() | Sort in increasing order | Build one or more keywords dynamically: This can in particular be useful for filling in the factor keyword FILTRE of IMPR_TABLE according to the context; one builds in this case a dictionary which is then supplied as an argument of the command. This: IMPR_TABLE( UNITE = unit, TABLE = tab, FORMAT = 'XMGRACE', FILTRE = (_F(NOM_PARA='NOEUD', VALE_K = 'N4',), _F(NOM_PARA='NOEUD', VALE_K = 'N4',),), NOM_PARA = ('INST', 'VMIS'), ) is equivalent to this: mfac = {‘FILTRE’ : [{‘NOM_PARA’:‘NOEUD’, ‘VALE_K’: ‘N4’}, {‘NOM_PARA’:‘INTITULE’, ‘VALE_K’: ‘exemple’},], ‘NOM_PARA’ : [‘INST’, ‘VMIS’], ‘UNITE’ : unit, ‘FORMAT’ : 'XMGRACE',} IMPR_TABLE( TABLE = tab, mfac ) The advantage being of course to be able to build the dictionary as one wishes. Note The factor keywords (here FILTRE) can be built by using _F(keyword = value), but it is more flexible to see them as a list of dictionaries.

u3.01.00 Description of the Code_Aster mesh file u3.01.00 Description of the Code_Aster mesh file Summary: This file makes it possible to describe a mesh of Code_Aster . It can be built by an automatic interface between a mesher and the code, but it can also be written by hand. It contains: - an optional title, - a list of nodes with their coordinates, - lists of mesh cells; each mesh cell is described by the list of the nodes which defines its topology, and its orientation, - node groups and mesh-cell groups. Note: A concept of type maillage, once read from the mesh file, can be enriched with the help of Code_Aster operators by information which cannot currently be described in the mesh file. This concerns in particular static substructuring. It is moreover possible, now, to create node groups or mesh-cell groups in the course of a study. > Table of contents 1 Structure of the mesh file The Aster mesh file is read from the first line up to the first occurrence of a line beginning with the word FIN . This keyword is mandatory. The Aster mesh file is made up of a succession of independent mesh sub-files. | FIN | | --- | The Aster mesh file is a formatted file, in the FORTRAN sense: - the line length is limited to 80 characters (any information from column 81 onwards is simply ignored); - the blank character ' ' and the comma ',' are the only separators recognised, - the character % is a reserved character used to indicate the beginning, up to the end of the line, of a comment, - the numerical data are interpreted in free format: 1 = 1. = 1.0 = 1.E+0 = .1E1 = 10.D-1 The mesh file must contain at least: - a sub-file of node coordinates COOR_2D or COOR_3D, defined by 2 or 3 real numbers in a single orthonormal Cartesian frame. - one sub-file per type of mesh cell used. It may contain, in addition, and this is recommended, a TITRE sub-file. It is practically indispensable to define, at the time of meshing, sub-files of mesh-cell groups GROUP_MA and sub-files of node groups GROUP_NO. It should be remembered that the assignment of a finite-element type can be done only on a mesh cell (or, exceptionally, on a node for the discrete elements) described in the mesh file. The loadings or the boundary conditions are assigned on mesh cells or on nodes according to the case. 2 Structure of a sub-file A sub-file begins with a keyword and is terminated by the imposed keyword FINSF : This description is sufficient for Aster . The most complete description is the following: - each sub-file comprises 3 parts: 1. the header of the sub-file, 2. the content of the information, 3. the end marker of the sub-file (FINSF). - MOTCLE and FINSF (end of sub-file) are mandatory because they delimit the sub-file inside the mesh file. - NOM is optional. When the keyword is GROUP_MA or GROUP_NO, if NOM is absent then the first character string encountered after these keywords will form the NOM of the GROUP_MA or of the GROUP_NO. By convention any character string which follows the character % is interpreted as a comment. 2.1 The header The role of the header is to provide global information on the content of the sub-file: | MOT_CLE | In addition to its role as a delimiter of the sub-file, it indicates the nature of the information which will follow. It must be found on the 1st line of the sub-file and left-justified . | | --- | --- | | NOM | it is used to designate a set of information. It must be found on the 1st line of the header of the sub-file. It is optional. | | | All the other keywords are currently ignored by the operator LIRE_MAILLAGE. | 2.2 List of the information These are items of information coming from a mesher and written in free format. The information which this file must contain defines the classical entities of the finite-element method: | nodes : | points defined by a name and by their Cartesian coordinates in 2D or 3D space, | | --- | --- | | mesh cells : | named topological figures, plane or volume (point, segment, triangle, quadrangle, tetrahedron, ...), defined by the ordered list of the nodes which constitute them and on which different types of finite elements, of boundary conditions or of loadings may be applied. The order of the nodes orients the mesh cell. This orientation must be established scrupulously because it is used in particular to define the orientation of the loadings (pressure, …). | One can also define groups of these topological entities. - node groups : named lists of node names, - mesh-cell groups : named lists of mesh-cell names. Systematically, whenever one has to refer to nodes (or to mesh cells), one will be able to refer to node groups (or to mesh-cell groups). The interfaces with the meshers automatically generate such groups (according to criteria specific to the mesher). These groups make it easier to assign the material characteristics on the mesh, the boundary conditions, or the printing of the results. Indeed, during such operations one refers to the nodes or to the mesh cells, which it is useful to describe by group. The operator of Code_Aster DEFI_GROUP U4.22.01 makes it possible to create groups a posteriori on any concept of type maillage already read. It will be noted that all the entities handled in the code (nodes, mesh cells, node groups, mesh-cell groups) are named and usable at any moment by their name ( 8 characters at most for the mesh cells and the nodes, 24 characters at most for the GROUP_MA and GROUP_NO). The “case” of the names is preserved: for example, 'GR_AB' is different from 'gr_ab'. The numbering of the entities is never made explicit: it is used only internally in order to point to the values of the different associated variables. 2.3 End of a sub-file It is the reserved and mandatory word FINSF which indicates the end of a sub-file, which begins with a MOTCLE. 3 List of the keywords (types of sub-files) | TITRE | Description of the mesh file, of a documentary nature. The interface operators with meshers build a title from information specific to each mesher | | --- | --- | | / COOR_3D | Description of the nodes by three spatial coordinates: name of the node described (or number interpreted as a name), 3 coordinates, | | / COOR_2D | Description of the nodes by 2 coordinates: name of the node described (or number interpreted as a name), 2 coordinates, | / POI1 points ) / SEG2 / SEG3 / SEG4 segments ) / TRIA3 / TRIA6 / TRIA7 triangles ) / QUAD4 / QUAD8 / QUAD9 quadrangles ) connectivité / HEXA8 / HEXA20 / HEXA27 hexaèdres ) des mailles / PENTA6 / PENTA15 / PENTA18 pentaèdres ) / TETRA4 / TETRA10 tétraèdres ) / PYRAM5 / PYRAM13 pyramides ) GROUP_MA Groupe de mailles (attention le nom est obligatoire) GROUP_NO Groupe de noeuds (attention le nom est obligatoire) - When a keyword has been read, it remains interpreted until the appearance of FINSF. - After an FINSF, any unrecognised keyword (typing error) is ignored and a message is issued. - COOR_2D and COOR_3D are mutually exclusive. - The presence of a coordinate system in the IDEAS universal file causes the IDEAS/Aster interface to stop. Notes 4 Description of the mesh cells The conventions for the description of the topology of the mesh cells in Aster are summarised here. The use of the mesh cells is given here for information; one must refer to the documentation specific to each command. | Mesh cell associated with one node (2D or 3D) | | | --- | --- | | POI1 | | | Mesh cell associated with one segment ( 2D or 3D ) | | | | --- | --- | --- | | SEG2 | | | | SEG3 | | | | SEG4 | | | | | | | | Orientation : The orientation is defined by the order of the vertex nodes This orientation may be supplemented by characteristics given according to the type of finite element assigned on the mesh cell by the factor keyword ORIENTATION of the operator AFFE_CARA_ELEM[U4.42.01]. | | | | Mesh cell associated with one triangle ( 2D or 3D ) | | | | --- | --- | --- | | TRIA3 | | | | TRIA6 | | | | TRIA7 | | | | Orientation: The orientation is defined by the order of the vertex nodes which are given so as to define the direct anticlockwise sense. This orientation may be supplemented by characteristics given to the elements by the operator AFFE_CARA_ELEM[U4.42.01], in particular for the shell elements by the factor keyword COQUE. | | | | Mesh u3.02.01 Interface of the GMSH mesh file with Aster u3.02.01 Interface of the GMSH mesh file with Aster Summary: GMSH is a tool for modelling, meshing and post-processing, distributed under the GNU-GPL licence (https://gmsh.info, executables, sources and documentation available on this site). The principle of the interface which makes it possible to use in Aster a file coming from GMSH is described here. This interface is implemented in Aster by the command PRE_GMSH U7.01.31. 1 Use of GMSH GMSH is a free or mapped meshing tool which incorporates a modeller and post-processing functionalities. The modeller, simple to use, makes it possible to prepare the meshing of structures by geometric constructions (creation of lines, surfaces, translations/rotations, extrusions…). The model of the structure can be built interactively (with the mouse) or else by a command file. The documentation of GMSH is available at this address: https://gmsh.info. The description of the geometry of the structure is contained in a .geo file; the mesh produced is saved with the extension .msh; this file will be converted by the command PRE_GMSH to the Aster format. 2 GMSH entities and Aster groups The GMSH modeller handles points, lines, surfaces or volumes as geometric entities (not meshed). The GMSH mesh is built by meshing, in this order, the lines, the surfaces and then the volumes supported on them. In general, one handles parts of the mesh in order to apply the material properties, the boundary conditions or the loadings. In order to access these sub-parts of the mesh, it is necessary to define “physicals” in GMSH. A “physical” is composed of one or more geometric entities. The GMSH–Aster interface produces a mesh-cell group for each “physical”: if “physical 21” is made up of two volumes, the mesh-cell group \mathit{GM21} contains the mesh cells of these two volumes. Note: In GMSH, one visualises the entities constituting a “physical” by the menu Tools/Visibility and by selecting the number. One can then use the command DEFI_GROUP in Aster in order to handle a more explicit mesh-cell group name. Warning: One must not create “physicals” grouping other “physicals”, because that would lead to the production of duplicate mesh cells. The number of the “physicals” must be less than 1000000. 3 Examples 3.1 GMSH geometry and mesh One creates a very simple geometry: a square of side 1 . Here, one creates the points, the lines and the surface; one could also have made it by translation/extrusion… NB: One creates a “physical” which contains the square surface of number 107. L=1; d=0.45; Point(1) = {0, 0, 0, d}; Point(2) = {L, 0, 0, d}; Point(3) = {L, L, 0, d}; Point(4) = {0, L, 0, d}; Line (1) = {1, 2}; Line (2) = {2, 3}; Line (3) = {3, 4}; Line (4) = {4, 1}; Line Loop (106) = {2, 3, 4, 1}; Plane Surface (6) = {106}; Physical Surface(107) = {6}; The mesh created with the anisotropic 2D algorithm is: The GMSH mesh file contains the description of the nodes and of the mesh cells: NOD 9 1 0 0 0 2 1 0 0 3 1 1 0 4 0 1 0 5 0.4999999999999931 0 0 6 1 0.4999999999999931 0 7 0.500000000000007 1 0 8 0 0.500000000000007 0 13 0.5000000000000001 0.5 0 ENDNOD ELM 8 1 2 107 6 3 13 1 5 2 2 107 6 3 8 1 13 3 2 107 6 3 5 2 13 4 2 107 6 3 13 2 6 5 2 107 6 3 6 3 13 6 2 107 6 3 13 3 7 7 2 107 6 3 7 4 13 8 2 107 6 3 13 4 8 ENDELM The syntax of this file is described in the section “File formats/Gmsh mesh file format“ of the GMSH manual. 3.2 Aster mesh file produced by the operator PRE_GMSH TITRE AUTEUR=INTERFACE_GMSH DATE=17/07/2003 FINSF % COOR_3D NBOBJ=9 %FORMAT=(1 NOM_DE_NOEUD,3 COORD) N1 0.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 N2 1.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 N3 1.00000000000000E+00 1.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 N4 0.00000000000000E+00 1.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 N5 4.99999999999993E-01 0.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 N6 1.00000000000000E+00 4.99999999999993E-01 0.00000000000000E+00 N7 5.00000000000007E-01 1.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 N8 0.00000000000000E+00 5.00000000000007E-01 0.00000000000000E+00 N13 5.00000000000000E-01 5.00000000000000E-01 0.00000000000000E+00 FINSF % TRIA3 NOM=INDEFINI NBOBJ=8 M1 N13 N1 N5 M2 N8 N1 N13 M3 N5 N2 N13 M4 N13 N2 N6 M5 N6 N3 N13 M6 N13 N3 N7 M7 N7 N4 N13 M8 N13 N4 N8 FINSF % GROUP_MA NOM=GM107 M1 M2 M3 M4 M5 M6 M7 M8 FINSF % FIN The eight triangles making up the meshed square are then accessible in Aster in the mesh-cell group GM107.

u3.03.01 Interface of the IDEAS mesh file with Aster u3.03.01 Interface of the IDEAS mesh file with Aster Summary: The purpose of this document is to describe the principle of the IDEAS (SDRC) interface with Aster . This interface is activated in Aster by the procedure PRE_IDEAS U7.01.01. The datasets of the I-DEASTM universal file read by the IDEAS– Aster interface are dataset 151 (title), datasets 15, 781 or 2411 (coordinates of the nodes), datasets 71, 780 or 2412 (description of the mesh cells), datasets 752, 2417, 2429, 2430, 2431, 2432, 2435 or 2467 (node groups or mesh-cell groups) and dataset 735 (nodes or mesh cells attached to the curves, mesh areas and mesh volumes). As a result, the I-DEASTM versions currently supported are versions 4, 5 and 6 as well as versions 1., 2., 3., 4., 5., 6., 7., 8., 9. and 10. of Master Series. 1 IDEAS vocabulary 'geometry' set of geometric entities on which the mesh is supported. They may be curves ('curve'), surfaces ('mesh area') or volumes ('meshvolume'). 'curve' line geometric entity which may be composed of sub-entities, segments, circular arcs, options. The mesh cells which are supported on these sub-entities are segments with 2 or 3 nodes. 'mesh area' surface geometric entity bounded by 'curves', on which the surface mesh cells are supported: triangles with 3 or 6 nodes or quadrangles with 4 or 8 nodes. 'mesh volume' volume geometric entity bounded by 'meshareas'. The volume mesh cells which are supported on these sub-entities are hexahedra with 8 or 20 nodes, pentahedra with 6 or 15 nodes or tetrahedra with 4 or 10 nodes. 'group' an arbitrary grouping (chosen by the user) of geometric entities, of nodes or of mesh cells; the user gives it a name. 'universal file' the formatted file produced by IDEAS constitutes the data file of the interface. It contains the whole mesh (nodes and mesh cells), the geometric entities, the groups and the geometric-entity–mesh associations. 'geometric entity – mesh association' list of nodes or of mesh cells supported on a given geometric entity. - for each 'curve', the nodes which compose it, - for each 'mesharea': - the nodes which compose it, - in 2D the mesh cells which compose it. - for each 'meshvolume': - the nodes and the mesh cells which compose it. - the nodes which compose it, - in 3D the mesh cells which compose it. 2 Purpose of the mesh interface The information contained in the IDEAS universal file (for versions 4, 5 and 6 and versions 1., 2., 3., 4., 5., 6., 7., 8., 9. and 10. of Master Series) is transcribed into the mesh file. This concerns in particular the coordinates of the nodes, the mesh cells, and the node groups and mesh-cell groups. These are most often simple transfers of sub-files, except for the mesh cells, where a permutation of the nodes is necessary. The names created by the interface are: - for the nodes: NO followed by the IDEAS node number, - for the mesh cells: MA followed by the IDEAS element number. The mesh cells are grouped into sub-files of homogeneous type: TRIA., QUAD., TETRA., PENTA., HEXA. - for the node groups or mesh-cell groups created by the user and named in IDEAS, the name is simply transcribed in upper case : - 8 alphanumeric characters at most (otherwise truncation of the name), - the underscore is permitted. Note The name of the group cannot begin with "COUL_xxx", otherwise it is ignored by the interface (an alarm message warns the user). - In IDEAS, one can assign a colour to each mesh cell generated (by default, the mesh cells are green). The colours are identified by a number (for example 7 for green). In order to keep this information in Aster , the interface PRE_IDEAS can generate mesh-cell groups of name "COUL_xxx" IDEAS colour number containing all the mesh cells of colour "IDEAS colour number". In order to generate these mesh-cell groups, the user must request it explicitly by CREA_GROUP_COUL = 'oui' in the command PRE_IDEAS. Without an explicit request from the user, these mesh-cell groups are not created, so as to limit the number of mesh-cell groups and so as not to increase the size of the mesh file unnecessarily. From the geometric-entity–mesh associations, the interface builds: - the GROUP_MA associated with the 'mesh volume' in 3D or else with the 'mesharea' in 2D. They bear the name M_VOLUi or M_AREAi for the original geometric entity, of number i. - the GROUP_NO associated with the 'mesh volume', 'mesh area' or 'curve', which bear the names M_VOLUi, M_AREAi, CURVEi according to the case. Note: The mesharea and the meshvolume no longer exist in versions 1., 2., 3., 4., 5., 6., 7., 8., 9. and 10. of Master Series. The user must therefore take care to define the node groups and the mesh-cell groups which he needs for his study. The mesh interface (PRE_IDEAS) does not transcribe the boundary conditions and loadings which may be present in the universal file. 3 Example: IDEAS mesh There also exists the node group FACE_INF 1 2 5 8 9 11 Aster mesh file produced by the operator PRE_IDEAS COOR_3D NO1 x1 y1 z1 … … … … NO12 x12 y12 z12 FINSF HEXA8 MA1 NO1 NO5 NO8 NO2 NO4 NO6 NO7 NO3 FINSF PENTA6 MA2 NO5 NO9 NO6 NO8 NO11 NO7 MA3 NO6 NO9 NO10 NO7 NO11 NO12 FINSF GROUP_NO NOM = FACE_INF NO1 NO2 NO5 NO8 NO9 NO11 FINSF GROUP_NO NOM = CURVE1 NO1 NO4 FINSF … … … … autres GROUP_NOpour CURVE2à CURVE11 GROUP_NO NOM = CURVE12 NO10 NO12 FINSF GROUP_NO NOM = M_AREA1 NO1 NO2 NO3 NO4 FINSF … … … … autresGROUP_NO pourM_AREA2 àM_AREA5 GROUP_NO NOM = M_AREA6 NO1 NO5 NO9 NO11 NO8 NO2 FINSF GROUP_NO NOM = M_VOLU1 % totalité des nœuds NO1 … … … … NO12 FINSF GROUP_MA NOM = M_VOLU1 % totalité des mailles MA1 MA2 MA3 4 Local numbering of the mesh cells of IDEAS and Aster Preliminary note : The numbers appearing on the diagrams which follow are the local numbers of the nodes. 4.1 Numbering of the TRIANGLES (TRIA6) 4.2 Numbering of the QUADRANGLES (QUAD8) Mesh cells of type QUAD9 are not available in IDEAS 4.3 Numbering of the HEXAHEDRA (HEXA8 - HEXA20) 4.3.1 HEXA8 4.3.2 HEXA20 4.4 Numbering of the PRISMS (PENTA6 - PENTA15) 4.4.1 PENTA6 4.4.2 PENTA15 4.5 Numbering of the TETRAHEDRA (TETRA4 - TETRA10) 4.5.1 TETRA4 4.5.2 TETRA10 5 Coordinate systems The IDEAS– Aster interface transcribes only the meshes whose nodes are defined by coordinates in a Cartesian frame.

u3.04.01 Interface of the GIBI mesh file with Code_Aster u3.04.01 Interface of the GIBI mesh file with Code_Aster Summary: The use of GIBI (mesher of CASTEM 2000) can be done on a Unix/Linux workstation, according to the versions available. The principle of the interface which makes it possible to use in Code_Aster a file coming from CASTEM 2000 is described here. This interface is implemented in Aster by the command PRE_GIBI U7.01.11. 1 Use of GIBI CASTEM 2000 is a structural analysis code based on finite elements, which has a set of functionalities dedicated to meshing in 2D and 3D. The whole of these meshing functions is known under the name GIBI. In the remainder of this document, the name GIBI will denote the set of meshing functions as well as the set of commands for the visualisation and the exploitation of the results. GIBI is available on a certain number of Unix/Linux platforms. It is a version distributed by EDF R&D/AMA within the framework of a contract with the CEA; it is available for download on the site https://www.code-aster.org. The memory allocated by GIBI is 20 mega-words by default. For certain applications it is necessary to increase this memory size. In order to do this, the variable ESOPE_PARAM must be defined in the following way: setenv ESOPE_PARAM 'ESOPE=x000000,NTRK=1024,LTRK=1048576' or according to the shell used: export ESOPE_PARAM='ESOPE=x000000,NTRK=1024,LTRK=1048576' where x is the number of millions of words that one wishes. The CEA produces a new version of GIBI every year. Before being put into service on the centralised server and being distributed, this version is tested by the code team on the whole set of the Aster tests. Thus the "standard" version is currently GIBI version 2000, launched interactively by the command gibi2000.x. 2 Documentation on the use of GIBI The documentation of GIBI can be obtained by executing GIBI with the following data file: NOTICE ; FIN ; One then recovers, in the job listing, the list of the chapters corresponding to all the operators of GIBI. GIBI has on-line documentation which makes it possible to obtain the syntax of each operator by the command: INFO name of the command ; but also the possibility of knowing the whole set of the operators dedicated to meshing, grouped by functionality (operators for the creation of points, of line entities, of surface entities and of volume entities …) by the command: INFO DEBU ; This information is also available from an Internet browser (the location depends on the local installation). 3 Advice on the use of GIBI for Aster - Do not forget that each command ends with a ";", - Code_Aster can reread the files created by GIBI having level 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 13. This level is linked to the change of format, - bear in mind that it is not possible to force the mesh to pass through a point or a line which does not appear on the outer contour. Plan the partitioning of the geometry accordingly, - bear in mind that GIBI orients the different mesh cells with its own conventions. Elements may thus be "turned over" (hence negative Jacobians and pressures the wrong way round!). In GIBI, the user has the operators INVERSE and ORIENTER available in order to modify the orientation of elements. One will advantageously refer to the command MODI_MAILLAGE (U4.23.04, keywords ORIE_PEAU_2D/3D) in order to act on the orientation of the mesh cells in Aster , - the operator PRE_GIBI assumes that GIBI has been run without error, that is to say that the second line of the .mgib file is "NIVEAU NIVEAU ERREUR 0 DIMENSION …" Otherwise, one carries out the interface all the same, while issuing an alarm, - the file containing the GIBI mesh must be produced by the command "SAUVER FORMAT maillage"; this is the only format reread by the interface PRE_GIBI. 4 Interface with Aster The interface with Aster is activated by the command PRE_GIBI U7.01.11. 5 GIBI and Aster meshing entities The GIBI mesher handles typed and named objects (cf. the GIBI user's guide). The types used are: - the integer, real, text constants, …, - the POINTS, - the MAILLAGES (set of mesh cells). The command PRE_GIBI has the effect: - of writing the points (GIBI) in the form of nodes ( Aster ): the names of the Aster nodes are of the form: {N}_{i} where i is the GIBI number of the corresponding point, - of writing the mesh cells ( Aster ) contained in the meshes (GIBI): the names of the Aster mesh cells are of the form: {M}_{j} where j is the order number of the GIBI mesh cell in the GIBI result file, - of writing GROUP_MA ( Aster ) corresponding to the meshes (GIBI) and with the same names, Note: The mesh-cell groups contain only the mesh cells which actually define the GIBI mesh. They do not contain the mesh cells of the objects referenced in this mesh (the edges, for example). - of writing GROUP_NO ( Aster ) reduced to a single node and whose names are the names of the GIBI points. One notes that PRE_GIBI does not generate any GROUP_NO containing several nodes. This would sometimes be very useful in order to impose boundary conditions on all the nodes of an edge. In order to do this, the user has available in Aster the command DEFI_GROUP, which makes it possible to create node groups from mesh-cell groups. The keyword CREA_GROUP_NO of the operator DEFI_GROUP U4.22.01 makes it possible to get round this obstacle. 6 Examples - for GIBI: A and B are named points. One therefore finds in the Aster mesh GROUP_NO of names A and B - for GIBI: \mathit{AB} , \mathit{CARRE} , \mathit{C1} , …, \mathit{C4} are named meshes. One therefore finds in the Aster mesh GROUP_MA of names: \mathit{AB} , \mathit{CARRE} , \mathit{C1} , …, \mathit{C4} Note: The interface writes only once mesh cells which may be identical (which sometimes happens with the "ET" operator of GIBI). This has the consequence that the names of the mesh cells {M}_{j} may have a "numbering with holes". One must not be concerned about it. - The orientation of the mesh cells is that given by GIBI. This may be of importance for certain changes: pressure, … One must be aware of the fact that the meshing operators of GIBI orient the elements (with rules specified in the documentation). Certain elements may be "turned over" with respect to others. Another set of GIBI commands could, for example, have generated the mesh: 6.1 Note concerning the POIN command of GIBI This command can produce results of a different type: - if this command makes it possible to recover a single point, for example: PA = toto POIN PROC A ; or PA = toto POIN INITIAL ; then \mathit{PA} is a named GIBI point. For Aster , one will have a GROUP_NO of name \mathit{PA} which contains only one node. - if this command makes it possible to recover several points: for example: PA = toto POIN DROIT A B 1.0D-2 ; then \mathit{PA} is a named GIBI mesh: This mesh is made up of POI1 mesh cells. For Aster , one will have a GROUP_MA of name \mathit{PA} which contains several POI1. In order to use this object as a GROUP_NO, one will have to use the factor keyword CREA_GROUP_NO of the command DEFI_GROUP. 6.2 GIBI command file OPTI DIME 2 ELEM TRI3 ; POINTS NOMMES: A = 0.0 0.0 ; B = 1.0 0.0 ; MAILLAGES: AB = DROI 2 A B ; CARRE = AB TRAN 1 (0. 1.); C1 C2 C3 C4 = COTE CARRE ; SAUVER FORMAT CARRE ; FIN; ------------------------------------------------------------------- 6.3 GIBI result file: (for information) ENREGISTREMENT DE TYPE 4 NIVEAU 11 NIVEAU ERREUR 0 DIMENSION 2 DENSITE 0.00000E+00 ENREGISTREMENT DE TYPE 7 NOMBRE INFO CASTEM2000 8 IFOUR -1 NIFOUR 0 IFOMOD -1 IECHO 1 IIMPI 0 IOSPI 0 ISOTYP 1 NSDPGE 0 ENREGISTREMENT DE TYPE 2 PILE NUMERO 1NBRE OBJETS NOMMES 6NBRE OBJETS 5 AB CARRE C1 C2 C3 C4 2 1 2 3 4 5 4 0 4 3 4 2 3 4 5 0 0 0 0 1 2 3 1 3 4 2 5 3 5 6 3 2 0 0 2 2 0 0 1 2 2 5 2 0 0 2 1 0 5 6 2 0 0 2 2 0 0 6 3 3 4 2 0 0 2 1 0 4 1 ENREGISTREMENT DE TYPE 2 PILE NUMERO 32NBRE OBJETS NOMMES 2NBRE OBJETS 6 A B 1 5 6 1 3 6 5 2 7 ENREGISTREMENT DE TYPE 2 PILE NUMERO 33NBRE OBJETS NOMMES 0NBRE OBJETS 1 21 0.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 1.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 5.00000000000000E-01 0.00000000000000E+00 5.00000000000000E-01 0.00000000000000E+00 1.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 1.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 5.00000000000000E-01 1.00000000000000E+00 5.00000000000000E-01 1.00000000000000E+00 1.00000000000000E+00 0.00000000000000E+00 ENREGISTREMENT DE TYPE 5 LABEL AUTOMATIQUE : 1 6.4 Aster mesh file produced by the operator PRE_GIBI

u3.11.01 Modellings POU_D_T, POU_D_E, BARRE u3.11.01 Modellings POU_D_T, POU_D_E, BARRE Summary: The four modellings POU_D_T, POU_D_E and BARRE correspond to the classical formulations of beam and bar elements, inspired by Strength of Materials. They can be used for three-dimensional problems in linear or non-linear isotropic mechanical analysis. 1 Discretisation 1.1 Degrees of freedom For the three beam modellings in three dimensions, the discretisation degrees of freedom are, at each node of the support mesh cell, the six displacement components (three translations and three rotations). These nodes are assumed to describe a segment of the mean fibre of the beam. For the bar modelling in three dimensions, the discretisation degrees of freedom are, at each node of the support mesh cell, the three translational displacement components. | Finite element | Degrees of freedom (at each vertex node) | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | POU_D_T | DX | DY | DZ | DRX | DRY | DRZ | | POU_D_E | DX | DY | DZ | DRX | DRY | DRZ | | BARRE | DX | DY | DZ | | | | 1.2 Support mesh cell of the stiffness matrices The support mesh cells of the finite elements, in a displacement formulation, are two-node segments SEG2: | Modelling | Mesh cell | Finite element | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | POU_D_T | SEG2 | MECA_POU_D_T | | | POU_D_E | SEG2 | MECA_POU_D_E | | | BARRE | SEG2 | MECA_BARRE | | 1.3 Support mesh cell of the loadings All the loadings applicable to the beam and bar elements are treated by direct discretisation on the support mesh cell of the element in a displacement formulation. No loading support mesh cell is therefore necessary for the edge of the beam or bar elements. 1.4 Main characteristics of the modellings The POU_D_E modelling (straight Euler beam) corresponds to the Euler–Bernoulli assumption, that is to say that the sections remain straight and perpendicular to the mean fibre (high-slenderness assumption). The POU_D_T modelling (straight Timoshenko beam) takes into account the effects of transverse shear. The BARRE modelling treats only the axial forces and strains. The beam with warping is dealt with in U3.11.04. 2 Assignment of the characteristics For these 1D structural elements, it is necessary to assign geometric characteristics which are complementary to the mesh data. The definition of these data is carried out with the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM associated with the following factor keywords: - POUTRE Makes it possible to define and to assign the characteristics of the cross-section and the orientation of the principal axes of inertia about the neutral fibre. Supported modellings: POUT_D_T, POU_D_E - BARRE Makes it possible to define and to assign the characteristics of the cross-section. Supported modelling: BARRE - ORIENTATION Makes it possible to define and to assign the principal axes of the cross-sections of beam-type elements. Supported modellings: POUT_D_T, POU_D_E Note on the discretisation: As regards the meshing of beams into mesh cells SEG2 , it is unnecessary to refine these elements excessively, since their integrated formulation makes it possible to obtain exact solutions at the nodes in linear statics R3.08.01. In modal analysis and in dynamics, care will be taken to mesh sufficiently to represent the expected modes, but without excess: the elements must remain of a sufficient length, depending on the dimensions of the section, so that the beam assumption is valid. For example, for a beam of length 1, and a circular section of external radius 0.05 and of thickness 0.01, 10 elements are sufficient to capture correctly the first 10 modes. But if one refines enormously, for example with 1000 elements, then each beam element is very short: length 0.001 for an external radius of 0.05. The element matrices are very ill-conditioned, in particular for the element POU_D_E (for POU_D_T the transverse shear terms improve the conditioning somewhat). On solution, one then loses 8 decimal places for the POU_D_E. 3 Supported loadings The loadings available are the following: - 'CONTACT' Makes it possible to define the zones subjected to contact conditions. Supported modellings: POU_D_T, POU_D_E - 'EPSI_INIT' Makes it possible to apply an initial-strain loading. Supported modellings: POU_D_T, POU_D_E - 'FORCE_ELEC' Makes it possible to apply the LAPLACE force acting on a principal conductor, due to the presence of a straight secondary conductor. Supported modellings: POU_D_T, POU_D_E - 'FORCE_POUTRE' Makes it possible to apply line forces Supported modellings: POU_D_T, POU_D_E,BARRE - 'INTE_ELEC' Makes it possible to apply the LAPLACE force acting on a principal conductor, due to the presence of a secondary conductor which is not necessarily straight with respect to this principal conductor. Supported modellings: POU_D_T, POU_D_E - 'PESANTEUR' Makes it possible to apply a gravity-type loading. Supported modellings: POU_D_T, POU_D_E, BARRE Note: Contact possible between a beam and a surface R5.03.50. 4 Non-linear capabilities 4.1 Constitutive law The constitutive laws specific to these modellings, usable via the keyword 'COMPORTEMENT' in 'STAT_NON_LINE' and 'DYNA_NON_LINE', are the following (Cf. U4.51.11): - / 'LEMA_SEUIL' , Supported modellings: POU_D_T, POU_D_E. - / 'VMIS_ASYM_LINE' . Supported modelling: BARRE. Note: . It is also possible, for these modellings using a one-dimensional stress state, to use the 3D constitutive behaviours (thanks to the De Borst method R5.03.03). 4.2 Strains Only the linearised strains (keyword 'PETIT' under 'DEFORMATION') are available in the constitutive relations (Cf. U4.51.11). 5 Examples of implementation: test cases - POU_D_T ◦ Linear statics DEMO004A: Analysis of a 3D truss without bracing, under self-weight and subjected to a point force. FORMA01A: Analysis of a piping run comprising an elbow subjected to a point force. ◦ Linear dynamics SDLL01A V2.02.01: Search for the natural frequencies of a short beam on simple supports. ◦ Non-linear dynamics SDNL103A V5.02.103: Analysis of the response of a column subjected to an arbitrary seismic loading. - POU_D_E ◦ Linear statics SSLL102A V3.01.102: Analysis of a clamped beam subjected to unit forces. ◦ Linear dynamics FORMA12A: Modal analysis of a beam (multiple modes). ◦ Non-linear dynamics SDNL105A V5.02.105: Impact of 3 beams against one another — analysis of the transient response by substructuring in the case where a non-linearity of impact type between moving structures is taken into account. - POU_D_T, modelling of elbows ◦ Linear dynamics SDLL11E: Analysis of the natural frequencies of a thin circular ring. - BARRE ◦ Linear statics SSLS110A V3.01.110: Analysis of a system of 3 bars in a U under self-weight. ◦ Non-linear statics SSLS111B V6.02.111: Analysis of three perfectly elastoplastic Von Mises bars.

u3.11.02 Modellings DIS_T and DIS_TR u3.11.02 Modellings DIS_T and DIS_TR Summary: This document describes, for the modellings DIS_T and DIS_TR : - the degrees of freedom carried by the finite elements which support the modelling, - the related support mesh cells, - the supported loadings, - the non-linear capabilities, - the test cases implementing the modellings. The two modellings DIS_T and DIS_TR make it possible to represent discrete elements in translation and in translation-rotation. They can be used for three-dimensional problems in linear and non-linear mechanical analysis. 1 Discretisation 1.1 Degrees of freedom For the two modellings in three dimensions, the discretisation degrees of freedom are, at each node of the support mesh cell, the three translational displacement components or the six components (three translations and three rotations). | Finite element | Degrees of freedom (at the vertex nodes) | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | DIS_T | DX | DY | DZ | | | | | DIS_TR | DX | DY | DZ | DRX | DRY | DRZ | 1.2 Support mesh cell of the stiffness matrices The support mesh cells of the discrete elements, in a displacement formulation, are two-node segments SEG2 or point mesh cells POI1 coincident with a node: | Modelling | Mesh cell | Finite element | | --- | --- | --- | | DIS_T | POI1 | MECA_DIS_T_N | | | SEG2 | MECA_DIS_T_L | | DIS_TR | POI1 | MECA_DIS_TR_N | | | SEG2 | MECA_DIS_TR_L | For the POI1 mesh cells, the forces are computed from the differences of the degrees of freedom of the node of the mesh cell with the fixed frame, whereas for the SEG2 mesh cells they are computed from the differences in degree of freedom between the two nodes. 2 Assignment of the characteristics For these discrete elements, it is necessary to assign geometric characteristics which are complementary to the mesh data. The definition of these data is carried out with the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM associated with the following factor keywords: - DISCRET . Makes it possible to define and to assign the values of the stiffness, mass or damping matrices. Supported modellings: DIS_T , DIS_TR - ORIENTATION . Makes it possible to define and to assign a local frame. Supported modellings: DIS_T , DIS_TR 3 Supported loadings - PESANTEUR. Makes it possible to apply a gravity-type loading. The supported modellings: DIS_T , DIS_TR 4 Linear and non-linear capabilities 4.1 Constitutive law The constitutive laws specific to these modellings, usable under COMPORTEMENT in STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, are documented in R5.03.17 Constitutive relations of the discrete elements, except for the law ASSE_CORN R5.03.32. The possible constitutive behaviours: - ELAS . In the general case, it is not necessary to assign an elastic constitutive behaviour to the discrete element. The operator STAT_NON_LINE carries out this assignment by default on all the mesh cells present in the model. This assignment is then overloaded when the keyword COMPORTEMENT is processed. On the other hand, if a discrete element is assigned a temperature and one wishes to take thermal expansion into account (only for a DIS_TR_L ), it is necessary to define the expansion coefficient \alpha and this is done by defining an elastic material. One must therefore define ALPHA=\alpha ; the keyword E is mandatory but its value will not be taken into account, see R5.03.17. Taking the expansion of the discrete elements into account is not possible with the operator MECA_STATIQUE unless ALPHA=0 . - ASSE_CORN . See R5.03.32 - ARME - DIS_CHOC - DIS_CONTACT - ELAS - DIS_VISC - DIS_ECRO_CINE - DIS_ECRO_TRAC - DIS_BILI_ELAS - DIS_GRICRA - DIS_GOUJ2E - CHOC_ENDO - CHOC_ENDO_PENA In addition to the assignment of the characteristics AFFE_CARA_ELEM, the use of the modellings DIS_T and DIS_TR with STAT_NON_LINE, DYNA_NON_LINE implies defining material characteristics, via DEFI_MATERIAU and AFFE_MATERIAU. With the material DIS_CONTACT and the constitutive behaviours DIS_CHOC and DIS_CONTACT , the elastic matrix is computed with the stiffness characteristic defined in AFFE_CARA_ELEM, whereas the tangent matrix is computed via the constitutive behaviour DIS_CHOC or DIS_CONTACT . 4.2 Strains The only strain available, used in the constitutive relations under the keyword DEFORMATION for the operators STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, is 'PETIT' (Cf. U4.51.11): The strains used for the constitutive relation are therefore the linearised strains computed on the initial geometry. 5 Examples of implementation: test cases - DIS_T - Linear statics SSLL100B V3.01.100: Linear static analysis of a structure made up of straight and curved beams subjected to a bending loading. - Non-linear statics SSNL118A V6.02.118: Non-linear static analysis of a bar subjected to a wind-velocity field. - Linear dynamics SDLD02A V2.01.002: Search for the frequencies and the vibration modes of a mechanical structure composed of masses and springs. - Non-linear dynamics SDND102B V5.01.102: Seismic response of a non-linear multi-supported mass-spring system. - DIS_TR - Linear statics SSLX100D V3.05.100: Analysis of a beam in bending whose model is composed of a mixture of 3D, shell and beam modelling. - Non-linear statics SSNL102A V6.02.102: Analysis of the non-linear behaviour of an assembly of angle sections subjected to a two-dimensional loading of tension and of moment. - Linear dynamics SDLD02C V2.01.002: Search for the frequencies and the vibration modes of a mechanical structure composed of masses and springs. - Non-linear dynamics SDND102B V5.01.102: Seismic response of a non-linear multi-supported mass-spring system.

u3.11.03 Modellings CABLE and CABLE_POULIE u3.11.03 Modellings CABLE and CABLE_POULIE Summary: This document describes, for the modellings CABLE and CABLE_POULIE: - the degrees of freedom carried by the finite elements which support the modelling, - the related support mesh cells, - the supported loadings, - the non-linear capabilities, - the test cases implementing the modellings. The modellings CABLE and CABLE_POULIE correspond to bar elements written specifically in order to take large displacements into account (cf. R3.08.02 and R3.08.04). They cannot be used for problems of linear mechanical analysis. 1 Discretisation 1.1 Degrees of freedom For these two modellings, the discretisation degrees of freedom are, at each node of the support mesh cell, the three translational displacement components. | Finite element | Degrees of freedom (at each vertex node) | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | CABLE | DX | DY | DZ | | | | | CABLE_POULIE | DX | DY | DZ | | | | 1.2 Support mesh cell of the stiffness matrices The support mesh cells of the finite elements, in a displacement formulation, are two-node segments SEG2: | Modelling | Mesh cell | Finite element | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | CABLE | SEG2 | MECABL2 | | | CABLE_POULIE | SEG3 | MEPOUL1 | | 2 Assignment of the characteristics For these modellings it is necessary to assign geometric characteristics which are complementary to the mesh data. The definition of these data is carried out with the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM associated with the factor keyword CABLE, which makes it possible to define and to assign a constant section. 3 Supported loadings The loadings available are the following: - 'CONTACT' Makes it possible to define the zones subjected to contact conditions. Supported modelling: CABLE - 'FORCE_POUTRE' Makes it possible to apply line forces Supported modelling: CABLE - 'INTE_ELEC' Makes it possible to apply the LAPLACE force acting on a principal conductor, due to the presence of a secondary conductor which is not necessarily straight with respect to this principal conductor. Supported modelling: CABLE. - 'PESANTEUR' Makes it possible to apply a gravity-type loading. Supported modellings: CABLE, CABLE_POULIE Note: - Follower load possible in the case of a loading of type FORCE_POUTRE. - Contact possible between a beam and a surface R5.03.50. 4 Non-linear 4.1 Constitutive laws The constitutive law specific to these modellings, usable under COMPORTEMENT in STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, is the following (Cf. U4.51.11): / 'CABLE' Supported modelling: CABLE 4.2 Strains No linear analysis is possible with these modellings (the analyses are necessarily carried out in large displacements). The strains used in the constitutive relation are the GREEN_LAGRANGE strains: keyword 'GREEN' under DEFORMATION (Cf. U4.51.11). 5 Examples of implementation: test cases - CABLE - Non-linear statics - SSNL100A V6.02.100: This test simulates the laying of a cable with two spans. u3.11.04 Modellings POU_D_TG, POU_D_TGM u3.11.04 Modellings POU_D_TG, POU_D_TGM Summary: This document describes, for the modellings POU_D_TG and POU_D_TGM: - the degrees of freedom carried by the finite elements which support the modelling, - the related support mesh cells, - the supported loadings, - the non-linear capabilities, - the test cases implementing the modellings The POU_D_TG modelling corresponds to a formulation of Timoshenko beam elements taking into account a modelling of the warping of the section (cf. R3.08.03). The POU_D_TGM modelling is based on the same formulation and makes it possible to take into account a non-linear constitutive behaviour of multi-fibre type. They can be used for beam problems in isotropic linear mechanical analysis and in elastoplasticity. 1 Discretisation 1.1 Degrees of freedom The degrees of freedom are, at each node of the support mesh cell, the six displacement components (three translations and three rotations) plus one component (GRX) relating to the warping of the section with respect to the neutral fibre (cf. R3.08.03). | Finite element | Degrees of freedom (at each vertex node) | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | POU_D_TG | DX | DY | DZ | DRX | DRY | DRZ | GRX | 1.2 Support mesh cell of the stiffness matrices The support mesh cells of the finite elements, in a displacement formulation, are two-node segments SEG2: | Modelling | Mesh cell | Finite element | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | POU_D_TG | SEG2 | MECA_POU_D_TG | | | POU_D_TGM | SEG2 | MECA_POU_D_TGM | | 2 Assignment of the characteristics For these 1D structural elements, it is necessary to assign geometric characteristics which are complementary to the mesh data. Supported modellings: POU_D_TG, POU_D_TGM • ORIENTATION Makes it possible to define and to assign the orientation of the principal axes of inertia about the neutral fibre. Supported modellings: POU_D_TG, POU_D_TGM 3 Supported loadings The specific loadings, available in AFFE_CHAR_MECA, are the following: • CONTACT Makes it possible to define the zones subjected to contact conditions. Supported modellings: POU_D_TG, POU_D_TGM • EPSI_INIT Makes it possible to apply an initial-strain loading. Supported modelling: POU_D_TG • FORCE_POUTRE Makes it possible to apply line forces Supported modellings: POU_D_TG, POU_D_TGM • PESANTEUR Makes it possible to apply a gravity-type loading. Supported modellings: POU_D_TG, POU_D_TGM 4 Non-linear capabilities 4.1 Constitutive laws The constitutive laws specific to these modellings, usable under COMPORTEMENT in STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, are the following (Cf. U4.51.11): / 'VMIS_CINE_LINE' Supported modelling: POU_D_TGM / 'VMIS_ISOT_LINE' Supported modelling: POU_D_TGM / 'VMIS_ISOT_TRAC' Supported modelling: POU_D_TGM / 'GRAN_IRRA_LOG' Supported modelling: POU_D_TGM Note: It is also possible for these modellings, which use a one-dimensional stress state, to use the 3D constitutive behaviours (thanks to the De Borst method R5.03.03). 4.2 Strains The strains available, used in the constitutive relations under the keyword DEFORMATION for the operators STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, are (Cf. u3.11.07 Modelling POU_D_EM u3.11.07 Modelling POU_D_EM Summary: The POU_D_EM modelling corresponds to the formulation of multi-fibre beam elements (beam of heterogeneous section divided into several fibres). They can be used for three-dimensional problems in linear and non-linear mechanical analysis. 1 Discretisation 1.1 Degrees of freedom For the multi-fibre beam modelling in three dimensions, the discretisation degrees of freedom are, at each node of the support mesh cell, the six displacement components (three translations and three rotations). These nodes are assumed to describe a segment of the mean fibre of the beam. | Finite element | Degrees of freedom (at each vertex node) | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | POU_D_EM | DX | DY | DZ | DRX | DRY | DRZ | 1.2 Support mesh cell of the stiffness matrices The support mesh cells of the finite elements, in a displacement formulation, are two-node segments SEG2: | Modelling | Mesh cell | Finite element | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | POU_D_EM | SEG2 | MECA_POU_D_EM | | 1.3 Support mesh cell of the loadings As for the classical beam elements (POU_D_E), all the loadings applicable to the multi-fibre beam elements are treated by direct discretisation on the support mesh cell of the element in a displacement formulation. No loading support mesh cell is therefore necessary for the edge of the beam or bar elements. 1.4 Main characteristics of the modelling The POU_D_EM modelling is based on the solution of a beam problem for which each defined section is divided into several fibres. Each fibre then behaves as an Euler beam, that is to say that the sections remain straight and perpendicular to the mean fibre (high-slenderness assumption). The section may be of any shape. 2 Assignment of the characteristics For this 1D structural element, it is necessary to assign geometric characteristics which are complementary to the mesh data. The definition of these data is carried out with the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM associated with the following factor keywords: • AFFE_SECT Makes it possible to associate a plane mesh of the section with a beam element. • AFFE_FIBRE Makes it possible to associate a section made up of one or more point fibres with a beam element. • POUTRE Makes it possible to associate a geometric torsion characteristic with a beam element. • ORIENTATION Makes it possible to "rotate" the plane mesh of the section about the axis of the beam. Notes on the characteristics of the modelling: - Within the framework of a multi-fibre type modelling, there are two "levels" of modelling. There is the so-called "longitudinal" modelling, which will be represented by a beam (with geometric support SEG2), and a plane modelling of the section (perpendicular to the SEG2). The operand AFFE_SECT makes it possible to associate a plane mesh of the section with a beam element. The operand AFFE_FIBRE makes it possible to associate a section made up of one or more point fibres (defined by their position and area) with a beam element. - In general, in the plane modelling of the section, several materials coexist. For example, in a reinforced-concrete section, there is both concrete and reinforcement. In that case, the operator CREA_MAILLAGE makes it possible to duplicate the finite-element support so that there is only one material per support. - The operand POUTRE is used to assign a geometric torsion characteristic (JX) which cannot be computed from the plane mesh of the section. If one uses the value GENERALE for the keyword SECTION of the operand POUTRE, one must give the characteristics (CARA) A, IY and IZ in addition to JX, because the operator AFFE_CARA_ELEM expects at least these four characteristics for a classical beam. The values (VALE) given to A, IY and IZ are not used by the POU_D_EM element, because they are computed from the plane mesh of the section. On the other hand, a check of the consistency of the information (AIRE and INERTIE) supplied on the one hand by A, IY, IZ and on the other hand by the keywords AFFE_SECT and AFFE_FIBRE is carried out. The error criterion is based on the relative error and is compared either with the default value or with that given by the user via the keywords PREC_AIRE and PREC_INERTIE. (Cf. command AFFE_CARA_ELEM, keywords PREC_AIRE and PREC_INERTIE of the operand POUTRE). - The operand ORIENTATION is used in general to "rotate" the plane mesh of the section about the axis of the beam (CARA 'ANGL_VRIL'). Indeed, by default, the axis x (horizontal) of the plane mesh of the section coincides with the axis y of the beam (see [Figure]). Figure 2-a: Default orientation of the plane mesh with respect to the beam element 3 Supported loadings The loadings available are the following: • 'FORCE_POUTRE' Makes it possible to apply line forces. • 'PESANTEUR' Makes it possible to apply a gravity-type loading. • 'ROTATION' Makes it possible to define the rotational speed and the rotation vector. The application of a thermal-expansion loading is carried out by defining the factor keyword AFFE_VARC under AFFE_MATERIAU U4.43.03. 4 Non-linear capabilities 4.1 Constitutive law The constitutive laws specific to this modelling, usable via the keyword 'COMPORTEMENT' in 'STAT_NON_LINE' and 'DYNA_NON_LINE', are the following (Cf. U4.51.11): - / 'CORR_ACIER' , - / 'MAZARS_UNIL' , - / 'VMIS_CINE_LINE' , - / 'VMIS_ISOT_LINE' , - / 'VMIS_ISOT_TRAC' , - / 'GRAN_IRRA_LOG' . 4.2 Strains Only the linearised strains (keyword 'PETIT' under 'DEFORMATION') are available in the constitutive relations (Cf. U4.51.11). 5 Examples of implementation: test cases Linear statics - SSLL111A V3.01.111: Static response of a reinforced-concrete beam (section in T ) with a linear constitutive behaviour, subjected to three successive load cases: a point force, the self-weight and a temperature rise. Non-linear statics - SSNL119A V6.02.119: Three-point bending test, static response of a reinforced-concrete beam (rectangular section) with a non-linear La Borderie constitutive behaviour. Linear dynamics - SDLL130B V2.02.130: Seismic response of a reinforced-concrete beam (rectangular section) with linear constitutive behaviour. Non-linear dynamics - SDNL130A V5.02.130: Seismic response of a reinforced-concrete beam (rectangular section) with non-linear constitutive behaviour.

u3.12.01 Modellings DKT - DST - Q4G - DKTG - Q4GG u3.12.01 Modellings DKT - DST - Q4G - DKTG - Q4GG Summary: This document describes, for the modellings DKT - DST - Q4G - DKTG - Q4GG: - the degrees of freedom carried by the finite elements which support the modelling, - the related support mesh cells, - the supported loadings, - the non-linear possibilities, - the test cases implementing the modellings. They can be used for three-dimensional plate problems R3.07.03 in linear mechanical analysis for all the modellings and in material non-linearity for the modellings DKT, DKTG and Q4GG only. Their use for shell problems is commonly accepted, considering that the plane of the finite element can be likened to a facet tangent to the middle surface of the shell (caution: only plane facets are permitted). The thermomechanical analyses are chained from the thermal shell finite elements (see U3.22.01). 1 Discretisation 1.1 Degrees of freedom For the three three-dimensional plate modellings, the discretisation degrees of freedom are, at each node of the support mesh cell, the six displacement components (three translations and three rotations) at the vertex nodes of the support mesh cell. These nodes are assumed to describe a facet tangent to the middle surface of the shell. | Finite element | Degrees of freedom (at each vertex node) | | --- | --- | | DKT / DKQ / DKTG | DX | DY | DZ | DRX | DRY | DRZ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | DST / DSQ | DX | DY | DZ | DRX | DRY | DRZ | | Q4G (Q4 \gamma )/ Q4GG | DX | DY | DZ | DRX | DRY | DRZ | 1.2 Support mesh cell of the stiffness matrices The support mesh cells of the finite elements, in displacement formulation, may be triangles or quadrilaterals. In the latter case, the mesh cells are assumed to be plane (4 coplanar vertex nodes): | Modelling | Mesh cell | Finite element | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | DKT | TRIA3 QUAD4 | MEDKTR3 MEDKQU4 | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | DKTG | TRIA3 QUAD4 | MEDKTG3 MEDKQG4 | | | DST | TRIA3 QUAD4 | MEDSTR3 MEDSQU4 | | | Q4G (Q4 \gamma ) | QUAD4 TRIA3 | MEQ4QU4 MET3TR3 | | | Q4GG | TRIA3 QUAD4 | MET3GG3 MEQ4GG4 | | 1.3 Support mesh cell of the loadings All the loadings applicable to the facets of the plate elements are treated by direct discretisation on the support mesh cell of the element in displacement formulation. No loading support mesh cell is therefore necessary for the faces of the plate elements. For the loadings applicable on the edges of the plate elements, a support mesh cell of type SEG2 can be used: | Modelling | Mesh cell | Finite element | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | DKT | SEG2 | MEBODKT | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | DST | SEG2 | MEBODST | | | DKTG | SEG2 | MEBODKT | | | Q4G (Q4 \gamma ) | SEG2 | MEBOQ4G | | | Q4GG | SEG2 | MEBOQ4G | | 2 Assignment of the characteristics For these plate or shell elements, it is necessary to assign geometrical characteristics which are complementary to the mesh data. The definition of these data is carried out with the command AFFE_CARA_ELEM associated with the following factor keyword: COQUE Makes it possible to define and assign to the mesh cells the thickness, the shear coefficient, the eccentricity, ... For the study of structures comprising multilayer materials, it is necessary to assign the characteristics of each of the layers (thickness, type of material) and their stacking (fibre orientation). The definition of these data is carried out with the command DEFI_COMPOSITE. 3 Supported loadings The available loadings are the following: FORCE_ARETE Makes it possible to apply linear forces. Supported modellings: DKT, DST, Q4G FORCE_COQUE Makes it possible to apply surface forces. Supported modellings: DKT, DST, Q4G, DKTG, Q4GG PESANTEUR Makes it possible to define the acceleration and the direction of gravity. Supported modellings: DKT, DST, Q4G, DKTG, Q4GG PRES_REP Makes it possible to apply surface forces. Supported modellings: DKT, DST, Q4G, DKTG, Q4GG PRE_EPSI Makes it possible to apply an initial strain loading. Supported modellings: DKT, DST, Q4G, DKTG, Q4GG The application of a thermal expansion loading is carried out by defining the factor keyword AFFE_VARC under AFFE_MATERIAU U4.43.03. 4 Non-linear possibilities For the modelling DKT only. 4.1 Constitutive laws Only the modellings 'DKT' and 'DKTG' have non-linear possibilities. The constitutive laws specific to this modelling, usable under COMPORTEMENT in STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, are the plane-stress constitutive relations available with the modellings 'AXIS' and 'C_PLAN' ( cf. U4.51.11). 4.2 Strains The available strains, used in the constitutive relations under the keyword DEFORMATION for the operators STAT_NON_LINE and DYNA_NON_LINE, are (Cf. U4.51.11): / 'PETIT' The strains used for the constitutive relation are the linearised strains. / 'PETIT_REAC' The strain increments used in the incremental constitutive relation are the linearised strains of the displacement increment in the updated geometry. Note: Warning: the analysis of the strains using PETIT_REAC is only an approximation of the large-displacement assumptions. It requires very small loading increments to be performed.
