Extract from sdls504a.mess Calling this operator is recommended as an a priori check/calibration of the model. It also makes it possible to define search intervals containing a reasonable number of eigenvalues (typically about forty modes) in order to optimise the costs of the subsequent modal operators and not to degrade the accuracy of their results. Typically, one advises searching for the modes in packets of about forty 3 . Beyond that, the consumptions in time and in memory are no longer optimal and the quality of the modes obtained is degraded. It is then better to use several frequency bands (or critical-load bands) directly with CALC_MODES and the option 'BANDE' split over several sub-bands, or by several calls to CALC_MODES U4.52.02. Ideally, in order to treat a standard GEP efficiently , one proposes to proceed in several steps: - Calibrate the zones of interest by pre-analyses using only INFO_MODE (in sequential mode or, if possible, in parallel) on given lists of frequencies (resp. critical loads); - Relaunch one or more CALC_MODES analyses with OPTION='BANDE' on the basis of these initial calibrations. To save time, one can even share (and this is strongly recommended!) part of the computational cost of the initial INFO_MODE by notifying to CALC_MODES the name of the sd_table generated. This chaining can thus make the extra cost of INFO_MODE negligible and guide the modal analysis effectively. On the intensive-computation side, the operator INFO_MODE, just as CALC_MODES with the option 'BANDE' split into several sub-bands, potentially benefits from two levels of parallelism (cf. keyword NIVEAU_PARALLELISME). Hence gains in time by a factor of up to 70 on a hundred processors and gains in peak memory of up to a factor of 2. Figure 3ab._ Two distinct counting problems: in a segment of the real axis and in a finite portion of the complex plane (for the moment only a disc). In the first case, when one seeks to count the eigenvalues strictly included in a segment of the real axis, one uses the so-called “Sturm” method; in the second case the APM method. Their theories and algorithms are detailed in the reference documentation R5.01.04. When one treats standard GEPs, the execution of this procedure generally 4 requires only one LDLT factorisation per mode (METHODE='STURM'). When they are scattered in the complex plane, the procedure is much more costly (METHODE='APM') because it requires, in general, hundreds of factorisations. In this case, it is therefore rather to be reserved for simplified problems of small size (fewer than 1000 degrees of freedom). Note that this latter APM method is still the subject of active research. Its robustness is therefore, for the moment, not guaranteed. It is to be used only after having taken care to read the associated documentation. 3.2 Characteristics of the modal problem: operands MATR_RIGI / MATR_A / MATR_MASS / MATR_RIGI_GEOM / MATR_B / MATR_AMOR / MATR_C The table below represents the operands to be used according to the type of the keyword TYPE_MODE. | TYPE_MODE | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 'DYNAMIQUE' | 'MODE_FLAMB' | 'MODE_COMPLEXE' | 'GENERAL' | | ♦ MATR_RIGI = A | ♦ MATR_RIGI = A | ♦ MATR_RIGI = A | ♦ MATR_A = A | | ♦ MATR_MASS = B | ♦ MATR_RIGI_GEOM = B | ♦ MATR_MASS = B | ♦ MATR_B = B | | Not applicable | Not applicable | ◊ MATR_AMOR = C | ◊ MATR_C = C | These operands make it possible to supply the matrices (assembled or generalised 5 ) characterising the modal problem. These matrices may be symmetric or not. They are real except the matrix \mathrm{A} which may be either real or complex. Supplying \mathrm{A} and \mathrm{B} makes it possible to define the generalised modal problem (GEP) (cf. R5.01.01) studied \mathrm{A}\mathrm{u}=\lambda \mathrm{B}\mathrm{u}({\mathrm{GEP}}_{\mathrm{dynamique}}) In the classical case of dynamics (TYPE_MODE='DYNAMIQUE'), \mathrm{A} is the stiffness matrix (real symmetric) and \mathrm{B} is the mass matrix (real symmetric). The eigenvalue \lambda is then related to the eigenfrequency f by the formula: \lambda ={(2\pi f)}^{2} . It is real and positive. In the case of the linear buckling theory (TYPE_MODE='MODE_FLAMB'), \mathrm{A}\mathrm{u}-\lambda \mathrm{B}\mathrm{u}=0({\mathrm{GEP}}_{\mathrm{flambement}}) \mathrm{A} is the stiffness matrix (real symmetric) and \mathrm{B} the geometric stiffness matrix (real symmetric). The eigenvalue \lambda is called the critical load. It is real. As mentioned in the previous table, these matrices will be supplied, respectively, for dynamics by MATR_RIGI / MATR_MASS and, in buckling, by MATR_RIGI / MATR_RIGI_GEOM. Only the so-called 'STURM' method is valid in these two cases. When one of the two matrices is no longer symmetric or contains complex terms (for example to take hysteretic damping into account), the eigenvalues are potentially complex. To treat this problem one must initialise TYPE_MODE to 'MODE_COMPLEXE' and only the APM method is then valid. Supplying \mathrm{A} , \mathrm{B} and \mathrm{C} makes it possible to define the quadratic modal problem (QEP) (cf. R5.01.02) studied (\mathrm{A}+\lambda \mathrm{C}+{\lambda}^{2}\mathrm{B})\mathrm{u}=0(\mathrm{QEP}) In this case, the eigenvalues are potentially complex. To treat this problem one must initialise TYPE_MODE to 'MODE_COMPLEXE'. Often \mathrm{A} is the stiffness matrix, \mathrm{C} a matrix taking into account viscous damping and/or gyroscopic effects and \mathrm{B} the geometric stiffness matrix. As mentioned in the previous table, these matrices will be supplied by MATR_RIGI / MATR_MASS / MATR_AMOR and only the APM method is valid. TYPE_MODE='GENERAL' makes it possible to solve an eigenvalue problem in the general case. One then assigns to the matrices \mathrm{A} , \mathrm{B} and/or \mathrm{C} the role that one wishes. As mentioned in the previous table, these matrices will be supplied by MATR_A / MATR_B / MATR_C. Depending on the case, only the Sturm method (if MATR_C is not supplied and if the other two matrices are real symmetric) or the APM method (all the other cases) is valid. 3.3 Operand TYPE_MODE ◊ TYPE_MODE= / ‘DYNAMIQUE’ [DEFAUT] / ‘MODE_FLAMB’ / 'MODE_COMPLEXE' / 'GENERAL' This keyword makes it possible to define the nature of the modal problem to be treated: pre-estimate the spectrum of vibration frequencies (classical case of 'DYNAMIQUE'), do so in terms of critical loads (case of the linear buckling theory 'MODE_FLAMB') or calibrate that of a non-standard GEP or of a QEP in a portion of the complex plane ('MODE_COMPLEXE'). One can also search for the eigenvalues and the associated modes of a general matrix system ('GENERAL'). For further details one may refer to the description of §3.2. Following this choice, the user must specify the characteristics of the control zone: - for 'DYNAMIQUE': list of frequencies via FREQ, - for 'MODE_FLAMB': list of critical loads via CHAR_CRIT, - for 'MODE_COMPLEXE': zone of the complex plane via TYPE/RAYON/CENTRE_CONTOUR, - for 'GENERAL': depending on the case, either one proceeds as for 'MODE_FLAMB' (if MATR_C is not supplied and if the other two matrices are real symmetric), or as for 'MODE_COMPLEXE' (all the other cases). 3.4 Operand FREQ ♦ FREQ = l_f List of frequencies (in Hertz) defining the intervals that one wants to calibrate \text{l\_f}={({f}_{i})}_{i} (one denotes by nb_freq the number of frequencies of this list). One then searches for the number of eigenvalues in the sub-bands [{\lambda}_{i},{\lambda}_{\text{i+1}}] with {\lambda}_{\text{ }}={(2\pi {f}_{\text{ }})}^{2} . This list must contain at least two values. These values must be arranged in strictly increasing order and all positive. This keyword must be used if TYPE_MODE=‘DYNAMIQUE’. Only the counting method of type STURM is then valid. Notes: - Each frequency is treated only once: as the lower bound of the first sub-band for the first of the list, as the upper bound of the following sub-bands for the other frequencies. In particular, if this frequency is judged too close to an eigenvalue, one shifts it (possibly several times cf. parameters PREC_SHIFT/NMAX_ITER_SHIFT etc.). This “shift” offset is always operated towards the outside of the sub-band under consideration. - If the shift of the lower bound makes it larger than the upper bound, the process stops in ERREUR_FATALE . - This mode of shifting makes the subsequent reuses of this sd_table by one or more CALC_MODES more robust and consistent. One avoids in particular the overlaps of sub-bands that could occur up to V10. - The initial bounds of each of these sub-bands are saved in the fields FREQ_MIN/MAX of each row of the table produced (cf. figure 2a). For each of these pairs, one mentions the bounds actually used by the Sturm test (that is to say after possible shifts), BORNE_MIN/MAX_EFFECT , as well as the number of modes found: NB_MODE . 3.5 Operands CHAR_CRIT CHAR_CRIT = l_c List of critical loads defining the intervals that one wants to calibrate \text{l\_c}={({\lambda}_{i})}_{i} (one denotes by nb_mode_flamb the number of critical loads of this list). One then searches for the number of eigenvalues in the sub-bands [{\lambda}_{i},{\lambda}_{\text{i+1}}] . This list must contain at least two values. These values must be arranged in strictly increasing order. They must be of real type. This keyword must be used if TYPE_MODE=‘MODE_FLAMB’ or if TYPE_MODE=‘GENERAL’ (if MATR_C is not supplied and if the other two matrices are real symmetric). Only the counting method of type STURM is valid. Notes: - Each critical load is treated only once: as the lower bound of the first sub-band for the first of the list, as the upper bound of the following sub-bands for the other frequencies. In particular, if this load is judged too close to an eigenvalue, one shifts it (possibly several times cf. parameters PREC_SHIFT/NMAX_ITER_SHIFT etc.). This “shift” offset is always operated towards the outside of the sub-band under consideration. - If the shift of the lower bound makes it larger than the upper bound, the process stops in ERREUR_FATALE . - This mode of shifting makes the subsequent reuses of the sd_table by one or more CALC_MODES more robust and consistent. One avoids in particular the overlaps of sub-bands that could occur up to V10. - The initial bounds of each of these sub-bands are saved in the fields CHAR_CRIT_MIN/MAX of each row of the table produced (cf. figure 2b). For each of these pairs, one mentions the bounds actually used by the Sturm test (that is to say after possible shifts), BORNE_MIN/MAX_EFFECT , as well as the number of modes found: NB_MODE . 3.6 Operands TYPE / RAYON / CENTRE_CONTOUR If TYPE_MODE=‘MODE_COMPLEXE’ or if TYPE_MODE=‘GENERAL’ (if MATR_C is supplied and/or if one of the matrices is non-symmetric or complex) ◊ TYPE_CONTOUR = 'CERCLE' [DEFAUT] ♦ RAYON_CONTOUR = rayon [R] ◊ CENTRE_CONTOUR = / centre [C] / 0.0+0.0j [DEFAUT] These keywords define the type of contour inside which one searches for the eigenvalues as well as its characteristics. For the moment one can choose only a contour of type 'CERCLE' (which therefore delimits the control disc). One mentions its centre (a complex number) and its radius (a positive real). Notes: - Strictly speaking, this radius must be greater than the “modal zero”. That is to say greater than the value below which one considers that an eigenvalue is zero or that two eigenvalues are coincident if one is speaking of their separation. - Unlike the values of FREQ, the units are not here in frequency, but in angular frequency if one makes the analogy with the DYNAMIQUE problem. As for a TYPE_MODE='MODE_FLAMB', the unit of the characteristics of the contour undergoes no transformation. This allows the APM method to treat all types of problems. - The table produced with the option TYPE_MODE='MODE_COMPLEXE' contains, in addition to the number of eigenvalues ( NB_MODE ), three reals making it possible to describe the search criteria for the APM method. The first two are CENTRE_R and CENTRE_I, the real and imaginary parts of the complex number that corresponds to the centre of the search disc. The third parameter, RAYON, is the radius (strictly positive real >1.D-2) of the disc. 3.7 Factor keyword COMPTAGE Once the type of control zone (segment or disc) has been defined, it remains to set the counting method and its parameters. ◊ METHODE = / ‘AUTO’, [DEFAUT] / ‘STURM’, / 'APM'. Si on traite un problème de type 'DYNAMIQUE' ou 'MODE_FLAMB', seule les méthodes 'STURM' et 'AUTO' sont autorisées. De même pour 'MODE_COMPLEXE' et 'APM'/'AUTO'. Dans le cas 'GENERAL', les trois méthodes sont disponibles et la valeur 'AUTO' prend alors tout son sens ! Elle choisit pour l'utilisateur entre STURM et APM suivant les caractéristiques du problème modal: - Either it is a standard GEP (two real symmetric matrices): STURM method. - In all the other cases (atypical GEP with a non-symmetric and/or complex matrix or QEP): APM method. Si on laisse le mode 'AUTO' paramétré par défaut, l'opérateur choisit automatiquement la méthode suivant le type d'étude choisie. On a laissé sciemment cette valeur, même dans les cas qui ne comportent qu'une seule alternative, pour faciliter l'ergonomie. Si on se trompe de METHODE, une alarme apparaît et l'opérateur choisit automatiquement la méthode la plus appropriée ou s'arrête en ERREUR_FATALE, suivant les cas de figure. Note: - One can use the APM method to count the modes of a standard GEP by setting TYPE_MODE='MODE_COMPLEXE'. This makes it possible to compare and validate the two counting methods (cf. test case SDLL123a). # Si TYPE_MODE=‘DYNAMIQUE’ ◊ SEUIL_FREQ = / f_seuil [R] / 0.01 [DEFAUT] ◊ PREC_SHIFT = / p_shift [R] / 0.05 [DEFAUT] ◊ NMAX_ITER_SHIFT = / n_shift [I] / 3 [DEFAUT] # Si TYPE_MODE=‘MODE_FLAMB’ ou 'GENERAL' (si MATR_C n'est pas renseignée et si les deux autres matrices sont symétriques réelles) ◊ SEUIL_CHAR_CRIT = / c_seuil [R] / 0.01 [DEFAUT] ◊ PREC_SHIFT = / p_shift [R] / 0.05 [DEFAUT] ◊ NMAX_ITER_SHIFT = / n_shift [I] / 3 [DEFAUT] These parameters are used only by the STURM method. The parameters SEUIL_ make it possible to define the “modal zero”, that is to say the value below which one considers that the eigenvalue is zero. If one is in dynamics one transforms this value into an angular frequency \mathit{omecor}={(2\pi \text{f\_seuil})}^{2} whereas in buckling one keeps it as it is \mathit{omecor}=\text{c\_seuil} . The other parameters, PREC_SHIFT and NMAX_ITER_SHIFT, are linked to the algorithm for shifting the bounds of the interval (cf. R5.01.04 §3.2) when one notices that they are very close to an eigenvalue. Roughly, these bounds {f}_{\min} (ou {\lambda}_{\min} en flambement) ou {f}_{\max} (resp. :math: {\lambda}_{max} ) are then shifted towards the outside of the segment by p_shift%. If the dynamic matrix thus rebuilt is still judged “numerically singular”, one shifts again after having issued an ALARME. One attempts this shift n_shift times. {{lambda}^{-}}_{min}={lambda}_{min}-max(mathit{omecor}{,2}^{(i-1)}text{x}{p}_{mathit{shift}}text{x}∣({lambda}_{min})∣) (ith attempt) {{lambda}^{-}}_{max}={lambda}_{max}+max(mathit{omecor}{,2}^{(i-1)}text{x}{p}_{mathit{shift}}text{x}∣({lambda}_{max})∣) (ith attempt) In fact, in dynamics as in buckling the shift is operated in the same way. Strictly speaking, in dynamics it is therefore not the frequencies that one shifts, but the angular frequencies. Another detail: the shift is in fact, for the sake of efficiency, dichotomic: p_shift% the first time, 2xp_shift% the second time etc. This process must make it possible to move quickly away from the “singularity zone” at lower cost. Conversely, one must not increase the values of these parameters too much, because by dint of shifts, the resulting bounds may turn out to be very different from the initial bounds. Furthermore, in order to remain consistent with the “modal zero” (denoted here omecor): - One does not shift by a value smaller than this minimum (hence the max in the formulae above), - If from the outset the assessed bound is smaller than this “zero” ∣{\lambda}_{\text{ }}∣ The APM algorithm implemented will converge only when 3 successive evaluations of the number of eigenvalues provide the same result. The differences between these three evaluations lie solely in the degree of discretisation of the contour. One starts by discretising with {k}_{-}=\text{nb\_point}/2 , then with k=\text{nb\_point} et enfin avec :math: {k}_{+}=2\text{nb\_point} . If these three levels of discretisation of the contour produce an identical estimate of the number of eigenvalues, the algorithm is considered to have converged. Its result is then this integer. Otherwise, one doubles these three levels of discretisation according to the following permutation {k}_{-}\leftarrow k , k\leftarrow {k}_{+} et :math: {k}_{+}\leftarrow 2{k}_{+} 6 If they are identical, convergence is reached, otherwise one continues. One repeats this dichotomic heuristic at most n_contour times. If this process has not converged or if its result is inconsistent (strictly negative integer), one stops in ERREUR_FATALE. 3.8 Operand INFO ◊ INFO = / 1 [DEFAUT] / 2 Indicates the print level in the MESSAGE file. 1: Printing of the result (and of the main steps of the algorithm if APM). 2: More detailed printing, rather for the developer. 3.9 Operand TITRE > The title that will be given to the table produced. 3.10 Factor keyword SOLVEUR ◊ SOLVEUR=_F(), On a accès à tous les paramètres des solveurs linéaires directs (METHODE='LDLT'/'MULT_FRONT'/'MUMPS') sauf ceux explicitement liés à l'étape finale de descente-remontée. Cette restriction ne concernent que les deux paramètres suivant du solveur MUMPS: POSTTRAITEMENTS et RESI_RELA. In parallel, one particularly recommends the setting 7 METHODE='MUMPS' and RENUM='QAMD'. Pour plus de détails sur les solveurs, on pourra consulter le document [:ref: U4.50.01 ]. 3.11 Operand NIVEAU_PARALLELISME ◊ NIVEAU_PARALLELISME = / 'COMPLET' [DEFAUT] / 'PARTIEL' When one treats problems of medium or large size (> 0.5M degrees of freedom) and/or when one seeks a good part of their spectra (> 50 modes), the use of parallelism provides appreciable gains in time and in memory. And this, with a functional behaviour and result accuracies unchanged with respect to sequential mode. The natural splitting of the INFO_MODE analysis into nb_sbande independent parts (number of sub-bands = nb_freq-1 or nb_mode_flamb-1) provides a first level of parallelism that is very efficient (in time). It does not affect the memory consumptions 8 . Furthermore, since the essential part of the computational cost is due to the numerical factorisation stage 9 of the linear solver, if one parallelises this stage via MUMPS (METHODE='MUMPS'), one adds notable gains in time and in memory. This is a second level of parallelism that can be activated. With the default value of this keyword (NIVEAU_PARALLELISME='COMPLET'), when the analysis is parallel, the two levels of parallelism are combined. Since the second (that of the linear solver) is less efficient than the first, it is triggered only if the number of processors allows it (nb_proc>nb_sbande) and if the linear solver selected supports MPI parallelism (SOLVEUR=_F(METHODE='MUMPS')). If one selects the other value of the keyword (NIVEAU_PARALLELISME='PARTIEL'), one benefits only from the parallelism of the linear solver (the second level). This may be of interest for testing methods or for focusing the gains on the reduction of the memory peak (after having tried the other levers proposed in the keyword SOLVEUR). For further information on the implementation of parallelism, one should refer to the documentation U2.08.06 or to the dedicated paragraph of the documentation U2.06.01. Figure 3.11-1. Example of the distribution of the INFO_MODE analyses on 8 processors with a splitting into 4 frequency sub-bands. Thus, by activating only the first level of parallelism, an analysis split into nb_sbande and parallelised on nb_proc=nb_sbande can gain in time at least a factor nb_sbande/2 (with no extra memory cost and no loss of accuracy). If one distributes the analysis over more processors (nb_proc>nb_sbande) by using the MUMPS solver (one thus adds the 2nd level), the gains in time will be improved by a factor close to 2 for each additional 2 nb_sbande processors [10]_ . And this, with memory gains that can go up to a factor of 2 [11]_ . In order to preserve the efficiency of the parallel analyses, one advises: - With 'COMPLET', to select a number of processors that is a multiple of the number of sub-bands. Typically 2, 4 or 8. This limits load imbalance. - With 'PARTIEL', to reserve at least 105 degrees of freedom per processor in order to feed the MUMPS linear solver sufficiently. The functional rules are the following, denoting by nb_proc the number of processors set (Astk options/mpi_nbcpu tab) and by nb_sbande the number of non-empty sub-bands: - With NIVEAU_PARALLELISME='COMPLET' (default) : very large gain in time / improvement of the RAM memory peak. This notion of generalised matrix has nothing to do with that of a generalised modal problem! Of course, in order to save computation time, one re-evaluates only for the new discretisation, the finest one. In order to reduce to a minimum the time cost of the (sequential) analysis phase of MUMPS. This setting is however done at the expense of the memory consumption. But this extra cost quickly proves to be compensated by the distribution of the data over the processors implied by the parallelism. Which is the case for CALC_MODES with OPTION='BANDE' split over several parallelised sub-bands. Stage of the linear solver that benefits the most from parallelism. On sufficiently large problems (N>0.5M), the parallel efficiency of the MUMPS factorisation phase is often close to 0.5 (especially with a crude renumberer of type 'QAMD' cf. §3.10). In INFO_MODE, the memory consumptions of MUMPS are particularly optimised: operation in IN-CORE does not consume more memory than OUT-OF-CORE (gain x3). This behaviour is suited to this operator. The gains that parallelism can provide it are therefore, in proportion, less important. 4 Examples 4.1 Example no. 1 Comparison of the two methods STURM and APM on the standard GEP of SDLD02a (for STURM the bounds are given in frequency). u4.52.02 Operator CALC_MODES u4.52.02 Operator CALC_MODES 1 Purpose Compute the vibration eigenmodes or the Euler buckling modes of a mechanical structure. The operator CALC_MODES solves, for this purpose, a modal problem which may be either generalised (GEP) [[R5.01.01]](https://code-aster.org/V2/doc/default/fr/man_r/r5/r5.01.01.pdf), or quadratic (QEP) [[R5.01.02]](https://code-aster.org/V2/doc/default/fr/man_r/r5/r5.01.02.pdf). The user specifies the mode search criterion (for example: over a band; in the vicinity of given values; etc.) by means of the keyword OPTION. Depending on the value of this keyword, the general analysis method (simultaneous iterations or inverse iterations) is then determined automatically. Within each of these two general methods, variants exist: - case of simultaneous iterations: subspace-type method (Bathe & Wilson, Lanczos or Sorensen), global QR-type method (QZ for small problems); - case of inverse iterations: direct method or method accelerated by the Rayleigh quotient. These variants are accessed with a factor keyword SOLVEUR_MODAL. In the case of an analysis of vibration eigenmodes, post-processing may also be carried out: normalisation of the modes according to a given criterion, filtering of the modes according to a given criterion, production of the modal parameters... This operator produces a concept mode_meca_ (dynamic case) or mode_flamb (Euler buckling case, only in GEP) or mode_gene according to the value entered under the keyword TYPE_RESU and the type of the input matrices of the modal problem. The concept mode_meca_ , or mode_flamb, contains the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors, and modal parameters, cf. [[R5.01.03]](https://code-aster.org/V2/doc/default/fr/man_r/r5/r5.01.03.pdf) _. To model hysteretic damping in the study of the free vibrations of a structure, the matrix \mathrm{A} may be complex symmetric U2.06.03 R5.05.04. This type of problem corresponds, in mechanics, in particular to: - The study of the free vibrations of a structure which is undamped and non-rotating. For this structure, one looks for the smallest eigenvalues or those which lie in a given interval in order to know whether an exciting force can create a resonance. In this case, the matrix \mathrm{A} is the material stiffness matrix, denoted \mathrm{K} , real symmetric (possibly augmented by the geometric stiffness matrix denoted {\mathrm{K}}_{g} , if the structure is prestressed), and \mathrm{B} is the mass or inertia matrix denoted \mathrm{M} (real symmetric). The eigenvalues obtained are the squares of the angular frequencies associated with the frequencies sought. The system to be solved may be written \underset{\mathrm{A}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{(\mathrm{K}+{\mathrm{K}}_{g})}}\mathrm{x}=\lambda \underset{\mathrm{B}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{\mathrm{M}}}\mathrm{x} where \lambda ={(2\pi f)}^{2} is the square of the angular frequency \omega , f the eigenfrequency and \mathrm{x} the associated eigen displacement vector. The eigenmodes handled (\lambda ,x) are real-valued. This type of problem is activated by the keyword TYPE_RESU='DYNAMIQUE' and generates a data structure of type mode_meca, mode_acou or mode_gene (depending on the type of the input data). - The search for a linear buckling mode . Within the framework of linearised theory, assuming a priori that the stability phenomena are adequately described by the system of equations obtained by assuming the linear dependence of the displacement with respect to the load level, the search for the buckling mode x associated with this critical load level \mu =-\lambda . This reduces to a generalised eigenvalue problem of the form: (\mathrm{K}+\mu {\mathrm{K}}_{g})x=0\mathrm{\iff }\underset{\mathrm{A}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{\mathrm{K}}}\mathrm{x}=\lambda \underset{\mathrm{B}}{\underset{\underbrace{}}{{\mathrm{K}}_{g}}}\mathrm{x} with \mathrm{K} the material stiffness matrix and {\mathrm{K}}_{g} the geometric stiffness matrix. The eigenmodes handled (\lambda ,x) are real-valued. This type of problem is activated by the keyword TYPE_RESU='MODE_FLAMB' and generates a data structure of type mode_flamb. Caution: - In Code_Aster, one produces the eigenvalues of the generalised problem, that is to say the variables \lambda . To obtain the true critical loads, the variables \mu , they must be multiplied by –1. Caution: - In GEP, to treat problems with complex modes (non-symmetric matrices and/or with complex values), one must use the modal solver with METHODE='SORENSEN' or 'QZ' . This operator also makes it possible to study the dynamic stability of a structure in the presence of damping and/or gyroscopic effects . This leads to the solution of a modal problem of higher order, called quadratic (QEP) R5.01.02. One then looks for complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors (\lambda ,\mathrm{x}) . - The problem consists in finding (\lambda ,\mathrm{x})\in (\mathrm{ℂ},{\mathrm{ℂ}}^{N}) such that: ({\lambda}^{2}\mathrm{B}+\lambda \mathrm{C}+\mathrm{A})\mathrm{x}=0 where typically, in linear mechanics, \mathrm{A} will be the stiffness matrix, \mathrm{B} the mass matrix and \mathrm{C} the damping matrix. The matrices \mathrm{A} , \mathrm{B} and \mathrm{C} are symmetric real matrices. The complex eigenvalue \lambda is related to the eigenfrequency f and to the reduced damping \xi by \lambda =\xi (2\pi f)\pm i(2\pi f)\sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}} . This type of problem is activated by the keyword TYPE_RESU='DYNAMIQUE' and generates a data structure of type mode_meca_c. The complex angular frequency is therefore \omega = i \lambda =\pm |\omega | \sqrt{1-{\xi}^{2}} + i | \omega | \xi Caution: - In QEP, to treat problems with non-symmetric matrices and/or with complex values, one must use the modal solver with METHODE='SORENSEN' or 'QZ' . - Buckling ( TYPE_RESU='MODE_FLAMB' ) is not allowed in QEP. - All the options work whatever the taking into account of the boundary conditions ( AFFE_CHAR_MECA or AFFE_CHAR_CINE ). The Sturm test [R5.01.04] _ is operative only in GEP with real symmetric matrices. Outside this framework (QEP, GEP with non-symmetric real matrices or with a complex symmetric matrix A ), the option ‘BANDE’ is prohibited and the post-verification based on the Sturm test is not activated (parameter VERI_MODE/STURM inoperative). To solve these generalised or quadratic modal problems, Code_Aster offers different approaches. This detection is carried out by comparing the loss of decimal places of the diagonal terms of this factorised matrix with respect to their initial values (in absolute value). If the maximum of this loss is greater than ndeci 7 , the matrix is assumed to be singular and one looks for a shifted value of the shift yielding an invertible matrix. For the GEPs, the parameters SEUIL_ make it possible to define the “modal zero”, that is to say the value below which one considers that an eigenvalue is zero. As a corollary, in certain processing of the operator, if the gap between two eigenvalues is less than this value, one considers that they coincide. One must therefore adjust this value according to the average amplitude of the eigenvalues sought. If one is in dynamics one transforms this value into an angular frequency: \mathit{omecor}={(2\pi \text{f\_seuil})}^{2} whereas in buckling one keeps it as it is: \mathit{omecor}=\text{c\_seuil} . For the QEPs, this value of the “modal zero” is used during the sorting carried out at the end of the modal analysis. During this sorting, one seeks to determine whether a mode is real (one does not keep it), complex conjugate (one keeps the one with positive imaginary part) or unpaired complex (one does not keep it). One then splits the analysis into several frequency sub-bands (cf. operand FREQ). On each of these sub-bands, a modal solver carries out the associated mode search. To do this, this modal solver makes intensive use of a linear solver. These two computational building blocks (modal solver and linear solver) are the stages which dominate the analysis in terms of memory consumption and time. It is on them that one must concentrate if one wants to reduce significantly the computational costs of this operator. Now, the organisation of the modal analysis over distinct sub-bands offers here an ideal framework for parallelism: distribution of large, almost independent analyses [11]_ . Its parallelism makes it possible to gain a great deal in time but at the price of an extra cost in memory [12]_ . If one has a sufficient number of processors (greater than the number of non-empty sub-bands), one can then switch on a second level of parallelism via the linear solver (if one has chosen METHODE='MUMPS'). This will make it possible to continue to gain in time but above all, it will make it possible to compensate the memory extra cost of the first level or even to reduce notably the sequential memory peak. Image 3.14-1- Example of distribution of the analyses of CALC_MODES on 8 processors with a splitting into 4 frequency sub-bands This double level of parallelism (activated by default via the keyword NIVEAU_PARALLELISME='COMPLET') then makes it possible to take advantage, in the best way, of both aspects. When one truly wishes to gain in memory peak because the analysis does not fit on the machine and one has tried, without success, all the other levers [13]_ , one may deliberately choose to limit the parallelism to the linear solver only [14]_ : NIVEAU_PARALLELISME='PARTIEL'. This works only with the parallel linear solver MUMPS. The functional rules are the following, denoting by nbproc the number of processors set and by nb_sbande the number of non-empty sub-bands (=nb_freq-1): - With NIVEAU_PARALLELISME='COMPLET' (default): very large gain in time / moderate improvement or deterioration of the RAM memory peak. Image 3.14-2- Scope of use with NIVEAU_PARALLELISME='COMPLET' . - With NIVEAU_PARALLELISME='PARTIEL' : moderate gain in time / large gain on the RAM memory peak. Image 3.14-3- Scope of use with NIVEAU_PARALLELISME='PARTIEL' . For an optimal use of the parallelism, it is therefore advised to: - Build relatively balanced computation sub-bands. To do this, one may therefore, beforehand, calibrate the spectrum under study via one or more calls to INFO_MODE[U4.52.01]. If possible in parallel mode. Then launch the CALC_MODES analysis in parallel according to the number of sub-bands chosen and the number of processors available. - Take sub-bands finer than in sequential, between 10 and 20 modes instead of 40 to 80 modes in sequential. The quality of the modes and the robustness of the analysis will thereby be increased. The memory peak will be reduced. One must however have enough processors available (and with enough memory). - Select a number of processors which is a multiple of the number of (non-empty) sub-bands. Thus, one reduces the load imbalances which harm performance. METHODE='TRI_DIAG' ndim=MIN(MAX(7+nf,mse nf),nactif ) avec mse=4 par défaut. METHODE='JACOBI' ndim=MIN(MAX(7+nf,mse nf),nactif) avec mse=2 par défaut. where nactif is the number of active degrees of freedom (that is to say the total number of degrees of freedom minus the number of LAGRANGE degrees of freedom and minus the number of linear relations which link degrees of freedom together, R5.01.01 §3.2) and mse is the proportionality factor set by COEF_DIM_ESPACE. If one solves a GEP, the dimension of the subspace is doubled. The values of these various parameters are printed in the MESSAGE file. - For the option 'SEPARE': having obtained an interval bracketing an eigenvalue, one takes for the computation of the mode the middle of the interval. During the computation of the mode, the value of the eigenvalue is further refined. This is the result of the inverse iteration proper. - For the option 'AJUSTE ': if the separation is not possible and if in a given interval there is more than one eigenvalue, one does not apply the adjustment method to this interval. On the other hand, one will carry out, during the computation of the modes, reorthogonalisations with respect to the previous modes contained in the interval (this makes it possible to compute modes associated with a multiple eigenvalue). 6 Modal parameters/ Norm of the modes/ Modal position On output from this operator, the real or complex eigenmodes are normalised to the largest of the components which is not a LAGRANGE multiplier. To choose another norm, one must use the factor keyword NORM_MODE inside CALC_MODES, or the command NORM_MODE U4.52.11 following CALC_MODES (one then has access to more functionalities). In the case of a dynamic analysis, the data structure mode_meca_ , and mode_gene, contains, in addition to the vibration frequencies and the associated mode shapes, modal parameters (generalised mass, generalised stiffness, participation factor, effective mass and effective inertia for the mode_meca case only). The definition of these parameters will be found in R5.01.03. In the case of a linear buckling analysis, the data structure mode_flamb contains only the critical loads and the associated mode shapes. In the case of a generalised dynamic analysis with real symmetric matrices, the modal position corresponds to the position of the mode in the whole of the spectrum defined by the initial matrices. In all the other cases, the modal positions are assigned from 1 to nf (nf being the number of modes retained) by classifying them in algebraically increasing order. All the modal positions are therefore positive. 7 Optimisation of the CPU performance 7.1 Parallelism of the linear solver The modal analysis calls on a linear solver. If one chooses the linear solver MUMPS with the factor keyword SOLVEUR, operand METHODE='MUMPS', one can activate its operation in parallel. For this one must use a parallel version of Code_Aster , and fill in the number of processors to be used. Empirically, the use of one processor per slice of 105 to 106 degrees of freedom that the model comprises gives good performance. In parallel, one also recommends the setting RENUM='QAMD'. 7.2 Computation of the modes by sub-bands If the problem to be treated is a GEP and one is looking for many modes over a given band, or if the number of degrees of freedom of the model is high (> 105), it is advised to split the global search band into several sub-bands, of 40 to 80 modes, as balanced as possible. The analysis will thus be more robust and faster, even by calling a CALC_MODES sequentially for each sub-band. For better ergonomics, the analyses on each sub-band can be carried out automatically and in a way that is transparent to the user, by giving the keyword FREQ a list of n>2 values. This moreover makes it possible to parallelise the processing of the various sub-bands, producing considerable gains on the CPU performance (a factor which may reach 10 to 20 on the computation time, and several tens of percent on the memory peak). For more details, one will refer to the generic documents U2.08.06 on parallelism, and U2.06.01 on the computation of eigenmodes. 8 Printout of the results To display the modal parameters associated with each mode and the coordinates of the modes, one must use the appropriate operator according to the type of analysis: - if the analysis corresponds to a mechanical mode ( mode_meca ), use the operator: IMPR_RESU U4.91.01; - if the analysis corresponds to a generalised mode ( mode_gene ), use the operator: IMPR_GENE U4.91.02. The commands are used in the following way: - Display of the modal parameters only in the form of a table: IMPR_RESU(RESU=_F(RESULTAT=mode, TOUT_PARA='OUI', TOUT_CHAM='NON'),) - Display of the modal parameters and of the eigenvectors: IMPR_RESU(RESU=_F(RESULTAT=mode, TOUT_PARA='OUI', TOUT_CHAM='OUI'),) 9 Sorting of modes / Characterisation of mode_meca_ For example, during seismic loadings in a modal analysis, the modal basis used must contain the modes which have a large unit effective mass in the direction of the earthquake. The factor keyword FILTRE_MODE makes it possible to extract, in the data structure of type mode_meca_ , modes which satisfy a certain criterion. One may also use the command EXTR_MODE U4.52.12 after CALC_MODES, in order for example to concatenate several data structures of type mode_meca_ . 10 Examples 10.1 Computation of the 5 eigenmodes closest to a given frequency mode=CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI=rigid, MATR_MASS=masse, OPTION =‘CENTRE’, CALC_FREQ=_F( FREQ=100., NMAX_FREQ=5 ) ); 10.2 Computation of the critical loads contained in a band mode=CALC_MODES( TYPE_RESU=‘MODE_FLAMB’, MATR_RIGI=rigid, MATR_RIGI_GEOM=riggeo, OPTION=‘BANDE’, CALC_FREQ=_F( CHAR_CRIT=(-1.E8,1.5E8)) ); 10.3 Chaining INFO_MODE+CALC_MODES (extract from SDLS504a) nbmod1 = INFO_MODE( TYPE_MODE='MODE_FLAMB', ... CHAR_CRIT=(-1.E+6,-5.E+5,0.0,1.E+5,1.1E+6),) RESULT0=CALC_MODES( TYPE_RESU='MODE_FLAMB', ..., OPTION='BANDE', CALC_CHAR_CRIT=_F( TABLE_CHAR_CRIT=nbmod1, CHAR_CRIT=(-1.E+06,1.E+05)), ) 10.4 Computation of the eigenfrequencies contained in the band [50 ; 150] Hz with the inverse iteration method mode=CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI=rigidite, MATR_MASS=masse, OPTION=’AJUSTE’, CALC_FREQ=_F( FREQ=(50.,150.)) ) 10.5 Computation of the eigenfrequencies closest to 20 and 50 Hz with the inverse iteration method, with acceleration of convergence by the Rayleigh coefficient mode= CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI=rigidite, MATR_MASS=masse, OPTION=’PROCHE’, CALC_FREQ=_F( FREQ=(50.,150.)), SOLVEUR_MODAL=_F(OPTION_INV=’RAYLEIGH’) ) 10.6 Splitting into several sub-bands Let the following sequence be given: mode=CALC_MODES( MATR_RIGI=rigi, MATR_MASS=masse, OPTION='BANDE', CALC_FREQ=_F( FREQ=(1.,3.,5.),) VERI_MODE=_F(), NORM_MODE=_F(NORME='TRAN_ROTA',), FILTRE_MODE=_F(CRIT_EXTR='MASS_EFFE_UN'), IMPRESSION=_F(CUMUL='OUI', CRIT_EXTR='MASS_EFFE_UN') ); One therefore wants to look for all the modes contained in the global band [1.,5.] Hz by splitting it into two frequency sub-bands: [1.,3.] and [3.,5.] . Once interpreted, the macro-command consists of the sequence of usual commands described below. - Stage 1: Determination of the number of frequencies in each sub-band table1=INFO_MODE( MATR_RIGI=rigi, > MATR_MASS=masse, FREQ=(1.,3.,5.)) [16]_ : nbmodeth If the global band is empty: ALARME or ERREUR_FATALE according to the value of CALC_FREQ/STOP_BANDE_VIDE. - Stage 2: Computation and normalisation of the modes in each sub-band [:ref: 17 ]_ and, by default, one does not carry out locally on each sub-band the Sturm post-verification test. # Si la sous-bande locale est vide: ALARMEou ERREUR_FATALE suivant la valeur de CALC_FREQ/STOP_BANDE_VIDE. mode_1=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=rigi, MATR_MASS=masse, OPTION='BANDE', CALC_FREQ=_F( FREQ=(1.,3.), TABLE_FREQ=table1),), VERI_MODE(STURM='NON')); mode_1=NORM_MODE( MODE=mode_1, reuse=mode1, NORME='TRAN_ROTA',); mode_2=CALC_MODES(MATR_RIGI=rigi, MATR_MASS=masse, OPTION='BANDE', CALC_FREQ=_F( FREQ=(3.,5.), TABLE_FREQ=table1),), VERI_MODE(STURM='NON')); mode_2=NORM_MODE( MODE=mode_2, reuse=mode2, NORME='TRAN_ROTA',); # Vérification par un test de Sturm global du bon nombre de fréquences calculées # Détermination de la plus petite (resp. grande) fréquence de la première (resp. dernière) sous-bande non vide: freq_ini(resp. freq_fin). # Calcul du nombre de fréquences comprises dans l'intervalle: :math: [\text{freq\_ini},\text{freq\_fin}] : nbmodeef. table2=INFO_MODE( MATR_RIGI=rigi, MATR_MASS=masse, FREQ=(freq_ini,freq_fin)) If this number of modes is different from the number of modes initially expected: ERREUR_FATALE . - Stage 3: Filtering, concatenation and printout of the computed modes. mode=EXTR_MODE( FILTRE_MODE=_F( MODE=mode_1, CRIT_EXTR='MASS_EFFE_UN'), FILTRE_MODE=_F( MODE=mode_2, CRIT_EXTR='MASS_EFFE_UN'), IMPRESSION=_F( CUMUL='OUI', CRIT_EXTR='MASS_EFFE_UN'), ); One simply sums the numbers of frequencies computed previously and stored in table1. In order not to repeat the preprocessing Sturm test specific to each sub-band.

u4.52.05 Operator MODE_ITER_CYCL u4.52.05 Operator MODE_ITER_CYCL 1 Purpose Compute the eigenmodes of a structure with cyclic symmetry. One computes the generalised components of the eigenmodes of the whole structure, by a cyclic substructuring method, from the modal base of a reference sector (cf R4.06.03). The axis of symmetry is the axis OZ. The modal base of the sector must be of type CLASSIQUE. The interfaces DROITE, GAUCHE and possibly AXE must be of the same type. The right and left sides are defined by the anticlockwise sense in the plane OXY. Produces a data structure of type mode_cycl. 2 Syntax mode_cycl = MODE_ITER_CYCL( ◆ BASE_MODALE = mode_meca, ◇ NB_MODE = int, ◆ NB_SECTEUR = int, ◆ LIAISON = _F( ◆ DROITE = text, ◆ GAUCHE = text, ◇ AXE = text, ), ◇ VERI_CYCL = _F( ◇ PRECISION = float (défaut: 0.001), ◇ CRITERE = "RELATIF", ◇ DIST_REFE = float, ), ◆ CALCUL = _F( ◆ / TOUT_DIAM = "OUI" (ou non renseigné), / NB_DIAM = int, ◇ OPTION = / "PLUS_PETITE" (par défaut), / "CENTRE", / "BANDE", # Si: equal_to("OPTION", 'CENTRE') ◆ FREQ = float, # Si: equal_to("OPTION", 'BANDE') ◆ FREQ = float, ◇ NMAX_FREQ = int (défaut: 10), ◇ PREC_SEPARE = float (défaut: 100.0), ◇ PREC_AJUSTE = float (défaut: 1e-06), ◇ NMAX_ITER = int (défaut: 50), ), ◇ INFO = / 1 (par défaut), / 2, ) ◆ : obligatoire ◇ : optionnel ⟐ : présent par défaut & : ensemble / : un seul parmi | : plusieurs choix possibles 3 Operands 3.1 Operand BASE_MODALE ♦ BASE_MODALE= bamo Name of the modal base of the sector built by DEFI_BASE_MODALE U4.64.02. 3.2 Operand NB_MODE ◊ NB_MODE= nbmo Number of eigenmodes of the sector to be used for the cyclic analysis.
