v4.22.100 TTNL100 - Nonlinear thermal source, homogeneous solution in space v4.22.100 TTNL100 - Nonlinear thermal source, homogeneous solution in space Summary: This test checks the thermal calculation in the presence of a nonlinear source loading, depending on the temperature. The reference solution is analytical. The part considered in the modellings consists of a single element whose dimensions do not matter to the solution. The following mesh cellss are checked: - Modelization A: - TRIA3, TRIA6, QUAD4, QUAD8 and QUAD9 for PLAN Modelling, - TRIA3,QUAD4 for PLAN_DIAG Modelling, - Modelling B: PENTA6 for 3D modelling Since the temperature is homogeneous in the element, the calculation can be considered as 0D. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The part considered in both modellings is a unique element. Since the temperature is homogeneous in the element, the calculation can be considered as 0D. 1.2 Material properties | \lambda =0 | thermal conductivity | | --- | --- | | \rho C=2 | volumetric heat | 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads Nonlinear volume source loading, temperature function: s(T)=2-2\times w\times T with w=2 Boundary conditions are adiabatic, which corresponds to the defect in Code_Aster . The [0.;1.] time range is discretized in 100 time step (duration of each time step equal to 0.01 ). 1.4 Initial conditions \mathit{T0}=0 in all the element. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution In this problem, the boundary conditions are adiabatic, the initial temperature is constant equal to {T}_{0} and the load is reduced to the heat source function of the temperature r(T)={r}_{0}-{r}_{1}T where {r}_{1} is positive for questions of thermal stability. These conditions ensure a homogeneous solution in space. The heat equation is reduced to: > \rho {C}_{p}\dot{T}={r}_{0}-{r}_{1}T ; T(0)={T}_{0} [éq1] Standardization can be reduced without loss of generality to the following equation: > \dot{u}=1-\omega u ; u(0)=0 [éq2] The solution of this differential equation of first order is then: > u(t)=\frac{1}{\omega}(1-{e}^{-\omega t}) Rather than going back from u solution from [eq2] to T solution from [eq1], we prefer to adopt the following set of parameters, without paying attention to the units, which leads to T=u : {T}_{0}=0 , {r}_{0}=\rho C and {r}_{1}=\omega {r}_{0} . 2.2 Baseline The test case is conducted with \omega =2 and the temperature at t=1 is examined in any node of the element. The data are as follows: | Thermal conductivity | LAMBDA | | | --- | --- | --- | | Volumetric heating capacity | RHO_CP | | | Initial temperature | {T}_{0} | | | Heat source | {r}_{0} {r}_{1} | 2. 4. | | Quantity tested | T ( t=1 ) | | --- | --- | | Reference value | 0.432332 | 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics PLAN Modelling is used and then PLAN_DIAG Modelling is used. 3.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh consists of a single mesh cell for each of the following types. | modellings | mesh cells | | --- | --- | | PLAN | TRIA3 TRIA6 QUAD4 QUAD8 QUAD9 | | PLAN_DIAG | TRIA3 QUAD4 | 3.3 Tested quantities and results The temperature at t=1 is tested in any node of the element. The solution conforms to the analytical value at less than 0.1%. 4 Modelling B 4.1 Modelling characteristics 3D modelling is used. 4.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh consists of a single mesh cell of the PENTA6 type. 4.3 Tested quantities and results The temperature at t=1 is tested in any node of the element. The solution conforms to the analytical value at less than 0.1%. 5 Summary of the results The results are consistent with the analytical solution.

v4.22.101 TTNL101 - Nonlinear thermal source in a bar v4.22.101 TTNL101 - Nonlinear thermal source in a bar Summary: This test checks the thermal calculation in the presence of a nonlinear source loading, depending on the temperature. The reference solution is analytical and variable in time and space. The part considered in the three modellings is a symmetrical bar composed of molten elements. The following mesh cellss are checked: - Modelling A: - QUAD4, QUAD8, QUAD9 quadrangles for AXIS Modelling - QUAD4 quadrangles for AXIS_DIAG Modelling - Modelling B: - HEXA8 hexahedrons for 3D_DIAG modelling - Modelization C: - TRIA3 triangles for AXIS Modelling - TRIA3 triangles for AXIS_DIAG Modelling - Modelling D: - QUAD9 quadrangles for linear AXIS_HHO Modelling - Modelling E: - HEXA8 hexahedrons for quadratic 3D_HHO Modelling - Modelling F: - QUAD9 quadrangles for constant AXIS_HHO Modelling - Modelling G: - QUAD9 quadrangles for cubic AXIS_HHO Modelling - Modelling H: - QUAD9 quadrangles for AXIS_HHO quartic Modelling Both ends of the bar are subject to the default adabadicity conditions. The heat source is a linear function of temperature. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A one-dimensional structure (a bar whose side faces are subject to adiabatic conditions) of \mathrm{2L} length occupying the [-L;L] domain is considered. Since the temperature is homogeneous in the normal directions at the bar, the calculation can be considered as 1D. 1.2 Material properties | \lambda =2 | thermal conductivity | | --- | --- | | \rho C=2 | volumetric heat | 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads Nonlinear volume source loading, temperature function: s(T)=2-2\times w\times T with w=2 Boundary conditions are adiabatic on side faces and temperature-type imposed zero at the end of the bar; a symmetry condition is implemented on the symmetry plane (equivalent to an adiabatic boundary condition). The [0.;1.] time range is discretized in 100 time step (duration of each time step equal to 0.01 ). 1.4 Initial conditions An initial analytical state is provided. See developments in the paragraph detailing the reference solution. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The bar is subjected to a heat source r(T)={r}_{0}-{r}_{1}T , where {r}_{1}>0 for thermal stability issues. Its initial temperature is {T}_{0}(x) and the ends of the bar are kept at zero temperature. The temperature evolution follows the heat equation: \rho c\dot{T}=\lambda {\nabla}^{2}T+r(T) ; T(x,0)={T}_{0}(x) ; T(-L,t)=T(L,t)=0 Standardization can be reduced without loss of generality to the following equation: \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\frac{{\partial}^{2}u}{\partial {x}^{2}}+1-{\omega}^{2}u ; u(x,0)={u}_{0}(x) ; u(-1,t)=u(1,t)=0 To solve this equation, we first look at the asymptotic solution {u}_{\infty}(x) which checks: 0=\frac{{\partial}^{2}{u}_{\infty}}{\partial {x}^{2}}+1-{\omega}^{2}{u}_{\infty} ; {u}_{\infty}(-1)={u}_{\infty}(1)=0 The solution of this linear differential equation of the second order is: {u}_{\infty}(x)=\frac{1}{{\omega}^{2}}(1-\frac{\cosh\omega x}{\cosh\omega }) The solution of the transient equation is then obtained by projection of v=u-{u}_{\infty} on the Laplacian's own functions on \left\rbrace -1,1\right\lbrace . To simplify the analysis, an initial condition {u}_{0} equal to the first mode of its own is adopted, namely: {u}_{0}(x)={u}_{\infty}(x)-\cos\frac{\pi x}{2} Only the first mode is activated, so we are reduced to the resolution of a differential equation in first order, to finally obtain the solution: u(x,t)={u}_{\infty}(x)-\exp(-{\omega}^{2}t-\frac{{\pi}^{2}}{4}t)\cos\frac{\pi x}{2} Finally, as before, we go back from u to T by adopting a set of specific parameters, without taking into account the units, so that T=u . For this, we take \lambda ={r}_{0}=\rho c , {r}_{1}={\omega}^{2}{r}_{0} , L=1 and {T}_{0}(x)={u}_{0}(x) . 2.2 Baseline The test case is conducted with \omega =\sqrt{2} and the temperature at t=1 is examined in an node of the (x=0) symmetry plane. v4.23.101 TTLP101 - Frusted plate at prescribed temperatures with exchange condition through crack lips v4.23.101 TTLP101 - Frusted plate at prescribed temperatures with exchange condition through crack lips Summary This test involves a square plate with a straight crack opening, subjected to a temperature gradient. A thermal exchange takes place between the lips of the crack (factor keyword ECHANGE_PAROI of the operators AFFE_CHAR_THER and AFFE_CHAR_THER_F U4.44.02). Three modellings are considered: - A Modelling: \text{FEM}\mathrm{2D} (mesh crack) - B Modelling: \text{X-FEM}\mathrm{2D} , crack in the middle of elements - C Modelling: \text{X-FEM}\mathrm{3D} , crack in the middle of elements 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The \mathrm{2d} structure is a unit square ( \mathit{LX}=1m , \mathit{LY}=1m ), with a straight crack opening to the right, located at mid-height. (Figure ) The left line is called the x=0 line , the right line is called the x=\mathit{LX} line and the bottom line is called the y=0 line . Figure 1.1-a : Geometry of the cracked square plate {P}^{+} is the point coordinates \left(\mathit{LX},{\mathit{LY}}^{+}/2\right) (located on the upper lip), {P}^{-} the point coordinates (\mathit{LX},{\mathit{LY}}^{-}/2) (located on the lower lip), and Q the point coordinates \left(\mathit{LX}/2,\mathit{LY}/2\right) (located on the crack tip). 1.2 Material properties Thermal conductivity: \lambda =1{\mathit{W.m}}^{\text{-1}}.{K}^{\text{-1}} Volumetric heating capacity: \rho {C}_{p}=2\mathit{J.m}-{\mathrm{3.K}}^{-1} Exchange coefficient between the lips of the h=2{\mathit{W.m}}^{\text{-2}}.{K}^{\text{-1}} crack 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The problem is solved on the time interval \left[0.s,1.s\right] discretized in 5 time step equal (of duration \Delta t=0.2s ). The default value is taken in THER_LINEAIRE of the parameter of the theta-schema: \theta =0.57 . The following temperature ramp shall be imposed on nodes segment \mathit{AB} (see Figure ): à t=0.s , \text{}\stackrel{̄}{T}{\rbrace ^{\mathit{AB}}=10°C ; à t=1.s , \text{}\stackrel{ˉ}{T}{\rbrace ^{\mathit{AB}}=20°C The following temperature ramp shall be imposed on nodes segment \mathit{CD} (see Figure ): à t=0.s , \text{}\stackrel{̄}{T}{\rbrace ^{\mathit{CD}}=20°C ; à t=1.s , \text{}\stackrel{̄}{T}{\rbrace ^{\mathit{CD}}=40°C Finally, on the lips of the crack, a Neumann condition of type exchange condition is imposed. 1.4 Initial conditions The initial state is determined by solving the stationary problem at t=0.s (with the boundary conditions given in paragraph 1.3.) 2 reference solution 2.1 Method of calculation The reference solution is obtained by refining the mesh Modelling A (elements classic with mesh crack): mesh regular compound of 500\times 500 QUAD4 (instead of 100\times 100 QUAD4 for mesh A) 2.2 Quantities and reference results The temperature at the end of the last time step ( t=1.s ) is tested at {P}^{+} , {P}^{-} and Q (see Figure ). | Identification | Reference type | Reference value | | --- | --- | --- | | Point {P}^{+} - \mathit{TEMP} | 'AUTRE_ASTER' | 29,156091860463 °C | | Point {P}^{-} - \mathit{TEMP} | 'AUTRE_ASTER' | 23,393394671258 °C | | Point Q - \mathit{TEMP} | 'AUTRE_ASTER' | 26,25259365185 °C | 3 Modelling A In this Modelling, the \mathrm{2D} structure is considered. v4.24.201 TTNP201-Thermal transfer with time-dependent conductivity v4.24.201 TTNP201-Thermal transfer with time-dependent conductivity Summary: This test consists of imposing variable conductivity time-dependent during a thermal transfer. A prescribed flow condition is applied to a edge of the wall and the temperature remains constant on the opposite edge. The conductivity increases with time and a temperature jump is observed on the edge where the flow is imposed. The problem is handled in PLAN, AXIS and 3D. The reference solution is obtained by the iterative method of Crank-Nicholson. The consideration of a time-dependent conductivity is tested. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A wall of thickness L=2m is considered. 1.2 Material properties The thermal properties are: - \rho \mathrm{Cp}=1J/{m}^{3}°C - \lambda (W/m°C) varies as follows: 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads On the \mathrm{SI} edge, a cooling flow of -1W/{m}^{2} is imposed. On the \mathrm{SE} edge, you will set a temperature of 100°C . 1.4 Initial conditions At the initial moment, the temperature is uniform and equal to 100°C . 1.5 Time-based discussion The calculation is performed on \mathrm{200s} with an time step of: 0,1s between 0 and \mathrm{40s} then 0,05s between \mathrm{40s} and \mathrm{80s} and finally 0,1s up to \mathrm{200s} . 2 reference solution 2.1 Method of calculation You must solve: \rho \mathrm{Cp}\frac{\mathrm{dT}(x,t)}{\mathrm{dt}}=\lambda (t)\frac{\mathrm{dT}(x,t)}{\mathrm{dx}} with the initial condition T(x,0)=100 and boundary conditions: -\lambda (t){\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\mid }_{x=0}=-1 and T(L,t)=100 This differential equation is solved with an iterative diagram of Crank-Nicholson [1] under scilab. 2.2 Quantities and reference results The temperature is observed at the edge of x=0 and in the middle of the x=\frac{L}{2} wall. When conductivity increases between 50 and 55 seconds, the temperature in the middle decreases more rapidly. The lost heat is spread to the edges where warming is observed. This phenomenon is also observed when drying calculation is done when the diffusion coefficient depends on temperature. We see then a re-wetting of the edge. For the test case reference, the temperature values in x=0 and x=\frac{L}{2} are recorded at different times corresponding to the appearance of the temperature jump at peak and at the end of the calculation. | | 50s | 51s | 72s | 200s | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | x=0 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | | x=L/2 | 0.0000 | Not tested | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 2.3 Uncertainties about the solution The resolution method requires small steps in time and space to correctly capture the temperature peak. Here we used \mathrm{dx}=0,05m and \mathrm{dt}=0,01s . 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. v4.26.101 TTNV101 – Concrete drying – Identification of parameters on the mass loss curve v4.26.101 TTNV101 – Concrete drying – Identification of parameters on the mass loss curve Summary: The objective of this test is to give an example of a simulation of concrete drying and the calculation of mass loss. The mass loss curve is often used to identify parameters of drying laws. The calculation of the mass loss (water) over time is done. A 3D sample is modelled. The drying law is SECH_GRANGER. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry One quarter of the 70\times 70\times 280\mathrm{mm} prismatic sample is considered. 1.2 Material properties In the drying equation: \frac{\mathrm{dC}}{\mathrm{dt}}-div\left[D(C,T)\mathrm{grad}C\right]=0 D diffusion coefficient will be of the SECH_GRANGER form: D(C,T)=A\exp(\mathrm{BC})\frac{T}{{T}_{0}}\exp\left[-{\mathrm{QSR}}_{K}(\frac{1}{T}-\frac{1}{{T}_{0}})\right] - A=2,5{10}^{-11}{m}^{2}/h - B=0.12 - {T}_{0}=273°K 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads Constant uniform temperature field over time of 20°C Concentration imposed on the edge of {C}_{\mathit{eq}}=29,31l/{m}^{3} 1.4 Initial conditions The initial water concentration is {C}_{\mathit{eq}}=106,42l/{m}^{3} 1.5 Transitory Drying is calculated over a period of 528h . 2 reference solution 2.1 Quantities and reference results The reference values are mass loss readings during the drying test from benchmark CONCRACK. To calculate the water loss of the numerical test piece at a given moment, the following calculations shall be made: 1. for each finite element, the integral of the water concentration on the volume of l-element: \underset{V}{\int}C\mathit{dV} , which is equivalent to the volume of water remaining (in l). 2. Somme des quantités d’eau restante \sum_{\mathit{éléments}}\underset{V}{\int}C\mathit{dV} : c’est le volume total d’eau restant dans l’échantillon (en l). 3. La concentration en eau moyenne (en l/m³) en divisant par le volume: {C}_{\mathit{moy}}=\frac{\sum_{\mathit{éléments}}\underset{V}{\int}C\mathit{dV}}{{V}_{\mathit{tot}}} 4. Levolume perdu (en l) est: {C}_{0}{V}_{\mathit{tot}}-\sum_{\mathit{éléments}}\underset{V}{\int}C\mathit{dV} et la masse perdue (en kg) est: {\rho}_{\mathit{eau}}({C}_{0}{V}_{\mathit{tot}}-\sum_{\mathit{éléments}}\underset{V}{\int}C\mathit{dV}) avec {\rho}_{\mathit{eau}}=1\mathit{kg}/l . 5. La perte de masse (%) est : 100\times \frac{{\rho}_{\mathit{eau}}({C}_{0}{V}_{\mathit{tot}}-\sum_{\mathit{éléments}}\underset{V}{\int}C\mathit{dV})}{{\rho}_{\mathit{beton}}{V}_{\mathit{tot}}}=100\times \frac{{\rho}_{\mathit{eau}}({C}_{0}-{C}_{\mathit{moy}})}{{\rho}_{\mathit{beton}}} avec {\rho}_{\mathit{beton}}=2410\mathit{kg}/{m}^{3} . v5.01.100 SDND100 - Drop frictional slider with Coulomb friction v5.01.100 SDND100 - Drop frictional slider with Coulomb friction Summary The one-way system with a degree of freedom consisting of a frictional contact mass on a rigid plane and a spring attaching to a fixed point is considered. The mass is released in an initial unbalanced position. It oscillates until complete stop at the end of the a finite time. The first two modellings are the transient response by modal recombination of the frictional slider, the third is the direct transient response, and the three calculations are compared with the analytical solution. Modellings A, B, D and F use DIS_CHOC behavior via DYNA_VIBRA operator, modellings C and G use DIS_CHOC behavior via DYNA_NON_LINE operator, and E Modelling uses DIS_CONTACT behavior via DYNA_NON_LINE operator. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Direction of movement: \theta =45° in the \mathrm{XY} plane 1.2 Material properties | spring stiffness: | k=10000N/m | | --- | --- | | Point mass: | m=1\mathrm{kg} | | gravity: | g=10m/{s}^{2} | | Coulomb coefficient: | \mu =0,1 | 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The system is based on the Z=0 plane on which it can slide with a Coulomb friction coefficient of \mu =0,1 . 1.4 Initial conditions Initial movement of the mass: {r}_{0}=0,85\mathrm{mm} according to the direction \theta . Initial zero speed. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution For a system without damping, the differential equation to be solved shall be written: \lbrace \begin{array}{}m\ddot{r}+kr=\mu \mid {F}_{n}\mid \\ r(t=0)={r}_{0}\ge 0\\ \dot{r}(t=0)=0\end{array} [bib1] The differential equation solution is shown to be: r(t)=\frac{\mu |{F}_{n}|}{k}+\left({r}_{0}-\frac{\mu |{F}_{n}|}{k}\right)\cos({\omega}_{0}t) with {\omega}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} The amplitude of the extrema, which comes from all {t}_{n+1}=\frac{n\pi }{{\omega}_{0}} , obeys the following recurrence law: r({t}_{n+1})={(-1)}^{n}\left[{r}_{0}-\frac{\mu \mid {F}_{n}\mid }{k}\right]\cos{\omega}_{0}t with n=1,2,\dots ,N such as ∣\frac{r({t}_{n+1})}{{r}_{0}}∣<\frac{\mu \mid {F}_{n}\mid }{k{r}_{0}} The movement stops when ∣\frac{r({t}_{n+1})}{{r}_{0}}∣<\frac{\mu \mid {F}_{n}\mid }{k{r}_{0}} at r({t}_{n+1}) position. 2.2 Baseline \theta =45° directional displacement values for the above r({t}_{1}),r({t}_{2}),r({t}_{3}),\mathrm{...} speed change moments. 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution analytical solution. 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. v5.01.101 SDND101 - Drop a spring mass system with impact v5.01.101 SDND101 - Drop a spring mass system with impact Summary This problem corresponds to a transient analysis by modal recombination of a nonlinear discrete system to an degree of freedom. Nonlinearity consists of a contact with impact on a rigid plane. The mass is launched with a nonzero initial speed against the obstacle. The initial game between the material point and the obstacle is zero. This problem allows testing the impact forces post-processing: impact speed, impact time ... 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry 1.2 Material properties The system consists of a mass m and a spring of stiffness k . The impact stop has an stiffness equal to {K}_{\mathrm{choc}} . | Mass | m=100\mathrm{kg} | | --- | --- | | stiffness | k={10}^{4}N/m | | Normal shock stiffness | {K}_{\mathrm{choc}}={10}^{6}N/m | 1.3 Initial conditions The system is initially in a stand-down position ( {U}_{0}=0 ) and has an initial speed \dot{{U}_{0}}>0 . An initial speed \dot{{U}_{0}}=1m/s will be selected for the application. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution During the impact phase, the system is solution of the differential equation: m.\ddot{u}+\mathit{k.u}+{K}_{c} }^{+}=0 with {u}_{0}=0 and \dot{{u}_{0}}=\dot{{U}_{0}} . }^{+} is the positive value of x . The analytical solution of this problem is: u=\frac{\dot{{U}_{0}}}{{\omega}_{c}}\sin({\omega}_{c}t) où {\omega}_{c}=\sqrt{\frac{k+{K}_{c}}{m}} . Speed cancels for {t}_{\dot{u}=0}=\frac{\pi}{2{\omega}_{c}} . The impact force is then maximum and is {F}_{\max}={K}_{c}u({t}_{\dot{u}=0})={K}_{c}\frac{\dot{{U}_{0}}}{{\omega}_{c}} . By construction, the duration of the shock is {T}_{\mathrm{choc}}=2{t}_{\dot{u}=0} . The system returns to the u=0 position with the -\dot{{U}_{0}} speed. In the u 0 domain and a {T}_{\mathrm{vol}} phase of free flight where the system describes a sinus arch in the u<0 domain. The pulse at each impact is: I=\underset{0}{\overset{{T}_{\mathrm{choc}}}{\int}}{K}_{c}u(t)\mathrm{dt}=2{K}_{c}\frac{\dot{{U}_{0}}}{{\omega}_{c}^{2}}=\frac{2m\dot{{U}_{0}}}{1+\frac{k}{{K}_{c}}} . 2.2 Baseline The reference results are the values of the maximum force moments, the maximum force value, the duration of the impact time, the value of the pulse and the impact speed and the number of elementary impacts for the first two oscillations of the system. 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution analytical solution. 2.4 Bibliographical references - G.JACQUART: post-processing of REP core and internal calculations under seismic stress - HP-61/95/074/A. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics The mass-spring system is modeled by element type POI1 to node \mathrm{NO1} . It is subject to x axis movement . The node \mathrm{NO1} is positioned in O=(0.0.0.) . A PLAN_Z (two parallel planes separated by a game) obstacle is used to simulate any shock of the mass-spring system against a rigid plane. It is chosen to take the \mathrm{Oy} axis for normal at the crash plane, i.e. NORM_OBST: (0., 1., 0.). To avoid being hindered by the rebound of the oscillator on the symmetrical plane, it is pushed back very far (see [Figure 3.1-a]). Therefore, it is chosen to locate the origin of the obstacle in ORIG_OBS: (-1. 0. 0.). Figure 3.1-a: Modeled Geometry The \mathrm{JEU} parameter is still to be set, which gives the half-range between the plans in contact. Here we want a zero real game, where \mathrm{JEU}:1 . If we want a real game of j , we need to impose \mathrm{JEU}:1+j in the case of the figure presented. Time integration is performed with the algorithm d-Euler and a time step of {5.10}^{-4}s . All calculation steps are archived. {\xi}_{i} reduced depreciation is considered to be zero for all calculated modes. 3.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh consists of an node and an mesh cell of the POI1 type. 3.3 Tested quantities and results For the first two shocks, the calculated values of the moment of impact, the maximum impact force, the impact time, the pulse and the impact speed are compared with the analytical values. The absolute extremum value of the impact force is also tested. v5.01.103 SDND103 - Axial dynamically-sustained pole v5.01.103 SDND103 - Axial dynamically-sustained pole Summary The answer is calculated for a post subjected to any seismic loading. The post is modelled by an unabated mass-spring system, its restraint with the ground by an effort-displacement nonlinearity. The discrete element in traction-compression, the calculation of eigenmodes and the calculation of the transient response by modal recombination with consideration of non-linearity of the force-displacement type are tested. The initial speed is taken not zero and the load is of the acceleration type imposed on the ground. The results obtained are in very good agreement with the reference results, which are analytical results. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The system consists of a ground-based pole subjected to seismic stress. It is modelled by a mass, its restraint with the ground by a {k}_{0} spring whose behavioral relationship reflects an effort-displacement nonlinearity. Characteristics of the pole: Length: L=\mathrm{2 }m ; section: S=0,3{m}^{2} . 1.2 Material properties Pole mass: m=\mathrm{450 }\mathrm{kg} . spring stiffness de restraint: {k}_{\mathrm{0 }}={10}^{5}N/m . 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads boundary conditions The only travels allowed are X axis translation: \mathrm{dy}=\mathrm{dz}=0 . The corrective force {F}_{c} due to nonlinearity of the soil is defined by the following relationship: {F}_{c}(x)=\frac{f({x}_{\mathrm{seuil}})}{{x}_{\mathrm{seuil}}}-f(x) with, if x>{x}_{\mathit{seuil}} , f(x)={k}_{0}\left[1–\frac{\mid x\mid }{{x}_{0}}\right]x We take {x}_{\mathrm{seuil}}={10}^{-6}m , {k}_{0}={10}^{5}N/m and {x}_{0}=0,1m . Therefore, the RELA_EFFO_DEPL operator's key word is used to specify the function: {F}_{c}(x)=\frac{{k}_{0}}{{x}_{0}}\mathit{x.}[\mid x\mid -{x}_{\mathit{seuil}}] if ∣x∣>{x}_{\mathit{seuil}} > {F}_{c}(x)=0 si ∣x∣\le {x}_{\mathit{seuil}} Charge The ground is subjected to an acceleration \gamma (t) in the direction x , built so that the displacement of the mass-spring system is sinusoidal x=\mathrm{a.sin}(\omega t) with a=0,01 and \omega =\pi /4 . 1.4 Initial conditions In the initial state, the system is released from its equilibrium position with a speed {v}_{\mathrm{0 }} : at t=0 , \mathrm{dx}(0)=0 , {v}_{0}=\mathrm{dx}/\mathrm{dt}(0)=a.\omega . 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution This test is further developed in the reference [bib1]. The fundamental equation of the dynamics, in relative movement of the mass-spring system relative to the ground is written: \ddot{x}+\frac{k(x)}{m}x=\gamma (t) . For a displacement of the form x=\mathrm{a.sin}(\omega t) and \ddot{x}=-a{\omega}^{2}\sin(\omega t) , the accelerogram form is obtained from the equation of the movement: \gamma (t)=a\sin(\omega t)\left[-{\omega}^{2}+\frac{{k}_{0}}{m}(1-\frac{\mid a\sin(\omega t)\mid }{{x}_{0}})\right] The basic frequency {f}_{0} of the unamortized oscillator is {f}_{0}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{{k}_{0}}{m}} . 2.2 Baseline Basic frequency {f}_{0} of unamortized oscillator. v5.01.105 SDND105 – Shock from point material against a wall with plastic blazing v5.01.105 SDND105 – Shock from point material against a wall with plastic blazing Summary: This test validates the behaviour of a shock-type obstacle with possible flaming. Resolution was performed with the DYNA_VIBRA operator using the FLAMBAGE keyword (modellings A, B, C and D) and with the DYNA_NON_LINE operator using the CHOC_ENDO_PENA (modellings E and F) behavior. The flashing start moment is calculated (this is the first moment when the impact force has passed the flashing threshold), the cumulative plastic deformation and the moment when it returns to the initial position. The results obtained are consistent with the analytical results. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry 1.2 Material properties For modellings A and B K={10}^{-7}N/m M=1\mathrm{kg} The {F}_{\mathit{ext}} reaction force depends on the wall compression following the following law: With: {K}_{1}=1N/m {F}_{\mathit{fl}}=1N {F}_{\mathit{seuil}}=0.5N {K}_{2}=0.5N/m For modelling C The force-compression relationship is shown in the figure below. With: {K}_{1}=1N/m {F}_{\mathit{fl}}=1N {F}_{\mathit{seuil}}=0.5N For modelling D The force-compression relationship corresponds to that used in Modelling C, but a damping is added. Before blazing this damping is 10.N/m.{s}^{-1} , then it is divided by two during blazing. 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The displacement of the M mobile mass is imposed on the x axis. 1.4 Initial conditions For modellings A and B At the initial moment, the moving mass is just in contact with the wall (initial zero) with an initial speed equal to 2m/s . The wall has not yet undergone plastic deformation (non-stripped wall). For Modelling At the initial moment, the moving mass is just in contact with the wall (initial zero) with an initial speed equal to 2.828427125m/s . In the initial state, the wall has not yet undergone plastic deformation (non-explosive wall). 2 reference solution 2.1 Method of calculation The problem is to analyze the response of a moving mass subjected to a non-zero initial speed and shocking against a wall following a constitutive law of the flaming type. The equilibrium equation of the system reads: M\frac{{\partial}^{2}x}{\partial {t}^{2}}+\mathrm{Kx}={F}_{\mathrm{ext}} The resolution of the process takes place in several phases: before blazing the wall, loading after blazing, unloading after blazing and free flight. 2.1.1 First phase Before the blazing, the reaction force is: {F}_{\mathrm{ext}}=-{K}_{1}x The solution of the equation is as follows: x(t)={A}_{1}\sin{\omega}_{1}t+{B}_{1}\cos{\omega}_{1}t With: {\omega}_{1}^{2}=\frac{K+{K}_{1}}{M} Taking into account the initial conditions: x(0)=0 and \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}(0)={v}_{0} We identify: {A}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{0}}{{\omega}_{1}} and {B}_{1}=0 Either: x(t)=\frac{{v}_{0}}{{\omega}_{1}}\sin{\omega}_{1}t The {F}_{\mathrm{fl}} flashing limit threshold is reached at the {t}_{\mathrm{fl}} moment, such as: x({t}_{\mathrm{fl}})={d}_{\mathrm{fl}}=\frac{{F}_{\mathrm{fl}}}{{K}_{1}} . D’où: {t}_{\mathrm{fl}}=\frac{1}{{\omega}_{1}}\mathrm{Arc}\sin(\frac{{F}_{\mathrm{fl}}{\omega}_{1}}{{K}_{1}{v}_{0}}) et \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}({t}_{\mathrm{fl}})={v}_{\mathrm{fl}} 2.1.2 Second phase The next phase is the loading phase after blazing; the reaction force is constant as long as the speed remains positive. This reaction force is: {F}_{\mathrm{ext}}=-{F}_{\mathrm{seuil}} and the solution of the equation s. With: {\omega}_{0}^{2}=\frac{K}{M} Like {\omega}_{0}^{2}\ll 1 , a limited development of the trigonometric functions can be performed. Either: x(t)={A}_{21}{t}^{2}+{B}_{21}t+{C}_{21} . Taking into account the initial conditions x({t}_{\mathrm{fl}})={d}_{\mathrm{fl}} and \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}({t}_{\mathrm{fl}})={v}_{\mathrm{fl}} , one obtains: > {A}_{21}=(\frac{{v}_{\mathrm{fl}}{t}_{\mathrm{fl}}}{2}-\frac{{d}_{\mathrm{fl}}}{2}-\frac{{F}_{\mathrm{seuil}}^{2}}{4M}){\omega}_{0}^{2}-\frac{{F}_{\mathrm{seuil}}}{2M} > {B}_{21}={v}_{\mathrm{fl}}+\frac{{F}_{\mathrm{seuil}}{t}_{\mathrm{fl}}}{M}+({d}_{\mathrm{fl}}{t}_{\mathrm{fl}}-\frac{{v}_{\mathrm{fl}}{t}_{\mathrm{fl}}^{2}}{2}){\omega}_{0}^{2} > {C}_{21}={d}_{\mathrm{fl}}-\frac{{F}_{\mathrm{seuil}}{t}_{\mathrm{fl}}^{2}}{2M}-{v}_{\mathrm{fl}}{t}_{\mathrm{fl}}-\frac{{d}_{\mathrm{fl}}{t}_{\mathrm{fl}}^{2}}{2}{\omega}_{0}^{2} The moment at which the speed is canceled is: {t}_{m}=-\frac{{B}_{21}}{2{A}_{21}} By neglecting the terms in {\omega}_{0}^{2} , we deduce: {t}_{m}={t}_{\mathrm{fl}}+\frac{M{v}_{\mathrm{fl}}}{{F}_{\mathrm{seuil}}} , and maximum displacement is: x({t}_{m})={d}_{m} This allows to obtain the plastic deformation cumulated: {d}_{p}={d}_{m}-\frac{{F}_{\mathrm{seuil}}}{{K}_{2}} 2.1.3 Third phase This phase corresponds to the discharge, the reaction force is: {F}_{\mathrm{ext}}=-{K}_{2}(x-{d}_{p}) The solution of the equation ssss written: x(t)={A}_{3}\sin{\omega}_{2}t+{B}_{3}\cos{\omega}_{2}t+\frac{{K}_{2}{d}_{p}}{K+{K}_{2}} With: {\omega}_{2}^{2}=\frac{K+{K}_{2}}{M} Taking into account the initial conditions x({t}_{m})={d}_{m} and \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}({t}_{m})=0 , we get: {A}_{3}=({d}_{m}-\frac{{K}_{2}{d}_{p}}{K+{K}_{2}})\sin{\omega}_{2}{t}_{m} and {B}_{3}=({d}_{m}-\frac{{K}_{2}{d}_{p}}{K+{K}_{2}})\cos{\omega}_{2}{t}_{m} . The solution of the equation ssss written: x(t)={A}_{4}\sin{\omega}_{0}t+{B}_{4}\cos{\omega}_{0}t The initial conditions are: x({t}_{d})={d}_{p} et \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}({t}_{d})={v}_{d}={\omega}_{2}({x}_{m}-\frac{{K}_{2}{d}_{p}}{K+{K}_{2}})\sin{\omega}_{2}({t}_{m}-{t}_{d}) This gives: {A}_{4}={d}_{p}\sin{\omega}_{0}{t}_{d}+\frac{{v}_{d}}{{\omega}_{0}}\cos{\omega}_{0}{t}_{d} {B}_{4}={d}_{p}\cos{\omega}_{0}{t}_{d}-\frac{{v}_{d}}{{\omega}_{0}}\sin{\omega}_{0}{t}_{d} Like {\omega}_{0}^{2}\ll 1 , by performing a limited development of the trigonometric functions up to order 2, the solution is as follows: x(t)={A}_{41}{t}^{2}+{B}_{41}t+{C}_{41} With: {A}_{41}=\frac{{\omega}_{0}^{2}}{2}[{v}_{d}{t}_{d}-{d}_{p}(1-\frac{{\omega}_{0}^{2}{t}_{d}^{2}}{2})] {B}_{41}={d}_{p}{t}_{d}{\omega}_{0}^{2}+{v}_{d}(1-\frac{{\omega}_{0}^{2}{t}_{d}^{2}}{2}) {C}_{41}={d}_{p}(1-\frac{{\omega}_{0}^{2}{t}_{d}^{2}}{2})-{v}_{d}{t}_{d} By neglecting the terms in {\omega}_{0}^{2} , we get: x(t)={v}_{d}t+{d}_{p}-{v}_{d}{t}_{d} . And we deduce the {t}_{0} moment of transition to the initial position ( x=0 ). Either: {t}_{0}={t}_{d}-\frac{{d}_{p}}{{v}_{d}} . 2.1.5 Reference solution of Modelling C The initial conditions selected allow to have a kinetic energy of 4J , which must lead to total compression of 6.5m and residual compression of 3.1m . 2.2 Quantities and reference results For modellings A and B The following quantities are intended to be tested: {t}_{\mathrm{fl}} : flashing start moment; {d}_{p} : cumulative plastic deformation; {t}_{0} : ironing moment at initial position (after blazing and discharge). v5.01.106 SDND106 – frictional slider with static and dynamic friction coefficients v5.01.106 SDND106 – frictional slider with static and dynamic friction coefficients Summary: This test case is designed to validate the functionality of non-linear friction by penalising, using two friction coefficients, a static (for adhesion phases) and a dynamic (for sliding phases). The system studied contains two degrees of freedom. Its evolution contains a transition of adhesion – slip and a transition of slip – grip. The reference solution is an analytical. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Figure 1.1-a : Schematic of test case. 1.2 Material properties The two masses are identical and are worth {m}_{1}={m}_{2}=m=5\mathrm{kg} . The stiffness placed between these masses is k={10}^{4}N/m . 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads {m}_{1} and {m}_{2} masses move according to \overrightarrow{x} only. The {F}_{N} normal force module is constant equal to {F}_{N}={10}^{4}N . The {m}_{1} mass is affected by a contact condition – friction. The friction coefficients 5 are: - in the static case: {\mu}_{S}=0,3 , - in the dynamic case: {\mu}_{D}=0,2 . In this Modelling, the system is divided into three phases: - A adhesion phase, during which the force exerted on the {m}_{2} mass is constant: F=3\cdot {10}^{3}N . - A sliding phase, starting at {t}_{1} , when the tangential force can no longer compensate for the pull force exerted by the spring on {m}_{1} . After arbitrary time ( {t}_{2}=0,2s ), the imposed force is set to 0 and the kinetics of the system then tend to 0. - A second adhesion phase, starting at {t}_{3} , when the speed of the {m}_{1} mass is canceled. 1.4 Initial conditions At the moment t=0 , both masses are at rest (moving and zero speed). 2 reference solution 2.1 Method of calculation The system pulse is noted {\omega}_{0} and is such that {\omega}_{0}^{2}=\frac{k}{m} . Adhesion phase At the moment t=0 , the {m}_{1} mass checks {x}_{1}(t)=0 \dot{{x}_{1}}(t)=0 and mass {m}_{2} checks {x}_{2}(t)=0 \dot{{x}_{2}}(t)=0 . The fundamental principle of dynamics applied to the {m}_{2} mass allows to write the following equation \ddot{{x}_{2}}+{\omega}_{0}^{2}{x}_{2}=\frac{F}{m} , and on the mass {m}_{1} the following equation {F}_{T}=-k{x}_{2} The general solution of {x}_{2} is the form: {x}_{2}=\tilde{A}\cos({\omega}_{0}t)+\tilde{B}\sin({\omega}_{0}t)+\frac{F}{(m{\omega}_{0}^{2})} where \tilde{A} and \tilde{B} are constants. Taking into account the initial conditions, the displacement of the {m}_{2} mass is therefore written {x}_{2}=\frac{F}{k}[1-\cos({\omega}_{0}t)] . This expression is valid until ∥{F}_{T}∥=\mu {F}_{N} In other words, until the moment {t}_{1} checking the following expression F[1-\cos({\omega}_{0}{t}_{1})]={\mu}_{S}{F}_{N} The sliding phase starts at {t}_{1} defined by {t}_{1}=\frac{1}{{\omega}_{0}}\arccos(1-{\mu}_{S}\frac{{F}_{N}}{F}) Slide phase At the moment t={t}_{1} , the {m}_{1} mass checks {x}_{1}({t}_{1})=0 \dot{x}{}_{1}({t}_{1})=0 The fundamental principle of the dynamics applied to the mass {m}_{1} allows to write the equation \ddot{x}{}_{1}+{\omega}_{0}^{2}{x}_{1}=\frac{-{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{m}+{\omega}_{0}^{2}{x}_{2} , and on the mass {m}_{2} the equation \ddot{x}{}_{2}+{\omega}_{0}^{2}{x}_{2}=\frac{F}{m}+{\omega}_{0}^{2}{x}_{1} . By changing variables \lbrace \begin{array}{}X={x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\\ Y={x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\\ {\Omega}_{0}=\sqrt{2}{\omega}_{0}\end{array} the previous system is written \begin{array}{}\ddot{X}=\frac{F-{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{m}\\ \ddot{Y}+{\Omega}_{0}^{2}Y=-\frac{F+{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{m}\end{array} For t\ge {t}_{1} , the general solution of X is the form X=\frac{(F-{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N})}{\mathrm{2m}}{(t-{t}_{1})}^{2}+\tilde{C}(t-{t}_{1})+\tilde{D} . and that of Y is of the form Y=\tilde{E}\cos({\Omega}_{0}(t-{t}_{1}))+\tilde{F}\sin({\Omega}_{0}(t-{t}_{1}))-\frac{F+{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{\mathrm{2k}} . Taking into account the initial conditions, the expressions of the constants \tilde{C} , \tilde{D} , \tilde{E} and \tilde{F} are: \begin{array}{}\tilde{C}=\dot{x}{}_{2}({t}_{1})\\ \tilde{D}={x}_{2}({t}_{1})\\ \tilde{E}=\frac{F+{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{\mathrm{2k}}-{x}_{2}({t}_{1})\\ \tilde{F}=-\frac{\dot{x}{}_{2}({t}_{1})}{{\Omega}_{0}}\end{array} {x}_{1} and {x}_{2} moves are deduced from previous expressions. Slide phase with loading F=0 from {t}_{2} (arbitrary but greater than {t}_{1} ) to the moment {t}_{3} (re-entry phase) The fundamental principle of the dynamics presented above is still valid. For the {m}_{1} mass, the verified equation is the same: \ddot{x}{}_{1}+{\omega}_{0}^{2}{x}_{1}=\frac{-({\mu}_{D}{F}_{N})}{m}+{\omega}_{0}^{2}{x}_{2} , and for mass {m}_{2} \ddot{x}{}_{2}+{\omega}_{0}^{2}{x}_{2}={\omega}_{0}^{2}{x}_{1} With the same variable change as before, the system is written \begin{array}{}\ddot{X}=-\frac{{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{m}\\ \ddot{Y}+{\Omega}_{0}^{2}Y=-\frac{{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{m}\end{array} For t>{t}_{2} , the general solution of X is the form X=-\frac{{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{\mathrm{2m}}{(t-{t}_{2})}^{2}+\tilde{G}(t-{t}_{2})+\tilde{H} The general solution of Y is of the shape Y=\tilde{I}\cos({\Omega}_{0}(t-{t}_{2}))+\tilde{J}\sin({\Omega}_{0}(t-{t}_{2}))-\frac{{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{\mathrm{2k}} Taking into account the initial conditions, the expressions of the constants \tilde{G} , \tilde{H} , \tilde{I} and \tilde{J} are: \begin{array}{}\tilde{G}=\dot{x}{}_{1}({t}_{2})+\dot{x}{}_{2}({t}_{2})\\ \tilde{H}={x}_{1}({t}_{2})+{x}_{2}({t}_{2})\\ \tilde{J}=\frac{{\mu}_{D}{F}_{N}}{\mathrm{2k}}+{x}_{1}({t}_{2})-{x}_{2}({t}_{2})\\ \tilde{J}=\frac{\dot{x}{}_{1}({t}_{2})-\dot{x}{}_{2}({t}_{2})}{{\Omega}_{0}}\end{array} {x}_{1} and {x}_{2} moves are deduced from previous expressions. 2.2 Quantities and reference results The quantities tested are the kinematics of the {m}_{1} and {m}_{2} masses at different times in the different phases of the Modelling. The following transition moments are also tested: - transition from adhesion to sliding phase ( moment {t}_{1} ) ; - transition from the sliding phase to the adhesion phase ( moment {t}_{3} ). 2.3 Uncertainties about the solution Analytical solution exact. 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. BOYERE: Shock and friction modelling in modal recombination transient analysis. Reference documentation of Code_Aster R5.06.03. September 2009. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics In this Modelling, the DYNA_VIBRA operator (see U4.53.03) is used with the DIS_CHOC relationship. The integration scheme is ADAPT_ORDRE2. In this Modelling, the force exerted on the {m}_{2} mass is canceled in {t}_{2}=0,2s . 3.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh contains 2 mesh cells discreet at one node (one for each mass) and 1 mesh cell discreet for the spring. 3.3 Tested quantities and results | Type | Instant ( s ) | quantity | Reference | Aster | Difference (%) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Analysis | 0.02 | {x}_{1} | | 2.0621E-05 | | | Analysis | 0.02 | {x}_{2} | 0.11221 | 0.11221 | 0 | | Analysis | 0.15 | {x}_{1} | 1.35332 | 1.35329 | -0.002 | | Analysis | 0.15 | {x}_{2} | 1.80751 | 1.80751 | 0 | | Analysis | 0.34 | \dot{x}{}_{1} | | -3.3802E-5 | | | Analysis | 0.34 | {x}_{2} | 3.96813 | 3.97012 | 0.05 | | Type | quantity (s) | Reference | Aster | % difference | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Analysis | {t}_{1} | 0.03512 | 0.03520 | 0.23 | | Analysis | {t}_{3} | 0.31492 | 0.31500 | 0.03 | 3.4 Remarks The difference in \text{\%} is not given for cases where the reference value is 0, but the absolute difference is in the order of {10}^{-5} . 4 Summary of the results This test case shows that the adhesion – slip and slip – adhesion transitions are well captured. It also validates the DYNA_VIBRA operator's ability to integrate problems in large translation movements.

When it touches the elastic ground, it is subjected in addition to the gravity to an effort of the type k.\delta x (configuration b). Once the rebound is complete, it is no longer subjected to the gravity (configuration a) with an initial speed {V}_{1} . Table 2.1.1-1 : Behavioural model Equation during free fall (configuration a): m.\ddot{x}=-m.g And so, by integration: x=-g.\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{V}_{0}.t The time of the fall is obtained by solving x=h : {t}_{\mathit{chute}}=\frac{1}{g}\left[{V}_{0}+\sqrt{{V}_{0}^{2}-2.g.h}\right] Equation during rebound (configuration b): m.\ddot{x}=-m.g+k.(h-z) And, therefore: x={C}_{1}\sin(w.\stackrel{~}{t})+{C}_{2}\cos(w.\stackrel{~}{t})+(h-g/{w}^{2}) Both constants are: {C}_{2}=g/{w}^{2};{C}_{1}=\frac{-1}{w}\sqrt{{V}_{O}^{2}-2.g.h} The time corresponding to the de-lamination is obtained by solving x=h : \tan\left(w.\frac{{\stackrel{~}{t}}_{\mathit{decol}}}{2}\right)={w}^{2}.\frac{{C}_{1}}{g} 2.2 Modelling B This case models a mass that bounces over an absorbent surface. 2.2.1 Baseline The mass is released with an initial speed {V}_{0} (configuration a), as long as it has not touched the surface, it only undergoes the gravity. When it touches the absorbent surface, it is subjected in addition to the gravity to an effort of the type k.\delta x+c.\dot{x} (configuration c). Once the rebound is complete, it is no longer subject to gravity (configuration a) with an initial speed {V}_{1} . Table 2.2.1-1 : Behavioural Model Equation during free fall(configuration a) m.\ddot{x}=-m.g And so, by integration: x=-g.\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{V}_{0}.t The time of the fall is obtained by solving x=h : {t}_{\mathit{chute}}=\frac{1}{g}\left[{V}_{0}+\sqrt{{V}_{0}^{2}-2.g.h}\right] Equation during rebound (configuration c): m.\ddot{x}=-m.g+k.(h-z)-c.\dot{x} And so: x=\exp\left(\frac{-c.\stackrel{~}{t}}{2.m}\right)\left[{C}_{1}\sin\left(\frac{\mathit{Rd}.\stackrel{~}{t}}{2}\right)+{C}_{2}\cos\left(\frac{\mathit{Rd}.\stackrel{~}{t}}{2}\right)\right]+(h-g/{w}^{2}) \textrm{avec} \stackrel{~}{t}=t-{t}_{\mathit{chute}} Constants are: {C}_{2}=g/{w}^{2};{C}_{1}=\frac{c.g-2.k.\sqrt{{V}_{O}^{2}-2.g.h}}{k.\sqrt{4.k.m-{c}^{2}/{m}^{2}}} The time corresponding to the de-lamination is obtained by solving x=h numerically. 2.2.2 Uncertainty about solutions No uncertainty (analytical solution). 3 modellings A et C With previous data: | Time [dry] | Depl [m] | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | | Time Fall = 0.54031242374329 | -2.0 | 1.0e-06 | | Time Deceleration = 0.88545615307643 | -2.0 | 1.0e-02 | | 1.0000 | -1.332162981855 | 1.0e-02 | | 1.1000 | -0.856394405035 | 2.0e-02 | Comparison of results with Modelling A with analytical solution. 4 Modelling B and D With previous data: | Time [dry] | Depl [m] | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | | Timefall = 0.54031242374329 | -2.0 | 1.0E-06 | | Times Deceleration = 0.92403882542 | -2.0 | 1.0E-02 | | 1.0000 | -1.88214079833 | 1.0E-02 | | 1.1000 | -1.81496422497 | 1.0E-02 | Comparison of results with Modelling B with analytical solution. 5 Summary of the results Very good agreement with analytical results.

v5.01.120 SDND120 - Transitional response of an anti-seismic patch v5.01.120 SDND120 - Transitional response of an anti-seismic patch Summary A non-seismic patch has been tested on a vibrating table. This test case is designed to reproduce this test numerically. The device is modelled by two unabsorbed spring mass systems, separated by a non-linearity of the anti-seismic patch type. The discrete element in traction-compression, the calculation of eigenmodes, static modes, and the calculation of the transient response by nonlinear modal recombination of the structure subject to an accelerogram are tested. The nonlinearity is of the ANTI_SISM type. The reference result is a MATLAB program. The results obtained are in very good agreement with the reference results. The calculated results are also compared with the measured forces and displacements on an experimental device (qualitative comparison only). 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry An anti-seismic patch is placed between two jaws (rectangles cut off on the following figure) which are placed on a vibrating table subject to an acceleration imposed in the direction X. It is modelled by a non-linearity of the "anti-seismic device" type placed on both sides of a mass-spring system. 1.2 Material properties The jaws that insert the device are each modelled by a mass-spring system: stiffness de restraint : k={10}^{10}N/m ; point mass: m=25\mathrm{kg} . The device tested is an anti-seismic patch of type JARRET. Its characteristics are as follows: - \mathrm{K1}=6.{10}^{6}N/m (RIGI_K1), - \mathrm{K2}=0,53{10}^{6}N/m (RIGI_K2), - \mathrm{Py}=1200 (SEUIL_FX), - C=0,07{10}^{5} (C), - alpha=0,2 (PUIS_ALPHA), - \mathrm{xmax}=0,03m (DX_MAX). 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads boundary conditions The only travels allowed are X -axis translations. C and D -points are clamped: \mathrm{dx}=\mathrm{dy}=\mathrm{dz}=0 . The other points are free to translate according to \mathrm{dx} : \mathrm{dy}=\mathrm{dz}=0 . Charge The point D is subject to a transverse acceleration in the x {\gamma}_{1}(t)=0,66\sin(\omega t)m/{s}^{2} direction with \omega =2\pi , the point C is fixed. 1.4 Initial conditions At the initial moment, the device is at rest: t=0 , \mathrm{dx}(0)=0 , \mathrm{dx}/\mathrm{dt}(0)=0 in all point. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The numerical values are compared to the experimental surveys and the reference solution obtained by a matlab script. The expression of the dissipation force in such a device is provided by the following formula [Peckan]: {F}_{D}={K}_{2}x+\frac{({K}_{1}-{K}_{2})x}{\sqrt{1+{(\frac{{K}_{1}x}{{P}_{y}})}^{2}}}+C\mathit{sign}(\dot{x}){∣\dot{x}\frac{x}{{x}_{max}}∣}^{\alpha} matlab script: | %test case for anti-sismic device clear; close all; %---direct calculation---- %initialization of the calculation parameters t0 = 0; tfinal = 1.; not = 0.01; tspan = t0: not: tfinal; y0 = [0 0 0]; y0 = y0'; options = []; %direct integration [t,y] = ode23('fonctsism1',tspan,y0,options); depl1 = y(:,1:1); depl2 = y(:,2:2); vit1 = y(:3,3); vit2 = y(:4,4); kk1 = 6.e6; kk2 = 0.53e6; py = 1200; c = 0.07e5; xmax = 0.03; alpha = 0.2; for tt = 1:1:length(tspan) depl21 = depl2(tt)1(tt); vit21 = g2(t2 x(t(tt2); gk(r(t2 k)g | function yp = functionism1(t,y,flag) % provisional initialization m1 = 25.; m2 = 25.; k1 = 1.e10; k2 = 1.e10; kk1 = 6.e6; kk2 = 0.53e6; py = 1200; c = 0.07e5; xmax = 0.03; alpha = 0.2; omega = 2 pi; % %---direct resolution---- x0 = (0.66 sin(omega t))/(omega omega); depl21 = y(2)-y(1); vit21 = y(4)-y(3); g1n = (kk1-kk2) depl21; g1d = sqrt(1+(kkk1/py) depl21)^2; g1 = g1n/g1; g2 = c sign(vit21) (abs(vit21 depl21/xmax)^ alpha; g0 = kk2 depl21; g1(kk1/py) depl21); g1(g = g0g + g | | --- | --- | 2.2 Baseline Maximum and RMS values of relative and absolute B displacements, and of the stress due to the anti-seismic patch. 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution The excitation imposed on the mass-spring system is an approximation of the displacement imposed on the experimental device. The uncertainty on the reference solution MATLAB is low. 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. PEKCAN, J.B. MANDER, M. EERI: The seismic response of a 1:3 scale model R.C. structure with elastomer spring lamps. - Earthquake Spexctra, vol. 11, N°2, pp. 249-267 - May 1995 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics Figure 3.1-a: Modelling of the seismic anti-seismic device The jaws that insert the device are each modeled by a discrete element at 3 degrees of freedom DIS_T. v5.01.121 SDND121 – Spring mass-responding system with forced excitation shock v5.01.121 SDND121 – Spring mass-responding system with forced excitation shock Summary: This problem corresponds to a transient analysis by modal recombination of a discrete nonlinear system to an degree of freedom. Nonlinearity consists of a contact with shock on a rigid plane. The mass is subjected to forced excitation. The problem is stiff, i.e. the stiffness is very different between the free flight phases and the contact phases. This problem allows to test the energy balance for the different patterns of temporal integration, as well as kinematics. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The structure is a rigid slider modeled by a single node. The slider is equipped with a spring reminder. It is subjected to an {F}_{\mathit{ext}}(t)=a\sin(2\pi ft) harmonic external force. It is carried a normal shock condition against a rigid plane, treated by penalization. Figure 1.1-a : Geometry 1.2 Material properties Properties of the structure : m=156\mathrm{kg} {k}_{\mathit{rappel}}=2\cdot {10}^{6}N/m Impact stop properties: {k}_{\mathrm{choc}}={10}^{10}N/m {c}_{\mathrm{choc}}=0\mathrm{Ns}/m {\mathrm{jeu}}_{\mathrm{choc}}=1\mathrm{mm} 1.3 Initial conditions, at limits and loading The slider leaves with zero initial conditions: {x}_{0}={x}_{t=0}=0 and \dot{x}{}_{0}=\dot{x}{}_{t=0}=0 . He's moving in one direction. The external force is sinusoidal: {F}_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)=\mathrm{Fa}\cdot \sin(2\pi ft) , with \mathrm{Fa}=3\cdot {10}^{3}N and f=5\mathrm{Hz} . 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution In a free flight phase, the equation of motion is written m\ddot{x}+{k}_{\mathrm{rappel}}x={F}_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) . Given the sinusoidal form of {F}_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) , this equation allows an analytical solution. It is possible to calculate numerically, with as great precision as you want, the {t}_{in} moment of input into the contact, checking x({t}_{in})={\mathrm{jeu}}_{\mathrm{choc}} . The m\ddot{x}+{c}_{\mathrm{choc}}\dot{x}+({k}_{\mathrm{rappel}}+{k}_{\mathrm{choc}})x={F}_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) is the same as the analytical solution. With the boundary conditions from the contact moment, the {t}_{\text{out}} is numerically calculated for the contact output moment. By doing so it is possible to obtain the complete solution of the problem. Note: The analytical formulae are not given here. Files containing formulae and allowing the calculation of the complete solution are attached with the command file. 2.2 Baseline The energy balance, the match between contact forces and kinematics, and kinematics are tested. For the energy balance, {E}_{i}^{\mathrm{cin}}=\frac{1}{2}m\dot{x}{}_{i}^{2} kinetic energies, potential {E}_{i}^{\mathit{pot}}=\frac{1}{2}{k}_{\mathit{rappel}}{x}_{i}^{2} , of {E}_{i}^{\mathit{choc}}=\frac{1}{2}{k}_{\mathit{choc}}{p}_{i}^{2} shock ( p is penetration; this expression is valid only if there is no shock damping), injected by the external force {E}_{i}^{\mathrm{inj}}=\sum_{j=1}^{i}{f}_{j}^{\mathrm{ext}}\dot{x}{}_{j+\delta \frac{1}{2}}\Delta t (with \delta =1 for Euler's schema, \delta =0 for the centered differences schema). The total energy {E}_{i}^{\mathit{tot}}={E}_{i}^{\mathit{cin}}+{E}_{i}^{\mathit{pot}}+{E}_{i}^{\mathit{choc}} is obtained. Finally, the overall error on the energy balance is calculated by {\mathit{erreur}}_{\mathit{globale}}^{\mathit{énergie}}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i}{({E}_{i}^{\mathit{tot}}-{E}_{i}^{\mathit{inj}})}^{2}}{\sum_{i}{({E}_{i}^{\mathit{inj}})}^{2}}} , which is ideally 0. For the matching of contact forces and kinematics, the quantity {\mathit{erreur}}_{\mathit{globale}}^{\mathit{force}}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i}{({F}_{i}^{\mathit{choc}}-{k}_{\mathit{choc}}{p}_{i})}^{2}}{\sum_{i}{({k}_{\mathit{choc}}{p}_{i})}^{2}}} is calculated, which is ideally 0. For kinematics, the calculated moments of input and output are compared to the analytical moments. 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution The solution is analytical in pieces. The moments of input and output of contact are determined numerically to the nearest {10}^{-9}s . 3 Modelling 3.1 Modelling characteristics The slider is modeled by an mesh cell to an node (type POI1), located at rest in O=(0,0,0) . The obstacle is of type 'PLAN_Z'. To avoid any shock with the symmetrical plane, the center of both planes is sufficiently shifted: ORIG_OBST=(-0.5.0.0.,0.,). As the real game between the slider and the right plane must be 1\mathit{mm} , an artificial game JEU=(0.5+Jeu_choc) is used. Figure 3.1-a : Modeled Geometry The time integration is performed over a duration T=4s either with the Euler schema or with the pattern of the centred differences ('ADAPT_ORDRE2' that is forced to a constant time step thanks to the parameters COEF_MULT_PAS=1.0, COEF_DIVI_PAS=1.0). The problem is stiff (the ratio of the stiffeners between the free flight and contact phases is about 5000), so we are forced to use a very low time step of \Delta t=4\cdot {10}^{-6}s . A calculation is also made with 'ADAPT_ORDRE2' actually variable steps, whose purpose is not precision, but simply checking the match between contact forces and kinematics. 3.2 Mesh characteristics > The mesh consists of a single node and a single mesh cell of the POI1 type. 3.3 Tested quantities and results 3.3.1 Energy balance and kinematics In the following tables, the values of the energy error and a few moments of contact input/output are given. - Euler diagram: | Values | Reference | Aster | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | {\mathrm{erreur}}_{\mathrm{globale}}^{\mathrm{énergie}} | 0 J | 0.092 J | 0.1 J | | 1st contact entry(s) | 2.4867876 E-02 s | 2.4868 E-02 s | 1.2E-5 s | | 1st contact exit (s) | 2.5260518 E-02 s | 2.5264 E-02 s | 1.2E-5 s | | last contact entry(s) | 3.886525493 E+00 s | 3.886528 E+00 s | 1.2E-5 s | | last contact exit(s) | 3.886916559 E+00 s | 3.886916 E+00 s | 1.2E-5 s | Table 4.1-1 : Results for the Euler scheme - Diagram of the centred differences: | Values | Reference | Aster | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | {\mathrm{erreur}}_{\mathrm{globale}}^{\mathrm{énergie}} | 0 J | 0.063 J | 0.1 J | | 1st contact entry(s) | 2.4867876 E-02 s | 2.4868 E-02 s | 1.2E-5 s | | 1st contact exit (s) | 2.5260518 E-02 s | 2.5264 E-02 s | 1.2E-5 s | | last contact entry(s) | 3.886525493 E+00 s | 3.886528 E+00 s | 1.2E-5 s | | last contact exit(s) | 3.886916559 E+00 s | 3.886916 E+00 s | 1.2E-5 s | Table 4.1-2 : Results for the pattern of centred differences 3.3.2 Adequacy between contact force and kinematics | Value | Reference | Aster | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | {\mathrm{erreur}}_{\mathrm{globale}}^{\mathrm{force}} | 0 N | 2.22 E-10 N | 1.E-8 N | Table 4.2-1 : Results for the matching of contact force and kinematics 4 Summary of the results The results are very similar to analytical solution, both for the Euler diagram and for the pattern of the centred differences. The stiffness change moments obtained by these two diagrams are identical. Energy balance sheets have an error of less than 0,1J in both cases. This value is to be relativized with the very low time step which tends to reduce differences, but such a low time step is necessary to deal with this stiff problem. Finally, there is a perfect fit (to the numerical accuracy close to) between contact forces and kinematics, which means that the processing of contact by penalisation is done correctly.

v5.01.122 SDND122 – Nonlinear mode calculation – 1 degree of freedom system impacting an elastic stop v5.01.122 SDND122 – Nonlinear mode calculation – 1 degree of freedom system impacting an elastic stop Summary: The objective of this test is to validate the nonlinear mode calculation with the MODE_NON_LINE operator. post-processings is also performed with CALC_STABILITE and REST_MODE_NONL. A analytical solution connecting frequency and energy is available for a material point that impacts against an elastic stop. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A system consisting of a spring fixed at one end and fitted with a point mass at the other end is considered. 1.2 Material properties spring stiffness: k=10N/m Mass: m=1\mathit{kg} Rigidity of the wall: K=50N/m 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The mass is fixed to one end of the spring and the other end is fixed. It moves in the direction u and can impact against the wall at e=0.01m of its equilibrium position. 1.4 Initial conditions For nonlinear mode calculations, the behaviour depends on the energy stored in the system. 2 reference solution The calculation of periodic solutions of the system characterizing the nonlinear mode [1] is being studied. 2.1 Method of calculation If u is noted the displacement of the mass and F the reaction force, the system equation is written: \ddot{u}(t)+\text{ku}(t)=-F(u(t)) Où: > F(u)=0 si u\le e > F(u)=K(u-e) si u>e The following initial conditions are assumed: > \dot{u}(0)=-\sqrt{\frac{2E}{m}} et u(0)=0 Where E is the mechanical energy stored. The problem is solved by considering two linear problems. The first corresponds to the free flight (excluding impact), and the second corresponds to the system with the solid mass at the wall (during impact). After calculation, the {T}_{1} duration of the free flight phase is obtained: > {T}_{1}=2\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\arccos(-e\sqrt{\frac{k}{2E}}) And the duration of the {T}_{2} impact is given by the following relationship: > {T}_{2}=2\sqrt{\frac{m}{K+k}}\arccos(ek\sqrt{\frac{1}{2E(K+k)}}) The frequency of the periodic solution is therefore equal to: N(E)=\frac{1}{{T}_{1}+{T}_{2}} The stability of the periodic solution is calculated based on Floquet's theory, by a Newmark diagram and a calculation at the own values. 2.2 Quantities and reference results The selected reference quantities are the frequency-energy torque and stability of the periodic solution obtained. The periodic solution is stable for frequency torque – energy such as: 0.644\mathit{Hz}<f<0.6475\mathit{Hz} et 6.2{10}^{-3}J<E<6.9{10}^{-3}J 2.3 Uncertainties about the solution The relationship between frequency and energy is obtained analytically. 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. MOUSSI, Analysis of vibrating structures with non-linearities located at play using non-linear modes. PhD Thesis 2013. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics DIS_T modelling is used. The system load is defined with the AFFE_CHAR_CINE operator. 3.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh contains 1 element of POI1 type and 1 element of SEG2 type. 3.3 Tested quantities and results The frequency value for a given energy is tested, and this frequency is obtained by interpolation from the table produced by MODE_NON_LINE. | Frequency ( \mathit{Hz} ) | Energy ( J ) | Stability of the periodic solution | | --- | --- | --- | | 0.64622 | 6.50108331624{10}^{-3} | STABLE | 4 Modelling B 4.1 Modelling characteristics DIS_T modelling is used. The system-related load is defined using the AFFE_CHAR_MECA operator. 4.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh contains 1 element of POI1 type and 1 element of SEG2 type. 4.3 Tested quantities and results The frequency value for a given energy is tested, and this frequency is obtained by interpolation from the table produced by MODE_NON_LINE. | Frequency ( \mathit{Hz} ) | Energy ( J ) | Stability of the periodic solution | | --- | --- | --- | | 0.64661 | 6.58129654238{10}^{-3} | STABLE | 5 Modelling C 5.1 Modelling characteristics DIS_T modelling is used. The system-related load is defined using the AFFE_CHAR_CINE operator. A further calculation of the results obtained with a first calculation of nonlinear mode is performed. To avoid overloading the test case, the stability calculation of the solution is not performed. 5.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh contains 1 element of POI1 type and 1 element of SEG2 type. 5.3 Tested quantities and results The frequency value for a given energy is tested, and this frequency is obtained by interpolation from the table produced by MODE_NON_LINE. | Frequency ( \mathit{Hz} ) | Energy ( J ) | | --- | --- | | 0.64610 | 6.47656819016{10}^{-3} | 6 Summary of the results This test case validates the nonlinear mode calculation operator (MODE_NON_LINE), the nonlinear mode stability calculation operator (CALC_STABILITE) and the periodic solution return operator (REST_MODE_NONL). The matrix of the system is quasi-singular, the value of the solution obtained may depend on the accuracy of the machine on which the calculation is initiated. The value of the relative frequency for a given energy is tested. This frequency is obtained by interpolation from the table produced by MODE_NON_LINE. It is found that the relationship between energy and frequency is always verified on the results obtained.

v5.01.124 SDND124 – Seismic Excitation of a Discreet Affected Behaviour DIS_ECRO_TRAC v5.01.124 SDND124 – Seismic Excitation of a Discreet Affected Behaviour DIS_ECRO_TRAC Summary: The response of the DIS_ECRO_TRAC nonlinear behavior model, formulated on discrete elements for mesh cells SEG2, is tested. DYNA_NON_LINE and DYNA_VIBRA operators are used for validation. Discrete d的elements response is analyzed for nonlinear constitutive law under seismic loading. The modellings and elements discreet tested are in \mathrm{3D} with DIS_T Modelling on a mesh cell SEG2. This behavior is also validated for non-dynamic stresses in the test case SSND117 V6.08.117 with the STAT_NON_LINE operator. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Description of the device The system studied is represented by the rheological model below. It is composed of a nonlinear element affected by the DIS_ECRO_TRAC behavior (between nodes N1 and N2), a mass assigned to node N2, d Figure 1.1-a: Model of the device. The equations governing the behaviour of nonlinear l-element are in R5.03.17. 1.2 modellings The modellings tested are on elements DIS_T, mesh cells SEG2. The features of the discreet elements are of the type: K_T_D_L. Note: The units of the parameters must be in accordance with the unit of forces, the unit of lengths R5.03.17. 2.68767E+03 | 9 Summary of the results These tests allow to check the smooth operation of the discreet elements with the DIS_ECRO_TRAC behavior in the context of use with the DYNA_NON_LINE and DYNA_VIBRA command. The behavior is tested: - in the x direction of the discreet, with isotropic hardening. - in the y and z directions, plane tangent to the discreet, with isotropic and kinematic nutring. The STAT_NON_LINE command uses an implicit algorithm and calculates 1281 time step, without any step adjustment. The DYNA_VIBRA command uses an explicit algorithm and adapts the step for the resolution of the schema in time, which leads to the calculation of 42796 time step. Although the number of time step in the DYNA_VIBRA study is 33 times higher than the number of STAT_NON_LINE studies, the DYNA_VIBRA command is 10 times faster in CPU time than the STAT_NON_LINE command. Note: kinematic hardening is not available in the local direction x of the discreet (no request and need to date).

v5.01.125 SDND125 – Treatment of localized nonlinear behaviors with DYNA_VIBRA v5.01.125 SDND125 – Treatment of localized nonlinear behaviors with DYNA_VIBRA Summary: In the context of the modernisation of the data structure architecture used for the calculation of transient response on the modal basis of a model with localised nonlinearities (operator DYNA_VIBRA), the implementation of data on nonlinear behaviour has been streamlined and a number of facilities have been provided for the post-processing stage. Thus, through a discrete system (mass-resort), this test case has as its main objective to expose the new data set of different localized nonlinear behaviors available in the DYNA_VIBRA operator, via COMPORTEMENT operand and keyword RELATION. The localized relationship between masses is used to model the following phenomena or devices in dynamic: - Modelling A: Frontal shock viaRELATION = ‘DIS_CHOC - Modelling B: Device representing linear flaming viaRELATION = ‘FLAMBAGE - Modelling C: Anti-seismic device viaRELATION = ‘ANTI_SISM - Modelling D: Device representing nonlinear viscoelastic behavior viaRELATION = ‘DIS_VISC - Modelling E: Device representing non-linear behavior viaRELATION = ‘DIS_ECRO_TRAC - Modelling F: Device representing a force-moving or moment-rotation relationship viaRELATION = ‘RELA_EFFO_DEPL - Modelling G: Device representing a force-speed relationship viaRELATION = ‘RELA_EFFO_VITE So it's a test case non-regression. Only calculation values have been recorded to check the consistency between different versions of code_aster. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The system consists of a set of 2 springs, 3 point weights, supported by 2 supports: Figure 1.1-1 > The system consists of the following elements: - a central mass mcenter of 10.0 kg in point N3; - Two mleft and mright weights of 4.5 and 3.7 kg respectively, fixed through two elastic springs each with a kouter rigidity of 103 N/m. - The system is unidirectional, the masses "slip" only in the X direction. > The coordinates of the points shown in the figure above are: | Nœud | X(m) | Y(m) | Z(m) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | N1 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | | N2 | 0.1 | 0.0 | 0.0 | | N3 | 0.2 | 0.0 | 0.0 | | N4 | 0.3 | 0.0 | 0.0 | | N5 | 0.4 | 0.0 | 0.0 | Table 1.1-1 The masses are linked by different phenomena and devices characterized by nonlinear behavioral relationships. 1.2 Boundary conditions and loads boundary conditions : All nodes with weights are free only in the direction X: \mathit{dy}=\mathit{dz}=\mathit{drx}=\mathit{dry}=\mathit{drz}=0 The nodes N1 and N2 are clamped: \mathit{dx}=\mathit{dy}=\mathit{dz}=\mathit{drx}=\mathit{dry}=\mathit{drz}=0 . Charge : The central mass is subjected to a temporal sinusoidal force (mono-sequence) in the form: A\sin(2\pi ft) . The frontal impact relationship is modelled via RELATION = ‘DIS_CHOC' and therefore characterized by a normal rigidity stiffness (shock Modelling with penalization) and a damping due to the relative movement speed between masses: - Shock between mleftet mcenter:normal rigidity {k}_{n} = 1.0E+7 (N/m) - Shock between mrightet mcenter:normal rigidity {k}_{n} = 3.0E+6 (N/m) > The physical distance between masses is 0.1m, corresponding to the distance between masses in the mesh. v5.01.126 SDND126 - Validation of DIS_ECRO_CINE in DYNA_VIBRA v5.01.126 SDND126 - Validation of DIS_ECRO_CINE in DYNA_VIBRA Summary: The DYNA_VIBRA operator has a keyword COMPORTEMENT to handle localized nonlinearities. One of these non-linearities is to impose the constitutive law DIS_ECRO_CINE on a mesh cell with a discreet element. The objective of this test is to validate this use by comparing the results with the DYNA_NON_LINE operator. In this test, it is a mass-spring system subjected to sinusoidal loadings on the different degrees of freedom. Il y a 4 modellings : - Modelling A: DIS_TR/SEG2 - Modelling B: DIS_T/SEG2 - Modelling C: DIS_TR/POI1 - Modelling D: DIS_T/POI1 This documentation is deliberately succinct. In the following we present only the displacement curves of the different degree of freedom by comparing the results obtained by DYNA_NON_LINE and DYNA_VIBRA. For information, we also trace the corresponding elastic behavior. Note that the results from DYNA_VIBRA are ever closer to those from DYNA_NON_LINE as the time step is reduced. 1 Comparison of results 1.1 degree of freedom DX 1.2 degree of freedom DY 1.3 degree of freedom DZ 1.4 degree of freedom DRX 1.5 degree of freedom DRY 1.6 degree of freedom DRZ

v5.02.112 SDNL112 - Vibration damage to a steam generator hanger v5.02.112 SDNL112 - Vibration damage to a steam generator hanger Summary This validation case is intended to verify the non-regression of the functions required for the vibrational damage calculations of the steam generator tubes: vibration fatigue and shock wear on an obstacle. The calculation of the vibration response is carried out by the ITMI method of Temporary Integration by Integral Method implanted in the DYNA_VIBRA operator. To this end, the nonlinear dynamic response of a steam generator tube subjected to external flow is studied. This tube is unstable and comes to impact a game holder. The effects of fluid-elastic coupling (variation in frequency and damping of the structure) are calculated primarily as a function of the flow rate, then the vibrational response of the structure at a given flow rate, and finally the impact wear or vibrational fatigue of the structure. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The structure studied is similar to the curved area of a steam generator tube. It is assumed to be clamped at both ends A and C ; these are supposed to correspond to the passage of the tube in the top interlock plate of a steam generator. At the point B top of the hanger (also called apex), the structure is guided in a game support. Figure 1.1-a: Diagram of the curved area of a GV tube, supposed to be clamped as the last interlocking plate, guided in a game holder The structure is assimilated to a circular cross section beam of total length of 1,74329m , which includes \mathrm{250,43 }\mathrm{mm} of right part at each end of the tube. External diameter of tube: \mathrm{22,22 }\mathrm{mm} Tube inside diameter: \mathrm{19,68 }\mathrm{mm} 1.2 Material properties The values of the characteristics of the different elements of the structure are as follows: Tube in Inconel 600 | E={\mathrm{2,02 10}}^{11}N/{m}^{2} | \nu =0,3 | \rho =\mathrm{8330 }\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} | | --- | --- | --- | | Internal fluid: | The internal fluid modelled is water under pressure at high temperature; its density {\rho}_{i} is assumed to vary linearly along the curved area, between A and C , from \mathrm{738,58 }\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} to \mathrm{731,16 }\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} . | | --- | --- | | External fluid: | The tube is assumed to be immersed in a diphasic mixture over its entire length; the flow of the mixture is transverse to the hanger in all point. The equivalent density of the mixture is obtained by using the formula: | {\rho}_{e}=\alpha {\rho}_{\mathit{gaz}}+(1-\alpha ){\rho}_{\mathit{liquide}} , where \alpha is the volumetric gas ratio. This density appears to be between 84\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} and 150\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} . An equivalent density is attributed to the dynamic system when calculating its modal base in fluid at rest; this equivalent density includes the density of the internal fluid, that of the structure and that of the external fluid; the inertial effect of the latter is evaluated by means of an added mass coefficient. 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The structure is clamped at A and C points. A game support is positioned at point B ( \mathrm{jeu}=\mathrm{1,20 }\mathrm{mm} ). A random load, distributed, transverse to the tube, is imposed on (A-C) . This load is defined, on the one hand by using a speed profile along the excited area, and on the other hand by using an adimensional spectrum of excitement. 1.4 Initial conditions The tube is initially at rest, resulting in zero displacements and speeds at the initial moment. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution See references [bib1], [bib2] and documentation of Code_Aster on dynamic nonlinear calculation algorithms with impact. 2.2 Baseline In the absence of available experimental results, only the non-regression of the results is tested. 2.3 Bibliographical references 1. GAY: "FLUSTRU Software Version 3.0.1, Note to the Policy - HT-32/97/014/A. 1. GAY, S. GRANGER: "Presentation of a non-linear fluid-elastic coupling method", HT‐32/94/015/A. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics The geometric and material properties of the model are those described above. The tube is modelled using Timoshenko's straight beam elements: POU_D_T. It is broken down into 60 elements over six sections. Nodes A and C are blocked in the x , y and z directions in translation and rotation. The damping of the fluid structure at rest is 0.4999 %. 3.2 Mesh characteristics The total number of nodes used for this mesh is 61. The mesh cells are 60 and SEG2 type. The mesh file is in ASTER format. 3.3 Steps of calculation The flow velocity profile and parameters taking into account fluid-structure coupling are defined using DEFI_FONC_FLUI and DEFI_FLUI_STRU operators. Modal parameters of the structure are calculated by taking into account the fluid-elastic forces using CALC_FLUI_STRU operator. The definition of random excitation is performed by using DEFI_SPEC_TURB operator. The excitation is projected on the modal basis using PROJ_SPEC_BASE operator. Modal response interspectrums are calculated using DYNA_SPEC_MODAL operator. The self-sensing spectrums of nodes are derived from this using REST_SPEC_PHYS operator. 4 Modelling results A 4.1 Test values The tests provide the non-regression of the code and cover eigenfrequencies, reduced damping and the RMS on the move. 4.2 Remarks The calculation is performed with 4 modes and a single flow speed of 4.811m/s . 5 Modelling B 5.1 Modelling characteristics The geometric and material properties of the model are those described above. The tube is modelled using Timoshenko's straight beam elements: POU_D_T. It is broken down into 60 elements over six sections. Nodes A and C are blocked in the X , Y and Z directions in translation and rotation. The fluid damping at rest of the structure is 0.4999 %. For the calculation of damage, the following fatigue curve (Wöhler type) is considered, giving the half stress amplitude as a function of the number of cycles: Note that this curve is not the actual fatigue curve for the material under consideration. 5.2 Mesh characteristics The total number of nodes used for this mesh is 61. The mesh cells are 60 and SEG2 type. The mesh file is in ASTER format. 5.3 Steps of calculation The flow velocity profile and parameters taking into account fluid-structure coupling are defined using FONC_FLUI_STRU and DEFI_FLUI_STRU operators. - The modal parameters of the resting water structure are calculated using the CALC_MODES operator. - Modal parameters of the structure are calculated by taking into account the fluid-elastic forces using the CALC_FLUI_STRU operator. - The definition of random excitation is performed using the DEFI_SPEC_TURB operator. The excitation is projected on the modal basis using the PROJ_SPEC_BASE operator. - Random excitation is calculated over a specified period, using the GENE_FONC_ALEA operator. - For temporal calculation, excitation functions are recovered and the time integration method is used by the integral method installed in the DYNA_VIBRA operator. This calculation allows the nonlinear dynamic response of a steam generator tube subjected to external flow to be studied. - The post-processing operator used to evaluate tube fatigue is then POST_FATIGUE. 6 Modelling results B 6.1 Test values The tests ensure the non-regression of the code and cover the movements and the cumulation of damage. 6.2 Remarks The calculation is performed with 4 modes over a total simulation time of 1 second. It is performed for a single flow speed ( \mathrm{4,811 }m/s ) by direct integration with the integral method. The tested values are the damage and the RMS interval of displacement for 1 and 100 cycles at the node of shock. The calculation time and the number of drawings allowing to define the excitation are too small to obtain a suitable statistical average representation of the random phenomenon. Therefore, this test case is only one test case of non-regression. To obtain more representative average values, it is sufficient to extend the calculation time and the number of drawings. 7 Modelling C 7.1 Modelling characteristics The tube is modelled using Timoshenko's straight beam elements: POU_D_T. It is broken down into 60 elements over six sections. Nodes A and C are blocked in the X , Y and Z directions in translation and rotation. The fluid damping at rest is 0.4999 %. 7.2 Mesh characteristics The total number of nodes used for this mesh is 61. The mesh cells are 60 and SEG2 type. The mesh file is in ASTER format. 7.3 Tested Features One way to test is to properly take into account the simple keyword GROUP_NO of the POST_USURE command. 7.4 Steps of calculation The flow velocity profile and parameters taking into account fluid-structure coupling are defined using FONC_FLUI_STRU and DEFI_FLUI_STRU operators. - The modal parameters of the resting water structure are calculated using the CALC_MODES operator. - Modal parameters of the structure are calculated by taking into account the fluid-elastic forces using the CALC_FLUI_STRU operator. - The definition of random excitation is performed using the DEFI_SPEC_TURB operator. The excitation is projected on the modal basis using the PROJ_SPEC_BASE operator. - Random excitation is calculated over a specified period, using the GENE_FONC_ALEA operator. - For temporal calculation, excitation functions are recovered and the time integration method is used by the integral method installed in the DYNA_VIBRA operator. This calculation allows the nonlinear dynamic response of a steam generator tube subjected to external flow to be studied. - The post-processing operator used to evaluate tube wear is then POST_USURE. 8 Modelling results C 8.1 Test values The tests perform the non-regression code and cover the movements as well as the next RMS displacement value. 8.2 Remarks The calculation is performed with 4 modes over a total simulation time of 1 second. It is performed for a single flow speed ( \mathrm{4,811 }m/s ) by direct integration by the integral method. The values tested are the wear power at the node shock. The calculation time and the number of prints that define the excitation are too small to obtain a suitable statistical average representation of the random phenomenon. That is why this test case is only one test case of non-regression. To obtain more representative average values, it is enough to extend the calculation time and the number of drawings. 9 Conclusion The sole purpose of this test case is to verify the non-regression of the GEVIBUS- Code_Aster calculation chains when using the DYNA_VIBRA operator jointly with the ITMI method of full-method time integration and post- fatigue and wear analysis operators. In view of the results obtained, the non-regression of Code_Aster can be considered to be provided for the moment.

v5.02.130 SDNL130 - Seismic response of a reinforced concrete beam (rectangular section) with nonlinear behaviour v5.02.130 SDNL130 - Seismic response of a reinforced concrete beam (rectangular section) with nonlinear behaviour Summary: The problem is to analyze the seismic response of a reinforced concrete beam. The \mathit{BA} beam behaviour is nonlinear. Two modellings are studied: - the beam is represented by R3.08.08 multifibre beam Modelling. The constitutive law of the concrete is Mazars in its version 1D R7.01.08 for Modelling A; - the beam is represented by elements DKTG. The nonlinear constitutive law used is GLRC_DM[R7.01.32] for Modelling B. 1 General characteristics 1.1 Geometry The geometry is identical to that of SSNL119 and SDLL130 test cases except for longitudinal frames which are all identical here: these are four \mathit{HA32} .
