v6.03.128 SSNP128 - Discontinuity validation of the element on a flat plate v6.03.128 SSNP128 - Discontinuity validation of the element on a flat plate DOC A SUPPRIMER Summary: The purpose of this test is to display an analytical solution to validate the quality of the discontinuity element (see R7.02.12 documentation for details on this element). The objective of this test is to verify that this model leads to a good prediction of the value of the displacement jump along a crack. To do this, we are looking for an analytical solution with an unconstant jump along a discontinuity that is compared with the numerically obtained solution. Furthermore, when we are looking for a numerical method, it is preferable to ensure the uniqueness of the desired solution. We will see that this is the case for the analytical solution presented if a condition relating to the maximum size of the domain studied according to the parameters of the model is verified. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry In the (x,y) Cartesian Coordinate System, consider an elastic rectangular flat plate noted \Omega =]0,L[\times ]0,H[ (see [Figure 1.1-a]). Note {\Gamma}_{0}=\left\lbrace 0\right\rbrace \times ]0,H[ the left side of the domain and \partial \Omega \mathrm{\setminus }{\Gamma}_{0} the additional part of the edge. Figure 1.1-a .1-a: Plate diagram Dimensions of the \Omega domain: L=\mathrm{1mm},H=2\pi \text{mm} 1.2 Material properties The material is elastic with a critical stress and a tenacity arbitrarily chosen: E=10\text{MPa},\nu =0,{\sigma}_{c}=1.1\text{MPa},{G}_{c}=0.9{\text{N.mm}}^{-1} 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The boundary conditions are determined by the analytical solution presented in the following part so that it leads to a crack with a non-constant jump along {\Gamma}_{0} . The load corresponds to a displacement imposed on the edges of the plate: (see [Figure1.3-a]). | u=U(x,y) | on \Omega /{\Gamma}_{0} | | --- | --- | | u={U}_{0}\delta (y)-(y) | on {\Gamma}_{0} | Figure 1.3-a: Schematic of loading The U,{U}_{0} and \delta values are set when building the reference solution in the next part. 2 reference solution In this part an analytical solution is displayed with a non-constant jump along {\Gamma}_{0} , then a single condition of the solution is given. 2.1 analytical solution The function d-Airy \Phi (x,y) governed by the \Delta \Delta \Phi =0 - \Omega - \Omega - \Omega - \Omega - \Omega - \Omega - \Delta \Delta \Phi =0 - \Omega - \Omega - \Omega - \Omega - {\sigma}_{xx} - {\sigma}_{yy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xx} - {\sigma}_{xx} - {\sigma}_{xx} - {\sigma}_{xx} - {\sigma}_{xx} - {\sigma}_{yy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - \Phi (x,y) - \Phi (x,y) - \Phi (x,y) - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xy} - {\sigma}_{xy} XX {\sigma}_{xy} XX {\sigma}_{xy} XXKK5XXXKK5XXXXXXXXXKKKK5XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXKKKK5XX {\sigma}_{xx}=\frac{{\partial}^{2}\Phi }{\partial {y}^{2}} , {\sigma}_{yy}=\frac{{\partial}^{2}\Phi }{\partial {x}^{2}} et {\sigma}_{xy}=\frac{{\partial}^{2}\Phi }{\partial x\partial y} éq 2.1-1 Choose a \Phi (x,y) bi-harmonic function defined by: \Phi (x,y)=\beta \frac{{y}^{3}}{6}+(\alpha x+\gamma )\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\eta xy with \alpha ,\beta ,\gamma and \eta arbitrary real constants. From this the stress field is derived after [eq 2.1-1]: \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}{\sigma}_{xx}& =& \alpha x+\beta y+\gamma \\ {\sigma}_{yy}& =& 0\\ {\sigma}_{xy}& =& -\alpha y-\eta \end{array} éq 2.1-2 By integrating elastic law, if E is noted the Young's modulus and \nu the Poisson's ratio (which is taken null), the displacement field is derived from it in \Gamma checking balance: u=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}u(x,y)\\ v(x,y)\end{array}\right\rbrace =\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}\frac{1}{E}(\alpha (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-{y}^{2})+x(\beta y+\gamma ))\\ -\frac{1}{E}(\beta \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\eta x)\end{array}\right\rbrace éq 2.1-3 Note, respectively, the {U}_{0} and U moves on {\Gamma}_{0} and \partial \Omega \setminus {\Gamma}_{0} given by [eq 2.1-3]. These are the boundary conditions leading to the stress field [eq 2.1-2]. From this data, it is easy to construct a displacement field with discontinuity on the edge {\Gamma}_{0} . Indeed, knowing the normal \sigma n stress on {\Gamma}_{0} that the F(y) notes, one obtains the \delta (y) displacement jump by inverting the exponential constitutive law Barenblatt: CZM_EXP type (see documentation on internal elements discontinuity and their behavior: R7.02.12): \delta (y)=-\frac{{G}_{c}F(y)}{{\sigma}_{c}\parallel F(y)\parallel }\ln(\frac{\parallel F(y)\parallel }{{\sigma}_{c}}) For all y in \left[0,H\right] . Thus, the new displacement imposed on {\Gamma}_{0} generating such a jump is equal to {U}_{0}-\delta . So we built a analytical solution of the flat plate checking the equilibrium and compatibility equations with a {\Gamma}_{0} discontinuity along which the \delta displacement jump is not constant. Let's remember the boundary conditions problem: \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}u=U(x,y)& \mathrm{sur}& \partial \Omega \setminus {\Gamma}_{0}\\ u={U}_{0}(y)-\delta (y)& \mathrm{sur}& {\Gamma}_{0}\end{array} éq 2.1-4 2.2 Uniqueness of the solution After building a analytical solution it is important to ensure that it is unique in order to compare it with the digital solution. See [bib2], that the uniqueness is guaranteed as soon as the following condition, on the geometry of the domain as well as on the material parameters, is verified: L<2\mu \frac{{G}_{c}}{{\sigma}_{c}^{2}} . éq 2.2-1 The dimensions of the plate and the material parameters given above verify this condition. 2.3 Bibliographical references 1. FUNG Y.C.: Foundation of Solid Mechanics, Prentice-Hall, (1979). 2. lantern J.: Energy formulation of rupture by models of cohesive forces: theoretical considerations and numerical implantations, Thesis of Doctorate of the University Paris13, November 2004. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics The idea is to perform a numerical simulation corresponding to the problem presented in the previous part and compare the results obtained. The discontinuity elements allows to represent the crack along {\Gamma}_{0} . These have for PLAN_ELDI modelling and CZM_EXP behavior. The other elements of the mesh are elastic QUAD4 models in D_PLAN Modelling. The d-Airy function parameters for the analytical solution construction are taken arbitrarily: \alpha =0{\text{MPa.mm}}^{-1},\beta =1/4\pi {\text{MPa.mm}}^{-1},\gamma =1/2\text{MPa}\text{et}\eta =0\text{MPa} 3.2 Mesh characteristics Mesh of the squared plate with 20 mesh cells in width and 50 in height is performed. elements with discontinuity along the {\Gamma}_{0} side with the normal directed following -X is available. This is done using CREA_FISS's CREA_MAILLAGE keyword (see U4.23.02 documentation). 3.3 Tested quantities and results | quantity tested | Type | Reference | Tolerance ( \text{\%} ) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Threshold variable: \mathrm{VI1} On the element \mathrm{MJ15} | 'ANALYTIQUE' | 0.49315 | 0.10 | | Threshold variable: \mathrm{VI1} On the element \mathrm{MJ45} | 'ANALYTIQUE' | 1.075 | 0.10 | | Normal stress: \mathrm{VI6} On the element \mathrm{MJ30} | 'ANALYTIQUE' | 0.4489 | 0.10 | 4 Summary of the results These results allow us to conclude that the internal discontinuity of element leads to a good approximation of the analytical solution. Furthermore, a study of mesh dependence was performed in [bib2]. It is found that the error made on the displacement jump decreases when the mesh is refined. This concludes that, despite a constant jump by element, this model correctly reproduces a crack with a non-constant jump by refining the mesh.

v6.03.130 SSNP130 - Detection of singularities in cracked plate v6.03.130 SSNP130 - Detection of singularities in cracked plate Summary: The purpose of this test is to test the detection of singularities in a cracked plate as well as the calculation of a size card (for a given target error). 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Geometry is a cracked plate with only the upper part modeled. 1.2 Material properties The massif consists of a linear isotropic elastic material: - Young's modulus isotropic elasticity: E=200000\mathrm{Pa} - Poisson's ratio : \nu =0,3 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads Unit pressure is applied to the top of the plate. For symmetry reasons, the crack ligament is blocked on the Y axis and the node at the end of the ligament is blocked on the X axis. 2 reference solution 2.1 Method of calculation When the exact solution of the problem studied has singularities, the convergence order of the elements solution is changed. Consider, for example, a problem of flat elasticity discretized with elements triangular p degree. If the exact {U}_{\mathrm{ex}} solution is regular, it is known that ([bib1]): {\parallel u-{u}_{h}\parallel }_{\Omega}={\parallel e\parallel }_{\Omega}\le C{h}^{p} éq 2.1-1 With C a constant, h the size of elements. Where {\parallel e\parallel }_{\Omega}\le C{h}^{p} is the contribution to energy error, i.e.: {\parallel e\parallel }_{\Omega}\le \frac{1}{2}\underset{\Omega}{\int}\varepsilon ({e}_{h})K\varepsilon ({e}_{h})d\Omega éq 2.1-2 However, if the exact solution has a singularity, for example if, locally near a point {M}_{0} , the displacement field is of the shape (with r and \theta polar coordinates near the point {M}_{0} ): {U}_{\mathrm{ex}}={r}^{\alpha}V(\theta )+W with 0<\alpha <1 eq 2.1-3 With V a function of \theta and W a constant. So we show that [bib1]: {\parallel {e}_{h}\parallel }_{\Omega}\le C{h}^{\alpha} éq 2.1-4 As a result, the rate of convergence of the overall energy error becomes independent of the p degree of the finished elements used and the same is true of the measurement of the error (for example, if p=1 or p=2 then \alpha =1/2 for a crack). Thus, at crack point the order of singularity will be 0.5, and away from singularity (where the element solution is regular the order of singularity is p (1 for linear elements, 2 for quadratic elements) 2.2 Quantities and reference results The value of the singularity in crack point (analytical solution), in its vicinity (non-regression) and away from the crack (analytical solution) will be tested. The size ratio to be applied to the mesh for a target error (non-regression) and the new size of the elements (non-regression) is also tested. It is noted that for Modelling A, the target error is the error (in amount of interest) on average displacement on the structure. For the other modellings, the error used is the energy standard error. 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution analytical solution et non-regression 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. v6.03.131 SSNP131 - Energy parameter identification Gp in 2D and 3D v6.03.131 SSNP131 - Energy parameter identification Gp in 2D and 3D Summary This non-linear quasi-static mechanical test allows the calculation of the {G}_{p} parameter from the energy approach of the elastoplastic rupture and the identification of critical values corresponding to the given experimental tenacity values. It requires the representation of the crack by a cut and the finely knitting of the vicinity of the bottom of the dent. It also requires the calculation of elastic energy on the virtual propagation zone of the dentaille, cut into "cops". Modelling A is done with quadratic elements \mathrm{2D} , in flat deformation. The mesh represents the so-called chip areas; the calculation of the parameter is done using the properties of the mesh (POST_GP and CALC_GP) or by automatic creation of these zones (CALC_GP). Model B is identical to model A, but uses any mesh; only the automatic definition of chips is used (CALC_GP). 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Uy = 0 \mathrm{CT25} test piece with a ligament length: a=27.5\mathrm{mm} ( a/W=0.55 ) is considered. On the z axis, the thickness is e=1\mathrm{mm} . \mathrm{CT25} test piece is modelled in flat deformations. Due to symmetry, half of this is represented in \mathrm{2D} . 1.2 Material properties Young's modulus: 214100 \mathrm{Mpa} Poisson's ratio : \nu =0.3 . The traction curve used is presented in the following table: | \epsilon | \sigma (\text{MPa}) | | --- | --- | | 0.003439678 | 740.6632663 | | 0.004628373 | 842.148772 | | 0.00607988 | 876.3117064 | | 0.007654628 | 895.2063119 | | 0.010417548 | 911.0718694 | | 0.014178015 | 925.022448 | | 0.017543214 | 935.2135771 | | 0.021942493 | 945.6948965 | | 0.027416704 | 960.732311 | | 0.033866984 | 975.8041996 | | 0.040205805 | 988.2450325 | | 0.046616375 | 1000.143035 | | 0.052903597 | 1010.004051 | | 0.058235889 | 1017.5664 | Table 1.1 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The load is of the displacement type imposed in an point located in the centre of the pin which is modelled by four unformable angular sectors. Half of the test piece is modelled, and a symmetry condition is applied to the ligament ( y=0 ). 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution in 2D The energy method of elastoplastic rupture based on the parameter \mathrm{Gp} [1], [2] is used. The bottom of the core is formed by a half circle of R radius. The \mathrm{Ze} zone of length \Delta l corresponds to the virtual propagation of the core and is cut into "cops". It determines at each moment the evolution of the quantity \mathrm{Gp}(\Delta l) defined by: \mathit{Gp}(\Delta l)=2[{W}_{\mathit{elas}}^{\mathit{traction}}(\Delta l)]/\Delta l where {W}_{\mathit{elas}}^{\mathit{traction}}(\Delta l) is the elastic traction energy calculated on the \mathrm{Ze} area. The maximum of this quantity shall then be calculated in relation to \Delta l , which is called " \mathrm{Gp} ". \mathrm{Gp}=\underset{\Delta l}{\mathrm{Max}}\lbrace \mathrm{Gp}(\Delta l)\rbrace The critical moment when the propagation of the defect will start is then the moment where the tenacity \mathrm{Kj}={\mathrm{Kj}}_{\mathrm{crit}} . It is said then that \mathrm{Gp} reaches the critical value " \mathrm{Gpc} ". 2.2 Bibliographical references 1. WADIER Y.: "Snapshot of the energy approach to elastoplastic rupture applied to cleavage rupture", Note EDF R&D HT-64/03/001/A, January 2003. 2. WADIER Y., LORENTZ E.: "Mechanics of rupture in the presence of plasticity: Modelling crack by a cut". C.R.A.S. t. 332, Series IIb, 2004. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics The crack is modelled by a 100 micron radius cut. \mathrm{Ze} zone of 2\mathrm{mm} length is divided into layers of d-elements of 20 microns thick (also known as "cops"). 3.2 Mesh characteristics Number of nodes : 9368 Number of mesh cells and types : 3350 TRIA6, 800 QUAD8 3.3 Tested quantities and results 3.3.1 Test values With the CALC_GP operator and definition of chips by the mesh: | Identification | Reference Aster | Tolerance (%) | | --- | --- | --- | | {G}_{P} at instant 4 at chip 8 | 0.022692041 | 0.010 | | {G}_{P} at instant 40 at chip 3 | 0.667072167 | 0.010 | With CALC_GP operator and automatic chip definition | Identification | Reference Aster | Tolerance (%) | | --- | --- | --- | | {G}_{P} at instant 4 at chip 8 | 0.0234148559 | 0.010 | | {G}_{P} at instant 40 at chip 3 | 0.674949376 | 0.010 | 4 Modelling B 4.1 Modelling characteristics This Modelling is two-dimensional, in flat deformations. In the case of the explicit mesh of the chips ( {W}_{\mathit{elas}}^{\mathit{traction}}(\Delta S) ), where the participation of spherical compression and compression in each specific deformation direction is removed, the elastic energy will be modified into an elastic energy of traction and by definition {W}_{\mathit{elas}}^{\mathit{traction}}(\Delta S)<{W}_{\mathit{elas}}(\Delta S) . 5 Summary of the results The tests are validated with an difference below 2nd-4%. v6.03.133 SSNP133 - Frustration of a hole plate with cohesive models v6.03.133 SSNP133 - Frustration of a hole plate with cohesive models Summary: This test allows to model the propagation of two cracks in an elastic hole plate. A Modelling: elements joint, CZM_LIN_REG cohesive law C Modelling: elements interface, CZM_OUV_MIX cohesive law D Modelling: elements joint, CZM_EXP_REG cohesive law E Modelling: XFEM Modelling, CZM_EXP_REG cohesive law. mesh conforming to cracks. F Modelling: XFEM Modelling, CZM_EXP_REG cohesive law. mesh triangles not compliant. G Modelling: XFEM Modelling, CZM_EXP_REG cohesive law. mesh unstructured. H Modelling: XFEM Modelling, CZM_LIN_REG cohesive law. mesh conforming to cracks. I Modelling: XFEM Modelling, CZM_OUV_MIX cohesive law. mesh conforming to cracks. J Modelling: XFEM Modelling, CZM_OUV_MIX cohesive law. mesh not compliant. The local numbering ad hoc of the cohesive elements (except X-\mathrm{FEM} ) is ensured by the MODI_MAILLAGE command and the ORIE_FISSURE keyword. The sudden opening of cracks is ensured by the control of the load available for each of these laws (see R7.02.11). 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry and loading A square plate on the 2000\mathit{mm} side with a R=500\mathit{mm} radius hole centred in the vertical direction and decentralized in the horizontal direction (see Figure 1.1-a). The plate allows a horizontal symmetry plane ( \mathit{AB}' ) passing through the centre of the hole. This symmetry can allow us to reduce our study to the upper half of the plate where possible. Figure1.1-a: Diagram of the hole plate, boundary conditions and loading. The elements is a single {F}^{i} load density, which is directed in the Y direction on the upper part of the domain. The strength of this force will be given by the load control (see R7.02.11). In addition, symmetry conditions (zero displacements following Y ) are imposed on the lower side of the elements cohesives. Finally, rigid body movements are blocked by imposing a zero displacement following X on the point P , the top of the hole. For modellings E to J, we have an X-FEM formulation: it is then necessary to model the entire structure for the moment. An interface is introduced on the right (AB') . It is recalled the approximation of the displacement field for nodes whose support is intersected by an XFEM interface : {u}_{h}(x)=\sum_{i}{\phi }_{i}(x){a}_{i}+\sum_{i}{\phi }_{i}(x){b}_{i}H(\mathit{lsn}(x)) In order to block rigid body movements, we want the interface to be a symmetry axis for the problem. If we consider {M}^{+} and {M}^{-} points immediately above and below the interface, we want {u}_{y}({M}^{+})+{u}_{y}({M}^{-})=0 . For a compliant interface, this implies {a}_{y}=0 on the nodes interface (Figure ). For a non-conform interface that intersects the edges in their middle, noting {N}_{\text{SUP}} and {N}_{\mathit{INF}} the nodes screws on either side of the crack (Figure ), this implies: {a}_{y}({N}_{\text{SUP}})+{a}_{y}({N}_{\text{INF}})=0 Figure 1.1-a : load with a crack conforming. Figure 1.1-b : loading for non-compliant cracks. 1.2 Material properties The values of Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, critical stress and tenacity of the material are selected as follows: \begin{array}{ccc}E=30000\mathit{MPa}& \nu =0.2& {\sigma}_{c}=0.2\mathit{MPa}\\ {G}_{c}=100\mathit{Pa.mm}& \text{}\mathrm{\Rightarrow }\text{}& \text{problème symétrisé}\\ {G}_{c}=200\mathit{Pa.mm}& \text{}\mathrm{\Rightarrow }\text{}& \text{problème non symétrisé}\end{array} These are "tests" values that do not correspond to any particular material. The purpose of the choice of cohesive parameters is to obtain a solution with a relatively coarse mesh. It is recalled that to ensure a correct solution (precision and good convergence) with these models, it is necessary that there are several elements in the cohesive zone (see U2.05.07 doc). v6.03.138 SSNP138 - 2D inclined crack with X-FEM v6.03.138 SSNP138 - 2D inclined crack with X-FEM Summary This test is intended to validate the calculation of stress intensity factors ( {K}_{I} and {K}_{\mathit{II}} ) with \text{X-FEM} in \mathrm{2D} , as part of the linear elasticity. This test is also intended to test the volume loadings of FORCE_INTERNE and gravity with the \text{X-FEM} method in \mathrm{2D} . This test involves a rectangular plate with a straight, inclined central crack, and subjected to traction loading on the lower and upper edges of the plate (modellings A C , D , E ) or subjected to a volume and clamped support on the upper part (modelling B ), or subject to lip pressure (modelling F ). Different modellingss are considered: 1. A Modelling: \text{X-FEM}\mathrm{2D} , surface loading on edges, mesh cells QUAD4, geometric enrichment 2. B Modelling: \text{X-FEM}\mathrm{2D} , volume loading, mesh cells QUAD4. geometric enrichment 3. C Modelling: \text{X-FEM}\mathrm{2D} , surface loading on edges, mesh cells TRIA3, geometric enrichment 4. D Modelling: \text{X-FEM}\mathrm{2D} , loading on the edges, mesh cells TRIA3, topological enrichment 5. E Modelling: \text{X-FEM}\mathrm{2D} , loading on the edges, mesh cells TRIA6, topological enrichment 6. F Modelling: \text{X-FEM}\mathrm{2D} , lip loading, mesh cells TRIA3, topological enrichment The validation is for stress intensity factors ( {K}_{I} and {K}_{\mathrm{II}} ), compared to analytical solution for modellings A , C , D , E , F and a non-regression solution for B Modelling. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The \mathrm{2D} structure is a rectangular plate ( \mathrm{LX}=0,2m , \mathrm{LY}=0,5m ), with a straight central crack, inclined at an angle \theta variable with respect to the horizontal axis (see v6.03.138-fissuree-plate-geometry). The crack length is constant ( a=0,04m ). In this test, the \theta angle will successively take the values: 0° , 15° , 30° , 45° , 60° for A and 0° Modelling , 45° for B Modelling . v6.03.143 SSNP143 – Validation of clavage/sawing for dam seal law v6.03.143 SSNP143 – Validation of clavage/sawing for dam seal law Summary: Two industrial procedures on dams are tested: clavage and sawing. The clavage is a pressure injection of concrete between the platings of a dam. It is an intermediate step in the construction of a vault dam, it is used to strengthen its seal after the construction phase of vertical plating. The sawing is a similar procedure during which the dam is sawn to release the stresses. This can occur before or after the watering. This test allows to validate both procedures by clavage/sawing between the two regular platings, which are either clamped on the ground and subjected to gravity force (modellings A, B, E, F, G, H), or compressed on the sides (modellings C and D). The procedure is defined via a PRES_CLAVAGE and SCIAGE key word in DEFI_MATERIAU for the material JOINT_MECA_RUPT/FROT. The corresponding laws bear the same names. The behaviour of the two-dimensional and three-dimensional joints, corresponding to modellings: PLAN_JOINT and 3D_JOINT. Modelling A: Industrial Clavage 2D; JOINT_MECA_RUPT law Modelling B: Industrial 3D clavage; JOINT_MECA_RUPT law Modelling C: 2D theoretical sawing; JOINT_MECA_RUPT/FROT laws Modelling D: 3D theoretical sawing; JOINT_MECA_RUPT/FROT laws Modelling E: 2D sawing; JOINT_MECA_RUPT law Modelling F: 3D industrial sawing; JOINT_MECA_RUPT law Modelling G: 2D sawing; JOINT_MECA_FROT law Modelling H: 3D industrial sawing; JOINT_MECA_FROT law For clavage, the thickness profile of the joints after clavage is compared with the results provided by another calculation code (SOURCE_EXTERNE GEFDYN) . For sawing a comparison is made with a theoretical estimate (modelization C and D). NON_REGRESSION tests are also carried out of the values of the thickness of the joint, together with corresponding forces. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry and loading Two dam pads are considered, represented by regular cubes of length L=\mathrm{5m} , height H=\mathrm{10m} and depth P=\mathrm{1m} . The distance between the pads is assumed not to be zero to simplify the generation of the mesh of the joints ( \epsilon =\mathrm{1mm} ). The clamped support varies according to the modellings. 1.1.1 modellings A,B,E,F,G,H The lower parts of the plots are clamped. The plots are subject to their gravity weights. The loading takes place in two stages: - The plots are balanced under gravity loading. The joint opens in the upper part because of the compression of the lower parts of the plots. One of the two industrial procedures is subsequently applied: - The clavage procedure is activated: "concrete is injected" between the PRES_CLAVAGE= 5{10}^{4}\mathit{Pa} pads. The profile of the joint thickness is then changed to obtain the clavage pressure on the crack lips. This profile is then stored by one of the internal variables to "memorize" the amount of concrete injected. - The sawing procedure is activated via SCIAGE key word. The thickness of the {\delta}_{\mathit{scie}} saw is selected so that the top part of the plot is only partially sawn. Drawing 1: Diagram of dam pads, boundary conditions and loading 1.1.2 modellings C,D The left side of the plot is clamped, while a displacement is applied to the right side of the plot. The sawing procedure is subsequently activated via the key word SCIAGE. The thickness of the {\delta}_{\mathit{scie}} saw is chosen so that the seal is only partially sawn. Drawing 2: modellings C and D, which allow the theoretical validation of sawing 1.2 Material properties The mechanical parameters of the plots (Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, density) are selected as follows: | E={3.10}^{2}\mathit{Pa} | \nu =0,25 | {\rho}_{b}=2400\mathit{kg}/{m}^{3} | | --- | --- | --- | The thickness of the saw varies according to the model. 1.2.1 Material JOINT_MECA_RUPT The normal stiffness equal to the tangential stiffness is taken for the joint. There is no tensile strength. The coupling between the normal opening and the tangential stiffness is chosen so that the tangential slope is zero as soon as the joint reaches the normal complete damage threshold. The breaking softening slope is five times steeper than the normal loading slope (see R7.01.25 document). After gravitational mechanical loading, the following is secured at a non-zero cladding pressure: | {K}_{N}={K}_{T}={10}^{12}\mathit{Pa}/m | {\sigma}_{max}=0\mathit{Pa} | \text{pena\_contact}=0.8 | | --- | --- | --- | | \alpha =1 | \text{pena\_rupt}=0.2 | \text{pres\_clav}={4.10}^{4}\mathit{Pa} | (NB: test values which do not correspond to any particular material) 1.2.2 Material JOINT_MECA_FROT For the friction law associated with the joint, "tests" are selected which do not correspond to any particular material. | {K}_{N}={K}_{T}/2={10}^{12}\mathit{Pa}/m | {\sigma}_{max}=3\mathit{MPa} | | | --- | --- | --- | | \mu =0.35 | \text{adhe}=1000 | \text{ecrouissage}=0.1{K}_{T} | 2 reference solution 2.1 Clash procedure We take as reference the solution given by the calculation code GEFDYN . This procedure has been validated on many industrial works. The opening of the seal after clavage is tested. 2.2 Sawing procedure As with sawing we do not have a solution from an external code. This is then theoretically validated in modellings C and D, which accept a \mathrm{1D} solution. First, a homogeneous compression {\delta}_{\mathit{impo}} is applied to the left side of the plot. The load is almost \mathrm{1D} and thus the stress equivalence is present in the joint and in the plot, allowing us to estimate the value of the stress applied \sigma : | {\delta}_{\mathit{plot}}+{\delta}_{\mathit{joint}}={\delta}_{\mathit{impo}} | \sigma 2L/E+\sigma /\text{pena\_contact}/{K}_{N}={\delta}_{\mathit{impo}} | | | --- | --- | --- | This gives: \sigma ={\delta}_{\mathit{impo}}/(\frac{1}{2LE}+\frac{1}{\text{pena\_contact}{K}_{N}}) Once the constraint is known, the constitutive law can be applied to find the joint opening: {\delta}_{\mathit{joint}}=\sigma /\text{pena\_contact}/{K}_{N} . v6.03.144 SSNP144 – Using a cohesive zone model with the X-FEM method v6.03.144 SSNP144 – Using a cohesive zone model with the X-FEM method Summary This test is designed to validate the constitutive law cohesive that is used during cracking of elements X-\mathrm{FEM} . This approach, described in R7.02.12, allows you to model the opening of an interface taking into account a cohesion force between the lips of the interface. Modellings A at K involves a parallelepipedic bar cracked over its entire section (i.e., interface), subject to a forced displacement, resulting in the separation of both parts of the structure in I mode as well as in \mathrm{II} mode. The influence of the refinement of the mesh and the type of elements used is studied. L Modelling tests the case of an interface that opens and closes in I mode. It is used simultaneously with penalised contact and control. Validation is done by comparing the Lagrangian contact and friction values with an analytical reference solution. 1 Reference problem 1.1 3D geometry The structure is a straight parallelepipeda with square base. The dimensions of the bar (see []) are: \mathit{LX}=\mathrm{5m} , \mathit{LY}=\mathrm{5m} and \mathit{LZ}=\mathrm{25m} . The interface is introduced by level set functions directly into the command file using DEFI_FISS_XFEM U4.82.08 operator. The interface is present in the middle of the structure through its representation by a level set \text{LSN} (see []) equation: \text{LSN}\text{(pour le plan de l'interface) :}Z-\frac{\mathrm{LZ}}{2} Figure 1.1-b Figure 1.1-a : Bar Geometry and Interface Positioning 1.2 2D geometry The structure is a rectangle. The dimensions of the bar (see []) are: \text{LX}=\mathrm{1m} , \text{LY}=\mathrm{5m} . The interface is introduced by a level set function directly into the command file using the DEFI_FISS_XFEM U4.82.08 operator. The interface is present in the middle of the structure through its representation by a level set \text{LSN} (see []) equation: \text{LSN}\text{(pour le plan de l'interface) :}Y-\frac{\mathrm{LY}}{2} Figure 1.2-a : Plate Geometry and Interface Positioning Figure 1.2-b : Evolution of the displacement jump imposed by pilotage as a function of the calculation moment 1.3 Material properties | Young's modulus: | \text{E = 0,5.E6P a} | | --- | --- | | Poisson's ratio : | \nu =0,0 | The presence of a cohesive law at the interface is indicated using the keyword RELATION='CZM_EXP_REG' when defining the contact area (command DEFI_CONTACT, factor keyword ZONE). The cohesive law then installed has for {G}_{c},{\sigma}_{c} and {\kappa}_{0} parameters, and is explained in detail in the R7.02.11 documentation | Tenacity: | {\text{G}}_{\text{c}}=\text{900 N/m} | (keyword: GC) | | --- | --- | --- | | Critical stress on rupture: | {\sigma}_{c}=\text{1,1.E6 Pa} | (keyword: SIGM_C) | | Energy regularization parameter: | {\kappa}_{0}=\mathrm{1,0E-3} | (keyword PENA_ADHERENCE) | Note: Les données matériaux n'ont bien entendu pas vocation à représenter un matériau en particulier. Elles sont uniquement destinées à des tests numériques de validation. 1.4 Boundary conditions and loads 1.4.1 Degrees of freedom enriched and boundary conditions Remember that moving under X-\mathrm{FEM} is the sum of a continuous displacement and a discontinuous displacement. In the case of an interface, without crack bottom, the approximation of the displacement is written as follows: {u}^{h}(x)=\sum_{i\in {N}_{n}(x)}{a}_{i}{\phi }_{i}(x)+\sum_{j\in {N}_{n}(x)\cap K}{b}_{j}{\phi }_{j}(x)H(\mathrm{lsn}(x)) Où: > {a}_{i} and {b}_{i} are the degrees of freedom moving node i , > {\phi }_{i} the form functions associated with node i , > {N}_{n}(x) is all nodes with point x in its support, > K is all nodes with a fully cracked support, > H(x) is the generalized Heaviside function defined by H(x)=\lbrace \begin{array}{}-1\text{si}x \mathrm{lsn}(x) is the normal level-set value at point x . For more details, refer to the X-\mathrm{FEM} R7.02.12 reference documentation. It is therefore possible to impose boundary conditions on total displacement (or physical displacement), on its continuous component or on its discontinuous component. We will first give different useful relationships between this physical displacement and the degrees of freedom existing in Code_Aster. Example: a edge of an mesh \mathrm{2D} any interface crossing: Figure 1.4.1-1: Arête intersectée par une interface Call {P}^{+} and {P}^{-} the geometric points that belong to the segment and are located just below and above the level set, respectively, and consider without loss of generality vertical displacements. We have: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\mathit{DY}({N}^{+})={a}_{y}^{+}+{b}_{y}^{+}\\ \mathit{DY}({N}^{-})={a}_{y}^{-}-{b}_{y}^{-}\\ \mathit{DY}({P}^{+})=\alpha ({a}_{y}^{+}+{b}_{y}^{+})+(1-\alpha )({a}_{y}^{-}+{b}_{y}^{-})\\ \mathit{DY}({P}^{-})=\alpha ({a}_{y}^{+}-{b}_{y}^{+})+(1-\alpha )({a}_{y}^{-}-{b}_{y}^{-})\end{array} The expression of the displacement jump for the ridge can be drawn from this: \mathrm{〚}\mathit{DY}\mathrm{〛}=\mathit{DY}({P}^{+})-\mathit{DY}({P}^{-})=\alpha {b}_{y}^{+}+(1-\alpha ){b}_{y}^{-} 1.4.2 Loading In I mode, the nodes on the lower side of the bar is clamped and vertical displacement is imposed on the upper side, as explained in Figure . In \mathrm{II} opening mode, the nodes located below the level set are clamped, and a vertical \mathit{DY} ( \mathit{DZ} in \mathrm{3D} ) shift is imposed from \mathrm{1,0E-13} to all nodes located above the level set. This ensures the nullity of the contact indicator at the interface level. We also impose pure shear at the cohesive area which, taking into account the notations of the figure, is imposed for each intersected edge: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\mathit{DX}({P}^{-})=\mathit{DX}({N}^{-})=0\\ \mathit{DX}({P}^{+})=\mathit{DX}({N}^{+})\end{array} Figure 1.4.2-1: Chargement appliqué, en mode I et en mode \mathrm{II} We see that this requires imposing restraints between degrees of freedom on both sides of the i edge that depend on the \alpha coefficient. In order not to unnecessarily weigh the command file, we will only test in \mathrm{II} mode meshes for which: - or all intersect edges are in their middle, i.e. for each \alpha =0,5 - either the interface is compliant, i.e. \alpha =1 In the first case, where all edges are intersected in their middle, we ensure the nullity of the contact indicator by imposing \mathit{H1Y}=5.E-14 on all nodes ends of the intersected edges by the interface. As far as shearing is concerned, we must impose the relationships: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\mathit{DX}({P}^{-})=\mathit{DX}({N}^{-})\mathrm{\iff }\frac{{a}_{x}^{+}-{b}_{x}^{+}}{2}+\frac{{a}_{x}^{-}-{b}_{x}^{-}}{2}={a}_{x}^{-}-{b}_{x}^{-}=0\\ \mathit{DX}({P}^{+})=\mathit{DX}({N}^{+})\mathrm{\iff }\frac{{a}_{x}^{+}+{b}_{x}^{+}}{2}+\frac{{a}_{x}^{-}+{b}_{x}^{-}}{2}={a}_{x}^{+}+{b}_{x}^{+}\end{array} We see then that if we impose the {a}_{x}^{+}={b}_{x}^{+} relationship then \mathit{DX}({P}^{-})=0 . If we then impose the {b}_{x}^{+}={b}_{x}^{-} relationship, we have more \mathit{DX}({P}^{+})=\mathit{DX}({N}^{+}) . In the second case, with mesh compliant interface, the jump is represented by the degree of freedom Heaviside at point confused with the interface and we must therefore impose \mathit{H1Y}=1.E-13 on nodes confused with the interface. As far as shearing is concerned, if {N}^{-} corresponds to the point confused with the {P}^{-} interface, we must impose: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}\mathit{DX}({P}^{-})={a}_{x}^{-}-{b}_{x}^{-}=0\\ \mathit{DX}({P}^{+})=\mathit{DX}({N}^{+})\mathrm{\iff }{a}_{x}^{-}+{b}_{x}^{-}={a}_{x}^{+}\end{array} We see then that if we impose the {a}_{x}^{-}={b}_{x}^{-} relationship then \mathit{DX}({N}^{-})=\mathit{DX}({P}^{-})=0 . If we then impose the {a}_{x}^{-}=\frac{{a}_{x}^{+}}{2} relationship, we have more \mathit{DX}({P}^{+})=\mathit{DX}({N}^{+}) . These two relationships are imposed for all nodes vis-à-vis mesh cells crossed by the interface. Note that in the command file, the syntax to impose these different degrees of freedoms differs depending on the operators. The DDL_IMPO factor keyword of the AFFE_CHAR_MECA operator allows to impose total displacement (or physical displacement) thanks to the DX, DY, and DZ keywords, as well as degrees of freedom discontinuous {b}_{i} keywords thanks to H1X, H1Y, and H1Z. On the other hand, the LIAISON_GROUP factor keyword allows to control degrees of freedom continuous {a}_{i} keywords through DX, DY, and DZ (not total displacement) as well as degrees of freedom discontinuous {b}_{i} keywords through H1X, H1Y, and H1Z. 1.5 Loading pilot For I mode, the control is performed on the vertical displacement jump. The \mathrm{DY} vertical displacement ( \mathrm{DZ} in \mathrm{3D} ) imposed on the nodes of the upper side of the bar is then unitary. The actual displacement intensity of these nodes is therefore known during the calculation via the ETA_PILOTAGE parameter. One of the SAUT_IMPO or SAUT_LONG_ARC -controlled drives is used, especially for \mathrm{XFEM} , on the normal \mathrm{H1Y} component ( \mathrm{H1Z} in \mathrm{3D} ), corresponding to {b}_{y} ( {b}_{z} in \mathrm{3D} ) with the above ratings, for all the interface intersect edges. For \mathrm{II} mode, the pilot is performed on the horizontal jump. The pilot is then performed in the same way as I mode, but on the \mathit{H1X} tangential component. Finally, for each of the opening modes, the controls used allow you to explore all phases of the constitutive law: elastic linear load, damage and discharge. The figures and represent the evolution of the shift jump according to the moment of calculation. To perform discharges, several calculation times (use key word) are performed to allow to change the value of the {c}_{\mathrm{mult}} coefficient (keyword COEF_MULT ) allowing to define the value of the \Delta {\delta}_{i} displacement jump increment to be imposed for a time step \Delta t via the steering equation. As the problem is uniform, this relationship is written in a simple way for SAUT_IMPO and SAUT_LONG_ARC: \Delta {\delta}_{i}{c}_{\mathit{mult}}=\Delta t . The PRED_ELAS type pilot is not yet tested for this case because it would require a return giving the possibility to fly in discharge, discussed in R5.03.80, with this type of pilotage. Figure 2-a : One-dimensional representation of Reference problem Let us express the movements of the different points of the structure: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}^{1}=0\\ {u}^{2}=L\epsilon \\ {u}^{+}=(L+\frac{a}{2})\epsilon \\ {u}^{-}=(L+\frac{a}{2})\epsilon +{[[u]]}_{n}\\ {u}^{3}=(L+a)\epsilon +{[[u]]}_{n}\\ {u}^{4}=(\mathrm{2L}+a)\epsilon +{[[u]]}_{n}\end{array} Now let's express the displacements of \text{N2} , \text{M+} , \text{M-} and \text{N3} points based on degrees of freedom X-\mathrm{FEM} . \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}^{2}={a}_{\mathit{y2}}-{b}_{\mathit{y2}}\\ {u}^{3}={a}_{\mathit{y2}}+{b}_{\mathit{y3}}\\ {u}^{+}=\frac{{a}_{\mathit{y2}}+{b}_{\mathit{y2}}}{2}+\frac{{a}_{\mathit{y3}}+{b}_{\mathit{y3}}}{2}\\ {u}^{-}=\frac{{a}_{\mathit{y2}}-{b}_{\mathit{y2}}}{2}+\frac{{a}_{\mathit{y3}}-{b}_{\mathit{y3}}}{2}\end{array} By reversing this system, we obtain: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{a}_{\mathit{y2}}=\frac{{u}_{2}}{2}-\frac{{u}_{3}}{2}+{u}^{+}\\ {b}_{\mathit{y2}}=-\frac{{u}_{2}}{2}-\frac{{u}_{3}}{2}+{u}^{+}\\ {a}_{\mathit{y3}}=-\frac{{u}_{2}}{2}+\frac{{u}_{3}}{2}+{u}^{-}\\ {b}_{\mathit{y3}}=\frac{{u}_{2}}{2}+\frac{{u}_{3}}{2}-{u}^{-}\end{array} The elastic law of the structure gives: \sigma =E\epsilon . The system balance gives \sigma ={t}_{c} . Finally, the cohesive constitutive law provides a relationship between stress and displacement jump. This relationship is different depending on whether the joint remains in its elastic domain or if it damages itself. If the joint remains in the elastic domain, the internal variable \alpha remains constant. We have {t}_{c}=\frac{{\sigma}_{c}}{\alpha}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}\alpha ){〚u〛}_{n} then . The movements of the different points of the structure are then written: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}^{1}=0\\ {u}^{2}=\frac{L}{E}\frac{{\sigma}_{c}}{\alpha}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}\alpha ){\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n}\\ {u}^{+}=\frac{L+\frac{a}{2}}{E}\frac{{\sigma}_{c}}{\alpha}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}\alpha ){\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n}\\ {u}^{-}=(1+\frac{L+\frac{a}{2}}{E}\frac{{\sigma}_{c}}{\alpha}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}\alpha )){\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n}\\ {u}^{3}=(1+\frac{L+a}{E}\frac{{\sigma}_{c}}{\alpha}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}\alpha )){\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n}\\ {u}^{4}=(1+\frac{\mathrm{2L}+a}{E}\frac{{\sigma}_{c}}{\alpha}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}\alpha )){\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n}\end{array} By injecting these expressions into the formulas giving {b}_{\mathrm{y2}} and {b}_{\mathrm{y3}} , we find that {b}_{\mathrm{y2}}={b}_{\mathrm{y3}} . So we have {[[u]]}_{n}={u}^{+}-{u}^{-}={b}_{\mathrm{y2}}+{b}_{\mathrm{y3}}={\mathrm{2.b}}_{\mathrm{y2}} . So the problem is completely determined for the degree of freedom {b}_{\mathrm{y2}} , corresponding to the half jump, and known at any moment thanks to the steering. If the seal remains damaged, the internal variable \alpha becomes equal to the {[[u]]}_{n} displacement jump. We have {t}_{c}={\sigma}_{c}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}{\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n}) then. The movements of the different points of the structure are then written: \lbrace \begin{array}{c}{u}^{1}=0\\ {u}^{2}=\frac{L}{E}{\sigma}_{c}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}{\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n})\\ {u}^{+}=\frac{L+\frac{a}{2}}{E}{\sigma}_{c}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}{\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n})\\ {u}^{-}=\frac{(L+\frac{a}{2})}{E}{\sigma}_{c}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}{\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n})+{[[u]]}_{n}\\ {u}^{3}=\frac{(L+a)}{E}{\sigma}_{c}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}{\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n})+{[[u]]}_{n}\\ {u}^{4}=\frac{(\mathrm{2L}+a)}{E}{\sigma}_{c}\exp(\frac{-{\sigma}_{c}}{{G}_{c}}{\mathrm{〚}u\mathrm{〛}}_{n})+{[[u]]}_{n}\end{array} By injecting these expressions into the formulas giving {b}_{\mathit{y2}} and {b}_{\mathit{y3}} , we find that {b}_{\mathit{y2}}={b}_{\mathit{y3}} . So we have {[[u]]}_{n}={u}^{+}-{u}^{-}={b}_{\mathit{y2}}+{b}_{\mathit{y3}}={\mathrm{2.b}}_{\mathit{y2}} . So the problem is completely determined for the degree of freedom {b}_{\mathit{y2}} , corresponding to the half jump, and known at any moment thanks to the steering. The displacement of all points below the level set is therefore zero and the displacement of all points above the level set is equal to the displacement jump. The cohesion force in the joint is therefore known as an explicit function of the jump itself known at any moment thanks to the steering. v6.03.148 SSNP148 - Calculation of stress intensity factor by stress regularization with ENDO_HETEROGENE v6.03.148 SSNP148 - Calculation of stress intensity factor by stress regularization with ENDO_HETEROGENE Summary: This test calculates the threshold for the propagation of a central crack in a plate of infinite length required by an infinite stress. In this case an analytical solution exists since the stress intensity factor can be calculated. This test gives a comparison between this analytical solution and the value of the stress intensity factor calculated from the regulated stresses (modelling D_PLAN_GRAD_SIGM). The objective of this approach is to validate the calculation method (Modelling D_PLAN_GRAD_SIGM and ENDO_HETEROGENE law. ) for cases where the characteristic length is small in front of the crack size and structure. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The l=\mathrm{6000mm} length domain is h=\mathrm{1000mm} height domain containing an initial vertical crack of \mathrm{2a} length. By symmetry condition, only half of the domain area is modeled (). Illustration 1: Geometry of test case 1.2 Material properties Elasticity parameters: Young's modulus {E}_{1}={20.10}^{9}\mathrm{MPa} , Poisson's ratio {\nu}_{1}=0,25 Law parameters ENDO_HETEROGENE : Elastic limit {\sigma}_{y}={10}^{18}\mathrm{Pa} Weibull m=2 Module Tenacity {K}_{c}=1000{\mathrm{MPa.m}}^{1/2} Sample thickness \mathrm{ep}=\mathrm{1m} \mathrm{GR}=121 seed Non-local model parameter: Characteristic length {l}_{c}=0,02m 1.3 Boundary conditions and loading Vertical displacements on the lower edge of the model are blocked and horizontal displacements on the left edge are imposed on the right edge of the model. The central crack is represented by a vertical band of elements finished broken ( i.e., d=1 ). The stress applied on the right edge varies from 0 to 10\mathit{MPa} during the calculation period, i.e. 1s . Illustration 2: Schematic of boundary conditions 2 reference solution For a central crack of \mathrm{2a} length in a bar of \mathrm{2b} thickness and infinite length required by an infinite {\sigma}_{\infty} constraint, the analytical stress intensity factor can be expressed by the following equation: {K}_{\mathit{Ia}}\approx \sqrt{\frac{\pi a}{\cos(\frac{\pi a}{\mathrm{2b}})}} Since in the case treated the crack is pressed in I mode, a stress intensity factor equivalent can be introduced for a given characteristic length [1]: {K}_{\mathrm{IIc}}=\frac{5\pi }{6\Gamma \frac{3}{4}}.\stackrel{ˉ}{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{Ip}}}\sqrt{\pi {l}_{c}} with \stackrel{ˉ}{{\sigma}_{\mathrm{Ip}}} the maximum main regulated stress at crack tip. To compare the numerical results with the analytical solution the \mathit{RKI}={K}_{{\mathit{Il}}_{c}}/{K}_{\mathit{la}} parameter is introduced. The above 2 equations were introduced into the command file of test case via table manipulations. The value of the regulated stress at the crack tip is extracted. The values of the analytical and numerical stress intensity factor are calculated in the command file. The ratio between the two values ( \mathit{RKI} ) is then calculated. This ratio was tested via the TEST_TABLE command. 3 Bibliographical references 1. Granet, Seyedi (2010) Probabilistic modelling of damage to geological barriers for deep storage of nuclear waste. Final report of BRGM in the framework of the ENDOSTON collaboration. Note HT64-2010-01265 2. Guy, N., Seyedi, D. M. and Hild, F., (2010). Hydro-mechanical modelling of geological CO2 storage and the study of possible caprock fracture mechanisms. Georisk. 4 Modelling A 4.1 Modelling characteristics The top half of the domain is meshed in elements triangular at 6 nodes. The mesh has 16602 TRIA6 triangles and 223 SEG2 triangles. The size of the central crack, a, is equal to 0,3571m . 1 time of 1s is modelled. 4.2 Results The horizontal displacements DX and the damage criterion (internal variable V1) are plotted on the figures and respectively at the end of \mathrm{1s} . Illustration 3: Horizontal Movements \mathit{DX} , t=\mathrm{1s} Illustration 4: Damage variable ( \mathit{V1} ), t=\mathrm{1s} 4.3 Test values The stress intensity value is tested via TEST_FONCTION. | Function | Instant | Reference value | Tolerance (%) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | \mathit{RKI}={K}_{{\mathit{Il}}_{c}}/{K}_{\mathit{la}} | 1 | 1 | 1.E-2 | 5 Summary of the results This test allows the threshold to be calculated for the propagation of a central crack in a plate of infinite length which is required by an infinite stress. We can compare the results obtained with an analytical solution: the results correspond. This test allows the validation of the D_PLAN_GRAD_SIGM model and the ENDO_HETEROGENE law.

v6.03.166 SSNP166 - Three-point bending beam v6.03.166 SSNP166 - Three-point bending beam Summary: The study of this problem allows to characterize the energy required to propagate a crack in a concrete beam. It allows to validate the constitutive law CZM_EXP_MIX by comparison with the experience of the overall Force-Movement behavior of a beam cut on two simple supports. It corresponds to one of the experimental essays of Per-Erik Peterson's thesis [bib1]. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry To validate the CZM_EXP_MIX cohesive law more specific to quasi-fragile materials, a concrete-cut beam subjected to 3-point bending is modelled, using experimental data from P.-E. Peterson's thesis [bib1]. This trial is one of the most frequent experimental references to validate models of surface or volume damage of concrete. A 2m length, 200\mathit{mm} height and 50\mathit{mm} thickness beam, cut in its middle on 100\mathit{mm} (half the height of the beam) is in single support on both ends. v6.03.176 SSNP176 – modellings D_PLAN_INCO_* type of near-incompressible elasticity v6.03.176 SSNP176 – modellings D_PLAN_INCO_ type of near-incompressible elasticity Summary: The objective of this test is to provide additional modellings D_PLAN_INCO_ verification on a model known to be analytical solution. It consists of two modellings: - Modelling A: D_PLAN_INCO_UPO Modelling test (so on linear elements) - Modelling B: Test on modellings D_PLAN_INCO_UP and D_PLAN_INCO_UPG(onquadratic elements) 1 Reference problem The Reference problem is inspired by an article by F. Auricchio et al . [1] which proposes an analytical solution. 1.1 Geometry A square of dimension 2m\times 2m is considered. v6.03.179 SSNP179 – Cook Membrane in Large Plastic Deformities v6.03.179 SSNP179 – Cook Membrane in Large Plastic Deformities Summary: The objective of this test is to provide additional verification of modellings of incompressible type on the problem of Cook's membrane which is a problem very often used to test numerical methods in the literature. 1 Reference problem The problem is the result of an article by J.C. Simo and F . Armero [1] . 1.1 Geometry The geometry can be viewed on the figure and will be used for all modellings. Figure 1.1-1: Géométrie de la membrane Coordinate of node A(48.60) and node C (24.30). 1.2 Material properties The material is elastic: - Elasticity module: E=206,9\mathit{GPa} - Poisson's ratio: \nu =0,29 The plasticity model is a Von-Measurement model with linear nonlinear hardening isotropic. The hardening curve is in the form: R(p)={\sigma}_{y,0}+Hp+({\sigma}_{y,\infty }-{\sigma}_{y,0})\ast (1-{\mathrm{e}}^{-\delta p}) - Elastic limit: {\sigma}_{y,0}=450\mathit{MPa} - Hardening limit: {\sigma}_{y,\infty }=715\mathit{MPa} - Saturation parameter: \delta =16.93 - Nutrient setting: H=129.2 The nut-cut curve was finely tabulated to properly describe the curve with the TRACTION key word. The deformation model used is GDEF_LOG. 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The left side of the membrane ( \mathit{DX}=\mathit{DY}=0 ) is clamped and a vertical surface force applied to the right side of the membrane ( \mathit{FY}=0,3125\mathit{kN}/\mathit{mm}\mathrm{²} ) is applied. 1.4 Extension to 3D The extension to 3D is obtained by extruding in the z direction (thickness 1\mathit{mm} ). Furthermore, the displacements according to DZ are blocked to return to the solution in flat deformations. 2 reference solution 2.1 Quantities and reference results The numerical solution of the article [1] gives: | Location | Instant | Component (DEPL) | Value | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Nœud A en (48,60) | t=1s | DX | -6.23907\mathit{mm} | | Nœud A en (48,60) | t=1s | DY | 7.00031\mathit{mm} | 2.2 Uncertainties about the solution The solution comes from another calculation code on a very fine mesh. 2.3 Bibliographic reference [1] Geometrically nonlinear enhanced train mixed methods and the method of incompatible modes , J.C. v6.03.180 SSNP180 - SCIENCE test Modelling with ENDO_LOCA_TC v6.03.180 SSNP180 - SCIENCE test Modelling with ENDO_LOCA_TC Summary: The constitutive law ENDO_LOCA_TC is validated by SCIENCE experimental tests. Two tests are modelled: a reinforced concrete beam in 4-point bending (test #1) and the same 4-point bending beam after heating at 170°C of its lower face (test #4). The beams have 5 m × 0.4 m × 1 m dimensions. The Modelling is D_PLAN (2D) where half of the test piece is used thanks to symmetry conditions. The steels (longitudinal frames and pins) are represented by bars and the restraint steel-beton is perfect. For concrete, the ENDO_LOCA_TC damage law is coupled with viscous regularization to improve robustness and reduce calculation times. In fine, the simulations give close results of the difference tests at the moment of plasification of the steels. For more results, a R&D note is available: 6125-1723-2023-00259. 1 Introduction ENDO_LOCA_TC was developed in 2022 as part of the NGC project. The SCIENCE test Modelling was done in 2022-2023 and the R&D note 6125-1723-2023-00259 summarizes the results obtained with different constitutive laws and configurations. The "High performance" case is given below. The objective of this validation case is to enrich the V&V file for this law. By agilers, it provides an example of the use of the law coupled with the viscous regularization to improve convergence and robustness of the calculation. 1.1 SCIENCE tests The European SCIENCE project (2013-2017) was designed to produce a dimensioning guide for the Steel-Concrete Structure (SCS) construction. The partners have conducted numerous laboratory tests to characterize the behaviour of the SCS but also on conventional reinforced concrete beams, with a view to comparison. The originality of this campaign lies in the fact that beams have been solicited by not only mechanical but also thermomechanical loads. This validation case focuses on the beam of 5 x 5 x 0.4 m. It consists of a concrete C33/37. It contains 2 sheets of 9 longitudinal frames of diameter 31.7 mm in B500B steel and pins of the same steel of diameter 11.9 mm. Illustration of the test piece's fittings Illustration of the railing in a section of the test piece The two tests selected shall have the following characteristics: - A mechanical (test 1) 4 point bending test in which displacement is imposed near the ends of the beam at a speed of 2 mm/min. The test bench is presented below; the supports are drawn in green, the cylinders in red. Illustration of the loading of the mechanical test No. 1 - A thermomechanical test (test 4) in which the beam is subjected to a bending preload of 4 points of 21 kN per cylinder in order to rigidize the built + test piece and then to a heating of the surface between the supports until it reaches about 170 °C and, finally, a bending test 4 points in the image of test 1. Illustration of the load of thermomechanical test No. 4 2 Reference modelling 2.1 Mesh A 2D Modelling of flat deformations was preferred to allow very fine spatial discretization without overly penalising performance. Due to the symmetry of geometry and loading, only half of the beam is modelled (therefore artificially a symmetrical distribution of damage is required). For modellings A and B, the mesh of the concrete domain consists of 1,368 mesh cells rectangular 3 to 4 cm with quadratic functions and 9 point Gauss integration scheme, V6.03.180-fig-mesh 2D. For C and D modelling, the mesh is linear, and the integration scheme is 4 Gauss points. mesh of the beam in 2D The longitudinal (black) and pins (violet and yellow) are represented by elements bars of the same size as the adjacent but linearly shaped mesh cells 2D concrete. The steel density per rebar is 7,103 mm2/m beam depth corresponding to 9 bars of diameter 31.7 mm over a metre depth. In this 2D model, which is based on an mesh whose length is the metre, the (fictive) depth is one unit length, i.e. one metre. To obtain a density of stiffness in tension identical to that of the actual rebar, an equivalent bar of section 7 103 mm2 must therefore be introduced into the 2D model. For the pins (14 bars of diameter 11.9 mm for a beam depth of 1 m), the steel density is 1,557 mm2 / m. Following the same reasoning as previously, the equivalent bar to be introduced into the 2D Modelling, is shown to be a squared-section, and the 2D-section is shown to be equal to that of section 2D, thus the 5-section is shown to be equal to that of section 2D. The only difference between the #1 test and the #4 test at the mesh level is the use of a linear mesh that includes only concrete for thermal calculation before performing a mechanical calculation chained to the previous mesh. The word "chained" indicates that the mechanical calculation includes at the input a thermal field from a previous calculation. The calculations are performed sequentially. 2.2 Boundary conditions and loads 2.2.1 Test 1 Test 1 is a "simple" 4-point bending test. The difficulty lies in the definition of boundary conditions and the application of the load. It was decided to control the average displacement on a line, consisting here of two mesh cells, that is 5 nodes (because the finished elements are quadratic). The kinematic relationship is applied: \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^NDY(k)=U_{imposé} ; N=5 where DY(k) is the displacement in the y (vertical) direction of the node d-indice k. In the case of the supports, U_imp=0; for the cylinders, U_imp=v t. The test lasts TFIN= 1.85 hours and the displacement at the verin is 200mm. The simulation is conducted only at the moment of platification of the steels, up to the moment 1400s corresponds to a required displacement of 35 mm at the cylinder level. We must not forget the symmetry condition on the right edge of the test piece where DX = 0 and the own weight of the beam. the V6.03.180-fig-CL_ test1 synthesizes the boundary conditions and loads of test number 1. Illustration of boundary conditions and the loading of the mechanical test (test n°1) 2.2.2 Test #4 The thermomechanical test simulation is performed in two stages: first a purely thermal calculation, followed by a mechanical calculation with the previously calculated temperature field (linking) input. The thermal calculation is performed with the load illustrated in V6.03.180-fig-CLTH_ test4: Illustration of thermal loading during thermomechanical test (test No. 4) The initial temperature is set at 25°C. The thermal boundary conditions are as follows: On the plane of symmetry a zero flow is imposed. On the lower side outside the heating zone, on the left end of the beam and on the upper side, convection exchange is possible with ambient air remaining at a temperature of 25°C. The convection coefficient chosen is h = 4 W/m2/K. On the heated part, in the absence of a document detailing this load, the following ramp is imposed (V6.03.180-fig-comparison_temperature): | Instant | Temperature in °C | | --- | --- | | 0 | 25 | | 3600 | 120 | | 7200 | 140 | | 10800 | 150 | | 21600 | 160 | | 32400 | 170 | | 36000 | 170 | Comparison between measurement and applied thermal loading (test #4) It should be noted that a nonlinear thermal calculation is carried out to integrate energy consumption by changing the phase of water at 100°C. The impact on the temperatures inside the beam is not negligible even if the impact on the mechanics is very limited. Thus, enthalpy is defined by: \beta(T)= \begin{cases}\int_{0}^{T} \rho C_{p}(u)du & \text { avec} & T 100°C\end{cases} With \rho the density of concrete, \rho {C}_{p} the density heat at constant pressure, L_{eau} the latent heat of water vaporization (2 257 kJ/kg) and m_{eau} the weight of water per cubic metre of concrete (136 kg). On the practical level, the nonlinear thermal calculation is based on the β(T) enthalpy data to be reported under DEFI_MATERIAU THER_NL. After , \beta(T) enthalpie has a discontinuity equal to the latent heat when L_{eau} m_{eau} β(T) = 100 °C. To facilitate convergence of the nonlinear thermal calculation, it was chosen to spread this discontinuity affine between 95°C and 105°C. In terms of mechanical loading: Mechanical preload in bending 4 points of 21 kN per cylinder, at a uniform temperature of 25°C. Temperature rise in the lower wall for eight hours and then maintain the set temperature during the 4 point bending test. It should be noted that for 8 hours the displacement of the cylinders is blocked at its value at the end of preload. Flexion 4 points by imposing a constantly increasing displacement of the cylinder from the preload position. The test is conducted at a speed of 1.92 mm/min. The measured displacements at the support level are on average 230 mm at the end of the test (i.e. at t = 10 hours). Taking into account own weight As in Test 1, the displacements imposed on the supports and cylinders follow. Furthermore, the symmetry condition on the right edge of the test piece (DX = 0) is applied. 2.3 constitutive law The reinforcements consist of an B500B steel. This paragraph focuses on the results with a comparison to the experimental data. 3.1 Overall response The amount of interest that is the subject of the trial / calculation comparison is the time of effort from which steels plasticize, i.e. 1,144 kN.m in the trial. The experimental and numerical responses are confronted V6.03.180-fig-test1_moment_deplacement: Test #1: Answer moment vs. Move The moment of plasification is very well predicted, with only 2% d-difference (1 163 kN.m vs. 1 144 kN.m). On the other hand, the numerical response is a little more rigid than the test, which results in a difference on the displacement of 30% (29.38 vs. 41.89 mm). Some elements explanation has been considered, but not yet conclusive: Uncertainties on material parameters Restraint steel Modelling – concrete (perfect grip) Modelling of support conditions Displacement measurement uncertainties (stiffness of the support and test machine) The reason that seems most relevant at the moment is the modelling of pins that drastically alter the overall response depending on their presence or their restraint with the frames. 3.2 Damage mapping For the damage distribution, presented in V6.03.180-fig-test1_carto_traction, it is consistent with a 4-point bending test with a strong damage around the upper steel, characteristic of a steel/beton detachment, then a development of damage from the upper to the lower representative part of the development of vertical cracks. This element being of degree 1, the total mechanical deformation will be constant in the element. The thermal field imposing linear deformation in the element will require a dilation coefficient and a thermal gradient large enough to make the total mechanical deformation sensitive to the imposed thermal field. v6.03.306 SSNP306 - Validation of the criterion for flaming by selective search of own values v6.03.306 SSNP306 - Validation of the criterion for flaming by selective search of own values Summary: This test allows the validation of the generalization of the flaming criterion (loss of solution uniqueness, presence of bifurcation) for mixed formulation models. The new criterion, which is written as a problem with the own sub-contraint values, is validated for the Modelling of non-local GRAD_VARI damage. The smallest modes of the GRAD_VARI formulation are compared with those of the local Modelling in the case of a homogeneous study. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Theoretical framework The usual flashing criterion results in a sign check of the smallest value of K\delta u=\mu \delta u tangent matrix. If \mu \le 0 the mechanical problem solution is no longer unique. For mixed formulations, the modes of the Lagrange coefficients must be eliminated, which leads us back to a problem with the stress modes. K(\begin{array}{}\delta u\\ \delta \lambda \end{array})=\mu (\begin{array}{}\delta u\\ 0\end{array}) is the new flashing criterion for mixed Modelling. In the case of GRAD_VARI the criterion is even more restrictive, as the constitutive law must also be taken into account to obtain physical modes. This must be possible to generalize to other types of modellings. The criterion is written as a problem with generalised own values: K(\begin{array}{}\delta u\\ \delta \alpha \\ \delta \lambda \end{array})=\mu (\begin{array}{}\delta u\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}) new flashing criterion for GRAD_VARI Modelling. This gives us two constraints of equality in the search for the moving mode. The first allows us to check the material constitutive law and the second equals the disturbances of damage to the nodes with that calculated locally at Gauss points. We validate the new flashing criterion by comparing the smallest modes of the GRAD_VARI formulation with those of the local Modelling in the case of a homogeneous study. Note: Technically to achieve this, the new RIGI_GEOM and DDL_EXCLUS commands have been added to the CRIT_STAB operator. In this case, they are used as follows: CRIT_STAB = _F( RIGI_GEOM = 'NON', # Required to then call DDL_EXCLUS DDL_EXCLUS = ('VARI','LAG_GV')) 1.2 Geometry Figure 1 : Problem representation in two quadratic mesh cellss 1.3 Material properties Damage law: material ENDO_FRAGILE Elastic characteristics: - E=3\cdot {10}^{4}\text{Pa} - \nu =0.25 Characteristics related to the damage law: - Elasticity limit: {\sigma}^{Y}=3.0\text{Pa} - Moisture pent : {E}^{T}=-1.95\cdot {10}^{3}\text{Pa} - Non-local features: {L}_{c}=1.0 ; r=100. 1.4 Boundary conditions and loads clamped support : Impaired \mathrm{DY}=0. on the bottom horizontal stop ( y=0. ) and \mathrm{DX}=0. on the left extreme node ( x=y=0. ). See Figure 1. Load 1 : {U}_{1} forced displacement on top horizontal stop ( y=1. ): \mathrm{DY}={2.10}^{-6}\text{t} Charge 2 : {U}_{2} displacement imposed on all nodes coordinates y=0.5 : \mathrm{DY}={1.10}^{-6}\text{t} 2 reference solution The same study is done in local and non-local. The smallest tangential operator values are compared with the standard local blazing criterion (which will be taken as a reference) and with the new non-local criterion. v6.03.505 SSNP505 - Multi-cracked bi-crack plate with X-FEM v6.03.505 SSNP505 - Multi-cracked bi-crack plate with X-FEM Summary: The objective of this test is to validate the multi-crack approach with X-FEM and junction. A flat deformation plate is required in bi-crack and shear. Eight cracks are introduced in the centre of the plate, two of which are joined. RAFF_XFEM is used to refine around crack bottoms and CALC_G to calculate stress intensity factors. A first test allows the contactless approach to be validated by comparing stress intensity factors with a semi-analytic solution. Then, in a second test, it is shown that the addition of contact, which corrects certain interpenetrations, influences the results. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A square plate on the 20m side is considered in flat deformations, centred in the (X,Y) marker. The cracks are defined by the A to J and A' to J' points, the coordinates of which are given in Table 1. | Items | X | Y | | Items | X | Y | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A | −3,0851 | 0,75 | | A' | 3,08512 | −0,75 | | B | 0,50000 | 1,13327 | | B' | −0,5000 | −0,3667 | | C | 0,20309 | 1,55730 | | C' | −0,2031 | 0,05730 | | D | −2,1454 | 1,09202 | | D' | 2,14543 | −0,4080 | | E | −1,3794 | 0,44923 | | E' | 1,37939 | −1,0508 | | F | −3,0851 | −0,25 | | F' | 3,08512 | −1,75 | | G | −2,3780 | 0,45711 | | G' | 2,37802 | −1,0429 | | H | −1,3794 | 1,09202 | | H' | 1,37939 | −0,4080 | | I | −0,5134 | 1,59202 | | I' | 0,51336 | 0,09202 | | J | −0,4397 | 0,79125 | | J' | 0,43969 | −0,7087 | Table 1: Coordinates of cracking points. MOËS "Large sliding contact long branched discontinuities xith X-FEM", rereading, 2012. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics The cracks are introduced with X-FEM using GROUP_MA_FISS and GROUP_MA_FOND operators' DEFI_FISS_XFEM operands. v6.03.507 SSNP507 - Stability of an undrained clay slope on the low foundation v6.03.507 SSNP507 - Stability of an undrained clay slope on the low foundation Summary: This test analyses the stability of a slope composed of undrained clay constructed on a weak foundation. The stability factor is calculated by the method (in English) CALC_STAB_PENTE macro-command. Undrained behavior, characterized by the significant volume compressibility of water, is nevertheless represented in this test by Annulment of the friction angle of Mohr-Coulomb law in total stress. Depending on the relationship between the cohesion of the slope and the foundation, one distinguishes two break-up mechanisms and a transitional point, corresponding to the different trends in the variation of the safety factor. By comparing the results of all the break-up mechanisms written in the literature, This test is used to validate the SRM method in the CALC_STAB_PENTE macro-command. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry and mesh Geometry of the slope studied The stability of a clay slope on a weak foundation is studied, whose geometry is shown in fig1-geom-ssnp507. The geometric parameter H is fixed at 3 m in this test case, which has no influence on the stability result since the cohesion of clay is assumed to be correlated with slope size. 1.2 Material properties Table 1 : Ownership of slope materials | | Foundation | Stage | | --- | --- | --- | | Density \rho (kg/m3) | 3000 | | | Young's modulus E (MPa) | 100 | | | Poisson's ratio \nu | 0,3 | | | Cohesion Force c (kPa) | 0.25\lambda\rho gH | 0.25\rho gH | | \psi dilatance angle (deg) | 0 | | | Friction angle \varphi (deg) | 0 | | The mechanical properties of the materials of the model are presented in Table 1. To simulate the undrained behaviour of clay, the angles of friction and dilatance I'm not good. So we find Tresca's criterion describing the soil's shear strength. The foundation weakness is described by the \lambda parameter defined as the relationship between the foundation cohesions and the slope: \lambda =\dfrac{{c}_{u2}}{{c}_{u1}} 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The boundary conditions applied to the model are: - Bottom of foundation clamped (DX=0, DY=0), and the vertical sides normally blocked (DX=0). The safety factor was calculated by both the SRM method ("strength reduction method") based on the elements method and traditional method assuming the sliding circles [2]. The results of both methods are consistent. 2.2 Baseline By varying the \lambda parameter between 0.25 and 4, the variation of the safety factor is traced according to the foundation-pent ratio, as illustrated in fig2-FS-varie. In the case of a weak foundation, the sliding circle deepens in the foundation so that the slope slides together with the foundation. The safety factor is increasing proportionally. The transition state corresponds to \lambda =1.5 , from which the security factor no longer depends on the ownership of the foundation. The non-regression results are ensured by testing the nodes two-way movements of the edge, H and I . These nodes positions are slightly different depending on the modellings, so you should not try to compare them between modellings. This test in curved geometry highlights the usefulness of certain matching parameters such as: - smoothing: this is a process of modification of normals that are used to write contact conditions. Although sphere meshes are symmetrical, in practice there is always a slight offset on the last point of the contact surface. Smoothing of normals allows us to find symmetry. This parameter is also useful for improving the geometric convergence of modellings using coarse meshes (this is the case of modellings \mathrm{2D} of this test). - Nodal pairing or average normal (slave master): not used in general, these two pairing options, such as smoothing, allow to find the symmetry of the problem. Modelling A where contact is replaced by a unilateral restraint also highlights the very important role played by geometric updating on the accuracy of the stresses. Indeed, this Modelling allows to remove the geometric non-linearity of this problem, so it provides an reference solution . Thus when comparing the results obtained on the same \mathrm{3D} problem by the modellings A, I and J, we find that: - the displacement values obtained by model I have differences up to 4% compared to the other two modellings - modellings A and J find the same Hertz pressure, while model I finds 10% lower pressure - in model I the geometric criterion is met to the nearest 5% whereas it is met to 1% in model J It therefore seems important to satisfy the geometric criterion as best as possible to obtain the best possible precision on the stress values.

v6.04.109 SSNV109 - Evaluation of cracking time (corrosion stress initiation) by BabY (Barbier-Bystricky) v6.04.109 SSNV109 - Evaluation of cracking time (corrosion stress initiation) by BabY (Barbier-Bystricky) Summary: The objective of this test is to capitalize the method of determining cracking time by the BabY (Barbier-Bystricky) model. The cracking time corresponds to the stress corrosion time. The cracking time obtained by the BaBy model is compared to the cracking time obtained by the index model. Model A proposes a determination of crack time by a simple post-processing of a static nonlinear calculation (decoupled method). 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A square plate of 50 mm side is considered, the top of which is dug by a disc of radius 40 mm, the centre of which is 80 mm from the bottom of the plate. The geometry is illustrated in the figure below. The top of the plate (line \mathit{CD} ) is in contact with the corrosive medium. The case is treated in axisymmetric, which amounts to considering a cylinder whose upper face is dug by a sphere. 1.2 Material properties The material is L-Alliage 600 at 350°C. Its behaviour is considered nonlinear visco-elastic, isotropic. The elastic properties are: - E=200000\mathit{MPa} - \nu =0,3 Visco-elastic behaviour is modelled by a Lemaitre law, whose parameters are: - n=3,77 - m=4,26 - K(T)=\mathrm{17,67.}\exp(\frac{47500}{8,31(T+273,15)}) with T in °C. For T=350°C , K=170182 The parameters to be entered in the DEFI_MATERIAU operator under the factor keyword LEMAITRE U4.43.01 are n , 1/m and 1/K . 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads As the case is axisymmetric, the x axis displacement on the \mathit{AC} side is blocked. To block rigid modes, the y axis displacement on the point A is blocked. The load consists of applying \mathit{BD} on the side of 0,1\mathit{mm} a displacement of 0,1\mathit{mm} on the x axis, gradually up to t=1h , and then the load is kept constant up to t=1000h . 2 reference solution 2.1 Quantities tested The quantities of interest are the cracking times obtained by the index method and by the BaBy (Barbier-Bystricky) model [1]. The crack time (in hours) of the index model is given by the following expression: {t}_{f}=\frac{10000}{{i}_{T}.{i}_{M}.{i}_{\sigma}} où - {i}_{T}={\mathrm{9,49.10}}^{15.}\exp(\frac{-22000}{T+273,15}) with T in °C. For T=350°C , {i}_{T}=4,41 - {i}_{M}=1 - {i}_{\sigma}={\mathrm{2,44.10}}^{-11}{\sigma}^{4} , with \sigma the largest main constraint (expressed in \mathit{MPa} ) The cracking time of the BaBy model is obtained by solving a coupled mechanical-corrosion problem. A simplified version of the problem resolution consists of decoupled equations and treating corrosion equations only in post-processing of a nonlinear mechanical calculation. This is the strategy adopted in model A. From the \sigma stress field, post-processing evolution of the p cumulative plastic deformation and {c}_{h} corrosive concentration is determined: \begin{array}{c}\dot{p}={(\frac{{\Vert \sigma \Vert }_{\mathit{VM}}}{K(T)(1-{c}_{h})})}^{n}.{p}^{-n/m}\\ \dot{{c}_{h}}=\frac{3}{2}\beta \dot{p}\frac{⟨1/3\mathit{tr}\sigma ⟩}{{\Vert \sigma \Vert }_{\mathit{VM}}}\end{array} then the cracking time is the time such as {c}_{h}({t}_{f})=1 . The \beta parameter is a material parameter identified from a creep experiment alone. This is \beta =889,5 . 2.2 Bibliographical references 1. Barbier, P. Bystricky, Application of the BaBy Model to Corrosion-Distributing Time Forecasts under Primary-Colored Alliage 600, Note EDF R&D HT-2C/97/048/A, March 1998 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics AXIS modelling is used. 3.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh is composed of quadratic mesh cells and is presented in the figure below. 3.3 Tested quantities and results The crack time is determined in each node of the line in contact with the corrosive medium. The crack times obtained are plotted according to the c coordinate in the figure below. The {t}_{f} crack time is tested at point C obtained by the index models and by the BaBy model. | Identification | Reference type | Reference value | | --- | --- | --- | | {t}_{f} to point C - Index model (in h) | 'NON_REGRESSION' | 94, 5785 | | {t}_{f} to point C - BaBy model (in h) | 'NON_REGRESSION' | 20,98 | 4 Summary of the results This test allows capitalization of the time-to-crack method by the BabY (Barbier-Bystricky) model. The crack time is the stress corrosion time. The crack time obtained by the BaBy model is compared to the crack time obtained by the index model.

v6.04.115 SSNV115 - Corrugated sheet in nonlinear behaviour v6.04.115 SSNV115 - Corrugated sheet in nonlinear behaviour Summary: This problem validates the constitutive law elastoplastic with Von criterion isotropic linear nutring for modellings R3.07.03 plates and R3.07.04 volume hulls where membrane and bending effects are also important. The geometry of the model respects 3 constraints: - the thickness is low to respect the thin shell hypothesis, - the problem must be flat deformation according to \mathrm{Oz} , - \mathrm{Oy} curvature is chosen to make both "flexion" and "membrane" meaningful. There is no analytical solution. Modelling A (2D D_PLAN) serves as a reference. The test has no physical significance and the values of the displacements obtained are very important in relation to the dimensions of the initial structure. This test is therefore more a test of non-regression and of inter-modellings comparison. The results (on displacement) differ from 2 to 3% between the modellings plate and the 2D reference. This difference reduces to 0.5% between the modellings volume shells and the 2D reference. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Characteristics of the hull: - h=0.05\mathrm{mm} thickness , - radius of curvature R=1\mathrm{mm} , - width L=\mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{CD}=0.1\mathrm{mm} , - position of the first curvature centre: , - the \alpha angle is chosen so that the top surface of the hull at point X is (y=0) , i.e. aligned with A and C , - position of second curvature centre: . 1.2 Material properties E=\mathrm{2 000}\mathrm{MPa} \nu =0.3 A constitutive law elasto-plastic with Von criterion isotropic linear hardening material is used: {\sigma}_{y}=100\mathrm{MPa} {E}_{T}:200\mathrm{MPa} . 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads - on \mathrm{AB} : clamped support: \mathrm{DX}=\mathrm{DY}=\mathrm{DZ}=\mathrm{DRX}=\mathrm{DRY}=\mathrm{DRZ}=0 , - on the whole hull: flat deformation according to \mathrm{Oz} or \mathrm{DZ}=\mathrm{DRX}=\mathrm{DRY}=0 , - on \mathrm{CD} : linear force (per unit length \mathrm{Oz} ) according to \mathrm{Ox} given by: {f}_{x}=50N/\mathrm{mm} It is equivalent to a pressure of {p}_{X}={f}_{x}/h=100\mathrm{MPa} exerted on the side \mathrm{CD} , - the load is applied gradually to the structure.
