v6.04.193 SSNV193 – Contact with static macroelements v6.04.193 SSNV193 – Contact with static macroelements Summary: The objective of this test is to validate the use of static macro-elements with unilateral contact in CONTINUE and DISCRETE formulation. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A cube on the 1m side is considered to be placed on a rigid plane. 1.2 Material properties The material is elastic isotropic with properties of: - E=209000\mathit{MPa} - \nu =0.3 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads On the upper side, a vertical displacement of -\mathrm{0.1m} is imposed. The rigid plane is clamped and a unilateral condition of contact between the cube and the rigid plane is imposed. 2 reference solution 2.1 Method of calculation The calculation is a calculation of non-regression between different situations. The reference calculation is done without static macro-element. 2.2 Quantities and reference results The displacement on the lower side of the cube, in the middle and the contact reaction is tested. Vertical displacement is necessarily zero (initial contact, rigid plane). 2.3 Uncertainties about the solution The displacement is a analytical solution. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics 3D modelling is used. 3.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh contains 1128 elements of type HEXA8. - The first calculation is made with contact in CONTINUE formulation and without macro-element; - The second calculation is made with contact in CONTINUE formulation and the cube is represented by a macro-element; - The third calculation is made with contact in DISCRETE formulation and the cube is represented by a macro-element; 3.3 Tested quantities and results The displacement and vertical reaction of point A is tested. First calculation (without macro-element) – Contact in CONTINUE formulation – Reference | Identification | Reference type | Reference value | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Point A - \mathit{DZ} | 'ANALYTIQUE' | 0 | 1.00E-012 | | Point A - \mathit{RZ} | 'NON_REGRESSION' | -1.380156E+009 | 1.00E-006 | Second calculation (with macro-element) – Contact in CONTINUE formulation | Identification | Reference type | Reference value | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Point A - \mathit{DZ} | 'ANALYTIQUE' | 0 | 1.00E-012 | | Point A - \mathit{RZ} | 'AUTRE_ASTER' | -1.380156E+009 | 1.00E-006 | Third calculation (with macro-element) – Contact in DISCRETE formulation | Identification | Reference type | Reference value | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Point A - \mathit{DZ} | 'ANALYTIQUE' | 0 | 1.00E-012 | | Point A - \mathit{RZ} | 'AUTRE_ASTER' | -1.380156E+009 | 1.00E-006 | 3.4 Remarks The three calculations give exactly the same results. 4 Summary of the results This test case shows the possibility of using static macro-elements to represent the rigidity of a structure subjected to unilateral contact, whatever the formulation of the latter (continuous or discreet). There are no restrictions on the conditions of use, potential contact surfaces may belong to the macro-elements. The complete model comparison/macro-elements static shows that the results are identical, both in motion and force.

v6.04.195 SSNV195 - Multi-crack bar with X-FEM v6.04.195 SSNV195 - Multi-crack bar with X-FEM Summary The purpose of this test is to test and validate the X-FEM functionality for multi-fabricated \mathrm{2D} and \mathrm{3D} structures. Overall, the SSNV173 V6.04.173 and SSNV182 V6.04.182 test essentials are re-established for a multi-frusted structure this time. This test involves a parallelepipedic bar, with the middle section clamped, having two cracks that cross it completely (we will then speak of interfaces), placed symmetrically on one side and the other of section clamped. The bar is subject to forced displacements, resulting in the total opening of the interfaces and the separation of the structure into three parts when pressed in traction, or the appearance of contact pressure when the pressure is compression. Two types of interfaces are considered, horizontal (one stage of elements is cut) and inclined (several stages of elements are cut, to test the proper management of the elements undercutting when several cracks are present in the structure. The case of an \mathrm{2D} plate with two interfaces is also studied. 1 Reference problem 1.1 3D geometry The structure is a straight parallelepiped square-based and healthy. The dimensions of the bar (see[Figure1.1-1)) are: \mathit{LX}=5m , \mathit{LY}=5m and \mathit{LZ}=50m . It has no cracks. The interfaces will be introduced by level functions (level set rated \text{LN} for normal level set) directly into the command file using DEFI_FISS_XFEM U4.82.08 operator. Initially, the interfaces will be horizontal, each one in the middle of the lower and upper blocks compared to clamped section (see [Figure1.1-2]). The equations of level functions for the two horizontal interfaces are therefore: \text{LN1}=Z-\text{LZ}/4 éq 1.1-1 \text{LN2}=Z-3\cdot \text{LZ}/4 éq 1.1-2 No tangential level is required since the TYPE_DISCONTINUITE='INTERFACE' key word is used, which allows a structure to be completely cut into three parts. 1) 2) Figure 1.1. Bar geometry and crack positioning For Modelling C, both interfaces will be tilted to rotations along the \mathit{OX} axis (see []). On this occasion, the correct functioning of X-FEM post-processing operators, which have undergone modifications during the transition to multi-cracking, is also tested. 1.2 2D geometry The structure is a healthy rectangle. The dimensions of the bar (see [Figure 1.2-1)) are: \mathit{LX}=5m and \mathit{LY}=50m . It has no cracks. The interfaces will be introduced by level set functions directly in the command file using DEFI_FISS_XFEM U4.82.08. By analogy with the \mathrm{3D} case, the interfaces are present in the media of both parts of the plate, separated by the line of clamped support (see Figure 1.2-a). The corresponding equations of the level functions are: \text{LN1}=\text{Y}-\text{LY}/4 éq 1.2-1 \text{LN2}=Y-3\cdot \text{LY}/4 éq 1.2-3 No tangential level is required since the TYPE_DISCONTINUITE='INTERFACE' key word is used, which allows a structure to be completely cut into three parts. 1) 2) Figure 1.2. Geometry of plate and position of crack 1.3 Material properties Young's modulus : E=100\mathit{MPa} Poisson's ratio : \nu =0.0 1.4 Boundary conditions and loads The nodes of the mid-bar surface is clamped (see [Figure 1.1-2] and [Figure 1.2-2]) while the movement is imposed on the lower and upper surfaces. The first step is to show the possibility of separating a structure into 3 parts following the introduction of two interfaces (the required displacements will open the interfaces) and in a second step we will prove the inclusion of the contact on the lips of two interfaces (the required displacements will close the interfaces). 2 Modelling A: Opening Horizontal Interfaces 2.1 Mesh characteristics Figure 2.1-1: Le maillage de la modélisation A The structure is discretized using elements HEXA8 finished. In the three directions of the selected reference system, 2\times 2\times 10 elements is then used, with a total of 40 elements finished (see []) The number of elements stages in the Z direction was chosen to avoid the enrichment of the same element by both interfaces. Indeed, in the implementation of the multi-cracking (see manual) you avoid approaching two cracks at less than 4 elements healthy in order to avoid conflicts when managing enriched degrees of freedom. Thus, by choosing 10 floors, you can both impose boundary conditions on the extreme mesh cells in the usual way and avoid that the characteristic enrichments of the X-FEM touch each other. The first interface will be introduced in the middle of the third floor while the second in the middle of the eighth. 2.2 boundary conditions In order to open both interfaces and to prevent rigid body movements, nodes from the median surface is embedded: GROUP_NO=SURFMED : DX = 0, DY = 0 et DZ = 0 For nodes belonging to the extreme surfaces (lower and upper) displacements are required as follows: GROUP_NO=SURFINF: DX = 0, DY = 0 et DZ = -DEPZ GROUP_NO=SURFSUP: DX = 0, DY = 0 et DZ = DEPZ The value of the displacement is \mathit{DEPZ}=3.{10}^{-3}m . The two extreme blocks of the bar can actually be moved in three directions by simply assigning a non-zero value for the degrees of freedom corresponding to \mathit{DX} or \mathit{DY} . 2.3 Analytical resolution The solution to such a problem is obvious. As explained for the test case SSNV173 V6.04.173, the solution is as follows: all the following moves x and y are zero, all the following moves z below the lower level-set are equal to the {u}_{z} displacement at the base of the structure, all the following moves z between the two level-set are zero and all the z moves above the upper level-set are equal to the {u}_{z} displacement at the top of the structure. 2.4 Tested quantities and results The displacement values after the convergence of the iterations of the STAT_NON_LINE operator are tested. The values determined in [§ 2.3] are verified. The result is visualized using post-processing operators. 3 Modelling B: Horizontal Closing Interfaces 3.1 Mesh characteristics and interface The mesh is the same as the Modelling A. The objective is to test the contact management on the interfaces represented with X-FEM, so only the boundary conditions have changed. 3.2 boundary conditions The boundary conditions will allow this time to test the consideration of the friction-free contact on the lips of the interfaces. So we keep the clamped support of the nodes belonging to the median surface but the displacements imposed on the nodes of the two extremes (lower and higher) will close the interfaces. So we will have: GROUP_NO=SURFMED: DX = 0, DY = 0 et DZ = 0 GROUP_NO=SURFINF: DX = 0, DY = 0 et DZ = DEPZ GROUP_NO=SURFSUP: DX = 0, DY = 0 et DZ = -DEPZ 3.3 Analytical resolution The interfaces being horizontal and the uniaxial and normal compression state at the interface, there is no possible slippage. The value of the contact pressure is checked and the solution of the problem is that of the same problem without interface, for each block on either side of the clamped surface. As shown for the test case SSNV182 V6.04.182 and given the geometry and boundary conditions described in §2.2, the contact pressure is given by: > \lambda =E\frac{\text{DEPZ}}{\text{LZ}/2} éq 4.3-1 With the numerical values previously introduced, \lambda =-12{.10}^{3}\text{Pa} . 3.4 Tested quantities and results The correct calculation process allows a priori to validate the correct contact management for multi-cracking. The contact components of the FISS_XFEM SD for each crack are managed correctly at the MODI_MODELE_XFEM and STAT_NON_LINE operators. A \theta =30° angle of inclination was chosen according to the rotation around the \mathit{OX} axis for both interfaces. Normal at the interfaces thus created is noted \mathrm{n} and the tangential vector is noted \tau : \mathrm{n}=(\begin{array}{c}0\\ -1/2\\ \sqrt{3}/2\end{array}),\tau =(\begin{array}{c}0\\ \sqrt{3}/2\\ 1/2\end{array}) éq 6-1 The new level functions introducing the two cracks in the command file are: \text{LN1}=\text{Z}-\tan\theta \cdot Y-(\text{LZ}/4-\tan\theta \cdot \text{LX}/2) éq 6-2 \text{LN2}=\text{Z}-\tan\theta \cdot Y-(3\cdot \text{LZ}/4-\tan\theta \cdot \text{LX}/2) éq 6-3 4.1 Figure 4.1-1: Maillage pourla modélisation CCaractéristiques du maillage Compared to modellings A and B, the number of elements in the Z direction (bar height) was multiplied by 2 to avoid the contiguousness of the elements enriched by the two inclined interfaces. Therefore, one has a mesh 2\times 2\times 20 elements HEXA8 (see []). 4.2 boundary conditions The boundary conditions allows for a mixed load: compression at the first interface and traction for the second. Thus, in addition to the clamped support of the nodes belonging to the median surface (as for the first two modellings), positive displacements are imposed in the Z direction for nodes belonging to the extreme (lower and upper) surfaces. For the upper block (interface 2), the analytical solution is for the displacement values of the nodes. The solution for the latter is identical to that of Modelling A and therefore we will only detail the analytical solution for the lower block. The interfaces are inclined and can be slipped. To avoid this, we force the adhesion by choosing a sufficiently high coefficient of friction of Coulomb. It can be drained (the fluid pore pressure does not vary during the test) or undrained (the valve is closed: the fluid pore pressure evolves in the sample). Here, we are interested in the drained case, simpler, because it does not involve the influence of the fluid pore pressure and modelisable by this pure mechanical calculation . In the model under consideration, the cubic element represents one eighth of the sample, so the limit conditions are as follows: - The symmetry conditions: - {u}_{z}=0 on mesh cell \mathrm{BAS} group - {u}_{x}=0 on mesh cell \mathrm{GAUCHE} group - {u}_{y}=0 on mesh cell \mathrm{DEVANT} group - Side pressure conditions: - {P}_{n}=1 on mesh cell \mathrm{COTE} group - The loading conditions: - {P}_{n}=1 on mesh cell \mathrm{HAUT} Group (phase 1) - {u}_{z}=-1 on mesh cell \mathrm{HAUT} Group (Phase 2) The load is carried out in two phases: - isotropic loading between t=-2 and t=0 where the pressure on the mesh cells \mathrm{COTE} and HAUT groups varies between p=0 and p={p}_{c} (isotropic preconsolidation pressure). In modellings A, B and C, the value of {p}_{c} is 50,100,200\mathrm{kPa} , respectively; - mesh-cell group \mathrm{HAUT} displacement varying between t=0 and t=10 from {u}_{z}=0 to {u}_{z}=-0.2 (total vertical deformation of 20\text{\%} ). 1.4 Results The solutions are post-treated with point C , in terms of Q equivalent stress , {\varepsilon}_{v} total volume deformation and ({r}_{\text{ela}}^{\text{s},m}+{r}_{\text{iso}}^{m}) isotropic and ({r}_{\text{ela}}^{d,m}+{r}_{\text{dev}}^{m}) deviatory nutring coefficients , depending on the {\epsilon}_{zz} axial deformation evolution The validation is performed by comparison with GEFDYN solutions provided by the École Centrale Paris. For modellings with GDEF_LOG operator, \underline{\underline{E}}=1/2\log(I+2\underline{\underline{\Lambda}}) logarithmic deformation is considered, with \underline{\underline{\Lambda}} the Green-Lagrange tensor. The density deformation in this case is obtained directly from the deformity gradient determinant, J=det(F) . 2 Modelling A 2.1 Modelling characteristics Model A is tridimensional and nonlinear static. First, a elastic preconsolidation ( \mathrm{ELAS} ) of the sample up to {p}_{c}=\mathrm{50kPa} (first phase of calculation) is performed. The vertical displacement imposed on the upper facet varies between 0. and -0.2 (second phase of calculation) in 100 time step between t=0 and t=10 . v6.04.198 SSNV198 – Dirichlet conditions with X-FEM in 3D v6.04.198 SSNV198 – Dirichlet conditions with X-FEM in 3D Summary The purpose of this test is to validate the imposition of Dirichlet conditions (taxed displacements) on nodes enriched by the X-FEM [bib1] method on a 3D academic case. This test involves a 3D structure with a flat, deep-right cracking opening. boundary conditions are applied to one side of the structure, containing enriched nodes. Several mesh configurations are tested and compared with the analytical solution. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The structure is a unitary cube ( \mathit{LX}=1m , \mathit{LY}=1m and \mathit{LZ}=1m ), with a flat crack leading to a=0,5m length , mid-height [ Figure 1.1-1.1-a ]. The face is called behind the face in the x=0 plane and the face in front of the x=\mathit{LX} plane . Figure 1.1- 1.1-a : geometry of cracked cube 1.2 Material properties Young's modulus: E=100\mathit{MPa} Poisson's ratio: \nu =0 . 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The load studied is a load that requires cracking in \mathit{III} mode (outside), without creating a displacement discontinuity. To do this, you will require a clamped support of the nodes of the rear side: \mathit{DX}=\mathit{DY}=\mathit{DZ}=0 and a displacement of the nodes of the front side in the normal direction (i.e. along the x axis ) \mathit{DNOR}={10}^{}6m . 1.4 Bibliography 1. GENIAUT S., MASSIN P.: eXtended Finish Element Method, Reference Manual Code_Aster , R7.02.12 2 Modelling A In this model, the crack is not meshed, and the mesh is selected so that the crack bottom is located in the centre of the elements containing the bottom. 2.1 Mesh characteristics The structure is modelled by a regular mesh composed of 5\times 5\times 5 HEXA8, respectively, along the x,y,z axes [ Figure 2.1-2.1-a ]. The crack bottom is therefore located at the centre of the elements containing the crack bottom. Figure 2.1- 2.1-a : mesh such that the bottom is in the centre of the elements 2.2 Tested Features The application of Dirichlet conditions is tested by AFFE_CHAR_MECA command on enriched nodes (here, nodes enriched by Heaviside function and other nodes enriched by asymptotic functions). This is done as for the classic nodes by keyword DDL_IMPO or FACE_IMPO. 2.3 Tested quantities and results The post-processing displacement values of nodes on which the conditions have been applied are tested. The post-processing displacement with X-FEM requires a specific reconstruction step, which does not retain the nodes groups. Therefore, nodes groups must be recreated on the mesh post-processed "fissured". Care must be taken to keep only the old nodes, and remove the new nodes, i.e. those that coincide with the intersection of the crack and the healthy mesh edges, from the group. This sorting is done by the name of the nodes: - N\dots for classic nodes, - \mathit{NX}\dots for nodes X-FEM that are not on the crack, - \mathit{NM}\dots and \mathit{NP...} For new nodes X-FEM that are on the "less" lip and the "more" lip. So we eliminate the nodes whose name starts with \mathit{NM} and \mathit{NP} . v6.04.201 SSNV201 – Block with slide contact interface with X-FEM v6.04.201 SSNV201 – Block with slide contact interface with X-FEM Summary This test case is designed to test and validate the GLISSIERE feature for contact with X-FEM. The main purpose of this test case is to prove that for an interface generated by X-FEM, where contact with option GLISSIERE is activated, there is no detachment of the surfaces in contact, they can only slide in relation to each other. This test involves a parallelepipedic block through a modeled interface with X-FEM. The block is subject to imposed displacements, which would result in the separation of the structure when the GLISSIERE option is not activated and the slipping of both blocks without release, when this option is activated. Digitally, the activation of this option is done after the contact is established, either initial contact imposed by the user (CONTACT_INIT='OUI'), or natural contact, resulting from the kinematic evolution of the structure. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The structure is a straight parallelepiped with a rectangular and healthy base. The dimensions of the bar (see[Figure1.1-1)) are: \mathrm{LX}=2m , \mathrm{LY}=4m and \mathrm{LZ}=10m . The interface (Figure 1.1-2) is introduced by level functions (normal level set noted \text{LN} directly in the control file using DEFI_FISS_XFEM U4.82.08 operator. The interface is defined as a horizontal crack, in the middle of the block following the \mathrm{OZ} direction given by the following level function: \text{LN}=Z-\mathrm{LZ}/2 éq 1-1 1) 2) Figure 1.1 Géométrie du bloc et positionnement de la fissure No tangential level is required since the TYPE_DISCONTINUITE='INTERFACE' key word is used, which allows the structure to be completely cut into two parts. 1.2 Material properties Young's modulus : E=100\mathrm{MPa} Poisson's ratio : \nu =0.0 Density: \rho =7800\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} 1.3 Boundary conditions and loading The nodes of the lower surface of the block is clamped (see Figures 1.1-1) by applying to the node group of the surface a load on the required movement: \mathrm{ENCASTR} : \mathrm{DX}=0 , \mathrm{DY}=0 et \mathrm{DZ}=0 . Two other loads on the required journeys are applied to the node group of the upper surface of the block: \mathrm{CHZ} : \mathrm{DZ}=\mathrm{DEPZ} et \mathrm{DX}=0 ; \mathrm{CHY} : \mathrm{DY}=\mathrm{DEPY} . The values of the required displacements are: \mathrm{DEPY}=\mathrm{DEPZ}=1.{10}^{-3}m . The loads are applied in three steps using the functions presented on the []. Figure 1.3-1: Variations des chargements en déplacements imposés By imposing this kinematic movement at the top of the block, we want to show the action of the GLISSIERE option. In the initial state, the contact is not affected on the lips of the crack (CONTACT_INI='NON') and therefore the two parts of the block will separate following the first loading step ( \mathrm{DZ}=\mathrm{DEPZ} ). They come back into the second step when they are brought together ( \mathrm{DZ}=-\mathrm{DEPZ} ). Once in contact, the GLISSIERE option activates and prevents the detachment following the normal direction ( \mathrm{OZ} ) during the third step, despite the imposed displacement ( \mathrm{DZ}=\mathrm{DEPZ} ), the tangential slide at the interface level remains possible ( \mathrm{DY}=\mathrm{DEPY} ). 2 reference solution The solution to such a problem is of course obvious. Step 1: Both parts of the structure are detached: the lower part has zero displacement and the upper part has an overall movement equal to the displacement imposed on the top of the structure. Step 2: There is no horizontal displacement. Vertically, both parts of the structure are linked and behave as a single compression block. The displacement at the interface is equal to the half of the displacement at the top of the structure and the displacement jump is zero. Step 3: Horizontally, the lower part has zero displacement and the upper part has an overall movement equal to the displacement imposed on the top of the structure. Vertically, both parts of the structure are bound and behave as a single pull block. The displacement at the interface is equal to the half of the displacement at the top of the structure and the vertical displacement jump is zero. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics 3D X-FEM Modelling is considered with contact consideration. The interface is introduced into the healthy mesh by the DEFI_FISS_XFEM operator. 3.2 Mesh characteristics The structure is discretized using elements HEXA8 finished. In the three directions of the selected reference system, 2\times 4\times 9 elements is then used to achieve a total of 72 elements finished (see []) The interface will be introduced in the middle of the fifth stage of elements following the \mathrm{OZ} direction. Figure 3.2-1: M aillage de la modélisation A 3.3 Tested quantities and results The POST_MAIL_XFEM operator allows the cracks to be broken by the X-FEM method. The POST_CHAM_XFEM operator then allows the X-FEM results to be exported to this new mesh. Both operators are only to be used after the calculation at post-processing views. They allow the nodes to be generated just below and above the interface and to display their movements. The values of the displacement are tested just below and above the interface after convergence of the iterations of the STAT_NON_LINE operator. v6.04.202 SSNV202 – Drained oedometric test with CAM_CLAY and MCC behavior models v6.04.202 SSNV202 – Drained oedometric test with CAM_CLAY and MCC behavior models Summary This drained oedometric compression test (in pure mechanical, equivalent to drained hydraulic conditions) validates the elastoplastic laws CAM_CLAY r7.01.14_ and MCC r7.01.48_, specific to soil behavior, presenting under this load a nonlinear elastic regime and a hardening plastic regime. Modelling A uses the CAM_CLAY model and pilotes the test by a monotonous, imposed displacement. Modelling C uses the MCC model and controls the test by a pressure imposed. For each of the two laws, the quantities calculated are compared with the results obtained either from the FLAC software for soil mechanics in Modelling A or from the results of a MTest calculation at the point hardware in Modelling C. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Height: h=1 m, width: l=1 m, thickness: e=1 m. 1.2 Material properties 1.2.1 Model CAM_CLAY The parameters specific to CAM_CLAY r7.01.14_ for Modelling A are: - \mu =276923 Pa, e_0=2 , \lambda =0.2 , \kappa =0.05 , M=1.02 , {P}_{cr}^0=5 kPa, K_{cam}=0 Pa, {P}_{trac}=0 Pa. > Note: > The initial vacuum index e_0 is associated with the initial porosity by the e_0=PORO/(1-PORO) relationship. 1.2.2 Model MCC The parameters specific to MCC r7.01.48_ are given in the following table for Modelling C. | Effect | Appellation | Definition | Symbol | Value | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Nonlinear isotropic elasticity | BulkModulus ShearModulus SwellingIndex | Compressibility moduleShield modulusElastic nonlinearity index | K \mu \kappa | 160 MPa100 MPa50 | | Initial elasticity | InitCritPress CritStateSlope TensileYieldStress | Initial critical pressureCritical state penetrating isotropic tensile elasticity | p_{c0} M \sigma_0 | 1 MPa110 kPa | | Kinematic-isotropic collision | IncoPlastIndex | Plastic incompressibility index | \beta | 50 | 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads An oedometric test consists of imposing a vertical load variation on the test piece while maintaining the lateral deformations zero. It can be drained (the fluid pore pressure does not vary during the test) or undrained (the fluid pore pressure changes in the sample). The case is examined here. The variation of the effective mean pressure, noted p' , is therefore equal to that of the total pressure p . In model A, the oedometric test is performed with a stress state initiated at \boldsymbol{\sigma}=-P_{conso}^0\boldsymbol{I} with {P}_{conso}^0=2P_{cr}^{0}-P_{trac} preconsolidation. The vertical load is controlled on a displacement from {U}_{z}=0 to {U}_{z}=-0.1 m (which corresponds to a maximum axial compression deformation equal to 10\% on the upper side of the cubic sample. In model C, the oedometer test is performed with an initially zero stress state. The vertical load is controlled by increasing the pressure force -\sigma_{zz} to 10 MPa before performing a discharge up to 10 kPa. > Note: > In Modelling A, the CREA_CHAMP operator defines the non-zero initial stress state \boldsymbol{\sigma}=-P_{conso}^0\boldsymbol{I} on all the element at Gauss points. 2 Modelling A 2.1 Modelling characteristics 3D Modelling | Number of nodes | 20 | | --- | --- | | Number of mesh cells | Type 1 HEXA 206 QUAD 8 | | DROITE | NO3, NO5, NO8, N10, NO12, NO15, NO17, NO20 | | --- | --- | | GAUCHE | NO1, NO4, NO6, NO9, NO11, NO13, NO16, NO18 | | DEVANT | NO6, NO7, NO8, NO11, NO12, NO18, NO19, NO20 | | DERRIERE | NO1, NO2, NO3, NO9, NO10, NO13, NO14, NO15 | | BAS | NO13, NO14, NO15, NO16, NO17, NO18, NO19, NO20 | | HAUT | NO1, NO2, NO3, NO4, NO5, NO6, NO7, NO8 | Modelling A with the CAM_CLAY 3D type is tridimensional and static nonlinear . v6.04.205 SSNV205 – Constant isotropic pressure drained cyclic shear test v6.04.205 SSNV205 – Constant isotropic pressure drained cyclic shear test Summary: The constant isotropic pressure drained cyclic shear test simulates the loss of stiffness from a soil as a function of the amplitude of the applied cyclic deformations, and also determines the dissipation introduced during loading cycles. In this case, the constitutive laws of Hudeux (modelization A) and Iwan (modelization B) are first examined. Two laws currently available in Code_Aster for the cyclic behaviour of granular materials. Next, the CSSM model (modelization C) designed around the general representation of granular geomaterials under monotonous and cyclic loadings is interested. In model A, the conduct of these tests also validates the introduction of the cyclic deviatory thresholds of the Hujeux behavior model. The results of the Code_Aster are compared with the results obtained with the GEFD yn software for the same behavior model. In model B, the results obtained with the Iwan model are compared with those of Modelling with the Hujeux model, considering similar behavioural curves for both models. In model C, the results obtained using model CSSM are compared with those obtained from material point calculations by Mtest. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A hardware element point is considered. 1.2 Material properties 1.2.1 Hujeux and Iwan's behavioural models The material's isotropic elastic properties are E=619.33 MPa and \nu =0.3 . v6.04.206 1 v6.04.206 SSNV206 - Triaxial test: LETK, LKR and NLH_CSRM models ­ 1 v6.04.206 SSNV206 - Triaxial test: LETK, LKR and NLH_CSRM models Summary This test is used to validate the LETK, LKR and NLH_CSRM models in rock mechanics. This is a triaxial test in pure mechanics or drained conditions. The calculations are performed only on the solid part of the soil without hydromechanical coupling. A containment level of 5\mathit{MPa} is applied. Due to symmetry, one only cares about the eighth of a sample subjected to a triaxial test. The Modelling is axisymmetric. 1 Description of modellings - Modelling A: The local model integration algorithm is explicit, classified as specific later: LETK model. - Modelling B: The local model integration algorithm is implicit with the local jacobian matrix obtained by disturbance: model LETK. - Modelling C: The local model integration algorithm is implicit with the local jacobian matrix obtained analytically: LETK model. - Modelling D: The local model integration algorithm is explicit, classified as specific afterwards. The load is applied 100 times slower to highlight the role of viscosity in the model: model LETK. - Modelling E: The local model integration algorithm is implicit with the local jacobian matrix obtained analytically. The load is applied 100 times slower to highlight the role of viscosity in the model: model LETK. - Modelling G: The local model integration algorithm is implicit with the local jacobian matrix obtained by disturbance, no temperature imposed: modelLKR. - Modelling H: The local model integration algorithm is implicit with the local jacobian matrix obtained analytically, no temperature imposed, no coupling between the plastic and viscoplastic mechanisms (COUPLAGE_P_VP = 0.): model LKR. - Modelling J: The local model integration algorithm is implicit with the local jacobian matrix obtained analytically, increasing temperature (0°C-100°C) imposed via AFFE_VARC: model LKR. - Modelling L: The local model integration algorithm is implicit with the local jacobian matrix obtained analytically. The load is applied 100 times slower to highlight the role of viscosity in the model, no temperature imposed: model LKR. - Modelling M: validation of the NLH_CSRM model. validate the LETK model in pure mechanics. Comparison between the two integration schemes allows to identify certain trends on convergence profiles. An explicit integration scheme allows for fine discretization of the load to guarantee converged results and a lower machine run time than the implicit scheme. However, it is difficult to quantify the level of finesse of the load to be applied to ensure the convergence of studies with an explicit integration scheme. The implicit integration scheme ensures a level of accuracy higher than the explicit scheme for the same load discretization. It also allows for a local tangential operator to be available. These advantages thus ensure that on a wide range of load discretizations a convergence on the results obtained with the implicit scheme is ensured. v6.04.208 SSNV208 – Drained Biaxial Test with Hujeux Law v6.04.208 SSNV208 – Drained Biaxial Test with Hujeux Law Summary A biaxial test in pure mechanics (equivalent to drained hydraulic conditions) is performed with the Hujeux law . The calculated solutions are compared with results from elements GEFDYN finished code from the École Centrale Paris. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The biaxial test is performed on a single finite element square isoparametric QUAD8, mesh cell group named \mathrm{BLOC} . The length of each edge is \mathrm{1m} . The different sides of this square are mesh cell groups named \mathrm{HAUT} , \mathrm{BAS} , \mathrm{DROIT} and \mathrm{GAUCHE} . The mesh-cell group \mathrm{COTE} also contains the mesh cell \mathrm{DROIT} and \mathrm{GAUCHE} groups; the mesh cell \mathrm{APPUI} group is the mesh cell \mathrm{BAS} group. 1.2 Material properties of the sand of Hostun The elastic properties are: - isotropic compressibility module: K=148\mathrm{MPa} - shear module: \mu =68\mathrm{MPa} The anelastic properties (model of Hujeux) are derived from the thesis of K.Hamadi [2] and correspond to sand d-Hostun slightly dense: - power of nonlinear elastic law: {n}_{e}=0. (linear elastic) - \beta =30. - d=2.5 - b=0.2 - friction angle: \phi =33° - characteristic angle: \Psi =33° - critical pressure: {P}_{\mathrm{CO}}=-400\mathrm{kPa} - Reference pressure: {P}_{\mathrm{ref}}=-1000\mathrm{kPa} - isotropic mechanism elastic radius: {r}_{\mathrm{ela}}^{s}={10}^{-4} - elastic radius of the deviatory mechanism: {r}_{\mathrm{ela}}^{d}=0.01 - {a}_{\mathrm{mon}}=0.017 - {a}_{\mathrm{cyc}}=0.0001 - {c}_{\mathrm{mon}}=0.08 - {c}_{\mathrm{cyc}}=0.04 - {r}_{\mathrm{hys}}=0.05 - {r}_{\mathrm{mob}}=0.9 - {x}_{m}=1. - \mathrm{dila}=1. 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The biaxial test presented here is carried out in D_PLAN Modelling. Normal shifts in the design of studies are therefore null. Vertical displacement is imposed on the test piece while maintaining the constant lateral pressure in the design of study. It can be drained (the fluid pore pressure does not vary during the test) or non-drained (the valve is closed: the fluid pore pressure evolves in the sample). Here, we are interested in the drained case, simpler, because not involving the influence of the fluid pore pressure. We then choose a model in pure mechanics. In the model under consideration, the square element represents a quarter of the sample. The boundary conditions are therefore: The symmetry conditions: - {u}_{y}=0. on mesh cell \mathrm{BAS} group - {u}_{x}=0. on mesh cell \mathrm{GAUCHE} group Side pressure conditions: - {P}_{n}=1. on mesh cell \mathrm{COTE} group The loading conditions: - {P}_{n}=1. on mesh cell \mathrm{HAUT} group - {u}_{z}=-1. on mesh cell \mathrm{HAUT} group The load is carried out in two phases: - An isotropic stress state, {P}_{o}=100\mathrm{kPa} , is initially assigned to the mesh cell \mathrm{BLOC} ; - Vertical displacement is imposed on the mesh-cell group \mathrm{HAUT} and varies between t=0. and t=10. from {u}_{y}=0. to {u}_{y}=-0.2 (total vertical deformation of 20\text{\%} ). 1.4 Results The solutions are post-treated with point C , in terms of {\sigma}_{yy} stress , {\varepsilon}_{v} total volume deformation and ({r}_{\text{ela}}^{\text{iso},m}+{r}_{\text{iso}}^{m}) isotropic and ({r}_{\text{ela}}^{d,m}+{r}_{\text{dev}}^{m}) deviatory nutring coefficients . The validation is carried out by comparison with GEFDYN solutions provided by the Ecole Centrale Paris ( http://www.mssmat.ecp.fr/-GEFDYN,016- ). The PDIL_ELGA elemental option calculation for this softening problem is also performed. This calculation option allows the maximum value to be estimated for the A1 regularization parameter of the R5.04.03 expansion second gradient media. This value is a function of the material parameters, the stress state and the values of the internal variables at the moment of calculation [1]. 1.5 Bibliographical references [1] Foucault A. " Modulation of the cyclical behaviour of earth works incorporating regularization techniques ". Thesis by Doctor, École Centrale Paris, Châtenay Malabry, France, 2010. [2] Hamadi K. " Modification of forklifts and instability in geomaterials ". Thesis by Doctor, École Centrale Paris, Châtenay Malabry, France, 2006 2 Modelling A 2.1 Modelling characteristics The Modelling is two-dimensional with D_PLAN flat deformations and nonlinear static. The vertical displacement imposed on the upper facet varies between 0 and -\mathrm{0.2m} in 280 time step between t=0. and t=10 . The automatic subdivision of the time step is enabled to manage non-convergence situations of local integration. The INDL_ELGA calculation option, which allows you to calculate the directions of the Rice tensor, is also enabled. The results provided by this option are tested in non-regression mode. The PDIL_ELGA calculation option, which allows the calculation of the A1_LC2 parameter, is also enabled. v6.04.214 SSNV214 - constitutive law BETON_RAG: cyclic loading of a concrete test piece v6.04.214 SSNV214 - constitutive law BETON_RAG: cyclic loading of a concrete test piece Summary: This document presents a test to validate the capabilities of the BETON_RAG behavior model, used to estimate the long-term behaviour of structures affected by the alkali-granulat reaction. The behaviour of a test piece under cyclic loading in single tensile mode is simulated. 1 Reference problem This test is intended to validate the damage part of the BETON_RAG behavior model. 1.1 Geometry The test is based on a single cubic finite element (1m x 1m). 1.2 Ownership of constitutive law Young's modulus: E=32000\mathrm{MPa} Poisson's ratio: \nu =0.2 Fragility parameter of tensile concrete: \mathit{MT}=1,7 Fragility parameter of compression concrete: \mathit{MC}=1,5 Equivalent tensile force of concrete: {\sigma}_{\mathit{ft}}=5.66\mathit{MPa} Equivalent stress of compression concrete: {\sigma}_{\mathit{fc}}=38.3\mathit{MPa} Angle of Drucker Prager's criterion: \alpha =0,15\mathit{rad} 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The load applied to nodes of the X=1m plane consists of two tensile loading cycles and then two compression loading cycles: | Moving Control1.traction {\epsilon}_{xx}=1,4{.10}^{-4} 2.relay to {\sigma}_{xx}=0 3.traction {\epsilon}_{xx}=1,0{.10}^{-3} 4.compression {\epsilon}_{xx}=-4,0{.10}^{-3} 5.relay to {\sigma}_{xx}=0 6.compression {\epsilon}_{xx}=-5,0{.10}^{-3} 7.traction {\epsilon}_{xx}=0 | | | --- | --- | The following boundary conditions are applied: - for nodes in the X=0 → DX = 0 - for node N1 (0, 0, 0) → DX = DY = DZ = 0 - for node N5 (0, 0, 1) → DY = 0 2 reference solution This test validates the model's ability to reproduce uniaxial cyclic loading. The imposed deformation steering allows you to traverse the entire curve, including the softening part. Here, the behaviour of a test piece subjected to a specific loading path creates a continuous rotation of the directions of the main stresses. 1 Reference problem In this test [Willam et al., 1987], the test piece is subjected to a specific loading path that creates a continuous rotation of the directions of the main stresses. v6.04.221 SSNV221 – Hydrostatic test with linear and parabolic DRUCK_PRAGER behavior v6.04.221 SSNV221 – Hydrostatic test with linear and parabolic DRUCK_PRAGER behavior Summary: The test case offers a purely hydrostatic loading for the Drücker-Prager law associated with R7.01.16. The formulation of this plastic law, often used for soils, is made both on the deviatoric and hydrostatic part; nevertheless, the criterion surface has a singularity for a purely hydrostatic stress state. This analytical test case is used to verify correct hardening in this singularity. The test is performed on a hardware point with the SIMU_POINT_MAT command. We work with imposed deformations. One test is performed with linear nutring (modelling A) and another with parabolic nutring (modelling B). 1 Reference problem 1.1 Material properties - Elastics : E=3000\mathrm{MPa} Young's modulus \nu =0,25 Poisson's ratio DRUCK_PRAGER linear(modelization A): \alpha =0,20 Pressure Dependence Coefficient {p}_{\mathrm{ultm}}=0,04 Ultimate cumulative plastic deformation {\sigma}_{Y}=6\mathrm{MPa} Plastic Constraint h=100\mathrm{MPa} Nutrient module DRUCK_PRAGER parabolic(modelization B): \alpha =0,20 Pressure Dependence Coefficient {p}_{\mathrm{ultm}}=0,04 Ultimate cumulative plastic deformation {\sigma}_{Y}=6\mathrm{MPa} Plastic Constraint {\sigma}_{Y}^{\mathrm{ult}}=10\mathrm{MPa} Ultimate plastic constraint 1.2 Loadings and boundary conditions The load is not monotonous: first, it is charged to the {\varepsilon}_{v1} density deformation, by exceeding the plasticization threshold, then it is discharged to a zero deformation level; then it is charged to the {\varepsilon}_{v2} deformation, thus exceeding the ultimate cumulative plastic deformation {p}_{\mathrm{ultm}} , above which it is found to be perfect plasticity; it is still discharged at zero stress (deformation equal to the plastic deformation {\varepsilon}_{v2}^{p} ) and it is reloaded later until the {\varepsilon}_{v3} deformation. The loading time (see ) is fictitious because the plastic laws are time independent. | t | {\varepsilon}_{v} | | --- | --- | | 0 | 0 | | 10 | {\varepsilon}_{v1}=0,018 | | 14 | 0 | | 26 | {\varepsilon}_{v2}=0,045 | | 30 | {\varepsilon}_{v2}^{p}=0,03667 | | 40 | {\varepsilon}_{v3}=0,06 | Table 1.2-1 : Volume deformation imposed. 1.3 Initial conditions All stress and deformation components are zero at the beginning of loading. 2 reference solution The Modelling checks the behaviour of the law with linear hardening. 2.1 Method of calculation The equations that interest us for the analytical calculation are ( {I}_{1}=\text{tr}(\sigma ) : stress tensor trace, {\varepsilon}_{v}^{p} : density plastic deformation): - Plastic constitutive law on the volumetric part: {I}_{1}=\mathrm{3K}({\varepsilon}_{v}-{\varepsilon}_{v}^{p}) - criterion surface, by posing zero stress of Von Bets ( {\sigma}_{\mathrm{eq}}=0 ) : F(\sigma ,p)=\alpha {I}_{1}-R(p) - relationship between volume plastic deformation and cumulative plastic deformation (internal variable of the plastic law): \dot{{\varepsilon}_{v}^{p}}=3\alpha \dot{p} - expression of the nutwork - Linear: \begin{array}{}R(p)={\sigma}_{Y}+hp\mathrm{si}p\le {p}_{\mathrm{ult}}\\ R(p)={\sigma}_{Y}+h{p}_{\mathrm{ult}}={\sigma}_{Y}^{\mathrm{ult}}\mathrm{si}p>{p}_{\mathrm{ult}}\end{array} - parabolic: \begin{array}{}R(p)={\sigma}_{Y}{(1-(1-\sqrt{\frac{{\sigma}_{Y}^{\mathrm{ult}}}{{\sigma}_{Y}}})\frac{p}{{p}_{\mathrm{ult}}})}^{2}\mathrm{si}p\le {p}_{\mathrm{ult}}\\ R(p)={\sigma}_{Y}^{\mathrm{ult}}\mathrm{si}p>{p}_{\mathrm{ult}}\end{array} It is observed that, as in the linear case, R(p)={\sigma}_{Y} if p=0 and one has perfect plasticity if p>{p}_{\mathrm{ult}} . 2.1.1 Deformation at initial elastic limit This deformation is obtained for {\varepsilon}_{v}^{p}=p=0 . If F(\sigma ,p)=0 is installed (plastic evolution) we have: {I}_{1}^{\mathrm{el}}=\frac{R(p)}{\alpha}=\frac{{\sigma}_{Y}}{\alpha} {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{el}}=\frac{{I}_{1}^{\mathrm{el}}}{3K} 2.1.2 Ultimate Deformation The ultimate deformation {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{ult}} is called the one obtained for p={p}_{\mathrm{ult}} . The {I}_{1}^{\mathrm{ult}} stress trace and the corresponding {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{pult}} plastic deformation are easily found: {I}_{1}^{\mathrm{ult}}=\frac{R(p)}{\alpha}=\frac{{\sigma}_{Y}^{\mathrm{ult}}}{\alpha} {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{pult}}=3\alpha {p}_{\mathrm{ult}} {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{ult}}=\frac{{I}_{1}^{\mathrm{ult}}}{3K}+{\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{pult}} 2.1.3 Deformation between the elastic limit and the ultimate deformation The cumulative plastic deformation is calculated first. - By combining the equations , , and with F(\sigma ,p)=0 for linear hardening we have: p=\frac{3KA{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{v1}}-{\sigma}_{Y}}{9K{\alpha}^{2}+h} - Combining the equations , , and with F(\sigma ,p)=0 for the parabolic hardening we arrive at the equation of degrade 2: {A}_{1}{\stackrel{ˉ}{p}}^{2}+{B}_{1}\stackrel{ˉ}{p}+{C}_{1}=0 \begin{array}{}{A}_{1}={\sigma}_{Y}{(1-\gamma )}^{2}\\ {B}_{1}=9K{\alpha}^{2}{p}_{\mathrm{ult}}-2{\sigma}_{Y}(1-\gamma )\\ {C}_{1}={\sigma}_{Y}-3K\alpha {\varepsilon}_{v1}\\ \gamma =\sqrt{\frac{{\sigma}_{Y}^{\mathrm{ult}}}{{\sigma}_{Y}}}\\ \stackrel{ˉ}{p}=\frac{p}{{p}_{\mathrm{ult}}}\end{array} The equations are then used and to find {\varepsilon}_{v}^{p} plastic deformation and {I}_{1} stress trace. If the material is discharged elastically until zero stress, there is a residual deformation equal to the plastic deformation; however, the compression material must be charged to obtain a total zero deformation. The second branch is also elastic, as the Drücker-Prager material cannot plasticize in hydrostatic compression. In the latter case, the trace of the stresses, negative, is: {I}_{1}^{c}=-3K{\varepsilon}_{v}^{p} 2.1.4 Deformation greater than ultimate deformation All the quantities of interest are easily found, as the stress trace is known a priori and equal to {I}_{1}^{\mathrm{ult}} . {\varepsilon}_{v}^{p}={\varepsilon}_{v}-\frac{{I}_{1}^{\mathrm{ult}}}{3K} p=\frac{{\varepsilon}_{v}^{p}}{3\alpha } 2.2 Quantities and reference results The K compressibility module is: K=\frac{E}{3(1-2\nu )}=2000\mathrm{MPa} 2.2.1 Deformation at the elastic limit For both modellings you can easily find: {I}_{1}^{\mathrm{el}}=30\mathrm{MPa} {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{el}}=0,005 2.2.2 Ultimate Deformation For both modellings you can find: {I}_{1}^{\mathrm{ult}}=50\mathrm{MPa} {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{pult}}=0,024 {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{ult}}\approx 0,03233 2.2.3 Deformation of 0.018 and zero deformation discharge This {\varepsilon}_{v1}=0,018 deformation value is greater than the {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{el}} elastic limit and less than {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{ult}} . First the plastic deformation accumulated with the equations and then the plastic deformation and stress trace is calculated: - Linear nutring: {p}_{1}=\frac{3KA{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{v1}}-{\sigma}_{Y}}{9K{\alpha}^{2}+h}\approx 0,019 {\varepsilon}_{v1}^{p}=3\alpha {p}_{1}=0,0114 {I}_{1}^{1}=3K({\varepsilon}_{v1}-{\varepsilon}_{v1}^{p})\approx 39,51\mathrm{MPa} - Parabolic nutring: {p}_{1}\approx 0.0192 {\varepsilon}_{v1}^{p}=3\alpha {p}_{1}\approx 0.0115 {I}_{1}^{1}=3K({\varepsilon}_{v1}-{\varepsilon}_{v1}^{p})\approx 38.956\mathrm{MPa} The trace of zero deformation stresses is: - Linear nutring: {I}_{1}^{\mathrm{1c}}=-3K{\varepsilon}_{v1}^{p}\approx -68,49\mathrm{MPa} - Parabolic nutring: {I}_{1}^{\mathrm{1c}}=-3K{\varepsilon}_{v1}^{p}\approx -69,044\mathrm{MPa} Indeed, the difference between parabolic and linear cases is very small. 2.2.4 Loading up to deformation of 0.045 and 0.06 The material is charged to the deformation values {\varepsilon}_{v2}=0,045 and {\varepsilon}_{v3}=0,06 , above {\varepsilon}_{v}^{\mathrm{ult}} . v6.04.222 FORMA04 - Practical work of the "Advanced use" training: Hertz contact v6.04.222 FORMA04 - Practical work of the "Advanced use" training: Hertz contact Summary: This TP deals with Hertz contact, one of the few non-trivial contact cases for which an analytical solution is available. The model consists of two half-spheres that come to contact one against the other. This simple test will illustrate the data of the contact, the different ways of solving the problem and finally the tools available to post-processing a contact calculation. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The model consists of two half-spheres. The problem is chosen to be treated in axisymmetric , so only quarter disks will be modeled. The geometric data are as follows: - Rayon of the spheres: R=50\mathit{mm} x y 1.2 Material properties The material is elastic linear: - Young's modulus: E=20000\mathit{MPa} - Poisson's ratio: \nu =0.3 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads - Next \mathit{DX} move blocked on \mathit{A1A2} axis (this condition is implicit in axisymmetric, however, it is imposed for points that would not be perfectly on the axis) - Next move \mathit{DY} imposed: +2\mathit{mm} on \mathit{A1B1} -2\mathit{mm} on \mathit{A2B2} 2 reference solution 2.1 Method of calculation In 1881 Hertz established a solution to the problem that bears his name under certain assumptions. Thus, assuming a friction-free contact and for which the a contact half width is very small in front of the R sphere radius ( a\ll R ), the contact pressure at the \mathit{C1} and \mathit{C2} points is: {P}_{0}=-\frac{E}{\pi (1-{\nu}^{2})}\sqrt{\frac{2h}{R}} where h corresponds to the imposed crash, which is 4\mathit{mm} here. The a contact half width is expressed in terms of the required crushing and sphere radius: a=\sqrt{\frac{\mathit{Rh}}{2}} The contact surface is a a radius disc, the pressure distribution as a function of the r radius in this area is as follows: \textrm{Si} r\le a 2.2 Quantities and reference results The pressure obtained at the centre of the contact area and the half-width of contact shall be compared to the above analytical solution. 2.3 Uncertainties about the solution None (assumed above). 2.4 References 3 Modelling A 3.1 Implementation of TP 3.1.1 Geometry 3.1.2 Read the full statement before you start Geometry is done with the Salome-Meca platform, Geometry module. The "Sketcher" tool (Menu New Entity → Basic → 2D Sketch) allows you to build the upper disc contour: A2 , B2 , D2 and C2 . The circle arc is made in 2 times so that the point D2 is created when building the contour. For B2D2 , you give the radius at 50 and angle at -45° using Direction and Perpendicular, and for D2C2 you give the radius at -50 and angle at 45° using Direction and Tangent. Then one can build a face from this contour (Menu New Entity → Build → Face). By symmetry, the second sphere (Menu Operations → Transformation → Mirror Image) can be generated by choosing the X axis to achieve symmetry. The two spheres have to be assembled to form only one GEOM object(Menu New Entity →Build →Compound ) . Warning: In this object, there are always two points, \mathit{C1} and \mathit{C2} , which overlap. On the contrary, the two points merge if the operation is Partition, Finally, you have to create groups on this geometry (with the names suggested in the figure above) (Menu New Entity → Group → Create Group).We draw attention to the fact that the groups are created last. - Create groups for \mathit{SPHHAU} and \mathit{SPHBAS} half-spheres surfaces - To create groups for point superimposed C1 and C2 , you use the feature to select a element slot from an GEOM entity: check " Only Sub-shapes of the Second Shape ", then for \mathit{C2} for example, select as " Second Shape " the upper half-sphere in the object tree, and only its points are highlighted. - Create groups for boundary conditions application: along the axis of axisymetry ( \mathit{A1A2} ) and on the upper and lower parts of the half-spheres ( \mathit{A1B1} and \mathit{A2B2} ). - For contact modelling, groups of mesh cells representing potential contact surfaces will be required: create \mathit{CONT}1 and \mathit{CONT}2 groups. 3.1.3 Mesh The Mesh module is used. The mail is set by the Mesh→ Create Mesh menu with the geometry to be meshed. The mesh will be made in triangles, and the assumptions of mesh automatic "Assign a set of hypotheses → 2D: Automatic Triangulation" will be used by choosing a maximum length of 2mm. The mail is calculated (MenuMesh→ Compute). The mesh contains about 3000 triangles and 1500 nodes. Then we will import the groups from geometry (Menu Mesh → Create Groups from Geometry). We will import mail in MED format. Illustration 3.1: mesh obtained for Modelling A 3.1.4 command file The AsterStudy module is used. Then in the left column, click on the Case View tab. The command file of the calculation case is set. (click right to CurrentCase and choose Add Stage). Note: To add commands: Commands Menu→ Show All. By using STAT_NON_LINE command, build command file relative to test case by not initially taking contact into account. - What is there on convergence?What should be done to converge? Index: How is the default convergence criterion built? > Help to build the command file: - Read mesh in MED format: LIRE_MAILLAGE command. - Set the material: DEFI_MATERIAU command. - Assign material to all elements: AFFE_MATERIAU command. - Set the finished elements used: AFFE_MODELE command to affect the MECANIQUE phenomenon and AXIS Modelling. - Assign boundary conditions / mechanical loads: AFFE_CHAR_MECA / DDL_IMPO for axial symmetry and unit-based required displacements which will then be multiplied by a ramp function over time. - Set the load ramp (imposed displacement) with the DEFI_FONCTION command. For example, the function varies between (\mathrm{0.,}0.) and (\mathrm{2.,}2.) . - Create time discretization using DEFI_LIST_REEL commands.For example, 20 steps from 0s to 2s. - Solve the problem with the STAT_NON_LINE command. We put COMPORTEMENT / RELATION='ELAS',the moment list previously defined in INCREMENT, the materials in CHAM_MATER, MODELE and also the boundary conditions and the loading (CHARGE + FONC_MULT) in EXCIT. Bonus Question: How many rigid body movements are there in axisymmetric Modelling? > Recall: a rigid body movement is a movement with zero deformation. Add the contact definition: orient the surfaces, define the contact load with the DEFI_CONTACT command and adapt the nonlinear solver options. - An alarm appears when calculating with contact. The default contact method will be retained at first ( FORMULATION='DISCRETE' and 'ALGO_CONT='CONTRAINTE' ). - Orient the normal mesh on contacts: MODI_MAILLAGE / ORIE_PEAU_2D command using CONT1 and CONT2 groups.The same name is retained for the mesh using weer. - Set contact: DEFI_CONTACT command. The default contact method will be retained at first (FORMULATION='DISCRETE' and 'ALGO_CONT='CONTRAINTE'). The CONT1 and CONT2 groups are assigned to the couple of contact areas (master and slave). - Adapt the contact option in STAT_NON_LINE. 3.1.5 Hertz pressure Numerical application: To calculate by hand with the problem data, the value of the Hertz pressure and the half-contact width (see Chapter 2). What do we see? Why this difference? Note: the component \mathit{SIYY} d u field SIEF_NOEU(calculated with the CALC_CHAMP / CONTRAINTE command) as contact pressure will be used as the first approximation. Trace the contact pressure as a function of radius in the contact area, compare it to the analytical solution. - Calculate the stress field by elements to nodes ( SIEF_NOEU ): command CALC_CHAMP / CONTRAINTE. - Create an node group with a curvilinear abscisse: DEFI_GROUP command. The same name will be retained for mesh with a rouse. The CREA_GROUP_NO / OPTION='NOEUD_ORDO' option will be used by giving the mesh cell group ( \mathit{CONT}1 ) and the point starting ( C1 ). - Extract the \mathit{SIYY} component from the SIEF_NOEU field in a table at the last moment: POST_RELEVE_T command. The name of the nodes group, the moment, the field and its component will be specified using EXTRACTION operation. - Create {\sigma}_{\mathit{YY}}=f(x) function: RECU_FONCTION command. We will define the curvilinear abscisse (ABSC_CURV) as PARA_X and SIYY as PARA_Y. - Build the analytical solution: - Calculate pressure at C1 and C2 points , {P}_{0} and contact half width a - Create the analytical formula:FORMULE command. It depends on the x curvilinear coordinate (NOM_PARA='x' / VALE='P0 sqrt(1.-x x/a/a)'). - Create a list of real values of x : DEFI_LIST_REEL command. For example, 100 values from 0 to 10mm. - Interpolation of the formula from the list of x : command CALC_FONC_INTERP. - Print both functions in XMGRACE format with the IMPR_FONCTION command. 3.1.6 Constraint of Von Mises Show Von stress Bets on the distorted configuration with Salomé. How does this constraint vary in the sphere? Where is the maximum? - The component VMIS_SG of the equivalent stress field SIEQ_NOEU calculated with the CALC_CHAMP / CRITERES command . The results can be printed in the format MED with the help of command IMPR_RESU to view the stress field in Results or in Paravis and the maximum position (Edit → Find Data menu). 3.2 Tested quantities and results | Identification | Reference type | Reference value | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | {\sigma}_{yy} point \mathit{C1} | 'ANALYTIQUE' | -2798,3\mathit{Mpa} | 1,0% | 4 Modelling B The mesh is the same model as the A model but it has been quadratic . 4.1 Implementation of TP 4.1.1 Continuous formulation Convert mesh from Modelling A to mesh quadratic in the Mesh module (Menu Modification → Convert to/from quadratic) To fully enjoy the quadratic elements and obtain a smooth pressure profile, it is important to place the nodes media on the geometry when converting (check the " Medium nodes on geometry " box when converting). Change the contact method and use the 'CONTINUE' formulation. See the contact pressure obtained using the degree of freedom LAGS_C field DEPL . Compare with the default contact method. What is the result of the method? Which method provides the best approximation? To obtain a correct pressure profile, a pattern of integrating the contact terms at Gauss points ( INTEGRATION='GAUSS' in the DEFI_CONTACT / ZONE command) must be used. To remove the alarm that appears with the default settings, it is necessary to impose REAC_ITER=1 under the factor keyword NEWTON command of STAT_NON_LINE (in continuous formulation, the tangent matrix is necessarily rebuilt with each iteration). 4.2 Tested quantities and results | Identification | Reference type | Reference value | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | \mathit{DEPL} {\mathit{LAGS}}_{C} point \mathit{C1} | 'ANALYTIQUE' | -2798,3\mathit{Mpa} | 3,0% | 5 Modelling C In this Modelling, a quadrangle mesh is made, with refinement near the contact area. 5.1 Implementation of TP 5.1.1 Realization of geometry In this Modelling, the geometry must be partitioned so that it can be gridded into quadrangles. In the GEOM module, an illustration of the possible partition is given in the figure: - Take the \mathit{SPHHAU} face and explain all of its points (New Entity menu → Explode: Vertex), then you get the 4 points A2 , B2 , C2 and D2 - Create M , N and P points to generate the partition lines in red(menu New Entity → Basic → Point): (0,25,0) , (25,25,0) and (25,50,0) - Generate partition lines (New Entity menu → Basic → Line) - Sheet music \mathit{SPHHAU} with the above lines (Menu Operations →Partition). - By symmetry, one can generate a new lower face(Menu Operations →Transformation →Mirror Image) choosing the X axis to achieve symmetry - The two new spheres have to be assembled to form only one GEOM object(Menu New Entity →Build →Compound ) . - Define all groups as in Modelling A, which will be needed to affect boundary conditions and loads (menu New Entity → Group→ Create Group) Figure 5.1: Upper disc sheet music 5.1.2 Mesh realization For the mesh, you choose to refine around the contact area using geometric progression on the circumference and radius. You may need to redirect certain segments in the Mesh module: - The mail is defined by the Mesh→ Create Mesh menu with the mesh geometry. The mesh will be made into triangles, and the assumptions of mesh will be used automatically "Assign a set of hypotheses →2D: Automatic Quadrangulation" by choosing the number of segments 15. - The sub-mesh(MenuMesh→ Create Sub-mesh) is defined with \mathit{CONT}1 and \mathit{CONT}2 groups. It is made using the Wire Discretization algorithm, the Start and End Length hypothesis (e.g. 0.2mm and 2.0mm) and the Advanced Propagation of Node Distribution on Opposite Edges hypothesis. v6.04.228 SSNV228 – Pre-voltage of a stud v6.04.228 SSNV228 – Pre-voltage of a stud Summary: This test illustrates the pre-voltage of a stud in Code_Aster. The methodology used is to apply a relative displacement between a d-group of the stud and a d-group of the nut (between the two faces that are normally threaded). Two modellings are proposed: - Model A : Manual displacement determination (use of DEFI_CONTACT ) - Model B : Automated determination of displacement using MACR_RECAL (use of DEFI_CONTACT ). - Model C : Manual displacement determination (use of DEFI_CONT ) 1 Reference problem 1.1 Methodology The pre-voltage setting consists of imposing a relative displacement between nodes of the nut and nodes of the stud. This relative displacement is imposed in the axis of the stud and must correspond to the desired tightening effort. This relative displacement is imposed via the keyword LIAISON_GROUP of the AFFE_CHAR_MECA_F command. For the user, it is therefore a question of determining the displacement to be imposed in order to find the desired clamping effort. To do so, the study must be replayed several times by changing the value of the relative displacement until reaching the desired clamping effort. This test case offers three modellings: - Modelling A : a model to illustrate a manual calibration (with DEFI_CONTACT ). - Model B : a model to illustrate an automated re-calibration (with DEFI_CONT ), - Modelling C : a model to illustrate a manual calibration (with DEFI_CONT ). Note: This method applies only to small movements. It assumes that the difference in movement between the nut and the stud is constant throughout the area. 1.2 Geometry The geometry, shown in the figure, is generated by the SALOME-MECA-2012.1 "Bride Calculation" tool. Dimensions, in millimetres, are shown in figure, which are the default values in the tool. Figure 1.2-a: Geometrics of flange and stud. Figure 1.2-b: Geometry parameters. 1.3 Mesh The mesh, shown in the figure, is also generated by the SALOME-MECA-2012.1 "Bride Calculation" business tool. It is linear and consists of 1108 hexahedrons and 70 prisms for 1821 nodes. Figure 1.3-a: mesh of flange and stud. 1.4 Materials The material is elastic and its properties are: E=200000\mathit{MPa} and \nu =0.3 . 1.5 Boundary conditions, contact and loading The boundary conditions blockings are as follows: - blocking of the degree of freedom DZ on the sides of the underside of the stud and the joint, - symmetry conditions via blocking of normal lateral surface displacement with bore, - symmetry conditions via blocking of normal lateral side movement without bore, - flatness condition of the cutting face of the tube in the \mathit{XY} plane by imposing an identical value for the degree of freedom DZ on all nodes on the face, - clamping condition via a zero difference between degrees of freedom DX and DY of the screw screw screw and nut nodes - 1.0E-06\mathit{Pa} pressure inside the tube. - contact condition between the sides of the joint and flange. The load corresponds to a relative displacement imposed on the nodes of the nut and stud. It is zero at the moment and is DEPL_R at the moment 1.0 . Note: The displacement is named DEPL_R in order to reuse the A Modelling control file directly with MACR_RECAL in the B Modelling. Indeed, the macro-command requires the presence of '__' at the end of the parameters to be re-calved. 1.6 Modelling The modelling is 3D. 1.7 Seeking effort An DEPL_R displacement corresponding to an average \mathrm{30 }\mathit{MPa} stress in the stud stem is applied, which is an effort resulting from: {F}^{\mathit{résultant}}={\sigma}^{\mathit{pré}-\mathit{tension}}.\pi .{R}_{\mathit{goujon}}^{2}/2=\mathrm{1695.6N} . Division by 2 takes symmetry into account. 2 Modelling A 2.1 Modelling characteristics This model illustrates the method of clamping a stud. It is to impose a relative shift between the nodes of the nut and stud and to calculate the resulting stress. The calculation is made by changing the value of DEPL_R until the resulting stress corresponds to the desired effort. The contact is modelled using DEFI_CONTACT and using the continuous method ( FORMULATION = CONTINUE ). 2.2 Tested quantities and results The recalibration is considered satisfactory when DEPL_R is 8.0E-3\mathit{mm} . This value allows to pre-tension the stud with an average stress of 30\mathit{MPa} in the stud. The resulting effort is compared to the effort sought. | Result | Reference | Reference value | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Resulting effort on the nut | ANALYTIQUE | -1695.6N | 1.0E-02 | Non-regression tests with 1.0E-6 tolerance are performed on the resulting forces of the following surfaces: - face of the nut in contact with the stud, - face of the stud in contact with the nut, - face of the underside of the stud, - face of the joint in contact with the flange, - face of flange in contact with joint. Note: the resulting stress calculated on each side is identical. 3 Modelling B 3.1 Modelling characteristics This Modelling illustrates the method of tensioning a stud by performing an automatic recalibration of the relative displacement value between the nodes of the nut and stud. To do this, the MACR_RECAL macro-command is used in a master file and Modelling A as a slave file. The function of the effort to be achieved is: CIBLE =DEFI_FONCTION( NOM_PARA='INST' , NOM_RESU='DZ' , VALE= (0.0 , 0.0 , 1.0 , F_RESULT ,), ) Call to the re-arrangement control: RECAL =MACR_RECAL( PARA_OPTI = _F(NOM_PARA='DEPL_R__' , VALE_INI= 0.004, VALE_MIN= 0.004, VALE_MAX= 0.012, ) , COURBE = _F(FONC_EXP= CIBLE, NOM_FONC_CALC='REACF' , PARA_X='INST' , PARA_Y='DZ') , ) In the slave file the calculation of reacf: REACF =POST_RELEVE_T( ACTION=_F(INTITULE='FZ_CEG' , OPERATION='EXTRACTION' , RESULTAT= RESU, NOM_CHAM='REAC_NODA' , RESULTANTE='DZ' , GROUP_NO='N_SCEG' , ) , ) 3.2 Tested quantities and results The recalibration is used to determine a value of DEPL_R close to 8.0E-3\mathit{mm} . v6.04.229 SSNV229 - Validation of ETCC formulas in DEFI_CABLE_BP and failure of a cable v6.04.229 SSNV229 - Validation of ETCC formulas in DEFI_CABLE_BP and failure of a cable Summary: The purpose of this test case is to bring elements validation of the DEFI_CABLE_BP operator for the calculation of voltage profiles in prestress cables in concrete structures. This is: - validate the ETCC formulae installed in Code_Aster that allow for the loss of tension by friction between cables and concrete, by recoiling at anchors, and by relaxation of steel, the material constituting the cables (modellings A and B); - validate the procedure developed to model the breakage of a cable with re-anchoring (keyword factor MODI_CABLE_ETCC of the DEFI_CABLE_BP command) (modelization C). The structure is a cylinder, containing ten prestressed cables in its thickness. The cables each describe a circle in a horizontal plane, and travel the structure along its length. All the cables are anchored on the same line. Modelling A allows the direct consideration of steel relaxation to be tested (approximate method). Modelling B allows the further modelling of steel relaxation by performing a short-term calculation and a long-term calculation that can be combined with the modelling of the removal and creep in concrete. In both cases, the results obtained are validated by comparison with those theoretically expected. Model C Modelling modeled the failure of one of the 10 prestress cables after the voltage setting. It was verified that the result obtained was in accordance with what was injected into the calculation. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry It is a concrete cylinder of height is H=10m and medium radius R=20.5m . The thickness of the veil is e=1m . Model studied The cables each describe a circle in a horizontal plane, and thus travel the structure along its length. All the cables are anchored on the same line. The 10 cables are spaced from 1m between z=-4.5m and z=4.5m . The right section of each cable is {S}_{a}=7.923{10}^{-3}{m}^{2} . 1.2 Material properties 1.2.1 Concrete material constituting the veil Elastic properties: | Young's modulus | {E}_{b}={3.10}^{10}Pa | | --- | --- | | Poisson's ratio | {\nu}_{b}=0,2 | 1.2.2 Steel material constituting cables Elastic properties: | Young's modulus | {E}_{a}=1,915{.10}^{11}Pa | | --- | --- | | Poisson's ratio | {\nu}_{a}=0,3 | Perfect parameters for estimating voltage losses: | Steel elastic limit constraint | {f}_{\mathit{prg}}=1,814.{10}^{9}\mathit{Pa} | | --- | --- | | Friction coefficient | \mu =0,17 | | Online loss coefficient | k=\frac{0,0015}{0,17}{m}^{-1} | | Steel relaxation at 1000 hours | {\rho}_{1000}=2,5\text{\%} | 1.3 Loading A normal tensile force is applied to both ends of each cable. The stress value applied in the steel is {\sigma}_{0}=0,8{F}_{\mathit{prg}}=1487,48\mathit{MPa} or {F}_{0}=11,785{.10}^{6}N voltage. The test results shall be carried out in accordance with the requirements of the Annex to Regulation (EU) No 1303/2013. For modellings A and B, the characteristics are evaluated after 65 years, i.e. t=569790h which corresponds to the NBH_RELAX parameter. For Modelling C, only friction and anchor loss are modelled. Then, it is assumed that a break in cable 5 occurs at the s=64,39m curvilinear abscisse and that the tension is re-anchored linearly over a distance of 20 m (on either side of the point fracture). Both modellings correspond to two methods of calculating prestress loss due to steel relaxation. - In model A, relaxation losses are considered by neglecting elastic losses (direct calculation with DEFI_CABLE_BP) either: {F}_{i}(s)={F}_{0}{\exp}^{-\mu (\theta +ks)}-\text{recul d'ancrage} And finally: F(s)={F}_{i}(s)-0,66{\rho}_{1000}.{\exp}^{9,1{F}_{i}(s)/{F}_{\mathit{prg}}}.{(\frac{t}{1000})}^{0,75(1-{F}_{i}(s))/{F}_{\mathit{prg}}}.{10}^{-5}{F}_{i}(s) - In model B, the losses by relaxation of steels are calculated from the voltage taking into account the elastic losses obtained by a previous calculation, where the cables were energized into 2 groups, i.e.: for Group 1 (unfair cables): {F}_{i}^{1}(s)={F}_{0}{\exp}^{-\mu (\theta +ks)}-\text{recul d'ancrage}-\frac{{A}_{p}{E}_{p}\Delta {\sigma}_{c}(x)}{E} for Group 2 (peer cables): {F}_{i}^{2}(s)={F}_{0}{\exp}^{-\mu (\theta +ks)}-\text{recul d'ancrage} et F(s)={F}_{i}^{1,2}(s)-0,66{\rho}_{1000}.{\exp}^{9,1{F}_{i}^{1,2}(s)/{F}_{\mathit{prg}}}.{\left(\frac{t}{1000}\right)}^{0,75(1-{F}_{i}^{1,2}(s))/{F}_{\mathit{prg}}}.{10}^{-5}{F}_{i}^{1,2}(s) The reference value was actually obtained by considering that the same elastic losses were present on all \Delta {F}_{\mathit{el}}(s)=\frac{{A}_{p}{E}_{p}\Delta {\sigma}_{c}(x)}{2E} cables. 2.2 Breakout modelling For Modelling C, the voltage profile was applied in a totally arbitrary manner. It is simply verified that the result of prestressing is well equal to the profile that was intended to be introduced. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Features of modellings The concrete wall is represented by elements 3D supported in both cases by mesh cells hexahedrals at 8 nodes: 10 mesh cells on a vertical generator, 4 mesh cells in thickness and 126 on the circumference. v6.04.230 SSNV230 - Validation of the constitutive law of 300 steels under 3D irradiation v6.04.230 SSNV230 - Validation of the constitutive law of 300 steels under 3D irradiation Summary: These elementary tests are designed to validate constitutive law IRRAD3M of \mathrm{3D} -irradiated steels by activating irradiation creep and swelling.
