v7.31.133 WTNV133 – Undrained Triaxial with Hujeux Law v7.31.133 WTNV133 – Undrained Triaxial with Hujeux Law Summary This test validates the implantation of monotonous deviatory mechanisms and the mechanism of cyclic consolidation of the Hujeux law. This is a triaxial test performed in undrained condition. The hydraulic coupling is taken into account, the sample is fully saturated, the skeleton and fluid are assumed to be incompressible. The containment levels applied are 50\mathrm{kPa} and 200\mathrm{kPa} . The results obtained with Hujeux's law are compared with results from elements GEFDYN finished code from the École Centrale Paris. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry It is a sample of cubic form in 1/8 representation using element \text{HEXA20} . 1.2 Material properties The elastic properties are: - isotropic compressibility module: K=516200\mathrm{kPa} ; - Shear module: \mu =238200\mathrm{kPa} ; - density 1: {\rho}_{s}=2500\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} . The anelastic properties of the cyclic Hujeux law are: - power of nonlinear elastic law: {n}_{e}=0,4 ; - \beta =24 ; - d=2,5 ; - b=0,2 ; - friction angle: \varphi =33° ; - Dilatance angle: \psi =33° ; - critical pressure: {P}_{\mathrm{c0}}=-1\mathrm{MPa} ; - Reference pressure: {P}_{\mathrm{ref}}=-1\mathrm{MPa} ; - isotropic mechanism elastic radius: {r}_{\mathrm{éla}}^{s}=0,001 ; - elastic radius of deviatory mechanisms: {r}_{\mathrm{éla}}^{d}=0,005 ; - {a}_{\mathrm{mon}}=0,008 ; - {a}_{\mathrm{cyc}}=0,0001 ; - {c}_{\mathrm{mon}}=0,2 ; - {c}_{\mathrm{cyc}}=0,1 ; - {r}_{\mathrm{hys}}=0,05 ; - {r}_{\mathrm{mob}}=0,9 ; - {x}_{m}=1 ; - \mathrm{dila}=1 ; The hydraulic properties are: - Biot coefficient: B=1 ; - the density of water: {\rho}_{e}=1000\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} ; - viscosity: \nu =0,001 ; - Intrinsic permeability: {K}^{int}=1{E}^{-8}{m}^{3}/\mathrm{kg}/s ; - Water compressibility module: {K}_{e}=1{E}^{+12}\mathrm{Pa} (compressibility coefficient 1/{K}_{e}=1{E}^{-12}{\mathrm{Pa}}^{-1} ) 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads 1.3.1 boundary conditions These are the symmetry conditions on the element, which represents 1/8 of the sample. The movements are blocked on the front ( {u}_{y}=0 ), left ( {u}_{x}=0 ) and lower ( {u}_{z}=0 ) sides. 1.3.2 Loading Phase 1: consolidation of sample to containment pressure {p}_{0} The sample is brought to a homogeneous state of isostatic effective stress {\sigma}_{xx}^{0}={\sigma}_{yy}^{0}={\sigma}_{zz}^{0}={\sigma}_{0} , by placing the pressure {\sigma}_{0} on the rear, right lateral and upper faces of the element, and by maintaining zero \mathrm{PRE1} water pressures everywhere. Phase 2: Undrained triaxial loading To obtain undrained conditions, zero hydraulic fluxes are imposed on all surfaces. By holding a pressure equal to {\sigma}_{0} on the rear and right side faces , a load of \Delta u shall be applied while moving equal to 0,02m on the upper side, in order to obtain a homogeneous deformation of the 2\text{\%} sample. 1.4 Results The solutions are post-treated with point C , in terms of equivalent stress of Von Mises Q ( =\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}({\sigma}^{d}:{\sigma}^{d})} ), effective isotropic pressure P ( =\frac{\text{trace}(\sigma ')}{3} ), plastic density deformation {\varepsilon}_{v}^{p} and ({r}_{\text{iso}}^{m}+{r}_{\text{ela}}^{\text{iso},m}) and ({r}_{\text{iso}}^{c}+{r}_{\text{ela}}^{\text{iso},c}) isotropic nutring coefficients and ({r}_{d}^{m}+{r}_{\text{ela}}^{d,m}) deviatory. v7.31.136 WTNV136 – 3D Modelling of clay swelling with GonfElas v7.31.136 WTNV136 – 3D Modelling of clay swelling with GonfElas Summary: This test allows the so-called "GonfElas" model to be validated. This nonlinear suction-dependent elastic model describes the swelling behaviour of certain types of clay. Typically it is used to model the behavior of compacted clay caps - or bentonite - used to close radioactive waste storage cells. It is a very simplified version (elastic part) of the Barcelona model. This model is written according to the following couple of variables: net stress and suction (suction is capillary pressure). This test represents the swelling pressure of a clay cell that is filled with water. This test case is the test case WTNA110 declination to a \mathrm{3D} geometry. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A cube of 1m on the side. 1.2 Material properties Elastic properties: E+150.{10}^{6}\mathrm{Pa} \nu =0.3 Model-specific parameters GonfElas: - {\beta}_{m}=0.1142 - Reference pressure A=1.\mathrm{Mpa} Hydraulic properties : | Liquid water | Volumetric mass ( {\mathrm{kg.m}}^{-3} ) Constant pressure heat ( {\mathrm{J.K}}^{-1} ) Thermal expansion coefficient of liquid ( {K}^{-1} ) Compressibility ( {\mathrm{Pa}}^{-1} ) Viscosity ( \mathrm{Pa.s} ) | 1.103 4180 10-4 5.10-10 10-3 | | --- | --- | --- | | Gas | Molar mass ( \mathrm{kg.}{\mathrm{Mol}}^{-1} ) Constant pressure heat ( {\mathrm{J.K}}^{-1} ) Viscosity ( \mathrm{Pa.s} ) | 0,002 1000 9. 10-6 | | Skeleton | Constant stress heat capacity ( {\mathrm{J.K}}^{-1} ) | 1000 | | Constants | Perfect gas constant | 8,315 | | Homogenized coefficients | Homogenized density ( {\mathrm{kg.m}}^{-3} ) Biot coefficient Van-Genuchten N \mathrm{Pr}(\mathrm{Mpa}) \mathrm{Sr} model parameters | 2000 1 1,61 16.106 0 | | Reference state | Porosity Temperature ( °K ) Capillary pressure ( \mathrm{Pa} ) Gas pressure ( \mathrm{Pa} ) | 0,366 303 0. 10 | 1.3 Initial conditions A t=0 : - \mathit{Pgaz}=1\mathit{atm} - S=0,5 (i.e. \mathit{Pc}=44,7\mathit{Mpa} and {p}_{w}=-44.6\mathit{Mpa} ) - Total compression stress equal to -1 atm. 1.4 Boundary conditions and loads All movements are blocked at the edge ( \mathit{DX}=\mathit{DY}=\mathit{DZ}=0 ). The flow is zero. The initial saturation is \text{50 \%} : saturation is increased and the evolution of total stress is monitored. By definition, the swelling pressure is the stress obtained with complete resaturation. For this purpose, a linear downward hair pressure load is imposed on the entire domain in \mathrm{1s} between 44,7\mathrm{Mpa} and -10\mathrm{Mpa} . 1.5 Bibliographical references 1. Gérard, P., Charlier R., Barnichon, J.D., Su, K. Shao, J-F, Duveau, G., Giot, R., Chavant, C. Collin, F. "Numeric modelling of coupled mechanics and gas transfer" Journal of Theoretical and Applied Mechanics, Sofia, 2008, vol. 38, No. 1, pp. 101-120. 2 Modelling A 2.1 Modelling characteristics 3D _HH2MS Modelling on 1 mesh cell HEXA20. 1 second is simulated by 500 time step. 2.2 Modelling result A Figure 2.2-a shows the evolution of total stress as a function of homogeneous hair pressure in all point. The post-treatment is done here at node N8 coordinates (0,5;0,5;0,5) . In the saturated part ( \mathit{Pc}\le 0 ), the decrease of the capillary pressure corresponds to an increase in water pressure and the total stress increases linearly. The slope of the curve is observed to be continuous. The parameters A and {\beta}_{m} were calculated to recover a swelling pressure of 7\mathit{MPa} . The purpose of this validation test is to test the correct consideration of the discontinuity of the pressure field in the massif on both sides of the fracture and the hydromechanical behaviour of the elements HM-XFEM. v7.31.145 WTNV145 - Application of a distributed pressure on the lips of a XFEM crack junction for hydromechanical cases v7.31.145 WTNV145 - Application of a distributed pressure on the lips of a XFEM crack junction for hydromechanical cases Summary: This is a first validation test to ensure the correct functioning of the extended elements finite method in the fractured saturated HM coupling model. In this test we are looking to verify that there is a discontinuity of the displacement field on both sides of the interface, compared to an analytical solution and the results obtained with a mechanical XFEM test (similar to ssnv203, modellings F and H) in the case where the pore pressure is taken uniformly throughout the field of study ( i.e in order to fit in a "classical" mechanical case without coupling). 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry of problem 2D (modelization A) This block is a square block on the L=10m side. This block has two discontinuities of the interface type (unmesh interface which is introduced into the model via the level-set via the DEFI_FISS_XFEM operator). The first is identified by the normal level-set of the {\mathit{lsn}}_{1}=Y-\mathrm{0.5X}-0.2 equation and crosses the block entirely in the horizontal direction. The second interface is identified by the normal level-set of the {\mathit{lsn}}_{2}=Y+\mathrm{0.5X}+0.2 equation. It connects to the lower lip of the first interface. The second interface therefore exists only in the part of the block such as {\mathit{lsn}}_{1}<0 . The point junction between the two interfaces checks {\mathit{lsn}}_{1}={\mathit{lsn}}_{2}=0 and has (-0.4,0) coordinates. This is a classic case of the BO-BG type which allows us to test the hydraulic law called by HYDR_VGM. It also allows the comparison of several numerical diagrams: elements finished and decentralized finished volumes. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The field studied consists of two media of 0,5m each. The material \mathrm{M1} will be called the open barrier ( \mathit{BO} ) and the material \mathrm{M2} geological barrier ( \mathit{BG} ) 1.2 Material properties This is only given the properties on which the solution depends, knowing that the command file contains other material data that play no role in the solution of the problem. | BO | | | | --- | --- | --- | | Liquid water | Density ( {\mathrm{kg.m}}^{-3} ) Viscosity | 1000 {10}^{-3} | | Homogenized parameters | Permeability K Porosity | {10}^{-20}{m}^{2} 0.3 | | Parameters of Van-Genuchten | N \mathrm{Pr} \mathrm{Sr} \mathrm{Smax} | 1,064 1,5\mathrm{Mpa} 0 0,999 | | Initial status | Pressure | {P}_{c}^{0}=89\mathrm{MPa}(S=0.77) {P}_{\mathrm{gz}}=1\mathrm{atm} | | BG | | | | --- | --- | --- | | Liquid water | Density ( {\mathrm{kg.m}}^{-3} ) Viscosity | 1000 {10}^{-3} | | Homogenized parameters | Permeability K Porosity | {10}^{-19}{m}^{2} 0.05 | | Parameters of Van-Genuchten | N \mathrm{Pr} \mathrm{Sr} \mathrm{Smax} | 1,7 10\mathrm{Mpa} 0 0,999 | | Initial status | Pressure | {P}_{c}^{0}=0(S=1.) {P}_{\mathrm{gz}}=1\mathrm{atm} | The saturation and permeability curves follow the Mualem-Van-Genuchten (HYDR_VGM) model. This nonlinear suction-dependent elastic model describes the swelling behaviour of certain types of clay. Typically it is used to model the behavior of compacted clay caps - or bentonite - used to close radioactive waste storage cells. It is a very simplified version (elastic part) of the Barcelona model. This model is written according to the following couple of variables: net stress and suction (suction is capillary pressure). v7.32.120 WTNP120 - Phase Appearance/Disappearance in a Diphasic Flow: Gas Injection in a Bar Saturated in Pure Water v7.32.120 WTNP120 - Phase Appearance/Disappearance in a Diphasic Flow: Gas Injection in a Bar Saturated in Pure Water Summary: This test represents the simulation of gas injection into a saturated geological environment. The purpose is to model and simulate the appearance of gas and the evolution of a water/hydrogen diphasic flow in a porous medium initially saturated with pure water. A "quasi"-1D situation is considered where the effects of gravity are neglected. The test case is presented in a 2D configuration but can be treated in an equivalent way as a 1D problem. This is a purely miscible hydraulic calculation. The geometry represented corresponds to a bar. The transfer terms are described by a model of Mualem Van-Genuchten. The problem is dealt with by the various diagrams available for the modelling of diphasic flows: the classic finished elements, the Decent Arest Finished Volumes, the mesh cell Decented Finished Volumes and mesh cell Centres Finished Volumes. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The domain is a [\mathrm{0m},200m]\times [\mathrm{0m},\mathrm{1m}] -sized bar: 1.2 Material properties This is only given the properties on which the solution depends, knowing that the command file contains other material data that play no role in the solution of the problem. | Liquid water | Density (k.{m}^{-3}) Molar mass (\mathit{kg}.{\mathit{mol}}^{-1}) Viscosity (\mathit{kg}.{m}^{-1}.{s}^{-1}) | 1000 {10}^{-2} {10}^{-3} | | --- | --- | --- | | Gas | Density (k.{m}^{-3}) Molar mass (k.{m}^{-1}) Viscosity (k.{m}^{-1}.{s}^{-1}) | 8{10}^{-2} 2{10}^{-3} 9{10}^{-5} | | Dissolved gas | Henry (P.{\mathrm{mol}}^{-1}.{m}^{3}) coefficient | 130719 | | Steam | Density (k.{m}^{-3}) | {10}^{-4} | | Homogenized parameters | Permeability k ({m}^{2}) PorosityGasick ({m}^{2}.{s}^{-1}) Fick Liquid ({m}^{2}.{s}^{-1}) | 5{10}^{-20} 0.15 0 0,45{10}^{-9} | | Parameters of Van-Genuchten | N {P}_{r} (\mathit{MPa}) {S}_{rl} {S}_{gr} \mathrm{Smax} {P}_{e} (\mathrm{MPa}) | 1,49 2 0,4 0 0,999 0 | | Initial status | Hair pressure (\mathit{Pa}) Gas pressure (\mathit{Pa}) | P_{c}^{0} = -10^{-6} P_{gz} = 0 | The saturation and permeability curves follow the Mualem-Van-Genuchten (HYDR_VGM) model. v7.32.121 WTNP121 – Modelling a straight-line compressible liquid (single phase flow) saturated bar v7.32.121 WTNP121 – Modelling a straight-line compressible liquid (single phase flow) saturated bar Summary: This test case has a dual objective: - validate the finite volume diagrams developed for diphasic flow modelling. - validate the Modelling Saturated hydraulic finite elements (modellings G and H) The diphasic problem here will be degenerated into a single phase problem known to the analytical solution. This is the one-dimensional Modelling of a water saturated bar subjected to pressure shock. 1 Reference problem The objective of this test case is to compare the solution obtained with the different finished volume diagrams to an analytical solution. 1.1 analytical solution The single-phase instationary and one-dimensional problem can be written in a general form of the type: N\frac{\partial P}{\partial t}-{K}_{\mathit{int.}}\Delta P=0 P(t=0)={P}_{0} P(t,x=0)=0 \frac{\partial P}{\partial x}(t,x=L)=0 This problem allows an analytical solution obtained by developing in series of Fourier. P={\sum}_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{{\mathrm{4P}}_{0}}{(\mathrm{2k}+1)\pi }\exp(\frac{-{K}_{i}}{N}{\omega}_{k}^{2}t)\sin({\omega}_{k}x) with {\omega}_{k}=(k+\frac{1}{2})\frac{\pi}{L} This series can be reduced to a finite K of terms, depending on the moment calculated. The number of terms is determined as follows: {n}_{x} is the number of {x}_{i} points where the solution is evaluated at a time t Installation: {a}_{k}^{i}=\frac{4}{(\mathrm{2k}+1)\pi }\exp(\frac{-{K}_{int}}{N}{\omega}_{k}^{2}t)\sin({\omega}_{k}{x}_{i}) So the solution can write: P({x}_{i})={\sum}_{k=0}^{K}{P}_{0}.{a}_{k}^{i} Choose K as: \frac{1}{{n}_{x}}\sqrt{{\sum}_{i=1}^{\mathit{nx}}{({a}_{k}^{i})}^{2}} \frac{\partial (\varphi {\rho}_{l})}{\partial t}-d({K}_{i}\frac{{\rho}_{l}{k}_{\mathrm{rl}}}{{\mu}_{l}}\nabla {P}_{l})=0 - Liquid is incompressible: {\rho}_{l}=\mathit{cst} - The matrix is compressible and the porosity evolves proportionally to the liquid pressure: \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial {P}_{l}}={E}_{m} The mass retention equation for the liquid is thus written: {\rho}_{l}{E}_{m}\frac{\partial {P}_{l}}{\partial t}-d({K}_{i}\frac{{\rho}_{l}{k}_{rl}}{{\mu}_{l}}\nabla {P}_{l})=0 1.3 Geometry We consider a \mathrm{1D} bar of \mathrm{5m} long. Specifically the mesh domain will make [\mathrm{0m},5m]\times [\mathrm{0m};0,05m] (in the case of triangle Modelling, it is important not to have triangles too "flat", so the choice of the height of the domain is not insignificant). v7.32.128 WTNP128 – Fluid-pressure concrete-coupling test v7.32.128 WTNP128 – Fluid-pressure concrete-coupling test Summary: The test presented here allows to check the correct functioning of the elements joints with hydromechanical coupling and use of cohesive laws. The modeled test is a corner crack test with fluid pressure in the crack. Comparisons with experimental and numerical tests are available for this trial. 1 Reference problem The "wedge splitting test" was initially proposed by Brühwiler and Wittmann to obtain a stable crack propagation and thus determine the fracture properties of the concrete. Slowik and Saouma then used this test to study the effect of fluid pressure in the crack. Segura and Carol modelled this fluid-pressure cracking test. The trial by Slowik and Saouma is repeated here. A device, known as a "coin", allows a force to be applied to the B and B' points (see figure ) to separate the sample in two. The experiment is controlled by the CMOD (Crack Mouth Opening Displacement), i.e. the displacement imposed between B and B' . 1.1 Geometry Figure 1.1-a : Sample Geometry Point coordinates (in \mathrm{mm} ): | | x | y | | x | y | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A | -50 | 51 | A' | 50 | 51 | | B | -50 | 138 | B' | 50 | 138 | | C | -50 | 150 | C' | 50 | 150 | | D | -150 | 150 | D' | 150 | 150 | | E | -150 | -150 | E' | 150 | -150 | | F | 0 | -150 | G | 0 | 0 | | H | 0 | 50 | I | 0 | 51 | The sample has a thickness of 100\mathrm{mm} . 1.2 Material properties - Properties of the interstitial fluid (liquid water): | Density | {1.10}^{-6}{\mathrm{kg.mm}}^{-3} | | --- | --- | | Viscosity | {1.10}^{-9}\mathrm{MPa.s} | Water is considered incompressible. - Properties of the massif : The concrete massif is elastic and has the following properties: | Young's modulus | 27500\mathrm{MPa} | | --- | --- | | Poisson's ratio | 0,2 | Given the time scales considered and the permeability of the crack very high compared, concrete is assumed to be waterproof. It is therefore modelled by classic elements D_PLAN. - Discontinuity properties: The discontinuity is broken down into three parts: - The rubber membrane that ensures the seal of the notch; - The notch in which constant pressure is imposed; - The crack path along which the crack spreads. The membrane has linear elastic behavior. The constitutive law JOINT_BANDIS is used with the \gamma =0 parameter to make it linear. The membrane properties are as follows: | Initial normal rigidity {K}_{ni} | 20{\mathrm{MPa.mm}}^{-1} | | --- | --- | | \gamma coefficient | 0 | For notch, CZM_LIN_REG law is used by initializing internal variables so that elementss are initially broken. For cracking, the CZM_EXP_REG law is used with the following parameters: | {G}_{c} cracking energy | 0,150\mathrm{MPa.mm} | | --- | --- | | Critical stress {\sigma}_{c} | 3,25\mathrm{MPa} | The numerical parameters of the elements joints with cohesive law are | PENA_ADHERENCE | {1.10}^{-3} | | --- | --- | | PENA_CONTACT | 1 | - Crack tip properties | Biot N module | 0,3{.10}^{-3}{\mathrm{MPa.mm}}^{-1} | | --- | --- | | Fictive OUV_FICT Opening | 10 \mathrm{mm} | 1.3 Initial conditions The fluid pressure is initially 0,21\mathrm{MPa} in the notch and 0,0\mathrm{MPa} in the future crack. 1.4 boundary conditions The mechanical and hydraulic boundary conditions are: - F : blocked movements in all directions and zero pressure imposed; - In the [\mathrm{GH}] notch: pressure imposed from 0,21\mathrm{MPa} ; - In the [\mathrm{HI}] membrane: pressure imposed by 0,0\mathrm{MPa} ; - In B and B' , the movements are symmetrical; - In B' , a force is imposed in the (\begin{array}{c}\cos(\alpha )\\ -\sin(\alpha )\end{array}) direction , the intensity of which is controlled by the \mathrm{DX} component of the point B' movement . At each t moment , the horizontal component of the B' displacement must be equal to {u}_{x}=-\frac{q}{2}t , where q is the loading speed . So the DDL_IMPO option is used. The solid is also waterproof and the fluid exchange between cracks and solids is blocked. The fluid pressures on the edges of the joint element and the hydraulic Lagrange multipliers are blocked at zero. 2 reference solution Reference solution was derived from the experimental results of Slowik and Saouma [2] 2.1 Bibliography 1. Brühwiler, E., Witmann, F. H., The edge splitting test, a new method of performing stable fracture mechanics tests, Engineering Fracture Mechanics ,1990,35,1/2/3,117-125 2. Slowik, V., Saouma, V. E., Water Pressure in Propagating Concrete Cracks, Journal of Structural Engineering ,2000,126,235-242 3. Segura, J. The adopted cohesive law is CZM_EXP_REG. The mechanical loading is slow: the loading speed {q}_{t} is 0,002\mu {\mathrm{m.s}}^{-1} . Time Discretization: 29 time step from 10s . 3.2 Tested quantities and results The results of numerical modelling are compared with those obtained experimentally by Slowik and Saouma. The figure shows the force applied by the corner as a function of the CMOD and the figure gives the pressure profiles in the crack. v7.32.130 WTNP130 – Calculation of hydraulic and thermal nodal forces on a bar v7.32.130 WTNP130 – Calculation of hydraulic and thermal nodal forces on a bar Summary: This test case models several hydraulic and thermal flows in a bar. v7.33.110 WTNA110 – axisymmetric Modelling of clay swelling with GonfElas v7.33.110 WTNA110 – axisymmetric Modelling of clay swelling with GonfElas Summary: This test validates the so-called "GonfElas" model. This nonlinear suction-dependent elastic model describes the swelling behaviour of certain types of clay. Typically it is used to model the behavior of compacted clay caps - or bentonite - used to close radioactive waste storage cells. It is a very simplified version (elastic part) of the Barcelona model. This model is written according to the following couple of variables: net stress and suction (suction is capillary pressure). 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry > Geometry is a square [1mx1m] 1.2 Material properties Elastic properties: E=150{10}^{6}\mathit{Pa} \nu =0.3 Parameters specific to the GonfElas model: {\beta}_{m}=0.1142 Reference pressure A=1.\mathit{Mpa} Hydraulic properties: | Liquid water | Volumetric mass ( {\mathit{kg.m}}^{-3} ) Constant pressure heat ( {\mathit{J.K}}^{-1} ) Thermal expansion coefficient of liquid ( {K}^{-1} ) Compressibility ( \mathit{Pa}-1 ) Viscosity ( \mathit{Pa.s} ) | 1.103 4180 10-4 5.10-10 10-3 | | --- | --- | --- | | Gas | Molar mass ( \mathit{kg.}{\mathit{Mol}}^{-1} ) Constant pressure heat ( {\mathit{J.K}}^{-1} ) Viscosity ( \mathit{Pa.s} ) | 0,002 1000 9. 10-6 | | Skeleton | Constant stress heat capacity ( {\mathit{J.K}}^{-1} ) | 1000 | | Constants | Perfect gas constant | 8,315 | | Homogenized coefficients | Homogenized density ( {\mathit{kg.m}}^{-3} ) Biot coefficient Van-Genuchten N \mathit{Pr}(\mathit{Mpa}) \mathit{Sr} model parameters | 2000 1 1,61 16.106 0 | | Reference State | Porosity Temperature ( K ) Capillary pressure ( \mathit{Pa} ) Gas pressure ( \mathit{Pa} ) | 0,366 303 0. 10 | 1.3 Initial conditions A t=0 : - \mathit{Pgaz}=1\mathit{atm} - S=0,5 (i.e. \mathit{Pc}=44,7\mathit{Mpa} and {p}_{w}=-44.6\mathit{Mpa} ) - Total compression stress equal to -1 atm. 1.4 Boundary conditions and loads All movements are blocked at the edge ( \mathit{DX}=\mathit{DY}=0 ). The flow is zero. The initial saturation is \text{50 \%} : saturation is increased and the evolution of total stress is monitored. By definition, the swelling pressure is the stress obtained with complete resaturation. For this purpose, a linear downward hair pressure load is imposed on the entire domain in \mathrm{1s} between 44,7\mathit{Mpa} and -10\mathit{Mpa} . 2 Bibliographical references 1. In the saturated part ( {P}_{c}\le 0 ) the decrease of capillary pressure corresponds to an increase in water pressure and the total stress increases linearly. The slope of the curve is observed to be continuous. The parameters A and {\beta}_{m} were calculated to recover a swelling pressure of 7\mathit{MPa} . When saturation reaches 1 (or capillary pressure 0), the swelling pressure is given by the following formula: \frac{{P}_{\mathit{gf}}}{A}=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{{\beta}_{m}}}+\frac{1}{2{\beta}_{m}} So we find the classic look of the swelling stress and we check that the curve cuts well the axis of the ordered ( {P}_{c}=0 ) with a value of 7\mathit{Mpa} . v7.33.112 WTNA112 – Thermal pressure of undrained saturated cylindrical test piece v7.33.112 WTNA112 – Thermal pressure of undrained saturated cylindrical test piece Summary: This is a problem of saturated and elastic THM. The temperature of a non-drained sample maintained at constant containment (constant total stress at the edge) is increased. The resulting water pressure then varies linearly with the temperature according to a coefficient of thermal pressure which is calculated analytically. The solution obtained here is therefore to be compared with an analytical solution. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A 1\mathit{cm} radius and 1\mathit{cm} height cylinder (i.e. a mesh corresponding to a square domain of 1\mathit{cm}\times \mathrm{1cm} , the Modelling being axisymmetric) is considered. 1.2 Material properties Argilite parameters are selected here to obtain a realistic thermal pressure coefficient. | Liquid water | Volumetric mass ({\mathrm{kg.m}}^{-3}) Constant pressure mass heat ({\mathrm{J.K}}^{-1}) Dynamic viscosity of liquid water (\mathrm{Pa.s}) Thermal expansion coefficient of liquid ({K}^{-1}) (if constant, see next section) Compressibility ({\mathit{Pa}}^{-1}) | {10}^{3} 4180 0.001 1.{10}^{-4} {K}_{e}=5.{10}^{-10} | | --- | --- | --- | | Solid | Young's modulus drained E(\mathrm{Pa}) Poisson's ratio Thermal expansion coefficient of solid ({K}^{-1}) | 3,14{10}^{9} 0.375 {10}^{-5} | | Reference state | Porosity Temperature (K) Liquid pressure (\mathrm{Pa}) | 0.18 273 0 | | Homogenized coefficients | Homogenized density ({\mathrm{kg.m}}^{-3}) Biot coefficient Intrinsic permeability ({m}^{2}) Thermal conductivity | 2410 0.6 {K}_{int}={10}^{-21} {\lambda}_{T}=1.61 | 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads It is imposed: - On the lower and left edges: zero displacements, zero hydraulic flow, zero thermal flow. These are symmetry conditions. - On the top and right edges: Total stress imposed on 12\mathit{MPa} , zero hydraulic flow, temperature imposed T(t) time function following a linear ramp such as: T(t)={T}_{0}+\frac{\Delta T}{{t}_{s}} where {t}_{s} corresponds to the simulation time (here {t}_{sim}=\mathrm{1h} ) and \Delta T the temperature variation imposed during this time (here \Delta T=40°C ). 1.4 Initial conditions P(x)=\mathrm{4MPa} and T(x)={T}_{0}=20°C everywhere. 2 reference solution It is called that the water mass input is written: {m}_{w}=\varphi .{\rho}_{w}.(1+{\varepsilon}_{v}) , which can be derived in the following form: {\mathrm{dm}}_{w}=d\varphi {\rho}_{w}(1+{\varepsilon}_{v})+d{\rho}_{w}\varphi (1+{\varepsilon}_{v})+{\rho}_{w}\varphi d{\varepsilon}_{v} with \varphi the Eulerian porosity. If we assume small movements, we will have: {\mathrm{dm}}_{w}=d\varphi {\rho}_{w}+d{\rho}_{w}\varphi +{\rho}_{w}\varphi d{\varepsilon}_{v} The variation in porosity is written according to the relationship: d\varphi =(b-\varphi )(d{\varepsilon}_{V}-3{\alpha}_{0}\text{dT}+\frac{{\text{dp}}_{w}}{{K}_{s}}) With {\alpha}_{0} the linear expansion of the skeleton (similar to the porous medium). It is recalled that the Biot b coefficient and the {K}_{s} solid grain compressibility module are connected to the "drained" compressibility module of the {K}_{0} porous medium, such as: b=1-\frac{{K}_{0}}{{K}_{s}} The variation in the density of water is also expressed as follows: \frac{d{\rho}_{w}}{{\rho}_{w}}=\frac{{\text{dp}}_{w}}{{K}_{w}}-3{\alpha}_{w}\text{dT} with the {K}_{w} water compressibility module and its {\alpha}_{w} expansion module. Finally, if the constitutive law is elastic, it is recalled that the deformation is related to the actual stress such as: d{\epsilon}_{V}=\frac{d\sigma '}{{K}_{0}}+3{\alpha}_{0}\text{dT} Furthermore, the wording in total constraint indicates that: d\sigma '=d\sigma +b{\text{dp}}_{w} , considering here that the medium is at constant containment, we have therefore: d\sigma '=b{\text{dp}}_{w} , which gives us the end d{\varepsilon}_{V}=\frac{b{\text{dp}}_{w}}{{K}_{0}}+3{\alpha}_{0}\text{dT} Now, you can inject (2), (3), (4) and (5) into equation (1) and you can obtain that: \frac{{\mathit{dm}}_{w}}{{\rho}_{w}}=(\frac{{b}^{2}}{{K}_{0}}+\frac{(b-\varphi )}{{K}_{s}}+\frac{\varphi}{{K}_{w}}){\text{dp}}_{w}+\varphi (3{\alpha}_{0}-3{\alpha}_{w})\text{dT} Considering that the medium is undrained, we have therefore: (\frac{{b}^{2}}{{K}_{0}}+\frac{(b-\varphi )}{{K}_{s}}+\frac{\varphi}{{K}_{w}}){\text{dp}}_{w}=\varphi (3{\alpha}_{w}-3{\alpha}_{0})\text{dT} What can be written in the form: {\text{dp}}_{w}=\Lambda \text{dT} With \Lambda the thermal pressure coefficient such as: \Lambda =\frac{\phi \left(3{\alpha}_{w}-3{\alpha}_{0}\right)}{\left(\frac{{b}^{2}}{{K}_{0}}+\frac{\left(b-\phi \right)}{{K}_{s}}+\frac{\phi }{{K}_{w}}\right)} It is noted that this coefficient shows the thermal differential ({\alpha}_{w}-{\alpha}_{0}) 2.1 Thermal dilation of constant water In case {\alpha}_{w}=\mathit{cte} the digital application is immediate. Digital application: With the data defined above, we obtain: \Lambda =2,25{10}^{5}\mathit{Pa.}{K}^{-1} This gives a pressure variation of \Delta T=40°C (i.e. a pressure of 13.01 MPa) for a temperature change of \Delta T=40°C . 2.2 Thermal dilation of water temperature function In this case, we will write \Lambda (T)=\frac{\phi \left(3{\alpha}_{w}(T)-3{\alpha}_{0}\right)}{\left(\frac{{b}^{2}}{{K}_{0}}+\frac{\left(b-\phi \right)}{{K}_{s}}+\frac{\phi }{{K}_{w}}\right)} et {\text{dp}}_{w}=\Lambda (T)\text{dT} To be able to incorporate this formula, thermal expansion of water is considered to be a linear function of the temperature such as {\alpha}_{w}=\mathit{a.}T+b . \Lambda (T) is also a linear function which is incorporated between the initial temperature T0 and the final temperature T1, giving: \Delta p=\frac{A}{2}.({\mathit{T2}}^{2}-{\mathit{T1}}^{2})+B(\mathit{T2}-\mathit{T1}) with A=\frac{3\phi a}{\left(\frac{{b}^{2}}{{K}_{0}}+\frac{\left(b-\phi \right)}{{K}_{s}}+\frac{\phi }{{K}_{w}}\right)} et B=\frac{\phi \left(\mathrm{3b}-3{\alpha}_{0}\right)}{\left(\frac{{b}^{2}}{{K}_{0}}+\frac{\left(b-\phi \right)}{{K}_{s}}+\frac{\phi }{{K}_{w}}\right)} Digital application: We're taking it here. a=2,63{10}^{-6} and b=-7{10}^{-4} which corresponds to {\alpha}_{w}(293)=6,67.{10}^{-5}{K}^{-1} and {\alpha}_{w}(333)=1,72.{10}^{-4}{K}^{-1} and are realistic values for water. Any calculation is made, for a temperature variation between 20°C and 60°C, a pressure variation of \Delta p=10,9\mathit{MPa} and therefore a final pressure of 14,9\mathit{MPa} . 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics A - 'AXIS_THMS' flat Modelling. 'ELAS' mechanical law. 'LIQU_SATU' coupling. - 20\times 20 elements \mathrm{Q4} equal width. - Thermal dilation of constant water 3.2 Modelling results A Time Discretization: 10 time step of 180s each. The solution calculated by Aster taking into account the movements of fluid and heat (diffusing phenomena), it is normal not to get exactly the reference solution. The differences remain very small. In theory the results should give exactly the same thing. The model differs slightly here, however, and the analytical solution indicated above is no longer entirely accurate, as it is not the isotropic relationship: d\varphi =(b-\varphi )(d{\varepsilon}_{V}-3{\alpha}_{0}\text{dT}+\frac{{\text{dp}}_{w}}{{K}_{s}}) The relationship used in this case becomes tensory (cf. doc R7.01.11) and is: d\phi =B:d\epsilon -\phi d{\epsilon}_{V}-3{\alpha}_{\phi }\text{dT}+\frac{{\text{dp}}_{\text{gz}}-{S}_{\text{lq}}{\text{dp}}_{c}}{{M}_{\phi }} with \frac{1}{{M}_{\varphi}}=(B-\varphi \delta ):{S}_{0}^{S}:\delta > where {S}_{0}^{S} the skeleton flexibility matrix, function of Young's modulus of the solid {E}^{S} matrix and Poisson's ratio of the solid {\nu}^{S} matrix. v7.34.102 WDNP102 – Reflection and absorption of a compression wave along a poroelastic column v7.34.102 WDNP102 – Reflection and absorption of a compression wave along a poroelastic column Summary: The efficiency of the elements paraaxials in hydromechanical modelling is tested. The case concerns the propagation of a compression wave in a poroelastic column. The wave is introduced and absorbed by the element paraaxial located at the base of the column after having reflected at its top. Two test cases are produced, one testing the 2D and the other testing the 3D. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The mesh of the poroelastic column is given opposite. The propagation axis is directed according to (\mathit{OY}) . The total height of the column is 25m , for 0.4m width. The first 5 meters from the bottom are discretized by elements of 1m thickness while the following 20m are discretized by elements of 0.2m thickness. The entire column contains 105 elements. mesh of the column 1.2 Material properties The material properties of coupled hydromechanical modelling are given in the table below. The linear, fully saturated, water-saturated, elastic porous material is assumed. From the following material properties, the speed of the compression waves is given by the relationship: {C}_{p}=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda +2\mu }{{\rho}_{\mathit{homo}}}}=534,14{\mathit{m.s}}^{-1} where \lambda and \mu are the Lamé modules. | Liquid water | Density {\rho}_{l} Compressibility {K}_{l} Viscosity \nu | 1000{\mathit{kg.m}}^{-3} 0,1\mathit{MPa} 0,001 | | --- | --- | --- | | Homogenized parameters | Intrinsic Permeability {K}^{int} Porosity \varphi Homogenized Density Mass {\rho}_{\mathit{homo}} | {10}^{-12}{m}^{2} 0,23 2105{\mathit{kg.m}}^{-3} | | Linear elastic solid skeleton | K Compressibility Module G shear module | 313,1\mathit{MPa} 215,6\mathit{MPa} | Table 1.2-1: Hydromechanical properties of the poro-elastic column 1.3 Boundary conditions and initials A compression wave in the column is to be propagated from bottom to top with a blockage of the upper part so that there is reflection of the wave at this point and inverse propagation from top to bottom. An absorbent border (element paraaxial) is placed at the base of the column in order to completely amortize the reflected wave. The column is subject to gravity, so geostatic conditions in both actual stresses and hydraulic pressure pre-exist initially in the column. The initial column balance is not obvious and requires the following procedure: - The base of the column, flanked by the element paraaxial (red), is blocked with very stiff springs. A prior static calculation ( Figure 1 ) allows to recover a field of stresses and hydraulic pressure in balance with the boundary conditions and loading; - Nodal forces (resulting from both mechanical and hydraulic forces, in green) are calculated in springs ( Figure 2 ); - These nodal forces are reinjected at the base where the springs are simultaneously deactivated by very low stiffness ( Figure 3 ). The boundary conditions thus defined allow to produce a perfectly balanced initial hydromechanical state; - Dynamic calculation can occur by injecting the wave from the element paraaxial ( Figure 4 ); To account for horizontal translation invariance (problem 1D), lateral displacements are consolidated by an restraint type LIAISON_DDL. v8.01.100 FDLV100 - Piston coupled to an incompressible fluid column v8.01.100 FDLV100 - Piston coupled to an incompressible fluid column Summary: This fluid field test (fluid-structure coupling) validates the modal-based mass calculation and performs, as part of a modal analysis, the calculation of the proper frequency of a piston-spring system coupled with an incompressible fluid column. To model the fluid, the elements thermal plane is used; to model the piston, 2D mechanical elements in flat deformation and a discrete element to model a spring. Finally, the fluid-structure interface is modelled by modified thermal linear elements to introduce an "acceleration" boundary condition into the fluid. The test case has only one model, two-dimensional. The specific frequency of the coupled system is found at 0.01% of the analytical result. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Steel pipe connected to the solid by a spring and coupled to an incompressible fluid column: | length: | L=1.0m | | --- | --- | | width: | d=0.25m | | \mathit{AB} width of piston: | 0.05m | Abscesses of points (in m ): | | A | B | L | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | x | –0.05 | | | 1.2 Material properties Fluid: Water : {\rho}_{0}=1000.0{\mathrm{Kg.m}}^{-3} Solid: Steel: {\rho}_{S}=7800.0{\mathrm{Kg.m}}^{-3} ; E=2.E11\mathrm{Pa} ; \nu =0.3 Resort connecting the piston to the massif: Discreet element of K_T_D_L type: K=(1.E5,1.E5,1.E5)N/m 1.3 Boundary conditions and loading Pressure (i.e. thermal analogy a zero temperature R4.07.03) is imposed in all nodes of the end of the fluid column. The spring clamped support is imposed on the massif and a displacement of the piston is imposed on \mathrm{Oy} . 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution Analytical calculus: When the structure vibrates in the fluid, it modifies the pressure field that obeys an equation of Laplace with boundary conditions from Von Neuman R4.07.03. In our case, given the symmetries of the problem, the pressure field depends only on the variable x and checks: \lbrace \begin{array}{cc}\frac{{\partial}^{2}p}{\partial {x}^{2}}=0& {(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x})}_{x=0}=-{\rho}_{f}{\ddot{x}}_{S}.n\\ p=0\text{en}x=L& \end{array} Thus, the pressure field is a function of the x affine. The two boundary conditions on the pressure involve: p=-{\rho}_{f}{\ddot{x}}_{S}.n(x-L) The pressure force on the structure is written: F=\underset{\Gamma}{\int}p(0)nd\Gamma =\underset{\Gamma}{\int}{\rho}_{f}L({\ddot{x}}_{S}.n)nd\Gamma Since the problem is one-dimensional, this force can be expressed algebraically according to the following acceleration component \mathrm{Ox} of the structure: F=-\ddot{x}\underset{\Gamma}{\int}{\rho}_{f}Ld\Gamma =-{\rho}_{f}Ld\ddot{x}=-{m}_{a}\ddot{x} with {m}_{a}={\rho}_{f}Ld This is the added linear mass of the fluid on the structure: it is noticed that it corresponds to the fluid mass in the column, that is to say the fluid mass displaced by the piston. The equation of the movement of the piston projected on \mathrm{Ox} is written (free vibration not damped due to the presence of the fluid): m\ddot{x}+Kx=F=-{m}_{a}\ddot{x}\mathrm{\iff }(m+{m}_{a})\ddot{x}+Kx=0 The proper frequency of this submerged system is thus written: f=\frac{1}{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{K}{m+{m}_{a}}} The effect of the fluid is therefore to lower the system's eigenfrequency in air. In Aster, the added mass matrix is determined on the modal basis of the structure in the vacuum: To calculate the added mass given above, the calculation of the proper mode of the piston-spring system is restricted to a unit-nominated translation movement: the modal base of the structure is therefore truncated to one mode in air (operator CALC_MODES option 'PLUS_PETITE'). This mode determines the added mass on the piston. K={10}^{5}N/m {m}_{a}=200\mathrm{kg}/m m=78\mathrm{kg}/m The proper frequency of the plunger-spring system is therefore f=3.018\mathit{Hz} 2.2 Baseline Analysis 2.3 Bibliographical references 1. A zero displacement of the cylinders is required according to \mathrm{Oy} . 1.4 Initial conditions Not applicable for mass-added calculation and modal analysis. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution Analytical calculus: It is assumed that the movements of the cylinders and the fluid are essentially plane. The longitudinal effects will be neglected in front of the transverse effects. The problem is two-dimensional. Given the symmetry, the reference used is a cylindrical (r,\theta ) marker linked to the central cylinder (see figure above). In this coordinate system and with this particular geometry, the normal \frac{\partial .}{\partial n} derivative is equal to the \frac{\partial .}{\partial r} derivative compared to r . In this part, the variable p refers to the hydrodynamic pressure field in the fluid created by the clean vibrations of the structures, {X}_{1/2} refers to the eigenmodes of the 1 or 2 cylinder, respectively. The eigenmodes of ({\Gamma}_{1}) and ({\Gamma}_{2}) border hulls in the absence of fluid are of the shape ( n refers to the order of mode): {X}_{\mathrm{1n}}(r)=\lbrace \begin{array}{}\cosn\theta \text{ou}\sinn\theta \\ 0\end{array} et {X}_{\mathrm{2n}}(r)=\lbrace \begin{array}{}0\\ \cosn\theta \text{ou}\sinn\theta \end{array} \theta is the azimutal angle. These modes are uncoupled of course. The first component corresponds to the normal displacement of the inner shell, the second to the outer shell. In the fluid volume, therefore, there are two problems to solve: > \Delta {p}_{\mathrm{1n}}=0 {(\frac{\partial {p}_{\mathrm{1n}}}{\partial n})}_{{\Gamma}_{1}}=-{\rho}_{f}\lbrace \begin{array}{}\cosn\theta \\ \text{ou}\\ \sinn\theta \end{array} {(\frac{\partial {p}_{\mathrm{1n}}}{\partial n})}_{{\Gamma}_{2}}=0 éq 2.1-1 et: > \Delta {p}_{\mathrm{2n}}=0 {(\frac{\partial {p}_{\mathrm{2n}}}{\partial n})}_{{\Gamma}_{1}}=0 {(\frac{\partial {p}_{\mathrm{2n}}}{\partial n})}_{{\Gamma}_{2}}=-{\rho}_{f}\lbrace \begin{array}{}\cosn\theta \\ \text{ou}\\ \sinn\theta \end{array} éq 2.1-2 The {p}_{\mathrm{1n}} field corresponds to the pressure field generated in the fluid if the {\Gamma}_{1} central shell vibrates alone, the {p}_{\mathrm{2n}} field is created by the {\Gamma}_{2} outer shell if it vibrates alone. The linearity of the Laplace equation allows each problem to be solved independently and then superimposed to find the total pressure field. The solution to the problem [eq2.1-1-o] is, in polar coordinates, of the [bib1] type: {p}_{\mathrm{1n}}(r,\theta )=\left\lbrace A{r}^{n}+B{(\frac{1}{r})}^{n}\right\rbrace \left\lbrace \begin{array}{}\cosn\theta \\ \text{ou}\\ \sinn\theta \end{array}\right\rbrace We must have n\ne 0 , because otherwise we have the non-conservation of fluid volume. A and B constants are determined by the boundary conditions: {(\frac{\partial {p}_{\mathrm{1n}}}{\partial n})}_{{R}_{1}}=-{\rho}_{f}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}\cosn\theta \\ \text{ou}\\ \sinn\theta \end{array}\right\rbrace et {(\frac{\partial {p}_{\mathrm{1n}}}{\partial n})}_{{R}_{2}}=0 The pressure field for each of the two problems is then found to be: {p}_{\mathrm{1n}}(r,\theta )=\frac{{\rho}_{f}{R}_{1}}{n}\frac{{(r/{R}_{1})}^{n}+{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{n}{({R}_{2}/r)}^{n}}{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{\mathrm{2n}}-1}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}\cosn\theta \\ \text{ou}\\ \sinn\theta \end{array}\right\rbrace et: {p}_{\mathrm{2n}}(r,\theta )=\frac{{\rho}_{f}{R}_{2}}{n}\frac{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{n}{(r/{R}_{1})}^{n}+{({R}_{2}/r)}^{n}}{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{\mathrm{2n}}-1}\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}\cosn\theta \\ \text{ou}\\ \sinn\theta \end{array}\right\rbrace The modal mass added coefficients {m}_{\mathrm{ijnm}}^{A} are calculated from the following formula R4.07.03 if i=1 or 2 , j=1 or 2 , (n,m) belongs to {i}^{2} . {m}_{\mathrm{ijnm}}^{A}={\int}_{{\Gamma}_{j}}{p}_{\mathrm{jn}}{X}_{\text{im}}(r).n({\Gamma}_{j})d{\Gamma}_{j} Indexation is a little more complex here than in the R4.07.03 formula: indices i and j refer to hulls et , and m and n indices are associated with the hull modes. It is noted that there are coupling modes of the various hulls, external and internal. On the one hand, the fluid does not couple different n index modes because the {\int}_{\Gamma}\cosn\theta \cosm\theta d\Gamma integrals are canceled; on the other hand, the fluid does not couple \cosn\theta and \sinn\theta modes because {\int}_{(\Gamma )}\cosn\theta \sinn\theta d\Gamma =0 . The only existing coupling is a coupling between the two hulls for the same modes. Each n mode is combined with a symmetrical 4 order matrix. A submatrix corresponding to the projection on n mode is written: {M}_{1}^{A}=(\begin{array}{cc}{m}_{\mathrm{11nn}}^{A}& {m}_{\mathrm{12nn}}^{A}\\ {m}_{\mathrm{21nn}}^{A}& {m}_{\mathrm{22nn}}^{A}\end{array}) The global matrix is written: \left[\begin{array}{cc}{M}_{1}^{A}& 0\\ 0& {M}_{2}^{A}\end{array}\right] with {M}_{1}^{A}={M}_{2}^{A} with {m}_{\mathrm{11nn}}^{A}=L{R}_{1}\underset{0}{\overset{2\pi }{\int}}{p}_{1}({R}_{1,}\theta )\left\lbrace \begin{array}{}\cosn\theta \\ \text{ou}\\ \sinn\theta \end{array}\right\rbrace d\theta Either: {m}_{\mathrm{11nn}}^{A}=\frac{\pi}{n}{\rho}_{f}{R}_{1}^{2}L\frac{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{\mathrm{2n}}+1}{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{\mathrm{2n}}-1} éq 2.1-3 We will get: {m}_{\mathrm{22nn}}^{A}=\frac{\pi}{n}{\rho}_{f}{R}_{2}^{2}L\frac{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{\mathrm{2n}}+1}{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{\mathrm{2n}}-1} éq 2.1-4 et: > {m}_{\mathrm{21nn}}^{A}={m}_{\mathrm{12nn}}^{A}=-\frac{\pi}{n}{\rho}_{f}{R}_{1}{R}_{2}L\frac{2({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{\mathrm{2n}}-1} éq 2.1-5 L is the height of the cylinder shells in the longitudinal direction. In our case, the n=1 modes of order of the hulls are considered only: they correspond respectively to the modes of translation of each of the hulls along an axis passing through the centre of the central tube: one takes those corresponding to the \mathrm{Ox} axis arbitrarily: the coefficients of added linear mass are written: {m}_{11}^{A}=\pi {\rho}_{f}{R}_{1}^{2}\frac{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{2}+1}{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{2}-1} {m}_{22}^{A}=\pi {\rho}_{f}{R}_{2}^{2}\frac{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{2}+1}{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{2}-1} {m}_{21}^{A}={m}_{12}^{A}=-\pi {\rho}_{f}{R}_{1}{R}_{2}\frac{2({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}{{({R}_{2}/{R}_{1})}^{2}-1} The equation of the generalized movement of the two coupled hulls is written: (\begin{array}{cc}{m}_{1}& 0\\ 0& {m}_{2}\end{array})(\begin{array}{}{\ddot{x}}_{1}\\ {\ddot{x}}_{2}\end{array})+(\begin{array}{cc}{k}_{1}& 0\\ 0& {k}_{2}\end{array})(\begin{array}{}{x}_{1}\\ {x}_{2}\end{array})=-(\begin{array}{cc}{m}_{11}& {m}_{12}\\ {m}_{12}& {m}_{22}\end{array})(\begin{array}{}{\ddot{x}}_{1}\\ {\ddot{x}}_{2}\end{array}) The pulses of the coupled system are given by the degree 4 equation: \det\left[(\begin{array}{cc}{m}_{1}+{m}_{11}& {m}_{12}\\ {m}_{12}& {m}_{2}+{m}_{22}\end{array}){\Omega}^{2}-(\begin{array}{cc}{k}_{1}& 0\\ 0& {k}_{2}\end{array})\right]=0 Digital application: {K}_{1}={10}^{7}N/m {K}_{2}={10}^{7}N/m {m}_{11}=33060\mathrm{kg}/m {m}_{22}=40004\mathrm{kg}/m {m}_{12}=–36200\mathrm{kg}/m Two frequencies are obtained: {f}_{1}=1.696\mathrm{Hz} {f}_{2}=4.128\mathrm{Hz} 2.2 Baseline Analysis 2.3 Bibliographical references R.J GIBERT. v8.01.103 FDLV103 - Concentric spheres separated by an incompressible fluid v8.01.103 FDLV103 - Concentric spheres separated by an incompressible fluid Summary: This test concerns the field of fluids in the inertial coupling aspect. v8.01.111 FDLV111 - Absorption of a pressure wave in a fluid column v8.01.111 FDLV111 - Absorption of a pressure wave in a fluid column Summary: The elements fluid-order 1 paraaxials are tested to apply absorbent conditions at the border of a finished mesh elements to simulate infinity in direct transient calculations. They are used to model an infinite fluid column, in 3D or 2D, in which a pressure wave is created using a piston. An interest is the non-reflection of the wave at the "infinite" end of the column. The two direct transient operators of Code_Aster , DYNA_VIBRA and DYNA_NON_LINE, are tested successively. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The system considered in the 3D case is that of a column of fluid with a square cross section and a piston of the same section animated by a rigid body movement according to the axis of the column. The lateral surface of the column is made up of a rigid, still guide. The absorbent elementss are placed on the opposite side of the piston to simulate the infinite character of the column in this direction. In the 2D case, the principle is identical with a column and piston supposed to be very wide, with only a vertical section Modelling (see diagram). 1.2 Material properties | Piston: concrete | | Audible wind: water | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | | | | | Density: | 2400{\mathit{kg.m}}^{-3} | Density: | 1000{\mathit{kg.m}}^{-3} | | Young's modulus : | 3,6{.10}^{10}\mathit{Pa} | Celerity: | 1500{\mathit{m.s}}^{-1} | | Poisson's ratio : | 0,48 | | | 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The lateral surface of the column of the fluid-structure elementss, which blocks the degrees of freedoms from zero displacements to reproduce the rigid wall condition, is provided. All nodes of the face of the piston in contact with the fluid are required to move according to x with the following temporal excitation function: 1.4 Initial conditions The piston is moved zero at the initial moment and the fluid is at rest. 2 reference solution The solution must show the absorption of an acoustic wave by the absorbent surface. The piston movement is a uniform translation according to the x axis. Given the symmetry of the problem around this axis, we will obtain an identical pressure field in all x=\mathrm{Cte} planes. Moreover, the absorbent boundary is orthogonal at this axis. Therefore, we study the absorption of flat pressure waves under normal incidence. The theory [bib1] says that with a fluid order 1 paraaxial boundary, this absorption is perfect. This is what we must check with this reference solution. Thus, by observing the evolution of the pressure in a given point of the mesh, we will focus on finding in the signal obtained the duration of the excitement and the return to rest after the passage of the wave, characteristic of its absorption. 2.1 Baseline This paragraph gives the results obtained with Code_Aster in this configuration. We check that they are satisfactory and take them as a reference for the future. They concern, for the 3D case, the pressure evolution in a point of the fluid located at 150m of the piston in the x direction and in the centre of the section in the yz plane. For the 2D case, the point is located at 40m of the piston in x direction and in the middle of the section in the y direction (in 2D, a shorter and refined mesh is taken). As expected, the width of the signal measured in both cases is identical to that of the excitation function. Physically, the compression due to the piston's advance is observed, then the depression corresponding to its retreat to its initial position. It is also clear that the return to rest immediately after the wave passage and the absence of a reflected signal at the end of the mesh are noted. 2.2 Uncertainties This is a numerical study result. Qualitative predictions are found. Numerical values are related to the accuracy of the calculation. Only the return to rest is clearly given by the analysis. 2.3 Bibliographical references 1. v8.01.113 FDLV113 - Pressure source in a fluid-filled ball in soil interaction - fluid - structure v8.01.113 FDLV113 - Pressure source in a fluid-filled ball in soil interaction - fluid - structure Summary: This test contributes to the validation of the Code_Aster - MISS3D chaining by the frequent method of coupling in soil-fluid-structure interaction (ISFS). This test allows you to consider all types of interface: soil-structure, fluid-structure, soil-fluid, free soil. It also allows you to test the loading by point pressure source in the fluid. It represents a ball, a hollow sphere of finite dimensions, filled with water. To have all types of interface, the lower half of the hollow sphere is modelled by Code_Aster as the domain "structure"; the upper half representing the domain "ground" of the same characteristics as the structure and the domain "fluid" is modelled by MISS3D. A source of harmonic pressure, of constant unit module for each frequency between 1\mathrm{Hz} and 30\mathrm{Hz} , is imposed on the center of the ball in the fluid medium. The radial displacement module obtained from the outside and inside the ball is tested against a calculated analytical solution. The concordance is correct provided that the effect of a parasitic resonance corresponding to the first proper frequency of the sphere with water mass added to the center is removed. This is possible by the introduction of a parameter RFIC in MISS3D. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Miss3D uses the frequent coupling method to account for the soil-fluid-structure interaction. This method, based on dynamic substructure, consists of cutting the study field into three sub-domains: - soil, - fluid, - structure. The result is 4 types of interface possible: - the soil-structure interface, - fluid-structure interface, - the ground-free interface. The soil, fluid, and structure The soil and structure are made of the same homogeneous material. In the coupled calculation Code_Aster -MISS3D, to represent the case of a hollow sphere of finite dimension filled with fluid, one models half of the solid medium as domain The fluid medium, which is inside the r=5m ray sphere, is taken into account with MISS3D. The solid medium occupies the volume between the {r}_{\mathrm{interne}}=5m and {r}_{\mathrm{externe}}=7m ray spheres. The domain 的structure Figure 1.1-a: Field of the ball of finished dimensions filled with fluid The elements interfaces are elements QUAD4 superfacial. The 的structure 的 domain (yellow in Figure 1-1.b) is modelled with elements HEXA8 density. The thickness according to radial direction is divided into four layers for a total of 1024 elements. The maximum size of the elements is 1.37m , which, with a secondary wave speed in the solid of 334m/\mathrm{sec} , must meet the 30\mathrm{Hz} frequency limit according to the criteria: {l}_{\text{elem\_max}}\le \frac{{l}_{\text{onde\_max}}}{8} f\le {f}_{\max}=\frac{{c}_{s}}{8{l}_{\text{elem\_max}}} Interfaces In Figure 1-1.b, the elements of the 4 interfaces are represented. There is a free surface area here. The ground-structure interface, in black, is discretized in 128 mesh cells and only includes the horizontal plane crown z=0 between 5m and 7m rays. The ground-fluid interface, in dark pink, and the fluid-structure interface, in blue, are discretized in 256 mesh cells. The free surface in green includes all the outer envelope of the upper half-sphere, also 256 mesh cells. Figure 1.1-b: Interfaces' superfacial models and meshes 1.2 Material properties The soil and structure The mechanical characteristics of the soil and structure used are those given in Table 1.1-a. | E | 700\mathrm{MPa} | | --- | --- | | NU | 0.2 | | RHO | 2500.\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} | | BETA | 0 | Table 1.2-a: soil and structural characteristics These characteristics induce shear wave speed: {c}_{s}=341.56m/s and compression wave speed: {c}_{p}=557.77m/s The fluid | Clerity | 150m/s | | --- | --- | | RHO | 1000.\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} | | BETA | 0. | Table 1.2-b: fluid characteristics A fluid speed characteristic lower than the compression shear wave speeds in the structure and soil is introduced to obtain resonances in the range of frequencies studied. 1.3 Boundary conditions and mechanical loadings A point fluid source condition is applied to the centre of the (000) coordinate ball with a P={P}_{o}\sin\omega t harmonic load whose {p}_{o} pressure module is unitary with a pulse that varies from 1\mathrm{Hz} to 30\mathrm{Hz} by 1\mathrm{Hz} steps. This corresponds to a Dirac at the initial moment in time. This returns to Code_Aster to insert the source coordinates into CALC_MISS under the SOURCE_FLUIDE key word. In order not to have a rigid body motion problem, the nodes of the mesh structure, which is located on the X , Y and Z axes respectively, were blocked ( Y and Z ), ( X and Z ), ( X and Y ). Thus, rigid body movements are prevented, while allowing radial movement. With respect to the ground-structure interface modes, it was noted that the static forced-type modes calculated with this boundary condition d-clamped support at the ground-structure interface cannot be a complete base for representing a spherical symmetry deformed. For this purpose, new static modes have been introduced into the modal base. The modes introduced are mode of type forced on the outer envelope of the lower half-sphere (in yellow in Figure 1.1-b). They correspond to a new limit condition of blocking according to the 3 degrees of freedom of all nodes of this surface, with the exception of its nodes intersection with the axes. For these nodes, the unit mode corresponding to the degree of freedom which is tangential to the surface is not used, because the displacement that is being sought does not have a component in this direction. Figure 1.3-a: Radial displacement measurement points The best result is obtained by using a modal base of Ritz without dynamic modes, and with the static modes completed as indicated above. Indeed, we have exactly the number of unknown displacements to determine to represent a spherical symmetry displacement, especially on the structure – fluid interface. 2 reference solution 2.1 Baseline The frequent coupling method between Miss3D and Code_Aster is described in the reference document [bib1]. The radial displacement module obtained from the outside and inside the ball is tested against a calculated and detailed analytical solution in an application study [bib2]. Pressure and development solutions depend only on radius and time. Total fluid pressure is considered to be due to the sum of two contributions: - {p}_{d} pressure due to the vibration of the wall at the interface with the solid medium, - {p}_{0} pressure due to the action of Dirac mass in the center of the sphere, in an infinite fluid - p={p}_{d}+{p}_{0} The Helmholtz equation of wave propagation in the fluid in the absence of a source is written in spherical coordinates after transformation of Fourier: \frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\frac{\delta}{\delta r}({r}^{2}\frac{\delta {p}_{d}}{\delta r})(r,\omega )+\frac{\omega}{{c}_{f}^{2}}{p}_{d}(r,\omega )=0 - By posing: {k}_{f}(\omega )=\frac{\omega}{{c}_{f}} , one obtains a solution of the form {p}_{d}=A(\sin\frac{({k}_{f}r)}{4\pi r}) , The solution for the {p}_{0} pressure is given by a function of Green and the pressure in the fluid is written: p=\frac{{e}^{i{k}_{f}r}}{4\pi r}+A(\sin\frac{({k}_{f}r)}{4\pi r}) The Navier equation of wave propagation in the solid in the absence of a source is written in spherical coordinates after transformation of Fourier and by changing variables u=\frac{\delta \phi }{\delta r} : \frac{{\delta}^{2}}{\delta {r}^{2}}(r\phi )(r,\omega )+{k}_{p}^{2}(r\phi )(r,\omega )=0 - By posing {k}_{p}(\omega )=\frac{\omega}{{c}_{p}} , one obtains a solution of the form: u=B\frac{{e}^{i{k}_{p}r}}{4\pi r}(\frac{i{k}_{p}r-1}{r})+C\frac{{e}^{-i{k}_{p}r}}{4\pi r}(\frac{-i{k}_{p}r-1}{r}) . The 3 unknown coefficients A , B and C are then determined from 3 limit conditions: - Continuity of normal movements at the \rho {\omega}^{2}u=\mathrm{grad}(p) ground-fluid interface for r={r}_{1} , - Continuity of normal stresses at the {\sigma}_{\mathrm{rr}}+p=0 ground-fluid interface for r={r}_{1} , - Zero radial stress on the {\sigma}_{\mathrm{rr}}=0 outer surface for r={r}_{2} , 2.2 Bibliographical references 1. It is important to have oriented the elements surface interfaces according to conventions described in document U2.06.08. 3.3 Tested quantities and results The tested values are m modules of the A (equatorial) and C (polar) responses for the 7-metre external radius. | Identification | Reference type | Reference | Tolerance | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | \mathrm{MDXA} ( 1\mathrm{Hz} ) | non-regression | 2.433100E-04 | 0.1% | | \mathrm{MDZC} ( 21\mathrm{Hz} ) | non-regression | 0.01679100 | 0.1% | | \mathrm{MDXA} ( 1\mathrm{Hz} ) | External source | 2.648E-04 | 9.0% | 4 Summary of the results The radial frequency-analytical displacement of A , B and C (positioned in Figure 1.3-a above) for 7m outside the post-contractor structure domain is represented in Figures 4a and 4b. The correct results are consistent overall. In particular, resonance frequencies generally are found to 19\mathrm{Hz} and 25\mathrm{Hz} despite a slight offset and the nonresonance displacements at points A and C in the equatorial and vertical planes. However, there is a significant difference in resonance amplitudes due to at least the previous slight offset. On the other hand, there is at least another disturbance with a parasitic resonance to 10\mathrm{Hz} . This frequency is the first specific frequency of the sphere with water mass added to the centre that can be found by a modal analysis calculation. The corresponding mode is a different incompressible fluid mode from the bulging modes sought here. This disturbance can be mitigated by the introduction of the RFIC parameter (here being 0.5) as given by MISS3D. The use of static modes forced on the outer envelope of the sphere is therefore exhaustive to represent spherical symmetry inflating modes, but it is therefore also likely to represent modes of another nature that may disturb the solution, notably at point B where no explicit limit conditions have been imposed to recover this spherical symmetry of displacements. The introduction of structural damping would also reduce the amplitude differences at resonance frequencies between analytical results and calculation. v8.01.114 FDLV114 - Seismic response of a cylindrical tank v8.01.114 FDLV114 - Seismic response of a cylindrical tank Summary: The objective of this test is to validate the seismic response of a cylindrical tank. In particular in model A, the impulsive contribution of the fluid contained in the reservoir is validated by an added mass method, the calculation of the participation factor and the actual modal masses of the wet modes. In the report [1], the details of the results are given, as well as the comparison with ANSYS and SYSTUS software or with the regulatory approach advocated by Eurocode 8. 1. v8.03.100 FDNV100 - Balking a water tank with elastic deformable wall v8.03.100 FDNV100 - Balking a water tank with elastic deformable wall Summary: This test, from the fluid-structure domain, proposes the implementation of a transient dynamic calculation (operator DYNA_NON_LINE) with consideration of a free surface. Given the absence of suitable reference values, it is test case non-regression. The stability analysis (with the keyword CRIT_STAB) is also valid for this fluid-structure problem. 1 Reference problem This test case, based on the model of the article [bib1], aims to test the correct consideration of a free surface in a fluid-structure calculation coupled with the DYNA_NON_LINE operator. 1.1 Geometry A parallelepipedic tank, filled with water, with external walls that are unformable, is considered. This rigid tank has a deformable inner plate, called \Gamma . It is clamped at its base at the bottom of the tank, with its vertical sides free. This flexible wall exceeds the free surface of a height of 12,9\mathrm{cm} : 1.2 Material properties The fluid (water) contained in the tank has the following characteristics: | density: | {\rho}_{f}=1000\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} | | --- | --- | | speed of sound: | c=1500m/s | The deformable wall is linear elastic (durumin): | density: | {\rho}_{s}=2787\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} | | --- | --- | | Young's modulus : | E=62,43\mathrm{GPa} | | Poisson's ratio : | \nu =0,35 | 1.3 Boundary conditions and loading 1.3.1 Dirichlet conditions The load defined here is of the type of displacement imposed on a surface. More precisely, the bottom of the container is considered to be only able to move according to the direction x . In this direction x , the system will be requested by imposing a time-based sinusoidal displacement of 1,7704\mathrm{Hz} frequency and 0,001m amplitude at the bottom of the tank. This displacement may be considered as a single-support type of stress applied by the base of the tank (seismic application). 1.3.2 Neumann conditions In superposition to the above-defined dirichlet surface condition, the model is also submitted to the gravity field (forced volume). Finally, the upper surface of the fluid domain is characterized by a free surface condition. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The only results of the literature [bib1] are modal types: eigenfrequencies and appearances of certain modes. Given the need to test the DYNA_NON_LINE operator, and given the relative complexity of the 3D model, it is not possible to find eigenfrequencies by transient analysis in a reasonable CPU time. Linear research is also used. For information, this type of analysis conducted with a random loading corresponding to a white noise requires, for probabilistic convergence reasons, a calculation for a physical loading time of 250s , which corresponds to a time CPU of a few hours. In order to have a calculation time of the order of a few minutes, it is mandatory to calculate the evolution over a short time (a few seconds). This restrictive framework does not allow to find precisely and in a way compatible with an automated post-processing the modal analysis results. The validation provided by this test can therefore only be of the non-regression type of the digital solution. Since the fluid-structure coupled computing features are already being tested for validation, this limitation to non-regression for this particular test case is not re-defining. As a further validation, the complete 250s signal calculation was performed. The spectra at the observation points showed a good match with the modal analysis results of [bib1]. To validate the stability analysis on this fluid-structure problem, we will use keyword CRIT_STAB from DYNA_NON_LINE. 2.2 Baseline The displacement values are tested at different times, depending on the x direction, for two points of the mesh: \mathrm{N145} and \mathrm{N3119} . These points are on the free surface, on either side of the deformable wall, as can be seen from the diagram in paragraph [§1.1]. As for stability, since the matrix of geometric stiffness is not to be used (which is unavailable for the elements DKT used here), the analysis can only be of the type looking for singularities of the stiffness matrix (so a clean value that tends to 0). The problem being linear elastic, one expects no instability and on the other, one should find the value of critical own (or critical load) as for the same model but without the fluid and worth -2,47726. This value of own will be the same in each step of calculation because the problem remains linear. 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution Digital solution (calculated with version 7.3.6 of the code). 2.4 Bibliographic reference 1. The stiffness and mass matrices of the fluid and fluid-structure coupling elements are tested. The free surface boundary condition is also tested. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry {L}_{a}=0.075 , {L}_{s}=0.025 , {L}_{e}=0.05m constant square section, a=0.05m or circular section (in the case axisymmetric) constant radius R=a=0.05m . 1.2 Material properties | Solid: E={2.10}^{11}\mathrm{Pa} | {\rho}_{s}=7800\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} | \nu =0.3 | | --- | --- | --- | | air : {c}_{a}=340m/s | {\rho}_{a}=1.2\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} | | | water : {c}_{e}=1400m/s | {\rho}_{e}=1000\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} | c=\mathrm{célérité}\mathrm{du}\mathrm{son} | c= speed of sound in the fluid 1.3 Boundary conditions and loading - For all M points on the (\mathrm{M1}\mathrm{M2}\mathrm{M3}\mathrm{M4}) side the pressure and displacement potential are zero (free surface condition), - For the solid P points, all degrees of freedom points are blocked except translation into x so that this solid behaves like a piston on the x axis. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution At low frequencies, the acoustic wavelengths of the movements envisaged are large compared to the characteristic dimension of the (\omega L/c\ll 1) fluid volume. The problem is therefore one-dimensional according to the x axis. It is shown [bib1] that a light fluid like air acts essentially as an added stiffness while a heavy fluid behaves only as an added mass. Therefore, the first specific frequency of the system can be calculated: \omega =\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} With: k={k}_{\text{air}}={\rho}_{a}{c}_{a}^{2}\frac{S}{{L}_{a}} Thus, we find: \omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\rho}_{a}{c}_{a}^{2}}{{L}_{a}\left({\rho}_{s}{L}_{s}+{\rho}_{e}{L}_{e}\right)}} Note: The first clean pulse \omega of the system checks well (\omega L/c\ll 1) . 2.2 Bibliographical references 1. v8.21.101 ADLV101 - Balking and acoustic modes of a water-filled parallelepipedic tank v8.21.101 ADLV101 - Balking and acoustic modes of a water-filled parallelepipedic tank Summary: This test, from the acoustic and fluid domain, is concerned with the search for the eigenfrequencies of a compressible fluid domain, including a free surface, contained in a rigid parallelepipedic tank. The modal analysis thus determines the first modes of stowage (in the presence of gravity) of the free surface of the fluid filling the tank, then the first acoustic modes. The first eight eigenfrequencies of stowage are found at less than 1% of the analytically calculated frequencies. The first two sound eigenfrequencies are found at less than 1% of the analytically calculated frequencies. The modellings proposed are: 的modelization E: PHENOMENE='MECANIQUE', elements fluid Serendip quadratic (p,\Phi ,z) ; 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry x y z Dimensions of the watertight and rigid tank: g Height: H=0.3m ; Length: L=0.8m ; Width: l=0.1m . 1.2 Material properties The modelled material is the homogeneous fluid contained in the tank: - density: {\rho}_{c}=1000\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} ; - speed of sound: c=1400m/s . The gravity is: g=9,81m/{s}^{2} . 1.3 Boundary conditions and loading The bottom and side sides are watertight and fixed. In fluctuating pressure + fluctuating displacement potential (P,\Phi ) in linear acoustics of a barotropic medium, it is therefore unnecessary to impose any condition on these walls. Similarly in fluctuating pressure formulation alone. The free surface subject to the action of the gravity is affected by linear modelling of (serious) sluggishing waves to the first order of AIRY (or STOKES) via elements finished (P,\Phi ,z) . However, if this phenomenon is neglected, in fluctuating pressure + potential formulation, the boundary condition: (P,\Phi )=(0,0) , cf. is affected over the entire free surface. [[R4.02.02]](https://code-aster.org/V2/doc/default/en/man_r/r4/r4.02.02.pdf). 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The reference [bib3] provides the general formula for the stowing modes of a compressible fluid domain comprising a free surface, contained in a rigid walled parallelepipedic tank: {f}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\sqrt{\pi g\sqrt{\frac{{i}^{2}}{{L}^{2}}+\frac{{j}^{2}}{{l}^{2}}}\tanh\left[\pi H\sqrt{\frac{{i}^{2}}{{L}^{2}}+\frac{{j}^{2}}{{l}^{2}}}\right]} where i and j are the whole orders of the longitudinal and transverse modes (number of nodal lines in each horizontal direction). Fluctuation pressure modes have an expression of the shape: {p}_{ij}(x,y,z)=\cos\left(i\pi \frac{2x+l}{2l}\right)\cos\left(j\pi \frac{2y+L}{2L}\right)\left(\cosh\left({\lambda}_{ij}(H-z)\right)+{A}_{ij}\sinh\left({\lambda}_{ij}(H-z)\right)\right) where {\lambda}_{ij} is the vertical wave number checking: {\lambda}_{ij}H\tanh\left({\lambda}_{ij}H\right)=4{\pi}^{2}{f}_{ij}H/g and with a checking coefficient: {A}_{ij}=-\tanh\left({\lambda}_{ij}H\right) .
