v8.21.102 ADLS102 - Meridian fluid-elastic oscillator v8.21.102 ADLS102 - Meridian fluid-elastic oscillator Summary: The objective is to calculate the displacement of the piston of a "merid fluid-elastic oscillator". It is a spring plunger coupled with a fluid contained in a rigid and fixed wall channel; the channel is crossed by a depressurization wave. The plan problem of this meridian model is considered. This two-dimensional problem is reduced to a one-dimensional problem by considering by approximation that the transverse flow speeds induced by the piston movement are instantly transmitted in axial speeds. Only one model is used. The mode calculation is in u,p,\phi formulation. Elements 2D is therefore used; these elements are based on mesh cells QUAD4 for fluid and piston, on mesh cells SEG2 for fluid and piston interface to account for fluid interaction structure (PHENOMENE=‘MECANIQUE The non-wave return boundary conditions are made by Modelling a shock absorber piston at each end; the excitation is achieved by applying a depression to the inlet piston. The fluid considered is water (chaud), the model schematizing fluid-structure interaction in the ring space between the core vessel and the core envelope during rapid depressurization. An exact analytical solution exists. Its comparison with the results produced allows to validate the consideration of the fluid coupling structure in 2D. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The meridian fluid-elastic d-oscillator model schematizing fluid-structure interaction in the ring space of the core-bulletin is described below. The meridian fluid elastic oscillator is a model of the reactor core ring-shaped space, consisting of an oscillator (lateral-spring track with a movable wall) coupled with a compressible fluid contained in a rigid and fixed wall channel. The channel is crossed by a depressurization wave. The [Figure] illustrates the model described. Maridian fluid-elastic oscillator global scheme The channel is rectangular cross section e \times H in size and the wall piston is rigid and is only moving on z perpendicular to a wall. A wave of depressurization arrives from the left; by going to the right (without possibility of return) this wave sucks the piston which, by its resulting displacement, generates waves propagating towards the ends of the conduit, supposedly infinitely long so that there is no reflection. A two-dimensional model of this system, as shown in [Figure], is being designed. Theoretical two-dimensional mechanical representation Its geometrical characteristics are as follows: - length of the wall piston: {2L}=5,0 \, m - fluid height: e=0,5 \, m - fluid width: H=1,0 \, m - fluid section: S=e \times H 1.2 Material properties The physical characteristics of the fluid material (hot water) in the tube are as follows: - density: {\rho}_{f}=0,75 \times {10}^{3} \, {kg}/{m}^{3} , - speed of sound: {c}_{f}=1,0 \times {10}^{3} \, m/s . The physical characteristics of the materials constituting the wall piston and the end pistons are only a formal role in the calculation, as the structure (the channel) is considered to be perfectly rigid. These physical characteristics of material are as follows: - Young's modulus E=2,0 \times {10}^{12} \,{Pa} , - Poisson's ratio \nu = 0,3 , - density {\rho}_{s}=0\, {kg}/{m}^{3} . 1.3 Characteristics of springs, masses and shock absorbers The characteristics of the wall plunger as an oscillator are as follows: - stiffness: K=5,0 \times {10}^{10} \, N/m - Mass: M=200,0 \times {10}^{3} \, {kg} - Depreciation: A = 0 \ {Ns}/m The characteristics of the end pistons as oscillators are as follows: - stiffness: k=0,0 \, N/m - Mass: m=0,0 \, {kg} - Depreciation: a={\rho}_{f} \, {c}_{f} \, S = 37,5 \times {10}^{4} \, {Ns}/m 1.4 Boundary conditions and loads The wall piston is infinitely rigid and its displacement is only on the vertical axis. The fluid length is infinite and there is no reflection of the end of the waves: this boundary condition is simulated in the model by a piston at each end, of zero mass, moving only on the axis of the x and equipped with an adequate shock absorber with a damping; these pistons are also infinitely rigid. A total reflection of the waves is made on infinitely rigid walls of the fluid tube. This condition is realized simply by omitting to model the wall by elements structure. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The purpose is to determine the z(t) time shift of the wall piston. The plane problem of this meridian model is considered to be the geometric, mechanical and fluid characteristics of which are described in [Figure]; the lateral piston is {2L} long. The two-dimensional problem is reduced to a one-dimensional problem by considering by approximation that \dot{z} transverse flow speeds induced by piston motion are instantly transmitted in axial speeds in the channel. Under the wall plunger, in a volume of dx extended control, one considers d\Omega = e \, dx . One can then write: d(\delta V) = \frac{1}{2e} \, d\dot{z} \, {dx} = \frac{1}{2e} \, \ddot{z} \, {dx} \, {dt} In the fluid, the velocity variation and the pressure variation in adiabatic evolution are connected by: d(\delta P) = {\rho}_{f} \, {c}_{f} \, d(\delta V) The pressure at the instant t in a point d-abscisse x results from the superposition of the propagation of all the elementary sources distributed on the piston. The coupling therefore consists in this: the movement of the \ddot{z}(t) acceleration piston induces a pressure field P(x,t) in the channel whose resulting stress on the extent of the piston itself acts in return on the dynamic of the oscillator. The geometric, mechanical and fluid characteristics of the model are presented in [Figure]. The piston and fluid are first considered to be at rest and a release of the oscillator is made at the moment t=0 by imposing an initial speed. The expression of the pressure in a channel point develops: P(x,t) = \frac{\rho_f \, c_f}{2 \, e} \, \int_{0}^{t} { \left[ \int_{-L}^{x} { \ddot{z} \left( \tau - \frac{\vert x - u \vert}{c_f} \right) du } + \int_{x}^{L} { \ddot{z} \left( \tau - \frac{\vert u - x \vert}{c_f} \right) du } \, d\tau \right] } z(0)=0 and z(t)=0 are available for negative t and z\left(-\frac{L-x}{{c}_{f}}\right)=0 since upstream of the piston (i.e. x between -L and L ) the amount in brackets is still negative. Similarly, z\left(-\frac{L+x}{{c}_{f}}\right)=0 is available. Finally, he comes: P(x,t) = \frac{\rho_f \, c_f^2}{2 \, e} \left[ 2z(t) - z \left( t-\frac{L-x}{{c}_{f}} \right) - z \left( t-\frac{L+x}{{c}_{f}} \right) \right] This expression is incorporated on x to obtain the result of the pressure forces on the piston: R(t) = -H \, {\int}_{-L}^{+L} {P(x,t)\, {dx} } = -2H \, {\int}_{0}^{+L} {P(x,t)\, {dx} } P(x,t) is paired in x , so just integrate on half the piston. Hence the expression of the resultant pressure forces on the piston in the hypothesis of small movements: R(t) = - \frac{H \, \rho_f \, c_f^2}{e} \, \left[ 2 \, L \, z(t) - c_f \, \int_{t-\frac{2\, L}{c_f}}^{t} { z(u) \, du } \right] The movement of the oscillator therefore follows the equation: M\ddot{z} + Kz + \frac{2 \, H \, L \, {\rho}_{f} \, {c}_{f}^{2}}{e} z - \frac{H \, {\rho}_{f} \, {c}_{f}^{3}}{e} \, \int_{t-\frac{2\, L}{c_f}}^{t} { z(u) \, du } = 0 or: M\ddot{z} - {F}_{int} - {F}_{cpl} = 0 if we put it down {F}_{int} = - Kz - \frac{2 \, H \, L \, {\rho}_{f} \, {c}_{f}^{2}}{e} z et {F}_{cpl} = \frac{H \, {\rho}_{f} \, {c}_{f}^{3}}{e} \, \int_{t-\frac{2\, L}{c_f}}^{t} { z(u) \, du } The case of the propagation of a steep front decompression wave \Delta {P}_{0} along the duct is now considered. At the moment t=0 , this wave attacks the wall plunger still at rest, creating an excitation force such as: {F}_{exc} = \left \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc} H \, {c}_{f} \, t \, \Delta {P}_{0} & \text{si}& t < \frac{2L}{{c}_{f}}\\ 2 \, H \, L \, \Delta {P}_{0} & \text{si}& t \ge \frac{2L}{{c}_{f}} \end{array} \right . The equation of motion then reads: M\ddot{z} = {F}_{int} + {F}_{cpl} + {F}_{exc} This equation is solved numerically for the presented characteristics of the meridian l-oscillator. 2.2 Baseline z(t) displacement of the wall piston. 2.3 Uncertainty of the solution analytical solution. 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. STIFKENS: "Transitional calculus in Code_Aster with vibro-acoustic elements". Internal note R&D HP-51/97/026/A. 1. TEPHANY, A. HANIFI, C. LEHAUT: "elements of fluid-structure interaction analysis in ring space core-cave in case of d的APRP" - internal note SEPTEN ENTMS/94.057. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics 3.1.1 Vibro-acoustic system equivalent to model In order to avoid the return waves from the ends of a necessarily finite dimension Modelling these ends are equipped with "piston-absorbent" systems as on the [Figure]. The channel is modelled over a total length of 28 \, m sufficient to obtain with certainty, at least the first two extrema of the piston displacement curve without disturbance of a reflection wave at the ends. Equivalent Vibro-acoustic System 3.1.2 Digital Modelling in elements finished We chose to model in 2D. For fluid : Modelling is in \left( p,\phi \right) formulation. v8.21.200 FDLL200 - clamped pipework and free by fluid beam-structure v8.21.200 FDLL200 - clamped pipework and free by fluid beam-structure Summary: The objective is to calculate the low frequency behaviour of a pipe filled with water. The pipe has a circular cross section; it is clamped at one end and free from the other. The elements of elasto-acoustic beam available in Code_Aster that takes into account the fluid interaction structure (PHENOMENE= 'MECANIQUE', MODELISATION= 'FLUI_STRU'). The boundary conditions are mechanical to simulate the structure's clamped support, and acoustic to simulate the fluid tank condition in this point (boundary conditions of zero pressure and zero fluid displacement potential). The fluid that is considered is a heavy fluid so as to highlight the phenomenon of coupling between the fluid column and the constitutive structure of the piping. The properties of the fluid and the material of the structure are chosen so that the speed of a wave spreading in the fluid is the same as the speed of a mechanical wave spreading in the piping. Under these conditions, the first mode of the structure resonates at the same frequency as the fluid column. Modelling A is based on a constant section and an exact analytical solution exists which provides the first eigenfrequency. Comparison with the results produced by Code_Aster (search for clean values) validates the consideration of fluid coupling structure in the longitudinal direction, with the transverse effects being non-existent in this model. This allows partial testing of the stiffness matrix and mass one. The modellings B and C are used to validate the case of variable circular sections. In the first section, the section is declared variable type (VARI_SECT='HOMOTHETIQUE' in AFFE_CARA_ELEM) but the parameters define a constant section. The solution is therefore the same as for Modelling A. In the last model, the section is actually variable and then only one test of non-regression is performed. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The pipe is a hollow cylinder with circular cross section, filled with fluid. Pipe characteristics: | length: | L=1,0m | | --- | --- | | outer diameter: | D=0,1m | | thickness: | \mathrm{ep}=0,01m | For Modelling C, the section that becomes variable is modified: the diameter varies from 0.1 to 0.11m while the thickness ranges from 0.011 to 0.01m. 1.2 Material properties The physical characteristics of the material constituting the tube are as follows: Young's modulus : E=1,0·{10}^{10}\mathrm{Pa} Poisson's ratio: \nu =0,3 density: {\rho}_{s}=1,0·{10}^{4}\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} longitudinal wave speed: {c}_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{E}{{\rho}_{s}}}=1,0·{10}^{3}m/s The physical characteristics of the fluid material in the tube are as follows: density: {\rho}_{f}=1,0·{10}^{3}\mathrm{kg}/{m}^{3} speed of sound: {c}_{f}=1,0·{10}^{3}m/s 1.3 Boundary conditions and loading - Move only on x axis. - Clamped support of the pipework in the end A . - Free pipe at the end B . - For the fluid tank condition A end. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The vibrational behaviour of a fluid-filled pipe is studied. The pipe is clamped at one end and free at the other end. The pipe section is constant and circular. The low frequencies of longitudinal pipe behaviour are examined. The following are defined: | Tube length: | L | | --- | --- | | Young's modulus of the hose: | E | | external diameter of the pipe: | D | | wall thickness: | \mathrm{ep} | | area of solid section: | {S}_{s} | | area of fluid section: | {S}_{f} | | speed in the pipe (structure): | {c}_{s} | | speed in the fluid: | {c}_{f} | The fluid and pipe characteristics were selected to have the following relationship: {c}_{f}={c}_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{E}{{\rho}_{s}}}=c=1000m/s In this particular case of equality of speed, it is shown [bib2] that the first frequency proper to the coupled problem is such that: \mathrm{tg}(\frac{\omega L}{{c}_{s}})=\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{s}}{{S}_{f}}.\frac{E}{{\rho}_{f}{c}^{2}}} It is valid in this case: f=157,94\mathrm{Hz} 2.2 Baseline Only one model is used. The calculation of the modes is in u,p,\varphi formulation. There is no reference solution in case the section is variable (modelization C). 2.3 Uncertainty of the solution analytical solution. 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. WAECKEL F., DUVAL C.: Note of principle and use of elements pipe implemented in Code_Aster . Internal Note R&D HP-61/92.138 2. DUVAL C. : Dynamic response under random excitation in Code_Aster . Internal note R&D HP-61/92.148 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics The Modelling of the elasto-acoustic beams is in u,\theta ,p,\phi formulation. It is done by assigning mesh cells type SEG2 (segments to 2 nodes) d-elements PHENOMENE= 'MECANIQUE', MODELISATION= 'FLUI_STRU'. The elements are assigned the characteristics of circular cross-section: | external radius | {R}_{\mathit{ext}}=0,100m | | | --- | --- | --- | | thickness | \mathit{ep}=0,010m | cf. [§1.1] | These elements are also assigned a mixed material of behaviour at the same time ELAS: | Young's modulus | E=1,0.1010\mathit{Pa} | | | --- | --- | --- | | Poisson's ratio | \nu =0,3 | | | density | {\rho}_{s}=1000\mathit{kg}/{m}^{3} | | et FLUIDE: | speed | c=1000m/s | | | --- | --- | --- | | density | {\rho}_{f}=1000\mathit{kg}/{m}^{3} | cf. [§1.2] | Degrees of freedom (DDL) translation into y and z (DY and DZ) and all degrees of freedom rotation (DRX, DRY and DRZ) of all nodes are blocked. For the fluid the tank condition at the end A is imposed by PRES= 0. and PHI= 0. on the node \mathit{NO1} . 3.2 Mesh characteristics The total number of nodes used for this mesh is 26. The mesh cells are 25 and SEG2 type. The mesh file is in ASTER format. 3.3 Calculation We want to validate the elements of elasto-acoustic beam. The frequency of the first axial coupled mode is calculated with the CALC_MODES operator. 3.4 Test values The test shall be conducted on the frequency of the first coupled axial mode of the fluid-containing piping. The relative tolerance of d-difference relative to the analytical value is 0.1 per cent. | Mode number | Analytical value | | --- | --- | | 1 | 157,93981\mathit{Hz} Value non-regression | 3.5 Note The reference values are both analytical values and those obtained by Code_Aster when test case is returned, which will allow the non-regression to be verified later in the evolution of the code. 4 Modelling B 4.1 Modelling characteristics The Modelling A is repeated by modifying only the report of the section of the piping. Under the keyword AFFE_CARA_ELEM, a case of variable cross section is declared with VARI_SECT='HOMOTHETIQUE', but with constant radius and diameter parameters. This is done to validate the variable cross section option, in the sense of the keyword, but by finding the same solution as for Modelling A. 4.2 Test values The test shall be carried out on the frequency of the first coupled axial mode of the piping containing a fluid which shall be identical to that of model A. The relative tolerance of d-difference relative to the analytical value is 0.1 per cent. | Mode number | Analytical value | | --- | --- | | 1 | 157,93981\mathrm{Hz} Value non-regression | 4.3 Note The reference values are both analytical values and those obtained by Code_Aster when test case is returned, which will allow the non-regression to be verified later in the evolution of the code. 5 Modelling C 5.1 Modelling characteristics Model A is repeated by changing only the circular section which becomes variable. The diameter ranges from 0.1 to 0.11m while the thickness ranges from 0.011 to 0.01m. 5.2 Test values The test is about the frequency of the first coupled axial mode of the fluid-containing piping. As the section is variable, it is no longer possible to compare with the reference solution and only the non-regression is verified for this Modelling. 6 Summary of the results It is found that the calculated frequency value of the first coupled axial mode reproduces the analytical value with a relative accuracy of 0.004% in the case of a constant cross-section.

v8.21.301 ADLV301 – Cavity-plate coupling problem v8.21.301 ADLV301 – Cavity-plate coupling problem Summary: The objective of this test case is to calculate the pressure fields in a cavity with one of the walls flexible, the other walls being perfectly rigid. The excitation is mechanical and consists of a point normal force applied to the flexible wall. Vibro-acoustic finished elementss are used (modelization A: 3D_FLUIDE and FLUI_STRU) The boundary conditions are purely mechanical, allowing to create a deformed on the flexible, distorted wall that is at the source of the acoustic field in the cavity. The transmission between the plate and the cavity field is managed by elements interface "fluid-structure", suitable for Modelling by elements finished vibro-acoustics. The cavity dimensions are large enough and the plate thickness is small to observe a non-negligible coupling effect. In addition, the excitation is de-activated to create a field of movement on the plate and a three-dimensional acoustic field in the cavity. An exact analytical solution exists. This test case allows you to validate the consideration of fluid-structure coupling. v8.21.312 ADLV312 – Water-filled flexible cylindrical tank v8.21.312 ADLV312 – Water-filled flexible cylindrical tank Summary: This test is for modal analysis of a water-filled tank. The fluid volume has a free surface. The tank is modeled by elements plate DKT and the fluid by elements vibro-acoustic 3D. The calculation of hydroelastic eigenmodes is not particularly relevant to the slurry modes with low strain energy vis-à-vis hydroelastic modes. To improve the identification of these modes, the generalised masses are calculated after imposing the standard on a given degree of freedom. The reference values of the eigenfrequencies are obtained numerically from modellings 3D and Fourier in the SAMCEF software. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Figure 1.1 Geometry of the problem Dimensions of the container: - height : \text{H}=0.3048\text{m} - medium radius : \text{R}=0.076073\text{m} - shell thickness : \text{e}=0.254\times {10}^{-3}\text{m} The ibre surface is located at Z=\text{H} . It is perpendicular to the Z axis. 1.2 Material properties The properties of the fluid filling the cavity are as follows: | Sound speed | {c}_{F}=1400{\text{m.s}}^{-1} | | --- | --- | | Density | {\rho}_{F}=1000{\text{kg.m}}^{-3} | The properties of the hull are as follows: | Young's modulus | E=2.06\times {10}^{11}\text{Pa} | | --- | --- | | Poisson's ratio | \nu =0.3 | | Density | {\rho}_{S}=7850.0{\text{kg.m}}^{-3} | 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads Clamped support at base: \textrm{En tout point tel que} Z=0 Fluid subject to a field of gravity: | In all point fluid | Gravity g=9.81{\text{m/s}}^{2} next Z | | --- | --- | 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The reference values for the eigenfrequencies are obtained numerically: the average of the results obtained from an analysis of Fourier and two 3D analyses is obtained. The formulation for the fluid is the same in all three cases: it is an incompressible fluid, discretized by a potential displacement. The hull of Fourier is of the Reissner type, the models of 3D hulls are of the Mindlin (3D-1) type and hybrid (3D-2) type, respectively. The analyses were carried out using the SAMCEF software. In each case, the meshes are refined until a stable solution is obtained. In order to improve the identification of these modes, the SAMCEF is identified in SAMCEF and the same is applied in the tests. This will allow the generalised masses to be compared. 2.2 Baseline The table below provides the reference values for the first mode of harmonics 2 to 7 (the harmonic "n" is in \cos(n\theta ) ). Relative the difference is calculated in relation to the numerical result furthest from the reference. | Harmonistic | Fourier ( \mathit{Hz} ) | Model 3D-1 ( \mathit{Hz} ) | Model 3D-2 ( \mathit{Hz} ) | Reference ( \mathit{Hz} ) | difference (%) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 4 | 71.2 | 71.5 | 70.8 | 71.2 | 1.0 | | 3 | 77.5 | 77.7 | 77.0 | 77.4 | 0.9 | | 5 | 98.8 | 99.6 | 98.3 | 98.9 | 1.3 | | 2 | 133.6 | 133.6 | 132.9 | 133.4 | 0.5 | | 6 | 147.3 | 149.4 | 146.6 | 147.8 | 1.9 | | 7 | 211.4 | 216.0 | 210.4 | 212.6 | 2.7 | 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution - The uncertainty varies from frequency to frequency. the difference relative the largest is less than 3% (see table above). 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics A Figure 3.1. mesh of Modelling A Only half of the tank is meshed. This model cannot be used to calculate the twist modes around the Z axis. The tank is regularly meshed with elements quadrangular plate (DKT Modelling). The fluid is meshed with elements fluid volume (3D_FLUIDE Modelling), the upper part is covered with a free surface layer of elements (2D_FLUI_PESA Modelling). The fluid-structure interface is lined with elements quadrangular coupling (FLUI_STRU Modelling). 3.2 Mesh characteristics Number of nodes: 2822 Number of mesh cells and types: 64 TRIA3, 1280 QUAD4, 512 PENTA6 and 2048 HEXA8 3.3 Tested quantities and results | Identification | Reference value | Reference type | Tolerance (%) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Mode 1 | 71.2 | 'SOURCE_EXTERNE' | 4.6 | | Mode 2 | 77.4 | 'SOURCE_EXTERNE' | 3.5 | | Mode 3 | 98.8 | 'SOURCE_EXTERNE' | 5.4 | | Mode 4 | 133.4 | 'SOURCE_EXTERNE' | 2.0 | | Mode 5 | 147.8 | 'SOURCE_EXTERNE' | 6.5 | | Mode 6 | 212.6 | 'SOURCE_EXTERNE' | 7.7 | 4 Summary of the results In this test, only the structural frequencies are tested; the frequencies of the free surface are not considered. v8.22.100 AHLV100 - Anechoic output waveguide v8.22.100 AHLV100 - Anechoic output waveguide Summary: A straight waveguide with anechoic output, rigid walls, whose propagation medium is "normal" air, is excited by a vibrating piston harmonically. The acoustic pressure field of the harmonic response for 13 different modellings is calculated by an acoustic formulation. The results are tested in 2 points at the inlet and 2 points at the outlet. They enable the validation of rigidity, mass, damping (impedance), source vector (normal speed imposed) and post-processings operators. The reference results are derived from an analytical calculation. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Tube with rectangular cross-section: | length: | L={l}_{x}=1.0m | | --- | --- | | height: | h={l}_{y}=0.1m | | width: | l={l}_{z}=0.2m | Point coordinates (in m ): | | A | B | C | D | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | x | | | 1.00 | 1.00 | | y | | 0.05 | | 0.05 | | z | 0.20 | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.10 | 1.2 Material properties Air: {\rho}_{c}=1.3\mathrm{kg.}{m}^{-3} {c}_{0}=343.{\mathrm{m.s}}^{-1} 1.3 Boundary conditions and loading | Normal inlet speed | V={V}_{n}\times \exp(i\omega t) with {V}_{n}=0.014{\mathrm{m.s}}^{-1} | | --- | --- | | | f=500\mathrm{Hz} | | Impedance at the \mathrm{CD} end | Z={\rho}_{0}.{c}_{0}=445.9{\mathrm{kg.m}}^{-2}{s}^{-1} | 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The general analytical solution for a waveguide is written: - for pressure: p(x,y,z)=A\exp(\mathit{ikx})+B\exp(-\mathit{ikx}) - for vibration speed: V=-\frac{1}{{\rho}_{0}{c}_{0}}\left(A\exp(\mathit{ikx})-\mathit{Bexp}(-\mathit{ikx})\right){e}_{x} - A and B are determined by boundary conditions: \text{En}x=0\to {V}_{n}={V}_{n0} \text{En}x=L\to p(L,y,z)=ZV(L,y,z)\cdot {n}_{L} This gives: A=B\left(\frac{Z-{\rho}_{0}{c}_{0}}{Z+{\rho}_{0}{c}_{0}}\right)\exp(-2\mathit{ikL}) Et: B=\frac{{\rho}_{0}{c}_{0}{V}_{n}}{\left(\frac{Z-{\rho}_{0}{c}_{0}}{Z+{\rho}_{0}{c}_{0}}\right)\exp(-2\mathit{ikL})-1} In the case studied, the output of the guide is anechoic , Z={\rho}_{0}{c}_{0} and therefore: p(x,y,z)={\rho}_{0}{c}_{0}{V}_{n}\exp(-\mathit{ikx}) V(x,y,z)=-{V}_{n}\exp(-\mathit{ikx}){e}_{x} For acoustic intensity: I=\frac{1}{2}p{V}^{\text{ }}=\frac{1}{2}{\rho}_{0}{c}_{0}{V}_{n}^{2}{e}_{x} That is, the active acoustic intensity uniform throughout the guide and parallel to the axis. The eigenfrequencies are given for the guide closed at both ends by: {f}_{m,n,p}=\frac{{c}_{0}}{2}{\left(\frac{{m}^{2}}{{I}_{x}^{2}}+\frac{{n}^{2}}{{I}_{y}^{2}}+\frac{{p}^{2}}{{I}_{z}^{2}}\right)}^{\frac{1}{2}} 2.2 Baseline Pressure at A,B,C,D points (for modellings A, B, C, D, E). Acoustic intensity at A,B,C,D points (for modellings A and C). Specific frequencies 2 to 9. 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution analytical solution 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. BOUIZI A. v8.22.101 AHLV101 - Anechoic output waveguide v8.22.101 AHLV101 - Anechoic output waveguide Summary: A straight wave guide with anechoic output, rigid walls, whose propagation medium is "normal" air, is excited by a harmonic incident wave, normal at the inlet face. The acoustic pressure field of the harmonic response is calculated using the elasto-acoustic formulation of displacement-potential displacement pressure. The tests concern six different modellings (elements three-dimensional, two-dimensional, and axisymmetric elasto-acoustic finished, and axisymmetric), they validate the stiffness, mass, impedance, and source vector matrices for the six modellings. The first three are for FORMULATION='U_P_PHI', the following three for FORMULATION='U_P' and the last three for FORMULATION='U_PSI'. The reference result is derived from an analytical calculation. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Tube with rectangular cross section: | length: | L={l}_{x}=1.0m | | --- | --- | | height: | h={l}_{y}=0.1m | | width: | l={l}_{z}=0.2m | Point coordinates (in m ): | | A | B | C | D | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | x | | | 1.00 | 1.00 | | y | | 0.05 | | 0.05 | | z | 0.20 | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.10 | 1.2 Material properties Air: \rho =1.3\mathrm{kg.}{m}^{-3} c=343.{\mathrm{m.s}}^{-1} 1.3 Boundary conditions and loading | Normal incident wave pressure at the inlet | {P}_{i}={P}_{0}\ast {e}^{i\omega t} With {P}_{0}=1.0\mathrm{Pa} | | --- | --- | | Frequency | f=500\mathrm{Hz} | | Impedance at the \mathrm{CD} end | Z=\rho c=445.9{\mathrm{kg.m}}^{-2}{s}^{-1} | 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The frequencies of the excitation are quite low and the waveguide is long enough in relation to its lateral dimensions to limit itself to the flat waves: the phenomenon is then identical at all points of a waveplane, i.e. does not depend on the coordinates describing the points of this plane, y and z for example. This hypothesis gives the well-known general solution of acoustic equations for both quantities pressure p and acoustic speed v : v=f(t-\frac{x}{c})+g(t+\frac{x}{c}) Et: p=\rho c\left[f(t-\frac{x}{c})-g(t+\frac{x}{c})\right] The guide is supposed to be closed at the L abscisse end on an {Z}_{L} impedance; there is reflection at the impedance level, which gives a g return wave. In each point of the guide, there is then superposition of the two f and g functions; by definition even the {Z}_{L} terminal impedance imposes on the point of L abscisse , between p and v the following relationship: \frac{{p}_{L}}{{v}_{L}}={Z}_{L} In the harmonic case f and g are written: \begin{array}{}f(t-\frac{x}{c})=I{e}^{i\omega (t-\frac{x}{c})}\\ g(t+\frac{x}{c})=R{e}^{i\omega (t+\frac{x}{c})}\end{array} where I and R are determined by the boundary conditions. In the calculation of the Z=\frac{p}{v} impedance in total point x the time variable this time disappears, according to the very calculation of impedances and is written: Z(x)={Z}_{0}\frac{I{e}^{-i\omega \frac{x}{c}}-R{e}^{i\omega \frac{x}{c}}}{I{e}^{-i\omega \frac{x}{c}}+R{e}^{i\omega \frac{x}{c}}} Terminal impedance becomes: {Z}_{L}={Z}_{0}\frac{I{e}^{-i\omega \frac{L}{c}}-R{e}^{i\omega \frac{L}{c}}}{I{e}^{-i\omega \frac{L}{c}}+R{e}^{i\omega \frac{L}{c}}} {Z}_{0}=\rho c is called iterative impedance. On the fluid border at the entrance of the guide the boundary condition of incident wave type imposed on {P}_{i}={P}_{0}{e}^{i\omega t} , obtains by writing at the border the following linear relation: p-\rho c{v}_{n}={P}_{i} where {v}_{n}=\mathrm{v.n} is the speed according to the n unit normal fluid. A final {Z}_{L}={Z}_{0} impedance value is also required at the end of the guide, making it an anechoic end. The terminal impedance is equal to the iterative impedance {Z}_{0} when R=0 , that is when there is no return wave ; then one has a pure progressive wave in the direction of the incident wave, that is: \begin{array}{}v=I{e}^{i\omega (t-\frac{x}{c})}\\ p=\rho cI{e}^{i\omega (t-\frac{x}{c})}\end{array} Thus the imposed incident wave relation () is written: p-\rho c{v}_{n}=p(x=0)+\rho cv(x=0)=2\rho cI{e}^{i\omega t} From where 2\rho cI{e}^{i\omega t}={P}_{i} is identified, the expression of the progressive pressure wave in the guide is derived when {P}_{i} is applied at the guide entrance: p=\frac{{P}_{i}}{2}{e}^{-i\omega \frac{x}{c}}=\frac{{P}_{0}}{2}{e}^{i\omega (t-\frac{x}{c})} 2.2 Baseline Pressure at A , B , C , D (for modellings A, B, C, D, E and F). 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution analytical solution. 2.4 Bibliographical references 1. v8.22.302 AHLV302 – Vibro-absorbent input anechoic wave guide v8.22.302 AHLV302 – Vibro-absorbent input anechoic wave guide Summary: The objective of this test case is to calculate the pressure fields in an anechoic output waveguide whose acoustic excitation is provided by an boundary condition of speed imposed on an absorbent panel defined in the input section. This test uses the elements vibro-acoustic finished: - Modelling A: 3D_FLUIDE, FORMULATION ='U_P_PHI' - Model B: 2D_FLUIDE, FORMULATION ='U_P_PHI' - Modelling C: AXIS_FLUIDE, FORMULATION ='U_P_PHI' - Modelling D: 3D_FLUIDE, FORMULATION ='U_P' - Modelling E: 2D_FLUIDE, FORMULATION ='U_P' - Modelling F: AXIS_FLUIDE, FORMULATION ='U_P' - Modelling G: 3D_FLUIDE, FORMULATION ='U_PSI' - Modelling H: 2D_FLUIDE, FORMULATION ='U_PSI' - Modelling I: AXIS_FLUIDE, FORMULATION ='U_PSI' An exact analytical solution exists. This test case allows you to validate the hardware properties definition features for a non-amortized fluid, boundary conditions definition in speed and impedance, as well as the tools for creating and assembling mass matrices, stiffness and acoustic damping. On the other hand, it allows you to validate the acoustic pressure calculation. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry Figure 1.1 Problem Geometry and Loading System Parallelipipedic cavity: - length : L={l}_{x}=1.0m - height : h={l}_{y}=0.1m - width: l={l}_{z}=0.2m Point contact details: - A : x=0. , y=0.05 , z=0.1 - B : x=0. , y=0.1 , z=0.2 - C : x=1. , y=0.1 , z=0.0 - D : x=1. , y=0.05 , z=0.1 1.2 Material properties The material properties are those of the air: | c=340{\text{m.s}}^{-1} | Sound speed | | --- | --- | | \rho =1.2{\text{kg.m}}^{-3} | Density | 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads Uniform unit speed and impedance: | x=0 input section | {V}_{n}=-1{\text{m.s}}^{-1}\text{à 500 Hz} {Z}_{n}=-1000{\text{kg.m}}^{-2}.\text{s} | | --- | --- | | x=1 input section | {Z}_{n}=-408{\text{kg.m}}^{-2}.\text{s} | 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution The p pressure field checks the Helmholtz equation on the x axis: \frac{{d}^{2}p}{{\mathit{dx}}^{2}}+{k}^{2}p=0 , x\in [0,L] In x=0 , you can find boundary conditions speed and {Z}_{\mathit{n0}} impedance imposed: p(x=0)={Z}_{\mathit{n0}}\left({V}_{n}(x=0)-{V}_{n}^{s}\right) what gives in terms of imposed administration: {V}_{n}(x=0)={V}_{n}^{s}+{A}_{\mathit{n0}}p(x=0) In x=L , the {Z}_{\mathit{nL}} impedance (or its reverse, {A}_{\mathit{nL}} admittance) is imposed: \frac{-\frac{\mathit{dp}}{\mathit{dx}}}{-i\rho \omega }={A}_{n}p The pressure in the waveguide is as follows: p(x)={C}_{1}{\mathrm{e}}^{-\mathit{ikx}}+{C}_{2}{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathit{ikx}} Thus, the pressure derivative can be expressed: \frac{\mathit{dp}(x)}{\mathit{dx}}=-{\mathit{ikC}}_{1}{\mathrm{e}}^{-\mathit{ikx}}+{\mathit{ikC}}_{2}{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathit{ikx}} Boundary conditions x=0 allows you to write: -{\mathit{ikC}}_{1}+{\mathit{ikC}}_{2}=-i\rho \omega {V}_{n}^{s}-i\rho \omega {A}_{\mathit{n0}}({C}_{1}+{C}_{2}) The boundary condition x=L allows you to write: {\mathit{ikC}}_{1}{\mathrm{e}}^{-\mathit{ikL}}-{\mathit{ikC}}_{2}{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathit{ikL}}=-i\rho \omega {A}_{\mathit{nL}}({C}_{1}{\mathrm{e}}^{-\mathit{ikL}}+{C}_{2}{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathit{ikL}}) These last two relationships allow to write a system of equations whose resolution allows to determine the constants {C}_{1} and {C}_{2} and thus the pressure and particle speed in any point of the waveguide. For simplicity, the analytical expression of the {C}_{1} and {C}_{2} coefficients is not provided here. 2.2 Baseline The pressure is calculated at A , B , C and D points. 2.3 Uncertainty about the solution - analytical solution. 3 Modelling A This Modelling concerns FORMATION='U_P_PHI'. 3.1 Modelling characteristics Figure 3.1. v8.22.303 AHLV303 - linear elasticity hollow sphere immersed in infinite fluid v8.22.303 AHLV303 - linear elasticity hollow sphere immersed in infinite fluid Summary: The objective of this test is to validate the IFS formulations with consideration of the Sommerfeld condition. This is an test case solution which is (semi) analytical 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry A hollow sphere of {R}_{\mathit{ext}}=1,4m external radius and {R}_{int}=1,0m internal radius immersed in water is considered to be infinite. But for the modelling of the problem, the fluid domain is truncated into a hollow sphere of {R}_{\mathit{bgt}}=3,0m external radius and {R}_{\mathit{ext}}=1,4m internal radius. 1.2 Material properties The structure is elastic isotropic with properties: E=210000\mathit{MPa} , \nu =0.3 and {\rho}_{s}=7850\mathit{kg}.{m}^{-3} The fluid is water which has {\rho}_{f}=1000\mathit{kg}.{m}^{-3} density. The speed of sound in this fluid is {c}_{f}=1500m.{s}^{-1} . The BGT condition is imposed (IMPE_FACE) with the following acoustic impedance: {Z}_{c}=3\times {\rho}_{f}+{\rho}_{f}{c}_{f}i . This quantity is, of course, complex. 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads The stress considered in the problem is a strictly radial {p}_{\mathit{imp}}=1,5\mathit{MPa} distributed pressure imposed on the {\Gamma}_{int} surface. 1.4 Initial conditions We start from a zero state (contraints, speeds, displacements and accelerations) 2 reference solution 2.1 Method of calculation The problem is spherical symmetry. So we place ourselves in the (r,\theta ,\varphi ) marker. We consider the case where {p}_{\mathit{imp}} does not depend on \theta , nor \varphi . This hypothesis allows us to express the analytical solution for the problem in harmonic and semi-analytical regime for the problem in transient by exploiting the symmetry of the problem. Indeed, by symmetry in the problem, the structure displacement s. {u}_{s}(r,\theta ,\varphi ,t)=u(r,t){e}_{r} And the sound pressure in the fluid: {p}_{f}(r,\theta ,\varphi ,t)=p(r,t) The deformation tensor of Green-Lagrange linearized is therefore given by: \epsilon (r,t)=\frac{\partial u(r,t)}{\partial r}(r,t){e}_{r}\otimes {e}_{r}+\frac{u(r,t)}{r}\left({e}_{\theta}\otimes {e}_{\theta}+{e}_{\varphi}\otimes {e}_{\varphi}\right) With an isotropic elastic material, the Cauchy stress is then: \sigma (r,t)=\left((\lambda +2\mu )\frac{\partial u(r,t)}{\partial r}+2\lambda \frac{u(r,t)}{r}\right){e}_{r}\otimes {e}_{r}+\left(\lambda \frac{\partial u(r,t)}{\partial r}+(\lambda +2\mu )\frac{u(r,t)}{r}\right)\left({e}_{\theta}\otimes {e}_{\theta}+{e}_{\varphi}\otimes {e}_{\varphi}\right) \lambda and \mu being the coefficients of Lamé. The expression of the preservation of the amount of movement allows to write: \frac{{r}^{2}}{{c}_{s}^{2}}\frac{{\partial}^{2}u(r,t)}{\partial {t}^{2}}-{r}^{2}\frac{{\partial}^{2}u(r,t)}{\partial {r}^{2}}-2r\frac{\partial u(r,t)}{\partial r}+2u(r,t)=0 With the speed of propagation of sound in the {c}_{s} structure which is: {c}_{s}^{2}=\frac{\lambda +2\mu }{{\rho}_{s}} \lambda and \mu being the coefficients of Lamé. \frac{1}{{c}_{f}^{2}}\frac{{\partial}^{2}p}{\partial {t}^{2}}(t,x)-\Delta p(t,x)=0 In spherical coordinates, the acoustic pressure propagation equation is written: \frac{1}{{c}_{f}^{2}}\frac{{\partial}^{2}p}{\partial {t}^{2}}(r,t)-\frac{{\partial}^{2}p}{\partial {r}^{2}}(r,t)-\frac{2}{r}\frac{\partial p}{\partial r}(r,t)=0 The condition of continuity of the normal stress on the surface {\Gamma}_{\mathit{ext}} is written as a scalar equation: (\lambda + 2\mu) \frac{\partial u(t)}{\partial r}_{r=R_{\text{ext}}} + 2\lambda \frac{u(t)}{R_{\text{ext}}} = -p(t)_{r=R_{\text{ext}}} The condition of the normal acceleration continuity on the {\Gamma}_{\mathit{ext}} surface is written: \frac{\partial^2 u(t)}{\partial t^2}_{R_{\text{ext}}} = -\frac{1}{\rho_f} \frac{\partial p(t)}{\partial r}_{R_{\text{ext}}} Pressure is imposed on the {\Gamma}_{int} surface and is written: (\lambda + 2\mu) \frac{\partial u(t)}{\partial r}_{r=R_{\text{int}}} + 2\lambda \frac{u(t)}{R_{\text{ext}}} = -p_{\text{imp}}(t) Finally, the Sommerfeld condition (non-reflection of the waves) is applied to the outer surface {\Gamma}_{\mathit{bgt}} : \underset{r\to \infty }{\lim}\left(\frac{1}{{c}_{f}}\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}(r,t)+\frac{\partial p}{\partial r}(r,t)\right)=0 2.2 Harmonic resolution The {p}_{\mathit{imp}}(t)={P}_{\mathit{imp}}{e}^{i\omega t} form is used here and the solution of the u(r,t)=U(r){e}^{i\omega t} and p(r,t)=P(r){e}^{i\omega t} form is sought. In this form, the partial derivatives in time are trivial. For example: u(r,t)=U(r){e}^{i\omega t}\to \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=i\omega U(r){e}^{i\omega t}\to \frac{{\partial}^{2}u}{\partial {t}^{2}}=-i{\omega}^{2}U(r){e}^{i\omega t} The problem is finding U and P that are solutions to the following problem: {r}^{2}\frac{{d}^{2}U}{{\mathit{dr}}^{2}}+2r\frac{dU}{\mathit{dr}}+\left(\frac{{\omega}^{2}}{{c}_{s}^{2}}{r}^{2}-2\right)U=0 Et: \frac{{d}^{2}P}{{\mathit{dr}}^{2}}+\frac{2}{r}\frac{\mathit{dP}}{\mathit{dr}}+\frac{{\omega}^{2}}{{c}_{f}^{2}}P=0 The solution to the problem () is written: U(r)=A(\omega ){j}_{1}\left(\frac{\omega}{{c}_{s}}r\right)+B(\omega ){y}_{1}\left(\frac{\omega}{{c}_{s}}r\right) Where {j}_{1} and {y}_{1} are, respectively, the spherical Bessel function of order 1 of the first type and the spherical Bessel function of order 1 of the second type. The solution to the problem () is written: P(r)=C(\omega )\frac{{e}^{-i\omega r/{c}_{f}}}{r}+D(\omega )\frac{{e}^{i\omega r/{c}_{f}}}{r} To find the values A(\omega ) , B(\omega ) , C(\omega ) and D(\omega ) . Limit conditions are used. In equation (), the term \frac{{e}^{-i\omega r/{c}_{f}}}{r} corresponds to the wave radially propagating towards infinity while the other term \frac{{e}^{i\omega r/{c}_{f}}}{r} is the reflection of the wave (to the source). As one imposes a condition of non-reflection, on the outer edge, this second contribution is null and so one has D(\omega )=0 . 2.3 Quantities and reference results To calculate the solution, you need to have an estimate of the functions of Bessel. This is used scipy, (special functions). We recover the displacement in two points: Uint on the surface of the structure {\Gamma}_{int} , Uext on the surface IFS {\Gamma}_{\text{ext}} . The pressure is raised Pext on the surface IFS {\Gamma}_{\text{ext}} and Pbgt on the outer surface {\Gamma}_{\text{bgt}} . | Real part | Imaginary part | | --- | --- | | | | | | | | | | | | | 2.4 Uncertainties about the solution None, the solution is analytical. 3 Modelling A 3.1 Modelling characteristics C_PLAN modelling is used. 3.2 Mesh characteristics The mesh contains 20 elements of type QUAD4. 3.3 Tested quantities and results We test the movement in the top left corner of the plate. | Identification | Reference type | Reference value | Creative decision | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Point A - \mathrm{DX} | 'ANALYTIQUE' | 12 | 5% | 3.4 Remarks This paragraph is optional. 4 Summary of the results

v9.01.100 SZLZ100 - Fatigue on a Decent Cycle v9.01.100 SZLZ100 - Fatigue on a Decent Cycle Summary: The purpose of this test is to calculate damage from a stress loading history and then from a deformation loading history. From a simple loading history defined by DEFI_FONCTION, the elementary cycles are extracted by the RCCM R7.04.01 cycle counting method, then the elementary damage associated with each cycle is calculated by interpolation on the Wöhler curve of the material (if load history in stress and interpolation on the Manson-Coffin curve of the material) (if load history in deformations). The Wöhler curve is defined by DEFI_FONCTION. L-interpolation is logarithmic in number of cycles at N rupture and on \mathit{Salt} alternating stress. The Manson-Coffin curve is also defined by DEFI_FONCTION. Finally, the total damage to the piece is determined by cumulating all the elementary damage by the Miner linear rule. In this test, the value of the average stress on the calculation of the elemental damage is also checked by the Wöhler method. A first calculation is performed without correction, a second with a correction by Gerber and the third with a correction by Goodman. In this simple example, extraction of elementary cycles and calculation of damage can be done manually, applying the algorithms presented in reference document R7.04.01. The results provided by the POST_FATIGUE operator are therefore very satisfactory. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The analysis is to determine the damage to a piece in an point to which the loading history is supplied. The stress loading history is considered to be the test of the Wöhler method and the elementary cycles are extracted by a cycle counting method, which is the RCCM method in this test. The elementary damage due to each elemental cycle is then calculated by interpolation on the Wöhler curve of the material. The Wöhler curve is filled as a point function by point, which gives the value of the number of cycles at break as a function of the \mathrm{Salt}=\frac{\Delta \sigma }{2} alternating stress. Interpolation is logarithmic on the abscisse and the abscisse and is allowed to extend linearly this function to the right and left. Three different calls to the POST_FATIGUE operator allow for the average stress of each elemental cycle to be taken into account. The correction adopted is that of the Haigh diagram, either to the right of Goodman or to the parable of Gerber R7.04.01. Total damage is determined by the Miner linear cumulation rule. The Manson-Coffin method of calculating damage is tested by considering the deformation loading history and extracting the elementary cycles by a cycle counting method, which is the RCCM method in this test. The elementary damage due to each elemental cycle is then calculated by interpolation on the Manson-Coffin curve of the material. The Manson-Coffin curve is provided as an point function by point, which gives the value of the number of cycles at breakage as a function of \frac{\Delta \varepsilon }{2} . Total damage is determined by the Miner linear cumulation rule. 1.2 Material properties The Wöhler curve of the material, which gives the number of cycles at break as a function of the alternating stress, is defined by point by point by: | \mathit{Salt} | | | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | N | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | | | | | | | | | \mathrm{Su} = material failure limit = 850. v9.01.101 SZLZ101 - Damage Calculation/RAINFLOW Method v9.01.101 SZLZ101 - Damage Calculation/RAINFLOW Method Summary: The purpose of this test is to calculate damage from a load history in stress. From a simple loading history defined by DEFI_FONCTION, the elementary cycles are extracted by the RAINFLOW R7.04.01 cycle counting method, then the elementary damage associated with each cycle is calculated by interpolation on the Wöhler curve of the material. Various possibilities are tested for introducing the Wöhler curve and for taking into account the elasto-plastic concentration coefficient. Finally, the total damage to the piece is determined by cumulating all the elementary damage by the Miner linear rule. This example is a validation test of POSTDAM software developed by the REME Department, provided in the validation manual of version 1.0 of this software. The results provided by the POST_FATIGUE operator are quite identical to those provided by POSTDAM software. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry The analysis is to determine the damage to a piece in an point to which the load history is supplied in stress. From a simple loading history defined by DEFI_FONCTION, the elementary cycles are extracted by the RAINFLOW R7.04.01 cycle counting method, then the elementary damage associated with each cycle is calculated by interpolation on the Wöhler curve of the material. Various possibilities are tested for introducing the Wöhler curve and whether or not an elastoplastic concentration coefficient is taken into account: - The Wöhler curve is defined as: \begin{array}{cc}{S}_{\mathrm{alt}}=\text{contrainte alternée}=1/2({E}_{C}/E)\Delta \sigma & X={\text{LOG}}_{10}({S}_{\mathrm{alt}})\\ N={10}^{\mathrm{a0}+\mathrm{a1X}+{\mathrm{a2X}}^{2}+{\mathrm{a3X}}^{3}}& D=\lbrace \begin{array}{}1/N\text{si}{S}_{\mathrm{alt}}\ge {S}_{I}\\ 0.\text{sinon}\end{array}\end{array} with: {E}_{C} = Young's modulus associated with the fatigue curve of the material, E = Young's modulus used to determine stresses, \mathrm{a0} material constants , \mathrm{a1} , \mathrm{a2} and \mathrm{a3} , and {S}_{I} the endurance limit of the material. - The Wöhler curve is defined in the same form and also takes into account an elasto-plastic concentration coefficient defined by: \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}{K}_{e}=1& \mathit{si}& \Delta \sigma <3{S}_{m}\\ {K}_{e}=1+(1-n)/(\Delta \sigma /3{S}_{m}-1)/(n(m-1))& \mathit{si}& 3{S}_{m}<\Delta \sigma <3m{S}_{m}\\ {K}_{e}=1/n& \mathit{si}& 3m{S}_{m}<\Delta \sigma \end{array} où {S}_{m} is the maximum permissible stress, and n and m two material-dependent constants. - The Wöhler curve is defined as the Basquin analytical form: D=A{S}_{\mathrm{alt}}^{\beta} Finally, the total damage to the piece is determined by cumulating all the elementary damage by the Miner linear rule. 1.2 Material properties Wöhler curve definition parameters: | \mathrm{a0} | \mathrm{a1} | \mathrm{a2} | \mathrm{a3} | \mathrm{Ec} | E | \mathrm{Sl} | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 55.81 | –43.06 | 11.91 | –1.16 | | | | Definition parameters of the \mathrm{Ke} elasto-plastic concentration coefficient: | \mathrm{Sm} | n | m | | --- | --- | --- | | | 0.3 | 1.7 | Wöhler curve definition parameters in Basquin analytical form: | A | \beta | | --- | --- | | 1.001730939 E-14 | 4.065 | History of loading | t | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | \sigma (t) | | | | 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution This test is based on the POSTDAM Software Validation Manual version 1.0. v9.01.103 SZLZ103 - RAINFLOW Method v9.01.103 SZLZ103 - RAINFLOW Method Summary: The purpose of this test is to test the RAINFLOW cycle counting method from a load history in constraints. The filtering functionality of the load history is also tested, and the consideration of a stress concentration coefficient {K}_{T} is taken into account. This example is a validation test of POSTDAM software developed by the REME Department, provided in the Validation Manual of version 1.0 of this software. v9.01.105 SZLZ105 - Cycle count by RAINFLOW and damage calculation v9.01.105 SZLZ105 - Cycle count by RAINFLOW and damage calculation Summary: Nearly static elastic linear transient problem in structural mechanics. Calculation of final damage in a element subjected to cyclic loading, with linear elastic behaviour. A planar stress model and a 3D model. This test validates the cycle counting method (RAINFLOW) installed in the CALC_FATIGUE operator and the method of calculating the stress damage imposed (Wöhler curve) or the strain imposed (Manson-Coffin curve). The reference solution is an analytical solution. It also validates the calculation of equivalent stresses and deformations using the options SIEQ_ELGA, SIEQ_ELNO, EPEQ_ELGA, EPEQ_ELNO, EPMQ_ELGA and EPMQ_ELNO. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Geometry 1.2 Material properties linear elasticity: E=1.\mathrm{MPa} \nu =0.3 1.3 Boundary conditions and loads - Blocked on 1-4 side following X - node 1 blocked on Y side . - Single unit traction on the 2-3 side. - Loading F(t) into saw teeth (according to the Downing and Societe 1982 Article) [bib1]. 1.4 Initial conditions No stress and deformation. 2 reference solution 2.1 Calculation method used for reference solution analytical solution - Calculation of stresses and deformations. For single-tension loading, a uniform uniaxial stress state is obtained in all point: \sigma =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\sigma & 0& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\\ 0& 0& 0\end{array}\right] et \varepsilon =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\varepsilon & 0& 0\\ 0& \gamma & 0\\ 0& 0& \gamma \end{array}\right] the equivalent quantities are therefore \lbrace \begin{array}{}{\sigma}_{\mathrm{VMIS}}=\mid \sigma \mid ={\sigma}_{\mathrm{TRESCA}}\\ {\sigma}_{\mathrm{VMIS}-\mathrm{SG}}=\sigma \end{array} et \lbrace \begin{array}{}{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{INVA}-2}=\frac{2}{3}\mid \varepsilon -\gamma \mid \\ {\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{INVA}-\mathrm{2SG}}=\frac{2}{3}\mid \varepsilon -\gamma \mid \ast \mathrm{sign}\left[\frac{\varepsilon +2\gamma }{3}\right]\end{array} - then manual calculation of the cycles by the RAINFLOW method, as well as loading amplitudes ( \frac{\Delta \sigma }{2} or \frac{\Delta \varepsilon }{2} ). | cycles | \Delta \sigma /2 | \Delta {\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{INVA}-2}/2 | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 2 3 4 | 1. 0.5 1. 3.5 | 0.8667 0.433315 0.8667 3.03335 | - Finally, these values are carried over to the Wöhler or Manson-Coffin curves to estimate unit damage at each i cycle, i.e. {\mathrm{Du}}_{i}=\frac{1}{{N}_{i}} ( {N}_{i} being the number of breaking cycles for a given amplitude), as well as the cumulative damage D=\underset{i}{\Sigma}D{u}_{i} (linear cumulation rule of MINER). v9.01.106 SZLZ106 - Fatigue under random solicitation v9.01.106 SZLZ106 - Fatigue under random solicitation Summary: The purpose of this test is to calculate damage from random solicitation, which is characterised by its spectral moments. From the spectral moments of random loading the average damage to the R7.04.02 structure is determined. Two methods of counting stress cycles are available for this purpose: - method of counting peaks of stress, - method of exceedances of a given level. Various possibilities of introducing the Wöhler curve and taking into account the \mathrm{Ke} elasto-plastic concentration coefficient are also tested. The reference results of this test are the values provided by POSTDAM software developed by the REME Department (EDF-DER-EP). The results provided by the POST_FATI_ALEA operator are quite identical to those provided by POSTDAM software. 1 Reference problem The analysis is to determine the average damage to a piece subjected to random loading. Random loading is fully characterized by the spectral moments of 0, 2, and 4: {\lambda}_{0} , {\lambda}_{2} and {\lambda}_{4} that are introduced under the keywords MOMENT_SPEC_0, MOMENT_SPEC_2 and MOMENT_SPEC_4. For the calculation of damage, a counting method must be chosen from the two available in Code_Aster : - method of counting peaks of stress, - method of counting the exceedance of a given level. The Wöhler curve of the material must also be introduced, which can be defined in three distinct mathematical forms: - point function by point, which gives the value of the number of cycles at break, depending on the {S}_{\mathrm{alt}} alternating stress, - Basquin analytical form: D=A{S}_{\mathrm{alt}}^{\beta} - analytical form {S}_{\mathrm{alt}} = alternating stress = 1/2({E}_{C}/E)\Delta \sigma X={\log}_{10}({S}_{\mathrm{alt}}) N={10}^{\mathrm{a0}+\mathrm{a1}X+\mathrm{a2}{X}^{2}+\mathrm{a3}{X}^{3}} | D= | 1./N | si {S}_{\mathrm{alt}}\ge {S}_{l} | | --- | --- | --- | | | 0. | if not | where {E}_{C} = Young's modulus associated with the material fatigue curve, E = Young's modulus used to determine stresses, \mathrm{a0} material constants , \mathrm{a1} , \mathrm{a2} and \mathrm{a3} , and {S}_{l} the endurance limit of the material. In addition, a \mathrm{Ke} elasto-plastic concentration coefficient may be used , defined by: \lbrace \begin{array}{ccc}{K}_{e}=1& \mathrm{si}& \Delta \sigma <3{S}_{m}\\ {K}_{e}=1+(1-n)/(\Delta \sigma /3{S}_{m}-1)/(n(m-1))& \mathrm{si}& 3{S}_{m}<\Delta \sigma <3m{S}_{m}\\ {K}_{e}=1/n& \mathrm{si}& 3m{S}_{m}<\Delta \sigma \end{array} where {S}_{m} is the maximum permissible stress, and n and m two material-dependent constants. In this test, for a single random load, the average damage is determined in ten separate configurations, depending on the shape of the Wöhler curve and the cycle counting method. 1.1 Material v9.01.108 SZLZ108 - Damage by TAHERI(TAHERI_MANSON and TAHERI_MIXTE) methods v9.01.108 SZLZ108 - Damage by TAHERI(TAHERI_MANSON and TAHERI_MIXTE) methods Summary: There are two modellingss: - Modelling A: This test is for the purpose of calculating damage from a purely uniaxial loading history in deformations by TAHERI_MANSON or TAHERI_MIXTE methods. - Modelling B: This test is for the purpose of calculating damage from a constant loading history by the three methods of counting RAIN_FLOW, NATUREL and RCCM. Taheri methods apply only to deformation loadings and do not allow the Manson-Coffin method to take into account the order of stress cycle occurrence. 1 Reference problem 1.1 Modelling A The analysis is to determine the damage to a structure subjected to a deformation loading history. The Rainflow method is used to determine the number of elementary cycles and the half amplitude of each cycle. For the loads considered, the Rainflow method determines 5 cycles of half amplitude: \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{1}}{2}=0.25 , \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{2}}{2}=0.25 , \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{3}}{2}=0.75 , \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{4}}{2}=0.25 et \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{5}}{2}=1.75 . Then the structural damage is calculated using the TAHERI_MANSON method and the TAHERI_MIXTE method. As long as the deformation amplitude of the various cycles applied to the structure remains increasing \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{1}}{2}\le \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{2}}{2}\le \mathrm{...}\le \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{n}}{2} , the TAHERI_MANSON and TAHERI_MIXTE methods are identical to the MANSON_COFFIN method (calculation of the number of cycles at break, {N}_{\mathrm{rupt}} , by interpolation on the Manson-Coffin curve and calculation of the damage by 1/{N}_{\mathrm{rupt}} ). However, if a i cycle has a half-amplitude \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{i}}{2} less than \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{i-1}}{2} , Taheri methods differ from the Manson-Coffin method. - The TAHERI_MANSON method is to determine a stress amplitude \frac{\Delta {\sigma}_{i}}{2} from \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{i}}{2} and {\varepsilon}_{\max} (maximum value of the deformation half amplitude encountered before the i cycle). To do this, the user must provide an \frac{\Delta \sigma }{2}(\frac{\Delta \varepsilon }{2,}{\varepsilon}_{\max}) tablecloth under the TAHERI_NAPPE operand. From \frac{\Delta {\sigma}_{i}}{2} , a half amplitude of \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{i}^{\text{ }}}{2} deformations is determined using a function introduced under the TAHERI_FONC operand. The value of the elemental damage of the i cycle is determined by interpolation of \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}_{i}^{\text{ }}}{2} on the Manson_Coffin curve. - For the 'TAHERI_MIXTE' method, the same procedure is followed for the determination of the \frac{\Delta {\sigma}_{i}}{2} stress half amplitude , and the value of the i cycle elemental damage is determined by interpolation of \frac{\Delta {\sigma}_{i}}{2} on the Wöhler curve. This method therefore requires the data of the curves of Wöhler and Manson_Coffin. The total damage is determined by linear accumulation of the elementary damage. 1.1.1 Material properties For the calculation of the damage of TAHERI_MANSON, the Manson_Coffin curve is required, a table sheet for calculating \frac{\Delta \sigma }{2} from ( \frac{\Delta \varepsilon }{2} and {\varepsilon}_{\max} ) and a function for calculating \frac{\Delta {\varepsilon}^{\text{ }}}{2} from \frac{\Delta \sigma }{2} . The table sheet (cyclic nutring curve with pre-lunching) is introduced under the TAHERI_NAPPE operand and the function (cyclic nutting curve) under the TAHERI_FONC operand. The Manson_Coffin curve is introduced into DEFI_MATERIAU. For the calculation of the damage of TAHERI_MIXTE, the Manson_Coffin curve, the Wöhler curve and a sheet (cyclic nutring curve with pre-nutting) are required to calculate \frac{\Delta \sigma }{2} from ( \frac{\Delta \varepsilon }{2} and {\varepsilon}_{\max} ). The sheet is introduced under the TAHERI_NAPPE operand. The Manson_Coffin curve and the Wöhler curve are introduced into DEFI_MATERIAU. 1.1.2 History of the load | t | | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | \varepsilon (t) | | 3.5 | | 3.5 | | 3.5 | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | 2.5 | | 0.5 | 1.2 Modelling B > The analysis consists of a special case where the loading history is constant (e.g., average load applied). v9.01.109 SZLZ109 - Lemaitre damage to post-processing v9.01.109 SZLZ109 - Lemaitre damage to post-processing Summary: The purpose of this test is to calculate the damage of LEMAITRE from any multiaxial loading history and the history of the cumulative plastic deformation.
